# Patrologia Latina, volume 61 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 61

**Complete Course of Patrology**, or universal library—integral, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes.

The first is an index of subjects, by consulting which everything that each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance. The second is an index of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, commented upon the individual texts of the books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete series in the several branches of ecclesiastical scholarship.

## Volume 61 of Patrology

Saint Paulinus of Nola; Claudius Marius Victor; Merobaudes the Scholastic; Saint Orientius; Saint Auspicius; Paulinus of Périgueux; Amoenus; Secundinus; Drepanius Florus; an uncertain author.

**One volume.**

Paris, sold by the publisher, in the street called d’Amboise, near the Barrière d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1847.

## The Series of Fifth-Century Poets Completed

And in a new and most accurate edition are presented the complete works of Saint Paulinus of Nola, Saint Orientius, Saint Auspicius, and also those of Claudius Marius Victor, Merobaudes, Paulinus of Périgueux, Amoenus, Secundinus, Drepanius Florus, and an uncertain author, revised and reproduced according to the highly celebrated editions of Muratori, Gallandi, and Margarini de la Bigne.

# Works of Saint Paulinus of Nola

[Column 0009]

## Dedicatory Letter

[Column 0009]

To the most illustrious and most reverend Lord, Lord Francesco Antonio Corrario, of the Capuchin order, patriarch of Venice, primate of Dalmatia, and so forth: Dionysius Ramanzini, printer, sends respectful greetings.

Those who seek favor from eminent men have been accustomed to offer them especially those gifts which they judge will be most pleasing and acceptable to their disposition. Therefore we ought not to be surprised that readers or spectators have sometimes seen coins or marbles given to some, gems and painted garments to others, or distinguished horses or weapons presented as gifts. People naturally accommodate themselves to the pursuits of those whom they admire and revere.

For my part, most excellent prelate, wishing to serve you according to the devotion of my heart, I could think of no other gift to send you than this book, which contains the writings of Saint Paulinus. This book is the best of my possessions, however small they may be, and I trust that it will also be very dear to you. Since you are endowed with every virtue and especially devoted to piety and religion, in these writings of so great and ancient a prelate you will recognize examples of every virtue and the most upright standard of piety and religion.

Meanwhile, other readers will approve my decision to inscribe these works to your name when they observe that you bear a certain likeness to Saint Paulinus, their author, if they compare the lives, pursuits, and praises of both. Paulinus was a senator and consul of the Roman state, most learned in human and divine letters. Setting aside the highest honors, he embraced a holier life and, having become bishop of Nola, enlarged the Christian world by his learning and example.

You, likewise, in the Venetian republic—which rivals the Roman republic splendidly—were born of a most illustrious family. Among your ancestors are counted Pope Gregory XII; Beriola, that eminent and celebrated woman, sister of the praised Gregory, mother of Eugene IV, and grandmother of Paul II; besides many other most eminent cardinals, renowned bishops, and distinguished commanders in war and peace, senators, procurators, dukes, whose names frequently occur in the annals.

You, I say, born in so great a republic from so noble a stock, like Paulinus—an immortal and most eminent senator of that same republic, supreme commander of its armies, and holder of every distinguished office on land and sea—having last administered the prefecture of Padua with distinction, despising all honors prepared for you and embracing the strictest rule of a holier life, entered the Capuchin order.

Yet you were later brought out from it so that you might preside over the Venetian see, in which two celebrated members of your family had once sat: Gregory himself, the twelfth of that name, when he governed Venice as bishop of Castello, and Gregory the patriarch, nephew by his brother of the pontiff just mentioned. Thus you spread the light of your virtue far and wide that you draw everyone’s minds into admiration of you.

The new honor of your dignity did not lead you away from the holiness and rigor of the discipline you had undertaken. Rather, steadfast in your purpose, you follow the ancient custom of the religious order you entered, living sparingly and austerely. You watch over the morals and instruction of those entrusted to your care, so that they may be weakened by no stain of vice or darkness of error.

Of your piety and charity, by which you most readily assist the needs of the poor and splendidly emulate Saint Paulinus, why should I say much, when it is evident to everyone how greatly you excel and shine in these matters? Yet I am not attempting here to heap praises upon you; that would be no small undertaking. I have merely said a few words about my judgment and duty, since I wished to adorn and dedicate this book with your distinguished name, knowing your intellectual refinement and piety.

Receive, therefore, this little gift of ours with a cheerful countenance, and may you yourself be willing both to love and to commend to others this most elegant and holy author.

Farewell, and may you prosper.

10 Kalends of July, 1736, on the feast of Saint Paulinus.

# Prolegomena

## Preface

[Columns 0011A–0014A]

[Column 0011]

No one who recognizes in Saint Pontius Meropius Paulinus either the learning and fidelity of a most eloquent writer or the divine mind and understanding of an outstanding poet can praise his works sufficiently according to their worth. Neither the nature of my undertaking nor the excellence of the most holy author himself permits me to commend him at length to readers. For that illustrious judgment has long been confirmed by many centuries and by the testimonies of so many other Fathers, especially Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine: that he was a man of the highest distinction in the Church.

But since I am now bringing all those testimonies together and making them public for the first time, I hope that, even if nothing else, I shall at least deserve praise for having served the interests of those who delight in reading the holy Fathers, in whose works all elegant learning and every memory of antiquity are contained.

Although I do not suppose that many will consider the labor I expended in collecting these materials worth much, and although I am not, as some now do, trying to hunt for fame among scholars by merely copying the bare compilations (συνταγμάτων) of others, I nevertheless see how much usefulness and benefit this very labor brings to the Christian cause and to Sacred Scripture. It makes available an edition of works which, although nearly unequalled in merit, had not yet appeared publicly both complete and finished in every respect.

To omit the earlier editions and speak only of the latest, the Paris edition, it had indeed been prepared with exceptionally learned and diligent care by the most celebrated priest, Jean-Baptiste Le Brun. It had been established according to the testimony of several manuscript codices and illuminated by brilliant notes and dissertations. Yet not merely one or two private letters, but four complete poems—the noblest part of the entire work—were missing, since the misfortunes of the times had not yet brought them to light. The edition was therefore as far removed from its natural completeness as a human body from perfection when both its face and its hands have been cut off.

It happened, however, that the distinguished Louis Antonio Muratori, the most fortunate investigator and interpreter of ancient monuments, recovered those four poems from the Ambrosian Library at Milan and repaired that loss. The loss was especially serious because the sequence of the birthday celebrations of Saint Felix had been interrupted; Paulinus had been accustomed to commemorate these annually in a special poem.

Since the matter was of such importance, and since the most learned man could not bear that monuments of such value to sacred and secular literature should continue to struggle against bookworms and moths, he published them in a separate volume of his *Anecdota*. Thus, at least as far as these *Natalitia* were concerned, the matter was saved. But because these scattered limbs were separated from the rest of the body, everyone wished that they might be reunited, so that, as with the works of the other Fathers, there might also be a complete edition of the works of Paulinus.

This is the usefulness toward which we have striven and the chief fruit of our labor: to ensure that new materials should be added in their proper order, and that their addition should receive the further advantage of being newly reviewed by the editor himself.

Accordingly, we turned to the distinguished Muratori and earnestly begged him to revise the dissertations and notes that he had printed on those poems many years earlier; to explain more fully whatever seemed to him to require fuller treatment; to change whatever seemed in any way to require alteration; and to contribute the whole to the public good, for which he is especially zealous.

He kindly agreed, as he is most ready for every upright and honorable scholarly pursuit. It was chiefly through his favor that this excellent work, polished with as much care as circumstances allowed, has appeared in public.

I shall now briefly explain how this was accomplished.

What had previously been contained in three quarto volumes we have included in a single volume. We divided the entire collection into two parts: one consisting of works in prose, the other of works in poetic meter. After these, as an appendix, we placed a few works of both kinds falsely attributed to Paulinus, together with the notes, dissertations, and commentaries of earlier editors, which the last Paris edition, published in 1685, reproduces with the greatest accuracy.

This means, in particular, all the care applied by the three learned priests of the Society of Jesus—Andreas Schottus, Heribertus Rosweydus, and Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius—when each prepared his own assigned portion.

In a word, we have been pleased to follow almost continuously the edition produced under the authorship of Bruni, preserving its sequence and arrangement, and arranging in accordance with its design the materials newly added.

Someone might have wished that, since we were bringing all these materials together in one volume, some features should be made more suitable to that purpose. We therefore did not wish to disappoint the reader or make him feel that his expectation had been frustrated. We placed the Life of the holy author before his writings and prefixed lists, or tables, both of the letters and of the poems to each part.

[Note: We have gathered all the indexes into one body at the end of this volume of the *Patrologia*. Editor.]

We also carried out other measures of this kind, so that elegance might be satisfied no less than usefulness, and so that nothing should be taken away from the reader’s pleasure, while everything that contributes to a more convenient reading of our author should remain connected in one continuous arrangement.

Indeed, no matter how much effort was possible, we have omitted nothing in the remaining matters that seemed relevant to equipping this new edition, in accordance with everyone’s wishes, as fully as possible and completing it in every respect. The reading itself, more than any commendation in words, will confirm this.

We shall think that we have received a great reward if we learn that our industry has been both pleasing and useful to those devoted to more solid learning. We shall continue striving so that each year something may emerge from our labor that will bring pleasure joined with usefulness, above all to students of sacred literature.

## Preface to the Paris Edition

[Columns 0013A–0016C]

[Column 0013]

Many know how highly the holy Fathers of the Church esteemed Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and his writings; all may learn this from the praises of him that will be set out below.

For a long time learned men had been distressed that the works of so great a man were so corrupt, and they ardently desired that someone should apply a healing hand to them. Moved by their counsels and authority, we undertook to restore them to their original purity. We gathered manuscript codices from every quarter, both from Gaul and from neighboring regions, by whose assistance the works have been enlarged and corrected.

The first edition appeared at Paris in 1516 from the press of Jodocus Badius Ascensius. In many places it was torn, in some mutilated, and even corrupted by Badius himself, who served as its censor.

The second edition followed, prepared by the Dominican Henricus Gravius, who in 1560 at Cologne, under the Cholinian press, purged the works of Paulinus of many errors by consulting ancient manuscript exemplars.

The third then appeared at Basel in 1569 among the *Orthodoxographi* collected by Johannes Jacobus Grynaeus. It seems to have been printed from manuscripts after the earlier editions.

The fourth edition was incorporated by the Jesuit Andreas Schottus, after collation with a manuscript codex, into the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* in 1618. He added Julian’s *Epithalamium*, which had not yet been printed.

The fifth and final edition was prepared at Antwerp in 1622 and entrusted to the Plantinian press by Heribertus Rosweydus of the Society of Jesus, a pious and learned man. He was, however, burdened by so many occupations that, when time did not suffice, he was often forced to rely upon the work of others and could apply only a substitute hand.

Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, of the same Society, certainly did not regard that edition as accurate. In his *Illustrated Paulinus* he brought forward much material for preparing a new edition of the works of Saint Paulinus. From that work, and also from the recent edition of the works of Saint Augustine, we have extracted whatever was relevant to our undertaking.

So that you may understand, benevolent reader, the nature and method of the service we have rendered, I shall briefly explain them here.

For six years we examined and carefully collated numerous manuscript codices for the correction of the works of Paulinus, comparing them with the printed editions. When anything more obscure or perplexing arose, we consulted learned men. We did not always prefer the reading that was clearer or more elegant, but rather that which, after comparison with other passages in his works, seemed to be the genuine diction of Paulinus.

We divided the entire work into two volumes. The first contains the undisputed works of Saint Paulinus, arranged for the first time according to chronological order, which we diligently sought to establish with the study and advice of a most learned man.

We added some letters; we divided several others into two, following the authority of manuscript codices; and in certain cases, on firm grounds, we combined two letters into one. Among these we placed, in its proper order, the one surviving sermon of Saint Paulinus, *On the Treasury*.

Moreover, we thought we would provide students with something both agreeable and useful if we inserted among these works the letters written to Paulinus or written by him in reply.

Next, we corrected the poorly arranged and disordered summaries of the letters, and printed passages of Sacred Scripture in italic type.

Since it is universally acknowledged that the dispositions and virtues of the holy Fathers can be discovered nowhere better than in their letters, anyone may readily behold in the letters of Paulinus the author’s character, eloquence, prudence, zeal, steadfastness of spirit, love of truth and piety, devotion to Sacred Scripture, humanity, modesty, truly Christian humility, and greatest charity, as well as his outward appearance and inner spirit.

In various letters authors spontaneously reveal and portray themselves in their natural colors. Nature, place, occasion, the kind of subject, and the persons involved all express them, even when they are not thinking of doing so. This is so true that Paulinus, who had refused his requesting Severus a portrait of himself, nevertheless painted himself so excellently in various passages of his letters that it was easy for us to reproduce his face from life on the basis of them: Letter 5, section 4; Letter 22, section 2; Letter 23, sections 10 and 23; and Letter 40, section 6. Uranium, sections 5, 6, and 7, also contributed something to the completion of the portrait, as did Fortunatus, Book II of *The Life of Saint Martin*, and the *Roman Subterranean*.

The letters are followed by poems purged of countless errors, enlarged by many verses, and elucidated by explanations. They contain many monuments of ecclesiastical discipline, antiquity, and history, as well as the principal precepts and counsels of the Gospel.

Furthermore, throughout all the works of Paulinus we marked frequent sections with numbered signs, so that the subsequent use of Paulinus and the investigation of passages might be easier. We explained the reasons for certain emendations in brief notes in the lower margins; in the side margins we explained some more obscure words. Additions are enclosed in round brackets.

The second volume contains works that are either doubtful or spurious. We appended the notes of various scholars, at the end of each of which the name of the author is printed. Our own notes are prefixed with the letter q.

There follow the praises of the most holy man, revised from various writers according to manuscript codices. These prepare the way for the Life of Saint Paulinus, newly composed from the works of the saint himself and of ancient writers.

Seven dissertations have been added. The first establishes the chronological order of the letters, the second that of the poems. The third, fourth, and fifth discuss Sulpicius Severus, Alethius, Victricius, and Aper, to whom Paulinus wrote. The sixth concerns the lost, doubtful, and spurious works of Saint Paulinus. The seventh discusses at length the disputed captivity of that same saint.

There follow the variant readings from manuscript and printed codices. Among them one may find corrections of lesser importance.

[Note: These variants, which had also been relegated to the end of the Veronese edition, we have restored beneath the text. Editor.]

Finally, so that nothing might be lacking in this last edition, we appended fifteen indexes.

The first presents this new order of the letters compared with the order previously in common use. The second contains the former order insofar as it can be reduced to the new one. The third consists of the names, arranged alphabetically, of those to whom Paulinus sent letters or from whom he in turn received them. The fourth presents the beginnings of the letters arranged alphabetically. The following four indexes concern the poems in the same way.

To these eight we added an alphabetically arranged list of the printed and manuscript codices by whose assistance we purged the text of Paulinus. The distinguished Emericus Bigotius of Rouen, well known to learned men, most courteously according to his custom supplied us with a considerable number of these, both from his own distinguished library and from several others.

We appended two indexes of the codices against which the individual letters were revised and the individual poems corrected.

These are followed by two further indexes of the passages of Sacred Scripture that are explained and cited in a distinctive manner.

[Note: We shall omit these indexes of Scripture, since they are to be copied later into the general Scripture index for the whole *Patrologia*. Editor.]

An index of words with unusual meanings is also added. The series is closed by a very full index of subjects.

Since the citations of various authors placed in the margins might otherwise cause difficulty, we wish to inform you that we used the Bordeaux edition of Ausonius, prepared by Vinetus in 1575; the Basel edition of Saint Jerome from 1565; the latest edition of Saint Augustine; the Antwerp edition of Sulpicius Severus from 1574; the Paris edition of Gregory of Tours from 1640; likewise the Paris edition of Saint Gregory the Great from 1605; and the Cologne edition of Binius’s Councils and Baronius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals* from 1609.

In words derived from Greek we used Greek orthography; in Latin words, the orthography displayed by the ancient manuscript codices, provided that in pronunciation there was no divergence from accepted usage offensive to the ear.

[Note: We too have preserved that orthography untouched. Editor.]

We would indeed have wished that a more elegant hand had revised these works of Paulinus, so that the industry of the labor might answer to the dignity and merits of so great a man. Since, however, we were led to undertake this work by the advice of learned men, whom it would have been irreverent not to obey, this alone remains for us: to commend the work to your humanity, dearest reader, and to ask you earnestly that, if you discover any errors in it, you attribute them not to an evil intention or negligence but to human weakness.

Moreover, join us, I beg you, in asking that God favor this work with a heavenly blessing, and that all into whose hands it comes may handle it with the reverence due to Paulinus and receive with appropriate piety a work suffused with the light of divine charity and filled with evangelical precepts and ecclesiastical discipline.

# Life of Saint Paulinus, Bishop of Nola

Composed from his own writings and from the monuments of antiquity.

## Chapter One

### The birth, family, and wealth of Saint Paulinus. Various men named Paulinus.

### 1

[Column 0015D]

Paulinus, who in ancient sources is also called Pontius [Note: Ausonius, Letter 23], and in manuscript and printed codices Meropius [Note: Paulinus, Letter 40], celebrated in the Church with so many and such great praises [Notes: Ambrose, Letter 30; Uranius, §9], was born of a most illustrious family, namely, of Roman senators on both his father’s and his mother’s side [Note: Chiffletius, *Paulinus*, p. 131].

[Column 0016D]

He was related to Melania the Elder, whose nobility was held in such high esteem at Rome [Note: Paulinus, Letter 29, §5], and also to Celsus, the son of Pneumatius, whose death he commemorated in a graceful and elegant poem [Note: Paulinus, Poem 32, v. 622].

### 2

[Columns 0016D–0017B]

Under the early emperors there were several men named Paulinus [Note: Ausonius, Letter 19]. Two were consuls under Constantine, in the years 325 and 334 [Note: Baronius, year 394, §78].

Among the patrician families that had first passed from idols to Christ, Prudentius counts the Paulini [Note: Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, p. 7]. Indeed, since the reputation of our Paulinus had already spread throughout the world, Cardinal Baronius rightly notes that Prudentius honored him with this family distinction [Note: Baronius, year 394, §79]. Baronius believes that our Paulinus belonged to the illustrious Anician family, because two Paulini who were consuls under Constantine bore the surname Anicius [Note: ibid.].

I would readily believe that the Paulini migrated from Rome to Aquitania, since Ambrose testifies that Saint Paulinus, in the splendor of his birth, was second to no one in the regions of Aquitania [Note: Ambrose, Letter 30].

A place called Paulinus’s Hill still remains at Bordeaux [Note: Vinetus’s notes on Ausonius, p. 465], and is believed once to have been the residence of this family.

There were also other Paulini in Aquitania related to Ausonius [Notes: Vinetus’s notes on Ausonius, pp. 128–129], among them Ausonius’s nephew Paulinus, whose poem entitled *Eucharisticon* survives [Note: see Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 420, observation 3]. Yet in the letters they exchanged, Ausonius and Paulinus do not say that they were bound by any relationship.

At Nola there were two other men of the same name as Saint Paulinus, one a presbyter and the other a layman, as will be demonstrated elsewhere [Note: Augustine, Letter 149, §34].

At the same time there lived in lower Aquitania a Paulinus, bishop of Béziers [Note: Hydatius, *Chronicle*; in French, *de Béziers*], who wrote a letter in 419 that has been lost.

There was also a Paulinus who was a disciple of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, and who wrote his life. It was while Paulinus was then a deacon and was bringing the accusation that Caelestius was condemned at the Council of Carthage in 411 [Note: *Life of Ambrose*; Augustine, Letter 175; Marius Mercator, *Commonitorium*, ch. 1; see Baronius, year 418, §§12 ff.].

Gennadius also mentions another Paulinus who wrote certain homilies. From the order of Gennadius’s catalogue, he seems to have flourished around the middle of the fifth century [Note: Gennadius, *Catalogue*, ch. 68].

At the end of that same century there lived another Paulinus of Périgueux, who composed in verse the life of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours [Note: see Dissertation 6, on doubtful works].

### 3

[Columns 0017C–0018A]

Our Paulinus was the son of another Paulinus [Notes: Ausonius, Letters 23 and 20], who prolonged his life to a very advanced age. It is plausible that this was Pontius Paulinus, founder of Bourg on the Garonne and prefect of the Gauls [Note: Sidonius Apollinaris, Poem 22], who left children to posterity; that, however, does not fit our Paulinus.

That Paulinus and his bride had professed the Christian religion is shown by the fact that our Paulinus sent one of his freedmen to Bordeaux to serve in the house of the Lord, assigning him services in memory of his parents [Note: Paulinus, Letter 12, §12].

Saint Paulinus had a sister, to whom he wrote several letters on contempt for the world [Note: Gennadius, *Catalogue*, ch. 48], and a brother who died before him, leaving children behind [Note: Ausonius, Letter 23]. This brother had been initiated into baptism by Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux. He had not, however, lived with the holiness demanded by the Christian religion, and had preferred present and perishable goods to heavenly and eternal ones. His death therefore deeply saddened his brother Paulinus, who commended his soul to the prayers of Delphinus and Amandus [Notes: Paulinus, Letters 35 and 36, §2].

Some claim that Ebromagus was Paulinus’s homeland [Notes: Sacchini, *Life of Saint Paulinus*; Paulinus, Letter 11, §14], but this is not sufficiently established.

He was born at Bordeaux [Note: Uranius, §1] in the year of the Lord 353, according to Chiffletius’s calculations and arguments [Note: Chiffletius, *Paulinus*, p. 130; see below, ch. 23], although Chiffletius says that he was born in 354.

He possessed a very extensive patrimony and immense estates [Notes: Gregory of Tours, *Confessors*, ch. 107; *Life of Martin*, 2, vol. VIII; Sulpicius, *Life of Martin*, ch. 26; Augustine, *City of God*, X; Eucherius, Letter to Valerian], both in the strength of his houses, the number of his slaves, and the number of those who honored him as their patron.

The nature of his estates may readily be inferred from the words of Ausonius [Note: Ausonius, Letter 23]. Calling Paulinus back from his retreat in Spain, he says:

> Lest we mourn the house torn away and scattered,  
> and the realms of the ancient Paulinus,  
> torn apart among a hundred masters.

### 4

[Columns 0018A–0018D]

While still living in the world, Paulinus inhabited a certain town belonging to his estate, called Ebromanum [Notes: Ausonius, Letters 21 and 22] or Ebromagus [Note: Paulinus, Letter 11, §14]; it is one and the same place.

Vinetus and Fronto Ducaeus, both natives of that region, suspect that the place was the village called Embrau, or Brau, below Blavia—which is four Gascon leagues distant—and below Bourg, formerly the proper domain of the Paulini, situated on the bank of the Garonne [Note: see note 30 on Paulinus]. They believe this to be the ancient Ebromagus.

But since the word *Bourg*, by which that place was designated, does not in any way approach Ebromagus after fifty years, the town of Bourg seems to me plainly different from Ebromagus.

Brau is undoubtedly the same town which the geographer Samson calls Braux in Votreziac among the Santones and says is one league distant from the Garonne [Note: Samson, B, p. 265]; whereas in ancient times Ebromagus was reached by boat, as Ausonius testifies [Note: Ausonius, Letter 22]:

> Carried all the way to your Ebromanum.

On this basis Samson insists that Ebromagus was not Brau but Bourg.

Nevertheless, nothing prevents the riverbed from having once been nearer to this town.

No one will be surprised that the region which he calls uncultivated and unpleasant—once adorned by the lavish expenditures of nobles—has lost its ancient beauty after twelve centuries of neglect.

The ancient itineraries place Ebromagus near Carcassonne [Note: see note 30 on Paulinus], which I consider entirely different from Paulinus’s Ebromagus.

Alingonum also, which is mentioned several times in the letters of Paulinus [Notes: Paulinus, Letter 20, §3, and Letter 12, §12], seems to have belonged to his estate. Today they call it Lengon, a town situated on the Garonne in the district of Bazas [Notes: see note 65 on Paulinus; Samson, A, p. 64]. Although it belongs to the diocese of the bishop of Bazas rather than to the archbishop of Bordeaux, to whom it seems to have belonged at that time, it was, by a gift of Saint Paulinus made before the year 670, the property of the canons of the church of Saint Severinus at Bordeaux.

Paulinus seems also to have possessed estates at Narbonne in Gaul [Note: Paulinus, Letter 5, §22], and likewise at Fundi in Latium [Note: Letter 32, §17], today in the Terra di Lavoro.

## Chapter Two

### The studies and learning of Paulinus. His teacher Ausonius.

### 1

[Columns 0018D–0019A]

From the monuments of Paulinus that survive, it is easy to recognize his natural gifts. Ambrose and Jerome raise him to the highest praises [Notes: Ambrose, Letter 30; Jerome, Letter 13].

He was exceedingly devoted to the liberal arts [Notes: Paulinus, Letter 8, §3, and Poem 10, v. 23], cultivated in every form of eloquence, and outstanding in poetic and oratorical fluency.

“I admired the wisdom of the world up to this point,” Paulinus himself says [Note: Letter 4, §2], “and through useless letters and a prudence rejected by God I was foolish and mute . . . once loquacious in the literature of human fables” [Note: Letter 40, §6].

2. He acquired an outstanding teacher in literary studies, Decimus Magnus Ausonius [Note: [Col. 0019] Auson. ep. 21 and 24.], renowned for poetic and oratorical ability among the leading men of his age. After having taught grammar and rhetoric for a long time, Ausonius was entrusted to the emperor Gratian for instruction and guidance [Note: [Col. 0019] Life, p. 1.]. Gratian subsequently raised him to the highest ranks of office: he became prefect of the praetorium of Gaul and Italy, and in the year 379 was appointed ordinary consul.

From his poems it is entirely clear that Ausonius was a Christian [Col. 0019B], and among the advantages of his country estate he expressly mentions its proximity to a church [Note: [Col. 0019] Auson. ep. 23.]. Yet most of his poems, by which he tried to turn our Paulinus away from his holy purpose of life, are more worthy of a pagan than of a Christian [Note: [Col. 0019] Baron. year 394, §§ 84–85.]. Compelled by his relationship and affection for Paulinus’s father, the elder Paulinus, he undertook to educate and raise the noble boy, teaching and shaping him with the diligence and industry of a teacher but with the humanity and devotion of a father. Thereafter he was accustomed to call him nothing other than his son [Note: [Col. 0019] Auson. ep. 23 and 24.], and to describe himself as his parent and foster-father.

For his part, Paulinus admits that he owed everything to Ausonius:

> To you I owe learning, dignity, and letters,  
> the honor of tongue, toga, and reputation.  
> I owe my advancement, elevation, and education to you—  
> my patron, teacher, father [Note: [Col. 0019] Paulin. carm. 10, line 93.].

[Col. 0019C] Elsewhere, too, he freely acknowledges that all he possessed—his good character and his studies alike—had arisen from Ausonius’s springs [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid., line 148.].

3. Although the works of Paulinus that we possess are splendid monuments of his learning, his homily *On Almsgiving*, or *On the Treasury* [Note: [Col. 0019] Paulin. 34 among the letters.], more clearly reveals the sweetness of Paulinian style, because its composition is tightly compressed and restrains the usual abundance and rapidity of his words in the letters.

Saint Ambrose strongly commends his outstanding eloquence, nobility, and natural gifts [Note: [Col. 0019] Ambros. ep. 30.]. In his *Chronicle*, Idatius calls him “most noble” and “most eloquent,” while Saint Eucherius calls him “a most abundant fountain of eloquence” [Note: [Col. 0019] Eucher. letter to Valerian.]. But Saint Jerome’s eulogy surpasses all others [Note: [Col. 0019] Hieron. ep. 13.]. Writing to him some time after his withdrawal to Nola, he says:

> I gladly read your book, which you sent me, wisely and elegantly composed for the emperor Theodosius [Col. 0019D], and I especially admired its divisions. Though in the opening sections you surpass others, in the penultimate sections you surpass yourself. The very style of your eloquence is compressed and polished; and although it shines with Ciceronian clarity, it is rich in maxims. For, as someone has said, speech lies prostrate when only its words are praised.
>
> Moreover, there is a great coherence among the subjects, and one thing depends upon another. Whatever you take from it is either the conclusion of what precedes or the beginning of what follows. Happy Theodosius [Col. 0020A], who is defended by such an orator of Christ! You have given brilliance to his purple and consecrated the usefulness of his laws to future ages. Well done in virtue: possessing such beginnings, what sort of seasoned soldier will you be!
>
> He testifies that nothing is lacking in him, provided an inward knowledge of the divine writings be added: “If you possessed this foundation—or rather, if it were as though the finishing hand were applied to your work—we would have no volumes more beautiful, more learned, more pleasing, or more truly Latin than yours” [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.].

After listing the chief lights of the Latin Church’s writers—Tertullian, Lactantius, Victorinus, Arnobius, Hilary, and Cyprian—and showing that each lacked something necessary for perfection, Jerome adds:

> I come to you yourself, and I shall ask you not to suspect flattery in our friendship; rather, think me mistaken or carried away by affection than believe that I would deceive a friend through flattery. You possess great talent and an infinite wealth of language; you speak easily and purely, and that very ease and purity are mingled with wisdom, for when the head is sound, all the senses are vigorous.
>
> If to this wisdom and eloquence there were added study of, or insight into, the Scriptures, I would see you shortly holding the citadel of our writers [Col. 0020B].

Elsewhere, too, he commends the beauty of Paulinus’s eloquence and his learning in secular literature [Note: [Col. 0019] Hieron. ep. 103 and 153.]. Erasmus calls Paulinus a “Christian Cicero” [Note: [Col. 0019] Erasmus, notes on Jerome, p. 107.].

Ausonius praises Paulinus’s learning in literature [Note: [Col. 0019] Auson. ep. 19 and 21.], but he exalts his poetic vein in an astonishing manner. Speaking of a poem written by Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0019] Aus. ep. 19.], he says that it was composed with such elegance that Paulinus alone seemed to have achieved what is contrary to the nature of things: brevity without obscurity.

> How skillfully and neatly you have done this, how rhythmically and sweetly! What shall I say now about your eloquence? I can confidently swear that no one among the young men of Rome is your equal in poetic expression. Certainly that is how you seem to me. If I am wrong, I am still a father [Col. 0020C] . . . Yet since I love you dutifully, I judge sincerely and severely.

He further praises the vigorous and sublime energy of Paulinus’s poems, saying that Paulinus reaches for the highest things without falling. Elsewhere he admits that his pupil had snatched the poetic palm from him [Note: [Col. 0019] Aus. ep. 20.]. In another letter, namely Letter 21, Ausonius says of another poem [Note: [Col. 0019] Aus. ep. 21.]:

> As for the poem’s delightfulness, its invention and continuity, I swear that it will never be imitable by anyone, even though people acknowledge that it ought to be imitated.

These poems, imitable by no one, have perished. Without doubt, Paulinus’s natural disposition and poetic vein were gentler and sweeter, and likewise more magnificent. Ausonius himself testifies that there was in him a certain honeyed modulation, and so forth [Col. 0020D] [Note: [Col. 0019] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 656, Rosweyde edition.].

Nor should the ability of the flourishing poet be judged from the poems that survive, composed with evangelical simplicity after he had renounced the Muses [Note: [Col. 0019] Paulin., carm. 10, line 19.]. Rather, we should consider that, since even these works are of such quality, something must have emerged as highly perfect while ambition was still burning, while the desire to please and the craving for fame were stimulating and sharpening his care, and while the vigor of his lofty intellect was at the same time raising his diction—something that deservedly pleased both learned people and the multitude.

4. While he was still living in the world, he reduced to an epitome three books of Suetonius, those which Suetonius had written on kings [Col. 0021A] [Note: [Col. 0021] Auson. ep. 19.], and composed a most delightful poem. That work of Suetonius Tranquillus has perished, and with it Paulinus’s *Epitome*, except for a few verses of Paulinus’s poem, which Ausonius praises and greatly exalts in Letter 19 to him.

Paulinus had also sent Ausonius another poem for correction [Note: [Col. 0021] Ibid.]. Ausonius promised to undertake the task, although, as he says, “the final hand has already been applied by you.” In turn, Ausonius sent him a poem composed by his own art in heroic meter.

5. Paulinus was not a particularly diligent investigator of history [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulin. ep. 28, no. 5.]. For in his earlier period, when he seemed to be reading what ought not to be read, he kept away from historical writers. It is evident from this that he was ignorant of geography: on Nicetas’s return from Nola to Scupi in Dardania, he directs the journey through the city of Tomi in Scythia [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulin. carm. 17, line 193.].

If we believe Jerome [Note: [Col. 0021] Hieron. ep. 153.], Paulinus was skilled in the Greek language. Paulinus, on the contrary, says that this language was unknown to him [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulin. ep. 46, no. 2.]. Nevertheless, in the same place he admits that he translated the works of Saint Clement into Latin, though not without errors [Note: [Col. 0021] Ibid.]. Let us therefore say that he was moderately instructed in Greek literature.

## CHAPTER III. Paulinus Marries Therasia. He Is Honored with the Consulship and the Highest Offices. He Forms Friendships with Many People.

1. Paulinus obtained Therasia as a wife, like himself, who brought him immense estates [Note: [Col. 0021] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107.]. She came very close to him in virtue and devotion and, differing in nothing from her husband’s purpose of fleeing the world, transferred her estates into the ownership of others and courageously followed her husband into retirement at Nola. Content there with a small plot of ground, she consoled herself with the services of charity, simplicity, and religion.

Thus she was a wife not like Eve, once a guide to softness for her husband [Note: [Col. 0021] Augustine, Letter 27, no. 2.], but one who recalled him to strength, restored and reunited to the bones of her husband by unity of heart and will. Joined to him by spiritual bonds all the stronger because they were chaste, she became a participant in his most holy love of God. Thus, in one marriage, both sexes found examples of trampling secular pride and of not despairing of Christian perfection.

Jerome calls Therasia “the holy sister of Paulinus” [Note: [Col. 0021] Hieron. ep. 13.], plainly because she led a continent life with him in solitude. She very diligently obeyed Saint Jerome’s counsels, avoiding the company of married women. Amid the jewels surrounding those women and their silken garments [Col. 0021D], she was never ashamed to wear humble clothing—partly because she avoided the companionship of noblewomen, and partly because she knew perfectly well that such companionship was a seedbed, in one case of repentance from her purpose and in the other of ostentation and pride.

For this reason, even when writing to bishops, Paulinus entered her name in the titles of his letters [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulin. ep. 3, 4, 6, 7, 26, 39, 40, 43, 44, 45.], and bishops writing back, on their part, continued to greet Therasia and Paulinus until the year 408 or 409 [Note: [Col. 0021] Augustine, Letters 31 and 95.].

That Therasia was an aid to Paulinus in virtue and in his conversion from the world to God can be inferred from the glorious insult of Ausonius [Note: [Col. 0021] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 662.]. Criticizing Paulinus as insufficiently constant in friendship, Ausonius attributes the cause to her, as though she were drawing him away, calling her a Tanaquil who would put herself forward through wisdom and knowledge of religious matters, command her husband, and for that reason be feared by Paulinus. Thus he snarls:

> If you fear betrayal, Paulinus, and fear  
> the charge against our friendship, your Tanaquil  
> must not know this [Note: [Col. 0021] Ibid.].

But Paulinus replies that his wife was not a Tanaquil but a Lucretia [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulin. carm. 10, line 192.]. Indeed, her divine wisdom and manly steadfastness are made clear by the fact that she gladly consented to a poor and harsh life with her husband, sold whatever resources she possessed, whether dowry or otherwise, and distributed the proceeds among the needy.

In Therasia’s name, Paulinus sent Bassula, the mother-in-law of Severus, a fragment of wood from the divine cross [Note: [Col. 0021] Letter 31, no. 1.], which Melania had brought from Jerusalem in the year 402.

One circumstance seemed to show Therasia less faithful to her husband, if Gregory of Tours is to be believed [Note: [Col. 0021] See below, chapter 8, no. 2.]. But Idatius, who assumes that she was still living in the year 423, after the death of Honorius, teaches in the same place that she did not depart from her husband in merits and devotion [Note: [Col. 0021] Idatius, *Chronicle*.]. It will be clear from what follows that she died in the year 426 [Note: [Col. 0021] See chapter 52, no. 2.].

After long prayers, a male child was finally born to them while they were living in Spain [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulin. carm. 32, lines 600 and following.]. But he was not destined to live: on the eighth day after his birth the boy completed his life and was buried at Complutum [Col. 0022C]. Whether they had other children is unknown.

2. At first Paulinus was occupied with the bustle of the forum and secular affairs, but from his earliest years he attained the highest levels of dignity and honor [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulin. ep. 5, no. 4.]. In the year 372, a certain Paulinus was prefect of New Epirus or Albania. If this was our Paulinus, he was nineteen, or at most twenty, years old [Note: [Col. 0021] Codex Theodosianus, Gothofred, vol. V, pp. 365–366.].

It is certain that he was consul before Ausonius, that is, before the year 379 [Note: [Col. 0021] Auson. ep. 20, 23, 25.]. But since his consulship is not recorded in the *Fasti*, it is necessary to say that he was substituted for the consul Valens, who died in the year 378, or for some other consul, rather than that he was an ordinary consul [Note: [Col. 0021] Paulinus, Chifflet, pp. 131 and 136.].

No one should be surprised that Ausonius called Paulinus’s name honored by the title of the *Fasti* [Note: [Col. 0021] Auson. ep. 20.], for it was customary for substitute consuls to be written in the *Fasti* alongside the ordinary consuls, and examples of this survive. This certainly should not have moved Baronius [Col. 0022D] to assert that Paulinus was ordinary consul in the year 375, since, according to Jerome’s testimony, no consul was appointed in that year [Note: [Col. 0021] Jerome, *Chronicle*]. Baronius himself both asserts and denies this in the same place [Note: [Col. 0021] Baronius, year 375, § 1.]. [Note: [Col. 0021] Ofg., vol. V, pp. 365–366.]

In the year 380 we read that Paulinus was prefect at Rome [Note: [Col. 0021] Baronius, year 394, § 82; and Chifflet, p. 131.]; it is easy to interpret this of our Paulinus. Ausonius calls himself the giver of his former honors [Note: [Col. 0021] Aus. ep. 21 and 24.], and it is clear that he enjoyed great favor and authority with the emperor Gratian from the fact that he taught and raised him. Paulinus, for his part, freely admits that he owed his honors and dignities to Ausonius [Note: [Col. 0023] Paulin. carm. 10, line 9.], whom he declares that he loved, honored, and continues to honor, and with whom he testifies that he was joined by an eternal covenant [Note: [Col. 0023] Carm. 11.].

3. Paulinus was joined in friendship not only with Ausonius but also with many others in the world [Note: [Col. 0023] Paulin. ep. 11, nos. 5 and 1.]. Among them was especially Sulpicius Severus, about whom more will be said elsewhere.

In an unfaithful world they had loved one another faithfully and reciprocally. Their love was so religious that no affection could be added to their mutual devotion except the charity of Christ, which alone surpasses every feeling and affection.

While still in the world, Paulinus had also known and loved Sanctus [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 40, no. 2.]; and from that time there had developed the relationship that arose between him, Jovius, and Aper.

## CHAPTER IV. How Paulinus Lived in the World. Through Various Labors and Afflictions, and Also through the Prayers of Saint Felix and Other Saints, He Is Converted to God.

1. It is not surprising that a man so remarkable, so learned, so wealthy, honored with so many dignities, endowed with such outstanding natural gifts, and equally lovable, should have been cherished by such great and numerous crowds of admirers and should have enjoyed such esteem among the nobles and such favor and applause among the multitude.

For this wisdom, this integrity of character, that beauty of eloquence, and that faithfulness in friendship which were praised in him shortly after his conversion [Note: [Col. 0023] Hieron. ep. 103.] had already been present in him. Hence Ausonius praises the elevation of his spirit and his generosity, by which he preferred to gratify his friends rather than indulge his own disposition [Note: [Col. 0023] Auson. ep. 21.]. He also commends the sweetness of their long-standing and mutual affection and holds him up as an example of perfected friendship [Note: [Col. 0023] Auson. ep. 23.].

He was gentle and kind even while living amid the pride of the world [Note: [Col. 0023] Uranus, § 5.]. His letters breathe this singular humanity and most charming character. He seems to indicate that, while still in the world, people considered him well conducted [Note: [Col. 0023] Paulin. carm. 10, line 133.].

Indeed, if he had committed any crime in his life, he would have mentioned it again and again in his writings, in which so many proofs of his humility are found. He laments that he spent his life in sins and rolled about in the world, in which, as he says, he had grown old among enemies [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 40, no. 6.]. He confesses with grief that, despite his great honor, he was a sinner and even a veteran among sinners [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 4, no. 2, and ep. 27, no. 3.]; he groans that he had suffered many shipwrecks amid the waves of the world [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 4, no. 4.]; and he trembles and fears God’s judgments. He laments that he had walked on an unfaithful road [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 11, no. 5.], lived on the food of death [Note: [Col. 0023] Carm. 10, line 135.], and been wise in folly before God [Col. 0023D]. From these things he draws abundant material for humility.

> “A veteran,” he says, “among sinners, I, wretched man, have until now admired the wisdom of the world, and through useless literature and rejected prudence I was foolish and mute before God” [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 4, no. 2.].

Yet he does not specifically identify any crime. It is therefore reasonable to believe that he had led in the world the sort of life led by so many mortals who, considering themselves irreproachable, have no serious doubts about their salvation because they are neither accused nor weighed down by visible and more serious crimes.

But the light of God that was shining upon Paulinus, and that caused him to think so humbly of himself, revealed something else. He had loved the world, and it was enough for him that he should mourn this until his final breath: what he had given to God alone, he had handed over to the devil, whose service he could not escape by his own power.

Moreover, the greater and more numerous his advantages of fortune and the flatteries of human prosperity, the more powerfully and tenaciously the vanity of the world held him bound to itself in chains [Note: [Col. 0023] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 660.]. Yet with Christ’s help he broke these bonds. Thus Christ’s glory triumphed all the more brilliantly, and the power of his grace appeared all the more effective, when so great a senator regarded as loss everything that others looked upon as the supreme good and considered it as dung, in order that he might gain Christ.

2. Since God often conceals the efficacy and power of his grace beneath afflictions [Col. 0024B], he used these means to convert Paulinus to himself. For, as Paulinus himself testifies [Note: [Col. 0023] Paulin. ep. 5, no. 4.], he was frequently exercised by labors and afflictions.

Perhaps, after Gratian’s death, he was compelled to undertake many journeys in order to escape the troubles of unsettled affairs. It seems that, in the year 387, these circumstances forced him to go to the court of Valentinian, at a time when he was known to Alypius, when Alypius was initiated at Milan through baptism [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 3, no. 4.].

Paulinus lived for a long time at Fundi [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 32, no. 17.], a town that he regarded as especially familiar and habitual. While still entangled in the cares of the world, he saw at Vienne the holy bishops Martin of Tours and Victricius of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 18, no. 9.].

Having experienced many hardships by land and sea [Note: [Col. 0023] Carm. 13, line 10.] [Col. 0024C], he moved more easily and readily toward contempt of the world and fellowship with Christ, withdrawing his mind from secular crowds and accommodating it to heavenly commands, as though he had departed by a road bordering on this purpose [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 5, no. 4.].

Moreover, a weaker body and an enfeebled flesh were wearing down his pursuit of pleasures [Note: [Col. 0023] Ibid.]. As we said above [Note: [Col. 0023] Chapter 3, no. 1.], his wife urged him toward devotion.

3. To these influences was added a great number of saints whose companionship he enjoyed. Among them was Saint Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 3, no. 4.], by whose affection he was nourished and strengthened in the faith, and whom he calls a father worthy of reverence and the author of all the good he possessed.

While still in the world, Paulinus was joined by an exceptional friendship to Saint Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, by whom he was baptized at Bordeaux, and to Delphinus’s successor, Saint Amandus, by whom he had been instructed in the salutary disciplines of the Christian religion. This will become clear from other evidence [Col. 0024D].

He calls Saint Martin a blessed father [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 18, no. 9.], wrote honorably of him everywhere, and paid him the highest honors. He recalls with joy that Martin loved him [Note: [Col. 0023] Ep. 32, line 33.].

Indeed, Paulinus was right to honor him with singular veneration. When Paulinus was suffering severely in one eye and a thick cloud had already covered its pupil [Note: [Col. 0023] Sulpicius, *Life of Martin*, chapter 21.], Martin touched the eye with a small brush and restored its former health, removing all pain [Col. 0025A].

Paulinus had not yet given such an illustrious example of evangelical poverty when Martin heard of it and commended him so highly [Note: [Col. 0025] Sulpicius, *Life of Martin*, chapter 26.]. It is not known where on earth that miracle occurred.

That Paulinus saw Martin and Victricius at Vienne is fully established, and we demonstrated it above [Note: [Col. 0025] No. 2.]. By that time Victricius, once a most glorious Confessor, had already been made bishop [Note: [Col. 0025] Paulin. ep. 8, no. 9.]. Paulinus therefore rejoiced that he could at least boast of having seen Victricius’s face in the flesh. At the same time, he mourned the negligence that had made him miss so great an opportunity, since, as he says, at that time not only the sins weighing upon him but also the cares of the world had cast him into darkness.

Nevertheless, he honored Victricius as fully as the opportunity allowed and commended himself and his family to his prayers forever [Col. 0025B].

4. But his principal patron was Saint Felix, priest of the Church of Nola. Felix had been made illustrious by the glorious title of confessor in the time of Decius, but he was made far more illustrious by the miracles that occurred repeatedly at his tomb. His name was celebrated throughout the Church, yet today he is known only through the writings of Saint Paulinus himself [Note: [Col. 0025] Carm. 29, line 5.].

Paulinus says that from his earliest years he had been dedicated by Christ to the service of this saint. Hence there is room for the conjecture that he had given himself to Christ from that time—that is, from childhood—if by the words “from his earliest years” he intended to indicate this.

No one will suspect that this is contrary to the truth if he remembers that Paulinus’s parents were Christians [Note: [Col. 0025] See above, chapter 1, no. 3.]. It is entirely probable that Paulinus arranged for them to be enrolled among the catechumens.

The statement could nevertheless refer to something else: namely, that in the year 394, fifteen years earlier [Note: [Col. 0025] Paulin. *On the Martyrs*, 13, line 7.], that is, around the twenty-seventh year of his age and in the year 379 of Christ, when he had come to Nola to the tomb of Saint Felix, he had dedicated his heart and prayers amid all the labors endured by land and sea.

At no time during that period, however, was Paulinus permitted to celebrate the feast day of that saint at Nola, on January 14, or to offer his devout prayers in person [Note: [Col. 0025] Carm. 12, line 13.]. The bones of blessed Felix rested in the countryside, five hundred paces from the city of Nola, and are still preserved there today [Note: [Col. 0025] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 681.].

During these fifteen years Paulinus undertook various journeys, was worn down by many afflictions, and was summoned into many dangers [Note: [Col. 0025] Paulin. carm. 13, line 10.].

## CHAPTER V. Paulinus Withdraws to Spain in Order to Renounce the World. At What Time He Received Baptism.

1. At last, when he seemed to have obtained rest from calumnies and journeys, was no longer occupied with public affairs, and had withdrawn from the bustle of the forum, he devoted himself to the leisure of the countryside and the worship of the Church, enjoying a tranquility established in the privacy of his household [Note: [Col. 0025] Paulin. ep. 5, no. 4.]. Thus, gradually withdrawing his mind from secular crowds and adapting it to heavenly commands, he moved more readily toward contempt of the world and fellowship with Christ, as though he had already departed by a road bordering on this purpose.

Paulinus’s first withdrawal seems to have taken place in Spain [Note: [Col. 0025] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, pp. 167 and 677.], where he spent at least four years, until the spring of the year 394 [Note: [Col. 0025] Chifflet, p. 163, no. 4.], and therefore seems to have gone there in the year 389 or 390 [Col. 0026A].

2. Up to this point we have made no mention of Paulinus’s baptism, because nothing is known about his age. He was initiated at Bordeaux into baptism by Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0025] Paulin. ep. 3, no. 4; and 10, no. 1.]. Paulinus indicates not only that he received from Delphinus the sacrament of salvation [Note: [Col. 0025] Ep. 20, no. 6.], but also praises him as having performed the offices of father, Peter, and fisherman:

> He cast the hook in order to draw me from the deep and bitter waves of this world, so that I might become a catch of salvation; that I might die to the one for whom I lived and live for the Lord, to whom I had been dead [Note: [Col. 0025] Ibid.].

These words clearly indicate that Paulinus had been granted the grace and effect of the sacrament of Baptism, and that at the same time as he was reborn he renounced the world. It is therefore highly probable that shortly before his withdrawal to Spain he was reborn through the life-giving waters.

But if he had believed that all his sins were absorbed in Baptism, why would he so often speak in his writings of sins and his former life in the world? When he explains to Ausonius the reasons for his changed conduct, he does not attribute the beginning of his holier life to baptism.

For this reason Chifflet places his renewal through divine washing as early as the year 379 or 380, when he dedicated himself entirely to Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0025] Chifflet, p. 140.]. Nor should anyone object that, on this assumption, sins committed after Baptism would have prevented him from attaining the rank of priest or bishop. For nowhere do we find him entangled in any canonical offense, and no one will deny that through his four-year withdrawal and renunciation of his possessions he atoned for his profane and secular life [Col. 0026C].

In any event, it is equally certain that Paulinus had already been baptized before he withdrew to Spain. There he remained for four years, absent from his homeland; during that period he sold his estates, distributed his possessions to the poor, and professed evangelical poverty. No one will deny that this happened in Spain.

Nor will anyone easily persuade himself that he did these things before being renewed by the spiritual washing. His assertion that he had been drawn by Delphinus from the bitter waves of this world is strongly opposed to such a view [Note: [Col. 0025] Ep. 20, no. 6.].

During these four years he wrote to Ausonius from Barcelona. While still a layman there, and later after he had been made a priest, he sent two letters to Sulpicius Severus [Note: [Col. 0025] Ep. 1, no. 10; Paulin. ep. 1, no. 10, and nos. 2 and following.]. The first has perished. In the second he warns Severus not to demand an account of the reason for the institution he had undertaken from profane persons; he encourages him to remain steadfast and invites him to join him.

There is therefore no basis for the conjecture that, after renouncing his possessions and dignities, Paulinus went to his homeland, Bordeaux, before he had been ordained a priest.

Paulinus’s brother had likewise been baptized by Delphinus [Note: [Col. 0025] Ep. 35.], as had Paulinus himself, who from that time calls the most holy bishop Delphinus “lord” and “father,” with the highest praise and reverence [Note: [Col. 0025] Ep. 17, no. 3.].

In the letters sent to him, the filial devotion and reverence of a son toward his parent shine forth so clearly [Col. 0027A] that nothing more gracious or more modest can be imagined [Note: [Col. 0025] Ep. 19, no. 1.].

He recognizes that he was born in Christ from Amandus and through Amandus [Note: [Col. 0027] Ep. 2, no. 4.]. It would be Amandus’s disgrace if Paulinus proved unworthy of so great a father, or his joy if Paulinus were known by good fruits to be a branch of that tree.

Through Amandus’s intercession, he says, the Lord was placed in the little boat of his heart through the sacrament of baptismal grace, and he calls himself Amandus’s planting in Christ [Note: [Col. 0027] Ep. 9, nos. 2 and 5.]. From this it may be inferred that Amandus was at that time a priest of the Church of Bordeaux, and that Paulinus owed him no small debt for his conversion, since Amandus instructed him in the elements of the Christian religion and perhaps lifted him from the sacred font.

## CHAPTER VI. How Paulinus Conducted Himself Immediately after His Withdrawal to Spain. Concerning His Son Who Died.

1. Paulinus, therefore, reborn from water and the Spirit and inflamed with love of perfect virtue, began, as we said above [Note: [Col. 0027] Chapter 5, no. 2.], to contemplate withdrawing to Spain, so that he might increase the grace he had received in baptism and dedicate himself entirely to God.

For a man entangled in so many necessities, so honored among his own people, and whose favor everyone eagerly sought, flight was altogether necessary [Note: [Col. 0027] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 667.].

He lived in cultivated and most pleasant places, not far from the sea and the cities [Note: [Col. 0027] Paulin. carm. 10, lines 182 and 216.]. Yet he already loved a solitary life and honored the holy anchorites with the greatest devotion and affection. As he says, they

> gaze upon God and, intent on seeing the depths of truth,  
> love leisure freed from empty cares;  
> they shun the noises of the forum and the turmoil of affairs,  
> and all occupations hostile to divine gifts,  
> to the commands of Christ, and to love of salvation.
>
> In hope and faith they follow God,  
> for the promised reward [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 164.] . . .

Yet it seemed that this conviction had settled in those

> to whom the whole light of truth and goodness  
> had already become clear—  
> the eternal age to come and the emptiness of the present.
>
> But the same did not then please me [Note: [Col. 0027] That is, “the same approval.”].

2. Shortly after he advanced toward a stricter life and his withdrawal to Spain, he seems to have composed certain poems that do not breathe the holiness found in his later writings, poems, and letters.

Among these we place a morning prayer to God in which he earnestly asks God for the honorable conduct of a man living in the world, through which he nevertheless promises himself eternal and blessed life [Note: [Col. 0027] Carm. 4, line 18.]. In that prayer he prays for a happy posterity for himself and his family [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 17.], from which one may infer that he then already had sons, or at least desired them [Col. 0027D].

The morning prayer to God that follows was apparently composed at about the same time [Note: [Col. 0027] Carm. 5.]. Yet in it greater devotion, deeper humility, and fear of God’s judgments shine forth. There he seems to indicate that sons had been born to him:

> May I be dear to my friends,  
> and always a father without the wound of that name [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 66.].

In the poem on Saint John the Baptist, which is a paraphrase of the Gospel [Col. 0028A] [Note: [Col. 0027] Carm. 6.], he seems to indicate that not long before he had devoted himself to a life of religious discipline and undertaken a stricter way of life. Departing slightly from the historical simplicity, he returns to the order of the narrative and adds:

> I hope that one day, with my strength made firm,  
> I may also drive strong chariots through this expanse.
>
> Now let us take up again the journey we have begun.  
> Let a mortal page speak of mortal things;  
> let divine things speak of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 175.].

The paraphrase of the first psalm seems, I think, to be one of the hymns that he composed while still inexperienced in theological mysteries [Note: [Col. 0027] Carm. 7.]. It is therefore not surprising if it appears to signify the error of those who, wrongly understanding the Apostle’s passage in 1 Corinthians 3, supposed that all Christians, even the wicked, would attain some sort of salvation, provided that they had preserved the faith intact, and would not be tormented by the punishments of the damned.

3. Since Paulinus had not yet entered upon the path of evangelical poverty before withdrawing to Spain [Note: [Col. 0027] Carm. 32, line 599.], I can readily believe that during that period a son was born to him. Paulinus ordered him to be buried at Complutum beside the bodies of the holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 605.], that is, as I think, beside the holy child-martyrs Justus and Pastor, whose memory is celebrated at Complutum, which the geographer Samso calls Madrid [Col. 0028B].

That boy had undoubtedly been initiated through baptism, since Paulinus calls him “pious posterity” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 602.] and makes him, together with the other baptized child Celsus, a participant in the glory of eternal life. Paulinus hopes that this drop of his own blood will help him, a sinner, so that, once his sins have been forgiven, he may one day be granted enjoyment of the same rest.

He had arranged the boy’s tomb beside the bodies of the holy martyrs so that, as he says, “from the neighboring blood and rank of the saints he might draw a new strength” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 606.].

After the boy’s death, no offspring remained to Paulinus. Nor do we dare assert that he ever had another son, since he himself calls this child one whom he had long desired [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid., line 601.]. From Paulinus’s final morning prayer, he seems to have had a son still living when he composed it [Note: [Col. 0027] Carm. 5, line 67.].

This, however, must be regarded as certain: he was bereft of his sons when he withdrew to Nola [Note: [Col. 0027] Ambros. ep. 30.]. He lacked the fruitfulness of children so that, through the sterility of his body, the fruitfulness of his soul might increase, and so that he might desire a better offspring of righteous deeds and a posterity of merits that would not perish.

He says that his son was taken from him by God [Note: [Col. 0027] Paulin. carm. 32, line 601.], because he was unworthy to rejoice in holy posterity.

[Col. 0028D] **4.** Some believe [Note: [Col. 0027] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 668.] that this occurred during his retreat in Spain, where he lived far from friends and acquaintances—not at Nola, where he could not have remained hidden from the Nolan people who knew him—that is, the event which Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 107, relates in these words:

> “Accordingly, he went away with his wife as though he were traveling to another region, possessing nothing except his own personal standing [*statum proprium*; reading uncertain]. After a long time, when he was being sought by inhabitants of his native region and could nowhere be found, a merchant from that city came to this town, [Col. 0029A] where the holy man was serving the heavenly Lord. When he saw him, he immediately threw himself upon the ground, embraced the holy man’s feet, and said: ‘THIS IS THE BLESSED PAULINUS, KNOWN THROUGHOUT THE WHOLE WORLD!’ He had been sought at length by his fellow citizens but could nowhere be found. When he recounted all his deeds, everyone who heard these things was astonished.”

## CHAPTER VII. Paulinus gives and consecrates himself wholly to God and embraces the monastic life

**1.** We have already observed above [Note: [Col. 0029] Chapter 5, § 1.] that Paulinus withdrew to Spain so that, by gradually drawing his mind away from worldly disturbances and adapting it to heavenly commandments, he might advance more readily and easily toward contempt for the world and fellowship with Christ. God is faithful to those who seek him, and he comes freely to their aid; he blessed and crowned the good will that he himself had inspired in his servant. Paulinus says:

> “After I grew old among my enemies and vanished in my thoughts, I lifted my eyes to the mountains, toward the commandments of the law; and, receiving the gifts of grace, I learned from where my help comes—from the Lord, who, not repaying according to iniquities, enlightened the blind, released the fettered, humbled the wrongly exalted, in order to raise up the humbly abased.” [Note: [Col. 0029] Paulinus, Letter 4, § 2.]

He completely changed the former life that he had led in the world, although he had not been regarded as depraved in it. This truly was “a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High,” which God alone could accomplish. [Note: [Col. 0029] Song 10, line 132; Letter 9, § 2; and Psalm LXXVI, 11.]

Fear of the final and terrible judgment had penetrated his heart. Therefore, writing to Ausonius, he says that he fears God as judge, terrified by the summons of that final trumpet; that he takes care lest death overtake him unprepared; and that he may be permitted to await that day of reckoning with a tranquil mind.

> At his coming, with trembling inward parts,  
> My credulous heart quakes, and my soul rejoices,  
> Already watchful for what is to come,  
> Fearing beforehand lest, bound by anxious cares  
> For its imprisoned body,  
> And weighed down by the burdens of worldly things,  
> If the vast trumpet should resound  
> Through the opened heavens,  
> It might not raise itself on light wings  
> To meet the King in the air. [Note: [Col. 0029] Song 10, line 304.]  
>   
> This is my fear, this is my struggle:  
> That the final day may find me, sunk in dark shadows,  
> Engaged in an unfruitful activity. [Note: [Col. 0029] Ibid., line 316.]

He also shows how the grace of Christ, wholly transforming a person, had entirely claimed Paulinus for itself:

> When, therefore, his radiance from heaven  
> Has flashed upon our inmost hearts,  
> He wipes away the sickly sluggishness of the body  
> And renews the mind’s condition;  
> He drains away everything that formerly delighted us  
> In place of chaste pleasure;  
> And, by the right of the Lord, wholly claims  
> Our hearts, our mouths, and our lives.  
> He wills that he be thought of, understood, believed in, and read;  
> He wills that he be feared and loved. [Note: [Col. 0029] Ibid., line 57.]

**2.** At the same time he changed his clothing and put on a new spirit. He firmly resolved to bid farewell to his household, his native land, and even his family, and to withdraw from the senate so that he might serve God more fervently; [Note: [Col. 0029] Jerome, Letter 13.] to profess the monastic life; [Note: [Col. 0029] Ambrose, Letter 30.] and to spend the remainder of his life in solitude near Nola, with his mind withdrawn from worldly disturbances, “abject and least in the house of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0029] Paulinus, Letter 14.]

For he ardently desired to submit his neck to the yoke of Christ, to serve God at the tomb of Saint Felix, to open the church doors, to care for the thresholds in the morning by keeping them clean, to guard the church at night with sacred vigils, and to end his life in this service. Indeed, he desired to begin his sacred servitude at least with the title and office of doorkeeper. [Note: [Col. 0029] Song 12, line 32; Letter 1, § 10.]

Moreover, he resolved to strengthen his soul through chastity and continence—virtues that even worldly athletes carefully preserve. He judged that he must guard them with still greater devotion while striving for that unfading crown, since even those who contend for a temporal and fragile crown cultivate them. [Note: [Col. 0029] Letter 24, § 9.]

Thus Therasia, formerly his wife, became his sister. [Note: [Col. 0029] Hydatius, Chronicle.] Paulinus, for his part, completely dismissed the Muses and poetic fables. Once he had dedicated his heart to Christ and wished to serve God alone with his entire being, he thought himself no longer permitted to occupy himself with vain and fictitious literature. He writes to Ausonius:

> Why do you command the Muses, dismissed from my care,  
> To return to me, Father?  
> The hearts dedicated to Christ  
> Refuse the Camenae and are closed to Apollo. . . .  
> God forbids his people, whether in leisure or business,  
> To devote themselves to vain and fictitious writings;  
> He commands us to obey his laws  
> And behold his light. [Note: [Col. 0029] Ibid., lines 20ff.]

After dismissing the Muses, he composed the poems he wrote both without literary learning and from evangelical simplicity and devotion. He had forgotten poets so completely that he did not even dare to name them; and he asked Severus’ pardon for having taken something from the poet Virgil, since such study was foreign to a monk. [Note: [Col. 0029] Baronius, year 394, § 83; Paulinus, Letter 22, § 3.]

## CHAPTER VIII. He sells his estates and distributes the money to the poor

**1.** “There is nothing remarkable,” says Jerome, “in feigning or displaying fasting with a gloomy and sallow face, while enjoying abundant income from one’s possessions and flaunting a shabby little cloak. Crates of Thebes did not think that he could possess both virtues and riches at once. We, stuffed with gold, follow the poor Christ and, under the pretext of almsgiving, cling to our former wealth.” [Note: [Col. 0029] Jerome, Letter 13.]

Paulinus did not fall into this vice. He changed his tunic together with his spirit. He did not seek glorious squalor while retaining a full purse; rather, with clean hands and a pure heart, he could glory in being poor both in spirit and in deeds.

He did not wait until the most violent storm of miseries drove him into the harbor of poverty, as happened to certain others of the same name; [Note: [Col. 0029] Augustine, Letter 149, § 34.] instead, he crossed by a calmer sea, because he saw danger precisely in calmness. Having heard the Savior’s sentence—“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me”—he turned the Gospel words into deeds. [Note: [Col. 0029] Jerome, Letter 13.]

These words, I say, entered Paulinus’ mind with ready and effective faith and continually resounded in the ears of his heart. What the rich man heard from the Lord’s mouth with sorrow, he did with joy. [Note: [Col. 0029] Gregory of Tours; Augustine, Letter 31, § 5.] He regarded this as necessary in order to forestall the justice of the coming Christ:

> This is my fear, this is my struggle:  
> That the final day may find me, sunk in dark shadows,  
> Engaged in an unfruitful activity,  
> Spending my lost years in empty cares.  
> For what shall I do if, while I close my eyes in sluggish prayers,  
> Christ, revealed to me from the heavenly citadel, flashes forth,  
> And, stunned by the sudden rays of the Lord  
> Coming through the opened heaven,  
> I seek, confused by the light poured upon me,  
> Some obscure and gloomy hiding place of night?  
> To prevent this from happening to me, whether through distrust of the truth,  
> Or love of the present life and delight in possessions,  
> Or care and labor, I resolved to forestall the danger  
> By a deliberate purpose and to complete my cares while life remained,  
> Entrusting future things to God through the ages,  
> And to await fierce death with a tranquil heart. [Note: [Col. 0031] Ibid.]

And again:

> The empty agitations stirred by the toil  
> Of the present life along its course  
> Faith in the future life with God abolishes.  
> It does not reject as profane or worthless  
> The riches that we seem to despise,  
> But teaches that they should be stored in heaven  
> As things more precious, entrusted to Christ our God,  
> Who promised to repay more than he received.  
> What has been scorned—or rather, deposited with him—  
> He will repay with abundant interest.  
> The faithful guardian, the good debtor,  
> Will return the increased sum to his creditors;  
> God will restore with interest  
> The abundant money that was despised. [Note: [Col. 0031] Paulinus, Song 10, line 67.]

He preferred poverty to riches, confident in Christ’s word by which he promised those who truly sought the kingdom of God and his righteousness that food and clothing would also be added to them. “Do you think,” he says, “that the person who trusts in the earth is richer than the person who trusts in God, or that the person fed by his own care is richer than the person fed by divine care? What can that wretched person possess who does not possess himself? For he does not possess himself who hopes more in himself than in God; and truly dead is the person who fears not living if he entrusts himself entirely to God and leaves himself in God’s hands.” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ibid.
