The text apparently reads *timet non vivere*—“fears not living.”]

**2.** Having therefore sold both his own resources and those belonging to his wife, he gave to the poor what he had converted into money. [Note: [Col. 0031] Ambrose, Letter 30.] He opened his granaries to the poor and made his storehouses available to travelers and strangers. It was not enough for him to feed those nearby unless he also summoned from every direction people whom he could feed and clothe. How many captives he redeemed! How many debtors entangled in obligations he freed from their creditors by paying the money owed! In a single transaction of charity he wiped away the debtors’ lamentations and restored the creditors’ joy. [Note: [Col. 0031] Uranus, § 5.]

“On one occasion,” says Gregory of Tours, “someone came to him asking for alms, and he said to his wife: ‘Go and give him whatever he needs.’ She replied: ‘We have nothing more than one loaf of bread.’ He said to her: ‘Go and give it to him; the Lord will provide us with food.’ But she, as though prudent and eager to preserve it lest anything be lacking, refused to hand it over. Before long she learned how much richer Paulinus’ faith was than the anxious concern of her own timid care.

“In the meantime, certain men arrived saying that they had been sent by their masters—perhaps by the administrators of Paulinus’ property—to bring him grain and wine, but that they had been delayed because a storm had arisen and had swept away one of their ships together with its wheat. Then the man of God turned to the woman and said: ‘Understand that you have now stolen one loaf from the poor man, and that is why this ship has sunk.’” [Note: [Col. 0031] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 107.]

Paulinus therefore redeemed his sins with countless coins and alms. Having scattered his possessions on earth, he migrated to heaven; indeed, he caused earthly things themselves to ascend into heaven, so that he might prepare an eternal dwelling there for himself. [Note: [Col. 0031] Fortunatus, *Life of Martin*, vol. VIII, p. 761.] Having become poor for Christ’s sake, he was himself richer in faith than before. “Freed from every desire, he follows the Master as a free man, thinking that by this means he is enriched with the riches of paradise, if he is seen to possess nothing transitory.” [Note: [Col. 0031] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 107.]

He became poor from being rich so that, relieved of a heavy burden, he might serve God more fervently; [Note: [Col. 0031] Ambrose, Letter 30.] and, naked following the naked cross, might climb Jacob’s ladder with greater freedom and lightness. [Note: [Col. 0031] Jerome, Letter 13.]

The illustrious Paulinus was the outstanding example of his age. Having cast away his immense wealth, he followed Christ and almost alone in those times fulfilled the evangelical commandments. [Note: [Col. 0031] Sulpicius Severus, Life of Martin, chapters 21 and 26.] He did not imitate others who were ashamed to appear especially devoted to the sacred religion. The fourth century was blessed to possess such a testimony of faith and virtue. [Note: [Col. 0031] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 107.]

Divine majesty granted Paulinus the privilege of fulfilling in practice what the Gospel had declared impossible. The fishermen, when the Lord called them, rejoiced to recall that they had abandoned their little boats and nets, that they had abandoned everything, and had followed the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0031] Augustine, Letter 31, § 5.] And truly, “he despises everything” who despises not only as much as he was able to have, but also as much as he wished to have. In what was desired, the eyes of God are witnesses; in what was possessed, those of human beings are witnesses as well.

Yet somehow, when superfluous and earthly things are loved, what has been acquired binds more tightly than what has merely been desired. . . . For it is one thing not to wish to incorporate what is lacking; it is another to tear away what has already been incorporated. The former are rejected like food; the latter are cut off like limbs.

**3.** Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0031] Jerome, Letter 103.] did not renounce all his goods at one and the same moment, for that was impossible, since he distributed to the poor the money he had obtained from the goods sold; and it is reasonable to believe that he sold his estates gradually and with a certain degree of caution, so that he could more easily support the poor. From his letters sent from Spain it is clear that he had already sold part of his possessions for the use of the poor before he left that region and entered the priesthood. [Note: [Col. 0031] Paulinus, Song 10, lines 81 and 328; Letter 1, § 7.]

It is highly probable that he began this process in that year, because in his fourth letter, written toward the end of 394, as we shall see elsewhere, he says that according to the flesh he had already reached the age at which the man healed by the apostles at the Beautiful Gate through the power of the word had been—that is, more than forty years old. [Note: [Col. 0031] Letter 4, § 3; Acts IV, 22, which says “more than forty years.”]

But in the birth of the soul, he says, he was still at the age of infancy: the age of the Innocents, who, when wounds were threatened against Christ, were sacrificed and with worthy blood went before the victim, the Lamb, inaugurating the Lord’s Passion. [Note: [Col. 0033] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 664.] This refers to the slaughter of the Innocents at the age of two. Since it cannot be interpreted as referring to his baptism, it must necessarily be understood of his adoption of a stricter way of life and his flight from the world. For even if we supposed that Paulinus received the priesthood toward the end of that year, no one, I think, would say that these words referred to the priesthood.

In another letter, also written in 394, he says:

> “Know that the very ancient sinner, recently brought out of darkness and the shadow of death, has breathed the air of life, and has recently placed his hand to the plow and taken up the cross of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0033] Paulinus, Letter 3, § 5.]

Elsewhere he humbly entrusts himself to Augustine to be educated, as one still an infant in the word of God and still nursing in spiritual age. [Note: [Col. 0033] Letter 4, § 3.]

## CHAPTER IX. Paulinus’ humility in renouncing his possessions

**1.** So illustrious and celebrated from its beginning, Paulinus’ virtue was the glory of Christ, the joy and example of the Church. Yet it was greatly exposed to vainglory, which could have undermined all his merits. “It is more beneficial,” says Augustine, “to hold earthly wealth humbly than to relinquish it proudly.” [Note: [Col. 0033] Augustine, Letter 31, § 6.]

Paulinus had dared to undertake so great a work, relying not on his own strength but on divine power and mercy. The one in whom he trusted was able to complete in him the work of his perfection, and what he had deigned to lay down and raise upon its first foundations, he could build according to its proper measurements and finish at the summit.

Paulinus regarded human glory with the greatest caution, as an enemy, and did everything as a humble disciple of Christ, meek in heart. Wisely and devoutly he understood that this glory was not his own—that is, human—but the Lord’s glory within him. Augustine bears this testimony to his virtue. Yet Paulinus himself is a faithful witness, for his writings clearly display charity and humility.

Everything breathes this pious humility, by which he continually begged God with groans and sighs not to lead him into temptation. [Note: [Col. 0033] Augustine, Letter 186, § 41.] His humility shines forth especially when he speaks of the possessions he had sold. He cheerfully acknowledges the Lord’s mercies and glories only in his praise, because if there was anything good in him, it came from God; and if anything was excellent, it came from God’s majesty. [Note: [Col. 0033] Paulinus, Letter 40, § 10.]

Thus his anxieties became light when he was praised. He was conscious of no goodness of his own, so that a flatterer might have pressed him as though he were being made to recognize it; for he knew that what was being proclaimed was not himself but the gifts and works of divine goodness. [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid.]

Nevertheless, when he was tested by these praises, he earnestly asked his friends to refrain from them, lest they sin “from charity against charity” by adding the burden of undeserved praise to the weight of his sins. [Note: [Col. 0033] Letter 24, § 1.] He regarded vainglory with the utmost caution and trembled at the sight of vanity, to use Augustine’s words. [Note: [Col. 0033] Augustine, Letter 31, § 6.]

“If,” says Paulinus, “we do not balance the movements of our minds by a firm standard, we shall take pride even in humility; and the appearance of devotion will vanish if inflation creeps in through praise of poverty. And what will it profit us to have been without riches if we remain rich in vices?” [Note: [Col. 0033] Paulinus, Letter 40, § 11; Song 24, line 301.]

Elsewhere he marvels that something should be considered a great achievement merely because he had purchased eternal salvation with perishable goods and exchanged transient things for everlasting ones; that he had sold earth in order to buy heaven, although God, having taken the form of a servant, had humbled himself, suffered the death of the cross, and bought him at a far greater price. [Note: [Col. 0033] Song 24, line 301.]

“O wretched human beings,” he says elsewhere, “we think that we give something; we conduct business and are considered generous, though we are proved to be exceedingly greedy. Indeed, we are more avaricious than the earth’s most covetous usurers, since it is a far greater thing to buy heavenly things with earthly things, and blessed things with miserable and impoverished ones, than to buy earthly things with earthly things and transitory things with things destined to perish, and to lend to the Lord rather than to a human being.” [Note: [Col. 0033] Letter 32, § 19.]

He says that this had been necessary for his salvation.

**2.** In public inscriptions he places himself among criminals and sinners who would redeem their crimes by pouring out money, while others called him perfect. [Note: [Col. 0033] Letter 32, §§ 3–4; Letter 24, § 2.] He considered that he had reached only the entrance and doorway, not the finish line. “The abandonment or disposal of temporal goods possessed in this world,” he says, “is not the completion of the race but its beginning; it is not the finish line but the gate.”

An athlete does not win when he strips himself, since he is made naked in order to begin the contest and is crowned only after he has competed lawfully. A swimmer also strips to cross the river lying before him; yet he will not swim across merely because he has divested himself with such preparation. He must cut through the force of the torrent with the exertion of his whole body, the skillful movement of all his limbs, the propulsion of his feet, the oaring of his arms, and the slipping of his side through the current, and must complete the labor of swimming.

In the same sense he continues, allegorically explaining Jacob’s wrestling at night with the angel, after he had crossed the torrent and sent ahead the burdens of his cares. [Note: [Col. 0033] Letter 24, § 7.] Writing to Augustine, he compares himself to a man who removes burdensome clothing in order to cross a river:

> “For this reason I have taken care to lighten myself of burdens and strip off the clothing that weighs me down, so that I may swim freely, with Christ commanding and helping me, across this surging sea which, amid all the coverings of flesh and the cares of the following day, separates us from God through the sins that rage between us.” [Note: [Col. 0033] Letter 4, § 4.]

He adds other comparisons of the same kind:

> “This is the pearl to be bought by expending patrimonies; but it is not immediately bought when its price has been prepared, because many difficulties intervene in this commerce. Either the sea lies between us, or a pirate intercepts us, or someone more eager arrives first, or a richer man is preferred. Therefore do not think that we have already acquired everything merely because you see that we have prepared the price. Nor have we yet built the house for which we have cleared the site, when we have removed visible riches, household goods, money, and patrimonies like filthy heaps and troublesome rubble, so that on a cleansed heart, as on living earth, we might lay the foundations of a more stable building.” [Note: [Col. 0033] Letter 24, § 20.]

By selling everything and distributing it to the poor, therefore, he thought that he had fulfilled only the first part of the evangelical commandment. When he saw that the words “Come, and follow me” (Matthew XIX, 21) still remained as a task of great difficulty, he feared that he might be unable to accomplish the second part.

“Consider,” he writes to his same Severus, “how great a task remains in the words, since the Lord of majesty adds: ‘And come, follow me’ (ibid.). Consider this difficulty above all, and measure it with an enlarged heart; then you will understand that greater causes for concern on our behalf remain for you than causes for rejoicing. The goods or burdens laid upon us easily fell away when we let down our cloak. What we had not brought with us into this world and could not carry out with us, we returned as though it were borrowed. We did not tear skin from flesh; we merely laid aside a garment from the body.” [Note: [Col. 0035] Letter 24, § 5.]

**3.** With diligent humility he explains that he has not yet sold everything. “We possess,” he says, “not only money, estates, and external resources, but also the internal riches of our soul, which truly constitute our substance. To sell these—that is, to alienate them from ourselves—is a far greater victory, since it is more difficult to separate what is innate and tear away what is fixed within than to reject what is attached externally.” [Note: [Col. 0035] Letter 40, § 11.]

Elsewhere he says:

> “Now it is necessary for us to pay to God what truly belongs to us, presenting our hearts, souls, and bodies as a living sacrifice, as it is written (Romans XII, 1), and building ourselves into a holy temple for him.” [Note: [Col. 0035] Letter 24, § 6.]

“Pray earnestly,” he says elsewhere, “that we may receive a heart worthy of so great a mouth or gift of God; and that we who have received contempt for our patrimony may also receive contempt for ourselves.” [Note: [Col. 0035] Letter 40, § 11.]

Above, we have also sufficiently demonstrated from Jerome that this man of fervent faith offered not only his riches but also himself to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0035] Jerome, Letter 34.] In opposition to the devil’s evasions, he did not offer merely “skin for skin”; he consecrated his flesh, heart, and bones, his soul and all his members, to God.

Paulinus teaches the same elsewhere:

> “The Lord set before us the way of life and the perfection of virtue not merely in selling estates and distributing their price, but in following him. And because he had said, ‘When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself’ (John XII, 32), for that reason he says, ‘Come, follow me’ (Matthew XIX, 21). Blessed is the person who follows at so close a distance that he can say, ‘My soul has clung to you’ (Psalm LXII, 9). This can be said only by that charity which is the fulfillment of the commandment and the fullness of the law (Romans XIII, 10); that is, by the charity which, arising from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy I, 5), so inserts and fastens itself to God that it can say, ‘And I am continually with you’ (Psalm LXXII, 23).” [Note: [Col. 0035] Paulinus, Letter 24, §§ 9, 11–12.]

Therefore, all our labor and the whole task lie in the observance of the commandments and the stripping bare of our heart. We cannot see its darkness or the hidden lairs of the enemy concealed within it unless the mind has been purified from concern for external things and turned inward upon itself.

God prepares us for the building of ourselves along the path by which he calls us after him, through the work by which he first persuades us to be freed from our possessions once they have been sold. Since care for or love of these things dulls the mind’s sight and draws the soul away from its inner regions toward external concerns, he also says to us through the Prophet: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm XLV, 11).

Does he not seem also to say here: “You cannot serve two masters” (Matthew VI, 24)? By these words he does not recommend idleness, since he urges us to pray and watch continually lest we enter into temptation (Matthew XXVI, 41). Rather, he commands us to be free from the world so that we may be occupied with him, and free from those affairs in which we are entangled while remaining idle toward God.

Therefore, as we build the newness of life within us, we must destroy our former state (Romans VI, 6). Since there can be no fellowship between darkness and light, or between Mammon and Christ (2 Corinthians VI, 15), we must exchange old things for new. We must reverse both our occupations and our leisure: we must become involved in the things from which we had been free, and be free from the things in which we had been involved. We must die to the things in which we lived and, conversely, live by those works and pursuits to which we had been dead; while alive, we had been dead, and by carrying out the works that bring death, we were living among the dead.

**4.** Paulinus, thinking so humbly of himself, placed himself above none of those who had retained their possessions. [Note: [Col. 0035] Paulinus, Letter 24, § 2.] He reflected that there are divisions of grace and measures of gifts, which the Lord, one and the same dispenser, works among the members of his body, distinguishing different members in his body by gifts according to his pleasure; yet he also builds one body from the diversity of its members, so that the grace of the sacred body may increase when manifold virtue is counted within a single structure.

Sulpicius Severus, whom an intimate friendship from their earlier life had joined to Paulinus, dedicated himself to God at the same time as Paulinus. Yet when he transferred his estates to the Church, he reserved for himself the right of use and enjoyment.

Paulinus, employing all the skill and ingenuity of his intellect, awarded him the palm. He said that it is harder to live without possessions while they remain than after they have been alienated, and harder to despise what one possesses than not to possess what ought to be despised. Thus, he said, there was no perfection in himself deserving praise, but rather weakness requiring excuse. [Note: [Col. 0035] Ibid., § 4.]

In the praises that Severus bestowed upon him, he also disparages himself in various ways:

> “Unless perhaps you do this as well according to a deeper plan of devotion: while in words you generously attribute to us goods that belong to others, you suggest the spur of shame, so that those who read may learn to be good as we ought to be, and may strive to express ourselves according to your words; and perhaps we may become what we are not, while we blush not to be what we are called. In the meantime, however, while our conscience does not acknowledge the truth of your words, modesty rejects your flattery.” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ibid., § 1.]

Many people would not be free from blame if they undertook a program of such perfection. For if exceptionally strong faith does not remain vigorous, and some misfortune occurs, many people are accustomed to fall in spirit and to become attached to longing for the goods they have distributed.

But Paulinus always showed himself equal, noble, and steadfast in his love of poverty and contempt for riches. When Severus, whom he had long been inviting to live with him at Nola, wrote that he believed Paulinus would soon become so poor that he would no longer dare to invite him, Paulinus replied that this was a jest of courtesy. [Note: [Col. 0035] Letter 11, § 13.] He confessed that he desired nothing more than the blessing of such freedom, since so intimate a circumcision was complete perfection.

“We have nothing,” he says, “except Christ; and see whether we have nothing, when we possess the one who possesses everything . . . and for whose sake, if we have nothing, we possess everything in him” (2 Corinthians VI, 10).

“Now, in this soil of thorns and labors, not even a clod from a little garden holds us in the earth’s mud. Would that no dust of sin clung to us in the same way! You commit an offense against the Lord himself”—that is, you sin—“if you think that the nourishment of mortal life will fail us only when God begins to be our possession” (Psalm XV, 5). [Note: [Col. 0037] “You commit an offense against the Lord himself,” that is, “you sin.”]

## CHAPTER X. Eulogies of the holy Fathers of the Church concerning Paulinus’ conversion and poverty

**1.** Paulinus’ deed, so illustrious and glorious, was praised throughout the world. [Note: [Col. 0037] Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues 3, chapter 20.] Almost all the most distinguished men of the Church who were then living admired it and celebrated it with abundant praise.

When Ambrose learned of it, he wished Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza, to share in his joy, knowing that Sabinus would certainly make much of so great a miracle. [Note: [Col. 0037] Ambrose, Letter 30.] Ambrose testifies that Paulinus’ wife did not depart from her husband’s purpose, and he especially emphasizes the nobility and virtue of a man so distinguished by the splendor of his lineage that he nevertheless confessed Christ so steadfastly before human beings and openly professed devotion to a holy religion and stricter discipline.

Augustine praises the magnitude and merit of this outstanding deed in a remarkable manner. [Note: [Col. 0037] Augustine, Letter 31, § 6.] He calls it the glory of Christ and says that it brought him wondrous joy to see Paulinus fulfilling the Lord’s words.

> “The brethren,” he says, “rejoice tirelessly and ineffably in such abundant and excellent gifts of God—in your goods.” [Note: [Col. 0037] Augustine, Letter 27, § 2.]  
>   
> “The brethren rejoice—not only those who live with us, and those who live anywhere and serve God together with us, but almost all who gladly know us in Christ. They greet, venerate, and desire your brotherhood, blessedness, and humanity.” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ibid., § 6.]  
>   
> “God is praised and blessed, whose grace has made you such. There Christ is invoked, that he may deign to calm the winds and seas for you as you make your way toward your own stability. To those who read, your wife seems not to have led her husband back toward softness, but toward strength, restored to the bones of her husband. . . . There the cedars of Lebanon, cast down to the earth and raised by the bond of charity into the construction of the ark, cut through the waves of this world without decaying. There glory is despised in order to acquire it, and the world is abandoned in order to possess it. There the little ones, and even the somewhat older sons of Babylon, are dashed against the rock—that is, the vices of worldly confusion and pride.” [Note: [Col. 0037] Augustine, Letter 27, § 2.]

**2.** Yet Augustine’s ardent love for Paulinus, visible in his first letter to him, written in 395, could receive no increase. [Note: [Col. 0037] Augustine, Letter 27.] From that time he commended to Paulinus those most dear to him, hoping that Paulinus would bring about their salvation both by his words and by his prayers. He begged and urged him to come to Africa, so that he might know how greatly he was loved and desired there.

In his second letter, inviting him to come to him, he appeals and pleads with him in these words:

> “I do not ask, entreat, and implore you immodestly to deign to come to Africa, which suffers from a greater thirst for such men than from the nobility of its dryness. God knows that we desire you to be physically present in these lands not only because of my longing, nor only because of those who through us have learned of your purpose, or have learned of it from anywhere through the report of your fame, but also because of the others who either do not hear of it or do not believe what they hear, yet may love it once they have learned the truth.” [Note: [Col. 0037] Augustine, Letter 31, §§ 4–5.]

Then, writing to his own Licentius, he says:

> “Go to Campania and learn from Paulinus, that distinguished and holy servant of God, how he has shaken off the great pride of this world with a neck all the more noble because it is humble, in order to subject it to the yoke of Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0037] Augustine, Letter 26, § 5.]

Elsewhere, recalling how securely Paulinus rejoiced when the Goths ravaged Nola, since he had nothing to lose, he calls him “from the richest of the rich, poor by choice, and abundantly holy.” [Note: [Col. 0037] Augustine, *The City of God*, chapter 10.]

Jerome extolled this renunciation of possessions with remarkable and well-deserved praises, and offered prudent counsels by which to moderate Paulinus’ charity. We have already mentioned some of these; we shall discuss the rest in their proper place. [Note: [Col. 0037] Jerome, Letter 13.]

To Julian, a most noble man, Jerome proposes the examples of Saints Paulinus and Pammachius. Having said that they could lead Julian to greater things by example and eloquence—that is, by deed and word—he adds:

> “Are you noble? So are they, but nobler in Christ. Are you rich and honored? So are they—but rather, from being rich and honored they became poor and without worldly glory, and for that very reason richer and more renowned, because they are poor and dishonored for Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0037] Jerome, Letter 34.]

### 3.

To these three teachers of the Latin Church must be added Martin, the bishop of Tours, a man of extraordinary holiness [Note: [Col. 0037] Sulpicius, *Life of Martin*, ch. 26.], who considered that age blessed because it had received such an example of faith and virtue. In his judgment, Paulinus, having cast aside his immense wealth and followed Christ, had almost alone in those times fulfilled the commandments of the Gospel. He continually challenged those who came to him—and especially Severus—with the authority and admiration he felt for Paulinus, crying out that Paulinus must be followed and imitated. Holding up his example, he said that the enticements of this world and the burdens of the age must be abandoned, so that they might follow Jesus freely and unencumbered.

When Paulinus had withdrawn to Nola [Note: [Col. 0037] Paulinus, Letter 5, §13.], all Campania venerated the work of God accomplished in him. Among Jerome’s works there is a letter which is rightly rejected as his. It was indeed written while Paulinus and his wife were still alive; Gennadius [Note: [Col. 0037] Gennadius, *Catalogue*, 49.] attributes it to the presbyter Eutropius, whom he places immediately after Paulinus in the order of his *Catalogue*.

[Note: [Col. 0037] Inter. ep. Hier. tom. IX, ep. 3, to the daughters of Geruntius.] After that author had said that the double tomb which Abraham provided for himself not only prefigured the tomb in which the bodies of dead people would be buried, but also signified the rest which he had obtained for himself through faith and contempt of wealth, he adds:

[Note: [Col. 0039] Letter 3 to the daughters of Geruntius.] “Our Paulinus too recently acquired this tomb for himself, together with his wife, by renouncing wealth; and, dying to the life of the world, they now rest from worldly works, as the Apostle says: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God’ (Colossians 3:3) . . . . This is that double tomb, of the outward and inward person, one rest . . . . These heads of households provided this double tomb for themselves: by abandoning the senate, honors, and riches, they appeared to be dead . . . . Behold one tomb in which the way of life of the old person, together with the toys of his nobility, is hidden.”

Saint Eucherius [Note: [Col. 0039] Idatius, *Chronicle*, year 423.], speaking of certain distinguished men who, despising wealth and offices, had abandoned everything for Christ, says:

“Paulinus too, the unique and blessed ornament of our Gaul, once possessed of an immense wealth of property and of an abundant fountain of eloquence, passed over so completely to our conviction and purpose that he sprinkled almost all the twenty-two regions of the world with his eloquence and works.”

Idatius, in his *Chronicle* under the year 423, says [Note: [Col. 0039] Tyro Prosper]:

“Paulinus, most noble and most eloquent, made still nobler by his conversion to God.”

Tyro Prosper gives this testimony concerning the same Paulinus:

[Note: [Col. 0039] Ambrose, Letter 30.] “By an admirable example, having sold everything, although he was master of innumerable estates, he chose religion unencumbered.”

## CHAPTER XI. The nobles and worldly men call Paulinus foolish. He steadfastly and courageously endures the mockery prepared for him.

### 1.

If, on the one hand, Paulinus’s conversion was a source of admiration and joy to the most eminent men of the Church [Col. 0039C], on the other hand it seemed intolerable to nobles and worldly men. “When the noblemen hear this,” Ambrose said, “what will they say?” [Note: [Col. 0039] Paulinus, Letter 5, §21.] “That a man sprung from that family, that lineage, that character, endowed with such eloquence, has withdrawn from the senate; that the succession of a noble family has been interrupted: they cannot endure it.”

Paulinus says [Note: [Col. 0039] Paulinus, Letter 11, §§3–4.] that the saying of Scripture applied to him: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matthew 10:36). For all the rich—his brothers, friends, relatives, freedmen, and slaves—deserted him and refused him the services they owed [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §5]. Moreover, because of Paulinus’s purpose, a separation arose between him and many with whom he had enjoyed the closest and dearest relationship [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §3]; changing their course, they broke away from him. From this he clearly understood how easily the bonds of flesh and blood could be severed.

“For where,” he says [Note: [Col. 0039] Paulinus, Letter 11, §4.], “is my blood relationship now? Where is the old friendship? Where are the former companions of my household? I have vanished before them all; I am a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother. My friends and those who were once close to me now stand far away” (Psalm 68:9; and 37:12 according to the Roman Psalter); “and, like a flowing river or a passing wave, so they pass by me, and perhaps they are confounded and ashamed, as it is written, to come to me.”

His brother was neglectful toward him [Note: [Col. 0039] Letter 1, §§2–3, 6]. Secular men not only despised and abandoned him, but also spread around, if I may put it so, profane or foolish words [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §§6–7]. They considered piety foolishness. They attacked God’s work in the deeds of his servant, because they despised him in their own actions; for they were unbelievers, or belonged to those who, while confessing Christ in name, denied him in practice.

### 2.

When Paulinus lived in solitude, he was less exposed to these contradictions. But Sulpicius Severus, who had followed him in his conversion, although at a lower rank [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §10.], had not left his homeland and labored greatly [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §§4 and 6.] to give an account of his own action and Paulinus’s. He complains about this in a letter addressed to Paulinus. In his reply, Paulinus shows from the sacred writings [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §2.] how grave their crime is, and adds:

“Close and hedge your ears, brother, with thorns” (Sirach 28:28) “against their words, which are thorns and arrows of the devil, who lies hidden in their hearts and secretly lies in wait to snatch away Christ’s poor man . . . . [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §3.] But you, man of God, flee from such people” (1 Timothy 6:11); “nor should you trouble yourself to give an account to those who think themselves wiser, since you know that the beginning of wisdom is with you, because you fear the Lord” (Psalm 100:10).

“If they consider what we are doing foolish, rejoice inwardly that you are doing the work of God and observing Christ’s commandment. Remember that God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1 Corinthians 1:27), and that what is foolish in God is wiser than men.

“To wish to justify yourself before such people is the same as being able to deny Christ himself. For those who are ashamed of his name before this world, he will be ashamed to confess as his own before the Father (Matthew 10:33). You, therefore, who, as you write, are laboring to give an account for my action and your own, what will you do if you fail to persuade men who dispute with you about the work of God—not for their edification, but for your destruction? You will blush and grow pale as an advocate of the worse cause; shaken, you will stumble in the way of the Lord, and fall back from heaven to earth if you destroy what you have built.

“It makes a great difference who these people are to whom an account must be given. If someone comes in a desire to learn and confesses his ignorance, scatter in him the seed of faith and expound the divine commandment. If he receives the word, you have won a brother for the Church and a sheep for Christ. But if he is not a pure shoot of good seed, but harmful grass—while the enemy of the heavenly householder by night sows weeds among the wheat (Matthew 13:25)—it meanwhile grows for its own burning . . . . Flee from him and drive him away from your conversation and presence, so that, if he cannot be healed by your faith, he may not wound you with his unbelief.

[Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §5.] “Even if he is your brother and friend, closer to you than your right hand and dearer than the light . . . . You must not fear the offense of such people. Indeed, we ought to desire it, because from their insults comes that reward which God promised in abundance in heaven (Matthew 5:12) . . . . What need have we of the world’s favor, which is hatred of Christ?

[Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §6.] “Let us therefore displease these people, and rejoice that we displease those whom God also displeases . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid., §7.] “Meanwhile let them enjoy their pleasures, dignities, and wealth—if indeed these things belong to them, since they prefer to have them there where we cease to exist, rather than there where we persist in existence. Let them keep their wisdom for themselves, and their happiness for themselves; let them leave us, as they suppose, our poverty and our foolishness. Let them be wiser, provided they are not children of light. Let them be wise in this generation of theirs, provided that in that regeneration of ours they are found to be without understanding. Let them now be blessed, or rather fortunate, flowing through every prosperity while the world smiles upon them; let them wear soft garments and be in the houses of kings, provided they are not in the labors of men and are not scourged with them. Let them be rich in the world, because they are needy before God . . . .”

[Note: [Col. 0041] Paulinus, Letter 1, §8.] “Would that we might be considered worthy, my brother, to be cursed, branded, crushed, and even killed in the name of Jesus Christ, provided Christ himself is not killed in us. Then at last we would walk upon the asp and basilisk and trample underfoot the head of the ancient dragon (Psalm 90:13). But we are still attached to the world as to a friend—which is worse—and delight in being praised in Christ, loving only his name; while we refuse to be saddened and afflicted, which would be more profitable.

“Remember the mustard seed, from whose seed we come: when it is crushed, it burns more intensely and is then roused to its full power. Therefore we ought to respond here to the nature of our origin, so that, crushed by hostile words, we may burn more fiercely for the faith; and that we may burn those very people who try to break us as though we were the smallest of things—namely, like the mustard seed, which is the smallest of seeds.

“But if those who are outside inquire from you about the reason for your holy work, and hurl poisoned tongues from their viperous hearts into your heart, do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine (Matthew 7:6).”

And in another letter to the same Severus [Note: [Col. 0041] Letter 11, §4.]:

“The world does not love us, but Christ loves us; man neglects us, but God loves us. A man’s enemies are those of his own household, but again, a man’s friends are those of God’s household.”

What he writes here to Severus, he repeats in writing to Aper, who, placed in the same persecution, endured everything courageously.

“You are now deserving of this grace from the Lord,” he says [Note: [Col. 0041] Letter 8, §2.], “that everyone should hate you; this would not happen unless you had begun to be a true imitator of Christ. For this world would hate nothing unless it saw it already alienated from itself and opposed to itself. Rejoice and exult: in your beginnings the virtue of perfection is already at work. It is clear how firmly you have believed in Christ, since it has already been granted to you to suffer for Christ . . . . O blessed insult, to displease together with Christ! We ought to fear more the love of those whom one pleases without Christ . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0041] Ibid., §3.] “Look from the beginning at the point from which we fell, and you will understand that by the counsel of divine wisdom and piety we are being restored to life: in Adam we fell through pride, and therefore we are humbled in Christ, so that we may wash away the sin of the ancient crime by the obedience of the contrary virtue; and that we who offended by pride may please by service.

[Note: [Col. 0041] Ibid., §4.] “Let us therefore exult and glory in him, who has made us both his battle and his victory . . . . Let us therefore be silent before those people, speaking to the Lord in the silence of humility and the voice of patience. Then he who is invincible will fight for us and conquer in us . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0041] Ibid., §5.] “As he loves the worker who cannot be put to shame, just as he loves the cheerful giver, so let us remain steadfast in the faith of truth and in the practice of righteousness. By our lives, better than by our words, we refute the hatred and insults of such people.”

## CHAPTER XII. Ausonius accuses Paulinus of fickle change and reproaches him for interrupting his correspondence. Paulinus declares his love and reverence for him.

### 1.

While Paulinus lived in solitude, he was less exposed to the opposition of his worldly friends. Nevertheless, in poems sent as letters, Ausonius reviled him, although Paulinus venerated Ausonius as a father. Ausonius [Note: [Col. 0041] Baronius, year 394, §85.], though a Christian, was still a carnal man, ignorant of the things of the Spirit.

Previously, Ausonius and Paulinus had frequently exchanged letters [Note: [Col. 0041] Ausonius, Letter 24]. But after Paulinus’s withdrawal to Spain, our Paulinus wrote nothing; and, as no letters were being delivered, rumor was already growing [Note: [Col. 0041] Ausonius, Letter 23.], it was firmly believed that he had decided to renounce the world and sell his patrimony. A false rumor also led people to believe [Note: [Col. 0041] Ausonius, Letter 25.] that he was living in vast solitudes, most remote from human society. Ausonius therefore sent him a lengthy letter [Note: [Col. 0041] Ausonius, Letter 23.] in which he complained that their friendship was being undermined and dissolved, and called him impious.

Then he solemnly appealed to him and begged him not to become implicated in that crime, and complained that he was living so far away in Spain. He described the quiet and pleasures of his villa among the Santones at Novero, which [Note: [Col. 0041] Vinet, note on Ausonius, p. 485.] is thought to have been the village of Novalarius, in French *les Nouliers*, near Saint-Jean-d’Angély. Among the advantages of this villa he mentioned the proximity of a church, but declared that he preferred his friend to all these things and called him to himself with vows and prayers.

This letter [Note: [Col. 0041] Paulinus, Poem 10, line 1.] was delivered to Paulinus when he had already spent four years in his Spanish retreat. Since Paulinus still sent no reply, Ausonius sent him another letter [Note: [Col. 0041] Ausonius, Letter 24.] in which, complaining again about his silence, he once more brought against him the charge of betraying their friendship. He also pointed out various ways in which Paulinus could write if he feared being betrayed. But he asked that Paulinus’s [Note: [Col. 0041] Ibid., line 31.] “Tanaquil” should not know of it; thus he called Paulinus’s wife by an insulting name.

I do not know whether Ausonius had Therasi[a] in mind, or the disturbances caused by Eugenius, who, as we believe, had not yet subjected Spain when Ausonius said that Paulinus feared his letters might be intercepted. He also wrote a third letter, which has been lost [Note: [Col. 0041] See Ausonius, Letter 25, line 1, and note, p. 568]. In it, I think, Ausonius complained that Paulinus had now been absent from his homeland for three years and begged him to return to the Muses.

He added a fourth letter [Note: [Col. 0041] Ausonius, Letter 25.], in which he continued to complain about the arrogance with which Paulinus disdained to reply. Finally, he added that the villages of Spain, the snow-covered regions of the Pyrenees, and the forests of the Vascones had changed Paulinus’s very sweet character; he called him mentally deranged, avoiding human gatherings and suffering from an illness of black bile. At last he begged the Muses to recall Paulinus to poetry.

### In the year of Christ 393

### 2.

We do not know whether Ausonius wrote other letters to Saint Paulinus in order to recall him from his stricter way of life. But God arranged that the poems—or rather, incantations—which were sent over different years should be delivered only very late [Note: [Col. 0043] Paulinus, Poem 10.], namely in the fourth year after Paulinus had received no letter from him, so that Paulinus, by then much stronger, might resist the snares and temptations of the lurking devil.

At last, four years later, he received three letters together: the one beginning [Note: [Col. 0043] Ausonius, Letter 24.], “The one next to our letter,” as will appear below; also the one beginning [Note: [Col. 0043] Ausonius, Letter 25.], “This fourth letter of mine to you”; and a third, which had been lost.

To these three letters Paulinus replied in a metrical letter [Note: [Col. 0043] Paulinus, Poem 10.]. Its opening elegy serves as a kind of preface, followed by iambic trimeters and dimeters in which he gives Ausonius his reasons for renouncing the Muses and abandoning his possessions. Then he shows how the grace of Christ, changing the whole person, had claimed him wholly for itself.

He admits that he owes everything to Ausonius and declares that he has always honored him, honors him now, and will continue to honor him with a devotion that will endure after death. Finally, he refutes Ausonius’s other complaints in these verses [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 81.]:

> Do not, I beg, think me sluggish or perverse  
> Because I am free for, or studying, or devoted to him,  
> Placing everything in him . . .
>
> But you complain that I remain withdrawn so long,  
> And in pious agitation grow angry.  
> This is useful, or necessary, or pleasing:  
> Whatever of these it may be, it is pardonable.
>
> Forgive the lover, if I do what is expedient;  
> Rejoice if I live as I please [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 97].

## CHAPTER XIII. Paulinus courageously refutes Ausonius’s complaints

### 1.

The iambic verses were followed [Note: [Col. 0043] Paulinus, Poem 10, line 14.] by hexameters in which he courageously refutes Ausonius’s harsh words in heroic verse [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 103.], beginning “I shall be absent from my native land.” This poem answers Ausonius’s fourth letter [Note: [Col. 0043] Ausonius, Letter 25.], “This fourth letter of mine to you,” and also the lost third letter, in which Ausonius complained that Paulinus had now been absent for three years. It also answers the second letter [Note: [Col. 0043] Ausonius, Letter 24.], “The one next to our letter,” in which Ausonius called Therasi[a] “Tanaquil.”

Since Paulinus says [Note: [Col. 0043] Paulinus, Poem 10, lines 222 and following.] that Ausonius names the little towns of Spain, while omitting the cities’ names—Caesaraugusta, Tarraco, and Barcino—which appear in Ausonius’s first letter [Note: [Col. 0043] Ausonius, Letter 23.], it is clear that Paulinus had not yet received that letter at the time.

After Paulinus first complained that Ausonius had not prayed to Christ, the author of our life, but to the Muses, asking them to recall Paulinus to poetry [Col. 0043D], he says that his conversion was truly a change wrought by the Most High, which God alone could accomplish. If there was anything in his disciple that Christ loved, Ausonius ought to rejoice, since, as his teacher, he would share in the praise and reward; otherwise he would lose the greatest rewards by condemning the good that had arisen from his own sources.

Paulinus says that he did not inhabit the solitary places customary among holy anchorites, whose virtue he was far from approaching. Nor did he suffer from the Bellerophontic fault, nor was his wife Therasi[a] a Tanaquil, as Ausonius had reproached him, but a Lucretia.

Hence Paulinus says [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 185.]:

> Would that righteous envy begin to assail me:  
> Under Christ’s name, insults will be welcome.  
> A mind made firm by God does not endure tender shame,  
> And this despised praise returns to me with Christ as judge.

At that time Paulinus was living in a most agreeable place not far from the sea [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 232.], and, as appears, in Barcino, where he remained that year and the following one, as will be demonstrated elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0043] Chapters 14 and 15.].

But even if he had lived among the snow-covered Pyrenees and in the vast forests of the Vascones—then in Spain—he would not have taken on barbarous manners. He writes to Ausonius that he does not approve of such jokes, though they had been permitted to Ausonius:

> Let many things be open to jokes; let it also be permitted to play with invented things.  
> But to blunt a grave tooth with a flattering tongue,  
> To play with burning flatteries, and to ferment ill-sweet  
> Jokes with the vinegar of biting satire—  
> This is often fitting for poets, never for fathers [Note: [Col. 0043] Paulinus, Poem 10, line 160].

He defends his wife’s honor [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 190.] and finally explains to Ausonius the reasons for his conversion, saying [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 293.] that he wished to flee the world and renounce his possessions so that he might safely meet Christ the Judge. But if anyone should judge it an error of mind to live according to Christ’s laws:

> I am glad of this, and do not regret this  
> Error. I care nothing if I am thought foolish  
> By those who pursue other things, so long as my judgment  
> Is wise to my eternal King [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 285].

Finally, he concludes his noble confession of Christ, and as it were fastens it with a beam-sized nail:

> If this pleases you, rejoice in the rich hope of your friend;  
> If it is otherwise, leave me to be approved by Christ alone [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., line 350].

### 2.

Paulinus also replied to Ausonius in another poem [Note: [Col. 0043] Paulinus, Poem 11.], “The Continuation of My . . . .” In it he no longer gives an account of the way of life he had undertaken; instead, he declares that he had always honored Ausonius with every service, honors him now, and will continue to honor him with a devotion that will endure after death, believing that the same affections would remain in souls separated from the body.

That poem [Note: [Col. 0043] Ausonius, Letter 23.] responds to Ausonius’s first letter and to any other letter in which Ausonius likewise accused Therasi[a] of ruling her husband. Paulinus perhaps received these two letters together sometime after the other three.

## CHAPTER XIV. Paulinus’s closest relationship with Severus

### 1.

We have already observed [Note: [Col. 0043] Chapter 9, §4.] that the friendship between Paulinus and Severus in the world had been exceptionally close [Col. 0044D]. Neither of them ever dissolved it afterward, because [Note: [Col. 0043] Paulinus, Letter 11, §6.] both turned equally to God and remained united forever in Christ, animated equally by his love, by one and the same purpose, and by the same moment of conversion.

Thus, when Sulpicius Severus—who gladly recognized in Paulinus a greater abundance of grace—had written to Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., §6.] that, of two men who had been in the field, one had been taken and the other left, Paulinus replied:

“Why do you speak harshly about us and falsely about yourself? [Note: [Col. 0043] Ibid., §§5–6.] We were indeed two individually, when rebellious flesh was at variance with the spirit within us . . . . We were two, but that was when we were joined to those other brothers; from them our present purpose brought about a division . . . .

“But now, by the mercy of Christ, who made both one, we are two who are one, because there is one spirit in two . . . . Therefore we ought to give even greater thanks to the good Lord, who deigned to look upon our humility: when he found us together in the field, he drew us together as twins from the womb of the flesh, and took us both together.

“For we were two in the field; but by the omnipotence of God—I dare say it—one of us was taken in such a way that neither was left . . . . Let us not be ungrateful to God, who did not take one of us, but took one in us.”

### 2.

This bond of friendship [Note: [Col. 0045] Paulinus, Letter 11, §5.] is common to all true Christians, but in Paulinus and Severus it was special and distinctive. Many spiritual men, and not a few saints, loved Paulinus for Christ’s sake. Their affection for Paulinus was very great, in place of his homeland, parents, and patrimony; nevertheless, he regarded the good things he had received from them as more generously and more precious compensated in his Severus.

“That special gift to us in you,” he says [Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid.], “is that our being predestined for one another in the closest love of Christ was also marked out by the friendship of our earlier life . . . . For we grew into the bond by which, through God’s intervention, we are now joined, through the habit of that former intimacy . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid., §4.] “If we count up in you all the good things we have received, we shall regard all that is ours as more generously and more precious compensated in you . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid., §3.] “In place of parents, brothers, and friends, you have been made for us by the Lord. Concerned with the care of parents, anxious with brotherly love, diligent with the whole faith of a genuine friendship, and pouring out toward us every affection of compassion, you visit us with constant letters and soothe us with the sweetest consolations.

[Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 23, §2.] “By your services toward our humility you had surpassed others; as we have often testified, you were more devoted than all our friends, more reverent than our relatives, more attentive than our brothers.”

For this reason he loved him above all.

“What are you trying to force from us,” he says to the same man [Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid., §1.], “that we should love you more? The sum cannot receive increase . . . . We cannot add to the fullness of our love for you. If the sea can overflow its barriers, and if all things that preserve their natural fullness can experience temporal increase, then our love for you too can be heaped up. We complete it at its end, when we love you as ourselves.”

For this reason [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 5, §22.] Paulinus presumed that he possessed the highest claim upon Severus’s heart.

### 3.

Paulinus and Severus shared the vow of withdrawing to Nola. In this year, 393, Paulinus wrote to Severus a letter which has been lost [Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid.]. In it he said that he was staying in the city of Barcino, where he had remained for a long time when Sulpicius Severus sent him a reply [Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid., §11.] from Elusio through one of his own men. This man reached Barcino on the eighth day; Barcino was approximately eighty-two leagues from Elusio.

The *Bordeaux Itinerary* places this Elusio in Narbonensian Gaul, about twelve leagues from Toulouse and at least thirteen from Carcassonne, near the city of Le Puy at the Lers, within the boundaries of the diocese of Toulouse.

## CHAPTER XV. At Barcino Paulinus is unwillingly initiated into the priesthood

### 1.

As was observed above [Note: [Col. 0045] Chapter 7, §2.], Paulinus had desired to hold the lowest place in the Church [Note: [Col. 0045] Paulinus, Letter 4, §4.]. He considered himself unworthy [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 2, §2.] to be placed among the priests, since he would not dare to become a member of the household of the Lord and solemnly bless the Lord.

If at last he were forced into the priesthood, because he considered himself unworthy of so sacred an office, he wished to be raised through the ranks little by little and to make himself more worthy through long service. He had resolved to serve God at the tomb of Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 1, §10; and Poem 12, line 36.], to open the church doors, care for the thresholds with cleanliness in the morning, guard them with sacred vigils at night, and end his life in that service.

“But the one who was pleased to set me apart,” Paulinus says [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 4, §4.], “from my mother’s womb and from the friendship of flesh and blood, and to draw me to his grace (Galatians 1:15), was also pleased to raise me, poor in every good merit, from the earth, and to bring me out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, so that he might place me with the princes of his people (Psalm 112:8) and assign my portion among the lot of priests.

[Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 2, §2.] “Thus, while I run after the fragrance of his ointments, I might become a drop of that ointment which descends upon Aaron’s beard (Psalm 132:2).”

When, therefore, he was attending the divine offices in the church at Barcino on the Lord’s Day on which Christ had deigned to be born in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 1, §10; Letter 4, §4; and Letter 2, §2.], he was suddenly seized by the force of the inflamed crowd, so that he might be ordained a presbyter, just as Augustine had experienced at Hippo three years earlier.

This struggle of the people caused Paulinus a great deal of trouble and distress, because he had decided to withdraw to Nola and was terrified by this as a new and unexpected determination of the divine will [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 1, §10.]. Moreover, he understood that if he were initiated into the priesthood in the church of Barcino, he would be bound to that church according to the canons; and because the resolve to lead a monastic life remained firmly fixed in his heart, he refused to consent to his promotion. At last, however, he was granted permission to devote himself to the service of the church he desired.

Thus, although he wished this cup to pass from him [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 2, §2.], nevertheless, knowing that Christ had said, “I have not come to be served, but to serve” (Matthew 20:28), he judged that he had to say to the Lord, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Finally, he allowed himself to be consecrated [Note: [Col. 0045] Letter 1, §10.] on the condition that he would not be bound to a particular diocese, but would be dedicated to the priesthood of the Lord alone and not also to a specific ecclesiastical place.

Thus Saint Jerome was ordained a presbyter at Antioch by Paulinus, bishop of that city, around the year 378. But [Note: [Col. 0045] Chifflet, p. 138.] our Paulinus became a presbyter in the year 393, if—as we think—he withdrew to Nola in 394; or in the year 392, if he withdrew to Nola in 393, namely in the year when he was preparing for the journey to Nola around the following Easter.

If [Note: [Col. 0047] Paulinus, Letter 1, §10.] “the Lord’s Day” on which he was made a presbyter designates Sunday rather than a feast day sacred to the Lord, we shall say that he was consecrated in the year 393 on a Sunday dedicated to Christ’s Nativity, since in that year 393 the Sunday letter was B and Sunday fell on 25 December.

He was therefore initiated into the priesthood by Lampius [Note: [Col. 0047] Letter 3, §4.], bishop of Barcino, who, as it seems, had succeeded Saint Pacianus, who had died under Theodosius before the year 392 [Note: [Col. 0047] Jerome, *Catalogue*, chapter 106.].

### 2.

He himself goes on to describe with what attitude of mind, submission, and reverence he bowed his neck beneath the yoke of Christ:

[Note: [Col. 0047] Paulinus, Letter 1, §10.] “Having given my neck to the yoke of Christ, I see that I am undertaking works greater than my merits and understanding; now received and inserted into the secret and innermost places of the most high God, I share in heavenly things and, brought nearer to God in the very Spirit of Christ, I live in spirit, body, and splendor.

“I scarcely yet grasp, in the narrowness of my mind, the meaning of the sacred burden; and, conscious of my weakness, I tremble at the burden of my office. But he who gave wisdom to the little ones (Psalm 18:8), and perfects praise for himself from the mouths of infants and nursing children, is able to complete his work in me and adorn the office, so that he may make worthy the one whom he called from unworthiness.”

Words worthy of a worthy and humble priest! How humbly he would serve at the altar and administer the mysteries of piety can be gathered from what precedes and immediately follows.

Thus he writes to Amandus shortly after his consecration:

[Note: [Col. 0047] Letter 2, §2.] “Therefore, having been anticipated by the Lord and seized by him whom we have not yet seized, we serve at God’s altar and minister at the saving table, already elders in name and office, but still infants in understanding and infants in speech.

[Note: [Col. 0047] Ibid., §3.] “That I may perform this ministry well, acquire for myself a good standing, and know how I ought to conduct myself in the house of God and handle the mystery of piety, pray, venerable lord and brother, and lord to us in Christ, to the Lord who is rich in every good thing, that we may abound in faith, speech, knowledge, and every diligence . . . .

“Moreover, instruct us often in your letters with the necessary supplements. Nourished by the words of faith and good doctrine which you have followed from childhood in the sacred writings, form us according to the rule of guidance; feed us with spiritual food, that is, the word of God, which is the true and living bread and the food of the righteous who live by faith.

[Note: [Col. 0047] Ibid., §4.] “Since, then, we have been made shepherds from sheep and placed upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, teach and strengthen my hands in the knowledge of building, so that from the stone which has been made the cornerstone I may learn to join the two walls together and construct bodies and hearts purified by faith into a holy temple and dwelling place of God; through the weapons of the Apostle, mighty through God, to lead captive every pride that raises itself against the knowledge of God and bring every understanding into obedience to Christ; to apply the evangelical axe to the roots of the trees; to kill the sinners of the earth [Col. 0048A] with the sword of the Spirit—that is, the word of God—and extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one with the shield of the catholic faith; and, when the battle has been fought, the course completed, the faith preserved, and the ministry fulfilled, to await that which the Lord, the just Judge, will render on that day to all who love his coming (2 Timothy 4:8).”

Paulinus’s humility also shines forth in the fact that he scarcely dared call Augustine his brother as a presbyter. He writes to him as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0047] Letter 4, §5.] “Therefore, not through my own presumption, but by the Lord’s pleasure and ordinance, claiming for myself the covenant of your brotherhood, I deem myself worthy of an honor of which I am unworthy, because I know for certain that, on account of your holiness, you do not set your mind on lofty things but associate with the humble.”

### In the year of Christ 394

## CHAPTER XVI. Paulinus invites Sulpicius Severus to withdraw to Nola. He writes to Amandus about his promotion to the priesthood.

### 1.

In this year, when Paulinus withdrew to Nola, we think that the first nativity poem in praise of Saint Felix belonged to January of the year of Christ 394 [Note: [Col. 0047] Chifflet, p. 145.], and that it was written in Spain. From there, as he was about to depart for Nola after the approaching Easter, he addressed his patron Felix as follows [Note: [Col. 0047] Paulinus, Poem 12.]:

> Now take thought for me, exhausted by immense longing;  
> Now, though late, remember and have mercy on your own.  
> Across the world the great expanse of sea keeps us far apart,  
> And hostile obstacles delay us, worn down as we are.  
> Open easy roads for us; and if an envious enemy  
> Blocks those hastening toward you, drive away the barriers in the way.  
> Stronger than adversity, advance your friends upon their journey.  
> Whether a land route pleases you, be a companion to your own  
> Along a safe embankment; or whether great confidence in you  
> Should persuade us to go by the long sea, grant that we may run  
> Over gentle waves, and summon servant winds from the stern  
> To serve your servants, so that, carried together to the Campanian shores  
> Under Christ’s guidance, we may soon be swept in eager course  
> To your heights, and that the harbor at your threshold  
> May be calm for us.

Not only the devil’s assaults were to be feared by Paulinus, but also the dangers of the war undertaken between Theodosius and Eugenius, the usurper of the Western Empire [Note: [Col. 0047] Ruffinus, Book II, chapter 33, and Ambrose, *On the Death of Theodosius*]. This war was not concluded until September of that year. This is perhaps the hymn [Note: [Col. 0047] Paulinus, Letter 3, section 6] which Alypius had read in that same year. We saw above [Note: [Col. 0047] Chapter 14, section 3] that Sulpicius Severus had written to Paulinus at Elusa in the preceding year that he had decided to renounce his possessions and flee from the world, and was laboring greatly to give an account of his action and Paulinus’s. Paulinus replied to him shortly before Easter and testified to the greatest joy at receiving his letter [Col. 0048D], by which he learned of Severus’s progress in piety; he also taught him how to answer those who despised them, as we reported above [Note: [Col. 0047] Canon 11, section 2]. He writes that he had been ordained a presbyter in such a way that he was attached to no church, and that thus the arrangement for fulfilling their common vow of returning to Nola remained intact. Accordingly, he urges Severus to come to Barcelona before the feast of Easter—which in the year 394 fell on 2 April—if he wished to celebrate the sacred festival with Paulinus himself as priest; or, at least, if he wished to meet him already on the road to Nola, to set out immediately after Easter [Col. 0049A]. For Paulinus had decided, once the Easter festivities had passed, to travel from Barcelona through Gaul into Italy. He says that he hoped his own fervent longing would inspire Severus not to postpone the journey beyond Easter; and he adds that the journey was short and easy, since Severus’s boy from Elusa had reached Barcelona in eight days. “But what are we to do about the distance?” he says [Note: [Col. 0049] Paulinus, Chapter 11, section 11]. “If you long for us, the road is short; it is long if you neglect us.”

2. At about the same time he wrote a second letter to Amandus, in which he says much about his ordination, matters that we related in the preceding chapter [Note: [Col. 0049] Chapter 15]. At one point he addresses several people in the letter [Note: [Col. 0049] Paulinus, Letter 2, section 4], evidently meaning either the clergy of the Church of Bordeaux or Bishop Delphinus himself. Paulinus seems to have maintained a correspondence with Amandus, [Col. 0049B] and to have received from Amandus a long-desired letter. Chiffletius interprets this letter as concerning Paulinus’s episcopate, not his presbyterate [Note: [Col. 0049] Chifflet, chapter 23, p. 177]. Some considerations support his opinion; nor would it be surprising if Paulinus had accepted the episcopate under the same force of popular pressure by which he had accepted the priesthood. Yet Paulinus himself states clearly enough [Note: [Col. 0049] Paulinus, Letter 2, section 4] that he had been made a shepherd from a sheep, and that he, a layman, had been placed upon the foundation of the apostles. He also indicates that he was a presbyter [Note: [Col. 0049] Ibid., section 2] in these words: “Now, in name and office, an elder …”

## CHAPTER XVII. Paulinus Comes to Italy. He Is Received Affectionately and Honorably by Saint Ambrose, but Badly by Siricius, the Roman Pontiff.

1. Everything supports the belief that Paulinus came through Gaul to Nola immediately after Easter, as he had planned. Some people [Note: [Col. 0049] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 679] think that he returned to this [Col. 0049C] region in order to arrange for the auction of the remainder of his possessions. He writes to Severus that he had old wine at Narbonne [Note: [Col. 0049] Paulinus, Letter 5, section 22], and asks him to arrange for its transport to Nola. At Narbonne he prepared to travel by sea to Italy. There, troubled by a storm, he called upon his patron Felix, as is evident from the natal poem for the following year [Note: [Col. 0049] Poem 13, verse 14]:

> And I entered the sea under your guidance, because concern for danger  
> yielded to love for you; nor was I without you, for I felt your  
> protection, overcoming through Christ in the Lord the sea’s harshness.  
> Because of you I always go safely both on land and on the waves.

Having entered Italy [Note: [Col. 0049] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 680], he saw Saint Ambrose. In a letter written that same year [Note: [Col. 0049] Paulinus, Letter 3, section 4], Paulinus says that he had been nourished by Ambrose in the faith and cherished by him in the priestly order, and that Ambrose had wished him to be counted among his clergy, even though he lived in different places. Baronius thinks that Paulinus accepted this favor, although it was contrary to the laws of the Church [Note: [Col. 0049] Baronius, year 394, section 89], and adds that Ambrose perhaps enrolled him among the Milanese clergy so that he might have a successor in his see. It is nevertheless certain [Note: [Col. 0049] *Life of Ambrose* 69, chapter 11] that Ambrose designated Saint Simplician as his successor. After Baronius [Note: [Col. 0049] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 680, and Chifflet, p. 142], some judged that Paulinus had come to Milan in order to see Ambrose; they should rather have said Florence, where Ambrose had already withdrawn in 393 in order to escape the tyrant Eugenius. Ambrose spent most of that period in Florence and did not return to Milan until August of the year 394 [Note: [Col. 0049] Baronius, year 394, sections 89 and 92; and Sacchini, p. 680].

2. Paulinus finally arrived at Rome, where, according to his merit and noble birth, he was received by the people with great honor and veneration—especially by Saint Domnio, a presbyter of the Roman Church, whom he calls “a most holy parent” [Note: [Col. 0049] Paulinus, Letter 3, section 3]—and by the distinguished Roman men Saints Pammachius and Macarius [Note: [Col. 0049] Letter 5, section 14; and Letters 13 and 49], as well as by a very large number of other servants of God. Yet he experienced the envy of certain clerics and even of Pope Urbicius, as Paulinus calls him—that is, Siricius, the Roman pontiff—which, Cardinal Baronius thinks [Note: [Col. 0049] Baronius, year 394, section 91], had been aroused because Siricius disapproved of Paulinus’s sudden ordination. For Siricius had exerted himself vigorously to suppress the wicked custom then spreading, by which laymen and even neophytes were hastily ordained priests; he had established fixed intervals through which one was gradually to ascend to the orders of the sacred service in accordance with ecclesiastical regulations. For that reason he may have said [Note: [Col. 0049] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 680] that he did not approve of Paulinus’s way of life, or perhaps [Note: [Col. 0049] Baronius, same place] he denied him a place among the presbyters in the Church, lest he should appear to approve Paulinus’s sudden ordination and himself weaken the laws he had promulgated. Yet if there had been any fault in this ordination, it certainly ought not to have been charged to Paulinus, who had done nothing through defiance, and whom everyone knew to have been initiated into the presbyterate against his will and by the force [Col. 0050C] of an inflamed multitude. General laws ought to yield in this singular circumstance, as had happened in the case of Ambrose. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0049] Sacchini, same place], at least Siricius’s ill-considered zeal cannot be excused.

From Paulinus’s Letter 5 to Severus [Note: [Col. 0049] Paulinus, Letter 5, section 14; and Baronius, same place], however, it can readily be inferred that the envy of certain clerics and of Siricius himself had been aroused because, when Paulinus arrived at Rome after so long an interval, everyone’s eyes were turned toward him. They were astonished at the spectacle of a senator, a consular man, a prefect, now made a presbyter and a monk—one who attained glory by despising glory. Consequently, both citizens and foreigners, bishops, clerics, monks, and laymen crowded to attend upon him and to send delegations. [Col. 0050D] Therefore he, a son of peace, peaceful in mind toward those who hated peace, did not answer minds so ill-disposed through envy with arguments, but with the silence of humility, keeping in his heart the Apostle’s words: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, this is not our custom” (1 Corinthians 11:16). Thus he thought that no more suitable remedy could be applied to them than a hasty departure from the City [Col. 0051A]. Eager, therefore, to leave Rome, he concealed himself in the desired bosom of his Felix, so that the envy nourished by his appearance and presence might be extinguished when its fuel was removed.

“Not long afterward,” he says [Note: [Col. 0051] Paulinus, Letter 5, section 13], “the distance from Rome extinguishes the fires of the jealous clerics, and all iniquity there closes its mouth, because, through our absence from that place, as though its fuel had been removed, the sluggish flame of hatred grows cold; nor does envy dare to burst into speech, although it gnashes its teeth, while, conscious of its own iniquity, it is itself ashamed and has no ready place in which to kindle the torches of its envious mind … Scarcely a faint rumor of these things reaches us, and from our ears, fenced about as they are with thorns, it is shut out like a cold breeze or the importunate buzzing of an idle gnat.”

The following passage in the same letter may perhaps refer to the same persecution [Col. 0051B] [Note: [Col. 0051] Ibid., section 7]: “The Lord himself has taught us to remain silent even in cases that provoke outcry. Therefore we silently endure his will and judgment; for he is powerful both to keep silent in us now and, when he wills, to plead for us.” The same matter [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 5, section 14] was becoming a great impediment to the glory of God and a detriment to the grace of the Lord, since that rumor concerning the Roman pontiff’s hostile attitude held back not a few people from following Paulinus’s footsteps. Yet it will become clear from what follows that Siricius’s jealousy was soon afterward quieted [Note: [Col. 0051] Chapter 22, section 2].

## CHAPTER XVIII. Paulinus Settles at Nola. The Life He Established There.

1. In a pleasant estate five hundred paces from the city of Nola, the bones of the blessed Felix, presbyter and confessor, rested [Note: [Col. 0051] Sacchini, *Life of Paulinus*, p. 681], and they are still preserved there today. It is impossible to say how Paulinus breathed again in that place, like a ship bringing its weary hull into harbor after the storm of the world; with what joys he overflowed; how he gave himself wholly to his most beloved patron and entrusted himself to him; and how he poured himself entirely into every excellence of holiness.

Nola is a celebrated colony in Campania, and a maritime one [Note: [Col. 0051] Ferrar’s *Lexicon*]. It lies eight leagues from Capua, or twenty thousand paces [Note: [Col. 0051] Paulinus, Poem 21, verse 404], or, according to Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, twenty-one thousand; and one hundred and sixty thousand paces, or sixty-four leagues, from the city of Rome. Yet Paulinus says that it is only one hundred and twenty thousand paces from Rome [Note: [Col. 0051] Poem 14, verse 67]. The city was especially commended by the tomb of Saint Felix, situated a short distance from it [Note: [Col. 0051] Poem 18, verse 166; Poem 24, verse 465]. A basilica had been built over the tomb [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 32, sections 10 and 13], and beside it stretched a building [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 29, section 13; and Poem 23, verse 400] raised above the ground, with an upper chamber and a portico interspersed with guest cells. On the opposite side there was another dwelling belonging to the same establishment, in which secular men sometimes lodged [Note: [Col. 0051] Ibid.]. All these buildings seemed to form another city [Note: [Col. 0051] Poem 18, verse 169].

There was also a little garden [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 11, section 14], which Paulinus called “Saint Felix’s garden” [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 5, section 14]. He describes it as so narrow [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 39, section 4] that it could scarcely produce or contain a single stalk. On the other side was an orchard [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 32, section 12], from which a private entrance opened into the basilica of Saint Felix. With Paulinus lived [Col. 0052A] certain servants of God, among them the Hebrews Proforus and Restitutus [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 5, section 19]. Paulinus called his dwelling a monastery [Note: [Col. 0051] Ibid., section 15], and called his community a “monastic brotherhood” [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 23, section 8], because all who lived there, devoted to monastic rules, pursued a stricter life. There [Note: [Col. 0051] Uranus, section 3] they celebrated the morning office at daybreak and the evening office at the lighting of the lamp.

2. Their manner of life can easily be gathered from one of Paulinus’s letters [Note: [Col. 0051] Paulinus, Letter 22, section 1]. After saying that he did not approve of having secular men as guests, he adds [Note: [Col. 0051] Ibid., section 2]:

> Let our fellow servants and fellow sufferers visit and revisit us—not proud in embroidered garments, but humble in bristling haircloth; not wrapped in a shortened cloak, but mantled in coarse woolen garments; not girded with a belt, but with a rope; not with the unseemly hairiness of the forehead on a shaven head, but with hair cut to the skin in chaste disfigurement, unevenly half-shorn, and with the forehead left bare by close shaving. Let them be unadorned with the ornament of chastity, decently neglected and honorably contemptible; let them even despise their body’s natural appearance for the sake of inward cultivation and deliberately disfigure themselves, so that they may wisely be dishonorable in appearance while becoming salvifically honorable in mind …
>
> Why should they rightly be angry with us if, in turn, the odor of their life stinks to us, while the odor of ours is death to them? They shudder at my fasting; I cannot endure their gluttony. They avoid the breath of a speaking monk; I flee the breath of a belching braggart. If the dryness of our throats displeases them, their gullets’ rawness displeases us. If the aridity of frugality offends them, the greediness of their bellies offends us.
>
> Let them therefore see us not drunk in the morning, but fasting in the evening; not bloated with yesterday’s wine, but abstinent today; not foolishly unstable from the excesses of gluttony, but soundly wounded by the vigils of holiness and soberly intoxicated—people whom frugality, not a chasm, makes stagger.

Paulinus not only postponed taking food until evening on the individual days of Lent [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 15, section 4], but even during the Easter season no one in the household dared to eat before the ninth hour [Note: [Col. 0051] Ibid.]. Throughout the whole year they ate in the evening [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 23, section 8], and their customary foods were herbs and small vegetables [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 19, section 4]. When Paulinus sent Severus rye bread as a blessing [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 5, section 21], he said that Severus would think it exceeded the measure of his humility; from this it follows that the ordinary bread on which he himself lived was not so delicate.

His moderation in food was extreme [Col. 0052D], both in the quality and in the quantity of food and drink. Speaking of Cardamatus, who was unaccustomed to such sobriety, he says that he was almost transformed [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 15, section 4]: “For,” he says [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 19, section 4], “as a constant participant at our little table, he so restricted himself to the measure of our throats that he did not avoid either our little vegetables or our little cups; this he will be able to demonstrate by the emaciation of his body and the pallor of his face.” Elsewhere he says [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 21, section 6]: “Although he was served with small and infrequent cups, barely touching his lips with their upper rims, he made no complaint about the hardship of an empty stomach or a dry throat.”

Nevertheless, Paulinus seems to have used a little wine even during Lent [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 15, section 4], something entirely foreign to the ecclesiastical discipline of the present age—unless we say that, being sick and weak, as he himself attests in his Letter 13 to Pammachius [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 13, section 2], he was able to follow the Apostle’s advice.
