He then speaks cheerfully of certain inventions [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 23, sections 6 and 9] with which Victor, whom we shall discuss more fully elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0053] Chapters 38, 39, and 47], had furnished him so that he might live more sparingly, simply, and austerely. Paulinus said that his own dishes were especially suitable for removing a senator’s fastidiousness [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 23, section 6]; yet, for a weak stomach, the foods he ate were probably rather heavy [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid., section 9].

He seems to have celebrated the divine praises at night [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 29, section 13]. His writings make it sufficiently clear that he was covered by a heavy sack made of goat hair and was pricked and tormented by the roughness of its bristles [Note: [Col. 0053] Poem 32, verse 451; and Letter 29, section 1]. When Severus sent Paulinus delicacies of this kind [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid.]—namely, cloaks woven from camel hair—Paulinus drew from these gifts abundant material for compunction and humility.

It is indeed something to marvel at: such austerity in so great a senator, who was not only naturally delicate but whose body was always weak [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 13, section 2]. We shall speak elsewhere of his various illnesses [Note: [Col. 0053] Chapters 26, 35, and 33].

## CHAPTER XIX. Paulinus’s Love of Poverty, Voluntary Bodily Affliction, Solitude, and Silence. Saint Augustine’s Judgment on His Letters.

1. His external surroundings were consistent with his austerity. Everything was simple, cheap, and breathing humility. From the beginning of his conversion he changed his silver household vessels [Col. 0053C] into wooden and earthen ones. He says that he loved the latter [Note: [Col. 0053] Paulinus, Letter 5, section 21] because earthen vessels, being related to Adam, were akin to him, and because the Lord’s treasure had been entrusted to vessels of that kind. He sent Severus a boxwood dish [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid.] as a gift for a spiritual banquet, so that Severus might be taught to use vessels of that kind instead of silverware.

The degree of poverty to which Paulinus reduced himself can be inferred from Letter 39 [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 39, section 4], where he represents himself as at one point needing salt because of poverty’s necessity. Severus admired his poverty [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 11, section 12], but denied that he could imitate it. Indeed, Paulinus had nothing except Christ [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid., section 14], yet considered himself to possess everything in him who possessed all things. He did not waver or despair in poverty, caring nothing for the morrow [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid.]. Nevertheless, he did not hesitate to invite friends to him, for he knew that God would assist him—he who had entrusted and surrendered himself wholly to God—and that the sustenance of mortal life would not fail those whose possession had become God.

He loved this poverty, voluntary bodily affliction, and humiliation, hoping thereby to obtain riches, glory, and eternal joys.

> Give me now, O God, to mourn, and with health-giving weeping  
> sow the seeds of eternal joy.  
> This I ask; let this mourning rather remain with me through my life,  
> in which whatever is present passes along a brief journey.  
> Go far away, you joyful ones; I prefer the company of those who weep,  
> so that with brief tears I may harvest long joys.
>
> If only, while I mourn, a rough sackcloth garment  
> covers and pricks me with the bristles of goat hair.  
> Then, with the Father appeased, the honors earned will be restored:  
> the ring, and the robe of joy will encircle me.  
> Then, with justice, O Father, you will slaughter a fattened calf for me,  
> if only, while fasting, I hunger for righteousness.
>
> I would rather endure hunger for bread than hunger for the holy word;  
> I do not want a house of wine; I thirst for the water of light.  
> Here let dreadful hunger torture me; here let shameful poverty  
> besiege me, contracted in mournful rags.  
> Here let a rich man pass before his own houses,  
> scorning even to satisfy me with crumbs.
>
> I do not want a garment of silk, glowing with Tyrian purple dye,  
> to burn against me through envy of the body destined to burn,  
> lest, after my purple coverings, an everlasting flame  
> surround me and I pay the price of my clothing in fire.  
> Here rather let us, wretched, lie on a foul heap of dung,  
> and let dogs lick our sores,  
> so that, after the mire of this sorrowful mortal life, a gentle angel may receive us  
> into peaceful encounters [Note: [Col. 0053] Poem 34, verse 445].

35 2. The cheerfulness and gracious sweetness breathed by his letters plainly demonstrate how much he delighted in the stricter way of life that he had chosen. Thus Augustine, describing in a few words the life which our Paulinus was leading in Campania, says [Note: [Col. 0053] Augustine, Letter 26, section 5]: “Now, with Christ guiding his journey, he rejoices in quietness and moderation.”

Nor was he greatly occupied with ecclesiastical affairs, although at the same time Saint Augustine thought that he was enjoying holy leisure [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 31, section 4], while he nevertheless had incredible occupations [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 95, section 9]. He devoted himself to solitude no less than to other works of penitence. For when he was apologizing to Pammachius because he had learned too late of the death of Pammachius’s wife, Paulina, he said [Note: [Col. 0053] Paulinus, Letter 13, section 2; Letter 5, section 7]:

> Nor should it seem that I heard of you late through negligence, since both the remoteness of the place and the nature of my chosen way of life defend me. Living withdrawn and silent, I can see only a few passersby, and I do not wish to ask about the holy brothers except those who are dear to me.

From this it can be inferred that the frequent crowds of visitors who came to the tomb of Saint Felix diminished nothing of his solitude and silence. He lived in a remote place, as he himself testifies elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid., and section 14], and remained silent in seclusion; and by this manner of life [Note: [Col. 0053] Augustine, Letter 26, section 5] he extinguished the fires of the jealous Roman clerics.

Above all, in the tranquility of solitude and the joy of peace before God, he devoted himself to giving thanks. Hence Augustine, writing to his Licentius, says: “Go to Campania; learn from Paulinus … learn with what resources of intellect he offers sacrifices of praise to Christ, returning to him whatever he has received from him, lest he lose everything if he does not place it in the one from whom he has these things.”

He was wholly occupied with the discipline and stripping bare of his heart [Note: [Col. 0053] Paulinus, Letter 24, sections 9, 13, and 14], so that he might evade the devil’s arrows. For this reason he had sold his estates [Col. 0054D] and freed himself from all other occupations, so that he might devote himself to this one thing.

3. In writing letters [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 13, section 1], his humility restrained the flowing vein of his pen on the one hand; at times, when he recognized the necessity of speaking, it allowed him to be carried farther by the flood of charity. How highly his letters should be valued may be learned from Augustine, who, after receiving Paulinus’s first letters, replied as follows [Note: [Col. 0053] Augustine, Letter 27, section 3]:

> I have read your letters, flowing with milk and honey, displaying the simplicity of your heart, in which you seek the Lord, thinking well of him, and offering him glory and honor … All who have read them are carried away, because they are themselves carried away as they read. It cannot be said how sweet the fragrance of Christ is, and how strongly it breathes from them. When those letters offer you to our sight, how greatly do they stir us to seek you! For they make you both visible and desirable. The more they in some way present your presence to us, the less they allow us to endure your absence. Everyone loves you in them and wishes to be loved by you. God is praised and blessed, whose grace has made you such.
>
> Those letters—letters of unfeigned faith, letters of good hope, letters of pure charity—how they breathe to us your thirst, and the longing and weariness of your soul for the courts of the Lord! What most holy love they exhale! What abundance of a sincere heart they pour out! What thanks do they give to God? What do they ask from God? Are they more flattering, or more ardent? More luminous, or more fruitful? For what is it that soothes us, so inflames us, so drenches us, and yet is so serene?

## CHAPTER XX. Paulinus Suffers the Troublesome Harassment of Carnal Desire, Calls upon God, and Despises Himself.

36 1. Augustine observes throughout Paulinus’s writings a piety that continually sighs [Note: [Col. 0055] Augustine, Letter 186, section 41], by which Paulinus prayed to God and begged with groans that he not be led into temptation. He guarded his heart with every watchfulness [Note: [Col. 0055] Paulinus, Letter 21, section 9], and his entire labor and complete task consisted in the discipline and stripping bare of his heart. Thus, with his mind cleansed of concern for external things and turned inward toward itself, he might see the enemy’s hidden lairs in his heart; what power the vices there possessed, how great the weakness of the virtues was, how prone his relapse into depravity was, and how necessary it was continually to entreat God. For this reason he writes to Severus [Note: [Col. 0055] Ibid., section 10]:

> I believe that you have already experienced how laborious and constant—indeed, daily—our struggle with this enemy is, and how many ambushes are involved in it: what power the vices possess there, how great the weakness of the virtues is, how prone its relapse into depravity is, and how sluggish its striving toward God. Now that discord of a different law, formerly closed within me, is opened to me; now I feel the force of the opposing law, which, as though laying a hand upon me, attempts to drag me captive into the law of sin. And I recognize that that blessed man burns because of my misery and, grieving for me because of my condition, cries out: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?”
>
> But that same Teacher restores and refreshes me, showing me a saving escape, provided that I have the will by which I may deserve to find perfection: the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. He must be entreated to prevail over our enemies and to make light abound over darkness; to destroy in us what is alien or our own, and to build what is his.

[Note: [Col. 0055] Ibid., section 20.]

> Just as, when rubble has been cleared away and the soil stripped bare beneath filthy masses, many tangled roots or remnants of trunks, remnants of thorns, or numerous creatures of a harmful kind—and especially the offspring or lairs of vipers—are discovered, so, once the possession and care of temporal things have been removed from our breast, and we are free to inspect our heart, we find in our thoughts the knots of long-standing crimes and the hiding places of spiritual enemies that formerly drew us outward. Now the inner house begins to appear to us, and in it creeping things whose number cannot be counted. Now the whole darkness of our misery is laid bare. Now at last we see how far we are from God and how dead we are in comparison with the living.

[Note: [Col. 0055] Ibid., section 21.]

> Understand these things, and, with an anxious heart, sigh for our sake.

When Severus once asked for an image of Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0055] Paulinus, Letter 30, sections 2 and 5], Paulinus seized upon this as an occasion to cast himself down and despise himself. Interpreting the request as concerning the inner man, and presenting the image of the heavenly man in himself as disfigured by earthly corruption, Paulinus ingeniously evaded it. He used the following words, which Augustine records in Letter 186, section 40 [Note: [Col. 0055] Ibid., section 2]:

> I am a poor and grieving man, still caked with the filth of the earthly image, and in my bodily perceptions and earthly actions I reflect more of the first Adam than of the second. How shall I dare to paint myself for you, when I am proved to disfigure the image of the heavenly man through earthly corruption? Shame closes me in on both sides: I am ashamed to paint what I am; I do not dare to paint what I am not. I hate what I am, and I am not what I love.
>
> But what will it profit wretched me to hate iniquity and love virtue, when I do rather what I hate and, sluggishly, do not strive to do what I love? I, divided against myself, am torn apart by inward war, while spirit fights against flesh and flesh against spirit, and the law of the body attacks the law of the mind through the law of sin.
>
> Wretched am I, who have not digested the poisoned taste of the hostile tree even by the wood of the cross. For that paternal poison from Adam endures in me, by which the father, transgressing, infected the whole of his race.

Nothing more beautiful can be written about the fault of our origin, nor can it be recognized more fully and abundantly that our nature was corrupted through that father of the human race and did not remain as it had been created [Note: [Col. 0055] Augustine, Letter 186, section 40].

Here Paulinus adds much more concerning human misery, groaning as he awaits the redemption of his body and recognizing that he is not yet saved in reality, but in hope. After humbly lamenting these things, he asks through such groans for assistance in advancing and living rightly [Note: [Col. 0055] Paulinus, Letter 30, section 5] that everyone might be moved by them [Note: [Col. 0055] Augustine, Letter 186, section 41]. In another letter he says:

> Who will rescue us from the coming wrath? Who will free us from ourselves, so that, cleansed of our own perceptions, we may be emptied of the material of heavenly wrath through purifying faith? For we feel within us the causes of eternal punishments, living roots of thorns and thistles in our heart.

2. With this same humility, scattered throughout all his writings, he says [Note: [Col. 0055] Paulinus, Letter 28, section 4] that he marvels at the charity and patience of his friends in enduring the burdensomeness of his writings—or, as he calls them, his foolishnesses. To Delphinus, by whom he had been baptized, he writes [Note: [Col. 0055] Letter 10, section 3] that he fears he will sadden Delphinus, whose mind rejoiced in the presumption of good hopes concerning him, when that expectation has been deceived, because, despite Delphinus’s instruction, example, and the sacraments he had conferred upon him, Paulinus had made no progress in virtue. Therefore, he says that Delphinus still has something to do for him by imitating the one who pleaded with the Lord of the vineyard for a reprieve for the barren fig tree.

After rejoicing with Severus over his piety toward his household and servants, Paulinus extols his happiness and adds [Note: [Col. 0057] Paulinus, Letter 27, section 3]:

> We confess that we groaned over our own unhappiness, since sterility had made our sins heavier than those of such sons; but we have become, as it were, consoled, because we judge that the good of your happiness is near to us.

[Note: [Col. 0057] Ibid., section 4.]

> Yet, lest our iniquity separate us from you by a wider interval, gird this whole selection of sacred youth, with whom you soothe God day and night, so that they may direct the battle-line of their prayers against our sins and entreat him to strengthen what the Lord has worked for us—that is, so that through your charity, in which we now rest and in which we glory, we may be refreshed and rejoice on that day.

Commending himself to Amandus’s prayers, he says [Note: [Col. 0057] Letter 12, section 10] that he is unworthy for his name to be brought by holy men into the divine ears, lest perhaps their lips become unclean when they name him.

Likewise, he writes to another presbyter [Note: [Col. 0057] Letter 43, section 6]:

> But because it is the last hour, and the axe has already been placed at the roots of the trees, threatening a just destruction to dry and wretched wood, I ask you to pray for pardon and an extension of time for me. Perhaps, with death postponed, I may receive the sap of fruitfulness through the diligence of your charity and the cultivation of my concern, so that divine fear may dig into my heart and necessary repentance may enrich my stock with the manure of humility. Then, awakened to watchful concern, I shall stand ready at every hour, and, while the Lord is absent, I shall be afraid, so that I may be secure when he arrives.

And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0057] Letter 19, section 2]:

> We love his coming, wretched as we are, through hope in his mercy, and we dread it, sinners as we are, through fear of his justice.

38 He preserves the same humility in his poems as in his letters. For when, in a certain poem, he had treated of the final judgment and David’s repentance, he adds [Note: [Col. 0057] Poem 32, verse 415]:

> What, alas, is it fitting for wretched me to do? From where shall I be cleansed?  
> How shall I make satisfaction? By what means shall I be saved?  
> My swollen heart needs tears; ashes dread food,  
> and pleasures delight me while my soul is hungry.  
> Who will show me a spring for streams of tears,  
> in which I may mourn my deeds and my days?  
> For according to the merits of a life spent in crimes,  
> I must weep rivers of tears for my immense wounds.
>
> Break the stone of my heart, Savior Jesus,  
> so that, softened, my inward parts may flow with a holy spring.  
> I pray you, O Christ, spring, be born within my fibers,  
> so that the living vein of your water may resound within me.

[Col. 0057D] When Paulinus had addressed Severus as “lord” in the heading of his letter [Note: [Col. 0057] Epist. 5, n. 20.] and had described himself as his servant, Paulinus altogether rejected this praise and did not wish to return it to Severus in his reply, because, he says [Note: [Col. 0057] Ibid.], “I thought it safer to write truthfully.” Therefore beware hereafter, now that you have been called from slavery into the freedom of Christ, of writing that you are the servant of a human being, a brother, and a fellow servant inferior to you; for to confer upon any human being—let alone a most wretched sinner—the honor due to the one Lord, the one Master upon earth, and the one God is rather the justification of the sin of flattery than of humility. “Love from a pure heart and an unfeigned faith” is sufficient; whatever goes beyond this is from evil.

Nevertheless, in accepting such praise he readily allowed it and extended the same courtesy to those with whom he was less familiar, preserving the custom and convention in a matter that was almost indifferent, and maintaining the honor due to them. He used to offer water to his guests’ hands [Note: [Col. 0057] Ep. 23, n. 4], so that at least in this small act of human service he might in some measure approach Saint Martin. But, made still lower in his own estimation by this same submission, he praises Victor, one of the common people who had performed certain charitable services for him, with extravagant commendation. “I dare,” he says [Note: [Col. 0057] Ep. 23, n. 3], “to confess to you a matter that is our burden, while concealing nothing from you about his virtues—things which I know for certain are your joy, since the good of your intimate friend is your portion.” [Note: [Col. 0057] Ibid., n. 4.] “He served me, then—yes, he served me; and woe to me in my misery that I permitted it. He served even a sinner, though he did not serve sin, and I, unworthy as I am, was ministered to by a servant of righteousness. Yet from this I hope for some relief from so great a burden: I did not arrogate to myself the service of my holy brother out of pride, but accepted it to testify to my love and to receive a blessing through faith. For that holy service in the name of God was a blessing to me, and his serving love was offered in the spirit of freedom. For this reason I accepted his voluntary goodness, and for his own benefit, presuming that he would be the more powerful in seeking pardon for me, the more merit he had acquired through works of religion. Surely by his prayers he will ensure that what accrued to his fruits even from me does not increase my burdens. For I confess that I loved the blessing in his service, fearing that, if rejected, it might withdraw far from me.”

He adds [Note: [Col. 0057] Ibid., n. 5] that Victor also wished to wash his feet; but Paulinus says that he yielded only once, following the apostolic example, because, venerating Christ in Victor, he wished that a better fellow servant might touch him with water as a remedy for his weakness. Although Paulinus’s eminent virtue turned everyone’s eyes and voices toward his admiration, amid these applauses he nevertheless took no complacency in his good works and declared himself an unprofitable servant [Note: [Col. 0057] Ep. 20, n. 4]. He placed all his hope in God’s power and mercy. From God he sought understanding for his journey, and from him he awaited the help by which he might travel that road. Indeed, even in his good works he feared God’s judgments. “Perhaps,” he said [Note: [Col. 0057] Ibid.], “the humility of our confession may establish us before the Lord as modest men, whom the usefulness of energetic service cannot commend as idlers.” 39

## CHAPTER XXI. [Col. 0058D] He considers himself unworthy to expound Sacred Scripture

1. Paulinus, always eager to remain hidden and not considering himself fit to treat the mysteries of the Christian religion with the authority of a teacher, was content with works of lighter labor. To the priest Desiderius, who had asked for an explanation of the words with which the patriarch Jacob blessed his sons, he humbly replied that he did not dare touch even with a finger the weight of such names and mysteries. “Concerning what you wrote to me,” he says [Note: [Col. 0057] Paulin. ep. 43, n. 3], “seeking sweet and abundant water in a bitter and parched stream, I return it to be explained rather by your grace; for I confess that I have not dared even with a finger to touch the weight of such names and mysteries. For I have read that ‘wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul’ (Wis. 1:4); and therefore, conscious of my wickedness, I could not trust in divine revelation, since my dark heart could not receive the light of understanding. But you, blessed man, a pure vessel suited to God, if you have received an understanding of that blessing by which the patriarch, illumined by the prophetic spirit while blind in body, addresses his sons, explain to me in your reply the mysteries of the kingdom,” and so forth.

A little later he asked Rufinus for an explanation of the same passage, saying: “I shall regard you as the author of great grace and praise if, for those who, thinking more highly of me than they ought, have judged that I should be consulted, I may give inept answers about divine matters from your spirit rather than from my own judgment.”” When in a certain poem he had treated extensively, in a grand and elevated style, of Christ’s death, he immediately accused himself as though conscious of rashness and pride [Note: [Col. 0059] Carm. 24, v. 307], and defended himself by an apology for the presence of Nicetas, which had aroused this unusual ardor in him [Note: [Col. 0059] Ibid., v. 315]. He adds [Note: [Col. 0059] Ibid., v. 320]:

> But I shall restrain my swelling breath; nor shall I, little as I am,  
> Breathe out great words above my station. I shall be returned, a little man,  
> To the earth I have left, and walk with the measured foot  
> Of modest song.

He writes to Augustine that he could praise the elder Melania in nothing holier or better than Augustine had spoken in her praise, so that, he says [Note: [Col. 0059] Ep. 45, n. 3], “since I, a sinner with unclean lips, could say nothing worthy, being far removed from the merits of her faith and the virtues of her soul, you, that man of Christ, a teacher in the Church of truth, with the grace of God directing you toward what is better, might be prepared as a worthier herald of such a manly soul in Christ—one who, as I have said, could perceive more closely her mind, strengthened by divine power, and praise her piety joined with virtue in worthier speech.”

2. The lower his estimation of himself, the greater was his reputation among others who consulted him about obscure matters, especially with Augustine, who asked Paulinus what activity the blessed would have in that age after the resurrection of the flesh. To this he replied [Note: [Col. 0059] Ibid.]:

> But I consult a spiritual teacher and physician concerning the present condition of my life, so that he may teach me to do God’s will, to walk after Christ in your footsteps, and to die beforehand by that evangelical death by which we anticipate the dissolution of the flesh through a voluntary departure—not by bodily death, but by decision—withdraw­ing from the life of this world, which is entirely full of temptations, or, as you once said to me, which is itself entirely temptation. Would that my paths might be directed after your footsteps, so that, following your example, I might loosen the old sandal from my feet, break my bonds, and exult as a free man in running the course by which I may attain that death through which you died to this world, so that you might live to God, with Christ living in you. His death and life are recognized in your body, heart, and mouth, because your heart does not savor earthly things, nor does your mouth speak the works of men; rather, Christ’s word abounds in your breast, and the Spirit of truth is poured out upon your tongue by the force of heavenly light, gladdening the city of God.

[Note: [Col. 0059] Ibid., n. 5.] “What virtue, then, produces this death in us, except love, which is strong as death? For it blots out and destroys this world for us in such a way as to accomplish the effect of death through the effect of Christ. Turned toward him, we turn away from this world, and while living for him we die to the elements of this world. Nor do we judge as though we were living in their presence and under their gaze, because our portion is the death of Christ. We do not grasp the resurrection from the dead in glory unless we imitate his death on the cross by mortifying the members and senses of the flesh, so that we may no longer live by our own will, but by the will of him whose will is our sanctification.”

Saint Augustine adapted himself to the meaning of this most modest man [Note: [Col. 0059] Ibid., n. 2]. Consulted by Alethius, Paulinus replied in these words [Note: [Col. 0059] Paulin. ep. 33, n. 2]:

> In the matters which you thought should be imposed upon me, judging me rich in poverty, you have indeed displayed the holy confidence of the purest love. Yet, as I understand, persuaded by the reputation of the Lord’s work, you have clothed yourself in the belief that, since God has deigned to inspire us with care for our redemption, we must also possess an abundance of intellect and speech sufficient for the fruitful work of the Lord. But a good desire, empty of great faith, has been deceived by hopes misled by empty opinions.  
>   
> Whence should I have so much water as your thirst requires? Whence such a cup as you may drink worthily? Whence such loaves as you ask for? Yet you yourself will be the author of your wrong for continuing to hunger, if, desiring the evangelical foods of light and life in the deep night of this world, you knock at the poor storehouse of a sleepy and needy friend, and, thirsting for rivers of living water, scratch at a dry little stream and attempt to squeeze moisture from a stone.  
>   
> Either there is no fountain within me because of the dryness of inspiration, or there is a bitter one because of the gall of wickedness. Would that your prayers and letters, so often devoted to me, might make it overflow and grow sweet through the wood of your faith and the sweetness of your eloquence.

Of the two little books composed by him—one of which was a panegyric, or apology, for the emperor Theodosius, whose desirability to learned men is made still greater by that magnificent approval of Saint Jerome—he writes thus to his Severus [Note: [Col. 0059] Epist. 28, n. 6]:

> To do something in accordance with your instructions, I have sent you some pieces which I fear may testify rather to my laziness or lack of judgment than to the marks of heavenly assistance, or at least to any evidence of human wisdom. Nevertheless, I have sent them to you—that is, I have entrusted my trifles to my own heart—not so that my darkness may pollute your understanding, but so that they may be cleansed by your understanding.  
>   
> I called them my trifles because they are made of my words and opinions. The subject itself, however, is holy and more worthy of your intellect and eloquence; even if it is clothed in my speech as in a dark garment, it nevertheless preserves the appearance of divine light and inward beauty, though amid the poverty of a needy household.

## CHAPTER XXII. [Col. 0060D] Paulinus’s devotion to the saints, especially to his most holy patron Felix. Every year he goes to Rome to venerate in person the sacred bodies of the apostles

1. How mindful he was of God’s benefits and what thanksgiving he poured out to God can readily be understood from the grateful and faithful service with which he served his most holy patron Felix [Col. 0061A], through whom he believed God’s gifts had been granted to him. He says that Felix’s birthday festival was a day of exultation and joy for everyone, but especially for himself:

> What Christ has given us through you,  
> Granting worthless flesh to a friend:  
> Not because you were worthy that such worthless servants  
> Should be deemed worthy to go with God, your companion, into eternal triumphs,  
> But because the good Father wished to enrich us, poor and unworthy of salvation,  
> So that, though perversely rich in sins, with wealth exchanged for better things,  
> We might receive Felix in place of all riches and all affections,  
> And in place of all noble titles and all empty honors,  
> Take him as our wealth, our fatherland, and our home.  
>   
> You are our Father, our fatherland, our home, and our substance;  
> Our cradle has been transferred into your bosom,  
> And your breast is our secure refuge. Here we grow well nourished,  
> And, changing our bodies into another form,  
> We strip off our earthly stock, and, when wings arise,  
> We are turned into birds through the divine seed of the word.  
>   
> Through you, as you lift the yoke, we know that Christ’s yoke is light; in you  
> Christ is gentle toward the unworthy and sweet to those who are bitter.  
> Therefore this day too must be held solemn by us,  
> Since it is your birthday: because, when you abolish our evils,  
> We die to the world so that we may be born to good things in Christ.  
> [Note: [Col. 0061] Paulin. carm. 15, v. 5.]

Paulinus had no doubt that Saint Felix loved him, at least as a master may deign to love a little dog [Note: [Col. 0061] Carm. 24, v. 602]:

> When my life, home, property, grace, glory, and bread  
> Are Felix, by God’s gift.  
> [Note: [Col. 0061] Ibid., v. 603.]

Since his own house adjoined this saint’s basilica, Paulinus very often calls Felix his “lord of the house,” as though he were the master of the building [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 5, n. 15; 18, n. 3; 28, n. 6; 32, n. 10, and Carm. 20, v. 109]. He likewise calls the house and little garden his own, and calls them Saint Felix’s dwelling and garden [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 5, n. 15 and 16]. On the vigil of Saint Felix’s solemnity he used to fast with his entire household; after the sacred rites had been performed in the evening and the assembly dismissed, he returned home and, after taking food, spent the whole or part of the night rejoicing in God with hymns and psalms [Note: [Col. 0061] Carm. 20, v. 111]. With body and spirit, as far as he could, he served that heavenly patron every day [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 28, n. 6]. Every year, however, he used to honor this saint’s birthday with a new birthday poem, paying with his sweetest tongue the tribute of voluntary service, offering Christ a sacrifice of praise, and rendering his vows to the Most High.

Fifteen birthday poems of his concerning Saint Felix survive. From them we possess the whole life of the confessor, his sacred struggles, and the miracles performed at his tomb. Thus, if our Paulinus owed the glory of his conversion to the most holy Felix, Saint Felix in turn owed his glory among human beings to Paulinus, who made the name of Saint Felix of Nola venerable and renowned far and wide throughout the world, both through the magnificence of his basilicas and through his poems. In what follows [Note: [Col. 0061] Chs. 42 and 43] we shall see how he enlarged and adorned his basilica.

Yet however devoutly he honored Saint Felix, and although with such a joyful heart he had devoted himself to God at Felix’s tomb for the whole course of his life, he nevertheless wrote to Augustine [Note: [Col. 0061] Aug. ep. 80, n. 2] that he had resolved to remain in that place, which he happily inhabited, only in such a way that, if anything else concerning him should please the Lord, he would place God’s will before his own. He likewise writes to Sulpicius [Note: [Col. 0061] Paulin. ep. 11, n. 14] that he was not held fast by a little clod of earth in his little garden, the only one of so many estates that remained to him. Nor did he honor Saint Felix alone: as his writings show, he also venerated the other saints with the greatest reverence, especially Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, and his disciple Clarus.

2. Every year [Note: [Col. 0061] Paulin. ep. 17, n. 2; 20, n. 2; 43, n. 1; 45, n. 1; and Aug. 95, n. 6] he went to Rome for the apostles’ birthday, out of veneration for the apostles and martyrs, to offer his vows at their sacred memorials. For this reason he says that he was accustomed to set out [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 17, n. 1] as summer was waning, though these words seem to denote nothing other than the whole summer.

It is more difficult to reconcile this with what he says in a certain letter dated on the Ides of May [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 45, n. 7 and 1], namely, that he went to Rome after the Lord’s Passover, according to his customary practice, to venerate the apostles and martyrs. For it cannot be said that he came to Rome twice each year [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 43, n. 3], since he himself calls his journey annual; Augustine likewise writes to him [Note: [Col. 0061] Aug. ep. 95, n. 6], “when you travel to Rome throughout the whole anniversary period.” Moreover, Paulinus’s twentieth letter to Delphinus [Note: [Col. 0061] Paulin. ep. 20, n. 2] clearly indicates that he went there only once each year.

Nor can it be said that the apostles’ birthday was so close to Easter, since he himself testifies that this festival was celebrated in summer; and there seems to be no basis for doubting that this birthday was that of Peter and Paul. For when he went to Rome after Easter, he does not say, as he does elsewhere, that he visited Rome for the apostles’ birthday.

It therefore seems nearer the truth that, when necessity compelled him that year to go to Rome shortly after Easter, and when he judged that he would not return there again for the apostles’ birthday, he regarded that journey, undertaken outside the customary season, as his regular one; and that he went to Rome intending to offer the saints then the veneration that he was accustomed to offer in June.

When he came to Rome in this way, he was overwhelmed by crowds of people [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 45, n. 1]. Before midday he spent his time in prayer at the sacred memorials of the apostles and martyrs [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 17, n. 2]. When he had then returned to his lodging, he was occupied by innumerable visits, brought about partly by friendship and partly by religion, so that only evening dissolved the gatherings and gave Paulinus’s spirit some relief. Although he spent ten full days there [Note: [Col. 0061] Ep. 45, n. 1], sometimes he had no opportunity to write a letter or to read anything continuously.

He had acquired this custom from the time of Siricius. For when he first went to Rome under Pope Anastasius in the year 399 [Note: [Col. 0061] Epist. 20, n. 2], he testifies that he made that journey according to his solemn custom. It therefore seems altogether probable that Siricius soon laid aside the jealousy with which he had burned against Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0061] See ch. 17, n. 2].

## CHAPTER XXIII. [Col. 0062D] Paulinus forms a friendship with Augustine and other saints in Africa

1. Paulinus had scarcely settled at Nola when, through his servant Julianus, who was returning from Carthage, he received a letter from Alypius [Note: [Col. 0063] Paulin. ep. 3, n. 1; Ibid., n. 2], by which Alypius joined friendship with him. He also received from him Augustine’s book *On True Religion* and four other works of Augustine against the Manichaean heresies. At the same time Alypius asked Paulinus to send him Eusebius’s history of all periods, which he could find at Rome in Domnio’s possession [Note: [Col. 0063] Ibid., n. 3]. From this it appears that Alypius believed Paulinus was not then living in Spain or Gaul, but at Nola or Rome.

At about the same time Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, wrote to him and mentioned certain matters concerning Augustine [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 6, n. 2]. Paulinus found that letter most welcome and regarded this benevolence toward him, shown by God’s friends in a distant land, as the favor of God, who repays him for the estates, fatherland, and parents he had abandoned for God’s sake [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 3, n. 1; 11, n. 3]. From that time onward he both greatly admired Augustine and honored him with deep affection.

He summoned from Rome Eusebius’s history of all periods—hence the delay in replying—and sent it to Aurelius, who was to return it to Alypius. Along with it Paulinus sent Alypius a letter, still extant, in which he asks him to recount the whole story of his life [Note: [Col. 0063] Ibid., n. 3]. He also sent him bread [Note: [Col. 0063] Ibid., n. 6], asking him to accept it as a *eulogia*, a practice that had become customary with Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0063] See note 8].

Augustine, among whom this custom had not prevailed, nevertheless sent Paulinus bread with a letter, at the end of which he wrote: “The bread which we have sent will become a richer blessing through the love of your kindness in receiving it” [Note: [Col. 0063] Aug. ep. 31, n. 9]. We may therefore rightly say that those loaves were blessed, as the word *eulogia* itself indicates.

When Paulinus sent five loaves to Romanianus, he wrote to him as follows [Note: [Col. 0063] Paulin. c. 7, n. 3]:

> So that the duty of brotherly kindness might not appear empty, from the provisions of the Christian campaign—for in its service we serve as soldiers for the ration of frugality—we have sent you five loaves, and likewise to our son Licentius. For we could not separate from the blessing one whom we desire to bind wholly to ourselves by the same grace.

We may therefore infer that these loaves were not sent indiscriminately to just anyone, but to the faithful generally; for it appears that Licentius had not yet been renewed in the waters of baptism [Note: [Col. 0063] Aug. ep. 36]. Paulinus says that the solidity of the Trinity was contained in this bread [Note: [Col. 0063] Paulin. ep. 3, n. 6], perhaps because it was threefold [Note: [Col. 0063] See note 7].

Paulinus calls Eusebius of Caesarea a venerable bishop [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 3, n. 3]. This proves what he himself admits [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 28, n. 5], namely, that he was inexperienced in history.

2. At about the same time he sent a letter to Augustine [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 4, n. 1 and 5], by which he sought to cement the love that he trusted had been formed between them by the Holy Spirit through Alypius. From Augustine he requested all the works he had written. He sent this letter before winter through one of his own men, to greet Augustine and the other beloved of God [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 6, n. 1].

Since this could have occurred neither before nor after the year 394 according to Augustine’s history, we are compelled to say that by this time Paulinus had already settled at Nola. It might reasonably also be believed that he had lived in that city as early as the year 393 and had been ordained priest in 392. But, with Baronius and Chiffletius, we preferred to assign this to the following year, because Alypius seems to have wished to form a friendship with him after learning that he had arrived at Nola.

If he received the sacred order of the priesthood on Sunday, 25 December, that date fell on a Sunday in the year 393, but not in the year 392. Moreover, the sequence of poems that Paulinus wrote each year in honor of Saint Felix readily accords with the history of the times in this manner.

He says that he was then of the age at which the lame man healed by the apostles Peter and John at the Beautiful Gate was healed—namely, forty years and more [Note: [Col. 0063] Epist. 4, n. 3]. Hence we concluded that he was born around the year 353, and thus was one year older than Augustine, who was born on 13 November 354.

In the anniversaries of his soul’s birth he says that this period was for him infancy, which, when wounds were aimed at Christ, was slaughtered and inaugurated the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0063] Ibid.]. By these words he seems to indicate the age of the innocents, namely two years, because of the words “from two years old,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0063] Sacchin. *Vit. Paulin.*, p. 664, and Chiffl. part 2, c. 5]. Accordingly, we have assigned to the year 392 both the decision he then undertook to renounce his possessions and what he says about his spiritual birthday. 44

## CHAPTER XXIV. [Col. 0064C] Paulinus writes to Jerome and receives a reply from him. He celebrates the panegyric of Theodosius

1. In that year, when Paulinus sent his servant to greet the saints in Africa [Note: [Col. 0063] Paulin. ep. 6, n. 1], perhaps at the same time and with the same intention he sent a certain Ambrose to Palestine [Note: [Col. 0063] Hieron. ep. 103, book III], and through him sent a letter and a small gift to Jerome, informing him that he wished to learn from him the mysteries of Sacred Scripture.

Those letters were most pleasing to Jerome. From their opening, which seems to indicate that no letters had previously passed between them, they displayed the character of an already tested and longstanding friendship, as well as Paulinus’s prudence and elegance of expression. A certain Eusebius, perhaps from Cremona, was also present with Jerome [Note: [Col. 0063] Ibid.]. Since he was already very well known and dear to Paulinus for other reasons, he commended him still further to Jerome by reporting the honesty of his character, his contempt for the world, his fidelity in friendship, and his love of Christ.

Jerome therefore sent him his 103rd letter concerning these matters [Note: [Col. 0063] Hieron. ep. 103]. In it he praises his zeal and ardor for knowledge, saying that no one can enter the Sacred Scriptures without someone going before him and showing the path. He refuses to call himself a teacher but promises to be a companion: they will seek together, ask together, and knock together.

Then he urges him to hurry and not to postpone matters by dragging one day after another; he should sell his possessions cautiously and step by step, or rather throw them away, and cut the rope of a little boat clinging to the shoal rather than merely loosen it. He should give himself wholly to God; Christ has other means by which to feed the poor. He should trust in Christ, not in possessions that might perhaps survive him.

By this holy exhortation Jerome indicates that he feared that, if Paulinus retained any of his former wealth and then devoted himself to it under the pretext of distributing it more wisely to the poor as alms, he might gradually become entangled in it again. Nor, throughout the whole letter, does he praise so extraordinary an act, whose outcome he did not yet clearly foresee.

Later, however, when he had certainly heard how willingly Paulinus had offered himself and his possessions to God, Jerome not only adorned him with extraordinary and unheard-of praises [Note: [Col. 0065] Hieron. ep. 13], but also advised him to moderate somewhat, with wise discretion, the zeal with which he distributed his possessions, rather than urging him to increase it.

Baronius thought that this letter had been written to another Paulinus, not to Paulinus of Nola. But those who examined the matter more carefully after him believed that the arguments on which his opinion rests should yield to those by which it is refuted [Note: [Col. 0065] Baron. an. 394, § 6; Sacchin. *Vit. Paulin.*, p. 634].

2. At about the same time Paulinus celebrated the panegyric of Theodosius, if we should accept Gennadius’s assertion [Note: [Col. 0065] Gennad. *Catal.*, c. 48] that this speech was dedicated by Paulinus to Theodosius himself. That emperor died on 17 January in the year 395.

The subject was supplied by the victories he won over the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.]. Eugenius was defeated only in September of the year 394. Endelechius, a friend of Paulinus and likewise a Christian, prompted him to compose this work [Note: [Col. 0065] Paulin. ep. 28, n. 6]. He is believed to have been Saint Severus Endelechius, some of whose poems still survive [Note: [Col. 0065] See note 125].

Paulinus undertook this labor from his friend all the more willingly because in Theodosius he praised not so much an emperor as a servant of Christ; not one powerful through the pride of ruling, but through the humility of serving; not a prince through kingship, but through living and ardent faith [Note: [Col. 0065] Paulin. ep. 18, n. 6]. He also shows that Theodosius conquered by faith and prayers rather than by arms [Note: [Col. 0065] Gennad. *Catal.*, c. 48]. In the speech he likewise commends the usefulness of the laws enacted by Theodosius [Note: [Col. 0065] Hieron. ep. 13].

“Happy Theodosius,” says Jerome in writing to Paulinus, “who is defended by such an orator of Christ. You have given splendor to his purple and demonstrated the future usefulness of his laws.” We have already reported the rest of what Jerome wrote in praise of that speech, which one might more accurately call an apology than a panegyric [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.].

Paulinus sent it to Endelechius [Note: [Col. 0065] Paulin. ep. 28, n. 6], though he did not publish it. He nevertheless sent copies of it to his friends—namely Sulpicius Severus and Jerome [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.; Hieron. ep. 13]. He prefixed to his little book, in place of a title, a letter in which he said that Endelechius had prompted this work.

Augustine had undoubtedly read that speech. But if the little book was the one *Against the Pagans* which Augustine requested from Paulinus in the year 396, and which he seems to imply was not yet completely finished [Note: [Col. 0065] Aug. ep. 31, n. 8], then Paulinus did not write it while Theodosius was alive, nor did he dedicate it to Theodosius, as Gennadius thinks.

Augustine seems to refer to this panegyric in the following words [Note: [Col. 0065] Aug. in Faust. 22, c. 76]:

> Christian emperors also, possessing complete confidence in piety toward Christ, won a most glorious victory over sacrilegious enemies who had placed their hope in the rites of idols and demons. The most open and well-known evidence of this—concerning which some have already committed a written account to memory—shows that the prophecies of demons deceived the former, while the predictions of the saints strengthened the latter.

By these words it is clear that he is referring to the defeat of Eugenius and Arbogastes.

Cassiodorus also mentions a book that Paulinus had written about Theodosius [Note: [Col. 0065] Cassiodor. *Div. Institut.*, book 1, c. 21], but he seems to have extracted what he reports about it from Jerome.

## CHAPTER XXV. [Col. 0066B] Concerning Paulinus’s relationship with Sanctus and Amandus

1. It cannot easily be determined whether that Sanctus Endelechius to whom Paulinus sent the panegyric of Theodosius was the same person to whom he wrote his fortieth letter. The name Sanctus was common to both.

Since it clearly appears that this Sanctus composed Christian hymns, some of which he had sent to Paulinus, this may persuade us that they were one and the same person. It is also clear that Paulinus began to love him while Sanctus had not yet been reborn [Note: [Col. 0065] Paulin. ep. 41, n. 1; Ep. 40, n. 2].

On the other hand, although in those times Romans were distinguished by many names, it nevertheless seems that the same name was always used in practice. Thus, since Paulinus always calls one of them Endelechius, while he always calls the other Sanctus whenever he repeats his name three or four times, it seems possible, not without foundation, to conclude that they were different from one another.

The following consideration supports this conclusion: Paulinus seems to indicate that, since his conversion to Christ, he had sent only one letter to Sanctus and had received from him only one, and a very brief one. Nor does he mention his panegyric, which he does not say that Endelechius had requested from him [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid., n. 1].

Who, then, that Sanctus was is not entirely clear, nor is it plainly established, except that when Paulinus speaks of the period during which he had served the corruption of the world [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid., nn. 4, 5, and 6], he seems to be speaking simultaneously of himself and of Sanctus.

2. Paulinus and Sanctus had continually loved one another with the friendship of human familiarity, which had no root in their hearts because it had not been built upon Christ [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid., n. 2]. It appears that they had sent one another many letters, yet Paulinus’s soul was not filled by them.

When Paulinus renounced the world, he did not likewise renounce Sanctus’s friendship; but he interrupted the service of letter-writing [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.]. He wrote to him only once and, after receiving from him a very brief letter, believed that he had discharged the debt of duty. Then he withdrew again into a sufficiently prolonged silence, until Sanctus, wounded by the arrows of Christ’s love, anticipated Paulinus in the sweetness of the word of God through the chaste and faithful language of a letter, as Paulinus himself testifies [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid., n. 4; Paulin. ep. 40, n. 2].

We may therefore judge that Sanctus, like Paulinus, had adopted a new way of life. Indeed, Paulinus says that love dwelt in him “from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith.” In his letter Sanctus honored Paulinus with words of blessing [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid., n. 3], because he had fulfilled Christ’s command to sell everything he possessed [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid., n. 11].

In writing to Paulinus, Sanctus had made a certain Amandus his associate—someone other than the bishop of Bordeaux—and it appears that this Amandus was not entirely known to Paulinus. Paulinus calls him “the blessed child of the Lord” [Col. 0067B] and asks him for his prayers [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid.].

Sanctus and Amandus had written on the back of their letter an index of Paulinus’s letters. Sanctus added several hymns that Paulinus had requested, among which, it seems, was the parable of the ten virgins [Note: [Col. 0067] Epist. 41, n. 1].

Paulinus was filled with immense joy when he received this letter [Note: [Col. 0067] Epist. 40, n. 1]. In the letter that he sent back to both men, he says that he counts it as the one letter returned to him by Sanctus, because he had once again received from him a letter with which his soul had been filled. He says that he was stirred by the desire for Sanctus’s letters, provided that Sanctus took care not to burden him with praises of which Paulinus considered himself altogether unworthy [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid., n. 3].

He then exhorts himself to piety in a splendid discourse, undoubtedly intending thereby to instruct Sanctus, whom he addresses in many passages. Concerning himself he speaks with his customary humility. It might seem that he was still creeping through the infancy of the spiritual life, unless the long silence that he had maintained with Sanctus led one to believe that he had already lived at Nola for many years [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid., nn. 1 and 3].

Yet he says that old age was not merely spreading white hairs over his head, but pouring them out [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid., n. 6]. We can only conclude that he wrote before he had been promoted to the episcopate, and therefore before the year 408, since the heading says that he wrote together with Therasia [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid., in title].

He says that he had received something from someone very dear to him who had traveled extensively [Note: [Col. 0067] Ibid., n. 6]. Without doubt he means Rufinus, who returned to the West only in the year 397.

3. After Paulinus had added, as it were, a conclusion to the letter, he once again [Note: [Col. 0067] Letter 41, no. 1.] undertakes another subject, namely the hymns which he had received from the Saint. This may properly be regarded either as a second part of the letter—for which reason they were formerly printed together—or as an entirely separate letter; and indeed [Note: [Col. 0067] Chiffl., part 1, chapter 24.] in certain manuscript codices they are read separately. We have therefore divided them into two. In this latter, the forty-first, he says that he was so forgetful of almost all his letters, which the Saint and Amandus had annotated on the back of the letter, [Note: [Col. 0067] Paulinus, Letter 41, no. 1.] [Col. 0068A] that he would not have recognized them as his own had he not trusted their letters.

## In the Year of Christ 395

### Chapter XXVI. Paulinus falls ill and sends a reply to Sulpicius Severus through Vigilantius

1. The poem [Note: [Col. 0067] Poem 13.] which Paulinus wrote in honor of Saint Felix when he celebrated his feast at Nola for the first time after settling there proceeded from the innermost feeling of joy. In it he pours forth full-hearted thanks to God, who had granted him what he had so long implored from Him in prayer. Toward the end [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place, verse 31.] he asks Saint Felix to entreat God that he may always remain in that harbor which, after overcoming so many and such great labors, he had at last reached.

His fifth letter appears to have been written in the second year after he had settled at Nola; [Col. 0068B] for this reason Chiffletius also unquestionably assigns it [Note: [Col. 0067] Chiffl., pp. 168 and 219.] to the year 395. From it [Note: [Col. 0067] Paulinus, Letter 5, nos. 9 and 10.] we learn that Paulinus had fallen ill, apparently [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place, no. 14.] in early summer. He says that by this illness [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place, no. 10.] God had chastised him in punishment for his sins, while [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place, no. 14.] all Campania was venerating in him the work of God the Savior. Throughout the whole period of his illness, the constant and diligent services of anxious bishops, clerics, monks, and often even laypeople celebrated him. Almost no bishop throughout Campania did not deem it his duty to visit him; and those whom illness or some other necessity detained sent clerics and letters in their place and were present through them. [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place.] The African bishops, too, sent people to revisit him in early summer. This could accord with the letters delivered to him by Aurelius and [Col. 0068C] Alypius in the year 394, if he was at Nola in 393, although the word “revisit” is not very appropriate to their first service, which they rendered to him through their own people and not through men sent by them for this purpose. It is therefore more probable that, as we have supposed, he came to Nola in 394 and fell ill in 395; and that at that time Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, whom Paulinus had sent to visit him in that very year 394, and perhaps some others with him, were present through certain men whom they had sent.

We shall see that Augustine wrote to him in that same year through Romanianus; yet it does not seem probable that his letter was delivered to Paulinus in early summer. He boasted of the services of good men, [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place.] but only in the Lord, whose grace he regarded as the work and gift at issue. He says that God’s grace had shone forth in the darkness, and that he had not lived obscurely in solitude because of the brilliance of God’s name. [Col. 0068D]

2. The letters of Severus brought him great and sweet consolation in his illness. As we have seen, they had planned to settle at Nola together, and Paulinus had urged him, for that purpose, either to meet him at Barcelona or to join him on the road. But [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place, no. 8.] in that year Severus suffered two illnesses when he wished to come to Paulinus. He was therefore compelled to excuse himself to him by letter. [Note: [Col. 0067] Same place, no. 1.] He wrote that he had recovered, [Note: [Col. 0069] Paulinus, Letter 5, no. 9.] and promised that many spiritual brothers would come with him. [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 15.] He extolled Paulinus’s virtue and conversion with the highest praises. [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 3.]

He sent this letter through some of his companions who were bound to him by virtue, namely [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 1.] through Vigilantius and another catechumen. Vigilantius suffered from fever in Campania even before reaching Paulinus. Paulinus reports nothing about him [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place.] except that he was baptized. Therefore, if he is the same man who later, as a presbyter, brought Paulinus’s letters to Jerome, and who subsequently disgraced his name by false doctrines, it is likely that he was ordained presbyter immediately after returning from Campania to Gaul.

Paulinus wondered that he and Severus had been afflicted by the same troubles at the same time. [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, nos. 9 and 10.] He says that this had not happened without the Lord’s will, since nothing occurs in the world without His command; and since He was the author of their inward unity, He would not have allowed their bodily condition to differ. Thus this fellowship in suffering brought them great and sweet consolation. Yet, so that the sign of their harmony might be even more pleasing to them, Paulinus felt himself restored by the very fact that Severus had written that he had recovered, so that, in some manner, he breathed again through Severus’s relief, [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 12.] just as through the prayers of the saints and of Sulpicius Severus himself, who had not known of Paulinus’s illness.

Paulinus remained ill for a long time, and could not easily restore the strength of his body, exhausted by illness and austerities. In that sickness he gloried, like Paul, through which he hoped he would be made strong; and the more his flesh was broken by adverse health, the more confidently he believed that spiritual virtue could not be overcome by it. His illness [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 11.] delayed his reply to Severus.

Vigilantius also suffered once again from the violence of fever. The catechumen who accompanied him did not fall ill. “Since he was not yet a member of our body,” Paulinus says, [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place.] “he did not feel our wounds. He remained healthy and free from our ailments, because flesh still foreign to our bodily fellowship could not feel the pain of a structure that was not yet its own.”

When Vigilantius began to recover, he wanted to proceed, but Paulinus kept him back against his will, withholding the letter until he had regained enough strength to undertake the journey—which, as the word “proceed” seems to indicate, Vigilantius was making on foot. At last, therefore, Paulinus gave him a reply for Severus, [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 1.] in which he gave the greatest thanks for Severus’s affection, “for which,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, nos. 2 and 3.] “God will reward you, whom you love in me, all the more abundantly because I have nothing with which to repay you.”

3. Paulinus writes to Severus [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 4.] that he will have to pay the penalty when he receives undeserved honors, and that his sluggishness and indolence are reproached him all the more for this reason. Then, with great humility and ingenuity, he attempts [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, nos. 5, 6, and 7.] to show that Severus’s conversion was a greater miracle than his own. Afterwards [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 8.] he turns to Severus’s promise to come to him and asks him to regard the two illnesses he had suffered as preliminary trials by which God had wished to test the steadfastness of his plan, not condemn it. He says that he does not fear that weak flesh will prevail as an obstacle to Severus’s desire, since faith would strengthen it, and so forth.

After speaking of Severus’s illness, he adds [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 13.] that love of peace ought to call him away from his homeland for a while, so that he might silence those who sought an opportunity to speak ill of him; Severus often complained of these people. He then relates [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 14.] how greatly he was scandalized by the Roman pontiff and by certain clerics at Rome. He again urges Severus to come and already imagines the joys he will experience when he welcomes him arriving with a company of God’s chosen ones.

“I shall place you,” Paulinus says to Severus, [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 15.] “as a tenant in the garden of my Felix, and free of charge.” Finally, after greeting Severus’s wife, whom [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 19.] he calls “his fellow-servant in the Lord,” and also Bassula, Severus’s mother-in-law, he says: “Take care, I beg you, not to write that you are a servant, and excuse this talkative letter. For while dictating, as I think of you and am wholly absorbed in you, it is as though I were speaking at length to you who are present, and I forget that I have been charged to bring the speech to an end.” [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 20.]

He asks him to accept the bread he is sending, along with a boxwood dish and other things; [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 21.] and he asks him to send him the wine which Paulinus believed he still possessed at Narbonne, saying that he would not fear loss even if he thereby made Severus his debtor for money. He entrusts this to him, confident that he possessed the highest claim upon Severus’s affection, since all Severus’s servants had deserted him. He does not report how he was doing at Nola, from which we may conjecture that Paulinus had written to Severus about this matter in the preceding year.

### Chapter XXVII. Augustine writes to Paulinus, who sends him another letter. Paulinus’s power over demons

1. We have observed that Paulinus wrote to Augustine toward the end of the preceding year [Note: [Col. 0069] Chapter 23, no. 2.] in order to establish a friendship with him—a friendship which Augustine readily granted to anyone, but which he owed especially to Paulinus, since there existed so many and such great proofs of Paulinus’s benevolence toward Augustine and of his love for Christ.

Indeed, nothing was dearer or more ardent than Augustine’s letter [Note: [Col. 0069] Augustine, Letter 27.] which he sent to Paulinus this year through Romanianus, a friend especially dear to him. In addition to what we have said above about Romanianus, Augustine testifies that he was held by an intense desire to see Paulinus. After pouring forth at length the joy he had received from Paulinus’s conversion, he says that he does not know what he can repay for Paulinus’s love, except that “I am wholly yours,” he says to him, [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place, no. 3.] “in Him to whom you wholly belong. If that is too little, I certainly have no more. Yet you have made it seem not too little to me: you honored me in that letter with such great praises that, when I pour myself out to you, I would prove myself not to have believed you if I were to think this too little for you.”

He then explains how Paulinus’s praises of him harmonized with his own consciousness of his sins, and resolves the conflict in this way: [Note: [Col. 0069] Same place.] “I shall not believe myself to be such as you think me, because I do not recognize myself as such; and I shall believe that I am loved by you, because I feel and clearly perceive it. Thus I shall be neither reckless toward myself nor ungrateful toward you.”

He promises that Romanianus, the bearer of these letters, will provide Paulinus with copies of his books. He speaks of them with profound humility and [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place and no. 6.] asks Paulinus to correct whatever might displease him. He also sends him [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 6.] a poem by Licentius, the son of Romanianus, and asks him, through the power of his instruction, to take responsibility for the salvation of father and son and strive to advance both in virtue.

He adds: [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 4.] “Do not believe whatever the father may perhaps have said in praising me, lest, if you judge me better than I really am, you fail to pray for me as much as I wish.” He also arranged for his own reply to Licentius’s poem to be delivered to Paulinus. In it [Note: [Col. 0071] Augustine, Letter 26, and Letter 27, no. 6.] he spoke in a truly marvelous and distinguished manner about “our Paulinus.” [Note: [Col. 0071] Augustine, Letter 26, no. 5.]

Finally, he begs and implores Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 6.] that, if he had any leisure from ecclesiastical duties, he would come even to Africa, so that he might see how greatly everyone thirsted for him. [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 2.] Finally, he sends many greetings to Therasia.

Romanianus, whom his own lawsuits had apparently drawn into Italy, did not deliver Augustine’s letter to Paulinus very quickly; he arrived at Nola only in the following year. The boy whom Paulinus had sent to Africa in the preceding year had not yet returned; nor, in all likelihood, had Augustine been among those who had sent people to visit him at the beginning of summer. Thus, since Paulinus had heard nothing about the letter written so many months earlier, he wrote a second reply before he had learned that Augustine had been promoted to the episcopate. This occurred toward the end of 395, when he addresses Augustine as “brother.” [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 2.] Paulinus sent his reply to Augustine through Agilis [Col. 0071C] and Romanus. [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 3.]

## In the Year of Christ 396

2. We extract no historical material from Paulinus’s third festival poem in praise of Saint Felix, [Note: [Col. 0071] Paulinus, Poem 14.] which we believe was published this year. It merely describes the notable miracles performed especially on this day upon those possessed by demons, [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, verses 23 and following.] and the crowd’s gathering for the solemnity. [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, verse 44.] He describes how the people covered the threshold of Saint Felix’s tomb with flowers, garlands, and wreaths, [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, verses 98 and following.] and how lights gleamed around the altars by night and day.

He then pours forth his vows to Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, verses 116 and following.] and prays that he may devote his service to him throughout a long life and complete his life at his tomb; [Col. 0071D] and that Felix may not refuse to carry his soul to Christ in a father’s embrace, so that by his merits and prayers Paulinus may at last deserve to be joined to the praised Lamb.

Some think that many of the miracles performed at Saint Felix’s tomb belonged to Paulinus. [Note: [Col. 0071] Sacchini, Life of Paulinus, p. 730.] For Gennadius asserts [Note: [Col. 0071] Gennadius, Catalogue, chapter 48.] that Paulinus was distinguished not only by learning and holiness of life but also by power against demons.

### Chapter XXVIII. Informed by Augustine himself of his promotion to the episcopate, Paulinus communicates his extraordinary joy to Romanianus

1. Romanianus, through whose agency Augustine had used the previous year to deliver his letter to Paulinus, [Note: [Col. 0071] Augustine, Letter 27, nos. 4 and 6.] approached him when he was already anxious about the return of the holy brothers Romanus and Agilis. They finally arrived [Note: [Col. 0071] Paulinus, Letter 7, no. 1.] after Romanianus’s departure, and through them Paulinus received letters from Augustine, now a bishop, and from other most distinguished men—namely Aurelius of Carthage, Alypius, Profuturus of Cirta, and Severus of Milevis, all likewise bishops.

Only Augustine’s letter survives; [Note: [Col. 0071] Augustine, Letter 31, no. 7.] it again concerned Licentius. Augustine wished to consider it as a response to Paulinus’s later letter, [Col. 0072B] and he testifies that, as in the earlier letter written the previous year, [Note: [Col. 0071] Augustine, Letter 27.] he was bound to Paulinus by equal affection and devotion. He deliberately used certain words of the Saint to whom he was replying, since they were exceedingly pleasing to him and [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place.] were both true and Paulinus’s own words.

He tells him [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 4.] how he had become bishop of Hippo, and that this office prevented him from visiting Nola. He therefore urges Paulinus much more strongly than in his earlier letters to come to Africa with his wife. [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, nos. 4, 5, and 6.] He takes the matter so far as to say that he believes they would do nothing less pleasing to God if they made the virtues infused into them known to everyone with as much zeal as the labor and ardor with which they had acquired them. From this anyone may easily perceive how highly Augustine esteemed the modesty of Paulinus and Therasia.

Gregory the Great appears to proceed from the same principles when he says: [Note: [Col. 0071] Gregory the Great, Pastoral Care, Book III, chapter 36.] “Whoever is now strong enough to trample down the desire for praise commits a fraud against edification if he conceals the good things he does. Like seed that has been cast, he withholds the roots from germination if he does not display the work that ought to be imitated.” And when he had objected to himself that Christ had given a commandment concerning the concealment of good works, he replies: [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place.] “Whoever, in a public good work, seeks not his own glory but that of the heavenly Father conceals what he does, because he has chosen to please only Him as his witness.”

2. In his letter Augustine commends to Paulinus a certain man named Vetustinum, who was traveling to Nola either to serve God with him or to be rescued, through the prayers of Saint Felix, from certain evils which would have drawn tears from the impious and which appeared to be scourges inflicted by God. [Note: [Col. 0071] Augustine, Letter 31, no. 7.]

He ordered three books of his work On Free Choice to be delivered to Paulinus, together with, as I conjecture, bread already blessed: “A fuller blessing will be made through the love of the recipient of your kindness.” [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 9.] Augustine also testified that he desired the work of the most blessed Pope Ambrose against the philosophers, [Note: [Col. 0071] Same place, no. 8.] although he had no doubt that Paulinus possessed all the writings of so great a man.

Augustine frequently cites this work in his later writings, including in the book entitled On Christian Doctrine, [Col. 0073A] which he may have composed two or three years later. [Note: [Col. 0073] Book II, chapter 28.] It is very plausible that Augustine obtained this work from Paulinus.

Augustine further says [Note: [Col. 0073] Augustine, Letter 31, no. 8.] that he had heard from the brothers—apparently Agilis and Romanus—that Paulinus was writing against the pagans. He therefore begs him not to hesitate to send him what he had written: “For your breast,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0073] Same place.] “is such an oracle of the Lord that we presume to receive from it answers both pleasing to us and fully explanatory of the most loquacious questions.”

I do not know whether this work may have been a panegyric of Theodosius. For when Jerome reports that Paulinus wrote an apology for this emperor and there discussed his laws, [Note: [Col. 0073] Jerome, Letter 13.] he could have defended here especially the laws enacted against the pagans and vindicated them from attack by answering the objections raised by the pagans against the Christian religion. [Col. 0073B]

3. The fact that Augustine had accepted the episcopate, and that God had deemed the African Churches worthy to receive heavenly words from his mouth, brought Paulinus the greatest joy. [Note: [Col. 0073] Paulinus, Letter 7, no. 2.] Immediately, after two days, he hastened to inform Romanianus by letter of the cause of his extraordinary joy. [Note: [Col. 0073] Same place, no. 1.]

He sent five loaves to Romanianus and his son Licentius, [Note: [Col. 0073] Same place, no. 3.] and at the same time—perhaps on the same sheet, or at least in the same packet—he replied to Licentius in prose and verse, at Augustine’s urging, to draw this young man’s mind away from the vanities of the world and urge him to provide for his salvation. [Note: [Col. 0073] Letter 8; Augustine, Letter 27, no. 6.]

### Chapter XXIX. Through Vigilantius, who conducts himself badly, Paulinus writes to Jerome. He applies himself to sacred reading with the greatest humility

1. There is no doubt that Severus and Paulinus exchanged letters with each other this year; those letters have been lost. As far as we can gather from [Note: [Col. 0073] Paulinus, Letter 17, no. 1.] other letters, Severus indicated that he despaired of being able to meet Paulinus at Nola, and that what remained to them was to refresh one another through the consolation of letters.

Nevertheless, Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0073] Letter 11, no. 12.] did not cease inviting him. Vigilantius must have delivered Severus’s letters to Paulinus if this was the same man who later traveled to Palestine, a journey which he could not have undertaken before the year 396. [Note: [Col. 0073] See Jerome, History.] There he delivered Paulinus’s letters to Jerome, who [Note: [Col. 0073] See Jerome, p. 75.] praised the distinguished piety and learning of so great a man, devoted for so many years to the service of Christ, with the highest commendations. [Note: [Col. 0073] Jerome, Letter 13.]

Paulinus asked him [Note: [Col. 0073] Same place.] what path he ought to take in his monastic state. He seemed also to be seized by a certain desire to travel to Jerusalem and visit the holy places, so that perhaps, by drawing closer to Saint Jerome, he might be instructed in those precepts concerning which Jerome had already received from him, in his earlier letter, the promise that he would instruct Paulinus in the reading of sacred Scripture.

Paulinus also sent him [Col. 0074A] his work on behalf of Theodosius. [Note: [Col. 0073] Same place.] In the same letter [Note: [Col. 0073] Letter 75.] he highly commended Vigilantius, who for this reason was received by Saint Jerome [Note: [Col. 0073] Letter 13.] with honor and great affection.

When a serious dispute had arisen between Jerome, John of Jerusalem, and Rufinus, [Note: [Col. 0073] See Jerome, History, sections 88 and 89.] Vigilantius became involved in this quarrel and controversy and spoke against Jerome. Nevertheless, he humbly sought pardon from him, found favor with him, then hastened to depart from Palestine. After returning to Gaul, [Note: [Col. 0073] Same place, section 144, and Jerome, Against Vigilantius.] he published a book against Jerome, who was compelled to reply.

Later Vigilantius also rose against the teaching of the Catholic faith and disseminated various errors, through which he rightly earned the title of leader of the heretics of Gaul. Behold the wretched condition of a man who failed to use for his salvation the divine benefit by which he had been joined to so many saints. Yet their affection was not without reward: they revered the virtue which they believed had been implanted in his soul and kindly excused in him those faults which they did not suppose would cause such great harm to the Church.

Whether Jerome sent a reply through Vigilantius to the letter of Paulinus which Vigilantius had brought is uncertain. [Note: [Col. 0073] Jerome, Letter 13.] Jerome said nothing against him and left it to Vigilantius’s discretion to report to Paulinus how he had been received. He nevertheless indicates clearly enough that something burdensome and unpleasant had occurred between them, while praising Paulinus very highly.

2. In these two letters [Note: [Col. 0073] Jerome, Letters 13 and 75.] Jerome assumes that Paulinus is to be instructed in the sacred Scriptures, meaning, it seems, the interpretations handed down by the Greeks. One can scarcely find any Father who makes more frequent use of the sacred Scriptures in his writings. He inserts them everywhere, alludes to them everywhere, and uncovers the most excellent insights, even in passing.

You will notice this from his earliest letters, so that no one can doubt that from the time of his Spanish retreat he devoted himself entirely to reading, examining, and meditating upon them, and that through the ardor of piety and love by which we attain their meaning he drew from them great sources of knowledge. Jerome himself, a few years later, acknowledged him to be learned in divine as well as human letters. [Note: [Col. 0073] Letter 153, volume III.]

Since Paulinus did not intend to instruct others, he undoubtedly devoted himself to the Scriptures for his own edification, with a simple contemplation of the truth rather than with a studied investigation of difficulties. For this reason, when consulted on such matters, he never dared to answer anyone, considering himself unworthy to have confidence in divine revelation. [Note: [Col. 0073] Paulinus, Letter 43, no. 3.]

With the greatest humility, in cases of doubt, he consulted those who were distinguished in the Church for their reputation for wisdom and knowledge. We shall later observe him doing this with Jerome, Rufinus, and Augustine.

When he once asked Augustine for an exposition of certain passages of Scripture, [Note: [Col. 0073] Letter 50, no. 1.] he said:
