“If these passages are perhaps clear but seem obscure to me, let none of the prudent sons who may happen to be standing around you from among our people at the hour of this little reading see me as foolish; rather, let him favor me because of the benevolence of fraternal love, by instructing me, so that I may become a participant in the vision of those who see, and that, through your teaching, I may contemplate, with minds illumined, the wondrous things of the law of the Lord.”

It appears that, while reading, he noted the things he did not understand so that he might seek their meaning from others. Before presenting a difficulty, however, he examined it so carefully that he came close to discovering its solution. Hence Augustine wrote to him: [Note: [Col. 0075] Augustine, Letter 149, nos. 2 and 34.]

“You have asked many questions, reminded me of questions that ought to be asked, and by asking have taught me … for when you discuss by questioning, inquire sharply, and teach humbly.”

### Chapter XXX. Paulinus writes to Saints Delphinus and Amandus. Severus sends him the Life of Saint Martin

1. In this year, it appears, Paulinus wrote his ninth letter to Amandus together with his tenth to Delphinus. We have already observed that, during Paulinus’s Spanish retreat, there had been an exchange of letters between him and Amandus; [Note: [Col. 0075] Chapter 16, no. 2.] this continued and was maintained at Nola, even with Delphinus. [Note: [Col. 0075] Paulinus, Letters 9 and 12; Letters 10 and 14.]

Delphinus’s letters were spiritual seasonings for Paulinus, since they were seasoned with the salt of spiritual wisdom with which Delphinus himself had been imbued at baptism, so that Paulinus might preserve its flavor. [Note: [Col. 0075] Paulinus, Letter 9, no. 1.] Paulinus, for his part, gave him replies full of a certain religious reverence, courtesy, and humility. [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place and Letter 10, no. 1.]

He dealt more freely with Amandus and set forth on paper, in a more familiar manner, the religious sentiments within him, in language indeed honey-sweet, although Paulinus otherwise calls it inept and rash. [Note: [Col. 0075] Letter 9, no. 4.]

When Amandus had shown Paulinus’s letter to the ears of their common father, Delphinus, that holy man asked Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place.] for letters seasoned with spiritual salt, in which, beyond the necessities of official duty, he would add some discourse from Scripture through which he might reveal the treasure of his heart. [Note: [Col. 0075] Letter 10, no. 1.]

Thereafter Paulinus wrote this genuinely pious and humble tenth letter. In it he says [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, nos. 1 and 2.] that Delphinus was certainly right to demand these things from him—as repayment of his deposit and as one awaiting the germination of seed—but that he feared he might produce thistles instead of wheat and thorns instead of grapes.

He then complains amicably to Amandus [Note: [Col. 0075] Letter 9, no. 1.] that he had shown his letters to Delphinus, and [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, nos. 2 and 5.] discusses with him various pious discourses, which are believed to be lacking something. [Note: [Col. 0075] Chiffl., p. 283; and Dissertation 1, article 10.]

After the death of Theodosius, in the year 395 or 396, Ambrose discovered the body of the martyr Nazarius at Milan. [Note: [Col. 0075] Life of Ambrose in Gaul, Book IX, chapter 1.] He arranged for some relics to be carried to Saint Paulinus, [Note: [Col. 0075] Paulinus, Poem 24, verse 436.] who received this gift with the greatest humility. From the same source he may also have received certain relics of Saints Vitalis and Agricola [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, verse 432.] and likewise of Gervasius and Protasius, the martyrs. [Note: [Col. 0075] Letter 32, no. 17.]

## In the Year of Christ 397

2. In the fourth festival poem in praise of Saint Felix, [Note: [Col. 0075] Poem 15.] which we assign to this year, Paulinus recounts the beginnings of the history of this holy confessor. He does so [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, verse 30.] not by invoking the Muses, but by invoking the divine name of Christ, who once loosed the tongue of the ass. He cites that poem in the one which he published the following year. [Note: [Col. 0075] Poem 16, verse 17.]

We assign to this year the eleventh letter to Severus, who not only took every opportunity to write to Paulinus, [Note: [Col. 0075] Letter 11, no. 4.] but also sent some of his own people to him. These men were afterward converted to piety through Paulinus’s holiness and example, so that Paulinus himself boasted of them as holy sons and a blessed offspring in the Lord.

Thus, through one of his servants, Severus sent him a letter this year. In it, [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place.] considering himself far inferior to Paulinus, he asserted that both had been found in the field—that is, on the broad road of the world—one had been taken up and the other left behind. [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, no. 6.]

He further confessed that he admired but also dreaded Paulinus’s poverty. He claimed that he wished for it but could not attain it: that, possessing food and clothing, he might be content with these, thinking of nothing beyond the day; he considered himself wholly unequal to imitating Paulinus in this. [Col. 0076B]

Then, [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, no. 13.] apparently in jest, he adds that he believed Paulinus would soon become so poor that he would no longer dare invite him; and he says that Paulinus had left Ebromagus for the sake of a little garden. [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, no. 41.]

He appears to have sent him at the same time [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, no. 11.] the Life of Blessed Martin, which he had written while Martin was still alive.

Paulinus began his reply with Severus’s affection for him, [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, nos. 1 and 4.] and thanks him for it at great length. He then praises Severus’s virtue with many commendations, into which he inserts the history of Martin. [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, nos. 5 and 11.]

He seems seriously to rebuke him for having spoken of poverty and thereby revealed himself to be weak in faith and distrustful of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, nos. 11 and 13.] He declares that, however poor he might become, he would never cease inviting Severus, and that he would urge him with the greatest earnestness. [Note: [Col. 0075] Same place, nos. 13 and 14.]

Since Severus gives no promise at all that he will come, we place the seventeenth letter only two years later.

We have already observed that the Life of Blessed Martin written by Severus was sent to Paulinus. Paulinus was the first to bring it to Rome, on the journey which he customarily undertook around the feast of Saints Peter and Paul. [Note: [Col. 0075] Severus, Dialogue 1, chapter 16.] Everyone thirsted for this book. Paulinus disseminated it throughout Italy and Illyria, [Note: [Col. 0075] Dialogue 3, chapter 20.] and his devotion to Saint Felix did not begrudge any glory to Blessed Martin. Indeed, he religiously revered and admired the outstanding virtues which God had infused into the soul of this holy bishop.

### Chapter XXXI. Paulinus wards off violence inflicted upon a most holy presbyter

1. We have assigned the twelfth letter to this year because of the affair of a certain presbyter, which is discussed toward its end. [Note: [Col. 0075] Letter 12, no. 11.] It is addressed to Amandus, who nowhere found the length of Paulinus’s letters burdensome; on the contrary, he requested new and longer ones. To satisfy his desire, Paulinus wrote this letter, longer than the others, [Col. 0077A] in which he elegantly sets forth an unjust humility and a holy pride, liberated from the vanities of the world and subject to the divine commandments. [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 12, no. 7.]

The bearer of this letter was Sanemarius, whom Paulinus had manumitted from slavery so that, under the authority of the Church of Bordeaux, he might serve in the house of the Lord through the duties assigned in memory of his parents. [Note: [Col. 0077] Same place, no. 12.] At the same time Paulinus wrote another letter to Delphinus, which has perished.

He asks Amandus to arrange that Sanemarius, through the services of the holy presbyter Exsuperius, receive a small plot of land from the Church’s estate, by which he might provide for his sustenance. Perhaps that field had been granted by Saint Paulinus to the church in which his parents were buried and whose administration was entrusted to Exsuperius. Baronius believes that this great man later became bishop of Toulouse. [Note: [Col. 0077] Baronius, year 405, section 61.]

2. Paulinus also treats with Amandus [Note: [Col. 0077] Paulinus, Letter 12, no. 12.] the case of a certain holy presbyter, venerable in life and age, who was suffering a grave wrong and exile from another’s house. [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 14, no. 4.] This was certainly Basil, the most distinguished presbyter of the Church of Capua, whom Paulinus discusses in letters written the following year. This man, I say, was [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 15, no. 2.] an old man of admirable piety, [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 14, no. 4.] whose house had been forcibly seized from him by the agents of certain rich men, who [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 15, no. 3.] possessed estates in Campania. Thus the afflicted [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 12, no. 2.] old man was compelled to live in another’s house as though in exile; nor were there lacking [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 15, no. 2.] wicked men who rejoiced in the venerable old man’s grief and misfortunes.

This wrong appears to have been committed by Christians who were responsible for the deed, since Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 3.] calls them his brothers and [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 12, no. 12.] sons. They frequently came to Bordeaux; [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 15, no. 3.] therefore Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 2; and Letter 14, no. 3.] judged that the assistance of Delphinus and Amandus should be sought, so that, having undertaken responsibility for the holy presbyter’s case, he might have their protection. [Col. 0077C]

Paulinus therefore sent a letter to Daducius, one of the principal men among them, [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid.] and sent it open to Amandus, so that he might recognize the importance of the matter and the need for prompt action. He asked him also to add to his own letter a recommendation from himself and Delphinus, to whom he was evidently writing; and he asked him to arrange that, if Daducius were in Gaul, Delphinus should have the letter delivered without delay by a trustworthy and energetic fellow-servant, by one of his own clergy, or by one of the men from Alingon. This certainly indicates that Paulinus had once possessed some right over this estate, which perhaps he had donated to the Church of Bordeaux, [Note: [Col. 0077] Vinet, notes to Ausonius.] and which, as we learn, had once belonged to that Church for many years.

Paulinus’s letter, [Note: [Col. 0077] Paulinus, Letter 15, no. 3.] joined with recommendations from Delphinus and Amandus, [Col. 0077D] achieved the desired outcome. God [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 14, no. 4.] rescued this poor presbyter from destitution, enlightened and humbled the proud hearts of the rich, who, by the just restoration of a small dwelling, prepared for themselves an eternal lodging in the heavenly tabernacle of the poor saint, from whom they in turn would receive hospitality.

Thus [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 15, no. 3.] they not only refrained from transgressing when they could have done so; [Col. 0078A] they even preferred, out of goodwill toward him, to do what was expedient rather than what was permitted. They ordered the house to be restored to the holy presbyter, even though he could not prove it to be his own, without any difficulty, so that, if he could not possess it by right, he might at least possess it as a gift from them.

Paulinus received the joyful news [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 2; and Letter 14, no. 3.] from letters sent by Delphinus and Amandus, who, as is likely, also sent him Daducius’s decree. Thus [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 15, no. 2.] the presbyter’s lament was turned into joy, and those who had rejoiced in his misfortunes were overwhelmed with shame. This most holy man [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 3.] proclaimed his gratitude for this generosity as though he had received an undeserved gift; and not he alone, but [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 2; and Letter 14, no. 4.] his entire household, rejoicing with the unanimous congratulations of the Church and city of Capua, did not cease blessing the Lord. [Col. 0078B]

Paulinus asks Amandus [Note: [Col. 0077] Letter 15, no. 3.] to love these noblemen beyond his customary affection and, if they should perhaps come to Bordeaux, to thank them in person also on Paulinus’s behalf, with all the affection of his mind and heart. Or, if their arrival should be delayed, he asks Amandus to send them the gratitude they deserved and the blessing merited by their deed, so that they might know and understand what an acceptable sacrifice to God they had offered through this obedience of their faith, by which, at the intervention of Delphinus and Amandus, they had received Paulinus’s petition favorably. Although, properly speaking, [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid.] Paulinus himself had decided to write them a letter when one of their household should travel from Campania to Bordeaux.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Paulinus consoles Pammachius on the death of his wife. From Delphinus’s illness he draws an occasion for humility. He writes Pope Anastasius on his behalf

1. Paulina, daughter of the holy Paula and wife of Pammachius, died [Note: [Col. 0077] See Jerome, History, § 107.] around the end of the year 397. Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0077] Paulinus, Letter 13, no. 2.] learned of her death only many months later, both because of the distance of the place and because news was infrequent. He learned it from a letter sent by a certain friend, [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 1.] namely Olympius, and this [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 2.] in winter. Prevented by the severity of the season and by his customary ill health from going to Pammachius himself, as he wished, he nevertheless felt his friend’s grief most deeply.

Since, therefore, he could not visit him, he wrote him a lengthy letter in which he first praised his pious tears at his wife’s funeral and then the alms he had distributed to the needy for the consolation of the deceased. This latter portion once occupied almost the whole of Letter 33, [Col. 0078D] which bore an inscription to Alethius. But Chiffletius [Note: [Col. 0077] Chiffletius, pp. 8 and 20.] has shown that this is plainly an error, and that the entire passage belongs to Letter 13, formerly Letter 37, which is addressed to Pammachius.

Paulinus had always remembered Pammachius, [Note: [Col. 0077] Paulinus, Letter 13, no. 2.] yet [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., nos. 1–2.] with appropriate humility he had maintained silence until urgent charity caused him to disclose the affection concealed in his heart. [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid., no. 1.] Olympius, from whom Paulinus had received news of Paulina’s death and whom he calls his brother, is called a bishop in the printed editions. From this Chiffletius concludes that Paulinus had already become bishop of Nola. He himself, however, admits that in a certain manuscript, namely the Regius manuscript, formerly belonging to the Putean brothers, the word “bishop” is absent. If it were to be supplied, it would be easier to believe that Paulinus, writing to a powerful lord, called him “brother bishop”—since Paulinus himself was both such a man and a priest—in an unusual expression, than to suppose that Paulinus had already been made a bishop at this time. For the latter view gives rise to difficulties from which Chiffletius could not extricate himself.

For when Paulinus says [Note: [Col. 0079] Poem 15, verse 3.] at the beginning of this year that Saint Felix’s birthday was dearer to him than his own birthday, I do not see what difficulty follows if we interpret it as referring to the day of Felix’s birth, [Col. 0079B] and likewise understand the solemnity he mentions as the feast day of Saint Felix, not of Paulinus, as Chiffletius rashly believed and accepted.

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 398

2. In his fifth birthday poem for Saint Felix, [Note: [Col. 0079] Poem 16.] Paulinus completed the history of this holy confessor, which he had begun in the poem [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., verse 17; and Poem 15.] of the preceding year. At the beginning of this year, or at the end of the preceding one, Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 17, no. 1.] received a letter from one of Severus’s servants, in which Severus promised that he would come to him during that very year. He had made this promise to undertake the journey [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., no. 3.] more than once. There is no doubt that Paulinus sent a reply, but it is missing.

He sent Severus’s servants back [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., no. 1.] before summer and the feast of Saint Peter. This year also, [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 19, no. 1.] namely two years before the Letter 19 that was written later, [Col. 0079C] we believe that Cardamates came to Paulinus during Lent [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 15, no. 4.] and brought letters from Delphinus and Amandus. [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 14, no. 1.] They informed him [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., no. 3; and Letter 15, no. 2.] that Basil’s case had been successfully resolved, of which we have said enough in the preceding year; and also about Delphinus’s prolonged [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 14, no. 3; and Letter 15, no. 1.] and serious illness, [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 14, no. 3.] in which he was afflicted by burning fevers and various humors. But through the same messenger [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 1, no. 3; and Letter 15, no. 1.] Paulinus learned both of his illness and of his recovery.

From this illness Paulinus drew a considerable occasion for humility, saying to Delphinus [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 14, no. 3.]: “If you scarcely escape chastisement without receiving blows, where shall we wicked and sinful men appear?”

[Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 17, no. 1.] Delphinus sent a very brief letter, but one most welcome to Paulinus. After Easter Paulinus replied to both men, [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 15, no. 4.] and undoubtedly sent the reply through [Col. 0079D] Cardamates, [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid.] whom he had retained until that time [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid.; and Letter 21, no. 5.] and who seems to have been his servant, and whom he had transferred to Delphinus and Amandus.

It may be conjectured that Cardamates had once performed as a mime and that he had been addicted to wine; [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 19, no. 4; and Letter 15, no. 4.] but under Amandus as his teacher [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 15, no. 4.] he was completely changed, so that he became a cleric and was received by Paulinus with brotherly affection. [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 19, no. 1.] Paulinus calls him a fellow-servant and boasts that [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 15, no. 4; and Letter 21, no. 6.] he had almost become his daily table-companion and had not fled from him. He says this especially to show how sober Cardamates had become. He adds, however, [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 15, no. 4.] that after Easter Cardamates complained that he did not take food until the day was declining toward evening.

To what clerical rank he was advanced is not known. In letters written two years later [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 19, no. 4.] he is said to have been made an exorcist by Delphinus. He was already an old man and had gray hair, yet he frequently traveled [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., no. 5.] from Nola to Bordeaux. When he claimed [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 15, no. 4.] that his wife was weak and therefore of no use to him, Paulinus, joking somewhat about him in his letter to Amandus, seriously asked that some little male slave or some young maidservant be provided for him.

Nicetas, bishop of Dacia, made his first journey to Nola in the year 398 or 399, since on his second visit [Note: [Col. 0079] Poem 24, verse 333.] he was present there four years later [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., verse 178.] for the feast of Saint Felix, on 14 February 402. [Col. 0080B] Perhaps there will be another occasion to speak at greater length about Nicetas; for now I will add only that Paulinus formed an extremely close relationship with him.

3. On 26 November, [Note: [Col. 0079] See Bollandus, Lives of the Saints, under 21 February.] Pope Siricius died. Anastasius, who succeeded him that same year, [Note: [Col. 0079] Paulinus, Letter 20, no. 2.] as soon as he began to have the power to offer Paulinus his affection, hastened to extend it to him with the greatest devotion. When Paulinus wrote to him about this promotion, [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid.] Anastasius was deeply pleased by this evidence of goodwill. Shortly after his ordination he sent letters in Paulinus’s name to the bishops of Campania, filled with religious devotion, piety, and peace, both to declare his own affection and to offer others an example of his benevolence.

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 399

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Theridius and Posthumianus, friends of Paulinus, and on Jovius, his kinsman

1. After Paulinus had, during the preceding two years, related in verse everything connected with the life of Saint Felix, in his sixth birthday poem [Note: [Col. 0079] Poem 18, verses 72, 155, and 93.] he commemorates Felix’s funeral and mentions both the tomb first erected for him and the magnificent church later built above it. He also recounts in general terms [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., verse 190.] the miracles that took place there; but at greater length he tells the delightful story of a certain peasant [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., verse 220.] whose oxen, carried off by robbers, were restored by Saint Felix. [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., verse 451.]

That same year, on the very night of Saint Felix’s feast, [Note: [Col. 0079] Poem 20, verse 107.] Theridius was wounded and miraculously healed; Paulinus elegantly describes this in verse the following year. This Theridius, whom [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., verse 106.] he calls his brother, [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid., verse 242.] had left his homeland some time earlier and, having faced the dangers of sea and land, had come to Nola, despising them, in order to dedicate himself to Saint Felix together with other servants of God.

He is unquestionably [Note: [Col. 0079] Letter 16, no. 1.] the Theridius whom Paulinus elsewhere associates with Posthumianus, calling them holy and religious men, [Col. 0081A] who had left their homeland—Gaul, as is probable—and had come to Campania for this very purpose. Elsewhere he speaks of Theridius, whom he calls his Theridius [Note: [Col. 0081] Poem 21, verse 381.]:

> A man, a gift to me from Christ,  
> a man of peace, a man of law, a man of grace,  
> my rest, my delight, my mind.

Yet this man appears to have remained at Rome and in his own home. We do not hesitate to believe that Posthumianus was the man who is most celebrated in the Dialogues of Sulpicius Severus. There it appears that he [Note: [Col. 0081] Sulpicius Severus, Dialogue 1, chapter 20.] was originally from Aquitania, had already made that journey to the East, and had known Jerome at Bethlehem.

By an unexpected gift of God, Theridius and Posthumianus [Note: [Col. 0081] Paulinus, Letter 27, no. 2.] came to Paulinus, who had not previously known them. He discovered that great virtue shone forth in them and, in the grace by which he considered himself blessed, reproached them only because they admitted that they lacked familiarity and acquaintance with Severus. [Col. 0081B] He gave those departing [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 16, no. 1.] from Campania for their homeland no instruction more earnestly than that they hasten to the presence and embrace of Sulpicius Severus, [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 27, no. 2.] and that in their homeland they place knowing him before all other concerns and occupations, so that they might, even late, make good the long loss they had suffered.

2. He also gave them a letter [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 16, no. 1.] to Jovius, a man of great distinction in Gaul and his relative, [Note: [Col. 0081] Poem 19, verse 163.] or kinsman by marriage. I cannot determine whether this was the same Jovius whom Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0081] Zosimus, Book 5, page 824.] calls distinguished for learning and other excellent qualities, when he reports that Constantine, emperor of the Gauls, sent him as an envoy to Honorius in 409; or whether he was perhaps that most noble Jovius of Gaul who assumed the purple [Col. 0081C] in 411 so that he might become emperor before his death. At that time there was also another Jovius, [Note: [Col. 0081] Catalogus of Godefridus, vol. 6, p. 368.] prefect of the praetorium under Honorius in 409, and a man of great distinction amid the disturbances of that period.

Whoever this Jovius was to whom Paulinus wrote, [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 16, no. 6.] he possessed the greatest prudence, both natural and cultivated. [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid.] He was wholly devoted to humane letters; he applied himself to reading the poets and read orators and philosophers extensively, retaining especially whatever was excellent in them. He knew both Greek and Latin, possessed an extraordinary abundance of eloquence and learning, and [Note: [Col. 0081] Poem 19, verse 10.] had acquired great distinction and renown through poetry.

He was endowed by nature [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., verse 79.] with an outstanding and lofty intellect. Yet he followed the Academic philosophers far too much. [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 16, no. 11.] In their arguments about divinity they were always seeking the divine, but never finding it, because they were neither pure and perceptive enough to see God nor humble enough to believe in what they had not seen.

Jovius held that secular learning ought to be placed after sacred learning, though he was less devoted to the latter than to the former. [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 16, no. 6.] He recognized Christ as the source of true light; and, through his affection for Paulinus, he professed himself devoted to the Christian name [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., no. 1.] and not opposed to monks. [Col. 0081D] But he did not follow the light he knew. As an excuse he claimed that he was not yet equal to it [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., no. 6.] and therefore not capable of God, because, being occupied with earthly affairs and concerns, he was kept from a higher contemplation of heavenly things as though by clouds placed between him and them. [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid.] He said that he was occupied with paying taxes, from which even the most powerful nobles were not exempt.

Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 16, no. 1.] had formed a friendship with him and never let an opportunity to write to him pass.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Paulinus writes Jovius an outstanding letter urging him to embrace Christian faith and piety

1. Some time earlier a ship [Note: [Col. 0081] Letter 16, no. 2.] heavily laden with silver had been violently tossed by a severe storm, yet had been preserved amid the sea’s whirlpools. It was cast upon a shore where Paulinus had a familiar town and Jovius had an ancestral estate. Thus, after the guardian of the silver had died, the cargo was nevertheless preserved amid winter storms and greedy sailors.

Of this silver Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., no. 1.] speaks as though it belonged exclusively to him, or at least was held in common by him and Jovius. He calls it “the silver of holy commerce.” From these words someone might perhaps suppose that Paulinus indicated that the silver had been intended for the poor. That is quite foreign to the true meaning. Besides, how would Jovius have acquired a share in it?

Paulinus learned from Jovius’s own letters [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., nos. 2 and 6.] how extraordinary was the preservation both of the storm-tossed ship and of the saved silver, in which so many signs of God’s providence toward human beings had shone forth. He wanted to use this opportunity, while congratulating Jovius on the preservation of the money, to urge him [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., nos. 1–2.] not to attribute God’s gift to chance, and not to recognize God’s beneficence as the work of empty powers of fate and fortune.

Jovius did not seize the splendid opportunity offered him to give thanks to God. Instead, he wrote to Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., no. 2.] that Paulinus was doing God an injustice by attributing to him diseases, shipwrecks, storms, and other evils of that kind—things more appropriate to Fate and Fortune, rival powers of God, than to God himself.

2. Paulinus replied to this letter [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., no. 1.] through Posthumianus and Theridius. He certainly did not wish to let pass the opportunity to write to Jovius through them, lest he seem to judge him averse to religious men. [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., nos. 2–3.]

He proves to Jovius that, since the world could have been created and preserved only by the one God, there can be no doubt that all movements and everything that takes place in it must be referred to God’s governance. If there are matters [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., no. 3.] whose explanations we cannot follow and understand, it is safer for us to believe that their reasons are higher than our senses and thoughts than to believe that they have no reasons at all.

Indeed, [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid., nos. 5–6.] what seems unable to accord with God’s goodness is most worthy of him, since through such things virtue is exercised or tested, and since the virtues of men so famous in history have shone forth only through labors and dangers. [Col. 0083A]

If by Fate [Note: [Col. 0083] Letter 16, no. 4.] are understood the effects of the stars, then the stars are indeed the smallest parts of this world of ours, and they obey God’s will. [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] Outside this meaning, Fate, the Fates, and Fortune are empty names. Since they have no visible form, they can produce nothing.

It is also remarkable that Plato himself [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] so misused human ears through the empty arrogance of his eloquence that he was not ashamed to insert into his writings the ridiculous refrain of an old woman’s tale, even though in those writings he dared to debate the divine nature.

After proving in this way [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., no. 5.] that God is the creator and lord both of us and of all things, he adds [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.]:

> And because, in all that he is, he is goodness, wisdom, and the source of reason, he establishes nothing except by reason, and he created all things for the material realization of his goodness. Let us devote all that we are to him; let us strive to learn what pleases him and take care to do it. Then, with a purified mind, looking more clearly, we shall see that this is the truth: that all things that exist are from God; and this is the consequence: that all God’s works are most beautiful. There is no evil whose author is good, for he has prepared all things throughout the world for our use and directs them toward our benefit. He so established the work of this universe that he created some things to serve, others to exercise, and others to rule.

Again he urges Jovius more forcefully [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., no. 6.] to obey the truth. He had neither lack of time nor lack of ability; occupations and taxes would not prevent him from learning God’s wisdom, since they did not keep him from studying Greek and Latin orators and philosophers.

“**You have leisure,**” Paulinus says, [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] “**to be a philosopher, but you do not have leisure to be a Christian. Change your judgment; change your eloquence. For you need not lay aside the philosophy of your mind, provided that you season it with faith and religion. Join yourself to the wise, so that you may be a philosopher of God and a prophet of God—wise not by seeking God but by imitating him—so that you may be educated not so much by your tongue as by your life, and so that you may discuss great things as well as do them.**”

In order to draw some solid benefit from the poets’ fables, [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] he says that the pernicious sweetness of empty literature and all the appearances of temporal things resemble either the roots of the Lotus-Eaters or the songs of the Sirens.

Moreover, he wishes that Jovius might be able to cast off everything completely, so that he might put on the one God and escape, naked if need be, from the mire of this world. [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., no. 8.] Yet he allows him [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., no. 9.] to share everything he possesses with God: he may retain what belongs to himself and his household, provided that he dedicates himself, his intellectual abilities, and the resources of his tongue to God.

“Immediately,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] “when you direct the eye of your mind toward the heavenly sanctuary, truth will open its face to you and will disclose you to yourself, because, when a human being refused to understand God, he became worthy of being stricken by ignorance of himself.”

He adds [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] that the human being, superior to all irrational creatures, is equal to all other creatures that are subject to the one God:

> By this moderation, he says, [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., no. 10.] the human being is held in balance: he neither falls away from the lot of salvation nor from the dignity of nature. He becomes conscious of truth, master of wisdom, servant of justice, free from error, and master of the vices to which the soul, when it does not serve God, is condemned to serve. Then, exiled from its proper condition, it is scattered through all the wandering paths of its own thoughts or of others’ opinions: wandering among philosophers, inquisitive among fortune-tellers, religious toward superstition, profane toward religion, always suspended between hope and fear in uncertain emotions. Hence it is carried about by every wind of every doctrine, because, empty of the fear of God, it has no head of wisdom.

He concludes [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., no. 11.] by urging him once more to send away the errors and ignorance of the philosophers and to retain from them only the abundance and adornment of language, as though he had carried off spoils from hostile arms:

> Thus, stripped of their errors and clothed in their eloquence, apply that cosmetic of eloquence by which empty wisdom deceives, clothing substantial things in it. Do not adorn an empty body of fictions, but a body filled with the marrow of truth; and do not meditate on matters pleasing only to the ears, but on those that will also benefit the minds of human beings.

3. In addition to that letter, in which Paulinus’s intellectual acuity and learning shine forth more clearly than elsewhere, he also dedicated a poem to Jovius [Note: [Col. 0083] Poem 19.], perhaps written somewhat earlier. In it he urges him [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., verse 148.] to devote his study and effort to writing about and praising the miracles and power of God. He says [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., verse 4.]:

> Begin to devote your heart wholly to divine things,  
> and raise your thoughts, lifted from earth, to God.  
> Soon a new light will rise before your eyes, with heaven opened,  
> and the Holy Spirit will enter through hidden passages  
> by a silent approach, and shake your inward parts  
> with a joyful breath. . . .
>
> How much greater glory will come to you from these beginnings,  
> in which, while exercising your tongue,  
> you will also educate your holy mind,  
> and gain both praise and life.  
> While you wisely read and write the true miracles  
> of the Most High God, [Col. 0084C]  
> you will learn to be nearer and dearer to God.  
> While, believing, you marvel at him,  
> you will begin to love him,  
> and by loving God you will be loved in return by Christ.

Paulinus further adds that Jovius should be taught [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid., verses 39 ff.] in the book of Genesis what the true origin of the world is; in John what should be believed about God and Christ; in the crossing of the Red Sea and the story of Jonah that God, not Fortune, rules the sea and storms; and in Joshua and Hezekiah that the sun and stars obey him, so that he may understand that the course of our lives is not governed by Fate.

What effect these things had on Jovius is not known. At least it is clear that through them Paulinus’s affection increased. [Col. 0084D] His poem to Jovius is sometimes attributed to Saint Mamertus, the brother of Claudianus, but this attribution appears to rest on no foundation.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Paulinus, ill, repeatedly invites Sulpicius Severus to visit him

1. Throughout the entire preceding year, from the departure of his servants until winter, Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0083] Letter 17, no. 1.] had awaited Sulpicius Severus. Since he had received no letters from him, either during the remainder of that year or at the beginning of the next, he believed that Severus had not written because he was about to arrive, and therefore expected him every day.

Accordingly, he set out for Rome [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] for the approaching venerable feast of the apostolic solemnity, [Note: [Col. 0085] Letter 20, no. 2.] following the customary practice of the feast, [Note: [Col. 0085] Letter 17, no. 1.] and expecting to embrace his beloved Severus. He was received by Pope Anastasius with kindness, deep affection, and honor; [Note: [Col. 0085] Letter 17, no. 1.] but he was unable to enjoy the sight of his Severus.

He therefore consoled himself with a letter delivered to him in Severus’s name. In it [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 4.] Severus pleaded his illness and removed Paulinus’s [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 1.] hope of his presence. Paulinus received the letter from a man whose clothing and appearance in no way suggested a monk, or one of those whom he and Sulpicius Severus were accustomed to employ for such exchanges.

He was in fact the servant of one of Paulinus’s friends, named Sabinus, who was closely related to Severus. When this became known to Paulinus on that occasion, he embraced Sabinus with an even greater affection. [Col. 0085B] I do not know whether his servant was that Marracinus whom Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0085] Letter 22, nos. 1–2.] depicts elsewhere in precisely the same way and whom he says brought him another letter from Severus.

Marracinus, however, appears to have belonged to Severus, who had ordered him to pretend to be a monk, as Paulinus testifies when he calls him an “unspiritual monk.” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid.] Sabinus asked Paulinus for letters to Sulpicius Severus, but, being extremely busy, [Note: [Col. 0085] Letter 17, no. 2.] he could not reply during the entire ten days he spent in Rome, much less after returning home. A serious and prolonged illness overtook him, but God, the life and resurrection of those who serve him, did not wish to deliver him over to death and rescued him, though stricken, because he hoped in God’s mercy.

When he had recovered, he wrote to Severus [Note: [Col. 0085] Letter 17, no. 3.] and complained that he had waited so long for him in vain. [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 1.] He asserted [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 3.] that he could not cast from his mind the hope that he would see and embrace Severus, since Severus had promised this so often. If he did not come, Paulinus said that Severus must be regarded as guilty before Saint Felix. Nor could Severus plead illness, since he made so many other journeys and repeatedly visited Martin at Tours, sometimes making several excursions there within a single summer. From this letter one cannot determine whether Martin was alive or dead.

Paulinus wrote through Amachius, Saint Delphinus’s subdeacon, who was very well known to Severus. It is probable that he also entrusted him with letters to Delphinus and Amandus. Of all the letters addressed to the two men, however, none survives that can be shown to have been written in this year rather than the next.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Paulinus writes to Victricius. He cultivates the friendship of Jerome and Rufinus

1. In this same year and period Paulinus wrote, through Paschasius, Letter 18, in which he mentions the same illness of his. [Note: [Col. 0085] Paulinus, Letter 18, no. 1; and Letter 17, no. 2.] We describe the history of this most illustrious confessor and bishop of Rouen in Dissertation 4, where we consider Saint Paulinus’s correspondence with him.

When Paulinus wrote to Victricius, he had learned the recent life of this most holy confessor and bishop [Col. 0086A] from Tychicus, whom he calls Saint Victricius’s dearest brother and faithful minister in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 4.] At that time [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 8.] he lamented the misfortune of his own negligence, because he had not sufficiently recognized or venerated Victricius’s holiness when he had formerly seen him at Vienna with Saint Martin and had not kissed his scars.

He had been seeking an opportunity to write to him, [Note: [Col. 0085] Letter 18, no. 1.] but none arose until what had not happened when he wished for it came to him when he did not expect it. This occurred at Rome, where Paulinus had gone. At that very time Paschasius, deacon of Saint Victricius of Rouen, encountered a certain catechumen, [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 3.] Ursus. In Paschasius’s [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 10.] kindness and favor, as though in a mirror reflecting certain traces of Saint Victricius’s virtues and graces, Paulinus says that he gathered these traces for himself.

Paschasius’s character proved him both a disciple of Victricius’s instruction and a companion of his journey: [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 1.] modesty of conduct, humility of heart, gentleness of spirit, steadfastness in the faith of the truth, and speech seasoned with salt in every respect. Therefore, beyond the grace of brotherly companionship in the sacred ministry of the diaconate, Paulinus received him with all the greater reverence and affection because Paschasius belonged to Victricius in clergy, body, and spirit.

When Paschasius wished to return from Rome to Victricius, Paulinus did not allow him to depart. Rather, by a kind of force of charity, he brought him to Nola, so that through Paschasius’s presence he might enjoy for a longer time, as it were, a portion of Saint Victricius’s grace.

Nevertheless, Paulinus lost no small consolation from Paschasius’s companionship, since at that time he was afflicted by bodily illness, as we observed above. [Note: [Col. 0085] Chapter 35.] Nor was Paschasius distressed and compassionate only on account of Paulinus’s illness; [Note: [Col. 0085] Paulinus, Letter 18, no. 3.] he was also deeply troubled by the severe illness of Ursus, whom he had kept as his inseparable companion on his journey. In Ursus, Paulinus says that he saw faith and charity in the Lord in their fullness.

At last, through Paschasius’s labor and faith—for the Lord wished to test the power that his holy confessor Felix possessed with him—Ursus, who had been ill to the point of death, found safety amid his danger. Through the hands of the deacon Paschasius, he was born to Christ and baptized on his sickbed, though Paulinus, already a presbyter, was present, and many other presbyters could have been available.

When Ursus had regained sound and vigorous health, and Paschasius was preparing to return to Victricius, Paulinus sent his Letter 18 to Victricius through Paschasius. In it, after excusing [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 1.] Paschasius for having been retained so long, he recalls that Victricius [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 4.] had spread the Gospel among the Morini and Nervii in Belgica and had established and formed the Church of Rouen.

Finally, after weaving together the history of his martyrdom or confession, [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 7.] he declares that he is held by the greatest desire to see him [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid., no. 8.] and wishes, in his presence, to admire and venerate Christ on his lips. He laments his own misfortune because, although he had once been at Vienna, this fruit had not been granted him, even though it had been within his reach. [Col. 0087A]

Here he says nothing about Victricius’s journey to Rome, which we shall demonstrate took place in 404.

## 2

At the close of this year [Note: [Col. 0087] Letter 20, §2], Pope Anastasius invited Paulinus to the annual commemoration of his consecration—a distinction which the supreme pontiffs were accustomed to extend only to their fellow bishops. Perhaps pleading the difficulty of winter, Paulinus did not attend; instead, in place of his presence he wrote the supreme pontiff a most humble letter. Anastasius received it with paternal feeling and was not offended by Paulinus’s excuse.

We have already observed [Note: [Col. 0087] Chapter 24, §1] that, from perhaps the year 394, Paulinus and Jerome were bound by the closest friendship. They continued in it during the following years, although nearly all the letters exchanged between them have perished [Col. 0087B].

From about this period there still survives a letter [Note: [Col. 0087] Jerome, Letter 153] from which it is clear that Paulinus had requested from Jerome his commentaries on the prophet Daniel. Jerome granted his request, but for certain reasons unknown to us delayed sending them. In 398 he attempted to undertake the work, but postponed it again in order to translate Origen’s books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*). Paulinus wrote to him again to urge him to write, and complained that Jerome was sending him only small and unpolished letters. Jerome therefore wrote him this letter, in which he excused himself for not having fulfilled his promise. He said that, because of lack of time, he refrained from writing very extensive and learned letters; moreover, since Paulinus frightened him by his eloquence and almost represented Cicero in the epistolary style, he feared that, when writing to him at greater length, he might send him more than could properly be approved [Col. 0087C].

He gave thanks for the little cap he had received from Paulinus. Paulinus proposed questions to him concerning passages that seemed to abolish free will and concerning the sanctification attributed by the Apostle to the children of believers. Jerome answered the latter question according to Tertullian’s opinion. As for the former, he referred Paulinus to Origen’s books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), whose recent translation by Jerome could be borrowed from Pammachius, although Greek copies were sufficient for him. In passing, he also stated that he did not reject everything Origen had written, as Jerome’s opponents accused him of doing, but repudiated only his erroneous doctrines.

Jerome said this because of his controversy with Rufinus, whose side Paulinus [Col. 0087D] and Augustine did not take. It is certain that Paulinus always loved Rufinus, who, having returned to the West at the end of 397, stayed nearly a full year at Rome; toward the end of that year he went to Aquileia and then returned to Rome. Paulinus surely refers to him [Note: Paulinus, Letter 40, §6; Col. 0087] when he says that he had heard some remarkable things about the pelican from a most holy and learned man, dear to him, who had learned much not only by reading but also by traveling.

# In the Year of Christ 400

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Paulinus writes to Delphinus of Bordeaux, Venerius of Milan, and Severus. He describes the story and shipwreck of Martinianus.

### 1

In the seventh poem on the birthday of Saint Felix [Note: Paulinus, Poem 10, verse 61; Col. 0087], Paulinus demonstrates this saint’s power against demons and specifically mentions a demoniac who had long been possessed [Note: same work, verse 84; Col. 0087]. The principal subject of the poem is the story of Theridius [Note: same work, verse 107; and Chapter 33, §1; Col. 0087], which had occurred the previous year.

Nearly two years earlier [Note: Letter 19, §1; Col. 0087], Cardamas had brought Paulinus a very brief letter from Delphinus. Since then Paulinus had received no letter from Delphinus [Col. 0088B]. Throughout the entire summer, Paulinus had been kept in suspense by his fruitless expectation of Uran(i)us’s arrival, from whom he expected to receive a letter from Delphinus. But Uran(i)us, neglectful of his duty, remained where he ought not to have been.

Paulinus did not take this man’s absence badly [Note: same place], since his arrival could have brought him no benefit. He was, however, deeply distressed that through his faithlessness Uran(i)us had caused Paulinus’s soul to waste away from prolonged hunger, far from the bread of Delphinus’s lips.

Since Paulinus had received no letter during the summer, he thought that the winter too would have to be spent in the same silence. But God, who gives food to the hungry, brought Paulinus—though he had not expected it, yet had desired it—comfort and joy through the sudden arrival of Cardamas, then an exorcist. Cardamas informed him of Delphinus’s health [Col. 0088C] and delivered to him letters from Delphinus and Amandus [Note: Letter 21, §§5–6; Col. 0087].

Paulinus replied to them. In almost the whole of the twenty-first letter to Amandus [Note: Letter 21, §6; Col. 0087], he praises Cardamas for being swift and light in his running. In the other letter, to Delphinus [Note: Letter 19, §§2 and 4; Col. 0087], he asks him to pray to God on his behalf, lest he stain the baptismal grace he had received through Delphinus’s ministry.

Although this letter is very long, because Paulinus rarely had an opportunity to write to Delphinus, he added a second letter [Note: Letter 20, §1; Col. 0087], certainly written between the anniversary of Anastasius’s consecration and the period when Paulinus was accustomed to go to Rome—that is, between the end of 399 and 29 June 400 [Note: same place, §2; Col. 0087]. We have assigned this date to certain letters of Paulinus to Delphinus and Amandus, although we do not assert that it is absolutely certain [Col. 0088D].

When Delphinus had charged Cardamas to inquire about Paulinus’s health [Note: same place, §1; Col. 0087], Paulinus wrote in the second letter to Delphinus that he was in good health, though not robust, and mentioned the benevolence of Pope Anastasius toward him [Note: same place, §2]. He added that, when he was in Rome, he would obtain from the supreme pontiff letters of recommendation by which Delphinus too would be commended [Note: same place].

### 2

Venerius, bishop of Milan and successor to Simplicianus, recently ordained, had written to Paulinus [Note: same place, §3; Col. 0087]. Delphinus had asked Paulinus to write to Venerius on his behalf. Paulinus did so, and instructed Cardamas, on his return journey, to pass through Milan and deliver his letter. Finally, if Venerius wished to write to Delphinus, Cardamas was to let him know that an opportunity was available [Col. 0089A].

Delphinus had informed Paulinus that he had arranged for the recently constructed basilica at Alingon to be completed, and that it had either already been dedicated or was soon to be consecrated [Note: Letter 20, §3; Col. 0089]. Paulinus rejoiced exceedingly, and from the words of this letter it appears that the basilica had been built at Paulinus’s expense. Delphinus had added that certain people were gnashing their teeth and wasting away with envy because of the construction of this new church [Note: same place, §4]. Paulinus replied that this was nothing new, nor was it surprising, since he trusted in the Lord. He therefore earnestly begged Delphinus, his spiritual father, to pray to God for his soul and for his progress in salvation [Col. 0089B].

### 3

There is no reason why we should not assign to this year the twenty-second letter to Severus, which must have preceded the twenty-seventh. Severus had entrusted a letter for Paulinus to Marracinus [Note: Paulinus, Letter 22, §1; Col. 0089], whom we mentioned above [Note: Chapter 35; Col. 0089]. When Marracinus arrived at Rome, he handed the letter to Sorianus, rejoicing that he would not be compelled to travel as far as Nola and appear before Paulinus. Sorianus, however, a very devout monk and truly spiritual man, had often heard Severus speak of Paulinus and was filled with longing for him. Rejoicing at the desired opportunity, he accepted the letter, carried it to Paulinus, and commended himself to him.

Accordingly, in replying to Severus [Note: Paulinus, Letter 22, §§2–3; Col. 0089], after Paulinus had sketched the portrait of an excellent and true monk, he states that the portrait is that of Sorianus, who was probably to deliver this letter. In this same year Paulinus began the great buildings that were completed three years later, toward the end of 402 [Note: Poem 25, verse 266; Col. 0089].

### 4

In a poem composed the following year [Note: Poem 23, verse 386; Col. 0089], Paulinus recalls that many people offered themselves each day before the altar of Saint Felix, in order to give thanks to him because, through God’s mercy and the help of that same saint, they had escaped unharmed from shipwrecks. I do not know whether this may allude to the story of Martinianus, which Paulinus describes to Cytherius in a poem whose date we cannot establish with complete certainty.

Cytherius was then a man distinguished in the world both by birth and by learning, and renowned for the offices he had attained [Note: Poem 21, verse 441; Col. 0089]. But God, who draws all things to himself and sometimes deigns to choose the powerful of the world, had enriched him with humility of heart so that he might grant him eternal elevation, and had stirred him to love the poor [Note: same work, verse 486; Col. 0089].

He was married to a wife [Note: same work, verse 689; Col. 0089] who raised their children in chastity [Note: same work, verse 695]. From the very beginning he had consecrated one of them to God [Note: same work, verse 715], and had entrusted him to Severus to be instructed and educated in salutary disciplines, so that one day he might deserve to serve among the clergy in the Church [Note: same work, verse 777; Col. 0089D].

Martinianus, of whom we are speaking [Col. 0090A], was dear to him but, as it appears, poor [Note: same work, verses 445 and 453; Col. 0089]. Paulinus calls him a brother, kindred in spirit and faith [Note: same work, verse 1], whose inward piety shone forth in his speech [Note: same work, verse 437]. He was filled with a great desire to visit Paulinus [Note: same work, verse 430], although Paulinus was unknown to him [Note: same work, verse 435]. For this reason Cytherius gave him a letter of recommendation [Note: same work, verses 432 and 4] so that he might approach Paulinus.

At first Martinianus wished to travel by land [Note: same work, verse 22]. But, not daring to undertake so long a journey on foot, he boarded a ship at Narbonne at the beginning of autumn [Note: same work, verse 259]. It is therefore clear that he, like Cytherius, was from Gaul. The wind was favorable. But the ship he had boarded, already worn out, sank in the middle of the night [Note: same work, verse 181], and all who were in it were drowned except those who took refuge in a small boat [Note: same work, verses 60 and following].

Martinianus, all the Christians, and certain unbelievers who were among them escaped unharmed. No believer was drowned; the Jews and schismatics, on the contrary, perished. The shipmaster, who was also a Novatian, was overwhelmed by despair, although he could have saved himself from danger.

Martinianus escaped almost naked [Note: same work, verses 253 and 272]. Having abandoned his possessions, and in his panic not knowing what he was taking with him, he had brought along a copy of the Apostle’s Epistles. It was placed at the very bottom of the boat and even in the water [Note: same work, verse 247]. Yet neither this inconvenience, nor the cold, nor the other circumstances of so great a misfortune awakened him from sleep until the boat reached the harbor—something that could not have happened by human means.

He landed at Massilia. There the solitaries, though abundant in charity, were poor and could give him nothing beyond shoes [Note: same work, verses 313 and 319]. Finally, lest he be regarded as one of those acephalous monks and impostors, or—as Paulinus calls them—greedy beggars [Note: same work, verse 329], who wander over land and sea, advertising themselves as shipwrecked men and selling their misfortune [Note: same work, verse 335], he was compelled to put out to sea again [Col. 0090C].

With favorable winds Martinianus reached Centumcellae [Note: same work, verse 364], from which he traveled on foot as far as Rome [Note: same work, verse 370]. He was received into the house of a certain Paulinus and Theridius, who were likewise dear to Saint Paulinus [Note: same work, verses 371 and 385 and following]; at that time Theridius was staying with our Paulinus at Nola.

In this city Martinianus found men he knew well and fellow countrymen. Paulinus, himself a Roman citizen, stripped him of his shipwrecked clothing and covered him with his own [Col. 0090D]. Martinianus then continued on foot toward Nola [Note: same work, verse 398].

At Capua, eight leagues distant from Nola, he hired for a small sum a mule returning without a load [Note: same work, verses 403 and following]. But he did not escape punishment for his laziness: when the mule was taken from under him, he fell face-first to the ground, sliding and being thrown among rocks and brambles. Yet he was not injured; our Paulinus attributed this to the protection of Saint Felix [Note: same work, verse 414].

At last he arrived at Saint Paulinus’s house [Note: same work, verses 435 and following]. Though previously unknown, as soon as he began to be recognized as Cytherius’s friend, he became exceedingly dear to Paulinus. He could give Paulinus no letter of recommendation, because he had lost both it and all his possessions.

Paulinus addressed this poem to Cytherius. After recounting the misfortune and the miracles by which God had rescued Martinianus from danger [Col. 0091A], he discusses at length the education of the son whom Cytherius had dedicated to God under Severus [Note: Poem 21, verses 496 and following].

About the same time Paulinus perhaps wrote the *Epithalamium of Julianus* [Note: Poem 22; Col. 0091], whom Augustine’s one hundred and first letter establishes to have been a deacon in 408 [Note: Augustine, Letter 101, §4; Col. 0091].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Through Victor, a disciple of Saint Martin, Paulinus writes several letters to Sulpicius Severus.

### 1

Severus, who was accustomed to write to Paulinus only once each year [Note: Paulinus, Letter 23, §2; Col. 0091], wrote again this year, apparently around winter, in order to show his affection for him more fully. In this letter he asked Paulinus to love him more and more [Note: same place, §1]. He extolled Paulinus’s virtue and his general renunciation of worldly goods with outstanding praise [Note: same place, and §2], while thinking humbly of himself.

He certainly acknowledged that he circulated, as far as he was able, the letters Paulinus sent him, and he sent him cloaks [Note: Letter 24, §1]. He chose as the companion of his solitude Victor—formerly girded with a sword—the spiritual son of Saint Martin and the companion of the blessed Clarus in holy living [Note: Letter 23, §3], to deliver this letter to Paulinus [Note: same place and Letter 25, §§1 and 3].

In this letter Severus had called Victor a man adorned with virtues [Note: see Severus’s letter preceding Letter 23; Col. 0091]. Paulinus therefore received him with intimate affection and great rejoicing, declaring that experience had shown him Victor to be truly a man of God: humble in heart, though not lacking in grace; a vessel of mercy and dwelling-place of the Most High, who receives him and delights in the peaceful lodging of a trembling soul [Note: Paulinus, Letter 23, §3].

Victor was a pure sheep, revealed not merely by his fleece—that is, by his monastic garment [Note: see note 127]—but by the spirit of gentleness and the modesty of Christ expressed in his speech and silence.

Victor, desirous of inward mastery and therefore untiring in bodily service, strove to render Paulinus the duties of the humblest and most abject servitude [Note: Paulinus, Letter 23, §4]. At Victor’s entreaty, Paulinus once allowed him to wash his feet and anoint his body with oil [Note: same place, §5]. He considered it no small blessing for himself to receive that holy service performed in God’s name, and in this way to show his affection for a man whose piety he venerated.

In return, wishing to taste at least a small drop of the sacred deeds of Saint Martin from Severus’s book, Paulinus, although Victor was unwilling, supplied water for his hands [Note: same place, §4]. Victor also taught him how to prepare simple foods and dishes at less expense and with less indulgence [Note: same place, §§6, 8, and 9]. Accordingly, for some time Victor practiced the culinary art for the entire household, assisted only by an old peasant, recently baptized, who belonged to Paulinus’s household [Note: same place, §9; Col. 0091D].

Paulinus asserts that Victor was extremely attentive to him, especially in cutting his hair [Note: same place, §10], which he did at Severus’s command, so that he might put his skill to Paulinus’s service [Note: Letters 30 and 33, §1]. From that time onward Victor very frequently traveled from Gaul to Nola, indeed making the journey every year [Note: Letter 50, §1; Col. 0091]. Therefore, writing to his Severus, Paulinus calls Victor his customary consolation. Apparently he made the journey on foot.

# In the Year of Christ 401

### 2

Paulinus probably replied to Severus through the same Victor at the end of 400, though more likely at the beginning of 401. First he highly commends Severus’s friendship and benevolence and declares his own in return [Note: Letter 23, §1; Col. 0091]; then he says much about Victor [Note: same place, §2 and following]. This constitutes the beginning of the twenty-third letter up to section 10, whereas earlier printed manuscripts made it the whole of the third letter to Severus. In those same printed editions the fourth letter began as follows [Note: same place, §10]:

> “I now come to Victor’s greater service toward me, his brother” [Col. 0092B].

But who cannot see, even from these opening words, the continuity with the preceding letter and that the two are one and the same? We have therefore constituted a single twenty-third letter.

In the latter part, after showing that we are bound to love God and our neighbor, Paulinus concludes with these words [Note: same place, §47]:

> “The more we glory in the Lord because of your love, which alone enables us to repay at least one of the many and immeasurable debts we owe to God, the more we acknowledge that, in all other good things, we have scarcely been initiated, even in a few, whereas in your love alone we confess ourselves to be perfect.”

Reminded at the end of that letter of the language of perfection and charity, Paulinus makes these words the opening of the twenty-fourth letter to Severus, which had previously been the second [Note: Letter 24, §1]. We have assigned it no title, because it was sent in the same packet as the twenty-third letter [Col. 0092C].

He also reproaches Severus for heaping upon him, out of great affection, unjust praise [Note: same place and §23; see the chronological order in Letter 24]. In order finally to make Severus desist, Paulinus greatly extols Severus’s virtue; while striving with all his strength to conceal his own, he conspicuously brings his own virtue into the light. This letter seems to me almost the holiest and most elegant of all.

In it he writes to Severus [Note: same place, §22]:

> “Meanwhile, while we are in the arena, while there are battles outside and fears within, do not think or speak lofty things on our behalf; rather, fear, cooperate in spirit with those who labor, and work together with them in prayer, so that he who chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong may also, through us, destroy the enemy and be our defender.”

> “Earnestly ask that he grant us understanding on this road by which he calls us; weaken in us the strength of sin, so that he may confirm the spirit of his virtue. Let us be stripped of crimes and clothed with virtues; let him aid us against our own desires, and not hand us over to the desires of our heart” [Note: same place, §23; Col. 0092D].

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Paulinus urges a soldier to renounce the world. He congratulates the hermit Sebastianus on his piety.

### 1

Paulinus composed the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth letters from conversations with Victor, but the year is not entirely certain. The twenty-fifth letter was addressed to an unknown nobleman [Note: Letter 25, §1; Col. 0093] who appears to have been a soldier wearing the military belt, and the prefect and patron of his native city [Note: same place, §8]; he was responsible for collecting military payments [Note: same place, §5]. He was in the flower of youth, married or of marriageable age [Note: same place, §7].

Victor had stayed with him while following the same way of life. Through Victor he became known to Paulinus, who thought it sufficient to send him a letter through Victor. In the letter he strongly urged him to abandon every earthly desire and henceforth serve Christ alone. It is conjectured from what follows that he had not yet been baptized: “When you have been converted, you will learn by reading,” and so forth [Note: same place, §5; Col. 0093A].

### 2

Sebastianus, the faithful servant of God to whom the twenty-sixth letter was addressed [Note: Letter 26, §1; Col. 0093], was sitting in seclusion beside a certain stream so that in that place he might devote himself to prayer and fasting. A certain deacon named Benedictus, who appears to have been his brother in flesh as well as in spirit, visited him there very frequently and supplied him with what was necessary for life.

Since Paulinus had learned about them from Victor—and from this it is inferred that they lived in Aquitaine—he wrote to Sebastianus, together with Therasia, to congratulate him on his piety and commended himself to the prayers of both men. “For this reason,” he says, “the merciful and compassionate Lord procures and grants his saints’ knowledge and love to his sinners, so that their most powerful advocacy may absolve even guilty persons without excuse from the condemnation deserved by their sins” [Note: same place, §5].

He greatly extols the piety of Benedictus and Sebastianus [Note: same place, §§2–3]. He says that one imitated John the Baptist crying out in the desert, while the other imitated Christ teaching in the temple [Note: same place, §4], so that at that time the deacons in Gaul appear to have preached to the people [Col. 0093C]. He calls Sebastianus a monk.

Yet because Sebastianus always shut himself away in the desert, I do not dare assert that he was the same monk Sebastianus who in 405 visited Sulpicius Severus to hear an account of the sacred deeds of Saint Martin [Note: Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* 2.1; Col. 0093]. Augustine likewise wrote to a certain monk named Sebastianus, who was also an abbot [Note: Augustine, Letter 248, note on the title].

## CHAPTER XL

The Goths spread terror in Italy. Paulinus writes to Severus through Posthumianus.

### 1

According to the chronology established above, the eighth poem on the birthday of Saint Felix [Note: Poem 23; Col. 0093] should be assigned to the beginning of 401. It entirely accords with the historical situation, for it was composed amid the turmoil of war and barbarian invasions [Note: same work, verse 75], specifically amid fear of the Goths [Note: same work, verse 12].

From the Chronicle of Saint Prosper [Note: Prosper’s *Chronicle*; Col. 0093] we also learn that Alaric, leader of the Goths, and Radagaisus ravaged Italy in 400. Jerome likewise tells us [Note: Jerome, *Against Rufinus* 3.6, vol. II; Col. 0093] that they besieged Aquileia in 400 or 401.

In that terror some people trusted in the legions, while others trusted in the fortifications of the cities, whose walls had been rapidly rebuilt [Col. 0094A]. Paulinus, however, relied solely upon the sign of the cross for defense and upon the protection of Saint Felix the confessor. For those who fear God are delivered from all the terrors of the world’s evils.

Thus the war that everyone feared did not prevent Paulinus from celebrating the feast of Saint Felix in his customary manner as a day of peace and joy [Note: Poem 23, verse 17; Col. 0093]. He merely devoted himself to prayer more fervently than in a time of peace [Note: same work, verse 67]. Moreover, because God usually rescues those who trust in his mercy from danger, Paulinus presumed that the barbarians could be driven back by Saint Felix, who terrified demons and performed so many miracles every day [Note: same work, verse 102].

In that poem he recalls the case of a neighboring peasant [Note: same work, verse 308] whom the devil, besieging him, was killing with dreadful hunger. Shortly before, the man had been restored to health, and at that time was cultivating his field with mind and body in sound and unimpaired health.

He likewise asserts that, by Saint Felix’s power [Note: same place, verse 415], a torrent that used to rush headlong upon the saint’s church and endanger the neighboring houses and Paulinus’s own house was made to follow a new channel, taking an unusual course by a long detour. He also says that a fire which seemed about to consume his entire house, while the wind remained completely still, burned only a modest portion of the roof [Note: same place, verse 400].

### 2

In this same year Paulinus wrote the twenty-seventh letter, in which he replies to several letters from Severus—at least two [Note: Letter 27, §2; Col. 0093]. He had received the first from Posthumianus and Theridius, and the second from Sorianus and Virinus [Note: same place, §1].

We have already seen [Note: Chapter 33, §1; Col. 0093] that, when Posthumianus and Theridius were setting out for Gaul, Paulinus instructed them to hasten to Severus’s presence and embrace [Note: Letter 27, §2], and to prefer knowing him to all their affairs and concerns at home [Col. 0094C]. They obeyed his commands.

They rejoiced greatly that they had followed Paulinus’s advice [Note: same place], for from Severus they received every service of the highest virtue and affection, and found in him even more good than they had expected. Severus, for his part, found them exceedingly religious and dear [Note: same place, §§2–3]. Moreover, it is clear from Severus’s dialogues how closely Severus himself and Posthumianus were bound by affection and friendship.

I do not know whether Paulinus, who had first obtained their company, had told them that he was again longing for them. It is certain that they visited him a second time [Note: same place, §1] and brought him a letter from Severus, in which Severus reproached Paulinus for having taken them away from him and left him alone [Note: same place, §2].

A few days after Posthumianus and Theridius returned, the arrival of the other brothers, Virinus and Sorianus, followed. They too brought him letters from Severus. In the twenty-seventh letter Paulinus promises to answer all these matters, but he does not satisfy all of Severus’s complaints in the first letter. Thus much appears to be missing from this twenty-seventh letter [Col. 0094D].

Not long afterward Posthumianus returned to Gaul. After bidding Severus farewell, he boarded a ship at Narbonne [Note: Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* 1.3; Col. 0093] in order to travel toward the East in this same year or, at the latest, the following year [Col. 0095A].

We refer to this return of Posthumianus to Gaul what Paulinus says [Note: Letter 28, §3; Col. 0095]: namely, that Posthumianus encountered Victor at Narbonne, whom Severus was sending to Paulinus to spend the winter with him. I think this happened around autumn [Note: same place].

Posthumianus sent Victor back to Severus, and Victor then set out again for Nola. Although he could have reached Paulinus when he was first sent there, he arrived only very late—at the beginning of winter, and, more precisely, as that winter was ending [Note: same place]. It is therefore more accurate to say that Posthumianus traveled to the East in 402.

# In the Year of Christ 402

## CHAPTER XLI

Paulinus is visited by Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, and by Melania. Consulted by Severus about certain difficult passages of history, he modestly declines to give an opinion; he also refuses Severus’s request for a portrait of himself.

### 1

In the ninth poem on the birthday of Saint Felix [Note: Poem 24; Col. 0095], Paulinus discusses at length the festivals of Christians. He first marks the Nativity of Christ, the Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost [Note: same work, verses 44 and following]. To these he adds the feast of Saint Felix [Note: same work, verse 149], which he himself celebrated with singular joy. Since he calls Felix his father [Note: same work, verse 180] and teacher [Note: same work, verse 269], he says that, in this year, the presence of Nicetas gave him a double birthday.

Nicetas had come to Nola four years earlier [Note: same work, verse 333], and Paulinus was filled with a considerable desire to see him again. Yet, after the joy he had received from the feast of Saint Felix, he did not dare hope that another joy would be added through seeing Nicetas, since his arrival seemed entirely prevented by the war and fear of the Goths [Note: same work, verse 339].

Accordingly, Paulinus, more inspired and encouraged than usual, published a poem in praise of Saint Felix, longer and loftier than those of the preceding years. From his more impassioned words it is possible to see how fiercely Paulinus himself burned with the desire for martyrdom [Note: same work, verse 289]:

> My life hung upon the wood,
>
> so that my life might stand for God. What shall I repay you,
>
> my Life, for my life, Christ? Unless perhaps I receive
>
> the cup of salvation, that my right hand may offer you,
>
> so that I may be cleansed by the sacred draught of precious death.
>
> But what shall I do? Even if I give my own body to the flames,
>
> and make myself vile in my own eyes, I cannot repay you
>
> what is owed by shedding blood, since I shall give myself to you
>
> in exchange for myself. And whatever I do in like return,
>
> I shall always be unequal to you, Christ;
>
> for you paid on my behalf debts that were mine,
>
> not yours, Christ, suffering for unrighteous servants.

He relates how he took Saint Nicetas with him to see the buildings not yet completed that he was constructing at the church of Saint Felix [Note: same work, verse 349]. He then describes them in a longer passage [Note: same work, verse 362]. At the same time he discussed with Nicetas the life of Saint Martin [Note: Letter 29, §14], whose history, handed down by Sulpicius Severus [Note: Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 3], he had read through and examined. Without doubt he had already partly explained it to Nicetas on his earlier journey, and perhaps through Nicetas’s efforts he disseminated the history of this most holy man throughout Illyricum [Col. 0096A].

When Nicetas returned to his own church, Paulinus composed the seventeenth poem [Note: Poem 17, verse 2], praying for his safe journey and intending it as a lasting monument to his immortal memory. It is uncertain to which journey of Nicetas the poem refers, the first or the second. It seems more likely to concern the year 398, when we observe no disturbance among the barbarians—unless it refers particularly to this period, when they were always standing under arms.

### 2

This year also brought Paulinus the most welcome pilgrimage of Saint Melania the Elder from Jerusalem to Rome [Note: Letter 29, §§6 and following]. As he was returning from Naples to Nola, he received her in his home with the greatest hospitality. For each part of this story, see Paulinus’s twenty-ninth letter [Note: Letter 29, §§6 and 8].

This distinguished widow brought Paulinus from Jerusalem a fragment of the wood of the divine cross, a gift from John, the illustrious bishop of Jerusalem [Note: Letter 31, §1]. She also gave him a tunic made of lambs’ wool [Col. 0096B]. After Paulinus had worn it for some time out of reverence, he sent it to Severus, to whom he had immediately intended it when he received it [Note: Letter 26, §5].

Melania arrived precisely during the days when Paulinus received Victor, whom Severus had sent—namely, as winter was ending [Note: Letter 26, §6; Letter 28, §3]. In a letter Severus warned Paulinus not to think him fatigued by the great number and quantity of volumes carried by Victor [Note: Letter 28, §4]. These volumes are understood to refer to the three letters from the preceding journey, all of them very long. On the contrary, Severus said that he had been wonderfully refreshed by them and asked Paulinus, if possible, to trouble him with even more writing [Note: Letter 29, §1]. He also praised the earlier writings in the highest terms.

### 3.

Severus also asked Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0095] Ep. 28, no. 3.] to instruct him, as a more learned man, in whatever matters concerning the annals not of one nation alone but of the human race had escaped him, since he was devoting himself to investigating them. He indicated that he was laboring especially over reconciling the chronology of the kings of Judah and Israel, a knowledge he needed in order to compose a universal history, which he extended to the year 400 and which he may have completed after that year.

He sent him [Note: [Col. 0095] Ep. 29, no. 1.] cloaks woven from camel hair. In the preceding year Severus had written this letter and had hoped that Victor would spend the winter with Paulinus and afterward return immediately. “For you,” Paulinus says [Note: [Col. 0095] Ep. 28, no. 3.], “truly fervent with the Spirit of God, will warm him more healthfully during the cold season with the fiery warmth of your faith; but I, being cold, will be more suited to his summer station.” Yet Paulinus says that Victor [Note: [Col. 0095] Ibid.], received as winter was ending, had necessarily to be detained through the spring months; and because the interval seemed short, while Paulinus himself had been extremely ill during that period and was unable to attend to the business of replying, he kept Victor through midsummer and did not allow him to leave until the end of summer, so that he might reach Severus in autumn and once again provide him with a winter companion.

To Victor he gave for delivery to Severus his twenty-eighth letter, to which he had appended [Note: [Col. 0095] Ibid., no. 6.] the *Panegyric on Theodosius* [Col. 0097A], not yet published, together with a poem on Saint Felix. Concerning the comparison of chronological reckonings from earlier times, he writes that he had never devoted himself to this study; but he had sent his little work to Rufinus. If Rufinus should not set forth these historical matters, Paulinus feared that he would seek them in vain from someone else in those regions; but if Rufinus should write back anything on the subject, he promised to forward it.
