[Note: [Col. 0097] Ep. 29, no. 5.] Paulinus sent Severus a tunic woven from lambs’ wool, which he said was for him a token received through Melania’s blessing. From the praises Severus had bestowed upon him [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., no. 1; and Ep. 28, no. 4.] he drew greater material for humility, as his reply clearly demonstrates. But he added a second letter to this earlier one, namely the twenty-ninth, in which [Note: [Col. 0097] Ep. 29, nos. 1 and 4.] from the cloaks woven of camel hair he takes occasion to confess himself a sinner in need of the garment and labor of penance, and explains this at considerable length. The remainder [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., no. 6.] consists of a eulogy of Melania, [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., no. 13.] for whom, since she was staying at Rome, he says he was anxious.

In this same year, and no later, Paulinus sent Severus his thirtieth letter, which Augustine [Note: [Col. 0097] Aug., Ep. 186, no. 40.] cited in discussing original sin. It has already been discussed above, chapter 20, no. 1.

### 4.

Severus had presumably requested [Note: [Col. 0097] Paulinus, Ep. 30, no. 2.] portraits of Paulinus and Therasia. Paulinus reproaches him for being irrational about this and for nearly becoming delirious through excessive affection. Ingeniously interpreting the request as referring to the inner person, he evades it, and with his customary elegance and holiness discusses the matter.

Finally he concludes by saying [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., no. 6.] that if Severus has so great a love for obtaining even visible consolations, he can, through the guiding lines of his mind, instruct painters—whether unskilled or ignorant of Paulinus and Therasia—to portray them, presenting to their memory the faces he wished painted, as though offering for imitation the features of those sitting before them.

“But if perhaps,” Paulinus adds [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid.], “a hand unskilled in understanding your word should err in its art [Note: [Col. 0097] Perhaps *artificis*, ‘of the artist,’ should be read.], it will paint us unlike others; yet for you, who always contemplate and embrace us in your mind, whatever faces its incompetence may paint under our name, we shall nevertheless be what your conscience knows us to be.”

Severus seems to have done this, since in the following year [Note: [Col. 0097] Ep. 32, no. 2.] he had Paulinus painted in a sacred building. We therefore infer that this letter was written in the present year, though it could not have been composed much earlier: the hope by which Severus had been encouraged to visit Paulinus was certainly cast down when he requested a portrait of Paulinus. It is not apparent by whom this letter was delivered [Col. 0097D], nor does it contain any historical information.

## CHAPTER XLII. Paulinus orders a new basilica to be built beside Saint Felix’s tomb and adorns it with various paintings.

### 1.

As we said above [Note: [Col. 0097] Chapter 37, no. 3.], Paulinus had begun in the year 400 to construct buildings adjoining the church of Saint Felix. He completed them in the third year afterward, namely 402 [Note: [Col. 0098A];] and we read that all, or at least some, were dedicated on January 14, 403 [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., verses 2 and 187.].

After Felix’s death [Note: [Col. 0097] *Carm.* 18, verse 170.] a tomb was erected which corresponded not to the merits of so great a man, but to the afflicted condition of the Church, oppressed by the persecutions of unbelievers. Yet the virtue of so great a man, enclosed in a small tomb, shone forth so wonderfully that within a short time [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., verse 170.] it was adorned with five basilicas, whose rooflines, visible from far away, presented the appearance of a city.

Paulinus discusses these five basilicas in his poems from the beginning of the year 399 [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid.], perhaps counting among them some chapel which, although it was not a basilica, could nevertheless have been called by that name. For when he speaks this year of the new basilica as completed [Note: [Col. 0097] Ep. 32, no. 10.], he says that it had been added to four ancient ones.

But those basilicas—four or five—which Paulinus had found at Nola when he arrived were not sufficient for the crowds flocking to Saint Felix’s tomb [Note: [Col. 0097] *Carm.* 18, verse 182; and *Carm.* 24, verse 491.]. He therefore ordered a new one to be built. Its apse, faced with marble from floor to walls, and its ceiling gleaming with mosaic, made it splendid. There the Trinity shone forth in its full mystery: the Father was signified by a voice thundering from a cloud, Christ by a lamb, and the Spirit by a dove. Moreover, a cross was surrounded by a crown and a luminous sphere; within the crown the apostles were represented in the form of a flock of doves. Then from the rock flowed four springs, beside which stood the four evangelists, the four living rivers of Christ. Verses inscribed there explained all these things.

Within the apse [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid.] there could be seen a *trichorum* (a three-apsed chamber), containing an altar beneath which sacred relics of apostles and martyrs had been deposited, together with a fragment of the wood of the cross which Melania had brought to him from Jerusalem in this very year.

The entire space of the basilica outside the shell of the apse [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., no. 12.] was expanded beneath a lofty, coffered roof by twin porticoes on either side, with a double row of columns extending through each arch. [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid.] Within the porticoes, four chambers inserted along each of the basilica’s long sides provided suitable places for those praying in private or meditating on the law of the Lord, and also for memorials of religious persons and family members—for rest in eternal peace.

Then, when [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., nos. 13 and 16.] the apse was widened into a curve within its spacious compass by two small apses on the right and left, the left one received those praying and meditating on the holy law, while the right was open to the bishop offering sacrifices of rejoicing. It resembled a venerable storeroom in which the vessels and ornaments of the sacred ministry were stored and from which they were brought forth to be carried to the altar.

### 2.

In this new basilica Paulinus wished the history of the Old Law—that is, [Note: [Col. 0097] *Carm.* 24, verse 517.] of the Pentateuch, Joshua, and Ruth—to be painted, [Note: [Col. 0097] Ibid., verse 58.] with explanatory captions added, for the benefit of those who gathered there every year from all directions for Saint Felix’s feast. Nearly all of them were peasants, and so rustic and inexperienced that they considered it an especially religious act to set up tables over the tombs of the saints and, indulging in banquets, spend the night in the basilicas amid repeated feasting and drinking.

“So they approve what the teachers who died condemned?

Does Peter’s table receive what Peter’s teaching rejects?”

Paulinus exclaims [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 568; 1 Peter 4:3.].

This abuse had already become widespread in the Church and had been abolished by Saint Ambrose at Milan, as well as by several bishops in other places [Note: [Col. 0099] See note 313.]. Augustine removed it from the African Church with every effort [Note: [Col. 0099] Aug., Ep. 22, and Sermons 5 and 101 *On Div*.], but more by teaching than by commanding, and by admonishing than by threatening.

Paulinus followed the same course with the same disposition: [Note: [Col. 0099] Paulinus, *Carm.* 24, verse 580.] he adorned the entire basilica with various paintings, so that the peasants might be drawn away from their drinking parties to contemplate these new works and, becoming more temperate, be converted to a holier life.

According to Paulinus himself [Note: [Col. 0099] Ep. 32, no. 13.], basilicas of this period generally faced east. Departing from common practice, however, Paulinus built the new basilica toward the church of Saint Felix.

A wall blocked the new basilica from the old one, with a certain monument and an apse placed between them. On the side of Saint Felix’s basilica, this wall was opened by three doors. Paulinus opened an equal number of entrances in the façade of the new basilica, and with three corresponding arches opened the whole of this basilica toward the basilica of the aforesaid confessor through a perforated screen. To those looking from either side into the other, this offered a most joyful view, like a threefold passageway.

[Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., no. 14.] At the very entrances of the new basilica, on the right and left, Paulinus painted a cross in vermilion, encircled by a ring-shaped flowering crown, with doves above it as a heavenly sign.

[Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., no. 15.] Within the screen, through which that short interval—rather separating than joining the neighboring basilicas—continued, a fountain flowed for washing the hands and rinsing the mouths of those entering the sacred buildings. [Note: [Col. 0099] See notes 41 and 169.] In that age such fountains were common before the opposite façades of churches, and they can still be seen in the atria of cathedrals and principal churches. [Note: [Col. 0099] See note 41.] Later these fountains were replaced by the vessel of lustral water customarily placed at the entrance of a church.

Besides the entrance on the side of Saint Felix’s basilica, another entrance was open [Note: [Col. 0099] Ep. 32, no. 12.], above whose door stood a crowned cross.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Paulinus adorns the ancient basilica of Saint Felix with paintings and surrounds it outside with numerous buildings.

### 1.

In addition to this new church, Paulinus adorned the aforementioned basilica of Saint Felix with new decorations [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 383.]. In its arched ceiling, carved coffering made ivory appear to be set in wood [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 385.], and lamps hanging from the roof above were held by bronze chains.

This basilica had stood with ugly pillars in a massive array [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 395; and *Carm.* 25, verse 200.]. After they had been transformed for the better, he supported it—if I am not mistaken—with marble columns as well [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 394.], thereby greatly increasing both its space and its light.

Verses still exist today in Saint Felix’s basilica [Note: [Col. 0099] See note 161.] unmistakably inscribed by Saint Paulinus’s hand [Col. 0100A], and they declare that the basilica had been made larger and brighter.

Paulinus also painted it [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 386; and *Carm.* 25, verse 212.], so that it appeared as new as the other basilica. In it [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 173.] he depicted the history of the New Testament; and beneath the altar table [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 403.] he deposited the ashes and relics of Saints John the Baptist, Andrew, Thomas, Luke, Agricola, Vitalis, Proculus, Nazarius, and Euphemia.

### 2.

This basilica had three entrances [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 456.]. Opposite the new basilica [Note: [Col. 0099] Ep. 32, no. 13.] there were three entrances. [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., no. 12.] On the other side there was a small door through which a private entrance opened from Paulinus’s garden.

In addition, two larger doors opened [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 374.] onto the principal atrium, in which [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 362.] there had formerly been a portico beneath a dark roof. Through Paulinus’s care and effort it increased in painted decoration and height [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 366; and *Carm.* 5, verse 8.], and it seems not to have been covered.

Not far from there was an old garden [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 367; and *Carm.* 25, verse 270.] and a mound of rubble. Paulinus ordered it cleared, and on that site [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 274.] he built new houses.

In addition, there was a certain open area [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 368.] which flooded the sacred building with abundant light. It was enclosed by porticoes and also by a double covering over chambers that converged through the vestibule [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 25, verse 56.].

There was also another, smaller courtyard, but richer in decoration, located farther within. It was joined, as it were, to three basilicas, opening from one point into different entrances to them all. It was further adorned with surrounding porticoes supported by marble columns. Upon these were upper chambers, roofed like sacred buildings beneath a double covering, with windows above looking toward the altar [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 400.]. Those who came to Saint Felix’s tomb to pray devoutly to God were lodged there [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 449.].

In the courtyard there were fountains of various and manifold forms, especially a brilliantly gleaming basin covered by a bronze tower with a gridded roof [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 25, verses 31 ff.]. Paulinus had constructed many cisterns [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 24, verse 470.] to collect rainwater and pour it into these fountains, since the city was far away and scarcely any aqueduct conveyed even a small drop there through a narrow channel [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 465.].

On another side a portico could be seen, supported in the middle by columns and opening into two spaces. Beneath its roof it joined halls separated from one another by an entrance [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 480.].

Another elongated building was also visible [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 484.], divided by several atria and offering a view of a meadow or field; it was enclosed by a fence so that the sacred buildings would not be exposed to profane eyes.

Paulinus further notes [Note: [Col. 0099] *Carm.* 25, verse 15.] several very narrow chambers, access to which was opened through three doors. [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 24.] The first was filled with the sacred deeds of Job and Tobias; the second was adorned with images of numerous martyrs of both sexes; in the third, the deeds of Judith and Esther had been elegantly rendered by the painter’s brush.

Within the interior of the larger court or church [Note: [Col. 0099] Ibid., verse 180.], set into its recess, there lay a chamber of greater height, beautiful from a distance beneath a starry dome and with three recesses. In its center a baptismal fountain shone, in which no one had yet been baptized; nor was there lacking an altar for celebrating the sacred mysteries [Col. 0101A].

This place may perhaps have been merely adorned, decorated, and renovated by Paulinus, since he admits [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, no. 1.] that Severus surpassed him in this respect because Severus had built a baptistery.

These are almost all the additions and decorations which our Paulinus, as far as we have been able to ascertain, describes as having been made by him in honor of Saint Felix, whom he had adopted as his patron. More penetrating eyes will not fail to discover further details.

### 3.

Paulinus testifies that these buildings were acceptable to God [Note: [Col. 0101] *Carm.* 25, verses 62 ff.], and this was also confirmed by a certain miracle.

In the middle of the courtyard, near the church doors, stood two old wooden houses. Their ugly obstruction blocked the view and ruined the beauty of all the works. Paulinus wished to remove them, but their owner swore that he would rather suffer death than leave the place.

“His voice indeed seemed contemptible;

but, I confess, it was the very thing

that wearied me with resentment, for I was tired

even of winning the quarrel,”

says Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0101] *Carm.* 25, verse 72.].

But [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., verses 75 ff.] one night, suddenly and unexpectedly, one of the chambers caught fire and blazed so fiercely that the church itself and the entire neighborhood were endangered. For a long time efforts to hold back the flames were fruitless, until Paulinus himself entered Saint Felix’s temple and poured forth humble prayers to God. Strengthened by the martyr’s prayers and also by the merits of the apostles whose ashes and relics lay hidden beneath the altar of the neighboring church, he later returned to the house and held out against the flames a fragment taken from the wood of the true cross. The flames immediately checked their advance and turned back toward the place from which they had arisen [Col. 0101C]; there, when their fuel failed, they were soon extinguished.

When morning came, only one house was found to have been consumed by the fire. But its owner, enraged because the house had been destroyed by such a pitiable—or, rather, marvelous—disaster, demolished the other one himself. Thus Paulinus obtained what he had wished without a lawsuit.

That other basilica in which we said that Paulinus had prayed and invoked the apostles seems to have been the new basilica he had built. Since we read that relics had already been placed beneath its altar, it is clear that it had already been dedicated at that time.

Besides the fragment of the wood of the true Cross which he placed beneath that altar [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, no. 11.], he had reserved another fragment [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 31, nos. 1 and 2.] from Melania’s gift to send to Severus in the following year. But whether that basilica was dedicated in this year or the next, it was certainly dedicated [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, no. 15.] by Bishop Paul, then bishop of the Nolani Church [Col. 0101D].

# IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 403

## CHAPTER XLIV. Paulinus likewise orders a basilica to be built at Fundi and sends Severus poems for the Primuliacum basilica.

### 1.

In addition to Paulinus’s customary festival, another solemnity was added this year [Note: [Col. 0101] *Carm.* 25, verse 2.], namely the dedication of all the works that had been added to the sacred building of Saint Felix and recently completed, shining forth everywhere with equal splendor; or at least the dedication of the baptistery [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., verse 186.] consecrated by the bishop (Paul) for the use of baptism and sacrifice, where he administered both sacraments on the same day.

For these new buildings and for the fire of the previous year, Paulinus composed a birthday poem in praise of Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0101] *Carm.* 25.], which has been transmitted to us complete. It includes pious reflections on the spiritual renewal of the Christian soul, and with this noble poem he concludes [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., verse 314.]:

> Let us not, then, remain old amid new buildings . . .
>
> Let the former life perish, let the future life perish no more;
>
> Let us willingly abandon the world, which must not be abandoned unwillingly,
>
> Unless we flee willingly; let us die, lest we die:
>
> Let us cover our deadly life with life-giving death;
>
> Let the earthly perish, let the heavenly image take its place;
>
> And let Adam be changed into Christ, and here too be transformed,
>
> So that we may be transformed there: whoever now remains himself
>
> Will remain the same and will never be changed from himself for eternity.

Paulinus also ordered a church to be built at Fundi [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, no. 17.], a town where he had once owned estates and maintained a family residence. Thus, as a token of civic charity, he gave a basilica to the town itself, since it needed one, having only a small and dilapidated building.

This later basilica does not seem to have been much larger than the earlier one, for Paulinus sometimes calls it [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid.] a “little basilica.” Its inscription, which he sent to Severus, shows how he painted the apse [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid.], and it is said [Note: [Col. 0101] See note 174.] that not long ago something from this painting was seen at Rome.

Paulinus placed beneath its altar the relics of Saints Andrew, Luke, Nazarius, Protasius, and Gervasius [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, no. 17.]. When this basilica was almost completed and was soon to be consecrated in the name of Christ, of the saints, of the holy martyr, and of the Lord of lords [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., no. 17; and Ep. 31, no. 1.] [Col. 0102C].

### 2.

This year Paulinus sent Severus his thirty-first and thirty-second letters [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, nos. 1 and 10.], since Severus too was devoting himself to building religious sites.

In particular, Severus had the baptistery of his basilica constructed [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., nos. 1 and 2.], decorating it on one side with images of Saint Martin and on the other with images of Paulinus. He also added certain poems [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., no. 4.], now lost, in which he spoke of light and honeycombs. When he wrote to Paulinus through Victor [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 28, no. 3.], who was to winter with Severus, he warned him that he would erase these poems if Paulinus sent others.

Victor added [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, no. 1; and Ep. 32, no. 7.] that Severus desired relics of saints to be deposited in this church. Paulinus informed him [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 31, no. 1.] that he had none left except those which he was reserving for the Fundi basilica, soon to be dedicated.

But the fragment of the wood of the true cross which remained to him from Melania’s gift [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., no. 2.] he sent, enclosed in a golden tube, to Bassula, Sulpicius Severus’s mother-in-law, in the name of his wife Therasia. This was equivalent to giving it as a gift to Severus himself. Accordingly, Paulinus testifies elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0101] Ep. 32, no. 7.] that he had sent it to Severus, and advises him to place it beneath the altar of the church among the other relics, unless he preferred to keep it for daily protection and healing [Note: [Col. 0101] Ibid., no. 8.].

He also explains [Note: [Col. 0103] Ep. 31, no. 2.] with what reverence he ought to handle so precious an object, and relates how the cross was discovered by Helena [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., no. 3.].

When space on the page allowed it, he began a long letter anew [Note: [Col. 0103] Ep. 32, no. 1.], in which he complains [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., no. 2.] that Severus had treated him either with excessive honor or with insult, since he had compared him with Saint Martin.

Later, however, he deliberately turned the discussion in that direction, as though Severus had displayed in Martin the pattern of justice and the perfection of the virtues, but in Paulinus the crushing awareness and confession of iniquity, so that Martin might be held forth as an example to the blessed and Paulinus to the wretched.

He sent him two epigrams expressing this idea and asked that, if Severus wished to place them in the baptistery, he nevertheless preserve his own poems.

He declares that he did all this [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., no. 4.] out of his supreme devotion to Severus, fearing sin more from failing to obey than from excessive speaking. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., no. 10.] he was induced, at Victor’s urging, to send verses for the two basilicas at Nola and Fundi, and also to compose new verses to be inscribed on the walls of Severus’s basilicas [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., nos. 5 and 7–8.], as well as on the tomb of Saint Clarus the martyr, who rested in one of them. Victor had supplied the subject matter by describing the work.

After Paulinus had said much about those material buildings [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., nos. 18 and 25.], he turned the discussion toward the spiritual meaning of building, about which, in his customary manner, he will speak splendidly.

## CHAPTER XLV. Paulinus writes to Alethius and Florentius, bishop of Cahors. The death of his brother.

### 1.

Perhaps on this same journey Victor, their common courier [Note: [Col. 0103] Ep. 33, nos. 1 and 2.], brought Paulinus a letter from Alethius [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., no. 2.], who, as I suppose, requested something from his scholarly labors. This token of goodwill was as sweet to Paulinus as it was unexpected, but Paulinus’s humility resisted Alethius’s request.

The thirty-third letter, in which Paulinus replies to Alethius, is incomplete. Its continuation, which concerns Saint Paula’s daughter, belongs to the thirteenth letter to Pammachius.

Chifflet supposes [Note: [Col. 0103] Chiffl., p. 47.] that Paulinus yielded to Alethius’s wishes and sent him the discourse on the Treasury, which in a Vatican manuscript is expressly addressed to Alethius.

But since Paulinus speaks to many people [Note: [Col. 0103] Paulinus, 34, no. 1.], I would call it a sermon to the people rather than a letter, although we have assigned it a place among the letters so that it might retain its numerical order.

Anyone could easily judge that Paulinus had at some time been asked by the bishop of Nola to teach the people especially the virtue and merit of almsgiving, for he was an excellent preacher and teacher. This discourse deals principally with that subject, and it is the most elegant and pleasing of all Paulinus’s works.

Its style is much purer than that of the letters. Since he was compelled to elaborate it carefully, its composition appears more restrained; in it he curbed the usual abundance and rapidity of his language in the letters.

It is entitled *On the Treasury* for no other reason than that it first speaks of the treasury. Following Tertullian, Paulinus calls it a table placed in the church on which alms distributed to the poor were stored.

Alethius is rightly and deservedly praised by Jerome [Note: [Col. 0103] See Dissertation 3, no. 2.] in the year 407, since he was distinguished by the character of so great a priest. Everyone agrees that after his brother Florentius died he became bishop of Cahors.

### 2.

Paulinus also wrote to Florentius. We mention this because the date of composition of the forty-second letter is not entirely certain; nevertheless, we think it was written around the year 405.

Paulinus received letters from Florentius [Note: [Col. 0103] Paulinus, Ep. 42, no. 1.], whom he had not previously known, filled with courtesy and kindness, as though an ancient bond of intimacy and familiarity had already existed between them.

Paulinus replied to him with equal kindness and generosity, and he rejoiced so much that he had gained the friendship of this bishop and had been enriched by his affection [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid.] that he offered abundant thanks to God for him.

We read nothing distinctive about this Florentius. Paulinus praises his letter magnificently [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., nos. 1 and 2.], saying that its discourse, seasoned with apostolic salt, expressed the flavor of the grace granted to him; just as the sweetness of his eloquence openly showed how sweet the Lord was in him.

Paulinus adds [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid., nos. 2 and 3.] that through the gentleness of a sheep and the innocence of a lamb Florentius had merited becoming a shepherd, and that his soul, elevated through humility and gentleness of heart, applied itself each day to drawing souls out of the bitter and deep waves of this age with the hook of saving speech [Col. 0104C], for this work he had been chosen to share the lot of the apostles.

Some people made this Florentius a bishop of Tibur [Note: [Col. 0103] See Chifflet, pp. 10–11.], because at that time a bishop of Tibur by that name was living. But the authority of three manuscripts, in which he is called bishop of Cahors, must be preferred to this slight conjecture.

### 3.

At the beginning of the following year Paulinus included Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, among the saints [Note: [Col. 0103] Paulinus, *Carm.* 30, verse 76.], whose relics commended those regions. We therefore should not assign the thirty-fifth letter to Delphinus to a later date than the present year [Note: [Col. 0103] Ep. 35.]. In it he replies to Delphinus’s extremely brief earlier letter, from which—or from some other indication—he had perhaps learned of his brother’s death around the same time.

For that reason Paulinus did not write a lengthy letter to Delphinus. He expressed only his grief—not so much at his brother’s death as at his conduct, which he mourned as inconsistent both with Christian piety and with his own wishes.

He asks Delphinus for prayers for his brother’s soul and for himself.

For the same reason he sent a somewhat longer thirty-sixth letter to Amandus [Note: [Col. 0103] Ep. 36, no. 2.].

# IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 404

## CHAPTER XLVI. Victricius, Aper, and Augustine write to Paulinus; he replies to them. Pelagius also writes to Paulinus.

### 1.

Of the poem which Paulinus issued at the beginning of this year in praise of Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0105] *Carm.* 27.] only a few fragments remain. They treat of the relics of the saints, which God scattered throughout the world as though to expiate it. Had the poem survived entire, it would have made known to us how great a terror the name of Alaric had brought upon Italy in the preceding year—Italy into which he had descended and from which he withdrew after the battle of Pollentia.

This year Victricius, bishop of Rouen, wrote to Paulinus through Candidianus [Note: [Col. 0105] Ep. 37, no. 1.], and Paulinus replied in his thirty-seventh letter. Let the reader consult Dissertation 4. Aper likewise wrote to Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0105] Ep. 38, no. 1.] concerning his conversion to Christ, and Paulinus replied to him in the same year in his thirty-eighth letter. For who Aper was and what intercourse he had with Paulinus, see Dissertation 5.

In this year, as it seems [Note: [Col. 0105] See Aug., Ep. 78 and chronological order.], the priest Boniface and a layman named Spes caused a very great scandal at Hippo. Since Augustine could not settle their dispute, or at least explain it to others, he ordered both men to proceed to a place famed for miracles, so that God might reveal the innocence or guilt of one or the other. He therefore sent them to the place where the body of blessed Felix of Nola was buried [Note: [Col. 0105] Aug., Ep. 78, no. 3.], because from there a more ready and trustworthy report could be written to him concerning whatever might be divinely revealed about the matter. Without doubt he said this out of regard for Paulinus, with whom it is probable that he always maintained the correspondence begun in 395, although no letter of his survives from 396 until this year.

The outcome of the dispute between Boniface and Spes does not appear. Perhaps on this occasion Augustine sent Paulinus the letter mentioned in the following year [Note: [Col. 0105] Aug., Ep. 80, no. 2.], in which, as it seems, he proposed a question about our obligation always to obey God’s will. Paulinus replied to him [Note: [Col. 0105] This letter of Paulinus is lost.] that he had resolved to remain in the place where he was happily settled, but that, should the Lord will anything else concerning him, he would prefer God’s will to his own. Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0105] Aug., Ep. 80, no. 2.] that Paulinus had spoken in his letter with a thoroughly Christian understanding and devotion, but too cursorily and briefly; and he wished that he had explained the point somewhat more fully, since the matter was to know the will of God which must be preferred to our own. We have neither Augustine’s letter nor Paulinus’s reply, which he probably sent through Celsus, a member of his household [Note: [Col. 0105] See below, no. 2.].

# IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 405

### 2.

Nothing remains to us of the poem Paulinus wrote this year in honor of Saint Felix. In the very first months Augustine sent Paulinus two letters [Note: [Col. 0105] Aug., Ep. 80, no. 1.]: one, now lost, through Fortunatianus, a priest of Thagaste travelling to Rome; the other through Celsus. Since Celsus was hurrying to return to Nola, Augustine at once wrote a few words [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid.], for Celsus did not give him the opportunity to write as much as he wished. Augustine asks Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid., no. 2.] to write back by what signs God’s will may be known in the circumstances of human life, in which it often cannot readily be discerned.

It is plainly apparent from that letter how highly Augustine valued Paulinus. He says [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid., no. 1.] that he could not, and indeed ought not, retain Celsus, who was better off with Paulinus than with himself. The African Church was often compelled, in many most serious emergencies, to send bishops to Italy; and it appears that nearly all these bishops went to Nola to greet Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid. and Ep. 95, no. 1.]. Augustine was consoled that Theasius and Evodius, both later confessors, continually saw Paulinus with the eyes of friends. The latter was most closely associated with Augustine. They had been delegated by the Council of Carthage to seek laws against the unbridled violence of the Donatists, and in this very year, in February, they obtained them.

They visited Paulinus; and Augustine, who was awaiting them, said when Celsus left [Note: [Col. 0105] Ep. 80, no. 1.] that Paulinus would come to him in the hearts and conversations of those bishops. Once he had been satisfied as far as possible by what they reported, he promised to send him a longer letter, a debt which he confessed he owed him. This letter does not now appear, nor does any one of those which they may have sent each other up to the year 408.

### 3.

Pelagius, who before his heresy became publicly known had been a friend of many holy men, was loved by Paulinus also as a servant of God. [Note: [Col. 0105] Augustine, Letter 186, §1.] Augustine says that he sent to Paulinus letters of this arch-heretic, [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid., §1.] in which Pelagius claimed that he sufficiently acknowledged grace, since he confessed that God had implanted in us the will and free choice. This appears to be the same letter to Paulinus, about 300 lines long—as Augustine himself reckons it—[Note: [Col. 0105] Augustine, *On Grace*, ch. 55.] which Pelagius produced in 417 to prove that his faith was sincere and orthodox. Augustine does not say that anything in that letter was absolutely evil, but maintains that Pelagius wrote in it about grace only in a very qualified and scarcely tolerable manner. Pelagius testified that he had written this letter about twelve years earlier, and therefore around the year 405. [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid.]

We discuss Aper’s conversion at length in Dissertation 5. Concerning his letter to Paulinus [p. 82], and Paulinus’s reply to him, we spoke in the preceding year. [Note: [Col. 0105] Chapter 46, §1.] Aper wrote to him again [Note: [Col. 0105] Paulinus, Letter 39, §2.] and complained that the possessions of his sons were the reason he was compelled to concern himself with earthly matters, since he ought to have sold them. He praised Paulinus’s poverty [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid., §3.] and described, in broad and powerful language, the garden at Nola. [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid., §4.]

Paulinus, in his own name and that of Therasia, replied to Aper and Amanda. [Note: [Col. 0107] Letter 39, title.] He urged them to draw from their lawful possessions as much as they could for the education of the soul; [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid., §2.] to consider themselves the field of Christ; and to offer God, the Lord, such cultivation of their hearts as they wished their own field to receive in order that it might bear fruit. [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid., §3.] Paulinus then humbles himself and speaks of his own temptations. [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid., §4.] Around this year Paulinus wrote Letters 40 and 41 to Sanctus and Amanda. See *Life*, ch. 25.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### Paulinus writes to Severus and Desiderius. Severus urges Posthumianus to visit Paulinus.

### 1.

Through Victor, Sulpicius Severus wrote to Paulinus in that year, as we believe. [Note: [Col. 0107] Paulinus, Letter 43, §§1–2.] We do not know the precise contents of the letter, except that he asked Paulinus to send Victor back to him as soon as possible, so that he might return in time for the vintage season. [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid., §3.]

Victor also delivered to him a letter from the presbyter Desiderius, who asked Paulinus to explain the blessings with which Jacob, when near death, blessed his sons. After spending a short time at Nola, Victor prepared to resume his journey, so that Paulinus wrote brief letters to Desiderius and Severus; both have been lost. [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid., §§1–2.] Perhaps at the same time, or shortly afterward, Letter 42 was written to Florentius, bishop of Cahors, concerning which we spoke at length above. [Note: [Col. 0107] Chapter 45, §2.]

But just as Victor was about to depart, sudden obstacles held him back, while winter closed navigation and the roads through fear. Because of these hindrances, necessity compelled him to remain at Nola until the end of winter. [Note: [Col. 0107] Letter 43, §1.] The danger that closed the roads was undoubtedly the fear that Roman or enemy armies might encounter the travelers on the way. This may be referred either to Alaric’s descent into Italy in 403 [Note: [Col. 0107] Prosper, *Chronicle.] or to that of Radagaisus in 405. Since we have assigned to the year 403 another letter of Paulinus to Severus, delivered to him by Victor, this fear must be referred instead to Radagaisus’s invasion, which caused far greater terror in Italy than Alaric did. Radagaisus’s army is said to have been destroyed only around wintertime. Even if it had existed earlier, however, Roman troops might still have been scattered in many places; and since most of them were barbarians, they could have frightened travelers.

### 2.

In that same year, apparently, Posthumianus returned from the East after spending the entire three years there. [Note: [Col. 0107] Sulpicius, *Dialogues* 1.2.] He reached Marseilles from Egypt on the thirtieth day, and on the tenth day from the city of Marseilles he reached the place where Sulpicius Severus lived. Posthumianus’s first conversations with Sulpicius Severus supplied the material for the *Dialogues*. Toward the end of those conversations, [Note: [Col. 0107] Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 3.17.] since Posthumianus was soon to return to the East, Severus urged him to travel through Campania, even though this would take him far out of his way:

> “Do not value the loss caused by such a great delay so highly that you fail to visit there the illustrious man praised throughout the world, Paulinus. I beg you, first read through for him the volume of our conversation, whether we completed it yesterday or spoke it today. You will report everything to him; you will recite the whole work to him, so that Rome may soon learn through him the holy man’s praises, just as he spread our first little book not only throughout Italy but also throughout all Illyricum. He, who does not begrudge Martin the glory, and who is a most devout judge of the holy virtues in Christ, will not refuse to compare our bishop with his Felix.”

When Paulinus died, he had with him a certain presbyter named Posthumianus. [Note: [Col. 0107] Uranius, *On the Death of Paulinus*, §2.] I cannot establish whether this was the same man who, after returning from the East, attached himself to Paulinus.

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 406

### 3.

The title of the thirteenth birthday poem [Note: [Col. 0107] Paulinus, poem 28, title.] in honor of Saint Felix, which according to the sequence of our history was written at the beginning of this year, is: “On the Destruction of the Gothic Army with Its King.” These words clearly indicate the disaster of Radagaisus. [Note: [Col. 0107] See note 329.] That disaster was always regarded as a clear and remarkable sign of God’s protection of the empire and of the Christian religion. The few verses that survive from this poem [Note: [Col. 0107] Poem 28.] show that Paulinus attributed the victory to the martyrs of Rome and of the empire. [Note: [Col. 0107] Chapter 47, §1.]

We have seen that Victor was sent to Paulinus in the preceding year by Severus and Desiderius, and that he was forced to wait at Nola until the spring weather arrived so that he could return to Gaul. While he was waiting, he was attacked by a very serious illness and brought to the point of death. Paulinus endured this affliction with compassion; although Victor was already sick beyond hope in everyone’s judgment, Paulinus nevertheless hoped for his recovery because of Severus’s faith and merits. In fact, Victor recovered, but he spent more time regaining his health than the illness itself had lasted; he was fully restored only near the feast of the apostles. Paulinus did not wish to send him away so quickly. He kept him until he could take him with him to Rome as his companion for the annual journey, so that Victor might depart from there on his return to Gaul and reach Severus in time for the vintage season—at the very time Severus had specified, [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid., §2.] but in the following year.

Paulinus gave Victor two brief letters, which he had written in the preceding year to Severus and Desiderius when Victor had wished to depart, to deliver to them. He also added two longer letters to the same men, written with his mind released and relaxed in leisure. The longer letter addressed to Severus was lost, and nothing remains of the letters he may subsequently have written to him. [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid., §§1–2.]

### 4.

In the Acherian *Spicilegium* we possess two letters addressed in Severus’s name to Paulinus. The first is certainly Severus’s letter to Paulinus, and for that reason we included it above. [Note: [Col. 0107] Chapter 38, §1.] The second also could have been sent to Paulinus, and it would be a notable testimony to his piety, since it is a thanksgiving made in the name of the writer and, apparently, of other country people, who had been taught the truth and the worship of God through his exhortations and had not been frightened by threats.

But since it is established that this letter is not by Severus, we do not dare, relying on this single authority, to attribute to Paulinus matters that perhaps do not suit him. When Paulinus had shown in his letter to Desiderius why Victor would not return until a year had passed, he excused himself with the greatest humility for the work Desiderius had requested, and asked him to explain the blessings of the twelve patriarchs himself. [Note: [Col. 0109] Letter 43, §4.]

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
### Paulinus obtains from Rufinus an explanation of the blessings of the twelve patriarchs. He writes to Aper and praises Melania’s son.

### 1.

Paulinus again requested this explanation of the blessings from Rufinus. [Note: [Col. 0109] Letter 46, §2.] In his forty-seventh letter to Rufinus he testifies that others had consulted him about it. [Note: [Col. 0109] Letter 47, §2.] Rufinus could not refuse him this exposition.

When Rufinus had written to Paulinus that he had come to Rome on certain business, [Note: [Col. 0109] Paulinus, Letter 46, §1.] Paulinus asked him in Letter 46 to explain the passage in which Judah is blessed by Jacob. [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid., §3.] He later wrote to him again and asked him to clarify this blessing in a threefold interpretation—historical, moral, and mystical. [Note: [Col. 0109] Gennadius, *Catalogue*, ch. 17.] Thus, after first offering an excuse, Rufinus finally complied and fulfilled Paulinus’s wishes. After receiving the first explanation of the blessing, Paulinus asked Rufinus to explain it as distributed among the other sons. Rufinus complied, and both works still survive, together with the letters he sent to Paulinus at the same time.

Therefore, leaving aside Gennadius’s authority, [Note: [Col. 0109] Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 4.] we cannot agree with Isidore, who assigns this work to Paulinus himself. Paulinus testifies that after some time he requested something of this kind from Rufinus; [Note: [Col. 0109] Paulinus, Letter 46, §3.] Rufinus, for his part, states that Paulinus had entrusted him with certain matters concerning the interpretation of Scripture. These works, however, do not survive.

From Paulinus’s earlier letter to Rufinus it is clear that Paulinus had translated something concerning Saint Clement. [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid., §2.] When Rufinus had therefore admonished him more seriously to devote himself more attentively to Greek literature, Paulinus replied that he could not fulfill this demand unless he enjoyed Rufinus’s company for a longer time and used him as his teacher.

Finally, Paulinus sent Letter 47 to Rufinus through Cerealis. Rufinus was then living in the monastery at Pinetum, from which he was soon to come to Rome in order to return to the East. This occurred around the year 409, as will at some point be demonstrated in the history of Jerome and Rufinus. [Note: [Col. 0109] See *History of Jerome*, §166.]

### 2.

We believe that in this same year, 406, Paulinus sent Letter 44 to Aper and Amanda. [Note: [Col. 0109] Paulinus, Letter 44, §1.] He had received a letter from them, which he greatly praised, and to which he said he could return nothing comparable. [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid.] At last he decided to compose his letter as a revision of their conversation, and, while again praising their letter to them, he used nearly the same words with which Augustine had written to him in the year 395. [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid., §2.]

He devoted the remainder of the letter to praising Amanda, who attended to the concerns of the world so that Aper could devote himself entirely to heavenly things and the duties of his ministry. [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid., §4.] Finally, he urged them to raise their children carefully and devoutly. [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid., §5.]

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 407

### 3.

Only certain fragments survive of the fourteenth birthday poem in honor of Saint Felix. [Note: [Col. 0109] Poem 29.] Paulinus seems to have written this poem solely to enumerate the benefits God had bestowed upon him through the help of this holy confessor. If it survived intact, we would gather much from it concerning Paulinus’s life. Even from what we possess, however, we can observe how grateful a spirit Paulinus received from God; this may rightly be attributed to Paulinus’s generosity and profound humility.

In this year also, as we believe, the elder Melania completed her journey to Africa. She perhaps carried to Augustine the letter [Note: [Col. 0109] Letter 94, §3.] in which Paulinus celebrated the virtues of this distinguished widow’s only son, who had died around the same time.

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 408

## CHAPTER XLIX  
### Paulinus writes to Augustine about Melania and receives a letter from him through Possidius. He praises many bishops of Gaul. Concerning Saint Venerandus of Clermont.

### 1.

As far as we can infer from what survives, Paulinus wrote the fifteenth birthday poem to relate the miracles of Saint Felix. [Note: [Col. 0109] Poem 30.] We know this to be the last poem about Saint Felix written by Paulinus—whether other poems have perished or whether he wrote nothing more about him. For it is clear that the disturbances that arose during the following three years could have turned Paulinus away from these spiritual recreations; after he became bishop, he considered that piety should be cultivated through other pursuits. At least he did not have enough leisure on Saint Felix’s feast day to apply his mind to writing verses.

From this year onward Paulinus had extraordinary occupations, [Note: [Col. 0109] Augustine, Letter 95, §9.] of which Augustine believed him to have been previously free. Driven by them, Paulinus perhaps had to hasten his customary pilgrimage to Rome earlier than usual. [Note: [Col. 0109] See ch. 22, §2.] He went there after Easter and returned before 15 May.

There the deacon Quintus, who had already spent some time in Rome, delivered to Paulinus a letter from Augustine, of which he was the bearer. [Note: [Col. 0109] Paulinus, Letter 45, §8.] But although Paulinus was extremely eager to read Augustine’s letter, he was unable to do so immediately. [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid., §1.] He waited until he could devote an entire day to this task during a halt on the journey, which he made in the town of Formiae, and feast upon the reading of Augustine’s letter as upon spiritual delights, freed from all the dross of cares.

Augustine had written to him about Melania’s constancy at the death of her only son. On 15 May Paulinus replied to Augustine with Letter 45, [Note: [Col. 0111] Paulinus, Letter 45, §8.] in which he continued to praise Melania. He also seems to believe that, after the resurrection, God will be praised by human voices by human beings in eternal life, but that this praise will far surpass human senses and human speech. [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid., §6.]

### 2.

Augustine replied to this letter in the following winter with Letter 95. Its bearer appears to have been Possidius, [Note: [Col. 0111] Augustine, Letter 95, §1, and marginal note.] who, while he was preparing to plead the case of his church of Calama before the emperor, took the opportunity to visit Paulinus gladly.

Around the same time Augustine sent a letter to Bishop Memor. [Note: [Col. 0111] Augustine, Letter 101.] There he discusses Memor’s son Julian, [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid., §4.] who was then a deacon and later became a heresiarch. Julian had been married to Ia, and Paulinus had written an epithalamium for Julian’s and Ia’s marriage on behalf of the father and son—the only such poem by him, just as by Augustine. We have therefore assigned it to the year 400 or thereabouts. [Note: [Col. 0111] See ch. 37, §4.]

### 3.

We may assign to this period, or rather to the year 409, the letter of the presbyter Paulinus cited by Gregory of Tours. [Note: [Col. 0111] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, ch. 13.] In it that author says:

> However the evils of the world may stand, this consolation remains for devout men: they enjoy, as though in the firmest protection, the support of illustrious bishops, most worthy of God, who were both exceedingly wise and most faithful guardians of the faith and religion.  
>   
> “You may see Exsuperius at Toulouse, Simplicius at Vienne, Amandus at Bordeaux, Diogenianus at Albi, Dinamius at Angoulême, Venerandus at Clermont, Alethius at Cahors, and now Pegasius at Périgueux.”

Rosweyde doubts whether that presbyter, the author of this letter, was our Paulinus. [Note: [Col. 0111] Note 176.] Chiffletius emphatically maintains that he was not Paulinus of Nola, [Note: [Col. 0111] Chiffletius, p. 11.] because, by distinguishing Pegasius from the others, the author sufficiently indicates that the others had already died; yet Paulinus of Nola does not seem to have survived them.

This is Chiffletius’s argument, but I do not agree with him, since Paulinus’s letter to Amandus, written before the year 404, by no means prevents Amandus and the other bishops from having died before the year 431. As for Gregory of Tours’s calling him a presbyter, this leads us to believe that Gregory designated Paulinus in the title of the letter as he actually was. Thus, if this letter is by our Paulinus—as we have no doubt it is—it must have been written before the year 410, when Paulinus already seems to have been a bishop.

Indeed, it is impossible for Amandus to have died before 410 if, as common opinion holds, he governed the church of Bordeaux before and after Severinus. And if Zosimus’s letters are not spurious, Simplicius was still living at Vienne in 417. [Note: [Col. 0111] Baronius, year 417, §§48, 51, in the appendix.]

Yet if Paulinus’s own text is carefully observed, anyone will see that Paulinus intended to describe the condition in which the Church then stood when he wrote. Accordingly, he listed living, not dead, bishops. That is why he does not say “you saw,” but “you may see,” which cannot refer to the dead. His use of the words “and now Pegasius” also seems to indicate that Pegasius was then a newly appointed bishop.

Therefore, since we believe that this Alethius, bishop of Cahors, was the man whom Jerome designates merely by the name “presbyter” in a certain letter that appears to have been written in 407, this letter does not seem to have been written by Paulinus except shortly before his episcopate, around 408 or 409.

Someone else will bring to light what history records about Exsuperius, Simplicius, and Amandus. We have discovered nothing about Diogenianus, Dinamius, or Pegasius. Concerning Alethius, see Dissertation 3, §2.

### 4.

Gregory says somewhat more about Venerandus. He was certainly a senator and probably a native of Clermont. He succeeded Saint Artemius and is counted as the seventh bishop of Clermont. Apart from Paulinus’s own testimony, we have no certain information about his deeds.

It is said that he died on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, and that his funeral rites were held the next day in the manner of a solemn procession on that feast. [Note: [Col. 0111] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, ch. 13.] Gregory of Tours asserts that many miracles were performed at his tomb. [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid., ch. 37.]

He was buried in a church that took his name and was enriched with the bodies of many saints, especially Saint Nepotianus, the fifth bishop of Clermont, [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid., ch. 37.] and Saint Liminius the martyr. [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid., ch. 36.] This basilica may still be seen in the gardens of the abbey of Saint Allyrius, [Note: [Col. 0111] Bollandists, 18 January, §6, p. 191.] but only very few relics of Saint Venerandus remain there, since the greater part was transferred on 22 December 1311 to the nearby church of Saint Allyrius, and the relics were placed separately in the shrine of Saint Allyrius.

At Clermont the memory of this translation is observed on 22 December, while the feast of the same saint is celebrated on 18 January. [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid., §§7, 1.] Saint Rusticus succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0111] Gregory of Tours, cited place, ch. 13.]

Around the year 408 Paulinus wrote Letter 46 to Rufinus, as discussed above in chapter 48, §1.

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 409

## CHAPTER L  
### Paulinus is made bishop of Nola. How he conducted himself in the episcopate.

### 1.

As we have already said, toward the end of 408 or at the beginning of 409 Augustine wrote Letter 95. [Note: [Col. 0111] Chapter 49, §2.] It is addressed jointly to Paulinus and Therasia, with epithets wholly worthy of Augustine’s affection for both. It does not appear from the letter that Paulinus was then distinguished by episcopal rank; otherwise a more honorific title would have been appropriate in the letter and would have been assigned to him by Augustine.

Rufinus supports our view. In replying to Paulinus’s Letter 47, written in 409, in the dedicatory letter of Book II of *The Blessings of the Patriarchs*, which he wrote during Lent of that year, [Note: [Col. 0113] See ch. 48, §1.] he calls Paulinus not a bishop but a brother.

However small a bishop’s diocese may be, a bishop does not seem to be free from business, as Paulinus appeared to Augustine to be in 408. Nevertheless, Augustine adds that he had been informed of Paulinus’s extraordinary occupations. This expression more likely denotes occupations arising from an unusual circumstance than those attached to the episcopate.

Just as Paulinus does not yet seem to have been distinguished by episcopal rank at the beginning of 409, so it is certain that he was already a bishop in 413, since Augustine gives him this title in Book I of *The City of God*, [Note: [Col. 0113] Augustine, Book I, ch. 10.] while reporting something Paulinus had done in 410. It may therefore reasonably be inferred that Paulinus was already a bishop in 410.

Moreover, Paulinus seems to have needed somewhere to take refuge in order to escape the hands of the Goths. Indeed, he fell into their hands unless he had been bound to feed his flock and retained by the bonds of episcopal office, from which he had been entirely free while he was a priest. In each of his letters he seems to have led a private life.

We also learn that Augustine was addressed by him as “brother” in a letter which we believe was written around the year 410. [Note: [Col. 0113] Paulinus, Letter 50, §18.] In his letters to Paulinus written around 413, and in his later works, Augustine always calls him a bishop, without mentioning his wife. It is therefore entirely probable that she had already died. [Note: [Col. 0113] Augustine, Letter 149, title.]

Chiffletius argues that Paulinus had been a bishop from the beginning of 397. [Note: [Col. 0113] Chiffletius, p. 153.] We believe that his arguments have been answered.

He could indeed have objected, with good reason, to the two letters to Victricius that we assigned to the years 399 and 404. In the published and manuscript copies, Victricius is called “brother” by Paulinus in Letter 37 of the year 404; [Note: [Col. 0113] Paulinus, Letters 37 and 18, titles.] and in Letter 18 of the year 399, according to the Vienna manuscript and others, he is likewise called “brother,” while some copies read “father.”

But this argument does not seem very weighty, since copyists can easily make this error, writing *fratri* (“to the brother”) instead of *patri* (“to the father”). Paulinus may also have addressed Victricius as “brother” merely as a term of friendship, just as Paulinus himself and Therasia, in Letter 45 sent to Augustine on 15 May 408, call Augustine “father,” “brother,” and “teacher.” [Note: [Col. 0113] Letter 45, title.]

If anyone should force us to maintain this point and admit that the two letters to Victricius were written after Paulinus’s episcopal appointment, they can easily be placed after the year 409. We assigned one to the year 399 solely because of a simple correspondence with Letter 17; the other was assigned to 404 because of the date of Innocent’s letter, which concerns Victricius’s journey to Rome, and because Paulinus says in his letter that Victricius had also come to Rome. Victricius could have undertaken two journeys.

Moreover, since we must partly or entirely remove the date of the letter of Innocent from the year 404, to which we assigned it—although not to 15 February—it must be placed on the same day of that month but in another year, perhaps 410, since Honorius spent the year 407 and part of 408 in Rome. [Note: [Col. 0113] Dissertation 4, vol. IV, §2.]

Nevertheless, the learned men whom we consulted judge that the disturbances which occurred in Gaul and Italy correspond most suitably with the journeys of Victricius and this exchange of letters as we have assigned them. History, however, records only two journeys to Rome undertaken by Victricius during the pontificate of Innocent under Honorius. For that reason we were compelled to assign Innocent’s and Paulinus’s letters to Victricius to the year 404.

Nor did we think that the matter should be decided solely from the use of the term “brother,” since we possess stronger arguments by which we can establish with certainty that episcopal rank had not been conferred upon Paulinus before 409. We should not therefore become entangled in this single difficulty concerning a title.

Our Paulinus was made bishop of Nola, as no one doubts. He seems to have succeeded Paul, who certainly governed this church in the years 402 and 403. [Note: [Col. 0113] See ch. 43, §3; ch. 44, §1, and elsewhere.] The church does not seem to have had a very large population, since Paulinus calls himself “the shepherd of a little flock.” [Note: [Col. 0113] Paulinus, Letter 49, §14.]

### 2.

Let us now learn from an eyewitness how he conducted himself in the episcopal office. [Note: [Col. 0113] Uranius, *On the Death of Paulinus*, §6.]

> When he was raised to the highest degree of priesthood, he did not wish to present himself as the kind of bishop whom anyone would fear, but made himself the kind of priest whom everyone would love. He was never so angry that he did not remember mercy in his anger. Indeed, that man could not be angry who disregarded insults and avoided hatred.  
>   
> He never sat in judgment without mercy, because he knew that mercy is better than sacrifice (Hosea 6:6). Every Christian judgment must be clothed in mercy, as venerable Scripture says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1).  
>   
> He also tempered justice with kinder intentions, knowing that just as the Holy Spirit favors equity and justice, so he graciously grants his own kindness to the merciful. Therefore he maintained strictness in examining justice, but displayed mercy in determining the sentence.

> O admirable man, worthy to be reckoned among all the virtues! For, following the examples of all the patriarchs, he was faithful like Abraham, trusting like Isaac, kind like Jacob, generous like Melchizedek, provident like Joseph, and rapacious like Benjamin: for he seized from the rich and distributed to the poor. Yet he is known to have benefited the rich more than the poor, because he benefited the poor in this world, but provided for the rich in the world to come. [Note: [Col. 0113] Uranius, §7.]

Even while dying, he received money brought from far away so that he could distribute it in alms. [Note: [Col. 0113] Uranius, *On the Death of Paulinus*, §4.] I admit that Jerome had advised him not to undertake the distribution of other people’s alms. But one thing is what prudence suggests to a private man who has recently devoted and consecrated himself to divine service; another is what piety suggests to a bishop already established in piety alone through a long exercise of virtue.

And in fact Paulinus’s piety was by no means imprudent. For the man who had sold the great estates that had been his and distributed the proceeds to the poor, when he later became a bishop did not despise the resources of the Church but administered them with the utmost fidelity. By doing this he sufficiently showed both that personal possessions ought to be despised for the sake of perfection and that the Church’s possessions, which are truly common, may be held without hindering perfection. [Note: [Col. 0115] Julian Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*, Book II, ch. 9.]

Saint Gregory of Tours asserts that the Church of Nola had great wealth, and that Christ fulfilled in Paulinus what he had deigned to promise through the Gospel to the man who had abandoned everything for him: “Whoever has left everything for my sake will receive a hundredfold in this life.” In my judgment, he would not easily have proved this; for Uranius continues as follows: [Note: [Col. 0115] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, §107; Uranius, *On the Death of Paulinus*, §7.]

> Therefore, as I began to say, he was gentle like Moses, priestly like Aaron, innocent like Samuel, merciful like David, wise like Solomon, apostolic like Peter, lovable like John, cautious like Thomas, a teacher like Paul, a seer like Stephen, fervent like Apollos. In concern and care for the churches, in faith and charity, he imitated all the apostles and bishops. He possessed all these qualities and faithfully preserved them throughout the time of his life. [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., §7.]

> And truly he was such a man that everyone loved him. He lived as an example to all in acquiring salvation and as a refreshment of consolation. These are not merely my words: all the provinces bear witness; the whole earth enclosed by the Roman world bears witness; even the barbarian nations to which the fame of Lord Paulinus had reached bear witness. [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., §8.]

> Nor was he loved by all without reason, since he was present to all. Whom did he fail to raise with his own hand when lying prostrate? Whom, when appealing to him, did he fail to console with a compassionate voice? He was pious, merciful, humble, and kind; he despised and looked down upon no one. He gave to all and indulged all. He encouraged the fearful and calmed the violent; he built up some by his words and others by his example; he helped some through letters and others through financial assistance.  
>   
> He admired no wealth or riches except those which Christ had promised to his saints. He defined the use of gold and silver and everything else in such a way that generosity claimed them for giving, not greed for keeping.  
>   
> In short, he possessed every good quality because he loved Christ. He had faith, gentleness, care for his neighbors, constant concern for the wretched, compassion for the weak, and regard for nothing except peace and charity. He alone begged so that everyone might abound.  
>   
> Finally, what place is there in the world, what solitude, what seas, that did not experience the benefits of Saint Paulinus? Everyone wished to know him; everyone desired to see him. Who came to him without joy? Or who departed from him without longing to return? For those who could not see him in person at least wished to touch his letters. He was gracious and gentle in his correspondence, sweet and most pleasing in his verses.  
>   
> What more can I say? Credulity would scarcely admit whatever is said about him, unless his deeds drove falsehood away.

## CHAPTER LI  
### Valgius, also called Victor, is the only person saved from a shipwreck. Nola is captured by the Goths. Another Paulinus takes refuge with Saint Paulinus. Augustine writes a letter to Saint Paulinus against the Pelagians.

90 1. Paulinus was already pastor of a small flock—that is, bishop of the Church of Nola—when the remarkable story occurred of Valgius’s rescue from shipwreck; after that disaster he took the name Victor. We cannot establish the date of this disaster with complete certainty. Paulinus recounts the circumstances of the story [Col. 0116B] in Letter 49 [Note: [Col. 0115] Paulinus, Letter 49, no. 14.]: how Valgius was rescued from shipwreck by Christ through the patronage of St. Felix. For this reason Valgius was perhaps compelled to come to Nola [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., no. 3.], where Paulinus says [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., no. 14.] that he was so astonished by God’s remarkable miracles that he was almost cruel toward the old man and wished to cut off part of his ear to preserve it, had there not actually been a wound in it. Paulinus himself appears to have washed the old Valgius, rescued from the shipwreck, in the waters of purification, and to have given him the name Victor in baptism [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., no. 2.].

The ship [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., nos. 1 and 15.], which belonged to a Christian named Secundinianus and in which Valgius was saved, reached the shore of Lucania and Bruttium without any loss of its cargo [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., nos. 8 and 15.], at the place where the estate of the Roman senator Posthumianus is washed by the sea [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., no. 15.]. Posthumianus’s agent immediately seized the ship [Col. 0116C] and, after capturing it, emptied it. Besides the public cargo, it contained many goods belonging to the sailors, including their wages and personal property [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., no. 1.]. Complaints about this robbery had already often been lodged before the provincial judge [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid., no. 13.], but the agent first resisted the provincial judge’s orders and his officers by force; afterward he fled to Rome, where Secundinianus and Victor also went.

In writing to Macarius, Paulinus begged him to bring Posthumianus back to the requirements of piety and the laws of justice, and to ensure that only what the agent had taken should be restored. As for imposing punishment upon him, Paulinus asked Macarius to refrain from that. This appears to have been the Macarius who, after serving as deputy of the prefects, was at this time highly distinguished in Rome for piety and learning, and to whom, as Augustine teaches [Note: [Col. 0115] Augustine, Letter 259, no. 1.], our Paulinus had given an extensive letter of consolation on the death of his wife [Col. 0116D].

**ANNALS OF CHRIST 410, 411, 412, 413**

2. The year 410 is famous for the devastation of Rome [Note: [Col. 0115] Theophanes and Crosius, book II, chapter 19; and book VII, chapter 39.]. In that year Alaric, king of the Goths, is said to have entered the city on 24 August and to have departed from it on the twenty-sixth of the same month [Note: [Col. 0115] Philostorgius, book XII, chapter 4]; afterward he ravaged Campania. The event mentioned by Augustine should surely be assigned to this period [Note: [Col. 0115] Baronius, year 410, §46]: namely, that Nola was besieged by barbarians, and that St. Felix appeared to the inhabitants of that city, to whom he had already offered so many proofs of his benevolence through repeated miracles. Augustine declares that he learned this not from common report but from reliable witnesses [Col. 0117A].

From this Baronius concludes [Note: [Col. 0117] Baronius, year 410, §46.] that, on this occasion, the citizens of Nola escaped unharmed—something Augustine does not assert. 91 Indeed [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, Book I of *The City of God*, chapter 10.], elsewhere Augustine explicitly states that the city was captured and devastated by the barbarians; Baronius likewise connects this event with the apparitions of St. Felix and assigns it to this period [Note: [Col. 0117] Baronius, year 410, §§45–46]. Paulinus himself was taken prisoner [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, cited passage.]. But since he had renounced the great wealth with which he had formerly abounded, and was now enriched by no other treasure than that of outstanding virtue, this calamity was certainly less harsh for Paulinus than for greedy men attached to life; indeed, the memory of his good works made it sweet to him, for he had deposited his resources through the hands of the poor in a place which the barbarians could not reach [Col. 0117B]. With these affections of faith and hope in his heart, he prayed to the Lord—as Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, cited passage.] that he had heard from him:

> Lord, do not let me be tormented on account of gold and silver; for you know where all my possessions are.

There can be no doubt that his prayers were heard, since Augustine adds that he knew of no one who, after abandoning his wealth for Christ, had been tormented by the barbarians as though he were still the possessor of money. This invasion and devastation by the barbarians kindled rather than extinguished Paulinus’s charity; indeed [Note: [Col. 0117] Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* III.1.], whatever he could possess as bishop, he distributed in alms for the relief of captives and the poor.

[Col. 0117C] 3. At about this same time Paulinus wrote Letter 50 to Augustine [Note: [Col. 0117] Paulinus, Letter 50.], proposing various questions to him, and Augustine immediately replied. When that letter was lost, Paulinus wrote to him again, and Augustine sent another reply, which was also lost. Undeterred by this, Paulinus wrote a third letter on the same difficulties, while contemplating some pious work. In 413 Augustine began his great work *The City of God*, whose opening chapters contain an illustrious testimony to Paulinus’s virtue [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, Book I of *The City of God*, chapter 10.].

**IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 414**

4. Augustine answered the questions proposed by Paulinus in Letter 149 [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, Letter 149.]. There is no doubt that Paulinus received it, since it has survived to our time. Near its end [Note: [Col. 0117] Ibid., no. 4.] we observe that our Paulinus then had with him another presbyter of the same name, as well as a third man of the same name who, having suffered the loss of his possessions through the calamities of the times, had taken refuge with our Paulinus and was trying to profit from his misfortunes under so great a leader [Col. 0117D].

He appears to have requested instruction from Augustine, but Augustine encouraged him briefly, in the letter addressed to St. Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, Letter 149, no. 34.], to give thanks to God for the condition in which divine Providence had placed him [Col. 0118A]. “For,” Augustine says, “he does not read or hear me teaching and explaining, or urging him by any exhortations, with richer benefit than he receives from seeing you live.”

Nothing historical is reported about Paulinus, bishop of Nola, for the years 415 and 416.

**IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 417**

5. We observed earlier [Note: [Col. 0117] Chapter 46, no. 3; and chapter 49, no. 2.] that our Paulinus had been bound by friendship to Pelagius before his errors became known, and also to Julian, bishop in Campania, who later became a most vigorous defender of Pelagian doctrine. In Paulinus’s own household—or at least in the city of Nola—certain people were stubbornly striving on behalf of the Pelagian error [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, Letter 186, no. 29.]. Therefore Augustine sent Letter 186, otherwise numbered 106, to 92 Paulinus [Col. 0118B], together with many writings against the Pelagians. Besides praying that they might be corrected, Augustine urged Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0117] Ibid., no. 2.] to be cautious not only in avoiding them but also in refuting those who had undertaken to defend Pelagius’s errors obstinately [Note: [Col. 0117] Ibid., nos. 37–38.]. Augustine even refutes them from Paulinus’s letters, especially from Letter 30, otherwise numbered 8, to Severus [Note: [Col. 0117] Ibid., no. 40; and Paulinus, Letter 30, no. 2.].

“For,” he says to him [Note: [Col. 0117] Augustine, Letter 186, no. 39.], “your letters breathe the purest fragrance of Christ, in which you appear a most genuine lover and confessor of that grace.”

Certainly no one recoiled from Pelagian doctrine more strongly than Paulinus. Yet it may be inferred from certain passages in his writings that he was not sufficiently removed from the error of the Semi-Pelagians, who asserted that the beginning of good will belongs to human beings [Note: [Col. 0117] Paulinus, Letter 10, no. 6; and *Poem* 11, lines 142 ff.]. At that time the presbyters of Marseilles had not yet raised this question [Col. 0118C], nor had Augustine disentangled and resolved it.

**IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 418**

6. Perhaps Paulinus had some part in the events conducted against the Pelagians in Rome and Ravenna in April 418. After these proceedings, Bishop Julian was expelled from his see for the Pelagian heresy by two edicts of the emperor Honorius. But no historical information about Paulinus is reported for this year.

**IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 419**

## CHAPTER LII. Paulinus is invited to the Synod of Ravenna to settle the schism of the Roman Church. Saints Eucherius and Honoratus establish a friendship with Paulinus.

1. After Pope Zosimus died toward the end of 418, a schism broke out and dissension arose among the clergy. The smaller party elected the archdeacon Eulalius as supreme pontiff, while the larger party elected the presbyter Boniface. Toward the end of March 419, the emperor Honorius summoned by letter the most holy bishops of the various provinces to a synod at Ravenna, so that they might bring such a great controversy to an end. He wrote first of all to St. Paulinus, bishop of Nola [Note: [Col. 0117] Baronius, year 419, §19.]; but Paulinus was entirely unable to attend because of bodily weakness [Col. 0119A].

When the synod announced for Ravenna was suspended and left unfinished through Eulalius’s rashness, and had not been brought to completion [Note: [Col. 0119] Baronius, year 419, §20.], the council was transferred to Spoleto, where it was to be held with a very large attendance on the Ides of June. The emperor Honorius—or rather his brother Constantius [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., §19.], the Patrician, who directed the affairs of the Empire—asked Paulinus to come [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., §24.] and therefore sent him a letter full of respect [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., §20.]. From it we can gather how highly Paulinus was esteemed and how great his merit was in his eyes. He first calls him a holy and venerable father, and then says that the council had been postponed because, in his absence through illness, it had been thought that nothing could be decided.

The letter is as follows, taken from a Vatican manuscript cited by Baronius under the year 419, §20.

[Col. 0119B] 93 **To the holy and venerable Father Paulinus, bishop.**

We were firmly convinced—according to another reading, *we held the firm opinion*—that nothing could be decided by those priests who had assembled for the synod, since Your Beatitude, prevented by a bodily disorder, was unable to endure the hardship of the journey. And because of the absence of the holy man, the vices rejoice, though they will not prevail; meanwhile, perverse and ancient ambition wishes to maintain a long contest with the blessed man and with holy living, so that, against these goods of apostolic teaching, it may suppose that confidence can be placed in walls raised through presumption and force. O truly worthy cause, which your blessed life designates as deserving only of a crown!

We therefore announce that the judgment has been postponed, so that the divine commands may be pressed upon us by the mouth of Your Reverence, since you have followed and fulfilled them; nor can another bearer of those precepts be found except one who has been approved as worthy of apostolic discipline [Col. 0119C].

Therefore, holy lord, deservedly venerable father, righteous servant of God, deign—disregarding the labor—to grant us this tribute of your visitation, this boon, if it may so be called, of a divine work: that, setting everything else aside, insofar as moderation and tranquility support it, you may benefit the synod and, without interruption, grant yourself also to our desires and to the blessing for which we long.

We do not know whether Paulinus decided to travel to the council. In any event, he did not undertake that journey, since on 7 April [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., §36.] the entire matter was settled in another way.

**IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 421 OR 424**

2. From the year 419 until 421, nothing historical is reported [Col. 0119D] about St. Paulinus. In 421 St. Augustine sent him, through the presbyter Candidianus, his book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* [Note: [Col. 0119] Augustine, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapters 1 and 18.]. Augustine made it lengthy because of his affection for Paulinus and his desire to converse with him at greater length; he wrote it around 421, or no later than 424. Augustine begs Paulinus to write back and tell him how he received the book.

To this period we should assign the correspondence that passed between Paulinus and the monks and solitaries of Lérins. This letter [Note: [Col. 0119] Paulinus, Letter 51.] was sent by Paulinus, already bishop of Nola [Col. 0120A], to Eucherius, who was not yet a bishop, while St. Honoratus was still abbot over the monks of Lérins; in 426 Honoratus was appointed bishop of the Church of Arles.

Everyone knows that St. Honoratus, having renounced the vanity of the world, withdrew to the island of Lérins on the coast of the maritime province and founded a monastery there, which later became extremely famous. St. Eucherius, later bishop of Lyon, having followed Paulinus in the same way of life [Note: [Col. 0119] Chifflet, p. 61.], likewise withdrew with his wife Galla to the island of Léro, now commonly called Sainte-Marguerite, near Lérins and separated from it by a narrow stretch of sea.

From there Eucherius sent certain men to visit Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0119] Paulinus, Letter 51, no. 2.]. Through divine grace they came to know one another, and they were joined by the bonds of Christ’s love.
