Through these men sent by Eucherius [Col. 0120B], Paulinus learned both his place of residence and that of the venerable Honoratus. From this it may be inferred that Honoratus was not yet famous in the Church at that time.

The letter that St. Paulinus undoubtedly sent to Eucherius at that time has been lost. Whether he then wrote to Honoratus is unknown. In the following year, however, Honoratus, encouraged by the example of St. Eucherius, sent three religious men from the holy number of his congregation to visit Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., no. 1.]. Eucherius did not know of their departure [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., no. 3.], and therefore 94 on this timely occasion he did not write back to Paulinus [Col. 0120C].

Nevertheless, Paulinus carefully asked these men how Eucherius was faring and, through this opportunity provided by the monks of Lérins [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., no. 2.], sent Eucherius a letter full of affection and love. In it he begs him, if God should thereafter provide a suitable opportunity through messengers of this kind [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid., no. 3.], not to be slow to write back, so that they might console one another solely through familiar affection, since he had no doubt about Eucherius’s most pious disposition toward him.

A few years ago, through the care of Chifflet, this letter was published from two manuscript codices. Anyone who knows Paulinus’s character and intellect will acknowledge that it bears the unmistakable stamp of Paulinus; we have added it to the Pauline letters. Paulinus addresses it to Eucherius and his wife Galla, yet nowhere in either the title or the letter does he mention Therasia. This is substantial evidence that she had already died. It can also be established that Therasia had died before Paulinus from the fact that Uranius, describing St. Paulinus’s final illness and death [Note: [Col. 0119] Chifflet, p. 215, chapter 34.], says nothing about Therasia [Col. 0120D]. If she had still been alive at that time, Paulinus would certainly, according to custom, have prayed for her welfare and would have entrusted something for the future to the surviving sister of his beloved wife.

**IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 431**

## CHAPTER LIII. The final illness and death of St. Paulinus.

1. Let us now come at last to the death of Paulinus, whose story was told by an eyewitness. Paulinus had long desired to fly from this world to his heavenly dwelling, so that he might have a home there with the saints [Note: [Col. 0119] Uranius, *On the Death of St. Paulinus*, no. 4.], when he was afflicted with an extremely severe pain in his side. Though already at the point of death, he was further exhausted by cauterizations administered at the excessive insistence of the physicians [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., no. 3.].

Three days before his death [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., no. 1.], two bishops came to visit him: St. Symmachus and the blessed Acindynus. Chifflet restored the latter name by a quite ingenious conjecture [Note: [Col. 0121] Chifflet, p. 192.] from the reading of the Medicean manuscript, since earlier printed editions had *Benedictus Hyacinthinus*. Since Uranius does not identify the sees either of St. Symmachus or of the blessed Acindynus [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., p. 193.], it is conjectured that they came from the neighborhood, and perhaps that the holy Symmachus was the bishop of Capua, whose name is borne by several churches in the city and province of Capua and whose feast is entered on 22 October in an old Capuan calendar [Col. 0121B]; but we are completely ignorant of the period in which he lived.

These two prelates came to Paulinus while he was struggling at the point of death, when everyone had already despaired of his recovery [Note: [Col. 0121] Uranius, no. 1.]. Yet Paulinus was so restored and refreshed by their arrival [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.] that, forgetting all bodily weakness, he displayed himself to them entirely as a spiritual and angelic being.

He ordered the sacred vessels and ecclesiastical ornaments to be brought before his bed, and together with the holy bishops he offered the sacrifice to God. At the same time, he restored to their former peace those whom, for the sake of ecclesiastical discipline, he had ordered to be 95 excluded from communion in the sacred mysteries. [Col. 0121C] When the holy bishop had celebrated all these things in joyful and perfect order, he suddenly began, in a clear voice, to ask where his brothers were. One of those standing nearby, thinking that he was asking about the bishops who were then present, said to him, “Look, your brothers are here.” But he replied, “I mean my brothers Januarius and Martin, who have just spoken with me and said that they would come to me shortly.”

Those standing around therefore realized that the man who had shone so greatly in virtue through the multiplied gifts of spiritual graces had been granted, before giving up his spirit, to behold with his bodily eyes these two most illustrious bishops at his death [Note: [Col. 0121] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107.]. The first was St. Januarius, bishop and martyr of Benevento, who died around 305 and was then glorifying the Church of Naples with his relics; the other was St. Martin, then bishop of Tours, a man apostolic in every respect and an illustrious glory and ornament of the Gallican Church [Col. 0121D].

It then became evident that Paulinus, although advanced in age, was no less beneficent and generous toward the poor. The presbyter Posthumianus [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.], perhaps the same Posthumianus whom we have mentioned once and again, reminded him that forty solidi were owed for garments distributed to the poor. Paulinus smiled gently and said to Posthumianus: “Be at peace, my son. Believe me: someone will come who will pay the debt of the poor.”

And indeed, after no long interval, a presbyter from the regions of Lucania entered. He had been sent by the holy bishop Exsuperantius and by his illustrious brother Ursatius, who sent Paulinus fifty solidi through him as a gift [Col. 0122A]. After receiving them, Paulinus gave thanks to God for not having abandoned one who hoped in his mercy. Of these fifty solidi he himself gave two, with his own hand, to the presbyter who had brought them; he ordered the rest to be returned to the merchants who had supplied the garments for the poor.

When night had succeeded day [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., no. 3.], he rested for a short time until midnight. He could not sleep thereafter, however, for the pain in his side grew worse and he was exhausted by the physicians’ cauterizations. One hour before dawn [Col. 0122B], the holy man awakened everyone, as he was accustomed to do, and celebrated the morning office according to the customary order. When day had come, he preached the peace of inheritance to the presbyters, deacons, and all the clergy, following the example of the Lord; afterward he remained silent until evening. Then, recognizing the time for the devotion of the lamps, he stretched out his hands and said, though in a weak voice, “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.”

After a period of silence [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.], around the tenth or eleventh hour of the night, while everyone present was watching anxiously, his little chamber was suddenly shaken by so violent an earthquake that those attending his bed, terrified and confused, all threw themselves into prayer [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.]. Those standing outside the doors knew nothing of it, for the earthquake was not public throughout the house but private within the chamber [Col. 0122C]. It foreshadowed the grief with which all would be afflicted at the death of this holy man.

2. He breathed out the spirit owed to God, received by angelic hands [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.]. When his blessed soul had flown to the joys of heaven, his face and entire body became so white and shining as snow that all who were present, amid 96 sobs and tears, blessed the Lord [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., no. 10.]. Everyone recognized his life from the merit of his death, and they proved the character of his death from the conduct of his life. Behold what almsgiving bestows; behold what kind of death it grants, and what treasures God gives to his saints who love him in the poor—not to those who gape greedily at the evil of avarice [Note: [Col. 0121] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107].

At Nola, in the basilica of St. Felix [Note: [Col. 0121] Uranius, no. 1.], he died a glorious death in 431, on 22 June [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., no. 12.]. His memory has been recorded in all the Martyrologies for this day [Note: [Col. 0121] Baronius, *Martyrology*, 22 June], and on that same day the Church celebrates his feast. At his death almost the whole world groaned; the faithful and the unbelieving wept [Note: [Col. 0121] Uranius, no. 4.]. Finally, not only Christians but also Jews and pagans came to his funeral in great mourning and with torn garments, and all with one voice lamented that they had been deprived of their patron, defender, and protector [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., no. 8.].

He was buried in the basilica of St. Felix [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid., no. 1.], to whom he had always rendered thanks to God and acknowledged gifts received through him as mediator and patron, and whose praises he celebrated with such joy and magnificence in his writings [Col. 0123A].

## CHAPTER LIV. After Paulinus has completed his life, the bishop St. John of Naples is summoned to heaven. Uranius writes the history of St. Paulinus’s death.

1. Uranius, who wrote about Paulinus’s death, recounts an apparition that is believed to have occurred in the year of Christ 432, shortly after Paulinus’s death [Note: [Col. 0123] Uranius, no. 11; and Chifflet, pp. 214–215.]. At that time the Church of Naples was governed by a bishop named John. During the night preceding Maundy Thursday of Holy Week, he fell asleep and saw St. Paulinus, as John himself reported, clothed and adorned with angelic dignity, holding in his hand a gleaming-white honeycomb, and saying to him [Note: [Col. 0123] Uranius, no. 11.]: “Brother John, what are you doing here? Release the bonds of your weariness and come to us now, for this food that I hold in my hand abounds among us.”

After saying this, he embraced Bishop John and placed part of the honeycomb in his mouth [Col. 0123B]. John desired its sweetness and fragrance so greatly that, if he had possessed the power during the vision, he would never have released the feet of St. Paulinus, which he held in his embrace.

He immediately awoke from sleep, and on that same day, Thursday, in good health, celebrated the solemnity of the Lord’s Supper. According to his custom, he served supper to the clergy and the poor. On Friday he devoted himself to prayer.

On Saturday, at the second hour of the day—that is, around seven in the morning—he went joyfully to the church. After ascending the tribunal, he greeted the people according to custom and announced peace to them. When the people had returned his greeting, he prayed; and when the prayer was concluded, he breathed out his spirit [Col. 0123C]. That day and the following night, however, the divine office was performed according to the usual custom. On the next day, the Sunday of the Resurrection, with lamps lit and a great procession of the newly baptized, accompanied by a multitude of people as far as the tomb, he received a glorious and praiseworthy burial.

This John is said to have been the fourteenth among the bishops of Naples [Note: [Col. 0123] Paulinus Chifflet, p. 198.]. Nothing is recorded about him except that he ordered the body of St. Januarius, which had been taken from Marcianus near Puteoli [Note: [Col. 0123] Gall, *Pouzzol*], to be transferred to Naples. He is said to have buried it with his own hand in the oratory 97 in which he himself was later buried [Col. 0123D]. I do not dare, however, to assert this translation as certain. It is said that the body of this saint was later transferred from that church to another.

Baronius observes [Note: [Col. 0123] Baronius, *Martyrology*, 22 June.] that several churches in Naples are dedicated to God under the name of St. John. He thinks that, because none of them is now called after John the bishop and all are called after St. John the Baptist, this resulted from the injuries of time and the scarcity of ancient records, so that churches once called St. John’s came to bear the name of St. John the Baptist [Col. 0124A]. We find examples of the same phenomenon elsewhere.

It is certain that John departed this life on Holy Saturday [Note: [Col. 0123] Chifflet, p. 215.], which in the year 432 fell on 2 April. But Baronius confesses that he does not know why his feast was transferred to 22 June, the day sacred to Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0123] Baronius, *Martyrology*, 22 June].

2. The body of St. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, is said to be preserved at Rome in the church of St. Bartholomew [Note: [Col. 0123] Baronius, cited passage.]. Immediately after St. Paulinus died, Pacatus undertook to celebrate his life in verse [Note: [Col. 0123] Uranius, title and no. 12.]. Whether he actually did so is uncertain, for no one mentions such a work; indeed, St. Gregory of Tours says that he had read nothing about St. Paulinus’s life [Note: [Col. 0123] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107].

From the title of nobility with which Uranius honors Pacatus [Note: [Col. 0123] Uranius, title.], it may be inferred that he was a layman of noble birth from Gaul, a Christian, and a poet of recognized merit in that age. He was descended from the distinguished orator Latinus Pacatus, who delivered a panegyric in Rome to the emperor Theodosius in 389, after the death of the tyrant Maximus.

Of Pacatus we know one thing with certainty: he asked 98 the presbyter Uranius to give him a faithful account of the death of St. Paulinus, which Uranius had witnessed [Note: [Col. 0123] Uranius, preface and no. 12.], as is clear from the following words: “We saw how the righteous man is taken away,” and “All with one voice lamented together with us” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ibid., no. 4 and no. 8].

Uranius therefore composed this account and dedicated it to Pacatus, whom he calls “the illustrious lord,” “venerable in Christ,” and “most beloved son” [Note: [Col. 0123] Uranius, preface; and ibid., no. 4.]. He urges him to hasten the gift of his distinguished work [Note: [Col. 0123] Ibid., no. 12.], so that, since he was preparing to sail, he might enjoy the very useful reading of the work before crossing the sea [Note: [Col. 0123] Chifflet, p. 192; and Baronius, *Martyrology*, 22 June].

Since Uranius begins his account with the arrival of the two bishops who came to visit Paulinus three days before his death, he appears to have belonged to the clergy of one or the other of them, rather than to the Church of Nola.

Some think that he was the same Uranius from whom Paulinus says he waited in vain for letters from Delphinus throughout the summer around the year 400, in Letter 19 [Note: [Col. 0123] Paulinus, Letter 19, no. 1.]. From that time onward, Uranius perhaps showed himself worthy of the holy man, who, because the letter had been delayed, had spoken harshly about him to Delphinus [Note: [Col. 0123] Ibid., no. 2.].

His writing was celebrated by the ancient Fathers. Gregory the Great quotes a fragment of it [Note: [Col. 0123] Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* III.12.], and Gregory of Tours indicates that he had a substantial account of Paulinus’s passing, in which the apparition of Saints Januarius and Martin is mentioned [Note: [Col. 0123] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107]. Isidore of Seville also mentions Uranius’s history of St. Paulinus’s death [Note: [Col. 0123] Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 4].

Chifflet offers an excellent discussion in *Pauline Illustrated* of the matters that some have wished either to add to or to remove from this account of Uranius [Note: [Col. 0123] Chifflet, pp. 179–180, 197, and 200].

[Col. 0125]

# EPITOME OF THE LIFE OF ST. PAULINUS

[Col. 0125A] 99–100

Paulinus, also called Pontius Meropius. Chapter 1, no. 1.

Descended on both his father’s and his mother’s side from Roman senators. Ibid., no. 2.

His father was Paulinus. Ibid., no. 3.

Born at Bordeaux in Aquitaine, at the end of the year of Christ 353 or the beginning of 354. Ibid. and chapter 23.

Educated by Ausonius in rhetorical and poetic arts. Chapter 2, no. 2.

He became suffect consul, not ordinary consul. Chapter 3, no. 2.

Very wealthy. Chapter 1, no. 3.

He married the pious and wealthy Therasia. Chapter 3, no. 1.

Through her exhortations and the support of holy bishops and presbyters, he was converted to Christ in his thirty-sixth year, at the end of 389. Chapter 4, nos. 2–3; chapter 5, no. 2.

Baptized by Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux. Chapter 5, no. 2.

He withdrew to Spain with his most pious wife Therasia, in an uncertain year but certainly before 390. Ibid., no. 1.

After living there for four complete years, he had a son, who died on the eighth day after his birth and was buried at Complutum. Toward the end of 389. Chapter 6, no. 3.

Paulinus devoted and consecrated himself to God and embraced the monastic life. Chapter 7, no. 2.

He sold his estates and distributed the money to the poor. In 392. Chapter 8, nos. 1–2.

At Barcelona, driven by a crowd led by the presbyter Lampius, he was ordained presbyter against his will on the Sunday of Christ’s Nativity, in his fortieth year. Toward the end of 393. Chapter 15, nos. 1–2.

He came from Spain to Italy and was received with great affection at Florence by Ambrose, who wished to enroll him among his clergy, so that, although he might live in different places, he would nevertheless be regarded as a presbyter of the Church of Milan. In the year of Christ 394, after Easter. Chapter 17, no. 1.

From there he went to Rome, where he was honorably received by the people and by distinguished men. He experienced the envy of Pope Siricius and of certain clerics of the Roman Church. Ibid., no. 2.

For this reason, a few days later he withdrew to Nola and settled there with his wife. In 395. Ibid.

He fell ill and was visited by bishops, clerics, and monks from Africa and Campania. Chapter 26, no. 1.

He obtained the restoration of a house that had been seized by force from Basil, the most holy presbyter of the Church of Capua. Chapter 31, nos. 1–2.

Pope Anastasius wrote to the bishops of Campania on Paulinus’s behalf. In 398. Chapter 32, no. 3.

Paulinus suffered from a severe and prolonged illness. In 399. Chapter 35.

He was visited by Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, and by the elder Melania. In 402. Chapter 41, nos. 1–2.

He built basilicas at Nola. Chapters 42 and 43.

Likewise, he ordered a church to be built at Fundi. In 403. Chapter 44.

His brother died. Chapter 45, no. 3.

[Col. 0126B] Paulinus was made bishop of Nola at the age of fifty-six. Toward the end of 408. Chapter 50, no. 1.

Nola was captured by the Goths, but no harm was done to Paulinus. In 410. Chapter 51, no. 2.

Two men named Paulinus took refuge with him, one a presbyter and the other a layman. Ibid., no. 4.

He was invited by the emperor to the Synod of Ravenna to settle the schism of the Roman Church. In 419. Chapter 52, no. 1.

Struck by an extremely severe pain in his side, he was visited by two bishops three days before his death. In 431, in June. Chapter 53, no. 1.

Together with them he offered the sacrifice to God before his bed. Ibid., no. 1.

He restored to ecclesiastical communion those who had been excluded from the sacred mysteries. Ibid.

The next day he celebrated the morning office with his clergy. Ibid.

And, having given peace to all the clergy of his Church. Ibid.

Around the tenth hour of the night, the chamber in which he lay trembled in an earthquake. Ibid.

Shortly afterward he gave his soul back to God, at the age of seventy-eight. In 431, on 22 June. Ibid., no. 2.

His face and entire body shone with snowy brightness. Ibid.

Pagans and Jews, with great weeping and torn garments, came together with the Christians to his funeral. Ibid.

He was buried at Nola in the basilica of St. Felix. Ibid.

The bishop St. John of Naples was summoned by him to heaven. In 432. Chapter 54, no. 1.

[Col. 0125]

# EULOGIES OF ST. PAULINUS FROM VARIOUS WRITERS, COLLATED WITH THE MANUSCRIPT CODICES

[Col. 0125]

101 **AUSONIUS, LETTER 20 TO PAULINUS**

(This fragment was revised against the Mariang manuscript and the editions of Gravius, Lyon, Poelman, Tollius, and Vinet.)

[Col. 0125D]

**Ausonius to Paulinus.**

The meter so advised that you should be

First, and should precede my name.

Although you are also first in the title of the *Fasti*, and although your curule ivory chair in Rome

[Col. 0126C] preceded mine,

And although the poetic palm that has long flourished for you

[Col. 0126D] is adorned with a ribbon, which my palm lacks,

We surpass you only in the honor of long-lived old age.

What does it matter? A crow is not for that reason before a swan.

Nor, because the Gangetic parrot lives a thousand years,

[Col. 0127A] does it defeat you, royal peacock, with your hundred eyes [some manuscripts: *pave*].

We yield to you in talent as far as we surpass you in age.

Our Muse rises to meet your Camena.

Live, farewell, and pile up as many coming Januaries [some manuscripts: *consere*, “join together”]

As our fathers or yours have joined together.

**AUSONIUS, LETTER 21 TO PAULINUS**
*(These fragments have been collated with the same manuscripts.)*

“More piercing than Parthian [arrows] and the darts of the Cydonians,

more swift than the wings of birds,

more rushing than the torrent-force of the plunging Po,

denser than the great strength of resounding hail,

more vibrating than the flames of flashing lightning;

now, borne through the air on Perseus’ winged sandals

and on the broad-brimmed hat of wealthy Arcadian [Mercury], fly . . .

I speak as far as Paulinus’ walls, Ebromagus.

[Col. 0127B] And presently, if now, with strength recovered,

he flourishes with the lively movement of a restored body,

soon ask back the mutual greeting that was commanded . . .

And say that he is well; say that his friend,

his neighbor, and your supporter commands you to say hello—

the author of your honor, the fosterer of your talent;

say also: teacher, father, say every

kindly and holy name of affection.

And having said ‘hail,’ say ‘farewell,’ and return at once . . .

Meanwhile bringing back some little gift

from the generosity of the musical storehouse.”

## AUSONIUS, LETTER 23 TO PAULINUS

*(These fragments have been revised against the manuscripts Lugdunensis, Poelmanianus, Reginensis, and the editions of Badius, Gravius, Ludovicus, Poelman, Schott, Tollius, and Vinet.)*

[Col. 0127C]

“Pauline, we are breaking apart the yoke that a certain balance

had sustained: what, lightly placed and bearable when joined,

gentle concord handled with evenly matched reins . . .

Pylades was yielding; and Damon, too, the glory of Phrygian Nisus,

was already less, fulfilling his pledged guarantees . . .

102 Paulinus and Ausonius, men whom the sacred

purple of Quirinus and the gold-covered cloak of the trabea

has veiled, ought not to yield through treachery to a foreign goddess.

Why do I complain? Why do I assail the crimes of the Eastern monster?

The bank of the setting Tagus wounds me; Punic Barcino wounds me;

the snowy ridges of the Pyrenees, spanning two seas, wound me . . .

Do you recognize [Note: [Col. 0128D] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions: ‘Will you recognize?’], sweetest Pontus, your own fault? . . .

Let us not mourn the house scattered and carried away,

nor the ancient realms of Paulinus, torn apart among a hundred masters;

[Col. 0127D] nor you, wandering through all the length of Spain,

forgetful of the ancient [bonds] and trusting foreign friends.

Hasten here, our glory, my greatest care;

summoned by vows, good omens, and prayers,

hasten.”

## AUSONIUS, LETTER 24 TO PAULINUS

*(These fragments have been collated with the manuscripts noted above and, in addition, with the Vossian manuscript.)*

“The complaint that had been nearest to our letter,

[Col. 0128A] I had believed, Pauline, could move you

and that gentle rebuke could draw out your voice [Note: [Col. 0127D] Some editions and manuscripts read ‘your . . . Muses.’].

But, as though devoted to sworn sacred rites,

you maintain profound silence and persist in the law of silence.

Is it not permitted? Or are you ashamed? . . .

If you fear exposure, Pauline, and dread

the charge of our friendship, let your Tanaquil know nothing of this.

You may disregard others, but do not disdain to address

your father in words. I am your fosterer, and he was

your first teacher, [Note: Thus the Reginensis manuscript and the editions of Badius, Lugdunensis, Tollius, and Vinet. Other copies read ‘of the ancients.’] your first giver of honors,

the first to lead you into the colleges of the Muses.”

## AUSONIUS, LETTER 25 TO PAULINUS

*(These fragments have been revised against the manuscripts Lugdunensis, Mariangonensis, and Reginensis, and against the seven editions noted above.)*

“This fourth letter has revealed to you the complaints of your acquaintances

[Col. 0128B] and, in gentle speech, chastises your inactivity;

but no page returns to me any dutiful service . . .

You have changed your character, sweetest Pauline . . .

Will Bilbilis, then, the glory and support of my fatherland and

[Note: The Mariangonensis manuscript reads ‘of the senate.’]

senate [Note: [Col. 0128D] The Mariangonensis manuscript reads ‘of the senate.’], or Calagurris clinging to its crags [Note: [Col. 0128D] Thus the Lugdunensis and Reginensis manuscripts with Poelman’s edition. Four editions read ‘Calagurris.’], possess you?

Or Ilerda, dry, looking down upon the rushing Sicoris

from ridges rough with exposed rocky ruins?

Here, Pauline, will you establish your trabea and Latin curule office,

and here bury your ancestral honors?”

## PRUDENTIUS, BOOK I AGAINST SYMMACHUS

“The ready faith of neither the Paulini nor the Bassi hesitated to devote itself to Christ and to raise the proud offspring of a patrician family for the age to come.”

103 ## HIERONYMUS, LETTER 13 TO PAULINUS

*(Collated with the Victorinus manuscript and the Mainz edition of 1470.)*

[Col. 0128C]

“A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, and a tree is known by its fruits. You measure us by your virtues, and, great as you are, raise up the lowly; you occupy the last place at the banquet so that, by the judgment of the master of the household, you may be advanced. For what, or how little, is there in us that we should deserve the praise of a learned voice, that with the mouth by which a most religious prince is defended we should, humble and insignificant as we are, be commended?

“Do not, therefore, dearest brother, measure us by the number of our years; nor reckon wisdom by gray hairs, but gray hairs by wisdom, as Solomon testifies: ‘The gray hairs of a man are his prudence,’ and so forth. Finally, having heard the Savior’s sentence, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor,’ [Col. 0128D] you turn words into deeds; and, naked, following the naked cross, you climb Jacob’s ladder more freely and lightly [Note: The Victorinus manuscript with the Mainz edition of 1470 reads ‘you ascend.’]. You change your tunic along with your spirit; nor, with a full purse, do you seek glorious filth, but with clean hands and a pure breast you glory in being poor both in spirit and in deeds . . .

“I gladly read your book, which you sent to me, wisely and elegantly composed for the emperor Theodosius; and I especially liked its division. Although in the first parts you surpass others, in the penultimate parts you surpass yourself. The very style of expression is compressed and polished; and, while it shines with Ciceronian purity [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads ‘shines forth.’], it is rich in maxims. For, as someone has said, speech in which only words are praised lies inert. Moreover, the sequence of the subject matter is strong, and each part depends upon the next. Whatever you have undertaken is either the conclusion of what precedes or the beginning of what follows.

“Fortunate Theodosius, to be defended by such an orator of Christ! You have ennobled his purple and consecrated the usefulness of his laws to future ages. Well done for your excellence: with such beginnings, what sort of seasoned soldier will you be? If only I were permitted to lead such talent, not through the mountains of Aonia and the peaks of Helicon, as the poets sing, but through Zion, Itabyrion, and lofty Sinai [Note: The Victorinus manuscript with the Mainz edition reads ‘to lead through the Scriptures.’]; if only I might teach what I have learned and, as it were, transmit the mysteries of Scripture from hand to hand, something would be born for us [Col. 0129B] that learned Greece did not possess . . . .

“If you had this foundation—namely, the divine Scriptures—or rather, if the finishing touch [Note: The same manuscripts read ‘were added to your work.’] were applied to your work, we should have no volumes more beautiful, learned, sweet, or Latin than yours. Tertullian is rich in maxims but difficult in expression. Blessed Cyprian, like a stream of the purest water, moves sweetly and peacefully; and although he is wholly occupied with exhorting to virtue [Note: [Col. 0129D] Thus corrected from the Victorinus manuscript and the Mainz edition; the earlier text read ‘exercise.’], being constrained by the hardships of persecution [Note: [Col. 0129D] The Victorinus manuscript and the Mainz edition read ‘of persecution.’], he did not discuss the divine Scriptures. The illustrious martyr Victorinus, crowned with martyrdom, cannot express what he understands. Lactantius, like a river of Ciceronian eloquence—if only he had been able to establish our doctrines as easily as he destroyed those of others [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads ‘to confirm’]. Arnobius is uneven and excessive, and confused because he has not divided his work [Col. 0129C]. Saint Hilary is raised on a Gallic cothurnus; and although adorned with the flowers of Greece, he is sometimes entangled in long periods and is far removed from the reading of simpler brothers [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads ‘the simple.’]. I say nothing of the others, whether dead or still living; concerning them others after us will judge on both sides.

“I shall come to you yourself, my fellow initiate, companion, and friend—my friend, I say, before I knew you—and I shall ask you not to suspect flattery in our intimacy. Rather, think me either mistaken or led astray by affection, than that I should deceive a friend by adulation. You possess great talent and an infinite supply of language; you speak easily and purely, and that very ease and purity are mingled with prudence, for when the head is sound all the faculties are vigorous.

“If to this prudence and eloquence you added either study or understanding of the Scriptures, I should see you shortly holding the citadel of our writers; [Note: The particle ‘and’ has been added from the Victorinus manuscript and the Mainz edition.] and, ascending with Jacob, singing upon the roofs of Zion in the upper rooms what you had come to know in the chambers. Gird yourself, I beg you, gird yourself. Life has granted mortals nothing without great labor” [Horace, Satires, preface to Book I].

“Let the Church regard you as noble, as the senate formerly did. Prepare for yourself riches that you may distribute every day and that may never fail, while your age is vigorous, while your head is not yet sprinkled with gray [Note: The Victorinus manuscript and the Mainz edition read ‘while gray has not yet come upon you.’]; before illnesses and grievous old age arrive, and labor and the harsh cruelty of death carry you off [Note: The Victorinus manuscript and the Mainz edition read ‘of harsh death’; Virgil]. I am content with nothing mediocre in you; I desire everything supreme, everything perfect.”

## HIERONYMUS, LETTER 34 TO JULIAN

“Nor is there any reason for you to excuse your nobility and the burdens of wealth. Look to the holy man Pammachius and Paulinus the presbyter, whose faith is most fervent; they offered to the Lord not only their wealth but themselves. Against the devil’s evasions, they did not offer skin for skin, but their flesh, bones, and souls consecrated to the Lord [Col. 0130B]; they can lead you to greater things both by example and by speech—that is, by deed and by word. Are you noble? So are they; but nobler in Christ. Are you rich and honored? So are they; rather, from rich and honored men they became poor and without glory; and for that reason they are richer and more illustrious, because they are poor and dishonored for Christ.”

## HIERONYMUS, LETTER 103 TO PAULINUS

*(These fragments have been revised against the Victorinus manuscript.)*

“Brother Ambrose, bringing me your little gifts, also delivered the sweetest letter, which from the beginning bore the marks of a friendship already tested by faith and of an old friendship. For that is a true relationship, joined by the bond of Christ, which is brought about not by household advantage, not merely by bodily presence, not by crafty and flattering adulation, but by the fear of God and devotion to the divine Scriptures [Col. 0130C]. Here you have your most loving brother Eusebius, who doubled for me the grace of your letter by reporting the propriety of your conduct, your contempt for the world, your fidelity in friendship, and your love of Christ; for the letter itself, even without him, displayed your prudence and the beauty of your eloquence.”

## AMBROSIUS, LETTER 30 (ALSO 36) TO SABINUS

*(Collated with the manuscripts Gemetensis, five hundred years old; Pratellensis, nine hundred; Vindocinensis, seven hundred; Saint Michael on Mount Tumba, four hundred; and Misericordia Dei, six hundred years old.)*

“I have learned that Paulinus, second to no one in the regions of Aquitania [Note: [Col. 0130D] Thus the Pratellensis, Gemetensis, Vindocinensis, Saint Michael on Mount Tumba, and Misericordia Dei manuscripts; none attests Baronius’s reading in the *Annals*.] for the splendor of his birth, sold his possessions, both his own and those belonging to his wife, and adopted this way of life for the faith, so that he might confer upon the poor what he had converted into money; and, himself made poor from rich, as though relieved of a heavy burden, he bade farewell to his household, fatherland, and even kindred, so that he might serve God more earnestly.

“He is said, moreover [Note: The particle ‘moreover’ has been added from four manuscripts.], to have chosen the seclusion of the city of Nola, where, fleeing the tumult, he spends his life. His wife also comes very near to his virtue and devotion, and does not differ from her husband’s purpose; finally, after transferring their estates into the ownership of others, she follows her husband and, content with a small patch of ground there [Note: We have corrected the text from the Vindocinensis manuscript. Others read ‘she will console herself’], consoles herself with the riches of religion and charity [Note: The Paris edition reads ‘simplicity’].

“They have no offspring, and therefore the posterity of their merits is desired. When the leading men hear [Note: [Col. 0131D] The Vindocinensis manuscript corrects in the margin: ‘heard . . . complain.’] of this, what will they say? That a man from that family, that lineage, that character, endowed with such eloquence, has withdrawn from the senate; that the succession of a noble family has been cut off; that this cannot be endured. And although they themselves shave their heads and eyebrows whenever they undertake the rites of Isis, if a Christian man, more devoted to the holy religion, should change his clothing, they cry out that it is an unworthy crime [Note: Thus restored from three manuscripts, Gemetensis, Pratellensis, and Michaelinus. Others read ‘they call it’].

“I certainly grieve that such observance should exist in falsehood and such negligence in truth, so that many who are more devoted to the holy religion are confused [Col. 0131B] at seeming so [Note: The Vindocinensis, Misericordia Dei, and Michaelinus manuscripts read ‘I shall confuse him’], not considering the voice of him who says: ‘Whoever is ashamed of me before men, I also shall be ashamed of him before my Father who is in heaven.’”

## AUGUSTINUS, LETTER 26 (ALSO 39) TO LICENTIUS

*(This fragment has been revised against the Benedictine edition, twenty-three manuscripts, and four editions.)*

“Go to Campania; learn from Paulinus, that outstanding and holy servant of God, how, with a neck all the more noble because it was humble, he unhesitatingly shook off the great pride of this world, so as to submit it to the yoke of Christ, just as he did submit it; and now, with him as the guide of his journey, he rejoices in quietness and modesty. Go and learn with what resources of talent he offers sacrifices of praise to Him, returning to Him whatever good he has received from Him, lest he lose everything if he does not store it up in the One from whom he has these things.”

## AUGUSTINUS, LETTER 27 (ALSO 32) TO PAULINUS

*(The fragments of this letter have been collated with the Benedictine edition, twenty-four manuscripts, and four editions.)*

[Col. 0131C]

“O good man and good brother, you were hiding my soul; and I tell it to endure that you still hide yourself from my eyes; it scarcely obeys—indeed, it does not obey . . . . Do not rebuke me, I beg you, with that holier gravity in which you prevail, and say that I am wrong to grieve because I still do not know you, when you have opened your mind for me to see—that is, your very inward self. For what if I had learned that you were my brother and beloved, and such a man in the Lord, somewhere in your earthly city, and you thought I would feel no grief if I were not allowed to know your house? How, then, should I not grieve that I do not yet know your face—that is, the house of your soul, which I know as I know my own?

“For I have read your letters, flowing with milk and honey, displaying the simplicity of your heart, in which you seek the Lord, sensing Him in goodness [Note: The printed editions read ‘and offering’; sixteen manuscripts read ‘and offering to Him’], and offering Him glory and honor. The brothers read them, and rejoice tirelessly and ineffably in such abundant and excellent [Col. 0132A] gifts of God, your good qualities. Whoever reads them is carried away, because, as they read, they themselves are carried away. How sweet is the fragrance of Christ, and how it exhales from them, cannot be said. When those letters present you so that you may be seen, how they awaken us to seek you! For they make you both visible and desirable. The love of everyone in them is directed toward you, and they desire to be loved by you. God is praised and blessed, by whose grace you are such a man.

“In them Christ is stirred up, so that He may deign to calm the winds and seas for you as you strive toward His stability. [Note: Thus twenty-one manuscripts. The printed copies have ‘so that He may deign toward His stability.’ One reading has ‘there the wife is stirred up, not the guide,’ and so forth.] The readers see there a wife, not a guide, brought back to firmness in her husband’s bones—not to soften him but to strengthen him—restored and returned to your union and bound to you by spiritual bonds all the stronger because they are chaster; with the duties owed to your holiness, we salute you both as one. [Note: Thus in three Vatican manuscripts and sixteen Gallican manuscripts. One Vatican manuscript reads ‘we salute you with one mind’; the earlier editions read ‘we salute you with one mouth.’]

“There the cedars of Lebanon, brought down to the ground and raised by the joined structure of charity into the building of the ark, cut through the waves of this world without decaying. There glory is despised in order to acquire it, and the world is abandoned in order to possess it. There the little ones, and even the rather large children, of Babylon are dashed against the rock—namely, the vices of worldly confusion and pride.

“Your letters offer these and similar, most sweet and most sacred spectacles to their readers: those letters, letters of sincere faith, letters of good hope, letters of pure charity. How they breathe forth your thirst and make us long for and pine after your soul in the courts of the Lord! What most holy love they exhale! What abundance of a sincere heart they pour forth! What thanks do they give to God? What do they obtain from God? Are they more soothing or more ardent? More luminous or more fruitful? For what is it that so delights us, so inflames us, so drenches us, and is so serene? What is it, I beg you, or what could I repay you for them, except that I am wholly yours in Him of whom you are wholly possessed? If that is too little, certainly I have nothing more . . . .

“The brothers—not only those who live with us, and those who live anywhere while serving God together with us, but nearly all who gladly know us in Christ—salute you, honor you, and long for your brotherhood, blessedness, and humanity. I do not dare to ask; but if you have leisure from ecclesiastical duties, you see what Africa thirsts for with me. [Note: The editions have ‘come and see what Africa feels with me.’ The manuscripts lack the words ‘come and’; they read ‘you see what,’ and three of them finally have ‘what it thirsts for with me.’ With this word Augustine beautifully alludes to the dryness of Africa, as he does again in Letters 31 and 42.]”

## AUGUSTINUS, LETTER 31 (ALSO 34) TO PAULINUS AND THERASIA

*(The fragments of this letter have been revised against the Benedictine edition, twenty-five manuscripts, and four manuscript editions.)*

[Col. 0132D]

“We received the holy brothers Romanus and Agile, who brought another letter of yours, repeating your words and returning them to you, and thereby a most delightful part of your presence; yet this made us all the more eager to see you, with great joy in the Lord. From whom, when, or how could you have given us, or we have demanded from you, such information about yourselves as we learned from their mouths by listening? There was also something that no writing can contain: such joy in the narrators that, through the very faces and eyes of those who spoke, we read you inscribed in their hearts with ineffable delight . . . .

“But although Christ’s yoke is gentle in itself and His burden light, nevertheless, because of our harshness and weakness, if this bond bites me or this burden weighs upon me, the comfort of your presence would make it, in an ineffable measure, more bearable and easier to carry, since I hear that you live more free and unburdened from such cares. Therefore I do not ask you immodestly [Col. 0133B], but beg, demand, and insist that you deign to come to Africa, which suffers from a greater thirst for such men than from the distinction of its dryness.

“God knows that we wish you to be bodily present in these lands not only because of my desire, nor only because of those who, through us or through rumor spreading everywhere, have learned of your purpose, but also because of the others, some of whom do not hear, and others who do not believe what they hear, but who nevertheless can love what they discover . . . .

“For it is one thing not to incorporate what is lacking, and another to tear away what has already been incorporated. The former are rejected like food; the latter are cut off like limbs. We therefore wish this glory of Christ to be brought before the eyes of our people also: in one marriage, examples set before both sexes of pride being trampled down, and of perfection not being despaired of . . . .

“I have learned from the brothers that you are writing against the pagans. If we deserve anything from your heart, send it freely for us to read; for your heart is such an oracle of the Lord that we may confidently expect from it answers both pleasing to us and fully explanatory against the most talkative questions.

“The most blessed brother Severus, bishop of the Church of Milevis, salutes your holiness with the duty he owes us. All the brothers who serve the Lord with us do likewise: they desire you as much as they salute you; they desire you as much as they love you; and they love you as much as you are good.”

## AUGUSTINUS, LETTER 80 (ALSO 65) TO PAULINUS AND THERASIA

*(This fragment of the letter has been revised against twenty-one manuscripts and four editions in the Benedictine edition.)*

[Col. 0133D]

“Now, therefore, I ask what I usually ask, so that you may do what you usually do. Pray for us, that God may see our humility and our labor and forgive all our sins. I wish to converse with you in writing about such matters, if you deign, as we could converse about if we were present before your senses.

“Behold, you solved that little question which I recently proposed, as though, being present to one another amid sweet conversation, I were putting it before you [Note: Some editions and manuscripts read ‘I were presenting it’; most manuscripts read ‘I were offering it’], with thoroughly Christian understanding and devotion [Note: This letter is not extant]; but you did so too hurriedly and briefly. For there the grace of your speech could have dwelt somewhat longer and more fully [Col. 0134A], if, after saying that you had decided to persevere in that place in which you are happily living, you had explained somewhat more clearly that, if anything else concerning you should please the Lord, you would prefer His will to your own. In what way are we to know the will of God, which must be preferred to our own will?”

## AUGUSTINUS, LETTER 95 (ALSO 250) TO PAULINUS AND THERASIA

*(This fragment has been collated with the Vatican exemplar and the Leuven edition of the Benedictine text.)*

“I asked you in an earlier letter what you thought the future eternal life of the saints would be like. But you answered me well: that one must still inquire about the condition of the present life.”

## AUGUSTINUS, LETTER 149 (ALSO 59) TO PAULINUS

*(These fragments have been collated with twenty-three manuscripts and four editions in the Benedictine edition.)*

[Col. 0134B]

“As far as I could, I did not fail your questions, aided by your prayers and by the very discussions you sent. For when you discuss by questioning, you inquire keenly and teach humbly . . . . No one reads or hears me teaching and discussing, or kindling them by any exhortations, with richer fruit than he observes you living.”

## AUGUSTINUS, LETTER 186 (ALSO 106), AGAINST THE PELAGIANS, TO PAULINUS

*(That fragment has been collated with six manuscripts and four editions in the Benedictine edition.)*

“Let us therefore pray for them, holy brother. You see, together with us, how bad an error holds them captive. Your letters exhale the purest fragrance of Christ, in which you appear as His most genuine lover and confessor [Col. 0134C]. But we thought we ought to speak with you at length on this matter. First, we did so because nothing is more delightful than grace—grace by which the weak are healed, grace by which the sluggish are aroused, grace by which those who are willing are helped. Then, so that, if by our arrangement, with God’s assistance, we could accomplish anything, your support might be employed not for your faith itself but for the defense of faith against such people, just as we too are aided toward this capacity by the letters of your brotherly affection.

“For what is richer and fuller than the truest confession, such as that in one of your letters where you humbly lamented that our nature has not remained as it was created, but has been corrupted through that father of the human race, saying:

“‘Poor and grieving, I am still thickly covered with the squalor of the earthly image, and in fleshly perceptions and earthly actions I bear more from the first Adam than from the second. How shall I dare to portray myself to you, when I am proved to be a defiler of the heavenly image through earthly corruption? Shame encloses me on both sides. I blush to portray what I am; I do not dare to portray what I am not. I hate what I am, and I am not what I love.

“‘But what will it profit miserable me to hate iniquity and love virtue, when I do rather what I hate and, sluggishly, do not strive to do what I love? I am divided against myself and torn apart by an inward war, while spirit fights against flesh, flesh against spirit, and the law of the body attacks the law of the mind through the law of sin.

“‘Unhappy am I, who have not digested within me the poisoned taste of the hostile tree even by the wood of the Cross. For that paternal poison continues in me [Note: In Paulinus it reads ‘from Adam’], by which the father, through his transgression, infected the whole of his race’ (From Paulinus’ Letter to Severus 30, also 8).

“And so forth, all the many things that you weave together [Note: [Col. 0135D] Thus three manuscripts; three others and four printed editions read ‘connect.’] concerning this misery with groaning, awaiting the redemption of your body and recognizing that you are not yet saved in reality but in hope. Yet perhaps, when you said these things, you transformed someone else into yourself; perhaps you do not suffer any troublesome and hateful vexations from the flesh lusting against the spirit, although you do not consent to it . . . .

“As for praying and groaning as you demand help for progress and right living, what letter of yours does not burn with this? [Note: The editions read, ‘Whom would your letter not strike?’ But the manuscripts read more aptly, ‘What letter of yours does not burn?’—that is, what does not proceed from your letters, and so forth. Benedictine editors.] What part of your speech, however extensive, does not scatter, with groaning devotion, what we say in prayer: ‘Do not lead us into temptation’? Let us therefore console one another in all these things, exhort one another, and, as the Lord grants, help one another.”

## AUGUSTINUS, BOOK ON THE CARE TO BE TAKEN FOR THE DEAD, TO PAULINUS

*(These fragments have been revised against two Vatican manuscripts.)*

“For a long time, venerable fellow-bishop Pauline, I have been in your debt for a reply, ever since you wrote to me through the people of our most religious daughter Flora, asking whether it benefits anyone after death that his body is buried near the memorial of some saint [Note: This letter is not extant]. That widow had asked this of you on behalf of her deceased son in those regions; and you had written back to console her, announcing also that the body of the faithful young man Cynegius, which she had desired with maternal and devout affection [Col. 0135C], had been placed, as she wished, in the basilica of the most blessed confessor Felix . . .

“You now have my answer to what you thought should be asked of me, such as I was able to give it. If it is more lengthy than necessary [Note: Thus two Vatican manuscripts. Another reads ‘enough’], forgive me; this happened because I wished to speak with you at greater length. I ask that you let me know by your reply how your venerable affection receives this book. Its bearer will undoubtedly make it more pleasing to you—our brother and fellow presbyter Candidianus, whom I came to know through your letters, welcomed with my whole heart, and dismissed unwillingly.”

## AUGUSTINUS, BOOK I OF THE CITY OF GOD, CHAPTER 10

*(This fragment has been collated with the Venetian edition of 1475.)*

“Thus our Paulinus, bishop of Nola, who from the richest of men became poorest by choice and most abundantly holy, when the barbarians ravaged Nola itself and he was held by them, prayed in his heart as we later learned from him:

“‘Lord, do not let me be tortured on account of gold and silver; for where all my possessions are, You know.’

“For he had all his possessions where the One who had warned him to store up and treasure them had told him to have them—the One who had foretold that these evils would come upon the world.”

## SULPICIUS SEVERUS, AT THE END OF THE DIALOGUES

*(That fragment has been revised against three German manuscripts, respectively eight hundred, seven hundred, and five hundred years old; two Jolian manuscripts, eight hundred years old; the Victorinus manuscript, six hundred; and the Bigotian manuscript, five hundred years old.)*

“But as you retrace your route, passing through various regions, places, harbors, islands, and cities, spread the name and glory of Martin among the peoples. Above all, remember not to pass by Campania; and even if your course is especially off the beaten track, do not let the expense of any great delay seem so significant to you that you fail to visit there the illustrious man Paulinus, praised throughout the whole world [Note: Thus restored from the three German, two Jolian, Victorinus, and Bigotian manuscripts. Some printed editions read ‘worthy of praise.’]. To him, I beg you, first unfold the volume of our discourse, whether it was completed yesterday or spoken today [Note: Thus emended from the seven manuscripts mentioned above]. You will report everything to him; you will recite everything to him, so that Rome may immediately learn through him the sacred praises of the man, just as he first spread our little book not only throughout Italy but also throughout all Illyricum. He, who does not begrudge Martin his glory and is a most devout judge of his holy virtues in Christ [Note: ‘in Christ’ is absent from one Jolian manuscript; in one German manuscript it has been added by another hand], will not refuse to compare our bishop with his Felix.”

## SULPICIUS SEVERUS, ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MARTIN, CHAPTER 21

*(This fragment has been revised against the German and Jolian manuscripts, eight hundred years old.)*

“Now when Paulinus, a man destined later to become an example of great importance, began to suffer severe pain in one eye, and a thick cloud had already covered its pupil, Martin touched his eye with a small brush [Note: Thus the Jolian manuscript. Other copies read ‘his eye’]; and, when all pain had been removed, restored its former health to him. [Note: One German manuscript reads ‘with a brush.’]”

## MARTIN, IN SULPICIUS SEVERUS’ LIFE OF HIM, CHAPTER 26

*(This fragment has been collated with four German manuscripts, respectively nine hundred, eight hundred, five hundred, and four hundred years old; the Jolian manuscript, eight hundred; the Victorinus manuscript, six hundred; and the Bigotian manuscript, five hundred years old.)*

“His speech among us was concerned with nothing else than abandoning the allurements of this world and the burdens of the age, so that we might follow the Lord Jesus free and unencumbered. He repeatedly placed before us the outstanding example of Paulinus, the illustrious man whom we mentioned above, who, having cast away immense wealth and followed Christ, alone among men of this age had almost fulfilled the evangelical commands. He cried out that we should follow him and imitate him, and that the present age was blessed to possess such a testimony of faith and virtue: for, in accordance with the Lord’s command, although rich and possessing many things, he had sold everything [Note: One German manuscript reads ‘by giving everything away’] and given it to the poor, accomplishing by his example what was impossible to do [Note: Thus one German manuscript with the printed editions. Six manuscripts read ‘having done’], and had made possible what was impossible [Note: One German manuscript reads ‘he did it.’]. [Note: Two German manuscripts wrongly read ‘the present age . . . a testimony.’]

“How great, moreover, was the gravity and dignity of his speech and conversation; how lively, effective, ready, and fluent he was in resolving questions concerning the Scriptures!”

## HONORIUS, THE EMPEROR, IN THE RESCRIPT BY WHICH HE INVITES PAULINUS TO THE SYNOD

*(From a Vatican manuscript, cited by Baronius under the year of Christ 419, no. 20.)*

“To the holy and venerable Father Paulinus, bishop.

“Our certain knowledge has been only this: nothing could be decided by those priests who had assembled for the synod, since your Blessedness, prevented by an illness of the body, was unable to endure the hardship of the journey. And because of the absence of the holy man, the vices are meanwhile rejoicing—perhaps, rather, raging—for a wicked and ancient ambition has long wished to contend with a blessed man and one of holy life, so that, against the goods of apostolic instruction, it may suppose that reliance should be placed upon walls erected through force and presumption.

“O truly worthy cause, which only the blessed life of your crown can mark out. We therefore announce that judgment has been postponed, so that divine commands may be spoken from the mouth of your Veneration, who have fulfilled them by following them. Nor can anyone else be their bearer who teaches those precepts except one who has been approved as worthy of apostolic disciplines.

“Therefore, holy lord, deservedly venerable Father, just servant of God, deign to grant us this gift of your visitation—if it may be called a gift of divine work—despite the labor you despise; so that, after all else has been set aside, insofar as moderation and tranquility support it, you may benefit the synod, without interruption, and deign to fulfill both our desires and the blessing [Col. 0137C] that we long for.”

## EUCHERIUS, IN HIS EXHORTATORY LETTER TO VALERIAN

“Paulinus also, bishop of Nola, a singular and blessed example for our Gaul, once possessing immense wealth and an abundant fountain of eloquence, passed over into our conviction and purpose in such a way that he sprinkled almost every part of the world with his eloquence and deeds.”

## PROSPER, IN HIS CHRONICLE, UNDER THE FOURTH YEAR OF ARCADIUS AND HONORIUS

“Paulinus, later bishop of Nola, chose religion unencumbered, after selling everything, although he had been master of innumerable estates.”

## IDATIUS, IN HIS CHRONICLE, UNDER THE THIRTIETH YEAR OF HONORIUS

[Col. 0137D]

“Paulinus, most noble and most eloquent, long ago made nobler by his conversion to God, an apostolic man, is renowned as bishop of Nola in Campania. Therasia, made his sister from his wife, equals him in the testimony and merit of a blessed life. The notable works of his own labor remain to be praised.”

## SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS, BOOK IV, LETTER 3

“Paulinus challenges.”

## SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS, POEM 9

“But do not try to compare with me

those whom, though myself much lesser, I adore even more:

112 Paulinus, Ampelius, and Symmachus,

Messala, of sufficiently profound talent,

and, in no respect, second to Martius.”

## GENNADIUS, BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS, CHAPTER 48

*(This has been revised against the German manuscript, one thousand years old.)”

Paulinus, bishop of Nola in Campania [Note: [Col. 0138D] Restored from a manuscript codex of Germanus, 1,000 years old. In the printed editions it formerly read *composed*.], wrote short works in verse, but many of them: a consolatory little book, in place of an epitaph, to a certain Celsus on the death of a Christian and baptized infant, fortified by Christian hope; several letters to Severus; and, before his episcopate, a prose panegyric to the emperor Theodosius on the victory over the tyrants, especially because he had conquered more by faith and prayer than by arms. He also composed a Sacramentary and a Hymnary. He likewise sent many letters to his sister concerning contempt for the world; and he published treatises on various subjects, treating different matters in diverse discussions [Col. 0138B] [Note: [Col. 0138D] This word is absent from the Germanus manuscript.]. Yet the chief of all his little works is his book *On Penance* and *On the General Praise of All the Martyrs*. He flourished in the time of Honorius and Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0138D] The Germanus manuscript reads “Theodosius.”], distinguished not only by learning and holiness [Note: [Col. 0138D] In the same manuscript the word “of life” is absent; but the words of Usuard in the Martyrology, taken from Gennadius himself, confirm that the word should be retained.] of life, but also by power against demons.

**AN ANCIENT AUTHOR AMONG THE WORKS OF ST. JEROME, VOLUME IX, LETTER 3, TO THE DAUGHTERS OF GERUNTIUS.**

This tomb our Paulinus himself recently purchased, together with the mother of his household, at great expense; and they, dying to worldly conduct, now rest from worldly works . . . This double tomb the heads of households whom we have mentioned provided for themselves: by abandoning the senate, honors, and riches, they seemed dead to those among whom they appeared to have been born, even while they were still living dead. Behold one tomb, in which the conduct of the old man, together with the playthings of his nobility, is hidden; the other will be when the body itself, which by nature’s law is destined to perish, dissolved, returns to the earth, concerning which it is written: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19); while the soul rests in refreshment.

**CASSIODORUS, *ON THE INSTITUTIONS OF DIVINE SCRIPTURE*, BOOK I, CHAPTER 21.**

(From the Fontanet manuscript, edited by Chifflet.)

He—that is, Jerome—sent his remarkable letter to Paulinus, formerly a senator and now a presbyter, teaching him how to read the divine Scriptures with due caution . . . For he wrote to a new reader of the divine law, who had been so thoroughly trained in secular literature [Col. 0138D] that he had also composed a prudent and elegant book on the emperor Theodosius.

**PAULINUS OF PÉRIGUEUX, BOOK II, *ON THE LIFE OF ST. MARTIN*.**

(This fragment was recently collated with a Germanus manuscript 800 years old.)

Indeed, a similar cure restored health to Paulinus,

Whom the glory of distinguished faith raised high,

Whose sight then lay hidden beneath a spreading cloud,

While darkness, extended through poured-in shadows,

Barred all light beneath a covering of blemishes.

A light sponge, applied with a gentle and delicate touch,

Drove it away when, through the gift of the blessed hand nearby,

It was soon brought close to his eye.

His sight, restored, now learned to bear the light,

And, marveling at the new brightness, received it.

Would that the medicine of our holy patron

Might likewise wish to touch the darkness of our heart with such light,

So that it might restore once more the mysteries of the ancient deed:

The name the same, the physician the same, and the cause [Note: [Col. 0139D] Thus corrected from an old Germanus manuscript. The former reading was *remedy*.] of the remedy the same.

**VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS, BOOK II, *ON THE LIFE OF ST. MARTIN*.**

And a sharp ray penetrated Paulinus’ eye,

Sunk in dreadful darkness, when hands were laid upon it;

A clear day shone forth when the cloud was wiped away;

Light flashed out, and his face, no longer dim, displayed a double brightness,

As a lamp from Martin’s fingers poured forth oil,

Its healing touch surpassing all eye-salves.

**MARTIN, IN FORTUNATUS’ *LIFE OF HIMSELF*, BOOK II.**

That illustrious Father who blessed the deeds of Paulinus

Flourished in Italy, where later Paulinus was bishop of Nola,

Where the Campanian region lies, under the highest ruler:

Rich in fields, wealthy in servants, abounding in heaps of wealth;

A man vast in fortune, lofty in household, full-voiced in speech;

Yet richer in faith, he made himself poor for Christ,

And gave countless coins to redeem those burdened by sins.

His wealth, scattered upon the ground, migrated to the stars,

And made sluggish lands ascend to heaven,

Standing in one place [Note: [Col. 0139D] Another reading: “must be given.”], and making brute creatures leap to the stars.

Thus, when Paulinus fulfilled what the Gospel records,

Martin admonishes all that such a man must be followed:

A rich man who was able to proceed along a difficult path,

And who, laying down his burden, ascended freely to the citadel,

Calling his followers to climb higher by his example.

**GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, BOOK II, *ON THE GLORY OF THE CONFESSORS*, CHAPTER 107.**

There was a man of venerable life, Paulinus of the city of Nola, born of a noble family. He obtained Therasia as a wife equal to himself; he possessed great wealth and was exceedingly rich and prosperous both in the ownership of estates and in the protection of his household. But when the Gospel reading first reached his ears in which the Lord rebukes the young man on account of his riches, saying, “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter [Col. 0139D] the kingdom of God,” he immediately sold everything he had and distributed it to the poor. Freed from every desire, he followed the Master unencumbered, thinking that by this means he would become rich in the treasures of paradise if he seemed to possess nothing transitory. The divine majesty granted him that what the Gospel had declared impossible he might deservedly fulfill in practice.

One day a man came to him asking for alms, and he said to his wife: “Go and give him what he needs.” She replied: “We have nothing more than one loaf of bread.” He said to her: “Go, hand it over; the Lord will provide us with food.” But she, being cautious and wishing to keep it in reserve lest anything be lacking, refused to give it. Meanwhile certain men arrived, saying that they had been sent by their masters to bring him a supply of grain and wine, but that they had been delayed because a storm had carried off one of their ships together with its wheat. Then the man of God turned to the woman and said: “Understand that you have now stolen one loaf of bread from the poor man, and for that reason this ship has been sunk.”

He therefore departed with his wife, as though traveling to another region, possessing nothing beyond his own condition. After a long time, when the inhabitants of his region were seeking him and could not find him anywhere, a merchant from that city arrived in the town where the blessed man was serving the heavenly Lord. When he saw him, he immediately threw himself upon the ground and embraced the saint’s feet, saying: “This is the blessed Paulinus, known throughout the world, whom his fellow citizens sought for a long time but were utterly unable to find.” As he recounted all his deeds, everyone who heard these things was astonished.

Before long, when the bishop of the city of Nola died, Paulinus himself was appointed in his place. That church possessed many riches, and the Lord fulfilled in him what he had deigned to promise through the Gospel: “Whoever has left everything for my sake will receive a hundredfold in this age, and in the age to come will possess eternal life.” Yet after he had assumed the episcopate he always showed himself humble, because he knew that he would be exalted before God if he pursued humility. The money from the revenues of the Church that came into his hands was immediately distributed to the poor.

His most chaste wife did not leave him. The holy man was possessed of remarkable prudence and trained in rhetorical literature. He shone so greatly in virtue through the multiplied gifts of spiritual graces that, as he was dying, he saw with his bodily eyes Martin himself and Januarius of Italy before he gave up his spirit; they had departed from this world before him. And because we had read nothing about the life of this blessed man, we have recorded what we learned through the report of the faithful when we wished to speak of almsgiving. There is, however, among us an extensive reading concerning his death; for that reason we have not followed his life in order.

Behold what almsgiving grants. Behold what treasures God bestows on his saints, who love him in the poor. Conversely, to those who greedily pursue the evil of avarice, he takes away what they wickedly desire, according to that saying of the holy Gospel: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. 25:29).

**GREGORY THE GREAT, *DIALOGUES*, BOOK III, CHAPTER 1.**

(This has been collated with the Bigot manuscript, 600 years old; two Jolian manuscripts; and the latest edition.)

When, during the time of the ravaging Vandals, Italy had been laid waste in the regions of Campania, and many people had been carried from that land into Africa, the man of God Paulinus gave to captives and the needy everything that he had been able to possess from his episcopal treasury [Col. 0141A] [Note: [Col. 0140D] Three manuscripts read “when.”] [Note: [Col. 0140D] We restored this from one Jolian manuscript. Another, and the printed editions, read “for the use of the bishop’s household.” The Bigot manuscript reads “for the bishop’s use.”].

When nothing at all remained that he could give to those who asked, a widow came to him one day. She reported that her son had been led into captivity by the son-in-law of the Vandal king, and she asked the man of God for his ransom, if perhaps his master might graciously accept it and allow him to return home. But the man of God, searching diligently for what he could give the woman who was asking, found that he had nothing with him except himself. He replied to the woman: “Woman, I have nothing that I can give; but take me myself. Declare me to be the slave belonging to you, and, so that you may recover your son, hand me over into slavery in his place.”

When she heard this from the mouth of so great a man, she thought it a joke rather than compassion. But he, being a most eloquent man and exceptionally well trained also in secular studies, quickly persuaded the doubting woman to believe what she had heard and not hesitate to hand over the bishop into slavery in exchange for the recovery of her son [Note: [Col. 0141D] From the Bigot manuscript and the new edition we restored “the bishop.” The former reading, “if I am,” was unsuitable; this may not, however, have been Gregory’s original reading.]. So both of them went to Africa.

As the son-in-law of the king, who held her son, was passing by, the widow presented herself to ask a favor. First she requested that he give her son to her [Note: [Col. 0141D] The printed editions read “his.” We restored “to her” from two Jolian manuscripts, in which the word “son” is absent; one of them reads “to be given.”]. But when the barbarian, swollen with proud arrogance and inflated by the joy of transient prosperity, disdained not only to do this but even to hear the request, the widow added: “Behold, I offer this man as his substitute; only show me mercy and return my only son” [Note: [Col. 0141D] The Bigot manuscript adds “my.”].

When he saw the handsome man, he asked what trade he knew [Note: [Col. 0141D] The Bigot and first Jolian manuscripts read “a man of handsome appearance.”]. The man of God Paulinus [Col. 0141C] replied: “I do not know any particular trade, but I do know how to cultivate a garden.” The pagan was very pleased when he heard that Paulinus was skilled in growing vegetables. He therefore accepted the slave and returned the son to the woman who had asked for him. After receiving him, the widow departed from Africa, while Paulinus undertook the care of cultivating the garden.

Whenever that same son-in-law of the king frequently entered the garden and asked for his gardener, and saw that he was a very wise man [Note: [Col. 0141D] We added “to be” from two Jolian manuscripts and the Bigot manuscript.], he began to abandon his familiar friends and converse more often with his gardener, taking pleasure in his conversation. Paulinus used to bring him vegetables and green herbs to the table each day, and, after receiving bread, return to the care of the garden.

When this had continued for some time [Note: [Col. 0142D] Thus read the three Jolian manuscripts and the Bigot manuscript together with the latest edition. The former reading was “was being done.”], he said one day to his master, who was speaking with him privately: “Consider what you are doing, and take thought for how the kingdom of the Vandals should be governed, because the king will soon die, and will die with all speed.”

When he heard this, since the king loved him above the others, he did not keep it silent but reported what he had learned from his gardener, namely, that he was a wise man. When the king heard this, he immediately replied: “I would like to see this man of whom you speak.” His son-in-law, the temporary master of the venerable Paulinus, replied: “He is accustomed to bring me green herbs for my meal. I shall therefore have him bring them to the table [Note: [Col. 0142D] The first Jolian manuscript and the new edition read “I will have him bring this man.”], so that you may recognize who has said these things to me.”

And so it happened. When the king reclined for his meal, Paulinus arrived from his work, carrying vegetables and various green things. When the king saw him, he suddenly trembled. He summoned his master, who was related to him through his daughter, and disclosed to him in secret what he had previously concealed, saying: “What you heard is true. Last night in a dream I saw judges sitting in judgment against me; among them this man was also seated, and, by their judgment, the scourge that I had once received was being taken away from me. But ask who he is, for I do not suppose that a man of such merit, apparently a commoner, is really one.”

Then the king’s son-in-law took Paulinus aside and asked who he was. The man of God replied: “I am your slave, whom you accepted as a substitute for the widow’s son.” When the other insistently demanded that he tell not who he now was but who he had been in his own land, and pressed him with repeated questioning [Note: [Col. 0142D] Thus restored from the Jolian and Bigot manuscripts. Otherwise: “through repeated questioning.”], the man of God, constrained by solemn adjurations and no longer able to deny who he was, declared that he had been a bishop.

When his master heard this, he was greatly terrified and humbly offered him the following, saying: “Ask whatever you wish, so that you may return to your own land from me with a great gift.” The man of God Paulinus replied: “There is one benefit you can confer on me: release all the captives from my city.” They were immediately sought out throughout Africa and, together with ships laden with grain, were released in his company as a recompense for the venerable Paulinus.

Not many days later the king of the Vandals died, and the scourge which, by God’s dispensation, he had received and retained for the punishment of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0142D] The first Jolian manuscript reads “which he had received, and which immediately followed,” instead of “which followed.”], to his own destruction, was taken from him. Thus it came about that Paulinus, the servant of almighty God, foretold the truth; and the man who had handed himself over alone into slavery returned from slavery to freedom with many others—imitating the one who assumed the form of a slave so that we might not be slaves of sin. Following his footsteps, Paulinus became a voluntary slave for a time, alone, so that afterward he might be free with many.

Concerning his death, it is also written at his church that, when he was struck by pain in his side, he was brought to his final hour. While his entire house remained standing firm, the room in which the sick man lay trembled when an earthquake occurred, and all who were there were shaken with great terror. Thus that holy soul was released from the flesh. And it happened that great fear seized those who had been able to witness the death of Paulinus. . . .

**JULIANUS POMERIUS, *ON THE CONTEMPLATIVE LIFE*, BOOK II, CHAPTER 9.**

(This fragment was checked against the Bigot manuscript, 800 years old; the Germanus manuscript, 800 years old; and the Jolian manuscript, 600 years old.)

[Col. 0143B] Finally, holy Paulinus, as you yourselves know well, sold the great estates that had belonged to him and distributed the proceeds to the poor. But when he later became a bishop, he did not despise the resources of the Church; rather, he administered them with the utmost fidelity. By this he clearly demonstrated both that personal possessions ought to be despised for the sake of perfection and that the possessions of the Church, which are truly held in common, can be possessed without hindering perfection.

**117 USUARD, IN THE MARTYROLOGY, JUNE 22.**

(From the Bigot manuscript, 600 years old.)

The tenth day before the Kalends of July.

At Nola in Campania, the birth into heaven of the blessed Paulinus, bishop and confessor, whom Saint Gregory mentions in the book of the *Dialogues*. He distinguished himself not only by learning and abundant holiness of life, but also by power against demons.

**DUNCALUS, *BOOK OF RESPONSES AGAINST CLAUDIUS, BISHOP OF TURIN*.**

Paulinus, a most learned and holy man, as many have testified concerning him, published a noble book divided into fifteen poems, in honor and praise of Saint Felix the martyr. In it he described the many miracles and virtues that, by the merits and intercessions of the saint, divine mercy grants to occur daily at his tomb, and especially on the anniversary of his birth into heaven. These things cannot easily be extracted or plucked out by anyone, because all of them—flowers, spices, roses, fragrant lilies—are sweet-smelling and honey-flowing . . . Hence we put forward the blessed Paulinus, endowed with holiness and wisdom, as a kind of most brilliant beacon and an impregnable tower [Col. 0143D], who discussed much on this subject in an exceptionally lucid and fertile discourse.

**JOHN THE DEACON, IN THE PROEM TO THE *LIFE OF ST. GREGORY THE GREAT*, TO POPE JOHN VIII.**

(Collated with the Bigot manuscript, 600 years old.)

Recently, while a reading about Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, was customarily being sung at the vigils of blessed Gregory, the Roman pontiff and apostle of the English people [Note: [Col. 0143] The Bigot manuscript reads “of blessed Gregory the pontiff, that is, the apostle of the English nation.”], you seemed, moved by some divine impulse, to ask the venerable bishops why so great a pontiff, who had composed the Lives of many saints, had lacked a record of his own deeds in his own Church alone—especially since among the Saxons and among the Lombards, a nation utterly hostile to him, he everywhere possessed distinction through his own deeds.

**ANONYMOUS, IN THE PROLOGUE TO THE WORKS OF ST. PAULINUS.**

(From a very old Cluniac manuscript, edited by F. Chifflet.)

Saint Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, Aquitanian by birth, but by the dignity of his family a most distinguished senator of the city of Rome, was moved—especially by the example and preaching of the blessed Martin, bishop of Tours, and of Delphinus of Bordeaux—together with Severus Sulpicius, an equally noble and learned man—was encouraged to exchange secular and married life for the richest poverty of Christian perfection.
