Trampling underfoot all the pomp and luxury of the world, he sold everything that he possessed in this world, according to the Lord’s commandment (Matt. 19:21), and distributed it to the poor.

Then, establishing a monastery near the city of Nola in Campania and practicing a holy life, he became bishop of that same city. Glorious, therefore, in word and example, and also in miracles, he was known to and closely associated with the blessed Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and others of his own time, whose gracious letters either to him or about him are read. After many struggles successfully endured for Christ, he completed a holy old age and rested in the Lord in the city mentioned above.

It is credible that this is the same Paulinus concerning whom blessed Pope Gregory, in the third book of the *Dialogues*, relates an extraordinary story of admirable virtue. For both the words of that same blessed Gregory, by which he records there, among other things, that Paulinus was a bishop of Nola, an ancient Father, and trained in secular studies, and the agreement of the times, seem sufficiently to affirm this. For around that period barbarians bursting forth from the African regions devastated not only Campania itself but almost all Italy, as the strength of the Roman Empire was failing—alas!

**JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, *BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS*.**

Paulinus, a presbyter, disciple of Saint Augustine of Hippo and afterward bishop of Nola in Campania, to whom many letters of Augustine and Jerome, as well as various treatises, are attributed, was a man exceptionally learned in the sacred Scriptures and second to no one of his time in secular literature. He shone forth no less by holiness than by learning. Of him blessed Pope Gregory writes in the third book of the *Dialogues* that he possessed such piety and compassion that, after spending all his property for the use of the poor and the liberation of captives, he even handed himself over into slavery in place of a widow’s son; and that he was eventually released from slavery, together with many captives, because of the merit of his life.

He wrote many volumes in both verse and prose, among which the following are attributed to him:

- *On the Sacraments*, one book;
- *Panegyric of Theodosius*, one book;
- *On Contempt for the World*, one book;
- *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, one book;
- Fourteen letters to Severus Sulpicius;
- *Life of St. Felix, Bishop of Nola*, one book;
- *On the Death of a Baptized Infant*, one book;
- *Hymns in Various Meters*, one book;
- *On Penance*, one book;
- *On the Praise of the Martyrs*, one book;
- [Col. 0145A] *Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He also published several other works that have not come to my notice. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 420.

**BAPTISTA MANTUANUS, CARMELITE POET, IN HIS *APOLOGETIC*.**

What should I say about Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, a contemporary and friend of Jerome? What can I say? Did he not produce poems of the greatest beauty, which still exist and will always exist? When I was still a young man and, according to the custom of that age, recoiled from ecclesiastical studies, I happened by chance upon those poems. Delighted by the sweetness of the verse, I gradually turned my mind toward divine subjects, and from that time became more devoted to sacred letters.

**AMBROSIUS LEO, *ON NOLA*, BOOK II, CHAPTER 13.**

It is well known where the chapel of the holy Paulinus is located: the building itself is a single structure without a separate cell. Attached to it is a large house which, when we were boys, served only as lodging for passing beggars; for this reason it was called a hospice, and the entire neighborhood acquired the same name. Now it has been converted into a monastery in which the priests of Saint Augustine reside.

In that chapel, ceremonies and fairs are held every year, with processions, spectacles, and a master of the fair, as will be explained more fully below. The saint, freed from slavery and returning from Africa to Nola, brought back with him all the Nolans who had been captured and were serving in Africa, liberated in his name. For when Paulinus was there the gardener of a certain ruler, and so forth . . .

When he returned, the Nolans welcomed the father of their city, who had deserved so greatly of the Nolaeans, with every display of ceremony and joy. Thereafter they honored that same day with fixed processions and festive spectacles, and the celebrations have continued down to our own time, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July until the tenth day before those same Kalends.

**PETRUS CRINITUS, *ON LATIN POETS*.**

(From the Badian edition, Paris, 1516.)

Pontius Paulinus, born of a noble family, is numbered among the poets who flourished under the rule of the emperor Gratian, such as Faustus, Tetradius, and Ausonius. He was from Bordeaux and excelled greatly in poetic ability. Some have thought that he was Ausonius’ nephew because Ausonius calls him “son” with a gracious and affectionate form of address; but this is not sufficiently established amid such confused and uncertain obscurity of the facts.

Among other works, Paulinus wrote a poem in hexameter verse on the kings, compiled from Suetonius Tranquillus, in which he achieved the highest praise, as Ausonius reports in these words: “You compressed Suetonius’ three books on the kings into an epitome with such elegance that you alone seem to have achieved what is contrary to the nature of things: brevity that was not obscure.”

Some poems of Paulinus are still read, in which extraordinary learning and incredible elegance appear. The same Paulinus also held distinguished and highly honorable offices, and was counted among the leading and most noble men.

**JODOCUS BADIUS ASCENSIUS, IN THE PREFACE TO THE WORKS OF ST. PAULINUS.**

[Col. 0146A]

Saint Paulinus, although he was thoroughly trained in pagan literature, nevertheless used riches in such a way that it may rightly be said that both that Peitho and the marrow of Suada sat upon his lips. For he teaches, moves, and affects the reader; indeed, he drives him wherever he wishes, beyond measure . . . To explain the life of blessed Paulinus briefly, I shall recount in a few words what I have been able to gather from his writings and those of others.

Born of distinguished parents, brought up in splendid circumstances, and endowed with remarkable talent, he devoted himself to refined literature under Decius Ausonius, the most charming poet of Bordeaux, to whom he was bound by an exceptional friendship because of the friendship and dealings between their fathers. As far as can be gathered from Ausonius’ verses, they either held the highest offices at Rome together or held them in succession. Hence the following from Ausonius to Paulinus, Letter 23:

> Paulinus and Ausonius, men whom the sacred  
> Purple of Quirinus and the gold-covered mantle  
> Of the military robe veiled.

Thus trained in deeper and more refined literature, he produced, with his fertile talent, remarkable poems, among them some on the Caesars drawn from Suetonius. Later, inspired by God, he was wholly converted to Christian piety. Taking Ambrose and Augustine as teachers, and lest he be turned away from Christian modesty by the splendor of his family or honors, he was sent by them to Barcelona. There, initiated into the sacred rites, he rejected all the pomp of the world and made his flowing and almost wanton vein grave and steady. He anxiously avoided every pagan observance, to such an extent that afterward he did not even dare to mention Virgil—a great example that one style suits a man initiated into sacred things, and another a man still devoted to profane matters. Hence he says himself at the beginning of his reply to Ausonius:

> Why do you command the Muses, father,  
> Whom I have renounced, to return  
> To my care?  
> Hearts dedicated to Christ  
> Deny themselves to the Camenae  
> And are not open to Apollo.

Yet in his poetry he retained such grace that one can easily recognize in him both rich fluency and extensive learning.

**HENRICUS GRAVIUS, IN THE PREFACE TO THE WORKS OF ST. PAULINUS.**

(From the Cologne edition, 1560.)

Blessed Paulinus, although he was by far the most learned and elegant of men, was nevertheless published in a remarkably corrupt state through the ignorance and recklessness of many. While this is certainly unworthy of all learned men, it was especially unworthy of Paulinus, who alone deserved to be preserved wholly uncorrupted because of the purity of his language and his other outstanding qualities. For what was purer than he? What more polished? What more dignified or ardent? If you consider the holiness of his life, who breathed Christ more vigorously? Who expressed him more fully in his life?

For this is especially remarkable, what Paulinus of Aquileia the deacon reports concerning him: “At that time,” he says (*Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 1), “when the Vandals, after capturing Rome together with the Moors, were ravaging the whole region of Campania and were destroying Nola in a miserable ruin, Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Nola, a most holy man and, as Gregory writes, most eloquent and especially learned in profane studies, though not without the prophetic spirit, had spent all his wealth on redeeming Christian captives. When he saw a widow bitterly mourning and lamenting her captive son, and could not bear the excessive tears mingled with compassion, he crossed with the widow to Africa, where the son was held captive; there, offering himself as a substitute, he redeemed the son and returned him to his mother. But because his holiness was revered even by the most barbarous men, he was ordered to return to his homeland with all his fellow citizens, who had been given to him as a gift.”

This also should by no means be passed over in silence: some maintain that this bishop of Nola was different from Pontius Paulinus, the praetorian man who compressed Suetonius’ three books on the kings into an epitome with such elegance that, as Ausonius testifies, he alone seems to have achieved what is contrary to nature: brevity that was not obscure. They were misled, I believe, by the fact that our Paulinus differed somewhat from the other in his manner of life and style of writing. But I shall explain briefly that these men were “erring completely from the path” (*τῇ πάσῃ ἱδῷ ἀφαμαρτάνεσθαι*, according to the proverb).

For Paulinus, born of distinguished parents, brought up in splendid circumstances, and endowed with remarkable talent, devoted himself to refined literature under Decius Ausonius, the most charming poet of Bordeaux, with whom he either held the highest offices at Rome together or held them in succession, as is clear from these verses of Ausonius addressed to him:

> Although your name in the title of the *Fasti* came first,  
> And your curule seat’s ivory preceded ours at Rome.

The same poet says:

> Paulinus and Ausonius, men whom the sacred  
> Purple of Quirinus and the gold-covered mantle  
> Of the military robe veiled.

Having become a Christian through divine inspiration, he took Ambrose and Augustine as teachers. They sent him to Barcelona, where he was initiated into the sacred rites, lest he be turned away from Christian modesty by the splendor of his family or honors. It is reported that after his conversion he rejected all the pomp of the world and made his flowing and almost wanton vein grave and steady; that he not only ceased to read pagan poets but was not even accustomed to mention them. Hence he sings of himself to the same Ausonius:

> Why do you command the Muses, father,  
> Whom I have renounced, to return  
> To my care?  
> Hearts dedicated to Christ  
> Deny themselves to the Camenae  
> And are not open to Apollo.

Since learned men everywhere lamented that this man had been corrupted in many places through the carelessness of scribes or printers, I thought I would perform a worthwhile service by publishing him after correcting him through study and labor, so that he might now be read more conveniently and understood more accurately.

**GREGORIUS FABRITIUS, *ON ST. PAULINUS OF NOLA*.**

(From volume I of the *Orthodoxographers*, Basel, 1569, p. 75.)

Pontius [Note: [Col. 0147D] Meropius.] Eutropius Paulinus, a native of Bordeaux, was born to a senatorial father. He possessed a large patrimony at Fundi in Campania, but, neglecting it for Christ’s sake, considered poverty preferable to riches. He had distinguished brothers, a very noble wife, Therasia, and good and eminent friends and relatives.

In the province of Tarragona in Spain he received the sacred orders from Lampius, bishop of Barcelona. At the beginning of his ministry, almost all the bishops of Campania, as well as some from Africa, visited him out of respect. At Nola he was presbyter under the two bishops Maximus and Quentus, whom he eventually succeeded with the consent of that Church and of the leading men.

He built the basilicas at Nola and Fundi, and adorned them not so much with architectural structures as with his ingenuity, adding various inscriptions in their several places. He himself possessed a humble little house near the temple of Saint Felix. In it there was an upper room raised and suspended above the ground, together with a nearby portico, near which were small cells intended for guests.

He did not gorge himself on the finest wheat bread or on Picentine loaves, as the priests of Vesta once did at Rome; nor did he have artichokes or pheasants set before him, as the priests of Cybele did there. Rather, he lived according to the moderate customs of his age, sparingly and frugally, using poor and inexpensive food—namely, gruels cooked not from fine wheat but from meal and millet, with little oil and abundant water. He also mixed beans with millet. For this reason he condemns the monk Marracinus, a glutton.

His cups were few and small, which he himself calls “the drippings of drinking vessels.” As witnesses to this frugality he cites his guests, the excellent priests Victor and Cardamates [Note: [Col. 0148D] They were not priests.]. Among the gifts he sent to foreign bishops who were his colleagues were wooden or earthen cups, and especially Nolan bread, which, as Leo Ambrosius writes, was highly praised and superior in crumb, whiteness, flavor, and softness.

In one passage he asks his own Sulpicius, the priest of Primuliacum, for old Narbonese wine—not drinking it from little ladles or from elephant vessels, the customary cups of the priests of old, but from small cups, a mixing bowl, or a beaker.

He was not strong in body and often suffered from poor health, not only at home but also on his travels. In his writings he rebukes the philosophers who defend fate and fortune, as in his letter to Jovius; and also wandering monks, who are no less flushed in their *armilausa* garment, as he calls it, than in their drunken faces, as in Letter 7 to Severus.

In religion he was steadfast and endured severe struggles for it. ([Note: [Col. 0148D] These statements are not certain.]) He was driven into exile by the Arians because he rejected their *ὁμοιούσιον* (“of similar substance”) and piously defended the *ὁμοούσιον* (“of the same substance”). Thrown into prison, he himself writes that he was saved through the favor of God’s angels. In the time of the Goths, he allowed himself to be sold in order to redeem a widow’s son, and was released by the savage enemy in admiration of his virtue.

Pope Anastasius commended him in his own letter to the bishops of Campania. He wrote ten books of the *Birthdays of Saint Felix*, a panegyric poem on the death of Celsus, and also works to Cytherius and Nicetas, as well as five books of letters. He also wrote a panegyric to the emperor Theodosius.

In his letters he treats historical subjects as well: the story of Melania to Severus and the shipwreck of Valgius to Macarius, in which the sweetness of the narrator is especially delightful. He reached a great old age and died under the emperor Marcian, around the year 458 [Note: [Col. 0149D] He died in the year 431.].

**ELIAS VINETUS, IN HIS NOTES TO AUSONIUS’ WORKS, ON ST. PAULINUS.**

(From the Bordeaux edition, 1575.)

The Roman consul was before Ausonius, as you will learn from Ausonius’s twentieth letter—that is, before the year of Christ 382—but an extraordinary consul, as we shall say; and he seems to have obtained that magistracy through Ausonius’s influence . . . I do not know where he died, unless perhaps at his own Nola, whence, Raphael Volaterranus writes, his body was transferred to Rome and placed in the church of Bartholomew.

## ANDREAS SCHOTTUS, ON THE LIFE OF BLESSED PAULINUS

*(From volume V of the Bibliotheca Patrum, Cologne edition, 1618.)*

[Col. 0149B] Paulinus’s father was consul at Rome with Julian, I suppose, in the year 1277 from the foundation of the City, in the year of Christ 325, in which year the first Council of Nicaea, of 318 Fathers, began to be held, as Onuphrius teaches in the Fasti. Paulinus the son, however, was born during the ninth consulship of Constantius Augustus and the second consulship of Gallus and Julian Caesar, in the year of Christ 357—or, as Victor Giselinus reckons in his prolegomena to Severus Sulpicius, in the year 348, in which the sacred poet Prudentius was also born, and Severus Sulpicius ten years later; in the year 1100 from the foundation of the City, when the councils of Ariminum and Seleucia were held.

Thus Paulinus was born of a consular family in the city of Ebromagus, not far from the borders of the Tarbelli and from Bordeaux—or rather from the river Garonne, along which he leads those coming from the Tarbelli most directly to Bordeaux. In that place he possessed estates left by his ancestors, no smaller than Ausonius’s estate at Lucaniacum [Col. 0149C], and, having Ausonius as his teacher, was educated together with his brothers. Nor do I doubt that he lived there for the greater part of his life, until, changing his way of life, he went away to Spain and settled with Lampius.

Here, then, Paulinus, throughout his fifth letter, never ceases to congratulate himself on the friendship cultivated with Severus from their earliest years with the greatest affection, and on that same friendship’s subsequent transformation from secular into spiritual. He very clearly suggests in the same words that Sulpicius at that time lived not very far from Ebromagus, probably on his ancestral soil. It is not difficult to conjecture that this was either Toulouse or a place near Toulouse, partly from Paulinus’s eleventh and twelfth letters (now the thirty-first and thirty-second), which mention the second basilica of Severus founded by Paulinus at Primuliacum, and partly from the third letter to his mother-in-law Bassula [Col. 0149D].

Ausonius writes in his twentieth letter that Paulinus was made consul while still a young man, but, I think, an extraordinary consul. For you will not find his name in the consular Fasti. Baronius conjectures from the Chronicle of Blessed Jerome that he was consul in the year of Christ 375. But he would scarcely have been twenty-five years old. In Baronius I find that Ausonius was made consul together with Olybrius four years later, in the year of Christ 379. He changed his style after having been initiated into the Christian mysteries and duly baptized, now fleeing the allurements of words. His letters sent in piety to Severus Sulpicius and others show that he loved sacred writings and devotion; and this is especially clear at the end of the sixth letter (now the first) to Severus [Col. 0150A]. Indeed, when Ausonius seriously urged him to return to poetry, he answered him as follows: “Why, having renounced,” and so forth.

Ausonius dedicated to him, as one who had once read and imitated Virgil but who, moved by a pious zeal, had now rejected him, the *Cento nuptialis* composed from Maro. Paulinus was baptized by Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, following the example of Severus Sulpicius, who, after his wife’s death, had renounced the world and joined himself to Saint Martin.

His wife was Therasia, a devout matron. With her consent Paulinus sold many estates and decided to renounce the world, as he writes in Letter 11 (now 31), “by selling the estates.” Ambrose mentions this in Book VI of his letters, Augustine in *The City of God*, chapter 10, and Severus in the *Life of Saint Martin*.

He first went to Vienne in Gaul, where he visited Blessed Martin together with Sulpicius. There, suffering from an affliction of the eyes, he was cured by Martin, and he formed a friendship with Victricius, who later became bishop of Rouen. From there he went to Milan, where he enjoyed an intimate relationship with Blessed Ambrose.

He also lived at Rome. Then he withdrew to Nola, as Ambrose records in his letter to Sabinus, Book VI, and as Paulinus himself records in the second *Natalis* to Saint Felix. Afterward he undertook a journey to Spain. Having traveled through Spain, he came to Complutum, where death took from him the firstborn son whom he had long desired by his wife Therasia. The child died on the eighth day and was buried there among the martyrs. They think that Paulinus then became known to Prudentius of Zaragoza.

At Barcelona he was ordained priest by Bishop Lampius, but on the condition that he be attached to no church, as he shows in his sixth letter to Severus. Ausonius, unable to bear his longing and wishing to draw him back to Gaul, pressed him through letters 21, 23, 24, and 25, accusing him [Col. 0150C] of being too devoted to his wife, whom he calls Tanaquil. Paulinus answered very wittily:

> “My wife is not Tanaquil, but Lucretia.”

At that time the tyrant Maximus killed Gratian, and Theodosius defeated Maximus. To Theodosius, the victor, Paulinus wrote a panegyric addressed to Endelechius, but it has perished.

By then Paulinus’s fame was celebrated throughout the world [Note: [Col. 0149D] Nola was not absent.], and, although absent, he was elected bishop of Nola in the year of Christ [Note: [Col. 0150D] This is not certain.] 395, at the age of thirty-eight. At Nola he completed the *Natalia* of Saint Felix from the second through the tenth. He had begun the first in Spain; from there he crossed to Italy and composed the eighth *Natalis*, in my opinion, in the year of Christ 402, when the Goths and Alans had occupied Spain. Bede the Venerable is said to have rendered these *Natalia*, piously composed in verse, into prose.

Under Innocent, created pope in the year of the Lord 404, the doctrine of Pelagius arose in the year 415. Paulinus’s rivals had also accused him of being suspect in this matter, but this one passage in the tenth *Natalis* seems sufficient to prove that he thought correctly:

> “And he who will reign together with God,  
> will receive the honor of co-rulership,  
> like Christ, but by Christ’s gift.”

And likewise Letter 2 to Severus, and Letter 11.

Concerning Paulinus’s offering himself as a substitute for the redemption of a widow’s son, since I see that the matter is disputed, I advise you to read Baronius under the year of Christ 431, in which year most people also think that Paulinus, having returned from Africa, died.

[Col. 0151A] Now let us say a few words about Severus Sulpicius, to whom most of Paulinus’s letters are addressed.

It is known from the annals that there were several Sulpicii, just as there were several Paulini. We are now speaking of Paulinus’s friend. Those who think that he was bishop of Bourges are mistaken, and that he lived until the year of the Lord 587. This friend of Paulinus was a priest of Primuliacum—not a bishop—and a disciple of Saint Martin. He also wrote Martin’s life with the greatest elegance, and flourished around the year of Christ 400. He built a basilica at Primuliacum, as Paulinus reports in Letter 12. You may gather the rest from Gennadius, from Victor Giselinus’s prolegomena to the works of Severus Sulpicius, and finally from Baronius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume V.

## CASPAR BARTHIUS, *ADVERSARIA*, COMMENTARY, BOOK XIII, CHAPTER 14

*(From the Frankfurt edition, 1618.)*

[Col. 0151B]

Among those distinguished in the poetic literature of Christians, you could place no one before Paulinus. His profound learning in secular literature fashioned his style, which he mingles excellently and agreeably with the treatment of divine mysteries without affectation. If you were to say that the apostles themselves, the heralds of God, wished to sing the praises of the Lord in Latin meters, you would certainly admit that they would have used such language.

It cannot be said how contemptuously such divine works are commonly regarded. For how few even among the learned, who otherwise roam through everything, remember these works twice or three times? Hence they require far greater diligence from those who bring them to light than has hitherto been thought necessary.

We have offered several specimens in these little books; in this chapter too we shall offer one, from the *Panegyric on Celsus*, which touches upon the highest mysteries of the Christian religion in smooth, learned, and rhythmical verse.

## JO. FREDERICUS GRONOVIUS, *OBSERVATIONS ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS*, CHAPTER 10

Nola has a witness to his office who was indeed later than Virgil, but also holier: it possessed him as a living man, as a teacher of sacred things, and as the builder of a sacred church. What great monuments of the beloved see! What letters, full of devout eloquence and devotion, he sent from there to the most distinguished men and women! What poems of lofty spirit, with which he consecrated that retreat and the *Natalia* of his Lord Felix!

This is the merit of the place: through him it is known, read, and seen throughout the world.

## CARDINAL PERRONIUS, *TO PLESSAEUS ON THE MASS*, FOLIO 403, ON SAINT PAULINUS

[Col. 0151D]

This delight of ancient Christian piety; this excellent and religious spirit, so loved and celebrated by Saint Ambrose, Saint Jerome, and the Church’s most flourishing age; this offspring and lesser likeness of Saint Paul; this second vessel of election, whose breast Saint Augustine calls, in Letter 34, the Lord’s oracle; whom Saint Gregory calls a man of God in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 1; whom Gennadius, in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, testifies to have been illustrious not only in doctrine and holiness of life, but also in power over demons; and of whom even the Centuriators of Germany are compelled to declare in Century 5, chapter 10: “His writings have been greatly approved by devout and learned men.”

## PHILIPPUS LABBEUS, *ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS*, VOLUME II

Paulinus, bishop of Nola, whom some hold to have been called by his full name Meropius Pontius Anicius Paulinus (others call him Eutropius or Neropus), was born in Aquitania Secunda around the year of Christ 353, either at Bordeaux or not far from it, in the town of Ebromagus, between Bourg and Blaye. He was a disciple of the poet Ausonius [Col. 0152B] and is said to have held the consulship at Rome in the year 375.

Then, having been baptized at Bordeaux by Saint Delphinus, bishop of that city, he withdrew with his most holy wife Therasia into the deserted regions of the Pyrenees and the fields of Barcelona. Thereafter he was ordained priest by Eulampius—or, correctly, Lampius—bishop of Barcelona, on the very Nativity of the Lord Christ, or, as he says in Letter 6 to Severus, “on the day when God deigned to be born in the flesh,” at the end of the year of Christ 393. This was nevertheless on the condition that he be attached to no church.

Therefore, leaving Spain, he went to Italy. From Milan, where he was most kindly received by Saint Ambrose, he entered Rome under the Roman pontificate of Siricius. Shortly afterward he came to Nola, the longed-for harbor of the Church of Saint Felix, in whose honor he poured forth many verses.

It is not known in what year he became bishop of Nola [Col. 0152C], nor what brought him to Africa, nor to which Vandal ruler. This much is certain: having returned from there, he died at Nola in the seventy-eighth year of his life, on 22 June in the year of Christ 431.

The following wrote about him: Saints Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory; Ausonius; Severus Sulpicius; Eucherius; Prosper; Hydatius; Cassiodorus; Gennadius, chapter 48 of his *Catalogue*; and Sigebertus, chapter 14. Sigebertus asserts two things, at least one of which is false—namely, that he wrote a life of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, addressed to Saint Augustine.

As for his further statement that Paulinus wrote a metrical life of Saint Felix of Nola, this may be understood as referring to the *Natalia*. Honorius of Autun and others also wrote about him; and so did Uranius, who was present at his death, although he wrote not so much a life as an account of his blessed passage to heaven.

## ISIDORE OF SEVILLE, *BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS*, CHAPTER 4

[Col. 0152D]

Uranius published an account of Paulinus’s death.

## URANIUS THE PRIEST, LETTER TO PACATUS ON THE DEATH OF SAINT PAULINUS, BISHOP OF NOLA

*(We have published this letter of Uranius in volume LIII of our *Patrology*, column 859; see it there.)*

## NOTICE OF THE EDITOR CONCERNING THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE WORKS

[Note: [Col. 0153B] It is worthwhile to preface a few remarks concerning the arrangement and typographical form of our edition of Paulinus’s works, so that, while reading this edition, everyone may in a sense reconstruct for himself a faithful image of the Muratorian edition, once he knows in which footsteps of that most distinguished man we have remained, and in which matters we have adopted another arrangement, consulting the greatest usefulness and convenience of readers.

The following points must therefore be carefully observed. In the Muratorian edition there are four series of annotations:

1. Citations and variant readings continuously written along both margins of each page opposite the text. Some of these, very few, are marked with asterisks; others, distinguished by letters, are almost infinite in number.

2. Notes and variant readings placed beneath the text.

3. The notes and observations of various scholars gathered together in a single body at the end of the works.

4. Variant readings from manuscript and printed books, which occupy a place between the indexes and the notes mentioned above.

Let us now compare that arrangement with ours [Col. 0154B]. [Col. 0154C] We wish therefore to inform the reader once and for all:

1. Whatever belongs to the first series of annotations has been transcribed by us partly within the text in brackets, and partly beneath the text with the superior letters, as they are called, or with prefixed asterisks.

2. The notes of the second series, likewise placed beneath the text, are marked by letters enclosed within parentheses.

3. The notes and observations of various scholars occupy with us the same place at the end of the works as they do in Muratorius.

4. The final series, to which the reader is referred by superior figures, has been divided by us so that the variants belonging both to the genuine and to the doubtful letters have been transcribed at the end of each respective group. A similar arrangement has been observed in setting out the variants of the poems.]

## THE FIRST PART OF SAINT PAULINUS

[Col. 0153]

## LETTERS (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0153] Additional notes to these letters were printed by Migne as a separate document in columns 419–438. Each superscript number in the text of the letters refers to the number of the note in that separate document.]

## LETTER I

[Note: [Col. 0153] Formerly numbered 6; the letter that was formerly 1 is now 5. Written at the beginning of the year 394, at the outset of his priesthood, shortly before Easter.]

[Col. 0153A]

### 1

Paulinus urges Severus Sulpicius, a priest of Primuliacum in Aquitania, not to abandon his chosen pursuit of perfection because of the criticism of wicked men. Inviting him to come to him, he explains how, while at Barcelona in Spain, he was suddenly seized by the force of the crowd and initiated into the priesthood against his will; at the same time he magnificently describes the dignity of that office.

**PAULINUS**, servant of Christ Jesus (see note 1), sends greetings to **SEVERUS**, his dearest brother according to the common faith in God the Father and in Christ Jesus our Savior.

How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth [Note: [Col. 0153] Psalm 118:103]. I plainly felt as though the faith of Holy Scripture had been poured like honey upon my inmost heart, the faith in which it is said: “Good words make the bones fat” [Note: [Col. 0153] Proverbs 15:30]—not, of course, those bones whose structure joins us together in bodily form [Col. 0153B], but those by which the steadfastness of the inner person is maintained: hope, faith, and charity. These are the inward parts of mercy, the bones of patience, and the members of every virtue.

You have enriched these bones, members, and inward parts with holy words of hope, faith, and charity. Through them you have taught me that the hope of your faith is directed toward the Lord, that the faith of your hope is steadfast in the Lord, and that the fullness of charity in Christ endures, just as God’s love toward us endures. To me, who was anxious and desirous, and who could believe nothing else concerning you—or rather, concerning God, who works and perfects his power in the weak—you announced the increase of your heavenly inheritance. You have secured it beneficially by reducing the burdens of the present life, purchasing heaven and Christ at the price of a fragile substance [Col. 0154A]—truly understanding the one who is “over the needy and the poor” [Note: [Col. 0153] Psalm 40:2; Matthew 25:40], whom you believed to be in Christ, and Christ in him, as Christ himself taught, hidden, nourished, and lent at interest.

### 2

“Let this be the odor of death unto death” to those who are perishing [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 Corinthians 2:16], to whom the flesh and cross of the living God are folly or a stumbling block [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 Corinthians 1:23], because for them the flesh and blood that they serve do not reveal that Christ Jesus is the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0153] Matthew 16:17]. For us, however, may faith in the divine flesh and death become an odor of life unto life.

Let not our feet be moved, dearest brother, from the ways of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0153] Psalm 16:5] or from the path of the narrow road [Note: [Col. 0153] Matthew 7:14], if at times the profane or foolish words of certain worldly people bark around us. For through the Holy Scriptures we have been sufficiently instructed both about them and about ourselves.

The blessed Apostle says of them to us that “in this we labor” [Col. 0154B] and are cursed, because we hope in the living God, “who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe” [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 Timothy 4:10]. He also foretold, from his own mouth in the Gospels, both the poison they utter in conversation and the punishments they deserve: “Woe to those who cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble! It would be better for that man if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the depths of the sea” [Note: [Col. 0153] Matthew 18:6; Luke 17:2].

But he says to us: “Blessed are you when people curse you, speak every evil against you, and reproach my name as though it were evil; rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0153] Matthew 5:11].

Holding fast to these words of the Lord, my brother, let us be confirmed in our faith [Col. 0155A] and disregard the reproaches and hatred of unbelievers. “They walk in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalm 81:5], because “the sun of righteousness has not risen for them” [Note: [Col. 0155D] So, Nobilius asserts in his scholia on the Septuagint version, in many books that he has read. It is so read in Augustine’s *Speculum* from the book of Malachi. In the Vulgate: “the sun of understanding.”] [Note: [Col. 0155] Wisdom 5:6; Malachi 4:2].

“The poison of asps is under their lips” [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalms 14:3 and 140:4]. It infects the mind and kills the soul if, received through the ears, it penetrates the heart. “Their heart,” divine Scripture says, “is vain, and their throat is an open sepulcher” [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalms 5:10 and 14:3].

Let us beware of their leaven, lest it corrupt the whole lump [Note: [Col. 0155] Galatians 5:9; 1 Corinthians 5:6]. For it is written: “The wicked shall not dwell near you” [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalm 5:6]. And again: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted” [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalm 17:26]. And: “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 Timothy 2:19].

Stop up your ears, brother, and fence them with thorns [Note: [Col. 0155] Ecclesiasticus 28:28] against their words, which are the thorns and arrows of the devil, who lies hidden in their hearts and secretly plots in concealment to seize Christ’s poor man [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalm 9:9 according to the Septuagint, corresponding to Hebrew Psalm 10:9] and hunt the Christian’s soul.

But, as it is written, their own iniquity will return upon their head, and they will fall into the pit that they themselves have made [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalm 7:16–17].

### 3

But you, man of God, flee from such people [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 Timothy 6:11]. Do not labor to give an account to those who think themselves wiser, since you know that the beginning of wisdom is in your possession, because you fear the Lord [Note: [Col. 0155] Psalm 110:10; Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10].

If they consider what we are doing foolish, congratulate yourself inwardly that you are carrying out the work of God and the commandment of Christ. Remember that God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 Corinthians 1:27], and that “what is foolishness of God is wiser than men” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ibid., verse 25].

To wish to be purified by such people is the same as being able to deny Christ himself. For he will be ashamed to confess his own before the Father if they are ashamed of his name before this world [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 10:33; Luke 9:26; Mark 8:38].

### 4

You therefore, who labor, as you write, to give an account for what you and I have done, what will you do if you fail to persuade people who dispute with you about God’s work—not for their own edification, but for your destruction?

You will blush; you will grow pale, as the advocate of the worse cause. Shaken, you will stumble in the way of the Lord, and, if you destroy what you have built, you will fall back from heaven to earth.

It makes a great difference who those people are to whom an account must be given. If someone comes with a desire to learn and confesses his ignorance, scatter in him the seed of faith and expound the divine commandment. If he receives the word, you have won a brother for the Church [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 18:15] and a sheep for Christ.

But if there is no pure shoot of good seed, and if, because of the enemy of the heavenly householder who comes by night and sows weeds among the wheat [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 13:25], there is a harmful plant and unhappy crop to be separated from the good grain at harvest time—material not destined for the granaries, but for the furnaces, to burn as fuel for eternal fire—then, while it grows toward its own destruction, flee from it and drive it away from your conversation [Col. 0156A] and your presence, so that, if it cannot be healed by your faith, it may not wound you through its unbelief.

### 5

Even if he is a brother and a friend, closer to you than your right hand and dearer than the light, if he is alien and hostile in Christ, let him be to you as a stranger and as a tax collector [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 18:17]. [Note: [Col. 0155D] So the manuscript copies and the editions of Rosweyde read. Other editions: “Let him be cut off.” [Col. 0156D] See our note on Letter 23, no. 12, and Letter 11, no. 7.]

Let the useless right hand that does not cling to you in the body of Christ be cut off from your body [Note: [Col. 0155] Ibid., verse 8], and let the harmful eye that darkens your whole body with its stain or blindness be torn out.

For it is better that one member perish for the salvation of the whole body than that, because of love for one diseased member, the whole body should go into Gehenna, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 5:29–30].

Nor should we fear the offense of such people. Indeed, we should desire it, since from their reproaches and curses is born the reward that God promised would be abundant in heaven [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 5:12; Luke 6:23].

“The disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord” [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 10:24; John 13:16]. And if they called the head of the household Beelzebub [Note: [Col. 0156D] So the manuscript copies of Reginensis and Viennensis read. The printed editions have: “they called”], how much more his household members [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 10:25]?

If they loved the Lord and God whom we follow, they will love us too; if they persecuted him, they will persecute us. What need have we of the world’s favor, which is hatred of Christ? “If you were of the world,” he says, “the world would love what was its own” [Note: [Col. 0155] John 15:19].

### 6

You therefore, who seek to give an account to people—to these unbelievers—consider what you desire: without doubt, the favor of people, that is, of the world. You cannot please it unless you choose to displease Christ.

“For if I pleased people,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0156D] “The Apostle.” We supplied this much-desired word from the Viennese manuscript], “I would not be the servant of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0155] Galatians 1:10].

Let us therefore displease these people, and congratulate ourselves that we displease those who also displease God. For, as you know, they are attacking not our work but the work of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, of almighty God. They despise him in their own actions and hate him in our works. Too late they will say: “Lord, when did we see you naked and not clothe you, hungry and not feed you, sick and not visit you?” [Note: [Col. 0155] Matthew 25:44, from verses 37–38].

Then they will hear: “Go into the eternal fire which God prepared for your father and his angels” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ibid., verse 41], because whatever they do not do for those in need, they deny to Christ, who, though he was rich, became poor so that by his poverty he might enrich us [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 Corinthians 8:9].

### 7

Meanwhile, let them enjoy their pleasures, dignities, and possessions, if indeed they are theirs [Note: [Col. 0155] Wisdom 2:6]—possessions which they prefer to have here, where we cease to exist, rather than there, where we continue to exist.

Let them keep their wisdom for themselves, and their happiness for themselves; let them leave us, as they think, our poverty and our foolishness. Let them arrogate to themselves, if they please, the wisdom of the very God whom, although they confess him in name, they deny in their conduct, having “the appearance of godliness but denying its power” [Note: [Col. 0157] Titus 1:16; 2 Timothy 3:5]. Let them reproach us with foolishness.

For the Lord says: “The children of this age are wiser than the children of light” [Note: [Col. 0157] Luke 16:8]; but he added: “in this generation.” Let them be wiser, so long as they are not children of light. Let them be wise in their own generation, so long as in our regeneration they are found without understanding.

Let them now be blessed—or rather, fortunate—in every prosperity, flowing along while the world flatters them [Note: [Col. 0157D] The Viennese manuscript has: “while the flattering world”]. Let them wear soft clothing and be in kings’ houses [Note: [Col. 0157] Matthew 11:8; Luke 7:25], so long as they are not in the labors of men and are not scourged with men [Note: [Col. 0157] Psalm 72:5].

Let them be rich in the world, because they are needy before God. Of them it is written: “The rich have become needy and hungry” [Note: [Col. 0157] Psalm 33:11]. But immediately afterward it is said of us: “Those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing” [Note: [Col. 0157D] The edition of Grinius and the Roman Psalter read: “shall not fail.” In the other psalters, the Vulgate, the Latin version of the Septuagint, and Augustine, “shall not be diminished.”] [Col. 0157B] [Note: [Col. 0157] According to the Roman Psalter.]

### 8

Would that, my brother, we might be judged worthy to be cursed, condemned, crushed, and even killed in the name of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0157] Acts 5:41], provided Christ himself is not killed in us.

Then at last we would walk upon the serpent and the basilisk and trample the head of the ancient dragon [Note: [Col. 0157] Psalm 90:13] (see note 59).

But we are still unbound toward a world friendly to us—which is worse—and delight in Christ, loving only to be praised in his name, while refusing to be saddened and afflicted, although that is more profitable.

Remember the mustard seed, whose seed we are: when it is crushed, it burns more strongly and is then finally roused to its power. Therefore we must respond, as it were, to our nature in this respect: crushed by hostile words, we must burn more intensely toward faith; and we must burn those very people who try to break us as the least of men—like the mustard seed, which is the smallest of seeds [Note: [Col. 0157] Matthew 13:31; Mark 4:31; Luke 13:19]. [Note: [Col. 0157D] The Viennese manuscript and the edition of Grinius read: “let us take care.”]

If those who are outside inquire of you about the reason for your holy work and hurl venomous tongues from their viperous hearts into your heart, do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs [Note: [Col. 0157] Matthew 7:6].

For what partnership can there be between the faithful and the unfaithful? What fellowship between light and darkness? What agreement between Christ and Belial? [Note: [Col. 0157] 2 Corinthians 6:14.]

### 9

You, however, soldier of Christ, armed by the Apostle with the helmet of salvation, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the sword of truth, and the power of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0157] Ephesians 6:14; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; Romans 15:13], stand steadfast in heavenly armor. Extinguish the enemy’s burning darts with the fountain of wisdom and the stream of living water within you.

Guard what has been entrusted to you; preserve the faith; pursue righteousness; hold fast to the charity of Christ; imitate patience; exercise yourself in godliness, which is useful for all things. Be sober; labor in all things; fight the good fight; complete the course, so that you may grasp that for which you have been grasped.

From now on the crown of righteousness will be laid up for you, which the righteous Judge, the Lord, will award on that day to those who love his coming.

But avoid those who do not endure sound doctrine, who are lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God [Note: [Col. 0157] 1 Timothy 6:20; 2 Timothy 1:14; ibid. 2:22; 1 Timothy 4:8; 2 Timothy 4:5; ibid., verse 8; ibid. 3:4], always advancing toward worse, deceiving and being deceived—people corrupt in mind and alienated from the truth, and for that very reason handed over to the desires of their hearts, to a snare and many desires that plunge those shipwrecked in faith into destruction and perdition [Note: [Col. 0157] 1 Timothy 6:9].

For they preferred the creature to the Creator [Note: [Col. 0157] Romans 1:25], that is, they valued the images of the nations, gold and silver [Note: [Col. 0157] Psalm 113:4], more highly than God. They preserve their souls in this world and lose them in Christ [Note: [Col. 0157] John 12:25].

“Depart from such people” [Col. 0158B] [Note: [Col. 0157] 1 Timothy 6:11], and avoid profane novelties of speech, lest you begin to grow sick over childish and vain questions or impious disputes about words, and lest you be endangered by false brothers or by ruined and rejected wise men [Note: [Col. 0157] 2 Timothy 2:23; 1 Timothy 1:4 and 4:7; Titus 3:9].

Otherwise everyone who sees you, with the devil mocking you (see note 2), may say: “This man began to build and was unable to finish” [Note: [Col. 0157] Luke 14:30].

Far be this from us, who, relying not on our own works or powers but on divine strength and mercy, have dared to undertake the work of perfection. He himself, who is almighty, is able to perfect in us the work of his perfection, and to build according to its proper measures and bring to completion the structure that he has deigned already to lay and raise with its first foundations [Col. 0158C].

For he himself, when his apostles were troubled by the magnitude of this work, deigned to say to them that this was impossible with human beings but not with God, with whom nothing is impossible for those who believe [Note: [Col. 0157] Matthew 19:26].

### 10

But, so that we may console one another with the words of the Lord and advance in our works, “Go out from your land” [Note: [Col. 0158D] So the manuscripts of Reginensis and Viennensis read. The word “your” is absent from the printed editions] “and from your kindred” [Note: [Col. 0157] Genesis 12:1 according to the Septuagint; Acts 7:3], imitating Abraham in his faithful departure, so that you may be worthy of the bosom of blessed Abraham [Note: [Col. 0157] Luke 16:22].

Hurry to come to us, to receive and give, for our common benefit, the additions of faith. For this is pleasing before God: “the brother who helps his brother will be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0157] Proverbs 18:19]. [Note: [Col. 0158D] This is how our Paulinus reads it in Letter 6, no. 3; Letter 3, no. 5; and Letter 40, no. 3, as does Saint Cyprian in Book IV, Letter 2, approximately halfway through.]

We are now staying in the city of Barcelona, as I had written before (this letter has been lost). After those letters in which you replied, on the Lord’s Day when he deigned to be born in the flesh, I was suddenly seized by the force of the crowd—as he himself bears witness [Note: [Col. 0158D] See Letter 2, no. 2, and Letter 3, no. 4]—but, I believe, by his own ordinance, and was initiated into the priesthood [Col. 0159A]. I confess that this happened against my will—not because I disliked the place, for I call him himself to witness that I desired to begin the sacred service even from the name and office of a church caretaker—but because, destined for another place and already settled and fixed in mind elsewhere, I trembled before this new and unexpected decision of the divine will.

Having therefore submitted my neck to the yoke of Christ, I see myself undertaking works greater than my merits and understanding. I have now been received and inserted into the mysteries and inner chambers of the most high God, sharing heavenly things, and, brought nearer to God, dwelling in the very spirit, body, and radiance of Christ.

My narrow mind can scarcely yet grasp the meaning of this sacred burden, and, conscious of my weakness, I tremble beneath the weight of my office. But he who gave wisdom to children and perfected praise for himself from the mouth of infants and nursing children [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalms 18:8 and 8:3] is able also to perfect his work in me and adorn the office, so that he may make worthy the one whom he called while unworthy.

Know nevertheless that, by the same Lord’s provision, the condition of our common vow remains secure. For I was induced to be consecrated in the Church of Barcelona on the condition that I would not be attached to that church, being dedicated only to the priesthood of the Lord, not to a particular ecclesiastical place (see note 3).

### 11

Come, then, if it pleases you, before Easter, which would be especially welcome to us, so that you may celebrate the holy feast with me as a priest. But if, with God’s favor, you already wish to meet me at the beginning of the journey, set out after Easter in the name of Christ.

Yet we trust in our Lord that he will kindle in you a more ardent longing for us, so that you will not endure to postpone bringing yourself to us beyond the time of Easter.

How long the journey is, the boy of your fellowship will report, since, as he said, he reached us from Elusio [Note: [Col. 0159D] The Viennese manuscript has “Clusio,” wrongly, instead of “Elusio,” as in the Bordeaux Itinerary] in eight days. For the road is so short and easy [Col. 0159C] that even in the Pyrenees it is not steep. The road between Narbonne and Spain lies there, more frightening in name than in actual mountain height.

But why concern ourselves with distance? If you long for us, the road is short; if you neglect us, it is long.

## LETTER II

[Note: [Col. 0159] Formerly numbered 23; the letter formerly numbered 2 is now 24. Written in the year 394, at the outset of his priesthood, around Easter.]

He informs the priest Amando, who later succeeded Saint Delphinus in the bishopric of Bordeaux, that he was made a priest against his will. He briefly describes the duties of the priestly office and asks for the help of Amando and Delphinus, through whom he had been born to God, in fulfilling them.

**To his most beloved brother in the Lord, AMANDO, PAULINUS.**
After some time we received letters from your affection; but the longer they had been desired, the more eagerly they were received by us. For cold water is sweeter to the thirsty, and good news from a distant land [Note: [Col. 0159] Proverbs 25:25.] is more pleasing; so the sweetness of your speech has fattened our bones [Note: [Col. 0159] Proverbs 15:30.] and satisfied our hungry soul with good things [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalm 106:9.]. What worthy response can we make to such expressions, weak in talent, dull of heart, meager in speech, and—as it is written—lazy bellies [Note: [Col. 0159] Titus 1:12.]? Yet although inferior in every respect, love alone makes us your equals. For we strive with equal devotion in the affection you have for us: an affection implanted in our inmost parts, fastened to our hearts, and mingled with the soul itself by the Spirit of the Lord, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalm 67:7.], who joins innumerable thousands of believers together in one heart, because the One fills all things in all [Note: [Col. 0159D] Thus the Vulgate and the Regius and Viennese manuscripts, which lack the particle “as” at the beginning of the following number. The printed editions read “he fills”; and in the following number, “as now.”] [Note: [Col. 0159] Ephesians 1:23.].

### 2

Now it has pleased this Lord to place his treasure in an earthen vessel [Note: [Col. 0159] 2 Corinthians 4:7.], [Note: [Col. 0159D] Thus the manuscript copies. The printed editions read “holy.”] who called me by his grace [Note: [Col. 0159] Galatians 1:15.], raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dungheap, to set him among the princes of his people [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalm 112:7.] and to clothe him with salvation among the priests [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalm 131:16.], so that, while I run after the fragrance of his ointments [Note: [Col. 0159] Song of Songs 1:3.], I might become [Col. 0160B] a drop of that ointment of his which descends upon Aaron’s beard [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalm 132:2.].

When, in view of the consciousness of my merits, I refused—or rather did not dare—to become a member of his household [Note: [Col. 0159] Ephesians 2:19.] and to bless the Lord from the springs of Israel [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalm 67:27.], I, a worm and not a man [Note: [Col. 0159] Psalm 21:7.], was suddenly forced, unwilling—as I confess—to submit, compelled by overwhelming pressure from the multitude. Although I desired that the cup itself might pass from me, I nevertheless had to say to the Lord: “Yet not my will, but yours be done” [Note: [Col. 0159] Matthew 26:42; Mark 14:36; Luke 22:42.], especially since I read that the Lord himself said of himself: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” [Note: [Col. 0159] Matthew 20:28.].

Thus, forestalled by the Lord and seized by him whom we have not yet seized, we serve at God’s altar and minister at the saving tables, already elders in name and office (see note 5), [Col. 0160C] but still children in understanding and infants in speech [Note: [Col. 0159] 1 Corinthians 14:20; 1 Timothy 3:13.].

### 3

So that I may discharge this ministry well, acquire for myself a good standing, know how I ought to conduct myself in the house of God, and handle the mystery of piety, pray, venerable lord and brother, [Note: [Col. 0160D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the editions of Badius, Gravius, and Schottus. “And lord” is absent from the Viennese manuscript and from Grinus’s edition. “I would delete it,” says Sacchini, “unless the repetition seems tolerable because it is made with a new meaning, the first occurrence referring to the dignity of the man.”] and lord in Christ to us, to the Lord who is rich in every good thing [Note: [Col. 0159] Romans 10:12.], that we may abound in faith, speech, knowledge, and every diligence, and, in addition, in your love for us, so that you too may abound in this grace [Note: [Col. 0159] 2 Corinthians 8:7.].

Moreover, instruct us often through your letters with the necessary supplements. For, nourished on the words of faith and good doctrine which you have followed from childhood in the sacred Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0159] 1 Timothy 4:6.], shape us according to the rule of right guidance; feed us with spiritual food [Note: [Col. 0159] Deuteronomy 8:3.], that is, with the word of God, which is the true and living bread [Note: [Col. 0159] Matthew 4:4.] and by which one lives more truly than by bread [Note: [Col. 0159] Luke 4:4.], since it is the food of the righteous who live by faith [Note: [Col. 0159] Romans 1:17.].

Nor should you be less attentive to the care of my instruction because, although separated by location in the Church, we are not separated in body. [Col. 0161A] For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings [Note: [Col. 0161] 1 Timothy 2:5.], who is the head of the Church. Since in it we are all one, we live as though in one house. Nor can we say that we are without you, since we are of one spirit and dwell in the One who is one. Therefore, preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, so that we may be one body and one spirit [Note: [Col. 0161] Ephesians 4:3.], so that, as members joined together, we may labor together [Note: [Col. 0161D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Grinus’s edition read “let us labor together”; this is sufficient to have noted once.], so that we may grow into the building up of that body [Note: [Col. 0161] Ephesians 4:12.] whose head is Christ.

### 4

Since, therefore, we have been made citizens from enemies (perhaps “guests”), neighbors from those who were far away [Note: [Col. 0161] Ephesians 2:17.], shepherds from sheep, and have been placed upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, instruct and strengthen [Note: [Col. 0161] Isaiah 35:3.] our hands in the knowledge of building, so that, by means of the stone that has become the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0161] Psalm 117:22; Matthew 21:42.], [Col. 0161B] I may learn to join the two walls together and construct bodies and hearts cleansed by faith into a holy temple and dwelling place of God [Note: [Col. 0161] Ephesians 2:21.].

Through the weapons of the Apostle, powerful before God, may I take captive every proud thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bring every understanding into obedience to Christ [Note: [Col. 0161] 2 Corinthians 10:5.]; apply the Gospel axe to the roots of the trees [Note: [Col. 0161] Matthew 3:10.]; and with the sword of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0161] Ephesians 6:17.], that is, with the word of God, slay the sinners of the earth [Note: [Col. 0161] Psalm 100:8.]; and with the shield of Catholic faith extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and, after fighting the fight, finishing the course, keeping the faith [Note: [Col. 0161] 2 Timothy 4:7.], and completing the ministry, await what the Lord, the just judge, will render on that day to all who love his coming [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid., verse 8.].

Therefore, seeing and holding me spiritually as your own and as abiding with you, [10] instruct me, help me, encourage me, and strengthen me. For, born to God in Christ from you and through you, I ought above all to be the object of your care, since I shall be your reproach if I am unworthy, or your joy if I am recognized as a branch from the good fruits of your tree.

## EPISTLE III (C)

[Note: [Col. 0161] Formerly 44; the one that was 3 is now 23. Written in the autumn of the year 394.]

He writes to Bishop Alypius about the books of Augustine that he had received, excusing himself for having sent Eusebius’s Chronicle to him so late. He wishes to be informed about Alypius’s origin and life, while in turn revealing some things about himself. He sends one loaf as a gift.

To the most deservedly honorable and most blessed father, ALYPIUS, PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1

This is true love, this is perfect affection, which you have shown to exist in you toward our lowliness, truly holy lord, deservedly most blessed and desirable. For through our man Julian, returning from Carthage, we received a letter bringing us so great a light from your holiness that we seemed not to recognize your love but to recognize it anew.

For this love flowed from him who predestined us for himself from the foundation of the world [Note: [Col. 0161] Ephesians 1:4; 1 Peter 1:2.], in whom we were made before we were born; because he made us, and not we ourselves [Note: [Col. 0161] Psalm 99:3.], he who made the things that are to come. Thus formed by his foreknowledge and work in the likeness of our wills and in the unity—or faith—of unity, joined together by a love that anticipated knowledge, we came to know one another before the Spirit revealed us to one another’s bodily sight.

Therefore we rejoice and glory in the Lord, who, one and the same, works his love everywhere throughout the world in his own people through the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon all flesh [Note: [Col. 0161] Joel 2:28.], making his city glad with the rush of the river [Note: [Col. 0161] Psalm 45:5.]. Among the citizens of this city he has deservedly placed you in a principal position [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript of Bigot reads “as the leader.”] with the princes of his people [Note: [Col. 0161D] This title, which today belongs exclusively to the Roman Pontiff, was once common to all bishops before Gregory VII, in 1073, as is known from the writings of the ancients, and especially from the letters of our Paulinus to Augustine, Delphinus, Alypius, Victricius, and Florentius.] upon the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0161] Psalm 112:8.]. He also wished us—whom he raised when we had been cast down [Note: [Col. 0161] Psalm 145:8, and 112:7.] and lifted from the earth when we were needy—to be counted among those belonging to your lot.

But we rejoice still more in that gift of the Lord by which he established us in the dwelling of your heart, and by which he deigned to insinuate us into your inmost parts, so that we may claim for ourselves a special confidence in your love. We have been challenged by such services and gifts that we cannot love you distrustfully or lightly.

### 2

For we have received the distinguished and exceptional work of your love and solicitude, composed in five books by our holy and perfect brother in the Lord Christ, Augustine [Note: [Col. 0162D] Four Vatican manuscripts add the particle “and.”]. We admire and esteem it [Note: [Col. 0162D] The same four Vatican manuscripts read “and receive.”] so greatly that we believe the words to have been dictated by divine inspiration.

Therefore, trusting in the acceptance of the unanimity we share, we have dared to write to him, presuming that through you we may both be excused to him for our ignorance and commended to his love, just as you have deigned to preserve us, even in our absence, through the services of all the saints. Without doubt you will take equal care that, through your holiness, they may greet one another by our attentions, and that we may be companions in the clergy of your holiness and rivals in faith and virtue in your monasteries.

For although you act among the people and over the people, governing the sheep of the Lord’s pasture [Note: [Col. 0161] Psalm 99:3.] with the vigilant watchfulness of a careful shepherd, yet by renouncing the world and rejecting flesh and blood, you have yourself made a desert for yourself: withdrawn from many, called among the few.

### 3

As a substitute, though in every respect unequal to you, I have, as you commanded, made provision for that history of all times by the venerable bishop Eusebius of Caesarea [Note: [Col. 0162D] So read the manuscripts and printed copies, except two Bigot manuscripts and the Benedictine edition, which mistakenly read “of Constantinople,” although it is established that Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was the author of this Chronicle.]. But the delay in obeying you arose because, on your instruction, since I did not possess this book myself, I found it in Rome with our truly most holy father Domnion. Without doubt he readily complied with me in this service, which I told him was to be conveyed to you [Note: [Col. 0163D] Thus the manuscripts, thirteen Gallican copies, and two Vatican copies. Two other Vatican copies read “I judged.”].

Yet because you also deigned to indicate your location to me, as you had instructed, we wrote to our venerable companion in your crown, our father Aurelius, in such a way that, if you were then staying at Hippo Regius, he might send you our letter and the parchment copied at Carthage.

We also asked the holy men, Comes and Evodius, whom we came to know from your account through the token of their love, to arrange for the copying themselves [Note: [Col. 0163D] Those same copies read “to write these things.”], so that Domnion would not be deprived of his book for any longer, and so that, once sent to you, it would not remain with you without necessity of being returned.

### 4

In particular I ask this of you, since you have filled me, undeserving and unsuspecting, with great love for you: in exchange for this history of the ages, relate to me the entire history of your holiness. Tell me, as Virgil says [Note: (Virgil, *Aeneid* 8)], “what your lineage is and from what home you come”; how, called by the Lord to so great a calling, from what beginnings, separated from your mother’s womb, you passed over to the mother rejoicing in the offspring of the children of God; and how, having renounced the lineage of flesh and blood, you were transferred into a royal and priestly race [Note: [Col. 0163] 1 Peter 2:9.].

For you indicated that you had already learned at Milan, when you were initiated there, about the name of our lowliness. I confess that I wish to learn this more inquisitively, so that I may know you in every respect and rejoice all the more if you were either invited to the faith by our father Ambrose, whom I must revere, or consecrated to the priesthood by him, so that we may both seem to have the same author.

For although I was baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and consecrated by Lampius at Barcelona [Col. 0163C] in Spain through the force of a suddenly inflamed crowd (see Epistle 1, no. 10), nevertheless I have always been nurtured in the faith by love for Ambrose, and now I am cherished in the order of the priesthood. Finally, he wished to claim me for his clergy, so that, although I live in different places, I might be reckoned his presbyter.

### 5

But lest you be ignorant of anything about me, know that I, a sinner of very long standing, not long ago brought out of darkness and the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0163] Psalm 106:14.], have breathed the spirit of life-giving breath, and that not long ago I laid my hand to the plough and lifted up the Lord’s cross [Note: [Col. 0163] Luke 9:62.]. May we be helped by your prayers, so that we may carry this through to the end.

This reward will be increased among your merits if, through your intercession, you lighten our burdens. For the holy person who helps one who is laboring—since we do not dare to call him a brother—will be exalted like a great city [Note: [Col. 0163] Proverbs 18:19.].

You indeed shine upon the mountain as a city built, or as a lamp lit upon a lampstand with sevenfold brightness [Note: [Col. 0163] Revelation 1:13.]. We hide beneath the bushel of our sins. Visit us by your letters and bring us into the light in which you yourself move, conspicuous upon golden lampstands [Col. 0164A]. Your words will be a lamp to our paths [Note: [Col. 0163] Psalm 118:105.], and the oil of your lamp will fatten our head [Note: [Col. 0163] Matthew 6:17.]. Faith will be kindled when we have received, through the spirit of your mouth, food for the mind and light for the soul.

### 6

May the peace and grace of God be with you, and may the crown of righteousness remain yours on that day, lord, deservedly most beloved, venerable, and greatly desired father.

We ask you to greet with great affection and salutary service our blessed companions and fellow-strivers in the Lord, your brothers—if they deign to accept us—both in the churches and monasteries: at Carthage, Thagaste, Hippo Regius, and throughout all your parishes, as well as in every place throughout Africa known to you where they serve the Lord in Catholic faith.

If you have received the parchment of the holy Domnion, you will deign to send us a copy of it. I also ask you to write to me which hymn of mine you have recognized [Note: [Col. 0164D] Two Bigot manuscripts read “have acknowledged.”]. We have sent one loaf to your holiness as a sign of our unity; in it too the wholeness of the Trinity is contained. You will make this bread an *eulogia*—a blessing—by deigning to partake of it.

## EPISTLE IV (C)

[Note: [Col. 0163] Formerly 41; the one that was 4 is now 23. Written together with the preceding letter, in the autumn of 394.]

He writes to Augustine, adorning him with elaborate praises for his five books against the Manichaeans, which he had received from Alypius. He sends him one loaf as a gift.

To his like-minded and venerable brother, AUGUSTINE, PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1

The love of Christ, which presses us [Note: [Col. 0163] 2 Corinthians 5:14.] and binds even those who are absent through the unity of faith, itself gave me the confidence to write to you after banishing shame, and through your letters made you intimate to my inmost being. I hold these letters for the time being in five books: they overflow with scholastic abilities and are sweet as heavenly honeycombs; they are medicines and nourishment for my soul.

We received these books as a gift from our blessed and venerable bishop Alypius, not only for our instruction but also for the benefit of the Church in many cities. I now have these books for reading [Note: [Col. 0164D] The Bigot manuscript reads “for study.”]; in them I take delight; from them I receive food—not the food that perishes, but that which produces the substance of eternal life through our faith [Note: [Col. 0163] John 6:27.], by which we are incorporated into Christ Jesus our Lord.

Our faith, which neglects visible things and longs for the invisible [Note: [Col. 0163] 2 Corinthians 4:18.], is strengthened by letters and examples of the faithful, believing all things according to the truth of almighty God through love [Note: [Col. 0163] 1 Corinthians 13:7.].

O truly the salt of the earth, by which our inmost hearts are seasoned so that they cannot vanish through the error of the world [Note: [Col. 0163] Matthew 5:13.]! O lamp worthy to be placed upon the lampstand of the Church [Note: [Col. 0163] Matthew 5:15; Mark 4:21.], pouring forth light far and wide upon Catholic cities from a seven-branched lamp fed with the oil of joy [Col. 0164D], while you disperse the dense darkness of heretics and, by the splendor of your brilliant speech, clear the light of truth from the cloud of darkness!

### 2

You see, my like-minded brother, admirable and worthy of welcome in Christ [Col. 0165A] the Lord, how familiarly I have recognized you, how greatly I admire you with astonishment, and with what great love I embrace you, as I daily enjoy conversation with your letters and feed upon the spirit of your mouth.

I would rightly call your mouth a conduit of living water and a vein of the eternal spring, because in you Christ has become a fountain of water springing up into eternal life [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thus the manuscripts and the Benedictine edition. But the printed editions, together with two Bigot manuscripts, read “of life.”] [Note: [Col. 0165] John 4:14.]. My soul has thirsted for him in you, and my land has longed to be intoxicated by the abundance of your river.

Therefore, since you have sufficiently armed me with this Pentateuch of yours against the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 0165D] By this expression Paulinus designates Augustine’s five books against the Manichaeans, as is clear from this letter, no. 1; Letter 6, no. 2; and Letter 3 to Alypius, no. 2.], if you have prepared any defenses against other enemies of the Catholic faith as well—for our enemy, who has a thousand arts of doing harm (Virgil, *Aeneid* 7, verse 334), must be overcome with as many weapons as he employs stratagems—I ask you to bring some out for me from your arsenal and not refuse to supply me with the weapons of righteousness.

[Col. 0165B] I am laborious, even now a sinner beneath a great honor [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thus seven manuscripts and the Benedictine and Rosweyde editions. Four manuscripts and three printed editions read “burden.” Sacchini says that “burden” fits the Gospel saying, “You who labor and are burdened.” Nevertheless, both the elegance of the books and the sense favor “honor,” because below, in no. 5, he professes to be a presbyter and adds that he is unworthy of so great an honor.], veteran in the number of sinners, but a new recruit in the incorporeal army of the eternal King.

Until now, wretched man that I was, I admired the wisdom of the world, and through useless writings and rejected prudence I was foolish and mute before God [Note: [Col. 0165] Romans 1:22.]. After growing old among my enemies [Note: [Col. 0165] Psalm 6:8.] and becoming vain in my thoughts [Note: [Col. 0165] Romans 1:21.], I lifted my eyes to the mountains [Note: [Col. 0165] Psalm 120:1.], looking toward the precepts of the Law and the gifts of grace. From there came my help—from the Lord, who does not repay according to iniquities [Note: [Col. 0165] Psalm 102:10.], who illuminated the blind [Note: [Col. 0165] Psalm 145:8.], loosed the one in chains, and humbled the one wrongly exalted so that he might piously raise up the one who had been humbled.

### 3

Therefore I follow, still with unequal steps, the great footprints of the righteous, if through your prayers I may attain that for which I have been apprehended by God’s mercies.

So guide the little one crawling on the ground, and teach me to walk in your footsteps. For I do not want you to consider my age according to bodily birth rather than spiritual rebirth [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thus the manuscripts, the Vatican copies, two Bigot manuscripts, and the Benedictine edition. The printed editions read “to consider age in me.”].

In the flesh I am already of the age of the man who was healed by the apostles at the Beautiful Gate through the power of the word [Note: [Col. 0165] Acts 4:22 says that he was more than forty years old.]; but in the birth of the soul I am still at the stage of infancy of that soul which, sacrificed to Christ with wounds not yet inflicted, went ahead as a victim in the worthy blood of the Lamb [Note: [Col. 0166D] Four Vatican manuscripts read “victim.” It is not objectionable if “worthy” is read as well.] and began the Lord’s passion.

Therefore, as I am still an infant at the word of God and nursing in spiritual age, raise me up, longing for your words, the breasts of faith, wisdom (perhaps “hope”) [Note: [Col. 0166D] Thus in all the printed editions and manuscripts. It would have been easy, with Sacchini, to correct this to “hope,” which both the subject matter and Augustine’s Letter 27, written in response to this one and using the same words in no. 3, show to be the reading.], and love.

If you consider our common office, you are my brother; if the maturity of your intellect and judgment, you are my father; and although perhaps younger in age, you are my elder, since gray-haired wisdom has advanced you to the maturity of merit and the honor of the elders [Note: [Col. 0166D] Thus two Vatican manuscripts and one Bigot manuscript together with the Benedictine edition. Nine manuscripts read “the honor of the elders.”].

Therefore cherish and strengthen me in the sacred Scriptures and spiritual pursuits. As I have said, I am still recent in these matters and, after long dangers and many shipwrecks, inexperienced through lack of practice, barely emerging from the waves of the world. You, who already stand upon solid shore, receive me safely into your embrace, so that in the harbor of salvation we may sail together, if you consider me worthy.

Meanwhile, as I strive to escape the dangers of this life and the depths of sins, support me by your prayers as by a plank, so that I may escape naked from this world as from a shipwreck.

### 4

For this reason I have taken care to lift burdens from myself and strip off the clothing that weighed me down, so that, by Christ’s command and help [Note: [Col. 0166D] Three Bigot manuscripts read “with the help of.”], I might swim unencumbered across this stormy sea of the present life, which lies between us and God, barking with sins, stripped of every covering of the flesh and of concern for the following day [Note: [Col. 0165] Matthew 6:34.].

Nor do I boast that I have accomplished this. Even if I could boast, I would boast in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0165] 2 Corinthians 10:17.], whose work it is to accomplish what it lies with us to desire [Note: [Col. 0165] Romans 7:18.]. But my soul still longs to desire the judgments of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0165] Psalm 118:10.]. See when he will attain, through the accomplishment of God’s will [Note: [Col. 0166D] The printed editions formerly read “the accomplished will of God.” Two manuscripts read “the accomplishment of God’s will”; two others, “the accomplishment of God’s will”; one Vatican manuscript, “by the accomplishment of God’s will.” We follow this last reading.], what he still desires to desire.

Yet, insofar as it lies with me, I have loved the beauty of the holy house, and, insofar as it was in my power, I had chosen to be cast off in the house of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0165] Psalm 25:8; Psalm 83:11.].
