But the one who was pleased to separate me from my mother’s womb [Note: [Col. 0165] Galatians 1:15.] and draw me away from the friendship of flesh and blood into his grace was also pleased to raise me, needy of every good merit, from the earth and draw me out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, so that he might set me among the princes of his people [Note: [Col. 0165] Psalm 112:8.] and place my portion in your lot, so that, with you advancing me by your merits, I might be made equal by association in office.

### 5

Therefore, not by my own presumption but by the Lord’s pleasure and appointment, claiming for myself the covenant of your brotherhood, I deem myself worthy of an honor of which I am so unworthy, because I know for certain that, in accordance with your holiness—for you understand truth [Note: [Col. 0166D] We have emended this from the three Bigot manuscripts and the Benedictine edition. The printed editions previously read “the truth.”]—you know not to think highly of yourself but to associate with the lowly [Note: [Col. 0165] Romans 12:16.].

Therefore I hope that you will readily and intimately receive the love of our lowliness. I trust that you have already received it through the most blessed priest Alypius, our father, because he deigns to do so. For without doubt he gave you an example from his own conduct of loving us, unknown to him and separated from him by a great distance of land or sea, before he knew us and beyond our merit. Through the spirit of true love, which is everywhere and is poured out everywhere, he was able to see us by loving us and reach us by addressing us.

He gave us the first proofs of his affection and the pledges of your love in the worthy gift of the books mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0167D] We have added this word from two Bigot manuscripts and the Benedictine edition.]. And just as he took great pains to ensure that we could not love your holiness moderately, but might know you not only through his words but more fully through your eloquence and faith, so we believe he took equal care that you, in imitation of him, might love us greatly in return.

May the grace of God remain with you eternally, as it does now, we pray, our like-minded brother in Christ the Lord, venerable and most deeply desired. We greet your entire household, every companion, and every fellow-striver in the Lord of your holiness with the greatest affection of united brotherhood. [16] We ask you to bless, by receiving it, the one loaf which we have sent to your love as a sign of our unity.

## EPISTLE XXVII (formerly XXXII): AUGUSTINE TO PAULINUS (C)

Augustine to Paulinus, embracing his goodwill and declaring a mutual love; with some remarks about Romanianus and Alypius, and also about Licentius, whose age he feared might incline toward the things of the world.

(See this letter among the Augustinian letters under number 27, volume XXXIII of our *Patrology*, column 107.)

## EPISTLE V

[Note: [Col. 0167] Formerly 1; the one that was 5 is now 11. Written in the year 395.]

[Col. 0167C] 20 Paulinus praises Severus and shows that he was converted to God by a greater miracle. He then urges him to come to him and sends a loaf and a boxwood dish, a mutual token of friendship.

To his brother Severus, PAULINUS [Note: [Col. 0167D] The Viennese manuscript adds: “and Therasia, sinners.”].

### 1

Did you think, dearest brother, that you needed to excuse yourself because you had not come to us yourself, according to your promise and our expectation?

Yet you came to us with the better part of yourself remaining where you were: your body alone stayed at home, while your will, spirit, and speech came to us. Indeed, you were not wholly absent even bodily, since in your children, who are joined to you in holy service in the Lord, members of your body came to us.

Therefore, truly holy brother, deservedly most beloved and like-minded with us in Christ, the crown of piety has already been stored up for you in heaven. The just Judge will give it to you on that day [Note: [Col. 0167] 2 Timothy 4:8.] and to all who, beside you, love their neighbor in Christ—or Christ in their neighbor—with perfect love.

For when we look at spiritual things through carnal ones, we easily infer from the evident love you show toward the brother whom you see that you possess that heavenly, faithful, and perfect love by which you love the God whom you do not see. We prove this by the obedience of faith, if, by loving one another [Note: [Col. 0167] 1 Peter 1:8.], we prove ourselves, as you prove yourself, disciples of that teacher who loved his own to the end and laid down his life for his friends [Note: [Col. 0167] John 13:1 and 10:15.], by the same power by which he also took it up.

### 2

Therefore, truly holy and deservedly blessed brother, in the land of the living you will have a place and reward above the queen of the South [Note: [Col. 0167] 1 Kings 10:1; 2 Chronicles 9:1; Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31.].

For although she was a sinner, being still a companion of the nations not yet visited by God [Note: [Col. 0167D] The words “by God” are absent from the Regius manuscript and from the editions of Badius and Schottus.], yet already a forerunner of those who were to be visited, she did not possess the written law but had the faith of the law engraved on the tablets of her fleshly heart by the spirit of counsel and piety.

Moved by concern for her own benefit and by the pursuit of a great and saving gain, she was roused from the farthest regions of the world and desired to hear divine wisdom, so that she might receive what she did not have and drink in the light of knowledge of which she was deprived.

Already then, clearly, the queen who was to come from the nations, desiring her future bridegroom, ran toward him, clothed in the varied, golden-woven garment of the Bridegroom-Christ whose fragrance spread far and wide through his prophet. She was forgetting both the people and her father’s house: barbarian in nation, not in spirit; openly a foreigner, but secretly a Jewess, longing to become a citizen of the saints.

Therefore she is judged worthy not only of the heavenly reward of blessed resurrection but also, by the very mouth of the Judge, of the authority of the apostles to judge the adulterous Jews, because, having marveled at Christ in Solomon [Note: [Col. 0167D] “In Solomon.” Thus the Regius manuscript and the editions of Badius, Gravius, Grinus, and Schottus, as elsewhere. The Greek text likewise reads Σολομών (“Solomon”), and Paulinus uses the form consistently; so too Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, verses 576 and 579, *Psychomachia*, verse 809, and *Diptych*, nos. 2 and 46. Gregory of Nazianzus also uses it several times in his poems, as does Drepanius Florus in his poem to Moduinus.], she had fulfilled, in the mystical image of the Church, the true affection of the heavenly queen.

Therefore, if a divine reward awaits her in the future, although even then she received in large part the reward she desired by obtaining the longed-for hearing of heavenly wisdom [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Regius manuscript reads “when she had obtained.” Schottus’s edition places in the margin “when she had obtained the desire.”], what rewards will finally be repaid to you, who desired me with equal grace and greater effort, because your present hope of benefit was less?

For what, I ask, did you have to desire in me? What did you hope to receive from me that you did not have? What good could you gain from conversation with an ignorant man? What benefit could there be in seeing a sinner? What could the wise receive from the foolish, the upright from the crooked, the blessed from the wretched, the strong from the weak, the rich in the Lord from the poor [Note: [Col. 0168D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Previously the text read “from the needy.”]?

### 3

Truly, you do not seek your own interests but those of Christ [Note: [Col. 0167] Philippians 2:4.], because you had as the motive either of your pilgrimage or of the distress of your own people not your own merit or advantage from me, but that love alone which is the fullness of the Gospel [Col. 0169A] [Note: [Col. 0169] Romans 13:10.].

Blessed are you because I have nothing with which to repay you. Yet it will be repaid to you in the resurrection of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0169] Luke 14:14.] by the one who testifies that he is loved and received in even the least of his own [Note: [Col. 0169] Matthew 25:40.].

Hence he also says—and, for any servant bearing his name, whether falsely or uselessly, making himself bound by his own words: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward.”

As for me, my burden will not be diminished because, though a sinner, I receive from a righteous man the honor due to the righteous. But for you, the righteousness of your opinion is to be credited as the reward of your goodness [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Viennese manuscript reads “to be credited in the rewarding of goodness.”], because, through a holy error but a true feeling of piety, you have honored the good Lord even in a bad servant.

### 4

What, then, shall we wretched men do, since we shall also have to render an account and suffer punishment for accepting undeserved honors, and since, though we are only hearers of the law, we are praised by those who are doers [Note: [Col. 0169] Romans 2:13; James 1:22.]?

All the more, therefore, our condemned sluggishness, the barrenness of our souls, and our hands dry in good works [Note: [Col. 0169] Luke 6:6.] will be reproached, when, through your speech, we hear truths due to worthy servants of Christ such as you are, and therefore false praises addressed to us; for, comparing your judgment with our actions, we do not find in ourselves what we hear said about us.

For what similar thing can we boast of? Although one ought to boast in the Lord, since we possess nothing except what we have received by his gift, nevertheless my more advanced age and the honored status I have enjoyed from my earliest years could have ripened my gravity. Moreover, a weaker body [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Viennese manuscript reads “an infirm body.”] and more exhausted flesh could have worn down my pursuits of pleasure; and life itself, repeatedly exercised amid labors and troubles, could have produced hatred of disturbing things and increased the practice of religion through the necessity of hope and fear of uncertainties [Note: [Col. 0169D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and four printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads the same through this point.].

Finally, when I seemed to have found rest from accusations and journeys, neither occupied with public affairs nor exposed to the noise of the forum, I practiced the leisure of the countryside and the worship of the Church in the chosen tranquility of domestic seclusion. Thus, as my mind was gradually withdrawn from worldly disturbances and adapted to heavenly commands, I had already, as it were, moved over from the neighboring road toward this purpose, more easily advancing toward contempt for the world and fellowship with Christ [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Regius manuscript reads “I may have moved away.” Three printed editions read “I may have fought.”].

### 5

You, dearest brother, have turned to the Lord by a still greater miracle, since you were in the prime of life, rich in praise, lightly burdened by patrimonial obligations, not impoverished in material resources, and still dwelling in the very theater of the world—that is, amid the public activity of the forum—while holding the palm of eloquence. In a sudden assault you shattered the yoke of sin’s slavery and broke the deadly bonds of flesh and blood [Note: So the manuscript copies. The printed editions have “fetters.”] [Psalm 115:17]. Neither the wealth amassed through marriage into a consular family, nor, after marriage, the freedom to sin, nor youthful age [Note: Thus *juventas* instead of *juventus* is used by Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book 2, line 1082: “... to which youth was subject.” On this word see N. Heinsius on Virgil and Claudian.] [Note: The Vienna manuscript and the editions of Grinius and Schott have *juventa*.] could recall you from the narrow entrance to salvation and the arduous path of virtue to that soft and spacious road of the many [Matthew 7:13]. Blessed are you, who fled from the counsel of the ungodly, refused to persist in the way of sinners, and disdained to sit in the seat of pestilence, so that in exalted humility you might recline at the feet of the Crucified.

### 6

You, therefore, are a true doer of the law and no deaf hearer of the Gospel [James 1:22]. You have crucified body and world, rejected the pleasures of youth and the evil joys of the present life as poisons and sorrows, and spurned the burdens of estates as though they were dung. Rightly, therefore, you received as an eternal mother a holy mother-in-law [Note: He means Bassula; see note 9.], more generous than any natural parent, because you had placed the heavenly Father before your earthly parent. Following the example of the apostles, you left your father in the tossing boat—namely, amid the uncertainty of this life, with the nets of his possessions and the entanglement of his patrimony—and followed Christ [Matthew 4:22; Mark 1:20; Luke 5:11] [Note: The word “having left” is absent from Schott’s edition.].

Nor did you accept from men a reputation for intellectual ability inferior to your domestic wealth; rather, nobly neglecting empty glory [Note: The Vienna manuscript adds “desire,” but incorrectly. Paulinus likes to speak in this way in Letter 38 to Aper, no. 11, “careful of yours”; in Letter 39, no. 1, “more careful of ours”; and no. 3, “careful of his own.”], did you fail to prefer the preaching of fishermen, drawn from your own writings, to all of Cicero’s. You fled to the silence of piety so that you might escape the tumult of iniquity. You wished to become silent before mortals so that you might speak divine things with a pure mouth, and cleanse a tongue polluted by doglike eloquence through the praises of Christ and the very remembrance of his holy name.

### 7

O true Israelite, who saw the God of Jacob with such faithful understanding [John 1:47], and, strengthened as though by the wrestling of the Lord himself [Genesis 32:24], prevailed against the ruler of this world and vanquished the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places [Ephesians 6:12] with the shield of faith and the weapons of righteousness; preferring to please Christ rather than human beings [Galatians 1:10]; preferring to be foolish in the eyes of human beings rather than before God: you preferred the scandal of the cross to all the eloquence and all the wisdom of this world, so that what is foolishness to those who are perishing [1 Corinthians 1:18] you might recognize as the power and wisdom of God, having been adopted by the Father of salvation, as is evident to all who are to be saved.

Blessed are you, brother, because flesh and blood did not reveal these things to you, but the Father who is in heaven [Matthew 16:17], through our Lord Jesus Christ, who overturns their wisdom and makes it foolish, and chose the weak and foolish things of the world in order to confound this world by those very things for which it scorns to know God [1 Corinthians 1:27] [Note: Thus the same manuscripts and printed editions. Other copies have “recognize.”].

Remember us, therefore, all the more, since you strive toward the power of intercession with richer merits. For although our lamp has already been lit in the light of Christ, we still lie hidden beneath the knot of sins. We desire to be brought out by the hand of you who shine conspicuously with the light both of faith and of grace and of works through the Lord’s seven lampstands [Revelation 1:20] [Note: The manuscripts read “to be led out”; the printed editions have “to be led down”], and to have our head enriched with your oil. Thus, instead of burning dimly with smoking flax—which nevertheless the merciful Lord does not extinguish [Note: See note 2]—we may burn brightly, not in darkness, but with the pure light of a faithful example, light that surpasses even others [Matthew 6:22].

Yet, because the Lord’s grace shines forth from darkness, we are not obscure through the glory of his name [Isaiah 42:3], even though, as you have heard, we live in retirement. For in our upper room we remain silent in seclusion, because, as the prophet says, it is good for a man to sit alone and be silent [Lamentations 3:28] [Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript and Schott’s edition. Other copies have “being silent,” which makes no sense.].

Therefore the Lord himself taught us to be silent even in cases requiring loud protest. Like a lamb before its shearer, he did not open his mouth [Isaiah 53:7]; yet he said: “I was silent; shall I always be silent?” [Isaiah 42:14, according to the Septuagint] [Note: Thus the Septuagint translators, Tertullian in *On Modesty*, shortly after the beginning, Cyprian in *Testimonies*, book 2, chapter 27, and our Paulinus in Letter 38 to Aper, no. 4.]. We therefore silently endure his will and judgment, for he is powerful both to remain silent in us now and, when he wills, to intercede for us [Romans 8:34].

### 8

Meanwhile, however, we perceive that our sins have harmed us in this respect: we did not deserve to see you. Moreover, we regard it as an additional burden of our misfortunes that we became the cause of your trials, in which, as you indicated, you endured double illnesses, being struck as many times as you attempted to come to us [Note: The manuscripts and the older printed editions consistently have *totius*—“of the whole”—wherever it occurs; noting this once is sufficient.].

But because the Lord himself often tests us, as it is written, “Our God tests us in order to prove our love” [Deuteronomy 13:3], by which we love one another in his peace, we place our hope in your faith rather than in our own. If the trial already undergone has produced testing in you [Romans 5:4], may the vows of love, proved in God, no longer be able to be frustrated [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript and Grinius’s edition. Other copies have “therefore.”].

For we know that the spirit within you is so ready that we do not fear lest ever-weak flesh prevail as an obstacle to our common desire. Strengthening it by faith, you will subdue it in spirit, so that what it cannot do of itself may be compelled to accomplish in Christ. If you say to it, “Do not fight against the spirit; be reconciled to your adversary on the way” [Matthew 5:25], then there will be peace for your bones; and when my heart rejoices in the living God, then my flesh too will rest in hope [Psalm 37:4; 83:3; 15:9].

### 9

Hold fast, therefore, brother, to what you hold, lest another receive your crown [Revelation 3:11]. It amounts to this: do not cease to desire what you have desired, and hold firmly to your unchanging resolve to come to us. He whose power and favor make it possible for us to accomplish prosperously what we piously desire will himself bring your religious efforts to the fruit of their vow. For we know that, for one who desires the good, all things proceed toward good [Romans 8:28] [Note: See Letter 47, no. 1.].

We too have received, with great gratitude as a sign of the concord that exists among us in all things, your letters reporting your illnesses. In ourselves we have experienced, according to the Apostle’s saying and sentiment, that the members of one body suffer together [1 Corinthians 12:26]. We felt ourselves restored by the very fact that you wrote that you had recovered, so that, though placed in different lands, we might experience the unity of the spirit working in us through a silent connection among separated bodies, sharing alike either in afflictions or in remedies.

### 10

Therefore, brother of one mind with us, and our better portion in Christ, lay aside any sadness you may have felt in pious concern because of the report of our chastisement. “The Lord chastising has chastised us, but he has not handed us over to death” [Psalm 117:18]. Visited by the healing hand of the Almighty, we were being sustained by hope of recovery from our present illness, while softening one another’s blows with mutual consolations.

The very fellowship of suffering brought us great and sweet comfort, since it seemed that the unity of our wounds had come together not without the Lord’s command—he without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground [Matthew 10:29]. Thus our recovery too began to proceed for both of us together, either because one breathed more freely through the relief afforded by the other, or because the Lord, author of unity, binding all his own together by one undivided spirit, would not permit our bodily constitution to differ.

### 11

Yet this was not the only reason that delayed our young men. Our Vigilantius, too, both before he reached us in Campania and after he arrived, suffered from the violence of fevers. Since he too was a fellow member, he shared sympathetically in our illness through shared suffering [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript, Schott’s edition, and the marginal reading of the Regius manuscript. Other copies have *solativo*, “as a consolation,” less suitably. The reading restored here is confirmed by what follows, “after the illness endured through common labor,” in section 12, and by Letter 2 to Amandus, no. 3, “that we may labor together for one another as fellow members,” and Letter 13, no. 3, “fellow members” and “a common member.”].

Finally, that catechumen, who was not yet a member of our body, did not feel our wounds. He remained healthy and free from our illnesses, because flesh that was still alien could not yet feel the pain of a body to which it did not belong. Therefore, when our Vigilantius began to be able to proceed, only then did I judge that the writings should be delivered.

We admit that both had been eager to hasten much earlier. But while the one who could not was rashly hurrying before recovering his strength, and the one who could was acting impiously [Note: Thus the Belgian and Regius manuscripts. See note 13.], we held both back by silence, against their will, though willingly in accordance with our judgment, because we were unable [to let them go].

### 12

Accordingly, as we wrote above, after enduring illness through common suffering, and being restored through the prayers of holy and beloved people—by your prayers also, as we believe, for the greatest part, while the Lord looked upon us with greater mercy—we remain nevertheless weak, our bodies still exhausted.

In this the Apostle teaches us to glory: weakness made him powerful, as he declares [2 Corinthians 12:10]. For the flesh [Galatians 5:17], which fights against the spirit, when it is broken by sickness, is likewise unable, with its strength broken, to overcome spiritual virtue.

Weak in the flesh, therefore, but advancing in spirit—the spirit that rejoices in the loss of the flesh and delights in the tribulation of what is, as it were, hostile material, growing strong as the body is subdued by weakness—we have sent this letter to comfort you, in the healthy and vigorous love that we have for you through the Lord Jesus, while for the present we hold yours. This will continue until we see you yourself, as you promised and as we never cease to hope from the Lord.

### 13

There are many things that should invite you to us and draw you away for a little while from your homeland, above all love of peace and escape from jealousy, which is most strongly kindled by the sight or proximity of a rival way of life.

At Rome, finally, the distance of the city extinguishes the fires of jealous clergy, and there all iniquity closes its mouth [Psalm 106:42]. For, with its fuel as though withdrawn by our absence, the sluggish flame of hatred grows cold. Envy does not dare to burst into speech, although it gnashes with its teeth [Note: Thus the Regius and Vienna manuscripts and four printed editions. Prudentius uses *frendit* in *The Crown of Martyrdom*, hymn 5, on Saint Vincent the martyr, line 393. Plautus also uses the same word. Rosweyde’s edition has *frendeat*, “may it gnash.”], while, conscious of its own iniquity, it is ashamed of itself and has no convenient place where it may kindle the torches of its livid spirit.

Yet the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, abounds in the hearts of many [Philippians 4:7], and all Campania venerates in us the work of God the Savior. At Rome, too, only a few, even within the clergy—the very group by which alone we seem to be scandalized—are stirred by the bite of envy.

But thanks be to the Lord, who has granted even me, his most wretched sinner, to say: “They hate me without cause” [Psalm 34:19]. For my part, however, I am peaceful in spirit even toward those who hate my peace [Psalm 119:7] [Note: The Vienna manuscript lacks “my.”]. If anyone wishes to be contentious, our custom does not accept it [1 Corinthians 11:16].

Yet even of those very people who are said to hate us and to exclude us from the fellowship of their holiness, only a faint report scarcely reaches us. From our ears, fortified by a hedge of thorns [Ecclesiasticus 28:28], it is shut out like a cold breeze or the troublesome buzzing of an empty gnat.

### 14

Our fellow servants, your young men, will be able to report more fully how much harm the proud separation of Pope Urbicius causes to us in the grace of the Lord [Note: This is a surname derived from the city of Rome. Thus Pope Zephyrinus is called “the Roman” by Optatus in book 1; likewise, the Council of Arles speaks of “Roman deacons,” that is, Roman deacons.].

During the few days they were here, they saw how regularly and diligently, throughout the whole period of our illness, the services of concerned brothers—monks, bishops, clergy, and often even laypeople themselves—were performed for us [Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript. Other copies have “our whole period.”]. In the presence of your unanimity, though in praise of the Lord’s grace, whose work and gift this too is, it may be said that scarcely any bishop throughout all Campania considered it right not to visit us. Those whom illness or some other necessity had detained nevertheless attended by sending clergy and letters in their place [See note 15].

The African bishops too sent people to visit us at the beginning of summer. Since this is so, you see how greatly you ought to hasten in humility toward us: both to remove a small opportunity from those who seek an opportunity, and, for the increase of grace and charity, to travel away from your homeland while you are still a stranger in the body, traveling away from Christ [2 Corinthians 5:6]. For Truth itself testifies that no prophet is accepted in his own homeland [Luke 4:24].

### 15

I admit that, although nothing could be given me more pleasing than your presence, my desire for your arrival has been kindled more intensely because you promised that many spiritual brothers would come with you. Will that time come, I ask, and will that day ever dawn when I may receive your brotherhood, arriving with a company of God’s elect, in the embrace of the common patron, my Lord Felix [See notes 16 and 17]? And what I now ask to obtain through his prayers, may we then rejoice together before him in the Lord, having obtained it in his presence?

When I have embraced all of you together and one after another, may I rightly say, while you sing in harmony: “This is truly the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” [Psalm 117:24], because “it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity” [Psalm 132:1] [Note: The manuscripts and the older printed editions consistently have “pleasant.”].

Then I shall lodge you not only as a resident in my monastery beside the neighboring Martyr, but also as a cultivator in his garden—and for free, because you have already received your denarius from the master of the household [Matthew 20:9]. This is in addition to those gifts that the same Lord, generous toward your wounds, has already given to the innkeeper [Luke 10:35], so that, healed with the oil of mercy and the wine of grace, you might be placed more usefully in the Lord’s vineyard with your body restored.

### 16

I seem already to see my little garden becoming more cultivated as the Lord’s laborers arrive with you and work alongside me. It is not difficult to imagine how readily those whom Christ chose for his vineyard will complete the labor of lighter cultivation [Matthew 20:4] [See Letter 49, no. 2]; he did not allow them to stand idle before God in the empty marketplace of this age.

Already, after the holy kiss, I imagine and contemplate the domestic joys that await me, when, with the spirit of charity making us drunk, we mingle sober joy in chaste cups, and celebrate holy feasts not in the leaven of wickedness but in the unleavened bread of sincerity [1 Corinthians 5:8]. We shall sing psalms to the Lord in hymns and spiritual songs, singing to God with tongues and hearts, and doing everything, in word or deed, in the name of Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him [Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16–17; 1 Corinthians 10:31].

May he who makes those of one mind dwell in a house [Psalm 67:7], as I hope, make us dwell among ourselves in him. He who made both one [Ephesians 2:14], and, when exalted, drew all things to himself [John 12:32], who, when humbled, made peace among all things [Colossians 1:20], reconciling the world to God—when he has filled our mouths with joy at the presence of your unanimity, we shall say: “The Lord has magnified what he has done for us” [Psalm 125:3]. In the abundance of our joy we shall bless you from the house of the Lord, because you are blessed by the Lord, you who have come in the name of the Lord.

May you receive the cup of salvation [Psalm 117:26; 115:13, 15], and eat the bread of the blessed in the kingdom of God [Luke 14:15]; for before the Lord Jesus you are our fullness and our joy.

### 17

Dare, therefore, to break forth—not relying on your own resources and strength, but trusting and leaning upon Christ. His rod and his staff comfort us [Psalm 22:4], sustain us, and guide us. He who bears our sorrows and has taken upon himself our infirmities [Isaiah 53:4], gives strength to the weary and strengthens weak knees [Isaiah 35:3]. He himself will establish your way, both undefiled and free from stumbling; he will gird you with strength and make your feet like those of a stag, so that you may exult like a giant to run the course [Psalm 17:33; 18:6] [Note: Paulinus uses the same expression in Letter 13 to Pammachius, no. 23. So too the Greek books, the Septuagint translators, and Augustine in his commentary on the Psalms; the Old Latin and Roman Psalters.].

Thus the weakness of fearful flesh will not be able to hinder you, since you walk not in the flesh but in the spirit [Note: The Vatican manuscript has “in the flesh.” Other copies lack the preposition *in*, which we have restored because it occurs in Paul. The reading is further confirmed by a similar expression in two Bigotian manuscripts of Paulinus’s Letter 50 to Augustine, no. 3, where we read: “because he walks not in the flesh but in the spirit.”].

For while we serve Christ through the service of the body [Romans 8:9], we make greater use of the command of the soul. Therefore, when our will is directed under Christ’s authority, the flesh obeys as its companion; the body draws strength from the soul’s courage, and the servant orders his obedience according to the master’s manner. Thus strength is perfected in weakness [2 Corinthians 12:9], while the soul, serving God in harmony with subdued flesh, fulfills the duties of strength through the ministry of weakness.

### 18

Pay attention, therefore, proceed prosperously, and the right hand of God will lead you wondrously. His mercy and grace will go before your face [Psalm 44:5; 88:15]. If you leave your home weak, you will gain strength as you go. For those who hope in the Lord will change their strength and take up wings like eagles [Isaiah 40:31].

If, then, you have a heart burning on the way [Luke 24:32], your youth will be renewed like that of an eagle [Psalm 102:5]. You will run and not grow weary [Note: Thus the Regius manuscript. Other copies have “you will not grow faint.” The reading restored here is confirmed by *Carmen* 32, line 118.]; you will walk and not fail [Isaiah 40:31]. Neither rod, nor bag, nor purse will weigh you down; neither sandals nor a double tunic will impede you [Matthew 10:10]. Having stripped off carnal bonds, so that you may be permitted to stand on holy ground with bare foot and loins girded [Exodus 12:11], with no money and no heavy belt, you will hasten to run your course, as the Passover of the Lord and Christ's work must be undertaken at the appointed time. God will make prosperous the journey of our salvation [Psalm 67:20].

Every valley will be filled, and every hill will be humbled [Note: Thus the Septuagint translators. The Vulgate has “will be exalted”], so that the rough places of iniquity may become level roads [Isaiah 40:4; Luke 3:4], lest anywhere you strike your foot against a stone [Psalm 90:11–12]. For he has commanded his angels to guard you in all your ways [Psalm 120:5]. The Lord himself will surround you as your protection with the shield of his peace, shining before you with the light of his countenance [Psalm 88:16] and spreading his protection over you in the shadow of his wings [Psalm 16:8], so that the sun will not scorch you by day, nor the moon by night [Psalm 120:6].

Everywhere he will guard and bless your going in and your coming out, so that in every place you may find a son of peace, and your peace may come upon every host [Luke 10:6].

### 19

If, while setting out, you should perhaps weep at the thought of dear people or the separation from familiar places, your temporal sadness will be changed into eternal joy. “Those who go forth,” he says, “went forth and wept, carrying their seeds; but those who return will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” [Psalm 125:6].

So you too, even if you weep as you come, will rejoice as you return, and in joy you will reap what you sowed in tears. May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit [2 Corinthians 13:13] be with your whole household, which is not made by human hands, because you are the temple of the living God, built upon the foundation of the apostles in Christ for God [1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19; Ephesians 2:20], my brother of one mind with me, venerable, dearest, and most desired by me.

I ask that our holy parent—your mother in Christ and co-heir, Bassula [Note: He means Bassula]—be greeted with the reverence she deserves. My fellow-servant in the Lord, Therasia, greets your brotherhood with the affection with which she venerates you. And on our behalf greet with great respect all the holy brotherhood whom we are sure live with you.

All who are with us in the Lord greet you, including, among the Hebrews, Proforus and Restitutus, who loves the Lord, loves you because he has found you in Christ, and greatly desires you.

### 20

In the title of the letter I was afraid to imitate your brotherhood, excellent in all things, because I thought it safer to write truthfully. Therefore, servant of Christ, called into freedom, beware hereafter of writing that you are the servant of a human being—of a brother and fellow servant inferior to you. It is more the sin of flattery than the justification of humility to attribute to any human being, not to mention a most wretched sinner, the honor owed to the one Lord, the one Master above the earth, and the one God.

“Love from a pure heart and an unfeigned faith” is sufficient [1 Timothy 1:5]; anything more is from evil [Matthew 5:37]. I beg you, brother, by the Lord, to examine my presumption concerning you in the spirit of revelation—or perhaps “relief” [Note: The text may read *relevation*, “relief,” rather than *revelation*.]. Otherwise I might fear your displeasure at a letter so talkative. Yet, in the presence of love, which bears all things [1 Corinthians 13:7], gratitude ought to increase precisely where irritation is usually produced, whenever no love moderates weariness.

For while dictating, as I think of you and am wholly absorbed in you, I speak as though I were conversing with you face to face across a long interval, and I forget that I have been required to bring the speech to an end.

### 21

We have sent you Campanian bread from our little cell [See note 18], relying so completely upon your merits in the Lord that we believed the bread’s own grace would be enough to carry it to you. Though you have already been filled with richer crumbs from the Lord’s table, deign to turn this bread, received from sinners in the Lord’s name, into a blessing.

And lest the wheat bread seem to you to exceed the measure of our humility, we have sent a boxwood dish as a testimonial of our wealth, so that you may receive it as a farewell gift [See note 19] of spiritual goodwill and have it as an example, if you do not yet use similar silver.

If you have a blackened one [See note 20], send it back to us in the little vessels that we entrusted to your boys, our sons [Note: The Vienna manuscript adds “your,” as Paulinus often does. See section 1 of this letter and *Carmen* 32, line 599.]. For we love earthen vessels, both because they are related to us according to Adam and because we have the Lord’s treasure entrusted to such vessels [2 Corinthians 4:7].

### 22

Moreover, because I am confident that I possess the highest authority over your heart, I ask that, if necessary, when freedmen, slaves, and brothers fail me, you devote your care to us and kindly arrange how the old wine—which we believe we still possess at Narbonne—may be brought to us.

Do not fear loss, holy brother, if you make us debtors even for money. For all our own have turned away from us; together they have become impious [Psalm 13:3; 52:4], and a man’s enemies are those of his own household [Matthew 10:36].

## Letter VI [Note: Elsewhere numbered 42; what was 6 is now 1. Written in the year 395.] (C)

### Paulinus writes again to Augustine, having received no reply from him, through others.

To the holy lord, brother, and brother of one mind with us, AUGUSTINE: PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1

For some time now, brother in Christ the Lord, my brother of one mind with me, ever since I recognized you, though you did not know it, in your holy and pious labors, and saw you though absent, I have embraced you with my whole mind and hastened to approach you through a familiar and brotherly conversation by letter [Note: Thus one Bigotian manuscript. It is the best reading, confirmed by Letter 13 to Pammachius, no. 2, “that I might visit you by a spiritual approach,” and Letter 11 to Severus, no. 3, “you approach us by letters.” Other copies have “to hear.”].

I believe that, by the hand and grace of the Lord, my words were brought to you. But because the boy whom we had sent before winter to greet you and other beloved people equally dear to God was still delayed [Note: Toward the end of the year 394], we could neither suspend our duty any longer nor restrain our great desire to hear from you. Therefore we have now written again, in case our earlier letter deserved to reach you—or, if it had not been fortunate enough to come into your hands, as our first letter.

### 2

But you, brother, judging all things spiritually [1 Corinthians 2:15] [Note: Thus the manuscript copies. The printed editions have “spiritually”], do not measure our love for you solely by our duty or by the timing of our letters. The Lord is witness—he alone and the same one works his love everywhere in his own people [1 Corinthians 12:1]. From the time when, through the favor of the venerable bishops Aurelius and Alypius, we came to know you through your labors against the Manichaeans, our love for you was so implanted in us that we seemed not to be taking up some new friendship, but to be recovering an old affection.

Thus, although we are inexperienced in personal conversation, we nevertheless do not write as though we were inexperienced in affection; and in spirit, through the inner person, we in turn recognize you as though anew. It is no wonder that we are present to one another though absent, and that we know one another though unknown, since we are members of one body [Romans 12:5; 1 Corinthians 12:12; 10:17], have one head, are drenched by one grace, live by one bread [See note 21], walk along one way, and dwell in the same house.

In short, in all that we are, with the whole hope and faith by which we stand in the present, we press toward the future. In spirit as well as in the body of the Lord we are one, lest we be nothing if we fall away from the One.

### 3

How little, then, is the bodily absence that begrudges us our presence with one another, except perhaps this temporal fruit by which the eyes of temporal spectators are nourished [Note: Thus two Bigotian manuscripts and the editions of Benedict and Gravius. See Letter 31, no. 5. Likewise, in accordance with the manuscript copies, *exspectare*—“to await”—instead of *spectare*, “to look at,” and *exspectator*—“one who awaits”—instead of *spectator*, “spectator,” occur very frequently in Augustine, volume 4. The same is found in the old Latin version of the Passion of the Holy Martyrs Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus, pages 261 and 268 of Bigot’s edition. Previously the reading was *spectatores*, “spectators.”].

Yet even bodily and temporal grace ought not to be called temporal among spiritual people, to whom the resurrection will also grant the eternity of their bodies. Thus we dare, through the power of Christ and the goodness of God the Father [Note: Fourteen manuscripts, including two Bigotian ones, have “goodness”], to presume upon this even though we are unworthy.

Would that the grace of God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, might grant us this gift as well: that we might see your face even in the flesh. This would not only bring great joy to our desires, but would also increase the light in our minds, and our poverty would be enriched from your abundance.

You can grant this even while absent, especially on the occasion when our sons, Romanus and Agilis, brothers of one mind with us and exceedingly dear to us in the Lord, whom we commend to you as though they were our other selves [Note: Two Bigotian manuscripts have “others,” plural], will return after completing a work of charity. We ask that they may especially experience your charitable affection.

For you know how lofty a promise the Most High makes to a brother who helps his brother [Proverbs 18:19]. Through them you can safely do so, if you wish to reward me with some gift of the grace given to you. Believe me: in the Lord they are one heart and one soul with us [Acts 4:32].

May the grace of God, as it is, remain with you forever, brother in Christ the Lord, brother of one mind with us, venerable, dearest, and most desired. Greet from us all the holy people in Christ whom you certainly have close to you. Commend us to all the saints, that they may deign to pray for us with you.

## Letter XXXI [formerly XXXIV], Augustine to Paulinus and Therasia (C)

Augustine offers Paulinus his grateful service for the second letter he received from him, and announces that he has been ordained co-bishop of Hippo with Valerius. He wishes that Paulinus himself might cross over to Africa, to the great consolation of Augustine and as an example to the other Christians.

[If you wish, read this letter among the works of Saint Augustine in volume 33 of our *Patrologia*, columns 121–125.]

## Letter VII [Note: Elsewhere numbered 46, part 1; what was 7 is now 22. Written in the year 396.] (C)

### Paulinus writes to Romanianus and congratulates the Church of Hippo because it has deserved Augustine as its fellow bishop.

To the deservedly praiseworthy and honorable brother ROMANIANUS: PAULINUS and THERASIA.

### 1

The day before we gave this letter, our brothers, whose arrival you saw us anxiously awaiting, had returned from Africa; and we had received letters from there—from Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Profuturus, O most desired of holy and beloved men, [See note 22] [Note: Profuturus seems to be the man praised in Augustine’s book *On the One Baptism against Petilian*, chapter 16, the bishop of Cirta to whom Augustine’s Letter 38 [formerly 149] was addressed. Finally, in Letter 158, no. 9 [formerly 258], among Augustine’s letters, Evodius reports that Profuturus, whom he had once known in the monastery, appeared to him in a dream and foretold something that was to happen. See note 22.], Severus [See note 23] [Note: Severus was bishop of Milevis, about whom Augustine writes in Letter 31, no. 9 [formerly Letter 34]. See note 23], and already from all the bishops together.

Therefore, rejoicing at the most recent messages of so many holy men, we hastened to report our joy to you also, so that, during your anxious exile, we might bring you the long-awaited news through the most festive indications. If perhaps you have learned the same things from the arrival of other ships, receive them again from us and rejoice anew, as though with renewed happiness.

But if this is the first report to reach you from us, rejoice that so much affection has, by Christ’s gift, been obtained for us in your homeland, so that whatever divine providence is accomplishing there, we may always know it to be marvelous—as it is written, “in his holy ones” [Psalm 67:36]—either first or among the first.

## 2.

But we write this not merely as something for which congratulations are due, that Augustine has received the episcopate; rather, we rejoice that the African Churches have deserved this providence of God, so that they might receive heavenly words from Augustine’s mouth. He, promoted in an unusual manner to the greater grace of the Lord’s office, was consecrated in such a way that he did not succeed a bishop in the episcopal chair, but joined him. For while Valerius remained in good health, Augustine became co-bishop of the Church of Hippo (see note 24). [Note: The printed editions added “bishop” here; since the word is absent from two Bigotian and Vatican manuscript witnesses and manuscript 4, the Benedictine edition expunged it.]

And that blessed old man, whose most pure mind no stain of envious jealousy ever sullied, now receives from the Most High fruits worthy of the peace of his heart: he who had simply wished for this man as his successor in the priesthood now deserves to have him as his colleague. [Note: Thus read the Vatican manuscripts 4 and two Bigotian manuscripts, with the agreement of the Benedictine edition. Other printed editions read “suppliciter,” “humbly.”] [Note: Thus read the Vatican manuscripts 4 and the Benedictine edition. The other codices read “mereretur,” “might deserve.”]

Could anyone have believed this before it happened? But here too, in this work of the Almighty, that evangelical saying may be uttered: “These things are difficult for human beings, but with God all things are possible” [Note: Matthew 19:26; Mark 10:27; Luke 18:27.].

Let us therefore exult and rejoice in him who alone works wonders [Note: Psalm 71:18], and who makes the like-minded dwell in one house [Note: Psalm 67:7, according to the Roman Psalter], because he himself has looked upon our lowliness and visited his people with goodness; he who raised up a horn in the house of David his servant [Note: Luke 1:69], and has now exalted the horn of his Church among his chosen ones, so that, as he promises through the prophet, he may break the horns of sinners—that is, of the Donatists and Manichaeans [Note: Psalm 74:11.].

## 3.

Would that our son Licentius’s ears might now be struck by this trumpet of the Lord, which thunders through Augustine; but may he hear with that ear through which Christ enters, and from which the enemy does not snatch away God’s seed [Note: Matthew 13:4; Mark 4:4; Luke 8:5.]. Then Augustine, the supreme priest of Christ, will truly seem so to himself, for he will feel that he has been heard by the Most High if the one whom he fathered for you as a worthy man in literature he also worthily begets for himself as a son in Christ.

For even now, believe me, he has written to us with the most ardent concern for him. We trust in almighty Christ that Augustine’s spiritual desires will prevail over our young man’s carnal desires. He will be conquered—even against his will, believe me, he will be conquered—by the faith of his most devoted father, lest an evil victory prevail, if he should prefer to conquer to his own destruction rather than be overcome for his salvation.

So that the duty of fraternal kindness might not appear empty, we have sent you and our son Licentius five loaves of the hardtack of the Christian campaign [Note: The manuscripts read *buccellato*. *Buccellatum* was the name for military bread, made approximately in the form of a small portion, so that it could be baked more thoroughly and preserved longer; Ammianus discusses it in Book 17. See the Benedictine Fathers’ notes on Augustine’s letters, p. 59.]. In this campaign we daily serve as soldiers for the ration of frugality. We could not separate from our blessing one whom we desire to attach wholly to ourselves by that same grace.

Let us nevertheless address a few words to him himself, lest he deny that what has been written to you has been written to him also; for what Aeschinus hears, Micio is said to hear as well [Note: Terence, *Adelphoe*. See note 25.]. But why should I speak of others, when we can say everything concerning our own son? To speak of others is not usually the mark of a sound mind—and by the grace of God we are sound and safe, since Christ is our head.

May we have you safe for very many years, and always blessed in Christ together with your entire household, as we desire, most worthy and most dearly desired lord and brother.

# Letter VIII: To Licentius

[Note: Formerly Letter 46, part 2; the letter formerly numbered 8 is now 30. Written and sent with the preceding letter in the year 396.]

Pauline exhorts Licentius, the son of Romanianus, for whom Augustine—once his teacher—had written, both in prose and verse, to despise the vanity of the imperial court and dedicate himself to Christ.

## 1.

“Listen, then, my son, to your father’s law” [Note: Proverbs 1:8], that is, to Augustine’s faith; and do not reject your mother’s counsels, since Augustine’s piety rightly claims that name equally for itself. He carried you, so very small, in his bosom, and, after you had first been imbued from infancy with the milk of secular learning, he now desires to suckle and nourish you for the Lord at spiritual breasts.

For he sees you grown in bodily age but still babbling in spiritual cradles, still an infant in the word of God, scarcely yet crawling in Christ with your first steps and faltering footprints—provided that Augustine’s teaching, like a mother’s hand and a nurse’s arm, guides the unstable child.

If you listen to him and follow him, let me again attract you with Solomon’s words: “My son, you will receive a crown of graces for your head” [Note: Proverbs 1:9, according to the Septuagint]. Then you will truly be that consul and priest who was not dreamt of in the phantom of sleep but formed by truth itself, when Christ fills empty images of false achievement with the solid effects of his own work.

For Licentius will truly be a priest and truly a consul if he clings to Augustine’s footsteps and to prophetic and apostolic disciplines, as blessed Elisha clung to Elijah [Note: 2 Kings 2:1], and as the young Timothy clung to the illustrious apostle, accompanying them inseparably along the divine paths. [Note: Vatican manuscript 4 and two Bigotian manuscripts read more sharply, “you, Licentius, will be”; the same manuscripts below read *adhaereat* (“may he cling”) and *discat* (“may he learn”).] Thus he will learn to deserve priesthood with a perfect heart and to counsel peoples for their salvation with the mouth of a teacher [Note: Six manuscripts, together with the Benedictine edition, read “of a teacher”; other manuscripts read “of a master.”].

## 2.

This is enough by way of admonition and exhortation. I think that with a brief speech and little effort you can be stirred, my Licentius, toward Christ, since from childhood you have been devoted to the studies of truth and wisdom—both of which are truly Christ—and to the supreme good of every good, kindled by the spirit and mouth of venerable Augustine [Note: We have added “supreme good” from four Vatican manuscripts, one Bigotian manuscript, and the Benedictine edition.].

If he has had little influence with you on your own behalf, what can I accomplish, so far behind him in time and so poor in all his resources? Yet because I trust both in the power of his ability and in the graciousness of your intellect, and hope that more and greater things have been accomplished in you than remain to be accomplished, I have dared to speak with a twofold purpose: both to make myself comparable to that man in my concern for you, through the affection owed to him, and to be counted—at least by my declared affection—among those who love your salvation.

For I know that the outcome of your perfection assigns the palm especially to Augustine [Note: The Benedictine, Grabe, and Rosweyde editions read “outcome”; twelve manuscripts read “affection.”].

## 3.

I fear, my son, that I have offended your ears by the harshness of my rash speech and inflicted the wound of my weariness upon your mind through your ears as well. But I remembered your letter—the poem of Licentius contained in Augustine’s Letter 26 [formerly 39]—in which I learned that you were familiar with musical modes. I myself was once not a stranger to that study at your age.

Thus, if I had wounded your mind in any way, I found a remedy for soothing it in the recollection of your letters, so that I might summon you to the Lord, the craftsman of every kind of harmony, by the measured sound of verse.

I ask you to listen with your ear. Do not reject the cause of your salvation because of my words, but gladly receive the pious concern and fatherly mind even in despised speech. The name of Christ, which is above every name [Note: Philippians 2:9], implanted in those words, makes such reverence due to them that a believer cannot despise them.

### 39–40

Come, then, break your delays and the tenacious chains of the world;

Nor fear the gentle yoke of the peaceful Lord.

Beautiful indeed, but wondrous are the things present to wandering minds;

Yet a wise spirit is not stunned by them.

Now Rome, powerful even to turn the strong,

Troubles you with various seductive forms.

But for you, my son, I pray that father Augustine

May always confront all the allurements of the City.

Looking upon him amid so many dangers

Of this fragile life, and holding him in your heart, you will be safe.

Yet this I shall repeat, and warn you again and again:

Flee the slippery path of harsh military service.

Honor is a seductive name; servitude is evil; the outcome is painful—

What now delights you to desire, soon makes you regret having desired.

It is pleasant to climb the heights; terror comes from descending the heights.

If you stumble, you will fall more disastrously from the summit of the citadel [Note: Two Bigotian manuscripts read “you fall.”].

Now false goods please you; now ambition,

Carried by every breeze, snatches you away,

And empty rumor bears its hollow vessel in a glassy bosom [Note: From Virgil.].

When the belt purchased at great cost

Has girded you with its ruinous heat,

And barren labor has broken you,

Then, too late and in vain, you will accuse your empty hopes,

And wish to break the bonds you are now weaving.

Then you will remember father Augustine in vain,

Grieving that you despised his truthful warnings.

Therefore, if you are wise and pious, boy, listen;

And receive the words of your fathers and the counsel of the old.

“Why draw your fierce neck back from the yoke? My burden is gentle [Note: Two Bigotian manuscripts and the Grabe edition read “my light burden.” I would read this way if the meter allowed it: the Vulgate has, at Matthew 11:30, “my yoke is easy and my burden is light.” Augustine likewise writes in Letter 31 to Paulinus [formerly 34], “Although Christ’s yoke is in itself gentle and his burden light”; and in Letter 26 [formerly 39] to the same Licentius, from which Paulinus took these words: “For his yoke is gentle, and his burden is light.” In the poem on John the Baptist, line 291, the reading is “a light burden.”], my yoke is sweet [Note: Matthew 11:30].” It is the pious voice of Christ: believe God,

And put your head beneath the yoke; give your mouth to gentle reins.

Place your lowered shoulders beneath the light burden.

Now you can do this, while you act as a free man, while no bonds restrain you,

No concern for a wife, no lofty honor.

This is true freedom: to serve Christ, and in him

To be above everything.

He serves neither human masters,

Nor vices nor proud kings—

he alone who has given himself to Christ the Lord.

Nor should the nobility seem free to you which you now

See carried loftily through the astonished City.

You see how free it considers itself,

That it disdains to bend its neck to God.

That man is wretched among many mortals, and even among slaves

He serves; he buys maidservants so that they may rule him.

Eunuchs know it, as do those who have endured great palaces,

And every Roman who, wretched by choice, suffers it.

At what cost in sweat and loss of dignity

Are the cloak there and the honor of office here obtained?

Yet even the powerful man who has bought himself a position

Higher than all others, so that he might serve no one,

Does not attain his goal.

When he has proudly proclaimed himself master of the whole City,

He serves demons if he worships images.

Alas! Do you linger in Rome for the sake of such men, Licentius?

And do you despise Christ’s kingdom in order to please them?

You call them masters and greet them with bowed neck,

Though you see them to be slaves of wood and stone.

They venerate silver and gold with a divine name;

That is the religion which the disease of greed loves.

### 41–42

May he love these men who does not love Augustine;

And may he not worship Christ who delights to worship them.

Therefore God himself says that no one can serve two masters [Note: Matthew 6:24],

Because one mind pleases God.

One faith, one God, and one Christ from the Father [Note: Ephesians 4:5];

There is no double servitude to one master.

For as great as the distance between heaven and earth,

So great is the difference between the affairs and dominions of Caesar

And those of Christ.

Rise from the ground—but now, while the spirit governs these limbs,

Penetrate heaven with your mind; no delay of the flesh impedes you.

Die even now to bodily actions, and clearly contemplate beforehand

The good things of heavenly life.

You are spirit, although you are held by a body, if now,

Victorious in pious thought, you destroy the works of the flesh.

These things, dear boy, compelled by faithful love [Note: Fifteen manuscripts and the Benedictine edition read *fido* (“faithful”); the other codices read *fidei* (“of faith”). See Poem 19, line 128, and note 334.],

I have written to you; if you receive them, you will be received by God.

Believe that Augustine is now doubled for you in me:

Receive two fathers with a single devotion.

Are we despised? You will be torn away from two with greater grief.

Are we heard? [Note: That is, the son. See Poem 18, line 226.] You will be a sweet pledge to two.

In you the joyful concern of two fathers has labored,

And it is a great honor for you to have gladdened two.

But when I join myself to Augustine, I do not claim to be equal

In merits; I compare myself only in my love for you.

For what can I pour out upon you, dripping from my poor stream?

Apart from me, you will be washed by a twofold river:

Brother Alypius is one, and Augustine the teacher;

The one shares your blood, the other is the sower of your intellect.

You are strong with so great a brother and teacher, Licentius,

And do you hesitate to follow the stars on such wings?

Whatever you do, let not the world hope to have you as a friend:

As a soul owed to Christ, you will not be given to the earth.

Although now you may contemplate marriage chambers and lofty honors,

You must one day be restored to your Lord.

I believe that two righteous men will overcome one sinner,

And that your brother’s desires and prayers will drive you away.

Therefore return: with the voice of a father and the blood of a brother,

Both priests order you to come back.

They call you back to what belongs to you, for now you seek what belongs to others [Note: Most manuscripts, together with the Benedictine edition, read “you seek”; one Bigotian manuscript reads “you have sought,” another “you forbade,” and Rosweyde’s edition “you have sought.”].

Seek these things again; hunger for these: these realms which hold you are more truly your own.

Do not wear away your time on foreign things.

If you do not want what is yours, will anyone give you what belongs to others?

You will not belong to yourself; sent far abroad,

Alas, you will live in exile from your own heart.

It is enough to have sung these things to a son with a concerned father’s care,

Since I wish or fear for you what I wish or fear for myself.

These things are for you: if you receive them, this page will one day bring life;

If you reject them, this same page will be a witness.

May Christ grant that you remain safe for me, dearest son,

And give you to himself as a servant forever.

Live, I pray—but live for God; for to live for the world

Is the work of death; true life is to live for God.

# Letter IX

[Note: Formerly Letter 22; the letter formerly numbered 9 is now 28. Written in 396.]

### 43

Delphinus had been urged by Amandus to ask Paulinus for some salutary instruction. Paulinus complains of this in writing to Amandus, excusing his own lack of skill and imploring their help; he again intersperses many wise observations for instruction in piety.

To the holy, truly like-minded, and deservedly most beloved Amandus, Paulinus.

## 1.

As I understand it, what I whisper in your ear you proclaim from the housetop [Note: Matthew 10:27; Luke 12:3]. Since you love me too much and take too much pleasure in your opinion of your inept brother, you do not hesitate to insinuate into the ears of our holy and venerable common father both the rashness of my ignorance and the audacity with which I dare, in my words, to slight you more than him.

For how would he have thought me capable of producing something in writing worthy of his spirit, unless you had persuaded him—thinking this more from affection than judgment—that my mouth too had been opened by the Lord among the mouths of the mute and infants [Note: Wisdom 10:21; Psalm 8:3], through whom the Almighty perfects his praise?

He therefore orders me to bring forth speech seasoned with spiritual—that is, his own—salt [Note: Colossians 4:6]. For he remembers that he sprinkled me with the salt of his word. Nor does he cease to do so: all his letters are spiritual seasonings for me.

For he himself is also the salt of the earth [Note: Matthew 5:13; Mark 9:49], conveying the living flavor of apostolic teaching. But I fear that I have not recognized his salt with an insipid heart, and that my mind may not perceive that with which it is seasoned [Note: Luke 14:34], so as to taste the Lord’s sweetness, if in it Delphinus’ flavor could have faded and its vigor grown dull [Note: Perhaps read *sit jam* (“may now be”); Sacchin.]. [Note: After “grown dull,” a note in the margin of the Viennese manuscript reads: “Much seems to be missing here from the letter, since the continuity is almost nonexistent.” Nevertheless, the Regius and Vatican manuscripts and the five printed editions contain nothing more.]

## 2.

Who has roused me to say, “There is a lion in the roads, but murderers in the streets” [Note: Proverbs 22:13 and 26:13, according to the Septuagint]? We are not awakened to the care and work of life’s provision by devotion to the mystical bee or by the example of the industrious ant [Note: Proverbs 6:6 and 30:25]; rather, “we sleep a little, we doze a little, we fold our hands a little” [Note: Proverbs 6:10–11 and 24:33, according to the Septuagint]. Meanwhile poverty meets us like a good runner.

And that rich man who became poor in order to enrich us, truly needy, by his poverty [Note: 2 Corinthians 8:9], seeing us lingering in our poverty, rightly cried out: “What profit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?” [Note: Psalm 29:10.] [Note: The Regius manuscript and three printed editions read “he cried out.”]

Would that, even while we say these things, we might be roused by the judgment of our own conscience and by the complaint of our own speech, so that at last we might be able to say: “Now we have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” [Note: Psalm 76:11]. [Note: The Viennese manuscript reads “we may be able”; the other codices read “we can.”] But we are lazy bellies [Note: Titus 1:12], and therefore our soul clings to the pavement [Note: Psalm 118:25], although long ago you said to it: “Rise from the dead, so that you may attain Christ” [Note: Ephesians 5:14]. [Note: Three manuscripts and three printed editions read “raise yourself”; two other editions read “rise.” Both readings are good. See Letter 32, note 20.]

Through the intervention of your faith, by the sacrament of grace, you have placed this Lord in the little boat of our heart (see note 26) [Note: Matthew 8:23]. But because through the sleep of our inertia he has fallen asleep in us, you must awaken him, so that he may rise to awaken our soul; command silence to the troubled winds of earthly thoughts, and settle the waves of our senses by the peace of his word, so that pure tranquility may arise in our heart. With the Spirit of truth as helmsman and the word of God as oarsman, may we be directed toward the harbor of our will [Note: Psalm 106:30].

## 3.

For what is our expectation except the Lord [Note: Psalm 38:8], Jesus, who is powerful enough to save us from faintheartedness and storm [Note: Psalm 54:9]? [Note: The old and Roman Psalters and Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms read “from faintheartedness.” The Septuagint and Hilary read “from faintheartedness of spirit”; the Vulgate has “from faintheartedness of spirit.” Jerome indicates to Sunia that this was added for the Greek *oligopsychia*. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it from the Greek *apo pneumatos*, “from spirit.”]

May he also heed your prayers, so that our flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath [Note: Matthew 24:20; Mark 13:18]—that is, during idleness in spiritual matters and the barrenness of good works. The Sabbath is idle, and winter is bare of things that are born.

Therefore, if we keep Sabbath not according to the flesh but spiritually, abstaining from every servile work, which is a life of sin—for the person devoted to it is truly a slave and does not remain in the house [Note: John 8:35]—then we keep the Sabbath [Note: Isaiah 1:13], not that which the Lord’s soul cannot endure, but that in which God’s rest is found: he rests in the humble heart of trembling servants [Note: Isaiah 66:2].

Then the winter storm will not overwhelm our flight, nor hold our feet—sluggish as though from cold—from the freedom of escape, if, rejoicing in hope and fervent in spirit [Note: Romans 12:11], with our hands not contracted by the frost of greed but open to the refreshment of mercy, that stealthy arrival of the final hour [Note: Luke 21:34] finds us covered and clothed with the saving garments of faithful works [Note: 2 Corinthians 5:3]. Thus we may be able to withstand his face of cold [Note: Psalm 147:17, according to the Septuagint]—he who now wishes us to be made ready in fear of his command, so that on the day of wrath he may find us acquitted. [Note: The old Psalter and Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms support “that we may withstand”; there it reads, “who will withstand?”]

## 4.

Therefore now favor us and pray that we may seize that for which we have been seized [Note: Philippians 3:12], and, stretching ourselves toward the prize of the heavenly calling, forget what lies behind. With the hand of the mind placed upon the plow of the cross [Note: Luke 9:62], I will not look back over furrows already made, but will consider those still to be plowed [Note: The Viennese manuscript and Schott’s edition read “let us look back … let us consider.”].

May we continue until we reach the mountains to which we have lifted our eyes, so that from there help may come to us from the Lord [Note: Psalm 120:1], who is wondrous among his saints [Note: Psalm 67:36]. These are the mountains of God, to which we are raised by the good work of a faithful soul.

For if we walk worthily in the way of truth, which is undefiled [Note: Psalm 17:31], then the Lord himself, who is the way and the truth [Note: John 14:6], will make our feet like those of deer and set us upon the heights [Note: Psalm 17:34, according to the Septuagint]. [Note: Thus read the Septuagint interpreters, the Greek books, the old and Roman Psalters, and Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms.]

For he says: “The high mountains are for the deer, and the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” [Note: Psalm 103:18]. If we flee from wickedness with the agility of deer, let us flee from Nebroth the hunter, who, as Scripture indicates, was a hunter against the Lord [Note: Genesis 10:9, according to the Septuagint]. [Note: The Vulgate reads “before the Lord.” Augustine, in Book 1 of his *Locutions on Genesis*, says that it is uncertain whether this can be understood as “before the Lord God,” since the Greek word *enantion* (ἐναντίον) is also customarily understood in that way. Augustine discusses the matter also in *City of God*, Book 16, chapter 4. Paulinus, however, interprets the word as “against,” in the sense of hostile or adversarial, as is clear from what follows, rather than “before” or “in the sight of.” Near the end of this letter he says that we should “resist hostile hunters.” The Regius manuscript and the editions of Bad., Grabe, and Schott read *Nebroth*; so too do older manuscripts of Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, line 143, and the Septuagint, which has Greek Νεβρώδ. Paulinus likewise uses *Nebroth* in Letter 38 to Aper, §9, and renders several other Old Testament names in Greek form, suggesting that he used Scripture in a Greek-based version rather than the Latin Vulgate. Thus he writes *Solomon*, not *Salomon*, following the Greek text.]

With Christ cooperating, let us ascend the heights of virtue through the teachings of the prophets and apostles, who are the mountains of God, those rich mountains. Then, as though looking down from a lofty crag upon the empty shapes of the passing world, we shall sing in a voice of exultation:

“I will exalt you, Lord, because you have raised me up above those who rise against me, and my eye has looked down upon my enemies” [Note: Psalm 67:16; 29:2; 17:49; 53:9].

From this mountain height, formed for humility of heart and fortified on every side by wholesome disciplines like thorns, we shall become like hedgehogs. Their little bodies, armed with a rough covering and natural spines, are protected against hostile attacks, whether the bites of dogs or the hands of human beings.

When, in our humility, we are armed by fear of God and by the grace of that humility, the rock is our refuge—that is, Christ, whose words are both our defenses and our darts against the devil [Note: Sirach 28:28]. With these we fence our ears against the wicked tongue and fix hostile vices within our hearts.

Thus, through spiritual observance and upright faith, we shall be both hedgehogs and deer: narrowed and humbled according to these lesser animals, we shall be hidden in Christ as in a rock of refuge; and, fortified by the word and Spirit of truth, we shall resist both the devil and the allurements of this world with a prickly defense.

## 5.

We shall imitate those greater beasts, swift of foot and lofty in horn, if we have firm feet for standing in the Lord’s way [Note: Psalm 17:34], and our footsteps are not moved from his path [Note: Psalm 16:5]. Let us use those same feet to flee sins and the harmful contagions of this age.

Let us bear the head of our salvation—which is the Catholic faith—simultaneously adorned and armed with the horns of good works, so that we may either resist hostile hunters or, crowned with deeds pleasing to God, be, above all, your joy and crown [Note: Philippians 4:1]. We are your planting in Christ and your daily labor for Christ.

For we do not doubt that you pray daily for us, so that that blessed change of the right hand of the Most High may be accomplished in us [Note: Psalm 76:11], and so that we may truly be able to say:

“My heart and my flesh have failed; God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion forever” [Note: Psalm 72:26].

For God will deign to be the God of our heart when our carnal heart has failed, destroyed by spiritual edification. Then we shall dare to call ourselves your portion in the land of the living [Note: Psalm 141:6], when, renewed in the sense of our mind [Note: Ephesians 4:23] according to Christ and after the heavenly image, we too shall be able to say:

“God is the God of our heart, and God is our portion forever” [Note: Psalm 72:26].

# Letter X

[Note: Formerly Letter 15; the letter formerly numbered 10 is now 29. Written and sent with the preceding letter in the year 396.]

To Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, by whom he had been baptized, Paulinus offers a profoundly devout apology for being less capable of treating passages of Sacred Scripture in letters, as Delphinus had requested. Delphinus is found entered in the Church calendars on the ninth day before the Kalends of January.

To the most blessed and peculiarly honored lord, always our father in the Lord Christ, Delphinus, Paulinus.

## 1.

We have received the letters of your holy affection, in which you order us to add to the letters we write to you some discourse from Scripture beyond the requirements of ordinary duty, so that it may reveal to you the treasure of our heart [Note: The Viennese manuscript reads “beyond duty, from Scripture.” The word “necessity” is also absent from the Regius manuscript, which has the erroneous reading “of duty.”].

Yet both the order of piety and the Apostle’s teaching require parents to store up treasure for their children [Note: 2 Corinthians 12:14]. Although you, as our father, made by the Lord and in the Lord, have always stored up good things for us and do not cease to store them up: in addition to that talent of saving grace which we received when you sealed us with it—not to hide in the ground or wrap in a napkin, but to place with the bankers [Note: Luke 19:13], so that it might be multiplied by abundant interest, or to distribute it at the proper time to those who sell oil to the wise, who must purchase it for the preparation of lamps at the bridegroom’s coming [Note: Matthew 25:9].

You also always store up treasure for us in another way, when you ask that something be added from the Lord’s treasures to the grace given to us through you. Would that we could receive as much as you are able to obtain for us!

For surely, conscious of this request and confidence of yours on our behalf, you ask—or rather ask again—that we speak something spiritual to you, worthy of the seed you have sown in us. Believing that, according to your faith, you have obtained what you have asked and continue to ask should be given to us, you desire to receive, through the evidence of our words, the result of your concern and prayer from the fruits of our heart and mouth. For “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” [Note: Matthew 12:34; Luke 6:45], and the flavor of the mind is tasted in speech.

## 2.

Your holiness therefore rightly asks again for the debt of your deposit and expects the sprout of your seed. But what can I do, a barren field? With what harvest can I answer you, when instead of wheat I have produced thistles, or instead of grapes, thorns [Note: Matthew 7:16]?

And so, conscious of an evil crop or fruitless tree, I put forward in my letters only the words required by duty, in order at least to satisfy the obligation of piety. Confounded by the shame of my inertia, I conceal a mind degenerate from your own, while, conscious of your excessive love for me, I fear that I may sadden your spirit, which rejoices in a presumptuous hope for good things from us, by disappointing its expectation.

You may be forced to say or write to me: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, but you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine” [Septuagint: “a foreign vine”] [Note: Jeremiah 2:21]. “I expected you to produce grapes, but you produced thorns” [Note: Isaiah 5:4, according to the Septuagint].

Would that they might at least be useful thorns, which provide a barrier against the wicked tongue for pious ears and protect faith in a cautious heart like a crop enclosed in a field [Note: Sirach 28:28 and 36:27; Matthew 13:7]. But, as I perceive, you have produced those useless and harmful thorns which choke the word and turn it into misery, while they still pierce hearts with carnal thoughts—like a rough bramble [Note: Psalm 57:10; see note 27].

[Note: Hilary, Jerome, and Augustine use a similar expression in their commentaries on the Psalms, where the reading is: “Before your thorns produce the bramble.” The old Psalter likewise reads: “Before your bramble produces thorns.” The Roman Psalter reads: “Before your bramble produces your thorns.” I would read “your bramble,” following the Greek text, unless Paulinus had said “rough bramble.” Arnobius has another reading: “Before your thorns produce brambles”; Eucherius, “the bramble”; Symmachus, “before your thorns have grown so that they become a bramble.” See note 27.]

## 3.

Therefore, most devoted father, you ask what more you can do for us that you have not already done. You have planted us in the house of the Lord [Note: Psalm 91:14], and, once planted, you built a wall of the seal of salvation around us, protecting us from the attack of the wild boar and from the ravaging of the fierce onager [Note: Psalm 79:14]. [Note: The Septuagint and Vulgate read “the solitary wild beast devoured it.” Here Paulinus has used a species for the genus; Jerome translated this verse from the Hebrew as “all the beasts of the field devoured it.” The onager is also used for various wild beasts, as in Psalm 103:11: “The wild asses await their food.” Some interpreters, however, think that the word there denotes an unknown bird, perhaps a griffin or some other creature related to other birds as the whale is to other fish.]

You also built a winepress and dug it, so that through a devout way of life we might pour out for you a kind of sweet vintage from your vine.
