You still have something to do, by imitating the one who asked the lord of the vineyard for a period of grace for the barren fig tree [Note: Three manuscripts—Regius, Vatican, and Viennese—together with Rosweyde’s edition, read this way. Certain printed editions have “threatened,” erroneously. One should read “a period of grace,” meaning a span of time for cultivation. See note 64], and by his promise postponed the cutting down that threatened the useless tree [Note: Luke 13:8].

Thus, let the care of your piety intervene for us as well, and let it ask that the axe placed at the roots of barren trees be suspended, either by an annual expectation of the Lord’s indulgence [Note: Matthew 3:10; Luke 3:9]. [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “ask and promise.”]

Promise the master of the household that your concern for us will be diligent, and offer continual prayers as that apostolic basket of evangelical manure [Note: Luke 13:8], so that the soil of our heart may grow rich and the crop of your sowing be nourished, or so that the tree of your planting may receive the sap of your fruitfulness.

Then, on the day of recognition—that is, of judgment [Note: See Letter 19, section 3]—when the sower and reaper will rejoice together, may you bring us too, in your fatherly bosom, among your sheaves, and claim from him the fruit of your cultivation, when you offer to him—who makes fruitful the labors of those who water and cultivate [Note: The word is “makes fruitful.” Since this verb may seem suspiciously active, the Fathers use it; Ambrose writes in his commentary on Psalm 36, “That good earth of the Lord makes fruitful without any labor.” Yet Paulinus’ meaning here is that he makes the labors fruitful. Sacchin.]—that which in us he may deign not to command be cut down for the fire [see Letter 11, section 7], but to reap for the granary [Note: Matthew 13:30].

# Letter XI

[Note: Formerly Letter 5; the letter formerly numbered 11 is now 3. Written in 397.]

How great is the superiority of Christian love over human ties, he shows by explaining allegorically the ancient sacrifices, in which a sacrifice to God must be offered in and from oneself; likewise he praises Severus for having written the life of Saint Martin, and finally, by inviting him to himself, gives a most beautiful reminder of the excellence of evangelical poverty. [Col. 0190C]

**PAULINUS to his wholehearted brother SEVERUS**

**1.** In the Lord God Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0190D] Thus three manuscripts, Cod. Reg., Vat., and Vien. In the editions, “God” is absent.] I perceive, and especially in you gladly experience, the gift and word of God, because nothing compares with a faithful friend, and the tongue of grace abounds in a good man [Note: [Col. 0189] Sirach 6:15]. For your consolation of love is like medicine of life to us; your words are like honeycombs; and good news concerning you from a distant land is to us like cold water to the thirsty [Note: [Col. 0189] Proverbs 16:24 and 25:25, according to the Septuagint]. When this report, both by its indication of your salvation [Col. 0191A] and by its expression of love, fattens our bones [Note: [Col. 0191D] The Vien. manuscript has *impinguat* (“fattens”).] [Note: [Col. 0191] Proverbs 15:30], it brings from this a great increase of joy and delight: namely, that it is conveyed and disclosed through our sons—your boys in the Lord—so that we possess not merely letters, but, in a certain sense, a part of your very side.

What shall we repay our Lord, besides all that he has repaid us [Note: [Col. 0191] Psalm 115:12], for this grace also, by which he has joined you to us—formerly most dearly loved by us in secular friendship—as our inseparable companion and partner in his own affairs, something we regard as of incomparable worth, binding us together in spiritual kinship?

“What is my mother, or who are my brothers?” [Note: [Col. 0191] Matthew 12:48.] Surely not those who are born from the will of the flesh and from the union of sleep, but those who are born of God [Note: [Col. 0191] John 1:13] through the wisdom of God, Christ: he who, remaining in himself, renews all things [Col. 0191B] and grants the power to become children of God [Note: [Col. 0191] Ibid. 1:12], coheirs of his kingdom. For this very purpose he was conformed to the body of our humility, so that he might conform us to the body of his glory; and, having torn us away not only from our own earth but also from our kindred, might transfer us into his lot and lineage.

By this gift he deigned to create us for himself [Note: [Col. 0191D] Thus the Reg. and Vien. manuscripts and four editions. The Rosv. edition has “to be created.”] and join us in the bond of his love. He had prepared us for this covenant through the intimacy of the flesh, which we now understand, and he has changed that former affection into an eternal relationship by a stronger love. For this is the love of Christ, which never falls away [Note: [Col. 0191] I Corinthians 13:8], because it flows from God and remains in God; and whoever it inhabits, it makes perpetual through its own eternity. It does not know how to become puffed up; it is free from deceit, pure from envy, emulous of God—not through exaltation of spirit, but through the spirit of gentleness and the emulation of devotion. For our Lord, as he himself attested and as we experience, is gentle and meek, and humble in heart [Note: [Col. 0191] Matthew 11:29]. [Col. 0191C]

**3.** In this respect, you, my brother begotten with me, surpass all the affection of bodily relationships toward me—not only for present assistance but also for everlasting companionship—by as much as you are my brother through a parent of greater worth than those whom flesh and blood alone join to me.

Where now is my blood relationship? Where is the old friendship? Where are the former companions of my household? I have vanished from the sight of them all, a stranger—as it is said—to my brothers, and a foreigner to the sons of my mother. My friends and former intimates now stand far away [Note: [Col. 0191] Psalms 68:9 and 37:12, according to the Roman Psalter]; and, like a flowing river or a passing wave, so they pass me by. Perhaps they are confused and ashamed, as it is written, to come to me: those who were near have become far from me, and those who were far have become near [Note: [Col. 0191] Psalms 37:12 and 107:10; Ephesians 2:13]. “Instead of fathers, sons have been born to you” [Note: [Col. 0191] Psalm 44:17].

Thus, in place of parents, brothers, and friends, you have been made for us by the Lord. You are anxious with the care of a parent, solicitous with fraternal affection, attentive with the entire fidelity of an unfeigned friendship, and poured out toward us with every affection of devotion; by your constant letters you visit us, and by your most tender consolations you soothe us.

**4.** Nor are you satisfied with revisiting us on every occasion unless you also send your boys. You choose as messengers not only servants but also holy sons, whose blessed offspring in the Lord brings you joy. Through their eyes you see us, and through their mouths you touch us. Their feet are beautiful to us, like the feet of those who proclaim good things [Note: [Col. 0191] Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15]. For they announce and bring us from you the things that make for peace, when they produce the works of the Lord—whether you perform them in the word of God or write them in the Spirit of the Word.

What riches, what precious gifts, what relationships could provide consolations so sweet? Leaving aside the consideration of those things which divine generosity promises for eternity [Note: [Col. 0191] Matthew 19:29], it is easy to consider how much more valuable are the things neglected here which are already repaid in this world. For what harm, I ask, do an unfeeling parent, a negligent brother, or a forgetful friend inflict on me, when all the loves attached to these names—whether of pledges or covenants—are abundantly repaid to me through you alone? Not to mention the many people, whether in our own land or in a foreign world, who resemble you in their devotion both to God and toward us: their affection, in place of country, parents, and estates, the grace of the one who repays grants us in abundance. If we reckon up in you alone the good things we have received, we shall judge that all that was ours has been compensated for us in you more generously and more preciously [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Vatican manuscript has “we shall think.”]

“Brother does not redeem; a man does not redeem” [Note: [Col. 0191] Psalm 48:8]. We may similarly say: The world does not love us, but Christ loves us. A man neglects us, but God loves us. “A man’s enemies are his household” [Note: [Col. 0191] Matthew 10:36], but again, a man’s friends are God’s household. We may have had good and great brothers, friends, and intimates; but it was not pleasing to the Lord that they should be so toward us. He chose you to give us as an inseparable brother and a most beloved intimate. We rightly love you as ourselves, because in Christ we have one heart and one soul with you [Note: [Col. 0191] Acts 4:32]. [Col. 0192C]

**5.** Therefore, what we said above briefly about the love of many who are likewise spiritual, we did not express suitably or worthily. For the same grace that we possess in you can correspond to us in the person of no one [Note: [Col. 0192D] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “in no person.”]. Even if others should deign to love the grace of the Lord in our humility [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Vien. manuscript reads: “the grace of the Lord to love our humility”], this particular gift in you is ours: we were predestined for one another in the closest love of Christ, and even the friendship of our former life marked us out for each other, while we were still lovers of the things from which we are now turned away through Christ.

Nevertheless, through the habit of that former intimacy we grew into this bond by which we are now joined through God’s intervention, so that, by loving one another faithfully even on the path of unbelief, we might learn also to love one another spiritually. For we always loved each other so religiously that no affection could have been added to our love for one another except the love of Christ, which alone surpasses every perception and affection.

Therefore we ought to give all the more earnest thanks to the good Lord: he deigned to look upon our humility and, finding us together in the field, drew us together from the womb of the flesh like twins and took us together. For, as you wrote, we were truly two in the field; but by the goodness and omnipotence of God, I would dare to say that one of us was taken in such a way [Note: [Col. 0193] Matthew 24:40] that neither was left behind.

For we were individually two when rebellious flesh disagreed with the spirit within us, and our outward self had no peace because it opposed the inward self. But now, through his mercy, who made both one [Note: [Col. 0193] Ephesians 2:14], we are two and yet one, because there is one spirit in the two; and there is no division between those whose body is one.

But this, as I said, is something we share with all our brothers in Christ [Note: [Col. 0193D] The Vien. manuscript has “with us”]. What is especially pleasing and worthy of special thanksgiving to us in you is that, in your friendship, we have received the most blessed gift of God: even if our journey had taken different directions, we would not have been separated from one another. We experience this loss, as you recognize, in the case of many of our once equally beloved companions [Note: [Col. 0193D] Thus the manuscripts and four editions. The Rosv. edition has “now”]. [Col. 0193C]

**6.** Truly, then, you are for us both parent, brother, and intimate, since, by doing in us the will of God and the fullness of the law [Note: [Col. 0193] Romans 13:10], you love us as yourself, our friend in the love of Christ and our brother in the regeneration of God.

Since you see and recognize this, why do you speak so harshly and falsely about us and about yourself, saying, “We were two in the field, and one was taken” [Note: [Col. 0193] Matthew 24:40]? Let us not be ungrateful to God, who did not take one of us, but took one in us.

We were two, but when we were being joined together with those brothers [Note: [Col. 0193D] The Rosv. edition formerly read *combinabamur* (“we were joined together”); the Schot. edition had *convivebamus* (“we lived together”). We have restored *combinabamus* from the Reg. manuscript and the Bad., Grav., and Grin. editions. This restored reading is confirmed by a new edition of Saint Augustine’s works, which has in *Confessions* 5.10.18: “And therefore I was still joining myself with their elect.” Paulinus here follows a reading of the Septuagint containing συνδυάσω (*syndyasō*, “I will join together”), just as Augustine does in Psalm 140.12, vol. IV, p. 1570. Thus, while the older manuscripts of Augustine’s works read *combinabam* and *combinabo*, we have written *combinabamus* here.] from whom we have been divided by this purpose: for the same Scripture sufficiently shows that “one” may be spoken not only of a single body but also of the unanimity of many [Note: [Col. 0193] Romans 11:7], when it sets forth these persons not as two individuals but as peoples, with the faith of the Gentiles and the remnant of the Jews demonstrating the point.

Likewise, the two women grinding, of whom one is similarly taken [Note: [Col. 0193] Matthew 24:41; Luke 17:35], seem, in my opinion, to represent the form of the Synagogue and the Church. For no other person is treated throughout the whole scope of the sacred Scriptures except either the distinction within the whole human race between believing and unbelieving peoples [Col. 0194A], or the twofold nature of every human being, composed of two substances.

Therefore, my brother, because we have always clung together in one heart, just as we now cling together in Christ, we have either been taken together or left together. We were taken not through our own merit but through the grace of God, whose gifts and calling are irrevocable [Note: [Col. 0193] Romans 11:29]; not through the privilege of works but through the faith of good will, by which we were equally inspired toward his love. Since it has appeared that we share one purpose and one time of conversion [Note: [Col. 0194D] The Reg. manuscript and the Bad., Grav., and Grin. editions have “way of life”], we ought together to glory and rejoice in him who justifies the ungodly through faith and gives food to every creature [Note: [Col. 0193] Psalm 135:25].

This is not the food that perishes, but that which is prepared for eternal nourishment—the kind that either the soul, active in the things of God, or the Catholic Church prepares. For it is the body of the true bread that came down from heaven [Col. 0194B] [Note: [Col. 0193] John 6:33] and gives life-giving food to those who hunger for righteousness. It does not stuff the flesh but strengthens the human heart.

This bread is also a fountain: the more it is eaten, the more it is hungered for; and the more it is drunk, the more it is thirsted for [Note: [Col. 0193] Sirach 24:29]. To eat this bread forever, let us grind good wheat in the bakery of this world: the faithful practice of obedience, and love in a pure heart and an unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0193] I Timothy 1:5].

**7.** Since you are full of this grace and virtue, you grind good grain for God, and present yourself to God as food to be eaten in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Whoever, by accomplishing his will, is changed into the members of his body is his food [Note: [Col. 0194D] The Reg. and Vien. manuscripts have “the fulfillment of his will”; five editions have “one who fulfills his will.” The Vien. manuscript below has “turns into.”]. The Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0194D] We have supplied *dicente* (“saying”) from the Vien. manuscript; the other manuscripts read *ipso* (“he himself”).] that whoever joins himself to God becomes one spirit [Note: [Col. 0193] I Corinthians 6:17].

We attain this if we bear the image of the heavenly one with the same care and diligence with which we bore the image of the earthly [Note: [Col. 0193] I Corinthians 15:49]. By imitating the imitator of Christ, we shall reach the imitation of God. We are a good fragrance to him in Christ [Note: [Col. 0193] II Corinthians 2:15] if we present a living sacrifice through rational service [Note: [Col. 0193] Romans 12:1], offering him pure fine flour, sifted from the inner recesses of ourselves by the mill of a pure heart.

Setting up a chaste altar in our breast, let us slaughter in our vices the animals prescribed by the law for sacrifice: let us offer the goat through the destruction of sin [Note: [Col. 0193] Leviticus 10:16], in which there is the odor of death; let us strike down the bull if we lay aside pride; let us sacrifice the sheep [Note: [Col. 0193] Leviticus 3:6] if, rejecting softness and sluggishness, we cast them out, not lukewarm in love but fervent in spirit.

Let us offer in ourselves also the lamb if we live without blemish, and the calf if we become little in malice, so that in the one we may reflect pure chastity and in the other the simplicity of a child.

I see you presenting such a sacrifice to God in the temple of your body, in the sanctuary of your heart, in the immolation of your flesh, and in the offering of your soul. You sacrifice the bull when, laid low in devout humility, you have struck down your lofty neck through the fear of God. You sacrifice the kid when, as a pursuer of justice, you kill all the works of the left side. You slaughter the sheep when, as a diligent worker and devoted student of the divine will and law, you overthrow in yourself inertia [Note: [Col. 0195C] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “of life”] and sluggishness like a soft animal.

You cut away from yourself the impediments of this life like wool—useful to the one who shears it, but burdensome to the one who carries it—with the shears of the heavenly word [Note: [Col. 0195C] Thus the Vien. manuscript. The other manuscripts have “you cut off.” The restored reading is confirmed by what follows] by which Christ holds us fast, seized between the Two Testaments. Either he strips us of secular burdens as of wool, or again, cutting away bodily vices from us as wool from diseased and soft sheep, he draws them into the garment of his body, which the work of believers covers. For, as we put on Christ [Note: [Col. 0195] Romans 13:14], so in turn we are clothed by Christ; he brings us down into the Church’s woven fabric and adorns us with the fringes of his garment.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] The Vatican manuscript and the Grin. edition have “just as.”]

[Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscripts have *abscidens* (“cutting away”), as do two editions. Thus also in Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 954, all the older manuscripts have *abscidere quidquam* (“to cut away anything”); likewise in *Peristephanon* 4.123, *abscisa papilla* (“the breast cut away”); in the hymn of Saint Romanus the Martyr, line 975, *Nervos abscideret* (“he might cut the sinews”); and in hymn 11.65, *Huic abscide caput* (“cut off his head”). Our manuscripts also have *abscidatur*, not *abscindatur*, in Paulinus’s first letter to Severus, section 5; and all the manuscripts and editions in letter 10.3 have *jubeat abscidi*, not *abscindi*.]

**8.** This shepherd has already shorn you, as I suppose, and placed you on his threshing floor, and drenched your fleece with heavenly dew. For both the grace poured into your mouth and, through your mouth, flowing like a stream from the fountains of Israel—or a *διώρυξ* (*diōryx*, “a channel or ditch leading from a river”), as it is written [Note: [Col. 0195] Sirach 24:41]—flows abundantly from paradise. This teaches us that the Lord descended upon you like rain upon a fleece [Note: [Col. 0195] Psalm 71:6] and gave you water from Jacob’s well [Note: [Col. 0195] John 4:6], because you too had become near to the Lord as one of the sons of Israel [Note: [Col. 0196C] The Vien. manuscript has “drawing near.”].

If, then, you have been completely shorn, you feel that you have received a double benefit: in the heat of the world you are light, and you gather the pasture of the word, sprinkled with the morning joy of dew [Note: [Col. 0196D] Thus the Reg. manuscript and the Bad., Grav., and Schot. editions. This is the most genuine reading. Paulinus likewise writes in letter 23 to the same man, section 38, “wounded by love,” and in *Natale* 6 of Saint Felix, poem 18, line 123, “surrounded by devotion.” The Vatican and Vien. manuscripts and the Grin. edition have “sprinkled with the dew”; the Rosv. edition, “scattered with dew.” Sacchin prefers the reading “the morning joy of dew.”] Nor are you scorched by the heat of the noonday demon [Note: [Col. 0195] Psalm 90:6], because you rest under the shadow of the Lord’s wings [Note: [Col. 0195] Psalm 16:8].

Meanwhile a tunic is being prepared for you from your own wool, in which you will be clothed on that winter’s day, so that you may be able to withstand the presence of its cold—provided that, when stripped of the body, you are not found naked of your works [Note: [Col. 0196D] We have supplied “from” from the Reg. and Vien. manuscripts and four editions].

Then Christ will in turn offer himself to you as sheep and lamb—the one who was led to slaughter for us and did not open his mouth before the one shearing him [Note: [Col. 0195] Isaiah 53:7], allowing his fleece, that is, the covering of his flesh, to be taken from him. For he laid down and took up again both his soul and his flesh for us [Note: [Col. 0195] John 10:17–18]. He is priest and sacrifice, lamb and shepherd: shepherd for his sheep, and lamb slain for his shepherds.

For the Lord himself is the sacrifice of all priests [Note: [Col. 0195] Hebrews 5:10]. Offering himself to the Father as a libation for the reconciliation of all, he was both the victim of his priesthood and the priest of his own victim. Now every new creature offers sacrifice to him as the one Lord of all, and priests are themselves sacrifices to him.

If we now offer ourselves to him to be shorn in the silence of humility and the patience with which he himself offered himself for us, he will take upon himself the burdens of our fleece. He will not disdain to carry the wool of his sheep, since he deigns to carry back to the sheepfold on his shoulders the very sheep whom he has recalled from error [Note: [Col. 0196D] The Vien. manuscript has “whom he had recalled.”] [Note: [Col. 0195] Luke 15:5]. [Col. 0196A]

**9.** And since he himself has no need of our goods [Note: [Col. 0195] Psalm 15:2], while we need all that belongs to him, he is good to us only for our good; he receives what is his as though it were ours, yet does not wish it to remain under his own legal claim, so that he may credit it to us as ours, although we have nothing unless we have received it [Note: [Col. 0195] I Corinthians 4:7], and cannot even exist without his command [Note: [Col. 0195] Acts 17:28].

Therefore, although we bring nothing into this world [Note: [Col. 0195] I Timothy 6:7], he supplies us with the substance of temporal things as fleece that may be shorn—not so that it may burden those whom he commands to be born free of encumbrances, but so that he may set before us material by which virtue can produce merit. It provides the means for us to display faith and devotion toward God, that is, the true Father and Lord, if we have available to us things empty or sweet which, when we prefer God to them, we neglect at the cost of a great reward [Note: [Col. 0195] Matthew 19:29].

And although, through his immense goodness, these things neither entered this world with us [Note: [Col. 0196C] I Timothy 6:7] nor can be carried away from it with us [Note: [Col. 0196D] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “which must be carried away.” The manuscript reading is confirmed by what follows, “we do not carry away with us”; the reading of the editions is confirmed by letter 16 to Jovius, section 8], nevertheless, if we obey his commands, they are so ordered that they may be changed for the better, and eternal things may be produced from temporal ones.

For things which, just as we did not bring them in, we cannot take away by our nature and by the passing form of this world [Note: [Col. 0195] I Corinthians 7:31], we transform through the work of almighty God in a blessed kind of commerce. We not only carry them away with us, but sow them beforehand and send them ahead of us into the bosom of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0196D] This word is absent from the Vatican manuscript] [Note: [Col. 0195] Galatians 6:8]. [Col. 0196B]

**10.** Hence, I think, it was prescribed that the lazy worker should not eat bread [Note: [Col. 0197] II Thessalonians 3:10]—not, of course, this bread of perishable food, but that by which one lives unto true life. For each person, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0197] Psalm 127:2, according to the Septuagint], shall eat from his own fruits and live by his works. Therefore each person’s work is his bread, and Christ is the true and living bread [Note: [Col. 0197] John 6:35].

The lazy worker cannot eat him, because he is also our Passover. We are commanded to eat it with all haste, prepared and girded, firmly shod, and without laying down from our hands the staffs [Note: [Col. 0197] Exodus 12:11]—that is, the works by which we rely and support ourselves—never relaxing them. For the time is short, and it is to our advantage to be free from anxiety, as the Apostle advises, because of the present necessity [Note: [Col. 0197] I Corinthians 7:26, 29, and 32], so that we may be found ready and may not fear opening to the Lord when he knocks [Note: [Col. 0197] Luke 12:36], dreading the consequences of sleep or negligence in our conscience.

This will profit us nothing if, despite all this, we are to be dragged away and brought to death after death, paying the just penalties of negligence and impiety—if we are found serving a master not our own, occupied more with the business of the world than with Christ’s, failing to open when the Lord knocks, and being led unwillingly to the Father.

Therefore we are instructed to labor and pray at the proper time for this—that is, for the soul [Note: [Col. 0197] Psalm 31:6]—the present time. We have been brought into the span of this time so that we may seek true life through this brief and passing life [Note: [Col. 0197] I Timothy 6:19].

The field and farm of this life is this world [Note: [Col. 0197] Matthew 13:38], or the human being himself who is sent into this world. God takes one [Note: [Col. 0197] Matthew 24:40] when, as we said above, he has made the two one by subjecting the flesh to the spirit. For in each of us, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0197] Galatians 5:17], there are two minds and two laws [Col. 0197C]. As these grind within us, acceptable or rejected fine flour is produced.

**11.** Your words testify that, the law of the members having been conquered [Note: [Col. 0197] Romans 7:23] and the outer man having been corrupted [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Vien. manuscript has “having corrupted the corruptible outer man”], you prepare pure dough [Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus the manuscripts and four editions. The Rosv. edition has “to prepare”] and become unleavened for Christ without leaven [Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus the same manuscripts and editions. The Rosv. edition has “to become”] [Note: [Col. 0197] I Corinthians 5:7]. Your speech is as eloquent as it is chaste [Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus the Reg. manuscript and four editions. Others have “fruitful.” Both words have been accepted. See “eloquence of speech,” letter 16 to Jovius, section 11].

You would not have been granted the ability to narrate Martin [Note: [Col. 0197] See letter 29, section 14] unless you had made your mouth worthy of sacred praises by a pure heart.

Blessed, then, are you, a man blessed by the Lord, who have reviewed the history of so great a priest and most illustrious Confessor with speech as worthy as your affection is just. Blessed also is he who, according to his merits, obtained a historian worthy of his faith and life: he is consecrated to divine glory by his merits and to human memory by your writings.

These words of yours too are fleeces, and cover the Lord Jesus with a most grateful garment [Note: [Col. 0198D] Rosweyde had conjecturally added “his limbs.” We have removed the word, since it is found in no manuscript]. They surround his beautiful furnishings and adorn them with the flowers of your intellect. On the day of recompense the Lamb will in turn clothe you with his own fleece, clothing your mortality over with his immortality [Note: [Col. 0197] I Corinthians 15:54]. [Col. 0198A]

**12.** Only remember us and look upon us—not looking backward [Note: [Col. 0197] Luke 9:62], but mindful of your friend. For it is certain that, as the more diligent farmer has more abundant crops, so the more swift runner will outstrip our slowness and reach the prize of the heavenly calling [Note: [Col. 0197] Philippians 3:14].

For I am weaker in mind than in body, and I follow you at a great distance, separated from you only by distance, not by the road [Note: [Col. 0198D] Thus the Reg. and Vien. manuscripts and the Bad. and Grin. editions. Others have “having been surpassed”]. I turn the same mill with a sick and unequal hand, your companion in the bakery, inferior in grain, because I grind tares mixed with wheat [Note: [Col. 0197] Matthew 13:25]. To have them all turned into grain, I need your prayers. Through them I hope to escape both my riches and my poverty, since both are harmful to me: I am poor in righteousness and rich in sin.

I would truly think myself rich in goodness if I were already as poor as you suppose. Yet here I shall briefly challenge you concerning your own words, by which you disagree with yourself. Even if you did not praise my virtues in me, since in your words you thought that you might credit me with those of another, how is it consistent for you both to declare that poverty is a virtue you admire and to confess that you dread it?

If you believe that this virtue has been granted to me, which you confess that you wish for but cannot attain—that, having food and clothing, I should be content with these [Note: [Col. 0197] I Timothy 6:8] and think about nothing beyond the day [Note: [Col. 0197] Matthew 6:34]—why do you think that I must be overcome by want, so that I should cease inviting you, whom I cannot help desiring? Or do you reveal yourself as so weak and distrustful toward Christ that you fear coming to a friend such as you describe, if you truly follow him who said, “Take up your cross, and come, follow me” [Note: [Col. 0197] Luke 9:23; Matthew 19:21]?

How else do you think Christ should be followed except by the rule he taught [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Vien. manuscript has “willed”] and the example he set forth? When he came among his own, he nevertheless had no place among them where he could rest his head [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Reg. manuscript adds “rights”] [Note: [Col. 0197] Matthew 8:20].

**13.** Imitate Christ’s imitator, so that, dead, you may live by crucifying yourself to the world and the world to yourself, dying daily through faith in the word and living in the word of faith.

For man does not live by bread alone [Note: [Col. 0197] Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4], especially the Christian, of whom it is specifically written: “He lives by faith” [Note: [Col. 0197] Galatians 3:12]. Did he say, “By bread”? Why, then, do you fear that I will hunger, if you have faith? Your bread is with you.

If you are fed by the word of God, you will not desire food for the belly. For God will destroy both it and the belly [Note: [Col. 0197] I Corinthians 6:13], while he builds himself up in us, provided that, rooted and established in his love, we remain [Note: [Col. 0197] Ephesians 3:17], and do not build our house upon the shifting sand of distrust [Note: [Col. 0198D] Thus the Vien. manuscript and the Schot. edition. Others have “wavering”] [Col. 0199A] [Note: [Col. 0199] Matthew 7:26; Luke 6:49].

Have we not believed him, and both sworn allegiance to him, who said: “Do not think about tomorrow; sufficient for the day is its own trouble. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” [Note: [Col. 0199] Matthew 6:34, 33; Luke 12:31]?

If you believe him, why do you fear hunger on account of the poverty of his brother, when you know that, secure in this word, he preferred poverty to riches? Or do you believe that the one who trusts in the earth abounds more than the one who trusts in God, and that the one fed by his own care abounds more than the one fed by divine care?

What does that wretched man possess who does not possess himself? For he does not possess himself who hopes more in himself than in God. Truly he is dead who does not fear not living [that is, perhaps, “who fears not to live”], if he entrusts and commits his whole self to God.

I therefore hope that what you wrote—that you believe I shall soon become so poor that I would no longer dare invite you—was rather a jest arising from your kindness than an expression of faithlessness. I confess that I desire nothing more than the good of such complete freedom, since so intimate a circumcision is full perfection.

Yet if you possess true faith in Christ, true admiration for the heavenly virtues in a human being, and true emulation of a person living in God [Note: [Col. 0199D] We have supplied *est* (“is”) from the Reg. and Vien. manuscripts], how could you not seek me all the more eagerly the more perfect you heard that I had become—unless you openly confess that you do not believe in your heart what you profess with your mouth [Note: [Col. 0199] Romans 10:10]?

But as a devoted follower of the most blessed Martin, you will be accused of fleeing from me as a sinner, not as a poor man. Certainly you would never have desired him if you had feared hunger for bodily food. [Col. 0199B]

**14.** For my part, since it is necessary that love, which is the fullness of the law [Note: [Col. 0199] Romans 13:10], should make the greatest progress in the advancement of spiritual work, I shall not cease both to desire you and to invite you, just as you desire me.

Come to us; if possible, hasten here. We have nothing except Christ—and see whether we have nothing, when we have the one who possesses all things.

For we did not leave Ebromagus [See note 30] for the sake of a little garden, as you write, but preferred the garden of paradise to both estate and homeland [Note: [Col. 0199D] Thus the Vien. manuscript. Others add “that one.” Both readings are good]. For the true home is more truly there where it is eternal; the truer homeland is there where the original earth and the principal dwelling are.

For if you believe—through the mercy of Christ, on account of whom, even if we have nothing, we possess all things in him [Note: [Col. 0199] II Corinthians 6:10]—then now, in this soil of thorns and labors, not even a clod of a little garden holds us as earth’s clay. Would that no dust of sin clung to us in the same way!

If you believe this good in the way you proclaim it; if you believe that I am in this condition, just as you write that you believe it; and if you nevertheless desire me less eagerly, then you are no longer sinning against me as a sinner, always and forever unworthy of your sight, but against the Lord himself—that is, you are committing an offense—if you think that the sustenance of this mortal life will fail us only when God begins to be our possession [Note: [Col. 0199] Psalm 15:5].

**EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0199] Formerly 21; the one formerly numbered 12 is now 32. Written in the year 397.] XII.**

[Col. 0200A]

Amandus had requested longer letters from Paulinus; accordingly, he writes this letter on the grace of God, no less devout than elegant, recalling God’s kindness and the profundity of the divine counsel concerning the salvation of humankind. He also teaches that one kind of humility is bad and one kind of pride good.

**PAULINUS to AMANDUS, holy, deservedly venerable, and most dearly beloved.**

**1.** I confess that I marvel at the holy kindness and patience of your love: although I am accustomed to make my letters to you exceedingly wordy and fuller of annoyance than grace, you nevertheless take from them a desire for my speech rather than weariness. For, by the favour of your writings, in which love from a pure heart and [Col. 0200B] unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0199] I Timothy 1:5] speaks sincere affection in the unleavened bread of truth [Note: [Col. 0199] I Corinthians 5:8] and in return stirs mine from the depths of my mind, you provoke and encourage me to frequent and more lengthy letters.

What then shall I do? Shall I comply with an abundance of letters? But you have no need of my good things [Note: [Col. 0199] Psalm 15:2], and it is fairer that I be enriched by you, because the rich ought to contribute to the poor, so that there may be equality [Note: [Col. 0199] II Corinthians 8:14]. Or shall I rather consult my own advantage and set a guard upon my mouth [Note: [Col. 0199] Psalm 38:2], that I may escape the danger of sin that arises from much speaking [Note: [Col. 0199] Proverbs 10:19]? But again I fear that I may be judged guilty of disobedience; and perhaps I shall offend more seriously if I fail you by not complying than if I fear for myself by not writing.

2. Therefore may the Lord grant me from the Lord an opening of the mouth toward you [Note: [Col. 0199] Ephesians 6:19], and may he set before my feet the lamp of his word [Note: [Col. 0199] Psalm 118:105], so that the night of my foolishness may be illumined like day [Col. 0200C] [Note: [Col. 0199] Psalm 138:12]. May he loosen my tongue for a good word, he who also opened the mouth of the she-ass [Note: [Col. 0199] Numbers 22:28] for human speech. For I too am one of those stones or beasts, in prefiguration of whom the she-ass then spoke, signifying that the mute nature of gentile hardness and stupidity, once tongues had been loosed by God, would speak [Note: [Col. 0199] Luke 19:40].

And, if it pleases you, let us extend the text of this letter from this very grace of God, because all our [Note: [Col. 0200D] Thus the manuscripts of Reg. and Vien. and four printed editions; edition of Grin., “prayer.”] discourse ought to be occupied with the commandments and praises of the Most High. Everything we speak, everything we live, must be rendered to him with perpetual thanksgiving, by whose work and gift we speak and live. For he made us, and not we ourselves [Note: [Col. 0199] Psalm 99:3]. He, I say, the Lord made us, and he also remade us from the beginning through all that he accomplished and spoke in his saints, preparing the mysteries of our salvation—that is, of the restoration of humanity.

For through the holy generation in Seth he immediately restored the righteous Abel [Note: [Col. 0199] Genesis 4:25]; Seth, formed with a countenance like his father’s in the image of God, reproduced his father. From there, flowing onward through the others from the first fountain, the stream of righteousness spread. And although, when the flood intervened, the seed of the whole world that had perished remained in one man—yet in a righteous one—the mystery of the one Redeemer was already at work, so that reconciliation might come through one, since offense had come through many [Note: [Col. 0201] Genesis 6:8 and 7:1; 2 Peter 2:5].

But when righteousness again declined in the progress of the human race, and nations and crimes increased together, lest the wickedness of the human race should once more deserve destruction, another was chosen to be called the father of faith, from whom both the promise of the kingdom and the seed of the eternal King would arise. Christ fulfilled this promise, multiplied through the faith of the nations: he was seen by the patriarchs, prefigured through the Law, foretold through the prophets, and himself appeared to fulfill the Law and the prophets, and to give through grace the healing which the Law had not been able to bestow through works [Note: [Col. 0201] Genesis 15:13; Romans 4:11; Galatians 3:7; James 2:21; Matthew 5:17; John 1:17].

3. For sin had already pervaded the whole body—that is, the entire human race [Col. 0201B] [Note: [Col. 0201D] Thus the manuscript of Reg. and four editions. Edition of Rosv., “the human race.” The reading we have restored is entirely correct, as will be clear to anyone who pays attention to what precedes and follows.]—so thoroughly that neither a poultice for the weak and wounded nor a bandage was of any use [Note: [Col. 0201] Wisdom 16:12]. For when the illness of vices had grown strong, a disease more powerful than remedies had excluded every treatment human aid could provide. Therefore he came—the one who is also to come—conformed to the body of our lowliness, so that he might conform us to the body of his glory [Note: [Col. 0201] Revelation 1:4; Philippians 3:21]. For no one except the craftsman has power over his work, and only the potter has authority over his clay [Note: [Col. 0201] Wisdom 15:7; Sirach 33:13; Jeremiah 18:6; Romans 9:21].

Thus the Lord of all, who had made everyone, deigned to descend to our condition and receive us into his body, so that he might remake us by the same art—or power [the source reads *vel*, “or,” in place of *et*, “and”]—by which he had made us. He came not in the sublimity of the Lord, which he was, but in the form of a servant, which he was not [Note: [Col. 0201] Philippians 2:7]. He who is the power of God and Lord of hosts, the helper and protector of all, became like a man without help [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 87:5]. He died for the sake of those who were to be liberated, although he was free among the dead. He was counted among the unrighteous, although he justifies the ungodly through faith. Like a sheep led to slaughter, that Lamb was led who takes away the sins of the world [Note: [Col. 0201] Isaiah 53:7, 12; 1 Peter 2:24; John 1:29]. He suffered death who grants eternity.

4. But in the cause of so great a plan and gift, it is the light of the one who illumines us from the eternal mountains that we must discern [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 75:5]. With eyes lifted toward them, let us see that we, by the very paths on which we had perished, have again been found: again from a tree, again from a virgin—but not again to be cast down by pride; rather, on the contrary, to return through humility.

For this reason the King of glory and Lord of majesty emptied himself, taking the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0201] Philippians 2:7], and covered his invisible greatness with visible abasement, so that he might raise us—outwardly lofty but inwardly crushed by that old disease of wrongly conceived arrogance—into the form of his exaltation by the pattern of our humility in him.

For in this the good Lord worked and works daily [Col. 0202A], so that we may attain the glory of divine conformity, if we follow the example of our conformity to Christ, recognizing that the measure of our nature has been tempered by the governance of the Most High. Thus we may be raised above ourselves by his grace, if we walk beside ourselves mindful of our own condition.

The prophetic word from Numbers sets us within this measure when it says: “We shall not turn aside to the right or to the left, but shall go by the royal road” [Note: [Col. 0201] Numbers 21:22; Deuteronomy 2:27]. This royal road is Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, tempering us between the divine and the human and leading us by the royal road to his kingdom. Thus, humble in heart but exalted in deed, we may be lifted away from the left—that is, from sins that drag us to death—and, recalled from excessive right-hand deviations—that is, from proud presumption—by the law of humility, may hold to a salutary middle course.

Otherwise, by lowering our eyes toward the earth [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 16:11], we may be compared with beasts that have no understanding [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 31:9]; or, by searching out things too high for us [Note: [Col. 0201] Sirach 3:22], we may become empty in our thoughts. Therefore, let us not be wise in lofty matters, but associate with the humble [Note: [Col. 0201] Romans 12:16]. Let us measure ourselves by the measure with which the Lord has measured us [Note: [Col. 0201] 2 Corinthians 10:13], so that we may be confined within ourselves and enlarged in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0201] 2 Corinthians 6:11].

Let us not be like those wise men of this age, whose wisdom the Lord rejected and destroyed, and whom through the folly of preaching he excluded [Note: [Col. 0201D] Manuscript Reg. and editions of Bad., Grav., and Schot.: “exhausted.”] [Note: [Col. 0201] 1 Corinthians 1:21] [Note: [Col. 0202D] Thus the Roman Psalter and Saint Hilary in his commentary on the Psalms]. “For,” he says, “they deliberated in order to hide snares” [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 63:6]. For evidently the whole art of philosophers labors at this: to obscure the light of truth by the assertion of fabrications, to entangle minds drawn away from the truth in the snares of empty disputes, to deceive them by the fraud of intellect, and to mislead them by the cosmetic of speech.

[Col. 0202C] 5. But after the light had arisen in the darkness, the merciful, compassionate, and righteous Lord [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 111:4], those who set their mouths against heaven in vain [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 72:9]—though ignorant even of earthly things and of their own nature—searched out the regions of the heavens [Note: [Col. 0202D] Thus the Vatican manuscript and the Latin text. Other codices: “they scrutinize.”], and sought God without God.

Therefore they failed, searching with scrutiny, and the arrows of children became their wounds [Note: [Col. 0201] Psalm 63:7–8]. For the Lord, who catches the wise in their own cunning [Note: [Col. 0201] 1 Corinthians 3:20], confounded them through the mouths of infants and sucklings. He established his kingdom not in speech but in power.

Hence I too, the least of all the Lord’s least ones, the most insignificant of the insignificant, and the most infantile of infants, dare to burst forth into a voice of praise [Note: [Col. 0202D] The word “his” is absent from the printed editions], giving thanks to the Most High Lord, because he has revealed to his little ones the mystery of the lofty devotion that he had stored up in the treasuries of his wisdom, and has hidden it from the wise of the world [Note: [Col. 0201] Matthew 11:25]. Thus this world would not glory in the vanity of its wise men, through which, darkness having been cast over it, it had not recognized the wisdom of God.

But Jesus, our peace, who came to make the two one [Note: [Col. 0203] Ephesians 2:14] and to establish all things in equality, destroyed the strong and chose the weak; he rejected the wise and assumed the foolish, so that there might be equality [Note: [Col. 0203] 2 Corinthians 8:14]. Thus there might be equality, with no one claiming anything as his own [Note: [Col. 0203D] We have added this word from the Vatican and Vien. manuscripts and the edition of Grin.], since every human being, possessing salvation and wisdom only through the divine gift, necessarily had to glory in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0203] 1 Corinthians 1:31].

Therefore let us rejoice with trembling in the Lord our God [Note: [Col. 0203] Psalm 2:11], who is humble in heart and exalted in majesty [Note: [Col. 0203] Matthew 11:29]. Let us have the same mind among ourselves as was in Christ [Note: [Col. 0203] Philippians 2:5]. As I said above, he bestowed on us the grace of salvation through the pattern of humility so that we, who had deserved to fall through the spirit of exaltation, might learn to rise again through humility of heart [Note: [Col. 0203D] Thus the Vatican manuscript. Other copies: “through a heart of humility.” The reading restored here is confirmed twice below, in section 8].

6. But the fact that the good Lord was crucified and rose again worked not only for the destruction of our death and the restoration of eternity, but also for the instruction of the present life, in which we acquire the merit by which possession of that eternally blessed life is prepared [Note: [Col. 0203] Romans 6:4; 1 Corinthians 6:14; 2 Corinthians 5:15; Colossians 3:1].

The Lord was therefore fastened to the cross. The Apostle teaches the mystery and plan of this devotion [Note: [Col. 0203] Ephesians 2:14]: “so that,” he says, “he might break down the dividing wall, destroy enmity, strip away the whole circuit of this world, and, taking captivity captive, triumph over the entire power of the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0203] Psalm 67:19; Ephesians 4:8]. He took upon himself, he says, “the likeness of sinful flesh” [Note: [Col. 0203] Romans 8:3]—not, certainly, the likeness of flesh, since God is truth in all things; and therefore the Word truly and bodily became flesh [Note: [Col. 0203] John 1:14]—but “in the likeness of the flesh of sin” [Note: [Col. 0203] Romans 8:3].

Thus, although he committed no sin through his inviolable and impassible nature, for our sake he nevertheless, as it is written, was made sin [Note: [Col. 0203D] Editions of Schot. and Sacchin.; other codices: “making sin.” The restored reading is confirmed by Letter 37, section 2], that is, he bore the sinner received in the form of a servant. He was made a curse for us so that he might release us from the curse of the Law [Note: [Col. 0203] Galatians 3:13]. “He condemned sin because of sin” [Note: [Col. 0203] Romans 8:3]—that is, he emptied out in that very flesh of Adam which he deigned to assume the material of sin that still lived in Adam’s flesh.

And so, destroying the dividing wall—that is, sin, which separated us from God—he made the two one [Note: [Col. 0203] Ephesians 2:14], not only so that the faith of Jews and gentiles might unite in Christ, but so that, in each one of us who believe, our nature might be reconciled with itself, and the discord formerly present within us, when the carnal soul resisted the spiritual inclination, might be dissolved by the peace of faith.

For now that ancient war, in which the law of sin resisted the law of God, is abolished in Christ [Note: [Col. 0203] Romans 7:21]. The spirit, serving God, disciplines the soul that has been subjected to it by faith, while, in turn, the flesh accompanying the soul that serves God ministers to it in every obedience.

7. For this reason, through the Lord’s passion and resurrection, we are instructed not only in the hope and faith of resurrection, [Note: [Col. 0203D] The word “but” is absent from the manuscript of Reg. and four editions] but also to know how to die not merely by the carnal dissolution of this life, but by a voluntary departure from this world; and, by dying to this world through faith, to be made alive to God.

For the life that loves this world is the death of the soul. Therefore the Apostle says to us: “Put to death your members on earth” [Note: [Col. 0203] Colossians 3:5]. He testifies that he himself dies daily, bruising his body, forgetting what lies behind, and stretching himself toward what lies ahead [Note: [Col. 0203] 1 Corinthians 9:27; Philippians 3:13].

In this he teaches both humility and exaltation. For the body cannot be crushed without the spirit of humility, nor can the soul rise to heavenly things without the mortification of the members. Yet even in humility we must preserve the proper measure, so that we humble ourselves to the one Lord only through divine fear: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” [Note: [Col. 0203] Deuteronomy 6:13 and 10:20; Matthew 4:7; Luke 4:8]. To serve him is freedom. For no one is subject to another who has subjected himself to God alone [Note: [Col. 0203] Romans 8:20].

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Thus the Vatican manuscript. Other copies: “But.”] Conversely, whoever wishes to be free from righteousness serves every lowly thing—whether spirits, other creatures, or his own vices and desires.

There is also a holy pride and an ungodly humility. For that pride which takes pride against this world, despises this age, and refuses to make use of all its greatness, sweetness, and beauty [that is, refuses to use them; see note 31], while intent on heavenly matters and subject to divine commands, is justified. But that humility is condemned which arises not from faith but from weakness of mind, which is brought before human beings [Col. 0204C] and cares more for human approval than for its own salvation: a servant of falsehood, an enemy of truth, deprived of freedom, subject to wickedness, mixing [Note: [Col. 0204D] The manuscripts of Vien. and Reg.: “water with wine.” The Latin text: “the force of water of flattery.”] water with wine [Note: [Col. 0203] Isaiah 1:22], that is, weakening the pure wine of truth [Note: [Col. 0204D] Thus the Vatican manuscript and the edition of Rosv. The manuscript of Reg. and four editions: “waters of flattery.”] with the watery substance of flattery.

It is especially against this sort of humility, it seems to me, that the saying is directed which pronounces woe on those who call evil good and bitter sweet [Note: [Col. 0204D] Thus the manuscripts of Reg. and Vien. with four editions. The Vatican manuscript and the edition of Grin., following the Vulgate and the Septuagint version, read: “calling evil good, sweet bitter, and proclaiming injustice to be justice.”] [Note: [Col. 0203] Isaiah 5:20], and who proclaim justice for the unjust. As you know, Truth also condemns such people through Solomon.

8. The blessed Psalmist rightly shapes us toward the balance of our proper moderation in a brief psalm, but one full of instruction, when in his prayers he sets forth the merit of humility [Note: [Col. 0203] Sirach 19:23], saying: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up. I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me” [Note: [Col. 0203] Psalm 130:1].

Then, having asked to be regarded because of the humility of his heart [Note: [Col. 0204D] Thus the manuscript of Regius. Other codices: “before”], he says: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul: as a child weaned from its mother, so you will requite my soul” [Note: [Col. 0205D] Thus the Septuagint, the old Greek Psalter, the Roman Psalter, Saint Hilary, and Saint Augustine in his commentary on the Psalms, as well as all printed and manuscript codices except Vien., which reads “upon his mother,” with the resulting interpretation found in the Vulgate] [Note: [Col. 0205D] Thus the Roman Psalter, the Septuagint, Saint Hilary, and, not much differently, Ambrose] [Note: [Col. 0205] Psalm 130:2, according to the Septuagint].

He asks for recompense because he did not think humbly but exalted his soul. Does the Prophet’s statement not seem to contradict itself unless we distinguish these things in understanding as they were distinguished in his own spirit and heart, so that they correspond to one another?

It was fittingly and humbly said in the fear of God, since he offered God, as he himself testifies, “a contrite spirit and a humbled heart” [Note: [Col. 0205] Psalm 50:19]. Yet, while preserving humility of heart, he also exalted his soul, not thinking humbly; for he did not set his mind on earthly matters, but had his mind fixed on God, considering it the one good to cling to God and to place his hope in God [Note: [Col. 0205] Psalm 72:28].

Hence the Apostle, who teaches us humility [Note: [Col. 0205D] We have removed the word “saying,” which is absent from the Vatican manuscript, appropriately], so that we may strive above all to be imitators of Christ, says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ, who did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0205] Philippians 2:5]. Yet the same Apostle urges us to exalt the soul toward heavenly and divine things when he says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, at the right hand and in the glory of God the Father” [Note: [Col. 0205] Colossians 3:1].

9. Therefore, holding to this rule both of humility and of exaltation, let us preserve each in its proper order and measure with devotion—for each, in the perversity I mentioned above, involves sin, but in the right direction in which we are instructed receives grace. Let us humble our hearts before God and exalt our souls toward the Lord our God. Let us fear nothing except him and love nothing above him.

Let us submit our necks only to his yoke, which is easy, and to his burden, which is light [Note: [Col. 0205] Matthew 11:29], so that, freed from every yoke of hostile power, we may be carried upward into heavenly things. For the yoke of our Lord is easy and his burden light for this reason also: because he raises us from earthly and infernal things [Note: [Col. 0205D] Thus the manuscripts of Reg. and Vatic. Other copies: “raises”] and lifts us to the heights of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0206A]. Every light thing, after all, seeks the heights and is borne upward by the vigor of its subtlety.

10. But the weights of sin, contrary to this grace, press us down and lead us into the lower regions. The weight of these things is testified by the Prophet when he cries out with a groan: “My iniquities have been piled upon my head, and like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me” [Note: [Col. 0206D] Thus the Roman Psalter, Saint Ambrose, and Paulinus, Letter 40, section 4] [Note: [Col. 0205] Psalm 37:5, according to the Roman Psalter].

But thanks be to the Lord Jesus our God, who is able to free us from this body of death [Note: [Col. 0205] Romans 7:24] through the abundance of his mercies [Note: [Col. 0205] Psalm 50:3] and the riches of his goodness [Note: [Col. 0205] Romans 2:4], by which he abounds beyond the abundance of our sins [Col. 0206A], and saves those who hope in him [Note: [Col. 0205] Psalm 16:7].

We believe that, with him, the watches of your prayers are also being kept for us. For we know that, having served him from childhood [Note: [Col. 0206D] It seemed natural to correct this according to the Vatican manuscript to “ministering”; Paulinus appears to have had in mind the Apostle’s passage in 1 Timothy 4: “You will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of faith.”] and having been nourished on the sacred writings, untouched by any stain of earthly conduct and [Note: [Col. 0206D] Thus the manuscripts of Reg. and Vien. with three editions. Other copies: “of the flesh.”] flesh, you found grace in the sight of the Most High.

For us, caught late from the forest of this age for the Lord’s flock or chariot, because our iniquities have multiplied beyond the hairs of our head [Note: [Col. 0205] Psalm 39:13], and we are unworthy for our names to be brought before divine ears, Otherwise your lips might become unclean when you name us [Note: [Col. 0205] Isaiah 6:5], and it might be necessary for your mouth to be touched with a fiery coal [Is the reading “reached” instead?]. Yet, whether in the humility or the confidence of the ancient prophet, you can say: “Lord, forgive them,” or “Blot me out of your book” [Note: [Col. 0205] Exodus 32:32].

He, sharing in divine conversation, neither neglecting his own salvation nor presumptuous before the Lord, dared to say this through profound skill in counsel, so that, when the just Lord threatened the sinful people with the death they deserved, he might offer his own destruction instead. Secure, evidently, in the justice of divine compassion, he sought that the Lord’s mercy should spare the unjust, while justice could not erase the just man.

11. By this same condition, constrain the Most High Lord on our behalf: while he cannot remove you from his book, may he receive the unjust through the intercession of his just servant. For since the one who is in us is greater than the one who is in this world [Note: [Col. 0205] 1 John 4:4], justice is stronger in defending sinners than iniquity is against the patronage of the saints.

I would like, as far as I can, to prolong my discourse further, were I not compelled by the failing paper and by fear of your weariness to set a limit to my words and bring the letter to an end. In all things, pardon my boldness, and answer me, so that I may be comforted and instructed by your letters.

12. Now we commend Sanemarius, the bearer of this letter [Col. 0206D] [Note: [Col. 0206D] We have corrected this from the manuscripts. It previously read “Marius, certainly.”], to your fellowship in a special manner, so that he may be placed in an appropriate position by you, just as we asked our holy bishop and father.

We have restored him as our fellow servant, having granted him freedom in the Lord. But let him serve you in the house of the Lord through the duties assigned to him in memory of our parents, so that through religious service he may deserve to obtain firm freedom under your protection.

Also approach the holy presbyter, our brother Exsuperius, so that he may receive from the Church’s estate a small plot of land on which to provide his livelihood. Furthermore, I ask that you arrange without any delay for my letter to our son Daducius, even if he is living in Gaul, to be sent by a faithful and diligent fellow servant from the bishop.

If he should perhaps be unwilling to employ a cleric, be so kind as to send one of the men of Alingon with your letters, by which our letter may be supported. From the letter I wrote to him you will learn that the matter is worthy of your intervention. Above all, speed is necessary, so that the most holy presbyter, who bears the burden I have described, venerable both in life and in age, may be freed as soon as possible from exile in other people’s houses.

## LETTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 0207D] Elsewhere numbered 37 and 33, part 2; the letter formerly numbered 13 is now 17. Written toward the end of the year 397.]

Paulina, the daughter of the holy Paula, had married Pammachius, a proconsular man, as Palladius says in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 122—or rather, according to Jerome, Letter 26, the great-grandson of consuls. When she died while still in the flower of youth, Pammachius mourned her with many tears and sought consolation through the most generous almsgiving to the poor. Paulinus both consoles and commends him under both aspects, repeatedly interweaving praise of the dead woman.

To his most beloved brother, deservedly worthy of praise and most venerable, Pammachius [Note: [Col. 0207D] Edition of Chiffl.: “To the Lord Pammachius, deservedly worthy of praise and honorable brother,”], Paulinus.

1. Just as until now I have kept the time for silence with fitting humility, so now I have recognized the time for speaking demanded by love, venerable and most beloved brother in Christ the Lord.

Recently I received from the writings of the holy man, our brother Olympius, our common friend [Note: [Col. 0207D] Thus the manuscript of Regius. Other codices add “bishop,” but without reason. See *Life*, chapter 32, section 1], news of your grief, as unexpected for me as it was unwished-for. In this matter, love would not permit me to withhold from you my fellowship in sorrow and the service of my voice [Col. 0207C] [Note: [Col. 0207D] We have added “then” and “but” from the manuscript of Reg. and the edition of Chiffl.], so that the feelings of private affection might fall silent; for the love of Christ our Lord and God, because in him and through him we are joined as members of one body, would not allow it.

For the Lord our God, who is equally our teacher of life and devotion, taught us through that heavenly vessel of his election to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep [Note: [Col. 0207] Romans 12:15], to sympathize with one another in turn, and to bear one another’s burdens. Thus, through mutual consolations, we might strengthen our common faith and warm hearts wearied by suffering.

God gave such value to this service that he promised to enlarge the one who performed it like a great city, declaring through the Prophet: “A brother who helps his brother will be exalted like a great city” [Note: [Col. 0207] Proverbs 18:19]—namely, because brotherly compassion brings protection to the soul in combat and, like a wall, resists the various blows of an afflicted mind.

2. But if perhaps it should be judged a fault rather than a grace that I have performed the duty of love late, please believe that I wrote as soon as I learned of it. Nor should I seem to have heard of your misfortune late through negligence, since both the remoteness of my location and the character of my undertaking defend me [Note: [Col. 0208D] Thus the manuscript of Reg. and the edition of Chiffl. Previously: “Nor should I seem to have heard late through my negligence of you.”].

Living in seclusion and silence, I can see only a few passersby, and I do not wish to ask about the holy brothers unless they are close to me. Yet I have always remembered you even in my silence. Now, when love seemed to demand it, I opened the affection hidden in my heart and expressed it through this letter to you, by which I have traveled by whatever path I could to your holy fellowship.

For I could not keep my body and my spirit within the same boundaries: my flesh, as always, weak during winter, refused to be moved farther away, while my spirit, always more ready, flew to you with burning desires [Note: [Col. 0207] Matthew 26:41], so that I might embrace in mind the one whom I could not hold bodily.

Thus, in the thirst of my longing, I ran to you [Note: [Col. 0207] Psalm 61:5], my brother, united and venerable in Christ. If you in turn look upon me in spirit, you will see and feel that I am wholly with you. For if it is true that we see and hear one another more through perception than through the senses, I am certainly present to you—and in the better part of myself—since I have come to you in spirit.

Unless we are present in this way, even when we are present in body, we do not prove our presence; our image is empty, while the mind is absent [Note: [Col. 0208D] Thus the manuscript of Reg. and the edition of Chiffl. Other copies: “so that we may be present…”].

Therefore I have offered a sealed gift of friendship [Note: [Col. 0208D] We have restored this from the manuscript of Reg. and the edition of Chiffl. Elsewhere: “a worthy gift.”], and have made it suitable to our faith, so that I might visit you by a spiritual entrance.

I ask that I may in turn deserve this favor from you: that, seeing me with your inward eyes, as though standing close by, speaking face to face and breathing alongside you in the anxiety we share, or congratulating you in the hope of faith upon your patience, you may receive and behold me as present in this discourse.

For a man’s speech is a mirror of his mind. The word of God itself confirms this, saying that “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart,” and that the treasure of the breast is made public through speech [Note: [Col. 0207] Matthew 12:34; Luke 6:45].

Therefore, in the truth in which we stand in Christ, receive through this letter the expression of my heart. Nor do I want you to measure our friendship by time. For this is not the kind that belongs to the world, which is more often begotten by hope than by faith; it is the spiritual kind, generated by God as its author and growing through the secret kinship of spirits.

Consequently, it does not grow toward love through long acquaintance, nor does it depend upon waiting for proof; rather, as is fitting for a daughter of truth, it is recognized at once as firm and great, because, born through Christ, it begins from fullness.

3. Embracing you, therefore, with this love, I venerate you as a member of Christ and love you as a member of myself. For how could those have anything but one mind who have one faith? How could those have anything but one spirit who have one God? And therefore how could their hearts differ in enduring affection when they are one body in the structure of belief?

I speak truly and do not lie: when I consider the movements of your soul, I feel my own inward parts also drawn along by your sighs and, as truly associated members, pierced by the pain of your wound. Yet the reflection upon your prudence and faith restores me no less than the concern for your grief afflicts me.

Indeed, I confess that I hesitated over whether I should offer words sorrowful in keeping with my affection for you, or rather words of congratulation in keeping with your faith. For I heard both of the calling of my holy sister to God and of your devoted piety in Christ. The head of the household through whom I wrote also reported your prudence and the holiness of your true love for your wife, Paulina.

You did not accompany her, as most mortals do, with tears alone, nor, as those without the hope of our faith are accustomed, with the empty honor of vain displays; rather, you followed her with salutary remedies and living works—that is, almsgiving [Note: [Col. 0209D] Thus the edition of Chiffl. Very appropriately; see note 91]. First paying the proper obligations of the flesh to the funeral rites, you honored the pious burial, drenched with devout tears and the abundant dew of love [Note: [Col. 0209D] Manuscript of Reg. and editions of Bad. and Grav.: “more religiously.”].

4. Therefore I shall first praise the work of this devotion in you. Scripture also shows that this is pleasing to God when it says: “My son, pour out tears for the dead, and, as though you had suffered terrible things, begin to mourn, and do not neglect his burial” [Note: [Col. 0209] Sirach 38:16].

Our patriarchs likewise provide examples of this religious observance. For our father in faith wept for Sarah, the mother of our calling [Note: [Col. 0209] Genesis 23:2], not from disbelief that she would be restored, but from longing for one who had gone before. For how could the father of faith and the first hearer of the blessed promise doubt the resurrection?

Yet, mindful of human nature, he did not neglect care for the body on account of the soul’s security. He purchased a field for a tomb and placed his dead wife in a costly resting place [Note: [Col. 0209] Genesis 23:9], teaching at the same time what such men—perhaps “the just,” as some suggest—ought to provide for themselves.

He who had gone forth from his native land and kin at the word of God [Note: [Col. 0209] Genesis 12:1], and had acquired nothing else from the regions he had traversed among foreign peoples, a stranger throughout the whole earth, nevertheless bought a single field for a tomb—that is, not a temporal but an eternal possession, not land for greed but for rest.

Jacob likewise honored his beloved and long-awaited Rachel with a celebrated tomb [Note: [Col. 0209] Genesis 35:19–20] and with an inscription—that is, an epitaph—in order both to discharge a religious duty toward his present grief and to testify to it for posterity.

Yet, with prophetic insight, he marked that place with an inscription of his wife’s death, foreseeing that the Law would be put to sleep by the birth of the Gospel. Through this mystery, the Patriarch’s wife, who in many places lived as an image of the Church, nevertheless, as I believe, dies as a type of the Synagogue and gives birth to a son of sorrow at the very place where, through the Virgin’s childbirth, an end was to be given to the Law. For Christ is the end of the Law [Note: [Col. 0209] Romans 10:4].

Tobit, moreover, teaches us a holy and sanctified hope through the care of burial. He was specially justified by the Lord and praised by the voice of the archangel because he had placed the burial of a poor man before his own meal [Note: [Col. 0209] Tobit 12:12]. Neglectful of his belly because he was attentive to his soul, he preferred to be hungry in body rather than in spirit, so that he might also be an example to us, teaching us to choose to fast from food for the flesh in order to bestow nourishment upon the soul.

Therefore, the religious observance of burial is good. Good are the tears of love, in which father Abraham led forth the mother of the promise. Good are the tears of devotion which righteous Joseph shed for his father [Note: [Col. 0209] Genesis 50:1]. Good also are the tears of prayer with which David watered his bed each night [Note: [Col. 0209] Psalm 6:7].

But why should I praise the tears of holy mortals? Jesus also wept for his friend [Note: [Col. 0209] John 11:35], deigning to take upon himself this sorrow from our misery, so that he might pour out tears for the dead man [Note: [Col. 0209D] Manuscript of Reg.: “shed”], and mourn with human weakness the one whom he was about to raise by divine power. Yet in that one man the merciful and compassionate Lord also lamented the entire condition of the human race, and with those tears wept for and washed away our sins [Note: [Col. 0209D] Thus the manuscript of Reg. and the edition of Chiffl. Previously: “and with those tears he wept for and washed away our sins.”].

5. Therefore your tears too, brother, are holy and devout, because they flowed from a similar affection and wept for a worthy companion of the chaste marriage bed—not from disbelief in the resurrection, but from the longing of love.

A beloved woman arouses glory in her husband when she is held by him [Note: [Col. 0209] Proverbs 11:16; Sirach 26:16], and therefore she also arouses longing when she is sent ahead. But she, as she always was, so will she remain forever a crown for her husband [Note: [Col. 0209] Wisdom 4:2; Proverbs 11:4], and her lamp will be extinguished at night [Note: [Col. 0209] Proverbs 31:18].

For, as it is written, she extended her arms toward useful works and opened her mouth wisely [Note: [Col. 0209] Proverbs 31:26]. She did good to her husband; she crowned you with glory and honor so that she might rejoice with you in the last days [Col. 0210C]. For this reason she is more worthy of tears [Note: [Col. 0209D] See note 10] than of mourning, and ought rather to be longed for steadfastly than lamented.

For the very reckoning of her merits, just as it imposes bitter grief upon the survivor because the righteous dead leave behind repentance, also provides abundant consolation to the faithful, because there is immortality in the memory of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0209] Wisdom 4:1].

Nor should a sharper sting of grief be inflicted upon you, holy brother, by the fact that she died in the first flower of life, since the divine word itself offers consolation for this very circumstance: “For if the righteous person is overtaken by death, he will be in refreshment” [Note: [Col. 0209] Wisdom 4:7].

### 6.

But lest she seem to you to have died prematurely, the same Wisdom proves to you in the words that follow that she was also an old woman:

> “Old age,” it says, “is honorable not because of long duration, nor reckoned by number of years. For,” it says, “gray hairs are understanding in human beings [Note: [Col. 0210D] Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. Paulinus has elevated *hominibus* (“for human beings”) in Greek fashion; the Greek has ἀνθρώποις (“for human beings”). The Vulgate has *hominis* (“of a human being”).], and the age of old age is an unblemished life.”

Therefore let us congratulate her on her deserved summons and mature end [Note: [Col. 0210D] Thus the Regius manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. Others read *accitui et fini* (“summons and end”).], who, although she was still green with the flower of her years, had nevertheless grown gray through the holiness of her conduct and adorned a girl’s age with the services of old age.

Thus even the very circumstances that wounded your spirit can bring you greater consolation: although you no longer possess such a holy woman, you have possessed her. It is common to you with everyone to have lost a mortal person; but it is granted to few, together with you, to have merited an excellent one. I am therefore less surprised that she did not remain long in this world and was summoned more quickly to Christ. For her soul was pleasing to God; and therefore, as it is written, he hastened to lead her out of the midst of iniquity, lest our malice change our understanding [Note: [Col. 0211] Wisdom IV, 14 and 11.]. For this whole world, as it is written, lies in the evil one [Note: [Col. 0211] 1 John V, 19.]; evil conversations frequently corrupt good morals [Note: [Col. 0211] 1 Corinthians XV, 33.]; and “whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0211] Sirach XIII, 1.].

Fearing delay on this account, and anxious about a prolonged end [Note: [Col. 0211D] We have emended the text from the margin of Grin’s edition. Previously it read *sene*, which made no sense.], a certain holy man prays to God to make known to him his end and the number of his days [Note: [Col. 0211] Psalm XXXVIII, 5.]. And when, through the revelation of the Spirit by whom he prophesied, he learned that his time had been prolonged, he groaned, saying:

> “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged!” [Note: [Col. 0211] Psalm CXIX, 5, according to the Roman Psalter.]

He testifies that this was the cause of his groaning and fear: that he dwelt [Note: [Col. 0211D] Saint Augustine, in his Commentary on the Psalms, says: “Cedar,” as far as we remember from the interpretation of Hebrew names, means “darkness.” The Vulgate has *I dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar*, contrary to all our manuscripts and printed books.] among the tents of Cedar—that is, in the darkness of this world. For *Cedar* in Hebrew is what in Roman speech is called *Obscurity*.

### 7.

Finally, David himself enacted the mystery of this truth in the case of two sons whom he lost, though they had different merits. He did not mourn the death of his beloved infant son, for whom he had wept while the child was ill, being certain that the infant had been transferred to the blessedness of eternal peace [Note: [Col. 0211] 2 Samuel XII, 22.]. But he lamented the dead Absalom, whom he had regarded as an enemy, because, conscious as a prophet of divine justice, he despaired of rest for the wicked and knew that the good of resurrection was not owed to a parricide.

Yet, as I have said, he had shed tears for that little son of his while the child was ill; he had exchanged royal clothing for black garments, supported himself with sackcloth, ashes, and fasting [Note: [Col. 0212D] Thus in the Regius manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. Previously it read *fletu* (“weeping”). Schott’s edition has *fultus* (“supported”).], and sent prayers to God. But after the illness of his son was ended by death, as though the subject of his anxieties had disappeared, he brought his mourning to the same end that the child had reached in living. Thus, when the son had been released from the body and the father from mourning, he simultaneously laid aside his sorrowful heart and clothing, ate food, resumed his customary dress, and brought his dust-covered head back under oil. When his servants asked him—astonished by this wholly unusual order of paternal affection, that the man who had mourned before bereavement should rejoice after bereavement—he replied:

> “I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.” [Note: [Col. 0211] 2 Samuel XII, 23.]

### 8.
