The Prophet-King, as I think, taught sufficiently what concern we ought to assume after the death of our loved ones: namely, that we should be troubled more about our own journey, on which we are following [Note: [Col. 0211D] Sacchini suggests *qui* (“which”) rather than *quo* (“on which”).], than about theirs, since they have already gone ahead and arrived.

It is pious to grieve over the removal of those we love; but it is holy to rejoice in hope and faith in God’s promises, and to say to the suffering soul:

> “Why are you sad, and why do you trouble me?” [Note: [Col. 0211] Psalm XLI, 6.]

Surely, “will not one who sleeps rise again?” [Note: [Col. 0211] Psalm XL, 9.]

A grateful joy is more acceptable to God than a prolonged sadness resembling complaint. For we are taught this by David’s example: we should not pour out empty tears. Such tears are indeed given uselessly to the dead, contributing nothing to one who has been taken away and burdening the one who remains.

Therefore David wept while his son was alive, but gave thanks when he had died, because while the child was still breathing he could obtain his departure [Note: See note 64.] through prayers and tears; but once the child had been summoned by God, he ought to give thanks, as he did, since there is no doubt that what pleases God is better than our petitions.

### 9.

Therefore, while preserving faith, let us pay the duties of affection; and while preserving affection, let us prefer the joys of faith. Let affection weep for a time, but faith ought to rejoice continually. Let us desire our loved ones as those who have gone before us, but let us not despair of receiving them again.

For our God is the God of the living, not of the dead [Note: [Col. 0211] Matthew XXII, 32.]. The Apostle says that the dead sleep in Christ [Note: [Col. 0211] 1 Corinthians XV, 18; 1 Thessalonians IV, 12.], so that you may understand death as a temporary sleep. For one who sleeps, awakening and rising follow naturally.

Since this is so, let us retain in love the longing born of familiar association with our loved ones, but let us draw consolation from our faith in the hope of resurrection.

### 10.

Therefore, dearest brother, just as you have used the authority of heavenly words and examples for the proper exercise of tears, so use it also to regulate them. For it is written:

> “There is a time for everything” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ecclesiastes III, 1, according to the Septuagint.];

and when the time for weeping has passed, the time for giving thanks has arrived.

Because the Lord is near, and divine Scripture, which permits us to draw out our tears as though evaporating our grief, also sets limits by prescribing a fixed time, it says that the bitterness [Note: See note 33.] of mourning is to be endured for one day [Note: [Col. 0211] Sirach XXXVIII, 15.].

O the riches of God’s goodness! How tenderly he guards us in this very matter! He is not grudging toward devoted affection, but conscious of our weakness and the regulator of every excess. He commands that tears be prolonged for the dead, but confines the bitterness of mourning to one day. He allows what eases grief and gives the soul room to breathe to continue; but he cuts short what wears down our mind with excessive and irrational torment, and what our frailty cannot endure for long.

But God’s own compassion explains this more fully in its own words. It adds:

> “And console yourself promptly because of your sorrow. For death hastens because of sorrow, and it will cover strength” [Note: [Col. 0211] Sirach XXXVIII, 19.].

For only that sorrow which is according to God is salutary. But the sorrow that is “according to human beings,” as the Apostle says—that is, carnal sorrow arising from weakness [Note: [Col. 0213D] The word *est* (“is”) was deleted on the basis of the Regius manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. We append the other part of the letter, which in some printed and manuscript books was addressed to Alethius under the same wording as Letter 33. See Dissertation 1, no. 13.]—produces death [Note: [Col. 0213] 2 Corinthians VII, 10.].

Although the author is different, Scripture agrees through both passages by the one Spirit and word of God: for true death is the covering-over of strength [Note: [Col. 0213D] Thus in the Viennese manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. Other manuscripts add *animae* (“of the soul”), which is of little relevance here.]. For if Christ is God’s strength and our life, you see that it is truly said that death hastens through that grief by which strength is covered [Note: [Col. 0213] 1 Corinthians I, 24; Psalm XLIII, 20; Colossians III, 4.]. The whole person is swallowed up, as it were by a gulf of hell, in an even heavier sorrow, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0213] 2 Corinthians II, 7.].

But thanks be to God, for my consciousness of your virtue and prudence shortens for me the burden and fear of this labor on your behalf. The light within you is too abundant to be covered by the darkness of sorrow. Rather, your virtue covers your sorrow more abundantly and swallows death itself and the force of harmful grief [Note: [Col. 0213D] This word, *tristitiam* (“sorrow”), has been added from the Regius manuscript and Chifflet’s edition.].

I do not grant this to you by my words, nor do I speak from conjecture about your virtue. Your works testify to this concerning you, and compel me to speak of what I know.

### 11.

For I shall now come to the praise of your works and turn from the holiness of tears to your acts of piety. You have paid what was owed to each part: pouring out tears for the body, and pouring alms into the soul. Truly conscious of the truth and a child of light, you wept where you knew death to be; where you believe life to be, you acted [Note: [Col. 0213] See note 91.]. You gave emptiness to empty things, but living things to the living.

Thus, like a rich man in the Apostle’s hall, you gathered the poor—the patrons of our souls—who, many of them, make their living from alms throughout all Rome [Note: [Col. 0213D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition. Otherwise, *Roma* (“Rome”).] [Note: [Col. 0213D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. Others read *stipem* (“alms”).] [Note: [Col. 0213D] Thus the Viennese manuscript, Chifflet’s edition, and Sacchini. Previously the text read *multitudinem* (“multitude”).] [Note: [Col. 0214D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition. Otherwise, *aulam* (“hall”).]. I feed with pleasure on the beautiful spectacle of such a great work of yours.

For I seem to see all those devout throngs of the pitiable multitude, those nurslings of divine compassion, flowing in dense ranks into the vast basilica of blessed Peter through that venerable royal gate [Note: [Col. 0214D] Thus in the Vatican and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s and Rosweyde’s editions. The Regius manuscript, together with four printed editions, reads *reginam* (“queenly”). It is the principal gate of the Vatican basilica, royal or queenly. See note 34.], which smiles from afar with its blue façade [Note: [Col. 0214D] Thus in the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and three printed editions. The Vatican manuscript and Rosweyde’s edition have *cerulea* (“azure”).] [Note: [Col. 0214D] See note 34.], so that the spaces both inside the basilica, before the doors of the atrium, and along the steps and open ground are constricted.

I see them gathered and arranged in orderly groups on couches [Note: [Col. 0214D] See note 35.], all being filled with abundant food, so that before my eyes appears the abundance of evangelical blessing and the image of those peoples whom the true bread, and Christ the fish of living water [Note: [Col. 0214] See notes 36 and 37.], filled with five loaves and two fish [Note: [Col. 0213] Matthew XIV, 19; John VI, 11.].

He did not, according to ordinary practice, produce food for human beings from created things, but, by a new gift, generated food already prepared for human beings. His covered hand, through divine provision, supplied visible dishes, and spiritual fecundity poured forth into bodily nourishment. From ineffable springs of bread and flesh he satisfied the peoples who were still hungry for faith, in hope of the fasting nations: satisfying hungry peoples bodily and watering them spiritually; replenishing what had been eaten by untraceable increase; supplying what was to be eaten; and bringing forth pieces to be bitten by those eating [Note: [Col. 0214D] Thus in the Viennese manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. Grin’s edition has *subcisiva*. Other manuscripts have *subcitiva*.].

Thus, as the food increased in the hands or mouths of those receiving it, they perceived the abundance of their provisions more than they saw it: what had been consumed returning with each bite, and what was being eaten appearing again beneath their teeth.

### 12.

For in your work you bore the example of the Lord himself. You ordered the crowd to recline on the ground; for Jesus too, as we read, commanded them to recline on the ground [Note: [Col. 0213] Matthew XIV, 19; Mark VI, 39; Luke IX, 14; John VI, 10.].

For the Lord himself was in you, and is in you, since no one performs Christ’s works without Christ. By his gift and blessing, you measured out through countless mouths of the poor the abundant loaves that you had received in his name, just as the disciples had received from him the loaves blessed for distribution [Note: [Col. 0214D] Manuscripts and printed editions read *demensus es* (“you measured out”), except Rosweyde’s edition, which has *dimensus es*.]. They ate and were satisfied; and what remained of the loaves they all took away, each with his baskets full [Note: [Col. 0213] Matthew XV, 37; Mark VIII, 8.].

But you gathered all the surplus of the spiritual fragments: from the twelve baskets, apostolic faith; from the seven baskets, spiritual grace. Christ worked no less wondrously in your loaves, transforming the bodily bread at your banquet into heavenly foods and preparing eternal satiety for you.

For you rightly recline with the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob at Christ’s banquet, clothed in the wedding garment [Note: [Col. 0213] Matthew XXII, 12; Matthew VIII, 11.]. For Christ reclines there with you in his poor, and in you the Son of Man has a place to lay his head [Note: [Col. 0213] Matthew VIII, 20.].

### 13.

It is pleasing even now to linger over the spectacle and praise [Note: [Col. 0213] See note 37.] of so great a work. For we praise not human works, but divine works accomplished through a human being.

What a joyful spectacle of this work of yours, as it is commonly called, “a purse” [Note: [Col. 0213] See note 38.], you, the sacred provider, displayed before God and his holy angels [Note: [Col. 0213] 1 Corinthians IV, 9.]! How greatly you lifted the Apostle himself with joy when you filled his entire basilica with dense gatherings of the poor:

- both where, beneath the height of its roof, the broad expanse opens through the middle of its lofty ceilings, flashing from afar with the Apostolic throne [Note: [Col. 0214D] See note 39.], dazzling the eyes of those entering and gladdening their hearts;
- and where, beneath the same mass of roofing, it spreads its sides in twin porticoes on either side;
- and where it extends along the shining atrium [Note: [Col. 0214D] See note 40.] and is spread out before the vestibule.

There the cantharus, serving our hands and mouths [Note: [Col. 0214D] See note 41.], pours forth flowing water; a dome crowned with solid bronze adorns and shades it, while, with mystical significance, four columns encircle the leaping waters [Note: [Col. 0214D] See note 42.].

Such ornament befits the entrance of a church, so that what is accomplished within through the saving mystery may be signified by a visible work outside the doors. For the temple of our body is also sustained by the fourfold foundation of the one faith of the Gospel. Since grace, through which we are reborn, flows from it, and Christ, through whom we live, is revealed in it, surely that fountain of leaping water, springing up into eternal life, arises for us in the four columns of life [Note: [Col. 0215D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition read *illuc* (“there”).] [Note: [Col. 0215] John IV, 14.]. It waters us from within and burns within us—if only [Note: [Col. 0215D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. Others read *possimus* (“we can”).] we can say, or may be worthy to feel, that we have a heart burning on the way [Note: [Col. 0215] Luke XXIV, 32.], kindled by Christ walking with us [Note: [Col. 0215D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition. Previously the text read *ambulante inflammatur* (“is kindled while [Christ] walks”).].

### 14.

What a joyful spectacle, then, you offered at that time to God, the angels of peace, and all the spirits of the saints [Note: [Col. 0215] 1 Corinthians IV, 9.]!

First, you celebrated the Apostle’s veneration with a multiplied devotion of wealth, bringing sacred victims and chaste offerings to God together with the most welcome commemoration of the Apostle himself. Then, through the munificence that followed, you offered yourself to Christ as a most acceptable sacrifice, with a pure heart and humbled spirit [Note: [Col. 0215] Psalm L, 19.]. In his tabernacles you sacrificed offerings of true rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0215D] Thus in the Old and Roman Psalters and in Saint Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms. The Septuagint and Vulgate have “of shouting” or “of cries.”] [Note: [Col. 0215] Psalm XXVI, 6.], refreshing and feeding those who, through the abundant blessing of praise, would sacrifice an offering to God [Note: [Col. 0215] Psalm XLIX, 14.].

How beneficially our City then resounded, when you poured out the entrails of your compassion to refresh and clothe the poor: restoring the pale bodies of the hungry, watering the dry throats of the thirsty, clothing the trembling limbs of those suffering from cold, and opening the harmonious mouths of all in blessing of God!

But while you warmed needy bodies, and your works returned to the better part of you through divine recompense, you fattened your own spirit instead, and refreshed the soul of your blessed wife. The hand of Christ poured into her what had been distributed by your hands to the poor, as bodily food was changed in the blink of an eye into heavenly nourishment.

And as much money as you had poured out with generous right hand, while the receiving hands were doubled, as a cheerful giver and tireless distributor, just so much was immediately carried by flying angels into the lap of the rejoicing Lord and stored up to be counted for you as thirtyfold fruit and return [Note: [Col. 0215] Matthew XIII, 8.].

Nor were riches alone added to your rewards; the grace of blessings was added as well. For the loud acclamation and prayer of the poor, by which God was blessed through your gifts, was reckoned to you as righteousness. The voices of the needy travel easily to the ear of God, because, as it is written, the prayer of the poor penetrates the clouds [Note: [Col. 0215D] The Septuagint and Vulgate have “the prayer of the one who humbles himself.”] [Note: [Col. 0215] Sirach XXXV, 21.].

### 15.

Rome, you could have no fear of those threats made against you in the Apocalypse, if your senators always offered such gifts [Note: [Col. 0215D] Thus the Viennese manuscript, Chifflet’s edition, and Grin’s edition in the margin; other manuscripts read *intentas* (“directed against you”). Saint Jerome likewise addresses Rome in Book II *Against Jovinianus*, at the end: “You can escape the curse that the Savior threatened against you in the Apocalypse through repentance, having the example of the Ninevites.” Chifflet.].

Truly, your nobility would then be noble: the consecrated fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob would receive it into their paternal bosoms; the prophets, apostles, and martyrs—that is, the senate of heaven—would acknowledge it; and Christ would clothe it, after its toga had not been defiled by the gore of impure blood, in the royal robe of the promised light [Note: [Col. 0215] Matthew XVII, 2.] and enroll it in the eternal white book—that is, the book of life [Note: [Col. 0215] Revelation XX, 12.].

Those would truly be rich riches, nourished not by the bloody cruelty of the ancient dragon but by the boundless goodness of God the Savior, if what is squandered badly on acquiring and feeding beasts or gladiators were instead given to one’s own salvation, and if life were dearer to us than destruction.

But through avarice and perverted generosity we are needy before God on our own behalf, and prodigal for the devil against ourselves. We count loss as gain and gain as loss. We do not take care to buy back our life cheaply, since we purchase death at great expense in place of life.

Our condition would be blessed if we feared displeasing God, or cared to please him, as much as we do human beings; if we dreaded Christ’s commandments as much as the hissing of the crowd; and if the praise that comes from God were valued as highly as this applause bought from the populace [Note: [Col. 0216D] Thus in the Viennese and Regius manuscripts. Other manuscripts read *tanti … quanti* (“as much … as”).].

### 16.

Blessed are you, who have not entered into such a council, nor sat in the chair of pestilence [Note: [Col. 0215] Psalm I, 1.], but have been praised in the seat of the Apostle and in the assembly of the Church—that is, in Christ’s theater—not amid seditious groups but amid companies blessing God, with God himself as spectator.

You are the Church’s provider, not an aspirant to earthly and empty glory, but a seeker of eternal praise [Note: [Col. 0216D] Thus in the Viennese manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. Previously it read *arenae* (“of the arena”).]. You buy neither gladiators nor beasts; rather, you stage a spectacle by which you may destroy the true gladiators—that is, the rulers of these darknesses—and by which you may overcome the true beasts, that is, every power of the devil, and trample the lion and the dragon underfoot without harm [Note: [Col. 0216D] Sacchini proposes emending *agis* (“you stage [a spectacle]”) to *alis* (“with wings”), prompted by the preceding statement in section 15 that money is badly squandered on acquiring and feeding beasts or gladiators. Moreover, Saint Jerome similarly calls Pammachius, in Letter 26, “a provider and candidate of the poor and needy.” See the very similar description. Sacchini.] [Note: [Col. 0215] Psalm XC, 13.].

Blessed are you, in whom the name of the Lord is blessed, and who have seed in Zion and household members in Jerusalem, who may in turn receive you into eternal tabernacles [Note: [Col. 0215] Luke XVI, 9.].

You will not fear the place of that rich man who, in Tartarus—that is, in the lower hell—and deservedly surrounded by fire in the outer darkness, begged that the tip of the finger of the poor man whom he had despised in this life might be sprinkled upon him. Father Abraham rightly answered him:

> “Remember, son, that you received good things during your life, and Eleazar bad things; but now he is being comforted and you are suffering.” [Note: [Col. 0217] Thus in the manuscripts and printed books. The same reading occurs in Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 20, *On the Maccabees*, and in Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 10, line 154. Nicolaus Heinsius notes that *Eleazar* is found in the manuscripts, and Saint Paulinus himself reads it in *Carmen* 32, *On the Death of Celsus*, line 582. The Greek text, however, has Λάζαρος (*Lazarus*), as do the Vulgate and the Vatican manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke XVI, 25.]

### 17.

For this reason, I think, those rich people should dread such an exchange of punishments and pleasures: those who, overflowing only for themselves and their vices, either lie upon hidden wealth without setting aside a share for the poor, or are deservedly poor in their evil extravagance and destined to be punished with eternal poverty. They have been so cheap to themselves in their love of luxury that they are shown to have considered a single day’s meal more precious than the life of all their time.

Such people, then, will not share forever in the heavenly goods of the poor whose earthly goods they did not know how to share here. Their tongues will burn more severely—those who now either shudder at or mock the infirmities of the poor, disdainful with deadly contempt and playfully harmful. They pass by and leave the sores of their neighbors to be licked by dogs, although every human being is by nature a neighbor to every other human being.

Are these not more truly to be called dogs—people who have not even imitated dogs in caring for and soothing human beings, and who command brothers, that is, those made kin by nature our mother, desiring at least to be filled (*saturari*) by crumbs falling from their table [Note: [Col. 0218D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Chifflet’s edition; other manuscripts read *satiari*, likewise “to be satisfied,” a variant distinguishable only in Latin.], not only to be excluded by closed doors but also to be driven away with savage beatings?

Therefore I believe that the rich man in the Gospel, when he was wholly tormented, as he cries out, in the flame of that fiery abyss, nevertheless asked for refreshment only for his tongue [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke XVI, 24.]. Without doubt, it burned more intensely because, with his proud and avaricious mouth, he had so often sinned against Eleazar, who lay before his door and had been left to the dogs.

For this reason we are also warned elsewhere to set a guard over our mouth [Note: [Col. 0217] Psalm CXL, 3.], Wisdom teaching through Solomon:

> “In the hand of the tongue are life and death.” [Note: [Col. 0217] Proverbs XVIII, 21.]

And elsewhere:

> “By your words,” he says, “you will be justified, or by your words you will be condemned.” [Note: [Col. 0217] Matthew XII, 37.]

### 18.

To you, therefore, brother united with me in Christ—to you, who share the fear of that punishment and fellowship with that place; whose mouth is full of blessing; whose wealth is the breasts of the poor; whose house is Christ’s lodging; who do not tolerate a beggar lying before your door while you feast [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke XVI, 20.], but instead gladly bring him beneath your roof, either to feast with you or to be filled while you yourself fast—to you belong a poverty blessed by freedom from sins and riches blessed in virtues.

You will rightly be counted among those poor whose is the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0217] Matthew V, 3.], and among those rich whose possession is a strong city [Note: [Col. 0217] Proverbs XVIII, 11, according to the Septuagint.], because you are rich in the spirit of God and poor in your own spirit.

God loves such rich people together with their poor and celebrates them in the sacred writings, ennobling them by the authority of the everlasting pages.

### 19.

For I want you to consider this very point: the names of those rich people whose crimes or punishments are recorded in Scripture are not given, because without doubt they were unworthy to be named in divine speech—people whom either the impiety of their lives erased or avarice destroyed.

Therefore the Lord had foretold of them through the Prophet:

> “I will not remember their names with my lips.” [Note: [Col. 0217] Psalm XV, 4.]

That is, through the words of the two immortal Testaments, which are rightly called the lips of the divine mouth, because they adhere to one another, are opened by one word of God, and through them God kisses us with the kisses of his mouth [Note: [Col. 0217] Song of Songs I, 1.].

Divine justice therefore did not wish those lips to be polluted by the names of the impious. For this reason the name of that rich man whose vanity and avarice are signified does not survive—the one who, with his life already consumed, was thinking about the resources of his life and was told:

> “Fool, this night your soul is being demanded of you; whose will those things be that you have prepared?” [Note: [Col. 0218D] Thus in the Viennese and Regius manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition. Other manuscripts have *expostulabitur* (“will be demanded”).] [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke XII, 20.]

Nor is the name of the rich man from Tartarus famous—the omission of whose name, when the poor man’s name is published, we understand not to have occurred by chance [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke XVI, 19.].

We also read of the blindness of the rich man who, boasting that he had fulfilled the Law, rejected the condition of attaining perfection because of his love of wealth, but we do not possess his name. For it says:

> “He had many possessions.” [Note: [Col. 0217] Matthew XIX, 22; Mark X, 22; Luke XVIII, 23.]

And therefore the sentence followed that almost closed the kingdom of heaven to every rich person, unless God, as the one who alone is good, had reserved for himself this gift: to enrich the rich by the will of the poor.

These, then, are the rich who are hated by God and erased from memory: those who have preferred perishable things to eternal ones (*praeverterint*, that is, *praetulerint*, “have preferred”; see *Carmen* 31, line 344) [Note: [Col. 0218D] We have emended the text from *Carmen* 6, line 21, and 23, line 303, although all manuscripts disagree; in them the reading *terrenis* seems to make no sense.], who preferred to trust in the earth rather than in God, heaping together food for moths and prey for thieves, and, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0217] Matthew VI, 19; Psalm XXXVIII, 7; Ecclesiastes II, 19; Sirach XI, 20; Luke XII, 21.], without knowing for whom they store up treasure—because they do not wish to understand to whom they owe their treasures, and are worthy not to know which heir will receive them, since they do not know from which giver they possess them.

For what do you have, O human being, that you did not receive? And because you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it [Note: [Col. 0217] 1 Corinthians IV, 7.] and grow proud of God’s own gifts?

The names of such rich people, my brother, are not written in the Gospel, because they are not found in the book of life either [Note: [Col. 0217] Psalm LXVIII, 29.].

### 20.

Finally, so that you may know that it is not riches but people who are either blameworthy or acceptable to God in their use of them, read how the holy fathers Abraham, Lot, and Job were made friends of God through their possessions [Note: [Col. 0217] Genesis XVIII, 3, and XIX, 2; Job XXXI, 16.].

For in the Gospel, where that Tartarean rich man who despised Eleazar has been passed over, we see Joseph of Arimathea called rich [Note: [Col. 0219] Matthew XXVII, 57.]. He is blessed, because he understood in a special way how to care for the needy and poor [Note: [Col. 0219] Psalm XL, 2.], honoring Christ’s body with devoted service [Note: See Letter 26, section 2.] [Note: [Col. 0219] Matthew XXVII, 58.]. He was not afraid to appeal to the judge for the sake of the Lord’s body, and, as a rich man, he used the costly expense of a precious covering and a new tomb in the Lord’s burial.

The sacred page will inscribe you under these names, and you will be counted among such rich people, whose riches you equal in spirit. They did not possess possessions as their own; rather, no one claimed anything as his own, and they considered nothing human alien to themselves—as did that former multitude, the first in faith, which had one heart, one soul, and all things in common [Note: [Col. 0219] Acts II, 44, and IV, 32.].

And consider the reason: you will easily judge that it is a crime like parricide to despise the poor according to our own will, when we see that God’s work has not separated them from us in any respect.

How do we exclude [Note: [Col. 0219D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts, Florus in the *Catena*, Book XI on Hebrews XIII, 1, and Chifflet’s edition. Other manuscripts read *excludamus* (“do we exclude”).] from our modest dwellings those whom God has enclosed together with us in the one house of this world [Note: [Col. 0219D] Thus Florus, the Regius and Viennese manuscripts, and the editions of Bad, Grav, and Chifflet. Otherwise, *concludit* (“encloses”).]? How do we disdain [Note: [Col. 0219D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition. Other manuscripts read *dedignemur* (“let us disdain”).] making participants in the use of earthly possessions those whom, even against our will, we have as partners in the unity of divine origin [Note: [Col. 0219D] Thus Florus of Lyons in the *Catena*, Book XI, from Paulinus on Hebrews XIII, 1–2; the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition. Other codices read *in una* (“in one”).]?

Keep this in mind: Abraham became God’s friend; by observing this, Lot escaped from Sodom [Note: [Col. 0219] Genesis XVIII, 3; Genesis XIII, 2.]; by following this, Job triumphed over the devil.

### 21.

Let us also open our dwellings to our brothers—either fearing danger by the example of the fathers mentioned above, lest, while excluding a human being, we perhaps repel an angel, or hoping to merit angelic guests by receiving every stranger’s arrival with ready kindness.

For when Father Abraham received strangers, he also received the Lord Christ with the angels, and in his hospitable tent he saw that day which the Savior displays openly in the Gospel in himself [Note: [Col. 0219D] This preposition has been added from Florus’ *Catena*, Book XI, the Viennese manuscript, and Chifflet’s edition.] [Note: [Col. 0219] John VIII, 56.].

The Sodomites were condemned for their injury to guests, while Lot merited liberation above all because of the affection by which he preferred his guests to his daughters [Note: [Col. 0219] Genesis XIX, 8.]. He was not impious but perfectly pious. He did not regard his daughters as worthless; rather, he earned his reward because he preferred the justice of charity—that is, fear of God—to domestic affection. By God’s command and through his spirit, he was serving the reception of guests.

Thus even then that mind fulfilled the perfection of faith of which we are told:

> “Everyone who has left brothers or sisters, or mother, or sons or daughters, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.” [Note: [Col. 0219] Matthew XIX, 29.]

The perfection of this mind—or the mind of this perfection—liberated righteous Lot from that Pentapolitan conflagration [Note: [Col. 0219D] That is, the burning of the five cities, from Greek *pente*, “five,” and *polis*, “city.” Likewise *pentapolis* in Natalis 8 of Saint Felix and *Carmen* 23, line 221.] from the beginning of the world [Note: [Col. 0219] Genesis XIX, 15.]. He merited, for his hospitable house, to receive by God’s gift the whole city as his household [Note: [Col. 0220D] Thus in the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and four printed editions. The Vatican manuscript and Grin’s and Rosweyde’s editions have *per hospitalem domum* (“through the hospitable house”).], because he alone in that incestuous and impious city had been pious and chaste, and, surpassing even piety itself in holiness [Note: [Col. 0219] See note 43.], did not hesitate, as far as it lay within him, to redeem the chastity of his guests by the chastity of his daughters.

Job, that man of the Lord—silver tested by fire—testifies that he had always been the eye of the blind and the foot of the lame [Note: [Col. 0219] Job XXIX, 15.]. He claims and receives the reward for these works in the very contest of his temptation.

He is stripped of the wealth of his inheritance, but not of his spirit; invulnerable in heart, he does not even sin with his lips [Note: [Col. 0220D] The Viennese manuscript has “nor does he sin with his lips.” The phrase is also absent from the Regius manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0219] Job I, 22.]. Stripped of the ambition of possessions, he is armed with the virtue of patience. Bereft of children, but not of the light of his heart, he embraces the children of his mind—that is, works of justice—and cries:

> “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I must return to the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0219] Job I, 21.]

> “We brought nothing into this world, and indeed we cannot take anything away.” [Note: [Col. 0219] 1 Timothy VI, 7.]

But because he had not lost his spiritual riches, he also recovered temporal riches as the prize of his patience. He was enriched twofold [Note: [Col. 0220D] The Regius manuscript and the editions of Bad, Grav, and Grin have *triplo* (“threefold”).], because he had been tested and purified sevenfold [Note: [Col. 0219] Psalm XI, 7.].

For, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0219] Psalm CXXVII, 2.], he had eaten the fruits [Note: [Col. 0220D] The Old and Roman Psalters, Saint Augustine in his commentary on the Psalms, and the old Latin books have *fructuum*. The Septuagint has *palmarum* (“of palms”); the Vulgate, *manum* (“of the hand”). Paulinus says *fructuum*, deriving it from the ambiguous Greek expression τῶν καρπῶν. According to Jerome in Letter 141, *karpoi* can mean both “fruits” and “palms” or “hands.” See note 44.] of his labors [Note: [Col. 0220D] See note 44.], laboring in pious works. For this reason he ate the fruits of his labors also in this world, receiving the rewards of his works.

22. You share the lot of these rich men because you remember God himself to be the source of your wealth, [Col. 0220C] free from avarice because you are a servant of righteousness. You use unrighteous mammon justly; you are not its captive but truly its master, because you are possessed by Christ, to whom captivity itself is captive [Note: [Col. 0219] Psalm 67:19]. Glory, therefore, in the Lord, because it was not flesh and blood [Note: [Col. 0219] Matthew 16:17], but he himself—Christ, who is the true light and wisdom of God [Note: [Col. 0219] 1 Corinthians 1:24]—who revealed to you the understanding of this providence. Through it you understand that Christ is fed, given drink, clothed, and visited in every needy and poor person [Note: [Col. 0219] Matthew 25:40], in accordance with those fathers whom, for the merit mentioned above, the Lord delivered on the evil day [Note: [Col. 0219] Psalm 40:2].

23. May the Lord himself preserve you, give you life, and make you blessed; may he now come to your aid upon your bed of pain [Note: [Col. 0219] Ibid., 3–4], and turn your devout mourning into holy joy. May he tear apart the sackcloth of your sorrow and restore to you the joy of his salvation [Col. 0221A] [Note: [Col. 0221] Psalm 30:12]. Confirming your principal spirit [Note: [Col. 0221] Psalm 51:14], may he strengthen your arms in prayer and almsgiving like a bronze bow [Note: [Col. 0221] Psalm 18:35]. May he make your feet like those of a stag, so that you may be swift both to flee the devil and to pursue Christ; and, with your footsteps fixed by the double nail of the two Testaments, may you stand firmly on the Lord’s way [Note: [Col. 0221] Sirach 5:12], your feet snatched by the Lord’s hand from falling and your eyes from tears [Note: [Col. 0221] Psalm 116:8]. Thus, together with your blessed wife, may you please 80 the Lord forever in the land of the living.

For it will happen to you according to your faith, because the Lord is faithful in his words [Note: [Col. 0221] Psalm 145:13]. He will remember your sacrifice forever, and your burnt offering will become fat [Note: [Col. 0221] Psalm 20:4]; and he, the rewarder of your investment, will receive you yourself as a living sacrifice, as a fragrance of sweetness, on that day when the creditor, richer than his debtors, will return to each person his [Col. 0221B] deposit with multiplied interest. Nor is the day of repayment far off, since the fields are already whitening with the approaching harvest [Note: [Col. 0221] John 4:35].

24. Meanwhile, promising yourself the riches that are to be received [Note: [Col. 0221D] Thus we have emended the text from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the Chifflét edition; this reading is confirmed by a thoroughly similar passage in the letter to Marcella, §8, where all the manuscripts read: “Confidently promise yourself, in joyful meditation, perpetual happiness in the goods to come.” The printed editions formerly had festina (“hasty”) here instead of festiva (“joyful”).] through joyful meditation, you will console your mind much more abundantly by faith in what is to come than by my speech or anyone else’s. For it is no slight pleasure to believing souls to anticipate, in sweet thought, the goods promised to the faithful and already to walk in paradise in spirit.

If it delights a farmer to admire the hope of a harvest in the standing grain while he awaits the fruit of his labor from the harvest, and if he bears the delay of the seasons more easily, in his eagerness for the fulfillment of his hopes, when he may feast his eyes while he waits for the outcome, how much greater a pleasure can we receive—although sinners, yet faithful little servants—to whom the care of the seed sown has been entrusted, not to the uncertain [Col. 0221C] faithfulness of earth, but to the unchanging truth of God, as we hope for what Truth itself promises?

25. For we do not gather what lies beyond human life from human opinions, the fabulous dreams of poets, or the phantasms of philosophers; rather, we draw our faith in things from the very fountain of truth. Who could know divine things better than God himself, who is conscious of his works and decrees?

We shall not falsely claim that souls pass into alien bodies and become monsters after death; nor that they will remain altogether without bodies, or perish within a body. Let the poets who have no prophets of truth flatter themselves with lies. Let the philosophers, who are not illumined by the testimonies of the apostles, be blinded by their wandering opinions. Let those who have no [Col. 0222A] hope console themselves in despair, saying: “Our time is the shadow of a passing thing, and there is no return at the end of our life, because it has been sealed” [Note: [Col. 0221] Wisdom 2:5], “and no one will return” (see note 45).

Blinded by the darkness of their wickedness and unbelief, they cannot say: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the light of the living” [Note: [Col. 0221D] Paulinus seems to have read ἐν αὐγῇ (“in brightness”) instead of the reading now found, ἐν γῇ (“in the land”). LATIN.] [Note: [Col. 0221] Psalm 27:13].

But we do not need such inadequate remedies, since Truth itself—the Word of God, God—both promised us the resurrection of the flesh unto eternal life by his teaching and proved it 81 by rising again. For the Son of God himself, through whom all things exist and without whom nothing exists, testified: “I am the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0221D] We have added this word from the Viennese manuscript and the Chifflét edition. It occurs both in the Greek text and in the Vulgate, and is required by what follows.] and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” [Note: [Col. 0221] John 11:25–26].

To establish this not by word alone, he sanctioned it by example. He showed the disciples his own human being, in whom the whole assumption of humanity resides, [Col. 0222B] raised from the dead, assigning in himself the proof of the flesh’s reality when he says to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands; and put your hand here and place it in my side; and do not be unbelieving but faithful” [Note: [Col. 0221] John 20:27], because “a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having” [Note: [Col. 0221] Luke 24:39].

26. Having, then, these testimonies, these proofs, this light of faith, on what grounds could we doubt the resurrection, which we have both heard from the Word of God and seen with the eyes of the apostles and touched with our hands [Note: [Col. 0221] 1 John 1:1]? We are so bound and grafted into God through Christ [Note: [Col. 0222D] Thus the Regius manuscript and the Chifflét edition. Florus of Lyon likewise reads this in the *Catena of Greek and Latin Fathers*, book XI, from Paulinus of Nola, under the title “From the Letter to Pammachius, on Ephesians 1:31 and 14, ‘You have been sealed,’ etc.” Elsewhere: *juncti* (“joined”).] that we possess the Holy Spirit as God’s pledge in our own land, the Spirit whom he gave us [Note: [Col. 0221] 2 Corinthians 1:22]; and that we have in God, as our pledge, the flesh of Christ. For it joins together that immense interval by which mortal [Col. 0222C] things are separated from divine things, intervening in the middle and between the two as a common mediator—like a bridge, so to speak—so that by his path earthly things may be joined to heavenly things, when the heavenly incorruption has flooded our corruptible nature, and immortality, as it is written, has swallowed up our mortal nature, and victorious life, having conquered death in Christ and proceeding from Christ, has swallowed death for us [Note: [Col. 0221] 1 Corinthians 15:54].

To attain this, we may doubt not the truth of so great a good but our capacity and merit. Let us do what Christ commanded, so that we may obtain what Christ promised. May his truth be present to us, and may our faith not fail him. He is life for all, the way for all, the door for all [Note: [Col. 0221] John 14:6]. He closes his kingdoms to no one, though he allows them to be seized by force [Note: [Col. 0221] Matthew 11:12].

27. Continue toward the goal for which you are running, so that you may grasp him by whom you have been [Col. 0222D] grasped; strive along the narrow way, so that you may arrive at the spacious possession of the inheritance of eternity [Col. 0223A] [Note: [Col. 0223] Matthew 7:13]. Already in Christ you possess a great pledge of yourself and a powerful advocate: your wife, who prepares for you in heaven as much grace as the wealth you supply to her from the earth [Note: [Col. 0223D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the Chifflét edition. Formerly the printed editions had “from earthly things.”]—honoring her, as I have said, not with empty mourning [Note: [Col. 0223D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts, the Chifflét edition, and Schott’s marginal reading. Others have “luxuries.”], but heaping upon her living gifts, with which she now rejoices. Already she possesses the benefit of your work in its fruit, though for now its gift to you remains in the seed. 82

28. She is already honored by your merits, already nourished by your bread, and abounds in your riches. Clothed in gold, she is surrounded by varied adornment [Note: [Col. 0223D] Rosweyde’s edition: “wrapped around.”] [Note: [Col. 0223] Psalm 45:10] and precious light. She does not need the finger of another hand to cool her; she herself is drenched by the dew of her own fingers—that is, by the works of your right hand.

You had not enriched her with so ample a dowry when she was marrying as you now enrich her while she rests. [Col. 0223B] For then she received only as much of your gifts as she could enjoy by wearing; now, whatever you bestow, she will possess all at once, rich in spirit with the pleasure of every sense.

Blessed is she who has so many advocates before Christ, and whose head is surrounded by so manifold a crown of illustrious gems—not woven with foreign flowers, but sparkling with lights of her own household. Truly that soul is precious to the Lord which draws its value from three pearls. She is the wife of faith, the sister of virginity, the daughter of perfection; Paula is her mother, Eustochium her sister [Note: [Col. 0223D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts: “Eustochia.”], and you her husband.

# LETTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Formerly numbered 18; the letter formerly numbered 14 is now 27. Written in the year 398, after Easter.]

He congratulates Delphinus on the restoration of his health, wisely explaining why evils befall the righteous. He also gives thanks for the settlement of the affair of the presbyter Basil.

To the most blessed and venerable father, always greatly desired by us [Note: [Col. 0223D] The printed editions: “most longed-for.”], DELPHINUS, PAULINUS.

[Col. 0223C]

1. We rejoiced at what was written and brought to us by Cardamates [Note: [Col. 0223] Psalm 122:1]. The message of your recovery, like the oil of gladness, made our bones fat, so that, filled with joy, we said: “The Lord has done great things with us” [Note: [Col. 0223] Psalm 126:3], he who visited us upon the bed of your pain [Note: [Col. 0223] Psalm 41:4]. Rising up in rejoicing at your health, we sang a hymn to our Lord, because he had rescued our eyes from tears [Note: [Col. 0223] Psalm 116:8], delaying you from your crown but reserving you for our assistance, so that, while your earnest prayers lighten our burdens and lead the way along our journey [Note: [Col. 0224D] The Viennese manuscript and Grin’s edition: “making shorter.” “Leading the way” is better in the other manuscripts, as the following makes clear.], we may run more swiftly in the fragrance of the Lord’s ointments. Though we have not [Col. 0223D] attained the fragrance that comes from your holiness by merit, we nevertheless pursue it in affection, hoping that through the inseparable bond of your love we may be led on to arrive, under your guidance, where you have [Col. 0224A] reached by your own effort.

For your illnesses 83 are not unto death, but for the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0223] John 11:4], so that they may bring perfection to your strength and strength to our weakness. Many examples from the patriarchs of the Lord’s saints already confirm us, lest we be troubled on your account.

2. Just as those fathers of faith, in addition to the other labors of their lives, even in that prophetic old age in which, enlightened inwardly, they already foresaw the eternity of the world and the succession of all ages [Note: [Col. 0223] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Other manuscripts: “they provided for.”], nevertheless, though their bodily eyes were weighed down by physical weakness, completed their spiritual virtue [Note: [Col. 0223] Genesis 27:1 and 48:10], so blessed Job was tested so that he might be proved, fought so that he might conquer, humbled so that he might be exalted, and wept so that he might rejoice [Note: [Col. 0223] Job 1:14; 2:7; 4:1; and 5:1].

And what of the Holy One himself, the Holy of holies? Did he not conquer precisely when he was judged, and [Col. 0224B], falling through death, rise again into glory? These things are encouragements to the strong amid the weaknesses of suffering and incentives to virtue for the weak. The strong man is made weak so that the weak may be strengthened and may learn, by imitating the robust, to overcome the struggles. Therefore the righteous person too is chastised, so that the unrighteous may be corrected.

3. Thus the bodily weakness of the saints accomplishes a double benefit: it exercises their spiritual virtue; and the person who prospers in his way [Note: [Col. 0223] Psalm 37:7] and, boasting in the strength of undisturbed health, says, “I have sinned, and what has happened to me?” [Note: [Col. 0223] Sirach 5:4], dares not flatter himself about bodily prosperity. Perhaps, restrained by fear of divine power, he will be corrected toward righteousness, while he rightly dreads the avenging hand of the heavenly Lord against impious deeds—a hand he sees to be severe even toward the righteous.

For if you scarcely escape without the blows of chastisement [Col. 0224C], where will we, the wicked and sinners, appear? [Note: [Col. 0223] Proverbs 11:31; 1 Peter 4:18.] We believe, however, that you have therefore suffered, in these recent times, more severe darts of bodily affliction than usual—formerly troubled by the heat of fevers, now by a disorder of the head—so that in that rest of the Lord you may be blessed to say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” [Note: [Col. 0224D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Latinius. The same reading occurs in five psalters, in the Vulgate, among the Septuagint, and in Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms. In the other manuscripts available to us was “into a place of refreshment.”] [Note: [Col. 0223] Psalm 66:12].

Rejoicing, therefore, in this mercy of God, by which he had looked upon our humility for our good so that we might gain the reward of very great anxiety, when you had at once disclosed to us both our concern for you and our reassurance, we received another gift of divine grace in the same letter: namely, the matter concerning our care for the house of the holy presbyter Basil, settled through your efforts just as we had wished.

[Col. 0224D] 4. May that entire blessing come upon your head and, woven over the crown of your [Note: [Col. 0224D] See note 6.] crown, blossom as its fullness. In you, not only those to whom the benefit belonged but almost all Capua, 84 and the city’s very celebrated church, rejoicing together in the presbyter’s happiness—blessed the Lord [Col. 0225A] and gave praise to God, who had helped the poor man out of poverty and humbled the proud hearts of the rich. Thus they too may have hope of an eternal dwelling in the city of habitation, since they were deemed worthy, through the intervention of your words, to be enlightened unto good understanding. By the just restoration of a small dwelling, they prepared for themselves an eternal lodging in the heavenly tabernacle of the poor saint, by whom they will in turn be received [Note: [Col. 0225] Luke 16:9].

# LETTER XV

[Note: [Col. 0225D] Formerly numbered 25; the letter formerly numbered 25 is now 10. Written in the year 398 and sent together with the preceding letter.]

He congratulates Amando because Delphinus, freed from a serious illness, has been restored to his former health; he gives thanks for the favor conferred upon Basil, the presbyter whom he had recommended; and he playfully jokes about Cardamates’ self-control.

To the holy, deservedly venerable, and most beloved brother AMANDO, PAULINUS.

[Col. 0225B]

1. We received Cardamates with the joy of love and the blessing of sweetness, bringing us every good thing: letters announcing your health, gladdening our hearts and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 19:9 and 11]. Their sweetness penetrated our inmost parts like oil; our humbled bones rejoiced [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 51:10], and with a voice of exultation we said to the Lord: “We have received your mercy, O God” [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 48:10], for you delivered the poor from the powerful [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 72:12] and the humble from the hand of one stronger than he [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 35:10, according to the Roman Psalter].

Everywhere causes for thanksgiving crowded into our minds: that we received your letters; that we found you mindful of us; that we heard, according to our prayers, that you were safe and well; and that we learned that [Col. 0225C] my lord and our father, Delphinus, had been healed of a serious and prolonged illness [Note: [Col. 0225D] The Regius manuscript: “his household.” The Viennese manuscript: “our Lord.”]. We rejoiced equally over both of you. For just as the same tribulation had worn him down in body and you in heart, so the same visitation had brought him divine aid upon the bed of pain [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 41:4] and you the refreshment of reassurance in the bed of compassion.

Nevertheless, when we considered his illness and your state of mind, our affection was pricked by the thought that during that time of your tribulation we might perhaps have been healthy and even cheerful. But thanks be to the Lord, who pardons the fault of ignorance and did not deal with us as we deserved. He anticipated our sorrow with thanksgiving, graciously arranging matters so that we should learn of the flight of your illness from the same messenger who announced the return of your health.

85 2. What shall I say about that work of your holiness by which you have contributed as much to the increase of our present grace as to the abundance of your eternal reward? [Col. 0226A] I mean the affair of the holy presbyter Basil: you turned his mourning into joy [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 30:12] and adorned his old age with abundant mercy [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 92:11]. In his tabernacle there has arisen a voice of joy and salvation [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 118:15], and he does not cease, together with his entire household [Note: [Col. 0225D] The Regius manuscript: “house.” Thus the ancient manuscripts and this same manuscript frequently.], to bless the Lord with the harmonious thanksgivings of the Church. The Lord has looked upon his humility [Note: [Col. 0225] Luke 1:48], bound up his wounds, and covered with shame those who rejoiced at his misfortunes [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalms 147:3 and 35:26]. Having torn apart the sackcloth of sorrow [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 30:12, according to the Roman and Old Psalters], he has girded him with the strength of joy.

3. Therefore, on behalf of those brothers of ours for whom we had previously asked that you be petitioned, we now ask your unanimity that you love them beyond your customary affection. If they should perhaps come to Bordeaux, as they usually do, then, in their presence, give them thanks also for the affection of our thoughts and inmost heart [Col. 0226B]. Or, if their arrival should be delayed, when the first opportunity presents itself, deign to send them the proper congratulations and the deserved blessing for their deed, so that they may know and understand what an acceptable sacrifice to God they offered through this obedience of their faith, by which they received our petition, through your intervention, as something that could be granted.

They have certainly brought us present joy through their devotion, but they have provided eternal benefit for their own salvation. Even if, in acknowledging justice, they did what was required—that is, ordered what belonged to another to be returned—they nevertheless deserve abundant gratitude for that very disposition of good will by which they could have transgressed but did not [Note: [Col. 0225] Sirach 31:10]. They preferred to do what was expedient rather than what was permitted, and they deigned to obey us with so open and pure a heart that there could be no dispute about their kindness.

For although they did not prove that the house was his by right, they nevertheless ordered it to be restored without difficulty to the holy [Col. 0226C] presbyter, so that, if he could not possess it by his own right, he might possess it nevertheless as a gift from them [Note: [Col. 0226D] We have added “his own” from the Regius manuscript and the Badaric and Grin editions]. Nor did they lose the credit of such holy generosity. The most holy man himself, for whom the Lord provided you as advocates according to your merit [Note: [Col. 0226D] Isaiah is called Hezekiah’s intercessor in the same sense in poem 23, line 195], gives thanks and praises you as though he had received an undeserved gift.

We have postponed replying to those brothers of ours for the present because, through their people who frequently travel from Campania, there will be no lack of more convenient opportunities to send a message immediately to wherever they are [Note: [Col. 0226D] The Viennese manuscript: “which may be directed.”].

4. As for Cardamates himself, we acknowledge that we owe no small debt of gratitude to your unanimity: we received him not only advanced in [Col. 0226D] service but also progressing in spirit. 86 For when he arrived during the days of Lent and we received him as a cleric with fraternal affection, he did not avoid the daily fasts, nor did he, as an evening guest, shrink from our poor little table.

And what is more remarkable, he was content with our cups, so that we understood that, in your holiness, he had been reformed, as he had learned from the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0227] 1 Timothy 5:23]; and that he was now intoxicated, no longer by a large measure but by a little wine [Col. 0227A] [Note: [Col. 0227D] Thus we have emended the passage from the two Regius manuscripts, the Viennese manuscript, and Grin’s edition. Formerly it read: “from the command, as the Apostle teaches . . . to be instructed to use wine,” etc. Both readings have been received.], with which the belly is not distended but the heart is gladdened—to sobriety (see note 46), belching forth to God a hymn from spiritual drunkenness.

The person who receives the Lord’s will with faithful hearing, recounts it in devout speech, and fulfills it with vigorous action, sings this hymn not only with his audible mouth but also in the silence of his heart. Blessed is the Lord, who does wonders [Note: [Col. 0227] Psalm 72:18]. He who turns the rock into waters [Note: [Col. 0227] Psalm 114:8] has made Cardamates a cleric, as we see, and, as we believe, a sober man [Note: [Col. 0227D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Others: “as we have seen.”].

For when the days of the Easter solemnity brought back the days of dining [Note: [Col. 0227D] The Viennese manuscript: “were recalling,” less well], he began around midday to murmur to us, saying: “My throat is parched like a potsherd, and my tongue has clung to my jaws” [Note: [Col. 0227] Psalm 22:16]. “My soul and my belly have failed, and from hunger and thirst my bones have clung to my flesh” [Note: [Col. 0227] Psalm 102:6].

We answered him: “My son, endure in humility, and let the desire of your belly not seize you” [Note: [Col. 0227] Sirach 2:4 and 23:6], because “man lives not by bread alone, but by every word of God” [Note: [Col. 0227] Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4; Luke 4:4]. But he, like a deaf man, did not listen; like deaf adders, he stopped his ears to us [Note: [Col. 0227] Psalm 58:5]—but in vain.

At the midday meal he wished to fill his belly, and no one gave him even a pod [Note: [Col. 0227] Luke 15:16], until the day declined toward evening (see note 47). Then, after the hymn had been sung, however sad he was from hunger for luncheon, he was reconciled with us by the refreshment of supper.

But lest by joking any longer we seem to do injustice to his gravity, which now rejoices more in driblets of cups than in streams of drunkenness, I shall speak seriously about his circumstances [Col. 0227C]: he asserts that his wife is disabled and therefore useless to him (see note 188). If this is so, I ask that some little servant be provided for him.

# LETTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 0227D] Formerly numbered 38; the letter formerly numbered 16 is now 20. Written in the year 399.]

87 He teaches Jovius, a distinguished man who attributed much to fate and fortune, that everything is subject to divine providence. He had already written to him on the same subject, perhaps in poem 19. Though praising him highly for his remarkable learning and eloquence, he deters him from reading the philosophers and urges him to read the sacred Scriptures.

To Jovius [Note: [Col. 0227D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the Badaric, Gravius, and Schott editions. Rosweyde’s edition adds “most distinguished.” The Vatican manuscript: “To Jovius, distinguished brother, etc.” Grin’s edition: “To Jovius, a most distinguished man, Paulinus.”], brother, PAULINUS sends greetings.

1. When our sons Posthumianus [Note: [Col. 0227D] The Viennese manuscript and three printed editions have “Posthumino,” incorrectly; all manuscripts and printed editions of Letter 49 to Macarius read “Posthumianus” and “Posthumianum.”] and Theridius [Note: [Col. 0228D] The Regius manuscript has “Theridianus,” incorrectly. This is the same Theridius about whom Paulinus writes in Letter 27, §1, and poem 20, line 107.] were returning from Campania, which they had visited for our sake, to their homeland, I thought it contrary to duty and affection not to write to your unanimity.

I was not merely guarding against seeming, through an unusual negligence toward you, to disregard the attention owed to everyone [Col. 0228A]; I was even more concerned lest I appear to judge your mind toward God wrongly if, carefully looking for every occasion to write to you, I passed you by without greeting through men of religion, as though you shrank from holy men—although you are certainly known to be devoted to the Christian name and, because of your love for us, to approve our own way of life.

Receive them, then, gladly—not approving them because of my letter, but approving my letter because of them. They have taken the greatest care in holiness to regard it as a religious duty either to revisit their homeland without approaching you or to approach you without my letter.

The character of these messengers seemed to me well suited also to this purpose [Col. 0228B]: to reply to something in that earlier letter of yours which you sent to me in response to my letter, in which I had proclaimed the evident benefit of divine power in the elements and God’s care for us. For surely you remember that, from your writings, I learned what I then answered in congratulation. I therefore urged you not to attribute God’s gift to chance; and perhaps you considered that the silver of that holy transaction had been preserved more by Fortune than by divine power amid winter storms and greedy sailors, after its guardian was lost, and that the ship had been cast onto that particular shore where a town familiar to us, and your patrimony, had received our property in its safest harbors [Note: [Col. 0228D] The true reading, confirmed below in §4: “Fate and Fortune and Chance”; and in poem 19 to the same man, line 98. The Viennese manuscript: “Fortune.”].

2. But you again complained more about the violence of the storm than you showed gratitude for God’s mercy. You subjected all the movements of the elements—among which only the divine hand can preserve human safety—and our actions, which the power of the supreme Lord [Col. 0228C] governs and turns or directs according to our merits, to the empty divinities of fate and fortune [Note: [Col. 0228D] Unless all the manuscripts opposed it, I would have followed Sachinus in reading “names,” since below, in §4, we find “empty names,” shortly afterward “hollow names,” and in §10 “empty names of chance and fate.”], as though to powers rivaling God.

Do not suppose that in this you have honored God. Rather, you have wronged him by refusing to acknowledge, as you should have done, that this was God’s benefit. You say that these things must therefore be separated from divine power because evils suit chance more than God. Yet there is no doubt that something is evil when it often brings danger or loss to human beings.

As I see it, you include among such evils storms, through which devastation is often suffered on land in the fields, or the distress of shipwrecks at sea [possibly: “the distress of shipwrecked people”]. But I see that this opinion arose from those teachers who, proud of their own wisdom and disdaining to seek God’s wisdom, live as exiles from the borders of truth. They assert their own opinions; having sent their minds out into the great void, they have vanished, as it is written and demonstrated, in their own thoughts [Note: [Col. 0229] Romans 1:21]; and they have fashioned God’s works and counsels according to their own judgments.

To them, the sea or sky may seem to be ruled and moved by chance. They argue that this world turns through random motions, either empty and without a ruler or neglected by an idle God; or that it was composed without an author and, just as it had no beginning, has no end. But corporeal nature does not permit this—the nature of this world, of which each of us is a part—because every structure is dissoluble. Or, more foolishly still, they want it to have created itself, as though anything could itself be the cause of its own birth, so that it would be at once creator and creature, maker and work. Yet it is obvious that these differ not only in name but also in kind and condition.

For who does not see that this corporeal world is governed by incorporeal power, and that the whole mass, infused and mingled with the great body of the universe by the divine Spirit, is moved by the mind by which it was made—to live, regulated for use, held together in its state, and ordered for endurance?

3. Since, then, it is evident that what is seen or sensed needs assistance from elsewhere in order to exist and remain, it cannot be doubted that it likewise needed assistance from elsewhere in order to be created. Since this is so, we must confess that everything arose from God. For no one except the impious can call it into doubt that the world was made with God as its author.

Accordingly, the winds and everything within the world that forms part of its mass, as it were the organs of its body [Note: [Col. 0229D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Others: “which are.”], must not be attributed to the rule of another. For the powers of God’s works—that is, the substance of all natures—could not endure to be ruled and held together amid such discord within themselves except by that one nature and power, namely, the one God, creator of all, by whom alone they could be made and ordered, and whose laws they must obey if they are to retain their proper state.

It is much more foolish to blame any nature and call it evil. For if everything is from God and God is good, then everything God made is certainly good. If, however, some things in the hidden ordinances of his decrees are higher than our senses and thoughts, and even if we cannot attain and grasp their rationale, it is nevertheless safer for us to believe that their reasons are hidden rather than that they have none. For we must not doubt that all God’s things [Note: [Col. 0229D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Other manuscripts added “are,” but we have removed the word as superfluous], though they are not clear to us, are nevertheless deliberate.

[Col. 0229D] 4. Therefore, if God, who created and governs the whole world, does so, where will chance, fate, or fortune rule, and over what creature? If they depend, as some maintain, on the movements or arrangements of the stars, they derive this power—which you make a rival of God—from little sparks that are not only smaller than God but also smaller than the world itself, indeed from lights that, as servants, adorn a third part of the world itself.

Certainly it belongs to divine power to disturb the elements, to excite the violence of winds when it is still or restrain it when aroused, and by the fury of storms either to expose mortals to danger or snatch them from it. Since every creature obeys this power [possibly: “lacks it”], being subject to the one Creator of all, how can divine force and power be assigned to things that lack not only the name [possibly: “the divinity”] of the Creator but even the appearance of a creature—empty names, lacking spirit or bodies, fitted merely to bear or signify things?

For although *fors* may be the word of someone expressing doubt, *fatum* the utterance of someone declaring, and *casus* the designation of things falling or happening, nevertheless, through the usage of ancient error born of ignorance of God, those devoid of reason fashion hollow names as though they were therefore divinities as well. In their foolish thoughts they give them bodily form [see Letter 49, §8], and, more foolishly than they fashioned them, honor them with divine worship.

Thus Hope, Nemesis, Love, and even Fury are worshiped in images; Occasion is consecrated with a bald back of the head; and your Fortune is represented, badly balanced upon a slippery globe [Note: [Col. 0229D] The Vatican manuscript: “is depicted.”]. With no less falsehood, the Fates are represented as spinning the lives of human beings from baskets or weighing them in scales.

Lest we attribute this madness to the common people or admire philosophers too much, it is reported that Plato too was raving—Plato, who, in the tenth book of the *Republic*, places the task of Necessity in the lap of an old woman and adds three daughters to her [Note: [Col. 0229D] Thus we have emended the text from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Schott’s edition. Our correction is further confirmed by Plato’s tenth book of the *Republic*, near the end, in these words: “The spindle, moreover, revolved upon the knees of Necessity. Above, upon each circle, a Siren was fixed, carried along with the sphere, uttering one voice and one tone; yet all eight together composed one harmony.” In Greek: ἐκ πασῶν καὶ ὀκτὼ οὐσῶν μίαν ἁρμονίαν ξυμφωνεῖν (“to make a single concordant harmony from all eight”). “The other three daughters of Necessity sat on thrones at equal intervals from one another, the Fates in white garments, their heads crowned: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos, who sing to the harmony of the Siren,” etc. In Greek: ὑμνεῖν πρὸς τὴν τῶν σειρήνων ἁρμονίαν (“to sing to the harmony of the Sirens”). The fourth printed edition has “singing together,” incorrectly.] singing in harmony, turning the spindle, and playing along the threads. In this way, he claimed, they fashioned human affairs by their wool-working and distinctly spun out each person’s allotted time [Note: [Col. 0229D] The Regius manuscript and the Badaric and Gravius editions: “marked out.”].

So great is the abuse produced in human ears by the arrogance of empty eloquence that he was not ashamed to insert into his writings—writings in which he dared to discuss divine nature almost as though he were personally acquainted with it—the ridiculous song of an old woman’s tale.

But in that discourse we should look only to the elegance of Attic speech, not to the harmony of an empty fable. Such things were composed merely to charm the ears; they ought not to overturn the foundations of understanding.

### 5

Rather, as reason and truth teach, let us refer to God himself all the works of God in which we exist and of which we are a part (from Virgil), and all his gifts by which, amid the uncertainties of this fragile and fleeting life, we are governed and preserved; and let us remove nothing from his power through our error, since, whether we wish it or not, he himself is, as he is the creator of all things, our Creator and God. [Col. 0230D]

And because [Note: This is the reading of the Schott edition; see Letter 23 to Severus, §1], whatever his greatness, he is goodness, wisdom, and the source of reason, he established nothing except by reason and created it as the material of his goodness [Latin: perhaps *memoriam*, “memory”]. [Col. 0231A] Let us devote to him all that we are; let us strive to learn what pleases him and take care to do it.

Then, looking more purely with a cleansed mind, we shall see this to be the truth: that all things that exist are from God; and this to be the necessary consequence: that all God’s works are supremely beautiful; and that there is no evil where the author is good—he who prepared all things throughout the world for our use and directs them for our benefit. Thus he established the work of this universe in such a way that he created some things to serve, others to exercise us, and others to rule.

Accordingly, by reason we rule over corporeal and animal natures. But, lest the very license of our power dissolve us, we are beneficially exercised by adversities—whether by demonic spirits, the difficulties of affairs, or often the movements of the elements themselves—so that, shaken by cares, prudence, and fear of the Divinity, we may be sharpened. [Col. 0231B] The security that ought rather to make us more grateful to the eternal Lord makes us negligent.

Hence the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, says that, by the hidden counsel of divine compassion and for the great benefit of human salvation, certain obstacles are placed in our paths and prosperity is changed into adversity—illnesses, losses, and dangers—because “tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces the testing of faith, and brings the reward of glory” [Note: Romans 5:3]. This, certainly, virtue cannot grasp unless it is victorious; and it will have no opportunity for victory unless it has first struggled against some difficulty.

### 6

When I consider that this could have been impressed upon your prudence—which you possess both by nature and through education—by the very writings which, if only you now subordinated them to sacred Scripture in devotion as you do in judgment, record that the virtues of distinguished men among commanders and philosophers attained noble renown only through toil and danger [Note: We emend *indicibus* to *in ducibus* from the Vienna manuscript and the Schott edition; the former reading has no sense; see note 48], I am greatly astonished that, in the clear truth of the divine gift, you wished to grope so blindly that you attributed to chance the astonishing rescue of the storm-tossed ship and the protection, arranged by evident signs, of our enterprise by divine providence on land and sea—and that you squandered so great an opportunity for proclaiming God. [Col. 0231C–D]

Raise your mind to the summit of wisdom and seek Christ, the very source of true light; he illuminates faithful souls and flows through chaste hearts.

You have taught that you perceive this yourself, although, as an excuse, you have claimed that you are still unequal to God and therefore incapable of him [Note: The Vienna manuscript together with the Grin edition reads “incapable”], because, occupied with earthly affairs and cares, you are shut off from the higher contemplation of heavenly things as though clouds lay between. [Col. 0231D]

Would that you could advance this claim as truly as you can express it eloquently. For the very fertility of your eloquence and learning proves that what you lack for sacred Scripture is willingness rather than either leisure or ability. I do not think you gathered such riches of speech or heart while asleep or occupied with something else. [Col. 0232A]

You breathe the flowers of all poets, overflow with the streams of all orators, and are also watered by the springs of philosophy; rich even in foreign literature, you fill what is Roman with Attic honeycombs.

Tell me, I ask, where was this tribute when you read Cicero and Demosthenes from beginning to end? Or when, already weary from the satiety of more familiar readings, you reread Xenophon, Plato, Cato, and Varro after completing them—and many others besides, whose names we perhaps do not even know, while you possess their volumes as well?

For occupying yourself with these things you are free and exempt; but to learn Christ—that is, the wisdom of God [Note: 1 Corinthians 1:24]—you are tributary and occupied. You have leisure to be a philosopher; you have no leisure to be a Christian.

Rather, change your opinion; change your eloquence. You need not lay aside the philosophy of the soul, provided that you season it with faith and religion; use it more wisely, interwoven with religion [Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript; the other manuscripts read, “and use it wisely, joined with religion”], so that you may be God’s philosopher and God’s prophet, wise not by seeking God but by imitating him; so that, learned not so much in tongue as in life, you may discuss great matters as you do them. [Col. 0232B]

### 7

Be a Peripatetic for God and a Pythagorean for the world; a preacher of true wisdom in Christ, and finally, silent before vanity, avoid this destructive sweetness of empty literature, like the Lotophagi—obliterators of their homeland through the sweetness of berries—and the songs of the Sirens, the melodies of harmful blandishments [Note: The Belgian manuscript, the Schott edition, and Fabricius read this way. Other copies read differently]. [Col. 0232C–D]

Since it is often permissible to adopt certain things from empty tales, as one may take some common proverbs into the service of serious and truthful discourse, I shall say that not literature alone but every form of temporal reality is for us a Lotos-eater or a Siren.

The pestilential sweetness of pleasures makes us forget our homeland, when it erases from the human being God, who is the common homeland of all; and the allurements of desires imitate that Siren story in the reality of their destruction. For what those Sirens are imagined to have been, the true allurements of desires and blandishments of vices really are: they possess seduction in appearance and poison in taste [Note: The Vatican manuscript has this reading, while other manuscripts prefer “for they have.”]; their use is reckoned as guilt, and their price as death.

We must flee these things with greater caution than Ulysses used—with not only our ears but also our eyes and mind sealed—as though passing swiftly by in a ship, lest, enticed by deadly pleasure, we be driven onto the rocks of crimes and, fastened to the cliff of death, suffer the shipwreck of salvation.

### 8

Would that we might escape from the brine of this world even naked, if, in this present time, while we drift amid bodily frailty and the slipperiness of possessions like sailors upon the unreliable framework of a decaying ship, we could strip ourselves for swimming of the encumbering impediments, as of wet garments; and if we would remember to seize the faith that saves, by which we rely upon the banner of the cross in the power of Christ God, as upon a plank of refuge. [Col. 0232D]

Thus may we obtain a solid hope from fleeting things and snatch something from the harmful substance of desires for innocence and salvation [Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript and Sacchini; the other manuscripts read “Because”]. [Col. 0233A] In this way, serving God and ruling over desires, let us limit our wants to what necessity requires; and, possessing necessary clothing, let us not seek superfluous adornments, because we are reminded that we brought nothing into this world and cannot take anything away [Note: 1 Timothy 6:7]. [Col. 0233D]

This truth has such force that even among the pagan philosophers—those who, with lofty intellects, reached the furthest boundaries of truth—they recognized that one could not devote oneself to wisdom, much less follow it, unless certain people threw the burdens of money into the sea as though they were dung [Note: The Schott edition reads this way; Rosweyde considers it the proper reading. Other copies have “the extremities of truth.”]. [Col. 0233]

### 9

But make a division with God, and, as though in mutual exchange, give thanks to the supreme Father, who nevertheless asks back from you only those things that he has given you by nature or added from without. You may possess all that you have, for yourself and your own, provided that you take care to acknowledge God as the giver of these things as well. [Col. 0233B]

For we possess nothing that we have not received [Note: 1 Corinthians 4:7], and, as I said, we came naked into this world [Note: Job 1:21]. Dedicate to God the capacities of your intellect and all the resources of your mind and tongue, offering him, as it is written, a sacrifice of praise [Note: Psalm 49:14], with eloquent speech and a devoted heart.

As soon as you direct the gaze of your mind toward the heavenly inner sanctuary, truth will open its face to you and will disclose your very self to you. For through knowledge of divine truth we also attain this: that we may know ourselves.
