From where, do you think, has such perversity of either pride or sloth grown among wretched mortals that, instead of worshiping God, they serve demons or the elements subject to them, venerating waters, fire, stars, trees, and images, with the most impious insult to the divine majesty? [Col. 0233C]

Whatever they worship in the name of demons or creatures, they honor servants. For this they deserve to be blinded by such darkness that, because they refuse to understand the true God, they are also punished by ignorance of themselves.

Faith liberates the enlightened human being from this, so that, understanding the order and measure of his kind, he may recognize that he is subject only to God, whose unity is constituted in ineffable Trinity; that he is equal to all other rational creatures; and that he is superior to all corporeal creatures.

### 10

Tempered by this moderation, a human being neither falls away from the lot of salvation nor abandons the dignity of his nature. He becomes conscious of truth, possesses wisdom, serves justice, is free from error, and is master of the vices to which the soul that does not serve God is condemned to serve. [Col. 0233D]

Then, exiled from its proper state, the soul is scattered through all the wandering paths of its own thoughts or others’ opinions: wandering through philosophers, inquisitive through soothsayers, religious toward superstition, profane toward religion, and always suspended between hope and fear in uncertain emotions.

Carried about by every wind of every doctrine [Note: Ephesians 4:14], because it is empty of fear of God and has no head of wisdom, it is like one “maimed in its faculties,” from which it might draw an understanding of things and in which it might establish a judgment [Note: The Vatican manuscript and Fabricius, together with the Rosweyde edition, read “lacking understanding.” The Regius and Vienna manuscripts, together with three editions, read “maimed in its faculties,” which is more accurate because it lacks a head. See note 50]. [Col. 0234A]

After it has uselessly wandered in thought through every region of heaven and earth and distracted itself, it establishes in visible creatures and empty names of accidents and fates the entire power by which the world is governed.

### 11

But let your mind, already kindled from heavenly seed and breathing a divine ardor, be directed by a preceding faith toward Christ, the citadel of wisdom [see note 11]. [Col. 0234B]

I endure seeing you possess, even in our studies, the eloquence of philosophers [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads: “the eloquence of philosophers to be possessed by you”], provided that you cease loving a wisdom opposed to truth. For it is better that I see you holding to the pursuit of divine things than disputing in pursuit of them.

Leave those men forever rolling in the darkness of ignorance, consumed by the contentions of learned loquacity and serving their own phantoms in mad dispute—always seeking wisdom and never finding it [Note: 2 Timothy 3:7]—because they do not deserve to understand the God whom they refuse to believe.

Let it be enough for you to have taken from them, as spoils from hostile arms, the abundance of their language and the adornment of their speech, so that, naked of their errors but clothed in their eloquence, you may apply that cosmetic of eloquence by which empty wisdom deceives to matters full of substance [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads: “being full of wisdom, adapt the embellishment of eloquence to realities.”]

Thus, adorning not an empty body of fictions but one filled with the marrow of truth, you may prepare what will be pleasing not only to the ears but also beneficial to the minds of human beings [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads: “you may publish.”]. [Col. 0234D]

## LETTER XVII

[Note: Formerly Letter 13; the letter formerly numbered 17 is now 19. Written toward the end of the year 339.]

He complains that Severus did not come to Saint Felix as he had promised, and warns him that, the more merciful the martyr is, the more he should fear offending him. He therefore urges him to come as soon as possible.

### PAULINUS TO SEVERUS

#### 1

We have grown weary both of inviting you and of waiting for you, and we have no prayers or words left to add to those that we have so often poured out in vain through petitions and letters. You have left us only this one resource of our mutual friendship, now that hope of one another’s presence has been cut off: we repay words with words, and we wish to be warmed at least by these consolations, although they bear no fruit.

Yet even in these you have begun to be sparing, now seeking us only when circumstances require it. For nearly two full years you have tortured us by keeping us suspended in daily expectation of seeing you.

We even brought that summer to a close—the summer that followed the return of our boys to you—waiting until winter should close the way, believing each day that it was dawning for your arrival. [Col. 0234C–D]

But since no indication of your delay had arrived, we consoled ourselves with the supposition that you had sent no one because you yourself would soon be present, even if late.

Meanwhile, as this summer too was passing away, still being soothed by that hope, or at least by that expectation, we set out for Rome for the venerable day of the apostolic solemnity, promising ourselves your arrival there in a meditation that was indeed dutiful but still festive. [Col. 0235A]

When the pleasure of our anticipated hope had been exhausted because you yourself were not there, we were not left entirely without consolation: we received your letter through Sabinus, a man very dear to us and our brother.

At first we were amazed that he was scarcely monastic in gait or clothing; moreover, his face was no less flushed than an *armilausa* [uncertain term; see note 67], and his cheeks were little spiritual. Only then did we realize that he was not one of our people, when, through him, the master of the courier demanded our letters back and we discovered that you were joined to him by the closest bond. From that moment we have embraced him as a friend with multiplied affection. [Col. 0235B]

#### 2

We had no opportunity, however, to write back from the City. For ten days we scarcely saw Rome—indeed, saw it without seeing it—and spent the very time before noon, for which we had come in fulfillment of our hopes, among the sacred memorials of the apostles and martyrs [Note: The Regius manuscript and the Schott edition read this way. Paulinus uses the same expression elsewhere. Other copies read “the time”]. [Col. 0235D]

Then, when we returned to our lodging, we were occupied by innumerable visits, occasioned partly by friendship and partly by religious devotion. We could scarcely be released by evening, when the gatherings ended and gave us some respite; thus, from lack of leisure, we necessarily postponed our duty.

After we had returned home, another delay arose: a recurring bodily illness, which examined us rather severely for no few days.

But he who is our life and resurrection [Note: John 11:25] visited our humility for good; and though he chastised us with chastisement, he did not deliver us to death [Note: Psalm 117:18]. “Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord” [Note: Tertullian has this form: “It is good to hope in the Lord,” Psalm 117:9; see also Psalm 31:10]. [Col. 0235C]

Therefore we were scourged as sinners and delivered as those who hope in his mercy, for he heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds [Note: Psalm 146:3].

#### 3

Now recovering through the strength and mercy of the Lord, we have written through Amachius, our beloved brother in the Lord, the subdeacon of our lord and father Delphinus, because the opportunity presented itself. Since he also claimed to be very well known to you, we thought him especially suitable to entrust with our letter to you.

We greet you as much as we love you in the Lord and still desire you. For we cannot yet tear from our hearts the hope by which we presume that, by the Lord’s gift, we shall see and embrace you in the seat and bosom of my lord, our common patron Felix [Note: The Regius manuscript and certain editions read this way. See note 52]. [Col. 0235D]

To him I have so often attested your vows and recounted your promises, whenever you remember what you pledged to me. [Col. 0236A] If we have deceived the martyr of truth, I do not think I alone should be judged guilty of this fault, since I promised what I believed.

But you, my brother, united with me and most beloved, while there is still time, take care lest you appear to have denied so great a confessor, a saint of such powerful favor with Christ.

#### 4

I do not know how you can plead illness rather than laziness, or an excuse based on circumstances or persons, when within a year you could have come to us and returned by the same route with which for so many years you have frequented the journeys through Gaul, and when, often making repeated excursions within a single summer, you visit Tours and more distant places.

I do not envy you (from Virgil); rather, I proclaim your devotion in the Lord—a devotion by which you admire and honor his servants.

I confess that it is just and deserved that Martin is frequently visited. But I say that it is unjust and harmful for Felix to be mocked by empty promises, or, by the careless pretense that a promise has already been forgotten, to be despised by the very person who honors Martin. [Col. 0236B]

With the same faith by which you hope for Christ’s grace in honoring Martin, fear Christ’s displeasure in offending Felix [Note: A more Latin expression, but…].

Perhaps your stronger mind, more robust soul, or powerful conscience of perfect love in Christ supplies you with such confidence that you think this offense—which, God forbid, you may have committed against my lord Felix—can be wiped away by compensation for the great merits of your faith and works.

You may promise yourself the most generous forgiveness, both from Felix’s own goodness toward you and from God and Christ, whose spirit he is—and you act faithfully in doing so.

But I confess that, either because of the weakness of my own infirmity I am so timid, or because of my excessive love for you, I fear even what is safe on your behalf. While I desire Christ’s grace to abound in you in every saintly matter, I do not wish you to encounter a stumbling block precisely in that matter in which God’s love is most distinguished and eminent.

I know that, according to the riches of God’s goodness, the bowels of compassion overflow also in my lord Felix. But, I ask you, love and fear this all the more because he is better and more forgiving. Such fear will bring you a great reward, so that you may be more anxious precisely where you can be more secure: namely, that you fear offending God’s dearest servant all the more readily because he deigns to forgive more readily.

For the one who does not know how to be offended is injured by a greater impiety, and the one who does not ask to be avenged is more gravely avenged by the Lord.

Consider this matter, I beg you, in the mutual affection of faith, and see whether you ought to excuse yourself as strong or distrust yourself as weak.

For our Lord is everywhere near us [Note: Luke 10:36], and he says: “In every place, while you are still speaking, behold, I am present” [Note: This sentence is absent from the Vulgate and is not found among the Septuagint]. And he says: “All things are possible to the one who believes” [Note: Mark 9:22].

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: Formerly Letter 18; the letter formerly numbered 18 is now 14. Written toward the end of the year 399.]

[Col. 0237A]

Paulinus excuses himself to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, for having kept the deacon Paschasius with him too long. He then vividly describes Victricius’s merits: how, while still a soldier, he showed himself in tortures to be a true confessor and martyr of Christ; how, after becoming bishop, he established and adorned the Church of Rouen; and how, in barbarian regions, he cultivated Christ’s faith and founded monasteries.

### PAULINUS TO VICTRICIUS, EVER MOST BLESSED AND VENERABLE FATHER

[Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “brother,” erroneously, since Paulinus, not yet a bishop, wrote to Victricius when he was already a bishop; see the Life of St Paulinus, ch. 50, §1.]

#### 1

What had for some time not happened despite our wishes suddenly, when we did not expect it, came about by the Lord’s gift: an opportunity was given us to write to your venerable holiness through a member of the household of faith—and especially through that brother who was alike yours and ours in the Lord [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “is”].

For, at Rome, when we had assembled for the most celebrated day of the apostolic festival, our blessed brother, the deacon Paschasius, came to us. Beyond the grace of our brotherly companionship in sacred ministry [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “as in the sacred mystery”], we received him with all the more reverence and affection because we learned that he belonged to the clergy, body, and spirit of your holiness. [Col. 0237B]

Yet we confess our coercion: although we approved his pious haste, prompted by a most rightful desire to return from Rome to your holiness, we embraced him in our love and brought him on to Nola.

We did so that the lodging-place of our humility there might be blessed, through his entrance, by some breath of your spirit, and that we might enjoy longer, as it were, some portion of your grace, seeing and keeping the man whom modesty of character, humility of heart, gentleness of spirit, faithfulness to truth, and speech seasoned in every respect with salt [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “prove”] showed to be both a disciple of your instruction and a companion of your journey [Note: The Regius manuscript and four editions read “companion of the journey”; the Vatican and Vienna manuscripts with the Grin edition read “companion of your life.” The former seems the truer reading and is confirmed by Letter 23 to Severus, §3, where Paulinus says closely similar things about Victor]. [Col. 0237C–D]

Therefore forgive our brother in us, or us in him. Whether his delay is blamed or our presumption censured, the Lord’s love will excuse either fault to you: by it he was compelled to comply with us, and we did not fear to seize and retain him as our own by right—not with obstinate arrogance, but with a pure heart and unfeigned faith [Note: 1 Timothy 1:5]—believing that what is yours is ours, and not doubting that you would reckon it reciprocally so: you would not consider that he had been absent from you [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “failed”] during the time when you knew that he had been with us.

For though we are separated bodily by intervals of regions [Note: The Regius manuscript reads “made unequal”], we are joined by the Spirit of the Lord, poured out everywhere, in whom we live and remain, as members of one body, having one heart and one soul in the one God [Note: Acts 4:32]. [Col. 0238A]

#### 2

Accordingly, beholding in a spiritual mirror your mind’s disposition toward us, and ourselves as mutually joined to you, we claimed for ourselves, from the affection of our heart, your united mind in retaining the brother [Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript and the Grin edition; others read “unanimous”]. The grace of the Lord, abundantly given to you, was itself effecting this: that you are loved even in the members of your body and in the fringes of your garment.

Yet we lost many days of his stay while the Lord, reproving us in his mercy [Note: Psalm 140:5], was chastening us with bodily sickness for our spiritual amendment. [Col. 0238B]

But he who consoles the humble [Note: 2 Corinthians 7:6] and heals the brokenhearted [Note: Psalm 146:3] consoled us by the presence of our blessed brother Paschasius. While we were refreshed in spirit by that presence, we were restored in body also; for a good friend is medicine for the heart, and Christ rightly stands between two brought together as one [Note: Matthew 18:20].

#### 3

Nor did he share and sympathize only in our own illness. During the grave and prolonged sickness of our most distinguished son Ursus, whom he had had as the inseparable companion of his pilgrimage, he was worn down as well.

In this we saw his faith and love in the Lord in their fullness. For as much as Ursus suffered in body, so much was Paschasius tormented in spirit.

Therefore the Lord looked upon Ursus in Paschasius’s humility [Note: Luke 1:48], adding this benefit also: though he had been sick unto death, through the faith and labor of Paschasius the Lord willed him to experience the power, with God, of his beloved holy confessor, our lord Felix; and he found safety from danger. [Col. 0238C]

For by Paschasius’s own hands he was born again, baptized on his bed, and restored. May the same Lord, who gave him back through the prayers of our holy brother Paschasius [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “through the prayers of our holy brother Paschasius”; the others, simply “through prayers”], through our shared concern, and above all through your church—which, without doubt, he always watches over in all who are yours, wherever they may be—bring him safely and soundly into your sight, free from sin and a servant of righteousness [Note: Romans 6:18]. [Col. 0238D]

We do not doubt that, if he is worthy to reach you, he too will make great progress in faith under Paschasius as his peer and under you as master of them both [Note: The Regius manuscript and the Schott edition read “peer”; compare Letter 32 to Severus, §17, “Gervasius his peer,” and Letter 45 to Augustine, §3, “Melania, a branch from the equal root of the saints.” Others read “father”; see note 55].

#### 4

For your beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, Tychicus [Note: The Vatican and Vienna manuscripts, with the Schott edition in the margin, read “Tychicus.” Other witnesses have “Titycus” and “Titius”; see notes 55 and 56], has made known to us—not so much praising you as preaching God in you—how many lights the Lord has kindled through you in regions formerly dark.

He who brings clouds from the ends of the earth [Note: Psalm 134:7] brought you too from the uttermost [Note: The Vatican manuscript and the Grin edition read “end”] edge of the world into the light of his people, and made the bright lightning into abundant rain. [Col. 0238D–0239A]

As once the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond Jordan, Galilee, and those who sat in the region of the shadow of death saw a great light [Note: Isaiah 9:1; Matthew 14:15], so now also in the land of the Morini [Note: See note 57], at the world’s farthest edge, which the roaring Ocean beats with barbarian waves, the peoples of remote nations—who sat in hiding places along the sandy sea-road beyond Jordan—rejoice that light has risen for them from the Lord through your holiness.

Before the boundaries of the desert grew rich there [Note: Psalm 64:13], they laid down their rough hearts at Christ’s entrance—that is, they cast them off.

Where once the unsafe wildernesses of forests and shores alike were frequented throughout [Note: The Regius manuscript and the Babylonian and Gravius editions read “throughout”] by foreign barbarians or resident robbers, now venerable and angelic companies of saints celebrate cities, towns, islands, and forests, in harmonious peace [Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript, supported by the Regius manuscript; others read “sounding together”], with numerous congregations in churches and monasteries. [Col. 0239B]

Although Christ works this among the peoples of all Gaul and everywhere among the nations—he who ranges through the whole world seeking those worthy of himself, passes through the nations into holy souls [Note: Wisdom 7:27], shows himself cheerfully in paths of uprightness [Note: Some Bibles read “his”; our manuscripts read “of uprightness”], and with every providence meets his lovers [Note: Wisdom 6:17]—yet in the remotest tract of the Nervican shore [Note: See note 58], which the faith of truth had formerly breathed upon but faintly and from which it especially chose you as a vessel of election [Latin: perhaps *te*, “you”], it first shone more brightly, glowed more ardently, and appeared more nearly in you. [Col. 0239C–D]

It chose you as the one in whom it might sanctify its name there, and through whose name its sound might go forth from the setting of the sun over all the earth [Note: Psalm 18:5].

#### 5

Finally, we now hear that Rouen, formerly little known even in neighbouring regions, is named with reverence even in distant provinces and numbered, with divine praise, among cities renowned for sacred places. [Col. 0239C]

Nor is this undeserved. By the merit of your holiness, it has brought to itself the very appearance of Jerusalem such as is remembered in the East, and also the presence of the apostles [Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript and Latinius; the earlier reading was “presence”]. They make a city foreign to their own memorials comparable to their own abodes by the affection of holy spirits and the effect of divine works, having found in you yourself a lodging most suited to them. [Col. 0239D]

For the friends of God and princes of the people of the true Israel—that is, of the people near to him [Note: Psalm 148:14]—delight to remain and work with you in that city, where, together with the holy angels, they are continually delighted day and night by the preaching of Christ the Lord. [Col. 0240A]

There, through the most devout hearts of believing servants, many friendly powers receive a welcome rest and a familiar lodging. There, amid the daily concord of those who sing wisely [Note: Psalm 46:8], through crowded churches and secluded monasteries, they delight in the most chaste hearts and voices of your sheep.

Now undefiled virginity keeps them in the temple of the sacred body, making them guests for Christ as he rests in chaste wombs.

No less does the integrity of widows, unconquered in holy works and pious ministry, feed them night and day, as does the hidden fellowship of spouses subjected to God. By diligent prayers this fellowship invites Christ, rejoicing in his works, to a visitation not of the marriage-bed but of the brotherly chamber; mingled in turn with him and his saints, it is united in the chaste intimacy of the visiting spirits by undefiled love [Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “is joined by chaste …”]. [Col. 0240B]

Now they are refreshed through the bowels of mercy and rest in children of piety and righteousness: they love you in all the children of your instruction, love Christ in you, and therefore work in your city especially the powers of God—that is, his power in Christ—so as to show that you are their companion.

#### 6

Grace and glory be to him who, not neglecting the works of his hands, wills every human being to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth [Note: 1 Timothy 2:4]. [Col. 0239]

Running through the whole world on the feet of the Gospel, he has also deigned to make you a beautiful foot for his word, so that in you he might rejoice like a giant to run his course, and to shoe your foot with the readiness of his Gospel of peace [Note: Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15; Psalm 18:6], so that through you also he might walk upon the asp and basilisk and trample the lion and dragon [Note: Psalm 90:13].

And lest so bright a lamp should lie hidden in darkness beneath the bushel of silence [Note: Matthew 5:15], by raising you to the apostolic see [Note: See Letter 3, §1] he set you aloft as though upon a lampstand, that you might shine upon the whole household with the illumination of many.

[Col. 0240C] 7. But by what roads did he lead you to the way of his truth? Instructing you through bodily duties in the spiritual matters of his power, at the beginning he created a soldier whom afterward he chose as a bishop; and he allowed you to serve under Caesar so that you might learn to serve God—so that, while exercising the strength of your body through military labor, you might strengthen yourself for spiritual battles, fortifying your spirit for confession and hardening your body for suffering. That this was the great design of divine providence concerning you was later made clear by your departure from military service and your entrance into the faith.

When, first inflamed by the love of Christ and at the Lord’s own ordering, on a distinguished day of military assembly you advanced onto the field in a certain public display of the deed [Note: [Col. 0240D] Two editions read “a display of his deed.” Both readings are good; the latter seemed more accurate.], girded with all the splendor of weapons which you had already rejected in your mind, and when everyone marveled at the most elaborate attire and terrifying equipment upon you, suddenly, while the army stood amazed, you turned [Note: [Col. 0240D] The manuscripts of the cathedral church of Rouen, of the collegiate church of Saint Mary of the Rotunda at Rouen, and the Rouen Breviary of 1491 read “having turned toward the army.”], you exchanged the military oath at the feet of the sacrilegious tribune [Note: [Col. 0240D] Those same manuscripts read “changing.”], and cast away the weapons of bloodshed, so that, putting on the weapons of peace, you might scorn to be armed with iron [Note: [Col. 0240D] The same manuscripts read “which.”], because you were armed with Christ.

And immediately, when the tribune had been driven into madness by the envy of the ancient serpent (see note 59), you were stretched out for scourging and broken by massive clubs; yet you were not conquered, because you leaned upon the wood of the cross. Then, when punishment was doubled upon your body, your limbs were mangled by terrible wounds and crushed beneath sharp fragments of pottery [Note: [Col. 0241D] Thus the Vatican, Vienna, C Rouen, M Rotunda, and B Rouen manuscripts, Bignaeus, and Rosweyde’s edition, with Grinius in the margin. But the Regius manuscript, together with the fifth editions, reads “laid beneath.”]. At that point Christ, whose bosom was your bed and whose right hand was your pillow, supported you more gently. Thus, before your wounds had even closed, restored for the greater enemy—made more ardent by the pain of those wounds rather than broken in courage—you leapt forth stronger; and when handed over to the commander, you triumphed more gloriously over the more powerful enemy [Note: [Col. 0241D] The C Rouen, M Rotunda, and B Rouen manuscripts read “gloriously.”].

Nor, after they had been overcome, did the attendants of the devil dare to inflict further tortures; but, as they contemplated a death sentence so that they might at least cease to be defeated by ending your bodily life [Note: [Col. 0241D] The same three manuscripts read: “Nor did the devil’s minion dare to inflict further tortures … he imposed the death sentence.” This reading seems more polished. Nevertheless, we have retained the common reading, since it rests upon the authority of the better manuscripts.], our Lord, strong and mighty, unconquered in battle [Note: [Col. 0241] Psalm 23:8.], confounded by conspicuous miracles hearts hardened beyond measure.

For the executioner who, along the road on which you, a sacred victim, followed your assailant, had insolently and threateningly violated your neck by daring to touch it, was feeling with his hand for the place of his blow [Note: [Col. 0241D] Those same manuscripts read “with his sword preceding.”]; immediately his eyes were struck out and he was smitten with blindness. O ineffable goodness of Christ, how great an affection he shows toward his own! He who asked forgiveness for his crucifiers [Note: [Col. 0241] Luke 23:34.] did not allow the injury done to his confessor to go unpunished; he who did not wish his own passion to be avenged immediately avenged the martyr’s insult. But that very anger is an act of mercy [Note: [Col. 0242D] So the Regius and Vienna manuscripts, together with Grinius’s edition. This reading is confirmed by Letter 29 to Severus, no. 8. The fourth editions read “that mercy is.” Both readings have been accepted.]. For one person was blinded precisely so that many might be enlightened; and perhaps the man who had lost the eyes of his flesh received the light of the mind.

Finally, immediately afterward, those who sadly carried out the duties of the savage guard saw, before their very eyes, the chains which they themselves had bound more tightly and pressed down to the bone—and which they had refused to loosen even slightly when you asked them as a favor—fall freely from their hands when your prayer had been turned toward God Christ. They did not dare to bind again what God had loosed, but ran fearfully to the commander, confessing God’s truth on behalf of the confessors. When this was reverently heard and believed, the commander reported it to his ruler with the testimony of the soldiers. And, so that his own sudden conversion from fury to clemency might also be counted among God’s miracles, he became a preacher of Christ [Note: [Col. 0242D] The C Rouen, M Rotunda, and B Rouen manuscripts read “which he had come to be.”]—he who had vowed to be Christ’s persecutor.

I think that the Lord had once filled him also with the Holy Spirit, like Saul [Note: [Col. 0241] 1 Samuel 19:23.], because he loved you as his own David [Note: [Col. 0242D] The same three manuscripts add “son.”]. Thus, just as that former king, while setting out to persecute the prophets, became a prophet, so that commander, sprinkled with the grace of the Lord which overflowed from the abundance of your faith, had come to punish a confessor but departed having himself become a confessor [Note: [Col. 0242D] Thus four manuscripts, together with B Rouen. The editions also read “a confessor.”]. For he believed; and those whom, in his fury, he had condemned as guilty, he sent away praising them as saints. He bore witness to the truth, although he had wished to punish the witnesses of faith.

8. Why, then, should we be surprised that you are so powerful in merits and so rich in graces, when this was your beginning in the virtues of Christ—something that for the few is the consummation of long labors? Shall we even now doubt that you are perfect, when you began from perfection? And if, after completing the contest, you are to be crowned lawfully, when you began to run from the crown?

Who would give us wings like those of a dove, so that we might fly to you and rest [Note: [Col. 0241] Psalm 54:7.] in the presence of your holiness; that, admiring and venerating Christ God present in your speech, we might wipe his feet with our hair upon your feet and bathe them with our tears [Note: [Col. 0241] Luke 7:38.], and upon those scars of yours, as though the marks of the Lord’s passion were impressed there, might lick them? For the wounds of a friend are sweeter than the kisses of an enemy [Note: [Col. 0241] Proverbs 27:6, according to the Septuagint.]. Woe to me, miserable sinner with unclean lips [Note: [Col. 0241] Isaiah 6:5, from the Septuagint version.], to whom this fruit has not fallen, although it was within reach.

9. I believe you deign to remember that long ago at Vienna I saw your holiness beside our blessed father Martin, to whom the Lord made you equal despite your difference in age. From that time, although I had encountered you only briefly, I nevertheless embraced you with great affection, and, as much as was then possible, revered your holiness. I entrusted myself and my companions to you forever—those who, although absent from you, nevertheless saw you through me, because in Christ who joins us we are one [Col. 0242C]. And now I rejoice that at least this much may be my boast: that I saw your face in the flesh. Yet I grieve over the negligence born of my unhappiness, because in ignorance I lost the opportunity for so great a good. At that time I was darkened not only by my sins, by which I am still oppressed, but also by the cares of this world, from which, by God’s favor, I am now free. I saw only the priest in you, what was outwardly apparent, and did not know how to see what was more distinguished: the living martyr.

10. Remember us, I beg you, on that day when angels will bring you to him, accompanied by the innumerable company of your merits, adorned with blessed ornaments, crowned alike with episcopal mitres and garlands, bearing the snow-white fillets of consecrated bishops [Col. 0242D] and the flowering purple robes of confessors (see note 60). Then the supreme purifier of his gold and silver will receive you yourself as silver tested in fire [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 11:7.] and gold proved in the furnace of this world [Note: [Col. 0243] Wisdom 3:6.], and the eternal King will set you as a precious pearl into his diadem.

Nor will the just Judge acknowledge that he owes you only the rewards of your own virtues, when he sees around you innumerable flocks of saints of both sexes, whom you daily beget for him through your teachings, a model for all of perfect virtue and faith. Brother Paschasius has also shown this: in his grace and kindness, as though reflecting in a mirror certain outlines of your virtues and graces, we have gathered them together [Note: [Col. 0243D] The Vienna manuscript and Grinius’s edition read “unity.”].

Truly blessed are you, parent of so many blessed ones, sower of so great a harvest, bringing to God from the fertility of your soil a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit [Note: [Col. 0243D] Thus the manuscripts and four editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads “thirtyfold.”] [Note: [Col. 0243] Matthew 13:8.] and destined to receive an equal measure from the varied fruits of your offspring [Note: [Col. 0243D] The Regius manuscript together with three editions reads “bringing forth.” Latin: perhaps “referring back.”].

The Most High has named you among the greatest of his kingdom. He granted you to make deed equal to word, so that your teaching may be your life, and your life your teaching. Thus no one dares excuse himself as a disciple under the pretext of difficulty, since he is first bound by the example of virtue.

# LETTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 0243D] Formerly Letter 17; the letter formerly numbered 19 is now 35. Written in the year 400 before June 29.]

Paulinus describes his joy at receiving a letter from Delphinus. He says that he is Delphinus’s planting and asks to be watered and cultivated by his words and prayers.

To the most blessed and singularly our lord, always our father in God Christ, DELPHINUS, PAULINUS.

1. We were waiting, like a thirsty threshing-floor [Note: [Col. 0243] Joel 1:20.], for the refreshment of your letters, and our soul, like land without water [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 142:6.], panted for your words with hearts thirsting for them. For nearly two years had already passed since, through our fellow-servant Cardamatus, you had sprinkled us with a few drops from your lips—few, indeed, but exceedingly sweet. Meanwhile we no longer hoped even to be touched by a drop of your speech, because, suspended all summer in the fruitless expectation of Uranus’s arrival (see note 61), we thought that we would have to spend the winter all the more in your silence.

And behold, the merciful and compassionate Lord, who gives food to the hungry [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 110:4.] and consoles the humble [Note: [Col. 0243] 2 Corinthians 7:6.], and is able to give us more than we hope [Note: [Col. 0243] Ephesians 3:20.]—what we desire—unexpectedly brought our Cardamatus to us again, although we were not expecting him but were wishing for him. As soon as the voice of your greeting came through him into our ears, our heart leapt for joy [Note: [Col. 0243] Luke 1:44.], and all our bones said: “Lord, who is like you?” [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 34:10.] “What is our lowliness, that you remember it and visit it?” [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 8:5.] “You have blessed our land, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 84:2.], “and you have given us drink from the torrent of your delight” [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 35:9.].

[Col. 0244A] [Note: [Col. 0244D] In all psalters, “Our lips will pour forth.”] Our lips will pour forth a hymn [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 118:171.] evening, morning, and midday. We will sing and praise the Lord, who grants us good things [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalms 20:14 and 12:6.]. For he sent a good messenger from a distant land [Note: [Col. 0243] Proverbs 25:25.], through whom we learned of the health of our sweetest and dearest father and received his message [Note: [Col. 0244D] The Vienna manuscript reads “letters.”]. Thus our heart was turned from the sadness of anxiety to the joy of security; and, as the anxious condition of our affection was changed for the better, on that day made festive for us by your letter, we rejoiced over the days during which the length of your silence had humbled us [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 89:15.].

2. Let us therefore confess the Lord’s mercies [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 106:8, according to the Hebrew.] and offer him a sacrifice of praise, because he has satisfied the empty soul [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 49:14.]—not, as we say with his favor, one empty of his grace, but fasting from the fruit of our desire—for it had long hungered for the consolation of your letters, which, as I have said, had been denied us for nearly two years.

May the Lord not count against them as sin their transgression—whose iniquity has lied to itself [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 26:12.]—and whose long hunger for the bread of your lips has wasted our soul.

[Col. 0244D] 105 [Note: [Col. 0244D] The Vienna manuscript reads “Let them remain.”] Let them remain where they wish, since they do not wish to remain where they ought to prefer to be. Let them do what is permitted to them, since they do not do what is expedient. Their addition to us, just as it could have contributed nothing good, will be able to take nothing away.

Would that our sins likewise caused us no harm, if they too, together with such neighbors, were removed far from us through the abundance of the mercies of him who does not repay us according to our sins, but, as a father has compassion on his son, so he has compassion on those who fear his name [Note: [Col. 0244D] The Vienna manuscript, together with five psalters, reads “those who fear.”] [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 102:10.] and hope in his mercy. We share in their company, because we love his coming in the miserable hope of his mercy and shudder as sinners in fear of his justice.

But, reconciled through your prayers to your children, may he not enter into judgment with his evil servants [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 142:2.], among whom we are the first, just as we are the last among the good. We even turn into an accumulation of condemnation the very glory by which we have received you in Christ and from Christ as the father of our regeneration, because we, useless servants [Note: [Col. 0243] Luke 17:10.] and degenerate sons, offer nothing worthy of you as a father to the Most High Lord. Even now we preserve in our heart the unhappy hardness of the wild olive, although long ago, through the goodness of the Lord, we appeared to have been torn away from the root of our kindred and grafted into your tree [Note: [Col. 0243] Romans 11:17.], from which we should draw the sap of your richness into the marrow of our soul and, rooted in the way of peace by the spirit of gentleness, recognize ourselves as shoots of the good olive through noble fruits [“Sacchin. ex” as printed].

3. But now, impoverished by the abundance of our vices and lacking our father’s goods, how shall we order our words on the day of recognition—that is, of judgment (see Letter 10, no. 3)—when we have not attained your virtues and bear no likeness from your stock by which we may be recognized as yours? [Note: [Col. 0245D] Thus the Vienna manuscript. Previously it read: “therefore that we may be recognized.” The phrase “on the day of recognition” has already preceded it.]

Who will rescue us from the coming wrath [Note: [Col. 0245] Matthew 3:7.]? Who will rescue us from ourselves, so that, cleansed from our own perceptions, we may be emptied by purifying faith of the material of heavenly wrath? For we feel within ourselves the causes of eternal punishments, while the roots of thorns and briars live in our hearts.

Our former growth of the old self, like the vine of Sodom, displayed a grape of gall through the bitter fruits of bodily life [Note: [Col. 0245] Deuteronomy 32:32.], and a mind drunk with the poisons of wickedness spewed forth the wrath of asps. But he who is powerful has done great things for us [Note: [Col. 0245] Luke 1:49.]; he sent from heaven and delivered us [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 56:4.]; he sent his mercy through you, renewed the face of our earth [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 103:30.], and made us your planting for himself in his vineyard.

Therefore, blessed and most revered father, you must continually and unceasingly pray to the Lord that he look down from heaven and visit these vines which your right hand planted [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 79:15.], so that, fastened to the true vine, we may live as branches pruned not for the fire but for fruit.

[Col. 0245A] 106 May he himself direct us—he who is both vine and life [Note: [Col. 0245] John 14:6 and 15:1.]—into every rule of his discipline and truth, watering us from his upper waters [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 103:13.] through your chaste and devout words, both fiery and sweet. For your words are drops of that willing rain which God set apart for his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 67:10.], which descended upon the fleece (see poem 22, line 157), being poured silently and gently upon the Virgin.

He is the one in whose showers we rejoice [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalms 64:11 and 71:6.] when he rises within us and lets fall upon the soul being reborn the first dew of his knowledge, so that he may heal all our sicknesses [Note: [Col. 0245] Isaiah 53:4–5; Psalm 102:3.]. For the dew that comes from him is health to us, because he is the fountain of life who sent his Word and healed us [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalms 35:10; 106:20.].

This Word of God is the willing rain, because not under compulsion as one subject to another, but by the consent of one equal to God, and in obedience to the duty of devotion, the Son humbled himself before the Father unto death, even death on a cross [Note: [Col. 0245] Philippians 2:8.], as he had said through the prophet: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 53:8.]. For the same Lord, both priest and victim, offered himself for us and by his own authority laid down his soul and took it up again [Note: [Col. 0245] John 10:18.]. Therefore this rain is willing: it poured itself forth of its own accord upon the parched lands, so that it might turn the desert into rivers [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 106:35.].

But how it was weakened, that one teaches who says: “For he was crucified in weakness” [Note: [Col. 0245] 2 Corinthians 13:4.]. And how it was strengthened and established [Note: [Col. 0245D] “Established.” Or “perfected”? The allusion is to Psalm 67: “And it was weakened; but you perfected it.”], you find in the same passage: “For,” he says, “he lives by the power of God” [Note: [Col. 0245] 2 Corinthians 13:4.].

4. Pray to this Lord until you prevail upon him, that he may not allow our fleeces—which he washed with your hands in the water of renewal, that is, baptism—to become dirty again, stained by our sins, or once more to be transformed after being dyed and infected by vices into purple [Latin: *phoenicium*; alternatively *phoeniceum*]. Rather, may he guard within us, through the watchfulness of your prayers, the gift of his grace; and may he not abandon the work of your hands in us until he ripens and perfects from us fruit and a crown for you.

Then, on that day, coming with rejoicing and carrying your sheaves in your filled bosom [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalm 125:6.], may you be able to say even concerning us, counted among your offspring and harvest [Note: [Col. 0246D] The Vatican manuscript reads “numbering.”]: “Behold, I and the children whom you have given me, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0245] Isaiah 8:18.].

But now fear of wearying you admonishes us—and not only that, but also fear of the sin which is not escaped through many words [Note: [Col. 0245] Proverbs 10:19.]—to place a bridle upon our mouth and, though belatedly, close the door of speech [Note: [Col. 0245] Psalms 140:3; Sirach 28:28.] with the ending of this letter.

Let the conclusion be a commendation of Cardamatus, whom we rejoice to have been renewed by the blessing of your hand, so that the dignity now assumed from the name of exorcist has given him reverence in place of the former lightness of his ridiculous stage-name. We were even more amazed and delighted that he also changed the disposition of his former condition through a religious office. For, as a constant participant at our table, he restricted himself to the measure of our appetite, so that he avoided neither our little vegetables nor our drinks. He can prove this by the attenuation of his body and the pallor of his face—unless, perhaps, on his return, he restored himself through the laborious journey and by renewing his former familiarity with his cups [Note: [Col. 0246D] Grinius’s, Schott’s, and Rosweyde’s editions add: “Farewell, father.”].

# LETTER XX

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Formerly Letter 16; the letter formerly numbered 20 is now 36. Written in the year 400 and sent with the preceding letter.]

Paulinus writes to Delphinus about the affection shown toward him by Anastasius, bishop of Rome, and Venerius, bishop of Milan. He congratulates him on the founding of the Church at Alingon and digresses to the spiritual temple which he wishes to be made within himself, so that Christ may dwell there.

To the most blessed and deservedly venerable father, DELPHINUS, PAULINUS.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] The Vienna manuscript reads: “To the most blessed and venerable, always most desired by us, and so forth.”]

1. It was indeed fitting for us, observing the teaching of wisdom, to impose a yoke upon our tongue and a scale upon our words [Note: [Col. 0245] Sirach 28:2.], so that we might avoid the doubled sin of both our many words and your weariness. But from the abundance of your charity our mouth is opened wide toward you [Note: [Col. 0245] 2 Corinthians 6:11.], and we cannot restrain the affection overflowing from our heart behind the closed door of our mouth, within the confines of a silent breast.

Therefore we speak to your venerable presence in another letter. For although the one in which we replied was so lengthy that it should be enough to fill you to disgust, nevertheless, since—as you recognize—we receive your conversations and return ours only after an exceedingly long interval of time, it is too little to speak to you in a single letter.

By this we give our soul some consolation, however slight: while we write letters to your affection, fixing our whole heart upon your face, we suddenly forget that you are absent and, as though lingering in conversation with you who are present, draw out our words at greater length. Thus, although we do not quench the burning thirst of our desires—for that is not even advantageous to us—we mitigate it by placing before our inner eyes the image of your appearance and conversation.

For although our dwelling-place may seem prolonged far from the places of your habitation [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalm 119:5.], our spirit is not separated from the embrace of your affection. For who, he says, will separate us from the love of Christ? If neither death nor life nor any other creature [Note: [Col. 0247] Romans 8:35.], how much less bodily absence, which cannot dissolve spiritual presence? For the stronger the spirit is than the flesh, the more powerful is the joining of souls than of bodies; and the presence of the inner persons is better than that of outward persons separated, who are often joined in place without cause if they are separated in mind.

For, he says, it is not the Jew who is one outwardly, nor circumcision that is in the flesh, but the Jew who is one inwardly, circumcised in spirit, not in the letter, whose glory is not from human beings but from God [Note: [Col. 0247] Romans 2:28–29.]. Therefore, by this same law—by which circumcision in the heart is truer than cutting in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0247D] The Vienna manuscript reads “circumcision.” The editions of Bade and Gravius read “joining.”]—and presence joined and held together in spirit is firmer than presence joined in the body, we are always with you, and you with us.

For although we are separated in face for a time—that is, divided and distant; see Letter 29, no. 9—we nevertheless remain always joined in heart within you, while you in turn dwell in our innermost being, both “to die with” and “to live with” [Note: [Col. 0247] 2 Corinthians 7:3.].

Since it belongs to the care and consolation of that same charity that we should become mutually aware of our actions, so that we may burn with more tolerable concern for one another when absent if we are not uncertain about each other, we inform your affection—which we know to be most solicitous about all our affairs—that, with Christ’s favor, we are well, as you pray, though not robust in body, yet sound.

We are “poor in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0247] Matthew 5:3.], not in our own spirit but in God’s, in need of his goodness and abounding in our own wickedness. This is what our Cardamatus reported, saying that you had ordered us to inform you from here also about our circumstances in the Lord.

2. Let your venerable presence know that your holy brother, Pope Anastasius of the City (see note 62), is exceedingly fond of our humility. As soon as he began to have the opportunity to offer us his affection, he hastened not merely to accept it from us but to thrust it upon us with the most devout kindness.

Not long after his ordination, he sent letters concerning us to the bishops of Campania, full of religion, piety, and peace, both to declare his own affection and to provide others with an example of his benevolence. Then, when we had come to Rome according to the customary solemn observance for the feast of the blessed apostles, he received us as graciously as he did honorably.

After some time, he even deigned to invite us to his own feast-day (see note 63), which he usually extends only to his fellow priests—that is, his suffragans. He was not offended by our excuse; rather, accepting the duty of our letter, which we had offered in place of our presence, he received us, though absent, with a father’s affection.

Finally, if the Lord grants us leave to return to him at the customary solemn season, I hope to obtain from him a letter to your holiness, through which he may also begin to commend us to you.

3. The new bishop of Milan, hitherto your son and now your brother, Venerius, had already written to us after his ordination. But since Cardamatus reported that you had also ordered this, we wrote to him through Cardamatus himself, so that he might know that the opportunity was available, if he wished to acknowledge the duty of the proper affection, to write to your blessedness and commend his beginnings to your heart.

We, however, rejoice and glory in the Lord, because you work visibly and invisibly for our salvation [Note: [Col. 0247D] Thus the Vienna manuscript. Previously it read: “you work for our salvation: you build our house.”], truly a good father and saving patron. Invisibly, you build us up through your prayers, asking that the kingdom of God be made within us; visibly, you work for us in the construction of churches, so that you may make us share with him whose house deserved to be visited by Christ, because it had received testimony from the devout people concerning the building of the synagogue [Note: [Col. 0247] Luke 7:5.]—which is now the Church.

We confess to your venerable piety that, as we read that portion of your letter in which you signified that, through your agency, a new daughter had been born in the name of the Lord for the Church at Alingon (see note 65) and had grown up until the day of its dedication, our spirit exulted in God our Savior [Note: [Col. 0247] Luke 1:47.] as though we were present among the gatherings of those dedicating it and were singing those words of prophetic joy from the Psalms:

“Rejoice in God our helper; take up the psalm and give the tambourine” [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalm 80:2.]. “Bring offerings and enter the courts of the Lord; worship the Lord in his holy court” [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalm 95:8, according to the Roman Psalter.]. Or that other saying of the same prophet: “Rise, Lord, to your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalm 131:8.]. “Let your priests be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice. Establish their day” [Note: [Col. 0248D] “Their own.” I would read “a festival,” since there is an allusion to Psalm 117: “Establish the solemn festival day.” Greek: ἐορτὴν, “festival.”.] [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalm 117:27.].

4. But since you have deigned to report that certain people on the side of him through whose envy death entered the world [Note: [Col. 0247] Wisdom 2:24.] gnash their teeth and waste away [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalm 111:10.], we are not surprised. For when the temple of God was being rebuilt in Jerusalem, the Assyrians were jealous [Note: [Col. 0247] 1 Esdras 4:4; 5:3.] and often tried to obstruct the rising structure by hostile incursions.

But because the one who is in us is mightier than the one who is in this world [Note: [Col. 0247] 1 John 4:4.], their desire will perish [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalm 111:10.], while ours will be strengthened, because we hope in his mercy, which never puts to shame those who hope in him [Note: [Col. 0247] Psalms 12:6 and 146:11.].

Let your holiness only pray, as you do, so that a house may be built in us by Christ and in Christ. For unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain [Note: [Col. 0249] Psalm 126:1.]. And unless this house is founded upon the rock, which is Christ [Note: [Col. 0249] 1 Corinthians 10:4.] [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 7:24.], it will not be able to withstand the winds of spiritual wickedness and the torrents of worldly temptations.

5. Pray that the Lord Jesus may enter our heart as into his temple [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 21:12.], brandish the scourge of his mercy with which he chastises every son whom he receives, and drive from the perceptions of our mind, as from the merchants of the temple, every traffic and contagion of iniquity [Note: [Col. 0249] John 2:15; Proverbs 3:12; Revelation 3:19.].

May he drive from us the oxen, the sellers of doves, and the tables of the money-changers, so that, cleansed from all impurity and greed, we may hold fast to the chaste simplicity of faith and love. For the figure of Christ is preserved wherever Caesar’s coin is driven out [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 22:21.]; where there are no oxen, the mangers are clean [Note: [Col. 0249] Proverbs 14:4, according to the Septuagint.]; and uncorrupted faith is retained where the dove is not sold.

[Note: [Col. 0249D] The Vienna manuscript reads: “For when we sin, we sell ourselves to the devil.”]

For unless we hand ourselves over to God, we sell ourselves to the devil. Hence the old man who gave himself over to the advice of the evil-speaking serpent [Note: [Col. 0249] Genesis 3:6.] is said to have been sold under sin [Note: [Col. 0249] Romans 7:14.].

Finally, as one who had been sold, he needed a Redeemer, who bought us at a great price [Note: [Col. 0249] 1 Corinthians 6:20.], so that we might no longer belong either to the devil or to ourselves. Changed from a brood of vipers into a royal and priestly race [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 3:7; 1 Peter 2:9.], we were made his blood: he took souls that had first degenerated from the noble institution of our origin and, while sin endured, had become worthless, and made them precious through the commerce of his blood, granting us, in his ungrudging mercy, to become his coheirs and children of God [Note: [Col. 0249] Romans 8:17.].

Let us exult and glory in him who became the refuge of the poor [Note: [Col. 0249] Psalm 9:10.] so that he might humble the eyes of the proud [Note: [Col. 0249] Psalm 17:28.]. Let us offer him both a temple in ourselves and a sacrifice, cleansing ourselves, if we can, from the old leaven [Note: [Col. 0249D] The Vienna manuscript reads “from the old.”], so that we may become unleavened [Note: [Col. 0249] 1 Corinthians 5:8.], and so that Christ, who was sacrificed for us, may himself feast within us.

6. Let us remember that, separated from the womb of the earth and from our kindred, we were made children of Delphinus, so that we might become those fish which traverse the paths of the sea [Note: [Col. 0249] Psalm 8:9.].

Let us remember that you have become for us not only a father but also a Peter, because you sent the hook to me [Note: [Col. 0249D] Thus the Vienna manuscript. The preposition *de* is absent from the other manuscripts.] so that I might be drawn out from the deep and bitter waves of this world and become a catch destined for salvation; that I might die to the nature to which I was living and live to the Lord to whom I had been dead.

But if I am your fish, I ought to carry in my mouth a precious coin [Note: [Col. 0249D] Thus the Vienna manuscript, better than the other manuscripts, which read “precious.”] [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 17:26.] in which there shines not Caesar’s figure and inscription [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 22:21; Mark 12:16; Luke 20:24.], but the living and life-giving image of the eternal King—namely, the faith of truth—which has impressed the coinage of your teaching [Note: [Col. 0249D] The Regius manuscript, together with four editions, reads “admonitions”; the Vienna manuscript reads “coinage.”] and the symbol of your ring upon the coin of my heart and the wax of my mind.

For your teaching is silver tested by fire, tried in the earth, purified sevenfold [Note: [Col. 0250D] Thus Paulinus reads in Letter 23 to Severus, no. 7. The Vienna manuscript, in accordance with the Vulgate and the old Roman, Gallican, and Septuagint Psalters, reads “seven times.”] [Note: [Col. 0249] Psalm 11:7.].

7. May the Lord grant through your prayers that I may be the coin of your coinage, the fish of your hook, the branch of your vine, the son of your chaste womb. For Delphinus’s sons will be reckoned among the sons of Aaron [Note: [Col. 0249] Lev. X, 1.]; but not with those who offered strange fire to the Lord and were kindled by divine fire—either the fire that they extinguished in their hearts, or the fire that they did not possess [Note: [Col. 0250D] We have added “or did not possess” from the Viennese and Regius manuscripts and the edition of Schott; this is confirmed by Epistle 44 to Aper and Amanda, §5.].

May your sons have a heart that is burning [Col. 0250B] [Note: [Col. 0249] Luke XXIV, 32.], not with the wicked fires of desires and worldly enticements, but with that fire which the Lord came to kindle in us, concerning which he says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire, if it is already kindled?” [Note: [Col. 0249] Luke XII, 49.] Therefore let neither avarice, nor the lust of the eyes, nor the harmful love of temporal things burn in us with a pestilential fire—for that fire is foreign to God. Rather, may our God himself, who is a consuming fire [Note: [Col. 0249] Heb. XII, 29.], recognize his own fire in us, so that we may say: “The Lord is our illumination and our salvation; whom shall we fear?” [Note: [Col. 0250D] The Viennese manuscript adds this phrase.] [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. XXVI, 1.]

This fire illuminates hearts and consumes sins; it extinguishes the darkness by which we are put to death and kindles the light by which we are given life. If our lamps are always burning with this fire [Note: [Col. 0249] Luke XII, 35.], we shall confidently say: “And if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, because you are with me” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. XXII, 4, according to the Roman Psalter.]. Illuminated by this fire, and inflamed by its heat toward a thirst for living water and a longing for the Lord, we shall truly say: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. XLI, 2.]. “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. XXXV, 10.] [Note: [Col. 0250D] Thus Augustine in his commentary on Psalm XXXV, verse 10. The verb “is” is absent from the Greek Septuagint.] [Note: [Col. 0250D] The Rosweyd edition adds at the end: “Farewell, father.”]

## EPISTLE XXI

[Note: [Col. 0249D] Otherwise numbered 24; the one that was 21 is now 12. Written in the year 400, at the same time as the two preceding letters.]

In the beginning and conclusion of the letter he explains the praises of Cardamas. Around the middle he magnificently describes the beginning of John’s Gospel and the evangelist himself.

To the holy, deservedly venerable, and most beloved brother AMANDUS, PAULINUS.

### 1

We marvel in the sacred history of the Kings at Asahel, that brother of Joab, who was swift of foot and light in his running, so that he rivaled deer and wild goats in speed [Note: [Col. 0251] II Kings II, 18.]. No less do we stand amazed, when reading, at that giant among the Philistines [Note: [Col. 0251] I Kings XVII, 4; II Kings XXI, 20.], who had grown beyond the stature and measure of the human body [Note: [Col. 0251D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Sacchinius. Other codices read “the measure.”]. His hands, armed with six fingers, and his feet, articulated with the same number of toes, made him stronger and swifter than the others. Yet against David, who fought by the hand of God and was always unconquered in the image of Christ, the hand and strength of no mighty enemy prevailed; for the proud exaltation of the devil was cast down in the great things belonging to others, while the saving form of God, powerful through humility, conquered in our little ones.

### 2

But let us return to the beginning of the letter, which we began from the feet [112], so that we may praise the Lord’s runner—namely, Cardamas, the servant of the Lord (see Epistle 40, §3)—by marked examples from the divine law of the swift men of old. That blessed swiftness of the youthful apostle in the Gospel also comes to our aid: he ran ahead to the Lord’s tomb, equal to Peter in eagerness to run but slower because of his greater age [Note: [Col. 0251] John XX, 4.], so that he might be the first to see the resurrection of the body—he who alone reclined upon the Lord’s breast [Note: [Col. 0251] John XIII, 23, and XXI, 20.].

From that breast he had drawn twin springs into the basin of his heart, and later, as herald of the Revelation—that is, the Apocalypse—and of the Gospel, he poured them out throughout the world. The bodily agility of his feet he afterward completed with spiritual speed, running with beautiful feet of speech throughout the whole world among its peoples.

### 3

He is remembered as the last writer of the Gospel, born into an age extending beyond all the times of the apostles. Thus, as the Chosen Vessel says of him, he added, as it were, a column [Col. 0251C] of support to the foundations of the Church, confirming the earlier Gospel writers with harmonious authority. He was the last author in chronological order, but first in the beginning of the mystery; for alone among the four rivers, flowing from the very summit of the divine Head’s fountain, he thunders from a lofty cloud:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” [Note: [Col. 0251] John I, 1; Gen. I, 1.].

He surpassed Moses, who extended the boundaries of knowledge—even to the beginning of the world and the origins of visible creatures—as far as the edge of his mind could reach. John, flying higher than the other evangelists, who began the Gospel of the resurrection either from the human birth of the Savior [Note: [Col. 0251] Matt. I, 1.], or from the figurative sacrifice of the Law, or from the prophetic proclamation of the precursor, John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0251] Luke I, 5; Mark I, 2.], penetrated even into the heavens.

Nor did he stop with the angels: he passed beyond the archangels and all the creatures above, the powers, principalities, dominions, and thrones [Col. 0251D], and directed his lofty mind toward the Creator himself. Beginning from that ineffable generation, he proclaimed the Son coeternal, consubstantial, co-omnipotent, and co-creator [Col. 0252A] with the Father, seeing God from God in the Holy Spirit; for in him the Trinity of the Godhead is fulfilled, and the one Godhead of the Trinity is seen.

The Spirit of God, like the Word of God, is each God, while the one Head remains; and, flowing from the one fountain of the Father, the Son by being born and the Spirit by proceeding will be distinct rather than divided, each person’s individual property remaining intact (perhaps the text should read *sunt*, “are”).

### 4

Thus blessed John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast [Note: [Col. 0251] John XIII, 23; and XXI, 20.] and had drunk from the very heart of the wisdom that created all things thoughts higher than those of every creature, intoxicated with the Holy Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God [Note: [Col. 0251] I Cor. II, 10.], made the beginning of the Gospel from the innermost and infinite source of all beginnings. By this single passage all the mouths of the devil that bark through the heretics are shut.

The first tongue of Arius is cut off; and the blasphemy of Sabellius is also emptied [Note: [Col. 0251D] Thus the Viennese and Regius manuscripts. In the others: “the blasphemies are emptied.”], when the same sentence of our Fisherman expresses both the unity of the Godhead in the Father and the Son and the distinction of their persons [Note: [Col. 0251D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. Other codices read “of the divinity.”].

In the same chapter Photinus too is cast out, that mad teacher who imagined only a human beginning in Christ; and Marcion, who separates the God of the Law from the God of the Gospel, is extinguished; and Mani, denier of the true Creator and inventor of a false one, is crushed, immediately confounded by the voice of that same heavenly Gospel.

I call this Gospel heavenly because its beginning starts from that origin which is above all the heavens and before all ages. For it hears from this Word of God, who is God: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Note: [Col. 0251] John I, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0252D] We restored this reading from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and four printed editions; Paulinus likewise says in Epistle 23 to Severus, §2, “the Word of God, God.” Rosweyd’s edition reads: “from this Word of God he hears.”].

But the Gnostic, who boasts in the name of false knowledge and turns every understanding of his perverse mind into certain airy phantoms, imagining bodily things spiritually, is compelled by the same author to believe in the flesh of Christ, when he says of the same Word who was God with God: “And the Word became flesh” [Note: [Col. 0251] John I, 14.].

Yet he did not become flesh as certain others, said to hiss like serpents, claim—as though he migrated from his own nature into ours. Rather, remaining in himself what he was, he began, for our sake, to be what he was not [Note: [Col. 0252D] We have added “in himself” from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the Grinarius and Schott editions.].

### 5

I am going much too far, while I so abuse your concord’s indulgence that I am not afraid either to weary you with many words or to err before you through foolishness. For I know that, although you are wise, you nevertheless willingly bear with your foolish fellow [Note: [Col. 0251] II Cor. XI, 19.], through that love which bears all things and never fails [Note: [Col. 0251] I Cor. XIII, 7.].

Still, I shall now say to myself, “I will guard the ways of my speech, lest I sin with my tongue” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. XXXVIII, 2.], and I shall descend briefly to Cardamas—that is, our Asahel—whose feet you have made like those of a deer [Note: [Col. 0251] II Kings II, 18.], renewing his youth like the eagle’s [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. CII, 5.] through the abundance [Col. 0253A] of your love, by which you established him, received in view of our humility, in the courts of the Lord’s house, so that he might be freer as a man once he had begun to be Christ’s freedman [Note: [Col. 0253D] The Viennese manuscript reads “fuller.”].

By this devotion you caused him to blossom again not only in spirit but also in body, so that, filled from your very inmost being with the affection with which you love us, he might bring your longings to us and in turn console ours. Moving almost ceremonially among us despite such great distances between our regions, he guards the difficult roads for the sake of your words [114] [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. XVI, 4.].

We believe that from the very letters of your holiness which he carries he takes wings like a dove [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. LIV, 7.], and that from your prayers he receives strength in his feet by which he may travel to us. Yet we rejoice with him over this very grace, by which he has been placed in so great a ministry [Note: [Col. 0253D] The Regius manuscript reads “service.”] [Col. 0253B] of love: that he may serve in freedom, run about in old age, and prefer to spend the rest of his earned leisure in the labor of pilgrimage rather than in sitting at home.

For he avoids treading the roads of the sluggish, strewn with thorns [Note: [Col. 0253] Prov. XV, 19.], lest he be turned into misery while the thorn of wretched anxiety is driven into him through the unproductive leisure of idleness. Thus the tireless man rejoices to run his course, lest, while sluggish idleness wears him down, the poverty that follows the lazy should meet him like a good runner [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. XXXI, 4; Ps. XVIII, 6; Prov. VI, 11.].

When he comes to us, how he bathes and fills our soul with joy through the good news of your health! He makes our bones fat [Note: [Col. 0253] Prov. XV, 30.] and becomes a voice of gladness in our tents [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. CXVII, 15.], when, our minds refreshed by the consolation we desired, we say: “The Lord remembered us and blessed us” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. CXIII, 12.].

### 6

Let us rejoice and be glad in him [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. CXVII, 24.], who grants a petition to the one who asks and gives us the desire of our soul, for he goes before us with the blessing of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. XX, 3, according to the Septuagint.].

What blessing can now be sweeter for us, or what sweetness more pleasant, than the fruit and consolation of love that comes to us in such abundance from your letters? In them we embrace pledges, as it were, both of your mouth and of your heart; for your words are the offspring of your soul: “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” [Note: [Col. 0253] Matt. XI, 34.].

Therefore we love Cardamas when he comes in your speech, and commend him to you when he departs in ours. He is worthy that his old age should rest in abundant mercy [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. XCI, 11.], since he labors for the sake of love, longing, and service [Note: [Col. 0253D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. The printed editions read “for charity.”].

Moreover, what we admired in him more than the speed of his gray hairs [Note: [Col. 0253D] Written in the year 400 at its end.], was that he advanced so far from the title of exorcist toward frugality that he did not shrink from being almost our daily guest. When he was sprinkled with rare and tiny cups, scarcely wetting the surface of his lips, he made no complaint about the hardship of an empty stomach or dry throat.

In every respect Cardamas appeared to us so pleasing that we saw in him a cleric commendable to human beings and an exorcist terrifying to demons. For the rest, brother, we commend both him and all our people and ourselves to you, so that through you we may be commended to the Lord by earnest prayers: that the freedom of all our people may serve the eternal Lord, and that our servitude in Christ may obtain the merit of eternal freedom.

## EPISTLE XXII

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Otherwise numbered 7; the one that was 22 is now 9. Written in the year 400.]

He elegantly describes the character of dissolute people, both secular and monastic, and teaches what sort of associates are suitable for monks.

To his like-minded brother SEVERUS, PAULINUS.

### 1

The letters that you had sent through that unspiritual monk of ours were intercepted and carried to us by a truly spiritual messenger, namely our son Sorianus. In him we perceived that the Lord had bestowed a twofold favor: first, lest he come to us empty of your conversation, since he had longed for us with affection infused from your own inmost being; and again, lest Marracinus bring us your letters.

Divinely inspired, as I believe, either by shame at seeing us or by reluctance to prolong his journey beyond Rome, he gave your letters in Rome to the brother mentioned above, rejoicing at the opportunity for the desired shortcut by which he thought he had secured himself against your commands, so that he would not be compelled either to pretend to be a monk, as you had ordered, or to see one in me, as was necessary.

Let him therefore keep his *armilausa* [Note: See notes 66 and 67.], his leggings, and his cheeks—of which he feared both to alter one and to lower the other [Note: [Col. 0254D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. The others read: “to change some, to remove others.”].

### 2

Let our fellow-servants and fellow-gray-haired companions approach and visit us—not proud in embroidered garments, but humble in rough hair shirts; not cloaked in a short *chlamys* [Note: See note 68.], but wrapped in little mantles; not girded with a belt, but with a rope; not wearing their hair long with the shameless brow of a shorn head, but with chaste unattractiveness having their hair cut close to the skin, unevenly half-shorn, and their foreheads left bare by close shaving.

Let them be unadorned with the adornment of modesty, modestly unkempt, and honorably despised. Even scorning the body’s natural appearance for the sake of inward discipline, let them deliberately disfigure themselves, so that they may become decently dishonorable in face while being salutorily honorable in mind [Note: [Col. 0254D] The Viennese manuscript reads “prudently.” We have retained the common reading, confirmed by Epistle 23 to Severus, §31: “modestly shameless, and piously improper.”].

The face, dress, and odor of such men produce nausea in those for whom the odor of death is an odor leading to life [Note: [Col. 0253] II Cor. II, 16.]; for whom what is bitter is sweet [Note: [Col. 0253] Isa. V, 20.], what is chaste is disgraceful, and what is holy is hostile.

Therefore it is right that we repay them in kind, so that their odor may be for us like the odor of death, and so that we may not cease to be the odor of Christ. For what right have they to be angry with us if, in turn, the odor of their life stinks to us, when our odor is death to them?

He loathes my fasting; I cannot endure his drunkenness. He avoids the breath of a speaking monk; I flee the breath of a belching braggart. If the dryness of our throat displeases them, the rawness of their appetite displeases us. If the aridity of frugality offends them, the greed of their bellies offends us.

Let them therefore see us not drunk in the morning but fasting in the evening; not swollen with yesterday’s wine but abstinent today [Note: See Carm. 6, verse 68.]; not madly unstable from the excess of lust, but wholly wounded by the vigils of decency and soberly intoxicated—made to stagger by restraint, not by an abyss of food.

### 3

We rejoice that we have received such a bearer of your letter. I ask that you receive him as though he had come to me from you. Among those who have come to me in place of your brotherhood, this man too must be counted, since the Lord, so that he might be counted by you in this way, entrusted him with your letters even without your knowledge.

I think that you too will assign to him the benefit of this divine grace, through whom it was also granted to you that your letters should be brought to us by a bearer who was not your own body. Yet, with his permission, I wish to praise Sorianus, lest you accuse me of him again [Note: [Col. 0255D] This is the reading required; Sacchinius should not be followed, since he thinks “Marracinus” should be restored in place of “Sorianus.” Who does not see that the words “his” and “him” refer to Marracinus, who was mentioned above in §1?].

I believe that by recalling the things in which one who is ashamed to be or appear to be a monk must necessarily glory, I praised him more than I blamed him. Finally, you remember that in Virgil the Fury is praised for the very things usually held against her. But do not slander me because I have taken something from a poet no longer belonging to our studies, as though I had violated my purpose. I attest that I did this on the authority of your example; for I possess your letter, whose closing words are:

“Live happily, you whose fortune has been fulfilled.”

VIRGIL, *Aeneid* III.

[Col. 0255C] And you also mentioned, in place of a domestic dwelling, the household hearth, recalling the prologue of Plautus.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Written at the end of the year 400.]

Severus sends Paulinus a cook suitable for preparing monastic food.

After I learned that all your cooks had resigned from your kitchen—for I suppose they disdained to provide service with cheap dishes—I sent you a little boy from our workshop, sufficiently trained to cook pale beans, season humble beets with vinegar and broth, and place cheap porridge before the hungry throats of monks; ignorant of pepper, unfamiliar with laserwort, fond of cumin, and exceptionally skilled at noisily working a mortar with sweet-smelling herbs.

He has one fault: he is no civil enemy of all gardens. If he is admitted, he will cut down everything nearby with his sword and will never be satisfied with the slaughter of mallows. Nor will he be troublesome to you when wood must be supplied to him: he will burn whatever is at hand, cut it down, and will not hesitate to lay hands upon the roofs and remove the ancient beams from the household shrines.

We wish you to have him, endowed with these habits and virtues [117], not as a slave but as a son in place of a slave, since you are not ashamed to be the father of the least. I would have been willing to serve you in his place; but if the will is a portion of the deed, simply see to it that amid your happy lunches and dinners you remember me. For it is more fitting to be your servant than the master of others.

Pray for me.

## EPISTLE XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Otherwise numbered 3 and 4; the one that was 23 is now 2. Written at the beginning of the year 401.]

He praises Severus’s affection; likewise he elegantly and piously commends Victor, whom Severus sent to him, and Victor’s service in preparing food according to monastic custom.
