From the barbering service Victor also performed for him, he discusses hair at length; and, after allegorically expounding the entire story of Samson and the sinful woman at Christ’s feet [Col. 0256B], he adds a thoroughly golden conclusion concerning the love of Christ.

To his brother SEVERUS, PAULINUS.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] The Viennese manuscript: “Paulinus, servant of Christ Jesus, to Severus, dearest brother according to the common faith in God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior, greeting.”]

### 1

Why do you compel us to love you more? The total admits no increase. If the sea can overflow its boundaries [Note: [Col. 0255] Prov. VIII, 29; Jer. V, 22.], and whatever things preserve their natural fullness can experience temporal growth [Note: [Col. 0256D] The Regius manuscript reads “in time.”], then our love for you too can be heaped up. We shall complete it at its limit when we love you as ourselves.

Thus, just as we cannot add a cubit to our stature [Note: [Col. 0255] Matt. VI, 27.], so we cannot add to the fullness of our love for you; yet we place no limit on our longing. You think that you satisfy us by this constant display of your honor and devotion, by which you try to compensate for your presence through such frequent letters. Rather, you trouble the appetite of our love, and you satisfy us less through the grace of your letters the more, through that very attentiveness and the humanity of your speech, you give us cause to long for you yourself, brother, so uniquely united with us in Christ.

For what can be done more diligently toward God and one’s neighbor than what you exhibit toward Christ in us? In him the twofold commandment of God is fulfilled: for he is both God to us by the majesty of his nature and, by assuming our nature, has become our neighbor.

As this advances in you, your love is brought to completion: its perfection is in him who is infinite [Note: [Col. 0256D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Other manuscripts, with Rosweyd’s edition, read “perfected in the infinite.”], because it reaches its end in Christ, whose greatness has no end [Note: [Col. 0255] Ps. CXLIV, 3.]. But our end in him must be that through him we may live without end.

For Christ is both our universal beginning, since all things are through him [Note: [Col. 0255] Rom. XI, 36.], and our particular summit, since he is the head of the body whose members we are [Note: [Col. 0255] Eph. I, 22; Col. I, 18.].

The Lord is sweet and upright, sweet to me in you; and what a great abundance of his sweetness you are to me! [Note: [Col. 0257D] Thus three manuscript codices. The printed editions read “of him?” or “For you are to me.”] [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. XXIV, 8, and XXX, 20.] For however great you are, in mind and speech alike, you are wholly longing. To me you taste of Christ’s sweetness, like a garden, like the fragrance of a full field [Note: [Col. 0257] Gen. XXVII, 27.], which you have gathered while running toward the fragrance of his ointments.

You too are a field belonging to him, who in turn is a field for us. For in him we sow, and from him we reap [Note: [Col. 0257D] The same Vatican manuscript reads “in him.”].

You are not a field rough with thorns, dry with sand, or harsh and bare with stones, in which the seed is either choked, abandoned, or scorched [Note: [Col. 0257] Matt. XIII, 4.]; you are that field which God blessed with the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth [Note: [Col. 0257] Gen. XXVII, 28.].

Therefore your tongue rains the word of God, and your heart, fertile for God, multiplies the seed it has received into spiritual fruit, so that the reaper may fill his hand with your fruits and the one who gathers sheaves may fill his bosom [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. CXXVIII, 7.]. That is, God himself, who is both the sower and the reaper of his word in us.

He is also the hand—he who is the right hand of God—which we fill with good works. He is likewise that bosom of Abraham in which we rest in return for our works [Note: [Col. 0257] Luke XVI, 22.].

### 2

Thus this God, abundant in your love for us, blesses, visits, feeds, and enlightens us not only through your letters but also through their messengers, opening to us by both gifts the good treasure of your heart. “For out of the abundance” [Note: See note 69.] “of the heart the mouth speaks” [Note: [Col. 0257] Matt. XII, 34.]; and, as the saying goes, “every living creature gathers to its kind” [Note: [Col. 0257] Sirach XIII, 20.].

Therefore God has blessed you, because the innocent and upright have clung to you [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. XXIV, 21, and XXV, 5.], and you do not sit with the ungodly [Note: [Col. 0257D] Thus the Vatican and Viennese manuscripts. The Regius manuscript and the printed editions read “you have not sat.”]. You hate iniquity and love your soul [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. X, 6; John XII, 25.], which you cast away in Christ so that, lost to this life, it might be preserved for eternal life, gaining itself by loss of itself if, through Christ’s love, it becomes worthless in its own eyes.

With this affection we smell the sweetness of your soul—worthless to you but precious to God—in the honeycombs of your mouth breathing Christ, and we bless the Lord, the Word of God, God [Note: [Col. 0258D] The manuscripts read thus. The Schott and Rosweyd editions read “we bless the gift of God, the word of the Lord”; three printed editions read “the house of God.”].

He, just as in that very man whom he bore, likewise passes through certain stages of bodily age in our minds: he is born, grows, becomes strong, and grows old. But we must pray that in us he not remain for long or forever a child, weak, and poor.

In you, as we rejoice to say—for your good is our glory—we recognize his progress: great in goodness, little in wickedness, old in wisdom, strong in faith, poor in the spirit of holy humility, and rich in love [Note: [Col. 0257] I Cor. XIV, 20.].

For by your earlier services toward our humility you had surpassed others: as we have often testified, more devoted than all our friends, more reverent than our neighbors, and more attentive than our brothers [Col. 0258A]. Now, in this exchange of our visitation, you have surpassed even yourself by your extraordinary kindness.

It was enough for us to earn your letters through annual journeys and to see those whom you sent, in whom we retained not only an image of your presence but also of your faith. Yet it was not enough for you to celebrate the established observance through its customary fulfillment.

Your great affection made the winter’s delay in keeping silent from us seem long [Note: [Col. 0258D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. The printed editions read “to be silent.”]. Your heart grew warm within you, and in meditation upon devotion a holy fire of good impatience blazed up in you [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. XXXVIII, 4.]. Nor was it enough to hasten the dispatch of your letters to us (Latin: perhaps *editionem*, “the sending”; see Epistle 5, §4), unless you also increased the grace of your speech by a chosen bearer drawn from your holy companions.

### 3

Blessed is the one whom you chose and took up for this service [Col. 0258B] [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. LXIV, 5.], by whom you lend to God at interest [Note: See note 70.]. For although we are sinners by the true confession of our conscience, you falsely think us holy, as you say, because of your opinion of our simplicity; nevertheless, you love us not with human love but with Christ’s love. Therefore you will receive a prophet’s reward [Note: [Col. 0257] Matt. X, 41.], because for Christ’s name you honor even non-prophets with the honor given to prophets.

We, however, deserve no comparable reward for the service by which we received brother Victor, who came to us in God’s name and as your representative, with intimate affection and great rejoicing. We did only what useless servants ought to do [Note: [Col. 0257] Luke XVII, 10.], because evident truth compelled us to receive and venerate in him a pure sheep.

He revealed himself not only as a sheep in its fleece but also as one whose spirit was gentle [Note: [Col. 0258D] Thus the three Regius, Vatican, and Viennese manuscript codices. The printed editions read “in the gentleness of his spirit.” The manuscript reading is confirmed by Epistle 19 to Delphinus, §2, “rooted in the spirit of gentleness on the way of peace,” and by Epistle 27 to Severus, §3, where nearly the same words are used: “poor in the spirit of gentleness.”], and who displayed Christ’s modesty in his speech and silence [Col. 0258C].

We truly recognized in him the pattern of the blessed saints Martin and Clarus, whose disciple, by your direction, we learned him to be, following his illustrious teacher at a short distance. Victor declared that he was the descendant of one of them through rebirth and the companion of the other on the way—the son of peace [Note: [Col. 0257] Luke X, 6.].

He was truly, as you wrote, a man humble in heart before God [Note: [Col. 0257] Matt. XI, 29.], not humble in grace: a vessel of mercy and a dwelling of the Most High, who receives him and delights in the peaceful hospitality of his trembling soul.

He brought us additional blessings beyond those twin blessings that he carried from you in letters and cloaks: blessings from the riches of his mind. He was most welcome to us not only in spiritual companionship but also diligent in bodily service. I dare to disclose a matter that burdens us, while concealing nothing of his virtues from you, since I know that they are your joy: for the good of one’s household is one’s portion.

### 4

He served me—yes, I say, he served me. And woe to me, miserable man, that I allowed it. He served a sinner, though he did not serve sin; and I, unworthy, was ministered to by a servant of righteousness.

Yet I hope for some relief from so great a burden, because I did not arrogantly claim the service of the holy brother, but accepted it to attest my love and, in faith, to receive his blessing [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Viennese manuscript reads “to arouse”; the Regius reads “to grieve.”]. For his holy service in God’s name was a blessing to me, and his loving service was a servant-act in the spirit of freedom.

For this reason I accepted his voluntary good deed [Note: [Col. 0259] Philemon 14.] for his own benefit, presuming that he would become more powerful in pleading for me the more merit he had acquired through religious works [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Vatican manuscript reads “religious.”]. Through his prayers he will certainly ensure that what came from me does not increase my burdens, since it also came from the fruits of his own works.

I loved, I confess, the blessing in his service, fearing that, if rejected, it would withdraw from me; for I held Scripture in mind: “He did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” [Note: [Col. 0259] Ps. CVIII, 18.].

Thus I gave myself entirely into his hands and inmost affections. Through the bowels of love, his servant hands anointed my limbs and applied themselves to my feet in washing [Note: [Col. 0259D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Others read “protected.”]. He was full of generous affection but seized the duties of a servant [Note: See note 71.], scarcely allowing me to pour water over his hands.

From your book [Note: See note 72.] I came to love this grace of service, so that I might at least taste a tiny drop from the sacred deeds of Martin. Every day he himself desired not only to wash my feet but, if I permitted it, to wipe my shoes as well—greedy for inward mastery and therefore tireless in bodily service.

### 5

But in the matter of washing feet, I confess that only once did I yield according to the apostolic example: I had read that the apostles offered their feet to the Lord for washing [Note: [Col. 0259] John XIII, 9.]. For they would have received no share in the inheritance except through the service of serving, since the good Lord and teacher of salvation bestowed the merit of ruling through the ministry of serving, and offered an example of human humility to those for whom he was preparing participation in divine sublimity.

When they perceived the mystery of so great a gift and understood the greatness of the good, those who at first had hesitated to offer their feet to the one who served now asked that not only their feet but their whole bodies, even to the head, be washed [121].

And I, venerating the Lord Jesus in brother Victor—for every faithful soul is from God, and the humble of heart is the heart of Christ [Note: [Col. 0259] Matt. XI, 29.]—confess that, as a remedy for my weakness [Col. 0259D], I desired that a fellow-servant better than I, with oil or water, should touch me.

My confidence in the help I sought was not fruitless. Like oil medicated by pious hands, the oil seemed to slip more gently into my marrow from the very gentleness of the one applying it, and my humbled bones rejoiced [Note: [Col. 0259] Ps. L, 10.].

“My soul, bless the Lord, and all that is within me, his holy name” [Note: [Col. 0259D] This is the reading of the Septuagint, the Old and Roman Psalters, and Augustine in his commentary on the Psalms.] [Col. 0260A] [Note: [Col. 0259] Ps. CII, 1.].

For this exercise of devotion, more beneficial to the renewal of my understanding than to my body, helped to invigorate my senses. The good brother, shaping my fragile limbs with his fashioning hand and setting them in order, also raised the strength of my mind by restoring my bones. Without doubt faith was working together with his hands: while the hand of the loving man guided my weak flesh, the grace of the believer washed my compassionate soul, and the oil of gladness, which outwardly was oil of health, came to be within me [Note: [Col. 0259] Ps. XLIV, 8.].

### 6

Now hear of another service of his toward our needs. Since he cared not only for our nourishment but also for our frugality, he taught us to take simple food easily: gruels cooked with a small quantity of oil and water. Yet he seasoned them with such abundant grace and such sweetness of charity that we did not long for cooks or condiments [Note: [Col. 0259] Ecclesiastes X, 1], because simplicity joined to charity mingled pure water with the oil of sweetness, which no annoyance of flies could spoil.

But as a spiritual cook he was more skilled at feeding the inner person, so that he might destroy the food of gluttony. He prepared our gruels not from fine wheat flour but from meal or millet. And lest he seem to deal more delicately with us in this respect—when he was preparing to initiate us into the monastic appetite [Note: See note 73]—he pounded beans together with millet, so that we might more quickly lay aside our senatorial fastidiousness [Note: [Col. 0260D] The Viennese manuscript reads *senatorum poneremus fastigium*, “we should lay aside the dignity of senators,” incorrectly. See St. Ambrose’s Letter 30 to Sabinus on Paulinus’s senatorial dignity; Jerome’s Letter 13 to Paulinus and Letter 3 to the daughters of Geruntius; and Ausonius’s Letter 25 to Paulinus.].

Yet in the blessing of sweetness we possessed the delicacies of the soul, rejoicing that our brother, even in bodily services, was spiritual and fed us with prophetic foods. For in the mixture of crushed ingredients he imitated those “bread[s] of tribulation” which the prophet Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0259] Ezekiel IV, 5] was commanded to prepare for himself from various kinds of grain and meal [Col. 0260C]. And, to signify the confusion of the Jews, who forgot God and “changed their glory into the likeness of a calf that eats grass” [Note: [Col. 0259] Psalm CV, 20], he was commanded to bake them in cow dung and, after they had been cooked beneath foul ashes, to eat them with tears [Note: [Col. 0260D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. The printed editions read “of captivity.”] in measured portions as captives.

Clearly, this was so that they might bodily foresee the punishment for their coming faithlessness, marked out in the prophet, and perhaps thus return to the Lord, if the wrath of the offended God should recall them to repentance—not only through what had been announced in words, but also through what had been represented in the bodies of the prophets.

### 7

Brother Victor therefore wished us to learn to humble the soul not only through fasting but also through food, and to eat sadly, in remembrance of former sins and with understanding of present ones, “the bread of sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0259] Psalm CXXVI, 2]. He spared us in part, however, mixing only beans with millet and millet-bread; though perhaps this was more a matter of forgetfulness than moderation. For the holy man, exercising faithful caution, would have feared to omit anything from Holy Scripture. And, to fulfill the prophetic bread’s entire recipe according to God’s word, he would also have mixed lentils, barley, and vetch into the [Note: [Col. 0261D] Thus the Belgian and Viennese manuscripts. Perhaps *crumilum* should be read. See note 74. The Regius manuscript has *crubilum*; Rosweyde’s edition, *cumulum*; Schott, in the margin, *cumerum*, as does Cauchius.] crumilum [Note: [Col. 0261] Ezekiel IV, 9] (see note 74), so that, as the heat outside their lips grew intense, the pot would crackle with fissures, as though the cooking of unlike fruits were resisting itself [Note: [Col. 0261D] So the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the editions of Badius and Schott. The editions of Grin and Sacchini have *sua*, “its own.” Rosweyde conjectured *vasis*, “of the vessels.”].

Nevertheless, filling a capacious vessel with the smaller number of grains, he brought us a dish smoking with a powerful aroma [Note: [Col. 0261] Thus the Regius manuscript and four printed editions. The Vatican and Viennese manuscripts and Schott’s and the Latin editions read “smoking.”]; and he filled not only the whole area of our little table but also the space of our cell with a pungent vapor.

And, to multiply the blessing for us, he brought to our little supper the meal of another prophet, so that he might set before us Elisha’s pot [Note: [Col. 0261] 2 Kings IV, 41]. Into it he put flour; he cooked in it not a poisonous herb but a seasoning of salvation, doing everything in the name of the Lord. Thus, safe and secure, we did not cry out to him, “Man of God, death is in the pot” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ibid., 40], because there is already life in our pot, since the Lord Jesus, the Word of God, became flesh and dwelt among us [Note: [Col. 0261] John I, 14].

And the earthen vessels of our body, which had slipped from his hands through the instability of our voluntary perversity and had been crushed by long-continued sins, he took upon himself, so that the Potter himself might renew them for better use [Note: [Col. 0261] Jeremiah XVIII, 6]. He himself was made from the clay of our body, as though a vessel—“a vessel ruined,” as he says [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm XXX, 13]—“in the likeness of sinful flesh,” so that “from sin he might condemn sin” [Note: [Col. 0261] Romans VIII, 3].

Therefore he says, “Moab is the pot of my hope” [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm LIX, 10], because he assumed a body not only from Judah but from Moab: that is, not only from the stock of the saints but also from that of sinners. Having, as it were, boiled away the rawness of our flesh in the pot of our humanity, he sanctified for us forever the food of his flesh. For, as he himself says, “his flesh is truly the food of life” [Note: [Col. 0261D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Grin’s edition; this reading is confirmed below, section 8, where the phrase “from the food, life” occurs.] [Note: [Col. 0261] John VI, 56 and 48].

This is also that “burning pot” according to Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0261] Jeremiah I, 13], burning up sins and consuming them with that fire of which he says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0261] Luke XII, 49]. May we desire that this fire also be kindled in us, so that we may be cooked in the pot of the Lord’s body—that is, in the Church. When our vices have been burned away and we have been purified, may we become silver tested by fire, approved by the earth, and purified sevenfold [Note: [Col. 0262D] Thus Paulinus in Letter 20 to Delphinus, section 6] [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm XI, 7].

Then may we remain in the same Lord not as branches destined to be burned, but as fruitful branches [Note: [Col. 0261] John XV, 2], that is, in the true vine. May that same Lord become for us the sweet cluster of grapes [Note: [Col. 0261] Numbers XIII, 24] which, suspended from the crossbeam of the cross, showed us both the fruit and the taste of the promised land. Thus we shall no longer pursue the worthless grasses of uncultivated soil, among which we might also risk plucking the poisonous clusters of wild vines [Col. 0261D].

This certainly happens to us when the soul, bristling with the thorns of worldly cares, whose cultivation is the word of God [Note: [Col. 0261] Luke VIII, 11], sighs over this brief life, barren of goodness. Amid useless activities we gather poisonous shoots—harmful sins—as though among wild grasses, and so cast death into the pot of our body or heart.

But thanks be to God, who has delivered us from “the body of this death through Jesus Christ our Lord” [Note: [Col. 0261] Romans VII, 24–25]. When he mingled the power of his Spirit with our weakness, and the word of God was poured into our inmost hearts, the bitterness of our wickedness and the barrenness of our uselessness were changed into sweetness and fruitfulness, as though by the sprinkling of life-giving salt that transforms them.

### 8

Let us return to Brother Victor, who, by the habitual practice of his service, which he performed in God’s name, made even the vessel of our little flour abundant with blessing, so that he gave us something also from the blessed jar of Elijah. This jar, filled by the sacred word to an unfailing sufficiency, enabled the heavenly prophet to feed the blessed widow of Zarephath with her sons during a three-year famine [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Kings XVII, 16].

In that widow, even then, Christ, through the prophet, was feeding his Church—not with grain but with the bread of the word. Of her he says, “Blessing his widow, I will surely bless her” [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm CXXXI, 15]—that widow whom the Apostle says, once her husband has died, is free to marry whom she wishes [Note: [Col. 0261] Romans VII, 3; 1 Corinthians VII, 39]. For when the law came to an end, whose end is Christ, the Church passed from grace into freedom and married Christ as though widowed from the law.

The oil of grace and the flour of blessing in this widow’s vessel have not now failed amid the hunger of all the nations outside [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Kings XVII, 16]. That ancient three-year famine aptly prefigured their wretched starvation of the food of life [Col. 0262C] and of faith in the Trinity.

But, to conclude this subject, our flour experienced the Lord’s grace in Brother Victor’s hand so fully that what previously scarcely sufficed for a few loaves [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Viennese manuscript adds “for a few”] now abounds even for gruels, and fills the monastic brotherhood, eager for its evening meal after the fast, with a double service: either with fermented rounds of bread or with loose meal [Note: [Col. 0262D] The editions of Badius, Grin, and Schott read “stuffs” or “fills out.”].

### 9

Yet although my Victor endeavored to accustom our stomach to stronger foods, the brother also prudently attended to our weakness in this matter: in consuming those gruels he filled up the deficiencies of our faith [Note: [Col. 0262D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Schott’s edition. Others read “in preparing them.” See note 16]. He completed the work of his hands with a single assistant for this dish, a man taken in from the countryside whom we nourish at home: old in bodily age but a child in understanding. For, as he was failing through old age, he was reborn through grace and blossomed from the oldness of the flesh into newness of life.

Brother Victor’s kitchen, together with its customary food [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Vatican manuscript reads “with food and suitable,” as though the man had been fattened from the country folk, and toothless.] and food suitable for him, fattened this man, who came from the country and was toothless.

“This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him. He delivered him from darkness and the shadow of death” [Note: [Col. 0263] Psalms XXXIII, 7, and CVI, 14]. Now sprinkled with hyssop and cleansed, he feasts in a voice of exultation and confession and cries:

“I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost. I will bless the Lord at all times. He gave me understanding, delivered me from the mire of filth, and put a new song into my mouth. I was young, and I grew old; yet my days did not fail in vanity. For he who is mighty has done great things for me. He gave me drink from the torrent of his delight, and my flesh blossomed again. He sent me abundant grain [Note: See note 76], and satisfied the hungry soul. Now my old age is in the mercy [Note: [Col. 0263D] So the Viennese manuscript; the Regius and Vatican manuscripts support this reading. In Psalm XCI, to which this alludes, the Greek reads ἐν ἐγέω, πίονι, apparently “in rich oil.” The printed editions have “in the mercy of fatness.”] of abundance, until I sleep and rest in peace [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read “in the length.”] for length of days” [Note: [Col. 0263] Psalms L, 9; CXVIII, 176; XXXIII, 2; XXXIX, 3; LXXVII, 33; Luke I, 49; Psalms XXXV, 9 and XXVII, 7; Psalm LXXVII, 25 according to the Roman Psalter].

### 10

I now come to the greater service of my victorious brother, by which he deigned to cut my hair with his own hands. Yet he wished me to owe this very benefit to you, saying, at your command, that he was revealing his art to me.

Therefore I asked him to pray, as you both have done, that what he accomplished with a skilled hand might be accomplished through the resources of prayer: namely, that once the Lord had been entreated by your prayers, our sins—through which we have a soul tangled with sins multiplied beyond the hairs of our head [Note: [Col. 0263] Psalm LIX, 13]—might be cut away not by a cutting made halfway [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Viennese manuscript reads “by cutting off.” Both readings are good. The Viennese reading is confirmed below, section 11: Samson, invincible while his hair was preserved, became captive when it was cut off], but destroyed to the very root, as though shaved by a razor [Col. 0263C].

Now we have a razor for cutting either salvation or destruction. Christ our God is the razor of healing and beauty: he circumcises our heart [Note: [Col. 0263] Colossians II, 11], shaves away our vices, smooths the head of the soul [Note: See Letter 41, section 3, and Poem 21, verse 537], and trims the face of the mind. He purifies and frees us, as he did that woman held captive under the law, from the dreadful hair of wretched slavery, so that, as she was about to pass into marriage with an Israelite man [Note: [Col. 0263] Deuteronomy II, 12], we may be stripped of the sins of our flesh as of barbarian hair and joined to the Lord.

Then, with our understanding renewed [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Viennese manuscript reads “renewed in understanding”], may we shine with untrimmed locks [Note: [Col. 0263] Numbers VI, 5] and consecrate our life to God in chastity and moderation, nourishing our Nazirite commitment.

### 11

We must beware, however, lest that hostile razor, which shaved the head of the human race after the first-formed parents had been deceived by its harmful fraud [Note: See note 78], rise against our own head—that is, against the faith by which Christ becomes our head—and strip us of spiritual grace, like that Nazirite’s hair.

The example of that sacred hero in the Book of Judges shows how much the hair benefits those who preserve it and how destruction follows when it is plucked away [Note: [Col. 0264D] Namely Samson, who is called a sacred warrior in section 20]: invincible while his hair was preserved, captive when it was cut off [Note: [Col. 0264D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the editions of Badius, Gravius, and Bignonius. The older manuscripts of Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 4, verse 123, have *abscisa papilla*, “the breast cut off,” as N. Heinsius notes there], and strong again when it grew back [Note: [Col. 0263] Judges XVI, 19].

Would that he had been as prudent in avoiding the woman as he was strong in strangling the lion [Note: [Col. 0263] Judges XIV, 6]. But he who had conquered through spiritual grace was overcome by weakness when he was defeated by carnal allure. This is necessarily suffered by those who do not subject their own woman—that is, the flesh—to her husband, the spirit, under God’s laws, and who, with yielding minds, submit to the burdens of their husband as though to a seductive wife [Col. 0264B].

They are degenerate from that Teacher—Paul; see Letter 30, section 5—who, as soon as he recognized Christ, did not yield to flesh and blood [Note: [Col. 0263] Galatians I, 16], even amid the first exercises of his warfare, victorious in a great struggle.

### 12

Let us therefore consider everything Samson endured after being corrupted by his faithless wife [Note: [Col. 0263] Judges XIV, 1, 16], because we sinners shall suffer spiritually the same things that he endured bodily and represented for our instruction.

For when Christ’s grace has been violated, just as Samson’s hair was cut, the enemy will mock us, take away our eyes, send us into prison, and assign us, like asses, to turn the millstones. Therefore the Lord warns us through the prophet, lest we make our neck, unsubmissive to the yoke of Christ, fit for an ass’s millstone [Note: [Col. 0263] Matthew XI, 29; XVIII, 6]: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” [Note: [Col. 0263] Psalm XXXI, 9].

For, as the same prophet says elsewhere, a human being who does not understand his honor—that is, the dignity of his nature, by which through reason he rules the other living creatures on earth—was made rational so that he might know and worship his Creator [Note: [Col. 0263] Psalm XLVIII, 13]. But when he abuses so great a gift of the Creator to license his error, he is compared with beasts and becomes like them.

We see this clearly fulfilled in the king of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0263] Daniel IV, 30]. Stripped of human understanding as punishment for impious stupidity and senseless pride, he endured these things with an animal’s heart.

Indeed, a human being placed in error and having fallen away from justice is justly deprived, like Samson, of both wisdom and the power of grace, and is punished with blindness and the millstone [Note: [Col. 0263] Judges XVI, 21]. For one who has deprived himself of the light of reason and cast himself into bodily slavery in the likeness of beasts is worthy of the work of beasts.

### 13

Consider the life of such mortals, and the entire image of a beast grinding at the mill will present itself to you [Note: [Col. 0265D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. The others read “may it appear.”]

Just as that *panis* [a materially uncertain reading] concerned the eyes of the body, so this man, with the eyes of his mind sewn shut by the filth of his life [Note: See note 79], wanders through the errors of his senses, as though around the winding paths of millstones. Wretchedly laboring at his station [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Regius manuscript and three printed editions read “turning about, deprived of his sight.” Grin’s edition has “he turns about, deprived of his sight.”], he is useless to himself and laborious for another.

He stands in the way of sinners [Note: [Col. 0265] Psalm I, 1], fettered by the chains of his desires. He himself is a prison enclosed by the darkness of his error and hardened by the filth of his conscience. Within himself he suffers the slavehouse of the mill. He turns the stone of his heart, hardened by the stubbornness of iniquity, like a millstone, producing flour for his enemies from the corrupted harvest of his soul.

For, as it is written, “the sinner runs from his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0265] Proverbs VII, 23, according to the Septuagint; see note 80]. Thus one who practices sin grinds hostile wheat from the mill of his life, so that he may feed the devil, for whom the soul that hungers for itself becomes bread.

But if, instead of always going onward, he sometimes turns back [Note: [Col. 0265] Psalm LXXVII, 39] and becomes spirit, then, as though his hair were restored, he will be renewed when grace blossoms again.

### 14

But, to weave an entire letter from the subject of hair, let us indulge the discourse and follow that strong man of the Lord to his end. For in his blindness and in his death we shall marvel at the sacraments of a divine mystery sketched beforehand.

When Scripture says [Note: [Col. 0265] Judges XVI, 30] that he struck down more enemies in dying than he had previously slain throughout his life, I think the primary interpretation should concern the power of the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0265D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and four printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads “to be interpreted”], through which the house of the devil fell and the kingdom of death was destroyed.

Although Christ always lived, as he lives, and before his bodily coming was with God the Father in the majesty of his nature as God the Word, nevertheless the power of death had reigned, raging with unrestrained license, through the ages arranged in their order from Adam to Moses [Note: [Col. 0265] Romans V, 14]. It had increased through sin understood from the law but not avoided.

The Son of God, King of kings and disposer of the ages, divided and overthrew this kingdom by his Passion. He became subject to the law in order to free those subjected to the law; he was made through a woman [Note: [Col. 0265] Galatians IV, 4], but a woman in sex and a virgin in giving birth, so that the Creator of both sexes might sanctify both by assuming manhood and being born through a woman.

Thus, by dying, he destroyed death itself, “abolishing in his flesh the enmity and making both one” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ephesians I, 14]—that is, humanity and God, whom God and the human being Christ Jesus joined in himself. In him he removed the discord of the two natures—that is, he set it aside [Col. 0265D]—and recognized the eternal covenant of unifying grace [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Regius manuscript has this reading; the others have “of life-giving grace.” See the preceding context].

A brother in the Levite and a brother in the priesthood passed by us, stripped and wounded by the robbery of the devil on the road; neither the law had redeemed them by sacrifices, nor the prophets [Note: [Col. 0265] Luke X, 31–32]. But that Samaritan did not pass us by, though for our sake he accepted even the insult of that name. He did not pass us by because he was not a hired servant but the true and good shepherd, who had come to lay down his life for the sheep [Note: [Col. 0265] John X, 18 and 12].

He pitied the wounded man, passed over and untreated by those who went before him, approached him, and received him upon his beast—that is, upon the incarnation of the Word. He entrusted him, with the oil of grace and the wine of his Passion, to the innkeeper [Note: [Col. 0265] Luke X, 34], that perfect teacher of the nations—that is, Saint Paul; see section 24, Letter 30, section 5, Poem 22, verse 178, and Poem 32, verse 353 [Note: [Col. 0266D] All manuscripts read *profecto*, “certainly.” We have emended this to *perfecto*, “perfect,” because Paulinus uses the same words twice in writing to his Severus, where all manuscripts consistently read “perfect teacher of faith and discipline” in the same letter, section 24, and in Letter 30, section 5, “he says, perfect teacher.”].

He healed him with the payment of a denarius in the two Testaments, and would repay him with abundant thanks for the fruits of blessed virginity and with innumerable crowns, because by adding this counsel to the commandment he contributed from his own resources [Note: [Col. 0266D] The Vatican and Viennese manuscripts read “in this”; this is not unsuitable if understood as “in this matter.”].

### 15

Therefore this was not a brother who differed from servants in condition as Lord and from mortals in nature as God. Yet he was also a human being, of whom it is written: “He is also a man, and who will know him?” [Note: [Col. 0265] Jeremiah XVII, 9; see note 81].

Nor, although divine mercy in the humility of his heart bestowed the name of brother upon servants, saying, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” [Note: [Col. 0265] Psalm XXI, 23], may he for that reason be called our brother in the sense permitted by our arrogance—not even because he deigned to become human. For even in becoming human he has nothing in common with us: without the ordinary process of our generation, he became flesh from the Holy Spirit, conceived and born while the virginity of his sacred mother remained undefiled.

Therefore, without any bodily intercourse of ours, he became our body and did not offer his own propitiation to God [Note: [Col. 0265] Psalm XLVII, 8], because he himself was the propitiation. Nor did he offer the price of redemption for his own soul [Note: [Col. 0265] 1 John II, 2], but for ours, because the Savior had no need of salvation.

We, sold under sin, needed the price of redemption [Note: [Col. 0265] Romans VII, 14]. Therefore, for our sake he became human, for our sake he took the form of a servant, and for our sake he became the son of a maidservant [Note: [Col. 0265] Philippians II, 7].

Although he is blessed and the sanctifier of the saints, for us he nevertheless became both sin and a curse [Note: [Col. 0265] 2 Corinthians V, 21; Galatians III, 13]—something he was not—in order to absolve us from both: we who through transgression were sin and through condemnation were a curse. He fastened both to the cross in his flesh [Note: [Col. 0265] Colossians II, 14].

Therefore, I think it was said: “A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem” [Note: [Col. 0265] Psalm XLVIII, 8]. Those whom a brother had not redeemed—that is, a prophet or legislator who was merely human—this human being redeemed, who was also God [Note: [Col. 0266D] Thus the Regius manuscript. The others read “these.”].

“For God,” he says, “was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” [Note: [Col. 0265] 2 Corinthians V, 19].

Only such a human being could prevail against the sentence of death and the sting of sin, abolish the record of death [Note: [Col. 0267] Colossians II, 14], and humble the accuser [Note: [Col. 0267] Psalm LXXI, 4]. Yet he confronted him not in the majesty of his nature but in the condition of ours, taking nothing from him by violent domination but overcoming him by the law of justice.

For since the woman had been deceived [Note: [Col. 0267] Genesis II, 13], and the man had been cast down through the woman, the enemy claimed all the offspring of the first human being under the laws of death as sinners—not indeed without a malicious desire to harm, but nevertheless by a perfectly just right of conquest. His power therefore had to remain until he killed the just man in whom he could point to nothing deserving death.

He was killed not only because he was without sin [Note: [Col. 0267D] All manuscripts read “without God,” which makes no sense. We have emended this to “without sin,” a certain conjecture, it seems, from the preceding and following context; the error arose from an abbreviation of the letters *delo*. Sacchini likewise suspects that *delicto*, “sin,” should be read slightly below, where the manuscripts and Rosweyde’s edition have *efferae Deo*, and four printed editions have *efferae a Deo*. He therefore insists that *efferae a delicto*, “savage because of sin,” must be read, but this is not convincing.] but also because he was born without lust, to which the enemy had subjected those whom he had seized. Thus, whatever was born thereafter, as the fruit of his own tree, he retained through a perverse desire to possess it, though by a not unjust right of ownership.

Most justly, therefore, he is compelled to release those who believe in the one whom he unjustly killed, so that they may both pay the debt of temporal death and live forever in him who paid on their behalf what he did not owe [Note: [Col. 0267] Psalm LXVIII, 5].

### 16

For this reason I think that he himself is also that lion [Note: [Col. 0267] Judges XIV, 8] in whose dead mouth we find food of honey. For what is sweeter than the Word of God? And what is stronger than the right hand of God?

Or in whose dead mouth are there honeycomb and bees, unless in the mouth of the one whose word contains the good of our salvation and the gathering of the nations? Many have rather placed the figure of the nations in this lion, because the people of the nations who believed had previously been a body of wildness but now belong to Christ.

In Christ, the Apostles, like bees amid the dew of heaven and the flowers of divine graces, prepared the honey of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0268D] The Viennese manuscript reads “brought forth”], as though food had come out of the mouth of one eating. For the nations, previously savage toward God, received the word of God with faithful hearts and brought forth the fruit of salvation.

Those who understand Christ more directly in this lion propose Samson as a figure of the Jews, so that the Jew might have killed that lion as Christ [Note: [Col. 0268D] Thus the Viennese and Regius manuscripts and the editions of Grin and Schott. The Regius manuscript together with four printed editions reads “might kill him.”]. They also assign this to the mystical preparation: precisely when Samson was seeking marriage, he killed the desired powerful beast, because the marriage established in Christ and the Church could not be confirmed [Note: [Col. 0267] Ephesians V, 32] unless the lion from the tribe of Judah had been killed [Note: [Col. 0267] Revelation V, 5].

The same Lord is both the lion who conquered and the lion’s cub [Note: [Col. 0267] Genesis XLIX, 9], voluntarily put to sleep and raised up by himself. Of him it is written: “Who will raise him up?” [Note: [Col. 0267] Psalm LIII, 8].

For, voluntarily sacrificing to the Father the offering of his body for us, he—the supreme and eternal priest [Note: [Col. 0267] Hebrews VII, 17]—as he himself testifies, took up his soul again by the same power by which he laid it down [Note: [Col. 0267] John X, 18].

This is the lion’s cub because he is the Son of God, and the same lion because he is equal to the Father. Therefore, as it seems to me, this saying applies more fittingly to this lion: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0267] Judges XIV, 14].

From whom else but our Savior, whose word is life, did this come? He both taught us this food by chewing it and supplied it by giving it. Or, if one prefers another interpretation, let food come forth from the eater because this lion from the tribe of Judah [Note: [Col. 0267] 1 Peter V, 8], victorious on our behalf, snatches us from the mouth of the hostile lion. He hunts in order to save; he captures in order to release; he breaks in order to strengthen; he chews in order to restore. He consumes in us what corrupts us.

Therefore let us desire to become the prey of this lion, lest we be the prey of the hostile lion. Let us become God’s food, lest we be food for the serpent. Let Christ eat us, lest the devil devour us. For when Christ eats, as I have said, what consumes us is consumed within us.

For Christ is life [Note: [Col. 0267] John XIV, 16], and we cannot lay aside this mortal condition unless we are swallowed up [Note: [Col. 0267] 1 Corinthians XV, 54], because Christ devours our death.

But we cannot be Christ’s food unless we do his will [Note: [Col. 0267] John IV, 34], so that he in turn may become food for us [Note: [Col. 0267] John VI, 48], in whom we always live if we live according to his commandments.

Thus sweetness comes forth from the strong when, through him, the bitterness of our wickedness has been changed into the sweetness of goodness, and we emerge as sweet food from his word: by eating us, he has consumed our sin and restored us to life.

He alone is strong—sweetly strong—who delivered the poor from the powerful miser [Note: [Col. 0267] Psalm LXXI, 12]. Through the mystery of his godliness he destroyed the wildness of my body by the death of his body; there he ate the food of life where the hunger of wretched death had been parching [Note: [Col. 0268D] The Viennese manuscript reads “where he was parched by the death of wretched hunger.”].

He changed offense into grace, sin into righteousness, weakness into power, death into life, shame into glory, and exile into a kingdom.

We used to hear, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” [Note: [Col. 0267] Genesis III, 19, according to the Septuagint]. Now we hear, “Your citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0267] Philippians III, 20; the Viennese manuscript and Grin’s edition read “we have heard”].

### 17

Therefore I think that the image unfolded in that Samson, whether with his hair restored or at his death, applies to every servant of Christ.

A person who has been overtaken by some sin [Note: [Col. 0267] Galatians VI, 1] and, through wholesome repentance, returns to the restoration of grace as though his hair were growing again, makes his arms like a bronze bow [Note: [Col. 0267] Psalm XVII, 35]—that is, exercising the faith of true hope and the hope of sincere faith. He also trains his hands for battle through works of devotion [Note: [Col. 0267] Psalm CXLIII, 1], whose practice is useful for all things [Note: [Col. 0267] 1 Timothy IV, 8].

Then, strong with the sinews of a good conscience and steadfast faith, he will dare to attack and will be able to overthrow the columns of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0268D] *Vertere* is used for *evertere*, a simple form for a compound; this is familiar to Paulinus and occurs once and again in Poem 32].

These are the columns of the enemy’s house upon which it rests. In that house the enemy, as though victorious over us, feasts and mocks his captives if he uses our limbs as weapons of his iniquity.

Therefore we cast down this enemy from his house [Note: [Col. 0269D] The Regius manuscript reads “from his house.” The ancients once used this form in the sixth case], through the destruction of the flesh that has been subjected. With its assistance, the enemy enclosed within us strikes our soul in an inward war. Made powerful through the crime of our will, he has our vices as his satellites against us and attacks our inner person through the service of the outer.

### 18

Let us remember the covenant by which, buried with Christ through the grace of baptism, we swore allegiance to the mysteries of the cross, so that we might no longer live as though alive in this world. Let us live now not ourselves, but Christ in us [Note: [Col. 0269] Romans VI, 4; Colossians II, 12; 2 Corinthians V, 15; Galatians II, 20].

When our head has been restored to honor, the devil’s house will fall, and the entire host of enemies will die together with the death of our sin.

Therefore, through Samson’s death I learn not only to die with my enemies—that is, to kill sin while mortifying my flesh, so that, my spirit surviving, I may triumph as victor in salvation and say to my soul, “Return to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” [Note: [Col. 0269] Psalm CXIV, 7]—but through Samson’s blindness also, in which he was captured only in his bodily eyes and did not lose his spiritual ones, I am enlightened toward good understanding [Note: [Col. 0269] Psalm CX, 10], so that from his example I may know what kind of eyes I ought rather to possess.

That man would not have invoked the Lord’s aid for his strength unless he had retained sound eyes of the mind. Christ is their light, and in his light we shall see light [Note: [Col. 0269] John VIII, 12; Psalm XXXV, 10].

If he always burns in the lamp of our body, then the works of darkness perish [Note: [Col. 0269D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts read “are destroyed”; immediately afterward the Viennese manuscript reads “will be sent out.”], and the prince of this world is cast out [Note: [Col. 0269] John XXXV, 12].

Not, of course, outside this world, which, as Scripture says, will be emptied in condemnation when it is judged together with the condemned [Note: [Col. 0269D] The Viennese manuscript reads “when it is judged with the judged.”], but outside our hearts, from which he is expelled if we receive Christ.

### 19

Since those who are of his party imitate him, let us imitate the Lord Jesus, who called us to share in the lot of his inheritance and commanded us to take up his easy yoke, so that he might shake off from us that heavy yoke of law and death [Note: [Col. 0269] John VIII, 44; Ephesians I, 11; Colossians I, 12; Matthew XI, 30].

The hair is also a yoke of lightness, for, as divine Scripture teaches us, the hair of the saints is light, while that of the impious is heavy [Note: [Col. 0269] 1 John V, 3].

The hair of the saints is either a sign of virtue, as in Samson, or of sanctification, as in Samuel. The other kind is either a burden, as in Absalom, or filth, as in Nebuchadnezzar [Note: [Col. 0269] 1 Samuel I, 11; 2 Samuel XIV, 26; Daniel IV, 30].

From this disagreement between human beings and their hair we learn to discern actions in the hair. For when the Assyrian king was condemned to solitude and wildness, the sorrowful mass of his uncut hair bristled into a lion’s mane. Thus, in bodily appearance also, he became a beast: exiled not only from his kingdoms but from human understanding, he represented a lion in his mournful hair, a vulture in his hooked claws, and an ox in his understanding and food.

He was made like many beasts in his punishment so that he would not bear the likeness of only one beast, having been like many in his behavior.

### 20

Yet, having at last come to understand God, and having been restored in mind and kingdom, he too became for us an example of faith, so that we may fear losing the kingdom that is within us by sinning and remember to regain it through repentance [Note: [Col. 0269] Luke XVII, 22.]. Nor could Absalom [Note: [Col. 0269D] Thus the Royal and Viennese manuscripts, with the editions of Badunus and Gravius; and so it is read in the manuscripts of Prudentius’s *Hamartigenia*, line 566, as N. Heinsius observes. The Septuagint translators, however, read Ἀβεσσαλὼμ (*Abessalōm*), and three printed editions read *Abessalom*.], although proud of his handsome body and head, say what Samson said [Note: [Col. 0269] II Kings XIV, 25.]: “If I am shorn, my strength will depart from me”; for he did not possess in his extremely beautiful hair that strength which was not of bodily locks [Note: [Col. 0269] Judges XVI, 7, according to the Septuagint], but of spiritual grace, which the impious man could not possess.

[Col. 0270B] For Christ is the power and wisdom of God [Note: [Col. 0269] I Corinthians I, 21.]; he did not enter a parricidal soul, because he did not dwell [see Note 82] in a body subject to sins [Note: [Col. 0269] Wisdom I, 4.]. Finally, the fact that his hair was cut off as though it were the mass of his iniquities is also demonstrated by the indicated necessity of shearing [see Note 83]. Thus you read:

> “He used to cut the hair of his head, because it weighed him down; and when he was shorn, he weighed the hair of his head, and it weighed one hundred and thirty-two shekels by the royal weight” [Note: [Col. 0269] II Kings XIV, 26, according to the Septuagint.].

How could it be expressed more clearly that the hairs are counted according to one’s deeds, when Scripture has marked upon the head of the impious man not some virtue but only a burden of hair? “He weighed,” it says, “the hair of his head.” For iniquity is glory to the impious man. Nor is he delighted only by the evil deed itself, but also—as someone has said—by the reputation of his wickedness. Hence you find this in the Psalms:

> “Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are mighty in iniquity?” [Note: [Col. 0269] Psalm LI, 3.]

For the light of the impious is darkness, honor is shadow, exaltation is transitory, and the devil is the head [Note: [Col. 0269] Psalm XXXIV, 6.]; therefore the hair is a burden. For this reason Scripture calls the hair of that parricide heavy with royal weight, that is, with devilish weight [Note: [Col. 0269] II Kings XIV, 26.].

For every impious man belongs to the devil’s kingdom. Thus also “those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matthew XI, 8; Luke VII, 25.], that is, in the houses of the rulers of this air [Note: [Col. 0269] Ephesians II, 2.] and of the leaders of spiritual wickedness. In their houses and kingdoms they live, either hard in impiety or soft in wantonness: their riches are sin, their paths slippery, their end destruction [Note: [Col. 0269] Philippians III, 19.], their glory in hell, their house in the grave [Note: [Col. 0269] Psalm XLVIII, 12.].

The hairs of such men are their crimes; and therefore they cannot be those hairs with which the holy warrior was loosening the cords of his enemies and new ropes as though they were soft threads [Note: [Col. 0269] Judges XVI, 9, and XII, 13.].

[Col. 0270D] Rather, they are those of whom it is written:

> “The cords of sinners have entangled me” [Note: [Col. 0270D] I have seen one manuscript of Paulinus that reads *circumplexi sunt mihi* (“have entwined themselves around me”). Five Psalters and St Augustine, in his commentary on the Psalms, read *circumplexi sunt me* (“have entwined me”). Psalm CXVIII, 61.].

[Col. 0271A] For the soul is both entangled and weighed down by its sins. The Prophet aptly proves this when he says:

> “My iniquities have been placed upon my head; like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me” [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Royal manuscript, with the editions of Gravius and Schottus, reads *plene* (“fully”). All manuscripts read *meas*; we have emended it to *meae*. For in Letter 12 to Amandus, no. 10, at the same scriptural passage, all printed and manuscript copies consistently read, as does the Roman Psalter: *Superposuerunt iniquitates meae caput meum* (“My iniquities have been placed upon my head”). St Augustine, with the old Psalter, reads: *Iniquitates meae sustulerunt caput meum* (“My iniquities lifted up my head”). St Ambrose reads *Superposuerunt*, and explains: *Iniquitates meae supertransierunt caput meum* (“My iniquities passed over my head”). Moreover, our Paulinus, Letter 40, no. 4, writes: *Superposuerunt iniquitates nostrae caput nostrum* (“Our iniquities have been placed upon our head”). See Note 83. Psalm XXXVII, 5.].

### 21

You see how heavy the sinner’s hair is. But the one whose hair is Christ leaps lightly and swiftly [Note: [Col. 0271] Psalm XXXVII, 5.], saying:

> “God, who girded me with strength and made my way blameless; who made my feet like those of a deer [Note: [Col. 0271D] Paulinus has this reading elsewhere, and so do the Royal and Viennese manuscripts. The other manuscripts read “of stags.”] and set me upon high places” [Note: [Col. 0271] Psalm XVII, 33.].

For, as I have said, the yoke and the hair of Christ are light [Note: [Col. 0271] Matthew XI, 30.], because, serving Christ, we do good works, by which, winged, we are carried aloft. Hence the Apostle also says to Christians who are still in the flesh:

> “But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0271] Romans VIII, 9.].

For the flesh subject to the soul subject to God passes into spirit—not by a change of substance, but of life. Therefore I desire both Samson’s death and his blindness, so that I may live and see for God. For perhaps, after recovering the strength that had been placed in his hair for the sake of the future mystery, he did not desire to recover his eyes at the same time as he had lost them, because that power of heavenly grace, sound in its inward lights, had no need of bodily sight.

### 22

Therefore, following this example, let us also blind our bodily eyes, with our senses intent upon the Lord, by turning away from worldly things—the eyes of which the Prophet desired to be deprived when he said:

> “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” [Note: [Col. 0271] Psalm CXVIII, 37.].

And the Lord himself, preferring blindness to the eyes of the Jews, says:

> “If you were blind, you would not have sin” [Note: [Col. 0271] John IX, 41.].

Let us remember by what ruin their eyes were opened in paradise—eyes that they had kept illumined by God for so long as they had kept them closed to sin [Note: [Col. 0271] Genesis III, 7.]. For only then did they drink in the shame of their nakedness, when they lost through the crime of transgression the chastity of a good conscience, by whose light they had been clothed.

Therefore it is the loss of the true light to use one’s eyes for the service of darkness, and to blind them to heavenly things by fixing them upon earthly things. Yet the soul is illumined by such blindness when it despises the world in order to behold God. For “everything that is in the world is the desire of the eyes” [Note: [Col. 0271] I John II, 16.].

Accordingly, the Apostle teaches that our vision must be veiled from this world and clouded for Christ [see Poem 21, line 667]—for him, that is, who “illumines every person coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0271] I John I, 9.], that is, the mind of every person who comes—and he draws us away from the sight of present things toward suspicion of eternal things, saying:

> “Do not seek the things that are in this world; for the form of this world is passing away” [Note: [Col. 0271] I John II, 25.].

And again the same Apostle says:

> “Seek the things above, where Christ is at the right hand of the Father” [Note: [Col. 0271] I Corinthians VII, 31; Colossians V, 1.].

For everything, as Ecclesiastes says, is vanity under the sun [Note: [Col. 0271] Ecclesiastes I, 14.]. Therefore truth is above the sun. Thus those who stand in the truth, although they live within the world in bodily habitation, are nevertheless above the world in heavenly conduct.

By the flight of the spirit they climb and surpass the choirs of the stars and the poles of heaven [Note: [Col. 0272D] The Royal manuscript reads “with the spirit flying”; this reading is confirmed below, no. 24, “lest, with the spirit exalted …,” and “lest, with knowledge puffing them up, they burst apart.”]. They live higher than the elements, not subject to the things and uses of the elements, but with their life fixed in Christ they become superior to the world, remaining in him who is God, blessed above all, forever [Note: [Col. 0271] John XV, 4; Romans I, 25.].

### 23

You see how the imitator of Christ [Note: [Col. 0271] I Corinthians XI, 1.] transfers us from mortal things to God, by teaching as well as by the example of virtue. He removes the veil from our heart, so that with unveiled face we may contemplate the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0271] II Corinthians III, 18.]. This glory is hidden from unbelievers by the veil of the Law, but is disclosed to believers through the revelation of the Gospel.

Therefore that bodily hair is no longer necessary for us. For, he says:

> “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things are new” [Note: [Col. 0271] II Corinthians V, 17.],

because light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart: the merciful and compassionate, the just Lord. “The Lord is Spirit. And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” [Note: [Col. 0271] Psalm CXI, 4; John IV, 24; II Corinthians V, 17.].

Therefore hair was once an honor, when that spiritual veil of the Law still had to be displayed even in bodily form. Now, however, it is a burden, since the sun of eternal freedom has shone forth and Christ has become our head, lifting us not only from the yoke but also from the burden of lowered heads [Note: [Col. 0271] Matthew XI, 29.].

For this reason we now dare, as free people, to proclaim in a voice of exultation and confession [Note: [Col. 0271] Psalm XLI, 5.]:

> “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” [Note: [Col. 0271] Psalm II, 3.].

For now is the acceptable time, now the day of salvation [Note: [Col. 0271] II Corinthians VI, 2.], since Truth is present no longer in the shadow of a cloud but in the light of its own body.

[Col. 0272D] And suitably, at the time of grace and in the outward appearance of freedom, the barber is at hand [Note: [Col. 0272D] The Royal manuscript, with the editions of Badunus, Gravius, and Schottus, reads: *et opportune ad gratiam, tempus, et species libertatis tonsori in promptu est* (“and suitably, for grace, time, and the appearance of freedom, the barber is at hand”). The Grinian edition reads: *ad gratiarum tempus et speciem libertatis tonsori in promptu est* (“at the time of graces and the appearance of freedom, the barber is at hand”).], to relieve us of the longer veil of hair upon our head, so that bodily appearance may also testify to the benefit of spiritual grace, and the brightness of an unveiled forehead may display the joy of inward freedom.

### 24

For women alone apostolic authority has left their hair [Note: [Col. 0272D] The Rosweyd edition reads “leaves it.”]. For although faith removes from them, as from us, the veil of the heart [Note: [Col. 0272D] So the manuscripts read: “removes.”], nevertheless the covering of the head and the shade of the forehead demand the ornament of modesty.

[Col. 0272D] Therefore the perfect Teacher of faith and discipline teaches that hair is unbecoming to a man, because the head of a man cannot be hidden: Christ is his head, and Christ is also that city built upon a mountain, in the Church, which is the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 0273] Matthew V, 14; I Corinthians XI, 3; Ephesians I, 22.].

Thus hair is unbecoming for a man but an adornment for a woman. For she is the head of no one, but by the adornment of honor she beautifies the man and supports, as though placed upon a foundation, the ordered structure of the body, which is woven from God as the head of Christ, Christ as the head of the man, and the man as the head of the woman.

Yet through the fellowship of the body and the interweaving of the members, Christ also makes her a participant in the supreme Head—in whom we are neither male nor female [Note: [Col. 0273] Luke VII, 38.].

Let women indeed have hair with which, following that evangelical sinful woman, they may dry the feet of Christ [Note: [Col. 0273D] The Rosweyd edition reads *tergant* (“wipe”); but *tergeant* (“dry”) is the truest reading, as is confirmed below, no. 35, and in Poem 32, *On the Death of Celsus*, line 542.], and with which they may cling to the feet of Wisdom, so that they may know how to love nothing but wisdom, embrace nothing but virtue, and kiss nothing but chastity.

And, sprinkled at least with the final dew of the heavenly word, let them say:

> “For the dew that is from you is health for us” [Note: [Col. 0273] Isaiah XXVI, 19.].

Let the hair of our women be the deeds of spiritual virtues, fasts, mercies, and prayers. Such hair also becomes men. Let Christ’s grace, not hair, adorn them; the jewel of chastity, not of stone; and let the ointment of works, not of scents, breathe fragrantly from them.

Let them remember that they are daughters of that daughter of the king whose entire glory is within [Note: [Col. 0273] Psalm XLIV, 14.]. Let them understand why the Apostle commanded them to be covered with a longer veil upon their head:

> “Because of the angels” [Note: [Col. 0273] I Corinthians XI, 10.],

namely, those prepared for seduction, concerning whom the saints will judge. For these attack weaker vessels with greater insolence, just as the serpent attacked Eve, not Adam [Note: [Col. 0273] Genesis III, 1.].

For this reason they are also forbidden to teach in the Church [Note: [Col. 0273] I Corinthians XIV, 34; I Timothy II, 12.], lest, with their spirit exalted, they dare to gaze upon the decrees of wisdom and, puffed up by knowledge, burst apart. [Note: [Col. 0273D] The Royal, Vatican, and Viennese manuscripts, together with the marginal reading in the printed editions, have this form. The printed editions read “puffed up by knowledge”; both readings are accepted.]

Certainly this serves to confound the wicked [see Note 86], if they see a woman conceal her thoughts in silence under the appearance of ignorance and confess the discipline of her understanding through a modest manner, so that the serpent does not dare to attack her again, despairing of capturing her.

### 25

The Apostle does not teach without reason that this should be done especially at the time when a woman either prays or prophesies [Note: [Col. 0273] I Corinthians XI, 5.]. For then she enters into spiritual conception. Therefore the tempter’s envy is aroused more strongly when, breathing toward the perfect man, she passes beyond the limits of her weakness.

That the Apostle has the same view of prayer as of prophecy is not surprising, since elsewhere he says that prayer is made in the Spirit:

> “For when we pray,” he says, “we do not know how we ought to ask, but the Spirit himself teaches us.”

Therefore, since spiritual conception also occurs in prayer, lest—as it is written—the enemy’s deceit and snare meet a woman acting beyond the limits of her vessel, the Apostle wishes her clothing to show that she has a power above her head, by which she may be governed and defended alike [Note: [Col. 0273] I Corinthians XI, 10.].

That very humility of heart gives her strength, pressing down the arrogance of knowledge with the rudder of discipline. He prefers her to fear rather than to presume lofty things; to be safer in silence through the fear of faith than learned with her tongue, needlessly pressing her forehead with her hair unless she also veils it with modesty [Note: [Col. 0273] I Timothy II, 9.].

### 26

Therefore, let every soul together strive to adorn itself with those hairs that God counts, as he himself says:

> “But even the hairs of your head are all numbered” [Note: [Col. 0273] Luke XII, 7.].

Of whose head would he deign to count the hairs more than of the one whose very crown he himself is the head? Of him it is said:

> “His head is like gold cephas” [see Note 87].

By this name I think a certain especially excellent and pure gold is more probably signified, like that mentioned concerning the land of Havilah [Note: [Col. 0273] Song V, 11, according to the Septuagint.]. For this gold is the form of the saints [Note: [Col. 0273] Genesis II, 12.], who shine like lights in the head of the body and are burning gold to God [Note: [Col. 0273] Revelation III, 18.].

For he found them—as it is written [Note: [Col. 0273] Wisdom III, 5.]—worthy of himself, having melted them through the trials of sufferings in the furnace of this world. In them he struck the sacred coin of his image, imprinting his word of truth upon their hearts and tongues. He appointed these same people as moneyers, so that, according to his likeness, they might mint coins acceptable to the Lord; and, once the image of Caesar had been abolished from us, they might stamp the living image of the eternal King [Note: [Col. 0273] Matthew XXII, 21.].

Thus, inscribed with the spirit of redemption, with our necks now freed from the yoke and our foreheads fortified by the title of salvation, we might sing [Note: [Col. 0273] Ezekiel IX, 4.]:

> “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0273] Psalm IV, 7.].

### 27

Therefore, with all our strength, let us strive to prepare ourselves so that we may deserve to be the hair and gold of the divine Head, who through God’s grace is Christ for us [Note: [Col. 0273] Ephesians I, 22.].

From that very Head springs the hair of which it is written [Note: [Col. 0273] Song IV, 1, according to the Septuagint.]:

> “His hair is like flocks of goats.”

And appropriately the flocks of Christ are designated by the name of those animals whose principal use is their milk [Note: [Col. 0273] Proverbs XXVII, 27.]. For everyone who believes that Christ is God embraces in devout faith the entire fullness of the Trinity in him whom the Father anointed with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0273] Acts X, 38.].

Therefore the mother of all living things [Note: [Col. 0273] Genesis III, 20.], the body of Christ, the Church, overflows with the sap of devotion, and her breasts are better than wine [Note: [Col. 0273] Song I, 1, according to the Septuagint.]. In this, I think, it is signified that the freedom of grace in the milk of mercy is sweeter than the austerity of the justice of the Law in the wine.

For he says:

> “The letter kills”—

you see the unmixed wine of judgment—

> “but the Spirit gives life” [Note: [Col. 0273] II Corinthians III, 6.],

you see the gift of the breasts and the effect of milk.

But let this be emended [see Note 88], as you understand it better, into that by which the first milk-draught of newborn creatures coagulates. [Note: [Col. 0274D] The Royal manuscript and the editions of Badunus, Gravius, and Schottus read “so that you may understand it more fully, the seed may be given.” Both readings are plausible. See Note 87.]

Good are the breasts [Note: [Col. 0275] John X, 10.], which the good Shepherd, who laid down his life for the sheep [Note: [Col. 0275] John X, 11.], milked for those infants for whom he perfected praise from the mouth, so that he might destroy the enemy of good and the defender of evil [Note: [Col. 0275] Psalm VIII, 3.].

### 28

From these flocks of goats came that man, a shepherd of the flock, who gave the little ones of Christ, not yet fit for solid food, nourishment in tender milk. To them he said:

> “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, nor are you even now able” [Note: [Col. 0275] I Corinthians III, 2.].

When we have grown through the nourishment of this milk, first establishing our steps through the conception of faith, we mature into the strength of youth. Then, with love and endurance strengthened through faith, we shall raise our hands to more vigorous action [Note: [Col. 0275D] Thus the Vatican and Viennese manuscripts read. Other manuscripts have: “and with endurance strengthened through faith and love.” Both readings are good.].

By works of virtue we shall live as though on stronger food, so that we may become those hairs of which it is written [Note: [Col. 0275] Song V, 11.]:

> “His hairs are fir trees, black” [see Note 88 bis], like a raven—that is, a crow.

But this is a good raven—not the one forgetful of returning to the ark, but the one mindful of feeding the prophet. The hairs that rival those fir trees are well compared to it, for he says that they are good and black fir trees, bringing the ships of Tarshish [Note: [Col. 0275] I Kings V, 8; II Chronicles IX, 21.].

Therefore this raven is now not a raven of night but of light; his hairs are of beautiful color. Thus the saints, a royal and priestly race [Note: [Col. 0275] I Peter II, 9.], are those by whom the divine Head is made purple with the splendor of its glory, since youthful grace particularly clothes flourishing age in this color.

### 29

It must nevertheless not be concealed that this bird is sometimes found in Scripture as an image of sin and sometimes as an aspect of grace. It appears deadly when it is brought forth for the punishment of the impious, because God sends evils—as it is written—through evil angels [Note: [Col. 0275] Psalm LXXVII, 49.]. Or it appears so when, as vengeance for a curse, it is said:

> “May the ravens of the valleys dig out the eye that mocks father and mother” [Note: [Col. 0275] Psalm CXLVI, 9.].

Yet the same bird is praiseworthy when it feeds the prophet with bread in the morning and meat in the evening, or when the young ravens call upon the name of the Lord.

Its color too is spoken of sometimes in connection with the saints and sometimes with the impious. The bride of Christ says that she is dark and beautiful, and the Lord has made darkness his hiding place. Conversely, the Apostle warns us not to be overtaken by darkness [Note: [Col. 0275] John XII, 35; I Kings V, 8.].

Nevertheless, those black and good fir trees bringing the ships of Tarshish [Note: [Col. 0275] Psalm XCI, 15.] correspond to her form, which is both dark and beautiful. For the saints are her members. Just as they are flourishing palms and multiplying cedars, so also they are black and good fir trees, because in the Church—that is, on the mountain of God—they rise high in the summits of their merits, like fir trees on their mountains.

And just as those trees are suitable for constructing ships, so they, the leaders of the people from the mountain of the Law, cut from Lebanon, covered the ark of the Lord—or the ship, that is, the Church, which was to sail through the floods of this world—with peoples shaped by the word of God. Joined together in the structure of love by the bond of faith, they taught it to cut through the waves of this world without rotting.

### 30

Even now, souls instructed in apostolic faith are black and good fir trees. They are black, as I think, no longer because of sin, but either because of their bodily dwelling or because they are darkened by the dust of inward discipline, like the dust of warfare, or by sweat covered with dust. Yet they are good because of their spiritual conduct even amid the nights of the body.

So too are they ships that float above the waves of the world. They are armed on the right and on the left with the oars of faith in truth and of righteous action, as it is written. They are directed by the word of God as by a rudder, spread open the folds of their senses to the breath of the Holy Spirit, and fasten the sail of their heart to the bonds of love, as with ropes to the yardarm of the cross.

They also have as their tree the branch from the root of Jesse [Note: [Col. 0275] Isaiah XI, 1.], which governs the entire four-oared vessel of our body. If, according to that poetic tale, we bind ourselves to it in prophetic truth—fastened by voluntary bonds, with not wax but faith blocking our ears, not the ears of the body but of the heart—we shall safely and harmlessly pass by the reefs of pleasure, like the rocks of the Sirens, which this world presents, variously suited to capture and equally suited to harm [Note: [Col. 0276D] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions, except for the Viennese manuscript, have “we pass beyond.”].

Let us bind ourselves to this tree with the strongest rope, bound in hope, faith, and love, believing in our hearts and confessing with our mouths the undivided Trinity, which is the threefold cord that is not broken.

With this cord let our works also be woven; by the rope of our faith let the tree be raised as the mast of love, and let the sails of our life be spread, so that we may be those fir trees which, woven into great rafts for the construction of the temple, were brought from Tarshish [Note: [Col. 0275] I Kings V, 8.]. Or let us ourselves be ships that imitate the one which once brought chosen gold and Tyrian wealth to Solomon [Note: [Col. 0275] I Kings IX, 29, and X, 22.]. Our commerce ought to be conducted with greater diligence and greater profit, since our eternal King Jesus is superior to that temporal Solomon.

“For behold,” he says, “something greater than Solomon is here” [Note: [Col. 0275] II Chronicles VIII, 18, and IX, 10; Matthew XII, 42; Luke XI, 31.]. He will not crush us with a violent breath among the ships of Tarshish [Note: [Col. 0275] Psalm XLVII, 8.], if we bring to him through the good action of our life the profit that is God’s most precious merchandise, so that he himself may receive his price from us. For he is also the pearl which the whole conduct of this spiritual commerce strives to acquire for itself.

If our means suffice to purchase it, we shall carry across this great and spacious sea not a burden that weighs us down but one that lifts us up [Note: [Col. 0275] Psalm CIII, 25.]. And if we deserve to carry the Lord, who sleeps within us because of our sluggishness, even while he sleeps, we shall dare to awaken him, so that, rebuking the winds of hostile spirits—or even of our own senses—he may save us from faintheartedness and storm [Note: [Col. 0277] Matthew VIII, 24; Mark IV, 38; Luke VIII, 23; Psalm LIV, 9.].

As we make our way toward his tranquility, he will make the seas calm, so that he may lead us, like cargo ships laden with his riches, to the harbor of salvation [Note: [Col. 0277] Psalm CVI, 30.], and joyfully place green crowns upon the prows victorious over the waves.

### 31

Let us also be his right hand [Note: [Col. 0277] Matthew XXV, 33.], who is wholly right hand, having nothing left-handed in our actions, so that we may deserve to stand at the right hand of the Judge—or rather to be the Judge’s right hand.

And on the day of recompense, may the Lord, who rewards, count our works as the hairs of his head [Note: [Col. 0277] Matthew X, 30; Luke XII, 7.], as he has already foretold in the Gospel, to be pronounced at the judgment [Note: [Col. 0277D] The Viennese manuscript reads “to be announced beforehand.”], and may he remunerate the merits of spiritual virtues with divine blessing and royal attribution [Note: [Col. 0277] The Vatican manuscript reads “with recompense.”]. [Note: [Col. 0277D] The Vatican manuscript reads “will be rewarded.” Paulinus uses this word actively elsewhere; see Letter 26 to Sebastian, no. 2.]

These are the most beautiful hairs of his head, like those of the woman who, in the figure of the Church, drenched and dried the feet of Christ with ointment and tears [Note: [Col. 0277] Matthew XI, 12.]. She pleased him not so much by the value of her gifts as by the affection of her service.

For the Lord loved in her not the ointment but the love by which, modestly immodest and devoutly shameless, without fear of reproach or rejection, she entered uninvited and boldly into the stranger’s house—that of the Pharisee—by the force with which the kingdom of heaven is seized [Note: [Col. 0277] Matthew XI, 12.].

Hungry for the heavenly word, she ran not to his food [Note: [Col. 0277D] The earlier reading was “wealth.” With Sacchini we emend it to “food,” a conjecture drawn with certainty both from what follows and from no. 42 below, where Paulinus says to the Pharisee: “I would rather be bound among her hairs to Christ’s feet than recline with you beside Christ among your dishes, without Christ.”], but to the feet of Christ. There she washed and nourished herself, and made those very feet, so to speak, her sanctuary and altar. Upon them she poured out her tears as a libation, offered ointment as a sacrifice, and sacrificed her devotion.

For “a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” [Note: [Col. 0277] Psalm L, 19.]. By offering this sacrifice to God, she obtained not only forgiveness of sins but also the glory of having her name proclaimed with the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0277] Matthew XXVI, 13; Mark XIV, 9; John XII, 3.].

### 32

And because she presented the image of the Church that was to be called from the nations, she bore in herself all the marks of the mystery of salvation. She was anointed with the chrism of her own offering; she had the tears of repentance as her bath and the inward parts of charity as her sacrifice.
