With hands and mouth she received in advance the living and life-giving bread—that is, she took it beforehand, and thus below she pre-tasted it. She also pre-tasted with thirsty kisses the blood of the cup before the cup became the cup of blood.

Blessed is she who tasted Christ in the flesh and in that very body received the body of Christ. Rightly was she preferred to the Pharisee, although he was feeding Christ: she who, fasting while the Jew feasted, served, as I have said, hungry not for food but for salvation [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Vatican manuscript and the Grinian edition read “she was hungry.” Both readings are good. The reading retained here is the truest, being confirmed by no. 40 below: “You feasted in order to become proud; she fasted in order to serve.”].

Blessed is she who deserved to be represented in the figure of the Church in this form also [Ambrose, Book VI on Luke VII], so that in the Pharisee’s house and at his banquet it was not the Pharisee but the sinful woman who was justified unto forgiveness. Her importunity obtained more than the Pharisee’s abundance.

For the order of the sacrament, arranged from the ages, required, in accordance with the prophetic blessing of our father Noah, that the dwelling of Japheth should pass into the tents of Shem—that is, that in the house of the Law and the Prophets the Church should rather be justified [Ambrose, Book VI on Luke VII], younger in the age of time but greater under the law of grace.

Hence the person of the Law itself, in John, declares [Note: [Col. 0278D] Following the Viennese manuscript, we have deleted the words *unde lex ipsa* (“hence the Law itself”), which seem to have been inserted by scribes in the other manuscripts.]:

> “He who comes after me has been made before me, because he was before me” [Note: [Col. 0277] John I, 30.].

### 33

And so that the Church might also correspond in figure to her Head, she had rightly assumed the form of a sinful woman [see Note 90], because Christ too assumed the form of a sinner.

But the Jew, who was to have neither head nor foundation in Christ, had anointed neither the head of Christ nor his feet. The evangelical woman had drenched both with precious ointments.

Therefore the Synagogue has from Christ neither the oil of grace nor the water of refreshment. In the person of that Pharisee, who bore its type, the water and the oil of charity dried up around him, although he stood beside the very source of the oil and the saving water.

Of this source the Prophet had foretold:

> “May the oil of the sinner not make my head fat” [Note: [Col. 0277] Psalm CXL, 5.].

But he could say to his Church:

> “You have made my head fat with oil” [Note: [Col. 0277] Psalm XXII, 5.].

She had brought not only the preparation but also the precious vessel containing the ointment, fragrant with the grace and power of many herbs or flowers mixed together.

Who but the Church could prepare such a thing? Fragrant with the varied flowers and juices of heavenly graces, she breathes forth to God countless sweetnesses from different nations and exhales the prayers of the saints, like spices burning in smoking bowls, through the Spirit of truth [Ambrose, Book VI on Luke VII].

The Bridegroom himself, rich in such floral fragrances and liquid dews, rejoices in her, addressing her tenderly in the words of the Song of Songs:

> “My dove, my perfect one, for my head has been filled with dew” [Note: [Col. 0277] Song II, 10, and V, 2, according to the Septuagint.].

God is the head of Christ, and his hairs are the elect of the saints, in whom the Father rejoices in Christ; “and my hairs are with drops of night.”

As we know, dew is not moisture from rain but refreshment by which grasses dried by the heat of day are restored. The earth is sprinkled with these bright drops of dew only on a clear night.

Hence it can be understood that those drops of night with which Wisdom rejoices that his head and hairs have been moistened represent the saints, whom the Apostle also shows shining like stars [Note: [Col. 0271] Philippians II, 15.], since stars likewise sparkle on clear nights, when dew falls.

But what night should be understood spiritually except the Passion of the Lord, which also illumined the day? Of it, I think, it is written:

> “And night shall be my illumination in my delights” [Note: [Col. 0277] Psalm CXXXVIII, 11.].

[Col. 0279A] But if you also regard this age as night, it has been cleared as though from clouds by the conversion of the nations, whose condition before faith bristled with darkness; and now, by the light of the Church, as by the mirror of a full and perfect moon, and by holy people, like stars pure in serenity [Note: [Col. 0279D] Thus read the Royal, Vatican, and Viennese manuscripts. The printed editions read *purissimis serenitate* (“in the purest serenity”).], the works of the faithful—by which each person, giving life to his soul, refreshes it from the thirst of its former dryness—distil like dew in this night of the age, as we have said.

### 34

And therefore Christ rejoices that his head is filled with such dew, and that the illuminator of our nights nevertheless rejoices that his hair has been drenched with the drops of our night [Note: [Col. 0279D] This is absent from Schott’s edition and from the Vatican manuscript, in which the whole passage reads: “And the illuminator of our nights rejoices that his hair has been drenched with the drops of our night.”] [Note: [Col. 0279] Song of Songs V, 2]; for that operation of the faithful—that is, mercy or almsgiving—is his refreshment and restoration (see note 91), by which either the brethren are helped or the needy are comforted.

For this reason, finally, he also rejected the voice of Judas, who, with his heart possessed by the spirit of the devil, begrudged Christ the woman’s ointment poured upon his feet [Note: [Col. 0279] John XIII, 2; Matthew XXVI, 10; Mark XIV, 6]. For by works of piety and mercy Christ is both anointed and enriched and nourished (see note 92). But the traitor, before he betrayed the Lord, betrayed his own faithlessness [Note: [Col. 0279] John XII, 6]. He was moved not by concern for the poor but by concern for his thefts; and the envy of his faithless mind judged that ointment—however precious, yet utterly cheap in comparison with the Lord’s blood—to be more valuable than the saving body, and he was indignant at the woman’s pious extravagance, although the Lord himself testifies that she was performing a good work upon him. He was teaching that care for the needy should be put second, but care for him alone should come first, thereby showing that with a perverse heart he had preferred mercy to faith (see note 93), although faith is the source of works, and the teacher himself surpasses his own commandments [Note: [Col. 0279C] The manuscripts and Schott’s edition read “so that.” The others read “as.”].

Except that in this also the son of perdition showed how cheaply he regarded Christ: he said that the ointment poured over Christ was being wasted [Note: [Col. 0279D] We have removed the particle “so that,” which was absent from the manuscripts]. And therefore he has no share in the value of Christ’s blood, because he cannot possess as redeemer the one whom he preferred to possess as merchandise; and rightly he is excluded from the commerce of life by the contractor of death, condemned by his own judgment, by which he sold for thirty pieces of gold the one whom the woman, as he himself had reckoned it, anointed for three hundred [Note: [Col. 0279] Matthew XXVI, 15; Mark XIV, 5; Luke XXII, 5].

But in this he was perverse: valuing the Lord himself cheaply, he appraised in a fleshly way that ointment which was being offered beforehand for his saving burial. Truly, like the devil, ignorant of God’s grace, in which there would be no portion for him, he valued highly—not through love but through envy—the price of his death, by which he saves us freely, although he bought us at great cost; he does not sell us [Note: [Col. 0279] I Corinthians VI, 20] (see note 94). For he wishes to make us precious through the cheapness of his own gift. He himself is more precious to us through this piety: that he wishes to be considered cheap, so that he may be bought by everyone.

For, he says, “he himself made the poor man and the rich man, and he cares equally for everyone” [Note: [Col. 0279] Matthew X, 8]. Hence he says: “You have received grace freely; give freely” [Note: [Col. 0280D] We have added “grace” from the Regius and Vatican manuscripts. See what follows] [Note: [Col. 0279] Acts III, 6]. Through this grace, Peter, rich in gratuitous gifts, though he possessed no money, endowed with health the lame poor man, who desired only a small alms.

### 35

Let us therefore be needy in avarice for gold, so that we may abound in grace; and, becoming cheap to this world through voluntary poverty, let us become precious ointment to the Lord. For we shall breathe forth Christ’s good fragrance to God if, carrying Christ’s death in our body, manifesting life in the Spirit, we give off the fragrance both of the Lord’s passion and of his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0279] II Corinthians II, 15; II Corinthians IV, 10; Matthew XVI, 7; Mark XIV, 3].

We shall pour ointment upon Christ’s body if we devote our substance and our life to faith in his truth and obedience to his commandment [Note: [Col. 0280D] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “in faith … and obedience.”]. Then we shall breathe out the fragrance of ointments filling the whole house in his body, if with perfect love we can ever say: “The world has been crucified to me” [Note: [Col. 0279] Galatians VI, 14]: to one who does not love riches (see note 95), nor the honors of the world; who does not love what belongs to himself, but what belongs to Christ [Note: [Col. 0279] Philippians II, 21]; who does not love what is seen, but what is unseen.

These will be our hair, serving as strength and holy ministry, with which we may wipe Christ’s feet [Note: [Col. 0280D] Thus the Regius manuscript together with the four printed editions. Other manuscripts read “wipe clean.” See note 24, where the form “may they wipe” occurs], break the cords of sins, and rejoice in the spirit of freedom, saying: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” [Note: [Col. 0279] Psalm CXV, 16–17].

### 36

But while there is time for running, while there is time for serving, let us nourish such hair; and let us imitate not only the love of that Gospel sinner, so that by great love we may wash away great debts, but also her persistence, so that we may seize salvation before the coming wrath [Note: [Col. 0280D] Thus the Regius and Vienna manuscripts. The very best reading, confirmed by what follows below in section 36 and above in section 4].

Seeking the bread of life opportunely and importunately, let us knock even at night at the householder’s door [Note: [Col. 0279] Luke XI, 5 and 8]. For he says: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy places” [Note: [Col. 0279] Psalm CXXXIII, 2]. As commanded, let us rub the thresholds of every wise person in Christ (see note 96), and everywhere let us seek the food of life; wherever we may find it, let us hunt for the word of God [Note: [Col. 0280D] Here and below we have restored “wherever” from the Regius and Vienna manuscripts; the reading is confirmed by what follows. The printed editions have “everywhere”]. Let us hang upon the lips of every believer, because the Spirit of God breathes upon every believer; and it is necessary that even from the least servant of God a drop of heavenly wisdom should distill, sprinkling the dryness of my heart with dew and overflowing for me as a drink of usefulness beyond the rivers of the wise men of this world. For I would rather speak five words in the law (see note 97) than many thousands in a tongue [Note: [Col. 0279] I Corinthians XIV, 19], just as I would rather live one day in the courts of the Lord than thousands in the tents of sinners [Note: [Col. 0279] Psalm LXXXV, 11], because “the Spirit breathes where he wills, and I hear his voice but do not know where it comes from” [Note: [Col. 0281] John III, 8].

Therefore, wherever I can, I will catch his breath; from wherever I can, I will gather even a faint exhalation. Wherever I hear that a just man has come either into the house of an unworthy person (see note 98) or into the house of a Pharisee, I will strive to seize the guest’s grace, and, if I can, to seize the kingdom of heaven. Wherever Christ’s name resounds for me, I will run; whenever I learn that Jesus has entered someone’s inner chamber, I too will hasten. When I find wisdom, when I find justice reclining in someone’s innermost room, I will run to Christ’s feet [Note: [Col. 0281] Matthew IX, 10], so that I may at least be marked by the very last trace of wisdom; nor will I disdain the feet. Rather, I shall desire that Christ touch my head even with his feet. She touched the fringe, and was healed; he healed others even by the passing shadow of an apostolic body [Note: [Col. 0281] Acts V, 15].

### 37

Let us spread out our hair before him (see note 99), that is, let us lay before him all the dignities of our insignia; and let us be cast down from ourselves, so that we may be exalted by him who dwells on high and looks upon the humble [Note: [Col. 0281] Psalm CXII, 5]. [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Vatican manuscript adds: “in heaven and on earth.”]

Let us confess our sins with tears, so that that heavenly Justice may say of us also: “She bathed my feet with tears and wiped them with her hair” [Note: [Col. 0281] John XIII, 5]. Perhaps for this reason he did not wash his own feet when he washed those of the disciples, so that we might wash them with our tears [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Vatican manuscript and Schott’s edition read “so that we might wash them,” which is correct if it agrees with the preceding reading of the Vienna manuscript. The Vulgate reading derives from Ambrose].

That soul was not of mediocre merit, of which Wisdom can say: “From the time she entered, she has not ceased to kiss my feet” [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke VII, 5]. [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Regius and Vienna manuscripts, together with Bad’s edition, read “that.”] What is this kiss except the eternal pledge of that love which covers a multitude of sins [Note: [Col. 0281D] I Peter IV, 8]?

The Church was already then preparing these kisses for her Bridegroom when she sang: “Let him kiss me from the kisses of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0281D] “From kisses,” according to the version of the Septuagint. In the explanation of Homily 1, Origen shows that it should be read in the plural, “from kisses”; Ambrose likewise uses the plural in his Commentary on Psalm CXVIII, Sermon 1, and in On Isaac, chapter 3] [Note: [Col. 0281] Song of Songs I, 1, according to the Septuagint]. This privilege the catholic love alone rightly claims for itself: unique and perfect, she seeks from the mouth of the Word kisses of truth from one man, so that she may not be polluted by the poison of heretical deceit through the kisses of alien and incestuous mouths.

### 38

Let us therefore imprint chaste kisses upon Christ’s feet, so that we may deserve to rise from the feet to the head; and, growing upward into the higher members of the body, let us now dare to approach his face and ask for kisses from his mouth. When, tasting God’s Word with a pure heart, we have tasted how sweet the Lord is, then let our soul, kindled with all the inward parts of its love for wisdom, be refreshed by a sweet ardor; and, pierced by the fiery arrows of the Lord’s love—which slays every other love of hostile pleasures—let it say with a contrite heart: “For I am wounded by love” [Note: [Col. 0281D] Previously it read *caritate* (“by love”). With the Regius manuscript we read *vulnerata caritatis* (“wounded of love”), according to the Septuagint version. This Greek construction was familiar to our Paulinus: thus in Letter 11 to Severus, section 8, he wrote “sprinkled with dew”; and in On the Nativity of Saint Felix 6, poem 18, line 123, “surrounded with piety.” See note 101] (see note 101) [Note: [Col. 0281] Song of Songs II, 5, and IV, 9].

Blessed, however, is the one who can also touch Christ’s feet with a kiss [Note: [Col. 0282D] The manuscript, together with the four printed editions, reads “to anoint.” “To anoint with oil” occurs in Ambrose, Book VI on Luke, chapter 7. But the reading we retain is more harmonious, and is confirmed by the preceding and following words] [Note: [Col. 0281] Isaiah VI, 7].

Who would burn my wretched mouth and cleanse my tongue with that heavenly coal, so that I might deserve at least to touch Christ’s heel with the very tip of my mouth, and, lowering my head, wipe his holy sole—that is, his footprints [Note: [Col. 0282D] The Vienna manuscript reads “holy sole.” See note 102]—so that Christ’s feet might rather wipe my head; and while I lick the divine feet, might I atone for unclean lips with chaste footprints—that is, feet [Note: [Col. 0282D] The Vienna manuscript reads “holy sole.” See note 102].

### 39

Let us therefore exhort one another, and vie with one another in saying: “Come, let us adore and weep before the Lord, who made us” [Note: [Col. 0281] Psalm XCIV, 6]. We shall sow our joys while we weep for him [Note: [Col. 0282D] Rosweyde’s edition reads “we were sowing,” mistakenly, against the other manuscripts. See what follows]; by anointing his footprints, we shall heal our wounds. For whatever we spend upon Christ, we spend rather for ourselves [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke VII, 38]. Finally, by pouring ointment over Christ, she washed herself; by wiping his feet, she cleansed her own sins; by loving him, she loved herself.

And therefore she deserved to hear: “Daughter, your faith has saved you” [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke VII, 50]—something that the one who was among the sons of the kingdom did not deserve to hear; and she was more justified by service than he by the banquet. For the Pharisee had not believed, but she did believe.

Finally, he was saying: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what sort of woman she is who touches him” [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke VII, 39]. And therefore he was not justified by the banquet to which he had invited Christ as though he were merely a man, perhaps reproaching him for having thought it so great a thing to take a poor man into his meals, although he was rich and Christ, for our sake, was poor [Note: [Col. 0282D] The Vienna manuscript, supported by the Regius manuscript, reads “because”] [Note: [Col. 0281] II Corinthians VIII, 9].

But she would not have hoped for the remission of sins through so much service, expenditure, and tears unless she had believed that God was in Christ. And so, even at the Savior’s final footprint, she found the source of her salvation.

### 40

Where will you boast yourself, wretched Jew? In your own house our sinful woman preceded you, entering into your labors. You feasted in order to become proud; she fasted in order to serve [Note: [Col. 0281] John IV, 38]. And the water that you refused to pour from your jars, she supplied from her own eyes. You did not wipe Christ’s feet even with a linen cloth; she wiped them with her hair [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke VII, 44]. You were unwilling even to touch with your hands those feet which you deemed unworthy; she did not cease to soothe them with kisses.

Yet surely you ought rather to have performed this service for a guest received into your house, if you had preserved the law of hospitality according to the example of the fathers. But it is enough for you, in your pride, to boast of your father Abraham [Note: [Col. 0283] Genesis XVIII, 3; XIX, 2; XXIV, 31]. And therefore she preceded you, who by faithful affection proved herself rather the daughter of your father. This very inhumanity also proves you degenerate from him: you disdained to wash the Lord’s feet, although Abraham washed the feet of angels, and the Lord himself washed the feet of servants.

Yet even then the father of faith washed Christ’s feet, whom, seeing with prophetic eyes as one of the three, he adored. And therefore he himself now rebukes you with his present voice: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0283] John VIII, 39]. And he adds: “He saw my day and rejoiced” [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Regius manuscript reads “he made blessed.” Thus Paulinus, Letter 49 to Macarius, section 5: “he made the poor in spirit blessed”]. Blessed, moreover, are those who did not see, but believed together with those who saw [Note: [Col. 0283] John XX, 29].

From this it is evident that faith has been acquired for us, while its nature has perished for you through unbelief [Note: [Col. 0283D] Thus the Vatican and Regius manuscripts. The printed editions add “not.” We have corrected to “through unbelief,” against all the manuscripts, in which the reading is “of unbelief,” with no sense or rather the contrary sense. See Letter 50, section 1].

### 41

Let them therefore keep their arrogance for themselves, their riches for themselves, their nobility and their righteousness for themselves—those who boast of Abraham as father more in the flesh than in the spirit, Jews uncircumcised in heart and in flesh alone [Note: [Col. 0283] John VIII, 39; Acts VII, 51; I Corinthians II, 2].

For us, both for salvation and for glory, Christ is sufficient—and Christ crucified. He raised us from stones to be children of Abraham, while, in contrast, those who are Abraham’s children became rigid into stones of our origin [Note: [Col. 0283] Matthew III, 9].

For us, Ephraim, the younger, advanced from left to right in blessing; but for them, in Manasseh, the one who by the presumption of age had stood at his grandfather’s right hand, the left hand transferred to his head marked out the mystery of the cross [Note: [Col. 0283D] Thus the Vatican and Vienna manuscripts. The printed editions mistakenly read “ministry”]. For the cross was a stumbling block to the Jews [Note: [Col. 0283] I Corinthians I, 23], but was to be the future glory of Christians; it would make that man who was on the right left, and me who was on the left right. For while the Jews sink down in our wilderness and we enter into their sown fields, they are through blindness what we were, and we are through grace what they were [Note: [Col. 0283] John IV, 38].

But we shall not rejoice in our salvation in such a way that we rejoice in your destruction [Note: [Col. 0284D] The Vienna manuscript reads “we rejoice”]. For we have been taught by the brother of your flesh, but the teacher of our spirit (see Letter 30, section 5), not to insult broken branches [Note: [Col. 0283] Romans XI, 18], because we ourselves have grown into the tree of your stock not through works but through the gifts of God’s mercies.

The common Lord, however, who is the Father of Christians—that is, the God of believers—is powerful to graft you again into the bosom of your native bark and to replant you in your own soil. He nourished us with the sap of your richness through the benefit of adoption, so that one root might sustain both of us, bearing fruit together for the Lord.

### 42

For the present I prefer the riches of our poor sinful woman, in tears and affection, to yours, in ungodliness and the letter; I prefer her fasting to your banquet [Note: [Col. 0283] Luke VII, 38]. I would rather be bound among her locks to Christ’s feet than recline with you amid your banquets beside Christ without Christ.

If I do not now possess ointment for Christ’s feet, at his coming I shall have no oil for my lamps [Note: [Col. 0283] Matthew XXV, 3]. And woe to me if my ointment is cheap (see note 103): it must be precious, so that I may deserve to be buried together with him in his burial; for unless I die together with him in his death, I shall not live in his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0283] Romans VI, 4].

Therefore let us love him whom it is our duty to love. Let us kiss him whom chastity may kiss. Let us be joined to him, to whom virginity has been married. Let us be subjected to him, beneath whom to lie is to stand above the world. For his sake let us be cast down, for whom falling is resurrection. Let us die together with him, in whom there is life.

### 43

And how worthily shall we be able to repay this Lord, in whom we live even though dead [Note: [Col. 0283] Colossians III, 3]? He who in turn deigns to be for us whatever we, his little servants, have been for him [Note: [Col. 0283] Luke XII, 37]. For he mingles himself with us and grafts us into himself, so that he may make what he received benefit us; and whatever is bestowed upon us—that is, upon his least ones—he counts as bestowed upon himself [Note: [Col. 0283] Matthew XXV, 40].

Thus, joining his own to his honor, he has shared with us almost all his names (see note 104). As he is called the power of God, so he deigns that we too should be power: “God is our refuge and strength” [Note: [Col. 0283] Psalm XLV, 2].

He is an inheritance for us, and we are an inheritance for him. For just as you have in Moses: “The people of Jacob became God’s portion” [Note: [Col. 0283] Deuteronomy XXXII, 9], so in the Psalms you have: “The Lord is my portion” [Note: [Col. 0283] Psalms CXVIII, 57, and CXLI, 6].

And just as he himself says of himself, “I am the light of this world” [Note: [Col. 0283] John VIII, 12], so he also said to his own: “You are the light of this world” [Note: [Col. 0283] Matthew V, 14]. “I am,” he says, “the living bread”; and we are all one bread. “I am,” he says, “the true vine”; and he says to you: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true” [Note: [Col. 0284D] Thus the Regius and Vatican manuscripts and Saint Ambrose, Book VI on Luke, chapter 9. The *l* better corresponds to the Septuagint edition: “I planted you as an entirely true and fruitful vine,” πᾶσαν ἀληθινὴν. The Vulgate has: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true seed.” Our printed editions read “a true vine.” See note 105].

Christ is the mountain of God, in whom it pleased God to dwell, and his saints are God’s mountains, rich mountains, from which he enlightens us wonderfully from the everlasting mountains [Note: [Col. 0284D] Paulinus reads θαυμαστὸς (*wonderful*) instead of θαυμαστῶς (*wonderfully*)].

Christ is the rock: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” [Note: [Col. 0283] I Corinthians X, 4]. He did not deny even his disciple the grace of this name, saying to him: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” [Note: [Col. 0283] Matthew XVI, 18].

### 44

But why are we surprised that he granted his own names to his servants, when he also shares with them his Father and his kingdom? For he gave to those who received him the power to become children of God [Note: [Col. 0283] John I, 12]; and, so far as it depended upon him, he said to all people: “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0283] Psalm LXXXI, 6].

But through the guilt of our own wills we die as human beings, and like one of the princes we fall [Note: [Col. 0285] Psalm LXXXI, 7]. For he was one of the princes of angels before he fell by being cast down and became the devil. To him it is said: “How Lucifer fell, who rose in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0285] Isaiah XIV, 1].

But we have not been condemned, as he was, to eternal destruction, because he was the author of sin and will be punished both for himself and for the human being, who perished through the same crime by which the devil destroyed him. Humanity, however, did not deserve to be utterly banished from paradise and become earth, because divine Justice judged it lighter to have sinned through another’s mind than through one’s own. It is more criminal to deceive than to be deceived, and to devise sin than to commit it.

Therefore the one who consented to the fraud was punished temporarily and for correction, but the inventor of death was destined for eternal punishment; the penalty of his sin will never cease, because he never ceases. And so, as it is written, it was not an angel or an ambassador but the Lord himself who came to raise the crushed and release the fettered [Note: [Col. 0285] Psalm LXLV, 8, according to the Roman Psalter], and to save what had perished [Note: [Col. 0285] Luke XIX, 10].

But in order to confound that deceiver of ours by a kind of reciprocal deception, the only-begotten Son of God, through the mystery of his mercy, deigned to assume the very nature of our weakness, so that the devil might be conquered through the nature he had deceived; and the devil, who always was and is under God’s power and laws, might be subjected to a human being.

### 45

What, then, shall we repay him for all that he has repaid to us [Note: [Col. 0285] Psalm CXV, 12]? He did repay us, but as a good Lord he repaid good for evil, although we had inflicted evil upon him for good. He blessed, and we cursed. He healed, and we blasphemed. He justified the ungodly, and was counted among the wicked [Note: [Col. 0285] Isaiah LIII, 12].

What, then, shall I return to him for my evils, which he endured, and for his good things, which he bestowed? What shall I repay for the flesh he assumed (see note 106), for the slaps, the insults, the scourges, the cross, the death, the burial? Granted, let us repay a cross for the cross, a funeral for the funeral; but could we repay what we have from him, through him, and in him—all things [Note: [Col. 0285] Romans XI, 36]? And even we who possess them exist from him [Note: [Col. 0285D] We have added “from him” from the Vatican manuscript and Grin’s edition]. For he made us, and not we ourselves [Note: [Col. 0285] Psalm XCIX, 3], and our soul is always in his hands.

Let us therefore repay love for debt, charity for gift, gratitude for money. For woe to us if we do not love.

### 46

When could I, wretched and needy as I am, hope to repay this Lord, whom even the apostles confess that they have not repaid? Listen, finally, to one of them confessing that he has not repaid him. He says: “Who first gave to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” [Note: [Col. 0285D] Thus the Vienna manuscript, the Greek text, the Vulgate, Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, section 17, and Ambrose, Book VI, chapter 7 on Luke. Other manuscripts read “and it is repaid”] [Note: [Col. 0285] Romans XI, 35] (Ambrose, Book VI on Luke, chapter 7).

Yet thanks be to him, who as a good creditor remits the interest on so great a loan to us and provides relief from an immeasurable obligation, asking of us only love for him. By placing this love in the chief position among his commandments, he shows how even the needy may discharge an otherwise insoluble debt to him.

Let no one therefore excuse himself on the grounds that repayment is difficult, because no one can say that he does not possess a mind. No sacrifices, no costly gifts [Note: [Col. 0285D] The Vatican manuscript and Grin’s edition add in the margin “journeys.” Sacchini says that this is not entirely without reason, since in ancient times journeys were necessary in order to go to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices. This does not please us. What, then, does “costly journeys” mean? The true reading is therefore “costly gifts,” which is confirmed by what was said above], no harsh labors are required of us. We have within us the means by which we may repay. Our affection is a thing within our power; let us devote it to the Lord, and we repay him.

Finally, David, delivered from the hand of all his enemies and seeking complete assurance of his salvation, did not repay with the riches of a kingdom but with the payment of his heart, saying: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” [Note: [Col. 0285] Psalm XVII, 2, according to the Roman Psalter].

### 47

I add something further: he who is the creditor will also become the debtor if, loving him, we pay with a free tribute of the heart the price of his goodness, which he grants to us without owing it.

He is also loved in our own selves, because he said that this would be the sign of his disciples: if they loved one another with the love with which he loved us [Note: [Col. 0285] John XIII, 35]—that is, so that we might have one heart and one soul in Christ [Note: [Col. 0285] Acts IV, 32]—and that each person should do for his neighbor what he wishes to be done for himself [Note: [Col. 0285] Matthew VII, 12].

For this reason we glory all the more in the Lord because of your charity, which alone enables us, to some extent, to repay one of the great and innumerable debts owed to God. In all other good things we scarcely profess to have made a beginning, even in a few; in your love alone we profess to be perfect:

## Letter XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0285] Formerly Letter 2; the letter formerly numbered 24 is now 21. It was written and sent together with the preceding letter, in the year 401.]

Severus had praised Paulinus because he had bestowed his resources upon the poor, so that he might serve Christ more devotedly. Paulinus replies that it is a matter of little importance if someone casts away his riches unless he renounces himself; and he teaches where the perfection of evangelical poverty consists. Then he enumerates how many dangers, how many snares, and how many enemies threaten those who serve Christ, to show that leaving external things behind is the beginning of the battle, not victory.

### 1

I still have something to say to you, although you receive it in the hidden repositories of letters and, as far as you are able, strive to proclaim it upon the housetops, as you yourself acknowledge [Note: [Col. 0286D] The Vienna manuscript reads: “although you who receive, in hidden places, the storehouses of letters …”].

But if, among the other absurdities of our loquacity, you bring out this complaint which we are now about to deposit with you and within you, you will at the same time publicize your own rashness. We are complaining of that rashness and composing this letter, having been reminded at the end of the preceding one of the word concerning charity and perfection, so that we might make this its beginning.

For this is the reason we reproach you, arising from the excessive affection of your unanimity: great love draws you even into the sin of lying. For whether I consider what you say about yourself or what you say about us—heaping our burdens up with unjust praises and diminishing your own with false reproaches—I accuse you of sinning against charity through charity.

“For charity,” he says, “is kind; charity does no harm to its neighbor” [Note: [Col. 0287] I Corinthians XIII, 4; Romans XIII, 10]. You show it to us as kind, as we experience it, and we glory in that. But take care lest you seem to act contrary to its rule by doing harm to your neighbors, upon whom you heap the burden of sins through the weight of undeserved praise [Note: [Col. 0287D] The Regius manuscript reads “heaping up”].

And as though you did not want the same thing for us as for yourself, if you consider it just to speak about us in such a way that you judge it useless for you to speak about yourself, you will rightly hear: “If you love rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” [Note: [Col. 0287] Genesis IV, 7, according to the Septuagint] (see note 107).

Unless perhaps you do this also out of a deeper plan of piety: by granting us in words goods that belong to others, you may be suggesting the spur of shame, so that, on reading what we ought to be, we may learn to be good and strive to show ourselves according to your words. Perhaps we may become what we are not, when we are ashamed not to be what we are called.

For the present, however, while conscience does not acknowledge the truth of your words, modesty rejects your flattery. As I said, this applies to you yourself: why do you dare to ascribe to us, as though we were victors after a completed contest, the palm of perfection, because we seem to have laid aside the entire burden of earthly possession—that is, to have deposited it [Note: [Col. 0287D] “That is, to have deposited it.” See poem 23, line 66]—while you, in contrast, lament that you are still wretched and clinging to the mud of infernal filth, because you seem not to have sold even one little estate, as you wrote, when you have nevertheless alienated even that one from your present ownership just as though it had been sold.

Thus you have become devoted to God twice over in the greater fruits of faith: by different acts of commerce but with one gain of life, within the limits of the same commandment, a seller and giver of estates and therefore a possessor without captivity of spirit; for even what you have reserved, the Church, as your servant, possesses on your behalf (see note 108).

### 2

Therefore weigh both our accounts and yours against the words of the Lord himself, lest you distrust yourself as though hindered, or congratulate us as though already free.

Consider that there are distributions of graces and measures of gifts. God, one and the same dispenser, works these in the members of his body, distinguishing different members in his body by gifts according to his will [Note: [Col. 0287] Romans XII, 4]. But he constructs one body from the diversity of its members, so that the grace of the sacred body may also be increased through this, if manifold virtue is counted within one structure [Note: [Col. 0287] I Corinthians XII, 4]; so that “the queen may stand at his right hand in golden fringes, clothed round about in variety” [Note: [Col. 0287] Psalm XLIV, 10 and 15, according to the Roman Psalter].

Consider now how much God has given you in that body. He has allotted you a portion also in the lot of those who lived perfectly under the law, possessing in such a way that they were not possessed by their possessions, and placing no love either of things or of relationships before the love and discipline of the Lord, as is shown in Job [Note: [Col. 0287] Job I, 21], Abraham, and Lot [Note: [Col. 0287] Genesis XII, 4]. But you are also a sharer in those whom the fullness of the Gospel perfects: you sold the estates that were the greater wealth and temptation.

### 3

Hence I trust that an equal rest is prepared for you in the midst of the divine lots, so that you may sleep, as it is written, “among the midst of the lots” [Note: [Col. 0287] Psalm LXVII, 4], that is, the Lord’s portions, which are understood in the two Testaments, from which the Lord’s inheritance and the fullness of the saints are completed.

For this reason I am ready to use the Lord’s word against you in the opposite sense, and to say to you: “In your brother’s eye you see the splinter of grace, and in your own you do not perceive the mass of that same good” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matthew VII, 3; Luke VI, 41], although, as I said, you have occupied both portions of the saints: a possessor in the estates you have retained, and perfect in those you have sold.

Therefore, even in the matter in which you appear to be a possessor, you are perfect in mind, freed from the bonds of possessions. Mindful of the shortness of time, you fulfill the Apostle’s saying [Note: [Col. 0287] I Corinthians VII, 39], so that, having, you do not have; for you have not for yourself, but for those who do not have.

You are a guest in your own house, so that you may be the house of guests. You are a stranger in your own homeland and an exile from this world, so that you may be an inhabitant of paradise and a citizen of the ancient homeland.

You do not occupy your dwelling with dining rooms, nor do you pack it with masses of household goods or money [Note: [Col. 0288D] The Vienna manuscript reads “with household furnishings”]. Rather, as the sole measurer of a corner, you fill it with strangers and the needy; you, yourself a fellow servant of your household servants, occupy the temporary habitation of your roof not as master of the house but as an empty hired man or tenant [Note: [Col. 0288D] Thus the Vatican manuscript and Grin’s edition. This yields a fine sense: “empty,” that is, “very poor.” Others read “you remain”], paying the Most High Lord the rent of a precarious dwelling [Note: [Col. 0288D] We have added this word from the Vienna manuscript. It is confirmed below in section 9] from the shared servitude of both your body and your soul.

### 4

But if, according to the measure of the work, the reward must be extended or contracted, and some compensation must be made between what has been done and what has not been done, then the condition of your mind’s perfection must be reckoned equal to the work of those who sold everything, because you have left nothing for yourself, either in ownership or, what is more, in your mind; you use the world as though you did not use it [Note: [Col. 0287] I Corinthians VII, 31].

And I do not know whether that constancy and firmness of your heart should be judged the stronger faith, by which you are not burned amid fires [Note: [Col. 0287] Proverbs VI, 27], are not caught among snares, touch pitch and are not defiled [Note: [Col. 0287] Ecclesiasticus XIII, 1], than that of those whom you consider strong but whom I judge weaker. For, not trusting their weakness, they hastened to alienate everything to which they feared they might cling.

You, therefore, are “free among the dead” [Note: [Col. 0289] Psalm LXXXVII, 6], since in earthly possession you are no longer earth, and you rise above earthly things [Note: [Col. 0289D] Thus the Regius and Vienna manuscripts. Three printed editions read “seed of the earth”; the Vatican manuscript and Grin’s edition read “earthly seed”]. You are not polluted by the contagion of corpses, nor do you dwell in the tombs of those cast down in sleep [Note: [Col. 0289] Psalms LXVII, 7 and LXXXVII, 6] (see note 109), because you have buried your life in heaven, the life that you have hidden in Christ [Note: [Col. 0289] Colossians III, 3].

Let us, however, not begrudge the perfection; rather, let us accept the pardon of weakness. For you cannot deny that it is stronger to lack possessions while they remain than after they have been alienated, and that it is stronger to despise what you possess than not to possess what you despise.

### 5.

Consider carefully the very words of the Lord concerning which you claim perfection for us, and you will see that you have treated beginnings as the end. “If you wish,” he says, “to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0289] Matthew 19:21.]. If he had ended his statement there, I would be falsely accusing you; indeed, I would gladly ask you, as a neighbor and fellow participant in the same endeavor, to congratulate me, since we would then be holding in our hands, as it were, the palm of a completed contest—the tenth drachma, so to speak, which had been lost in our first ancestor according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0289] Luke 15:8.], but which, though still within the house, had at last been found after the lamp of the saving word was lit. But when you see how substantial a word remains, since the Lord of majesty himself adds, “And come, follow me” [Note: [Col. 0289] Matthew 19:21.], consider rather the difficulty of this command and measure it with an enlarged heart. Then you will understand that greater reasons for anxiety about us remain for you than reasons for congratulation.

For the good things, or burdens, laid upon us easily slipped away when we let our cloaks fall back; and what we had not brought with us into this world, nor could carry out with us [Note: [Col. 0289D] So the manuscripts Reg. and Vien. In the others, “take away.”], we returned as though it had merely been borrowed. We did not tear away skin from flesh, but laid aside a garment from the body [Note: [Col. 0289] 1 Timothy 6:7.].

### 6.

Now it is necessary for us to render to God what is truly ours—that is, to present our hearts, souls, and bodies as a living sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0289] Romans 12:1.], as it is written, to the Lord; and to build ourselves for him as a holy temple [Note: [Col. 0289] Ephesians 2:21.], upon the cornerstone who gave us in himself the pattern of our sanctification and said: “Be holy, for I am holy” [Note: [Col. 0289] Leviticus 11:44.].

What favor, then, is ours if we have been faithful only in what belongs to another, unless we serve from what is our own—that is, from the free choice of the will, loving God with all our heart and with all the powers of our soul, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0289] Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37.]? To this affection the prophet urges us when he says: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” [Note: [Col. 0289] Psalm 53:8.]. For this is acceptable and pleasing before God: that our good be voluntary [Note: [Col. 0289] Philemon 14.].

Thus may we receive what is ours—the house of paradise, that is, and eternal life—in which we were created. If, purified from possession of this earth into which we came under condemnation, we recover that inheritance, then truly, restored from exile to our homeland, or brought back from a distant sojourn to our native home, we shall be able to say: “The Lord is my portion in the land of the living” [Note: [Col. 0289] Psalm 141:6.].

### 7.

For this reason, abandoning or disposing of the temporal goods possessed in this age is not the completion of the course but its entrance; it is not the finishing mark but the door. An athlete does not win when he strips himself; he is stripped so that he may begin to fight and, when he has competed lawfully, receive the crown [Note: [Col. 0289] 2 Timothy 2:5.]. A swimmer likewise strips himself in order to overcome the river lying before him. Yet merely because he has divested himself with all this preparation, he will not swim across unless, by the exertion of his whole body, the carefully coordinated movement of all his limbs, the thrust of his feet, the rowing of his arms, and the gliding of his side, he cuts through the current’s force and completes the labor of swimming.

### 8.

I see, nevertheless, that the blessed patriarch Jacob also foreshadowed for us the order of this undertaking [Note: [Col. 0289] Genesis 32:24.]. I read that, after crossing the torrent and sending ahead the burdens of his concerns—that is, the impediments of bodily possessions and relationships—he remained alone at the site of the tent and wrestled with God. When he prevailed in obtaining the blessing, he received the name Israel, consecrated to heaven and earth.

Although this chiefly appears to be a foreshadowing of the saving mystery—namely, that Jacob prevailed with the Lord in the figure of the Jews, that is, through the offspring of his body, just as that people prevailed in procuring the Lord’s passion from Pilate, as it is written when they said, “Crucify, crucify,” and, he says, “their voices prevailed” [Note: [Col. 0289] Luke 23:21.]—nevertheless, in the present argument this history seems useful only insofar as it produced an image of the evangelical command. From that example we understand that we cannot be adequately prepared to contend with God. We contend with him, of course, when we strive to fulfill his word and endeavor, by imitating him, to prevail in divine virtues.

Accordingly, to take up the path of life, to seize God’s word, and to prevail in attaining the kingdom of heaven—which “has suffered violence since the days of John and is seized by those who use force” [Note: [Col. 0289] Matthew 12:13.] [Note: [Col. 0289] Luke 16:16.] [Note: [Col. 0290D] We have added this word from manuscript Vien. The Reg. manuscript reads: “is hindered by force and seized by those who use force,” which is suitable.]—we cannot be fit for this unless, before the evening of our death, we send ahead everything that, whether through love or concern, adheres to us and impedes or delays us on the journey through this age. From then on, throughout the entire night of this age, we must strive with anxious persistence in spiritual works and pursuits to seize and hold Christ; nor must we be torn away from Christ’s love, as Jacob was not torn from his embrace, until we wrest from him the blessing [Note: [Col. 0289] Genesis 32:26.].

And would that, as a mark of the saving struggle, he might strike the sinew of our thigh with fear of his majesty. When that sinew is numbed, the strength of the flesh will be weakened, and spiritual grace will grow strong.

Yet in Jacob, as a figure of Jewish barrenness and corruption, the sinew of the struck thigh withered. It signified that portion of his children which, degenerating from the faith of the fathers, ceased to be fruitful for God. Hence you have the saying: “She who was fruitful in children has languished” [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Samuel 2:5.]; and, straying from the commands of its author, it limped along the paths of its error.

### 9.

Nevertheless, we too must take care not to appear barren in the sight of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Kings 16:21.], nor limp with a weakened foot upon his path. Rather, though unfruitful in bodily offspring, let us draw that stupor of the ancestral thigh from the blow of the divine hand toward the rigor of self-restraint. Let us strengthen the soul through chastity, rendering it powerless against the desires by which the strength of faith is weakened. As the Apostle teaches [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Corinthians 9:25.], even athletes of the flesh guard themselves carefully (see note 110); therefore we who struggle for that unfading crown must preserve chastity with still greater diligence, since it is cultivated even by those contending for a temporal and perishable crown.

Accordingly, when we are about to fight before the Lord in the theater of this world, under the gaze of human beings and angels [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Corinthians 4:9.], let us strip off hostile burdens, so that we may be clothed with healing burdens [Note: [Col. 0291D] So manuscript Vat. and the Grin. edition. Other codices read “works,” a reading that may be supported by the word used below, “laboring.” See whether perhaps “healing resources” should be read, as in poem 18, line 159; poem 23, line 381; and poem 30, line 31. For a copyist’s error from *opibus* to *operibus* is easy.]. For he who says, “Come, follow me,” wishes to prepare us precisely for this [Note: [Col. 0292D] We have added this word from manuscript Vien.]. [Note: [Col. 0291] Matthew 8:22; Mark 2:14 and 10:21; Luke 5:27 and 18:22.]—so that we may seize him in whom we have ourselves been seized by him.

He who calls us to the place where he sits at the right hand of God [Note: [Col. 0291] Mark 16:19.] in the glory of the Father says to everyone: “Come to me, you who are burdened and laboring, and you will find rest for your souls” [Note: [Col. 0291] Hebrews 1:3; Matthew 11:28.]. For he wishes every human being, insofar as it depends on him, to be saved [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Timothy 2:4; John 3:13; Philippians 3:21.], he who made them all.

For this reason also he descended to us, so that we might ascend to him. He was conformed to the body of our flesh, which was enslaved to sin, so that he might conform us to the body of his flesh, which committed no sin, and so that we might truly be restored to our original glory, if through imitation of Christ we take on the divine likeness.

For Genesis itself, which recounts the work of the divine hand, shows that in Adam only the image remained to us (see note 111) [Note: [Col. 0291] Genesis 1:26; 2:7.]. In the account of the making of the human being, likeness is mentioned together with the image of God; but in the following chapter, where the human being already made is said to have been created only in the image of God, the foreknowledge of what was to come plainly indicates that likeness was destined to be withdrawn from the one who was about to sin, so that it might be reserved for human beings in Christ. Through the obedience of his devotion, Christ reconciled to the Father the world that the disobedience of the first ancestor had alienated [Note: [Col. 0291] 2 Corinthians 5:19; Romans 5:19.].

Therefore the Lord himself, emptied into the form of a servant, received again the likeness of God, which the servant had clearly lost through desire for the Lord’s equality [Note: [Col. 0291] Philippians 1:7.]. The human being who had fallen through pride by the deceit of the devil rose through faith in the humility of the Lord, in the humiliation of the Most High Lord, when the devil had been overthrown.

Thus he, grieving for us and becoming obedient for our sake unto death, even death on a cross [Note: [Col. 0291] Philippians 2:8.], set before us the way of life and the perfection of virtue—not merely in selling estates and distributing their price, but in following him.

And because he had said, “When I have been lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” [Note: [Col. 0291] John 12:32.], he therefore says, “Come, follow me” [Note: [Col. 0291] Matthew 19:21.]. Blessed is the one who follows at so close a distance that he can say: “My soul clings after you” [Note: [Col. 0291] Psalm 62:9.].

Only that love can say this which is the fulfillment of the commandment and the fullness of the law: love which, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0291] Romans 13:10; 1 Timothy 1:5.], so inserts and fastens itself into God that, loving nothing outside God, it says: “And I am continually with you” [Note: [Col. 0291] Psalm 72:23.].

Our entire labor, therefore, and our complete task consist in guarding and stripping our heart. We cannot see the darkness or the hidden lairs of the enemy concealed within it unless the mind has been cleansed of concern for external things and turned inward toward itself. For it was not said without reason: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” [Note: [Col. 0291] Proverbs 4:23.].

### 10.

I believe you have now learned by experience how laborious and continual—indeed, daily—the struggle with this enemy is for us, how many ambushes are laid within it, how much force vice possesses there (that is, its power; see section 23), how much weakness virtue has, how readily the soul relapses into perversity, and how sluggish is its striving toward God.

Now that discord of a divided law, formerly closed within me, is opened to me. Now I feel the power of the opposing law, which, as though laying hands upon me, strives to drag me captive into the law of sin [Col. 0292C]. And I recognize that the blessed man burns rather because of my misery, and, grieving for me because of my condition, cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0291] Romans 7:24.]

But the same Teacher revives and restores me, showing me a saving escape, provided that willingness is present in me, so that I may deserve to find perfection through the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. He must be entreated to prevail over our enemies and to abound beyond the darkness [Note: [Col. 0292D] Manuscript Vien. reads, “to overcome the darkness.” The reading we have retained is excellently confirmed by Letter 12 to Amandus, section 10, where we read, “the riches of his goodness, with which he abounds beyond the abundance of our sins.”]; to destroy in us what belongs to another or to ourselves, and to build what belongs to him.

We know that the friends of God have obtained this through prayer. They allowed their hearts to be searched when they said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts” [Note: [Col. 0291] Psalm 50:12.]; [Note: [Col. 0292D] Manuscripts Reg. and Vat. and the editions of Bad., Grav., and Schot. read “who.”] and, once he has entreated him, he confidently says: “Test me, Lord, and know my heart; and see whether there is in me any way of wickedness” [Note: [Col. 0291] Psalms 25:2 and 138:23.].

But lest he appear to have obtained this confidence in himself through his own virtue rather than through the grace of God, he says the same thing: “For you, Lord, have possessed my inward parts” [Note: [Col. 0291] Psalm 138:13.]. For, as the Lord himself said, we can do nothing without him, because he is the true vine [Note: [Col. 0293] John 15:5.] and we are his branches.

If we remain in his love, we shall not wither, living from the sap of the eternal root. Nor shall we be cut off and cast into the fire by anger; rather, we shall be pruned for fruitfulness by discipline, as the edge of the evangelical pruning-hook purifies us, so that, with the luxuriance of our branches chastened, we may sprout more fruitfully.

### 11.

Therefore, as he is about to begin his cultivation in us, he says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0293] Luke 12:49.]. He wishes thereby to cleanse our heart, burdened with sins like a field bristling with thorns, burning us in our vices and illuminating us in our understanding.

The pious cultivator pursues in us the roots of our former actions with the saving pruning-hook [Note: [Col. 0293D] So manuscript Reg. and the Grin. and Schot. editions. Others read “torch,” less suitably. See the preceding and following context.], so that the fiery word may set alight whatever stubble remains from the old harvest and prepare our soul, like a field, for new sowing. Freed of thorns by the plowshare pressed into them by the divine word, it may pour forth a joyful crop of virtues and multiply fruits worthy of the heavenly granaries once the roots of harmful weeds have been destroyed.

But because we are not only God’s agriculture but also his building, cultivated and constructed by his grace, Spirit, and word [Note: [Col. 0293] 1 Corinthians 3:7; Ephesians 2:21.], he prepares us for building along the path by which he calls us after himself, through the work by which he first advises us to be released from our possessions.

Since concern for or love of these things dims the mind’s very sight [Note: [Col. 0293D] Manuscript Vien. reads, “touches closely.”] and draws the soul away from its inward parts toward external things, he also says to us through the prophet: “Be still, and see that I am God” [Note: [Col. 0293] Psalm 45:11.].

Does he not seem here also to say: “You cannot serve two masters” [Note: [Col. 0293] Matthew 6:24.]? By this word he does not recommend idleness, since he commands us to pray and keep watch continually, lest we enter into temptation [Note: [Col. 0293] Luke 22:40.]. Rather, he commands us to be free from the world so that we may be occupied with him; to be free from those affairs by which we are entangled and made idle toward God [Note: [Col. 0293] Romans 6:6.].

### 12.

Thus, as we build the newness of life in ourselves, it is necessary that we destroy the old. Since darkness can have no commerce with light, nor mammon with Christ [Note: [Col. 0293D] So manuscript Vien., with *b* changed to *u*. The editions read, “it is expedient for us to avoid old things.” Manuscript Reg. reads, “it is necessary,” and so on, as in the editions. Paulinus seems to have written what we have inserted into the text; the preceding and following context confirm it.], we must exchange old things for new. We must reverse the manner both of our occupation and of our leisure: we must become involved in the things from which we had been free, and be free from the things in which we had been involved. We must die to the things by which we lived, and conversely live for those works and pursuits to which we had been dead; while alive, we had been dead, and while performing works that put us to death, we would live among the dead [Note: [Col. 0293D] So manuscript Vien. Other codices read, “of the living.”].

Hence the holy Teacher (see Letters 23, section 14, and 37, section 3) makes the humane and reasonable demand that, just as we presented our members to serve iniquity, so now we should present those same members as servants of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0293] Romans 6:13.]. We must change our pursuits when we change our masters.

For by exchanging masters we do not lay aside either slavery or freedom. We acquire only happiness, changing both slavery and freedom for the better: when we break the bond of iniquity, submit ourselves to the yoke of righteousness, and are restrained by divine fear, we begin—having turned the path straight—to be free from sin, to which we had been enslaved in miserable freedom while rebelling against righteousness.

### 13.

Now, therefore, servants of God and rebels against this world, we enter the contest; trusting in the Lord, we challenge as an enemy the one whom we once served.

You surely recognize, my brother—for I speak as a fellow soldier who has shared the experience—how great our discord is and how great is the enemy within us: not flesh and blood, but, as the Apostle says, invisible powers and spiritual wickedness [Note: [Col. 0294D] So the manuscripts read. The editions have “wickednesses … spiritual.”] [Note: [Col. 0293] Ephesians 6:12.], which conspire with the agencies of carnal vices [Note: [Col. 0294D] Manuscript Vien. reads, “may reach.”].

Hence they are also called “the rulers of darkness” [Note: [Col. 0293] Ephesians 5:8.], because, according to the Apostle, sinners are called darkness, and demons rule over them as over beings like themselves.

But the whole form of this world, which is passing away [Note: [Col. 0293] 1 Corinthians 7:31.] and entices hearts through the eyes, spread out before us in devilish nets, is, in whatever form it appears, a snare for the mind and a sword.

Let us believe the prophet, because we walk in the midst of traps, and life is spent among swords concealed by deadly deceptions [Note: [Col. 0293] Psalms 22:4 and 30:5; Wisdom 14:11; Ecclesiasticus 9:20.].

This world receives us, flourishing with varied pleasures and poisoned with deceptive allurements. The serpent assails us with innumerable ambushes: it has a thousand names and a thousand arts of harming. Often it attacks us with open combat and assails us with glowing weapons if it cannot capture us in hidden snares.

For the sharp arrows of the mighty one [Note: [Col. 0294D] The Regius manuscript, together with the Bad. edition, reads “powerful.” Thus Augustine reads Psalm 44:6 according to the manuscripts of better quality: “Your arrows are sharp, exceedingly powerful”; and it is easy to see from the interpretation itself that Augustine read it this way.] come with burning coals of desolation [Note: [Col. 0293] Psalm 119:4.]. These burn our soul with the harmful fires of desire and drive it from the dwelling of the Holy Spirit.

When this occurs, various guests enter us, and a person’s own household becomes his enemies [Note: [Col. 0293] Matthew 10:36.]. Now they inflate us with the wind of ambition, now apply the torches of lust, now bind us with the chains of avarice. Avarice alone, armed with every crime, is sufficient—if it captures us by itself—for the devil’s wickedness and for the human being’s death.

### 14.

What, then, are you doing, unhappy human being, placed—or perhaps mingled [Note: [Col. 0294D] Perhaps “mingled” should be read.]—among so many enemies? How will you, weak as you are, resist the strong; unarmed, the armed?

Blessed Job, wounded by many weapons of the devil yet uninjured in heart, cries out: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb” [Note: [Col. 0293] Job 1:21.]. Who, then, will arm me against all these hosts of the aerial enemy [Note: [Col. 0294D] That is, of the devil. See Ephesians 2:2, “the prince of the power of the air.”], lest naked, as I came, I return to the earth?

Behold, I breathe again; I am strengthened; I rise up. “The Lord is my light, the Lord is the defender of my life. Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear” [Note: [Col. 0295] Psalm 26:1, according to the Septuagint.].

Nor, if I lack weapons of my own strength, will I despair. I have Christ’s arsenal, from which I may take the weapons of light, with which I may storm the rulers of darkness and the armies of night opposing me in the heavenly places [Note: [Col. 0295] Romans 13:12; Ephesians 6:12.]—that is, in the spiritual way of life, which they strive to overthrow with earthly enticements.

But against these enemies my armor-bearer and standard-bearer will be the one who was a chosen vessel for God. He will fasten my loins with the belt of chastity, fit the helmet of salvation upon my head, and enclose my breast in the breastplate of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0295] Acts 9:15; Ephesians 6:14; Isaiah 59:17.].

He will protect me entirely with the shield of faith and arm my right hand—or rather, arm me whole, made into Christ’s right hand—with the sword of the Spirit and the word of truth. Then a thousand will fall at my side and ten thousand at my right hand [Note: [Col. 0295D] So manuscript Reg. and four printed codices, the Old Psalter, and Augustine in his Commentary on the Psalms. Paulinus likewise read this in Letter 37 to Victricius, section 4, and poem 21 to Cytherius, line 627.] [Note: [Col. 0295] Psalm 90:7.].

He will shod my feet with readiness for the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0295] Ephesians 6:15.], so that, with my step firmly planted, I may walk unharmed over the thorns and thistles of this earth, and with a protected foot proceed safely over the rough places of the narrow path.

Without fearing the bite, I will crush the subdued head of the enemy serpent [Note: [Col. 0295] Genesis 3:15.] with the very heel that he watches in ambush.

I do not arrogantly claim this for myself as though it arose from the boldness of my weakness; rather, I promise it to every believer through the power of Christ. As he calls things that are not as though they were [Note: [Col. 0295] Romans 4:17.], so he is powerful—as he always has been and is now—to destroy the strong and lofty things of this world through his weak and humble ones [Note: [Col. 0295] 1 Corinthians 1:27.].

For this reason he gave us a Teacher who had him as the one he imitated, through whom we might reach imitation of the Lord himself. The Teacher teaches me to stand in the battle line, to run in the stadium, and to struggle in the contest, “buffeting” [Note: [Col. 0295D] Greek: ὑποπιάζων. Paulinus uses the same reading according to the force of the Greek text in Letter 12 to Amandus, section 7, and Letter 50 to Augustine, section 13. See note 112.] his body and making it livid (see note 112), forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead [Note: [Col. 0295] Philippians 3:13.].

### 15.

Thus founded upon the rock, so that he may glory even in weaknesses and, when he is weak, may then be powerful—powerful in every respect [Note: [Col. 0295] 2 Corinthians 12:10.]—as he himself professes [Note: [Col. 0295] Philippians 4:13; Hebrews 2:18.], in him who strengthens his own [Note: [Col. 0295D] Manuscript Vien., the Grin. edition in the margin, and the Vulgate read, “strengthens.”]—namely, Christ, who fights for us and conquers in us—this was the reason the Apostle said: “Run in such a way that you may all attain” (see note 113) [Note: [Col. 0295] 1 Corinthians 9:24.].

In an earthly contest the opposite occurs, where a struggle cannot end except through unequal fortune among the contestants, so that the glory of one is the disgrace of another. But in Christ, because we who are many are one [Note: [Col. 0295] Romans 12:5.], we all run as one; the course of all is directed toward one common good. Therefore it is said to us: “Run in such a way that you may all attain.”

For, as the same Apostle says, there can be no division in the body whose head is Christ; the one structure of its members accompanies him as their common summit. Since its members cannot disagree with one another, let us run together [Note: [Col. 0295] 1 Corinthians 9:24.], so that all may attain, without jealous rivalry and with victory shared equally. Thus, just as in the contest of running we are Christ’s labor, so at the finish of reaching the goal we may be Christ’s triumph, and he may bless us with the crown of the year of his goodness [Note: [Col. 0295] Psalm 64:12.].

### 16.

I see, however, that in this contest it is no less advantageous for us to conquer than to be conquered, because both an enemy and a friend dwell within us.

Who is friendlier to me than the spirit that opposes the flesh, lest it drag me into the law of sin? Or who is more hostile to us than the flesh, which lusts against the spirit for our destruction?

Therefore I prefer the wounds of a friend, which Christ received in order to heal me [Note: [Col. 0295D] Manuscript Vien. reads, “which he accepted in order to heal mine”; not an unsuitable reading.], to the voluntary kisses of an enemy [Note: [Col. 0295] Proverbs 27:6, according to the Septuagint.]. Through the allurements of its pleasures, the flesh, with its evil counsel, flatters me so as to betray me into captivity to enemies prepared for my capture, like that parricidal kiss of Judas [Note: [Col. 0295] Matthew 26:49.].

Yet the Lord did not receive that kiss in order to accept the peace of the betrayer, but in order to recover his own from the one who had been alienated.

It is also salutary to retain that other example as a model of perfect goodness: in the same spirit in which he commands us to love our enemies [Note: [Col. 0295] Matthew 5:44.], he gave the enemy a friendly kiss of peace, returning love for hatred, though he received hatred in return for his love [Note: [Col. 0295] Psalm 108:5.] [Note: [Col. 0296D] So manuscripts Reg. and Vien., together with the Bad. and Grin. editions. Others read “to hold.”].

### 17.

It is therefore easy to distinguish: the devil and the flesh contend with one another [Note: [Col. 0296D] Manuscripts Reg. and Vat. and the Grin. and Schot. editions read “the devil.” See note 2.]. It is better to be conquered by good than to conquer through evil [Note: [Col. 0296D] Manuscript Vien. reads, “it is good to be conquered … evil.”].

Thus one seems defeated in this world when another takes away his tunic [Note: [Col. 0295] Matthew 5:40.]; but in Christ he triumphs when he lets the one who took away his tunic have his cloak as well.

To return injury for injury is human vengeance [Note: [Col. 0295] Ibid., verse 44.]; but to love even an enemy is heavenly vengeance.

To sell one’s patrimony and give to the poor [Note: [Col. 0295] Matthew 19:21.] is folly to this world but wisdom to God. Conversely, to cling to riches, increase money through interest, enlarge possessions by auctions, and extend boundaries by force is industry and profit in this world, but before God it is crime and punishment.

Thus, if you conquer through evil, though victorious you have been defeated, because when you conquered through wickedness, you were overcome by desire.

But when defeated, you will conquer if you yield to what is just and the divine will prevails over your own will [Note: [Col. 0296D] Manuscript Vat. reads, “you conquer if you yield to what is unjust.” The Grin. edition reads, “you conquer if you yield to what is just,” which amounts to the same thing as being conquered by good and is opposed to the preceding “if you conquer through evil,” Sacchinus.].

Let us therefore be emptied of our own powers, so that we may be filled with divine ones. Let us be conquered in body so that we may conquer in salvation.

Let us remember that we are members of the one who conquered when he was judged, who overcame by yielding, and who, by falling into death, rose again into glory, establishing the rising of our resurrection from the setting of his passion [Note: [Col. 0297] Romans 6:4.].

### 18.

Let us follow this Lord who calls us, who teaches us to conquer by yielding and to live again by dying (see Letter 44, section 7), killing in us that by which we are put to death and bringing to life that by which we live.

This is our God; no other shall be compared with him, who was seen on earth and lived among human beings.

Because flesh and blood cannot reveal this to us, he therefore says: “Be still, and see that I am God” [Note: [Col. 0297] Psalm 45:11.].

At this point I am stirred to the boldness of questioning, so that I may say: Who are you, God, who made heaven and earth and appeared in the bush; who performed great deeds in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham [Note: [Col. 0297D] We have corrected this expression in the text, although the manuscripts and printed editions read “Canaan.” See note 114.], and terrors in the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0297] Genesis 1:7; Exodus 3:2; Acts 2:30; Psalm 105:21–22.]?

Even now everyone believes that you are God—not only the Jews, however much they love you with their lips while being far from you in their hearts [Note: [Col. 0297] Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8.], as a people formed under the law, but also the Gentiles living without the law, who by natural perception confess the one Lord of supreme power [Note: [Col. 0297] Romans 2:14.].

What difficulty, then, is there in seeing that you are God, when the heavens declare your glory [Note: [Col. 0297] Psalm 18:2.] and your invisible attributes are seen and understood through the things that have been made [Note: [Col. 0297] Romans 1:20.]?

What prevents us from possessing you? What hinders us from attending to other matters, when even people occupied with affairs can readily behold God’s manifest truth and see the evident light of supreme providence?

“Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night” [Note: [Col. 0297] Psalms 18:3 and 45:11.]. Yet I am commanded to be still so that I may see that you are God, when even the nights know this light—that is, even the rulers or servants of darkness [Note: [Col. 0297] Ephesians 6:12.].

### 19.

But it is not without reason that the truth, which has often revealed itself through many conspicuous signs of divinity, testifies that it can be perceived only when stillness has been secured.

It is immediately evident that God is God. As I have said, every soul sees this; no mind is darkened with respect to it; even the faith of unbelievers perceives it [Note: [Col. 0297D] So manuscript Vien. Others read “receives it.”].

But that God is in Christ, or Christ in God, is not seen by one who is occupied and surrounded by a cloud of earthly cares [Note: [Col. 0297D] Manuscript Vien. reads, “occupied and surrounded …,” not unreasonably. We have retained the common reading because the phrase “when even people occupied with affairs can readily … see the light” occurred shortly before.].

For the Word made flesh is folly to the wisdom of this world [Note: [Col. 0297] John 1:14.]. Therefore it pleased God, in order to confound the wisdom whose pride did not recognize God’s wisdom, to save believers through the folly of preaching [Note: [Col. 0297] 1 Corinthians 1:21.].

### 20.

This, then, is that treasure of the field for the sake of obtaining which the field itself must also be purchased [Note: [Col. 0297] Matthew 13:44.]. The price of our salvation consists in confessing that God, the Son of God, came in the flesh to save the flesh. This is the pearl to be bought at the cost of patrimonies squandered.

But it is not immediately bought once its price has been prepared, because many difficulties intervene in the transaction itself [Note: [Col. 0297] Matthew 13:46.]. Either the sea lies between, or a robber intercepts it, or one more eager arrives first, or a wealthier person is preferred.

Therefore do not suppose that we have already purchased the gem merely because you see that we have prepared its price. Nor should you suppose that we have already built the house for which we have merely cleared the site, when we have removed visible riches, household goods, money, and patrimonies like filthy heaps and troublesome rubble, so that in a cleansed heart, as in living earth, we might lay the foundations of a more firmly established building.

But just as, when the soil has been stripped bare by the removal of rubble, many knots of tree-trunks, remnants of ruins, animals of harmful kinds, and especially the offspring or lairs of vipers are discovered beneath the unclean masses [Note: [Col. 0297D] Manuscript Vat. reads, “a fierce serpent.”], so, when possession and concern for temporal things have been removed from our breast and, free from the things that drew us outward, we devote ourselves to inspecting our heart, we discover in our thoughts the knots of long-standing crimes and the hiding places of spiritual enemies [Note: [Col. 0298D] So manuscript Vien. The others read, “for the inspection of our heart, now vacant from these things that were drawing us outward.” The Schot. edition has “being vacant.”].

Now the inner house begins to appear to us, and there are creeping things without number [Note: [Col. 0297] Psalm 104:26.] [Note: [Col. 0298D] So the Old Psalter and Augustine in his Commentary on the Psalms.].

Now the whole darkness of our misery is laid bare. Now at last we see how far we are from God and how dead we are in comparison with the living.

[Col. 0298C] 21. Understand these things, and, with anxious heart, sigh with concern for us, foreseeing that praise is sung at the end [Note: [Col. 0298D] Thus the Viennese manuscript and Sacchinus thought it should be read. Other codices have *curam* (“care”).], so that, by the grace of the same Lord, we may be brought to perfection in the spirit with which we began [Note: [Col. 0298D] Thus the Vatican and Viennese manuscripts; the printed editions have *coepti sumus* (“we have begun”).], and may obey the command to the end—the command which we seem to have obeyed at the beginning of our undertaking. For he gives counsel, not a command, who does not say, “Be perfect,” but, “If you wish to be perfect” [Note: [Col. 0297] Matthew 19:21.], because freedom of the will, when it is good, is above the law: it is not compelled but persuaded, and is itself a law to itself.

How great it is to follow Christ you can gather from the Apostle’s statement: “Whoever says that he follows Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” [Note: [Col. 0297] 1 John 2:6.]. 161 But how Christ walked, another teacher explains: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0297] Isaiah 53:9.]; “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” [Note: [Col. 0298D] Thus the Regius manuscript and four printed editions. The Viennese manuscript has *non maledixit* (“he did not curse”). Rosweyde’s edition has *non maledicebat* (“he was not cursing”).]; “but he handed himself over to death, to the one judging unjustly” [Note: [Col. 0299D] The Viennese manuscript has *judicantibus* (“to those judging”).] [Note: [Col. 0299] 1 Peter 2:22.].

But we can also learn from his own actions and commands how he walked. For he came for this purpose: to set before us his life as a pattern and mirror of life. “I have not come,” he says, “to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matthew 5:17.]; and he himself also teaches what this fulfillment is: “Unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matthew 5:20.]. To fulfill means to add what is lacking. The law said, “You shall not kill” [Note: [Col. 0299] Exodus 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:17.]; but he says, “Nor shall you be angry with your brother without cause” [Note: [Col. 0299D] According to the Greek text, εἰκῆ (“without cause”). So too the Greek Fathers and some Latin writers: Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 2.56 and 4.31; Chrysostom, on Matthew; Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus* 3; Hilary, commentary on Matthew; and Augustine, *Sermon on the Mount* 1.] [Note: [Col. 0299] Matthew 5:22 and 28; Romans 2:29.].

The law forbids adultery, but Truth itself condemns the curious gaze upon women.
