From this you see how much greater faith is than the law—faith whose praise comes not from human beings but from God—because the circumcision of the law is outward, while that of faith is inward. The law breaks off the branches of sin [Note: [Col. 0299D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. Others have *praestringit* (“cuts short”).]; faith uproots its roots. It makes us pure not only in our actions but also in our thoughts, so that we may truly be restored to our primordial dignity—that is, to the likeness of God—cleansed not only in body but also in heart. Hence the Apostle testifies that, having put off the form of the earthly human being [Note: [Col. 0299D] The Viennese manuscript has *imaginem* (“image”).], we put on the heavenly one; and elsewhere he declares that the person clothed with Christ is the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0299] Colossians 3:10; Romans 13:14; 1 Corinthians 11:7.].

22. Consider, then, how much we must do if we are to traverse the length of this journey—not, as you say, already perfected, but, as we find, only begun. We are commanded to surpass the righteousness of the law, so that we may become the righteousness of God [Note: [Col. 0299] Matthew 5:20; 2 Corinthians 5:21.]; and the law must be for us not an action imposed from without, but a law residing in the will. To follow Christ is to imitate God. [Note: [Col. 0300D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. The reading *et* (“and”) also appears in the Regius manuscript and three printed editions.] And he who wishes us to be more righteous than the very law of his righteousness, and perfect like his Father [Note: [Col. 0299] Matthew 5:48.], demands that we not merely flee human faults but also fulfill divine virtues.

Since you see that this is so difficult for those engaged in the contest, how great is its glory for those who, after exhausting themselves in the struggle, are victorious. While we are still in the arena [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Scamma*: a place enclosed by ditches where gladiators fought.], while there are battles outside and terrors within [Note: [Col. 0299] 2 Corinthians 7:5.], do not meanwhile think or speak lofty things on our behalf; rather, fear [Note: [Col. 0299] Romans 11:20.], share spiritually in the labor of those who are struggling, and cooperate through your prayers, so that through us also he may destroy the enemy and the avenger [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Defensorem*: “defender.” In Greek, ἐκδικητήν, which has the same meaning as “avenger,” as also in Romans 12:19. Thus too the Old Psalter and the Roman Psalter have “defender,” as does Augustine in his commentary on the Psalms. See note 115.] [Note: [Col. 0299] Psalm 8:3.], who chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong [Note: [Col. 0299] 1 Corinthians 1:27.].

23. Beg humbly that he grant us understanding on this road [Note: [Col. 0299] Psalm 31:8.], on which he calls us, so that we may see that he is God [Note: [Col. 0299] Psalm 46:11.], he who was crucified in our weakness but lives by the power of God [Note: [Col. 0299] 2 Corinthians 13:4.]. May he weaken in us the power of sin (see no. 10), so that he may strengthen the spirit of his power. May he turn our poverty and our abundance around: may we abound in the righteousness of which we are in need, and be in need of the wickedness in which we abound. Let us be stripped of crimes and clothed with virtues.

May he help us against our own desires, and not hand us over to the desires of our heart [Note: [Col. 0299] Romans 1:24.]; and against flesh and blood, the devil and death, may he give us victory, as he gave Abraham victory (see note 116) over the four kings, whom that father of faith overcame through this mystery. Thus may our faith, if it has been strengthened by the principal Spirit, bring under the word of God the four elements of our body [Note: [Col. 0299] Genesis 14:15; Hebrews 7:1; Romans 4:16; Psalm 51:14.].

And just as Abraham was victorious for his brother when five kings had been defeated (see note 117), so faith, victorious for the soul, which flourishes through the same number of senses, will triumph over the outer human being, in whom the form of the four kings is contained, since he is composed of the same number of elements. But just as Abraham conquered his adversaries not through the multitude or strength of legions, but already then through the mystery of the cross—whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter Τ in the number three hundred (see note 118)—[Note: [Col. 0299] Ezekiel 9:4.] so, by the power of this mystery, the ark, constructed with three hundred cubits in length (see note 119), overcame the flood, so that now the Church sails across this age.

In the same way, relying not on our own resources or strength but on the single knowledge of the Crucified One, let us lift our eyes toward him, so that he may make his mercies wondrous over us—he who saves those who hope in him [Note: [Col. 0299] Psalm 17:7.]. For he is the Lord who shatters wars, mighty in battle [Note: [Col. 0299] Psalm 46:10 and 24:8.]. He gave us both the confidence to fight and the way to conquer when, carrying human nature already triumphant in himself, he said: “Stand firm, because I have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0299] John 16:33.].

EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0299D] Formerly numbered 39; the one that was 25 is now 15. Written in the year 403.] XXV (C)

[Col. 0300C]

He urges a nobleman, whose name is unknown, to pass from the profane service of Caesar to the sacred warfare of Christ, and warns him not to postpone his conversion out of confidence in his age or love of the world.

1. Although I am unknown to you in person, I have already come to know you in my heart. For my beloved son in the Lord, Victor, by reporting to me your religious way of life, enabled me to know you although absent and to begin loving you as one who would become a fellow member in Christ. He also told me how, in the secular military service in which you are still held, he had been your companion and comrade in your tent. For this reason I have been all the more confident in writing to you through him.

I hope that you too will come from that same road to our road, since you have sent this man from among your companions ahead to us. The Church holds him as your pledge, so that after him it may receive you also. For nothing can or should be preferred to the one who is the true Lord, the true Father, and the eternal Emperor. To whom could we devote our life more rightly than to him from whom we received it and to whom we owe it to the end, since it is by his gift that we live?

If, however, we serve him in this world, then we shall deserve to pass over to him. But if we love this world more and prefer to serve Caesar rather than Christ, afterward we shall be transferred not to Christ but to Gehenna, where the cause of the rulers of this world is decided.

2. Therefore we must not prefer to God affection, homeland, honors, or riches, because it is written: “The form of this world is passing away” [Note: [Col. 0301] 1 Corinthians 7:31.]. And those who have loved this world will perish with it. Therefore the Lord himself, in the Gospel, solemnly declares and says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple” [Note: [Col. 0301] Matthew 10:37–38; Luke 14:27.].

Regarding the riches of this world, which some embrace and love as the highest and most necessary good, he says: [Note: [Col. 0301D] The Victorinus manuscript and six printed editions add *Quia* (“because”).] “Treasures will not profit the wicked, but righteousness delivers from death” [Note: [Col. 0301] Proverbs 10:2, according to the Septuagint.]. And again, through the prophet, he says: “All who had exalted themselves through gold and silver have been destroyed” (see note 120) [Note: [Col. 0301] Zephaniah 1:11.].

In the Gospel he also cries out and condemns the rich of this world, saying: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have your consolation. Woe to you who are filled, because you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, because you will mourn and weep” [Note: [Col. 0301] Luke 6:24–25.].

3. Therefore do not continue to love this world or its military service, because, according to the authority of Scripture, whoever is a friend of the world is an enemy of God [Note: [Col. 0301] James 4:4.]. And whoever serves with the sword is an agent of death. Whoever sheds his own blood or that of another will receive the fruit of his military pay. For he will either be held guilty through the outcome of death or through the crime itself: since in war a soldier—who nevertheless fights not so much for himself as for another—must either, when defeated, encounter his own death, or, when victorious, incur responsibility for another’s death. For he cannot be victorious unless he has first become a shedder of blood.

Therefore the Lord says: “You cannot serve two masters” [Note: [Col. 0301] Matthew 6:24.]. But since one must serve a single Lord [Note: [Col. 0301D] The Vatican and Victorinus manuscripts, together with six printed editions, read *Deo* (“God”). But the argument requires *Domino* (“Lord”), lest what is to be concluded be assumed. Sacchinus.], I think it is easy to discern whom one ought rather to serve: God or Mammon, Christ or Caesar. Caesar himself strives to be Christ’s servant, so that he may deserve to be king of some peoples.

For no earthly king is lord of the whole earth. Christ, however, is Lord and King of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0301D] The two words *Dominus et* (“Lord and”) are absent from the Victorinus manuscript and from the Mainz, Roman, Erasmus, and Ponce editions.]: because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made [Note: [Col. 0301] John 1:3.]. He is King of kings and Lord of lords [Note: [Col. 0301] Revelation 17:14.]; on earth, in the sea, and in the depths he does whatever he wills [Note: [Col. 0301] Psalm 135:6.].

4. Let us therefore follow him and serve him in the army; [Note: [Col. 0301D] Thus the Vatican and Victorinus manuscripts together with Rosweyde’s edition. Sacchinus remarks that the military terms fit together excellently. In six printed editions the reading is *cui conjunctus* (“to whom joined”), which is never disjoined. The reading retained here is the truest. So too *discingitur*. In Prudentius, *discingitur* means the same as “is disarmed,” *Psychomachia* 634: “All Terror is unbelted”; and ibid. 824: “that the unbelted youth may hasten to its seat.”] his soldier is never unbelted, who grants those who serve him the glory of eternal life, the honor of the heavenly kingdom, the riches of his inheritance, and an everlasting share in divine knowledge.

It is written: “Whoever loves money will not be justified; and whoever covets earthly possessions will, as it is written, fall in them” [Note: [Col. 0302D] In Greek, πεσεῖται (“will fall”); the Vulgate has *corruet* (“will collapse”). Erasmus’s edition has *implicabitur* (“will be entangled”).] [Note: [Col. 0301] Ecclesiasticus 31:5; Proverbs 11:28.].

For in Ecclesiasticus divine Wisdom speaks through Solomon: “Many have been endangered because of gold, and their destruction has taken place in its presence. Gold is the wood of his stumbling, and it casts down those who pursue it. Yet no one who is not foolish will perish through it” [Note: [Col. 0302D] According to the Greek text I would read: “Many have been brought to ruin because of gold,” supported by the Victorinus manuscript and the Roman edition, which have “Many have been enriched because of gold.” The Vulgate has “Many have been given to the fall of gold.”] [Note: [Col. 0301] Ecclesiasticus 31:6–7, from the Septuagint.].

Therefore flee from it, son, as from the face of a serpent [Note: [Col. 0301] Ecclesiasticus 21:2.], trusting Christ, who in the Gospel declares to all people: “A person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” [Note: [Col. 0301] Luke 12:15.].

5. But perhaps confidence in your age, the accumulation of honors, or increases in wealth troubles you, so that you say: “I am still young; now is the time for me to serve for a while, take a wife, and have children, and afterward serve God.” To this it is not I but the Lord who responds—the Lord who speaks through his prophets and apostles [Note: [Col. 0302D] The Victorinus manuscript and the Roman and Mainz editions read *Propheta* (“prophet”).]. And the Wise Man says: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, lest his anger suddenly come” [Note: [Col. 0302D] The Victorinus manuscript and the Roman, Mainz, and Ponce editions have *tardaris* (“be delayed”).] [Note: [Col. 0302D] Ecclesiasticus 5:8.].

In the Gospel he shows with what zeal we must hasten toward conversion when he says: “From the days of John until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” [Note: [Col. 0301] Matthew 11:12; Luke 16:16.]. Such violence is pleasing to God: it harms no one and is committed to the detriment of no one. Turn your hands toward this seizure, which involves no crime and brings salvation.

And what have you to do with managing the pay—or perhaps the accounts—of soldiers amid the envy and violence of extortion [Note: [Col. 0301] Luke 3:14.], when perhaps, for the sake of your honor, you are also a moderate collector of debts? You can be violent without anyone’s envy and with the grace of God, so as to seize the kingdom of heaven. It allows itself to be taken away, and Christ rejoices to have it invaded, because in the abundance of his love and power he is capable both of giving what he possesses and of obtaining what he has given.

For when he grants his saints to reign in his kingdom, he himself will reign in those whom he has taken as companions of the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0303] Revelation 1:6.]. For it is written both that the kingdom of God will be with the saints and that the saints themselves are the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0303] Revelation 20:6.]. With God’s favor, when you have converted, you will learn this by reading and understand it by believing.

6. Who would dare boast of the first flower of youth? Divine Scripture [Note: [Col. 0303D] We have deleted *namque*, because it was absent from all our manuscripts.] warns us, saying: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” [Note: [Col. 0303] Isaiah 40:6, from the Septuagint version.].

Therefore the Prophet, desiring rather those things in which the eternal glory of the restored body may remain after the resurrection, cries out: “How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0303] Psalm 84:2, according to the Septuagint, the Old Psalter, and the Roman Psalter.].

7. Regarding the bonds of marriage and the other cares of temporal things, as thorny as they are empty, the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0303] 2 Corinthians 13:3.]—in whom Christ speaks—warns us not to make futile vows for the long duration of this world. He commands us to recognize that the time has been shortened, and says: “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they were not weeping; those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing; those who buy as though they possessed nothing; and those who use this world as though they were not using it” [Note: [Col. 0303] 1 Corinthians 7:29.].

By saying this he shows that those who are free should not become entangled, since he advises those who are entangled to be freed. If, then, you are already perhaps bound to a wife, do not seek release [Note: [Col. 0303D] Thus the Victorinus manuscript, four printed editions, and the Vulgate, in accordance with the Greek text; better than Rosweyde’s edition, which has *absolutionem* (“release”).] [Note: [Col. 0303] 1 Corinthians 7:27.]. But if you are still free from a wife, do not seek entanglement.

The Apostle does not say this in condemnation of marriage, since he compares the sanctity of this covenant with the great mystery of Christ and the Church. Rather, he says it because of the impending necessity, asserting that it is good for a person to be as he himself was. “I want you,” he says, “to be without anxiety” [Note: [Col. 0303] 1 Corinthians 7:32.]; that is, to think about nothing except God and our salvation.

For a wife and children, although they too are pledges given to us by God, are nevertheless burdens of the gravest cares. Hence the same Apostle says: “Such people will have tribulation in the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0303D] Thus the Victorinus manuscript and the Mainz edition, supported by four other printed editions, which have *carnes* (“flesh”). Rosweyde’s edition has *carnis*. Our reading is confirmed by what follows.] [Note: [Col. 0303] 1 Corinthians 7:28.], because our fleshly relationships, the dearer they are to us, the more they torture and weary us.

For once a wife has been taken, children are first desired; if they are not born, their barrenness is mourned; if they are born, bereavement is feared. Consequently the soul never rests so completely in fleshly affections that it is free from suffering. It is always exposed to misery, whether it loves its relations while fearing to lose them or hates them while wishing to lose them. Miserable is the person who loses a good wife; more miserable the one who possesses a bad one. Between these two contingencies, much happier is the person who knows neither (see note 121).

The same is true of children. Parents are very often wretched either because they have beloved children from whom they are bereaved, or because they have such children that they are forced to envy those who have none.

8. Listen, then, my son, and incline your ear to me, and break every bond that holds you entangled in this world. Exchange your military service for something better, so that you may begin to serve the eternal King. And now, as I hear, you who are an assistant and [Note: [Col. 0304D] The Victorinus manuscript and the Roman, Mainz, Erasmus, and Ponce editions have *tutator* (“protector”).] guardian of citizens, become Christ’s companion.

Moreover, in this military service you customarily hope for promotion in office, so that you may become protectors (see note 122). But if you prove yourself before God, you will begin to have God himself as your protector. See to what kind of military service I invite you as a fellow soldier: what you wish to be for a human being, may God be for you. If you begin to follow him and to serve in his company, the end of your military service will be a kingdom—not of earth and time, but of eternity and heaven.

EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0303D] Formerly numbered 40; the one that was 26 is now 40 and 41. Written in the year 401.] XXVI

Sebastian the hermit and Benedict the deacon have been highly praised: Sebastian for his way of life, Benedict for his care in supplying what Sebastian needs. Paulinus asks them to intercede with the Lord for himself and Therasia.

To the holy and most deservedly beloved brother SEBASTIAN, PAULINUS and THERASIA send greetings in the Lord Christ.

1. Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who chose you and took you up as a vessel of his election, and set you apart from the womb of your ancient mother, and gave you the wings of a dove, so that, flying far away from the noise of this world, you could say: “Behold, I have flown away in flight, and I have remained in solitude” [Note: [Col. 0304D] The five Psalters and Saint Augustine, in his commentary on the Psalms, have *elongavi* (“I have withdrawn”).] [Note: [Col. 0303] Psalm 55:8.].

Although your solitude is not solitary—for it is not deserted but secluded, withdrawn from the darkness of this world, frequented by the light of God, shunned by raging demons, and cultivated by rejoicing angels. Our Lord God himself has granted us, though separated from you by a long distance, to draw near to you in love through the good fragrance of the knowledge of you [Note: [Col. 0304D] Thus the Victorinus manuscript together with two printed codices. Others have *bonae* (“of good”).], which we received through our beloved brother in the Lord, Victor.

He told us both about the work of your chosen way of life and about the secrecy of your tabernacle: that, as an energetic imitator of the ancient saints, you had established a peaceful dwelling and spiritual camp beside a stream most pleasing to you, just as the sons of the prophets once did beside the Jordan under the leadership of Elisha [Note: [Col. 0305] 2 Kings 6:2; 2 Kings 4:8.]; and that your brother Benedict the deacon served you in the manner of that woman of Zarephath or the Shunammite.

Blessed is the one to whom the Lord commanded, as to one of the birds of heaven, to feed you like Elijah, secretly seated beside the stream, with the bread of compassion [Note: [Col. 0305] 1 Kings 17:4.]; and to fly back repeatedly to your cell in service of this ministry, like Noah’s dove bringing a fruitful branch of pious growth [Note: [Col. 0305] Genesis 8:11.].

[Col. 0305B] 2. May you be blessed by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0305] Psalm 113:15.], who makes those of one mind dwell in a house [Note: [Col. 0305] Psalm 68:7.], and who has doubled the bond of brotherhood in you. He made you brothers in the womb of the Church and distinguished you by different duties under one faith, so that, under different forms of service, each of you might nourish the other.

You would help him with spiritual weapons through fasting and prayer, while he would sow heavenly goods for himself in you as he supplied you with bodily food—not because you lacked the nourishment of perishing food, since your hunger hungers for righteousness and the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0305] Matthew 5:6.]. Nevertheless, because the same Lord who made what is within also made what is without, and because “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” [Note: [Col. 0305] Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:38.], he rewards the soul that lives by the Word of God, which is Christ God, the true and living bread [Note: [Col. 0305] John 6:41.], with such service that it serves your body—that is, the earthly weakness within you—with modest foods, while he himself is nourished by the abundance of your fasts.

For this reason he said: “Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” [Note: [Col. 0305] Matthew 4:4; Luke 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3.]. Because he took account of the weakness of our substance, lest it should hunger, the Creator himself thereby showed that bread is necessary for the flesh also.

3. But lest we place care for the body before care for the soul, which is nourished by the word of God, he taught that human life is not established by bread alone [Note: [Col. 0305D] The Victorinus manuscript reads: “He showed that human life does not consist in bread alone.” Hence the negative [should be read as referring to him]: although the soul’s care does not seek bread, he taught that bodily nature requires it.], though the body’s nature demands what the soul’s care may not seek.

Therefore blessed is he for whom the necessity of your condition contributes to the wealth of the soul: for you are still human and must be fed with this visible bread, even though inwardly you are filled with that eternal bread. Spiritual strength would not advance if bodily weakness were not present beneath it. Nor would the ministry of the faithful be effective if fraternal poverty did not often provide material for ministry.

Hence the Apostle says that there will be an exchange among the saints, when he encourages the Church toward the consolation of this blessing and says: “Let your abundance be for their need, so that their abundance may become a supplement to your need” [Note: [Col. 0305] 2 Corinthians 8:14.].

4. I still dare to say that in each of you there is a different representation of John and of the Lord (see *Vita* chapter 39, no. 2): John crying out in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0305D] Six printed codices add *vox* (“voice”), less correctly.] [Note: [Col. 0305] Matthew 3:3; John 7:28.], and the Lord teaching in the temple. One of you has been called to the service of ministry, the other to the freedom of the monk.

Yet both have been summoned into one kingdom and glory of God. Both are free, because both are under grace; both are servants, because both are under the law of faith. Both are free from sin and servants of righteousness. Both, in fasting, make the day belong to the Lord; both, at feasts, give thanks to the Lord in sincerity, to him who gives food to all flesh [Note: [Col. 0305] Psalm 136:25.] and gives living food—the true righteousness—to those who hunger [Note: [Col. 0306D] “Righteousness.” This is the true reading and agrees with Sacred Scripture; in Greek, τὴν δικαιοσύνην (“righteousness”). The Victorinus manuscript and four printed editions have *vitam* (“life”). The former reading is further confirmed by no. 2 above: “your hunger hungers for righteousness and the kingdom of God.”] [Note: [Col. 0305] Matthew 5:6.].

One of you has heard the command to say: “I will enter the altar of God, to God who makes my youth rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0305] Psalm 43:4.]. The other has learned from the same prophet to say: “I am solitary until I pass over” [Note: [Col. 0305] Psalm 141:10.].

5. Since, then, you have been chosen and loved by the Lord so that each of you may bear the other’s burdens [Note: [Col. 0305] Galatians 6:2.], and since, through the perfect love by which you nourish, support, instruct, enrich, and complete one another, you fulfill the law of Christ, pray for us. Join together the strong hands of your prayers, so that you may overcome the multitude of our sins.

For this reason the merciful and compassionate Lord arranges and grants his saints’ knowledge and love to his sinful people: so that a powerful intercession may absolve even guilty persons who have no excuse from the merits of condemnation.

May you remain in the kingdom of the Lord—which he has made to exist within you through the indwelling pledge of the Holy Spirit, in whom you cry, “Abba, Father” [Note: [Col. 0305] Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6.]—blessed sons of piety, peace, and light.

EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0305D] Formerly numbered 14; the one that was 27 is now 37. Written in the year 401.] XXVII

He rejoices at receiving news from Severus; clears himself regarding the men who were taken away; and continues to praise Severus with the greatest affection and self-abasement.

To his entirely united brother, the venerable and always most longed-for SEVERUS, PAULINUS.

1. “I will bless the Lord at all times” [Note: [Col. 0305] Psalm 34:2.]. I will not forget his acts of recompense, because he does not deal with us according to our sins [Note: [Col. 0305] Psalm 103:3 and 10.]. Through the constant and numerous consolations of your fellowship he satisfies our longing. Within a few days, we received the return of our holy and mutually beloved brothers, Posthumianus and Theridi (see *Carmen* 22, verse 381, and *Vita* chapter 33, no. 1), followed by the arrival of other brothers, Virinus and Sorianus.

Thus, almost at one and the same time, a very abundant harvest of joys came to us, when all those whom we have mentioned as having arrived together made the grace of their presence sweeter to us through letters expressing your fellowship. Therefore our spirit rejoiced in the Lord, and our mouth was enlarged over our enemy [Note: [Col. 0307] 1 Samuel 2:1; Luke 1:47.], who was not allowed to say, “I have prevailed against them” [Note: [Col. 0307] Psalm 13:5.]. Rather, the desires of our longings had prevailed, so that we received from you what we had desired—namely, the judgments and words of the one who is the greatest care of our soul.

2. Therefore, so that we may owe one another nothing except mutual love, as commanded [Note: [Col. 0307] John 15:17; Romans 13:8; 1 John 3:23.], I will answer all your letters. First I will answer the one I received first, in which you complain to me about the men through whom you had written, asking why I had either left you alone or taken them away from you.

But you will recognize that I can be blamed on neither count: I have never placed a limit on my longing for you, nor have I ever disputed with you over their possession. Otherwise I would willingly have yielded your right to you, if possession of them had previously been yours.

They would not have been alienated from me by remaining with you, since you are wholly mine in Christ the Lord, through whom I am in turn yours. Nor would I have gained as much grace by receiving them as I would have lost if I had taken from you companions, however desirable, on the path of salvation. Indeed, I would judge myself entirely worthy of being deprived of your love if I preferred any good for myself rather than for you.

But when I discovered that, by an unexpected gift of the Lord, they had come to me as people such as they soon afterward proved to be to you, I even envied myself for having been happier than you in this respect, so that I had obtained—or had first recognized—men more worthy of your sight and companionship.

Finally, so that I might enjoy as soon as possible, with you as my companion, the grace by which I considered myself blessed, I reproached those who were present [Note: [Col. 0307D] Thus the Regius manuscript, and thus Paulinus in Epistle 49 to Macarius, no. 5: “he rebuked the sea.”] because they admitted that they lacked familiarity and acquaintance with you. I gave those who were departing no more earnest instruction than that they should hasten to see and embrace you, and should place knowing you before all the affairs and concerns of their homeland, so that they might at last repair their long delay.

And, thanks be to the Lord, we received them as they came in exultation [Note: [Col. 0307] Psalm 126:6.], bringing back a great sheaf of joy from the field full of the fruits of their life—this joy arising from their awareness of the great acquisition they had believed in you, an acquisition which they had sought above all others.

What thanks did they give first to God, who had not merely satisfied but surpassed their longing, so that they found more good in you than they had expected? What thanks did they give us, who had been the authors of so great an acquisition for them? What thanks did they give themselves, because they had obeyed us for their own gain?

[Col. 0307D] 3. It is impossible for me to say how great a pleasure they poured into me when they reported your actions and words, and your perfect heart through the knowledge of divine love. They declared that Martin wholly breathed in you, Clarus flourished in you (see note 124), and the Gospel ripened in you: humble yet exalted, poor yet rich, servant yet free, a fellow servant with servants, servant to brothers, rich to the poor in the depths of mercy, poor in spirit to the rich in the gentleness of humility, humble through the virtue of piety, lofty through the sublimity of virtue, servant of God, and free from Mammon.

They thoroughly anointed our head with the oil of joy [Note: [Col. 0307] Psalm 23:5.]. For this reason all our inward parts blessed the Lord [Note: [Col. 0307] Psalm 103:1, according to the Old Psalter and the Roman Psalter.] with a double cause for thanksgiving: we understood that we had done you a great service by making known to you the most beloved brothers, as you have proved them to be; and we saw that they rejoiced for themselves over their knowledge of and love for you, as a gift from God.

What is more, amid the works and gifts of God in you, how greatly they also admired your young men, who flourish around you like young olive trees [Note: [Col. 0307] Psalm 128:3.]. Our God has made you to them what he himself is to all: so that they fear you as a true master and love you as a father [Note: [Col. 0307] Malachi 1:6.].

Yet, in their account, we confess that we groaned over our own misfortune, because our more serious sins had made us barren of such children. But we became, as it were, comforted [Note: [Col. 0307] Psalm 126:1.], because we judge the blessing of your happiness to be near us.

4. But lest our iniquity separate us from you by an even longer interval, muster for us the entire chosen band of sacred youth with which you soothe God day and night, so that they may direct the ranks of their prayers against our sins and plead for us. May the Lord confirm what he has done for us [Note: [Col. 0307] Psalm 68:29.]; that is, may we, through your love in which we now rest and in which we glory, be refreshed and rejoice on that day.

EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0307D] Formerly numbered 9; the one that was 28 is now 48. Written in 402, toward the end of summer.] XXVIII

171 He praises Victor, through whom they sent letters to one another, to Severus, and excuses the delay in sending him back. He has woven the entire letter with the most sacred thoughts and words, inserting beautiful comparisons of Christ as fire, foundation, door, bread, and so forth. Since Severus had requested some of Paulinus’s works, he sends him two little books. One was the *Defense of Theodosius*, praised so highly by Saint Jerome (Epistle 13 to Paulinus), whose loss everyone laments; the other was a collection of birthday poems about Saint Felix.

To his holy brother and fellow soldier in fellowship, SEVERUS, PAULINUS.

1. Victor returns from me to you, so that he may return from you to me: Victor, our common pledge, our faithful companion, and our customary solace; Victor yours in me, and mine in you; Victor, the foot-courier—or two-footed post-horse—of our letters; Victor, conqueror of the longest roads; rightly to be called at once both victor and vanquished, because he is vanquished by the love with which he conquers difficult roads and great labors—he who eats his bread in the sweat of his face [Note: [Col. 0307] Genesis 3:19.]—so that he may refresh us by his yearly journeys between us, tirelessly [Note: [Col. 0308D] Thus the Vienna manuscript, Schott’s edition, and Latinius; the Vatican manuscript has *favente*, “favoring,” in which [he is] untiring.] carrying and bringing back the commerce of letters by which, as though paying a tax of duty owed, we weigh out to one another mutual visitation in our minds and inmost affections.

Blessed by the Lord be the boy Victor; may his land not bring forth thorns and thistles for him [Col. 0309A], because he is diligent [Note: [Col. 0309] Genesis 3:18.]. For the ways of the sluggish are paved with thorns [Note: [Col. 0309D] Thus the Septuagint translators, Aquila, Theodotion, and Paulinus in Letter 21 to Amandus, §5.] [Note: [Col. 0309] Proverbs 15:19, according to the Septuagint.]. But our Victor does not say, “There is a lion in the roads” [Note: [Col. 0309] Proverbs 22:13 and 26:13.], because he is so straightforward that he walks confidently [Note: [Col. 0309] Proverbs 10:9.], faithful and chaste, so that he does not fear the terror by night or the arrow flying by day [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 90:6.].

Therefore the Lord guards him in all his ways and commands angelic sentinels, lest he anywhere strike his foot against a stone; nor will a serpent lying in wait on the road bite his heel [Note: [Col. 0309] Genesis 49:17.], for he will tread upon and crush it harmlessly with feet shod for the course of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0309] Ephesians 6:15.]. I shall therefore praise and bless in the Lord the feet of our Victor, and I shall dare to say also of these feet: “How beautiful are the feet that proclaim peace to me” [Note: [Col. 0309] Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15.] from you, when they announce your safety and peace in you, when they announce your faith, through which Christ—our peace—dwells in you. He also makes both things one in us or among us [Col. 0309B] [Note: [Col. 0309] Ephesians 2:14.]: whether because we two are one in heart; or because we make both substances, soul and body, one, Christ fusing us by the fire of his Spirit, of which he says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth; and what does the good Lord desire except that it be kindled” [Note: [Col. 0309D] The Vatican manuscript reads *quia*, “because,” twice.] in us, that it may illumine our darkness and consume our sins? For “the Lord our God is a consuming fire” [Note: [Col. 0309] Deuteronomy 4:24; Hebrews 12:9.].

May the Lord grant me that the consuming fire may also be made in me and for me. May my heart burn with this fire as my eternal light, lest my soul burn with the same fire as everlasting punishment. For in this fire the day of the Lord will be revealed, and the fire will test what sort of work each one of us has done [Note: [Col. 0309] 1 Corinthians 3:13.].

2. Let us pray to this Lord that he teach us to do his will, and that his good Spirit lead us into the right way [Col. 0309C] [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 142:10–11, according to the Roman Psalter.], lest our labor be found to be wood, hay, and stubble [Note: [Col. 0309] 1 Corinthians 3:12; 1 Peter 2:5.]; but rather that we may be found to be silver, gold, precious stones, and living stones in the walls of that heavenly and free Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0309] Galatians 4:31.], which is built as a city whose fellowship is altogether one [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 121:3.].

For the inhabitant of this city is shown to be one in three; hence it is called “the city of the great King,” “the city of our God,” and “the city of the Lord of hosts.” The Lord himself, as it is written, founded it forever [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 47:2 and 9.]. Christ has become not only the foundation of this city, but also its tower and gate. “No one,” he says, “can lay any other foundation than the one that has been laid,” and he is for us “a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0309] 1 Corinthians 3:11; Psalm 60:4.]. He says: “I am the gate of the sheep” [Note: [Col. 0309] John 10:7.]; “no one can come to the Father except through me” [Note: [Col. 0309] John 14:6.].

If, then, our house and mind are founded upon him, and a work worthy of so great a foundation is built upon it [Col. 0309D], he himself will be for us the gate into his city, and he will rule us forever [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 47:15.]. He will place us where there is pasture—we whom he has already begotten for himself through the water of refreshment [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 22:2.]—and nourish us with saving banquets [Col. 0310A] at the table he has prepared for us in the presence of those who trouble us.

Of this table he says: “Blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0309] Luke 14:15.]. For Christ is both the kingdom and the bread with which we are filled, while the serpent wastes away; Christ Jesus, the food of our life, is the serpent’s hunger and punishment. He became our food so that, living by that bread [Note: [Col. 0309] John 6:35.] and walking according to him, we may be able, with the Apostle, to say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0309] Philippians 3:20.].

When we taste and seek the things above [Note: [Col. 0309] Colossians 3:1.], we cease to be earthly, so that we are no longer food for the serpent, who in turn was given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia [Note: [Col. 0309] Genesis 3:14; Psalm 73:14.], so that he might be eaten by those whom [the printed text breaks off: *EDIT.*]. This, by contrast, is salutary for us: we eat Christ and are swallowed up by Christ, who swallows up our mortality because he is life, so that he may clothe us with immortality [Note: [Col. 0309] 1 Corinthians 15:53.] [Col. 0310B] and conform us to his image [Note: [Col. 0309] Romans 8:29.]. He has given us power to tread without harm upon every power of the enemy [Note: [Col. 0309] Luke 10:19.] through the same grace by which he gave those who believe in his name power to become children of God [Note: [Col. 0309] John 1:12.], a name that is above every name [Note: [Col. 0309] Philippians 2:9; Matthew 5:14.].

Let us dwell in him, because he himself is also the city that cannot be hidden, because it is set upon a mountain [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 86:1 and 5.], whose foundations are on the holy mountains. The Most High himself founded this city, as it is written: “Wisdom built herself a house” [Note: [Col. 0309] Proverbs 9:1.].

This is that house not made with hands. If we dwell in it by such works as may make us worthy to become fellow citizens of the saints, our work will not burn up [Note: [Col. 0309] 2 Corinthians 5:1; Ephesians 2:19.]. That wise fire, passing us through its examination, will not surround us with harsh heat to punish us; rather, receiving us as those who have been approved, it will caress us with a gentle touch [Col. 0310C], so that we may say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” [Note: [Col. 0309] Psalm 65:12.].

3. But so that the letter may end with the same name with which it began, I shall return to our Victor, for whom I owe you an apology. Do not blame his feet because he returns to you later than agreed: he remained with us longer not through the fault of laziness, but out of zeal for obedience. Consider, however, not the time when you announced that he had been dismissed, but when you sent him; and you will see that my reckoning stands according to the agreed alternation by which we were to retain Victor between us.

For he was not with us, as you had written, to spend the winter; rather, as he reported, he had been sent back to you from Narbo, where he had met our brother Postumianus [Note: [Col. 0310D] Thus the Regius manuscript and four editions. This is the most authentic reading. Rosweyde’s edition has *nunc*, “now.” The Viennese manuscript reads: “sent back by you, then he set out again to you,” which is erroneous.], and then set out from you again at a time when he could have reached me directly.

Since he was received when winter was already passing [Col. 0310D], I necessarily had to keep him during the spring months. Because the interval seemed short, and the Easter solemnity would soon bring it to an end, and because I had been extremely ill throughout that period and was unable [Col. 0311A] to undertake the business of replying, I added delays from the summer days of his stay, so that I might make it up to you if I used as much of your time in him as you had occupied of the winter days.

Accordingly, I shall agree that, if he reaches your fellowship in the autumn, he may once again spend the winter with you. You see that this was arranged by the Lord’s decision in such a way that the periods of our common friend’s time, which we had mutually allotted to one another, might be exchanged—without violating the faith of our agreement—to the greater advantage of this man. For now it has aptly been reversed, so that what you had written indulgently toward me and at your own expense might more truly come to pass.

You, burning with a wholesome spirit, will warm him more beneficially during the cold season with the fiery heat of your faith [Note: [Col. 0311] Romans 12:11.]; whereas I, being cold, will be more suited to provide him a station during the summer.

4. Would that I were at least cold rather than lukewarm [Col. 0311B] [Note: [Col. 0311] Revelation 3:16.], so that I might not make my Lord vomit and might relieve the heat of my neighbor! But as things stand, I produce disgust through my satiety for those who use the time of my sojourn. I am needed neither by those who are cold nor by those who are hot; through the lukewarmness of my scanty faith I deserve to be vomited out by those who have tried, in hope of spiritual sweetness, to taste the flavor of my companionship.

All the more I marvel either at your desire to seek out, or your patience in enduring, the nuisances of my foolishness. Would that I incurred as little sin from excessive speech [Note: [Col. 0311D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts read *accederet*, “might accrue.”] as you are heaped with a great reward for such tireless love [Note: [Col. 0311] Proverbs 10:19.].

As though you had not been wearied but rather refreshed by the great number and abundance of the volumes previously sent through our Victor, you have again asked through the same book-carrier that, if I am able, I should become still more troublesome to you by my writings [Col. 0311C] [Note: [Col. 0311D] The Viennese manuscript reads *possem*, “I might be able.”].

5. Moreover, flattering yourself too generously about your poor friend, you ordered me to teach you what you had forgotten from the annals not of one nation but of the human race, as though I were especially learned. But he whose hunger knocks at a poor friend’s door [Note: See poem 24, line 613, and Letter 32, §12.] and searches an empty storeroom has himself to blame. I have never devoted sustained study to investigating and collecting such matters.

Indeed, even in earlier times, when I seemed to read things that ought to be neglected rather than read [Note: [Col. 0311D] The Viennese manuscript and Schott’s edition read *negligenda*, “things to be neglected.”], I kept away from historical writers. Nevertheless, now that I am attending to your work—you indicated that, for the benefit of our faith, you were occupied in examining and comparing the records of past times—I sought from the richer treasury of our unanimous brother what I did not possess myself.

I sent the very note that you had enclosed in your letter as a memorandum to the presbyter Rufinus, the spiritual companion of the holy Melania [Note: [Col. 0311D] It previously read “of Melania.” We have corrected it from the Regius manuscript [Col. 0312D] to “of the holy Melania.” Our correction is confirmed by several passages in the letters of Saint Paulinus. See note 138.], truly holy and devoutly learned, and for that reason bound to me by intimate affection.

If he does not publish the causes of those gaps in history that rightly disturb you—arising from disagreement in the reckoning of years or reigns—he who is rich in both scholarly and sound letters (that is, in humane and sacred letters; see Letter 44, §1), in Greek as well as Latin, I fear that we shall seek them in vain from anyone else in these regions.

But if he fulfills my confidence in him, I shall, at the first opportunity, if the Lord permits [Note: [Col. 0312D] The Viennese manuscript reads *siverit*, “if he permits.”], forward to your fellowship whatever he writes back to me concerning this matter.

6. Meanwhile, to do something in response to your instructions, I sent some things that I fear may prove testimonies rather of my idleness or ignorance than insignia of heavenly ministry—or at least demonstrations of human wisdom. Nevertheless, I sent you, that is, entrusted to my heart, my trifles [Col. 0312B] [Col. 0312C], not so that my darkness might pollute your understanding, but so that it might be dissolved by your understanding.

I called them my trifles with respect to my words and ideas. Their subject matter, however, is sacred and more worthy of your talent and eloquence. Even though it is clothed in my speech as in a dark garment, it nevertheless preserves the appearance of divine light and inward beauty, despite the poverty and worthlessness of its furnishings.

You therefore have two little books from me. One is a birthday poem in verse, concerning my solemn song to my Lord Domnaedius, to whom I render daily with body and spirit, and yearly with my tongue, the sweetest tribute of voluntary servitude, sacrificing to Christ on the feast of his consecration a sacrifice of praise and paying my vows to the Most High [Note: [Col. 0311] Psalm 49:14.].

The other little book is among those that I seem to have written to my blessed—in other words, Christian—friend Endelechius [See note 125], though I cannot be proved to have published it. He was the author of this little work in the Lord, as his own letter, which is placed at the head of my book as its theme, shows.

I confess that I gladly undertook this labor at a friend’s request so that in Theodosius [See note 126] I might proclaim not so much an emperor as a servant of Christ; not powerful through the arrogance of ruling but through the humility of serving; and a prince not by his kingdom but by his faith.

**LETTER XXIX** [Note: [Col. 0311D] Formerly numbered 10; the one formerly numbered 29 is now 38. Written toward the end of the summer of 402.]

He rightly interprets the camel-hair cloaks sent by Severus as suitable for him, a penitent in need. To the same man, as an innocent, he sends a tunic received from Melania, whose praises he elaborates at length.

**PAULINUS to his unanimous brother SEVERUS** [Note: [Col. 0312D] The Viennese manuscript has: “Pauline, servant of Christ Jesus, to Severus, his dearest brother in God the Father and Christ Jesus, greetings.” Grinius’s edition has: “Pauline to Severus.”]

1. You tempered the excessive love in your letters, which spoke of our burden, with the appropriate and measured kindness of gifts for our benefit. For you sent cloaks woven from camel hair to sinners who needed both the prayerful lamentation of supplication and the clothing of need. As we lie prostrate before the Most High, they admonish us with useful goads: we are pierced by the roughness of the bristles, and are impelled to be pierced by horror at our sins and inwardly crushed in spirit, while the garments wear us down outwardly [See note 127].

Much benefit for the strengthening of faith is also derived from their use through the remembrance of the holy men of old. Elijah comes to mind, translated [to heaven], and John, sent beforehand: the one was girded with a belt rough with bristles; the other was clothed in camel hair, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0313] 2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6.].

We also remember David and all his gentleness, by which, offering God a contrite and humbled heart, he clothed himself in sackcloth and covered his soul in fasting [Note: [Col. 0313] Psalms 131:1; 50:19; 68:11; 31:1.], so that he might cover it with spiritual fullness. From this we learn that the soul’s garment is that fasting by which we abstain from everything forbidden by divine law.

We learn the same from the stripping of our first parents, who, after they had ceased from the forbidden food and begun to fast, were found naked [Note: [Col. 0313] Genesis 3:7.] [Col. 0313B]. The prophet himself also teaches us by what sort of fast he protected his soul from the nakedness of shame, when he says to the Lord: “I have kept my foot from every evil way, so that I may guard your word” [Note: [Col. 0313] Psalm 118:101.].

2. From this same woolen gift of yours, that camel from the Gospel is also brought before us: it passes more easily through the eye of a needle than a rich man enters the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0313] Matthew 19:24; Mark 10:25.] [Note: [Col. 0313D] All manuscripts read this, except the Viennese, in which “that camel is introduced” appears.].

Reflecting on our riches, which now remain only in sins, and recognizing that we cannot aspire to the virtues of those divine men, we desire at least that the grace of the tax collector may come to us. In a contrite heart he accused himself before God, repeatedly struck his afflicted breast with his hand, and, with his eyes lowered by shame of conscience, did not dare to raise them toward heaven [Note: [Col. 0313] Luke 18:13.].

With the iniquity of his vices resembling the camel’s back, he so compressed himself into the humility he owed and directed himself along the leveling path of a repentant soul that he inserted himself into the eye of the needle—that is, the way of the word or of the cross, which leads to life by a narrow path [Note: [Col. 0313] Matthew 7:14.]—and penetrated the ears of God. For, he says, “the prayer of the one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds” [Note: [Col. 0313] Sirach 35:21.].

By contrast, that rich Pharisee, carried along by the spirit of his boasting, who, because he was a debtor according to the law of works, could not claim the due service as though he had voluntarily done more than was owed [Note: [Col. 0313D] The Viennese manuscript reads *computatione*, “reckoning.” We retain the true reading, which is confirmed in §4: we cannot claim the due service; and in Letter 50, §3, concerning “the Pharisee on the reckoning of his righteousness.”], made himself his own herald and another’s accuser. He came to God rather to confront him than to ask him, and could not enter, because narrow spaces do not accommodate those loaded with baggage. He could not be received where narrow humility had gathered itself, and where the narrower still narrowness of a contrite heart had penetrated [Note: [Col. 0314D] Thus the Regius and Vatican manuscripts: *angusto*, “in a narrow place,” that is, in a confined space or narrow entrance. The sense is clearer than in the printed editions, which have *angusta*.].

3. May your prayers intervene, so that the needle of the Lord’s cross may be inserted into my soul, torn apart by much corruption and rashly entangled with the thorns of my thoughts, and may it mend me with the thread of the saving word.

I consider faith and the word of Christ’s cross to be this needle, by which the fabric of our life is renewed and our mind is pierced [Note: [Col. 0314D] The Viennese manuscript reads this. The others read *mors*, “death.]” [Col. 0314A], and by which we ourselves are brought to God through the intercession of the Mediator.

In him and through him is that opening also, because through him and in him that way to life is desirable to many but passable by few. Through it humbled iniquity enters more easily than proud righteousness [Note: [Col. 0313] Matthew 7:14.].

For this reason we owe you, as spiritual physicians, greater gratitude: you confer even bodily gifts upon us with spiritual benefit, sending us these cloaks as an incentive to prayer and a garment of humility, like a basket of manure sent to that barren fig tree [Note: [Col. 0313] Luke 13:8.].

In this, it seems to me, the eternal usefulness of holy humility is indicated: it makes the barren soul fruitful, lest, pleasing itself like that Pharisee [Note: [Col. 0313] Luke 18:11.] in the empty appearance of arrogance, it luxuriate like an unhappy tree in useless foliage, without fruit [Note: [Col. 0313] Matthew 21:19.] [Col. 0314B].

How good and useful such manure is for cultivating salvation, we are taught in blessed Job [Note: [Col. 0313] Job 2:8.], who, after he sat upon the dung heap, ceased to be tested. For perfect humility had consumed the envy of the tempter, which can more easily rise than fall.

One sitting in dung has nowhere to fall from, but has from where to rise—through him who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap [Note: [Col. 0313] Psalm 112:7.] and casts the proud into dung [Note: [Col. 0313] Job 40:6.], because, as it is written, everyone who is proud is unclean before God. Therefore, before God, the accuser of his own iniquity is more righteous than the proclaimer of his own righteousness. The one accused himself by praising himself; the other defended himself by accusing himself.

4. Therefore, flattering ourselves in nothing concerning our works, let us always commend our spirit into his hands [Note: [Col. 0313] Psalm 30:6.], because with him is the fountain of life [Note: [Col. 0313] Psalm 35:10.]. Let us ask him for understanding of our journey, since the steps of a man are directed by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0313] Psalm 36:23, according to the Septuagint.].

But even if, through his help, we are able to carry out his commandments, we must still confess our uselessness [Note: [Col. 0313] Luke 17:10.], because we cannot claim the service that is owed if we merely perform the commands. For a useless and wicked servant is one who adds nothing voluntarily and affectionately to the necessary duty owed, and will have no basis for hoping for a reward if he has merely paid the obligations of his condition.

Therefore, even when we fulfill the commandments, let us fear, as I often write to you, always saying to the Lord: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” [Note: [Col. 0313] Psalm 142:2.].

The humility of our confession may perhaps establish us as modest before the good Lord; but the usefulness of energetic service will not be able to commend us as idle [Col. 0314D]. The Ninevites also prove how great a remedy for the sinner there is in divine mercy [Note: [Col. 0313] Jonah 3:10; Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32.]: he should spare himself nothing. Reconciled to God through the support of repentance, they deserved to escape the destruction that had been announced to them [Col. 0315A], because by torturing themselves with voluntary mourning they forestalled the divine sentence with their own.

5. Although we judge ourselves worthy neither in words nor in deeds, nevertheless by the one resource of love—in which alone we are your equals—we have sent you a tunic. Deign to receive it as a piece of cloth gathered from the worthlessness of manure, taken from my own use. For this too accords with your innocence: woven from the tender fleece of lambs, it caresses the touch.

I add further to its value and grace that, to make it more worthy of your use, it is a pledge to me from the blessing of the holy and illustrious woman among God’s saints, Melania [Note: [Col. 0315D] Thus Schott’s edition, correctly. See note 138.]. Hence it seemed more worthy of you, whose faith is closer to hers than our blood is.

I confess, however, that I ventured to put it on first—although I had destined it for you as soon as I received it—by inaugurating it with my own wearing. I knew that I would do you a greater service by this affront than if I had honored you with its untouched newness. At the same time, I might thus anticipate for myself a blessing as though it came from your garment, so that I could boast of being a participant in your clothing, clothing myself, by God’s favor, in the tunic that was destined for your use as though it had already been used by you.

6. The Lord added this grace to your gifts and letters: our brother Victor happened to arrive precisely on the days when we welcomed that holy woman herself, returning from Jerusalem after five five-year periods. But what a woman—if she may be called a woman—so manly a Christian!

What shall I do here? Fear of intolerable tedium forbids me to add further to these volumes; but the dignity of the person, or rather the grace of God, seems to demand that I not pass hastily over the memory of so great a soul. For a little while, therefore, let me turn the course of my speech toward telling you about her.

Sailors, when they see some notable place on the shore, do not pass it by; instead, they draw in their sails somewhat or suspend their rowing and feed their eyes by delaying to look. In the same way, I shall turn aside the course of my speech, so that I may seem to repay your illustrious book with some corresponding subject and eloquence, if I follow this woman—lower in sex but, through her virtues, a soldier of Christ like Martinus—who, though descended from a noble line of consuls, made herself nobler by despising bodily nobility.

7. I think that this too belongs to the fullness of divine grace: I begin to praise the holiness of one whose lineage is worthy of praise. But that I have adopted this order not so much from rhetorical instruction as from Gospel examples, I have the most learned Luke as my witness [Note: [Col. 0315] Luke 1:5.]. He disclosed the merit of the blessed Baptist through the splendor of his origin.

And lest you think that he mentioned the noble parent of the Lord’s forerunner merely for the sake of historical narrative, he links together the venerable insignia of ancient nobility and each person’s lineage, saying that the priest Zechariah was “of the division of Abijah” [Note: [Col. 0315] Luke 1:5; 1 Chronicles 24:40.].

I believe that he added the name derived from the priestly insignia in order to show through it the dignity of his merit: undoubtedly, among the Hebrews it was a mark of distinction, and he had obtained and exercised the honored priesthood by lot from that division [Col. 0316A].

Finally he adds: “And his wife was of the daughters of Aaron” [Note: [Col. 0315] Luke 1:5.]. You see that the evangelist, by commemorating the saint’s birth [See note 128], made a statement about his merits, placing ancestral names before those whose personal merits he was about to praise. “And,” he says, “his wife was of the daughters of Aaron.”

He increased the priest’s merit by recalling the nobility of his marriage. In praising his life, he first praised his lineage, so that he might appear more venerable as one who answered the holiness of holy parents with an innate holiness, as though by a certain inheritance of righteousness. He carried on that principal name of Aaron among priests, both in the office of honor and in the wife’s lineage.

And she, who in harmony with her husband bore the yoke of truth on the journey, was chosen to give birth by the angel of whom it is written: “Behold, I will send my angel before your face” [Note: [Col. 0315] Malachi 3:1; Matthew 11:9; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:26.]. She was made more worthy than the priestly husband and than the son who was to be preferred among the prophets, since not only a life of righteousness but also the distinction of her family had made her suitable for divine gifts.

The two evangelists also begin their accounts of the Lord’s birth—not only of that birth which flows from the divine source, but also of this one by which the Son of Man deigned to be born—by counting his ancestors from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0315] Matthew 1:1; John 1:1.]. Each writer, with equal faith and dignity, reports a different stream of bodily blood.

For it was fitting that the only-begotten Son of God, the firstborn of all creation and head of the entire body, should also hold the primacy in the dignity of bodily lineage. As he was the Son of God, ineffably born in heaven before the ages, so on earth he also claimed for himself the highest titles of illustrious ancestry, a noble offspring of both kings and priests, as the two authors testify [Note: [Col. 0315] Matthew 1:1; Luke 3:23.] [Col. 0316C].

For this reason, in praising earthly nobility in the aforementioned servant of God, we shall not seem to be using a rule foreign to us rather than our own. It is clear that the Lord contributed this also to the glory of her work, so that the world—which boasts in such titles—might be more thoroughly confounded. What human vanity uses to despise God, she instead used to despise the world.

At the same time, the authority of a salutary example might be made greater for humbling the eyes of the proud: a woman of higher rank, cast down on account of her love for Christ into the practice of humility, was sublimely humbled [Note: [Col. 0315] Psalm 17:28.]. She might rebuke sluggish men by her strength in a weak sex, and, rich though impoverished and noble though humbled, confound arrogant persons of either sex.

8. Thus, during the consulship of her grandfather Marcellinus [See note 129], having endured marriage while still in early youth amid the ambition of lineage and the luxury of wealth, she soon became a mother—but did not long enjoy that happiness of mortals [that is, for a long time; see poem 32, line 593]—so that she might not love earthly things for long.

Besides the other bereavements that, together with her husband, she had mourned after the fruitless labor of miscarriages, her troubles increased to such a degree that within a single year she lost two sons and her husband, with only one small child left to her, more as a reminder than as compensation for her affections.

But while the Lord was providing for us, from the seeds of our evils, the causes of heavenly blessings, she conceived divine piety through the losses of human affection. She was made wretched so that she might become blessed. She was struck so that she might be healed: “For I strike, and I heal,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0317] Deuteronomy 32:39; Psalm 76:10.].

So great is the mercy of the supreme Father that even his anger arises from mercy; therefore he chastises so that he may spare [Note: [Col. 0317] Revelation 3:19.]. Finally, the blessed Apostle was blinded so that he might be enlightened [Note: [Col. 0317] Acts 9:8.]; the persecutor fell so that the apostle might rise; on the journey he found a new road, and on the path of impiety he recognized the way of peace.

Thus the good Lord has until now continually bestowed these same acts of his mercy even upon us, the least of his servants, working the Father’s works, as he himself testified [Note: [Col. 0317] John 5:17; 9:4; 10:25; 12:10; 15:24.]. In his fatherly mercy he also corrected this holy woman—not because he found her faithless, but in order to make her perfect [Note: [Col. 0317] Proverbs 3:12.]—and struck her with trials in mercy [Col. 0317B], so that he might crown her with patience. For “he scourges every son whom he receives” [Note: [Col. 0317] Hebrews 12:6; Revelation 3:19.].

Therefore, as the companion of three funerals in a mournful procession [Note: [Col. 0317D] The Regius manuscript and the editions of Badius and Gravius read *luctuosa ambitu*, “in a mournful procession.” Grinius’s edition reads *luctuosa obitu*, “in mournful death.”], widowed and bereaved alike, she came to Rome with her only child, more an inciter than a consoler of tears [Note: [Col. 0317D] We have restored this from the Vatican and Viennese manuscripts. Others read *solatore*, “consoler.”]. Perhaps, while still unable to understand his own life, the infant already had enough understanding to grieve another’s death; or perhaps, in ignorant and unharmed infancy, he laughed in pitiable play amid his mother’s lamentations.

## 9

Instructed by these lessons, she acquired for herself and her son the saving knowledge not [Note: [Col. 0317D] Thus emended from the Vatican manuscript. So too the editions of Grinarius, Schottus, and Latinius. Other manuscripts read: “to end.”] to trust in the fragile world but to place one’s hope entirely in God, whom alone we cannot unwillingly lose: so that, by neglecting her little child, she might love him, and by relinquishing him, retain him; for she would possess him more securely absent, after commending him to the Lord, than she would embrace him present if she had entrusted him to herself.

She imitated, insofar as her circumstances allowed, the faithful vow of barren Hannah [Note: [Col. 0317] 1 Samuel 1:11]. For destructive fertility had brought this woman close to barrenness; and fearing that, once her fertility had been exhausted, she might become what Hannah had been before she obtained fertility, she dedicated to God, with a similar affection, a different kind of gift. The one was concerned about a child already born, the other about conceiving one; the one so that she might begin to be a mother, the other so that she might not cease to be one.

If this is judged dissimilar because her son was not, as Hannah’s was, placed in the temple to serve the Lord [Note: [Col. 0317] 1 Samuel 3:1], while also enjoying the world’s wealth and honors, nevertheless, by a contrary compensation of piety and faith, the two seem to be made equal. For this woman paid to the Lord concerning herself what glorious Hannah paid concerning her son. Hannah’s Samuel, given in fulfillment of her vow, was later repaid to her in several children; for this woman, her only child was the sum of her offspring and the end of her grief.

Hannah was consoled by her firstborn’s service in the temple, by her other children at home, and by the fact that even the consecrated son himself was not far distant—that is, not separated by a great distance [Note: [Col. 0318A] See Epistle 20, no. 1]—as she regularly returned to visit the temple. But this woman, once she had torn her only child from her breast and cast him into Christ’s bosom, so that the Lord himself might nourish him [Note: [Col. 0317] Psalm 54:23], gave him nothing thereafter of her own anxious care, judging it an act of distrust if she herself cared for one whom she had entrusted to Christ.

How great was the faith with which she did this can be seen from the fact that, although Rome abounded in powerful and illustrious relatives, she did not deign to entrust her little child to any of them—even, as the saying goes, to be fed, educated, and protected. So certain was she that he had been received by Christ, and therefore she deserved to regain him because she had refused to enjoy him; and now, through the pious faith by which she had not desired him after leaving him with God, she deserved to see him again.

Thus he who is powerful did great things for her [Note: [Col. 0317] Luke 1:49; Ephesians 3:20], being willing to grant even greater gifts to believers who dared to hope for them. In this way he added to her the sight of her son in this place, just as he gave Solomon, because he had chosen to ask for wisdom, the other riches which he had not requested—precisely because he had not desired them [Note: [Col. 0317] 2 Chronicles 1:10; 1 Kings 3:23; Wisdom 7:11]. Having rewarded her good understanding [Note: See Epistle 26, no. 2], by which she had preferred the highest things to the lowest, he poured lesser gifts over greater ones.

Thus the man who had chosen to be a petitioner for the highest things deserved to become the possessor of all riches. By this example we are all admonished to be wise when we are taught what to choose. For if we put lesser things before greater, and the lowest goods—that is, earthly things—before the highest, heavenly things, then, as punishment for our foolish desire, we shall be deprived of every good, both highest and lowest. We shall rightly fail to receive the things we have not desired, and deservedly be defrauded of those things whose love, wrongly directed, led us to neglect better gifts [Note: [Col. 0318D] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read “we neglect”].

So also father Abraham received the only son whom he offered to God [Note: [Col. 0317] Genesis 22], because he promptly offered what had been requested. The Lord was satisfied with the sacrifice of piety perfected in the heart; and therefore, when the angel’s hand intervened and caught the father’s right hand already brandished to strike, he placed beneath the victim a ram suddenly prepared, so that neither a victim would be lacking to God nor a son to the father.

At the same time, so far as the image permitted, the mystery destined to be fulfilled in Christ was represented in Isaac and formed in the ram: for that lamb, later to be sacrificed in Egypt as a figure of the Savior [Note: [Col. 0317] Exodus 12:3], was already foreshadowed in an animal of its own kind—that is, in the ram which appeared as a victim in Isaac’s place, so that it might go before Christ as a figure of him. Thus a ram was found for him to whom the fullness of the mystery was not owed; but he was slain for whom the perfection of the sacrament had been reserved.

## 10

She endured many struggles against the envious dragon even in the very beginnings of this campaign. The envy of her jealous enemy did not allow her to depart easily and peacefully; rather, the entire power of her noble relatives armed itself to hold her back and attempted to obstruct her purpose and oppose her departure.

But she, already strengthened beyond the power of temptations, loosened both her bodily bonds and the bonds of affection; and while everyone wept, she joyfully set sail. She steadfastly confronted the waves of the sea, lest the waves of the world overcome her, and she sailed on. Changing at once her world and the world’s city, she chose the city of Jerusalem as a spiritual gift, in which she might be a pilgrim away from the body, an exile from her fellow citizens and a citizen of the saints [Note: [Col. 0319] Ephesians 2:19]. Wisely and devoutly she wished to serve in this city, which is subject to service, so that she might be able to reign in that city which is free.

## 11

Among the many virtues she possessed, I shall at least proclaim one of them, by which all her works may be judged.

In the time of Valens, when the fury of the Arians, with the emperor himself as an accomplice of its impiety, was persecuting the Church of the living God, she was a leader—or a participant—among all who were striving on behalf of the faith. She received fugitives, or accompanied those who had been seized. When she had received into hiding men who, because of their conspicuous faith, were persecuted with even greater hatred by the heretics, and who were exposed by the envy of those concealing them [Note: [Col. 0319D] Thus the Vatican manuscript. Other copies read “were covered”], she was ordered, as though defying the public law, to be dragged out and to suffer the penalties which awaited those men, unless she preferred to betray them.

She came forward fearlessly, eager for suffering and exulting in the insult of public condemnation. Though she had not been expected to be dragged away, she hastened ahead of those who would drag her to the judge. He, overcome by reverence for her presence, did not carry out the anger of unbelief, while admiring the boldness of her faith.

During that same period she fed for three days, from her own bread, five thousand monks who were in hiding, so that through her hand the Lord Jesus might once again feed the former number in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0319] Matthew 14:21]—with a mercy all the more generous then because those who were hidden were sheltered with less freedom than those who once gathered voluntarily to the Lord in liberty and peace.

Yet she was neither afraid of being discovered as she confidently rendered the forbidden service, nor willing for the glory of the deed—that is, of the almsgiving [Note: See note 91]—to be recognized; nevertheless, she was revealed by the greatness of her work. She was glorious among human beings by as many witnesses as there were people whom she fed, while God alone was conscious of the deed.

Let us consider what merit this possessed. Since, in the history of the Kings, the man is celebrated who fed one hundred prophets of God hidden from the anger of an equally impious king [Note: [Col. 0319] 1 Kings 18:13], should we doubt that this woman, in a similar work, often surpassing that number by a thousand times, produced a hundredfold harvest [Note: [Col. 0319] Matthew 13:8]?

## 12

I shall now pass over the rest of her affairs and periods of her life; and I shall cross the very sea by which she sailed on her return, so as to imitate her course, in order to bring my account to its conclusion more quickly by describing her arrival among us, at which I was a witness of God’s great grace.

She was conveyed to Naples, a city separated by a short distance from Nola, where we live—that is, distant from it [Col. 0319A]. There she was welcomed by the meeting of her sons and grandsons, and soon hurried on to Nola, to the lodging of our humility. She arrived there surrounded by an imposing retinue of her wealthy descendants.

We saw the glory of the Lord in the journey of mother and sons: it was one journey, but their manner of travel was utterly different. She sat upon a lean and inferior little donkey [See note 130], while senators, honored and wealthy, who could be surrounded by all the pomp of this world, followed her in swaying carriages, on caparisoned horses, in gilded litters, and with many wagons; the Appian Way—that is, the Appian road [Col. 0319D]—groaned and glittered.

Yet the grace of Christian humility shone more brightly than the splendors of vanity. The rich admired the holy poor woman, while our poverty laughed at them. We saw a spectacle worthy of God’s world-confounding power: purple, silk, and gilded furnishings serving old and black rags.

We blessed the Lord, who makes the humble and the exalted wise [Note: [Col. 0320D] The word “wise” is absent from the Viennese manuscript] [Note: [Col. 0319] 1 Samuel 2:7], who fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty [Note: [Col. 0319] Luke 1:53].

Yet in those rich men, on that same day, we marveled at a poor spirit derived from their mother’s possessions: they took greater pride in their holy mother’s poverty than in their own visible abundance. It seemed to be the glory of the Lord at work that we saw our poor little woman’s riches in her sons, so that she might already receive the fruit of her faith, when she herself looked down upon her victory over the vanity of this world, seeing close at hand all that she had left for Christ and had persevered in despising [Note: [Col. 0320D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts read “perseveres.” I would read “had persevered”].

Her sons, dressed in silk and accustomed, each according to his sex, to shine in a toga or a stola, rejoiced to touch with their hands that coarse tunic, like the threads of sackcloth, and the cheap little cloak. They eagerly spread their garments beneath her feet—garments of wool, gold, and precious workmanship—and wore them out beneath her feet [Note: [Col. 0320D] Thus the Vatican manuscript, with the support of the Sacchin manuscript; the Regius manuscript. The Viennese manuscript reads “to cover.” Others read “to conceal”], judging themselves cleansed from the contamination of their wealth if they were worthy to gather any dirt from her most wretched clothing or from her footprints.

## 13

Our little dwelling, which extends farther from the earth, suspended as an upper room, with a single portico inserted between the cells for guests [Note: [Col. 0320D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and four printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads, incorrectly, “with one upper room and a portico”], provided, as though enlarged by the grace of the Lord, ample space not only for the saints—many of whom accompanied her—but also for the throngs of those rich men, who were not incapable of such narrow quarters [Note: [Col. 0320D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Gravius read “not capable,” incorrectly. See the preceding context].

Near it, the lofty buildings of our Lord Felix echoed with the voices of groups of boys and girls. Nor did the guests of that same dwelling, although their purposes were discordant, make a disturbance; rather, in those guests too, religious modesty imitated the silence of our discipline. Even if, sunk in sleep by sluggish stomachs, they seemed not to join in harmony with those keeping vigil, they nevertheless did not dare to be discordant with the devout voices, being restrained by faithful fear. Thus, when the tumult of secular crowds had been subdued by the pleasing voices of those singing psalms, they too joined in the song, though silently.

But, to return to the Lord’s perfect dove, know that this great virtue of God in a frail woman is nourished by fasting, rests in prayer, has bread in the word, clothing in a garment, a bed in a cloak and blanket; that what is hard on the earth becomes soft in writing, by which the delight of reading mitigates the harshness of a rigid bed [Note: [Col. 0321D] The Regius manuscript and the editions of Badæus, Gravius, and Schottus read “will,” a reading that does not displease Sacchinus, as in Epistle 12 … “the will to meditate on the law”]. For the holy soul, to keep vigil in the Lord is to rest.
