This daughter of Zion has possessed and desired such things until now; now the daughter of Babylon—that is, Rome [See Epistle 47, no. 1, and note 131]—possesses and admires her. For now the city itself is, in many respects, more a daughter of Zion than a daughter of Babylon; and therefore it marvels at her, living in the obscurity of humility and the light of truth, offering the wealthy encouragements to faith and the poor the consolation of narrow circumstances.

Yet, although she is at present burning amid the Roman crowds, in the quiet and refuge of her life near Jerusalem, she cries:

> Alas for me, that my sojourn has been prolonged!  
> Is it for this that I have been delayed, that I should now dwell with the inhabitants of Kedar? [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 119:5.]

For, as I have learned, among the Hebrews this name signifies “obscurity.” Therefore I think she should be congratulated on the virtues mentioned, but feared on account of her present dwelling, lest so distinguished a soul contribute more to Rome than she draws from Rome. Let her therefore sit beside the rivers of Babylon in such a way that she remembers Zion [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 136:1]; and, with the organ of her body suspended from all the snares and allurements of hostile Babylon, established in the steadfastness of her purpose as upon willows that always live by their native moisture, may she never cease to flourish. Let the constancy of her faith and the grace of her virtue endure, so that her leaf may not fall [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 1:3], and so that, just as her life is admired on the journey, her praise may be sung at its end [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 113:1].

## 14

I could not bear, brother, for you not to know these things. So that she might know God’s grace in you more fully, I revealed you to her more by your speech than by mine. I myself recounted to her the story of our Martin [Note: [Col. 0321D] Thus Paulinus, in Epistle 11 to the same Severus, no. 11, “to relate Martin.” The Viennese manuscript reads, “For I myself read to her the history of our Martin,” since she was most devoted to such matters. See note 132].

By this means I revealed you also to the venerable and most learned Bishop Nicetas [See note 133], who had come from Dacia and deservedly aroused the admiration of the Romans, and to many saints of God—boasting in truth no less as your herald than as my own. For it is glory to me to have you loved and cherished, since a life in harmony with your speech testifies that you are a servant of the truth.

May the Lord grant us on that day mercy from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0321] 2 Timothy 1:18], through this grace of which he himself is the author; so that, just as we are now refreshed in the depths of your love, we may likewise be refreshed from deserved flames by the finger of your lot [Note: [Col. 0321] Luke 16:24]. For I hope that, with the Lord’s indulgence, we shall have, as those who love you dearly, the support of your righteousness, even if, unworthy as we are, we dare not hope to share your crown.

# EPISTLE XXX

[Note: [Col. 0321D] Formerly 8; the one formerly numbered 30 is now 39. Written in the year 402.]

Severus had requested a portrait of Paulinus. On the occasion of this request, Paulinus censures his excessive affection and cleverly eludes the request by discussing the inner and outer human being.

To his holy brother and kindred in spirit, Severus: Paulinus.

## 1

It was said to the blessed Apostle: “Many writings are driving you mad” [Note: [Col. 0321] Acts 26:24]. The true madness of those people is apparent in this: the wisdom of God which Paul proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0321] 1 Corinthians 1:23] was foolishness to them, because, empty of faith in the truth, they were not worthy to understand that Christ is the wisdom of God.

But although, with Christ favorable to me, I differ from those people, to whose unbelief that teacher of health—Saint Paul [See Epistle 30, no. 5]—seemed mad, I shall nevertheless, by the liberty of our kindred affection, which is made closer by our unity of faith, appropriate a resemblance of the word, not of the mind, and say:

“Severus, my Severus, your great affection almost makes you delirious; and in your concern for me, your little one—not in age, but in understanding [Note: [Col. 0322D] Thus we have emended from the Regius manuscript and the four printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads “in age”]—you become, like a grandfather concerned for a late-born grandson, so excessively loving that, forgive me for saying so in deference to your wisdom, you become foolish.”

## 2

What answer should I give you concerning that request by which you ordered our portraits to be painted and sent to you? I beg you, by the heart of our affection: what consolations of true love are you seeking from empty forms? What sort of portrait do you wish us to send you—the image of an earthly human being or of a heavenly one [Note: [Col. 0321] 1 Corinthians 15:47]?

I know that you desire that incorruptible appearance which the heavenly King has loved in you. For no other form can be necessary for you from us than that form according to which you yourself were formed: the form by which you love your neighbor as yourself and do not wish to excel us in anything, lest any inequality appear among us.

But I am poor and sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 68:30], because I am still hardened by the squalor of an earthly image, and in my fleshly perceptions and earthly actions I bear more of the first Adam than of the second. How shall I dare to have myself painted for you, when I am proved to stain the image of the heavenly one with earthly corruption?

Shame confines me on both sides. I am ashamed to paint what I am; I do not dare to paint what I am not. I hate what I am, and I am not what I love. But what will it profit wretched me to hate iniquity and love virtue, when I do rather what I hate and, being sluggish, do not strive to do rather what I love?

I am torn apart by an inner war within myself, while spirit fights against flesh and flesh against spirit [Note: [Col. 0321] Galatians 5:17], and the law of the body, through the law of sin, attacks the law of the mind [Note: [Col. 0321] Romans 7:13].

Wretched man that I am! I have not yet digested the poisonous taste of the hostile tree by the wood of the cross. For that ancestral poison of Adam endures in me, with which the father of the human race infected all his offspring by his transgression [Note: [Col. 0321] Genesis 3:6]. Thus I, who by the natural good of innocence had eyes of the mind open to innocence and closed to iniquity, drank a deadly knowledge through the choice between good and evil: blinded and perversely enlightened alike by the ill-fated food of the forbidden grove—that is, tree or fruit.

## 3

Would that at least I had cleansed the guilt of unlawful desire by this remedy: having received through taste the harmful knowledge of good and evil [Note: [Col. 0323D] Thus we have emended from the Viennese manuscript and Grinarius’s edition. Others read “the innocent knowledge”] [Note: [Col. 0323] Genesis 2:9], would that I had chosen the good instead! Especially since I had heard God’s saving counsel urging me, when water and fire, life and death had been set before me, to stretch out my hand rather toward the water and choose the gift of life.

But my guilt increased from the crime of foolishness into audacity: although I had received the choice of both good and evil [Note: [Col. 0323D] We have added “and evil” from the Viennese manuscript. The addition was necessary and is confirmed by what precedes—“the choice between good and evil” in no. 2—and by what follows in no. 3, “having received … the knowledge of good and evil”], I preferred to desire what was harmful.

What pardon for sin, then, is available to wretched me, for whom no excuse of ignorance remains? I recognized the good and did evil, although it was equally within my power to do good, had I not despised the soul’s welfare through the fault of my will. By that will I admitted what was not expedient, failing to restrain what was permitted.

Therefore I justly lost those eyes of innocence with which I did not see evil, and received instead these eyes, by which sin is recognized, as a punishment of conscience for iniquity.

## 4

For Scripture declares that the first parents of the human race both saw and did not see. “For the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes to behold” [Note: [Col. 0323] Genesis 3:6, according to the Septuagint]. It says, “She saw”: therefore she had eyes. And what does it add next? “When they had eaten, their eyes were opened” [Note: [Col. 0323] Ibid., 7]. Were they therefore blind? How are we to understand this? For blindness and sight of the eyes cannot coexist in the same body. Yet certainly there is something blind in us even when we see, and conversely something seeing even in the blind.

For this reason I think that the Lord said: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” [Note: [Col. 0323] John 9:39]. For he came into this world to seek what had perished [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 19:10] and to restore light to what had been blinded [Note: [Col. 0323] John 8:12]. Accordingly, one in need of this physician cries in the Prophet: “Enlighten my darkness, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 17:29]. For the merciful and compassionate Lord, who arose as a light amid the darkness of human blindness [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 111:4], came to raise those who had been cast down [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 145:8], loose those in bonds, and enlighten the blind [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 7:21]. How, then, had he come to blind those who saw?

Yet in the Gospel we are taught that he restored sight to many blind persons and took it from no one. But just as it is written in the Law, “I shall kill, and I shall make alive” [Note: [Col. 0323] Deuteronomy 32:39], and likewise in the Gospel that he is set “for the fall and for the rising again of many” [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 2:34], so too is this: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” [Note: [Col. 0323] John 9:39]. Therefore the Lord came so that the old things might pass away and new things arise [Note: [Col. 0323] Revelation 21:5]. And what he had said was fulfilled: “I shall kill, and I shall make alive” [Note: [Col. 0323] Deuteronomy 32:39]. For by assuming our old human being he put it to death, fastening it to the cross; stripping himself of flesh, he exposed principalities and powers, triumphing openly over them in himself [Note: [Col. 0323] Colossians 2:15]. And from the resurrection of the dead he gave life to the new human being, ascending on high [Note: [Col. 0323] Ephesians 2:6] and seating him in heavenly places.

## 5

Thus he came so that the blind might be enlightened and those who see might be blinded: so that our eyes, which had been opened for transgression, might be blinded, and, conversely, those which had been blinded might be opened. For I am rightly blind if I do not see sin, and rightly sighted if I discern righteousness. Pray therefore, my brother, that the Lord may work both things in me: that he may blind my seeing self, lest I see vanity [Note: [Col. 0324D] The Viennese manuscript reads twice, “may see.”], and enlighten my unseeing self, that I may see righteous ordinances [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 118:37]. May he kill in me the old human being with its deeds [Note: [Col. 0323] Colossians 3:9], so that my flesh may bloom anew in Christ and my youth be renewed like an eagle’s [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 102:5].

For this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 76:11], when we shall be changed [Note: [Col. 0324D] The Viennese manuscript reads, “when we are changed.”] from ourselves into that human being who was created according to God [Note: [Col. 0323] Ephesians 4:24], whose image is heavenly, putting off him who is corrupted according to the desires of error [Note: [Col. 0323] Ephesians 4:22]. May God, I pray, break this image in me and reduce our image—that is, the earthly image [Note: [Col. 0323] 1 Corinthians 15:49]—to nothing in the city of the surrounding multitude [Note: [Col. 0324D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Others read “circumstance.”]; and may he restore and perfect in us his own image [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 72:20], in which we are not ashamed to be portrayed, and which bearing, we may truly say: “My heart and my flesh have failed; God is the God of my heart and my portion for ever” [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 72:26, according to the Roman Psalter].

For when, through the good change which comes to a human being from the right hand of the Most High [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 76:11], my heart and my flesh have failed—that is, the acts of my will and the fruits of my flesh—then, freed from bodily bonds and cleansed from my own heart, I may dare to say: “God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever” [Note: [Col. 0323] Psalm 72:26]. Would that the saying of the evangelical Symeon might be fulfilled in me, that Christ may become for me a fall and a rising again [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 2:34]: a fall to my outer self and a resurrection to my inner self; so that sin may fall in me, which stands while the soul falls, and that immortal self may rise, which fell when sin rose. For the standing of the outer self is the fall of the inner; and therefore, when the outer self is weakened, the one within is renewed day by day [Note: [Col. 0323] 2 Corinthians 4:16]. In this sense the perfect teacher—that is, Saint Paul [See Epistle 23, no. 14]—says: “When I am weak, then I am powerful” [Note: [Col. 0323] 2 Corinthians 12:10].

## 6

But thanks be to the Lord, because he has painted our images in the more enduring and living painting—not on perishable panels or in melting wax, but on the fleshly tablets of your heart [Note: [Col. 0323] 2 Corinthians 3:3]. There, having impressed us and made us conformable to your soul, joining us together in the unity of faith and grace [Note: [Col. 0324D] The Regius manuscript reads “faith.”], you will behold us not only here but also in the eternal age, in an indivisible and ever-present contemplation.

Here also, if such great love seeks even visible consolations, you will be able, through the guiding lines of your mind, to direct painters who do not know us or lack skill, setting before them your memory—in which you have us painted—as a model to be imitated, like the faces of those sitting before one’s eyes. But if an unskilled hand in the art should perhaps err through ignorance of the meaning of your word [the text perhaps reads *artificis*, “of the artist”], it will paint us unlike others. Yet for you [the text perhaps reads *autem*, “however”], as you contemplate and embrace us in your mind, whatever faces its incompetence may have painted under our name, we shall nevertheless be ourselves in your consciousness.

# EPISTLE XXXI

[Note: [Col. 0325D] Formerly 11; the one formerly numbered 31 is now 44. Written in the year 403.]

At the dedication of a basilica he sends Severus a particle of the most holy cross and teaches with what reverence it is to be kept. He then appends the history of the cross’s discovery.

To Severus, his brother and kindred in spirit: Paulinus.

## 1

Brother Victor, among other accounts of your works and vows, reported to us that you desire, for the basilica which you have recently founded at Primuliacum [See note 137], larger than the earlier one, a blessing from the sacred relics of the saints, with which your domestic church may be adorned, as is worthy of your faith and grace. The Lord is witness that, if we had possessed even a scruple [*scrypulum* for *scrupulum*] of sacred ashes beyond what was necessary for the basilica which is shortly, in the Lord’s name, to be completed and dedicated by us [Note: [Col. 0325D] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read “will be.” Both readings are good.], we would have sent it to your kindred spirit. But since we had no abundance of this gift, and Victor said that he had abundant hope of the same grace from holy Silvia [Note: [Col. 0325D] The Vatican and Viennese manuscripts read “was saying.”], who had promised him relics of many martyrs from the East, we found something worthy to send you both for the sanctification of the basilica and for increasing the blessing of the saints’ ashes: a portion of a particle of the wood of the divine cross.

The blessed Melanius [See note 138] brought this good thing to us from Jerusalem as a gift from the holy bishop John there [Note: [Col. 0326D] Thus the Viennese manuscript. Other manuscripts read “Melania.” The former reading is certainly correct. See note 138.], and sent it especially to our venerable sister Bassula—that is, Therasia, Paulinus’s wife—his fellow servant in the common service. But what is given to one of you belongs to both of you, because in each of you one principle remains [Note: [Col. 0325] Galatians 3:28], and faith abolishes sex, by which you both come together into a perfect man [Note: [Col. 0325] Ephesians 4:13].

Receive, therefore, from brothers of one mind, who desire fellowship with you in every good thing, receive a great gift in a small thing. In a segment, an almost atomic fragment of a short splinter, receive a protection for the present and a pledge of eternal salvation. Let not your faith be narrowed by fleshly eyes which see a small thing; rather, let its inward vision behold in this least fragment the whole power of the cross. When you consider that you see that wood on which our salvation, on which the Lord of majesty, hung while the world trembled, rejoice with trembling. Let us remember the rocks split at the sight of this cross; and, at least by emulation of stones, let us cleave our hearts with divine fear. Let us also reflect that the veil of the temple was torn by the same mystery of the cross [Note: [Col. 0325] Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38], and understand that the rending of that veil was displayed beforehand so that, hearing the voice of the Lord and the mystery of immense piety, we may not harden our hearts [Note: [Col. 0325] Psalm 94:8], but may be separated from fleshly things and tear the veil of unbelief, so that, with the face of the heart unveiled, we may see the sacraments of God’s saving gifts [Note: [Col. 0325] 2 Corinthians 3:18].

## 2

Nor do we write this to you so that you may imitate this arrangement by which we have enclosed a thing of so great a blessing in a little golden tube. Rather, by such adornment we have imitated your faith, so that we might send you your own pattern in the appearance of gold. For we know that, like gold tried by fire [Note: [Col. 0325] Revelation 3:18], you have the kingdom of God within you [Note: [Col. 0325] Luke 17:21; Luke 16:16]—that is, faith in the cross, by which the kingdom of heaven is stormed. For, he says, “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” [Note: [Col. 0325] Romans 8:17]. Therefore we have sent you in the Lord the gift of the saving wood, not for the strengthening of faith, since you have anticipated sight by faith, but on account of the merit of the faith which, received by hearing [Note: [Col. 0325] Romans 10:17], you prove by deed [Note: [Col. 0326D] The Viennese manuscript and the editions of Grinarius and Latinius read “by deed.” Bignaeus reads “by deeds.”], so that you may possess bodily the cross which you hold in spirit and bear by the strength of your purpose [Note: [Col. 0325] Galatians 6:14].

## 3

But because faith itself seems to require this, I think it not out of place, since it is worthy to be known, to recount the particular history of the cross after the time of the Passion—how it was revealed and found. If this is unknown, it is easy to see how difficult it would be to prove that this wood is that of the Lord’s cross. For it is certain that, if it had come into the hands of the Jews, who took every precaution against faith in Christ, it would have been broken up and burned. Nor would those who sealed the tomb [Note: [Col. 0325] Matthew 27:66 and 28:13] have been negligent in destroying the cross; nor could they have endured the Passion of one whose resurrection, proved by the tomb emptied despite their seals being broken open [See note 139], they cannot endure being venerated, being venerated while his cross survived.

Why, then, is it now asked where it was hidden [Note: [Col. 0326D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts, with three printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition has the erroneous “which.”], since, unless it had lain concealed, it is evident that it would have been destroyed, especially in those times of persecution which followed Jewish hatred and almost surpassed its cruelty? For we can readily infer by conjecture with what force those would have cut down the cross had they seen it standing, who persecuted even the place of the cross. For the Emperor Hadrian, thinking to destroy the Christian faith by outrage done to the place, consecrated an image of Jupiter at the place of the Passion [See note 140]; and Bethlehem was profaned by a shrine of Adonis. Thus, as though the root and foundation of the Church might be removed, idols were worshipped in the places where Christ was born in order to suffer, suffered in order to rise, rose in order to reign, and was judged in order to judge [Note: [Col. 0327D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the marginal reading of Grinarius’s edition read: “he rose to reign as judge,” or “the king might judge me, wretched one.” The received reading is more elegant.].

Wretched me! The almighty Lord did not refuse to endure even these things for us: that where he had hung crucified for the salvation of humankind, he should there be scorned by human sacrilege. Above the cross—at which, when the world was shaken, the sun withdrew, and the tombs burst open in the resurrection of the dead, the nature of things had trembled—stood the image of a demon, and the altar of that image smoked with the pyres of beasts. The name of God was ascribed to statues of the dead, while the God of the living [Note: [Col. 0327] Matthew 22:32; John 11:25], who is also the resurrection of the dead, was blasphemed with the reproach not only of a dead but of a crucified human being.

At Bethlehem too, where the ox had known its owner and the ass its Lord’s manger [Note: [Col. 0327] Isaiah 1:3], there the leaders of humankind, denying that the Savior was God, worshipped the notorious loves and deaths of human beings. Where the cradle of the eternal King, revealed by a new star, had been adored by supplicating Chaldeans with their wealth [Note: [Col. 0327D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts, with two printed editions, read “where the cradles [were] supplicating.”] [Note: [Col. 0327D] Thus emended from Grinarius’s edition, and this is certainly how it should be read. See what precedes and follows. Other manuscripts read “they adored.”], Romans consecrated barbarous lusts. Where shepherds, with the host of angels, singing in heavenly joy, had greeted the newborn Savior on that illuminated night [Note: [Col. 0327] Luke 2:13], prostitutes joined with half-men bewailed Venus’s lover. Alas! What human piety could compensate for this impiety? Where the sacred infancy of the newborn Savior had cried, there the infamous rite howled with the wanton lamentations of those who feigned Venus’s griefs; and where a Virgin had given birth, adulterers were worshipped.

4. This crime of the preceding age remained into the time near our own, under Constantine, who deserved to be the foremost prince among Christian rulers no less through his own faith than through that of his mother Helena [Col. 0327C]. She, inspired by divine counsel—as the outcome showed—when she recognized Jerusalem by name, [Note: [Col. 0327D] In all printed editions this passage is mutilated and corrupt. Since we could not restore it from the manuscripts, we consulted Sulpicius Severus, to whom this letter was sent, in *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 48, where it is certain that he inserted from this letter what he says about the discovery of the holy cross. Thus, without adding anything of our own, we corrected the passage from Sulpicius Severus, with the help of the manuscripts: “who, reigning as Augusta together with her son, asked him,” etc. For in Sulpicius, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 48, we read: “Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, who reigned as Augusta together with her son, when she desired to recognize Jerusalem,” etc. In the Regius and Vatican manuscripts and in the printed editions: “reigned together”; in the Viennese manuscript: “asked him.” Before this stood: “by name, reigned together, so that for herself,” which made no sense.] who was reigning as Augusta together with her son (see note 141), asked him to grant her permission to cleanse all the places there marked by the Lord’s footprints and distinguished by memorials of his divine works from every contact with profane impiety, by destroying temples and idols, and to restore them to her religion, so that at last the Church might be celebrated in the land of its origin.

Accordingly, with the emperor son’s ready consent, the Augusta mother, having opened her treasuries for holy works, exhausted the entire imperial treasury. With as much expense and magnificence as a queen could command and religion required, she covered and adorned with basilicas all the places in which the Lord our Redeemer had completed the saving mysteries of his goodness, incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension on our behalf.

It is remarkable, moreover, that in the basilica of the Ascension that place alone from which he ascended after being received into the cloud, carrying captive our captivity in his flesh [Note: [Col. 0327] Acts 1:9; Ephesians 4:8; Psalm 68:19], is said to have been so consecrated by the divine footprints that it has never permitted itself to be covered with marble (see note 142) or paved [Note: [Col. 0328D] The Viennese manuscript reads “pavimentari.” But *paviri* is the correct reading, confirmed by poem 25, line 40: “spacious, paved in the middle . . .” The footprints of Christ impressed in the earth on the Mount of Olives are also mentioned in the book *On Hebrew Places* among Jerome’s works; in Augustine, *Tractate 47 on John*, no. 4; in Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 48; and in Bede, *On the Names of Places* in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7.]—the ground always rejecting, once shaken off, whatever human hands have attempted to place there in their zeal for adornment.

Thus, throughout the entire space of the basilica, it alone remains green in the form of its own tuft of grass; and the sand, at once visible and close at hand to those who venerate it, preserves the impressed imprint of the divine feet and the dust trodden by God (see poem 15, line 291), so that it can truly be said: “We worshipped where his feet stood” [Note: [Col. 0328D] The Viennese manuscript adds “in that place.”] [Note: [Col. 0327] Psalm 132:7.].

5. But in the history of the cross, hear of a great and truly divine miracle.

That venerable queen, when she came to Jerusalem, diligently and devoutly [Note: [Col. 0328D] We have corrected this from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. Previously it read “to those places.” See note 4, “all the places there.”], inquisitive about all the divine monuments there and in the surrounding area, and desiring to draw with her eyes the faith she had received through pious ears and writings, began with the utmost zeal to seek the Lord’s cross.

But what path or method of discovery could there be, when no suitable guide could be found, after antiquity had effaced the memory and care of religious conscience or observance, and the long duration of impious superstition had obliterated them? Yet the Lord, who knows and bears witness to everything hidden from both earth and human hearts, granted the faithful woman the Holy Spirit through her pious devotion. Under his inspiration, when she had diligently and fruitlessly searched for something divinely removed from human awareness, she sought only to become certain of the place of the Passion.

Accordingly, she sought out not only men among the Christians who were full of learning and holiness, but also the most learned among the Jews, as witnesses to their own impiety—the impiety in which those wretched people glory—and summoned and gathered them in Jerusalem. When all had together confirmed the place of the testimony—that is, of the martyrdom or Passion, as above—she immediately ordered work to begin digging at the very place, doubtless driven by the impulse of the revelation conceived in her mind.

Soon, with both the citizens and the military force prepared, she quickly completed the labor of this undertaking; and, contrary to everyone’s expectation but in accordance with the faith of the queen alone, when the depths of the earth had been opened by a deep excavation, the secrets of the hidden cross were revealed.

But when three crosses were found together, just as they had once stood fixed for the Lord and the thieves, the joy of their discovery began to be confused by anxious doubt, through the justified fear of the devout: lest perhaps they should choose the gibbet of a thief in place of the Lord’s cross, or, by rejecting the saving wood as a thief’s stake, profane it.

The Lord faithfully regarded the devout anxieties of those who were fervently concerned, and poured the light of this decision especially into the mind of the woman who was the leader of so holy a solicitude, so that she ordered a recently dead man to be sought out and brought in.

There was no delay: the order was carried out. The corpse was brought in; it was laid down, and one of the crosses was brought near it, and another. But death rejected the wood of the criminals [Note: [Col. 0329D] The Viennese manuscript reads “of those crosses.” The Regius manuscript, together with four printed editions, reads “of those criminals.”].

Finally, the resurrection revealed the Lord’s cross. At the touch of the saving wood, death fled, the corpse was shaken free [that is, the dead man was restored to life], and the body was raised upright. While the living trembled, the dead man stood; freed from his funeral bonds, like Lazarus once, he immediately walked alive among his onlookers [Note: [Col. 0329D] Thus the Regius manuscript with three printed editions. This is the correct reading. Other manuscripts read “spectators.” See letter 6, section 3.] [Note: [Col. 0329] John 11:44.].

6. Therefore, after the Lord’s cross had been hidden for so many ages, concealed from the Jews at the time of the Passion, and certainly not revealed to the Gentiles when they were digging earth for the construction of the temple itself, was it not kept hidden so that it might now be found when devoutly sought?

Yes: as was fitting for Christ’s cross, Christ’s cross was found and authenticated by the proof of resurrection. Soon it was consecrated with worthy ceremony—that is, with honor and pageantry—and a basilica was built at the place of the Passion. Gleaming with gilded ceilings and rich with golden altars, it preserves the cross, placed in a secret shrine. Each year, when the Lord’s Pascha is celebrated, the bishop of the city himself brings it out for the people to venerate, leading the worshippers.

Except on this day, when the mystery of the cross itself is celebrated, the cross—which is the cause of the sacraments and is brought forth as a kind of mark of the sacred solemnity—is not displayed, unless exceptionally devout persons request it: those who have traveled there for this sole reason, so that its unveiling might be offered to them as the reward of their distant pilgrimage.

They say that this can be obtained only through the bishop’s favor. By his gift alone, small fragments of this same sacred wood are granted to be possessed as a great favor of faith and blessing. This cross, possessing living power within insensible matter, lends its wood almost daily to countless human petitions, yet suffers no diminution (see note 143) and remains as though untouched, even when portions are taken daily and it is always venerated as whole [Note: [Col. 0329D] Thus the Regius manuscript and Latinius: the correct reading. Other manuscripts read “for those taking a portion, and always venerating it whole.”].

Indeed, it drank this imperishable power and indestructible solidity from the blood of that flesh which, though it suffered death, did not see corruption [Note: [Col. 0329] Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27.].

We hope that for you also it will become not only a memorial of blessing but a seedbed of incorruption [Note: [Col. 0330D] The Regius manuscript reads “will become”; the Vatican manuscript, “fruit,” in which reading “memorial” and “seedbed” will be genitives. —Sacchini.], so that the sight of it may kindle your faith also through remembrance of that blessed thief [Note: [Col. 0329] Luke 23:43], who, having turned his thievery to good purpose, anticipated by the faith of a moment and the instant of his confession the long roads traveled by the saints through great labors, and not undeservedly was the first to seize and piously plunder the kingdom prepared from the beginning for the apostles and martyrs themselves, as he says [Note: [Col. 0329] Matthew 25:31].

For when he saw Christ crucified, in the likeness of his own punishment, in that condition in which even the faith of the disciples had been shaken and faltered, he nevertheless confessed him as he truly was, the Lord of majesty [Col. 0330B]. Asking that he be remembered in the kingdom of God, he believed in the glory of the resurrection before the resurrection itself—a resurrection which the apostles, after it occurred, believed not only by seeing but by experience.

Yet they too were doubting not so much the resurrection of the flesh as the nature of the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0329] Luke 24:39; John 20:27]. For, since they were destined to be sent throughout the world to instruct all nations, they had to receive the faith to be proclaimed not only with their ears but also with their eyes, so that what they had learned more firmly they might teach more steadfastly [Note: [Col. 0329] Matthew 28:19.].

# LETTER XXXII

[Note: [Col. 0329D] Formerly number 12; what was number 32 is now number 42. Written in the year 403 and sent with the preceding letter.]

He reproaches Severus, by whom he had been painted with Saint Martin beside the sacred font. He sends verses to be inscribed, showing that the painting was made so that Paulinus might serve as an example for penitents and Martin for the innocent. He describes the basilica of Saint Felix built by himself and sends the epigrams inscribed on the basilicas at Nola and Fundi. Then he eloquently commends works of mercy and the building of the spiritual temple in the soul.

1. When these little verses had been inserted [Note: [Col. 0330D] The Viennese manuscript reads “composed.” The Schott edition has “reviewed” in the margin.] into the open page, the page prompted tongue and hand to occupy the vacant space, and something occurred to my mind that I should write [Note: [Col. 0330D] The Viennese manuscript reads “came to mind.”].

For I rejoice greatly that we have shown one likeness of our heart and body, and also of our works and vows, by adding basilicas to the Lord’s sheepfolds at the same time. But you, in fact, built even a baptistery placed between two basilicas, so that in the construction of these works also—works visibly built—you might surpass us.

But thanks be to the Lord, who gave us the means by which we could regard being defeated as victory. For we conquer by our desire, in which we are conquered by grace, by him whom we place before ourselves in judgment but equal ourselves to in affection.

You are the one of whom we speak; you, I say, are the greater and better part of us. You are our rest, our joy; in you is the reclining of our head and the dwelling of our mind. This will remain ours not only in the present time but, as we hope and trust in the Lord, perpetually, through his gift, in his body and spirit [Col. 0331A]. Therefore, if by the Lord’s grace you accomplish anything more, you certainly act with us and surely for us.

2. But I fear that in your works—by which you straighten the crooked ways of the secular world and level its slopes—you may mingle a stumbling-block, because of that affection toward us about which I am always complaining: namely, that you darken the splendid titles of your devotion in Christ with our names and insert this injustice into your righteous labors, polluting the holy place even with the faces of the unrighteous.

Rightly is Martin painted in the place of refreshment—that is, the baptistery—because he bore the image of the heavenly man through perfect imitation of Christ, so that for those laying aside in the font the oldness of the earthly image, the likeness of the heavenly soul might appear for imitation.

But what place is there for us, who are equal neither to infants in innocence nor to adults in wisdom, and who are distinguished from the spotless by our wickedness and from the perfect by our weakness? What fellowship, then, is there between light and darkness [Note: [Col. 0331] 2 Corinthians 6:14], between wolves and lambs, between serpents and doves—that is, between us and Martin?

Have you not mixed a cup of milk and gall? Yet it is good that, unlike liquids confused together in one cup, when human beings are placed together in the same place while differing in merit, the sweetness of the good is not poisoned by the bitterness of the evil. Rather, the opposite occurs: when a sinner is set beside a righteous man, he appears more filthy, and when a righteous man is compared with a sinner, he shines more brightly.

I am therefore less disturbed by the error of your affection, because you have done no injury to that blessed man; rather, you have contributed to his glory, so that a venerable face might be painted opposite a contemptible one, and his splendor might shine more clearly by comparison with darkness—he who also shines with conspicuous brightness among the splendors of the saints [Note: [Col. 0331] Psalm 110:3.].

Indeed, unless I knew that you had designed this painting out of the intense devotion of your excessive love for us, I would accuse you of malice and cunning: you would have placed the persons of our humility, darkened by the night of our souls, opposite the holy head on the facing wall, so that you might paint him alone while disfiguring us—whom, rightly, anyone who saw Martin’s face would spit upon—and expose us to the disgrace of a ridiculous comparison.

But lest this contrivance of yours, born of affection, be mocked on our account—for, deceived by your great love for us, you represent us falsely—although it truly can and ought to be mocked,

3. I have sent you only a few lines about this sort of painting of yours, so that the reasoning behind your plan might be revealed: in your wholesome concern for the instruction of new people, you had set before them widely differing images, so that those emerging from the sacred font might see equally what to avoid and what to follow.

Here they are; if you approve, use them:

> Whoever has washed souls and limbs in the baths,  
> See the paths set before you toward good deeds.  
> Martin stands as the rule of the perfect life;  
> Paulinus teaches how you may earn pardon.  
> Look to the one, you sinners, and to the other, you blessed;  
> Let the one be an example for the holy, the other for the guilty.

Again, on the same subject:

> Rich in possessions for Christ, poor for himself, beautiful Severus  
> Established these heights beside the sacred fonts.  
> And because he was building a heavenly hall for deeds  
> By which human beings might be renewed through the font and God,  
> He painted, worthy of the sacraments, twin images,  
> So that the reborn person might learn the gifts of life.  
> The venerable image of the man bears witness to Martin;  
> The other form represents humble Paulinus.  
> The one arms faith with examples and bold words,  
> So that he may bear the undefiled palms of merit.  
> The other teaches that, by redeeming his crimes with scattered coins,  
> A person should value wealth less than his own salvation [Note: [Col. 0331] That is, money. See appendix to letter 1, section 6.].

4. Certainly it is now clear that you should not be mocked but rather praised, if for this sole reason you seem to have painted us close together while making us utterly unlike: so that in Martin the form of justice and the summit of virtues might be seen, while in us the wearing-down and confession of a guilty conscience might appear, making an example available both to the blessed and to the miserable.

In him, courage would offer a mirror; in us, cowardice would find consolation. Those who were able to fulfill the command through virtues would look upon him; those who wished to bring a remedy to their crimes would be consoled in us. For those deprived of confidence in their innocence and bound by the chain of wickedness, redemption alone can help, as it helps captives.

Nevertheless, I ask you not to turn my obedience into a crime if, as you announced, you remove those verses of yours—those of light and praise. I ask this modestly rather than threaten it in earnest. And if you decide that these verses should be added, let the others remain, so that they may be like jewels set among these, giving value to what is base and marking off darkness from what is bright.

With permission granted, I have allowed my tongue to speak—not, in accordance with the prophet [Note: [Col. 0331] Psalm 39:2.], so that it might remain in its rest and guard my ways, but rather [Col. 0332C] to break the reins of the guard set over it, while serving you. I love you so much that I feared sinning more by obeying you than by speaking at length [Note: [Col. 0331] Proverbs 10:19.].

5. For this reason I have also assigned verses to your basilicas, as votive inscriptions for the sacred fonts. If I seem to have spoken aptly in them, this too is due to our brother Victor, whose eyes and words allowed me to see everything that you have done and are doing in Christ the Lord. Therefore you will regard as their author the verses that I have also inserted concerning the basilicas, since he dictated their subject matter by recounting your deeds.

The following verses, then, are for the baptistery itself; the preceding ones concern only its painting:

> Here the generating fountain of souls to be restored  
> Sends forth a living river in divine light.  
> The Holy Spirit descends from heaven into this sacred stream,  
> And joins the holy waters to the heavenly fountain.  
> The water conceives God, and with life-giving streams  
> Brings forth offspring from eternal seed.  
> Wonderful is God’s goodness! The sinner is plunged beneath the waters;  
> Soon he emerges from the same water justified.  
> Thus a person, having undergone both a fortunate death and birth,  
> Dies to earthly things and rises to everlasting ones.  
> Guilt perishes, but life returns; the old Adam dies,  
> And the new Adam is born to eternal dominion.

The following verses concern the painting of the basilicas:

> Pure in body, mind, and faith, a most chaste inhabitant of Christ,  
> Joyful Severus built these houses for God.  
> He himself, wholly alive as God’s temple with Christ as his guest,  
> Carries within his humble heart the Lord who rejoices.  
> Behold, as though under a threefold name, he worships one mind:  
> Thus he consecrated a threefold work in a sacred structure.  
> He gave the people broad roofed heights in twin buildings,  
> So that the number might correspond to the sacred laws.  
> For one faith in Christ joins  
> The two Testaments, covenanted through the one God who bears them,  
> He established the fountain between two halls  
> Of differing roofs, beneath a towered covering.  
> So that Mother Church might joyfully receive in her twin bosoms  
> The new offspring whom the water has brought forth.  
> A double hall beneath roofs, as the Church is in the Testaments;  
> Yet one grace of the font is present for both.  
> The ancient Law confirms the new, and the new fulfills the old:  
> In the old there is hope; in the newness, faith.  
> But the grace of Christ joins old and new;  
> Therefore the fountain was placed in the middle space.  
> From there the fatherly priest leads infants from the sacred font,  
> White in body, heart, and clothing [Note: [Col. 0333] See note 144.],  
> And, surrounding the inexperienced lambs at festive altars,  
> He moistens their unformed mouths with health-giving food.  
> Hence the elder [Note: [Col. 0333] That is, those recently initiated. See poem 25, line 211.] rejoices with the assembled crowd:  
> The sheepfold bleats “Alleluia” in its new choirs.

6. When I had given you these verses concerning the works made by your united labor [Col. 0333B], I could not remain silent about that unmade grace of God in your domestic church, through which he granted you Clarus as a perpetual guest there.

Accordingly, I dared to compose and send you verses in memory of that holy man—not because I could say anything worthy of his divine merits, but to express my great affection for his soul. As you recite them before the Lord, to his holy soul, which always dwells with you in the Lord (see poem 24, line 438), you will excuse my boldness and commend my devotion.

> As his name is bright in title, so is Clarus bright in mind’s light.  
> This presbyter is covered here, but his frail limbs are covered by the tomb;  
> His mind, freed from the prison of the body, rejoices among the stars,  
> Having received a pure place among the seats of the proven righteous.  
> His holy bones rest beneath eternal altars,  
> So that, while pure gifts are offered to holy Christ,  
> His soul may be joined to the divine sacred fragrances.

Again, on the same man; read whichever you prefer. But I know that you ought to hesitate here—not about choosing some verses for the inscription, but lest you do injury to any holy man of God:

> Here lies the presbyter Clarus, in merit and in name,  
> Martin’s companion in devotion and his partner in the measure of merit.  
> The house is worthy of the pious altars beneath which his limbs  
> Are buried lifeless [Note: [Col. 0333D] “His lifeless limbs are buried.” See the same Greek construction in poem 22, line 53. Four editions have “lifeless,” incorrectly; for *artus* is not expressed in the singular.], while his spirit rejoices in the ether  
> And joins the disciple with his like master above the stars.  
> Bright in faith, most excellent in conduct, brightest in fruit,  
> You who make the title of your name equal to your merits,  
> Chaste altars fittingly veil your body,  
> So that the altar of God may cover Christ’s temple.  
> But since you do not occupy this seat in which your body lies,  
> You whose spirit flies among the heavenly realms because of your merits,  
> Whether you recline in the bosoms of the fathers, or are placed beneath  
> The Lord’s altar, or are nourished in the sacred grove,  
> Wherever you are placed in the region of heaven or paradise,  
> Blessed beneath eternal peace, you live on;  
> Receive these good prayers of sinners who ask,  
> That you may remember Paulinus and Therasia.  
> Love them through Severus, who conveys their requests,  
> Those whom you did not know in the body, though they are so meritorious.  
> Let shared love, in harmony, be the fuel for both  
> Of an everlasting covenant in the Lord.  
> You cannot tear apart those who are joined: if you draw one,  
> He will draw with him the one who clings to him wherever he is carried.  
> Therefore embrace the brothers who are inseparable together;  
> As we are, so love us by making us your companions.  
> Thus God summoned us; thus Martin loved us;  
> Thus you too, Clarus, protect your equals together.  
> Equal not in merits but in love: you, holy one, will have power  
> To pray that we may become equal in merits,  
> If, together with Martin, you labor in shared devotion,  
> So that your prayers may overcome our crimes;  
> And that together we may be led into the lot of your Severus,  
> And your wing may always protect us within its embrace.

7. If the Lord grants the desire of your souls according to your faith, adding to the adornment and sanctification of your works so that you may obtain sacred ashes from the relics of holy and glorious apostles or martyrs—for we have learned that, in anticipation of this wish, you have prepared at Primuliacum another basilica of ours, larger than the former one—we consider it worthy of your work of faith and of the exceedingly famous dedication of your faithfully completed work, and fitting for the relics of the saints, that you should also venerate what we have sent from the cross, deposited and consecrated there together.

If this pleases you, the following verses, if you wish, will announce your decision:

> Venerable altars cover the divine covenant,  
> With martyrs placed together with the sacred cross.  
> All the martyrdoms of saving Christ come together:  
> The cross, the body, the blood, and God himself, the martyr.  
> For God always preserves his gifts for you [Note: [Col. 0333] Perhaps “for us.”];  
> And where Christ is, there are the Spirit and the Father.  
> Thus where the cross is, there too is the martyr; where the martyr is, there too is the cross,  
> Which was the pious cause of the saints’ martyrdom.  
> The cross brought forth food for mortals, and crowns  
> For those who share in the Lord as his servants.  
> On the cross was fixed the flesh on which I feed; from the cross came the blood.  
> It flows as the life by which I drink and wash my heart.  
> Christ, may these gifts of yours come together for Severus,  
> And may this recipient be a witness of your cross.  
> May he live by your flesh; may your blood provide him cups;  
> May he live and act in your word.  
> By whatever means you saw your companion Martin ascend with Clarus,  
> May he too be carried there by your gift [Note: [Col. 0334D] Thus the Viennese manuscript, supported by the Regius manuscript. Other copies read “joined.”].

8. But if you would rather have this blessing from the cross readily available for daily protection and healing, so that, once placed in the altar, it may not always be at hand when use requires it, that grace is sufficient also for the consecration of the basilica—namely, the Lord together with the apostles and martyrs. If their venerable ashes are placed beneath the altars without the company of the cross (see note 147), this inscription will indicate those covered here:

> The pledges of the saints veil the divine glory of the altar-table,  
> Brought forth from apostolic bodies.  
> The Spirit, present with the Lord’s healing powers,  
> Proves the sacred ashes living through their works.  
> Thus doubled grace breathes upon pious prayers,  
> Worked below through the martyrs and above through the sacred rites.  
> The prayers of the priest and the welfare of the living are helped  
> By the precious death of the saints in a little dust.

9. You have here verses unworthy indeed of your holy and magnificent works, but suited to your persuasion—your tendency to believe in me more than I believe in myself. If you are not ashamed to have them inscribed for viewing on the walls of your domestic church [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts, together with four printed editions, read “for viewing.”], I shall have my revenge.

For I believe that even then you will blush at my foolishness and repent of your desire and insistence, when you see the buildings, still shining in the spotless beauty of your work, darkened by the doggerel of my folly and—as a word worthy of my verses may put it—turned into kettles [see note 148], while many laugh or feel nauseated in embarrassment.

Nor will you be able to conceal the matter so that the reader thinks you the author, since the folly, known to no one in you, could inform the reader that he should not attribute my poem—that is, my crime—to you. Yet you will still be blameworthy either as the betrayer or as the writer.

But lest anyone judge me unjust according to the rule that says, “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” [Note: [Col. 0335] Tobit 4:16], you will prove with present evidence that you had already endured the same thing from me in my basilicas. In this way you will also show our harmony: whether through favor or injury, by comparing me with yourself, I have sinned with the same recklessness in your buildings as in my own.

But let our Victor be considered the author or defendant in this matter—whether it be favor, in keeping with your exceedingly patient attitude toward me, or injury, in keeping with the unworthiness of my gift. He, the most holy interpreter of our affection, presumed that he would return to you more welcome from us the more heavily he returned oppressed beneath the unjust burden of our foolishness.

He also wished to add this to his bundles, carrying you the verses and paintings of our basilicas together. And rightly he will do so if, bringing himself to you exhausted and bent beneath this complaint, he cries:

> “Behold, because of the words of your lips I have walked difficult paths” [Note: [Col. 0335] Psalm 16:2];

and cries:

> “Sinners have built upon my back, who prolonged their iniquity through so many letters” [Note: [Col. 0335] Psalm 133:3.].

10. Thus I have also received this mound added to my sins, so that I might render to a brother exceedingly eager for such a burden—the burden by which his soul might be lightened while his body was weighed down—the injury he desired.

For this request of his seemed truly to fit our harmony: he maintained that your knowledge of our buildings in the Lord ought to be made so complete that you would wish us to indicate yours in inscriptions and paintings.

Persuaded by this reasoning, I took care to join our basilicas to yours in writing, just as they are joined in the time of their construction and the character of their vow, so that our union might also be represented here—a union joined in souls but separated by places. In this way, these buildings too, which we have constructed in the Lord’s name and by the same spirit, though separated by different regions, will appear joined to one another, as it were, by the sequence of the same letter [Note: [Col. 0335D] Thus the Rosweyde edition. This is the correct reading, confirmed by poem 25, lines 12 and 57. Three manuscripts together with four printed editions read “marked.”].

That basilica, then, which has now been dedicated in the name of the Lord Christ God [Note: [Col. 0335D] We have added “God” from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. This reading is confirmed by section 12, line 1.] to my lord and our common patron [Col. 0336A], and which has been added to his four basilicas, with the relics of apostles and martyrs consecrated beneath the altars in a threefold apse (see note 149; perhaps *trichoram* should be read; see note 150), is venerable not only through the honor of blessed Felix.

Its apse, marble-paved on floor and walls, is brightened by a mosaic-decorated vault (see note 151), whose painting has these verses:

> The Trinity flashes forth in its full mystery.  
> Christ stands as the Lamb [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 152.]; the Father’s voice [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 153.] thunders from heaven;  
> And the Holy Spirit flows through the dove [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 154.].  
> A crown [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 155.] encircles the cross with a radiant sphere;  
> And the apostles are the crown of that crown.  
> Their figure is in the choir of doves [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 156.].  
> The pious unity of the Trinity joins with Christ,  
> Bearing in itself also the emblems of the Trinity:  
> The Father’s voice reveals God, and the Spirit;  
> The cross and the Lamb confess the holy victim.  
> Purple and palm indicate kingship and triumph.  
> He himself stands above the Rock [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 157.], the Rock of the Church,  
> From which four resounding fountains [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 158.] flow—  
> The living rivers of Christ’s evangelists.

11. On the lower band, where a plastered ledge inserted between the wall and the vault joins or divides their boundary, this inscription indicates the holy relics deposited beneath the altar:

> Here are devotion, here nourishing faith, here Christ’s glory;  
> Here the cross is joined to its martyrs.  
> For a great pledge of the cross is a short splinter from its wood,  
> And the entire power of the cross is in this tiny fragment.  
> This [Note: [Col. 0336D] We have retained this reading according to the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the Schott edition. It is the truest reading. Other manuscripts read “of Melania.” See note 138.] gift of holy Melania [Note: [Col. 0335] Note 138.], brought to Nola,  
> Came from the supreme city of Jerusalem,  
> The greatest good.  
> Holy altars veil a twofold honor for God,  
> Joining apostolic ashes with the cross.  
> How well the bones of the devout are joined to the wood of the cross!  
> May those piously slain on the cross find rest in the cross!

12. The entire space of the basilica outside the apse (see note 159) is expanded beneath a high, coffered roof by twin porticoes on either side, through which a double row of columns extends beneath each arch.

Small chambers (see note 160), four of them inserted along the long sides of the basilica within the porticoes, provide secluded places for those praying or meditating on the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0335] Psalm 1:2], and also suitable places for the memorials of devout and beloved persons, for the rest of eternal peace.

Each chamber is marked above its threshold by two verses. I did not wish to insert them in this letter (see note 161), but I have written those belonging to the entrances of the basilica itself, since, if you wish to use them, they could also suit the doors of your basilicas. For example:

> May peace be with you, whoever enters the inner chambers of Christ God  
> With a heart made pure by peaceful devotion.

Or this, concerning the sign of the Lord—that is, the sign of the cross—painted above the entrance in the form indicated by the verses:

> See the cross of the Lord, crowned, standing above the courts of Christ,  
> Promising lofty rewards for hard labor.  
> Take up the cross, whoever wishes to win the crown.

At the other basilica, whose private entrance opens from the little garden or orchard, these verses open the more secluded door (see letter 28, section 5, and poem 24, line 613):

> Enter the heavenly ways through pleasant green spaces,  
> Worshippers of Christ; and it is fitting to enter here from joyful gardens,  
> From which a holy passage into paradise is granted as a reward for merits.

The same door is marked by other verses on the inner face of its entrance:

> Whoever leaves the house of God with vows fulfilled in due order,  
> Return in body, but remain in heart.

13. The front of the basilica does not, as is more customary, face east; rather, it is directed toward the basilica of my lord, blessed Felix, looking toward his memorial—that is, his tomb.

Nevertheless, within its spacious enclosure the apse opens broadly in a curve with two small apses on the right and left (see note 162). One of them is open to the bishop offering the sacrifices of jubilation [Col. 0337B]; the other, with its capacious curve, receives those who pray behind the priest.

With a most joyful prospect, this entire basilica opens at once toward the basilica of the aforesaid confessor [Note: [Col. 0337D] We have corrected this from the Viennese manuscript. Previously it read “in the basilica.”] through three equal arches, with a screen allowing light through (see note 165), by which the roofs and spaces of the two basilicas are joined to one another in turn.

For because a wall, blocked by the intervening apse of a certain monument, separated the new basilica from the old, it was opened at the side of the confessor by as many doors as the new basilica was opened at its front by entrance doors. It thus presents the appearance of a threefold passageway (see note 166), looking from either basilica into the other, as is indicated by the inscriptions placed between the two sets of doors.

Accordingly, at the entrances of the new basilica itself are these verses:

> The nourishing house opens to those entering through a triple arch [Note: [Col. 0337] Note 167],  
> And the threefold door bears witness to pious faith.

14. Likewise, on the right and left, these epigrams are painted above crosses in red pigment:

> The lofty cross is encircled by a crown of flower-bearing wreaths,  
> And, stained with the Lord’s poured-out blood, it glows red.  
> The doves that sit above the heavenly sign  
> Proclaim to the simple [Note: [Col. 0337] Note 168.] that the kingdoms of God are open.

Again, on the same subject:

> Through this cross kill us to the world, and the world to us,  
> Giving life to the soul through the death of sin.  
> You too will make us, Christ, doves pleasing to you,  
> If your peace flourishes in pure hearts [Note: [Col. 0337D] With Sacchini, we have corrected this, against all the manuscripts; the sense requires it, and the two preceding verses in section 12 confirm it. Previously it read “a part.”].

15. Within the very screen—by which the intervening space that formerly separated the neighboring basilicas is continued—these verses are inscribed opposite the new basilica, above the central arch:

> When Jesus, our peace, dissolved the wall in the middle,  
> and, removing the division by the cross, made two into one,  
> so now, once the separation of the old roof has been destroyed,  
> we behold the roofs of the gates joined by a covenant.  
>   
> A shining vessel, flowing with pure water, bathes  
> the holy courts for the servants and washes the entrants’ hands  
> with its ministering stream. [Note: [Col. 0337] Note 169.]

The twofold people adore Christ in the hall of Felix,  
which Paul the priest governs with apostolic speech. [Note: [Col. 0337] Note 170.]

These epigrams, each marked by two little verses, are likewise above the other arches, on the right and left. [Col. 0338A] On one:

> A new light opens before astonished eyes, and, standing  
> on a single threshold, one sees both halls at once.

On the other:

> The twin halls have opened through six arches, [Note: [Col. 0337] Note 167.]  
> and, through their mutual thresholds, marvel at each other’s worship.

Likewise, on the same arches, at the front that opens toward the basilica of the lord Felix, these verses are placed above the central passage:

> You whom devoted faith urges the dense peoples  
> to celebrate as blessed Felix, with voices from every side,  
> pour the assembled crowds through the three broad entrances:  
> however numerous they may be, the courts will stand open and spacious,  
> joined to one another by open arches facing them,  
> which Paul the bishop dedicates to everlasting use.

On the others, these two:

> Having departed from the ancient sacred hall of Felix,  
> pass over into the new roofs of Felix.

[Col. 0338B] Likewise:

> One faith, which under a threefold name worships the One,  
> receives the like-minded through a threefold entrance.

16. In the two sacristies, which I said above were situated near the apse, these verses indicate the function of each. On the right of the apse:

> This is the place of the venerable storehouse, where the sacred  
> furnishings of the nourishing ministry are stored and brought forth.

[Note: [Col. 0337] Note 171.]

On the left of the same apse:

> If anyone possesses a holy desire to meditate on the Law,  
> here, seated, he will be able to devote himself to the sacred books. [Note: [Col. 0337] Note 172.]

### On the Basilica at Fundi

17. Let us now leave this basilica at Nola and cross over to the one at Fundi. Fundi is the name of the town, which was no less familiar to me while the estate remained in my possession than I found it commonly used there. Therefore, whether as a pledge, so to speak, of civic affection, or as a memorial of my former patrimony, I desired to give a basilica in the town itself, since it was in need of one, having only a small and ruinous building. For this reason I also thought that these verses should be added, which we prepared for the dedication of the basilica in that town. It is still under construction, but, by God’s favor, its dedication is near.

What chiefly persuaded me to do this was that my Victor took particular pleasure in the picture designated for the apse of this building, and wished to carry it to you, if perhaps you should choose to paint it—one of two—in your more recent basilica, in which he likewise indicated that an apse had been made. But whether I ought to say *in hac apside* or *in hac abside*, you may decide; I confess that I do not know, since I do not remember ever having read this form of the word.

This little basilica too will be consecrated by the sacred ashes of the blessed relics of apostles and martyrs, in the name of Christ, the Holy One of saints, the Martyr of martyrs, and the Lord of lords. For he himself testified that in turn he would be the Confessor of his confessors. Therefore, for the sake of the painting, the title has been doubled here. [Note: [Col. 0338D] We have emended this in accordance with the Viennese manuscript. The other editions, except …] [Col. 0339A]

### On the Painting

> The labor of the saints and their reward properly belong together:  
> the lofty cross, and the sublime crown, the reward of the cross.  
> God himself, the author both of the cross and of the crown,  
> stands amid the heavenly grove of flowering paradise.  
> Beneath the bloodstained cross Christ stands in a snow-white lamb,  
> the Lamb given as an innocent victim to an unjust death.  
>   
> [With a winged one?] whom the holy Spirit gently drenches as he gapes,  
> while the Father crowns him from a radiant cloud. [Note: [Col. 0339] Note 174.]  
> And because he stands like a lofty judge upon a high rock,  
> goats, a discordant breed among the twice-twin sheep,  
> surround the throne: the Shepherd turns away the goats on his left  
> and embraces the deserving lambs on his right.

### On the Relics

> Behold, beneath the blazing altars, a royal covering of purple  
> marble conceals the bones of the righteous.  
> Here grace displays apostolic powers  
> more mightily through its pledges in a little dust.  
> Here are Father Andrew, and Luke of great renown,  
> and the martyr Nazarius, illustrious through his blood; [Note: [Col. 0339] Note 175.]  
> and those whom God reveals to his Ambrose after long  
> ages: Protasius together with his companion Gervasius.  
> Here one little casket embraces the pious company together  
> and contains such great names within its narrow space.

18. In the meantime, my brother, I had fashioned these and other visible works of this kind on earth through earthly labor. But blessed is the Lord day by day, who alone does wonders [Note: [Col. 0339] Psalms 67:20; 71:18; 113:8.]. Just as he turns rock into a pool of water, so he changes earthly things into heavenly ones; and he deigns to make with us this exchange of his possessions, both here and there, so that what I had physically fashioned on earth might secretly be built through him in heaven, to be revealed to us when we shall see in appearance (or: “face”) [Note: [Col. 0339] 2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 Corinthians 13:12.] what we now perceive through faith.

Thus here we sow, and there we reap [Note: [Col. 0339D] Previously *metemus*, “we shall reap.” Our correction is supported by what follows.]; here we scatter, and there we gather; here we live, and there we dwell; here we gird ourselves, and there we serve as soldiers; here we fight, and there we conquer—or, if we conquer here, there we are crowned. Thus what we construct here with our hands, there we store up through faith.

And although these buildings of ours are earthly, if they are erected with spiritual desire and zeal, they are a blessed preparation for heavenly dwellings [Note: [Col. 0339] John 14:2.]. For while we build these in the Lord through the attainment of faith, we ourselves are built by the Lord through the progress of that same faith.

That evangelical centurion [Note: [Col. 0339] Matthew 8:5.] is also an example to us of the certain hope of an eternal reward, to be received especially on account of this work. In order to obtain his son’s healing, and to have the Lord Jesus himself as the herald of his faith, he achieved such particular merit because the Lord’s people—who at that time still existed only among the Jews—supported him by bearing witness to the synagogue that he had built [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 7:5.].

[Col. 0339D] 19. Why, then, do we wretched people now sit idle and yawning [Note: [Col. 0339] Matthew 20:6.], and stand empty-handed in the tumultuous marketplace of this age like laborers who have not been hired? Or, if we consider that the master of the household owes us his denarius because we have been hired to work in his vineyard, do we even propose to charge this to the Lord as though it were something owed, while presenting as a favor what will benefit him rather than us?

O wretched human beings! We believe that we are giving him something; we conduct business and are thought generous, although we are proved to be exceedingly greedy—and indeed more greedy than the most rapacious moneylenders of the earth, inasmuch as it is a greater bargain to buy heavenly things with earthly things, and blessed things with miserable and needy possessions, than to purchase earthly things with earthly and transitory things destined to perish, and to lend to the Lord rather than to a human being. [Note: [Col. 0339] See Note 70.]

The Law condemns anyone who lends his money at interest and accepts gifts against the innocent [Note: [Col. 0339] Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36; Deuteronomy 23:19; Psalm 14:5.]. Behold, the grace of the Gospel shows us how these same crimes may be transformed into innocence and holiness, and how a recompense of reward rather than punishment may follow, if only they are converted by the saving desire of faith toward the divine commandments. Lend your money at interest—but to Christ—and the interest will be saving interest [Note: [Col. 0339] Proverbs 19:17; Sirach 29:1.].

[Col. 0340B] 20. Likewise, in this age judges who are corrupted by gifts from the accused are condemned [Note: [Col. 0339] Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19.]. But whoever has been overtaken by some sin and, distrusting your innocence, brings the price of your salvation to our Judge, need not fear that you are committing against God’s justice the offense of corruption. Christ gladly accepts from you the price of your salvation, because he prefers mercy to … [Note: [Col. 0339] Hosea 6:6, according to the Septuagint; Matthew 9:13.]

But perhaps you ask where you will find him, and by what means you can corrupt one whom you do not see. “Rise,” he says, “you who sleep, and raise yourself from the dead, and you will touch Christ” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ephesians 5:14.]. That is: shake off the sleep of carnal inertia, raise your mind, weighed down by earthly thoughts, from dead concerns—that is, from carnal conduct—and lift and direct your soul toward the Lord, and you will touch Christ.

By doing his commandments, you will see him in every poor person; you will touch him in every guest, because he himself testifies that whatever is done in his name for one of his least ones is done for him [Note: [Col. 0339] Matthew 25:40.]. Behold, it is now clear to us how you may see the invisible and grasp the incomprehensible.

Therefore, let us now be poor here, so that there we may become rich [Note: [See] Epistle 40, section 7.]. Now let us weep, so that then we may rejoice. Now let us hunger, so that then we may be filled. “At all times,” he says, “you have the poor with you” [Note: [Col. 0339] Matthew 26:11.]. You see that we have no excuse ever to postpone benevolence, since, if our will is not lacking, the poor person is always at hand.

21. Let us therefore confidently lend now to the needy, and, in his poor, to Christ, so that we may be able to share in his abundance and glory among them. For this reason the Lord himself gives the warning: “Make friends for yourselves from unrighteous mammon.” [Col. 0340D] You see how the Almighty makes light from night and justice from iniquity? “So that,” he says, “when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 16:9.].

Because the human race is ordered by a kind of alternation between abundance and want—as the Gospel passage about the rich man in the underworld and the poor man above makes clear [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 16:19.]—we should understand the plan of the common Creator, by which he prepared the rich for the poor and the poor for the rich: so that the abundant substance of the rich might be nourishment for the needy, and the needy person might be material for the wealthy person’s justice.

Thus, as the Apostle said [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 Corinthians 8:14.], equality may come about; and, when their present want is recompensed in that age by eternal riches, their abundance may overflow into our want, if our abundance here has lent itself to their need.

Let us therefore sow carnal things for them, so that we may reap spiritual things from them. Let the hand labor now over earthly things, so that then the soul may be refreshed by heavenly things. Let present hope build the future reality. Let us make here dwellings that will shelter us there. Let the poor person be fed here, where he is in need while I am rich, so that he may feed me there, where he will be filled while I am in need.

See the spiritual exchange; and, if you can, deny that we are greedy when we sell earth and tribute so that we may purchase the kingdom’s exemption from tribute together with eternity.

[Col. 0341B] 22. We cast down fragile sand in order to lay the foundation of an eternal house, and with worthless cement we reach the stars [Note: [Col. 0341] Genesis 11:4.]. From such materials we do not vainly contrive to build that tower of confusion and pride which must be destroyed; rather, we are founded upon the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0341] Ephesians 2:20.], so that through it we may rise into the fullness of him who is the tower of strength against the enemy [Note: [Col. 0341] Psalm 60:4.].

He himself commands us to build this tower [Note: [Col. 0341] Luke 14:28.], after first calculating the expense, lest, exhausted by an interrupted construction, we should incur the stigma and deserved ridicule of reckless negligence, having begun rashly in vain. Our expense, however, is firm faith. Therefore, whoever believes according to the truth of God, having the Lord Jesus as his hope, resources, and strength, has his whole building, compactly joined together, grow [Note: [Col. 0341] Ephesians 2:21.] and rise upward into the fullness of God.

Thus, unless the Lord builds the house, we shall sweat in vain, building with labor [Note: [Col. 0341] Psalm 126:1.]. But lest, even after the building has been completed with the Lord’s cooperation, we should let our idle hands fall back in security, divine Scripture adds that, unless God himself guards the house once built, the watchfulness of those who guard it will keep watch in vain [Note: [Col. 0341] Ibid.].

23. Let us therefore pray to the Lord that, while we build for him outside the dwellings that are seen, he may build within us those that are unseen—namely, that house which, as the Teacher says (that is, Paul; see Epistle 23, section 24), is not made with hands [Note: [Col. 0341] 2 Corinthians 5:1.]. Having entered it at the last, we shall understand it, seeing face to face what we now see in a riddle and know only in part [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 Corinthians 13:12.].

But now, while we still dwell in the tabernacle of this body, living as though beneath the skins of that ancient tabernacle and in tents in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0341] Exodus 25:40 and 26:30.], let the word of God go before us through the arid land of this world—either in a pillar of cloud [Note: [Col. 0341] Exodus 23:20; 13:21 and 14:19.], to cast its shadow over our heads on the day of battle [Note: [Col. 0341] Psalm 139:8.], or in a pillar of fire, so that we may recognize his heavenly way upon earth [Note: [Col. 0341] Exodus 13:21; Psalm 66:3.].

Let us pray that through these tabernacles of the Church we may now enter as far as the house of God [Note: [Col. 0341] Psalm 41:5, according to the Roman Psalter.], where the Lord himself—the supreme stone, made for us by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0341] Psalm 117:23.], cut from the mountain and likewise enlarged into a mountain—stands as the stone that is marvelous in our eyes.

[Col. 0342A] May he himself be both the foundation and the summit of our building, because he himself is its beginning and its end. Upon that same rock—for Christ too is the rock—apart from which no one can found a stable house, let our hands not gather straw, hay, and stubble, as servants in Egypt did into a basket. Let us not, as they say, wash bricks for muddy buildings of sordid works, nor, bent beneath the burdens of servile labors, turn our backs away from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0341] Psalm 80:7.]. [Note: [Col. 0341D] We have restored this reading on the basis of the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and four printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition has *qui* (“who”).]

For just as he refreshes those who turn toward him with light, so he afflicts those who turn away with blindness.

24. Let us see, then, what we builders can construct upon the divine foundation from our fragile and earthly substance that is worthy of it [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 Corinthians 3:10; 1 Peter 2:5.], so that, made alive by the chief cornerstone himself, we may be fitted as stones into the structure of the heavenly temple.

Let us smelt the gold of our understanding and the silver of our speech in Christ, so that, purified by him in the furnace of this world [Note: [Col. 0341] Wisdom 3:6.], he, the examiner of souls pleasing to himself, may make us gold refined by fire and coin worthy of his image; and let us bring ourselves to him as precious stones fashioned from works of light.

Let us be neither dull through the hardness of wood in our hearts, nor dry through the hay-like barrenness of our works, nor unstable and weak in faith or love through the lightness of straw. Rather, let us pray to the Most High for that peace of our building [Note: [Col. 0341] Psalm 121:6.] by which our work of free choice may be prepared so as not to burn, and may rise secure through peaceful activity; the peace in which that wall was once made into a temple wall, so that no hammer, axe, or any iron vessel might be heard within it [Note: [Col. 0341] 2 Kings 6:7, according to the Septuagint.].

Nor, as later in the restoration of the same temple, should hostile Persian resentment and an enemy assault obstruct and interrupt the structure as it rises [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 Esdras 4:4.]. For we shall be completed as a house of prayer and peace if no concern of carnal thoughts cuts us down and no tumult of the world disturbs our quiet.
