The hammer for us is concern for food and concern for clothing; the axe and iron for us are the desire for temporal things, nocturnal fear of the dead, hostile envy, and the affairs of this world. Through concern for its evils or love of its goods the soul is entombed and the mind fettered; and the peace of good will, which is strengthened when the senses are composed in religious silence, together with the concentration of prayer, which is directed unhindered from a free and pure heart, is torn apart by the clamor of carnal cares—as though by a hammer resounding or an axe striking.

But because the one who is in us is greater than the one who is in this world [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 John 4:4.], the Lord is able to crush Satan beneath our feet [Note: [Col. 0341] Romans 16:20.], so that this prophecy may also be fulfilled for us: “The hammer of the whole earth has been shattered” [Note: [Col. 0341] Jeremiah 50:23.].

25. It is beneficial for us, moreover, that the Lord Jesus often revisit the temple of our heart once it has been built, coming with the scourge of his fear, so that he may cast out from us the money-changers’ tables and the sellers of oxen or doves [Note: [Col. 0341] Matthew 21:12; Mark 11:15.]. Let our spirit conduct no commerce of greed, and let no sluggishness in our thoughts stable oxen there, because “where there are no oxen, the stalls are clean” [Note: [Col. 0343] Proverbs 14:4, according to the Septuagint.].

Let us not be sellers either of our innocence or of divine grace, lest we make the house of prayer a den of thieves [Note: [Col. 0343] Matthew 21:13; Luke 19:46.]. For when every leaven of wickedness has been cleansed from our minds [Note: [Col. 0343] 1 Corinthians 5:7.], our Lord Jesus Christ will gladly walk within us; and Wisdom, the power of God, which heals all our diseases [Note: [Col. 0343] Psalm 102:3.], will stroll as it were in those five porticoes [Note: [Col. 0343] John 5:2.].

For in our soul also many lie sick and weak, as once in that portico beside the pool that formerly healed. [Note: [Col. 0343D] The Regius manuscript reads: *quae si audiat*, “which, if it hears.”] If the word of God approaches it, by its healing command it will drive away the leprosy of greed, the rust of envy, the blindness of intemperance, the madness of anger, and the paralysis of lust. Having restored us not only to the health of innocence but also to the strength of patience, it will immediately command us not merely to rise from the bed of weakness but also to take up the bed itself, so that, now strong, we may carry what carried us when we were weak [Note: [Col. 0343] John 5:8.].

This is certainly fulfilled also in the spiritual kind of our sickness and health: formerly, devoted to our flesh as to a bed, we lay bound in the chains of vices and in weakness of virtues; afterward, our inner self having been renewed through the word of God by the grace of Jesus Christ into a good and incorrupt mind, in health we take up that bed and carry it by the prevailing spirit, bearing that flesh itself wherever we wish.

In it we were weak, waiting for another’s help, always forestalled by the swiftness of those who occupied the pool; for there was no one to extend a hand or to save us. Until he himself came—greater than legates and angels, since he is the Lord of prophets and angels—and in mercy took upon himself all our weakness [Note: [Col. 0343] Isaiah 53:4.], cleansed it by assuming it, filled the hungry soul with good things, and commanded us to go into our house, that house which, as I said above, is not made with hands [Note: [Col. 0343] 2 Corinthians 5:1; Psalm 117:15, according to the Roman Psalter.].

In it the voice of joy and salvation will dwell, and Christ himself will be, for all his own, dwelling, kingdom, and king, as the Apostle testifies: “For we shall always be with the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0343] 1 Thessalonians 4:16.]. To him be honor, glory, and power forever.

## LETTER XXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0343D] It appears to have been written in the year 403.]

He writes to Alethius, who had requested some work from Paulinus, and says that he is not sufficiently capable of satisfying his desire. This Alethius later succeeded his brother Florentius in the bishopric of Cahors. (See Dissertation 3, section 2.)

To the blessed, deservedly venerable, and most beloved brother Alethius [Col. 0343D] (see Note 176, “Paulinus”).

1. Thanks be to God, who through the words of your letter manifested to me the fragrance of his grace in you [Note: [Col. 0343] 2 Corinthians 2:14.]. For through my dearest brother in God, my Victor, who serves God in this ministry so as to serve brotherly love, and who, though separated from us by long distances across the earth [Col. 0344A]—that is, separated and distant; see Epistle 29, section 9—offers himself as an untiring courier in his annual journeys and, through his most religious services, supplies spiritual affection in place of the bodily labor of those who visit one another: through this brother and fellow servant in the Lord, who is common to us and united with us—for he boasts that he is as acceptable to you through the grace implanted in him as he is to us—through him, I say, I received, holy and venerable brother, your letter, a gift as sweet as it was unexpected.

In it the good treasure of your heart became apparent to us [Note: [Col. 0343] Matthew 12:35.], so that I rightly rejoiced when I received the blessing of your service, having looked upon the face of your inner self through your most chaste expression and recognized how great a help from the Lord you provide for me.

2. But in the matters which you, a wealthy appraiser of my poverty, thought should be imposed upon me [Col. 0344B], you certainly displayed the holy confidence of the purest love. Yet, as I understand it, persuaded by the reputation of the Lord’s work, you were led to suppose that, in proportion to the work of the Lord by which he has deigned to inspire us with concern for our redemption, we also possess abundant resources of intellect and speech. 213 But a hope beguiled by empty opinions has deceived your good desire, grounded in great faith.

From where could I obtain as much water as your thirst requires? From where such a cup as you could worthily drink? From where such loaves as you request [Note: [Col. 0343] Luke 11:5.]?

But you yourself will be the author of your own injury if you continue to go hungry, for, desiring the Gospel’s food of light and life in the deep night of this age, you knock at the poor storehouse of a sleepy and impoverished friend. Thirsting for rivers of living water [Note: [Col. 0343] John 7:38.], you scratch at a withered vein and try to squeeze moisture from a pumice stone.

Either there is no spring within me because of the dryness of inspiration—or, as the Latin and Sacchini suggest, perhaps because of “folly”—or else there is a bitter spring of wickedness within. May your prayers and letters, offered to me more frequently, cause it to overflow and grow sweet [Note: [Col. 0343D] We have emended this from the Viennese manuscript and the Chifflet and Schott editions. The Regius manuscript and three printed editions have “that they may sweeten it by overflowing.” Rosweyde has “that they may sweeten it abundantly.”] through the wood of your faith and the sweetness of your speech [Note: [Col. 0343] Exodus 15:25.], so that, through the word of God which you, as a good minister, draw forth from your pious mouth, my heart may be struck as by the prophet’s rod [Note: [Col. 0344D] All manuscripts except the Vatican and Rosweyde have *corde*, “heart”; those two have *virga*, “rod.”] [Note: [Col. 0343] Exodus 17:6.].

(The rest is lacking.)

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Elsewhere, Letter 34. Perhaps written in 403 and sent with the preceding letter.]

## XXXIV. SERMON ON THE TREASURY

(See Note 177.)

He eloquently, learnedly, and piously commends benevolence toward the poor.

1. It is not without purpose, my dearest brothers, that a manger is provided for beasts, nor does it lie there merely to be looked at; for it is a kind of table, arranged by human reason even for irrational creatures, so that quadrupeds may receive food from it. But if those who have taken care to build mangers neglect to bring in fodder, the beasts will more readily waste away in the impoverished stall, and hunger will consume the animals that are not being fed.

Those, however, will suffer a loss proportionate to their negligence or greed, who have taken the trouble only to prepare the manger but have failed to provide for its being filled. For together with the dead animals they will lose the use of the manger, rightly bearing two serious losses because they spared the one necessary expense of supplying it.

We must therefore beware, beloved, following this example, lest we suffer damage to our soul and loss of salvation by neglecting the table placed by the Lord in the Church for the needy—a table at which we gaze with disdainful eyes or pass by with dry hands. May such a contagion be far from your souls, I beg you.

For the cancer of greed easily spreads into a heart fortified by no compassion, binds the captured soul with serpentine chains, and, if the hostile serpent finds it stripped of good works and overflowing with wealth—the material of captivity, that is, with unproductive riches—he keeps it bound.

Let us therefore not permit the Lord’s table to be left both empty for us and vacant for the needy, standing only for the sake of sight and not of use, lest the groans forced from the hungry by our negligence be turned back against us. For “whoever despises the poor provokes,” as it is written, “the one who made him” [Note: [Col. 0345] Proverbs 14:31 and 17:5.]—that is, the common Creator of all. Just as he rejoices in the nourishment of the needy, so he is saddened by their wasting away.

2. Let us therefore rouse ourselves from the sleep of inertia and, whether to shake off the torpor of negligence or to break the chains of greed, carefully examine all the words, commandments, promises, works, and counsels of our Savior and God. Let us consider with ourselves why this table has been set out, and by whose authority, in the courts of the house of the Lord, before the eyes of all his people; and, what must especially be considered, for whose benefit, by what grace, and toward what fruit it shines and stands open. [Note: [Col. 0345D] We have emended this from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the Gravina, Schott, and Chifflet editions. Two other printed editions have “to whom it belongs.” Rosweyde has “to whom it belongs.”]

Consult the very oracles of truth, and the prophet will answer you: “Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God” [Note: [Col. 0345] Proverbs 19:17.]. This, then, is the table of the heavenly moneychanger, building a treasury of life and conducting God’s lending in order to acquire the pearl [Note: [Col. 0345] Matthew 13:45.]. For whoever lends to the Lord’s poor [Note: [See] Note 70.] awaits from the Lord the repayment of an eternal reward.

The blessed Apostle Paul also teaches us, and testifies that, amid all his concerns for the Churches, he had no small care for the poor. For he says: “Only that we should remember the poor, which very thing I was eager to do” [Note: [Col. 0345] Galatians 2:10.]. Elsewhere he cries: “We brought nothing into this world, and indeed we cannot take anything away” [Note: [Col. 0345] 1 Timothy 6:7.]; and again: “What do you have that you did not receive?” [Note: [Col. 0345] 1 Corinthians 4:7.]

Therefore, beloved, we are not to be restricted as though the goods were our own, but are to lend from what has been entrusted to us. “A stewardship,” he says, “has been entrusted to us” [Note: [Col. 0345] 1 Corinthians 9:17.]: the eternal possession is the common interest of temporal money, not of private property.

If you recognize that what is yours on earth belongs to you only temporarily, you will be able to make it perpetual for yourself in heaven. If you remember in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0345] Matthew 25:14.] those who received the Lord’s talents and what the master of the household, on his return, repaid to each, you will know how much more useful it is to place money at the Lord’s table so that it may be multiplied than to preserve it through barren faith [Note: [Col. 0345D] We have retained the Vulgate reading until greater clarity emerges from the manuscripts. The Regius and Viennese manuscripts read: “which, through barren faith, they remember as hateful; therefore …” Chifflet’s correction reads: “which, through barren faith, you, miser, remember as hateful to lend, kept without any return for the creditor … to the great loss of the useless servant, solely for the increase of his punishments”; this correction is not satisfactory.]

3. Hurry, therefore, to deserve rather to hear that voice: “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matthew 25:21.], than that other one: “Wicked and lazy servant, out of your own mouth I judge you” [Note: [Col. 0345] Luke 19:21.], and the rest that are familiar; the useless servant being sent into outer darkness and his talent being given to the one who had grown rich through multiplying what had been entrusted to him. For “to everyone who has,” he says, “it will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matthew 25:29; Luke 19:26.].

Let us also remember that widow who, neglecting care for herself and thinking only of the future, emptied the whole substance of her livelihood, as the Judge himself testified: “Others,” he says, “gave from their surplus; but she, perhaps poorer than many of the poor, for whom two small coins were her entire wealth” [Note: [Col. 0345] Mark 12:43; Luke 21:3–4.], was richer in spirit than all the wealthy. Looking only to the riches of an eternal reward and greedy for the heavenly treasure, she renounced for herself all at once the whole of that substance which is taken from earth and returns to earth.

She sent what she had, so that she might possess what she had not seen. She sent corruptible things, so that she might acquire immortal things. That poor woman did not despise the order and arrangement established by God concerning the reception of what was to come. Therefore the one who established it himself did not forget her; and the Judge of the world himself anticipated his own judgment [Note: [Col. 0346D] We have restored this reading from the Viennese manuscript and the Chifflet edition, as required by the sense. Other editions have “preceded.”], proclaiming in the Gospel the one whom he will crown at the judgment.

4. Let us therefore lend to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0346D] The Regius manuscript and five printed editions have “from good things”; both readings have been accepted. The reading adopted here, from the Viennese manuscript and the Chifflet edition, is confirmed by what follows and by sections 6 and 7.] from the Lord’s gifts, for we possess nothing without his gift, and without his will we ourselves do not exist. And especially what should we regard as ours, since we do not belong to ourselves under a greater and particular obligation? We are not merely made by God; we have also been bought [Note: [Col. 0345] 1 Corinthians 6:20.].

Let us rejoice that we were bought at a great price—indeed, by the blood of the Lord himself. By that price we cease to be cheap and for sale, because freedom is more precious than servitude. For one who is free in this way is nevertheless a slave of sin and a captive of death.

Let us therefore return the Lord’s own gifts to the Lord. Let us give to him who receives in every poor person; let us give, I say, rejoicing, and receive from him with exultation. For he is pleased by such an act of apparent injury, that we should use good works to force our way into his kingdom and break open heaven’s gates.

Our Lord, who alone is good, as there is one God [Note: [Col. 0345] Matthew 19:17.], desires to receive not from a spirit of greed but from a spirit of generosity. For what does he not have, who has given everything? Or what does he not possess, who possesses those very people who possess? “For all the mighty men of riches are in his hands.” Yet in his immeasurable justice and goodness he wishes gifts to be made to him in return from his own gifts, so that, because he is good, he may provide you with the material for showing benevolence toward him; and, because he is just, he may make it your merit to receive worthily.

5. The treasures of his goodness therefore lie open, and the riches of his kindness are at hand, so that no one need wait to receive, but each may freely seize as much as he wishes. For the good Lord made us for this purpose: that we might be good for our own good. What external good could he need, who in his entirety is goodness and blessedness [Note: [Col. 0347] Psalm 15:2.]?

For this reason, beloved, insofar as it lies with him, he wants every human being to be saved [Note: [Col. 0347] 1 Timothy 2:4.], because he loves his own work in every person. And he is lavish with you from his riches, provided that you yourself are not envious and greedy toward yourself concerning those things that God made yours—not so that they might be a cause of death for you, but so that they might be the price of life.

O abundance of God’s goodness! He wishes to be repaid with interest from what he himself has bestowed; he desires to become the debtor of his own gifts, so that with great profit he may repay you your interest.

6. Hurry, then, brother, to bind such a generous debtor to yourself that he may call you his friend instead of his servant [Note: [Col. 0347] John 15:15]; and, having found you faithful in your earthly coins, may make you rich from his heavenly treasures. Do not tremble, do not delay, do not spare. Be forceful toward God; seize the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0347] Matthew 11:12]. He who forbids the touching of what belongs to another rejoices when his own possessions are seized; and he who condemns the rapacity of greed praises the theft of faith.

Your guests have long been standing at your doors, awaiting the proper time and the master of the feast. You delay your guests: hurry anxiously, lest they remain fasting too long; and lest their injury rouse the one who made them and who made them poor in order to benefit you [Note: [Col. 0347] Proverbs 14:31]. For the almighty Lord could have made everyone equally wealthy, so that no one would need another; but in the design of his infinite goodness the merciful and compassionate Lord arranged matters in this way, so that he might test your disposition through them. He made one miserable so that he might recognize the merciful person. He made one needy so that he might exercise the wealthy.

Your brother’s poverty is the material of your riches, if you understand the words, “He who has regard for the needy and poor” [Note: [Col. 0347] Psalm 40:2]. Do not keep solely for yourself what you have received, because for this reason God has bestowed upon you in this world a share belonging to that other person: so that whatever you offered from his gifts to those in need by your voluntary goodwill would become a debt owed to you, and so that in turn, on the eternal day, he might enrich you from that person’s share. For through them Christ now receives, and then he will repay on their behalf.

The rich man of the Gospel and Eleazarus—now no longer a beggar in Abraham’s bosom—teach us this. Eleazarus, who in that painful place received refreshment amid the burning rich man’s poverty [Note: [Col. 0347] Luke 16:24], teaches, I say, by this example that a reciprocal allotment has been made for the human race here and there: that there the poor will be repaid what here appears to have been denied them; and, conversely, that the rich who here were destitute toward the poor will gain nothing from the poor’s blessedness. Perpetual beggary together with an abundance of punishments will be rendered as a deserved vengeance for the wrong done to the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] The Regius manuscript reads *Eleazar*. So also in Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 10, verse 154. N. Heinsius asserts in his notes that *Eleazar* is read in the manuscript codices: an indeclinable name, used for *Lazarus*, concerning whom Luke writes in the Gospel, chapter 16, verses 19 and following. See what we said about this word in Letter 13 to Pammachius, section 17.]

7. Therefore, “walk,” as it is written, “as children of light in the light, while you have the light” [Note: [Col. 0347] John 12:35]; and act in this way, Christian, while the day for repentance and foresight is available, so that you may deserve to hear from the Lord: “Well done, good servant, because you have been faithful in a little, I will set you over much” [Note: [Col. 0347] Matthew 25:21; Luke 19:17].

See, then, and attend to this word, brother, and do not neglect the grace offered to you. Do not descend empty-handed into the house of Christ [Note: [Col. 0347] Exodus 23:15], which is the Church of the living God [Note: [Col. 0347] 1 Timothy 3:15]. If from your many possessions you give even a little, you have prepared for yourself a great increase in what remains. Very many are waiting for you, and depend upon your arrival, looking about to see when you will appear. The prayers and vows of all the needy and weak are directed toward you.

Take care lest you force such devout affections to change, and lest they turn their prayers into complaints; and lest the groans uttered against you, which the necessity of suffering people, when you show no mercy, wrings from their exhausted bodies, strike and provoke the Father of orphans, the judge of widows, and the compassionate God of the poor [Note: [Col. 0347] Psalm 67:6].

8. Beware of loving only yourself, if you love yourself, because such love is wickedness; and “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul,” as it is written. But “the fullness of the law is love of neighbor” [Note: [Col. 0347] Psalm 10:6; Romans 13:10; Luke 10:36], since every human being is kin to every other by nature.

Therefore, care for yourself and for the poor equally, so that you may imitate the imitator of Christ, caring for what is useful not for yourself but for others, so that God may care for you more earnestly [Note: [Col. 0347] 1 Corinthians 10:33]. Consider, then, by how great a crime—pride or greed— you separate yourself from the one whom God has joined to you by his work.

Refresh the hungry soul, and you will not fear, on the evil day, the anger that is to come. For he says: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” [Note: [Col. 0347] Tobit 4:11; Psalm 40:2].

Work, then, and cultivate this region of your land, brother, so that it may produce for you a fertile harvest, full of the fatness of grain, yielding you, with great interest, a hundredfold fruit from the multiplied seed [Note: [Col. 0347] Matthew 13:8]. In seeking and pursuing this sort of possession or investment, greed is holy and salutary. For such desire, which earns the kingdom of heaven and longs for an everlasting good, is the root of blessings.

Desire, therefore, such riches, as was said above, and possess an inheritance of this kind, which will pay you a hundredfold return [Note: [Col. 0348D] The Viennese manuscript and Chifflé’s edition read *penset* (“pay”); the Regius manuscript, together with four printed editions, reads *creditos pensitet* (“repeatedly pay what has been entrusted”).], so that you may also increase your heirs with you in everlasting goods.

For this possession is truly great and precious [Col. 0348], since it does not burden its possessor with worldly accumulation but enriches him with eternal income. It flows with milk and honey, and it offers its farmers sweet nectar of liquids poured forth through radiant channels—not pressed from beehives or cattle [Col. 0349A].

9. But, beloved, provide not only that you may seek eternal goods, but also that you may deserve to avoid countless evils, through present vigilance and diligent practice of justice. For we need great help and protection, and we require the advocacy of many unceasing prayers.

Our adversary does not rest; the ever-watchful enemy lies in wait for our destruction and blocks all our paths [Note: [Col. 0349] 1 Peter 5:8]. He carefully explores everyone’s exits and entrances; he attaches himself as an inseparable companion to each person’s footsteps [Note: [Col. 0349D] The Viennese manuscript and Chifflé’s edition read *saepe se gressibus* (“often [attaches] himself to the steps”), but the reading retained here is better and more correct. See what precedes and follows.]; he sets a hedge before our departures and inserts it among our feet, so that, unwary even on level ground, you stumble upon a hidden roughness.

Thus it is written: “There are ways that seem level to human beings, but their ends lead to hell” [Note: [Col. 0349] Proverbs 14:12 and 16:25]. If, secure on level ground and unwary on slippery ground, you fall, he immediately rushes upon you and presses down the fallen person; nor does he refrain from leaving you until he has broken and devoured you.

Beware, then, on every side; whenever you place your foot, look all around. For the devil threatens from every direction, like a lion prepared for prey [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 16:12]. Do not even trust your own earth, with your foot poised—or rather, protected—to tread upon it [see Note 178]. For, acknowledging the first father’s sin in all human flesh, it carries out the Creator’s sentence, fertile in thorns and thistles [Note: [Col. 0349] Genesis 3:18], and in serpents and wild beasts.

Moreover, many crosses, countless dangers, the corruption of diseases, the fires of fevers, and the weapons of pains assail our souls in this world; the torches of desires are kindled [Note: [Col. 0349D] The Regius manuscript and Chifflé’s edition read *accedunt* (“are added”), a reading which seems erroneous to us.]; traps lie hidden everywhere, drawn swords bristle on every side; life is spent amid ambushes and battles, and we walk over fires hidden beneath treacherous ashes.

10. Therefore, before you are driven by chance or by your own deserts into the stain of any of such great sufferings, hurry to be received and loved by the physician, so that in the time of need you may have a remedy of salvation prepared [Note: [Col. 0349] Ecclesiasticus 38:1].

It is one thing when you alone pray for yourself, and another when a multitude trembles before God on your behalf. You are silent, and, while you are silent, they cry out for you [Note: [Col. 0349D] These two words are absent from the Viennese manuscript and Chifflé’s edition.]. They see you, and they smile. They find you, and they greet you. Forgetful of their own poverty and weakness, their bodies are strengthened by your health, and their souls are invigorated by your presence.

You are, for them, a fertile field; you are a fruitful estate [Col. 0349]—and they, in turn, are for you a wealthy and precious possession. They place you before their own children, and each one prays for your salvation before his own, or together with, or even before, his own salvation [Col. 0350A]. Not neglecting themselves, but transferring their love, each person loves himself in you and prays for your life as for his own, because your fruit is his life and your riches are his wealth [Note: [Col. 0349D] Thus the four printed editions together with the Vatican manuscript. This is the best reading. But in what sense do the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflé’s edition read, “your riches are his wealth, rich in poverty”? The Regius manuscript reads *pauvertatis* (“of poverty”).]—and your poverty is his wealth.

In every church they pray for you; in every street they rejoice for you. In every place, at the remembrance of your name, they rise up blessing the Lord, and they kiss you, though absent, in their hands. They always see you, and never fail to see you, because they embrace you in their minds as we behold those who are absent.

For you are inscribed and stamped upon their hearts by your great kindness toward them. They do not fear hunger, secure in the food you provide; nor do they fear winter, because you forestall and exclude winter by preparing clothing. Blessed is the person whom the returning Lord will find doing this [Note: [Col. 0349] Matthew 24:46].

**LETTER XXXV**  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] Formerly Letter 19; the letter formerly numbered 35 is now 43. Written in the year 403.]

Paulinus commends to Delphinus’s prayers the soul of his deceased brother and himself.

To Delphinus, always most blessed, venerable, and greatly desired by us [Note: [Col. 0350D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. The printed editions have *desideratissimo* (“most longed-for”).], Father, PAULINUS.

We received the brief letter of your holy affection, rich in feeling, with great affection and with a heart wholly as full as our longing. But because there is a time for everything [Note: [Col. 0349] Ecclesiastes 3:1, according to the Septuagint], now, in a time of grief, it has seemed appropriate that there should also be a time for shortening our discourse.

We confess that we are deeply saddened—not so much by the bodily death of our brother as by his spiritual negligence. Remembering more the concerns that had to be left here than the remedies that had to be provided there, he put off what should have been put first and placed first what should have been put off [Note: [Col. 0349] 2 Corinthians 12:14]. He ought to have cared for those more important things on his own behalf, and not neglected these temporal matters for the sake of his children.

Therefore, we ask you, in your fatherly affection and sympathy for our grief, to remember that he was once begotten by God’s grace as your spiritual son, and that for this reason this matter belongs especially to your care, lest we, whose fatherly devotion used to glory in us as sons, disgrace you by squandering the substance of our inherited portion [Note: [Col. 0349] Luke 15:13].

Rather, may it be granted you through your prayers that, distilling for his soul even from the smallest finger of your holiness [Note: [Col. 0350D] The Regius manuscript reads *destillans* (“distilling”). Thus all the manuscripts in Letter 23 to Severus, section 33, at the end: “as dews distill in this night of the age”; and section 36: “to distill a drop of heavenly wisdom.” Both readings have been accepted. See Letter 19, section 3.], you may sprinkle it with a drop of refreshment [Note: [Col. 0349] Luke 16:24]. And may divine mercy, with your intervention, come to our aid while there is still time, as we return to you and cry out: “Father, we have sinned against heaven and before you; we are no longer worthy to be called your sons” [Note: [Col. 0349] Luke 15:18].

May we not be overwhelmed by shame at returning because we have squandered the substance of the eternal Father, which our sins daily dissipate; and may we not, while dwelling in a far country [Note: [Col. 0350D] We have corrected the text from the Viennese manuscript, which reads *commorati* (“having dwelt”). Chifflé’s edition reads *commorantes* (“dwelling”). Previously it read *commorantium* (“of those dwelling”).], be led—God forbid—to the custody and food of swine, which are unworthy of us [Col. 0351A].

**LETTER XXXVI**  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] Formerly Letter 20; the letter formerly numbered 36 is now 43. Written in 403 and sent together with the preceding letter.]

He commends to the prayers of Amandus, presbyter of Bordeaux, the soul of his brother and himself. That Amandus later succeeded Saint Delphinus in the bishopric of Bordeaux, and he too is numbered among the saints in the Roman Martyrology on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.

To the holy, deservedly venerable, and most beloved AMANDUS, PAULINUS.

1. We tasted the sweetest flavor of your mouth in the brief discourse of your holiness. For just as a drop of honey has the same taste as the whole honeycomb, so even in a single word the trickle of your tongue conveys the entire flavor of your holy soul. Whatever is brought forth from a good treasury is good and precious [Note: [Col. 0351] Matthew 12:35; Luke 6:45].

A pearl is not worthless because it is small; rather, it is more precious for this reason, because even in its small size it possesses great value, so that, as the authority of the Gospel also testifies [Note: [Col. 0351] Matthew 13:46; Matthew 13:32], it is sought even at the cost of estates being squandered. And the mustard seed, which appears smallest among seeds, nevertheless becomes the greatest among garden plants.

Since the word of this seed has been sown in you and flourishes in your heart, from which you possess a heart burning on the way of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0351] Luke 24:32], your brief discourse therefore contains and supplies us with both the sweetness and the vigor of the heavenly word, so that we too may be seasoned with the salt of your wisdom [Note: [Col. 0351] Colossians 4:6].

2. Therefore, in this letter we too shall imitate the frugality of your speech, even if we are unable to imitate the fullness of your meaning [Note: [Col. 0351D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *valemus* (“we are able”).]. We shall respond only to this, which, especially as we wrote these words, was a principal concern for us: the recent pain of our brother’s separation.

Although we know that he has been taken from this world for a time and that we must soon follow him there, we mourn his death for the more genuine reason that, from what he himself did—or rather, from what was arranged at the end of his life [Note: [Col. 0351D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscript codices. The printed editions read *ad* (“according to”).]—we perceived that his actions were more in keeping with our sins than with our prayers. He preferred to pass to the Lord as a debtor rather than as one released from debt.

For this reason we earnestly ask you—since you deign to be our brother in the Lord—to help your brothers in unity [Note: [Col. 0351] Proverbs 18:19] and thereby increase the reward of your faithful merits: sympathize with our weakness on his behalf and join us in the labor of prayer, so that the merciful and compassionate God, who does all things in heaven and on earth and in the sea and in the abysses [Note: [Col. 0351] Psalm 134:6], may refresh his soul with drops of his mercy through your prayers.

For just as the fire kindled by him burns down to the depths of hell [Note: [Col. 0351] Deuteronomy 32:22], so without doubt the dew of his forgiveness will also penetrate the underworld, so that, in the dewy light of his compassion, we who burn amid fiery darkness may be refreshed [Note: [Col. 0351D] Rosweyde’s edition reads “may be refreshed.”].

3. Pray also for us, that we may not die in our sins. May the Lord make known to us our end, so that we may know what is lacking in us [Note: [Col. 0351] Psalm 38:5] and hasten to complete what remains; so that we may not be turned back in the midst of empty days [Note: [Col. 0351] Psalm 101:25], weaving a spider’s web through empty works [Note: [Col. 0351] Job 8:14], but may our days be found full in us.

May we be “children of a hundred years dying” [Note: [Col. 0351] Psalm 89:9 and 72:10; Isaiah 65:20]—that is, children in malice and mature in understanding [Note: [Col. 0351] 1 Corinthians 14:20]. May it happen that, when dead, we leave the living an example of good conduct and a saving repentance; and may our mourning not exceed seven days [Note: [Col. 0351] Ecclesiasticus 22:13], if we agree on the way of this life with our adversary [Note: [Col. 0351] Matthew 5:25]—that is, with the Spirit and word of God, which oppose us when we sin.

For the Spirit also convicts the world concerning sin [Note: [Col. 0351] John 16:8 and 15:22]. And the word of God, as the Lord bears witness in the Gospel, if we do not obey it, will be our accuser and will hand us over to the Judge, the Word [Note: [Col. 0351] Matthew 5:25], who will demand an accounting of his talent down to the last farthing. Unless, through the practice of piety, which is useful for everything [Note: [Col. 0351] 1 Timothy 4:8], he receives double interest on his money [Note: [Col. 0351] Matthew 24:51 and 25:27], he will place the portion belonging to idle faith with unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0351] Luke 19:23], because the person who bears dead faith without works under the empty name of Christian is close to an unbeliever [Note: [Col. 0351] James 2:17].

This is the fool whose mourning lasts for all time [Note: [Col. 0351] Ecclesiasticus 22:13], because, lacking the fear of the Lord, he has not grasped the head of wisdom. He has become the tail [Note: [Col. 0351] Deuteronomy 28:44], because he does not dwell in the midst of the house; and, loving iniquity, he hates his own soul [Note: [Col. 0351] Psalm 101:7 and 10:6]. Handed over to the minister of the prison of hell, he is cast into the outer darkness [Note: [Col. 0351] Matthew 22:13], because he has lived according to the outward person [Col. 0352C].

Therefore, he must be mourned without end, because he will be condemned to eternal fire and will die without end [Col. 0352].

4. Let us therefore have peace with the Lord [Note: [Col. 0351] Romans 5:1]—not the peace of this world [Note: [Col. 0351] John 14:27], which is friendly to sins and at odds with God, but the peace of Christ, which agrees with God and conforms us to Christ, if our soul clings to the word of God [Note: [Col. 0351] 1 Corinthians 6:17].

Thus, through the intervention of the Mediator, who is our peace, we may become one with God, because “he made both one” [Note: [Col. 0351] Ephesians 2:14], joining in himself the discordant natures of God and humanity; and in us he makes two into one, namely, the flesh consenting to the spiritual soul.

Then the fire will remain in our midst, if the agreement of these two within us—or of those three spirits (see Note 179)—invites him to establish [Note: [Col. 0351D] We have corrected the text from the Viennese manuscript. Rosweyde’s edition reads, “or the harmony of these two in us, or of the three spirits who breathe together.” Sacchini reads, “with the spirit of the three.” See Note 176.] in our heart a dwelling pleasing to himself, with the Father and the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0351] John 14:23]. And in turn may he lead us where he is, saying: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” [Note: [Col. 0351] Matthew 25:21].

[Note: [Col. 0352D] The Grinian and Rosweyde editions add at the end: “I wish you well.” Since these words are absent from the manuscripts and from three printed editions, we have removed them.]

**LETTER XXXVII**  
[Note: [Col. 0353D] Formerly Letter 27; the letter formerly numbered 57 is now 13. Written toward the end of 404.]

[Col. 0353A]

He grieves that, because of his sins, Victricius, when he came to Rome, did not reach him. He praises him for his apostolic ministry of evangelizing and for enduring the harassment of his opponents. Finally, he exhorts him to steadfastness in sound doctrine and in every virtue.

To VICTRICIUS [Note: [Col. 0353D] The Viennese manuscript reads: “To the holy, deservedly venerable, and most beloved brother Victricius, Paulinus.”], his brother in unity, PAULINUS.

1. Just as cold water is to the thirsty and good news from a distant land [Note: [Col. 0353] Proverbs 25:25], so the discourse of your holiness was refreshment and restoration to us. We received it by letter from the hand of our most beloved bearer, our son Candidianus: we rejoiced in his grace, because, for the sake of the words of holy lips, he compelled the sluggish beast of his frail flesh, relying not on strength but on faith, to travel the difficult roads [Col. 0353B] [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 16:4].

Without doubt, strengthened through your prayers—as though with the wings of a dove or the feet of a deer [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 54:7 and 17:34]—to fulfill the ministry of charity, he received strength; and then, in his small body becoming like a giant, he rejoiced to run the course [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 18:6]. He filled our soul with the blessing of sweetness, bringing us letters more desirable than gold and the most precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 18:11].

Through them, the holy and sweet breath of your blessedness changed our mind, bitter from sins, into the sweetness of spiritual joy, like that bitter water (*merram*) [Note: [Col. 0353D] All the codices read *myrrham*. We have corrected it to *merram* (“bitter water”) from the German manuscript in the poem *On the Return of Nicetas*, line 32. The same form appears in manuscript codices of Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 56. See Note 244.] in the hand of Moses [Note: [Col. 0353D] The Viennese manuscript reads, “that hand of Moses.”] through the wood of the mystery [Note: [Col. 0353] Exodus 15:25], which became sweetness.

For we had drawn bitterness from our sadness that you had not come to us from Rome by the short journey we expected, although you had reached Rome after crossing such vast stretches of land. I confess that I was not only saddened but also ashamed by the loss of this good. Never had my sins been revealed more clearly to me, I will not say to others, than by the fact that they had deprived me of the light of your face when you were so near.

Could the hand of God, which had led you so far, have been unable to bring you near? But our sins, set like a great wall against our desires, separated us from you [Note: [Col. 0353] Isaiah 6:5, from the Septuagint version]. Woe to me, miserable sinner with unclean lips, who dare to say that you were near us, or that we were near you, when, even if you had come all the way to us, we would nevertheless have been equally far from your holiness. For such a great distance and remoteness of virtues and merits could not have been made equal or joined merely by place.

2. Nevertheless, the work of this piety would have increased the fruits of your holiness [Note: [Col. 0353D] The Viennese manuscript reads *accederet* (“would approach”); perhaps the correct reading is *accessisset* (“would have increased”).], and your reward in heaven would have grown from so devout a labor, if, by visiting our weakness in person and with your own hand, you had fulfilled that saving word of the Lord: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” [Note: [Col. 0353] Matthew 9:12].

For I do not want you, blessed man of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0353D] The Vatican manuscript reads “blessed man in the Lord.” Both expressions are customary with Paulinus and the holy writers.], to be so confident about us that you think all the diseases of our soul have already been healed—the diseases in which we sinned and continue to sin against the Lord.

Although the supreme maker of ointments, who prepares various sweet fragrances of saving ointments and virtues as remedies for our salvation, has compounded the medicine of our life not only from the outpouring of his Spirit but also from the assumption of our body, becoming, as it is written, sin for us through the likeness of sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0353] 2 Corinthians 5:21] in the reality of our flesh, so that he might condemn sin from sin [Note: [Col. 0353] Romans 8:3]—that is, so that he, free from sin, might first condemn the root of our sin from the material that had previously been sinful, erasing through the blood of his Passion the written decree of death that stood against us [Note: [Col. 0353] Colossians 2:14]—and he destroyed in himself the hostility by which sins had separated us from God [Note: [Col. 0353] Ephesians 2:16], triumphing over the hostile powers in his flesh [Note: [Col. 0354D] The Viennese manuscript reads: “he destroyed … and triumphed …”], nevertheless he gave us an example of living and conquering within ourselves the spiritual and invisible enemies in the spiritual and invisible battle waged between the law of the mind and the law of the flesh, which seeks to take us captive under the law of sin [Note: [Col. 0353] Romans 7:23].

3. But pray to God, and implore him to take up arms and shield, rise to our aid, and say to our soul: “I am your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 34:2–3], lest our way become darkness and slippery ground, lest the shadow of death cover us, and lest the enemy say: “I have prevailed against them” [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 12:5].

Stretch out, then, on our behalf, the bow of prayer, so that we may not turn into a twisted bow [Note: [Col. 0354D] The Vatican and Regius manuscripts read “with you aiming.”]. May God arise within us, so that our enemies may be scattered [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 77:57 and 67:2]; for, because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 11:6], whose companions we are, the Lord has risen to turn our evils back upon our enemies [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 53:7] and to save sinners, of whom we are the chief [Note: [Col. 0353] 1 Timothy 1:15], as the least of Christ’s servants, who cannot even do what we owe [Note: [Col. 0353] Luke 17:10].

Yet we ought also, from our devotion, to add some voluntary gift beyond what the law requires, as the Master himself did—he whose imitator you are. Though he had the right to live from the Gospel, he nevertheless did not wish to use his right; and, foregoing what was permitted [Note: [Col. 0354D] “Foregoing what is permitted,” that is, not using it. The same sense occurs shortly afterward in “the foregoing of permitted things,” and in Letter 49 to Macarius, section 14, *non abutendum*. Likewise in Letter 12 to Amandus, section 7: “There is a holy pride that is proud of this world … and does without all its great, sweet, and beautiful things.”], he found an opportunity to increase his reward with Christ, so that he might provide the Gospel without expense [Note: [Col. 0353] 1 Corinthians 9:18 and 4:12; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8].

4. Your holiness, however, possesses the glorious wealth of Christian poverty not only through foregoing permitted things and abstaining from visible advantages [Col. 0355A], but, as I have learned, also through the multitude of your opponents and the endurance of trials. For false witnesses rose up against you, and iniquity lied to itself [Note: [Col. 0355] Psalm 26:12].

But no knot in the reed or blemish in the light could be found. Your lamp was not hidden under a bushel; it stands out and shines brightly upon the holy lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house [Note: [Col. 0355] Matthew 5:15; Mark 4:21; Luke 11:33], and serve as fuel for lighting many lamps for the Lord.

Therefore your lampstand remained unshaken and firm, though human hands were pushing it so that it might fall. You did not deserve that it should be shaken into ruin by the hand of the one who holds the seven stars and walks among the seven golden lampstands, holding in his mouth a two-edged sword [Note: [Col. 0355] Revelation 2:1 and 1:16]. With this sword he armed the right hand of your mind, so that you might victoriously extinguish the enemy’s fiery darts with the blazing torch of both Testaments [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Regius manuscript reads *facie* (“face”); the Viennese, *acie* (“edge”).] [Col. 0355B] [Note: [Col. 0355] Ephesians 6:16].

Let a thousand fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand [Note: [Col. 0355] Psalm 90:7], but let them not approach you. The truth of God will cover you with an impenetrable shield, so that the bows of those who are said to have sharpened the swords of their tongues against you may be weakened.

Their blows have been weakened like the arrows of children [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Vatican manuscript reads *jactus* (“throws” or “shots”).] [Note: [Col. 0355] Psalm 63:4 and 9]; nor could they find a place to wound the body enclosed by the powerful weapons of God.

For the Lord is your protection [Note: [Col. 0355] Psalm 26:2; 2 Timothy 1:11], and the Lord is the illumination of your heart. He instructed you in the spirit of truth, so that in Paul’s doctrine you might be a teacher of the nations, proclaiming with faith and truth—not in the inflation of knowledge or in loftiness of speech [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Viennese manuscript and Schott’s edition read “proclaiming.”]—the mystery of Christ, judging that among human beings you knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified [Note: [Col. 0355] 1 Corinthians 2:1].

5. Since, then, your faith and confession testify—as we believe and trust—that the coeternal Trinity is one in divinity and substance, in work and kingdom; and since you confess the Father as God, the Son as God, and the Holy Spirit as God, as he is who is, who was, and who is to come [Note: [Col. 0355] Revelation 1:4], who sent you, as he sent Moses and the apostles [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Viennese manuscript reads “the Apostle.”], to evangelize the nations with the good things of the Lord;

since you teach these things just as you yourself have been taught by God, joining the unity of the Trinity without confusion and distinguishing the Trinity of that unity without separation [Note: [Col. 0355] Exodus 5–10; Matthew 28:19; Acts 1:8], so that no person is confused with another and the one God shines forth in every person of the three;

and since the Son is as great as the Father and as great as the Holy Spirit, while each always remains distinct by the particularity of his own name and preserves an undivided harmony in equality of power and glory—

6. We are certain that you also proclaim the Son of God in such a way that you are not ashamed to confess him as the Son of Man: truly human in our nature, just as truly God in his own.

But he was the Son of God before the ages, because he is himself the Word of God, God who was in the beginning with God, equally God [Note: [Col. 0355D] Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and five printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads “almighty.” Thus Paulinus says in Letter 21 to Amandus, section 3: “the Son co-almighty with and co-creator with the Father.”], co-almighty and co-worker with the Father. For through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made [Note: [Col. 0355] John 1:3 and 14].

And this Word, through the mystery of immeasurable compassion, became flesh and dwelt among us. He assumed not merely the flesh of our body, but the whole human being, by assuming both our body and our soul; and a rational soul, which, according to God’s natural workmanship, possesses mind implanted within it.

Otherwise we shall fall into the darkness of Apollinaris, if we say that the human being assumed by God possessed a soul empty of the human mind, like that of cattle and beasts [Note: [Col. 0356D] Thus the Vatican and Viennese manuscripts. Other codices read “we have erred.”]. The Son of God necessarily assumed the human being whom he took upon himself in the truth by which he is truth and by which he created humanity—he assumed the whole human being, so that he might renew his work with complete salvation.

Our salvation is not complete unless it is whole. For the Son of God would have assumed not a human being but some other animal of an irrational creature, if the soul of the human being assumed had not possessed its own human mind. And, contrary to the nature of the human race, the firstborn of all creation, that human being assumed into the form of perfect humanity, would have needed his own mind to such an extent that he would be said to have possessed a mind not from the human spirit but from the divine.

That is what is said by the mouths of those in whose hearts this poison is conceived, so that even Truth would have lied. But near you and within you is the word of truth and the truth of God.

Nor do you lack the Holy Spirit, since you confess, believe, and proclaim that the Lord Jesus, the Son of God, remains God in the glory of God the Father and at the right hand of his power, King of kings, and that, through the resurrection of the dead, he is present as judge of the living and the dead.

7. Remember us, and glory according to the Apostle, because this brief trial has produced for you an eternal weight of glory [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 Corinthians 4:17] and has laid up for you the crown of righteousness, which you will receive from the hand of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 Timothy 4:8].

The battle has been permitted to arise as material for your victory, so that, in accordance with your blessed teacher Paul, you may also glory in your sufferings [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 Corinthians 12:9]; and, opening your mouth wide against your enemies, say how you have labored in patience, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as a deceiver and yet truthful; as unknown and yet recognized; as chastised and not killed; as sorrowful and always rejoicing; as needy and yet enriching many [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 Corinthians 6:6].

For this very trial of your holiness has benefited many for the advancement of the Gospel [Col. 0356D] [Note: [Col. 0355] Philippians 1:12], because no one has been put to shame through you, while the grace of Christ and the truth of your faith shine forth—not only in the soundness of your teaching but also in the power of the conduct that belongs in heaven [Note: [Col. 0355] Philippians 3:20].

“For the kingdom of God,” he says, “is not in speech but in power” [Note: [Col. 0355] 1 Corinthians 4:20]. What, then, is in question, when in you that which excels in word also excels in deed? [Note: [Col. 0356D] The Viennese manuscript reads *queritur* (“is sought” or “is asked”).] Who could doubt that the faith of truth dwells in the spirit of one whose life displays the power of faith? [Col. 0357A]

**LETTER XXXVIII**  
[Note: [Col. 0357D] Formerly Letter 29; the letter formerly numbered 38 is now 16. Perhaps written in 404.]

227. He commends Aper’s distinguished transition from the forum and tribunal to Christ; he advises him not to be surprised, but rather to rejoice that for this reason he is despised and hated by the world, since from the beginning Christ has suffered such things in his own people. He concludes that, with whatever zeal one has served human affairs, one must serve divine things. Aper subsequently advanced in every virtue and became a presbyter; he earned a place among the saints on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

To the holy, deservedly venerable, and dearly beloved brother Aper, Paulinus.

1. I rejoiced in what you wrote to me [Note: [Col. 0357] Psalm 121:1], and, in accordance with your faith, which you conceived in your heart and attested with your mouth, if the Lord’s grace makes me a participant in so great a spirit, I hope that “we shall go into the house of the Lord.” And, contemplating together in the face of truth the things we have received in common hope and faith [Note: [Col. 0357D] Thus we have emended from the Viennese manuscript. Others read, “we command.”], we shall sing a hymn to our God with harmonious exultation, saying to the Lord: “We believed that we were ashes and earth” [Note: [Col. 0357] Genesis 3:19; Sirach 10:9], if at this time our feet are so firmly established in the courts of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0357] Psalm 121:2] that in deed and action we cease to be earth and ashes [Note: [Col. 0357] Genesis 18:27]. Thus, in a spirit of humility, let us remember and acknowledge before the Lord that we are earth, so that through him we may not deserve to be what, through the condemnation of sin, we are, but may instead be reconciled by grace.

Blessed are you, brother, and it shall be well with you [Note: [Col. 0357] Psalm 127:2], because you have learned—not through flesh and blood, but through the revelation of the Spirit of the heavenly Father [Note: [Col. 0357] Matthew 16:17]—what you have confirmed, at the most holy conclusion of your letter to me, that you hold with unshaken faith and profess with a free voice: Jesus Christ crucified, the Son of God, God, before whom every knee of those on earth, in heaven, and under the earth is bent [Note: [Col. 0357] Philippians 2:10] [Note: [Col. 0357D] So the Viennese and Regius manuscripts. Other codices read “is bent”; both readings are accepted.]; and whom every tongue confesses to be at the right hand of the power and in the glory of God the Father.

You embrace this Lord and our God, because “no other shall be reckoned beside him” [Note: [Col. 0357] Baruch 3:36, according to the Septuagint], with the whole mystery of hidden devotion. You believe—and, as you believe, proclaim—that he is the Lord and God, the Son of God before the ages, made from the seed of David [Note: [Col. 0357] Romans 1:3] in this age, and now, through the resurrection of the dead, living forever in himself as the hope of human eternity. And yet you call yourself unformed and a child before God? Indeed, I believe that in one respect you have become a little child—but in malice; whereas in understanding you are perfect, as I learn from your profession of faith [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Corinthians 14:20]. For the knowledge of the truth that you have grasped in a brief statement is the fullness of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0357] 2 Corinthians 13:3].

And therefore the very teacher of the nations, the chosen vessel and vessel of God, who professes that Christ speaks in him and that he possesses the Spirit of God [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Corinthians 7:40], does not glory in lofty speech [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Corinthians 2:1] or in knowledge of the law. Rather, he declares that he has rejected and counted as refuse all the glory by which the wisdom of Jews and philosophers is puffed up [Note: [Col. 0357] Philippians 3:8], so that he may gain Christ, and, by forfeiting that knowledge, obtain the gain of this apparent ignorance, saying: “I know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Corinthians 2:2].

Since in him the entire fullness and perfection of wisdom and knowledge is contained [Note: [Col. 0357] Colossians 2:3] [Note: [Col. 0358D] We have added the particle “so that” from the Viennese manuscript], he mocks this world and, looking down with a loftier spirit upon its letters and all its wisdom as vanity, says: “Where is the scribe? Where is the wise man? Where is the investigator of this age? Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish?” [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Corinthians 1:20] [Note: [Col. 0358D] We have retained the reading of the Vulgate, supported by the authority of the manuscripts: “despising the wisdom of the world as vanity with a loftier spirit.” The Schott edition reads “the vanity of the wisdom of the world”; the Latin edition, “the vanity of wisdom.”]

He also shows the cause of this error: the wisdom of this age deserved to be struck down in such a way that it became foolishness before God, because, through the arrogance of wisdom as though it were their own—although no one possesses anything unless he has received it—God’s wisdom seemed foolish to them [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Corinthians 4:7]. Thus, rightly according to God’s justice, in an exchange of foolishness and wisdom, those who seem wise to themselves not through God’s gift but through some supposed good of their own are condemned as fools.

2. For this reason I rejoice all the more in your single-mindedness: you rejected that wisdom which God had condemned, and you preferred to associate with Christ’s little ones rather than with the wise of the world [Note: [Col. 0357] Matthew 11:25]. From this you now deserve this grace also from the Lord: that, as you have piously boasted and judged worthy to indicate, everyone should hate you. This would not happen unless you had begun to be a true imitator of Christ. For this world would not hate what it saw as already alien to itself and opposed to it [Note: [Col. 0357] John 15:19].

Rejoice and exult: even in your beginnings, the power of perfection is already at work. It is clear how firmly you have believed in Christ, since you have already been granted to suffer for Christ. See what the Lord himself says, and understand how blessed you are: “Do not be surprised,” he says, “if the world hates you, because it hated me before you” [Note: [Col. 0357] John 15:18]. For “if you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” [Note: [Col. 0357] John 15:19]. And again: “A servant is not greater than his master. If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more his household?” [Note: [Col. 0357] John 15:16].

Consider now whether, as servants, we may refuse to suffer for the Lord what the Lord previously endured for us, his servants. O blessed injury—to be displeasing together with Christ! We must fear more the love of those with whom one is pleasing without Christ. “Do I not hate those who hate you?” he says; and he adds: “With perfect hatred I hate them” [Note: [Col. 0357] Psalm 139:21–22]. What association can we have with those whose lot is separate from ours?

229. 3. You rightly glory, most venerable brother, and say in exultation that you yourself believe this to be proof to you that you are a Christian: those who loved you have begun to hate you, and those who feared you have begun to despise you. You are also conscious within yourself that, if you were still so important in your own estimation, they would love and honor you just as they used to.

Rejoice, therefore, and exult, for “your reward is abundant in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0359] Matthew 5:12]. They have not begun to hate you, but him who has begun to be in you [Note: [Col. 0359D] The Vatican manuscript reads, “him who is in you.”]. His work in you is both the humility they despise and the chastity they detest. Recognize with gladness that in this good you share the lot of the prophets and apostles: in the prophet, when he says, “They were slandering me because I pursued righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0359] Psalm 38:21, according to the Roman Psalter] [Note: [Col. 0359D] Thus Saint Ambrose and the Roman Psalter. The Septuagint, the Old Psalter, and Saint Augustine read, “I pursued righteousness.” The Arabic and Ethiopic Psalters and Apollinaris’ paraphrase agree with this reading. The Vulgate has, “I followed goodness.”]; and in the Apostle, who says: “We have become the refuse of all” [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Corinthians 4:13]; and again, the same witness declares: “We have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Corinthians 4:9].

From the beginning of the ages, Christ suffers in all his own. For he is himself the beginning and the end [Note: [Col. 0359] Revelation 1:8]: veiled in the Law, revealed in the Gospel, always wondrous and patient, and triumphing in his saints, the Lord [Note: [Col. 0359] Psalm 67:36]. He is in Abel, slain by his brother [Note: [Col. 0359] Genesis 4:8]; in Noah, mocked by his son [Note: [Col. 0359] Genesis 9:22]; in Abraham, wandering as an immigrant [Note: [Col. 0359] Genesis 12:10]; in Isaac, offered up; in Jacob, serving [Note: [Col. 0359] Genesis 27:43]; in Joseph, sold [Note: [Col. 0359] Genesis 37:28]; in Moses, exposed and driven into exile [Note: [Col. 0359] Exodus 2:3]; in the prophets, stoned and sawn apart [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Chronicles 24:21]; in the apostles, tossed about on land and sea [Note: [Col. 0359] Acts 7:57]; and frequently slain amid the many and varied crosses of blessed martyrs [Note: [Col. 0359] Hebrews 11:37].

He is therefore still carrying our weaknesses and sickness [Note: [Col. 0359] Isaiah 53:4], because he is always the man placed in affliction for us and knows how to bear weakness [Note: [Col. 0359] 2 Corinthians 12:9], which without him we can neither bear nor understand. He is still enduring the world for us and in us, so that by enduring it he may destroy it and perfect power in weakness.

He suffers reproaches in you also, and this world hates him in you. But thanks be to him, because he conquers when he is judged [Note: [Col. 0359] Psalm 51:6; Romans 3:4]; and, as you hold in Scripture, “the Lord triumphs in us under the appearance of servitude” [Note: [Col. 0359] 2 Corinthians 2:14], acquiring the grace of freedom for his servants. He does this through the mystery of his devotion, by which he assumed the form of a servant and deigned to humble himself for us even to death on a cross [Note: [Col. 0359] Philippians 2:7], so that through visible humility he might work inwardly in us that invisible sublimity in the heavens.

Consider from the beginning from what height we fell, and you will understand that by the counsel of divine wisdom and devotion we are restored to life [Note: [Col. 0359] Genesis 3:5]. In Adam we fell through pride; therefore we are humbled in Christ, so that we may wipe away the sin of our ancient crime by obedience to the contrary virtue. We who offended through pride make satisfaction by serving.

4. Let us therefore exult and glory in him, who has made us participants in both his battle and his victory, saying: “Stand firm, because I have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0359] John 16:33].

230. And in the Book of Kingdoms I likewise hear the prophet speaking to King Jehoshaphat when he was terrified by the great burden of war and the vast multitude of enemies: “Thus says the Lord: Do not fear or be dismayed before this multitude, for the battle is not yours but the Lord’s” [Note: [Col. 0359] 2 Chronicles 20:15, according to the Septuagint]. Moses likewise had already said: “You shall be silent, and the Lord will fight for you” [Note: [Col. 0359] Exodus 14:14].

Therefore let those who trust in their own strength or wisdom, and those who glory in the abundance of their riches [Note: [Col. 0359] Psalm 49:7, according to the Roman and Old Psalters], sharpen against us, as they wish, the weapons of their teeth, and the arrows of their words; let them pour forth the poisons of an evil treasure through viperous tongues. They have the Lord answering them on our behalf: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” [Note: [Col. 0359] Isaiah 42:14] (See Letter 5, section 7.)

Let us fence our ears with thorns, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0359] Sirach 28:28]—that is, with the word of God and faith in the word. These firmly protect the crop of our life with innocence and patience [Note: [Col. 0359] Sirach 36:27], and they resist the devil, who seeks by his deceits an entrance into our inmost parts, as thorns resist thieves. And the innermost parts of the king’s enemies—that is, lovers of Christ’s enemies, namely, the detractors of Christians—are pierced by the contemplation of our life and steadfastness.

Let us therefore be silent toward such people, speaking to the Lord in the silence of humility and the voice of patience. Then he who is unconquered will fight for us [Note: [Col. 0359] Exodus 14:14], and he will conquer in us. Then the prince of these darknesses will be cast out [Note: [Col. 0360D] The Regius manuscript reads “is sent away.”] [Note: [Col. 0359] John 12:31]. He is cast out not from this world but from the human being, when he is shut out from us by faith entering within and gives place to Christ, whose dwelling casts out sin and becomes the exile of the expelled serpent.

5. In such suffering the prophet teaches us what we ought to do, saying: “But when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” [Note: [Col. 0359] Psalm 35:13, according to the Roman Psalter]. In this way we may destroy our detractors by the very appearance of humility that troubles them, and they may be all the more confounded before the Lord because they remain in the guilt of their former pride, while we ourselves glory all the more in that by which they are confounded in us.

God loves an unashamed worker as he loves a cheerful giver [Note: [Col. 0359] 2 Timothy 2:15; 2 Corinthians 9:7]. Therefore, steadfast in the faith of truth and in the practice of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Corinthians 15:58], we refute the hatred and insults of such people better by our way of life than by our words. For “he who hates discipline will cast your words behind him,” as it is written [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Peter 2:15; Psalm 50:17]; and “he who reproves a fool brings insult upon himself” [Note: [Col. 0359] Proverbs 9:7].

6. Let orators keep their letters, philosophers their wisdom, the rich their riches (see Letter 23, section 41), and kings their kingdoms. For us, Christ is glory, possession, and kingdom; for us, wisdom is found in the foolishness of preaching [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Corinthians 1:21]; for us, power is found in the weakness of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0359] 2 Corinthians 12:9]; for us, glory is found in the scandal of the cross [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Corinthians 1:23], by which the world is crucified to me and I to the world [Note: [Col. 0359] Galatians 6:14], so that I may live to God—yet no longer I, but Christ in me [Note: [Col. 0359] Galatians 2:20].

We have been buried with him [Note: [Col. 0359] Romans 6:4; Colossians 2:12], and in him we are now hidden from the eyes of this world, so that together with him we may be revealed in the world’s own shame, when, remembering the things it now accuses us of, it will say: “These are the ones whose life we considered madness; how have they been counted among the children of God?” [Note: [Col. 0361] Wisdom 5:4]

In the meantime, dearest brother, let them enjoy their glory and their life; let them possess their fruits, since they will quickly fall like the vegetables of the fields [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 37:2], and their days pass away like a shadow [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 144:4]. Their hope is confined within the limits of this age, because they possess neither faith in the truth nor the will to believe. Intent only on present things, they surrender themselves to greed and lust rather than believe in God, since the fear of the Lord brings an end to both desires; and this fear is confirmed by faith in Christ, through which we learn to recognize the truth either in contempt for temporal things or in the desire for eternal goods.

Because they are alienated from him, and because Christ is the truth [Note: [Col. 0361] John 14:6], they must remain in the blindness of these wretched errors, thinking the fragile solid and the solid empty, laughing at what is true as though it were vain, and marveling at what is vain as though it were true.

If they wished to understand in order to act well [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 36:4], and would lift their eyes—which they have set on turning toward the earth [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 16:11]—toward the salvation of righteousness, and would raise themselves even a little above the ground (Virgil), they would easily be enlightened by the conversions of those very people whom they disparage as empty and foolish.

For the Lord, as it is written, releases those in chains, and the Lord gives sight to the blind [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 146:8]. And again: “The law of the Lord is blameless, restoring souls; the testimony of the Lord is trustworthy, granting wisdom to the little ones” [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 19:8, according to the Roman Psalter].

It is God’s work to change a human being, because he alone can restore what he made [Note: [Col. 0361D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts, together with three printed editions, read “whom he made.” Both readings are good; the Vulgate is more polished and more expressive.]. This is what Christ, the wisdom of God, has long been accomplishing throughout the whole world: carrying himself everywhere among the nations by the will of the Word and pouring himself into chosen souls [Note: [Col. 0361D] The Septuagint and Vulgate read, “transferring himself into holy souls.”] [Note: [Col. 0361] Wisdom 7:27], so that, as the prophet said, he might hold primacy in every nation [Note: [Col. 0361] Sirach 24:10].

7. Since the day of recognition—that is, of judgment—now draws nearer each day (see Letter 19, section 3), and every hour brings us closer to judgment, the good Lord strives and hastens to snatch us from the coming wrath and to lead us away from the embrace of this harmful and viperous generation, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0361] Matthew 3:7].

For this reason, in every place, more signs and extraordinary wonders occur each day, so that he may save every human being, insofar as it depends on him [Note: [Col. 0361] 1 Timothy 2:4]. He displays in a few what may benefit all, if they are willing. The example of a few is sufficient for the instruction of all; it is set before both groups, as an example to those who believe and as a testimony to those who harden themselves (or: “to those who are hardened”).

Therefore, if those who are inwardly offended by the person whose outward appearance they behold possess any human understanding, let them marvel at you and praise God. Let them not consider this most blessed transformation of your mind and life an error born of your foolishness, but let them understand that it is the power of God’s wisdom.

For the wiser and more learned they remember you to have been than others, the more evident to them should be the working of God’s power: a prudent person cannot be turned from the course or position of his own judgment except by Wisdom itself in its supreme form—God in Christ, the power of powers, the mind of minds, the Lord of majesty, the exalted arm—in which, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0361] Luke 1:51], the proud are scattered by the thought of their hearts, the mighty are brought down from their thrones, and the humble are exalted.

By this arm—that is, by Christ—the hungry are filled with good things, and the rich are sent away empty. We see this happening in you also. Look into yourself, for in that same person you will find both things that God casts down and things that he exalts.

8. You have been overthrown from pride and taken up into humility; you have been brought down from the unjust throne of power so that you might be placed upon the throne of peace and righteousness. You have been emptied by the rich so that you might be enriched in the poor. You have been emptied of that superfluous fullness of self-display so that, hungering for righteousness, you might be filled with the true goods of holy poverty.

Where are you now, that formerly terrible man—whether an advocate before tribunals or a judge upon them? Where is that neck of yours, then more truly, as you now falsely said of yourself, a fat bull’s neck? How has it become gentle and thin beneath the yoke of Christ, since you were converted and groaned [Note: [Col. 0361] Matthew 11:29], and God was pleased with you as with a young bull-calf [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 69:32]?

With the bull’s neck laid down [Note: [Col. 0361D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts read “having become,” a reading that could be admitted because it is confirmed by what precedes. The received reading seemed more accurate.], you have been broken into the meekness of that ox which recognized its owner [Note: [Col. 0361] Isaiah 1:3]. Blessed are the eyes of those who behold these wonders of God in you, even if those most wretched people see and yet do not see.

9. “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly” [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 55:7] to you and rest in your presence and conversation, feasting upon a voice of exultation and confession [Note: [Col. 0362D] The Rosweyde edition incorrectly reads “of exaltation”; the other codices, five Psalters, the Vulgate, and Letter 9 to Amandus, section 4, read “of exultation.”] [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 42:5].

I shall see you, yet not you; I shall see a calf arising from a lion; I shall see Christ in Aper: now, by a reversal of ferocity and strength, a boar toward the world, but a lamb toward God. For you are no longer a boar from the forest [Note: [Col. 0361] Psalm 80:14], but a boar from the grainfield [Note: [Col. 0362D] From the Regius manuscript and the Grin edition we have restored “because,” required by the second member of the sentence. Previously it read “who.”], because you are enriched with the good fruits of discipline, and you are nourished in the fruitfulness of virtues. You are armed with the teeth of the two Testaments to tear apart the nets of the hunter Nimrod (see Letter 9, section 4) [Note: [Col. 0361] Genesis 10:9]; and all those weapons that you proudly carried for the world, you now humbly turn against the world.

Now you are truly wise, truly eloquent, and truly powerful: you are foolish and mute to this world, so that, eloquent and wise through his gifts, you may serve God, the author of your tongue and mind.

10. Now, instructed in divine law, you may plead your case on your own behalf, and, as a more just judge, judge yourself. In yourself, or concerning yourself, pronounce judgment, so that you may deserve to be acquitted all the more; and make yourself worthy not only of pardon but also of glory, when you stand beside yourself by accusing yourself and sanctify yourself by condemning yourself.

You understand that it is not what pleases human beings but what pleases God that is holy and innocent. Therefore, as you write, you are now a rare visitor to cities. You have come to love the familiar solitude of the silent countryside (see note 180), not preferring leisure to duty or withdrawing from the usefulness of the Church, but now almost avoiding the disturbances of the courts, rivals to the tumult of churches and their restless councils.

I judge that this very thing is being prepared for greater usefulness to the Church: you devote yourself, according to a healthy plan, to holy instruction; and, intent upon spiritual studies, for which solitude is a friend, you daily form Christ within yourself and confirm him [Note: [Col. 0363D] We have added the particle “and” from the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and four printed editions; from the same manuscripts and the Grin edition we have restored “you form … and confirm.” The Rosweyde, Gravis, and Schott editions read “forming … and confirming.”]. Thus, as a more useful servant and a more learned teacher, you may make yourself worthier of the position to which God’s will has appointed you [Note: [Col. 0364D] Thus we have emended from the Regius manuscript and four printed editions. The Rosweyde edition reads “to him.”], being powerful alike in deed and word. In this way, with tongue and mind in agreement, you may present yourself as a true model of apostolic discipline, both a doer and teacher of the Lord’s command [Note: [Col. 0363] 2 Thessalonians 3:9]. Only then will it be clear that you are a priest by divine judgment, not by human approval.

11. Believing that this is already proved by your faith and life, I ask and earnestly beg you always to include us in your prayers and, whenever there is an opportunity, to make an effort to visit us by letter.

I demand this service from you not so much out of eagerness to receive the obligations of office as from a desire to refresh my spirit, so that I may receive both the consolation of charity and joy at once, when I read and see that you remember me amid holy occupations, are diligent in your own spiritual progress, and possess an understanding of a heart burning toward God.

I no longer assess you by your discourse about virtue—that is, by your preaching of Christ—but by the virtue of that discourse itself: whether by speaking and living alike you confirm that you believe Jesus Christ crucified to be Lord and God.
