For we ought to bear the image of the heavenly man with the same disposition with which we previously bore the image of the earthly man [Note: [Col. 0363] 1 Corinthians 15:49].

Otherwise, who will give us what belongs to us, if we have not been as faithful in what is ours as we were in what belonged to another? [Note: [Col. 0363] Luke 16:12] For we were made for this: to be good and to serve our Creator. By living contrary to his commands through the fault of our will, we shall act not only against life but also against our own nature; and therefore we shall be compared to beasts that have no understanding [Note: [Col. 0363] Psalm 49:13 and 32:9; Tobit 6:17].

Nevertheless, God’s goodness makes this agreement with us: after granting us pardon for our former impiety, it is content that we should be servants to him for our own sake in the same way that we formerly presented ourselves as servants to the devil against ourselves. The Apostle says that, just as we presented our members to serve iniquity, so we should present those same members to serve righteousness [Note: [Col. 0363] Romans 6:19]. That is, we should delight in the Lord with the same affection with which we delighted in sin. Let us pursue the kingdom of God as eagerly as we pursued worldly rank; and finally, let us care for heavenly goods as diligently as we cared for earthly ones.

EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0363] Formerly 30; the one formerly numbered 39 is now 25. Written in 405.] XXXIX (C).

He teaches Aper how the field of the heart is to be cultivated; here he applies Joel’s words about the caterpillar, locust, grub, and rust with great beauty to the four passions of the soul.

To the holy, deservedly venerable, and dearly beloved brothers Aper and Amanda, Paulinus and Therasia, sinners.

1. To others, revenue from estates is paid in the customary installments. For us, whose possession in Christ is your love, revenue is drawn from the services of your affection and reckoned in the graciousness of your letters.

Thanks be to our Lord God, who, repaying living goods for dead and perishable ones, has also bestowed you upon us as a most abundant estate. For just as in earthly matters an estate is more valuable when it either answers the hopes of its greedy farmer with flowing fertility or charms the eyes of its delicate owner with beauty, so now, in our spiritual estates—that is, in the holy brothers whom the charity of Christ has joined to us and given us as an eternal possession—the more fertile field is judged to be the person who is more attentive to us and more fruitful for us in administering saving benefits.

Since this is so, consider how large a mass of such a possession we possess in you, since, beyond the affection that you pour mutually upon us, you contribute other gifts, equal to which we cannot be, through the abundance of your speech and the riches of your mind.

The services and words of your letters, which you lavishly pay us in an annual provision [Note: [Col. 0364D] The Viennese manuscript reads “you expend”], show how broad a possession and how fertile a land you are for us before God. Already you are producing the thirtieth fruit through your mutual continence, approaching the sixtieth through daily increases of shared faith, and promising the hundredfold from virginal offspring [Note: [Col. 0363] Matthew 13:8; Mark 4:8; Luke 8:8].

2. You write that the possessions of your children are obstacles to your purpose, since they are the cause of the necessity by which you care for earthly things while desiring heavenly ones. We judge instead that these have been placed before you by divine providence as abundant material for exercising faith and perfecting virtue.

Since the entire possession of the world appears to have been established for the human being and subjected to the human being [Note: [Col. 0363] Genesis 1:26], who can doubt that throughout every place in the world and every part of nature, benefits have been prepared for humanity—benefits from which we may receive not only bodily profit but much more readily discern spiritual profit?

Therefore Wisdom itself, the maker of things, which orders all things gently, says through Solomon that agriculture was created by the Most High [Note: [Col. 0363] Wisdom 8:1], so that you may cultivate it not only with bodily but also with spiritual devotion.

Finally, it shows how much can be drawn from the countryside for the education of the soul when it sends its followers to the ant and the bee [Note: [Col. 0363] Proverbs 6:6 and 30:25; Sirach 11:3], both of which are creatures of the countryside: the one provident of the fruits of life, the other a worker among the flowers for honey.

And in the Gospel the Lord taught many things through rural examples [Note: [Col. 0363] Luke 13:6; John 4:45; Mark 13:28; Luke 21:29; Matthew 24:40; Matthew 13:25], demonstrating the signs of the last times through the fig tree and the regions already yellowing with the approaching harvest. He warned that we must learn in the field, so that in spirit we may beware lest the enemy sow fraudulent imitation into our faith, just as he sows weeds among wheat.

Thus he called us his field and showed himself to be the sower of our life; and he expressed the distinctions among souls through the various qualities of lands. Let us beware lest we be barren; let us cultivate ourselves also for the fruitfulness owed to God and useful to us, through devoted study of the law of the Lord.

3. Therefore, when you are in the field and look upon your countryside, consider that you yourself are also Christ’s field, and look upon yourself as upon your own field. The appearance you ask your farm manager to produce in your field—such cultivation render to the Lord God in your heart. Understand that whatever pleases or displeases you in your field likewise pleases or displeases Christ in your soul.

If it is foul with sins like thickets and is not watered by prophetic or apostolic clouds, it will be condemned to dry desolation when grace abandons it. But if, attentive to itself, it cultivates itself through frequent prayers, is enriched by the sacred Scriptures, impresses the plow of the cross upon the innermost heart [Note: [Col. 0365D] The Viennese manuscript reads, “and impresses the plow of the cross into the innermost heart”], uproots its thorns with the rake of divine fear, and is burned in its faults by God’s fiery word while being illumined in its understanding, then the master of the household will necessarily delight in walking through your heart and traversing all the regions of your soul.

And, rejoicing with you on your behalf, he will say to you, if you appear to be a diligent cultivator of yourself: “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your lord, because you have been faithful in a little; I will set you over much” [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 25:21; Luke 19:17].

4. But what shall we ourselves answer—who, giving sound counsel to the strong while ourselves weak through a perverse arrangement—say on our own behalf, since we are as poor spiritually as you suppose us to be, humble not through strength of mind but through lack of strength?

That narrow little garden which, though powerful, you describe with your broad mouth—scarcely fertile and spacious enough for a single stalk—we ourselves are; and, as the prophet said [Note: [Col. 0365] Isaiah 51:20, according to the Septuagint], we are tasteless beyond a half-cooked beet (see note 182). Let us ensure that in our house that one stalk is not the only tasteless one.

The one who did not receive salt through the necessity of poverty or through the fault of frugality is more excusable. We, rather, have been boiled; we are more culpably tasteless, because, with foolishness overflowing from voluntary sins, the apostolic salt has lost its savor [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 5:13], and spiritual seasonings have fled from the face of our sins.

But unless we are refreshed by your prayers, not even that single stalk will remain green in us, and when we are utterly abandoned, even the tasteless vegetable will be lacking.

5. Pray, therefore, that the harmful caterpillar may not ravage the shoots of our soul; that the devouring locust may not consume the crop of our mind; that the sluggish grub may not settle upon our inmost parts; and that rust, the last companion of these little creatures, may not eat away the innermost fibers of our life [Note: [Col. 0365] Joel 1:4].

For evil beasts press upon our inner being, and troublesome birds frequently attack it, so that, if they can, they may snatch away from us the seed of the word.

But thanks be to God that we have not fallen beside the road from the hand of the sower; rather, we have been sown on the road itself [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 13:4]—that is, we have been established in the bosom of the Catholic mother. To prevent us from being cast out as abortions, we need her mercy, so that she may grant us understanding on this road on which she commanded and enabled us to walk, and may establish his eyes over us, lest we become like the horse and mule that have no understanding [Note: [Col. 0365] Psalm 32:8].

6. But let us return to the language of our husbandry. Our God and Father is himself the farmer; our saving God is the true vine [Note: [Col. 0365] John 15:1]; and the Holy Spirit is the waterer of souls.

Therefore, through your prayers, may it come about for us that the supreme master of the household, the heavenly farmer, and the diligent gardener may visit, frequent, and mark the garden of our soul, like that garden in which he taught, prayed, and rose again [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 26:36 and 28:6; Mark 14:32].

May he strengthen in us the bond of his charity, so that we may live as branches remaining in him. May he command his clouds to rain upon us and remove from our heart the passions of wicked bodily thoughts, those creatures hostile to good fruits.

May the prophet’s word not come to pass in us: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the grub ate; and what the grub left, the rust ate” [Note: [Col. 0365] Joel 1:4].

For there are in our body just as many principal incentives to vice: hope, fear, joy, and sorrow, by which the human race is especially disturbed—two belonging to the present and two to the future. To the present belong distress of spirit and joy; to the future, fear and hope. Therefore we must beware lest, while fleeing from one of these vices, we fall into its opposite.

### 7

Therefore, in the caterpillar, locust, grub, and rust, the passions of our affections are to be understood. Some of these cling briefly to the heart; others gradually grow, and, if they are not cast away, reach to the marrow and drink up all the soul’s sap. Consider, then, how these monsters of vices correspond to one another in our hearts, just as the vices of monsters occur among crops.

For example, if I desire something forbidden and immediately cast the thought away, it is a caterpillar sitting on a leaf. [Note: [Col. 0366D] The Royal and Viennese manuscripts read “and having been shaken off”; the editions of Grin. and Latin. read “which, having been shaken off.”] If I cast it away but the thought returns, and begins to be rejected yet increasingly returns, it is a locust flying away and coming back. But if it begins to linger and has more opportunity for eating than for flying away, it is called a grub. And if that grub, which does not fly away sufficiently but rather sits, is not cast away, it turns into rust; and once it has become thoroughly embedded, it is driven out of the soul no more easily than from straw—or only with difficulty.

### 8

I fear that, while I weary you by talking too much, I myself have settled upon you more unpleasantly than a locust or a grub. [Note: [Col. 0366D] The Viennese manuscript reads “Shake it off.”] Shake me off, then, like a caterpillar, and cast this little page far away, lest through prolonged contact with my discourse you gather the rust of my ignorance, by which the brightness of your hearts may lose its luster and the vigor of your mind grow dull. [Col. 0367A] Yet forgive us this one fault by which we weary you so heavily, because we abuse your patience by the permission granted by charity; and we trust that your breast is so filled with love for us that it cannot receive offense from us, even if we commit an injury by which we might deserve to give offense—if you could ever be offended by us, even when we deserved it.

## LETTER XL (C)

[Note: [Col. 0367] Elsewhere 26, part 1; but the letter formerly numbered 40 is now numbered 26. Written about the year 405.]

Sanctus and Amandus had heaped great praises upon Paulinus in a letter sent to him. In reply, he supplies them with sharp goads toward perfection. At the beginning he treats, from the sacred Scriptures, of the fact that there is a proper time for everything. Then, from Psalm 101, he adds a moral interpretation of the pelican, the night-bird, and the solitary sparrow. Finally, using the praises bestowed upon him as an occasion for humility, he attaches much concerning the divine grace to which we owe everything, the watchfulness necessary on the way of the spirit, and the perfect renunciation of self.

**MEROPIUS PAULINUS AND THERASIA, TO THE HOLY BROTHERS SANCTUS AND [Note: [Col. 0367D] Thus the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts, together with the edition of Chiffl. The edition of Rosv. reads: “to the holy brothers in the Lord Christ, greetings.”] AMANDUS, GREETINGS IN GOD CHRIST.**

### 1

“There is a time for everything, and a time for every matter under heaven” [Note: [Col. 0367] Ecclesiasticus 3:17]; for above heaven there is no time, since eternity has no time—the eternity which the Creator also gave to creatures in heaven, while he alone possesses eternity in its proper sense and dwells in inaccessible light. For true eternity exists nowhere except in him, who alone is what he is, as he himself said: “I am who I am.” (All other things, unless they are in him, are not.) Therefore, there is a time for everything under heaven: a time for leisure and a time for work; a time for silence and a time for conversation; a time for hunger and a time for feasting. Just as until now it was a time for us to fast from your words, so now the time has arisen for us to be fed by them. You have nourished us with your letters, sweet with the word of God [Col. 0367C] and anointed with the oil of gladness, with which we gladly anoint our head [Note: [Col. 0367D] Thus the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts, together with the edition of Chiffl. Rosv. reads “we have joined.”] [Note: [Col. 0367] Matthew 6:17]; for in you there is no deceitful work of the olive [Note: [Col. 0367] Habakkuk 3:17], in whom love dwells from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0367] 1 Timothy 1:5]. But because no one who is very hungry can be satisfied with a single loaf, we confess that we are not yet filled, but rather stirred up to desire your letters by that one letter of yours—which we count as one because we have so far received only one such letter from you, one by which our soul might be filled as with fat and abundance [Note: [Col. 0367] Psalm 62:6].

### 2

Nevertheless, although among our duties there have been changes of times—“a time to keep silence, and a time to speak” [Note: [Col. 0367] Ecclesiasticus 3:7]—there was not likewise a time for loving and a time for neglecting. For some time ago, as you undoubtedly recognize, holy brother, I began to love you; and I continued to love you, although not with that love which belongs to Christ, but with the friendship of human familiarity, which has flattery on its lips but no root in its heart, because it is not founded upon the rock, which is not built in Christ. Thus, shaken at times by any wind of frivolity, it is dissolved; and, holding only a brief flower through temporal favor, it quickly withers like grass and quickly falls like the flower of the field [Note: [Col. 0367D] The Septuagint, Vulgate, Roman and Gallican Psalters read “the vegetables of herbs”; the Old Psalter and Saint Augustine in his Commentary on the Psalms read “the vegetables of the meadow.” Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine in the *Speculum* read “green vegetation.”] [Note: [Col. 0367] Psalms 36:2 and 128:6]. But the love of the Lord endures forever; by it we are bound together both to live together and to die together, because the love of Christ is strong as death [Note: [Col. 0367] Song of Songs 8:6]. For just as the law of death, once broken, so also the chain of love testifies that love and death possess equal force. For as the prophet says: “Who is the man who will live and not see death?” [Note: [Col. 0367D] We have corrected this from the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl., in accordance with the Greek text and the Vulgate; Augustine likewise frequently reads it this way in his Commentary on the Psalms. The edition of Rosv. reads “who lives.”] [Note: [Col. 0367] Psalm 88:49], so the Apostle also cries out: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” [Note: [Col. 0367] Romans 8:35.] [Note: [Col. 0368D] The Cluniac manuscript and the edition of Chiffl. read: “Therefore a richer fruit of this love will come to you, who, wounded first, have gone before us in the blessings of sweetness,” etc.]

Therefore, blessed one, a richer fruit of this love will come to you, who, wounded first by the arrows of this love, went before us in the blessing of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0367] Psalm 20:4] through the chaste and faithful words of your letters, in which your tongue distilled honey and milk from the word of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0367] Song of Songs 4:11].

### 3

I had previously written to your kindred spirit; and when I had received from you your brief letter in return for the one which I myself had sent, [Note: [Col. 0368D] So the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts, together with the edition of Chiffl. Other manuscripts read: “the brief letter which you yourself had sent.”], I poured myself once more into prolonged silence, as though I had discharged the obligation of duty. But, with Christ keeping watch, you began again more vigorously to flourish in wisdom in your own mind, awakening in us the observance of love, lest it fall asleep into the death of forgetfulness. And because my inhumanity toward you had been great, your humanity toward me overflowed all the more.

For you multiplied your efforts to enrich me through the affection and service of your love, by which you took the blessed servant of the Lord, brother Amandus, as your companion in our visitation and appointed him for us [Note: [Col. 0368D] The Vatican manuscript reads “you opposed.” The Cluniac manuscript and the edition of Chiffl. read “you appointed a strong patron of salvation,” less suitably.] as a powerful patron. We trust, indeed, that just as he has become your partner in writing to us, so also he may be your companion in praying for us. Spiritual brotherhood demands that, just as you have one spirit in faith and confession of Christ, so you should have one love and one labor in defending your neighbors [Note: [Col. 0368D] The Cluniac manuscript reads “in supporting them.” The Vulgate reading is more correct.]. Therefore you will reap a common reward abundantly from the supreme rewarder, exalted in his towers, because “a brother helping a brother will be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0367] Proverbs 18:19].

Provided, however, that you remember always to pray and sigh for us alone, and henceforth take care not to burden us with words that pronounce us blessed, lest you perhaps acquire a stumbling-block for yourselves by calling sweet what is bitter [Note: [Col. 0367] Isaiah 5:20]. For you have read that praise belongs to the upright and truly holy [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 32:1], not to sinners placed in the gall of bitterness [Note: [Col. 0369] Acts 8:23], nor even to those still bound by no slight bond of iniquity [Note: [Col. 0369D] The Cluniac manuscript and the edition of Chiffl. read “bound fast.”], so that contrition and misery may already be lacking in our ways [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 13:3] [Note: [Col. 0369D] The Cluniac manuscript and the edition of Chiffl. omit “already.” Three other manuscripts—the Nol., Vatic., and Vien.—include it; this is probably erroneous.].

### 4

Nevertheless, contrition must also be present in our minds, because “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 50:19] [Note: [Col. 0369D] Thus the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl. Saint Paulinus likewise has this reading elsewhere, in Letter 49 to Macarius, section 13, and Letter 50 to Augustine, section 2. The edition of Rosv. reads: “a contrite heart … he will not despise.”]. And who will give us a heart of flesh [Note: [Col. 0369] Ezekiel 36:26], so that, when the hardness of our feeling has been softened, we may feel the arrows of the Lord fixing our flesh with holy fear [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalms 118:120; 119:4], and, when the pain of our wounds has been awakened, we may weep before the Lord who made us [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 94:6]?

May Jeremiah lend us that fountain of tears [Note: [Col. 0369] Jeremiah 9:1] with which he lamented his day and his people; may David also pour over us the rivers of his eyes [Col. 0369B], with which he watered his bed [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 6:7]; indeed, he washed not only the cheeks of his face but his whole couch with overflowing tears. For our iniquities have been placed upon our head, and they have multiplied beyond the hairs of our head [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 37:5 according to the Septuagint Psalter; Psalm 39:13]. In us there are more works of iniquity than of justice. Therefore our scars have become putrid and worse because of the face of our folly [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 37:6 according to the Roman Psalter] [Note: [Col. 0369D] Thus in the Roman and Hebrew Psalters, and in Saints Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine in their commentaries on the Psalms.], and our bones have grown old because we kept silence before God [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 31:3]. Adding iniquity upon iniquity [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 68:28], although we had determined to turn our eyes toward the earth [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 16:11], we raised them late and with difficulty toward the mountains of God, from which our help comes from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 120:1], who alone is powerful to heal all our diseases [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 102:3, according to the Roman Psalter] and to rescue us from this body of death [Note: [Col. 0369] Romans 7:24] [Note: [Col. 0370D] The Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts read “by which”; the Nol. manuscript reads “because.”].

Bound through Adam, we are released through Christ [Col. 0369C], provided that we bear the image of the heavenly man as faithfully as we bore that of the earthly [Note: [Col. 0369] 1 Corinthians 15:49]. That is, provided that we serve justice and truth for our salvation as faithfully as we served injustice and inhumanity for our death. For the Apostle demands from us the human response: just as we presented our members to serve iniquity for destruction and disgrace, so let us present those same members to serve justice [Note: [Col. 0369] Romans 6:19] for life and glory. We carry with us the fruit of those works of which we are now ashamed.

### 5

But thanks be to the grace of the Wisdom of God, Christ God, who, remaining in himself, makes all things new and orders all things gently [Note: [Col. 0369] Wisdom 8:1], so that there may be a time for everything [Note: [Col. 0369] Ecclesiastes 3:17]: a time to kill and a time to heal; a time to laugh and a time to weep; a time to build and a time to destroy [Note: [Col. 0369] Ibid., verses 3 and 4]. [Col. 0369D] May the time for killing, destroying, and laughing have now passed from us, I pray; and at last may the time for healing, building, and weeping have arrived. For behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation [Note: [Col. 0369] 2 Corinthians 6:2]. The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us cast off the works of darkness and take up the weapons of light [Note: [Col. 0369] Romans 13:12]. Let us walk as children of the day in the light, for behold, our enemies have prepared arrows in their quiver, to shoot in the darkness [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 10:3]. They will not be able to shoot those who are placed in the light, before they strike, if they are foreseen and easily avoided by those who take precautions.

Yet the order of both times can be joined together in the very same work, so that the times distinguished above may operate in us together. For in what we are made alive, we are killed; or in what we are killed, we are made alive through him who said: “I kill, and I make alive” [Note: [Col. 0369] Deuteronomy 32:39]. Unless Christ kills us, we shall not live. Of him it is written: “The Lord kills and makes alive” [Note: [Col. 0369] 1 Kings 2:6], because unless he has destroyed our sins, he will not make our souls alive. Therefore the prophet says to him: “I have risen, and I am still with you. If you kill the sinner, O God” [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalms 138:18–19].

We shall rise, emerging from the mud of filth and the shadow of death, and we shall remain with him if he kills the sinner within us and creates the just person, because the cup of our weakness is in the hand of the Lord, in which he humbles one and exalts another [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 74:8]. Unless the outward person is humbled, the inward person is not exalted. Thus the times for killing and healing, or for destroying and building, come together in one work [Note: [Col. 0369] Ecclesiastes 3:3], when the life of sin is destroyed in us so that the life of justice may be built. The new cannot be built unless the old is destroyed; nor can we love Christ unless we begin to hate mammon [Note: [Col. 0369] Matthew 6:24]. Nor shall we be able to rejoice in that age unless we mourn in this one, because “those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 125:5, according to the Roman Psalter].

### 6

Therefore that prayer of the poor man who is anxious and mourning from the Psalms is fitting for us now, since our days have almost failed like smoke [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 101:4], while our wickedness has not yet failed. For behold, he has made our days old, extending them through the course of life; old age does not merely sprinkle our head with gray, but drenches it [Note: [Col. 0370D] Thus the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl. Before this, the edition of Rosv. read “pours forth.”]. Yet we still spend our time with the childish perceptions of spiritual infancy, crawling with its first efforts; and only now, scarcely beginning to speak in the word of God, we loosen a mute and unformed tongue for the sacred Scriptures, our soul wailing as it utters its first sounds. Once eloquent in the literature of human fables, we now stammer in the utterances of truth: wise in folly and foolish in wisdom; strong in vices and still tender in virtues [Col. 0371A]; scarcely beginners, with a will just being born for justice, yet veterans in an age consumed by sins.

For a long while, as you know, holy and blessed brother, we grew old in rolling about in this world among our enemies. Would that we had grown old for our enemies, so that the life of that spacious journey might now have failed us in our leisure, and our youth might be renewed in Christ like that of the eagle [Note: [Col. 0371] Psalm 101:7], so that we might strip off the old age of the old man and put on that new man who was created according to God [Note: [Col. 0371] Ephesians 4:24].

But if we cannot yet be like the pelican of solitude, when will it be that we become like the night-bird in its dwelling [Note: [Col. 0371] Psalm 101:7]? When shall we be awakened to that vigor of exalted mind, so that, flying with spiritual alacrity and carried on the lofty wing through the heights of the virtues [Note: [Col. 0371D] We retain the Vulgate reading. The reading of the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts, “and perfected at the lofty end of the virtues,” is not satisfactory; nor is Chiffl.’s correction, “carried through the lofty end,” acceptable.], we may be able to say: “I kept watch, and became like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” [Note: [Col. 0371D] From the Cluniac, Nol., and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl. we have restored “a solitary sparrow upon the roof”; thus Paulinus reads here, in sections 8 and 9, and likewise in Letter 49 to Macarius, section 5.] [Note: [Col. 0371] Ibid., verse 8].

Let us consider here, if you please, in what manner the prophetic utterance arranges these kinds of birds, and in this order, under the person of the poor man who is anxious—that is, the penitent—reduced to poverty of hope through some fall. You endure, I think, the loquacity of my foolishness, which you have provoked to your own disparagement. For I learned from a certain holy, most learned, and very dear man, Rufinus, who came to know many things not only by reading but also by traveling, that the pelican is a bird common in Egypt, or in those nearby deserted regions along the Nile, and that it fattens itself by feeding on snakes whom it has defeated in combat [Note: [Col. 0371D] Thus the Vatican manuscript and the edition of Rosv. The Cluniac, Nol., and Viennese manuscripts, together with the edition of Chiffl., read “which it has defeated by fighting,” less suitably.]. Thus it fights in order to conquer, and when conquered it dies; but when victorious it both escapes death and obtains food.

As for the word “night-bird,” he more correctly maintained that it should be *nycticora* [Col. 0371C], and he seemed to demonstrate this by a plausible argument. He said that the bird placed here is the one we call the owl, because it secretly sings and flies at night, and because, amid the darkness of night in which nearly all animals are shrouded, it is illuminated. Hence *nycticora* is more appropriate than *nycticorax*: *nycticorax* means “night-raven,” whereas *nycticora* means “seeing by night,” because the pupil of the eye is called *kórē* (κόρη) by the Greeks. It is plainly evident that the owl has nothing resembling a raven. Moreover, as I said, it is clear that, like certain other birds, it sees better in the darkness of night and is blinded in the light; it experiences night as day and uses light as night.

### 7

Now, therefore, my blessed ones, see how this bird corresponds to the sorrowful poor man—that is, the penitent—impoverished in the riches of grace (see Letter 32, section 20), mourning, with a conscience aware of his miserable falls, the losses of his glory, laboring in his wretched affliction and groaning, striving to recover the life of his soul through the death of his own flesh, and eagerly seeking, through the expenditure of prayers, the support of groans, and tears, remedies for wounded salvation.

How aptly such a poor and sinful person is called an Egyptian or nocturnal bird! For he who separates himself from the common assembly of the Church to mourn and confess his sins, and sorrowfully shuts himself within the prison of his cell, withdrawing from this world in flight so that he may remain in the solitude of lamentation, and there struggle against the desires of his flesh and battle in spiritual combat to crush his sins, certainly becomes like the pelican of solitude both in dwelling and in battle. He imitates that bird hostile to serpents by fighting against the devil himself and the rulers of darkness, in order to conquer the sins and thoughts of the flesh.

And if he conquers in that contest, he will live as the survivor of his enemies. He seeks food for himself from his victory, because he acquires the reward of life by conquering sin and the devil, whom, together with the whole army of spiritual wickedness, we experience crawling by various devices toward our destruction amid the daily dangers within us. But thanks be to God, who gave us victory through Jesus Christ our Lord, so that we may walk upon the asp and basilisk and trample the lion and dragon [Note: [Col. 0371] Psalm 90:13].

Therefore let us fight against such rulers of darkness—that is, against the powerful sinners whom the Apostle calls darkness [Note: [Col. 0371] Ephesians 6:12]—with whom we have a striving in rivalry for salvation. Pray that, while we live in the desert of this world, we may remove these serpents by the example of that saving bird [Note: [Col. 0372D] The Nol. manuscript reads “of the solitary one.” But the adjective “saving” is appropriate, since it removes serpents.]. When they have been crushed and devoured through victory, as though the cloud of darkness had been dispersed, our inner person will be illuminated. Then it will become like the night-bird in its dwelling—that is, in the house of the Lord—so that amid the darkness of this world it may direct the sharp vision of a purified mind, and, enlightened with such eyes, may say according to the prophet: “For the darkness will not be darkened by me, and night will be illuminated like day” [Note: [Col. 0371] Psalm 138:12] [Note: [Col. 0372D] Thus we correct the text from the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl.; our correction is confirmed by Letter 41, section 2: “the inner eye is illumined.” The edition of Rosv. reads “illuminated.”].

This occurs when both substances in a human being are brought into harmony, so that even the flesh, having been imbued with an earthly nature, passes over to the soul’s harmony with a spiritual disposition. Then night will be illuminated like day, when the flesh also becomes spiritual, like the soul [Note: [Col. 0372D] The same manuscripts read both “is illuminated” and “is made.” Both readings are good.].

### 8

[Col. 0373A] If, through your prayers, it is granted that, in crushing the viperous enemy [Note: [Col. 0373D] Thus corrected from the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and Chiffl. The edition of Rosv. reads “the pelican.”], we may imitate the pelican of solitude and see with the eyes of the night-bird amid the darkness of this world, then, when our feet have been established in perfection and we have been set upon the heights of perfect virtue, watching in prayers and meditating on the law of the Lord, we shall become like the solitary sparrow upon the roof [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 101:8], with body and spirit harmonized [Note: [Col. 0373D] The Vatican manuscript reads “according to the will of God.”] in the will of God; and rightly we shall say: “I am solitary until I pass over” [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 140:10].

And who is this sparrow, in whom there is the form of perfection, except that sparrow who found a house for himself and made a nest for himself with the turtledove—your altars, O Lord of hosts [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 83:4]? Perhaps this is one of those two sparrows, one of which does not fall upon the earth without the will of the Father [Note: [Col. 0373] Matthew 10:29]. This highest sparrow fell in the body, but he also rose again. He fell by the consent of his will, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross [Note: [Col. 0373] Philippians 2:8].

This sparrow is that Wisdom which gladly shows herself to those who seek her along the ways; now she meets them at the gates, now encounters them in the streets; now, high upon the walls or towers, she calls her lovers to herself and invites them into the heights of her dwelling places [Note: [Col. 0373] Proverbs 8:2], so that she may fulfill her word, because, when exalted, she draws all things to herself [Note: [Col. 0373] John 12:32] [Note: [Col. 0373D] Thus the Cluniac, Nol., and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl. Other copies read “and, when exalted, draws all things to herself.”].

Who will give us wings like those of a silvered dove [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 54:7; and 7:4], so that, winged by the pure words of the Lord, words tested like silver in the fire [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 11:7], we may fly toward the prize of the heavenly calling, following this singular sparrow—the only-begotten Son of God—who flies above all things, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 112:5]. [lacuna] And he who descended into the lower parts of the earth is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens, leading captivity captive, so that he might fulfill all things [Note: [Col. 0373] Ephesians 4:8–10].

If we are able to follow this sparrow through direct imitation, walking in the same footsteps in which the beautiful feet of those who proclaim the gospel have entered [Note: [Col. 0373] Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15], then, established on high, we shall be able to say: “I kept watch, and became like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 101:8, according to the Roman Psalter].

### 9

Nevertheless, even when we have advanced to the heights, let us remember that word of the Lord: whoever is on the roof must not return to his house to take away his vessels [Note: [Col. 0373] Matthew 24:17]; that is, we must not turn back into ourselves and retrieve carnal works, like vessels left below. For he says: “No one who puts”—that is, places; the Greek has *epibalōn* (ἐπιβαλών)—“his hands to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0373] Luke 9:62].

But even if we have been upon the roof—that is, if we have flown above our earthly nature and refused to yield to the flesh—let us fear, following the example of birds, falling back down to low things. [Col. 0374A] For it is written that “the nets are spread for birds not without cause” [Note: [Col. 0373D] Greek: ἀδίκως. The Septuagint and Lucifer read “not unjustly.” Greek Fathers commonly cite the passage this way, as does Blessed Cyril in *Commentary on John*, book II, chapter 54, and others.] [Note: [Col. 0373] Proverbs 1:17, according to the Septuagint]. And we know that fowlers, thus lying in wait for the simplicity of birds, place snares upon the ground; [Note: [Col. 0373D] Thus the Vatican manuscript and the edition of Rosv. The Cluniac, Nol., and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl. read: “and they usually lay down birds, deceived by the bait scattered with fraud,” etc.] they often bring down birds by bait, or by the enticement of a hidden lure strewn with deceit, and entangle the trusting ones in snares concealed beneath a treacherous covering of turf.

But let us, armed with faith and enlightened by truth, speak against the fowlers of spiritual wickedness, who solicit us by similar means through the allurements of this world: “In the Lord I trust; how can you say to my soul: ‘Fly away to the mountain like a sparrow’?” [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 10:2]; “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 6:9].

Therefore let us pray to the Lord, who enlightens every person coming into this world [Note: [Col. 0373] John 1:9]. I think that “every person” is said because no one is truly human unless he recognizes God, and unless he has rather deserved to be recognized by God. Those who do not recognize him, “compared with senseless beasts, have become like them” [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 48:13].

Let us, therefore, justified by faith through his great mercy from our ungodliness, and not by works, run into the fragrance of his ointments [Note: [Col. 0373] Song of Songs 1:3], so that from his name we may draw the fragrance of life and become a fragrance of Christ, good to God [Note: [Col. 0373] 2 Corinthians 2:15], having been given to drink [V. note 183], as it is written [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 115:13], from the wine of ointments, from the cup of salvation. In it he himself, like a perfumer, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus [Note: [Col. 0373] Ecclesiasticus 49:1], mixes fragrant ointments, distributing his gifts to each person as he wills [Note: [Col. 0373] 1 Corinthians 12:11], so that all things may be fulfilled in all [Sacch. reads “may be fulfilled.” See Letters 42, section 2, and 43, section 3], and may manifest in us the fragrance of his knowledge. For “his name is ointment poured out” [Note: [Col. 0374D] Nobilius says that he found this reading in some copies in his scholia on this verse. Our Paulinus repeats the same reading of the verse at the end of Letter 41 to the same persons, section 3; hence we have corrected the text, following the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chifl. Previously it read “to him.”] [Note: [Col. 0373] Song of Songs 1:2].

So that this name may be invoked upon us [Note: [Col. 0373D] James 2:7] and may always be named in us, let our citizenship be in heaven [Note: [Col. 0373] Philippians 3:20]. For thus we shall become like the solitary sparrow upon the roof [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 101:8], if we neither think about nor seek the things that are on earth, but those that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0374D] The edition of Chiffl., together with the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts, reads “is seated at the right hand of the Father.”] [Note: [Col. 0373] Colossians 3:2], observing our actions with innumerable eyes and watching this contest in which, while walking in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0373] 2 Corinthians 10:3].

### 10

For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against invisible enemies and against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places [Note: [Col. 0373] Ephesians 6:12]. Not that wicked spirits act in the heavenly places, but that they oppose those who live in a heavenly manner. Let us therefore put on the weapons of light [Note: [Col. 0373] Romans 13:12], and in our God let us cross that wall [Note: [Col. 0373] Psalm 17:30] which separates us from God. Let us not fear the adversary, violent in spiritual nature, because “power is made perfect in weakness” [Note: [Col. 0373] 2 Corinthians 12:9].

Nor is a man powerful through his own strength; rather, the Lord makes his adversary weak. The Lord of hosts, the King of glory, himself confounded that adversary by such a form of combat on our behalf that, on the cross of Christ, it was not divine power but human weakness that overcame him. Let us therefore follow the triumphant Jesus, and let his truth surround us as a shield of faith, so that we may not fear the terror by night or the arrow flying by day. A thousand will fall at our side and ten thousand at our right hand [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 90:5–7]—not by our power, but by the power of Christ, whose battle is the battle we fight and whose crown is the crown by which we conquer. For we are members of his body, provided that we mortify our members on earth so that they may become weapons of justice. Girded with these, let us provide Christ, his angels, and you with a joyful spectacle of our contest; and, flying out of the snare of the hunters, let us sing with chattering thanksgiving:

“Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been set free, because our help is in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 123:7–8].

For no other name has been given under heaven to human beings [Note: [Col. 0375] Acts 4:12], by which we must be saved [Note: [Col. 0375D] Thus the edition of Chiffl. together with the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts. The edition of Rosv. read, with different punctuation, “to be made.” We have adopted this reading.].

Triumphing in this name, let us confess the mercies of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0375D] Thus Paulinus himself reads in Letter 19 to Delphinus, section 2, following the Psalter’s translation from the Hebrew; whereas in four other Psalters and in Saint Augustine’s Commentary on the Psalms, “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies” is read four times—in verses 8, 25, 21, and 31.] [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 106:8], and let us glory in his praise [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 105:47], not in our own.

For, as the prophet says, if there is anything good in us, it is from him; and if there is anything best, it is from his majesty [Note: [Col. 0375D] We have added the particle “in” from the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and the edition of Chiffl., which read “if there is anything good in us, it is from him; and if anything best, it is his.”]. For “he made us, and not we ourselves” [Note: [Col. 0375D] Psalm 99:3]. Therefore Paul also says: “What do you have, O man, that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0375] 1 Corinthians 4:7]. In this he urges that “the one who glories should glory in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0375C] 1 Corinthians 1:31].

Therefore our distress is now light when we seem to be praised, since we are conscious of no good of our own, so that the one who praises us may press upon us as though we recognized it with embarrassment. For we know that it is not we ourselves who are being proclaimed, but the gifts and works of divine goodness. If any good is seen or believed to be in us, it belongs to him who alone is good [Note: [Col. 0375] Matthew 19:17], and from whose fullness we all receive [Note: [Col. 0375] John 1:16], being sprinkled according to the capacity of our merit or faith. For the dew that comes from him is health for us, and we rejoice in his showers [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 64:11].

Therefore even this error by which you praise us will be harmless to us. Moreover, such devout faith will heap up an abundant reward for you, because, in judging us to have been made good—though we regard ourselves as wicked and as perverse members of this world’s depraved generation—you believe in almighty God, who is able to justify the ungodly, bring the dead to life, illumine darkness, and make crimson white [Note: [Col. 0375] Isaiah 1:18].

11. Therefore pray earnestly that we may receive a heart worthy of God for so great a mouth or gift of God; and that, having received contempt for patrimony, we may also receive contempt for ourselves. For we walk along a narrow road and, as it were, walk precariously on a suspended rope; unless we set our feet with a sure balance, so that we do not turn aside to the right or the left, the enemy will easily drive us into the ruin of one side or the other. Therefore Wisdom sings to us in Solomon: “Do not turn away from the Lord, lest you fall” [Note: [Col. 0375] Sirach 2:7.]. For the Lord Christ himself is the way, the truth, and the life [Note: [Col. 0375] John 14:6.], who says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” [Note: [Col. 0375] Proverbs 4:23.], since through the very paths of the virtues we can slip into vices. Unless, as I have said, we direct the movements of our minds and weigh them with a sure steadiness, we shall take pride from humility itself; and the appearance of piety will vanish if conceit steals in under the praise of poverty. And what will it profit us to have done without riches if we remain rich in vices?

Therefore, we ask you not to flatter us on the basis of that word of the Lord, “Sell what you possess,” since we have done so; for greater is what follows: “And come, follow me” [Note: [Col. 0375] Matthew 19:21.]. It is easy to see how great a thing it is to follow Christ, so that a human being may imitate God. But you also know this: “God has spoken once; I have heard two things” [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 61:12.]; for this saying too, like almost all divine Scripture, opens into a forked path: “Go and sell all that is yours.” For we possess not only money and estates, external goods, but also the inward riches of our soul, which truly constitute our substance. To sell this—to alienate it from ourselves—is a greater victory, the greater the difficulty of separating what is innate from what has been added, and of tearing away what is fixed within rather than casting off what is attached externally.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] We have corrected this from the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition, in which *mutat* stands for *vincit*. Previously it read: “For if he conquers himself,” which made no sense.]

He conquers and overcomes himself who renounces his own ways and disowns himself, so that he may fulfill that most powerful word of God: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” [Note: [Col. 0375] John 12:25.]. Remembering these words of the Lord, let us pour out our soul into him, and he himself will nourish us, cherish our life hidden in himself, and reveal himself with glory—provided that we pray for this same soul at the opportune time, now in this world. “For in hell, who will confess to you?” [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 6:6.] Let us die to sins here, lest we live there in punishments. For the death called the second death is nothing other than a life of punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] Thus we restored the reading from the same manuscripts. In Rosweyde’s edition: “we shall pour out.”]

248 12. Let us therefore beware of the lower hell, where Gehenna will torture body and soul, while the sinner’s soul dies eternally, yet sensation remains and the material of corruption endures. For the dead too, as it is written, will rise incorruptible [Note: [Col. 0375] 1 Corinthians 15:52.], not with the immortality of glory but of punishment. “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0375] Romans 7:24.] The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 23:8.], who broke iron bars [Note: [Col. 0376D] In accordance with the Greek text, the Vulgate, the Cluniac, Nolan, and Viennese manuscripts, and Chifflet’s edition, we have corrected *ferreos* (“iron”). Rosweyde’s edition previously had *aereos* (“bronze”).] [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 106:16.], and humbled the slanderer [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 71:4.], so that he might raise me from the gates of death, so that I might recount his wonders at the gates of the daughter of Zion [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 9:12 and 15.]. May the Lord bless you from Zion; may you see the good things of Jerusalem; and may you pray for us all the days of your life [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 127:5.], so that our common portion may be in the land of the living [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 141:6.].

## LETTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 0377] Formerly numbered 26, part 2; the letter formerly numbered 41 is now 4. Written and sent with the preceding letter around the year 405.]

Paulinus had been warned by Sanctus to prepare his lamp diligently while there was still time. Taking this as his occasion, he develops the Gospel parable of the lamps and of the five wise and five foolish virgins with great piety and ingenuity.

### 1

We read on the back of the letter the list of letters that you indicated were mine [Note: [Col. 0377D] Thus the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition; Rosweyde’s edition has “you judged.” The Nolan manuscript has “you indicated.”]. In truth, I was so forgetful of nearly all of them that I would not have recognized them as mine had I not trusted your letters. From this I received an even greater proof of your affection, because I realized that I was better known to you than to myself.

I rejoice that I have received the hymns I had desired. By this gift, holy brother, you reminded me to prepare my lamp diligently while there was still time, lest I be shut out with the foolish if I did not meet the bridegroom with the wise. Pray, moreover, that our souls may be both virgins and fruitful: virgins without sterility, fruitful without corruption.

For by this mystery also, in the Law, the man who did not give seed in Israel was accursed; and in the Gospel the wise virgin is called such [Note: [Col. 0377D] We have added the word “is called” from the Cluniac manuscript and Chifflet’s edition.] because, having procured oil, she awaits the bridegroom’s arrival with vigilant care, her lamp anointed [Note: [Col. 0377D] Thus we have restored the reading from the Nolan and Vatican manuscripts. The very true reading is taken from Matthew 25 and is confirmed by section 2 and Letter 23, section 42. Other manuscripts have “having anointed her face,” less appropriately; for Christ did not command in the Gospel that the virgins awaiting the bridegroom’s arrival should anoint their faces, but that they should have oil in their lamps.] and burning, and already kindles for him, when he comes, a light that cannot be extinguished, fed by rich fuel.

### 2

Therefore let our mind be fruitful for God and bring forth the fruits of life in good works. Let the spirit also be a virgin, so that it is corrupted by no enticement of the world and remains undefiled by every stain of vice. For those foolish virgins seem to me to be souls that are sterile in virtues [Note: [Col. 0377] Matthew 25:3.], while those wise virgins are souls incorrupt in vices.

Finally, five are assigned to each of the two classes of virgins, so that it may be understood to refer to the integrity or corruption of the human senses. For we are all endowed with five senses, through which we have received either life or death. Concerning these the grieving prophet says: “Death entered through your windows” [Note: [Col. 0377] Jeremiah 9:21.].

Let us block those windows with the fear of God, so that we may be deaf and blind to all the forms and voices of this world. Let us hedge our ears with thorns against an evil tongue and seductive melodies [Note: [Col. 0377] Sirach 28:28.]. Let us turn our eyes away, lest they see vanity [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 118:37.]. Let us also block our nostrils, lest we draw in the odor of death from the corruption of this world. Nor should disease enter through taste by the lure of the appetite, and the foods of desires [Note: [Col. 0378D] The Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition have *cibus* (“food”), less appropriately.] weaken the strength of self-restraint. Nor should we flatter the body with soft clothing, nor allow illicit touches and embraces to tear apart our fleshly limbs, improperly handled beneath delicate coverings [Note: [Col. 0378D] The Viennese manuscript and Chifflet’s edition have *descateant*, mistakenly. The Cluniac manuscript has *descatent*.].

Thus it will come about that, in each of us, all five senses remain wise virgins, chaste and imbued with the faithful oil of teaching; having stored oil in their vessels, they will rest in secure expectation, soon and easily ready to prepare their lamps when they are awakened by the first commotion of the approaching bridegroom.

For among the vast populations of the Church, in which not only virgins—whose number is nevertheless countless—but also married women and widows are seen to differ in their conduct and their fruits, I do not think that the five foolish virgins and the equal number of wise virgins have been set forth for any other reason than this: each class represents a different person within the totality of the people, while the number is contained individually in everyone according to the interpretation stated above. Each person has within himself either foolish or wise virgins, according to the quality of his senses: where the senses are prudent, virginity is wise; where they are inert, it is foolish.

For this reason the foolish, like the wise, are likewise called virgins despite their great difference from one another: according to the flesh, virginity is sterile and unfruitful; according to the spirit, fruitful chastity is present.

Therefore the wise do not have sterile virginity, because they are wise; nor do the foolish have fruitful virginity, because they are foolish. Their form seems to me to be the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God, and the wisdom of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0377] 1 Corinthians 3:19.], which is truly a foolish virgin [Note: [Col. 0378D] The Cluniac manuscript and Chifflet’s edition have: “because it is not subject to the law and wisdom of God. Its lamp is easily extinguished.”], because it is not joined and subject to the law [Note: [Col. 0377] Romans 8:7.] and wisdom of God. Its lamp is easily extinguished [Note: [Col. 0377] Proverbs 20:20.], because it has no oil of truth; it is empty of the Holy Spirit, by whom the inner eye is illumined and the head of the soul is enriched with oil [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 140:5.], that is, our faith, for which oil is the infusion of heavenly teaching [Note: [Col. 0377] Song of Songs 1:2.].

### 3

Therefore let the oil of the sinner not enrich our head, nor let dying flies destroy the oil of sweetness. Let Christ always be our head, and let the oil never fail from our head, because “his name is ointment poured out.” Then we shall be wise virgins with all our senses perfected [Note: [Col. 0378D] The Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition have “with all our senses perfected.” Both readings are good.], if the Wisdom of God remains in us, through which fruitful virginity was also created in the body.

I weary you excessively, and presume too much upon the patience of your affection. But I ought to listen to Solomon speaking in the Wisdom of God, so that, even to those most beloved, I may advance the foot of my word more sparingly, lest they grow satiated and hate me [Note: [Col. 0379D] The Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition have: “I ought to listen to Solomon speaking in the Wisdom of God.”]. Yet I know that just as no one can hate his own inward parts, so neither can you hate our humility, which you have mingled with your own inward parts.

May the peace, love, grace, and humility of Christ the Lord Most High abound in you, blessed brothers, rightly venerable [Note: [Col. 0379D] Rosweyde’s edition has “and most beloved,” and adds: “Farewell in the Lord.”] and most beloved.

## LETTER XLII

[Note: [Col. 0379] Formerly numbered 32; the letter formerly numbered 42 is now 6. Written around the year 405.]

He rejoices that he has gained the friendship of Florentius, bishop of Cahors; he commends him and asks his prayers, while interweaving splendid praises of Christ.

To the most blessed and rightly venerable [Note: [Col. 0379D] Thus the Regius, Vatican, and Viennese manuscripts and the editions of Badius, Grinæus, and Rosweyde—and correctly so, since Paulinus, not yet a bishop, wrote to a bishop. The editions of Gravius and Schottus have “brother.”] father FLORENTIUS (see note 184), PAULINUS.

### 1

We rejoice in the Lord that we have been visited by the letters of your holiness and summoned to accept, through the sudden gift of God, the full confidence of your friendship as though it were long-standing, although previously we had enjoyed neither acquaintance nor favor with you. “Wine and a friend grow old together, and you will drink it with pleasure” [Note: [Col. 0379D] Sirach 9:15.]. Behold, your holiness has surpassed this saying of the prophet: you have begun to love us with such perfect affection that, at the first novelty of this alliance, you have given us the sweetness of an established love. We do not need to wish for an increase of affection whose fully ripened maturity we experience already in its abundant beginnings.

Thus we can compare the abundance of your soul to great springs, which, bursting forth with a widely poured-out mouth at their source, are immediately rivers at their birth.

Blessed, therefore, is the Lord, who has caused such grace to abound over our sins that, although we were not worthy even of your acquaintance, he has enriched us with your love; and, though until now we lacked the lesser good of bodily acquaintance with you, he has granted us so much greater a gift in you, by how much spirit is a nobler substance in a human being than flesh.

Therefore our heart rejoices, and with a mouth filled with joy we say: “The Lord has done great things for us” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 125:3.], because you have gone before us with the blessing of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 20:4.], through holy words and, like silver purified and tested [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 11:7.], by visiting us, as I have said, and rousing us from the stagnation of our laziness to observe your affection.

In this we were not sleeping in drowsiness, but were silent in ignorance. Therefore let the name of the Lord be blessed [Note: [Col. 0379] Job 1:21; Psalm 112:2; Psalm 103:31.], and let him rejoice also in this work of his mercy, by which, to those who were ignorant of your face in the flesh, he has shown instead that form of your mind in which you have been more beautifully fashioned in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0380D] Paulinus has almost the same wording in Letter 13 to Pammachius, section 2. Yet these words are found neither in the Septuagint nor in the Vulgate, where the passage speaks of a person’s entrance and declares something about him.]

For, he says, “a man’s speech reveals him, and the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” [Note: [Col. 0379] Matthew 12:34; Luke 6:45.].

### 2

Your speech, seasoned with apostolic salt, expressed to us the flavor of the grace given to you [Note: [Col. 0379] Colossians 4:6.]. From the drops falling from your lips we tasted how sweet the Lord is in you [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 33:9.], you who have been made and set as head of the people, chosen from among the sheep to be a man of the flock, so that you might rule the sheep of his pasture, he who laid down his life for his sheep [Note: [Col. 0379] 1 Samuel 15:17; 1 Samuel 16:11; Psalm 77:70; John 10:15.].

The same one, both lamb and shepherd, will rule us forever: he made us sheep from wolves, and is now the shepherd of these sheep for their protection, for whom he was a lamb offered in sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0379] John 1:29; Isaiah 53:7.].

This Lord and God of ours, therefore, who was seen on earth and lived among human beings [Note: [Col. 0379] Baruch 3:38.], is, for our sake, sheep and shepherd in us, because he rules us within by an invisible staff and saving rod. Thus even if we walk in the shadow of death, we do not fear evil, because God is with us [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 22:4.], that Emmanuel [Note: [Col. 0379] Isaiah 7:14.], the Lord of majesty and the son of a handmaid—one by nature, the other by becoming [Note: [Col. 0380D] The word “other” has been restored twice from the Regius manuscripts, while the Viennese manuscript and Rosweyde’s edition have “one by nature, the other by becoming.”].

He is at once the creator and redeemer of humanity, God from God, human being for humanity; Son of God before the ages, son of man for the world [Note: [Col. 0379] Matthew 1:16; Luke 2:7.]; the form of a servant for the freedom of servants; and he became poor so that by his poverty he might enrich the poor [Note: [Col. 0379] 2 Corinthians 8:9.]. For he is rich toward all in every good thing [Note: [Col. 0379] Romans 10:12.]; he is fulfilled in all things [Note: [Col. 0379] Ephesians 1:23.], the fullness of divinity [Note: [Col. 0379] Colossians 2:9.], the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far away upon the sea [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 64:6.], our saving God, mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus [Note: [Col. 0379] 1 Timothy 2:5.], who is in the glory of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0379] Philippians 2:11.], God blessed above all forever.

### 3

This is the one who graciously admitted you into the lot of his apostles [Note: [Col. 0379] Acts 1:20; Colossians 1:12.], so that by their craft you might become a fisher of human beings [Note: [Col. 0379] Matthew 4:19.] and draw out with the hook of saving speech from the bitter and deep waves of this world a catch for God, destined to be given life rather than destroyed—as indeed you do every day.

This is the God who made you a helper in his building and cultivation [Note: [Col. 0379] 1 Corinthians 3:9.], who deigned to insinuate the love of our humility into the height of your soul through the humility of your heart, because without doubt, through the gentleness of a sheep and the innocence of a lamb, you have deserved to become a shepherd.

This God, I say, who deigns to make you one who loves us, will act not according to evil desert but according to the riches of his goodness. Thus may aid for us from the protection of your prayers, and reward for you from your great love even for lesser neighbors, be increased [Note: [Col. 0379] Matthew 25:40.]. May he make you perpetually mindful of us and mingle concern for our salvation with all your prayers and offerings, lest this great outpouring of your affection—in which we glory in the Lord—become an offense to us if we cover ravenous beasts of untamed senses with the clothing of sheep [Note: [Col. 0381] Matthew 7:15.].

Pray, therefore, until you prevail, that our heart may be blameless in the sight of the Lord, so that we may not be put to shame or dragged along with those who speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts [Note: [Col. 0381D] Psalm 27:3.]. Let us be of one mind in tongue and thought; let us believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto life [Note: [Col. 0381] Romans 10:10.].

Only then will the devotion with which you love us return fruitfully to you, if your prayer for us is so effective that, transformed from our earthly appearance into your likeness, we bear with equal truth the image of the heavenly human being [Note: [Col. 0381] 1 Corinthians 15:49.].

### 4

Then we shall truly be blessed by your love if you obtain that we not be unlike your love. Yet in this we do not extend our desire arrogantly, as though we hoped to reach the summit of your merit. Rather, enclosed within the goal of salvation, may we follow the footprints of truth along a straight path, according to the form of your faith; and may our end itself be what our beginning is—the head and foundation of his body, Christ the rock [Note: [Col. 0381] Revelation 1:8; Ephesians 1:22; 4:15 and 5:23; Colossians 1:18; 1 Corinthians 3:11; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Matthew 7:24; Luke 6:48.].

That rock follows us, thirsting for righteousness amid the deserts of this world, with a continuous spring, and refreshes us with sweet drink, lest we be burned by the heat of carnal desires. That is the rock upon which a house, once established, does not collapse; that is the rock from which, when its side was pierced by the lance, water and blood flowed [Note: [Col. 0381] John 19:34.], so that it might pour forth for us together saving springs: the water of grace and the blood of the sacrament, which is both the fountain of our salvation and its price.

253 ### 5

But woe to me, a sinner! How far have I advanced—or rather, how far have I slipped? While I address you at length, seeking to earn your protection for my sins, or rather against my sins, when you devote yourself to prayer, I heap up through my loquacity the very burden that I ask to have diminished by your prayers, as though I had forgotten the written word: “You will not escape sin through much speaking” [Note: [Col. 0381D] Thus the Septuagint and Saint Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, book 3, article 103.] [Note: [Col. 0381] Proverbs 10:19, according to the Septuagint.].

And what shall I do? With what mouth shall I ask to be cleansed? By what reasoning will you defend me, when knowingly and deliberately I have committed what contradicts the prophetic word, so that by the sin of many words I have injured both myself and wearied your holiness?

I shall cling entirely to this offense, nor will even your prayer be able to cover me unless you yourself first forgive me this fault of my injury to you; and, as blessed Job was commanded to do for his talkative friends [Note: [Col. 0381D] Thus the Regius and Vatican manuscripts together with four printed editions. The Viennese manuscript and Grinæus’s edition have: “as blessed Job was commanded …”], offer God a sacrifice of reconciliation on my behalf [Note: [Col. 0381] Job 42:8.].

For I claim so much from your affection that I presume this excess of speech will, through your indulgence, pass harmlessly for me; I do not doubt that you possess as much patience as you possess love.

## LETTER XLIII (C)

[Note: [Col. 0381] Formerly numbered 35; the letter formerly numbered 43 is now 50. Written in the year 406, around the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.]

He excuses Victor for having returned late, attributing it to the winter weather and Victor’s poor health. Then, with outstanding humility, he refers back to Desiderius the priest the interpretation of the patriarchal blessings that had been proposed to him; and he himself wisely explains the curse pronounced by the Lord upon the fig tree.

To the holy and rightly venerable brother, and most desired [Note: [Col. 0381D] The Viennese manuscript has “most desired”; the Regius manuscript bears this heading: “Here begins the second letter to Desiderius.” Nevertheless, the first letter to Desiderius, which Paulinus mentions at the beginning of this Letter 43, is absent from the Regius manuscript, and this letter is missing. See *Life*, chapter 47, sections 1 and 3.] Desiderius (see note 185), desired by my desires, PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners, send greetings in Christ the Lord.

### 1

Long ago we had given brother Victor a brief letter for you (this letter is not extant), and I wanted him to deliver it also to your holiness, so that it might itself testify to its bearer that his delay among us was not voluntary.

This was the reason for its brevity: shortly after his arrival, Victor, hastening back from us to you, had hardened himself with such determination to resume his journey that he scarcely allowed us the opportunity to write even a brief letter to you.

Meanwhile, as he was setting out, sudden obstacles in circumstances drew him back, since winter closed navigation and fear closed the roads [Note: [Col. 0382D] The Regius and Viennese manuscripts have “closed.”]. Hindered and recalled by these things, he yielded to necessity and imposed a long delay, although, when asked to postpone his departure, he had refused to postpone it out of love. During these delays he was also ill, and indeed suffered so severely that, brought back from the gates of death, he spent more time recovering his health than the illness itself had lasted.

Afterward, when the feast of the apostles was already near, we thought it inhuman to send him away. Thus we added, by our own decision, this brief delay to the longer delays that he had given to the necessities mentioned above, so that, after celebrating the apostolic solemnity as a companion in our vows and annual journey, he might return to you as the messenger of this business of ours.

### 2

Certainly, we composed the letters he has for our blessed brother Severus at different times, according to the urgency of each departure, as their varied style will show. The shorter letters (those letters have perished) Victor demanded as though he were in a hurry and standing at the threshold of departure; the longer ones we wrote once we had begun to feel secure about his lengthy stay, with our minds relaxed and released into leisure [Note: [Col. 0382D] The Viennese manuscript has “we took care.”].

Our brother Severus had written to us that we should send him back to you immediately, and had fixed the time in such a way that he would be returned in time for the vintage season. Since we were unable to obey him in this, we tried at least to offer obedience in this form: that, if he did not receive Victor as arriving in the same year he had expected, he might nevertheless receive him as arriving at the same season he had ordered.

If he does not wish to attribute Victor’s delay to the necessities I have explained, let him charge to my fault the fact that Victor remained behind. Yet Victor owes even his delayed return to Severus’s prayers, because, when he was already completely prostrated by illness, I hoped for his recovery from Severus’s faith, whereas I despaired of it on the basis of my own merits.

Through these events I saw Victor’s innocence being scourged, so that my iniquity might be punished in him, since divine justice was taking vengeance on what was wrong in my love. Love also stirred punishment within me, so that I might endure, with compassion in my inward parts and soul, the affliction that this man, united with me in spirit, suffered in his body.

### 3

As for what you had written to me through him, seeking sweet and abundant water in a bitter and dry stream [Note: [Col. 0383] James 3:11.], I return it to be explained by your grace rather than by mine. For I confess that I have not dared even to touch with my finger the weight of such names and mysteries.

I have read that “wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” [Note: [Col. 0383] Wisdom 1:4.]. Therefore, conscious of my wickedness, I could not presume upon divine revelation, since my dark heart could not contain the light of understanding.

But you, blessed man, a clean vessel fit for God: if you have received an understanding of that blessing with which the patriarch, illumined in bodily blindness by the prophetic spirit, addresses his sons, explain to me in your reply the mysteries of the kingdom and the sacraments hidden from the ages [Note: [Col. 0383] Genesis 49:2.] and revealed for the ages in Christ Jesus.

In him the varied form of all the saints converges: he is represented in the patriarchs, speaks in the prophets, works in the apostles, and is fulfilled in all things in all [Note: [Col. 0383D] Thus the Regius manuscript together with the editions of Gravius and Schottus. Other copies have “he fills all things.” Paulinus also uses *is fulfilled* elsewhere instead of *fills*, see Letter 40, section 9, and Letter 42, section 2.], because in him the whole fullness was pleased to dwell [Note: [Col. 0383] Colossians 1:19 and 2:9.], who is the beginning and the end of all things [Note: [Col. 0383] Revelation 1:8.].

But if you have not yet received this—perhaps because, while you believe that the gifts granted to me, your neighbor, are already prepared in your own ready storehouse, you have delayed asking the Lord for them specifically—then ask, and you will receive according to your faith and your soul. The purer it is in its members, the more lively it is in understanding; and the cleaner it is in heart, the more capable it is of Christ, who is possessed by the humble and seen by the pure in heart [Note: [Col. 0383] Isaiah 66:2; Matthew 5:8.].

### 4

But so that you may bear with less displeasure having been deceived in your opinion of me by my poverty, consider that you have suffered from me what the Lord himself suffered from that fig tree to which he approached hungry and, finding no fruit, struck it with the word of his mouth. Thus what had been barren by the Lord’s blessing [Note: [Col. 0383D] *Benedicto*, that is, “by blessing,” so that it corresponds to the curse that follows. The Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Schottus’s edition mistakenly have “blessed by the Lord.”] became dry through his curse [Note: [Col. 0383] Matthew 21:19; Mark 11:14.].

But I beg your brotherhood: although you have found me like that unfortunate tree, do not strike me with a similar word, lest I dry up completely and, empty of the fruit I owe, be stripped even of the covering of leaves—that is, the foliage of grace [Note: [Col. 0383] Ezekiel 18:31.] (see Song 32, verse 46, and Letter 30, section 4).

But then, reflecting that the Lord is merciful and compassionate and wills no one to die in death [Note: [Col. 0383D] Thus the Vatican and Viennese manuscripts with Grinæus’s edition: “that is, he does not wish anyone to die an eternal death, although he dies naturally.” Other manuscripts have: “he does not wish one who is dying to die.”], and that in cursing the tree he condemned not his own creation, but the tree’s defect, the enemy of his planting [Note: [Col. 0384D] We have corrected this from the Viennese manuscript. The correction is confirmed by Letter 40 to Sanctus and Amandus, section 7: “a flying creature hostile to serpents.” Previously it read “the fault of the planting.”], I ask you instead to curse my sterility, so that no fruit may ever grow from it and fruit may be able to grow from my very self for God.

For the destruction of my sterility is beneficial to me, so that the fruitfulness of the Lord’s planting may revive in me. As the vice by which I am made unfruitful dies, may I grow green again for my cultivator through the return of good will, so that, when the Lord hungers for my life, he may himself find me offering him the fruits owed to him on fertile branches.

### 5

But in this same tree Mark added the basis of a significant question. While the other evangelists speak in agreement of the cursed and withered fig tree, he said something deeper. After stating that the Lord did not find fruit on that tree, he added what seems to excuse the tree, saying: “For it was not the season for it to bear fruit” [Note: [Col. 0383] Mark 11:13.].

If this is so, the tree seems to have been cursed without cause. It was free from the fault of sterility if, because the season of the year was not yet right, it did not have fruit ready—not unfruitful through defect, but unripe because of the season.

But what the Apostle says about cattle we can also apply to wood, so that we may say: “Is God concerned about trees?” [Note: [Col. 0383] 1 Corinthians 9:9.] It was certainly written for our sake, since God always wishes to find his food in us. For he has a field and a vineyard in us. In his threshing floor he winnows us; in us he cleanses the grain; in us he separates the chaff [Note: [Col. 0384D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “scatters.” See note 186.]; he burns the weeds [Note: [Col. 0383] Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17.].

Therefore, in that tree he hungered for the salvation of the human being and sought from humanity the fruit owed to him. Yet when he came to what was his own, his own people did not receive him [Note: [Col. 0383] John 1:11.]; and the barren synagogue of the unbelieving Jews did not return the harvest of faith that he had sown among them through the Law and the Prophets.

He came to their tree, seeking from the children of his planting the sweet food of the expected shoot. But it, having withdrawn the fruits of piety, gave him gall for food [Note: [Col. 0383] Matthew 27:34; Mark 15:36.], and, when he asked for grapes, offered him thorns; it gave the very planter of the good vineyard, the true vine itself and the cluster of sweetness, acrid vinegar to drink [Note: [Col. 0383] John 15:1; Luke 23:36.].

Therefore their table was turned into a snare for them [Note: [Col. 0383] Psalm 68:23.], their grape became bitterness, and the wrath of dragons their incurable wine [Note: [Col. 0383] Deuteronomy 32:32, according to the Septuagint.].

### 6

But you, my brother, pray to the Lord that our vine may not spring from the vineyard of such people, since their shoot from the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts degenerated into the vineyard of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0383] Isaiah 5:7.].

Unless the Lord had left us, on the branches of the apostles and from the roots of the patriarchs, a nursery of life from which the salvation of the nations could sprout and in which the vein of blessed seed could endure, we should have been altogether like Sodom and Gomorrah in the fullness of wickedness [Note: [Col. 0383] Romans 9:29; Isaiah 1:7.].

But because it is the last hour [Note: [Col. 0385] 1 John 2:18.] and the axe has already been placed at the roots of the trees [Note: [Col. 0385] Luke 3:9.], threatening a just destruction to dry and wretched wood, I ask you to pray for indulgence and an extension of time for me.
