With death delayed, perhaps I may receive the sap of fruitfulness through your diligent love and the cultivation of my concern; may divine fear dig around my heart, and may necessary repentance enrich my root with the manure of humility [Note: [Col. 0385] Luke 13:8.].

Then, awakened to vigilant concern, may I stand ready at every hour [Note: [Col. 0385] Luke 12:40.], and, while the Lord is absent, remain fearful, so that I may be secure when he arrives. At every time, every day, may Christ find me fruitful for him—that is, may I never appear unripe for any work of his will.

But if, perhaps, in a season of anger he should desire his peace from me, may my mind not be unripe for harmony because of the bitterness of anger; nor may I wait for the sun to set upon my anger [Note: [Col. 0385D] The Viennese manuscript has “upon anger.”] [Note: [Col. 0385] Ephesians 4:26.], lest my life set, if evening closes the day before peace has extinguished my fury.

7. As for what I said about anger, understand it as having been said about every kind of vice. For I think this is what the Lord meant when he sought fruit from that tree before its proper season. Surely he who knows the secrets of the heart [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 43:22, according to the Septuagint], and who perceived human thoughts, did not fail to see what was placed before human eyes; nor was he inferior in human understanding, so as to be unaware of the season of the year known even to little children and to demand the fruit of autumn in spring. Rather, the Craftsman and Creator of our salvation, whose whole life and conduct on earth was for us a model of behavior and morals, [Col. 0385C] arranged his invisible purposes visibly for this reason, and in irrational creatures expressed for the rational soul the image of his own shaping [Note: [Col. 0385D] Thus emended from the Viennese manuscript. This correction is confirmed by Letter 44 to Aper and Amanda, no. 2: “Your letters have expressed to me the face of your heart.” Other manuscripts read *rationalis*, through the concurrence of the following letter *s* [Col. 0386D].], so that by the marked signs of his works and words he might instruct us in everything conducive to our salvation. This is what he wished the evangelist to make us understand by indicating that he had not sought fruit from the tree in its own season, so that every human being might recognize that he owes fruit to God at every season. For the good Lord, who prepares mortal humanity for immortality, already in this age wishes a person to assume the appearance of perpetuity, so that he may not bear fruit only at a particular season, but may be ripe for him at every season—he with whom, or in whom, he is to remain outside time.

## LETTER [Note: [Col. 0385] Formerly 31; the letter that was formerly 44 is now 45. It appears to have been written in the year 406.] XLIV. (C)

He most beautifully praises the power and sweetness of divine grace breathing through Aper’s letters, and no less charmingly celebrates the diligence of Amanda, formerly Aper’s wife and now his sister, through which she managed the household affairs and provided her husband with leisure for divine pursuits. At the same time he advises them how their children should be trained. From this letter it is clear how the wives of presbyters lived.

To the holy, deservedly venerable, and most beloved brothers APER and AMANDA, PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners. [Note: [Col. 0386D] In Rosweyde’s edition the words “and most beloved … sinners” are absent. Four printed codices have: “To the holy and deservedly venerable and most beloved brother Aper, Paulinus and Therasia.”]

### 1

Who would give me a fountain of your letters, so that I might answer your letters, woven together with the varied flowers of spiritual graces, and no less eloquent and abundant in divine speech than in scholarly discourse (see Letter 28, no. 5), flowing as though from the land promised by God with the milk of devotion and the honey of wisdom? You have sucked both honey and oil from the firm rock, that is, Christ the Lord, who is the foundation of the eternal house. Upon this foundation you have begun to build the edifice of salvation through living works, and you are endeavoring to build upon it not wood, hay, or straw, but gold, silver, and precious stones [Note: [Col. 0385] Deuteronomy 32:13; 1 Corinthians 10:4; 1 Corinthians 3:12]. For, laying aside with the old person the hardness, dryness, and frivolity of your former heart, you have become a moist tree, which, growing green beside the neighboring watercourses, will yield its fruit in its season [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 1:3], and will never be deprived of the honor of its leaves.

Your understanding is gold tested by fire, and your speech is silver purified sevenfold. Shining with spiritual grace, it brings forth the Lord’s pure utterances [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 11:7] from a pure heart and a tongue that reveals the heart. You preserve a good and firm treasure in an earthen vessel, though not in a fragile faith; for your mind is the vessel of the grace entrusted to you, and, strengthened within bodily frailty by the princely spirit [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 51:14], it provides a solid custody for the divine gift.

I am poor and sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 69:30]; how shall I answer the wisdom that commanded me to put my hand to the table of a powerful man (see note 187), on the condition that I should know myself thereby made a debtor to an equal provision? For you have become for me the table of a powerful man. You have placed before me rich foods that, while I was hungry, easily seized me into every aspect of your words, as into the varied tastes and sights of choice delicacies. Remembering my appetite more than my poverty, I dared to partake of what I cannot prepare in equal measure.

What, then, shall I do? From whom shall I ask or borrow either the furnishings with which I might, in worthy splendor, rival the banquet hall of a rich man, or the expenses with which I, a poor man, might feed the rich man (see poem 21, line 853)? Who will help me in the obligation of this debt except you, Lord Jesus, who always bind yourself as a debtor to every poor person who lends to you [Note: [Col. 0385] Proverbs 19:17], and promise that you will repay those who now have no ability to repay [Note: [Col. 0385] Luke 14:14]?

Come to my aid now, and, on account of my poverty, pay my debt to your Aper from your riches. Water his streams and multiply your offspring in him [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 65:11, according to the Roman and Old Psalters], so that in your house he may be like a fruitful olive tree [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 52:10], may blossom like a palm, and may multiply like a cedar of Lebanon.

### 2

But I shall return to your letters, in which I rejoice like one who has found abundant spoils [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 119:162]. Although I can return nothing comparable from my own words, nevertheless, as hungry people do when, after digesting the abundance of a sumptuous banquet, they begin again to hunger from their poverty, they console their hunger by remembering their former fullness and feed their empty soul with the present thought of the absent feast, so I shall weave this letter through a reconsideration of your speech and recount my delight, giving you nothing. I shall speak not so much of my wishes toward you as of my experience of you.

For your letters have expressed to me the face of your heart—those letters of good hope, letters of sincere faith, letters of pure charity. What love of the holiest kind they breathe! How sweetly and abundantly the fragrance of Christ diffuses through them! [Note: [Col. 0387D] In Augustine, Letter 27 to Paulinus, no. 3, the reading is: “How great an abundance of a sincere heart boils forth?”] How great an abundance of a sincere heart boils forth? How they breathe forth to us your thirst, and the longing and weariness of your soul for the courts of the Lord! What thanks they offer to God! What things they obtain from God! What spectacles of God’s graces flowering in you, and of virtues already at work, they offer to me as I read!

### 3

There the little ones—or even the grown children of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0387D] The Viennese manuscript reads “adults”]—are dashed against the rock [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 137:9]: namely, the vices of worldly confusion and pride, which faith, when it engages them, will overcome more easily if, by striking them against Christ at their beginnings, it forestalls them while their weakness is still developing.

There, too, the cedars of Lebanon, laid low upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 29:5] and raised up in the structure of the ark by the joining of charity, cleave the waves of this world with incorruptible strength. There Christ appears to have been aroused, calming the winds and the seas for you [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 8:26; Luke 8:24], so that he may guide the course of your direction toward his stability.

He already has passage in the ship of your body and a pillow in your heart, because there the sparrow has found a house for itself [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 84:4], and in you he has a place to lay his head [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 8:20].

There, too, your wife—not a leader toward softness or greed for her husband, but one who has led him back to continence and strength—has been restored into the bones of her husband [Note: [Col. 0387] Genesis 2:23]. [Note: [Col. 0387D] We have added *dux* (“leader”) from twenty-one manuscripts, against which Augustine’s Letter 27 in the Benedictine edition was compared. This word was absent, Sacchinus says, but the sense seemed to require it; Augustine’s Letter 32 (now 27), from which this most beautiful whole passage was taken, has it, with the praises which Augustine had given Paulinus and Therasia transferred to Aper and his wife.] In a great imitation in a great imitation of that divine marriage of God with the Church, she is wonderful [Note: [Col. 0387] Ephesians 5:32]. Christ’s charity has gathered and restored her into your unity [Note: [Col. 0387D] Augustine reads this way in Letter 32, no. 2, from which Paulinus drew this passage. Rosweyde’s edition had *reductam*, “led back,” instead of *redactam*, “gathered together.” Both readings are good.] and joins her to you with spiritual bonds all the stronger because they are chaste, as you have passed from your own body into his.

### 4

Blessed are you by the Lord, who made both one [Note: [Col. 0387] Ephesians 2:14–15], joining two in himself, he who alone does marvelous things [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 72:18], who transforms not only souls [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 23:3] but also affections, temporal things into eternal things. [Note: [Col. 0388D] So read the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. This reading is more elegant than the Vulgate, which has “changing temporal things into eternal.”] Behold, you remain the same spouses you were, but not spouses in the way you were spouses; you are yourselves, and yet not yourselves. And just as you no longer know Christ according to the flesh, so you no longer know one another according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0387] 2 Corinthians 5:16].

This is the change brought about by the right hand of the Most High [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 77:11], which, remaining itself, renews all things and turns the sea into dry land [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 66:6], constraining the streams of vices into the dryness of continence.

Blessed among women, and through this devotion also faithful and most acceptable to the Lord, she has set herself against the necessities of the world for your sake, like a tower fixed immovably upon a rock amid storms. Truly, founded upon that very rock on which a house built will not fall [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 7:24], with the solid footing of an energetic mind, she has become for you a tower of protection (or “of strength”) from the face of the enemy [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 61:4], breaking the waves and whirlwinds of the world by the opposition of her devoted service. Thus, withdrawn from the open sea, you may exercise a safe vessel of an unshaken mind in the harbor of the Church through continual meditation on heavenly studies and works, as though by a certain oar of salvation. [Note: [Col. 0388D] We have deleted the particle *in*, which is absent from the Vatican manuscript and Grin’s edition.]

“For bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but piety is profitable for all things” [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Timothy 4:8]. This has subjected you to Christ: you prefer to lie in the house of the Lord rather than to stand out in the tents of sinners [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 84:11]. And your fellow servant has pledged herself to bodily labors, from spiritual affection, for the sake of your soul [Note: [Col. 0388D] The Vatican and Viennese manuscripts, with Grin’s edition, read “in bodily labor, but with spiritual affection”], making her service the price of your freedom—not serving the world in worldly affairs [Note: [Col. 0387] 2 Timothy 2:4], but serving Christ, for whose sake she suffers the world, so that you may not suffer it.

Truly, according to the divine work and word, she has been made for your assistance [Note: [Col. 0387] Genesis 2:18]. With her orientation toward you, she depends upon your command; she stands in your position, walks in your footsteps, draws life from your soul, and gives herself for your life, so that she may be refreshed in your life [Note: [Col. 0387] Genesis 3:16]. She attends to the concerns of the world so that you need not attend to them [Note: [Col. 0388D] Here the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Grin’s edition add: “she attends to them so that you may attend to them”]; she appears to possess so that you may not be possessed by the world, but may be possessed by Christ.

It is not a discordant will that separates her from your purpose; rather—and this is more remarkable—a harmonious faith divides her in action while joining her in intention. For, managing without captivity of spirit the material burden of captivity in the freedom of the spirit, she has strengthened her hands for the work of virtue; she has extended her arms toward useful things, girded her loins firmly, and, not eating the food of idleness, she has become for you like a ship that brings merchandise from afar. By this necessary division she renders to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, so that through you she may minister to God the things that are God’s [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 22:21; Mark 12:17; Luke 20:25].

For when she has given the tax to whom tax is owed, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0387] Romans 13:7], then, opening her hands to the poor [Note: [Col. 0387] Proverbs 31:20, according to the Septuagint] and extending the fruit of her labor to the needy, she pays a spiritual tribute. She contributes the income from her possessions to the pay of your service, more eager for saving loss than for deadly profit.

“Such a woman—her husband’s heart trusts in her.” For she does good to her husband all the days of her life, and not evil, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0389] Proverbs 31:12–13, according to the Septuagint]. Therefore you are not anxiously occupied with what is done in your earthly house; you energetically and freely carry out what is done in the heavenly house.

Nor are you put to shame when you speak with your enemies in the gate [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 127:5], because the woman of wisdom—such as has been given to you—[Note: [Col. 0389D] So the manuscripts read: “that is, the woman of whom the wise man speaks in Proverbs.” The editions read “the wise woman.”] makes you watchful at the doors of the Church.

“She made double cloaks for her husband,” it says [Note: [Col. 0389] Proverbs 31:22, according to the Septuagint]. Does she not seem to weave for you these double cloaks, purple or linen garments for herself [Note: [Col. 0389D] Thus restored from the Viennese manuscript. Previously the text read “for you”?], when her faith doubles your grace because a good woman is a crown to her husband [Note: [Col. 0389] Proverbs 12:4]? And, in turn, your honor is purple for her, because, with the Lord’s grace moderating [Note: [Col. 0389D] The Vatican and Viennese manuscripts read “with the Lord’s grace tempering.” Both readings are accepted], clothed simply in the unity of faith, you put on one another through the working of spiritual virtues.

You are her head in Christ [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 Corinthians 11:3], and she is your foundation. Through her work your foot stands on the way of the Lord; and, made a participant with your head, she will be incorporated into the body of the Lord by the joint structure of faith. For, despite the diversity of your responsibilities, yet with the agreement of a harmonious mind and with the judgment of your purpose joined together [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Vatican manuscript reads “joined to the judgment of your purpose.” The Regius manuscript reads “to … a joined judgment.”], while you faithfully [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 Corinthians 9:17] and diligently exercise the stewardship entrusted to you as a multiplier of your master’s talents [Note: [Col. 0389] Matthew 25:15], she does not treasure on earth what she labors to produce from earthly things [Note: [Col. 0389] Matthew 6:19], but lends it at interest to your works rather than to the ruinous profits of greed [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Viennese manuscript and Grin’s edition read “lends it at interest.” Both readings are good].

Therefore “the fruit of her hands will be given to her, and her husband will be praised in the gates of the daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0389] Proverbs 31:31, according to the Septuagint], in the Lord. He prepares for you, from the different labor of the same work but with equal devotion, a harvest sown for a common reaping, so that on that day you may come together in rejoicing, bringing your sheaves [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 126:6]—she as the minister of the seed, and you as the minister of its sowing.

She will not be deprived of sharing your reward through the merit of this exchange, by which, obeying not her own will but your salvation, she demonstrates through the proof of this very work the judgment of her faith. She makes it sufficiently clear how much she judges contempt of the world preferable to its use: she has chosen spiritual things for you, preferring you to herself, rather than preferring this world to Christ.

### 5

May the Lord increase you and your children [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 115:14]. For the mercy of the Lord will raise up children for parents who have earned it [Note: [Col. 0390D] Thus emended from the Viennese manuscript. The previous reading was “has raised up.”], as it is written, and they will be enriched with the Lord’s goods.

I hope that, just as your wife is like an abundant vine at the sides of your house [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 128:3], overflowing for you with the fruits of devotion, so that a thousand may fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 91:7], so your children also may deserve to surround the Lord’s table with you like young olive plants. I think that you now feed them on the foods of divine wisdom and your good conduct, like young eagles being fed, so that they may learn already to consume and devour spiritually the flesh stripped of its prey by their parents—that is, the carnal hostilities that oppose the spirit—and then fly upward with the oars of their wings strengthened in virtues above.

Let them be brought up like the sons of the prophets, who, turning away from the tumultuous habitation of the city in order to compose the soul in the peace of silence, marked out secluded dwellings for themselves beside the bed of the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Regius manuscript, together with four editions, reads “peace,” incorrectly. The Viennese manuscript reads “the peace of silence,” turning away from the sea] [Note: [Col. 0389] 2 Kings 6:2].

Let them be consecrated like the sons of Aaron—not like those who, kindling strange fire for the Lord, were burned by divine fire [Note: [Col. 0389] Leviticus 10:1], fire of which they themselves were deprived—but like Eleazar and Ithamar, deservedly perpetual successors to their father’s dignity, because they were not degenerate heirs of holiness.

### 6

It seems to me that anyone kindles a strange fire who, lighting in the sanctuary of his heart the fire of some bodily or worldly desire, dares to approach the altars of the Lord. They receive only the kindling of that fire of which he says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire, if it has already been kindled?” [Note: [Col. 0390D] Paulinus consistently reads this way. The Vulgate has “unless it be kindled.”] [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 12:49]

With this fire, Lord Jesus, always kindle us, so that we may be enlightened in understanding and consumed in vices; for this fire alone, which comes from you, will resist the eternal fire.

Having hearts burning on the way of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 24:32], we kindle for the Lord not a strange fire but his own. Protected by this fire amid the fires of the world, like the boys in the furnace amid the flames hissing with violent force, we shall be sprinkled with dew [Note: [Col. 0389] Daniel 3:24], and amid the fires, which refresh us, we shall sing a hymn to the Lord while the Son of God sings with us [Note: [Col. 0389] Matthew 18:20]. For he himself said that he would always be present wherever two or three are in agreement.

Therefore we trust that he also dwells in the midst of your household, where in you and your children there is formed one assembly of numerous souls. We pray that you may join us to it—absent only in body, but present spiritually [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Viennese manuscript reads “joined together”—and water not only by your word but also by your prayer the little garden of our thirsty soul, which we cannot cultivate with our own hands because we are weak, nor with hired hands because we are poor. And we do not find the way by which we may seek your way, because we cannot dig and are ashamed to beg [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 16:3].

[Col. 0390D] 263 Therefore we need the help of your prayers all the more urgently. For who would hire useless laborers, or give to those who do not ask? Nevertheless, those who possess poor and uncultivated fields, when they have despaired of receiving fruit from their own labor or hand, turn all their hopes toward divine assistance; and often, when the result granted corresponds to their faith, religion compensating for diligence, pious prayers have helped those whom careful cultivation abandoned.

### 7

Pray, therefore, that the almighty Lord, who placed rivers in the desert, may turn our dry land into outlets of waters [Note: [Col. 0391] Psalm 107:33, 35]; may strike and break through the hardness of our heart, so that he may turn this rock also into a pool of water [Note: [Col. 0391] Exodus 17:6].

Would that he might sprinkle us with the dew [Note: [Col. 0391] Judges 6:37] with which he made that mystical fleece in the threshing floor [Note: [Col. 0391D] The Viennese manuscript reads “of the threshing floor.”]. For the dew that comes from him is health to us.

Pray, I say, that, having deigned to enter our little garden, he may command the north wind to rise and the south wind to come [Note: [Col. 0391] Song of Songs 4:16], so that, as they breathe vital breezes, our seedlings may live (see Letter 24, no. 18).

But if, having entered his vineyard, he finds our tree without fruit, may he spare it from being cut down; and, with mercy delaying the sentence, may he trust the gardener who promises that through his diligence fruit will be extracted from the barren fig tree [Note: [Col. 0391] Luke 13:8].

For the Lord himself, who intercedes for our sins and calls things that are not as though they were [Note: [Col. 0391] Romans 4:17], is powerful enough to make a fruitful tree even of us, the needy and dry, and to enrich the empty soul with the fatness of his word as with a basket of manure.

For it is written: “The regions of the desert will grow fat from his grace” [Note: [Col. 0391D] So the Old and Roman Psalters read, as do Hilary and Augustine in his commentary on the Psalms; they appear to have read ὄροι (*oroi*, “regions” or “mountains”) for ὄρη (*orē*, “mountains”). The Vulgate has “the beautiful places of the desert.” See note 192] [Note: [Col. 0391] Psalm 65:13, according to the Roman Psalter].

This basket of manure, which makes a barren tree fruitful, seems to me specifically to be spiritual humility. Through it, by distressing our heart with repentance for past vanity, we empty out what is vain and receive the sap of virtue; through it we, who were barren in works of righteousness, are made fruitful.

It is therefore good for us to enter our retreats and humble our soul in fasting—the fasting by which one abstains from the works of darkness—so that from the manure of this humility, which is despised by the world but dear to God, it may be raised up by him who lifts the needy from the earth and raises the poor from the dung heap [Note: [Col. 0391] Psalm 113:7].

The grace of God be with you.

## LETTER [Note: [Col. 0391] Formerly 44; the letter that was formerly 45 is now 3. It appears to have been written in the year 408, on 15 May.] XLV. (C)

Giving thanks to Augustine for a book or letter received from him, he continues his praise of the elder Melania and of her only son Publicola, recently deceased, and discusses certain matters concerning the future activity of the blessed in heaven after the resurrection.

[Col. 0391D] To the holy man of the Lord, most blessed, uniquely one in heart with us, and venerable father, brother, and master, AUGUSTINE, bishop: PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1

“Your word is always a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” [Note: [Col. 0391] Psalm 119:105]. Thus, whenever I receive letters from your most blessed holiness, I feel the darkness of my ignorance dispelled; and, as though the collyrium of illumination had been applied, I see more clearly with the eyes of my mind, once the night of ignorance has been driven away and the mist of doubt wiped off [Note: [Col. 0392D] Thus emended from the Phimarcon manuscript and the Benedictine edition; this is the most correct reading. Previously the text read *delectationis*, “of delight”]. Although I have often experienced this gift bestowed upon me through your letters, I did so especially through that little book of your recent letter, whose bearer was as welcome to me as he was worthy: our brother Quintus, a deacon and a man blessed by the Lord (see note 193). Though a long interval had elapsed since he had come to Rome, when, according to my customary annual practice, I had gone there after the Lord’s Passover to venerate the apostles and martyrs, he brought us the blessing of your lips.

Yet the time he had spent at Rome without my knowledge was effaced: he seemed to me wholly fresh from your presence. When I first saw him, I could scarcely believe that he had then just come to me from you, as he offered me in your words the full fragrance of your sweetness, fragrant with the chaste perfume of heavenly ointment. I confess, however, to your venerable unanimity that I could not read the book itself at Rome as soon as I received it. There was such a crowd there that I could neither examine your gift attentively nor enjoy it as I wished—that is, by reading it continually once I had begun. Therefore, as commonly happens, in the confident expectation of a prepared feast I restrained the hunger of my eager mind; and, although I held in my hand the breads of my desire in the book I was to devour—which, when I later devoured it, was most sweet to me both in mouth and belly—I easily held back my mouth, gaping for the honeycombs of your letters, in the sure hope of taking my fill. I did so until I left the City and devoted to this whole work the day which we spent at a stopping-place on the journey in the town of Formiae, so that I might feast freely on the spiritual delights of your letter, delivered from every dreg of care and the stifling of crowds [Col. 0392C] 265.

### 2

What then can I, humble and earthly, reply to this wisdom given you from above, which this world does not comprehend and which no one knows wisely unless he is made wise by the wisdom of God and speaks eloquently through God’s Word? Since, therefore, I have proof of Christ speaking in you [Note: [Col. 0391] 2 Corinthians 13:3], I will praise your words in God [Note: [Col. 0391] Psalm 56:11] and will not fear the terror of the night [Note: [Col. 0391] Psalm 91:5]. For in the spirit of truth you have taught me the wholesome moderation by which the mind may be governed amid the declining things of mortal life. By it you saw that the blessed mother and grandmother Melania wept at the bodily death of her only son, Publicola: with a silent grief indeed, yet not with a grief dry of maternal tears.

As one whose spirit was nearer to hers, or more equal to it, you understood her restrained and grave tears more deeply. Preserving the strength of a manly mind, you regarded from the likeness in your own heart the maternal heart of a woman perfect in Christ more fittingly and on equal terms. Thus you perceived that she wept first under the movement of natural affection, and then under the sting of a weightier cause: not so much because, in the human sense, she had lost in this present world her only son, who had died under the condition of mortality, as because he had been overtaken, almost, in worldly vanity. Since the ambition of senatorial rank had not yet left him, she grieved that he was not to be considered taken up in accordance with the holy covetousness of her vows, so as to pass from the glory of conversion to the glory of resurrection and to win, with his mother, a common rest and crown—if, in the life of this world, following his mother’s example, he had preferred the sackcloth to the toga and the monastery to the senate.

### 3

Nevertheless, that same man, as I think I have previously reported to your holiness [Note: [Col. 0393D] Thus the Phimarcon manuscript and the Benedictine edition; elsewhere: “I have reported, in accordance with the wish of your holiness”], departed enriched with such works that, if he did not wear the nobility of his mother’s humility in clothing, he nevertheless preferred it in his mind. For he was so gentle in character and humble in heart according to the Lord’s word [Note: [Col. 0393] Matthew 11:29] that he may deservedly be believed to have entered into the Lord’s rest: “For there is a remnant for the peaceable man” [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 37:37], “and the meek shall inherit the earth” [Note: [Col. 0393] Matthew 5:4], pleasing God in the land of the living [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 115:9].

Certainly he also fulfilled the Apostle’s saying not merely in the silent disposition of his mind but in visible offices of religion [Note: [Col. 0393D] Thus the Benedictine edition; Rosweyde’s edition has “religious”; Sacchinus, “of religion”]. Though he was a colleague in the rank and honor of the great men of this world, he did not, as one glorious upon earth, set his mind on high things [Note: [Col. 0393] Romans 12:16]; rather, as a perfect imitator of Christ, he condescended to the lowly and persevered all day in showing mercy and lending [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 37:26; Psalm 112:5]. Hence his seed has become mighty on earth [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 112:2], among those gods, the mighty of the earth, who have been greatly exalted [Note: [Col. 0393D] The word *gods* is added from the Benedictine edition after comparison with manuscripts] [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 47:10], so that even the blessed visitation of his family and household reveals the man’s holy merit. “The generation of the upright shall be blessed”: glory that does not fall away, and riches that do not slip away, are in his house [Note: [Col. 0393D] Thus the Benedictine edition; previously the text read “of the house”]—in the house built in heaven, not by the labor of hands but by the holiness of works.

But I refrain from recounting more about the memory of a man as dear to me as he was devoted to Christ, since I believe that in earlier letters I have already related not a few things about him; nor can I proclaim anything better or holier about the blessed mother of this son and the holy branches from the same root, Melania (see note 138), than your holiness has deigned to say and expound concerning her. For since I, a sinner with unclean lips, could say nothing worthy of her, being far from the merits of her faith and the virtues of her soul, you, that man of Christ, a teacher of Israel in the Church of truth [Note: [Col. 0393D] This word is inserted from the Benedictine edition; compare Paulinus, Letter 50 to Augustine, no. 2], were, by God’s grace providing something better, prepared as a worthier herald of a soul so manly in Christ: you could behold her mind, strengthened by divine power, with a kindred spirit, as I have said, and praise in worthier speech the piety mingled with her strength.

### 4

You have deigned to ask me what the activity of the blessed will be in that age after the resurrection of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0394D] We have deleted the word “our,” absent from the Phimarcon manuscript and the Benedictine edition and wrongly added in Rosweyde’s edition]. Yet I consult you, the spiritual teacher and physician, about the present state of my life, that you may teach me to do God’s wills, to walk in your footsteps after Christ, and first to die by that evangelical death [Note: [Col. 0394D] Thus the Phimarcon manuscript and the Benedictine edition; Rosweyde’s edition has “this evangelical death”], by which we anticipate bodily dissolution through a voluntary departure: withdrawing from the life of this world not by death, but by a judgment, though it is wholly full of temptations, or, as you once said to me, is wholly temptation.

Would that my ways might thus be directed after your footsteps, so that, following your example, I may loose the old shoe from my feet, break my bonds, and rejoice in freedom to run the way; thus I may attain that death by which you have died to this world in order to live to God [Col. 0394B], with Christ living in you. Both his death and his life are known in your body, heart, and mouth: your heart does not savor earthly things, nor does your mouth speak the works of men; rather, Christ’s word abounds in your breast [Note: [Col. 0393] Colossians 3:16], and the Spirit of truth is poured forth upon your tongue with the rush of the heavenly river, making glad the city of God [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 46:5].

### 5

What power produces this death in us except charity, which is strong as death [Note: [Col. 0393] Song of Songs 8:6, according to the Septuagint]? For it so obliterates and slays this world for us that, through affection for Christ, it accomplishes the effect of death. Turned toward him, we are turned away from this world; living for him, we die to the elements of this world. Nor do we make decrees as though living in the sight and view of those elements [Note: [Col. 0394D] The Phimarcon manuscript reads “and use”; Rosweyde’s edition has *decernimur*, “we are distinguished,” wrongly. We have emended to *decernimus*, “we decree,” as the reading must be; the reference is to Colossians 2:20: “If therefore you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why do you still make decrees as though living in the world?”] [Note: [Col. 0393] Colossians 2:20]. For our portion is Christ’s death; we do not attain his resurrection from the dead in glory unless, with the members and senses of the flesh mortified on the cross, we imitate his death in this world [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Thessalonians 4:3]. Thus we may no longer live by our own will, but by the will of him whose will is our sanctification, and who therefore died and rose again for us, so that we may no longer live for ourselves but for him who died and rose again for us. He gave us the pledge of his promise in his Spirit, just as he placed the pledge of our life in heaven in his body, which is the head of our body.

Therefore the Lord is now our expectation [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 39:8], and the substance made by him is with him, in him, and through him: he who was conformed to the body of our humility, in order to conform us to the body of his glory and seat us with himself in the heavens [Note: [Col. 0394D] Thus the Benedictine edition and Paulinus, Letter 11, no. 2. Rosweyde’s edition instead has: “who was conformed to the body of his glory, that with him …”] [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Thessalonians 4:16]. Accordingly, those found worthy of eternal life will be in the glory of his kingdom, that they may be with him, as the Apostle says, and remain with him, as the Lord himself said to the Father: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” [Note: [Col. 0395] John 17:24].

### 6

Without doubt this is what you have in the Psalms: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; throughout the ages they will praise you” [Note: [Col. 0395] Psalm 83:5]. I think, however, that this praise is to be uttered by the voices of those singing together—even though the bodies of the saints who rise again will be transformed, so that they will be like the Lord’s body as it appeared after the resurrection. In that body, certainly, a living image of the human resurrection shone forth, so that the Lord himself, in that very body in which he had suffered and risen again, might be a kind of mirror of contemplation for all.

When he had risen again in the same flesh in which he had died and been buried, he repeatedly displayed before the eyes and ears of human beings the full functions of all his members [Note: [Col. 0395C] The Phimarcian manuscript and the Benedictine edition have *collatus* (“displayed,” “presented”), by comparison.]. But if angels also, whose nature is simply spiritual, are said to have tongues with which they sing praises to the Lord their creator and never cease to give thanks, how much more will human beings—although their bodies after the resurrection will already be spiritual, yet with all the members of glorified flesh remaining, and with their forms and proportions preserved in every member—have tongues in their mouths and utter voices with their speaking tongues, by which they may express in words the divine praises, or the affections of their senses and joys [page 268]?

Perhaps the Lord will also add this to the grace and glory of his saints throughout the ages of his kingdom: that they sing with tongues and voices so much nobler as they will have advanced through blessed transformation toward a more blessed nature of their bodies. Thus, established already in spiritual bodies, they may perhaps speak not in human but in angelic and heavenly speech, such as the Apostle heard in paradise [Note: [Col. 0395] 2 Corinthians 12:4].

And perhaps for this reason he testified that those utterances were ineffable to a human being, because among the various kinds of rewards new tongues are already being prepared for the saints. Human beings of this age are not yet permitted to use them, so that those who are immortal may speak with tongues now suited to their glory. Of these it is said: “For they will cry out and sing a hymn” [Note: [Col. 0395] Psalm 64:14]—undoubtedly in the heavenly places, where they will be with the Lord and delight in the abundance of peace [Note: [Col. 0395] Psalm 36:11], rejoicing before the throne, casting bowls and crowns before the feet of the Lamb, and singing to him a new song. Joined to the choirs of angels, powers, dominions, and thrones, they too, with the cherubim and seraphim and those four living creatures [Note: [Col. 0395C] We have added from the Benedictine edition the words “singing together with an unceasing voice.”], will say with an unceasing voice: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” [Note: [Col. 0395] Psalm 6:3], and the rest, which you know.

### 7

This, then, is what I, that poor and needy man—that foolish and little one of yours whom, as a truly wise man, you are accustomed to bear—ask you to teach me concerning your knowledge or opinion on this matter. For I know that you have been enlightened by the spirit of revelation from that very leader and source of the wise, so that, just as you have come to know the past and see the present, you may also judge what you think about the voices of these heavenly creatures—or even of those who act above the heavens in the presence of the Most High—and by what instruments those everlasting voices are finally expressed.

Although the Apostle, by saying, “If I speak with the tongues of angels” [Note: [Col. 0395] 1 Corinthians 13:1], seems to have shown that they possess a speech proper to their nature, or, so to speak, to their race—a speech as much higher than human senses and utterances as the angelic creature and its rank surpass mortal inhabitants and earthly dwellings [Note: [Col. 0395C] Thus we emend the text from the Phimarcian manuscript and the Benedictine edition. Previously it read “in the heavens.”]—perhaps nevertheless he called the languages of angels “tongues” with reference to different kinds of voices and speech. He does the same when, discussing the variety of spiritual gifts, he counts kinds of tongues among the gifts of grace, thereby signifying that it was given as a sign that individuals might speak in the language of many nations.

But the voice of God, often sent forth to the saints from a cloud, shows that speech can exist without a tongue. For the tongue is a member of the body, small yet great [page 269]. But perhaps for this very reason—because God placed the function of the voice in this member—he also called the speech and voices of the bodiless angelic creature a “tongue,” just as Scripture customarily assigns the names of bodily members even to God according to the forms of his activity [Note: [Col. 0395C] The passage has been corrected from the Phimarcian manuscript; the Benedictine edition reads likewise. Previously it read: “because in this member, in which is the function of the voice, God can also create speech and voices in the body of angels, he called them a tongue”—an entirely erroneous reading. See what precedes in section 6.]. Pray for us, and teach us.

### 8

Our dearest and sweetest brother Quintus returns to us from you as slowly as he hastens to return from us to you. His urgency in demanding letters speaks through this letter, which is more frequently marked with erasures than composed in verses [Note: [Col. 0395C] That is, the urgency of the demander caused the sheet to be covered with erasures rather than to be a polished letter. The Benedictine edition reads: “excessive haste made the sheet”; this makes no sense. The author of the Gallican translation of Saint Augustine’s letters thought that *scheda* should be replaced by *schedia*, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts; but wrongly. Here *scheda* means a sheet of paper or an impromptu little book, not sufficiently polished, such as those we set aside as though we were going to reread them. See Quintilian, book 1, chapter 18, and Martial, book 4. Nor, in our view, should certain corrections by that translator be admitted in Saint Paulinus’s letters 3.2.1, 5.2, 3, and Saint Augustine’s letter 91.5, since in these passages the sense of our edition is excellent and supported by manuscript authority. Furthermore, concerning the letter 3 passage mentioned above, see letter 29.7, where Paulinus uses a similar expression in speaking of the priest Zechariah.], because of the urgency of the person who demanded it. He came to us on the day before the Ides of May to ask for written replies, and obtained permission to be sent away on the Ides before the sixth hour. Consider, then, whether by such testimony I have commended or accused him. For perhaps—or rather, without doubt—he will be judged more worthy of praise than blame, since from the darkness, which we are in comparison with your light, he hastened back most justly to his own light.

## LETTER XCV (formerly CCL). AUGUSTINE TO PAULINUS AND THERASIA (C)

[Col. 0397A]

Augustine, in reply to the preceding letter, discusses the condition of the present life, as well as the quality of the bodies of the blessed and the functions of their members after the resurrection.

(This letter is found in volume 33, column 351, of our *Patrologia*.)

## LETTER XLVI

[Note: [Col. 0397] Formerly 47; the letter formerly numbered 46 is now 7 and 8. Written around the year 408.]

### 274

He asks Ruffinus to teach him Greek letters. He admits that he did not translate Clement correctly and asks for an exposition of verse 11 of chapter 49 of Genesis.

### PAULINUS TO HIS BROTHER RUFFINUS, GREETINGS

#### 1

Even brief letters from your devoted friendship are a great refreshment to us, just as thirsty soil is revived by dew when rivers are scarce. Therefore, although your letter was brief, because it was yours and came through the boy who is the child of us both, we confess that it restored us [Col. 0397B]. Yet our affection is troubled again, because even now, amid the heat of anxiety and uncertainty about delays, you have decided to travel to Rome. May the Lord grant that we may soon rejoice in the outcome of our affairs through the Lord: so that, just as we sympathize with those who are anxious, we may also share in their happiness, and may nevertheless begin to hope for the fruit of your presence if you begin to be certain about your own decision—or about the Lord’s will concerning you.

#### 2

As for what you deign to urge upon me with that affection by which you love us as you love yourself—that I should apply myself more attentively to the Greek language—I gladly accept the advice, but I cannot fulfill it, unless perhaps the Lord assists my desires so that I may enjoy your companionship for a longer time. For how can I make progress in an unknown language [page 275] if there is no one from whom I can learn what I do not know?

I believe that in my translation of Saint Clement [see note 195], besides the other failures of my talent, you particularly noticed this poverty of my ignorance: that I translated certain passages whose words I could neither understand nor express by grasping their sense—or, to speak more accurately, by guessing it [see note 196]. All the more, therefore, do I need the mercy of God, so that he may grant me a fuller supply of you; for to a poor man it will be riches to gather, with the eager mouth of a starving heart, the crumbs falling from a rich man’s table.

#### 3

At the time when this writing was being composed, that passage from Genesis happened to fall under my eyes while the appointed reading was being made—the chapter in which Judah is blessed by Jacob [Note: [Col. 0397] Genesis 49]. Since the Lord had provided this most appropriate opportunity, I thought it right, after so long, to knock at the doors of your heart.

Therefore, if you love me—or rather, because you love me greatly—I ask you to write to me and explain to me as you understand it the blessing of the patriarchs. And if you yourself know anything difficult to understand in them and worthy of knowledge, I would have you make it known to me. In particular, however, I ask about the passage in which he says: “Binding his colt to the vine, and the colt of his she-ass to the tendril” [Note: [Col. 0397D] Nobilius notes in his scholia on the Septuagint that Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine read *ad vitem* (“to the vine”), whereas the Septuagint and Saint Cyprian, book 1 *Against the Jews*, read *ad helicem* (“to the tendril”). In Greek: τῇ ἕλικι. The Vulgate has *ad vitem*.] [Note: [Col. 0397] Genesis 49:11, according to the Septuagint]—who is his colt, and who is the colt of the she-ass? And why is his own colt bound to the vine, but the colt of the she-ass to the tendril?

## LETTER XLVII

[Note: [Col. 0397] Formerly 48; the letter formerly numbered 47 is now 46. Written in the year 409.]

He commends Cerealis to Ruffinus. He asks that Ruffinus visit him while passing through; [Col. 0398A] at the same time he requests that the remaining blessings of the patriarchs be explained, so that he may answer the presbyter Desiderius. See letter 43, sections 3 and 4.

### PAULINUS TO HIS BROTHER RUFFINUS, GREETINGS

#### 1

Although your son Cerealis left me uncertain when he said that he would proceed to you at the time when he was returning to Saint Peter, nevertheless, since he is equally yours and ours, we judged that not writing to you through him would be as blameworthy for us as it would be sad for you. Therefore, preferring to risk the loss of this little sheet, if he should perhaps not see you, rather than—as we trust—the loss of our duty if he should visit you, we entrusted this letter not to chance but to faith.

For we believe that both our message and our son’s journey should be directed toward you by the Lord, since for those who desire what is good everything works together for good [Romans 8:28; see the same passage in letter 5.9]. He desires you as much as one ought to be desired [Col. 0398B] by someone who understands his own advantage in sharing your company. Therefore I presume that, according to his faith and piety, his desire will be fulfilled in good things, will reach you, and will remain with you; and through you both our saving support before the Lord will be doubled for us.

For you will have gained so good a son, companion, disciple, and helper; and you, granted to him by the Lord as a father and teacher of every good thing, will have added the strength of spiritual grace to the effective power of his prayers. As for us, although because of your affection it is presumptuous to suppose that, when you return to the East, you will not depart without visiting us, we nevertheless fear because of our sins that even if the daughter of Babylon so near to us—that is, Rome; see letter 29.13—should turn you aside, you may not come.

Therefore we entrust our desires and prayers to the Lord, asking him to act for us not according to our merit but according to our desire, and to direct your way to us in his way of peace. For those who do not walk in that way have been condemned to a reprobate mind, and do not deserve to desire you.

#### 2

Because of the importunity with which I have been accustomed to knock at your door even in the middle of the night, and because fear of rejection has compelled me to modesty and restraint in making requests, I now entrust this task concerning myself to you: the twelve blessings of the patriarchs, whose beginning—the prophecy concerning Judah—you have already published in written pages composed according to the prescribed threefold interpretation. May you deign to explain the blessings distributed among the remaining sons, so that through you I may become aware of the truth and have you as the author of great grace and praise.

Then, when those who think highly of me beyond my deserts—or perhaps the text has an addition such as “thinking above me”; something seems to be missing—have thought it necessary to consult me concerning this work—or perhaps “concerning its difficulty”; see letters 43.3–4 and 50 [Col. 0398D], section 15—I may answer them with what is divine and inspired by your spirit, rather than with the foolishness of my own understanding.

## FRAGMENT OF LETTER XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0397] Around the year 409. The letter formerly numbered 48 is now 47.] [Note: [Col. 0397] This has been taken from Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book 2, chapter 13.]

He praises the most illustrious bishops of his age.

For if you see these priests worthy of the Lord—Exsuperius of Toulouse, Simplicius of Vienne, Amandus of Bordeaux, Diogenianus of Albi, Dynamus of Angoulême, Venerandus of Auvergne, Alethius (also called Alithius) of Cahors, or now Pegasius of Périgueux—whatever the evils of the age may be, you will certainly see men most worthy to guard the whole faith and religion.

## LETTER XLIX

[Note: [Col. 0399] Formerly 36; the letter formerly numbered 49 is now Appendix 1. Written in the year 409 or later.]

### 277

He describes the immense miracles by which the old man Valgius, later called Victor, was saved from shipwreck, and asks Macarius to protect both him and his patron Secundinianus from human harassment.

### TO MACARIUS [see note 197], PAULINUS

#### 1

To proclaim the works of the Lord is honorable [Note: [Col. 0399] Tobit 12:7]. This was the reason for this letter, because, as you will acknowledge, the affair of Secundinianus, the master of the household of this man whom I commend to your friendship, cannot be narrated without the glory and praise of the Lord.

For just as he said in the Gospel, “My Father is still working, and I am working” [Note: [Col. 0399] John 5:17], so he acts even now. The good Lord does not cease to arouse and truly challenge our faith by evident proofs of his truth. Thus God our Savior, appearing to us in various proofs, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0399] Acts 1:3], works for us by land and sea; and what he does for individuals he directs toward the faith and salvation of many.

Consider how admirable and worthy of proclamation is the work that the Lord Jesus performed with his holy angels for one old man. This is the story of the aforementioned friend and brother of ours, a man faithful in Christ.

During the preceding winter, he was compelled in Sardinia, together with the other shipmasters, to receive on his own vessel grain to be transported to the imperial storehouses. Without awaiting the customary season for sailing [see notes 64 and 198], before the summer weather, he sent the loaded ship out under the pressure of public authority.

Immediately, as he himself reported to me, a storm arose in the nearby strait. It drove back from their appointed courses a fleet of many ships that had rashly left the harbor and broke them upon the shore. They attempted to anchor his ship in a certain place on that island called the Pulvini, so that it would not likewise be driven onto the rocks. But when the violence of that same winter prevailed and the cables broke, the sailors lowered a small boat—either to assist in holding the ship more securely by renewing and setting the anchors deeper, or to rescue themselves, if possible, from the ship’s danger.

The storm, it is said, immediately seized them together with the frail refuge of their little boat, drove them onto the rocks, and overwhelmed them beneath the waves. They left behind one old man from the entire number of sailors, assigned to bail out the bilge—either because, overcome by fear, they had forgotten him, or because they despised him as a worthless life. Meanwhile the ship, abandoned by sailors and anchors, was carried out into the open sea.

#### 2

The old man, unaware that he had been left behind, felt himself being tossed and rolled. He emerged from the innermost part of the ship and saw everything empty, the sea everywhere and sky everywhere. When solitude added both fear and danger to his misery, he passed six days and nights fasting.

“For bread day and night there were tears for him” [Note: [Col. 0399] Psalm 41:4]. Then, when he already desired death more than life and longed for the end of the soul’s sufferings, the merciful and compassionate Lord deigned to approach him closely and revive him with the food of his word.

The old man himself, still weeping, recounts the blessedness of his peril. One cannot hear the story without tears of heart and joy of spirit: how Christ approached him and addressed him; how, strengthened by Christ’s encouragement, he cut down the tree, when cutting it down was the means of saving the ship; and how, although many men of great strength could scarcely do what was required without endangering themselves and the ship, he, alone and weak, did not dare to undertake it but nevertheless dared through the word of God.

Twice only, and lightly—as though the axe had touched rather than struck it with an old man’s hand—the mast sprang from the wound and was thrown far outside the ship into the waves, where it fell safely.

Then, in the various duties required by the tossing of the sea and the equipment of the ship [see note 199], whenever it was necessary to rig the *artemon* sail or empty the bilge—that is, to drain and exhaust it—he was called by the name Victor by the Lord and was merely ordered to extend his hand, as though beginning the task, toward whatever work was required [see letter 5.16].

Among the many and varied miracles of God concerning this old man, this gift of God also ought not to be passed over: he received a name by which he is now reckoned among the reborn and is recorded by human beings and angels. For by his pagan name he was called Valgius; now he is called Victor by the Lord, and he is victorious in the Lord. The Lord gave him this name, suited to his works, because through Christ’s help he triumphed at sea over storms and shipwreck, and recently on land, through the same grace, over sins and the devil. Thus he was to be wholly renewed in Christ and remain neither in the old name nor in the old man.

#### 3

What marvelous faith and ineffable devotion belong to the Lord and Savior, who, if the old man happened to be slow to rise for his duties because he was sluggish with sleep, gently awakened him by stroking his ear lest he start awake in alarm, while with a soft hand he first touched him lightly [Note: [Col. 0400D] Thus the royal manuscript, together with the editions of Grinarius and Schottus. Three printed editions read *leniter*, “gently.”]!

When the old man, making a slight effort, immediately saw that his first attempt had been completed by angelic hands, he had scarcely touched the rope—as though he were about to draw it—when he saw the sail already spread upon its yards. The topsail (*supparum*) stood; the ship was making sail.

Water entering through the ship’s cracks had threatened to sink it. After one or two brief draws from the pump had removed the moisture [see note 201] and the ship had been dried, he had nothing left to do. He was astonished that his labor had been taken from him without labor and that his task had been anticipated by a hidden hand. Yet “hidden” is hardly the right word for what provided such manifest assistance.

Nor were the actual workers concealed from the eyes of the simple and innocent old man. For he often saw armed soldiers—obviously from the army of heaven—keeping watch over the ship and carrying out every duty of sailors.

Indeed, no sailors but angels were suited to that ship, whose helm was held by the governor of the world. The Lord himself sometimes sat at the stern, radiant in countenance and shining in hair, as he is described in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0399] Apocalypse 1:44]; at other times he appeared with the venerable face of his confessor and friend, my lord and our common patron Felix [see note 16]. He sat, as sailors say, by the steering oars, or rather in place of the steering oars, which the ship had lost together with its anchors and sailors on that shipwrecked shore.

It was an unhappily fortunate ship: in place of all the men and equipment it had lost, it obtained either the Lord’s martyr or the martyr’s Lord. The old man, weeping with joy, relates that he was accustomed to fall at the feet of the one who sometimes steered as Lord and sometimes as martyr. He says that, drawn to him by his especially familiar invitation, he was blessed even upon his knees and in the sacred bosom, and that he had the pillow of his reclining head perfumed by divine breathings.

#### 4

Should we doubt that the bosoms of the patriarchs are open to the faithful servants of Christ, when his boundless goodness cherished even this man, then a catechumen, either in his own bosom or in that of his saint?

For he himself was present in his saint, who, as you know, said to the Father: “The glory that you gave me I have given them, so that they may be one, just as we are one. I in them, and you in me” [Note: [Col. 0401] John 17:22].

And again he said to the apostles, in whom he spoke to his entire body: “Behold, I am with you every day, until the end of the age” [Note: [Col. 0401] Matthew 28:20].

He proves this to us every day through the visible power working in the hands of his apostles and martyrs, so that we may believe that God’s Son and our Lord Jesus, reigning in heaven at the Father’s right hand through the resurrection of the dead [Note: [Col. 0401] Mark 16:19], is Lord of the living, not of the dead [Note: [Col. 0401] Matthew 22:32; Mark 12:27].

Therefore, when he cherished the old sailor in the likeness of his holy confessor, he himself was present in his saint. He soothed the exhausted and dejected man with gentle words and refreshed him not more with food than with speech, because he himself is the true bread that came down from heaven [Note: [Col. 0401] John 6:41] to give food to every flesh [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 135:25].

For he loves his work in every human being and wishes every human being, insofar as it depends on him, to be saved [Note: [Col. 0401] 1 Timothy 2:4]. The giver of life, who is life in his entirety, did not make death and does not rejoice in the destruction of the living [Note: [Col. 0401] Wisdom 1:13]. He prefers mercy to sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0401] Matthew 9:13], does not show partiality [Note: [Col. 0401] Matthew 22:16; Mark 12:14; Luke 20:21], made all people, but judges them according to their merits, because God is judge.

#### 5

Finally, the sailor was not made lower in his eyes by the disaster of shipwreck, by old age, or by poverty. Rather, Christ was moved by all those things for which his companions had despised him, and the divine compassion was stirred.

For his eyes always look upon the poor. Certainly this poor man also cried out, and the Lord heard him [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 33:7]. Perhaps the Lord himself, together with the danger that occasioned the prayer, dictated prophetic words to him, so that he cried out:

“Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul. I have come into the depths of the sea” [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 68:2–3]; “let not the storm of waters overwhelm me, nor the abyss swallow me” [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 68:16]. “Let your mercy quickly anticipate me” [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 78:8], before I am fixed in the mud of the deep and the pit closes its mouth over me [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 68:3 and 16].

“Look upon me, for I am alone and poor” [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 24:16]. “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness, like a night-bird in a dwelling, and in my ship I am like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 101:7–8].

The Lord heard him and had mercy on him. He sent angels around him, and became his salvation [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 29:11; Psalm 33:8]. He commanded the storm, and it stood still as a breeze [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 106:29]. He rebuked the sea, and its waves were silent; he led him through many waters [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 105:9], so that he saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 106:24].

He fed him with the fat of wheat, and while Christ spoke with him he was filled with honey, as though it came from a rock [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 80:17]. He looked upon the humble, he who blessed the poor in spirit [Note: [Col. 0401] Matthew 5:3]. He addressed the weeping man, he who promised consolation to those who mourn. And he who gives fullness to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness refreshed and fed this failing man from himself, for he is bread, righteousness, and the fountain of life.

He showed him no other compassion than that with which he pitied every human being tossed about on the sea of this world, in the devotion with which he surrendered himself to the Father even unto death on the cross. For one human being is a portion of the whole, and the whole is the image and cause of one human being.

#### 6

Finally, while governing not only the ship but also the man for whose sake he guarded the ship, and while distributing within him the distinct duties of flesh and spirit [that is, different duties; see letter 50.13], he ordered him to rest securely at night and to remain watchful and attentive by day, promising that he would keep watch in place of the sleeping man and work together with the one who was awake.

You will recognize in these words the Lord’s disposition, by which he always nurtures our hope without relaxing our vigilance: he cares for weak flesh in such a way that the spirit does not cease to be ready. Therefore he allowed the old man to sleep in his exhaustion, but he did not allow even the old and weary man to be secure without the task of keeping watch, lest he be dissolved into inert sleep and begin to sleep not only in body but also in mind.

Fearing this, a certain saint said: “Enlighten my eyes, O Lord, lest I ever sleep unto death” [Note: [Col. 0401D] Thus the royal manuscript and the editions of Badanius, Grinarius, and Gravellius. In Greek, εἰς θάνατον, “unto death.” The Rosweyde and Schottus editions have *in morte*, “in death.”] [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 12:4]. For the torpor of souls is a stain close to death. And then the enemy will say, “I have prevailed against him” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ibid., verse 5], if sleep has also overwhelmed the eyes of the mind.

We therefore recognize that the same Lord was present to the old man who said to his drowsy disciples: “Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation” [Note: [Col. 0401] Matthew 26:41]. And again he said to those who were already watching, secure in the strength of those who had been awakened: “Sleep now and rest” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ibid., verse 45].

Elsewhere he teaches that this was spoken not so much about bodily sleep as about steadfastness of faith, saying: “Stand firm, because I have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0401] John 16:33]. For this is the true rest of a human being: to enjoy peace with a united heart, steadfast in faith and secure from every enemy through Christ’s victory. For he himself is our rest [Note: [Col. 0401] Ephesians 2:14], who is our peace; indeed, he watches for us so that he may rest in us, and he now commands us to watch in expectation of perpetual rest.

#### 7

The Lord himself deigned to perform in this one old man these same gifts of his compassion, which he wishes to be enacted throughout the world. Stern with tenderness and indulgent without dispensing with the restraint of fear, he plucked the man’s ear in order to shake off bodily sleep; he offered his bosom in order to provide perpetual rest.

For twenty-three days the man was excluded not only from the land but also from human beings, the plaything of every wind, an exile from every land [Thus the poem *Carmen* 21, verse 222], a guest upon a foreign sea and deprived of human society, wandering amid waves and sea-monsters in the uncertain lodging of a roaming ship, exhausted by fasting, old age, and fear.

Tell me, I ask you, did he endure all this by his own natural strength? Who, then, could fail to see that God was in him? I mean the God who alone performs wonders [Note: [Col. 0403] Psalm 71:18], who calls what does not exist as though it existed [Note: [Col. 0403] Romans 4:17]. By his aid the ship moved through the entire hidden sea, as though empty and guided by an invisible helmsman, yet advancing under its heavy burden. With the man and the grain shut inside its chambers, it floated like that ark pregnant with the seeds of the world during the Flood [Note: [Col. 0403] Genesis 7:17]. Though tossed upon one sea, it did not alter its course with the storms.

#### 8

First it was driven toward the City and saw the lighthouse of the Roman harbor. Then it skirted Campania over long stretches; changing winds carried it across to the shores of Africa. From there it was again carried away and passed through Sicily.

Around Sicily, the straits are said to be driven into whirlpools and eddies by frequent islands, and even under a helmsman ships must pass dangerous courses amid the islands’ winding passages and obstacles. Yet the old man, in a ship that traveled quietly and without mishap, passed through them so directly that, as though the ship were divine and made wise by a spirit sent from heaven, it spontaneously avoided what had to be avoided, sought what had to be sought, and turned usefully and skillfully through the necessary channels.

At last, on the twenty-third day, with the Lord already showing mercy, it was to bring an end to its wanderings and dangers on the shores of Lucania.

As it approached those shores, the eternal Lord—so that his unfailing goodness might continue to perform his wonders to the end of the voyage he had undertaken—sent fishermen out from the shore in two small boats. They had been impelled by a silent prompting of his inspiration to come toward the ship. When they saw it from a distance, they were initially frightened and fled, for they later reported that it appeared full of armed men and like a Liburnian warship.

Then, recalled at length by the old man’s loud and repeated cries, they considered the matter among themselves. Since the Lord was acting in this way, they understood that they had nothing to fear from the ship to which they were being summoned. They approached it and scarcely believed the old man’s assurance that the vessel they had seen surrounded from afar was empty of soldiers until they had boarded it and trusted their own eyes.

The old man then welcomed them with the meal which, at the Lord’s command, he had prepared the day before. As a generous reward, he filled them with abundant loaves from the provisions of the lost sailors and bestowed them upon them.

Rejoicing in this payment, they served him with their little boats and towed the ship into its harbor. It was like a veteran returning from a great war, crowned after the battle: a ship that had survived shipwreck and conquered winds and waves, with the towline leading it forward.

What would the vanity of those people have done with this ship—those who, in the error by which they worship everything they fashion, consecrated in fabulous writings the vessel built by the unfortunate Argonauts, and still believe that they see it in the heavens and count it among the constellations?

With no less madness, do they venerate the ship that carried the dragon from Epidaurus, deluded by the very one whose embodied phantom they carried, fashioning it through foolish thoughts [Note: [Col. 0403D] Thus the royal manuscript, the Schottus edition, and Paulinus, letter 16.4, “they fashion into an embodied appearance through foolish thoughts.” The Rosweyde edition here has “a corporeal phantom.”]—the serpent?

#### 9

But let us flee from what is fictitious and foreign, and let us not mix the lies and poisons of the perishing with the light of our truth.

We have our own ships, so that we may use examples worthy of truth and belonging to our own tradition. We have Noah’s ark [Note: [Col. 0403] Genesis 7:15]. We also have the ship of Tarshish [Note: [Col. 0403] Jonah 1:3] and the Tarshish ship [Note: [Col. 0403] Acts 27:6].

But the first ship—the one in which the avenging and guarding sea-monster received the fugitive prophet [see note 204]—can be compared with this ship only insofar as it was endangered before the casting of lots [Note: [Col. 0403] Jonah 1:4].

The third ship, however, agrees with my example in this respect: it carried an apostle and martyr, and for his sake, and in him, received Christ—or rather, Christ gave the entire company of the ship, which was destined to perish, back to him [Note: [Col. 0403] Acts 27:24].

#### 10

Let us therefore set before our mind and contemplate with our inward sight the most beautiful spectacle of a divine work: one ship snatched from the shipwreck of many ships and all their sailors, traversing different seas with one old man, alone upon the open sea, and in it alone—

That ark of the Flood will then appear before our eyes as an image of the Church, floating solidly throughout the whole world above the submerged earth, amid the single surface of the sea spread everywhere [Note: [Col. 0403] Genesis 7:17], amid the waters poured out from heaven and the abyss. In a smaller model, this ship bore its image in many ways.

For just as the ark was full of seeds of every kind [Note: [Col. 0403] Genesis 6:20], so this ship was full of various kinds of produce [Col. 0404C], with, besides its public cargo, many provisions and private goods belonging to the sailors [page 283].

The ark carried one family for the restoration of the human race; this ship carried one man for the faith of many [Note: [Col. 0403] Genesis 7:7; 1 Peter 3:20]. A dove brought the branch of peace to the ark [Note: [Col. 0403] Genesis 8:11]; the Lamb bestowed peace upon this ship. A bird entered the ark as an image of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0403] Genesis 8:9]; Christ came to this ship through the image of his confessor.

Let us also consider Jonah’s ship: we shall see that this one was preserved by the same power through a more generous gift and a greater miracle. The former was saved with everyone except one man; this one was saved with everyone lost except one man who remained.

But this ship also seems to have imitated that harmless devourer of the living prophet, the sea-monster, when it likewise carried a man shut within its belly through the depths of the sea [Note: [Col. 0403] Jonah 2:1] and set him safely upon the shore. Just as that beast, fasting despite its prey, restored to God—at whose command it had received him—the undigested man shaken out from the prison of its spacious belly by commanded heaves, and, when the mystery of the saving Passion had been fulfilled, vomited him forth on the third day into the hope of resurrection [Note: [Col. 0403] Jonah 2:11; Matthew 12:39].

### 11.

But happier was the company of that ship which was granted to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0403] Acts 27:24]—not, indeed, on account of its own merits, for they too deserved shipwreck, since they had sailed contrary to the Apostle’s advice. Yet from this also we may boast of a vessel in divine works: although its men lacked an advocate like him, nevertheless God himself, the Apostle’s God, was present as pilot in that single sailor, and through whom it deserved to be rescued for the sake of one innocent man (Sach.: perhaps, “by whom”); whereas that other ship, which had first received the Chosen Vessel in chains, did not deserve to be freed because of the Apostle’s contempt and imprisonment, having been condemned on the charge of confinement.

That company of the ship seems to me to have been delivered because of the mystery of grace, so that they might escape naked from the shipwreck of the ship they had boarded [Note: [Col. 0405D] The royal manuscript reads *addictae*.]; that is, so that the whole and sound ship, presenting the complete figure of the Church’s faith, might receive those who had been freed from the sin of the flesh of the former ship—that is, of Adam [Note: [Col. 0405] 1 Peter 3:21]—and cleansed by the very waves through which they had escaped [Note: [Col. 0405D] So the royal manuscript. See what follows. Previously: “they escaped.”], lightened of all the secular burdens they had thrown into the sea, and stripped of the old man’s garment, heavy and soaked with waves as with sins—and carry them safely into the harbor, and to Rome.

In these matters, likewise, mystical interpretations are formed. For the changed ship signifies life renewed in Christ; and the harbor of salvation, as Greece bears witness, is Rome, the name of virtue. Let us therefore bless God and rejoice in our God, who dwells on high and regards the lowly [Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 112:5]; in whom there is no pleasure in the strength of a horse or in the tents [Note: [Col. 0405D] Elsewhere, “pipes.” See note 205] of a man, but in the lowly and those who fear him [Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 146:10, according to the Roman Psalter]; and who, as he has shown even in this old man, heals all the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds [Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 146:3].

### 12.

I feel, brother, that I am chattering too much, but I ask you to bear with me a little longer. For I should like to ask whether you would prefer any dignity of this world to the divine favor with which this old man has been honored. Do those seem happier to you who shine in purple, drink from jeweled vessels, are supported by the toga, and are adorned with the *palmata*—men who rule over fellow mortals, even over many better than themselves, yet are slaves to their desires and possessions; insolent because of God’s gifts toward God; poor in Christ; rich in sin; barren in life; fruitful in death?

What harm, I ask, did it do this old man that he bore the role of a *sentinator* (a bilge-worker), the most contemptible among sailors, had poor clothing, and wore a Sardinian *mastruca*? He was clothed in stitched skins when the Lord of hosts, the King of glory, both blessed him with his speech, enlightened him with his gaze, and lulled him in his embrace—surely loving in him also the fact that he imitated Elijah’s *melote* (see note 206) and the hairy garment of John the Forerunner [Note: [Col. 0405] 2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6].

A great part of the world considers it the height of blessedness to see the king of this world at close range and to be splashed by even his wearisome conversation; and, if it cannot obtain this otherwise, it buys it even at the cost of losses. Once it has attained it, it forgets not only other people but even itself. How much happier in dignity is this man, whom the King of kings honored? How much nobler in nobility is he, whom Christ acknowledged? How much richer in wealth is he, to whom the goods of so many saints were conferred together, so that he saw Christ as Israel did, spoke face to face with the King of heaven as Moses did [Note: [Col. 0405] Genesis 32:30; Numbers 12:8], and rested with almost the same intimacy in Christ’s bosom [Col. 0406A] as John reclined upon his breast [Note: [Col. 0405] John 13:23]?

Finally, he received a new name, just as did the friends of God whom you know well in the patriarchs and the apostles [Note: [Col. 0405] Genesis 17:5 and 32:28; Mark 3:16]. A little earlier I asked you whether you would prefer to be granted this grace above all the glory of this world. Indeed, I think that even the rulers of these darknesses [Note: [Col. 0405] Ephesians 6:2], if they should be permitted to see him, would prefer the blessed misery of our old and poor man to their own wretched felicities and joys destined to be mourned forever.

### 13.

Perhaps you will ask by what merits this old sailor, who had always remained in the darkness of ignorance and was as remote from works of righteousness as from knowledge of the truth, seems to have obtained what is readily granted to very few laborers, although they endured the whole burden and heat of the day from the morning watch until night [Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 129:6; Matthew 20:12].

The Apostle will surely answer you: because the graces and gifts of God are irrevocable [Note: [Col. 0405] Romans 11:29], and because no flesh will be justified by works [Note: [Col. 0405] Romans 3:20]. This is the time of grace, and faith is reckoned for righteousness, because sons of Abraham are raised up daily from stones [Note: [Col. 0405] Matthew 3:9].
