Now is the acceptable time, now the day of salvation [Note: [Col. 0405] 2 Corinthians 6:2], when we offer sacrifices of peace and praise; and the sacrifice acceptable to God is a contrite spirit [Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 50:19].

And in man there is the temple of God [Note: [Col. 0405] 2 Corinthians 6:16], and in the believing heart things that bring salvation, and in purified breasts the holy of holies. Therefore he who does not despise a contrite and humbled heart [Note: [Col. 0406D] So the royal manuscript; Paulinus likewise elsewhere. See Letter 40, section 4. Rosweyde’s edition: “a broken heart.”] [Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 50:19, according to the Roman and Old Psalters] accepted our old man, pleasing to him by his natural gifts, as a sacrifice of sweet fragrance [Note: [Col. 0405] Ephesians 5:2].

For he is said always to have been so pure in spirit, through his innate simplicity, that he did not know how to sin. Now, in the extreme old age of his life, he is a child and little one in wickedness [Note: [Col. 0405] 1 Corinthians 14:20], bearing not only the infancy of grace but also of understanding. For recently, as I said above (section 2), he was reborn in Christ and consecrated to the Lord, through whom he escaped the evils of life and the waters of death.

### 14.

Receive him, therefore, joyfully in the Lord, as a good fragrance of Christ [Note: [Col. 0405] 2 Corinthians 2:15], as the lamb of the month of new things, which, for the harmony of your fellowship, I have sent to you as a spiritual gift—a spotless lamb from the rough offspring of Mother Church, with shining fleece, offered by a shepherd of a small flock but a giver of a great pledge, as a *xenium* [Note: [Col. 0406D] The royal manuscript reads *exenium*. See note 207] (see note 207).

For I judged no one more worthy of such a gift than you, who, according to God’s grace and working, would know how both to behold and to receive him. I seem to see with what joy, wonder, and faith you will hear about him and behold him himself, when you consider that he sailed with angels, that a martyr served as his pilot, that he slept in Christ’s bosom, that Christ tugged his ear in play, and gave him a name.

I confess my affection to you: while I marvel too greatly at and love such remarkable works of God in a man of our own time, I was almost cruel toward the old man himself. For I kept tugging his ear so persistently that I nearly wore it away. I would even have cut off part of one ear, if the wound in him had not been for me a matter of affection and a pledge.

No other affection draws people to Jerusalem except the desire to see and touch the places in which Christ was bodily present, and to be able to say of their own experience: “We entered his tabernacles and worshiped where his feet had stood” [Note: [Col. 0407] Psalm 131:7]. Although this passage also has a higher interpretation (see note 208), nevertheless, when circumstances require it, the simple literal sense must not be rejected—that is, it must be used; or, “one ought not not to use it,” as the note explains [Note: [Col. 0407] That is, “it must be used,” or “one ought not to refrain from using it.” See note 31].

If, then, it is a religious desire to see the places where Christ entered, suffered, rose again, and from which he ascended, and to take and possess from those very places even a little dust (see note 209), or from the wood of the cross at least something like a splinter [Note: [Col. 0407B] See note 210], and if this is a blessing, consider how much greater and fuller a grace it is to behold a living old man, by the testimony of divine truth.

If the manger of the one born [Note: [Col. 0407] Luke 2:7], the river of the one baptized [Note: [Col. 0407] Matthew 3:13], the garden of the praying Teacher [Note: [Col. 0407] John 18:1], the courtyard of the one judged [Note: [Col. 0407] Mark 15:16], the pillar of the one scourged, the thorn of the one crowned [Note: [Col. 0407] John 19:2], the wood of the one hanged [Note: [Col. 0407] John 19:17], the stone of the one buried [Note: [Col. 0407] Mark 15:46], and the place of the one raised and carried away [Note: [Col. 0407] Mark 16:6] are honored as memorials of a former divine presence, and living proofs confirm by present faith the ancient truth in lifeless objects, how reverently ought this man to be regarded—the man whom the Word of God deigned to address, from whom the divine face did not conceal itself, to whom Christ showed now his martyr, now himself!

In his living body, as in living earth, we see the footprints of the Lord’s body impressed, if with faithful eyes and spiritual vision we read through what in him Christ’s bosom and Christ’s hand touched; if with our own hands we often stroke the white hair that frequently lay upon the Lord’s knee and often grew warm in the Lord’s bosom, and if we often touch the little ear that heavenly fingers, while the Lord was joking, pulled [Note: [Col. 0407D] The royal manuscript, together with two printed editions, reads *jacente* (“while lying”), incorrectly; hence Sacchinus reads *Domini jacenti* (“of/to the Lord lying”).].

### 15.

You have my *xenium*, dear brother [Note: [Col. 0407D] The royal manuscript reads *exenium*.]. Consume it in the spirit of charity; and if you have grown nauseated by the bitterness of my loquacity, temper your distaste with the sweetness of the Lord’s grace and of this heavenly history.

I know for certain that you will seek and desire some means by which you may exercise toward this man the charity with which you love Christ. The opportunity is at hand: apply the zeal of your pious devotion and, with the full force of your faith, assist his patron Secundinianus, to whom Christ almighty has restored the ship saved for this man’s sake, when he had already despaired of it.

For you will be defending Christ’s gift. Do not allow the envy of the devil, through an unscrupulous man, to rob Secundinianus of what God gave him back from the shipwreck, or to deny that it was given to him.

It is said that the procurator of our Christian brother Postumianus is the man who seized that ship after it had drifted ashore on the coast of Bruttium, where a senator’s estate reaches the sea. More avaricious than the sea, and conducting piracy on land without a *myoparo* (see note 211), he took possession of it and emptied it. Even now it remains empty on that very shore, bearing witness to the loss of the cargo, preserved in vain upon the sea and lost upon the land.

Complaints about this robbery have repeatedly been lodged before the provincial governor, but our Pharaoh hardened his heart. Perhaps this is so that wonders may be performed in him. When summoned through official channels, he first rebelled by force and afterward fled to Rome.

This necessity compelled my Secundinianus to travel to the City by land with his one sailor. I have no doubt that our brother Postumianus will be moved both by your intervention and by his own faith and justice. Therefore we must intervene with such moderation—which you will certainly exercise [Note: [Col. 0407D] So the royal manuscript; the printed editions read “which you should exercise.”]—that, even if no one reminds you, you will defend and excuse before the excellent Senator, that is, the Christian man, his accused client, with equal diligence; so that the robber himself may find the profit of impunity sufficient, while we are content to receive from God himself his gifts.

## LETTER L [Note: [Col. 0407] Elsewhere numbered 43; the letter formerly numbered 50 is now Appendix 2. Written around the year 410.]

Several questions are put to Augustine, first about the Psalms, then about the Apostle, and finally about the Gospel.

## CHAPTER ONE. Questions from the Psalms

### 1.

I shall propose a few matters that have now come to mind as the bearer of this letter hastens toward the ship, while I too hurry because of his own haste, lest you send me a reply without a little crown of supplementary discussion.

If these matters are perhaps clear, though they seem obscure to me, let none of the prudent sons who may happen to be standing around you during this brief reading of ours laugh at my foolishness. Rather, let him favor me with the goodwill of fraternal charity by instructing me, so that I may become a participant with those who see and, through your teaching, join those whose minds are enlightened and who contemplate the wonders of the Lord’s law.

### 2.

Tell me, therefore, blessed teacher of Israel, what is meant by what is said in the fifteenth psalm: “He has made all his desires wonderful among them, for the saints who are in his land.” Their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened [Note: [Col. 0407D] “For” has been added from two Bigotian manuscripts and the Benedictine edition].

Whom does he call saints? Who are the saints in the land? Does he mean those Jews who, as children of Abraham according to the flesh and not children of the promise, are excluded from the seed that was called in Isaac [Note: [Col. 0407] Romans 9:7]?

Are they called “saints in the land” [Note: [Col. 0407] Psalm 15:3] because they are holy by carnal descent, but earthly in life and understanding, because they think earthly thoughts and, through carnal observance, grow old in the antiquity of the letter, not being reborn into a new creation [Note: [Col. 0407] Galatians 6:15]? They did not receive him [Note: [Col. 0407] John 1:11] through whom old things passed away and became new [Note: [Col. 0408D] We have removed the word “all,” which was absent from two Bigotian manuscripts and the Benedictine edition] [Note: [Col. 0407] Revelation 21:4–5].

Perhaps he calls them saints in this psalm in the same way that, in the Gospel, he calls certain people righteous, where he says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” [Note: [Col. 0407] Matthew 9:13]—that is, those righteous people who glory in the holiness of their descent and in the letter of the law.

To them it is said: “Do not glory in your father Abraham, because God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0409] Matthew 3:9; Luke 3:8]. Their pattern is set forth in that Pharisee [Note: [Col. 0409] Luke 18:11] who, as though the Lord did not know, recalled and proclaimed his own righteousnesses in the temple—not praying to be heard, but demanding, as though it were a debt owed for merit, a reward for works that were indeed good, but performed without gratitude toward God.

For what righteousness had built, pride destroyed; and he did not keep even this silent, but shouted it aloud, so that it might become clear that he was not speaking to divine ears, since he also wanted to be heard by human beings. Therefore he did not please God, because he pleased himself. “God has scattered the bones of those who please themselves. They were confounded,” he says, “because God despised them” [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 52:6]—he who does not despise a humble and contrite heart [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 52:19].

### 3.

Finally, in the very Gospel parable [Note: [Col. 0409] Luke 18:10] in which the persons of the Pharisee and the tax collector are contrasted, the Lord himself clearly shows what he receives in a person and what he rejects, as it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” [Note: [Col. 0409] James 5:6].

Therefore he declares that the tax collector went away from the temple more justified through his confession of sins than the Pharisee through the reckoning of his righteousnesses. Rightly that self-praiser, rejected, departed from the presence of God. Though, even in his very name, he displayed knowledge of the law, he had forgotten the Lord speaking through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” [Note: [Col. 0409] Isaiah 66:2].

The tax collector, however, is received as the accuser of himself in his contrite heart, and obtains forgiveness for his confessed sins because of the grace of humility; while that holy Pharisee, such as the Jews are holy, carries away a burden of sins acquired through his boastful display of holiness.

The Jews in question are certainly his likeness—those of whom the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0409] Romans 10:3] that, desiring to establish their own righteousness, which is from the law, they were not subject to the righteousness of God, which is from faith, the faith that was reckoned to our father Abraham for righteousness [Note: [Col. 0409] Romans 4:2], not from works, because he believed God according to the omnipotence of God. With God, the one who truly is righteous is the one who lives from faith [Note: [Col. 0409] Romans 1:17].

He is not holy in the land but in heaven, because he does not walk in the flesh but in the spirit, whose citizenship is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0409] Philippians 3:20]. He does not glory in circumcision of the flesh but in circumcision of the heart, which is performed invisibly not by the letter but by the spirit; therefore his praise is not from human beings but from God [Note: [Col. 0409] Romans 2:28].

### 4.

Then, concerning what he joins in the same verse—“He has made his desires wondrous among them” [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 15:3]—I believe he says this because he first kindled for them the lamp of the law and gave them commandments for living. “He made known,” he says, “his ways to Moses and his desires to the children of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 102:7].

Then he worked out among them the sacrament of his own piety [Note: [Col. 0409] 1 Timothy 3:16], God born in the flesh from a Virgin among their people, and made man from their flesh, from the seed of David [Note: [Col. 0409] Matthew 1:1].

Then there were the mighty works of healing that he performed among them and before them. Yet through these he was not merely disbelieved; he was also blasphemed by them when they said: “This man, if he were from God, would not heal on the sabbaths” [Note: [Col. 0409D] Two Bigotian manuscripts read “would not have healed”] [Note: [Col. 0409] John 9:16], and, “He casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” [Note: [Col. 0409] Matthew 12:24].

Because of this mind, blinded by hardened impiety, their infirmities and darkness were multiplied [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 15:4].

### 5.

But what does he mean when he says: “Afterward they hastened”? Did they hasten to repentance, like those in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0409] Acts 2:37] who, pierced by the preaching of blessed Peter, believed in the one whom they had crucified [Note: [Col. 0409D] So two Bigotian manuscripts and the Benedictine edition; elsewhere, “whom they crucified”], and, hastening to be cleansed from so great a sin, ran toward the gift of grace [Note: [Col. 0410D] So the Benedictine edition together with two Bigotian manuscripts; others: “they ran together”]?

Or is it because the powers of the soul are strengthened by faith and love of God, whereas, being empty of both, those impious people suffered multiplied infirmities of soul, seized by deadly sicknesses because of their impious crimes?

For Christ is the light and life of believers [Note: [Col. 0409] John 8:12; 14:6], and healing is under his wings [Note: [Col. 0409] Malachi 4:2]. It is therefore no wonder that their darkness and infirmities were multiplied unto destruction, since they did not receive life and light, nor did they wish to remain under his wings.

As he himself, weeping, testifies in his Gospel, he often wished to gather them under his wings, as a hen gathers her chicks [Note: [Col. 0409] Matthew 23:3; Luke 13:34], but they were unwilling.

After their infirmities had multiplied, where did they hasten? Perhaps toward shouting for the Lord’s cross and extorting it from Pilate, despite his resistance, by their wicked cries, so that they might fill up the measure of their fathers [Note: [Col. 0409] Matthew 23:32]; so that these people might kill the Lord of the prophets, whose fathers had killed the prophets themselves, by whom it had been announced that he would come as the Savior of the world.

“Afterward they hastened” [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 13:3]. For “their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace”—that is, Christ, who says: “I am the way” [Note: [Col. 0409] John 14:6].

### 6.

In the following psalm I desire you to explain to me what is meant by: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things. They have been satisfied with swine,” or—as I hear it written in certain Psalters—“They have been satisfied with sons, and they have left what remained for their little ones” (see note 212).

### 7.

Again, in another psalm I am accustomed to marvel, understanding the Son to be speaking to the Father, in Psalm 58, where, concerning the Jewish enemies of whom he had said above, “Behold, they will speak with their mouth, and a sword is in their lips,” he says a little later: “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law” [Note: [Col. 0410D] So Augustine and Hilary, together with the Old and Roman Psalters, according to the Greek: τοῦ νόμου σου, “of your law”]. “Scatter them by your power and bring them down, Lord.”

We see this fulfilled in them down to the present day. For they have been brought down from their former glory, living dispersed among all nations, without a temple, sacrifices, or prophets [Col. 0410D].

But why should we wonder that through the prophet he was already asking that they not be killed, when, at the very time of his Passion, as they were leading him to the cross, he prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0411] Luke 23:34]?

Yet I confess that what he added—“Lest they ever forget your law” [Note: [Col. 0411] Psalm 58:12]—is obscure to me, as though their life, even without faith in the Gospel, were necessary on account of this. What benefit is it to them for salvation—which is sought only through faith—to occupy themselves with remembering and meditating on the law, unless perhaps it is for the honor of the law itself or of Abraham’s race [Note: [Col. 0411] Genesis 22:17]?

Perhaps it is so that, even in the earthly portion of his carnal seed, which seems to be counted like the sand of the sea, the letter of the ancient law may persist [Note: [Col. 0411D] Thus the Gravius and Benedictine editions and two Bigotian manuscripts; Rosweyde’s edition reads “and perhaps”], lest some, by reading the law, be enlightened unto faith in Christ, who is the end of the law and of the prophets [Note: [Col. 0411] Romans 10:4] and shines forth, prefigured and foretold, throughout all their books.

Or perhaps it is because from those impious people the generation of the elect is to come—those chosen from each tribe and designated in groups of twelve thousand. The revelation of blessed John [Note: [Col. 0411] Revelation 7:5], through the voice of the announcing angel, bears this testimony concerning them: they will cling more familiarly and entirely without stain to the company of the eternal King, free from human union.

Of them he says especially: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, because they have not defiled themselves with women; for they are virgins” [Note: [Col. 0411] Revelation 14:4].

### 8.

In Psalm 67, besides other matters, this is exceedingly obscure to me: “Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins.” What does the phrase “the hairy crown of those who walk in their sins” mean? For he did not say, “the crown of the head,” but “the crown of the hair,” which is without sensation. Does he wish to indicate a man filled with sins? It is written: “Every heart is in anguish, from the feet to the head.”

And a little later, what does he mean by: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him himself” [Note: [Col. 0411] Psalm 67:24]? From whom himself? Can the Gentiles, whom he himself calls dogs in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0411] Matthew 15:26], be called God’s dogs?

Or perhaps he calls those people God’s dogs who may be considered such if they live like Gentiles while bearing the Christian name, whose portion is placed with unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0411] Matthew 24:51], because they deny by their deeds the God whom they worship with their words [Note: [Col. 0411] Titus 1:16]?

## CHAPTER TWO. Questions from the Apostle

### 9.

These matters, for the moment, concern the Psalms. Now I shall propose whatever questions I have about the Apostle.

In the Letter to the Ephesians he says what he had said in another letter concerning the degrees or orders of God’s dispositions, as the Holy Spirit works divisions of graces: “He gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints” [Note: [Col. 0411] 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11], and so forth.

I wish you to distinguish for me, amid this diversity of names, what particular function or grace belongs to each name. What is proper to apostles, what to prophets, what to evangelists, what to pastors, and what to teachers? For in all these different names I see an office of teaching that was similar and almost one and the same.

I do not think that the prophets whom the Apostle placed after the apostles are those who preceded the apostles in the order of time, but those to whom, already under the apostles, there was granted by grace either the interpretation of the Scriptures, the inspection of minds, or the prediction of future events.

Thus Agabus perceived what was to come: he foretold both the impending famine and what blessed Paul would suffer in Jerusalem, announcing it in words and showing it by the sign of Paul’s belt [Note: [Col. 0411] Acts 21:11].

I wish to understand what distinction there is specifically between pastors and teachers, since both names are usually assigned to the leaders of the Church.

### 10.

Likewise, concerning what he says to Timothy—“Therefore, first of all I ask that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people”—I ask you to explain what distinction there is among this diversity of words, since everything he says should be done seems to me to belong to the office of prayer.

### 11.

Likewise, concerning what he says to the Romans, I ask and beg you to explain this to me. I confess that I am very blind in this statement of the Apostle concerning the Jews, where he says: “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers” [Note: [Col. 0411] Romans 11:28] [Note: [Col. 0412D] Thus the Benedictine edition and two Bigotian manuscripts; Rosweyde’s edition reads “they are beloved.”].

How are these same people enemies for our sake, for us who have believed from among the Gentiles—as though the Gentiles could not have believed unless the Jews had not believed? Or was the one God, creator of all, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth [Note: [Col. 0411] 1 Timothy 2:4], incapable of acquiring both peoples unless he possessed one in place of the other?

Then, “beloved for the sake of the fathers”: how, or from where, if they do not believe and persist in being enemies of God? “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and do I not waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred” [Note: [Col. 0411] Psalm 138:21].

I certainly think that this is the voice of the Father speaking to the Son through the prophet in the same psalm, where above he had said concerning the portion of believers: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored by me; their rule has been greatly strengthened” [Note: [Col. 0411] Psalm 138:17].

What benefit does it bring them for salvation—which is obtained only through faith and the grace of Christ—if they are beloved by God because of the faith of their fathers [Note: [Col. 0412D] Thus the Benedictine edition and two Bigotian manuscripts; Rosweyde’s edition reads “they are beloved.”]? For what purpose are those loved whom it is necessary to condemn because, through their own unbelief, they differ from the faith of their prophetic and patriarchal ancestors and are enemies of the Gospel of Christ?

If they are beloved by God, how will they perish? And if they do not believe, how will they not perish? If they are loved for the sake of their fathers without personal merit, how will they not also be saved for the sake of their fathers?

Yet even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were among them, they would not save their impious children; they alone would be saved [Note: [Col. 0411] Ezekiel 14:14].

### 12.

Draw another, still more obscure matter for me from the depths, and bring it into shallow water. In the Letter to the Colossians I cannot understand at all what he says: “Let no one deceive you, wishing in humility and the religion of angels, walking in things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head.”

Of which angels does he speak? If of hostile and evil ones, what is their religion, or what is their humility? And who is this teacher of deception who, under the pretext of some angelic religion, teaches as though they were seen and known things that he has not seen?

Without doubt these are heretics, who both follow doctrines of demons [Note: [Col. 0413] 1 Timothy 4:1] and bring forth inventions conceived by their spirit, pretending that phantasms they have not seen were visions, and sowing them through pestilential arguments in hearts ready to believe evil.

These are the people who do not hold fast to the head—that is, Christ, the source of truth; whatever opposes his teaching is madness. They are the blind guides of the blind [Note: [Col. 0413] Matthew 15:14], of whom I think it is said: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” [Note: [Col. 0413] Jeremiah 2:13].

### 13.

Then, in the following chapter [Note: [Col. 0413D] Two Bigotian manuscripts and the Benedictine and Gravius editions read “in the following chapter”], he added: “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle—things which all perish in their use—according to human commandments and doctrines. These things have indeed an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, but not in any honor, for the satisfying of the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0413] Colossians 2:21].

What are these things, concerning which the Teacher of truth—Saint Paul (see Letter 30, section 5)—testifies that they have an appearance of wisdom, and yet denies that the truth of religion itself is present in them? Is he perhaps speaking of things such as those about which he says to Timothy: “Having an appearance of piety, but denying its power” [Note: [Col. 0413] 2 Timothy 3:5]?

I therefore ask you to explain these two passages of the Letter to the Colossians to me word by word, because laudable things have been mixed with things deserving execration. For what is as laudable as an appearance of wisdom? And what is as execrable as the superstition of error?

Humility too, both pleasing to God and especially praiseworthy in true religion, is attributed to them together with an appearance of wisdom. Yet concerning their doctrines and practices we are told: “Do not touch, do not taste—things which lead to destruction” [Note: [Col. 0413] Colossians 2:21], because they are not from God; and everything that is not from faith is sin [Note: [Col. 0413] Romans 14:23].

God has destroyed the counsels of the wise, who through carnal prudence are foolish before God; for the fleshly mind cannot be subject to the law of God [Note: [Col. 0413] Romans 8:7]. He knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain [Note: [Col. 0413] Psalm 93:11].

I ask what sort of humility and what kind of appearance of wisdom he says is present in the superstition arising from human doctrines.

And what does he mean by: “In not sparing the body, not in any honor, for the satisfying of the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0413] Colossians 2:23]? I understand this very poorly, because in the same sentence there seems to me to be a great distinction (see Letter 49, section 6).

I think he is speaking of some fabricated or useless abstinence, such as heretics commonly affect, when he says, “in not sparing the body.” But when he adds, “not in any honor,” he means that, while not practicing the appearance of a holy work in the faith of truth, they perform it without the honor or fruit of any glory, thereby completing a great condemnation of their perverse error, since they transform themselves into ministers of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0413] 2 Corinthians 11:15].

But what he adds—“for the satisfying of the flesh”—seems contrary to what he says, “in not sparing the body.” For it seems to me that the person who does not spare the body is one who subdues the flesh with fasts, as the Apostle says: “I bruise my body and bring it into servitude” [Note: [Col. 0413] 1 Corinthians 9:27] (*hypōpiazō*, Greek ὑπωπιάζω; Vulgate: *castigo*). The satisfying of the flesh is foreign to such a practice.

Unless perhaps he called even the care taken to satisfy the flesh—which is especially disgraceful in those who make a show of religious observance—not sparing the body, in accordance with that honorable command which he gives elsewhere, that each person should know how to possess his own vessel honorably [Note: [Col. 0413D] 1 Thessalonians 4:4], and should present his body as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 0413] Romans 12:1]: “not for the satisfying of the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0413D] So the manuscripts together with the Benedictine edition; Rosweyde’s edition reads “in the satisfaction of the flesh”], because bodily distension destroys the soul’s sobriety and is hostile to chastity.

[Column 0414B] 14. It remains for me to offer Your Blessedness something also from the passages of the Gospels—not, indeed, as much as ordinarily occurs to one reading at leisure (for now I shall not have time to search through scattered books, or to stir up my memory by recalling them), but I shall inquire about the few things that come to mind at the moment of dictation. Concerning the form of the resurrection, if you still have copied out among your papers the letter—not large, but full of instruction in the faith—which you sent in reply to my second consultation while you were wintering at Carthage [Note: [Col. 0413D] Manuscripts 15, “I was wintering.” See note 213] [Note: [Col. 0414D] Thus four Vatican manuscripts, one Bigot manuscript, and the Benedictine edition; another Bigot manuscript reads “kept.” The Rosweidian edition reads “left.”], I ask you to send it to me; or at least to rewrite it for me, which is easy for you. For even if it no longer exists in writing, perhaps because it was a short letter and, as something hastily composed, was neglected among your books, renew it for me with the same meaning, ready from the treasury of your heart, and send it to me among the other replies that, I hope, you will give me. May Christ grant both you and me a span of days [V. note 64], so that I may receive these things, by which your labor may bear fruit in me, according to the following passages of Scripture. Concerning them I questioned you, who see as though through God [Note: [Col. 0414D] Thus we have corrected the text from four Vatican manuscripts and the Benedictine edition. Previously it read, “it must be believed”], so that I might hear what God speaks to me in you or through you [Note: [Col. 0413] Psalm 84:9].

15. I ask you to make clear to me how or for what reason the Lord, after the resurrection, was both unrecognized and recognized—first by the women who came to the tomb, then by the two men on the road, and afterward by his disciples. For he rose in the same body in which he had suffered. How, then, was the form of that same body not the same as it had been? Or, if it was the same, how was he not recognized by those who knew it? I believe, however, that there is a sacramental meaning in the fact that he who had not been recognized by those walking on the road was revealed in the breaking of bread [Note: [Col. 0413] Luke 24:30]. Nevertheless, I wish to hold this according to your understanding, not my own.

16. And concerning what he said to Mary: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.” If she was not permitted to touch him while he stood close by, how would she touch him once he had ascended to the Father—unless perhaps by an advance in faith and an ascent of the mind, by which God becomes distant from or near to a human being? Or perhaps she had doubted concerning Christ, whom she had thought to be the gardener [Note: [Col. 0415D] Two manuscripts read “you who see as though God”; some printed editions, “according to God.”]. For that reason, perhaps, she deserved to hear: “Do not touch me” [Note: [Col. 0415] John 20:17]. She was judged unworthy to touch Christ with her hand, since she had not yet apprehended him by faith, nor understood that he was God, because she had thought him to be the gardener—the one concerning whom she had shortly before heard from the angels: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” Do not touch me, therefore, because I have not yet ascended for you to the Father, to whom I still seem merely human; later you will touch me, when by believing you have ascended to the recognition of me.

17. Tell me also what you think concerning the words of the most blessed Simeon, so that I may follow your understanding. When he had come into the temple, moved by the Spirit, to see Christ according to God’s oracle, and had received the infant Lord into his arms and blessed him, he said to Mary: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed; and your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” [Note: [Col. 0415] Luke 2:34–35]. Are we to believe that he prophesied here concerning Mary’s passion, which is nowhere written? Or rather concerning her maternal affection, by which afterward, at the time of the Passion, as she stood beside the cross to which the one whom she herself had borne was fastened, she was pierced by the pain of a mother’s entrails; and the cross’s sword, which had pierced her son according to the flesh while she watched, penetrated her soul?

For I see that the Psalms also say concerning Joseph: “They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul” [Note: [Col. 0415] Psalm 105:18], just as Simeon said in the Gospel: “And your own soul a sword will pierce” [Note: [Col. 0415] Luke 2:35]. He does not say “the flesh,” but “the soul,” in which the feeling of affection is contained and in which the sting of pain operates like a sword—whether someone is afflicted by an injury to his flesh, as Joseph was, who endured not death but the sufferings of injuries, being sold into slavery and bound as a criminal [Note: [Col. 0415D] We have deleted the particle “in,” which was absent from the manuscripts and from the Gravian and Benedictine editions.] [V. Carm. 21, verse 752], and cast into prison [Note: [Col. 0415] Genesis 37:28 and 39:20]; or whether someone is tormented by the sadness or pain of an inward affection, as happened to Mary [Note: [Col. 0415] John 19:25]. Her maternal mind had certainly led her to the Lord’s cross, where at that time she thought only of the son of her own body, so that, when she saw him dead, she might mourn with human weakness and gather him for burial, presuming nothing concerning his resurrection, since the punishment of the Passion placed before her eyes blinded her to faith in the wonder that was to follow [Note: [Col. 0416D] Six manuscripts read “which”; eight others, “by which.” See note 214].

Although the Lord did console her as she stood beside his cross—not trembling with the weakness of one who was dying, but, since he willingly underwent death and held it in his power, full of the strength of one who lives and the steadfastness of one who would rise again—he reminded her from the cross, saying of the blessed apostle John: “Woman, behold your son”; and likewise to him, standing there: “Behold your mother” [Note: [Col. 0415] John 19:26]. Having now passed from the human frailty by which he had been born of a woman, through the death of the cross, into the eternity of God, so that he might be in the glory of God the Father, he assigns to a human being the obligations of human affection. From among his disciples he chooses the younger, so that he might fittingly entrust a virgin mother to a virgin apostle [Note: [Col. 0416D] Five manuscripts read “he chooses one younger than his disciples.”].

In the same statement he teaches two things together, leaving us a model of devotion: while caring for his mother, he ensures that, although he was leaving her bodily, he would not abandon her in his care; indeed, he would not be leaving her bodily either, because the one whom she saw dying she would soon see risen again. And, consigning under this utterance a saving sacrament of his devotion—one that concerned the faith of all—through the hidden reasoning of divine counsel, he assigned to John a mother to be regarded as a mother and consoled in his place, and in turn entrusted to her a new son in place of his own body—or, so to speak, begot one for her [Note: [Col. 0416D] Thus two Bigot manuscripts; previously it read “indicating.”] [Col. 0416B]. In this way he showed that, apart from himself, who had been born from that virgin, she had neither had nor had any other son; for the Savior would not have been so greatly concerned for her desolation [Note: [Col. 0416D] Thus several manuscripts and printed editions. The Benedictine edition, together with Bigot manuscript I, reads “desolation”], if he had not been her only son.

18. But let us return to Simeon’s words, at the conclusion of which I confess that my understanding grows dim. “And your own soul,” he says, “a sword or sword-blade will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” [Note: [Col. 0415] Luke 2:35]. According to the literal sense, this is completely obscure to me, since we nowhere read that the most blessed Mary was killed, so that that holy man might seem to have prophesied a future suffering for her from a bodily sword.

But consider also what he adds: “So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” [Note: [Col. 0415] Psalm 7:10]. “For God searches hearts and reins,” he says. And concerning the future judgment the Apostle says: “For then God will bring to light the things hidden in hearts and the secrets of darkness.” Likewise the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0415] 1 Corinthians 4:5], expressing spiritually the heavenly weapons with which we must arm ourselves within, calls the word of God “the sword of the Spirit.” Concerning this he says to the Hebrews: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword; it reaches,” he says, “to the division of soul and spirit,” and the rest that you know.

What wonder, then, if the fiery power of this word, whose edge is sharper than a two-edged sword [Note: [Col. 0415] Ephesians 6:17; Hebrews 4:12], pierced both the soul of holy Joseph long ago and afterward that of blessed Mary? For we know that iron passed through neither his body nor hers. And so that it may become still clearer that the prophet used “iron” in place of the sword of the word, he immediately adds in the following verse: “The word of the Lord set him on fire” [Note: [Col. 0415] Psalm 105:18]. For the word of God is both fire and sword, the Word himself, God, saying both concerning himself. “For I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it already be kindled?” [Note: [Col. 0415] Luke 12:49]. Elsewhere he says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” [Note: [Col. 0415] Matthew 10:34]. You see that he designated the one power of his teaching under the different names of fire and sword.

Or how would the suffering or tribulation brought upon Mary through the sword persist? Therefore I wish to know what this had to do with Mary: “so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” [Note: [Col. 0417] Luke 2:35]; or where it became apparent that, because her soul had been pierced either by a bodily sword of iron or by the spiritual sword in the word of God, the thoughts of many hearts were thereafter revealed.

Explain this conclusion of Simeon’s words to me above all, for I do not doubt that it is clear to your holy soul, which through the purity of its inward eye has deserved the illumination of the Holy Spirit, through whom it can search out and behold even the deep things of God. May God have mercy on me through your prayers, and may he make his face shine upon me by the lamp of his word [Note: [Col. 0417] Psalm 67:2], holy Lord, most blessed brother, united with me in the Lord Christ, my teacher in the faith of truth and my protector in the depths of charity [Note: [Col. 0417D] Several manuscripts, including two Bigot manuscripts, add “of Christ” [Col. 0418D].].

# LETTER 149 (formerly 59). AUGUSTINE TO PAULINUS. (C)

[Col. 0417B]

Augustine replies to the questions proposed by Paulinus above in Letter 1, concerning the Psalms, the Apostle, and the Gospel.

(See this letter among Augustine’s letters in volume 33 of our Patrologia, column 630.)

# LETTER [Note: [Col. 0417] Added to this edition. Written between the years 409 and 426] 51

[Col. 0417B] 313. He writes to Eucherius and Galla, living on the island of Lero, as a testimony of affection and love, and praises them highly. He asks them for letters as a sign of mutual friendship.

To the holy, deservedly praiseworthy and venerable, and most beloved sons, Eucherius and Galla, Paulinus, bishop.

1. Blessed is the Lord our God, who grants the wish of one who longs, and always surpasses our prayers and answers our prayers. He has deigned to provide me, when I did not expect it, with an opportunity as timely as it was desired, through the religious young men, my sons and our fellow servants in the Lord, Gelasius, Augendus, and Tigridius. Our praiseworthy and illustrious brother in Christ and fellow presbyter, Honoratus, sent them from the holy and most chaste company of his community to revive my humility by the example of your affection [Note: [Col. 0417D] The Vienna manuscript reads “to seek.”], at the prompting of the Lord.

When I anxiously inquired, out of the charity owed to your merits, about your activity and well-being—for I could not doubt your pious and heavenly activity—they gave me the answer that refreshed my soul: with God’s favor, they had left you safe and sound, occupied in the works and pursuits of your venerable purpose, seeking heaven with one heart, having abandoned earthly things.

2. For I remembered that my sons, whom you had sent a year earlier to visit my humility for my sake [Col. 0417D], had made known to us both the place of your dwelling and that of the venerable Lord Honoratus. They said that you lived nearby, separated by only a short stretch of sea, on the islands likewise named Léron and Lérina. Therefore, when these sons of ours said that they had come from the island called Lérins, I recognized and easily recalled the neighboring island whose name I knew, and in which I already knew that your holiness remained in refuge from the tumult of this world.

Knowing, therefore, that the service of my letter would be pleasing to your affection, since it was also owed by me to you as an enduring expression of gratitude, I gladly embraced this opportunity afforded by my spiritual sons, so that they might carry my letter to your blessed unity in the Lord Christ. They received this task most readily, as sons or ministers of obedience, taught by God or according to God.

Receive, then, in these small words the marks of my smallness, but of no small charity; and retain these writings of mine as tokens, as it were, of your souls and as testimonies of my feeling and love toward you. 314

3. I hope, through the mercy of Christ the Lord, that you may receive these words of mine in safety; and if he grants an opportunity thereafter, through messengers of this kind, may you be willing to reply without delay. Without a doubt your affection would also have done this through these sons of mine, if you had known that they were setting out for me. For when I asked them about this, since I knew that you were neighbors, they said that they had sailed from their monastery without your knowledge.

Nevertheless, just as the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power [Note: [Col. 0417] 1 Corinthians 4:20], so charity, in whose perfection and fullness the kingdom of God is contained or acquired, consists in the treasury of the heart and in the power of faith. In exchange for your familiar grace, I desire the writings of your unity. Moreover, trusting in the most pious affection of your souls, I do not doubt that I remain joined even to your silent minds. For it is not through human friendship but through divine grace that we have made ourselves known to one another and have been joined through the depths of Christ’s charity.

Therefore it is necessary that perpetual harmony remain between our hearts, since it has been joined together by Christ, its author. What force or forgetfulness could separate what God has joined?

4. May the Lord bless you from Zion, with the blessing by which the man who fears the Lord is blessed [Note: [Col. 0417] Psalm 128:5 and 4], as perpetual spouses and parents, together with the most noble offspring of your holiness, blessed with you by God. May you see the good things of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0417] Ibid., 5], and may you both deserve to dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days [Note: [Col. 0417] Psalm 23:7], holy sons, deservedly venerable, loved by me with intimate affection and always to be desired.

# THE PASSION OF SAINT GENESIUS OF ARLES (C, G, S)*

1. From the beginning, all the zeal of the faithful and all the writings of religious people ought to have celebrated and exalted the most blessed Genesius, the proper and native son of the city of Arles, its martyr, its nursling by right of birth, and its patron by the virtue of his death. In this way the glorious proofs of so great a merit, recorded in the trustworthiness of written accounts and entrusted to living memorials, might reach posterity undefiled and whole—things that admiration would always make new and veneration would prove ancient.

But because successive generations, during the uncertain span of life, preferred to hand these things down to one another in mutual memory rather than commit them to writing, it is now necessary to transmit the same matters to future ages in faithful writings [Col. 0419A] 315, lest those events which are still reported from living recollection as they occurred should, when the trustworthiness of transmitters and recipients fades with time, be believed fictitious.

2. Saint Genesius, therefore, in the early flower of youth, undertook the apprenticeship of provincial military service. He embraced that part of the office with such zeal and skill that he could render the words of advocates either by the unprecedented speed of shorthand signs or match the sound of their voices by the dexterity of his right hand, prefiguring an image of his future spiritual glory: he who would hear the divine commands swiftly would receive them in the faithful signs of a devout mind.

It happened, however, that while he was carrying out the office of secretary before the tribunal, orders of persecution were issued under an unjust and sacrilegious command. His devotion to God rejected them in hearing, and his holy hand refused to impress them upon wax tablets. Therefore, throwing the tablets at the judge’s feet, the mind already consecrated to the Lord rejected the sacrilegious service.

And so that the martyr’s conduct might in no respect deviate from the evangelical commandments—which either permit or command us to avoid the onslaught of persecution—he hid himself for a short time from the rage of the raging judge, changing not only his hiding place but even his city [Note: [Col. 0419] Matthew 10:24]. For it is also written elsewhere: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” [Note: [Col. 0419] Matthew 26:41].

When the judge ordered him to be seized immediately and brought before him, but the search did not reach the hiding place that had been arranged, he commanded the most savage ministers of punishment to kill him with the sword wherever he was found. When the blessed Genesius learned this, either through secret messengers or by rumor, he changed his various places of concealment—as the outcome shows—not from weakness of spirit but from trembling of the flesh.

3. Meanwhile, although it was unnecessary, he was concerned to confirm the faith he had presumed upon. Since he had not yet been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he asked, through trustworthy intermediaries, the bishop of the Catholic religion for the gift of baptism. But the bishop, whether prevented by the pressure of time or distrustful of the young man’s age, deferred his ardent desires, and faithfully explained that the ready shedding of blood for Christ would also grant the complete consummation of this sacrament.

This hesitation of the priest, however, was, as I judge, provoked and arranged by the prompt will and judgment of God, so that human offices would cease around his solemn consecration, for whom the double grace of a single baptism was being prepared: water and blood from the two sides of Christ [Note: [Col. 0419] John 19:34].

4. 316 But the Lord, who through the Holy Spirit was preserving the mysteries of the future martyr, had either made him steadfast for the suffering he was to undergo or had seen that he was steadfast. Nor did he allow the crown to be delayed, when he saw that victory was ready. Accordingly, he delivered him to his executioners and displayed him to those whose eager cruelty was thirsting for him.

When Genesius saw that he had been discovered, at the Lord’s prompting he made for the Rhône and entrusted his holy limbs to the river, so that there an unseen Baptist might cleanse him from mortal contagion, as though in the waters of another Jordan. Through a mutual and alternating mystery, he consecrated both his body with the waters and the waters with his body.

This was surely the reason that he reached the far side with the aid of swimming: as the most blessed Peter had done, when he was making his way to Christ, he was able to walk over the surface of the deep waters [Note: [Col. 0419] Matthew 14:29; John 21:7].

After he had crossed immediately to the farther bank of the river, secure under Christ’s guarantee that he would undergo the promised reward of suffering, the executioner caught up with him at the place that the Lord had chosen for the shedding of his glorious blood and that is now frequented by continual prayer and vows that are never frustrated. With the desired stroke of the sword he released the soul hastening to God from the bonds of the body by which it had been held. As each substance returned to the elements of its own origin, he entrusted the earthly limbs to the earth and sent the heavenly spirit to heaven.

5. Yet the faithful servants of God of that time took care that both banks of the river, encircled by twin cities, should be protected by one martyr. Leaving behind traces of consecrated blood at the very place of his blessed Passion, they transferred his honored relics to the other side of the river, so that Saint Genesius might be present on both sides: there through his blood, here through his body.

6. Recognize all these things faithfully, as they happened, whether learned by discovery or reported by tradition, with willing and devout minds—you who knew them; and you who did not know them, acknowledge them. Contemplating with the eyes of your minds the glory of so great a martyr, which increases through each succession of years and will live through eternal ages, let each of you prepare your hearts according to his strength for similar things, should faith require it.

And pray that blessed Genesius, standing before the throne of the Lord until the time of his vindication, may protect the priests, ministers, clergy, all of us, and also the one who composed these things for your instruction. Amen.

In long periods of this sort, some inconsistency is not unusual even among great writers, and Paulinus may have admitted it deliberately or inadvertently. Since, however, it seemed more likely that the word had fallen out through scribal error, we considered it most convenient to supply it from the Second Letter to Timothy, from which this whole passage is taken. There is a similarly abrupt passage below, in Letter 10: “Know now this”; and so forth; “Therefore this”; and so forth.

3. Sacchinus: “Should *animo* be added, rather than *sensu*? Since the sense of soul and body is being compared, *sensus* does not seem to be used here for ‘soul’; nevertheless, I would change nothing. For it is certain that *sensus* is understood as mind or the inward faculty of perception both in Sacred Scripture—for example, ‘he opened their understanding’—and by the holy Fathers, especially Paulinus, as in the letter to Ausonius: ‘the sense, fired and penetrating the secrets of heavenly things.’ Since *sensus* is something common to the interior and exterior, it is better attributed absolutely to what is primary. Indeed, Paulinus seems here to understand it as a certain faculty of perceiving present things. His meaning, therefore, is: ‘If it is true that we see and hear by an inward power rather than by our eyes and ears,’ and so forth.”

Three editions have *dispositio seculi* (“the arrangement of the age”), incorrectly. Ducaeus wrongly restored *dispositi a seculo* (“arranged from the age”) from the Putean manuscript, now the Royal manuscript; for the reading is *a seculi*, from which the final letter *s* could easily have fallen out through the copyist’s carelessness because of the conjunction of the following letter. Therefore, since Paul [Ephesians 3:9], Ambrose in the cited passage, and Grin’s edition have *a seculis* (“from the ages”), and four codices support it, we have restored this reading. See note 89.

[Col. 0430] 22. The Royal manuscript and three editions read *Sufficit* (“it suffices”).

[Col. 0430] 23. The Royal manuscript and four editions read *adversum* (“against”).

[Col. 0430] 24. The Vienna manuscript reads *sed illi* (“but to him”).

[Col. 0430] 25. The Royal manuscript and four editions read *operam* (“effort, service”).

[Col. 0430] 26. Schott’s edition reads *stantibus* (“to or for those standing”). Paulinus often uses a compound for a simple verb, just as he uses a simple verb for a compound.

[Col. 0430] 27. The Royal manuscript and three editions read *habeat* (“may he have”).

[Col. 0430] 28. Schott’s edition reads *transibo* (“I shall cross, pass over”).

[Col. 0430] 29. The Vienna manuscript reads *quod* (“which, because”).

[Col. 0430] 30. The Gravius, Grineus, and Schott editions read *Neapolin* (“Naples,” accusative).

[Col. 0430] 31. The Royal manuscript and the Badian, Gravius, and Grineus editions read *quidem in eo* (“indeed in him or it”).

[Col. 0430] 32. The Royal manuscript and four editions read *supra* (“above”).

[Col. 0430] 33. The Royal manuscript and the Badian, Gravius, and Grineus editions read *vertere* (“to turn”).

[Col. 0431] 34. The Vienna manuscript reads *nesciret: et ut* (“would not know; and so that”).

[Col. 0431] 35. Thus all witnesses except Rosweyde, which reads *diligite* (“love!”), apparently a printer’s error.

## IN EPISTLE XXX

[Col. 0431] 1. The Royal manuscript reads *artior* (“narrower, stricter”).

[Col. 0431] 2. The Royal manuscript and three editions read *Ipso* (“by him or it”).

[Col. 0431] 3. The Royal manuscript and the Badian and Gravius editions read *adversum* (“against”).

[Col. 0431] 4. The Royal manuscript and four editions read *suppetet* (“will be available, suffice”).

[Col. 0431] 5. The Royal manuscript reads *ignorantia excusatio* (“ignorance [is] an excuse”).

[Col. 0431] 6. The Royal manuscript reads *quia id* (“because that”). Both readings are good.

[Col. 0431] 7. Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *quod bona* (“because good things” or “which good things”).

[Col. 0431] 8. Schott’s edition reads *certe esse* (“certainly to be”), not badly.

[Col. 0431] 9. The Gravius and Grineus editions read *illuminare* (“to illuminate”).

[Col. 0431] 10. The Vatican manuscript reads *Atque* (“and also”).

[Col. 0431] 11. The Royal manuscript and Badian edition read *transduxit* (“led across, transferred”).

[Col. 0431] 12. The Vatican manuscript reads *refloreat* (“may it flower again”).

[Col. 0431] 14. The Vienna manuscript reads *Deo* (“to or for God”).

## IN EPISTLE XXXI

[Col. 0431] 1. The Royal manuscript and three printed editions read *reversatae* (“turned back”); perhaps *reservatae* (“preserved”) should be read, as the sense seems to require. Sacchinus says that the history tells how the cross was preserved after the time of the Passion and finally discovered.

[Col. 0431] 2. The Vienna manuscript reads *quia difficulter* (“because with difficulty”).

[Col. 0431] 3. The Royal manuscript reads *omittenda* (“to be omitted”).

[Col. 0431] 4. The Royal manuscript reads *obdita* (“hidden”).

[Col. 0431] 5. The Vienna manuscript reads *Facili* (“easy, readily”), not badly.

[Col. 0431] 6. The Vienna manuscript reads *potuisset* (“could have”); the Royal manuscript, *possit* (“may be able”).

[Col. 0431] 7. Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *Deo* (“to or for God”).

[Col. 0431] 8. Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read *requisiisset* (“had sought”).

[Col. 0431] 9. The Vienna manuscript reads *testificatio* (“testimony”); the Royal manuscript and four editions, *testificatione* (“by testimony”).

[Col. 0431] 10. The Royal manuscript and the Badian and Gravius editions read *revelata est* (“was revealed”).

[Col. 0431] 11. The Royal manuscript and Grineus’s edition read *repositam* (“placed back, stored”).

[Col. 0431] 12. The Vienna manuscript reads *Domini* (“of the Lord”).

[Col. 0431] 13. The particle *in* (“in”), absent from the printed editions, was inserted from the Royal and Vienna manuscripts.

[Col. 0431] 14. *Qui* (“who”) is absent from the Royal manuscript and four printed editions.

## IN EPISTLE XXXII

[Col. 0431] 1. The Vienna manuscript gives this letter the title *Severo fratri unanimo Paulinus in Domino Deo Jesu Christo* (“Paulinus to Severus, his brother of one mind, in the Lord God Jesus Christ”). Rosweyde’s edition has *Severo fratri unanimo Paulinus* (“Paulinus to Severus, his brother of one mind”). We deleted the title because it is absent from the Royal manuscript and because this letter was sent with Letter 31 in the same packet. See Dissertation 1.

[Col. 0431] 2. We restored this reading from the Royal and Vienna manuscripts and four printed editions. Rosweyde reads *tu es is* (“you are he”).

[Col. 0431] 3. Schott’s edition reads *sic habe* (“take it thus”).

[Col. 0431] 4. The Vienna manuscript reads *Sequentes basilicarum sunt* (“the following belong to the basilicas”).

[Col. 0431] 5. The Royal manuscript and five printed editions read *sanctum mole* (“holy by its mass”); *sanctum* is not bad, if it refers to the work.

[Col. 0431] 6. Latinius reads *niveo* (“snow-white”).

[Col. 0431] 7. The Vatican manuscript reads *Tunc senior* (“then the elder”).

[Col. 0431] 8. The Royal manuscript and Poelman’s edition read *pio … Christi* (“pious … of Christ”).

[Col. 0431] 9. The Vatican manuscript reads *Divinae* (“of the divine”), which Sacchinus explains as “of the soul.” The now common readings are preferable, however, because the sacred Eucharist is meant, as also below in the epigram *Divinum veneranda* (“venerating the divine [mystery]”), in the following *Pignora sanctorum* (“relics of the saints”), and elsewhere.

[Col. 0431] 10. The Royal manuscript reads *eligas* (“may you choose”).

[Col. 0431] 11. The Royal manuscript and the Badian and Gravius editions read *aequiperas* (“you equal”), as they do throughout.

[Col. 0431] 12. Sacchinus asks whether *participes* (“participants”) should be read, so that it also joins with *sumus* (“we are”).

[Col. 0431] 13. The Vienna manuscript reads *ascivit* (“adopted, associated”).

[Col. 0431] 14. The Royal manuscript and the Badian and Gravius editions read *qui* (“who”).

[Col. 0431] 15. The Vatican manuscript reads *sacrum* (“sacred”).

[Col. 0431] 16. Sacchinus suggests *nobis* (“for us”).

[Col. 0431] 17. The Royal manuscript reads *socium* (“companion,” accusative).

[Col. 0431] 18. Barthius judges that *Pulvere functorum* (“with the dust of the dead”) should be read.

[Col. 0431] 19. The Royal manuscript and the Badian, Gravius, and Grineus editions read *et cum* (“and with”); Schott reads *sed cum* (“but with”).

[Col. 0431] 20. The Vienna manuscript reads *quod* (“which, because”).

[Col. 0432] 21. Elsewhere the reading is *fabricaverunt* (“they built”).

[Col. 0432] 22. Thus the Royal and Vatican manuscripts with Rosweyde. The Vienna manuscript and four editions correctly read *in tot epistolis* (“in so many letters”).

[Col. 0432] 23. Thus Rosweyde. Three manuscripts and four editions read *consignata* (“sealed or marked together”). Sacchinus says this might mean joined to the letter by the same seal. I nevertheless strongly prefer *contignata* (“joined by beams”), which Paulinus describes in *Natal Poem* 10:

> “Rival roofs are joined by interlaced beams.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Through the meeting beams of connected buildings.”

[Col. 0432] 24. The Vatican manuscript and Poelman read *ipsa petra* (“the rock itself”). Sacchinus says that the sense seems to require the verses to be separated by some interval, since they were probably inscribed in different places in the apse.

[Col. 0432] 25. The Royal manuscript and four editions read *parietes* (“walls”).

[Col. 0432] 26. The Vienna manuscript reads *Hierusalem* (“Jerusalem”).

[Col. 0432] 27. The Royal manuscript and four editions read *alterae* (“the other,” feminine).

[Col. 0432] 28. Rosweyde alone reads *ostiolum* (“little door”).

[Col. 0432] 29. The Vienna manuscript reads *ad interiorem sui frontem* (“toward its inner façade”).

[Col. 0432] 30. Du Cange judges that *parat* (“prepares”) should be read.

[Col. 0432] 31. The Royal manuscript reads *alia post* (“other things afterward”).

[Col. 0432] 32. The Vienna manuscript reads *munimenti* (“of the fortification, protection”).

[Col. 0432] 33. The Royal manuscript and the Badian and Gravius editions read *quod* (“which, because”).

[Col. 0432] 34. Latinius thinks *diatreta* (“pierced or openwork vessels”) should be read.

[Col. 0432] 35. The Royal manuscript and three editions read *utrumque* (“each of the two, both”).

[Col. 0432] 36. The Vienna manuscript, supported by the Royal manuscript, reads *animas* (“souls”).

[Col. 0432] 37. We emended the text thus with Sacchinus. Previously it read *potius* (“rather”).

[Col. 0432] 38. Thus the manuscripts. The printed edition reads *dissidium* (“division, disagreement”).

[Col. 0432] 39. The Royal manuscript reads *in alio* (“in another”).

[Col. 0432] 40. The Vatican manuscript reads *vultus* (“face, countenance”).

[Col. 0432] 41. The Royal manuscript reads *circa absidam* (“around the apse”). Both readings are good.

[Col. 0432] 42. The Royal manuscript reads *absidae* (“of the apse”).

[Col. 0432] 43. Thus all manuscript and printed witnesses. Poelman’s margin reads *meditandi in lege* (“of meditating on the law”), as do some library inscriptions.

[Col. 0432] 44. The Royal manuscript reads *paramus* (“we prepare”).

[Col. 0432] 45. The Royal manuscript reads *absida* (“apse,” nominative or ablative).

[Col. 0432] 46. The Royal manuscript reads *si forte et jam* (“if perhaps even now”); the Vienna manuscript, *si forte eam* (“if perhaps her or it”).

[Col. 0432] 47. The Royal manuscript reads *recte* (“rightly”).

[Col. 0432] 48. That title is absent from the Royal manuscript and four printed editions.

[Col. 0432] 49. The Vatican manuscript reads *Haec simul* (“these things together”).

[Col. 0432] 50. The Vienna manuscript reads *visibile* (“visible”).

[Col. 0432] 51. This was emended from the Vienna manuscript, and Latinius also judges it should be read so. Previously the reading was *laborem* (“labor”).

[Col. 0432] 52. Schott’s edition reads *moliebar* (“I was undertaking”), and below *molior* (“I undertake”).

[Col. 0432] 53. Thus all witnesses. Sacchinus says the sense may be “from the fact that we have obtained faith.” He asks whether *ex affectu* (“from affection”) should be read, since *affectu fidei … fidei profectum* would answer elegantly as “from affection for faith … progress in faith.”

[Col. 0432] 54. Sacchinus explains it as “deservedly,” an expression especially common among historians, though he thinks it more likely that Paulinus himself wrote *merito* (“deservedly”).

[Col. 0432] 55. The Royal and Vienna manuscripts corruptly read *si conductos nos* (“if us, hired or brought together”).

[Col. 0432] 56. The Royal and Vienna manuscripts incorrectly read *patrifamilias* (“to the father of the household”).

[Col. 0432] 57. Sacchinus explains *gratum* as what is advantageous to someone. The ancients often contrasted *jucundum* (“pleasant”) with *gratum* (“beneficial”), referring the former to pleasure and the latter to use. St. Ambrose says in his praise of Satyrus: “Public service is more pleasant in prosperity and more beneficial in adversity.” Hence the old reading, also in the Vatican manuscript, should not be changed to *gratuitum* (“gratuitous”) or *gratis* (“freely”), though at first sight the sense seemed to demand it.

[Col. 0432] 58. Schott’s edition reads *fenerari* (“to lend at interest”).

[Col. 0432] 59. The Vienna manuscript and four editions read *adfers* (“you bring”).

[Col. 0432] 60. The Royal manuscript reads *magis vult* (“wishes more”).

[Col. 0432] 61. The Vienna manuscript incorrectly reads *corripias* (“may you rebuke or seize”). See the preceding discussion.

[Col. 0432] 62. The Royal manuscript reads *attingis* (“you touch, reach”).

[Col. 0432] 63. The Vienna manuscript reads *Operando in praeceptis* (“by working in the commandments”).

[Col. 0432] 64. We deleted *et* (“and”), which was absent from the manuscripts.

[Col. 0432] 65. Sacchinus says the sense seems to require *et nunc egeno* (“and now to the needy man”).

[Col. 0433] 66. The Royal manuscript and three editions read *illic carnalia* (“there, carnal things”).

[Col. 0433] 67. The Vienna manuscript reads *rem futurorum* (“the substance or matter of future things”).

[Col. 0433] 68. Thus the Royal and Vienna manuscripts and four editions, correctly. See below.

[Col. 0433] 69. The Vatican manuscript reads *frustratae* (“frustrated, disappointed,” feminine plural or genitive singular).

[Col. 0433] 70. Four editions incorrectly read *Spiritus* (“Spirit”).

[Col. 0433] 71. The Royal manuscript reads *ut umbret* (“so that it may shade”).

[Col. 0433] 72. We added *et* (“and”) from the Royal and Vienna manuscripts.

[Col. 0433] 73. *Ab* (“from, by”) is absent from the Royal manuscript.

[Col. 0433] 74. The Vienna manuscript reads *monetam imaginis suae dignam* (“coinage worthy of his own image”).

[Col. 0433] 75. The Royal manuscript and four editions read *male cura, aut bene amore* (“by evil care or good love”). The Vatican manuscript reads *mali cura, aut boni amore* (“by care for evil or love of good”).

[Col. 0433] 76. Sacchinus suggests *anima tunditur, mens conciditur* (“the soul is pounded, the mind is struck down”), since an axe and hammer are under discussion. Yet fetters also suit love, and it is unusual to mix a literal word into an allegory, especially one that appears almost proper rather than figurative.

[Col. 0433] 77. The Vienna manuscript reads *sapientia et virtus Dei* (“the wisdom and power of God”).

[Col. 0433] 78. The Royal manuscript reads *sanitatis nostro genere* (“of health in our kind”), a compressed or corrupt phrase.

[Col. 0433] 79. Schott’s edition reads *interiore homine, sanati* (“healed in the inner person”).

[Col. 0433] 80. The Royal manuscript and the Badian and Gravius editions incorrectly read *tulimus* (“we bore”). See the preceding discussion.

[Col. 0433] 81. We deleted *Amen* at the end of this letter. It is absent from the manuscripts and appears to have entered the printed editions from Scripture.

## IN EPISTLE XXXIII

1. This title is absent from the Royal manuscript and the editions of Badian and Gravius. Grin’s edition has: “Paulinus to Alethius, bishop and brother of Florentius.”

2. The Royal manuscript has *eloquium* (“utterance,” “speech”).

3. The Royal manuscript and the editions of Badian and Gravius have *qui nobis* (“who for us …”).

4. Grin’s edition has *aut tale* (“or such a thing”), supported by the Royal manuscript.

## IN EPISTLE XXXIV

1. Grin’s edition has “Homily, etc.” The Viennese manuscript and Florus of Lyon, in *The Catena on the Epistles of Paul*, book II, together with Chifflet’s edition, have: “Sermon of Saint Paulinus, bishop, concerning the treasury.” Three printed codices have “Epistle, etc.” Rosv’s edition has: “Epistle XXXIV, or Declamation concerning the Treasury.”

2. Thus the Royal and Vienna manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition. Others have *vincula* (“chains,” “bonds”).

3. Thus the same codices. Others have *quod quam maxime* (“which as much as possible”).

4. The same codices have *Dominum fenerat* (“he lends at interest to the Lord”). The others have *Deum fenerat* (“he lends at interest to God”).

5. The Royal manuscript and the editions of Badian and Gravius have *trapezetae* (“bankers,” “money-changers”).

6. Grin’s edition has *ferens* (“bearing”).

7. Four editions add *Deo* (“to God”).

8. “On earth yours”: that is, if you recognize that money on earth is yours only temporally, only for a time, you will be able to make it perpetual in heaven.

9. The editions of Badian and Gravius have *Dominicorum talentorum* (“the Lord’s talents”).

10. Thus we emended from the Vienna manuscript and Chifflet’s edition. The previous reading was *superantes* (“surpassing”).

11. Thus we restored it from those same two witnesses. The previous reading was *quo digne* (“by which worthily”).

12. Grin’s edition has: *Propterea … obstringo* (“Therefore … I bind”).

13. The Viennese manuscript has *te expertus fidelem, de suis coelestibus thesauris te divitem faciat* (“having found you faithful, may he make you rich from his heavenly treasures”). The Royal manuscript and Chifflet’s edition have *te expertum fidelem de suis coelestibus thesauris divitem faciat*, incorrectly.

14. The Royal manuscript has *quid* (“what”); the editions of Badian and Gravius have *quod* (“which,” “because”).

[Col. 0433] 15 The Vienna manuscript and the edition of Chifflet: “it may be seen.”

[Col. 0433] 16 Thus the Regius and Vienna manuscripts together with Chifflet’s edition. The others: “on the evil day, from anger.”

[Col. 0433] 17 The editions of Badius and Gravius: “he endures to omit.”

[Col. 0433] 18 Thus the Vienna manuscript together with the editions of Gronovius and Chifflet. Elsewhere: “they kiss.”

[Col. 0433] 19 The Regius manuscript: “more forcibly.”

Sacchini: “I read *epibatae*.” The Vulgate reading, *aditae*, makes no sense; *abditae* was close at hand, since what had been the Apostle’s prison seemed to have been submerged and hidden in the deep. But that reading appeared more ingenious than true. *Perditae* was related to it, as in the poem to Cytherius: “The captain himself, leader of the ruined raft.” *Obito*, that is, “shipwreck,” suggested itself, as in the letter to Jovius: “Let us undergo the shipwreck of salvation.” Likewise *navitae*; finally, “safe and naked,” which, according to what we have adopted, was by no means displeasing.
