# The Later Part of the Works of Saint Paulinus

[Col. 0437]

## Poems (C, G, S)*

[Note: [Col. 0437] Additional notes to these poems were printed by Migne as a separate document in columns 709–718. Each superscript number in the text of the poems refers to the number of the note in that separate document.]

## Poem I [Note: [Col. 0437A] Written before the year 390.]

[Col. 0437A] While Paulinus was still living in the secular world, he sends birds to Gestidius.

### 327–328. Paulinus to his deservedly revered lord Gestidius

It is indeed an affront to a master of a household abounding in maritime delicacies to offer him anything earthly and rustic. But, both to give me an occasion for conversing somewhat with your harmonious spirit and to make it seem that I am adding some service to this discourse, I have sent you a few little fig-peckers among the very few that the boys bring in the evening—birds whose small number embarrassed me, so that I also appended more words in little verses, as though I were going to make up the number by loquacity. But since both things are blameworthy, you, by kindly and familiarly forgiving both, will arrange matters so that neither the smallness of the gift seems inhuman nor the chatter odious.

So take these birds, fattened in the thorny countryside,

Which, while the clever fowler hides beneath a covering of flint,

Pretending a bird and deceiving it with a similar whisper,

He hangs in trusting flocks upon limed branches.

[5] Then, bringing back the slender prey, though not a small gift,

He arranges the fowling on tablets, and first the rich

[Col. 0439A] Row shines, gradually thinning toward the bottom of the little board,

So that leanness may offend less; the favor of fattening,

Placed before the eyes, delights them with the plump bird.

## Poem II [Note: [Col. 0439D] Written before the year 390.]

[Col. 0439D] While still living in the secular world, he sends oysters to the same Gestidius.

So that the dear gift of a poor friend may please you,

Do not reckon as gifts the rich presents you send us.

For what worthy return can I make to you for those fish,

Which the nearby shore, rich in its deep waters,

[5] 329–330 supplies you, distinguished by marvelous appearance and form?

But for me, scarcely in the deep, through rocky channels,

Is a rare *sphondylus* [Note: [Col. 0439D] See note 216.] produced amid dark seaweed.

Thus sharing with you, I have sent you twice five

And twice three shells, fragrant with the nectar of the sea,

[10] [Col. 0439B] Which a very sweet substance fills with two-colored flesh.

I gladly ask you to accept them; do not disdain as worthless

What is small only in size, but measure it by great affection.

## Fragment of Poem III [Note: [Col. 0439D] Written before the year 390.]

On kings collected from Suetonius.

[This was added from Ausonius’s Epistle 19 to Paulinus.]

Europe and Asia, two of the earth’s greatest

Limbs, to which Sallustius hesitantly adds Libya [Note: [Col. 0439D] That is, Africa. See Poem 27, verse 73, and note 217.]

As attached to Europe, so that it may be called the third,

Were ruled by many whose fame has obliterated them,

[5] And whose barbarian names Roman tongues do not transmit:

Illibanus, Avelis the Numidian, and Vonones the Parthian,

And Caranus, who received the name of kings from Pella,

And Nechepsus, who taught the Magi empty mysteries;

[Col. 0439C] And Sesostris, who soon afterward ruled without a name.

[10] [lacuna]

The bold man who gave names to the Icarians’ sea,

And he who skillfully sailed to the Chalcidian citadels.

## Poem IV [Note: [Col. 0439D] Elsewhere numbered 3; what was 4 is now 5. Written around the year 390.]

Shortly after his conversion from secular life, in this prayer he asks God for honorable conduct and prays for a happy future for himself and his family.

### Morning Prayer to God

Almighty Father [Note: [Col. 0440D] The Hieronymian manuscript of Alexander and three editions—those of Gravius, Poelman, and Schott—in their margins have: “Almighty, known to me only through the worship of the mind.”] of all things, to whom belongs supreme power,

Hear me if I ask what is right: may no day be sad for me,

And may no night break my peaceful rest.

May I not desire what belongs to others, but may my own possessions also benefit

[5] Those who supplicate; and may no one hold prayers wishing harm to me,

Or hold prayers that would harm me. [Note: [Col. 0439D] See Poem 3, verse 64.] May there be no power

[Col. 0439D] To wish evil, and may a tranquil power to do good be present.

May my mind be content with its own lot, not devoted to shameful gain,

And, conscious of its goodness, may it overcome bodily allurements

[10] In a chaste bed; may it hate shameful jokes and obscene words,

That evil tongue, ever guilty of pouring out poison,

Which is greatly pleasing to malicious ears.

[Col. 0440A] May I not be afflicted by anyone’s death, nor grow through anyone’s funeral.

May I never envy anyone, nor ever lie.

[15] May my household be joyful; may a satisfied servant delight in unbought banquets,

And a faithful companion, a polished attendant,

An obedient wife, and children dear because of their mother.

May God grant these things on account of chaste conduct; these ways of life

Promise you perpetual life throughout the ages to come.

## Poem V [Note: [Col. 0439D] Elsewhere numbered 4; what was 5 is now 6. Written around the year 390.]

[Col. 0439D] He enumerates various attributes of God and prays for grace from God by which he may avoid sins, so that he may meet God’s judgment securely.

### Another Prayer to God

Almighty [Note: [Col. 0440D] See note 218.] Father, the one God of all things, whom I worship in mind,

[Col. 0440B] Unknown to evils and unknown to none of the devout;

Without beginning or end, older than the age,

Than whatever has been or will come; whose form and nature

[5] Neither mind can comprehend nor tongue express;

Whom only the righteous are permitted to see and hear face to face

Commanding, and to sit beside the Father on his right hand;

The maker himself of all things, himself the cause of things being created;

Himself the Word of God, God the Word, existing before

[10] The world that he was to make; begotten at that

Time when time did not yet exist; brought forth before

The Morning Star and the red East illuminated heaven;

Without whom nothing was done, through whom all things were made, whose

[Col. 0440C] Throne is in heaven, and to whom earth is subject as he sits,

[15] As are the sea and the unconquerable chaos of dark night;

Himself moving all things without rest, giving life to the lifeless;

God from the unbegotten Father [Note: [Col. 0440D] See Poem 6, verse 168.], who, offended by the deceit

Of the proud people, called the nations into kingdoms:

To be worshiped through the better offspring of an adopted race.

[20] Whom our forefathers were permitted to see; when that Divinity was seen,

It was granted that the Father too was seen—he who bore our defilements

And, suffering the mockery of cruel death,

Taught that the way to eternal life could be retraced.

Not merely that the soul could return, but that with the whole body

[25] It could enter the heavenly regions, leaving behind the empty

Mystery of the tomb, covered over in the vacant earth.

Son of the Most High Father, and our salvation in our age [Note: [Col. 0440D] See Poem 10, verse 5]:

[Col. 0440D] Father, to whom the Father entrusted all his own powers,

Holding nothing back through envy, full of gifts,

[30] Open the way to my prayers, and carry these things to the Father’s ears.

Father, grant me an unconquered mind against every crime,

And avert from me the serpent-like wickedness of harmful poison.

[Col. 0441A] Let it be enough that the serpent destroyed ancient Eve

And joined Adam to her in deception [Note: [Col. 0441D] See note 219.]. We, the late seeds of descendants,

[35] An age foretold by truthful prophets,

Must avoid the snares in which the death-dealing serpent entangles us.

Open the way by which, after the bonds of my sick body,

I may rise on high: by which the milky path of the pure heavens

Surpasses the wandering lights of the windy moon:

[40] By which the pious leaders departed, and by which formerly

Whole in body, carried in a four-horse chariot, [Note: [Col. 0441D] See note 220.]

Elijah penetrates beyond the upper air, with Enoch preceding him

In his solid body.

Father, grant me the hoped-for breath of eternal light,

If I do not swear that stones are gods, and, looking up to one altar

[45] Of the One who must be revered, bring undefiled offerings of life;

[Col. 0441B] If I acknowledge you as Father of the Lord and of the only-begotten God,

[Note: [Col. 0441D] See Poem 24, verse 93.] And him who, mingled with both,

Hovered above the watery waves as Spirit.

Father, grant forgiveness, and cleanse my tortured heart,

[50] If I do not seek you in the entrails of animals or in poured blood,

Nor infer the divine power from hidden entrails.

333–334 If I abstain from crime [Note: [Col. 0441D] See the Appendix to Epistle 2 to Celantius, note 6.], yet am myself liable to error;

And if I desire more than I trust that I shall be found good and pure,

Deign to accept my confessed soul; if I curse perishable limbs,

[55] And if I repent in silence, and fearfully my deepest understanding

Anticipates the late torments and punishments of Gehenna,

And my wounded mind suffers its own spirits as shades.

Father, grant that these prayers may be made certain [Note: [Col. 0441D] See Poem 14, verse 43.] by my supplication:

[Col. 0441C] Let me fear nothing and desire nothing: let me consider this enough,

[60] Whatever is enough; let me desire nothing shameful, nor let me myself

Be a cause of shame; nor let me do to anyone what at the same time

I would not wish done to me; nor let me be wounded by a real crime,

Nor stained by uncertainty: the suspected person seems to differ little

From one truly guilty. [Note: [Col. 0441D] See Poem 4, verse 6.] Let there be no power

[65] To do evil, and may a tranquil power to do good be present.

May I be content with modest food and clothing, and dear to my friends;

And may I always be a father without injury to this name.

May I suffer neither in mind nor body; may all my limbs

Perform the functions of rest; nor, wounded in any part,

[70] [Col. 0441D] May use desire anything that has been lost.

May I enjoy peace and act without fear; may I regard no earthly marvels as extraordinary.

When my final hour comes,

May a life conscious of its goodness neither fear death nor desire it.

When, with your indulgence, I appear pure from hidden things,

[75] I shall look down upon all things, when the sole pleasure will have been

To hope for your judgment; while it postpones its appointed time

[Col. 0442A] And the day delays, drive far away the savage

Ambusher, the serpent, with its seductive errors.

These pious prayers, yet trembling with sorrowful guilt,

[80] Christ [Note: [Col. 0442D] The printed editions of Gronovius, Poelman, and Schott have “Son” in their margins, as in verse 26.], propitiable before the eternal Father,

Commend them before the eternal Father, O Savior, God and Lord, Mind, Glory, Word,

The Son [Note: [Col. 0442D] The same codices together with Gravius in their margins: “The Son, true from the true.”], and true light from true light,

Remaining with the eternal Father, reigning throughout the ages;

Whom the people celebrate [Note: [Col. 0442D] Only Rosweyd’s edition has “they celebrate,” incorrectly, since the following verse has “he strikes”; here the people is singular.] in harmonious song,

[85] And strikes the air with answering voices: Amen.

## Poem VI [Note: [Col. 0441D] Elsewhere numbered 5; what was 6 is now 7. Written around the year 390.]

[Col. 0442B] On Saint John the Baptist, Christ’s Forerunner.

Highest Father of all things, eternal power of heaven,

With whom our salvation and the glory of the saints are, O Christ,

And Spirit, equally joined to the Father and the Son,

Who rule minds and tongues and supply strength,

[5] Which faith alone has earned; to whom full power belongs

To infuse understanding into beasts and voice into the mute,

Grant that John, drawn from the Evangelical spring,

May make verses flow in our dry stream.

He was indeed as great as it was possible to give the world,

[10] He who commanded such a man to be born through new miracles;

Yet it is permitted for the great to devote modest care,

And heavenly beings do not disdain humble praise:

It is also part of merit to celebrate the merits of the devout.

I shall sing nothing new now, nor anything of my own: the prophets spoke

[15] [Col. 0442C] All things beforehand, and holy men in unrestrained speech

Consecrated the promised birth, life, and death:

If that was death which deserved heaven through blood.

335–336 We have vowed only to unfold those words in melodious rhythms

And to relax the minds of readers through verse:

Thus—for it is permitted to compare great things with small, ancient with new,

[20] Perfect with unlearned, eternal with perishable [Note: [Col. 0442D] See Epistle 13, note 19.]—

Whatever the earlier writers said under God’s inspiration,

The venerable name of David adapted to the lyre,

Composing harmonious melodies with a heavenly plectrum.

It is also permitted for us to remember God, although hearts covered

[25] [Col. 0442D] With many crimes can receive heavenly understanding.

Zacharias, once a priest from the Syrian people,

Attended to the temples entrusted to him with solemn preparation.

His life, piety, faith, dignity, and modesty were worthy of God;

His gracious wife, worthy of obedience to God,

[30] Elizabeth, descended from an ancient stock of holy men,

And equal to such a husband in virtues.

[Col. 0443A] But—what earlier generations counted a reproach in mothers—

Being without offspring, she led a sorrowful old age in barrenness,

And the passing of time had shut out every hope of children.

[35] By chance the whole people was bringing the customary sacrifice to God,

And the high priest had kindled the sacred fires more abundantly,

Adorning the innermost altars with divine flames.

Behold, beside the sacred altar [Note: [Col. 0443D] That is, nearby. See Poem 9, verse 52.] a heavenly messenger

Stood forth, distinguished in clothing and venerable in face,

[40] And showed by countenance and appearance that he had been sent from heaven.

Then he opened his holy breast to such words:

Receive, priest beloved by the heavenly Lord,

The commands of the eternal God, whose care for the devout

Is perpetual, who, as a constant guardian in a pure breast,

[45] [Col. 0443B] Has known how to bestow merited love upon the holy.

First of all: he does not wish your family to have perished

With its seed extinguished, and he has made the womb

Of your wife fertile, although it had already ceased in exhausted old age.

Why, then, do you doubt, even with mortal understanding,

[50] That God can do all things? But you will believe; he will prove it.

A blessed child will be born, worthy of so great a sponsor,

An enduring child who, immediately from his earliest age,

Greater than you, will possess in an unconquered breast sacred powers,

Beyond those of his father, by the gift of his Creator.

[55] Nor is it truly within your choice and authority

What first name you should give the child at birth: God himself,

Who orders him to be born, likewise orders him to be John.

This title of a name, an immense succession of merits,

[Col. 0443C] Which only he who will grant it, and allot you joys

In so great a child, could foresee before the child was born—

[60] But he will not grant you merely a glory enclosed

Within one household; that would be a small glory.

Rather, as great as the world stretches from birth

To the late twilight of ending light,

The whole world will rejoice with you in your offspring.

[65] What wonder? He will be free from all the dregs of vices,

Leading a heavenly life without stain or crime,

Keeping his temperate breast free from maddening wine [Note: [Col. 0443D] See Epistle 22, note 2.],

And avoiding every cup of evil-counseling juice.

And when he promises salvation to the human race even after its errors,

[70] Whoever is renewed from the holy water,

He himself will have nothing in him that needs purification.

[Col. 0443D] And so that I may not tell you more through various circumlocutions,

You, learned priest, cannot be unaware of the merit of Elijah,

Who, with the law of hated death remitted,

[75] Leads eternal life with his own body,

Whom a fiery chariot carried to the high heavens,

A mass of flaming horses gathered in swift movement [Note: [Col. 0443D] Thus the Lyon edition. Rosweyd’s edition: “made fiery.”].

337–338 Your son will equal him in the distinction of his merits,

[80] And will possess an equal share of both praise and virtue.

Therefore, for thanks commensurate with so great a gift,

[Col. 0444A] Do not leave your wavering faith in suspense, lest the anger of the favoring God,

Once aroused, decree a deserved punishment after the rewards.

He spoke, and the winged being slipped away into the thin air,

[85] And from afar filled the air with a fragrant sacred scent.

The priest stiffened, bewildered in his trembling mind,

And while his hesitant heart revolved the promise,

While he distrusted himself as having deserved so great a favor—

That he should be the concern of the Most High God,

[90] That a messenger dismissed from high heaven should bring

Such clear commands from his Lord to so humble a servant—

And feared that he was playing games,

He thought those things dreams, while he judged his own conduct

More sparingly than was fair and refused to admit that he had deserved it.

[95] Faith itself makes him faithless: while he refuses to believe

Himself worthy of belief, he earns punishment through disbelief.

Immediately his tongue was fastened to his doubting palate,

[Col. 0444B] And, forgetful of its movement, the organ that fashioned speech,

Stuck together in sluggish numbness, unable to articulate a sound.

And while he desired to recount the miracles to his people,

[100] His attempt was in vain, and with his mouth fixed he fell silent.

Sadly he departed and turned his grief over within his imprisoned mind,

Praying in the secrecy of his heart for pardon for his errors.

How great is God’s compassion! How readily the Divinity can be entreated!

It is enough to have repented. The appointed order of time by which he grants what is certain

[105] Rolls onward, and the pregnant womb—wondrously—swells,

And Elizabeth’s devout entrails bear a sacred burden,

And a youthful gift comes forth in exhausted old age.

Then another—Saint Gabriel, who had been the same messenger

To Zacharias—pondering much greater things,

[110] Sets out toward Mary [Note: [Col. 0444D] In the word *Mariam*, Prudentius in *Psychomachia*, verse 88, and Paulinus often shorten the second syllable. See Poem 22, verse 153.], who, betrothed to a husband

But more greatly chosen by God, was destined to give birth to the world’s salvation.

[Col. 0444C] The chaste virgin guarded her unstained modesty.

After a splendid heavenly form stood before her eyes,

She lowered her modest gaze

[115] And tinged her shining cheeks with suffused crimson.

He said: “O girl more blessed than all virgins in the world,

Whom the circle of the whole sun encompasses,

And [more blessed] than all who were before, who are now, and who will follow;

Chosen by the great God, so that you may be called the mother

[120] Of him whose father he also is! Come, blessed one, conceive this burden,

Unpolluted by a man and free from all intercourse,

Pregnant through the Word of God: let your womb provide a body

For him who made heaven, earth, the sea, and the stars;

Who always was, and now is, and in every age

[125] Always will be: Lord of the world and creator of light,

[Col. 0444D] Himself the light of heaven, through you will put on mortal limbs

And enter the eyes and assemblies of human beings.

Lift up an undisturbed spirit to the reward of such great praise;

He who willed it will give you both strength and faith

[130] —for he rules all things and governs them by his command—

To be your son, although he was the Son of the Lord.”

He had spoken, and at the same time left the earth and vanished from sight,

Seeking the accustomed heaven with an easy movement.

God’s commands are fulfilled, and the girl believes immediately;

[135] Her ready faith increases both her merit and her former life.

[Col. 0445A] The elements hidden under silent causes fashion the divine body,

And the sacred burden grows:

339–340 The devout womb nurses the heavenly Lord.

Meanwhile the offspring, although not yet born,

[140] Urges holy Mary to go forth and visit Elizabeth,

Who, already venerable through long age,

Was carrying the child beloved by the Lord whom she was to bear.

The mother listens to her child—so great is the power of faith [Note: [Col. 0445D] See note 334.],

And she comes as commanded. John moved his mother’s

[145] Womb and filled her breast with divine understanding.

Already a prophet, not yet born, enclosed within the womb,

Already he saw what had happened before and what was to come.

When from afar she saw Mary shining with the light of conception,

[Col. 0445B] She hurried forward swiftly to meet her,

[150] And, extending her arms in reverence, she said:

“Hail, O mother of the Lord; hail, devout virgin, ”

Free from the marriage chamber and ignorant of intercourse with a man,

Yet destined to bear God: such was the value of her chastity,

That you might bear the titles and honors of an untouched woman and a wife.

[155] Why is honor paid to me, who have not earned it and am not worthy of so great a gift?

Why is the glory of heaven, brought down to our household gods and humble dwelling,

Bringing light only into our obscure inner rooms?

But may he, gentle and gracious, be present with his worshipers,

[160] And, being begotten, grant this favor also—the favor which he had granted before.

She spoke, and embraced him, joining her arms around him;

And now, having worshiped God, she gave kisses to the holy womb.

Come now, guilty Judaea, stained with the blood of your king,

If no credence is to be given to the words of those who came before,

[165] If you believe that the holy prophets can deceive,

And if the impious cruelty of a perverse people thinks that even Moses

Could deceive David—believe the unborn child:

Confined in his mother’s womb, John teaches what he sees through his mother’s holy mouth.

[170] Who, I ask, taught him—while the virgin holds him in her chaste womb—

How great a birth awaits the new ages?

But what is hidden from the holy is revealed, and what is unseen by the profane is exposed.

Yet once she had gone beyond the appointed limit, her course sought the broad fields,

And, forgetting me, she dared to run farther ahead.

[175] I hope that one day, when my strength has been firmly established,

I shall be able to drive chariots through this space as well.

Now let us resume the journey begun: let mortal language speak of mortal things;

Let divine things be spoken by the Lord.

And now, when the time prescribed by nature had fully elapsed,

[180] The illustrious child is brought forth from the mature womb,

And steadfast faith fulfills the great promise of God, which had not been believed,

And the infant born confirms it.

The relatives who lived nearby gather according to custom,

To fit to the child a name derived from the names of his ancestors,

[185] Choosing names sought from their combined reasons;

But his mother, conscious of the heavenly command given through the child,

Denies that the choice has been left to her relatives.

Therefore it seems best to consult the father, who had long been shut up in silence,

The sole means of expressing the message that his tongue could not utter,

If a letter could signify it.

He is consulted, takes tablets, and writes “John.”

Everyone is astonished, and recalls that no earlier name

Had been prescribed from the lineage of his ancestors.

How much power late faith possessed! For because his right hand recorded

[195] What his mind had believed, the punishment of sin was remitted.

The barriers of his bound tongue are loosened.

Now the old man answers with his voice, and reveals to his relatives

The commands of God long kept hidden, and promises what is to come,

While confirming what has already happened. Who could doubt that such a one would be

[200] Able to be born by an extraordinary birth,

When the law of nature had been set aside by the Lord’s commands?

He placed before all eyes an example of unbelief worthy of universal remembrance,

Whether in the punishment of the parent or in his forgiveness:

At once fear and hope press upon their minds, from opposite sides.

[205] Meanwhile the time of the cradle passes. In the child himself

The clear form of divine power appears.

Cajoling words and laughter are silent, and uncertain murmurs cease:

Seriousness, the forerunner of a playful mind,

Already shapes the tender mouth for future conduct.

[210] Then, when the child had fixed his first footsteps

With steady effort, and his words began to mark out articulate speech,

It was his custom either to listen to the sayings of his holy parent,

Or to learn by heart the celebrated deeds of ancient men,

Or the laws that God himself had established through Moses as interpreter,

[215] Which the sacred page of stone preserves.

He would recall and study these and whatever else might strengthen his tender mind:

For he must not be thought ignorant of earlier things,

Since the Lord had granted him knowledge of things to come.

But after age had added strength to his limbs—

(For his mind, full of God, had outstripped his slow-growing years)—

[220] He resolved that he must learn those things which human beings cannot teach:

At the same time, he resolved to avoid foods

And drink, and the harmful contagions detrimental to holy life.

Therefore he left the dwelling of his holy, though immaculate, parent

[225] And fled the crowds of human beings and harmful gatherings,

Making his way alone toward the trackless regions of the earth,

Where his undefiled mind could see only itself,

And, free from cares, devote itself to sacred commandments.

His garment was woven from the bristles of a shaggy camel,

So that, in opposition to luxury, it might harden his tender limbs

[230] And repel heavy sleep from his mortified body.

A cheap belt bound it around his stiffened loins.

Wild honey provided him with easy nourishment,

As did fruits and herbs that had sprung up on uncultivated rocks,

[235] And running water relieved his parched thirst.

What place is there here for vices? What access could depraved desire

Find among these sacred things and inner sanctuaries of the mind?

Where could one sin who desires nothing? Where could wicked feeling

Tend in secret, when one needs nothing at all?

[240] Thus the first human beings lived, and the author of the world had given them

These customs for ages yet to come,

Until ill-advised pleasure inserted itself,

And with it brought luxury and the love of possessing.

Hence hatred, hence quarrels, hence deceit, envy, and anger,

[245] Slaughter, weapons, bloodshed, conflict, battles, and deaths:

Hence the offense against God, which savage Tartarus will atone for.

But why do I accuse common guilt so excessively,

When I myself am forgetful of myself, whom it is not right to burden with what I have committed,

But rather to hope for forgiveness? [Note: Thus the editions of Lyon and Rosweyde, *mirabimur* (“we shall marvel”). See verses 254 and 285.]

Rather, let us marvel at the more excellent, unconquered,

And inimitable example of the ancient age,

The demigod-like man who, free from every stain,

Though he tortured his own body with such savage punishments,

[255] Prescribed what should become of us even after our sins:

[343–344] But after, by such means, strengthening his unconquered mind,

He had spent a long period of time and had resolved the questions

That had to be sought, a voice issued from heaven to him:

“Beloved prophet, enough time has now been spent

[260] For you to benefit yourself. The time has come for you to use what has been given to you

So that it may benefit others, and preserve what has already been lost.

Go, therefore, to the holy waters of the pure Jordan.

Here wash away the sins of every human being

Who regrets the offenses of his former life

And at last turns his thoughts toward better things.

Whoever, with faithful mind, believes that you can erase his offenses

[265] In the holy washing, that person will be reborn,

Provided that a life follows which proves that the washed have condemned their former life.”

John obeyed what he had heard with a servant’s mind,

And immediately descended to the banks of the river at the command.

Here he proclaims the commandments of God in reverent speech,

And pours new salvation into the hearts of believers.

He washes away the offenses of believers with the water poured over them,

Absolves human beings from fear, and remits their punishments,

[275] And extinguishes fire with water. He urges forgetfulness of errors,

And grants new bodies to a new life.

O Father, O eternal creator of human beings and of all things,

By how many stages does your mercy show restraint! What father has ever

Endured forgiving his erring child so many times?

You give the human race understanding, by which they may know good and evil.

[280] Not enough: you bind them with the bonds of a law to be preserved,

And set punishments before the wicked and rewards before the just.

Who has rejected this as well? Whenever one wishes to return,

Forgiveness is at hand: behold, the holy washing is open,

Which renews life and erases former deeds,

And makes new human beings. What more do we seek?

And yet there is still further forgiveness: if anyone should violate

This gift as well, having fallen through a polluted body.

Although his error may already have advanced very far,

Let him stop and return: once he has condemned himself,

[290] He has deserved to be absolved. If he repents, the guilt is annulled.

O truly, as you say, a light burden, and a gentle yoke

That clings to us, when one human being is forgiven so many times!

And yet we continue to err, nor is there any end to crime

Among the human race. But your praise increases, for the greater

[295] The guilt of the offender, the greater the glory of the one who spares him.

Therefore let every mind give thanks to you, and every tongue sing

As much as the human race can,

And, if it cannot succeed in pleasing you, let it at least strive to become pleasing.

If we spread our sails, an immense depth opens

For praising you, gracious Father. But the mind, conscious of so great a burden,

[300] Trembles, and, not unaware of its own powers,

Considers the matter and leaves what ought to be said to those more worthy.

Let us return to the work begun: this task is for you, holy John,

By which you renew minds purified through washing.

This was not the first pronouncement of the Lord by which he gave you warning,

Sending a clear voice through the clouds:

Many ages earlier God had spoken through the mouth of the holy prophet Isaiah,

The greatest prophet of the ancient age:

“I shall send before your eyes, my son, a minister,

[310] Who, clearing the packed roughness of the roads for your steps,

Will make the lofty mountains sink down;

He will likewise make the depressed valleys rise up.

He will straighten what is crooked here,

And smooth what is rough and hard,

And compel the entire world to become level.”

[315] [345–346] Then, I ask, gracious John, gift of the supreme Father,

Do you come with Christ, promised by him

Who sent the Son? Then, O prophet foretold by the prophets,

Have you shared in the honor of an angelic name?

Through you the first mercy of God reveals itself;

The first authority to grant forgiveness has been entrusted to you.

When many crowds sought new miracles from Christ,

Christ said of you: “It has been granted to see such a man,

A prophet whom no earlier age had seen.

I say that, among mortals born from women,

And among those whom the customary manner of human birth will produce,

There will be no one able to place himself before John.”

This is what he reports about you who sees every hidden thing

Of the human heart and all the stretches of the ages in their succession,

Perceiving them as we see the things placed before our eyes.

## POEM VII [Note: Formerly 6; what was 7 is now 8. Written around the year 390.]  
### Paraphrase of Psalm I

Paulinus, at that time inexperienced in theological mysteries, thought that all Christians, even the wicked, would obtain a certain salvation, provided that they preserved their faith unharmed.

Blessed is the man who has kept his life far apart

From the gatherings of the ungodly,

Who has not remained in the way of sinners,

Nor sat in the seat of pestilence,

[5] But, with all his heart fixed upon the law of God,

Turns over the commandments of life night and day,

And cultivates his mind with chaste teachings.

He will be like a tree that, standing near a river,

Is nourished by the moisture of the bank,

And in its proper season will yield abundant fruit,

And, with foliage that never falls,

Will stand ever green, a living tree with vigorous branches.

This glory will not follow the wicked,

But just as the wind carries away a spark of dust,

So anger will sweep the wicked from the face of God.

Therefore the scattered groups of human beings throughout the world

Will be divided in this order,

So that the wicked may not rise for judgment,

Those who denied God the worship owed to him,

[20] But may rise to be punished. For, seeing their own crime,

They will not need an inquiry to expose it,

Since they will bear before them the mark of approaching death,

Not carrying on their foreheads the sign of salvation.

But the sinner, though not yet ungodly—

And that is a great multitude—

Will not rise to glory,

But will rise to be assigned to examination.

For the judge cannot sit with the righteous,

When he must render an account of his own deeds,

And be proved or convicted according to his varied actions.

Without the law, those ignorant of the law will fall everywhere;

The one who has fallen under the law will be judged by the law.

Through the whole work the judging fire will pass:

Whatever the flame does not burn but proves

Will be weighed out as an everlasting reward.

[35] Whoever has done things destined to be burned will suffer loss,

But he himself will escape through the fires.

Yet, miserable, bearing the marks of a scorched body,

[347–348] He will retain life, though he will not retain glory;

For, though conquered in the flesh, he has not been converted in mind,

Even if he has denied the faith owed to the law,

After repeatedly falling into many crimes.

Yet, still bearing the eternal name of faith,

He will never be excluded from the bounds of salvation.

Therefore let us all now, in this age,

While life runs on and the day of our age remains open,

Tread straight paths with firm foot,

And not be carried away along the slippery breadth of the road.

It is better to fight our way along the narrow path

And enter through laborious exertions.

God gladly recognizes the ways of the good,

But the easy path of the wicked will be destroyed.

## POEM VIII [Note: Formerly 7; what was 8 is now 9. Perhaps written around the same time.]  
### Paraphrase of Psalm II

Why did the nations rage, and why did the peoples

Meditate on empty things? The rulers stood together with kings,

Driven against the Lord and Christ, bringing madness.

“Let us break their bonds, let us shake off their yokes!”

[5] He who remains in eternal command over all the heavens

Will mock them, and speak justly in anger,

And with a terrible word of threat will disturb the wicked.

But I am the King created by him with equal dominion;

I proclaim the Lord’s command upon holy Zion.

The Lord himself said to me: “You are my Son;

Today I have begotten you. Ask: let me make you heir of the nations,

[10] And let your possession be spread over all the earth.

You have an iron rod, because by powerful right

You rule the swelling peoples throughout the whole world,

Breaking their hardened hearts like vessels

Fashioned from baked clay, so that you may remake them for the better.”

And now, all of you kings, turn your minds toward submission,

And you who govern obedient human hearts by judgment

And hold the reins of affairs:

Serve God in fear, and, faithful amid fear,

[20] Rejoice. Let discord become harmonious,

Joining unlike emotions within a single breast,

So that fear may not afflict your minds, nor joys dissolve

Because they lack the cheerful security of freedom from death.

Learn justice and take up upright conduct,

Tremble before the just God and rejoice in the benevolent one,

Lest at some time God become angry with the world because of your deserts,

And you perish, justly driven away from the righteous way.

From now on hasten to recoil from the wicked path.

Behold, soon, when the great anger of the Mighty One has blazed forth,

He will sift the whole world by divine judgment,

And separate the chaff for the fire, the grain for salvation.

Then blessed are all whose faithful hope is in him.

## POEM IX [Note: Formerly 8; what was 9 is now 10. Perhaps written around the year 390.]  
### Paraphrase of Psalm CXXXVI

We sat beside the unknown rivers of savage Babylon,

Captives, the people of Judaea, weeping piteously.

As we carried our ancestral Zion in our remembering hearts,

And sighed for exile as a deserved punishment from just anger,

[5] Where willow trees planted along the sluggish bank

Provided friendly shade for the foreign peoples.

There, amid the walls of the Assyrian city,

Having forgotten joyful voices amid mournful silence,

We hung our instruments from the branches of the willows.

For harsh anger gave us a painful grief,

Because the impious enemy who had taken us from our homeland

[10] Ordered us to sing for his pleasure

Those songs accustomed to be sung in the holy temple.

Therefore shall we sing divine praises and songs suited to chaste choirs

Amid barbarous rites and loathsome tombs,

And amid altars kindled with mournful fires—

Alas, rejoicing evilly in our sorrow?

Shall we turn our holy ritual into wicked luxury,

Playing mystical songs for a hostile game?

With what mouth, wretched people, shall we now sing sacred hymns?

In what place does Babylon demand songs from Zion?

But foreign soil does not receive the Lord’s song;

The sacred voice turns away from unworthy ears.

Yet if, as a more violent master over captives, you persist,

And if you have so great a desire to know holy Zion,

If you continue to compel me to speak what is not yours,

And to tell you what the songs of holy Zion are,

Hear what the avenging God promises the captive city.

Do not hope, wicked man, to enjoy this triumph for long,

By which you command a sacred hymn to be betrayed to you:

Behold what the Lord’s hymn is, what the songs of Zion are:

“If I forget you, my walls, let you, Jerusalem, be my concern;

May my right hand become forgetful of me,

May my tongue cling, dry, to my jaws,

Unless I embrace you with eternal love,

And unless, at the beginning of the promised kingdom,

At the beginning of my joy, I remember

To place you, Jerusalem, before all lands.”

Remember also the descendants of Edom, so that, in turn,

They may look upon our day in shame, when your people

Will inhabit bright Jerusalem within eternal walls—

The people who now, forgetful of you, cruelly threaten your destruction,

Saying: “Tear down and empty the hated city completely by hand,

Until no traces remain and the walls are reduced to emptiness.”

Unhappy daughter of wretched Babylon, blessed is the one

Who will repay you for what you have done against us.

No less blessed will be the one who seizes your little ones

And dashes your children against the solid rock.

If you desire to be blessed after Babylon’s stock has been extinguished,

Break by faith the crimes beginning to flare within you like first flames;

For the rock, Christ, is already near. With strong arms

Dash the serpent’s offspring against him.

For Babylon means “Confusion”; its daughter is the flesh,

The mother of sins, which leads a crowd harmful to salvation

To sow evils through bodily members.

[351–352] These things must be conquered by you if you wish to conquer death.

For if such enemies, shut up within your bones,

Are allowed to gain strength by growing,

You will conquer them only through a difficult struggle.

Seize them while they are small,

While the infancy of vices, still raw from the womb of the heart,

Yet creeps through your captive breast and tender limbs.

Unless you take precautions, once strengthened by force

It will kill the soul united with vices through earthly descent.

Therefore do not spare slaughtering such a band.

It will not be a crime for you to destroy a people destined to harm,

And to drench the avenging rock in evil blood:

The just man rejoices when the impious offspring falls.

For the devout man is purified all the more by this slaughter,

If he destroys the sins that dominate his own members,

And triumphs in Christ over the broken multitude of vices.

## LETTER XXIII [Note: Apparently written in the year 390.]  
### Ausonius to Paulinus

Paulinus, living in Spain, is addressed by Ausonius, who attributes his conversion to fickleness of mind. He reproaches him for interrupting his letters and invites him to return to him.

### Ausonius sends greetings to Paulinus

“We are shaking off, Paulinus, the yoke that a certain balance had supported:

A light and tolerable burden when placed upon joined shoulders.”

(See this letter among the Ausonian letters under number 23, in volume XIX of our *Patrology*, column 932.)

## LETTER XXIV [Note: Written in the year 391.]  
### Ausonius to Paulinus

Ausonius again complains of Paulinus’ silence and lays the blame for the violated friendship upon his wife, Therasia.

### Ausonius sends greetings to his Paulinus

“I had believed that the complaint contained in our preceding letter

Might bend you, Paulinus.”

(This letter may be read among the Ausonian letters under number 22, in volume XIX of our *Patrology*, column 931.)

## LETTER XXV [Note: Apparently written in the year 393.]  
### Ausonius to Paulinus

Since Paulinus answered nothing, Ausonius complained for a third time in a letter written in the year 392; that letter has been lost. He writes this fourth letter to him on the same subject.

### Ausonius sends greetings to his Paulinus

“This fourth letter has revealed to you my familiar complaints, Paulinus,

And provokes your sluggishness with a gentle discourse.”

(See this letter among the Ausonian letters under number 24, in volume XIX of our *Patrology*, column 934.)

## POEM X [Note: Formerly 9, 10, 12. Written in the summer of 393.]

Paulinus, now spending his fourth year in Spain, received the four letters mentioned above. This poem responds to the first, the third—which has been lost—and the fourth.

### Paulinus to Ausonius

[361–362] This is now the fourth summer to return to the harsh reapers,

And so many times winter has grown stiff with white frost,

Since no letter has come to me from your mouth,

And I have seen no writing marked by your hand,

Ever since, happy with a life-giving little book,

A letter finally gave me gifts long denied and multiplied.

For the letter blossomed with threefold variety of composition,

But the page, in its threefold abundance, was a poem.

Certain sweet things, rendered somewhat bitter by many complaints,

An anxious affection had mingled with criticism.

[363–364] But to me the gentleness of a father, more than the harshness of a critic,

Was pleasing, and I weighed the harsh words against the gentle ones in my mind.

These matters must nevertheless be restored to their proper place,

And must be handled in a more serious tone by an avenging heroic measure.

Meanwhile a lighter iambic line runs ahead a little,

Reporting our reciprocal words with measured step.

Now the elegiacs bid you farewell, and, having spoken that farewell,

As they have done for others, they fall silent after beginning their advance.

[Note: Here poem 10 formerly began.]

“Why do you command the Muses, father, who have renounced me,

To return to my care?

Hearts dedicated to Christ deny the Camenae,

Nor do they open to Apollo.

Once there was between you and me a harmony equal

Not in resources but in devotion:

To rouse deaf Phoebus from his Delphic cavern,

To invoke the Muses as divinities,

To seek, from groves or mountain heights,

The gift of speech granted by the gift of God.

Now another power moves my mind, a greater God;

It demands other ways of life,

Reclaiming from a human being what belongs to itself,

So that we may live for the Father of life.

It forbids us to devote ourselves to empty things,

Whether in leisure or in activity,

Or to fictional writings;

It commands us to obey its laws

And to behold its light.

The clever skill of the philosophers, the art of rhetoricians,

And the inventions of poets obscure that light,

For they fill hearts with false and empty things,

And merely train tongues,

Bringing nothing that contributes to salvation,

Nothing that reveals the truth.

For what good or true thing can those possess

Who do not possess the source of the highest truth

And goodness, God,

The nourishment and fountain of truth and goodness?

No one sees him except in Christ.

He is the light of truth, the way of life,

The power, mind, hand, and strength of the Father,

The sun of justice, the fountain of blessings, the flower of God.

Born from God, the creator of the world,

The life of our mortality and the death of death,

He is the teacher of virtues,

And God for us, and for us a human being.

By clothing himself with us, he stripped himself,

Joining human beings and God

In a union directed toward both.

Therefore, when his heavenly radiance has flashed into our hearts,

He wipes away the sickly sluggishness of the body

And renews the condition of the mind.

He drains away everything that formerly served

As a substitute for chaste pleasure,

And wholly claims for the Lord by his right

Our hearts, mouths, and time.

He wishes himself to be thought of, understood, believed in, and read;

He wishes to be feared and loved.

The empty passions aroused by the labor of present life

Along the pathway of the present age,

Faith in the future life with God abolishes.

Those things which we seem to scorn

He does not reject as profane or worthless possessions,

But warns us to place them in heaven as more precious things,

Entrusted to Christ God,

Who has promised more than he has received.

What is despised or more greatly set aside for him in the present

He will repay with abundant interest.

The good debtor, a faithful guardian of what has been increased for his creditors,

Will return the money;

God will restore with abundant interest

The much money that has been scorned.

Do not, I beg you, think me lazy, perverse, or impious

Because I am free for him, or study him, or devote myself to him,

And place everything in him.

For how can piety be absent from a Christian?

To be a Christian is itself mutual evidence of piety;

To be impious is not to be subject to Christ.

When we learn to possess this piety, can I fail to display it to you—

That is, to my father—

To whom God willed that I owe all sacred obligations and cherished names?

To you I owe education, rank, learning,

The honor of language, the toga, reputation,

Advancement, distinction, and instruction;

To you, my patron, teacher, and father, I owe these things.

But you reproach me for remaining away so long,

And angrily do so from a pious impulse?

It is useful, necessary, or pleasing:

Whatever of these it may be, it is pardonable.

Forgive me, if I do what is expedient as one who loves;

Rejoice if I live as I wish.

[Note: Here poem 12 formerly began.]

For a full three-year cycle I have been absent from my ancestral lands,

And you rebuke me, moved by holy complaints,

Because I have read another world through wandering errors,

Having first forgotten the cultivated fellowship of your life.

I embrace the feelings of a father that deserve to be welcomed,

And the anger that deserves my gratitude while affection remains safe.

But I would rather, my father, that you demand my return

From a place from which it could be granted.

I shall believe that I must be recalled by you

When you pour out prayers that are not fruitless before divine things,

A suppliant to the Muses of Castalia, whose divinity has been turned away.

It is not through these divinities that you will restore me to my fatherland and to you.

Whatever is granted, a light breeze will carry away into nothingness

(You call upon the Muses by names without divinity,

You appeal to them deafly and ask nothing).

These prayers are seized by the storms of the winds,

They cling to empty clouds because they have not been sent to God,

And they do not penetrate the starry court of the heavenly King.

[367–368] If you care about my return, look to him and pray to him

Who shakes the fiery heights of heaven with his thunder,

Who flashes with triple fire and does not mingle empty murmurs,

Who sufficiently bestows suns and rains upon heaven,

Who, above all that exists, is wholly and everywhere in all things,

Christ, infused into all things, governs all things,

Who holds and moves minds, who arranges our times

And places. If he establishes things contrary to our prayers,

He must be turned by prayer toward what we wish.

Why do you accuse me? If you disapprove of the course I follow

With God as its agent, the author whose will it pleases

To form or change my thoughts must first be accused,

If it is permitted.

For if you consider what I formerly was, what you know me to have been,

I shall freely confess that I am no longer the person I was under that former condition,

When I was not considered perverse,

Though I was perverse, seeing through the darkness of falsehood,

Thinking folly about God to be wisdom, and living upon death’s fodder.

For this reason it is right to forgive me all the more,

Because through this I am more readily granted recognition

And renewal by the highest Father,

Since what is being done is not done according to my former way.

Having confessed these things, I do not think I shall be called guilty

Of having changed my mind for the worse,

Since I have freely professed

That I did not change my former life by my own mind.

I confess that a new mind has seized me—

A mind that once was not mine,

But now is mine through God, its author.

If he has seen anything in my conduct or intellect worthy of his service,

The first grace and the glory owed belong to you,

Whose instruction has produced what Christ would love.

Therefore you should give thanks rather than complain,

Because that Paulinus of yours, born from your studies and character,

Whose parent you do not deny yourself to be,

Even when you believe me to have been perverse,

Has so changed my purposes that I have deserved to belong to Christ,

Although I am the son of Ausonius.

He will bring your praise its own rewards,

And will first offer you fruit from your own tree.

Therefore, I ask you, think better things and do not lose

The greatest rewards,

By condemning the good things that have sprung from your own sources.

For my mind is not wandering,

Nor is my life a flight from the human beings among whom I share,

Where, as you write, the rider of Pegasus lived in the caves of Lycia,

Although many worship remote places under the agency of divinity,

As the celebrated philosophers of old did for the sake

Of their studies and Muses.

So now too those who have taken Christ into their chaste minds

Frequently practice this—not because they are poor in spirit,

Nor because, learning savagery, they choose to live in deserted places,

But because they have turned toward the stars,

And, gazing upon God, strive to perceive the depths of truth.

They love leisure freed from empty cares;

They recoil from the noise of the forum, the turmoil of affairs,

And every business hostile to divine gifts,

To the commands of Christ, and to the love of salvation.

They follow God in hope and faith,

With the promised reward as their sure recompense,

Which the reliable author will return to those who do not despair,

Provided that present things do not conquer them through empty possessions.

Let them scorn what they see, so that they may deserve what they do not see,

Penetrating the hidden heavenly things with a sense set ablaze.

For perishable things lie open to our eyes,

But eternal things are denied to them;

And now we follow in hope what we see with the mind,

Scorning the varied appearances of things,

And the bodily forms that wrongly trouble our good senses.

Nevertheless, this judgment seemed to have pleased those

To whom the whole light of truth and goodness had already become clear,

The eternal future age and the emptiness of the present.

But since I do not possess the same glory, why should I possess the same reputation?

The faith of my vow is equal, but I am cultivating pleasant things,

And now I am settled upon the pleasant shore

Of a wealthy coast; whence this hasty catalogue of places—

What envy is it?

Would that righteous jealousy begin to criticize me;

Insults uttered under Christ’s name will be pleasing.

A mind made firm by God does not endure tender shame,

And this praise, though despised, returns to me with Christ as judge.

Therefore, revered father, do not rebuke me as perversely turned

By these studies, nor criticize me on account of my wife

Or because of a fault of mind.

My mind is not the anxious mind of Bellerophon,

Nor have I Tanaquil for a wife, but Lucretia.

Nor, as you claim, have I now forgotten my ancestral heaven,

Since I regard the supreme Father;

Whoever worships him alone truly remembers heaven.

Believe me, therefore, father: we are neither forgetful of heaven

Nor living without a mind,

Though we move among human places.

The very pursuits of the devout bear witness to human character;

For an impious people cannot know the supreme God.

Are there not many regions and many places

Uncultivated by human pursuits and lacking laws,

Where the countryside lives by rustic custom?

Or what harm can depravity, foreign to honorable things, do?

Why do you set before me the vast forests of Vasconia

And the snowy settlements of the Pyrenees,

As though, fixed at the very threshold of the Spanish region,

I were to live in exile,

And there were nowhere for me, in countryside or city,

Where wealthy Spain stretches endlessly across the world,

Looking upon suns that have sunk?

But suppose fortune had made me live on the mountains of robbers:

I was not steeped in a barbarian household,

Nor changed into the very colonists among whom I lived

With a shared savagery.

A pure mind does not admit evil,

Nor do stains lightly sprinkled cling to its fibers.

Thus, whoever leads a life pure of crime in the Vasconian forest

Among wicked people takes no contagion of character

From an inhuman host.

But why should it be a crime for me to bear that name,

When I inhabit, as I inhabited before, different regions

Joined to proud cities and crowded with prosperous cultivated peoples?

And suppose that my life had been spent on the Vasconian coasts:

Why would the barbarian people, migrating into our customs,

Not rather lay aside their savage ways, shaped according to mine?

For because you place my dwellings among the remote Iberian cities,

And in your poem enumerate deserted towns,

You reproach me with mountainous Calagurris,

Bilbilis hanging from its sharp cliffs,

And the hill of fallen Herda (Ilerda),

As though I lived in exile in these houses and cities—”

371–372 Beyond human dwellings and roads, do you, ignorant of the Spanish world, suppose these are the resources of Iberian land—where that Atlas stood, weighed down beneath the burden of the sky—the mountain now the farthest portion and boundary of that land, which with its lofty summit divides two-sea Calpe? [230]

Does it mark only Bilbilis, Calagurris, and Ilerda?

Caesaraugusta is assigned to it, as is pleasant Barcino, and Tarraco, looking down upon the sea from its distinguished headland.

Why should I enumerate the cities distinguished by land and walls, wherever fortunate Spain stretches toward two seas, wherever Baetis enlarges the Ocean and Hiberus the Tyrrhenian Sea, and fills the broad division of the separated waters, setting its own boundary at the limit of the world?

Would you, illustrious lord, if you wished to write about the region where you live, prefer to pass over shining Burdigala and describe the Boii, blackened by hardship?

And when you lavish your leisure upon the Marojalic baths, and grant yourself life among shady groves, cultivating dwellings joyful in their locations and wondrous in their construction—

[245] would you describe black huts and *mapalia* woven of straw, and claim to inhabit deserts worthy of fur-clad Bigerri?

And you, consul, who despise the proud walls of your Rome, would you disdain sandy Vasatas?

Or because your fertile countryside grows green in the fields of the Pictones, should I complain that you have transported the Ausonian curule chairs here to Raraunum, and that an old cloth has made the bordered robe shabby?

The robe that nevertheless shines, in the august city of Latian Quirinus, among the Caesars, with an equal title and palm-bearing distinction, venerable in its worn gold for its long-standing splendor,

[255] preserving the honor of flourishing and enduring merit.

Or when you dwell upon the heights of the Lucanian estate, rivaling the roofs of Rome, with the place itself supplying the material that marks it as nearby, are you said to live in the Condatinian district?

[260] Let much be open to jokes; let it also be permitted to play with inventions.

But to strike a harsh tooth with a soothing tongue, to play with burning flatteries, and to ferment viciously sweet jokes in the vinegar of biting satire—this often becomes poets, but never befits parents.

[265] For faith and filial devotion require that, when rumor insinuates into chaste ears some tale that weaves evil, the good intention of a father’s mind not allow it to be fastened upon him or fixed in his heart, so that the malicious, ill-omened tale of the crowd may not have grounds, by its rumor, to bend a life of previously established conduct. Changing one’s life is not always a crime; indeed, to turn it rightly is praiseworthy.

When you hear that I have changed, look for my zeal and duty.

If what is wrong is changed into what is right, profane conduct into religious, luxury into frugality, and shameful conduct into honorable conduct;

if I live sluggishly, inactive and obscure, pity your companion who has been perverted into evil.

Although anger may rouse a gentle father to restore a fallen friend to upright conduct and, through stern admonition, repair him into something better,

[275] yet if you hear the same things that I have read and follow—that I have vowed my heart to the devout God, following the venerable rule of Christ with obedient faith, persuaded by God’s commands that eternal rewards are prepared for mortals and purchased through present losses—

I do not think that this displeased a sound father so greatly that he would believe it an error of mind to live for Christ as Christ ordained.

[285] I am glad of this, and do not regret the “error” of being foolish in the eyes of those who pursue other things, so long as my judgment is wise before my eternal King.

Brief is whatever a human being is: the frailty of an ailing body, the setting of time, dust and shadow without Christ.

[290] Whatever he approves or condemns is worth only as much as the judge himself.

He dies, and his own error accompanies him; and, when he dies, his judgment passes away with its judge.

But unless, while the present time is granted us, anxious care leads us to live according to the command of the Lord Christ,

[295] too late will be the human being’s complaint once he has been stripped of his limbs, when he fears the light insults of human speech because he failed to fear the grave anger of the divine Judge—

the One whom I believe to be seated at the right hand of the eternal Father’s throne, set over all as King, and who, as the years pass, will come to judge all nations with balanced judgment and render their rewards according to their various deeds.

I believe this, and, fearing it, I labor with eager haste, if only I may be released from guilt before death releases me.

At his coming my heart, believing with trembling fibers, quakes; my soul rejoices, already cautious of what is to come, fearing beforehand lest, bound by anxious cares for the sickly body and weighed down by worldly burdens, it should be unable—if the great trumpet resounds from the opened heavens—to rise on light wings into the presence of the King,

[310] flying among the honored thousands of the saints in heaven,

who, light through the empty air and unbound by the fetters of the world, will raise their feet to the lofty stars with easy effort, borne through the heavens on tender clouds,

so that in the midst of the air they may worship the heavenly King and join their shining ranks to Christ adored.

[315] This is my fear, this is my labor: lest the final day find me asleep in dark shadows, engaged in barren activity, wasting my time amid empty cares.

For what shall I do? If, while I doze in sluggish expectation, Christ, revealed to me from his heavenly citadel, should flash forth,

and, blinded by the rays of the Lord coming through the suddenly opened heaven, I should confusedly seek refuge from the dark and gloomy night in the light poured upon me?

[325] So that neither distrust of the truth, nor love of the present life, nor pleasure in worldly things, nor the labor of cares might bring this upon me, I decided to forestall the event by my resolve and to end my cares while life remains;

entrusting what is to come to God, and awaiting fierce death with a tranquil heart.

[330] If this is pleasing, rejoice in the rich hope of your friend.

If it is otherwise, leave me only to be tested by Christ.

## POEM XI

[Note: Written toward the end of the year 393. It answers Ausonius’s second letter in the following poem.]

### PAULINUS TO AUSONIUS

You remember my prolonged silence of speech, though you never remain silent; you reproach me for the leisure I have chosen in hiding places, and add to this the charge of neglected friendship.

You accuse me of fearing marriage, and hurl a harsh verse into my innermost being.

Spare, I beg you, from wounding your own man; do not mix bitter things into words meant for a father, like wormwood into honey.

It has always been, and remains, my concern to honor you with every duty and to respect you with faithful affection.

[10] I have never allowed your favor toward me to be stained by even the slightest blemish; I have always feared offending you by my very expression or injuring you through some careless gesture.

Whenever I approached you reverently, I composed my features with special care and shaped my face into a joyful expression,

[15] lest some false suspicion should lead you to suppose that I carried a cloud contracted in my silent heart against a holy father.

My household has honored and continues to honor you by this example, and so great is our agreement in love for you

as it is also in united devotion of mind to Christ.

[20] What jealousy, I ask, has covered your heart against your own people?

By what rumor did an easy report burst into your pious ears, strike your mind, and, contrary to the faith proved by your ancient devotion, stir up new wounds,

so that it might injure a peaceful father through malicious counsel?

[25] But my mind, conscious of unfeigned simplicity, and my devotion, not guilty of neglect toward a father, reject every undeserved charge and cannot endure to be touched by a false accusation.

Indeed, one who is free from guilt is violated all the more grievously by an unjust wound, being as tender toward offense as he is free from blame.

[30] You complain that I have thrown off the yoke by which I was joined to you in learned studies.

I assert that I did not even bear it; for equal partners submit to equal yokes. No one couples the strong with the weak, nor can the reins be harmonious if the measure of the yoked animals is unequal.

[35] If you pair a calf with a bull, or a horse with a wild ass;

if you compare coots with swans, and a nightingale with a magpie;

hazel trees with chestnuts, and viburnums with cypresses,

compare me with yourself: scarcely could Tully and Maro sustain an equal yoke with you.

If I am joined to you in love,

[40] I shall dare to claim only this much—that I am your equal partner:

a sweet friendship contends, with modest reins against great ones, with you, bound to me by an eternal covenant,

and equal in the constant laws of loving one another in return.

Neither hostile rumor has loosened this yoke from our necks,

[45] nor has long absence from our lands broken it.

Nor will it destroy it, even if I am removed throughout the whole world or through the whole of time.

I shall never live divided from you in spirit; life itself will depart from my body before your features depart from my heart.

[50] Through all that has been granted and appointed to mortals as an age,

as long as I am held enclosed within my closing body,

wherever I may be separated throughout the world,

and not far away in place or removed from the light,

[55] I shall hold you implanted in my very being,

see you in my heart, and embrace you in my devoted mind,

present to me everywhere.

And when, released from the bodily prison,

I have flown beyond the earth,

wherever the common Father shall have placed me beneath the heavens,

[60] there too I shall carry you in my spirit.

The same end that will release me from my body

will not release me from love of you.

For the mind, which survives its fallen limbs

and endures from its heavenly stock,

[65] must retain its perceptions and affections

just as it retains its life,

and, as it cannot die, so it cannot forget:

living forever and remembering.

## POEM XII

[Note: Also numbered 14; what was formerly 12 is now 10. Written in the year 394, on January 14.]

### FIRST BIRTHDAY POEM OF SAINT FELIX

In this poem, written in Spain on January 14, 394, shortly before he set out for Nola, he implores the aid of Saint Felix, so that he may arrive safely at his tomb.

Illustrious Confessor, Felix in merits and in name,

mind powerful through devotion, mind dwelling near the highest heaven,

and no less experienced in power throughout the earth,

you who confessed Christ the Lord with steadfast voice,

[5] and, by despising cruel punishments, deserved to escape them,

when, by your own will, commanded to release your devoted soul to Christ through every torment,

you left your limbs empty for the raging lictors,

borne, bloodless, into the heavenly honor of martyrdom.

[10] O father, O lord, grant your consent, although we are unworthy servants,

so that at last, while we drag out this life in a fragile body,

in the desired dwellings where you rest in your palace,

we may be permitted to celebrate this day, present our devout vows before you,

and rejoice among the joyful tumult.

[15] Let it now, I beg, be enough that I have endured this punishment for so many years—

as many years as we have lived without you because of our deserved impiety—

far from your dwelling, alas, although not distant from you in mind.

Now aid desires exhausted by immeasurable time;

now, even if late, remember and have mercy on your people.

[20] Throughout the world, which separates us far away by the vast expanse of sea,

and through the hostile obstacles that hold us back, worn down by them,

open easy roads for us; and if an envious enemy obstructs those hastening toward you,

remove the barriers set before us, stronger than our adversities,

and speed your friends upon their journey.

[25] Whether the route by land pleases you, be a companion to your people upon a safe road;

or whether great confidence in you persuades us to travel by the long sea,

grant us passage over gentle waves,

and summon favorable winds for your servants from the stern,

so that, borne together under Christ’s guidance to the Campanian shores,

we may soon be carried swiftly to your heights

[30] and find a calm harbor at your threshold.

There we shall bear a sweet yoke, a light burden, and a gentle service beneath you as lord.

Although, being just among the unjust, you have no need of servants,

nevertheless you will endure and love those who, whatever they may be, have been dedicated to you by Christ’s gift,

[35] and you will allow us to serve at your doors, to care for your thresholds in the morning with cleanliness,

and in turn to guard them at night with devout watches;

and in this service to close our deserving life when our bodies are weary.

## POEM XIII

[Note: Also numbered 17; what was formerly 13 is now 21. Written in the year 395, on January 14.]

### SECOND BIRTHDAY POEM OF SAINT FELIX

[Note: He gives thanks to Saint Felix because, through his aid, he reached Nola safely, and describes the gathering of the people at Saint Felix’s tomb on his feast day.]

Felix—rightly so, and by name as well; by name and likewise by merit—

the blessed day returns on which Christ, the Most High, received you, who had confessed him, into his heavenly palace as your homeland.

The time has come to pour out full thanksgiving to you with complete vows.

[5] O father, O lord, best of lords though we are unworthy servants,

at last our prayer has been heard: within your thresholds we may celebrate your birthday.

Three lustrums have passed since, on that solemn occasion, I consecrated my heart’s vows to you in your presence,

[10] as you know what labors, by land and sea, kept me far from your dwelling in a distant world.

For I have always called upon you as near to me everywhere, amid the hardships of the road and the uncertainties of life.

And I entered the seas under your guidance, because concern for danger yielded to love of you, and not without you:

[15] I experienced your protection, overcoming the harshness of the sea in the Lord Christ.

Always, because of you, I was safe on land and on the waves.

[Note: “Ask him, I pray, to be serene toward your people in eternal mercy and peace—you, Felix, who stand by his great name.”]

[20] Now it is a pleasure to release our minds into overflowing joy,

since at last this dear day has dawned here among those present,

always and eternally to be celebrated by us throughout the world,

the day that consecrated you upon earth and raised you to the stars.

Behold, the many-colored crowd paints the roads with its varied procession:

[25] in one city we marvel at countless cities.

O fortunate Nola, fortunate in your Felix as protector,

illustrious in your holy citizen, secure under a heavenly patron,

and, after Rome herself, having received the second place in distinction.

You who formerly stood first only through imperial power and victorious arms,

[30] now also stand first among the world’s apostolic tombs.

Be good and fortunate to your people, and entreat the powerful Lord

that, through the gift of Christ’s favor,

after we have passed through the waves of the sea and also the waves of the world,

we may stand peacefully in your harbor.

[35] Upon this shore I have securely moored my fleet;

in you may the anchor of my life be fixed and at rest.

## POEM XIV

[Note: Also numbered 18; what was formerly 14 is now 22. Written in the year 396, on January 14.]

### THIRD BIRTHDAY POEM OF SAINT FELIX

[Note: He displays Saint Felix’s power against demons and implores his intercession with God.]

The feast day comes from heaven, most celebrated on earth,

celebrating Felix’s birthday—the day on which he died bodily upon earth

and was born to Christ among the heavenly stars,

having attained the heavenly honor of martyrdom without bloodshed.

[5] For the Confessor dies, having won punishments not by his own choice,

God accepting his faithful spirit in place of blood;

he who searches the hidden heart regards those prepared to suffer

as equal to those who have suffered,

content to have proved their inward devotion;

with just piety he remits the punishment of the flesh.

Martyrdom without slaughter is pleasing:

if mind and faith burn readily for God, willing to suffer is enough,

and the testimony of the vow is the highest proof of merit.

Therefore this day, which brought Felix back to heaven on high through so great a gift,

is this day of sacred solemnity.

[15] For after the solstice at which Christ was born in the body,

and, with the new sun, changed the season of the cold winter,

providing mortals with a saving birth,

as the day advances he ordered the nights to diminish with it;

from that time the light that rises for us on the twentieth day

marks the stellar honor of Felix’s merit.

Finally, this day shows that his merit is in no way inferior to that of those who shed their blood,

in its testimony, title, and virtue alike received,

since by the power of his authority he exercises demons

and releases bodies bound by them.

[25] For the pestilential rulers confess, with mournful cries,

that Felix presses upon them in their blind punishments;

they testify to hidden crosses with open groaning,

and reveal him—veiled from mortal eyes but manifest to the ears—

as present with great divine power,

[30] when, caught within the bodies they have seized, they cry out and prove

that Christ shines in his holy servant,

through the trembling blows of their limbs and the turning of their heads.

They torture themselves with their own torments, though not their own bodies,

and, crying their own pains through alien mouths,

they ask forgiveness from those who pray:

the avenger is hidden; punishment is visible.

Then, if a more violent enemy has bound some people with a heavier affliction,

this day releases them through divine grace.

[40] It is then possible to see everywhere chests purified by sacred healing

prostrate themselves at the thresholds, already restored in mind,

already giving thanks in their own voices.

The trembling crowd of those with open mouths gathers;

amid the rejoicing, tears spring forth from everyone.

God is believed to be present there for all;

Felix is the glory of the immense Christ.

The nurturing day is celebrated by great assemblies; all

[45] utter vows made secure at the sacred doors.

Everything rejoices on earth and in heaven; heaven itself seems to smile with its open skies.

The air breathes spring through its silent breezes,

and the Milky Way encircles the joyful sky.

There is no limit to the peoples gathering in dense procession,

[50] nor any rest: they hasten from night into the light,

and are impatient to await the day.

Their eager vows break through the delay of night,

and torches defeat the darkness with their flames.

It is a pleasure to behold one city crowded with many cities,

and so many swarms driven together by one vow.

[55] The peoples of Lucania gather; the Apulian youth gathers,

and the Calabrians, and all whom either tide washes,

the wave that resounds around Latium on the left and on the right.

And wherever prosperous Campania rejoices in six cities,

as though in its own festivals, those whom wealthy Capua possesses within its broad walls,

[60] those whom beautiful Neapolis possesses, or whom Gaurus nourishes,

those who cultivate the joyful Massic fields,

those who drink from Ufens and Sarnus,

those of the dry Tanagro,

and those who inhabit the fertile fields watered by the Galēsus,

those whom powerful Atina sends, and those whom mother Aricia sends.

[65] Rome herself, powerful through the sacred monuments of the heavenly leaders,

Peter and Paul, gladly grows less crowded in honor of this day,

pouring thousands out through the Capenian Gate toward the walls of friendly Nola;

in a dense procession she sends twelve times ten thousand,

and the Appian Way lies hidden beneath the crowds gathered along it.

[70] Nor are there fewer people setting out from the opposite region:

the rough roads of mountainous Latium are traversed,

by those whom lofty Praeneste and fertile Aquinum sustain;

by those whom ancient Ardea sends from its suburban shores;

by those who have left the city of Cales and twin Teanum,

or whom stern Auruncus or the rugged Apulian inhabits.

[75] Here too a crowd from olive-bearing Venafrum gathers;

the hardy Samnites leave their mountain towns.

Devotion has conquered the difficult road;

the love of Christ conquers everything, and so does nurturing faith.

It persuades minds and places hardened by hardship to endure bitter things,

and to lay aside their harsh and rigid hearts.

[80] One day calls everyone, and one Nola receives them all;

its thresholds are wholly filled with its own people and spacious enough for everyone,

so that you might believe that the walls have expanded for their countless guests.

[85] Thus Nola rises up in the likeness of Rome.

You too, after the City, have received the second place in distinction:

for formerly you stood first only through imperial power and victorious arms,

but now also among the world’s apostolic tombs.

You too, beneath a twofold honor, wear everlasting crowns,

embracing your Felix first as priest and later as martyr throughout all time;

with twofold merit you touch heaven, rightly the mother of your divine friend.

[90] First, the nurturing priest, celebrating your altars with devout worship,

established you and ruled you with peaceful governance.

From this point onward Felix also adorns you with an everlasting name.

For he, consecrated in your bosom, brings you the honor that is your due, his holy bones laid to rest in a fragrant tomb.

[100] Now golden thresholds are adorned with snowy veils,

and shining altars are crowned with dense lamps.

Lights are kindled with fragrant waxed papyrus;

they gleam night and day, so that night shines with the brightness of day,

and day itself, illustrious with heavenly honor,

shines more brightly, doubling its light with countless lamps.

[105] We too are fortunate, to whom it is granted to see this day in person,

to celebrate it, to behold our patron’s rewards,

to give thanks to Christ for such great gifts to his servant,

and to rejoice amid the joyful tumult.

Bring praise to God, boys; fulfill your devout vows,

and together offer festive songs in chaste dances.

[110] Scatter flowers upon the ground; cover the thresholds with garlands.

Let purple spring breathe even in winter; let the year be full of flowers

before its appointed day; let nature yield to the holy day.

The earth owes crowns to the martyr’s tomb.

But sacred glory of light surrounds him above,

[115] flowering with the twofold crown of war and peace.
