Ask for this day, I beg, serene with eternal peace together with us,

so that, when it returns, we may again be permitted to rejoice,

and here to render yearly vows and songs at your festivals,

under the tranquil favor of Christ appeased.

[120] This is our love, this is our labor; these are the vows of your people.

Receive them and commend them to God,

so that, when our diligent service has been rendered to you through a long age,

you may finally release with a kindly hand the children made pleasing by their devoted service,

[125] and not refuse to carry the souls of your people, set before your eyes,

to the countenance of the shining Lord, in his paternal embrace.

Entreat him—merciful in goodness, but fearsome in majesty—

to repay what is due to us through your prayers and merits, which are full,

when you too, Felix, as a great portion of the devout,

will accompany the reigning Lamb.

Ask that we be placed among the flock of sheep,

so that the judgment of the highest Judge may grant us once again to you as this gift,

and not assign us, ungrateful for blessings, to the left among the goats,

but rather place us on the right, in the portion of salvation,

[135] among the generous flock and join us to the praised lambs.

## POEM XV

[Note: Also numbered 19; what was formerly 15 is now 32. Written in the year 397, on January 14.]

### FOURTH BIRTHDAY POEM OF SAINT FELIX

[Note: He describes Saint Felix’s lineage and origin, and his holy duties in the Church.]

My annual vows return, and with them the yearly obligations of my tongue:

your birthday, O Felix, most illustrious in Christ,

dearer to me than my own birthday,

on which, however many the public crowds’ joys may be,

[5] there is something special for your people,

because Christ has given us to you, having bestowed flesh upon a lowly friend.

Not because you were worthy of servants so lowly—although deemed worthy to go as God’s companion in eternal triumphs—

but because the good Father wished to enrich us,

poor in righteousness and unworthy of salvation,

[10] so that, with our riches of crimes turned into something better,

we might receive Felix as our wealth, homeland, and household,

in place of all riches, all affections,

and all empty noble titles and honors.

[15] You are father, homeland, household, and substance to us;

our cradle has been transferred into your bosom,

and your breast is our nest.

Here, well nurtured, we grow,

and, changing our bodies into another form,

we cast off our earthly stock,

and, as wings come upon us,

we are transformed into birds through the seed of the divine word.

With you lifting the yoke, we recognize Christ’s yoke as light;

in you Christ is gentle to the unworthy and sweet to the bitter.

Therefore this day too must be solemn for us,

[25] since it is your birthday:

because, by abolishing our evils,

we die to the world so that we may be born to what is good in Christ.

Rise, therefore, lyre, and stretch yourself with all your fibers.

Awaken the force of my soul; let my inward parts be roused by silent song.

Let the love of speech strike the not-silent lyre of my heart with plucked fingers;

let the lyre of my mouth resound beneath the plectrum.

[30] I shall not summon the phantoms of the Castalian Muses, the prophets’ goddesses,

nor call deaf Phoebus from the Aonian rock.

Christ is the inspirer of my song;

through Christ’s gift I, a sinner, dare to speak of holy and heavenly things.

Nor is it difficult for you, Almighty One, to release my mouth into learned measures,

you who command the mute to speak, the dry to flow, and the hard to be dissolved.

[35] For you made the she-ass resound in speech,

and the suckling infants to utter perfect praise to you,

and you dissolved solid rock into rivers,

and commanded dry land without water to remain in sudden streams,

watering the desert in hope of the peoples.

[40] Into their parched souls your devout grace flowed;

Christ, the living rock pouring forth from a spring, refreshed them.

Therefore I, the least part of humanity, relying on this gift,

though dry, beg for living draughts of your dew, O Christ.

Give me a word from your fountain; for without you I cannot speak of you;

for the praise of your martyr is also your praise—

you, Almighty, make human beings capable of divine things,

and, overcoming the strong by means of the weak, triumph over flesh,

overcoming the aerial rulers.

Come, then, that under your guidance I may proceed from the beginning

to tell of your Felix, whose noble lineage came from the East.

For no other land suited Felix’s homeland more than the land that bore the patriarchs

and the holy prophets, sacred vessels of Christ.

[55] From there, pouring out his rivers through apostolic tongues,

the sound of the Gospel flowed throughout the whole world.

From there Felix, destined for God, came through his father to Italy,

although he had not yet been born;

so that, born in our lands through affection,

he might remember no people as his birthplace except us.

Thus Father Abraham, following the Lord’s commands,

changed his ancestral lands for foreign soil,

and planted the sacred seed among the fields of the Canaanites.

From there, as his offspring entered foreign lands,

a mystical origin transmitted Felix to us,

whom perfect faith, proceeding from that root,

brought forth as a devout vein of faith for us.

Felix now too rests with his flesh laid aside,

his spirit living in Christ.

Through the merits of his lofty power,

he transforms the hardness of stones into the goodness of life,

raising them up as Abraham’s seed.

[70] Born, therefore, of a Syrian father in that city,

he honored beloved Nola under the image of his homeland,

blessing his dwelling with a pleasing seat.

Left with much gold, he flourished in wealth,

although he was not the sole heir.

With his brother Hermias, who bore his father’s name,

he divided earthly riches;

Felix alone obtained heavenly things.

A contrary judgment divided the two brothers:

[80] the world carried Hermias away,

while Christ took Felix for himself.

The one preferred perishable things, the other solid things;

the one clung to present realities, the other turned only toward heaven,

changing inheritances into kingdoms.

The one was heir only of his own father, the other a co-heir of Christ.

But who would marvel at such varied offspring from one blood,

when among the sacred records of the ancient fathers one reads

that Rebecca complained to God of the struggles of her pregnant womb,

lamenting the conflict of her burdened belly?

[90] Even then there raged within the holy mother’s womb

the discord that now rages within the womb of the world.

The shaggy treachery of the Jews, following bristling Esau,

was devoted to serving the lesser people.

But for us, through the smoothness of Jacob,

the better-born follow the gentle paths of peace along the way of light.

Thus blood unlike in character came from the equal blood of brothers:

Hermias, like harsh Edom, pursuing earthly things,

grew squalid, captive within the empty image of the world,

and chose the hard fields of his Idumaean father,

living by his own sword, and the labor of vain things—

## Editorial apparatus and notes

- [Cols. 0457D–0458D, on *Caesarea Augusta cui … Barcino amoena*:] This is the reading of the editions of Constantine, Poelman, and Vinet, with the Royal manuscript and the editions of Schott and Rosweyd. The latter read: “Augusta, to which pleasant Barcino [belongs].”

- [Col. 0458D, on *Baetis*:] The first syllable is wrongly shortened, since it is a diphthong; it is read long by Lucan, Statius, Silius, and all poets. To preserve the metrical rule the editor would read: “Where Baetis enlarges the Ocean and Hiberus the Tyrrhenian [Sea].” This denotes two rivers: Baetis empties into the Ocean, Hiberus into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Nevertheless, the received reading has been retained, since the authority of all manuscripts supports it as probably Paulinus’s.

- [Col. 0457D:] See note 227.

- [Col. 0458D, on *texta*:] Thus the Royal and Vossian manuscripts and the printed editions of Gravius, Poelman, and Schott in their margins; see Nicolaus Heinsius’s notes on Ovid. Others read *tecta* (“roofed”), with Rosweyd.

- [Col. 0457D:] See note 228.

- [Col. 0457D:] See note 229.

- [Col. 0459D:] See note 230.

- [Col. 0459D, on *Rauranum*:] Three manuscripts—Lyons, Royal, and Vossian—together with the marginal readings of Gravius, Poelman, and Schott, read *Raraunum*. See note 230.

- [Col. 0459D, on *Ausonias huc devexisse curules*:] The Lyons and Vossian manuscripts and the marginal editions of Poelman and Schott read *heu devenisse* (“alas, to have come here”). The Vossian manuscript reads *secures* (“axes”), not badly; see note 231.

- [Cols. 0459D–0460D, on *veteri panno*:] All manuscripts read *fano* or *phano*. One must certainly write *veteri panno* (“old rag”). Ancient writers commonly use *pannus* for a patchwork garment or a torn garment sewn from patches. Thus in Petronius: “A rag holds barbarous battles in contempt”; and: “Eloquence alone shudders in frosty rags.” Hence *pannucea Baucis* in the *Satyricon*. *Pannus* and purple are sometimes opposed, whence the proverb “to sew a rag onto purple.” Here likewise the bordered robe and the rag are opposites. Compare Paulinus, Poem 21 to Cytherius, line 477, “Purple and rags come together into one flock,” and Letter 29, §12, “We have seen purple furnishings served by old rags.”

- [Col. 0460D, on *bona voti / mens patris*:] Poelman and Rosweyd read *noti*. Heinsius proposes that one should read *f. voti … patrii* [the abbreviated reading is materially uncertain in the printed apparatus].

- [Col. 0460D, on *scaevo*:] Thus the Vossian manuscript. Other manuscripts read *saeva*, erroneously. See “*scaeva fabula*,” Poem 11, line 44.

- [Col. 0460D, on *flectere vitam*:] Thus all manuscripts. It would not be bad if *vitae* were read.

- [Col. 0460D, on *itidem*:] Thus the Vossian manuscript and the Lyons edition; elsewhere *id idem* (“the same thing”).

- [Col. 0460D, on *pio Deo*:] Sacchini and Nicolaus Heinsius suspect that *pie* should be read; but compare above “to pious Christ,” Letter 32, §6.

- [Col. 0460D, on *Persuasumque*:] The Lyons and Vossian manuscripts read *sedet* (“is established”).

- [Col. 0460D, on *sano parenti*:] The Royal manuscript with five editions reads *sancto* (“holy”).

- [Col. 0460D, on line 287:] The Vossian manuscript reads: “Whatever man is, [he is] a man of a sick body.”

- [Col. 0461D, on *obscura et tristia noctis*:] “Of dark … night” would not be displeasing; compare Poem 5, line 15.

- [Col. 0461D:] Poem XI was written toward the end of 393.

- [Col. 0461D, on *et in Christo*:] Five editions with the Lyons manuscript read: “in devotion to Christ, to be worshipped with minds joined together.”

- [Col. 0461D, on *quo rumore*:] The Royal manuscript reads *pium* (“pious”).

- [Col. 0462D, on *immunis*:] Five editions read *merito* (“deservedly”).

- [Cols. 0461D–0462D, on *aedona parrae*:] See note 232. The Royal manuscript and three marginal printed editions read *picae* (“magpies”).

- [Col. 0462D, on *nec orbe longe*:] The Lyons, Schott, and Vinet editions read *longum*; Poelman reads *longo*. Sacchini suggests perhaps *nec ore longe*, since *orbe* precedes, or *nec orbe longe, nec remotum limine*.

- [Col. 0461D:] “Just as [it retains] its own life”: poetic license.

- [Col. 0461D:] That is, it cannot forget; see Poem 9, line 23.

- [Col. 0461D:] Poem XII was also numbered 14; what was 12 is now 10. Written in 394, 14 January.

- [Col. 0462D:] The first three lines printed by Rosweyd are absent from German manuscript no. 540; the second and third are absent from the five editions.

- [Col. 0462D, on *Dominum Christum*:] German manuscript no. 540 reads *Jesum non vincta voce* (“Jesus in an unfettered voice”).

- [Col. 0463D:] The following three lines, together with lines 15–17, 19–20, 22–27, 29, and 30, are absent from the five editions.

- [Col. 0463D, on *in aula*:] See Poem 32, line 544.

- [Col. 0463D, on *reddere coram*:] See Poem 13, line 9.

- [Col. 0463D, on *tanto*:] The German manuscript reads *tanto* (“by so great [an expanse]”).

- [Col. 0464D, on *a puppi suggere ventos*:] The five printed editions read *a puppibus aggere* (“from the ships’ bank”).

- [Col. 0464D, on *sub te domino*:] The German manuscript reads *domine* (“O lord”).

- [Col. 0464D, on *munditie*:] The German manuscript reads *munditiis* (“with cleansings”).

- [Col. 0463D:] Poem XIII was also numbered 17; what was 13 is now 21. Written in 395, 14 January.

- [Col. 0463D, on *inter tua limina*:] The editor restored *inter* (“among/within”) from the German manuscript and the five editions. Rosweyd had corrected it to *intra* (“within”); Heinsius, however, attests *inter viscera* from older manuscripts in his notes on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 4, line 20, rather than *intra*.

- [Col. 0463D, on *coram*:] See Poem 12, line 13.

- [Col. 0464D:] Some printed editions read *Semper ego* (“I always”). The following six lines are added from the very ancient German manuscript. The next seven lines, absent from the five editions, also occur in that manuscript.

- [Col. 0463D:] Poem XIV was also numbered 18; what was 14 is now 22. Written in 396, 14 January.

- [Col. 0463D, on “birthday”:] See Beleth, *De divinis officiis*, chapter 4.

- [Col. 0465D:] Thus the manuscripts.

- [Col. 0465D:] This verse is added from the German manuscript: “if mind and faith burn readily for God.”

- [Col. 0465D, on *rettulit*:] The same manuscript reads *condidit* (“placed/founded”).

- [Col. 0465D, on *recepta*:] The German manuscript reads *recepti*; not badly.

- [Col. 0465D:] See note 233.

- [Col. 0466D:] This verse was added from the German manuscript. Previously the text read: “with assemblies, by speech they rejoice upon earth, and smile,” etc.

- [Col. 0465D, on *rata postibus*:] See Poem 5, line 58, and Poem 16, line 10.

- [Col. 0465D, on *aestus uterque*:] That is, the sea.

- [Col. 0466D, on *monimentis*:] Thus the German manuscript with the editions of Gronovius and Poelman. Others read *monumentis*.

- [Col. 0466D, on *honore diei*:] Thus the German manuscript and the marginal Schott edition, by synaloepha; this is unusual. Previously the five editions read *Dei*, which supports this reading; Rosweyd reads *die*, without sense.

- [Col. 0465D, on *ponere*:] That is, “to lay aside”; see Poem 17, line 248.

- [Col. 0466D, on *Nola assurgit*:] The German manuscript reads *adsurgis* (“you rise”).

- [Col. 0467D:] These three lines are absent from the German manuscript. With a few words changed, they already occur in the second *Natalicium* of Saint Felix, lines 28–30.

- [Col. 0467D, on *Nunc*:] The German manuscript, with the editions of Gravius and Schott, reads *Nunc* (“now”).

- [Col. 0467D:] See note 234.

- [Col. 0467D:] See notes 235 and 236.

- [Col. 0467D, on *Plus micat*:] The German manuscript has only a lacunose reading, “[lacuna].”

- [Col. 0467D, on *pariter*:] That is, “together”; see Poem 15, line 334.

- [Col. 0467D:] See note 237.

- [Col. 0468D, on *placidos*:] The German manuscript reads *placitos* (“pleasing”).

- [Col. 0468D, on *Absolvas*:] The editor emended to *absolvas* from the German manuscript and the five editions; Rosweyd reads *absolvat* (“may he release”).

- [Col. 0468D, on *lenis*:] The German manuscript reads *lenis* (“gentle”).

- [Col. 0468D, on *dextrae*:] The German manuscript with the five editions reads *dextrae* (“of the right hand”). Rosweyd’s punctuation is corrupt: “in the portion of salvation, to the generous flock.”

- [Col. 0468D, on *piorum*:] The German manuscript reads *piorum* (“of the devout”).

- [Col. 0467D:] Poem XV was also numbered 19; what was 15 is now 32. Written in 397, 14 January.

- [Col. 0468D, on *inopes justi*:] The German manuscript reads *aequi* (“of equity”). *Justi* means “of justice/righteousness.”

- [Cols. 0467D–0468D, on *Felicem opes*:] “Riches.” Thus two German manuscripts and the marginal Schott edition, correctly: it means “substance,” and *opes* has already occurred. Compare the eighth *Natalicium* of Saint Felix, line 356: “the riches of Felix.”

- [Col. 0469D, on *plectro*:] Rosweyd reads *cor* (“heart”).

- [Col. 0469D, on *sanctum*:] One German manuscript reads *sancta* (“holy things”).

- [Col. 0469D:] Numbers 22:28.

- [Col. 0469D:] Psalm 8:3.

- [Cols. 0469D–0470D, on *Aerios proceres*:] This verse is absent from one German manuscript. The other reads *Aerios proceres*, correctly—that is, demons. Paulinus favors this expression: in Letter 24 to Severus, §14, “the aerial enemy,” and in Letter 23 to the same, §20, “the princes of this air.” Elsewhere the reading is *Assyrios proceres* (“Assyrian princes”).

- [Cols. 0469D–0470D, on *sua flumina*:] Rosweyd reads *fulmina* (“thunderbolts”), against the other manuscripts and printed editions. Both readings are good.

- [Col. 0470D:] These two lines are added from two German manuscripts.

- [Col. 0469D:] See note 334.

- [Col. 0469D, on *Hermiam mundus abegit*:] That is, “the world carried him away.”

- [Col. 0470D, on *hic solida*:] Here Paulinus makes a syllable naturally short but long by position because of the two following consonants. See the same license in Poem 24, line 508.

- [Col. 0470D, on *Hispida … Perfidia*:] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *hirtis sectantibus Esau*, with bad punctuation. But what does “shaggy treachery” mean? Perhaps *perfidiae* should be read.

- [Col. 0470D, on *laevem per lenia*:] Thus the German manuscripts with the Schott edition. Others read *laevia*.

- [Col. 0470D, on *praelegit*:] Restored from the old Badius edition. Elsewhere *jura* (“laws/rights”).

[The supplied source ends incompletely.]

[100] Enduring a barren military career, he who had yielded to Caesar’s arms performed Christ’s duties as a private man.

But my Felix, born to take up the weapons of the eternal King, passed into the name of his father Israel:

From childhood his devout mind, feeding upon heavenly things, trained itself to serve God; nor was grace lacking,

[Col. 0470D] and in proportion as his heart thirsted, so generously did his spirit, gaping for light, draw in the gifts of God. In his earliest years he served as a reader. [Note: [Col. 0469D] See note 238.]

Then he advanced to the office whose duty, with faithful voice, was to adjure the evil and drive them out with sacred words.

Because he carried out this office with conspicuous virtue worthy of his merit, [Note: [Col. 0471D] We have emended the text on the basis of two German manuscripts; Sacchinus thought this should likewise be read. The former reading was *regebat* (“he governed”), which is erroneous, for one does not say that an exorcist “governs” his office.] he obtained by right the venerable insignia of the priesthood;

His merit adorned the honor with a mind worthy of the position.

But lest the sacred head alone be adorned by a fillet, [Note: [Col. 0471D] Thus we have restored the text from two German manuscripts. The former reading was:

“But lest the sacred head of the man alone be covered by a sacred fillet.”

Aldhelmus, *Poem on the Apostle Paul*:

“Whom the sacred fillet accompanies with virginal modesty.”

The same should be written from the manuscripts, as the distinguished J. F. Gronovius points out in *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 15. Aldhelmus, *On Eustochium*:

“The fillet which chaste youth adorned.” [Col. 0472D]] there also arose a nobler reason for doubling the crown.

[115] The savage rage of the profane broke out in furious madness;

When the devout Church was shaken by sacrilegious war, [Note: [Col. 0471D] See note 239.] impiety especially demanded from the whole people those whose piety was most distinguished.

[120] Then the aged Maximus, bishop, was shaping the city of Nola by sacred laws with calm speech, powerful through the priest Felix. [Note: [Col. 0472D] German manuscript 1 reads *Nolam qui* (“Nola, who”). Thus read two German manuscripts and the editions of Gravius and Schottus in their margins; others read *et placido* (“and with calm”). One German manuscript, with the editions of Grinæus and Poelman, reads *formabat*; the other reads *firmabat* (“was strengthening”); others, *formavit* (“formed”).]

He embraced and cherished him with fatherly affection as though he were his own son, and was fostering him as heir to his see. [Note: [Col. 0472D] Other copies read *vovebat* (“he was promising”). See note 240.]

Driven out by a sudden storm, [Note: [Col. 0472D] One German manuscript reads “in the midst of the storm.”]

[125] he sought deserted places without yielding in faith.

Then Felix, all the more resplendent because the bishop had been sought, stood alone in opposition to the swords and was attacked by the envy of faith; [Note: [Col. 0471D] See note 334.] nor was honor taken into account;

Faith alone was greater than honor, because it was the cause of faith. [Note: [Col. 0471D] See the same note.]

[130] Then, when the livid dragon stirred up his weapons and sought him, wishing to overthrow that through which we rise—and himself fell—

Felix alone, or first among the people, as the summit from the body, was singled out for the savage punishments while the bishop fled.

Everyone strove to overcome him;

[135] They attacked him as though he were a lofty citadel besieged within its walls, piling up a mass of assaults; once its defenses were overcome, the rest of the city would already fall in an easy, prostrate ruin. [Note: [Col. 0472D] Thus two German manuscripts. The printed editions read *constrata* (“laid low”).]

O madness worthy of the faithless! They believe that faith can be extinguished in one man, though the whole world has believed it.

[140] Alas, wretched impiety, blind in infernal darkness, where are you rushing? Against whom are you directing your weapons?

Do you believe that God can be contained in one mortal, and that, if you destroy the body, you can at the same time abolish divine power and mind?

That power which moves through the members of the world, through which you yourself were born,

[145] and unworthy are nourished; whose divine will determines whether one conquers or is conquered; by whose power even one man is stronger than countless others:

[393–394] Armed with piety, though unarmed, he prostrates those armed with iron but unarmed in heart before Christ, [Col. 0471D] while conquering faith, conscious of heavenly truth, [Note: [Col. 0472D] One German manuscript reads *prosternet* (“will prostrate”); the others read *prosternit* (“prostrates”). See what follows.]

[150] that faith, heavenly and comparing the life to come with the present height, carries the mind, victorious over the conquered body, joyfully back to God and conveys it among the rejoicing stars.

What good does it do, then, that in such a huge mass of madness you seek the devout Felix?

Within him, hidden in God, an unconquered mind remains; nor does the earthly nature of man alone resist you now:

[155] God himself opposes you, whom you seek; and Christ himself, O ancient serpent, offers himself to your poisons through the bodies of his servants, binding you in your own snares. [Note: [Col. 0471D] See note 59.]

[160] And through the appearance of death overthrowing you, triumphing over death.

But error, with its own furious goads, urged their savage hearts to burn with a bloody thirst and to demand holy blood as though claiming the prize of crime. [Note: [Col. 0472D] Two manuscripts and five printed editions read *suis* (“its own”); others read *suus* (“his own”).]

[165] Therefore, when Nola received the sacrilegious fury and was alarmed by swords directed against her devout citizens, [Note: [Col. 0472D] Thus we have emended the text from two German manuscripts. The former reading was *Intentusque ... ensis* (“and the sword, intent ...”).]

the venerable Felix was sought throughout the shaken city.

Nor did he flee, already breathing the stars with lofty inspiration and sharpening his mind for battle with silent goads;

[170] Fearless, he guarded the trembling shepherd’s fold, following the example of the Lord, ready to give his life for the flock. [Note: [Col. 0471D] John 10:15.]

Therefore, eagerly, he stood like a wall against the savage enemies;

And, with his faith flourishing, he renewed his strength with advancing years, his mind wholly among the stars, mindful of Christ and forgetful of time,

Carrying God in his heart and Christ filling his breast.

[175] He no longer contained himself; he seemed holier and greater, with a starry honor shining in his eyes and face. [Note: [Col. 0471D] Poetic license. See poem 25, line 98.]

At once he is joyfully seized and dragged by the savage hands of the raging men; [Note: [Col. 0472D] This is emended from two German manuscripts and Schottus’s edition; others read *Pertrahitur* (“he is drawn through”). The correction is confirmed by Letter 29 to Severus, §11.] but—such is the custom of the unjust enemy, for whom it is a greater task to destroy our souls than our bodies [Note: [Col. 0472D] Two German manuscripts read *animos* (“minds”); elsewhere *animas* (“souls.”)]—

[180] he first delays him before the sword with terrors and rises toward death through successive stages of punishment.

The first order of torment is woven from the prison.

Iron chains are joined to the dark bars;

Steel stands upon his hands and neck, and his sinews grow stiff as his feet are stretched apart. [Note: [Col. 0471D] See note 241.]

[185] Fragments of pottery are scattered beneath him, so that the painful bed, with its sharpness, keeps sleep away.

Yet the confessor is not without rest or deprived of light, for Christ, already joined with him in all things, suffers with him;

For him the more severe punishment multiplies green crowns, while with an expansive mind he traverses the heavens.

[190] Although confined in a shackled body, his free spirit flies ahead into the innermost sanctuary of highest Christ, his soul already anticipating its rewards with steadfast prayers.

Thus blessed suffering pressed Felix with sacred punishments, heavy chains, and a dark prison:

As many punishments as his subjected flesh had taken upon itself from man, so many palms of victory his endurance received from Christ.

[195] Meanwhile Maximus, sick in the mountains beneath the sun, [Note: [Col. 0473D] See poem 16, line 8.]

content with having escaped the savage hands and faces of the executioners,

[200] endured a different martyrdom, but no lighter, than if he had given his neck, limbs, and body to tortures or fires:

A sharper care for his flock burned and afflicted him; he was scorched by the fire of cold and stiffened by the chilly dew of heaven;

Without bread and shelter alike, he joined night and day in uninterrupted prayer, keeping both periods awake with attentive devotion.

While lying on thorny ground, his limbs were pierced by the thicket, and he fought inwardly and outwardly against anxieties,

[210] he bore the thorns of sorrow in his grieving breast.

Covering hard things with hard things, he lightened the torment of his limbs through the bitter anguish of his mind, and the pain of his heart shut out awareness of bodily suffering. [Note: [Col. 0473D] One German manuscript reads *corporis* (“of the body”) rather than *corporei* (“bodily”).]

Yet the sick substance of his earthly body—although the strength of his soul remained unshaken, faith scorning the flesh as it fell— [Note: [Col. 0473D] German manuscript 1 reads *superante* (“prevailing”); both readings are good.]

[215] overcome by winter and hunger, worn down by his harsh bed, and with his body failing, was leaving his spirit behind;

The cold drawn more deeply from the empty marrow of the exhausted old man drove life away through his frozen blood.

[220] The compassion of the supreme Father was moved by so great a bishop and did not allow the body to be consumed by an obscure death.

Although he could have fed him, as he had fed Elijah, by sending birds bearing food through the trackless wilderness, [Note: [Col. 0473D] German manuscript 1 reads “and likewise the holy man.”]

and could also have covered him, as Moses, in a hidden tomb,

[225] God had granted this gift to one friend alone, whom he hides in secret earth because such a burial was rightly fitting.

So great was the honor of that body, which had shone face to face and, through the word of God, had discharged mortal obligations, that it enjoyed God alone as witness of its tomb. [Note: [Col. 0473D] See poem 32, line 15.] [Note: [Col. 0473D] Thus emended from two German manuscripts. The former reading was *tanti*, which makes no sense.]

[230] Therefore the gentle Father, looking with serene eyes upon the priest and confessor, could no longer endure him wasting away in silent forests;

And because he was preparing to join a worthy companion to worthy merits, he chose Felix from the entire number of the prison,

[235] to whom he might entrust this task: to lift the limbs of the kindly old man, restore his spirit, bring him back refreshed,

and return comfort to the astonished sheep of their beloved shepherd.

Therefore an angel came, shining through the silent night, and addressed Felix alone among the entire multitude of imprisoned criminals;

[240] his holy piety had made him guilty. The horror of the dark prison fled.

At the voice and light of the sacred messenger Felix trembled, shaken from sleep, and listened to the word with faithful ear.

At first, as though receiving the commands of God in the form of a deceptive dream, he stood anxiously amazed;

[245] he excused himself, saying that he could not follow because the chain prevented him and because he was held both by the prison enclosure and by the guard of the secured prison.

But the divine voice rebuked him for delaying and ordered him to rise, his chains shaken loose.

[250] And suddenly, when the supple chains flowed from his hands, his neck, released from the iron yoke, rose of its own accord;

His feet sprang forward, their sinews freed from the stock.

Wonderful faith! With the prison doors unlocked while the locks remained intact, the guard asleep, he fearlessly went out through the doors;

[255] and a path was made through the very men by whom the way was closed.

The angel went before him, and through the friendly silence of the quiet night the angel was Felix’s light and road.

Is Christ not present as one in every saint? Just as the same Spirit lives in all those born in Christ, so the very grace of the devout is in harmony.

[397–398] I see an ancient pattern returning in a recent history: Peter, commanded to depart amid the exalted company of the twelve disciples, [Note: [Col. 0474D] We have restored *bisseno* (“of twelve”) from two very ancient German manuscripts. The printed editions read *princeps super* (“the chief above”).] his chains falling away of their own accord,

he came out of the closed prison, following the angel who went before him and led him away after stealing him from Herod as prey.

[265] So my Felix, led forth by God, through the doubled darkness of prison and night—dark to the others but illuminated for him alone—passed safely by the guards,

keeping his steps steady, and, directed along unknown paths, went to carry out the command.

After he had traversed the secret, trackless countryside, he found the place where the exhausted old man was; sorrowfully he saw him drawing faint sighs with a feeble breath. [Note: [Col. 0474D] One German manuscript reads *rura* (“countryside”); another, *jura*; the printed editions, *pura*. The correction is confirmed by Poem 20, line 29, *avia rura*.]

[275] As soon as he recognized the limbs of his beloved father, he poured himself into an embrace and kissed the familiar face. [Note: [Col. 0474D] One German manuscript reads *rura* (“countryside”); another, *jura* (“rights”); the printed editions, *pura* (“pure [places]”). The correction is confirmed by Poem 20, line 29, *avia rura* (“trackless countryside”).]

He tried to restore warmth to the cold limbs by cherishing them and, with repeated breath from his panting mouth, to return living sensation to the body as it grew warm.

But the body moved neither at his shouting nor at his touch.

[280] It was already like a corpse; nevertheless, a slight breath at the last extremity of life and a tremor within the vital organs gave signs of life.

Anxious at this sight, devout Felix tore at the bloodless limbs; seeing the face yellow with hunger, he had nothing with which to aid one so needy:

Neither fire nearby nor food close at hand, by which he might restore the man wasting from hunger and stiff with cold.

As he sought and entreated Christ with many prayers, asking by what means or by what path he could fulfill the command entrusted to him,

the Almighty suddenly produced a cluster of grapes from the thorns [Note: [Col. 0476D] Thus two German manuscripts and the editions of Gravius and Schottus in the margins. Five printed editions read *vitibus* (“from vines”).]

[290] and ordered it to hang nearby at the level of his head, so that he could easily pluck the spontaneously produced food from the accessible branch. [Note: [Col. 0475D] See poem 16, line 168.]

Thus refreshed by divine aid, Felix rejoiced in his devout mind over the gift that had been offered.

He brought the cluster, plucked by his hand, to the dying man’s mouth;

[295] but since the old man’s teeth were already clenched and he could neither feel the sweetness nor take nourishment,

Felix squeezed the moist berries and let the flowing juice drip in, separating the dry lips with his finger;

Until, with God breathing upon his sick efforts and his hand struggling, he loosened the rigid opening a little

[300] and gave the open mouth a narrow passage through which the dissolved grape might pour its small drop of moisture.

Then the senses of the soul, warmth in the bones, and light in the eyes returned, and life returned entire.

The tongue, which had been stuck fast by the dry throat, resumed its accustomed speech after the slippery moisture opened the path of the voice.

[305] Thus, reviving, he saw close before him the most familiar face, the face of his own Felix, and embraced him in turn.

He complained that Felix had been slow:

“For a long time,” he said, “the Lord had promised that you would already be here with me, my Felix, my portion;

[310] Felix, my chief pledge—what, I ask, caused so great a delay, or where did they hold you?

[399–400] Although I yielded for a time in this fragile body, I remained faithful in a steadfast heart.

The place and my present condition themselves show you that I did not flee from fear of death, nor put my soul before Christ;

[315] I fled not because I loved life, but because I feared this fragile weakness of the body. [Note: [Col. 0475D] See Poem 21, line 603.] Yet had faith been worthless to me and this life dear, [Note: [Col. 0476D] One German manuscript reads *cara* (“dear”); others *carum*, wholly incongruously.] I could have sought shelter and lived safely in another city.

I sought unknown mountains and barren deserts, laying my gentle neck in the lap of the Lord,

so that I might die with him as my witness, or be fed by him.

Nor was this confidence in us vain: behold, you see that the Almighty was present, and chose to send you to me, [Note: [Col. 0475D] That is, “he chose.” See poem 32, line 522, and letter 32, section 6.]

[325] through you to restore his gifts to me.

Use, my son, the commands that entrust you with the work of piety, and, taking me upon your shoulders, carry me back to our common fold.”

Felix, eager and rejoicing in the desired gift, took up the beloved burden as though it were the light burden of Christ;

[330] he carried it with such swift running that one might think he himself was being carried rather than carrying.

Indeed, Christ himself carries the one who carries, and God added wings to his feet, swift with devotion. [Note: [Col. 0476D] German manuscript 1 reads *volucer* (“swift” or “winged”). Two German manuscripts and the editions of Grinæus and Poelman read *et pedibus* (“and to [his] feet”), which is better; others read *it pedibus* (“he goes on foot”).]

In that same night one man received so many gifts at once. [Note: [Col. 0475D] Poetic license. See letter 32, note 5, line 8.]

[335] And Felix at once fulfilled them all: commanded to break his chains, he restored the priest and carried him back refreshed.

He set him down safely beneath the roof of his own house, the only dwelling protected by an old woman.

So lofty was Maximus, and so great in this confessor’s merit, that a household crowd and great wealth had dwindled for him to one old woman.

[340] Felix knocked at the door and awakened her.

Terrified at the first sounds, she scarcely recognized the familiar words; she received her master into the open house, trembling in voice and step, old age shaken by fear. [Note: [Col. 0476D] German manuscript 1 reads “astonished.”]

Felix said to her:

“Take this deposit, which the stars of the night, conscious of it, and the hands of the angel under Christ their leader entrust to you through me.

Receive in your faithful lap this jewel of the Lord, which at the end of time you are to return unharmed to us, with the Lord as judge,

[350] the Lord who now witnesses your receiving it.”

At these words Maximus intervened and, calling back his own Felix, said:

“You too, my son, receive in return the gift, restored to health, which he commanded me to give back to you—the one who commanded you to come to me when I had been laid down.”

Then he placed his right hand on the head of his beloved Felix, asking at once for all the gifts of Christ:

[355] as that venerable father Isaac blessed his son with the dew of heaven and the abundant fruitfulness of the earth, [Note: [Col. 0475D] Genesis 27:28.]

so Maximus, with a fatherly and apostolic voice, blessed Felix with Christ’s blessing and enriched him;

[360] he crowned him with the honor of an unfading crown and enriched him with everlasting wealth, which we too now behold.

# POEM XVI [Note: [Col. 0475D] Elsewhere numbered 20; what was 16 is now 12. Written in the year 398, on January 14.] — NATALITIAL POEM V ON SAINT FELIX

[Col. 0476D]

It continues the history of Saint Felix.

[401–402] Times succeed times; summer departs and comes again.

Each day, by driving on the next, flees and turns the world;

[Col. 0477A] all things pass away, but the glory of the saints endures in Christ, who renews all things while remaining in himself. [Note: [Col. 0477D] One German manuscript reads *ipse* (“he himself”); both readings are good.]

[5] At last, then, the day has come around and is born for me—the day desired throughout the whole year—which renews the sweet festival and my vows;

the day that demands from me solemn gifts, recalling the birthday on which thousands of countless peoples rejoice;

the day whose special joys touch me, on which I owe to offer the due gifts of my serving tongue to my Felix, to whom I am devoted with a mind consecrated in the Lord Christ.

It is permitted me to celebrate him, holy, through annual songs of loving service.

Therefore I shall speak of his merits and the causes of his merits,

[15] through which he obtained the rewards of heavenly praise, eternal days, and the name of great honor.

The preceding book has already published for you the first acts of the martyr. [Note: [Col. 0477D] That is, *Natalitial Poem* 4. The same two German manuscripts read *primus* (“first”), and rightly so in this sense: the preceding first book—that is, the book immediately before this one—has already set forth for you the acts of the martyr.] It told where he was born, what his family was, how he was raised in his studies, and by what progression he was afterward called through sacred duties

[20] to prefer serving Christ eternally rather than wandering along his father’s paths through the byways of the world.

For his father had served under Caesar with a veteran’s arms.

We also recounted the punishments endured in the dreadful prison, which the confessor underwent, prepared even to suffer death,

[25] had not God, forestalling the swords, released him, sent forth from wicked chains, and called him to other duties;

so that he might first return to the sacred episcopal court, [Note: [Col. 0478D] German manuscript 1 reads *pius* (“devoutly”).] while Maximus, driven away by the advancing enemy, was breathing his last in the sunlit wilderness. [Note: [Col. 0477D] See poem 15, line 98.]

[30] Felix carried him on his own body, by command, and placed him, carried thus, in the shelter of a poor dwelling.

Having rendered him these services and been blessed by the holy old man’s blessed mouth, he departed.

For a few days he remained hidden in silence beneath his own roof,

[35] not silently wearying the heavenly Lord in his mind, but striking at him with direct prayer as it pierced above the stars, calling upon him through his proximate merit and asking that peace might proceed.

Meanwhile the days passed; peace seemed to be returning.

At last Felix left his hiding place and, trusting in the calm sky, began to return joyfully to the joyful brothers and to entrust himself to the peaceful city.

[Col. 0477D] Christ’s sheep rejoiced at the return of their shepherd.

He soothed the frightened flock after the recent storm with heavenly exhortations, and, guiding their anxious hearts with his word,

[45] strengthened them with the love of faith. [Note: [Col. 0477D] See note 334.]

He taught them to despise both the bitter and the sweet things of the world;

He taught that one must not yield to terrors and urged them to bring their breasts readily before the very fires or swords.

[403–404] He himself added weight to his words, as a confessor who had suffered what he taught others to endure;

[50] in speech and example alike he was a teacher to all.

That Evil One did not endure this long. He bristled with black hair and inflated his neck with raging poisons; [Note: [Col. 0478D] We have emended the text from two German manuscripts, against the printed editions, which erroneously read *rapidis* (“swift”). See line 199, *rabida monstra* (“raging monsters”), and elsewhere, *rabidis lictoribus* (“raging executioners”).]

He injected his own venom into their criminal breasts,

[55] so that Felix’s grace might burn their blackened minds.

He inserted goads, and the fury of envy blazed in their wicked minds.

The shameless rage assailed the first house; impious passion for crime burned in all. [Note: [Col. 0478D] One German manuscript reads *vipereus* (“viper-like”). Six editions read *improba* (“shameless”); three marginal editions, with two German manuscripts, read *primum* (“first”).]

[Col. 0478B] Impiety thirsted for Felix.

But he happened to be absent from his own house, standing safely in the middle of the city,

surrounded, as was his custom, by brotherly friends and sowing devout words in the ears of the believing people.

[60] Behold, they came upon him, seeking him with swords drawn.

Suddenly either their hostile hearts or this man’s face were changed: in their frenzy they did not recognize the familiar man.

They ask where Felix can be found, and Felix is both seen and not seen; he himself is not himself a man: although near, he is far away.

The same man became both unknown and known to his fellow citizens;

[70] faith distinguished his face for those who believed, but to his enemies he was another man.

He himself perceived Christ’s favoring plan; smiling, he answered their questions:

“I do not know the Felix whom you seek.”

At once they passed him by; he departed from the street, while the Lord mocked and frustrated the gaping dogs.

[75] They had not gone far when, as they asked in what district Felix might be, someone rebuked them and gave them information, unaware of the reason and believing that they were mad with frenzy:

They had not seen the man close at hand, though they had spoken directly with him.

[80] Struck by the novelty of the deception and now more furious, they quickly returned and ran along the very tracks of the man.

They were already drawing near, but Felix, warned by the approaching tumult of the city and by the uproar of the astonished crowd all around,

turned aside from the threatening blows and withdrew obliquely a good distance away.

[85] For he had found a place which, by chance, in an open stretch, offered escape. [Note: [Col. 0478D] Two German manuscripts read: *E spatio, nanctusque locum qui forte paventi*; three marginal editions: *paventi*.]

Though drawn away from the busy city, he was nevertheless not far from the dark pursuers; slipping away close beneath the conspicuous gaze of those following, he had somehow avoided their hostile swords.

[90] Yet he was bound to be captured, since that place offered no barrier to resist the wicked.

No doors protected it: opening onto the public roadway was a half-ruined, ill-omened wall, broken by the fragments of the fallen structure.

[95] But the divine hand placed itself between the saint and his enemies and enclosed the place with a wondrous defense.

There were no heaps of stones and no iron-barred doors, the human devices by which we close courtyards;

Instead, a dirty mound suddenly thickened with rubble,

[100] and a spider, commanded to do so, stretched its trembling webs and built them throughout the open space, giving the deserted ruin the appearance of decay. [Note: [Col. 0479D] Two German manuscripts read *intutum* (“unprotected”); both readings are good.]

[405–406] When this confronted the threatening men, they were stunned, and, standing fixed in place, said to one another: [Note: [Col. 0479D] The printed editions read *simul et* (“and at once”). From two German manuscripts we have restored *sibimet* (“to one another”), that is, “they said to each other.”]

[105] “Is it not madness to attempt an entrance or believe that any man has entered here, where the smallest worms have left signs?

Little flies break these webs; yet we foolishly suppose that a man has passed through closed spaces, without breaking so delicate a fabric despite so large a body?” [Note: [Col. 0480D] Thus two German manuscripts. Schottus’s edition nearly agrees, reading *per clausa* (“through closed places”). Others read *praeclusa* (“blocked off”).]

“That man is now more deservedly in our hands—the informer who cunningly led us into the wilderness by deceitful trickery,

[110] and, having turned us elsewhere, falsely claimed that Felix was hiding in this place, so that by wicked deception he might divert our weapons from the fugitive’s head, being friendly to him.

Let us therefore withdraw. To remain here longer will be a laughingstock to the crowd, and our mad error will be noted:

We have directed our steps to search for the man’s hiding places where the untrampled ground shows inaccessible recesses blocked either by a rotten mass or by little spiderwebs.”

[120] Without delay they departed quickly in different directions, growling.

But, as Scripture sings, [Note: [Col. 0479D] Psalm 2:1 and 4.] Christ from his heavenly citadel laughed at them as they madly threatened.

He had hidden his own Felix beneath sacred wings.

Safe in the Lord’s embrace, Felix joyfully scattered the gleaming weapons with his helmet and shield of faith, [Note: [Col. 0479D] See note 334.]

[125] and, as a confessor, carried the sword of the word in his mouth.

With hands armed by piety and a breast chaste and full of God, he was protected by the breastplate of distinguished merit.

[Col. 0479D] O divine Wisdom, rich in many forms,

[130] always confounding the mighty things of the world through the weak!

Scarcely do peoples defend themselves with lofty walls, and even those who trust in strong fortifications are often overwhelmed by the enemy;

Cities are stormed from mountains that oppose them.

Now God also protected the saint from armed men by means of a spiderweb;

[135] the enemy was halted by delicate nets, and iron force yielded to an aerial thread.

Human salvation is empty; my strength is no strength for me if I lack the strength of God.

What are the vast powers of giants? What are the kings of Egypt? Where is mighty Jericho? [Note: [Col. 0480D] Two German manuscripts read *Hierico* (“Jericho”).]

[140] Their own glory, in which they swelled with pride, brought ruin upon them all and proved empty.

Nor did divine power break these things through their own strength, but rather through the weak.

That giant died by the sling of a shepherd boy like a dog;

That city was brought down by the sound of trumpets;

[145] that proud king lay upon the shore, paying for his kingdom’s wealth in naked death.

So when Christ is with us, a spiderweb is a wall;

But from him whom Christ abandons, a wall will become a spiderweb. [Note: [Col. 0480D] German manuscript 1 reads “a wall.”]

[150] When the crowds had departed and silence had come, and deep night had supplied the faithful darkness of escape, Felix came out and changed his hiding place.

He sang to the Lord:

“Even if I enter the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, because your right hand is with me; I shall go through the underworld not deprived of light.” [Note: [Col. 0479D] Psalm 22:4.]

[155] Thus, guided by God, he reached a remote *compluvium*—a cramped place among narrow dwellings—where an old cistern lay dry beneath a deep roof. [Note: [Col. 0479D] See note 242.]

Nearby lived a woman, a holy servant of God, who, without knowing that the confessor was concealed there, fed Felix as though she knew it in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0479D] That is, “nearby.” See poem 21, line 305, and poem 22, line 118.]

[407–408] I shall sing of the marvel: the Lord’s ingenuity fed his fosterling through one who unknowingly fed her own.

[160] Now diligently she brought bread, now other foods which she had customarily baked for herself;

In a divine transport of mind she carried provisions to the place where Felix, hidden by the Lord, lay concealed.

[165] Yet she did not know when she entered with them, nor when she departed from there; she remembered neither her own entrance nor her exit. [Note: [Col. 0480D] Two German manuscripts read “when she had departed.”]

Whenever she had brought the prepared food, although she was serving the saint with her own hands, she remained unaware of so great a service and could not know in her heart

That she was doing this not by her own intention but by Christ’s divine power.

At the place of his hiding, at the narrow opening above its mouth, she would enter and leave the food she had brought;

[175] believing that she had placed it in her own house, she always departed remembering what was to be put away and immediately forgetting what had been put away.

O woman blessed by God, like one of the birds that once fed the prophet carried away from the world.

You too fed a martyr in a secret dwelling, like a bird obedient to the Lord;

And, though unaware of the saint, conscious of your service. [Note: [Col. 0480D] Two German manuscripts read *conscia servitii* (“conscious of your service”); the editions read *quod* (“because/that”).]

[180] What you did, and for whom you ultimately served, you will joyfully learn at that time when God himself, through Christ, returns to you the crown of righteousness for his confessor.

Then Felix himself will report to you before Christ the judge the meals you provided,

Which God transferred to the sweet service of the consecrated martyr, just as once, with an angelic hand suspended through the empty air, he sent food baked for reapers to the hungry prophet among ravening beasts;

[190] not savage beasts, because holy faith had conquered the lions and sacred fasts restrained their hungry jaws.

They say that for six full consecutive months he lived without human company beneath that dark and narrow roof,

[195] needing no human help and always abounding in Christ’s consolation.

It is said that during that time Christ often deigned to visit him with his own speech;

Often fed him with his own hand and gave him drinks from heaven—not rainwater, which the clouds pour out everywhere for all,

[200] but dew which grace sent specially from heaven to Felix alone. [Note: [Col. 0481D] Thus we have emended the text from two German manuscripts and four printed editions. The Rosweyde edition reads *quam* (“which”), incorrectly. One German manuscript reads *defudit* (“poured out”).]

For, as often happens, summer was then parched by excessive suns, and the well too had dried up, the well that had supplied the hidden man with the drinks already obtained.

But lest bodily thirst burn him, he who thirsted for Christ and endured this punishment of his afflicted body,

A thin cloud, carried through the clear sky and gathered into a small globe, [Note: [Col. 0481D] Thus one German manuscript, better than the printed editions, which read *tenuem* (“thin”). This line is missing from another German manuscript.]

poured a sweet liquid into the thirsty mouth through the narrow rain-cistern, as though pressed out by hand.

[210] It refreshed him with the milky juice of a heavenly fleece, as it must be called.

What wonder, then, if Christ now nourishes one freed from earthly stain, [Note: [Col. 0481D] Thus we have restored *terrena labe* (“from earthly stain”) from two German manuscripts; the true reading is confirmed below by line 272, *terrenae contagia ducere labis* (“to contract the contamination of earthly stain”). The former reading was *mole* (“mass”).] when the Holy Spirit nourished him while he was placed in a body,

[409–410] and when bread for him was God himself, the heavenly bread on which every angel feeds?

When this period had passed, peace returned and sheathed the swords.

[215] God warned Felix to come out of his hiding place—he who had until then closed his peaceful ears to the world’s uproar, drawing forgetfulness over human affairs. [Note: [Col. 0482D] Two German manuscripts and Schottus’s edition read *qui* (“he who”); others read *qua* (“by which”). The same two manuscripts then read *et patria* (“and [in] his native city”), whereas other copies read *ut* (“as”).]

When he emerged as something new into the light for those who already despaired,

[220] he seemed to his native city like one returned from the dead.

Many hesitated to recognize him and, after first asking, said:

“Is this truly your face? Are you, blessed Felix, being restored to us after so long a time?

From what region do you come? Were you given by heaven, or from paradise?

[225] Restored to earth, are you revisiting our dwellings?”

He confirmed their faith, saying that he was present before them in his own body, that he had lived preserved by God;

He gave joy to everyone and was celebrated by the entire people in praises and for his merits.

[Col. 0482A] Maximus had died, having fulfilled a long lifetime as bishop. [Note: [Col. 0482D] Thus two German manuscripts. The editions read *largum* (“long”).]

[230] The people needed the guidance of a shepherd. [Note: [Col. 0481D] That is, “the people.” See poem 23, line 27.]

The entire flock bleated the name of Felix, whom Christ had crowned with the confessor’s wreath of victory.

The people’s voice proclaimed him a saving teacher, and his life harmonized with his teaching.

But, so that this too might bring him the palm of righteousness, he restrained his lofty merit with a quiet heart and, considering himself unworthy, did not dare to grow in honor.

[235] He testified that this honor was owed more to the aged Quintus, because that man had previously earned the rank of presbyter, his companion in honor.

This arrangement lasted for seven days.

[240] Therefore under this bishop Felix also lived as a presbyter, and he grew in merits though he did not wish to grow in office.

Quintus himself, as though inferior, observed him in all things, and possessed Felix’s mouth and tongue.

He governed the flock through office; Felix governed it through speech.

[245] Grace increased holy Felix with many other virtues of Christ, and in peace he subdued no lesser battles than those he had fought as a confessor with powerful arms.

He had despised bodily safety during the grievous storm, and, likewise, had despised wealth and honors;

In secure peace he was cautious—not secure in possessing merit, but more watchful in guarding the good things of life after he had overcome the dangers of death, fearing the reefs even amid calm waters.

[Col. 0482C] We have said how he trampled death and ambition.

[255] Now learn another palm of the confessor.

He conquered avarice.

For, rich in his ancestral wealth, he had inherited and possessed many estates and houses. [Note: [Col. 0482D] Two German manuscripts read *domusque* (“and houses”); these manuscripts consistently have *domus* where the others have *domos*.]

The confessor had been proscribed, but after peace was restored, he was permitted, if he wished, to demand back his own rights.

[260] Yet he preferred to heed the Teacher’s word—“All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial” [Note: [Col. 0481D] That is, the apostle Paul. See letter 30, note 5.]—and to prefer what was useful to what was lawful.

As though he feared contracting the contamination of earthly stain, he recoiled from reclaiming the estates he had lost under legal title.

Many pressed him, especially Archelais, [Note: [Col. 0482D] Two German manuscripts read *Archelaus*; Paulinus may perhaps have used this form, as he uses *Melanius* for *Melania*.]

a wealthy widow, as holy in faith as she was distinguished by ancestry,

[265] who revered holy Felix with faithful devotion and was in turn dear to him.

She honored him according to his merit and, as they say, treating him as a companion joined to herself by right,

Often wearied his devout heart with repeated complaints about why he refused to have his due and readily available rights returned,

[270] which, once received, he could distribute to the needy, with great interest accruing as his reward.

She often offered him many gifts from her own possessions; but he, content with a devout disposition in all things,

[Source ends here.]

With a tranquil heart he smiled at feminine anxiety,

himself fully conscious of the heavenly blessings

which he held as compensation for earthly things.

Therefore, when his dear friends pressed him, he replied:

[280] “Do you compel me to seek again earthly things and lose the eternal?

It is better that wealth be absent while life is safe than to be wealthy and lose life:

I shall be poor in possessions, but rich in God, for I shall possess Christ in poverty.”

The grace of Christ will enrich the poor in worldly goods. [Note: [Col. 0483D] Thus manuscript 1 of the German codices; better than the others, which read *ditavit* (“enriched”).]

Holding to this resolve, he himself cultivated with his own hands three lean acres of land, [Note: [Col. 0483D] Two German manuscripts read *modici*, “small,” instead of *macri*, “lean.”]

[285] [Col. 0483B] not possessing them under his own legal title, but farming them as a tenant,

without a servant, the owner of a poor garden. Yet even these meager resources,

rich in his poverty, he placed at the disposal of the Lord; with the poor

he always shared the vegetables he had gathered, and with the poor his table.

[290] A single day consumed his care in securing the necessities of life.

A single garment covered him, and often scarcely even that.

If he had two, he clothed a naked man with the better one.

Often he transformed the rags of the wretched with a new garment.

The poor man, changed from blackness by Felix’s clothing,

[295] shone forth; while Felix, beneath the beggar’s covering,

grew dark, adorning his mind with an unadorned body.

Living in this devotion, mature before God, and having completed

his years and merits in full, he closed the seasons of his life,

and changed, rather than closed, the ages of his devout life.

## POEM XVII

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Formerly 30; what was numbered 17 is now 13. It appears to have been written in the summer of 398.]

### TO NICETAS, RETURNING TO DACIA

[Col. 0483C]

He accompanies Saint Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, who had appeared at the feast of Saint Felix’s nativity, as he departs, with extraordinary praises.

413–414

Are you already leaving, and in haste abandoning us—

us whom, though you leave in this one region,

you will always carry with you,

bound to you in our minds without end?

Are you already departing, recalled from afar

by the land that you inhabit? Yet here also you remain,

holy Nicetas, [Note: [Col. 0483D] That is, “you stay.”] since we hold your departure

[8] within our hearts.

Go, mindful of us; and as you depart, remain present in spirit,

implanted in our minds in turn.

Draw along, and carry with you,

[12] those whom you bear within yourself.

O land and peoples, too blessed,

whom, returning from us, you will soon approach;

whom Christ will visit, coming with your foot,

[16] and with your mouth.

You will go far to the northern Dacians;

you will go, to be seen in Epirus twice over,

and you will pass through the Aegean waves

[20] to Thessalonica.

But now, once you have reached land, the first road

will carry you across a broad, spacious plain,

where the fleeces of Canusium glow,

[24] dyed with medicinal purple.

But when the road has extended a little farther,

may Christ, I pray, grant you gentle weather,

and may a light breeze blow, without cloud,

for the dry lands of Calabria.

Just as, by the hands of the ancient prophet,

through the sacrament of the cross, when wood was cast into the water,

the liquid of Marah was sweetened [Note: [Col. 0483D] Exodus 15:25.] and the bitter waters were set aside [Note: [Col. 0483D] That is, “removed.”],

[32] so may the heavens be tempered for you now,

and the air, made mild beneath a light clear sky, [Note: [Col. 0484D] The German manuscript reads *ut* (“that”).]

may breathe health-giving breezes

[36] through pure currents.

The air that is usually heavy with the breath of marshland,

carrying the foul odors of snakes,

and dissolving swollen bodies into sickness

[40] with its thick wind—

may the Lord, powerful over all things, command it to flee

or to change; and now may it offer his priest

the breath of health

[44] in its breezes.

Just as, when Egypt was once perishing,

covered by the darkness of night and dense shadows,

where the sacred people of the living God dwelt,

[48] there was light for the world,

[Col. 0484C] so now, throughout the whole world, this appearance is displayed,

when the devout portion of holy faith shines through Christ,

while error overwhelms the rest

[52] with darkness.

So, wherever your journey carries you,

may the Lord prosper all things for Nicetas,

until he is borne joyfully to his desired homeland,

[56] to his native city.

Go, Nicetas, along the road by which you are returning in safety;

with Christ accompanying you, make prosperous progress,

you whom your people, long wearied,

[60] seek night and day.

They call you back, as a field thirsts

for rain enough to lighten it,

and as young calves, their mothers’ milk held back,

[64] seek their mothers again.

Therefore, by the just prayers of your people,

who rightly seek back their father,

we are compelled, though defeated and still unsatisfied,

[68] to yield to their desire.

And because the hope of holding you is now being snatched away,

affection urges us to favor what pleases you.

Although we have hated those roads [Note: [Col. 0485D] A poetic license. See note 342.]

[72] which carry you away,

we hate and love those same roads.

We hate them because they draw you away; we love them

because, from far away, they have brought us the sight

[76] of your face.

The roads which we once prayed might be constricted by prevailing love, [Note: [Col. 0485D] The German and Royal manuscripts read *peradstricti*. But *prius stringi* better corresponds to what follows, *nunc sterni*.]

we now pray may be made easy and spread out for you,

with the name of highest Christ going before you over land and sea.

[80]

May he make the whole road level for you,

restrain the lofty mountains, fill the hollow valleys,

smooth the rough places,

[84] and join the gaps.

May the unmarried bands of brothers and sisters,

as you are carried through Hydruntum and Lupiae, [Note: [Col. 0485D] Manuscript Germanensis reads *Lipias*. The Royal manuscript, together with four printed editions, reads *Lepias*.] [Note: [Col. 0486D] The German manuscript reads *ambiant*.]

surround you, singing the Lord

[88] with one voice.

Who would give me wings like a dove? [Note: [Col. 0485D] Psalm 54:7.]

Then I would swiftly be present among those choirs,

who, singing of God and Christ with you as their guide,

[92] strike the stars.

But although I am held by the sluggish bondage

of an ailing body, still in spirit I fly forth

after you, and with the Lord and with you

[96] I sing hymns.

For inwardly entangled with your thoughts,

when you sing and pray,

with your prayer concerning yourself and with your voice

[100] we too are brought forth.

Then, when the sea passes beneath the land, the broad expanse of the Adriatic gulf will yield;

there it will lie down, and beneath a gentle west wind

[104] the sails will swell.

417–418

You will glide upon the resting sea,

and, in the beloved ship bearing the title of salvation [Note: [Col. 0485D] See note 245.], armed

with the victorious cross as your mast [Note: [Col. 0485D] See note 246.], you will go across the waves,

[108] safe from the southern winds.

The joyful sailors will sing their customary cry [Note: [Col. 0485D] See note 247.],

turning it into hymns with varied melodies,

and with pious voices they will lead the winds, their companions,

[112] out upon the sea.

Before them all, like a trumpet resounding,

the tongue of Nicetas, modulating Christ,

will sing—David, the eternal harpist, [Note: [Col. 0486D] The Rosweyde edition reads *alternis*. We have corrected this from the German manuscript, with the support of the Royal manuscript and the Bad., Grav., Schot., and Poelm. editions, which prefer *aeternis*, “in eternal [things],” though this makes no sense. Sacchini: “I read *aeternus*. And indeed David is most aptly called the eternal harpist, since he sings through the mouths of all who chant his psalms; he achieved not only that God should be praised by him personally in heaven, but also on earth through others, forever and unto ages of ages, which he desired and promised while he lived.”—The text has *Psallet aeternus citharista*, “the eternal harpist will sing.”]

[116]—throughout the whole sea.

The terrified sea-monsters will hear “Amen,”

and happily, from far away, will swim toward

the priest singing to the Lord,

[120] the playful creatures of the deep.

Everywhere dolphins, raising their open mouths,

will play around him, though without a voice;

yet, rivaling human tongues, they will express

[124] their joy.

For what does not taste and live for God,

by whose word all things were sown?

Therefore the depths of the sea know God’s praise,

[128] and the mute creatures proclaim it.

The beast of the ancient prophet bears witness to us [Note: [Col. 0485D] Jonah 2:1.],

roused from the deep at the Lord’s command

to receive the man who had been swallowed,

and then

[132] to return what it had taken in. [Col. 0486B]

But now, savage itself, it will devour only with its ears

the sacred songs of our prophet [Note: [Col. 0486D] The German manuscript reads *Carmina* (“songs”).];

it will fill its unfed belly

[136] with song as food.

Wherever you may go—along the road and over the waves,

over land, if need be, and through enemies—

you will go armed with the helmet of salvation,

[140] with Christ upon your head.

May Raphael, sent forth, fly to you, as once to Tobias among the Medes [Note: [Col. 0485D] Tobit 5.];

may that angel himself attend Nicetas

[144] all the way to the Dacians.

May that same Leader lead his servant,

he who once led Jacob to safety

from the face of his threatening brother [Note: [Col. 0486D] The German and Royal manuscripts read *superbi*, “proud”; all the printed editions read *minacis*, “threatening,” which better suits the scriptural sense.],

[148] God, the guide of Jacob [Note: [Col. 0485D] Genesis 28:13.].

For Nicetas too is an exile;

what the patriarch once did, he does continually,

fleeing from the world to the lofty

[152] walls of heaven.

And those steps by which Jacob saw

angels coming and going in opposite directions [Note: [Col. 0485D] Genesis 28:12.],

this man strives by a life surpassing the clouds

[156] to climb. [Note: [Col. 0486D] Thus the German manuscript; others read *contentus* (“content”).]

419–420

Hastening to the stars by the ladders of the cross,

where God, leaning down with flashing radiance

from his thrones, looks upon the various labors

[160] and battles of the mind.

And you, Nicetas, rightly named,

victor over the body, like the man called

Israel because he saw the highest Creator

[164] with his lofty heart [Note: [Col. 0487D] Genesis 32:28.],

my Nicetas is approved as

a true Israelite, without deceit,

who sees God, Christ, with the light

[168] of steadfast faith. [Note: [Col. 0487D] The German manuscript and the Grin. edition read *solido*, “steadfast.”]

May this God, who is always our way,

be our companion and go before us;

may the Word be a light for our paths

[172] and a lamp for our feet [Note: [Col. 0487D] Psalm 118:105.].

Through the blind and obscure channels of this age,

may we be guided by the torch of true light,

until we are permitted to touch

[176] the desired harbors of salvation,

which we now seek across the surging sea,

while we drift amid the turbulence of a wandering mind,

borne in a fragile body,

[180] as in a frail boat.

But with the cross at the helm guiding this vessel,

we now spread the pious sails of our hearts within us,

while Christ, with a favorable wind,

[184] brings the shore back to us.

Therefore may that same Leader now accompany you

on the road along which you hasten in returning;

may he bring you, Nicetas, safely

[188] to your ancestral threshold.

But once the strait has been crossed, the labor of the roads

on land remains, so that you may be carried

to the fortunate shores to which you have been appointed

[192] as priest.

[Col. 0487C] You will walk through the Philippaean fields of Macedonia,

through the city of Tomis,

and you will go to Scupi, [Note: [Col. 0487D] See note 259.]

near the homeland of your Dardanian host.

[196] O how that land will then resound

with joy, when you teach its frozen peoples

to submit their savage necks to gentle Christ!

And wherever Boreas binds the rivers

[200] in thick frost on the Rhipaean shores,

there you will melt rigid minds

with heavenly fire.

For although hard in land and spirit,

and harder than their own snows, the Bessi,

now become sheep under your guidance,

[208] are herded into the hall of peace.

Those necks which, always untamed by war,

refused to submit to servitude,

now, subdued beneath the yoke of the true master,

[212] rejoice to bow.

Now the Bessus exults, richer in the reward of labor:

what he once sought with hand upon the ground,

he now gathers as gold in heaven

[216] with his mind.

421–422

O transformations of things! O well-changed appearance!

The mountains once impassable and bloody

now shelter converted robbers,

[220] disciples of peace among the monks [Note: [Col. 0487D] See Epistle 31, section 12.].

Once a place of blood, now a land of life,

the pious band of robbers is turned toward heaven,

and Christ favors this plundering seizure of

[224] the kingdom above.

Where once there had been the custom of wild beasts,

there now the practice of angels flourishes;

and the righteous man lies hidden among those caves

[228] in which the robber himself once lived.

That old plunderer becomes prey for the saints,

and the murderer groans over his transformed losses:

stripped by right, as Christ strips away

[232] the weapons of crime.

In a reciprocal downfall, envious Cain perishes;

Abel, restored to life, feeds

the lambs redeemed at the price of poured-out

[236] blood [Note: [Col. 0487D] Genesis 4.].

Well done, Nicetas, good servant of Christ,

who grants you to turn stones into stars

and to build sacred temples from living stones.

[240] You traverse pathless glades and vast mountain ridges,

while seeking a road; and, overcoming the sterile forest

of an uncultivated mind,

[244] you turn it into fertile fields.

The whole region of Borra calls you father [Note: [Col. 0487D] The German manuscript reads this way. Other manuscripts incorrectly read *Boreae*, “of Boreas.” The Schot. edition has *Borrhae* in the margin. We have corrected the text from the very ancient German manuscript to *Borrae*, all the more confidently because, apart from the metrical necessity, N. Heinsius notes that the same word was restored in older manuscripts of Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 847: “the icy land of Borra.”]

At your words the Scythian is softened,

and that savage people, divided against itself, under your guidance

[248] lays down its fierce hearts. [Note: [Col. 0487D] That is, “lays them aside.” See Poem 14, line 81.]

The Getae come running, and both Dacians—

the one who dwells in the middle of the land,

and the other, the cap-wearing inhabitant of the riverbank, rich in many oxen [Note: [Col. 0488D] We have corrected this from the German manuscript. Previously the text read *pelleatus*. The correct form is *pilleatus* or *pileatus*: Ulpian uses *pilleari* in the *Collation of Mosaic Law*, title 2, in the sense “to be given a cap.” See also Henricus Valesius’s notes on the excerpts, p. 205 B, *De Legationibus*. But see note 251 for the meaning of *pilleatus* here.] [Note: [Col. 0487D] See notes 250 and 251.],

[252]

You make wolves produce calves,

and you make the lion, joined to the ox,

feed with straw, and open the safe hollows

[256] of vipers to little children [Note: [Col. 0487D] Isaiah 11:7–8.].

For you persuade wild beasts to mingle

with the gentle flock, their savagery driven away,

and with polished speech you imbue

[260] the savage minds of human beings.

Through you, in a mute region of the world,

the barbarians learn to echo Christ

with a Roman heart,

[264] and to live in the peacefulness of chastity.

Thus the wolf is gentle in your fold,

the lion feeds in harmony with calves,

and the little one, drawn from the fierce serpent’s caves,

[268] plays with the asp.

423–424

You turn the clever gatherers of gold [Note: [Col. 0489D] That is, those who gather gold from veins of ore.] into gold,

and you yourself imitate the Bessi [Note: [Col. 0489D] See note 252. The printed editions read *versos*; there is no doubt that, with the German and Royal manuscripts, *Bessos* must be read. Some codices read *imitare in ipsis*.]

from whom, as your living Word digs, you extract

[272] living gold.

Storing up these riches for the eternal Lord [Note: [Col. 0490D] The German and Royal manuscripts read *condis . . . cumulas*; other codices, more aptly, read *condens . . . cumulans*.],

and piling up the sacred talent through these profits,

you will hear: “Enter joyfully

[276] into the everlasting joys of your Lord” [Note: [Col. 0489D] Matthew 25:21.].

When the gracious house, filled with a holy assembly of brothers,

has received you among its choirs,

then, dear to us in the devotion of your heart,

[280] hide us within yourself.

For thanks be to God, who has bound us to you

with so great a love, through hidden chains

which no force can sever,

[284] so that nothing can break the inward bond.

Therefore, embracing your beloved heart without end,

we cling to you in a faithful noose;

wherever you go [Note: [Col. 0490D] All manuscripts except Rosweyde read *Quaque*; Rosweyde reads *Quoque*. Both readings are sound. See Poem 16, line 116.], we shall be your companions, [Note: [Col. 0489D] A poetic license. See note 342.]

[288] following you in mind.

The love of Christ, poured abundantly from heaven,

so binds our hearts together within,

that even when you have departed far away,

[292] we shall not be carried off into a distant world:

No age will ever cause us to slip away from you; no other world, nor death, shall tear us away. [Note: [Col. 0490D] These four lines have been added from the German manuscript, in which they were entirely necessary to complete the sense. They are absent from the other manuscripts, including the 800-year-old Royal manuscript.]

[Col. 0489C] Though the life of the body dies,

the life of love will live.

[296] While we inhabit these burdensome limbs,

we shall always honor you with a mindful mind. [Note: [Col. 0490D] The German manuscript reads *memores* (“mindful”).]

You will seek that we may be with you together

[300] in everlasting time. [Note: [Col. 0490D] The same German manuscript reads *Tu pete ut simus*, “Ask that we may be,” instead of *Tu petes simus*, “You will ask that we may be.”]

For virtue, exalted by its merits,

will set you upon a lofty summit,

and in the city above the living

[304] will add you to its great towers.

We, separated from you by places as much as by merits,

will look up humbly from afar to our exalted patrons [Note: [Col. 0490D] The German manuscript reads *patronum*, “patron,” not badly.],

while you, far away, among the sacred choirs,

[308] will regard us as companions.

Who will give us this on that day—

that we may stand beneath the shadow of your side,

and that the breeze of your rest

[312] may temper our burning? [Note: [Col. 0489D] Luke 16:24.]

Then, I pray, remember us in your great mercy,

and, reclining in the lap of the holy Father,

with a dew-filled finger [Note: [Col. 0489D] See Poem 20, line 270.]

[316] dispel the flame raging against us.

Now go happily nevertheless; and, as you depart,

always return here to us in spirit.

Be with us, even when you come

[320] to your ancestral city.

425–426

For God has not made you the teacher

of one people only, nor given you citizenship

in one land only: behold, our homeland

[324] claims you as its own.

Now divide your affections equally between the two,

and in love for us, your fellow citizens,

remain with your face in both places,

[328] a citizen of both lands.

Perhaps this homeland should be considered the greater,

where you are contained not within structures made by human hands,

but inhabit a living city

[332] of human hearts.

As you are a bishop, so you are a worthy guest

of gracious Christ, because, sharing in Christian minds,

you dwell as an inhabitant

[336] in the Lord’s temple.

Now farewell to us; and, mindful of us

through every age, good to the end,

complete your good course

[340] and receive the crown appointed for the just.

## POEM XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0489D] Formerly 21; what was numbered 18 is now 14. Written in the year 399, on January 14.]

### A SIXTH BIRTHDAY POEM ON SAINT FELIX

On the death, tomb, and miracles of Saint Felix.

[Col. 0490C]

By sacred right, the law laid upon me requires

that I celebrate this day every year.

My speech, serving it, demands from my mouth

the solemn gift of speaking Felix in verse,

of shaping my joy in votive song,

[5] and of singing the great merit of my beloved Patron,

through whom, seeking the heights by a difficult path,
