along a road open to few, he entered the citadels above.

I beg you, brothers, agree with my songs

and rejoice together with me;

pour forth your hearts in chaste delight.

[10] Holy joys and chaste songs suit the faithful:

for whom among human beings is it lawful—

for whom, when Christ is both love and fear—not to rejoice today,

and to come forward without fulfilling his vow?

With whatever resources of ability, speech, and means a person can,

how could he fail to rejoice, when the heavenly ministers rejoice with Christ,

[15] and even the elements themselves reveal it in festive color?

[Col. 0491A] Behold the joy of the world shining forth

in the splendor of the day, glittering with sacred adornments.

Everything is filled with joyful brightness;

the rain is stilled beneath delicate clouds,

and the earth is covered with a snowy garment.

[20] Snow covers the earth, the ground, the forests, the roofs, and the hills;

all things bear witness to the hoary honors of the old saint.

They show that Felix possesses both angelic light and peace

in the tranquil realm of the devout,

where milky fleeces glide through the silent sky.

[25] Christ, God of Felix, be present; now give me speech.

God who is Speech, give me speech;

Wisdom, give me a clear mind.

Human eloquence cannot adequately speak your praises [Note: [Col. 0491D] Thus two German manuscripts. The printed editions read *facunde*, “eloquently.”],

for the joys of your saint are your own.

[Col. 0491B] Let others bring precious gifts and surpass me

in the expense of their service;

let them bring beautiful coverings for the doors, [Note: [Col. 0491D] See note 253.]

[30] whether splendid with pure linen

or embroidered with colored figures.

427–428

Let others polish smooth inscriptions with pliant silver

and cover the sacred thresholds with affixed plates.

[35] Let others light candles decorated with paintings [Note: [Col. 0491D] See note 254.]

and attach many-wicked lamps to the hollow ceilings,

so that hanging torches may wave their trembling flames.

Let them strive to drench the martyr’s tomb with nard,

and bring perfumed ointments to the holy sepulcher.

[40] I yield indeed to many richer than I in gold [Note: [Col. 0491D] Manuscript 1 of the German codices reads *vano*, “empty,” instead of *auro*, “gold.”],

those whose heavy purses are relieved of bronze

and who fill the needy by opening their rich storehouses,

who stand before him, pledging their souls

with various gifts, [Note: [Col. 0491D] See note 255.] equal in devotion though different in means.

[45] Let them offer rich dishes of food,

broad curtains depicting deer and wild beasts—

abundant gifts, certainly, but reciprocal ones.

I, naked of possessions [Note: [Col. 0491D] Two German manuscripts read *nullus*, “no one,” or “none.” Both readings are good. The Vulgate is confirmed by Poem 18, line 337: “the nakedness of oxen.”], serve with my tongue,

paying what I owe from myself,

and offering myself for myself, though I am an unworthy victim.

Nor will I fear being despised, since Christ does not despise

[50] the offerings of a poor servant;

he who joyfully accepted the two bronze coins

as the praised widow’s contribution.

At that time, the wealthy too were bringing many gifts to God,

filling the sacred treasuries with great talents.

[Col. 0491D] But Christ was watching, examining the hearts of those who offered;

he awarded the widow the palm.

She had sent into the sacred treasury

[55] the means of her daily sustenance, two coins,

which constituted her entire property [Note: [Col. 0491D] That is, goods or wealth.],

without anxiety for her body.

Therefore, from the very mouth of the Judge who was to come,

she deserved to receive beforehand the praise of her deed,

[60] before the day itself,

and to be preferred to those whose gold she had surpassed by her offering—

a poor old woman, but prodigal in faithful devotion.

Therefore, good brothers, to whom this honor and this shared devotion belong,

lend attentive ears with peaceful minds,

and listen willingly not to who I am, but to whom I shall speak.

[63] I shall speak of things that ought to be despised,

yet are also worthy of wonder:

despised according to my ability,

but wondrous according to the merit of blessed Felix.

It is not possible to speak of them without praising Christ,

because whatever we marvel at in this man comes from him,

[70] from whom virtue comes to the devout,

and through whom life comes to the buried.

In earlier little books I sang of his homeland, lineage, and deeds,

and, recounting the saint from his whole origin [Note: [Col. 0491D] Two German manuscripts read *duxi*, “I led/recounted,” instead of *dixi*, “I said.”],

I described Felix until the time of his perfect life

came to an end,

and, having laid aside his body and left the earth,

he hastened by his merits toward fellowship with the eternal kingdom.

[75] But tombs do not conceal the limbs of the devout and their merits in the same way.

The life of souls survives after the bodies have been laid aside;

it experiences the fruits sought through the body,

and, not dead after bodily death,

the soul experiences good things with joy,

[80] while the tormented soul experiences evil things—

fruits which, when restored to the very body in the time to come,

it will reap together with the reunited body,

in a common and undivided reception.

My material, therefore, is extensive;

and as long as time lasts, so long will words remain.

If only I might tell the deeds of Felix,

and proclaim throughout the whole world

[85] the names of his merits—

if only my speech had as much capacity [Note: [Col. 0492D] Two German manuscripts and five printed editions read *pateat*; two manuscripts add after it, *si copia tanta sit oris* (“if there were such abundance of speech”).]

as there remains a store of deeds and merits.

For from the time when this day first placed Felix

in a blessed end,

when it gave his flesh to the earth

and his soul to the stars,

[90] almost every day since then seems to be at work

through God’s confessor.

And Christ proves him alive without his body,

to show that the power of the devout remains greater in death

than the force of the wicked remains in life.

Behold, you see the tomb covering the sacred bones of the martyr,

and the silent body preserved beneath the marble that covers it:

[95] [This line has been added from German manuscript 2.]

“No human eye sees the body in which he exists.”

His limbs lie hidden in the place where they were laid;

his peaceful flesh rests,

[Col. 0492D] deposited in the sure hope of renewed life.

Why, then, does such terror surround the threshold?

Who drives so many crowds here?

What hand presses the demons,

[100] seizes them against their will,

and compels them—though they protest with rebellious voices—

all the way to the martyr’s tomb,

where it makes them stand fixed, as it were, at the sacred threshold? [Note: [Col. 0493D] Manuscript 1 of the German codices reads *fixus limite*, “fixed at the boundary.”]

I look back upon that day,

which was mournful when it abandoned the world,

but joyful in heaven,

when God, Christ, received the beloved soul, [Note: [Col. 0493D] One German manuscript reads *acceptum* (“received”).]

taking it from its chaste mouth.

He added adornment to the heavens,

yet did not deprive the earth of its pledge:

the inhabitants above enjoy Felix in spirit,

while we enjoy him in body.

The spirit of his powerful soul lives there,

[110] while his merit remains here;

but it is pleasing to present the whole honor

of the blessed funeral which Nola offered.

For the devoted city had lost a priest

venerable in sacred office and years,

but it was to have him as its patron in heaven;

[Col. 0493B] hope consoled its love. [Note: [Col. 0493D] Thus two German manuscripts. Others read “but hope consoles love.”]

Therefore, with all the crowds by which it was surrounded,

it poured forth its faithful people

and ran to perform its duty.

[115] Then grief and devotion joined together in every heart [Note: [Col. 0493D] Thus two German manuscripts and the Grin. and Poelm. editions. Others read “in the breast.”];

faith mingled with devotion both rejoiced and grieved.

Although it believed that Felix had been summoned by Christ

and lifted above the heavens,

it nevertheless grieved that it was being left

[120] without so great a teacher.

And the one consolation of love that remained

in the holy funeral and procession was this:

after the bier carrying the body had been placed

in the place where it was to be buried,

the people, surrounding the body in a dense throng,

crowned the limbs lying there on every side.

[125] A pious struggle of loving people took place:

each strove to press against the others

and to stand nearer to the relics,

and rejoiced to touch the body with his hand.

Nor was it enough to have seen it once;

they were glad to remain there continually,

[130] fixing their eyes upon the exposed limbs

and, wherever access was given, pressing kisses upon them.

The harmonious crowd gave Christ the praise he deserved

and undertook the sacred honor of Felix’s throne.

Wherever the region beyond the walls and buildings lay vacant,

a field spread out there, smiling with joyful turf,

[135] blossoming more richly in that place [Note: [Col. 0494D] Thus two German manuscripts; the printed editions read *liberius* (“more freely”).],

as though already aware that the world would always honor

the venerable tomb. [Note: [Col. 0494D] Thus the Grin. and Poelm. editions, supported by German manuscript 2. Others read “the tomb worthy of veneration.”]

The earth rejoiced to be blessed by the sacred body,

and spread itself with fragrant grasses,

[Col. 0493D] in the pleasant adornment of spring [Note: [Col. 0494D] German manuscript 1 reads *amoeno*, “pleasant,” instead of *veris*, “with spring flowers.”]

more worthy of the martyr who had been buried there. [Note: [Col. 0494D] Thus two German manuscripts and the printed editions; they read *humato*, “buried,” instead of *humando*, “to be buried.”]

431–432

But as he ascended the heights on a tranquil flight,

and had been taken up from his chaste body,

the joyful throng of the devout received him

[140] as it came to meet him among the heavenly clouds.

The bands of the sevenfold angelic choirs of heaven,

coming to meet him at every gate wherever heaven lies open,

carried him joyfully in a starry triumph

[145] into the presence of the King and before the face of the highest Father.

They adorned your sacred head with a snowy crown.

Yet the Father also added a rose-colored one

at Christ’s indication,

and doubled the snowy coverings with purple attire.

Both honors were deserved by his merits. [Note: [Col. 0494D] Sacchini, together with the Schot. edition, writes in the margin *pro meritis*, “according to his merits.”]

For he took bright garlands,

as though transferred to heaven by a peaceful death,

[150] yet he equally deserved the purple of one who had been slain—

he who died as a confessor.

Therefore he possesses the rewards both of the one who suffered,

because of the ready virtue he displayed,

and of the one who died in peace;

nor is he deprived of the honor and adornment of peace,

because he did not die in combat.

[155] Thus established justice completed the pious funeral

and covered the corpse in the tomb. [Note: [Col. 0493D] That is, the corpse or lifeless body. See Poem 32, line 41.]

But the grace divinely implanted in his holy limbs

could not die, be covered, or be concealed with the flesh.

Immediately, behold, a light flashed forth from the bones laid there, [Note: [Col. 0494D] Two German manuscripts read *emicuit lux* (“a light flashed forth”).]

[160] and from that time onward has never ceased

to give signs of his powerful merit through healing works.

That same light will shine throughout the age,

for as long as the world exists,

a guardian of the holy ashes through the ages.

It proves the life of the dead martyr;

and, working Christ’s blessings at Felix’s tomb,

[165] it spreads the wondrous name of Felix

through all the lands far and wide.

It ennobles Nola above all other cities,

a city made worthy of so great a guest.

The grace of Christ has so expanded it through Felix’s merits

[Col. 0494C] that, enlarged by new citizens and walls,

[170] there is now even a city here where at first there was a poor tomb,

which, in savage times,

when religion was considered a crime,

had been narrowly built by the trembling people of the Lord

amid swords and fires,

[175] as a later age handed down the ancient account,

it had enclosed a great light beneath a small roof.

That sacred corner, once the sole possessor

of so great a deposit,

aware of the hidden light,

stood like a fountain within spacious buildings

and remains like a jewel set among roofs,

[180] spreading broad courtyards around the sacred tomb

through five basilicas,

whose roofs, visible from far away,

present to the eyes the appearance of a great city.

Yet, however spacious those heights may be,

they are surpassed by the crowds.

For as faith grows,

Christ’s grace overflows,

[185] granting Felix to live among the peoples

through a healing gift.

Even after the age of his body has passed,

he himself presides, holy, over his own bones.

The bones of his holy body in the tomb

are not buried beneath the dust of death;

rather, endowed with the secret seed of eternal life,

[190] they breathe the life-giving fragrance of his victorious soul,

through which powerful healing is granted

to the sick who pray.

One may infer how much virtue and glory

will surround the bodies when they rise again,

when so great a grace encircles the buried,

[195] and how brightly the bodies will shine

with renewed beauty,

when so great a light is present in hidden ashes.

What sort of crowns will be sufficient for us, insignificant as we are,

when even their ashes provide benefits to the living?

It is often a joy to behold the miraculous spectacles

of those who come to seek healing in various ways,

[Col. 0495B] each receiving what is suited to the requests of their vows.

433–434

You may also see country farmers

[200] carrying not only their cherished children

in a father’s embrace [Note: [Col. 0495D] That is, children. See lines 226 and 228.],

but often bringing sick animals in their hands as well,

and entrusting them confidently to the saint,

as though he were visibly present.

Soon, trusting in the healing granted in answer to their vows,

they rejoice in the God whom they have experienced,

and already believe the animals healed;

[205] and, in fact, they often lead their beasts home joyfully,

healed within a short time beneath that very threshold.

But since it would be lengthy and pointless

to pass through all the miracles Felix performs

in the name of Christ,

I shall bring forth one remarkable deed

[210] from among countless similar ones—

a deed depending upon one case,

though the same power accomplished them,

different in their circumstances.

Open your hearts, I pray;

you suffer only a brief inconvenience

while I recount a great work

in a few small words.

[215] And remembering the widow mentioned at the beginning of my speech,

whom God, looking at the value of her spirit rather than her gift,

preferred to those who gave much,

though she gave everything—

bear with me too as I speak of great things in a modest account.

For my words are like those small coins:

devotion has made them worth their weight in gold. [Note: [Col. 0495D] See note 256.]

[220] A certain man, poor in property [Note: [Col. 0495D] That is, in possessions.],

of plebeian birth and rustic in appearance,

supported his narrow poverty with a pair of oxen,

earning a meager livelihood from their labor.

Sometimes he was accustomed to yoke them to wagons,

[Col. 0495D] hauling loads for hire along an agreed route;

at other times, he rented them out for work beneath another man’s plow,

[225] obtaining from his poverty a return for his labor.

His whole hope and property lay in that pair.

He had no offspring dearer to him,

nor was he dearer to himself than they.

He regarded them as his children [Note: [Col. 0495D] That is, children. See line 200.];

and he cared no less to feed his young oxen

than to raise his beloved children.

Indeed, he was more sparing toward his children

[230] than toward the cattle.

He did not feed the animals on cheap grass

or barren straw,

but, cold himself, he sheltered them beneath a sunny covering,

and, hungry, he fed them on grain denied to himself and his children.

[Col. 0496A] Needy for himself but rich in them,

he was nourished by the abundant labor

that satisfied the needy man.

[235] These, then, the dear supports of his life [Note: [Col. 0496D] One German manuscript reads *sibi* (“to himself”).],

a wretched man, buried in unusually heavy sleep one night,

lost when they were driven away by the silent theft of a robber.

Rising at daybreak,

he first went inside, as usual, to yoke them,

only to find the stalls empty.

[240] Then he searched outside in the familiar fields in vain.

At once, weary from fruitless wandering here and there,

when he saw no certain tracks by which to identify them,

and his search, its hopes exhausted, had failed,

he despaired of human assistance.

But, filled with devotion,

[245] and with God inspiring him,

he raised his mind, bowed down within his broken heart,

toward heaven.

Then, with his heart restored,

and faith anticipating the fulfillment of his prayer,

he drank in the hope of obtaining what he had vowed.

He quickly sought the sacred court of Felix,

[250] entered the holy hall with great tears,

threw himself down before the doors,

and pressed kisses upon the doorposts [Note: [Col. 0496D] See note 257.].

He drenched the whole ground with tears,

lying prostrate before the holy threshold,

and demanded from pious Felix, as from a guardian,

the young oxen stolen by night.

Scolding him, he mingled words of prayer with complaints:

[255] “Holy Felix of God, sustenance of the poor,

ever Felix to the wretched,

and ever rich toward the needy,

God appointed you as rest for the weary,

relief for the afflicted,

and healing for sorrowful hearts wounded by grief.

435–436

[260] Therefore, as though trusting in a father’s embrace,

poverty, bowing its head, reclines upon you. [Note: [Col. 0496D] Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.]

Holy Felix, always compassionate toward my labors,

now that I have been forgotten by you—

why, I ask, or to whom have you abandoned me in my nakedness?

I have lost the dear young oxen,

your gifts,

[265] which I used often to commend to you as a suppliant.

Your care always guarded them with favor

and fed them for me.

Your protection kept them safe,

and your sufficient right hand made them strong and prosperous—

those whom this night has taken away from me in my misery.

Alas, what shall I do now?

Where shall I go in my deception?

Whom shall I accuse?

[270] Or shall I complain to you about yourself,

and accuse my patron of having forgotten me?

You allowed such deep sleep to creep over me as I lay asleep

that I did not perceive robbers breaking through my barriers.

Did you not shatter my hardened heart

with some terror?

Did you not give light to the darkness

[275] and to the theft?

Or did you not take care to reveal the fugitives

by any sign?

How shall I run about?

Where shall I be carried?

Everything is blind…

Built all around with hiding places; now even my own dwelling seems

Closed to me, where, with my charges taken away, I am left desolate.

I have nothing that I would wish to possess; nothing that, sweet to one who sees it,

[280] [Col. 0497A] Sweet to one who labors, might offer an unfailing grace,

Delighting the poor man with the wealth and yield of his little estate.

Where shall I, miserable, seek them now? When, or anywhere,

Shall I find such creatures again? Or from where shall I procure them once found?

They alone were the rustic wealth I possessed,

[285] The riches of my contented poverty. Give them back to me, then—

I do not want others. Nor will I seek them in any other region;

They are owed to me here: these doors will restore them,

At which I, suppliant, hold you fast yourself, and cling to you.

Why should I seek, or where, thieves whom I do not know?

[290] This man is my debtor; I shall hold the very guardian as the thief.

You, holy one, are answerable to me, conscious of them:

[Col. 0497B] I hold you; you know where they are, you who see all things, hidden and revealed,

In the light of Christ, and perceive what is far away,

And apprehend them, while God contains all things within himself.

[295] And therefore hidden thieves, in whatever hiding place

They may lurk, are not concealed from you, nor can they escape from you—

You whom one hand already holds. God is one and everywhere:

Christ’s right hand is gentle toward the devout, but an avenger against the wicked.

Give me back, then—give me back my oxen, and punish the thieves.

[300] But I am not seeking the guilty; let them go. I know your ways,

Holy one: you do not know [Note: [Col. 0497D] One German manuscript and four editions read *mala facta*, “evil deeds.”] how to requite wrongs with evil;

You prefer to correct the wicked by pardon rather than destroy them by punishment.

Let us therefore come to an agreement: divide with me

What is yours and what is mine; let my advantage remain unharmed through you,

[305] [Col. 0497C] And let your clemency justly defend its share;

Let your judgment stand with its scales held level:

Release the guilty to yourself; return the young oxen to me.

Behold, you hold the agreement; your servant now has no reason

To delay before you. Hasten to free me from such great cares.

[310] For my fixed resolve remains never to depart [Note: [Col. 0497D] That is, “to withdraw.”]

Until you come to my aid, nor to be torn away from this doorway.

If you do not hurry [Note: [Col. 0497D] One German manuscript and five editions read, “If you do not hasten.”], I shall lay down my life upon this threshold,

And you will no longer find anyone to whom, though restored late, you may return them.

Such things he spoke in a plaintive voice, but with faithful heart,

[315] Weeping and praying without end throughout the whole day.

The martyr gladly heard the weeping man; playing with his Lord,

437–438 He laughed at his own reproaches.

[Col. 0497D] Moved by the faith of the petitioner, not by the bold complaint of one in grief,

He hastened to bring help; the delay lasted only a few hours.

[320] Meanwhile, as the day slipped away and evening had already arrived,

He set no limit either to his prayers or to his tears; one

Voice remained fixed upon the doors: “I shall not be rescued from here.

Here I shall die unless I immediately receive the cause of life

Here at this very place.” At last, however, when the advancing night

[325] [Col. 0498A] Was compelling the sanctuaries to ever greater security, and he,

Forgetting the hour but remembering his loss, pressing his face

Against the doors, was barring the entrance with his whole body,

A violent hand assailed him, though his ears had vainly been assailed with many cries.

At last a crowd tore him away as he resisted, and drove him far

[330] From the holy sanctuary.

Driven out by the keepers, he wept still more bitterly, and mourning his own

Dwelling, sought his home. The silences of night resounded with his lament,

And the lonely places echoed far and wide with his loud complaints:

Until, unwillingly, he reached it; and entering the dark interior

[335] Of the silent hut, once again, from the very entrance of the roof,

As he saw the oxen’s manger bare, and no bells giving forth

The sounds they used to make when shaken upon the oxen’s necks,

Or when their hollow bronze was struck more softly by their sluggish tongues,

[340] [Col. 0498B] While the herd, brought back, ruminated its food in its throat,

He renewed his mourning more heavily, as though a wound had been reopened.

Although anxious care denied his afflicted heart rest,

He nevertheless gave this solace to his sleepless grief:

He stretched his body upon the places where his oxen had been stalled,

[345] And lay upon them; his limbs, broken by the hard bed,

Were not pained—the very injury pleased him. He did not shrink from

The position or the filth of the dirty stall, because it brought back

The familiar smell of his beloved herd, and no stench stinks to one who loves.

If the tracks they had left with their final steps

[350] He saw, then, feeling with his hand, he traced back the marks where they had trodden,

Groaning, and rubbed again with all his limbs

The signs of their feet, now cold. And although he was far away in body,

[Col. 0498C] He sent his mind, consecrated to Felix, to Felix’s holy sanctuary,

Calling upon Felix with tears, calling upon Felix by name;

[355] Nor did he despair of help, nor spare to pour forth his prayers.

Night, having crossed the middle of the sky, had covered the whole world

With sleep-bringing peace; everything was silent in slumber,

And only hope and concern for his own affairs kept him awake.

Suddenly he heard a noise before his doors,

[360] And the doors resounding as they were struck. Terrified and distraught,

He cried out, believing that thieves had come again:

“Why do you cruelly wish to break empty doors in vain?

I have no ox left; what more do you seek?

[Col. 0498D] Others have gone before you; only my life remains,

[365] Left to your companions as worthless booty.”

He said this in fear; but the sound at the threshold did not cease.

As it grew more frequent, and no voice of those striking the doors

Answered him, he approached, suspended in hesitant steps,

Put his anxious ear to the doors, and inserted his gaze through the cracks

[370] And the openings of the barriers, where the white light of the sky

Shimmered through the darkness. [Col. 0499A] He examined the scene for a long time;

Nor yet did he trust what he saw. For in the faint light of night

Clear certainty does not belong to the eyes; nevertheless, amid the shadows,

The bodies of those striking the doors began to dispel his trembling fears

[375] 439–440 And, in their new forms, to promise hope of good.

He sees that it is not men who are striking; but what he sees to be real

He does not dare to believe. I shall tell of great things,

Though they are small miracles to God, at whose command every living creature

Of every kind has the sense with which the Creator himself

[380] Endowed it. Behold, a pair of oxen,

Carrying a mind guided by the divine will, had come through unknown paths

By night to a familiar house without any driver,

As though by their own will—yet not by their own will, since through the action

Of the divine will Felix, guiding them with hidden reins,

[385] Had driven them away from the robbers by a stronger hand.

And after they had reached the thatched roof of their accustomed shelter,

Rejoicing in their return and fearing the hands they had experienced,

They shook the doors with their joined foreheads,

[390] As though they feared a robber threatening them by their own choice,

And used their horns as hands, so that they might rouse their master by the sound.

But he, terrified again by the tumult hostile to his doors,

[Col. 0499C] Feared even what was safe. Wisdom inspires the brute

To sense the reason for delaying his course,

And to unlock the understanding of the master who fears.

He was waiting for them to utter a lowing by which, their fear dispelled,

[395] He might safely open the entrance to the young creatures outside.

Seeing the unexpected signs of the divine gift,

He still stood transfixed; even his joy disturbed his trembling.

He dared not believe; he feared not to believe; he saw

Before him, [Note: [Col. 0499D] Three manuscripts and Schott’s edition read *Comminus*, “near at hand,” and wrongly suppose that the text should read *caligare*, “to grow dim.” See poem 32, verse 203.] and thought that his sight was failing. As he looked back upon himself,

[400] He doubted that he could have deserved so much.

But then, reflecting on the one from whom he had hoped for it,

He dared to believe, recognizing the deeds of Felix, his patron.

Already the dawn was reddening as the twilight broke through,

[Col. 0499D] And the stars were growing faint as the last darkness fled.

In the dim light, or with the shadows just beginning to brighten,

[405] The indistinct colors of things had begun to reveal themselves.

Then at last, when the oxen’s familiar appearance became clear,

And their hair first began to shine before his eyes,

He exulted, now certain, removed the bolts from the barriers,

And opened the doors, creaking on their loosened hinge.

[410] As he did so, the two young oxen rushed in together

[Col. 0500A] And anticipated the efforts of the man who was still opening the door.

The doorposts easily yielded when the barrier was moved aside.

Immediately, upon the very threshold, they recognized their master,

Offered to them in joy, and, delighted, licked him in turn.

[415] They flooded the hands that stroked them with their lips [Note: [Col. 0500D] Thus we have corrected the text from one German manuscript. Another reads *inhumant*, perhaps meaning “they make moist.” The former reading was *inudant*.],

And stained all his clothing with foamy kisses,

While, gently pressing against their embracing master's dear neck,

They softly caressed his kindly breast in tender alternation [Note: [Col. 0500D] Thus two German manuscripts. The editions read *complectentes*, “embracing.”]

Nor did the horns of his beloved herd wound him.

He brought their brows together as though they were soft against his breast,

[420] [Col. 0500B] And the tongue which, when licking, scrapes even wild pasture

Did not seem rough to his hands.

Yet amid all this, the faithful rustic, with no unworthy heart,

Remembered his duty, and did not concern himself with the panting

441–442 First to lead the oxen into the stalls, and afterward, once the labor

[425] And hunger, to restore them with food, rather than take them with him

To the place from which he had received them.

So he came, leading them back, and did not conceal his joy in silent prayers.

As he reported the matter, he drew dense crowds after his words;

And he entered the holy sanctuary while everyone marveled.

[430] The creatures whose loss he had lamented the day before,

He led forth present on this day; he displayed the triumph

Of the holy martyr to the people. The young oxen themselves were led

Through the midst of the gathering, now the booty of thieves,

And now the spoils of Felix. The great crowd made room for those passing,

[435] And Christ’s glory was celebrated in silence

[Col. 0500C] In the cattle.

But the man who had been the cause of so great a gift from the Lord,

Standing in the midst of the threshold and weeping again—but now from joy—

Offered the vows owed to the Saint, not with heavy bronze,

Nor with a silent gift,

[440] But pouring forth a living offering of tongue and mind,

With pious voice bearing witness to the poor man’s generous honor.

As debtor, he paid Christ sufficiently with this pledge,

To whom the spotless sacrifice of his praise is enough.

“Behold, Holy One, I bring your captives to you as victor

[445] Before all the people, and as a suppliant once again entrust them to you to be kept safe:

Preserve those whom you have deigned to restore after their abduction.

Yet now, good Martyr, look upon me also:

For you see that what you must do still remains for you to do in me,

[Col. 0500D] Who stand near your threshold with eyes almost blinded;

[450] For I have immersed my eyes in abundant weeping,

Weeping not only because of my loss but even amid my joy.

You have removed the cause of my tears; now remove the wounds

That have arisen from my tears. Have pity, Holy One, on the loss

Of my oxen, and now likewise pity the loss of my eyes.

[455] [Col. 0501A] You restored the cattle to me; give my eyes back as well.

For what good is it that they have been restored,

If, while my sight is failing, I am absent from those present?

The people standing there laughed at him as he made these complaints.

But the ears of the Martyr, approached from afar in secret,

[460] Received the pious words of the foolish suppliant,

And soon the sacred right hand restored his eyes to health.

Then, rejoicing that he had recovered both his sight and his oxen,

He returned home, while the people praised God,

And the joyful victory of his twofold prayer followed him.

## Muratori’s Prolegomena to the Three Following Natal Poems of Saint Paulinus

[Col. 0501]

443–444 At last I have brought to light four poems of Paulinus, bishop of Nola, [Note: [Col. 0501] He means Natales XI, XII, and XIII, together with Paulinus’ final poem. These four short works have these prolegomena prefixed to them in volume I of Muratori’s *Anecdota*. EDIT.] long desired by all lovers of letters and long mourned as lost. The ravages of cruel time had until now begrudged us these monuments of so great a man; among its illustrious acts of plunder, it had also carried off this great treasure of eloquence.

It is certainly most grievous that so many riches of the ancient Fathers have perished—riches by which both ecclesiastical history and the doctrines of the Catholic faith could have been successfully advanced. Yet it is especially in the loss of those works composed by the most eloquent and holiest Fathers that it is fitting for our grief to exercise itself, since with their aid it would have been lawful for us to overthrow the heterodox of our own age and recall them to a better way of life.

How great our Paulinus was as orator, poet, and saint is attested both by his writings and by the testimony of all distinguished writers. I shall not address his outstanding holiness, since it has found sufficiently evident eulogists in Saint Ambrose, Letter 30 to Sabinus; Sulpicius Severus at the end of the *Dialogues*; Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107; Gregory the Great, Book III of the *Dialogues*; and others who have recounted his deeds; moreover, he is still commended in the ecclesiastical calendars.

It must surely seem remarkable that a man once elevated to senatorial rank and to the consulship itself, and distinguished by immeasurable wealth, should have renounced the world so completely that he became an example of holiness for the whole Christian commonwealth, as Augustine says in writing to him in Letter 34 and in Letter 39 to Licentius.

Jerome praised his excellence in oratory in Letter 13, in these words:

> If the final hand were added to your work, we would have nothing more beautiful, nothing more learned, nothing sweeter, and nothing more truly Latin than your volumes.

He then adds:

> You possess great talent, an infinite abundance of language, and you speak easily and purely, and so forth.

I omit the rest, so that I may demonstrate his excellence in poetry through the great testimony of a great man.

Ausonius held Paulinus dear among the few, and was always wholly occupied with ensuring that honors should be secured for him and that his name should be commended to fame. Thus, writing to him in Letter 20, he says:

> And the poetic palm that has long flourished for you  
> Is adorned with the ribbon that my palm lacks.  
> We yield to your genius as far as we surpass you in age;  
> Our Muse rises up to your song.

From this you may learn how great Paulinus’ reputation was in poetry, since Ausonius, otherwise a most distinguished poet, rose to meet him.

The same Ausonius, in Letter 1 to Paulinus, says:

> Now what should I say about your eloquence? I can swear with certainty that no one among the Roman youth is your equal in poetic eloquence.

But I do not wish to weave a panegyric sufficient to praise such a great man. I shall therefore turn to explaining the sequence of his books.

Fifty of his letters to various persons survive, together with various poems, especially ten *Natales* composed in honor of Saint Felix. These and other short works of the holy bishop were often committed to print, though the Antwerp edition of 1622 is considered the most attractive of all, since it is rich in the notes of Fronto Ducaeus and Heribert Rosweyde, as well as in a life of Paulinus composed by Father Sacchini.

Finally, in Paris in 1685, the works of Paulinus were published in two volumes, revised against manuscript codices and illustrated with the notes of various scholars, through the efforts of Johann Baptista Le Brun. To my great regret, these volumes have not yet been placed in my hands.

Peter Francis Chiffletius, a distinguished man of letters of the Society of Jesus, had also published in 1662 a book entitled *Paulinus Illustrated*, in which he had treated the life and books of this saint with great learning.

Yet no one had hitherto had the opportunity to see those poems which I am the first to bring forth from the hidden recesses of the Ambrosian Library.

Paulinus testifies in his ninth letter to Severus that he was accustomed to compose a *Natalitium* poem for Saint Felix every year. It was believed that only ten of these *Natales* existed when Dungalus’ book was brought to light. Dungalus flourished around the year of Christ 821 and wrote against Claudius of Turin concerning the veneration of sacred images; he dedicated the work to the emperor Louis the Pious and his son Lothair.

There the eloquent and pious author mentions many poems of Saint Paulinus, among them excerpts from *Natales* XI, XIII, XIV, and XV, by which the veneration of sacred images and relics is wonderfully confirmed. Our library also preserves a very ancient copy of this author.

From Dungalus’ testimony, then, it became known that Paulinus had composed other *Natales* as well. The value of the fragments increased the thirst for more: after seeing a few drops of water, the entire fountain immediately became the object of our desire.

Therefore, while I was examining the very extensive series of manuscript codices preserved in the Ambrosian Library, an ancient volume fell into my hands containing poems by Venantius Fortunatus, Prosper, Juvencus, Arator, and other ancient Christians. There I found thirteen *Natales* of Saint Paulinus written out. When I compared them with the fragments of Dungalus, I immediately congratulated myself and the world of letters on the discovery of the genuine offspring of so great a writer.

The codex breathes venerable antiquity. Its square, extremely small characters, distinguished from one another by straight lines with marvelous elegance, were, in my judgment, produced in the ninth century.

Until now it had been believed that Paulinus sang fifteen *Natales*, since Dungalus expressly quoted poems both from XIV and from XV. But either that author, or the scribes who copied him, were deceived. For the poems reported as taken from *Natalis* XIV must altogether be assigned to XIII; our codex and the order of the events establish this.

Accordingly, the *Natalis* called XV by Dungalus must here be numbered the fourteenth; we deeply regret that it was not copied in our parchment manuscripts.

Furthermore, in our codex the first and second *Natales* are confused together, and for that reason the remaining poems differ in number by one from the editions. Thus the poem called the seventh here is numbered the eighth elsewhere, and the others proceed in the same order. This was caused by the carelessness of the copyists, since the first and second must be completely distinguished from one another.

The praised codex is followed by another poem of Paulinus without a title, which I have also brought forth, as it is filled with profound learning.

After this appears the life of Saint Martin with the following title:

> Here begins the work of Paulinus of Périgueux, in verses, on the Life of Saint Martin the Bishop.

Thus the opinions of Bellarmine, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Sirmond, in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris; Labbe, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; and others are confirmed. They make the author of these poems Paulinus of Périgueux—*Petricorius* or *Petricordius*—who flourished thirty or forty years after the death of our Paulinus.

Ughellus, in volume VI of *Italia Sacra*, wrote carefully that the author of those poems was Saint Paulinus the Younger, likewise bishop of Nola. For the latter was raised to that episcopate at least around the year 520 after Christ, whereas Petricordius, as I have said, certainly wrote around the year 460.

For the rest, I cannot sufficiently wonder why some have partly neglected these *Natales* and others have protected them with the greatest zeal. Bede, Notker, Ado, Marcellus the ancient presbyter, Gregory of Tours himself, and others cited in the *Acts of the Saints* under 14 January, illustrated the life and miracles of Saint Felix. Yet none of them seems hitherto to have seen more than the ten *Natales* that had been published, since they display only the miracles praised in those poems. They would surely have related others as well if the remaining three or four had been available to them.

Hardly one Dungalus has been found who made any mention of these poems.

We therefore hope that learned men will receive our labor all the more willingly, since we have at last wrested from the voracity of time a treasure so long taken from us and almost abandoned to despair.

I judged that all these matters should be clarified, as far as possible, through learned notes and discussions: first, lest these poems should be thought in any respect inferior to Paulinus’ remaining works, which have until now appeared adorned by the labor of scholars; and second, so that some satisfaction might be rendered by me to the merits of his poetry.

To say nothing of what may be brought forward from these poems against the innovators who reject the veneration of relics and saints, nowhere will one find greater learning than in at least these three poems. Here pagan superstition is explained; here the monuments of the saints are interpreted; and Paulinus’ deeds, gathered together as though into a single compendium, will furnish writers with an illustrious sequence of learning.

As for the years in which these *Natales* were recited, I think we should accept the opinion proposed by Chiffletius in part 2, chapter 9 of *Paulinus Illustrated*: namely, that the first belongs to the year 394 after Christ, when Paulinus had not yet moved to Nola; the second falls in the year 395, when the saint had already returned to Nola; the third in the year 396; and so with the rest, since Paulinus sang a *Natalis* every year.

This is proved above all by *Natalis* XIII. There the splendid victory over the Goths and the slaying of Rhadagaissus are mentioned. These events occurred in the year 405, when Stilicho II and Anthemius were consuls, as Prosper testifies in his *Chronicle*. Consequently, *Natalis* XIII refers to the following year, 406.

If, then, the *Natalis* is assigned to each successive year, after the preceding years have elapsed, one will find that the first falls in the year 394; similarly, the eleventh must be assigned to 404 and the twelfth to 405.

I wish to warn readers of only one thing: I deliberately transcribed these verses together with the errors of the copyists. For the most learned men often complain that faith has not been preserved toward manuscripts, and that genuine readings are usually corrupted by the opinion or audacity of emendators.

For this reason I have left certain passages to be corrected by the ingenuity of others, while in some places I have also applied my hand in the notes.

*(Thus far Muratorius. Let us now hear Johann Aloysius Mingarellius, from whose edition we have preferred to transcribe the three *Natales* in question. EDIT.)*

## Preface to Paulinus’ Natal Poems

[Col. 0503]

### 1

Long ago Ludovico Antonio Muratori, a man distinguished both for talent and for learning, published from a codex of the Ambrosian Library three poems of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, concerning Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0503] Volume I of the *Anecdota*, published at Milan in 1697.]. Previously, only certain fragments of them had existed in Dungalus’ book, which he wrote against Claudius of Turin concerning the veneration of sacred images [Note: [Col. 0504] This book is found in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* and is entitled *Responses against the Opinions of Claudius*.]. For this reason Muratori earned the greatest gratitude among men of letters and was adorned with great praise by Casimirus Oudinus and others.

But when he came upon a copy that was everywhere full of errors and in some places mutilated and incomplete, it was entirely impossible for him to publish the poems in a thoroughly corrected form. Since, therefore, I myself have had the codex before me, with whose help it was possible to remove very many errors and add several verses not previously published, I decided to publish the poems once again in this volume of our *Anecdota*.

### 2

The codex I used is on paper and was, in my opinion, written in the fourteenth century by Lippo Platesio [Note: [Col. 0505] On the first page of the codex an old hand has written: “This book belongs to … written by Lord Lippo de Plathesiis, a devout and learned man.”].

It first contains thirteen poems of Paulinus concerning Saint Felix, followed by other poems of Prudentius, whose index you will find on the final page [Note: [Col. 0505] The following was once written at the beginning of the codex:

> In this book … the following works are arranged in order. First, fourteen books composed in verse by Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor of the city of Nola. They were composed over fourteen years, one for each feast, and their subject is Saint Felix the presbyter, confessor, and patron of the city of Nola, together with his feast, which is wintry, namely on 14 January—the day of Saint Felix *in Pincis*, presbyter and martyr at Rome. Among these poems are many passages about God, the saints, and other spiritual and devotional matters.
>
> The *Apotheosis* follows, that is, Prudentius’ work on the Divinity, by that most distinguished poet. Also Prudentius’ poem or book against the heretics called Patripassians … the same author’s book against the Unionites … the same author’s poems or book against the Jews … the same author’s poem or book against the heretics and unbelievers called Homuncionites … the same author’s book on the nature of the soul … the same author’s book against the Phantastics … his *Marciogenia* … his book against the Marcionites … the book called *Psychomachia*.

Verse 506: “Teque sacris, psalmisque simul devota litante” (“and while a devout woman offers sacrifice to you with sacred rites and psalms together”). Verse 521: “amne refuso” (“with the river poured back”). Verse 555: “Per totam vigiles” (“watchful throughout the whole”). Verse 564: “irrepsit rudibus” (“it crept in among the unlearned”). Verse 581: “pictura ludere” (“to play with painting”). Verse 629: “vigilare parato” (“prepared to keep watch”).

### 11

In poem 10, our codex reads:

Verse 2: “solennia voto” (“the solemn rites by vow”). Verse 10: “Illic adjunctis” (“there, with [them] joined”). Verse 25: “lumine Tobis” (“with the light of Tobias”). Verse 32: “culmine turris” (“at the summit of the tower”). Verse 40: “A tribus egressus” (“having gone out from the three”). Verse 45: “interpositisque columnis” (“with columns interposed”). Verse 47: “Aspectare lacus” (“to look upon the lakes”). Verse 59: “spatiabile pandit” (“he opens a space for walking”). Verse 151: “quam liquerat illis” (“which he had left to them”). Verse 188: “castifico socians” (“joining in chastity”). Verse 234: “Et moribus istius aevi” (“and in the customs of this age”). Verse 276: “post corporis usum” (“after the use of the body”). Verse 282: “terra, quis in me Rubus” (“earth, what thorn is in me”). Verse 314: “Ut qui corde” (“so that he who in heart”).

### 12

These are the matters that we judged should be noted in the first ten poems of Paulinus.

As for the three final poems, which we are now publishing again, in them we have corrected more than three hundred passages. In addition, after verse seventy in the thirteenth poem we have added fifty-three verses that were missing from the codex of the Ambrosian Library used by Muratori.

We have illustrated this addition of ours with brief explanatory notes; the other poems we have not treated in the same way, because they have already been explained with great clarity by Ludovico Muratori.

You will recognize from its reading how valuable the addition itself is. But this must not be passed over here: Paulinus cites the Book of Tobit and the book entitled *Ecclesiasticus*—books that the heterodox reject as apocryphal—as sacred and divine writings. We shall demonstrate this in the notes.

13. And here I would bring this preface to an end, were it not necessary to say something about the title I have used for these poems. For they are commonly entitled *Natalis I*, *Natalis II*, and so on. Muratorius certainly entitled them in this way. But I have never been able to approve that title, for many reasons.

First, although Paulinus wrote a poem every year for the day of Saint Felix’s death—or, to speak more correctly with the Church, for his *natalis*—I do not understand how the poems themselves can be called *Natales*. Dungalus, in the book I mentioned, frequently brings forward these very poems of Paulinus, yet nowhere calls them *Natales*, but always either *books* or *poems*. The scribe of our manuscript initially entitled them as follows: “Poem on the Life of Saint Felix, of the first year; poem of the second year,” and so forth. Later, however, as though he had become dissatisfied with this title, he wrote: “Book I, Book II,” and so forth. The name *Natalis* nowhere occurs in his writing.

But why say more? Paulinus himself, although he mentions these poems in many places, does not call them *Natales* even once, but rather *little books* or *natalitial little books*. Thus, in poem 12, verse 306, he sings:

> But what has passed, preserved always in the present,  
> shall be sung before our little books.

And in poem 13, verse 52:

> And because those things were said by me  
> more fully in earlier little books.

And verse 55:

> This little book I shall weave with a grateful mind.

And verse 104:

> Let the heroic head be, and the foundation, of the little book.

Indeed, in his letter 28 to Severus he spoke in the same way:

> “You therefore have from me,” he says, “two little books: one in natalitial verse, concerning my solemn song to my Lord of the House—thus Paulinus calls Saint Felix, as though he were the Lord of the shrine—to whom I pay each day with body and spirit, and each year with my tongue, on the day of his consecration, the sweetest tribute of voluntary service,” and so forth.

I thought it right to mention these few matters to you, most courteous reader, before you come to Paulinus’s poems themselves. For what need was there for me to say more, since Muratorius has written so much about them with the greatest learning? Farewell.

## POEM XIX. POEM XI

**On Saint Felix**

[Note: In the manuscript of the library of Saint Salvator at Bologna—which I shall call our manuscript—the first poem of Paulinus on Saint Felix is entitled: “The poem of the blessed Meropius Paulinus, bishop of Nola, on the life of Saint Felix, of the first year. Book I.” This eleventh poem, however, is entitled: “Here begins Book XI.”]

[Col. 0509A]

**447–448.** If the stars could be lacking to the sky, if grasses to the earth,

if honey to the honeycombs, water to the springs, milk to the rich udders,

so could praise of the righteous cease from human tongues,

in whom are found both the virtue of life and the glory of death:

[Note: Dungalus cites the first six verses of this poem in his *Responses against the Opinions of Claudius of Turin*. These earlier poems were also quoted by the deacon Dungalus, who in the ninth century of Christ wrote a book *On the Cult of Images* against Claudius of Turin and dedicated it to the emperors Louis and Lothair. His following most distinguished words ought certainly to be placed before the eyes of all:

“Paulinus,” he says, “a bishop, a most learned and holy man, as many have testified concerning him, published a noble book divided into fifteen poems, in honor and praise of Saint Felix the martyr. In it he described how many miracles and acts of power, through his merits and intercessions, divine mercy grants daily to take place at his tomb, and especially on his annual feast day. It cannot easily be excerpted or culled by anyone, because everything in it consists of flowers, spices, roses, sweet-smelling lilies, and honeyed words.”

I have already observed in the preface that Dungalus was mistaken when he asserted that Paulinus composed fifteen *Natales*, whereas he actually wrote only fourteen. Dungalus himself thoughtfully divided one of them into two. — MURATORIUS.]

[5] God himself, for whom they were willing to bargain away their lives,

and by dying to seal the faithful devotion of the peoples,

and to purchase a sacred kingdom with precious blood—

blood by which, when the martyrs poured it over the whole world,

they became heavenly seed for countless nations.

[Note: In Muratorius’s manuscript *fuere* is read; the difference is of little consequence.]

[10] Of these, Felix, a confessor from the number of the noble,

was given to this city, and his name shone far and wide throughout the world.

[Note: Dungalus cites this verse and those that follow up to verse 19.]

[Col. 0509B]

Nola, made the home of his buried body, rejoices as though in a star that is her own.

For every martyr, wherever he lies committed to the earth,

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript reads *jacet* (“lies”), while ours reads *manet* (“remains”); Dungalus also read as in our manuscript.]

[15] is at once the star of the place and the healing-power of those who worship him.

[Note: I have followed the reading of our manuscript. Muratorius’s manuscript reads *locis* (“of the places”); Dungalus reads as does our manuscript.]

[Col. 0510A]

For the Creator, taking pity on the world darkened by ancient gloom

and on languishing souls throughout the earth,

arranged the sacred monuments of the righteous across the lands,

so that he might scatter the lights of the stars throughout the night-sky.

[20] And although one faith, equal grace, and kindred virtue

remain among all the martyrs, nevertheless we see

different forms of their works appearing in them all.

Here, in silent tombs,

[Note: Our manuscript has *tacitum* (“silent,” neuter); Muratorius’s reading seems preferable.]

we cultivate, mindful, a lofty merit; elsewhere we marvel

at conspicuous powers, signs that cry aloud.

[25] Wherever, I believe, harsher impiety holds greater sway,

there illness demands greater aid;

or wherever error, still blinder, drags on

the deep night of unbelief, and faith struggles sickly

within a wavering people, there it is altogether fitting

[30] that greater lights be kindled, that God illuminating the darkness of the world

may destroy it, and that minds, their astonished eyes opened,

may direct their fearful gaze toward the rays

of divine truth itself, release them from foul darkness,

and anoint them with the healing eye-salve of Christ.

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript has *medentes* (“healing”); but *medentis* (“of the healer”), as in our manuscript, must be read. The meter itself also requires this.]

[Col. 0511A]

[35] This healing is wrought through the apostolic arts for curing the senses, upon a holy whetstone, because Christ’s yoke is gentle and his burden light for those now turned toward Christ in pure light and with hearts suffused with evangelical nourishment.

By this the mists are well cleansed, those which the loves

[40] of the deceiving world draw across the inner sight;

those loves which, without a helmsman, drive wandering senses

around the great void, and blunt them, seized by heavy darkness,

with soft enticements, so that they may break the strength of life

and pursue wandering processions through slippery pleasures.

[Note: This is how it is written in our manuscript. Muratorius’s manuscript reads *cavas*, that is, “empty,” as Muratorius correctly explains in the following note:

“*Cavas*, that is, ‘empty.’ Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> And unless her learned companion should remind  
> the insubstantial lives, without bodies, to flit  
> beneath the hollow semblance of their forms,  
> she would rush upon them and vainly strike the shadows with her sword.

And elsewhere:

> Black night flies around with hollow shadow.”]

[45] **449–450.** Therefore the Lord, healer of every kind of illness,

wishing to turn diseases away from us,

brought forth holy physicians for mortal sufferers

among various peoples, with saving compassion.

And, so that divine power might display its healing more clearly,

he placed them in the more important cities;

and although some small towns retain certain martyrs,

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript and Dungalus read *martyres*; our manuscript reads *martyras*.]

God brought the eminent ones themselves within broad walls,

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript originally read *ad proceres*. Muratorius rightly suspected that *at proceres* should be read; this is found both in our manuscript and in Dungalus.]

and distributed a few of them among various regions,

[Col. 0512A]

yet before their death he made them teachers throughout the whole world.

Therefore he fixed Peter and Paul in the city of Rome,

[Note: Saint Leo, in his sermon on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, aptly says: “The most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, is sent to the citadel of Roman power, so that the light of truth, which was revealed for the salvation of all nations, might spread more effectively from that very head throughout the body of the world. See the rest.” — MURATORIUS.]

[55] because the head of the world needed chief physicians,

sick with many vices and blind with darkness.

But God is more powerful to restore our salvation

than Satan is still to hold those captured by his deceit:

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript reads: “rather than Satan still hold those captured,” and so forth.]

[Note: I have followed the reading of Muratorius’s manuscript. Ours has *teneri* (“to be held”).]

the darkness of the world grows thin, and now, through nearly all places,

[60] piety has prevailed, and life has conquered death.

As faith increases, defeated error falls away,

and, with scarcely anyone now left to crime and death,

all Rome is reckoned under the holy name of Christ,

[Note: Paulinus’s words should not be taken so strictly that we suppose no pagans then remained in Rome. The dominion of superstition did not fall at a single stroke; rather, through the favor of time, what could not immediately be achieved by the proofs of the faith or the examples of the emperors after Constantine was eventually accomplished. Certainly consuls, senators, and other magistrates were still chosen from among the pagans almost down to this very period, that is, to the year of Christ 404. Indeed, Paulinus himself, while not yet freed from pagan religion, had proceeded to the consulship. Several laws issued during these same years by the most devout emperors, by which paganism was being struck down, sufficiently indicate that, to use Tacitus’s phrase, its “great day” had not yet been imposed upon it. On this matter see the Theodosian Code, title “On Pagans,” and so forth. Moreover, in the year 410—only six years ago—Rome was destroyed by the barbarian invasion under Alaric, giving Saint Augustine the occasion to write his distinguished books *On the City of God*, in order to defend the Christian faith against pagan insults. The great doctor says in Book I, chapter 1:

“Are not even those Romans hostile to the name of Christ, whom the barbarians spared on account of Christ? The places of the martyrs and the basilicas of the apostles bear witness to this; during the very devastation of the City they received within themselves those who fled there, both their own people and strangers”—that is, pagans living in Rome.

— MURATORIUS.]

mocking the fictions of Numa and the prophecies of the Sibyl.

[65] And when the devout crowd returns “Amen”

to the priests throughout the numerous folds of the reigning God,

[Note: I have corrected the reading from our manuscript. Muratorius reads *ferat* (“may it bear”) instead of *refert* (“returns”). It became customary in the primitive Church for the people, after the sacred prayers of the bishop, to respond with one voice, “Amen.” Saint Justin Martyr offers an excellent passage on this subject in the *Second Apology for the Christians*—which should really be called the first:

“When he”—that is, the bishop—“has finished the prayers and the eucharist, all the people present acclaim with joyful approval, saying, ‘Amen.’”

The ancient teacher Tertullian likewise repeats this below. In *On the Spectacles*, chapter 25, he says to a Christian: “With the mouth with which you have uttered ‘Amen’ to the Holy One, do you wish to give testimony to a gladiator?” Paulinus himself, speaking of God in the *Morning Prayer*, says:

> Whom the people celebrate in measured song,  
> and with the answering voices of “Amen” strike the air.

See also Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book II, chapter 5. — MURATORIUS.]

and the shout of praise to the eternal Lord strikes the heavens,

the Capitol trembles, holy, shaken at its summit.

[Note: Or should we read *fulmine*, “by lightning”—that is, by the thunderous force of devout voices? — MURATORIUS.]

[Col. 0512B]

In their empty temples, the idols tremble,

their decaying shrines struck by devout voices

[Note: Saint Jerome has nearly the same words in the preface to Book II of his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians: “The faith of the Roman people is praised. Where else do people rush to the churches and the tombs of the martyrs with such zeal and such numbers? Where else does ‘Amen’ resound like heavenly thunder, and the empty temples of idols shake?” — MURATORIUS.]

[70] and driven by the name of Christ.

[Col. 0513A]

The demons flee in terror from the abandoned sanctuaries.

The livid serpent hisses in vain with bloody mouth,

mourning human salvation with his starving throat.

And, at the same time, lamenting that he has now been deprived

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript had *quem* (“whom”); ours has *jam* (“now”); Muratorius had suspected that the latter should be read.]

[75] of the blood of animals, the plunderer circles the dry altars in vain.

Thus God, granting his holy gifts to the remaining lands as well,

scattered his mighty members throughout the cities of the world.

Thus he gave Andrew to Patrae,

[Note: Patrae is a city of Achaea. Andrew is said to have completed his martyrdom there in his Acts, in Surius, volume VI. Jerome, in Letter 148 to Marcella, says: “Jesus was present everywhere: with Thomas in India, with Peter in Rome, with Paul in Illyricum, with Titus in Crete, with Andrew in Achaea.” See Baronius in the *Roman Martyrology*, and Florentinus in Jerome’s *Martyrology*. — MURATORIUS.]

and John to Ephesus,

[Note: A thousand records testify that John died at Ephesus. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.35, reports the letter of Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, in which the same is asserted. See Baronius in the *Martyrology* under 27 December. Hence the celebrated Church of Ephesus, counted among the apostolic churches, once claimed a primate or exarch subject to no patriarch. Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 36, says: “Are you near Achaea? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi and Thessalonica. If you can travel to Asia, you have Ephesus.” To these Venantius Fortunatus may fittingly be added, singing in Book VIII, poem 4:

> Noble Achaea sends forth its own Andrew;  
> venerable Ephesus, distinguished by its merits,  
> sends John.

— MURATORIUS.]

[Col. 0514A]

so that together they might care for Europe and Asia,

[80] and scatter the heavy darkness through such great lights.

**451–452.** Parthia embraces Matthew,

[Note: Marcus Antonius Columna, in his *Life and Deeds of Saint Matthew*, says: “Historians certainly agree on this: that the blessed Apostle was crowned with martyrdom in the royal city of Ethiopia, and that his sacred body long remained there.” I could accept this as the place of his martyrdom, since the Metaphrast supports it, together with Venantius Fortunatus in Book V, poem 1:

> Matthew by his speech tempers Ethiopian vapors,  
> and pours living streams over the scorched land.

But Columna is mistaken about the place of burial. For how could our Paulinus have said that Parthia contained Matthew’s tomb if it had been established in Ethiopia? The Parthians and Ethiopians are too different for their names to be confused. Let us hear Venantius again, in Book VIII, poem 4:

> From there India sends Bartholomew in triumph,  
> and lofty Naddaver sends the distinguished man Matthew.

He suggests the same thing in the following poem:

> Those whom Patrae, Ephesus, and Naddaver’s citadel hold.

To reconcile such eminent men, I would suppose that Naddaver was a city situated in Parthia, to which Saint Matthew’s bones were transferred after his death. Why should we accept Abdias, universally judged an apocryphal writer, who places this city in the Ethiopian region? If such authorities are to be followed, I would also set aside Dorotheus as a pseudonymous writer, together with the author who, in his book *On the Twelve Apostles*, says that Matthew died at Hierapolis of Parthia—or at Hierapolis of Syria, as William Cave reports in a certain fragment in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. But Paulinus is openly supported by an Anonymous author quoted by Oecumenius, who says: “Matthew the Evangelist handed down the Gospel written in the Hebrew language. He fell asleep in the city of Hiera in Parthia, and was buried there.” Hippolytus, in his *Catalogue of the Twelve Apostles*, writes: “Matthew fell asleep at Hierea, a city of the Parthians.” Freculphus, Book II, chapter 46, marks Matthew’s tomb in this way: “He first preached the Gospel in Judaea, then preached in Macedonia; he rests in the mountains of the Parthians.” C. V. Bollandus, under 24 February, reports from a thousand-year-old manuscript a notice concerning the burial places of the holy apostles; there it says: “The feast of Saint Matthew the apostle, who suffered in Persia.” Jerome’s *Martyrology*, edited by Florentinus, has: “In Persia, the feast of Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist.” Another very ancient catalogue in Florentinus, p. 159, likewise attests that Matthew suffered in Persia. Parthia certainly bordered Persia; indeed, as Pliny says in Book VI, chapter 25, “the name of Persia was long ago transferred to the Parthians.” And Parthia included Persia, as my learned friend C. V. Baudrand also noted in his geographical dictionary. Thus another argument supports my opinion when, with Paulinus, I affirm that Matthew was buried in Parthia. It is also clear that the holy apostle preached among the Parthians, so it is reasonable to believe that, after his death, disciples whom he had left there could have honored him and carried his bones to the city of Naddaver.

— MURATORIUS.]

India, Thomas,

[Note: Among other authorities, Saint Jerome testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that this apostle died there; he also assigns the city of Calamina as the place of his martyrdom. His body was later transferred to Edessa, as may be seen in Baronius’s *Martyrology* under 3 July. The notice cited by Bollandus also asserts this: “The feast of Saint Thomas the apostle in India, and the translation of his body to Edessa.” — MURATORIUS.]

Lebbaeus to Libya,

[Note: Lebbaeus is the same as Thaddaeus, who is also called Judas by another name. Saint Jerome, on Matthew chapter 10, says: “Ecclesiastical history records that the apostle Thaddaeus was sent to Abgar, king of the Edessenes, in Chosidena”—rather, Osrhoene should be read—“and that he is called Judas of James by the evangelist Luke and elsewhere Lebbaeus, which means ‘little heart’; and he must be believed to have had three names.” But the other writers disagree with Paulinus about the place where his sacred body is preserved. Venantius Fortunatus, Book VIII, poem 4:

> From there joyful Persia sends Simon and Judas,  
> twin lights, upward from her opened breast.

Dorotheus of Tyre, in his book *On the Twelve Apostles*, says: “Judas of James, who is also Thaddaeus and Lebbaeus, preached the Gospel of the Lord to the Edessenes and throughout Mesopotamia. Under Abgar, king of Edessa, he was killed at Berytus and buried with honor.” Florentinus, in his notes on Jerome’s *Martyrology*, produces certain very ancient martyrologies in which Thaddaeus is said to have been killed in Persia or in the Persian city of Suanis. I would understand these as referring to the place of his death, and Paulinus as referring to the place of his tomb. — MURATORIUS.]

the Phrygians received Philip,

[Note: We also learn from Venantius Fortunatus that Philip was buried at Hierapolis in Phrygia:

> Blessed Hierapolis, fulfilling her desires,  
> brought forth Philip for her people.

Add Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “The apostle Philip preached the Gospel of the Lord Jesus in Phrygia. He was buried honorably at Hierapolis with his daughters.” See Baronius’s *Martyrology* under 1 May. — MURATORIUS.]

Crete took Titus,

[Note: Jerome, the other writers, and the Menologia teach that Titus was bishop of Crete and was also buried there; there is no need to rehearse the same matter again. — MURATORIUS.]

and Boeotia the physician Luke.

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript reads *Boethia*; ours reads *Boetia*. Dungalus corruptly read this verse as follows: “Crete took Titus for itself, Antioch, and Ostia, Luke.” Until now we had taken the corrupt reading from Dungalus, since it occurs in his manuscripts, especially in the oldest one in our library: “Crete took Titus for itself, and Antioch, and Ostia, Luke.” Rosweidus says in his notes on this passage: “It is strange that Paulinus should assert that Luke’s relics are preserved at Antioch and Ostia, when the Roman Martyrology on 9 May says that his relics were transferred from Achaea to Constantinople. Unless he means only that Antioch and Ostia had Luke as an excellent disseminator of the Gospel, perhaps they obtained some of his relics from elsewhere.”

But we owe the restoration of this passage to our manuscript. Luke was in fact buried in Boeotia, or Achaea. Gaudentius of Brescia, in a sermon delivered at the dedication of a church, reports that John was buried at Sebaste in the province of Palestine, Thomas among the Indians, and Andrew and Luke at Patrae, a city of Achaea. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, later mentions the transfer of Luke’s relics, together with the bones of the apostle Andrew, from Achaea to Constantinople. Other evidence may be added. Thus one may convict the pseudo-Dorotheus of error when he imagines that Luke died and was buried at Ephesus.

In another place Paulinus also applies the title “physician” to Luke, namely in *Natalis* 9:

> Here Luke is physician first by his art, then by his speech:  
> Luke is twice a physician.

— MURATORIUS.]

[Col. 0515A]

Mark, bestowed upon you, Alexandria,

[Note: This is how it is read in our manuscript; Muratorius’s manuscript has *Alexandria*. Mark founded the Alexandrian Church after being sent there by Saint Peter, and blessed it both with his blood and with his tomb. Jerome and all the martyrologies teach this. — MURATORIUS.]

so that, when the ox had been driven away,

[Note: The worship of Apis was once famous among the Egyptians; they represented him in the form of an ox. Each year a long series of ceremonies was performed in his honor. Solinus, chapter 32, says: “Among all the things Egypt possesses that deserve mention, they especially marvel at the ox. They call it Apis. They worship it as a god, distinguished by a white mark naturally formed on its side, which resembles the shape of the horned moon,” and so forth. I could compose a lengthy account of these Egyptian superstitions, but it is preferable to refer the reader to the material collected by Vossius in his books *On Pagan Theology*, Salmasius in his *Exercises*, Pliny in his commentary on the passage of Solinus cited above, Diodorus Siculus, Book I, Eusebius of Caesarea, *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 11, Herodotus, and others. I shall also make further observations on these matters in the fourth poem of Paulinus. — MURATORIUS.]

[85] **453–454.** Egypt, mad in Apis, would no longer worship cattle, nor would Crete worship Jupiter,

her fellow citizen, wrongly buried there,

[Note: When the Gospel was brought by Titus into a Cretan city, Jupiter was driven from it. If this passage is referred to the Egyptians, it concerns Jupiter Ammon, whom they honored with the highest reverence. Plutarch, in *On Isis and Osiris*, says that Ammon is “the distinctive name of Zeus among the Egyptians”; that is, the proper Egyptian name for Jupiter. Herodotus, in Book II, says: “For the Egyptians call Ammon Zeus”—“the Egyptians call Ammon Jupiter.” — MURATORIUS.]

[Note: The pagans themselves acknowledge that Jupiter was king of Crete, was buried there, and was raised to divine status by the unhappy error of the gentiles. Among them Lucian, in *On Sacrifice*, says:

> The Cretans, for their part, say that Zeus not only was born and raised among them, but also show his tomb.

Callimachus likewise says in his hymn to Jupiter:

> Cretans are always liars, for they built  
> your tomb, O lord; but you did not die—  
> you are eternal.

See Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*; Demetrius of Scepsis in the scholia on Apollonius, Book III; and the other mythographers. — MURATORIUS.]

Nor would the Phrygians celebrate the Cybelean rites with emasculated Galli,

[Note: The Cybelean days were festivals of Cybele, or the great Berecynthian Mother of the Gods. Her priests, called Galli, were compelled to deprive themselves of their male organs in memory of Attis. Our Paulinus says in poem 4:

> Here too he has a mother captured by love of a shepherd,  
> but a better Shepherd, who wished to preserve a chaste purity,  
> and scorned the goddess whose savage hand  
> cut off the virile members, and so forth.

“Even now the eunuch priests mourn their shameful mysteries,” and so forth.

Lucan also mentions the Galli in Book I:

> And the Galli, whirling their hair,  
> sang bloody, mournful songs to the peoples.

Herodian, Book I, says: “The Phrygians once celebrated orgies beside the river Gallus, from which the priests of Cybele are also called Galli.” See Panvinius, Book II of *A Description of the City of Rome*, and what I reported concerning the fourth poem. I have also said more about the Galli and Archigalli in a certain inscription of Julian the jurist, which I shall publish in a new collection of inscriptions. — MURATORIUS.]

soothing their impure mother with a foul wound,

[Col. 0516A]

until at last Ida would leaf out upon chaste mountains,

[Note: Cybele was especially worshiped by the Phrygians on Mount Ida, because there she had carried on her abominable love-affair with Attis. Virgil refers to this in Book X of the *Aeneid*:

> The nurturing Idaean mother of the gods.

Cybele is also thought to have received her name from Cybelus, a mountain of Phrygia. — MURATORIUS.]

[90] bringing back pines untouched, their crowns secure;

[Note: “The pine is under the protection of the Mother of the Gods,” says Servius on Virgil’s Book IX, where Cybele addresses Jupiter:

> A pine-wood, beloved by me through many years,  
> was a grove on the highest citadel.

Arnobius likewise says in Book V *Against the Gentiles*: “What is the meaning of that pine which, on fixed days, you always bring into the shrine of the Mother of the Gods?” And near the end of the same book: “That pine which is solemnly carried into the sacred rite of the Mother—is it not an image of the tree beneath which Attis, having cut off his generative organs, took his own life? And is it not the tree which they say the goddess consecrated as a consolation for her grief?” On these matters see much in the works of the distinguished men, especially Benedict Bacchini, dearer to me than all others, in his special dissertation *On Sistra*. — MURATORIUS.]

Nor would Greece any longer consult its many silent Delphoi,

[Note: I corrected the text from our manuscript, which has *mutos*. Muratorius’s manuscript reads *multos*, but Muratorius rightly suspected that *mutos* should be read.

“We know only one Delphi, famous for the oracle of Apollo. What, then, is meant by the mention of many here? Paulinus seems to have spoken poetically at this point, so that by ‘Delphoi’ he might mean the oracles, or the temples especially dedicated to Phoebus. This is characteristic of poets. We also know that several sanctuaries were dedicated to Apollo Pythius, and that in ancient times Delphi was called Pytho. Pausanias, in his account of Phocis, says: ‘At a later time the inhabitants called the city not only Delphi but also Pytho.’ Therefore it would not be unreasonable to understand by ‘many Delphoi’ here the many temples of Apollo Pythius. Orosius, Book I, Cedrenus, and Nicephorus Callistus, Book I, chapter 17, report that the Delphic demon fell silent when Christ was born. They say that, when asked the reason for his silence, he replied:

> A Hebrew child, God himself, who governs the gods,  
> commands me to yield my seat and return sadly beneath Orcus.

I would therefore suppose that the text contains an error, and that *mutos* should be restored in place of *multos*. — MURATORIUS.]

but, scorning her own Olympus, would tread higher upon Sion,

where Christ, the hill’s fosterling, raises his gentle yoke from a lofty summit.

[Col. 0517A]

[Note: That is, “sharpens” or “raises to a point.” Silius Italicus, Book V:

> And gradually sharpening through the middle of the belly,  
> he joins the compressed peaks.

Caesar also uses *fastigatus* of a gently sloping hill in his *Commentaries*. — MURATORIUS.]

[95] Diana too fled Ephesus as John drove her out,

accompanied by her own brother, whom Paul,

commanding in the name of Christ after Python had been driven out, banished.

[Note: Acts XVI contains the following: “As we were going to prayer, a certain girl who had a spirit of Python met us. She brought her masters much profit by divination,” and so forth. “But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit: ‘I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her’; and it came out at that hour.” Apollo Pythius was famous for his oracles; therefore those possessed by an evil spirit and bursting into prophetic utterance were said to have the Pythian spirit within them. When Paul expelled it from the woman, Paulinus rightly recalls that Apollo was driven away. The title “Pythian” was derived either from Python, who was killed, or from *πυθέσθαι*, “to inquire,” and so Phoebus acquired it from consulting the oracle. — MURATORIUS.]

Satan fled from Egypt,
