[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript reads: “Egypt too fled”; ours: “fled from Egypt.” Both readings are plausible.

The number of Egyptian gods was infinite. Diodorus Siculus gives a long list of them in Book I of his *Library*; Juvenal, Satire 5, says:

> Who does not know, Volusius Bithynicus, what monsters  
> mad Egypt worships? One part adores the crocodile;  
> another fears the ibis stuffed with snakes;  
> the golden image of the sacred ape shines.

Tertullian, chapter 34 of the *Apology*, says: “Egypt is permitted the power of such vain superstition, consecrating birds and beasts, and condemning to death anyone who kills one of these so-called gods.” See Lucian, *On Images*; Clement of Alexandria, Book III of the *Paedagogue*, chapter 2; Minucius Felix, in the *Dialogue*; and especially Constantine Manasses in his *Annals*, where he says that the Egyptians worshiped:

> Cats and monkeys,  
> ibises and goats, oxen, dogs, and crocodiles,  
> and other abominations arising from their madness.

Hence Saint Jerome, Book IV of his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 11, said that the Egyptian people were so devoted to idolatry and the most foolish superstition that they consecrated hawks, owls, dogs, goats, and asses under the divine name, and so forth. — MURATORIUS.]

where he had taken a thousand forms,

[Note: This is how it is written in our manuscript; Muratorius’s manuscript has *sub mille figuris* (“under a thousand forms”), which is a corrupt reading.]

[100] and had fitted a thousand names to various monsters,

so that he might fashion holy Joseph into Serapis,

hiding the venerable name beneath a death-dealing name.

[Note: I corrected the text from our manuscript, which has *abscondens* (“hiding”). Muratorius’s manuscript reads *abscindens* (“cutting off”).]

Yet the very form of the image itself taught the truth,
[Col. 0518A] Since a modius remains upon his head, because once, when grain had been gathered before the famine at the Lord’s inspiration, he fed innumerable peoples of Egypt from abundance and satisfied barren years with rich plenty.

[Note: Serapis was represented with a modius placed upon his head. This image may be found in Cartarius, *De imaginibus deorum*, and in Fulvius Ursinus, on Scipio’s coin. Rufinus, cited above, says in the same place: “After this, the head is torn from the neck and dragged away with the modius pressed down.” And below: “Others think him Jupiter, upon whose head a modius has been placed.” Suidas, under the word “Serapis,” likewise says: “Some said that he was the Nile, because he had a modius upon his head.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.20, mentions this false god, but places a basket rather than a modius upon his head. The Egyptian temple of Serapis stood until the time of Theodosius. It was then destroyed and lay in ruins, as the historians Rufinus, Socrates, and others relate. Casalius, *De profanis ritibus* 13, displays an image of Serapis; but since its head lacks a modius, I am uncertain whether it is an image of that deity. Certainly the learned Patinus presents several figures of Serapis in *Numismata imperatorum*, p. 153, under Titus and Hadrian, and all of them can be seen with the modius. Plutarch also touches on this in his treatise *On Isis and Osiris*. MURATORIUS.]

But lest the holy man should thereafter be worshiped with profane honor, the hidden mind of God sharpened the devout hearts of the people with its goads, and, after Serapis had been overthrown

[Note: I think this should be read as in our manuscript. Muratorius’s manuscript has *averso* (“turned aside”).]

and shattered,

[Note: This alludes to an event completed in his own age; for the statue of Serapis was overthrown under the Emperor Theodosius the Great. MURATORIUS.]

it closed the worship of the wicked demon.

Not Isis, wandering through the Pelusian groves, sought Osiris,

[Note: Osiris was killed by Typhon and torn to pieces. Isis, having avenged her murdered husband with mourning and wailing, sought his remains and, when she found them, restored them to the tomb. Hence the Egyptians repeated this profane rite every year. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX:

“And royal splendor, with which were the barking Anubis,  
holy Bubastis, Apis of varied colors,  
and the sistra; nor was Osiris ever sought by his own people.”

Minucius, in the *Octavius*: “Consider finally the sacred rites themselves and the mysteries themselves: you will find mournful endings, fates, funerals, lamentations, and the wailing of miserable gods. Isis mourns and beats her breast as she seeks her lost son with her Cynocephalus and other priests; and the wretched devotees of Isis beat their breasts and imitate the grief of the most unhappy mother. Soon, when the little one has been found, Isis rejoices, the priests exult, and the Cynocephalus, the discoverer, boasts.” But why does Minucius call him the lost son? The ancients all testify that Osiris was Isis’s husband, and especially Synesius in *On Providence* and Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris*. It is not worth dwelling on this, since the Egyptians themselves are found to disagree so greatly in the history of their rites that they do not even offer fables seasoned with wit, but produce the most ridiculous nonsense. Lactantius supports Minucius in *Divine Institutes* I.21, where he says: “The rites of Isis concern the fact that she either lost or found her son; for her priests beat their own breasts and lament; then the boy is brought forth as though he had been found, and mourning is changed into joy.” I suspect that Horus was called the lost son of Isis, and that he was sought by her at the same time, from Athanasius’s words in his *Oration against the Gentiles*: “Even now in Egypt the customary mourning for Osiris, Horus, Typhon, and the others is performed as for those who have been lost.” Certainly, even now in Egypt, a solemn lamentation is performed for Osiris, Horus, Typhon, and others as though they had been lost and destroyed. MURATORIUS.]

[Col. 0519A] She seeks him with bald-headed diviners,

[Note: Lampridius, in his life of Commodus: “He practiced the rites of Isis, so that he even shaved his head and carried Anubis.” Spartianus repeats this in his life of Pescennius Niger: “We saw him carrying the rites of Isis, to which Commodus was so devoted that he even shaved his head and carried Anubis.” Jerome, on Ezekiel XIII: “It is plainly shown that we must not be like those with shaven heads, such as the priests and worshipers of Isis and Serapis.” Ambrose likewise, in his letter to Sabinus: “They shave their heads and eyebrows whenever they undertake the rites of Isis.” Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, gives the reason for this ridiculous custom. On the word “bald,” Martial’s epigram is relevant, XII.29:

“The bald-headed linen-wearers flee, and the sistrum-bearing crowd,  
when Hermogenes stood among the worshipers.”

MURATORIUS.]

who, beating their breasts, lament another’s grief with their own sorrow.

[Note: Julius Firmicus, a most distinguished writer, summarizes the essence of the Isiac rite in *On the Error of Profane Religions* 2 with these words: “In their inner sanctuary they have a buried image of Osiris. They bewail it with annual lamentations and shave their heads, so that, disgraced by the shame of their king’s miserable fate, they may mourn it with the disfigurement of their heads; they beat their breasts, tear their arms, and reopen the scars of ancient wounds, so that through their yearly mourning the ruin of the deadly and pitiable death may be reborn in their minds.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I: “The priests of Isis, their bodies shaved bare, beat their breasts and lament as she herself had done when she lost her son.” According to Lampridius, Commodus also compelled the devotees of Isis to beat their breasts with pine cones almost to the point of death. Athenagoras, in his *Apology*: “The Egyptians beat their breasts in their sacred rites.” MURATORIUS.]

Then, their mourning put to sleep, they likewise enact

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *planctu* (“wailing”); ours has *luctu* (“mourning”).]

empty joys, pretending that they have found what they sought through the same deception by which, wandering about, they sought what they had not lost.

[115] Alas, into what abyss of folly do minds sink,

457–458 empty of the light of God! For what, I ask, is more blind than those who seek what was not lost, find what nowhere remains, and mourn for what causes no grief to those whom they lament?

[120] Choose what you will do, miserable error. What do you worship? Or what do you mourn? The things you join together do not belong together: mourning does not follow honor. You worship lamentations and believe that what you regard as divine must be mourned. If they are gods, they are not miserable;

[125] but if they are miserable, they are not gods: they are human, and miserable. Therefore pity those who have suffered mortal things, or worship the gods with joy; for this madness is plainly blind—either to worship the miserable or to mourn the blessed.

[Note: Firmicus’s words in *The Error of Profane Religions* 8 supplied Paulinus with this passage: “If those whom you worship are gods, why do you mourn them? Why do you lament them with yearly mourning? If they deserve tears and mourning, why do you heap divine honor upon them? Make one of two choices: either do not mourn them, if they are gods, or, if you think them worthy of mourning and tears, do not call them gods, lest the majesty of the divine name be polluted by your mourning and tears. Heraclitus likewise objects to the Egyptians in Epiphanius, *Ancoratus* 106: ‘Another Heraclitus says to the Egyptians: If they are gods, why do you lament them?’” MURATORIUS.]

Is Isis therefore a goddess? A woman a goddess? If she is a goddess, she has no body, and sex is absent without a body, or offspring without sex;

[Note: The poem is corrupt. With the words emended, I would read it as follows:

“Is Isis therefore a goddess? A woman a goddess? If she is a goddess, she has no body;  
and does she have sex without a body, or a body without sex?”

This would give the sense: If Isis is a goddess, how can she possess a body, since divinity is understood to reject the body? If you say that she is without a body, how can she have sex without a body? It would be preferable, however, to read *partum habet* (“she has offspring”). MURATORIUS.]

offspring is absent.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *pars habet*, a reading plainly corrupt; it should be read as in our manuscript, whose reading I have adopted.]

How, then, does she possess the Osiris whom she seeks?

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *quaerat* (“may seek”); ours has *quaerit* (“seeks”), which I follow. MURATORIUS proposes the following correction:

“How, then, does she possess him, when she seeks Osiris,  
or where she should seek him, the goddess does not know?”]

And where she should seek him, the goddess does not know. But a goddess can never be a mother or a woman. For God is one;

God is triune in power, one Father and one Son in him: from him, together with the Father, proceeds one Spirit of the Word.

[Note: Here the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Word. If you think the passage should be read otherwise, so that “of the Word” refers to the Father, then “from him” would have to refer to the Son, from whom the Spirit would proceed; and this passage could therefore also be used as an argument for the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. Saint Augustine nevertheless supports the former interpretation in *Tractate* 99 on John, where he says: “Why should we not believe that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, since he is himself also the Spirit of the Son?” But see what I have noted below. MURATORIUS.]

These three names are always one God.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *trina* (“threefold”), but this is corrupt. Muratorius therefore judged the passage should be emended: “This one God is always under three names.” The reading of our manuscript, however, should not be altered; it has: “These three are always the names of one God.”]

God is the one nature alone: what the Son is, and what the Spirit and the Father are. But the Son is born from the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father,

[Note: In the earlier centuries of the Church, when the question whether the Holy Spirit also proceeded from the Son had not yet been raised as a controversy—for, as Bellarmine says, the heretics conceded it, as was demonstrated from Basil’s *Against Eunomius* II at the Council of Florence—the Catholics were content to say that the Son proceeded from the Father. Yet they never dared to affirm that he proceeded from the Father alone; indeed, many explicitly wrote that the Spirit proceeded from the Son, as Bellarmine, *On Christ* II.24–25, Leo Allatius, and others demonstrate with many examples.

In the remaining books of my *Anecdota* I shall publish Venantius Fortunatus’s exposition of the *Quicumque* Creed, in which this too will be expressly found. In another very ancient manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, written more than a thousand years ago, I likewise found the same creed, where the familiar words occur: “The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, not created, not begotten, but proceeding.” It is therefore permissible to silence the complaints of the Greeks and of the innovators, who think that the phrase *Filioque* was added late. Nothing therefore prevents us, as I said above, from hearing some of the ancients say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father; although they are silent about the Son, their silence offers no opposition to us.

Thus we may also hear Bachiarius, a very ancient philosopher who, as far as can be gathered from Gennadius, flourished in the fifth century. In his *Apology* he mentions the Father, but not the Son. With God’s favor I shall likewise publish this *Apology* in my *Anecdota* as an exceptional secret of antiquity.

I have also observed that in the exposition of the Faith attributed among Saint Jerome’s works to the presbyter Rufinus, and likewise in the creed attributed by some to Jerome, by others to Pelagius, and in a very ancient Ambrosian manuscript to Pope Damasus, the phrase *Filioque* is not added as it appears in printed editions, but was inserted by later copyists who were excessively scrupulous. I refer the reader to the second volume of the *Anecdota*, where these matters are treated more fully.

For now it is enough to observe that this Paulinus elsewhere affirms the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, if indeed he sings in *Natalis* IX:

“the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Only-begotten and from the Father.”

That is, from the Only-begotten offspring, who is none other than the Son. I am certainly surprised that no one has noticed the testimony of so great a writer. MURATORIUS.]

Nothing here has any common or similar nature among created things.

[140] But powerful Carthage flourishes through the martyr Cyprian,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *Et* (“and”); ours has *Ast* (“but”). Dungalus, who cites this verse and the two immediately following, reads *At* (“but”).

The holiness and reputation for learning of Cyprian spread so widely throughout the world that in ancient times his solemn festival was famous not only among the Latins but also among the Greeks. Some sermons of Saint Augustine and two of Saint Maximus on him are extant. In the remaining books of my *Anecdota* I shall also publish five others by that same bishop of Turin in praise of Saint Cyprian. MURATORIUS.]

whose fountains, poured forth alike from his mouth and his blood, made fertile the sands of thirsty Libya.

Not far from there, the White Mass, assembled from martyrs, raised Utica high by a great heap of venerated slaughter;

[Note: Utica is famous among African cities for the death of Cato, as well as for its size and antiquity. Appian writes of it: “Utica, after Carthage, is the greatest city of Africa.” Under Valerian, three hundred martyrs—or, according to the various martyrologies, or Saint Augustine’s *Tractate on Psalm* XLIX, one hundred and fifty-three—were cast into a furnace and gloriously died. Hence the sacred ashes were held in the highest veneration. See Baronius, *Martyrology*, 24 September; Prudentius, hymn 13 on Saint Cyprian:

“The bodies are white; whiteness carries their minds heavenward;  
thereafter the white mass deserved to be named throughout every age.”

MURATORIUS.]

[145] raised up the martyrs with a great heap of venerated slaughter;

459–460 for one mound of blessed turf, covering many bodies, lifted its head high above the fields and testified by the lofty mountain of its tomb to their merits.

From there Africa, long already fertile for God and Christ,

[150] multiplies abundant fruits from so great a seed and gives birth to distinguished teachers in word and faith.

[Note: By God’s love, since Paulinus considered it somewhat improper to extol living saints with praises, he at least praised them by silence. Here I am certain that he alludes to Saint Augustine, who at that time was illuminating Hippo, indeed the whole world, by word and faith; perhaps also to the distinguished man Alypius, then bishop of Thagaste. Paulinus embraced all of them in close friendship. Consult the friendly letters of Augustine and Paulinus. MURATORIUS.]

[Note: Dungalus cites this verse and the five that immediately follow.]

Nor did grace shine less brightly in the lands of the West. Ambrose stands forth for Latium; Vincent for Iberia.

[Note: No one among the ancients failed to raise Ambrose, so great a teacher, with worthy praises. I shall cite Venantius Fortunatus, book VIII, poem 4, to remedy the injury done him. He commends Vitalis and the others whom beloved Ravenna buries:

“Gerunsius, Vitalis, and the others whom dear Ravenna buries,  
Ambrose, your own, Milan.”

Thus the passage had been corrupted; but from an excellent manuscript of the Ambrosian Library I restore the genuine reading: “Gerbasius, Ambrose,” and so forth. Fortunatus is referring to Saint Gervasius, whose body, discovered by Ambrose, Paulinus mentions below. MURATORIUS.]

Gaul took Martin; Aquitania took Delphinus.

[Note: I shall not pile up further material to illuminate the memory of Saint Martin. Obtain his deeds from Paulinus of Petricordia, Sulpicius Severus, and other great writers. It is enough to note that so great a man departed to heaven only a few years ago. Whether the year was 397, or rather 400 or 401, I leave to others to investigate. MURATORIUS.]

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *Aquitanica*; ours has *Aquitania*, which I approve. Dungalus nevertheless reads *Aquitanica*. Delphinus was bishop of Bordeaux and a very close friend of our Paulinus. Five letters of Paulinus to him still survive, in which our poet also testifies that he was baptized by this holy man. From this you may learn that Delphinus was no longer among the living in the year 404, since Paulinus here lists men distinguished by a reputation for holiness after their death. MURATORIUS.]

[155] And many other seeds of the saints, scattered richly throughout those same shores in tombs that have been established, illuminate the whole world with heavenly virtues and drive the ancient dragon from the entire earth—

the dragon who, under a thousand names of gods, which he himself took from dead mortals and gave to his own, holds the chief’s grim kingdom in the empty air and, hostile to us, hovers over the demons.

[160]

[Note: Something seems to be missing.]

Thus our own Nola also, through the loving mercy of Christ,

[165] deserved to be fortified by the tomb of Felix and cleansed at the same time, because it lay dying in the night, mingled with the blind ruins of the world.

[Note: Our manuscript wrongly has *iam* (“already”) for *simul* (“at the same time”); I emended it from the Muratorian manuscript. Dungalus wrongly reads: “And the world, itself dying, lay in the night.”]

Long polluted by worshipers of stone, it contained a brothel of Venus,

[Note: An old riddle, applied to a certain woman named Clodia, reads: “Coan in the dining room, Nolan in the bedroom.” By the agreement of the learned, this means nothing other than that Clodia behaved at table and among her guests with such lascivious speech and brazen words that she entirely displayed Venus, who was worshiped on the island of Cos; but in the bedroom she indulged in every kind of lust according to the custom of the Nolan women.

Indeed, Nolan lasciviousness passed into a proverb, and therefore Ausonius, in epigram 70, casts the foulest love affairs in the face of a certain Crispa with these words:

“And the fatal luxury that Nolan excess branded.”

The peoples of Campania, among whom were the Nolans, were anciently called Oscans—that is, something like “obscene”—as the words of Porphyrion, the very ancient scholiast on Horace, testify; and Festus asserts that the Oscans were especially addicted to filthy lusts. Paulinus therefore rightly says that Nola contained a brothel of Venus. MURATORIUS.]

and the madness of Bacchus.

[Note: Ambrose Leo, book III, final chapter, on Nola, elegantly describes the vintage of that region. Among other things he says: “But on the day when they make the vintage for each person, and throughout the whole vintage season, the grape-gatherers seem to be filled with the god Bacchus and utterly frenzied.” He adds: “Their shouting surpasses every human capacity and is scarcely credible to those who hear it, for it is altogether the shouting of madmen. In the very field where they gather grapes, they continually shout obscene things while harvesting, naming the most shameful parts by their own names; they cry out that they desire the most disgraceful Venuses, boast of them, threaten with them, and so forth.”

Who would have believed that such remnants of paganism could have endured so long in those regions, so that even in our own times orgies were celebrated there and Bacchus was worshiped under merely an altered name? The utmost disgrace for the people! For what, to speak with Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier* 6, should be thought among the people of the true God of something introduced by the devil’s recruits, dedicated to them from the beginning, and even then initiated into idolatry by idols—idols that are still alive? MURATORIUS.]

[170] The gods of the wretched were these, and lust joined to madness celebrated impious rites with filthy ritual.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *Numen* (“a deity”); ours has *Numina* (“deities”).]

And what place was there here for a life in which shame was nowhere found and no fear existed? For who would fear to sin here, where bloody madness and incestuous lust were the rites of religion, and crime was regarded as a deity by those who believed that any deity existed in crime?

[175]

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has “They were religions,” which is plainly corrupt. Our manuscript has “It was the religion.” But to preserve the meter I think it should read “They were the religion.”]

462–463 And there was someone regarded as more sacred than the whole company, whoever had been more deeply inflamed by the polluted rites of Venus.

And he, filled with God and happier than the rest,

[Note: Our manuscript has *at ille*; the Muratorian manuscript has *et ille*. I have followed the latter reading.]

[Note: Our manuscript has *esse* (“to be”); but from what verb does this *esse* depend, unless one supplies “was thought”? I have followed the reading of the Muratorian manuscript. MURATORIUS.]

who, driven more savagely against himself by the demon poured into him, and sacrificing to the frenzied rites with his own wounds,

[Note: Our manuscript has exactly this reading. The Muratorian manuscript has the corrupt *propriis litans furalia sacrae*.]

deserved to lose his sound mind through the wounds by which he was made mad.

[Col. 0525A] O mind worthy of blind spirits, and gods worthy of serving those who have turned away from God! Venus and the grove may be their god;

[Note: The groves, also called sacred precincts, were commonly worshiped among the ancients with great superstition. There was the grove of Aricia, where Diana’s image was hidden; the grove of Mars among the Athenians; and many other groves are mentioned throughout the sources. Ovid, *Fasti* II:

“A dark grove lay beneath the Aventine’s shade of holm oak;  
seeing it, you might say: ‘A deity is present.’”

Claudian, *Rape of Proserpina* III, mentions a venerable grove near the river Acis and adds that the place possessed a deity and religious sanctity. Propertius, book IV, elegy 10: “Withdraw from the revered grove.” I shall add Apuleius, *Apology*, p. 377, who says: “He gives no first fruits of field, vine, or flock to the rural gods who feed and clothe him; no shrine is established in his farm, no place or consecrated grove.” This is enough on a matter sufficiently well known. Pinto Ramirez has illustrated it above all others in *Sacred Spicilegium*, treatise I, chapter 6; consult him. MURATORIUS.]

let drunken folly and impious love sanctify them; let them worship what has been cut off, and let the wretched call the shame of their foul error the mysteries of the Mother.

[Note: Both among the adherents of Isis and in the Orgies this wicked rite had become established: the male genitals, which the ancients called the Phallus, were worshiped. Diodorus, *Library* I, explains all this: “They say that Osiris’s genitals were thrown by Typhon into the river, because none of his companions wished to recover them. Isis nevertheless recovered them and bestowed divine honors upon them. For she ordered their adorned image to be worshiped in temples, and ensured that it should be most highly honored in the ceremonies and sacrifices performed for that god. Therefore the Greeks too, after they had received from the Egyptians the solemnities of Bacchic rites and Orgies, honor that member in the mysteries, initiations, and sacrifices of this god under the name Phallus.” MURATORIUS.]

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *miserique*; ours has *miserumque*.]

[185] Such is the fitting faith of those who, in the nourishing light of truth, in the laws of chastity, and in the great name of Christ, possess no faith and no love; and therefore no price for their unworthy life exists in Christ’s blood.

Let the belly be their god, or the other pleasures of the flesh,

[Note: This alludes to Paul’s words in Philippians III about the enemies of the cross of Christ: “Their end is destruction, their god is the belly,” and so forth. MURATORIUS.]

for whom God himself is not God, in whom there is no glory in the cross of Christ, because the virtue of the cross does not deign to approach degenerate minds.

[195] Hence blessed Felix, like the other martyrs in different parts of the world, was a physician to the Nolans, and remains a perpetual source of healing through this power.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *beatus*; both readings are plausible.]

Nor only for the Nolans: to all by whom he is invoked he will grant salvation by this privilege, if the nourishing faith of the cross is present in the breast of the suppliant.

[Note: Our manuscript has *assit*; the reading is *adsit*.]

This faith heals and purifies the human race. Where this medicine is absent, the kingdom of every evil will linger, and it will never cease there:

Cypris will reign through adulteries, and Lyaeus through frenzies,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *Cypres*; it should be *Cypris*, as in our manuscript.]

[205] wherever the modesty of Christ and the ardor of the cross are absent.

For divine fire is present wherever the power of the cross, burning through faith within, torments hearts that are conscious of evil and brings the soul to life after its vices have been slain in the flesh.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *beatus*; both readings are plausible.]

[Note: Our manuscript has *iis* for *his*. Yet, just as *iisdem* in verse 259 has two syllables, Paulinus may have used *iis* as one syllable. See also verses 268 and 313, and poem 10, verse 331.]

Long crushed beneath these enemies and corrupted by such plagues,

[210] Nola asked for a great remedy.

[Note: Our manuscript has *pascebat*; it is plainly necessary to read *poscebat* (“asked for”).]

And therefore, as God weighed both its peril and its need, it received the physician Felix, who could conquer every ancient destruction in the dark hearts of the wretched

[Note: After *atris* (“dark”) the Muratorian manuscript has this verse: “For those who had believed that there was one deity in crime.” We have discussed this verse on the preceding page.]

463–464 and, stronger by the virtue of his lofty merit,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *altis*; ours has *alti*.]

[215] cut through the hardened tissue drawn over putrid ulcers, so that he might press out the pus gathered in swollen corruption through the ruptured cavities, and then fill the wound’s hollow with a scar formed by smooth skin.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *suffusa labe* (“steeped in corruption”); our manuscript corruptly has *suffusus a labe*.]

Thus, when Felix shone among the Nolans like a star in darkness, coming from the mouth of God and carrying in his mouth the word of healing,

[220] as the morning star, serene like the sun that is about to rise, extends a joyful beam at dawn and, newly arisen, shines before the western stars as the messenger of the day that is about to dispel the night.

[Note: Our manuscript has *praefulget in astris* (“shines before the stars”); the Muratorian manuscript has *praefulgurat astris* (“flashes brightly among the stars”).]

[225] So now, with the Gospel shining throughout the whole world and God soon to judge all lands, the banners of his coming are displayed everywhere,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *propitiante Deo* (“with God propitious”); our manuscript’s *propiante Deo* is the truer reading. See poem 12, verse 409.] and through his friends Christ flashes forth his own signs.

[Note: This is elegantly used, following the example of better writers. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII:

“Aeneas presses on against him and brandishes his spear.”

Again in the same book:

“Here and there he hates delay and brandishes his spear.”

This was indeed modeled on the Greeks, but it is used with great elegance. MURATORIUS.]

Among these he wished Felix to shine before us in this region,

[230] so that by this star he might drive away our shadows and by this means also drive the ancient demons from the city,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *Daemones*; ours has *Daemonas*.]

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *decerperet* (“tear away”), which seems corrupt; our manuscript’s *depelleret* (“drive away”) is preferable.]

so that, when such inhabitants had been driven from the human heart, God might enter as a dweller into pure minds,

[Col. 0527A] and, our chains having been loosed by the change of fortune through piety, our former bonds might now press upon our former lions,

[235] who, conquered, roar in vain with savagery against Christ’s sheep.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *vincta* (“bound”); our manuscript’s *victa* (“conquered”) is the better reading.]

This grace still remains for us: it releases us from sins when the prayer of the saints entreats it, and by the same saints, as avengers, it binds those who once used to bind us;

[240] it torments the enemies who used to torture us.

Now, like thieves caught when the light has been brought in, they are handed over to chains; now they endure the fiery whips of the righteous as they deserve, or, already thrust miserably into the prisons of hell,

[Note: Our manuscript has *inferni*; I prefer the Muratorian reading, *infernis*.]

they tremble, acknowledging that the Lord’s judgment is near—a judgment bitter only to themselves and to all those whom a savage will has turned toward Satan and a life competing with Satan has joined to him.

There are the human companions of wickedness; here, the companions of punishment.

[245] Behold the day accepted by God: now the true light of salvation flashes; we see that everything has at last been set right.

Deceits have fled; Bel has fallen; error has perished. The demons who were worshiped throughout the temples as though they were gods are now tortured helplessly throughout God’s temples. And those who dared to assume divine honors

[255] are now punished and subdued by the human race.

[Note: The most devout emperors Constantine and his successors issued many laws against the pagans, which will be evident to anyone consulting the Theodosian Code, title “On Pagans,” and related sections. These laws entirely forbade the rites of the gentiles and the worship of demons, which I think our poet alludes to here. MURATORIUS.]

For these demons, whom we now see tormented in Felix’s celebrated church, crying out and being dragged about through the bodies they have seized,

[Note: Paulinus sings elsewhere of Saint Felix’s marvelous power to drive away unclean spirits, especially in *Natalis* III, where he says:

“He displays the martyr’s merit when, by his powerful right,  
he torments demons and releases bodies bound by them;  
for the deadly princes confess with mournful cries  
that Felix presses upon them with blind torments,  
and with open groans they testify to hidden crosses.”

MURATORIUS.]

are held bound within the very bodies into which they thrust themselves and in which they willingly found human punishment as their own.

[260] Now, therefore, the persons of the guilty howl amid their punishments—those who had been gods through a false divinity

[Col. 0528A] and who, before the worship of God, had surrendered living men to a pretended divinity, seeing nothing heavenly for themselves. Now, when the true faith has been revealed by the light of Christ, they cannot endure the dead bodies.

[Note: Dungalus cites this verse and the four immediately following.]

[Note: Dungalus wrongly reads the verse as: “They had been absent, and those who, by a false name, had given living men,” and so forth. I would rather write: “by a false divinity, while alive.” In his fragments Dungalus has: “by a false name, the living.” MURATORIUS.]

But to make it clearer that the demons who are now tortured before the doors or tombs of the saints are the same as those for whom the human race once sacrificed as slaves and, in its madness, offered sacred honors,

[265] the very character of their voices demonstrates it; for they often groan in such a voice that you recognize the fury familiar from their cries.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *litabat* (“sacrificed”); ours has *libabat* (“offered”).]

Thus, commonly, as though their loosened mouth had been opened more widely,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *disoluto*; this is entirely corrupt.]

they gnash their teeth, foam at the lips, and bristle with their hair.

[Col. 0528B] And when a hand seizes their hair, they are thrown upward,

[275] and, hanging by one foot, they stand upon their hair. Meanwhile, remembering the ancient sacred rites in which they used to lick the entrails of slaughtered animals or feed upon libations,
and lead lascivious dances, crowned with ivy, in processions,

[Note: In the Dionysiac rites it was customary to bind ivy around the head. Hence Seneca, *Oedipus*, act 2, in the chorus: “You restrain your head with a Tyrian mitre and bind your soft brow with fruitful ivy.” He says this of Bacchus. Statius likewise, book 1 of the *Silvae*, poem 2, line 233: “And the company crowned with ivy.” See Delrio’s commentary on Seneca at this passage, and the other mythographers. To avoid seeming tedious on a sufficiently familiar matter, I shall say no more. MURATORIUS.]

even now bearing witness that those rites were theirs,

[280] in which the drunken crowd raised frenzied uproars:

they imitate the cry “Euhoe, Bacchus,” [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *Euhoe Bacchisonum* (“Euhoe, sounding of Bacchus”) for *Euhoe Bacche sonum* (“the sound ‘Euhoe, Bacchus’”), a reading perhaps more correct.] with broken, breathless voices,

and toss their necks in a slow rotation.

But because the lifetime of a single mortal [Note: Our manuscript has *mortalis* (“of a mortal”), which seems to me the correct reading, although the Muratorian manuscript reads *mortalibus* (“for mortals”), and the final syllable of *mortalis* is short.]

could not suffice to cleanse, in a few years of bodily life,

the contagion drawn out over so long a time,

the confessor Felix, and priest, a teacher by his speech,

a martyr in title [Note: Felix of Nola’s torments and passion Paulinus had described in the preceding Natalicia; they are also set forth in the published Acts. Yet that holy man did not die in the persecution. Hence he is called a martyr only in title, as elsewhere one is called a martyr without bloodshed. In the early Church the name of martyr was also given to those who survived tortures, as is plainly gathered from Tertullian’s book *To the Martyrs*. Cyprian addressed Letter 9 to the martyrs and confessors of Jesus Christ, and in Letter 12 says: “On this matter I have written also to the clergy and to the martyrs and confessors.” Likewise, in Letter 15: “I wrote letters by which I recalled the martyrs and confessors, as far as I could by my counsel, to the Lord’s commands.” Thus some were distinguished by the appellation of martyr while still living, because they had confessed Christ most steadfastly even to the shedding of their blood. Cyprian writes on this matter in the cited Letter 30: “We should further like to learn whether martyrs become martyrs for any other reason than that, by not sacrificing, they preserve the Church’s peace even to the shedding of their blood.” MURATORIUS.], a priest deservedly and by office [Note: Here “priest” must be understood as “bishop,” since Saint Felix was called a presbyter above. In truth, this holy man had labored so greatly for Christ’s flock that he deserved the name of bishop. Thus Paulinus, *Natalia* 13, says that a bishop’s crown was added to Felix’s heavenly crown. See what I noted there at line 568. MURATORIUS.];

the Almighty Lord caused his bodily life to continue for Felix

[Col. 0529A] by a better path,

[290] extending the healing deeds of the laboring martyr,

so that, buried, he might celebrate those same powers

which, while remaining in the flesh, he exercised through Christ’s power;

and thus, though dead, he would not be absent from the city,

since the spirit placed there would be present as its healer,

while only the beloved patron’s face,

[295] withdrawn for a time, would be hidden from the desires of his loving people;

but ready medicine for the sick would always

be available for their salvation.

Thus an everlasting honor and glory surrounds holy Felix

with merits that flourish without end [Note: So the Muratorian manuscript. Our manuscript mistakenly reads *sinper* (corrupt) instead of *sine fine* (“without end”).]:

[300] and although, hidden by age-old time [Note: Dungalus also transmitted the following seven verses, which Rosweide had thought should be assigned to *Natalicia* 9; but their proper position is evident. In the old manuscript of Dungalus preserved in the Ambrosian Library, they are found explicitly cited from *Natalicia* 11. MURATORIUS.],

he lies concealed beneath the earth’s covering,

in which he was mortal,

yet, with God giving life, and surviving in his limbs,

the grace that breathes divinity into the martyr’s bones

[Col. 0529B] glorifies them among the peoples,

by the merit of the buried man who lives on:

[305] and it adores the brief throne of the great confessor [Note: It is worth observing the words with which Paulinus expresses the veneration due to the saints. Certainly he says that their tombs are adored:

“And it adores the brief throne of the great confessor.”

If one adds to this all the other testimonies of Paulinus on the subject, one will surely wonder at the complaints of innovators, who are so enraged by the same veneration of the saints that is still preserved in the Catholic Church. Paulinus and the other saints must therefore, whether they wish it or not, be counted among idolaters, since a blind people loudly declares that we are everywhere afflicted with this disease. MURATORIUS.]

continually gathered from various lands [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *confecta* (“assembled/completed”) instead of *congesta* (“gathered together”). Our manuscript’s reading is better.]

in assembled crowds.

But God, as the creator of all human beings,

granted to all the world this power to proceed from the saints:

so that blessed martyrs might now bring pious gifts

from their tombs,

[310] and, though buried, might be able to heal the living.

[467–468] Nor was this gift sufficient for the Lord:

that the martyrs should illuminate places only by their name

or by their wealth.

From those same tombs, in his mercy,

he multiplied and bestowed upon many peoples

[315] monuments of the righteous as well. [Note: [Col. 0529D] So our manuscript: *monumenta*. Muratorius reads *monimenta* (an alternative spelling of “memorials”).]

I shall relate the various causes from which,

at the beginning, this blessing arose in different lands.

Since the first faith had not spread equally

throughout the whole world,

martyrs had been absent from many regions of the earth [Note: So the Muratorian manuscript. Our manuscript reads *affuerant* (“had been present”) instead of *abfuerant* (“had been absent”); this reading does not please me.]

and therefore, I think, by a great gift

[320] this was pleasing to Christ, who now inspires the powerful,

as first occurred under Caesar Constantine,

now [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Muratorian manuscript reads *tunc* (“then”) for *nunc* (“now”), a reading not to be despised.] revealing it to his servants, so that they might transfer martyrs [Note: [Col. 0529D] Muratorius’s manuscript reads *Martyres* for *Martyras* (alternative accusative plural forms, “martyrs”).] summoned from their former seat [Note: [Col. 0529D] Our manuscript reads *priorum* (“of the former ones”) instead of *priori* (“former,” agreeing with “seat”); this reading pleases me less.] to new dwellings in the earth—as we know was done long ago by the holy bishop Ambrose [Note: He relates the celebrated discovery, accomplished in his own time, of the bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius, which befell Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Concerning it Saint Augustine, *Confessions*, book 9, chapter 7, writes: “Then you revealed by a vision to your aforesaid bishop, Ambrose, the place where the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius lay hidden, which for so many years you had kept incorrupt in the treasury of your secrecy.” Sidonius Apollinaris, book 7, letter 1, calls Ambrose “the discoverer of two martyrs.” See also Ambrose himself, Letter 14 to his sister Marcellina, and the other Paulinus in his *Life of Ambrose*. John Peter Puricelli, who has treated the affairs of Milan more accurately than anyone, discusses the matter at great length in his dissertation on Nazarius and in the *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*. Our poet recalls that Ambrose sent him the relics of these saints in Letter 12 to Severus; for, while listing the relics he himself deposited in the Fundanian basilica, he says:

“Those whom God reveals to his Ambrose after long ages—
Protasius with his companion Gervasius.”

MURATORIUS.],

who, supported by such a gift,

[Col. 0530B] after the bodies previously unknown had been discovered,

and Christ had revealed them to him [Note: Saint Augustine, in addition to Ambrose himself in Letter 14 to Marcellina, also testifies—as we have just seen—that the bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius were revealed to Saint Ambrose in a vision. Yet the famous Calvinist minister Molinaeus, book 7 against Perron, chapter 11, rejects the entire history of this discovery as a collection of fabricated fables. Surely a man deprived both of judgment and of understanding, who dared to portray such great authorities, witnesses of this most devout event, as utterly impious impostors. Saint Augustine again asserts that the event occurred by divine agency in book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 8, where, speaking of the bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius, he says: “While they lay hidden and were entirely unknown, they were revealed to Bishop Ambrose in a dream and found.” MURATORIUS.]

he transferred them to their altered sanctuary.

He confounded the queen [Note: The empress Justina was infected with the Arian error, as Paulinus, who recorded Ambrose’s life in writing, explicitly tells us. Justina hated Ambrose and greatly strengthened his enemies. But when she saw so great a miracle performed through the most holy bishop, she thereafter restrained her fury and ceased persecuting the Catholics. Augustine also relates this in book 9, chapter 7 of the *Confessions*: “Therefore you opportunely brought it forth to restrain the royal, though female, fury,” and so forth. “Hence the mind of that enemy of his—Justina, namely—although it was not inclined toward the health of belief, was nevertheless restrained from the fury of persecution.” MURATORIUS.] who was raging with a ready voice [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *luce*, “by light.” Our manuscript’s reading is more correct.]

For [Note: [Col. 0530D] Dungalus quotes this verse and those following through verse 362.] when [Note: [Col. 0530D] Both Muratorius’s manuscript and ours have *cum* (“when”). Dungalus reads *dum* (“while”).] Constantine was founding the city

[330] of his own name, and was the first of the Roman kings

to bear Christ’s name, he received divine counsel in his mind,

so that, since he was then building walls rivaling

the magnificent works of the Roman city,

[Col. 0531A] he might also follow the city of Romulus

in these endowments,

[335] and, rejoicing, fortify his walls

with apostolic bodies.

Then he brought Andrew [Note: Authorities differ remarkably in assigning the date when the bodies of Saints Andrew and Timothy were transferred to Constantinople: some assign the pious work to Constantine, others to Constantius. Yet I judge it certain that it occurred under Constantine, since Jerome expressly reports it in two places. In *Against Vigilantius* he says ironically: “The Emperor Constantine was sacrilegious, who transferred the holy relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy to Constantinople.” And in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Luke: “He was buried at Constantinople, to which city, in Constantine’s twentieth year, his bones were transferred from Achaea together with the relics of the apostle Andrew.” It is true that the same writer, in the additions to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, under the nineteenth year of Constantius, writes: “The relics of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople”; but the error should be attributed to copyists rather than Jerome’s memory. Peter Damian, Sermon 16 on Saint Mark, says: “In the twentieth year of Caesar Constantine, Luke was transferred from Achaea to Constantinople together with the sacred relics of the blessed apostle Andrew.” Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* 4.60, says: “He therefore reserved for himself here, for the fitting time of his own death, a place sharing the title of the Apostles, as his own resting place.” The supplied Latin paraphrase reads: “He therefore prepared a place for himself here by divine dispensation for the approaching day of his death, known by the name of the Apostles, for his own tomb.” Constantine therefore ordered the church of the apostles Andrew and Luke to be built, so that both the apostles’ bones and his own body might rest there. Many others, and better authorities, report this; but I refer the reader to Du Cange, *Constantinopolis Christiana* 4.5, who examined the matter more diligently than anyone. MURATORIUS.] from Achaea

and Timothy from Asia; thus, with twin towers [Note: Saints are rightly called the bulwarks and towers of kingdoms. Compare Basil the Great, Oration on the Forty Martyrs: “These are they who guard our region and, like connected towers, provide security against the assault of enemies; they do not shut themselves up in one place, but, having become guests in many places, adorn many homelands.” Theophried, abbot, Sermon 1 on Holy Relics: “To each place, as also to ours, he provides abundantly great relics of saints, so that, while they are worthily and familiarly honored by the inhabitants, those inhabitants may be strengthened by their perpetual protection.” MURATORIUS.], stands

Constantinople [Note: The learned Du Cange proves at length that Constantine’s city was called the second and new Rome, in book 1, chapter 6 of his *Constantinopolitan Christian History*. Socrates, speaking of Constantine in book 1, chapter 16, says: “He legally decreed that it should be called a second Rome.” The law was engraved on a marble column; this is also asserted by the *Alexandrian Chronicle* and Theophanes under Constantine’s twenty-fifth year. The Second Ecumenical Council, held in Constantinople in the year 381, grants the bishop of Constantinople privileges of honor after the Roman bishop, “because it is itself the new Rome.” Claudian, appropriately in relation to Paulinus’s words, sang in book 2 against Rufinus:

“The city also which is called the rival of great Rome.”

See Gothofredus on book 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Law of Italy*. MURATORIUS.]

the great city’s rival head,

more truly resembling Rome in the height of its walls,

[340] [469–470] because God compensated it with Peter and Paul

in equal ambition, since it deserved to receive

Paul’s disciple together with Peter’s brother.

How great a benefit for the duties of our life

grew along this road through the long distances of the earth,

[345] the places themselves still teach today,

where the broad wagon, bearing that blessed burden, [Note: [Col. 0532C] The other Paulinus also taught us, in his Life of Saint Ambrose, that saints’ relics were customarily placed on litters for transfer. Speaking of the translation of Saints Protasius and Gervasius, he says: “But when the bodies of the holy martyrs were raised and placed on litters, we are told that the illnesses of many were healed there.” MURATORIUS.]

came to rest at stations,

wherever there was a lodging for the holy bodies

and a resting place for those carrying

the sacred ashes,

with wondrous signs crying out [Note: After these words, verses seem to have fallen out. MURATORIUS.]

[350] For there [Note: So Muratorius; our manuscript reads *illis* (“for/in those”), a less satisfactory reading; Dungalus likewise reads *illic* (“there”).] the divine hand was at work [Note: So our manuscript; Muratorius’s manuscript reads *operata* (“having worked”) rather than *operosa* (“active”), as does Dungalus.] with healing power

along all the roads,

wherever the holy bodies impressed their living footprints

upon the sacred route.

Therefore, when faith gave the faithful companions permission,

they wished to pluck for themselves certain pledges

[355] from the holy bones, a fruit deservedly obtained [Note: The reading of this passage is corrupt in Dungalus.]

so that, as the reward and payment of their service,

each might carry home protections for his own house [Note: So our manuscript. Muratorius reads *referret*, “he might carry back,” instead of *referrent*, “they might carry back”; Dungalus also reads that way.]

From then on the sacred ashes were scattered like seeds of life

in different places,

and wherever a tiny fragment of bone fell, [Note: [Col. 0532D] Dungalus incorrectly reads *quacunque* (“wherever”) for *quaque* (“and wherever”).]

[360] a small drop from the modest store of the sacred body

fell among the peoples: [Note: [Col. 0532D] So our manuscript. Muratorius, however, reads *Decidit. ingentes illic pia gratia fructus*, etc.: “Fell. There pious grace [produced] great fruits,” instead of *Decidit in gentes: illic pia gratia fontes*, “Fell among the peoples: there pious grace [produced] springs.” Dungalus also has the former reading.]

there pious grace produced springs

and the drop of ash generated rivers of life.

From there, too, an abundance of Christ flowed down to us,

rich even in small things;

for here we also received this [Note: The verse should be emended from *nam hoc quoque*, “for this too,” to *Nam nos quoque*, “for we too”: “For we too received [the relics] here.” MURATORIUS.]

[365] the sacred relics of apostolic flesh [Note: Paulinus often testifies that several relics of the apostles were deposited in the Nolan basilicas. Speaking in Letter 12 to Severus about the relics deposited in the basilica dedicated to Saint Felix, he sings:

“The altars consecrated to God veil a twofold honor,

joining apostolic ashes with the cross.”

Speaking of the Fundanian basilica, he says:

“Here grace displays apostolic powers

in great pledges within a little dust.

Here are Father Andrew and Luke of great name.”

MURATORIUS.]

in a little dust, [Note: [Col. 0532D] Muratorius’s manuscript reads *pulvere Patrum* (“in the dust of the Fathers”) instead of *pulvere parvo* (“in a little dust”).]

which Felix—the holy one, lord and father of our household, guardian of our soul and protector of our salvation—received close by in the neighboring sanctuary,

which, more recent in age than his other halls, [Note: [Col. 0533B] This is the same basilica that he described in Natalis IX to Bishop Nicetas. He indicates that it had scarcely been completed then by these verses, in which he congratulates Nicetas on arriving at an opportune time, so that:

“The bishop may aid the unfinished work with prayers,
And dedicate it when finished.”

He then describes it in most elegant verses and, listing the relics placed there, adds:

“For the apostles’ ashes too, deposited beneath the heavenly table,
[Col. 0533C] Give forth, amid the holy offerings of sacred dust,
A gentle fragrance of dust breathing toward Christ.”

He designates this same basilica in Natalis X with these words, mentioning the same apostolic ashes:

“Therefore, united only in faith and suppliant prayer, we run
To the nearby threshold of my Felix; and from there
With equal vows we hasten to the adjoining hall,
And ask healing from the power of the apostolic ashes.”

MURATORIUS.]

[370] preserves his small ashes and great honors,

and is itself more greatly preserved by its patron guardians.

For let it not be thought that they ever need to be preserved:

they are accustomed to preserve others, nevertheless,

and, in their fatherly love, they graciously care for the welfare

of their foster children,

[375] and deign to order the protection of places dedicated to them [Note: [Col. 0533C] I do not know what the heterodox are muttering against the dedication of our churches, since we dedicate them to God in honor of the saints. But let them observe, I ask, how strongly Paulinus supports our custom. MURATORIUS.] [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *diligere*, “to love.”]:

that such devotion exists in the holy spirits,

wondrous signs of faith have demonstrated.

Therefore [Note: Muratorius reads *Inde* (“from there/therefore”) instead of *Unde* (“whence/therefore”).] I shall now briefly recount a recent work:

for it is worthy that the gifts of Saint Felix

[380] should be brought forth in rejoicing words

on his own festival.

I shall speak of no foreign place or event

from ancient time [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads “I shall speak of no foreign matters.” Our manuscript’s reading is more graceful.]

[471–472] but shall relate a work recently accomplished

within our own borders and in this very sanctuary,

which you may perhaps be glad to recognize [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *agnoscere*, “recognize,” rather than *renoscere* (also “recognize,” a different formation).],

because the event occurred in the full light of day.

[385] I believe that scarcely anyone among you is unfamiliar with it,

since flying rumor has carried the news

through distant regions [Note: Muratorius reads *ivit*, “went,” instead of *ierit*, “may have gone”; I prefer that reading.].

Certainly, some of you were present in this city

at the very time when it happened:

a thief, driven by unlawful impulses in his mind,

[390] stretched greedy hands toward the sacred gifts.

The wicked madman chose, from all the splendid furnishings

of the venerable sanctuary, one object as booty:

a cross [Note: The Muratorian manuscript read *cruce* (“by/with a cross,” ablative). Muratorius rightly substituted *crucis* (“of a cross,” genitive), as in our manuscript.],

unaware that it would be his own evidence,

not his plunder,

just as a ravenous fish swallows the hook,

only to be caught by the bait that it has seized.

[395] What, I ask, impelled, armed, blinded, and hurled that robber into so great a daring [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *tam grandis* (“so great,” nominative or genitive) instead of *tam grandi* (“with so great,” ablative). Our manuscript’s reading seems preferable.], so that, though his heart was struck, he did not flee either the guards’ watch or—even more—the reverent altars that conceal [Note: [Col. 0534B] Rosweide, in the additions to his notes on the passage in Paulinus, Letter 12 to Severus, “With the relics of apostles and martyrs consecrated within the apse beneath three-apsed altars” (*Reliquiis apostolorum et martyrum intra absidem trichora sub altaria sacratis*), [Col. 0534C] judges that in the Church’s earliest times there was only one altar in churches. Salmasius, on Solinus’s Polyhistor, page 1213, says: “The talk of three-apsed altars is nonsense. In Paulinus’s time there was only one altar in churches.” He then corrects the quoted words to *intra absidem trichoram sub altari sacratis*: “consecrated within the three-apsed apse beneath the altar.” Yet it is not so certain that only one altar was set up in ancient sacred buildings. Paulinus himself mentions, in one basilica:

“The reverent altars which cover the sacred ashes.”

He himself says in Letter 12 to Severus:

“The reverent altars cover the divine covenant,
With the martyrs laid together with the sacred cross.”

Again:

“The altars sacred to God veil a twofold honor,
Joining the apostles’ ashes with the cross.”

It is true that the requirements of verse could have prompted Paulinus to use the plural for the singular. But I shall show that he used the plural also in prose. [Col. 0534D] In the same letter he discusses consecrating a single basilica, for which the martyrs’ relics were sufficient: “If the venerable ashes of these martyrs,” Paulinus says, “are placed beneath the altars without the company of the cross, this explicit inscription will indicate it.” Again, in Letter 11 to Severus, he says of the basilica built at Jerusalem by Helena Augusta: “And soon, with a worthy surrounding enclosure, the basilica built at the place of the Passion is consecrated; glittering with gilded ceilings and rich in golden altars, it preserves the cross placed in a hidden sanctuary.”

But let us hear also the great Ambrose, in Letter 4, book II, to Marcellina. He relates the celebrated defense of the Portian basilica against the Arians. Shut inside with the people, he fearlessly withstood armed men forcibly sent in, when suddenly it was announced that the emperor had restored peace: “The soldiers,” he says, “vied with one another in announcing this; rushing to the altars, they signified the token of peace with kisses.” There was therefore not one altar, but several. Saint Gregory the Great, book V, Letter 50 to Palladius, mentions a church in which thirteen altars were placed. The same can be observed in the cemeteries, [Col. 0535B] which served as churches under pagan rule. Aringhus describes one of these in Roma Subterranea, book III, chapter 22, and points out not a few altars placed above martyrs’ tombs. [Col. 0535C] How much more usual must this have become when freedom was restored to religion and several saints’ bodies were often deposited in one and the same church! I hasten to other matters. MURATORIUS.]

[Note: It was customary for the bodies or bones of martyrs to lie beneath every altar. Indeed, altars could not be consecrated without them. This is expressly stated in canon 14 of the Fifth Council of Carthage, which forbids the practice. Saint Jerome, against Vigilantius, says ironically: “The Roman bishop therefore acts wrongly, who offers sacrifices to God over the venerable bones of the dead Peter and Paul—which, according to us, are bones to be venerated, but according to you are worthless dust—and considers their tombs to be Christ’s altars.” The Seventh Ecumenical Council, canon 7, says in Greek: “A bishop who consecrates a church without holy relics shall be deposed, as one who has transgressed the ecclesiastical traditions.” Other councils established the same. I must not omit the notable passage of Saint Ambrose in his letter to Marcellina. After describing the discovery of Saints Protasius and Gervasius, he says that he spoke thus to the people: “Let the triumphant victims enter the place where Christ is the victim. But he is upon the altar, who suffered for all; these are beneath the altar, who were redeemed by his suffering,” and so forth. MURATORIUS.]

the sacred altars,

and breathe forth the power of the sacred dust—nor did their pre-eminent character, by divine power alone, or at once by their appearance and value, drive him away [Note: The word *pretio*, “value,” is absent from Muratorius; I have supplied it from our manuscript.]

For many other ornaments were present there,

as you know [Note: Consult dissertation 16, *On the Ornamentation of Churches*, which I have reserved for the end of the book in order not to make the notes too long. MURATORIUS.],

in that very place—objects he might have taken

to spare the gold of the cross;

for inside there lay hidden sacred vessels

assigned for the celebration of the holy rites.

But, besides the ornaments of the sanctuary itself,

there were gifts of various forms,

as is customary,

set out here, which you see there every day,

or fixed all around the building

in diverse arrangement [Note: So our manuscript. Muratorius’s manuscript reads *dimenso* (“measured”) instead of *diverso* (“varied”). Candelabra were used in Christian worship from ancient times. I sufficiently demonstrated this in the preface to the dissertation. It is useful now to add the authority of Saint Clement in his letter to James. Although I scarcely think that letter a genuine work of so great a pontiff, it was nevertheless venerable among the ancients. He says: “As for the sacred vessels, they are to be treated as follows: the altar covering, the *canthara*, the candelabrum, and the veil, if worn out by age, are to be given to the fire.” How magnificent the candelabra were, learn from the fact that they are said to have been constructed like columns. MURATORIUS.]

like columns of candelabra.

[410] They bear painted candles [Note: So our manuscript. Muratorius reads *exstare*, “to project,” instead of *exstante*, “projecting.” I would not dare either to correct or alter *exstante*; let others decide. Candles were also once painted, and this custom continues in the Church. Paulinus, *Natalia* 6:

“But others light their lamps with painted candles.”

MURATORIUS.]

projecting from their tips,

so that the lights may be enclosed in fragrant papyrus [Note: Paulinus likewise sang in *Natalia* 3:

“They burn fragrant lights in wax-coated papyrus.”

It was customary among both pagans and Christians to surround a reed of papyrus-like material with wax and form candles from it. Pliny, book 16, chapter 27, speaking of reeds, says: “After their bark is removed, they serve candles and lights and funerals.” There are also verses of Antipater preserved by Suidas on this subject:

“A lamp clad in wax, the smoky light of Cronus,

bound with reed and slender papyrus.”

I translate them thus: “A lamp wearing a waxen garment, the burning lamp of Saturn, bound with reed and delicate papyrus.” MURATORIUS.]

[Col. 0535B] In the middle space, fixed to the lofty ceiling [Note: Virgil, book 1 of the *Aeneid*, says:

“Lamps hang from the lofty ceilings,

burning.”

Paulinus himself, *Natalia* 6:

“And they attach many-branched lamps to the hollow ceilings.”

And *Natalia* 9:

“And above, hanging from bronze spirals,

lamps are held beneath the roof,

and in the open space wandering lights sway

on loosened ropes;

a light breeze agitates the flowing flames.”

MURATORIUS.]

hollow lamps hung from bronze supports,

which, in the form of a tree, [Note: [Col. 0536C] He vividly describes the lamps called *lumiere* in Italian, which are customarily made at Milan with marvelous craftsmanship. These consist of several branches or arms extending from a single stem, or in a circle from a central ring. Each branch bears its own candles at the top; hanging all around, they carry crystal beads [Col. 0536D] in such a way that the light striking them is multiplied in splendid variety. MURATORIUS.]

stretch out arms on flexible, vine-like branches,

[415] and at the very top the branches bear

glass cups like their own fruit [Note: Our manuscript reads *calillos* (a defective form). Muratorius reads *caliclos*, which I approve as a shortened form of *caliculos* (“little cups”).],

and, as though blossoming in spring, flower with burning light.

With dense flames on many branches they imitate the stars,

distinguish the heavy darkness with their numerous light,

[420] and paint the delicate air with flowering sparks.

While they tremble, they flash their liquid locks repeatedly,

and, scattered through the darkness of night

by their constant torches,

they mingle uncertain light with shadows

and disturb the air with wavering appearances.

[425] Although he saw these things openly available to him, [Note: [Col. 0536D] Muratorius’s manuscript reads *Iste ergo* (“that man therefore”) instead of *Ergo isthaec* (“therefore these things”). Our manuscript’s reading is more correct.] he judged it safer, and easier to steal—because it involved less guilt and value—to make off with a light silver lamp hanging farther from the altar’s edge [Note: Lamps were hung beside the altar even in Paulinus’s time. Hence he says in *Natalia* 3:

“The bright altars are crowned with dense lamps.”

MURATORIUS.] [Note: Muratorius reads *emendare*, “to repair.” Our manuscript has *emandare* (“to send away,” as written), which seems worth retaining. Unless perhaps we prefer *amandare*, “to send away,” as below at line 658.]

But the wretch, ambitious and proud even in his crime,

[430] scorned to steal silver as though it were a contemptible offense,

and boldly stretched out his hand toward the golden lamp,

which he had seen artfully decorated

with various gems [Note: Muratorius reads *et variis* (“and with various”); our manuscript has *e variis* (“from various”). Both readings are possible.],

and had filled his heart with great desires,

so that he might alike rejoice in riches,

in gems and in gold.

[435] But so great a crime accumulates [Note: Muratorius reads *cumulatus*, “heaped up”; our manuscript has *cumulatur*, “is heaped up.” I prefer the former reading.]

upon the wicked man with its immense weight:

he remained burdened by sin, though light in bronze.

The sacrilegious man is met by his punishment;

his booty abandoned the robber.

Stripped of the stolen plunder, though not of his crime,

he lives poor in its gain,

but abounding in the wound of his fraud.

[440] Yet I think that he was permitted to undertake this crime only by the great power and plan of Christ [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *adesse*, “to be present”; but *adisse*, “to undertake,” as in our manuscript, is correct.],

so that, because he had conceived the thought

of taking something from the sacred things,

he might be allowed to come to those objects

where his impiety would be more conspicuous.

[445] A few days earlier he had fled there [Note: The immunity, or asylum, of churches is illustrated by many examples in Gothofredus, volume 3 of the Theodosian Code, title 45, book 1, *On Those Who Flee to Churches*. Later the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian established this in book 4 of the same title: “Let the temples of the Most High God be open to those who fear.” They decree that not only the altars but also the area surrounding the temple’s oratory be made available for the protection of fugitives, and so forth. The same is expressed in another law of Theodosius the Younger; on this, consult the cited Gothofredus. MURATORIUS.]

pretending that he was fleeing military service,

and, received as a guest in friendship

by the custodians of the sanctuary [Note: *Aedituus* was also called *aeditimus* among the ancients, and this name designated the guardian of a sacred building. The term passed from the pagans to the Christians. The *aeditui* are none other than doorkeepers, whose order flourished in the Church of God from its very beginnings. Thus among the Greeks the order of doorkeepers is called “the order of the temple guardians” (*Νεοκόρων τάξις*), a name that properly means *aeditui*. A passage of our Paulinus in Letter 6 to Severus will be illuminated by this. He says: “I confess that I was seized by a sudden force of the multitude, though I believe by God’s own ordering, and was unwillingly initiated into the presbyterate—not because I despised the place (for I call God to witness that, both by the name and by the office of temple guardian, I desired to begin sacred service), but…” You see, then, that even in Paulinus’s time the office of doorkeeper was the first grade of the clergy. MURATORIUS.],

who cared for the sacred sanctuary.

He concealed himself there for almost a month,

taking his rest and sleeping [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *ubi*, “where”; both readings are possible. In the law mentioned above, the emperors granted immunity not only to the church itself but also to many places adjoining it, and they give this reason for their piety: “We grant this breadth of space so that no fugitive may be permitted to lie down or spend the night in the temple of God itself or at the sacred altars, whether in the morning or in the evening.” Thus this thief did not usually sleep inside the basilica. MURATORIUS.],

while he had also observed the guards’ schedules.

And when he had selected [Note: Muratorius reads *coepisset*, “had begun”; that reading is plainly corrupt.]

the quiet hours for his contemplated crime [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *placitas*, “approved”; our manuscript’s reading is better.],

he silently took up the crime at night,

without difficulty or noise,

shut in behind closed doors, as one of the servants

among whom he was a guest,

once those servants, the guards not wakeful amid the silent shadows, had begun to take their first sleep [Note: From this we learn that doorkeepers were required to sleep in the churches at night and keep watch there. Consult Hallier, part 2, article 1, chapter 1, *On Sacred Election*, and Morinus, *On the Sacrament of Orders*. This custom is still preserved in the metropolitan church of Milan. MURATORIUS.]

and to snatch sleep,

[455] carrying forgetfulness to their burdened cares.

He took the place suited to his crime [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads, somewhat differently, “he took the place for his crime.” I would prefer *sumpsit*, “he took,” rather than *sumens*, “taking.”]

where he knew that a little device, [Note: [Col. 0537D] Muratorius’s manuscript reads *quam* (“which,” accusative feminine); ours has *qua* (“where”).]

left out according to custom during the night [Note: [Col. 0537D] Muratorius’s manuscript reads *adpositam* (“set beside/placed ready”) for *expositam* (“set out”).]

for preparing the lamps,

provided ready steps as a ladder [Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads *paratam*, “prepared.”],

and had then been left behind

by the careless caretaker [Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *jam* (“already/now”) instead of *tunc* (“then”).]

[460] It was in the shape of a cross, as it is still now: [Note: [Col. 0537D] Muratorius’s manuscript reads *qua* (“where/by which”) instead of *quae* (“which,” feminine nominative), and that indeed seems the reading to adopt. *Instar* here must be understood as “image, form, or figure.” It occurs elsewhere in this Natalis:

“Yet first, because the matter requires it,
I shall describe the shape of the cross itself.”

In Natalis XIII:

“This blessed boy will be to the Lord
An image of that very tree.”

[Col. 0538B] That is, an image. This word belonged also to better Latin usage. Virgil, Aeneid VI:

“What a likeness there is in him!”

That is, a model. Ulpian, in the law Si stipulatio, Digest, On Notice of New Work, says: “If a certain model is set before us, and, as it were, a representation of the work has been made.” MURATORIUS.] a straight upright of continuous rod, bearing a pair upon a transverse crossbar [Note: A transverse *limes* is nothing other than a crossbeam, which forms the lateral arms of the cross. Below he describes it thus:

“And where it has its summit, it is joined by a transverse bar.”

Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 118 on John, says: “The cross is broad in the transverse wood, by which the hands of the one hanging are extended.” Two of these *cantharuli* were therefore placed upon the lateral arms of the holy cross. Aringhus presents an elegantly worked cross in book 2, chapter 22, page 381 of *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, on whose arms two candelabra can likewise be seen. I believe that Paulinus’s *cantharuli* were placed on the cross in this fashion, since no mention occurs of chains by which they were supported, as we shall see shortly in the case of another. Hincmar, bishop of Reims, says in the *Life of Saint Remigius*, in Surius under 13 January: “Then, taking a cloth from the blessed tomb, they arrange it in the form of a bier; and, lighting candles upon the crosses and upon the candle-bearers, they raise their voices in song.” MURATORIUS.]

Cantharulos [Note: [Col. 0538C] In Muratorius’s manuscript *cartarulos* was read. But *cantharulos* must be read, as it stands in our manuscript—an emendation that Muratorius had conjectured.—The word necessarily requires correction, and *cantharulos* must be restored. *Canthari* were a kind of lamps suspended in churches, like other lamps. Anastasius the Librarian often mentions them, and explicitly under Sylvester: “A *pharus-cantharus* of the purest gold before the altar, in which genuine nard oil burns, where candles burn.” Under Leo III: “*Canthara* having gilded silver tapers in their midst.” *Pharocanthara* also occurs elsewhere, as does *canthara cerostrata*. The distinguished Joannes Ciampinus, an ornament of the City and of letters, displays the form of *canthari* in his outstanding work on mosaics. More often, however, I think the word designated candelabra. In this sense the name *canthari* continues in the Rituals of the Ambrosian Church. Beroldus, the most ancient writer of this rite, preserved in the metropolitan archive and in the Ambrosian Library in manuscript, frequently uses the word to designate candelabra. I shall transcribe a few passages. In the rites of Holy Saturday he says: “Then two deacons from among those standing around light the candles which they hold with the *canthari*, from the fire that is upon the larger candelabrum.” Below: “Two deacons carry two candelabra, which are called *canthara*, with candles burning above them.” Likewise, on Easter Day: “The deacons carry candelabra, which are called *canthara*.” And many similar passages occur elsewhere. MURATORIUS.]: one hanging by a little chain from the crossbar,

supports it; in these three small cups [Note: [Col. 0538D] Muratorius has: “supports it in three. In these cups,” etc. But our manuscript seems to me more correct.] inserted [Note: [Col. 0538D] The Muratorian manuscript has *incerta* (“uncertain”). But our manuscript has the better reading.] lights shine

[Col. 0539A] when the feast-day brings them forward [Note: [Col. 0539C] From this you may learn that candles were accustomed to be lit even during daytime services. On this subject consult Dissertation XVI. The lights are said to shine “uncertainly” because, although lit during the day, they are so overpowered by the strength of the sunlight that the wax scarcely seems to be burning. MURATORIUS.]; but then, without any use

[465] for light, they remained suspended merely for appearance [Note: [Col. 0539C] Our manuscript has *manebat* (“it remained”); Muratorius has *manebant* (“they remained”).].

But a little before, an unbroken silver cup, fitted for use,

had hung before the splendor of the cross by that same light [Note: [Col. 0539C] Muratorius has *de limine* (“from the threshold”)].

The thief immediately extinguishes it, shining with an unwelcome light to him—for he knew that this too

often tends to die when a thoroughly dried wick

[470] buries the light, after the oil has been consumed, deep into the night [Note: [Col. 0539D] Our manuscript erroneously has *conderat* (“had hidden”).],

and that the watchman would not be surprised if he happened to see darkness

drawing down the roof beneath an extinguished lamp [Note: [Col. 0539D] Muratorius has *culmine* (“from the roof’s summit”). But the reading of our manuscript should be retained.],

thinking that the night had come by its usual course, not been made by crime.

[475] [Col. 0539B] Therefore, not like a thief—for he was a robber—but like a guard,

the confident robber removes his unlawful booty,

and does not flee but remains undaunted. One chamber, hidden among many,

conceals him [Note: [Col. 0539D] Refer to Dissertation XVII, where I also showed that private persons found places for burial even in churches, and at the same time explained this word as far as possible. MURATORIUS.]; one of many such chambers, set all around along the sides of the great buildings,

provide secret lodging [Note: [Col. 0539D] Muratorius has *secura* (“safe”). But the reading of our manuscript is more elegant.] for the buried.

[480] In one of these the thief hid [Note: [Col. 0539D] The Muratorian manuscript has *abditur* (“is hidden”), a reading that may perhaps be better.]; and when he saw

that the barriers of the open hall stood ready to be passed, he sprang out through the opened chamber.

477–478 Leaving his hiding place, he carried away his crime; he was preparing to go

to Rome, as he later confessed when captured,

there to conduct the commerce of his unspeakable fraud.

[485] [Col. 0539C] Meanwhile, unknown to our people, that night and

the whole following day passed [Note: [Col. 0539D] The Muratorian manuscript has *obit* (“passes away”). The reading of our manuscript is more harmonious.]. Late, when they had completed their customary evening duty,

they set up the steps; but when he began to climb to make

the lamp, he found nothing: the customary staff of the cross

remained stripped of its beautiful jewel.

[490] [Col. 0540A] The wretched men are frightened [Note: [Col. 0539D] Muratorius has *pallescunt* (“grow pale”), which is more pleasing.], and, though they know that guilt

rightly attaches to them [Note: [Col. 0539D] Muratorius has *posse* (“can”). Our manuscript has *jure* (“rightly”).], do not dare

to reveal the loss; trembling, they depart and flee, pursuing

the runaway robber. Nowhere do they find any trace of his flight;

all go in different directions,
