[495] and search the harbors situated along different shores.

Eight days—or ten—passed while they searched in vain,

and, when all had now returned empty-handed from the investigation [Note: [Col. 0539D] Muratorius has *recursis*. But the reading of our manuscript is much more elegant.],

one boy among the searchers, himself unsuccessful in his labor,

returned along the long road after his effort had been poured out in vain [Note: [Col. 0540C] Our manuscript has *fusus* (“poured out”). But the reading of Muratorius’s manuscript is much better.].

[500] And, already approaching Nola, he stopped upon the very

roadway, and with a great groan and abundant tears,

calling Felix by name, presumed with faithful heart

that he would not return home except with the cross. Then, having completed

the journey, he promptly retraced his steps; and at once he met

[505] a certain man who knew the thief—not as a thief, but almost as a fellow citizen.

Our man first asked him where the traveler

had come from; the other answered. Again he was asked about the thief [Note: [Col. 0540C] Muratorius has *rogatus* (“when asked”). But it must be read as it stands in our manuscript.],

whether he had seen him. He replied that the thief was staying

nearby, in that very region [Note: [Col. 0540C] In Muratorius’s manuscript the verse is defective: “*Inde locis agere, et regio prope ipsos*.” The passage must therefore be emended from our manuscript.], which, while they were speaking, lay near Mount Vesuvius [Note: [Col. 0540C] Muratorius has *ipsos* (“them”). Our manuscript has *illos* (“those men”). I would prefer to read *ipsos*.] [Note: [Col. 0540D] Muratorius’s manuscript reads *Besaevo*; ours has *Vesero*. Everyone knows that in later centuries B was used for consonantal V. Thus below, poem 12, verse 313, Muratorius’s manuscript had *Veneventum* for *Beneventum*.—Following the usage of some Greeks, consonantal V is pronounced as B. Among them Vesuvius is not infrequently called Βεσύβιος and Βέσβιος. Aulus Gellius’s remark on Virgil’s verse, “The shore neighbouring the Vesaevan ridge,” is famous: he says that the poet first wrote “Nola’s ridge,” but, because the people of Nola denied him the favour of water he requested, substituted *ora* (“shore”) for *Nola*. We preserve the author’s account. Ambrose Leo, book II *On Nola*, chapter 3, likewise teaches that Mount Vesuvius is five Roman miles from Nola. MURATORIUS.],

[510] five miles from the city of Nola. But the approach of evening

postpones the plan. They agree that tomorrow’s light should again

join the two men; morning comes, and the guide returns.

[Col. 0540C] He leads our men onward; the thief is captured, and the booty is recovered.

[515] By chance that sacred day had dawned which brought the birthday

of blessed Priscus, whom Nola also celebrates; although he,

the bishop of Nuceria, had held his see in another city [Note: [Col. 0541C] There were two Nucerias: one in Umbria, the other in Picenum. The latter is here intended, expressly called Nuceria of the pagans; its bishop was Saint Priscus. Ughellus, in volume VII of *Italia sacra*, reports the following about him: “Saint Priscus is considered the first bishop of this church, crowned under Nero; his feast is celebrated on 9 May in the Roman Martyrology, concerning which see Baronius in his notes, and he is its patron saint.” Yet nothing concerning this saint occurs in the present Martyrology; thus Ughellus may be suspected of having been mistaken and of having remembered Baronius and his notes in place of Ferrarius. A cathedral was dedicated to him by the people of Nuceria, and he has always been regarded among them as their patron. The learned Henschenius and Papebrochius discuss this saint under 9 May in the *Acta Sanctorum*, though they acknowledge that his history is uncertain, as is also the date of his martyrdom. I congratulate the people of Nuceria that I was the first to bring from darkness the memory of so illustrious a bishop, so many centuries old. For how celebrated must he have been, whose birthday was observed not only at Nuceria but also in other cities in the time of Paulinus! MURATORIUS.] had occupied,

behold, the very church of Saint Felix,

which the people then crowded with solemn honor [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Muratorian manuscript has *stipavit* (“had crowded”).],

[520] after the bishop had already concluded the sacred rites and dismissed

the devout congregation. At the divinely appointed moment, as the people

were going out to meet him, the thief is suddenly brought in,

his thievish hands bound and tied behind his back.

The people are filled with joy, the robber with terror;

[525] and the whole city runs together to see the strange spectacle.

The raging crowd, driven by popular hatred, advanced against him;

joy and anger mingled the sorrowful tumult [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Muratorian manuscript has *incertos* (“uncertain”) instead of *maestos* (“sorrowful”), which stands in our manuscript.].

I feared, I confess, that the devil might perhaps, through the envy

by which he usually violates a procession with blood,

[530] seek to heal one wound by inflicting a worse.

[Col. 0541B] The thief is snatched from the people and confined in that very chamber

479–480 (as perhaps happens to a criminal after capture), in which

he had hidden with the stolen cross. When the cross was later found,

he too was shut up there, so that he might remain alive. Then, having regained his senses [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Muratorian manuscript has: “Then I, with my mind restored,” etc. But the reading of our manuscript should be retained.],

[535] he himself, as the guilty man, began to recount his crime,

and, confessing, described in wondrous fashion how, during those

eight or ten days in which he had intended to go to Rome,

his feet had been drawn backward so that, always preparing to go,

he always returned, continually retracing his steps

[540] to that same region of Vesuvius [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Muratorian manuscript has *Besaevi*, as above in verse 510.], where he had been commanded to be confined as though in a prison,

by an angel’s hand weaving the bonds. Yet he thought himself,

poor man, to be master of his own will [Note: [Col. 0541D] Muratorius reads *tui* (“of yours”), which is perhaps a typographical error.], because he seemed

free in body; although, without any visible chain,

[545] [Col. 0541C] a stronger right hand held him by secret bonds.

Felix, the avenger, bound him with a punishment suited to his error,

and whirled the madman around in such a frenzy [Note: [Col. 0542C] Muratorius has *mentem* (“mind”), but *amentem* (“madman”) is preferable.],

that, always departing, he never went away; and whenever

he began to leave with a leaping step, he returned.

[550] Marvelous faith! He went while standing still; he remained while moving,

[Col. 0542A] unaware that the very thing for which he was preparing to flee

was made the means of preventing his flight, and that his chains remained

with him—the crime he himself had committed becoming his own chain [Note: [Col. 0542C] Our manuscript has *insumptamque* (“and taken up”), but the reading *inruptamque* (“and unbroken”) is required by the sense.].

For he had placed in the bosom of his garment the weight of the booty

[555] he had shut inside it, and, eager [Note: [Col. 0542C] The Muratorian manuscript has *avidam* (“eager,” feminine). But it must be read as in our manuscript.], as though captured in mind,

to seek a hiding place, he wandered nevertheless through open fields;

thinking that he was concealed, he stood exposed upon the clear expanse [Note: [Col. 0542C] Both the Muratorian manuscript and ours have *in aequore claro* (“upon the clear expanse”). Muratorius comments on this passage: “Certainly a copyist’s error, written instead of *aethere* or *aere claro* (‘clear air’).” But, with all due respect to that most learned man, I think there is no error here. It is established that the most elegant poets—Virgil, Ovid, and others—use *aequor* sometimes for a level field, sometimes for the air.].

Thus the impiety conscious within him had so blinded his mind

that, while fleeing, he could not escape, and, while wandering, could not hide.

[560] With his perceptions at odds, fear on one side and bewilderment on the other

had confused his guilty soul; he avoided the beaten roads;

inactive, he feared approaching secluded thickets;

[Col. 0542B] even in the forests he feared that the very silence

might somehow cry out his crime, or he thought that dreadful shapes,

the avenging monsters of wild beasts, might confront him.

[565] Then the wretched man, diverted from the crowded roadway [Note: [Col. 0542D] Muratorius has *seductus* (“led aside”). The reading of our manuscript, *sejunctus* (“separated”), is more accurate.], wandered off the road

nearby, walking in a certain field [Note: [Col. 0542D] The Muratorian manuscript has *devius in quodam* (“wandering in a certain [place]”). Our manuscript has *devius in id quod* (“wandering into that which”). I follow the former reading.],

pretending to be secure to those who did not know him,

while beneath his heart he concealed fear [Note: [Col. 0542D] Muratorius has *sed corde* (“but in his heart”). Our manuscript has *sub corde* (“beneath his heart”).],

and pressed his crime beneath his clothing. For, high up,

[570] he had placed the gold, shut within the folds of his tucked-up garment,

suspending the flowing robe with his thigh left bare.

For he had not dared to entrust the theft even to the silent earth, or, in the manner of robbers, to hollow caves, greedily fearing evidence that would betray the entrusted fraud.

Therefore the impious robber had constructed for himself

a storehouse of crime [Note: [Col. 0542D] The Muratorian manuscript has “he had constructed this punishment for himself,” and Muratorius emended it to “the robber had constructed this punishment.” The reading of our manuscript seems more correct.], and was deservedly bound by such fear:

he believed that no one else shared in his wretched theft,

[580] that he alone bore the contagion of so great a crime,

[Col. 0543A] and that the folds of his garment would become the custody of the theft [Note: [Col. 0543B] Paulinus has just described the tunic used by ordinary people. On this subject Quintilian, book XI, should be heard: “He who has no right to the broad stripe should gird himself so that the front of his tunic reaches a little below the knees, and the back to the middle of the calves.” The Romans girded their tunics and, as they wished, drew them up or let them down; sometimes they loosened them so much that, a fold being formed, they could conceal something there. Paulinus says above:

“High up,

he had placed the gold, shut within the folds of his tucked-up garment,

suspending the flowing robe with his thigh left bare.”

Plutarch in his *Life of Coriolanus* likewise shows that this was customary. He says that candidates in ancient times went to the assemblies without tunics, lest, with gold concealed in them, they should purchase votes: “They wished the candidate to come forward ungirded and without a tunic before the citizens.” Ovid, *Amores* I:

“Why do you command the boy to prostitute himself for Venus’ price?

He has no fold in which to conceal the payment.”

Horace, *Satires* II.3:

“I have seen him carry things in a loose fold, give them away, and play.”

On this subject consult Octavius Ferrarius, *De re vestiaria*. MURATORIUS.],

in which his hand had dared the sacrilegious theft.

He himself would carry his own burden, and alone would be weighed down;

he would pollute himself with the deadly load of his booty,

[585] so that nothing in him would remain free from impiety.

Having enclosed the plunder taken from the sacred buildings

in his girded clothing, he would bind it tightly [Note: [Col. 0543D] Muratorius has *contingeret* (“would touch”). Our manuscript has *substringeret* (“would bind tightly”).],

and himself display the sign by his own chains.

For shortly afterward, when captured, he changed his belts into bonds;

[590] and when the gold fell from the loosened folds of his ungirded garment,

he was bound by the very strap with which he had been girded,

and by which he had boldly stretched out his hands toward the sacred gifts.

Captured by the knot of his own thong,

he brought them back with his hands empty of booty but full of the strap [Note: [Col. 0543D] Muratorius has *rete* (“net”). Our manuscript has *reste* (“strap”), which is preferable.].

[595] [Col. 0543B] But if we wish to examine more deeply the entire sequence

of the exact order, and observe it more and more in every detail—

both where the crime lay hidden and by what device, once concealed,

it became visible [Note: [Col. 0543D] Muratorius has “where the crime lay hidden, and by what art it was concealed.” Both readings are plausible.]—

we shall discern the wondrous workings of God’s hand

upon Felix. We have already said much about how, while fleeing, he did not flee;

[600] how, with his steps turned back, he repeatedly retraced the courses

he had traveled along his own tracks, rolling his journey back in vain,

shut out from distant places and driven back toward the nearby ones [Note: [Col. 0543D] Muratorius has *recursus* (“having returned”). But the reading of our manuscript pleases me more.].

[Col. 0544A] Now I shall commemorate another deed of Felix, which the right hand of Christ

[605] brought forth to display the merit of his beloved servant:

a miraculous sign of equal wonder,

which the trembling culprit himself disclosed by confessing his daring deed [Note: [Col. 0543D] Muratorius has *auso* (“deed”). Both readings are plausible.].

But first, since the matter requires it, I shall explain

the form of the cross itself, which painting has also been accustomed

[610] to represent in two shapes [Note: [Col. 0543D] Muratorius has *pingere* (“to paint”).], either as two-horned upon an upright staff,

or spread through five rods into three horns.

The form of the cross is composed in a double shape. Now

it assumes the appearance of a ship’s mast, with its yards,

[Note: [Col. 0544B] Muratorius reads *antemnae*. In our manuscript it is written in such a way that one might read either *antennae* or *antemnae*. I think *antennae* should be read.—Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*, says: “We plainly see the sign of the cross in nature, when a ship is carried along with its sails swelling.” The author of the poem *On Easter*, attributed to Saint Cyprian but vindicated for Bede of Poitiers by Victorinus, writes:

“This form of a tree rises from a single trunk,

and soon extends its arms into two branches,

just as full yards stretch heavy sails.”

Saint Justin, *Apology* II: “Consider whether all things in the world are governed without this shape, or can have any participation in it. For the sea is not divided unless this trophy, which is called the mast, remains safe in the ship.” Author of Sermon 56 in volume III of the works of Saint Ambrose—whether he was Saint Maximus or Ambrose—asserts this clearly. Origen, *Homily 8 on Various Matters*, says: “The yards of ships, or the horns of sails, fly beneath the figure of our cross.” MURATORIUS.]

or, existing as the sign which the Greeks customarily use for three hundred,

[615] [Col. 0544B] it explains the figure when joined to a single upright shaft,

and wherever it has a summit, it is joined by a crossbar.

Now the same cross [Note: [Col. 0544C] The monogram was a concise written form of the name of Christ. It was customary on ancient standards called *labara*, but Constantine the Great used it especially for a more sacred purpose; from that time he was the first among Christians to give his name to it. Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* II.8, says that this sign was considered “more precious and holier than the others.” See Gretser, in his excellent work *On the Holy Cross*, book II, chapters 38 and following. The notorious heretic Brentius asserted that the monogram had no form of a cross, but signified only the word “Christ.” See how our Paulinus refutes him when he says:

“Now the same cross, composed in a different arrangement,

speaks of the Lord as Christ through the monogram.”

This plainly represents the form of a cross. The monogram was formed as follows. MURATORIUS.]

composed in a different arrangement,

speaks of the Lord as Christ through the monogram.

For the sign by which the Latin reckoner denotes twice five,

[620] [Col. 0544B] is written by the Greeks as chi, and the central rho [Note: [Col. 0544D] Perhaps it should read: “And the middle is rho,” or rather, “And the middle [letter] is rho.” MURATORIUS.],

[Col. 0545A] whose apex and marks it holds [Note: [Col. 0545B] To form the Greek name of Christ, *Χριστός*, seven elements are involved, though they are better called six, since one sigma serves in both places. Since Paulinus counts ΧΡΙΤΟ, however, he adds nothing concerning sigma. Should *signa* be corrected to *sigma*? This letter was formerly written in two forms: sometimes Σ and sometimes Ϲ. The former is observable on older Greek coins; the latter, according to Spanheim, *Dissertation II on the Excellence and Use of Coins*, became so customary after the time of Domitian that scarcely any trace of the former can be detected. These signs, XC—that is, ΧΡΙϹΤΟϹ, “Christ”—also occur in certain Christian inscriptions. But how is this sigma expressed in the monogram? To make true what Paulinus sings here:

“And thus the six elements, by which the name

is expressed more sublimely than every name,

come together beneath a single sign.”

And below:

“Thus one expresses six signs together.”

For no Σ is visible there. Therefore I think that the other form of the same sigma, namely C, was placed in the monogram, if we take it as part of the straight line and part of the curved line that constitute rho. Or rather, C—that is, sigma—is formed in the semicircle of the letter P, namely in C, which, if reflected, displays the true C. Paulinus cannot otherwise be explained. MURATORIUS.],

which, when bent back toward the curved staff itself,

makes an ο, as though completing a circle [Note: [Col. 0545C] Both the Muratorian manuscript and ours have *facit ω*. But *facit ο* must be written, as Muratorius rightly observes. In the word *Χριστός*, which Paulinus has in view, there is no omega (*ω μέγα*) but an omicron (*ο μικρόν*).].

For the rigid upright line makes the ι [Note: [Col. 0545C] Our manuscript has *obstipuus*. But *obstipus* must be read, as Muratorius reads it.], which in Hellas [Note: [Col. 0545D] Muratorius has *Ellade*. But *Hellade* should be read, as in our manuscript, since ἡ Ἑλλάς is written with the rough breathing.] is iota.

Tau [Note: [Col. 0545D] Our manuscript has *taut*, but incorrectly.—If, after placing the iota, you put a transverse line upon its summit, you obtain T; one part of it, bent into a curve, will then provide the whole P. I have noticed that on ancient *labara* the upper line of rho sometimes extends slightly to the left; Paulinus also calls this extension “short.” For examples of this observation consult Aringhus, *Roma subterranea*, book IV, chapter 27, pages 175 and 178; book VI, chapter 50, page 685; book III, chapter 22, page 524. Aringhus also presents a ring on which the monogram is expressed in such a way that the complete tau can likewise be seen there. Thus you will find six letters drawn in the monogram, as Paulinus asserts below. Neither the sense nor the meter is consistent here. It is therefore better to read: “Tau: the same stylus, drawn backward with a short point.” There *the same* refers to *stylus*: the same stylus I forms tau. MURATORIUS.]—the same stylus, itself drawn backward with a short point [Note: [Col. 0546B] The Muratorian manuscript has: “Tau: the same stylus itself drawn backward from the short summit.” Our manuscript has: “Taut: the same stylus itself drawn backward with a point.” Both readings are corrupt, as the meter shows. I have therefore combined a third reading from the two, which seems to me genuine. Muratorius had emended it as follows: “Tau: the stylus itself drawn backward with a short point.” But the first syllable of *acumine* is short.]—

[625] produces it; and thus the six elements by which the name

is expressed more sublimely than every name

come together beneath one sign, and one letter is formed by three rods [Note: [Col. 0546B] The Muratorian manuscript has *formatur* (“is formed”). Both readings are plausible.—Two rods combine to constitute X, while only one forms P. From this Paulinus draws forth the sublime mystery of the Trinity. The following verses teach that X consists of two rods:

“And this is the mystery: that, in both rods,

their summits, drawn upward to an equal end,

rise; while below, standing apart at equal distance,

they stand on equal feet and are joined together at the middle.”] as a letter.

Thus one sign expresses six marks, so that one through three rods

may signify that the Lord is at once three and one.

[630] [Col. 0545B] And God is in Christ, whom, having assumed a body,

the harmony of the threefold mind willed to be born for us.

[Col. 0546A] This is also the mystery: that in both rods

their summits, spread apart, rise to an equal end,

while below, standing apart at equal distance,

[635] they stand on equal feet and are joined by a central bond,

and, separated, face one another with equal summits [Note: [Col. 0546C] Muratorius’s manuscript has *summi* (“of the summit”). Our manuscript has *summis* (“with summits”), which Muratorius himself had suspected should be read.].

When these meet at the intermediate point [Note: [Col. 0546C] For these two words, *his intermedio*, both the Muratorian manuscript and ours have the three words *has inter medio*. The text should apparently be read as Muratorius emended it.],

the rod, like a royal scepter, rises more proudly,

signifying that Christ God reigns over all.

[640] who, on the cross spread through the four outer ends of the wood [Note: [Col. 0546C] Is the monogram normally formed from *lignum* (“wood”)? Do not believe it. I therefore think that *extima signi* (“the outer extremities of the sign”) should be read here. MURATORIUS.],

reaches the world measured out in four regions [Note: [Col. 0546D] Saint Ambrose—or, more accurately, Saint Maximus—in Sermon 56 writes: “The heavens themselves have also been arranged according to the figure of this sign; for since they are divided into four parts, namely east, west, south, and north, they are contained as though by the four angles of a cross.” Gregory of Nyssa, in his homily on Christ’s Resurrection, says this concerning the cross mentioned by the Apostle: “For he knows that the figure described with four horns proceeding from the middle declares the power and providence of him who hung upon it.” Saint Jerome—or whoever the author may have been—in his commentary on Mark 11: “What else is the appearance of the cross than the square form of the world?” MURATORIUS.],

so that he may draw peoples from every quarter to life.

And because through the death of the cross Christ God became all things to all,

[Col. 0546B] he stands as the beginning of life’s rising and the end of evils,

[645] with alpha surrounding the cross, and omega, formed by three rods,

[Col. 0547A] completing a shape different in each of the two letters [Note: [Col. 0547B] Three rods compose A. Two meet at the summit and embrace a third within their curve. Likewise omega, drawn in such a form, displays three rods, through which the great mystery of the Trinity is revealed. MURATORIUS.], through a threefold arrangement [Note: [Col. 0547B] The Muratorian manuscript has *trina* (“threefold”). Both readings are plausible.],

because the one mind and threefold power are perfect.

Alpha likewise is Christ to me, and omega he who embraced

equally the highest and lowest ends of the exalted and the humble,

[650] conqueror who grasped both the infernal and the heavenly,

and, breaking open the abysses, entered the heavens laid open,

bringing back victorious salvation after death had been overcome.

And when victory joined him to the right hand of the Fatherland,

485–486 he established a bodily trophy in the heavenly seat [Note: [Col. 0547B] So the Muratorian manuscript reads. Our manuscript has *trophaeum*. [Col. 0547C] I prefer the former reading. Dungalus cites these two verses, 654 and 655, in reverse order.—Thus our manuscript reads, in accordance with true orthography. Bulengerus, in his treatise *On the Spoils of War*, thinks *trophaeum* should be read because of established usage, though he does not deny that *tropaeum* is more correct. The word came from Greek, where it is written τρόπαιον, namely *tropaeum*. Gerardus Joannes Vossius defends this reading in his *Etymologies*. Certainly ancient manuscripts read it so; I have consulted them, and the oldest Virgilian manuscript in the Florentine library of the Grand Duke, preserved under the care of the distinguished and exceptionally eminent scholar Antonio Magliabechi, has *tropaeum*, not *trophaeum*. The inscriptions on marble do not disagree. See Dausquius on orthography. MURATORIUS.],

[655] and fixed the banner of the cross above all the stars.

That image, therefore, which the thief, driven by greedy

frenzies, had torn down uselessly from its hanging hook,

[Col. 0547B] and, with polluted hand, removed from the holy church,

has through this work been completed, so that, composed in wondrous forms,

[660] it represents both images of the eternal cross [Note: [Col. 0547C] The cross described by Paulinus was not a mere monogram; rather, it was also joined to the ordinary image of the cross. I have examined all the examples of monograms, both on ancient coins and on funerary monuments, yet I have not been permitted to find the two images joined together in this way. Only one outstanding testimony to this learned construction occurs in Aringhus, *Roma subterranea*, book II, chapter 10, page 311. There he presents an image of a marble sarcophagus excavated from the Vatican cemetery, on which the figures of the twelve apostles are elegantly drawn. In the middle between them appears the form of a jeweled cross, exactly as the ordinary cross is formed, namely with a transverse piece of wood. From the upper summit of a straight shaft rises the sacred monogram, surrounded by a beautiful crown. I suppose that the cross of Paulinus was constructed after this model. MURATORIUS.]:

[Col. 0548A] so that, if one now wishes to look closely at it,

clear proof is ready for the eyes; for, restored, it shines in the very place

where it had formerly been fixed, and adorns with the sign of piety the face of the altar enclosed by a veil [Note: [Col. 0547D] Both the Muratorian manuscript and ours have *clausi*. Muratorius suspects that *clausa* should be read, understanding *lege dum*: “while the altar’s face is closed.” Paulinus may perhaps have written: “with the altar’s face closed by a veil,” which would produce a clearer sense. Altars were accustomed to be closed with a veil, after the model of the veil formerly placed before the Holy of Holies in Solomon’s temple, 2 Chronicles 3; this was called περιπέτασμα τοῦ ἀδύτου, “the veil of the sanctuary.” Theodoretus, *Ecclesiastical History* I.31: “And the divine altar was adorned with royal curtains.” The Council of Toledo, chapter 7: “Those who, carried away by mad presumption, strip the altars bare and remove their sacred coverings.” Anastasius, under Stephen II, says: “Around the altar he made eight curtains.” Likewise: “Upon the altar in the church of Saint Lawrence he made a covering.” MURATORIUS.]

altar’s face [Note: [Col. 0548B] Crosses were placed on altars in ancient times, whatever the heterodox may mutter. Saint John Chrysostom, in his sermon that Christ is God, says: “The cross upon the sacred table.” Especially noteworthy on this matter is the passage of Sozomenus, *Ecclesiastical History* II.3, where he relates that a certain Probanius, who had become a Christian from paganism but did not yet acknowledge the power of the cross, was shown in a vision Σταύρου σύμβολον τῶν ἀνακειμένων ἐν τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ τῆς ἐνθάδε ἐκκλησίας—“the sign or image of the cross placed upon the sacred altar of that church.” The most mendacious Centuriators, century 4, chapter 13, call this story superstitious and alien to the age of Constantine, alleging that Sozomenus invented it or foolishly accepted it as true. But their calumnies do not concern us. Sigebert, under the year A.D. 451, shows that a golden cross was on the altar when the bishop of Casatentum celebrated Mass. Gretser correctly observes this in book II, chapter 13, *On the Holy Cross*. Add also what is found in canon 3 of the Council of Tours, held in A.D. 567—not, as some think, 570: “That the body of the Lord be placed on the altar, not in an imaginary arrangement, but under the title of the cross.” This canon certainly must be understood of a cross placed on the altar. From this Paulinus’s poem on the cross receives its illumination:

“He adorns the face of the altar with the sign of piety.”

MURATORIUS.] adorns with the sign of piety.

[665] Therefore the same image displays that form of the cross

which marks the balanced scales, poised upon an even beam [Note: [Col. 0548D] The manuscript read: “which marks the scales, balanced upon an equal thread,” etc. I have emended it. See again what I discussed in Dissertation XXI. MURATORIUS.] [Note: [Col. 0548D] The Muratorian manuscript corruptly has: “which marks the scales of the balanced, poised upon a thread,” etc. Our manuscript has: “which marks the scales, balanced upon an even beam,” etc., the form in which Muratorius had emended it.],

and represents the yoke, joined to its harmonious pole [Note: [Col. 0548D] Both the Muratorian manuscript and ours have *subreptoque*. Muratorius thinks *subrectoque* should be read, and I agree.—I have judged that *subrectoque jugum* (“with the yoke raised upright”) should be written, not *subrepto* (“with the yoke snatched away”), as in the manuscript. Consult the same Dissertation XXI. MURATORIUS.],

or the lofty tree with transverse branches, which imitates the eyes

joined at the brow above the face [Note: [Col. 0548D] Concerning these matters see the preceding dissertation, XXI. MURATORIUS.],

[670] the tree upon which the Lord hung

while the world trembled, pouring out innocent blood for the sinner.

To this solid cross a double rule, with its weight,

[Col. 0548B] joins the small crown at the end of the extended metal [Note: [Col. 0548D] Crosses surrounded by crowns were customarily painted. Paulinus teaches the same in Letter 12 to Severus, where he says: …].

Crowned, behold, the cross of the Lord standing above the courts of Christ,

Promising lofty rewards for arduous labor; take up the cross, whoever wishes to take away the crown.

[Col. 0549C] In the same place:

The lofty, flower-bearing cross is encircled by a wreath-like crown.

Again:

A crown surrounds the cross in a radiant circle,

And the apostles are crowns for that crown.

Concerning crowns likewise surrounding the cross, the following is found in the same place:

The labor of the saints and their duly corresponding reward,

The lofty cross, and the sublime crown that is the cross’s recompense.

Gregory of Nazianzus expressed the same in *Against Julian*, Oration 1: “The reported thing is that, while he was sacrificing, the entrails displayed a crowned cross” (Τὸν δ᾽ οὖν λεγόμενον, ὅτι θυομένῳ τὰ σπλάγχνα τὸν σταυρὸν ἀναδείκνυσι στεφανούμενον). They report that, when Julian was sacrificing, the entrails of the victims showed him the image of a crowned cross. Examples of such crosses occur on the coins of several Christian emperors. See what Aringhi has in *The Christian Catacombs of Rome*, and Gretser, *On the Holy Cross*, book II, chapter 11, and Rosweyde’s notes on Paulinus’s much-praised letter, drawing on Gretser. — Muratorius.] lies beneath it, encircled with various gems.

[675] This cross of the Lord too, as though girded with a diadem,

Shines forth in the eternal image of the life-giving wood.

That thief, from the whole of his theft,

Left this one piece untouched by the iron with which he had broken the rest,

And when, as the captured and disrobed man’s garments fell away,

[680] The fragments of the plunder slipped down and fell.

The sight of the matter then confused the hearts of the discoverers themselves

With bewilderment. They rejoiced at what they had found, but grieved that it was broken; then they began

To seek the reason, marveling at the thief—cautious and daring at once—

[685] Blind in what he had broken, yet cautious in what he had left behind.

Then, before the astonished men, he confessed both his crime and the divine power:

487–488 For in his mind he considered the whole matter: yet this one thing

[Col. 0549B] He had preserved through divine power, by which the cross, enclosed within it,

By its inactive strength prevented any bold thief from touching it.

He himself confessed the crime of his mind and the power of the cross,

Declaring that whenever he had armed his hands against it,

[690] The crown joined to the cross by a common fastening had, as though shattered,

Each time refused to fall when the blow rebounded.

While his feeble arms had grown numb, their sinews loosened.

Here I would like briefly to denounce the wretched thief.

Unhappy man, what madness had so turned your mind

That, rebuked by so great a light of truth,

You did not hasten to retrace the whole investigation,

Flying back quickly so that you might willingly return the stolen object?

[700] Did such power oppress your avaricious mind with darkness

That you dared to hide in your lap that part

Which, because God barred it, you had so often feared to violate?

Tell me: where did that fear of yours flee, and from where?

Again, how did reckless audacity so perversely persist in your mind—

[705] You fearful, yet likewise contemptuous, departing different in the appearance of the same crime—

And, mixing faith with treachery in a divided heart,

You believed that with fearful iron you could touch

The power of the cross and Christ’s inviolable sign,

[710] Yet, fearing what you recognized, you denied it by carrying it away?

Nevertheless, your impiety neither benefited you nor us;

Rather, you confessed your folly and made the divine signs

Exult in the great triumph of the cross.

So let us cease attacking the thief who has now been captured,

[715] For the poverty resulting from his deceitful plunder is punishment enough.

Now I turn my words to you, venerable cross of God,

And shall conclude my speech with grateful praise.

O great cross, the piety of God; cross, glory of heaven;

Cross, eternal salvation of humankind; cross, terror to the wicked,

[720] And strength to the righteous, light to the faithful. O cross,

You who granted God, in the flesh, to serve salvation on earth,

And granted humankind, in God, to reign in heaven;

Through you the light of truth was revealed, and impious night fled.

You destroyed, for believers, the temples torn from the nations;

[725] You are the harmonious clasp of human peace,

Reconciling the mediating human being through Christ’s covenants.

You became the stairway of humanity, by which it may be carried into heaven.

Be forever a pillar to the godly, and an anchor to us,

So that our household may stand firm and our fleet make a good voyage,

[730] Fixed in faith upon the cross, or receiving a crown from the cross.

## The Poems of Saint Paulinus, Bishop of Nola

### Muratorius’s Preface to Saint Paulinus’s Twelfth Nativity

[Col. 0551]

489–490 Saint Paulinus composed this Nativity in the year of Christ 405. It contains three miracles of the blessed confessor Felix. A certain man had vowed a pig to the blessed confessor and, after distributing small portions of the victim among the poor, was leaving, believing that he had fulfilled his vow. Miraculously struck from heaven, he fell from his horse and complained that his feet were afflicted by hidden fetters. He was carried back to the basilica of Saint Felix. There he appeased the saint by prayers and by distributing the meat, and was divinely restored to his former health. Some farmers from Apulia attempted to drag another pig, vowed to Saint Felix, to Nola. The animal, weighed down by fattening, resisted their pious desire and lost the use of its legs at the beginning of the journey. These men, intending to complete their vow by another means, proceeded to Saint Felix. Without their knowledge, the pig was carried to Nola of its own accord for many miles, with no human leading it. Everyone marveled at the miracle, and the unexpected victim fed the poor of Nola. The final prodigy happened to other farmers. They too vowed a heifer to the glorious confessor. She refused to be harnessed to the cart and, driven mad, escaped from her masters’ hands. Thereafter she accompanied their journey of her own accord and, miraculously tamed, presented herself to the axe. Paulinus sings of all these events at length and with elegance.

### Poem XX: Song XII on Saint Felix

[Note: In our manuscript this poem bears the title: “Book XII begins.” See what we said on the title of the preceding poem.]

[Col. 0551A]

Often good masters serve their beloved dependants

With a pious mind, and protect their slaves, subject to them, with ancestral affection;

They show especially attentive care in nurturing those

Whom, as they examine their circumstances, they see to be more in need of help and lacking in resources.

[5] And if one of them wishes to perform some vow,

As customary human practice solemnly requires,

But is unable to carry it out with the resources of the poor,

The impoverished servant is assisted by his master’s zeal:

The rich master, possessing the means that the poor man lacked,

[10] Provides the expense for the feast that must be enlarged.

This condition has been granted to me under the patronage of Felix:

Let nothing come from myself, so that everything may come to me through him.

For now, at his Nativity—as indeed in earlier years,

In which this day has flourished for me—

[15] I had no means by which to prepare the customary feast of the vow,

And the day was approaching, while no resource was yet available to me

From any source. Suddenly, behold, the generous patron provided

The means with which I might set out a plentiful meal:

He gave two pigs at once, together with a nurse.

[Note: In Muratorius’s manuscript, *cum junice* (“with a young cow”) appears instead. Both readings are plausible. *Junix* is a female bovine of tender age, one that has ceased to be a calf but has not yet reached full size. Persius, satire 2: “When so many udders of young cows melt for you in the flame.” Plautus, *Miles Gloriosus* 6: “How soon the young cow will return to the stall for fodder.” Papias: “*Junices*, young cattle.” Alexander the Medical Writer, book II of *Affections*: “Such things as beef, and feet from a young cow.”]

[20] Their flesh fed the poor, while we took our material from those same animals,

Since through those very beasts God had recently displayed

Miracles through remarkable signs,

Teaching human beings, by a profound design, to attend to Christ,

491–492 And not to place the desire for meat above faith.

[Note: Paulinus often uses this word with a long final syllable. In the *Panegyric*: “And the human race everywhere without the law of faith.” In *Nativity* V: “Exulting with helmet and shield of faith.” And elsewhere. — Muratorius.]

For, as a lamentable reproach to our greed,

The sequence that follows will teach that God gave the highest signs

Through animals lacking human reason.

[Col. 0552B] I shall sing no fiction, although I use the art of poetry;

I shall narrate history faithfully, without the poet’s deceit.

[30] For it would be wrong for a servant of Christ to utter falsehood:

Let such arts please the nations, who worship what is false.

But for us there is one art: faith—and Christ, the musician—

Who taught a wondrous peace to arise within himself

From a once discordant harmony, which he brought together as one body

[35] By assuming humanity, and which joined the gracious God

With infused power, so that he might establish two in himself

And make natures, once far apart, one.

So that God might be human, the one who is God became human through himself,

He who is God, born from God the Father, to whom grace is not something added

[40] But nature, since he is the only heir of the supreme Father,

Possessing alone by right what, as a gift, he grants to those

To whom gracious faith has given the power to deserve divine things.

He, therefore, is truly our musical author;

He is the true David, who restored the lyre of this body,

[45] Long lying in its decayed framework,

Silent through strings broken by ancient sin:

by assuming it, the Lord repaired it for his own use,

And, joining mortal beings to God, made all things of the created order

Bloom again in the likeness of their first form,

[50] So that everything might become new, with age passing away from all things.

God himself, the master who would renew this lyre,

Himself hung it upon the wood of the tree,

And, by the cross destroying sin in the flesh, made it new.

Thus he fashioned a mortal lyre suited to heavenly rhythms,

[55] One lyre from peoples of many kinds,

Joining peoples of every race into one body.

Then, with the strings aroused by the plectrum of the Word,

The voice of the Gospel’s tortoise-shell lyre fills all things

With the praise of God: throughout the world Christ’s golden lyre

[60] Resounds in countless tongues with a single melody,

And new songs answer God on evenly tuned strings.

[Col. 0553C] But let me return to what I began; for the time and hour have come

To offer you the promised feast,

To set before you breakfasts to be received chastely through attentive ears.

[65] I shall not repeat from ancient times what I am about to say.

I shall speak of something witnessed here only a few days ago.

A certain newcomer from the territory of the city of Abella

Had come to our dwelling to fulfill a vow pleasing to himself.

He had prepared a pig with careful attention,

[70] And, having delayed it for a long time so that it might grow both in years and in fatness,

Had brought it here from that place. When he arrived,

He slaughtered the fat animal according to the custom of one making a vow.

The report had stirred in his own people a sharp hunger

For the poor man’s great [or: “for the great need of the poor”]—

[Note: This passage is very corrupt in Muratorius, who reads in the Ambrosian manuscript: “The report had greatly inflamed among his people a fierce hunger,” and so forth. Our manuscript has: “The report had stirred in his own people a great hunger,” which is much more corrupt, though it is nevertheless corrupt. The error can be removed if *magna* is read as *magni* or *magnae*.]

[Col. 0554C] Their mouths gaped with hunger and with great hope of a share;

[Note: Both Muratorius’s manuscript and ours have *ora* (“mouths”). Muratorius thought the passage should be emended and read *ore* (“with the mouth”), because he had adopted the corrupt reading of the preceding verse. But it should be read *ora*.]

The old men stretched their throats toward the rich banquet,

[Note: Muratorius reads *fauces* (“throats”), since he had previously read *hiantes* (“gaping”). Our manuscript has *faucem* (“the throat”). As I said, both readings are plausible.]

[75] And the mouths of all were gaping toward the sumptuous feast.

Meanwhile the impoverished donor, without equitable division,

Divides the cut-up meat, takes for himself half the pig’s head,

And cooks only the innermost parts of its opened belly,

Dividing among the poor only the vital organs of the slaughtered pig,

[80] While keeping the whole body for himself,

And thinks he has fulfilled his vow; happily, he begins to return,

Daring to place the remains upon his pack animal

And, in them, to carry home the sacred pledges of his fulfilled vow,

Foolishly believing that he was carrying home the same thing.

[85] In those remains the avaricious man carried the loss of his soul

And the obstruction of his journey.

Finally, before he had been allowed to travel even a thousand paces,

In the open daylight, on a level embankment,

With no darkness to frighten him and no rough ground to trip him,

He fell from his horse and, as though fixed to the earth,

[90] Could not rise again to stand upright with restored strength.

He began to cry out that his feet were bound,

And, lying there, proved it, as though his soles had been joined by fetters.

Another wonder was joined to this event by chance:

While a sorrowful crowd of his relatives stood around him,

As he lay there in such weakness,

[95] The animal, upon which only the pork remained as a burden,

Without its rider and abandoned by its driver,

Of its own accord held itself back, with no one turning its rein,

As though it had recognized by itself the cause of the obstacle

Or had seen someone blocking the road along which it had begun to travel.

[100] Thus it fled along the road and turned back its course,

And with hurried steps ran back again to the hospitable dwelling,

Outstripping everyone whose attentive concern held them beside

The fallen man, who, as though his body were gradually broken,

[105] Struggled forward, though his stiff knees refused to let him proceed,

Confessing in tearful speech alike the unseen bonds upon his feet,

The desert of his fall,

And the cause of his punishment.

While the faithful band carried his sick body in the open daylight,

[Col. 0555A] Supported by hands burdened with their weight,

They brought him back to the sacred courts,

Praying that he might be restored at the very threshold

Of the physician Felix and might soon find there

[110] A sure remedy.

As the crowds carried him among their hands and through their throngs

Into the sacred courts, they marveled at him;

There, arranged in three groups along the long benches,

[Note: In the ancient churches a threefold gathering of people could be seen, all arranged along long benches and devoting themselves there to pious prayers. See Dodwell, *Cyprianic Dissertation* 5, no. 24. Perhaps each was supported from the revenues of the churches. First the old men are mentioned, then the pitiable crowd of the poor, and finally the gray-haired mothers. Of the first group I have nothing to say except that I believe they served the churches, so that, after the manner of the ancient law, they might bring offerings to the altar. This custom is still preserved in the metropolitan church of Milan, and they are called *veglones* by our manuscript of Beroldus, as also in several other ancient documents. That the poor were customarily fed from church revenues is explicitly taught by the Council of Antioch, canon 25; Chrysostom in many places; Possidius in the *Life of Saint Augustine*; and countless other Fathers, so that the matter needs no further clarification. — Muratorius.]

[115] The old men, the pitiable crowd of the poor,

And the gray-haired mothers sitting in the same company were astonished.

[Note: I consider it almost certain that deaconesses are meant here, whose rank and function flourished in the Church for many centuries. Only women of quite advanced age were admitted to this office, according to the Apostle’s instruction in 1 Timothy 5: “Let widows be chosen who are not less than sixty years old and have not been married twice.” Tertullian confirms this in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, book 27, as does the Theodosian Code, law 27, *Concerning Bishops and Clergy*. Hallier, *On Sacred Elections*, part 2, section 5, chapter 2, and Morin, *On the Sacred Orders*, provide further information about their ministry. I am certain that traces of them remain in the rites of the Ambrosian Church, since those widows here called *veglonissae* serve by carrying offerings to the sacred altar; this was likewise the function of ancient deaconesses, as Saint Jerome teaches in his commentary on Matthew 13. Both these women and those others were supported from the revenues of the church, as is attested by canon 103 of the Council of Carthage IV, the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book III, chapters 1, 2, and 3, and Balsamon in his commentary on chapters 18 and 24 of Basil’s letter to Amphilochius. Among others, hear Saint Jerome on Isaiah, chapter 3: “Nor is a widow supported with ecclesiastical provisions unless she is sixty years old.” — Muratorius.]

Moreover, many people whom their devotion had brought

From distant lands to the various holy buildings

Witnessed the remarkable pious event, since at the same time—

Indeed, on the same day—the transformation was so extraordinary.

[120] The same man who shortly before had departed from those very thresholds

On his own feet now returned,

And was carried in on another’s feet, hanging upon a supported body.

Elsewhere, the horse stood before the guesthouse doors,

Still laden with pork, with none of his companions attending it,

[125] Laden with the pork,

And no one known to him stood beside him

Who might undertake to relieve him of his burden

And lead the returning animal into familiar shelter.

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript reads *illi* (“to him”), whereas ours has *illa* (“that woman/that one”). The latter reading appears corrupt.]

Nevertheless, as though endowed with human reason,

[130] It stood like one seeking its own people and at once awaiting them,

Keeping its tracks firmly fixed in that place.

At the same time, flashing its ears and breathing through its nostrils,

It sought the familiar scents of accustomed people.

It was astonishing to the guests what the horse’s flight and condition might be,

[135] And the unfamiliar form of the event made the animal, known to its friends, seem uncertain,

Nor was anyone a witness of what had happened,

While everyone crowded inside around the man

Who had been carried by their hands into the sacred court

Of the martyr, where, sick, he had fallen before the holy threshold,

[140] His body thrown down, clinging to the doors,

Kissing them as a suppliant and washing them with his tears.

[Note: It was customary among Christians to press kisses upon the sacred doors of churches. Saint John Chrysostom, *Homily 30 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians*: “We are the temple of Christ. Therefore we kiss the vestibules of the temple and its entrance, as we kiss one another. Do you not see how many people also kiss the vestibules of this temple—some bowing down, others holding them with the hand and bringing the hand to the mouth?” Prudentius expresses the same more clearly in hymn 2, *On Saint Lawrence*:

“Even the lights of the Senate,

Once luperci and flamines,

Kiss the shrines

Of apostles and martyrs.”

Paulinus below:

“While he clings to the very doors

Of holy Felix and wipes them clean with kisses.”

The same author had said in *Nativity* VI:

“You lie before the doors and press kisses upon them,

And water the whole ground with tears,

Stretched upon the earth before the holy threshold.”

— Muratorius.]

Recognizing himself and confessing that his own head was the source of his suffering,

He uttered such complaints while accusing himself:

“O me, who have deserved to undergo such punishment,

[145] Wretched in this place, where, if any wretched person comes,

He is made happy! But I confess that I have rightly and deservedly

Received and suffered destruction equal to my wickedness,

So that, as the guilty one, I may now be punished within these very thresholds,

Burning as pain simultaneously scorches and constricts my feet—

[150] Feet by which, alas, madman that I was, I violated faith

Through fraud in the offering of the vowed gift,

Turning the gift into a loss of salvation.

Yet there is, there is something, I confess, that I can say:

Now, by a welcome exchange, sad things are being changed for me into gladness,

[Col. 0557B] And, as my mind already looks toward better things,

[155] The punishments themselves have begun to grow sweet to a mind looking toward better things, though my afflictions remain unbroken,

From which this very grace now comes to me:

That I have been permitted, wretched as I am, so quickly

To touch again the venerable threshold of Felix.

For if this misfortune had been absent or light,

[160] So that I could have continued along the course I had begun,

Then I would have been more unfortunate because of my prosperity:

My guilty fault would have remained to harm me,

And I would not have felt the wound driven inward into the bones of my soul

By rebellious flesh.

The strength of an uninjured body would have concealed

[165] The distinction of an unjust desert,

And a hardened mind would have bound me, inactive, in guilt,

Unless punishment had bound me after my fall.

[Col. 0557C] Therefore, powerful physician in the name of the Lord Christ,

Felix, let this now be enough for you and for the powerful Lord:

That not anger but mercy friendly to salvation

[170] Has brought about my punishment,

So that, with my body bound by guilt, it might loosen the guilt.

Behold, you have rightly drawn back the evil servant

And the voracious runaway,

By imposing fetters as punishment for his crime.

I am held as an unhappy debtor, bound, constricted, and burned,

[175] Set before everyone as an image of divine fear.

Attend to these things, all of you with trembling minds,

Which you now see me, wretched as I am, bear as an example for the rest.

For is anyone free from this error? Yet it pleased God

That an example should be made in one person,

So that my punishment might serve as a warning

[180] To those for whom there is no correction.

But now spare your wretched servant, I beg you, excellent Felix.

497–498 Spare me willingly; favor me and come to my aid:

My final anguish presses me to repeat my loud prayers.

Come quickly, lest death overtake the physician who delays.

But I know that the hand of the Lord—

The hand that strikes and, in its customary manner,

[185] Will also spare me—

Only do you now hasten to loosen for me, exhausted

And already giving way, the chain

Which you see, holy one, while I feel it.

Just as, secretly and silently, you bound the limbs of the fugitive

[Col. 0558B] With a hidden fetter,

So loosen, by invisible healing, the man who has returned.”

[190] While he cried out these words, clinging to the very doors

Of holy Felix and wiping them with kisses,

The pious crowd both saw and heard him amid the astonished groups.

Even as he lay there, he was raised up by hope,

And rebuked all delays and the tardy services of his companions.

[195] He ordered the pig to be brought immediately

And all its portions soon to be restored to the poor.

He asked that only enough be granted him to live

And that he be nourished by the satisfaction of the needy.

His companions hastened, vying with one another, to carry out his faithful commands.

They went to the familiar guesthouse;

There the burden was removed from the animal,

[200] The meat was cut into pieces,

And the divided portions were cooked over foaming fires.

[Note: Muratorius’s manuscript reads: “And the divided portions were cooked by the fire amid foaming liquids.” I have followed the reading of our manuscript.]

The cooked pieces were carried in numerous broad dishes.

The hunger of the poor was satisfied, and they returned thanks,

Giving words to God and asking forgiveness,

So that, having been appeased, they might be reconciled to the giver.

[205] There was no delay: as soon as the obligation of the vow had been discharged,

That debtor, inside, was released from the fitting structure of his chains;

And when, by the Lord’s mercy, his feet had been restored,

He flew out like a free horse or a bird released from nets,

And ran like a leaping stag.

[210] A wondrous faith is placed before the eyes.

Everyone rejoiced at God’s mercy, so readily bestowed and so powerful,

And at the merit of Felix, so great that Christ was present before them in him,

Powerfully directing both events according to the merits of human beings,

[Col. 0559A] So that he might be a physician to the repentant and an avenger to the wicked.

[215] Consider how great was the injustice of that fraudulent act,

By which the wretched man had earlier divided among the needy

What he ought to have returned entirely,

And had consumed only the head and intestines of the pig,

[220] While, heedless and wicked, he had made the remaining portion

Of the whole body his own.

Yet through the very thing by which he had become wretched,

He was soon made blessed,

As God’s blow of mercy exchanged guilt for him.

For such is God’s judgment:

Thus God, the arbiter, father, and king, regulates the weights of his lofty judgment,

[225] So that with measured examination he may balance justice peacefully for all,

And that a power tempered with kindness may warn the accused with a goad

Before destroying them with a thunderbolt,

So that, if the blow of the scourge sent beforehand proves beneficial,

[Col. 0559B] May the salvation entrusted to the sluggish person return safe.

[230] But if anyone, warned by the sacred terror of the scourge,

Refuses to feel the blow, he will depart unhealed;

And, reserved for death, will experience wrath in its fullness.

Thus the man who had first been wretched,

And soon afterward himself blessed,

Was healed in both flesh and soul by such a remedy.

[235] But because he recognized the cause,

And, recognizing it, repented while lying there,

He found in himself the care he deserved,

And in a short time experienced both outcomes,

Which divine peace and divine wrath preserve according to a just law:

The right and the work of vengeance,

So that punishment may rightly remain for the proud who are guilty,

[240] While mercy may preserve those who confess, having taken pity on them.

499–500 Therefore, released from his fetters, he joyfully retraced his steps,

The same man who had quickly changed from whole to weak and quickly from weak to free,

Returning from captivity with a joyful voice,

Exulting like the man whom Peter and John once ordered,

[245] At the word of the Lord, to rise up with strong feet in a leap—

The man who had been lame from his mother’s womb.

[Note: That is, “limping.” The word is certainly novel and unworthy of Paulinus, concerning whom Saint Jerome wrote in letter 13 to the same man: “If only the final hand were put to your work, we would have nothing sweeter, nothing more Latin, than your volumes.” Should one read *plaudentem* (“clapping”) or rather *claudum ante* (“formerly lame”)? The story is well known from Acts of the Apostles, chapter 3. — Muratorius.]

This poor man too, worthy of the threshold of the Beautiful Gate,

[Note: In Acts: “Whom they placed every day at the gate of the temple called Beautiful” (Ὃν ἐτίθουν καθ᾽ ἡμέραν πρὸς τὴν θύραν τοῦ ἱεροῦ τὴν λεγομένην ὡραίαν). — Muratorius.]

Whom God himself—the God of Peter and of Felix—

Has now healed among us by the same power of his word,

[250] Healed from a fall as he once healed the lame man

From the womb. By this power he now departed joyfully,

He who had poured out mournful prayers inwardly over his wound,

And behold, with a sound body, returned thanks outwardly.

What could I give back to Felix, my patron?

[255] What fitting thanks could I return to him for so great a gift,

Having so quickly been healed from so great a wound?

[Additional editorial notes omitted above, in source order: At line 683, Muratorius’s manuscript reads *cum*; but *tum* is to be read, as in our manuscript. At 487–488 Muratorius’s manuscript reads *Mente etenim consederat: hoc tamen unum*. Yet the verse limps; Muratorius therefore emended it to *Mente etenim placida consederat: hoc tamen unum*, adding *placida* himself. But it must be read exactly as in our manuscript. At 690 Muratorius’s manuscript, whose reading I have adopted, has *quotiensque manus armasset in illam*; our manuscript reads *quotiensque manus armasset, ut illam*, etc. The reading *ceu fractas* likewise follows the Muratorian manuscript; ours has *ceu fracta*. At 700 Muratorius’s manuscript has *avaris*; our manuscript’s *avarum* should be retained. At 705 it has *speciem*; I think *specie*, as in our manuscript, should be read. At 709 it has *confringere*, perhaps the better reading, for *contingere*. At 711 the word *profuit* was absent from Muratorius’s manuscript and was supplied by him; rightly, since it is also in ours. At 714 our manuscript has *cessere*; Muratorius’s has *incessere*, which I think should be read. Dungalus cites this verse and those following down to the end of the poem. At 719 Muratorius’s manuscript has *hominis*; our manuscript’s *hominum*, also read by Dungalus, is better. At 725 it has *medii*, a reading I prefer, though Dungalus reads *medium*. At 730 Muratorius’s manuscript has *nixa*, ours *fixa*; Dungalus too reads *fixa*. It reads *Et de cruce*, whereas ours has *vel de cruce*, which must be read or the verse limps; Dungalus too reads *vel*.

At line 2 of the present poem, the conjunction *et* is absent from Muratorius’s manuscript. At 9 ours reads *quo* for *queis*, but the former reading seems genuine. At 15 Muratorius has *voti*; perhaps *votis*, as in ours, should be read. At 17 Muratorius reads *Unde dapem instruerem, geminos dedit una*; the verse consequently limps, and it should be read as emended from our manuscript. At 25 Muratorius reads *Et pecora*; ours, *Per pecora*, must be read for the sense to stand. At 32 Paulinus had said the same in *Nativity* IX: “Thus God, the sole arranger and judge of all-sounding harmony, moves it through all the bodies of things.” Below, in *Nativity* XIII, he repeats the image of the lyre: “Let us all make from ourselves one lyre, a song composed of diverse strings.” At 34 our manuscript reads *Disparis harmoniae: quo tamquam corpus in unum*, etc.; Muratorius’s reading, which I have followed, is far more elegant. At 40 Muratorius reads *Solum et habens*; ours is much more elegant. At 45 it reads *patri*; our reading is better. At 48 ours reads *reviviscere*; I prefer Muratorius’s *revirescere*, since the second syllable of *reviviscere* is long. At 65 ours has *non*, Muratorius *nec*. At 70 Muratorius has *illuc*; I prefer our *illinc*, namely, “from the city of Abella.” At 72, for the practice of vows and offerings made to saints, see Dissertation XVIII. At 74 Muratorius reads *hiantes*; either reading is possible. At 77 three verses were absent from Muratorius’s manuscript and have been supplied from ours; its scribe passed from the first *dividit* to the second. At 80 Muratorius has *et* for *ac*, a matter of no consequence. At 91 Muratorius’s manuscript had *conjunctis*; *junctis*, as in ours and as Muratorius himself emended it, is demanded by metre. At 102 it has *ad hospita tecti*; ours is better. At 103 it has *quae*; *quem*, as in ours, must be read. At 105 Muratorius’s manuscript reads quite differently, *Caecaque vincla, pedem amissum, meritumque ruinae*; I prefer our reading. At 107 it reads *Illius, et poenae, lacrimosa voce fatentem*.

At 110 both manuscripts read *certam*; nevertheless I prefer Muratorius’s conjecture *certum reperire*, an entirely Greek and poetic elegance. At 125 Muratorius has *nec* for *neque*, which makes no difference. At 135 our manuscript’s *Ambigui nova forma feri* is plainly corrupt; Muratorius’s reading has been followed. His manuscript corruptly has *neque quisquam erat inde Accidui*. He noted that word and error required correction; but *inde* must be corrected from our manuscript, not *accidui*: just as in *Nativity* IV, verse 291, Paulinus makes *attiguum* from *attigit*, so here he makes *acciduum* from *accidit*. At 138 Muratorius reads *sacram* for *sanctam*. At 143 Muratorius reads *Hic ego*; ours has *o mihi* for *heu mihi*. At 145 it reads *Factus et inde miser*; ours has *hac in sede miser*, which pleases more. At 148 it has *ipse*; our *ipsa* is much more beautiful. At 156 it reads *quod factum mihi nunc*; our text should be read. At 162 it has *mansissetque*; Muratorius rightly emended it to the reading in ours. At 167 it has *in Domino*; I prefer our *in Domini*. At 170 it has *devinctam ut corpore*; I prefer our reading. It also reads *culpam solveret*, while ours has *culpa solveret*. At 171 it has *servumque, fugamque voracem*; ours is better. At 175 it reads *Mentibus haec trepidis omnes*; both readings are excellent. At 178 it has *Et praejudicium*; our reading seems preferable. At 185 ours reads *Parcit, in ore tuo est: citus ergo patronus adesto*; I judged the passage should be emended from Muratorius’s manuscript. At 187 ours has *aperto*; I emended it from Muratorius’s manuscript. At 200 Muratorius reads *Et divisa coquit lymphis spumantibus ignis*; I have followed our manuscript. At 205 ours has *compago*; I emended it from Muratorius’s manuscript. At 212 ours has *assit*. At 215 ours has *sit*; I emended it from Muratorius. At 217 ours reads *istis*; Muratorius’s *istic* must be read. At 219 Muratorius has *reliquum*; this appears to be a printer’s error. At 225 Muratorius has *tacitam*, ours *placidam*; the latter seems better. At 227 it reads *Ante reos moneat, stimulo quam fulminet ullo*; I think our reading should be read. At 228 the entire verse was corrupt in Muratorius’s manuscript, which read *Ut si profuerit praemiis, sine verberis icta*; I emended it from ours. At 230 Muratorius has *sacri*, ours *sacro*; either is possible. At 235 both manuscripts have *sed*, but Muratorius would prefer *se*, which I too approve. At 236 ours reads *merito curam sibi memet in ipso*; Muratorius’s is very different: *meritum curae sibimet simul ipse*. At 237 ours has *inque brevem expertus*; I have followed Muratorius’s *inque brevi est expertus*, required by both metre and sense. At 238 Muratorius has *omne*; *omnes*, as in ours, must be read. At 239 it has *uti*; I removed this error by following our manuscript. At 243 it has *insultans*. At 246 it has *exsurgere*. At 250 it has *excessu*, ours *de casu*. At 251 it has *ista*, ours *qua*. At 252: “Or *moestus*?” At 255 it has *pro tanto munere dignas*; I have followed our manuscript.]

I did not pay a physician’s fee, nor endure the grievous discomforts of a sickbed,

nor medicines administered through scalpels or fire,

nor bitterly biting juices from various plants.

[Note: Pliny the Elder’s complaints against physicians, in Book XIX, chapter 1, are exceedingly well known; nor did Leonardus a Capua, the most expert medical philosopher of our age, receive less applause for his book *On the Uncertainty of Medicine and Medicaments*, which in recent years we saw prohibited, to our regret. I should like to add Bernardinus Ramazzinus, a most distinguished man who deserved excellently of medicine: in his dissertation *On the Constitutions of the Years* 1692, 1693, and 1694, no. 25, he becomes somewhat indignant with cruel physicians and elegantly censures their uncertain method of treatment, calling fortunate the rustic people who trust their parish priest more than a physician. The very learned Harvey, too, not long ago published a dissertation *On the Deceits, Lies, etc., of Physicians*. St Bernard, in Letter 321 to the brothers of St Anastasius, says: “For this reason it is quite unfitting for your religious profession to seek bodily medicines, nor is it expedient for salvation.” In the same place he teaches rather that recourse should be had to spiritual remedies, in which there is a power greater than that of human remedies. John Molanus vainly attempts to soften this passage of the mellifluous doctor in his *Diary*, chapter 34. St Jerome likewise relates in the *Life of Hilarion* that a woman who complained that she had spent all her substance upon physicians was brought to this saint; Hilarion said to her: “If you had distributed to the poor what you lost by giving it to physicians, the true physician Jesus Christ would have cured you.” Muratori.]

[260] A medicine more savage than the diseases and wounds themselves had attacked my body, as happens to those whom a suspect human hand visits with its art,

and continually handles, trembling, with uncertain relief.

Now, carried within a short time to the very throne of holy Felix

[Note: Our manuscript mistakenly has *ad illum*, “to him.” I follow the reading of the Muratorian manuscript.]

[265] and thrown down upon that threshold, broken upon marble as cold as it was hard,

I lay there suffering; and prayer was my only speech,

faith alone my medicine. I saw no one coming,

yet I felt a physician. And who was this physician, unless Christ himself,

[270] or Felix, powerful through Christ and bearing the name of Christ?

I felt neither of them at that time, and yet he himself was present in both,

as though he might quickly rebuke me, a sinner, and heal me in my pain.

Equal was the manner, though differing in appearance, of the Lord who chastised me

[275] and spared me. The healer and the avenger were hidden from my eyes;

punishment and remedy shone forth.

Now, with my vows completed in their full order,

I shall go home rejoicing in my physician, and safe under the protection

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *totusque*, “entirely safe,” but incorrectly; I have corrected it from our manuscript.]

of Felix, my patron forever. I shall no longer fear

[280] any dangers of the road that may meet me, as before;

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads: “I shall fear no danger any longer.”]

for danger will be absent, since the cause of danger has been removed.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript reads: “for danger will be absent, since there is no cause of danger.” I approve the reading of our manuscript because of the words that immediately follow.]

My faith, not yet fulfilled, had bound me, and now fulfilled it has released me.

Yet, I beg you, let your faith, rightly fulfilled, bind me to you;

[Note: This verse was missing from Muratori’s manuscript; I added it from our manuscript. The Muratorian manuscript instead read: “For the danger will be absent, since there is no cause of danger. Yet faith not fulfilled will bind me: let your…”]

let your love, Felix, always bind me. Weave this chain for me,

[285] so that neither death nor life may ever release me from you.

But all who saw my sufferings,

and in your merit saw the mighty hand of Christ exalted

with great signs, must recognize

[290] how much good my suffering provided for them, so that now

they may beware of sparing their earthly possessions,

and, while seeking profits, acquiring losses to their salvation.

For if it was wrong for me to have deprived the poor of food

by withholding the flesh of a worthless animal, what shall we say of those

[295] who embrace riches with excessive love?

Who lie upon metals dug up and buried together with their hearts,

and, by keeping these superfluities hidden away, show that they protect them

far from their proper use?

What will they do? What will they say to you, Christ, on their own behalf—

those who have seized so great a portion from the needy

[300] and have secured no salvation for themselves from their surplus?

One messenger departs. Now we shall set out the pleasant dishes of a second course;

but although we shall again serve the same flesh seasoned

with a different sauce,

[305] I shall unfold once more for you the remarkable work that Felix performed with the swine,

with marvelous novelty.

The earlier event occurred first, but, having been passed over in our earlier books,

it shall now be sung as though preserved for the present time.

It does not matter at what time the deed was performed;

[310] for the worker is one and the same through the changing years—

Christ, who performs different miracles of his saints’ praise

throughout all lands.

Certain farmers from our own region, cultivating fields farther away

in Apulia, beyond the city of Beneventum,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *Veneventum*. See what we said on *Carmen* 11, verse 510.]

[315] selected from a bristly herd one pig, still young,

whose tender muzzle was pressing the milk-filled teats,

[Note: *Sumen, suminis*, “udder,” is so called from sucking. Lucilius, *Satires*, Book IV, quoted by Nonius:

“Yet if no woman can be so hard-bodied,

nevertheless, shaken by a tender arm,

she grows weak, and the more generous hand of the nursing woman rests upon the teat.”

Lampridius, in the *Life of Alexander Severus*: “He ordered that no one should kill a sow with teats, no one a suckling.” Casaubon, in his notes, explains *suminatam* as “fattened,” but nevertheless thinks the sense better if the text is corrected to read: “No one should kill a sow with teats.” In fact, *sumen* is properly used of a sow’s breasts, and from them a sort of forcemeat was made, often mentioned by Pliny and Martial. Salmasius, commenting on the same passage of Lampridius, thinks *suminatam* should be understood as a sow, and *lactantem* as a young pig. Pliny, Book XI, chapter 37, asserts that *sumina* formerly came under the name “abdomen.” I leave consultation of him open to everyone. Muratori.]

and, having tended it with great care for a long time,

fed the pig as a vow and began to lead it, prepared,

to the sacred court of holy Felix,

so that, slaughtered from its large body, it might feed many needy people.

[Note: Votive offerings customarily brought for the support of the poor are mentioned repeatedly by Paulinus, because such offerings greatly pleased the martyrs. Indeed, the practice of agapes was once praised in the Church; by this name pious banquets held within churches were distinguished. At them the poor shared in the tables of the rich, and the fervor of charity was nourished. But since many inconveniences arose from them, agapes were removed from Christian gatherings. The practice of offerings nevertheless continued to some extent, and St Augustine records that offerings made in honor of the martyrs were mentioned in *The City of God*, Book VIII, chapter 7; the poor were also invited to share in them:

“Whatever,” he says, “is presented as the service of the devout at the places of the martyrs is an adornment of memorials, not sacred things or sacrifices of the dead as though they were gods. Those, too, who bring their meals there—something which better Christians do not do, and which in most regions is not customary—when they have set them out, pray and remove them so that they may eat, or distribute some of them to the needy; they wish these offerings to be sanctified there through the merits of the martyrs in the name of the Lord.” Muratori.]

[320] and the martyr might rejoice in feeding the satisfied poor.

But the pig, heavy with excessive fat,

could not long carry itself, its weight exceeding the strength of its feet;

at the very beginning of the road it collapsed under its own weight,

and afterward could not be moved by voice, hand, or goad.

They left it lying there;

[325] its sorrowing owners entrusted the abandoned animal to their hosts.

Their anxious minds wavered between alternatives:

their pious hearts did not wish to turn back from the path of their vow,

yet they were ashamed to go far again to Felix’s revered threshold,

empty-handed and without the promised gift.

Thus a decision remained fixed in their perplexed minds:

[330] they should choose from the same stock as many younger pigs

as the one pig had advanced in years,

so that, through many small animals, they might weigh out one large one.

Thus they came to this sacred place, and, their vows fulfilled,

returned to their lodging, which was not nearby.

For at that time, by chance, the houses around the martyr’s court

[335] had been filled and crowded with their customary throngs.

[Note: Paulinus often remarked how great a multitude gathered to venerate St Felix. In *Natalis* III, after listing many peoples who converged on Nola for this reason, he adds:

“One day calls them all, and one Nola receives them all;

its thresholds are wholly full of its people and spacious enough for everyone,

so that you might think the walls expanded for countless guests.

Thus Nola rises in the image of Rome.” Muratori.]

Therefore, at some distance from here, in a secluded countryside,

they were content to enter a remote hut,

where in the morning they planned to set out on the return journey,

when the first dawn, in labor, began to redden the day.

The hut’s door was open.

[Note: [Col. 0564C] The Muratorian manuscript was corrupt here, reading *tuguri forte aperti*. We restored *tuguri fore aperta* (“that the hut’s [door] would be open”) from our manuscript.]

[340] The host, a man, came out from the roofed dwelling,

and saw the familiar pig standing before the doors,

prepared for slaughter in a wondrous manner,

as though it were saying that it had been sent by the Lord and was present.

[Note: [Col. 0564C; line 345] Our manuscript reads *astare* (“to stand”), while the Muratorian manuscript reads *adstare* (“to stand by”). The former reading is better.]

Like one greeting him, it licked the feet

of its rejoicing master and, with a gesture,

grunted softly at the one who had nourished it.

[345] Gentle, it sniffed and, moving its snout, gave kisses;

and, as though it recognized that it owed the offering to its master,

it thrust itself forward and invited the slow knives with its throat.

Under whose guidance, I ask, did it travel roads through unknown lands?

What feet did it use, so that it could run so far,

when, after only short stretches at the beginning of its journey,

it had collapsed beneath the mass of its flowing fat?

[Note: In our manuscript verse 355 is placed after verse 356. It is written there as follows: “It failed beneath the mass of its flowing fat, which, after short stretches at the beginning of the roads…” But I preferred to follow the reading of the Muratorian manuscript.]

[350] Certainly no human hand carried so great an animal along a lengthy road;

no lap carried it, nor did its own mind compel it

to penetrate so extensive a road through an unknown region.

Even human beings, although endowed with sound reason

and able to be guided through unknown places by an interpreter’s speech,

[355] if they lack a guide by whom the road may be made clear to them,

blindly become entangled in error in foreign lands.

Who, then, directed the animal’s journey?

Whence did it gain the will to follow its masters,

or even the understanding to do so?

[360] Aware that it had been compelled for a long time toward the vow,

whence did this care arise in the animal—

a care that rarely rouses the faithful—

so that, as though guilty of a personal act,

the lazy pig, enclosed by fear,

[365] might remain behind,

and, by remaining withdrawn and then coming,

seek to atone for its fault and compensate for the vice of sluggish idleness,

although it followed its masters only belatedly?

The marvelous event is plain:

[370] a prodigy was granted by heavenly authority to such a bold undertaking,

so that the pig alone might make the long journey,

and possess such intelligence that, along a straight path,

it could find its way through unknown spaces.

And what of this even greater marvel:

[375] that, arriving here from the Trans-Beneventine territories,

it was not caught by the public paved road

running boldly across the raised embankment,
