nor by the frequent traffic it encountered anywhere,

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *seu strata*, while ours has *constrata*. Roads were formerly called *stratae*, hence the Italian word *strada*, because they were paved with stones. Thus Paulinus, *Natalis* XIII:

“When, breathing silently into my mind, you ordered me

to prepare and pave the road leading to your dwelling.”

The same saint, in the poem to Cytherius, concerning the Appian Way:

“After this he begins to proceed toward us by the road

whose embankment the stone paves,

to which its builder Appius gave his name.”

Tibullus, writing to Messalla, likewise says:

“For here the hard gravel, heaped up by your wealth,

is spread, and here the stone is joined by fitting craft.”

Therefore Procopius, Book II *On the Persian War*, p. 46, says: “A paved or stone-laid road is called in the language of the Latins *strata*.” Nor was this an invention of the later centuries, but the Latins of the better age themselves used the word. Virgil says in the First Book of the *Aeneid*, “the paved roads.” Lucretius likewise:

“And now we see the stone-paved roads,

worn down beneath the feet of the people.”

Hence our *Natalis* XI:

“He avoided the paved roads.”

*Strata* was also used in Paulinus’s age without any additional word, for in Book VI of the Theodosian Code, concerning imperial images, issued by the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, we read: “Far be it from us to count the construction of public roads, bridges, and paved ways among sordid duties.” See Gothofredus on the same law; Du Fresne, *Glossarium Latinitatis*, under STRATA; Isidore, Book XV, chapter 16; and Juvencus, Book II. Muratori.]

[380] whether it traveled along hidden woodland paths,

where no human hand with iron, nor any wild beast with its bite,

came in its way.

What hand alone guided it, or protected it as it went?

Surely, hidden by some cloud, it deceived the eyes;

[385] carried through the air—or rather coming by wind than by its feet—

it suddenly descended at the Lord’s lodging itself

and stood before the unknown threshold as a four-footed guest.

I shall tell of another wonder, close to this one.

Some people, likewise setting out from a distant place,

[390] had raised a young heifer, separated by breed from the herd,

kept apart from its mother’s nursing breast,

and dedicated as a votive gift to our poor—

the many poor whom, gathered there in a great crowd,

the bounty of Felix feeds through the generous aid of many.

[395] When the heifer had already exulted in its adult limbs

and, its body fully developed, had become fit to fulfill the vow,

they wanted to bring it forward from the house.

But since it seems to be the custom of those who carry their vows

to the martyrs from far away to fulfill them,

they attempted to harness it to the wagon by which they were to be conveyed,

[400] and attempted to attach it to the yoke,

although it was unaccustomed to this, yet already gentle

and previously subdued to human uses.

Its masters had taken it small from the herd,

mingled it with their household and food,

and therefore, thinking that its wildness had been tamed,

[405] expected it readily to submit beneath the yokes

and offer its docile neck.

They soothe it with a caressing hand and try to draw it into the narrow harness.

At first, trusting that these familiar touches are playful,

it consents and follows those calling it.

[410] But when it saw the reins brought close to the yoke

and felt the straps being prepared for its neck,

indignant at the trickery and suddenly transformed,

it became wild.

It accepted neither the yoke upon its neck nor the bonds around its throat,

and, with its handlers defeated and the straps thrown back,

[415] it sprang away from the group that tried to retain it.

It sought the distant fields,

fleeing its masters and the familiar dwelling.

Nor did it, after the manner of wild animals,

snatch itself out of human sight

and hide the fugitive in blind woodland paths.

[420] Rather, fleeing its masters, it stood at a distance as they departed,

and fled in such a way that it would not endure being left in the countryside.

Finally, when it saw a wagon joined to a pair of oxen

and moving along, it understood its human purpose,

and, as though conscious that it owed itself to the vow,

began to become a companion to those setting out.

[425] It did not remain far away as their companion;

it disdained to go at the slow pace of the wheels,

but, as though exulting in its running,

it overtook the groaning procession of the heavy wagon,

flying ahead and looking back at the wheels.

It no longer feared being forced beneath the yoke.

[430] It became friendly with what it had previously hated,

and went before the wagon,

until they came to the sacred court of Felix.

[Note: The word *est* is absent from the Muratorian manuscript; this is of little importance.]

There it voluntarily stopped its step,

attached itself to those calling it,

and, as though bound by the vow,

[435] rejoiced to stand in the very place

where it owed its own slaughter as a victim.

That rebellious creature, not subject to human bonds,

was led to a peaceful death without resistance,

submitting its undefiled neck to the axe,

providing food for the poor from its slaughtered body,

and gladly pouring out its blood for the vow of its masters.

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *dolos*, “tricks,” while ours has *dolis*, “at the tricks.” The reader may judge which is better.]

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *vinctum*, “bound,” while ours has *junctum*, “joined.”]

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *currere*, “to run,” while ours has *tendere*, “to proceed.”]

[Note: Our manuscript has *comis*. I think *comes*, “companion,” should be read, as in the Muratorian manuscript. The first syllable of *comis* is long.]

[Note: The Muratorian manuscript has *insultante*, “exulting,” while ours has *exultante*. Both readings are plausible.]

[507–508] Why this? Is there perhaps, as the Apostle says,

any concern for animals on God’s part?

[Note: St Paul, First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter IX: “For it is written in the law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.’ Is God concerned with oxen?” Muratori.]

But he who made everything for our sake

works everything for us, the author of all things,

and through animals that do not know what they are doing

performs signs for our benefit,

stirring our dull minds by manifest wonders

to strengthen faith and trust in the truth,

so that human beings, with tongues freed for speech,

may not remain silent about the Lord,

whom mute creatures proclaim through signs.

## Textual apparatus for the pig episode, lines 291–341

[Col. 0561D; line 291] The Muratorian manuscript reads *malo* (“evil” or “misfortune”); the reading of our manuscript, *malum* (“wrong” or “evil”), is better.

[Col. 0561D; line 294] The Muratorian manuscript reads *vano* (“vain”); ours reads *multo* (“great” or “much”).

[Col. 0561D; line 304] Our manuscript reads *nobis* (“for us”). But *vobis* (“for you”) should be read, as in the Muratorian manuscript.

[Col. 0562D; line 318] The Muratorian manuscript reads *sancitam* (“sanctioned”). But *sacratam* (“consecrated”), as in our manuscript, should be read.

[Col. 0563C; line 320] The Muratorian manuscript reads *Sed grave sagina* (“But heavy with fat”), a wholly corrupt reading; I therefore emended it from our manuscript to *Sed gravis arvina* (“But the pig, heavy with fat”).

[Col. 0563C; line 320] The Muratorian manuscript corruptly had *porcus superante pedumque*. I emended the passage from our manuscript to *porcus superante pedum vim* (“the pig, its weight exceeding the strength of its feet”).

[Col. 0563C; line 328] The Muratorian manuscript reads *rursus* (“again”) for *rursum*; this makes no difference.

[Col. 0563C; line 328] Our manuscript corruptly reads *longo* (“long”) for *longe* (“far”).

[Col. 0563D; line 330] The Muratorian manuscript has *Et* (“And”); ours has *Ut* (“that” or “so that”), which I approve.

[Col. 0563D; line 331] In *totidém*, Paulinus made one syllable out of two. —Muratori.

[Col. 0563D; line 331] The Muratorian manuscript corruptly reads *eadem de grege* (“the same [number] from the herd”). I restored the passage from our manuscript as *eadem de gente* (“the same [number] from the stock”).

[Col. 0563D; line 332] The Muratorian manuscript reads *legunt* (“they choose”); the text has *legant* (“that they should choose”).

[Col. 0563D; line 333] The Muratorian manuscript reads *ineptus* (“inept”); ours has *iners sus* (“the sluggish pig”), which is the correct reading.

[Col. 0563D; line 337] The Muratorian manuscript reads *huc* (“to here”); ours has *hunc* (“this”), in *sacrum hunc … locum* (“this sacred place”).

[Col. 0563D; line 339] Our manuscript reads *aulas* (“courts”). I preferred the Muratorian manuscript’s *aulam* (“court”).

[Col. 0564C; line 340] Our manuscript corruptly reads *denseta*; the text has *densata* (“made dense” or “crowded”).

[Col. 0564C; line 341] Our manuscript reads *praeterea* (“besides”). I prefer the Muratorian manuscript’s *propterea* (“therefore”).

## Textual apparatus for the pig and heifer episodes, lines 345–440

[Col. 0564C; line 347] The Muratorian manuscript reads *se missum Domino* (“sent to the Lord”). I approve the reading of our manuscript, *se missum a Domino* (“sent by the Lord”).

[Col. 0564D; line 358] Both our manuscript and Muratori’s have *subegit* (“compelled” or “made [it] penetrate”), although Muratori would prefer to read *coegit* (“drove” or “compelled”).

[Col. 0564D; line 361] Our manuscript corruptly reads *Per que ignota rei*. The text must be read as in the Muratorian manuscript: *Perque ignota regi faciles interprete lingua* (“and [those] easily guided through unknown places by an interpreter’s speech”).

[Col. 0564D; line 363] The Muratorian manuscript reads *extremis* (“remotest”) for *externis* (“foreign”). I prefer the reading of our manuscript.

[Col. 0564D; line 365] The Muratorian manuscript reads *paratum* (“prepared”); ours has *coactum* (“compelled”).

[Col. 0564D; line 368] The Muratorian manuscript reads *astu* (“by cunning” or “by a device”). The printed note then says that *astu*, as in our manuscript, should be read, although the main text has *actu* (“by an act”); the note is internally inconsistent and its reported forms are retained here.

[Col. 0564D; line 369] Our manuscript reads *sancto subjecta timore* (“subjected by holy fear”). I preferred the Muratorian manuscript’s *sancto sus cincta timore* (“the pig encompassed by holy fear”): to what noun could the feminine adjective *subjecta* refer? To *pecus* in line 367? But *pecus* there is neuter. Thus anyone wishing to read *subjecta* for *sus cincta* would have to read *pecudi* (“to the beast,” feminine dative), rather than *pecori* (“to the beast,” neuter dative), in line 367.

[Col. 0565C; line 374] This verse limped in the Muratorian manuscript because the word *tanto* (“so great”) was missing; I supplied it from our manuscript.

[Col. 0565C; line 377] The Muratorian manuscript reads *quod et hoc quam grande* (“and what [is] this, how great”). I followed our manuscript’s *quid et hoc tam grande* (“and what of this so great [a marvel]”).

[Col. 0565C; line 378] The Muratorian manuscript reads *Trans Veneventanis*; the text has the compound *Transbeneventanis* (“Trans-Beneventine”).

[Col. 0566C; line 380] Muratori reads *numquam caepere* (“never caught”). Ours reads *nusquam cepere* (“caught nowhere”), which I follow.

[Col. 0566C; line 381] The Muratorian manuscript corruptly had *igitur* (“therefore”). *Egit* (“it pursued” or “traveled”) must be read, as in our manuscript.

[Col. 0566C; line 385] The Muratorian manuscript had *aera* (“air,” accusative). Muratori correctly emended it to *aere* (“through the air”), as in our manuscript.

[Col. 0566C; line 386] Our manuscript reads the whole verse *Et subita hospitium domini delapsus ab aura* (“And, suddenly gliding down from a breeze, [it came] to the Lord’s lodging”). I preferred the reading of the Muratorian manuscript used in the text.

[Col. 0566C; line 390] The Muratorian manuscript reads *hac* (“from this”); ours has *huc* (“to here”), which I follow.

[Col. 0566C; line 391] The Muratorian manuscript reads *lactentis* (“suckling”); I emended it from our manuscript to *lactantis* (“nursing”).

[Col. 0566D; line 393] The Muratorian manuscript reads *ista* (“that”); I removed this corruption by following our manuscript’s *istic* (“there”).

[Col. 0566D; line 399] The Muratorian manuscript read *plaustrum subjungere* (“to yoke the wagon”). Muratori emended it to *plaustro subjungere* (“to yoke [her] to the wagon”), but the phrasing still gaped. The reading must be *plaustro subjunctam* (“yoked to the wagon”), as in our manuscript.

[Col. 0566D; line 400] The Muratorian manuscript reads *submittere* (“to place beneath”); the text has *subjungere* (“to yoke”). Either reading is plausible.

[Col. 0566D; line 401] I emended the text from our manuscript. The Muratorian manuscript reads *tamen ut mitem jam mente subacta* (“yet, as gentle, now subdued in mind”) for *tamen ut mitem, jamque ante subactam* (“yet as gentle and already subdued”).

[Col. 0566D; line 405] The Muratorian manuscript reads *in artum* (“into a narrow space”) for *in arctum* (“into the tight harness”).

[Col. 0566D; line 417] The Muratorian manuscript reads *adstans* (“standing by”) for *astans* (“standing”).

[Col. 0568B; line 440] I emended *ignaras* (“unaware”) from our manuscript; the Muratorian manuscript has *ignotas* (“unknown”).

# Muratori’s Preface to St Paulinus’s Thirteenth *Natalis*

[Col. 0567]

[509–510] Beyond the other *Natales*, the thirteenth is unquestionably the most distinguished, both because of the abundant learning and the deeds of Paulinus explained there at length, and because of the eminent men and pious women who, established at Nola, were present while the bishop recited the poem and increased the value of the solemnity.

The year in which the *Natalis* was delivered was the year 406 of the common era, as Chiffletius proves by solid arguments in the second part of his *Pauline Illustrated*, and as Prosper’s *Chronicle* confirms. For there Radagaisus is said to have been utterly defeated with his army during the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius, namely in the year 405. Paulinus therefore sings of peace restored to Italy in the following year, and the *Natalis* must accordingly be assigned to 406.

Let us now see who those distinguished men and women were in whose presence our poet recited this most elegant poem. The following verses show that there were ten together with Paulinus:

“Therefore, nine parents with their joined offspring,

let us be, in harmonious hearts, like a single lyre.

Let Aemilius come as the tenth.

Then at last the mystical law will sing in us

with its complete number.”

Let us recall their names individually. First of all are mentioned:

“Turcius with pious countenance, and Suecrius in the flower of youth.”

Turcius is the same as Apronianus, a man of senatorial rank, who is later commended in these verses:

“Apronianus, glory of the Turcian race,

a boy in age, but an old man in the understanding of the flesh.”

Suecrius—if this name is correctly transmitted in the manuscript—either represents Asterius, the son of the Turcius Apronianus just mentioned, of whom Paulinus later says:

“But another light equal to mine shines for me in Asterius,”

or else Pinianus, a man of senatorial rank, who appears shortly afterward.

Two girls follow:

“Two girls likewise,

Alfia, such as that sister of Philemon once was,

noble in title, whom Paul’s Epistle records;

and with her Eunomia, already a maiden betrothed

to everlasting chambers in heaven.”

The name of one girl is clear: Eunomia, whose parents were Turcius Apronianus and Avita. The name of the other must be supplied: it was Melania the Younger, whose mother was Albina. Only she could be called a girl because of her tender age and her mother’s presence.

This is expressed more clearly below:

“For these mothers there are two pledges, three in one sex:

a double flower, Melania’s offspring, and Eunomia.”

“Melania’s offspring” is used for Melania, either because she was descended from the son of the elder Melania, or, more correctly, according to the custom of poets—especially Greek poets—who commonly use similar expressions instead of a proper name. Thus Homer has βίη Πριάμοιο, “the strength of Priam,” that is, Priam; ἶς Τηλεμάχοιο, “the strength of Telemachus,” that is, Telemachus; and Lucretius has “the strength of the spirited horse,” meaning the horse; while Virgil has “the strength of the fragrant hounds,” meaning the hounds.

Since it is certain that Melania is meant here, I became uncertain about the name Alfia. For Philemon’s sister was not called Alfia but, in Greek, Ἀπφία, and correctly Appia in the Latin Vulgate. If this is the intended meaning—“such as Appia, the sister of Philemon, was”—the name must be corrected and Appia restored.

I am more inclined, however, to the view that Alfia was also a name of Melania, and that a comma should be placed after Alfia. This name was known to the ancients, as many inscriptions show, and the text itself seems to support this interpretation: when it later says, “and with her Eunomia,” it strongly suggests that the name of the other girl had already been expressed above.

Next comes Albina, the mother of that same Melania:

“Albina is first of the chorus.”

And later, when speaking of Melania, he joins Albina with her mother.

Then follows Haerasia:

“Equal is Haeresia,”

or, as we shall say in Dissertation 5, this may be Therasia, and the text should accordingly be corrected:

“With Therasia, her equal.”

She was the wife of Paulinus in the world, and afterward, together with him, embraced a most devout continence and continued to live at Nola.

Another woman, Avita, is then mentioned:

“To her her sister is joined in the yoke, so that she is the third leader,

Avita, mother of the hymn-singing choirs.”

Avita was the wife of Turcius Apronianus and bore him two children, Asterius and Eunomia, mentioned above.

After these comes Pinianus, a man of senatorial rank, the husband of Melania the Younger:

“To him draws near his companion, joined by an equal yoke,

Pinianus, younger in age, equal in faith.”

He forms an equal yoke with Turcius, for both were married.

If Paulinus himself and Aemilius are added to these, there can be no doubt that they are the ten whom the poet indicated in the verse quoted above.

With this established, it becomes clear why he sang:

“Therefore this entire company is: three names among the mothers,

four among the children, and two among the fathers.”

Albina, Avita, and Therasia were the mothers. Although Therasia was not then distinguished by any child known to have been born to her, her age and the son whom she had once received in Spain identified her.

The two daughters belonged to the mothers: Melania to Albina, and Eunomia to Avita. Paulinus expressed this more clearly:

“For these mothers there are two pledges, three in one sex:

a double flower, Melania’s offspring, and Eunomia.”

Two male sons follow, namely Pinianus and Asterius. The latter acknowledged Turcius as his natural father, while the former acknowledged Paulinus as his spiritual father. Hence the saint says:

“With Paulinus as father, this Turcius too is equally a father;

but my age makes me a father, and offspring makes him one.”

Thus four children and two fathers are plainly identified.

We have treated all these persons individually in separate dissertations, to which we refer the reader.

In any event, the fame of Paulinus’s holiness and the most devout life he led had brought those distinguished Romans to Nola, so that, having renounced the world, they might live there with one heart for themselves and for God.

Paulinus was evidently professing the monastic life there, and many wished to learn under his direction the beginnings of a better and safer discipline.

This explains why St Augustine, who was himself a bishop, called Pinianus “brother”; the holy doctor would certainly not have addressed him by that name unless Pinianus had been at least a lay monk.

The author of St Melania’s *Life*, in Surius under 31 January, says that Pinianus and Melania sailed to Sicily partly to sell the estates they possessed there and partly to visit the most holy bishop Paulinus, who was their father according to the spirit.

See how perfectly everything agrees.

That author is mistaken, however, in suggesting that this illustrious company went to Paulinus merely out of a sense of duty. They undertook that journey both to avoid the Goths, who were threatening the city, and to dedicate their lives there forever to the service of Christ.

Certainly Paulinus says:

“Therefore Felix, at Christ’s command, hid these people in his own bosom;

he received them beneath his roofs,

and took them with me as everlasting guests.”

Further on he adds:

“We received our companions into our dwelling,

and now, by equal right, we hold the rights of Felix;

joined to the bosom of Felix our father,

we are cherished as his pledges.”

So conspicuously had Paulinus—formerly a man of the highest nobility and wealth—renounced secular affairs that he alone was almost proposed as an example of perfection.

See Augustine’s Letter 34 to Paulinus, and Letter 39 to Licentius, and again Letter 59 to Paulinus himself. Consult Jerome likewise in Letter 34 to Julian, and Sacchinus in the second part of his *Life of Paulinus*.

The reason why this distinguished company did not remain long at Nola seems to have been the renewed movement of the barbarians. Later, in the year 410, threatening Italy with slavery, they entered the city itself with a most disastrous assault, filling it with slaughter and plunder, and laying waste even Campania.

In this *Natalis*, moreover, many passages are offered to illuminate the deeds of so great a bishop. I have treated all of them, as far as my powers allowed, in Dissertation 9 and those that follow.

# Poem XXI. Thirteenth Song on St Felix

[Note: In our manuscript the title of the poem is: “Here begins Book XIII.”]

[Col. 0571A]

[513–514] Bright peace, welcome to us, leads the year

in the season’s change, after the winters have passed,

with tranquil light.

[Note: In the preceding year, that is, in the year of Christ 405, during the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius, a great victory over the Goths was won, as Prosper asserts in his *Chronicle*. Therefore Paulinus sings that peace was restored to Italy in the present year, 406. I added “welcome,” so as to complete the poem, which is defective in the manuscript. Muratori.]

[Note: I corrected this passage from our manuscript. In the Muratorian manuscript the verse was defective and read: “Bright peace, welcome in place of the season, leads the year.” Muratori had supplied the word “welcome” after “peace” on his own.]

It opens to peoples in safety the day marked by the honor of holy Felix,

while Felix, rejoicing, urges us to celebrate with serene minds,

[Note: [Col. 0571C] I corrected this passage from our manuscript; the Muratorian manuscript corruptly read *signatumque pio* for *signatamque diem* (“and the day marked”).]


after the dreadful darkness of war has been wiped away,

because he himself, together with Fathers Paul and Peter

and the blessed brother martyrs,

entreated the King of kings, by his gracious favor,

to prolong the times of Roman rule,

[10] and to drive away the Getae, already pressing at the very jaws of the city,

turning against them the destruction or bondage

that they were threatening as the final fate of the Roman kingdom.

[Note: Paulinus is supported by Orosius, Book VII, chapter 37 of the *History*, who says the same concerning Radagaisus, king of the Goths: “When he was threatening the Roman strongholds, a gathering of all the pagans into the city took place.” And below: “Having now entered the bosom of Italy, he was shaking Rome, trembling with terror, from nearby.” St Augustine touches upon this Gothic invasion in *The City of God*, Book V, chapter 23: “When Radagaisus, king of the Goths, with a huge and monstrous host already stationed near the city, was threatening Roman necks.” Muratori.]

[Note: Orosius, cited above, agrees with Paulinus: “Radagaisus, as is customary among barbarous peoples, had vowed to offer to his gods the blood of the entire Roman race.” Muratori.]

Now, therefore, with fear driven away,

[Note: [Col. 0571D] The Muratorian manuscript reads *et* (“and”). I emended it from our manuscript, which has *ut* (“as”), yielding “as after the rains.”]

as after the rains it is pleasant to look upon the expelled clouds

and compare present events with past ones,

[15] what a dreadful night there was through those days

that have now flowed away, when the year had passed,

while madness, kindled by the movements of divine anger,

burned in the cities of Latium after an enemy had been sent against them!

[Note: Our manuscript mistakenly has *milibus*, “thousands,” instead of *in urbibus*, “in the cities.” I therefore followed the reading of the Muratorian manuscript.]

Now likewise, having witnessed the power of tranquil Christ,

[20] let us consider his gifts:

[Note: [Col. 0571D] The Muratorian manuscript reads *munere* (“gift,” singular). I followed our manuscript’s less obscure *munera* (“gifts,” plural).]

when the impious king and his enemies were slain together,

[Note: Let us again hear Orosius, who attests Radagaisus’s death in these words: “Then King Radagaisus, placing his sole hope in flight, secretly abandoned his men and fell among ours; he was captured by them, held for a short time, and then killed.” Augustine likewise, in the passage cited, affirms that this barbarian was killed. Muratori.]

victory restored peace to the young Augustus;

[Note: Honorius Augustus was born during the consulship of Richomer and Clearchus, namely in the year of Christ 381, as Marcellinus in his *Chronicle*, Hydatius, and Socrates, Book V, chapter 12, assert, although Claudian, in the Fourth Consulship of the same Honorius, seems to contradict this. Therefore in the year 405 he completed his twenty-first year and entered his twenty-second. Nevertheless Paulinus calls him a boy, certainly with poetic license. See what I noted below on verse 158. Muratori.]

and, though still young in years, he prevailed by strength of arms,

[Note: Our manuscript lacks the little word *et*, “and,” which I supplied from the Muratorian manuscript.]

through the power of God,

and broke mortal forces,

while Christ overcame the sacrilegious tyrant.

[25] But why should I now say more about this?

Does not the commonwealth show that this was not merely the work of my Felix?

[Note: Muratori reads the single word *respublica*, “commonwealth.” Our manuscript has two words, *res publica*, and I think that is how it should be read.]

For this, indeed, has been secured through many patrons,

so that Roman safety and public life might endure.

[Note: Dungalus quotes this verse and those that follow, up to verse 36.]

[Note: All who have touched upon this victory of the faithful Romans admit that the Goths were astonishingly slaughtered or reduced to chains. St Augustine, *Sermon* 29 on Luke: “God shows that temporal salvation itself is not in these sacrifices; he changes earthly kingdoms themselves. Radagaisus was defeated, with the Lord’s help, in a wondrous manner.” And Orosius, in the passage cited: “Radagaisus, terrified by divine action, was driven into the Faesulan mountains.” Muratori.]

Here were Peter, here Paul, the leaders; here were all the martyrs.

[30] Whom the expanse of the great City contains in countless numbers,

**[Col. 0572C] Note:** Dodwell, a learned man among the Protestants, published a dissertation *On the Scarcity of Martyrs*; but this Paulinus alone shows how far he departed from the truth, when he affirms that countless martyrs existed in a single City. Prudentius fully agrees, in Hymn 11 to Valerian, concerning Hippolytus:

> We have seen countless ashes in the holy City of Romulus,  
> O Valerian, sacred to Christ.

The same author, in his hymn on Saint Laurence:

> Scarcely is it known by report  
> how full Rome is of saints,  
> how the City's soil blossoms,  
> rich in sacred tombs.

Saint Leo the Great likewise transmitted this. — MURATORIUS.

and whom the Church venerates within the bounds of Romulus among peoples spread over countless regions, all kept watch together in earnest prayer. My Felix here, like one of them, played a great part in those prayers; but the sum of the petition’s benefit is referred to all, and is claimed as belonging to no one individually.

**[Col. 0572D] Note:** In our manuscript and in Dungalus it is written *limite* (“boundary”); in Muratorius’s manuscript, *lumine* (“light”). I prefer the former reading.

[35] Therefore I shall draw back my foot; for, having said enough about what would contribute nothing distinctive to Felix’s merits, I could not nevertheless keep silent, because a share of praise also belonged to Felix: the supreme power, and Christ God, the mighty King of kings, had granted one common favor to all the saints, among whom He kindly heard Felix, mingled with the suppliant flock, with equal benevolence.

**[Col. 0573B] Note:** I have emended *hinc* (“hence”) from our manuscript; Muratorius has *hoc* (“this”) instead of *hinc*.

**[Col. 0572D] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript and Dungalus have *his* (“these”); our manuscript has *hic* (“here”). Neither reading seems objectionable.

I shall therefore refrain from adding public gifts to private ones, and shall sing of Felix’s personal honors and publish what he himself specifically accomplished in these places.

**[Col. 0573B] Note:** Our manuscript erroneously has *gerit*; I have therefore followed Muratorius’s manuscript, which reads *egerit*.

From where, then, shall I begin the weaving of my song? What good deeds of Felix shall I recount? What many things he performs everywhere shall I explain? Or shall I speak of his household gifts, of which I am his particular debtor?

I shall rather repeat what I remember was bestowed upon me and mine, and because these matters were spoken of by me more fully in earlier little books; what he granted partly to others and partly to us, from these riches which he lavishly bestowed upon us, I shall now weave this little book with a grateful heart.

**[Col. 0572D; 515–516] Note:** I have emended this from our manuscript. Muratorius’s manuscript has *locutum*.

And, contrary to my usual practice, I shall change my manner with varied modulation; just as he himself supplies me with varied subjects every year, so I shall change my meters, and, under one sequence, proceed not under one single rule of verse.

**[Col. 0573B] Note:** Paulinus treated the other *Natales* in heroic verse; he completed this one in varied meters. I believe he was led to this choice so that he could include the name of Pinianus in the poem, since it could not be incorporated into hexameters without violating the meter. Thus Rutilius Namatianus, in his *Itinerary*, unable to commend the name of Volusianus to his poem without violating the laws of prosody, was content to testify to his desire. He says:

> I would wish to embrace the true name in song,  
> but the harsh rule of meter rejects certain feet.

This is that Rufius Volusianus, the uncle of Albina, who will be mentioned below. On him, consult my Dissertation IV. — MURATORIUS.

[60] For, since new flowers, two shoots of Christ, have sprung up in the fertile field of holy Felix—Turcius, with pious speech, and Suerius, in his flourishing age—and likewise holy mothers and similar maidens:

**[Col. 0573C] Note:** Our manuscript reads *Turtius*, but this is erroneous. See Dissertation I. — MURATORIUS.

**[Col. 0573C] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript reads *Suecrius*; ours, *Suerius*. Let the reader consult Dissertation II. — MURATORIUS.

Alfia, such as that sister of Philemon once was, noble in the title by which Paul’s Epistle marks her,

**[Col. 0573C–0574D] Note:** Both Muratorius’s manuscript and ours have *Alfia*. Muratorius considers, in his preface to this poem of Paulinus, that *Alfia* was also a name of the younger Melania, and that she is designated here; thus, after the word *Alfia*, a punctuation mark or comma should be supplied, and Philemon’s sister should be compared with Alfia, or Melania herself. For, he says, since Paulinus later says “and Eunomia,” he strongly suggests that the name of another girl had previously been expressed.

I confess that I reluctantly disagree with so great a man; yet, if I may freely say what I think, I can scarcely be persuaded that the younger Melania was also called Alfia. Augustine, Jerome, our Paulinus in his letters, Palladius, and other ancient writers often mention this most holy woman, yet none of them ever calls her Alfia.

It therefore seems probable to me that the name *Alfia*, both in the Ambrosian manuscript used by Muratorius and in ours, has been written corruptly and incorrectly, and that we should read *Apphia*, such as that sister of Philemon was. Thus the sister of Philemon would be indicated by the name Apphia, who is called *Appia* in the Vulgate translation of the New Testament.

The passage of the Apostle Paul to which Paulinus refers reads as follows in the Greek text:

> Παῦλος δέσμιος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ, καὶ Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφὸς Φιλήμονι τῷ ἀγαπητῷ, καὶ συνεργῷ ἡμῶν, καὶ Ἀπφίᾳ τῇ ἀγαπητῇ·

That is:

> Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon, the beloved and our fellow worker, and to the beloved Apphia.

In the Vulgate translation, however, the word “sister” is added; Paulinus too appears to have read that addition there. Since Paul calls Philemon’s sister Apphia, it is possible to conjecture that Paulinus wrote, “Apphia, such as she was,” and that copyists transcribed *Alfia* instead of *Apphia*. If someone prefers to think that Paulinus wrote *Appia*, as the name is read in the Vulgate translation, I shall not object.

But, one may say, after Paulinus had written “and the similar maidens, Appia, such as she was,” he shortly afterward adds, “and Eunomia.” It must therefore be certain that, besides Eunomia, the name of another girl who was at Nola with Turcius, Suerius, and Eunomia had previously been expressed.

I could reply that immediately before the words “and the similar maidens” Paulinus had written:

> In the fertile field of holy Felix  
> new flowers have sprung up, shoots of Christ:  
> Turcius with pious speech, Suerius in flourishing age.

Accordingly, he could rightly have added afterward:

> And Eunomia also.

Yet, to conceal nothing, I believe that several verses are missing between verses 65 and 66, or between 63 and 64, both in Muratorius’s manuscript and in ours. For if you read this passage attentively from verse 60 to verse 71, you will find its meaning entirely mutilated and incomplete.

and Eunomia, now a virgin pledged to eternal bridal chambers in heaven, whom Christ, snatched from her mother’s breast and made pleasing to Himself by His love, devoted to Himself in haste,

**[Col. 0574D] Note:** I have discussed this holy virgin at greater length in Dissertation III. — MURATORIUS.

[Col. 0574B] and anointed her with the perfume of His name; hence, her hair stained and her chaste head anointed with holy merits, she breathes forth the sacred fragrances of her heavenly Bridegroom.

**[Col. 0574D] Note:** This passage was extremely corrupt. Muratorius’s manuscript reads *Tincta comas animae, et mentis caput uncta pudicum / Debere quemquam plandere, et confidere*. Thus fifty-three verses were missing there, which I am the first to publish.

**[Col. 0574D] Note:** The pious custom of Christians referred to here will be illustrated below in the note on verse 315. For the present, Prudentius may suffice, in his hymn to Saint Laurence:

> We see illustrious houses,  
> noble in either sex,  
> offering the pledges  
> of their most distinguished children  
> as votive gifts.

— MURATORIUS.

**[Col. 0575B–D] Note:** Ancient writers mention two women bearing the same name, Melania: one is called the elder, the other the younger. The elder is highly praised by Augustine in a letter to our Paulinus, by Paulinus himself in Letter 29 to Severus, and, to omit others, by Palladius in his *Lausiac History*.

This celebrated matron had a son whom Chiffletius calls Publicola. Muratorius, surprised by this, says: “I do not know, then, on what authority Chiffletius calls him Publicola.” Yet that learned man seems to have taken the name from Palladius’s *Lausiac History*. When Palladius speaks of this elder Melania, he writes (chapter 117):

> Καὶ τὸν Ποπλίπολα δὲ υἱὸν κατηχήσασα τὸν νεώτερον, ἤγαγεν ἐπὶ τὴν Σικελίαν,

that is:

> “After instructing her younger son Poplicola in the mysteries of the Christian faith, she led him to Sicily.”

Melania’s son Poplicola, or Publicola, therefore married the most noble young woman Albina and had by her the younger Melania, of whom Paulinus speaks here. I therefore cannot accept what the monks of Saint-Maur wrote in their notes on Augustine’s Letter 124, namely, that Albina was the daughter of the elder Melania.

For Palladius, speaking of the elder Melania in chapter 118, writes:

> Στηριξασα δὲ καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ἐκγόνην Μελανίαν τὴν νεωτέραν σὺν τῷ αὐτῆς ἀνδρὶ Πινιάνῳ· κατήχησεν δὲ καὶ Ἀλβίναν τὴν ἑαυτῆς νύμφην, γυναῖκα δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτῆς·

that is:

> “After strengthening her own granddaughter, the younger Melania, together with her husband Pinianus, she also instructed Albina, her daughter-in-law, the wife of her son, in the mysteries of the faith.”

To return to the younger Melania: she is numbered among the holy women in the Roman Martyrology. Ancient writers call her now *Melania*, now *Melanium*, and in Greek Μελάνιον, just as the names Glycerium, Dorcium, Philotium, and Eustochium occur for women in Terence and other writers. The name *Melanius*, which Rosweyde mentions in his notes on Paulinus’s Letter 44, appears fictitious.

Here Paulinus forms the genitive *Melani* from *Melanium*, imitating the ancient poets, among whom we read *benefici* for *beneficii*, *ingeni* for *ingenii*, and so forth.

[70] She is Melania’s sister, together and, as it were, her daughter, having found in her a rejoicing and kindred guide.

**[Col. 0576B] Note:** Eunomia was certainly not the younger Melania’s blood sister. Eunomia’s parents were Turcius Apronianus and Avita; Melania’s were Publicola, the son of the elder Melania, and Albina. I therefore think that Paulinus calls Eunomia Melania’s sister because she was her cousin. Eunomia’s mother Avita was the sister of the elder Melania, as Palladius testifies in chapter 118; the elder Melania was the grandmother of the younger Melania.

**[Col. 0576C] Note:** Eunomia was obedient to Melania as to a parent, so to speak.

These two, bound together by divine gifts, bear upon their cultivated minds and beautiful breasts, like living necklaces, the various gems of virtues.

[75] A numerous company of nobles follows them, and the sacred throng of the virgin band, matching them in a single fleece.

**[Col. 0576C] Note:** By “nobles” Paulinus means Pinianus, Aemilius, and others who lived a most holy life at Nola together with Paulinus himself.

Here Christ joyfully hears Eunomia, taught by Melania and, under her guiding voice, shaping the vessels of the psalms in modest melodies, because, while God supplies the melody, the little leader guides the blessed companies of saints with her chaste voice.

**[Col. 0576C] Note:** Paulinus seems to have had in mind Psalm 70: “For I too will give thanks to you, in the vessels of the psalm, for your truth.”

**[Col. 0576C] Note:** When Paulinus wrote this poem, Melania was approximately twenty-four years old. She was born around the year 382, as Tillemont proves; Paulinus recited this poem in 406, as Muratorius demonstrates.

This grace, therefore, as I pondered it, suggested to me that I should imitate a garden distinguished by flowers of many kinds in a poem varied by many meters:

**[Col. 0576C] Note:** This verse requires emendation, for it limps metrically.

[85] just as I admire Felix’s bosom, flourishing with the wealth of varied light, like a rich estate filled with many guests sent into it under Christ’s guidance; and pray that Father Felix, with a dense company of children born to him, may rejoice that dwellings have suddenly expanded their bounds throughout all his cells and that his sober, chaste roofs at last resound in fitting melodies with voices their own,

[90] and that he himself, with a full bosom, may marvel at pupils worthy of his hospitality and souls equal in virtue though different in sex:

just as an old man rejoices, on a fertile hill of olives, seeing young shoots from Christ’s divine seed planted among his own fields.

**[Col. 0576C–D] Note:** This expression is taken from Psalm 127, where we read: “Your children shall be like young olive trees.”

**[Col. 0576D] Note:** He calls Saint Felix “the elder”; in *Carmen* 11 he had called him a presbyter, for *presbyteros* is rendered in Latin by *senior*, “elder.”

[95] Therefore let the ground of my new poem flower into a fresh meadow; and, in praise of the Lord, who is the creator of speech and of every kind of art, let music run in varied meter as His servant.

Now let elegiacs succeed interwoven iambics; let a heroic line be the head and foundation of the little book.

**[Col. 0576D] Note:** Before this verse, our manuscript reads “Here begins Book XIV,” as though another poem began here; but this is plainly false from the preceding verses 103 and 104.

[100] Let the sacred day shine forth, to be celebrated with chaste joys and offerings.

**[Col. 0576D] Note:** “Offerings of praise,” or rather Eucharistic sacrifices.

The sacred day of Felix has shone forth in praise.

What I have called “in praise,” call “in death,” because the death of the pious may rightly be called praise—the precious offering rendered to the Lord God.

[105] Hence the prophet too says, in the word of God, that praise is given to a life proved worthy at its end.

**[Col. 0576D] Note:** Paulinus seems to refer to Tobit 3: “Everyone who worships you knows this for certain: that if his life is tested, it will be crowned.”

And the divine word, by Solomon’s mouth, teaches that no one should be praised before death,

**[Col. 0576D] Note:** Paulinus refers to Ecclesiasticus 11: “Before death, praise no one.” Many Fathers of the Church attributed the book called Ecclesiasticus to Solomon, although it appears to have been written by Jesus son of Sirach.

although some conduct deeds in this life that deserve praise, and praise cannot be prepared elsewhere than in this age, to be sung at the end.

[110] But I believe that, since the whole condition of this life hangs in a slippery state, changing and uncertain, and turns our brief age upon a wheel,

rising and falling along the rough roads by which the course of this age must be unfolded,

[115] therefore provident wisdom, our teacher, warns us not to applaud or trust ourselves or anyone else before the end,

**[Col. 0577B] Note:** Here the fifty-three verses that I supplied from our manuscript end.

[120] however uprightly one may proceed along an honorable path, but always to fear a stumble,

until, after completing the course all the way to the goal, one seizes the palm of the glory sought.

**[Col. 0577C] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript has *martyres*; ours has *martyras*.

Therefore we, all their descendants, celebrate the blessed martyrs whom perfect virtue raised to a heavenly crown,

[125] with the just proclamations of honor due to them, confessing the Christian name;

for by pouring out their blood on behalf of holy faith they planted the good of eternal fruit,

[130] so that, if we walk in the footsteps of the martyrs, we may enjoy rewards equal to those of our parents.

**[Col. 0577C] Note:** I have followed the reading of our manuscript; Muratorius’s manuscript has *partis*.

Hence, for the saints—whether confessors or consecrated witnesses through suffering—

**[Col. 0577C] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript has *sive*; but *seu*, as in our manuscript, must be read, for the meter requires it.

**[Col. 0577C] Note:** The Greek word *μάρτυρ* (*martyr*) means “witness” in Latin. The Greek word, however, is more frequently used. Augustine expressed the meaning of the term in Book XXII, chapter 76, *Against Faustus*: “Through whose confessions, sufferings, and deaths it pleased God to bear witness to this; they are called martyrs, which in Latin means witnesses.” Isidore, Book VII, chapter 11: “They are called martyrs, or witnesses, because they endured sufferings for the testimony of Christ.” — MURATORIUS.

[135] faithful peoples, rejoicing in Christ’s honor, celebrate with solemn joy the sacred days on which, having completed the day of mortal life by a life-giving death, they passed from the world’s pollution to God,

**[Col. 0577C–D] Note:** How explicitly Paulinus here teaches, praises, and recommends feast days instituted in honor of the saints is plain even to the dim-sighted. Elsewhere he touched on the matter; here he attests it in full encomiums. Yet, though this pious practice was once approved by the judgment of the whole Catholic Church, Luther shamelessly says in his booklet *On the Form of the Mass*: “We think that all feasts of the saints ought altogether to be abolished”; and in *On the Ceremonies to Be Observed in Churches*: “Let feasts of the saints universally be abolished.” Not a few heterodox persons join him. We Catholics, thinking with Paulinus and the other holy Fathers, shall celebrate the sacred feasts of the saints; they, under Luther’s leadership, will offer this new doctrine to the credulous. — MURATORIUS.



[140] Such is this holy day of Felix, on which the old man once closed his bodily life, having previously completed the battles of confession;

but, consecrated by an unbloody departure, after his battles, victorious, he was received on the day of peace,

[145] when Christ called him; rejoicing, he left the earth and made his passage into the heavenly dwellings,

not deprived of a martyr’s crown, because in his mind he had carried the vow of suffering.

**[Col. 0577D–0578C] Note:** Elsewhere we have indicated that Saint Felix did not complete his life by martyrdom; for this reason he is called in *Natale* XI “a martyr in praise,” and elsewhere “a martyr without blood.” In *Natale* VI Paulinus sings this very thing about Felix, taken up into heaven:

> Then they crowned his sacred head with a snowy crown,  
> yet the Father also added a rose-colored one, at Christ’s sign,  
> and doubled his snowy coverings with purple attire,  
> since his merits earned both honors. For he received the shining wreath  
> as though transferred into heaven by a peaceful death,  
> but likewise deserved the purple of a slain martyr,  
> since he died a confessor.

— MURATORIUS.

For often the soldier entered the contest with strength and returned as a confessor, having always conquered the enemy;

[150] but God, content with his prepared mind, preserved him, not denying him the martyr’s crown but adding also the crown of a bishop,

**[Col. 0578C] Note:** Felix rightly obtained this crown in heaven because on earth he had refused the one offered to him. After the death of Saint Maximus, the people sought him as bishop; but he—as Paulinus says in *Natale* V—

> As though unworthy, he does not dare  
> to increase in honor,  
> and testifies that it is more due  
> to the old Quintus.

Thus, even under this bishop, Felix lived as a presbyter and increased in merits, since he did not wish to increase in rank.

— MURATORIUS.

so that, having won the palm in an unbloody battle, he might possess the reward of his struggle,

[155] crowned twice over: with the purple laurel of confession and with the ribbon of peace upon the priestly robe—Felix, confessor and presbyter of God.

[160] This, then, is the day which we recall each year with vows.

**[Col. 0578C] Note:** The sacred day of Saint Felix is celebrated on the day after the Ides of January, as it was also in Paulinus’s time. Wandelbert provides confirming testimony:

> It is known to be the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February,  
> Felix the holy confessor honors it.

— MURATORIUS.

It is not the day of his struggle but of his burial,

**[Col. 0578D] Note:** I have corrected this from our manuscript; Muratorius’s manuscript has *annus*.

on which, the substances having been separated from one another, the soul flew to God, while the flesh, returned to the earth, rested hidden in the tomb.

**[Col. 0578D] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript has *anima*; but *animae*, as in our manuscript, must be read.

[165] And rightly this day is called the birthday of the saints,

**[Col. 0578D–0579C] Note:** Among the ancients it was customary to express the day of a saint’s death by the name “birthday,” because on that day they were truly born into heaven. Our poet says in *Natale* III:

> The festive day comes to heaven, most famous on earth,  
> celebrating Felix’s birthday, on which he died to earth in body  
> and was born to Christ among the heavenly stars.

Saint Augustine—or whoever else may be the author of Sermon 10 on the Saints—gives the same explanation: “We rightly celebrate as the birthday of those whom the world of eternal life brought forth more blessedly than the birth from a mother’s womb brought them forth for the world.” Eusebius Gallicanus, or Caesarius, Homily 50 on Saint Genesius: “We call the sufferings of blessed martyrs birthdays, because when the life of martyrdom and faith of glory consign them to death, it gives them birth into eternity.” Add to these Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 129; Beleth, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 4; Amalarius, Book IV, chapter 35, *On Church Offices*; Rabanus, Book II, chapter 43, *On the Institution of the Clergy*; Honorius of Autun, Book III, chapter 17; Albinus, *Commentary on the Gospel of John*, Book VI, chapter 38; and many others. Consult Dissertation XIX below concerning these matters. — MURATORIUS.

is marked out, on which, having completed the law of the flesh, they are stripped of the bonds of bodily mortality,

[170] and are born to God in the heavenly kingdoms, carrying with them the joyful hope of resurrection.

[175] I have always honored this day in such a way that I would regard it more as my birthday than the day on which I was born to no purpose.

**[Col. 0579C] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript erroneously has *legendus*; I have therefore emended it from our manuscript.

For that day is more worthy of mourning for me—

**[Col. 0579C] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript has *dignus*, so the verse limps there. It must therefore be read as *dignius*, as in our manuscript.

the day on which I was created for this world,

**[Col. 0579C] Note:** Both Muratorius’s manuscript and ours have *istum*.

[180] when, a sinner, I fell from the womb of a sinful woman, conceived in dark iniquities, so that my mother might give birth to me already guilty.

Therefore let the day on which I, wretched, was born from the wicked for iniquities be accursed.

**[Col. 0579C–D] Note:** He imitates holy Job, who cursed the day on which he was born. Besides Origen—or whoever that author may have been—in Book III on Job, Saint Gregory must be heard in Book IV of the *Moralia*, chapter 7, explaining Job’s words and concluding: “What, then, is it to curse the day of one’s birth, except openly to say: ‘May the day of change perish, and may the day of eternity break forth’?” It is also useful to quote Philip on this passage. This Philip, mentioned by Gennadius and a disciple of Saint Jerome, wrote a commentary on Job, which a hostile age has deprived us of. I shall publish some fragments of it, taken from a very ancient Ambrosian-library manuscript written in Saxon characters, in the remaining books of the *Anecdota*. I do not wish to omit one here:

> Some say that the times of human birth cannot be cursed because they have passed. Certainly they are cursed superfluously, because their course has already been completed. But the saints, filled with the spirit of prophecy, curse the day of human birth; and they do this not without their own tribulation. For, in compassion, they feel within themselves the sentence of God’s death imposed upon the human race, and so forth.

— MURATORIUS.

[185] But blessed for me is this birthday, on which my patron was born in the heavens—Felix, who arose to that power by which he might cleanse me of my filth,

and, having redeemed me, release me from my bonds and set me free from the sorrowful death of my birth.

**[Col. 0579D] Note:** Our manuscript has *laxatum*, but that reading is erroneous; I have therefore corrected it from Muratorius’s manuscript.

The same day always returns for all, when the year has completed its cycles around the world:

[190] Yet it changes each year, as grace renews the diversity of gifts which Christ gives to His companion Felix, so that Felix may grant them to me; it is not the same day that comes to everyone, but brings varied themes for my songs.

Let us therefore see what new thing this year has brought me, from which I may blossom in new utterances.

[195] I shall not go far, nor seek for myself something absent in time or place from the past.

The gifts themselves are present and held close at hand:

you all see the gifts given this year, joined together in one bosom of Felix—

**[Col. 0579D] Note:** Thus this holy company of Romans had come to Nola in the year 406. — MURATORIUS.

[200] Christ’s servants, formerly nobles of the earth, but now destined inhabitants of heaven,

whom Christ Himself, who had made them rich,

**[Col. 0579D] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript has *creavit*; ours has *crearat*. I prefer the latter reading.

made poor in this world, so that, cast down from the citadel of earthly honor, He might carry them into His kingdom.

[205] Turcius Apronianus, the glory of the Turcian family, a boy in the understanding of the flesh but an old man in his senses,

**[Col. 0580C] Note:** Our manuscript erroneously has *Appronianum*. Concerning him, see Dissertation I. — MURATORIUS.

noble in the ancient lineage of the toga, but nobler in the name of Christian,

**[Col. 0580C–D] Note:** It is highly worthy of notice that Turcius is here called a boy; below, however, Paulinus says that Pinianus was younger than Turcius in age. Pinianus was living around the year 406 in his thirtieth year and somewhat beyond. For when the author of Saint Melania’s Life, under 31 January in Surius, says that Pinianus vowed continence to God together with Melania when he had passed his twenty-fourth year, and when this occurred in the year of the Lord 399, as I have shown in Dissertation VI, it plainly follows that in 406 Pinianus was at least thirty years old.

Since Turcius is also called a boy, although he was older than Pinianus, the word “boy” seems to have been considerably extended by Paulinus. Below he applies the same designation to Pinianus, to Julian in his epithalamium, and to the emperor Honorius when the latter was twenty-two years old. I do not know whether this usage was current among Greek or Latin authors; but in the sacred Scriptures those who had already reached manhood are sometimes called boys. I would perhaps believe that Paulinus uses the word of those who had recently received baptism. For in Letter 36 to Macarius he says of an old man recently baptized: “Now a boy in the extreme old age of life, and a little child in wickedness, he bears the infancy not only of grace but also of mind.”

— MURATORIUS.

[210] who, with the glory of an ancient and a new birth mingled together, is an old senator of the curia and a new senator of Christ,

his companion approaches him under an equal yoke.

Pinianus is younger in age, equal in faith,

[Col. 0580D] **Note:** Our manuscript has *quo*; I preferred to follow the reading of Muratorius’s manuscript.

[215] and himself a young man distinguished by ancient blood,

**[Col. 0580D] Note:** The word *deerat* was missing from Muratorius’s manuscript, causing the verse to stumble. I supplied it from our manuscript.

**[Col. 0580D–0581C] Note:** Our manuscript erroneously writes *Pinnianus*. Concerning this distinguished man, consult Dissertation VI below. — MURATORIUS.

the first-born son of a consul in the foremost City.

**[Col. 0581C] Note:** Why does he call him a consul in the leading City—that is, in the City of Rome? Could it be that at that time consuls existed elsewhere, so that the name of the City was added to distinguish them? Indeed, this was so. In the most distinguished cities of the Empire, the supreme magistrates were called consuls after the example of Rome. Ausonius taught us that consuls were established at Bordeaux, in *On Distinguished Cities*, at the end:

> I love Bordeaux; I honor Rome; in the former I am a citizen,  
> consul in both. Here is my cradle, there the curule chair.

Gruter records seven inscriptions, on page 429 and following, erected for a certain Lucius Licinius, who had been consul three times at Barcelona. He likewise mentions another consul in the colony of Astigi, Allius Mamercus, consul six times, on page 351, no. 5. Sidonius Apollinaris was similarly called consul, although in reality he had performed this office only in his own country. — MURATORIUS.

**[Col. 0581C] Note:** Our manuscript erroneously has *primi genitus*.

[220] That Valerius, of consular lineage,

who first held the name in the Latin lists of magistrates, whom Rome, after expelling the kings, added to Brutus,

is now the distant ultimate ancestor of this Christian consul Valerius.

**[Col. 0581D] Note:** Publius Valerius later acquired the surname Poplicola and was counted among the first consuls. All the chronological records, Livy, Plutarch in his *Life* of him, Sigonius, and the other Roman historians teach this. He publicly praised Brutus, his colleague, who had been pierced by an enemy spear, and enacted laws in favor of the people. Pinianus descended from this family. — MURATORIUS.

O happy bloodline! Although that man, misled by pagan error, performed this good deed of his lineage, he does not grasp it, submerged in the dark lake of hell;

[225] but we, contemplating with faithful light the things of the past and the present condition of humanity, marvel at the works of the lofty Creator,

and, prepared through the lines of mystical successions from ancient ages, we are astonished at the pious sons of the impious.

**[Col. 0581D] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript has *terrore*; ours has *errore*.

Nevertheless, even in the darkness of impious minds we see seeds of light flash forth,

[230] in the very age of the ancient night,

by which the mind and will of the pagans, although subject to the law of nature, were proved capable of some good.

**[Col. 0581D–0582C] Note:** There is a sharp dispute among historians of the Pelagian and Jansenist controversies: namely, whether pagans could perform any good work by the sole light of nature, or whether all their deeds deserved the name of sin. On this question one should read the great defender and glory of Augustine, Cardinal Noris, in his *Vindiciae Augustinianae*, section 4; Gonet, *On the Necessity of Grace*, disputation 1, section 5, article 3; Macedonius, in his book against Calvin; and many other eminent theologians.

The Apostle writes in Romans 2: “Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law.” Saint Augustine, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapters 27 and 28, asserts that some good works are performed by unbelievers, and adds the reason: “For the image of God in the human soul has not been so completely worn away by the stain of earthly desires that no outlines of it have remained.”

Hence Paulinus agrees that among the Gentiles certain seeds of light flashed forth, and that for this reason most authorities concede that they received some reward in this world from God when they acted according to the teachings of nature. — MURATORIUS.

[235] Hence, in some of their descendants today, the lineage of their ancient fathers answers from time to time,

as when the supreme ancestor of my present Pinianus, chosen to vindicate his citizens’ liberty after the harsh reigns of the kings, foreshadowed the birth of this descendant,

**[Col. 0582C] Note:** That is, after the harsh rule of the kings, whom Rome had long obeyed. — MURATORIUS.

[240] who, pursuing arrogance in an ancestral spirit but for a worthier cause, drove servitude away from himself, victorious over his own body,

having expelled the kingdom of the devil from his own limbs,

[245] now, through spiritual peace, the chaste liberty of the faithful soul tramples upon the yoke of sin.

And this boy, serving as Christ’s consul, reflects something of that ancestor:

[250] in providing for those who are to be freed, he performs for God the pious office of redemption.

**[Col. 0582C] Note:** Muratorius’s manuscript has *ope*, which makes the verse stumble if read that way. Therefore *opere*, as in our manuscript, must be read.

In this he emulates his ancient ancestor:

[255] he frees his household servants from servitude, just as that man freed his fellow citizens.

But what the other accomplished in Rome, and in one small city during its earliest years, this man now performs in many cities established throughout a different world,

[260] benign everywhere toward his own people and toward strangers.

For he drives the servile yoke from the necks of very many children,

**[Col. 0582C–D] Note:** Florus, Book I, chapter 9, narrating the expulsion of the kings from Rome, says:

> “Now free, the Roman people first took up arms against foreigners for liberty, then for their boundaries, next for their allies, and afterward for glory and empire, since neighboring peoples continually provoked them everywhere; for there was no tract of their native soil without hostile territory immediately beyond it, and, placed as though at a crossroads between Latium and the Etruscans, they rushed out through every gate against the enemy,” and so forth.

— MURATORIUS.

**[Col. 0582D] Note:** Our manuscript has *et una parvula*.

[265] and releases with gold from the chain of debt those who are bound by money in the darkness of prison.

**[Col. 0582D] Note:** I have corrected this from our manuscript. Muratorius’s manuscript erroneously reads *Nam et libertorum*. Consult Dissertation VI. — MURATORIUS.

Thus Felix hid these men, sheltered within his own bosom, in his own dwellings, at Christ’s command,

and with me took them as everlasting guests.

[270] Now, joyful in having these helpers on both sides, I dedicate a vow in a single voice of three,

with one person speaking in the spirit and affection of three.

**[Col. 0582D] Note:** The remainder is missing from our manuscript. It is greatly regrettable that Lippus Platesius did not transcribe the whole poem, for his help would have enabled us to remove several other errors found in Muratorius’s manuscript. From this point to the end of the poem, we present Muratorius’s text and notes, which it would now be unnecessary to mark with his name. — EDITOR.

Magnify God with me, and, wise and honorable boys, sing psalms with unanimous songs.

Let the ten-stringed instruments resound as the psalteries are struck,

[275] and let discordant strings come together in equal melodies.

Thus let the lyre of our holy fellowship ring out,

as though a threefold tongue sounded with one mouth.

[Col. 0583A] For we are the same three in number, one in mind,

[280] and many souls come together in these three.

The heavenly book preserves their names, inscribed there:

the first of the choir is Albina, and Haerasia her equal.

This sister is joined to this yoke, so that she may be the third leader  
of the company, Avita, mother of hymn-singing choirs.

These mothers have two pledges of one sex among their three children:  
[285] a twin blossom, the offspring of Melania, and Eunomia.

These same women are also pledges to us men; for those whom sex  
separates, piety unites.

With Father Paulinus, this man Turcius is likewise a father to me;  
but age makes me his son, and offspring makes him my father.

[290] From different generations we join our names into one;  
[Col. 0583B] and though neither of us is an old man, we are nevertheless alike.

Thus this entire company consists of three mothers in all,  
four among the children, and two among the fathers.

For from this group comes the boy, Melania’s husband in the body of Christ,  
[295] to whom God granted a name from the pine,  
so that, born as a child of eternal life, he might receive his name  
from that tree which remains ever green.

For the pine, standing with its crown always in flower,  
[Col. 0584A] is ever fond of adorning the lofty ridges;

[300] it does not change its appearance with the seasons, for beneath the heat  
and beneath the snow it remains equal to itself in its green foliage.

Within, beneath its rough covering, the fertile tree bears  
the soft milk of its powerful nut as food.

Its rich wood sweats fragrant resin,  
[305] so that the tree is not barren even in its very timber.

This tree, therefore, is an image of the eternal body:  
beautiful, fruitful, living, lofty, fragrant, green.

In the likeness of this tree, that blessed boy will belong to the Lord,  
so that enduring grace may remain with him.

[310] Now planted by God, he grows in holy progress,  
[Col. 0584B] and, fruitful, raises his pine-like head high.

Here, in my own flock, my son stands foremost;  
but in Asterius I have another light equal to him.

His parents, united in true devotion,  
[315] together dedicated this infant as sacred to Christ,

so that, marked out like Samuel from his earliest years,  
he might grow as one vowed to the holy life, with God sustaining him.

[Col. 0585A] With Christ’s name as father, he uttered his first murmurs,  
and the Lord’s name was his first speech.

[320] Now, born for God and for the heavenly kingdoms,  
he shines equally in name and in speech with a starry radiance.

Pious grace made this boy both son and brother to his father,  
for they were born alike in the holy stream.

Those whom nature had divided by rank, God, in his gracious gift,  
[325] will bring as brothers into his own kingdom.

Therefore, all nine parents, together with their united offspring,  
let us be as one lyre, harmonious in heart;

let us all make of ourselves one cithara,  
a song composed of different strings.

[330] Let Aemilius come as the tenth. Then at last, with the number complete,  
the mystical law will sing within us.

[Col. 0585B] For at the head of this number, in the peaceful shell,  
a living string will proclaim the work that brings salvation.

Felix will be the plectrum of this cithara. With this plectrum  
[355] Christ, rejoicing, will strike the ten-stringed cithara.

When Christ plays upon it, this cithara within us will sound  
[527–528] complete harmony, with perfect meaning.

Thus may our peace be consonant with God in all our fibers,  
so that we may be united in body, mind, and faith.

[340] For such a man fills the cithara with the holy laws,  
ordered in every measure for life.

His life agrees in all things with the sacred law;  
for every string will sing with an unbroken breath.

[Col. 0585C] Now to you, venerable father, eternal patron,  
[345] my protector and Felix, dearest to Christ,

I shall return your gracious words with words of my own,  
for you have bestowed many gifts upon me of many kinds;

[Col. 0586A] all that belongs to the present life, and all that produces  
hope for the future—I remember that I owe to you, since Christ

[350] made me your bondsman from my earliest years.

If eloquence flowed for me in river-like streams,  
and if I possessed a thousand mouths and a hundred tongues,

perhaps, even filled to overflowing by these resources,  
I could not recount all the gifts of Felix,

[355] how many the Lord Christ bestowed upon his friend  
and how many, as a confessor, he poured forth upon me, his servant and fosterling.

The gifts I might mention first, though different, are equal  
and meet together in greatness and weight; yet among them

I cannot decide which I should remember before the others.

[360] The abundance of material bewilders the judgment that might easily distinguish them.

If, beginning from the very origin, I were to review everything  
that he provided for me with equal affection at different times,

[Col. 0586B] I could count the hairs of my own head  
before I could recount your gifts toward me, good Felix.

[365] You first cast, if I may approach heavenly things,  
the seeds of salvation for me through saving causes.

For when, as a boy, I had been brought from the western shores of Gaul,  
as soon as I touched your threshold with trembling steps,

seeing the admirable proofs of holy works  
[370] teeming before your doors, where you are enclosed in buried bodily form,

and spread far abroad through the greatness of your merits,  
I drank faith in the divine name with my whole heart,

and, rejoicing in your light, I loved Christ.

Under your leadership I bore the fasces of office in my earliest years,  
[375] and while you guided my hand and guarded my salvation,

I remained pure from the shedding of human blood.

[Col. 0586C] Then also I cut the first offerings of my beard [lacuna]  
[529–530] before your throne, as though you yourself were clipping it;

then, as a pledge of honor already offered to your seat,  
[380] [Col. 0587A] I fixed habitations to be measured out in the Campanian fields,

you laying the foundations of the future dwelling of your servant.

When, silently breathing concern into my mind, you ordered me  
to fortify and pave the road leading to your couches,

and to raise, adjoining your buildings, a roof extending at length,  
[385] beneath which the earlier use of the needy had dwelt,

the house, built afterward beneath a double roof, grew  
and now remains as a guest-house for our cells.

The portico beneath it serves poor invalids,  
and we, dwelling in the roofs added above,

[390] sustain them in their lodging and provide wholesome fellowship  
for our wounds in one shared seat,

so that in turn we may offer friendly comforts to one another;  
may they, praying, strengthen our foundations,

[Col. 0587B] while we shelter the brotherly bodies of the poor beneath a roof.

[395] Therefore, when, released from the sixfold burden of rule,  
I laid down an axe unstained by any slaughter,

at your recall to the shore of my native land  
I was restored to my anxious mother. From there I went

[400] across the Pyrenees as a foreigner to my Iberian relatives.

[Col. 0588A] There you allowed me to be joined in marriage according to human law,  
so that you might purchase the life of two people,

and so that, through the yoke of the flesh, the salvation of two souls,  
doubled, might compensate for the salvation of one that had been deferred.

Although from that time my life ran by another path  
[405] and I lived elsewhere, far away in another world,

where the waves of the Ocean Sea resound all around,  
yet in Gallic thought I was never separated from this seat;

I always clung to Felix’s breast,  
and in turn I felt Felix standing by our affairs

[410] for every good purpose, in all things, at home and abroad,  
to bring them to completion. He was my means and my defense.

Felix alone was my resource, through the propitious divine power of Christ,  
always turning away what was adverse and granting what was prosperous.

[Col. 0588B] You, Felix, were always fortunate for me, so that I might not be wretched;  
[415] as a perpetual father and guardian, you were present through your devotion.

And when I was troubled by the blood of a slain brother,  
and a brotherly cause brought danger upon my kinsman,

[531–532] when the governor had already come against my property,  
[Col. 0589A] you, father, rescued my neck from the sword and my patrimony from the Treasury,

[420] and preserved me and my possessions for Christ the Lord.

For what counsel Christ then used to bring help  
to my affairs and to my life, and how Felix’s care powerfully assisted me,

the great outcome of events afterward made clear:  
my circumstances and my view of life were transformed,

[425] when faith renounced the world, my homeland, and my house,  
[The text reads *Prodita*, “given up/brought forth,” with uncertain syntax] business was transacted in various lands,

and, with everything sold, the cross that had to be carried was purchased.

Thus earthly property purchased the hope of the heavenly kingdom;  
for the hope of faith is stronger than the substance of the flesh.

This hope, founded upon God, gives birth to an everlasting possession;  
[430] but the fleshly possession destroys the heavenly hope.

Yet if, by conquering faith, it overcomes even that possession,  
it does not immediately remove it, but reforms it, rightly transformed,

according to divine law, transferring it from the fragile to the eternal  
and setting it, removed from earthly things, in heaven,

where Christ, the faithful guardian, keeps what has been entrusted to him.  
Nor does he merely preserve the deposit in the amount

[435] in which he received it from here; rather, multiplying it,  
he returns the talents entrusted to those who have believed with interest,

and makes himself the possession of believers.

And what possession could be more precious than this?

If the whole world had been my private property,  
would that possession have been preferable to the Lord Christ?

[440] And who made me the possessor, even in hope, of so great a possession?  
Who compelled me to despise that possession for Christ,

so that Christ might become my possession?

Who but you, always my great power, Felix,  
enemy of my sins and friend to my salvation?

[Col. 0589C] You changed my homeland for me with a better provision,  
[450] giving yourself to me in place of my homeland.

You broke our bonds of flesh. You freed us from the stain  
of our fallen blood and from the shores of our native land,

and made us emigrate into your lineage  
and hope for heavenly things with great courage.

You changed our ancestral records from those of wicked mortals  
into the company of the heavenly Lord’s friends,

[455] names marked in the everlasting book;  
by transferring the source of our mortal origin,

you will have us erased from death and enrolled in salvation.

What comparable possession did I have when I was said to be a senator,  
[533–534] such as I now possess here, when I am called poor?

[460] Behold: through so many halls of the blessed martyr,  
broad in their spaces, lofty in their roofs,

adorned with deeply recessed ceilings, watered with streams  
and encircled everywhere by porticoes,

whatever is honored, celebrated, and possessed  
under the blessed name of Felix throughout these places—

[465] all of it is my house. There is no place  
joined to and incorporated into his buildings

[Col. 0590B] that does not lie open to me as though it were my property.

But why should I boast of this gift, if I possess  
only the visible stone roof of my beloved Felix as a native guest?

[470] How much greater is what I possess: Felix himself, by God’s gift, is my house;  
in him my life lives, and it possesses a house that will fall in no age.

For the fact that Felix’s house is also my house,  
through his permission, which grants me the lawful reins of his authority,

our boldness proves even by these services:  
we have received our fellow guests into the roofs,

and now, with equal right, we hold Felix’s rights;  
[480] our children, whom you know and see,

are joined and cherished in the lap of Father Felix,  
now quartered with me within Felix’s own roofs,

watching over their lodgings, having forgotten the lofty roofs  
of former houses and remaining more safely in narrow cells

near the martyr, with ambition rejected.

[485] For Christ is near the humble and turns away from the lofty;  
he frequents more willingly the cramped beams of a poor hut

than the exalted heights of proud possessions.

Therefore, to compare the roofs I now inhabit  
with the lofty buildings I now possess or remember having possessed,

[490] if you wish, compare them with one another through fair judges.

[Col. 0591A] What house is so beautiful? What field so fertile? Or what possession  
in mortal life was ever given to me by Christ in this poor dwelling,

through whom Felix, rich in inexhaustible return,  
abounds as my possession?

But if I review my estates from the old reckoning,  
[495] whatever was once great for me in any land,

it was merely earth, and the empty appearance of a windy shape;  
whether it was gold or gems, that furniture

was of little value to the good, but precious poison to the greedy.

And now I am bereft of wealth—or rather,  
[500] free from condemned burdens.

Freed from the anxiety of possessing, I enjoy secure poverty;  
no hostile bonds of those who follow wealth hold me fast,

so that they might restrain me when naked. Easily and lightly he departs  
from the body whom no alluring love chokes,

the image of a deceiving world appearing in various forms.

O poverty of Christ, venerable to me and more precious than the whole world,  
[535–536] rich with heavenly treasure,

you strip those whom you deprive of wealth, cleansing them  
as though from the refuse of earth;

you destroy earthly things within us and, in their place, build eternal things  
[510] as the price of life.

You truly reverse loss by a novel reversal,  
so that money kept may be loss of gain to us,

while money not kept may be gain;  
but when the same money is poured out in a perverse way, it is loss.

For it does no good to pour out one’s possessions  
without the name and command of Christ;

[515] [Col. 0591C] for what is spent on profane vices truly perishes.

Luxury and ambition, diseases of great danger,  
balance the crime of avarice,

because the same cause of death lies beneath both,  
which stained desire and the seductive craving for worldly things

[520] bring to completion.

With these riches, good Felix, you wish to make me poor,  
so that you may make me rich in life

and free me, through a poor manner of life, from the death  
that the world’s rich must suffer without end,

for whom the deadly use of gold gives birth  
to eternal fires shared with the worms.

You do not wish us merely to dwell in joined roofs,  
but you prepare to nourish us for fellowship with yourself

in eternal life and to lead us to the form  
that you, perfected under the image of the Lord Christ,

[530] once bore on earth as a rich man who became poor.

For who remains unaware of your poverty, which you gladly embraced  
as a confessor after your wealth had been proscribed for the holy name,

and which you, Felix, continued to practice into old age  
in the rented garden?

[535] Therefore you strive to make all whom you receive  
beneath a hospitable roof like yourself through holy poverty;

for a dissimilar form could not coexist with you.

For as much as a wolf differs from a lamb and light from darkness,  
so greatly do the rich man’s way and Christ’s way diverge.
