[540] For the broad road lies open, slippery with its downward slope,  
and descends into hell; along it the rich drive the greedy,

hurled into Tartarus beneath the weight of their own burdens.

But the road that belongs to Christ, open to holy confessors  
and martyrs, provides a difficult path for the few.

[545] Therefore this road does not admit the heavily burdened;  
it excludes those weighed down by baggage.

[Col. 0592C] For this reason it is fitting that the servant and follower  
of the blessed martyr be bound to him,

stripped of troublesome shackles, made lean by saving poverty,  
and made light, so that he may enter through the narrow gate

[550] [Col. 0593A] and climb the Lord’s lofty mountain.

But why, foolishly, should I distinguish the weights of possessions?  
I count these among your great gifts, best of fathers.

However great these things may be for me, they are still small,  
[537–538] if I speak of what is greater. For what portion is this

[555] of the reckoning of your works toward us,  
this gift that you gave us land for hospitality

and enabled us to build dwellings for habitation,  
when you, father, gave us your own heart?

For what but your inmost heart did you disclose to us,  
when you deigned to open the innermost parts of your tomb,

[560] [Col. 0593B] Saint, for reasons arising from the hidden dust,  
and by so great a sign wished to show us bound to you in special love,

so that, gracious one, with the ash of your dust suddenly appearing,  
you wished the silent and fixed resting place of your body

through so many past ages  
[565] to be preserved in our time?

Therefore I shall briefly read in his praises those riches of Felix,  
as though they were lesser gifts,

many of which he has already bestowed upon us, received into his lap,  
[Col. 0594A] as his attentive care does not cease to pour upon us

[570] countless gifts from his abundant resources.

He provided not only what the use of the body requires,  
but also what now wins us grateful renown

and preserves our honored name after us.  
He added these things so that he might allow his halls,

never before enclosed by such works,  
to grow through our labor, built anew or restored,

[575] with porticoes and houses.

He also revealed to us the secrets of his own tomb.  
I shall speak of this venerable gift in few words,

so that the likeness of his great devotion may shine forth:  
he deemed us worthy of such great love

[580] that, allowing our eyes near the revered mystery,  
he disclosed his bones to us

as though he were bringing them forth from his own marrow.

[Col. 0594B] Therefore I shall tell you the whole story in due order,  
by which he granted us to see what lay near his limbs

[585] and to touch the very chest of his resting body.

The appearance of the place remains known to all: above the very throne  
of the hidden martyr, with the side of the tomb closed by a grille,

there is, in the middle, a kind of marble panel,  
covered with an attached layer of silver.

[590] This surface of the slab is open on both sides,  
[539–540] providing openings beneath for the nard poured into it,

[Col. 0595A] through which the medicinal breath coming from the holy ashes’ seat  
sanctifies the hidden things.

These openings, suddenly, drank the liquids poured into them  
in their customary manner, the earth beneath the tomb absorbing the cups.

Those who had supplied the place with nard, preparing to empty it,  
found instead, when the openings had been filled in a wondrous new way,

[595] a heap of sand bursting forth in place of the nard.  
They drew back their hands in fear, filled with much dust,

from the throat of the tomb.

The new event disturbed everyone  
and kindled an eagerness to investigate the cause

of the sudden miracle. They therefore decided upon a fixed day  
to search out the innermost chamber after removing the marble.

[605] [Col. 0595B] For an exceedingly anxious concern feared this:  
that perhaps the dust of the holy body contained something

which the hand, drawn up from the tomb through the open holes,  
had sucked in and carried away,

clotted together with varied filth, with little bones  
and fragments mixed with rubble.

Hence, through mutual conversation, people feared  
that perhaps some little creature, shut up in hidden cavities,

[Col. 0596A] was spitting out the sacred ash from the holy flesh  
farther within,

as monsters in deserted fields are accustomed  
to dig into the earth with sharp beaks

and scatter black heaps around their holes;

[615] so, from within the hidden interior of holy Felix,  
the wondrous eruption of earth had, with intervals of days,

made the matter all the more astonishing.

Therefore, on the appointed day, the useful undertaking,  
productive of many results, was begun.

The bishop sent all the presbyters to us.  
Before their eyes the craftsmen’s hands set to work,

[620] carrying out the priests’ commands. Their first task  
was to remove the grille from the place;

then, in the next stage, to raise the panels attached to it  
by loosening the nails.

But when we saw the chest beneath the marble covering,  
remaining in place with the structure of the shrine unbroken,

[Col. 0596B] [541–542] then secure faith drove the danger of error  
from our doubting hearts,

when touch and sight proved that, with the shrine unharmed  
and the tomb unbroken,

the martyr’s body was enclosed on every side  
by a strong defense,

[630] and had not been exposed to any profanation;  
and that the bones, worthy of retaining the honor

of their holy flesh, were there—bones to which the holy Spirit  
never ceases to be present,

from which living grace stands forth for pious tombs,

[Col. 0597A] proving that those who have died in Christ  
are buried without death,

their bodies sleeping peacefully for a time.

Therefore, after restoring the honor of Felix’s tomb,  
we leave everything carefully secured,

so that until the day of the Lord, when, with Christ as prince,  
the glory due to the saints raised together

[640] will shine, his bones may rest undisturbed in their own dwelling;  
and may the peace awaiting the holy soul in the heavenly region

also hold the venerable body on earth.

What remains for me still to report?  
As though I had even adequately produced what I have sung,

or had recounted in full speech  
all the abundant gifts of my patron!

[Col. 0597B] Many things lie hidden, yet all remain fixed for us  
in our remembering heart;

many have already been mentioned, and more remain  
to be mentioned.

But the rule governing the book’s limits warns  
that the greatest matters must be selected from the many.

[650] After all the works had been constructed—works that appear to stand  
in lofty forms throughout the halls

and whose vestibules are widely enclosed  
by projecting porticoes—

the only gift still lacking seemed to be water;  
all these roofs appeared to pray for it together

[655] to the grieving inhabitants.

Even I, I confess, had begun to accuse my Felix  
in a complaining voice,

as though he were sluggishly attending to these prayers,  
because he allowed the sharing of water with us

[543–544] to be denied for so long by the neighboring city.

[Col. 0597C] But, as we hurried along with unconsulted minds,  
he was weaving delays into suitable times

[660] through a wiser plan. For in proper order  
the sequence of the works rightly demanded

[Col. 0598A] that priority be given to the completion of those undertakings  
which his diligent care was preparing

around the holy halls of the venerable martyr  
through labor of many kinds.

And when divine grace had given the finishing touch  
to the works already made,

[665] then, with the vows completed in their full order,  
he would cause the enclosed springs to flow into the courtyards.

Finally, when this entire work stood complete and prepared,  
our parched thirst for the long-deferred vow was not extinguished;

[670] soon, when God willed it, the people’s previously harsh hearts  
gave easy consent with willing minds.

Let me now speak of the gift of water. Give me now, Felix,  
as you intercede with the Lord,

that my word may flow with as easy an eloquence  
as you have made the springs flow in abundance

[675] [Col. 0598B] into your vestibules and houses.

Everything that the gracious Lord, with your support,  
has granted and increased for us,

he adorned with such a gift,  
by which he brought springs to thirsty fields.

Christ again flowed from the breast of the pious rock,  
recalling the gift of ancient devotion,

[680] so that he might sprinkle with an extraordinary stream  
all the dry sand that had previously lain parched,

and make the waterless earth flow with sudden currents;  
and in the holy halls of his Felix,

where peoples of different nations had gathered as guests,  
he caused new cups to run abundantly with streams,

[685] through wells, basins, and capacious tanks.

Who would grant you, supreme Fount, to water my desert  
and break through the pumice-stone of my heart,

[Col. 0598C] to establish a house from the rock, and to let me drink from you  
a stream that would produce in my dry breast

[690] a living vein of water springing up eternally?

[Col. 0599A] Yet this small drop of eloquence too, with which I speak of you,  
is surely drawn from the source from which rivers also overflow.

For who could speak even a little of you without you,  
O Christ, supreme power of the supreme Father?

Christ himself inspires the speaking of you, by whose light  
we behold the equal light of Father and Son,

[695] so that, with the holy Spirit guiding and breathing upon us,  
we may confess Christ as God together with the Father.

But since, while I carry the name of the living fountain upon my lips,  
a drop has fallen into my mouth from the river of the Word,

perhaps my lips will henceforth convey some flavor of it;  
and now my tongue, no longer dry in the gift of water,

[700] but as though more richly moistened, will speak.

After all the works had been provided,  
which appear so numerous,

[Col. 0599B] this place demands that the name of devoted Abella  
be inserted in the verses;

she seems worthy of the honor of this name,  
so that she too may be praised in Felix’s praise,

because for the honor of Felix she willingly undertook the labor,  
considering it rest and reward

[710] to sweat beneath the heat among the steep rocks.

[545–546] This city is indeed small in its walls,  
but great in its service to the holy bier.

This city of ours, lying six miles from Nola,  
stands amid high mountains,

from which it draws the waters that rise nearby  
and receives them into a single channel.

[715] From there, through inserted pipes, it first claims the flowing water for itself,  
and then lets the remaining stream flow to the city of Nola,

watering many estates  
throughout the fields.

[Col. 0600A] But let me return to the thanks due for this work.

For she generously provided welcome labor  
for the aqueduct,

which long age had broken,  
to call it back to its vessels and channels.

The place, set among high cliffs,  
was accessible by no road or path,

and even pack animals could not penetrate it.  
The steepness of the immense mountain

[725] made it difficult to find a hand ready for the work,  
even for payment.

This makes Abella’s honor of reward all the greater,  
because, readily serving the holy honor of Felix,

she devoted her unstinting hands  
with overflowing devotion.

It was possible to see anxious crowds from the entire people,  
[Col. 0600B] from every rank and class, summoned together with one mind,

joyfully rushing at the new morning to the work,  
and eagerly competing to climb the highest peaks,

with baskets borne upon necks bent beneath heavy loads,  
and rubble carried through the thorny heights;

[735] beneath the burning sun they repeated their frequent journeys,  
and throughout the entire length of the day,

as long as summer delays it,  
they stretched the late hours from dawn to evening.

Vigilant in spirit, their bodies scarcely restored  
by the brief night,

they rose again before daybreak  
to their builders’ tools,

[740] and, with God giving them strength, felt no labor.

At last the grace of the great work advanced so far  
that, as though it were a game, the entire undertaking

was completed in a few days  
and brought to its end by a finished work.

The channel-form, long interrupted by decay,  
[745] [Col. 0601A] was restored from the distant mountains;

water gathered everywhere from little springs  
received from different rocks

was brought back to the thirsty cities that had once drawn from it,

[547–548] and, through the channel’s course extending over many miles,  
flooding the precinct of our Felix,
it joyfully filled a new basin with its abundant stream.

And, as proof of the divine gift,  
a more abundant stream flowed here in the summer months

than had previously been accustomed to flow  
from winter rains.

Here, Nola, I shall now rightly declare you guilty  
before our common patron,

[755] and, remaining calm in spirit,  
I shall pretend that the patron is moved by gentle affection,

rebuking his little daughter in the voice  
of an old complaint.

[Col. 0601B] For when I rightly sought from you, Nola,  
a share in the fountain,

you, disturbed by fear, acted as though you were harshly denying me  
hospitality in our common water;

forgetting to consider divine rights,  
you thought my prayers depended upon human strength,

[760] and, having forgotten Felix, believed that you would give yourself to me.  
And if you granted it, you mournfully complained

that soon your homeland would be left dry,  
when the water had been withdrawn.

You often condemned this as well,  
stirring up a commotion,

not knowing that the springs had been advanced  
through divine resources,

[765] as you have also learned by experience. For soon God himself,  
the creator, reproved minds that were sluggish in trusting Christ,

when, after peace had been agreed,  
you piously shared with Felix

the use of the river, now held in common;

[770] thereby, through an overflowing goodness,  
he all the more clearly reproved your complaint.

He did not, as you feared, make you thirsty  
by dividing the water;

rather, as author and sustainer alike of things and human beings,  
he who created everything by his word

[775] showed you that the water was his own property,  
which, because you distrusted the Lord, you denied to his friend

as though it belonged to him.

You certainly saw—for the event itself compelled you to admit it—  
the sublime rights of the eternal Father,

[Corrupt fragment: *Cis potens ... meritum*, “Cis [unclear] ... powerful ... merit ...”] when abundant [water], beneath the heat,  
[780] flowed forth,

and, through the holy loss by which you had given a portion  
to the martyr’s halls,

the sudden channels grew;  
when the fountain’s breast was released in its own throat,

[Col. 0602A] the ordered streams were returned to you with much increase  
and flowed into your walls;

and at the very time when you had so often been accustomed  
to suffer as the possessor of water in need,

God returned in abundance what he had received from you.

Water flowed abundantly for your drinks and baths.

What gift, then, shall I return to you for so great a gift,  
poor Abella in resources?

At least, by proclaiming your name in my song  
and marking it with praise,

[790] I shall repay you with the honor of this reward:  
may you always be written as added to the praises

of holy Felix, and may you be remembered  
as the fosterling of so great a patron,

whose greatest share of gifts has become yours.

[Col. 0602B] Now this labor of yours, to which the spirit of Felix impelled you—  
so that, with your whole people and civic order in harmony,

you undertook a work requiring  
great exertion,

[549–550] its hardship doubled by the summer season—

has enabled you to uncover the course of the ancient structure  
among the rugged heights,

[800] a course known in past ages but now,  
for want of water, without use;
by removing the dense accumulation of forests  
lying hidden everywhere between the vast ridges,

you have restored its long-forgotten function;

you have gathered the scattered veins  
that were deeply swallowed by pumice-like sands,

[805] compelled each stream of water to follow its own former tracks again,  
and carried it back to the mouth of its mother-channel;

[Col. 0602C] you have made the canals, long empty because their flow had ceased,  
overflow with the returning current;

and you have flooded Nola, long complaining  
because its springs had been withdrawn,

[810] with a river it had already despaired of.

She now enjoys Felix’s waters—for this abundance  
does not belong solely to the city itself,

which has recently acquired the flowing water of Felix—  
and, in return for a modest drop,

[815] she has been enriched through divine power  
with abundant streams.

Therefore, Nola, cherish the little Abella with me  
as a mother,

for although you recognize that she too is yours,  
[Col. 0603A] and although she is your daughter,

she is nevertheless the mother of your waters,  
from whose native mountains all your abundance flows,

through which you had formerly been proud  
and through which afterward you became a better servant.

[820] Rejoice, therefore, my Nola, and congratulate yourself,  
exulting in the powers poured forth by Christ,

who, through his beloved friend Felix,  
fashioned and increased you,

with nature serving and his mighty hand  
deepening your beauty.

Look upon your face, which now shines with renewed splendor,  
so that you may recognize whether you have given anything

[825] to Felix’s honor,  
or whether you are rather adorned by Felix,

heaping upon you the gifts of God.

Where the rough stone once lay parched  
in the naked fields,

now, with the soil moistened,  
renewed grace grows green.

[830] Nor has Felix’s merit poured forth for you, Nola,  
only these springs, through the rich grace of Christ;

he has also led here to your walls  
the springs that flow from heaven,

and, placing them in the rejoicing lap of Felix,  
has ordered them to stream through many cities

[835] in overflowing rivers from your city.

I speak of these servants of Christ,  
equal in splendor before God and equal in nobility of Christ’s name,

born just now within your boundaries:  
Albina with her mother,

pledges of all the saints and joys of heaven,  
and the blessed pair of Pinianus and Melania, joined in marriage.

[840] God made these both the children of Felix  
and breasts,

breasts flowing with the milk of divine goodness,  
from which every poor person receives nourishment flowing forth,

and every rich person likewise receives saving instruction.

Behold, these are fountains from the pious stream of Christ,  
which do not flow through the earth in a visible torrent,

[845] but abound with the living water of compassionate devotion.

Grant, Christ, that these fountains may gush forth  
with eternal abundance in the breast of your Felix,

and that these channels may never be weakened  
by any constellation.

[551–552] Flow always into hearts dedicated to you, Christ;  
and grant your Felix, concerning the sinners entrusted to him,

so that your devotion may never withdraw  
the fountain of this help from our inmost hearts,

[855] and so that Felix himself, a generous fountain from your fountain,  
may flood us abundantly;

may your fountain, Christ the King, always leap up within us,  
and may Felix obtain for us, who are wretched and needy,

to live happily by the lot of your name.

[Note: [Col. 0583B]]

**Line 278, “For there are three.”** I explained all this in the preface to this Natalis.

**Line 281, “Albina.”** Let the reader consult Dissertation IV, where much is said about this distinguished woman.

**Line 281, “Equal and Herasia.”** It should certainly be read *compar Therasia*, or *cum pare Therasia*—“Therasia, her equal” or “with her equal, Therasia.” See Dissertation V.

**Line 283, “Avita.”** I also devoted Dissertation III to her.

**Line 285, “A twin blossom.”** I explained the whole matter in the preface to this poem.

**Line 291, “Both alike.”** I would rather favor this reading: *sed tamen ambo patres*—“but nevertheless both fathers.”

**Line 294, “Melania’s husband.”** Refer to what I treated more fully in Dissertation VII.

**Line 298, “For the pine is always.”** Virgil, in the *Culex*:

> The ever-green bumastus and the always flowering pine.

Columella, discussing bee fodder in Book IX, says:

> After these, there should frequently be a shoot of greater growth, such as rosemary and either kind of clover; for one is cultivated and the other grows wild. Likewise, there should be the evergreen pine and the lesser holm oak.

Peter Victorius, Book XXV, chapter 5 of the *Variae Lectiones*, and Pontanus in his commentary on Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book IV, line 112, interpret this passage of Columella not of the pine tree but of a certain kind of shrub in which perpetual greenness resides. Salmasius, in his commentary on Solinus, page 279, thinks that both in Virgil and in Columella one should read *tinus*, “laurustinus,” not *pinus*, “pine.” But these eminent scholars are refuted by Paulinus’ testimony, which plainly calls it a tree, not a shrub, when he speaks of the ever-flowering pine:

> So that, born as a child of eternal life,  
> he might receive his name from that tree which remains ever green.

He explains this more fully below. La Cerda, commenting on the cited passage of the *Georgics*, proves that the pine was devoted to ornamental purposes and often found a place in gardens—namely for the benefit of bees, to which Virgil and Columella assign the ordinary pines.

**Line 304, “Its resin sweats.”** Thus it is read in our manuscript and in the ancient manuscripts, although Stephanus preferred to write *teda* without the diphthong. *Thaeda* is called in Greek δαῖς, or δᾳς, meaning “torch” or “lamp.” It is the resinous disease of the pine: when that tree luxuriates through an excessive abundance of sap, the sap changes into a woody, oily material suitable for burning. Theophrastus, *On the Causes of Plants*, Book V, chapter 15:

> Perhaps there is also some kind of tree that, without being diseased but flourishing abundantly, undergoes this process, as does the poplar, when its roots have been changed into torch-wood.

Torches were made from this wood, and they were especially accustomed to be carried at weddings. Hence Ovid, *Heroides* 12, says, “the pine torch.” Columella, Book V, chapter 10:

> Drive a wedge into a split of pine torch-wood.

Salmasius discusses torches at length in his commentary on Solinus, chapter 33.

**Line 312, “My son.”** The author also indicates that Pinianus was Paulinus’ spiritual son. In the life of Saint Melania preserved by Surius under 31 January, the author speaks of Pinianus and his wife Melania, who had gone to Sicily to visit the most holy bishop Paulinus, saying:

> So that they might visit the most holy bishop Paulinus, who was their father according to the spirit.

**Line 313, “Asterius.”** Much is said about him in Dissertation II.

**Line 315, “Infant.”** The heterodox of our own times sometimes attack monasticism and the vows of religious people. But the Christians of earlier centuries did not think this way, since they were accustomed to dedicate boys and girls to God from their very cradles. Paulinus affirms this about Asterius, and had earlier said of Eunomia:

> And Eunomia, the maiden already pledged to eternal  
> bridal chambers in heaven, whom Christ, snatched from her mother’s breast,  
> dedicated to himself in haste, made pleasing by his love.

Augustine, in Psalm 75, intimates this same practice to us: “Some vow virginity from the beginning of life, so that they experience none of the things that those others experienced and abandoned; and these have vowed something very great.” Thus the most illustrious holy virgins—Thecla, Agnes, Cecilia, Agatha, Catherine, and others—were dedicated to God, as they say, from their tenderest infancy. Saint Melania likewise, the wife of Pinianus, as her Acts record under 31 January in Surius, dedicated her daughter to God when scarcely born:

> A girl was born to her. As soon as she saw the light, she was consecrated to the Sun of chastity, Melania offering to the Lord her first-fruits—the daughter whom he had given her—so that, even though she had known marriage, she might seem to accord the highest value to virginity.

From this it will be very easy to explain a passage of Hincmar, bishop of Reims, in the Life of Saint Remigius, where he says that this holy man, after ministering for twenty-two years in the clerical state and seventy-four years as bishop with the greatest continence, returned his body to the earth in the ninety-sixth year of his life. For Remigius was consecrated to God scarcely after birth, and therefore Hincmar reckons the years of his clerical service from the very day of his birth.

mike

[Col. 0585C] Verse 318. “Parent of Christ.” In place of “parent of Christ” I restore “parent of God.” But below the phrase is repeated:

> And now, God being the parent.

[Col. 0585C] Verse 321. “Starry.” *Asterius* is derived from *astron*, that is, “star”; hence Paulinus says that the name Asterius is “starry.”

[Col. 0585C] Verse 326. “Therefore nine.” See the preface to this poem.

[Col. 0585C] Verse 330. “Aemilius.” You will find an extensive discussion of him in Dissertation VIII.

[Col. 0585C] Verse 344. “Now to you.” Dungalus, in his reply to Claudius of Turin, cites these verses from Natalis XIV and likewise admits that he took other verses from that same Natalis. Yet, through the benefit of our manuscript, all of them are recognized as belonging to one and the same Natalis XIII. Hence arose the error that Paulinus composed fifteen Natalices, whereas in fact only fourteen should be counted.

[Col. 0585D] Verse 351. “If for me with river.” Our poet imitates the more celebrated poets, who used expressions of this kind. Homer:

> Οὐδ᾽ εἴ μοι δέκα μὴν γλῶσσαι, δέκα δὲ στόματ᾽ εἶεν,  
> Φωνὴ δ᾽ ἄρρηκτος, χάλκεον δέ μοι ἧτορ ἐνείη.

> “Not even if I had ten tongues and ten mouths, an unbreakable voice, and a heart of bronze.”

Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> Non mihi si linguae centum sint, oraque centum,  
> Ferrea vox.

> “Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, and a voice of iron.”

Ovid, Book I of the *Tristia*, Elegy 4; Silius, Book IX; Claudian, in the *Panegyric on Olybrius and Probinus*; and others have sung the same theme. Persius, however, in Satire 5, seems to mock this convention, saying:

[Col. 0586C]

> Vatibus hic mos est centum sibi poscere voces,  
> Centum ora, et linguas optare in carmina centum.

> “It is the custom of poets to demand a hundred voices for themselves, a hundred mouths, and to wish for a hundred tongues for their songs.”

[Col. 0586C] Verse 367. “For when a boy.” Some have called into question whether Paulinus was born in Aquitania. But, apart from other authorities that establish it, the matter is asserted here:

> For when a boy, brought from the western shores of the Gauls.

Paulinus therefore derived his birth from Gaul. It is also asserted below:

> When you called me back to the shore of my former native land,  
> I was restored to my anxious mother.

Here he speaks of his own journey to Gaul, where he also indicates that his parent was still living. He adds that, although residing in Spain, he lived with a Gallic mind. Moreover, Paulinus has already testified above that he went to Nola while still a boy, addressing Saint Felix as follows:

> To you Christ gave me as a servant from my earliest years.

[Col. 0586D] Verse 374. “Under your leadership, the fasces-bearing.” I have treated Saint Paulinus’s consulship at length in Dissertation IX.

[Col. 0586D] Verse 376. “Pure from human.” The poem must be emended, and the word “blood” must either be removed or placed earlier in the metre. I would prefer:

> I remained pure from the stain of human slaughter.

[Col. 0586D] Verse 377. “Then also the first.” A metrical foot is missing from the verse. Either the epithet must be joined to “offerings,” or something else must be inserted, for example:

> Then also, as is customary, the first offerings of the beard.

It was the custom among the ancients, when young men first emerged from the class of ephebes, to shave the beard and dedicate it to some god or to the household gods. Theseus went to Delos for this purpose, as Plutarch relates in his *Life*. Statius, *Thebaid* VIII:

> One was feeding his cheeks to Phoebus, another his hair to Bacchus.

Dio, speaking of Nero in Book LXI, says:

> Τρίχας ἐς σφαιρίον τι χρυσοῦν ἐμβαλὼν ἀνέθηκε τῷ Διὶ τῷ Καπιτωλινίῳ.

> “Throwing the hair into a certain golden ball, he dedicated it to Jupiter Capitolinus.”

Suetonius had recorded the same thing in these words:

> “At the gymnastic games that he held in the enclosure, amid the preparations for the sacrifice, he placed his first beard, enclosed in a golden box and adorned with the most precious pearls, and consecrated it to Jupiter Capitolinus.”

On this custom, see Bisciola, *Horæ Subcesivæ*, Book VII, chapter 5; Alexander ab Alexandro, *Dies Geniales*, Book I, chapter 26, and Book III, chapter 27, and elsewhere; Caelius Rhodiginus, Book XIX, chapter 22; Tiraquellus, *De Jure Primigeniorum*; Hadrian Junius, Book II *De Coma*; and others. What the pagans did was also transferred to Christians, as we learn from this evidence. The pagans dedicated the beard to their gods; Christians dedicated it to the holy martyrs or to God himself. From the Life of Saint William the Duke, edited by the distinguished Mabillon, chapter 23, we learn that the beard was consecrated to God by monks who placed it there. Among Christians the beard was blessed when it was cut. Adhemar of Chabannes, in Besly, page 328, says of Bishop Jordan:

> “On the following day he ordered the beard to be blessed and cut off.”

On this custom, consult Du Fresne, Dissertation 22 on Joinville, page 273. Paulinus therefore wished his first beard to be cut before Saint Felix’s tomb, and perhaps dedicated it to the holy confessor.

[Col. 0587D] Verse 380. “To the Campanians.” Return to what I treated at greatest length in Dissertation X, so that I need not become excessively tedious here.

[Col. 0587D] Verse 395. “Therefore, when twice three.” Saint Ambrose, Letter 58:

> “I know,” he says, “that many pagans used to boast that they had brought back the axe unstained with blood from the administration of a province.”

For these offices of Paulinus, see Dissertation X below.

[Col. 0587D] Verse 397. “Of the former native land.” Namely, Gaul or Aquitania, from which Paulinus had derived his origin.

[Col. 0587D] Verse 398. “Thence his kinsmen.” Paulinus was born at Bordeaux, the most celebrated city of Aquitania, as Uranius testifies in his Life; or at Hebromagus, a settlement near that city, as Ausonius suggests in his letter to the same Paulinus. Hence Paulinus calls his kinsmen Iberians.

[Col. 0587D] Verse 400. “There, in marriage chambers.” Paulinus received Therasia, concerning whom see Dissertation V, as his wife. With very probable conjecture, she was born in Spain, and her native city may perhaps have been Complutum. For in the *Panegyric on Celsus*, Paulinus says of the son born to him:

> “Whom we entrusted to our kinsmen in the city of Complutum,  
> joined to the martyrs by the bond of a tomb.”

[Col. 0588B] Verse 406. “Where the sea of Ocean.” The verse can easily be emended, for Paulinus never devised the word *unditus*; rather, some word must be changed. The most elegant poet Peter Bernardonius, a man of the highest talent, thinks the verse should be read:

> “Which is beaten round by the resounding surge of Ocean’s sea.”

Accordingly, he also thinks the preceding verse should be corrected so that the sense is coherent:

> “And I would inhabit another shore, far removed.”

But what region of Spain did Paulinus inhabit? Let us hear Ausonius, who complains of this to our poet in Letter 24:

> “Punic Barcelona wounds me,  
> and the snowy ridges of the two-shored Pyrenees wound me.”

And below:

> “Now for you beyond the Alps, beside the marble Pyrenees,  
> lie Tarragona, near the Caesarean and Augustan house,  
> and Barcelona, added to the shell-bearing sea.”

Yet these cities are washed only by the Tyrrhenian Sea, not by Ocean. I think that Paulinus lived chiefly in Vasconia. This was a part of Spain near Ocean, on the borders of Aquitania. The poet himself confirms this in Letter 4 to the same Ausonius:

> “Why do you set before me the vast forests  
> and snowy hospices of the Pyrenees in Vasconia?  
> Fixed, as it were, at the very threshold,  
> I shall dwell in a region of Spain.”

Nevertheless, Paulinus did not remain there so exclusively that he failed often to visit the rest of Tarraconensian Spain. Other poems of his same work suggest this. I proceed to other matters.

[Col. 0588D] Verse 418. “Now a governor.” Governors were appointed over the provinces of the Roman Empire, possessing supreme authority over offenders and property. There is a title in the Theodosian Code, Book I, *On the Office of the Governor of a Province*, where more is said about them. They are also discussed in Book I, *On the Office of the Prefect of Africa*, section “God Has Given Us”; in the law *Illicitas*, *Digest*, *On the Office of the Governor*; and in other imperial edicts. See Gothofredus in the *Notes on the Notitia Dignitatum*, Panciroli on the *Notitia of Both Empires*, and Bulengerus in *The Roman Empire*.

[Col. 0589C] Verse 426. “He conducted business.” I would prefer *egi commercia*, “I conducted business,” as also in the following poem: *distractis omnibus emi*, “having sold everything, I bought.”

[Col. 0589C] Verse 439. “And to those who trust.” I would add *ipsum*, so that the poem is complete:

> “By interest he will make a fortune for himself from those who borrow.”

[Col. 0589D] Verse 446. “My great power.” An imitation of Virgil. Venus says to Cupid in *Aeneid* I:

> “Son, my strength, my great power, you alone.”

Statius, *Thebaid* I, introduces Venus speaking in this way:

> “But he shall be given to the young man for whom you, my son, desire to be my highest power.”

[Col. 0589D] Verse 449. “You, bodily, to us.” He indicates the holy resolve of chastity by which, together with his wife Therasia, he had dedicated himself to Christ. For, in order to be promoted to the priesthood, he had to be separated from his wife’s bed. This ancient practice of the Church is found reinforced by many conciliar canons. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius:

> “Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are chosen either as virgins or widowers, or at least, after the priesthood, they remain chaste forever.”

[Col. 0590C] He repeats this frequently, especially against Vigilantius. Arator the Subdeacon, chapter 30:

> “The gracious faith of the Church now commands  
> that her pontiffs be chaste without end.”

Several writers have discussed this question at length, especially Bellarmine, Book I *On Clerics*, and Allatius, *On the Agreement of the Two Churches*. For this reason Idacius says in his Chronicle that Therasia was changed from Paulinus’s wife into his sister.

[Col. 0590D] Verse 483. “With a neighboring martyr.” Paulinus wrote in Letter 10 to Severus that the elder Melania had been received in these same Cells:

> “Our hut, suspended above the ground and extending farther through one upper room, with a portico placed between guest cells, provided, as though enlarged by the grace of the Lord, ample space not only for the saints who accompanied her in great numbers, but also for the crowds of those wealthy people, whom its narrowness did not exclude.”

[Col. 0590D] Verse 486. “Narrow beams.” A *tigillum* is a small beam, or a little transverse timber, and therefore the sense does not fit very well. I prefer to emend it to *magis arta tegella*, “a still narrower little roof.” *Tegellum* means a small covering or little roof. This better agrees with the poet’s intention.

[Col. 0591C] Verse 494. “With inexhaustible return.” *Reditas*, not *redditus*, was used by the best authors for income or proceeds. Ovid, Book IV of the *Pontic Letters*, Elegy 5:

> “Or may he arrange the revenues of the people that have been put up for auction.”

Velleius Paterculus speaks of “richer revenues” in Book II of his *History*, and Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 37, mentions “the revenues of the people.”

[Col. 0591C] Verse 496. “Whatever was great.” Paulinus must once have been a remarkably wealthy man. Besides other authorities, Ausonius clearly suggests this in Letter 24 to the same man:

> “Lest we mourn the scattered and plundered house,  
> and the realms of ancient Paulinus, broken among a hundred masters.”

Saint Eucherius, in his letter *On Contempt of the World*:

> “Paulinus also, bishop of Nola, a singular and blessed example of our Gaul, once possessing an immense assessment of wealth…”

Venantius Fortunatus, in Book II of the Life of Saint Martin, says this about Paulinus:

> “Rich in fields, wealthy in servants, rich in heaps of treasure,  
> a man vast in census, rich in house and rounded in speech;  
> richer still in faith, he becomes poor to himself for Christ,  
> and gave countless coins that redeem sins.”

I pass over Augustine, Book I, chapter 10, of *The City of God*; Prosper in his Chronicle under the fourth year of Arcadius and Honorius; Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107; and the rest.

[Col. 0591D] Verse 503. “The light burden easily departs.” Saint Jerome, in Letter 13 to our Paulinus:

> “Finally, when you heard the Savior’s saying, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess and give to the poor, and come, follow me,’ you turn words into deeds; and, naked, following the naked cross, you climb Jacob’s ladder more freely and lightly.”

[Col. 0591D] Verse 514. “Nor without a name.” Saint Jerome likewise, Book III on Matthew:

> “Christ did not say, ‘You who have left everything’—for the philosopher Crates did this, and many others despised riches—but ‘you who have followed me’: this is proper to the apostles and to believers.”

[Col. 0592C] Verse 515. “And to the command for anyone.” Something is missing from the poem. I would write: *Praeceptoque ejus cuiquam*, “and to his command for anyone.”

[Col. 0592C] Verse 526. “Joined.” Perhaps *junctos*, “joined,” should be read.

[Col. 0592C] Verse 530. “Once rich.” Paulinus had said the same of Saint Felix in Natalis IV:

> “Left rich in much gold,  
> he flourished in wealth, although he was not the sole heir.  
> Hermias, with his brother who bore the same name as their father,  
> divided the earthly riches; Felix alone  
> obtained the heavenly things.”

[Col. 0592D] Verse 534. “Felix, a tenant.” Of the same holy confessor Paulinus says in Natalis V:

> “He himself cultivated three acres of lean soil,  
> not holding them under his own right, but as a tenant farmer;  
> he tended them by his own hand, without a servant,  
> the owner of a poor garden.”

Bede and Marcellus the presbyter say the same in the Life of Saint Felix.

[Col. 0592D] Verse 539. “They separate only so much.” *Dispescere*, “to disagree,” is an unusual word. Perhaps *tantum discordant*, “they differ only so much,” should be read, as the preceding poem teaches, where the wolf is said to be at odds with the lamb.

[Col. 0592D] Verse 545. “This way, furfos.” I approve here the conjecture of Peter Anthony Bernardonius, a most charming poet and, above all others, my intimate friend. He thinks *fartos*, “stuffed,” should be read, the letters in the manuscript having been slightly corrupted. This word properly means “full” or “heavy with food,” and suits the poet’s intention perfectly.

[Col. 0593B] Verse 563. “Through so many ages past.” Consult Dissertation XIV, in which I discuss Saint Felix. There we said much against the common opinion concerning the date of his martyrdom.

[Col. 0593B] Verse 588. “With a railing.” The tombs of men distinguished for holiness were customarily surrounded by railings. Paulinus, Natalis VII:

> “Snatched from the crowd, and brought near the sacred doors,  
> the body was turned before the railings.”

Gregory of Tours, Book VI of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 10:

> “Those thieves, placing a railing at the window of the apse, which stood above the tomb of a certain dead man…”

Paul, in the little book which he presented to Saint Augustine, Sermon 31 *On Various Matters*, says:

> “Every day I prayed with great tears in the place where the memorial of the most glorious martyr Stephen is. On Easter Sunday, as others who were present saw, while I was praying and holding the railing with great weeping, I suddenly fell.”

Saint Ambrose, in his letter to Marcellina:

> “When even the clergy were afraid, I ordered the earth to be dug up at the place before the railings of Saints Felix and Nabor…”

The other Paulinus repeats the same account in the Life of Ambrose. Our author, below, speaking of opening Saint Felix’s tomb, says:

> “Their first task is  
> to remove the railings from the place.”

[Col. 0593C] Verse 588. “Let it be some kind of covering.” I wrote this, whereas the manuscript had *Sed pagina quaedam*, “But some kind of covering.” The tombs of the saints were formerly covered with silver or gold. Famous is the altar here at Milan where the bodies of Saints Ambrose, Protasius, and Gervasius are buried, which Archbishop Angilbert covered with golden plates. In 1468, according to Spondanus, *On Sacred Cemeteries*, Book I, part 3, chapter 4, a very white marble chest was found in Rome, in the chapel of Saint Petronilla. It contained two wooden coffers, one larger and the other large enough for a child; both were covered with silver plates and marked with the sign of the cross. Sometimes the chests themselves were made of silver; examples may be found in Aringhi, *Subterranean Rome*. In 1695, at Pavia, beneath the confession or altar of Saint Augustine, a similar sarcophagus was discovered containing two coffers, one of them made of the purest silver. It was long disputed whether Augustine’s bones were enclosed within it; the matter remains uncertain.

[Col. 0593D] Verse 590. “Open with a double mouth.” The tombs of the saints were constructed so that the bodies, enclosed in small coffers, lay deeply below; in the upper part, however, one or two openings were made in the pavement. In the Life of Saint Quintinus, under 31 October in Surius and in other writers, such an opening is called a little window. The railings mentioned above were placed around it. A representation of this kind can be seen in the tomb of Saint Charles here at Milan. Through these openings pallia, handkerchiefs, *brandea*—a name by which certain cloths were known among the ancients—and oils were inserted, so that they might be imbued through contact with the tomb by all the power flowing from the saints’ relics.

Gregory of Tours, Book II *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 46, says of the tomb of Saint Venerandus:

> “Above it, anyone who wishes may insert his head through the little window, praying for whatever necessity compels him.”

The same author, Book I *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 37, describing the tomb of Saints Peter and Paul:

> “Whoever wishes to pray approaches the tomb after the railings surrounding the place have been opened; then, when the little window has been opened…”

Metaphrastes, in Surius under 11 July, relates the discovery of Saint Euphemia’s relics. In her tomb there was a chest with a small opening. Once, when I too, unworthy though I was, dared to put my hand into it and touched the little coffin, I sensed a good fragrance and apprehended grace.

[Col. 0594C] Verse 591. “Offering what had been poured in.” It was a pious custom among Christians to bring oil or nard to the tombs of the saints; the power of healing was communicated through these liquids. Here is what Paulinus says of this nard:

> “Coming from the sacred ash’s hidden resting-place,  
> it sanctifies and heals with the secret breath of the spirit.”

They used to carry back the nard that had been poured in, inserting vessels and drawing it out:

> “And those who had given it to the place, preparing to drain the nard,  
> so that they might now carry it away for themselves.”

He had said in Natalis VI:

> “They hasten to bathe the martyr’s tomb with nard  
> and carry back the healing ointments from the holy sepulchre.”

I could prove with many examples what cures the oil and nard carried away from the tombs of the holy martyrs accomplished. Augustine alone will suffice. In Book XXII, chapter 8, of *The City of God*, he says this about a certain dead child:

> “While the body lay lifeless and the funeral rites were being prepared by those groaning and weeping, one of his friends, amid words of consolation, suggested that the body be anointed with the oil of that same martyr. It was done, and he came back to life.”

On this custom and the power of blessed oil, let the Agiomachi see how rightly they themselves malign it. We hasten to other matters.

[Col. 0595B] Verse 592. “Which came from the sacred ash.” This matter is wonderfully illuminated by the poems of Paulinus of Petricordia, Book V *On the Life of Saint Martin*, where he says:

> “For, as the faithful often do with devoted hearts,  
> they fill vessels with oil, brought for the preservation of health,  
> either to offer to righteous men or to place in holy  
> and reverenced places, where the present working  
> of the martyr reveals patrons proven by their power.  
> In these places, where the surrounding neighborhood provides it,  
> they pour peaceful liquid into clean vessels,  
> destined to be changed by the dew poured from above,  
> through which heavenly grace flows into the holy substance.”

I say nothing of the remaining passages to be read in that author.

Verse 598. “Instead of nard, with a dart.” A corruption may perhaps lie hidden here. I would explain *jaculum* as a vessel or some sponge inserted through the opening into the sepulchral chest, so that the nard or oil poured in might be drawn out from it. For *jaculum* is something made to be thrown, as Varro attests. Thus Plautus, *Truculentus* 3, calls a net a *jaculum*:

> “They test whether you will be kind or a good fellow,  
> like one who prepares a casting-net for a fishpond;  
> when the net has sunk, he draws it away.”

I would nevertheless emend the passage with only a few changes:

> “With wondrous novelty, the heap is filled,  
> instead of nard, with little vessels.”

The form *vasclum* for *vasculum* is permitted by syncope, just as the ancients used *maniplis* for *manipulis*, *duxti* for *duxisti*, *dispostus* for *dispositus*, *tablis* for *tabulis*, *soldis* for *solidis*, and hundreds of similar forms. This reading is wonderfully confirmed by the poems of the other Paulinus cited recently:

> “They pour peaceful liquid into clean vessels.”

[Col. 0595D] Verse 599. “With much dust.” Nevertheless, it was customary in antiquity to carry away dust from the tombs of the saints, and it possessed no less power of healing than the relics themselves. Bede, Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 3, describes the tomb of the blessed bishop Chad as follows:

> “The place of the tomb is a wooden coffin made in the form of a little house, with a covered opening in the wall, through which those who come there out of devotion may insert their hand and take away a portion of the dust.”

On this subject, consult John Ferrandus of the Society of Jesus, Book I, chapter 3, of his *Investigations into Relics*.

[Col. 0596B] Verse 603. “To search out and the innermost.” That is, “the inward part.” The adjective *penitus* is not without good examples. Plautus, *Asinaria* 3:

> “Come, please, by Hercules, right out from the innermost jaws.”

Catullus, in the wedding poem:

> “But no less than yours, a flame burns in my inmost breast—  
> indeed, more deeply within.”

Hence *penitissimus* and *penitior* occur in the older Latin writers.

[Col. 0596C] Verse 605. “Lest anything.” The manuscript has *Et quid*, “And what.” I have emended it.

[Col. 0596C] Verse 621. “The commands of priests.” In the earliest centuries of the Church, the title “priest” was customarily applied only to bishops. This practice was gradually weakened, and the term was then widely extended to presbyters. Hence Rabanus, Book I *On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 5:

> “A priest may be called either a bishop or a presbyter.”

Honorius of Autun had preceded him in Book I, chapter 182. Among the ancients—Cyprian, Augustine, and others—this title was always, or generally, reserved for bishops. Saint Ambrose, Book V, Letter 30:

> “Saint Damasus, priest of the Roman Church.”

Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107, speaking of our Paulinus:

> “When the priest in the city of Nola died, he himself was appointed in the bishop’s place.”

Paulinus himself, speaking in the *Epithalamium* of Aemilius, bishop of Beneventum, says:

[Col. 0596D]

> “Born later but senior, because as priest in his see  
> he bears apostolic gray hair in his breast.”

Above:

> “The holy pledges of the priest, joined  
> by a venerable covenant.”

This refers to Bishop Memor. On this matter, see also La Cerda, *Sacred Adversaria*, chapter 39, no. 13. Presbyters were called priests of the second order, as may be seen in Sidonius, Letter 25, Book IV, and elsewhere. Bishops, however, were called priests of the first order. Nevertheless, the word here could signify the presbyters themselves, since it is expressed in the plural and at that time only one bishop is mentioned at Nola. I would not dare to assert this; rather, I would be inclined to restore *sacerdotis* for *sacerdotum*.

[Col. 0596D] Verse 628. “With the throne unharmed.” Dungalus incorrectly attributed the following eight verses to Natalis XIV. See how much more correctly they now appear.

[Col. 0597C] Verse 639. “Raised together.” Since in Paulinus’s time it was not yet established whether the souls of the righteous were admitted to the vision of God and everlasting glory immediately after death or only after the Last Judgment, I suspected that Paulinus had remained uncertain on this question and had here followed the examples of certain other Fathers who were likewise undecided. From this verse I thought I had sufficiently detected his opinion, and still more clearly from Letter 12 to Severus, where he sings of Clarus, a holy man already dead:

> “Whether you rest in the bosoms of the Fathers,  
> or are buried beneath the altar of the Lord,  
> or are nourished in the sacred grove,  
> wherever in the region of heaven or paradise you are placed,  
> blessed Clarus, you live beneath eternal peace.”

[Col. 0597D] But the distinguished Father Eustachius of Saint Ubaldus, of the Congregation of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, a man of refined learning, pointed out to me that Paulinus, if his words are carefully weighed, held a sound view. And indeed we can easily persuade ourselves that in this verse the holy poet indicated that complete blessedness which the saints will enjoy after the final day of judgment, when their bodies too have been glorified. The verses recently cited to Severus testify only that Paulinus was uncertain about the place where the souls of the faithful are now detained. For he is far from denying that glory is granted to the saints before the resurrection of their bodies; indeed, he explicitly asserts it when he says:

> “Wherever in the region of heaven or paradise you are placed,  
> blessed Clarus, you live beneath eternal peace.”

For this reason he implores his aid with God. Paulinus often sings of Saint Felix as restored to heaven. In Natalis I he says:

> “Borne without bloodshed to the martyr’s heavenly honor.”

Natalis III:

[Col. 0598C]

> “He died, and was born to Christ among the heavenly stars,  
> attaining the martyr’s heavenly honor without bloodshed.”

Natalis VI explicitly testifies to Saint Felix’s glory:

> “The heavenly beings enjoy Felix in spirit;  
> here we possess his body, while there the spirit  
> of his powerful soul lives, and here his merit.”

He says that the dead Felix was carried by angels

> “into the presence of the King and before the face of the supreme Father.”

He presents him as endowed with three crowns and adds:

> “Thus he possesses the rewards of what he endured,  
> which was accomplished by ready courage;  
> nor is he without the honor and adornment of peace.”

Therefore Paulinus appears to have been somewhat uncertain about the place where the souls of the faithful are detained, but not about their blessedness.

[Col. 0598D] Verse 655. “I myself also, I confess.” Paulinus touched on this shortage of water in Natalis IX:

> “Perhaps, amid these spectacles, you eagerly ask  
> from what source this area, rich in fountains, is to be filled,  
> when the city is far away and there is scarcely any watercourse from the city  
> to send a scant drop here through a narrow channel.  
> I shall answer: we trust nothing to our own right hand,  
> we place no confidence in earthly aid;  
> we have entrusted everything to mighty God  
> and look for fountains from heaven.”

[Col. 0598D] Verse 685. “Through wells.” It was the practice at Nola to receive water brought by aqueduct into wells and reservoirs, so that it might provide relief in summer. Capaccio, at the end of his *History of Naples*, speaking of the water brought to Nola from the city of Abella, says:

> “It not only waters the countryside, so that, when led through channels, it is poured into wells found everywhere, and the people of Abella are refreshed with the greatest pleasure during the summer heat by the goodness and coolness of its waters, but it is also conveyed, for a price, to the cisterns of the Nolan people.”

[Col. 0599C] Verse 695. “Your own self, you.” The reading and sense lie in considerable obscurity. I leave the attempt to cure the passage to others.

[Col. 0599C] Verse 705. “The name of Abella.” *Abella*, not *Avella*, must be read. As Cluverus observes in *Ancient Italy*, Book IV, page 1185, Ptolemy and Strabo write Ἀβέλλα, not Ἀουέλλα. On an ancient marble inscription preserved by Capaccio one reads *POPULUS ABELLANUS*, “the people of Abella.” Virgil likewise mentions Abella in *Aeneid* VII:

> “And those who look down upon the walls of honey-bearing Abella.”

Servius, however, commenting on this passage of Virgil, advises reading *maliferae*, “apple-bearing,” since Punic apples grow at Nola. See also Justin, the epitomator of Trogus, Book XX, and Pliny, Book III, chapter 5.

[Col. 0599C] Verse 711. “A great sacred bier.” I have not yet been able to discover what holy body was formerly buried at Abella, despite the labor expended on this matter by the most learned man, and one to whom I owe much commendation, Hercules Barussius. While he was at Naples, he neglected no effort in his attempt to reach knowledge of this matter. Our manuscript reads:

> “But a great [thing] will bring me to the saint.”

I supplied the deficiency in the final word and, as the metre advised, removed *mihi*.

[Col. 0599D] Verse 712. “The city by its construction.” There may perhaps be an error in the word, but I do not dare remove it. Two Abellae can now be counted: one new, the other old. The former is scarcely six thousand paces distant from Nola; the latter, as Capaccio says in Book II, chapter 30, of his *History of Naples*, reveals ancient remains not far from the new city, clearly marked by the ruins of walls and towers and enclosed within a circuit of about twenty-four stadia.

[Col. 0599D] Verse 713. “High-jutting mountains.” Capaccio says in the passage cited:

> “Abella sits in a theatre of mountains and hills on the Campanian plain. Although the mountain ridges grow cold in winter, it is nevertheless so fanned by the pleasantness of the air that the inhabitants never fear the injuries of the cold.”

[Col. 0600C] Verse 714. “Draws water close at hand.” On the streams that descend from the mountains of Abella and are conveyed as far as Nola, Ambrose Leo, *On Nola*, Book I, chapter 1, and Capaccio in the passage cited should be consulted.

[Col. 0600C] Verse 715. “Through inserted cups.” The glossaries and other lexicographers are silent about what *calix* means in aqueducts. Frontinus, however, teaches us in his *Aqueducts of Rome*:

> “A *calix* is a bronze measuring device inserted into a channel or reservoir. Pipes are attached to it. Its length must be no less than twelve fingers, and its aperture—that is, its capacity—must be as large as has been prescribed. It appears to have been devised because the rigidity of bronze, which is difficult to bend, cannot easily be loosened or tightened.”

The author cited below also uses the word:

> “The superintendent should take care that the *calix* of the prescribed measure be marked in the presence of surveyors.”

And again:

> “Care must also be taken with the placement of the *calices*, so that they are arranged on a level and the *calix* of one is not placed lower and that of another higher.”

Finally, he reports this point:

> “In some pipes, not even *calices* were installed.”

[Col. 0600D] Verse 721. “Grateful works.” I think this should be read instead of the manuscript’s *gratis operis*, “of free work.”

[Col. 0600D] Verse 733. “Baskets.” A *cophinus* is a little wicker basket or something similar. The word occurs not only among the Evangelists but also in the better Latin authors. Juvenal, Satire 3, verse 13:

> “Now the grove of the sacred fountain and the shrines are rented to Jews, whose household goods are a basket and hay.”

He repeats the same point in Satire 6, verse 542. For excellent learning about the basket—namely, that it was a sign of Jewish servitude—see Laurentius Ramirez de Prado, *Pentecont*, chapter 40. In the following verse I read *vectis* for *vectos*.

[Col. 0600D] Verse 744. “And the channels.” *Formae* are constructed and arched channels, as Vitruvius says. Sidonius Apollinaris uses the term in Book VIII, chapter 7:

> “I seemed likely to drain not only his channels but even his sea-battles.”

Frontinus, Books I and II; Cassiodorus, Letters 21 and 31; Symmachus, Letter 33, Book X; Ammianus, Book XXVIII; and others mention them. The anonymous author *On Aqueducts* says:

> “Now let us list the names of the waters brought for the uses of the eternal City through the construction of channels.”

Palladius, Book IX, title 11:

> “If water is conveyed through a channel, the conduit must be solidified so that it cannot escape through cracks.”

Hence the magistrate called the *comes formarum*, “supervisor of the channels,” and the *curator formarum*, “curator of the channels,” appears not infrequently in ancient inscriptions. On this, see the distinguished Du Fresne in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*.

[Col. 0601D] Verse 748. “Through many thousands.” I do not know whether *milia* for *milliaria* was known to the better authors, but it was used in the age of Paulinus. Our poet had used it above:

> “Our city lies six thousand [paces] from Nola here.”

I also find it used by Rutilius Namatianus, Book II, who flourished in Paulinus’s time:

> “The stone marked with the words ‘many thousands’  
> seems to provide intervals of road for the weary.”

[Col. 0602C] I think this word was brought into Latin from Greek. Among the Greeks *mílion* was used for a thousand paces; Strabo uses the word in Book VII. Suidas says of it:

> Μίλιον μέτρον τῆς γῆς. Τὰ δέκα μίλια ἔχουσι σταδία πʹ.

> “A *mílion* is a measure of land. Ten *mília* contain eighty stadia.”

For this reason, at Constantinople the place from which roads were measured, and where the milestones of journeys stood, was called a *milliarium*, after the Golden Milestone formerly erected at Rome. On this, see the learned Du Fresne, Book I of *Christian Constantinople*, chapter 24. Palladius, Paulinus’s contemporary, therefore uses *milii* for *milliarium* in *The Lausiac History*, chapters 6, 20, and 77; his very ancient Latin translator retained the word. In our manuscript this word is written with a single *l*. I have not altered it, since it comes especially close to the Greek form.

[Col. 0602D] Verse 763. “You believed.” Perhaps the word requires some emendation. Certainly the sense could be made clearer.

[Col. 0602D] Verse 789. “Poor in wealth.” Silius Italicus also touches upon Abella’s poverty in Book VIII:

> “Sorrento, and Abella, poor in the furrow of Ceres.”

[Col. 0603D] Verse 820. “The abundance that you had been.” Thus it stands in the manuscript.

[Col. 0603D] Verse 826. “You repented.” *Poeniteo* was used by the older Latin writers, and Paulinus therefore uses it elegantly as well. The testimony is the very ancient Priscian, Book XI *On Participles of Tense and Form*. Speaking of impersonal verbs, he says:

> “It must nevertheless be known that all these forms are found in usage among the ancients with the perfect declension, as Capro testifies: *pigeo*, *pudeo*, *taedeo*, *poeniteo*.”

The very learned Michael Maddius, son of the distinguished Carolus Maria Maddius and thoroughly versed in both languages, also informed me that he had read *poenitebunt* in Pacuvius.

[Col. 0603D] Verse 840. “Of Pinianus.” That is, “of Pinianus,” who perhaps was the son of another Pinianus, according to the rule governing patronymic names. See what I said in Dissertation VI.

POEM XXII. [Note: [Col. 0604D] It was formerly appended as Letter 16. It has been placed here. Written before the year 400, perhaps in 398 or 399.]

He teaches Jovius that all things are subject to divine providence, while fate and fortune are nothing. He urges him to read Holy Scripture.

> Now I promise myself that you will place your poems  
> in the sacred books, and that, set aflame by the power of Christ’s God,  
> you will loosen your eloquent lips before the supreme Father.

> Begin to devote your heart wholly to divine things,  
> and raise your thoughts, lifted from earth, to God;  
> soon a new light will arise for your eyes, with heaven opened,  
> and the sacred Spirit will enter through a silent passage  
> and shake your innermost being with joyful breath.

> Come, then, stretch the lyre; strike your fruitful breast,  
> producing great things. Let the resources devoted  
> to customary songs depart: a greater order of things  
> is being born for you.

[Col. 0604D] Note: The Vienna manuscripts read *subjectos*, “subject”; the Regius manuscript and the edition of Poelman read *subreptos*, “stolen.”

[Col. 0604D] Note: Thus the Vienna manuscript and the edition of Schott, volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 978. Other copies read *operta*, “covered.”

[Col. 0604D] Note: The Vienna manuscript reads *facundum*, “eloquent.”

[Col. 0604D] Note: The Vienna manuscript reads *vomens*, “pouring forth.”

Not merely the judgment of Paris, nor the wars of the giants,

shall you falsely sing: let this once have been a childish game

of yours; such amusements suited a little boy.

[15] Now, since you are more mature in spirit and further advanced in years,

[Col. 0604B] disdain the frivolous Muses with a mature heart,

receive a subject such as your age, now suited to chaste character,
and the venerable pattern of your utterance fittingly demand;
and conceive divine thoughts.

[20] If you have gained some distinction and a name

from false things—greatness from empty matters—

when you sang fabricated tales in ancient poems,

or recounted earthly deeds while praising the insignia

of triumphant kings,

you are not, in truth, worthy to derive glory from those works,

which you adorned more by the lavishness of your words.

How much greater glory will accrue to you from beginnings

in which, while exercising your tongue, you will also educate

your holy mind, and at once gain praise and life?

And while, with understanding

[Note: The Viennese manuscript reads *caute*, “cautiously.”],

you read and write the miracles of the Most High

[30] [Col. 0604C] true God, you will learn to be nearer and dearer to him:

while believing in him, you will marvel at him,

and you will begin to love him; and by loving him,

you will be loved again by Christ.

Until now that trumpet of your voice has been employed

for empty purposes;

let your person now sound forth the divine deeds

in a loftier manner.

[35] Do you wish to know the causes of things and the world’s beginnings?

[Note: The Viennese manuscript reads *volens*, “wishing.”]

Do not, wandering aimlessly, seek innumerable worlds—

the dreams of Epicurus—

which a madman supposes to be produced by atoms as parents

through the void, and seek them with your breast straying

into emptiness.

Moses, revered under the ancient name of lawgiver,

who, composed and orderly, recounts the world from its first origin,

will relieve you of these vain concerns:

he will teach you of the human being formed from clay

and breathed upon by the sacred breath,

[Col. 0604D] 553–554 breathed upon by him as a gift, and of the fact that by this gift

you are higher on earth than all creatures that breathe.

[45] Do not despise yourself as though you were Pyrrha’s stones

or Prometheus’ clay,

for the supreme hand fashioned you sublime in face and spirit,

and judged you worthy of his own image.

There too you will learn

[Note: Thus the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Schott’s edition, p. 978; other manuscripts likewise read *ibidem*, “there.”]

—for do not go on assigning our free will to the fates—

what judgment bound us to death

and under whose law we live.

[50] If you cast your mind higher than heaven

and desire to know what exists, or what existed before the ages,

John teaches you what lies beyond both world and ages

[Note: John 1.].

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word:

God rejoiced with the Word beside him;

and the Word was both the Word of God and God himself.

This Word exists without whom nothing exists,

through whom all things were made and endure,

who governs everything, to whom all things are subject and obedient,

[Col. 0605B] and every nature, prostrate before God in eternal service,

worships the divinity of the begotten and the begetter

[Note: So the Viennese manuscript. Other manuscripts read: “the name of the begetter of the begotten.”].

[60] And now every tongue among the nations confesses

the Lord Jesus, reigning in the majesty of the Father—

in whose name our salvation is founded and our faith stands,

reaching toward the ages of eternal life

[Note: Philippians 2:1.]

Strengthened by his divine gift, we attain,

through chaste deeds, to overcome our frail nature

and break the bonds of harsh death;

and to live in the body not according to bodily laws,

following the divine footsteps of Christ, God’s Son,

while the mind governs soul and body under sacred armor.

[70] For the mind, subject to God, receives the weapons of salvation,

and exercises dominion over its own soul and flesh;

and each person becomes master of himself by right:

whoever dedicates himself wholly to the one Lord

becomes ruler over his own limbs,

invincible to vices and a hater of wickedness.

[75] Stronger against adversity through the virtues,

a true human being, because powerful in mind,

he possesses the light of reason;

without struggle he restrains his servant senses

and guides his breast with gentle reins.

You, whose noble mind burns with the fire

of heavenly seed

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “of light.”],

[80] ascend in spirit to the heavenly recesses,

and place your head in the Lord’s bosom.

Soon Christ, generous, will offer his breasts,

overflowing with sacred milk, to your eager mouth,

and will flood your mind with divine light,

so that, once the great darkness has been dispelled,

you may behold the awesome ordinances of God—

the ordinances by which Christ, the all-parent wisdom,

always remaining in himself, continually renews all things.

And, as he wills, God himself, arbiter of his own works,

preserves and changes their forms,

and extends or shortens the times of life,

[Col. 0606A] governing heaven, sea, stars, and winds

[90] by the power through which he made them.

The great outcome of Egypt teaches this:

the tyrant submerged when the sea flowed back

[Note: Exodus 14.];

and earlier, he himself experienced the grievous upheavals

of all the elements, so that everything trembles before him

and everything serves him.

For at one time the common earth held the Jews,

the only nation then chosen by God

[Note: Psalm 75:1.];

yet God’s grave anger against proud enemies

ran distinct among peoples mingled together.

Now I know you will not say that uncertain chance

drives the storms and agitates the sea,

when you read that, once commanded to withdraw,

the sea withdrew,

[100] and that a road lay open through the rigid waters,

with the waters standing dry on either side,

and that, when the sea was again released at the command

and by the rod of the holy prophet,

it returned to its liquid depths

[Note: Exodus 14.].

In both cases the power of the sea obeyed,

so that a path might be given to the holy

and vengeance to their enemies.

[105] What of the prophet fleeing to Tarsus,

who, cast into the sea by the lot of danger,

was seized by a great beast with its spacious jaws

and vomited forth unharmed from its vast belly

[Note: So the Regius manuscript and Schott’s edition; the Vatican manuscript reads “hurled out,” while others read “vomited out.” See note 258.]

[Note: Jonah 1.]?

Does this not teach that the sea and the stars move

under God’s dominion?

For, fleeing God in vain—no one escapes him

who holds all things—he stirred the anger

of heaven and sea at once.

For the nature of the omnipotent Lord,

recognizing the rebel,

feared, as though conscious of its own safety,

to carry the guilty man,

and bound the fugitive with winds and waves.

This prophet, chosen by God to terrify peoples

[115] sinning at the warning,

after proclaiming grave destruction,

breaking the guilty and turning away the anger

of the deity,

washed away its crimes with abundant tears; and Nineveh, rightly changed,
escaped the final day

[Note: So the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and Schott’s edition, p. 979. Five printed editions read “of Nineveh.”]

[Note: Isaiah 38:5.].

Did that king have a fate who, with death near,

[120] prayed to the Lord, whom he knew to be the only one

able to bend his own decrees,

so that he might extend his completed life farther,

and deserved to live through three lustrums,

surviving beyond his own years

and living through ages not allotted to him?

Shall we now admire Plato weaving three Fates

[Note: See note 259.],

[125] or the measures of Aratus,

or the painted stars of Manetho?

Let them tell, I ask, where they then placed the swift hours

at their birth,

and through which signs the stars traveled,

when pious Hezekiah, praying with faithful devotion

[Note: So Badaric’s and Sachin’s editions. Other manuscripts read “of faith.” Paulinus always lengthens the second syllable in *fidei*.]

[Note: The Vatican and Viennese manuscripts read *precatu*, “by prayer”; this reading too may be accepted.],

[Col. 0607A] turned the courses of the stars

and disturbed the pathways of heaven

[130] by his commands, with the sun’s light driven backward

[Note: From the Viennese manuscript and Sachin we have emended this to *jussis*, “by his commands,” that is, “he disturbed the pathways of heaven by his command, with the sun driven backward.” The command is mentioned because he himself chose the sign. Formerly the text read *jussi*. The Regius manuscript has *jussit*, incorrectly.]

[Note: Joshua 10:12.]?

Or when, at the command of the holy leader,

the same delayed sun stood still through the night,

extending the day so that the victory of the sacred people

might be accomplished,

it stood with the circle of heaven turned back

[Note: So the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and the editions of Gronovius and Poelmann. The Vatican manuscript and three printed editions read “with the sphere of heaven shaken back.”]

so that the increased light might embrace great triumphs?

[135] What of Christ, the offspring, power, and wisdom of God—

does he not sufficiently remove our anxieties

from vain errors?

And by warnings and deeds alike he teaches us

that one God rules all things,

and that we should think nothing occurs without the mind

of God the Sovereign:

he says that not a leaf falls from a tree

[140] nor a bird from the air without his command.

When the Almighty lays the sea low by his word,

or treads upon it with his foot,

and by his word drives away diseases,

or compels demons,

or restores departed souls to dead bodies,

and commands those long lifeless to go forth

from opened tombs,

[145] restoring the buried when life returns—

does the author who alone governs all nature and life

not sufficiently reveal his own power

[Note: Matthew 10:29; Luke 8:24; and Matthew 14:25; likewise 4:24; Luke 7:15; John 11:39 and 44.]?

To reading and writing these things, I pray, devote

your study and labor;

sing of the great beginnings of the Thunderer’s works,

[150] write of the beginnings of created things by the Word,

and of chaos before day,

and of the first twilight of light;

then, through the sacred books, you will learn

what elements God spoke or brought about

through the successive ages,

as Moses taught when they were inscribed

on the legal tablets,

[155] or what the new law of the evangelical Testament

marks out, revealing mysteries of Christ previously concealed

[Note: So the Viennese manuscript. Other manuscripts read *Christo*, “to Christ.”].

Then I shall truly call you a divine poet,

and I shall drink your poems as though they were sweet water,

when your verses, singing again the Lord Christ,

shall offer me nectar drawn from the highest springs,

[160] and shall testify that your mind is powerful in God,

so that from you I may receive both the riches of your mouth

and those of your mind.

And him whom I rejoice to have joined to me

by a kindred covenant

[Note: So the Regius and Viennese manuscripts and three printed editions. Others read “joined by a relative.”],

[Col. 0607D] and whom I congratulate as a kinsman under holy religion,

[165] I shall embrace as a holy brother

with an everlasting pledge,

even when the bonds that must be released with the mortal body

have been dissolved.

[Note: These lines are absent from the Viennese manuscript. Schott’s edition has: “Farewell, happy Jovi, in Christ Jesus our Lord.”]

Read happily, Jovi, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## POEM XXIII

[Note: Formerly numbered 22; what was formerly 10 is now 16. Written in the year 400, on January 14.]

### On the Nativity of Saint Felix: Poem VII

Saint Felix frees those possessed by a demon. He restores an eye to Theridius.

Spring opens the voices of the birds;

my tongue has its own spring in Felix’s nativity,

on whose day winter itself blossoms with light,

while the peoples rejoice.

Even if the season, amid the deep frost,

still leads the year through the midst of winter,

[5] on this day, nevertheless, pious joys

make spring joyful for us.

Winter-sorrow yields as cares are driven from the breast;

the clouds of sadness flee from the serene heart.

Just as the gentle swallow recognizes the days,

and the white-winged bird with black wings,

and the turtledove, kindred of the pious dove,

and the acalanthis, which sings only in new spring

among the thickets,

and the birds that now wander mute beneath rough hedges,

but soon rejoice everywhere at returning spring,

[15] each as varied in voice as in many-colored wings—

so too I recognize this day,

which the holy annual festivals renew

with due honor to great Felix.

Now peaceful spring is reborn for me

as the rejoicing year returns;

now I delight to release my mouth in measured song

and fulfill my vows in song,

and to make my voice bloom with new utterances.

[20] Christ, God, flow into my heart,

and satisfy me, thirsting for the heavenly springs.

[Col. 0608C] But even a drop of you sprinkled upon my marrow
will be a light.

For what is astonishing if, with a little dew,

you fill even a very small soul,

when, made human in a small body,

you filled the world with eternal seed

and saved the whole orb with a single drop of blood?

Grant my request, Fountain of the Word,

God the Word,

and, like that spring bird just now,

make my voice melodious with a sweet sound—

that bird which, hidden beneath green foliage,

customarily charms the trackless fields

with many kinds of melody,

and through a single tongue pours forth

not a single kind of voice,

changing its song.

A bird of one color in its feathers,

but variegated in its utterances:

now it rolls out smooth melodies,

now draws out sharp hisses in long sounds;

[Col. 0608D] 559–560 then again begins a plaintive song,

[Note: Thus restored from the German manuscript; formerly the text read *sicut*, “as.”]

[35] and, suddenly cutting off its lament at the end,

[Col. 0609A] deceives astonished ears

with its broken melody.

But may your grace, Christ, flow continually from you for me.

And nevertheless I pray that I may be granted

the power to vary my melodies after the manner of that bird,

and now to bring forth my promised songs,

even if with one mouth and changing Muses,

because rich grace always adds varied subjects

to the wondrous powers of the Lord,

which Christ God repeatedly performs in his dear Felix,

bringing forth bright miracles through signs of salvation.

[45] That day is seen, accustomed to being observed

by the whole brood of vipers,

when he drives on savage demons

and beats the clamorous enemies

with an unseen hand

[Note: We have emended this from the German manuscript and Schott’s edition in the margin. The five printed editions incorrectly read “when he knew”; Rosweydus therefore corrected it to *communes*. See note 260.].

Yet it is marked by something extraordinary

in this very power:

although throughout the entire year

he torments the demons

[50] and orders them to depart from human bodies,

he nevertheless prolongs the affliction of many,

so that the longer punishment may harass the wicked enemies—

like those who deserved to become vessels for evil,

so that, as healing is delayed,

they may pay their entire guilt more fully

over an extended period

[Note: So the German manuscript and the editions; “by decree.”]

[55] Or perhaps he wishes to show indulgence to this nativity,

so that on other occasions he may help only a few,

and, in his kindness, bestow more gifts

on his own birthday.

For when this day draws near

as the year slips away,

then he presses upon them more frequently

and more severely.

Then you may see the sick hosts

being driven together more densely,

and salvation being sought

more urgently as the festival approaches.

[60] Then the demons, inflamed more fiercely than usual,

burn, howl more pitifully,

and, overcome by greater force,

groan under their final torments.

They are not allowed to depart easily

through a simple expulsion,

but, first driven about by strange

and varied punishments,

[Col. 0609C] 561–562 they are lifted high,

suspended and shaken higher than usual

in the empty air,

and cling to hidden bonds,
