enduring a penal delay through the void.

Although the bodies are not their own,

their punishment exhausts the tormented enemies.

[70] They are released from punishment

when bodies appear to suffer punishment,

and the immune souls [of the afflicted persons]

watch torments inflicted on limbs not their own.

A human being, when the demon is captured,

goes free;

[Note: We have added this line from the German manuscript. Formerly it read *Liber egit*, “the free man acted,” because.]

the appearance of punishment is confined to the body;

sensation is absent,

because the suffering is not the human being’s,

but the demon’s.

[75] Why do you insult us, bitter enemy?

What hope do you place in us?

Behold, the Evil One, by the craft of our Redeemer,

you are in turn toyed with as a mocker;

your deceit falls back upon your own bonds:

you seize, but are seized;

you bind, but are bound.

The trapped human being becomes a snare,

and his prey deceives the robber.

While the captive seeks the forbidden food of the body,

he, himself captive, devours the deadly hook.

[Col. 0610A] Yet I shall proclaim things witnessed

even more remarkable than these.

Before all the others, I shall relate how the man

whose limbs an ancient enemy possessed

was seized from the suffering crowd

and brought before the sacred light

of the holy martyr.

He was brought to the consecrated grating

before the saint’s doors,

and, with his body turned,

was suspended by his feet,

looking upside down toward the roof.

What is still more astonishing and sacred

[Note: See note 261.],

[90] is that the whole sacred body is veiled with a chaste covering—not with garments fallen back over the face and stiffly held there, nor with garments sewn to the feet—

[Note: Instead of “as a covering.”],

so that reverence for the divine work

might remain in the covered body;

and so that the demon, though suffering punishment,

might not take pleasure in exposing modesty

through naked limbs,

but might be tortured more severely

by the honor preserved intact.

[95] Although the coverings remained properly in place

on the inverted limbs,

these things are marvelous and great:

who can deny it?

Yet because they are more familiar through experience,

they seem less astonishing when heard,

however reverend they may be to behold,

and however great in deed.

Therefore listen, I pray,

to the small and at once new deeds of my patron,

which the Lord Christ performs in him

through manifold power,

by all of which he seeks to confirm one faith in us:

so that, through manifest proofs,

we may see the hidden God present,

and may recognize the heavenly Lord,

who created all things by his Word,

caring for human affairs and minds

with paternal concern.

[105] Let my brother Theridius provide

the opening of my narrative.

For what work of Felix should I undertake to sing,

what should I take up first or rather,

than what Dominaedius himself performed
for me in my own house?

From that night to this one,

a year has now fallen.

You know the custom by which we fast

before the day,

and, after tasting the sacred offerings late in the evening,

each of us returns to his own home.

Then, once the gatherings had dispersed

from the Lord’s temple,

after rest had been granted to our weary bodies

and food had been taken,

we began to rejoice in hymns to God

and prolong the night with psalms.

Meanwhile my brother, having withdrawn

from the friendly choir,

so that, with the air blowing outside,

he might drive away the heat

given off by the smoky room

with its waxed papyrus,

went out into the portico,

which extends beneath the narrow covered passage.

[120] Although the path lay dark at night,

with no light to illuminate it,

he nevertheless went with fearless step

through familiar doorways—

alas, for he was unaware of the danger nearby.

In the middle of the building,

between the roof and the ground,

a lamp customarily hung from a rope,

which swayed there.

A three-pronged iron fitting was attached

to the upper strand,

and into it was inserted

the penetrating handle of the glass lamp;

the broad-rimmed vessel was secured

on every side by three hooks.

The water below was completely white,

while olive oil floated yellow upon the water.

[130] The liquid stood in the liquid;

the slippery oil floated above

the water beneath it,

and the two fluids did not combine.

It is remarkable that the oily substance floated,

and that the dense material, once dissolved,

did not break apart the element,

but that the light substance supported the thick,

so that the water was thinner than the solid stream,

and, resting beneath the oil,

served as the foundation for the liquid.

Such discord among the fluids,

though they were mixed together inside,

shone visibly,

so that you could see the liquids remain distinct,

each preserving the color of its own fluid

within the vessel’s common interior

[Note: The German manuscript reads “preserves.”].

[140] A three-footed lead support was submerged in the middle,

and above it rose a hollow point

surrounded by an oiled wick.

The wet wick received the liquid fire

in its slender flame,

and, surrounded by the expanse

of the stagnant olive oil,

the thin lamp-wick gleamed

in the glass vessel.

[Col. 0611B] 563–564 Its sharp light, trembling from the top,

cast a gentle brightness

into the shadowy inner rooms

and opened the dense darkness

with calm radiance.

But by the time this night had passed,

the flame had already gone out,

for the boys, keeping vigil, had prolonged the hours,

and the light had failed when it had consumed its thirsty oil.

[150] But the boy who had removed the lamp

after its light was extinguished,

and who had loosened the rope

when he took it down,

neglected to tighten it again

with the customary knot.

Hence the rope hung lower,

drooping in a low curve,

deprived of its welcome light

and full of blind danger.

For the top of the noose

was armed with toothed hooks

that threatened those approaching;

and then it was disastrously in the way

of my brother—

almost disastrously,

but, by Christ’s command, beneficially,

for he turned a deadly accident

into joys worthy of remembrance.

[160] Therefore—behold Christ’s hand—

that hanging rope,

lower than usual in the darkness,

hung below its accustomed height

in the empty air.

From the region of the head,

with equal balance,

it had come to occupy the position

in which it stood.

Thus, alas, it received the approaching face

securely upon the point of its threefold hook,

[165] [Col. 0611D] and the hook caught the eye as it met it.

The blade slipped inward beneath the tender eyelid;

in that place the cautious hand of a physician

can scarcely guide the soft mass

with trembling care

and draw back the eyelid

with a gentle movement.

[170] Struck suddenly by so violent a blow,

he cried out,

and, confused, carried his trembling hands

to the eye itself.

At the same time, with his eye closed, he held the iron,

so as to restrain it,

or, if it fell, to catch the falling eyeball.

The globe, preserving the inmost organ of sight,

lies hidden within a smooth little sac,

filled with liquid:

the white lies beneath the glasslike image of the black pupil

[Note: That is, the pupil.].

[175] [Col. 0612A]

Here, like a marrow-root entering the eye,

it supports the eye

and nourishes it with the moist substance of the veins,

while the springs of the eyes remain fixed

beneath their matching star.

But if, by chance, the membrane of the eye’s fluid,

split by severe disease or by a blow,

should unfortunately rupture,

this globe leaps forth,

and, deprived of its nourishing fluid,

abandons the little dry hollow

emptied of its light.

Meanwhile the boy, startled by the cry

of the suffering man,

ran up, leaving his bed

as sleep fled from him,

and held out toward his face

the lamp he had lit.

[185] The man had covered his face with his hands

and, with his head thrown back,

looked upward like a young man struck by lightning

[Note: See note 264.],

so that, keeping his body balanced,

he might hold the rope motionless,

guiding his trembling limbs

according to the wound’s demands.

He feared that an opposite movement

might widen the wound,

and, because one eye alone remained free,

he guarded against danger to the corresponding side

with the eye of the captive.

Yet he did not dare touch the iron

in order to draw it out,

lest, by pulling the blade,

he should extract the eyeball

which still clung to it;

nor could he any longer endure

the delay caused by the weapon fixed beneath the eye,

but, despairing of human medical aid,

Felix was soon summoned

and came with divine help.

[200] Hanging there in so great a wound,

he called upon him

and brought forth his lament in these words:

“Alas for me!

How greatly my sins weigh upon my labors,

that I have deserved so great a wound

with Felix as my patron,

and, moreover, have had to suffer it

on the very birthday of Felix!

Alas, a great criminal,

whom punishment strikes at the very time

when he is accustomed to be released from punishment.

[205] 565–566 Holy one, I beg you, come to the aid of your servant.

I know that you stand near, and that from the neighboring shrine you have heard the weeping of your unhappy disciple.

[Note: So the German manuscript and three editions. Two printed editions read “this one.”]

Whether now, joined close to the exalted side before the throne of the great King, you receive in God’s ear, venerable confessor and friend, this voice of your poor servant through the clouds, you do not disdain it, but seek there the salvation which, through Christ’s mercy, you may bring to me.

[214] Therefore come, Felix,

everlasting patron of my soul,

now come as physician for my bodily danger.

[215] [Col. 0612D] Come, I pray,

and place your holy hands before the threatening fall

of the eye.

Draw out the fixed iron that you see,

which I do not dare to remove with my own hand,

lest, while trying to release myself from the weapon,

I strip myself of my eye

[Note: See Letter 13, note 4.].

[220] For I feel the thunderbolt driven deeply into me,

the nail inserted beneath the hidden recesses of the eye,

so that only the divine hand,

which formed our very eyes,

and the right hand which also gave you power

through healing strength,

by which, while tormenting them,

you subdue the black demons,

and by which, through the great name of Christ,

you can drive away every torment

of our perishable body—

only that hand,

with the omnipotent Lord presiding over it,

can take me up to be healed.

[225] May my crimes not overcome you,

but rather, defeated by you,

may they fall.

For I confess that I am more deserving

of this wound

than of the gift of gentle Christ.

But remember the word and deed of the Lord himself,

who redeemed the sinner’s life by dying.

If you wish to pass judgment upon me

according to the law of justice,

I deserve to be punished not with one eye alone,

but with both,

so that my face may be such

as my dark heart is within—

a man who uses his bodily eyes wickedly,

blind in righteousness

though sighted in iniquity

[Note: Virgil, Book 8.],

and who admits that a sinner ought to be one-eyed.

[Col. 0613B] [If it is fitting that one such as yours should be so,

then, bound by whatever crime,

he becomes worthy of pardon

once he has begun to be yours:]

[240] and so, as I began some time ago,

I have become one of your people.

I did not follow them out of love

for my native soil,

but from the desire by which I came

to dedicate myself to you, holy one,

through the despised dangers of sea and land.

Following the example of the good man,

I broke the bonds of kindred soil

so that I might serve you,

together with those companions

with whom I boast that I am also yours.

Show this also through your help,

so that I may not lose the eye

fastened by so great a wound.

[245] Give, I pray, to your unworthy servant

so noble a gift for the praise of the Lord.

Grant this distinction to your holy day:

that the one whom the glory of Christ,

confessed by you,

has made the nativity of eternal light

throughout the ages,

I may likewise possess and celebrate

as the nativity of my eye—

Felix, and the light received by me from Felix.”

[Note: These three verses were supplied by the German manuscript.]

[255] While he wept such words in simplicity,

behold, the helping hand of blessed Felix

soon appeared,

and, breathing silently upon the doubtful mind

of the one who feared,

strengthened both his mind and his hand,

so that he would not be afraid

to draw out the iron safely.

He scarcely attempted it,

and, like a slippery hook,

the hook fell from the eye

without the eye following it.

Only the fluid that followed

vomited forth in tears

the inflammation that had festered there.

Soon, cleansed of so great a night of danger,

the eye shone with so pure a brightness

as it still appears now in health,

gleaming through the eternal gift of Christ

[Col. 0613D] 567–568.

[265] And I think it shines more brightly than usual today,

because the very day that restored it

has added light to it.

Therefore, faithful people,

now contemplate in your minds

the likeness of so great a danger,

and together weigh the working

of so great a gift.

A man mature in age and dignified in body

had clung to the hook of the cord

like a fish to a fishing line.

[270] Suspended in place of the lamp,

he hung in the open air,

but not by his own will,

with the eye stretched open

as the nail caught beneath the eyelid.

The nail, hooked beneath the eyelid, did not inflict a wound, because the divine hand restrained it—the hand that had made the blade harmless there and its weight light; yet we cannot endure even oppressive rheum, an intolerable eyelash, or the smallest grain of sand

[Note: See Poem 15, line 334.].

[280] Who would believe that so heavy an iron,

with its curved point,

and additionally smeared with the hardened grime

of the lamp,

fixed in place,

could for so long press upon the delicate pupil

without harm,

and leave sight uninjured by any wound?

What hand so subtle in its fingers,

or what skill of healing,

could insert itself into so narrow a space,

where the eyelid and eye meet,

and, passing unharmed between both passages,

through the fragile channel between the two,

suspend the iron—

the iron whose entire surface

was enclosed by a thick solid covering—

fixing it upon the eye’s orb by its edge

without injuring it with a wound?

[285] What hand could do this

except the hand that made all things?

That Spirit of God,

penetrating everywhere through all the natures of things,

more subtle than anything delicate,

which restored sight to the blind,

and made the blind from birth

possess new light,

filling out the face of an incomplete body

by the Creator’s art,

through which he perfects the whole world—

that Son of God,

the hand and wisdom of the Father,

the all-parent source of things,

Christ, their sustaining power.

[295] He himself once formed that man

in the womb of a mother not yet complete,

so that afterward,

having himself become human and Creator,

he might add this admirable work

to his divine signs,

filling empty eye-sockets with sight.

Finally, spitting upon the ground,

he makes mud,

by which he restores to the believing disciple

the sight denied him at birth.

With the same material

[Note: See Poem 15, line 334.],

he adorns the defective part

of the half-completed human being,

whom he formed in his entire body,

[305] to prove that he himself had come

in our flesh—

he who, together with God the Father,

had formed Adam from clay

and with his breath fashioned him

in the image shared by them.

He himself, the Maker, our light, God,

willed to adorn the nativity

of his friend Felix

with such a great healing,

so that by a powerful gift

he might display the sublime merit

of the confessor,

not that he might increase the honor

of the martyr by this work—

the martyr to whom long ago

he granted immense palms

with noble titles

in a blessed name,

which the mercy of the Lord Christ

continually extends through all his tireless virtues.

[315] But God wished to give us,

at this particular time,

a special joy,

and to grant his own servants

such a sign through their own patron,

performing it for those who are his own,

by which he might reveal us

as the heavenly Felix’s own disciples,

and teach us to live

in accordance with his merit and care.

While preserving our salvation

through him as guardian,

he more often drives away

the hostile enemy

from our bodies and minds alike

when danger comes by night.

[325] Finally, we now rejoice

in the honor brought by our danger,

[Col. 0615A] 569–570 and, seeing with equal sight the eyes

of the man whom we had seen disfigured

when he had almost lost one of them,

we rejoice to the depths of our hearts

over this brother restored to health

[Note: The Belgian and German manuscripts and three editions read “as this guest bears witness.” The usual reading seemed more elegant and truer. See note 262.]

[Note: See note 265.],

whom Christ has given to us

as a gift so great

[Note: So the German manuscript and the editions of Grin and Poelmann, and very suitably. Other manuscripts read: “whom that one has given to us with such good things.”].

[330] By right I may regard this man

as equal to my own eyes,

in whose light Felix’s hand

shines as my glory in Christ.

O fortunate accident,

good wounds,

sweet danger,

through which I learned

that I am under the care of a martyr.

For it was so great a thing

for me nearly to lose my eye

[335] that now I have light from the light of Felix

[Note: The German manuscript reads “by the gift.” Both readings are good.].

## POEM XXIV

Paul writes to Cytherius about Martinianus’s shipwreck, praising him for having entrusted his son to be educated by Sulpicius Severus.

### Meropius Paulinus to Cytherius, brother in Christ, greetings

[Col. 0615B]

My brother Martinianus in spirit,

and my true brother in the one faith,

whom you had sent to come to us,

having accompanied him with eloquent letters,

[Note: Schott’s edition reads “whom you had ordered.”]

we have now received—

scarcely restored to possession of his own safety,

but with his written message emptied of words,

yet full as an indication of your love,

as though we had received your own mouth.

And we read, both in mind and ear,

a letter more truthful than writing,

marked from your heart.

Then, clasping one another’s right hands,

we give them in the kiss of sacred peace,

[15] and offer God a sacrifice of praise,

returning thanks to Christ.

For he delivered our man safely from the sea,

and he entered our threshold as a guest—

having suffered terrible things,

yet having experienced miracles amid dangers.

Having departed from his homeland

for a reason known to you,

he had chosen to travel on foot.

But, judging the distances of land

that he would have to cover with him

to be too long,

he changed his decision about the journey

and preferred the idle nausea of voyaging

to the labor of his feet.

From Narbo he set out

across the savage sea,

trusting himself to a fragile vessel.

[30] Hence, this lazy traveler,

having reversed his course,

became repentant of sailing.

And when, having advanced from the mainland

along the shore,

he proceeded into the open sea,

already in dense night—

yet made bright by a serene sky

and the calm sea’s smiling—

when the stars alone

were arranging the course,

[35] and the moon was absent from the sky,

the ship, suddenly,

after a long period of use,

was abandoned by the wear of carrying passengers.

Its side came apart at the loosened joints,

and it began to admit the waves

through the cracks.

[40] Calm had lulled everyone into sleep,

and only the helmsman remained awake.

As he securely sailed his ship through gentle shallows,

he was cutting a foamy path,

[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII; see note 267.]

and with his whistle called up

stronger winds to advance the course.

Meanwhile the ship began to sink lower

as its own bilge increased,

and as its planks loosened more widely,

a greater volume of water rushed in.

[50] Where previously there had been no waves

from the open sea,

waves arose within the ship,

and, already washing beneath

the sleeping men’s limbs,

the wet chill awakened them.

As one perceived it,

soon another did too,

and fear shook sleep from everyone.

They were afraid with the terror of death,

yet still did not understand

the causes of their fear.

By what route could the wretched men

flee the hostile sea?

They were drowning in their own ship.

[60] If the open sea were boiling

and stirred by winds,

safety might be found in the ship.

But with the sea poured into the inside

of the hull,

where could life be preserved?

What harbor was there for them,

when there was a sea in the ship itself,

which, pressing in upon them,

was killing them?

[65] [Col. 0616C] But God, for all of them,

offered wind, harbor, and safety—

he extended his fatherly hand,

and amid the high ridges

of the deep whirlpool

he spread out the bosom of his mercy,

[70] into which he received those

falling into the broken jaws of death,

and placed them in the shallows of life.

A following boat belonging to the quadrireme’s equipment

had been prepared for this rescue,

so that it might receive those

whom God had chosen to save

from that company of sailors

[Note: That is, “number.”],

and might take aboard those

whom he had selected

[Note: That is, “chosen.”], while it swam close beside

the ship as that vessel split apart at sea.

[75] The ship’s own master,

Novatianus,

when he first put out into the open sea

with the shore left behind,

carrying a torn faith in his heart,

a man of death

and thinking according to his usual manner

of what was suitable for death,

wanted the boat to be a share of the burden.

He quickly hastened to climb aboard it,

[85] but, when the final danger pressed upon him,

he tried to drive it away,

so that, once the rope by which it was attached

had been cut,

it might be released into the sea.

[Note: Formerly numbered 13; what was formerly 21 is now 18. Probably written in the year 400.]

But overcome by the voices of many

who opposed him,

he remained unsuccessful on both sides,

because the judgment of everyone prevailed—

a judgment made stronger by Christ’s authority—

so that the little boat

might soon serve as a saving refuge,

surviving after the stern had been submerged

[Note: See note 268.].

The appearance of this shipwreck

was unprecedented:

the ship was dying,

but the sea was at peace.

[Col. 0617B] 573–574 Outside, in the strait,

tranquillity was seated;

[100] inside the ship, there was a storm.

Neither rocks nor a gale had broken the vessel.

Rather, stronger than these,

old age had loosened the firm strength

of the wood,

with the iron nails wearing away

and time consuming the timbers

[Note: That is, oak.].

[105] The sky shone with serene features

[Note: The Regius manuscript and five editions read “with clouds.”],

and the sea gleamed with stars.

But what did the cheerful calm

of the winds and sea

offer those whom the transport

of the disintegrating vessel

was abandoning in the depths

of the marble-colored sea?

The wave drank the ship,

and the ship drank the wave;

they were swallowed up,

and they swallowed the waters.

The sailors, intoxicated by the draught of salt water,
Tragically they are slain by drunken excess.

[115] For the other ships the gentle water smiled,  
but against that vessel it raged alone.  
Yet in the peril of so many one may discern  
the action of a heavenly judgment.

The common danger of death awaits all  
whom one ship carries;  
but behold, they are divided by differing fates,  
assigned to death and to life.

[125] Lest this be thought to have been randomly imposed  
upon the good together with the wicked,  
it is certain that no Christian perished,  
whereas the faithless died.

For either the Jew perishes with his wicked heart,  
or he is guilty of proud schism.  
Whomever the right faith of Christ has marked,  
life acknowledges as its own.

[130] Yet there were people added to the Christians  
who had not yet been consecrated by this name;  
the joined escape saved them from the deep,  
because they had clung to the Christians.

For, among the faithless multitude of sailors  
(“multitude,” that is, number; see verse 74 and poem 10, verse 71),  
no believer was drowned.

[135] Thus God displayed, in a few persons,  
the clear truth of the great mystery:  
at the end of the world, when the nations are divided,  
there will be discrimination among all,

when the avenging angel passes over the faces  
marked beforehand with the sign of the cross  
(Revelation 7:2–3).

[145] So in that ship no one endowed with truth  
was handed over to death.  
The impious lived joined to the Christians,  
while light overcame night.

For death was powerless by its force to join the Christians  
to the dead  
(the Royal manuscript and Schott’s marginal edition read *Mor cassa virtutis fuit*, “death was void of power”; see note 269).  
The sign gleams upon the Christians’ foreheads,  
by which death, subdued, has fallen.

[150] The shipmaster himself, commander of the doomed vessel,  
was the first among those who perished.  
For before the shipwrecked man perished in the sea,  
he had already suffered shipwreck in his mind.

Twice submerged was that man: the keel  
plunged him beneath the waves, and error plunged him into hell.  
He could have torn himself away from danger,  
but his head, already owed to death,

[155] his mind held captive by deserving bonds of avarice,  
bound him fast to the end.  
For, lest the ship and its cargo survive,  
he preferred death to safety.

When Martinianus, already mingled with the men  
whom the final thread of life was drowning,  
heard the sound of the tumultuous crowd,  
he was roused from the sleep of death.

[165] Then, exhausted, he lay withdrawn  
in the hollow of the prow,  
secure in his innocence;  
like Jonah once hidden in the ship’s belly,  
he was breathing heavy sleep.

But awakened by the mournful cries  
of those perishing on every side,  
and shaken in all his limbs by the feet of the crowd,  
he sprang up from his hard bed  
(the reading is emended from Schott’s marginal edition, following Heinsius’s note on Prudentius; *ejulatus flebiles*, “plaintive wailings,” has the same sense; compare poem 14, verse 26, *tristi clamore*, “with a sad cry”).

[175] Since most had been submerged within the ship’s womb,  
he joined the sailors who were still moving swiftly  
along the edges of the sides and planks,  
where they normally run to raise the sails  
or lift them with poles.

The ship, covered by the whirlpool,  
still floated upon its outermost planks.  
As they searched this route for a way of salvation,  
Martinianus joined them,

[180] and, through Christ’s action, escaping from the circle of death,  
became a companion to those who were getting away.  
He leapt from the distant ship into a small boat,  
which became a harbor for many.

He had almost remained abandoned to death,  
about to be swallowed by the sea with the fleet,  
had not Christ, as though grasping him with his own hand,  
snatched him from the pit of death.

[190] As Joseph once fled the raging woman  
after throwing off his garments,  
so this man, leaving everything behind,  
escaped naked from the treacherous vessel  
(Genesis 39:12).

And as once the beast, obeying the command,  
received Jonah in its open mouth,  
and, through its widely gaping slippery throat,  
carried him into its belly,

[200] devouring his unharmed body  
with its tooth held back,  
but not consuming the one it devoured  
(Jonah 2:1),

so the boat that came toward him  
received him as he fell headfirst  
from the high ship into the waves,  
and carried him safely through the night  
in its faithful bosom until it brought him to harbor  
(*tuto* is emended with J. F. Gronovius, *Observationes ecclesiasticae*, ch. 10; compare Letter 4, section 4, *tuto excipe sinu*, and Letter 16 to Jovius, section 1, *tutissimis sinibus exceperat*).

[205] But after mention had been made of the great prophet,  
in whom the image of the holy mystery  
preferred the death of three days’ burial  
to restored salvation,

I wish, following briefly along the trail  
of the poem, to return to Jonah  
(Matthew 12:40).

The Lord’s wonderful design: submerged in the sea,  
he floats untouched by the waves.  
He lives though swallowed, and the one who swallowed him remains,  
while fasting from its living food.

[215] Though he is prey, he is not food for the beast;  
the beast’s belly serves him as a dwelling.  
O worthy prison of God’s holy fugitive!  
He is captured in the sea, from which he had fled,

and, cast into the belly of the vast beast,  
is held in a living prison.  
Thrown from the ship, he perishes—and sails upon the waves;  
an exile from the land and a guest of the sea.

[225] He walks about within the cave of the beast’s body,  
a captive and yet a free defendant.  
For free upon the waves, within the sea  
and outside the sea (we have added *et* from Schot’s edition so that the verse would scan; Barthius advises this reading; see note 271; see also verse 34),

he swims within the swimming beast.  
Although enclosed in a body, he escapes from it  
by his spirit, flying toward God.

[230] The body is held within a body,  
but earthly bonds do not restrain the mind’s flight.  
Enclosed in the belly, he breaks open his prison through prayer,  
and reaches the ears of God;

free in prayer, yet bound from escape,  
he proves himself through his faith.

For the man who had thought to evade God by sea  
and to conceal himself from God in a ship  
must now believe that, even within the beast  
submerged in the sea, the judge is present.

[240] Now I must bring back the pliant step of my poem  
to my Jonah, whom the capacious boat  
received in the manner of the whale,  
and, enclosed within its belly, carried him—  
trembling with cold and fear—  
and restored him safely to land.

[245] He tells a wondrous story: throughout that time,  
from the moment he leapt headlong from the high stern  
and fell into that little boat,  
he came to the place

where the boat had drawn much water  
through its cracks, in the foul pool of the bilge.  
At once God warmed his chilled limbs  
and lulled him into holy rest.

[255] Naked and wet—conditions from which sleep usually flees—  
he slept more softly than in a bed.  
Throughout the entire interval in which  
he was carried back to the shore,  
he remained given over to sleep,

and was awakened neither by the water  
with which he was soaked, nor by the frost  
that his nakedness had drawn upon him.  
Although it was the mild autumn season,  
for shipwrecked men it was winter,

[260] since the harsh loss of their ruined coverings  
and the icy trembling shook them.

Receive another astonishing detail, beloved brother,  
from which you may gather the grace shown to the faithful Martinianus,  
and praise God and embrace the holy brother:

[265] As soon as he sensed the vessel drawing toward the harbor  
over the shore’s resounding sand,  
when sleep departed he at last became aware of himself,  
and awoke  
(the text has been emended in accordance with the Royal manuscript; previously it read *expergitus*, “having awakened”).

Then he touched against his breast  
the Letters of the Apostle.  
In his fear, though unaware of what he was doing,  
he had taken this book while leaving his possessions behind.

[275] Or perhaps that book, alive through the Holy Spirit,  
had clung to him without his realizing it.  
Consider, I beg you: who but Christ  
gave this protector to his own minister?

The book itself testifies that,  
at that moment of danger,  
he had not even thought of remembering  
to take away the little book entangled among his baggage.

[285] And if the thought had entered his mind in fear,  
he would not have had the leisure to search for it.  
But Paul the teacher was present  
in the body of his own writings  
(see Letter 30, section 5),

loving the reader of his writings  
with a pure heart,  
and drawing him away from the hand of death.  
God once more granted Paul the rescue  
of men to be brought out from the bottom of the sea.

[290] The power of grace that once operated  
in the Apostle Paul himself while he was sailing  
now, through his writings, interceded  
for Martinianus and the others  
(see note 361)

who had then escaped together with the Christians,  
making one danger safe from another,  
just as he had separated the faithful shipwrecked men  
from the wicked.

[300] Thus, when the galley reached the shore  
and set down the drenched men—  
men clinging to life and seeking it at once—  
they begged for help toward safety,

lest, delivered from the waves to the harsher land,  
they should perish from cold and hunger.

But nearby, on the soil of the Gauls,  
Massilia, daughter of the Greeks,  
a city nourished by the holy Church,  
opened its human bosom.

[305] Approaching this city,  
the shipwrecked men report their misfortune  
(the Royal manuscript and five printed editions read *naufragii*, “of shipwreck”; Ducaeus suggests *naufragi*, “the shipwrecked men,” as perhaps preferable).  
They ask to be fed and sheltered.

The brotherhood receives Martinianus  
(*ἀδελφότης*, “brotherhood”; see note 272),  
warms him under its roof and gives him food.  
But though rich in charity,  
they offer the poor man only a small donation.

[315] The generous affection makes up for the small gift (see note 273):  
through prayer they enrich their guest,  
and send him away, rich in spiritual provision,  
with their peace.

He was nevertheless given cheap shoes,  
so that he would not travel with a sailor’s bare feet,  
although he would rather have been warmed barefoot  
than, while cold, have shoes put on.

[320] Yet, though he had endured the sea,  
he rejected the shame of traveling overland naked,  
also considering that people might think  
he was pretending to be naked for profit,

if, clad in a cloth garment, he were to pass through  
fortresses, villages, and towns—  
the kinds of places through which greedy beggars  
who wander by sea and land are accustomed to travel,

[330] selling, by perjury, both the name  
and the misfortune of monks or shipwrecked men  
(see note 274).

But although this man was truly a Christian  
and truly shipwrecked,  
taking care not to be thought like deceivers  
and not wishing others to be deceived,

[335] he did not want an impostor to acquire for himself  
the new name of a traveler without means.  
He preferred, while sailing, to suffer the loss of life  
rather than, while walking, the shame of his appearance.

Thus, dirty in his cloth but bright in his footwear,  
he chose to float again.  
He returned to the harbor and preferred the safe road of land  
to the unsafe road of the sea  
(the gloss “and of the land” comes from Schot’s edition; the expression may be poetic license; *praevertit* means “preferred,” see Letter 13, section 19).

[345] So that, sheltered in the ship,  
he might reach the shores of his desire,  
like an unencumbered sailor,  
and escape the shame of nakedness  
from the fellowship of nautical nakedness.

God the King, favoring the faithful man’s steadfastness,  
follows his daring faith.  
Changing the order of events,  
he balances hard adversities  
with the favorable circumstances that follow.

He prepares the ship, planked with solid timber  
(see verse 103 and the variant readings),  
to carry him onward.  
He commands peace to the storms,  
drives away the clouds,

[355] and directs the course in a breeze.  
He so tempers sky and sea with calm  
that the voyage does not become stalled by peace,  
nor does dangerous speed drive the vessel forward  
with a heavy gust.

Thus, with Christ gently favoring him,  
he crosses the harsh sea  
and approaches a more distant harbor  
from the city called Centumcellae  
(see note 275),

[365] from there to be carried farther by ship  
so that he might enter the harbor of the lighthouse  
(see Letter 49, section 8).

Hardly believing that he had reached  
the shore of the land he had desired,  
he joyfully leaves the ship and sets foot on the ground,  
and hastens on foot to Rome.

[370] There he finds the friendly homes  
of brothers and fellow citizens,  
a welcome guest.  
He breathes freely in spirit,  
rests in body,  
gives and receives joys.

Those who share his homeland  
restore themselves to one another,  
and confess their thanks to God.

Martinianus, rejoicing in his sorrow,  
reports what he has endured to the brothers.  
They mingle tears with their very congratulations,  
pouring them forth from their hearts.

[380] My own Theridius was then away from me,  
a man whose gift came to me from Christ,  
a man of peace, a man of the law,  
a man of grace, my rest and delight, my very mind.

In the City, I, Paulinus, his fellow guest in devout mind,  
was maintaining a house  
(compare Letter 16, section 1, and Letter 27, section 1).  
There, he strips Martinianus  
of his shipwrecked clothing  
and covers him with his own garment.

[390] He doubles the gift of the tunic  
with which he had dressed his companion  
by the gift of a cowl.  
Then the giver himself, in turn,  
remained as a shipwrecked man in a single garment.

After this, he begins to make his way to us  
along the road paved with flint,  
to which its builder Appius gave his name.  
He wears down the road that wears down others:

[395] the navigator who had come in worn clothing  
wears down his feet as a traveler  
(the note explains *exterit* as “wears down”).

But lest even this road be entirely free  
from its usual misfortunes,  
he did not escape unharmed the judgment  
that makes one reluctant to undertake the journey.

Twenty miles from the city of Capua,  
which was the site of my residence,  
he found an unburdened mule—  
as pack animals are accustomed to be led home—  
and sat down after hiring it cheaply  
for the short journey.

[410] Soon, halfway along the road,  
the mule was frightened;  
its rider was thrown off at a distance  
when the mount was pulled away beneath him.

He fell upon his face,  
but did not injure his face.  
Thrown among rocks and brambles,  
he bruised neither his features on a thorn  
nor his limbs on a stone,  
because he was received by the hand of Felix.

[415] Felix, who would not allow  
a brother already approaching his house  
to encounter misfortune,  
or to suffer danger within his own boundaries,  
drove away the hostile force of envy.

He brought this faithful man,  
who had obtained his wish,  
into his own home as a confessor,  
and the gracious patron welcomed the guest  
into the house beside our dwelling.

[425] When asked, he reports his homeland  
and recounts his misfortunes;  
he announces good news about you.  
As he repeats a few words from your writings  
(*λόγους*, “words” or “discourses”),  
it is as though he had sprinkled honey upon his lips.

Thus, offering me the sweetest taste  
from drops of your honeycombs,  
he made me desire your letters still more,  
which I had longed for but had not received.

[430] But when he himself came as the cause of the letters,  
and I saw your letters—not written in ink by a pen,  
but inscribed in the mind of a good brother  
with the stylus of the spirit—

he who had previously been unknown,  
as soon as he became known,  
began to become most dear.  
Grace shone from within him,  
announced by the speech of his mind.

[440] “Every good person,” he said,  
“brings forth good things from what is good,  
and you recognize the tree by its fruit.”  
Thus this man, sweet in speech,  
chaste in faith,  
and radiant with honorable bearing,

flowed into our inward parts  
with the sweet stream of kindly charity.

Moreover, by rightly boasting that he was your friend,  
he gave further reason to love him.  
For night and light have no harmony,  
nor does the wolf agree with the lamb.

[450] Hence the prophet also says:  
“Just as birds of a kind  
fly together into one flock”  
(see note 276),  
so righteousness always joins itself  
to the good according to a fitting likeness of character.

Thus a kindred mind  
has woven Martinianus, far away,  
to be your equal;  
and the love shown toward such men  
is a mirror of the mind and an image of your faith.

Blessed is God, the author and fountain of the saints.  
He no longer chooses only  
the foolish and weak things of the passing world  
to overthrow the world’s greatness;

[460] but, as he himself said,  
now drawing everything upward  
and claiming the world’s heights.

Since he made both the small and the great,  
his grace joins both together.  
Those whom the Creator fashioned  
in one work,  
he restores through one gift.

[465] A common unbelief has enclosed everyone,  
so that faith may heal everyone,  
so that every world may be subjected to God,  
and every tongue and rank  
may confess that the one Jesus reigns  
in the glory of the Father.

[475] By now even the mighty of the age  
bend their knees to him  
and surrender their necks to God.  
Rulers confess Christ as King  
and submit their scepters to the cross.

Purple robes and coarse garments  
come together as one flock,  
in harmony under God the shepherd.  
Christ is the common kingdom,  
one blood for all,  
for the highest and the lowest alike.

He enriched you, splendid in the world’s  
glorious honor, learning, and household,  
with a humble heart,  
so that he might grant you eternal exaltation,

[485] and so that, as a fellow heir of the heavenly rich,  
you might be a lover of the poor.

Blessed are you now, poor in spirit  
but rich in the hope in which the poor rejoice—  
those who, deprived of the slippery goods of the world,  
will enjoy the joys of heaven.

Among them, in the deep bosom  
of Abraham the father,  
God prepares a hidden place  
far from the fire of the rich  
and a place refreshed by the dews of life  
(see Letter 49, section 6).

[495] A distinguished pledge of so great a hope  
now flashes for you with a great guarantee:  
the offspring of your lineage,  
planted for the Lord in the courts of Jerusalem  
(see Letter 18, section 5, and the variant readings).

For, to make you like the faithful father,  
he asked a son from you,  
counting your seed among the seed of Isaac  
and desiring him as Isaac himself.

You, an imitator of Abraham’s charity  
(the Royal manuscript and five editions read *Abramiae*, “of Abraham”),  
gave him as a living sacrifice,  
and, handing him over to God,  
already slew him for yourself,  
so that you might possess him more securely alive.

[510] Now this boy remains both a stranger to you  
and your own, deprived of the earthly world.  
He came forth from his mother’s womb  
before he knew either father or mother,  
before he could understand good  
or distinguish evil.

Blessed, he chose the good.  
Now, a little child, he plays in God’s palace  
and sings with his nursing mouth:

“From my mother’s womb,  
and from the first day,  
you, Christ, have been my protector”  
(Psalm 70:6).

[515] You have also heard what is said of the blessed:  
“Your offspring shall be powerful”  
(Psalm 111:2).

You have this saying also:  
“From the fruit of your womb  
I will place upon my throne”  
(Psalm 131:11).

Although this saying of David sounds of Christ,  
it also sings in Christ of those  
who will be placed upon God’s throne  
in the fellowship of Christ’s body.

[525] Your association with Anna  
is also laid out through the example of the sacred child.  
Samuel and this boy grew in God’s temple:  
now a lamb, later a shepherd.

Let the diligent hands of his mother weave for him  
an ephod suited to his stature,  
which spiritual instruction may weave  
with sacred threads in God’s word.

Let he himself be embroidered  
in the golden fringes of the heavenly Queen’s garment,  
and let the Nazarene adorn for Christ  
his holy head with growing hair  
(see note 277).

[535] Let the beautiful head of his soul,  
its hair of virtue,  
be armed with painstaking faith  
(that is, with good works and faith).

May no razor ever come upon it  
to the destruction of his hair.

And as Samson, powerful through the strength of his hair,  
was endowed with sacred might,  
so may he overthrow the strangled lion  
with the strong arms of his prayers,

[545] and pluck the sweet fruit  
of noble victory from the mouth of the dead.

But warned by that example,  
let him beware of entering foreign covenants.  
The Philistine woman is the carnal law to me,  
deceitful with flattering nets.

If that law is stronger than the law of the mind,  
it will drag him into the rights of sin.  
By words that persuade evil,  
with the sweet art of deceit,  
it makes the manly mind effeminate;

[555] it blinds the eyes of the mind,  
shaves the head,  
strips faith and disarms it.

In this respect I do not want our boy to be Samson,  
nor let him be joined to the union  
which captivity, weakness, and blindness  
immediately follow.

Although Samson afterward recovered his strength  
when his hair grew again,  
and, led by the hand from the mill  
to serve as a spectacle for hostile triumph,

[565] while physically blind but seeing inwardly,  
called upon God as avenger,  
and, strength restored with his hair,  
cast down the hostile house.

When his stronger hand enclosed its columns  
in a heavy embrace,  
the roof, its supports torn away from the ground,  
fell upon them.

[575] Even in death the mighty hero of God  
mingled his enemies with the ruin.  
By a glorious death he balanced for himself  
the disgrace of a conquered life:  
he who had lived as a slave  
while the enemy exulted  
fell victorious when the enemy was crushed.

[580] Dying, he killed more thousands  
than he had slain while alive.

I want our son to imitate him in this way:  
through death, to conquer death;  
while remaining in the flesh,  
to overcome the flesh and live for God,  
crushing the sins of the flesh.

[585] But I do not want him, overcome by the pleasures of the flesh  
through the deceit of a harmful woman,  
to surrender his mind,  
and afterward become stripped of the power of grace  
before his enemies  
(Ducaeus proposed emending *postea*, “afterward,” to *praeda*, “prey”; all manuscripts retain *postea*; see note 278).

Let him be Samuel in this respect:  
holy continually,  
with his hair never cut,  
weaving an unbroken sacred age  
through all the seasons of his life.

Let him weigh his infancy, begun in servitude,  
all the way to old age.

[595] Let him kill Amalek,  
and in holy severity sacrifice to God  
the sins of the flesh;  
when these have been destroyed,  
the devil too will perish,  
hateful to God forever.

Let Saul fail in this respect,  
and let David reign.  
Let the small overthrow the lofty,  
so that he is not high in the spirit of pride,  
nor envious through the evil of jealousy;

but, bearing lofty virtues  
in a humble heart  
(that is, humility of heart; see poem 15, verse 318),  
let him ascend the throne of the kingdom.

Let him follow those deeds of Samson  
that came earlier,  
and, like new ropes,  
break the bonds without betraying his faith.  
Let the cowardly man not lose his hair:

[610] with the strength of heavenly works in his hair,  
he will break the ropes set before him,  
pull up the stakes,  
and overthrow a thousand men  
subdued by one right hand.

For our strength and our head is Christ God,  
who is both the right hand  
and the strength of God.  
By his power we conquer the serpent  
that attacks us with a thousand deceits.

[615] Let the soul be strong,  
mortifying its own donkey,  
the sluggish beast of the body  
(see note 279).

Let the body’s moisture,  
consumed by sober labors,  
make the face livid with pallor,  
and let victorious chastity,  
through afflicted flesh,  
consume the fires of sin  
(see note 280).

[625] For as our outer self is corrupted  
by the wearing down of continence,  
so the inner self, powerful through the body’s weakness,  
is renewed  
(2 Corinthians 4:16; 12:10).

Then a thousand at his side  
and ten thousand at his right  
will fall by the parched jaw  
(Psalm 90:7),

if our jaw is kept sound through idleness,  
though use in eating makes it mobile.  
For the license of a well-nourished body  
is blunted by fasts.

[635] Then triumph and a fountain arise for us  
in our dried bones.  
The jaw that gave a weapon  
to the warrior in battle  
gives a drink to the man who thirsts.

The fasting bones,  
dead of the flesh’s moisture,  
are watered by the Holy Spirit.

But the deeds formerly performed  
by the saints as figures  
were written down as actions for us  
(1 Corinthians 10:11),  
so that what our fathers carried out in the body  
we might carry out in the spirit.

[645] The old things have passed;  
everything has become new.  
Truth has emptied the shadow.  
The day of salvation is already here;  
winter is departing,  
and the earth is blooming with flowers  
(Song of Songs 2:11).

The voice of the turtledove has already been heard;  
it announces that the season of pruning is at hand.

Let us therefore feast without the old leaven  
on the unleavened bread of truth  
(1 Corinthians 5:8),  
because Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed,  
and the kingdom of God is within us.

[655] Therefore, freed from the old laws,  
we no longer live in shadow.  
Christ God himself has lifted us, whom  
the cloud of the law  
and the yoke of ordinances,  
as though a burden of hair, had weighed down,  
and he has become a head for his redeemed.

With this head we walk freely,  
having conquered the grim-headed dragon  
(Psalm 90:13).

The burden of hair and the shade over the head  
suited those whose hearts were covered by a veil,  
obscuring the sacred mysteries.

[665] But we, with the veil of the letter removed,  
see the truth cleared of clouds  
in the light of his body,  
with the face of faith revealed  
(see Letter 23, section 22).

Let our boy, therefore,  
a pupil of both law and grace,  
be prepared by both for spiritual glory,  
so that he may bring forth old things and new  
(the reading has been corrected from the Royal manuscript and five editions, as required by the meter; Rosweyde’s *veteri* is erroneous).

[675] Let him grow strong in chaste deeds,  
and know no destructive iron  
(that is, what causes harm; see verse 703 and note 281),  
so that he may preserve his faith intact  
from the sword of harmful doctrines.

But let him again,  
with his mind unveiled by the evangelical light from above,  
lay aside the hair of burden and covering  
(that is, let him put it off; see poem 14, verse 81),  
as a servant of faith and free through faith.

[680] Let the pedagogical law nourish him first  
with the milk of the prophets’ breasts.  
Let sweet grace feed him  
with the bread of angels  
and honey from the rock  
(Psalm 80:17).

Let him be intoxicated  
with a cup that makes sober,  
from the fountain of the Holy Spirit.

[690] And soon, joined to sons,  
may you flourish like a palm for God.  
And behold, your wife, yoked with you in Christ,  
may abound like a fruitful vine  
to your household and to God  
(Psalm 127:3).

May she be a strong rib for you  
at the sides of your house  
(see note 282),  
bearing a husband’s cares  
and caring for faith,  
the holy wife’s crown,

nourishing children in chastity,  
children bringing new life to God.

For I believe that this shoot,  
spread from your vine,  
will be so firmly established by God  
that, being itself a branch of its root,  
it will draw its own offspring along with it.

[700] As once, by God’s providence,  
Joseph, a boy torn away  
and sold into slavery,  
was sent to fields of grain  
(that is, fruitful fields; see verse 674),  
to go before both his father and his brothers,

and soon, when famine was to overtake the world,  
to become the provider of his father and brothers,

so perhaps this son of yours,  
sent ahead into the holy house of bread  
(Bethlehem),  
has gone before you,

[710] to feed both his parents and his brothers  
during the famine of this world,  
where the earth is generous in producing thorns  
and lacks the fruits of good things.

He may also be called sold to a eunuch,  
since he is a servant of chastity;  
and he has been handed over  
to the authority and power of Severus,  
a eunuch for the sake of God’s kingdom.

[720] Nourished by him,  
may he grow strong in faith  
and in manly charity,  
and reject with chaste, proud disgust  
the seductive splendor of the ensnaring world,  
as he would an immodest woman.

May he avoid it in naked flight,  
and prefer to suffer salutary punishments  
to deadly pleasures  
(*antevertit* means “preferred”; see verse 344).

[725] As that man once did,  
so let this one now endure prison  
for the sake of chastity.  
From youth, let him sit apart,  
shut away in a silent house;  
let him love the dwellings of quiet solitude,  
and hedge his ears with thorns.

Let him prefer a house of mourning  
to houses of food,  
so that he may sow joy through tears.  
Let him bind himself voluntarily  
with harsh laws,  
so that he may loosen the bonds of guilt,

[735] and put the fetter of patience upon himself,  
wandering neither in place nor in mind.

Then he will deserve to draw lofty things  
from what is low,  
because he who brings down the proud  
raises up the humble,  
and, giving grace to the small,  
resists the arrogant.

[740] Thus Joseph was first made small,  
so that he might become great.  
Had he not been a servant,  
he would not have become powerful  
in the land of his servitude.

Where he had endured servitude and prison,  
there he obtained kingship and wealth.  
By enduring the bonds of injustice,  
he gained the rewards of justice.

[750] Let this man also be an approved guardian  
of his own body,  
so that he may keep the prison’s doors.

If, through fear of Christ,  
he has restrained the vices of the flesh,  
he will rule as though over prisoners  
(see Letter 50, section 17; see the same work, verse 871),

over others still enclosed  
in the world’s prison  
and bound to the age—  
while he himself is free.

He will be both teacher and guardian  
of those entrusted to him.  
For the man who rightly guards himself  
has custody of others as well,

not so that he may wish them  
to remain in the prison’s darkness,  
or wish free men to remain bound,  
but so that by his example  
he may teach those received by him  
to strip off the chains of the world.

[765] Once freed from his own bonds,  
he will easily teach them  
to be released from sin.  
A good man, governor of his own mind,  
will also govern the ship of the Church  
(see note 239).

For how can he preside over his neighbors  
who does not know how to preside over himself?

But my speech has slipped and run farther afield.  
I shall return to my Joseph.

[775] Let him bloom with the flower  
of holy grace,  
like a lily of paradise.  
Let him drink chastely from a pure heart  
the wisdom of heaven.

Let him give answers to doubtful mortals,  
a mysterious interpreter of God,  
and, as the glory of a good reputation shines forth,  
become known in the king’s household.

Pleasing the king through a spirit of wisdom,  
let him be chosen as leader of the kingdom;  
let him go forth as chief administrator  
of the royal possessions,  
overseer in the great house.

But let him wear a linen robe  
and a golden chain,  
fitting insignia for Christ.  
Let him put on a garment woven  
from heavenly grace,  
clothed in innocence.

[785] A robe woven of linen  
signifies unbroken faith,  
held by a steadfast thread,  
for linen threads are said to be stronger  
than hempen cords.

In place of a chain,  
let the exceedingly sweet yoke of golden charity  
surround his neck  
(Matthew 11:30),  
a yoke that is pleasant to Christ  
and not burdensome in weight,  
which binds the necks without pressing them.

[795] Among these gifts,  
let him also receive the ring,  
the sign of royal authority.  
Adorned with the threefold gift of the Trinity,  
let him be carried in a royal chariot.

For Christ’s flesh is the royal chariot,  
and the holy body is the Church,  
in which God, the driver of Israel,  
is carried among thousands rejoicing  
(Psalm 67:18; see note 283).

Imitate Christ: do good, avoid evil,  
live heaven’s life on earth  
(Psalm 36:27).

[805] Then the King himself will place you  
in his chariot  
and give you a share in the kingdom.  
He will entrust you  
with the highest laws of his kingdom  
and open his treasures to you.

But first he will grant worthy pledges,  
so that, adorned with royal insignia,  
you may ascend the king’s lofty throne  
and open the royal storehouses:

[810] the necklace of wisdom,  
the robe of glory,  
and the ring of faith.

But just as that powerful man  
was a foreigner throughout the whole land of Egypt,  
so let this man, stronger than the powers of the world,  
be strong over Egypt,

[820] yet be a stranger to the Egyptians’ home,  
mingled with them in such a way  
that he is not mixed with them.  
Let him remain distinct as holy,  
even though he lives in a common place,  
and not derive his origin from an unholy people.

Only in this way, as though situated in Egypt,  
let him dwell in the world  
(the Royal manuscript and four editions read *Nam tunc in isto*; Schott’s edition reads *Nam nunc*).  
yet be foreign to the world’s affairs,  
an inhabitant of the heavenly city.

Living in the flesh,  
let him live outside the life of the flesh;  
walking according to the law of the mind,  
let him traverse for himself  
the whole land of the kingdom entrusted to him  
in the sacred books.

[830] As that pious man of God, Joseph,  
traveled through the boundaries of Memphis,  
and, enlarging the granaries,  
stored up abundant wealth of fertility,  
rich in the good of overflowing years  
and feeding the barren seasons,

so let this man of ours  
travel through the kingdom of God  
in the sacred Scriptures.

For Scripture, breathed by the Holy Spirit,  
is the mother of the everlasting kingdom.  
Let him, providing through spiritual care,  
build broad granaries of the mind,

[840] so that, with his heart enlarged,  
he may store abundant nourishment  
for everlasting life.  
And when he has made his land rich  
with living substance,

then you, so that you may enjoy  
the power of your son,  
will go as an old man, like Israel,  
and enter joyfully,  
summoning at the same time  
the whole company of your kin.

[850] Your son will feed your old age  
in the king’s house with his share of bread  
(see note 284).

As the young eagle is said  
to feed its parents in turn  
(see Letter 44, section 1),  
so may mutual care nourish the parents,

whom the weakness of old age  
makes featherless again  
and brings back to the nest to be fed,  
until, feathered anew,  
they are clothed again in bodily strength  
and flourish with new wings.

[860] By a new reversal according to nature,  
old parents become nestlings to their children.  
But when youth, having cleansed away their weakness,  
has made them swift and new,  
they begin, under the instruction of their offspring,  
the rowing of wings long unused through old age  
(the word *longo*, “long,” is absent from the Grin. and Poelm. editions; no remedy could be found for the incurable defect).

Mingling with their nurturing young,  
they fly through the air with gentle force.  
They delight to cut the clear path  
through the serene sky  
with slow tracks on high.

[870] Peacefully fanning the open air,  
equal wing to equal wing,  
while they follow one another  
and alternately lead the way  
(see verse 752),  
they crown the circuit with a garland.

The winged birds speak silently  
of the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom  
(see note 285).  
They explain the sacred image  
(that is, the example or likeness; see poem 18, verse 181, and note 286)  
of the powerful cross,  
their bodies suspended upon wings.

The circular flight, turning in its circuit,  
promises the reward of labor.

[880] Thus may this child,  
a son of graces  
(see note 287),  
a forerunner of your salvation,  
be a spiritual rival  
of the birds traveling through the high clouds.

Supported by horns and wings  
of the lofty cross,  
may he fly into a crown of glory.

He has been derived from his own fountain,  
so that the whole fountain may flow into its channel;  
and may you follow your descending rivulet,  
so that a river may flow forth from all  
(the verse has been emended from Schott’s edition and the Royal manuscript; previously it read, “so that he may go to all the rivers”).

[890] Blessed offspring, holy root,  
and fruitful branches of a good tree:  
you gave a son to God to raise,  
and he nourishes you in this way,  
so that he may in turn nourish you in your old age  
(the Royal manuscript and the Badian, Gravian, and Schot editions read *canus puer*, “an aged boy”; Sacchinus considers this not entirely inappropriate, recalling: “The senses of a man are gray, and old age is a life without blemish,” Wisdom 4:9).

A little one is a teacher to the aged,  
and, through the admirable mystery of piety,  
has become a parent to his parents.

Then all of you, the entire company of the saints,  
will go toward that body of the Head  
(that is, Christ; see poem 17, verse 140, and poem 22, verse 148),  
where the faithful will gather like eagles;  
and you too will go there flying.

[900] Those will not be able to go  
whom the weight of their patrimonies prevents  
from being lifted from the earth.

When the trumpet has first resounded in heaven  
as a sign for the dead to be raised,  
these men, now bloated with the spirit of pride  
and puffed up with hollow riches  
(that is, empty riches; see poem 22, verse 139),
They will remain lying in chains, nor will they free themselves from their own

[Note: The Regius manuscript and four editions read *vitiis* (“vices”). Sacchinus asks: “Or *divitiis* (‘riches’)?” But I think *vinculis* (“chains”) is correct, both for the meter and for the allegory.]

chains,

By which unbelievers are now bound, as they wish,

[910] Then, when they do not wish to be held,

Because, laden and weighed down by their possessions,

[Note: That is, by riches.]

The rich of the perishable world

Will not be able to carry their tender clouds

To meet God the King;

[915] But, stumbling in the mud of their own filth

And weighed down by the masses of their wealth,

From the world’s southern blaze a sudden

[Col. 0632D] Ruin of death will crush them.

May God the Lord, I beg, not admit the rod of such men

Into his own portion;

Nor allow us to stretch our hands

Toward the fruits of these rich men.

[Col. 0633A] You, therefore, with great concern in my heart,

601–602 Make yourselves light for Christ.

[925] And now, freed from the burdens of want,

Release your feet from their chains,

So that you may be clothed in abundant light;

Be naked to the world,

So that, when the prince of this world comes, he may find nothing

[930] Of his own in you.

And may the clouds, bearers of the devout,

Easily lift you in their slender bosom, free from the weight of pressing possessions

And pure from the stain of crimes;

and, borne to meet the Bridegroom-King, may God

[935] Flood you with his splendor,

So that the bright glory of everlasting life

May swallow up your mortal state,

[Col. 0633B] And, restored to the heavenly image,

May fashion you into lordly beauty,

So that you may live through everlasting time, like perpetual angels,

With God the King.

## POEM XXV

[Note: Formerly 14; but since what was 22 is now 20. Written around the year 400, before 408.]

### THE EPITHALAMIUM OF JULIAN AND IA

[Note: See Notes 288 and 289.]

Paulinus teaches Julian, the son of Bishop Memor, and Ia how they ought to conduct themselves in marriage, how to establish their household, avoid the pomp of the world, decline honors, and so forth.

Kindred souls are joined in chaste love,

A virgin boy of Christ, a virgin girl of God.

Christ God, lead these equal doves to your reins;

And guide their gentle necks submitted to the yoke.

[5] [Col. 0633C] For your yoke, Christ, is light: with ready will she

Receives it and bears it with love’s easy obedience.

Against unwilling hearts the pious burden of the chaste law is heavy;

For the devout, it is sweet to overcome the work of the flesh.

Let the wantonness of the foolish crowd be far from these bridal chambers—

[10] Juno, Cupid, Venus: names of lust.

The holy pledges of the priest are joined in a venerable covenant:

Let peace, modesty, and piety come together.

For the love of piety is at once the honesty of love,

And peace is the harmonious bond of marriage before God.

[15] God himself consecrated the work of this covenant with his own voice,

And by his divine hand established the pair of human beings.

And in order to designate their indivisible love more clearly,

He made two remain from one flesh.

[Col. 0633D] For while Adam lay asleep, a rib was taken from his side,

[Note: Genesis 2:21.]

[20] And immediately he took for himself the mate made from his bone.

Nor did he feel the loss of his side, its flesh being restored in turn,

And he recognized what had been doubled;

Seeing another self proceeding from himself in a shared body,

He immediately became the prophet of himself with a new voice.

[25] “This,” he said, “is flesh from my flesh; this bone from my bones

[Col. 0634A] I recognize as mine; this is the rib of my side.”

[Note: Genesis 2:23.]

Now, therefore, since under an ancient image the holy covenant

Is enacted through Aaronic pledges,

Let serious joys be stirred by tranquil prayers;

[30] Let Christ resound everywhere in the voice of the devout people.

Let no crowd run riot through the decorated streets;

Let no one cover the ground with leaves, or the thresholds with foliage.

603–604 Let there not be a fanatical crowd of Christ-worshipers through the city;

I do not want profane ambition to defile the devout.

[35] Let no air be fragrant with foreign perfumes;

Let everything smell of the cleanliness of chastity.

There is one perfume for the holy: that which, poured out in Christ’s name,

Breathes God forth in chaste fragrance.

[Col. 0634B] I do not want dishes adorned with superfluous gifts;

[40] Integrity is adorned by character, not by wealth.

The holy priest’s daughter-in-law and the consecrated matron

[Note: In Schott’s edition from a Belgian manuscript; Rosweyde’s edition has *sacratis*, erroneously.]

Will now receive the dowry of pure light.

Let her shudder at garments enclosed in gold or purple:

For her, God’s pure grace is a golden garment.

[45] Let her reject necklaces set off with various gems,

So that she herself may be a noble gem for the Lord God.

Let her say that the neck consecrated to bearing the yokes

Of Christ the Lord should not be oppressed by the weight of hateful greed.

Let her, adorned more inwardly, be cultivated so as to please;

[Note: That is, adorned.]

[50] Let her mind be adorned with saving gifts.

Let her not desire the price of stones, nor silken fleeces,

[Col. 0634C] Nor squander her revenues uselessly,

But let her soul be adorned with chaste virtues, so that she may be

Not costly to her own ruin, but precious to her husband.

[Note: This expression is familiar to Paulinus, especially in this poem. See verse 64, verse 162, and Letter 32, note 6, verse 11. Schott’s edition reads *animus* (“mind/spirit”).]

[55] For whenever the pomp of bodily splendor is cultivated,

A person, devalued, becomes cheap in worth;

And the mind, blinded by the evil desire of a perverse wish,

Grows filthy amid the bright trappings of the body,

Nor perceives how shameful an adornment the wicked person wears,

[60] So that he is lighter than his own clothing, who pleases himself with clothing.

[Note: The same license is found in Prudentius, Book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 611, and Book II, verses 48 and 79.]

Let it be far from her to appear the daughter of an idolatrous temple,

Having become the daughter of an apostolic household.

Let her not fashion her skin falsely with cosmetics,

Nor her eyes with black powder, nor dye her hair with yellow color.

[65] Despising nature’s pure beauty through proud

[Col. 0634D] Guilt, she condemns within herself the work of God.

In vain will a woman boast that she is chaste

Who adorns herself with so many adulteries.

But you, young men of Christ, flee everything whose price lies in its loss,

[70] Whose use lies in destruction.

Believe the divine words: from these adornments

A material of punishment arises for the greedy.

Isaiah [Note: Isaiah 3:24.] threatens that those who now wear

Silks mixed with purple will be girded with a stiff rope;

[75] Those who drag shining tunics of purple, rattling with gold,

In flowing folds with their trailing hem;

Girded with ropes, carrying sacks without end,

They will grind great stones in the prison of the mill.

And those who enlarge a head heaped with groomed hair (*pastis*)

[Note: See Notes 290 and 277.]

[Note: Rosweyde’s edition reads *passis* (“spread out”). Both readings are good. See Note 290.]

[80] Will wear baldness upon their uncovered crowns.

Flee adornment of this kind, O new bride

Of a holy husband: such things please empty minds.

Then [Note: Thus we have emended the text, following J. F. Gronovius in *Observationes Ecclesiasticae*, chapter 10; Paulinus’ meaning and the following sense require this. Previously the reading was *quoque* (“also”).] do not wish to be recognized by your fragrant clothing and hair

By your scent, wherever you walk.

Nor, with a piled-up mass and torturing arrangement of braided hair,

Sit with your head built up into a tower.

[Col. 0635B] Do not become, through your splendor, the deadly and wicked

Head of enticement for many whom you have wrongly aroused.

Nor should you desire, even by the enhancement of your own body,

[90] To please a husband whose mind is foul.

You also, holy young man, devoted to consecrated books,

Scorn the care of bodily adornment.

For Christ has richly repaid you, adorning

Your beautiful soul with everlasting riches,

[95] And has adorned you both together with chaste gifts:

Hope, piety, faith, peace, and modesty.

The word of God is silver, and the Holy Spirit is gold;

The bright works of goodness are jewels for the mind.

If modest attire offends honorable minds,

[100] [Col. 0635C] And if proud hearts rejoice in being courted for their price,

Let the examples of the holy remove that shame,

And the chaste simplicity of the first human beings.

Look upon the ancient parents in the seat of paradise,

Whose entire world was one field.

[105] Yet sheep’s skins were their coverings.

Are you now ashamed of garments woven from combed wool?

When beautiful Rebecca came as a bride to holy Isaac,

[Note: Genesis 24:65.]

She was simply covered with a veil of modesty.

[Note: See verse 96 and Letter 23, notes 24 and 25.]

She is not read to have come adorned with various little stones,

[110] But clothed in a mantle laid over her;

With that veil of modesty she covered her face,

The virgin bride, fearing the face of the bridegroom offered to her.

Or will the virgin dancer Herodias be more pleasing,

[Col. 0635D] Who obtained the Baptist’s death as the price of her feet?

[115] Thus the impious girl avenged her mother’s lustful anger,

So that she might receive a head as the price of sensuality.

That very head concerning which the herald’s voice had proclaimed

To the crowds that the Lamb of God was near;

[Note: That is, nearby. See Poem 16, verse 158.]

From what source did she deserve such great wickedness, unless from seductive adornment,

[120] Impious dancer, daughter worthy of her father?

Yet by this crime she overcame him and compelled him, unwilling,

[Col. 0636A] Into the deed through the allurements of her pleasing body.

For by the nimble art of her feet she brought the guests,

Worthy of the wicked king’s banquet, to assent.

For if she had fastened a golden plate around her delicate feet,

[125] So that she might play more wantonly with painted heels,

And had drawn a flowing garment with a curling train,

Her forehead glittering with gems, her hair flowing down behind,

She would not, entering minds already corrupted,

[130] Have prevailed so craftily in accomplishing the unspeakable deed.

Herod himself, too, proud in royal clothing,

Swelled madly with sacrilegious breath;

Lifted up by his attire and forgetful of divine honor,

He perished foul with a wound pouring forth worms.

[Note: Herod’s death.]

[135] He paid a fitting penalty for his deeds, dying foully from his ulcer,

[Col. 0636B] He who had believed himself a god because of the honor of his clothing.

But grant that royal trappings suit the frenzied

Hearts which, with Pharaoh, stand opposed to us: what has

The empty glory of worldly kingdoms to do with our realm,

Or holy light in common with adverse darkness?

Let the cleric love a wife made beautiful by the adornment of Christ,

And love her beauty in the light of the heart;

And let the reader learn from heavenly history that she was made

A help to her husband by divine gift.

[145] And, in turn, so that the woman may be equal to her holy husband,

Let her receive Christ in her spouse with a humble mind,

So that, woven together into a holy body,

605–606 The husband may be her head, while Christ is his summit.

[Col. 0636C] In such a marriage Eve’s servitude ceased,

[150] And free Sarah made herself equal to her pious husband.

Under such a law Jesus, as the marriage broker,

Stands beside those marrying, and changes water into wine.

It is fitting that Mary, the mother of the Lord, be present at these marriages,

[Note: See Poem 6, verse 110.]

She who bore God while her virginity remained safe.

[155] For God himself built for himself, in the consecrated virgin,

A fitting temple by a secret rain-channel;

He descended in a silent gliding, just as rain from a high

[Col. 0636D] Cloud falls upon the fleece in silent dew.

For no one has ever been aware of this mystery,

By which God assumed humanity from a virgin mother.

O new devices of the Lord for human salvation!

[Col. 0637A] Without intercourse, a woman becomes fruitful in her womb.

She is a bride only in relation to a man, not subject to a husband,

And a mother by childbirth, not a woman by sexual union.

[165] She was a wife by covenant, but was not a wife in body:

Untouched by a man, she was a mother to the child.

A great sacrament, by which the Church marries Christ,

[Col. 0637A] And at the same time is the bride and sister of her Lord.

A bride as a wife; a sister because she is not subjected.

[Note: A verse is missing.]

[170] Hence she remains a mother through the seed of the eternal Word,

Conceiving peoples and likewise giving them birth.

Thus sister and wife, because she unites in mind

Without bodily use, and her husband is not a man but God.

Through this mother the old man is generated equally with the infant.

[175] This offspring has neither age nor sex.

For this is the blessed generation of God, which is not

Of human seed, but of a heavenly kind.

Hence the Teacher says: For now there is neither female nor male

[Col. 0637B] In Christ, but the same body and one faith.

[180] For we are all one body: all are members of Christ,

And Christ is the head of the body for them.

[Note: Galatians 3:28; 1 Corinthians 12:27.]

And because we have now put on Christ, we put off Adam;

Immediately we move toward an angelic form.

Therefore this work is for all who are born through baptism:

[185] It is perfected so that each sex may receive the complete man,

And so that Christ, the common head, may stand as all things in everyone,

The King handing his members over to the Father’s kingdom.

The fragile age of marrying or being married now departs,

When all have been fashioned into an eternal body.

[190] [Col. 0637C] Therefore, remembering me, live always as an inviolate pair:

Let the cross be your revered yoke.

As children of that mother, who is bride and sister,

Assume hearts worthy of these pious names,

And come together with Christ, your brother and Bridegroom,

[195] So that you may be one flesh of the eternal body.

Let this love bind you, by which the Church binds Christ,

[Note: Thus emended from Schott’s edition; Rosweyde’s edition reads *qui*. See the following verse.]

[Note: See Note 239.]

And by which Christ in turn cherishes her with love.

May the bishop himself, your father, bless you;

May he himself sing holy songs before you with hymn-sounding choirs.

[200] Lead your children, gracious Memor, before the Lord’s altars,

And commend them in prayer with a sanctifying hand.

[Col. 0637D] But what fragrance comes gliding through the air to my nostrils?

From where does unexpected light seize my eyes?

Who is that man who approaches from afar with peaceful steps,

[205] Whom the grace of Christ accompanies in such abundance?

Whom a blessed company surrounds with heavenly disciples,

607–608 Presenting the likeness of an angelic host?

[Col. 0638A] I recognize the man whom divine fragrances accompany,

And upon whose face a heavenly splendor shines.

[210] This is that man, rich in the abundant gift of the Lord Christ,

The man Aemilius, rich in heavenly light.

[Note: See Note 292.]

Rise, Memor; honor the father, embrace the brother:

In Aemilius one name belongs to both for you.

Memor is both younger and older: a wondrous gift

[215] And work of the great God; the younger one here is the father.

Born later, he is the elder, because, as a priest, he bears

An apostolic hoariness in his breast.

He is both Memor’s son and brother; he rejoices to be present

As the common father of himself and of his pledges.

[220] [Col. 0638B] Justice and peace embrace one another in twin exchange,

When Memor is joined to Aemilius in harmony.

The bishop’s headband joins pontiffs in divine honor;

Piety joins equals in human affection.

Hence Memor, mindful of his duty, in due order

[125] Hands over to Aemilius the dear pledges.

He joins the heads of both beneath marital peace,

And with his right hand veils those whom he sanctifies by prayer.

Christ, hear the priests; Christ, hear those who pray,

And grant favor to pious vows offered in sacred supplication.

[230] Inspire with holiness, Christ, the newly married by the holy bishop,

And by chaste hands assist their pure hearts,

So that there may be harmony of virginity in both,

Or so that both may be the seed of holy virgins.

[Col. 0638C] This is the first stage of their vows: that their bodies,

[235] Unacquainted with the flesh, may remain so; but if they unite bodily,

May the offspring to come be a chaste priestly line,

And may the house of Aaron be entirely the house of Memor,

And may this house of Memor be the house of those belonging to Christ.

Remember also Paulinus and Therasia,

[240] And Christ will remember Memor forever.

## POEM XXVI

[Note: Written in the year 401, on January 14.]

### EIGHTH BIRTHDAY POEM ON SAINT FELIX

While the Goths were ravaging Italy, Paulinus places his trust in the protection of Saint Felix. He recounts some of Felix’s miracles.

Behold, after the year has run its course,
