[Col. 0638D] The day brings back a shining light in Felix’s name.

It was a time when one could bring forth joys in happy words,

If anxious times allowed joyful voices.

[5] Yet this day, although amid battles, will still be for us

A day of joy and peace. Let dreadful wars roar far away;

Let untroubled peace be present in our minds.

A mind accustomed to releasing its heart in devout prayers

Does not forget the sweet practice of joy,

[10] And rejoicing chastely in festive days before the Lord.

[Col. 0639A] Therefore, drive away the unwelcome sadness, although the season is sorrowful;

Good joys, sweet words—

Let us love everything devout and joyful on Felix’s day,

On a birthday without end, because on this day Felix was born

[15] Into everlasting ages, when, having completed the span of his bodily life,

[Note: See Notes 331 and 332.]

He migrated into eternal life in heaven.

Therefore let gloomy fears depart, and let joys return to restored

Hearts; [Note: The German manuscript reads *figant* (“may they fix”), but read *fugiant* (“may they flee”); the sense requires it: “all sorrow should flee the holy day.”]

It is fitting to drive every sorrow from the holy day,

609–610 Whose glory, through the ages, makes the day of so great a confessor

[20] Shine out as distinguished among all days,

[Col. 0639B] And adorns it with thronging peoples.

If I were living under the evil yoke of Getic arms

On this day [Note: Supply “day”], I would celebrate joyfully even among the savage Alans;

And if chains with many links weighed upon my neck,

[25] The enemy would not bind my spirit to my captive limbs;

With an unconquered heart [Note: The German manuscript reads *vincto* (“bound”).] piety would proudly trample

Grievous servitude. Even amid barbarian bonds,

Free love would sing my vows with willing speech.

Now, therefore, although wandering rumor through various lands

[30] Strikes fearful ears with terrifying reports,

Still, our steadfast trust in the Lord Christ

May strengthen us and arm our minds planted firmly on an upright foot.

[Col. 0639C] Let black dread not cast clouds over this light,

Which God makes serene through Felix’s heavenly honor.

[35] As once the lawgiver Moses, in the land of the Pharaoh,

Consecrated the sacred Passover under the first law,

[Note: The same German manuscript reads “Moses.”]

[Note: Exodus 12.]

And holy Judea—although an impious enemy forced them

To hasten their flight by overwhelming force—

Bold in the freedom of a devoted heart,

[40] Did not abandon the commanded solemn rite, though fear disturbed it;

But, trembling and fleeing, performed the divine festival,

Feasting in joyful assemblies on the life-giving lamb,

And, already victorious through the prefigured blood of Christ,

Led joyful dances in triumph over conquered Pharaoh.

[45] For this reason, remembering their flight, the Jews even now eat unleavened bread,

[Col. 0639D] Retaining the people only in name,

Because once, driven from Egypt by unleavened loaves,

They made their escape; now, with similar signs,

But through ancestral rites that are empty Sabbaths,

[50] They recall the pleasing traces of ancient fear.

For in vain they practice the old law under an empty image,

Since Christ, offered to the Father as one sacrifice for all,

Has fulfilled the true Passover for us;

And since the body of life is present, the shadow of the figure perishes.

[55] [Col. 0640A] Thus, in this troubled time, let us all joyfully celebrate

The feast of the beloved martyr with devout hearts,

Joining our efforts in cheerful piety.

Perhaps this piety will give us greater salvation,

If for this reason we choose to lay aside our cares,

[60] So that we may bring joyful hearts to the confessor,

Whose honor pleases God, because as a martyr he despised

His own honor for the name of the Lord Christ,

Making himself less valuable in his own eyes so that he might be more precious to Christ.

Therefore let us be pleased to rejoice in such a patron,

[65] And, laying aside our cares, celebrate the birthday

Of the martyr who sleeps in blessed peace.

[Note: That is, “having laid aside.” See verse 59.]

[Col. 0640B] He too will be present to the devout, if the impulse

Toward joy now proves stronger than the cause of fear,

Which, spreading over the heart, brings minds to consternation.

[70] Believe that foreign peoples are not to be feared for their weapons

Or their strength—those whom, because of our crimes,

The anger of God, offended by us, stirs up,

So that through fear of death he may awaken sluggish hearts to concern for life.

Therefore let us fear the gentle God in the savage enemy;

Let fear of the enemy be far from us. Since, by not fearing God,

[Note: This verse was added from the German manuscript.]

(whom in lax peace we neglect, though we deserve to dread him),

let us at least tremble under the compulsion of force.

[Col. 0640C] 611–612 Let us appease him by humble sorrow, whom we, proud because of immediate prosperity,

Scorn when he brings us joy.

[80] Let us recall [Note: That is, remember or review.] the ancient examples of holy fathers,

Who, enduring the blows of wars sent against them,

Prepared no defenses in weapons or walls.

There is no salvation in hoping for salvation through human resources.

Nor can mortal things drive away death.

[85] Therefore, since it is a time for concern, let it be a time for concern in prayer

To the heavenly Lord, from whom sorrowful or joyful things are prepared,

Who alone, by his heavenly authority, can provide them;

So that, when our cares have been exhausted, joys may be renewed.

For God, the judge, governs and varies human affairs

[90] In such a way that clouds always follow clear skies,

And rains again flee when serenity returns.

How great is the power of prayers, what medicine it is to weep before God,

Let sorrow-preserved Nineveh teach,

[Note: Jonah 3.]

[Col. 0641A] And Amalek, overcome by the prayer offered by the old man Moses,

[Note: Exodus 17:11.]

[95] And cursed Haman, destroyed by the holy prayer of Esther,

[Note: Esther 7.]

Who, by a fitting reversal of punishments, alone drank the impious draught

Which he had wickedly mixed for the holy,

And from the just cross

[Note: The printed editions read *populo* (“for the people”). We have emended this from the German manuscript to *famulo* (“for the servant”), namely Mordecai, for whom Haman had prepared the gallows. See Esther 7:10; it does not refer to the Jewish people, whom Haman had ordered to be killed and destroyed by the sword on the appointed day. See Esther 3.]

That he had set up for the Lord’s servant, he himself hung.

Therefore let faith founded upon God strengthen trembling

[100] Hearts, and in a sorrowful time let it confidently

Anticipate security, trusting in God, because there is no reason for fear

Except to fear God; whoever does not fear him alone

Rightly fears everything. Let them trust in legions,

And provide refuge in walls rebuilt with restored masonry,

[105] [Col. 0641B] Those in whom there is no trust in Christ the Savior;

Us the sign of the unconquered cross and confession fortify,

And, armed in mind with God, we do not seek bodily weapons;

Although we may appear unarmed in our limbs,

[110] We nevertheless carry weapons with which, even under serene peace,

We fight in spirit against incorporeal enemies.

Now there is need of God as helper, and he alone is to be feared,

Without whom weapons fall, and through whom weapons are made firm;

He himself is a tower within your walls, who without walls

[115] Will be a wall. From now on let us recall the deeds of our fathers

Recorded in sacred books, and consider who possessed the stronger defense:

Those whom a city surrounded with great

[Col. 0641C] Walls but without God, or those whom divine power

Enclosed with its accompanying favor without a city’s walls.

I mean that city which fierce Jesus destroyed,

[Note: Joshua 6.]

[120] Having changed his proper name through the name of his valor,

And which he did not subdue according to the customary practice of warfare,

As a leader usually does, laboring through a long siege;

But by divine aid, brandishing weapons through sacred mysteries,

Yet not employing them, with the army’s weapons silent,

[125] He circled it while every hand was at rest, and for seven days

Repeated seven circuits around the walls.

He captured the people [Note: That is, the populace. See Poem 16, verse 230.] by the power of the potent number,

And by the trumpets of the priests, with terrifying blasts,

Imitating the thunderbolts of heaven’s wrath.

[130] Then the people who trusted in riches and in the city

[Col. 0641D] Perished, buried together amid their own houses.

Rahab alone, the prostitute who maintained chaste faith

Among a wicked people, did not trust in her walls to escape,

613–614 But, having obtained the reward of piety through God’s piety,

[Col. 0642A] Was a safe hostess to the Lord’s servants under her roof,

And, having concealed them piously, deceived the wicked citizens,

A false deceiver through a good fraud, lying with faithful intention.

Because she had been faithful to devout guests but unfaithful

To her profane fellow citizens, she found life, homeland, and house

[140] Immediately, when everything had been despised and God preferred,

In the Lord, who showed her kindness.

If she had placed her defense in the city,

She would have fallen amid the ruins of her ancestors,

Undefended by God. But the mystical prostitute, foreseeing Christ,

Who would redeem defiled peoples with blood,

[145] Marked her own roof with a crimson fleece,

And received her salvation while her homeland perished;

Signifying that those will be sheltered amid the world’s collapse

Whom the blood of the unconquered cross marks. From this learn how much

[Col. 0642B] The blood itself is worth, whose image was saving.

It has always been effective to trust in Christ for every good:

To entrust everything to God is the source of virtues;

To place God alone above all things; such faith has always been

The strongest weapon above everything. With such strength that little boy

[155] Was mighty: scorning weapons, he struck down the armed giant

By the power of a stone.

[Note: 1 Samuel 17:49.]

Faith is always armed; we have never known faith

To need weapons. A faithful rod split the sea,

Which drowned the wicked ruler together with weapons empty of faith.

[Note: Exodus 14.]

Faith also clothed women with masculine valor:

[160] Holy faith enabled a woman to kill

Terrifying Sisera, piercing his temples with a stake,

And Judith, through the cunning art of modesty,

Deceived Holofernes, who terrified peoples far and wide with his hand.

[Note: Judith 13.]

She laughed, unpolluted in the impure bedroom,

[165] And, victorious after beheading the barbarian leader, drove his camp to flight.

Unarmed faith is armed with God.

[Note: See Note 334.]

Through the strength of faith Ezekiah, with a few men, was stronger than that man with thousands,

Sennacherib, whose Babylon and wealthy Nineveh

Were his kingdom.

[Note: 2 Kings 19.]

He had stirred up Assyrian forces and Median kingdoms,

[170] And, trampling every surrounding kingdom with great legions,

Was advancing against the holy city of the Lord,

Attacking one city with the whole mass of his wars.

While he prepared these impious plans, their fulfilment being held back

And hindered by God, he sent ahead writings

[175] [Col. 0642D] Full of harsh threats, which Ezekiah, grieving, took up

Around the altars, and, while reciting the savage words,

Washed them with tears, prostrate and praying,

[Note: Perhaps *levans* (“lifting”) should be read. Sacchinus says: “It is not displeasing to understand that he washed the writings with tears.” But I would readily read *levans* (“lifting”), prostrate, so that he may be understood to have lifted them when, as Isaiah says, he spread them before the Lord; and, prostrate, prayed.]

And, together with the black-clad people, moved God.

With one prayer he struck down from afar the Assyrians,

Victorious through so vast a slaughter, while God fought,

Having gained such an advantage that he did not know

The enemy whom he would defeat.

For after Ezekiah’s plaintive weeping crossed the stars,

And after complaints sent heavenward from his humble heart

Moved the ears of the supreme Father with a devout voice,

[185] As the gates of heaven opened, a winged angel descended,

Drawing along the air through which he passed,

Armed with the sword of the word, and struck the impious camp,

Triumphing in the silent slaughter of the sleepers,

He gave one hundred and eighty thousand over to death,

[190] And one night alone witnessed so great a war.

In the morning the threatening king still rises; then, wretched,

[Col. 0643B] With his soldiers destroyed and his forces empty, he flees with a sparse band,

Fleeing from Ezekiah, only to be slain far off in another land—

Ezekiah, whom just before he had threatened with his chains in person.

[195] Then, just as Isaiah was Ezekiah’s intercessor,

So let Felix be our intercessor with the Lord at this time.

Let us cast our cares and pour our fears into him.

Our burden will be a light load for him,

Because what is a burden to the small is light to the great.

[200] Thus God himself took upon himself human sins, but did not absorb them,

And, suffering death, did not bear guilt upon the cross;

He destroyed it, so that on the cross he might restore my life;

He was made guilty so that I might not be guilty;

[Col. 0643C] He died condemned among the wicked so that he might distinguish us from the wicked.

The Lord died for me a pious death, so that I might live for him,

And might always deserve to live the life of the living one.

Thus Felix, honoring the greater ones in his body,

The martyrs—in whom Felix is distinguished by outstanding strength,

Shining among the sacred lights of the divine head—

[210] Is rightly strong before God, because he suffered near to Christ.

Let us hasten to this patron with hope united;

He will receive our complaints with peaceful piety,

And while we celebrate his birthday in triumph,

He, pious in his lofty merits, will plead our prayers,

[215] And in turn will weep for us, because with devoted minds

We rejoice for him. This is not a new concern among the saints:

To entreat God for sick sinners,

And through the force of good merit to overcome an evil desert.

Thus we read that Moses, praying for the sinful people,

[220] Extinguished the grave anger of the eternal Avenger.

[Note: Exodus 32.]

And when a fiery rain was flooding the Pentapolis,

[Note: That is, the five cities. See Letter 13, note 21; Genesis 19.]

Lot, fleeing, separated little Zoar from wicked Sodom.

[Col. 0644A] By the power of a chaste prayer he freed the city,

And took it as his chosen dwelling, because, pure in his chaste home,

[225] He had remained an upright inhabitant of an impure land,

Living amid Sodom’s houses but a stranger in morals.

Why should I speak of heaven’s being shut and opened by Elijah’s prayers,

And of famine remaining on the earth through the holy-speaking

[Note: Thus in Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 1006: “holy-speaking Luke.”]

Prophet’s sublime utterance, and salvation returning?

[230] As the ancient age once possessed such men, so now our age,

Having obtained Felix as its salvation, should ask for everything it dares,

And, trusting in such a patron, hope for whatever it desires.

Holy one beloved by God, Felix, you are God’s right hand;

[Col. 0644B] Be, I pray, our most strongly fortified tower.

[235] For the God of Abraham is your God, and the God of Isaac

And the God of Israel is your God: he who divided the Red Sea,

And sweetened the bitter spring;

He who gave manna from heaven, gave quail from the south,

And watered the thirsty ground when struck by the rock;

[240] He is your God, who went before the people following him through the deserts,

And changed the column set before them by night and day

According to the alternating law of time;

Who, for forty years amid the deserts,

Fed the people with angelic bread from heaven,

[245] And refreshed the thirsty with the rock split into streams.

Ask, I beg, that Christ may come peacefully to our side;

[Col. 0644C] He is your God, through whom the strong Jesus commanded the sun and moon

To stand still for his victories.

[Note: Joshua 10:13.]

And when the Lord has granted prosperity to the Roman kingdom,

[150] Command the elements, Felix, to serve our good;

Let the day advance, increasing while the stars stand still;

Let the sun stand still for you, and the moon in harmony.

Let it remain fixed, suspending the stars in their course,

617–618 Until Roman victory reaches its conclusion.

[255] As Daniel once in Assyrian Babylon subdued the lions

By victorious prayer poured forth,

[Note: Daniel 14.]

So for you, Felix, let savage barbarism be subdued

When Christ breaks it;

And let your captives lie around your footsteps,

Just as wild beasts once lay around the prophet,

[260] And, changing nature through God, licked the feet

Of the one praying with kindly tongues,

So that he might condemn savage men in their cruel minds

By the human peace of beasts.

Thus the flame also confounded the cruel tyrant,

[265] as he watched the furnaces serve the holy boys,

The accused innocents sing, and their ministers burn.

How will wretched kings be able to defend themselves,

Who, so degenerate in human understanding, have raged against those

Whom both the beasts’ ferocity and the flames spared?

[Col. 0645A] But just as, while the boys sang eternal hymns,

[270] A dewy spirit dispersed the burning fires,

[Note: Daniel 3:50. See Poem 17, verse 315, and Note 293.]

So may Felix’s grace, through a peaceful breath,

With God breathing upon us, temper the fires of war;

Suppressing the fires that have arisen in Roman lands,

May it now cool our anxious heats in peaceful calm,

[275] And release our weary hearts from cares extinguished.

But why, foolishly, as though I were an ignorant stranger to you,

And forgetful of you, do I ask you for help in needy circumstances

By the examples of ancient fathers,

Which, with God granting it to you, you will cause to yield to us?

[280] The examples of your virtues are enough for me, Felix;

And Christ pours heavenly gifts upon you no more sparingly

[Col. 0645B] Than upon the fathers, whose noble descendant you are.

For Felix, you are equally a son of the patriarchs

And of the apostolic line, no degenerate heir

[285] Of such great seed; as a confessor of holy law and faith,

[Note: See Note 334.]

You, a holy man, carry signs that rival your ancestral virtues.

Nor, if the appearance of your deeds differs,

Is your virtue unlike theirs; grace is different among you,

But glory is equal, since there is one source for all the holy

[290] And sacred martyrs. Their deeds were different

Because the times were different, and deeds differing in their causes

Do not converge in their signs;

By God’s heavenly gifts they are equal in merit.

If Felix did not do everything that Daniel did,

Or endure everything, and did not have this man’s den

[295] Nor were terrible lions surrounding him,

[Note: Daniel 6:22.]

[Col. 0645C] Nor did Daniel suffer, for his Lord’s name,

The blows, chains, fears, and night of the dark prison

Which Felix endured in terror. He who closed the jaws of beasts,

Making them gentle for the praying prophet;

[300] he who made the fires mild for praying boys

And gave them moist garments amid the furnaces—

he himself granted Felix power by his lofty right

To command the pestilential legions of Satan.

Among these Felix restrains all beasts

[305] And all fires.

For what serpent is not present here? What beastly crowd is not here?

Finally, I shall speak of one among many,

So that from one case one may learn that demonic minds are beastly.

[Col. 0645D] A certain man, not long ago, was so swollen with a monstrous

Demon that he no longer merely consumed familiar human foods,

[310] Or, if a great table were set before him with abundant fare,

Swallowed it down easily;

He also snatched hens from the threshold of the inhabitants,

And as soon as he had seized them, tore them apart with his swift mouth,

And devoured them, feathers and all, without choking.

[315] [Col. 0646A] Indeed, he thirsted even for the putrid discharge of a corpse,

[Note: That is, of a dead corpse.]

619–620 Licked bones, and chewed the discarded carcasses of beasts,

An obscene fellow-guest of dogs. Now, freed from so great a demon,

Behold, sober, he cultivates a farm leased from afar.

And, restored to himself by God’s care in the holy house of Felix,

[320] He shows clearly enough by this evident sign

That Felix is strong through his merits and through the name of Christ:

He tames savage beasts and conquers flames.

Tell me, you who are present as witnesses of Felix’s deeds:

Does he not tame beasts and fires when he drives out demons,

[325] Who shatter souls through vices and bodies through diseases,

[Col. 0646B] And devour them through sins?

When he tortures and drives these away, does he not tame beasts and fires?

Felix, the fiery avenger of the fiery host, rages—and the harmful flame—
The fire of God overwhelms it: the fire of darkness is conquered

[330] by the fire of holy light; the demon flees, and God enters.

And the man becomes a well-ordered house, a happier dwelling,

having been defiled by its loathsome tenant, with God as its possessor.

God is a bright and healing fire: my Felix burns with this fire,

so that he may extinguish the frenzied demon,

and refresh the loosened man with his blazing enemy.

[335] Wonderful hand! Thus, with a mighty rod and lofty power,

Felix intervenes within a single body, where hostile spirits

have been mingled in an inimical alliance;

[Col. 0646C] he enters into the hidden recesses of the breast

and separates the subtle airs, distinguishing the soul from the demon.

When the demon has been driven out, the mind receives the man again,

restored to freedom. This work is like that other work of his,

by which the image of the cross changed bitter myrrh (*merra*) into drink for the people

through the sweetness of the sacred tree.

[Note: [Col. 0646D] We emended this word, as also in line 345, from Poem 17, line 32, in accordance with the German manuscript. See there, and also note 244.]

Thus Felix, powerful in piety, because he is the noble

[345] confessor of the cross, changes the man himself,

as though he were the bitter cups of the bitter myrrh.

The man who now, swollen with a bitter demon,

was belching a viper’s taste through foaming lips,

repeatedly exhaling it with convulsions of his sides

and the spasms of his distended throat,

[350] now, wholly or alone a man returned to his own rights,

tastes sweetness, breathes health, and speaks peacefully.

[Col. 0646D] Therefore the hand of virtue also encircles Felix.

Then he devours the various arts of the dark prince,

as Moses’ magical rod devoured the dragons

[Note: [Col. 0646D] Exodus 7:12.]

[355] Behold, we see that the powers of the heavenly Lord

correspond to Felix’s merit, and that the forms of his works

are likewise in harmony; and whatever examples of God

the holy fathers have produced while in the body,

[Col. 0647A] Felix, living without a body, performs in Christ,

powerful in his distinguished spirit,

[360] while the bones of his body lie at rest,

displaying before the day of his return by clear signs

what sort of crown he will bear according to his merits,

when Felix shall stand complete in his restored body.

All the saints, each with his own light, will shine;

[365] equal in splendor, though their radiance is not the same,

and, with Christ as judge, one will not increase

at the expense of another’s merit:

Christ will be kingdom, light, life, and crown to all.

Observe their distinct deeds, yet united in honor,

the teachers of the Old and New Testaments,

[370] in whom the one Wisdom gave the two laws.

And thus equal glory weighs their various virtues.

[Col. 0647B] Peter did not cleave the sea with his rod;

nor did Moses walk upon the liquid waters;

yet the honor of both shines equally,

because the same author enabled each

[375] to cleave the waters with a rod and to tread the streams—

the God who is the God of the ancient saints,

and himself the God of the new;

the one to whom the Law was given—the same one from whom grace came;

the God of Daniel and the God of the three youths;

the very God of Felix, himself no lesser God.

[380] In holy Felix God is still God himself;

through him he exercises good gifts

and healing powers on land and sea.

For every day we are witnesses:

from every side, in frequent assemblies,

we see vows of gratitude offered for the restoration of the healthy,

[Col. 0647C] or the sick seeking and requesting various cures

[Note: [Col. 0647D] The editions of Gronovius and Schottus add *sentire* in the margin.]

[385] We also see many brought from a foreign shore,

prostrate before the sacred altar of the holy martyr,

while they give thanks and recount the dangers they have endured.

They testify that, when their ship was struck by violent storms,

they were rescued through the mercy of God,

and, as though by Felix’s own hand leading them forth,

emerged from the depths of the sea

[390] and received a peaceful salvation when all hope was gone.

By Felix’s merits both the waters and the flames give way.

To say nothing of the earlier proofs of his powerful merit,

we know by experience: fear still quivers in our minds

from the recent terror, as we remember the fires

that almost consumed us, the witnesses to which we were.

[395] However thoroughly the flames were extinguished,

their traces still glow again and again,

and heap up in our minds a great love for Felix.

[Col. 0647D] We saw him almost bodily present in action,

holding out his hands against the flames

and protecting our thresholds, joined to his;

the flame, as though terrified by the face

of the holy man standing close and almost touching it,

shrank back from seizing the ridge of our roof,

[400] and burned at close quarters in the neighboring hut,

bringing ruin upon it.

I shall speak of wonders: the air stood motionless, without wind,

and no breeze gave any trembling to the leaves of the woods,

so that the swift fire could not advance farther,

flying along the interwoven beams of the neighboring houses.

But when the winds had fallen, the flame refused to go on,

[Col. 0648A] and, its fuel consumed, died away in languor.

In the same way, Felix, deliver us from dangers by your aid;

may evils not approach our houses;

and, driven far away through you,

may the dreadful wrath of the bloody scourge resound no more.

Clothe yourself also with that power for warding off wars

by which you made the river, rushing badly down from the neighboring hills—

when, swollen by sudden rains and overflowing in a torrent,

it so often hurled itself headlong upon your threshold,

[415] violently shaking the dwellings joined to your house

with its vast waters—you made it change its course

by turning the river into another path,

so that now a new channel leads it raging

through an unfamiliar region,

and it avoids our roofs by a distant course.

[420] In the same way, now turn away from our places

the battles advancing in a warlike stream.

[Col. 0648B] Let the impious hand keep away from the sacred boundaries,

which your grace has made a rampart.

Let enemies fear this dwelling of yours as demons do,

and let neither blood violate it,

which flame and flood alike flee.

# POEM XXVII

[Note: [Col. 0647D] Written in the year 402, on January 14.]

## ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT FELIX. POEM IX

He treats of the solemn festivals of Christians. He receives with extraordinary praise Saint Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, returning to Nola for a second time for the feast-day of Saint Felix.

[623–624] You who are born for me in a tardy dawn,

and soon, hastening toward sunset, flee away?

You are a day weary of returning, winged for departure.

For, while the wheel of the slow year turns laboriously,

[5] [Col. 0648C] I endure you as you linger through long periods,

with my breast intent and longing with earnest prayers.

How I would wish you to shine before me through all your days!

Or, whenever you come, could you compensate for your delays

so that you might stretch out the light across the summer hours,

[10] or make amends for that day which,

by ordering the stars to stand still,

wearied the world with its long light

and doubled human labors by prolonging the night!

Now the law of wintertime, with its swift course,

takes you, dear day, away from us too quickly,

[15] and winter, swift in light but sluggish in darkness,

forces the hours to be shortened.

But it is well that your sun, Felix,

whose unfailing grace gleams by the illumination of Christ,

shines with his own natal radiance

and is never hidden by sunset,

the splendor of eternal honor.

[20] O fleeting day, glide away; I shall not call you back.

I shall no longer complain that you are brief,

because, without you, Felix himself always shines before me

with undying light.

If the birthday is absent, there is something greater:

the light of this birthday is continually present in him.

For he does not become holy on the day

whose honor is the reason for celebrating the day.

And if the crowd makes a birthday surpass other days,

because it runs more densely than usual to the sacred thresholds,

we see Felix’s birthday being celebrated almost always

by crowds packed together.

For what day, I ask, rises empty of vows,

or with only a sparse multitude?

[30] [Col. 0649A] Yet I shall confess that this day rightly retains

a special distinction,

because once his earthly vesture had been laid aside,

when his age was complete,

it was the day on which Felix was summoned

to the high stars, to be kept in a blessed dwelling.

[35] For this reasoning strengthens faith:

it distinguishes times by fixed titles

and marks sacred festivals through the annual cycle—

[Note: [Col. 0650D] We corrected the reading to *ad* (“at”) from the German manuscript; previously it was *aut* (“or”).]

days on which, once, the ancient fathers trembled

before the miracles of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Exodus 14:22 and 27.],

terrible to the wicked on the left,

yet always to be celebrated by the devout;

because they were favorable to the holy

and harsh to the wicked.

The land of Memphis bears witness,

and the sea then made into dry ground for the holy,

but into a watery expanse for the wicked;

[Col. 0649B] and the other events like these, performed by God

in Egypt and through many regions,

are recalled by us with remembering love.

Thus the divine gifts of Christ are likewise proclaimed

[Note: [Col. 0649D] See note 295.]

[Note: [Col. 0650D] The German manuscript reads *munera*, less suitably.]

so that all may venerate the day on which,

born of a Virgin,

God assumed a human being for the sake of all

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Matthew 1:16.];

and the day on which the Magi,

bringing mysterious gifts under the star’s guidance,

humbly saw him as a child

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Matthew 2:11.];

or the day on which the Jordan,

trembling as John baptized him,

washed him who sanctified all its waters

for the renewal of the nations

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Matthew 3:16.];

[50] or, again, the day made more sacred by that sign

through which God first performed his work,

when, by changing the waters,

he exchanged them for wine’s exceedingly sweet nectar

[Note: [Col. 0650D] The German manuscript and Grinonius’s edition read *perdulcis*; but *praedulcis* is familiar to Paulinus. See Poem 21, line 792, and Poem 32, line 220.]

[Note: [Col. 0649D] John 2:9, 11.]

What of the Paschal feast?

For certainly, every day,

throughout all lands, the Church continually proclaims Easter,

proclaiming the Lord’s death on the cross,

and, from the cross, life for all.

[55] [Col. 0649C] Yet this great sacrament of piety toward all

[Note: [Col. 0649D] See note 296.]

is celebrated yearly, in the appointed month,

by the whole world, everywhere, with equal service;

the eternal King, risen in his renewed body,

is worshiped

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Matthew 28:6.].

This solemn day follows:

we count seven weeks,

and the festive light returns to the peoples—

the day on which the holy Spirit,

once sent down from heaven above,

divided tongues with fiery light

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Thus emended from the German manuscript. The printed editions read *flumine*, “with a stream.”],

and the one God himself ran through different mouths,

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Thus emended from the same manuscript. The printed editions read *divisa*, “divided.”]

[65] sounding languages of every kind with one voice,

granting all the ability to utter words they had not known,

so that each person might recognize his own people

in a foreign mouth

and hear a foreign speech in his own mouth

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Thus the German manuscript; the printed editions read *nesciret*, “might not know.” BIGN suggests, perhaps, *resciret*, “might recognize.”].

[Col. 0650A] The barbarian himself sang familiar things

in languages unknown to him,

speaking words foreign to his own people;

[70] but in everyone one Spirit praised the one God

with varied voices

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Acts 2:2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11.].

As when, striking strings with the blow of a single plectrum,

a player sets discordant strings in motion;

or as one who presses his blowing lips to joined reeds,

though he produces one song from one mouth,

does not produce a single sound,

but, by his skill, the master regulates different tones,

[75] guiding the sharp openings with his breath,

and with nimble fingers controlling them,

closing and opening them,

so that the sweet sound flows swiftly into and back out of the chambers;

as the melodious breath runs through the Aeolian passage,

and the living pipe releases songs that burst forth;

[80] so God, the one director and arbiter of all-sounding harmony

[Note: [Col. 0649D] See note 298.],

moves throughout all the bodies of things

the harmony that he himself regulates.

God is the maker of all nature and of art,

the source of every work and its end,

making good things and preserving what has been made;

[Col. 0650B] himself abiding in himself, in the mutual piety

by which the Father reigns in the Word

and the Son in the Father.

Without him nothing was made;

through him all things sown stand fast in him;

the same one renews everything through the ruling Word.

He, by the purple cross and the crimson dye of precious blood,

[90] rose on swift ascent into the heights,

flying above the Cherubim through the high cloud,

and sat at the Father’s right hand

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Mark 16:19.],

and from there poured heavenly gifts upon his own

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Thus the German manuscript and the editions of Gronovius, Poelman, and Schottus. Two others read *et in servos*, “and upon the servants.” Both readings have been received.],

the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Only-Begotten and the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Greek: Μονογενής, “Only-Begotten.” See Poem 5, line 47.]

[Col. 0650C] Although he is God himself, coming from God

and present everywhere,

he nevertheless descended there in visible form as fire,

where the united assembly of the apostolic youth was gathered.

Then, with a new sound, when many men from the city

had been brought together from every nation,

he sat like a flame upon them all;

and at once, in all of them,

with one breath yet with differing sound,

[100] as one who easily plays lyre strings with a plectrum,

he sang the same proclamations through divided tongues,

striking various human organs with voices

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Acts 2:2, 4, 6.].

When such intoxication filled their chosen minds,

their hearts drunk with God

belched forth sacred praises from fasting throats.

Who will pity me and give me a drink

from this stream that sobers drunkenness?

[Col. 0650D] [627–628] Therefore, just as the Lord distinguished the heavens by stars,

the fields by flowers, and the years by seasons,

so he himself distinguished the seasons by festive days,

so that sluggish minds, through the observance of daily duties,

might at least, by the distinction of these days,

after an interval, gladly perform the sacred solemnities

when they return,

and prepare their inactive minds for the annual festivals of the Lord,

because they are continually reluctant to serve undefiled justice.

For those accustomed to sin,

to spare themselves from sin is labor.

One runs down every valley;

there is no escape by running up the ascent.

Hence the path of falling is easier,

and the path of life more difficult:

the former accommodates many,

the latter is steep and narrow for the few.

Therefore the good Lord, so that he may cover everyone

with the wings of his mercy

and enable the weak to strive toward the citadel of virtue,

gave the days of the saints suitable intervals:

[Col. 0651B] so that at least through modest observances

those who are not wholly exiled from the region of salvation

might touch the outermost garment of Christ,

and the sacred fringe might heal them.

They lodge within the perpetual stalls of life,

not far, though distant from the first rank, from the second.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] The German manuscript reads: “For the first step of life is …”]

For the first step toward heaven

is to weave all one’s days together in continuous goodness

and to celebrate Christ’s holy Easter

through the whole of time with pure devotion.

[130] But if a mixed crop sprouts thistles for me,

and an uncultivated heart is pricked

by the thorn of earthly toil,

let me at least strive to offer myself to the Lord

on his festive days,

so that I may touch the borders of life, even in part,

and not be dragged with my whole body

into the fellowship of death.

[Col. 0651C] Although, then, we who dwell nearby

in constant attendance may enjoy the honor of our patron saint,

whom a devoted multitude always celebrates with us

even without his birthday,

nevertheless, so that we servants may be released from our cares by our master's own festivals

and sing our vows,

[140] I shall go first in this joy,

as my brothers sing,

and lead the company like a standard-bearer.

For although crowds from various regions of the people

pour forth pious joys today with equal vows,

it is nevertheless fitting that I rejoice on this day

more abundantly and more conspicuously:

for no one is more deeply bound in debt to him than I,

to whom this day, under a private and special star,

has brought forth such an everlasting patron.

Hail, dear day; hail, my light; hail,

always a festival day for me.

[Col. 0651D] But this year you have shone upon me more brightly,

[150] because, together with Felix’s honor,

you bring back Nicetas,

so that today I may possess a double birthday

through the love of two saints:

I celebrate the departure of the martyr,

taken from the body,

and the return, in a body present before me, of the priest,

behold, satiated, I worship him

[Note: [Col. 0651D] That is, “I honor him.” See note 299.].

[155] [Col. 0652A] I receive Christ, who dwells within him,

as he makes his way into my humble breast

[Note: [Col. 0651D] That is, “turning aside.”].

Let my soul now rejoice

and say what the bride once sang,

lovingly vocal to her loving Lord:

“The rain has gone; winter has departed;

the voice of the turtledove sounds in our land;

the vine gives forth its fragrance,

[160] and we marvel at the flowering lilies of heaven on earth”

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Poetic license. Song of Songs 2:11–12; Virgil, *Eclogue* 1. See note 300.].

From where, I pray, has the sky suddenly changed its season?

Spring has gone

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Perhaps *obit*, “has died.”],

and flowers are seen in the frozen fields?

[Note: [Col. 0652D] We restored this reading despite the manuscripts; for what sense is there in “the joined company of the Lord”? See note 300.]

Nicetas is present, the anointed companion of the friends of the Lord Christ.

Hence winter blossoms into spring for us;

hence everywhere the living breeze breathes fragrant vapors.

[165] [629–630] This comes from the heart of the blessed spirit’s field.

A life of chastity and a mind clear in transparent truth

make Nicetas into flowers and springtime spices

[Note: [Col. 0652B] The German manuscript reads *Christi*, “of Christ.”]

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Song of Songs 2:11–12; Virgil, *Eclogue* 1.].

What worthy gift could I, poor, foolish, and small,

produce either with heart or mouth

for so great a gift?

Now Felix himself is needed for this task,

so that he may receive from Christ what he may himself impart to me,

and so that I may give worthy thanks for his gifts.

And now I would wish that living rivers

of perennial water might flow from my breast,

[175] so that, not by my own mouth,

but by Christ’s gift,

I might be able to recount my joy,

which Christ’s gift pours more abundantly than usual

into my peaceful breast,

and doubles Felix’s birthday for me

through manifold love.

I see Nicetas returned before my present eyes

[Note: [Col. 0652D] The same manuscript, together with five printed editions, reads *Niceten*; the nominative is *Nicetes*.];

and, seeing the father whose love rules in me

above all others,

I myself become Nicetas,

[Col. 0652C] bearing in my mind the likeness of his blessed name,

which now triumphs through the victory of my prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Thus restored from the German manuscript and the marginal readings of the editions of Gronovius and Schottus. The others read: “Therefore, seeing him from far away after a long time …”]

[185] Seeing him, after a long time and from far away,

come on your birthday, most illustrious Felix,

shall I not confess that he arrived under your guiding hand?

For who could fail to see, in so clear a sign,

that this came about through your prayer—

that I, who could scarcely obtain what I desired in my vows,

or at least fix it in my sleep,

should once again hold Nicetas before my eyes,

on Felix’s very birthday,

both in sight and in embrace,

[190] and again sing my due praises beneath his gaze,

with you, Felix, as my auditor?

But what shall I do? I ask.

I sit as a poor man at a rich man’s table

and, miserable, dare to thrust my hand into the feast

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Proverbs 23:1.];

nor do I consider that I ought, in turn,

to prepare things like those I consume

and offer a word worthy of such a judge.

Therefore, holy one, give to your needy servant

so that I may speak things worthy of you as patron,

and, daring as your friend,

say things equally worthy of your friend

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Thus restored from the German manuscript. Previously *usus*, “having used.”].

[200] Felix, I ask your parents together with you

for what they ask in their prayers.

I ask your forebears, Felix, to join you in your prayers.

What prayers of yours I speak of are my own;
indeed, these are more truly my prayers.

But lofty honor refuses earthly joys to you.

Yet because our joys are the fruits of your victory,

may you deign to regard the prayers of your people

as your own prayers.

[205] Therefore, Felix, I also beseech your parents:

be present here, too, and now ask them

to be present when called.

You who inhabit the joyful heavenly gardens of paradise

[Note: [Col. 0653D] The German manuscript reads *coelitus*, “heavenly.” See Poem 21, lines 775 and 873.],

and you who rest beneath the lofty altar of the Lord,

beautiful choir of the apostolic host,

and first people of the patriarchs,

two choirs of leaders whom God marked with twelve names in each company,

the fathers whom he calls to the heavenly kingdom

for the nations and peoples:

you also, holy prophets, I humbly beseech—

[Col. 0653B] you who foretold that God would be in our flesh;

and you, martyrs,

who, with bodies slaughtered and blood poured out,

testified to the Lamb, both killed and living;

all one offspring from the divine springs,

whom pious Abraham, holy Isaac, and gentle Jacob

begot for God through numberless seed,

[220] whom they begot for God through seed beyond number,

twofold in its heavenly and mortal merits,

equaling the stars of heaven and the sand of earth—

I certainly believe that you have gathered from every side

for this day, out of love for Felix,

[631–632] to celebrate the honor of your fellow confessor.

[225] Yet I do not regard myself as possessed of so great

a presumption of honor

that I should therefore immediately pray

for all the saints to breathe into my senses,

as though I were worthy of so great a gift,

so that the voice of the turtledove

which the rejoicing earth heard throughout the world

might resound through my mouth.

[230] But because a divine voice suits Felix’s honor,

and because Nicetas,

the Lord’s servant and priest,

has just been sent to me from a distant land

and has come for this day—

a man as good in his eloquent speech

as he is holy in his victorious spirit

and in his conquered body—

[235] O that one of the Cherubim, swift as lightning

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Isaiah 6:6. See note 301.],

might carry from the Lord’s distant altar

a coal taken up with tongs

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Thus the German manuscript and Rosweyde’s edition. The others, wrongly, read *hac ferat*, “may carry this.”],

and burn the sinner’s excessively fat lips,

so that, with my mouth cleansed of its clotted impurities,

I might not draw what I have heard from my own mouth,

but from the auditor’s mouth,

and then utter it more worthily through my own.

May the harsh and sickly speech of a foolish sinner

neither violate nor wound pure and learned ears!

[Col. 0653D] But since my teacher himself sits beside me,

I shall frequently behold him with reverent gaze,

situated close by and opposite me.

Perhaps, from the mouth of the wise man,

I shall conceive fruitful thoughts

in my barren breast,

as once Jacob’s exhausted flocks conceived

from the shepherd’s displayed rods.

For Nicetas, blessed by the Lord, is gentle like that man;

like Israel, he is also a shepherd of sheep and goats

before the pool of living water.

But here too he chooses for himself

three rods from three kinds of tree,

with one purpose;“

and, when they have been placed in the water,

he calls the flock,

makes them conceive as they come together,

and marks the offspring conceived through the three rods with color.

Thus, from rods whose bark has been scraped away

[Note: [Col. 0653D] That is, “cut into.”]

and varied,

the marked offspring of the holy flock is shown to be Christ's offspring

[Note: [Col. 0654D] The German manuscript reads *Christi* (“of Christ”).].

[255] But it is not the mark of Laban's flock, but the mark of life.

For it will be a mark of death

not to be marked with Christ

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Thus emended from the German manuscript and Schottus’s edition. The others read *novatos*, “renewed.”].

So grace renews barren souls

in the threefold name,

and the Spirit, the male,

fills them through union with the Word.

The Church, fertile in a virgin womb and mother of salvation,

marks within herself the offspring conceived for God

[Note: [Col. 0653D] See note 302.]

[Note: [Col. 0653D] See note 239.],

while, intent upon the three rods,

she drinks the moist seeds of the Word,

and her face is marked with eternal light

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Psalm 4:7.].

[Col. 0654B] Hence the barren woman bore seven,

and the abundant woman failed,

as God enlarged the lowly

and diminished the proud

[Note: [Col. 0653D] 1 Samuel 2:5.].

Thus, when I saw Nicetas,

as though I had found a spring,

I ran like a thirsty sheep to living waters—

parched,

and at once I felt my breasts begin to swell.

For a long time I attentively gazed

at the mouth of the teacher who was feeding me.

I looked upon the various rods

that he carried in his learned breast,

and, with fixed eyes,

drank in their visible color.

My mind, moistened by dew,

sprinkled me with divine drops.

Yet, since mention has been made of the three rods,

if it pleases you,

let us still examine the mysteries of the kingdom.

[275] The patriarch chose three rods for himself

from three different trees:

the fragrant storax,

the smooth plane,

and the firm nut tree

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Thus emended from the German manuscript and five editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads *storace*, “storax.”].

[Col. 0654C] The Spirit is in the plane,

the Virgin in the storax,

and Christ in the nut tree.

[633–634] For the plane spreads its broad branches

into shady shelter.

The Spirit formed Christ in the Virgin

who was overshadowed by the Holy Spirit.

And I think the rod of storax

belongs to David’s tree,

which produced the Virgin,

who gave birth to the fragrant flower.

The rod of the nut tree is Christ,

because in nuts there is food within,

a shell outside,

and a bitter rind over the green skin.

See Christ, God, veiled in our body:

in frail flesh he is food through the Word,

and on the cross he is bitter.

The hard outer surface is the word of the cross,

and the food of the cross

is the heavenly marrow of Christ enclosed in flesh.

Yet he is sweet through the cross as well,

because through the tree he brought forth life.

Our God is Life:

my Life hung upon the wood

so that my life might stand before God.

What shall I repay you, Life,

for my life, Christ?

Unless perhaps I receive the cup of salvation,

with which my right hand may offer you a drink,

so that I may be washed by a sacred draught

of precious death.

[Col. 0655A] But what shall I do?

Even if I give my own body to the flames

and make myself worthless in my own sight,

I cannot pay you what I owe

by pouring out my blood,

because I would give myself to you in exchange for myself.

Whatever I might do in return,

I shall always remain unequal to you, Christ,

because you paid on my behalf

what I owed, not what you owed,

suffering for sinful servants.

[300] What love can measure up to yours?

You became my likeness, Lord,

so that I might become your likeness as a servant.

Is it considered a great thing

to purchase salvation for oneself

from a perishing possession?

To exchange perishable things for the eternal,

to sell earth and buy heaven?

Behold, at what a price God bought me:

through the death of the cross,

suffering and humbled in the likeness of a servant,

[Col. 0655B] so that he might buy worthless servants

with precious blood.

But what shall I do?

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Thus we emended from the German manuscript; elsewhere, *toto* (“wholly”).]

I recklessly rise into the unsafe heights,

daring to entrust my fragile self to a wing.

As is my custom,

singing the birthday of the distinguished martyr

with lighter material,

I suddenly sprang upward,

flying above the stars,

and, sending my bold speech forth,

stretched my mind toward the source of all things.

Where have I obtained this courage?

What breeze lifts me proudly on high?

I do not recognize my swelling breast;

a greater mind is moving me.

I feel Nicetas, who sits close beside me,

touches me,

and breathes near my joined side.

[Col. 0655C] The keen breath of the one breathing beside me

enters me

and awakens the unusual, powerful fire

of one who meditates,

bringing warmth to my cold limbs

by applying its fuel.

[320] But I shall restrain my swollen breaths,

and, small as I am,

I shall not hope to speak great things beyond my powers

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Thus the German manuscript together with Schottus's edition. The others read *spirabo*, “I shall breathe.”];

I shall return to the ground I left

and proceed with the measured step

of a modest poem.

Although I cannot proclaim Felix’s lofty merit

without praising God,

you, holy Nicetas, receive me into your fatherly embrace.

While I am supported by your learned breast,

let me rest my head upon your tender heart.

May your salt season me, foolish as I am,

and may your rich vein water my thirsty senses

with an unending stream.

I shall speak again with joy,

and, still scarcely believing in this gift,

I shall ask again and again:

Tell me, please—have you returned?

Do I really hold you yourself, Nicetas,

on whom, sick at heart,

I have depended through nights and days

with my spirit wasting away?

At last you have come back to me

in the fourth year of your departure.

But thanks be to Christ,

because, even if late,

he has brought you back.

[0335] How I feared that an enemy

might hold you fast in the middle regions,

severed from us by an opposing cloud of wars!

[Col. 0656A] [635–636] But, with your desires overcoming all obstacles,

you broke through the bonds that confronted us.

Neither the sea nor any labor held you back,

nor Gothic fears,

nor the cold hard to endure on long roads

[“figora” is probably an OCR error for *frigora*, “cold.”].

[340] Truly, Nicetas, amid such circumstances

you were both conquered and conqueror

through kindly affection;

strong and weak at once,

yet powerfully both.

Conquered by friendship,

conquered by love of Felix,

you conquered harsh labors

through tender devotion.

[345] Come now, holy father,

give me your ear and your hand.

Let us bind our joined hands

in mutual bonds,

and, with our right hands linked

in alternating alliance,

let us sow varied conversations

as we walk at leisure.

[Col. 0656B] It pleases me to recount everything together
and to show my father
[350] our activities throughout the entire time

during which he was absent.

For to whom could I more properly unfold my deeds

and recount what Felix’s hand has worked for us

than to one who cares for us?

He is equally our teacher and father,

and therefore may approve what has been well done

and condemn what has been badly done;

[355] may correct our errors

and calmly arrange what must be done;

may aid the imperfect with his prayers,

and, as priest, dedicate what is complete.

Thus he may move back and forth

through Felix’s buildings,

as though he carried Felix himself

in his entire breast

and might boast of himself

in his patron’s hall.

[360] Therefore come, father,

and join your step to mine

[Note: [Col. 0656D] The German manuscript reads *gressu*, “with your step.”]

while I lead you around the work,

taking you through each part.

Behold, you see this portico,

which the first doorway receives:

formerly it was buried beneath a dark roof;

now the same structure has grown,

with new colors and a roof.

[365] But where, enclosed by a square covering,

the vestibule opens its central space to the sky,

there was formerly a poorly cultivated little garden.

A worthless plot of ground,

with a few vegetables,

served no purpose.

Meanwhile, the desire arose in us

to build this work in that place

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Thus the German manuscript; five printed editions read *ipso*, and Rosweyde's edition *isti*, incorrectly.];

for the place itself seemed to demand this cultivation,

so that, with the venerable martyr’s shrine

opened from afar opposite the doors,

a happier honor might illuminate it,

and its open, bright double-front

might flood the interior through the arches

with abundant light,

turned toward the visible face of the tomb,

[375] [Col. 0656D] where the martyr lies sleeping,

his body laid to rest.

There Felix, set before the threshold

of his shining throne

[Note: [Col. 0655A] See notes 304 and 39.],

looks forth rejoicing

through the two pairs of doors opened to the light,

and delights that his walls are overrun

by pious assemblies,

and that the spacious halls are opened wide

as crowds break through the many entrances.

The shrine itself,

where the tomb of the consecrated martyr stands,

has recovered a new appearance,

cleansed of age.

[Col. 0657A] Three craftsmen’s hands,

working with different ornaments,

adorned it:

the artisans of the double ceiling and of marblework,

and the painter with images bearing divine faces.

Behold how great the splendor is,

as though in a renewed shrine,

smiling from the carved coffered ceiling

with its rippling panels

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See note 305.]

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See note 306.].

In the wood, ivory is imitated.

Above the roof, hanging lamps

are held by bronze spirals,

and in the empty space

their wandering lights sway

from slackened cords;

a light breeze disturbs their wavering flames.

[390] [637–638] What formerly stood upon pillars

is now supported by columns,

and, having changed its metal,

has rejected its cheap cement

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See note 307.].

[395] But let us return again to the halls.

Look again at the cells

set upon the long porticoes

beneath a doubled roof—

dwellings to be apportioned fittingly to the good,

those whom the zeal for prayer,

not the care of drinking,

has led here to the just honor of holy Felix.

For, like upper rooms joined beneath sacred roofs,

they look down through windows from above

upon all the altars,

beneath which the bodies of the saints have their resting place.

For apostolic ashes too,

laid beneath the heavenly altar,

offer sacred libations of dust,

an odor pleasing to Christ

[Col. 0657D] [Note: The German manuscript reads *sacra sui*. The four printed editions read *sacra Deo*, “sacred things to God.”].

[405] Here is Father Andrew;

here is the man who, sent as a fisherman to Argos,

taught vain-speaking tongues to fall silent.

After he had freed the peoples

from the nets of wicked error

and drawn them into Christ’s nets,

he condemned Thessalian Patras

with the blood he shed.

Here too is John,

the Lord’s forerunner and Baptist,

at once the sacred door of the Gospel

and the boundary of the Law.

He too, coming as a guest

to Felix’s halls,

as bearer of his own ashes honors a brother’s burial.

[415] Beside him lies Thomas,

uncertain under his double name, Didymus

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See note 308.].

Christ permitted him,

through the hesitation of his fearful mind,

to doubt for the sake of our faith,

[Note: [Col. 0658D] From the German manuscript we have added these two lines, which complete and restore the sense formerly interrupted.]

so that we too, strengthened by this guide,

might confess, while trembling,

that Jesus, both Lord and God,

lived after death in the body,

showing the living wounds of his flesh.

[420] And when the day comes

on which God will come manifest

in open light,

the frightened will recognize,

shining in the flesh he suffered,

the one whom the rebellious crucified.

Here is the physician Luke,

first in his art and then in his speech—

Luke, twice a physician:

once he treated the sick in body

with earthly means,

and now he has composed medicines for sick minds

in the two books of life.

[425] Beside these, equal in piety, faith, virtue,

and crown, are the martyrs:

Agricola,

and Vitalis, who clings to Proculus.

And Euphemia the martyr,

who on Chalcidian shores

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See note 309.]

marks the shore as sacred

with the blood of a virgin.

Bologna houses Vitalis, Agricola, and Proculus,

whom their sworn faith in piety

called to the arms of martyrdom;

and equal victory covered them

with saving palms,

their renowned bodies pierced

by beam-like nails

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See note 310.].

Here too is the martyr Nazarius,

whom, through the faithful gift

of noble Ambrose,

I received with submissive mind.

He too deigns to be a fellow-guest

beneath Felix’s roof

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See Poem 21, line 385, and Letter 32, no. 6.],

and adds his brotherly dwelling

to these private quarters

[Note: [Col. 0658D] The German manuscript reads *domus*, “homes.”].

[440] Although all the saints throughout the whole world

are together one through the one God,

through whom they are presented everywhere

as the members of his body,

nevertheless places are owed to the bodies of the saints.

It is not merely in the place where the whole body lies

that the grace of those laid there lives;

[445] rather, wherever a pious part of the body

or a hand is present,

it bears witness before God

to the proofs of the blessed one’s merit.

Great power in the small dust of the saints

proclaims the force of the apostolic body,

with the Word as witness

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See Poem 18, line 147.].

Whoever lives chastely in these upper dwellings
will therefore be near these saints.

And the foreigner who, though far away,

is driven by upright devotion

and hastens to the holy shrine,

when he wishes to approach Christ

in secret prayer,

whether he wants to utter his vows by day or by night,

may emerge without delay

from the adjoining threshold

[Note: [Col. 0657D] See Poem 15, line 291.].

[455] Marvel also at this:

the lofty house of the martyr

opens through three thresholds

according to the law of the sacrament

[Note: [Col. 0658D] Thus emended from the German manuscript with Sacchinus. Previously *quo*, “which.”].

For he confessed one king

under a threefold name.

And the house, its joined masses woven together,

is marked by a sacred bond;

for although the structures have several roofs,

the holy house of peace is nevertheless one,

and concord among many members

forms one body,

whose structure stands with Christ as its summit

[Note: [Col. 0658D] The German manuscript reads *compago suo stat*, “its structure stands.” See Poem 17, line 140.].

Perhaps, as you eagerly gaze upon these sights,

you will ask from where this courtyard,

rich in so many fountains,

is to be filled,

since the city is far away

and there is almost no water conduit from the city

[Col. 0658D] [639–640] [465]

Let it send down here a small drop through a narrow channel.

I shall answer: that we place no trust in our own right hand, put no confidence in earthly aid, but have entrusted everything to the mighty God and look to heaven for its fountains.

[470] Finally, we have built cisterns everywhere beneath the roofs, ready to receive streams poured forth by God from the clouds; from these the hollowed marble basins may flow together with full rims [Note: [Col. 0659D] That is, simultaneously. See poem 14, line 109.]. If, moreover, a shortage of water should sometimes occur, the court will still be pleasing to behold with its vessels arranged in orderly variety, distinguished by different forms, by the shapes of its basins, and by its flowering borders of painted design.

For you remember also, in Solomon’s great temple, how beautiful the dry sea was [Note: [Col. 0659D] See note 311.]: the wise king gave it in solid bronze and suspended it upon bronze bulls.

[480] Look now at the other side: so that there may be a single portico and a wall with columns standing in the middle, dividing the space into two, the roof joins halls separated by entrances. It is time to pass with wandering eyes into this building, which, opened along its entire length, gains from the light of heaven the expanse of its roof; this opens out into adjoining courts, joining the separated sections through inserted arches, and provides the people with a spectacle of a watered field (though walls enclosed by a constructed fence surround it, so that the sacred buildings may not lie open to profane eyes), while the open vestibule protects the covered spaces from the wind.

Nor should you marvel that sacred enclosures grow in extent. Everywhere grows the power of the glory of eternal Christ: the honor of the saints is heaped up, and the one God is recognized by all. For the Holy Spirit illumines the world, and the Son, heir, reigns with the coeternal Father. From there, having spread the holy light of truth, grace multiplies among the peoples the seeds of eternal life.

[495] And because the good shepherd increases his sheep, lofty Christ favors the broadening of the sheepfolds along with the growth of the redeemed flocks [Note: [Col. 0659D] Three editions read *fovet* (“fosters”); Sacchinus thinks *facit* (“makes”) should be read. [Col. 0660D]].

[500] Enter this place, bishop, chanting psalms and hymns; bring my prayers before the Lord, and join your joys to my prayers as you celebrate the feast of our common patron. At the proper time you will pray for the sinner to the Lord rejoicing in the honor of his confessor.

[Col. 0659D] Under his guidance your prayers will be carried along the descending path; blessed, he will go before you to the divine ears, and, while you offer sacred psalms together with devout service [Note: [Col. 0660D] Thus we have restored the reading from the German manuscript and four printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition reads “with sacred psalms and service.”], Christ will descend with tranquil power,

641–642 [Note: [Col. 0659D] See the same license in poem 15, line 81.] so that he may veil the people and the temple in sacred darkness,

[510] [Col. 0660A] pouring a snow-white cloud through the covered sanctuary.

Now I want you to see the paintings in long processions along the colored porticoes, and to weary your slightly upturned neck as you read everything with your face tilted back. Whoever sees these things and recognizes the truth in the empty figures will feed his trusting mind with an image that is not empty [Note: [Col. 0660D] The German manuscript reads *pascit* (“feeds”).].

For the painting, in faithful sequence, contains everything that the elder Moses wrote in five books, and everything that Jesus, marked with the Lord’s name, accomplished. Under his leadership the Jordan, its current suspended and its waves fixed, stood still before the divine ark.

[520] A new power divided the river: one part stood still with the stream opened up [Note: [Col. 0660D] Thus we have restored the reading from the German manuscript; previously the text read *recurso*. See Joshua 3 and Augustine on Psalm 113:13.], while the other part of the river ran on, flowing into the sea. It left the riverbed bare; and where the strong current had rushed, its force had piled the restrained waters high above, so that a threatening mountain of water hung on its trembling structure, looking down upon feet crossing over the dry depths, while dusty human footprints passed dry-shod through the middle of the river over its hard mud [Note: [Col. 0659D] Joshua 3:15.].

Now, with attentive eyes, run over the brief book that distinguishes Ruth’s period—the period ending with the Judges and beginning with the Kings. This history seems short, but it marks the mysteries of a great conflict, in which two sisters tear themselves apart in opposite directions.

[535] Ruth follows the holy mother whom Orpah abandons; one daughter-in-law displays treachery, the other faith. One prefers God to her homeland, the other her homeland to life [Note: [Col. 0659D] Ruth 1:14; 2:11.].

Does not this division, I ask, remain throughout the whole world—one part following God, while another part rushes headlong through the world? Would that an equal portion belonged to death and salvation!

[540] But the broad road receives many, and irresistible error sweeps those who slip along in easy ruin down its slope.

Perhaps it will be asked for what reason this plan of procedure was adopted by us [Note: [Col. 0659D] See poem 10, line 12.]: to adorn sacred buildings, in an unusual fashion, with figures represented as living.

[545] Hear me, and I shall try briefly to explain the reasons. It is obvious to all what glory of the holy Felix draws the crowds here, but the gathering here is greater still. The rustic population, not lacking in faith but untrained in reading, long accustomed to serve profane rites, is at last converted to Christ as a stranger, while it gazes in wonder at the works of the saints displayed in Christ.

See how many gather from every countryside, and how piously they wander, deceived in their uneducated minds. They have left distant homes and despised the frosts, not cold in their fervent faith; and now, look, they extend their wakeful celebrations through the entire night.

[555] Joy keeps sleep and darkness away with torches.

[Col. 0661A] If only they carried on these celebrations with sound prayers and did not mix their own cups with those at the thresholds of the saints [Note: [Col. 0661D] See note 312.].

[560] However much this fasting company may resound with more fitting service, it also makes the holy hymns ring out in chaste voices and offers the sober praise sung to the Lord. Nevertheless, I think such small joys, which they draw from modest feasts, should be forgiven, because error has slipped into their uneducated minds; simplicity, unaware of so great a fault, does not fall from piety, though it wrongly believes that the saints rejoice at tombs drenched with the breath of wine.

643–644 Do the dead, then, approve what the teachers condemned? Does Peter’s table receive what Peter’s teaching rejects [Note: [Col. 0661D] 1 Peter 4:3. See note 313.]?

[570] Everywhere there is one cup of the Lord, one food, and one table and house of God. Let them sell their wines in taverns [Note: [Col. 0662D] The German manuscript, together with four editions, has *Discedant* in the margin (“Let them depart”).]. The church is the holy house of prayer: depart from the sacred thresholds [Note: [Col. 0661D] That is, “withdraw”], serpent. This is not a place where wicked amusement is owed to you, but punishment. You mix mockery with your prayers, enemy; you howl discordantly amid torments, yet sing among the cups.

You fear Felix, you foolishly despise Felix; drunk, you insult him, guilty, you pray; and, wretched man, you revel under the very judge whose vengeance punishes you in your burning state.

[580] Therefore we thought it a useful work to adorn all Felix’s buildings with sacred painting, so that the colored likeness set before the astonished minds of the country people might perhaps catch them by these spectacles, and captions placed above might show in writing what the hand has displayed.

While everyone in turn points out and rereads the painted scenes for himself, they either remember their food more slowly or feed their pleasing fasts with what delights the eyes. Thus a better practice may enter the astonished minds, while painting deceives hunger. As one reads the sacred stories, the nobility of chaste deeds slips in, introduced through pious examples; sobriety is drunk in with open mouth, and forgetfulness of excessive wine enters.

While they spend the day looking on for a longer time, the cups grow fewer, because the time is prolonged by the miracles, and only a few hours remain for the feasters.

[Col. 0661D] From what remains of the things we see accomplished and painted, I offer you material for prayer on my behalf, asking you, while carrying out the work of Felix, to pray earnestly for me.

[600] It is fitting that the one whom you accompany in pious thought you should also reproduce in the image of your mind and follow in spirit, equal in love toward me. For I, wretched man, do not doubt that I am loved by the martyr, who has deigned to love even a little dog.

Since Felix, by God’s gift, is my life, my house, my possessions, my favor, my glory, and my bread, ask him, as my patron,

[605] that my foundations may be laid upon the holy mountains [Note: [Col. 0661D] Psalm 86:1.] and that the tower already begun may be completed without a breach in its structure.

From Genesis, I ask you, gather this meaning for prayer: let me not remain earthly Adam [Note: [Col. 0661D] 1 Corinthians 15:48], but be born from virgin earth, and, with the old self laid aside [Note: [Col. 0662D] Perhaps *exposita* (“laid aside”), or *ex posito*. Here *exponere* is used for *deponere*, as also in poem 23, line 66.], let a new image be formed.

[610] Let me be brought forth from my own earth and be unlike my own race; let me hasten to the honey-sweet rivers of the bride’s land, preserved from the fire of the Chaldean furnace.

Let me be hospitable to those under my roof, like Lot, with my doors always open [Note: [Col. 0661D] See Letter 18.11, note 5.], so that I may be freed from Sodom; and let me not turn my eyes backward,

[615] lest, lacking the salt of the heart, I be turned into a pillar of salt [Note: [Col. 0662D] Genesis 19:22.].

Let me be offered to God as a living sacrifice, like the boy Isaac; and carrying my wood, let me follow the gracious Father beneath the cross. Let me find wells; but, I pray, let jealous Amalek not bury them and blind the living water [Note: [Col. 0662D] See note 314.].

[620] Let me be a fugitive from the world, as blessed Jacob was a fugitive from his brother Esau; and, weary, let me place beneath my head the stone destined for consecration, and rest in Christ.

Let me possess chaste love, and also dread sinful love; so that, like the unviolated Joseph,

[625] I may escape the enticements of the flesh, freed from bodily bonds, and leave my carnal spoil to the world, free from crime.

645–646 For the time to embrace is far off; the final day is at hand. The Lord is already near; it is already time to rise from sleep and keep watch, ready for the Lord’s knock.

[630] Let me have a good departure from Egypt, so that, penetrating the surges of the tossing heart under the guidance of the law, I may escape through the Red Sea and sing the Lord’s triumph when Pharaoh has been drowned. With a supplicant vow, trembling in exultation and rejoicing with fear,

[635] I commend my labors to his holy gifts [Note: [Col. 0662D] Ecclesiasticus 3; 1 Corinthians 35; Romans 1:7; Luke 12; Exodus 7:14.].

[Col. 0662D] Support with prayer, Nicetas, what I pray for; and all of you who have gathered here together for holy religion, devoted to the Lord and giving thanks, say with me:

[640] “These things, O Christ our God, we make for you with slender and simple resources on our behalf; for you, supreme Creator, cannot be contained by works made by hand, nor can the world in its entirety contain you, for whom heaven is narrow and the earth a point.

[Col. 0663A] But bearing devoted service to your saints without end, we honor the great with a small tribute,

[645] hoping through those intercessors that you will place in us the completed summits of your works, and that, as inhabitant, you will be present in minds that have been built up.”

# POEM XXVIII [Note: [Col. 0664D] Written in the year 403, on January 14.]  
## ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT FELIX. POEM X

He enlarges the old basilicas of Saint Felix with new buildings; he constructs a new and magnificent one, with a baptistery; and he adorns them with paintings and epigrams. The new basilica is consecrated by Paul, bishop of Nola, and on that same day the sacraments of baptism and the Eucharist are administered there.

In the old, a new thing is born for us through its accomplishment, and familiar solemnities grow through an unfamiliar rite. At once they double for me the material of a poem and the gracious birthday of Felix: in his buildings this newly born work,

[5] which you see shining forth with equal splendor among lofty structures raised everywhere, has recently been born.

Here vestibules, broadly surrounded by long porticoes [Note: [Col. 0663D] See note 315.], are opened beneath a roofed court with an open impluvium [Note: [Col. 0663D] That is, an atrium. See notes 167 and 316.] [Note: [Col. 0664D] The German manuscript reads *incloso tecti* (“with the roof enclosed”); five printed editions read *in clivo* (“on the slope”). See notes 167 and 316.], and at the same time their entrances open the courts to the stars above.

[10] There halls joined to one another are connected with the walls; with their open breadth both spreading apart and coming together, they rival one another, joining their roof ridges with interwoven beams. Varied and beautiful in equal ornament, they stand forth in marble, painting, coffered ceilings, and columns.

Among them, even the small chambers vary in grace. In the porticoes—where one continuous portico extends farther in a single uninterrupted stretch—three closely placed fronts open the chambers set along its side,

[Col. 0663C] and three doors open through running railings [Note: [Col. 0663D] See note 317.].

[20] Pious names mark the central chambers with painted martyrs, whom equal glory redeemed despite their different sex. But the two chambers open on the right and left are adorned by faithful painting with two cycles of stories.

One is filled with the sacred deeds of holy men: Job tested by wounds and Tobit restored to sight. The other is occupied by the lesser sex: renowned Judith, together with the powerful queen Esther.

The inner court smiles with varied ornament, joyful above the roofs and open to the clear light of day,

647–648 [30] with fronts, and below encircled by white columns [Note: [Col. 0663D] That is, made of marble.].

[Col. 0663D] In its open space a shining basin stands, covered by a bronze tower with a latticed summit. The remaining vessels stand beneath the open bronze, set around little fountains in a pleasing and varied arrangement. The work of art differs, but the vein of metal agrees. A single stream flows from different mouths, through a larger opening.

This court, joined to three basilicas, is open to all and spreads different entrances from a single one. Likewise, from the three it receives into one embrace those who have come out, into a spacious central pavement.

[Col. 0664A] Yet through five rows of shining groups of basins [Note: [Col. 0663D] See note 318.], a compressed series of marble, constructed with marvelous artistry, opens itself to wandering eyes.

[45] But in the surrounding porticoes there is abundant room for walking, for leaning against the railings between the columns when tired, and from there watching the flowing streams at play; for seeing the ground wet while one’s feet remain dry; for observing without stepping on the pavement; and for admiring the fountains springing up with a gentle murmur.

This convenience is available not only for the pleasures of winter,

[50] because in the heat the shade of the roof is equally welcome,

[Col. 0664B] (As sunny places please in cold weather, so dry places please in the rain.) [Note: [Col. 0664D] This line is added from the German manuscript.]

On the other side an exterior court lies open, likewise enclosed by porticoes, smaller in ornament but larger in surface.

[55] In front of the sacred buildings it spreads out a vestibule visible from a distance. With its double covering of chambers constructed from the interlocking beams of joined buildings, it imitates the appearance of a fortress wall and broadly opens a forum conspicuous for its meeting places.

[60] What sign the venerable Felix recently displayed in this place I shall tell in a swift account.

In the middle of the field, opposite the thresholds of the venerable hall [Note: [Col. 0663D] That is, near them.], two wooden beams, joined together, stood there, obstructive in their position and ugly to behold.

[65] [Col. 0664C] They destroyed all the beauty of the works, wickedly blocking the view with their foul obstruction [Note: [Col. 0663D] French: “which obstructed the view.”]. For the door of the open basilica, darkened by the short hut placed between, stood uselessly closed.

When we wished to remove this obstruction confronting us, the people who had marked out their dwellings there gave us their answer: they swore that they could sooner bargain away their lives than be forced to migrate from the site.
