Their words certainly seemed contemptible; but, I confess, I myself was reluctant to provoke resentment, for I was weary even of winning a quarrel.

[75] Meanwhile, one night, when they had just begun to take their first rest [Note: [Col. 0664D] Thus we have corrected the reading from the German manuscript. Previously it read *prima*, erroneously. [The corrected reading is *quadam* (“on a certain”).]], as the sleepers began to fall quiet, behold: a spark leaping from the abandoned hearths set fire to one of the chambers. In the hiding place of the chamber itself, among the straw and hay into which it had perhaps fallen, it kindled a sudden blaze. Soon, spreading through the hut, as it gained strength from the dry fuel,

[80] it seized an immense flame from the fragile tinder. With an easy slide it burst through the rotten timbers of the old roof and twisted the raging fire into great whirlwinds; it mixed a hot cloud through the air and drew the stars away beneath black smoke.

The fire itself added a terrible roar, resounding with a heavier crackling of the fragile material [Note: [Col. 0665D] The same German manuscript reads “with a crackling.”].

649–650 It encircled all the houses marked out by the neighboring inhabitants, and even the fields farther away from the village.

[90] The vapor blew upon them so fiercely, the dreadful light struck them so fiercely; it sprinkled the roofs situated near and far alike; and with sparks flying widely, there was a fiery rain. So suddenly were we roused by mournful cries from every side, and by the monstrous light poured around the buildings,

[95] that, seeing everything around us shining as though exposed, we thought that all things were being seized and consumed by flames, and that the very halls of the saints were simultaneously boiling in so great a fire. From all the roofs at once those flashes were reflected, filling even distant places with scattered fires and terrifying the countryside with vast clouds of flame [Note: [Col. 0665D] The German manuscript reads “the fields nearby.”].

[100] So each person feared that the neighboring houses were close to him, and that burning heat was bringing torches directly to his own dwelling, drawing foul air with dreadful odors [Note: [Col. 0665D] Thus the German manuscript reads, together with the editions of Badius and Schottus; the other manuscripts read “hostile.”].

We were frightened: with greater danger approaching our houses, we did not rely on our own resources. For where would there be strength in our weak hands sufficient to extinguish so great a mass of fire? The flame, growing greater through its own fuel,

[105] and suddenly arising from a little beam, was spreading over all the roofs at once with threatening fire [Note: [Col. 0666D] The German manuscript reads “the flame.”].

[110] Therefore we ran, relying only on faith and a suppliant prayer, to the nearby threshold of my Felix. From there, with equal prayers, we hurried to the adjoining hall, and sought healing from the power of the apostolic ashes, placing our faces beneath the altars.

[115] Returning to my house, I bring out a small piece of wood, but one of great power for salvation, taken from the eternal cross. Holding it in my hand, I thrust it from a distance against the opposing flames, as though holding a shield before my breast with which to protect myself and drive back the enemy, checked by the joined boss.

[120] Believe me, and do not offer thanks to me, but render them to Christ; give the Omnipotent his due praise. For our salvation rests upon the cross and name of Christ. From that source we received faith, and in this danger our faith, resting upon the cross, proved effective; the flame recognized our salvation [Note: [Col. 0665D] That is, the cross, which is our salvation.].

[125] It was not my voice or right hand that terrified the fire, but the power of the cross. In the very place from which it had risen, the cross compelled the flame, enclosed within its prescribed boundary, to stand still [Note: [Col. 0665D] That is, to be halted.] and to be extinguished as its roar died away; it compelled the storm, born from ash, to return to ash.

[130] How great is the power of the cross, that nature should abandon itself! The fire that devours all wood is itself burned by the wood of the cross.

Many hands then sprinkled the fire with repeated vessels, wishing to overcome the blaze with abundant water. But although the rain was weighed against exhausted springs, the fire nevertheless, with greater force, overcame all the water while the tired men scattered it. We extinguished fire with wood; what water could not conquer, a small splinter overcame [Note: [Col. 0665D] See note 319.].

[135] After the fear had departed and the laboring light had restored the desired day, we went out to inspect what the night had done and, although the flames had been extinguished, to observe with secure eyes the traces of the fire still smoking far and wide.

[140] We believed that we would see extensive damage to the buildings, remembering the great terror and fire. But our expectation quickly diminished when we saw what had happened:

[145] nothing had been burned except what ought to have burned. We saw that one of the two lodgings had caught fire,

651–652 lodgings which our own hand would have removed had the fire not done so. Yet even this was a kindness that Felix provided for us, anticipating our labor with useful flames and granting us the savings of construction.

The fire, having overcome one house there, did not allow the other house, equal to the burned one, to remain as an obstruction before the similarly double-open doors,

[155] but so that this same fire might punish the occupant, while preserving for him what he himself would soon destroy.

For the man who had recently preferred his own hovels to the sacred buildings [Note: [Col. 0666D] Thus we have emended *gurgustia* from the German manuscript; the editions read *dictis*.] was first punished by the fire in one of them; then he himself began to destroy another beam with his own hand and swiftly completed his own losses, lamenting his beloved houses and empty affections [Note: [Col. 0666D] The German manuscript reads “houses.”].

When he saw the burned and demolished buildings together, he marveled at unequal ruins in a similar heap, a two-colored ruin composed of rubble and ash [Note: [Col. 0666D] The same German manuscript reads “joined together in a two-colored ruin.”].

[165] Seeing that he had yielded this triumph to us without a quarrel, he accuses only himself, since no grace of service remained for him and the confusion of punishment remains.

Now that the fronts have been opened by the removal of the obstruction, let us walk about within them in speech and in spirit, rejoicing in their spaces, and let us proceed into the sacred halls.

[170] Let us admire the sacred monuments of ancient figures, and in the three spaces read the two Testaments. Let us also discern this principle with clear sight [Note: [Col. 0666D] The German manuscript reads *credentes . . . certo* (“believing … certainly”).]: that the new law is painted in the old buildings, and the old law in the new. For in the old there is equally useful newness, and in newness there is antiquity.

[175] Thus there may be both new life and hoary wisdom; that we may draw from a double age a balance of mind, old in gravity and young in simplicity, joining a different age to our own character.

There is also, far within the larger hall’s inner space, an attached chapel [Note: [Col. 0667D] See note 320.], as though a daughter of that building,

[180] beautiful with a starry dome [Note: [Col. 0667D] Thus corrected from the German manuscript; for the chamber set within the recess of the larger hall could not have been spacious, as the printed manuscripts imply. Rather, it is “like a daughter of its roof, beautiful beneath a starry dome.” What *tholus* means is discussed in note 321.] [Note: [Col. 0667D] See note 327.], curved into three recesses with its spaces arranged. In its middle shines a fountain of piety, wonderfully renewing and being renewed at the same time.

[185] For today a twofold renewal accompanies it twice over, while the bishop there performs the two offices of Christ. He dedicates the venerable shrine to two uses, joining pious sacraments to a cleansing bath.

Thus the sacrifice renews the temple, and grace renews the fountain.

[190] And the new fountain, renewing the human being, both receives and gives a gift—or rather, although through use it ceases to be new, it begins to impart divine use to mortals. For the fountain itself, once sent into service for renewal [Note: [Col. 0667D] Thus corrected from the same German manuscript. Previously it read “sent into one use for renewal,” which made no sense.],

[195] ceases to be new, but through such a gift it is always to be used and never ceases to renew the old.

Behold this gift of the Lord, this image in which the same person becomes new through Christ’s gift and the old person perishes, as you see the repaired roofs of Felix’s twin hall:

[Col. 0667C] 653–654 what had been old now appears to stand forth as new.

[200] Formerly they stood in a shapeless row of massive pillars; now, supported in their renewed arrangement by better columns, they have gained both space and an increase of light. Having laid aside their neglected condition, they have taken back their youth.

For in these buildings too a double pleasure for the eyes shines forth: the roofs renewed with new material rival one another in equal brilliance; the ages of the buildings differ, but their appearance agrees. The work of the old and of the recent builders comes together; one beauty adorns both works in a similar aspect; what was founded long ago joins what is new.

[210] There is no distinction for the eyes: a single beauty shines [Note: [Col. 0668D] Thus corrected from the German manuscript; that is, the old building which he had adorned with paintings shone with the same beauty as the new one. For what would “old age shines as one” mean, as the printed manuscripts read?]

[Col. 0667D] in aged and new places. The black horror is hidden, and painting has restored a youthful brightness to the old roofs by pouring over them a flowering variety of colors.

[215] Thus the time of the buildings is confused, and newness shines outward on the walls while antiquity lies hidden within. Painted youth covers the face of old age; an age grown old has blossomed again into a child’s face [Note: [Col. 0668D] Thus the German manuscript reads; the editions have “an aged face.”].

So they are old and new at once, neither equally new nor equally old. They are both the same and not the same, a form of the good that is to come and of the good that is present. For even now it is useful for us, after wiping away the filth of our former life, to be renewed in a pious mind, to follow Christ, and to prepare ourselves for the kingdoms.

[220] Then also, when renewed life is granted [Note: [Col. 0667D] See note 322.], that order of the risen will be counted superior which, having clothed its flesh in a splendid garment,

[225] will change its flesh’s servile form by the image of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0668D] Thus corrected from the German manuscript. See what precedes and follows. Previously it read “he changed.”]. Conformed to God, it will receive the honor of reigning with him, like Christ, yet by Christ’s gift.

[230] This same image teaches us to lay aside the old form, to wear the new, and to erase what lies behind; to turn the mind toward what is to come from God; to bring fitting forgetfulness to former concerns; and to introduce into the spirit concern for the heavenly kingdoms.

We must die to human affairs and the loves of this age in mind before we die in body; nor should we be released from the bonds of the body before we are released from crime. Therefore let us be renewed in our perceptions and hasten to shake the earthly actions of the terrestrial image far from our bodies,

[240] casting off our garments, so that, cleansed of the filth of body and soul, we may restore our bright clothing [Note: [Col. 0668D] Thus corrected from the German manuscript. Rosweyde’s edition has “with filth shaken from the heart”; two editions, “shaken off”; three, “shaken from the heart.”].

Let us flee not only the sin committed but also the sin contemplated, like a deadly breath from a corpse, blocking our nostrils against its foul odor.

Solomon warns us to fear sin and to shudder at it like the face of a serpent [Note: [Col. 0667D] Ecclesiasticus 21:2.], saying that it has the teeth of an armed lion. And truly so: like a savage mouth, it devours the soul conquered by sick pleasure of the body [Note: [Col. 0668D] The German manuscript reads “will.”],

[245] and the dragon, having slain it, leads it away as food for itself [Note: [Col. 0668D] The German manuscript, together with three editions, reads “having conquered it.”]. It devours the peoples of Ethiopia, not scorched by the sun,

[250] 655–656 but blackened by vices and darkened by crimes.

Such Ethiopians the serpent eats; in them it has food which it is permitted to seize [Note: [Col. 0669D] Thus restored from the German manuscript. The others read “which is condemned.” See note 323.]. For by one name God called the sinner—and the serpent’s food—“earth”; and therefore, while devouring sins, the sinner is devoured by the dragon.

[255] The time has come to change our ways, to rise from sleep [Note: [Col. 0669D] Romans 13:11.], and at last to keep watch for God, while in turn sleeping with respect to those actions over which a mind dead to Christ keeps watch.

If God’s teaching from the light of the Word does not open our understanding, at least let us take examples from these very buildings. Let stones and timbers be teachers for the dull, so that we may produce in faith a work like the one we have made here by hand.

[260] Though the labor of mind and hands is not one and the same, a similar principle of work arises from unequal causes. Behold, look: I shall prove that dissimilar forms meet in a similar appearance.

Many remember the state of the place where the new buildings now stand. For it is only a short time since all the works that now remain completed were begun. The third year brought them to completion after two years of labor, through the prayers of the saints and the aid of Christ.

[270] Part of the space had been a small garden, part a heap of rubble, which the united labor of the people removed. It tore out the worthless plants and weeds,

[Col. 0669C] so that the court might lie open, cleansed, with a polished surface. Now it shines, spread broadly across a surface adorned with marble stones, having forgotten its former cultivation.

[275] How well it has changed its appearance! After the use of manure it bears marble ornament [Note: [Col. 0669D] The German manuscript reads *ornatu* (“ornament”).]; after worthless cabbages, Parian shells [Note: [Col. 0669D] Thus we have emended *Brassica* from three printed editions, supported by the German manuscript. Rosweyde reads *Brassicla*; others, *Brassida*.]; and it shines with waters, though it once shone with filth.

In what way, then, will this building now offer me a model by which I may cultivate, build, and renew my perceptions, and construct a dwelling fit for Christ?

The answer is ready: what my earth is, what the rubble in me is, and from what source thorns arise in my field. The earth is the heart; guilt is the evil rubble of the heart.

[285] Idle luxury, impure love, and stained lust are the rubble of the soul. So too are anxious care for the body, devouring envy, greedy hunger, heavy anger, and light-minded hope;

[Col. 0670A] extravagant ambition for what is one’s own and thirst for what belongs to another are thorns in the mind [Note: [Col. 0670D] The German manuscript reads “of the soul.”], because they always torment wavering souls with empty goads. The miserable fear of lacking burns them continually, as does the miserable eagerness to possess.

Thus, even amid wealth, they are poor; like that Tantalus among the waters, they thirst and do not possess what they seem to possess.

[295] For they are afraid to use their possessions and leave them stored away; while they prepare provisions, they lose the time of living.

These thorns, then, and this rubble must be cleared from rough minds; and the first root of all crimes must be torn out from the fibers [Note: [Col. 0670D] Thus the German manuscript, the Latin edition, and three printed editions. Others read “first,” incorrectly.],

[Col. 0670B] from which the unhappy tree grows [Note: [Col. 0670D] Thus the German manuscript. The printed editions read “because,” incorrectly.]. Struck by the Lord’s axe at its root,

[300] let it fall [Note: [Col. 0669D] Matthew 3:10.], so that it may never sprout in our fields.

If, once the fuel has been cut away from us, this root dries up, every wickedness will fall and every vice will perish. All evils will follow the collapse of their mother,

657–658 and when their tree dies, its fruit will perish with it.

[305] Then, once the house has been well cleansed, it will be built in the garden, and the structure of divine design, founded on living soil, will rise well into the heights. Christ himself will raise columns within us and loosen the old pillars that obstruct the soul.

[Col. 0670C] The King will make space for himself in our perceptions, so that he may walk in them, as Wisdom once used to lead his healing steps with pious speech through Solomon’s five porticoes,

[310] healing bodies by touching them [Note: [Col. 0670D] The German manuscript reads “healing.”] and teaching hearts [Note: [Col. 0669D] John 5:2–3.].

Let us not, therefore, be old among new buildings, so that Christ, who dwells in hearts, may renew new hearts.

For a tear in something new and old joined together is made worse, and new wine is properly put into new wineskins [Note: [Col. 0669D] Matthew 9:16–17.]. Let the former life perish, lest the future life perish.

[315] Let us willingly leave the world, since it must be abandoned unwillingly unless we flee it willingly. Let us die, lest we die; let us cover mortal life with life-giving death.

Let the earthly image perish, and let the heavenly image enter; let Adam be transformed into Christ, and let us also be changed here, so that we may be changed there. Whoever now remains the same in himself

[325] will not be changed from himself forever [Note: [Col. 0670D] Thus the German manuscript. The printed editions read “in eternity.”].

# POEM XXIX [Note: [Col. 0671D] Added here. Moreover, poem 26 is now poem 27. Written in the year 403. These verses still exist today in the same basilica.]  
## ON THE BASILICA OF SAINT FELIX AT NOLA, ENLARGED BY HIMSELF

Previously the place was small, too narrow for sacred rites and unable to open its hands to suppliants. Now it offers spacious altars to the people for sacred services within the shrine of the central martyr.

[5] Everything renewed for God is pleasing; Christ always renews all things and increases them into a greater abundance of light. Thus, honoring the throne of his beloved Felix, he has enlarged it both in splendor and in space.

# POEM XXX [Note: [Col. 0672D] Elsewhere numbered 26; but what was 27 is now 28. Written in the year 404, on January 14.]  
## ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT FELIX. POEM XVIII. FRAGMENTS

### On the relics of the saints spread throughout the world

If stars could be absent from the sky, grass from the earth, honey from honeycombs, water from springs, and milk from swelling breasts,

then the tongues of the righteous could cease from praise; in them God himself is both the power of life and the glory of death—God for whom they chose to bargain for life and, by dying, to establish the pious faith of peoples.

[5] [lacuna]

Of this number, Felix, a distinguished confessor, given to this city, has shone far and wide throughout the world under the title of his name. But Nola, the home of his burial,

[10] [Col. 0671C] like a star belonging to itself, applauds.

For every martyr, wherever he has been assigned to remain, is at once the star of that place and the healing of those who worship him.

For the Creator, pitying the world darkened by ancient gloom and the souls languishing throughout the earth,

[15] thus arranged the monuments of the righteous throughout the lands, so that he might scatter them like the lights of the stars across the nighttime sky.

[lacuna]

659–660 Desiring, therefore, to drive these diseases away from us, the Lord, healer of every kind, brought forth holy physicians for suffering mortals among various peoples, physicians rich in saving piety.

[20] [Col. 0671D] And so that divine power might display its care more clearly, he brought them into the more important cities. Although some towns retain martyrs in small communities, God brought others into the leading cities with broad walls; and those who had completed their lives he distributed among a few regions,

[25] though before their death he had given them as teachers to the whole world.

Thus he established Peter and Paul in the city of Rome, because the head of the world needed the chief physicians.

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

[Col. 0672A] [lacuna]

Thus, granting his holy gifts also to the remaining lands, God scattered his great limbs throughout the cities of the world.

[30] Thus he gave Andrew to Patras and John to Ephesus, so that through them he might heal Europe and Asia together and dispel the heavy darkness through such great lights.

Parthia embraces Matthew, India Thomas; Libya received Lebbaeus, and the Phrygians received Philip.

[35] Crete took Titus for itself, and Antioch and Ostia took Luke [Note: [Col. 0671D] See note 324.]:

Mark was given to you at Alexandria, so that, once the ox had been driven away,

[lacuna]

For while Constantine [Note: [Col. 0671D] See note 325.] was founding the city of his own name, and was the first of the Roman kings to bear the name “Christian,” he received a divine plan in his mind:

[40] since he was then building walls rivaling Rome’s magnificent walls, he would also make that city follow Rome in these endowments;

so, rejoicing, he fortified his walls with apostolic bodies. Then he transported Andrew from Achaea,

[45] and Timothy from Asia. Thus Constantinople, with its two such towers, rises as a rival capital to great Rome:

more truly resembling Rome in the height of its walls because God, with equal ambition, compensated it with Peter and Paul—since it deserved to receive Paul’s disciple together with Peter’s brother.

[50] [Col. 0672C] How much usefulness for the duties of our life has grown through the long divisions of land along this route of the saints,

the very places still show today, where that capacious wagon, bearing its blessed burden, came to rest at its appointed stopping-place.

[55] At every interval where there was either a lodging for the holy bodies or a resting-place for those carrying their consecrated ashes, wondrous signs cried out.

For the divine hand worked there along every road with healing power, wherever the holy bodies impressed their living footprints upon the sacred route.

[60] Therefore, when faith had prompted it, an opportunity was granted to the faithful zeal of the companions, so that they might wish to gather from the holy bones a worthy benefit,

as though each might carry home, as the reward of his service and the payment for his labor,

[65] a protection for his private household.

From then on the sacred ashes were scattered in different places like seeds of life; and wherever a little dew fell from a tiny bone, a small portion of the holy body,

there pious grace produced vast springs and rivers of life from a drop of ash.

[Col. 0673A] [lacuna]

But powerful Carthage rejoices in the martyr Cyprian, whose fountains, poured forth alike from his mouth and from his blood,

made fertile the thirsty sands of Libya [Note: [Col. 0673D] That is, Africa. See Poem 3, line 2.]

[lacuna]

[661–662] Nor did grace shine less brightly in the western lands:

[75] Ambrose stands for Latium, Vincent for Iberia;

Gaul received Martin, Aquitaine Delphinus.

And many other seeds of the saints, scattered abundantly throughout those same regions in established tombs,

illumine the whole world with heavenly powers.

[lacuna]

[80] Thus our own Nola, through the love of the compassionate Christ, deserved to be fortified by the tomb of Felix,

[Col. 0673B] and at the same time to be purified; for the world, mingled with blind ruins, and the city itself dying in an equal darkness, lay there.

[lacuna]

Those persons who, by the power of a false divinity, had been gods now howl in torment;

and those who, under a deceptive name, had surrendered living human beings to themselves, seeing nothing heavenly before the worship of God,

now, when true faith has been made manifest in Christ’s light, cannot endure the buried dead.

[lacuna]

Christ is likewise Alpha [Note: [Col. 0673D] See note 326.] and the Greek ο (“O”), who at once embraces the highest and lowest boundaries of the universe;

[90] victor, he seized both the regions below and the heavenly realms alike;

and, having shattered the abysses, he entered the opened heavens,

bringing back victorious salvation after death had been overcome.

[Col. 0673C] And when victory joined him to the Father’s right hand,

[95] and he fixed the banner of the cross above all the stars [Note: [Col. 0673D] See note 327.],

he established the bodily trophy in the heavenly seat.

[lacuna]

Now I turn my words to you, venerable cross of God [Note: [Col. 0673D] See note 328.],

and, giving thanks, I shall conclude my speech with your praise.

O great cross, God’s compassion; cross, glory of heaven;

[100] cross, eternal salvation of humankind; cross, terror to the wicked,

and strength to the just, and light to the faithful: O cross,

you granted God, in the flesh on earth, to serve salvation,

and humankind, in God, to reign in heaven!

Through you the light of truth appeared; impious night fled.

[105] You destroyed the shrines torn down for believers among the nations;

you are the bond joining human peace,

[Col. 0673D] reconciling humanity through the covenant of Christ the mediator.

You became the step by which a human being may be carried into the heavens.

Be always a column and anchor for us, your pious servants,

[110] so that our household may remain secure, our fleet be well guided,

with faith fixed upon the cross, or with the crown obtained from the cross.

# POEM XXXI [Note: [Col. 0674D] Formerly 27; but since what was 27 is now 28. Written in the year 406, on 14 January.]

## A NATALICIUM POEM ON SAINT FELIX, POEM XIX. FRAGMENT.

[Col. 0674A]

## On the destruction of the army of the Goths together with its king [Note: [Col. 0673D] See note 329.]

For this cause was indeed commended to many patrons,

so that Roman safety and the life of the state might endure.

Here were Peter, here Paul, the leaders; here all the martyrs,

whom the circuit of the great City holds together in countless number,

[5] and whom the Church [Note: [Col. 0673D] See note 239.] venerates throughout the Romulean boundaries,

with her frontier spread through innumerable peoples.

Together they maintained anxious vigils with fervent prayer.

My Felix was among them like one of their number;

he was a great part of their prayers, but the chief object of the petition

[10] [Col. 0674B] is referred to all, and not as a private request to any one.

# POEM XXXII [Note: [Col. 0674D] Formerly 28; but since what was 29 is now 30. Written in the year 407, on 14 January.]

## A NATALICIUM POEM ON SAINT FELIX, POEM XX. FRAGMENTS.

Saint Felix is thanked most generously for the gifts and benefits received through his intervention with God.

[663–664] Now to you, venerable father, eternal patron,

my protector and Felix, most dear to Christ,

I shall return grateful words in a changed form of speech.

You have bestowed many gifts upon me through various benefactions.

[5] I remember that I owe you everything that produces the affairs of the present life and the hope of the future;

for Christ gave me into your possession from my earliest years.

If eloquence flowed for me in river-like streams,

and I had a thousand mouths and a hundred tongues,

[10] [Col. 0674C] perhaps even, refreshed by these resources poured from a gathered fountain,

I could not run through all the gifts of Felix,

all that the Lord Christ bestowed upon his friend,

and that the confessor transmitted to me, his servant and foster-child.

[lacuna]

If, returning to the beginning, I should review everything

[15] that he granted me with equal kindness at different times,

I could count the hairs of my own head

before I could recount your gifts toward me, good Felix.

[lacuna]

With its throne unharmed and its tomb never cracking,

the body, everywhere enclosed by solid protection,

of the martyr and his merit has been open to no defilement;

and the bones are worthy to preserve the sacred honor of his flesh,

because the Spirit never ceases to be present with the saints.

[Col. 0674D] Hence living grace abides in pious tombs,

which proves that all who have been buried in Christ are without death,

[25] their bodies sleeping for a time in peaceful slumber.

# POEM XXXIII [Note: [Col. 0674D] Formerly 29; but since what was 30 is now 17. Written in the year 408, on 14 January.]

## A NATALICIUM POEM ON SAINT FELIX, POEM XXI. FRAGMENTS.

It recounts the miracles of Saint Felix, by which the sick are healed and bodies possessed by demons are set free.

Come now, verses: let the articulated voice of my modest offering flow. Be present, Felix, rich cause of my speaking,

and enter my heart with silent breath.

Your spirit will run through my mouth; be a fountain

[5] for my words. I shall indeed be a reed-pipe for your streams,

which you will offer me from the river of the divine word.

[lacuna]

Rise, therefore, and enter my breast with your gentle breath,

O father Felix, lord and patron;

you are my household, my medicine, and my wisdom, Felix.

[10] Now sharpen my mind, dulled by long periods of idleness,

and invigorate my heart by your fiery light.

[lacuna]

But my speech is not to be poured into this expanse

so that I may run through the merits or miracles of the saints,

[Col. 0675B] and try to weave into verse all that God has done and continues to do through all the saints

from the beginning of creation,

things that the human mind cannot grasp and the tongue cannot express.

[665–666] And what wonder is it if a single sheet in an entire volume cannot contain

what the whole world itself cannot contain?

For the Maker of the world is greater than the world—the God himself, the king

[20] who fills earth and heaven, whom this world cannot contain;

the saints contain him—not by the vastness of the body,

but because they are humble in devotion and capable through a pure heart.

[lacuna]

Now, therefore, so that I may recount the divinely wrought deeds of my patron Felix,

[25] [Col. 0675C] or the benefits of life he has conferred upon me,

or those which, by heavenly aid, he bestows upon many,

he does not cease to confer pious gifts almost every day,

granting various gifts through signs:

the order of his merits demands that Christ be praised.

[30] I shall seem to praise not a human being, but rather him

through whom Felix is mighty, possesses his venerable name,

and gives healing powers by which he visits sick bodies

and releases captive souls by the force of the dark spirit,

with God prevailing. Nor does Felix work Christ’s gifts only through this power;

[35] generous Felix performs many other gifts of Christ,

and triumphs most powerfully over the serpent-like enemy.

# POEM XXXIV. ON SAINT FELIX, A NATALICIUM POEM. FRAGMENT OF UNCERTAIN AUTHORSHIP.

[Col. 0675D]

The power of Saint Felix at his tomb; the frequent gathering of the people to him.

Although he was hidden from ancient times in a tomb,

and, since he was mortal, lay concealed beneath the earth’s covering,

yet his living grace, made vigorous by God and surviving in his limbs,

enlightens the peoples with the divine breath of the martyr’s bones,

[5] [Col. 0676A] through the merit of the one buried yet living,

and the gathered crowd, continually brought together from various lands,

worships the brief throne of the great confessor [Note: [Col. 0675D] That is, honors it. See Poem 27, line 154.]

# POEM XXXV [Note: [Col. 0676D] Formerly 15; but since what was 32 is now 3.]

## A PANEGYRIC ON THE DEATH OF THE BOY CELSUS

He consoles Pneumatius and Fidelis, the parents of the boy Celsus, for the death of their son.

Celsus was formerly a boy of illustrious fathers and ancestral name,

but now he lives in the height of true merit:

Christ the Lord enriched him with so great a gift

that, though inexperienced in years and newly come to the waters, he might die [Note: [Col. 0675D] That is, die. See note 330.],

[5] and that grace, doubled for the infant in the span of life and in the font of baptism,

might bear him onward to God.

Alas, what shall I do? I struggle, hanging in uncertain affection:

shall I rejoice, or grieve? The boy deserves either response.

His love urges tears, and love urges me to rejoice,

[10] but faith commands rejoicing, while devotion commands weeping.

I mourn that so small and sweet a pledge was granted to his parents

for so brief a period of time [Note: [Col. 0675D] See Poem 24, line 37.].

Again, when I turn over the everlasting blessings of eternal life

that God prepares in heaven for the innocent,

[15] I rejoice that he died after completing his brief mortal age [Note: [Col. 0675D] See the following line, Poem 15, line 228, and note 331.] [Note: [Col. 0675D] See note 332.],

so that he might quickly enjoy the divine riches.

Nor, mingled with the wicked, would he long drag out earthly contagions

[667–668] in the fragile lodging of his body.

But, polluted by no crime of this world,

[20] [Col. 0676C] he would more worthily hasten toward the eternal Lord.

Therefore the infant was owed to God rather than to us,

and truly, on our behalf, he was pleasing to God.

The little boy had begun to enter his eighth year,

driving the first stages of life in swift chariots.

[25] He already bore the childish yoke upon his tender neck,

subject to the harsh commands of the grammarian.

Whatever the boy was taught, while his teacher marveled,

was insignificant beside his teachable nobility of intellect.

His parents rejoiced with anxious foreseeing hearts,

[30] even while they feared the envy directed against so great a gift.

Nor was there a long delay: Christ God, summoning to heaven the soul pleasing to him,

took it with deserved honor,

and snatched it away suddenly [Note: [Col. 0676D] The edition of Rosweyde has *subitam*. But, following the Royal manuscript and four editions, we restore with Sacchini *subitum*, used for *subito*, just as Paulinus used *longum* for *longe* in Poem 35, lines 593, 613, and 630, and *aeternum* in Poem 22, line 241.]

[Col. 0676D] so that it might be more worthy

to live joined with the assemblies of the pious.

[35] The cause of death was fluid suffused into his throat,

which, swelling heavily, inflated his milk-white neck.

From there it was driven back, but, sliding inward, it fled

into the depths of the body and struck life from the entrails.

The earth received its portion in the buried flesh;

[40] the spirit, borne away, departed into an angelic bosom.

The parents led the empty funeral of the deserted child [Note: [Col. 0675D] See line 278.]

with tears, lest devotion become a fault.

[Col. 0677A] For it is impious devotion to mourn a blessed soul

and a guilty love to weep for one rejoicing in God.

[45] Is it not clear how much sin is drawn forth by such devotion?

We are accused of holding faith deceitfully,

or of rejecting God’s laws in rebellious error,

if what pleased the Lord does not please us.

It is more just to mourn those human darknesses

[50] that degenerate souls make for themselves,

forgetful of their first origins in the heavenly image,

which the compassionate Father recalls to his kingdoms.

Because of whose love the Son took on my limbs,

conceived of a virgin, born a human being from a virgin,

[55] undergoing all that belongs to humanity, and in one body

[Col. 0677B] taking upon himself all the servants of all things [Note: [Col. 0677D] That is, “through all things.” See note 333.].

For he who was God, reigning in the form of God with God the Father as king,
took the form of a servant
and destroyed the guilt

[60] by which the human servant had once been held subject to punishment and death.

The Lord, having become our flesh under the appearance of a servant,

restored the servant to freedom.

So that the heavenly image might return to me through Christ,

who stripped the earthly Adam on the cross [Note: [Col. 0678D] Thus we have emended the text from Schott’s edition together with Barth. Paulinus uses the word similarly elsewhere, Poem 23, line 219: “I shall strip away by the light,” and Letter 24, no. 2. Otherwise, “Adam stripped himself.”].

[65] Therefore that Creator of mine bore my flesh and my death,

and by death redeemed his precious work.

Previously he had given me many promises of salvation,

[Col. 0677C] and commandments by which I might be directed through good deeds.

But because I had not cleansed, by laying on the medicine of the law,

[70] the ancient wounds of the first father,

and because I had not believed that I should await the gifts of God

announced beforehand by prophets from the divine mouth,

and because the human race, everywhere without the law of faith [Note: [Col. 0677D] See note 334.],

[669–670] had sunk into darkness, its salvation despaired of,

[75] while sin likewise ruled in our body,

death in sin, and the demon in destruction,

and sad fear and miserable error gave captive humanity

an even deeper plunge into death.

Meanwhile the Father himself, having compassion from high heaven

[80] on the deadly falls of erring humanity,

could not endure the serpent ruling cruelly over those falling into death,

and sent the Son for the accomplishment of every good.

He obeyed willingly, God in complete concord with the Father,

[Col. 0677D] caring for their common undertaking with equal devotion.

[85] He came and became human, and, perfect in both natures,

[Col. 0678A] showed God to be present in fragile flesh [Note: [Col. 0677D] That is, “in fragile flesh.” See Poem 15, line 318.].

He made use of human functions, but from within he displayed

the signs of God through healing commands.

With a human voice he taught divine things, and bodily

[90] performed mortal actions, yet without sin.

For, intent only on restoring his own work to himself,

he came to assume nature, not vice.

For the good One, good by nature, made the human being good and for good things;
the human being corrupted himself by a fall of mind.

[95] Therefore the maker of human beings came in mortal flesh,

but was not made human with mortal guilt.

For he could not erase sins unless he were free from them,

nor could he release the guilty if he too were guilty;

[Col. 0678B] nor would death yield to a sinner, since, as one bound,

[100] it lawfully held him in the chains of sin.

Rightly, therefore, Tartarus yielded to Christ who burst it apart,

since in him it found nothing that it could bind.

And death itself, in turn made guilty of unjust judgment,

was rightly subjected to the human being whom it had killed through crime.

[105] The serpent grew pale with envy, seeing the infernal barriers opened, with the law reversed, for the human being restored from below;
and, in turn bound, it saw a mortal released from death,

and the body, shaken free, rise from the earth,

and, moreover, saw the risen one ascend into heaven.

[110] Livid, it snarled in vain with its savage tooth.

And now it wastes away, since, as the company of the pious grows,

the destroyer itself is destroyed through Christ [Note: [Col. 0677D] That is, the serpent.].

[Col. 0678C] Therefore he healed the faults of my soul,

and took upon himself the sicknesses of the body, human from his mother, God from his Father.

[115] He bore the weaknesses, indeed, but also the natural functions of flesh,

and displayed the bodily affections.

With human senses he eats and drinks, and lowers his eyes

in sleep; he grows weary while traveling along the road [Note: [Col. 0677D] For *lassatur*, “is wearied.” See Letter 5, no. 18.].

As a human being, he sheds tears for a dead friend,

[120] whom he himself, as God, soon raises from the tomb [Note: John XI, 35 and 44.].

“A human being is carried by boat, and God commands the south winds,”

and the human being crosses the sea by God’s power [Note: Matthew XIV, 32 and 29; XXVI, 38.].

With a human mind he trembles at the hour when death is near;

with the mind of God he knows that the time of death has come.

[125] On the cross he is human; from the cross God terrified the earthly world;
as a human being he suffers death, but death itself suffers God [Note: Matthew XXVII, 51.].

As a human being he hangs on the cross; as God, from the cross he forgives crimes [Note: That is, “pardons,” a simple form used for a compound.];

and by dying he destroys the life of sin.

And, treated as one of the accused [Note: Mark XV, 28.], and judged worse than a robber,

[130] [Col. 0679A] whom Judaea preferred to the pious Lord [Note: Matthew XXVII, 21.],

he grants the believing robber the heavenly kingdom,

and, while still enclosed on earth, opens paradise [Note: Luke XXIII, 43.].

It is therefore fitting for us to strengthen our spirits, raise our minds,

and thrust cowardly fears from our hearts.

[135] For our sake, behold, that Son of God laid down his soul and took it up again,

[671–672] the Son through whom God created all things.”

God, the victor, achieved a triumph over our death,

and carried our body with him into the stars.

It was not enough that, for our sake, he drained away all mortal things

[140] so that he might remove our wounds through his own wounds.

But, so that anxious care might not suspend me in doubtful thought,

[Col. 0679B] he rose in the body in which he had fallen.

Clear faith became visible to mortal eyes: he himself was seen after death,

such as he had been before death.

[145] For he willingly presented himself to his doubting disciples,

and offered himself for examination by their eyes and hands [Note: John XX, 20.].

Nor was the apostle’s doubt without God’s purpose [Note: See Poem 27, lines 417 and following.],

so that no one might doubt that he lived after death.

He strengthened faith through doubting: while hesitant Thomas

[150] is challenged at close quarters, every human being is instructed.

What Thomas is commanded to see and touch face to face [Note: John XX, 27.],

I learn to believe with steady and steadfast faith:

that the death of human beings has been subdued by the death of Christ crucified,

[Col. 0679C] and that hope of resurrection has been established for bodies;

[155] for our bodies, because Christ the victor rose in this flesh which I bear,

in which I die.

He teaches me and presents his limbs to me, who doubted on my behalf;

he proves solid flesh, structured upon bones,

and further displays the wounds of his side and hands,

[160] and commands the doubting fingers to be inserted into them.

“See,” he says, “here is my side, and my palms and feet;

here are the nails of the cross, here is the path of the spear.

Here it is evident that the very living structure of my whole body

stands intact in sinews, bones, mouth, and skin [Note: John XX, 27; Luke XXIV, 39.].”

[165] Therefore hold the faith that you see, and also that

[Col. 0679D] you touch, and drive doubtful thoughts from your hearts.

Be witnesses to all of such great salvation,

and release the hearts of all human beings from fear.

Let the fear of death perish for everyone, and let the hope

[170] of resurrection likewise animate all peoples.

Yet this salvation belongs to those who believe, who with faithful hearts

will receive what you see with your eyes.

[Col. 0680A] For after I had achieved a triumph over conquered death,
“Death, overcome [Note: [Col. 0680D] Thus we have restored the reading from Schott’s edition; Paulinus elsewhere has a different allusion to Hosea XIII, 14: “From the hand of death I shall free them; from death I shall redeem them; I shall be your death, O death.” The reading fits well: “Death, overcome, died,” when life restored to life stands. Formerly the text read *abiit* (“has gone away”); see below, line 186, *obita morte* (“death having been undergone”), and line 187, *mors ruit* (“death falls”).], has perished; salvation, restored to life, stands.

[175] I gave life from death; by dying I subdued death.

And I restored the human race through blood [Note: Hosea XIII, 14].”

Having overcome the sin of the flesh in the flesh, I destroyed

the material of guilt and brought forth righteousness.

Death fell in the body; life rose in the body;

[180] the human being revived in the flesh in which he had previously died.

And now, behold, carrying the restored Adam in my body,

I present him as victor over death and the serpent.

What consolations, I ask, will be sufficient for us, or what rest

will heal our weary spirits,

[185] if such a great medicine cannot heal the sick,

a medicine that teaches lives to return after death [Note: See line 174 and Poem 27, line 568.]?

[Col. 0680B] Grief, depart; fear, withdraw; guilt, flee: death collapses,

life has risen, and Christ calls into the stars.

Having undergone my death, dead for me and victorious for me,
[190] “so that the death of sin may be the life of God for me.

Finally, from the cross he led the saved robber through an open

[673–674] passage to where paradise is found [Note: Luke XXIII, 43.],”

by this gift giving a sign both that he can cleanse sins

and that faith can overcome the boundaries of the forbidden grove.

[195] By such examples, with so great a guarantor of salvation,

it is fitting for the uplifted to turn their sorrow into joy [Note: See line 407.].

Let us drive complaining griefs from our ungrateful hearts,

and let pure eyes return, cleansed.

[Col. 0680C] Let us believe of Christ what we have seen in him:

[200] that we too shall rise in the same bodies in which we died,

and then, covered with the garment of divine beauty,

take on a changed, angelic form.

But if such darkness obstructs minds,

and sluggish sensation grows dull in an unresponsive body,

[205] so that, because divine things are concealed from bodily eyes,

you say that the writings contain no faith at all,

let Paul teach that the things which are seen are not eternal;

eternal things are hidden from human eyes.

Foolish one, look upon earthly things; believe heavenly things;

[210] contemplate the world with your sight, God with your mind.

Hence faith is precious; for just as grace will no longer be grace

if it is attributed to merits,

so there is no faith unless it believes what it does not see

[Col. 0680D] and follows the eternal reality under the guidance of hope.

[215] Miserable mortals, complaining race, finally strip off your impious hearts and soften your minds.

“Alas, how long, I ask, will you seek falsehoods with a heavy heart

[Col. 0681A] and, foolishly, love slippery things [Note: Psalm IV, 3]?”

Change your paths, break the bonds of death,

[220] and offer your necks free to the exceedingly sweet yoke.

Take up divine chains in place of freedom:

they release from crime and bind through devotion.

You who follow darkness wander in the open light,

and because you see at night, you act blind in the light [Note: That is, in the day.].

[225] Therefore let us open the eyes and ears of our minds to Christ,

so that the mind closed by sin may be open to God.

For all things whose promises God now reveals to bodily sight
and whose hidden things he clearly displays
reflect everywhere the form of resurrection [Note: Prudentius, *Hymn* 10 of the *Cathemerinon*],

[230] in every body, in seeds upon the earth, and in the stars of heaven.

Nights and days, risings and settings, alternate in turn:

[Col. 0681B] I die at night; I rise in the day.

I sleep, lulled by the image of bodily death;

I am awakened from sleep as from destruction.

[235] What of crops, what of the leaves of the woods, what of the seasons?

Surely everything dies and returns according to these laws.

In spring, a new image of resurrection for all things

returns, made alive after winter’s death.

What the human being, to whom the bodies of the world are subject, will do once,
all things beneath heaven frequently do.

But they ask in what body every dead person will be restored [Note: That is, made whole. See line 308.],

or in what manner a human being will come from ashes.

If the things marked out by the sacred prophets are not enough,

silent things proclaim faith: believe what is visible.

[245] [Col. 0681C] See how no seeds emerge from their own fields

unless they first perish, released into corrupt decay [Note: See note 335.].

You sow naked seeds; you reap them clothed [Note: See note 336.]; you cast dry grains,

and reap those same grains multiplied in fruit.

O perverse faith of ours, and our unbelief—

[250] that we trust the earth and doubt God!

Nor has the earth either dared or been able to promise anything with sure assurance,
and often the field has deceived us,

scarcely returning the seeds entrusted to it; yet, deceived,

[675–676] I do not hesitate to believe in the hope of a harvest.

[255] Nor am I reluctant to spend certain labor for uncertain crops,

and to trust naked things to the naked soil.

But if earth can return corrupted seed

(which nevertheless it does by the law of the eternal Lord),

is it believed to be difficult for the Omnipotent to restore us,

[260] [Col. 0681D] made from nothing, from something?

I did not exist, and by God’s making I was born so that I might exist;

now, from my own seed, I shall be again.

For although bones may be reduced to fine ash,

the dust contains the seeds of the complete body.

[265] And even when the earth, emptying the tombs,

has swallowed the ashes mixed with their kindred soil,

[Col. 0682A] then too the Omnipotent preserves what seems to vanish

from human bodily eyes,

and on the great day we shall see the bodies

[270] that we now think have been consumed rise whole for God.

Nothing perishes for him, since whatever exists anywhere

is enclosed in the embrace of the Creator.

Those whom rivers, the sea, and fish have swallowed,

those whom birds and wild beasts have torn apart,

[275] all of them the earth owes to God; for those whom the water submerged,

the earth received, whether on the shore or on the sea floor.

Although it is one earth, it covers, not in one tomb,

the bones of a mangled corpse scattered in different places [Note: That is, “of a body.” See line 41.].

[Col. 0682B] And because both the consumed and the consumer fall together

[280] into the same lap of earth, where death brings them down,

or because, through the discharge by which animals cleanse themselves,

they return the limbs swallowed with digested food,

the human body is transferred through another body,

yet does not lose the power of its own kind.

[285] But although human limbs transferred into the earth through the limbs of beasts

remain safe in living seed,

and when the beast dies, the one that happened to have human flesh as food,

the arrangement is divided.

For a human being is an animal endowed with reason, and therefore

[290] as king he surpasses other animals in bodily form.

[Col. 0682C] Thus, although the same substance may be given as prey

to dumb animals, it refuses to be united with them by chance.

Only that flesh will receive the power of resurrection
which has been the vessel of a rational soul [Note: That is, the body. See line 310.],
[295] so that, in a restored structure, it may receive the soul returning to it,
in a covering no longer destined to fall.

And just as here mind and flesh are joined in every action,

so they will be joined for the eternal day,

so that they may reap, in shared fruit, the rewards of their deeds,

[300] sharing in merit, whether in the place of light or of fire.

Therefore, although we and all breathing creatures

have been allotted one bodily material,

we are not, once released by death,

recalled in vain, deprived of the soul, from flesh’s setting;

[305] but when the trumpet sounds and the earths everywhere return

[Col. 0682D] our bodies from their hidden seeds,

with body, mind, and soul joined again in their covenant,

we are presented whole before God the Lord [Note: See line 241.].

If you doubt that ashes can be gathered back into bodies,

[310] and souls made to return to their vessels [Note: That is, bodies. See line 294.],

“Ezekiel will be your witness; to him long ago

the Lord disclosed the whole form of resurrection.

There you will see throughout the entire field [Note: [Col. 0682D] See Letter 24, no. 18.]
[Col. 0683A] the dry remains of ancient human beings come to life,

[315] and the bones, scattered broadly across the field,

ordered to run of their own accord toward their joints,

and, in their marrow-filled inner parts,

to put forth sinews;

then to draw skin over them, covered with flesh; and, more swiftly than speech, with the limbs completed in order,

[320] new human beings will stand forth from ancient dust [Note: Ezekiel XXXVII.]”

And lest you perhaps think that this is merely a vain vision,

although it is plainly the sacred Prophet’s vision,

receive an even greater and complete witness concerning these things:

for the Lord of the prophets himself speaks:

[325] “I am life; whoever believes in me, though not destroyed by death,

will live blessed in light shared with me [Note: John XI, 25 and 26.]”

Finally, what he said by his word, he proved by his power,

recalling his own human being from the abyss [Note: [Col. 0684D] We have emended the text from the Royal manuscript, and Paulinus likewise has it in Poem 27, line 92. All editors of the editions—and Rosweyde himself—had substituted *erebis*, troubled by the short second syllable in *abysis*; but here that word should not be written with double *ss*. Elsewhere Paulinus similarly says *Eclesia*, with the first syllable short, for *Ecclesia*.].

Although at that time Christ did not give signs only in his body,

[330] when he died victorious upon the cross.

For, when he opened Tartarus as the shaken earth revealed it,

and released Adam, bound in the prison of hell,

“the buried, risen again, broke through the split rocks,

and a new dome (*tholus*) [Note: [Col. 0684D] Schott’s edition, together with Sacchini, has *chorus*; I have not dared to emend it against the authority of the other manuscripts.] flourished in the holy city [Note: Matthew XXVII, 52 and 53.]”

[335] Many saw the renewed bodies of the ancient pious,

brought to life by God’s descent.

Then too the world, blinded by the returning light,

feared to atone for its crime in eternal night.

Then, when the altars were stripped bare after the veil had been shaken aside,

[340] they lost the sanctity of the sacred inner shrine;

so that it might be shown that the temple was to be emptied of divinity,

and that the holy place would become profane through a hostile hand.

This was taught under a Roman leader after the great destruction,

when temple, citizens, city, and sacred rites had been overthrown.

[345] For it was right that Judaea, for whom Christ was not her own victim,

and through whom Christ was a victim,

deprived at once of the seat and place of her ancient rites [Note: That is, “stripped.”],

having denied the faith, should lose every sacred thing.

For Christ is the end of the law: because foretold by the faithful law,

he became, by coming, the law of the law,

[350] prescribing an end to the ancient law and the law of faith [Note: See note 334.],

and establishing a perfect law for the nations.

Hence the Teacher [Note: See Letter 30, no. 5.] says: “The old things have flowed away;

once the ages have been completed, all things new enter everywhere [Note: II Corinthians V, 17.]”

[355] [Col. 0683D] “And now, with face unveiled, we gaze upon the open vision

of God in Christ, in the glory of his own light [Note: II Corinthians III, 18.]”

And I think that the mysteries of the veil torn in the temple

also signified that grace which he bestowed.

For just as the sanctuary became visible when the veil was torn,

[360] so faith opens for us the hidden things of the law.

[Col. 0684A] “Hence Moses is read beneath the ancient veil [Note: Exodus XXXIV, 33.]”

still covered for the Jews by a cloud upon the heart,
which Christ, in whom I believe, removes from the lights of my mind,
dispersing the shadowy appearances.

[365] And he teaches that he himself was veiled in the ancient shadow of the law,

and is now revealed in the face of the body.

Such as the prophets who came before sang that he would be,

such as he appeared before apostolic eyes,

such as the Jews, though seeing, did not perceive,

[370] [679–680] with minds dulled by their own impiety;

and such as, although we have not seen him in the body,

we behold by believing, through inward light.

For what the truthful Teachers testify that they saw

and touched, I touch and see by faith.

[375] And by believing, it is evident that all can know Christ,

who blinds impious hearts through their faithlessness,

and pours his light through faithful hearts,

so that he may dwell in and glorify souls that please him.

Therefore, my brothers, my care, my heart,

[380] gladden your grieving spirits with this faith.

Drive away sadness, teachable ones, through faithful devotion,

and, trusting in God, put on joy.

Unhappy grief and senseless sorrow befit those

for whom no hope remains, because there is no faith.

[385] Alas for me! How foolish it is to trust one’s empty eyes,

to despair of God, and to trust bodily things!

Let inward stupor and an incurable heart possess those

who, abandoning their true senses,

[Col. 0684C] are disowned by a mind faithless toward God, and whose lot,

[390] separated from Christ, falls into infernal darkness.

May the Apostle, the consoler by God’s mouth, be present for us;

may Christ, who loves us, teach us through the Gospel;

may the examples of the fathers and the proclamations of the prophets,

may the book of apostolic history strengthen us [Note: Acts I.],

[395] in which we see Christ bodily go back to the stars
and carried into the heavens in the embrace of a cloud,

and are commanded to hope that he will return from heaven

such as we saw him go to the Father in heaven.

Everything now hangs upon his coming;

[400] every hope and faith gazes eagerly toward this King.

And now, as the end of the final age approaches,

the ages are bringing forth their transformation into new things.

[Col. 0684D] All the true oracles in the sacred books admonish us

to believe what has been foretold and prepare ourselves for God.

[405] Hasten, I beg you, while opportunity is offered here,

to provide for good things and guard against evil.

Turn your perverse cares [Note: See line 196.] with a converted heart;

faith shows that it is useful to weep.

[Col. 0685A] It is beneficial to mourn over sin and wash away

[410] wounds contracted through guilt with abundant tears.

“As he moistened his bed every night

with much groaning, David, strong in humble heart [Note: Psalm VI, 7].”

“If that king beloved by God ate ashes

and mixed his drink with tears [Note: Psalm CI, 10],”

[415] what should I, wretched as I am, do? From where shall I be purified?

How shall I make satisfaction? By what means shall I be saved?

My heart, hard as pumice, needs tears;

it shudders at ashes for food, while delights please a hungry soul.

Who will point out to me a spring for rivers of tears,

[420] [Col. 0685B] with which I may mourn my deeds and my days [Note: Jeremiah IX, 15.]?

For according to the merits of a life spent in crimes,

I must weep rivers of immense wounds.

Break the stone of my heart, Savior Jesus,

so that, softened, my inner parts may flow with a holy spring;

[425] you, Christ, I beg, O fountain, grow within my fibers,

so that a living vein of your water may resound for me.

For you are the fountain from which life flows, from which grace pours,

from which light is spread among all peoples.

“Those who drink you, Christ, refreshed by the sweet stream,

[430] will thirst no longer, and yet they will still thirst [Note: John IV, 13.]”

For those whom the abundance of the divine Word has satisfied,

681–682 Its sweetness makes them thirst still more when they have drunk.

[Col. 0685C] Therefore, O Lord God, may their souls always hunger and thirst for you, the bread and fountain of salvation;

[435] May no fasting hunger, nor parching thirst, consume their life, if the mind eats and drinks you.

Ever-flowing, you are always drunk; and, more lavish than the exhaustion of those who drink, you surpass both crowd and thirst.

For you, Christ, are wholly sweetness, God, and love;

[440] Hence you can fill us ever more, rather than satisfy us.

You flow into greedy desires, always to be thirsted for;

You are received, yet love is never satisfied;

And thus devotion is perfected, so that you may be loved without end,

Christ, who will give your own people life without end.

[445] Grant me now, O God, to mourn, and with saving tears

To sow the seeds of eternal joy;

This I ask; rather, may this mourning remain with me throughout the age

[Col. 0685D] In which whatever exists passes along a brief path.

Go far from me, you joyful ones; I prefer the company of those who weep,

[450] So that through brief tears I may attain lasting joys.

If only, while I mourn, a rough sackcloth garment

Made of goats’ hair will cover and prick me,

Then, when the Father is appeased, the honors I have earned will be restored to me,

And a ring will be given me, and a robe of joy will encircle me;

[455] Then, with good reason, Father, you will slaughter for me a fattened calf,

[Col. 0686A] If only, fasting, I hunger for righteousness.

I prefer to endure hunger for bread rather than hunger for the holy Word;
I want no house of wine; I thirst for the water of light;

Here let dreadful hunger torment me, here let shameful poverty

[460] Besiege me, contracted beneath miserable rags;

Here, though a rich man pass before his own house,

Let him disdain to satisfy me even with his crumbs.

I do not want a garment of silk, glowing with Tyrian purple,

[465] To burn upon me, while my body’s impending destruction is envied;

Lest, after purple robes, everlasting flame

Surround me, and I pay the price of my clothing in fire.

Here rather let us, wretched, lie upon a foul

[Note: [Col. 0686D] I have thought this should be restored from the EDIT. Schot. in the margin. Other manuscripts read *in agmine*; but I do not see what a foul heap of dung would be.],

Heap of dung, and let dogs lick our sores,

So that, released from this sorrowful life by a peaceful death,

[470] A gentle angel may receive us for the coming meeting,

[Col. 0686B] And, rejoicing, set us down in the bosoms of the patriarchs,

Far from the open-mouthed abyss where Gehenna rages.

I do not speak of the frightening fictions of poets that terrify children:

The dog barking at the gates with three muzzles,

[475] Charon terrifying the shades with grim squalor,

The Eumenides, fierce with serpent-entwined hair,

Tityos, the everlasting food of the accursed vulture,

Tantalus, parched with thirst amid the waters,

The wheel turning without end, and the rock rolling back,

[480] And the empty jars of the sweating Danaids.

These things the poets, poor in truth, sang in their vainness,

They who did not hold Christ, the source of truth.

But God taught us the truth, himself the sower of his own works,

Declaring all the truths to us.

[485] [Col. 0686C] Learn from the Gospel the dwelling of the poor man and the dwelling of the rich:

“The poor man lies in Abraham’s bosom; the rich man lies in fire.

When justice reverses their lots, he who had wept here

Rejoices there; and, while the poor man is full, the rich man is in want.

The one enjoys good rest; the other groans amid flames;

[490] The rich man receives punishment for his wealth; the poor man receives wealth.

683–684 The rich man begs the poor man for a little drop,

The man whom he had despised when he was begging above.

Therefore, for the man burning below, not even a small poor man

Dripped a drop of refreshment from his finger,

[495] Because not even a crumb from the rich man’s great banquets

Had fallen into the mouth of the hungry poor man [Note: [Col. 0686D] Luke XVI].”

By these admonitions let us learn to live a holy life in Christ [Note: [Col. 0686D] See poem 26, line 206],

To practice righteousness, and to assign a portion to the poor.

[Col. 0686D] You who find the poor man repulsive, who shudder when you see the needy,

[500] And regard the approach of a devout beggar as an evil omen;

You who marvel at yourself, shining in costly clothing,

And do not see that you are foul in your inward dress—

You carry in your mind everything that horrifies you in the poor man’s body,

[505] Fouler than rags, rich in sores;

You despise touching the blind man and avoid the leper;

Avaricious rich man, you cherish your own leprosy.

He is wretched and weak in the eyes of men; but you

[Col. 0687A] Are vile before God through the weakness of your soul.

Wicked man, you despise the needy person who shares your nature,

[510] And through avarice make him excluded from his portion.

Whatever, unjust man, overflows for you without any useful purpose,

Whatever you hide beneath a dug-up clod, belongs to the poor.

Why do you hold what belongs to another? With what hope do you retain what must be abandoned,

Neither returned to its rightful owners nor possessed by you?

[515] You who find the poor man repulsive, who, though rich in name, witless,

Raise your sad eyebrow with a wrinkled [Note: [Col. 0687D] That is, furrowed.] forehead,

And do not deign even to call “human beings” those

Whom you see not floating in similar luxury—

Look at the form in which that Son of God came:

[520] “Though he was rich, he became poor in the world” [Note: [Col. 0687D] II Corinthians VIII, 9].

[Col. 0687B] “And when he came, God chose not the lofty but the lowly things of the world,

To destroy the strong through the weak” [Note: [Col. 0687D] I Corinthians I, 27].

Let no one now rejoice in wealth as rich, or in strength as powerful,

Nor in great intelligence as wise.

[525] Let no one trust in his own resources [Note: [Col. 0687D] See poem 27, line 468], or applaud himself,

Since everything has been sown or given from God the fountain.

Christ became the refuge and person of the needy;

To the rich he is a disgrace, to the poor a glory.

Let us run after his ambrosial fragrances,

[530] So that the smell of death may flee far from us.

Who will grant me the pouring out of precious nard from alabaster,

And the washing of the Lord’s sacred feet with tears [Note: [Col. 0687D] Luke VII, 38]?

I beg you, my beloved concerns, devote yourselves to devout cares,

[Col. 0687C] And give yourselves, with your whole mind, to union with God.

[535] “The time is at hand; the Lord is already near: hurry to prepare yourselves

For the meeting with the King, while the brief hour remains open” [Note: [Col. 0687D] Romans XIII, 11].

Use your resources with kindly devotion,

And tear out the root of evil from your breasts.

Enclose the price of your life in the hearts of the poor,

[540] And anoint your heads with devout expenditures.

Licking the chaste footprints of the Lord Christ,

Wipe them with your hair [Note: [Col. 0687D] See Letter 23, note 35]; wash them with your eyes.

If your desire is to enjoy the Most High without end,

Act so that the same palace [Note: [Col. 0687D] That is, heaven. See poem 13, line 3] may stand open to you.

[545] For the one whom holy faith, a life ignorant of sin,

And a devout mind have enclosed in a chaste body—

[Col. 0687D] Certain is the faith that he will possess that realm above,

Where the altar of God protects the holy with fire.

“We do not wish, therefore, good brothers, that you should grieve over your pledge [Note: [Col. 0687D] That is, son. See poem 18, line 200]

[550] As those who have no hope;

For if your faith is certain that Christ Jesus

Died and now lives in the citadel of God,

[Col. 0688A] 685–686 So also the Father will bring with Christ, when he returns,

All those who rest in living faith.

[555] For that teacher teaches this in the word of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0688D] Paul. See Letter 30, note 5, and line 353],

Under whose guidance we strive to travel the starry ways:

Those whose life has been completed in Christ

Will have everlasting life with Christ.

And when the chief angel has sounded the sign of the approaching Lord

[560] From the Father’s high seat,

Those who first died in Christ will rise,

Deemed worthy to go to meet God in the clouds” [Note: [Col. 0688D] I Thessalonians IV, 13–16].

And when all shall live again in the flesh in which they lived,

“Not all, with their bodies changed, will be light” [Note: [Col. 0688D] I Corinthians XV, 5].

[565] “For we shall rise again, but we shall not all be changed”—

[Col. 0688B] This will be the distinction among the nations before God.

The bodies even of the profane will rise incorruptible

From their tombs, food for long punishment.

For them life will be to die without end, and death to live in torments,

[570] And, while their flesh endures, to feed their own crosses.

Each sinner will produce his own executioners from his own body,

And will be food for his own worms [Note: [Col. 0688D] See note 338].

But those whom devotion has raised through heavenly action

Will bear the marks of participation with God the King;

[575] And, clothed in divine light, their bodies

Will live forever conformed to Christ the Lord.

“Since this is so, take comfort from these words” [Note: [Col. 0688D] I Thessalonians IV, 17],

And refresh faithful hearts with hope of the truth;

[Col. 0688C] And believe that the common pledge [Note: [Col. 0688D] See line 549] of the Most High,

[580] In the light above, enjoys the milk and honey of the living.

Or Abraham tenderly cherishes him, received into his bosom,

And gentle Eleazar feeds him with the dew of his finger [Note: [Col. 0688D] Luke XVI, 23–24];

Or he is with the children of Bethlehem in paradise,

Whom wicked Herod struck down in his jealousy [Note: [Col. 0688D] Matthew II, 16],

[585] He plays amid fragrant groves and weaves crowns

As rewards to honor the martyrs.

Mixed among such companions, he will accompany the King, the Lamb,

The infant added to the virgin ranks.

Celsus, child, inhabitant of the pure land of the blessed;

[590] Celsus, sorrow to fathers, glory of your fathers;

Celsus, love and longing, and light of your own;

Celsus, a brief grace to us, but a long one to you.

Yet your grace may also live long for us [Note: [Col. 0688D] See line 613 and Letter 29, note 8],

[Col. 0688D] If you remember us before the Lord.

[595] For in you, a little one in years but great in merits,

Life was brief in time, but powerful in devotion.

For God declares that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those

Who were such as you were in mind and faith as children;

Such as that other one of ours was—he who was yours, of blessed

[600] Name, summoned at the time when he was given,

The long-desired offspring, yet not granted to us,

So that we, unworthy, might rejoice in devout posterity.

We believe that he, Celsus, plays with you

As a participant in the eternal green meadows of joy and life,

[605] He whom we entrusted in the city of Complutum,

Joined to the martyrs by the bond of a neighboring tomb [Note: [Col. 0689B] See note 339];

So that from the nearby blood of the saints [Note: [Col. 0689B] See note 340] he may draw

That by which he may cleanse our souls in the fire.

For perhaps one day, even for us sinners,

[610] This little drop of our blood will be light.

Celsus, help your brother, laboring with shared devotion,

So that there may also be a place for us in your rest.

Live as partners; live forever, brothers,

And inhabit together places worthy of joy;

[615] [Col. 0689B] 687–688 And, equal in innocent merits, overcome the sins of your parents,

You infants, by your chaste intercessions [Note: [Col. 0689B] See poem 24, line 293, and poem 1, Appendix, line 74, and note 341].

[Col. 0690A] As many years of life as you had, Celsus, so many days of life

Were drunk in by him; but he is younger, since he is healthier in precedence.

For he is younger in that he lived less; nevertheless, in that he departed first,

[620] He is now your elder there.

Celsus, stand by with your brother and your own people—for we are joined to you;

For we are your blood from our father.

With your father Pneumatius, and likewise with your mother Fidele,

Speak also of your own Paulinus and Therasia,

[625] So that through your common prayers, with Christ showing mercy,

We too, Celsus, may have the protection of you.

Yet it remains for us also to make the effort by which

[Col. 0690B] We may follow you with equal simplicity.

Then we shall be able to live as companions of sweet Celsus [Note: [Col. 0690B] Thus we restore the ancient and most genuine reading from the Belgian and Royal manuscripts and from EDIT. Schot. in the margin. All printed editions read *possimus*. See note 342.],

[630] And to be equal forever to the sweet pledge [Note: [Col. 0690B] See line 613].

## Preface to Saint Paulinus’ Last Poem

[Col. 0689]

[Col. 0689] 689–690 This most distinguished poem of Saint Paulinus follows the thirteenth Nativity in our manuscript. It contains much learning and the customary spirit of the most eloquent poet. It is directed first against the Jews and then against the Gentiles, whose deities, varied philosophy, and many errors it observes.

I believe that this work is certainly indicated in Saint Augustine’s Letter 34 to Paulinus, where he writes:

“I have learned from the brothers that you are writing against the pagans. If we deserve anything from your heart, send it without reserve, so that we may read it; for your heart is such an oracle of the Lord that we confidently expect from it answers both pleasing to us and most fully explanatory of the most talkative questions.”

Perhaps Augustine thought that Paulinus had resolved to overthrow the whole superstition of the Gentiles; but such a plan had not occurred to the sacred poet, who merely wished to explain, not refute, the madness of the pagans. Rumor suggested otherwise to Augustine, so it is not surprising that he says he expects from Paulinus explanations of the most talkative questions.

Certainly, if Paulinus had undertaken to write some outstanding work against the pagans, Gennadius, when reviewing his writings, would have made some mention of it. We must therefore conclude that a small work on this subject was composed by that same saint, of the kind represented by this poem.

Indeed, the time at which this little work was composed also seems to support our conjecture. “In the consulship of Olybrius and Probinus,” Prosper says in his *Chronicle*—that is, in the year of the Lord 395—“Augustine, a disciple of the blessed Ambrose, outstanding in eloquence and learning, was ordained bishop at Hippo Regius in Africa.”

Augustine informs Paulinus of his ordination as something recently accomplished in the same letter cited above, when he says:

“You ought to infer how much care for the Church occupies me from this: the most blessed father Valerius would not allow me to remain merely his presbyter unless he imposed upon me the greater burden of the co-bishopric,” and so forth.

Therefore this letter of Augustine was undoubtedly written either toward the end of 395 or at the beginning of the following year. For, as Chiffletius demonstrates in part 2, chapter 8 of *Paulinus Illustratus*, Augustine’s ordination occurred after the middle of December of that same year, 395.

Thus in this year our Paulinus was fighting against the pagans in writing. He had withdrawn to Nola toward the end of A.D. 394, and there, having hastened the decision of his conversion, had undertaken the most excellent discipline of Christian life.

He touches on this same decision at the beginning of the poem in these words:

“I examined, I confess, all the sects, Antonius;

I sought very much, I ran through each one in turn,

But I found nothing better than to believe in Christ.”

The following verses establish this even more fully:

“All these things I had previously undertaken, when the holy Church,

Having received me—long uncertain and driven by so many storms—

Into the safe harbor of salvation,

After wandering waves, stationed me in a tranquil seat,

So that now, the cloud of evils having been wiped away,

I might hope for clear light at the promised time.”

[Col. 0691] And below:

“May he who has now taken away the error of our mind

Here happily open for us the gates of paradise by a better path.

Our faith is devoted to one sure foundation.”

[Col. 0691] See how Paulinus discloses to us his withdrawal to Nola and the new way of life he had recently chosen for himself.

Therefore, since Paulinus composed these verses at the time when he had devoted his whole mind to Christ and his faith—that is, in A.D. 394 or 395—you see that they fall within the period mentioned above, when Augustine is also said to have learned that Paulinus was writing against the pagans.

Who that Antonius was to whom Paulinus dedicates his poem, I cannot guess. At first sight of the work, I suspected that *Antonius* should be read *Ausonius*, for Paulinus had once been bound to Ausonius by the closest intimacy and had addressed him in not a few poems that still survive.

But the exchange of affection between these two excellent men had long since been interrupted, and our poet would surely have used other words if he had been writing to Ausonius, once his teacher and almost his parent.

I do not doubt that this Antonius was enrolled among the Christians, since David is brought forward to him as an example.

“And lest you dislike my unfolding such poems,

David himself asked for the lyre with tuneful voice,

By whose example we sing small things about great ones.”

Since it is therefore uncertain whether Ausonius embraced the religion of Christ, and since not a few passages in his poems are unbecoming to a Christian poet, I do not think that he is indicated here.

## The Last Poem (C, G)*

[Col. 0691A]

693–694 I examined, I confess, all the sects, Antonius;

I sought very much, I ran through each one in turn;

But I found nothing better than to believe in Christ.

I have arranged to write all this in a gentle verse,

[5] And lest you dislike my unfolding such poems,

David himself asked for the lyre with tuneful voice,

By whose example we sing small things about great ones,

Saying what must be shunned, pursued, and honored,

Although in all things both the matter and the reason may be approved.

[10] At first the Jewish people were not moved even by God’s wondrous grace;
