For although they had then been rescued from wicked Pharaoh,

And had crossed the sea on foot, while a shining pillar

Went before them as guide, who saw the hostile horsemen swallowed up,

[Col. 0691B] And for whom nothing was lacking even in the deserted fields,

For whom manna ran from heaven, and a spring from the rock,

After these things they themselves denied God, who had provided so greatly,

And, while seeking another deity with mad hearts,

Lost the gold which they had cast into the fire.

[Col. 0692A] The pagan likewise worships the stones he has carved,

[20] And makes for himself what he himself ought to fear.

Then he worships images, which he fashions from bronze in such a way

That, whenever he wishes, he can send the fabricated objects into coinage,

Or often transform them into more shameful shapes.

From this he slaughters miserable sheep, and in the warm lungs

[25] 695–696 He seeks the minds of the gods, whom he supposes to be angry,

And begs for human life from the death of an animal.

What pardon does he ask to be forgiven, who seeks forgiveness through blood?

For what sort of thing is that? How foolish? How deserving of condemnation?

When almighty God once formed human beings,

[30] [Col. 0692B] A human being dares to form God. And lest crimes be lacking,

The master even sells this god, and the buyer purchases him.

Should I believe that philosophers possess any reason,

[Col. 0693A] Who lack reason, whose wisdom is vain?

They are Cynics, resembling dogs, as their name reveals.

[35] There are also uncertain followers of Plato’s doctrine,

Whom the substance of the soul, long sought, disturbs,

As they are always discussing it, yet unable to define it;

Hence they delight in describing Plato’s book on the soul,

Which contains nothing certain within it except its title.

[40] There are also the Physicists, so called from nature,

Whom an ancient, crude, and unformed life pleases.

For one of them, once carrying a staff and an earthen vessel,

[Col. 0694A] Thinking that only the staff was useful and only the vessel worth possessing,

The staff as a source of support and the vessel as a means of drinking—

[45] When he saw a farmer standing and drawing water with hollowed hands

For drinking, broke the earthen vessel,

And, throwing it far away, declared that superfluous things should be removed.

697–698 A peasant taught him that he could dispense with that object as well.

These men neither drink wine nor are nourished by bread as food;

[50] They do not recline on a bed, nor ward off the cold with clothing,

And, ungrateful to God, reject what he has provided.

What shall I say of their various sacred rites? Shall I speak of the temples

[Col. 0695A] Established for gods and goddesses? First, what do they wish the Capitoline gods to be?

This god, the god’s wife, and the god’s own sister,

[55] Whom Virgil, their authority, marks by saying: “Both sister and wife.”

More is reported of Jupiter: that he violated his own daughter

And gave her to his brother;

And that, in order to seize other women, he changed his own form into various shapes;

Now he was a serpent, now a bull, now a swan, and now a tree.

[60] [Col. 0696A] By changing himself, he himself reveals what he was;

Another’s form pleased him more than his own.

More shamefully than these, he fashioned himself as an eagle

And entered into the boy’s wicked embraces. What does the crowd of worshipers say?

Let it either deny that he is Jupiter or admit this disgrace.

[65] 699–700 He certainly has a name that cannot be justified by reason.

They perform sacred rites to Jupiter and call him “Jupiter Best and Greatest,”

[Col. 0697A] They petition him, and place Father Janus first in order.

This Janus was a king, a prudent man who made the Janiculum

From his own name; and because he could look upon many things in the future,

[70] The ancients painted him with a double form,

And the old Latins called Janus “two-faced.”

[Col. 0698A] Since he came by ship to the Ausonian shores,

A coin was first struck for him with this honor,

So that one side might display a head and the other might carve a ship.

[75] Remembering this, whatever coins they now mark

701–702 They call “heads” and “ships,” from that ancient event.

[Col. 0699A] What do they expect from Jupiter, who is second after the king,

And who is placed upon the lips of those who pray during sacrifices?

This one also has a mother captured by a shepherd’s love,

For the shepherd existed before Jupiter, or Jupiter himself;

But the shepherd acted more nobly, wishing to preserve his chaste modesty,

And rejecting the goddess, who cruelly cut off his manly parts

So that he might never touch the marriage-bed of another,

Since he had refused to enter hers.

[85] Yet did the just judgment of the gods accomplish this,

That he should not become a husband who had not become an adulterer?

Even now eunuchs lament their shameful mysteries,

And there are men whom these contagions transform;

Within, they worship some secret thing as though it were something greater,

[90] [Col. 0700A] And call it holy; if a chaste man wishes to approach it,

He will be profane. Thus the priest himself more strictly

Avoids intercourse with women but undergoes intercourse with men.

O blind mind of men! The stage of their sacred rites always provokes laughter,

Yet they do not withdraw from this error.

[95] 703–704 They say that Saturn is the father of Jupiter, and that he devoured

His children before him, then later vomited the wicked food from his belly;

But afterward, through his wife’s stratagem, he swallowed a stone

Substituted for Jupiter;

Had she not done so, Jupiter would have been consumed.

[100] They call him Chronos, and fictitiously name him Chronos, because time

Consumes what it creates and promises again what it has consumed.

Why, however, do they contrive a name indirectly in place of time?

They also say that, because he often feared his offspring,

He was cast down from heaven by Jupiter and hid throughout the fields

[105] Of Italy, and that Latium was therefore so called at that time.

Great gods, both of them! One is hidden beneath the earth;

The other could not discover the hiding places of the earth.

Hence the ancient Quirites established the evil of the Latiarian rite,

So that a sacrificed human being might satisfy an empty name.

[110] What darkness of mind is this? What thoughtless hearts?

What they worship is nothing, and bloody rites are performed.

[Col. 0702A] What of the fact that they also conceal the Unconquered One in dark caves,

705–706 And, though they cover him in darkness, dare to call him the Sun?

Who would worship light secretly, or hide the heavenly star,

[115] Unless the cause were evil things in the world below?

What of the fact that they do not conceal the Isiac rattle and the dog’s head any more,

But place them in public places?

I do not know what exactly they seek; they rejoice when they find it,

And then lose it again, so that they may seek it again.

[120] [Col. 0703A] What wise person could tolerate this—that they seem to shut up the Sun,

While these others openly display the monsters of their own gods?

What has Serapis deserved, that he is so mangled by them

Through various and shameful places? At one moment he becomes a beast,

Then a dog, then the shameful corpse of a donkey,

[125] Now a man, now bread, now languid with diseased body.

While they do such things, they confess that he feels nothing.

What shall I say also of Vesta, whom the priest himself denies

Knowing what she is? Yet in the innermost sanctuaries within

[Col. 0704A] They pretend that an inextinguishable fire is always preserved.

[130] Why is she a goddess and not a god? Why is fire said to be female?

This woman, as Hyginus relates,

707–708 Once wove a garment from a new thread,

A garment named from her own name, which she herself gave

To Vulcan, who at that time had shown her how

[135] To guard covered hearths. He, delighted with the gift,

Offered it in turn to the Sun, through whom he had previously discovered

The adultery of Mars. Now every credulous crowd

Hangs garments from the Sun during the Vulcanalia;

And, to mark Venus, Adonis is then also carried;

[140] [Col. 0705A] Then they cast dung, and throw him himself in place of dung.

If you examine everything, it seems even more laughable.

Another thing is added: the maidens whom they call Vestals,

Are said to carry five-yearly meals to a dragon.

Yet he either does not exist, or, if he exists, he is the devil himself,

[145] Previously the enemy and instigator against the human race.

And they venerate him who now, in the name of Christ,

Both trembles and hangs, and confesses all his deeds.

What kind of mind do human beings possess, that they call false things true,

Worship what must be abandoned, and abandon what must be worshiped?

[150] [Col. 0705B] It will now be enough for us to recount their empty terrors.

All these things were mine before. When I attained the clear light, the holy Church

709–710 Received me—long uncertain and driven by so many storms—

Into the safe harbor of salvation,

And, after wandering waves, placed me in a tranquil seat,

[155] So that now, the cloud of evils having been wiped away,

I might hope for clear light at the promised time.

That earlier salvation, which forgetful Adam lost,

[Col. 0706A] Will rise again, rescued from the rocks—

Then under evil’s persuasion, now with Christ as helmsman—

And will remain forever.

[160] For our ruler governs all things in every direction in such a way

That he who has now taken away the error of our mind

May here happily open for us the gates of paradise by a better path.

Our faith is devoted to the one sure God;

For God is one, and the Son is of one substance;

[165] He is one in both: one might, one power.

For Christ, the Word of God, sprang forth from the Father’s breast,

And always existed; he did not come forth as though newly born,

But, proceeding from the mouth, removed that empty chaos,

And took away the shapeless chasm of woven night,

[170] Distributed the sea, lands, air, and heaven among their places,

And gave them a double light when the darkness had been driven away.

But when all things marveled at the new Sun rising,

[Col. 0706B] These four drew their beginnings from various elements.

There are human beings on earth; stars have been added to heaven;

[175] A bird hangs in the air; a fish swims in the liquid sea.

Thus he adorned each element with its own forms,

Bound them together, although diverse, and joined what was distinct;

And he separated what had been joined, though now divided things cohere.

For Ocean encloses the earth; the sea is enclosed; the air itself

[180] Is enclosed in the middle beneath the heavenly axis.

This heaven also, which we see high above,

[Col. 0707A] Is below six others, rising at equal intervals,

And beyond the seven thrones, beyond so many heavenly kingdoms,

There is the remaining region, which rises above everything,

[185] Which surpasses the heights, which stretches everywhere upward,

Which extends without end, which no mind can encompass:

It is the dwelling of inaccessible light, the seat of the mighty

Holy God, from which he sees from afar the things he made subject to him.

711–712 Thus all things remain established, while the Spirit surrounds all things—

[190] These same things whose use has been granted to us,

Which the lower vault of heaven encompasses with its great circuit.

Although all things are distant from one another, they are held together in peace.

Finally, they have one name: together they are the world.

The Greeks of old also called this *cosmos*;

[195] [Col. 0707B] Hence, distinguishing the two languages in this way,

He called it *cosmos* from adornment, and “world” from light.

For wherever the sun shines, the whole had been lying in shadow,

And it remains an example whenever night befouls everything,

Teaching what grace of light has been given out of darkness.

[200] He who made all these good things, who thus works everywhere,

[Col. 0708A] Is God from the heart of God, the Spirit from his mouth,

The holy speech of the Father, the maker of so many things.

Let no pagan boast if he avoids idols

And thinks it sufficient to believe in one divine power.

[205] What will that man worship as God, who does not worship his Word?

Who does not venerate his Power with equal honor?

And whoever confesses that God is invisible and incomprehensible—

If he also considers Christ, he will find the same to be true,

Since no one can comprehend the Word,

[210] No one can see him; only his works are visible.

In the Father the Son, and in the Son the Father, made all things,

And whatever he gave through power, he protects through devotion.

Thus the Savior was and will remain throughout the ages,

[Col. 0708B] He who removed errors, who made the truth visible,

[215] And, having appeased the Father, restored the perishing world.

Nor is it surprising that he governs all things, since he created all things,

Who gave everything from nothing, and preferred light to darkness,

And ordered day to follow night;

And, because he was in the flesh, forgives the sins of the flesh.

[220] [Col. 0709A] For he sees frail humanity readily falling,

Yet, reproving it, he will grant one pardon to all.

(I shall speak of a new thing, nor will I regret having said it:)

He will be more merciful than just. For if, finally, he wishes

[225] To be just, no one will escape punishment without guilt;

For the just one condemns evil, but the merciful one forgives everything.

He does this so that the gifts of the coming life may stand firm,

713–714 And that what guilt took away, indulgence may restore.

If these things are not granted to the people who ask,

Then scarcely anyone will be free from every offense

[230] Who could, having earned it, attain the promised light.

Then it will be possible to touch the kingdoms of heaven in joy;

Then death itself will be able to die, when for all time

[Col. 0709B] Everlasting life shall exist, because then in the blessed seat

There is no place for sin, where there is no desire.

[235] Such great glory remains reserved for the faithful people.

He grants still more and gives this greater gift as well:

[Col. 0710A] That the sinner who repents, though previously fallen,

Is not counted among the multitude of sinners;

For punishment is sufficient when his own guilt causes him sorrow;

[240] Fear is his proper penalty; he endures tortures

As though he were already suffering what he confesses he deserved.

What could be better, or what could be more restrained?

He judges, investigates, chastises, spares, and honors—

He who overcomes all things and is not overcome even by anger itself.

[245] We already see that this is true of the present, and it will be true of the future;

For when he often gathers threatening, terrifying clouds,

And flashes with excessive fire in holy terror,

And thunders with mournful rains and black clouds,

Every race fears destruction; but the power of life

[250] Will cease, and at the same time heaven and minds will grow clear.

This too he commands us to hope for—the one who now proves

[Col. 0710B] That he can destroy all things, if he refuses to wish to destroy them.

Thus salvation to be renewed is shown in the age to come,

And the eternal mercy of the eternal God will remain.

[Col. 0709] 715–716 After these distinguished poems of Saint Paulinus, it would have been pleasing to append a certain hymn which two ancient manuscripts of the Ambrosian Library affirm was composed by that same most holy poet in praise of Saint Ambrose. Its beginning is:

“Sing, all peoples,

A praiseworthy miracle,

Which was given to the Church

Tossed about in the world.”

That hymn, however, is the very one still used by the Ambrosian Church, and which is read in its Breviaries, polished and restored through recent editorial effort.

Yet since the hymn contains a great deal of barbarous diction and pays no regard to meter, it is utterly clear that it not only differs from the style of our Paulinus but was plainly a lowly product of a later age.

It is indeed established, on the testimony of Gennadius, that Paulinus composed a hymn-book; but this work was intercepted by the most devouring passage of time, and every educated person will easily recognize that this little work is not a fragment of it.

I therefore append dissertations, which I have worked out to the best of my ability so that greater light might shine upon Paulinus’ poems.

Some of them will be dedicated to the most learned men. I have thought they should be distributed according to the order of the poems under discussion, without making any selection among those distinguished men.

Would that this kind of labor be received by the most humane readers with an even and grateful spirit! Then I too shall rejoice over the plan I have undertaken, and my mind will be summoned to undertake greater things in the future.

[Note: [Col. 0691B]

Verse 1. *Antonius.* Who can tell me whom Paulinus is addressing here? Vossius demonstrates in book IV, chapter 5 of *The Art of Grammar* that the nominative was used for the vocative by the ancients.

[Col. 0691B] Verse 13. *Who saw them swallowed.* Unless Paulinus has used poetic license, something is lacking from the meter. Perhaps *mersos* should be read instead of *mergi*.

[Col. 0691B] Verse 15. *And a spring.* Here too the verse is somewhat defective. I would write:

“Manna for whom came from heaven, for whom a spring …”

[Col. 0691B] Verse 21. *He fashions from bronze.* Tertullian, in his *Apology*, chapter 13, made the same accusation against the pagans:

“You treat your household gods, whom you call Lares, with household authority, pledging them as security, changing them sometimes into a cooking pot from Saturn, sometimes into a ladle from Minerva, according to how each has been worn down and battered, as each master has discovered the holiest one through household necessity. You likewise defile the public gods by public law, whom you hold as taxable property in the auction hall. If the Capitol or the vegetable market is sought, under the same crier’s proclamation, under the same spear, under the same notation of the quaestor, the divinity is assigned and leased.”

The cooking pot mentioned by Tertullian, which was a vessel for filth, is modestly indicated by Paulinus in these words:

“Or often transform them into more shameful shapes.”

[Col. 0692B] Verse 24. *And the minds of the gods.* The Gentiles foolishly sought the minds of the gods in the entrails of slaughtered animals. Ovid, book V of the *Metamorphoses*:

“Even the diseased fiber had disclosed signs of truth

And the gods’ warnings.”

Seneca, himself a pagan, also condemned this same error. *Natural Questions*, book II:

“You make God excessively idle, and a servant of petty matters, if you arrange dreams for some and entrails for others,” and so forth. Consult J. Caesar Bulenger, *On Magic*, etc.

[Col. 0692B] Verse 31. *He even sells.* To this belong again the passages we recently cited from Tertullian. Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religion*, chapter 16:

“God was sold so that he might benefit the buyer, and the buyer humbly worshiped whatever he had shortly before seen put up for auction.”

[Col. 0692C] Verse 32. *Should I believe that philosophers.* Saint Eucherius wrote elegantly on this subject in the *Exhortation to Valerian*. Among other things he says:

“It will quickly become clear to you how much our teachings—that is, the teachings of devotion and truth—ought to be preferred to those teachings of the philosophers. In theirs, virtue is either only sketched or wisdom is false; in ours, completed righteousness and solid truth are contained. Hence it is permissible to say that others have appropriated the name of philosophy, while we possess the life. For what sort of teachings about living can they give? They do not know the cause,” and so forth.

[Col. 0693A] Verse 34. *They are Cynics.* These philosophers were commonly called *κυνικοί* (*kynikoi*), that is, “canine,” *ἀπὸ τοῦ κυνός* (*apo tou kynos*), “from a dog.” Diogenes Laertius says the following in the Life of Antisthenes:

“Κατῆρξε πρῶτος τοῦ κυνισμοῦ”—“He first established the Cynic sect, and was its leader.”

Hence Ausonius sings of him:

“I was the first inventor of Cynicism. What is this reasoning?

Alcides is said to have preceded me by much.

Once I was second, with Alcides as my teacher;

Now I am first in Cynicism, and he is that god.”]

Laertius himself, in the Preface, asserts that the Cynics were so called from their disgraceful behavior: “And from mockery, as the Cynics [are so called].” Suetonius, in his *Life of Vespasian*, says that when Demetrius the Cynic met him on the road after his condemnation, and did not deign either to rise or to greet him, even barking something or other, Vespasian was content to call him a dog. Augustine also writes elegantly on this subject in *The City of God*, book XIV, chapter 20: “Those dog-like philosophers—that is, Cynics—failed to see this: in bringing forward arguments against human modesty, what else did they produce but a dog-like, that is, an unclean, doctrine?”

[Col. 0693B] **Verse 35. “Following uncertain [doctrines].”** Plato adhered to Socrates, and for that reason Laertius ranks him among the Socratics in the Preface. But when he had “established the ancient Academy” (*Τὴν ἀρχαίαν Ἀκαδημίαν συστησάμενος*), he laid the foundations of a new sect. Hence the sect of the Platonists. Strictly speaking, however, these men were called Academics. Laertius, in his *Life of Plato*, says: “He was buried in the Academy, where he had spent most of his time philosophizing; hence the sect that proceeded from him was called Academic” (*Ἐτάφη ἐν τῇ Ἀκαδημίᾳ, ἔνθα τὸν πλεῖστον χρόνον διετέλεσε φιλοσοφῶν, ὅθεν καὶ Ἀκαδημαϊκὴ προσηγορεύθη ἡ παρ’ αὐτοῦ αἵρεσις*). Augustine, *The City of God*, book VIII, chapter 12: “When Speusippus, Plato’s sister’s son, and Xenocrates succeeded him in his school, which was called the Academy, both they and their successors were for that reason called Academics. Later, however, the most distinguished philosophers, who chose to follow Plato, did not wish to be called Peripatetics or Academics, but Platonists.”

[Col. 0693C] **Verse 35. “The uncertain doctrine.”** Prudentius writes in the *Apotheosis*:

> Consult the ravings of bearded Plato,  
> Consult also the shaggy Cynics whom he imagines, and the sinews  
> Which Aristotle has woven with a twisted whirl.

[Col. 0693C] **Verse 36. “Long sought by the soul.”** The verse is somewhat defective. I would write:

> Whom the substance long sought by the soul troubles.

[Col. 0693D] **Verse 39. “Who, beyond the title.”** Plato’s book is certainly an excellent and most celebrated one, in which he discusses the immortality of the soul. But if it is compared with the assertions of the Christians and the most certain proofs of our faith, it contains nothing certain within it. For a pagan, situated so far from true religion, it was a great marvel of wisdom not to put forward an entirely laughable opinion concerning the soul’s continued existence. Yet how many errors he made in this matter is not for me to investigate here; I merely point out that much of what is said there is advanced uncertainly. The most learned writer Theodoret, in his fifth discourse against the Greeks, examines Plato’s opinion with great acuteness and repeatedly finds it wavering. He further adds:

> “And although the very wise Plato, after discussing at length the immortality of the soul” (*Καὶ ὁ μὲν σοφώτατος Πλάτων περὶ τῆς ἀθανασίας τῆς ψυχῆς παμπόλλους λόγους διεξελθὼν*), “did not persuade even Aristotle, his student, to accept this position” (*οὐδ’ Ἀριστοτέλη τὸν φοιτητὴν ἔπεισε τόνδε στέρξαι τὸν ὅρον*).

Acciaiolus translates it thus: “Plato, indeed, the wisest of men, who discussed the immortality of the soul in many discourses, did not persuade even Aristotle, his pupil, to accept that position.”

[Col. 0694B] **Verse 40. “There are also physicists.”** *Physis* (*φύσις*) is the Greek word for “nature” in Latin. Hence *physicists*, or natural philosophers. Laertius, in the Preface, says: “And those who dealt with nature were called physicists” (*Καὶ οἱ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς περὶ φύσιν πραγματείας φυσικοὶ προσηγορεύθησαν*). Others too were called physicists because they wrote about the nature of things.

[Col. 0694B] **Verse 42. “For one of them, a staff.”** Laertius, in the *Life of Diogenes*, says: “Once, seeing a boy drinking with his hands, he threw the cup out of his wallet” (*Θεασάμενός ποτε παιδίον ταῖς χερσὶ πῖνον, ἐξέρριψε τῆς πήρας τὴν κοτύλην*). “Once Diogenes saw a boy drinking from his hollowed hand and threw away the cup taken from his wallet.” The entire company of writers assigns this deed to Diogenes, especially Seneca in letter 90 and St. Jerome in book II *Against Jovinian*, who agree with Paulinus that it was not a boy, as Laertius says, but a peasant who was Diogenes’ teacher. Since this man had been a pupil of Antisthenes, the leader of the Cynics, and since, as a follower of Cynic philosophy, he deserved above all others the name “Cynic,” I am certainly surprised that Paulinus, expressly distinguishing the Cynics from the physicists, later attributes this deed of Diogenes to one of the physicists.

Nor should anyone reply that the ancients practiced philosophy in three divisions, and that consequently physics, being one of the three, also belonged to the Cynics. For the Cynics rejected this part of philosophy and devoted themselves exclusively to ethics. These are Laertius’ words concerning Menedemus: “They are therefore content to remove logic and natural philosophy, and to devote their attention solely to ethics” (*Ἀρέσκει οὖν αὐτοῖς [κυνικοῖς] τὸν λογικὸν, καὶ τὸν φυσικὸν τόπον περιαιρεῖν, μόνῳ δὲ προσέχειν τῷ ἠθικῷ*). What Paulinus adds, however, applies altogether to the Cynics, not to the physicists.

[Col. 0694C] **Verse 49. “They drink no wine.”** Laertius explicitly records this about the Cynics in the *Life of Menedemus the Cynic*: “Some of them use even herbs and altogether cold water” (*Ἔνιοί τε γοῦν καὶ βοτάνοις, καὶ παντάπασιν ὕδασι χρῶνται*). Most also use herbs and cold water. And concerning Diogenes, in his *Life*, he says: “At home he taught people to serve food, being content with simple fare, and to drink water” (*Ἐν οἴκῳ τε ἐδίδασκε διακονεῖσθαι λιτῇ τροφῇ χρωμένους, καὶ ὕδωρ πίνειν*).

[Col. 0694D] **Verse 50. “Nor do they recline on a bed.”** The famous tub of Diogenes the Cynic is still known, in which that philosopher reclined day and night. Other Cynics imitated him. Chresolius, in *Mystagogy*, book IV, chapter 20, section 3, says of them: “For the sake of utterly empty glory, the Cynics slept on grassy couches or on the bare ground, so that by this harshness of life and affected endurance they might turn everyone’s eyes upon themselves.” They too therefore used to lie upon a cloak spread beneath them, as Martial suggests when speaking of a Cynic in book IV, epigram 52:

> Whom the *abolla*, the wife of a naked couch, covers.

A coarse cloak was called an *abolla*.

[Col. 0694D] **Verse 50. “Nor cold.”** The Cynics lacked clothing suitable for warding off the cold; for, being without a tunic, they used only a cloak. St. Cyprian rebukes their shameless display of an exposed and almost naked chest. See Augustine, book XIV of *The City of God*, chapter 20.

[Col. 0694D] **Verse 51. “And ungrateful to God.”** Seneca rightly says in *On the Shortness of Life*, chapter 14, that the Cynics went beyond human nature. So many bodily hardships sought by these philosophers were miracles of arrogance rather than of true wisdom. Diogenes once declared that he was trampling on Plato’s pride; Plato replied, “Yes—but with another kind of pride.” Tatian the Assyrian should be consulted on this subject in his elegant *Address against the Greeks*.

[Col. 0695B] **Verse 53. “What the Capitolia are.”** Since the passage is mutilated and without punctuation (as the entire manuscript lacks punctuation), it is not easily disentangled. I would nevertheless add *est* twice and punctuate it as follows:

> What are the Capitolia? First:  
> For these there is a god, and a god’s wife, and they wish  
> Her herself to be his sister.

[Col. 0695B] **Verse 54. “And her own sister.”** Virgil, whom Paulinus cites here in book I of the *Aeneid*, introduces Juno speaking of herself as follows:

> But I, who walk as queen of the gods,  
> Both sister and wife of Jupiter.

Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 1 against Julian*: “Juno, sister and wife of great Jupiter” (*Ἥρα τοῦ μεγάλου Διὸς ἀδελφὴ, καὶ ὁμόζυγος*). Augustine reproaches the pagans for this shamelessness in book IV, chapter 10, of *The City of God*. Minucius likewise says: “You worship incestuous gods joined to their mother, daughter, and sister.”

[Col. 0695B] **Verse 55. “Vergilius.”** Thus the manuscript reads. Politianus, in *Miscellanies*, epistle 2, chapter 77, and book V, epistle 3, proves by clear testimony that *Vergilius*, not *Virgilius*, ought to be written. Many inscriptions and very ancient books likewise have this form. Caelius Rhodiginus, book VII of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 4, and Manutius in his *Orthography*, citing other examples, defend the contrary opinion. Their arguments should be reviewed in Dausquius’ *Orthography*, where *Virgilius* sounds more correct.

[Col. 0695C] **Verse 57. “To have violated his daughter.”** Everyone will acknowledge that no other woman than Proserpina is meant here—Jupiter’s daughter by Ceres—for she was afterward given in marriage to Pluto. But who asserted that Jupiter violated her? Eusebius of Caesarea, book II of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, says:

> “Ceres gives birth and the daughter is brought up; then Jupiter, her begetter, again has intercourse with Proserpina, his own daughter, after her mother Ceres, having forgotten his former crime; and he has intercourse with her after taking the form of a serpent” (*Κυεῖ μὲν ἡ Δημήτηρ, ἀνατρέφεται δὲ ἡ κόρη· μίγνυται δ’ αὖθις ὁ γεννήσας οὑτοσὶ Ζεὺς τῇ Φερεφάττῃ τῇ ἰδίᾳ θυγατρὶ, μετὰ τὴν μητέρα Δηὼ, ἐκλαθόμενος τοῦ προτέου μύσους, καὶ μίγνυται δράκων γενόμενος*).

That is: “Ceres gave birth, and the daughter was brought up; then Jupiter, who had begotten her, after her mother Ceres, again had intercourse with Proserpina, his own daughter, forgetting his former crime, and, having taken the form of a serpent, violated her.” Eusebius drew this account, in nearly the same words, from Clement of Alexandria in his *Exhortation to the Gentiles*. To this you may add Arnobius, who treats the matter at length in book V *Against the Gentiles*.

This passage sheds light on a passage of Ovid in book VI of the *Metamorphoses*. In reviewing Jupiter’s adulteries, he says:

> How golden fire deceived Danaë and the daughter of Asopus,  
> A shepherd Mnemosyne, and a many-shaped serpent Deois.

Here *Deois* is Proserpina, Ceres’ daughter by Jupiter. For Ceres is called *Dēō* in Greek, from *dēō*, “I find,” and from this the patronymic name *Deois* was transferred to Proserpina. Orpheus—or whoever the author may have been—says that Liber was born from this abominable intercourse, and Diodorus Siculus agrees with him in book III of his *Historical Library*.

[Col. 0695D] **Verse 59. “Now a serpent.”** Jupiter assumed the form of a serpent when, as we have just seen, he had intercourse with Proserpina; that of a bull when he carried off Europa; that of a swan when he deceived Leda; and finally that of a tree—unless perhaps *aurum* (“gold”) should be read here for *arbos* (“tree”)—when the abominable adulterer lay with some other woman. Ovid expresses these and other transformations in book VI of the *Metamorphoses*:

> He made Leda recline beneath swanlike wings;  
> When, concealed in the image of a beautiful satyr,  
> Jupiter filled fair Antiope with twin offspring;  
> He became Amphitryon when he possessed you, Tirynthian woman;  
> How golden fire deceived Danaë and the daughter of Asopus,  
> A shepherd Mnemosyne, and a many-shaped serpent Deois.

A certain Greek poet also playfully expressed these matters in two verses:

> Zeus became a swan, a bull, a satyr, gold, for love  
> Of Leda, Europa, Antiope, and Danaë.

Nazianzenus also wittily mocks Jupiter’s shamelessness in *Oration 1 against Julian*: “Jupiter becomes everything through impurity and uncleanness” (*Τὰ πάντα γίνεται δι’ ἀσέλγειαν καὶ ἀκαθαρσίαν ὁ Ζεύς*). Consult Arnobius, Lactantius, Clement, and other very ancient Fathers for more on this subject.

[Col. 0696B] **Verse 62. “More shamefully than these, an eagle.”** In the form of an eagle, Jupiter carried off Ganymede. Virgil says of this in book III of the *Aeneid*:

> Whom the winged bearer of Jupiter  
> Carried aloft from Ida in his hooked talons.

Some, however, make Jupiter himself, transformed into an eagle, the author of this abduction. There is a Greek verse:

> “Zeus came as an eagle against godlike Ganymede” (*Ἀιετὸς ὁ Ζεὺς ἦλθεν ἐπ’ ἀντίθεον Γανυμήδην*).

“Jupiter, having become an eagle, flew to beautiful Ganymede.” Ovid likewise says in book X of the *Metamorphoses*:

> The king of the gods once burned with love for Phrygian Ganymede,  
> And found something that Jupiter would rather be  
> Than what he was. Yet he deigned to become no bird  
> Except one that carries his thunderbolts to earth.

This is the meaning of our Paulinus in this passage.

[Col. 0696C] **Verse 64. “Or deny that he is Jupiter.”** St. Justin Martyr, in his *First Apology*, which has until now been regarded as the second, speaks as follows:

> “Let such a thought concerning the gods be far from a self-controlled soul: namely, that Jupiter himself, whom they regard as the ruler and begetter of all things, was a parricide and the son of such a father, and, overcome by love and by the pleasure of wicked and shameful desires, went to Ganymede and to the many women who had been violated in adultery” (*Ἀπείη δὲ σωφρονούσης ψυχῆς ἔννοια τοιαύτη περὶ θεῶν, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν ἡγεμόνα καὶ γενήτορα πάντων κατ’ αὐτοὺς Δία, πατροφόντην, καὶ πατρὸς τοιούτου γεγονέναι, ἔρωτί τε κακῶν καὶ αἰσχρῶν ἡδονῶν ἥττων γενόμενον, ἐπὶ Γανυμήδην, καὶ τὰς πολλὰς μοιχευθείσας γυναῖκας ἐλθεῖν*).

Lactantius, after mentioning the rape of Ganymede, adds: “Let us see whether he who did this is the greatest; certainly he is not the best.” See also Augustine, book VII, chapter 9, of *The City of God*, and Arnobius, book III *Against the Gentiles*.

[Col. 0696D] **Verse 65. “He certainly bears the name.”** Since Jupiter has so many acts of disgrace—being one who assaults whole families with his violations—and since the pagans often regard Jupiter as their enemy without cause, Paulinus says that the name *Jupiter* is wholly unfitting for this god. Or, as Lactantius explains in book I, chapter 11, of the *Divine Institutes*: “Cicero interprets Jupiter and Juno as having been named from *juvare*, ‘to help,’ and Jupiter is called as it were ‘helping father.’ This name is utterly inappropriate to God, because helping belongs to a human being who contributes some assistance to one who is alien to him and receives a small benefit.” He then proceeds to show how little this designation suits the supreme God.

[Col. 0696D] **Verse 66. “And Jupiter Best.”** Pliny says in the *Panegyric*: “He is worshiped under the name first of Best, then of Greatest, as the father of men and gods.” This was Jupiter’s principal title, and it occurs very frequently among ancient writers. Lactantius is relevant to our subject in book I of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 10, where he says: “What of all these matters is the father Jupiter, who in the solemn prayer is called Best and Greatest?” And below: “Let us see whether he who did these things is the greatest; certainly he is not the best.” Arnobius likewise says in book I *Against the Gentiles*: “Since Jupiter is regarded by you as both Best and Greatest.”

[Col. 0697B] **Verse 67. “Father Janus.”** As Brissonius teaches in book I of *Legal Formulas*, the ancients began their prayers with Janus. Martial, speaking of this deity in book X, epigram 28, writes:

> Most beautiful sower of the years and of the shining world,  
> Whom public vows and prayers name first.

Aurelius Victor, in his *Brief History of Rome*, says: “In every sacrifice they gave Janus the first place, to such an extent that even when sacrifice was offered to other gods, after incense had been placed upon the altars, Janus was named first, with the title ‘Father’ added.” Paulus, the abbreviator of Festus, under the word *Chaos*, says: “Hence Janus is named with the aspiration removed, because he was the first of all, the first to whom supplication was made.” Arnobius, speaking of him in book III, says: “And thus, according to you, he is believed to be a god, whom you place before all others in your prayers.” Hence Ovid, book X of the *Fasti*:

> Why, although I appease the powers of other gods,  
> Do I first bring incense and wine to you, Janus?

Consult Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 9; Horace, book I, epistle 16; Servius on book VII of the *Aeneid*; and others.

[Col. 0697B] **Verse 69. “The Janiculum.”** Cyprian, speaking of Saturn in his book *On the Vanity of Idols*, says: “When Saturn had been driven out, Janus received him as a guest; from his name the Janiculum was called.” Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 2; Arnobius, book I; and Augustine, book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 4, assert the same. Virgil likewise says in book VIII:

> This citadel Janus the Father, this one Saturn founded;  
> The former was called Janiculum, the latter Saturnia.

Minucius says: “Therefore, because his hiding place had been safely concealed, he preferred it to be called Latium; and the city Saturnia, from his own name, and the Janiculum, Janus, each left to posterity as a memorial.” I am surprised that Dionysius of Halicarnassus, otherwise such an accurate writer of Roman antiquities, recorded that it was founded by Romulus, son of Aeneas and brother of Ascanius and Remus: “A city named Aeneia after its father, which was later called the Janiculum” (*Αἰνείαν πόλιν ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς, τὴν ὕστερον κληθεῖσαν Ἰάνικλον*).

[Col. 0697C] **Verse 69. “Who, since he knew many things to come.”** This too is the opinion of others, who assert that Janus was represented with two faces because he looked toward the past and foresaw the future. Ovid in book I of the *Fasti*, Macrobius in book I of the *Saturnalia*, Augustine in book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, and others devised different explanations, which will be available to anyone wishing to review them in their books. Macrobius, however, in the book just mentioned, especially chapter 7, supports Paulinus.

[Col. 0697D] **Verse 71. “Two-faced Janus.”** Numa was the first of all to dedicate the temple of Janus Geminus. Velleius, book II, calls him this: “Closed Janus Geminus gave evidence of assured peace.” Pliny, book XXXIV, chapter 7: “Moreover, Janus Geminus was dedicated by King Numa.” The same writer, book XXXIII, chapter 2, says: “The mark of bronze was, on one side, Janus Geminus, and on the other, a ship’s beak.” Paulinus’ following verses refer to this. See also Varro, book IV of *The Latin Language*; Suetonius, *Life of Nero*, chapter 14; and Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 9.

[Col. 0697D] **Verse 73. “A coin bears this.”** Plutarch writes on this subject in the *Roman Questions*: “Why does the ancient coin have on one side the two-faced image of Janus and on the other the engraved stern or prow of a ship? Is it, as most people say, in honor of Saturn, who crossed over to Italy by ship?” (*Διατί τὸ παλαιὸν νόμισμα πῆ μὲν εἶχεν Ἰάνου διπρόσωπον εἰκόνα, πῆ δὲ πλοίου πρύμναν, ἢ πρώραν ἐγκεχαραγμένην; πότερον [ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ λέγουσιν] ἐπὶ τιμῇ Κρόνου πλοιῳ διαπεράσαντος εἰς Ἰταλίαν*).

That is: “Why does the ancient coin have on one side the image of two-faced Janus, and on the other an engraved ship, either its prow or its stern? Is this, as the common opinion holds, done in honor of Saturn, who crossed to Italy in a ship?” Plutarch himself says that this explanation is not altogether satisfactory; nevertheless, highly respected authors accepted it. Ovid, in book I of the *Fasti*, addresses Janus in these words:

> But why is one side marked with a ship on bronze,  
> While the other bears a two-faced form?

Janus replies:

> The reason for the ship remains. By ship the sickle-bearing god  
> Came into the Tuscan river, after wandering through the world.  
> But grateful posterity fashioned the stern in bronze,  
> Bearing witness to the arrival of the guest-god.

Paulinus, however, seems to disagree with others here, since he attributes the arrival in Italy to Janus himself, whereas others refer it to Saturn. Athenaeus, in book XV of the *Deipnosophists*, asserts that such coins were used not only in Italy but also in Greece. He says: “Many cities throughout Greece, and those in Italy and Sicily, engrave upon their coins a two-headed face, and on the other side either a raft, a wreath, or a ship” (*Τὰς κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα πολλὰς πόλεις, καὶ τὰς κατὰ τὴν Ἰταλίαν, Σικελίαν, ἐπὶ τοῦ νομίσματος ἐγχαράττειν πρόσωπον δικέφαλον, καὶ ἐκ θατέρου μέρους ἢ σχεδίαν, ἢ στέφανον, ἢ πλοῖον*).

Coins of this kind are still seen among collectors of antiquities, especially in the possession of the most distinguished man, the Count of the Holy Roman Empire Francesco Mediobarbo Birago, who owned a very extensive treasury of numismatic material and in past years published a highly praised work on imperial coins, by which he wonderfully enlarged Occo’s work. But alas for our misfortune! This most learned man was taken from the living in the present year and left learned men greatly desiring his presence.

[Col. 0698C] **Verse 75. “Nomismata.”** The forms *numisma* and *nomisma* are both used. The first occurs in Horace, book II, epistle 1, and in Martial, book I, epigram 40. The second occurs in ancient glosses and in the most distinguished authors. Certainly it conforms better to Greek orthography, which has *nómisma* (*νόμισμα*).

[Col. 0698C] **Verse 76. “These heads and ship.”** Among Italian boys there is a game called *giocare a testa o arma* (“to play heads or arms”), or *a testa o croce* (“heads or cross”), and among the French *jouer à croix ou pile* (“to play cross or pile”). It is the same game as that played among the ancients. Here is an authority. Aurelius Victor—or whoever the author of the book may be—in *On the Origin of the Roman People* says: “Janus is also said to have shown the practice of marking bronze and striking it into the form of coin, on which his head was impressed on one side and a ship on the other, the ship in which he had arrived there.” Thus this author agrees with Paulinus concerning Janus’ arrival. He adds: “Hence gamblers, after placing down a coin and covering it, give their fellow players the choice of declaring what they think lies beneath it, a head or a ship; which the common usage of the present day corruptly calls *naviandi*. Correct this word *naviandi* and restore *navia*.”

Macrobius agrees in book I, chapter 7, of the *Saturnalia*: “When Janus first marked bronze, he also preserved reverence for Saturn in this respect: since Saturn had been brought there by ship, on one side the likeness of his head was represented, and on the other a ship. That bronze was marked in this way is still understood in the game of chance, when boys toss coins into the air and shout ‘heads’ or ‘ship,’ in a game that bears witness to antiquity.”

Andreas Schottus says that *naviam*, not *navim*, is read in full in four manuscripts of Pithaeus. I would rather read *navia* or *navium*, since the meter of Paulinus’ verse unshakably requires it. Certainly Joannes Isaac Pontanus read *navia* in the 1597 edition of Macrobius.

[Col. 0699B] **Verse 77. “Second after the king.”** Saturn reigned before his son Jupiter. Afterward, when he was expelled by his son, he left him the reins of either the heavenly or the earthly kingdom. Lactantius, book I, chapter 11, of the *Divine Institutes*, says: “I see that one god was king in the earliest times and another in later times. It may therefore happen that there will later be yet another. But divine rule is either always unchangeable, or, if it is changeable—which cannot be the case—it is always changeable.” Hence the reign and golden age of Saturn are attributed to Saturn’s rule.

[Col. 0699B] **Verse 78. “And he who is approached with sacrifices.”** He repeats what he had indicated above: namely, that the prayers and vows of the pagans began with an invocation of Janus and then turned to Jupiter—something that certainly never suited the greatest of the gods and ruler of all.

[Col. 0699B] **Verse 79. “Here he also has a mother.”** Rhea, or Cybele, the mother of Jupiter, fell in love with the shepherd Attis. He, unwilling to listen to the shameless goddess, was castrated. Ovid says of this in book IV of the *Fasti*:

> The Phrygian boy, remarkable for his beauty in the deep forests,  
> Joined the tower-crowned goddess in chaste love.

Minucius, in the *Octavius*, reproaches the pagans for this deed of the goddess: “It is shameful to speak of Cybele of Dindyma, who, because she was herself deformed and old—as the mother of many gods—and could not entice her adulterer, whom she had unfortunately favored, into intercourse, mutilated him, so as to make him, of course, a eunuch.” Augustine, book VI, chapter 7, of *The City of God*, says: “These are the rites of the Mother of the gods, where Attis, a beautiful young man loved by her and mutilated through feminine jealousy, is mourned in the misery even of the mutilated men whom they call Galli.”

[Col. 0699C] **Verse 80. “For the shepherd is earlier.”** The theology of the gentiles consists of such great entanglements and contradictions that no one can easily extricate himself from it. Eusebius of Caesarea, book II, chapter 4, of the *Preparation*, where he discusses the theology of the Phrygians, says that Cybele was seized by love for Attis before the marriages of the gods. Yet as many heads, so many opinions.

[Col. 0699C] **Verse 80. “Or Jupiter himself.”** *Jovis* is correctly used in the nominative case. According to Priscian, among the ancients *Jovis* alone was said, from *juvare*, “to help,” and when another word was added it became *Jupiter*, as if “Jovis pater,” or, as Lactantius more plausibly thinks, “helping father.” The nominative *Jovis* occurs in Hyginus’ book of *Myths*, in Nonius Marcellus, and in other authors whom you may consult.

A certain very severe French critic, N. A., denies the four books *On the Creed for Catechumens* to Augustine, since their style seems to him to differ from Augustine’s and indeed to depart from the principles of the grammarians. Among his examples he cites this: “There it is imagined that Jupiter has Juno as his sister and wife,” and he objects to the use of *Jovis* in the nominative case. But he is mistaken, since this use of the name is found among the most authoritative writers and therefore does not discredit Augustine. Content with this, we proceed to other matters.

[Col. 0699D] **Verse 81. “But better.”** Might it be preferable to read: “But better”?

[Col. 0699D] **Verse 87. “Half-men.”** These are the Galli, priests of the Mother of the gods, who castrated themselves in memory of Attis’ emasculation. Lactantius, book I, chapter 17, says: “The Mother of the gods both loved a handsome young man and, catching him with his mistress, made him a half-man by cutting off his virility. And for that reason her rites are now celebrated by the Galli priests.” After exposing Cybele’s impurity, Minucius adds: “Because of this story the Galli and the half-men worship her by the punishment inflicted on their bodies. These are no longer sacred rites but tortures.” See Juvenal, satire 2, and Paulinus himself, *Natales*, book XI.

[Col. 0700B] **Verse 88. “Nor are there lacking men.”** Augustine’s entire book VI of *The City of God*, as well as other passages, is devoted to refuting this vanity and evasion of the pagans. They used to claim that these old-womanish tales were full of inner mysteries, and that philological truths lay hidden within them. Yet they were confounded by their own arguments. “Then,” says the holy doctor in chapter 8, “if these rites, which are proved to be fouler than theatrical indecencies, are excused and cleansed on the ground that they have their own interpretations, why should poetic tales not likewise be excused and cleansed?” and so forth.

Gregory of Nazianzus, in *Oration 1 against Julian*, after listing certain pagan superstitions, adds:

> “Let these things be wheeled before the spectators of the wonderful teachings of theology; then let allegories and monstrous interpretations be devised for them, and, straying from the matters before it, let the discourse descend into abysses and plunge over cliffs of a contemplation that possesses no firm standing” (*Ταῦτα ἐπεισκυκλείσθω τοῖς θαυμαστοῖς τῆς θεολογίας ἀκροαταῖς, εἶτ’ ἐπινοείσθω τούτοις ἀλληγορήματα, καὶ τερατεύματα, καὶ τῶν προκειμένων ἐκπίπτων ὁ λόγος εἰς βάραθρα χωρείτω, καὶ κρημνοὺς θεωρίας οὐκ ἐχούσης τὸ στάσιμον*).

[Col. 0700C] **Verse 92. “And suffers the virile [parts].”** I suspect that a verse is missing here, for the sense remains ambiguous. Certainly the word *abscindi* (“to be cut off”) is entirely necessary here for the meaning to be: “and suffers the virile parts to be cut off.”

[Col. 0700C] **Verse 94. “The stage provokes laughter.”** Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 13, has this striking passage: “O sad consolation of criminal desire! O belief of men deserving lamentation! You have made a theater out of heaven and led wandering minds through abrupt precipices in cruel ruin.” And below: “Transfer the temples to the theater instead, so that the secrets of these religions may be presented on the stage; and, so that impiety may omit nothing, make actors into priests.” I pass over Augustine, letter 5 to Marcellinus, and book VII, chapter 26, of *The City of God*, as well as Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 15.

[Col. 0700D] **Verse 95. “Saturn.”** Hesiod recounts the matter at length in the *Theogony*, as does Natalis Comes in book II of his *Mythology*, along with the other writers who pursued the learning of pagan theology in their works.

[Col. 0700D] **Verse 100. “And this Chronos.”** It should have been written *Cronos*; for Saturn is *Κρόνος* in Greek. But because he is said to signify time, he is also called *Χρόνος*. Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 22; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I of the *Roman Antiquities*; Cicero, book II *On the Nature of the Gods*; and others discuss this. Arnobius, however, rejects this designation entirely in book III *Against the Gentiles*: “For if this name signifies Time, as the Greek interpreters maintain, so that what is *Chronos* is taken to be *Cronos*, there is no Saturnian name. For who is so mad as to say that Time is a god?” and so forth.

[Col. 0701A] **Verse 101. “What creates, consumes.”** He has elegantly rendered a verse of Orpheus—or Onomacritus—about Saturn, in his hymn:

> “Who consumes everything, and himself again increases everything” (*Ὃς δαπανᾷς μὲν ἅπαντα, καὶ αὔξεις ἔμπαλιν αὐτός*).

“Who brings forth all things, consumes them, and all things again.” In place of *promittit* (“promises”), I would read *remittit* (“restores” or “sends back”).

[Col. 0701B] **Verse 105. “And therefore Latium.”** Virgil, speaking of Saturn in book VIII of the *Aeneid*:

> And he preferred that it be called Latium,  
> Because he had lain safely hidden in these lands.

[Col. 0701B] **Verse 108. “The Latian evil.”** This was the most savage sacrilege of paganism. A human victim was sacrificed to Jupiter, whom they called *Latiaris*. Tertullian reveals the matter in chapter 9 of the *Apology*: “Behold, in that most religious city of the pious descendants of Aeneas there is a certain Jupiter whom they drench with human blood in his games.” La Cerda gives an excellent explanation of the passage.

Minucius says: “Even today Jupiter Latiaris is worshiped by the Romans through homicide; and, as is worthy of Saturn’s son, he is fattened with the blood of a wicked and guilty man.” Elsewhere: “When he is drenched with blood under the title Latiaris.” Porphyry, book II *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, says:

> “And even now, who does not know that in the great city a human being is sacrificed at the festival of Jupiter Latiaris?” (*Ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν τίς ἀγνοεῖ κατὰ τὴν μεγάλην πόλιν τῇ τοῦ Λατιαρίου Διὸς ἑορτῇ σφαζόμενον ἄνθρωπον*).

Prudentius, book I *Against Symmachus*:

> Human blood is poured out as a gift to Latiaris.

St. Athanasius, in his *Oration against the Gentiles*, says: “The ancient Romans also worshiped the so-called Latiarian Jupiter with human sacrifices” (*Καὶ οἱ πάλαι δὲ Ῥωμαῖοι τὸν καλούμενον Λατιάριον Δία ἀνθρωποθυσίαις ἐθρήσκευον*). Tatian, *Against the Greeks*: “Among the Romans I found Jupiter Latiaris delighting in human gore and in the blood shed through murders” (*Εὑρὼν δὲ μὲν Ῥωμαίοις τὸν Λατιάριον Δία λύθροις ἀνθρώπων, καὶ τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνδροκτασίων αἵμασι τερπόμενον*). Thus, among the Romans, Jupiter Latiaris was appeased with human blood and gore poured out through homicide.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book IV of the *Roman Antiquities*, records that these rites were performed for Jupiter Latiaris, but does not mention this victim. From this learn that *Jupiter Latiaris* is the more correct form, rather than *Latialis*, as some deny.

[Col. 0701C] **Verse 112. “And Invincible.”** Above all among the Persians, the worship of the Sun was practiced. They called him Mithras and added to him the title “Invincible.” More is found in Gruter, pages 33 and following. Inscriptions occur in Reinesius dedicated to *Deo Invicto*, *Deo Invicto Mithrae*, *Soli Mithrae*, *Soli Invicto*, and *Soli Invicto Mithrae*. Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 5, asserts that Jupiter was divided into two powers, one of which—that is, the masculine power—was called Mithras.

Herodotus, speaking of the Persians in book I, says: “They sacrifice to heavenly Aphrodite, whom they call Mithras” (*Θύουσι δὲ οὐρανίῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ, ἣν καλέουσι Μίθραν*). Nicetas, in his notes on Nazianzenus, says: “Some regard Mithras as the Sun, others as the kidney of fire, and others as a certain special power” (*Τὸν Μίθραν οἱ μὲν τὸν ἥλιον, οἱ δὲ τὸν νεφρὸν τοῦ πυρός, ἄλλοι ἰδικήν τινα δύναμιν ὑπολαμβάνουσι*).

Since I see that Mithras signifies not only the Sun but something else as well, I can easily explain the inscription in Gruter, page 22, no. 12. It reads: *D. I. M. ET. SOLI. SOCIO. SAC.*, that is, “Sacred to the Invincible God Mithras and to the Sun, his companion.” Here Mithras seems to signify another deity, distinct from the Sun, not the Sun himself regarded as a foreign god, as Reinesius thinks in inscription 48, class 1.

The ancient inscriptions also contain: *NANNAE SEBECIO. DEO MITHRAE*. J. Caesar Bulengerus, chapter 4 of book I *On Lawful and Unlawful Magic*, thinks that all these words refer to the Sun Mithras. I, however, think that the marble was dedicated to three gods: *Nanna* is the name of Diana Nannaea, whom Jerome and Josephus mention in book I, chapter 6, and book II, chapter 1, of the *Maccabees*. *Sebecius* should be understood as Jupiter Sabazius, of whom Orpheus, or Onomacritus, says in his hymn:

> Hear, Father, son of Cronus, glorious Sabazius,  
> Illustrious divinity.

For I do not know on what authority Heinsius, in his *Sacred Aristotelian [Works]*, also called Bacchus Sabazius. But enough of this.

[Col. 0702B] **Verse 112. “Spelaea.”** This is the Greek word *σπήλαιον*, which in Latin means “cave”; nevertheless, the Greek name has also been tolerated by Ausonian ears. Virgil, *Eclogue* 10:

> It is settled: in the forests, among the caves of wild beasts.

Claudian, *On the Getic War*:

> The caves of wild beasts,  
> To be feared.

The sacrifices of Mithras were performed in the most secret caverns. Among his worshipers, the mysteries received there were preserved in religious silence. Those wishing to be initiated into these rites also underwent testing through many tortures. Hence Suidas, under the word *Mithras*, says:

> “No one, therefore, could be initiated into him unless, after passing through certain stages of punishment, he showed himself holy and free from passions” (*Οὐκ ἂν οὖν εἰς αὐτὸν δυνήσαιτό τις τελεσθῆναι, εἰ μὴ διά τινων βαθμῶν παρελθὼν τῶν κολάσεων δείξει ἑαυτὸν ὅσιον καὶ ἀπαθῆ*).

The same is confirmed by Nazianzenus, *Oration* 3; Lampridius in his *Life of Commodus*; and Tertullian, chapter 15 of *The Crown*. His words are: “Be ashamed, you Roman fellow-soldiers of his, now to be judged no longer by him but by some soldier of Mithras, who, when he is initiated in the cave, and so forth.” St. Justin Martyr, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, twice says that the rites of Mithras were performed “in a place which among them is called a cave” (*Ἐν τόπῳ ἐπικαλουμένῳ παρ’ αὐτοῖς σπηλαίῳ*).

See Jerome’s letter to Laeta; Reinesius, class 1, no. 48, *Inscriptions*; Bulengerus, book I, chapter 4, *On Lawful and Unlawful Magic*; Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, synthesis 1, chapter 6; Salmasius on the *Historia Augusta*, folios 349, 382, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0702D] **Verse 113. “And which conceal.”** It seems preferable to write: “and they cover each one in darkness.” Nevertheless, the sense is satisfactory.

[Col. 0702D] **Verse 115. “May conceal.”** *Celo*, used for *lateo* (“to lie hidden”), is an unusual verb. I find it used only with the meaning “to cover” or “to conceal.” Yet the very learned Michael Maddius, worthy offspring of the distinguished Carlo M. Maddius, pointed out to me that in Plautus’ *Bacchides*, act III, scene 2, one reads:

> Whatever you may be, I warn you: you will not conceal it.

And Lambinus’ Scholiast explains it thus: “You will not deceive; you will not remain hidden.” Certainly, if you insist that the pronoun *te* (“you”) is to be understood here, I too shall understand the pronoun *se* (“itself”) in Paulinus’ verse. If anyone preferred to emend the passage, I would read:

> May he conceal in the infernal regions within himself the cause of these evils.

[Col. 0703A] Certainly, in the manuscript it is written not *malarum* (“of evils,” feminine) but *malorum* (“of evils,” neuter).

[Col. 0703A] **Verse 116. “Isiac.”** In the rites of Isis, sistra were shaken, and the doglike head of Anubis was displayed. Lucan, in book VIII, encompasses both matters:

> And the semidivine dogs, and the sistra that command mourning.

Ausonius, writing to our Paulinus in letter 25, says:

> The Mareotic sistra stir the Isiac tumult.

Moreover, Anubis was also called *Cynocephalus*, a name expressing his form. Athanasius, in his *Oration against the Greeks*: “Anubis, the Cynocephalus among the Egyptians” (*Ὁ παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις Κυνοκέφαλος Ἄνουβις*). “Among the Egyptians, Anubis with a dog’s face.” Ovid, book IX of the *Metamorphoses*:

> With whom were the barking Anubis,  
> The sistra, and Osiris, never sufficiently sought.

On the sistra, consult Laurentius Pignorius in *The Isiac Table*, and the excellent dissertation of the most learned and distinguished Benedict Bacchini.

[Col. 0703B] **Verse 118. “I know not what.”** Paulinus expressed a passage from Minucius. Minucius says: “Soon, when the little boy is found, Isis rejoices and the priests exult. The Cynocephalus, the finder, boasts, and every year they do not cease either to lose what they find or to find what they will lose.” Julius Firmicus, chapter 2: “You find nothing here except something that you must either seek again or mourn.” Paulinus himself, *Natales*, book XI:

> For what, I ask, are they more blind than those  
> Who seek what they have not lost,  
> And find what nowhere remains?

[Col. 0703C] **Verse 122. “What did Serapis deserve?”** I willingly confess that I find the passage difficult here. Paulinus is referring to a certain festival day on which Serapis was compelled to assume many forms. Yet I find no trace of this custom anywhere. Certainly Macrobius and Plutarch, in the book *On Isis and Osiris*, depict Serapis as having no other form than human. “Everywhere the image of Osiris is human in form” (*Πανταχοῦ ἀνθρωπόμορφον Ὀσίριδος ἄγαλμα*). The solution must therefore be awaited from more learned men.

[Col. 0703C] **Verse 127. “What shall I say of Vesta?”** Some have thought that Vesta herself is the earth; others, that she is the guardian of all houses; still others believed that through her the pure fire of the ether was signified. Hence Orpheus said that she dwelt not in the Sicilian regions but in the ether:

> Hestia, queen, daughter of mighty Cronus,  
> Who hold the central dwelling of the greatest everlasting fire.

“Vesta, queen, daughter of mighty Saturn, who inhabits the central region of the great ether and fire.” Others have held other opinions, so that it is not surprising if our author claims that even her priests did not know what she was.

[Col. 0703D] **Verse 130. “Why is fire female?”** Above, you saw from Orpheus that Vesta is understood as fire. I now add Ovid, book VI of the *Fasti*:

> Understand Vesta as nothing other than living flame.

Yet earlier he had said:

> Vesta is also Earth . . .

Augustine, book IV, chapter 10, of *The City of God*, says: “They regard the same Earth as Ceres and the same also as Vesta,” although they often maintain that Vesta is nothing other than fire. He repeats the same point in book VII, chapter 16. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* and book II *On the Laws*, Diodorus, and others. Paulinus therefore marvels and laughs that fire is called female.

[Col. 0704B] Verse 131. Hyginus. Julius Hyginus was a freedman of Augustus and a friend of Ovid. He wrote the book of *Fabulae*, which still survives. Yet I was unable to find there the passage cited by Paulinus. He also wrote books of *Genealogies* and a book *On the Household Gods*, cited by Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.14; a book *On the Properties of the Gods*, likewise attested by Macrobius III.8; and *Miscellaneous Questions*, mentioned by Fabius, Gellius, and Diomedes—all of which the devouring power of time has denied us. From these books, without doubt, our Paulinus drew the learning displayed here.

[Col. 0704B] Verse 138. “They hang them for the Sun.” The Vulcanalia were festivals in honor of Vulcan. They are mentioned in the oldest calendars in Gruter, pp. 133–135, and in another similar calendar in Dempster, *Roman Antiquities*, supplements to chapter IV of book IV. They were celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. Columella agrees with this in *On Agriculture* XI.3: “Moreover, for Augustus, the third sowing occurs around the Vulcanalia.” Varro also mentions it in *On the Latin Language*.

In antiquity it was customary among idol-worshippers to hang garments for false gods. Aristophanes, in *The Birds*:

> Τίς δὲ θεὸς  
> Πολιοῦχος ἔσται, τῷ ξανοῦμεν τὸν πέπλον;

“What god, then, will be guardian of the city, for whom shall we spread out the robe?” That is: “For which god shall we hang the garments?”

Apuleius, *The Golden Ass* VI: “You see splendid gifts and strips of cloth embroidered with gold, fastened to the branches of trees and to doorposts.” Alexander ab Alexandro III.18: “In certain other mysteries, the custom is recorded that the garment in which someone is initiated should be dedicated to temples and divinities.” Pinto Ramirez gathers this and other material in *Sacred Spicilegium*, treatise 1, chapters 2 and 22, §15.

Yet I had been unable to find garments dedicated specifically to the Sun anywhere, until the most learned abbot Francesco Blanchinus, whose care the eminent Othobonian library has been entrusted, informed me through the distinguished Ciampini that Herodotus contains a passage on this subject. It is in book II, where he speaks of King Necho:

> Ἐν τῇ δὲ ἐσθῆτι ἔτυχε ταῦτα κατεργασάμενος, ἀνέθηκε τῷ Ἀπολλωνι πέμπψας ἐς Βραγχίδας τὰς Μιλησίων.

“Having happened to accomplish these things in this garment, he dedicated it to Apollo, sending it to the Branchidae of the Milesians.”

[Col. 0704D] Verse 139. “Adonis is carried.” There were indeed Adonia among the pagans, that is, festivals sacred to Adonis, mentioned by Aristophanes in *Peace* and by Ovid in *Metamorphoses* X, in the verse spoken by Venus:

> “He will perform annually the semblances of our mourning.”

The solemnities of Adonis were especially celebrated at Alexandria, as Natalis Comes states in *Mythology* V.16, and his image was carried with great ceremony. But here another occasion is plainly indicated on which the image of Adonis was carried—namely, during the Vulcanalia themselves, for he says: “Then Adonis too is carried.” The story of Venus and this boy is famous.

[Col. 0705B] Verse 140. “Then they throw dung.” The gods of the nations were customarily dishonored with dung. The recently mentioned abbot Blanchinus, prefect of the Othobonian library, through the distinguished Jo. Ciampinus, drew my attention to a verse of Orpheus, or Onomacritus, concerning a similar rite. It is found in Gregory of Nazianzus, *Against Julian*, invective 1:

> Ζεῦ κύδιστε, μέγιστε θεῶν, εἰλυμένε κόπρῳ.

> “Most glorious Jupiter, greatest of the gods, smeared with dung.”

Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, synthesis 2, chapter 5, quotes this same verse, but judges that the expression “smeared with dung” no more concerns Jupiter Stercorarius than Virgil’s words about Jupiter:

> “And, infused throughout his limbs,  
> Mind moves the whole mass and mingles with the great body.”

As though in both places Jupiter were said to be enveloped in the hidden workings of nature. But the Latin verses have no connection with the Greek ones, and the dung with which Jupiter is said to be smeared is wholly incompatible with such an explanation. There were also gods called Stercorean; and, as Selden notes in the same place, Beelzebub means “Lord of dung,” while Rabbi Abraham Benkattun explains Exodus 23:33 as follows: “You shall not allow those who worship foreign or dung-gods to dwell among you.”

But why did Adonis endure dung? I believe I have found the reason. Some identified Adonis with the seed of wheat; among them the Scholiast on Theocritus writes:

> Ὁ Ἄδονις, ἤγουν ὁ σῖτος ὁ σπειρόμενος ἓξ μῆνας ἐν τῇ γῇ ποιεῖ ὑπὸ τῆς σπορᾶς etc.

“Adonis—that is, the wheat that is sown—spends six months in the earth beneath the sowing, etc.”

Dung, therefore, is as appropriate to Adonis as to wheat. Since there was hostility between Vulcan and Venus’s lovers, Adonis was consequently mistreated when Vulcan’s rites were being celebrated. I consider these the more probable reasons why he was compelled to undergo such shameful treatment during the Vulcanalia.

[Col. 0705D] Verse 143. “Quinquennial banquets.” Hear Lipsius, chapter 10, *On Vesta and the Vestal Virgins*: “There is something obscure or clouded in what is found in certain acts of Sylvester: that he closed the dragon’s mouth and condemned him to perpetual imprisonment, and that food was customarily supplied to him by the virgins of Vesta on every Kalends. For who among the ancients records anything of this kind? I see that great men therefore reject or discard it as false.” While I was hesitating, I wondered whether Tertullian had looked toward this passage in *To His Wife* VI.6, in these words: “At Rome, those who handle the image of that inextinguishable fire, while caring for the omens of their own punishment together with the dragon himself, are judged concerning virginity.” Thus Lipsius.

But you should consider how much weight all this receives from Paulinus. As for why he calls them “quinquennial banquets,” I confess that I have not yet understood it. Our manuscript does indeed read *quinquennis*; but neither the meter nor the sense permits this reading, and it has been written for *quinquenneis*.

[Col. 0706C] Verse 149. “Who must be abandoned.” Minutianus has a similar passage: “Is it not ridiculous either to mourn what you worship or to worship what you mourn?”

[Col. 0706C] Verse 151. “I first considered everything.” No one will deny that one or more verses are missing here; for the preceding words remain uncertain and require a similar sense to complete them: “All these things I formerly turned over in a doubtful mind and did not know how to approve, when I obtained the clear light, etc.”

[Col. 0706C] Verse 153. “Church.” Paulinus pronounces this word in the same way elsewhere for the sake of the meter. In the *Epithalamium*:

> “A great sacrament, by which the Church is wedded to Christ.”

> “Here let love bind you, by which the Church binds Christ.”

Likewise in *Nativity* IV and elsewhere. The Anonymous author also used it in book II *Against Marcion*, in the verses attributed to Tertullian:

> “Thus the Church too proceeds according to the apostolic word.”

[Col. 0706D] Verse 161. “As now.” He indicates the time when he was committing these things to writing, namely the year 395; for Paulinus had recently moved to Nola in order to devote himself there to a religious and devout manner of life. See what I discussed in the preface to this poem.

[Col. 0706D] Verse 176. “Thus the elements.” There will scarcely be anyone to whom Paulinus’s view does not seem novel. Clearly he distinguishes the sea, lands, air, and heaven under the name of the elements, and gives no thought whatever to fire. This is an attractive and worthwhile subject for investigation. Let the reader therefore consult Dissertation XX, which I included for the purpose of clarifying this distinctive aspect of his learning.

[Col. 0706D] Verse 180. “The air is enclosed in the middle.” Far be it from us to suppose that our Paulinus accepted that imaginary sphere of fire which Aristotle and his followers cleverly devised and still approve. He therefore declares that the air is enclosed not by those fictitious flames, but by the ether or heaven.

[Col. 0707B] Verse 183. “And after the seven thrones.” We commonly say that there are not merely seven heavens but nine beneath the empyrean. Seven of them contain the wandering stars, as the verse has it:

> “Cynthia, Mercury, Venus, and the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn.”

The eighth is occupied by the fixed stars; the ninth is the *primum mobile*, or first moved heaven, which the empyrean follows. Nevertheless, Paulinus expressly holds that seven heavens exist before the empyrean. How, you ask? I answer: by poetic license. For among poets the dwelling of the supreme God is placed in the eighth heaven, namely, the starry heaven. Virgil, *Aeneid* X:

> “The father of the gods and king of men summons the council  
> To the starry seat.”

Sidonius Apollinaris, in the *Panegyric of Avitus*, on the council of the gods:

> “The stars themselves are the pavement; now the Father,  
> Tranquil, seats himself upon his golden throne.”

Euripides, in *Ion*, calls it:

> Διὸς πολύαστρον ἕδος

> “Zeus’s many-starred seat.”

To this add Chrysostom, *Oration II on the Nature of God*, and others. This was also the view of the ancient Christians. Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, lists among imaginary heresies a discussion of the diversity of the heavens in chapter 46, and says:

> “Whether, therefore, someone wishes to accept six heavens according to David and this firmament as the seventh, he does not err; for Solomon speaks of three heavens, namely, heaven, and the heaven of heaven. The apostle Paul likewise confesses that he was caught up to the third heaven. Whether, therefore, someone accepts seven, as David does, or three, or two, he does not err.”

[Col. 0707D] Verse 188. “From where, far away.” He imitates Virgil, who sings thus in *Aeneid* X:

> “The father of the gods and king of men summons the council  
> To the starry seat, from which, high above,  
> He surveys all the lands and the camp of the Dardanians.”

Let us also hear here the leading poet of the Italians, in book I of *The Hierusalem Delivered*:

> “When from the lofty throne the eternal Father,  
> Who is in the purest region of heaven,  
> Cast his eyes downward, and in a single moment, with one  
> Glance, saw what the world contains within itself.”

[Col. 0707D] Verse 191. “He encompasses the City.” Poets have made the boundaries of the Roman Empire identical with those of the world. Rutilius, in the *Itinerary*, says elegantly:

> “While you offer the conquered the fellowship of your own law,  
> You made a city of what had previously been the world.”

The Scholiast on Dionysius’s *Description of the World*:

> Ὅπερ δὲ πόλις τοῖς αὐτῆς ὁρίοις, καὶ χώραις ἐστὶ, τοῦτο ἥδε ἡ πόλις τῆς  
> ἁπάσης οἰκουμένης, ὥσπερ αὐτῆς χώρας ἄστυ κοινὸν ἀποδεδειγμένη.

> “What any city is within its own boundaries and territories, Rome is this for all the provinces of the inhabited world, having been established as the common city of the entire inhabited earth.”

Hence Rome is called by Claudian “she who spreads her empire over all.” Thus Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 5, said that Rome was the one homeland of all peoples throughout the whole world. For more, consult Bulenger, *On the Roman Empire* II.5.

[Col. 0708B] Verse 195. “Hence thus.” He would prefer *Hunc ita* (“him thus”).

[Col. 0708B] Verse 196. “Cosmos, from adornment.” Among the Greeks, *kosmos* means ornament. Paulinus thinks that the name for the world, which the Greeks call *kosmos*, derives from this meaning, because the world is truly a beautiful arrangement of ornaments. Others derive the etymology of the name from *kosmos* meaning order or measure, since the world is genuinely a condition of things joined and ordered together. Tertullian, *Against Marcion* V, agrees with our poet: “Therefore, to say something about this unworthy world, whose name among the Greeks is also one of ornament and cultivation, not of filth.”

[Col. 0708C] Verse 196. “The world from light.” Honorius of Autun, *Image of the World* chapter 1; Isidore, *Etymologies* III.28 and XIII.1, think that *mundus* was so called as though from *movendus*, “to be moved,” because it is in perpetual motion. But Varro, Cicero, Pliny, Paulus the Jurist, and others more correctly hold that it was named from cleanliness or elegance. Paulinus approaches this etymology when he says that the world is called *mundus* from light.

[Col. 0708C] Verse 201. “This is God.” That is, the divine Word and Son of God, through whom, as he sang above, all things were made, and without whom nothing that was made was made. The manuscript reads: “This god from the heart.” I supplied the word *est* (“is”). The verse nevertheless still limps; I could add another *est*: “This is the Spirit of the mouth.”

[Col. 0708D] Verse 202. “The structure of things.” Sipontinus taught that *fabrica* is properly used for a workshop. The word may perhaps be understood in that sense here. In my judgment, however, either an error has entered the manuscript or some verse has fallen out.

[Col. 0708D] Verse 203. “Nor the pagan.” For more on this name, consult the great father of the *Annals*, Baronius, in the *Martyrology* for January 31; Gothofredus on book VI, title 10, of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Pagans*; and other writers. In the fourth century of the Christian era, this name began to be applied to gentiles, since they continued to practice their profane religion in villages and rural districts.

[Col. 0708D] Verse 203. “If he avoids.” The manuscript read: “If anyone avoids idols.” I have emended it.

[Col. 0708D] Verse 204. “By divine power.” I preferred to write this instead of *nomine* (“by name”), as the manuscript has it.

[Col. 0708D] Verse 213. “The verse ‘Savior.’” The word *versus* does not please me much. Perhaps *verus* (“true”) should be written.

[Col. 0709B] Verse 249. “Life, power.” I leave it to others to remove this error.

---

# VARIANT READINGS IN THE POEMS OF ST. PAULINUS OF NOLA, FROM MANUSCRIPT AND PRINTED COPIES (C)

## In Poems I, II, and IV

[Col. 0709B] 1. Line 10, *quasi vero numerum* (“as though truly a number”). Barthius thinks that *quasi verum numerum* (“as though a true number”) should be read.

[Col. 0709B] 2. Verse 5, *mira* (“marvelous”). The editions of Schott and Vinet have *miros* (“marvelous,” masculine plural).

[Col. 0709C] 3. Verse 6, *alto* (“high”). Schott’s edition has *acto* (“driven,” or “done”).

[Col. 0709C] 4. Verse 15, *epulis alludat* (“may allude to the banquets”). Vinet’s edition has *epulisque adludat* (“and may play upon the banquets”).

[Col. 0709C] 5. Verse 18, *tribuat* (“may grant”). The editions of Schott and Vinet have *tribuit* (“he grants” or “he granted”).

## In Poem V

[Col. 0709C] 1. In the title. Grin’s edition has: “Prayer of Pontius Paulinus of Bordeaux to Almighty God.”

[Col. 0709C] 2. Verse 33, *perdidit* (“destroyed” or “lost”). This is found in the edition of Rosweyde, in Latinius, and in three editions in the margins. But four editions have *prodidit* (“betrayed” or “handed over”).

[Col. 0709C] 3. Verse 35, *aetas* (“age”). Three editions in the margins have *olim* (“once” or “formerly”).

[Col. 0709C] 4. Verse 41, *aethera* (“ether” or “heaven”). Three editions in the margins have *aera* (“air”).

[Col. 0710B] 5. Verse 52, *errori ipse* (“he himself to error”). The editions of Grin and Poelmann in the margins have *errorique* (“and to error”).

[Col. 0710B] 6. Verse 64, *male … bene* (“badly … well”). The editions of Gravius, Poelmann, and Schott in the margins have *mala … bona* (“bad things … good things”).

[Col. 0710B] 7. Verse 75, *voluptas* (“pleasure”). The same manuscripts in the margins have *voluntas* (“will”).

## In Poem VII

[Col. 0710C] 1. Verse 22, *imminentem* (“impending”). Schott’s edition in the margins has *eminentem* (“standing out” or “prominent”).

[Col. 0710C] 2. Verse 38, *vitam tenebit* (“he will preserve life”). These psalms, and likewise the poem on St. John the Baptist, are, I think, among the hymns composed while he was still inexperienced in theological mysteries. It is therefore not surprising if this error is indicated here: those who misunderstood the passage in 1 Corinthians 3 thought that Christians, even if wicked, would not attain salvation provided only that they had kept their faith unharmed. — SACCHIN.

[Col. 0711A] 3. Verse 48, *per arctum* (“through the narrow place”). The Royal Manuscript has *per artum* (“through the confined place”).

## In Poems VIII and IX

[Col. 0711A] 1. Verse 9, *almum … Sion*, and in the following poem, verse 3, *patrium … Sion*, masculine because of the mountain. Alternatively, read *almam*, *patriam* (“nourishing,” “ancestral,” feminine). — SACCHIN.

[Col. 0711A] 2. Verse 49, *elidet* (“will dash out”). Schott’s edition in the margin has *allidet* (“will dash against”), from the Vulgate.

[Col. 0711A] 3. Verse 60, *praeripe* (“snatch away”). The Royal Manuscript, together with five printed editions, has *praecipe* (“command”), incorrectly.

## In Poem X

[Col. 0711A] 1. In the title. Rosweyde’s edition has: “Paulinus to Ausonius, greetings.”

[Col. 0711A] 2. Verse 5, *felix cum* (“happy when”). The editions of Gravius, Poelmann, and Schott in the margins have *felix quam* (“happy whom”).
