[Col. 0711A] 3. Verse 9, *multimodis* (“in many ways”). SACCHIN: “I would prefer *multa modis*, that is, ‘with much charm of rhythms and verses, anxious piety had mingled some sweet and somewhat bitter things with the complaints of censure.’”

[Col. 0711B] 4. Verse 13, *referenda* (“to be referred” or “reported”). The editions of Lyon, Vinet, and Gravius, Poelmann, and Schott in the margins have *retegenda* (“to be uncovered”). SACCHIN: “Perhaps *regerenda* (‘to be related again’).”

[Col. 0711B] 5. Verse 18, *aliis* (“to others”). SACCHIN: “The sense shows that this should be read. Five editions have *alias* (‘otherwise’), incorrectly.”

[Col. 0711B] 6. In the same place, *silent* (“they are silent”). Four editions have *secent* (“they cut off”).

[Col. 0711B] 7. In the same place. We deleted after verse 18: “Farewell, illustrious lord,” because it was absent from the Lyon manuscript and from the editions of Poelmann and Vinet. I suspect that it was taken from that verse of Paulinus, “Or do you, illustrious lord, …,” by those who confused all these writings and defiled them with new and false titles.

[Col. 0711B] 8. Verse 38, *nubilant* (“they cloud”). The editions of Poelmann, Schott, and Vinet have *nubilent* (“may they cloud”), incorrectly.

[Col. 0711B] 9. Verse 41, *Nihil adferentes* (“bringing nothing”). The Royal Manuscript and four editions have *Nihil ferentes* (“carrying nothing”).

[Col. 0711B] 10. Verse 42, *Quod veritatem detegat* (“which reveals the truth”). The Royal Manuscript and the editions of Gravius and Schott in the margins have *Aut veritatem non tegant* (“or let them not conceal the truth”).

[Col. 0711B] 11. Verse 43, *queant* (“may be able”). The Royal Manuscript has *queunt* (“are able”).

[Col. 0711C] 12. Verse 52, *virtutium* (“of virtues”). Thus the Lyon and Royal manuscripts and Vinet’s edition. Gravius, Lyon, Poelmann, and Schott substituted *virtutis est* (“is of virtue”).

[Col. 0711C] 13. Verse 69, *Abolet* (“he abolishes”). The Lyon edition has *Horret* (“he shudders”).

[Col. 0711C] 14. Verse 70, *videmur* (“we seem”). Schott’s edition in the margin has *jubemur* (“we are commanded”).

[Col. 0711C] 15. Verse 75, *Coelis* (“to the heavens”). The Royal Manuscript has *Coelo* (“to heaven”).

[Col. 0711C] 16. Verse 75, *praesens* (“present”). Schott’s edition in the margin has *praestans* (“excellent” or “outstanding”).

[Col. 0711C] 17. Verse 106, *mota pietate* (“piety having been moved”). Three editions in the margins have *nota pietate* (“with known piety”).

[Col. 0711C] 18. Verse 113, *reduces* (“you bring back”). The Royal Manuscript and the Badian edition have *reducis* (“you lead back”).

[Col. 0711C] 19. Verse 116, *vota* (“vows”). The editions of Lyon, Poelmann, Gravius, and Schott in the margins have *verba* (“words”).

[Col. 0711C] 20. Verse 135, *Stulta Dei sapiens* (“wise, yet foolish before God”). The Royal Manuscript and Schott’s edition in the margin have *Stulta Deo sapiens* (“wise, yet foolish to God”). The editions of Gravius and Poelmann in the margins have *Stultus desipiens* (“a foolish fool”), incorrectly; for this was taken from Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 3, verse 19.

[Col. 0711D] 21. Verse 138, *istis* (“to these”). The Royal Manuscript and the Badian and Schott editions in the margins have *istic* (“there”).

[Col. 0711D] 22. Verse 142, *cepit* (“he took”). The Lyon edition has *flexit* (“he bent” or “turned”).

[Col. 0711D] 23. Verse 157, *in antris* (“in caves”). The Royal Manuscript and the Badian and Schott editions in the margins have *in agris* (“in fields”).

[Col. 0711D] 24. Verse 161, *agitare frequentant* (“they frequently pursue”). The Lyon and Poelmann editions in the margins have *habitare frequentent* (“they frequently inhabit”).

[Col. 0711D] 25. Verse 166, *strepitusque* (“and the noise”). The Royal Manuscript and the Badian edition have *strepitumque* (“and the noise,” accusative).

[Col. 0711D] 26. Verse 178, *sedisse* (“to have sat”). Vinet: *sedere* here means “to please,” as also in the following letter, verse 11.

[Col. 0711D] 27. Verse 182, *voti* (“of the vow”). The Lyon and Schott editions in the margins have *veri* (“of the truth”).

[Col. 0711D] 28. Verse 183, *acta*. This is a Greek word, ἀκτή, meaning “shore” and a maritime place. — VINET.

[Col. 0711D] 29. Verse 213, *inter iniquos* (“among the unjust”). The Royal Manuscript with Poelmann’s edition has *integer aequo* (“upright among the just”).

[Col. 0711D] 30. Verse 231, *notatur* (“is marked”). The Vossian manuscript has *notantur* (“are marked”).

[Col. 0712A] 31. Verse 234, *terris et moenibus* (“with lands and walls”). That is, “with territory.” Heinsius thought *turritis moenibus* (“with towered walls”) should be read.

[Col. 0712A] 32. Verse 247, *tuae* (“your”). The editions of Gravius, Poelmann, and Schott in the margins have *altae* (“high”). The Royal Manuscript has *potens* (“powerful”).

[Col. 0712A] 33. Verse 254, *in attrito longum* (“long in what is worn away”). The editions of Vinet, Gravius, Poelmann, and Schott in the margins have *nativo longe* (“far in what is native”).

[Col. 0712A] 34. Verse 273, *mutatur* (“is changed”). The Royal Manuscript and the Badian edition have *mutatus* (“changed”).

[Col. 0712A] 35. Verse 278, *At si* (“but if”). The Royal Manuscript and the Badian edition have *Aut si* (“or if”).

[Col. 0712A] 36. Verse 305, *id jam* (“that now”). Thus restored from the Lyon and Vossian manuscripts and Vinet’s edition. Others have *haec jam* (“these things now”).

[Col. 0712A] 37. Verse 308, *possit* (“may be able”). The Royal Manuscript and four editions have *posset* (“might be able”).

[Col. 0712A] 38. Verse 323, *illato* (“having been brought in”). The Royal Manuscript and four editions have *inlato* (“having been brought in”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0712A] 39. Verse 326, *Curarumve* (“or of cares”). The Royal Manuscript has *Curarumque* (“and of cares”).

[Col. 0712A] 40. Verse 328, *Commissisque Deo* (“and having been entrusted to God”). The Royal Manuscript with the editions of Schott and Vinet has *Communique Deo* (“and to the common God”).

## In Poem XI

[Col. 0712B] 1. Verse 16, *suspicicio* (“suspicion”). Five editions in the margins have *suspectio* (“suspicion”).

[Col. 0712B] 2. Verse 17, *colitque* (“and he worships”). The editions of Lyon and Vinet have *coletque* (“and he will cultivate”).

[Col. 0712B] 3. Verse 22, *Irrupit* (“he burst in”). The Royal Manuscript with five printed editions has *Inrupit* (“he burst in”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0712B] 4. Verse 28, *vero* (“truly”). Five editions in the margins have *merito* (“deservedly”).

[Col. 0712B] 5. Verse 29, *Vulnere tam tenera* (“with a wound so tender”). The Lyon Manuscript and Poelmann’s edition in the margin have *Vulnere tam tetro* (“with so foul a wound”).

[Col. 0712B] 6. Verse 31, *Hoc nec* (“but not this”). Thus the Royal Manuscript and the Badian and Lyon editions. Others have *Hoc ne* (“whether this”).

[Col. 0712B] 7. Verse 39, *Sustineant* (“may they endure”). The Royal Manuscript has *Sustineat* (“may he endure”), incorrectly.

## In Poems XII and XIII

[Col. 0712B] 1. Verse 10, *annue* (“grant assent”). The German Manuscript and the Badian and Gravius editions have *adnue* (“grant assent”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0712B] 2. Verse 13, *reddere coram* (“to return before”). Three editions have *nostra* (“our”).

[Col. 0712B] 3. Verse 19, *Consule jam vel sero* (“consult now, even if late”). These two verses are absent from the five printed editions, which read *Consule et obtritis* (“consult, even amid the crushed”). They survive in the German Manuscript.

[Col. 0712C] 4. Verse 2, *Qui* (“who”). The editions of Grin and Poelmann have *Cui* (“to whom”).

[Col. 0712C] 5. Verse 10, *Ex illo qui me* (“from the one who me”). Five editions have *Ex illo quo me* (“from that by which me”).

[Col. 0712C] 6. Verse 12, *nam te mihi … vocavi* (“for I called you to me …”). Five editions have *nam me tibi … vocasti* (“for you called me to you …”).

## In Poem XIV

[Col. 0712C] 1. Verse 4, *nanctus* (“having obtained”). Thus the German Manuscript.

[Col. 0712C] 2. Verse 8, *Aequiparat* (“he makes equal”). Three editions have *Aequiperat* (“he makes equal”).

[Col. 0712C] 3. Verse 9, *remittit* (“he releases”). The German Manuscript has *remittat* (“may he release”).

[Col. 0712C] 4. Verse 15, *Nam post* (“for afterward”). The German Manuscript and five editions have *Quam post* (“which afterward”), incorrectly.

[Col. 0712C] 5. Verse 19, *vicesima* (“twentieth”). Thus the German Manuscript with five printed editions. Rosweyde’s edition has *vigesima* (“twentieth”).

[Col. 0712C] 6. Verse 37, *munere* (“by a gift”). The German Manuscript has *numine* (“by divine power”).

[Col. 0712C] 7. Verse 58, *Et qua bis ternas* (“and by which twice three”). The German Manuscript has *Et bis ter denas* (“and twice three tens”).

[Col. 0712C] 8. Verse 88, *est prima* (“is first”). The Badian and Gravius editions have *es prima* (“you are first”).

[Col. 0712C] 9. Verse 135, *laudatisque* (“and having praised”). Thus the German Manuscript. The editions have *laudatis* (“you praise” or “having praised”).

## In Poem XV

[Col. 0712D] 1. Verse 8, *dignate Deo* (“O one deemed worthy by God”). Two German Manuscripts have *dignante Deo* (“with God deeming worthy”).

[Col. 0712D] 2. Verse 37, *lactentes* (“suckling”). Two German Manuscripts have *lactantes* (“giving milk”).

[Col. 0712D] 3. Verse 38, *et solidam* (“and solid”). Thus two German Manuscripts. The editions have *ac solidam* (“and solid”).

[Col. 0712D] 7. Verse 110, *pellere* (“to drive away”). Thus the two German Manuscripts, and the editions of Gravius, Schott in the margins, and Latinius. Five printed editions have *vellere* (“to tear away”).

[Col. 0712D] 8. Verse 112, *nanctus* (“having obtained”). Thus the two German Manuscripts. The printed copies have *nactus* (“having obtained”).

[Col. 0712D] 9. Verse 118, *omni* (“every”). German Manuscript 1 has *omnis* (“every,” nominative).

[Col. 0712D] 10. Verse 126, *antistite* (“high priest” or “bishop”). Two German Manuscripts have *antestite*, and likewise below and in *Nativity* 5.

[Col. 0712D] 11. Verse 129, *tantum quia* (“only because”). German Manuscript 1 has *quia tantum* (“because only”).

[Col. 0713A] 12. Verse 140, *infernis* (“to the infernal regions”). German Manuscript 1 has *inferni* (“of the infernal regions”).

[Col. 0713A] 13. Verse 162, *flagrare* (“to burn”). German Manuscript 1 has *flagrans* (“burning”).

[Col. 0713A] 21. Verse 244, *velut eludentis* (“as though mocking”). German Manuscript 1 has *veluti ludentis* (“as though playing”).

[Col. 0713A] 22. Verse 249, *assurgere* (“to rise up”). Two German Manuscripts with Gravius’s edition have *adsurgere* (“to rise up”), and likewise everywhere.

[Col. 0713A] 23. Verse 251, *ferrato exuta* (“stripped of the iron”). German Manuscript 1 has *ferroque exuta* (“stripped of the iron”).

[Col. 0713B] 24. Verse 261, *abire* (“to depart”). Two German Manuscripts with five printed editions have *adiri* (“to be approached”). In the margin of one German Manuscript, however, a later hand has written *abire*.

[Col. 0713B] 25. Verse 268, *Illustrata* (“illumined”). Two German Manuscripts and Gravius’s edition have *Inlustrata* (“illumined”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0713B] 26. Verse 276, *tentat* (“he attempts”). Two German Manuscripts have *temptat* (“he attempts”), and likewise elsewhere.

[Col. 0713B] 27. Verse 285, *comminus* (“at close quarters”). The same manuscripts always have this form. The printed editions have *cominus*.

[Col. 0713B] 28. Verse 294, *Decerptumque* (“and plucked away”). The editions of Gravius, Poelmann, and Schott in the margins, together with two German Manuscripts, have *Demessumque* (“and reaped”).

[Col. 0713B] 29. Verse 296, *victus* (“food” or “conquered”). German Manuscript 1 has *gustus* (“taste”).

[Col. 0713B] 30. Verse 318, *atqui* (“but indeed”). Two German Manuscripts have *atquin* (“but indeed”).

[Col. 0713B] 31. Verse 320, *cara* (“dear,” feminine). Thus one German Manuscript. The others have *carum* (“dear,” neuter).

[Col. 0713B] 32. Verse 341, *excitat* (“he arouses”). German Manuscript 1 has *suscitat* (“he raises up”).

[Col. 0713B] 33. Verse 343, *assumit* (“he takes up”). Two German Manuscripts have *adsumit* (“he takes up”), everywhere.

[Col. 0713C] 34. Verse 352, *o mi nate* (“O my son”). One German Manuscript with five printed editions has *o mihi nate* (“O my son”).

## In Poem XVI

[Col. 0713C] 1. Verse 10, *rata debeo* (“I owe what has been ratified”). German Manuscript 1 has *debeo sacra* (“I owe sacred things”).

[Col. 0713C] 2. Verse 21, *errare vias* (“to wander through paths”). German Manuscript 1 has *servare vias* (“to preserve the paths”).

[Col. 0713C] 3. Verse 48, *aut gladiis* (“or with swords”). Thus the two German Manuscripts and the editions of Grin and Poelmann. Others have *et gladiis* (“and with swords”).

[Col. 0713C] 4. Verse 49, *verbis* (“with words”). In one German Manuscript, after this verse appears the gloss: “Did you not carry this upward with your own body?”

[Col. 0713C] 5. Verse 70, *persensit* (“he fully perceived”). Five editions have *praesensit* (“he perceived beforehand”).

[Col. 0713C] 6. Verse 74, *Illudente* (“while mocking”). Two manuscripts have *Inludente* (“while mocking”). Below: *Inridebat* (“he mocked”).

[Col. 0713C] 7. Verse 79, *loquelis* (“with speeches”). Two German Manuscripts have *loquellis* (“with speeches”) throughout; likewise below, *querellis* (“with complaints”).

[Col. 0713C] 8. Verse 93, *Nam* (“for”). German Manuscript 1 has *Jam* (“now”).

[Col. 0713C] 9. In the same place, *rostra* (“beaks” or “rostra”). Schott’s edition in the margin has *strata* (“roads” or “strewn”).

[Col. 0713C] 10. Verse 99, *sordidus* (“filthy”). Two German Manuscripts have *sordibus* (“with filth”).

[Col. 0713C] 11. Verse 103, *obstupuerunt* (“they were astonished”). German Manuscript 1 with four printed editions has *obstipuerunt* (“they were astonished”).

[Col. 0713D] 12. Verse 117, *Scrutatum* (“examined”). German Manuscript 1 has *Scrutari* (“to examine”).

[Col. 0713D] 13. Verse 143, *gigas* (“giant”). Two German Manuscripts have *gigans* (“giant”).

[Col. 0713D] 14. Verse 152, *Illa* (“she” or “that”). German Manuscript 1 has *Ille* (“he” or “that”).

[Col. 0713D] 15. Verse 166, *illo* (“with that” or “to that”). Paulinus uses it likewise elsewhere, in Letter 24.9 and Letter 31.6. German Manuscript 1 has *illuc* (“to that place”).

[Col. 0713D] 16. Verse 171, *hoc* (“this”). German Manuscript 1 has *haec* (“these things”).

[Col. 0713D] 17. Verse 173, *strictae* (“tight” or “drawn”). German Manuscript 1 with the editions of Grin and Poelmann has *structae* (“built” or “constructed”).

[Col. 0713D] 18. Verse 192, *totos perhibent* (“they declare all”). Thus the two German Manuscripts. The editions have *perhibent totos* (“they declare all”).

[Col. 0713D] 19. Verse 206, *afflicti* (“afflicted”). Two German Manuscripts have *adflicti* (“afflicted”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0713D] 20. Verse 238, *prior* (“earlier”). German Manuscript 1 has *prius* (“earlier”).

[Col. 0713D] 21. Verse 241, *qui* (“who”). German Manuscript 1 has *quia* (“because”).

[Col. 0713D] 22. Verse 257, *patriis* (“ancestral”). German Manuscript 1 has *patris* (“of the father”).

[Col. 0713D] 23. Verse 264, *prisco* (“ancient”). German Manuscript 1 has *claro* (“illustrious” or “bright”).

[Col. 0713D] 24. Verse 265, *stemmate* (“by lineage”). One German Manuscript has *nomine* (“by name”).

[Col. 0713D] 25. Verse 273, *posset* (“could”). German Manuscript 1 has *possit* (“may be able”).

[Col. 0714A] 26. Verse 275, *sensu* (“by sense”). Schott’s edition in the margin has *censu* (“by judgment” or “assessment”).

[Col. 0714A] 27. Verse 287, *sed et has* (“but these also”). German Manuscript 1 has *sed eas* (“but them”).

## In Poem XVII

[Col. 0714A] 1. Verse 3, *adnexa* (“joined”). The Royal and German Manuscripts and five printed editions have *adnixa* (“leaning upon” or “joined”).

[Col. 0714A] 2. Verse 4, *futuros* (“future,” masculine plural). The German Manuscript has *futurus* (“future,” masculine singular).

[Col. 0714A] 3. Verse 13, *terra* (“earth”). Thus the German Manuscript. The editions have *terrae* (“of the earth”).

[Col. 0714A] 4. Verse 29, *antiqui* (“ancient”). The Royal Manuscript and five printed editions have *antiquis* (“ancient,” dative or ablative), incorrectly.

[Col. 0714A] 5. Verse 71, *oderimus* (“we shall hate”). Thus the Royal and German Manuscripts with three editions. The editions of Grin and Poelmann have *execremur* (“we may curse”), because they objected to the lengthened third syllable. But see note 342.

[Col. 0714A] 6. Verse 111, *in aequor* (“upon the sea”). The German Manuscript has *per aequor* (“across the sea”).

[Col. 0714A] 7. Verse 134, *devorabit … saturabit* (“he will devour … he will satisfy”). Schott’s edition has *devoravit … saturavit* (“he devoured … he satisfied”).

[Col. 0714A] 8. Verse 153, *ille vidit* (“he saw”). The German Manuscript has *vidit ille* (“he saw,” with reversed order).

[Col. 0714A] 9. Verse 173, *secli* (“of the age”). Four editions have *mundi* (“of the world”).

[Col. 0714A] 10. Verse 187, *reddat … tutum* (“may he render … safe”). The German Manuscript has *reddi … tutus* (“to be rendered … safe”).

[Col. 0714B] 11. Verse 199, *colla* (“necks”). The German Manuscript has *corda* (“hearts”).

[Col. 0714B] 12. Verse 214, *exsultat* (“he rejoices”). The German Manuscript has *exsultet* (“may he rejoice”).

[Col. 0714B] 13. Verse 264, *vivere* (“to live”). The German Manuscript has *quaerere* (“to seek”).

[Col. 0714B] 14. Verse 296, *vivet* (“he will live”). The German Manuscript has *vivit* (“he lives”).

[Col. 0714B] 15. Verse 302, *imponet* (“he will place”). The same manuscript has *imponit* (“he places”).

## In Poem XVIII

[Col. 0714B] 1. Verse 6, *qua fert* (“by which it carries”). German Manuscript 1 has *quo fert* (“by which it carries”).

[Col. 0714B] 2. Verse 11, *Nam cui* (“for whom”); *Non gaudere* (“not to rejoice”); *Qua quis* (“by which each”); *Coelicolas* (“the dwellers in heaven”). In two German Manuscripts and in the editions of Grin and Poelmann, these four verses are arranged in this order. In others: *Qua quis*, *Nam cui*, *Non gaudere*, *Coelicolas*.

[Col. 0714B] 3. In the same place, *Christus* (“Christ”). German Manuscript 1 has *Sanctus* (“Holy One”).

[Col. 0714B] 4. Verse 12, *vacuum* (“empty”). German Manuscript 1 has *vacuus* (“empty,” masculine).

[Col. 0714B] 5. Verse 15, *Ipsa* (“she herself”). German Manuscript 1 has *Ipso* (“by itself” or “he himself”).

[Col. 0714B] 6. Verse 33, *poliant* (“they polish”). German Manuscript 1 has *aedificant* (“they build”).

[Col. 0714B] 7. Verse 34, *praefixis* (“having been fixed beforehand”). German Manuscript 1 has *perfixis* (“having been fixed”).

[Col. 0714B] 8. Verse 39, *Et medicata* (“and having been healed”). German Manuscript 1 and four editions in the margins have *Ut medicata* (“so that, having been healed”).

[Col. 0714C] 9. Verse 42, *laxant* (“they loosen”). German Manuscript 1 has *laxent* (“may they loosen”).

[Col. 0714C] 10. Verse 45, *cervis aulaea ferisque* (“curtains with stags and wild beasts”). The German Manuscripts have *ceras aulaeae lucernas* (“wax candles, curtains, lamps”). Schott’s edition in the margin has *ceris aulaea lucernis* (“curtains with wax lamps”).

[Col. 0714C] 11. Verse 57, *nil* (“nothing”). German Manuscript 1 has *nihil* (“nothing”).

[Col. 0714C] 12. Verse 81, *metet* (“he will reap”). German Manuscript 1 has *metat* (“may he reap”).

[Col. 0714C] 13. Verse 83, *O si dicere* (“O if only to say”). Thus Schott’s edition in the margin. Five editions with one German Manuscript have *hoc quod dicere* (“this which [he is] to say”); another German Manuscript has *hoc qui dicere* (“this who [is] to say”).

[Col. 0714C] 14. Verse 86, *operum* (“of works”). German Manuscript 1 has *operis* (“of the work”).

[Col. 0714C] 15. Verse 141, *aethereas* (“heavenly”). Two German Manuscripts have *aetherias* (“heavenly”).

[Col. 0714C] 16. Verse 149, *Nam* (“for”). German Manuscript 1 has *Jam* (“now”).

[Col. 0714C] 17. Verse 150, *leto* (“death”). German Manuscript 1 with five editions has *laetus* (“joyful”).

[Col. 0714C] 18. Verse 155, *justae* (“just”). German Manuscript 1 has *justa* (“just,” neuter).

[Col. 0714C] 19. Verse 169, *hic etiam* (“this one also”). Four editions have *haec etiam* (“this also,” feminine).

[Col. 0714C] 20. Verse 196, *Sufficient* (“may they suffice”). German Manuscript 1 has *Sufficiunt* (“they suffice”).

[Col. 0714C] 21. Verse 198, *accommoda* (“fitting things”). German Manuscript 1 has *adcommoda* (“fitting things”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0714C] 22. Verse 208, *nomine* (“by name”). German Manuscript 1 has *numine* (“by divine power”).

[Col. 0714D] 23. Verse 234, *exsaturabat* (“he fully satisfied”). Thus the two German Manuscripts. Others have *exaturabat* (“he satisfied”).

[Col. 0714D] 24. Verse 258, *medelam* (“remedy”). Two German Manuscripts have *medellam* (“remedy”), and likewise elsewhere.

[Col. 0714D] 25. Verse 260, *pauperies … inclinata* (“poverty … inclined”). German Manuscript 1 has *paupertas … adclinata* (“poverty … inclined”).

[Col. 0714D] 26. Verse 272, *claustra* (“barriers” or “enclosures”). German Manuscript 1 has *clausa* (“closed things”).

[Col. 0714D] 27. Verse 282, *quando vel usquam* (“when or anywhere”). Two German Manuscripts have *aut ubi quando* (“or where, when”).

[Col. 0714D] 28. Verse 306, *vendicet* (“may he claim”). Two German Manuscripts have *vindicet* (“may he claim”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0714D] 29. Verse 310, *nusquam* (“nowhere”). Two German Manuscripts have *numquam* (“never”).

[Col. 0714D] 30. Verse 313, *reductos* (“brought back”). Four editions have *juvencos* (“young bulls”).

[Col. 0714D] 31. Verse 322, *affixi* (“fixed”). Two German Manuscripts and the editions of Grin and Poelmann have *adfixi* (“fixed”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0714D] 32. Verse 329, *revellit* (“he tears away”). German Manuscript 1 has *repellit* (“he repels”).

[Col. 0714D] 33. Verse 340, *escas* (“food”). German Manuscript 1 has *herbas* (“herbs” or “grass”).

[Col. 0714D] 34. Verse 350, *Aspicit* (“he looks upon”). German Manuscript 1 has *Respicit* (“he looks back” or “regards”). Twenty-eight verses are missing here in the other German Manuscript.

[Col. 0715A] 35. Verse 351, *et refricat* (“and rubs again”). German Manuscript 1 and four editions have *et spirat* (“and breathes”). But *refricat* should be read, as Barthius advises. [Col. 0715A] 36. Verse 358, *solum* (“alone” or “only”). German Manuscript 1 has *sola* (“alone,” feminine).

[Col. 0715A] 37. Verse 359, *pro postibus* (“before the doorposts”). German Manuscript 1 has *de postibus* (“from the doorposts”).

[Col. 0715A] 38. Verse 366, *sed* (“but”). German Manuscript 1 has *et* (“and”).

[Col. 0715A] 39. Verse 387, *culmea tecti Culmina* (“the thatched peaks of the roof”). One German Manuscript has *culmine tecto Culmina* (“the peaks on the roof’s summit”).

[Col. 0715A] 40. Verse 404, *speraverit* (“he will have hoped”). German Manuscript 1 has *speraverat* (“he had hoped”).

[Col. 0715A] 41. Verse 409, *reserare* (“to open”). Two editions have *servare* (“to preserve”).

[Col. 0715A] 42. Verse 437, *ostentat* (“he displays”). German Manuscript 1 has *ostendit* (“he showed” or “shows”).

[Col. 0715A] 43. Verse 446, *honorem* (“honor”). German Manuscript 1 has *amorem* (“love”).

[Col. 0715A] 44. Verse 454, *prope* (“near”). German Manuscript 1 and three editions have *pro* (“for” or “before”).

[Col. 0715A] 45. Verse 459, *itidem* (“likewise”). German Manuscript 1 has *iterum* (“again”).

[Col. 0715A] 46. Verse 460, *pecudes* (“cattle”). German Manuscript 1 has *illos* (“those”).

[Col. 0715A] 47. Verse 467, *Inde* (“thence”). German Manuscript 1 has *Unde* (“whence”).

[Col. 0715A] 48. Verse 468, *Collaudante* (“while praising together”). Two German Manuscripts have *Conlaudante* (“while praising together”), an orthographic variant.

## In Poem XXII

[Col. 0715B] 1. Verse 13, *fuerit* (“may have been”). The editions of Gravius and Poelmann have *fuerat* (“had been”).

[Col. 0715B] 2. Verse 34, *Persona divinos* (“sound forth divine things”). Correctly, *tuba persona* (“let the trumpet sound”). Schott’s edition in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and the Cologne edition, volume V, p. 978, have *Personuit vanos* (“he sounded empty things”).

[Col. 0715B] 3. In the same place, *celsius intonet* (“may he sound more loftily”). Schott’s edition, p. 798, has *celsior intonat* (“he sounds loftier”).

[Col. 0715B] 4. Verse 45, *Ne te ceu* (“lest you, as”). Thus the Viennese Manuscript. Others have *Nec te ceu* (“nor you, as”).

[Col. 0715B] 5. In the same place, *Promethei* (“of Prometheus”). The Royal Manuscript with the Badian edition has *Promethi* (“of Prometheus”).

[Col. 0715B] 6. Verse 93, *tremant … ministrent* (“may they tremble … may they serve”). Schott’s edition, p. 979, has *tremunt … ministrant* (“they tremble … they serve”).

[Col. 0715B] 7. Verse 112, *tutum* (“safe”). The Viennese Manuscript has *totum* (“whole”).

[Col. 0715B] 8. Verse 115, *monitu* (“by advice”). The Royal Manuscript has *monito* (“by the advice”).

[Col. 0715B] 9. Verse 119, *morte propinqua* (“with death near”). Thus emended from the Royal and Viennese Manuscripts and Schott’s edition, p. 979. Others have *morte propinquae* (“of near death”).

## In Poem XXIII

[Col. 0715C] 1. Verse 24, *Et minimam* (“and the least”). The German Manuscript has *Tu minimam* (“you, the least”).

[Col. 0715C] 2. Verse 36, *Attonitas* (“stunned”). Barthius thinks *attentas* (“attentive”) should be read.

[Col. 0715C] 3. Verse 39, *et jam mihi pacta* (“and now promised to me”). The German Manuscript has *et pacta quotannis* (“and promised every year”).

[Col. 0715C] 4. Verse 40, *Camoenis* (“to the Muses”). The German Manuscript has *loquellis* (“with little speeches”).

[Col. 0715C] 5. Verse 53, *ut meritum* (“as deserved”). The German Manuscript has *ob meritum* (“on account of merit”).

[Col. 0715C] 6. Verse 56, *quo* (“by which”). Thus emended from the German Manuscript and Schott’s edition in the margin. Previously it was *quod* (“which”).

[Col. 0715C] 7. Verse 95, *tegmina* (“coverings”). Thus the Belgian and German Manuscripts and three editions in the margins. Five printed editions have *tegmine* (“with a covering”).

[Col. 0715C] 8. Verse 148, *Hoc* (“this”). The German Manuscript has *Haec* (“these things”), perhaps *Hac* (“by this”).

[Col. 0715C] 9. Verse 161, *submissior* (“more submissive”). Thus the German Manuscript. Others have *summissior* (“more submissive”), an orthographic variant.

[Col. 0715C] 10. Verse 214, *patronus* (“patron”). The Badian and Schott editions in the margins have *patrone* (“O patron”), not improperly.

[Col. 0715D] 11. Verse 232, *moriendo* (“by dying”). The German Manuscript has *veniendo* (“by coming”).

[Col. 0715D] 12. Verse 287, *opertu* (“by a covering”). The German Manuscript with five editions has *operti* (“covered”).

[Col. 0715D] 13. Verse 289, *hoc potuit* (“this was able”). Thus the German Manuscript with Schott’s edition. The other manuscripts have *haec potuit* (“this was able,” feminine).

[Col. 0715D] 14. Verse 303, *reddat* (“may he render”). The German Manuscript and five editions have *reddit* (“he renders”).

[Col. 0715D] 15. Verse 308, *formaverat* (“he had formed”). The German Manuscript has *formaverit* (“he may have formed”).

## In Poem XXIV

[Col. 0715D] 1. Verse 18, *Intrarat* (“he had entered”). The Royal Manuscript has *Intraret* (“he might enter”). The Badian edition has *Intrabat* (“he was entering”).

[Col. 0715D] 2. Verse 29, *piger* (“sluggish”). Thus the Royal Manuscript and four editions in the margins. Five editions have *pio* (“devout”).

[Col. 0715D] 3. Verse 31, *Jamque* (“and now”). Five editions have *Namque* (“for”).

[Col. 0715D] 4. In the same place, *littorum* (“of shores”). The editions of Grin and Poelmann have *littore* (“on the shore”).

[Col. 0715D] 5. Verse 37, *temporis longo* (“with a long duration of time”). The true reading; likewise in poem 32, *exiguo temporis* (“with little time”). Three editions have *tempore ab longo* (“from a long time”).

[Col. 0715D] 6. Verse 103, *robora* (“strengths” or “oaks”). The Royal Manuscript has *robura*. And likewise elsewhere.

[Col. 0716A] 7. Verse 123, *permixtim* (“mixed together”). The Royal Manuscript has *permixte* (“in a mixed manner”).

[Col. 0716A] 8. Verse 165, *excitat* (“he arouses”). Three editions have *eripit* (“he snatches away”).

[Col. 0716A] 9. Verse 249, *cymba* (“boat”). The Royal Manuscript has *cumba* throughout. Prudentius likewise says *cumba* more than once, in *Peristephanon*, hymn 5, on St. Vincent the Martyr, verse 450, and in the *Diptych*, no. 35, etc.

[Col. 0716A] 10. Verse 254, *Dormisse* (“to have slept”). The Royal Manuscript has *Dormire* (“to sleep”).

[Col. 0716A] 11. Verse 315, *largos* (“generous” or “abundant”). SACCHIN: “Perhaps *largo … affectu* (‘with generous affection’)?”

[Col. 0716A] 12. Verse 321, *excalceus* (“unshod”). The Royal Manuscript and five editions have *excalcius* (“unshod”); and below, *calciari* (“to be shod”), always.

[Col. 0716A] 13. Verse 353, *paginatam* (“paged” or “joined into pages”). BARTHIUS: instead of *compaginatam* (“joined together”).

[Col. 0716A] 14. Verse 364, *Centumcellas*. The true reading. Five editions have *Centumcellis*. See note 275.

[Col. 0716A] 15. Verse 497, *Hierusales*. Thus in Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 813: “Then Hierusalem, illumined in the temple.” See Letter 18.5.

[Col. 0716A] 16. Verse 530, *Ephod*. The Royal Manuscript and three editions,
Ephot.

[Col. 0716A] 17 Verse 535, *Nazaraeus* (“Nazarene”). The Regius manuscript, together with edition 4, has *Nazarenus* (“Nazarene”).

[Col. 0716B] 18 Verse 577, *qui* (“who”). The Regius manuscript and five editions have *quia* (“because”).

[Col. 0716B] 19 Verse 719, *irretientis . . . illicem* (“of one ensnaring . . . [a] holm oak”). The Regius manuscript and five editions have *inretientis . . . inlicem* (“of one ensnaring . . . [a] holm oak”).

[Col. 0716B] 20 Verse 723, *letalibus* (“deadly”). This was restored in this form, since previously it had incorrectly been *laetalibus*.

[Col. 0716B] 21 Verse 871, *praeeunt* (“going before”), with the first syllable long, as above: *Quasi vinculatis praeerit* (“He will preside as over bound men”), verse 752.

[Col. 0716B] 22 Verse 873, *Utroque* (“in either way”), correctly used adverbially. Elsewhere *Utraque* and *Utraeque*, incorrectly.

[Col. 0716B] 23 Verse 894, *senibus* (“old men”). Schott’s edition has *senes* (“old men”).

[Col. 0716B] 24 Verse 925, *egentibus* (“the needy”). Schott’s edition has *urgentibus* (“pressing”).

[Col. 0716B] 25 Verse 935, *Sponsoque vectos obviam regi Deus* (“And God [brought] those conveyed to meet the bridegroom and king”). The editions of Bad., Grav., and Schott have *Sponsoque reginae obviam vectos Deus* (“And God [brought] those conveyed to meet the bridegroom and queen”). The editions of Grin. and Poelm. have *Sponsoque regi* (“and with the bridegroom to the king”), incorrectly. The Regius manuscript has *regis* (“of the king”).

[Col. 0716B]

## In Poem XXV

1. Verse 41, *sacerdotis* (“of the priest”). Schott’s edition has *sacerdotum* (“of the priests”).

2. Verse 42, *accipiet* (“he will receive”). Schott’s edition has *accipiat* (“let him receive”).

3. Verse 43, *inclusas* (“enclosed”). Schott’s edition has *inlusas*.

[Col. 0716C] 4. Verse 147, *Crescat ut* (“so that it may grow”). Schott’s edition has *Crescat et* (“and may it grow”).

5. Verse 186, *stet* (“may it stand”). Schott’s edition, in the margin, has *sit* (“may it be”).

6. Verse 187, *deserit* (“abandons”). Schott’s edition, in the margin, has *desinit* (“ceases”).

[Col. 0716C]

## In Poem XXVI

1. Verse 59, *deponere* (“to lay down”). Thus the German manuscript and Rosweyd’s edition. Five editions have *cognoscere* (“to know”).

2. Verse 170, *circum* (“around”). Four editions have *circa* (“around”).

3. Verse 176, *circa* (“around”). Four editions have *coram* (“before”).

4. Verse 195, *Isaias* (“Isaiah”). Bad.’s edition has *Esaeas*; Schott’s has *Isaeas*. This name is written in various ways: *Esaias* in the version of the Seventy translators, and in Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, books III and IV; in Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 5; in Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 16; and elsewhere. It appears as *Ezias* in Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 591, and in Alcimus Avitus, *Poem on the Praise of Virginity*.

[Col. 0716C] 5. Verse 197, *ipsum* (“himself/itself”). Three editions, in the margins, have *istum* (“that one/that”).

6. Verse 335, *Laxatumque* (“and loosened”). Bad.’s edition has *Lassatumque* (“and wearied”).

7. Verse 286, *aram* (“altar”). The editions of Grin. and Poelm. have *aulam* (“hall”).

[Col. 0716D]

## In Poem XXVII

1. Verse 8, *posses* (“you might be able”). The German manuscript has *possis* (“you may be able”).

2. Verse 32, *in alta* (“into the heights”). The German manuscript has *ad alta* (“toward the heights”).

3. Verse 35, *sacrosque* (“and sacred [masculine]”). The German manuscript has *sacrasque* (“and sacred [feminine]”).

4. Verse 48, *trepidans* (“trembling”). The German manuscript has *trepidus* (“tremulous”).

5. Verse 79, *Aeolio* (“Aeolian”). The German manuscript has *aerio* (“airy”).

6. Verse 84, *Fons opere, et finis, faciens* (“A source by work, and an end bringing about [something]”). The German manuscript has *Fons ope, fonsque opere; et faciens* (“A source by aid, and a source by work; and bringing about [something]”).

7. Verse 91, *seditque* (“and he sat”). The German manuscript has *sedetque* (“and he sits”).

8. Verse 92, *profudit* (“he poured forth”). The German manuscript has *profundit* (“he pours forth”).

9. Verse 96, *Pubis apostolicae concors* (“in agreement with the apostolic youth”). The German manuscript has *Plebis apostolicae consors* (“a companion of the apostolic people”).

10. Verse 100, *pectine* (“with a comb”). The German manuscript has *plectine*.

11. Verse 108, *ipse* (“he himself”). The German manuscript has *ipsa* (“she herself”).

12. Verse 110, *saltem* (“at least”). The German manuscript has *saltim* (“at least”); *semper* (“always”) is also reported.

13. Verse 134, *nec* (“and not”). Thus the German manuscript. Previously it was *ne* (“lest”).

14. Verse 151, *Nicetam* (“Nicetas”). Five editions have *Nicetan*, and likewise below.

15. Verse 175, *possem* (“I might be able”). The German manuscript has *possim* (“I may be able”).

[Col. 0717A] 16. Verse 176, *enarrare* (“to recount”). The German manuscript has *narrare* (“to relate”).

17. Verse 190, *Nicetam* (“Nicetas”). Three editions have *Nicetan*; two have *Niceten*.

18. Same place, *rursus* (“again”). The German manuscript has *rursum* (“again”).

19. Verse 194, *assideo* (“I sit beside”). The German manuscript has *adsedeo* (“I sit beside”).

20. Verse 204, *digneris* (“may you deign”). The German manuscript has *dignaris* (“you deign”).

21. Verse 215, *caesis* (“having been cut down”). The German manuscript has *scissis* (“having been split”).

22. Verse 218, *lenis* (“gentle”). Five editions have *levis* (“light”).

23. Verse 283, *cortex* (“bark”). The German manuscript has *cortix*.

24. Verse 292, *te mea* (“you, my [feminine]”). The German manuscript and the editions of Grav. and Schott, in the margins, have *me tua* (“me, your [feminine]”).

25. Verse 295, *nec* (“and not”). The German manuscript has *neque* (“nor”).

26. Verse 346, *Nodemus* (“let us bind”). Four editions have *Nos demus* (“let us give”).

27. Verse 387, *quantus* (“how great”). The German manuscript has *quantum* (“how much”).

28. Verse 389, *superne* (“from above”). The German manuscript has *superno* (“heavenly”).

29. Verse 399, *Duxerit* (“he will have led”). The German manuscript has *Duxerat* (“he had led”).

30. Verse 414, *Parte sui* (“by a part of himself”). Thus the German manuscript, Rosweyd’s edition, and Latinius. The editions have *Parta sua* (“his own part”) and *Parte sua* (“by his own part”), incorrectly.

31. Verse 421, *Et* (“and”). The German manuscript has *Ut* (“so that”).

32. Verse 442, *debita* (“owed”). The German manuscript has *reddita* (“given back”).

[Col. 0717B] 33. Verse 445, *quacumque* (“at whatever [time/place]”). Five editions have *quocumque* (“in whatever place”). **Sacchini:** either it is understood as *loco* (“place”), or rather one should read *quacumque*, that is, “at whatever time.”

34. Verse 450, *aget* (“he will do”). The German manuscript has *agit* (“he does”).

35. Verse 452, *volet* (“he will wish”). The German manuscript and five editions have *velit* (“he may wish”).

36. Verse 460, *Sint* (“let them be”). The German manuscript has *Sunt* (“they are”).

37. Verse 489, *sacra tecta* (“sacred roofs/buildings”). The German manuscript has *sacramenta* (“sacraments”).

38. Verse 546, *agat* (“he may do”). The German manuscript has *agit* (“he does”).

39. Verse 553, *decepti* (“deceived”). The German manuscript has *direpti* (“plundered”).

40. Verse 560, *haec* (“these things”). Thus the German manuscript together with four editions. Previously Rosweyd’s edition had *hic* (“here/he”).

41. Verse 569, *Mensa Petri* (“Peter’s table”). Five editions have *Mensque Petri* (“and Peter’s mind”).

42. Verse 581, *illudere* (“to mock”). The German manuscript and five editions have *ludere* (“to play”).

43. Verse 585, *explicuit* (“he unfolded/explained”). The German manuscript has *explevit* (“he fulfilled”).

44. Verse 587, *Sunt* (“they are”). Thus the German manuscript. The editions have *Sint* (“let them be”).

[Col. 0717C] 45. Verse 591, *potatur* (“is drunk”). Five editions have *suadetur* (“is advised”).

46. Verse 595, *superant* (“surpass”). The German manuscript has *subeunt* (“go beneath/approach”). Four editions have *suberunt* (“they will be beneath”).

47. Verse 596, *Quod superest ex his quae facta et picta videmus* (“What remains of these things that we see made and painted”). The German manuscript and five printed editions have *Quae superest his quae facta et quae picta videmus* (“What remains for these things that we see made and that we see painted”).

48. Verse 601, *mei* (“of me”). The German manuscript and five editions have *Dei* (“of God”).

49. Verse 609, *exposito* (“having been set forth”). The German manuscript has *exposita* (“having been set forth [feminine]”).

## In Poem XXVIII

[Col. 0717C] 1. Verse 2, *ritu* (“by ritual/custom”). The German manuscript and the editions of Grav. and Schott, in the margins, have *voto* (“by a vow”).

2. Verse 10, *adjunctae* (“having been joined”). The German manuscript has *adjunctis* (“having been joined [plural/dative or ablative]”).

3. Verse 11, *sinu* (“in the bosom”). The German manuscript and five editions have *situ* (“in position”).

4. Verse 16, *qua* (“by which”). The German manuscript has *quo* (“by which [masculine/neuter]”).

5. Verse 17, *protenditur* (“is stretched forth”). The German manuscript has *pertenditur* (“is extended”).

[Col. 0718A] 6. Verse 25, *Tobit* (“Tobit”). The German manuscript has *Tobi*.

7. Verse 29, *super* (“above/on”). One edition of Rosweyd has *supra* (“above”).

8. Verse 43, *mira spatiantibus arte* (“with wonderful skill for those walking about”). The German manuscript together with Schott’s edition has *mirum spectantibus apta* (“wonderfully suitable for spectators”).

9. Verse 47, *jocos* (“jokes/games”). The German manuscript and the editions of Grin. and Poelm. have *lacus* (“lakes”).

10. Verse 65, *foedo* (“by the foul thing”). The German manuscript and Schott’s edition, in the margin, have *foedaque* (“and foul things”).

11. Verse 67, *interjectu* (“by an interposition”). The German manuscript has *interjactu*.

12. Verse 89, *vico* (“in the village”). Five editions have *vicis* (“in the villages”).

13. Verse 115, *saluti* (“for salvation”). The German manuscript has *salutis* (“of salvation”).

14. Verse 146, *flagrasse* (“to have burned”). The German manuscript has *flagrare* (“to burn”).

15. Verse 150, *Utilibus* (“useful things”). The editions of Bad. and Grav. have *Utilius* (“more usefully”).

16. Verse 157, *mulctatus* (“punished”). The German manuscript has *multatur* (“is punished”).

17. Verse 167, *dimoto* (“having been moved away”). The German manuscript has *demoto* (“having been removed”).

18. Verse 176, *Ut* (“so that”). The German manuscript has *Et* (“and”).

19. Verse 245, *dicens* (“saying”). The German manuscript has *dicitque* (“and he says”).

[Col. 0718B] 20. Verse 251, *Aethiopas* (“Ethiopians”). The German manuscript has *Aethiopes* (“Ethiopians”).

21. Verse 264, *operis* (“of the work”). The German manuscript has *operum* (“of the works”).

22. Verse 275, *priores* (“the earlier ones”). The German manuscript has *prioris* (“of the earlier one”).

23. Verse 283, *nascuntur* (“are born”). Thus the German manuscript and five editions. Rosweyd’s edition has *nascantur* (“may be born”).

24. Verse 294, *servata* (“having been preserved”). The German manuscript has *reserata* (“having been unlocked”).

25. Verse 300, *Icta* (“struck”). The German manuscript has *Jacta* (“thrown”).

## In Poem XXXV

[Col. 0718B] 1. Verse 76, *in peccato daemon* (“a demon in sin”). Thus the manuscripts of Poelm. and Regius, and three editions in the margin, together with Rosweyd. But five editions have *in peccatis, hostis* (“in sins, the enemy”).

2. Verse 78, *praecipitare* (“to hurl headlong”). A verb of active force used in place of the passive; for *praecipitari* (“to be hurled headlong”) ought to have been written. Barthius noted many examples of this kind, and of this same verb, in *The Venatics* and Apuleius.

3. Verse 144, *ante obitum* (“before death”). Thus the Regius manuscript and three editions in the margins, together with Rosweyd. Five editions have *ante fuit* (“it was before”).

4. Verse 246, *labe* (“by stain”). Barthius read *tabe* (“by corruption”).

[Col. 0718C] 5. Verse 256, *frugibus* (“fruits/crops”). The Regius manuscript has *fructibus* (“fruits”).

6. Verse 409, *juvat* (“it helps/pleases”). Schott’s edition, in the margin, has *lubet* (“it pleases”).

7. Verse 419, *suggeret ad lacrymarum, etc.* (“will provide for tears, etc.”). Three editions have *suggereret lacrymarum ad, etc.* (“would provide tears for, etc.”). Both readings are good.

8. Same place, *flumina* (“rivers”). The editions of Bad. and Grav. have *lumina* (“lights”).

9. Verse 452, *teget* (“will cover”). Schott’s edition has *tegit* (“covers”).

10. Verse 455, *mactabis* (“you will sacrifice”). Schott’s edition has *mactabit* (“he will sacrifice”).

11. Verse 456, *esuriam* (“hunger”). Thus the Regius manuscript and four editions. Rosweyd’s edition has *esuriem* (“hunger”), incorrectly.

12. Verse 581, *Aut illum gremio exceptum fovet Abramio* (“Or Abraham cherishes him, received into his bosom”). Thus, together with Rosweyd’s edition, the Regius manuscript. Five printed editions have *Aut illum gremio fidei pater excipit almo* (“Or the father of faith receives him in his nourishing bosom”).

13. Verse 603, *viretis* (“in the green places/groves”). The Regius manuscript together with the editions of Bad. and Schott, in the margin, has *virectis* (“in the green places/groves”).

14. Verse 624, *Dic et* (“say also”). The editions of Grin., Poelm., and Schott have *Dices* (“you will say”).

# Appendix of the Works of Saint Paulinus, Containing Doubtful, Foreign, and Falsely Attributed Works

[Col. 0717]

## Letters

[Col. 0717]

### [Letters.(C,G,S)\*]

[Note: [Col. 0717] Additional notes on these letters were printed by Migne as a separate document in columns 735–738. Each superscript number in the text of the letters refers to the corresponding note in that separate document.]

## Letter I [Note: [Col. 0717D] Also numbered 49.]

[Col. 0717D]

The author discusses the good of tribulation, through which he congratulates Marcella on having advanced in the pursuits of piety [Note: [Col. 0717D] See Dissertation 6, no. 2.]

### 1

The love of Christ has given our humility great confidence to write to your veneration [Col. 0718D]; it has made you humble in heart through piety and rich in works of blessing. For such a reputation of the holy riches of your faith has gone forth that it has reached even us, who are placed far away, and by hearing of the grace of God has fattened our bones as with the oil of gladness. [Note: [Col. 0719C] Thus three manuscript codices, Jol. 1 and Victor. 2, together with the Mainz, Roman, and Ponce editions. But Rosweyd’s edition has *gratia* (“grace”).] [Note: [Col. 0717D] This letter was attributed to Paulinus by the Roman associate, when volume IX of Jerome either preferred Jerome himself or an uncertain author. Since Paulinus lived chiefly at Nola, and Rome, where Marcella lived, is nearby, Paulinus could not have been far from her unless he wrote to her when he first embraced a stricter way of life in Spain. Rosweyd.] For your goodness has become known to us, because the Lord has illumined his face over you. He separated you from the womb of your kindred and your land—not geographically, but in the spirit of good will—in order that, from earthly riches, he might make you faithful to him and a participant in those riches in heaven, concerning which it is written: “Wise women built houses for themselves” [Note: [Col. 0719] Proverbs XIV, 1, according to the Septuagint.].

Having heard these things about your heavenly happiness, we poured out our hearts before God and, feasting in a voice of rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm XLI, 5.], said: “The Lord puts to death, the Lord gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back. The Lord makes the rich poor; he exalts the humble” [Note: [Col. 0719] I Samuel II, 6.], because “the cup is in the hand of the Lord; he humbles this one and exalts that one” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm LXXIV, 9.]. Although this seems to pertain to the whole mystery of the kingdom, nevertheless it can also be referred specifically to your grace: by the great counsel of the Lord’s mercy you have been exalted in order that you might be humbled, and, having been humbled, in order that you might be exalted. [Note: [Col. 0719C] The Jolian and first Victorine manuscripts have *humilieris . . . exalteris* (“you may be humbled . . . you may be exalted”).] [Note: [Col. 0719C] We have added this from three manuscript codices, Jol. 1, and Victor. 2, together with the Mainz, Roman, and Ponce editions. See what follows.]

### 2

For we do not fail to know, venerable sister and blessed daughter, your former glory in this world. Indeed, we also saw you at the time when royal kinship surrounded your household, distinguished by those honors that are destroyed. For although these honors too are bestowed by the Most High Lord, since “all authority is from God” [Note: [Col. 0719] Romans XIII, 1.], nevertheless the things conducted under this world are fleeting and fragile, whose outward form passes away like a shadow.

Therefore we admire all the more the grace that has been given to you, and we glorify the Lord in you, who placed you amid the labors of human beings and visited you with the saving scourge of a father’s affection, so that, afflicted in a few things, he might order many things well for you, as the Apostle testifies: “In this world we are chastened, so that we may not be condemned with this world” [Note: [Col. 0719] I Corinthians XI, 32.]. Hence David also says: “Let the righteous man chastise me in mercy and rebuke me; but let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm CXL, 5.].

Thus, undoubtedly, you have learned in your spiritual studies that it is also written in Solomon: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves and scourges” [Note: [Col. 0719] Proverbs III, 32, according to the Septuagint.]; “he disciplines every son whom he deigns to receive” [Note: [Col. 0719] II Corinthians XI, 30.], to be directed toward eternal life. The Apostle is not ashamed of this, nor is he crushed by it; rather, he glories and becomes powerful in his weaknesses. To strengthen us by his example, he confesses and proclaims this about himself—even though an ascent had been opened to him as far as the third heaven, and although that fiery sword could not exclude him from the entrance to Paradise, where he had heard a mystery ineffable to every tongue [Note: [Col. 0720C] The Jolian manuscript together with the Mainz edition has *patuerat* (“had been opened”).]. Yet, lest he be exalted because of the greatness of the revelations, he reports that he was governed by the Lord’s direction—by whom he had been glorified so greatly—so that, when an angel of Satan was placed as a thorn for his flesh, that is, as bodily tribulation [Note: [Col. 0720C] Thus the same codices. Others have “bodily affliction.”], he might be beneficially humbled and not vainly puffed up. “Because of this,” he says, “I besought the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” [Note: [Col. 0719] II Corinthians XII, 8.].

### 3

Therefore, instructed by such a teacher and author [Note: [Col. 0719] See Paulinus, Letter 30, no. 5.], place your confidence, daughter, in the virtue of patience and the hope of eternal glory, as you have begun to do, and glory in your past sufferings, remembering also the words of that same teacher. For, faithfully, as one acquainted with heavenly mysteries [Col. 0720A], he testifies that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0719] Romans VIII, 18.]. “Tribulation,” he says, “produces patience; patience, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts” [Note: [Col. 0719] Romans V, 3.], in which love [Note: [Col. 0720C] We have added this word from three manuscript codices and four printed editions.] we are rooted and endure all things.

Therefore David also says: “I shall love you, Lord, my strength” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm XVII, 2, according to the Roman Psalter.]. For love of the Lord is the strength of salvation, because “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God” [Note: [Col. 0720C] Three manuscripts together with the Mainz edition have *caritate* (“love”); others have *dilectione* (“love”).] [Note: [Col. 0719] I John IV, 16.]. The prophet too, knowing that “the momentary tribulation of this world produces an immeasurable weight of eternal glory,” as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0719] II Corinthians IV, 17.], that holy king says in the psalm, in order to be judged worthy to be refined by the test of temptations: “Test me, Lord, and try me” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm XXV, 2.].

Hence again that same psalmist of ours [Note: [Col. 0720C] The Jolian manuscript and the Mainz edition have *psalmigraphus* (“psalm-writer”).], as though repenting of the glory of this world, confesses when he says: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm CXVIII, 67.]. And because he had been healed by humiliation, he immediately says: “Therefore I kept your word.”

For this reason the prophet says again: “Give us help from tribulation”; and: “The salvation of man is vain” [Col. 0720B] [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm LIX, 13.]. For human salvation is vain when it is thought to exist only in this mortal life, of which it is said to man: “Man’s days are like grass” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm CII, 15.].

And indeed, holy daughter, you have also been taught by experience to prove the saying, because “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the word of the Lord, and he who made it, remains forever” [Note: [Col. 0719] Isaiah XL, 6–8.]. [Note: [Col. 0720C] These words were added as far as “Therefore” from three manuscript codices and the Mainz edition.] So too the Lord himself remains forever, he who is before the ages. Therefore it was truly said: “The salvation of man is vain” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm LIX, 13.], because all things beneath heaven are vain. Hence you have in the Psalms: “Every living man is wholly vanity” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm XXXVIII, 6.].

### 4

But what class of people he means by this, he teaches in what follows: namely, those who are vainly troubled by love of their riches, at which, like blind beasts, they gape without end in their desire to acquire and accumulate, “storing up on earth and not knowing for whom they gather them” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ibid., 7.]. “He will leave his riches to strangers,” he says [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm XLVIII, 11.]. And when their days have failed in vanity, all of them—carried off to the underworld, not masters but slaves of their riches—will find nothing there in their hands [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm LXXV, 6.], because they sent nothing ahead except the merits of eternal punishments.

But that is not [Note: [Col. 0720C] The Jolian manuscript has *vacua* (“empty”).] the vain salvation of man of which it is said: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm III, 9.]. And again: “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm XXXVI, 39.]. Therefore hope placed in God will not disappoint [Note: [Col. 0719] Romans V, 5.], because the salvation hoped for in Christ and bestowed by Christ is not vain.

### 5

Therefore, because you have received help from tribulation [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm LIX, 13.], so that you would not desire the human day or rejoice in the vain salvation of man, glory in the Lord and bless him who granted you understanding [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm XV, 7.], so that you would not persist in standing in the way of sinners, nor remain among the children of this generation, for whom there is no salvation [Note: [Col. 0719] Psalm CXLV, 3, according to the Septuagint]. For they grow strong in their vanity, forgetful of truth. While they trust in the abundance of their riches, they do not make God their helper.

But for you a lot has fallen in the inheritance of Jacob, and your eyes have been enlightened for recognition of the truth, so that you might understand that “a little for the righteous is better than the many riches of sinners” [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm XXXVI, 16.].

[Col. 0721A] Therefore the merciful and compassionate Lord [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm CX, 4.], because he prepares his inventions for such people in order to extend human life, permitted you to be tossed by the waves and winds of this age, so that, having experienced shipwreck, you would thereafter beware of undergoing similar danger. Thus everything that you have suffered was, as you understand, indeed wounds to your body, but also remedies for your soul.

### 6

Perform your works in the circumcision of your heart, so that your glory may not be from human beings but from God [Note: [Col. 0721] Romans II, 29.], who “casts the powerful down from their seat and exalts the humble; he fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty” [Note: [Col. 0721] Luke I, 52.].

God, Lord of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0721] I Samuel II, 3.], see how he has changed your great glory by recompense [Note: [Col. 0721C] Thus three manuscripts and the Ponce edition. This reading is confirmed below, in no. 8: “which will be recompensed to you by God.” The Roman edition has *repensatione* (“repayment”); Rosweyd’s edition has *compensatione* (“compensation”).], preferring that you become a participant in heavenly things rather than remain until the end among earthly things, so that you might pass from human dignity into the kingdom of God.

Indeed, God graciously offers many people, captivated by the vanity of this age, similar aids for attaining eternal salvation. But [Note: [Col. 0721C] We have restored this from three manuscripts, Victor. 2, and Jol. 1 [Col. 0721D], and from the printed editions of Mainz, Ponce, and Rome; previously most copies had “despising.”] most people, with the sound counsels of their minds overcome by the cares of riches [Col. 0721B] and bodily pleasures, do not wish to understand so as to act well; they prefer to wander with the many along the broad road of destruction rather than find the narrow path with the few [Note: [Col. 0721] Matthew VII, 13.].

Therefore you also, most blessed woman, to whom it has been granted not to be hardened by pious chastisement but to be corrected, and not to glory in riches but to place your hope and substance [Note: [Col. 0721] See Letter 32, no. 3, verse 18.] in God, and to be separated from the lot of sinful rich people [Note: [Col. 0721D] This word is absent from two Victorine manuscripts and the Mainz edition.], whose heart is like mud because they sink their heart, like their treasure, into the earth: pass over to the lot of the blessed poor, whose form Christ assumed and “became a refuge for the poor” [Note: [Col. 0721D] Thus the editions, in agreement with the Greek and the Vulgate. Two Victorine manuscripts have *pauperi* (“for the poor man”); the Jolian manuscript has *pauperum* (“of the poor”).] [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm IX, 10.]. Not the rich, but the poor are blessed, for he declares that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them [Note: [Col. 0721] Matthew V, 3.].

### 7

It is therefore now your task, in great thanksgiving, to confess and sing praise to the Lord. As we have heard, you have been so adorned in both dress and heart with humility that David’s words are fitting for your tongue and mind: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications” [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm CXVIII, 71.].

You will also truly be able to add what immediately follows [Note: [Col. 0721D] This word is lacking in the Mainz edition and in the Jolian and first Victorine manuscripts. The other Victorine manuscript has *jure* (“rightly”).]: “The law of your mouth is good for me, above thousands of gold and silver” [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm CXVIII, 72.]. For you have chosen to place your treasures in the commandments of the Most High.

We too, rejoicing with you, say in the words of the prophet: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; be glad, daughter of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0721] Zechariah II, 10, according to the Septuagint.], and forget the evils that arose for you from the good things of this age, since you have chosen for yourself the good portion that will not be taken away from you [Note: [Col. 0721] Luke X, 42.].

For no one can take away the treasures stored in Christ’s bosom [Note: [Col. 0721D] The Jolian manuscript together with the Mainz edition has “hidden treasures”; but “You have chosen to place your treasures in the commandments of the Most High” has already preceded.], nor overthrow the house founded upon the very cornerstone.

You have not placed your building upon rotten wood, fragile straw, or withering hay, on unstable sand; rather, upon the immovable foundation that is Christ, “besides which no one can lay another foundation” [Note: [Col. 0721] I Corinthians III, 11.], you have begun to build in Christ with silver, gold, and precious stones [Note: [Col. 0721] Ibid., 12.]; the transmitted *inconsummandum* (“not to be completed”) is syntactically uncertain.

And because you are completing this building—for it is God’s building [Note: [Col. 0721] Ibid., 9.]—that wise architect applies himself to your work, teaching you to run the good course, to forget what lies behind, and to stretch toward the prize of the heavenly calling [Note: [Col. 0721] Philippians III, 13.], so that you may grasp that for which you have been grasped, and receive the crown of righteousness and the diadem of glory from the hand of the Lord.

And when that great day begins to be revealed in fire [Note: [Col. 0721] I Corinthians III, 13.], your work will not be consumed by the testing of the wise fire [Note: [Col. 0721D] We have corrected this from three manuscript codices and the Roman and Ponce editions. The printed editions previously had “by the test of the consuming fire.” But the restored reading is entirely correct, and is confirmed by a very similar passage in Letter 28 to Severus, no. 2: “This is that house not made by hands; if we dwell in it through works by which we may deserve to become fellow citizens of the saints, our work will not burn. And that wise fire, passing us through its testing, will not surround us for punishment with harsh heat, but, receiving us as approved, will touch us gently with a soothing caress,” etc. The wise fire also appears in Augustine; it is called wise because, as though by a certain wisdom infused into it by God, it distinguishes those whom it ought to test from those whom it ought to burn. See Paulinus, poem 7, verses 32 and following.], but will be tested [Note: [Col. 0721] See Letter 28 to Severus, no. 2.].

May your lamp not be extinguished, but shine among the brighter stars, among those who “will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0721] Matthew XIII, 43.], and “like the moon perfected forever” [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm LXXXVIII, 38.], whom the sun will not burn by day, nor the moon by night [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm CXX, 6.]. For they will remain in Jerusalem, that heavenly city, [Col. 0722B] for which the Lord himself, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0721] Revelation XXI, 23.], will be both name and light.

### 8

Therefore, seeing and foreseeing in the spirit of revelation [Note: [Col. 0722D] One Victorine manuscript has: “that a great harvest of everlasting joys may blossom for you.” The Vulgate confirms the reading we retain, as does the passage in Letter 13 to Pammachius, no. 23. Nor is the day of recompense far away, since the fields already whiten with the approaching harvest.], that a great harvest of everlasting joys is blossoming for you, we rejoice in the Lord and, rejoicing in your fruits, sing in the voice of the psalm of gladness [Note: [Col. 0722D] Three manuscripts together with the Mainz edition have *dicimus* (“we say”). But *canimus* (“we sing”) agrees better with “the voice of gladness” and with the verse of the psalm to which he alludes.]: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his desires” [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalm CX, 2.].

For his goodness has greatly abounded [Note: [Col. 0721] See Letter 42, no. 1.] beyond your tribulations, since he has called you into their lot with everlasting joy, a heavenly inheritance, royal honor, and a place in the super-judicial assembly.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] One Victorine manuscript has *Tolerandae . . . humilitatis passiones* (“The humiliations of suffering must be endured”); the Jolian manuscript has *Toleratae* (“having been endured”).]

The humiliations of suffering that God will recompense to you must be endured in this age. And you, blessed woman, likewise [Note: [Col. 0722D] The Roman and Ponce editions have *consolare* (“console yourself”) between these words; the received reading is supported by manuscript authority and confirmed by the passage from the letter cited above, no. 24.] console yourself in the meantime with these words, so that you may both forget your former sorrows and, strengthened in the present undertaking by which you have raised your hands to works of salvation with a perfect heart, confidently promise yourself, in festive meditation, perpetual happiness in future blessings [Note: [Col. 0721] See Letter 13, no. 24, and Letter 17, no. 1.], and run ahead of yourself into heaven with an eager spirit [Note: [Col. 0722D] The Jolian manuscript together with the Roman and Ponce editions has “carrying a spirit”; the text has a lacuna.].

Thus, while you remain bodily on earth, may you already reach Christ in mind; and while you strive to imitate Christ and cling to his footsteps, having laid aside the burdens, impediments, and chains by which the rich of this age are held—those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0721] Psalms LXXXVII, 7, and CVI, 10.]—may you, already liberated and unencumbered, accompany the crucified Lord of majesty.

No one can bear his image unless in this age he makes himself naked and dead, so that, according to the Lord himself, he may say: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” [Note: [Col. 0723] John XIV, 30.]; or, according to the prophet David: “I have become like a dead man among the living” [Note: [Col. 0723] Psalm LXXXVII, 6.], so that, among the dead, you may be free and able to say with the Apostle: “Yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me” [Note: [Col. 0723] Galatians II, 20.]. [Note: [Col. 0723D] These two words are absent from three manuscript codices and two editions.]

Rejoice, because you have become like the glorious Judith, powerful among the virtues of chastity through the merits of uncorrupted widowhood, and like the venerable Anna, devoted to prayer night and day in the chastity of fasting.

## Letter II [Note: [Col. 0723D] Also numbered 50.]

The author teaches the noble matron Celancia, who had earnestly asked him about this subject, how to live her life in holiness and devotion amid honors, riches, and the burdens of marriage. He urges her to read divine Scripture; and, warning her not to be proud of the nobility of her lineage, teaches where true nobility lies and also what she owes her husband. Finally, he rebukes her for having vowed chastity to God without consulting her husband. (See Dissertation 6, no. 2.)

### 1

It is an old and celebrated saying of Scripture that there is a modesty by which glory and grace are found, and there is again a modesty that ordinarily gives birth to sin [Note: [Col. 0723] Ecclesiasticus IV, 25.]. Although the truth of this saying shines clearly enough by its own light for everyone’s understanding, it has nevertheless, somehow, become more closely known to me in the present case.

Provoked to write by your letters, which begged this of me with remarkable entreaties, I confess that I hesitated for a long time over my reply, with modesty commanding me to remain silent. Yet the faithful eagerness of your prayers [Note: [Col. 0723] That is, your earnestness.] resisted it most forcefully and compelled me; and the humility of the one making the request fought fiercely with my hesitation. With a great violence of faith it beat upon the barriers of my mouth. While different reflections thus balanced my wavering mind between the two alternatives, modesty almost excluded the duty of writing.

But the saying of the Wise Man that I quoted above armed me to drive away useless modesty and undo harmful silence. For I saw that the very reason for writing was so honorable and so holy that I believed I would sin if I remained silent, recalling to myself this passage of Scripture: “A time to be silent, and a time to speak” [Note: [Col. 0723D] Ecclesiasticus III, 7.]. And again: “Do not withhold a word in the time of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0723] Ecclesiasticus IV, 28.]. And that of blessed Peter: “Always ready to give satisfaction to everyone who asks you for an account” [Note: [Col. 0723] I Peter III, 15.].

### 2

For you ask—indeed, you ask earnestly and insistently—that we establish for you from the holy Scriptures a definite rule by which you may order the course of your life; that, having learned the Lord’s will, amid the honors of the world and the allurements of riches, you may love rather the furnishings of good character; and that, being established in marriage, you may please not only your spouse but also the one who granted the marriage.

Not to satisfy so holy a request and so pious a desire—what else is that than not to love another’s progress? I shall therefore obey your prayers and strive to encourage you, prepared as you are to fulfill the Lord’s will, by the Lord’s own sayings.

For the true Lord and Teacher of all is the one who commands us to please him and teaches us how we may please him [Note: [Col. 0723] Matthew XIX, 17.]. Let him therefore shape you; let him teach you—the one who, when the young man in the Gospel asked what he should do to deserve eternal life, immediately set forth the divine commandments, showing us that the will of the one from whom we hope for rewards must be done.

For this reason he testifies elsewhere: “Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0723] Matthew VII, 21.]. This plainly shows that we do not earn the greatness of so great a reward by confessing God alone, unless works of faith and righteousness are joined to that confession.

### 3

For what sort of confession is it that believes in God in such a way as to count his command as nothing? Or how do we say sincerely and truly, “Lord, Lord,” if we despise the commandments of the one whom we confess as Lord?

Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?” [Note: [Col. 0723] Luke VI, 4.] And again: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” [Note: [Col. 0723] Matthew XV, 8.]. And again he speaks through the prophet: “A son honors his father, and a servant fears his master. And if I am Father, where is my honor? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?” [Note: [Col. 0723] Malachi I, 6.].

From this [Note: [Col. 0723D] The Jolian manuscript has *patet* (“it is evident”).] it is clear that the Lord is neither honored nor feared by those who do not do his commandments. Hence it is said more explicitly to David, who had committed sin: “And you counted the Lord as nothing” [Note: [Col. 0723D] From the Jolian manuscript we have restored *Dominum* (“the Lord”) in accordance with the Greek. Previously the text had *Deum* (“God”). The Vulgate and Septuagint have “you despised the word of the Lord.”].

And the word of the Lord comes to Eli: “Whoever honors me, I will honor; but whoever treats me as nothing will be reduced to nothing” [Note: [Col. 0723D] Lucifer’s version has: “and whoever despises me will be reduced to nothing.”] [Note: [Col. 0723] I Samuel II, 30.].

## 4.

And are we secure and well-disposed, we who through each and every sin [Note: [Col. 0724D] The Jolian manuscript adds “of God” (*Dei*). The Roman and Poncian printed editions read: “through each and every sin” (*per singula quaeque peccata*).] and each and every commandment dishonor the most merciful God, provoke the Lord [Note: [Col. 0724D] The two Victor manuscripts, Jolian manuscript 1, and the Roman and Poncian editions add “the Lord” (*Dominum*).] to anger, and, by treating his command with the utmost arrogance, commit an outrage against such great majesty? For what could ever appear so arrogant, or indeed so ungrateful, as to live contrary to the will of him from whom you received life itself? What could be more contemptuous than to despise the precepts of him who commands something for the very purpose of having grounds on which to reward us? For God does not need our obedience; rather, we need his command.

“His commandments are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; for in keeping them there is great reward” [Note: [Col. 0723] Psalm 18:11.]. And therefore he is angry with us, and the immeasurable goodness of God is all the more offended, because we despise it even at the cost of forfeiting so great a reward. We treat not only his commands [Note: [Col. 0724D] Three manuscript codices, Victor and Jolian, with the Roman edition, read as above; Rosweyde’s printed edition has *imperata*, “things commanded.”] but also his promises as nothing. Hence that saying of the Lord must often—indeed always—be turned over in our minds: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” [Note: [Col. 0723] Matthew 19:17.]. For this is the whole concern of the Law with us; this is what the prophets teach, what the apostles teach; this is what both the voice and the blood of Christ demand from us. He died for all for this reason: so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them [Note: [Col. 0723] 2 Corinthians 5:15.].

To live for him means nothing other than to keep his commandments, which he entrusted to us for observance as a sure pledge, so to speak, of his love. “If you love me,” he says, “keep my commandments. And whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me.” And again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words” [Note: [Col. 0723] John 14:15 and 21.].

True love possesses great force. And the one who is perfectly loved claims for himself the whole will of the lover [Col. 0724D] [Note: [Col. 0724D] So read all the manuscripts except Rosweyde’s edition, which has “vindicates.”]. Nothing is more commanding than love. If we truly love Christ, if we remember that we were redeemed by his blood, we ought to wish and do absolutely nothing more than what we know him to wish.

## 5.

There are two kinds of commandments, in which the whole of righteousness is contained: one consists in prohibitions, the other in commands. Just as evils are prohibited, so good things are commanded. In the former case inactivity is required; in the latter, exertion. There the mind is restrained; here it is stirred up.

There, doing something is blameworthy; here, failing to do it is blameworthy [Note: [Col. 0725D] Thus the Julian manuscript follows appropriately from what precedes, whereas elsewhere the reading is: “here, to have done; there, not to have done.” The same manuscript adds after “is blameworthy”: “The person who desires life and wishes to see good days.”]. Hence the prophet also says: “Who is the person who desires life and wishes to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good” [Note: [Col. 0725] Psalm 34:13–15.]. And the blessed Apostle says: “Hating evil, clinging to what is good” [Note: [Col. 0725] Romans 12:9.].

This twofold and distinct command, namely, that of prohibiting and that of ordering, has been imposed upon everyone by an equal right. Neither virgin, widow, nor married woman is free from this command. In every calling and in every rank, it is an equal sin either to do what is forbidden or not to do what is commanded. Do not let yourself be deceived by the error of those who, according to their own judgment, choose which of God’s commandments they will chiefly perform and despise others as worthless and insignificant; nor do they fear that, according to the divine sentence, by despising what is least they may gradually fall away.

## 6.

It is characteristic of the Stoics to abolish distinctions among sins, to judge all offenses equal, and to make no distinction between a crime and a mistake [Note: [Col. 0725D] Paulinus, poem 5, line 52: “If I abstain from crime, I am nevertheless liable to error,” etc.]. They make no distinction between a heinous offense and an error [Note: [Col. 0725] Jerome, in Book II Against Jovinianus, and Augustine, Letter 167 (formerly 29) to Jerome, refute this Stoic opinion.].

We, however, although we believe that sins differ greatly—for we also read this—nevertheless say that it is very useful for caution to guard even the smallest sins as though they were the greatest [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Julian and first Victor manuscripts read “to fear the smallest as though they were the greatest.”]. For we abstain from any offense all the more easily the more we fear it; and the one who fears even small offenses does not quickly advance to greater ones.

Indeed, I do not know whether we can call any sin slight when it is committed in contempt of God. The wisest person is the one who considers not so much what has been commanded as who commanded it; who thinks not about the magnitude of the command but about the dignity of the one commanding.

## 7.

Therefore, as you build a spiritual house—not upon the lightness of sand but upon the solidity of rock—let the foundation of innocence first be laid, upon which you can more easily raise the lofty summit of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Julian manuscript reads: “upon which the lofty summit of righteousness may more easily rise.”]. For the greater part of equity has been fulfilled by the one who has harmed no one. Blessed is the person who can say with holy Job: “I have harmed no human being; I have lived justly with everyone” [Note: [Col. 0725] Job 27:6.].

Hence he spoke boldly and frankly to the Lord: “Who is he who will bring a judgment against me?” [Note: [Col. 0725] Job 13:19.] That is: Who can appeal to your judgment against me and prove that I have injured him? It belongs to a most pure conscience to sing confidently with the prophet: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” [Note: [Col. 0725D] So read the Roman and Poncian editions and the Victor manuscript, in accordance with the Greek and the Vulgate. See the same passage at the end of the letter, no. 32. Rosweyde’s edition has “your house.”] [Note: [Col. 0725] Psalm 101:2.].

Therefore the same man says elsewhere: “God has not defrauded those who walk in innocence of good things” [Note: [Col. 0725D] In Greek, Κύριος οὐχ ὑστερήσει τὰ ἀγαθά: “The Lord will not withhold good things.” The four Psalters and Augustine on the Psalms read: “He will not deprive.”] [Note: [Col. 0725] Psalm 84:13.].

Accordingly, the Christian soul must drive away malice, hatred, and envy, which are either the greatest or the only seeds of doing harm. It must guard innocence not only with hand or tongue but also with the heart; and it must fear doing harm not only by deed but also by intention. For insofar as the matter concerns sin, the one who intended to harm has also done harm.

Many of our writers define as absolutely and wholly innocent the person who harms no one even in failing to do good [Note: [Col. 0726D] The printed editions of Erasmus and Rosweyde omit “Many” (*Multi*).]. If this is true, then rejoice at the consciousness of your innocence only if, when you are able, you do not cease to help. But if these things are separate and distinct—if not harming is one thing, which you can always do, and doing good another, when you are able; if not doing evil is one thing and doing good another—then let this thought return to you: it is not enough for a Christian to fulfill one part of righteousness, when both are commanded.

## 8.

For we must not look to the examples of the multitude, which, following no discipline of conduct and holding to no order of life, is guided less by reason than carried along by a kind of impulse [Note: [Col. 0726D] The first Victor manuscript, together with the Roman and Poncian editions, reads: “For it is not fitting that we should look to the life of the wicked multitude, which …”]. Nor should we imitate those who, under the Christian name, live a pagan life and bear witness to one thing in their profession and another in their conduct; as the Apostle says, “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” [Note: [Col. 0725] Titus 1:16.].
