A Christian must be distinguished from a pagan not only by faith but also by life, and a different religion must be shown through different works. “Do not be yoked,” says the Apostle, “with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” [Note: [Col. 0725] 2 Corinthians 6:14.] [Note: [Col. 0726D] Thus three manuscript codices and the Roman edition read *luci*, “light,” in accordance with the Greek and the Vulgate. Rosweyde’s edition has *lucis*, “of light.”]

## 9.

Let there therefore be the greatest separation between us and them [Note: [Col. 0726D] The Julian manuscript reads “let it be distinguished”; two Victor manuscripts, together with the Roman and Poncian editions, also read “let it be distinguished.”]. Error and truth are separated by a clear distinction [Note: [Col. 0725] This figure of speech is very familiar to Paulinus.].

Let those who do not possess the promises of heaven set their minds on earthly things. Let those who do not know eternal life devote themselves wholly to this brief life [Note: [Col. 0726D] The Julian manuscript reads: “who do not know eternal life.”]. Let those who think sins go unpunished not fear to sin. Let those who do not hope for future rewards serve their vices.

But we, who confess with the purest faith that every person must be revealed before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil [Note: [Col. 0725] 2 Corinthians 5:10.], must be far from vices. For the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” [Note: [Col. 0725] Galatians 5:24.]. Those who profess themselves disciples of truth must not follow the wandering crowd.

## 10.

Certainly the Savior displays in the Gospel two ways of life and paths of living that diverge in opposite directions: “How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it” [Note: [Col. 0726D] The Julian manuscript adds: “saying, ‘How broad and spacious is the way …’”] [Note: [Col. 0725] Matthew 7:13.]. And again: “How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” [Note: [Col. 0725] Ibid., 14.].

See how great the separation between these ways is, and how great the difference. The one leads to death; the other reaches toward life. The former is celebrated and trodden by many; the latter is scarcely found by a few [Note: [Col. 0726D] The same manuscript reads: “it is celebrated by more and held by many.”]. For the former, because of habitual vices, is more downhill and smooth, and, like a path made pleasant by the flowers of sensual pleasures, easily draws to itself the multitude of travelers. But the latter, unfamiliar in its track of virtues and more gloomy and rugged, is chosen only by those who care less for the pleasure of the journey than for the benefit of the destination.

The excessive habit of vices makes the way of virtues harsh and unpleasant for us. But if that habit is transferred to the other side, then, as Scripture says, the path of righteousness will be found easy [Note: [Col. 0726D] The Roman and Poncian editions read: “you will find … the path of righteousness easy.” This passage is also cited by Augustine in On Nature and Grace, chapter 69, at the end. The Latin version according to the Septuagint reads: “They would certainly have found the paths of righteousness easy.”] [Note: [Col. 0725] Proverbs 2:20, according to the Septuagint.].

Let us therefore now examine the order of our life and learn, with conscience as our witness, which road we are chiefly walking. Everything we do and everything we say belongs either to the broad way or to the narrow. If, with the few, we find the narrow road and a certain slender path, we are moving toward life; but if we accompany the way of the many [Note: [Col. 0727] Perhaps: “we go along the way of companions.” See what follows.], then, according to the Lord’s judgment, we are going toward death.

## 11.

If therefore we are possessed by hatred and envy, if we yield to desire and greed, if we prefer present advantages to future ones, we are walking along the spacious way. For we have a multitude of companions in these things, and are surrounded on every side by dense ranks of people like ourselves.

If we wish to satisfy anger and lust, to avenge an injury, to answer abuse with abuse, and to be hostile in spirit toward an enemy, we are likewise carried along with the many. If we either flatter someone ourselves or willingly listen to a flatterer [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Roman and Poncian editions read: “but if we show favor.”], if favor prevents us from speaking the truth and we fear offending people’s feelings more than speaking sincerely [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Julian manuscript reads: “than speaking to the Lord”; likewise, “we go along the way of the many.”], we too belong to the way of the many. We have as many companions as there are outsiders to the truth.

But, on the other hand, if we are strangers to all these vices [Note: [Col. 0728D] The Julian manuscript reads: “we are free from them.”], if we present a pure and liberated mind, and, having trampled down every desire, strive to be rich in virtues alone, we are pressing along the narrow way. For this way of life belongs to the few. It is exceedingly rare and difficult to find suitable companions for this journey. Indeed, many pretend to travel by it, but through various bypaths of error return to the way of the multitude. Therefore we must fear that those whom we think we have as guides on this straight path may prove to be companions in error.

## 12.

If, then, examples are found that lead us along this way and hold to the straight path of the Gospel, they should be followed. But if such examples are lacking, or are thought to be lacking, the pattern of the apostles has been set before everyone.

Paul, the chosen vessel, cries out and, calling us as though to this narrow road, says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0727] 1 Corinthians 4:16 and 11:1; Philippians 3:17.].

Certainly, greater than all other examples, the example of the Lord himself shines forth. In the Gospel he says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0727] Matthew 11:28.].

If it is dangerous to imitate those of whom you doubt whether they ought to be imitated, then it is certainly safest to imitate him and follow the footsteps of the one who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0727] John 14:6.]. For the one who follows the truth never goes astray [Note: [Col. 0728D] The manuscripts add “in imitation.”]. Hence the Apostle John also says: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked” [Note: [Col. 0727] 1 John 2:6.].

And blessed Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judged him unjustly. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0727] 1 Peter 2:21.].

## 13.

Let every excuse for error cease; let the shameful consolations of sinning be removed. We accomplish absolutely nothing when we defend ourselves by the examples of the multitude, and, often counting the sins of others as our consolation, say that we lack people whom we ought to follow.

We are directed to the example of the one whom everyone admits must be imitated. Therefore let it be your chief concern to know the divine law, through which you can, as though seeing them present, behold the examples of the saints and learn from its counsel what must be done and what must be avoided.

For filling the mind with divine utterances and continually meditating in the heart on what you wish to carry out in action is the greatest aid to righteousness. To a still inexperienced people and to persons unaccustomed to obedience, the Lord commanded through Moses that, as a memorial by which they might remember the Lord’s commandments, they should have, on each fringe of their garments, insignia with scarlet and hyacinth-colored thread [Note: [Col. 0728D] The Julian manuscript reads “the whole”; the first Victor manuscript reads “twisted.”] [Note: [Col. 0727] Numbers 15:38.]. Thus, even when their eyes happened by chance to look here and there, remembrance of the heavenly commandments might arise. The Lord rebukes the Pharisees because they began to wear these fringes through a perverse practice—not as a reminder of God’s commandments but for their own display [Note: [Col. 0727] Matthew 23:5.], so that the people might judge them holy because of their supposedly greater diligence in observance.

## 14.

But for you, who now keep not the commandments of the letter but of the spirit, the memory of the divine commandments must be cultivated spiritually. You must not merely remember the Lord’s commandments frequently; you must think of them constantly. Let the divine Scriptures therefore always be in your hands and be continually turned over in your mind.

Do not think it sufficient to retain God’s commandments in your memory while forgetting them in your actions. Rather, know them for this purpose: so that you may do whatever you have learned must be done. “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified” [Note: [Col. 0727] Romans 2:13.].

The broad and boundless field of the divine law stretches out, blooming with various testimonies of truth like heavenly flowers, and nourishes and refreshes the reader’s mind with wondrous delight. To know all these things continually and turn them over within oneself is a great benefit for preserving righteousness.

But as a kind of concise reminder, you should choose and inscribe upon your heart that saying of the Gospel which the Lord’s mouth offers as a summary of the whole of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0728D] The Julian and first Victor manuscripts, together with the Roman and Poncian editions, read “of the Lord.”]: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” [Note: [Col. 0727] Matthew 7:12.].

Expressing the force of this command, he adds: “For this is the Law and the prophets.” The forms and parts of righteousness are infinite; it is difficult not only to pursue them with the pen but even to grasp them in thought. Yet this one brief saying embraces them all and, by the secret judgment of the mind, either acquits or condemns the hidden conscience of human beings.

## 15.

For every action, every word, and even every thought, let this saying be reconsidered [Note: [Col. 0727] See below, no. 29.]. Let it stand ready for you like a mirror, always placed at hand, showing the quality of your will, and either reproving you for an unjust deed or making you glad because of a just one.

Whenever you have toward another the disposition that you wish another to maintain toward you, you are holding to the way of equity. But whenever you are toward another as you wish no one to be toward you, you have abandoned the path of righteousness.

Behold the entire lofty and difficult matter of the divine law; behold why we complain to the Lord about harsh commands and say that we are burdened by the difficulty or impossibility of the commandments. It is not enough that we fail to do what is commanded: we even declare the one who commands to be unjust, when we complain that the very author of equity has commanded things not only difficult and arduous but impossible.

“Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” [Note: [Col. 0727] Matthew 7:12.]. He wishes love to be joined and bound among us through mutual benefits, and all people to be united with one another by reciprocal affection, so that, when each person provides for another what he wishes everyone to provide for him, the whole of righteousness—and this command of God—may become the common good of humankind.

And what astonishing mercy of the Lord! What ineffable goodness of God! He promises us a reward if we love one another—that is, if we provide to one another those things of which we in turn have need—and yet with an arrogant and ungrateful spirit we resist the will of him whose command is itself a benefit [Note: [Col. 0728D] Four of the same manuscripts read “with the most arrogant spirit.”].

## 16.

Never slander anyone, and do not wish to appear praiseworthy by criticizing others. Learn instead to order your own life rather than attack another’s. Always remember the saying of Scripture: “Do not love to slander, lest you be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0729D] The Latin version according to the Septuagint reads “lest you exalt yourself.” Thus Saint Cyprian, Book III of the Testimonies, in many manuscripts; for in some it reads “lest you be uprooted.” The Greek word ἐξαρθῇς supports both interpretations.] [Note: [Col. 0729] Proverbs 20:13, according to the Septuagint.].

Very few renounce this vice, and rarely will you find anyone who wishes to make his own life so irreproachable that he does not gladly criticize another’s. So great is the appetite for this evil that even those who have withdrawn far from other vices nevertheless fall into this one as into the devil’s final snare.

But avoid this evil so completely that you not only refrain from slandering yourself but never believe anyone else who slanders. Do not lend authority to slanderers by your agreement, lest you nourish their vice. Scripture says: “Do not agree with those who speak evil against your neighbor, and do not take sin upon him” [Note: [Col. 0729D] The first Victor manuscript, together with the Roman and Poncian editions, reads “through them”; the Julian manuscript reads: “and do not take sin against them.”] [Note: [Col. 0729] Sirach 28:28.].

And elsewhere: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue.” Hence blessed David, enumerating various forms of innocence and righteousness, did not remain silent about this virtue either, saying: “He has not received reproach against his neighbors” [Note: [Col. 0729] Psalm 15:3.]. For he himself not only resists but also pursues the slanderer. He says: “The one who slanders his neighbor secretly, him I pursued” [Note: [Col. 0729] Psalm 101:5.].

This is certainly a vice that must be extinguished above all and entirely excluded by those who wish to train themselves in holiness. Nothing so unsettles the mind, nothing makes the mind so changeable and fickle, as readily believing everything and following the words of slanderers with reckless assent. From this arise frequent dissensions; from this, unjust hatreds. This is what often makes even the closest friends enemies, when a malicious tongue separates souls that are indeed harmonious but too credulous.

By contrast, there is great peace of mind and great seriousness of character in not rashly hearing anything sinister about anyone [Note: [Col. 0729D] Thus according to the Julian and first Victor manuscripts. Previously the reading was “something.” See no. 23.]. Blessed is the person who has so armed himself against this vice that no one dares to slander in his presence.

If only we were this diligent not to believe slanderers indiscriminately! Then everyone would fear slandering, lest by slandering they make not others but themselves despicable. But this evil is so widespread, and this vice burns so fiercely in many, because it is gladly heard by almost everyone.

## 17.

Flee also the flattering speeches and harmful deceitful caresses of flatterers as though they were certain plagues of the soul. Nothing corrupts people’s minds so easily; nothing wounds the spirit with so sweet and gentle a blow.

Hence a certain wise man says: “The words of flatterers are soft, but they strike the innermost parts of the belly” [Note: [Col. 0729] Proverbs 26:22.]. And the Lord speaks through the prophet: “My people, those who call you blessed mislead you and confuse the paths of your feet” [Note: [Col. 0729D] The Roman and Poncian editions read “disturb.”] [Note: [Col. 0729] Isaiah 3:12, according to the Septuagint, and 9:16.].

In many people, especially in our own time, this vice reigns; and what is most serious, it is regarded as a form of humility and goodwill. As a result, anyone who does not know how to flatter is thought either envious or arrogant.

It is indeed a great and subtle art to praise another in order to commend oneself, and, by deceiving, to bind the deceived person’s mind to oneself. This vice is especially practiced by selling invented praise for a definite price.

What great frivolity of mind, what great vanity, it is to abandon one’s own conscience and follow another’s opinion—an opinion that is fabricated and feigned—to be swept along by the wind of false praise [Note: [Col. 0730D] The Roman and Poncian editions read “the wind of false flattery.” This reading could be accepted, since no. 30 has “to deceive by feigned flattery.”], to rejoice in one’s own deception, and to accept mockery as a benefit?

Therefore, if you truly wish to be praiseworthy, do not seek human praise. Prepare your conscience for him who will both bring the hidden things of darkness to light and reveal the purposes of hearts; and then your praise will be from God [Note: [Col. 0729] 1 Corinthians 4:5.].

## 18.

Let your mind therefore be attentive and watchful, always armed against sins. Let your speech in all things be measured and sparing, and let it indicate the necessity of speaking more than the desire to speak. Let modesty adorn prudence, and let shamefacedness—the quality that has always been especially characteristic of women—surpass all virtues in you.

Consider long beforehand what ought to be said; and while still silent, take care lest you regret having said something. Let thought weigh your words, and let the mind’s balance regulate the office of the tongue. Hence Scripture says: “Melt down your silver and gold, make a balance for your words, and straight reins for your mouth; and take care lest you slip with your tongue” [Note: [Col. 0730D] The Julian and first Victor manuscripts read “in your tongue,” as in the Vulgate.] [Note: [Col. 0729] Sirach 28:29.] [Note: [Col. 0729] Greek: καταύησον, “melt down.”]

Never let an evil word proceed from your mouth [Note: [Col. 0730D] The first Victor manuscript reads “a curse”; another Victor manuscript reads “a cursing.”], when, as an increase of kindness, you are even commanded to bless those who curse. “Be compassionate, modest, humble, not repaying evil for evil or cursing for cursing, but, on the contrary, blessing” [Note: [Col. 0729] 1 Peter 3:9; Romans 12:17.].

## 19.

Let your tongue be wholly unacquainted with lying and swearing. Let your love of truth be so great in you [Note: [Col. 0730D] The same manuscripts, together with the Poncian and Roman editions, read “of truth.”] that whatever you say you consider sworn. Concerning this the Savior says to his disciples: “But I say to you, do not swear at all” [Note: [Col. 0729] Matthew 5:34.]. And shortly afterward: “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no’; whatever is more than these is from evil” [Note: [Col. 0729] Ibid., 37.].

In every action and word, therefore, let a quiet and peaceful mind be preserved; and let the presence of God always confront your thoughts. Let the mind be humble and gentle, and raised up against vices alone. Let neither pride lift it up, nor greed bend it, nor anger hurl it down.

For nothing should be calmer, nothing purer, nothing finally more beautiful than the mind that must be prepared as a dwelling place for God. He is not pleased by temples shining with gold or altars adorned with jewels, but by a soul adorned with virtues. Therefore the hearts of the saints are called the temple of God, as the Apostle affirms when he says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” [Note: [Col. 0729] 1 Corinthians 3:17.].

## 20.

Let nothing be more excellent to you than humility, and nothing more lovable. For it is the chief preserver and, as it were, guardian of all virtues. Nothing makes us so pleasing both to human beings and to God as this: that, though great in the merit of our life, we are lowly in humility. Therefore Scripture says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” [Note: [Col. 0729] Sirach 3:20.].

And the Lord speaks through the prophet: “Upon whom else shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my utterances?” [Note: [Col. 0730D] Thus the Jolian and Victor manuscripts and the Roman and Poncian editions, as in Letter 50, no. 3; Rosweyde’s edition has *verba mea*, “my words,” instead of *sermones meos*, “my utterances.”] [Note: [Col. 0729] Isaiah 66:2.].

Nevertheless, pursue humility not the kind that is displayed and feigned through bodily gesture or a broken tone of speech, but the kind expressed by the pure feeling of the heart. For it is one thing to possess virtue, another to possess the likeness of virtue; one thing to follow shadows of realities [Note: [Col. 0731D] So read the same manuscripts. Rosweyde’s edition has “the shadow of realities.”], another to follow the truth.

That pride is much more deformed which hides beneath certain signs of humility. For somehow vices are more shameful when they conceal themselves under the appearance of virtues.

## 21.

Never set yourself above anyone because of nobility of birth, nor consider people of humbler origin and lower station inferior to you. Our religion does not know how to accept persons or social conditions; it examines the minds of individuals and judges slave and noble according to their character.

The only freedom before God is not to serve sins. The highest nobility before God is to be illustrious in virtues.

Who among men was nobler before God than Peter, who was a fisherman and poor? Who among women was more illustrious than blessed Mary, who is described as the betrothed of a craftsman? Yet to that poor fisherman the keys of the heavenly kingdom are entrusted by Christ [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Jolian manuscript reads “are given.”] [Note: [Col. 0731] Matthew 16:19.]; and this betrothed of a craftsman deserved to be the mother of the one by whom those very keys were given.

For God chose the lowly and contemptible things of this world [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 Corinthians 1:28.], so that he might more easily bring the powerful and noble to humility.

Indeed, anyone else boasts in vain about the nobility of his ancestry, since all who have been redeemed by the one blood of Christ possess equal honor and the same value before God. Nor does it matter in what condition a person was born, since all are reborn equally in Christ. Even if we forget that we were all generated from one ancestor, we must at least always remember that through one person we are all regenerated.

## 22.

Beware lest, if you begin to fast or abstain, you think that you are already holy. For this virtue is an aid, not the perfection of holiness. You must take even greater care lest the fact that you despise what is permitted give you a certain security about what is forbidden.

Whatever is offered to God beyond what justice requires ought not to hinder justice but to assist it. What good does it do for the body to be weakened by abstinence if the mind swells with pride? What praise will we deserve for the pallor of fasting if we are livid with envy? What virtue is there in not drinking wine while becoming drunk with anger and hatred?

Then, I say, abstinence is excellent; then the chastisement of the body is beautiful and magnificent, when the mind is fasting from vices [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Julian manuscript reads “pure.”]. Indeed, those who practice abstinence responsibly and intelligently afflict their flesh precisely so that they may break the pride of their soul. They descend, as it were, from a certain height of self-contempt and arrogance in order to fulfill the Lord’s will, which is perfected above all in humility.

For this reason they withdraw the mind from various desires for food, so that all its power may be occupied with the desire for virtues. Then the flesh feels less the labor of fasting and abstinence, while the soul hungers for righteousness.

Paul, the chosen vessel [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 Corinthians 9:27.], when he disciplines his body and brings it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be found disqualified [Note: [Col. 0731D] Rosweyde’s edition reads “while.”], does not do this merely for chastity, as some inexperienced people think. Abstinence assists not only that virtue but all virtues altogether.

Nor is the Apostle’s great or complete glory simply that he does not fornicate. Rather, he does this so that his mind may be trained through the discipline of the body. The less he desires anything from sensual pleasures, the more he is able to think about virtues; so that the Teacher of perfection [Note: [Col. 0731] See Letter 30, no. 5.] may not show himself imperfect in anything; so that the imitator of Christ [Note: [Col. 0731] See Letter 45, no. 3.] may not do anything outside the command or will of Christ; and so that he may teach no less by example than by word.

Then, after preaching to others, he might not himself be rejected [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Roman and Poncian editions add “by the Lord.”], and might hear with the Pharisees: “For they say and do not do” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matthew 23:3.].

### 23

It is both an apostolic precept and example that we should take account not only of conscience but also of reputation [Note: [Col. 0731D] The same manuscripts read *curemus*, “let us take care.”]. It is not an empty teaching, devoid of benefit, that the Teacher of the Gentiles gives here: for he wishes outsiders also to advance toward faith through the works of the faithful, so that the discipline of religion itself may commend religion. Therefore, just as he commands us to shine as lights in the world [Note: [Col. 0731] Philippians 2:15], in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, so that unbelieving minds may detect the darkness of their ignorance by the light of our actions, so he himself says to the Romans: “Providing what is good, not only before God but also before human beings.” And elsewhere: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and the Church of God, just as I in all things please everyone, not seeking what is useful for myself but what is useful for many” [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 Corinthians 10:32–33].

Blessed is the person who has ordered his life so holily and so gravely that nothing sinister can even be fabricated about him; for the greatness of his merit battles against the will of his detractors, and no one dares to invent what he thinks no one would believe. But if attaining this is difficult and exceedingly arduous, let us at least apply such care to our life that evil minds may find no occasion for slander; let no spark proceed from us by which the flame of an evil reputation may be kindled against us. Otherwise, we are angry with our detractors in vain if we ourselves supply them with material for detraction [Note: [Col. 0732D] Thus the manuscripts of Julianus and Sacchinus. Others read *ipsis*, “to them.”] [Note: [Col. 0732D] The manuscript of Julianus, together with the Roman and Poncian editions, reads *materias*, “materials.”].

But if, while we carefully and anxiously provide for everything honorable and place the fear of God before all our actions, they nevertheless rage against us, let our conscience console us. It is then most safe and most secure when it has not even given occasion for anyone to think evil of it. For the prophet pronounces woe upon those who call good evil, who call light darkness, and call what is sweet bitter [Note: [Col. 0731] Isaiah 5:20, according to the Septuagint.]. The Savior’s saying, therefore, will apply to us: “Blessed are you when people curse you while lying” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matthew 5:11]. Let us act now so that no one can speak evil of us without lying.

### 24

Manage your household with such diligence that you nevertheless grant some leisure to your soul. Choose a suitable place, somewhat removed from the bustle of the household, into which you may withdraw as into a harbor from the great storm of your cares, and in the tranquility of seclusion calm the waves of thoughts stirred up outside. Let there be there such devotion to sacred reading, such frequent turns of prayer, and such firm and concentrated reflection upon the future, that you may easily compensate for all the occupations of the remaining time by this period of leisure. We do not say this in order to draw you away from your own people; rather, we want you to learn there, and meditate there, what sort of person you ought to show yourself to your own.

### 25

Govern and cherish your household in such a way that you wish to appear more a mother to your people than their mistress, and demand their respect by kindness rather than severity. The obedience that proceeds from love is always more faithful and more welcome than that which proceeds from fear [Note: [Col. 0732D] The manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus read “is received.” The Roman and Poncian editions read “is obtained.”]. Above all, in the honorable and undefiled marriage, let the order of the apostolic rule be maintained.

### 26

First of all, let the husband’s authority be preserved, and let the whole household learn from you how much honor it owes him. Show him to be master by your obedience; show him to be great by your humility. You yourself will be more honored in proportion as you honor him more. For, as the Apostle says, “the man is the head of the woman” [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 Corinthians 11:3]; and the rest of the body is adorned by nothing more than by the dignity of the head. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Women, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0731] Colossians 3:18].

The blessed apostle Peter also says: “Likewise, let women be subject to their husbands, so that even if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives” [Note: [Col. 0732D] These two words, which occur in all our manuscripts, are absent from the printed edition of Rosweyde.] [Note: [Col. 0733D] Thus the manuscripts of Julianus according to Scripture. Others read “of the woman.”] [Note: [Col. 0733] 1 Peter 3:1]. If, then, honor is owed even to pagan husbands by the right of marriage, how much more must it be rendered to Christian husbands?

### 27

And to show with what ornaments women joined to husbands ought also to be adorned, he says: “Their adornment should not be outward, consisting in the braiding of the hair, or the wearing of gold, or the arrangement of clothing, but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is precious in the sight of God” [Note: [Col. 0733] 1 Peter 3:3]. For in this way holy women who hoped in the Lord once adorned themselves, subject to their own husbands, just as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him her lord.

In giving this command, he does not order them to be filthy with squalor and covered with rough scraps of cloth [Note: [Col. 0733D] Thus the Roman and Poncian editions. Earlier the text read “to be covered with squalor and dirty rags.”]; rather, he forbids extravagant and excessively refined adornment, and commends simple ornament and dress. Concerning this the Chosen Vessel also says: “Likewise, women should adorn themselves in becoming clothing, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but—as is fitting for women professing chastity through good works” [Note: [Col. 0733] 1 Timothy 2:9].

### 28

I have found you inflamed with an extraordinary ardor of faith, and for several years now resolved to practice continence and consecrate the remainder of your life to chastity. This is a sign of a great spirit and an indication of perfect virtue: suddenly to renounce a pleasure once experienced, to flee the familiar enticements of the flesh, and to extinguish the flames of still-warm youth through love of faith.

But I also learned something else, which troubles and torments me considerably: namely, that you began to preserve this great good without the consent and agreement of your husband. The apostolic authority absolutely forbids this; in this one matter it has subjected not only the wife to the authority of the husband but also the husband to that of the wife. “The wife,” it says, “does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” [Note: [Col. 0733] 1 Corinthians 7:4].

But you, as though forgetful of the marriage covenant and unaware of this agreement and legal right, vowed chastity to the Lord without consulting your husband. Yet what still lies in another’s power is promised at peril; and I do not know how welcome a gift can be if one person offers something belonging to two. We have already both heard and seen many marriages torn apart through ignorance of this kind; and—painful to recall—adultery committed on the pretext of chastity. For while one party abstains even from what is lawful, the other has fallen into what is unlawful [Note: [Col. 0733] See Augustine, Letter 262 (formerly 199), to Ecdicia.].

And in such a case I do not know who ought to be accused more, who deserves greater blame: the husband who, rejected by his wife, commits fornication, or the wife who, rejecting her husband, in a certain sense thrusts him toward fornication.

To make you recognize what truth holds concerning this matter, I must set down a few passages from divine authority. The rule of apostolic teaching neither equates the works of continence with marriage, as Jovinian did, nor condemns marriage, as Mani did. Thus the Chosen Vessel and Teacher of the Gentiles proceed temperately and midway between the two, granting marriage as a remedy for incontinence and encouraging continence toward its reward. His entire meaning in this matter is that chastity should be proposed with the agreement of both parties, or at least that the common marital debt should be discharged by both.

### 29

Let us now set down the Apostle’s own words and reconsider this entire matter from its beginning [Note: [Col. 0733] See above, section 15.]. He speaks to the Corinthians: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman” [Note: [Col. 0733] 1 Corinthians 7:1]. Although he has praised chastity here, nevertheless, lest anyone seem to think that he forbids marriage, he adds: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” [Note: [Col. 0733D] These words are enclosed in brackets because they do not appear in the manuscripts or in the three printed editions.]: “Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; and the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the woman. Do not defraud one another.”

And again, lest by saying so much in favor of marriage he seem to exclude chastity, he continues: “Unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” Immediately, as though retracting what he had said—“for a time” [Note: [Col. 0734D] The Roman edition reads “returns to it.”]—lest he appear to teach not perpetual but only temporary and brief continence, he says: “Because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by concession, not by command.”

By the words “for a time,” therefore, he teaches that chastity should be attempted, so that, at determined intervals, as though their strength in continence had been tested, both parties may promise without danger what must always thereafter be observed by both. But what he wants absolutely, he states plainly: “I wish that all people were as I myself am”—that is, that they live in continual and perpetual chastity.

### 30

Do you see how cautiously, prudently, and without giving anyone an occasion for scandal the Teacher [Note: [Col. 0733] See Letter 30, section 5.] established his judgment concerning chastity? He did not wish so great a good to depend upon the rashness of one person when the consent of both ought to bind and confirm it. And truly, what is firmer or safer than a chastity begun by the considered decision of two and preserved by both as something held in common?

Nor should one party be concerned only for herself, but each should mutually encourage the other to persevere in virtue. For in this, as in other good things, it is not merely beginning but completing that deserves praise.

As you understand, our discourse has long been moving through a rugged and difficult place, and it dares not incline wholly to either side, since it fears both equally. From our difficulty recognize your own peril: we preferred perhaps to sadden you by speaking the truth rather than deceive you with false flattery [Note: [Col. 0734D] This word is absent from Rosweyde’s edition.].

As you see, there is a double and equal evil, and danger on both sides: you are constrained and bound from both directions. To despise and reject your husband altogether is plainly contrary to the Apostle’s judgment. But to abandon the chastity you have preserved for so long and fail to render to God what you promised is something to fear and dread. As the saying goes: “You will easily turn a friend into an enemy if you do not render what you promised.”

For Scripture says: “If you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay in fulfilling it, because the Lord your God will surely require it of you, and it will be counted as sin for you” [Note: [Col. 0733] Deuteronomy 23:21, according to the Septuagint; Ecclesiastes 5:3]. Therefore he says: “Show your husband the honor that is due, so that from both of you you may be able to render to the Lord what you vowed” [Note: [Col. 0733] 1 Corinthians 7:4].

We do not distrust his conscience, if only you had waited a little—not because we wish to draw you away from the good of chastity, but because we wish to urge his mind with all our strength toward the oracle of chastity, so that he may offer God a voluntary sacrifice as a pleasing fragrance; so that, with the mind stripped of all worldly restraints and bodily pleasures [Note: [Col. 0734D] The Roman edition reads “may be able to,” producing: “so that the mind, stripped of all restraints … may be able.” Both readings are good.], you may be able to cling more fully to the Lord’s commandments.

Yet lest you think that anything has been said carelessly by us, we have instructed you by testimonies from the divine Scriptures, just as the Apostle also says: “And the two shall be one flesh” [Note: [Col. 0733] 1 Corinthians 6:16]; “no longer one flesh, but one spirit” [Note: [Col. 0733] Matthew 19:6].

### 31

“This mystery is great,” and the way of chastity is arduous; but the rewards are great. The Lord calls us in the Gospel, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Note: [Col. 0733] Matthew 25:34].

The same Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” [Note: [Col. 0733] Matthew 11:28–30].

The same Lord says to those who will be on his left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. I do not know you, workers of iniquity. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0735] Matthew 25:41].

All those people will lament and mourn who entangle themselves in the cares of the present life so completely that they forget the future; those who, overcome as though by a sleep of ignorance and false security amid the waves, will be overtaken by the Lord’s coming. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts become weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life; lest that day come upon you suddenly. For like a snare it will come upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” [Note: [Col. 0735] Luke 21:34]. And again: “Watch and pray” [Note: [Col. 0735] Matthew 24:42 and 25:13], for you do not know when the time will be.

### 32

Blessed are those who await that day in such a manner and watch for it so attentively that they prepare themselves for it every day; those who, not flattering themselves with their past righteousness, are renewed in virtue day by day, according to the Apostle. For the righteousness of a righteous person will not benefit him from the day on which he turns away from righteousness [Note: [Col. 0735] 2 Corinthians 4:16]. Nor will the iniquity of an unrighteous person harm him from the day on which he turns away from iniquity [Note: [Col. 0735] Ezekiel 18:24].

Therefore, neither should a holy person be secure so long as he remains in the contest of this life, nor should a sinner despair, since, according to the prophet’s statement just cited, he can make himself righteous in a single day. Rather, the whole span of your life is the time in which you strive, so that you may accomplish righteousness and, trusting in past righteousness, may not become more lax.

But, as the Apostle says: “Forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, the prize of the heavenly calling” [Note: [Col. 0735] Philippians 3:13–14], knowing that God is written to be the examiner of hearts [Note: [Col. 0735] Proverbs 24:12; Acts 1:24]. For this reason he takes pains to keep his soul clean from sin. Hence it is written: “Guard your heart with every vigilance” [Note: [Col. 0735] Proverbs 4:23]. And again: “The Lord loves pure hearts; and all the blameless are acceptable to him.”

Therefore act so as to order the remainder of your life without offense, so that you may safely sing with the prophet: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” [Note: [Col. 0735] Psalm 100:2]. And again: “I will enter the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth” [Note: [Col. 0735] Psalm 42:4]. For it is not enough to have begun; to have completed is righteousness.

---

## VARIANT READINGS IN THE LETTERS OF THE APPENDIX FROM MANUSCRIPTS AND PRINTED EDITIONS

### IN THE FIRST LETTER

1. Column 721: *etenim*, “for indeed.” Rosweyde’s edition: *enim*, “for.”

2. Ibid.: *Dominus*, “the Lord.” Thus the manuscripts of Julianus and the two manuscripts of Victorinus, together with the Mainz edition. Rosweyde’s edition: *Deus*, “God.”

3. Ibid.: *ab utero*, “from the womb.” Thus the same four manuscripts. Rosweyde’s edition: *ex utero*, “from the womb.”

4. Column 722: *a Deo est*, “is from God.” We deleted *Domino*, “from the Lord,” which was absent from the two Victorinus manuscripts and the Mainz edition.

5. Column 723: *esse*, “to be.” It is absent from the manuscript of Julianus and the Mainz edition.

6. Ibid.: *fatetur et praedicat sibiipsi*, “he confesses and proclaims to himself.” Sacchinus: Something seems to be missing, perhaps “that the tribulation had been salutary.”

7. Ibid.: *excellentiam*, “excellence.” The manuscript of Julianus: *extollentiam*, “exaltation.”

8. Ibid.: *manet*, “remains.” Two Victorinus manuscripts: *permanet*, “continues to remain.”

9. Column 724: *verbum autem Domini*, “but the word of the Lord.” We added *autem* from the Roman, Erasmian, and Poncian editions.

10. Ibid.: *in quas*, “into which.” Two manuscripts together with the Mainz edition: *in quo*, “in which.”

11. Ibid.: *belluae caecae*, “blind beasts.” Sacchinus: I would prefer *caeci*, “blind.”

12. Ibid.: *diem, et*, “the day, and.” The particle *et*, “and,” was added from the Roman, Erasmian, and Poncian editions.

13. Ibid.: *in vanitate sua*, “in their vanity.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *in vanitates suas*, “into their vanities.”

14. Column 725: *divitum*, “of the rich.” The manuscript of Julianus: *divite*, “with a rich person.”

15. Ibid.: *ut coenum*, “like mud.” Two Victorinus manuscripts: *ut cinis*, “like ashes.”

16. Ibid.: *beatorum*, “of the blessed.” Others: *beatam*, “blessed.”

17. Ibid.: *ornata*, “adorned.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *honorata*, “honored.”

18. Ibid.: *justificationes tuas*, “your justifications.” Three editions: *mandata tua*, “your commandments.”

19. Ibid.: *congratulantes*, “rejoicing with.” The manuscript of Julianus: *gratulantes*, “congratulating.”

20. Column 726: *super infirmam arenam aedificium*, “a building upon weak sand.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *infirmum super arenam aedificium*, “a weak building upon sand.” Both readings are good.

21. Ibid.: *quos etiam*, “whom also.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *quas jam*, “whom already.”

22. Ibid.: *uret*, “will burn.” The Julianian manuscript together with the Mainz edition: *exuret*, “will burn up.”

23. Ibid.: *inter*, “among.” The manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus 1 and the Mainz edition: *in*, “in.”

24. Ibid.: *Deo*, “God.” The manuscript of Julianus: *Domino*, “the Lord.”

25. Column 727: *et umbra*, “and shadow.” The editions and Poncian edition: *et in umbra*, “and in shadow.”

26. Ibid.: *nocte ac die*, “night and day.” The manuscript of Julianus and the Mainz edition: *die ac nocte*, “day and night.”

### IN THE SECOND LETTER

1. Column 727: *inveniatur*, “may be found.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *invenitur*, “is found.”

2. Ibid.: *soleat*, “is accustomed.” The same manuscripts: *solet*, “is accustomed.”

3. Ibid.: *quadam fidei*, “of a certain faith.” The manuscript of Julianus: *quodammodo*, “in a certain way.”

4. Ibid.: *sic*, “thus.” The manuscript of Julianus: *sane*, “indeed.”

5. Column 728: *me crederem*, “I would believe myself.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *me omnino crederem*, “I would believe myself entirely.”

6. Ibid.: *violenter*, “violently.” The same manuscripts: *vigilanter*, “vigilantly.”

7. Ibid.: *implendam*, “to be fulfilled.” The same codices: *implendum*, “to be fulfilled,” masculine or neuter.

8. Ibid.: *ipsius*, “of himself.” The manuscript of Julianus: *jam piis*, “now for the devout.”

9. Ibid.: *et docet*, “and teaches.” Three editions: *etiam docet*, “also teaches.”

10. Ibid.: *Deo credit*, “believes God.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *Deum credit*, “believes in God.”

11. Ibid.: *imperium*, “command.” The same manuscripts: *imperia*, “commands.”

12. Column 729: *pretiosum multum*, “very precious.” Three editions: *pretiosum nimis*, “exceedingly precious.”

13. Ibid.: *illa immensa Dei bonitas*, “that immense goodness of God.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *illa immensitas, illa immensa Dei bonitas offenditur*, “that immensity, that immense goodness of God, is offended.”

14. Ibid.: *eam*, “her/it.” The manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus 1: *eum*, “him/it.”

15. Ibid.: *ducimus*, “we lead.” The manuscript of Julianus: *ducentes*, “leading.”

16. Ibid.: *hoc apostoli*, “this of the Apostle.” The manuscript of Julianus: *et apostoli*, “and of the Apostle.”

17. Ibid.: *efflagitat*, “he urgently demands.” The manuscript of Julianus: *flagitant*, “they demand.”

18. Ibid.: *illis*, “to them.” The manuscript of Julianus: *ipsis*, “to those very persons.”

19. Column 730: *mandatum*, “commandment.” The manuscript of Julianus: *imperatum*, “commanded.”

20. Ibid.: *libera*, “free.” The manuscript of Julianus: *secura*, “secure.”

21. Ibid.: *Dominum*, “the Lord.” The manuscript of Julianus: *Deum*, “God.”

22. Column 731: *voto*, “by a vow.” The manuscript of Julianus: *voluntate*, “by will.”

23. Ibid.: *quod semper*, “which always.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *cum semper*, “since always.”

24. Ibid.: *Deum confitentur se nosse*, “they confess that they know God.” The manuscript of Julianus: *confitentes se nosse Deum*, “confessing that they know God.”

25. Ibid.: *et*, “and.” The manuscript of Julianus: *enim atque*, “for and also.”

26. Ibid.: *Illi terrena sapiant, etc.*, “Let them savor earthly things, etc.” Sacchinus: This figure is very familiar to Paulinus, as will be clear to an attentive reader.

27. Ibid.: *aeterna nesciunt*, “they do not know eternal things.” The manuscript of Julianus: *aeternam nesciunt vitam*, “they do not know eternal life.”

28. Ibid.: *autem sunt*, “but are.” Thus the manuscript of Julianus. Others: *enim sunt*, “for they are.”

29. Column 732: *omne enim quod*, “for everything that.” The manuscript of Julianus: *omne quodcumque*, “everything whatsoever.”

30. Ibid.: *ad haec*, “to these things.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *ad hoc*, “to this.”

31. Ibid.: *remaledicimus*, “we return the curse.” Three editions: *maledicimus*, “we curse,” less well.

32. Column 733: *idoneos*, “suitable.” The manuscript of Julianus: *et unius*, “and of one.”

33. Ibid.: *per hanc ducant viam*, “may lead them by this way.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *per hanc viam ducant ad vitam*, “may lead them by this way to life.”

34. Ibid.: *reficiam vos*, “I will refresh you.” Three editions: *requiescere faciam vos*, “I will make you rest.”

35. Ibid.: *Apostolus*, “the Apostle.” This word is absent from the manuscript of Victorinus 1. The manuscript of Julianus: *sanctus*, “holy.”

36. Ibid.: *ambulavit*, “he walked.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *ambulabat*, “he was walking.”

37. Ibid.: *pro nobis*, “for us.” The Roman edition: *pro vobis*, “for you.”

38. Ibid.: *nostram*, “our.” The manuscript of Julianus: *nostri*, “of us.”

39. Ibid.: *mittimur*, “we are sent.” The manuscript of Julianus: *nitamur*, “we strive.”

40. Column 734: *ostentationem*, “display.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *ostensionem*, “showing.”

41. Ibid.: *de majoris observationis diligentia*, “concerning the diligence of greater observance.” The manuscript of Julianus: *de majoribus observationibus sancti a populis*, “concerning the greater observances of the holy man by the peoples.”

42. Ibid.: *spiritualiter excolenda est*, “is to be cultivated spiritually.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *specialiter excolenda sit*, “should be cultivated particularly.”

43. Ibid.: *cogitanda*, “to be considered.” The same codices: *recogitanda*, “to be reconsidered.”

44. Ibid.: *compendiosum quoddam*, “a certain concise [account].” The Roman, Erasmian, and Poncian editions: *compendiosum locum, quoddam*, “a certain concise passage.”

45. Ibid.: *quae ad totius*, “which [pertain] to the whole.” The Julianian manuscript: *quae superans potius*, “which rather surpasses.”

46. Ibid.: *persequi*, “to pursue.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *prosequi*, “to follow.”

47. Ibid.: *Ad omnem igitur*, “Therefore, with every.” These words are absent from the Julianian manuscript up to *En totum*, “Behold, entirely.”

48. Column 735: *irreprehensibilem*, “blameless.” The manuscript of Julianus: *inreprehensibilem*, “blameless.”

49. Ibid.: *de consensu tribuas*, “you grant with consent.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *de nonsensu tuo tribuas*, “you grant from your foolishness.”

50. Ibid.: *dinumerans*, “counting.” The manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus 1 together with two editions: *tenuntians* [uncertain reading].

51. Ibid.: *proximo suo*, “to his neighbor.” The manuscript of Julianus: *proximum suum*, “his neighbor.”

52. Ibid.: *excludi*, “to be excluded.” The manuscript of Julianus: *excludatur*, “let him be excluded.”

53. Column 736: *maliloqua lingua*, “a foul-speaking tongue.” The Roman edition: *maliloqui lingua*, “the tongue of foul speech.”

54. Ibid.: *loquendi magis*, “of speaking rather.” The Erasmian edition: *magis loqui*, “to speak more.” Sacchinus: The reading is not to be rejected, since it indicates the necessity of speaking rather than the desire to speak. That is, speech should be so sparing that necessity, rather than inclination, seems to speak.

55. Column 737: *animus, ac*, “the mind, and.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *animus tuus, ac*, “your mind, and.”

56. Ibid.: *nihilque*, “and nothing.” Thus three manuscript codices. Others: *nihil*, “nothing.”

57. Ibid.: *faciat*, “may do.” The manuscript of Julianus: *facit*, “does.”

58. Column 738: *cum virtutum*, “with virtues.” Erasmus: *quae virtutum*, “which [are] of virtues.”

59. Ibid.: *obscuriores*, “more obscure.” The manuscript of Julianus: *pauperiores*, “poorer.”

60. Ibid.: *adjuvare*, “to help.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *juvare*, “to help.”

61. Column 739: *ne*, “lest.” The manuscript of Julianus: *ne forte*, “lest perhaps.”

62. Ibid.: *facit*, “does.” The manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus 1: *efficit*, “brings about.”

63. Ibid.: *unde et ipse*, “hence he himself also.” The particle *et*, “also,” was added from the Poncian and Roman editions.

64. Column 740: *Apostolus*, “the Apostle.” This word is absent from the manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus and from the Roman edition.

65. Ibid.: *decorari debeant*, “ought to be adorned.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *decorare se debeant*, “ought to adorn themselves.”

66. Column 741: *miro fidei ardore*, “with extraordinary ardor of faith.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *mirae fidei ardore*, “with the ardor of extraordinary faith.”

67. Ibid.: *quoque simul didici*, “I also learned.” We added *simul*, “also,” from the manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus and four editions.

68. Ibid.: *objicit*, “thrusts forward.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *objecit*, “thrust.”

69. Column 742: *Loquitur*, “He speaks.” Three editions add *enim*, “for.”

70. Column 744: *uno die*, “in one day.” The Roman and Poncian editions: *una die*, “in one day.”

# POEMS

[POEMATA (C, G, S)]

[Note: [Col. 0737] Additional notes to these poems were printed by Migne as a separate document in columns 741–744. Each superscript number in the text of the poems refers to the corresponding note in that separate document.]

## POEM I [Note: [Col. 0737D] Elsewhere numbered 31.]

He urges his wife to dedicate herself wholly to God [Note: [Col. 0737D] See Dissertation 6, section 2.].

### 745–746

Come, now, I beg you, my companion  
inseparable in my affairs,  
let us dedicate our trembling, brief life  
to the Lord God.

[5] You see the days hastening on  
with swift rotation,  
and the fragile limbs of the world  
diminishing, perishing, slipping away.

Everything we possess flees,  
and flowing things do not return;  
they draw our greedy and wandering minds  
after an empty appearance.

Where now is the image of worldly things?  
Where are the riches of the mighty,  
whose delight it was  
to seize captive souls?

[Col. 0737D] Once he turned the earth with a hundred plows;  
now he strains to have a pair of oxen.  
Often carried through cities in magnificent carriages,  
now, sick and exhausted, he reaches his empty country estate on weary feet.

He who once plowed the sea before him  
with ten lofty ships [Note: [Col. 0738D] Thus three German manuscripts, the manuscript of Julianus, and Victorinus 1. Another manuscript, together with Rosweyde’s edition, reads *alta*, “high.” See the preceding text.],  
now climbs into a tiny boat  
and steers it himself.

The condition of fields is not the same,  
nor of any cities;  
everything rushes headlong toward its end.

[25] By sword, plague [Note: [Col. 0737D] See Poem 24, line 304.], famine, chains, cold, and heat,  
a single death snatches wretched human beings  
in a thousand ways.

Wars roar everywhere; madness rouses everyone,  
and countless kings press arms  
against other kings.

Impious discord rages through the confused world;  
the final peace has departed from the earth—  
all that you see.

And even if ages remained  
after the completed cycle of time,  
or if the world could possess long days,  
we should nevertheless watch for our own setting  
and each person should look toward the end of his own life.

[35] For what does it profit me that rivers,  
in a long course, forever flow downward  
with waters that are never exhausted,  
that many centuries have surpassed  
the ancient forests [Note: [Col. 0738D] We emended *silvae*, “forests,” from four manuscripts. Rosweyde’s edition reads *silva*, “forest.”],  
and that flowering fields endure in their own places?

These things remain,  
but our ancestors did not remain.

[Col. 0738D] I pass my life as a guest  
of a short span of time [Note: [Col. 0737D] See Poem 35, line 12.].

Therefore we were not born here  
for nothing through the ages—  
ages that perish for us  
and in which we perish—  
but so that in this life  
we may deserve eternal life,  
and so that long rest may follow  
a brief labor [Note: [Col. 0738D] Thus four manuscripts. Rosweyde’s edition: “so that rest may follow.”].

### 747–748

And yet this labor may perhaps be harsh  
for the rebellious [Note: [Col. 0738D] The manuscripts of Julianus and the two Victorinus manuscripts read *sit*, “may be,” and the following verses seem to depend on it.],  
and savage hearts may think  
the laws severe.

[Col. 0739A] Yet this burden is not heavy  
for a gentle back;  
a kindly yoke does not hurt  
a gentle neck [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Poem 24, line 792, and Poem 25, line 4.].

God is to be loved  
with the whole mind  
and with the whole strength of the heart;  
care for one’s fellow human being  
is enjoined as the second duty.

What one would not wish done to oneself,  
one should do to no one;  
when injured, one should not seek revenge.

Content with little, let one avoid being thought lofty;  
let one not fear being despised,  
and let one not delight in despising.

[55] Sparing, speaking truth,  
chaste in mind and body,  
let one live an innocent life  
as a lover of peace.

Let the kindly person give his own possessions  
to all whom he sees in need;  
let him not desire what is not his,  
and let him distribute what is his.

[Col. 0739B] What, I ask, is considered difficult  
in these commandments?  
Or what is there that faith could not accomplish [Note: [Col. 0740D] Two manuscripts of Julianus and Victorinus 1 read *habere*, “to have,” instead of *obire*, “to accomplish.”]?

Those who believe that the holy prophets  
sang what is true,  
and who do not doubt  
that God’s words endure;

those who see Christ suffering  
the penalties of the cross,  
the final pains of death,  
in the full honor of the exalted Father;

and those who await him,  
terrible with great majesty,  
keeping vigil with well-filled lamps—

for such people earthly things are worthless,  
heavenly things lie open,  
and they do not make themselves  
captive servants of this age.

[70] The world’s deceptive wisdom  
has not ensnared them,  
nor have sterile cares  
fixed themselves in their hearts [Note: [Col. 0740D] Thus we emended from four manuscripts. Rosweyde’s edition reads *curae*, “cares.”].

They have trampled governments and offices,  
the gifts of the unlearned crowd,  
and the riches that the world  
has made seeds of crimes,

seeking heaven with holy ambition  
through the suffrages of Christ  
and the applause of angels [Note: [Col. 0739D] See the same license in Poem 24, line 293, and Poem 35, line 616.].

[75] Neither harsh labor conquers them,  
nor alluring pleasure.  
They desire to seek nothing  
and fear to lose nothing.

Everyone who belongs to Christ  
hates everything that is not Christ,  
establishing himself in Christ  
and wishing to carry Christ within himself.

[Note: [Col. 0740D] Thus restored from three manuscripts: one German manuscript and two Victorinus manuscripts. Previously the text read: “That God of heaven, creator of things and of earth.”]

He, God, creator of things,  
of heaven and earth,

[80] was born human for my sake  
from a holy Virgin [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Poem 35, line 54.].

He offered his back to whips,  
his cheeks to blows,  
his face to spittle,  
and did not refuse to be nailed to the cross.

Not that God had to endure anything  
through such patience,  
since his riches neither increase nor diminish,

but so that what was corrupted in me  
might be overcome in him;  
I became a member of Christ’s body,  
and he became a member of mine.

[85] He bore me when he died;  
he bore me when he rose,  
death having been conquered,

[Col. 0739D] and with himself he carried me  
above the stars to the Father [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ibid., line 138.].

[Col. 0740A] What, then, for so great a hope  
would I refuse to endure [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ibid., lines 154 and 170.]?  
Or what will separate me  
from the Lord?

Apply fire, torturer;  
search my entrails with your hand:  
my limbs, once released,  
will escape your punishments.

If I am shut in a blind prison [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Poem 15, line 195.]  
and I am bound with chains,
I will approach God,  
free in the exaltation of my mind.

[95] If the executioner prepares  
to cut off my neck with his sword,  
he will find me unafraid:  
swift death, brief punishment.

### 749–750

I do not fear exile;  
there is one home for everyone [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Poem 35, line 457.].

I disdain hunger;  
the Lord’s word becomes food for me [Note: [Col. 0740D] Thus restored from the German manuscripts, the manuscript of Julianus, and Victorinus 1. The other Victorinus manuscript, together with Rosweyde’s edition, reads *sit*, “may be.”].

Nor does this confidence in myself  
arise from myself;

[100] You, Christ, grant me speech,  
and you grant me the ability to suffer.

We dare nothing in ourselves [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Poem 26, line 31, and Poem 30, line 105.],  
but we trust in you,

who command us to fight  
and make us conquer [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Letter 38, section 4.].

Therefore God is my only hope;  
to believe in him is life.  
He has made me a citizen  
of another homeland [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Poem 17, line 322.].

[105] Ordered by the lot of my ancestors  
to pass through the setting world,  
I go as an immigrant soldier  
under Christ’s sacred standards.

Nor do I doubt that by a brief right  
I possess earthly things;  
I will use my own possessions  
as though they were not my own.

I will not marvel at riches,  
nor pursue any honors;  
I will not fear poverty  
with Christ as my wealth.

With whatever mind I stand amid adversity,  
with that same mind I will use prosperity;  
evils will not conquer me,  
nor will good things capture me.

[115] I will always give thanks to Christ,  
I will always give him honor [Note: [Col. 0740D] Thus the German manuscripts and Victorinus 1. Other manuscripts read *honores*, “honors.”];  
the praise of the Lord  
will always live upon my lips.

[Col. 0740C] You, my faithful companion,  
gird yourself with me for this struggle,  
which God has provided  
as aid for the weak.

Hold back the proud in anxiety;  
comfort the grieving.  
Let us both be an example  
of a devout life.

Be the guardian of your guardian;  
render mutual service.  
Raise up the one who falls;  
rise by the help of the one who raises.

So that not only our flesh  
may be the same,  
but also our minds,  
and so that one spirit  
may nourish us both.

## POEM II: On the Name of Jesus

(Added here from Bartholomew’s *Adversarial Commentaries*, book 34, chapter 1. See Dissertation 6, section 2.)

### 751–752

The festal day desires to be celebrated with sacred pages;  
put away profane books.

The beginnings of the Name  
which Christ commands to be worshiped  
must be consecrated in a hymn  
[Note: [Col. 0740D] The manuscript reads *luminis*, “of light.” Our correction is confirmed by lines 12, 33, 37, 50, and 64.].

[5] Christ is nectar in the mouth,  
honeycomb upon the tongue,  
living ambrosia in the throat;

the blessed lotus in the breast,  
from which, once tasted,  
you cannot bear to depart  
[Note: [Col. 0741C] The lotus is a tree whose fruit is exceedingly sweet. See Paulinus, Letter 16, section 7.].

Honey in the marrow,  
serene light in the pupils [Note: [Col. 0741C] That is, in the eyes, as in Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, lines 308, 374, and 382.],

the sound of life in the ears.

When this Name is heard,  
[Corrupt words: *Elin ve*] the plectrum  
of sweet eloquence returns.

Through a wandering course,  
through slippery misfortune,  
through the temptations of the Evil One [Note: [Col. 0741C] That is, of the devil; this expression is familiar to Paulinus.],

[15] through thirst and hunger,  
through heat and cold,  
a powerful balm is provided  
for those who are dead.

Does dreadful despair  
shake the inmost chamber of the mind  
because of the mass of sins [Note: [Col. 0742C] *Peccaminum*, “of sins.” Thus Prudentius in *Apotheosis*, line 915, and in *Cathemerinon*, hymn 9.]?

Does inherited depravity rage  
in the deepest inward parts?

[20] Does lust kindle its torches?

Does the desire for gold  
urge the tender heart  
to gather by right and wrong?

Does the mind burn with the gluttony  
of a stinking throat, ruined  
by Venus and Bacchus [Note: [Col. 0742C] The manuscript reads *horret*, “shudders,” which gives no acceptable sense.]?

[25] Does the bloodstained avenger  
drag anger along,  
ready to extinguish it with his sword [Note: [Col. 0741C] That is, to extinguish it. A simple verb is used for a compound, as often in Paulinus.]?

Does he command the infliction  
of a terrifying misfortune  
that one could have avoided badly?

Does powerless violence  
cast out patience  
and seek lost weapons?

[30] Does perverse obstinacy,  
not long fortunate in its errors,  
shake faith [Note: [Col. 0741C] Poetic license. See Poem 24, line 494.]?

This Name, when heard,  
comes for salvation;  
this Name takes away every poison.

[35] Limbs possessed,  
and the spirit tormented  
by an utterly impure demon,  
obtain healing through this Name—  
this very Name—  
and return upward from the underworld.

Bodies devoted to tombs  
by an evil incantation [Note: [Col. 0741D] See Dissertation 6, section 2.],  
bodies bound by a magical spell [Note: [Col. 0742D] *Sago*, that is, “by magic.” Saint Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book 4, chapter 8, section 33, in most printed editions reads “songs of magical art.” The manuscripts read *sagae*, “of magic,” twice.],

shake off the treacherous power  
of the binding disease,

[Col. 0742A] and, made sound,  
return home [Note: [Col. 0741D] That is, “return.”].

### 753–754

The one whose joints,  
loosed limb by limb,  
it commands to sit upon his bed,  
weak;

[45] the one whom blindness,  
the most wretched of all crosses,  
condemned to another person’s foot;

the one lame in both knees,  
whom it commands to come—
The whole city sees it,

[50] and those who celebrate the name of God can return home on their own feet.

Hail, Apollo indeed, illustrious Paean,

striker of the infernal dragon.

Sweet is your quiver [Note: That is, of the New Testament.] of Testimony,

which consists of four men;

[55] an arrow dipped in prophetic honey,

feathered with the oracles of the Fathers;

a bow resounding with the strength of the Father,

a sinew powerful in miracles,

they have laid low the ancient serpent by their death [Note: See note 59.]

[60] Io, noble triumph!

Hail, blessed victory [Note: The manuscript reads *seculis*.] of the age,

opening the blessed era.

Hail, you whom all heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings

hear as they bend the knee.

[65] Hail, one, one, one God in Trinity;

hail, one Trinity in one.

This, when the light has risen from the eastern horizon

and begins its daily course;

this, when the setting sun plunges beneath the sea in its chariot,

[70] consecrates me with its blessing,

O victorious Crucified One, expiator of sins,

[Note: See poem 24, verse 573.]

life almighty in death,

when at the final hour I am summoned away,

from the abyss overwhelmed by evils,

[75] may this blessing lead me across to you;

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Meanwhile grant what is useful. Nor …”]

while my flesh is given to the earth,

so that the delay may not torment my troubled mind,

bound in a foul-smelling prison. [Col. 0741]

INTO THE FIRST POEM OF THE APPENDIX: VARIANT READINGS FROM MANUSCRIPTS AND PRINTED COPIES

[Col. 0741] [Col. 0741D]

IN APPENDIX POEM I

1. Verse 2, *irremota*. Four manuscript copies have *inremota*.

2. Verse 13, *rerum est*. The word *est* has been added from four manuscript copies.

3. Verse 19, *magnificis*. Four manuscripts have *magnificas*, incorrectly.

4. Verse 32, *Aut*. We have restored this from the German manuscript. Others have *Ut*.

5. Verse 40, *Exigui*. Three manuscripts have *Exiguam*, incorrectly.

6. In the same place, *temporis*. Manuscript 1 of Victor has *corporis*.

7. Verse 50, *secunda*. Three manuscripts have *secundi*.

8. Verse 54, *libeat*. Four manuscripts have *soleat*, incorrectly.

9. Verse 64, *excelsi*. Four manuscripts have *celsi*.

10. Verse 75, *vincit*. The Joliet and German manuscript copies have *vicit*.

11. Verse 100, *tribuis*. The German and Joliet manuscripts have *tribues*.

12. Verse 117, *Sollicita*. The German and Victor manuscript 1 have *Sollicite*.

DISSERTATIONS ON THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF SAINT PAULINUS  
(BY LEBRUN)

DISSERTATION ONE. ON THE LETTERS

[Col. 0744]

[Col. 0743A] 755 All the letters that Paulinus wrote before his conversion have completely perished. In order to establish the chronology of the letters that survive and were written after his conversion, we place Paulinus’s withdrawal to Spain after his conversion in the year 390. See chapter 5 of the *Life of Saint Paulinus*, no. 1, and chapter 15, no. 1.

At the end of the year 393, Paulinus was ordained presbyter at Barcelona by Lampius, bishop of Barcelona, on Christmas Day. See chapter 15 of the *Life*, no. 1. Somewhat after his ordination, namely at the beginning of the year 394, shortly before Easter, he wrote from Barcelona Letter 1 to Sulpicius Severus. In it he informed him of his promotion to the priesthood and invited him to celebrate the sacred Easter festivities with him at Barcelona, where Paulinus was the priest. 756 See Letter 1, nos. 10 and 11, and *Life*, chapter 16, no. 1.

We place approximately around Easter the letter written on the same consecration to the presbyter Amandus, Letter 2. See nos. 2, 3, and 4, and *Life*, chapter 15, no. 2, and chapter 16, no. 2.

In the same year, 394, shortly after Easter, as Paulinus had arranged (see Letter 1, no. 11, and *Life*, chapter 16, no. 1), he departed from Barcelona and came to Italy, where Ambrose received him with great affection. See *Life*, chapter 17, no. 1, and Letter 3, no. 4. From there he went to Rome, where he experienced the envy of certain clergy and of the Roman pontiff himself. See *Life*, chapter 17, no. 2. From there he withdrew to Nola, where he remained and sent Letters 3 and 4 to Africa: one to Alypius, his father—that is, his bishop, for he had doubtless learned that Alypius held this dignity from the letters which he declares he had received from Alypius, 757 Letter 3, no. 1; the other to Augustine, his brother, whom he had heard was still a presbyter and with whom, as he says in no. 4, he was equated by sharing the same office. From Letter 3, no. 2, we learn that this fourth letter was sent together with it. From the beginning, however, of Letter 6, which Paulinus certainly wrote to Augustine at the beginning of the year 395, we learn with certainty that this same letter to Augustine, namely the fourth, and also the other to Alypius, the third, were sent before the preceding winter—that is, in the autumn of the year 394.

We place Augustine’s Letter 27 to Paulinus at the beginning of the year 395. For, after receiving Paulinus’s letter written before winter, Augustine entrusted this letter for delivery to Romanianus, as he indicates in no. 4. Romanianus, to whom Letter 7 was addressed, was sailing to Italy on family and domestic business, perhaps in the spring of that year 395, certainly while Augustine was not yet bishop, as appears from Saint Augustine’s Letter 31 to Paulinus and Paulinus’s Letter 7 to Romanianus. See *Life*, chapter 27, no. 1.

Also in the year 395, the second year after Paulinus had withdrawn to Nola, he wrote Letter 5 to Severus through Vigilantius. In it he replied to Severus, who had excused himself for not previously having been able to come to Paulinus at Nola because of two illnesses (see *Life*, chapter 16, nos. 1 and 2), as he had intended. See *Life*, chapter 16, no. 1. Paulinus also discusses his own illness and recalls how the bishops of Africa and Campania, at the beginning of summer, sent their clergy in their place to attend him while he was confined by illness. See Letter 5, no. 14, and *Life*, chapter 26, no. 1. He then relates how greatly he had been scandalized at Rome by certain clergy and by the supreme pontiff himself. See Letter 5, no. 13; *Life*, chapter 17, no. 2; and above, section 3.

Paulinus wrote Letter 6 before he had received from Romanianus Augustine’s reply mentioned above, Augustine’s Letter 27. That holy man, inflamed by an extraordinary longing for Augustine from reading Augustine’s work, saw that the messenger whom he had sent to Africa before winter was delayed on the journey and was uncertain whether his letter had been delivered. Unable to suspend his duty any longer, he therefore sent Augustine a second letter through Romanus and Agilis, to testify both to the devotion and respect of his own mind toward Augustine and to his most ardent desire to see him. See *Life*, chapter 27, no. 1.

Augustine, now a bishop, sent Paulinus the letter numbered 31 in the new edition of Saint Augustine, after receiving Paulinus’s later letter; he had it immediately carried back to him through Romanus and Agilis. In this letter he informed Paulinus of his promotion to the episcopate, so that Paulinus would understand that he could no longer contemplate traveling to Italy to visit him; and he invited Paulinus, who was freer from ecclesiastical cares—for Paulinus was not yet a bishop—to cross over to Africa.

Augustine’s promotion occurred as Christmas approached, as appears from Homily 25, among the fifty, chapter 3, and certainly before the year 397, in which the Third Council of Carthage, celebrated on September 1 or August 28, decreed that the conciliar decrees should be read before bishops or clergy were ordained. This decree was established at Augustine’s request, and he also subscribed to that council. But we have not yet sufficiently determined which of the years 395 and 396 was marked by Augustine’s ordination. 758 Prosper writes, under the consulship of Olivrius and Probinus—that is, in the year of Christ 395: “Augustine, a disciple of the blessed Ambrose, outstanding in marvelous eloquence and learning, was ordained bishop at Hippo Regius in Africa.” All who have written Augustine’s biography have regarded this clear authority as a valid chronological epoch, fixed and entirely unquestionable; hence it is improper to depart from it. This letter to Paulinus, therefore, sent by Augustine as a recently ordained bishop, had to be assigned to the beginning of the year 396. From this, too, the dates of several earlier and later letters had to be determined.

When Romanus and Agilis returned from Africa, Paulinus could not refrain from immediately sharing with Romanianus the most welcome news he had received from them concerning the holy men, and especially Augustine’s promotion to the episcopate. Two days after their return he sent Romanianus Letter 7 on this very matter, congratulating him—as it was fitting that he should rejoice—with the holy man of God. See *Life*, chapter 29, no. 3.

In the commonly published editions of Paulinus and Augustine, Letter 8 to Licentius was joined to the preceding letter to Romanianus and ran on continuously with it. Since the Cluniac manuscript, of excellent quality and great antiquity, and one Bigotian manuscript of Saint Augustine’s letters, six hundred years old, presented this commonly printed letter to Romanianus as divided into two, we too divided it into two: the first addressed to Romanianus, the second to Licentius, his son, who was to receive his own letter from his father’s hand.

Since the two letters were sent in the same packet, no title was attached to the second except “To Licentius,” which is found in the Cluniac and Bigotian manuscripts. The first letter ends with this auspicious prayer: “May we have you safe for very many years, and always blessed with your whole household, as we desire, in Christ, my lord brother, most deservedly to be honored and most dearly desired.” The second begins with the words, “Hear, therefore, son, the law of your father,” that is, of Augustine, and ends with an excellent poem exhorting him to flee the world. Each has its own subject.

The subject of the first is: writing to Romanianus, Paulinus congratulates the Church of Hippo because it has deserved to have Augustine as a fellow bishop. The subject of the second is: Paulinus exhorts Licentius, son of Romanianus, for whom Augustine, formerly his teacher, had written, both in prose and in verse, to despise the arrogance of the imperial court and dedicate himself to Christ. Everyone can see that these are two letters.

Paulinus wrote Letters 9 and 10 in the same year, 396, to the presbyter Amandus and Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, and sent them together. See *Life*, chapter 30, no. 1. Not far from the beginning of Letter 9, in the Viennese manuscript, an asterisk has been placed beside these words: “and strength could have been weakened.” * “Who aroused me as I spoke?” etc. [Col. 0745C] In the margin is then written: “Here much seems to be missing from the letter, because there is almost no continuity.” The conjecture of this annotator is strengthened by the fact that Paulinus, who at the beginning of this letter had addressed Amandus individually, from the asterisk to the end addresses several people, as though he were speaking to a crowd and resembling one preaching to the people. If this defect exists, it is extremely ancient, since it is found both in the very old Regius manuscript, in the Vatican manuscript, and in five printed editions.

We assign Letter 11 to Severus to the year 397. See *Life*, chapter 30, no. 2. In it Paulinus declares that he will never cease inviting 759 Severus and urging him with the greatest earnestness. Since Severus by no means promises that he will come, we therefore place Letter 17 only two years later.

We have assigned Letter 12 to Amandus to this year, 397, because of the affair of the presbyter Basil, which is discussed near the end. See *Life*, chapter 31, nos. 1 and 2. The bearer of this letter was Sanemarius, whom Paulinus had made a freedman from slavery so that he might serve in the house of the Lord under the authority of the Church of Bordeaux, with duties assigned in memory of his parents. See *Life*, chapter 31, no. 1, and Letter 12, no. 12.

Paulina, daughter of Saint Paula and wife of Pammachius, died around the end of the year 397. Paulinus learned of her death only many months later, both because of the distance and because messengers were scarce; he learned it from a letter of a certain friend, Olympius, and this was in winter.
