Prevented by the severity of the season from visiting Pammachius, as he wished, he wrote him the lengthy Letter 13. First he praises his pious tears at his wife’s funeral; then he praises the almsgiving he had expended for the consolation of the deceased. The latter section formerly occupied almost the whole of Letter 33 in the commonly printed editions and formed the latter part of the letter to Alethius. See *Life*, chapter 32, no. 1.

This error arose either from the carelessness of copyists or, more probably, from the negligence of binders, who sewed together the leaves or gatherings of books in the wrong order, so that what should have come later occupied the earlier place, or what should have come earlier occupied the later place. This kind of confusion seems to have arisen because in ancient times pages were never, or only rarely, distinguished by numbers or gatherings by letters, as they are now.

When such confusion had entered one principal copy of this letter, it passed from it into another derived from it. The unequal page divisions in different copies concealed the error: the connection in the principal copy, which viciously joined the end of one page to the beginning of another, fell within a page of the copy. Thus Paulinus’s letter of consolation to Pammachius on the death of his wife Paulina was split into two parts. The first ended abruptly with these words: “But this, as the Apostle says, which is according to man—that is, arising from weakness—is carnal sorrow.” The latter was joined to the letter to Alethius and began with the words “brings about death”; it ended with: “For she is the spouse of faith, the sister of virginity, the daughter of perfection; Paula her mother, Eustochium her sister, you her husband.”

The commonly printed editions, drawn from various manuscript copies, presented the first part; the Regius manuscript likewise preserves it. From this it may be understood that the latter part of the letter formerly addressed to Alethius does not belong to Alethius: writing to Alethius, Paulinus says that he was separated from him by long distances across the earth, Letter 33, no. 1, whereas Paulinus was at Nola only a three-day journey from the city of Rome. In fact, it can be discovered that Alethius was in Gaul when Paulinus wrote to him, from the brother Victor mentioned there, who offered himself as a tireless annual messenger to Alethius, Severus, and Desiderius, his Gallic friends.

Moreover, the first part of the letter to Alethius contains not a single phrase suggestive of consolation. The part formerly placed later, however, was addressed to some son-in-law of Paula, whose 760 wife—who died in the flower of her age—had Eustochium as her sister and Paula as her mother, as the conclusion of the letter states; this man was then living at Rome and distributing very generous alms there to the poor.

Thus the letter to Alethius in the commonly printed editions was a cento composed of two parts: the first to Alethius, living in Gaul and brother of Florentius, bishop of Cahors, as will be shown in Dissertation 3, no. 2; the second to a certain son-in-law of Paula devoted to feeding the poor at Rome.

The error was discovered from various manuscript copies. A bold ancient copyist, by whose hand the Cluniac manuscript was written, noticed that the sense did not hold together. At the junction of its two parts, he cut out approximately nine lines so that some meaning might appear on either side, and concluded the letter to Alethius with the words, “by the wood of your faith and the sweetness of your eloquence.” He then appended the consolation to Pammachius, beginning: “To Pammachius, a brother deservedly to be praised and honored, Paulinus. Thanks be to God, for the consciousness of your virtue and prudence makes my labor and anxiety shorter”; and so on to the end: “Paula her mother, Eustochium her sister, you her husband.”

But far more useful to the public was the scrupulousness of others who did not allow even a syllable of the ancient exemplar—although, as we have said, it had been disordered by the binder—to disappear without reproducing it. In this way they left a scar from which the wound could eventually be recognized and healed.

That scar appears after the words “with a stricken heart,” or, as the Regius and Viennese manuscripts have it, “with a stricken heart” [the manuscript reading is *percusso cordis*], and immediately before what follows, “brings about death.” In this interval Rosweyde inserted an asterisk in the Antwerp edition, adding in the margin: “Not a little is missing”; nevertheless he asserted that the entire following section, to the end, was addressed to Alethius.

More correctly and truthfully, the Viennese manuscript records in that same interval: “Here the end of the preceding letter is missing, and the beginning of the following letter, which is written to Pammachius.” Thus the two Viennese and Cluniac manuscripts agree in confirming that the latter part of the letter commonly addressed to Alethius was given by Paulinus to Pammachius.

Furthermore, Florus of Lyons composed a *Catena* on all the letters of Paul from the Greek as well as the Latin Fathers, excluding Augustine, and divided it into twelve books. The eleventh of these books consists entirely of works by Paulinus, bishop of Nola. There he cites two notable passages from this letter formerly believed to be Alethius’s, under the title “From the letter to Pammachius.”

The first passage concerns Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 1, verses 13–14: “You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance.” Florus writes: “From the letter to Pammachius: Thus we have been bound and grafted into God through Christ, so that we hold God’s pledge, etc., up to ‘the possession of the eternal inheritance,’ Letter 13, nos. 26 and 27.” These words appeared under the title of the letter to Alethius in the Antwerp edition of 1622, page 300.

Florus also cites, on Hebrews chapter 13, verses 1–2, “Let brotherly love remain, and do not forget hospitality,” the following from Paulinus: “From the letter to Pammachius: And consider the reason. You will easily judge that the poor are despised by our will with the crime of murdering brothers, although we see that they are in no way separated from us in God’s work, etc., up to ‘receiving the rewards of their works,’ Letter 13, nos. 20 and 21.”

These very words, which Florus attributes to Paulinus’s letter to Pammachius, are found in the letter addressed to Alethius in the same 761 Antwerp edition, from line 25 of page 295 to line 20 of page 297. Therefore nothing remains doubtful: Florus believed that the former latter part of the letter addressed to Alethius belonged to the letter by which Paulinus consoled Pammachius.

Florus also clearly shows that he recognized only one letter of Paulinus to Pammachius. He says that he is citing the two passages from “the letter to Pammachius”; if he had thought there were several, he would certainly have distinguished them by number, as he did when he cited other letters of Paulinus. Nor, as far as I know, has anyone else recognized two letters to Pammachius. And there will not be two if these are proved to be two parts of one and the same letter.

It is certain from what has been said that the first part is missing from the letter to Pammachius which formerly appeared under the title of the letter to Alethius. This is especially clear from the note in the Viennese manuscript and from its abrupt and unintelligible beginning. For what do the words “brings about death” refer to, unless to something preceding that completes the sentence?

It is equally certain that the latter part is missing from the other letter which is prefaced in the commonly printed editions by the title “To Pammachius.” We are convinced, however, that if the latter part is joined to the former, not even a letter or stroke will be lacking for the letter’s completeness.

These parts coalesce and bind one another by a threefold connection. The first is the passage of the Apostle, 2 Corinthians chapter 7, verse 10: “But worldly sorrow brings about death.” At the end of the commonly printed letter to Pammachius, Paulinus says: “But this, as the Apostle says, which is according to man—that is, arising from weakness—is carnal sorrow.” Then, at the beginning of the latter part of the letter formerly addressed in the printed editions to Alethius, we read: “Brings about death.” We join the passages so that the Apostle’s text is completed: “But this, as the Apostle says, which is according to the human person—that is, arising from weakness—is carnal sorrow, brings about death.” The matter is settled.

The second connection lies in these words of the latter part: “Although under a different author, nevertheless Scripture agrees through both by the one Spirit and word of God.” Do you ask which two sacred writers are mentioned here? Go to the end of the first part. There Paulinus cites Ecclesiasticus, chapter 38, verse 19: “For from sorrow death hastens, and it covers strength.” He adds the passage of the Apostle: “That which according to man—that is, arising from weakness—is carnal sorrow brings about death.” Thus he concludes: “Although under a different author—namely, Jesus Sirach and Paul—Scripture agrees through both by the one Spirit and word of God: for true death is the covering over of virtue,” etc.

But here is a third connection, even stronger, arising from the author’s idea and the arrangement of the entire work. At the beginning of the first part Paulinus had proposed to praise two things in Pammachius: first, his pious tears at the funeral of his wife Paulina; then, the alms he had expended for the consolation of the deceased. For he says (Letter 13, nos. 3 and 4):

“For just as I heard of the calling to God of my holy sister, so I also heard of the devotion of your piety in Christ … that you accompanied your wife … not empty of tears or attended with the vain honor of empty pomp; but, following her with saving remedies and living works—that is, with alms—after first rendering to the flesh the proper rites at the funeral, and honoring the burial with devout tears and the abundant dew of charity, you more religiously paid the honors of the funeral. Therefore I shall first praise this work of piety in you,” etc.

Then, not far from the beginning of the latter part assigned to Alethius, Paulinus says (Letter 13, no. 11): “For now I shall come to the praise of your works, and shall pass from the holiness of your tears to your pious actions.” From there to the end, he praises Pammachius’s generosity toward the poor even more magnificently than his pious tears. 762

It will now be useful to view the letter itself, Letter 13, fully joined together and revised from several ancient manuscripts, in one continuous text, so that from it the logic of the whole argument and the order and connection of all its parts may become clearer.

In the year 398, as we believe, Cardamas arrived at Paulinus’s house during Lent and brought him letters from Delphinus and Amandus. These informed him that the affair of Basil had been successfully handled, of which we spoke above in connection with Letter 12, and also of Delphinus’s prolonged and serious illness. Through the same messenger, however, Paulinus learned both of the illness and of the recovery. After the Lord’s Easter he replied to Delphinus and Amandus in Letters 14 and 15. The bearer was the same Cardamas, whom Paulinus had kept with him for that period. See *Life*, chapter 32, no. 2; Letter 14, nos. 1 and 3; and Letter 15, nos. 1, 2, and 4.

Theridius and Posthumianus had visited Paulinus. When they were returning to Gaul, he gave through them, in the year 399, a letter to Jovius, a distinguished man in Gaul and his relative. See Letter 16, no. 1, and *Life*, chapters 33 and 34.

Throughout the preceding year, 398, from the departure of his boys until winter, Paulinus had awaited Sulpicius Severus. Since he had received no letters from him, either during the remainder of that year or at the beginning of the next (see Letter 17, no. 1), he believed that Severus had not written because he was about to arrive, and therefore awaited him every day.

Accordingly, in the year 399 he set out for Rome as the feast of the Apostles approached, following his customary practice and presuming that there he would embrace his dearest Severus. Pope Anastasius received him with great affection and honor. But he was not granted the enjoyment of seeing his Severus. He therefore consoled himself with a letter delivered to him in Severus’s name, in which Severus pleaded illness and deprived him of the hope of his presence [the reading is somewhat uncertain]. See Letters 17, nos. 1, 2, and 4, and *Life*, chapter 35.

Paulinus received this letter from a man related by marriage to Sabinus Severus. Occupied at Rome for ten full days, he could not write a reply; still less could he do so after returning home, where a serious and prolonged illness confined him. When he recovered, he wrote through Amachius, Saint Delphinus’s subdeacon and a man well known to Severus. See Letter 17, no. 3, and *Life*, chapter 35.

We place in this same year and period Letter 18 to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, in which Paulinus mentions this same illness. The bearer of the letter was Paschasius, Saint Victricius’s deacon. When Paulinus encountered him at Rome, he brought him back with him to Nola, together with Urso, a catechumen of the Church of Rouen, who was worn down by a very serious illness while staying with Paulinus; Paschasius was thus detained at Nola.

Since Urso was in sound and robust health, and Paschasius was considering his return, Paulinus sent through him Letter 18 to Victricius. In it he excuses himself for having detained Paschasius so long and describes the life of the illustrious confessor Victricius, as he had learned it from Paschasius. We present it in Dissertation 4.

Almost two years earlier, Cardamas had brought Paulinus a very brief letter from Delphinus. See Letter 19, no. 1. At the end of the year 399, in winter, the same Cardamas—then an exorcist—again delivered Paulinus letters from Delphinus and Amandus and 763 informed him of Delphinus’s health. See Letter 19, no. 1, and Letter 21, nos. 5 and 6.

Paulinus replied to Amandus in Letter 21, in which he praises Cardamas, and to Delphinus in Letter 19. Although this letter is very long, since Paulinus rarely had an opportunity to write to Delphinus, he added another letter, certainly written between the anniversary of Anastasius’s election and the time when Paulinus customarily went to Rome—that is, between the end of the year 399 and June 29 of the year 400. See Letter 20, nos. 1 and 2, and *Life*, chapter 37, no. 1.

We have assigned a date within this period to several letters to Delphinus and Amandus. When Delphinus had instructed Cardamas to inquire about Paulinus’s health, Paulinus writes in Letter 20 to Delphinus that he was in good health, though not robust, and mentions the benevolence of the supreme pontiff Anastasius toward him. See Letter 20, nos. 1 and 2. We have already observed this in connection with Letter 17; see also *Life*, chapters 35 and 37, no. 1. Everyone recognizes from what has been stated above that Cardamas was the bearer of these letters.

There is no obstacle to assigning Letter 22 to Severus to this year; it must have preceded Letter 27. Severus had given a letter to Paulinus through Marracinus. See Letter 22, no. 1. When Marracinus arrived at Rome, however, he handed it to Sorianus, being unwilling to come into Paulinus’s presence. Sorianus, a deeply devout monk, rejoiced at the desired opportunity to see Paulinus, undertook to carry the letter, and brought it to Paulinus, to whom he commended himself.

Accordingly, in replying to Severus, Paulinus first sketches the image of a true monk and then says that this image is Sorianus, who would probably carry Paulinus’s letter. See *Life*, chapter 37, no. 3, and chapter 35, as well as Letter 22, nos. 2 and 3.

Severus, who was accustomed to write to Paulinus only once a year, wrote again this year, apparently around winter, in order to give stronger proof of his affection and to request reciprocal affection from Paulinus. He sent him a cook named Victor, suitable for preparing the monks’ food: Victor was the companion of his solitude, formerly girded with a sword, the spiritual son of Saint Martin, and the companion of the holy man Blessed Clarus, whom Severus had described in his letter as adorned with virtues.

Victor practiced the culinary art in Paulinus’s household for some time and cut Paulinus’s hair. See *Life*, chapter 38, no. 1; Letter 23, nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, and 10; and the letter preceding Letter 23.

If it was at the end of the year 400, but more probably at the beginning of the year 401, Paulinus replied to Severus through the same Victor. He highly commends Severus’s friendship and goodwill, declares his own reciprocal affection, and then discusses Victor at length. This constitutes the beginning of Letter 23 through no. 10, which formerly made up the whole of Letter 3 to Severus in the commonly printed manuscripts. In those same printed editions and manuscripts, a fourth letter began as follows: “I now come to Victor’s greater service toward me as a brother.” But who cannot see from these opening words the continuity with the preceding letter and that the two are one and the same? We have therefore constituted one Letter 23.

In the latter part, after showing the necessity of loving God and one’s neighbor, he concludes with these words: “The more we glory in your love in the Lord, which alone makes us discharge one of the great and countless debts we owe to God. For in all other good things we scarcely profess ourselves initiated, and then only among the few; in your love 764 alone we profess ourselves perfect.”

Reminded at the end of that letter of the word “perfection,” and specifically of the word “love,” Paulinus begins Letter 24, which had previously been the second in the printed editions. We have prefixed no title to it because it was sent in the same packet as Letter 23. See Letter 24, no. 1. He also reproaches Severus for having heaped upon him, with great affection, unjust praises in a certain letter that has perished—plainly a different letter from Paulinus’s Letter 23. See Paulinus’s Letter 24, nos. 1 and 23, and *Life*, no. 2.

Paulinus composed Letters 25 and 26 from conversations with Victor; we therefore assign them to the year 401, when Victor stayed with Paulinus for some time. See *Life*, chapter 38, no. 1, and chapter 39, no. 1. Letter 25 is addressed to a certain nobleman whose name is unknown. See *Life*, chapter 39, no. 1. Letter 26 was addressed, apparently, to Sebastian, a hermit in Aquitania. See *Life*, chapter 39, no. 2.

Those letters had occupied a place among the commonly printed letters of Saint Jerome. That they are Paulinus’s is shown both by their style and by the person of Victor. Gravius, Schottus, and Rosweyde placed them among Paulinus’s letters; Erasmus likewise judged them to be Paulinus’s in his edition of Jerome. But, most noteworthy of all, the very first Roman edition of Saint Jerome’s letters, in the year 1468, assigns the letter to Sebastian to Paulinus and Therasia, and it was published under their names.

In this same year Paulinus wrote Letter 27, in which he says that he will reply to several letters from Severus, no. 2—at least two, the first of which he had received from Posthumianus and Theridius, and the second from Sorianus and Virinus. See Letter 27, no. 1, and *Life*, chapter 40, no. 2.

Since he promises to reply to all these letters from Severus (Letter 27, no. 2), and since he satisfies not merely all of Severus’s complaints in the earlier letter, much seems to be missing from this Letter 27. See *Life*, chapter 40, no. 2.

In the year 402, Melania the Elder came from Jerusalem to Rome, and when she was returning from Naples to Nola, Paulinus received her with the greatest courtesy. See Letter 29, nos. 6 and 8, and *Life*, chapter 41, no. 2. This distinguished widow brought Paulinus a fragment of the wood of the divine Cross, a gift from John, the illustrious bishop of Jerusalem, and gave him a tunic made from lambs’ wool. Ibid.

Around this same time Victor, sent by Severus, arrived at Paulinus’s house—that is, as winter was ending. See Letter 29, no. 6; Letter 28, no. 3; and *Life*, no. 2. Severus was sending him cloaks woven from camel hair. Letter 29, no. 1.

Severus had written this letter in the preceding year, hoping that Victor would spend the winter with Paulinus and return immediately afterward. See Letter 28, no. 3. But Victor, who had arrived as winter ended, Paulinus detained through the spring months. Ibid. And because even this seemed a short period to Paulinus, who had been so weak during that time that he could not write a reply, he also kept Victor through the middle of summer and did not allow him to leave until the end of summer, so that he would reach Severus in autumn. See Letter 28, no. 3.

Paulinus gave him Letter 28 to carry to Severus, together with the *Panegyric of Theodosius* and a certain poem on Saint Felix. Letter 28, no. 6. He added another letter, namely Letter 29, and sent to Severus a tunic woven from lambs’ wool, saying that it was for him a pledge of Melania’s blessing. See Letter 29, no. 5.

From the cloaks woven from camel hair that Victor had brought from Severus 765 at the beginning of the year, Paulinus took the occasion to confess himself a sinner who needed the garb and labor of penitence. See Letter 29, nos. 1, 4, and 5, and *Life*, chapter 41, nos. 2 and 3. The remainder constitutes a panegyric of Melania. Ibid., no. 6, and *Life*, chapter 41, no. 3.

Also in this year, and no later, Paulinus sent Letter 30 to Severus, which Augustine cited when treating original sin. Since Severus had requested portraits of Paulinus and Therasia, apparently in this Letter 30, and Paulinus had refused, Paulinus nevertheless allowed Severus to dictate their portraits to painters, presenting the painters with a memory of the way in which he wished them depicted. See Letter 30, nos. 2 and 6, and the *Life*.

Severus seems to have done this, since in the following year he arranged for Paulinus to be painted in a sacred building. See Letter 32, no. 2, and *Life*, chapter 44, no. 2. From this we infer that Letter 30 was written in this year, though it could not have been composed much earlier. For the hope by which Severus had been led to visit Paulinus was certainly dashed when he requested Paulinus’s portrait. It is not apparent who delivered this letter. See *Life*, chapter 41, no. 4.

Pauline ordered a church to be built at Fundi, a town where he had formerly possessed estates and a family residence. When this basilica was nearly completed and soon to be consecrated, in the year 403 (see Ep. 32, no. 17; Ep. 31, no. 1; and Life, chap. 44, no. 1), he sent Letters 31 and 32 to Severus, who was likewise occupied with the construction of religious buildings. See Ep. 32, nos. 1 and 10. Severus took particular care to complete the basilica’s baptistery, which he decorated on one side with images of Martin and on the other with images of Paulinus. See Ep. 32, nos. 1–2. Victor, sent by Severus to Paulinus, asked him for relics of the saints to be deposited in a church constructed by Severus. Since Paulinus had none except those which he was reserving for the Fundanian basilica, soon to be dedicated, he gave Victor a fragment of the wood of the true cross, enclosed in a little golden tube, which he had received as a gift from Melania. See Ep. 31, no. 1. Since the page was still open, he began another, longer letter, [Col. 0751B] Letter 32, in which he complains that Severus had treated him either with excessive honor or with an insult, since he had compared Paulinus himself with Saint Martin, and so forth. See Ep. 32, nos. 2–3. Paulinus sent these letters through Victor. See Life, chap. 44, no. 2.

Perhaps on this same journey Victor, their common courier, brought Paulinus a letter from Alethius; and through the same Victor Paulinus seems to have sent Alethius a reply, Letter 33, which is not complete. See Ep. 33, nos. 1–2, and Life, chap. 45, no. 1. Some think that Paulinus also sent Alethius the discourse on the Treasury, or On Almsgiving, which is expressly addressed to him in a Vatican manuscript. See Life, chap. 45, no. 1. We have assigned this discourse a place among the letters, as Letter 34, so that it might retain its proper number. Who that Alethius was may be seen in Dissertation 3, no. 2.

In Poem 27, published at the beginning of the year 404, Paulinus counts Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, among the saints; his relics gave distinction to these lands. [Col. 0751C] Accordingly, Letter 35 to Delphinus, which responds very briefly to his earlier letter, cannot be assigned later than the present year, 403. From that earlier letter—or perhaps from some other indication—Paulinus had learned at about the same time of the death of Delphinus’s brother; he asks Delphinus for prayers for his brother’s soul and for himself. For the same reason he sent Letter 36 to Amandus.

In the year 404, Victricius, bishop of Rouen, sent Paulinus a letter through Candidianus (see Ep. 37, no. 1), to which Paulinus replied in Letter 37 toward the end of 404. See Dissertation 4, chapter 3, no. 2, for the date assigned to this letter.

Aper had written to Paulinus about his conversion to Christ. See Ep. 38, no. 1. In this year, 404, Paulinus replied to him in Letter 38. See Dissertation 5 for who this Aper was and what correspondence Paulinus had with him.

Aper again wrote to Paulinus in Letter 39 and complained that his sons’ estates were the cause of the necessity that forced him to concern himself with earthly affairs, since he ought to have sold them. [Col. 0751D] Paulinus replied to Aper and his wife Amanda on this matter, in his own name and that of Therasia, in the year 405, as may be inferred from the dates of the letters sent in both directions.

There had formerly been an exchange of letters between Paulinus and Sanctus, before Paulinus converted to Christ. See Ep. 40, nos. 1–2 and 6. Shortly after his conversion he wrote to Sanctus, and thereafter surrendered himself to a prolonged silence. Ibid., no. 3. The long silence that Paulinus had maintained with Sanctus from that time onward leads us to believe that he wrote this Letter 40 after he had already been living at Nola for many years. Add that in it he says that old age not only scatters white hairs over his head but drenches it with them. Ibid., no. 6. We can only judge that he wrote it before he was promoted to the episcopate, and therefore before the year 409, since he writes together with Therasia (see the heading of Ep. 40), and certainly after the year 397, when Rufinus returned to the West. Rufinus is surely the person he indicates [Col. 0752A] when he writes to Sanctus and Amandus that he had received something from a very learned and dear friend who had traveled widely. We therefore place it around the year 405.

After Paulinus had appended what was almost a conclusion to this Letter 40, he took up another subject, namely the hymns he had received from Sanctus. This may elegantly be regarded as a second letter added to the first without any title; and in fact the two are read separately in the Cluniac and Viennese manuscripts. In the Viennese manuscript, Letter 41 is separated from Letter 40 by fourteen other letters; in the Cluniac manuscript, although the latter follows the former immediately, it is distinguished from it by this separate title: “Letter of Saint Paulinus to I know not whom,” the name being suppressed. In the Viennese manuscript, however, the first letter of all is entitled “To Sanctus and Amandus”; eight letters to Sulpicius Severus follow, then three to Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, and an equal number to Amandus; finally comes the notice: “On the back of the letter we read, under the title: Likewise another letter of the same Paulinus, XVI.” Who those [Col. 0752B] Sanctus and Amandus were may be seen in chapter 25 of the Life of Saint Paulinus, nos. 1–2.

We think that Paulinus wrote Letter 42 to Florentius, bishop of Cahors, in the year 405 or thereabouts. See Life, chap. 47, no. 1, and chap. 45, no. 2.

In the year 405, Victor, sent by Severus to Paulinus, brought another letter from that same Severus, in which he asked Paulinus to have Victor meet him when the vintage season arrived. See Ep. 42, nos. 1–2. At the same time Victor delivered a letter from the presbyter Desiderius, who asked Paulinus for an interpretation of the blessings that Jacob, when near death, bestowed upon his sons. Ibid., no. 3. Shortly after his arrival at Nola, Victor prepared to resume his journey, so that Paulinus had time to write only brief letters to Desiderius and Severus (ibid., nos. 1–2); both letters have been lost. But just as Victor was about to depart, sudden obstacles held him back, since winter and fear closed navigation and the roads. [Col. 0752C] Thus prevented, he was forced to postpone his departure until the end of winter. Ibid., no. 1.

The danger that closed the roads was undoubtedly fear that Roman or enemy armies might meet him on the way. This may be referred either to Alaric’s descent into Italy in the year 403 or to that of Radagaisus in 405 (see Prosper, Chronicle). Since we have assigned to the year 403 another letter from Paulinus to Severus, delivered to him by Victor, we think that this fear should be referred to the invasion of Radagaisus, which caused much greater alarm in Italy than Alaric had done. Radagaisus’s army is said to have been destroyed only around winter (ibid.). Although it may have been present earlier, Roman troops—who might still have been scattered in many places and who for the most part were barbarians—could also have inspired fear in travelers. Victor was therefore compelled to wait at Nola until the spring weather of 406 arrived, so that he could return to Gaul.

While he was waiting, he was attacked by a most serious illness and brought to the point of death, with everyone despairing of his recovery. See Ep. 43, no. 1. He did recover, but spent more time restoring his health than he had endured in illness [Col. 0752D] (ibid.), and was completely restored only shortly before the approaching feast of the Apostles. Ibid. Paulinus did not wish to dismiss him so soon, but kept him until he could take him with him to Rome as his companion on his annual journey. From there Victor was to depart and return to Gaul, and meet Severus when the vintage season arrived—at the very time Severus had specified, but in the following year only. Ibid., II. 2.

The two brief letters that Paulinus had written the previous year to Severus and Desiderius, when Victor wished to depart, he gave to Victor to deliver (ibid., nos. 1–2; and Life, chap. 47, nos. 1 and 3); but he added to them two longer letters addressed to the same men. Ibid., no. 2; and Life, chap. 47, no. 3. The longer letter to Severus has been lost, nor does anything remain of whatever he may subsequently have written to him. The letter to Desiderius, Letter 43, survives. In it Paulinus humbly declines to answer the question proposed concerning the blessings of the patriarchs; he requested their explanation from [Col. 0753A] Rufinus and finally obtained it, as we shall see in Letters 46 and 47.

We observed in connection with Letter 39 that Paulinus wrote to Aper and Amanda in the year 405. He sent them another letter, Letter 42, which cannot be placed before the year 406, since a letter from the same Aper and Amanda to Paulinus intervened; Paulinus praises it highly and says that he could not return anything comparable. See Ep. 44, no. 1, and Life, chap. 48, no. 2.

Paulinus gives the month and day on which he sent Letter 45 to Augustine in section 8, in these words: “On the day before the Ides of May, the deacon Quintus came to us to request a reply, and on the Ides he obtained permission to depart before the sixth hour.” Augustine himself indicates the year in Letter 95, no. 1, when he writes: “Accordingly, concerning this joy in which our brother Possidius shares with you: when you have heard from him what sorrowful cause compelled him, you will recognize that I have spoken this with complete truth.”

That sorrowful cause which compelled Possidius to sail to Italy was none other than the calamity and destruction inflicted upon his Church [Col. 0753B] at Calama by pagans in June of the year 408. As Possidius departed, this reply was undoubtedly entrusted to him for delivery to Paulinus, or at any rate was sent not long after his departure. Augustine wrote it while wintering at Carthage, as appears from Paulinus’s Letter 50, no. 14—that is, at the beginning or end of winter; for in midwinter he was at Hippo, according to Letter 97 of Saint Augustine, no. 3. Unless, perhaps, “midwinter” signifies a time especially unfavorable for navigation.

We observed in connection with Letter 43 that Desiderius, a presbyter in Aquitania, had asked Paulinus for an interpretation of the blessings of the patriarchs, and that Paulinus had declined to provide it. Later, when Desiderius asked him again, Paulinus requested this explanation from Rufinus; in his Letter 47 to Rufinus he testifies that others had also consulted him about it. For when Rufinus wrote to Paulinus that he had come to Rome on certain [Col. 0753C] business (see Ep. 46, no. 1), around the year 407, Paulinus asked him in Letter 46, no. 3, to explain the chapter in which Judah is blessed by Jacob.

Afterward he wrote him Letter 47, asking him to elucidate this blessing by a threefold interpretation (see Gennadius, Catalogue, chap. 17): historical, moral, and mystical. Thus, after first offering an excuse, Rufinus finally complied and yielded to his wishes. See Ep. 47, no. 2. Once he had received the explanation of this blessing, Paulinus first asked Rufinus to explain it as distributed among the remaining sons. Ibid., no. 2. Rufinus complied, and both works, together with his letters to Paulinus, still survive.

Paulinus sent this final Letter 47 to Rufinus through Cerealis. Rufinus was then living at the monastery of Pinētum, from which he was shortly to come to Rome before returning to the East, around the year 409. You will learn these matters more clearly from the History of Jerome and Rufinus, which, God willing, the most learned and dearest of my friends will publish. See, however, Life [Col. 0753D] of Paulinus, chap. 48, no. 1, and chap. 50, no. 1.

Sacchinius doubts whether these two letters to Rufinus are by our Paulinus. He says that their style seems to him more likely to have been deliberately fashioned by someone in imitation of Paulinus than to be Paulinus’s genuine style. See Sacchinius, Life of Paulinus, near the end, p. 739. I myself do not possess such penetrating judgment that I can discern what difference there may be between this style and Paulinus’s genuine style. I could easily persuade myself that the only foundation for the doubts entertained by some concerning these letters was a preconceived hatred of Rufinus. For some think that Rufinus could not safely have been loved after the controversy arose and Rufinus was alienated from Jerome, although the friendship of Augustine and Paulinus for both [Col. 0754A] men suffered no diminution on that account.

But from the evidence cited above it is clearer than daylight that these letters were written by our Paulinus to Rufinus.

We place Letter 48, of which we give a fragment, at the end of the year 408, or rather at the beginning of 409, shortly before Paulinus’s episcopate, for the reasons given by us in chapter 49, section 3, of the Life of Paulinus, where we discuss at length this letter, which some have rejected.

We demonstrate in the Life, chap. 50, no. 1, that Paulinus had already become a bishop by the year 410. Since in Letter 49 to Macarius, concerning the story of Valgius’s rescue from shipwreck—the man who later took the name Victor (Ep. 49, no. 2)—he calls himself the shepherd of a small flock (ibid., no. 14), there is no room for doubt that this letter to Macarius was written when Paulinus was already a bishop, not before the year 409, but either in that year or later, since we cannot establish the exact date of the event. See Letter 49 for the course of this story, and Life, chap. 51, no. 1, for who that Macarius was.

[Col. 0754B] It appears that this Letter 50 of Paulinus to Augustine was written somewhat later than Augustine’s Letter 95, composed toward the end of the year 408, since in section 14 Paulinus asks that another copy of the reply already sent to him be transmitted. It was somewhat earlier than Augustine’s Letter 149, written around the year 414, since between this letter and that one several letters passed back and forth, including Augustine’s reply to the questions that Paulinus here proposed; all of these letters, however, have been lost. Compare Augustine’s Letter 149, no. 1.

Augustine’s Letter 149 to Paulinus can scarcely be placed before the year 414. First, several letters that have been lost passed back and forth between it and Letter 50, which Paulinus answered in the year 410 and whose questions Augustine again addresses, as appears from section 2. Second, in section 32 mention is made of Urbanus, bishop of Sicca; if he is the same Urbanus as the presbyter mentioned in Augustine’s Letter 143, no. 1, he had not yet attained episcopal rank toward the end of the year 412. [Col. 0754C] It can scarcely be placed later, since the deacon Peregrinus, who had departed together with Urbanus when Urbanus went to assume the burden of the episcopate, had not yet returned to Hippo when Augustine dictated this letter, as he states at its end.

Letter 51 was sent by Paulinus, now bishop of Nola, to Eucherius, who was not yet a bishop, sometime between the year 409 and the year 426, while Saint Honoratus was still abbot over the monks of Lérins. In 426 Honoratus was appointed bishop of the Church of Arles. This Honoratus had withdrawn to the island of Lérins, off the maritime coast of the province, and had founded a monastery there. Saint Eucherius, later bishop of Lyons, withdrew with his wife Galla to the island of Lerō, now commonly called Sainte-Marguerite, near Lérins, separated from it by a narrow stretch of sea.

Honoratus, who had become known to Paulinus through men sent by Eucherius, sent three monks from his community to greet Paulinus [Col. 0754D] in the following year, prompted by the example of Saint Eucherius. See Ep. 51, no. 1. Through this welcome opportunity provided by the monks of Lérins, Paulinus sent Eucherius a letter full of affection and love (ibid., no. 2), which anyone who knows his character and intellect will acknowledge as thoroughly characteristic of Paulinus. It is addressed to Eucherius and his wife Galla.

Rosweyde doubts whether the story of Saint Genesius the martyr is a genuine work of our Paulinus. He thinks it could be attributed to a certain Paulinus, bishop of Béziers, who held that office in the year 420. Nevertheless, the work is commonly attributed to Paulinus of Nola, and indeed there is nothing to prevent its being assigned to him, although we do not see what occasion he had for composing the narrative. We have found no argument by which to determine its date.

## SECOND DISSERTATION. ON THE POEMS

[Col. 0755]

[Col. 0755A] 770 To Gestidius, to whom Paulinus sent birds and oysters, we attribute two poems written before Paulinus’s conversion, since they contain none of the flavor of Christian piety that can be detected in his other poems composed after his conversion. See Life, chap. 5. This places them before the year 390.

While he was still living in the world, Paulinus reduced to an epitome three books that Suetonius had composed on kings and produced a most delightful poem. Suetonius Tranquillus’s work On the Kings has perished, and with it Paulinus’s Epitome, except for a few verses of the Pauline poem which Ausonius praises and magnificently extols in Letter 19 to that same Paulinus. We give a fragment of this poem, which we know with certainty was written before the year 390. For from the time he converted to Christ Paulinus was far removed from this kind of writing; he renounced the Muses and the fictions of poets, as may be inferred from his Poem 10 to Ausonius, verses 19 and following.

A short time after he had advanced to a stricter way of life and [Col. 0755B] withdrawn to Spain, Paulinus composed certain poems which do not breathe the holiness found in his later writings and poems. Among these we place the Morning Prayer to God. In it he earnestly asks God for the honorable conduct of a worldly man, from which, nevertheless, he promises himself an eternal and blessed life, verse 18.

Another Morning Prayer to God was also composed around the same time. In it, however, greater piety, deeper humility, and fear of God’s judgments shine forth. In verse 67 he sufficiently indicates that a son had then been born to him: “May I always be a father, without blemish to this name.”

Since in Poem 32, verses 599 and following, he says that he had a son in Spain whom, after eight days from his birth, he ordered to be buried at Complutum there (ibid., verse 605); and since it is clear from the Life of Paulinus, chap. 5, no. 1; chap. 6, nos. 2–3; chap. 14, no. 3; chap. 15, no. 1; and especially chap. 16, no. 1, that he spent four full years in Spain, from the year 389 until the spring of 394, [Col. 0755C] when, deprived of his child, he withdrew to Nola, this poem must be placed within that interval. We have therefore assigned it approximately to the year 390.

In the poem on Saint John the Baptist, Paulinus seems to indicate that he had not long before devoted himself to a more attentive religious observance and adopted a stricter life, Poem 6, verse 175: “I hope that I shall be able, with strength once established, to…” [The quotation is incomplete in the supplied text.] We therefore judge that the poem was written around the year 390.

We assign the Paraphrase of the First Psalm to this period. Its author was still inexperienced in theological mysteries, since it contains the error of those who, misunderstanding the Apostle’s passage in 1 Corinthians 3, thought that all Christians, even the wicked, would attain a certain salvation and would not be tormented by the punishments of the condemned, provided only that they had preserved the faith intact.

We have placed Poems 8 and 9, on Psalms 2 and 136, whose precise date we cannot establish, after the preceding poem, [Col. 0755D] because their subject is the same and Paulinus perhaps composed them at the same time.

We have already observed in connection with Poem 5 that Paulinus, after converting from worldly life, withdrew to Spain with his wife and spent four years there, from the year 389 until the spring of 394, when he withdrew to Nola. During these four years Ausonius wrote several letters to Paulinus while he was living in Spain. In Letter 23, apparently written in the year 390, Ausonius attributes Paulinus’s conversion to fickleness of mind, reproaches him for interrupting their correspondence, complains that he lived so far away in Spain, and invites him to return to him. This letter was not delivered to Paulinus while he was living in Spain until the fourth year. See Poem 10, verse 1, and Life, chap. 12, no. 1.

[Col. 0756A] Since Paulinus did not reply, Ausonius wrote again in the following year, Letter 24, complaining of his silence and charging him with betraying their friendship. He suggests various ways of writing so that Paulinus’s wife Therasia—whom he maliciously called Tanaquil—would not know of it, Letter 24, verse 31.

Apparently in the year 392 he also wrote a third letter, which has perished. In it, I think, Ausonius complained that Paulinus had now been absent from his homeland for three years and pleaded with him to return to the Muses. See Ausonius, Letter 25, verse 1, and Vinet’s Notes, p. 568.

Since Paulinus, who had received no letters from Ausonius, still did not respond, Ausonius sent him Letter 25 again in the year 393. In it he continued to complain of the arrogance by which Paulinus disdained to reply. Finally he added that the villages of Spain, the snowy regions of the Pyrenees, and the forests of the Vascones had transformed Paulinus’s exceptionally gentle character. He said that Paulinus was mentally disturbed, avoided gatherings of people, and suffered from black bile; at last he begged the Muses to recall Paulinus to poetry.

We assign these three letters to different years both because of the distance between the places—for Ausonius lived in Aquitania and Paulinus in Spain—and because Ausonius, waiting day by day for Paulinus’s replies, wrote again only after a considerable interval. [Col. 0756B] At last, four years later, Paulinus received all three at once: the one beginning “The last letter which was ours,” as will appear below; the one beginning “This is the fourth letter to you”; and another which has perished. See Life, chap. 12, no. 2.

In that same year, 393, during the summer (see Poem 10, verse 1), Paulinus also replied to these three letters in verse, in Poem 10. Its beginning is an elegy serving as a kind of preface, followed by iambic trimeters and dimeters in which he explains why he had renounced the Muses and abandoned his possessions.

The iambic verses were followed by hexameters (see Poem 10, verse 14), in which he vigorously refutes Ausonius’s harsh words in heroic verse, beginning “Do not reproach me with my ancestral…” (ibid., verse 103). In this way he responds to Ausonius’s Letter 25, “This is the fourth letter to you,” to the third letter that has perished, and to Letter 24, “The last letter which was ours,” [Col. 0756C] in which Ausonius called Therasia a Tanaquil (ibid., verse 31).

The letters which earlier printed manuscripts divided into four under various new and false titles should be counted as only two. The first of these contains the following three poems: the elegiac poem “The Fourth Returns”; the iambic poem “Why Have You Renounced”; and the hexameter poem “Do Not Reproach Me.” An old manuscript of Lyons appended the iambic poem to the elegiac one. This is certainly the iambic poem that Paulinus said he would place before the heroic poem in the final elegies. Thus the heroic poem by which he intended to defend himself is the one beginning “Do not reproach me with my ancestral….”

There was therefore a single letter containing these three poems, and Paulinus himself makes this sufficiently clear in his elegiac preface. Since Paulinus says in Poem 10, verses 22 and following, that Ausonius names the little towns of Spain by the unspoken names of the cities Caesaraugusta, Tarraco, and Barcino, and since these are found in Ausonius’s first letter, it is clear that Paulinus had not yet received that letter at the time.

[Col. 0756D] In addition, Paulinus replied to Ausonius in another poem beginning “The succession of my…,” toward the end of that same year, 393, since he returned to Nola in the spring of the following year. See Life, chapters 16 and 17, no. 1. This poem responds to Ausonius’s Letter 23 and to another letter in which Ausonius accused Therasia of exercising authority over her husband; Paulinus seems to have received these together somewhat later with the three other letters. See Life, chap. 13.

Paulinus testifies that each year he honored the birthday of Saint Felix, celebrated on January 14, with a new birthday poem, paying it as though it were an annual tribute. Ep. 28, no. 6. It appears that this continuous series of fifteen poems was begun by Paulinus before he returned to Nola and Saint Felix, indeed that it was begun in Spain when he was preparing for the journey to Nola. This is evident from the first birthday poem, which we therefore think belongs to January of the year 394, because no one doubts—and we demonstrate—that Paulinus began to live at Nola [Col. 0757A] toward the end of that same year. See Life, chapters 16, 17, and 18, no. 1.

Accordingly, the second birthday poem belongs to the year 395, the third to 396, and so successively until the tenth and final poem, which must be associated with the year 408. See what is said concerning the second and third poems in Life, chap. 26, no. 1, and chap. 27, no. 2.

The fourth birthday poem on Saint Felix was published at the beginning of the year 397, according to the sequence established by us in connection with Poem 12.

Paulinus composed the fifth birthday poem on Saint Felix at the beginning of the year 398. See what we said above concerning Poem 12.

The date of Poem 17, addressed to Nicetas on his return to Dacia, must be established from the order of the birthday poems in honor of Saint Felix. In the ninth birthday poem, verse 333, Paulinus says, “At last you have come, returned to me [Col. 0757B] in the fourth year.” Since that poem was published at the beginning of the year 402, Nicetas’s first arrival at Nola must be assigned to the year 398. Paulinus indicates that Nicetas departed in the summer in Poem 17, verses 26, 33–36, and that on his second journey he was present there four years later, on the feast of Saint Felix in the year 402. See Life, chap. 41, no. 1.

The sixth birthday poem on Saint Felix is placed by us at the beginning of the year 399, according to the sequence indicated above in connection with Poem 12.

We observed above, in Dissertation 1, that Letter 16 to Jovius was sent concerning Fate and Fortune. From that same letter, section 1, it may be inferred that Paulinus had shortly before written to him on the same subject, perhaps the poem under discussion. It could therefore be placed in the year 398 or at the beginning of 399, since Paulinus’s Letter 16 to him was written in the year 399, as we demonstrate in Dissertation 1, in connection with Letter 16, and in Life, chap. 33, no. 1, and chap. 34, no. 2; [Col. 0757C] or in the year 399, if it was sent together with the letter.

Paulinus must have composed the seventh birthday poem on Saint Felix in the year 400, according to the sequence established by us in connection with Poem 12.

In Poem 26, namely the eighth birthday poem of Saint Felix, which Paulinus composed at the beginning of the year 401, he mentions in verse 386 that most people offered themselves each day before Saint Felix’s altar, to give thanks to him because, through God’s mercy and the aid of that same saint, they had escaped unharmed from shipwrecks that threatened their lives. He may perhaps allude to the story of Martinianus, which Cytherius describes in Poem 21; thus that poem may have been written in the preceding year, 400.

Julianus, the son of Memorius the bishop, was married to Ia. Paulinus was a friend of both father and son, just as Augustine was. He composed in verse an Epithalamium for the marriage of Julianus and Ia. In order to establish its date, we must observe that around the year 408 Augustine wrote to his father, the bishop Memorius, and there mentioned his son Julianus, who was then [Col. 0757D] a deacon (see Augustine, Letter 101, no. 4) and later became a heresiarch. See Augustine, Books 6 Against Julian. Since he was a deacon in the year 408, this epithalamium must be assigned to the year 400 or thereabouts. See Life, chap. 59, no. 2, and chap. 51, no. 5.

According to the chronology established thus far, the eighth birthday poem of Saint Felix must be assigned to the beginning of the year 401. Its historical setting agrees completely with this: it was composed [Col. 0758A] amid the turmoil of war and barbarian incursions (Poem 23, verse 75), specifically amid fear of the Goths (ibid., verse 22). From Prosper’s Chronicle we learn that Alaric, leader of the Goths, and Radagaisus ravaged Italy in the year 400; Jerome likewise tells us that they besieged Aquileia in the year 400 or 401. See Jerome, Against Rufinus III.6, vol. II.

Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, had already come to Nola four years earlier, as we observed above in connection with Poem 17. He came to Nola again and was present for the feast of Saint Felix on January 14 in the year 402. See Poem 27, verse 333; Ep. 29, no. 14; and Life, chap. 41, no. 1. Poem 24 agrees perfectly with the sequence established above for Poems 12 and 17.

The tenth birthday poem on Saint Felix was published at the beginning of the year 403, according to the same sequence.

In Dissertation 1 and Life, chapter 44, we observed that in the year 403 Paulinus sent Letter 32 to Severus, who was engaged in building basilicas. He sent him [Col. 0758B] epigrams for the Nolana and Fundanian basilicas, which he had just constructed, to be inscribed on the walls of the church at Primuliacum. See Ep. 32 and Life, chap. 44, no. 2.

Since the few verses that we add to Paulinus’s works did not suit the church at Primuliacum, Paulinus did not send them to Severus, who was building a new church where there had previously been none (see note 161). It is therefore clear that they were composed in that same year, 403.

At the beginning of the year 404 Paulinus wrote the eleventh birthday poem on Saint Felix, according to the sequence established above in connection with Poem 12.

Nothing remains of the twelfth birthday poem, which Paulinus wrote in honor of Saint Felix in the year 405. The title of the thirteenth, composed at the beginning of the year 406 according to the sequence of our history, is: “On the Destruction of the Gothic Army Together with Its King.” These words clearly indicate the defeat of Radagaisus. See note 329. The few surviving portions of this poem prove that Paulinus attributed this victory to the martyrs of Rome and of the [Col. 0758C] Empire. See Poem 28.

We place the fourteenth birthday poem on Saint Felix in the year 407, according to the sequence established by us in connection with Poem 12.

The fifteenth birthday poem on Saint Felix is inferred to have been written in the year 408 from the sequence established in connection with Poem 12. We know that this was the last poem published by Paulinus on Saint Felix—whether other poems have perished or whether Paulinus wrote nothing further about him. For it is clear that the disturbances that arose during the following three years could have turned Paulinus away from these diversions of the mind; and once he had attained the episcopate, he certainly considered that piety should be cultivated through other pursuits. See Life, chap. 49, no. 1.

We have not been able to assign a definite place or date to the fragment of an uncertain birthday poem on Saint Felix.

We cannot establish by any argument a definite date for this panegyric On the Death of the Boy Celsus. [Col. 0758D] We know only that it was written between the year 393 and the year 413. In verses 599 and 600 it mentions a son who died in Spain and was buried at Complutum—that is, the son who died between the years 389 and 394, as we demonstrated above in connection with Poem 5. In verse 624 it designates Paulinus’s wife Therasia, who, it is entirely probable, had already died by the year 413. See Life, chap. 50, no. 1.

## THIRD DISSERTATION

## ON SAINT SULPICIUS SEVERUS, DISCIPLE OF THE BLESSED MARTIN

[Col. 0757]

1. The name of Sulpicius Severus is found in various Martyrologies on 29 January, where he is identified as a disciple of St. Martin and bishop of Bourges (Bituricensis). As for his episcopate, the most learned authorities agree with Gennadius, who attributes to him only the rank of presbyter. They believe that he was called bishop of Bourges because he was not distinguished from another of the two bishops of that Church who also bore the name Sulpicius—one of whom lived under Guntram in 585, the other under Dagobert in 680. Indeed, the silence that Sulpicius Severus imposed upon himself toward the end of his life [Col. 0759A] is less compatible with someone who had assumed episcopal office.

But whether the man celebrated on 29 January (Bolland., *Acta Sanctorum*, 19 January, vol. II, nos. 12, p. 968) was one of the two bishops of Bourges or the disciple of St. Martin: those who revised the Martyrology under Urban VIII embraced the former opinion; and (ibid., no. 10) on that very day the Church of Bourges now venerates the earlier of those two men. We read that none of the ancients assigned the surname Severus to this Sulpicius; and the fact that most Martyrologies, including the Roman Martyrology since the time of Urban VIII, give the name “Severus” without the surname “Sulpicius” is of the greatest importance. (Ibid., no. 2.) Writers of a later age dispute among themselves whose the name Severus is: some assign it to the later bishop without foundation (Bolland., on 17 January, nos. 1 and 6, pp. 165–166); Bollandus assigns it to the earlier, guided by the sole consideration that it cannot belong to the later one.

Gregory of Tours speaks of the earlier as a good man, but reports nothing distinctive about him [Col. 0759B]; nor is anything known about him from other authors. I would not readily believe that anyone could prove that the Church of Bourges had always venerated this man. (The same author, on 29 January, no. 17, p. 969.) Guibert, believed to have died in 1208, indicates that the feast of Sulpicius Severus, the blessed disciple of St. Martin, which he himself had attended at the Major Monastery, was celebrated on 29 January with a solemn office; yet he calls him bishop of Bourges. The monks of the Major Monastery, however, seem to have honored him not because he had been bishop of Bourges, but because he was a disciple of St. Martin, their founder (ibid., no. 15, p. 968), and because he had established his residence among them, as they maintained. Yet the praises with which Gennadius (*ch. 19*) and Paulinus of Périgueux (*Metr.* 5), sixty or eighty years after his death, celebrated him sufficiently show the extent of the honor in which he was always held by the Gallican Church.

Guibert testifies that at the Major Monastery a written Life of him was preserved [Col. 0759C] (Bolland., loc. cit., no. 14); from this it is clear that the monks honored the feast day of Martin’s disciple on 29 January. Accordingly, the Martyrology of the Gallican Church not unjustly assigns his feast to that day (ibid., no. 12). Be that as it may, it is entirely right and fitting to venerate a man through whose conversion, life, extraordinary penitence, silence, and piety—celebrated with the highest praises by the holiest men—the Gallican Church was not only glorified, but also through whose writings the other faithful were edified and the most learned were filled with admiration.

The Church’s constant reverence for the memory of Sulpicius Severus would shine forth through stronger evidence if it could be established that he was the Severinus of whom Gregory of Tours (*On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 5) relates two miracles: through his prayer a tree began to wither and then to grow green again, and a lily placed upon his tomb flowered each year on the very day of his death. Rosweyde, on the basis of many conjectures (see note 13), thinks that they were the same man. Gregory of Tours (loc. cit., §§ 50–51) [Col. 0759D] indeed asserts that this Severinus was a presbyter distinguished by the nobility of his birth, who spent his resources on feeding the poor and had caused two churches to be built on his rural estate, in one of which he had been laid in a tomb.

The only difficulty for Rosweyde is the place of residence. Sulpicius Severus seems to have lived near Toulouse, whereas the Severinus of whom Gregory speaks lived within the territory (see note 137 to Paulinus) [Col. 0760A] of the city of Georreta, in the village of Sexciacum or in the neighboring districts. Nevertheless, no argument proves that Sulpicius Severus maintained a residence near Toulouse beyond the year 405. He could subsequently have changed his place of residence and withdrawn to another estate of his own, perhaps with the intention that the Pyrenees would protect him from barbarian incursions, or for other reasons.

In fact, everything Gregory of Tours testifies about him fits more closely with the course and later development of Sulpicius Severus’s life than with the condition in which he is known to have been before 405. Up to that point he appears to us as a solitary man, occupied only with the care of himself and his household, or at most with a few friends who shared his private life; for he calls a certain Calippianus his presbyter. Severinus, however (*Dialogue* I, p. 306), was plainly engaged in pastoral ministry, since every Sunday he celebrated Mass in two churches eight leagues apart (Gregory of Tours, loc. cit., § 50). He had evidently ordered basilicas to be built on his estates [Col. 0760B] (ibid.), and it is sufficiently clear that these were not the churches Paulinus mentions in his letters 31 (no. 1) and 32 (nos. 5–6), since the churches built by Sulpicius Severus seem to have been close to one another.

For this reason also it may be conjectured that Sulpicius Severus is meant by the name Severinus: according to Samson’s *Geography*, there is in the territory of Beorreta a town called Severus in its own right, and three leagues from it, in the district of Arminiacum, lies the village of St. Justin. This may perhaps be the village of Sexciacum where, according to Gregory of Tours (*On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 49), St. Justin the presbyter rested, at whose tomb many miracles occurred. Gregory nowhere records when that Justin, Severinus, and also the presbyter Misilinus lived; through the merits of Misilinus, notable miracles likewise took place in the village called Talva, in the same region, where he had been buried. On our Sulpicius, see Saussay in the *Gallican Martyrology*, and Peter of Natalibus, book III, chapter 67.

## On Alethius

2. Jerome writes to Algasius as follows (Ep. 151, at the beginning):

> I am sufficiently astonished that, after leaving nearby the purest spring, you have sought the waters of our little streams so far away. Here you have the holy presbyter Alethius, who, as they say, can resolve what you ask by living speech and prudent, eloquent discourse. Therefore let him cure our bitterness with his nectar-like honey and restrain the phlegm of old age with the vigor of youth.

Paulinus, I think, wrote to this same Alethius (Ep. 31), whom he addresses in the title as “the blessed and deservedly venerable brother,” to excuse himself for some little work that Alethius had requested from him. He sent the letter through Victor, his customary courier to Gaul, as appears from other passages in Paulinus; from this it may be inferred that Alethius lived in that same region.

Gregory of Tours (*History of the Franks*, book II, ch. 13) cites our Paulinus’s letter 48, in which Paulinus lists Alethius, bishop of Cahors, among the most holy bishops of Gaul, worthy of the Lord and guardians of the whole faith and religion in the Church’s troubled circumstances [Col. 0760D]. It is sufficiently plausible that Paulinus wrote to this same Alethius from the letter itself, in which he is designated a bishop, just as Amandus and others who were bishops are so designated when Paulinus wrote to them. In the Cluniac, R.g., and Viennese manuscript codices, he is also called, in the title of letter 33 (see the title, *Life*, ch. 45), the brother of Florentius, bishop of Cahors, whom he perhaps succeeded.

# FOURTH DISSERTATION. ON ST. VICTRICIUS

## Chapter One. The history of St. Victricius, bishop of Rouen. He lays down his arms and suffers for Christ, who protects his innocence by miracles.

1. Victricius seems to have been born (Paulinus, Ep. 18, no. 1) somewhere within the boundaries of the Empire, from which God brought him forth into the light for his people. He was younger than Martin, who was born in 316 or 317 (ibid., no. 9). By the Lord’s appointment Victricius became a soldier (ibid., no. 7); he served the emperor, and in that very military service first entered the faith (ibid.).

When he was first inflamed with love for Christ, he rejected military service in his mind, and on a day of great significance for the military council suddenly removed his arms, throwing them at the feet of his tribune. When the tribune was driven into a frenzy, Victricius was stretched out for scourging, beaten with clubs, and, still covered with injuries, was thrown into prison and rubbed against sharp fragments of pottery; before his wounds had closed, he was presented to the Count (Paulinus, Ep. 18, no. 7). The Count, apparently, had come to torture him. Paulinus says that Victricius triumphed over that more powerful enemy (ibid.), from which it may be inferred that the Count subjected him to torture. The guards did not dare to inflict further torments (ibid.), but Victricius was condemned to death.

Then God visibly confounded his enemies by miracles. While Victricius was being led to the place of execution, the executioner walking before him touched his neck with his hand in mockery, as though feeling out the place for his blow. Immediately his eyes were knocked out and he was struck blind (ibid). He was blinded so that many might be given sight, and perhaps so that he himself might receive the light of the mind.

The guards had refused to loosen the chains that bound him more tightly (ibid.), even when Victricius asked this as a small favor. But when, in their sight, he directed a prayer to God, they saw the chains spontaneously slip free from his hands [Col. 0761B], and the soldiers did not dare fasten them again. Instead, they ran in fear to the Count, confessing the truth of the miracle. The Count himself, by God’s providence changed from fury to clemency, accepted the soldiers’ testimony and sent him to the emperor. The emperor, as is probable, did not keep the confessor as a criminal but released him as a holy man.

2. Paulinus, who reports these events, does not say whether Victricius wished merely to abandon his arms in order to devote himself entirely to God, or whether the soldiers had tried to compel him to do something contrary to religion, as happened under the emperor Julian. Nor does he say whether he was condemned as a deserter or for the Christian religion.

At the beginning of his account only the first cause is presented. If Victricius had been condemned as a Christian under Julian, the Count, as is probable, would not have released him while praising him as a holy man (ibid., no. 7), whether before receiving the emperor’s order to release him or after receiving it.

Elsewhere Paulinus says that the Count wished to be Christ’s persecutor against Victricius and wanted to punish witnesses to the faith (ibid., no. 4); he calls the tribune, at whose feet Victricius threw down his arms, a sacrilegious man (ibid.), and the soldiers who tortured him servants of the devil. This may indeed seem strange if they knew Victricius only by the name of a soldier who wished to lay down his arms. Nor should he apparently have been honored with the title of confessor and martyr, by which Paulinus repeatedly adorns him (ibid., nos. 7 and 9), for all that he endured on this account. Moreover, many others seem to have been condemned for the same reason as Victricius and released together with him; Paulinus calls all of them confessors (ibid., no. 7).

For these reasons Baronius was led to assert that Victricius suffered under Julian (Annals, 362, § 264), and the Roman Martyrology assigns his feast day to 7 August. If he suffered under a Christian ruler and only in order to devote himself entirely to God, no more outstanding example could demonstrate how much force a person must exert upon himself to obey grace, and even to lay aside offices that are not in themselves wholly harmful. It also becomes evident that God can crown in heaven people who are guilty under civil laws that the Church cannot defend by her own laws.

St. Martin was thrown into prison (Sulpicius, *Life of Martin*, book III) because he no longer wished to remain under arms, but not principally for that reason; for his life was not placed in danger. Victricius’s virtues corresponded to this illustrious beginning, which is the completion of long labors in a short space (Paulinus, Ep. 18, no. 8). He always appeared powerful in merits and rich in graces (ibid.), and Paulinus asserts that God made him equal to Martin in merits (ibid., no. 9). By refusing what was permitted and abstaining from conveniences, he maintained the glorious wealth of Christian poverty (Ep. 37, no. 4), and the power of faith shone throughout his whole life (ibid., no. 7).

## Chapter II. Victricius is made bishop of Rouen. He makes his Church illustrious through piety. He preaches the faith in Belgica.

1. God did not wish Victricius’s virtue to lie hidden beneath the bushel of silence (Paulinus, Ep. 18, no. 6); he therefore raised him upon the lampstand of the apostolic see, the Church of Rouen (ibid., no. 5). This happened before Paulinus was free from the concerns of this age (ibid., no. 9), that is, before the year 390. At that time Paulinus saw him at Vienne, at St. Martin’s. Although he knew him then only as a bishop, not as a martyr, he nevertheless showed him every courtesy, commended himself and his people to his prayers, and embraced him with a truly exceptional affection.

Sulpicius Severus (*Dialogue* 3, ch. 2) relates that the bishops Valentinus and Victricius were present when a certain father brought to Martin at Chartres a twelve-year-old girl to be healed. Martin wished to attribute the miracle to the two bishops, claiming that he was far inferior to them in holiness and that they could do everything. But the two bishops, together with the girl’s father, implored Martin; and after dismissing the crowd, while the two bishops and the father were present, he restored the girl to health. This Victricius was certainly the bishop of Rouen, since among the other bishops of Gaul we know of no one else of that name.

2. After Victricius was made bishop, he announced the mystery of Christ in faith and truth, not in inflated knowledge or lofty speech (Paulinus, Ep. 37, no. 4), judging that he knew nothing among human beings except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. God granted him what he ordinarily grants only to men of exceptional holiness (Ep. 18, no. 10): to make his words equal to his deeds, and to instruct by life as well as by speech. Thus no one could excuse himself on the grounds of difficulty when Victricius’s example had first imposed the obligation.

In this way he became the blessed father of many blessed people (ibid.). He gathered around him countless holy flocks of both sexes, whom he had begotten for Christ through his wise institutions and to whom he was both a rule of faith and an example of perfect virtue. He also gave his Church the appearance of that first Church of Jerusalem (ibid., no. 5), and every kind of virtue seemed to flourish in it.

Very many daughters preserved inviolate virginity; Christ alone was their guest and bridegroom. Countless widows served the Church day and night through holy works, devoted ministry, and constant service, overcoming the assaults with which the devil tormented their bodies. Many married people professed a hidden brotherhood and, through assiduous prayers, invited Christ to visit them and bless their chastity. Others in turn trained themselves both in conjugal chastity and in continence.

Everywhere the bowels of mercy were opened (ibid.). Day and night the name of Christ the Lord resounded through continual preaching. In the many churches and monasteries, sacred hymns were sung in daily concert (ibid.), and the saints rejoiced in chaste hearts and voices, both in heaven and on earth.

For this reason Paulinus adds that the apostles, having found in Victricius a most suitable lodging for themselves (ibid.), worked together with him and demonstrated through the effect of divine works that their spirit was present in that Church, although their relics were elsewhere. They rested in the children of piety and justice (ibid.); they loved Victricius in all the children of his instruction and loved Christ in him. To testify that they regarded him as a sharer in their glory, they performed wholly divine miracles especially in his diocese.

Thus through the zeal and care of St. Victricius (ibid.), Rouen, previously a city known only by a modest reputation in the neighboring regions, began to be reverently named even in distant provinces and to be counted, with praise to God, among cities distinguished by holy places.

3. Victricius became not only a companion of the apostles through the dignity of the episcopate, but also because God made him—as I put it in Paulinus’s words—a beautiful foot of his word (ibid., no. 6), kindling a bright flash of light in regions previously obscure (Paulinus, Ep. 18, no. 4), among distant peoples who sat in the region of the shadow of death; he made him a cloud pouring abundant rain upon the deserts, and finally a teacher and instructor of the nations (ibid.).

Under Diocletian, the faith of truth had already breathed upon the Morini and Nervii in Belgica with a faint spirit (ibid), but it had made no progress because of the negligence of pastors and the frequent incursions of barbarians. God chose Victricius above all as a vessel of election (ibid.), in which he might sanctify his name there. In him the faith of truth first shone more brightly and appeared more closely, and charity grew warmer.

Finally, where once deserted and equally unprotected forests and coasts were frequented by foreign barbarians and native brigands, then venerable and angelic choirs of saints, cities, towns, islands, forests, monasteries, and churches filled with numerous peoples celebrated divine praises in harmonious peace (ibid., no. 4). “His sound has gone out into all the earth,” and the name of God was sanctified (ibid.).

## Chapter III. Paulinus writes to Victricius. Victricius is accused concerning the faith. He comes to Rome and writes to Paulinus.

1. Victricius had very probably already preached as a bishop in the regions mentioned above. The last news Paulinus had heard of him was when he wrote to him in the year 390. Tychicus had brought Paulinus this information (Paulinus, Ep. 28, no. 4); Paulinus calls him the dearest brother of St. Victricius and a faithful minister in the Lord.

At that time Paulinus lamented (ibid., no. 9) the negligence resulting from his own unhappiness: he had not sufficiently recognized or venerated Victricius’s holiness when he had once seen him at Vienne with St. Martin, and had not kissed his scars. He was seeking an opportunity to write to him (ibid., no. 1), but none was granted until what had not happened when he hoped for it came to him when he did not expect it: Paulinus had gone to Rome, and not long afterward (ibid., no. 3) encountered a certain catechumen named Ursus, together with Paschasius, a deacon of St. Victricius of Rouen.

Paulinus says that in Paschasius’s kindness and favor, as though in a mirror reflecting certain traces of St. Victricius’s virtues and graces, he recognized those qualities (ibid., no. 10). His modest conduct, humility of heart, gentleness of spirit, constancy in the faith of truth, and speech seasoned with salt in every respect proved him to be both a disciple instructed by Victricius and a companion on the journey (ibid., no. 1).

Accordingly, in addition to the grace of fraternal companionship in the sacred ministry of the diaconate, Paulinus received him with all the greater reverence and affection because Paschasius belonged to Victricius’s clergy, body, and spirit. Paulinus did not allow him to depart from Rome, although Paschasius wished to return to Victricius (ibid.), but by a sort of violence of charity brought him to Nola, so that he might enjoy for a longer time, through Paschasius’s presence, a kind of share in St. Victricius’s grace.

Paulinus nevertheless lost no small consolation from his companionship, for at that time he was suffering from bodily illness (ibid., no. 2). Nor was Paschasius troubled and sympathetic only during Paulinus’s illness; he was also overcome by grave sickness in the case of Ursus, whom he had kept as an inseparable companion of his pilgrimage. In Ursus, Paulinus says, he saw faith and charity complete in the Lord (ibid., no. 3).

At last, through Paschasius’s labor and faith—by which the Lord wished to test the power of his holy confessor Felix with him—Ursus, who had been sick unto death, found safety from his danger. Through the hands of the deacon Paschasius he was begotten for Christ and baptized in his bed (ibid.), even though St. Paulinus, already a presbyter, was present, and many other presbyters could have attended.

When Ursus had recovered sound and vigorous health, and Paschasius was planning to return to Victricius, Paulinus sent through him his letter 18 to Victricius (ibid., no. 1). In it, after excusing Paschasius for having been detained with him for so long, he speaks of the Morini and Nervii, whom Victricius had begotten for Christ through the Gospel (ibid., no. 4), and describes how Victricius had formed the Church of Rouen (ibid., no. 3), as we related above (ch. 2, no. 2). Finally, after weaving together the history of his martyrdom or confession (Ep. 18, nos. 6–7), Paulinus indicates that he is held by an intense desire to see him (ibid., no. 8). He says nothing in this letter about Victricius’s journey to Rome, which, as we shall soon demonstrate, took place in 404.

2. After the war against Alaric had ended, Honorius came to Rome in the final days of the year 403, where he remained at least until 25 July 404. At the same time Victricius of Rouen went there, and himself witnessed the great labors and zeal with which the Roman pontiff Innocent urged the emperor not to drag ecclesiastical men into civil burdens and public offices (Innocent, Ep. 2 to Victricius, ch. 11).

Paulinus speaks of this journey of Victricius to Rome (Paulinus, Ep. 37, no. 1). He had hoped that Victricius, who had traveled across so many expanses of land from Rouen to Rome (ibid.), would come to Nola by a short route. When Victricius did not come, Paulinus admits that he was not only saddened but also confounded by the loss of this blessing. Never had his sins been revealed so clearly to himself or to others as when the hand of God, which had brought Victricius so far, did not permit him to come nearer to Paulinus.

The purpose for which Victricius undertook this journey is not entirely clear, unless we say that he was drawn there by the lying tongues of malicious people who envied his holiness (ibid., no. 4). He seems to have been accused (ibid., nos. 6–7; Chifflet, p. 177) of holding an incorrect view of the faith. In writing to him, Paulinus therefore explains the Catholic faith at length, especially concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation (Paulinus, Ep. 37, nos. 5–6).

God allowed him to suffer this injury (ibid., no. 7) so that he might again rejoice in victory and receive a crown after departing victorious from the battle. He was thereby permitted, in the words of blessed Paul, to say that he fought on the right and on the left with the weapons of righteousness, through dishonor and good repute, through glory and disrepute (ibid).
