The arrows of unjust tongues could find neither a place to wound in his body, which was enclosed by the powerful armor of God, nor a blemish in his light (ibid., no. 4). For who could doubt that the faith of truth dwelt in his spirit (ibid., no. 7), when the power of faith could be seen in his life? Nor was anyone confounded in him who had formed a truer judgment of him; indeed, this new proof of his faith and virtue benefited many for the advancement of the Gospel (ibid.).

The reason Victricius came to Rome is not publicly known; nor is it sufficiently established, as we have said, whether he was brought there by the accusations of wicked men. Be that as it may, in Rome the praise of his doctrine and virtue was certainly greatest in everyone’s mouth. Only a few days later, in a letter sent to him, Pope Innocent praised him (Innocent, Ep. 2) for having attained the praise of a true bishop in the direction of doctrine, the virtue of his conduct, and the instruction of others according to the rule of the Church. He found nothing in Victricius’s teaching that conflicted with the sacred Scriptures.

3. Not long after his return to Rouen, Victricius sent Candidianus to Italy with a brief letter for Paulinus (Paulinus, Ep. 37, no. 1). Paulinus received it with extraordinary joy; it completely wiped away his former grief that Victricius had not come to him (ibid., no. 1). Nevertheless, in his reply he complains of this most sweetly and humbly, declaring that this consolation was owed to him as a sinful and sick man (ibid., no. 2).

“For I do not want you,” Paulinus says (ibid.), “to be so secure concerning us that you think that all the ailments of our soul have now been healed—those in which we have sinned and continue to sin against the Lord.””

In his customary manner he adds much on this subject and asks for Victricius’s prayers (ibid., no. 1). The rest of the letter concerns the persecution he had endured (ibid., nos. 4 and 7).

Around the year 404 Augustine speaks (*On the Care for the Dead*, ch. 18) of a certain presbyter Candidianus, whom he had come to know through Paulinus’s efforts and through whose ministry Augustine sent Paulinus his book *On the Care for the Dead*. The bearer of Victricius’s letter to Paulinus had not yet attained the dignity of the presbyterate, since Paulinus calls him “son” (Paulinus, Ep. 37, no. 1); and at that time he seems to have belonged more to Victricius than to Paulinus.

## Chapter IV. Pope Innocent I of Rome writes to Victricius.

1. Victricius perhaps entrusted letters to Pope Innocent to this same Candidianus. He wished to learn from the pontiff what rule and practice the Roman Church followed concerning discipline and the regulation of morals (Innocent, Ep. 2 to Victricius, at the beginning).

He complained (ibid.) of the perverse conduct of certain people who, fearing no divine judgment but seeking popular favor, presumed to violate the Church’s sacred and ancient decrees, without any regard for its sanctity. He therefore desired that the discipline of the Roman Church be observed in his own province.

Innocent agreed to this most equitable request and sent Victricius a book (ibid.) which he calls the *Regulary* (*Regularis*), as a teacher and admonisher. In it he did not wish to impose new precepts, but to have everyone observe those things that had been neglected through the negligence of some and those established by apostolic and patristic tradition, with due regard for divine judgment.

Innocent says that he sent these regulations so that he himself would not appear, through his silence, to favor errors and abuses. He also instructs Victricius (ibid.) to make them known to his suffragan bishops and neighboring Churches, so that the practice of the Roman Church might be understood and followed by all who had undertaken responsibility for instructing Christians. Through observing these rules, they would easily arrive at knowledge of the other decrees not recorded here.

This *Regulary*, which Innocent says he sent with his letter, seems to me to be nothing other than the decrees so closely attached to the letter itself that they appear to constitute a part of it. The first of these forbids anyone to dare ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan, or to have him ordained by a single bishop.

The second prohibits admitting to the clergy anyone who, after the remission of sins in baptism, had borne the military belt of secular service. It is clear that only penance excluded a person from the clergy, even if he had not professed secular military service.

The third, which Dionysius Exiguus adds to the second (Canon Code, p. 197), establishes that cases or disputes among clerics, both of higher and lower rank, are to be settled by the bishops of the same province—with no prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, as Justellus’s edition has it, p. 197. Those who transfer judgment of their case to other provinces are to be deposed from the clergy. As for more serious cases, once the bishops have rendered judgment, they are to notify the supreme pontiff according to custom and, apparently, according to the decree of the Council of Sardica.

The fourth, fifth, and sixth decrees prohibit ordaining clerics who have had a second wife, or a widow, or a divorced woman, whether after or before baptism, contrary to Jerome’s position (Ep. to Oceanus). Innocent asserts that this was observed by each bishop.

The ninth decree prohibits deacons and priests from having intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of their ministry. Clerics of lower rank seem to have been permitted to use marriage at will, except those, as Innocent says in chapter 10, who had spent a long time in monasteries, where they had devoted themselves to perpetual continence. It would have been contrary to reason if they had lost, after being placed in a higher rank, what they had long preserved.

In the same article he notes that men who had been corrupted before marriage did not receive the Church’s blessing when they took wives; and that those who had not remained virgins before baptism, when they were admitted to the clergy, promised according to the ancient use and practice of the Church that they would not contract marriage.

The seventh article forbids anyone to ordain a cleric from another Church unless that cleric’s bishop, prevailed upon by entreaty, should consent; and it forbids one Church to receive a cleric rejected by another.

The eighth states: Those returning to the Church from the Novatians or Montanists—that is, the Donatists—are to be received only by the laying on of hands, except those who, after passing from the Catholic Church to them, were rebaptized. Such people are not to be admitted without a prolonged satisfaction of penance.

In the eleventh article Innocent warns Victricius not to make clerics of municipal councillors or persons occupied with any public functions, since rulers sometimes recalled them from the priesthood in order to subject them to duties in which they provided entertainments—namely, public games—which were unquestionably invented by the devil. At the same time he recalls to Victricius’s memory what he himself had seen while staying in Rome.

The twelfth decree establishes that women who have spiritually married Christ and have deserved to be veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or secretly violate themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has withdrawn from the world. Women who marry another man while their husband is still alive are to be regarded as adulteresses, and they are not to be permitted to perform penance unless one of the two men has died.

The thirteenth decree establishes that those who marry after promising, in a profession of virginity, to remain perpetually virgins must perform penance for some time, even if they had not been veiled.

2. The final two articles are cited from Pope Innocent I’s letter to Victricius of Rouen at the Second Council of Tours, where they are approved. The heretics of our own time use these last two articles very foolishly to disparage this letter of Innocent (Baron., year 404, §122). Others reject it entirely (Coc. p. 106) and insist that it is not Innocent’s, because it reproduces Siricius’s letter word for word. But since Innocent wished to renew the ancient rules and make the discipline of the Roman Church known, he could not have done this better than by transmitting the ordinances of his predecessors. Therefore no one can rightly doubt either the letter of Siricius, praised by the Council of Telepte and by Ferrandus, or the Decretal Letter of Innocent, which Dionysius Exiguus inserted in full into the code of the Roman Church and which was cited in 570 by the Second Council of Tours and by many others (Blond., *De Decretis*, p. 551).

The greater difficulty concerns assigning the date on which the letter was written—it is dated 15 February (*Ep.* 2 of Innocent, at the end)—because the letter states that Victricius had been a witness to the many troubles with which the Roman pontiff had beset the emperor then present (ibid., c. 11). We must therefore suppose that Victricius was in Rome at the same time as Honorius, who did not arrive there until December of the year 403. From the poem which Claudian composed about that journey for his sixth consulship, it is clear that Honorius had never previously come there since he had been made emperor. Moreover, Innocent did not become pope before the year 402. If, then, Victricius was in Rome in December 403, who would suppose that Innocent wrote to him on 15 February 404?

One possibility might be that Victricius, still staying in Rome, requested this instruction from him and received it from him in the form of a letter, so that it might carry greater authority. But from these words, “which you yourself, when you were staying with us, came to know” (ibid., c. 11), it is clear that Victricius had already left the city at that time; and in fact Innocent states that these decrees were sent by him in a letter. The words, “for you assert that certain persons existed” (ibid., at the beginning of the letter), sufficiently indicate that the pontiff was not responding to what Victricius had said in person, but to what Victricius had written afterward.

Accordingly, if we place Victricius’s departure from Rome at the end of March 404—a date that cannot be set earlier, since Victricius must have written from Rouen to Rome and Innocent must have taken some time to prepare his reply, which he could not have sent before that year on the fifteenth day before the Kalends, not of March but of January—that is, on 18 December, the matter can be explained. In certain editions and in the Justel manuscript, the date on which this letter was written is not found, although the other letters are each assigned to their respective times.

Indeed, what follows—“Therefore this rule” (ibid., at the end of the letter), and so forth—appears to have been excerpted from certain other writings, nor does it in any way cohere with what precedes, unless the whole letter is understood to concern this rule. History tells us nothing more about Saint Victricius, whom the Church celebrates among the confessors of Christ on 7 August. His body is said to have been transferred to Braine and placed in the Church of Saint Remigius (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 559).

# FIFTH DISSERTATION. ON SAINT APER

## CHAPTER I. The Life of Saint Aper, Bishop of Toul. Whether He Was the Same as Aper, Paulinus’s Friend

If Aper the monk, who in the year 404 or the following year took part in the Gallic conference from which Sulpicius’s *Dialogues* were composed (*Dial.* 3, c. 1), was the same person to whom Paulinus wrote, Paulinus did not write to him later than the year 404. But it is sufficiently probable that he was not the same person. Since the man to whom Paulinus writes was a nobleman and a priest, Paulinus would not have designated him merely by the name “monk.” We therefore know nothing certain about the date of his conversion or of the letters which Paulinus wrote to him.

Another difficulty remains: whether he was the bishop of Toul among the Leuci who bore the same name and appears in the martyrologies on 15 September. Baron supposes that he was the bishop of Toul in his *Martyrology*. Chiffletius asserts that no one doubts this (Chiffl., *Paulinus*, p. 177); but the title “bishop” (ibid.), which was formerly assigned to him in the title of the commonly circulated twenty-ninth Pauline letter, really means that he became a bishop later, if he was not one at that time.

The Sammarthani, on the other hand, argue (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 1095) that Paulinus could not have written to Aper, bishop of Toul, because, they say, he had died before Sidonius became bishop. We do not see what follows from this, unless we suppose with them that Saint Aper did not obtain the episcopate until after the death of Ursus, the successor of Auspicius. If we make that supposition, it will be clear that he did not become bishop until toward the end of the fifth century; hence he was not a contemporary of Paulinus, since Auspicius was alive in the time of Sidonius (*Sidonius*, ep. 7, 10, and 17, with the note), around the year 470.

To this very strong argument, by which Aper of Toul is distinguished from Paulinus’s contemporary, may be added the earlier manuscript *Life of Aper*. It states that Aper was born to Christian parents, lived in the greatest piety from infancy, and from youth onward advanced in virtue throughout the remainder of his life; that his reputation led to his being elevated to episcopal office. This agrees with great difficulty with what Paulinus says. Paulinus describes his friend as enslaved, in the manner of the age, to its vices (*Pauline Epistle* 38, no. 1), and as having performed not only the role of advocate but also that of judge (ibid., no. 8). His mind and life, however, were soon changed (ibid., no. 7); God began to dwell in his heart through grace (ibid., no. 3); and he had possessed the hardness of heart, dryness, and frivolity of the old man (*Epistle* 44, no. 1).

After his conversion, Aper also testified to Paulinus in a letter that he held with unshaken faith that Christ was the Son of God and that he had been crucified (Ep. 38, no. 1). Paulinus replied that blessed is the one who, through the revelation of the Spirit of the heavenly Father, has learned these truths and has embraced Jesus Christ in the entire mystery of hidden piety. These words suggest that he was a recent Christian, or at least a recent Catholic. For who could easily understand such statements of a catechumen who had been nourished in the Christian religion from infancy, even if not yet baptized, as many were at that time? Who, moreover, would readily believe that the *Life of Aper* praises a catechumen about whom the following things are especially reported: “From childhood he received the rudiments of heavenly training; he was always a worshiper and distinguished devotee of the Christian religion, wholly attentive to churches and holy places,” and so forth?

If, therefore, anyone maintains that Aper, Paulinus’s friend, was a bishop, it must be said either that the history of that *Life* is wholly false or that much is missing from it. For it does not seem to possess the character of an original history; indeed, it describes his virtues in general and at length, while saying little about his deeds. The death of the judge of Châlons is sufficiently contrary to common belief; and when the *Life* touches upon a certain circumstance concerning Aper’s death, it bases it on common opinion: “it is said.” Nevertheless, I would call this *Life* correctly and piously composed.

It designates cities by their ancient names—for example, “Augusta of the Leuci” and “the city of the Leuci”—which is not customary among authors of the sixth century and later. Nor does it report miracles as the most certain proofs of the bishop’s sanctity. It also notes how carefully Aper guarded against being led into error by the activity of heretics. Such prudence is scarcely found among those who lived after the heresies had been extinguished—that is, after the middle of the sixth century.

It should nevertheless be noted that, in his catalogue of the bishops of Toul, P. Cointius, who lists those who lived from the time of Auspicius down to the year 550, says nothing about Aper. He evidently considered him earlier than Auspicius.

## CHAPTER II. The Conversion of Aper and His Wife Amanda

Let us return now to Paulinus’s friend. He was a rich, wise, and eloquent man (*Pauline Epistle* 38, no. 7), distinguished for prudence and learning (ibid.); but he was so proud that Paulinus compares him to a fat bull, as Scripture says (ibid., no. 8). He married a woman named Amanda (*Epistle* 39, in the title), by whom he had several sons and a daughter (ibid., nos. 1 and 2).

He had been an advocate and a judge in the courts (*Epistle* 38, no. 8)—what Paulinus calls “the wicked seat of power” (ibid.), just as secular dignities are called by Augustine “the magistracies of Babylon” (Aug., on Psalm 61, no. 8). He lived in Gaul, since after his conversion he maintained his correspondence with Paulinus only by an annual exchange of letters (*Pauline Epistle* 39, no. 1).

Without doubt, while Aper and Paulinus were still living in the world, they knew one another; and Paulinus seems to have written him certain letters (*Epistle* 38, no. 11) in which he urged him to embrace the Christian faith. At last, however, the power of divine wisdom and the operation of heavenly power shone forth in him (ibid., no. 7), since nothing but supreme Wisdom can turn a prudent man from the course or position of his own judgment, and so forth.

Taught by heavenly light, he learned to hold and profess the truth of Christ with unshaken faith and in a free voice; he immediately changed his mind and his life. Converted, he groaned and became acceptable to God. “You have been torn down from the proud,” Paulinus says to him (ibid., no. 8), “and taken up into the humble. That neck has become teachable and slender beneath the yoke of Christ. Having laid aside the neck of the bull, you have been broken into the gentleness of that ox which recognized its owner; now, from a lion, a calf; and, with ferocity exchanged for virtue, a boar to the world, a lamb to God. All that pride which you formerly displayed on behalf of the world you now turn against the world in humble arms.”

He laid aside with the old man the former hardness, dryness, and frivolity of his heart (Ep. 44, no. 1), those unhappy fruits of sin. “Now you are truly wise,” Paulinus says to him (Ep. 38, no. 9), “truly eloquent, and truly powerful: to this world you are foolish and mute, but to the author of your tongue and mind you are eloquent and wise. Serve God with his own gifts; now, better instructed in divine law, plead for yourself as your own advocate, and, as a more just judge, judge yourself. Pass sentence upon yourself and concerning yourself, so that you may deserve more to be acquitted and make yourself worthy not only of pardon but also of glory, since you stand by yourself in accusing yourself and sanctify yourself by condemning yourself—understanding that holiness and innocence consist not in what pleases human beings but in what pleases God.”

He was now growing rich in the good fruits of learning and seeking nourishment in the fruit of virtues; and he armed himself with the teeth of both Testaments to tear apart the devil’s nets. He rejected and spurned the wisdom of this world, which God had called foolish (ibid., no. 7), because he had arrogated to himself what he had received from God; and he preferred fellowship with the little ones of Christ to fellowship with the wise of the world.

Made mute to this world (*Pauline Epistle* 38, no. 9), he embraced the humility despised by the proud (ibid., no. 3), and humility itself as a way of life (ibid., no. 5). He was emptied of wealth so that he might become rich in poverty (ibid., no. 8), and emptied of that excessive fullness of superfluous display so that he might be filled with the true goods of holy poverty.

But he could not reach the renunciation of possessions that had been proposed to him (Ep. 39, no. 2), nor imitate Paulinus in it. Although he desired heavenly things with a free inclination, he was nevertheless compelled in some measure to care for earthly matters because of his children’s property. His wife either went before him or followed him on the straight path of virtue. She was not a guide to softness and avarice (Ep. 44, no. 4), but rather, like one who restored strength to the bones of her husband, she guided him toward fortitude.

Both professed continence (Ep. 39, no. 1) and chastity (ibid., no. 3) together. They no longer knew one another according to the flesh, but passed from their own union into the body of Christ (Ep. 44, no. 3); and, in the great emulation of the divine marriage with the Church, they were joined to Christ by bonds of love, all the stronger because they were purer.

## CHAPTER III. Aper Is Advanced to the Priesthood. His Wife Frees Him from Domestic and Civic Affairs

Although Aper seems to have received Paulinus’s letters only at the very beginning of his conversion, he had already been promoted to the priesthood (*Paulinus*, Ep. 38, no. 10). In that position, like a throne of peace and justice, he had been placed not only by divine will (ibid., no. 8), but also there installed by human election.

There is certainly no reason for us to be surprised that people should choose for advancement to the priesthood men who had distinguished themselves not only by eloquence and wisdom but also by great virtues in the administration of civil affairs, even though they were thereby doing violence to the men themselves and resisting the laws of the Church. If such compulsion is wholly detestable and intolerable in those who thrust themselves from secular life into the Church, who are not divinely called but inflamed by desire, and who seize—rather than attain—the height of honor, a work and burden feared even by angelic shoulders, how praiseworthy and holy, by contrast, is that compulsion by which the people urge to the priesthood and insist on the promotion of those whom God has shown worthy of so great an honor, such as Ambrose, Paulinus, Germanus, and other men of this merit.

Aper must certainly be counted among them. The holiness of his life shows that he was not advanced to the priesthood through secular ambition. He was a rare visitor to cities and loved the private solitude of the quiet countryside (*ibid.*, no. 10). “You do not prefer leisure to business,” Paulinus says to him (ibid.), “nor withdraw yourself from ecclesiastical usefulness; rather, you are already avoiding almost all the disturbances of the law courts, the rival commotions of the churches, and their restless assemblies.

“I believe that what you are preparing for the greater uses of the Church is this: with sound judgment you devote yourself to the instruction of holiness, intent upon spiritual studies, for which solitude is a friend. You form and daily strengthen Christ within yourself, so that you may become both a more useful servant and a more learned teacher, and may make yourself more worthy of the position to which you have been placed by God’s will; powerful alike in deed and word, so that your tongue and mind may agree, and you may present yourself as a true pattern of apostolic discipline, an agent and teacher of the Lord’s command.”

He had withdrawn to his estate (Ep. 39, no. 3), and seems to have cultivated the field with his own hands (ibid.). From Paulinus’s letters (ibid. and Ep. 38, no. 10), it appears that he spent at least that entire year in this retreat. When it had ended, he exercised the stewardship entrusted to him as a diligent multiplier of his master’s talents (Ep. 44, no. 4).

He kept his wife and children at home (ibid. and no. 5). There he lived a life free from every disturbance and withdrawn from the waves of the sea (ibid., no. 4), exercising in continual meditation on heavenly studies and works, as though by a kind of oar of salvation, the secure vessel of an unshaken mind in the harbor of the Church.

He freely carried out what belongs to the heavenly household (ibid.), unconcerned about what was being done in his earthly household, trusting in his wife’s faith and prudence. She intended to attain the same happiness as he, though through a different form of life and solicitude (Ep. 44, no. 4). Occupied with bodily labors, she attended to secular business so that her husband might attend to Christ (ibid.); she did not prefer this world to Christ, but her husband to herself (ibid.). For she did not cling to her own will in this matter; rather, she cared for his salvation, to whom, as nature and circumstance required, she owed obedience (ibid.). Thus, while she served secular business, she served not the world itself but Christ.

She considered that she would be faithful and most acceptable to God (ibid.) if, established like a tower on an immovable rock, she opposed herself to the needs of the world and to the storms that might disturb the tranquility which her husband enjoyed with gladness.

The following words suggest that Aper left to his wife the possession of his estates—that is, the property of his children:

“She takes care of the cares of the world,” Paulinus says to Aper (ibid.), “so that you need not care for them. She seems to possess, so that you may not be possessed by the world and may be possessed by Christ. A will not discordant with your purpose does not separate her from it; rather—and this is more remarkable—a concordant faith divides in action those who are united in will.

“For, managing a thing subject to captivity without captivity of the soul, in freedom of spirit, she strengthened her hands for the work of virtue. She extended her arms toward useful things, girded her loins with strength, and did not eat the bread of idleness. She became for you like a ship that brings its merchandise from afar, rendering by a necessary division to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, so that through you she may minister to God the things that are God’s.

“For when she has paid tribute, as it is written, to the one to whom tribute is owed, then, opening her hands to the poor and presenting the fruit of her labor to the needy, she pays a spiritual tax. She supplies the income from the estate as the wages of your service, more eager for salutary loss than for deadly profit. For she does not store up on earth what she produces from earthly fruits; rather, she lends it at interest to your good works instead of to the destructive profits of avarice.”

## CHAPTER IV. Paulinus Reflects on Aper’s Conversion and Fortifies Him against the Persecutions of the World

Paulinus says (Ep. 38, no. 6) that God, whose work it is to change a human being—because he alone can restore what he alone made—performed at that time more extraordinary signs of grace than usual, signs that convert the souls of sinners, as though he had hastened to rescue his own people from the coming wrath.

In this, Paulinus could contemplate not only himself and his wife Therasia, Sulpicius Severus, dearest to him, and Aper, to whom he was writing, together with Aper’s wife, but also Pammachius, Pinianus and his wife Melania the Younger, Constans and Macarius, who had discharged very great offices, and many others unknown to us. Among them should be added Germanus of Auxerre, who was summoned from the offices and dignities of the world into the clerical order by the Saint in a wholly unheard-of and extraordinary manner.

In these holy persons God displayed examples of virtues especially useful to many (ibid., no. 7). For the greater their natural wisdom and prudence, the more evident was the operation and power of God in their conversion. For this reason Paulinus wished that he had wings, so that he might fly to Aper, rest in his company, and praise God with his whole heart (ibid., no. 9).

But his conversion was an example to some (ibid., no. 7) and a testimony against others who were hardened and rejected. Those whose hope was confined within the limits of this age (ibid., no. 6), and in whom the fear of the Lord had not yet brought an end to lust and avarice, regarded Aper’s conversion as an error of folly (ibid., no. 3). They despised his humility, by which their pride was destroyed (ibid., no. 5), and detested the chastity which he had embraced (ibid., no. 3).

The world hated him (ibid., no. 2) when it saw him alienated from itself and opposed to its morals; and by that very jealousy of its own, the world proved Aper to be a true servant of God. In his beginnings the power of perfection was already at work (ibid.), but he was now able to resist temptations. He considered himself blessed because the world hated him, since he was serving Christ.

For this reason he believed himself a Christian: those who had loved him had begun to hate him, and those who had feared him had begun to despise him (ibid., no. 3). He was conscious that, if he had remained the same person he had formerly been, they would likewise have continued to love and honor him as they had been accustomed to do.

Aper had written these things to Paulinus (ibid.) in a letter which he sent to him from the silent seclusion of his countryside (ibid., no. 10). In it, without doubt, he related the entire course of his conversion. At the end of the letter he affirmed (ibid., no. 1) that he held the Catholic faith with an unshaken mind and professed it in a free voice; he also said that in it he was still inexperienced and a child before God (ibid.).

Paulinus rejoiced greatly at what Aper had written to him (ibid.). Since he had no wings with which to fly to him and congratulate him face to face on this happiness, he expressed his judgment of it in an outstanding and elegant letter. In it he tells Aper that it was evident how firmly he believed in Christ (ibid., no. 2), and that from the beginning he had been granted the gift of suffering for Christ.

He urged him to endure this persecution (ibid., nos. 2 and 7), which Paulinus himself had once suffered; to overthrow his adversaries with the firmest humility (ibid., no. 3); to confound their hatred and slanders by the conduct of his life rather than by words of the tongue; and to speak to the Lord through the silence of humility and the voice of patience.

He then turned to that remarkable transformation which the Lord had wrought in Aper (ibid., nos. 7 and 10). Toward the end he exhorted him to show himself diligent in advancing in piety (ibid., no. 11), and to delight in the Lord with the same affection with which he had once delighted in sin. He added:

“I earnestly ask you to include me in your prayers and, whenever occasion permits, to take care to revisit me by letter.”

Paulinus sought Aper’s letters in order to refresh his spirit, and he was filled with the greatest joy when he learned that Aper was advancing in spiritual knowledge (ibid.).

Aper most willingly obeyed Paulinus. In fact, we see him writing to Paulinus every year, for Paulinus says that Aper maintained this correspondence with him by an annual exchange of letters (*Epistle* 39, no. 1). From this correspondence there also arose the two letters which Paulinus and Therasia wrote to Aper and Amanda, which we assign to the years 405 and 406.

Since the barbarians invaded Gaul toward the end of the year 406 and devastated it within a very short time, and since Constantine, after Honorius had been removed, brought all of Gaul under his power in the year 407, it seems that this very welcome correspondence between Paulinus and his friends in Gaul must have ended in the year 406 or at least at the beginning of 407.

This is what we have to say about the life of Aper. We do not dare assert that he was the same person as the bishop of Toul, about whom the *Annals* likewise say nothing. The martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, and Bede include him among the holy bishops on 15 September.

The church which he himself had begun to build near Toul was immediately given his name, although it is corruptly called by the French name Saint Epure. It is now a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. The Sammarthani also note (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 1095) that there is an abbey of nuns in Cologne bearing this name, as well as a parish in the city of Nancy.

Salvianus, who flourished at Florence from the year 430 to the end of the fifth century, writes one letter to Aper and Verus, his friends (Salvian., Ep. 3, pp. 212–213), in which he professes himself far inferior to them. He asserts that they had attained the crown of virtually all humility and of almost every good work, and that the dignity of their conduct so freed them from every suspicion that one would plainly believe that whatever they did had been done entirely rightly.

# SIXTH DISSERTATION. ON THE LOST, DOUBTFUL, AND SPURIOUS WORKS OF SAINT PAULINUS

1. We have discussed at sufficient length, in the First and Second Dissertations, those works of Saint Paulinus which remain; but many truly distinguished monuments have perished.

Besides his panegyric for the emperor Theodosius, mentioned by Saint Jerome in his thirteenth letter to Paulinus, *On the Institution of a Monk*; by Cassiodorus in Book II of the *Divine Institutes*; by Gennadius in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*; by Trithemius; and by Paulinus himself in Letter 28 to Severus, no. 6;

besides the various letters which have perished, to Augustine (see *Life*, c. 51, nos. 3 and 4), Jerome (ibid., c. 36, no. 2), Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux (ibid., c. 31, no. 1), Venerius, bishop of Milan (ibid., c. 37, no. 2), Sulpicius Severus—at least four letters (ibid., c. 29, no. 1; c. 32, no. 2; c. 47, nos. 1 and 3)—Desiderius the presbyter (ibid., c. 47, no. 1), Macarius (Augustine, Ep. 259, no. 1), Sanctus (see *Life*, c. 25), and Ausonius (Ausonius, Ep. 24), together with many others;

besides the homilies which he delivered to the people, at least from the time when he became bishop, and which certainly deserved to be transmitted to posterity;

Gennadius (*Catalogue*, c. 48) writes that he gave his sister many letters concerning contempt for the world. He also attributes to him a *Sacramentary*, which, if it existed, would certainly be a distinguished monument of antiquity, from which we could gather the ancient practice of the Church and its external ceremonies in the administration of the sacraments.

The same Gennadius testifies that Paulinus also composed a *Hymnary*. I believe that this consisted of natal poems for Saint Felix.

But most especially to be regretted is the lost book *On Penance and on the General Praise of the Martyrs*, which the same Gennadius calls the chief of all Paulinus’s works. Trithemius and Bellarmine also mention it (*Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*).

In addition, his work against the pagans, which he was writing around the year 395, has perished. Augustine says that he learned of it (Ep. 31, no. 8; Ep. 42, no. 1) and testifies that he greatly desired it.

Gregory of Tours also cites a letter of Paulinus in which it is said that Saint Martin had received several relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.

From Paulinus himself (*Pauline Epistle* 46, no. 2, and *Life*, c. 48, no. 1; see note 195), we further infer that he translated into Latin certain works of Saint Clement the pope.

## On the Letters to Marcella and Celancia, etc.

2. In the latest edition of Saint Paulinus’s works, published at Antwerp in 1622 (Rosweyde, edition, pp. 412 and 419), letters to Marcella and to Celancia were included; these are also found among the works of Saint Jerome.

The letter to Marcella, concerning the endurance of adversity, seems to us, as it did to Sacchinus (*Life of Paulinus*, pp. 733–734), especially close to Paulinus’s diction. Yet it is certainly not easy to reconcile it with the history of our Paulinus, as Rosweyde also observed (see the note on the Appendix to this letter, no. 1).

At the very beginning of Marcella’s conversion, when she was afflicted, the merciful Lord came to her aid and gave her a devout consoler. Although he was far away (Appendix, Ep. 1, no. 1), when he heard of the greatest benefits of divine mercy bestowed upon her, learned what her condition was, and learned of the tribulation that had befallen her, he composed this eloquent letter to her in a spirit of congratulation.

In it he urges her to hope for eternal life and to practice the virtue of patience which she had displayed (ibid., nos. 3 and 6), and to confess to the Lord with great thanksgiving that he had recalled her from the lot of rich sinners to the lot of blessed poor people, whose form Christ assumed (ibid.).

From the letter itself it may be inferred that this had happened in the early years, when Marcella had devoted herself to divine service. If she had not previously undertaken the decision to vow herself to God, at least that event—whatever it may have been—gave her sharper incentives to works of piety and caused her to hold her purpose more firmly and profess it more freely.

Nevertheless, certain things in the letter seem capable of being referred to the end of her life and to the time when Rome was captured by Alaric, during which she truly suffered in the body (Jerome, Ep. 16). But would the letter have remained silent about such harsh calamities and the innumerable evils that so many and such great provinces had to endure, and which the capture of Rome itself produced?

Jerome testifies concerning this calamity (Ep. 16) that it did not make her poor but found her poor, and that it could not take away from her the goods which she had once voluntarily abandoned.

It is entirely unclear whose this letter is. In no manuscript is it inscribed with the name of Paulinus. It is counted among Jerome’s spurious works, and rightly so, since it does not have the flavor of Jerome’s style.

Erasmus, in his note on Jerome’s letter, judged that its style was not unlike Paulinus’s, since it is gentle and devout, anointed with the grace and love of the Holy Spirit, and rich in passages from Scripture. Marianus Victorius reached the same judgment.

Rosweyde included it in his edition of Paulinus’s works (Rosweyde, edition, p. 412). Yet in his notes he raises against himself the objection that Paulinus, living at Nola, could not have said—as the author of this letter asserts—that he was far away (Appendix, Ep. 1, no. 1) from Marcella, who was living at Rome. Rosweyde seems to resolve the difficulty by judging that Paulinus could have written it from Spain at the beginning of his conversion.

We do not readily accept this, however, since Paulinus was not converted until around the year 390, many years after Marcella’s piety had become conspicuous. Yet he writes to her as though she had only recently entered upon the path of virtue, and as though he possessed authority over her—something that accords poorly with Paulinus’s humility.

Moreover, when he discusses wealth and human ambition, he would, in my judgment, have related at least something about himself. I therefore think that Erasmus’s judgment should be followed: amid so many and such great writers of this age, we would search foolishly for the author of this letter.

If anyone wishes to regard it as a work of Paulinus, since in style, language, and thought—as we have noted in the margin—it differs very little from the Pauline letters, it must be said that it was addressed to another Marcella, not to the woman to whom Jerome wrote so often and whose life he described in Letter 16 to the virgin Principia. We summarize that life briefly:

“Saint Marcella, daughter of Albina, a noble Roman woman, first deprived of her father and then, in the seventh month after her marriage, deprived of her husband, rejected the proposal of the consul Cerealis, who sought her in marriage. Instructed by the Alexandrian bishops Athanasius and Peter, she was the first woman in Rome to profess the monastic life. There, instructed by Saint Jerome, she lived together with the virgin Principia. Her chief achievement is said to have been that she expelled the errors of the Origenists from the City and traveled to Jerusalem for the sake of piety and religion. She died a few days after Rome was captured by the Goths.” (Marianus Victorius, note on Jerome’s Epistle 16.)

The later letter to Celancia is certainly a distinguished monument of antiquity, both because of the elegance of its style and because of its subject. It contains excellent instructions for the education of a mother of a household.

It is addressed (Appendix, Ep. 2, no. 2) to a most noble matron who, while holding the honors of the world, was married to a man and to a Christian man (ibid., no. 26). Several years earlier she had resolved upon continence in her mind (ibid., no. 27), and had begun to preserve chastity without any agreement or consent from her husband and without having made a vow.

Paganism does not yet seem to have been abolished at the time when this letter was written (ibid., no. 8), although it is certain that the letter was sent after the time of Jovinianus (ibid., no. 28).

The letter could therefore be attributed to Paulinus, since the chronology fits. Moreover, if we believe Erasmus (Erasmus, vol. I on Jerome, p. 106) and Sacchinus (Sacchinus, *Life*, p. 733), it contains many marks of Paulinus’s style.

Nevertheless, within this stylistic elegance there is a certain gravity too remote from Paulinus’s liveliness and fluency of expression, as well as a different manner of rendering passages from Holy Scripture, for this letter to be assigned to him. Sacchinus, indeed (ibid. and p. 734), judges that it is not his, saying: “Nothing seems sufficiently clear to us.”

Paulinus’s exhortatory poem *To His Wife* (Appendix, poem 1), urging her to dedicate herself to God, which Rosweyde had included among Paulinus’s works (Rosweyde, edition, p. 643), comes sufficiently close to Paulinus’s own style and language. The reader himself will observe this in several passages of the poems.

But since it is attributed to Prosper in four manuscript codices and to Paulinus in none, and since it does not at all correspond to Paulinus’s history, we do not dare assert that it is a work of Paulinus. The poem is certainly excellent and very pleasing; its poetry also flows more sweetly and freely than that of Paulinus’s other poems.

What can disqualify this poem from being Paulinus’s, however, is that it describes the whole world amid that general overturning and confusion of affairs which the empire of the West experienced from the year 407 onward (Appendix, poem 1, verses 5 and 7). But at that time Paulinus had no need to exhort himself and his wife to Christian living or to indicate how they should use their possessions (ibid., verses 57 and following).

Arbogast caused the greatest disturbances in the West when, on 15 May 392, he ordered the younger Valentinian to be strangled and placed the diadem upon Eugenius. But the poem gives no outline of these events.

It is found among the poems of Prosper, to whom Rosweyde and others deny it and attribute it to Paulinus. Labbaeus disagrees with them (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*), but refutes their opinion with no arguments.

Appendix, poem 2, might appear to be a paraphrase of the praises that St. Bernard wrote concerning the name of Jesus; and therefore its author would seem not to have lived earlier than the twelfth century, if anything in the style suggested barbarism. Yet it approaches elegance somewhat; and, were it not for this paraphrase of Bernard, anyone could readily believe Paulinus to have been its author. For why should Bernard, who gathered so many sentences from authors whom he does not name and produced so many arguments concerning the name of Jesus, not have excerpted anything from Paulinus?

Caspar Barthius encountered this poem in a parchment manuscript of the Carthusian monastery near the German city of Strasbourg, among poems by various authors, and inserted it in book XXXIV, chapter 1, of his *Adversaria Commentaria*, assigning it to our Paulinus. Whenever you compare it with any of the distinguished Christian poets, you will see that it is inferior to none in genius; but to me its phrasing [Col. 0774C] and character so strongly resemble Paulinus that, when compared with his writings, you will find nothing in it that is not similar to them. After Barthius, the most learned men whom I consulted, and those most skilled in poetic art, judged likewise, among them the Reverend Father Commirius, S.J., and Nicolaus Heinsius shortly before his death.

The words *Illa Felix errorum non diu*, verse 32, plainly violate the rules of meter; yet I do not sufficiently see what should be put in their place, nor by what means the passage can be corrected without another book. I am in no way persuaded that so conspicuous a blemish proceeded from the author, but rather from ignorant copyists. The words *de cantatis diro carmine corporibus* plainly refer to the dead, whom magical song was customarily used to summon from their tombs. I think he wrote *Sono sago*, that is, “by the song of witches”: *Corpora cantata diro carmine et sono sago*—“bodies enchanted by an evil song and by the sound of a witch”—*devota bustis*, that is, “already dead.” See whether perhaps verse 76 should be read: *Carne interim terrae data*, or *Caro interim terrae data*—“Meanwhile, the flesh having been given to the earth,” or “Meanwhile, the flesh given to the earth”—*Ne*, etc. Barthius thinks that this poem was composed for the Easter celebrations (*Advers. Comment.*, book XXXIV, chapter 1).

[Col. 0774D]

### 3.

Some have suspected that Epistles 126 (otherwise 45) and 243 (otherwise 38) among St. Augustine’s letters belonged to our Paulinus. But the Louvain theologians and the Reverend Benedictine Fathers object, since Possidius lists them in his *Index*, chapter 7, and Bede, citing them in his commentary on I Timothy 5 and II Corinthians 5:15, recognizes them as Augustine’s.

Almost no one is now unaware that the life of St. Ambrose and the six books of poems on the *Life of St. Martin*, once falsely attributed to Paulinus of Nola, were composed by other Paulini. The former of these was only a deacon in 411, when our Paulinus had already been raised to episcopal dignity; the latter, on the other hand, was writing around the year 480.

Baronius has the following to say about Paulinus, the author of the *Life of St. Ambrose*, under the year of Christ 397, § 36:

> “That Paulinus who wrote down the deeds of Ambrose was manifestly a very different person from Paulinus, bishop of Nola, is clearly shown by his own statement. For when he testifies that at this time he was serving in the Church of Milan as a cleric of a lower order, under the care, as he says, of the deacon Castus, and that he was Ambrose’s secretary, who cannot see that this man was different from Paulinus of Nola, who had already four years earlier been ordained a priest and at this time was living in the territory of Nola, where he had already remained for three years? The name deceived many people. But because both men were known to have been joined to Augustine by friendship, they thought that the same man who committed the deeds of Ambrose to memory was Paulinus of Nola. Even if the strongest other arguments were lacking, the very great difference in their manner of expression certainly distinguishes them. Moreover, the man who, at Augustine’s request, wrote the life of that most holy man states that toward the end of Ambrose’s life he was staying in Africa, at Carthage, when he relates the divinely inflicted punishment upon Mauranus, who had spoken against Ambrose. It is therefore not surprising that he became known to Augustine, who could also have known him earlier, when he was living at Milan.”

And in § 27:

> “For this reason I have sometimes thought that this very man was that Paulinus who, later promoted to the diaconate, rose up as a most vigorous opponent of the Pelagian heresy, when he first acted energetically at Carthage against Coelestius in the council of bishops. For those proceedings, recited by St. Augustine, survive; they indicate that through his efforts Coelestius was first condemned at Carthage and afterward at Rome, when a petition against him was presented to Pope Zosimus.”

Anyone who wishes to know more should consult Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, book IV, and Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 420, observation 1.

Franciscus Juretus was the first to have the six books *On the Life and Miracles of St. Martin* printed. He attributed them to St. Paulinus of Nola, supported by the testimony of Gregory of Tours, who writes as follows in book I, chapter 2, of *On the Miracles of St. Martin*:

> “The blessed Paulinus also, bishop of the city of Nola, after writing in verse five books on his virtues, which Severus collected, included in the sixth book of his work those miracles that occurred after his death.”

A little later the same Gregory adds [Col. 0775C]:

> “Paulinus wrote these things in verse in the sixth book of his work, having received from St. Perpetuus, bishop, a little memorandum concerning them.”

Now Perpetuus became bishop of the Church of Tours sixty-four years after Martin’s death, as Gregory of Tours himself testifies in book I, chapter 61, of *On the Miracles of Martin*, and likewise in book X, chapter 31, of his *History of the Franks*. There, listing the bishops of Tours in order, he says:

> “Perpetuus was ordained sixth after the blessed Martin. He too was, as they say, of senatorial descent, extremely wealthy, and possessed estates in many cities.”

Sidonius Apollinaris likewise, in book IV, letter 18, calls Perpetuus the sixth bishop after Martin; and Sigibert mentions the same Perpetuus in his *Chronicle* around the year of Christ 472. It is therefore plainly evident either that the words “bishop of the city of Nola” were added and interpolated by some incompetent copyist, or that Gregory of Tours made a foolish mistake and contradicted himself. For if Perpetuus was ordained the sixth bishop after Martin sixty-four years after Martin’s death, around the year 470, and was still alive in 472, how could Paulinus, who died in 431, have written the sixth book of a *Life of St. Martin* for him?

Furthermore, the six books *On the Life of St. Martin* cannot be by St. Paulinus of Nola, since their author mentions Paulinus of Nola in book II and declares himself to bear the same name. Bellarmine supports this opinion in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, observation 2, on St. Paulinus of Nola. The very praise of Paulinus is also sufficient to establish that the writer is not the same man. Would one who had conquered pride and vanity, with such a humble spirit, boast of himself as

> “the distinguished man of faith, whom glory raised high”  
> (*Life of St. Martin*, book II)?

Yet Juretus, bound by prejudice [Col. 0776B], says: “Observe that this Paulinus seems to be praising his own faith.” Rather, observe that because he thinks so magnificently of Paulinus of Nola, this Paulinus cannot be Paulinus of Nola. In any case, I do not think it necessary to produce further arguments to confirm that this is not the Nolan Paulinus.

In the *Book of Rules* (*Appendix*, part 4, p. 81), which St. Benedict of Aniane, abbot, collected in the ninth century, there is a fragment by a certain Paulinus, under the title: “Response of St. Paulinus to the monks concerning penance.” It answers the question: “How ought monks to do penance?” It presents an eloquent author, but, in my opinion, not Paulinus of Nola. For Paulinus of Nola would not have made the absolutely certain statement that from the day on which someone renounced the world, his sins committed in the world after receiving baptism were no longer to be remembered, although he had promised God that he would thereafter practice righteousness; nor would he have said that such a person ought not to hesitate to receive the Lord’s body (*Ibid.*, p. 82). For who could ever affirm that this agrees with our Paulinus [Col. 0776C], who, after becoming a monk and priest, so often grieves and groans over the sins he committed in the world?

Finally, we must remember the statement of Sidonius Apollinaris (*Book IV*, letter 3, p. 90), who, assigning his own gifts to individual Fathers of the Church, says that Paulinus challenges him. This must be understood as referring to Paulinus’s exceptional sharpness, and to the most gracious power by which, when people read his writings, he challenges, attracts, and inflames them to obey Christ and observe his commandments exactly.

# SEVENTH DISSERTATION. ON THE CAPTIVITY OF ST. PAULINUS

[Col. 0775]

## Paulinus Gives Himself as a Substitute for a Captive. The Time at Which This Captivity Occurred.

### 1.

We know nothing from history about Paulinus of Nola between the year 414 and the year 417. The remarkable example of charity that Gregory the Great relates of him (*Dialogues*, book III, chapter 1) seems capable of being assigned to this interval. It is certainly unsuitable to refer it to Paulinus’s later years, since he still had enough strength to cultivate a garden and, in this exercise, displayed a handsome appearance of face characteristic of youth. Up to the year 413, however, we see each individual year so fully accounted for by his relations with Gaul and with Augustine that we cannot find a period of absence to which even one year could be assigned. Nor does Augustine seem to have known and understood the very distinguished deed of his friend; certainly, if he had known it, he would not have been silent about it in his book *The City of God*.

The story may be summarized as follows. Gregory the Great recounts its individual parts in *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 1:

> “When the Vandals were ravaging Campania in Italy and carrying many captives away into Africa, Paulinus, having spent all his possessions in works of piety, was asked by a widow to ransom her captive son. He gave himself into slavery in his place and devoted himself in Africa to cultivating the gardens of the son-in-law of the king of the Vandals. When the Vandal had taken him into his power, he entrusted him with the care of a little garden. Since Paulinus pleased his master by the reports he gave concerning his daily labor, his master willingly and frequently invited him to conversation. On one occasion, while they were speaking alone together, Paulinus warned him to take thought for his own affairs and to consider the condition of the Vandals, since their king, his father-in-law, would soon die.
>
> “The man reported this to the king. Wishing to see the author of the advice, the king came to lunch at his son-in-law’s house, since Paulinus used to bring vegetables to his master when he was dining. Moved by the sight of him, the king confessed to his son-in-law that he had seen this same Paulinus and several others sitting as judges during the night, and that they had taken the whip from his hands. Paulinus was then compelled to say that he was a bishop. When the king ordered the captive Nolan citizens to be sought throughout Africa—for Paulinus had humbly begged for their freedom—he sent them back honorably to Nola with the bishop, loading with grain the ships in which they had arrived.”

### 2.

No one doubts that this story is burdened with serious difficulties. In Paulinus’s time the Vandals did not come into Italy; they scarcely had time to occupy Africa, much less to cultivate gardens there. Moreover, King Genseric, under whose rule they were brought there, died long after Paulinus. We must therefore admit that Gregory was mistaken in certain parts of this story, as sometimes happens in accounts of the deeds of others transmitted through reports, even when the events themselves are entirely true. Gregory says in what manner he learned the story.

After Procopius (*Vandalic War*, book I, chapter 2), Chiffletius rightly observes (*Paulinus Illustratus*, p. 187) that Goths, Vandals, Gepids, Sarmatians, and other peoples are referred to by writers under one name, since they were all sprung from one people, contemporaries, fellow soldiers, trained under the same laws, equally supporters of the Arian heresy, and speakers of one language, which they call Gothic [Col. 0777B].

Since Nola was captured by the Goths in 410 (see *Life*, chapter 51, note 2), and no other barbarians came—or could have come—to Campania in Paulinus’s time, that great crowd of captives which, according to Gregory the Great, was carried into Campania by the Vandals must be referred here. Gregory adds that they were transported to Africa, since the Vandals had long possessed their royal seat there; but at that time they did not yet rule there. It is therefore much more probable that the captives were carried away with the Gothic army, which crossed from Italy into Gaul in 412 and into Spain three years later, or that they were sold to other barbarians.

It is possible, however, that the man for whom Paulinus surrendered himself as a slave came into the hands of the Vandals in this way, since they had inhabited Spain from the year 409 onward. As for the prince whose death Paulinus foretold, among the many different leaders of those peoples who were regarded as kings, some unknown one may have died in 415 or 416; for Paulinus’s captivity cannot be extended to a later period.

### 3.

Hydatius, in his *Chronicle* around the year 416 or 417, speaks of a certain Fredibald, king of a Vandal people, who was captured without a battle by Constantius and sent to Honorius. Perhaps he died a few days later. If this event occurred only in 417, Paulinus could nevertheless have foretold it near the end of 416 as imminent.

We read that Ataulf, Alaric’s brother-in-law and king of the Goths, died in 415. But since the Goths had crossed into Spain somewhat earlier, they had not yet begun thinking about the cultivation of gardens. Chiffletius (*loc. cit.*, pp. 188–189) asserts that Paulinus surrendered himself into slavery in 409 or 410 and foretold Alaric’s death. Yet it is certain that Paulinus was at Nola when it was plundered by Alaric around the month of September, and Alaric died not long afterward.

Nor can one say that Alaric’s son-in-law had been a ruler in Africa from the year 408, as Chiffletius supposes, and that in 410 Paulinus could freely have been taken away from him and handed over to Alaric, the enemy of the most savage empire. These suppositions appear fabricated and entirely improbable [Col. 0777D].

Baronius (*Annals*, 431, § 191) asserts that Genseric, king of the Vandals, ravaged Italy in 428 or 429 and carried captives away from it, and that Paulinus foretold the death of Guntharius. Relying on the authority of Procopius, he maintains that Guntharius brought the Vandals into Africa together with his brother Genseric. But the Vandals could not have traversed the sea before they had occupied Africa. Prosper states (*Chronicle*, 427) that at the time when they crossed from Spain into Africa they did not yet know the art of navigation.

Procopius (*Vandalic War*, book I, chapter 3), whom Baronius follows as his guide, says that Guntharius was then still a boy and therefore did not have a son-in-law. It is also certain that Guntharius, or rather Gundiacrius—for this is how some writers call him—had already died in 427 or 428, before the Vandals crossed into Africa. Hydatius confirms this. Procopius himself testifies (*Ibid.*) that the Vandals of his own time believed this; nor do Victor of Vita or the other writers indicate that the Vandals came into Africa under any leader other than Genseric.

If, therefore, Paulinus was made captive under Guntharius, he was certainly in Spain, not in Africa, as Baronius maintains. It would then have to be said that Paulinus, seventy-five years old, worked as a gardener (Chiffl., *loc. cit.*, p. 180), which is in no way plausible.

### 4.

I do not know whether the circumstances of another Paulinus, who is said to have been appointed bishop of Nola somewhat after our Paulinus, would agree any better with Gregory’s account. Even if they did, however, no one will think that so distinguished a deed—one that must be proposed to all as a remarkable example of charity—should be attributed to anyone other than the man from whom such great works of divine charity proceeded at the very beginning of his conversion, when grace seemed to cooperate with him.

To forestall the objections that might be brought against this interpretation of the story—namely, that a bishop ought not to leave his people, nor prefer the freedom of a private captive to the eternal salvation of his entire flock—it will be sufficient to answer that Gregory (*Dialogues*, book III, chapter 1), who knew the rules of the Church and the duties of bishops extremely well, praised that astonishing, admirable, and altogether unheard-of deed, from which anyone could learn the greatest lessons of virtue.

“In this,” he says (*Ibid.*), “he imitated the one who took the form of a slave, so that we would not be slaves of sin.”

St. Eulogius (*To Flora and Maria*, tome IX, p. 312, *Library of the Fathers*), a distinguished martyr of the ninth century, uses almost the same words when proposing this example to virgins detained in prison for Christ. There he calls St. Paulinus a bishop of remarkable holiness and incomparable merit.

Some writers (Ambrose, Leo, book II, *On Nola*, chapter 13, and Chiffl., p. 259) relate that St. Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, returned with all the Nolans liberated in his name and, having deserved so well of his fellow citizens, was received by them with such pomp and joy that thereafter they honored, and still honor, that same day with fixed processions, festivals, and spectacles. This observance lasted from the tenth day of June, on which he is said to have returned to the city, until the twenty-second, on which he died.

From a Medicean manuscript containing Uranius’s account of Paulinus’s death addressed to Pacatus—and in which the story extends from the widow’s son, whom St. Paulinus ransomed by exchanging himself, to his return from Africa to Nola—Baronius argues (*Annals*, 431, § 195, in the appendix) that St. Gregory copied from Uranius, word for word, the story that we included among the *Elogia*. But this did not persuade Sachinus (*Life of Paulinus*, pp. 721–722), who always attributes the story to St. Gregory the Great; nor did it persuade Chiffletius (pp. 179–180), who very effectively refutes Baronius’s arguments and reasoning.

For Gregory himself (*Dialogues*, book III, chapter 1) says that he did not excerpt this story of Paulinus’s captivity from anyone’s writings, but heard it from elderly men, whose testimony he admits he could not reject.

If this captivity occurred between the year 414 and 417, it is reasonable to believe that Augustine had already written to Paulinus about it no later than the beginning of 417, since in Letter 186 (formerly 106), written around the middle of that same year, he says nothing at all about the captivity.

[Col. 0779]

# DISSERTATIONS ON THE POEMS OF ST. PAULINUS  
*(By Ludovico Antonio Muratori)*

# FIRST DISSERTATION. ON TURCIUS APRONIANUS

[Col. 0779]

[Col. 0779A] 799

The family of Turcius Apronianus is famous among the ancient Latins. After Glandorpius, the Apronian family was treated with especially refined and vigorous scholarship by the eminent Norisius in *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, Dissertation 4, chapter 2, § 1. The Turcian Apronian Asterian family was therefore extremely distinguished at Rome, as the cardinal cited there says.

Under Julian Augustus, L. Turcius Secundus Apronianus flourished as prefect of the city. An inscription concerning him is found in Gruter, p. 476, no. 7, and another on p. 647, no. 6. Another Gruterian inscription, on p. 165, no. 2, from Fano, must also be referred to him, although until now it has been presented incorrectly, as though it had been dedicated to *Divo Augusto*. The Ambrosian sheets of the Library, the oldest of all, provide the true reading. From them I have drawn much material for the adornment of my collection of unpublished inscriptions, which, if the gods favor me, I now intend to communicate to the world in a suitable volume. The marble and its annotation read as follows:

[Col. 0779B]

At Fano, on a partly ruined arch shattered by engines of war during the war of Pius II against the people of Fano, 1462.

**To the divine Augustus, the pious Constantine, father of the lords.**

What is found in Gruter follows in the middle and below the marble. The marble had earlier been placed in honor of Augustus; then, as frequently happens, another inscription was joined to the same marble, which Turcius Secundus Asterius wished to dedicate to Constantine the Great.

There were other Turcii Aproniani, or Asterii, whom one may see in the work of Norisius, never sufficiently praised. There, from an ancient Vergilian manuscript of the Medicean Library, is presented an inscription of Turcius Rufius Apronianus, *vir clarissimus*, who entered upon the consulship in the year of Christ 494; the inscription was written in the hand of that same Turcius.

Let us now return to our Turcius. Paulinus commends him as follows:

> The glory of the Turcian family, Apronianus,  
> A boy in age, an old man in the understanding of the flesh,  
> Noble through the ancient lineage of the toga,  
> But nobler still in the name of Christian;  
> He who, with the glory of an old and a new birth combined,  
> Is an old senator of the curia, but new in Christ.

Thus this Turcius was enrolled among the senators [Col. 0780A] and had recently professed the Christian religion. Apronianus owed his conversion to Christ to the piety of the elder Melania, who led him from the pagan peoples into the arms of Christ.

I have Palladius as the authority for this in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 118, where, speaking of the elder Melania’s return from Jerusalem to Rome, he says:

> “While she was there, she instructed through catechesis the most blessed and highly esteemed man Aprianus—one must read *Apronianus*—who was a pagan, and made him a Christian.”

Melania returned to Rome in the year 397, according to the calculations of Baronius and Pagius. Thus Apronianus renounced paganism after that time.

He was also among the few friends of Rufinus of Aquileia. The elder and younger Melania had cultivated this intimacy, and Rufinus held the first place in honor and esteem among them. Hence, having become his supporter, Apronianus had also closed his mind against Rufinus’s erroneous doctrines.

In the year of the Lord 399, Jerome composed a letter to Pammachius and Oceanus in which he corrected certain opinions and slanders of Rufinus. [Col. 0780B] But, as the eminent Norisius says in book I, chapter 2, of his *History of Pelagianism*, as soon as Jerome’s letter was delivered to Pammachius, Apronianus—who was most zealously attending to Rufinus’s cause—sent a copy of it to his teacher at Aquileia.

In response, Rufinus immediately composed two books of invective against Jerome and dedicated them to our Apronianus. They begin as follows:

> “I have read through your writings, dearest Apronianus, which you sent on to me after you had transmitted them from the East to the most noble man Pammachius from a good friend and brother—that is, Jerome.”

Now let us see what concerns his wife.

Palladius preserves the following information for us in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 134:

> “I also saw the blessed and God-worthy Avita with her husband Primianus.”

So it stands in the printed books; but the passage must be corrected, and *Apronianus* must be read instead of *Primianus*. Heraclides, in the *Paradise*—a book that, with a few changes, is the same as Palladius’s *Lausiac History*—writes in chapter 39:

> “I saw a certain Avita, worthy of God, with a man named Aprenianus, her husband, and their daughter Eunomia.”

Here too the name is erroneous, and *Apronianus*, not *Aprenianus*, must be read. [Col. 0780C]

Thus Avita, who was likewise present to Paulinus and of whom I shall speak below, was the wife of Apronianus. He had two children by her, namely Eunomia and the boy Asterius. Let us first consider the latter.

# SECOND DISSERTATION. ON ASTERIUS, THE SON OF TURCIUS APRONIANUS

[Col. 0779]

[Col. 0779C] 802

This Asterius must certainly be distinguished from Turcius Apronianus, both so that the number given by Paulinus in the following verse may be correct:

> Thus, together with their offspring, the parents are nine in all,

and because this is expressly asserted in the preceding words:

> With Father Paulinus, this Turcius too is equally a father,  
> But my age and offspring make him a father.

Turcius did indeed have another child, namely Eunomia, but Paulinus had first assigned her to Avita as mother:

> For these three mothers there are two children of one sex:  
> A twofold blossom—Melania’s offspring and Eunomia.

[Col. 0780C]

Therefore Asterius was the son of Turcius Apronianus, bearing a surname evidently proper to the Turcian family. The poet repeats this still more explicitly below, after speaking of his own son Pinianus in Christ, in these words:

> But in Asterius I have another light equal to mine.  
> His parents, united in true piety,  
> Consecrated him as an infant to Christ,  
> So that, like Samuel marked out from his earliest years,  
> He might grow, devoted to holiness, with God nourishing him.  
> Holy grace made this boy a brother to his father.  
> For they were born in the same sacred stream;  
> Those whom nature [*na ura* in the text] had separated in rank,  
> God, in his gracious gift, will lead as brothers into his kingdom.

[Col. 0781A]

Here Asterius is mentioned as having been washed, together with his father Turcius Apronianus, in the sacred font of baptism. Nor had this happened long before, since Asterius’s age did not permit it; and the recent circumstance noted concerning Turcius does not indicate otherwise. He is called an old senator of the curia, but new in Christ, and had become far more illustrious through the glory of his new birth.

The following verse may perhaps also be understood of this Asterius:

> Turcius with pious face, Suecrius in the flower of life.

The father Turcius is mentioned first, then the son, who is also called Suecrius, unless this name refers rather to Pinianus. I admit that this surname was sufficiently foreign among Romans of that age, and so I am easily led to suspect a corruption of the text. Perhaps *Syagrius* should be read, which copyists could easily have changed into *Suecrius*. We have two consuls bearing this surname in the *Fasti*, in the years 381 and 382. Ennodius also calls the Syagrian family the treasure of the Church in his *Epiphanius*.

The aforementioned Cardinal Norisius, in *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, Dissertation 4, chapter 2, § 1, praises Hydatius for mentioning in his *Chronicle* Asterius in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Honorius—that is, in the year 420 of our era—and again in the seventeenth year of Valentinian III, namely 440. He also praises Renatus Profuturus in Gregory of Tours, book I of the *History of the Franks*. These authors mention two Asterii under Honorius and his successor Valentinian, who served in Spain as masters of both military branches.

Another Asterius is also recorded in the *Fasti* as consul in the year of Christ 449. But I readily persuade myself that none of these was our Asterius, since, as they say, he had been consecrated to God by his parents from his tenderest years and was being raised for priestly honor, as we learned above from Paulinus.

# THIRD DISSERTATION. ON AVITA AND EUNOMIA

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781B] 803

Avita was the wife of Turcius Apronianus, and their children were the Asterius mentioned above and Eunomia. Paulinus writes of her as follows:

> His sister is joined to him in the yoke, so that Avita may be the third mother  
> Of the hymn-singing choirs in the procession of the company.

Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 134, calls this woman blessed and counts her among women distinguished by the holiness of their lives. His words are:

> “I also saw the blessed and God-worthy Avita with her husband Primianus—one must read, as I said above, Apronianus—and their daughter Eunomia, pleasing God in all things. They had evidently been transferred from a dissolute and pleasure-loving life to an honorable and continent way of life. They too were deemed worthy to fall asleep in Christ, free from every sin, fighting perfectly in the contest, and leaving their lives in good remembrance.”

The same Palladius, in chapter 118, after reporting that the elder Melania had brought Apronianus back to the Christian faith, adds:

> “She also persuaded him to live continently with his wife, his sister Avita by name.”

From this we learn that Avita was the sister of the elder Melania and that, after her admonitions, she observed continence. If this passage of Palladius did not stand in the way, I would have explained the word *sister* in Paulinus so that Avita would be called the sister of the Albina mentioned above. But we are compelled to understand it either as a relationship of affinity that existed between her and Albina, or as a similarity of age or character between them; the word permits several interpretations.

Since the elder Melania returned to Rome in the year of Christ 397, we must admit that Avita and Turcius embraced continence after that time. Consequently, Eunomia and Asterius, their children, must have been born before the year already mentioned.

Heraclides describes Avita in the *Paradise* in the same words as Palladius:

> “I saw Avita, worthy of God, with a certain Aprenianus—read *Apronianus*—her husband, and their daughter Eunomia, so pleasing to God that they deserved to be transferred to heavenly life before his sight. For they too, now at the final end of nature, rest in Christ; they have been freed from the bonds of all sins and have always possessed knowledge and understanding of divine things.”

It is therefore established from these statements that Turcius and Avita were Eunomia’s parents. Paulinus speaks of her as follows:

> And Eunomia too, already a maiden betrothed  
> To eternal bridal chambers in heaven, whom Christ,  
> Snatched from her mother’s breast, in hastening love  
> Consecrated as pleasing to himself.

He mentions her likewise below. It is especially worthy of notice that Paulinus here indicates that Eunomia and Asterius, as children, were dedicated to Christ from infancy. I have explained this custom of the ancient Christians somewhat in the notes.

# FOURTH DISSERTATION. ON ALBINA

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781C] 804

Albina too was held in the highest esteem among the ancients, a woman distinguished both by birth and by holiness. Let us first see what Paulinus says of her:

[Col. 0781D]

> Albina is first in the choir, together with her father Therasia.

And below:

> I speak of these servants of Christ,  
> A noble pair before God, a pair distinguished in the name of Christ,  
> Albina and her mother, newly born in your regions.

The parents of this most illustrious woman became known through the scholarship of the most distinguished Cardinal Norisius. In the *Acts of St. Melania the Younger*, presented under 31 December in Surius, Melania’s *θεῖος*—that is, her maternal uncle—is called Volusianus. From this, the excellent scholar concluded that Albina was the daughter of Rufius Ceionius Albinus, who was the brother of Rufius Ceionius Volusianus. He therefore judged that this illustrious woman belonged to the Ceionian family.

He observed this with great learning in a certain short work. From my manuscript notes I shall not hesitate to append an unpublished fragment of an inscription concerning Rufius Volusianus. With God’s favor, I shall soon publish it as well in a proper collection of unpublished marbles. It is found in the pavement of the Lateran basilica at Rome:

[Col. 0782D]

**RUFIUS VOLUSIANUS, V. C. [vir clarissimus, “most distinguished man”], X. VI.  
RUFIUS FESTUS, V. C. [“most distinguished man”], XV SEPT.  
SEBASMIUS, PHILOS… [philosopher]  
…  
PONT. M. [chief pontiff]  
BRITTIUS PRAESENS, V. C. [“most distinguished man”], P. M.  
EVACRIUS, PHILOSOPHUS [philosopher]…  
FL. ATTICUS, V. C. [“most distinguished man”]…**
Melania the Elder, a woman of illustrious rank, after her husband had been taken from the living, saw that she had one surviving son as the sole remnant of her offspring. Chiffletius, a man of distinction from the Society of Jesus, calls him Poblicola (whether correctly, I do not know). He grew up and, having acquired an exceptional reputation in the City, became prominent among the foremost through his wealth. We owe all this to Paulinus in Letter 10 to Severus, where he says much about Melania and her son. This man later joined Albina to himself in marriage; from this we can easily estimate how great was the nobility with which she was endowed, since she obtained as her husband a man of the highest nobility, distinguished by grandfathers who had been consuls. From this marriage came Melania the Younger, who likewise was present at Nola, [Col. 0783A] and concerning whom there will be discussion below.

According to what the Metaphrast teaches in Surius under 31 January, this Melania was of the most illustrious family: her parents belonged to the first rank of the Roman Senate. Thus, from these words also, one sees what distinguished cradle the holy woman Albina received. Let us now examine what Palladius reported about her. In the *Historia Lausiaca*, chapter 118, speaking of Melania the Elder, he says:

> After she had also strengthened her granddaughter Melania together with her husband Pinianus, and had instructed her daughter-in-law Albina, the wife of her son, in catechesis, and had persuaded all of them to sell what they possessed, she led them out of Rome and brought them to the honorable and tranquil harbor of life.

In chapter 120, speaking of the granddaughter of Melania the Elder, he adds:

> She also had with her her mother Albina, [805] who likewise practices ascetic discipline and likewise distributes her money separately.

Heraclides repeats the same account in the *Paradise*, chapter 42, in these words:

> Having therefore instructed these people together—that is, her granddaughter Melania and her husband Pinianus, and also Albina, her daughter-in-law, that is, the wife of her son—she taught them in every respect. [Col. 0783B]

Albina, then, was the daughter-in-law of Melania the Elder, since she had married her son and borne Melania the Younger. This close blood relationship was the reason that Albina, Melania the Younger, and her husband Pinianus always kept their household and their hearts united. Accordingly, all of them together undertook a pilgrimage to Africa, which the Metaphrast also records in the *Acts of Saint Melania* under 31 January in Surius.

The principal purpose of the journey was to visit Augustine, who was living at Hippo. There Pinianus endured no small disturbances, when the people of Hippo wanted by every means to compel him to accept the priesthood. For this reason Saint Augustine sent a letter to Albina, who was staying at Tagaste, in which he excused the popular uprising and especially cleared himself before her.
