This is Letter 225 in the Antwerp edition.

The holy Doctor also sent another letter, Letter 227, to Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania, in which he excused himself for not yet having been able to meet them. According to the great father of the *Annals*, this took place in the year 409, or later, as some believe.

These three distinguished companions also undertook another pilgrimage to Jerusalem, where they greeted Saint Jerome. Jerome, writing at the same time to Alypius and Augustine in Letter 79, adds:

> Your holy common children, Albinus, Apinianus, and Melania, send you their warmest greetings.

Rosweydus, in his notes to the *Lives of the Fathers*, p. 1005, adds the following concerning this Albina:

> Saint Jerome speaks of her in various letters.

But this is not entirely correct, for he confuses this Albina with Albina, the mother of Marcella. Baronius had warned that this confusion must be avoided in his remarks on the year 408. Above, in Augustine’s Letter 227, and now in the highly praised letter of Jerome, you have seen *Albinum* written in place of *Albina*. Baronius, restoring *Albinam*, says that the manuscripts should be corrected; [Col. 0784A] Rosweydus, however, p. 703, in his notes to the *Lives of the Fathers*, considers this restoration unnecessary, since at that time women’s names were also sometimes expressed with masculine endings. He proves this by the example of Melania, who was occasionally called *Melanium*.

With due respect to so great a man, I cannot accept this opinion. The circumstances are different, and the origin of the name is different. This usage did not attach to Latin names, but rather to Greek names introduced into Latin. Donatus the Grammarian says in Book V *On Gender*:

> Some nouns are neuter in their ending but feminine in meaning, such as *Phronisium*, *Glycerium*, and *Sophronium*; these are names of women.

Priscian likewise asserts in Book V that women’s names can end in *-um*, as in *Glycerium mea*, *Dorcium*, and *Philotium*. These are indeed all names of women, but each derives from a Greek origin. The name Albina, however, proceeding from Latin sources, could not without boldness—and without the danger of obvious ambiguity—be changed into *Albinum*. Such a practice was permissible among the Greeks, but not among the Latins. Moreover, the names used as examples are expressed only with a neuter ending; [Col. 0784B] Albina, on the other hand, has the form of a masculine name, so that no comparison can be drawn between them.

It should further be known that the very charming name Albina first provoked a sharp dispute among the greatest scholars. The eminent Norisius once wrote, in his celebrated work *On the History of Pelagianism*, that the title of Augustine’s book *On the Grace of Christ* should not be corrected where it reads: “Albine, Piniane, et Melania.” He followed the traces of Rosweydus.

Father Macedus, a man of great reputation and the author of many substantial volumes—though one often misses sound judgment in him—rose against the opinion of the most distinguished Norisius. He judged that, instead of Albina, the mother of Melania the Younger, the name *Albinus* referred to some man: either her father, father-in-law, uncle, Pinianus’s maternal or paternal uncle, some cleric, or whatever else he fancied.

The same eminent cardinal nevertheless established with irrefutable arguments, in two treatises composed on this subject, that our Albina is meant there. I could add further evidence from Saint Paulinus, [Col. 0784C] but one observation will suffice. The eminent scholar himself writes somewhere that in two Medicean manuscripts Jerome’s letter quoted above reads as follows: “Albina, Apinianus, and Melania send you greetings”; I have also observed this reading in a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library.

Possidius, Augustine’s contemporary and saintly associate, likewise teaches us that the reading at Augustine should be *Albina*. In reviewing Augustine’s works, he reports a letter entitled: “To Albina, Pinianus, and Melania.” Moreover, the learned Benedictine Fathers, in the excellent edition of Saint Augustine prepared in recent years, read *Albina*, not *Albinus*, and support this reading with the authority of several manuscripts.

Therefore, everywhere one should read *Albina*, not *Albinus*, and Baronius’s correction should be accepted.

# FIFTH DISSERTATION. ON THERASIA

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783C] In the best manuscript, from which I produced my restored text of Saint Paulinus, the words are divided in such a way that one reads *compar et haerasia*. But who is this Haerasia? I nowhere find mention of a woman of that name. The manuscript must therefore be corrected, and the reading should be either *compare Therasia* or *cum pare Therasia*.

I have a similar verse of Paulinus in Letter 12 to Severus, where he says:

> After long ages he reveals  
> Protasius with his companion Gervasius.

She was the faithful and most devout wife of our Paulinus in the world. Later, together with him, she professed celibacy and chose for herself a way of chaste and religious life, while her husband devoutly undertook the duties of the priesthood.

Idacius, in his *Chronicle* under the thirtieth year of Honorius, says:

> Paulinus, most noble and most eloquent, formerly made still nobler by his conversion to God, an apostolic man and distinguished bishop of Nola in Campania, had Therasia, who, from being his wife, became his sister, equal to him in the testimony and merit of a blessed life.

See how Idacius extols her chastity when he asserts that, from being Paulinus’s wife, she became his sister. Gennadius likewise, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, mentions several letters that Paulinus wrote to his sister concerning contempt for the world. I think that this sister may have been none other than his wife Therasia. A poem on this subject still exists, though some manuscripts wrongly attribute it to Saint Prosper.

I infer that this holy woman was Spanish, since she entered into marriage with Paulinus there. The saint himself sings of this:

> Across the Pyrenees I went, a pilgrim among the Iberians.  
> There you allowed me, under human law, to be joined in marriage,  
> So that you might purchase the life of two,  
> And through the double yoke of the flesh the salvation of souls  
> Might compensate for the salvation of one, long deferred.

Below he suggests that he and Therasia had jointly undertaken a vow of chastity:

> You broke for us  
> The bonds of the flesh.

This most devout woman was still alive when this *Natalis* was recited, and indeed remained alive later. This is established from Paulinus’s Letter 44 to Saint Augustine, which bears the names of both Paulinus and Therasia, and was written in the year of Christ 416 and thereafter, as Chiffletius correctly proves in Part 2, chapter 34. Therefore, in the year 406, when Paulinus recited this passage, Therasia was still living with him. See Sacchinus’s *Life of this Saint*, where there is further information about Therasia.

# SIXTH DISSERTATION. ON PINIANUS

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785A] His name is famous in ecclesiastical history. I shall recount his achievements as briefly as possible.

Paulinus has left us evidence that Pinianus belonged to a most distinguished family, for he descended from Valerius Poplicola, who is counted among the first consuls of the City. Pinianus therefore belonged to the Valerian family. It is pleasant to hear Paulinus:

> His companion draws near him under an equal yoke,  
> Pinianus, younger in age, equal in faith,  
> Himself also a young man distinguished by ancient blood,  
> The firstborn of a consul in the imperial City.

[Col. 0785B]

> That Valerius, bearing consular descent,  
> The first to hold the name in the Latin annals,  
> Whom Rome, after the kings were driven out, added to Brutus,  
> The final ancient source of the lineage  
> Of this Christian consul Valerius.

Do you hear Pinianus called *primigenus*, that is, the firstborn son of a certain consul? The same is asserted in the *Life of Melania the Younger* in Surius under 31 January, in these words:

> Her fiancé was comparable to Melania in family, age, and every other respect. He was born of consuls and had only recently passed beyond boyhood. His name was Apenianus—that is, Pinianus—and he was about seventeen years old.

But which consul was this? I confess that I am left in darkness. The official lists are silent, and the writers say not a word. Palladius nevertheless asserts in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 119, that Pinianus was the son of Severus, who was one of the prefects—or rather, an ex-prefect. Heraclides likewise, in the *Paradise*, chapter 49, calls him the son of Severus, the former prefect.

In contrast, the aforementioned author of Saint Melania’s *Life* makes him the brother of Severus, for he says:

> But he brought against them the formidable weapon of Apenianus’s—namely, Pinianus’s—brother Severus, by whom he thought that he could shake the tower of their steadfast mind.

Thus this Severus, who had been a brother, had become an enemy. [808] The same author repeats this further below.

I think the matter can be reconciled if we say that Pinianus was the son of Severus, and that from this Severus another Severus, Pinianus’s brother, was born. Since the Valerian family produced Pinianus, it follows that his father was named Valerius Severus, just as his brother was also named Severus, the two being distinguished only by their name or praenomen.

But again I am distressed to find myself uncertain, since nowhere do I discover a Valerius Severus who was consul at this time. I therefore hold that Pinianus’s father must have been designated not as an ordinary consul but as a suffect or honorary consul. If this is so, it is not surprising that his name was consigned to oblivion.

A certain L. VALERIUS SEVERUS is mentioned in Gruterus, p. 49, no. 4, and p. 566, no. 6. But whether he has anything to do with this Severus, I do not know.

In Dissertation 2, on Asterius, I noted that this verse was corrupt:

> Turcius with pious countenance, Suecrius in flourishing youth.

I proposed the conjecture that *Syagrius* should be read, since these letters could very easily have been confused through their similarity of sound. What if that verse referred to Pinianus, and the most distinguished man also bore the cognomen Syagrius? Perhaps we would then have found his father distinguished by an ordinary consulship; for in the years 381 and 382 two Syagrii—distinct from one another, as the distinguished Pagius maintains in the prolegomena to his Dissertation on Hypatius, no. 27—were elevated to this office.

If this were true, Pinianus would have to be called Valerius Syagrius, and one of those consuls would have to be accepted as his father. Since I do not fail to recognize that many objections may stand in the way of this conjecture, it is enough for me merely to have mentioned it; let better arguments be expected from others.

From these considerations it is certainly clear that our Pinianus was also called Valerius. The great father of the annals, Baronius, under the year of Christ 385, produces from a Vatican manuscript letters written by the Emperor Valentinian to Pinianus, prefect of the City, concerning the election of Syricius as supreme pontiff. The same Pinianus is addressed in Law 13, *On Physicians and Professors*, of the Theodosian Code, issued in 387; in Law 4 of the Theodosian Code, *On Agents in State Affairs*, issued in the same year; and in Law 13 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Privileges of Those Serving in the Sacred Palace*, promulgated in 386.

Baronius and Gothofredus, in their notes on these very laws, consider this Pinianus to be the same as our Pinianus, namely, the husband of Melania the Younger. The same opinion is repeated by this celebrated jurist in the *Prosopography of the Theodosian Code*.

I shall demonstrate that such eminent men have formed an insufficiently supported opinion. Poplicola—as Chiffletius calls him—the father of Melania the Younger and father-in-law of Pinianus, died before May of the year 399, as the most distinguished Cardinal Norisius proves excellently in a certain short work.

The author of Saint Melania’s *Life* relates that she and her husband Pinianus had considered embracing the celibate life, but that Melania’s parent opposed so holy a plan. The author adds:

> Then Melania’s father died. Once the one who had prevented them had been removed, when God willed it and the time called for it, they immediately departed from the great city, bidding farewell to urban crowds and disturbances. When they began this angelic form of life, Pinianus was twenty-four years old and Melania twenty.

Thus, if one counts six years backward from the year of Christ 399—the period during which Pinianus’s marriage with his wife lasted—one arrives at the year 393, when he married Melania, being, as the same author says, about seventeen years old. Again, counting backward from 393 to the year 385, when he is thought to have held the urban prefecture, one clearly discovers that Pinianus would then have been about nine years old.

Everyone can therefore see how rashly Baronius and Gothofredus made our Pinianus prefect of the City. The urban prefecture was a great burden and rejected youthful shoulders, as can be seen in Guido Pancirolus’s notes on both empires and in Gothofredus’s *Notitia Dignitatum*.

This may also be inferred from Paulinus’s silence. Why would Paulinus, when praising Pinianus and composing everything in order to praise him, have passed over this honor without mention? That was not Paulinus’s custom.

But someone will ask: Who was that Pinianus distinguished by the urban prefecture? I willingly confess that I do not know. Yet why should we not believe that he was a kinsman, and perhaps the father, of our Pinianus, since Heraclides calls Pinianus the son of the former prefect Severus, and Palladius calls him the son of Severus, who had been one of the prefects?

This Severus could have used Pinianus as a cognomen. Paulinus’s words seem to me to prove this remarkably:

[Col. 0786D]

> Blessed Piniades, Melania’s equal in covenant.

The word *Piniades* certainly denotes Pinianus according to the pattern of patronymic names: “the son of Pinianus.” Thus we have seen that Pinianus married Melania the Younger.

They remained married for six years. After that, embracing continence and renouncing their enormous wealth—which surpassed that of everyone except the Emperor—they devoted everything to the support of the poor. Both Palladius and the author of Saint Melania’s *Life* reveal this, in harmony with what Paulinus sings:

> And in this the boy reflects something of that parent,  
> This young servant of Christ, performing the office of a consul,  
> Who, caring for the liberation of others, dispenses a holy gift  
> Through the work of redemption before God.  
> For from the necks of very many freedmen  
> He drives away the servile yoke with sacred wealth,  
> Whom, bound by debt in the darkness of prison,  
> He releases with gold from the chain of interest.

[Col. 0787A] You will find the remaining deeds of Pinianus, a man of illustrious rank—how he went to Tagaste and experienced the disturbance of the people who wanted him initiated into the sacred ministry, and how he undertook journeys to Jerusalem and then Constantinople—in Baronius under the years of Christ 409 and 419, except that several chronological errors in the *Annals* must be corrected from the *Pelagian History* of the most distinguished Cardinal Norisius.

I would like to add one point: some call this most noble man Apenianus, others Alpinianus, and some Pimanus. They are all mistaken. His true name was Pinianus, as Paulinus makes perfectly clear when, playing on his name, he compares him with a pine. He says:

[Col. 0788A]

> For here is the boy, Melania’s husband, in the body of Christ,  
> To whom God granted a name derived from the pine,  
> So that, as a boy, he might receive the name from that tree of eternal life  
> Which remains ever green without end.

For the pine endures with its crown ever in bloom.

Augustine held Pinianus so dear that he dedicated two books to him against the Pelagians. Jerome also treated him with the greatest friendship, and for this reason he may rightly be called a man of outstanding distinction in his age.

Let us now return to his wife Melania.

# SEVENTH DISSERTATION. ON MELANIA

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787B] Melania the Elder, a woman of illustrious rank, had one son. Chiffletius calls him Poblicola. He married Albina, and by her had Melania, who is therefore called the Younger, as the granddaughter of Melania the Elder. She later married Pinianus, a man of illustrious rank, and always remained at his side as his faithful companion.

An anonymous author recorded in writing the life of this exceptionally distinguished woman, who was enrolled among the saints. The work appears in Surius under 31 January, and there one should read about her astonishing virtues.

She burned with such love of continence that from the very beginning of their marriage she persuaded her husband to embrace it; nevertheless, she did not fulfill her vow until only after six years. The aforementioned author says:

> When they began this angelic form of life, Pinianus was twenty-four years old and Melania twenty.

Melania fulfilled this holy purpose in the year of Christ 399. In that year her father ceased to live, and he had always opposed the pious vows of the married couple. I indicated this in the preceding Dissertation. Now, however, in order to remove the chronological error of the distinguished Joannes Baptista le Brun—who prepared the latest edition of Saint Paulinus’s works, which I long sought but have not yet obtained—I think it necessary to investigate more carefully the year in which Melania’s father died.

Saint Paulinus expressed his death in Letter 44 to Saint Augustine. Augustine subsequently replied in Letter 250, in which the great Doctor writes, among other things:

> Therefore, concerning the joy that is with you, when you have heard from brother Possidius himself what sorrowful cause compelled him, you will know me most truly, and so forth.

The sorrowful cause that compelled Bishop Possidius to sail to Italy is reported by Augustine himself in Letter 202 to Nectarius. The pagans living at Calama in Numidia had attacked Possidius himself, who was their bishop, and sought to kill him. Augustine writes that this crime had been committed against the most recent laws enacted against the pagans by the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius.

The laws that Augustine mentions were promulgated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, during the consulship of Manlius Theodorus—that is, in the year of Christ 399—as he himself also testifies in Book XVIII, chapter 54, of *The City of God*, and as we learn from the Theodosian Code.

Again, the time of Possidius’s voyage can be established from Augustine’s Letter 254 to Nectarius. There he says:

> For I had written back when the holy brother and my fellow bishop Possidius was still with us and had not yet sailed.

He continues:

> I received the letters which you graciously returned to him on my account on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, almost eight months after I had written.

Therefore Possidius had crossed over to Italy after the Kalends of June, at which time we learn from Augustine that an uprising had been stirred up against him, in the year of Christ 399; and he had returned to Africa in the following year before the sixth day of the Kalends of April.

Augustine therefore wrote Letter 250 in reply to Paulinus in the year 399, the same year in which Paulinus had sent him Letter 44 and announced the death of the father of our Melania. These observations were made with great learning by the eminent Cardinal Norisius in a certain short work.

Accordingly, the aforementioned letter of Paulinus must be assigned to the year 399, not to 409, as the recent commentator on Paulinus, Brunius, supposed. For this reason, in that same year 399 Melania and Pinianus undertook their vow of continence. [811] After distributing their enormous wealth among the poor, they both devoted themselves to holy pilgrimages.

First they went to Nola to Paulinus, then to Sicily, afterward to Africa, and finally to Jerusalem and Constantinople. Their deeds are to be sought in Baronius’s *Annals*.

As for her name, I see that she is sometimes called *Melania* and sometimes *Melanium*. If we trust Rosweydus, in his preface to Palladius’s work, p. 703, and in his notes on Paulinus’s Letter 44, she was also called *Melanius*. But I do not accept the opinion of this most learned writer. For where has he found this name used except with a neuter or feminine ending? Among the Greeks one finds Μελάνιον (*Melanion*), and among the Latins only *Melanium*.

In Letter 44 Paulinus says of Melania the Elder:

> I could praise nothing better or holier concerning the blessed mother of this son and likewise the root of branches of saints than Melanium.

In Letter 12, as the manuscripts prefer:

> This was brought to Nola as a gift for holy Melani.

In *Natalis* XIII he often repeats:

> Melani’s double flower, the offspring of Eunomia.

> For here is the boy, Melani’s husband, in the body of Christ.

> Blessed Piniades, Melani’s equal in covenant.

Augustine likewise inscribes Letter 227:

> To the dearest brothers, *Albinae, Piniano, et Melanio*.

Palladius also gives this title in chapter 117:

> Περὶ τῆς μακαρίας Μελανίου — On the blessed Melanio.

# EIGHTH DISSERTATION. ON AEMILIUS

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787D] Finally Paulinus says: “Let Aemilius come as the tenth.” Aemilius was living at this time—that is, in the year of Christ 406—as a very devout man and, as the Metaphrast calls him in the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*, bishop of Beneventum. Ughellus consequently included him among the bishops of the Beneventan Church.

There was the closest friendship between him and Paulinus, and for that reason no one will deny that he is indicated in these verses. In the year 405, as Baronius writes, Aemilius undertook an embassy to Constantinople on behalf of Saint John Chrysostom, carrying letters from Pope Innocent and others.

The deacon Theodore of the Roman Church says in his *Dialogue* apud Palladius:

> Having received the letters of the Emperor Honorius, Pope Innocent, and the bishops of Italy—Chromatius of Aquileia, Venerius of Milan, and the remaining bishops—together with the synodal memorandum of the whole West, the holy men Aemilius, Cythegius, and Gaudentius, bishops, with the presbyters Valentinianus and Boniface, proceeded to Constantinople under official authority.

The Metaphrast gives a similar account in the aforementioned *Life of Chrysostom*.

Aemilius became no less famous through this embassy than through the poems of our Paulinus. Julian, son of Memorius, bishop of Capua, who later became an exceedingly shameless and fierce defender of Pelagian doctrine and raged against Saint Augustine in pointed books, had already married. Aemilius, together with Memorius, Julian’s father, honored these nuptials by his presence, and Paulinus celebrated them in an elegant epithalamium.

Among other things, our poet says:

[Col. 0789A]

> Who is that man who approaches from afar with tranquil steps,  
> Whom the abundant grace of Christ follows?  
> Whom a blessed company surrounds with heavenly attendants,  
> Presenting the likeness of an angelic host?  
> I recognize the man whom divine fragrances accompany,  
> And whose face shines with a heavenly splendor.  
> This is the man, this is Aemilius,  
> Rich in the abundant gift of the Lord Christ,  
> Rich in the light from above.

The time at which Paulinus recited this epithalamium is entirely uncertain, and it will be easier for me to refute another man’s opinion than to establish my own.

The eminent Cardinal Norisius, in Book I, chapter 18, of his *Pelagian History*, considers Julian to have entered marriage after Aemilius had returned from his embassy to Constantinople and had been restored to his see—an event which perhaps occurred in the year 407. Garnerius, a man of distinction, likewise asserts in Dissertation 2, chapter 6, addressed to Marius Mercator, that the event took place in 408; he is not without followers in this opinion.

I, however, regard it as almost certain that Julian had entered into this marriage with Ia before the year 399. When Paulinus composed the poem in question, Julian was a cleric and was counted among the readers. For the holy poet says:

> Let the cleric love a wife made beautiful by Christ’s assistance,  
> And love the beautiful woman with the light of his heart.  
> Let the reader learn from the heavenly history  
> That she was made the wife of the man by divine gift.

Julian later, either after his wife’s death or after separating from her by mutual agreement, enrolled himself among the deacons.

Saint Augustine, writing to Memorius, Julian’s father, in Letter 131, says:

> For the preceding five works will scarcely seem worthy of reading and reflection to our son and fellow deacon Julian—for he too is now serving alongside us.

The year in which Augustine wrote this can be established from the words of the same letter:

> It was exceedingly ungrateful and hard-hearted that holy brother and fellow bishop Possidius, in whom you will find no small presence of us, should either fail to learn of you, who love us so greatly, or learn of you without our letters.

Augustine had instructed Possidius by letter, when he was sending him from Africa to Italy, to enter into friendship with Memorius, or Memor. Possidius sailed after the Kalends of June in the year 399, as I have sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding Dissertation.

Therefore, before this year Julian had not merely celebrated his marriage with Ia; he had also been released from it and bound himself to the ministry of the diaconate. From this one can see how poorly Garnerius argues in the work cited when he supposes that Aemilius had died before Paulinus composed the epithalamium and that the sacred poet had fictitiously invented his presence at Julian’s wedding.

Although, if the poems are consulted, the foundations of this dream immediately collapse, the learned man’s opinion is still found to be inconsistent with our calculations, since Paulinus teaches us that Aemilius lived even after these nuptials.

The eminent Cardinal Norisius, in his distinguished *Pelagian History*, Book I, chapter 18, follows Julian’s career. With his customary learning, he proves that Julian later became bishop of Eclanum and at the same time establishes that our Aemilius was the father of Ia, who became Julian’s wife.

But let the distinguished cardinal pardon me if I do not readily accept his opinion. I do not see upon what foundations this judgment rests. Nevertheless, perhaps the eminent writer advanced his assertion from the following passage. Paulinus says:

> The mitre joins bishops in divine honor;  
> Piety joins fathers in human affection.

[Col. 0789D]

> Memorius, mindful of his duty, with proper order  
> Hands over the precious pledges to Aemilius.

The cardinal says that Memorius and Aemilius are here called the fathers of Julian and Ia. But the great writer will derive nothing from this, since he admits that he corrected the earlier poems and consequently adapted them to his opinion. The word *fathers* is absent from all the published and manuscript copies of Paulinus; they read *equals*.

Nor do the following poems establish his case. He adds that Paulinus predicts to both bishops, as fathers of the betrothed, a long succession of descendants in these verses:

> A chaste priestly offspring shall be the future line,  
> And the entire house of Aaron shall be the house of Memorius.

After considering the meaning of the words, I think that the prophecy must certainly be referred to Memorius alone. The offspring to come was to be a priestly line that would proceed from Julian, his son. For this reason you hear only the house of Memorius named: following the example of Aaron, our poet wishes priestly, or episcopal, honor to be perpetuated in it. He says nothing about Aemilius’s house, to which a priestly line ought not to have been added.

But what supports my conjecture? The epithalamium itself. There we read:

[Col. 0790B]

> The holy pledges of the priest, joined by a venerable covenant,  
> Are united.

If Ia had also been the daughter of a bishop, why would Paulinus have called her the pledge of a priest, not of priests? Below she is likewise called “the holy daughter-in-law of the priest,” and:

> Having become the daughter of an apostolic family.

This woman is said to become a daughter of an apostolic family, which indicates that she had not previously belonged to it.

Nowhere is Aemilius named as her father; Memorius, however, appears everywhere. To him alone Paulinus also refers the whole sum of his wishes:

> May this house of Memorius be the house of Christs.

The following verses must also be considered, from which one can easily conclude that Aemilius was Memorius’s brother. Listen:

> Rise, Memorius, honor your father, embrace your brother;  
> In Aemilius one name belongs to you both.  
> Memorius is younger and older; wondrous is the great  
> Gift and work of God: the younger is the father.  
> Older in birth, because as a priest he bears  
> In his heart the apostolic dignity of age.  
> He is Memorius’s son and brother …

Aemilius was Memorius’s brother, but younger by birth, and therefore he is called the younger. He had obtained the episcopal insignia before Memorius and was consequently called the elder and the father.

It was indeed customary for bishops to call one another brothers. Someone might therefore interpret Aemilius’s being called a brother as resulting from his being a bishop, and his being honored with the title of father from his being the older bishop.

But who does not see that such an interpretation destroys the force of the antithesis? The same meaning could be applied to countless bishops, since one is often promoted to the episcopate younger and another older.

It remains, then, that Aemilius was Memorius’s own brother. This appears more consonant with Paulinus’s eloquence, and he calls it “the wondrous great gift and work of God.”

But if this is true, how can we now make Aemilius’s offspring married to Julian—that is, cousins of the first degree to one another? Under Christian laws, marriage in the second degree of consanguinity was always forbidden; and if we trust Saint Ambrose in Letter 66, it was not practiced even among the Hebrews. The Council of Epaon, assembled in the year 517 of our era, utterly condemns such marriages in canon 28. The Second Council of Tours repeats the same judgment in chapter 12, as does the First Council of Paris in canon 4, and Gregory the Great in chapter 6 of his *Responses to Augustine’s Questions*.

Therefore Ia’s father was not Aemilius, for he would not have given his daughter in marriage to his brother’s son.

Moreover, since Baronius seems to place our Aemilius’s embassy to Constantinople on behalf of John Chrysostom in the year 405, with his dispatch there in the following year, I do not see how Paulinus can present him as being at Nola in 406. There is no time to reexamine Baronius’s calculations.

If, however, those calculations are correctly established, we must understand that Aemilius was absent from Nola in that year, and that the sacred poet therefore said, “Let Aemilius come.” His absence is also suggested by Paulinus’s silence. For if so great a man had been present, why would Paulinus have dispatched his praises in so few words? This was not Paulinus’s custom.

But enough has been said about Aemilius.

# NINTH DISSERTATION. ON THE HONORS OF SAINT PAULINUS

[Col. 0791]

Franciscus Sacchinus, a man of distinction from the Society of Jesus, once committed the life of Saint Paulinus to writing. It was certainly a work worthy of such a learned man. Yet he allowed the distinguished work to be brought to light with such humility that the author’s name was concealed in silence.

Rosweydus communicated this *Life* to us in his 1622 edition of Paulinus’s works, and recent Parisian printers have again sent it to press. But since the four poems that I was the first to publish had not yet become known, you will find not a few things missing there that must be supplied in our style; you will also find certain passages there that require correction.

I therefore undertake the work so that the memory of so great a bishop may become more illustrious for later ages. I hope that I shall most easily accomplish this through the benefit of *Natalis* XIII.

The family of the Paulini was once counted among the leading families of the City. A succession of illustrious men, an abundance of public offices, and an immense accumulation of wealth commended the glory of this most distinguished house.

Our Paulinus came from it, although he first saw the light in Aquitania. Whether Bordeaux or Hebromagus provided him with his cradle, he was certainly born in that province. Some have doubted this, but they are refuted by the clearest evidence.

Uranius, a presbyter and contemporary of Paulinus, says in his letter to Pacatus concerning Paulinus’s death:

> Saint Paulinus the bishop was born in the Gallic city of Bordeaux.

Ausonius, also his teacher in his early years, suggests the same in Letter 21. But let us hear Paulinus himself, than whom no witness is better. He admits that as a boy he migrated from Gaul to Italy:

> For as a boy I was brought from the western shores of Gaul.

And more clearly below:

[Col. 0791C]

> Therefore, when, twice ten times, I had been raised up  
> And had laid down the burden of authority, with no murder staining my conduct,  
> You calling me back to the shore of my former native land,  
> I was restored to my anxious mother.

The only native land that the poet mentions is Gaul, to which he calls the Iberians and the Pyrenees neighboring. Therefore he adds:

> From there I went to the neighboring Iberians,  
> A pilgrim across the ridges of the Pyrenees.

Therefore, although he was living in Spain, he still gloried that he had always remained Gallic in spirit. I have noted all these points in order to answer the opinion of those who wish Aquitania in Paulinus’s age to have been distinct from Gaul. Sirmond, a distinguished member of the Society of Jesus, defends this view in his note on Sidonius’s poem 17, and it also seems to me to rest on sound foundations. For Aquitania at that time was counted among the five provinces which are found distinguished from Gaul in the Council of Valence in A.D. 374, in the letter of the tyrant Maximus to Siricius in A.D. 385, in Symmachus, [Col. 0791D] Book IV, Letter 30, in the Council of Turin in A.D. 399, and elsewhere. On this subject consult Gothofredus, Book XVI of the Theodosian Code, title 10, *On Pagans and Sacrifices*, law 15. Sulpicius Severus, *History*, Book II, distinguishes the Aquitanians from the Gauls when he says: “But this seemed unbecoming to our people, that is, to the Aquitanians, Gauls, and Britons.” Ausonius writes at Arles:

> Which Gaul enjoys, and Aquitania in her joyful lap.

Yet even among the Aquitanians the name “Gauls” remained in use after the establishment of the five provinces, as one learns from Uranius and from Paulinus himself. Indeed, the same Sulpicius Severus, speaking of Nitiobrix—plainly an Aquitanian—in Book II of his *History*, says: “Saturninus, bishop of the people of Arles, an overbearing man, was oppressing our Gauls.” And below: “It was agreed by everyone that through the favor of Hilary our Gauls had been freed from the pollution of heresy.” The ancient *Notice of the Satrapies*, or provinces, which is read appended to Ptolemy’s books in ancient manuscripts and is cited by Salmasius on page 611 of *On the Suburban Church*, [Col. 0792A] lists in Europe Γαλλὶαν Ἀκουιτανίαν, “Gaul Aquitania.” There is no time to add more. Let us now examine the honors conferred on Paulinus.

First, he was enrolled in the senatorial order. Ausonius, writing to him while he was living in Spain in Letter 25, says:

> Then will Bilbilis, or Calagurris clinging to its rocks, possess you—my glory, my country’s glory, and the pillar of the Senate?

Uranius writes in his *Life*: “Let us say nothing of the nobility of his family, shining remarkably in the senatorial purple through both his paternal and maternal ancestry.” Paulinus himself writes in *Natale* XIII:

> Who had anything like this when I was called a senator?

Paulinus was also advanced to the consulship. Until now, however, we had only Ausonius as a witness to this fact. He says in Letter 20:

> Ausonius to Paulinus: The metre so prompted that you should be first, and that your name should precede mine.  
>   
> Although in the title of the *Fasti* too you are earlier, and at Rome the ivory of your curule chair preceded ours.

Then in Letter 24:

> Paulinus and Ausonius, men whom the sacred purple of Quirinus and the gilded covering of the trabea have clothed, ought not to yield to the intrigues of a foreign goddess.

And likewise in Letter 25, to the same Paulinus, established in Spain:

> Are you setting up here, Paulinus, your trabea and your Latin curule chair?

Yet since the remaining authors do not say a word about Paulinus’s consulship, and the *Fasti* themselves are entirely silent, some deny Paulinus this dignity and attempt to evade Ausonius’s words by various replies. But Paulinus himself speaks on his own behalf when he addresses Saint Felix:

> I take you as my guide: in my youth I held the fasces-bearing honor;  
> under your direction of my hand and preservation of my safety,  
> I remained pure from the guilt of human bloodshed.

816. This fasces-bearing honor is the consulship, whose distinctive insignia consisted in the carrying of the fasces. Paulinus conducted himself so peaceably in it that he declares himself clean from every act of slaughter. There is a celebrated question whether this consulship was ordinary or suffect. Baronius and Sacchinus embrace the former opinion. But the latter, whose advocate is Chifflet in Part II, Chapter 2 of *Paul the Illustrious*, seems to me more substantial. He holds that Paulinus was made suffect consul in the Christian year 378, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, after the consul Valens Augustus had been killed by the Goths. He rightly criticizes Baronius, who conjectures that Paulinus was ordinary consul in the year 375, although both the *Fasti* and Jerome and Prosper affirm that that year lacked consuls.

The most distinguished Antonius Pagius, in the prolegomena to his *Dissertation on Hypatius*, number 26, investigates Saint Paulinus’s consulship and, rejecting the opinion that it was ordinary, says: “That Paulinus was suffect consul, as the same Chifflet writes, must by no means be believed. During these times, when there were ordinary consuls, honorary consuls, not suffect consuls, were in use.” But the most learned writer is refuted by Paulinus himself. For when Paulinus admits that he abstained from human slaughter and that the direction of his right hand was granted him by Saint Felix, he clearly claimed not merely the honor of the consulship but also the power that accompanied the true consulship.

Senator describes the insignia of an honorary consul in Book VI of the *Variæ*, Letter [lacuna]. In that formula these words occur: “But now you receive these things more happily, since we bear the labors of the consuls, while you possess the joys of their dignities.” And below: “Paint your broad shoulders with the varied color of the palmata; ennoble your strong hand with the victorious staff; leave your own house even in gilded shoes; climb the curule chair, striving through many steps in proportion to its grandeur, so that in leisure you may deserve what we, as rulers, undertake through the greatest labors.”

[Col. 0793A] Behold: honorary consuls are granted no power and no right over the lives of men; behold, no carrying of the fasces is granted them, whereas Paulinus elsewhere affirms that he held the fasces-bearing honor. For this reason an honorary consul is called by Procopius, *Gothic War*, Book III, ὕπατος καλούμενος μόνον, “a consul in name only,” and Cassiodorus says that he lies idle. Furthermore, let someone show that the names of such consuls were ever entered in the *Fasti*. Certainly no example will be produced, while from the words of Ausonius quoted above we know that Paulinus was entered in them. Therefore Paulinus’s honorary consulship must be rejected; and if he was not an ordinary consul, we must at least admit him to have been suffect.

I do not wish to pass over two verses which seem to shed considerable light on the date of this consulship. They are:

> Then also the first offerings of my newly grown beard  
>   
> [Col. 0793B] I cut before your throne, as though you yourself were shearing it.

[Col. 0794A] After mentioning his consulship, Paulinus adds these words, by which he shows that he first shaved his beard at Nola, before the tomb of Saint Felix. The sequence of events, arranged according to chronological order in this *Natale*, plainly suggests that this occurred after the completion of his consulship. If this is true, let us see in what year of life Roman youths used to cut their first beards. Macrobius, a contemporary of Paulinus, in Book I, Chapter 6 of *The Dream of Scipio*, discussing the number seven, teaches that the beard was customarily cut after three periods of seven years—that is, after twenty-one years. This opinion was accepted by the more learned. Therefore, if Paulinus was consul in the year 378, he would not have advanced to that office in his twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth year, but three or four years earlier. Nevertheless, since several examples teach us that Romans were accustomed to cut their beards in whatever year they wished, I conclude that this is a fluid and weak argument. Otherwise, I am almost certain that Paulinus went to Nola in the year 379 and consequently, in his twenty-fifth year and somewhat beyond, was advanced to the consulship.

# TENTH DISSERTATION. SAINT PAULINUS, CONSULAR GOVERNOR OF CAMPANIA

[Col. 0793]

After Paulinus confessed that he had first grown his beard at Nola, he continues singing as follows:

> Already then, having sent ahead the pledge of a settled residence through my office,  
> I fixed dwellings to be measured out in the Campanian regions,  
> with you founding the future quarters of your servant.

I understand some dignity to be signified here. But what dignity? I offer my conjecture. Namely, after completing his consulship, I believe that Paulinus became consular governor of Campania. Under the rule of the emperors, several provinces still remained under senatorial administration; they were called either proconsular or consular provinces. The former, as the most distinguished of all, were usually entrusted to men most worthy by reason of an ordinary consulship already held. Consular provinces, however, were assigned both to men who had completed a consulship and to men who had not held one at all.

There is no time to investigate whether Bulenger’s opinion is sufficiently certain when he says in Book IV, Chapter 36 of *On the Roman Empire*: “Persons are called consular because they have held the consulship, not because they govern consular provinces.” Certainly, as I was saying, there were many consular governors who had never held the consulship. Campania had its own consular governor, and he was so distinguished that the other consular governors held office in imitation of him, as the *Notice of the Western Empire* teaches us.

The custom still observed at that time—that the administration of a province should be entrusted to men of illustrious rank after they had held the consulship—therefore suggests that Paulinus was none other than the consular governor of Campania. He accordingly indicates that he fixed dwellings in the Campanian regions and settled specifically in the city of Nola.

Above, we said that Chifflet’s opinion seemed stronger to us, namely that Paulinus held the consulship in the Christian year 378. This now becomes clearer. In the Second *Natale* he himself says to Saint Felix:

> Three long periods of five years  
>   
> have passed since, on those solemn occasions,  
> I dedicated my vows to you in your presence, and my heart in your presence.

The Second *Natale* falls in the year 395. If one counts back three lustra, that is, fifteen years, one arrives at the year 380, in which Paulinus testifies that he was present at Nola. Therefore in that year he was consular governor of Campania and dedicated his heart to Saint Felix.

I am also convinced that Paulinus departed for that province in the preceding year, namely 379. For this reason he says that he was present at the festival of Saint Felix only in the year 380: in 379 he could not have hastened so early to his new dignity as to attend the feast of the holy martyr. It was celebrated on the day after the Ides of January, and therefore, while he was still at Rome, he could not so quickly have freed himself from the duties following his completed consulship and from other domestic affairs that he could have attended the feast of Saint Felix in that same year. Thus he accomplished this in the following year.

If Paulinus went to Campania in the year 379, it plainly follows that his consulship must be assigned to the year 378, since immediately after the consulship the administration of some province was customarily entrusted to consular men.

“But why,” you will ask, “did Paulinus settle at Nola rather than at Capua, which was regarded as the capital of Campania?” I believe that consular governors were free to remain in whatever city they preferred, provided that they stayed within the limits assigned to their province. Thus, in the *Acts of Saint Januarius and His Companions*, those saints are said to have been brought before Timothy, governor of Campania, who lived at Nola, not Capua.

Having considered these dignities of Paulinus, we must subject two laws recorded in the Theodosian Code to examination. They are Laws 4 and 5, Title 5, *On Stage Performers*, and they are headed “To Paulinus, prefect of the City,” under the consulship of Gratian V and Theodosius Augustus and Augustus, that is, in the year 380 of our era.

Baronius argues from these laws, under the year 394, that our Paulinus was granted the urban prefecture. But I do not see what documentary evidence could have enabled him to assert this. If we are to proceed by such conjectures, there is nothing to prevent us from also making Paulinus governor of New Epirus, since a rescript of the elder Valentinian addressed to a certain Paulinus who held this dignity in the year 372 is preserved in the Theodosian Code, Book 22, *On Bishops*. With much stronger reason we could make him prefect of the Augustal province, since in the same Code there are Laws 10, *On the Faith of Witnesses*, and 22, *On Receivers*, dated to the years 385 and 386 and addressed to a Paulinus who held a similar office. Yet the great historian of the *Annals* did not dare to assert this.

Therefore, since Paulinus himself—who otherwise records his honors—nowhere claims that this dignity fell to him, I think we must depart from Baronius’s opinion. Chifflet is less satisfactory, although we owe him much in the history of Paulinus. In Part II, Chapter 2 of *Paul the Illustrious*, he attempts to prove from the laws just cited that our Paulinus was appointed urban praetor in the year 380.

The headings of these laws are worded as follows: “To Paulinus, P. V.” Even the less learned understand these words as “prefect of the City,” not “praetor of the City.” From this opinion Chifflet rushed headlong into another. Having established this imaginary praetorship of Paulinus, he necessarily supposes that Paulinus had been curule aedile, since the aedileship, as Paulus Manutius observes in his book *On Roman Laws*, customarily preceded the urban praetorship by two years.

But the distinguished scholar is strangled by his own calculations. If the aedileship precedes the praetorship by two years, and the praetorship likewise precedes the consulship by two years, as the same Manutius observes in the same work, together with Rosinus and Dempster in *Roman Antiquities*, Book VII, Chapter 9, and other writers who have pursued Roman learning in their works, then if Paulinus became consul in 378, as Chifflet himself believes, how could he also have been curule aedile in that same year and urban praetor in the year 380? This reverses the order of Roman dignities.

But, as we said above, those laws clearly refer to a certain Paulinus who was prefect of the City, not urban praetor; and our Paulinus was neither of these, as his own silence sufficiently clearly indicates. Rather, I believe that the Paulinus referred to in these laws is the man mentioned in Gruter’s *Inscriptions*, page 343, who is called PRAEF. URBI.

# ELEVENTH DISSERTATION. ON THE REMAINING EVENTS IN PAULINUS’S LIFE

[Col. 0795]

We have seen, if I am not mistaken, that Paulinus was consular governor of Campania. Let us now examine what he did after this dignity. These are his words:

> Therefore, when I had been relieved of the sixfold fasces of authority,  
> I laid down the axe, unstained by any slaughter,  
> and, as you recalled me to the shore of the land  
> that had once given me birth,  
> I was restored to my anxious mother . . .

I would interpret the sixfold fasces of authority as six years, or perhaps six months, during which Paulinus may have administered Campania in the office of consular governor. Although Law 4 *On the Julian Law on Bribery* in the Theodosian Code forbade the repetition of the fasces of consular office, and although this office must be believed to have lasted only two years, or at most three, nothing is thereby established against us. For that rescript was issued only in the year 416, under Honorius and Theodosius; indeed, the same law asserts that such offices had customarily been repeated, provided that the emperor granted permission.

It is true that consular governors were also granted the right to the fasces. This is evident from the law recently cited, and Gothofredus demonstrates it from other laws in the *Notice of Dignities*. It might therefore seem that six fasces were granted to them by distinction from the consuls, to whom, as Silius says in Book IV,

> This first office granted the right to have twelve fasces precede.

Let the learned decide what they think more sound; I shall not delay over it.

From Campania, therefore, Paulinus proceeded into Gaul, [Col. 0795C] where his mother was still alive. The poet continues:

> From there, a stranger, I visited the neighboring Iberians  
> beyond the ridges of the Pyrenees.

From Gaul Paulinus migrated to Spain, and he seems to have remained there for a long time. Sacchinus, a most learned writer on the life of Paulinus, lacking knowledge of the Thirteenth *Natale*, writes as follows: “He lived for some time at Rome. From there, for nearly fifteen years, he traveled as a stranger through Italy, Gaul, and Spain, by land and sea, occupied partly with public affairs and partly—unless my conjecture deceives me—with domestic matters.”

Paulinus did not travel for fifteen years, since the office of consular governor restrained him in Campania for several years. Moreover, this wandering is greatly exaggerated, since it was undertaken neither from curiosity nor for public affairs.

William Cave is more plainly mistaken in his *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*. Speaking of Paulinus, he says that the honor of the consulship fell to him in the year 375, and adds: “In the following year, preparing to visit foreign regions, he traveled through almost all the provinces of the West. He spent nearly fifteen years on these journeys.” But Paulinus left Italy much later, nor did he travel through almost all the provinces of the West.

What he did in Spain he himself explains:

> There you allowed me to be joined in marriage according to human law,  
> so that you might purchase the life of two,  
>   
> 820 and through the yoke of the flesh the doubled salvation of souls  
> might compensate for the salvation of one that had been delayed.

Theresia, a woman distinguished in birth and piety, became his wife. One may infer that she was from Complutum because Paulinus, in the *Panegyric on Celsus*, at the end, said that his son too was born and died in that city.

Theresia had already been washed in sacred baptism and professed the Christian name. Paulinus says that he alone had delayed his salvation, and in fact he was baptized many years later by Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux.

The verses that follow testify that our poet had a brother. This brother, killed for some reason unknown to me, left Paulinus many troubles. The treasury was not pursuing only his wealth and extensive inheritance; a deadly sentence also threatened his innocent life. Yet the patronage of Saint Felix was present to the suppliant, and through his aid both Paulinus’s property and his life escaped unforeseen danger.

It is pleasant to hear the holy poet himself:

> When I was suffering because of the blood of my murdered brother,  
> and the fraternal cause was bringing danger upon me,  
> and the governor had already come for my property,  
> you, Father, rescued my neck from the sword and my inheritance from the treasury,  
> and reserved both me and my possessions for Christ the Lord.

Who this brother of Paulinus was has not yet become known to me. Nevertheless, I readily believe that he was the same man whom Paulinus mentions in Letter 19 to Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux. There is no mention there of any killing, because Delphinus had already been informed more fully of the entire affair. But when Paulinus admits that he was deeply grieved and would therefore write only briefly, it is clear that some great cause of sorrow had befallen him, and this could scarcely have been anything other than the killing of his brother.

He wrote about this same fraternal death in Letter 20 to Amandus, where he mentions the recent grief caused by the loss of his brother. If these things are true, the anachronism of the distinguished Joannes Baptista le Brun must be corrected; to him we owe the latest edition of the works of Saint Paulinus, and he assigns both letters to the year 403. These two letters were written around the year 393, since it is clear from this *Natale* that the killing of Paulinus’s brother occurred while Paulinus was still living in Spain.

In the letter to Amandus the pious man says: “Pray also for us, that we may not die in our sins. May the Lord make known the end of our life, so that we may know what is lacking to us and hasten to complete what remains.” Here he implies that his holy vow of poverty had not yet been fulfilled, and that he had not yet departed from Spain.

In any case, this misfortune so struck Paulinus’s spirit that he firmly resolved to renounce the world, chiefly impelled to this by his devout wife. Having therefore matured his plan and sold everything for the support of the poor, he struck a great covenant with heaven and finally withdrew to the city of Nola. He sings all this himself:

> For what help Christ then brought to my affairs and to my life,  
> and how the powerful care of Felix was present,  
> a great outcome after the event has shown:  
> my lot and the purpose of my life were changed  
> when, by a sworn pledge, I renounced the world, my homeland, and my home.

The Sammarthani, in *Gallia Christiana*, in the notice of the archbishopric of Bordeaux concerning the life of Saint Delphinus, make Paulinus still live in Spain in the year 396. Yet it is as certain as anything can be that he had bid farewell to those regions in the year 394.

# TWELFTH DISSERTATION. ON THE DATE OF PAULINUS’S ASSUMPTION OF THE EPISCOPATE

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797A] 821 Our Paulinus had scarcely settled at Nola when, released for every kind of piety, he entirely renounced the world. Already a presbyter, he lived in the monastery he had built from its foundations, becoming an outstanding example of holiness to others. His virtues recommended him so greatly that, at length, by the unanimous desire of the people, he was sought as bishop of Nola.

But in what year of our era did this occur? I shall investigate very briefly. He certainly held this office by the year 409, or at the latest 410, since Saint Augustine calls him bishop of Nola in Book I, Chapter 10 of *The City of God*, while recounting the tortures inflicted on him by the barbarians who devastated Campania—an event that occurred in the year 410.

From this, as I believe, the new editor of Paulinus, Joannes Baptista le Brun, whom I have learned of from another source, places the beginning of Paulinus’s episcopate in the year 409. P. Sacchinus, in his *Life*, at the beginning of Part III, thinks that Paulinus ascended the episcopal see as soon as the bishop of Nola died. Chifflet, however, in Chapter 12 of Part II of *Paul the Illustrious*, believes that this dignity was conferred on him approximately two years after his withdrawal to Nola, namely around the year 397.

I cannot accept the opinion of this last writer, since no compelling evidence is offered in its support. The argument he draws from the letter to Pammachius is weakened by the authority of the better manuscripts. His second argument is this. Paulinus says in the Fourth *Natale*, which was recited in the year 397:

> Your birthday, O Felix, dearest to Christ,  
> is dearer to me than my own birthday. On it,  
> however numerous the joys among the countless crowds may be,  
> there is something special belonging to you, because Christ has granted us  
> to be yours, having bestowed us, though worthless, upon his friend.

Chifflet affirms that these words must be understood of Paulinus’s ordination as bishop, because in ancient times *natales* were also called the ordinations of bishops: “For if anyone interprets it as referring to Paulinus’s first emergence into the light, at which there would be public rejoicing among countless crowds, he would surely inflict no slight injury on Paulinus’s monasticism and modesty.”

But the distinguished man has not calculated correctly. The phrase “on which” refers to the birthday of Saint Felix, not to Paulinus. Moreover, Paulinus’s own birthday means nothing other than the day on which he first came into the light, which the ancients customarily celebrated every year with solemn ceremony. This will be absolutely clear from the Thirteenth *Natale*, where Paulinus repeats these same words:

> I have always honored this day in such a way  
> that I would rather regard it as my birthday  
> than the day on which I had been born in vain.

The remaining evidence makes the matter still clearer. Chifflet’s entire structure, and his lengthy reflections on this passage, therefore collapse.

In Letter 16 to Delphinus, Paulinus says of Anastasius, pope of the City: “He also deigned to invite me to his birthday, an honor which he usually extends only to his fellow priests.” This letter was written in the year 399. Therefore, at that time, Paulinus was still excluded from the number of bishops, since he distinguishes himself from the number of fellow priests—which at that time meant the same as saying “fellow bishops.”

[Col. 0797D] The replies Chifflet offers to clarify this argument can easily be rejected.

A letter of Paulinus to Severus was also sent in the year 402, Letter 12. In this letter Paulinus inserted several epigrams inscribed on the basilica he had recently built at Nola. One of them reads:

> The twofold people worship Christ in the hall of Felix,  
> which Paul, the priest, governs with apostolic speech.

And another:

> Paul, the bishop, dedicates this for eternal use.

Therefore in the year 402 Paul was sitting as bishop at Nola, not Paulinus. Chifflet vainly attempts to evade these most explicit words.

I shall also supply other arguments. In writing to Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, Paulinus always calls him, and especially in the year 403, “venerable father.” He would not have done this if he himself had been a bishop, since it was customary in those times for bishops to call one another brothers. Consult, I beg you, Letter 16 to Delphinus, where he says: “The bishop of Milan, your son, Venerius, had also written hitherto; now he is your brother,” and so forth.

You see that Venerius, as soon as he entered the episcopate, began to be called Delphinus’s brother. Since Paulinus also distinguishes himself from Delphinus, he clearly had not yet been girded with the episcopal insignia.

Let us produce still clearer evidence. In the year 404 Paulinus recited the Eleventh *Natale*. In it he says much about a thief who had recently plundered sacred objects. The wicked robber, captured not without a miracle, is brought to Saint Felix:

> after the bishop had already dismissed the pious congregations at the end of the sacred rites.

These are the words of our poet, who thereby distinguishes himself from the bishop of Nola at that time.

The Thirteenth *Natale* also reveals the matter plainly. When the people of Nola conceived the idea of opening the tomb in which the bones of Saint Felix rested, Paulinus says:

> The bishop sends all the presbyters to them.  
> Before their eyes the craftsman’s hand applies itself  
> to carrying out the commands of the priest.

Paulinus composed this *Natale* in the year 406. I am almost certain that the event described there had recently occurred, for the holy poet would not have kept such a great undertaking silent for long. Therefore, since another bishop is explicitly said to be sitting at Nola, Paulinus had not yet ascended the episcopal chair even in the year 406.

Furthermore, if Paulinus had received this eminent dignity, why would he have passed over it in the Thirteenth *Natale*? There he spares no words in recounting the honors conferred on him and the deeds of his life, yet would he have left this greatest office unmentioned? I cannot believe it.

Whether he became bishop only in the year 409, I admittedly cannot determine with certainty. Nevertheless, we must now accept the opinion of the most learned le Brun, who, I am persuaded, made this assertion not without strong arguments, or at least conjectures.

As for the claim of Ambrosius Leo in Book II, Chapter 12 of *On Nola*—namely, that Paulinus had previously been bishop of the Church of Fundi—this should be regarded as the dream of an otherwise learned author.

The brevity I have adopted does not allow me to pursue the remaining events of Paulinus’s life and his admirable holiness. Yet if anyone undertook that task, he would reap an abundant harvest from the Thirteenth *Natale*. I now proceed to describe his piety as expressed in the buildings he completed at Nola.

# THIRTEENTH DISSERTATION. ON THE BUILDINGS FOUNDED AT NOLA BY PAULINUS

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797D] 823 At least three visits of Paulinus to Nola must be counted. The first occurred when he was still of childish age and had scarcely arrived in Italy from Gaul, as he indicates in these verses to Saint Felix:

> For, a boy brought from the western shores of the Gauls,  
> as soon as I touched your threshold with trembling step—

This is why, addressing the holy confessor himself, he sings again:

> Christ gave me to you  
> as your servant from my earliest years.

His second journey to Nola took place when, after holding the consulship, he became consular governor and undertook the administration of Campania. For he says:

[Col. 0799A]

> Already then, having sent ahead the pledge of a settled residence through my office,  
> I fixed dwellings to be measured out in the Campanian regions,  
> with you founding the future dwelling of your servant.

Paulinus spent a long time at Nola, as the dignity he had assumed required. As the miracles performed daily through Saint Felix stood before his eyes, he began to consider converting from paganism to the Christian faith. Therefore, having been enrolled among the catechumens, he judged, as I believe, that he should immediately undertake certain works of piety.

About five hundred paces from the city of Nola lay the resting place of Saint Felix’s bones, where an illustrious basilica is still visited. Paulinus therefore paved the road leading there, in order to provide for the convenience of the crowds who came in abundance. Thus he addresses Saint Felix himself:

> When, inspiring me with silent care in my mind,  
> you commanded me to pave and lay down a road leading to your dwelling.

Nor was the pious man content with this. At the same shrine of blessed Felix he wished to construct a magnificent house. This building extended over a considerable distance, and a place was first assigned for the use of the poor. From this one may also learn how great Paulinus’s piety was, although he had not yet been led into Christ’s flock through the waters of baptism.

Let us hear him speaking again:

> And beside your roofs, over a long stretch,  
> a covering rose, beneath which the poor first  
> found their dwelling.

At last Paulinus’s third arrival at the city of Nola occurred when, having renounced the world and poured out his wealth upon the poor, he chose the retreat at Nola in order to dedicate himself to Christ alone and establish and pursue a holier life. This took place in the year 394.

At that time Paulinus turned himself to every work of piety and regarded nothing as more important than promoting whatever would increase the honor of Saint Felix. His first task, as I believe, was to enlarge the house built during his second visit. He therefore constructed other roofs above the earlier walls and improved the old buildings so that they could suitably serve as his dwelling.

After assigning the poor to cells beneath the portico, he established lodging for himself in the upper building. Hence he sings:

> After this, with its covering doubled, the constructed house grew,  
> which now remains a lodging for our cells;  
> the portico, placed beneath, serves the sick poor,  
>   
> 824 while it supports us, who inhabit the roofs built above.

Below he further praises the beauty of this building:

> Behold, through so many halls of the blessed martyr,  
> spacious in their extent and lofty in their roofs,  
> adorned with deeply recessed ceilings,  
> watered by streams and crowned with porticoes.

Yet Paulinus had arranged the building in such a way that, despite its very spaciousness, he wished there to be humble cells for himself and his guests—cells that displayed no ambition, but rather condemned the enormous houses of the powerful. Hence, speaking to the people about his illustrious guests, he says:

> Those whom you see, and who now, in these very dwellings of Felix,  
> have set up their lodging with me,  
> have forgotten the lofty roofs of their former homes  
> and live in narrow cells beside their humble neighbor.

After recounting these things, Paulinus adds another work:

> When all the structures of the works that seem to stand  
> had been built, arranged in different forms, high throughout the halls,  
> and surrounded widely by porticoes extending around  
> the vestibules, everything seemed to be covered by the hands of water,  
> as though praying for the sorrowful inhabitants.

He therefore conceived the desire to bring to the basilica of Saint Felix from the town of Abella the longed-for aqueduct, which had been interrupted by the passage of time. A long stretch intervened along the route, namely five thousand paces. But the holy man was not deterred by the difficulty of the undertaking. Despite the opposition of the Nolans, who vainly resisted and rejected the benefit of the sacred shrine, he opened broad channels.

The people of Abella contributed their labor to the work, and he became so ardent that at last he brought an immense quantity of water to the appointed place. These matters are described at great length in the always-praised Thirteenth *Natale*.

The brevity I have adopted does not permit me to pursue Paulinus’s other buildings. I shall merely mention that he founded several basilicas, all of which you can find described by him in Letter 12 to Severus.

The most important among them was the basilica dedicated, as he says, to Dominaedium, the common patron, in the name of the Lord Christ. Ambrosius Leo, Book II, Chapter 11 of *On Nola*, maintains that Paulinus dedicated this basilica to God Almighty. “For,” he says, “God was then called Domnedius, a word which we hear preserved to our own time in the mouths of those who swear by and invoke God.”

But he does not touch upon the true meaning of the word. By Domnedius Paulinus understands Saint Felix. The word signifies simply “lord” or “patron,” as I shall likewise prove in a sermon of Saint Maximus of Turin, which I shall publish, together with several other sermons by the same bishop, as unpublished material in the remaining books of the *Anecdota*. There Domnedius is used for “Lord.”

Paulinus also shows that he meant Saint Felix in Letter 9 to Severus, where he calls the solemn hymn composed in honor of the same holy confessor a song to Domnedius; and in Letter 28 to Victricius he mentions Domnedius, his most beloved holy confessor Felix. The expression occurs elsewhere as well.

Nor does the same Leo speak more accurately in Book II, Chapter 12, when he asserts that the basilica of Saint Felix had anciently stood within the circuit of the city of Nola. In fact, it was at a considerable distance from the city, approximately one thousand paces.

The same site is now visited as a distinguished sanctuary of holiness in the place called the cemetery, commonly *Cimitino*. For its description one may consult Capaccio, *History of Naples*, Book II, at the end; the distinguished Sarnelli, in *Clerical Mirror*, in the life of Saint Felix; Pacichelli, in his Italian letters; and several others.

# FOURTEENTH DISSERTATION. ON SAINT FELIX OF NOLA

[Col. 0799]

[Col. 0799D] 825 It has pleased me to make a few observations here also about Saint Felix, whose fame for miracles was once so celebrated that peoples flocked to him from every direction, and scarcely any region of the world was thought not to venerate that saint. His deeds were committed to writing by Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 104; Bede; Marcellus, the most ancient presbyter; Ado; Notker; and others. Yet our Paulinus preceded them all as a master, for in his *Natalia* he gathered together the life of Felix and the miracles performed through him. The most learned Fathers of the Society of Jesus, who prepare the *Acta Sanctorum* with incredible diligence and erudition, brought all these materials together. Nevertheless, because the *Natalia*, now published for the first time, were unknown to them, they omitted other miracles that Paulinus had sung and that everyone may now recall. [Col. 0800D] In the thirteenth *Natale* the holy poet describes a remarkable event: the tomb of the blessed martyr had almost been opened when dust suddenly burst forth from the upper parts of the venerable sarcophagus. I have no exact knowledge of when this occurred. Yet I should think that it happened a few months before the year 406, since Paulinus would not have passed over so great a gift in the preceding *Natalia* had the event taken place much earlier.

Having seen this, I proceed to examine when Saint Felix ceased to live. The distinguished scholar Bollandus, in the life of that saint for 14 January, § 6, writes as follows:

> The age of Saint Felix is not stated by Paulinus. Christophorus Phreislebius absurdly writes that he lived around the time of Theodosius. Henricus Fabricius thinks that he died about the year of Christ 300; but what peace then existed for the Church? Heraeus places him around 310; Michael Monachus not long after the year 312, when peace was granted to the Church. This is also the opinion of others, and it is a plausible one.

But I am compelled to depart from the opinion of so many authors. Paulinus says in the thirteenth *Natale*:

> You wished to reveal it through so great a sign,  
> so that, O gracious one, you might wish that the long-hidden and fixed resting-place  
> of your body, after so many past centuries, should suddenly be preserved in our age  
> when a cloud of dust arose.

And below:

> He further allowed that his courts, never built throughout so many past centuries,  
> might be enlarged or renewed—constructed by our work with porticoes and dwellings.

Saint Felix therefore did not die around the year of Christ 312. For how can the “so many past centuries” mentioned here be accommodated to the age of Constantine, from which Paulinus was separated by not even one century? In the eleventh *Natale* he likewise said:

> And although, hidden in tombs from ancient time,  
> he lies concealed beneath the earth’s covering,  
> as he was when mortal,

[Col. 0801B] But let us bring forward another passage from the sixth *Natale*, which Bollandus, along with others, might also have noticed. Our poet describes the Nolan countryside in which Saint Felix had been buried:

> Where at first a poor tomb, which in a savage age  
> (when religion was a crime), beneath the threat of profanation  
> the Lord’s trembling people had built amid swords and fires,  
> as ancient tradition handed down to later generations, [Col. 0802A] 826  
> had enclosed a vast light beneath a small roof . . .

If Felix died not long after the year 312, when peace was granted to the Church, as Bollandus believes, why is that poor tomb said to have been built in a savage age, when religion was a crime and the Lord’s people lay trembling amid swords and fires threatened by tyrants? Why is the memory of this tomb said to have been handed down from ancient times to later descendants? Certainly we are altogether forbidden to understand these statements as referring to the time of Constantine.

Pauline likewise says in the sixth *Natale*:

> This same light, guardian through the centuries of the martyr’s sacred ashes,  
> proves the life of the martyr who has fulfilled his course.

Here we learn that Felix’s tomb stood “through the centuries,” not merely through one century. Let us therefore conclude that Felix of Nola, harassed during the earlier sufferings of the Church, gave his soul back to heaven when peace followed. The matter seems to have occurred in the second century of Christ rather than the third, since so many centuries appear to have elapsed between him and Paulinus. Hence several anachronisms in Ughelli’s *Italia sacra* must be corrected. For he asserts that Saint Maximus, bishop of Nola and Felix’s companion in martyrdom, died when Diocletian’s persecution was abating; he also says that Saint Quintus—we know that Saint Felix likewise lived under him—flourished in the year of Christ 320, and that another Saint Felix, the first bishop of Nola, died crowned with martyrdom in the year 259. The ages of these saints must instead be assigned to earlier times.

# FIFTEENTH DISSERTATION. ON SAINT PAULINUS’S *NATALE* XI, VERSE 324: THE YEAR IN WHICH THE BODIES OF SAINTS PROTASIUS AND GERVASIUS WERE DISCOVERED THROUGH SAINT AMBROSE

[Col. 0801]

To the most learned man Nicolaus Rubinus, ordinary canon and theologian of the metropolitan church of Milan.

I have no doubt, most wise Rubinus, that you will receive my Paulinus with willing spirit and open heart—not only because, as though restored after a long exile and victorious over hostile time, he will now be able to circulate in the hands of the learned, but also because he has emerged from the Ambrosian library, to which you have bound yourself by everlasting affection. Yet I think that you will chiefly congratulate me on my good fortune because in the works of that same saint you will discover some mention of Saints Protasius and Gervasius. For although your exceptionally gifted intellect embraces the whole sea of ecclesiastical learning, you have devoted yourself so diligently to investigating and understanding Milanese affairs that you seem to have given yourself entirely to these matters, while treating the rest only cursorily.

Therefore, since I have undertaken to investigate the year in which the bodies of these saints were divinely discovered, my opinion on the matter could surely have been offered to no one more appropriately than to you. Our Puricellius, a man deserving eternal praise, judged in *Dissertatio Nazarena*, chapter 39, that the year of Christ in which this occurred was 387. Having treated the matter with diligent care and study, he transferred at length into his volume every argument that he observed to support his position. Yet the arguments opposed to his view are so numerous that I am compelled altogether to dissent from it and to affirm that Protasius and Gervasius were discovered by the great bishop Ambrose not in 387 but in 386.

The celebrated history is thus related by Paulinus, the friend and contemporary of that same Ambrose:

> As we know it once happened under the holy bishop Ambrose,  
> who, supported by such a gift,  
> after those previously unknown had been revealed to him by Christ as their guide,  
> transferred them into a changed sanctuary,  
> and by the ready light confounded the raging queen.

The first argument of Puricellius’s opinion, then, was Saint Augustine’s baptism; once its date was known, the date of the martyrs’ discovery would also become clear. He placed the holy Doctor’s washing in the saving water in the year of Christ 388. [Col. 0802B] But it will first of all be shown that this is contrary to the true calculations of history. The very learned man enlisted as defenders of his opinion the weighty authorities of Baronius, Pennottus, and several others; yet it will be demonstrated that their support added little strength to his case.

When Augustine recalls his baptism in book IX, chapter 7 of the *Confessions*, he writes:

> It was, of course, about a year, or not much more, after the time when Justina, the mother of the boy Valentinian, was persecuting your servant Ambrose on account of her heresy, etc. At that time it was arranged that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, so that the people might not waste away from the weariness of grief. At that time, through a vision, you revealed to your aforementioned bishop the place where the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius were lying concealed, etc.

Thus a year, or not much more, had elapsed between the discovery of the saints and Augustine’s baptism. Therefore, if we can establish the year in which Augustine was baptized, we shall necessarily arrive at the knowledge of the other year.

Ludovicus ab Angelis, in book III, chapter 4 of *The Life of Saint Augustine*, reasoning from the fact that the great annalist places Justina’s fury against the Catholics and the discovery of the saints in the year 387, considers Saint Augustine’s baptism to have occurred in that same year. But his calculations are faulty, since Augustine plainly testifies that a year and more intervened between the translation of the martyrs and his baptism, as I have said.
