Saint Augustine was born, as everyone now agrees against Baronius and his followers, in the year of our Lord 354, on the Ides of November. Yet in book IX, chapter 11 of the *Confessions*, he says that his mother Monica “flew to the heavenly realms in the thirty-third year of my age.” Her death occurred in the same year in which Augustine received baptism. For afterward he had taken leave of Milan in order to cross over to Africa, and had gone directly to the mouth of the Tiber, intending to entrust himself to the sea. Elsewhere also he repeats that he was cleansed in the sacred waters in the thirty-third year of his age; the Roman Church itself likewise transmits this in the lessons of its Breviary.

Augustine’s thirty-third year began to run on the Ides of November in the year 386. His baptism therefore must be placed between that day and the Ides of November of the following year, 387. Since Possidius teaches us in the life of that saint that Augustine received the water of salvation as the holy days of Easter approached, it is plainly inferred that he went to the sacred font on Holy Saturday of the year 387.

Let us also bring forward another argument. Augustine remained in Italy for at least one year after his baptism. For, apart from his stay at the Tiber and in other places, he remained for a long time at Rome, where, as he admits in book I, chapters 7–9 of the *Retractations*, he wrote *On the Customs of the Manichaeans*, *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, the *Dialogue on the Soul*, and three books *On Free Will*. He then returned to Africa.

Let us hear from him when he himself says that he arrived there. In book III, chapter 25 of *Against the Letters of Petilianus the Donatist*, he writes:

> When I came to Milan before the consulship of Bauton—for this consul held office in the year of Christ 385—and recited a panegyric to that consul on the Kalends of January, before such a great assembly and in the presence of so many people, in keeping with my profession at that time as a rhetorician, and after that journey returned to Africa only after the death of the tyrant Maximus . . .

Maximus died on 28 August in the year of Christ 388, as Idacius in his *Chronicle* and Socrates in book V, chapter 24 attest; Gothofredus also bears witness to it in his *Chronology of the Theodosian Code*, on laws 6 and 7 of the title *On Invalidating Acts Performed under a Tyrant*. Augustine therefore returned to Africa in the year 388 and, for that reason, had been baptized in the preceding year, 387.

The distinguished man P. Eustachius a S. Ubaldo, to whose benevolence and learning I confess that I owe much, very soundly attacks Macedus and Desnos in *Quodlibetal Regulations*, doubt 7, no. 53, because they make Augustine’s stay in Italy after receiving baptism extremely brief. Yet I cannot approve his own opinion, when he supposes that the holy Doctor received the grace of baptism in 388, that his mother Monica died in 389, and that Augustine then set out for Africa.

For why would Augustine, in designating the year of his voyage, have referred to the death of Maximus if it had already occurred in the preceding year? Why would he have said “after the death of Maximus,” which means “immediately after the death of Maximus”? As for the death of Saint Monica, it is as certain that it occurred in 387 as anything can be. Augustine’s thirty-third year ended in that same year on the Ides of November, and his thirty-fourth began. Therefore, since, as we have seen, Augustine himself asserts that he was deprived of his mother in the thirty-third year of his age, Saint Monica’s death must be assigned to the year 387 itself.

Moreover, Augustine did not first go to Rome, as Baronius, Torellus, Ludovicus ab Angelis, and many other learned men have held, but went directly from Milan to Ostia on the Tiber. For in book IX, chapter 10 of the *Confessions*, he says:

> At Ostia on the Tiber, where, withdrawn from the crowds after the labor of a long journey, we were preparing ourselves for the voyage, etc.

Do you see that Augustine went there after a long journey? He had come from Milan, not from Rome; for those traveling from Rome to the mouth of the Tiber would not have needed the labor of a long journey. There, therefore, five days after his arrival, she was confined by fever, and on the ninth day of her illness Saint Monica flew to heaven in the year 387.

The reason why the learned Father Eustachius and other writers extended her death into later years was the day on which she is solemnly commemorated, namely 4 May. Since each of them persuaded himself that Monica had died on that day, and since that day perhaps passed in the city of Milan in the year 387, they postponed her death to other years. Yet the eminent Cardinal Norisius had observed in a certain short treatise that Saint Monica’s feast day must be referred to some translation of her relics or to another cause; and after him the distinguished Fathers of the Society of Jesus, in the *Acta Sanctorum* for 4 May, pointed this out. They also acknowledge that the cult of Saint Monica was introduced into the Church only about five hundred years ago.

That Augustine approached baptism in 387 can also be inferred from chapter 31 of Possidius’s *Life*. He says of the holy Doctor:

> He lived seventy-six years, and in the clerical or episcopal office for nearly forty years.

Before beginning the sacred duties of the clergy, he had lived in the countryside around Tagaste for approximately three years, having withdrawn from worldly cares, as Possidius says in chapter 3. Augustine therefore spent approximately forty-three years in Africa after returning there from Italy. Since he certainly died in 430, it is clear that the great Doctor left the city of Tagaste in at least the year 388. If both endpoints are included, the interval from that year to 430 yields the approximately forty-three years mentioned above; this cannot be done if his departure for Africa is placed in 389.

If Augustine went to Africa in the year of Christ 388, then he had been washed in the baptismal water in the preceding year, 387. This truth is further supported by the eminent Cardinal Norisius in a certain short treatise; by Ludovicus ab Angelis, book III of *The Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 4; by Herrera in the *Alphabet of Augustine*; by Torellus, volume I of *The Augustan Centuries*, under the year 387; and this opinion is now strengthened by the judgment of nearly all the more learned authorities.

It therefore occurs to me, most learned Rubinus, to wonder with you, quite properly, why the most devout Cistercian Fathers living in the Ambrosian monastery caused the following inscription to be placed on the front of the chapel called Saint Augustine in the year of our Lord 1677:

[Col. 0804B]

> THE DIVINE AUGUSTINE, CALLED TO THE RULE OF FAITH THROUGH SAINT AMBROSE, IS HERE WASHED IN HEAVENLY WATER IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 388.

It is certainly grievous that a public monument, destined to be transmitted to distant descendants, was displayed with such confidence that no account was taken in it of true chronology. More grievous still is the fact that our mutual friend provided the occasion for such an anachronism.

As for the place where Saint Augustine received baptism, please pardon me, as one who has danced outside the choir; and let the distinguished Fathers pardon me as well if I agree with Landulfus, who flourished in the eleventh century and is preserved under the name of Datius in an Ambrosian manuscript, when he writes of Saint Augustine:

> At the Font, which is attributed to Blessed John, with God’s help he was baptized and confirmed by Blessed Ambrose, with all the faithful standing by and witnessing, in the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity.

This church of Saint John at the Font once stood between the Greater Church and Saint Thecla’s, as the highly learned Puricellius demonstrates in *Dissertatio Nazarena*, chapter 39, no. 21, and in *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 300. He also denies that Augustine’s baptism took place in the aforementioned church of Saint Augustine. Petrus Paulus Bosca, a most eloquent man, believes in his *Ambrosian Martyrology* for 5 May that the ancient tradition must be followed.

But what weight, I ask, does such a tradition possess when it is supported by no testimony of the ancients and is expressly cut down by their testimony? Joseph Vicecomes, once a doctor of the Ambrosian college, also taught with great learning in his book *On Baptism*, chapter 8, that in ancient times there was only one baptistery in each city—a custom that still continues in some places—and I have observed that in former times the sacrament of baptism was administered only by bishops. Consequently, there was no need for several baptisteries; one alone was sufficient.

This baptistery at Milan was called the Basilica of Saint John at the Font; in other cities as well, baptistery basilicas were distinguished by that name. Thus at Rome the church of Saint John the Baptist, called the Lateran, contained the baptistery; and at Ravenna Saint John in the Font served the same purpose, as the distinguished man and my devoted patron Joannes Ciampinus noted in chapter 25 of volume I of *Ancient Monuments*.

Saint Ambrose writes in epistle 13 to Marcellina:

> After dismissing the catechumens, I was handing over the Creed to some of the candidates in the basilica of the baptistery.

Surely anyone who established several baptisteries at Milan in Ambrose’s age would seem to be acting contrary to Ambrose himself. For why would it be called simply “the Basilica of the Baptistery” if there had not then been only one at Milan? That building would have needed another name so that it could be recognized among the other baptistery basilicas.

There was therefore one baptistery at Milan, which they called the church of Saint John at the Lesser Fonts; and we rightly suppose that Saint Augustine was there endowed with baptismal grace. Do not reply, on the basis of Ennodius, Landulfus, and others, that there were formerly two baptisteries in this city, or that there was another at the Portiana basilica, which was once metropolitan, as Carolus a Basilica Petri teaches in his *History of Milan* under the life of Saint Castritianus. By the time of Ennodius, several baptisteries had already begun to be used in cities; this was entirely unfamiliar in Ambrose’s age. Nor is there any memory, among either ancient or recent writers, of another baptistery at the Portiana basilica.

Indeed, the most accurate investigator of Milanese affairs, Camillus Sitonus, Doctor of Both Laws, soundly suspects that this basilica was not metropolitan at all. Rather, the Intramural Basilica, which Saint Ambrose calls the Greater Church in epistle 13 to Marcellina, should be considered to have once performed this function.

I omit other matters, lest I be found to have wandered too far from the path or to have become more tedious than is fitting.

Having therefore established Augustine’s baptism in the year 387, it remains for us to assign the discovery of Saints Protasius and Gervasius to the preceding year, 386, whereas Puricellius, along with others, assigned it to 387. As I said above, this must necessarily be admitted on the basis of Saint Augustine’s words.

But I also have Saint Ambrose standing on my side, and from his books I shall elicit that the event occurred in 386. In that same year in which the discourse *On Not Handing Over the Basilica* was recited by the holy Doctor, the aforementioned martyrs were discovered. For in the preceding year the Augusta Justina had begun to exercise the violence of her spirit against the Catholics.

In that discourse the great bishop says:

> If anyone has confidence, let him come here; let him not seek the favor of those who court approval, now that the emperor’s judgment has been bent, as he has made clear by the law he issued, by which he attacks the faith.

Ambrose mentions a law of the emperor recently promulgated, by which the faith was attacked. But what law was this? It was the final law of the Theodosian Code, *On the Catholic Faith*, issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of February at Milan, under the consulship of Honorius, the noble boy, and Evodius—that is, in the year of Christ 386. There the Arians were granted permission to assemble in the churches of the Catholics; there the Council of Ariminum was approved. Ambrose referred to this in the following words:

> Is anyone, then, to follow this law, by which the Council of Ariminum is confirmed, in which Christ was called a creature?

The discourse was therefore recited in that same year, 386, during the days of Easter, not in 387, as Puricellius and Baronius maintained. Ambrose would not have said that the emperor’s judgment had already been bent if the holy bishop had delivered the speech in 387—that is, one year and several months after the law had been issued and while it remained in force.

The same chronological point is established by Saint Ambrose’s second embassy to the tyrant Maximus. In 387 Valentinian and Justina sent him as their envoy to Trier to the tyrant. The holy man was dismissed without accomplishing his mission, returned to Italy, and wrote letter 56 to Valentinian, in which he says:

> Be safer against a man who conceals war beneath the cloak of peace. Therefore the emperor sent another lord as envoy to Maximus to confirm peace. Maximus received him with great honor and dismissed him; then he followed close behind with an army, occupied the Cottian and Julian Alps, and advanced as far as Aquileia. When this was reported to Valentinian, Augustus, fearing for himself, took flight toward Thessalonica.

The emperor appears to have abandoned the West in September, since on the seventh day before the Ides of that month he issued a law at Milan—law 4, *On the Principal Agents in Public Affairs*, in the Theodosian Code.

If in the year 387 the sacred remains of Gervasius and Protasius had been translated on 19 June, how could Justina so quickly have honored Ambrose, a man who had been hostile to her up to that point, with the office of envoy? And how could the embassy of that same Ambrose, followed by that of Domninus, and Maximus’s invasion of Italy have occurred within a period of three months?

Certainly, for anyone who considers the distances involved, the conclusion must be different: namely, that the bodies of the saints were discovered in the preceding year, 386, and that the other events connected with Maximus occurred in the following year.

Paulinus again suggests this in the *Life of Saint Ambrose*. After recounting this discovery, he adds:

> Saint Ambrose, the bishop, having thereby become a man of greater humility, preserved the grace granted to him by the Lord; and each day he grew in faith and love before God and men.

He then says that Ambrose undertook his embassy to Maximus. Since Ambrose grew each day in faith and love before God before he went as envoy to Trier, a considerable period intervened between the discovery of the martyrs and the embassy undertaken; therefore all these events did not occur in the single year 387.

The arguments I have brought forward thus far receive their greatest support from the *Chronicle of Prosper*. In the edition of Labbé, volume I of the *New Bibliotheca*, the events are arranged as follows:

**No. 2.** Justina, the mother of Valentinian, favoring the Arians, heaps various kinds of insults upon Ambrose and the Church of Milan. The relics of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius are first discovered at Milan by Ambrose. The hymns of Ambrose are composed, which had never before been sung in Latin churches with musical melodies.

**No. 3.** Maximus invades. Valentinian flees to Theodosius. Augustine, teaching rhetoric with great distinction at Milan, abandons the schools and turns to the true faith, although he had previously been a Manichaean.

**No. 4.** Theodosius crossed into Italy with an army and killed Maximus.

832 Do you see how the entire sequence of years is preserved here? The second number refers to the year 386, and there the relics of the saints are said to have been discovered; in the third, that is, in the year 387, Augustine’s baptism is recorded; and only in the fourth number is Maximus’s death assigned to the year 388, just as the other chroniclers have stated.

But the time now demands that I commend the greatest defender of this opinion, the eminent Norisius, in his short treatise *On the Journeys of Saint Augustine*. Since I have advanced so far through that great man, the glory due to him must be acknowledged, and it must be admitted that his support gives this opinion exceptional weight. I have also observed that the distinguished Antonio Pagius, in his *Criticism of Baronius* under the year of Christ 387, and Hermantus in his French *Life of Saint Ambrose*, fight on our side. Who, I ask, would now disdain to subscribe to such men—and to men of such stature?

But I do not wish to abuse your patience any longer, most illustrious Rubinus, lest whatever I may have gained by my profession of devotion be lost through excessive loquacity. Would that you too might someday contribute your efforts to the dignity of the city of Milan and, by bringing your studies into the public light, reveal the brilliance of your intellect. Then the republic of letters would look upon you as the most learned illuminator of so great a city and certainly could not thereafter desire a more distinguished one. Farewell.

# SIXTEENTH DISSERTATION. ON SAINT PAULINUS’S VERSE 402, “FOR MANY OTHER THINGS REMAINED,” ETC., *NATALE* XI

[Col. 0805]

## On the Ornamentation of Temples among the Ancient Christians and on the Daytime Use of Candles in Them

To the distinguished and most learned man Antonio Magliabechi, librarian of the Most Serene Grand Duke of Etruria.

If I were to appoint you judge, most illustrious Magliabechi, in some matter of learning, even your opponents could not take offense at my choice, since I would be summoning a most learned man and a pillar of the republic of letters to that tribunal, from which a sound judgment would immediately be expected.

And indeed I should now like to entrust you with such a task, since I have resolved to speak about the sacred ornaments of churches—not merely to illuminate my Paulinus, but also in part to answer the customary slanders of the innovators.

Cardinal Baronius, a man deserving eternal praise, established with great force of learning in his *Annals* under the years of Christ 57 and 58 that churches had formerly been filled with many and very costly ornaments. Not many years ago, Johannes Henricus Ottius, a Calvinist, dared to attack the opinion of so great a man in a book entitled *A Perpetual Historical-Theological Examination of the Annals of Cardinal Baronius*. I shall speak neither from malice nor with the intention of provoking envy against the author: that book promised much with a great opening, but most amusingly produced a ridiculous mouse. Indeed, if someone undertook to offer another examination in response to that examination, he would run out of ink and paper sooner than he would cease correcting its errors.

For the present I have decided to refute the part that concerns the ornaments of sacred buildings, relying especially upon Paulinus, for no one has left these matters expressed more fully or clearly for future centuries.

Ottius praises Alexander Severus, a pagan emperor, because he forbade gold to be brought into temples, citing for this purpose these verses of Persius:

> Tell me, pontiffs, what is gold doing in sacred rites?  
> Surely we commend upright and chaste morals to the gods.

He then adds: “But do, pray, compare these things with the temples and monasteries of modern Papists.” Under the year 58, § 36, after quoting Acts 20:8—“There were not a few lamps in the upper chamber where they were assembled”—he writes: “From this Baronius wishes to foist upon us the use of candles, lamps, or lights, and, like another candle-bearer, to bring it from the midst of Judaism and paganism into the Christian world.” He then proceeds to show that candles formerly lit in churches were employed not in daytime services but at night.

That costly ornaments formerly existed in sacred buildings, and that they were decorated with gold and silver, is attested by Paulinus in the sixth *Natale*:

> Let others bring costly gifts, and surpass me  
> in the expense of their service—those who bring beautiful coverings  
> for the doors, whether shining with pure linen  
> or dyed with colored figures woven into the fabric.  
> Let them polish smooth inscriptions in supple silver  
> and cover the sacred thresholds with plates fixed before them.

In the eleventh *Natale*, among other objects marked by no lesser value, a golden cross is described in these verses:

> For many other things remained, as you know, in that very place—  
> ornaments which it would have taken in order to spare the gold of the cross;  
> for inside lay hidden the sacred vessels  
> appointed for the sacrificial rites.

By the final verse I think nothing other than chalices is meant, from which the faithful drank the Lord’s blood, together with other sacred vessels of this kind. There were also silver lamps:

> It would have been a lesser crime, and a lesser expense,  
> to repair with silver a lamp hanging farther out  
> from the edge of the altar and light in weight.

And below:

> The silver cup is continuously suitable for use.

The cross itself, which Paulinus describes so beautifully, was not merely heavy with gold; it also increased in value by bearing a crown elegantly adorned with jewels. Speaking of the gold objects—that is, the cross and the golden crown—to which the thief extended his right hand, he says:

> Which, at the same time, he had seen skillfully marked  
> with various precious stones.

Again the holy poet asserts that the crown was heavy with jewels:

> A small crown lies beneath, encircled with various gems.

He also describes lamps at considerable length:

> In the middle of the space, fixed to the high ceilings,  
> hollow bronze supports for lamps hung down.

Likewise, in the ninth *Natale*:

> Above the roof  
> hanging lamps are held by unfamiliar spirals,  
> and in the empty space wandering lights sway from slackened cords;  
> a light breeze troubles the wavering flames.

In the third *Natale* he had described the abundance of lamps around the altars:

> The bright altars are crowned with dense lamps.

In the seventh *Natale*, as is his custom, he vividly describes a glass lamp; and in the eleventh he displays before everyone others fashioned from metal. Our poet reports these and other things, although he sometimes refrains from describing what the people themselves could see, lest he burden his hearers with tedium. Therefore, for the sake of brevity, he says:

> Gifts were placed there according to custom—those which you see there,  
> ready for use every day.

The mention of candelabra in the following verses is especially notable:

> Or, fixed around all the columns  
> in measured order like candelabra,  
> they rise, painted, bearing candles on their points,  
> so that fragrant lights may be given back by enclosed papyrus wicks.

We thus see expressed how numerous and how costly the ornaments of sacred buildings were at that time. It is useful to add certain passages drawn from elsewhere, lest I present Paulinus in isolation.

Theodoret, book I, chapter 31 of his *History*, writes:

> Διεκοσμεῖτο δὲ καὶ τὸ θεῖον θυσιαστήριον Βασιλικοῖς τε παραπετάσμασι, καὶ κειμηλίοις λιθοκολλήτοίς χρυσοῖς.

> The divine altar was also adorned with royal curtains and with golden treasures set with precious stones.

Eusebius, in book IV, chapter 59 of the *Life of Constantine*, describing the Church of the Apostles at Constantinople built by that emperor, asserts that the entire interior roof was covered with gold.

Aurelius Prudentius, likewise a contemporary of Paulinus, in the *Peristephanon*, in the hymn to Saint Lawrence, presents the tyrant as saying:

> It has been revealed that this is the custom  
> and practice of your rites,  
> this the discipline of your covenant:  
> bishops gladly cause the sacred blood  
> to smoke in silver cups,  
> and fixed candles  
> to stand in gold at nocturnal rites.

Thus, even while the threats of pagans against the Christian religion were raging, the Church used costly vessels. This was indeed done secretly because of fear, but it was nevertheless done.

Saint Augustine, in book III against Cresconius, chapter 29, quotes the following from the proceedings held under the consulship of Constantine Augustus Maximus and Constantine, the junior noble Caesar—that is, in the year of Christ 320, as Valesius correctly establishes, not 306, as Baronius thought:

> After the matter had been exposed, empty cupboards were found in the library. There Sylvanus produced a silver vessel with an inscription and a silver lamp. But it had also previously been written down that two golden chalices and likewise six silver chalices had been handed over by that same Sylvanus.

Augustine reports this to prove that Sylvanus had been an informer during the time of persecution.

Anastasius Bibliothecarius—or the ancient author of the *Book of the Popes*—mentions the following, among other golden and silver vessels, under Saint Sylvester:

> He gave a silver paten weighing twenty pounds, two silver cups, each of which weighed ten pounds, two silver pitchers, etc. He offered seven bronze candelabra before the altars, each ten feet in height, etc.

Athanasius also mentions candelabra in his letter to the Orthodox.

The celebrated statement of Saint Ambrose appears in book II, chapter 28 of *The Duties*, and Gratian also reports it in canon *Aurum*, 12, question 2. He says there:

> The Church possesses gold, not in order to hoard it but to distribute it, etc. What will you say? “I was afraid that the temple of God would lack ornament.” It will answer: “The sacraments do not seek gold, nor do they please by gold—things which are not bought with gold,” etc.

He continues and states plainly that the sacred buildings possessed costly furnishings, approved by universal consent, and nevertheless designated for the support of the poor.

These, most learned Magliabechi, are the testimonies of venerable antiquity that we can oppose to the innovators who slander the ornaments of our churches. Why, then, do the heretics bring satirical attacks against us and sing a foolish pagan refrain? They ask what gold is doing in temples; but Joannes Tomcus Bosnensis, in his *Oration for Church Ornamentation*, chastises them most elegantly.

As for the second part of my subject, in which Ottius contends that candles and lamps were accustomed to be lit in churches only at night, behold, I bring Paulinus forward as our advocate. He says in the third *Natale*:

> The bright altars are crowned with dense lamps;  
> fragrant lights are burned from waxed papyrus wicks;  
> they shine by night and by day. Thus night and the splendor of day  
> gleam, and day itself, illustrious with heavenly honor,  
> shines more brightly, doubling its light with innumerable lamps.

Nothing clearer could be found. In the eleventh *Natale* he also says:

> In these little cups uncertain lights gleam  
> when the festal day arrives.

And below he mentions a little cup intended for the continuous use of light:

> The silver cup is continuously suitable for use.

It also shone by night and by day; and a thief extinguished it when it was shining with an unwelcome light to him.

I therefore think that a distinction should be made among the lamps of the ancients in the same way as among the lamps and lights of our own age. Some lights served the nighttime, others the daytime; all, however, had been devised for the worship of the temple. The lamp that was just said to shine when the festal day arrived was deprived of this function at night. Hear the following verses:

> Then, however, unused  
> it remained hanging, merely for appearance’s sake, as a light.

Above he had described other lamps intended to illuminate the night. But Ottius assigns these night lamps to the necessities of those performing sacred rites, not to the worship of the church. The Calvinist is mistaken: when this thief approached to commit his theft, that lamp was providing no light for the performance of any sacred rite. Indeed, we clearly recognize that it customarily burned every night, even throughout the whole night; for, speaking of the vessel, he says:

> The robber immediately extinguishes it at once, as it flickers with a light troublesome to him; for he knew that it too often used to die when the thoroughly dry wick prolonged the light far into the night, the olive oil having been consumed.

Thus lamps were customarily used for the pious worship of religion and the sacred building at night no less than during the day. [Col. 0809C] Nothing more explicit than this can surely be found. I shall add also the testimony of Venantius Fortunatus, who flourished one century after Paulinus. In book V, poem 5, he describes the feast of the Ascension and the crowds rushing to the church, and says:

> From every side a waxen light, snatched up in the hand, challenges the stars,  
> So that you might think their hair was being drawn out along with the stars.  
> From one side the color of milk-white garments, from the other the radiance of lamps  
> Is drawn forth, and the day is painted with varied light.  
> The priest himself was shining among the candelabra.

Now I shall deal with Baronius’s arguments. He praises Epiphanius’s letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, where he says:

> When I had come to the village called Arablatha, and, passing by, had seen there a lamp burning, and had asked what place it was, and had learned that it was a church, etc.

This happened during the day, Baronius says; for at night it would not be surprising to have seen many lamps everywhere. It is nevertheless established by the testimony of several ancient Fathers that candles were customarily burned in churches as a laudable practice; proving this would be [Col. 0809D] superfluous. Yet Ottius repeats Jerome’s authority, sufficiently explained in that same place by the father of the Annals, and here places his entire hope of victory. Saint Jerome says in his treatise *Against Vigilantius*:

> We do not light candles in broad daylight, as you falsely accuse us of doing, but so that by this consolation we may moderate the darkness of night and keep watch by the light, lest we sleep with you, blind, in the darkness.

But if some people do this because of the ignorance and simplicity of secular persons—or certainly of religious women, concerning whom we may truly say, “I bear witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge”—for the honor of the martyrs, what do you lose by it?

Here, however, it must be observed that Jerome could not have denied that candles were lit during the day, since we have already established beyond doubt that this was customary both in the West and at Jerusalem. Jerome himself says in the same passage:

> Throughout all the churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, lamps are lit while the sun is already shining—not, of course, to dispel darkness, but to display a sign of joy.

[Col. 0810B]

[Col. 0810A]

Vigilantius himself would have been utterly out of his mind if, having found that this custom existed nowhere, he had nevertheless produced the following words with puffed-up cheeks:

> We see masses of candles being lit while the sun is shining.

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, older than Jerome, in the preface to his *Catecheses* and elsewhere; Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome’s contemporary, in *Oration* 40; and others testify that lamps were customarily lit in the administration of baptism. Thus the daytime use of candles could not be denied.

The reason why they were lit had therefore supplied Vigilantius with an opportunity for slandering Catholics. He believed that religious peoples did this as though they thought the martyrs required some illumination and light in order to be blessed. I do not present my own conjecture, but Vigilantius’s actual slander. These are the words of that same heretic:

> Such people render great honor to the most blessed martyrs, whom they think must be illuminated by the most worthless little candles, although the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, illuminates them with all the splendor of his majesty.

Jerome therefore replies that people led by this motive do not light candles in broad daylight, but as a sign of joy, as he proves below by Gospel examples; nor, under this perverse belief, do they customarily light lamps at night because they suppose the martyrs require them, but so that the darkness of night may be moderated by this consolation, lest they sleep blind with Vigilantius in the darkness. He then continues: if there were some among secular people and religious women who did this for the reason that had occurred to Vigilantius, Jerome excuses them and demonstrates that the act was performed with zeal for God and without guilt. “If they do this,” he says, “what do you lose by it?” The apostles once complained that the ointment was being wasted, but they were corrected by the Lord’s voice; for Christ had no need of ointment, and the martyrs have no need of the light of candles.

Here again Vigilantius’s mind is plainly revealed. He believed that the faithful lit candles for the sole reason that the martyrs needed that light, and Jerome therefore rebukes him by means of the example he gives. If Christ, who had no need of ointment, praised the woman who anointed him, why should we not also commend a Christian who lights candles for martyrs who are in no way in need of light? They do not do this, however, according to knowledge. All of that is true: [Col. 0810C] earthly light contributes nothing to the blessedness of the saints. But what follows from that? The faith of those who light the candles benefits them. “Whoever lights candles,” the outstanding doctor says below, “has his reward according to his faith,” as the Apostle says: “Let each person abound in his own understanding.”

Do you call such people idolaters? Jerome had said the same thing in his letter to Riparius:

> Are candles lit before the tombs of martyrs signs of idolatry?

Ottius continues and praises these words of Lactantius from book VI, chapter 2:

> Is a person to be considered sound in mind who offers candles and the light of candles as a gift to the author and giver of light?

He says that this displeased the papists so much that they counted the proposition among Lactantius’s errors, and that they defend the cause of the pagans against the Christian teacher. These are illustrious calumnies maliciously hurled against us. No one even among the heterodox is thought to exist who does not recognize numerous blemishes in Lactantius. One who has fallen into more serious errors could also have stumbled into this lesser one. Yet Lactantius is not [Col. 0810D] deserving of censure here—as all Catholics, I think, will agree—but rather his censors deserve correction.

He is arguing against the pagans and vigorously attacking their blindness. For, led by that blindness, they offered the light of candles to God as though he were dwelling in darkness and needed light. Here are Lactantius’s clear words:

> They therefore sacrifice rich and fat victims to God as though he were hungry;  
> They pour out wine as though he were thirsty;  
> They light lamps as though he were dwelling in darkness.

He presses the same point elsewhere, as may be seen in the same author. If some of our own people criticize Firmianus here, they show themselves worthy of censure in this matter, just as they have shown themselves worthy of it in many others, as Possevinus’s testimony demonstrates.

I do not deny, however, that this may provide some heretic with an opportunity to attack the Catholic use of candles. But let them consider whether they can fight against us with the same weapons Lactantius used against the pagans. We offer lights to God, the Father of lights, as an act of honor, not to drive darkness away from his eyes. This should be excused rather than censured in Lactantius, who had [Col. 0811A] not yet been imbued with solid principles of faith and entered the arena against the pagans; he was concerned with preparing a defense for the sacred religion while overthrowing its adversaries. “Would that,” Jerome wrote concerning him to our Paulinus in letter 13, “he had been able to confirm what is ours as easily as he destroyed what was alien.”

Ottius therefore perversely asserts that we have taken up the cause of the pagans against a Christian teacher. He is no more sensible in bringing a lawsuit against us because we derive the Catholic use of candles from the idolaters and the Hebrews. Many things were transferred to us from the pagans and the Jews, yet these things do not arouse the disgust of the acatholics themselves; rather, they inspire them with the greatest veneration. Why, then, do they seize upon this practice to accuse us?

I shall confront them with Jerome, who speaks as follows about the intended use of candles:

> I do not deny that all of us who believe in Christ came out of the error of idolatry; for we are not born Christians, but reborn as Christians. And because once we worshiped idols, should we therefore not worship God, lest we seem to venerate him with an honor like that given to idols?  
> That was done for idols, and therefore it must be detested; this is done for martyrs, and therefore it must be accepted.

[Col. 0811B] [Col. 0812A]

Augustine likewise, in book XXI of *Against Faustus*, chapter 10, forestalls the objection of heretics of this sort when speaking about the sacrifices of pagans and Jews:

> There is as much difference between the sacrifices of the pagans and those of the Hebrews as there is between a mistaken imitation and an anticipatory prefiguration. Just as the virginity of nuns is not to be despised or detested merely because there were also Vestal virgins, so the sacrifices of the fathers are not to be condemned merely because there are also sacrifices of the pagans. For just as there is a great difference between those forms of virginity, although the only difference is to whom each is vowed and rendered, so there is a great difference between the sacrifices of the pagans and those of the Hebrews, precisely because the sole difference is to whom they were sacrificed and offered: the one to the proud impiety of demons, the other to the one God, etc.

What, then, will the heretics mutter in response to this, most illustrious Magliabechi? They have heard the testimonies of the ancients affirming the daytime use of candles; they hear our Paulinus, than whom no one contends better against them on this issue. If they believe that so many saints should be cast onto the register of transgressors, let us leave them to their learning, since they dare even greater things.

Farewell.

## SEVENTEENTH DISSERTATION  
### On Saint Paulinus’s Verse “A Small Chamber from Many,” etc., *Natalis* XI

### On the Tombs of the Ancient Christians

[Col. 0811B]

To the most distinguished and learned man, John Ciampini of Rome, master of briefs of grace, major abbreviator of apostolic letters, and referendary in both signaturas.

Among some people an opinion has arisen, most learned Ciampini, namely that in ancient times it was by no means permitted to bury the bodies of Christian believers in sacred buildings, because this is found to have been forbidden by certain imperial edicts. Hence the excellent writer Cabassutius, commenting on canon 6 of the Council of Nantes, says: [Col. 0811C]

> It was only later that the practice was received into the churches of burying the bodies of the faithful within the precincts of the temples.

He concedes that this custom became established in the time of Gregory the Great, since it is clearly inferred from Gregory’s *Dialogues*. In support of this view people cite canon 36 of the First Council of Braga, where the burial of the bodies of the faithful within basilicas is forbidden, and canon 17 of the Council of Tribur, convened in the year 893, which likewise prohibits it. They also cite law 2, *On Sacred Churches*, which reads as follows:

> Let no one suppose that the seat of an apostle or martyr has been granted to human bodies;

and the final law of the Theodosian Code, *On the Violation of Tombs*, expressed in these words:

> Μηδεὶς ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ ταπτέτο νεκρὸν  
> Let no one bury a dead person in a church.

[Col. 0811D] Kepper, a heterodox writer, in book I, chapter 15 of his *Ecclesiastical Politics*, after producing similar authorities, descends to this remarkable conclusion:

> But once, as superstition increased, sacred rites for the dead began to be performed under Gregory the Great, and then the monks and priests built cemeteries near the churches so that they could perform those rites more easily and make greater profit.

This is also the spiteful opinion of many innovators concerning us. But after the most learned Spondanus, I shall strive to prove by solid testimonies that this heretic and his followers are plainly mistaken, and that among the ancients it was customary—and not without commendation—to bury the bodies of the faithful in sacred buildings. I shall also demonstrate fully that the practice of the present age agrees with that of antiquity.

These are Paulinus’s verses:

> A small chamber from many, which, set on every side  
> Against the great roofs along their sides, provide  
> Secure lodging for the buried.

These chambers were certainly in the basilica itself and formed part of it. Paulinus had said that a thief was enclosed when the doors of the basilica were shut, and that when they were opened he fled in the morning:

> In one of these a thief lies hidden; and when in the morning  
> He sees the barriers of the hall standing open, he springs out through the unbarred entrance.

[Col. 0812B] They seem to me to be nothing other than what we call *cappelle* in Italian, “chapels.” I prove this again clearly from Paulinus’s letter 12 to Severus. He says:

> The entire space outside the apse of the basilica extends beneath a lofty, coffered roof, with twin porticoes on either side, through which a double row of columns is aligned beneath each arch. Four chambers within the porticoes, inserted into the long hidden recesses of the basilica, provide places for those praying or meditating on the law of the Lord, and also suitable places for the memorials of the devout and of family members, for the rest of eternal peace.

Here again you see that the tombs of Christians were located in these chambers. [Col. 0812C] These small chambers, or rooms, were inserted into the sides of the basilica and were undoubtedly arranged in the same order in which the chapels of the present age can be seen to be arranged. For the porticoes mentioned there, within which the chambers were located—what else are they than what we now call the lateral naves of the basilica?

Twin naves of this sort, situated on either side outside the principal apse of the church, distinguished by their lofty and magnificent construction and their columns, may be seen in the enormous and marvelous metropolitan church of Milan; and for you, living in the Eternal City, many examples are available all around you.

But, to reach the meaning of the chambers Paulinus mentions more clearly, here is the testimony of Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Pope Sergius:

> He diligently renewed and repaired the roof and all the chambers surrounding the basilica of the blessed Apostle Paul.

From the same author, in his account of Marcellinus, we learn that the dead were buried in these chambers:

> He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla, in a distinguished chamber.

[Col. 0812D] The Greeks too used the word “chamber” in the same sense. An anonymous writer, *On the Holy Places*, chapter 1, cited by the distinguished Du Fresne in his *Glossary of Medieval and Low Latin*, says:

> Καὶ εἰς τὸ μέσον τῆς τρούλλας εἰς τὸ ἔδαφος κουβούκλιον πέτρινον ὡραιότατον·  
> And in the middle of the rotunda, upon the ground, lies a most beautiful stone chamber.

The same anonymous writer, chapter 15, reports:

> Τὸ μνημεῖον τῆς Ῥαχὴλ κουβούκλιον πέτρινον·  
> Rachel’s monument is a stone chamber.

The Greeks also called these chambers *οἰκίσκοι*, “little houses” or “small chambers.” Saint Nilus, in his description of the church built by the prefect Olympiodorus, says:

> Ἐν δὲ τῷ κοινῷ οἴκῳ πολλοῖς καὶ διαφόροις οἰκὶσκοις δίειλημμένῳ ἀρχεῖσθαι ἕκαστον οἰκίσκον πεπεγμένῳ τιμίῳ σταυρῷ etc.  
> In the common building, divided into many different small chambers, each chamber rises, containing within it a venerable cross, etc.

Thus, since memorials of the devout, or tombs, were placed in these chambers, it is clearly evident that the tombs of the faithful were located in basilicas. [Col. 0813A]

There was also another pious custom among Catholics, dating from the very beginnings of the Church: martyrs were buried in sacred buildings, as I observed in my notes on that verse in *Natalis* XI:

> Which cover the sacred ashes,

where I also indicated that it was not permitted to consecrate churches without the bodies of some martyrs or some relics. That is entirely certain and beyond all doubt.

There was yet another practice among the faithful: they took every care to have their own bodies placed beside the bodies of the holy martyrs, because they believed that through the prayers of such powerful intercessors they would receive stronger assistance from God. Paulinus, in the *Panegyric on the Boy Celsus*, says this about his deceased son:

> Whom we committed in the city of Complutum, joined to nearby martyrs by the bond of a tomb,  
> So that he might draw from the neighboring blood of the saints that which cleanses our souls in the fire.

When Saint Augustine was asked by Paulinus himself whether it benefits anyone after death that his body is [Col. 0813B] buried near the memorial of some saint—these are his words in book V of the *Retractions*, chapter 64—he wrote an entire book, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*. There he says:

> This the widow mentioned by you had asked on behalf of her deceased son in those regions; and you had written back to console her, also informing her that the body of the faithful young man Cynegius had been placed where his mother, with maternal and pious affection, desired it to be, namely in the basilica of the most blessed confessor Felix.

Augustine there approves this pious custom and affirms that it was practiced not only by this faithful young man but by all the faithful. At the end of the book the great doctor adds quite explicitly:

> When someone is buried near a martyr’s memorial, this alone seems to me to benefit the deceased: that, by commending him also to the patronage of the martyrs, the affection of supplication on his behalf may be increased.

Thus each person was buried near the tombs of martyrs, and for that reason within the precincts of the churches.

Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, bears witness to this in sermon 55:

> For this reason our ancestors provided that we should join our bodies to the bones of the saints, so that while hell fears them, punishment might not touch us; while Christ illuminates them, the darkness of shadows might flee from us.

Thus, resting with the holy martyrs, we escape the darkness of hell through their own merits, though as companions in holiness.

Maximus flourished in the fifth century of our era. Since he says that our ancestors provided that our [Col. 0813C] bones be joined to the bones of the saints, it immediately becomes clear that in the earlier centuries of the Church it was customary to place the bodies of Christians in churches.

To spare myself many examples, I shall offer a few from this practice, not taken from distant places but arising at Milan. Saint Ambrose, while still alive, had designated for himself a place of rest in the Ambrosian basilica beneath the altar, where he later placed the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. In his address to the people concerning these same martyrs he says:

> I had destined this place for myself; for it is fitting that a priest should rest where he was accustomed to offer sacrifice. But I yield the place on the right to the sacred victims. This place was owed to the martyrs.

Saint Satyrus, the brother of [Col. 0813D] Ambrose, a man counted only among the laity, obtained a similar place of rest. For his devoted brother placed him in the tomb of Saint Victor, and verses were added to the tomb, also reported by Dungalus:

> Ambrose bestowed upon Uranius Satyrus, at the martyr’s left side,  
> The final honor due from a brother.  
> This is the reward of his merit: that the moisture of sacred blood,  
> Penetrating the neighboring remains, may wash them clean.

Another monument of no lesser antiquity and value is found in the Ambrosian basilica: the pious virgin Manlia Daedalia’s sarcophagus, marked with these verses:

> The limbs that lie in the tomb at the martyr’s left—  
> It is worthwhile, reader, for you to know who they are.  
> Noble in birth, wealthy in resources, and mother to the needy,  
> The consecrated virgin Manlia Daedalia.

For the remaining verses, consult Gruter’s volume of *Inscriptions*. Saint Marcellina also found rest beside the tomb of her brother Saint [Col. 0814A] Ambrose; since this is perfectly clear, it requires no proof.

All these persons, as ecclesiastical usage required, either designated for themselves during life a burial place within the precincts of sacred buildings or obtained one after death through the efforts of others. I am therefore astonished that Cabassutius should have reached this conclusion:

> Constantine Augustus was buried not in any other part of the church than the vestibule; and I think the same should likewise be judged concerning bishops.

Yet it is so certain that Saint Ambrose and other faithful people placed their ashes beside the bodies of the holy martyrs that there is no room for hesitation. Since the holy martyrs rested beneath the altars of churches, who does not see that Christian believers too—not to mention bishops—found burial in the innermost parts of sacred buildings?

Everyone can see how recklessly the canon of the Council of Mainz is brought forward to establish the contrary; Gratian also reports it in chapter *Nullus*, question 2, canon 13. It is expressed in these words:

> No dead person is to be buried within a church except bishops, abbots, worthy presbyters, [Col. 0814B] or faithful laypeople.

From this we learn that faithful laypeople too, apart from bishops and priests, were customarily brought into churches after death. So far is this from suggesting the contrary.

The canon therefore concerns only unbelievers, heretics, or even laypeople who were insufficiently devout—for example, those who died without repentance, were devoted to usury, were murderers, or were afflicted with similar vices—and establishes that such persons must be entirely excluded from sacred burial in a church.

If certain canons and imperial laws were promulgated against this pious custom, the only reason was that the mass of tombs and corpses in sacred buildings was increasing excessively. Christians were therefore restrained to some extent, since a sacred place outside the church opened another field for graves.

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, in the *Life of Saint Remigius* published by Surius, volume I, mentions a certain little church in which, and in the courtyards surrounding it, there had been from ancient times a cemetery of the church of Rheims. You see, therefore, that from ancient times—that is, before the time of Saint Remigius, who lived in the fifth century of Christ—tombs of Christians had been established both in the churches themselves [Col. 0814C] and around them.

Gothofredus, commenting on book IX, title 17 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Violation of Tombs*, says:

> It should be observed that although, as the Christian religion grew strong, the burial of the relics of saints within cities came to prevail contrary to the law, and little churches, or martyria, were often built beside such tombs—in which emperors at Constantinople, and soon afterward priests, were buried by a special privilege—private individuals were nevertheless not permitted the same.

This is appropriate to the meaning of the law, and I willingly subscribe to it. But from this we learn that the burial of the faithful was indeed forbidden for a time in urban churches, because both ancient pagan ordinances and the edicts of Christian rulers had stipulated that a tomb should not be granted to the dead within cities. But whoever, in the face of so many testimonies of antiquity, dares deny that burial in churches outside the city—of which nearly all churches in the first age of the Christian religion were of this kind—was not forbidden, shows little sense.

Finally, I have not forgotten what you presented in your excellent [Col. 0814D] work, volume I, chapter 17, *On the Illustration of Cemeteries*. But it would be useless labor to employ your own work against you. I shall therefore introduce only Onuphrius Panvinius, a man of such distinction in the science of antiquities, who proposed a book *On Cemeteries* in his additions to Platina.

He teaches that cemeteries were not only churches and basilicas, but had something more than urban churches: namely, Christian tombs, which could not be made within the city. He confirms this with countless examples, which I leave to those who wish to consult him and Spondanus in his book *On Christian Tombs*.

From this, therefore, most learned Ciampini, unless my judgment deceives me, it becomes clear how unjustly Kepper and others attack the tombs of Christians. It was certainly not in the time of Gregory the Great—that is, in the seventh century of our era—that the faithful began to claim places near churches for their tombs, as those foolishly assert who wish to heap odium upon us. Rather, already in the earliest centuries of the Church it was accepted among many that they should be buried within the basilicas themselves.

If, after everything I have related here, you add your judgment, with the great learning in which you excel, [Col. 0816A] I shall rejoice exceedingly—not so much because I have overthrown the calumny of the heretics as because I have pleased you.

Farewell.

## EIGHTEENTH DISSERTATION  
### On Saint Paulinus’s *Natalis* XII

### On Vows and Votive Offerings of Christians Made in Veneration of the Saints

[Col. 0815A]

To the distinguished man Father William Bonjour of the Order of Hermits of Saint Augustine.

The offerings that the Catholic people dedicate to some saint for the sake of a vow and veneration were once mocked by Erasmus, a man of considerable learning but excessive boldness, who on occasion served religion poorly. In the colloquy entitled *The Shipwreck*, he undertook to criticize this pious custom of the Church, thereby gaining no small favor [Col. 0815B] among the heretics who followed him.

But relying on the testimonies of the ancient Fathers, and above all on one pronouncement of Saint Paulinus, I have decided to blunt such a great appetite for slander, without forgetting either brevity or modesty. My purpose is both to strike down at a single blow the calumny that I see pleasing modern innovators and to confirm more firmly, by the authority of the ancient Fathers, the veneration of the saints.

I thought I should offer this brief inquiry to you, most illustrious Bonjour, so that among the cultivated people of the republic of letters it might become clear with what zeal and with what reverence of mind I pursue your learning. For when that dissertation of yours appeared, the one you composed on the worship of Joseph, the most chaste man, under the name of Serapis, and in which you will understand that Paulinus of Nola also subscribed, I was immediately carried away into the greatest admiration of you.

And indeed, what may not be expected from you when you reach more mature years, if at so flourishing an age you have already shown yourself so deeply imbued with philological learning? Yet this would have brought you little praise had you not made your learning still more illustrious through modesty and [Col. 0815C] kindness. The former now compels me to restrain my praise of you; the latter has given my own writings the courage and confidence to approach you.

But let us now fulfill what we have undertaken.

In ancient times various offerings were customary. Some consisted of bread and wine, which were transferred to the use of the unbloody sacrifice. Concerning these the Second Council of Mâcon, chapter 4, says:

> Therefore we decree that on every Sunday the offering of the altar be presented by all men and women, both bread and wine.

Cyprian, in his book *On Works and Almsgiving*; Augustine, or another author, in sermon 215 *On the Seasons*; Eligius of Noyon in his treatise *On the Rectitude of Catholic Conversion*, volume I; Augustine Bona in book I, chapter 23 of *Liturgical Matters*; and many others have likewise mentioned this custom.

Other offerings consisted of oil or wax for lamps. Apart from the author of sermon 215 *On the Seasons*, canon 4 of the Apostles speaks of these in the following words:

> Μὴ ἐξὸν δὲ ἔστω προσάγεσθαί τι ἕτερον πρὸς τὸ θυσιαστήριον, ἢ ἔλαιον εἰς τὴν λυχνίαν, καὶ θυμίαμα τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ἁγίας προσφορᾶς.  
> Let it not be permitted to offer anything else at the altar except oil for the lamp and incense at the time of the sacred offering. [Col. 0815D]

Other offerings consisted of sacred vessels, vestments, and ornaments. The Greeks call these *ἀναθήματα*, “dedicated offerings” or “votive gifts.” Anastasius the Librarian, Coccius in volume II, book VI, article 15, Raynaudus in section 2, point 3 of *Heteroclite Spiritual Matters*, and others speak of them at considerable length.

Finally, Paulinus teaches us of another kind of offering: those made to the saints from a vow or out of veneration. These consisted of all sorts of things, so that sacred religion might accommodate itself to the devotion of everyone. The rich contributed lavish gifts; the poor offered whatever they possessed, however small, in the service of the blessed.

These gifts too were not without a vow. Whenever someone implored the aid of a saint in escaping dangers, he was also accustomed to bind himself by a vow to the saint who was to provide protection. I leave it to our theologians to demonstrate [Col. 0816A] how correct the use of such vows is—although they are called vows somewhat improperly. I have not set myself so large a harvest. Here we are seeking the fact, not the law; and at once Paulinus comes forward as a brilliant witness to the matter in *Natalis* XII, speaking as follows:

> A certain stranger had come here from the territory  
> Of the city of Abella, to fulfill a vow pleasing to himself  
> At our shrine. Here, taking careful pains, he had prepared a pig  
> And brought it along, delaying it for a long time so that it might grow  
> In both years and fatness. When he arrived,  
> The fat animal was slaughtered according to the custom of those who make vows.

Here our poet clearly indicates the ancient custom [Col. 0816B] of those who made vows to God in honor of the saints. He repeats below:

> And he thinks that he has fulfilled his vow.

Likewise:

> In which, alas, the madman, deceiving the pledged gift of his vow,  
> Violating his faith, turned it into a loss of salvation.

And elsewhere:

> As soon as the obligation of the vow was discharged,  
> That debtor within is released from the deserved binding of a chain . . .

This is the first miracle of Saint Felix, who punished the inhabitant of Abella for defrauding his vow. The second is related by Paulinus with his characteristic eloquence and verbal ornament, where he again makes an excellent mention of votive offerings made in the worship of Saint Felix. Let us hear him sing:

> Certain farmers from our region, living farther away,  
> Cultivating fields across the Apulian countryside beyond Beneventum,  
> Selected for themselves from the bristling herd, among many offspring,  
> [Col. 0816C] One animal. For a long time they cared for it  
> And fattened the pig as a votive offering; then they began  
> To lead it, prepared, to the consecrated sanctuary of Saint Felix.

He adds:

> Their anxious mind wavers in uncertainty;  
> For pious hearts do not wish to turn back from the path of their vow,  
> Yet they are ashamed to go again a long distance  
> To Felix’s revered threshold empty-handed, without the devoted gift.

The pig had become weighed down by the burden of its fatness. For that reason the same farmers selected other, smaller pigs, so that they might fulfill the vow completely. Paulinus therefore says:

> What their devoted faith, bound by the debt of an obligation,  
> Thought it could accomplish by this means, preparing to hasten it:  
> To balance one excellent animal with several modest ones.  
> Thus they came here to the sacred place, their vows fulfilled . . .

Paulinus mentions a third miracle in these verses:

> For some men, who had come here from an equally distant place,  
> Had raised a heifer separated from its kind,  
> [Col. 0816D] Hidden away from the nursing breast of its mother,  
> Nourishing it from the first as a votive offering  
> Pledged to our poor.

He also says in *Natalis* VIII:

> For every day we are witnesses: from every side, in frequent gatherings,  
> Either vows give thanks for restoring the healthy,  
> Or the sick ask for various cures and experience them.

These vows to the saint were conspicuous because offerings were added to them. All of them went toward feeding the poor, so that the martyr might rejoice in a poor person who had been satisfied. The sacred poet teaches us this through these three examples, and he also states clearly that these vows were made to the martyrs. Let us hear him:

> But the custom seems to be that those who make vows  
> Carry their vows far away to be fulfilled  
> To the holy martyrs . . .

Apart from these, other vows were customarily made to the saints that did not involve such offerings. Some vowed that they would visit the basilicas of the blessed; others that they would celebrate their feast days. The same Paulinus will provide examples of these vows. [Col. 0817A]

He was living in Spain when he first composed a *Natalis*, and he had vowed to undertake a journey to the city of Nola in order to visit Saint Felix. Thus he says:

> And in the shrine where you rest,  
> May I be permitted to celebrate this day, to render my pious vows  
> Before you, and to rejoice among the rejoicing crowds.

In *Natalis* II, after he had returned to Nola, he writes the same thing:

> Three lustres have passed in the long course of time  
> Since, in your presence, on these solemn occasions,  
> I dedicated my vows to you and my heart in your presence.

In *Natalis* IV he says:

> My annual vows return.

Likewise in *Natalis* V:

> The day desired each year, which renews  
> The sweet festival and my vows.

[Col. 0817B] [Col. 0817C]

If someone insists that the vows mentioned in these verses should be understood as nothing more than simple prayers, let him answer me this: did Paulinus pour out prayers to Saint Felix only on the saint’s birthday? He certainly will not affirm that. For Paulinus says in *Natalis* IX:

> For what day, I ask, rises empty of vows,  
> Or rare amid great crowds?

The vows renewed on that day were therefore poems that our poet vowed to Saint Felix each year. He himself leaves this explicit in *Natalis* VI:

> By a pious right a law has been imposed on me: each year to celebrate this day,  
> With eloquence serving it; the solemn duty requires from my mouth  
> That I name Felix in verse,  
> And modulate my joy in a votive song.

Here is a poem as a vow; here is a promised and owed gift to Saint Felix.

Observe also how well this same Paulinus distinguishes these vows from the votive offerings described above. He speaks as follows in the cited *Natalis*:

> Weeping again, but with joy, he brings back the vows  
> Now owed to the saint—not with heavy bronze, nor with a voiceless gift,  
> But with a living gift, poured forth from tongue and mind.

To Paulinus, who has completed the matter thus far, it is pleasant to add other witnesses to our purpose, so that the truth may be brought more fully into the light.

Saint Pope Damasus also composed an epigram on Saint Felix of Nola, whose final verses are as follows:

> Under your guidance I was saved and broke the bonds of death;  
> With these verses I, Damasus, suppliant, repay my vows to you.

Prudentius offers something similar in his hymn on Saints Hemeterius and Chelidonius:

> The inhabitants throng the sands stained with sacred blood,  
> Attending with voice, with vows, and with gifts.

Here, unless I am mistaken, we see mention both of pure vows and of offerings. Gregory of Tours, however, in Book II of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 37, says that they “gave thanks to the Lord and, promising vows to the blessed confessor [Martin], joyfully announced [the matter] to the king,” etc. Saint Augustine, in Book II *Against Faustus*, introduces that same heretic objecting to us as follows: “You have turned idols into martyrs, whom you worship with similar vows.”

Especially excellent for this subject is the testimony of Eusebius of Caesarea. After affirming in Book XIII, chapter 7, of his *Preparation for the Gospel* that we honor the saints as soldiers of true piety, and finally as friends, he adds:

> “Hence, too, it is our custom to go to their tombs and to make our vows beside them.”

For some might think that the expression “our vows” (*τὰς εὐχὰς*) means prayers. Permit me, therefore, to explain the force of this word, so that it may become clear that among the Greek Fathers *εὐχή* properly means a vow, while *προσευχή* means a prayer or supplication. Henri Estienne proves this with numerous examples in his *Thesaurus of the Greek Language*, and I shall reinforce it with two especially clear testimonies.

Gregory of Nyssa, in his second homily *On the Lord’s Prayer*, commenting on Matthew 6, “when you pray,” says: “He did not say, *ὅταν εὔχησθε*, that is, ‘when you make vows,’ but *ὅταν προσεύχησθε*, that is, ‘when you pray,’ etc.”

But what is the difference between these terms? *Εὐχή*, that is, a vow, is a promise of some thing which is dedicated in the name of piety and set apart for sacred purposes; *προσευχή*, that is, prayer, is a petition for blessings which is offered to God with supplication, etc. He then adds: “In many passages of Scripture one may see this meaning of *τῆς εὐχῆς*, that is, of ‘vow,’ etc.”

Saint Augustine speaks no less plainly in Letter 59, written to our Paulinus, where he says:

> “For the term which they call *εὐχή* Scripture rarely uses in such a way that it is understood as ‘prayer’; rather, and much more commonly, it calls a vow *εὐχή*, while it always calls prayer *προσευχή*.”

And below:

> “Moreover, if, as I have said, Scripture more commonly calls a vow *εὐχή*, then, apart from the general term for prayer, that prayer is properly to be understood which we make for a vow, that is, *πρὸς εὐχήν*.”

Everything offered to God is vowed, especially the offering of the holy altar, etc.

But let us return to our subject and once again bring forward vows made to the saints. The Council of Nantes, canon 20, speaks as follows:

> “Let it be forbidden to all that no one, when asking elsewhere for his own health, make a vow or carry a candle or any gift, except to the church of the Lord his God.”

I certainly cannot agree with the distinguished Du Fresne, who in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin* thinks that the term “vows” here signifies the festivals of the pagans. For the candles and other gifts offered to the eternal Godhead for the recovery of health, which are mentioned here, sufficiently show that such vows are to be understood as votive tablets. Clearly, in ancient times no less than in our own, it was customary to hang such tablets before God and blessed men.

Hear the outstanding testimony on this subject of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, who, as you know very well, wrote about the middle of the fifth century. These are his words in Homily 8 *On the Martyrs*, addressed to the Greeks:

> “That those who make faithful promises obtain what they ask is openly attested by their offerings, which declare the healing received. Some bring representations of eyes, others of feet, and others of hands; some are made of gold, others of silver.”

Zenobius Acciaiuoli translated the passage as follows:

> “That those who have prayed piously, faithfully, and devoutly obtain precisely what they desire is especially attested by those who discharge the offerings owed for their vows—clear evidence, indeed, of health obtained. For some hang up likenesses of eyes, others of feet, and others of hands, made of silver or gold.”

The aforementioned Theodoret adds much more, which for the sake of brevity I shall now pass over.

One may also find an illustrious memory of such vows in Paulinus, in *Natalis* III, among those verses which we have now restored or added to the edition from our very ancient manuscript. They are these:

> “The gracious day is celebrated by great assemblies; all  
> Dedicate their answered vows at the sacred doors; all rejoice …”

Here votive tablets are plainly being mentioned—tablets which were hung upon the sacred doors of the basilicas. For to dedicate vows is the same as to hang up vows. They are called “fulfilled,” that is, heard and granted, after the manner of Ovid’s verse in Book I of the *Fasti*:

> “And may each goddess make the prayers fulfilled.”

In memory, therefore, of the gifts received from God through the intercession of Saint Felix, and as a token testifying that the vow had been heard, tablets were carried to the sacred doors of the churches. If Erasmus had taken these matters into consideration, he might perhaps have spared his wit and would not have attacked with such biting sarcasms the use—approved by the Catholic Church up to that time—of votive offerings or tablets made to the saints.

In any case, if this custom does not suit recent innovators, they must also bring an action against the most ancient Fathers, from whom, though they are surpassed in holiness and learning, they will just as easily be defeated in matters of piety. Farewell.

# NINETEENTH DISSERTATION. ON VERSE 87 OF SAINT PAULINUS’S *NATALIS* XIII

## On the Birthdays of the Holy Martyrs

[Col. 0819A]

To the distinguished man Antonio Felice Marsili, archdeacon of the cathedral of Bologna.

Long ago, most distinguished Marsili, together with the eminent father of the *Annals*, Baronius, and many others, I had believed that all the birthdays of the saints which are set out in the ecclesiastical calendars designated, if not invariably, at least very frequently, the day of their death. I was led to this opinion all the more readily because I had noticed with particular care that the Church herself sometimes warns us when the solemn celebrations of the saints fall on a day other than that of their death. For then, by slightly altering the hymns or prayers, that teacher of all the Churches showed that it had departed from the ancient custom.

But the celebrated writers Father Papebrochius first, and afterward Father Pagius, warned me in past years that I had remained too long in error. Papebrochius says in his *Chronological Endeavor concerning the History of the Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 25:

> “Thus, even to the present day, with few exceptions, almost all the ancient Roman bishops are honored on a day other than that on which they are said to have died.”

Pagius, following Papebrochius’s footsteps, says in his *Baronian Criticism* under the year of Christ 67, no. 18:

> “The days on which the holy pontiffs are honored, or which the martyrologies and other writers assign to their death or burial, usually have nothing in common with the day of their death or burial.”

Indeed, he goes further in the following section, declaring that the other saints are subject to the same rule. He says:

> “The saints, therefore, are generally honored on days other than those on which they departed for their heavenly homeland.”

And below:

> “Hence, few saints are honored on the days on which they died.”

I had scarcely adopted this new opinion and begun to follow such great men completely when I noticed that it was more strongly confirmed by Paulinus’s testimony; and, after submitting the matter to examination, I understood that this recent view rested on weak foundations. What I have therefore been able to discuss at leisure concerning these matters I now place before your eyes, more likely to bring me the merit of obedience than the praise of learning.

First, however, I shall make some observations on the feast days of the saints, so that it may immediately become clear that their institution favors our position. For all the solemn observances introduced into the Church of God in ancient times referred to the very day on which the holy martyrs had completed the course of their lives and, restored to heaven, had first received the reward of the death they had endured.

A famous passage occurs in Saint Cyprian’s Letter 37 to the priests and deacons, where he earnestly urges them to record the days on which each of the martyrs had departed from the living. Finally, he says:

> “Record also the days on which they depart, so that we may be able to celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs.”

He adds that Tertullus had written and was writing to him, reporting the days on which “our blessed brothers, through the glorious outcome of their death, passed in prison to immortal life,” and that “offerings and sacrifices are celebrated here by us in commemoration of them, which we shall soon celebrate with you, with God’s protection,” etc.

In Letter 34 the same Cyprian says:

> “As you remember, we always offer sacrifices for them whenever we celebrate the sufferings of the martyrs and their anniversaries in solemn commemoration.”

Let us offer an even earlier testimony on this subject, namely, the letter of the Church of Smyrna concerning the martyrdom of Saint Polycarp, which has survived to our own times among the sacred fruits of antiquity. The most devout men say:

> “We placed the bones of the holy martyr in a tomb, more precious than jewels and gold. There, when we gather together as far as we are able in exultation and joy, the Lord will grant us to celebrate the day of his martyrdom as a birthday feast.”

Thus, even in apostolic times, this day devoted to the commemoration of the martyrs was called a “birthday,” and among the ancients that term designated only the day of the saints’ death.

First let us hear Paulinus speaking in *Natalis* XIII:

> “And deservedly this birthday is marked out for the saints,  
> on which, having fulfilled the law, they are stripped  
> of the bonds of bodily mortality  
> and are born to God in the heavenly kingdoms.”

Because the holy martyrs were then born into heaven, the name “birthday” was given to the day of their death.

Saint Peter Chrysologus says in Sermon 129:

> “When you hear of the birthday of the saints, beloved, do not think that this means the day on which they are born in the flesh upon earth, but the day on which they are born from earth into heaven, from toil into rest,” etc.

Eusebius of Gaul, or Caesarius, says in Homily 50 *On Saint Genesius*:

> “We call the sufferings of the blessed martyrs birthdays—the days on which the life of martyrdom and the faith of glory, by delivering them over to death, gave birth to them for eternity.”

Saint Augustine, Sermon 1 *On the Saints*; Pope Nicholas in his *Response to the Questions of the Bulgarians*, chapter 5; Rabanus, Book II *On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 43; Radulphus Flavius, Book VII, chapter 2, on Leviticus; Amalarius, Book IV *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 35; Beleth, *On Divine Offices*, chapter 4; and others hold the same opinion.

From the agreement of these authors it is clear that in ancient times only those days were marked with solemn honor and consecrated to the memory of the saints on which the saints themselves, through the benefit of the death they had endured, had been restored to heavenly rest.

Paulinus provides particularly clear testimony on this point, for in *Natalis* XIII he says:

> “Therefore, for the saints, whether confessors,  
> the faithful peoples honor with solemn rejoicing  
> the sacred days on which, having completed the day  
> of their mortal age through life-giving death,  
> they passed from the world’s stain to God,  
> rejoicing in Christ’s honor.”

Thus, whenever we encounter the word “birthday,” whether in ancient martyrologies or among the Christian Fathers, we ought immediately to understand the feast day on which the death or burial of some saint is recalled annually with solemn vows. From this the martyrologies derive their origin, and from this the ecclesiastical calendars derive their beginnings.

I believe that it must be consistently affirmed that it was only in the later centuries of the Church that another day came to be devoted to the commemoration of a saint instead of the day which annually renewed the memory of his death.

Gregory of Tours, in Book II *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, chapter 29, records that in the time of Saint Germanus—that is, in the fifth century of Christ—the solemn day of Saint Julian the martyr was instituted. The blessed martyr’s day of death was unknown; hence the people, anxious and uncertain, were impeded in their devout observances. At last divine assistance was granted to those who were ignorant, and the sought-for day became known through a revelation from heaven.

The author cited above says:

> “The people, ignorant of the time of this festival, were sorrowfully suspended in uncertainty, not knowing on which day the blessed martyr ought to be honored for the glory of his virtue and suffering; and this ignorance lasted until Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, etc.”

Then he said: “Let us pray, and perhaps the power of the Lord will reveal this to us.” When they had done so, at dawn he declared that the festival was to be celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

If in ancient times it had been permissible to celebrate the commemoration of the saints on whatever day one preferred, the people would not have been so slow to establish Saint Julian’s solemn observance, nor would they have investigated with such diligence the time at which the glory of his passion should be recalled.

Accordingly, observe that all the writers who committed the martyrologies to public records had chiefly this before their eyes: that the days of the saints’ deaths should be expressed as accurately as possible.

Saint Gregory the Great, in Letter 29 of Book VII to Eulogius of Alexandria, says:

> “We have the names of almost all the martyrs, with their sufferings arranged according to individual days, collected in a single book, and on each day we celebrate the solemnities of Mass in their honor.
