The same volume does not indicate how each suffered, but merely records the name, place, and day of the passion.”

On this subject Ado, archbishop of Vienne, writes in the preface to his *Martyrology*:

> “For the days of the martyrs to be recorded with the greatest accuracy, although they are commonly found confused in the calendars, assistance was provided by the martyrology sent from Rome to Aquileia.”

Bede, who was earlier than Ado, says in the catalogue of his works:

> “A martyrology of the birthdays of the holy martyrs, in which I carefully endeavored to record, for those whom I could find, not only on what day but also by what kind of contest, or under which judge, they conquered the world.”

All these statements are directed toward demolishing one of Pagius’s arguments. He says:

> “The saints were generally honored on days other than those on which they departed for their heavenly homeland, either because during the time of persecution it might have been difficult to record with sufficient accuracy the days on which they suffered,” etc.

But how diligent Christians were in recording these days has already become clear from the testimonies of the writers cited. Let Chrysostom also be heard, in Homily 26 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “Indeed, even the monuments of Christ’s servants are illustrious, for they have gained possession of the royal and ruling city of all; and the days of their death are known to all, since festivals are celebrated throughout the whole world.”

Let us therefore hold it as certain that formerly almost no feast days were instituted in the Church of God except those on which the departure of the saints from this life was annually commemorated.

But I hear someone asking why ancient martyrologies sometimes disagree among themselves, and why the acts of the saints likewise often fail to agree with the martyrologies themselves. If the sacred calendars represented only one day of death, either those acts would be untrustworthy, or the martyrologies themselves would be contending with one another over the truth.

As I explain the various causes of this discrepancy, I shall also proceed to show that it is not so great as to justify the conclusion reached by Pagius—that scarcely any of the saints’ days of death are now observed. We do not deny that the feasts of some are celebrated not on the very days of their martyrdom; we merely maintain that this happens rarely and almost always with the martyrology itself providing the warning. This is likewise the opinion of Florentinius in note 11 on the *Hieronymian Martyrology*, and of Peter Damian in the work entitled *The Lord Be with You*.

I therefore think that the first reason why the memory of certain saints is celebrated on a day other than that of their death may be assigned as follows: in ancient times, during Lent, either no ferial days or very few admitted the commemoration of saints; consequently, it was necessary to transfer their honors to other days outside Lent.

Thus the feast of the Annunciation was transferred from March 25 to December 18 by the Tenth Council of Toledo, canon 1; and no other reason intervened. The Council of Laodicea, canon 51, decreed that the birthdays of the martyrs should not be celebrated during Lent, but that their memory should be observed only on Saturday and Sunday. The same rule appears in the *Capitula* of Martin of Braga, chapter 48:

> “It is not permitted to celebrate the birthdays of the martyrs during Lent, but offerings may be made on Saturday and Sunday only for their commemoration.”

If, therefore, the birthdays of the saints fell during Lent on a Saturday or Sunday, their commemoration was permitted; on the other days it was forbidden. Hence certain blessed persons are honored on days other than those on which they departed from the living, because the anniversary of their death could not be celebrated on account of Lent.

I certainly do not believe that this custom prevailed everywhere. In the Ambrosian Church, however, it was so constant that even now no saint’s feast is celebrated during the Lenten fast; instead, feasts which otherwise would have been celebrated at that time are transferred to other days. On this subject Charles Guyet of the Society of Jesus should be consulted, *Heortology*, Book II, chapters 2 and 3.

Second, the birthday of a certain saint might be occupied by a more important feast. Thus the feast of Saint Basil was transferred from January 1 to June 14, and that of Saint Remigius from September 15 to October 1.

The translation of a saint’s relics could likewise cause a day other than the day of death to be devoted to his commemoration. Let us consider several matters relevant to this point.

Paulinus is a particularly clear authority that the sacred relics of the martyrs began to be transferred only under Constantine. In *Natalis* XI he says:

> “When this was first done under Caesar Constantine,  
> who then revealed to his servants that the martyrs, summoned,  
> should be transferred from their former resting place  
> to new dwellings in the earth.”

That the precious remains of the saints began to be transferred to various places so late seems to have been caused by the rule of the pagans. For it is established that under the ancient law of the Romans the transfer of dead bodies was forbidden, as Digest 11.7.39, *On Religious [Places]*, and Pliny, Letter 73 of Book X, make clear.

But scarcely had the faith of Christ raised its head under Constantine when the triumphant relics of the martyrs began to be conveyed here and there for the assistance of the peoples. Paulinus says again:

> “From that time the sacred ashes, like seeds of life,  
> were scattered through different places; and wherever  
> a tiny drop fell from the small portion of the sacred body,  
> there pious grace produced mighty springs  
> and rivers of life from a drop of dust.”

Cardinal Baronius, under June 15 in the *Martyrology*, and Azor, Volume I of the *Moral Institutions*, Book IX, chapter 8, question 11, believe that the bodies of the blessed began to be transferred into Gaul and throughout the West only from the time when the Franks, having liberated the Roman Church from the Lombards and other tyrants, made the pious traffic in relics free.

But both Paulinus and countless examples can persuade us that this custom existed many centuries earlier, so that it is astonishing that such learned men should have adopted this opinion. Let one read Gregory of Tours, and the matter will become clear.

The term “translation” does not refer to every conveyance of relics, but only to the removal of sacred remains from one place of proper burial to another. Thus, although the body of Saint Ignatius the martyr was carried to Syrian Antioch by human effort immediately after his slaughter, in the year of Christ which Baronius estimates as 110, it could less appropriately be called a “translation” of his relics.

Such translations subsequently became so celebrated that the Church began solemnly to commemorate them every year, and mention of them is sometimes found in the martyrologies. Accordingly, after Florentinius, the learned Pagius suspected that the days of translations had sometimes been substituted for the days of the saints’ deaths.

I have no time to examine this question fully, but I shall not pass over what Guyet says on the same subject in Book II, chapter 2, question 3, of his *Heortology*:

> “But, as far as one may conjecture, perhaps a greater celebration was appointed for the aforementioned days because the birthdays of those saints occurred during Lent, during which period, as we have observed, people formerly abstained from the celebration of feasts.”

But let us now approach the heart of the controversy and storm its citadel. Most wise Marsili, will you really think that Pagius immediately reached the truth when he adopted that severe and absolute opinion according to which scarcely any birthdays—or days of death—of the saints are now observed? I certainly do not think so.

He followed this opinion in order to provide support for his calculations in the chronology of the Roman pontiffs. How well this succeeded may be learned from certain examples, and we shall examine only those Roman bishops.

I could never persuade myself that the Roman martyrology could be so carelessly mistaken, or could mislead us so completely, that those whom it usually presents to us in the saints’ feasts as having died on particular days must be judged to have died on entirely different days. For what could have been so many serious and frequent causes by which the practice of earlier centuries in honoring the birthdays of the saints was completely eliminated by the Roman Church and the authority of the martyrology everywhere thrown into confusion?

Let us now examine Pagius’s own calculations.

Saint Linus died in the year of Christ 67, namely two years after the deaths of Peter and Paul; his death is recorded both in the Roman and other martyrologies and in the chronicle of the ancient pontiffs under September 23. What does Pagius say about this?

> “It must not be thought that Linus passed to the blessed on that day, since the days on which the ancient pontiffs are honored in the martyrologies, and on which they are said to have been buried in the fuller Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs, usually refer to some translation of their relics.”

Saint Cletus is also honored on April 26, Saint Anacletus on July 13, Saint Evaristus on October 26, Saint Telesphorus on January 5, and Saint Soter on April 22. All the martyrologies agree with the ancient chronicle of the pontiffs in assigning these days; nevertheless, Pagius repeats the same refrain, namely, that on these days we should not believe that the deaths of these saints occurred, but rather that some translation took place.

Let the distinguished man pardon us if we openly declare that the explicit testimony of the Roman Church and other writers deserves belief more readily than his bare opinion. Indeed, whom should one heed more, when investigating the day of death of the supreme pontiffs, than the Roman Church, which once witnessed their struggles, recorded them, and transmitted them to posterity in the martyrologies?

Philosophers rightly hold that the assertion of one person—or even of many—is worth more than the opinion of one person who denies the matter in question without offering any argument. For what can a man establish who presents as his reason and argument the very point under dispute?

Let us examine the remaining evidence. Saints Peter and Paul are honored on June 29; Saint Clement on November 23; Saint Alexander on May 3; Saint Hyginus on January 11; Saint Pius on July 11; Saint Anicetus on April 17; Saint Callistus on October 14; Saint Urban on May 25; Saint Fabian on January 20; Saint Lucius on March 4; Saint Stephen on August 2; Saint Sixtus II on August 6; Saint Dionysius on December 26; Saint Eutychianus on December 8; and Saint Caius on April 22.

They are honored on these days in the public records, and that their martyrdom or burial occurred on those same days is clearly attested not only by the Roman martyrology but also by the so-called Hieronymian Martyrology, Ado, Bede, Notker, Wandelbert, the chronicle of the ancient pontiffs, Anastasius, and many others.

Therefore Pagius was compelled to surrender to the agreement of so many ancients in assigning the birthdays of these pontiffs. On what grounds, then, could so learned a man adopt the view that so few of the blessed were solemnly honored on the very day of their death, when so many of the Roman pontiffs alone are commemorated on those same days?

Indeed, these examples ought to have moved him, so that if he thought some feast days could not be questioned rashly, he would explain them according to the established usage of the martyrology, rather than being led by a weak opinion.

Nor shall I hesitate to mention a matter which caused him considerable difficulty. The death of Saint Sixtus is recorded in the Roman, Hieronymian, and Usuardian martyrologies, in those of Ado, Rosweyde, Wandelbert, and many others, under April 6; but Anastasius, Florus, and a few writers of little authority mention it under April 3.

Pagius, however, says that neither day refers to Sixtus’s death, since, if one calculates the years of his pontificate, he observes that his martyrdom must have occurred on July 3.

It is not my purpose to assess how slippery are the foundations on which he relies, or how unstable his rule is in the chronology of the pontiffs. I shall nevertheless offer a few remarks to complete what concerns Sixtus.

The chronicle attributed to Damasus says of him:

> “Sixtus: ten years, three months, twenty-one days. He lived in the time of Hadrian, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus to that of Verus III and Ambibulus.”

Pagius replies:

> “An error has entered the numbers; it should read ‘two months and one day,’ as it appears in the fuller chronicle of the ancient pontiffs, in the Palatine catalogue, and in two Corbie catalogues.”

Since, according to that same chronicle of Damasus, Saint Alexander, who preceded Sixtus in the pontificate, suffered martyrdom on May 3 in the year of Christ 116, Pagius therefore thinks that Sixtus’s death must be moved to July 3 of the year 126.

But first, greater diligence is needed from Pagius in presenting the ancient testimonies. For the Corbie catalogues which he adduces in support of his correction, and which are found in Papebrochius’s *Chronological-Historical Endeavor* after the Life of Saint Felix IV, read differently and give Sixtus in these words:

> “Sixtus: 10 years, 3 months, 22 days; the eighth day before the Ides of April.”

Thus these catalogues too agree with the Roman martyrology in assigning Saint Sixtus’s day of death.

Next, was there no interval between the death of Saint Alexander and the election of Sixtus, as it is called, during which the see was vacant? Certainly, according to Anastasius and other witnesses, twenty-seven days intervened. Why does Pagius not include these days in his calculation?

Finally, if Sixtus was elevated to the pontificate in the year of Christ 116, on May 3 itself, the day on which Saint Alexander ascended to the blessed, why does the Chronicle of Damasus count his years not from the year 116 but from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus, which falls in the year of Christ 117?

I shall say confidently what I think: the Chronicle of Damasus has, by universal agreement, an uncertain author and is filled with many errors, which Pagius himself and others must repeatedly correct in order to derive any benefit from it. What confidence, then, can be placed in a work that errs so often? I believe that those whom I see trusting this one writer in pontifical chronology are easily wasting both oil and labor.

Even by Pagius’s own admission, under the year of Christ 130, no. 3, it is clear that the intervals between pontificates are altogether unknown to us. They are indeed recorded, as he says, both in the *Book of the Pontiffs* and in the fuller chronicle of the ancient pontiffs; but, besides the fact that the authors of these books disagree, the vacancy of the see was not copied from certain records but calculated by the authors themselves.

Why, then, does Pagius labor so greatly to derive the dates of elections and deaths from those same authors? Why is the authority of the Roman martyrology so readily attacked?

I therefore am persuaded that Saint Sixtus either died or was buried on April 6, and that the period of the holy pontiff’s tenure should be reckoned backward from that day.

I now turn to Pope Eleutherus. Pagius does not deny that he was buried on May 26, the day on which he is honored by the Roman Church, although the testimony of certain writers tends in another direction.

As for Saint Victor, Pagius does not dispute that he died on July 28, the very day on which the Roman martyrology, the fuller chronicle of the ancient pontiffs, the ancient catalogues, Anastasius, other martyrologies, and Henschenius testify that he is honored. Therefore the Hieronymian Martyrology, Papebrochius in his *Chronological-Historical Endeavor*, and the few others who assign the death of this saint to another day should not be followed.

His successor Zephyrinus is said in all the martyrologies except the Hieronymian, and in the records of the other writers, to have gained the palm of martyrdom on August 26. Pagius, however, calculates from the uncertain and fluctuating years of his pontificate that he died on July 12.

Yet the very learned man will prove nothing against the agreement of so many records unless he first produces some certain author who securely records both the pontificate and the intervals between pontificates without error. Certainly he cannot do this, while reliable writers—preeminent both in number and authority—fight on our side.

Since Saint Pontianus died in exile in Sardinia, it is not surprising that his death is assigned here and there to various days.

Pagius also learnedly demonstrates, against Papebrochius, that Saint Cornelius ceased to live together with Saint Cyprian on September 14, the very day on which all the martyrologies say that they suffered death.

Saint Felix is assigned by almost everyone to May 29; but relying on his own calculations and on the testimony of the Hieronymian Martyrology, Pagius asserts that he died on December 22. Nevertheless, since the chronicles and catalogues disagree greatly among themselves in assigning the duration of his pontificate, I do not know how much confidence he can inspire.

Thus far, most learned Marsili, throughout the first three centuries of our era we have seen several holy pontiffs, according to Pagius’s own agreement, receive the crown of martyrdom on the very days on which they are honored.

Since he cannot prove by any solid arguments that the deaths of the very few who remain occurred on days other than those on which they are honored, it follows that we should place greater trust in the Roman martyrology than in the flimsiest arguments of others.

I therefore repeat the complaint made earlier: why did Papebrochius and Pagius declare that so few of the blessed are now honored in the Church of God on the day of their death, when so many of the pontiffs alone are commemorated in this manner contrary to their opinion?

Indeed, it would not be difficult to overthrow this recent opinion with many more examples, if leisure permitted. For the present it will suffice to observe one thing: namely, that Eusebius, in the book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, which is customarily appended to Book VIII of the *History*, preserved the memory of the martyrdoms of several persons and also recorded the day of their martyrdom.

Those days agree exactly with the testimony of the Roman martyrology.

Saints Alphaeus and Zachaeus are honored on November 17. Eusebius says of them:

> “On the seventeenth day of the month called Dios—which among the Romans is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December—they are beheaded.”

The commemoration of Saint Procopius falls on July 8, on which day the blessed martyr received burial, entirely in agreement with what Eusebius records when he says that Procopius died “on the eighth day of the month Desius, which among the Romans is the seventh day before the Ides of July.”

Similarly, the days of death recorded by Eusebius for Saints Dionysius, Timolaus, Agapius, Apphianus, Theodosia, Silvanus, Hadrian, Eubulus, and many others agree with their present feast days, as the Roman martyrology demonstrates.

If the genuine acts of the martyrs still existed and deserved the same confidence as the celebrated writer Eusebius, we would almost always read in the martyrology that the birthdays of the saints had been correctly recorded. For who does not know that the acts of the martyrs, often produced in later centuries, are frequently of weak authority and for that reason cannot be reconciled with the most reliable martyrologies?

But I fear that I have caused your ears more annoyance than is proper, most distinguished Marsili, by bringing before you documents which may seem slight to a man of such exceptional learning, or, at the very least, cannot be unknown to you.

You established that most learned academy in your house for this one purpose: to illuminate the more obscure matters of ecclesiastical history and of the sacred canons and rites. You carried out that work so happily and wisely that our Bologna cannot venerate you sufficiently, while the entire republic of letters cannot admire you enough.

Would that it might one day be permitted us to see those outstanding dissertations, commended to the public presses, by which you resolve the principal ecclesiastical controversies. Then the Church would rejoice not so much in its own profit as in congratulating you on such an abundance of learning.

How long, I ask, will you allow the desires of the learned to be tormented by delay? We repeatedly beg you at last to renounce the counsels of your modesty, and meanwhile I shall not cease earnestly to ask you to receive this dissertation with the kindness which is customary with you.

# TWENTIETH DISSERTATION. ON SAINT PAULINUS’S LAST POEM

## Paulinus’s View of the Elements Examined

To the distinguished and most learned Joseph Ferrarius, general vicar of His Eminence Cardinal Federicus Caccia, archbishop of Milan.

I should seem to have treated Paulinus, the glory of all the Muses, badly if I passed over without greeting his singular opinion concerning the elements; and I should now regret my silence all the more seriously if I allowed an entirely suitable occasion for displaying my devotion toward you and your virtues to slip so easily away. I perceive that it would greatly contribute to the glory of the holy bishop and to my regard for you if I demonstrated that he was not among the least in philosophical disciplines; and to a man distinguished by excellence both in philosophy and in the other arts capable of forming our minds, I shall present this further virtue of Paulinus. Indeed, as Boyle said in *Chymico-Physical Doubts and Paradoxes*, part 1, Dialogue: “Opinions concerning the elements are as important among the doctrines of physics as the elements themselves are among the bodies of the universe.” Why, then, should I now abandon Paulinus, whom I have followed in other matters, when he speaks in the assembly concerning the elements?

You will notice a most beautiful question in his final poem, since there the holy doctor places heaven, not fire, among the elements. When the common crowd of philosophers hears this, may the gods so love me, they will scarcely restrain themselves from laughter—or certainly from astonishment. They acknowledge only the customary four elements, namely earth, water, air, and fire; whatever appears different from these either drives a cross into their minds, already preoccupied with their opinions, or baffles their minds, already preoccupied with their opinions, or seems to them more like a monstrosity than something resembling the truth.

For this reason I thought it worthwhile to clarify Paulinus’s opinion rather than leave it to anyone’s immediate judgment, lest the learning of so great a Father be less understood by some, be given a bad reputation, or even be hissed off the stage. Let us first examine his words:

> And he distributed the sea, the lands, the air, and HEAVEN among their places;
>
> These four he drew forth as beginnings from diverse things.
>
> There are human beings for the lands, and the stars have been added to HEAVEN;
>
> The bird hangs in the air, the fish swims in the liquid sea:
>
> Thus he adorned each of the ELEMENTS with its proper forms.

He describes below the structure and position of the elements:

> For Ocean encloses the earth; the sea is enclosed; air itself
>
> Is enclosed midway beneath the heavenly axis.

This, plainly, and nothing else, is the opinion of Paulinus. He counts heaven, not fire, among the elements. Indeed, Paulinus openly shows that the imaginary sphere of fire which Aristotle devised above the region of air, and which we all learn about, was not at all to his liking, since he says not a word about it.

But on what grounds did Paulinus adopt such an opinion? I shall investigate it as best I can. First, however, as I begin a discussion of the elements, I readily confess that I do not wish to enter the arena against the opinions of others, and much less against the Peripatetics, since I must take account of brevity, and since the doctrines of those philosophers have already been examined with sufficient learning by the most eloquent philosophers of our age, among whom Helmont, Gassendi, and Boyle stand out as unquestionably exceptional minds.

Accordingly, we shall pursue only the opinion of Paulinus; and, unless my judgment deceives me, I affirm plainly that it rests upon the authority of Sacred Scripture. For according to Scripture, fire is by no means counted among the elements. Saint Peter says in the Second Epistle, chapter 3:

> “Awaiting and hastening the coming of the day of the Lord, on account of which the heavens, burning, shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with the heat of fire.”

There the Apostle distinguishes the elements from fire, since he teaches us that by fire they are either to be consumed or transformed into something better.

“But heaven too,” you will insist, “is distinguished there from the elements.” I do not see this. For Peter had spoken above in this way:

> “But the day of the Lord will come like a thief; on it the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.”

Did you notice that here too the earth is distinguished from the series of the elements? Yet since it cannot be argued from this that earth is not an element, it will likewise not be absurd to affirm the same concerning the heavens. For Saint Peter mentions the changes of heaven and earth, which will show that the final day of judgment is at hand, in such a way that he seems not to distinguish them from the elements but to describe them individually for the sake of clearer explanation.

What is more, I have discovered that other adherents of the Christian faith were by no means opposed to Paulinus’s opinion. Gennadius, presbyter of Massilia, writes in *The Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 69:

> “Let us not believe that the elements—that is, heaven and earth—are to be abolished by fire, but that they are to be changed into something better.”

Philaster, bishop of Brescia, a man known among the ancient Fathers for holiness and learning, counted heaven among the elements in *On Heresies*, chapter 46:

> “Scripture declares that on the first day heaven and earth were made; these two are the elements.”

The most eloquent writer Theodoret likewise demonstrates most openly that this opinion had taken hold of him, in Sermon 3, *To the Unbelieving Greeks, Concerning Angels*. He says of God:

> **Πάθη τινα συνεκλήρωσε τοῖς στοιχείοις, ἵνα τὸ μὲν κάλλος αὐτῶν, καὶ τὸ μέγεθος θαυμάζεσθαι παρασκευάσῃ τὸν ποιητήν· τὰ δέ γε συνεζευγμένα παθήματα κωλύει τὴν θείαν αὐτοῖς προσφέρειν προσκύνησιν.**
>
> “He joined certain qualities to the elements, so that, by contemplating their beauty and greatness, human beings might be led to marvel at their Maker; while the defects and affections joined to them would restrain them from offering them divine worship.”

He then gives examples not from fire but from the heavens, in which the sun and moon at times suffer eclipse. He adds the weaknesses of the air, earth, and waters, thereby correctly showing that each of the elements possesses its own defects.

The same author confirmed this opinion in Sermon 4, *On Matter and the World*. There he says:

> **Τούτους δὲ τοὺς ὅρους ἔστιν ἰδεῖν τὰ ἄψυχα στοιχεῖα φυλάττοντα.**
>
> “It is possible to see these boundaries being guarded by the lifeless elements themselves.”

He gathers many things in proof and, in concluding, first brings forward these statements:

> **Διά τοι τοῦτο, καὶ ἡ γῆ μεμένηκεν οἵαπερ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐγεγόνει. Καὶ ὁ ἀὴρ ἣν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐλάχε φύσιν, ἄσυλον διετήρησε. Καὶ ἡ θάλαττα οὔτε σμικρύνεται, οὔτε αὔξεται. Καὶ ὁ ἥλιος τήκειν οὐ δύναται καὶ διαλύειν ὃ θέει στερέωμα etc.**
>
> “For this reason the earth has remained even to the present day just as it was constituted at the beginning; and the air has preserved inviolate the nature it received at the beginning; nor does the sea either grow or diminish; and the sun cannot melt or dissolve the firmament through which it runs.”

Thus Theodoret counted heaven among the elements. It should also be observed that, when speaking of them, he made no mention of fire.

Certainly, some among the ancients existed who thought that heaven should be called an element without excluding fire, and for that reason devised a fifth element. Hear Lucius Apuleius in *On the World*:

> “The mutual connections of the elements are intertwined through close affinities, and five pairs are joined by bonds arranged in such a way that the lighter cling even to the heavier. Earth contains water within itself, and water, as some think, carries earth. Air is generated from water; fire is formed from the density of air; while aether in turn, together with those immortal fires, is kindled by the vitality of God.”

Apuleius plainly makes five elements, joined together by five connections. The following words, which he had discussed above, bring the matter into the clearest light:

> “Heaven itself, the stars that bear the heavens, and the whole stellar structure are called aether—not, as some think, because it is fiery and burning, but because it is always whirled along in rapid courses. It is not one of the four elements known to everyone, but something entirely different: fifth in number, first in order, divine in kind, and inviolate.”

Nothing more evident could have been produced from which we might learn that aether was the most excellent of the elements.

Hence some assigned aether to Jupiter. Saint Augustine censures them in *The City of God*, book 4, chapter 10, in these words:

> “We understand Jupiter in the aether, Juno in the air. These two elements are joined together. The sea is assigned to Neptune, and the earth to Pluto.”

Then the great doctor laughs at the claim that Juno is said to be joined to Jupiter, Salacia to Neptune, and Proserpina to Pluto:

> “For if these things were so, the ancients would have declared that there were rather three elements of the world, not four, so that the individual marriages of the gods might be assigned to the individual elements.”

Ludovicus Vives, a highly learned man, believes in his notes on this passage that Augustine understood earth, water, air, and fire by the four elements. Augustine’s meaning, however, is different. There he says nothing about fire, but speaks only of aether, which he had asserted was designated by the name of Jupiter and counted among the elements by the ancients. He then adds that the more recent pagans differed from them, since they joined Jupiter to Juno—that is, air to aether—and consequently, by combining the two into a single element, held according to their opinion that there were only three elements.

We have gradually disclosed what opinions concerning the elements were held by the ancients. We shall now clarify the matter more fully and repeatedly show that Gassendi, otherwise a most learned man, departed from their opinion in his interpretations.

Empedocles, in Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, book 1, chapter 3, says:

> **Τέσσαρα γὰρ πάντων ῥιζώματα πρῶτον ἄκουε·**
>
> **Ζεὺς αἴθηρ, Ἥρη τε φερέσβιος, ἢδ᾽ Ἀϊδωνεὺς,**
>
> **Νῆστίς θ᾽ ἣ δακρύοις τέλλει κρούνωμα βρότειον.**
>
> “First hear of the four roots of all things:
>
> ethereal Jupiter, life-bearing Juno, and with them Dis,
>
> and Nestis, who with her tears moistens the mortal springs.”

Gassendi says in *Physics*, book 3, section 1, chapter 2, that by the name of Jupiter fire is meant here without obscurity, perhaps following Plutarch, who says concerning these verses:

> **Δία μὲν γὰρ λέγει τὴν ζέσιν, καὶ τὸν αἰθέρα.**
>
> “By the name of Jupiter he means heat and aether.”

But the learned man is mistaken, together with Plutarch. The aether marked by the name of Jupiter in Empedocles differs greatly from the element of fire. It is heaven itself, concerning which we have just heard Apuleius speaking, and we shall introduce others who speak of it as well.

Orpheus—or whether that man was Onomacritus—in a hymn to Rhea lists four elements:

> **Ἐκ σοῦ γὰρ καὶ γαῖα, καὶ οὔρανος εὐρὺς ὕπερθεν,**
>
> **Καὶ πόντος, πνοιαί τε.**
>
> “For from you arose earth, and the broad heaven above,
>
> and the sea, and the breezes.”

Here you see that for Orpheus οὔρανος—that is, heaven—is what aether is for Empedocles. Why, then, does Gassendi think that heaven is to be understood as fire, and aether likewise taken for fire?

Indeed, in the same book he says concerning these verses:

> “Clearly, by the name of heaven he understood fire because of the fires appearing in it.”

But when a mind is already preoccupied by its own opinions, everything, however different, seems to support them—just as it sometimes happens through a defect of the eyes that we see what appears nowhere, while things that really exist are presented to our fixed gaze in a false image or with altered colors.

For were the ancients really so impoverished in words that, when they wished to describe the element of fire, they were forced to misuse the word “heaven”? Euripides, according to Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Physicists*, book 2, believed that everything was generated from aether and earth:

> **Αἴθερα, καὶ γαῖαν πάντων γενέτειραν ἀείδω.**
>
> “I sing of aether and earth, the mother of all things.”

Gassendi adds in the same place that by the name aether fire must be understood, or at least that this may be understood from Aristotle’s own interpretation in *On the Heavens*, book 1, chapter 3, and *Physics*, book 4, chapter 5.

But it is false that aether in Euripides means the same as fire, and that this interpretation ever entered the mind of the Stagirite. Aristotle says nothing whatever about this matter in *Physics*, book 4, chapter 5. In *On the Heavens*, book 1, chapter 3, he is so far from taking aether for fire that he establishes it as entirely different from fire. His words are:

> **Διόπερ ὡς ἑτέρου τινὸς ὄντος τοῦ πρώτου σώματος παρὰ γῆν, καὶ πῦρ, καὶ ἀέρα, καὶ ὕδωρ, αἴθερα προσωνόμασαν τὸν ἀνωτάτω τόπον ἀπὸ τοῦ θεῖν αἰεὶ τὸν ἀΐδιον χρόνον, θέμενοι τὴν ἐπωνυμίαν αὐτῷ. Ἀναξαγόρας δὲ κατακέχρηται τῷ ὀνόματι τούτῳ οὐ καλῶς, ὀνομάζει γὰρ αἴθερα ἀντὶ πυρός.**
>
> “For this reason, since the first body is something different from earth, fire, air, and water, they called the highest region aether, deriving the name from its always running through eternal time. Anaxagoras, however, uses this name incorrectly, for he calls aether fire.”

Gassendi, that eloquent philosopher, declared that this aether, which we heard counted among the elements, was nothing other than fire, on Aristotle’s authority. But how correctly and accurately he did so is now evident to everyone. In reality, the philosopher devised nothing less than such a doctrine.

Let us perceive more clearly what Aristotle’s opinion on this matter actually is, so that we may more forcefully overthrow Gassendi from the opinion just mentioned. Hear his clear words in *On the World*, chapter 2:

> **Οὐράνου δὲ, καὶ ἄστρων οὐσίαν μὲν αἴθερα καλοῦμεν, οὐχ ὥς τινες διὰ τὸ πυρώδη οὖσαν αἴθεσθαι, πλημμελοῦντες περὶ τὴν πλεῖστον πυρὸς ἀπηλλαγμένην δύναμιν· ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ ἀεὶ θεῖν κυκλοφορουμένην, στοιχεῖον οὖσαν ἕτερον τῶν τεσσάρων, ἀκήρατόν τε καὶ θεῖον.**
>
> “We call the substance of heaven and the stars aether—not because it blazes as something fiery, as some have thought, grievously mistaken concerning a power most removed from the nature of fire, but because aether is always running in a circular motion, being an element different from the four, both incorruptible and divine.”

Moreover, Aristotle says in *On the Generation of Animals*, book 2, chapter 3, that a certain warm substance is present in the seed of animals, corresponding to **τῷ τῶν ἄστρων στοιχείῳ**, “the element of the stars.”

Therefore, most eloquent Ferrari, I cannot sufficiently marvel at why such a great crowd of philosophers, which follows Aristotle as its teacher, has treated this element with such contempt that they have not deigned to include even a mention of it in their books. What clearer opinion of Aristotle could be produced than this?

Plutarch himself, in book 1 of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, reports that Aristotle taught:

> **στοιχεῖα τέτταρα, πέμπτον δέ τι σῶμα αἰθέοιον ἀμετάβλητον**
>
> “Four elements, and a fifth, a certain unchanging aetherial body.”

Thus, if anyone in the future asks how heaven, or aether, is designated by the name of an element, or what our Paulinus meant by this opinion, the answer will be ready: namely, that aether is a certain exceedingly subtle substance endowed with perpetual motion, which contributes to the generation of things and the constitution of bodies, just as earth and water do.

For this reason, I think, Lucretius calls aether exceedingly fluid and diffuse in book 5. Likewise Orpheus, or Onomacritus, believed that everything is nourished by aether, when he says that the universe was constituted:

> **Ἐκ πυρὸς, ἐξ ὕδατος, καὶ γῆς, καὶ παντοτρόφ᾽ αἴθρης.**
>
> “From fire, water, and earth, and aether that nourishes all things.”

The same author lists four elements in his hymn to Love:

> **Αἴθερος οὐρανίου, πόντου, χθονὸς, ἤδ᾽ ὅσα θνητοῖς**
>
> **Πνεύματα.**
>
> “Of heavenly aether, the sea, the earth, and life-giving breath for mortals.”

Here too I do not approve Gassendi’s interpretation. He thinks that fire must be understood by the name aether, although the substance referred to here is the one said in the other, highly praised poem to nourish all things, and is explicitly distinguished from fire.

For what the highly learned Francesco Patrizi says in *Panaugia*, book 7—“The whole aether, according to the wisdom of the ancient Greeks, is fire”—departs so far from their opinion that it requires no refutation.

Once these matters have been observed, some light will shine upon Virgil, who sings in book 2 of the *Georgics*:

> Then the almighty Father, aether, descends in fruitful rains
>
> into the lap of his joyful consort, and, mingled
>
> with the great body, nourishes all the great offspring.

Pacuvius likewise transmitted the same thought in *Chryses* in the clearest words:

> What our people call heaven, the Greeks call aether.
>
> Whatever this may be, it gives life to everything, forms, enlarges,
>
> nourishes, sows, buries, and receives everything into itself;
>
> and it is likewise the Father of all.

You see, therefore, that among the ancients heaven—or aether, or that substance which Sextus Empiricus, in book 2 of *Against the Physicists* and elsewhere, calls **κυκλοφορητικὸν σῶμα**, “a body mobile in circular motion”—was regarded as an element. Accordingly, when you hear them list aether together with earth, water, and air, you will understand that they designate not fire, as Gassendi believed, but an element different from fire.

I omit many further matters relating to this question, mindful of brevity, and observe only one thing by way of conclusion. That subtle matter which Descartes, a man of supreme genius, seems to have been the first of all to devise so astonished the Peripatetics by its novelty that they cry out that it is an audacious fiction to be expelled from the schools. But is it not, with its name slightly changed, the same as the aether of the ancients, the same diffuse substance from which all things are formed and nourished?

Let our age marvel at or condemn Descartes; he must share the common lot with the ancients, since, having borrowed from them an ingenious or daring opinion, he sought a name for himself through imitation rather than invention.

And that aetherial substance which the physician Robert Fludd established among the first principles of things—was it not first taught by the authors whom I have praised, and from them transferred into the books of that most acute man? Truly, what Ecclesiastes says in chapter 1 is correct: “There is nothing new under the sun”; and in the cultivation of the sciences scarcely anything can be devised that was not at some time produced in the schools of the ancients.

These are the matters, most learned Ferrari, that I thought should be added to the verses of Paulinus, and which now await the support of your learning. Indeed, it is not the least of your distinctions that you have given your name to the more refined study of philosophy and that, among the series of other sciences with which you are adorned, you have cultivated this one as well, so that you appear no less skilled in natural philosophy than in divine and human law.

You have therefore encouraged me to add such ornaments to my discussion so that it might approach you. Now, by your excellence in humanity, you will ensure that the devotion of one who approaches you does not fail to meet with good fortune. Farewell.

## TWENTY-FIRST DISSERTATION. ON THE NOLAN CROSS

So that I might not linger too long in the notes, I thought it appropriate to bring together here everything that seemed relevant to discuss concerning the cross described by Paulinus.

In former times two forms of the cross were commonly constructed. One was called *commissa*: an upright piece of wood was set up, and another, shorter piece was joined to it above, at its very summit, transversely, so that nothing of the upright wood projected above it. The other was *immissa*: a transverse piece was placed across the upright one in such a way that it intersected it.

The first is represented by the letter T; the second is commonly found in churches and in other Christian monuments. It is uncertain to which of the two Christ was affixed, although the highly learned Lipsius, in book 1, chapter 10, of *On the Cross*, and Gretser, in book 1, chapter 3, of *On the Holy Cross*, contend on firm grounds that this distinction belongs to the *immissa* cross.

Setting aside the question, I shall pursue the form of the cross mentioned by Paulinus and briefly investigate what kind it was. He describes the appearance of the cross in general in *Natales* 11 and says:

> The form of the cross is composed in a double fashion, and now
>
> it unfolds the appearance of a ship’s yard by the likeness of a naval mast,
>
> or, existing with one upright trunk, it displays
>
> the sign customarily used by the Greeks to mark three hundred,
>
> and, wherever it has a summit, it is joined by a transverse bar.

Here is a distinct image of each kind of cross. The *immissa* is understood from the appearance of a ship’s yard or naval mast; Gretser produced a brilliant work on this subject, worthy of preservation, and Bosius, in book 1, chapter 5, of *The Triumphant Cross*, Lipsius, in book 1, chapter 9, of *On the Cross*, and many others have discussed it.

The *commissa* cross, however, is represented by the sign customarily used by the Greeks to mark three hundred, namely by the letter Tau. Paulinus used this example more than once. In his second letter to Sulpicius Severus he says:

> “Christ conquered the hostile rulers not by numbers or the strength of legions, but already then through the mystery of the cross, whose form is expressed by the Greek letter Tau, the number three hundred.”

Saint Augustine likewise says in Sermon 1, *On Time*, for the Monday after the Lord’s Passion:

> “The holy Gideon therefore foresaw the mystery; at last he chose three hundred men for battle, to show that the world was to be freed from the attack of grave enemies not by the multitude of numbers but through the mystery of the cross. For the three hundred in Greek displays the likeness of the cross in Tau.”

Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book 1:

> “For the Greek letter Tau itself, and our T, is the form of the cross.”

When the temple of Serapis was destroyed under the Emperor Theodosius the Great, Egyptian hieroglyphic letters were found there which bore the image of a cross, as Rufinus, book 11, chapter 29, of his *History*, Sozomen, book 7, chapter 13, Socrates, and Suidas testify. Kircher reproduces their form in *Interpretation of the Egyptian Obelisk*, hieroglyph 5, with signs entirely corresponding to our T.

The ancient author Julius Firmicus seems likewise, if I am not mistaken, to describe a cross of this kind in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, when he says:

> “The horns display nothing other than the venerable sign of the cross. By one extended and upright horn the world is supported, the earth is held together, and by the union of the two that run sideways the east is touched and the west is raised, so that the whole world is fixed in a threefold stability, etc.”

For this reason Paulinus called the cross a two-horned one standing upon a staff, and in these words expressed a *commissa* cross, which, as he adds below, is:

> Fixed upon one trunk,
>
> and wherever it has a summit, joined by a transverse bar.

Having made these observations concerning the *commissa* cross, let us seek from Paulinus a description of that cross which the most depraved thief removed from the Nolan basilica—or stripped of its pendant ornament. His words are:

> Therefore the same form displays that shape of the cross
>
> which depicts a balance suspended from an evenly poised cord;
>
> and, with an upright pole beneath it, forms a harmonious yoke,
>
> or the tree, with transverse horns, imitates the eyes which, from the brow, join the face.

From this I infer that the Nolan cross was fashioned in a form resembling the *commissa*. Let us examine the individual details.

If you raise an upright trunk and place upon its summit a balance hanging with equal pans on either side, you will certainly obtain the form of the cross in question, since the upright trunk and the arms of the balance present the letter T to anyone looking at them.

Again, if you consider the straight pole of a chariot with a yoke placed at its summit, you will see that it likewise displays a figure of the cross very similar to the letter T.

Finally, if you inspect a human face and consider the arrangement of the eyebrows, nose, and mouth, does not the same figure of the cross present itself to our eyes?

Nevertheless, I admit that Paulinus’s meaning cannot be established with complete certainty here, since the form of a pole with a yoke added to it represents, in our time, a cross more like the *immissa* than the *commissa*. By contrast, the human face bears more resemblance to the latter than to the former, since above the eyes, at the smooth and level forehead, no sign rises that appears to project as a third horn of the cross.

Let others judge this matter. My present opinion is that the Nolan cross was fashioned in a form resembling the *commissa*, perhaps after the likeness of the Labarum, whose image, besides Baronius, is presented by Bosius in book 7, chapter 13, of *The Triumphant Cross*. It is preferable, however, to await a more exact judgment from others.

## TWENTY-SECOND DISSERTATION. A GLEANING FROM THE LOST WORKS OF SAINT PAULINUS

Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, lists the works of Saint Paulinus in these words:

> “Paulinus, bishop of Nola in Campania, composed in verse brief but numerous works; and for a certain Celsus he wrote, in the form of an epitaph, a consolatory little book concerning the death of a Christian and a baptized infant, fortified by Christian hope. He wrote several letters to Severus; and before his episcopate, in prose, a panegyric to the Emperor Theodosius concerning the victory over the tyrants, especially because he conquered more by faith and prayer than by arms.”

This is the panegyric about which Jerome, writing to Paulinus himself in letter 13, said extraordinary things in his praise, thereby arousing in us an intolerable longing for it.

Gennadius continues:

> “He also composed a sacramentary and a hymnal. He sent many letters to his sister concerning contempt for the world, and published treatises on various subjects, dealing with different matters in various discussions. His chief little works, however, are a book on Penance and one on the general Praise of All the Martyrs.”

O loss insufficiently lamentable! We have lost the latter works, and I do not know whether it will ever be possible to restore them.

There is in the Ambrosian Library a very ancient codex, which I would believe to have been written in the eighth or even seventh century. Its characters approach the script of the Merovingian age and display something of the Saxon style, examples of which the distinguished Mabillon has shown us in his highly praised work *On Diplomatics*.

This codex contains sayings of the ancient Fathers and explanations of certain passages of Scripture. Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory occupy the greater part, while the most recent author among them is Isidore, bishop of Seville.

I encountered in it certain fragments of Saint Paulinus, which now seem appropriate to make public. Among the passages I judged especially worthy of notice are these words:

> “After the Passion and Ascension into heaven, Christ, just as Elisha ascended to Bethel—that is, to the house of God—turned and cursed the Jews forty-two years after his Ascension, and sent two bears, that is, two dreadful kings, Vespasian and Titus. Coming forth from the forests of the nations, they struck them down in a cruel slaughter.”

Petavius, the leading chronologist, proves in book 11, chapter 17, of *On the Doctrine of Times*, and elsewhere, that Jerusalem was overthrown by Titus in the year 70 of our era; the other writers agree with him.

If, therefore, you count forty-two years backward from that year—the interval which Paulinus affirms occurred between the destruction of Jerusalem and the Lord’s Ascension—you arrive at the year 28 or 29 of the same era, if both terminal years are counted. Thus, according to Paulinus, in the Dionysian year 29 Christ the Lord ascended into heaven after completing his Passion.

Eusebius of Caesarea, in his *Chronicle*, says that this city was captured in the forty-second year from the fifteenth year of Tiberius, and correctly so. In fact, the year 29 of the common era fell in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, in which year the two Gemini served as consuls.

Since, however, Eusebius believed that Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, he therefore says in book 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History* that Jerusalem was captured by Titus forty complete years after the crime committed against Christ. Paulinus does not follow him in this opinion, since his words clearly show that Christ was crucified and taken up into heaven in the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

For the rest, almost all the ancient Fathers who placed Christ’s Passion under the consulship of the two Gemini—that is, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius—are found to agree with Paulinus: Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the *Stromata*; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 8; Lactantius, book 4 of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 10; Sulpicius Severus, book 2 of the *Sacred History*; Saint Augustine, book 18, final chapter, of *The City of God*—although in that same passage he appears to contradict himself; Paulus Orosius, book 7 of his *History*; Africanus, cited by Saint Jerome in his commentary on chapter 9 of Daniel; and very many others. Some more recent writers also join them.

Clement of Alexandria, in book 1 of the *Stromata*, taught specifically that forty-two years elapsed from Christ’s Passion to the destruction of Jerusalem. He says:

> “From the Passion of Christ to the overthrow of Jerusalem there are forty-two years and three months.”

Saint Jerome likewise says in his commentary on chapter 1 of Zephaniah, verse 17:

> “After forty-two years from the Lord’s Passion, Jerusalem was surrounded by an army, and its destruction was completed with haste.”

He repeats this in letter 150 to Helbia, question 8.

This opinion—that Christ’s Passion occurred in the fifteenth year of Tiberius and in the year 29 of our era—now has few followers. Yet it was once so famous that it is not surprising that Paulinus subscribed to it.

What will seem surprising is that a certain Gallic writer, to whom we owe a critical examination of Saint Augustine’s works, concealed or ignored this opinion so completely that he declared it could never have occurred to Augustine.

Among the works of this great doctor there is a sermon entitled:

> “On the Passage Written Concerning Saint Elisha: ‘Go Up, Baldhead, Go Up,’ etc.”

Among other things it says:

> “What is meant by ‘Go up, baldhead, go up, baldhead,’ except ‘Ascend the cross at the place of Calvary’? And pay attention to this, brothers: just as under Elisha forty-two boys were torn to pieces, so after forty-two years from the Lord’s Passion two bears came, Vespasian and Titus.”

He then adds the devastation of Jerusalem by the Romans and says:

> “After forty-two years, that sacrilegious people received from the two bears, Vespasian and Titus, what it deserved.”

The writer just mentioned takes this as an opportunity to hiss the sermon off the stage and deny it to Augustine. He says that the statement is entirely foolish, since Jerusalem was destroyed not forty-two, but thirty-six or thirty-seven years after Christ’s Passion; that this is an enormous chronological error, and consequently that the sermon is unworthy of Augustine.

He is mistaken and might appear a stranger to the reading of the ancient Fathers, since, as was observed above, most of them held that Christ suffered under the consulship of the two Gemini—that is, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius—and Saint Augustine was especially among them.

From that year to the destruction of the holy city it was necessary to count forty-two years. If this opinion conflicts with the learned views of the most recent chronologists, neither Augustine nor Paulinus should be blamed for it, since they favored a common and widely held opinion.

That sermon therefore does not dishonor Augustine for this reason, although I too am entirely certain that it did not come from his pen, but rather was extracted from the lost works of Paulinus. This becomes immediately clear to anyone reading these fragments.

To return to the fragments themselves: the final three undoubtedly derive from the book on Penance, which we heard Gennadius praise above all the others. I believe that the remaining pieces were taken from lost letters or from another work of Paulinus.

I could not restrain myself from mentioning a wholly charming but apocryphal letter which, in a beautifully ornamented manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, is called the sixty-fifth among the letters of Jerome and bears this title:

> “Likewise Jerome: On the Twelve Doctors.”

It begins as follows:

> “Do you now wish me, my brother, to tell you clearly and precisely, as though concerning the luminaries that shine throughout the entire firmament of the world, something about those writers who were able to bring forth for us, toward the splendor of spiritual contemplation, much concerning the obscurities that impede understanding because of the carnal mind?”

Such thickets of words and circumlocutions immediately warn us that this work is by no means Jerome’s.

There a judgment is pronounced against Augustine, Hilary, Origen, Ambrose, Eusebius of Caesarea, Heliodorus, and Dardanus. Then the ill-disposed author spews forth the following against our Paulinus:

> “Paulinus thought he should become a teacher, though he had not first been a disciple; he attempted to make fruit arise without a root. Therefore his writings require neither a writer nor paper.”

He then gives his verdict on Pelagius, Jovinian, Julius Africanus, and a certain Fannonius, an unknown writer.

But this letter is so far from being attributable to Jerome that it is wholly alien to his style, judgment, and holiness.

I thought that corrections and additions to the remaining *Natales* of Paulinus should be appended to this foolish fabrication. For after comparing the copies hitherto committed to print, especially the Antwerp Plantin edition of 1622, with the outstanding Ambrosian codex, I observed that certain verses were missing and that certain others should be restored to a better form.

I therefore present these observations, which may perhaps be of considerable use to someone who prints the works of Paulinus, so that the honor of so great a writer may increase day by day.

## EXCERPTS FROM THE LOST WORKS OF SAINT PAULINUS (C, G, S)*

The Lord commanded the ravens to feed Elijah, who was sitting at the brook Cherith. It is certainly a remarkable thing that an unclean bird should provide the means of life for a holy man. Therefore, if we too, despising even our own possessions, imitate Elijah’s poverty, believe what I say: unclean animals—that is, sinful human beings—will minister to us with devoted service.

Why do we read that Elisha, gentle and mild, handed little children over to beasts? The prophet Elisha bore the figure of Christ. Indeed, his name is interpreted as “Salvation of God.” But what else is the salvation of God than his Son, who is also the Savior of the world?

The little children, mocking the salvation of God in the person of Elisha, represented the Jews, who cried out, saying, “Go up, baldhead, go up!”—because Christ was going to ascend the cross at the place of Calvary.

“And he turned,” Scripture says, “and cursed them in the name of the Lord. And two bears came out of the forest and killed forty-two children.”

So Christ, after his Passion and Ascension into heaven, just as Elisha ascended to Bethel—that is, to the house of God—turned and cursed the Jews forty-two years after his Ascension, and sent two bears, that is, two dreadful kings, Vespasian and Titus. Coming forth from the forests of the nations, they struck them down in a cruel slaughter.

The righteous man falls seven times a day, and rises again. If he falls once and again, how can he be called righteous? He is called righteous because, when he falls, he is raised up. The number seven, moreover, teaches rest. Whoever falls on the seventh occasion ought to beware lest he fall any further. He should already have taken care after the first fall; but because God is merciful, he patiently bears such falls, so that a person may repent even on the seventh occasion. But if someone, becoming more negligent, passes beyond the number of resurrections, he cannot be called righteous; rather, because of the multitude of his sins, he is counted among sinners.

A person sins in two ways: by deliberate intention and by accident—that is, one may wish to sin, while another is overtaken by sin. But accidental sin is divided in two ways: through ignorance and through weakness. [Col. 0834C] Judas sinned deliberately, saying: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” What he intended, he willingly carried out, and therefore received the fitting reward of his most criminal will. Peter, however, denied the Lord through weakness, fearing death, although he had promised that he would undergo death for Christ. But because he had suddenly been overcome, he deserved swift pardon for his fall. Paul, on the other hand, became a persecutor through ignorance and was healed by rapid forgiveness, himself also testifying: “I persecuted the Church of God, but I received mercy, because I did it in ignorance.”

You see, then, that some fall unwillingly, while others are struck down by their own will. There are also two things in a person: forgetfulness and ignorance. A person forgets God when he deliberately plans to sin; but he is ignorant when he transgresses because he has been overtaken—for example, one person commits fornication willingly, while another, resisting fornication, is overcome through weakness. The sin of both is indeed one, but their penance will not be equal, because the former sinned willingly, whereas the latter, unwillingly overcome in the struggle, succumbed. Do you see what distinction there is in sin? Behold how [Col. 0834D] the righteous man falls and, when the Lord extends his hand beneath him, is saved, and so forth.

Let us assist God’s will with our own power, so that by his power he may favor our will, because it is written: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” To will and to run is ours; to show mercy is God’s, as the Truth itself also testifies through the apostles: “Without me you can do nothing.” And Paul says: “What do you have that you did not receive? If you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” And so forth.

Therefore, if anyone has provoked God, let him imitate the example of Moses, who erased the guilt of doubt by the satisfaction of repentance and humility. If anyone incurs the crime of sacrilege, let him imitate Aaron, who, cleansed of the crime of transgression through the remedy of confession and humility, deserved the primacy of the priesthood. If anyone has committed adultery and murder, let him consider David and do penance, and, having been made healthy by this medicine, remain in the fear of [Col. 0835A] God. If anyone has been overcome in confession and, yielding to torture, has become a betrayer of the faith, let him imitate Peter, who denied the Lord. Going outside—that is, departing from faithlessness—let him weep bitterly and return to the faith. In the case of great sins, the offenses of great men are [Col. 0836A] displayed, so that if some weak or humble person should err, by looking to the example of great men he may find an easy entrance to life and turn to faith and repentance, and so forth.

[Col. 0835]

NOTES AND OBSERVATIONS ON THE WORKS OF ST. PAULINUS.

[Col. 0835]

ON THE FIRST LETTER.

[Col. 0835A] 869 Note 1. “To Severus.”—This Severus is called Sulpicius by Gennadius in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 29; Gregory of Tours likewise designates him in no other way in Book I of *The Miracles of St. Martin*, chapter 1, and in Book X of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 31. Others prefer him to be called Sulpicius Severus; this is also the form given by the standard heading of his letter to Aurelius the deacon, and likewise of his letter to his mother-in-law Bassula. Although Paulinus always simply calls him Severus—and this is also generally the practice in Gregory of Tours—he nevertheless introduces himself in the dialogues under the single name Sulpicius. Since, then, in the same period he is sometimes called Severus and sometimes Sulpicius, *haplōs* (simply), it appears that authors did not always use a person’s proper name when they set down only one name, after each person had come to have only one proper name. See Francis Sylvius, *Second Century of Progymnasmata*, chapter 41, where he shows that a surname was often placed before a personal name.

He was Aquitanian by birth, as he himself admits in *Dialogue* 1, chapter 20, and as Gennadius also says. Indeed, he was from the Nitiobriges, since in Book II of his *Sacred History* he calls Phoebadius—who was bishop of Agen in Gaul, according to Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 108—his own bishop. It is well known that Agen was in the territory of the Nitiobriges.

He lived chiefly at Elusa, as Paulinus states in Letter 6, or at Primuliacum, as the same author says in Letters 11 and 12; see there where these places were situated. It can also be inferred from Severus’s letter to his mother-in-law Bassula that he lived at Toulouse.

He was not bishop of Bourges, as many learned men have thought, but only a presbyter, as Gennadius testifies. He lived sometimes at Primuliacum and sometimes at Elusa, as the letters of Paulinus already cited indicate. ROSWEYDUS.

Note 2. “When the Devil [*Zabulus*] attacks.”—That is, the Devil. Paulinus almost always uses this term, following the earlier Fathers, who expressed it in this form. Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, chapter 6: “Why do you fall through the Devil and with the Devil into ruin?” Thus the most ancient books read it; this spelling also occurred in other passages of Cyprian in older editions, where *diabolus* now appears. In the same author, the author of *The Book on Gamblers*, chapter 3: “Stripped by the darkness of the Devil, they join hands with one another”; and several times in the same book. Hilary, on Matthew 24, canon 26: “He shows that the Devil is a thief, ever watchful to carry away our spoils.” The same author, on Matthew 12, canon 12: “He indicates that the whole power of the Devil was crushed by him in the first temptation.” Ambrose, *On the Faith to Gratian*, Book V, chapter 1: “He struck down and crushed that savage beast, namely the Devil, prostrated in the latter days by the venerable passion of his body.”

A church hymn concerning St. Michael:

> Michael, who by his strength crushes the Devil.

The Claromontane manuscript glosses: “*Zabulus*, the Devil.” The Aquicinctine manuscript glosses: “*Zabulus*, Satan, the adversary.” Likewise: “*Zabulum*, an abode of beauty,” where the former is Greek and the latter the Hebrew word *zabulon*, which St. Jerome, in *On Hebrew Names*, says means “an abode of strength,” or “the flow of night.” The true derivation of *zabulus* is that which learned men have already proposed: from *diaballō*, in Aeolic *zaballō*; hence, just as *diabolus* comes from the former, *zabolus* comes from the latter. ROSWEYDUS.

Note 3. “Dedicated only to the priesthood of the Lord, and not also assigned to the title of a church.”—A person who was not ordained presbyter for a definite title of this or that church was said to be ordained *apolelymenōs* or *apolytōs cheirotoneisthai*, “absolutely.” This was later forbidden by canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon:

> No one is to be ordained absolutely, whether presbyter or deacon, unless specifically in a church of a city or village; and those who are ordained absolutely, the holy synod decreed that such an imposition of hands is to be considered invalid.

Writing on this passage, Zonaras says that formerly, when presbyters were ordained, the name of the title or church to which they were ordained was expressly stated:

> And just as now the person ordaining each of the chief bishops says that he has been appointed bishop of this particular city, so formerly everyone who was ordained priest or deacon was simply called the priest or deacon of this particular church.

I have rendered the wording literally, so that it may be clear that the title was pronounced by the ordaining bishop, although Zonaras likewise testifies that this practice had fallen into disuse in the case of presbyters and deacons. See Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 1, chapter 33, where canon 26 of Chalcedon is corrected. DUC. See C. Cangius, *Latin Glossary*, under the word “TITLE,” volume III, page 1134.

Note 4. “On Eluson.”—Paulinus was staying in the city of Barcelona. This messenger had reached him on the eighth day after setting out from Eluson and had crossed the Pyrenees, the barrier between Narbonese Gaul and the Spanish provinces. The author therefore indicates that Eluson was a city of Narbonese Gaul. The Bordeaux Itinerary, edited by P. Pithoeus, confirms this, calling it *Elusio*: “City of Toulouse, 7 leagues; Elusone, 9 miles; village of Ebromagus, 10 miles; city of Narbonne, 15 miles.” Thus it places Eluson between Toulouse and Narbonne in Narbonese Gaul, while it places Elusa between Bordeaux and Toulouse in Aquitaine and Novempopulana. Elusa must therefore be distinguished from the city of Elusio; nor should one agree with Abraham Ortelius and other more recent geographers, who think that Paulinus corruptly reads *de Elusone* instead of *de Etusa*, and who read in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XV: “In Narbonese Gaul are Elusa, Narbonne, and Toulouse.” On the contrary, Marcellinus must be corrected from Paulinus, since Elusa is not in Narbonese Gaul—or else nothing in Marcellinus need be altered. DUC.

Joseph Scaliger writes in the prolegomena to his *Correction of Chronology* that Eluson was a town with an ancient fortress on the borders of the Nitiobriges, where they are separated from the Petrocorii by the river Dragutus; it is now commonly called Lausun. ROSWEYDUS.

ON LETTER II.

Note 5. “We have served at God’s altar and ministered at the saving tables, now elders in name and office.”—*Senior*, “elder,” means *presbyter*, from the Greek word *presbytēs*. St. Cyprian, Letter 75: “For this reason it is necessarily our practice that every year the elders and overseers come together to arrange those matters entrusted to our care.” Prudentius, in the *Passion of St. Hippolytus*: “The elder is offered, bound in chains.” He had previously called Hippolytus a presbyter. CHARLES CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume III, page 809.

ON LETTER III.

[Col. 0837A]

Note 6. “To the venerable companion of your crown, our father Aurelius.”—“Crown” means clerical, priestly, episcopal, or pontifical dignity, because the crown is the principal insignia of the clergy and priesthood. St. Augustine, Letter 147 to Proculianus: “Your people appeal to us by our crown; our people appeal to you by your crown.” By this word, too, the supreme pontiffs and bishops were addressed as an illustrious title of honor. Ennodius, Book IV, Letter 22 to Pope Symmachus: “May the mercy of your crown, when invoked, raise up the little ones.” The bishops of Tarragona, Letter 2 to Pope Hilary: “Offering, in the provincial language of letters, the services owed to your crown.” Anastasius, in his account of Pope Cornelius: “Cornelius replied: ‘I received letters from the crown of the Lord—that is, from the bishop Cyprian—not against the commonwealth.’” Marculfus, Book I, formula 26, entitled “A Brief Memorandum to a Bishop”: “We have sent this memorandum to the crown of your blessedness.” St. Jerome uses the expression frequently in Letter 81; Paschasinus of Lilybaeum in his letter to Leo; Florianus in his letter to Nicetius; the deacon Quodvultdeus in his letter to St. Augustine, volume VI of the works of that same Augustine; Sidonius, Book VI, Letter 4; Paulinus of Nola, Letter 18 to Delphinus; Braulio of Zaragoza in his letter to Isidore of Seville; Fortunatus in the letter prefixed to his books on the *Life of St. Martin*, and in Book V, in his letter to Martin, bishop of Gaul; St. Bernard, Letter 205 to the bishop of Rochester; and others. CANGIUS, volume I of the *Latin Glossary*, page 1225.

Note 7. “One loaf … in which also the fullness of the Trinity is contained.”—Was this loaf divided into three parts so as to represent the Trinity? Augustine recognizes the Trinity in three loaves in *Sermon 171 on the Season*, on Luke 11: “Which of you will have a friend?” He comments as follows:

> He does not ask for three loaves without a sacramental meaning, because one guest was present through the grace of kindness, but the substance was the Trinity. Was not one guest present in the three who came to Father Abraham? Guest and friend, diner and dweller; and all the services of hospitality were offered to him in the Trinity, because the glory of the Trinity shines forth. The father brought a threefold calf; the future mother, who was to bear a son, mixed three measures of fine flour; for her the father sacrificed a lamb; and she had already made the body of Christ a sacrament in the Trinity.

The same author, *Sermon 29 on the Words of the Lord*, chapter 3:

> When you have reached the three loaves—that is, the food and understanding of the Trinity—you have both what will sustain you and what will nourish you, and so forth. There is bread, and there is bread, and there is bread: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit.

ROSWEYDUS.

ON LETTER IV.

Note 8. “The one loaf which we sent as a token of unity.”—It was customary among the holier Fathers to send one another bread as a symbol of unity and unanimity, also called *eulogiae*, and to exchange them with one another. Paulinus, Letter 1 to Severus: “We have sent you Campanian bread from our cell as a *eulogia*.” The same author, Letter 45 to Alypius: “We have sent one loaf to your holiness as a token of unity, in which also the fullness of the Trinity is contained. You will make this loaf a *eulogia* by the graciousness of receiving it.” The same author, Letter 46 to Romanianus: “So that the service of brotherly kindness might not appear empty, from the provisions of the Christian campaign—in whose service we daily labor for our frugal ration—we have sent you and our son Licentius five loaves together.” Augustine, Letter 34 to Paulinus: “The bread we have sent will become a richer blessing through the love of your kindness in receiving it.” Christ instituted the Eucharist in bread for this reason, as will be explained in Letter 6. ROSWEYDUS.

ON LETTER V.

Note 9. “The holy mother-in-law.”—He means Bassula, the mother-in-law of Severus, concerning whom he says below in this same letter: “I ask you to greet with the reverence she deserves our holy parent, our mother in Christ, your fellow-heir”; and in Letter 11, speaking to Severus about a fragment of the Holy Cross which Paulinus’s wife, Therasia, had sent to Bassula: “She sent this specifically to our venerable sister Bassula, the common fellow-servant.” Among Severus’s letters, the third is addressed to his mother-in-law Bassula. ROSWEYDUS.

[Col. 0838A] Note 10. “O true Israelite.”—Thus in Letter 36, now numbered 49, he says that he might see Christ as Israel did. He is clearly alluding to the etymology of the name Israel, which Eusebius gives in Jerome’s *On Hebrew Names*: “Israel, which is interpreted as ‘Seeing God.’” Nazianzen, *Oration 2, On Theology*; Hilary, on Psalm 13; Philo, in *On the Flight* and *On Abraham*; Basil, in his commentary on Isaiah 1, likewise give: “Israel, which is interpreted, ‘Seeing God.’” Jerome repeats the explanation in his commentaries on Amos 4, Hosea 8, and Jeremiah 31.

Nevertheless, in his *Questions on Genesis* the same Jerome considers this etymology not so much true as forced, although worn smooth by universal usage. He declares that he is guided rather by the authority of the angel, who gives this explanation: “You have been strong against God.” Thus Aquila translates: “Because you have ruled with God.” The Septuagint and Theodotion: “Because you have prevailed with God.” For *Sarich*, or *Sar*, from which the word Israel is derived, means “prince.”

Our most learned Delrius therefore corrects this passage in that way, and he also thinks that Jerome spoke here not so much from his own opinion as from that of others. I do not agree with him, however, since it is clear that Jerome generally expressed his commentaries on the prophets from the volumes of the Greek Fathers without examining their opinions, whereas in his *Hebrew Questions* he followed the more learned Hebrews. More recent scholars likewise agree with them concerning this etymology of Israel, including Pagninus and others. They point out that if, following the opinion of the ancients, we say that Israel is as though it were *Is roch el*, “a man seeing God,” then it would have to be written with *shin*—that is, with the point on the right horn—whereas in all books it is written with *sin*, that is, with the point on the left horn. It is therefore better derived from the verb meaning “to rule” and “to prevail.” DUC.

Note 11. “By the Lord’s sevenfold candlesticks.”—Revelation 1:12: “And I turned and saw seven golden candlesticks, and in the midst of them one like the Son of Man.” It is correct, however, that the editions of Badius and Gravius read *septena* (“sevenfold”) rather than *septem* (“seven”). DUC.

Note 12. “With smoking flax.”—This is correctly written instead of *ligno* (“wood”), which appeared in the Paris edition. Thus Isaiah 42:3: “He will not extinguish smoking flax.” DUC.

Note 13. “Impiously, who was strong.”—The earlier reading was *impari aequivalebat* (“he was equivalent to the unequal”), from which a Roman friend conjectured that the text should read *faciebat ire par ei qui valebat* (“he made him equal to the one who was strong”). This is an entirely plausible conjecture: it has a very suitable meaning, does not conflict with Paulinus’s style, arises naturally from the common reading, and introduces no difficulty. Nevertheless, the reading supplied by manuscripts B and P seems preferable. In this way the members of the period correspond better with one another, as do the return of each adverb and the very sound of the composition—all of which bears the stamp of Paulinus’s style: “Vigilantius, sick, was rashly hurrying; the catechumen, strong, was impiously hurrying”—that is, he did not yet possess the compassion of Christian devotion and had not learned to sympathize with the sick, because, as Paulinus says, he was not yet a member of our body. ROSWEYDUS.

Note 14. “The fires of the jealous clergy at Rome.”—Baronius, volume IV of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year of Christ 394, in the tenth year of Pope Siricius, comments on this passage and on the one that immediately follows, concerning Pope Urbicius:

> I think you now understand whom Paulinus means by Pope Urbicius: no one other than the pontiff who then presided over the Roman Church, Siricius himself, whom Paulinus was forced, as he says, to endure as hostile to him without any cause. It plainly happened that holy Paulinus had just cause to complain of Pope Siricius and certain other clergy of the Roman Church, about whom we have also seen St. Jerome complain, as we have often said above. Thus Siricius happened to acquire a bad reputation in this respect, because he was angered against men so distinguished in holiness and learning and so universally esteemed.
>
> But for what reason? Was it because he did not receive Paulinus among the clergy of the Church, knowing that he had been ordained by another? Is this what Paulinus means by “the proud discrimination of Pope Urbicius”?
>
> Or perhaps Siricius was angry with him because, immediately after being ordained, he became a presbyter from a layman? To prevent this from being done by any bishop, Siricius, in a letter addressed to the orthodox, had issued a warning with solemn protest. But if this was the offense, the blame should have been placed on Lampius, the bishop of Barcelona. For Paulinus, as he himself repeatedly testifies, suffered violence. Yet even in so great a man this was a pardonable matter, as it was in Ambrose and others who, unwillingly, were advanced from the ranks of lay catechumens not merely to the presbyterate but even to the episcopate.
>
> But since Paulinus himself attributes all that he suffered at Rome solely to jealousy and envy, this offers no slight reason for thinking that, when Paulinus arrived in Rome after so long an interval, everyone’s eyes were turned upon him. People were astonished at the spectacle of a former consul made a presbyter and soon to be transformed into a monk, while both citizens and foreigners flocked to him in great numbers and vied in performing services for him.
