His fame aroused them as if by a trumpet-call, and there was a great rush from every quarter to visit him—not only of Roman citizens but also of foreign bishops hurrying from overseas regions, and not merely on private business but also in the performance of public embassies. All these many and great circumstances, he says, stirred the envy of some, brought on jealousy, and provoked anger. As a son of peace, he thought that the only suitable remedy for minds so badly affected was to depart from the city without delay. He proposed that Severus do the same, since Severus was then being harassed in his own country by the same blows of envy.

ROSWEYDUS.

Note 15. “The African bishops also to us.”—Below, in Letter 46 to Romanianus, Paulinus mentions the African bishops from whom he had received a letter: “From there we had received letters, namely from Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Profuturus, Severus, now all bishops together.” ROSWEYDUS.

Note 16. “Of my patron, Domnaedius Felix.”—The same author, Letter 13, *Panegyric* 3, on Felix:

> We are allowed both to celebrate the day and to behold the rewards  
> of the Patron . . . .

And frequently in *Natalis* 7, and likewise in *Natalis* 8.

Among ancient Christians, “patrons” meant especially the saints who provided protection. Thus in Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, chapters 4 and 18; Ambrose, *On Luke*, Book X, chapter 21; Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymns 1 and 2; St. Eulogius, *Apology*, and elsewhere. CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume III, page 205.

Note 17. “Of my *Dominaedium*, Felix.”—He calls Felix of Nola *Dominaedium*, as though meaning “lord of the shrine,” or “lord of the Nola basilica.” Thus in Letter 9: “The birthday hymn from my solemn celebration to my Domnaedius”; and in Letter 10: “In it the roofs of our neighboring Domnaedius Felix resounded with the voices of choirs of boys and virgins”; and in Letter 12: “That basilica, which is now celebrated as dedicated in the name of the Lord Christ to our Domnaedius, our common patron”; and in Letter 28, addressed to Victricius: “Whom the Lord wished to experience as powerful with him, his holy confessor, our beloved Felix, our Domnaedius.”

Likewise in *Natalis* 7:

> Rather than what he himself performed for me in my own buildings,  
> the same Domnaedius did.

I would not mention this unless I saw that Ambrose of Lyons had fallen into error here in Book II of *On Nola*, chapter 11. He thought that in Paulinus’s time the Nolan people called God *Domnaedius*. “We hear,” he says, “that this word has been preserved in the mouths of those who swear by and invoke God down to our own time.” The Paris edition is also incorrect in giving *Domini ac Ducis* (“of the Lord and Leader”) here instead of *Domnaedii*. ROSWEYDUS.

Note 18. “We have sent you Campanian bread from our cell as a *eulogia*.”—Private *eulogiae* were gifts that bishops and presbyters freely gave and received from one another. They were consecrated by the blessing of those who sent them and were generally loaves of blessed bread. They were also sent along with letters of greeting, a formula for which Marculfus provides in Book II, formulas 42–44. St. Basil, *Rule*, chapter 133; Paulinus of Nola, in his letter to Alypius and in his letter to Romanianus; St. Fructuosus, *Rule*, chapter 23; the *Rule of St. Columbanus*, chapter 10; the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 76; Gregory of Tours, Book IV of his *History*, chapter 16; Book V, chapter 14; Book VI, chapter 5; Book VIII, chapters 2 and 20; Book X, chapter 16; *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 31; Fortunatus, Book XI, poems 8 and 11; Hincmar of Reims, *Capitularies to the Presbyters of His Parish*—that is, his diocese—chapters 7 and 16; and many others discuss such *eulogiae* and blessed loaves.

The name *eulogiae* was also applied to the loaves that were offered in the church for sacrifice and blessed, from which a portion was selected for making the body of Christ. These *eulogiae* were distributed to those who, because of some impediment, were not prepared to receive Communion on feast days and Sundays, according to the decree of Pope Pius preserved in Burchard, Book V, chapter 27, and the Council of Nantes, chapter 9. They were even distributed to catechumens, who had no right to receive the Eucharist; for them the *eulogiae* served in place of a sacrament, or even as a kind of sacrament, as St. Augustine calls them in Book II of *On the Remission of Sins*, chapter 26—using the term in a looser sense, since the bread was sanctified by prayers.

For this reason, the making of blessed bread is forbidden on Easter Day and on the festivals when Christians customarily and ought to receive the body of Christ. This is stated in the synodal injunctions of Peter of Collemedio, archbishop of Rouen—a practice still observed on Easter Day in that diocese. The bread was distributed after Mass by the priest to all those present, shortly before dismissal. Pope Leo IV, *On Pastoral Care*: “Distribute *eulogiae* to the people after Mass on feast days.” They were received with great submission of spirit and reverence from the hand of the priest, after first saluting it with a kiss of the mouth, as Cabasilas testifies. For, as St. Augustine says in Book II of *On the Remission of Sins*, chapter 26: “Although this bread is not the body of Christ, it is nevertheless holy, and holier than the foods by which we are nourished.” Hence Pachymeres, Book V of his *History*, chapter 8, calls it *theios artos*, “divine bread.”

Accordingly, just as the sacred Eucharist was eaten by those who had fasted, so if someone had not fasted and received it, he gave it to someone nearby to eat. Allatius, Book III of *On the Agreement of the Western and Eastern Churches*, chapter 9, section 1, and Goar in his commentary on the *Euchologion* report that this is still observed in the Greek Church.

Pope Pius, martyr, also discusses *eulogiae* distributed after Mass in Book II of his *Five Books*, chapter 117; and Hincmar, drawing on him, in the *Capitularies Given to the Presbyters of His Parish* in the year 752, chapter 7:

> From the offerings brought by the people and left over after consecration, or from the loaves that the faithful bring to the church, or indeed from their own loaves, the presbyter is to have cut pieces placed in a clean and suitable vessel, so that after the solemn celebration of Mass those who were not prepared to communicate may receive *eulogiae* from them every Sunday and on feast days. The priest is first to bless what he intends to distribute as *eulogiae*, using these words, and then distribute it to those who are to receive it, and so forth.

The Council of Nantes, held in 895, chapter 9, and Regino, *On the Life and Conduct of Presbyters*, chapter 61, contain the same provisions.

Balsamon, in his commentary on canon 2, appears to attribute the first institution of *eulogiae* to the Synod of Antioch held under Constantius; but the writings show that they were already in use earlier. See St. Augustine, Book III against Petilianus, chapter 16. These matters concern the public *eulogiae*, which were distributed to the people after the sacred liturgy had been completed. CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, pages 290–291, volume II, note 2. Anyone wishing to know more about the various kinds of *eulogiae* should consult the same *Glossary*, on the same pages and those following.

Note 19. “*Apophoretum*.”—Thus it was formerly written, *apophoretum*, from Greek *apophorēton*. Note that *apophoreta* means gifts customarily carried away from a banquet in Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter 55; *Vespasian*, chapter 29; Martial, in the heading of his final book; Lampridius, in *Elagabalus*; and the ancient scholiast on Juvenal’s *mustacea*, Satire 6. It also means gifts given at the distribution of presents and in wishes for office and honors, in Symmachus, Book XI, Letter 81; Book V, Letter 56; and Book IX, Letter 59. The ancient Fathers used the word for spiritual banquets and sacred gifts.

Concerning banquets, Ambrose, in *Exhortation to Virgins*, says:

> Those who are invited to a great banquet customarily carry away gifts with them. Therefore, since I was invited to the Bolognese banquet at which the translation of the holy martyr Agricola was celebrated, I have reserved for you *apophoreta* full of holiness and grace.

He repeats this in Letter 55, when he had brought back with him from Bologna to Milan relics of the nails, blood, and cross of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola. The same author, in his commentary on chapter 1 of St. Paul’s Letter to the Romans: “All who are invited to the Gospel receive double *apophoreta*: they receive remission of sins and become children of God.” Zeno of Verona likewise, in Sermon 1 to the Neophytes after baptism, speaking of the spiritual banquet to which the holy men of the Old and New Testaments contribute their portions, treats Zacchaeus’s final contribution as an *apophoretum*: “Zacchaeus without delay pays out fourfold *apophoreta*.”

Concerning the triumphs of rulers and great vows, Ambrose, in *Exhortation to Virgins* on the translation of St. Agricola:

> Triumphs of rulers customarily have *apophoreta*; and these are triumphant *apophoreta*. For the palms of the martyrs are the triumphs of our Christ.

The same author, in his commentary on chapter 3 of St. Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians:

> Just as in great vows the greatest *apophoreta* are given, so, when Christ’s magnificent mystery was revealed, human beings were given so distinguished a gift as the cause of joy and gladness—a gift sufficient for their saving abundance.

Augustine, Letter 179: “We received with the greatest joy the *apophoretum* of the veil,” understanding this as the gift sent to him by Proba and Juliana in honor of the solemnity when the veil of virginity was given to Demetrias.

Since Paulinus was sending Severus a boxwood dish as an *apophoretum*, it is not irrelevant that Isidore notes, in Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4, concerning eating vessels:

> The Greeks named *apophoreta* from carrying away fruit or something else; for it is flat.

ROSWEYDUS.

Note 20. “*Nigellatum*.”—Peter Danesius, formerly a professor at Paris, wrote the following note in the margin of his book, as our Fronto points out:

> I think that by *signinum nigellatum* he means those earthen vessels that Italians commonly call porcelain. They are made from crushed shells mixed with lime; although they are white on the outside, when held up to bright light they display within, as though transparent, dark little figures to the viewer.

So he wrote. If this interpretation is accepted, both *nigellatum* and the little vessels must be understood as referring to the same objects, through which he wished certain other things that he had entrusted to his boys to be sent. But another interpretation might be that Paulinus wants a *nigellatum* sent to him in the little vessels entrusted to the boys—that is, in earthen vessels, as he explains immediately afterward. Therefore, if someone understands *nigellatum* as black wine, oil, or some kind of sauce, he will perhaps not depart from Paulinus’s meaning. Certainly such things were commonly stored in earthen vessels. It is also well known that people frequently sent one another sometimes oil and sometimes brine, as is clear from Ausonius, Letter 21 to Paulinus. Oil was often used by monks. Paulinus, Letter 3 to Severus: “In my concern for frugality, he taught us to take simple food easily, with porridges cooked in a small quantity of oil and plenty of water.”

Someone might perhaps understand *nigellatum* as a dark vegetable, which is customarily seasoned and preserved in earthen pots. See Columella, Book XII, chapter 56. More probably, however, *nigellatum* means oil made from black cumin, *melanthion* in Greek, hence *melanthine oil*, in Actuarius, Book VI, chapter 10 of *The Method of Treating Disease*. Paulinus, subject to various illnesses, needed medicinal oil; hence in Letter 3 to Severus he praises Victor’s service because Victor anointed his limbs. ROSWEYDUS.

ON LETTER VI.

Note 21. “Let us live on one loaf.”—He means the Eucharist, which Christ instituted in bread and wine as a symbol of unity. Cyprian, Letter 63 to Caecilius, chapter 6:

> Just as many grains, collected, ground, and mixed together, make one loaf, so in Christ, who is the heavenly bread, we should know that there is one body, to which our number is joined and united.

The same author, Letter 76 to Magnus, chapter 2:

> When the Lord calls his body bread, formed from the union and gathering together of many grains, he indicates our people, whom he bore, as united; and when he calls his blood wine, pressed from many clusters and grapes and gathered into one, he likewise signifies our flock, joined together by the mingling of an united multitude.

St. Chrysostom says admirably, Homily 24 on chapter 10 of the First Letter to the Corinthians:

> “For what do I mean by communion?” he says. “We are that very body. What, then, is the bread? The body of Christ. And what do those who partake become? The body of Christ—not many bodies, but one body. For just as bread, composed of many grains, is united so that the grains are nowhere visible, although they themselves remain, while their distinction is not apparent because of their joining together, so we too are joined to one another and to Christ. For you are not nourished from one body and he from another, but all of us from the same body.”

Augustine, *Monday of Easter, On the Sacraments of the Faithful*, preserved by Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 3, chapter 36:

> This bread indicates unity. So too the wine was in many grapes, and now it is one—one in the sweetness of the cup after the pressure of the winepress.

The same author, *Tractate 26 on John*:

> For this reason, as the men of God before us also understood, our Lord Jesus Christ commended his body and blood to us in those things that are brought together into one from many. One thing is made into one from many grains; another flows together into one from many grapes.

Earlier in the same passage:

> The body of Christ cannot live except from the Spirit of Christ.

Hence the apostle Paul, explaining this bread to us, says: “One bread, one body are we, though many.” O sacrament of devotion! O sign of unity! O bond of charity!

And shortly afterward:

> The Jews were indeed quarreling with one another because they did not understand the bread of concord and did not wish to receive it. For those who eat such bread do not quarrel with one another, because “one bread, one body are we, though many.”

The same author, Letter 59 to Paulinus:

> Everything that is offered to God is vowed, especially the offering of the holy altar. Through this sacrament our greatest other vow is proclaimed: that we vow to remain in Christ, namely, in the joining together of Christ’s body. The sacrament of this is that “one bread, one body are we, though many.”

The same author, on Psalm 147:

> “One bread, one body are we, though many.” He himself says this. Therefore, if one bread is the whole body of Christ, the members of Christ are pieces of bread.

For this reason they formerly sent bread to one another as a symbol of unity and unanimity, as I have explained in the fourth letter. ROSWEYDUS.

ON LETTER VII.

[Col. 0842D]

Note 22. “Of Profuturus.”—There is a letter of Augustine to him, Letter 149, in which Augustine calls him “brother,” indicating that he was a bishop. Augustine relates the death of Megalius and that Profuturus was being appointed his successor in the primacy. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 23. Severus

Paulinus and Therasia, in their letter to Romanianus (Epistle 46): “We had received letters from holy and most beloved men there [from Africa], namely Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Profuturus, Severus—now all bishops together.” This Severus was bishop of Milevis, whom Augustine mentions in Epistle 34, writing to Paulinus and Therasia: “The most blessed brother Severus, our fellow-student and bishop of the Church of Milevis, well known in that same city, greets your holiness with the duty he owes us.” Severus himself, in Epistle 37, professes that he had been Augustine’s disciple: “Thanks be to God, brother Augustine, whose gift is whatever good and joyful things there are in us” [Col. 0843A]. Augustine replies to him in Epistle 133. He mentions the same Severus as bishop of Milevis in Epistle 129 to Olympius; and in Epistle 110—which is rather a record of proceedings, in which Severus designated Eradius as his successor—he mentions Severus as already dead and says that he appointed as his successor the man whom Severus himself had designated. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 24. “Augustine is a co-bishop”

The word *co-bishop* is used for the bishop whom we call a coadjutor, as also in St. Augustine’s Epistle 34. See what Charles du Cange writes about *chorepiscopi* in the *Glossarium Latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 969.

### Note 25. “For it is said to Aeschinus what Micio hears”

This is expressed in proverbial form, from Terence’s *Adelphi*, where Aeschinus was adopted by his paternal uncle Micio. ROSWEYDUS.

## IN EPISTLE IX

### Note 26. “That you may touch Christ”

It is written in Ephesians 5:14: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you.” Some of the ancients, such as Ambrose in his Commentary on this epistle and Augustine on Psalm 3, translate it: “Rise from the dead, and Christ will touch you”—that is, *ἐπιψαύσει*, says Beza, not *ἐφάψεται*, as Erasmus thought. Yet Erasmus could have defended himself against Beza by the testimony of St. Jerome, whose words in Commentary 877 indicate that he had heard someone debating this passage in church who said that the reading should not be *ἐπιφαύσει σοι* (“Christ will shine upon you”) but *ἐφάψεταί σου* (“Christ will touch you”).

Nevertheless, I think we should assent to neither reading, but rather follow the authority of St. John Chrysostom, who wrote as follows in Homily 18 on the same Epistle to the Ephesians:

“Some say, ‘And you will touch Christ’; others say, ‘Christ will shine upon you’; but the latter is more correct,” since he adds: “Depart from sin, and you will be able to see Christ.”

As for what Beza puts forward, *ἐπιψαύσει τοῦ Χριστοῦ* (“he will touch Christ”), it is acknowledged by none of the ancients, so far as I know. For Ambrose, whom he cites, has in his Commentary the reading that we have given. Chrysostom favors Paulinus, but prefers the common reading; Epiphanius likewise defends it in *Against Heresies* 46. DUC.

## IN EPISTLE X

### Note 27. “As if it were a buckthorn”

It should be read this way, not “branch,” as the first edition had it. The passage is Psalm 57:10. Gregory of Nyssa, on that psalm:

“The most difficult species among thorns is the buckthorn (*rhamnus*), whose points are sharp, whose projections are continuous, injuring those who approach them, and whose wounds are poisonous.”

Augustine, in the same place: “What is a buckthorn? It is a kind of thorn. Certain thorns are said to be extremely dense.”

St. Jerome, on Habakkuk 3: “The buckthorn is full of thorns and resembles a hedgehog” [Col. 0843D]. And on Haggai 2: “The buckthorn is a thorny shrub, a little tree interwoven with thorns and hooks, which seizes whatever it touches, wounds what it has seized, and delights in the blood of the wounded.” ROSWEYDUS.

## IN EPISTLE XI

### Note 28. “Or *διορυξ*”

Someone had written in the Paris edition, after the end of the epistle, *διωρυχή*. Perhaps *διορυγή* would be better, since this word signifies a ditch or trench, whereas *διωρυχή* means a breach made by piercing through walls.

In this passage, unless I am mistaken, St. Paulinus is imitating that passage in Genesis 2 concerning the river which flowed out of paradise and divided into four heads. It must indeed be admitted that *διορυγή* signifies a ditch, as Plutarch, among others, teaches at the beginning of his *Life of Fabius Maximus*: “For even to the present day ditches are called *διόρυγες*.” But in the old manuscripts of Plutarch it is written *διόρυγες*: “For even to this day *διόρυγες* are called ditches.” These words were omitted by both Latin translators, Guarino and Cruserius, [Col. 0844A] but not by the French translator Amyot.

The word *διώρυξ* is also used for a ditch drawn from a river, and this is the reading found here in manuscript P., where the form “Israel dioraχy” occurred. Ecclesiasticus 24:41: “And I, like a ditch from a river, and like an aqueduct, went out into paradise.” The Latin Vulgate has: “I, like a river’s *dioryx*, and like an aqueduct, went out from paradise.”

It should be noted that, although Paulinus’s wording, “flows from paradise,” agrees less well with the Greek text now extant—*ἐξῆλθον εἰς παράδεισον*, “I went out into paradise”—it nevertheless agrees with the Vulgate, “I went out from paradise,” perhaps because his author read *ἐξῆλθον ἐκ παραδείσου*. DUC.

### Note 29. “Upon his own shoulders”

This parable of the shepherd carrying the sheep back to the fold upon his shoulders was formerly represented on sacred chalices. Tertullian, in *On Modesty*, chapter 6:

“Let the very paintings on your chalices come forward, if even in them the interpretation of that sheep will shine through—whether it points to the restoration of a Christian or of a pagan sinner.”

In the same work, chapter 10:

“Perhaps that shepherd whom you depict on the chalice will intercede for him,” and so forth; “you drink nothing more willingly than the sheep of second repentance.”

Christ frequently appears in this form in the Roman sacred sculptures. It was formerly represented by Philip Winghius, a diligent investigator of every kind of antiquity, whose print the brothers Antonius and Hieronymus Winghius—equally devoted to and admiring of ecclesiastical antiquity, the former abbot of Liessies and the latter a canon of Tournai—sent to me.

After the example of Christ carrying the sheep upon his shoulders, certain bishops, both formerly and today, to whom the pope grants this privilege, wear upon their shoulders a pallium made of sheep’s wool. Isidore of Pelusium splendidly explains its symbolism in Book I, Epistle 136, to Count Herminus:

“The bishop’s *omophorion*, being made of wool rather than linen, signifies the skin of the sheep. The Lord sought that sheep when it had gone astray, found it, and lifted it upon his own shoulders. The bishop, being a type of Christ, fulfills his work and shows everyone through his vesture that he is an imitator of the good and great shepherd, who has undertaken to bear the weaknesses of the flock.

“And pay close attention. For when the true shepherd himself arrives through the opening of the venerable Gospels, then the bishop rises and lays aside the garment of imitation, thereby declaring that the Lord himself is present—the leader of the pastoral art, both God and master.”

[Col. 0844D] In a similar manner Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, writes in his *Ecclesiastical Theory*:

“The *omophorion* with which the bishop is clothed signifies the skin of the sheep. When the Lord found it wandering, he lifted it upon his shoulders and numbered it together with those that had not gone astray.”

He also adds why the pallium is marked with crosses:

“It has crosses because Christ himself carried his cross upon his shoulder. Moreover, those who wish to live according to Christ lift his cross upon their shoulders—that is, affliction; for the cross is a symbol of affliction.”

For more on the archiepiscopal pallium, see the writers on sacred rites. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 30. “Ebromagus”

Our fellow citizen Ausonius mentions this Ebromagus in Epistle 22 to Paulinus: “Now carried as far as your Ebromagus.” I consider this reading preferable to the others mentioned by the most learned Elias Vinetus, whether one reads *Ebromagus*, *Hebromagus*, or *Ebromagum*. Many towns and cities of this kind occur in Aquitaine and throughout Gaul, ending in the word *magus*, such as Argantomagus, Cassinomagus, and Carantomagus, as is clear from the *Itinerary of Antoninus* and the Peutinger Map.

In compiling his *Geographical Treasury*, Ortelius thinks that this city is called Eburomagus on that map. But since the map places Eburomagus between Lactora and Carcassonne, while the *Jerusalem Itinerary*, published with Antoninus, places it between Elusio and Carcassonne, it plainly seems to be a different city from this Ebromagus.

Joseph Scaliger, in Book II, chapter 9 of his *Readings on Ausonius*, thinks it was a town at the confluence of the Duranium [Col. 0845B] and the Garonne. Because it was enlarged in the manner of a fortress with public granaries and towers by Pontius Leontius, one of Paulinus’s descendants, it was called Burgus. But since he supports his conjecture with no authority, it seems preferable to agree with Elias Vinetus, who, following the traces of the ancient name, suspects that a village called Embrau, situated below Burgus and below Bravia on the bank of the Garonne, is the ancient Ebromagus.

Yet neither of them, while investigating the true location of Ausonius’s estate at Lucaniacum, noted that the name is still retained by a village situated on the left bank of the Duranium as it flows into the Ocean, commonly called Lugagnac. We know that this place lies in the territory of the most illustrious Lord Barraldius, who, while acting as vice-admiral of Aquitaine and exercising command at sea, recently won a notable victory over the pirates who had made the whole Aquitanian region unsafe.

Our fellow countryman Joseph Scaliger wrongly places Ausonius’s Lucaniacum in the territory of the Meduli, as though it bordered the Boii, although his Epistle 6 contradicts this: there it is situated not far from the port of Condate and consequently on the bank of the Duranium, near the city now called Libourne. The same conclusion follows from Epistle 22 to Theon.

Yet neither the Meduli nor the Boii extend beyond the Garonne or as far as the Duranium, and Scaliger is not even consistent with himself. For in chapter 9 of Book II of his *Ausonian Readings* he wishes Lucaniacum to have been situated on the bank of the Duranium, but in chapter 14 he places it not far from the bank of the Garonne. DUC.

## IN EPISTLE XII

### Note 31. “He makes use of sweet and beautiful things”

Pauline uses—indeed, I might say misuses—the unusual word *abuti*. For here *abuti* means “to use,” whereas elsewhere it means “not to use.”

Thus, below, in Epistle 27, he praises St. Paul as one who was “abusing what was lawful,” that is, abstaining from the payment for the Gospel which he could lawfully have received. Likewise, in the same place, he praises Victricius for abstaining from lawful things: “Your holiness possesses the rich glory of Christian poverty not only through the disuse of lawful things but also through abstinence from visible advantages.”

Again, in Epistle 36: “Nevertheless, even in the simple, literal sense, when circumstances require it, one must not *abuti*.” In this passage *abuti* means “to use,” just as earlier it meant “not to use.”

Augustine also used the word in this sense in Epistle 59 to Paulinus, and he explains St. Paul’s passage in Colossians 2:22: “All these things are for destruction through abuse.” He explains it as follows:

“All these things,” he says, “contribute rather to destruction when one abstains from them superstitiously, so that a person *abuses* them—that is, does not use them according to the commandments and doctrines of men.”

In Greek St. Paul has: *Ἅ ἐστι πάντα εἰς φθορὰν τῇ ἀποχρήσει*—“which are all destined for destruction through use.” The Latin translator of the Vulgate has: “Which are all for destruction through use itself,” as though he had read *χρήσει*, although *ἀπόχρησις*, or “abuse,” can also mean consumption through use, as in Plautus’s *Asinaria*, Act I, Scene 3: “Where are those things I gave before? They have been used up.” Nonius Marcellus explains the passage in this way.

Boethius likewise says in Book VIII of Cicero’s *Topics*: “We use those things which remain for us when we use them, but we abuse those things which perish for us when we use them.”

An anonymous author, *On Boundaries*, derived from the second book of Frontinus, writes: “Then, in many places, they do not place the sacrificial boundary markers at the end, but wherever the convenience of the sacrifice advises that they be placed—that is, in a place where the sacrifice can conveniently be *abused*.” Here my very dear Rigaltius, in his *Glosses on the Surveyors*, interprets *abuti* as “to consume by fire.” ROSWEYDUS.

## IN EPISTLE XIII

### Note 32. “To Pammachius”

Palladius, chapter 122:

“A man of proconsular rank, named Pammachius, approached him [Pinianus, living as an ascetic in the fields of Campania and Sicily]. After renouncing the world, he led a most excellent life. While still alive he distributed part of his wealth, and at his death he left the remainder to the poor.”

Jerome, in the preface to Daniel:

“I beseech you, most learned Pammachius, and Marcella, the unique example of Roman holiness.”

Augustine, Book II *Against Pelagius*, chapter 3:

“The holy presbyter Rufinus, who remained at Rome with St. Pammachius.”

Baronius, in volume V, under the year of Christ 410, the ninth year of Pope Innocent, the sixteenth of Honorius, and the third of Theodosius, when the city was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths, places Pammachius’s death on the basis of Jerome’s preface to Book I of his *Commentary on Ezekiel*:

“Behold, suddenly the death of Pammachius and Marcella, the siege of the city of Rome, and the falling asleep of many brothers and sisters were announced to me.”

His memory is preserved in the Martyrology on the third day before the Kalends of September. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 33. “The bitterness of mourning”

This corresponds to the Latin Vulgate of Ecclesiasticus 38:17: “But because of slander, bear his mourning bitterly for one day.” The Septuagint has:

“Make the lament bitter, and perform mourning according to his worth for one day.”

And in verse 19:

“For from sorrow comes death, and sorrow of heart will bend strength.”

The Latin Vulgate has: “For from sorrow death hastens, and it covers strength.”

This agrees with Paulinus’s text as though it had *καλύψει* (“it will cover”), rather than *κάμψει* (“it will bend”). This is evidence that he had read the Greek text of Ecclesiasticus exactly as the author of the Vulgate had read it. Therefore the Latin translations of Scripture should not immediately be corrected or altered on the basis of the published Greek text, since the authors of those translations may perhaps have used another, more ancient Greek manuscript. DUC.

### Note 34. “Through that venerable royal gate”

He means the principal gate of the basilica of the Apostle St. Peter. Formerly *regia*, used absolutely, meant the royal or principal gate of a temple, monastery, or dining hall, as I showed in the *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers* from the *Life of Mary of Egypt*, Ennodius, Gregory of Tours, and Anastasius the Librarian.

To these examples I now add the following. Eusebius, Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4, calls the central gate *βασιλίς*, “royal.” Perhaps Isidore also refers to this in his *Glosses*: “Tullia, central, royal,” so that he designates the central or royal gate.

The manuscript *Rule of the Master*, chapter 30: “Then, when the royal doors have been closed by the doorkeepers, they too lie down on their beds and, in silence lasting through the hours of the night, seek sleep.”

Chapter 47: “Lest, when we praise God with the tongue alone, we admit God only through the royal gate of our mouth.”

Chapter 67: “So that they may appear, when entering through the threshold of the outer royal gate of the monastery to seek prayer, to fulfill the Rule.”

Chapter 95: “A cell shall be established for two brothers advanced in age near the royal gates of the monastery.”

In the same work: “The royal gate of the monastery shall have outside an iron bell on a small support, so that, when it is struck by someone arriving, the arrival of anyone who comes may be announced to those inside.”

Anastasius the Librarian also seems to be understood in this way in his account of Leo III: “At the entrance of the basilica, above the great royal gates, he made images of silver.” Again: “In the basilica of the Mother of God, at the manger, at the entrance to the manger, he made royal gates covered with the purest silver, weighing altogether 127 pounds; above these royal gates he placed a small veil, bordered all around with gold embroidery. He also placed three other Tyrian veils above the great royal gates at the entrance of the basilica, with a border of gold embroidery.”

Our Bulengerus, in Book II, chapter 57 of *On the Gifts of the Pontiffs*, understands *regiae* in the first passage of Anastasius to mean certain magnificent projecting structures on which images and statues could be placed; in the second, he understands them as ornaments of gold and silver. But since so many authors cited above use *regiae* for principal gates, why should one seek an authority for another meaning? Certainly, veils hung above the royal gates or doors, as Anastasius mentions here, can be seen in certain Roman monuments preserved from antiquity, some impressions of which I possess. ROSWEYDUS.

That in the Middle Ages *regia*, without an accompanying qualification, customarily meant the principal gate is shown by Rosweydus in this passage and in the *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers*, from Ennodius, Gregory of Tours, Anastasius the Librarian, and other writers.

But I would not dare affirm, without another example, that the principal gate of the Vatican basilica was at some point called “the queen,” although the older editions prefer that reading, as does the Putean manuscript, an excellent and very ancient codex now called the Regius.

Otherwise, whatever may have been the popular usage, Paulinus could with equal justification have called that principal gate either “the queen,” without further qualification, or “the queen of gates,” just as Statius called the Appian Way “the queen of roads” in Pollius’s Surrentine villa. CHIFFLETIUS, in *Paulinus Illustrated*, pp. 42–43.

### Note 35. “Through the reclining places”

We infer that this word refers to tables. Among the Latins, *accubita* and *accubitus* are known to mean what the Greeks call *ἀνακλιντήρια*, or reclining couches, as they are called by Abbot Wilramus in chapter 2 of his commentary on the *Song of Songs*. The familiar term here derives from reclining at table.

Hence *accubitus* and *accubita* came to mean the meals themselves in Isidore, Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, and in Papias, p. 135.

The use of these reclining places is ancient. Since the early Christians used to celebrate communal meals, as signs and inducements of mutual charity—which they therefore called *ἀγάπαι*—with one another on the principal solemnities of the year, and consequently even within the churches themselves, this practice was later disapproved with respect to the place where the meals were held.

For it was forbidden by frequent canons of councils to “eat together and …” or “hold agapes” within the sacred buildings themselves, as may be observed from the Council of Laodicea, canon 28; the Council in Trullo, canon 74; the Council of Auxerre, chapter 9; the Council of Aachen, chapter 80; St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, in the *Capitularies*, chapter 21; and Atto, bishop of Basel, in the *Capitularies*, chapter 22. Such practices had a certain pagan character, since it was customary among pagans to hold public banquets in their temples during their festivals, as Ammianus, Book XX, and Tertullian, *On Banquets*, teach.

These solemn meals subsequently began to be celebrated not in the churches, but in buildings attached to them for this purpose, which they named after the reclining couches. Anastasius the Librarian mentions this custom, which was introduced later, especially in his account of Pope Leo IV, p. 178, where he observes that such meals were particularly celebrated at the Nativity of Christ.

The same Anastasius mentions such dining buildings attached to churches in his accounts of Gregory III, p. 74, and Leo III, pp. 129 and 178. CANGIUS, *Constantinople Sacred*, p. 130.

### Note 36. “Christ, the fish of living water”

Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 1:

“But we little fishes, after the example of our Fish, Jesus Christ, are born in the water.”

Optatus, Book III *Against Parmenianus*, concerning Christ:

“This is the fish who, through invocation, is introduced into the waters of the font at baptism, so that what had been water may also be called a pool from the fish. The name of this fish, according to the Greek designation, contains within one word, through its individual letters, a host of holy names: for *ἰχθύς* in Latin is Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.”

Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 23, refers this to the prophecy of the Erythraean or Cumaean Sibyl:

“If you join the first letters of these five Greek words, *Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτήρ*, which in Latin are ‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior,’ they form *ἰχθύς*, that is, ‘fish.’ In this name Christ is mystically understood, because in the abyss of this mortality, as in the depth of the waters, he was able to remain alive—that is, without sin.”

The Greek verses in which these words are represented acrostically by the Sibyl can be found in Eusebius’s *Oration of Constantine*, chapter 18.

Bede, on Luke 24:

“What else are we to understand by the roasted fish except the mediator between God and human beings, the man who suffered? Having deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race, he wished to be caught in the snare of our death and, as it were, roasted in tribulation at the time of his Passion.”

The same author, on John 20: “The roasted fish is Christ who suffered.”

For an explanation of how the spiritual person is a roasted fish, see Athanasius, in the work circulated under his name, Question 79.

To remind Christians of Christ or of baptism, Clement of Alexandria once advised them, in Book III of the *Instructor*, chapter 11, to have a fish engraved on their rings. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 37. “You were presenting a spectacle, a sacred producer”

I hope I shall be forgiven if, since there is incidental mention here of a producer of spectacles, I call attention to a passage in 2 Maccabees 4:19, where the five-year contest at Tyre is discussed. The Greek text reads:

“The impious Jason sent *θεωρούς* as envoys from Jerusalem to Antioch, carrying three hundred silver drachmas for the sacrifice of Heracles.” The old Latin version reads: “The wicked Jason sent from Jerusalem sinful men carrying three hundred silver didrachms for the sacrifice of Hercules.”

I greatly fear that something is defective in “sinful men.” I suspect that the translator wrote *spectatores*, “spectators,” intending thereby to render the Greek *θεωρούς*, deriving it from *θεᾶν*, “to look upon.” The oldest manuscripts and editions likewise have this reading.

The Sixtine edition, prepared by Cardinal Caraffa, translates *θεωρούς* as “ministers”; the Plantin edition gives more fully, “agents of sacred affairs.”

*Θεωροί* means both “spectators” and “producers of spectacles,” or administrators of sacred matters. The latter meaning suits this passage.

Hesychius: “*Θεωροί*: those who consult oracles, spectators, and those who care for sacred things.”

Again: “*Θεωρούς*: observers, inspectors.”

Suidas: “*Θεωροί*: those sent to sacrifices and festivals.”

Again: “They are called *θεωροί* not only the spectators, but also those sent to God [whether to produce games or to consult oracles], and in general those who guard or take care of divine matters; for they called care itself *ὤρη*.”

Pollux, Book I, chapter 1, §18:

“Properly, the oracle from Delphi is called Pythian, and those who consult it are called *θεωροί*.”

More precisely, the Pythian oracle at Delphi and those who consult it are called *θεωροί*.

The same author, Book II, chapter 4, §7:

“For those who go to Pytho are *θεωροί*, and the road to the oracle and the ship called a *theoris* derive their names from going, hastening, or traveling toward God.”

For those who go to Apollo at Pytho are *θεωροί*, that is, spectators—or rather, consultants of oracles. The road is called the “spectator’s road,” and the ship a *theoris*, because it is driven, hastens, or travels toward God.

When I once proposed this conjecture of mine to our Serarius, he immediately condemned his own suggestion, by which he had proposed reading *precatores*, “supplicants.” Prevented by death, however, he could not correct it. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 38. “From this purse of yours, as the saying goes”

This is spoken proverbially when someone does something at his own expense. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 39. “And shining from afar with the apostolic throne”

Take care not to understand *solium* here as the apostolic seat or chair. He means the place where the bodies of the apostles are buried.

Thus Paulinus writes in *Natale* 9, p. 609:

“Felix, who shines before the threshold of his radiant throne.”

And in a fragment of *Natale* 9, concerning the humbler tomb of Felix of Nola:

“And the gathered throng from various lands continually worships the small throne of the great confessor.”

And in the poem transcribed by P. Sirmond from the suburban church of St. Felix and appended to Sidonius, Book IV, Epistle 18:

“Thus also honoring the throne of beloved Felix.”

Ambrose calls this a lofty floor, in the Christian monuments published by Gruter, concerning the throne of Nazarius:

“And the lofty floor with the martyr’s remains.”

This place was also called a confession. The Roman Martyrology, on the day before the Nones of July: “When he was praying at the confession of Blessed Paul on the eighth day of the Apostles.”

Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book X, Epistle 2:

“We possess something belonging specifically to the apostles, provided that it is not made alien by the divisions of sin, since fortunate Rome has deserved to have within her territory those confessions which the whole world longs to see.”

The word is frequently used by Anastasius the Librarian, for example in his accounts of Pope Hilary, Sixtus, and others.

This place was in the apse. Evodius, Book I, chapter 3 of *The Miracles of Blessed Stephen*:

“When the relics had been placed in the apse above the veiled chair.”

Gregory of Tours, *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 96:

“He was seated before the glass apse in which the holy limbs of Albinus were enclosed.”

The same author, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, in his account of Gregory, bishop of Langres, whose relics Bishop Tetricus wished to transfer:

“He laid the foundations before the altar of the basilica, constructed an apse with marvelous workmanship, and vaulted it.”

Nor was it far from the altar, since according to the ancient custom the bodies of martyrs were buried beneath the altar, in accordance with the passage in Revelation 6:

“I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony that they bore.”

Hence Anastasius the Librarian joins the confession to the altar in his account of Sixtus III:

“He made the confession of Blessed Lawrence the martyr with porphyry columns, and adorned the screen, the altar, and the confession of the holy martyr Lawrence with the purest silver.” ROSWEYDUS.

See Note 304.

### Note 40. “Why, gleaming in the outspread atrium”

This was a marble portico, now largely ruined, of quadrangular form, which Pope Domnus adorned with such magnificence that it was called a paradise.

Paul the Deacon describes the place in Book V, chapter 31:

“Domnus, pontiff of the Roman Church, magnificently paved with white marble stones the place called Paradise, before the basilica of Blessed Peter.”

Attilius Serranus says the same in chapter 1 of *The Seven Churches of Rome*, where he discusses St. Peter’s church in the Vatican.

I do not know whether that place came to be called Paradise for this reason from the time of Domnus, or Donus, the pope. Anastasius has a statement comparable to that of the Deacon in his account of Donus [Col. 0649C]:

“He paved with great marble stones the upper atrium of Blessed Peter the Apostle, called Paradise, which is before the church and forms a four-sided portico.”

Aimoinus repeats this in almost the same words in Book IV, chapter 35.

Leo Marsicanus also mentions the Paradise before St. Peter’s church in Book II, chapter 9 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, while discussing the burial place of the emperor Otto II:

“Returning to Rome, he died at that same time and was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus in the atrium of the church of Blessed Peter the Apostle, on the left as one enters the church itself, in Paradise.”

The epigram found in Gruter’s inscriptions, p. 1173, under the heading “In the Paradise of Blessed Peter,” should also be referred to the atrium or Paradise of the Vatican church. Read the explanation of Paradise in the following verses:

“Although illustrious faith, with much light from the hall,

and the merits of the place, ennoble the work still more,

nevertheless these beautiful things possess a special grace,

and precious art captures the eyes of those who behold them.

John adorned this work, whom the summit

of the city’s pontifical office duly crowns.”

[Col. 0849D] Likewise, in the Lateran church, under the same heading, “In the Paradise,” there are four different epigrams in which porticoes and fountains are mentioned.

By Roman custom, the atrium before a church was called this even elsewhere outside Rome. Leo Marsicanus, Book III, chapter 26 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, concerning the church of Monte Cassino rebuilt, or rather constructed, by Abbot Desiderius:

“He also made an atrium before the church, which by Roman custom we call Paradise.”

The same author, Book IV, chapter 8, while discussing Elgaita, the wife of Duke Robert, who wished to be buried there:

“She asked to be buried in the Paradise of the church, before the basilica of the Apostle Peter.”

Likewise, the spacious area—as James de Bruel notes in his commentary on Aimoinus—which lies in Paris before the principal church of Blessed Mary and is commonly called *le parvis*, is called Paradise in the ancient charters of that place. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 41. “The *cantharus*, ministering to hands and mouths”

Josephus Vicecomes, Book I of *On the Ancient Rites of Baptism*, chapter 6, cites this passage as referring to the baptistery of the Vatican church, since Paulinus says that it stood in the atrium or vestibule, where baptisteries were formerly erected.

But since Paulinus himself specifies the use of this water—namely, washing the hands and mouths—it is clear that this was a different fountain from the baptistery. Accordingly, Baronius, in volume IV of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 384, the eighteenth year of Pope Damasus, the ninth of Valentinian, and the sixth of the emperors Theodosius, believed that Prudentius had led him to identify the baptismal fountain of the Vatican church at the tomb of St. Peter. He therefore recognizes here another fountain, distinct from the baptismal one, which he likewise attributes to the work of Damasus.

Josephus is similarly mistaken when he applies this passage to Sidonius, Book II, Epistle 2 to Domitius:

“An exterior pool, or, if you prefer a Greek term, a baptistery, adjoins this basilica on the eastern side.”

These are ornaments of a private villa. He gave it the name “basilica,” but here the word does not mean a church; it signifies a private and magnificent house.

Among the ancient Christians it was common to have fountains or *canthari* before a church for washing the hands and mouth. Eusebius, Book X, chapter 4:

“He placed there symbols of sacred purifications, setting up fountains directly in front of the temple, providing an abundant flow of water, so that those proceeding inward into the precincts of the sacred enclosure might wash themselves.”

Fountains flowing from the front of the temple were installed, overflowing with water, so that all who entered the sacred precincts of the temple might wash away the dirt from their bodies [883]; these fountains represented the holy washing of baptism.

In the same way Leo constructed a fountain with a *cantharus* before the basilica of St. Paul outside the Ostian Gate for this purpose. Our Sirmondus was the first to publish the following eight-line poem concerning it in his edition of Ennodius:

“The water washes away the stains of the flesh, but faith,

purer than the stream, cleanses sins

and purifies souls.

Whoever enters the venerable shrine of Paul,

approaching with your own merits, humbly wash your hands in the fountain.

Long neglect had deprived the water of its flow;

now the *cantharus* pours it forth for you with full mouth.

The provident care of the shepherd Leo

has given these abundant streams to the sheep of Christ.”

Ennodius’s poem 149, entitled *On the Fountain of the Baptistery of St. Stephen and the Water Flowing through the Columns*, should be understood as referring to a similar fountain. Such fountains were arranged in temple atria for the use of those entering.

Paulinus himself writes above, in Epistle 12:

“The gleaming *cantharus* bathes the sacred courts with its waters and washes the hands of the entering people with its ministering stream.”

For formerly Christians washed their hands before the doors of the temple, so that they might be reminded of inward purity. Tertullian suggests this in *On Prayer*, chapter 11:

“What reason is there to pray with hands washed but with the spirit defiled?”

Among the pagans also, temples once had shrines with such fountains. Isidore, Book XV, chapter 4:

“The ancients called those temples *delubra* which had fountains where people washed before entering; they were called *delubra* from washing.”

This is taken directly from Servius on *Aeneid* II:

“Some say that a *delubrum* is the place before a temple where water flows, from washing.”

Likewise, on *Aeneid* IV:

“It was called a *delubrum* because of the pool in which hands are washed.”

The poets’ books are full of descriptions of this pagan rite.

Among Christians, the fountains placed before temples were later replaced by a vessel of holy water, intended to cleanse lighter sins, customarily placed at the vestibule of the temple, with which the faithful sprinkled their faces.

Such a basin appears to be the one recently excavated at Constantinople and reproduced in Gruter’s *Inscriptions*, p. 1046, no. 9, bearing this inscription:

“Wash away sins, not only the face.”

This was taken from Book VI, chapter 13 of the *Anthology of Ancient Epigrams*, as the most learned Rigaltius observed. It appears there among the “crab” verses, composed with remarkable skill by retracing, so that the same verses can be read backward without changing the letters. Sidonius calls such verses *recurrentes*.

This poem was written on the tomb of Diomedes. I believe that he was St. Diomedes the physician, since sickness is mentioned there; he suffered martyrdom at Nicaea during the time of Diocletian. His memory is celebrated in the Greek *Menologion* on 16 August, and from there in the Roman Martyrology.

Cedrenus, in his account of Basil, mentions a temple erected at Constantinople to the martyr Diomedes, which Basil adorned with the most splendid gifts. ROSWEYDUS.

See Note 304.

### Note 42. “With four columns”

At the time of Paulinus this *cantharus* was indeed surrounded by four columns. But afterward Symmachus adorned it with eight porphyry columns, as it is seen today. Attilius Serranus says this in the place cited.

Anastasius, in his account of Symmachus, gives only the following: “He adorned the *cantharus* of Blessed Peter, together with the four-sided portico, with marble.”

The Bertinian manuscript of Anastasius, in the account of Stephen—where the book also ends—adds the following unpublished words after “having completed”:

“Meanwhile, in the atrium before the doors of Blessed Peter the Apostle, which is called the four-sided portico, he restored eight marble columns of extraordinary beauty, carved and arranged above in squares, and placed a bronze covering above them.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 43. “Surpassing piety in holiness.”

In the editions of Badius and Gravius, the reading is *civitate pietatem* (“piety by citizenship”); but in the Paris edition it was emended—perhaps by a typographical corrector—to *pietate civitatem* (“the city by piety”). The very learned Cauchius conjectured that the reading should be *ipsam superans pietate pietatem* (“surpassing piety itself in piety”). The true reading of manuscript P. is *sanctitate pietatem* (“piety in holiness”), evidently referring to what he said shortly before: that he preferred justice born of charity to domestic piety. He evidently chose to look after the chastity of his guests rather than that of his daughters, as paternal affection urged. DUC.

### Note 44. “The labors of the fruits.”

He translated it as it appears in Hilary, Augustine, Prosper, Cassiodorus, and the Old Psalter. The difference arises from the ambiguous word *καρπῶν* (*karpōn*), which signifies the junction of the hand with the elbow, and also “fruit.” Jerome, Letter 141: “When the Latin translators, deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, interpreted *καρπούς* as ‘fruits’ rather than ‘hands’”; but in the Gallican Psalter and the Latin Vulgate, *Τοὺς πόνους τῶν καρπῶν σου φάγεσαι* is translated, “You shall eat the labors of your hands,” and Jerome likewise translates it from the Hebrew. DUC.

### Note 45. “It has been sealed.”

Wisdom 2:5: *Σκιᾶς γὰρ πάροδος ὁ καιρὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀναποδισμὸς τῆς τελευτῆς ἡμῶν, ὅτι κατεσφραγίσθη, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἀναστρέφει.* “For our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no reversal of our end, because it has been sealed, and no one returns.” Thus the Latin Vulgate, and it referred the verb *ἐσφραγίσθη* (“was sealed”) to *ἀναποδισμός*, which means “return,” not “impediment,” as it was printed in the Basel Bibles. Paulinus, however, referred it to *τελευτή*, “end,” saying that the end had been sealed—a metaphor, as Vatablus says, drawn from things that are sealed in order to make them valid and secure. Thus the end is said to be sealed because it cannot be changed, and the return is closed off, since, as the poet says, “from there they deny that anyone returns,” nor is one allowed to retrace one’s steps from death. DUC.

## IN LETTER XV

### Note 46. “To become intoxicated.”

The passage appears to have been taken, like several others, from St. Ambrose, who says in Book I, near the end, *On Faith to Gratian*: “The cup that gladdens the human heart intoxicates sobriety, exhales the drunkenness of faith and true religion, and pours in the drunkenness of chastity.” I have also read in him, “It intoxicates unto sobriety.” SACCHINUS.

### Note 47. “Toward evening . . . . . sad from hunger for the midday meal, we might be appeased by the refreshment of the evening meal.”

It was customary among the ancients to refresh the body only once each day, toward nightfall. See Book I of St. Augustine’s *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, chapter 33, volume I.

## IN LETTER XVI

### Note 48. “Of illustrious men among generals or philosophers.”

ROSWEYDUS, “in indexes”: “I do not understand it.” Stephanus Claverius, commenting on Claudian here, thinks that “indexes” signifies nothing other than the titles and coats of arms of nobility. Tibullus:

> What each index signifies beneath the image.

But what if we read the whole passage as follows? “By whom the outstanding virtues of illustrious men among generals or philosophers are remembered as having shone forth into noble fame only through labors and dangers.” Philosophers, certainly, shone through labors; generals, through dangers. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 49. “The furthest lines of truth.”

ROSWEYDUS reads *extremae* (“of the furthest”) rather than *extremas* (“the furthest”). Is *extremas* correct? Terence, *The Eunuch*, Act IV, scene 2:

> Certainly, at the farthest line,  
> To love is not nothing.

Nannius, *Miscellanea*, Book I, chapter 20, explains this as “at the furthest rank or order.” “It is,” he says, “that part of the theater where the spectators sit, first divided into wedges, and then into rows, as though into separate partitions, so that if crowding should arise anywhere it might not flood the whole theater and afflict all the spectators.” Hence Ovid’s phrase to a girl avoiding another’s company:

> The line compels us to be joined.

Thus *ultima linea* means “the last row,” whence also:

> Death, the final line of all things.

Erasmus and others explain it differently, writing about the circus; those authors should be consulted by anyone eager to investigate the matter. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 50. “As though with mutilated senses.”

ROSWEYDUS’s edition reads *carens sensibus* (“lacking senses”). Thus it is found in the Vatican manuscript and in Fabricius’s edition, before the reading *quasi truncis sensibus* (“as though with mutilated senses”) was published. The latter, however, is also correct. Claudian, *The Gothic War*:

> Surely the kingdom will fall to the Rhone,  
> Though the city has been granted to northern peoples,  
> And a trunk will survive, deprived of its head.

Curtius, Book VII: “He ordered the trunk to be buried after the head had been cut off.”

### Note 51. “I suffer from abundance.”

In Greek, *ἐκ περιουσίας* means “out of abundance.” Nor is Claverius’s reading, *Patior esse copiam* (“I suffer that there is abundance”), necessary. Thus Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, Book I, chapter 6: *Ἔξεστι δὲ ἡμῖν ἐκ περιουσίας πρὸς τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας ἐπαποδύσασθαι.* “It is permitted us, as though from an overflowing abundance, to engage those who delight in finding fault with others.” ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XVII

### Note 52. “In the seat and bosom of Lord Felix.”

Among writers of the Middle Ages, learned men long ago observed that the title *domnus*—formed by removing one letter from *Dominus*, “Lord”—was held in special veneration and was commonly bestowed upon those holding ecclesiastical office or distinguished by holiness of life. Thus Gregory the Great, Paulinus of Nola, Evodius, Fortunatus, Nicetius of Trier, Avitus of Vienne, Gregory of Tours, Ennodius, Ivo of Chartres, and others frequently apply it to bishops. CANGIUS, *Glossary*, vol. II, p. 161, no. 1.

### Note 53. “In every place, while.”

In the prophet Isaiah 58:9, we read only this in the Septuagint: *Ἔτι λαλοῦντός σου ἐρεῖ, Ἰδοὺ πάρειμι.* “While you are still speaking, he will say, ‘Behold, I am here.’”

Chrysostom, in his homily *On Various New Testament Passages*, 28, “What Sort of Wives Should Be Taken,” quotes it somewhat differently, as though it read *λαλοῦντός σου ἐρῶ*, “While you are speaking, I shall say.” In his homilies on Psalm 4 and in Homily 79 among those that follow the homilies to the Antiochenes, he likewise cites this passage of the prophet in the same sense, to show that God hears prayers in every place, although he does not add the words “in every place” as though they belonged to the text of Scripture: “For is there a human being from whom you must request a place? God is always near. For while you are still speaking, I shall say, ‘Behold, I am here.’ Whether you are in the forum, or on the road, or wherever you may be, by invoking God you can obtain what you ask.” It is likewise cited by Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 3. DUC.

## IN LETTER XVIII

### Note 54. “To Victricius.”

He was the eighth among the bishops of Rouen, whose memory is celebrated in the Roman Calendar on 7 August: “At Rouen, Saint Victricius, bishop, who, while still a soldier under the same Julian, cast aside his military belt for Christ, was subjected to many tortures by the tribune, and condemned to death. But when the executioner who had been sent to kill him was struck blind, he himself escaped free after his bonds had been removed. Later, having become bishop, he led the untamed peoples of the Morini and Nervii to faith in Christ by preaching the word, and finally rested in peace as a confessor.” These details are sketched from Paulinus’s Letter 18 to Victricius. A decretal letter of Pope Innocent also survives, addressed to him, as Letter 2. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 55. “Like Paschasius.”

DUC.: The manuscript P. more correctly reads *pare Paschasio*, that is, “as his companion and comrade,” just as the same Paulinus says in Letter 12 to Severus:

> Those whom God, after long ages, reveals to his Ambrose,  
> Protasius together with his companion Gervasius.

ROSWEYDUS: The reading *patre* (“father”) may be retained. For Paschasius truly was Ursus’s spiritual father. A little earlier: “For, begotten through the hands of this very man, he returned baptized in his little bed.” Thus Paulinus also calls Delphinus, who had administered baptism to him, his father.

### Note 56. “Your Tychicus.”

Thus the Vatican and Vienna manuscripts. DUC: Manuscript P. reads *Tyticus tuus*, “your Tyticus.” I therefore suspect that *Tychicus* should be read, as in the Apostle, Ephesians 6:21: “Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you.” DUC.

### Note 57. “In the land of the Morini.”

Augustine appears to refer to this in Letter 80 to Hesychius: “We now know that the Church has already reached even the shores of the Ocean in the western regions.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 58. “Of the Nervian shore.”

This reading must be retained, since the manuscripts agree. Thus we find *Nervicanus tractus* (“the Nervian district”) and *Nervicanus limes* (“the Nervian frontier”) in the *Notitia of the Empire*. It should not be changed to *Ebruicanus*, as Scaliger thought in Book II, chapters 6 and 14, of his *Readings on Ausonius*, and as our Brouwer subsequently did in his notes on Fortunatus, Book III, poem 8. Just as Paulinus’s published reading gives light to the *Notitia*, so the *Notitia* gives light to Paulinus.

Our Brouwer also cites from the Acts of Saints Quintinus, Crispinianus, and Macra, Rictius Varus, prefect of the Nervian frontier. Ortelius likewise prefers the Nervian shore to the Ebruican shore in his *Geographical Thesaurus*, as does Velserus in his explanation of the first Peutinger map, chapter 5. I also see that in the later edition of his *Readings on Ausonius*, Scaliger omitted the entire passage about the Ebruican shore in chapter 6, although he retained it in chapter 14. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 59. “And the tribune, aroused to madness immediately by the envy of the ancient serpent.”

Thus in Revelation 20:2: “The ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan.” The words *antiquus* (“ancient”) and *vetustus* (“old, ancient”) frequently occur in the books of the early Christian theologians when the devil is being discussed.

Paulinus of Nola himself, speaking of the same being, uses the expression in Letter 1, no. 8, “the head of the ancient dragon”; in Letter 13 to Pammachius, no. 15, “the bloody savagery of the ancient dragon”; in the *Natale* of St. Felix 4, verse 157, “ancient serpent”; and in *Natale* 7, verse 83, “the older enemy.”

The other Paulinus, of Petricordia, writes in Book III of *The Life and Miracles of Saint Martin*:

> He said to the ancient serpent, “Stretching . . . . .”

And in Book VI:

> As the ancient serpent seized the poison of the curse.

The holy Fathers use the same expression. St. Leo the Great, Sermon 3 *On Lent*: “The ancient enemy never ceases to spread the snares of sin everywhere before us”; and in the letter to Demetrias, attributed elsewhere to St. Prosper: “The ancient enemy rages more wickedly.”

Jerome, in his letter to Theophilus: “No longer does the ancient serpent hiss.” Augustine, on Psalm 30: “We have another enemy, the devil, the ancient serpent.” Gregory the Great, Homily 27 on the Gospels: “When doing these things, the ancient enemy does not care to remove earthly things, but to strike charity in us”; and similarly a little earlier. Also Homily 34 on the Gospels, near the beginning: “That ancient enemy who desired through pride to be like God”; and so very frequently in the *Moralia*.

Bernard, Sermon 1 *On Holy Easter*, near the beginning:

> Do you not remember, ancient serpent,  
> How confused you departed long ago  
> When you had dared to say, “Cast yourself down”?

### Note 60. “The brilliant purple robes of confessors.”

The word *confessor* is often used with various meanings. It frequently denotes those who publicly confessed Christ before tyrants, were subjected to some form of punishment, and, having survived, died a peaceful death. Sometimes it denotes singers and psalmists, who occupy a lower rank among the clergy, as in canon 11 of the Council of Carthage and in the Sacramentary of St. Gregory the Great. At times it also denotes monks who, in order to expiate their sins, undertake confession or penance and, having renounced secular life, enter the monastic life. Occasionally it is used for the confessor to whom sins are disclosed.

Here, however, it chiefly refers to those confessors who ended their lives by martyrdom for Christ, whom they had publicly confessed and proclaimed.

Besides John of Antioch and the Eastern synod, in the letter to Cyril cited by Facundus of Hermiane in Book VIII, St. Ambrose says in Book II *To the Emperor Gratian*: “Already, almighty God, by our destruction and our blood we have sufficiently washed away the slaughter of confessors, the exiles of priests, and the crime of such great impiety.”

## IN LETTER XIX

### Note 61. “Uranius.”

Baronius, volume V, under the year A.D. 431, thinks that this Uranius was the man who, as a disciple of Paulinus, commended his death to posterity in a written record. His account survives in Surius, volume III of *The Lives of the Saints*, under 22 June. ROSWEYDUS.

See this account immediately after the encomia, before the Life of St. Paulinus.

## IN LETTER XX

### Note 62. “That Anastasius was most devoted to our humility.”

Baronius, volume V, under the year A.D. 398, in the fourth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, writes of Pope Anastasius I: “Meanwhile, Pope Anastasius, at the very beginning of his pontificate, took great care to correct as soon as possible those things that he had learned had been improperly done during the time of his predecessor. For since he knew—as has been said in its proper place—that Siricius, whom he succeeded, had treated St. Paulinus, a most distinguished man who had embraced the monastic life together with his wife Therasia and withdrawn to the territory of Nola, somewhat ungenerously, as soon as he had been raised to the papal throne he sent most courteous letters to the bishops on Paulinus’s behalf. Thereafter he never missed any opportunity of visiting him with every kind of service.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 63. “On his own anniversary.”

Just as emperors formerly celebrated the beginning or anniversary of their reign, so Roman pontiffs were accustomed to celebrate the anniversary of their see or episcopate.

Pope Sixtus, in a letter to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, in A.D. 430: “The whole brotherhood has gathered at the blessed apostle Peter: behold an audience assembled in harmony, suited to those who are to hear. Our co-bishops had him as a witness of their rejoicing, whom we have as the beginning of our honor. For he himself presided over the holy and venerable synod that my anniversary had gathered, with the Lord’s favor—for so it must be believed.”

The same pope, in a letter to John, bishop of Antioch: “The whole brotherhood that had gathered for my anniversary heard how, with me presiding over the Apostolic See, they rejoiced in the good of the human race.”

Pope Hilary, in a letter to the bishops of the province of Tarragona: “When your letters had been read at the gathering of the brothers whom the celebration of my anniversary had assembled.”

This celebration was counted among the solemn occasions, as is shown by what Anastasius the Librarian reports in the *Life of Hadrian I*: “Finally, his blessedness also made a larger lamp in the same church of Blessed Peter in the form of a cross, hanging before the presbytery and containing one thousand three hundred and seventy candles. And he established that this lamp should be lit four times a year: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, on the anniversary of the apostles, and on the anniversary of the pontiff.”

On the first anniversary of the see, sermons were delivered by the bishops themselves. Thus Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 7; likewise Gregory of Nyssa, volume II of his works; Chrysostom, volume V of his works; and Ennodius, *Sacred Speech* 5. Sometimes they were praised in panegyrics by others: thus Bishop Peter by Chrysologus in Sermon 107, and Laurentius, bishop of Milan, by Ennodius in *Sacred Speech* 1. Indeed, bishops also delivered a sermon on the yearly anniversary of their see. Augustine, Homilies 24 and 25 from Book I of the *Homilies*; Leo, Sermons 1, 2, and 3. Likewise, in the thirtieth year of the anniversary of Epiphanius’s priesthood or episcopate, Speech 9 was delivered by Ennodius in Book I of the *Poems*. See Ferrarius, Book II *On the Rite of Sacred Sermons*, chapter 35.

However the anniversaries of individual bishops may have been celebrated among their own people, only the anniversary or see of Peter was venerated by all. Augustine, Sermon 15 *On the Saints*, on the feast of the Chair of St. Peter: “The institution of today’s solemnity received the name ‘chair’ from our elders, because it is reported that Peter, the first of the apostles, received the chair of the episcopate on this day. Rightly, therefore, the churches celebrate the anniversary of that see which the Apostle accepted for the salvation of the churches.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 64. “If the Lord grants a period of leave.”

*Commeatus* means a span or period of time, as in the same Paulinus, Letter 10 to Delphinus, no. 3: “He begged the Lord of the vineyard for a respite for the barren fig tree.” It also means permission or the opportunity to carry something out; sometimes it means permission to depart, as in Letter 49 to Macarius, no. 1; at other times it is used for refreshment. But among Christian writers it very often means an extension of life, or an opportunity obtained from God to prolong life. This passage must be understood in the last sense, as also in Letter 50 to Augustine, no. 14: “Christ granting me and you a period of days,” and most clearly in Letter 13 to Pammachius, no. 8: “Because he could obtain a period of life for his son who was still breathing.” Paulinus the other uses it in the same sense in the *Life of St. Ambrose*. Marius Mercator, *Notes*, chapter 7: “But if God grants a prolongation of life and allows time for revising these excellent books of yours . . . . .” St. Fulgentius, Letter 1 *On the Marriage Debt*: “I was so suddenly seized by a bodily illness that the violent excess of the fever would have taken away from me the extension of my present life, unless, and so forth.”

### Note 65. “To the Church of Alingon.”

The other passage in Letter 21 to Amandus must be emended from this place: “deign to send one of the Alingon people.” For there is a port of Alingon, of which Sidonius Apollinaris writes in Letter 12 of Book VIII to Trigetius: “After this you tread the port of Alingon so slowly, as though you now had to set out for the Danubian frontier against the incursions of the Massagetae.”

Today it is called Lengon, a town situated on the left bank of the Garonne as it flows toward the Ocean, seven leagues from Bordeaux. It now belongs to the diocese of the bishop of Bazas, not to that of the archbishop of Bordeaux; as for civil authority, it belongs to the counts of Bénauge and Candale, after it was transferred to them by the soldier Arnaldus Gartia through hereditary succession or purchase.

Gabriel Lurbaeus writes in his *Chronicle of Bordeaux* that as early as A.D. 1170 the town of Lengon had been granted under feudal tenure by the college of canons of the church of St. Severinus, built in the suburb of Bordeaux, to the same Gratia and his descendants, on the condition that they pay twelve lampreys each year to that college on the appointed day.

Thus, although this town was taken from the successors of St. Amand, the archbishops, and withdrawn from their ecclesiastical jurisdiction, it nevertheless returned to the successors of St. Paulinus, whose civil authority governs it, since the same counts of Candale are lords of that fief and residence which once belonged to the Paulini and which is still called the “Height of Paulinus” at Bordeaux. Under that name they hold the foremost place among the citizens of Bordeaux.

The village called Alinganiensis, which Ortelius cites from Gregory of Tours, has no relevance here; it is located in the territory of the city of Tours, not near the Garonne, in chapter 16 of the *Miracles*. DUC.

## IN LETTER XXII

### Note 66. “Let him keep his armilausa for himself.”

Paulinus also used this type of expression, *sibi ergo habeat armilausam* (“let him keep his armilausa for himself”), elsewhere, as in Letter 4: “Let the Jews, in the flesh alone, keep for themselves their arrogance, their riches, their nobility, and their own righteousness; for us Christ is sufficient for salvation”; and in Letter 6: “Let them keep their wisdom and their happiness for themselves; let them leave us our poverty, as they suppose it to be, and our foolishness”; and in Letter 29: “Let orators keep their literature for themselves, philosophers their wisdom, the rich their riches, kings their kingdoms; for us Christ is glory, possession, and kingdom.”

He imitates Plautus, in whose *Curculio* the young Phaedromus says:

> Let kings keep their kingdoms for themselves, the rich their riches;  
> Let them keep their honors, their virtues, their contests, their battles,  
> So long as they refrain from begrudging me.

In the same author, the household Lar delivers the prologue in the *Aulularia*, and this is mentioned at the end of the letter. But the following words of Aeneas bidding farewell to Helenus are from Virgil, *Aeneid* III:

> Live happily, you whose fortune  
> Has already run its course.

DUC.

### Note 67. “His armilausa.”

He used this same word in Letter 13: “Since, moreover, his face was no less red than an armilausa.” Isidore counts it among kinds of clothing in Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22: “The garment commonly called *armelausa*, because it is divided and open in front and behind, and closed only at the shoulders, as though *armiclausa*, with the letter *c* removed.”

The old interpreter of Juvenal, Satire 5, verse 143: “A green cuirass, a green armilausa.” The learned Rigaltius cites a passage of Mauritius from the *Strategics*, from which we infer that it was a kind of shorter military garment. Accordingly, Paulinus assigns military—not monastic—boots to this courier.

Thus Mauritius writes: *Ποῖα δεῖ φορεῖν ἱμάτια τοὺς πεζούς, εἴτε ζωστήρια Γοτθικὰ, εἴτε ἀρμελαύσια ἔχουσι . . . μέχρι τῶν γονάτων.* “What clothing should infantrymen wear, whether Gothic girdles or armelausia . . . reaching to the knees?”

Suidas, in the *Etymologicum*: *Ἀρμελαύσιον παρὰ τὸ ἄρμα τὸ ἐπάνω τῶν ὅπλων.* “An armelausion, from the *arma*, the covering worn over weapons.”

It is therefore clear that this garment did not extend below the knees and was similar to the garment worn by cavalrymen over their armor, distinguished by their insignia, which is commonly called a coat of arms, *cotte d’armes*. DUC.

### “Armilausa.”

An armilausa is a military cloak worn over the cuirass. Paulinus likewise makes it a military garment here and in Letter 13: “Since, moreover, his face was no less red than an armilausa.”

The *Passion of St. Boniface the Martyr*, published by Holstenius: “He is a square-built man . . . dressed in a scarlet armelausia.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Gregory II, p. 70, concerning Liutprand, king of the Lombards: “And thus he was moved by pious admonitions to such great contrition that he removed what he had been wearing and placed before the body of the Apostle his cloak, armilausa, belt, sword, and gilded blade.”

Some have also given the canons’ *almucia* the name *armilausium*. CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, vol. I, p. 336.

### Note 68. “Nor with a short chlamys.”

Nonius shows that the *chlamys* was properly a military garment when he writes that it was called a *paludamentum*; so does Herodian, Book VII: *Πορφυρᾷ χλαμίδι περιβαλεῖν*—“to clothe the emperor in a purple military cloak,” as the soldiers said. Plautus also introduces a soldier wearing a chlamys in the *Pseudolus*.

We therefore infer that these *curtalini* had served in the military, as the jurists also indicate when they cite Law 14 *On the Privileges of Those in the Sacred Palace*, where the military service of the *cohortalini* is mentioned, as well as Law 26 *On the Cohortals of the Emperors* and Law 3 *On the Officials of Provincial Governors*. For *cohortalini* were attendants and officials of magistrates who governed the provinces.

Brissonius also cites an old Glossary: *Cohortalinus, εὐτελὴς θυρωρὸς τοῦ πραιτωρίου*, that is, “a lowly doorkeeper of the praetorium.”

The outstanding jurist Cujacius, writing on Book X of the Code, title 23, likewise says that *cohortales* were the permanent attendants of governors. He then cites a passage from Book XLV of the *Basilica*, title 1, where Thalelaeus, following Patricius, defines *cohortalini* as *beneficiarii* who care for the stations of horses: *Ὁ δὲ μακαρίτης Πατρίκιος τοὺς κορταλίνους καλεῖ μὲν beneficiaros, λέγει δὲ φροντίζειν αὐτοὺς τῶν ἀλλαγῶν τῶν ἵππων.* “The late Patricius calls the *cortalini* *beneficiarii*, and says that they take care of the changing of the horses.”

The *cortalini* are therefore the same people who are called *cohortalini* in the Code. For what the older Latin authors called *cohors* or *chors*—namely, an enclosed place on an estate, surrounded by buildings, in which livestock is kept in confinement—later writers called *curtis*, that is, a part of an estate or the estate itself.

Thus in the books of the Feudal Law, those who sell an estate are said to sell a *curtis* or *allodium*. Likewise Godefridus the monk writes in his *Annals*: “Hidden in a certain estate of the monks of Evera.” In the Bavarian Laws, chapter 14: “If anyone enters another’s estate”; and in the Alemannic Laws, title 10, Helmodus, cited by Fr. Hotomanus in his book *On Feuds*, *History of the Slavs*, Book I, chapter 14: “Besides other things, he possessed two noble estates”; and chapter 32: “The king was staying in the royal estate of Hilgelstein.” The abbot of Ursperg likewise uses the word in his account of Frederick I.

As the same Hotomanus notes, *curtis* is used for an estate, just as things are often named from their principal part. Then magnificent rural houses were also called *curtes*, as were royal estates—the palaces of princes in towns and cities. Hence later Greek historians and jurists also called the imperial court *κόρτη* and *κούρτη*.
