Codinus, *On the Offices of Constantinople*: *Ὑπηρετοῦσι δὲ οἱ κορτινάριοι εἰς τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως σκηνὴν ἥτις κόρτη ὀνομάζεται.* “The *cortinarii* serve in the emperor’s tent, which is called a *corte*.”

Thus, just as authors confuse *cohors* and *curtis*, it is probable that Paulinus here called the officials and attendants of princes or governors by both names, *cohortalini* and *curtalini*. DUC.

## IN LETTER XXIII

### Note 69. “Out of abundance.”

The first passage is Matthew 12:34; the second is Ecclesiasticus 13:19. The Author has combined them from two verses of Scripture: *Πᾶν ζῷον ἀγαπᾷ τὸ ὅμοιον αὐτοῦ καὶ τῷ ὁμοίῳ αὐτοῦ προσκολληθήσεται ἀνήρ.* “Every animal loves its kind, and a man will cling to one like himself.”

This proverb became current among the pagans. Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* 8: *Ὅμοιον ὁμοίου ἐφίεται;* “Like seeks like.” And Agathon in Plato’s *Symposium*: *Ὅμοιον ὁμοίῳ ἀεὶ πελάζει.* “Like always draws near to like.” DUC.

### Note 70. “You lend to God at interest.”

Our Paulinus uses *foenerare* with the accusative, whereas others say *foenerare alicui*, “to lend money at interest to someone.” The same Paulinus, Letter 32, no. 19: “It is greater to lend to the Lord than to a human being.” Also in the sermon *On the Treasury*, among the letters, no. 2: “He lends to God at interest.” And shortly afterward: “For whoever lends to the Lord’s poor.” And no. 5: “Let us therefore lend to the Lord from the Lord’s gifts.”

Cyprian likewise, *On the Dress of Virgins*: “Lend your wealth to God; feed Christ.” Thus the manuscript codices read, as J. F. Gronovius notes in *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 1. The same Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*: “When someone shows mercy to the poor, he lends to God.” Augustine, Sermon 65: “It is sufficient for the glory of the giver . . . that mercy lends to God, that it feeds Christ in the poor.” And Sermon 1 on Psalm 48, no. 9: “Lend to Christ at interest; let him receive a little on earth, so that he may repay you much in heaven.”

Martial likewise joins this verb with the accusative, Book I, epigram 77:

> This one woman lends to all the gods at interest.

### Note 71. “The preemptor of servile tasks.”

I am entirely convinced that *praereptor* or *praecerptor* must be read. By his diligence, Victor was snatching and seizing in advance from Paulinus every service of serving. Thus in Letter 4 to Severus: “I shall strive to anticipate the favor owed to a guest.” And in Letter 36 to Macarius: “Amazed that the labor had been taken from him without labor.” Manuscript B. had *praereptor*. So also in Ambrose, Book VI on Luke, chapter 7: “to anticipate the favor owed to a guest.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 72. “For from your book.”

He means Severus’s book *On the Life of St. Martin*, where, in chapter 26, he recounts Martin’s humble service toward him: “He himself offered water for our hands.” Paulinus imitated this conduct toward Victor. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 73. “For the appetite of the monks.”

*Orexis* means an appetite or craving for food, from the Greek *ὄρεξις*. John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Book VIII, chapter 6: “Those whom they wish to burden more heavily, after loading them with larger cups, they stuff and distend with smaller ones; and until they shake off their ravenous appetite—perhaps *rabidam* should be read, as in Juvenal—they think that something has been taken away from friendship or festivity.” CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, vol. III, p. 63.

### Note 74. “He would have mixed it into a crumilum.”

The learned Cauchius was troubled by the reading *in crumilum* in an old manuscript; in another, including the Put., *in crubilum* was read. For this reason he suspects that it should be corrected to *in cumerum*, citing passages of Festus and Horace. I do not agree with him at all, but understand the received reading as follows: Paulinus means that this spiritual cook would readily have added to the beans and millet the remaining kinds of grain or seed mentioned by Ezekiel—namely, lentils, barley, and vetch—in a heap, that is, so that those porridges of beans and millet might be increased by this addition and thereby equal Ezekiel’s loaves.

Thus Cicero, *Against Rullus* 2: “Let the spoils of our generals be added to the heap.”

The passage in Ezekiel is chapter 4:9: *Λάβε σεαυτῷ πυροὺς, καὶ κριθὰς, καὶ κύαμον, καὶ φακὸν, καὶ κέγχρον, καὶ ὄλυραν, καὶ ἐμβαλεῖς αὐτὰ εἰς ἄγγος ἓν ὀστράκινον, καὶ ποιήσεις αὐτὰ σεαυτῷ εἰς ἄρτον.* “Take for yourself wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt; put them into one earthen vessel, and make them into bread for yourself.”

Here Paulinus translates *ὄλυρα* as “vetch.” Jerome says: “What we have translated as vetch, the Septuagint and Theodotion rendered *ὄλυρα*; others think it is oats, others rye.”

See also Isaiah 28:25. The same Cauchius emended the words *sed farina confecit aut milio* (“but he made it with flour or millet”) to *sed panico confecit aut milio* (“but he made it with panic grass or millet”), which he judged more appropriate; and shortly afterward: “He introduced beans into the panic grass.”

I, however, by no means reject the received reading *panicio*, since Isidore supports it in Book XVII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3: “*Panicium* is so called because in many regions people are sustained by it in place of bread, as though it were *panis vicium*, ‘a substitute for bread.’” Pliny, however, gives the more accurate etymology in Book XVIII, chapter 7: “*Panicum* is named from its panicles.” DUC.

### Note 75. “Crumilum.”

Thus we restored the reading from two Belgian and Viennese manuscripts. Gregory of Tours uses the same word in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 98: “He asserts that he had stayed within the territory of Autun and had often eaten with him in this little vessel either vegetables or cooked *crumelum*.”

What *crumilus* or *crumelus* is, however, I do not sufficiently understand. Perhaps *grumulum* should be read. For the diminutive *grumulus* is formed from *grumus*, meaning any heap or pile. From *grumus* comes the French word *grumeau*. See Dacerius on Festus under the word *grumus*, p. 170. Earlier, Rosweyd’s edition had *in cumulum* (“into a heap”).

### Note 76. “A provision of grain.”

This is taken from Psalm 77:25, where the Vulgate has *cibaria* (“food supplies”); but the Roman and Gallican Psalters, as well as Cassiodorus together with Paulinus, have *frumentationem* (“a provision of grain”). The Greek is *ἐπισιτισμός*. Hesychius: *ἐπισιτισμόν, ἐφοδιασμόν*—“a provision, a supply.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 77. “In rich mercy, until, and so forth.”

Paulinus, or the author of the Latin version that he followed, evidently found in the Septuagint text *ἐν ἐλέῳ πίονι* (“in rich mercy”); hence the Old Psalter and Augustine have, in Psalm 91:2, “in rich mercy.” The Latin Vulgate has “in abundant mercy.”

In other Greek books the reading is *ἐν ἐλαίῳ πίονι*, “in rich oil,” which agrees with the Hebrew, from which Jerome translated “in abundant oil.” Theodoret, following Symmachus: *Ἡ παλαίωσίς μου ὡς ἐλαία εὐθαλής;* “My old age is like a flourishing olive tree.”

The same Paulinus below, Letter 24: “May his old age rest in abundant mercy.” DUC.

### Note 78. “In the first-formed.”

Thus the Greek Fathers call Adam and Eve, the first parents, created by God himself. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* III: *Οἷς κατηκολούθησαν οἱ πρωτόπλαστοι τοῦ Θεοῦ.* “Those whom the first-formed of God followed.”

St. John Chrysostom, Book I *On Providence*: *Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τοῦ παραδείσου τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐξέβαλε τὸν πρωτόπλαστον.* “For this reason he also expelled the first-formed man from paradise at the beginning.”

And Book II: *Ἐπὶ τὸν τοῦ πρωτοπλάστου ἔλθωμεν παῖδα.* “Let us turn our attention to the son of the first-formed man.”

Cyprian, *On the Dress of Virgins*: “In nearly all the Scriptures God speaks to the first-formed man.” DUC.

### Note 79. “Covered over.”

Instead of *oculos mentis obsitus* (“the eyes of the mind covered over”), which appeared in the Paris edition, we have emended the text from the manuscripts and older editions to *oculos mentis obsutus* (“the eyes of the mind stitched shut”), for Paulinus likes to speak in this way: *κατὰ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς συνεῤῥαμμένος*, “stitched together over the eyes,” as the Greeks say *ἀποῤῥάπτειν στόμα*, “to stitch the mouth shut.”

Thus in Letter 6: “The Pyrenean barrier lies terrifyingly between us, more a name than a mountain range”; and in Letter 7: “His hair cut close to the skin.”

Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “Sadder, and her shining eyes suffused with tears.”

### Note 80. “The sinner runs for his soul.”

After much labor we finally found where this was written, namely Proverbs 7:23: *Οὐκ εἰδὼς ὅτι περὶ ψυχῆς τρέχει.* “Not knowing that he is running for his soul.”

The Latin Vulgate: “And he does not know that it concerns the danger of his soul.” This agrees with the expression of the Greeks, among whom *τρέχειν τὴν ἐσχάτην* is proverbial for “to encounter the utmost danger,” and *τρέχειν περὶ ψυχῆς*, with *κίνδυνον*, *δρόμον*, or *ἀγῶνα* understood: “to run a danger, a race, or a contest for one’s life.”

Budaeus cites Gregory Nazianzen, *Against Julian*: *ᾜσθετο πολλῶν τῶν περὶ ψυχῆς τρεχόντων.* “He perceived that many were running the danger of their souls.”

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* III: *Ὁ δὲ ἕτερον νῦν τὸν ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀγῶνα τρέχει.* “Now he is running another contest for his life,” that is, he is being brought into mortal danger. DUC.

### Note 81. “And he is a man, and who will know him?”

The passage is Jeremiah 17:9: *Βαθεῖα ἡ καρδία παρὰ πάντα, καὶ ἄνθρωπός ἐστι, καὶ τίς γνώσεται αὐτόν;* “The heart is deep beyond all things, and it is a human being; who will know it?”

Jerome, following Symmachus: “The heart of all is inscrutable; but who is the man who can discover it?”

Theodoret, in his commentary: *Ἀνθρώποις μὲν, φησίν, ἀκατάληπτα τὰ τοῦ πέλας βουλεύματα, κέκρυπται γὰρ τὰ τῆς καρδίας κινήματα.* “The thoughts of one’s neighbor, he says, cannot be comprehended by human beings, for the movements of the heart are hidden.”

Although most understand this to refer to any human being, they also explain it of Christ—who, although he is human, is not known because of his hidden divinity—together with Paulinus: Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 14, and Book III *Against Marcion*, chapter 7; Cyprian, Book II, chapter 10 *Against the Jews*; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 30; Ambrose, *On the Instruction of a Virgin*, chapter 16; Augustine, Book III *Against Faustus*, chapter 11; and Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 13. DUC.

### Note 82. “Because it did not dwell.”

Wisdom 1:4: *Εἰς κακότεχνον ψυχὴν οὐκ εἰσελεύσεται σοφία, οὐδὲ κατοικήσει ἐν σώματι κατάχρεῳ ἁμαρτίας.* “Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sin.”

The typographical correctors had placed *non habitabit* (“it will not dwell”) in this passage, since the Scripture reads *κατοικήσει*. We restored *habitabat* (“it dwelt”) from Badius and Gravius. DUC.

### Note 83. “It bears witness to what was indicated.”

The older editions incorrectly had *judicata testatur* (“it bears witness to what was judged”) instead of *indicata* (“what was indicated”). This is what was written, although Paulinus departs from it slightly because his memory failed him, namely in the added detail concerning the weight of the hair.

2 Samuel 14:26: *Ὡς ἂν ἐκείρετο, ὅτι κατεβάρυνεν ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν, καὶ ἔστησε τὴν τρίχα τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ διακοσίους σίκλους, ἐν τῷ σίκλῳ τῷ βασιλικῷ.* “Whenever it was cut, for it became heavy upon him, he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels, according to the royal shekel.”

The Latin Vulgate differs in no respect: “Two hundred shekels by the public standard,” just as *ἡ λεωφόρος* is called “the royal road.” DUC.

### Note 84. “My iniquities have risen above my head.”

In verse 5 of Psalm 37: “For my iniquities have risen above my head” (*Ὅτι αἱ ἀνομίαι ὑπερῆραν τὴν κεφαλήν μου*). Ambrose likewise translated it: “My iniquities have risen above my head,” and explains: “They have passed beyond my head and tower over me, so as to weigh down my understanding.” Saint Augustine has: “They have lifted up my head.” The Vulgate reads: “They have gone beyond my head.” Consequently, all earlier editions should be corrected where they have the accusative *iniquitates meas* (“my iniquities”) here in Paulinus, instead of the nominative *iniquitates meae* (also “my iniquities,” as the subject). DUC.

[Col. 0860A] ### Note 85. “For dew.”

The passage is Isaiah 26:19: “For the dew that comes from you is healing for them” (*Ἡ γὰρ δρόσος παρὰ σοῦ ἴαμα αὐτοῖς ἐστι*). “The dew that comes from you is healing for them.” The Vulgate has: “For the dew of light is your dew.” Pagninus and Vatablus: “As the dew of plants, so is your dew.” This difference arises from the Hebrew *oroth*, a plural form that may be translated either “lights” or “plants.”

An elegant comparison is enclosed in this ambiguous word, as though he were saying: Just as the dew of light, or the dew before dawn, is most welcome to plants and wild herbs and makes them revive, so your dew, falling upon dry bones, will make them live again. See our Gaspar Sanctius in that place. Paulinus also uses it below, in letters 17, 26, and 31; in the last of these passages consult our Fronto. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 86. “For the confusion of evils.”

That is, of demons, whom he here calls angels prepared for seduction. Accordingly, many of the Fathers understand “evil” in Matthew 6:13, “But deliver us from evil” (*ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ*), as referring to the evil one; likewise in Matthew 5:37: “Whatever is more than these is from evil” (*ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ*); and in chapter 13:19: “The evil one comes” (*ὁ πονηρός*).

Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter 2: “But deliver us from the evil one”—that is, do not lead us into temptation by permitting us to fall under the evil one. In his book *On Prayer*, chapter 8, he had said: “But lift us up from evil.” Chrysostom, Euthymius, and Theophylact likewise interpret the passage in Matthew 6 in this way.

Again, Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 5: “So that the evil one, having recovered his prey, may rejoice against his Lord.” The same author, *On Patience*, chapter 11: “Let us therefore strive to endure the things inflicted by the evil one”; and chapter 14: “The evil one was being dismembered when Job, with great composure, restrained the filthy overflow of his ulcer.” He uses the expression frequently throughout that book.

The same author, *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 5: “Will a Christian be helped by that evil one?” The same, book 2 *To His Wife*, chapter 6: “Everything foreign, everything hostile, everything condemned and inimical to salvation, was introduced by the evil one”; and he uses the same expression several times in that book.

Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, chapter 10: “When, in our temptations, nothing is permitted to the evil one unless power is granted to him from that source”; and he uses the expression several times in the same place. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 87. “As gold cephas.”

We have restored this reading from manuscript P and the edition of Badius, whereas the Parisian and Gravian editions had *aurum paz* (“gold paz”), perhaps because the Hebrew in Song of Songs 5:11 is read as *roscho ketem paz*: “His head is pure gold,” as Pagninus translates it; or, as Montanus has it, “a mass of pure gold.” Aquila likewise rendered it in Greek as *λιθέα χρυσίου*, “a stone or mass of gold,” while Theodotion has *ἐπίσημοι ἐν χρυσίῳ*, “distinguished in gold.”

Kircher, in his Hebrew Index, incorrectly has *χρυσίον κεφαλή*, “gold of the head.” For the Septuagint wrote *χρυσίον κεφάζ*, “gold cephas,” as is clear from Gregory of Nyssa’s thirteenth homily on the Song of Songs. He explains *κεφάζ* as “unadulterated and free from every foreign mixture, pure and clean, and genuine.” Ambrose, in the fifteenth section of his commentary on Psalm 118, has: “His head is gold cephas.”

Accordingly, Aquila also said “stone-gold”; Symmachus, “golden stone,” signifying stable and eminent wisdom. Perhaps the most holy man was deceived because he thought that the Hebrew text contained the word *Cephas*, which means “rock” and from which Saint Peter the Apostle received his name. But only the word *kethem* means a lump or mass of gold, or a piece of pure gold such as Indian gold; therefore it is joined with the word *pas*, which likewise denotes refined gold.

Some therefore think that the word *κεφάζ* was formed from the two terms *kethem* and *pas*, or *phas*, as the ancient Hebrews read it. Others, among whom is our Delrio, believe that the Septuagint wrote *χρυσίον ἐκ φάζ*, “gold from Phas,” that is, gold brought from that region, and that the word later deteriorated into *κεφάζ*. Pagninus likewise thinks that *Ophas* in Daniel 10:5 is the name of a place, since Jeremiah 10:9 reads: “Silver from Tarshish and gold from Ophaz.” The Septuagint has: “From Tharsis gold will come from Mophaz” (*Ἀπὸ Θαρσὶς ἥξει χρυσίον Μωφάζ*).

Symmachus, on Proverbs 8, has: “My fruit is better than gold of Ophaz” (*Κρείσσων καρπός μου χρυσίου Ὠφάζ*).

Others derive the term from a root meaning “to strengthen” and “to confirm,” since gold becomes more solid when it is purified. The true reading, therefore, is *cephas*, since Paulinus follows the Latin edition of Scripture translated from the Greek text of the Septuagint. DUC.

**“Gold cephas.”** The Viennese manuscript has *aurum ophaz*, “gold ophaz.” Thus, in Daniel 10:5, the Septuagint has: “His loins were girded with gold ophaz.” But here the Vatican Septuagint manuscript and the Royal manuscript, together with the three printed editions, have *cephas*. Ambrose, in *On the Death of Valentinian* and in Sermon 15 on Psalm 118, has *cephas*, interpreted by Aquila as “rock-gold” and by Symmachus as “golden stone”; he also has it in book 2 of *On the Holy Spirit*, in the preface. The true and best reading is therefore “gold cephas.”

[Col. 0860D] ### Note 88. “But let this be corrected so that you understand it better.”

Thus read the Vatican and Belgian manuscripts. Previously it stood, as in the Putean manuscript: “But let this, as you prefer it to be understood, be given as seed.” Our Fronto thought the passage obscure and believed that Paulinus was perhaps speaking of human semen as a coagulating agent. Certainly Columella, when discussing cheese, writes that a certain “seed” is used for rennet. So far he.

Since Paulinus here mentions milk and wine, as well as the first milk of newborn creatures, and since it is clear from ancient authors that newly born and newly baptized children were formerly given milk and wine, someone might perhaps think that Paulinus is alluding to that custom—a custom that still continued in Gaul in the age of Hugh of Saint Victor, when the Eucharist was administered to newly born children under the appearance of wine. Indeed, he says that even in his own time pure, unconsecrated wine was given in place of the blood of Christ, and that he wished this practice to be abolished.

Thus he writes in book 1 of *Ceremonies, Sacraments, and Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 20, speaking of someone newly baptized:

“If his health permits, he ought to receive the sacraments of unity, that is, the body and blood of Christ. The same sacrament, in the form of blood, is to be administered to newly born children by the priest’s finger, because such children can naturally suck.”

Augustine, *To Boniface Against the Pelagian Heresy* (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, chapter 22):

“In the Church of the Savior, infants believe through others, just as they contracted from others the sins that are remitted in baptism. Nor should you think that those can have life who are deprived of the body and blood of Christ, since the Lord himself says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood’ (John 6), and so forth.”

Therefore, if it can be done without danger, according to the Church’s original institution, the sacrament of the Eucharist should be given to children in the form of blood. Hence ignorance, while retaining the form but not the substance, gives them wine in place of blood. I would consider this entirely superfluous if it could be abandoned without scandalizing the simple. But if danger threatens either in reserving Christ’s blood or in administering it to children, it seems preferable to refrain.

Nor should Augustine’s preceding words frighten you. Elsewhere, in his sermon *On Infants*, as though defining the matter, he says:

“No one should in any way doubt that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the body and blood of the Lord at the moment when, in baptism, he becomes a member of Christ’s body; nor is he excluded from sharing in that bread, even if, before eating that bread and drinking the cup, he departs from this world established in the unity of Christ’s body.”

If this rite was practiced in Gaul even in Paulinus’s time, and he wished it to be corrected, this may perhaps shed some light on this obscure passage.

That the practice formerly prevailed in Gaul, whereby wine was given to the newly baptized, continued even in our own age in the church of Dordrecht, as William Lindanus reports in book 4 of the *Panoplia*, chapter 25.

If the interpretation just given is still unsatisfactory because it mentions only wine and not milk, and because Paulinus here seems to speak of a mixture of two forms—for he asks that this be corrected, by which the first milk of newborn creatures is made to coagulate, yet he has mentioned both milk and wine, assigning wine to the Old Testament and milk to the New—if, I say, the preceding interpretation is insufficient, Paulinus may perhaps have alluded to the custom by which, formerly, wine mixed with milk was offered to the baptized after baptism.

Saint Jerome mentions this in his commentary on Isaiah 55, explaining the passage in which we are invited to buy wine and milk. He writes:

“Wisdom too mixed the wine in her cup, inviting all the fools of the age and of the world who lack wisdom to drink; and so that we may buy not only wine but also milk, which signifies the innocence of little children. This custom and type is still preserved today in the churches of the West, so that wine and milk are given to those reborn in Christ.”

Concerning this milk Paul also said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3). And Peter: “As newborn infants, desire rational milk” (1 Peter 2). Hence Moses, understanding wine and milk in relation to Christ’s Passion, bears witness in mystical language: “His eyes are graceful from wine, and his teeth are white from milk.”

Since Paulinus in this letter praises milk so enthusiastically, and celebrates the good breasts of grace in the Church above the wine of the law, perhaps he was astonished that milk mixed with wine was given to the baptized and wished this rite to be corrected in accordance with Severus’s view.

Nor does Jerome seem to have said without reason that this custom was observed in the churches of the West. For it is not easy to find it practiced in the churches of the East. As for what Joseph Vicecomes asserts in book 5 of *On Baptism*, chapter 44—that the custom was known and mentioned by Clement of Alexandria in book 1 of the *Instructor*, chapter 6—I fear that he is mistaken.

Clement certainly relates various things about milk while explaining 1 Corinthians 3 against certain Gnostics who insisted that milk signified something imperfect; but he does not say that the practices he describes were used in the Church. In the same place he says that milk was mixed with water. Who, however, would claim that this was a Greek baptismal rite?

Because Clement’s passage is well known and may serve to illuminate the sacramental rite formerly observed in the Western Church, of which Paulinus here seems to be reminding us, I shall set it out:

“Indeed, milk is also mixed with sweet wine. The mixture is beneficial, as though passion were being blended into incorruption. For the milk is made to curdle and separate by the wine, and whatever in it is adulterated is drawn off through a channel. In the same way, the spiritual fellowship of faith with the passible human being, causing carnal desires to curdle and flow away, gathers the human being into eternity, making him immortal through divine things” (*Ναὶ μὴν ἐπιμίγνυται τὸ γάλα καὶ οἴνῳ τῷ γλυκεῖ· ἐπωφελὴς δὲ ἡ μίξις καθάπερ ἀνακιρναμένου τοῦ πάθους εἰς ἀφθαρσίαν· ἐξοῤῥοῦται γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ οἴνου τὸ γάλα καὶ σχίζεται, καὶ ὅ τί περ αὐτοῦ νόθον, τοῦτ᾽ ἀποχετεύεται· κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ δὲ τῆς πίστεως ἡ κοινωνία ἡ πνευματικὴ πρὸς τὸν παθητὸν ἄνθρωπον, τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἐξοῤῥοῦσα, εἰς ἀΐδιότητα συστέλλει τὸν ἄνθρωπον, τοῖς θείοις ἀπαθανατίζουσα*).

Clement of Alexandria, *Instructor*, book 1, chapter 6.

“Moreover, milk is also mixed with sweet wine. The mixture is beneficial, as though affection were being blended into incorruption. For the milk curdles and separates through the wine, and whatever in it is adulterated is led out as through an aqueduct. In the same way, the spiritual fellowship of faith with the passible human being, causing carnal desires to curdle and flow away, gathers the human being into eternity, making him immortal through divine things.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 88 bis. “His locks are black fir trees.”

Song of Songs 5:11: “His locks are like raised palm shoots, black as a raven.” But the Septuagint has: “His curls are *elatae*; black as a raven” (*Βόστρυχοι αὐτοῦ ἐλάται, μέλανες ὡς κόραξ*).

Others translate: “His locks are the fruit of the palm, black as a raven.” It must be observed that both in the Latin Vulgate and in the version made from the Greek, the word *elatae* signifies the fruit of the palm, not a kind of palm that is taller than others, as some think.

For *ἐλάτη*, in Galen, means “the tender shoot of the palm” (*τὸ ἁπαλὸν ἐκβλάστημα τῆς φοίνικος*). Dioscorides, book 1, chapter 124:

“The palm, which some call *elaten* or *spathen*, is the covering and calyx of the fruit of palms that are still flowering” (*Φοίνιξ, ἢν ἔνιοι ἐλάτην ἢ σπάθην καλοῦσι, περικάλυμμά ἐστι τοῦ καρποῦ τῶν φοινίκων ἀκμὴν ἀνθούντων*).

Marcellus calls it the garden-like covering of a palm that is still flowering. The rind of this *elatae* is black and somewhat reddish-yellow.

Pliny, book 12, chapter 24:

“There is also a tree used for the same perfumes, which some call *elaten*, we call the fir, and others call the palm or *spathen*.”

Andrew Matthiolus, writing on Dioscorides, warns that Pliny in this passage confused the covering of the fruit of a palm still in flower with the fir tree, deceived by the similarity of the terms. From this our Delrio concludes that Pliny misled the holy men Ambrose—in book 2 of *On the Holy Spirit* and in section 15 on Psalm 118—as well as Paulinus, and caused them to translate the word as “fir trees” when they encountered Greek copies in which the word “palms” was absent.

I do not agree with him. I think both men should be acquitted of error, since the testimony of the best authors establishes that the Greek word *ἐλάτη* has two meanings: “fir tree” and “fruit of the palm,” but not the palm tree itself, as Pliny seems to have thought.

Genesis 21:15: “She threw the child beneath a fir tree” (*Ἔῤῥιψε τὸ παιδίον ὑποκάτω ἐλάτης*).

Ezekiel 31:8: “And the fir trees were not like its branches” (*Καὶ ἐλάται οὐκ ἐγένοντο ὅμοιοι κλάδοις αὐτοῦ*).

Isaiah 41:19: “I will set a fir tree in the desert” (*Στήσω ἐν ἐρήμῳ ἐλάτην*).

Pagninus translates from the Hebrew: “His locks are curly, black as a raven.” But when he translates from the Septuagint as “His locks are pliable,” in my judgment he is mistaken, first because all the books have *ἐλάται*, not *ἐλαταί*, as in Numbers 16:38: “Make hammered plates” (*Ποίησον λεπίδας ἐλατὰς*); and secondly because the word *βόστρυχοι*, “locks,” cannot be joined with *ἐλαταί*, since the latter belongs to a different grammatical category. The Latin version used by Paulinus suffers from the same defect.

The phrase is “black locks,” not “black fir trees”: in Greek it is *Βόστρυχοι ἐλάται μέλανες ὡς κόραξ*. Thus the locks may be called black, but not fir trees. Ambrose likewise did not think it necessary to examine the received translation. DUC.

[Col. 0863B] ### Note 89. “Established through the ages.”

Thus reads manuscript P. The Apostle’s similar passage in Ephesians 3:9 supports this reading: “The administration of the mystery hidden through the ages in God” (*Οἰκονομία τοῦ μυστηρίου τοῦ ὑποκεκρυμμένου ἀπὸ αἰώνων ἐν τῷ Θεῷ*). DUC.

### Note 90. “The form of a sinful woman.”

This appears to have been expressed from Ambrose, book 6 on Luke, chapter 7:

“She”—the Church—“rightly assumes the appearance of a sinful woman, because Christ too assumed the form of a sinner.”

The things that follow in Paulinus concerning the manifold sweetness of flowers and fragrances are likewise found in the same passage of Ambrose. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 91. “The activity of the faithful.”

That is, mercy. For the holy Fathers properly used the verb “to act” and its derivatives of works of mercy.

Soon afterward Paulinus has: “For by works of piety and mercy.”

Letter 10, concerning Melania feeding five thousand monks in Egypt: “Although she did not wish the glory of her activity to be recognized, the magnitude of her work nevertheless revealed it.”

Letter 12: “By acting according to his commandments, you will see him in every poor person.”

Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 23, speaking of someone who had sworn by pagan gods and had given a written guarantee to a lender:

“Let us pray to the Lord that the necessity of such a contract may not surround us. And if this should happen, let him give the brothers an opportunity to act, or give us the constancy to break every necessity.”

He wishes this sin to be redeemed by action, that is, by almsgiving.

The same author, book 4 against Marcion, chapter 16: “For even if the goodness that acts toward strangers is greater.”

Cyprian, following the footsteps of his teacher, in *On the Lapsed*, chapter 13:

“Let the work of mercy be done unhesitatingly and generously; let all one’s resources be expended for the healing of the wound; let the Lord, who will judge us, be lent money from our wealth and resources.”

And shortly afterward:

“He can mercifully forgive the repentant, the one who acts, and the one who asks.”

The same author, *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 1:

“Among us, unity has been so diminished that the generosity of our activity has also been weakened.”

The same author, letter 52, chapter 9:

“For the washing away and cleansing of your sin, act generously and frequently.”

He also gave a particular book the title *On Work and Almsgiving*. Likewise, the first chapter of the third book of the *Testimonies* to Quirinus begins with “the goodness of work and mercy,” and the second with “work and almsgiving.”

Pontius, in the *Life of Cyprian*:

“Thus, by the generosity of abundant works, that which is good toward all was accomplished.”

Optatus, book 3 against Parmenian, speaking of the envoys sent to Africa by the Emperor Constans to relieve the poverty of the people and establish concord, calls them “workers for unity.”

Prudentius too, in the *Psychomachia*, sets “Activity,” or almsgiving, and compassion against Avarice:

“When suddenly, roaring, Activity sprang into the middle of the field.”

Here Aldus, Antonius Nebrissensis, and Georgius Fabricius incorrectly substituted *Compassion*, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts.

Pamelius is not without reason in suspecting that the name “mercy” was given to activity because almsgiving is among the chief good works. Or did the term perhaps arise from the mention of almsgiving in Matthew 26:10 and Mark 14:6: “She has performed a good work upon me”? ROSWEYDUS.

[Col. 0864A] ### Note 92. “Christ lends at interest and is fed.”

The older editions of Badius and Gravius, together with the Parisian edition, consistently read *serenari* (“to be cleared”); manuscript P has *foeneratur* (“lends at interest”). Storms are said to become clear not only among poets but also in Pliny, book 2, chapter 6, as are the clouds of the human mind. Yet Paulinus’s expression is more familiar when discussing almsgiving and generosity toward the poor, as manuscript P has it: “he lends at interest.”

Letter 34: “He wishes to borrow from what he himself has bestowed,” that is, to receive a loan in return.

The same passage: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to God,” that is, he gives a loan to God. Ambrose expressed this in *On Churches Not to Be Handed Over*: “He who gives to the poor lends to God”; the Latin Vulgate has the same in Proverbs 19:17.

For in both cases the expression is joined with the word even among good Latin authors. Martial, book 1, epigram 77:

“This woman alone is wise; she lends at interest to all the gods.”

Chalderinus comments on this passage:

“She is so rich that she can lend money at interest to all the gods.”

Nevertheless, “to lend at interest” does not always mean to lend at interest or usury. Although Festus says that *foenus* is the offspring of money, the Greek *δανείζεσθαι* likewise often means nothing more than simply to receive a loan, while *δανείζειν* means to give a loan.

Thus Plutarch’s *On Avoiding Debt* may refer either to borrowing at interest or to receiving an ordinary loan. Deuteronomy 28:12:

“You will lend to many nations, but you will not borrow” (*Καὶ δανειεῖς ἔθνεσι πολλοῖς, σὺ δὲ οὐ δανειῇ*).

The Latin edition of Sixtus V has: “You will lend at interest to many nations, and you yourself will borrow from no one,” as though it meant: You will be pressed by no necessity, since you will abound in every good. Nor does the verb *lavah* mean “to lend at interest,” but “to give a loan,” lest the Jews claim that usury had been permitted to them.

Thus, in Psalm 3:5, the same verb is translated into Greek as *κιχρᾷν*: “A good man is one who shows mercy and lends” (*Χρηστὸς ἀνὴρ ὁ οἰκτείρων καὶ κιχρῶν*).

Paulinus, letter 12: “Let us lend to Christ in his poor.” But in the same passage the manuscript reading seems preferable: “How much greater it is to lend to the Lord than to a human being,” rather than the Vulgate reading, “and to the Lord rather than to a human being.” Otherwise, “to lend at interest” may mean to give generously in any manner, as Pliny says in book 2, chapter 6: “The sun lends its light to the other stars.” DUC.

### Note 93. “He would have preferred mercy to faith.”

Ambrose, book 6 on Luke, chapter 7:

“She preferred mercy to faith, which has merit only when it is preceded by faith.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 94. “He who bought at a great price does not sell.”

Ambrose, in the same place:

“Christ wishes to be valued at so cheap an auction that he may be bought by everyone, so that no poor person may be deterred,” and so forth.

“He himself bought us with his precious blood; he did not sell us.”

See the same author, book 3 of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 18, not far from the end. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 95. “To one who does not love riches.”

Ambrose above:

“To one who does not love riches, who does not love the honors of the world, who does not love what belongs to himself but what belongs to Jesus Christ; who does not love visible things but invisible things; not to one who desires life, but to one who hastens to depart and to be crucified with Christ to the world.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 96. “Rubbing the thresholds of the wise, as commanded.”

The Wise Man commands this in Ecclesiasticus 6:36:

“If you see a prudent man, rise early to go to him, and let your foot wear down the steps of his doors” (*Ἐὰν ἴδῃς συνετόν, ὄρθριζε πρὸς αὐτόν, καὶ βαθμοὺς θυρῶν αὐτοῦ ἐκτριβέτω ποῦς σου*).

Augustine likewise, in his seventh treatise on John, translates *βαθμοὺς θυρῶν* as “the threshold of his doors.” DUC.

### Note 97. “In the law.”

We conjectured that Paulinus had read *διὰ τοῦ νόμου*, “through the law,” in 1 Corinthians 14:19, instead of *διὰ τοῦ νοός μου*, “through my understanding.” Unless, perhaps, he wrote “from my understanding,” not “in the law,” in order to express the received Greek reading, as though it were *ἐν νόμῳ*. DUC.

### Note 98. “Wherever, even into the house of an unworthy man.”

The passage is taken directly from Ambrose, book 6 on Luke, chapter 7:

“Wherever you hear that the righteous man has entered, whether into the house of an unclean man or into the house of a Pharisee, strive to seize the grace of your host; seize the kingdom of heaven.”

Hence Paulinus also took what follows here. Ambrose writes:

“Wherever you hear the name of Christ, hasten there; wherever you learn that Christ has entered the inner house of anyone, hasten there yourself. When you find wisdom, when you find justice reclining in someone’s inner chambers, hasten to his feet—that is, seek even the lowest part of wisdom. Do not despise the feet. She touched the fringe and was healed.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 99. “Let us spread out his hair.”

Ambrose, in the same place:

“Spread out your hair; lay before him all the dignities of your body. These are no ordinary hairs, since they can wipe Christ’s feet. He bears witness to this—the man who could not be conquered as long as he had his hair” (Judges 16). “Finally, it is not fitting for a woman with shorn hair to pray” (1 Corinthians 11). Let her indeed have hair with which to enfold Christ’s footprints, with the locks of her beauty and adornment to wipe the feet of Wisdom, so that at least with the final dew of divine power they may become moist; let her fasten her kisses upon the feet of righteousness. ROSWEYDUS.

[Col. 0865B] ### Note 100. “For perhaps this is why, and so forth.”

Ambrose, in the passage cited:

“And perhaps this is why Christ did not wash his own feet: so that we might wash them with our tears. Good are the tears that can not only wash away our sin but also water the footprints of the heavenly Word, so that his steps may abound within us.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 101. “Wounded by love.”

Manuscript P has: “I am wounded by love,” literally from the Greek *Τετρωμένη ἀγάπης ἐγώ εἰμι*. Ambrose likewise expresses it in the later *Apology for David*, chapter 10: “I am wounded by love.” Others have “wounded by love,” as in the Basel edition and in the same Ambrose’s commentary on Psalm 118, section 15. DUC.

### Note 102. “To wipe the holy soles.”

That is, the footprints: the lower part of the foot is meant, which others call the sole.

Ambrose, Sermon 74: “The way of life, where the Lord rose again, became known, worn smooth by the soles of many.”

Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book 5: “For me, the hardened sole of my shoe is my footwear; the earth is my bed.”

Lucretius, book 4:

“I travel through the pathless regions of the Pierides,

Previously trodden by the sole of no one.”

DUC.

### Note 103. “If my ointment should be cheap.”

Ambrose above:

“I poured ointment upon the Lord’s body? It begins to give off fragrance, though it was thought to be dead. Therefore let each person strive to purchase, through his labor and effort in virtue, an alabaster vessel of ointment—not some cheap and common ointment, but precious alabaster ointment, and pistic ointment.

“For if someone gathers the flowers of faith and proclaims Jesus Christ crucified throughout the whole Church—which is Christ’s body, dead to the world and resting in God—he pours out the ointment of his faith. The entire house of the Lord begins to smell of the Passion.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 104. “Their names.”

Ambrose, book 6 on Luke, chapter 9:

“Great is Christ’s grace, since he bestowed nearly all titles upon the disciples themselves.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 105. “Every true one.”

The Vatican manuscript has: “Every true one.” Thus, in Jeremiah 2:21, the Septuagint reads: “A fruitful vine, wholly true” (*Ἄμπελον καρποφόρον πᾶσαν ἀληθινήν*), “a fruitful vine, wholly true.”

Ambrose likewise reads it this way in book 6 on Luke, from which Paulinus expressed much of the present passage. And what is said shortly afterward about the rock, by which he did not deny his disciple the grace of this name, is taken word for word from the passage of Ambrose just cited. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 106. “What in return for the flesh he assumed?”

This is sketched from Ambrose, book 6 on Luke, chapter 7:

“What shall we offer in return for the injury of the flesh he assumed? What in return for the blows, the cross, the death, and the burial?”

The rest of what follows on this page in Paulinus is almost word for word from Ambrose. ROSWEYDUS.

## In Letter 24

### Note 107. “If you love rightly but divide wrongly, you have sinned.”

He uses the passage from Genesis 4:7 by what is called accommodation. Thus the Septuagint has:

“Is it not that if you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned? Be still” (*Οὐκ ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγκῃς, ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἥμαρτες; ἡσύχασον*).

The Vulgate has: “If you do well, will you not receive?” These words are spoken to Cain, because in a correct division the first things should be preferred to the second, heavenly things to earthly things, not earthly things to heavenly things.

Ambrose, book 2 of *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 6:

“So that first things may precede second things, and second things may not precede first things; and so that heavenly things may be preferred to earthly things, not earthly things to heavenly things.”

Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 18 on Genesis:

“He offered whatever happened to come to hand, displaying no care or precision in his choice, when he ought to have offered the most precious things.” DUC.

[Col. 0866A] ### Note 108. “May the Church possess you while you serve her.”

What Paulinus writes here about Severus—how he preserved his possessions not for himself but for the Church—Prosper (read: Julianus Pomerius) writes similarly about Paulinus and Hilary, bishop of Arles, in book 2 of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 9:

“Saint Paulinus sold the great estates that had been his and distributed them to the poor. But after he had become a bishop, he did not despise the resources of the Church; rather, he administered them with the utmost fidelity. By this action he clearly showed both that personal possessions ought to be despised for the sake of perfection and that the common possessions of the Church may be held without hindering perfection.

“And what of Saint Hilary? Did he not likewise leave all his goods either to his relatives or distribute them to the poor after selling them? Nevertheless, when by the merit of his perfection he became bishop of the Church of Arles, he not only possessed what that church then had but also increased it by accepting numerous inheritances from the faithful.” ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 109. “Nor do you dwell in the tombs of sleepers.”

God says that he is provoked by those who dwell in tombs and sleep in the shrines of idols, in Isaiah 65:3. The Septuagint has:

“And in tombs and caves they sleep because of dreams” (*Καὶ ἐν τοῖς μνήμασι καὶ ἐν τοῖς σπηλαίοις κοιμῶνται διὰ ἐνύπνια*).

Saint Cyril of Alexandria explains this as: “Deceived by dreams and apparitions, and investigating knowledge of future things.”

Procopius has: “In tombs because of necromancy” (*Ἐν μνήμασι διὰ τὰς νεκυομαντείας*).

He seems to have taken this from Theodoret, whose words are found in the Royal manuscript catena:

“They follow the apparitions that occur in dreams, and for this reason they even consent to sleep beside tombs” (*Ταῖς καθ’ ὕπνους γενομέναις φαντασίαις ἀκολουθοῦσι, καὶ τούτου χάριν καὶ παρὰ τοὺς τάφους καθεύδειν ἀνέχονται*).

Jerome adds:

“In the shrines of idols, where they were accustomed to lie upon the skins of sacrificial victims so that through dreams they might learn the future—a practice that pagan error continues to celebrate in the shrine of Aesculapius even today.”

What Pliny says—“in the tombs of sleepers cast out”—seems to have been taken from the Roman Psalter, where Psalm 87:6 reads:

“Like the wounded, cast out and sleeping in the tomb.”

The Roman Greek edition renders it:

“Like the wounded, cast out and sleeping in the grave” (*Ὡσεὶ τραυματίαι ἐῤῥιμμένοι καθεύδοντες ἐν τάφῳ*).

Ambrose likewise recognizes the phrase “cast out,” as does Apollinaris:

“Just as the wounded, cast out and uncared-for, sleep around the tombs” (*Οἷάπερ οὐτηθέντες ἀκήδεστοι περὶ τύμβους εὔδουσι*). DUC.

### Note 110. “Athletes of the flesh.”

Concerning the continence of athletes, Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 3:

“They say that not a few athletes abstain from sexual intercourse, practicing self-control on account of bodily training” (*Φασί δὲ καὶ ἀθλητὰς οὐκ ὀλίγους ἀφροδισίων ἀπέχεσθαι δι’ ἄσκησιν σωματικὴν ἐγκρατευομένους*).

Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, chapter 3:

“Indeed, athletes too are separated for stricter discipline, so that they may devote themselves to building strength. They are restrained from luxury, from more pleasant foods, and from more agreeable drink; they are compelled, tormented, and exhausted.”

See also Basil, homily *On Not Clinging to Secular Things*; John Chrysostom, Homily 23 on 1 Corinthians and Homily 8 on the First Epistle to Timothy. DUC.

### Note 111. “That in Adam only the image has remained for us.”

Like many of the Fathers, Paulinus distinguishes the image from the likeness. He wishes the latter to have been lost through Adam’s sin, while the former remained.

Hence, in letter 2 to Severus:

“That we may truly be restored to our primordial dignity, that is, to the likeness of God.” ROSWEYDUS.

[Col. 0867A] ### Note 112. “Making his body livid.”

These words express Paul’s statement in 1 Corinthians 9:27:

“I bruise my body and bring it into subjection” (*Ὑπωπιάζω τὸ σώμα, καὶ δουλαγωγῶ*).

It is as though he were saying: “I make my body livid and reduce it to servitude.” Beza testifies that this was likewise printed in Latin in the Claromontane manuscript: “I make it livid.” The translator of Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 72, has: “I make my body livid.” Paulinus himself again has it in letter 43 to Augustine, which is letter 58 among Augustine’s letters.

Hesychius and Suidas:

“*Ὑπώπια* are swellings that arise beneath the eyes.”

Julius Pollux:

“The marks of blows that appear beneath the eyes” (*Τὰ ὑπὸ τοὺς ὦπας τῶν πληγῶν ἴχνη*).

In the old Glossary: “*Ὑπώπια*, bruises,” that is, parts around the eyes battered by blows and made livid.

Hence *ὑπωπιάζειν* is properly an athletic term meaning to bruise the part beneath the eyes—or any other part of the body, as boxers were accustomed to do with their fists and boxing gloves.

Thus it is written in Chrysostom, Homily 22 on 1 Corinthians, where he explains it:

“I restrain and subject myself with many labors and much sweat” (*Καταστέλλω καὶ ὑποτάττω μετὰ πολλῶν ἱδρώτων*).

The same appears in Theophylact and Oecumenius.

In other authors one reads *ὑποπιέζω*, that is, “I press down, crush, harass, or oppress by throwing down,” which is a term used of wrestlers. This reading is found in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 3; Gregory of Nazianzus against the Eunomians; Basil; and Theodoret’s commentary.

The Royal manuscripts have *ὑποπιάζω*, which is a Doric form.

The Apostle uses both comparisons, that of boxers and that of wrestlers; Cyprian, *On the Singularity of the Clergy*, expresses both words by “I afflict,” and the author of the Latin Vulgate by “I chastise.” DUC.

### Note 113. “So that you may apprehend.”

In Paul, the statement is simply:

“Run in such a way that you may obtain” (*Οὕτω τρέχετε, ἵνα καταλάβητε*).

“Run in such a way that you may comprehend”; nor is the word *ἅπαντες*, “all,” added in 1 Corinthians 9:24.

Nevertheless, some interpreters draw the same meaning from this passage, such as Theodoret:

“There, although many compete, only one is proclaimed victor by the herald; here, however, each of those who compete well is deemed worthy of the proclamation” (*Ἐκεῖ πολλῶν ἀγωνιζομένων, εἷς ἀνακηρύττεται μόνος, ἐνταῦθα δὲ τῶν καλῶς ἀγωνιζομένων ἕκαστος ἀξιοῦται τῆς ἀναῤῥήσεως*).

Jerome, letter 28:

“Our master of the games is not envious, nor does one person’s palm prepare disgrace for another; he desires all his athletes to be crowned.”

What follows—“There cannot be a division in the body”—cannot have been drawn from anywhere except 1 Corinthians 12:25:

“So that there may be no schism in the body” (*Ἵνα μὴ ᾖ σχίσμα ἐν τῷ σώματι*),

or “division” or “dissension.” There he is speaking about the human body, but verse 27 adds: “Now you are the body of Christ.” DUC.

### Note 114. “In the land of Ham.”

Elsewhere, “Canaan.” It should be corrected to “in the land of Ham,” from Psalm 105:22:

“Marvelous deeds in the land of Ham” (*Θαυμάσια ἐν γῇ Χάμ*),

that is, in Egypt; and Psalm 104:23: “Jacob was a resident in the land of Ham.” But the land of Canaan is Palestine. Leviticus 14:34: “When you enter the land of Canaan, which I will give you.”

Unless perhaps this was an author’s *μνημονικὸν ἁμάρτημα*, a “memory error,” so that he wrote “Canaan” instead of “Ham.”

Shortly afterward he says “with the patrimonies squandered,” that is, dispersed by sale. Thus Cyprian, citing Matthew 13:44 in *On Work and Almsgiving*, said:

“The merchant of heavenly grace, having dispersed all his possessions, ought to purchase the precious pearl from the value of his patrimony.” DUC.

### Note 115. “That he might destroy the enemy and the defender.”

Our Vulgate has *avenger* instead of *defender*, with the Greek *τιμωροῦντα*—which should be read as *ἐκδικητάν*. But “defender” was current in Paulinus’s time, as is clear from Severus Sulpicius, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 7.

When that remarkable support from the sacred Scriptures came to Martin’s aid in his election to the bishopric of Tours, a certain Defensor, a bishop of that name who had strongly opposed Martin’s election, was confounded. For, as Severus says, when the reader whose duty it was to read that day was prevented by the crowd and failed to appear, and the ministers were thrown into confusion while they awaited the absent reader, one of those standing nearby took up a Psalter and seized upon the first verse he found.

The psalm was:

“From the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, so that you might destroy the enemy and the defender” (Psalm 8:3).

When this had been read, the people raised a shout and the opposing party was confounded.

This method of seeking to discover the divine will was once employed by many. Thus Clovis, the first Christian king of Gaul, when preparing an expedition against the Arians, sent messengers to the basilica of Saint Martin so that from there he might receive some omen of victory (Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book 2, chapter 37).

He received one. For when the messengers entered, these verses were being sung:

“You have girded me, Lord, with strength for battle; you have thrown down beneath me those who rise against me; you have given me the backs of my enemies, and you have destroyed those who hate me” (Psalm 17).

Thus King Meroveus of the Franks arranged for three books to be placed at the tomb of Saint Martin: a Psalter, a Book of Kings, and a Gospel-book (the same author, book V, chapter 14). From the Psalter this verse emerged: “Nevertheless, because of their deceitfulness you set evils before them” (Psalm LXXII), and so forth. From the Books of Kings: “Because you have forsaken the Lord your God” (II Chronicles VII), and so forth. From the Gospels: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over” (Matthew XXVI), and so forth.

Likewise Gregory of Tours himself (the same author, book V, chapter 49), when he saw Plato the archdeacon and Gallienus being carried off by force by Leudastes, opened the Psalter and read: “He led them out in hope, and they did not fear; and the sea covered their enemies” (Psalm LXXVII). Then Leudastes’ ship was sunk, while the other survived.

Heraclius reviewed his army for three days; afterward, when he opened the inviolate Gospels of God, he found that he was being instructed to winter in Albania. Cedrenus, in the thirteenth year of Heraclius; and from him Baronius, volume VIII, under the year 622. Does that passage in I Corinthians XVI apply: “Or shall I even winter?” Or the passage in Titus III: “For I have decided to winter there”?

Pauline himself explains how the devil is both “enemy” and “defender” in Letter 4: “That he might destroy the enemy of good and the defender of evil.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 116. “As he gave to Abraham.”**—You may see this expressed from Paulinus in Eucherius—whoever that Eucherius may be; certainly he is later than that famous bishop of Lyon, since he cites Gregory the Great—in book II of his *Commentaries on Genesis*, chapter 17:

“But what did this victory of Abraham over the five kings signify? Those kings, whom the father of faith overcame in a mystery, signify nothing other than that, if our faith has been confirmed in the principal Spirit, it should subjugate to the word of God the five senses of our body.”

Isidore reproduces this in exactly the same words in his *Commentaries on Genesis*, chapter 11; but instead of “in a mystery” he reads “in battle.” Paulinus is more correct, and here, more in accord with the sense of Holy Scripture, has Abraham’s victory over four kings, referring it to the four elements of the body. For Abraham truly defeated the four kings who had taken Lot captive. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 117. “And just as he was victorious on behalf of his brother, who had been defeated in the company of five kings.”**—This reading was ingeniously devised by our Roman friend for the present passage from traces of the ancient reading. Previously there was only: “Victorious over neighboring kings,” which could be tolerated, as appears from Eucherius, p. 898, and Isidore, who present the passage as follows:

“For just as he emerged victorious over his kinsman’s enemies among the kings, so faith, victorious on behalf of the soul, will triumph over the external man.”

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 118. “By the Greek letter T.”**—Eucherius and Isidore also transferred this material into their commentaries. Eucherius there also explains the number 318, which Paulinus omits here—unless this passage was omitted by scribes because of the difficulty of the Greek numerals, iota and eta, which form the abbreviation of the name Jesus:

“But the fact that he conquered the hostile princes not by a multitude or by the strength of legions, but only with three hundred and eighteen companions, was already then imagined as a figure of the holy cross [which is expressed by the Greek letter T, and by the name JESUS—written in Greek characters as ι and η, and interpreted as ‘Savior’—whose numerical value is 318]; this signified that the passion of Christ would free us from the domination of the five bodily senses, which had previously overcome us, held captive by various vices.”

In Eucherius I have restored *imaginabatur* from Isidore, since it was lacking there and was necessary to complete the sense.

[Col. 0869A] Just as Eucherius and Isidore extracted their material from Paulinus, so Paulinus adapted certain things from his very close friend Ambrose. Ambrose writes in the prologue of his book *On the Faith*, addressed to Gratian:

“You ask me, holy emperor, to compose a little book on the faith, as you are about to set out for battle. For you know that victory is ordinarily sought more through the emperor’s faith than through the soldiers’ valor. Abraham too led three hundred and eighteen men to battle, and returned with trophies from countless enemies. By the sign of the Lord’s cross and name, after subduing the strength of the five kings and their victorious troops, he both avenged his kinsman and earned a son and a triumph.”

The same author, *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 3:

“He counted three hundred and eighteen, so that you might know that not the quantity of the number, but the merit of election, is expressed. For he chose those whom he judged worthy of the number of the faithful, those who would believe in the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Three hundred is signified by the Greek letter T; eighteen expresses the sum of ι η—that is, the name JESUS. Therefore, by the merit of faith,” and so forth.

This passage should accordingly be read in this way. Faustus of Riez likewise writes *On the Holy Spirit*:

“We call it a sacred number, because the three hundred—in Greek reckoning—show the sign of the cross, namely T, while the eighteen display the name of Jesus, namely ι η, which must be adored.”

Tertullian similarly, in book III of *Against Marcion*, chapter 4, refers Gideon’s three hundred companions to the mystery of the cross:

“For by this sign he felled heaps of robbers,

Engaging the people of Christ without a great army,

With three hundred horsemen”—

the number represented by the Greek letter Tau.

Augustine likewise writes in Sermon 108, *On the Season*:

“Gideon chose three hundred men for battle, to show that the world was to be delivered from the assault of powerful enemies not by the multitude of numbers, but by the sacrament of the cross. For three hundred, in the Greek T, display the likeness of the cross.”

A little later he continues:

“Gideon prefigured the Lord our Savior. And because three hundred, according to Greek reckoning—indicating the letter T—form a cross, Gideon then, with three hundred men, rescued the people of the Jews from the most savage nations, just as Christ later, through the mystery of the cross, delivered the whole human race from the power of the devil.”

Gregory the Great likewise writes in book XXX of the *Moralia*, chapter 17:

“The number thirty is contained in the letter Tau, which has the appearance of the cross. If what projects from the cross were added above its transverse line, it would be not merely the appearance of a cross but the cross itself. Since, therefore, this number three hundred is contained in the letter Tau, and through the letter Tau the appearance of the cross is displayed, it is not without reason that those who followed Gideon among these three hundred were designated as those to whom it was said: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (Luke IX).”

Isidore repeats the same words in chapter VII of his *Commentary on Judges*.

Ambrose explains the passage of John XII—“For he could have been sold for three hundred denarii”—by the same mystery in book VI of his *Commentary on Luke*, chapter 7. He says:

“The three hundred pieces of money declare the emblem of the cross.”

ROWSEYDUS.

**Note 119. “By the power of which mystery, in three hundred cubits …”**—Isidore recognizes the same mystery in the three hundred cubits of the Ark, in chapter 7 of his commentary on Genesis:

“Indeed, in these three hundred cubits too the sign of the wood of the Passion may be displayed. For the number of the letter T itself demonstrates the sign of the cross, through which, having been made partners in Christ’s Passion by baptism, we receive the length of eternal life.”

Bede repeats this in exactly the same words in his *Questions on Genesis*, where he more correctly has *quo* (“by which”) instead of *per quod*. The letter T must nevertheless be supplied in his text, since it is absent there. ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXV

**Note 120. “They were exterminated.”**—The passage occurs in Zephaniah I, 2:

> Καὶ ἐξωλοθρεύθησαν πάντες οἱ ἐπηρμένοι ἀργυρίῳ.

“And all who were raised up by silver were exterminated.”

The Latin Vulgate has: “All who were wrapped in silver perished.” A similar thought occurs in Ecclesiasticus XXXI, 5:

> Ὁ ἀγαπῶν χρυσὸν, οὐ δικαιωθήσεται, καὶ ὁ διώκων διαφθορὰν, αὐτῆς πληθήσεται.

“He who loves gold will not be justified, and he who pursues corruption will be filled with it.” The Vulgate has: “will be filled with it.” DUC.

[Col. 0870A] So too in Baruch III, verses 18–19:

“Those who hoard silver and gold, in which human beings place their trust—and they were exterminated.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 121. “Is sufficiently more fortunate.”**—Authors sometimes like to speak in this way, joining *magis* (“more”) or *satis* (“sufficiently”) to a comparative degree: “more stronger.” Here *satis* means “very,” as in Cyprian, Letter 20: “letters sufficiently sober”; in Julius Capitolinus, in *Marcus Antoninus*: “sufficiently noble”; in Aelius Spartianus, in *Severus*: “sufficiently devoted to his studies”; and in Rufinus, addressed to Gaudentius: “not even to depart from sufficiently expressive speeches.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 122. “That you may become protectors.”**—Suidas:

> Προτέκτωρ εἶδος ἀξιώματος Ῥωμαικοῦ.

“Protector: a type of Roman dignity.”

The *Glosses of the Basilica*:

> Πριμοσκουτάριοι, ὑπερασπισταὶ οἱ νῦν λεγόμενοι Προτέκτορες.

“Primoscutarii: defenders, now called Protectors.”

Menander, *On Embassies*:

> Προτέκτωρ δηλοῖ παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις τὸν εἰς τοῦτο καταλεγόμενον ἀξίας, τὸν βασίλειον προσκεπαστήν.

“Among the Romans, *protector* signifies one enrolled in this rank of dignity, the royal defender.”

They were established by Gordian the Younger. Cedrenus writes:

> Μετὰ δὲ τοῦτον ἐβασίλευσεν Ἰουνίωρ μῆνας τρεῖς, ὃς πρῶτος ἐποίησε κανδιδάτον καὶ προτέκτορας.

“After him Gordian the Younger reigned for three months; he was the first to institute the *candidati* and the Protectors.”

Protectors are frequently mentioned by Ammianus: the *domestici* in books XIV, XV, XVIII, XXI, and XXVI, and the commander of Mesopotamia in book XVIII. ROSWEYDUS.

**Protectors.**—The guards of the emperor’s person, who protected the emperor’s side, as described in book IX of the Theodosian Code, *On Protectors*. Cedrenus says that Gordian established their corps. It was regarded as an order far more distinguished than the other palace corps, so much so that Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, was first a protector and then a tribune, and nearly all serving soldiers aspired to this office.

Julius Firmicus, book III of the *Mathesis*, chapter XIV:

“He will make shield-bearers, or Protectors of the emperors, or men who by their personal watch will safeguard the rulers.”

[Col. 0870C] CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume III, p. 448.

## IN LETTER XXVI

**Note 123. “Sebastian.”**—This Sebastian may perhaps be the man mentioned by Severus in *Dialogue* 3, chapter 1:

“While I was saying these things, and Gallus was already prepared to relate his story, a crowd of monks burst in: the presbyter Evagrius, Aper, Sebastian, and Agricola.”

ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXVII

**Note 124. “The flourishing Clarus.”**—Clarus is mentioned several times by Paulinus. Paulinus wrote his epitaph, which appears in Letter 12. He was buried in Severus’s private church, as stated there. Severus mentions him in Letter 2 to the deacon Aurelian concerning the death of Saint Martin, and in the *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 25. His solemn commemoration is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 8 November, and he is assigned to Tours. ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXVIII

**Note 125. “Endelechius.”**—Our Sirmond notes concerning this Endelechius in Letter 8 of book IV of Sidonius. This Endelechius, who held a rhetorician’s chair at Rome, is mentioned in an old annotation to an Apuleian manuscript in the Vatican Library:

“I, Sallustius, read and corrected this successfully at Rome, in the consulship of Olybrius and Probinus, declaiming a controversy in the Forum of Mars before the rhetor Endelechius. I revised it again at Constantinople, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.”

This was the holy Severus Endelechius, a Christian orator and poet, whose short poem *On the Deaths of Cattle* survives. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 126. “Theodosius.”**—Jerome mentions, in Letter 13 to Paulinus, books composed by him in honor of Theodosius, which he says were composed with intelligence and elegance. Cassiodorus also mentions him in book I of the *Sacred Readings*, chapter 21; likewise Gennadius, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, chapter 48, calls the work a panegyric on the victory over the tyrants. ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXIX

**Note 127. “We are pricked by the harshness of the bristles.”**—“Formerly monks wore garments made from camel hair, as is evident from this passage and from Sulpicius’ *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 7, in his description of the monastic order established by Saint Martin:

‘Most of them,’ he says, ‘were clothed in camel hair; a softer garment was regarded there as a crime.’

Paulinus of Périgueux, book II of the *Life of the same Saint Martin*:

> For many, a garment was woven from camel’s bristles,  
> that with gentle goads it might prick their wakeful limbs,  
> and, pricking the flesh, exclude light sleep,  
> lest soft things foster a body’s softness,  
> and a loose garment billow in wanton folds.

I therefore suspect that the monks’ hair shirts and the canons’ *almuces* derived their origin from this practice, since they too formerly wore garments made of skins close to the body, following the example of Saint John the Baptist, who was clothed in camel hair and girded with a leather belt around his loins, as Matthew, chapter III, and Mark, chapter I, testify. Paulinus also, in Letter 49 to Macarius, no. 12, speaks of Vagium as clad in sewn skins and imitating the clothing of John the Forerunner with a bristly garment.”

**Note 128. “To the birth of the holy one, having made an addition to his merits.”**—In manuscript P, now the Royal manuscript, the reading was *natalium sanctis dictionem*, as also in the manuscript mentioned by Cauchy; hence he conjectures that it should be corrected to *sanctis adjectionem fecisse meritorum* (“having made an addition of merits to the saints”). With less alteration, however, I would willingly substitute *sanctis auctionem fecisse meritorum* (“having increased the merits of the saints”). What follows supports this conjecture of ours: “He increased the priest’s merit by recalling the nobility of his marriage.” DUC.

Paulinus here also favors Cauchy’s reading no less strongly. For the preceding words are: “adding a name from the episcopal insignia.” Nevertheless, I retain the common reading and understand *dictionem* in the sense in which it is used by Ennodius. Our Sirmond restored this usage splendidly in Sidonius, book VIII, Letter 11:

“When he had undertaken the work he had proposed, he varied his ethical diction according to the character of the person, the time, and the place.”

Previously the passage read incorrectly, “and here addition”; “a correction worthy of cedar” is appropriate. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 129. “With Marcellinus the consul as grandfather.”**—EDIT. Grin. in the margin: “Marcellinus and Probinus were consuls in the year of Christ 342, in the time of Constantine and Constantius.”

Schot. EDIT. in the margin: “Jerome thinks that she was Marcellinus’ daughter; but Rufinus, in the second of his *Invectives against Jerome*, calls her his granddaughter.”

**Note 130. “On a cheaper little donkey.”**—There was no reason for some people to add in the margin: “Others read *burdico*.” The word was known not only to writers of that age but also to earlier authors. It does not mean *burrhus*, *pyrrichus*, or some kind of red garment, as certain people wrote in their notes on Saint Jerome’s letters; nor was the name derived from Buris, a city of Achaea, as Erasmus thinks, from which little donkeys were supposedly sent. Rather, the ancient commentators on Horace’s Ode 27, book I, explain that *manni* are horses, and small ones are called *burdi* or *buridi*. In *Epode* IV: “*Manni* are horses which we commonly call *burdones* or *burichi*”; and in Letter 7 of book I: “*Mannis*, small horses, *burichis*.” An old glossary has: “*Mannis*: βουρίχοις.”

This caused certain people, in two passages of Saint Jerome where *manni* are mentioned, to add *buricis* in the margin. The word later slipped into the text, as in the commentary on chapter X of Ecclesiastes:

“Inflated by sudden dignity from the devil, they tread the public roads on *manni*, which they commonly call *lubrici*.”

So reads the old Frobenian edition; more recent editions have “which they commonly call *burici*.” In the edition of Marianus Victorius, however, this gloss has been removed. In Letter 26 Jerome likewise writes:

“When you see platters smoking, when you see silver weighed out, when you see hot *burici*—that is, *manni*—and long-haired boys and costly garments.”

But Erasmus testifies that the word *burici* is absent from certain manuscript books. In the excellent book of V. C. Nicholas Fabri, *the blessed one*—τοῦ μακαρίτου—it nowhere appears, and it seems to have been stitched in to indicate what Jerome calls *manni*, namely, small and extremely cheap hired horses.

Our Aquitanian and French dialects have retained the word, but only to designate donkeys, which they call *bourriques* and *ocurriquets*. DUC.

**Note 131. “Daughter of Babylon.”**—Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 397, says:

“Since he calls that city the daughter of Babylon, while nevertheless saying in many places that it displays the daughter of Zion, I think you can easily understand that, through this variation in the name of the one city, pagans and Christians are distinguished: Rome is called Babylon insofar as pagan impiety still prevailed in it; but Zion in many places, since it abounded in Christians among whom the worship of the true religion shone forth.”

I think rather that at this time Paulinus, like Jerome, called Rome Babylon because of the disturbances and temptations that were abundant at Rome, whereas Jerusalem was at peace—as Paulinus clearly says here. Thus Jerome, in Letter 17 to Marcella, written in the names of Paula and Eustochium in order to summon her from Rome to Jerusalem, sets before her the disturbances of the City. He does the same in Letter 18, which he writes in his own name to the same Marcella. See these matters explained at length against the calumnies of the heretics in my *Anti-Capellus*, chapter 5. ROSWEYDUS.

[Col. 0872B] **Note 132. “I recited Martin.”**—That Paulinus was the first to make Martin’s Life known to the city of Rome is attested by Postumianus in Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 16:

“Your most devoted Paulinus was the first to introduce him to the city of Rome.”

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 133. “Nicetas, who had come from Dacia.”**—Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 397, derives Nicetas’ first arrival in Rome from the number of the *Natalitia* of Saint Felix published by Paulinus, as follows:

“When Paulinus, writing to Severus in Letter 28, testifies that he had decided to compose every year in verse the birthday poem of the same Felix, it will clearly be possible to count the years in their proper sequence from the number of those poems. But since the ninth *Natalitium* published by Paulinus mentions Nicetas’ later arrival at Nola, and says that it occurred four years after his earlier arrival, it must be affirmed that his first arrival took place at the time when the fifth *Natalitium* was composed. For concerning his later arrival, when he recalls the earlier one, these are the verses in *Natalitium* 7:

> At last you came, restored to me in the fourth year;  
> yet thanks be to Christ, who brought you back, though late.

Since, therefore, his first arrival must have occurred at the time of the fifth published *Natalitium*, it remains to determine in which year of the Lord this most likely happened.

It can be understood from Paulinus himself that these *Natalitia* must be numbered beginning with the last year in which, while still detained in Spain, he was preparing to travel to Rome. That was the year of the Lord 393. In the following year, when he had already gone to Nola for the birthday of Saint Felix, he published the second *Natalitium* in sequence. But when, as his testimony makes clear, he had already spent a year with the same Felix in the Nola estate, and had received a legation from the African bishops—which was in the year of the Lord 395—he wrote the third *Natalitium*. In the following year, namely the year after that, he wrote the fourth. Therefore it must necessarily be said that in this very year, 397, the fifth *Natalitium* was elaborated; and it is equally necessary to affirm that Nicetas’ arrival took place at that time, since from the fifth *Natalitium* to the ninth there are four years, the period by which Nicetas postponed his return to Italy.”

ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXX

**Note 134. “But poor me.”**—From this point to “that he who by nature,” Augustine cites the passage in Letter 106 to Paulinus. In some books it is wrongly addressed to Boniface. Augustine himself mentions it as a letter sent to Paulinus in book XXI of *The Gift of Perseverance*:

“Was it not many years ago that I published the very letter which I wrote against the Pelagians to holy Paulinus, bishop of Nola, a letter which they have only recently begun to oppose? Let them also examine the one I sent to Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church, when we were engaged in our fiercest struggle against the Pelagians, and they will find it like that one addressed to Paulinus.”

Prosper also mentions it in chapter 43 of his *Against the Collator*:

“Leaving aside, then, those volumes in which, from the beginning of his episcopate, long before the opponents of grace arose, he argued on behalf of grace, let the three books he wrote to Marcellinus be read, and let the letter to holy Paulinus, bishop of Nola, be reconsidered.”

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 135. “May he reduce it to nothing.”**—These are the words of Psalm LXXII, 20:

> Ὡσεὶ ἐνύπνιον ἐγειρομένου, Κύριε, ἐν τῇ πόλει σου τὴν εἰκόνα αὐτῶν ἐξουδενώσεις.

“As a dream when one awakens, Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.”

The expression “in the city of the surrounding enclosure” is taken from Psalm XXX, 22:

> Ὅτι ἐθαυμάστωσε τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ ἐν πὸλει περιοχῆς.

“For he has made his mercy wonderful in a fortified city.”

Literally, “in a city of fortification”; Felix Pratensis likewise translates it from the Hebrew in Psalm LIX, 2:

> Τίς ἐπάξειμε εἰς πόλιν περιοχῆς;

“Who will lead me into a fortified city?”

In IV Kings XXIV, 10:

> Ἦλθεν ἡ πόλις ἐν περιοχῇ.

“The city was surrounded by fortifications.”

The Hebrew word is translated as *ὀχύρωμα* (*ochýrōma*), “stronghold, defense, fortification,” in Zechariah IX, 3. In this passage of Psalm XXX, Theodoretus cites Symmachus:

> Ὡς ἐν πόλει περιπεφραγμένῃ.

“As in a city surrounded by fortifications.”

In Augustine and in the old Psalter, *περιοχῆς* is translated *circumstantiae* (“surrounding enclosure”), just as by the author of the Latin Vulgate in Psalm CXL, 3:

> Καὶ θύραν περιοχῆς περὶ τὰ χείλη μου.

“And a door of enclosure around my lips.”

DUC.

**Note 136. “Nor with melting wax.”**—Basil, *Homily against the Sabellians*, p. 805:

> Ξύλα καὶ κηρὸς, καὶ ζωγράφου τήχνη τὴν εἰκόνα ποιεῖ φθαρτὴν φθαρτοῦ μὶμημα.

“Wood and wax, together with the painter’s art, make the image corruptible, a likeness of a corruptible human being.”

They used to paint with wax and burn the painting in, as Pliny teaches in book XXXV, chapter 11; and in book XXI, chapter 14, he writes that wax is drawn into various colors with pigments. Hence *κηρογραφία* (“wax painting”) denotes this kind of art, and *κηροχυτεῖν* means “to pour and melt wax.” For this reason, when the Greek Fathers discuss paintings, they also mention wax.

Chrysostom, in the homily *That the Old and New Testaments Have One Lawgiver*:

> Ἐγὼ καὶ τὴν κηρόχυτον ἠγάπησα γραφὴν εὐσεβείας πεπληρωμένην.

“I too loved the wax-poured painting filled with piety.”

And in the homily *On the Basin*, or *On the Washing of Thursday*:

> Οὐ σανίδα τιμῶσιν οὐδὲ τὴν κηρόχυτον γραφὴν ἀλλὰ τὸν χαρακτῆρα τοῦ βασιλέως.

“They do not honor a tablet, nor a wax-poured painting, but the image of the emperor.”

Both passages are cited in the Seventh Ecumenical Council, session 4, where the other translator perhaps more accurately renders *κηρόχυτον* as “an image cast from wax,” or “an image composed of molten wax.” DUC.

## IN LETTER XXXI

**Note 137. “Primuliacum.”**—The same place is mentioned in Letter 12 to Severus:

“We have learned that you have prepared another basilica at our Primuliacum, larger than the former one.”

It must have been not far from Eluson, among the Nitiobriges, where Severus lived chiefly.

In Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 50 and 51, there is mention of a certain Severus who was a presbyter in the territory of Bordeaux, within the boundary of the city of Beorreta, in the village of Sexciacum. He was of noble birth and built two churches on the site of his rural estate.

Our Severus likewise built two basilicas for Paulinus in different places: one mentioned by Paulinus in Letter 12 to Severus, though the place is not specified; and another, larger than the former, at Primuliacum, which he mentions in the same place. If the locations could be made to correspond, it would be necessary to regard the two Severuses as one and the same. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 138. “The blessed Melanius.”**—So reads the Viennese manuscript, and so it should be read. Because of this illustrious woman’s outstanding qualities of mind and exceptional virtues, Paulinus gave her a masculine name, refusing even to call her a woman. Thus he says in Letter 29, number 6:

“To whom at last—a woman? if she may be called a woman who is so manly a Christian.”

For this reason Paulinus himself, in Letter 28 to the same Severus, number 5, speaks of “holy Melani,” according to the reading of the Royal manuscript. Likewise, in Letter 29 of the same author to the same person, number 5, Schott’s edition has *Melanii*. In Letter 32 to the same person, number 11, verse 5, the Royal and Viennese manuscripts, as well as Schott’s edition, read *Melani sanctae*. And in Letter 45 to Augustine, number 3, we read: “of the blessed mother of this son … Melanio.”

I think the reader will not find it unwelcome if, to establish our correction, I insert here something from the *Adventoria* of the Augustinian Henry Noris addressed to Father Francisco Macedo:

“When,” he says, “I examined the heading of Saint Augustine’s books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*—‘Most sincere brothers, beloved by God, Albine, Piniane, and Melania’ [the Latin address uses these forms]—I did not accept Baronius’s correction, by which, under the year 409, he thought *Albina* should be substituted for *Albine*, unless, he adds in the same place, there was there a son Albinus in addition to the mother Albina. For in that period women’s names were not always expressed with feminine endings. Paula’s daughter had a name with a neuter ending, namely Eustochium. Indeed, I affirmed that women’s names were then customarily expressed by the holy Fathers with masculine endings. Thus I showed that the mother of the younger Melania, Albina, was commonly called *Albinus* in the nominative case. Apart from the heading of the book *On the Grace of Christ*, Augustine gave Letter 227 this heading: *Albino, Piniano et Meliano* (“To Albinus, Pinianus, and Melianus”), where it is certain that one must read *Melanio* (“to Melanius”). Jerome, in Letter 79, says: ‘Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania greet you.’ Possidius of Calama, in his catalogue of the books of the holy Doctor of Hippo, writes that the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin* were sent to Pinianus, Albinus, and Melania.
