Thus the Fathers who flourished in the year 400 wrote the name of the most noble woman Albina.”

Anyone who wishes to learn more should consult the same most learned Henry Noris the Augustinian, in the *Adventoria* addressed to Father Francisco Macedo, where he discusses at length the heading of Saint Augustine’s book *On the Grace of Christ*: “To Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania.” Concerning Melania, see Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 117 through 214. See Note 194.

**Note 139. “Having been broken open.”**—This is the more accurate reading, so that the reference may be understood as being to the Jews, who, after breaking open and unsealing their own marks—for the Jews fortified the tomb, sealing the stone with guards, Matthew XXVII—found the tomb empty, yet did not believe in the resurrection. Thus writes our Gretzer in volume II of *On the Cross*, in connection with this letter of Paulinus.

Bignaeus, in the Paris edition, advises restoring *indiscussis* (“unbroken,” “unopened”), so that the reference may be to Christ rising from a closed tomb whose seals had not been opened. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 140. “The statue of Jupiter.”**—Apart from Rufinus, Socrates, Theodoret, and Sozomen, whom someone added in the margin of the Paris edition, Eusebius—older than all of them—in book III, chapter 25 of the *Life of Constantine*, testifies that a statue of Venus, not Jupiter, had been erected at the place of the Lord’s Passion and burial:

> Δεινὸν ὡς ἀληθῶς ταφεῶνα ψυχῶν κατασκευάζουσι νεκρῶν εἰδώλων, σκότιον. Ἀφροδίτης ἀκολάστῳ δαίμονι μυχὸν οἰκοδομησάμενοι.

“They truly built a dreadful and abominable tomb of dead idols, and constructed a dark recess for the wanton demon Venus.”

The translator omitted the word *σκότιον* (“dark”), which, if referred to *μυχόν* (“recess”), would indicate a dark and gloomy recess. Or rather, in place of *σκότιον* one should read, as in Sozomen, book II, chapter 11, *ζώδιον*; or at least, as another reading of Christophorson has it, *ζόανον ἱδρύσαντο*, “they set up an image.”

Thus Eusebius’ passage should be corrected as follows:

> Νεκρὸν εἰδώλου ζόανον Ἀφροδίτης ἀκολάστῳ δαίμονι, καὶ μυχὸν οἰκοδομησάμενοι.

“They built a tomb of souls, and a dead image of an idol for the wanton demon Venus, and constructed a recess.”

In this way the passage agrees with what follows in Paulinus: “the statue of the demon stood, and the altar of the statue smoked with the burial-offerings of cattle” (for this seems preferable to reading, with Cauchy, “the burial-offerings smoked”), “and the name of God was borne upon statues of the dead.”

See also Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 28.

These things also agree with the statue of Venus and with the mourning that Paulinus later says was performed by prostitutes who mourned Venus’ lover together with effeminate men. Such mourning is also mentioned in Ezekiel, chapter VIII, verse 14:

“And behold, women were sitting there mourning Adonis.”

The Septuagint has:

> Καὶ ἰδοὺ ἐκεῖ γυναῖκες καθήμεναι θρηνοῦσαι τὸν Θαμμούς.

“And behold, women were sitting there mourning Thammuz.”

Theodoret says:

> Ὁ Θαμμαοὺς ὁ Ἄδῶνις ἐστι κατὰ τὴν Ἐλλάδα φωνήν.

“Thammuz is Adonis in the Greek language.”

Jerome, in his commentary:

“According to the pagan story, in the month of June Venus’ lover and a most beautiful young man was killed. They call that same month of June by his name and celebrate an annual festival for him, at which women mourn him as though dead; afterward he is sung and praised as returning to life.”

Plutarch, in his *Life of Alcibiades*:

> Ἀδωνίον γὰρ εἰς τας ἡμερας ἐκείνας καθηκόντων εἴδωλα πολλαχοῦ νεκροῖς ἐκκομιζομένοις ὅμοια προὔκειντο ταῖς γυναιξι, καὶ ταφὰς ἐμιμοῦντο κοπτόμεναι, καὶ θρήνους ᾖδον.

“When the Adonia occurred on those days, women everywhere displayed images resembling the dead who were being carried out for burial; they imitated funerals by beating themselves and sang dirges.”

DUC.

It may be that Paulinus made a *μνημονικὸν ἁμάρτημα* (“a mnemonic error”), unless the place of the Passion is understood broadly enough to include the place of the Resurrection. For a statue of Jupiter was placed at the latter, whereas a statue of Venus was placed at the place of the Passion.

Jerome, in Letter 13 to Paulinus, *On the Institution of the Monk*:

“From the time of Hadrian to the reign of Constantine, for approximately one hundred and eighty years, a statue of Jupiter was worshiped by the pagans at the place of the Resurrection, and a marble statue of Venus on the rock of the Cross. The authors of the persecution thought that they could undermine our belief in the Resurrection and the Cross if they polluted the holy places with idols.

“Our Bethlehem, now the most august place in the world, concerning which the Psalmist sings, ‘Truth has arisen from the earth’ (Psalm XLVIII; see Jerome on chapter VIII of Ezekiel), was overshadowed by a grove of Thammuz, that is, Adonis; and in the cave where Christ once whimpered as an infant, Venus’ lover was mourned.”

Alexander the monk, in his homily *On the Discovery of the Holy Cross*, and George Hamartolus in his *Chronicle* likewise testify that a statue of Venus was placed at the site of the Passion. Hence Mount Calvary seems to have been called *Venerarium* from this statue of Venus.

Ambrose, on Psalm XLVII:

“The Lord suffered, according to the region of the heavens, in the Venerarium, which was located on the northern side.”

Mount Calvary, however, is on the northern side. See our Gretzer, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 62. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 141. “He reigned with him.”**—The most learned Cauchy proposed the reading: “she asked her son to grant her [permission].” We suspected that, with less alteration, it should read: “she asked the Lord.” But conjectures must be dismissed, since it is clear that Paulinus is following the wording of Sulpicius Severus, whom he had previously mentioned in connection with his *Annals* or history, concerning events “which have passed from the annals not of one nation but of the human race,” unless both writers drew the narrative from the records of some other historian.

Thus Sulpicius writes in book II of his *Sacred History*:

“For Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine, who, as Augusta, reigned with her son, desiring to recognize Jerusalem, destroyed the idols and temples found there.”

The passage should therefore apparently be restored as follows:

“When she recognized Jerusalem, she asked her son, with whom she reigned under the title Augusta, to grant her permission.”

A little later Paulinus accordingly adds: “with the ready assent of her son the emperor, the Augusta mother.”

Constantine therefore wished his mother Helena to be called Augusta. For this reason she is said to have reigned with her son when she recognized Jerusalem—that is, when she revisited the holy places, as Ambrose says in his sermon on the death of Theodosius; and he confirms the truth of this history by his authority. DUC.

**Note 142. “Never covered with marble.”**—The Reverend Father Franciscus Canillacius, a priest of our order, testified to us that this miracle persisted into our own age, when, on his journey to Constantinople, he visited those holy places as a pilgrim to fulfill a vow.

Sulpicius Severus also recounts another miracle concerning the same footprints, which we must not omit, since Paulinus adds a similar one concerning Christ’s cross. Sulpicius says:

“Although the faith of those who flock together daily eagerly carries away what has been trodden by the Lord, the sand nevertheless suffers no loss.”

Paulinus below:

“This cross, indeed, lends its wood daily to the countless vows of human beings, so that it suffers no loss and remains, as it were, untouched, daily divided among those who take from it and always whole for those who venerate it”—or, as should be read, “daily divided … always whole.”

DUC.

Jerome, in his book *On Hebrew Places*:

“To the east of Jerusalem, with the torrent Cedron flowing between, where the Lord’s last footprints impressed upon the earth are still shown today, although the same earth is daily taken away by believers, those same holy footprints nevertheless continually recover their former condition.”

Severus, book II of his *Sacred History*:

“It is remarkable that the place where the divine feet last stood, when the Lord was lifted into heaven on a cloud, could not be made continuous with the pavement and the rest of the paved surface.”

Paulinus, book V of the *Life of Saint Martin*:

> Or here the happy earth received  
> Christ, returning joyfully to the stars,  
> his final footprints;  
> and, preserving the gifts of that holy touch,  
> whatever the hand had contrived for ornament  
> it disdainfully scattered far from its sands.

Bede, *On the Holy Places*, chapter 7:

“The Lord’s last footprints, where he ascended, with heaven opened above, are visible. Although earth is taken away from them daily by believers, they nevertheless remain and retain the same appearance, as though marked by impressed footprints.”

This should be considered all the more miraculous because, during the siege of Jerusalem, this mountain was occupied by the Roman army. Who could doubt that much was then overturned and dug up there? Yet this place remained unharmed after so much time. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 143. “So that it suffers no loss.”**—Cyril, *Catechesis* 10, infers Christ’s divinity from this multiplication and dispersion of the cross, which nevertheless always remains whole:

> Τὸ ξύλον τὸ ἅγιον τοῦ σταυροῦ μαρτυρεῖ, μέχρι σημερον παρ’ ἡμῖν φαινομενον, καὶ διὰ τῶν κατὰ πίστιν ἐξ αὐτοῦ λαμβανόντων, ἐντεῦθεν τὴν οἰκουμένην πᾶσαν σχεδὸν ἤδη ἐπλήρωσαν.

“The holy wood of the cross bears witness to Christ, appearing among us to this day, and among those who receive from it here in faith and have by now filled almost the whole world.” [The printed Greek has “through those who receive from it” and a plural verb, “they have filled.”]

ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXXII

[Col. 0876C]

### Note 144. “Infants in snow-white … clothing”

The same Paulinus, in Letter 49 to Macarius, no. 14, writes of Valgius, recently baptized:

> “I have sent him, as a spiritual gift, to your unanimity: an immaculate offspring of Mother Church, in the rough fleece of shining wool, a shepherd of a small flock but a giver of a great pledge.”

Here the reference is to the white, or shining garment, which the newly baptized put on as a symbol of the purity and innocence they professed. For immediately after they emerged naked from the font, they were clothed in a white robe.

Learned men commonly suppose that Christians were clothed in white garments after baptism for this reason: as Saint Paul says to the Ephesians, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” This is also the interpretation of Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book I, chapter 6. Hence the new light of baptism is called “illumination” in the *Theodosian Code*, in Greek φώτισμα (*phōtisma*). See Theodulf of Orléans, *On the Order of Baptism*, chapter 14. [Col. 0876D]

Saint Zeno of Verona, Letter *Invitatorium* 2, “To the Font”:

> Indeed, you are plunged naked into the font,  
> but soon you rise from it clothed in an ethereal garment.

Lactantius, poem *On the Resurrection*:

> The shining army comes forth from gleaming waters.

The Roman *Ordo*:

> And the infants themselves, after baptism, are brought before him, that is, the bishop; and he gives each one a white robe, a chrismal, and ten siliquae, saying: “Receive this white and undefiled garment, which you are to carry before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ for everlasting recompense.”

The Council of Rouen, in the year 1050, canon 19:

> Let the baptized be presented for eight days in white garments, with burning candles, in the same church [where they received the grace of regeneration and where they are parishioners].

Conrad of Ursperg, under the year 1124:

> Let them bring their children to baptism on Holy Saturday of Easter and Pentecost, with candles and with the *cappa* called the white garment, accompanied by their sponsors; and, having clothed them in the garment of innocence, let them bring them to church each day until the eighth day of that Saturday and take care to attend the celebration of the divine service. [Col. 0877A]

Here he calls the garment a *cappa*, whereas others call it a *chrismal*. The white garments were provided at the Church’s expense, as Gregory the Great suggests, book VII, indiction 1, Letter 2.

There is frequent mention of this kind of white garment of the baptized among writers: Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapters 1, 2, and 5; Saint Cyril, *Catechesis* 4; Jobius in Photius, no. 223; John Moschus, chapter 207; Socrates, book VII, chapter 17; Saint Augustine, Letter 168 and Sermon 137 *On Time*; Saint Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*; Prudentius, book I *Against Symmachus*; Gregory the Great, book VII, indiction 2, Letter 5; Fortunatus, book V, poem 4; Gregory of Tours, book V, chapter 11, and *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 1; Lambert, *Life of Saint Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne*, no. 21; Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Institution of the Clergy*, book I, chapter 29; Amalarius, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapters 29 and 33; Honorius of Autun, book I, chapter 243; Durandus, book VI of the *Rationale*, chapter 82; and the Council of Ypres, in the year 1288, chapter 17, and elsewhere.

Some writers, however, call into question what is reported concerning the nakedness of those being baptized and of the baptized, at least in the case of the female sex. Yet this is expressly reported also of women by Chrysostom in his letter to Innocent; by John Moschus, chapter 3; by Cyprian, or the author of the book *On the Singular Life of Clerics*; and in the Fourth Council under Mennas, session 5, p. 751, Cologne edition, 1618.

CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, vol. I, p. 121.

### Note 145. “That they might be sacred ashes”

The dedication of churches could not take place without the relics of saints.

The Seventh Synod, canon 7:

> A bishop who consecrates a church without holy relics shall be deposed, as one who has transgressed the ecclesiastical traditions.

Balsamon, book I, *Responsa* 38:

> There is a great difference between churches consecrated through the *enkaenia*, the opening ceremonies, the enthronement, the anointing with holy chrism, and the deposition of the holy relics of martyrs, and those which have not been sanctified in this way. [Col. 0877C]

Ambrose, Letter 85 to his sister Marcellina, concerning the relics of Gervasius and Protasius:

> When I had dedicated the basilica, many began to appeal as with one voice, saying: “Dedicate the basilica as they do in Rome.” I replied: “I shall do so if I find relics of martyrs.”

Metaphrastes, June 19, in Surius, concerning Theodosius, who had taken portions of Gervasius and Protasius and gone to Constantinople:

> Before this great city he therefore raises for them a beautiful and elegant church, and deposits in it the sacred relics of the martyrs, as a treasure worth more than thousands of gold and silver pieces, as the divine David says [Psalm 118].

Paul the Deacon, concerning Justinian:

> The *enkaenia* of the saints took place at Constantinople, and the relics of the apostles Andrew and Luke were deposited there. Bishop Menas proceeded with the holy relics, seated in an imperial golden carriage adorned with jewels and holding three cases of the holy apostles on his knees; and thus he celebrated the *enkaenia*. [Col. 0877D]

ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 146. “The cross, the body, the blood—the martyr himself is God”

Our Brouwer, in his commentary on Fortunatus, book III, poem 25, understands this as referring to the body of Christ formerly placed on the altar beneath the cross. The rite is mentioned by the Second Synod of Tours, held in the year of Christ 570, during the pontificate of Pope John III and the sixth year of King Charibert, canon 3, where it decrees:

> Let the body of the Lord be placed on the altar, not in an imaginary arrangement, but under the title of the cross.

Accordingly, in the passage already cited, Fortunatus praises Felix, bishop of Bourges, who had made a sacred reliquary or tower for the body of the Lord:

> How well the joined ornaments become it, so that great pearls  
> and golden gifts may adorn the consecrated Lamb’s body.  
> Let Solomon’s metal vessels yield to chrysolites;  
> art and faith make this more pleasing.  
> These gifts, O Christ, which Felix has given to you,  
> are like those which the shepherd Abel once gave from his flock.  
> And you, who see his heart, make him equal in piety  
> to the widow of Sarepta, who gave her two coins.

Gregory of Tours, book I *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 86, likewise mentions a similar tower in which the ministry of the Lord’s body was kept. He relates a miracle in which a tower slipped from the hands of an impure deacon and of its own accord passed through the air back to the altar.

ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 147. “With the apostles and martyrs, whose venerable ashes are placed beneath the altars”

In former times the relics of the saints were not placed above the altars, but beneath them and within them, as may be seen in Augustine, Sermon 32 *On Various Subjects*, chapter 3; Gregory of Tours, book X of the *History*, chapter 31, and book I *On Miracles*, chapter 63; and very frequently in our Paulinus in this same letter, as well as in *Natale* 9 of Saint Felix, verses 401–402:

> The entire altars look out through windows from above,  
> beneath which within they have given the bodies of the saints their place.

[Col. 0878B]

Veils were also hung around the altar, so that dust might not settle on the cases containing the holy relics; hence the altar hangings used today. I recently saw such a veil, hung as an altar hanging before the table of the high altar, in the church of the town of Galardon, four leagues from Chartres.

### Note 148. “Caccabata”

That is, “blackened.” Paulinus means that his verses darken the walls of the church rather than illuminate them. The word passed into use as an insult.

In the *Lives of the Fathers*, book VI, Pelagius’s booklet 15, no. 29:

> They have done you a good turn, you ash-colored and blackened one.

The subject is Moses, an Ethiopian hermit. In no. 25, concerning Macarius, falsely accused of fornication:

> And they hung blackened pots and the handles of vessels around my neck.

Hence Zeno of Verona, Sermon 6 to the newly baptized, calls black bread *caccabaceus*:

> The breeze did not spoil them, bitter smoke did not stain them, nor did frost crush them; and, what is more, they rose without leaven. Certainly they are not blackened; not stale, not burnt, not raw, not moldy: they have the color of milk, and the taste of milk.

Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 41, calls the movement of matter, according to Hermogenes’ view, *caccabaceus*, because it was turbulent, like a boiling pot.

John Filesacus, book I of the *Selecta*, chapters 3 and 14, derives *caccabata*, meaning “chattering and frivolous,” from the verb κακκαβίζειν, the cry of partridges.

But Paulinus clearly contrasts the blackness, or darkness, of his verses with the brightness of the new walls, newly faced; and Zeno contrasts the milk-white color with the blackness of *caccabaceus*.

ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 149. “Within the apse”

The larger shell-shaped recess of the altar, called κόγχη by Greek writers, was commonly called *absida* or *apsis* by Latin writers of the later period. Paulinus expressly confuses the apse with the shell in Letter 12, now numbered 32. Walafrid Strabo is not inconsistent with this when he says, in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 6, that an apse is an exedra separated from the church and is called in Greek κύκλος.

Strictly speaking, however, the shell and the apse were different. The *apsis* properly is a semicircle, ἡμί¬κυκλος, which rises upward from the lower part of the θυσιαστήριον, or altar, and curves into an apse, arch, or semicircle. The shell, on the other hand, is the inner part of the apse, vaulted, curved, and hollowed above in the form of a shell.

Thus Paulinus correctly distinguishes the apse from its inner vault:

> The apse, marble-covered on floor and walls, is brightened by a vault adorned with mosaic.

Paulinus also notes that *apsis* and *absis* are both commonly used. If there were several altars in a church or sacred building, each had its own apse. Leo of Ostia, book III, chapter 28:

> Each altar had its own apse.

It should also be noted that writers very often call the shell itself, or the sacred table itself—that is, the altar—an *apse*. For example, they write of relics of saints being placed in apses, although it is well known that these were customarily deposited beneath altars and within altars.

CANGIUS, *Christian Constantinople*, book III, pp. 45–46.

### Note 150. “The trichora beneath the altars”

The word *trichorum* is rare and has no single fixed meaning.

Spartianus, in his *Life of Pescennius Niger*:

> His house may still be seen today at Rome, in the Campus of Jupiter. It is called the Pescennian, and in it he placed his statue in a trichorum.

Isaac Casaubon comments on this passage:

> “In a trichorum,” that is, in one of the trichora.

The houses and palaces of the great commonly consisted of three distinct parts: one stood opposite the person entering, while two were at the sides. Architects called these three-part houses *trichora*, τρίχωρα.

Statius Papinius, in his poem on the Tiburtine villa of Manlius Vopiscus:

> Why should I now marvel at immense structures,  
> or at buildings separated by divided trichora?

Our architects today call them pavilions, because the separate roofs of these sections—for we commonly call the sections of a building its bodies—rise in such a way that, as in the arrangement of a military camp, there are an equal number of distinct pavilion gables.

Thus Casaubon, and not entirely incorrectly.

Claudius Salmasius interprets the same passage differently:

> “In a trichorum,” he says, means “on the gable.” For statues were customarily placed on the gables of magnificent houses, as also on the gables of temples.

Vopiscus, in the *Life of Florianus*:

> The image of Apollo, which they worshiped, was found placed on a couch at the very top of the gable, without anyone’s hand having put it there.

The gable was called *trichorum* because of its triangular shape; for τρίκωρον and τρίγωνον mean the same thing.

Galen, in his *Lexicon of Hippocrates*:

> A roof-gable is that part of the roof raised upward like a triangle.

For among the ancients all roofs of buildings were either flat or gabled. But Claudius’s interpretation is less correct.

What a *trichorum* is can be learned nowhere better than from this passage of Paulinus:

> The relics of the apostles and martyrs, consecrated in a triple apse beneath the altars.

He means that within the larger apse there were two other apses, beneath each of which stood an altar; or rather, that one altar stood in the middle of the trichorum, or between the three apses—that is, in the middle of the larger apse, yet positioned so as to face the two lateral apses as well.

Spartianus likewise seems to be understood in this way: the statue of Pescennius Niger was placed in the trichorum, that is, in the middle of the trichorum. The entire place, consisting of three apses or sections, was called *trichorus* or *trichorum*.

I have said “one altar” because in the earliest periods of the Church there was generally only one altar in churches. This is clear from the church at Tyre built by Paulinus, bishop of that city. Eusebius, book X, chapter 4:

> And he placed the holy altar of the holy of holies in the midst of all.

That is, he placed the altar, like the holy of holies, in the middle of the sanctuary.

Later, explaining this mystically, he says:

> But what is the august, great, and unique altar except the pure holy of holies of the soul of the common priest of all?

The august, immense, and single altar therefore signifies nothing other than the pure holy of holies of the soul, which is the common priest of all.

Nor should it be surprising that here you find *altars* in the plural, for shortly afterward the poem likewise says:

> The altars veil a double honor sacred to God,

although the preceding line reads:

> This inscription indicates that the holy of holies has been deposited beneath the altar.

Just as in the church built by Paulinus there are three apses, so formerly there were three or even more in other churches.

Anastasius the Librarian, in his life of Hadrian:

> He constructed three apses in the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

The same writer, in his life of Leo III:

> In the greater dining hall he made an apse of remarkable beauty, decorated with mosaic, and two apses, shining with marble and painting, on the right and left.

Again, in the same place:

> With a mosaic apse; and also ten other apses, on the right and left, painted with various scenes.

Paulinus appears to call these apses also *shells* in this same letter, no. 13:

> With two small shells on the right and left, the apse is widened and curved within its spacious circuit.

Earlier, in no. 12, he acknowledged the shell that is itself the apse.

The following passage from Paulinus’s *Natale* 10 may perhaps also be relevant:

> There is also, in the inner recess of the greater hall,  
> a distant chamber set within it, as though its daughter,  
> beautiful beneath a starry dome, and curved with threefold recess,  
> arranged in its several divisions.

Dioscorides will also shed light on our *trichorum*. In book I, chapter 133, concerning acacia:

> In autumn it bears a seed smaller than a lentil, in joined pods capable of containing three or four seeds.

In book IV, chapter 167, concerning spurge:

> At the ends of its branches it bears a round fruit, like a caper, divided into three chambers, in which three small seeds, larger than bitter vetch, are separated from one another by intervening coverings.

Here you see three-celled receptacles called τρίχωρα.

The ancient glossographers, although often barbarous in other respects, seem to have had this passage of Paulinus before their eyes and to have explained it correctly.

The manuscript Camberon Glossary:

> *Tricora*: three chambers, or apses.

The manuscripts of the Aquicinctine Glosses:

> *Tricora*: three chambers, or three apses.

The manuscript Utrecht Glossary of the monastery of Saint Jerusalem:

> *Tricorium*: a place vaulted beside the fire for dining.

Papias the Vocabularist:

> *Tricora*: three chambers or apses.

The same writer:

> *Tricorum* is a place where people dine beside the fire; a high rock.

The *Catholicon* of John of Genoa:

> *Trichorum* is formed from *tris* and *chorus*. It is called *trichorum, -i*, and *trichorium, -ii*, that is, a place beside the fire for dining, having three chambers or apses; and the syllable *cho* is short.

The vocabulary of Gerard of Schueren:

> *Trichorum, -i*, and *trichorium, -ii*: a dining place beside the fire, having three vaulted sections.

It should be written τρικωρον, not τρίκορον, as the Genoese would have it. For *τριχορον*, with short *cho*, is something else, whence *τριχορία*. A collection of words printed after the invention of typography changed *trichorium* into *tritorium*. *Tritorium* is said to be a place beside the fire for dining, having three chambers or apses, according to Hugutio.

Yet *tritorium* seems rather to mean a dining room or chamber in which there are three couches; it is formed from *tris* and *torus*, with *-rium* added. You see how the barbarous vocabularists guess, though they nevertheless touch upon the matter in some fashion.

Just as they called a place with three chambers or recesses a *trichorum*, so they called a church with eight recesses or separate spaces an *octochorum*.

Among the Christian monuments in Gruter’s *Thesaurus of Inscriptions*, p. 1166, no. 8, there is a poem by Ambrose of Milan in the church of Saint Thecla at the Font:

> A church with eight recesses has risen for holy uses,  
> and the octagonal font is worthy of this gift.  
> This number suited the hall of sacred baptism,  
> for through it true salvation returned to the peoples,  
> through the light of the rising Christ, who broke open  
> the prison of death and raises the lifeless from their tombs.

Here you see that, as a symbol of the eighth day—that is, the resurrection—both the octochorum church and the octagonal font were raised for Christ.

Do not be troubled by the shortened *cho* and *go*, since in Greek they are written with omega. Sacred writers commonly attend more to accent than to quantity.

ROSWEYDUS.

[Col. 0880D]

### Note 151. “Illuminated with mosaic”

What Paulinus here calls *illudere musivo*, “to illuminate with mosaic,” others call *depicting with mosaic*.

Spartianus, in the *Life of Pescennius Niger*:

> We see him painted in mosaic in the Commodian Gardens, in the curved portico, among the closest friends of Commodus.

Gregory of Tours, book V of the *History*, chapter 45:

> He built a church, supported it with columns, varied it with marble, and painted it with mosaic.

Thus the passage should be emended on the basis of Aimoinus, book III *On the Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 42.

This kind of mosaic painting frequently appears in the lives of the popes by Anastasius. Hence *musivarius* in law 1 of the *Code* concerning exemptions of craftsmen, as law 2 under the same title in the Theodosian Code shows that it should be read: “from mosaic work.”

ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 152. “Christ stands as a lamb”

Soon afterward Paulinus writes:

> Beneath the blood-red cross Christ stands in a snow-white lamb.

In ancient times Christ was very frequently represented in the form of a lamb, because John the Baptist designated him in this way, in John 1. The Quinisext Council of Constantinople, held in 692—whatever authority that council may have had—preferred a true image of Christ, canon 82.

Although that council forbade the painting of a lamb, the contrary practice nevertheless always prevailed in the Western Church. Sacred Scripture commonly uses the lamb to represent Christ’s humility and gentleness.

Christ represented in the form of a lamb frequently appears in the *Lives of the Popes* by Anastasius the Librarian. A lamb beneath a cross stands on an altar stone at Besançon; Chifflet reproduces its image on p. 208. Likewise, a lamb beneath a cross, standing upon a rock, appears in Jacobus Bosius, book VI *On the Triumphant Cross*, chapter 12. It sends forth five springs: one from its breast and one from each foot, signifying the five wounds of Christ.

Two lambs beneath a cross, facing one another, are found at Narni in the church of Saint Januarius, where Saint Cassius was also buried; Baronius cites this in his entry for June 29 in the *Martyrologium*.

I think, however, that the two lambs more likely signify the faithful, or the newly baptized. Thus Paulinus writes in this same letter:

> And surrounding the rough lambs around the festive altars.

Unless perhaps Cassius himself, who is thought to have constructed his own tomb and epitaph, represented himself and his wife by the two lambs. For the epitaph cited by Baronius under June 29 in the Roman Martyrology, which stands at Narni in the cathedral church above the door of the crypt of Saint Juvenal—where the body of Saint Cassius is also believed to rest—mentions his wife Fausta, buried there as well.

ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 153. “The Father’s voice thunders from heaven”

Soon afterward Paulinus writes:

> The Father’s voice reveals God.

Joseph Scaliger, in his explanation of a coin of the emperor Constantine of Byzantium, thought that God the Father was represented in these paintings by the words emerging from a radiant cloud: “THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.”

But John Macarius, *ho makaritēs*, who inspected various monuments of sacred antiquity at Rome, assured me that God the Father was represented by a hand emerging from a cloud, and the Son as though being designated by it.

Certainly a hand emerging from a cloud is often found on ancient monuments in circumstances not unlike this. Shortly afterward, no. 17, where the Father crowns from the cloud the Son represented in the form of a lamb, I think that only a hand extended from the cloud, holding a crown, was shown:

> Beneath the blood-red cross Christ stands in a snow-white lamb,  
> upon whom the holy Spirit descends in peaceful flight,  
> and the Father crowns him from a radiant cloud.

The cross in the apse of the church of Saint Clement is relevant here: above the cross is a hand with a crown. The place of the Lamb is occupied by Christ crucified. I think that Christ was put in the place of the Lamb because the Quinisext Council of Constantinople—whatever its authority—had decreed that henceforth Christ should be placed in the Lamb’s position. The apse may indeed have been decorated by Nicholas I, as the inscription seems to indicate; he lived not long after that council.

[Col. 0881D]

An extended hand from heaven frequently appears on ancient coins and monuments.

A coin of Constantine the Great, in Eusebius, book IV *On the Life of Constantine*, chapter 73:

> Figures were already being engraved upon coins: on one side they represented this blessed man of ours with his head covered; on the other, seated like a charioteer in a four-horse chariot and received from above by a right hand extended from heaven.

A reproduction of this coin is found in Baronius, vol. III, under the year 337 of the Christian era, no. 468.

Hands from heaven with crowns above the head of Arcadius are represented on a coin of that emperor in Baronius, vol. V, under the year 395, and in our Gretzer, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 15. The same appears above the heads of Eudoxia and Placidia in Gretzer, in the same place, chapter 16.

In Chifflet’s *Besançon*, part 2, chapter 12, there is a monument of Count Warnarius, who rests at Palm, where a palm or hand is extended from heaven as a sign that he should restore the monastery of Palm, which had formerly been destroyed; they say that this was once revealed to him.

In Gruter’s *Thesaurus of Inscriptions*, p. 1158, no. 8, an onyx is presented bearing the letters GERBA. PROTA., designating Saints Gervasius and Protasius. They stand beside a church or altar, where a hand is extended from heaven, perhaps indicating the revelation of the relics granted to Ambrose.

Scaliger says nothing of this in his *Index of Christian Matters*, either because he did not understand the mystery or because he was hostile to relics.

ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 154. “And through a dove”

That the Holy Spirit was formerly represented in the form of a dove is shown by the Council of Constantinople held under Mennas in the year 536. In session 5, in a letter of the clergy of Antioch concerning the sacrilege of Severus, we read:

> He appropriated, together with the other objects, the golden and silver doves hung above the divine fonts and altars as representations of the Holy Spirit, saying that the Holy Spirit ought not to be represented in the form of a dove.

A golden or silver dove was rightly hung above the sacred fonts because the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove above Christ after his baptism, Matthew 3; and because the Holy Spirit makes the waters fruitful. Hence Paulinus writes:

> The Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon this stream  
> and wedded the sacred waters to a heavenly spring.

The council also reports that doves were hung above altars. This practice had already been customary with Basil the Great, who placed the Eucharist inside a golden dove and hung it above the altar, as is related in chapter 6 of his *Life* by Amphilochius. The custom still continues in many churches in our own temples.

Since the cross follows here, I suspect that the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, was seated upon the cross. Certainly, according to an ancient rite of the Church, doves were seated upon crosses or flew above them.

A dove flies above a cross in the apse of the Lateran church, reproduced by Jacobus Bosius, book VI *On the Triumphant Cross*, chapter 12. A dove appears above a cross on an altar stone in Chifflet’s *Besançon*, p. 208. The most ancient image of a dove on the gable of a cross was found at Malipur, or the city of Saint Thomas, as recorded by Jerome Osorius, *On the Deeds of Emmanuel*, book III; Maffeius, *Indian History*, books I and XII; Ciacconius, *On the Signs of the Cross*, chapter 35; and Baronius, vol. I, under the year 57.

Saint Thomas was killed during the worship of this cross. No one should therefore suspect that the cross on which the dove stands was placed over Saint Thomas’s tomb, as the Lombards placed poles with doves over the graves of those who had died abroad. Paul the Deacon records this in book V of the *History of the Lombards*, chapter 54:

> The place itself is called “At the Poles” because poles—that is, beams—formerly stood there erected, and for this reason they were customarily placed there according to Lombard usage. For if anyone had been killed in some region, whether in war or in any other way, his relatives fixed a pole within their tombs, and at its summit placed a dove made of wood, turned toward the region in which their beloved had died, so that it might be known in what direction the deceased rested.

Nicetas also reports, in book V of the *Greek-Latin Law*, *Responsa*, book I, that certain pagans sacrificed doves at the tombs of the dead.

Beware here the extremely false conjecture of Joseph Scaliger. In his commentary on the silver coin of the emperor Constantine of Byzantium, shown to him by Marquard Freher, he writes the following after explaining an ancient image of the Trinity through the words “lamb, dove” borrowed from Paulinus, though he does not name him:

> These were the simplest symbols of those times, when Christians dared to paint forms of things or animals, but not human forms. They carved or painted an anchor, a ship, a fish, and a dove, but not a human being. “For,” says Clement, “the faces of idols must not be impressed, since even looking at them is forbidden.”

Scaliger is both mistaken and misleading. Clement is not discussing sacred images there, but the engraving of a seal on a ring. He does not want Christians to have the image of an idol—Neptune, for example—but rather that of some object or animal that might suggest a good meaning.

The passage is in book III of Clement’s *Paedagogus*, chapter 11:

> Let our seals be a dove, or a fish, or a ship running before a favorable wind, or the musical lyre used by Polycrates, or the nautical anchor engraved by Seleucus. If someone is a fisherman, he will remember the apostle and the children drawn up from the water. For the faces of idols must not be impressed, since even looking at them is forbidden. Nor should one engrave a sword or bow for those who pursue peace, or drinking cups for those who practice self-control. Many of the dissolute keep naked images of those whom they love, or of their mistresses, so that even if they wished to do so, they could never allow forgetfulness of their erotic passions to enter them, because the constant reminder of their licentiousness keeps them mindful of it.

Once the passage is carefully examined and read through, it is clear how perversely Scaliger transfers what is said about idols to images of the saints.

If, says Clement, anyone takes pleasure in carving some symbols on the seals of rings, let him engrave those which suggest a mystical meaning, such as a dove, a fish, or a ship, so that we may remember the apostle Peter, who became a fisher of human beings, and the children who are lifted from the baptismal font.

Perhaps the dove is also mentioned with reference to baptism, both because doves were formerly accustomed to be hung above baptisteries, as we have already shown, and because the dove brought an olive branch from the Flood to the ark, as a symbol of baptism.

Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 3:

> Noah sent out a dove, which is said to have returned with an olive branch. Do you see the water? Do you see the wood? Do you see the dove, and do you doubt the mystery? The water is that in which the flesh is immersed so that sin may be washed away. Every vice is buried there. The wood is that on which the Lord Jesus was suspended when he suffered for us. The dove is that in whose form the Holy Spirit descended, as you learned in the New Testament; it inspires peace in your soul and tranquility in your mind.

Cyril, *Catechetical Lecture on Illumination* 17:

> According to some, that dove upon Noah partially represented this event. For just as through wood and water salvation came to them, and for us the beginning of a new birth, and the dove returned to him toward evening bearing an olive leaf, so, they say, the Holy Spirit also descended upon the true Noah, the author of a second birth.

The ring of Polycrates also recalls fishing, since it is said to have been thrown into the sea and then recovered by fishermen in a fish. From this passage of Clement we learn that a lyre was engraved upon it. Perhaps the lyre also recalls the lyre of David, with which he praised God.

The ship may recall the Church, whose type was borne by the ark, as Prosper testifies in *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 4. The fishing boat mentioned in Matthew 5 also bore the figure of the Church and of the cross.

Augustine, Sermon 22 *On Various Subjects*:

> It is therefore necessary that we be in the ship—that is, that we be carried by the wood—so that we may cross this sea. The wood by which our weakness is carried is the cross of the Lord, on which we are marked, so that we may be rescued from the engulfing waters of this world.

Further on in the same sermon:

> The Jews did to the Lord whatever they wished, because he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. But afterward he rose from the dead, so that he might pray alone for the disciples established in the Church as in a ship, carried by faith in his cross as by a piece of wood, and endangered by the temptations of this age as by the waves of the sea.

I remember seeing a ship represented on the gems of the ancients.

Hervetus translated this passage of Clement as “a ship carried through the air by the wind.” The Florentine Greek text had οὐροδρομοῦσα; hence Sylburgius thinks οὐριοδρομοῦσα should be read, meaning “carried by a favorable wind.” But οὐρανοδρομοῦσα is found in the Palatine manuscript, and in the manuscript from which the Florentine edition derives there may perhaps have been written οὐροδρομοῦσα, which has the value of οὐρανοδρομοῦσα. Thus someone might understand it as the ship Argo borne through heaven.

How foolishly Scaliger says that in Paulinus’s time, whose verses concerning the cross, the lamb, and the dove he cites, Christians did not dare to paint human forms, Paulinus himself reveals and refutes. In this very Letter 12, from which Scaliger drew his material, Paulinus mentions Saint Martin painted by Severus in the church together with an image of Paulinus:

> Martin stands beside him, the model of a perfect life;  
> Paulinus teaches you how to earn forgiveness.  
> Sinners look upon the one, the blessed upon the other;  
> let the former be an example for the saints, the latter for the guilty.

[Col. 0884C]

In *Natale* 10 of Saint Felix he likewise mentions martyrs of both sexes painted above the royal or central doors, as well as other saints of the Old Testament—Job, Tobit, Judith, and Esther—painted above the lateral doors or arches.

One is ashamed and annoyed by Scaliger’s absurdities, although he is the god of critics. Bellarmine, book II *On Images*, chapters 9 and 10, proves at length that human forms of the saints were represented in every age before Paulinus. See Gretzer, vol. III, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 26.

ROSWEYDUS.

From Letter 12, now numbered 32, of Paulinus to Severus, it appears that the Lord’s body was placed beneath a cross, or beneath the figure of a cross, in a ciborium. This is confirmed by the Second Council of Tours, canon 3, which decrees:

> Let the body of the Lord be placed on the altar, not in an imaginary arrangement, but under the title of the cross.

That is, it was placed beneath the ciborium itself, not in what we call a tabernacle, which is termed an “imaginary arrangement,” namely, a work fashioned in gold or silver and decorated with various figures and images.

It follows that the most holy Eucharist, formerly kept for the journey as a viaticum beneath the ciborium itself in a pyx, hung beneath the cross, a practice still observed in many of our churches, especially cathedrals. The sacred pyx hung from a dove, through which it is clear that the Holy Spirit was symbolized among Christians.

The Fifth Council of Constantinople, session 5, mentions such golden and silver doves suspended above altars, sacred tables, and even the fonts of baptisteries. The session contains the complaints of the clergy against Severus, who had removed the doves from the altar and baptistery.

Among Latin writers, the suspension of doves above altars is chiefly gathered from Paulinus, in the passage cited above, where he describes the entire arrangement of the altar; and also from the testament of Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, in volume V of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*.

Udalricus further confirms this custom in book II of the *Customs of Cluny*, chapter 30:

> The deacon removes the aforementioned pyx, together with the dove hanging above the altar.

And in book I, chapter 9:

> When the hosts have been consecrated, four are exchanged with those which are continually kept in the pyx and the golden dove hanging above the altar, especially for the sick, so that whatever may happen to them, a viaticum may be ready at hand.

Finally, Anastasius mentions such doves suspended above altars in his accounts of Popes Hilary and Innocent. From these sources it is abundantly clear that this custom prevailed in both the Eastern and Western Churches.

CANGIUS, *Christian Constantinople*, book III, pp. 55–56.

### Note 155. “The cross with a crown”

There are two forms of the crowned cross in Paulinus. He presents the first here, when a shining circle surrounds the cross:

> A radiant globe encircles the cross with a crown.

Such a cross, enclosed as if by a luminous rainbow-like circle, appeared to the Jews in the year of Christ 363, when, under the leadership of Julian the Apostate, they undertook to restore the Temple at Jerusalem. Gregory of Nazianzus speaks of it in this way in Oration 2 against Julian:

> And what was still more extraordinary and conspicuous: a light stood in the heavens, outlining the cross; and that which previously on earth had been despised by the impious—both its form and its name—was now displayed equally to all in heaven, and became for God a trophy of victory over the ungodly, higher than every trophy.

What Gregory says may be translated as follows: “What was even more marvelous and clearer was this: a light stood in the sky, describing the cross in a circle. But that name and figure, which had previously been despised by the impious on earth, is now shown to everyone alike in heaven, and becomes for God a trophy of the victory won against the ungodly, loftier and more distinguished than every trophy.” [Col. 0885B]

To this one may refer the crosses said to be enclosed within a circle. Such a crowned cross, according to our Maffei (*History of India*, book XII), belonged to the apostle Thomas: it was carved on a square stone, sprinkled with drops that were blood-red and appeared fresh, and was likewise enclosed in a stone circle.

A similar cross appeared to Julian the Apostate while he was performing his impious rites, as Gregory of Nazianzus asserts (*Oration 1 against Julian*). The augurs regarded it as an ominous sign, although Julian himself tried to evade its significance:

> The report, then, is that, while Julian was sacrificing, the entrails of the victims displayed a cross crowned with a wreath. This inspired the others with terror and anxiety, and with a recognition of our power; but to the teacher of impiety it supposedly gave courage, as though we had been circumscribed and enclosed on every side. For this is how he improvised an interpretation of the cross and the circle.

Such crosses are also seen on the coins of Christian emperors, generally surrounded by a crown of oak leaves or flowers. One occurs on a coin of the emperors Zeno and Valentinian, in Lipsius, book III *On the Cross*, chapter 16; another on coins of Eudoxia and Valentinian III, in our Gretzer, volume III, *On the Cross*, book, chapter 16; others on those of Pulcheria and Majorian, chapter 17, and of Julius Nepos and Zeno, chapter 18. [Col. 0885C]

Such crosses, painted in miniature and surrounded by a crown or circle, are commonly depicted on the walls of churches being consecrated. Pamelius, *Liturgical Works*, volume I, page 502, wishes Paulinus to have alluded to this when he says:

> On the right and left, with crosses painted above in vermilion.

Yet in Paulinus the crown does not surround the cross; rather, it is placed upon its summit, as the following passage makes clear.

[Col. 0885D]

It is remarkable that crosses surrounded by a circle were known long ago among the Egyptians, such as those shown on the Bembine Tablet of Isis in Jacobus Bosius, book V *On the Triumphant Cross*, chapter 6. In chapter 10 he also reproduces a saltire cross enclosed within a circle, taken from the obelisk of Augustus and Constantius, and teaches that the circle is a symbol of eternity.

Paulinus presents the second form of the crowned cross, in which a crown is placed upon the very summit of the cross, in these verses:

> The lofty cross is encircled by the circle of a flower-bearing crown.

Likewise:

> The labor of the saints and their reward properly belong together:  
> the lofty cross, and the sublime crown, the price of the cross.

Such was the cross on Constantine’s military standard, as Eusebius testifies (*Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 25):

> It was a tall spear covered all over with gold, having a transverse arm constructed in the shape of a cross; above, at the very summit of the whole, a crown woven of precious stones and gold had been fastened.

The shaft was long and upright, entirely covered with gold; it had a transverse arm constructed in the form of a cross. Above, at the summit of the whole structure, a crown was attached, skilfully woven of precious stones and gold.

ROSWEYDUS

We read in ecclesiastical authors that crowns were formerly offered to churches by princes and great men and hung above the sacred table.

CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, p. 38.

**Note 156. “Whose figure is in the choir of doves.”** —On Paulinus’s cross, doves surrounded the crown of the cross and, as it were, crowned the crown itself. They numbered twelve, expressing the number of the apostles.

By contrast, on the cross that stands in the curve of the apse of the church of Saint Clement, twelve doves perch upon the cross, while a crown surrounds them. You may see a reproduction of it in Jacobus Bosius, *On the Triumphant Cross*, book VI, chapter 11. It seems to be the same cross that the most illustrious Cardinal Borromeo sent to our Gretzer. Certainly the doves stand alternately in Bosius in the manner described by Gretzer in volume III, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 33.

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 157. “It rises above the rock.”** —What is stated here about Christ, the rock, and the four springs, as well as about the palm in the preceding verse, is represented in a marble sarcophagus at Rome, excavated from the ground of Saint Peter’s basilica in the year 1590, and likewise in another sarcophagus there. Philippus Winghius drew them with his own hand, and I possess the drawing.

Paulinus had a similar scene painted in mosaic in the apse chamber of the church of Saint Felix.

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 158. “From which four sounding springs flow.”** —In Bosius, book VI, chapter 12, *On the Triumphant Cross*, you will find a reproduction from the apse of the Lateran church, where the cross stands upon a rock from which the four rivers of Paradise flow.

In the same chapter Christ is shown standing with a jeweled cross upon the rock, from which four rivers flow. This monument once belonged to Sextus Petronius Probus and stood behind the tribune of the ancient basilica of Saint Peter; it has now been transferred to the nave of the new basilica.

See Baronius, volume IV of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 395, where you will find another similar monument, although in neither case are the rivers well represented. Bosius represented them well.

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 159. “The entire space outside the shell of the basilica.”** —A little later he says:

> With two small shells on the right and left, the apse, hollowed out within its spacious compass, is widened.

You see that in both passages the shell belongs to the apse.

Among the Christian monuments in the *Treasury of Inscriptions*, page 1168, no. 4, I find the following poem concerning a similar shell:

> The shell that rises above the sacred altar had lost  
> the daylight beneath the old roof’s trailing fabric.

It was the part of the temple where the sacrifice was offered.

Evagrius, book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 30, says of the church of Holy Wisdom at Constantinople:

> Its length, from the door opposite the sacred shell, where the bloodless sacrifice is celebrated, to the shell itself, is 190 feet.

Hence, in the Bertinian manuscript Glossary: “Apse: sanctuary.”

Germanus, archbishop of Constantinople, explains the mystery of the shell or apse in his *Ecclesiastical History and Mystical Theory*:

> The shell is like the cave at Bethlehem where Christ was born, and like the cave where he was buried.

Anastasius the Librarian formerly translated this passage, in an unpublished version, as follows:

> The shell is in the likeness of the cave that was at Bethlehem, in which Christ was born, and in the likeness of the cave in which he was buried.

ROSWEYDUS.

See Note 320 on *Natale* 10 of Saint Felix, V, 181–182.

**Note 160. “Four chambers inserted within the porticoes along the long sides of the basilica, providing secluded places for those praying or meditating on the law of the Lord, and also suitable places for the memorials of religious persons and relatives, for the repose of eternal peace.”** —Such chambers were oratories into which people withdrew to pray privately. From these chambers, or private oratories, came the origin of our chapels, which surround both sides of a church—as they are now called.

In Paulinus’s time the bodies of religious persons were already being buried in these private oratories or chambers.

Anastasius the Librarian, in his life of Marcellinus, says: “He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla, in a distinguished chamber.” In his life of Sergius: “He zealously renewed and repaired the roof and the chambers that are situated all around the same basilica of Saint Peter.” The same Anastasius mentions such chambers elsewhere more than once.

From this practice, in subsequent centuries, there seems to have arisen the extremely bad custom of indiscriminately burying the bodies of all sorts of people in churches, provided that they paid a certain sum for the right of burial. Thus what was formerly granted on the basis of merit is now granted for gold—a practice which, in the judgment of the holy Fathers, is no different from selling the sacraments of the Church.

**Note 161. “Whom I did not wish to insert in these writings.”** —Other verses still exist today in the suburban basilica of Saint Felix. Our Sirmondus transcribed them in his notes on Sidonius, book IV, letter 18. He was a most diligent investigator of every kind of antiquarian matter.

Paulinus did not send these verses to Severus because they did not suit his church: Severus was building a new church where there had previously been none. The verses are as follows:

> Previously the place was small, too narrow for sacred rites,  
> and unable to open its hands to those who prayed.  
> Now it provides the people with spacious altars  
> for sacred services, in the embrace of the central martyr.  
> All things renewed by God are pleasing; Christ always renews all things  
> and enlarges them into an increase of light.  
> Thus, honoring the throne of beloved Felix,  
> he brought it forth alike in splendor and in spaciousness.

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 162. “With two shells on the right and left.”** —Thus the apse of the church built by Saint Paulinus is called *diconchus*, or rather *triconchus* if the larger shell is included as well, because of the vaults shaped like shells.

So also *triconchus* occurs in the Alexandrian Chronicle under the thirty-ninth year of Theodosius, when a solemn commemoration of the litany was held on account of an earthquake: “the litany in the triconchus before the Ides of November.” Thus: “of the litanies in the triconchus, on the eighth day before the Ides of November.”

Likewise, a *heptaconchus* was a dining room supported by seven shell-shaped vaults, in the palace of the emperor Justinian called the Hormisdas, as stated in the account of the conference held at Constantinople with the Severians during the pontificate of Pope John II.

The Bertinian manuscript Glossary also recognizes small shells in the apse: “Apses: broader small shells.”

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 163. “One of them is open to the bishop sacrificing sacrifices of jubilation.”** —Here Paulinus is speaking of the two smaller shells. I think that instead of *patet* (“is open”), one should read *parat* (“prepares”), since the bishop does not sacrifice in this shell but in the middle and larger shell. Rather, the prothesis prepares or sets out the sacrifices of jubilation for the bishop who is sacrificing—or, more properly, who is about to sacrifice.

For since in both shells the things necessary for performing the sacred liturgy were prepared—in the prothesis, the host and wine; in the diaconicum, vestments, books, vessels, and ecclesiastical implements—the two were consequently called “preparatory rooms” in the Roman Order:

> The subdeacon then receives the chalice and gives it to the acolyte, who returns it to the preparatory room,

that is, to the prothesis, where the chalices and other vessels used for the sacrifice were stored. This can be amply demonstrated from the sacred liturgies.

CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book III, pp. 59–60.

**Note 164. “The other, after the sacrifice, receives those who pray in its capacious bosom.”** —After the sacrifice had been completed, the priests and deacons withdrew there and devoted themselves to reading the sacred books.

Codinus, in his *Book of Offices*, chapter 15, no. 4, clearly teaches that such readings took place in that shell when he says that the emperor withdrew into the church of Holy Wisdom and there listened to the prayers of Basil the Great, read aloud by the patriarch, “near the diaconicum”—that is, beside the shell called the *diaconicum*. For not far away stood the emperor’s seat, from which he listened to the reading of the sacred books.

This shell was therefore called the *diaconicum* because it was, in a certain sense, an appendage of the larger diaconicum or sacristy. In the latter, ecclesiastical vestments and the sacred implements, as they are commonly called, were kept; from it the things necessary for performing the sacred liturgy were brought out and carried into this shell, which was therefore called the diaconicum. For in it they put on the sacred vestments: both the priest who was to celebrate and the deacons who were to minister to him.

Since the larger diaconicum was also called the *skeuophylacium*, the smaller diaconicum, or shell of the diaconicum, is sometimes likewise called the *skeuophylacium*. Thus the prayers that in the liturgies of Saint Mark and Saint James are said to be performed “in the diaconicum” after the sacrifice has been completed are said in the liturgy of Chrysostom to be performed “in the skeuophylacium.”

Finally, the same shell was called the *metatorion*, just like the larger diaconicum.

Some, however, maintain that the entire space of the *bema* outside the altar curtains, and therefore outside the larger shell, was called the diaconicum. Since only priests were permitted to stand within the curtains—or *parapetasmata*, of which we shall speak shortly—that portion of the bema was properly called the *hierateion*. The remaining part was assigned to the deacons, who, according to the demands of their office, needed to stand at both shells, namely the prothesis and the diaconicum.

Symeon of Thessalonica, in his *Book on the Temple*, says that no one was permitted to sit in the sacred synthrone except priests, and not even deacons, for whom another place was assigned: the diaconicum, that is, the place where they were permitted to sit.

It seems, however, that the altar curtain itself was also called the diaconicum, as if the whole space of the bema extending outside the altar curtains were the diaconicum. In it they were permitted to stand and move about according to the requirements of their office, but they were not permitted to enter the sanctuary. The same arrangement applied to subdeacons in the corresponding spaces of the bema, while subdeacons and readers stood in the *solea*, outside the barriers of the bema, as the same Thessalonicus teaches.

From this we may understand the ruling of canon 21 of the Council of Laodicea, which says that subdeacons may not stand within the barriers of the bema:

> Servants must not have a place in the diaconicum.

That place was permitted only to deacons.

This is the proper way to understand the canon, even though Balsamon and Zonaras interpreted “diaconicum” as referring to the office of a deacon.

Isidore Mercator clearly supports the former interpretation, translating *diaconicum* as “sacristy”:

> “The sacristy,” he says, “which the Greeks call the diaconicum.”

The same words occur in the Council of Arles, canon 66. Thus by “sacristy” he understood the shell that the Greeks call the diaconicum, which took its name from the deacons who ministered there, as we have observed.

It is scarcely credible that *diaconicum* should here mean an exedra outside the building, since all the ministers of the church were permitted to stand there, and all the clergy proceeded from it to the altar.

As for the provision of the Second Council of Arles, under Pope Siricius, canon 15, which forbids deacons to sit among the priests in the sacristy, this seems to refer either to the larger diaconicum—the sacristy or vesting room—in which priests or bishops withdrew to deliberate about ecclesiastical matters, while either attending to greetings or hearing legal cases (perhaps business matters); or rather to the smaller diaconicum, that is, the shell which the Greeks call the diaconicum.

For in this diaconicum, when priests put on the sacred vestments before celebrating or perform other matters relating to the sacred liturgy, they are forbidden to sit there with the priests, out of reverence for the priestly character.

CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book III, pp. 60–61. See his *Latin Glossary*, volume III, p. 770.

**Note 165. “Through the translucent screen.”** —The screen is also mentioned in basilicas by Anastasius the Librarian, in his life of Sixtus III:

> He made the Confession of Blessed Lawrence the martyr with porphyry columns, and adorned the screen, altar, and Confession of the holy martyr Lawrence with the purest silver.

Our Bulengerus, book III *On Temples*, chapter 14, understands *transenna* to mean a gallery extending outside the church, across which one passes beneath a roof. “It is,” he says, “a sort of upper walkway inserted between the two basilicas.”

Nicolaus Perottus, bishop of Sipontum, likewise understands *transenna* in this way in his *Cornucopia*, in his note on Martial’s epigram 41, *On the Kingdom*.

In this passage of Paulinus, however, it seems to me that *transenna* was some kind of latticework.

You will learn what a *transenna* was from no better source than Eusebius, book X, chapter 4, in his account of the church at Tyre built by Paulinus, bishop of that city, when he speaks of the atrium:

> Having enclosed the place in a square form with columns rising on every side, he surrounded and confined the intervening spaces with wooden latticework, fashioned like a net and extending to a moderate and proportionate length.

The place of the atrium or vestibule—Christophorsonus incorrectly calls it the sanctuary—was enclosed on every side in the form of a square by lofty columns. Their middle spaces were surrounded by partitions of wood, latticed like a net or screen, extending to a moderate and uniform length.

Later, speaking of the sanctuary, Eusebius says:

> Again, he enclosed these things also, so that they might be inaccessible to the multitude, with wooden lattices, worked out to the highest degree of delicate craftsmanship, so that they offered a marvelous sight to those who looked upon them.

He again surrounded the place so that it could not be approached by the common people and the crowd, using wooden latticework so skilfully made that it offered a wonderful spectacle to the observer.

The same author, book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 59, speaking of the church of the Apostles at Constantinople, founded by Constantine the Great, says:

> He surrounded the chamber on every side with reticulated work, embossed and fashioned from bronze and gold.

He clothed the inner part of the building all around with reticulated work, skilfully made of bronze and gold.

Just as here there are three arches with a screen, so in *Natale* 10 there are three doors with latticework:

> And they open three doors with running latticework.

The Latin-Greek *Onomasticon*, formerly published at Strasbourg in 1536, gives: “*Transenna*, κιγκλίς,” meaning a latticed gate or latticed doors.

So too in Pollux, book VIII, chapter 10, and in the interpreter of Aristophanes: “κιγκλίδες, the doors of the law courts,” called by the Romans καγγελλωταὶ or καγκελωταὶ—that is, latticed doors.

In the present passage *transenna* refers to an arch or doorway; in the circus it referred to the starting barriers.

The old Greek-Latin Glosses give:

> βρόχος ἐν ἀφετηρίαις τεταμένος: *transenna*,

that is, a rope stretched from one end to the other at the starting barriers or gates.

The old Latin-Greek Glosses give:

> *Transenna*: ὕσπληξ, παλλαγεμάππαρίου σημεῖον.

Our Bulengerus, *On the Circus*, chapter 11, reads ἀπαλλαγή, meaning “the release of the horses,” and μαππαρίου σημεῖον, “the signal of the napkin.” This does not mean that the napkin and the *transenna* were identical, but that when the napkin was released, the line was immediately stretched out. The starting barriers of the circus were also latticed.

Callisthenes, in his *Life of Alexander the Great*, says:

> The starting barriers of the lattices were opened.

That is: “The latticed starting gates were opened.”

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 166. “It offers a *diatrita* appearance to those looking from one side to the other.”** —What a *diatrita* appearance is can be seen clearly enough from Paulinus’s description.

Vitruvius, book IX, chapter 4, likewise uses *species* when a thing is viewed as turned toward some particular side.

Among physicians, *diatritos* means something else: either a three-day fast or a tertian fever.

ROSWEYDUS.

Read *diatretam* for *diatritam*. *Diatretus* means perforated or carved, from the Greek διάτρητος.

Here it denotes what we call in French a building with an open-work appearance, as Vitruvius uses the word in book IX, chapter 4. A *species diatrita* is, in our language, a *face à jour*: an open-to-light façade pierced with windows and doors.

CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume II, p. 86, no. 1.

**Note 167. “The gracious house is open to those entering through a triple arch.”** —The same Paulinus says below:

> Three times the halls opened in pairs through paired arches.

Before the western porticoes of the principal churches there is a large square court, or atrium, which is the chief ornament of church vestibules.

Some also give such courts before sacred buildings the name *aula*.

Our Paulinus calls these atria *impluvia* in *Natale* 10, verses 8 and following:

> There, surrounded on every side by long porticoes,  
> vestibules roofed with open courts are laid bare;  
> and at once the atria open both the stars to the eyes  
> and the courts to those entering.

[Col. 0890A]

There were many passageways, closed by elegant gates. This can still be seen in cathedral churches. Paulinus says of them in *Natale* 10, verses 37 and following:

> Joined to three basilicas, the court is open to all;  
> from one place it opens different entrances to everyone,  
> and likewise receives into one embrace  
> those who have come out from the three, across its spacious pavement.

In the arch of the church—as Paulinus calls it—the hands of those whose crimes were public were laid upon them; there the public penitents stood. This can be seen in the commentators on the divine offices.

The custom is still observed by many cathedral churches on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, in the public reconciliation of penitents. Among them are the metropolitan and primatial church of Rouen and the cathedral churches of Évreux, Chartres, Uzès, and Saint-Pons-de-Thomières.

Partly from CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, p. 20.

[Col. 0890B]

**Note 168. “They reveal them in simplicity.”** —Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 3:

> Our dove has a simple house, always in a high, open, and light-filled place.

Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 6:

> The dove is a simple and joyful creature, not bitter with venom, not savage with bites, not violent with the tearing of its claws. It loves human dwellings and knows the fellowship of one house. When they give birth, they produce their young together; when they travel, they keep together in flight; they live their life in common fellowship; by the kiss of the mouth they recognize the harmony of peace; and in all things they fulfil the law of unanimity. This is the simplicity to be recognized in the Church, this the charity to be maintained: that love of brotherhood should imitate the doves, and that gentleness and mildness should equal those of lambs and sheep.

Cyril, *Catechetical Lecture* 17:

> Perhaps he descended in the form of a dove, as some say, a pure dove, as a symbol of innocence, cooperating with prayers for children born and for the forgiveness of sins.

“He descended perhaps in the form of a pure dove,” as some say, like something innocent, because of the pure and guileless little children who are born of the Holy Spirit, and because forgiveness of sins is obtained through prayer.

The same author wishes this to have been foretold figuratively in *Song of Songs* 5:12:

> Your eyes are like doves beside abundant waters.

In *Catechetical Lecture* 18, on Isaiah 66:8, “Who are these?”:

> Clouds, because of the spiritual reality; doves, because of innocence.

“Clouds because of the spiritual reality, doves because of simplicity.”

Augustine, book II *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 45:

> Catholic discipline therefore teaches that the Christian mind must first be nourished by simple faith, so that it may be made capable of understanding the highest and eternal realities.

The same author, *Against the Fundamental Epistle*, chapter 4:

> For in the Catholic Church, to pass over the most sincere wisdom, to the knowledge of which only a few spiritual persons attain in this life, so that they may know it, although only in a small part—for they are human beings—yet without doubt, the rest of the multitude are made most secure not by keenness of understanding but by the simplicity of belief.

See Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 2, where he gives two reasons why some do not believe simply: the simplicity of divine works and the magnificence promised in their outcome. He illustrates this by the simple arrangement of baptism, from which eternity nevertheless follows.

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 169. “With the river as minister.”** —You may learn why Christian churches placed canthari and basins filled with water, or even fountains, at their entrances from Saint John Chrysostom’s sermon 25 *On the Words of the Apostle*, in the volume containing the homilies on various passages of the New Testament, p. 369:

> Just as it is customary for fountains to be present in the courtyards of houses of prayer, so that those who are about to pray to God may first wash their hands and then raise them in prayer, so our fathers placed the poor before the doors in place of fountains, so that, just as we wash our hands with water, we may first cleanse the soul through acts of kindness and only then offer our prayers.

DUC.

In the middle of the court or atrium of the church of Holy Wisdom at Constantinople, Justinian established a *phiala*. They called it a basin or fountain where perennial waters sprang up, from which the people might wash. For, as Eusebius says in book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4, it was not permitted to enter the holy places “with unclean and unwashed feet.”

In this *phiala* of Holy Wisdom there were other fountains, or wells, which supplied water for washing to the people entering the church.

Eusebius, in the passage just cited, teaches above all that public baths and washing places were situated before the vestibules of sacred buildings, in his description of the church at Tyre. Paulinus likewise refers to them in letters 12 and 31 and in *Natale* 9 and 10. In Paulinus, the structure is called a *cantharus* and is sometimes described as covered by a solid bronze dome rising to a peak. Canthari are receptacles for water from which the water flows.

The same Paulinus, *Natale* 10:

> The inner court smiles, adorned with varied decorations.

See what follows. For before entering the church, the faithful washed their faces and hands with this water, which was blessed by the priest.

Hence Paulinus writes to Severus:

> The shining cantharus washes the sacred courts for the servants with its waters,  
> and with the river as minister it washes the hands of those entering.

These waters of the fountains were consecrated and blessed every year on the vigil of the feast of the Theophany, and sometimes on the feast day itself. The order of this blessing is found in the Greek *Euchologion*.

Among the Latins, holy water, which is customarily placed at the doors of churches, took the place of these fountains, as those who have written about ecclesiastical rites explained long ago.

CANGIUS, *Constantinople Christian*, book III, chapter 22, pp. 21–22.

I think that Johannes of Avranches, later archbishop of Rouen, had this washing in mind in his *Book on the Divine Offices*, on Christmas night, p. 34. After the nocturnal offices, before treating of the office of the Mass at cockcrow, he says: “Let clergy and people go out to wash.”

Hence, I think, the fountains beside cathedral and principal churches. See Note 41.

**Note 170. “Paul, apostolic.”** —It seems that Paul presided over the bishopric of Nola when Paulinus wrote this; here Paulinus calls him a priest, and shortly afterward a bishop, which in Paulinus’s time amounted to the same thing.

Our Roman friend suggested that “Paul” here might perhaps mean Paulinus. Yet at this time Paulinus does not seem yet to have been a bishop. This may be gathered from letter 16, where Anastasius had invited his fellow priests to his birthday—that is, the bishops of Campania—and notes that he himself had been invited contrary to custom, since such invitations were normally extended only to fellow priests.

In this letter 12, Paulinus describes the church at Nola that he built himself; he also mentions its construction in *Natale* 9, on the occasion of Nicetas’s second arrival. But Nicetas’s first arrival occurred before Anastasius became pope, if Baronius correctly calculates the chronology in volume V of the *Annals* under the year 397. The second arrival occurred four years later, and that basilica had already been completed before Nicetas’s second arrival; Paulinus led him through it in *Natale* 9.

Unless perhaps Paulinus was made bishop in the second or third year of Anastasius, the matter is entirely uncertain.

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 171. “This is the venerable storehouse where the sacred procession of the holy ministry is deposited and from which it is brought forth.”** —In the bema, where the sacred table or altar stood, there was a larger shell with two smaller ones attached: one on the right, toward the north, and the other on the left, toward the south, of the altar.

The Greeks call the shell situated on the right or north the *prothesis*, as if one were to say “presentation” or “table of presentation,” taking its name from the ceremony performed there.

“For in it,” says Allatius, “before the Mass, the priest and those ministering with him prepare all the things necessary for completing the sacred rite, such as bread, wine, and other items. When this has been done, they withdraw to the sacred table, where the sacred liturgy begins.”

Paulinus calls both shells the *secretarium*. He describes the use of the first, or prothesis, as follows: “This place,” and so forth, as above.

In letter 12 to Severus—now letter 32—speaking of these two shells, he says:

> One of them is open to the bishop sacrificing sacrifices of jubilation.

I think that *parat* (“prepares”) should be read instead of *patet* (“is open”).

CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, p. 59.

**Note 172. “If anyone has a holy desire to meditate on the law, here, seated, he can attend to the sacred books.”** —It has already been observed above that Paulinus called the shells attached to the larger one *secretaria*. Accordingly, the *paratorium* is the same as the *secretarium*.

That ecclesiastical books were kept in this shell is taught by Paulinus himself when he describes its use:

> If anyone has a holy desire,

and so forth, as above. For sacred readings took place in this shell, and the sacred books were publicly read there after the liturgy had ended.

If I am not mistaken, Paulinus himself sufficiently indicates this. After saying that one of the shells prepares for the bishop, who is sacrificing, the sacrifices of jubilation, he adds:

> The other, after the sacrifice, receives those who pray in its capacious bosom.

CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book III, p. 60.

**Note 173. “The title has been doubled.”** —One title concerns the painting, the other the relics. I have therefore supplied each with its own inscription, which had previously been lacking.

ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 174. “The bird by which he is gracious.”** —This part of the sacred painting, in which the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, pours water over the gaping lamb, still existed at Rome in a sarcophagus in the house of Bernardo Biscia near the Sapienza in 1591, when Philippus Winghius copied it. The brothers of Winghius mentioned above preserve his reproduction.

ROSWEYDUS.
