**Note 175. “And Luke the martyr, with his great name.”** —Baronius, in the Roman Martyrology under 18 October, reads the words together as “Luke the martyr” and believes that Paulinus held Luke to have suffered martyrdom. Our Servius follows him in his *Evangelical Apparatus*, adding that Paulinus also calls Luke a martyr in *Natale* 9.

But neither passage decisively proves that Luke suffered martyrdom. In the first passage, “martyr” may refer to Nazarius, as we printed it from the older editions. In the second, there is no mention of martyrdom in the poems concerning Luke—unless one wishes to call him a martyr because he is placed among martyrs there.

He could also have been called a martyr because he suffered much for the name of Christ, as the Roman Martyrology states. In this sense Paulinus also calls Felix of Nola a martyr in *Natale* 9:

> This too makes the lofty house of the martyr Felix shine.

Some ancient writers nevertheless stated that Luke truly was a martyr. This matter will be discussed more suitably elsewhere.

It might seem that when Paulinus calls Luke “great in name,” he was alluding to the fact that *luca* or *lucanus* was formerly used in Italy for something great, because Lucania had enormous herds, as Lucilius testifies:

> Whom not even bulls born in the Lucanian mountains  
> could drag forward with their powerful necks.

Hence, in Ennius, quoted by Varro in book VI *On the Latin Language*, *luca bos* means “a great ox,” or an elephant. Lucretius used the term in the same way in book V, and Silius in book VI.

See Varro in the cited passage, where he gives three reasons why an elephant was called a *luca bos*. Of these, Verginius’s explanation is the most pleasing: because the largest quadruped in Italy was an ox, and because elephants were first seen in Lucania during the war against Pyrrhus, they called the elephant a *luca* or Lucanian ox.

Baronius misunderstood Varro’s meaning in volume I, under the year of Christ 58, no. 34, when, in connection with Saint Luke, to whom an ox is attributed, he cites Varro as though Varro asserted that an ox was called *luca* in Italy. For it is not the ox that is called *luca*; rather, the elephant is called the *luca bos*.

ROSWEYDUS.

**IN LETTER XXXIII**

[Col. 0893A]

**Note 176. “Alethius.”** —I do not know whether this is the same man who was bishop of Cahors in Paulinus’s time, whom Paulinus—if the author is indeed our Paulinus—mentions in a letter of which only a fragment survives in Gregory of Tours, book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 13:

> What sort of bishop this Venerandus was, the presbyter Paulinus bears witness, saying: “For if you see these priests worthy of the Lord—Exuperius of Toulouse, Simplicius of Vienne, Amandus of Bordeaux, Diogenianus of Albi, Dynamias of Angoulême, Venerandus of Clermont, Alethius of Cahors, or now Pegasius of Périgueux—you will see that, whatever the evils of the age may be, they are assuredly the most worthy guardians of the whole of faith and religion.”

Although Florentius was bishop of Cahors in Paulinus’s time, as is clear from the preceding letter, Alethius succeeded him afterward.

The first edition of Paulinus here reads: “Alethius, bishop, brother of the man mentioned above.”

ROSWEYDUS.

See *Life of Saint Paulinus*, chapter 48, no. 3.

**IN THE THIRTY-FOURTH SERMON ON THE GAZOPHYLACIUM**

[Col. 0893B]

**Note 177. “Of the gazophylacium.”** —Formerly there was in churches a place called the *gazophylacium*, where alms intended for distribution to the poor were stored. It is frequently mentioned in the sacred writings.

Chrysostom, in the volume *On Various Passages of the New Testament*, homily 22, *On Almsgiving and the Collection for the Saints*, first warned the people of Antioch—not of Constantinople, as Franciscus Bernardinus Ferrarius supposed, in book II, chapter 10, *On the Ancient Ecclesiastical Epistolary Genre*, and book I, *On the Rite of Sacred Sermons*, chapter 26—to set aside privately something for the poor.

That the homily was delivered at Antioch is clear from the conclusion of the letter, where he says that Jerusalem was supported by alms from that city, as stated in Acts II.

> Let each person’s house therefore become a church in this manner, with sacred resources stored within. For the gazophylacia that are situated here are a symbol of these things.

“Let each person’s house therefore become a church in this manner, preserving sacred resources within itself. Indeed, the gazophylacia that are in the churches represent those resources.”

Augustine, on Psalm 63:

> What is the gazophylacium? The treasury of God, where those things were collected that were sent for the needs of the servants of God.

Possidius, *Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 24:

> When he was speaking in church about the gazophylacium and the sacristy neglected by the faithful, from which the necessities of the altar are brought, he used to admonish them. He also told us that the blessed Ambrose had once treated the same subject in church in his presence.

The Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 93:

> Offerings from dissenting brothers are to be received neither in the sanctuary nor in the gazophylacium.

Gazophylacium—Pauline here also calls this a table. Tertullian calls it an “ark” in *Apology*, chapter 39: “Even if there is some kind of chest, it is not collected from the ordinary sum, as though from a redeemed religion,” as also in Augustine at the passage cited; Cyprian calls it a *corbona* in *On Works and Almsgiving*, chapter 5: “Do you think that you are celebrating the Lord’s feast, when you do not regard the *corbona*?” There he also calls it a gazophylacium. [Col. 0893D] ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 178. “With your step suspended—or rather, secured—for treading.”** —I corrected the text conjecturally in this way. Previously it read: “with your step suspended in a monument for treading,” which made no sense. A Roman friend corrected it to “in a moment.” My conjecture is true, as Paulinus himself will perhaps say; for in Letter 2, p. 29, line 22, he has: “With a secured foot I shall enter safely.” ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXXVI

**Note 179. “Let the agreement of the three spirits invite him.”** —The meaning is this: Christ—of whose presence the two disciples going to Emmaus said, “Was not our heart burning within us?”—will also remain with us if the two things within us, or rather the three, namely body, soul, and spirit, judge that he should be invited. For he himself said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.” See Letter 3 to Aper [Col. 0894A] [now 44], “Having a burning heart,” etc. That the Fathers were accustomed to distinguish those three elements in a human being from 1 Thessalonians 5 is clear. See Paulinus himself, Letter 2 to Amandus [now 12], “With the spirit serving God,” etc. SACCHINUS.

## IN LETTER XXXVIII

**Note 180. “The secret retreat of the silent countryside.”** —These were the beginnings of a religious life. Jerome relates something similar about his teacher, St. Gregory of Nazianzus, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 117: “After ordaining a bishop in his own place, he practiced the life of a monk in the countryside.” Sophronius said: “He led a monastic life in the country” (*Ἐν ἀγρῷ μοναδικὸν βίον ἀπηνέγκατο*). Gregory, in his *Life*, says: “He came to Arianzus, a village of Cappadocia, which he possessed because it had fallen to him from his paternal inheritance” (*Ἔρχεται εἰς Ἀριανζὸν χωρίον Καππαδοκίας, ὅπερ ἔκτησεν ἐκ πατρικοῦ κλήρου*). Possidius, chapter 3 of the *Life of St. Augustine*: “It pleased him, after receiving the grace of baptism, to return to Africa and to his own home and estates. Once established there for three years, and having already withdrawn from secular cares, he lived for God with those who adhered to him, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord through fasts, prayers, and good works.” [Col. 0894B] DUC.

See, concerning this retreat for meditation, the elegant and exact treatise of our Father Julius Nigronius, which is sixth among the ascetical works. ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XXXIX

**Note 181. “If it lies waste, as though foul with brambles, and is not watered by prophetic or apostolic clouds, it will be condemned to arid solitude when grace abandons it.”** —“Waste” is used especially of fields that are not cultivated. The Cartulary of Vendôme, charter 237: “While it was cultivated in ancient times, it paid a census of twelve denarii; now, however, because it is waste, it yields no census, but is an allod.” The Cartulary of the Church of St. Stephen of Limoges, in the year 1081: “Gosbert, the archdeacon, caused the whole land of Mount St. John to lie waste.” CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, vol. III, p. 1260.

[Col. 0894C] **Note 182. “Beyond the half-cooked beet.”** —Where the Vulgate reads Isaiah 51:20, “Your sons have slept at the head of all the roads, like a wild ox ensnared,” the Greek of the Septuagint reads: “Your sons, sleeping at the end of every road, like a half-cooked beet, full of the Lord’s fury” (*Οἱ υἱοί σου καθεύδοντες ἐπ᾽ ἄκρου πάσης ἐξόδου, ὡς σευτλίον ἡμίεφθον, οἱ πλήρεις θυμοῦ Κυρίου*).

St. Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah: “Instead of ‘half-cooked beet,’ the other interpreters translated ‘a wild ox captured and ensnared,’ which in Hebrew is called [Hebrew term absent or illegible]. This species of newly born animal is listed among the clean animals in Deuteronomy 14; for it the Septuagint, apparently through the Syriac language, took *thoreth*, which is called a beet. Whoever wavers midway between vices and virtues, and approaches the service of God with a divided heart, is called a half-cooked beet.”

Cyril: “Those who are slack in understanding and whose mind is loosened are like a half-cooked beet” (*Οἱ παρειμένοι τὰς φρένας, καὶ ἐκλελυμένοι τὸν νοῦν ὡς σευτλίον ἡμίεφθον*). Those who are remiss in spirit and weak in mind are like a half-cooked beet.

Beets, moreover, are tasteless unless seasoned with pepper. Martial, book XIII, epigram 13:

> To make the foolish beet dishes of fools taste good,  
> How often will the cook demand wine and pepper!

Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 87: Octavian Augustus regularly uses *betissare* for “to languish,” which is commonly called *lachanissare*. *Λάχανον* in Attic Greek means “beet,” and *λαχανίζειν* means “to languish.” The Glossary has: *λαχανίζουσι*, “they stagger.” DUC.

## IN LETTER XL

**Note 183. “Having been drugged … with wine and ointments from the Lord’s saving cup.”** —In common usage *potionatus* means “carried off by poison”; here, however, the word has the opposite meaning and is derived from the true verb *potionare*, “to take medicine.” It should likewise be understood in this latter sense in the charter of Cardinal Octavian apud Ughelli, vol. III of *Sacred Italy*, p. 635: “We receive the sick and those who are, as it were, gravely weakened, medicated and bled,” etc.

## IN LETTER XLII

[Col. 0895A]

**Note 184. “To Florentius.”** —This Florentius was the bishop of Cahors, as can be gathered from all the headings of the manuscript and printed copies of this letter. The Regius manuscript: “Here begins [the letter] to Florentius, bishop of the city of the Cadurci.” The Viennese manuscript: “To Florentius, bishop of Cahors.” The Badian edition follows the Regius manuscript but adds “letter.” Gravius likewise has: “The letter of the divine Paulinus,” as does Schottus: “of the holy [Pauline],” etc. All copies read “of the city of the Cadurci”; but in the Grinian edition: “To Father Florentius, bishop of the Cadurci, Paulinus.”

Pamelius, vol. I of *Liturgics*, pp. 507, in the section on the fifth century, cites this letter of Paulinus with the heading “to Florentius, bishop of Tibur,” instead of “of Cahors”; where he got this I do not know. But since he also says there that Pope Innocent wrote his eighth letter to this Florentius, bishop of Tibur, it is easy to see that Pamelius altered Paulinus’s transmitted heading on that basis. Moreover, Innocent also wrote letters to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, whom Paulinus likewise mentions. This may have been Pamelius’s reason for changing the heading. ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XLIII

**Note 185. “To Desiderius.”** —This is the Desiderius to whom Severus dedicated the *Life of St. Martin*. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 186. “He separates the straw.”** —Thus read the Regius and Viennese manuscripts. The printed editions have *disjicit*, “he scatters,” but *dissicit paleas* means “he separates the straw from the grain.” According to John of Genoa, *dissicere* means “to remove, to separate”; sometimes also “to scatter, to disperse.” Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 1: “You, Christ, scatter sleep”; and in the book *Peristephanon*, in the hymn to St. Lawrence the archdeacon, verse 209:

> When disease scatters the limbs.

For this is how it is read in the oldest manuscript copies, as N. Heinsius testifies in his notes. Add Paulinus of Petricordia, books III, V, and VI, *On the Life of St. Martin, Bishop of Tours*, based on five very ancient manuscripts collated by Franciscus Juretus.

## IN LETTER XLIV

**Note 187. “At the table of a powerful man.”** —Something similar occurs in Ecclesiasticus 13:12: “When a powerful man invites you, withdraw” (*Προσκαλεσαμένου σε δυνάστου, ὑποχωρῶν γίνου*). And chapter 31:13: “You have sat at a great table; do not open your throat over it” (*Ἐπὶ τραπέζης μεγάλης ἐκάθισας; μὴ ἀνοίξῃς ἐπ᾽ αὐτῆς φάρυγγά σου*). And verse 16: “Wherever he looks, do not stretch out your hand” (*Οὗ ἐὰν ἐπιβλέψῃ, μὴ ἐκτείνῃς χεῖρα*). And verse 20: “If you have sat among many, do not be the first to stretch out your hand” (*Καὶ εἰ ἀναμέσον πλειόνων ἐκάθισας, πρότερον αὐτῶν μὴ ἐκτείνῃς τὴν χεῖρά σου*). Perhaps our author formed this sentence by combining these passages, as far as the evidence of our books allows us to determine. DUC.

**Note 188. “Wife.”** —Here Paulinus is speaking of Amanda, the wife of the presbyter Aper, who was a *presbyterissa*. *Presbyteras* or *presbyterissas* were the wives of presbyters, namely of those who, by mutual agreement, had renounced marital relations and devoted themselves to divine worship, becoming priests or bishops. Otto, bishop of Vercelli, Letter 8: “We may also consider them presbyteresses or deaconesses who were joined in marriage to presbyters or deacons before their ordination, and whom they must afterward govern chastely,” etc.

Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 11: “There a certain presbyter governed the church entrusted to him with great fear of the Lord. From the time he received ordination, he loved his presbyteress as a sister, but feared her as an enemy, and never allowed her to approach him closely.” It should be observed here that such presbyteresses lived chastely in the same building in which their husbands lived; Gregory says that this was prescribed by the canons of the Church in book VII, letter 39, where, after forbidding bishops to live with women, he adds: “With this sole provision, that, as canonical authority has decreed, they should not abandon their wives, whom they must govern chastely.”

This agrees with law 43 of the Theodosian Code, *On Catholic Religion*, and with the Second Council of Tours, canon 19. But that such cohabitation was sometimes dangerous is shown by the example related by Flodoard, book I of his *History of Reims*, chapter 14. Hence the Third Council of Toledo, canon 5, says that it is preferable for presbyteresses to live in another house. The author of the book *On the Singularity of Clerics*, among the works of St. Cyprian, expresses the same view: “When I see that many Christian husbands and wives, jointly intending continence, choose separate dwellings, so that, by agreement in their common vows, without the irritation of presence and with harmonious withdrawal, they may attain their purpose.” See Gregory of Tours, book I of his *History*, chapter 39.

At the Second Council of Arles, chapter 3, such presbyteresses are called converted wives; they were permitted to live in the houses of clerics, like mothers, grandmothers, and sisters, but on the condition that the men abstain from their wives, as stated in the First Council of Tours, chapter 2; the Council of Auvergne, chapter 13; the Fourth Council of Orléans, chapter 17; and the Council of Auxerre, chapter 21. They were not even to share a common bed or cell, as stated in the same passages of the Councils of Orléans and Auxerre, and in the Second Council of Tours, chapter 19. They were further commanded to live as sisters by the Council of Auvergne, chapter 19, and the First Council of Mâcon, chapter 11.

Nevertheless, presbyters were permitted to live in the same house with their wives, provided that they had the testimony of another cleric, by which the purity of their life might be made more evident. See the Council of Gerunda under Pope Hormisdas, chapter 7; the Third Council of Braga, chapters 1 and 4; and the Second Council of Tours, chapters 12 and 19. But St. Gregory of Nazianzus, St. Chrysostom, and St. Basil criticize this practice and custom of cohabitation.

Finally, if a presbyter’s wife survived her husband, she was forbidden to marry another man. Thus the First Council of Orléans, chapter 13; the Council of Epaon, chapter 2; a fragment of the Council of Lérida cited by Surius after the Council of Lérida; the Roman Council under Pope Zachary, canon 5; the Council of Verberie in 752, canon 3; and others.

Perhaps for this reason *presbyteresses* came more generally to mean all elderly widows who devoted themselves to sacred exercises in the Church. Manuscript glosses on the Council of Laodicea, canon 11: “Presbyteresses, that is, elderly widows.” Isidore Mercator and Ferrandus the deacon likewise say, canon 221: “Women whom the Greeks call presbyteresses, but whom we call elderly widows, converts, and matricularies.”

These presbyteresses, or *presbyterissae*, as they are called in the Roman Order, wore clothing much more modest than that of other women, as Gregory the Great teaches, book VII, letter 7. Regarding their ministries, Atto, bishop of Vercelli, says in Letter 8: “For just as those who were called presbyteresses had undertaken the task of preaching, commanding, or teaching, so the deaconesses had undertaken the duty of ministering or baptizing; but this is now no longer expedient.”

The synod of Trullo, canons 12 and 13, also discusses presbyteresses or the wives of presbyters, as does Pope Leo VII in his letter to Gerhard, archbishop of Lorch, p. 11. CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, vol. III, pp. 408–410. See the same *Glossary*, under the word **SISTERS**, vol. III, p. 903.

**Note 189. “In work.”** —This reading is better than *in opere*, “in the work.” It expresses the text of the Septuagint, which Paulinus follows, Proverbs 31:17: “She strengthened her arms for work” (*Ἤρεισε τοὺς βραχίονας αὐτῆς εἰς ἔργον*); and verse 19: “She extends her forearms toward useful things, and strengthens her hands at the spindle” (*Τοὺς πήχεις αὐτῆς ἐντείνει εἰς τὰ συμφέροντα, τὰς δὲ χεῖρας αὐτῆς ἐρείδει εἰς ἄτρακτον*); and verse 27: “She did not eat sluggish foods” (*Σῖτα δὲ ὀκνηρὰ οὐκ ἔφαγε*). On this passage Flaminius Nobilius annotates: “A loaf of laziness” (*Ἄρτον ὀκνηρίας*). Paulinus said, “food of laziness.” The Latin Vulgate: “She does not eat idle bread.” DUC.

**Note 190. “Mercy … will raise up children,” etc.** —These words seem to have been drawn from nowhere else than the same book and chapter of Proverbs, which contains the praises of the generous and munificent widow, chapter 31:28: “Her almsgiving raised up her children, and they grew rich” (*Ἐλεημοσύνη δὲ αὐτῆς ἀνέστησε τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐπλούτησαν*). So reads the Roman edition, with which Paulinus agrees, not the Complutensian edition, which has *ἀνέστησαν τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς*, “her children rose,” but the Latin Vulgate, “Her children rose.”

A little later, when he speaks of the sons of the prophets, he touches on the story recorded in 4 Kings 4:38 and 6:4: “When they had come to the Jordan, they were cutting wood. It happened, however, that when one of them had cut down a piece of timber,” etc. But in Paulinus it should perhaps be corrected to “to compose the soul by the peace of silence,” not “the peace of silence.” For he says in Letter 1 to Aper: “Avoiding the disturbances of the churches and their restless councils.” DUC.

**Note 191. “For the dew that comes from him is healing.”** —This is Isaiah 26:19: “For the dew that comes from you is healing of the soul” (*Ἡ γὰρ δρόσος παρὰ σοῦ, ἴαμα ψυχῆς*). The Latin Vulgate has: “For the dew of light is your dew.” Likewise Proverbs 16:24: “Their sweetness is healing of the soul” (*Γλύκασμα δὲ αὐτῶν, ἴασις ψυχῆς*). He cited the same passage from Isaiah earlier in Letter 17 to Delphinus, where he likewise reads: “For the dew that comes from him.” DUC.

**Note 192. “The boundaries of the desert will grow fat.”** —Psalm 64:13 has the expression “the boundaries of the desert will grow fat.” It appears that the translator whom Paulinus follows read *Πιανθήσονται ὅροι τῆς ἐρήμου*, “the boundaries of the desert will grow fat,” as did Hilary, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Arnobius, and Ambrose in *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 15; this is also what appears in the Roman Psalter. But in the Gallican Psalter, which is found in the Vulgate, the reading is *τὰ ὡραῖα τῆς ἐρήμου*, “the beautiful things of the desert.” The Roman Septuagint, from the Vatican manuscript, has *τὰ ὄρη τῆς ἐρήμου*, “the mountains of the desert,” as does Apollinaris: “the rich mountains of the desert.” St. Jerome, from the Hebrew, has “the pastures of the desert”; Aquila and Symmachus have *νομαί*, “pastures.” DUC.

## IN LETTER XLV

**Note 193. “Quintus the deacon.”** —Augustine mentions him in Letter 59 to Paulinus: “The Lord quickly gladdened us by the very favorable arrival of our brother and fellow presbyter Quintus, and of those who sailed with him.” He had carried Augustine’s letter to Paulinus and brought Paulinus’s reply back to Augustine. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 194. “Melanius.”** —He means Melania herself, who is variously called Melania, Melanius, and Melanium. The same applies above in Letter 12. The manuscripts preferred:

> This was brought to Nola by the gift of holy Melanius.

See my *Preludes to Book VIII of the Lives of the Fathers*, no. 6.

Augustine appears to be understood in the same way in Letter 227: “To our dearest brothers Albinus, Pinianus, and Melanius.” I read this as *Melania*. He means Albina and Melania, when they were staying with Alypius, bishop of Thagaste in Africa.

Could these women, Melania and Albina, have been called Melanius and Albinus because of the manly courage by which they overcame every passion and the world, just as the Phrygians were called Phrygians because of the effeminacy of Phrygia? This could be confirmed from the *Life of Eugenia*, chapter 7. When Eugenia, wishing to conceal her sex, said that she was called Eugenius, St. Helenus replied: “You rightly call yourself Eugenius, for you act manfully; let your heart be strengthened for the faith of Christ. Therefore you are rightly called Eugenius.”

Similarly, St. Francis called the distinguished Roman matron Lady Jacoba not “Lady Jacoba” but “Brother James,” because of the uprightness and holiness of her life, as Bartholomeus of Pisa relates, book III, *Conformities*, part 2. ROSWEYDUS.

See Note 138.

## IN LETTER XLVI

**Note 195. “In the translation of St. Clement.”** —Does he mean the Roman Clement or the Alexandrian? I understand him rather to mean Clement of Rome, who wrote ten books of the *Recognitions*, which Paulinus may have undertaken to translate at the request of Rufinus.

Certainly, this translation appears to have reached Rufinus. When Rufinus found it inadequately executed, he urged Paulinus to devote more careful study to Greek literature. Paulinus himself admits this in this very letter. It follows that Rufinus either interpolated Paulinus’s translation or translated those Clementine books anew. In any case, these books circulate today through Rufinus’s translation, dedicated to a bishop named Gaudentius, whether of Brescia or Novara one cannot determine, since both men were prominent in Italy in Rufinus’s century.

[Col. 0898A] Rufinus undertook this translation at the request of the virgin Silvia. I believe this is the woman whom Palladius calls Silvania in chapter 142 of the *Lausiac History*, Heraclius calls Silvania in chapter 42 of the *Paradise*, and Paulinus calls Silvia in Letter 11 to Severus.

Gennadius also admits in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* that Clement was given Latin form by Rufinus. Rufinus himself, in his letter to Macarius concerning the corruption of Origen’s books, mentions the books called *Ἀναγνωρισμός*, that is, *Recognition*, which Clement of Rome wrote, although he acknowledges that they were corrupted by heretics. In his preface to them he calls them *Ἀναγνώσεων*, “books of Recognitions.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 196. “Having grasped the sense more than the words.”** —Paulinus admits that, since he could neither fully understand nor express the words, he tried, according to his own judgment, to sketch their meaning. Rufinus, however, also tried to express the words, as he acknowledges in his dedicatory letter to Gaudentius: “In the rest, as far as we were able, we took pains not to depart either from the meanings or even from the words and turns of phrase.” From this one may perhaps infer that Rufinus undertook a new translation. ROSWEYDUS.

## IN LETTER XLIX

**Note 197. “To Macarius.”** —I think this is the Macarius mentioned by Palladius in chapter 123, when he lists those who visited Pinianus, now living on estates in Campania, now in Sicily, for the sake of sacred asceticism: “Likewise, a certain man named Macarius, from the vicariate.” He means that Macarius had held the office of Roman vicar.

Thus Paulinus rightly urges him to assist Secundinianus, who was reclaiming a shipwrecked vessel and its cargo from the agent of the senator Postumianus. The agent had seized it after it had drifted onto the Bruttian coast and reached his master’s estate. That agent, when summoned by the provincial judge, had first rebelled by force and then fled to Rome.

Rufinus dedicates his apology for Origen to this Macarius, whom he calls “a man of desires” and “most faithful.” Of his writings Gennadius says in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 28: “Macarius wrote in the city of Rome a book against the mathematicians, in which, through his labor, he sought the consolations of Eastern literature.” Jerome alludes to this in his second apology against Rufinus: “Therefore, unless he had come from the East, that most learned man would still be lingering among the mathematicians,” clearly referring to the Roman Macarius, whom Rufinus held in the closest friendship and whom he drew away from the mathematicians.

This Macarius is different from Macarius the Roman, whose *Life* appears in the *Lives of the Fathers*—the Macarius whom Baronius confused with another in the Roman Martyrology on 2 January, as I have shown in my commentary on Book I of the *Lives of the Fathers*. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 198. “The customary grain supply.”** —This was the Sardinian grain supply by which ships imported grain into Italy. So also the Alexandrian grain supply. Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 20: “He was captivated by the measured praises of the Alexandrians who had gathered at Naples for the arrival of the new grain supply.” ROSWEYDUS. See Note 64.

**Note 199. “With various duties, as the tossing of the sea and the equipment of a ship require.”** —Since this concerns an old man who performed every nautical duty in order to escape shipwreck, it is useful here to record what Augustine says about the new song, the return to the heavenly homeland, and the dangers of life, chapter 2, vol. IX. Under the metaphor of naval equipment and instruments, he elegantly exhorts us to board the ship promptly, in which we may sail to our heavenly homeland:

“Let us prepare the rigging; let us seize and board the ship of faith and the cross together. Let the anchor of our hope of salvation not be absent. Let us stretch out the ropes, the various virtues; let us gather the sails of charity; let us call upon the favorable wind, the word of God. Let us empty the bilge of sins; through almsgiving let conscience be cleansed.

“Let nothing impede the course of our voyage; let us work with our hands as we are able. The man who said, ‘With my hands before him through the night, and I was not deceived’ (Psalm 76), was emptying the bilge with his own hands. Let us not neglect our sins: they are small, but they are many. A single powerful wave rushing in overwhelms the ship and threatens shipwreck; but water flowing in through cracks and reaching the bilge does the same thing unless it is repeatedly drained. Therefore let the bilge be emptied; let mercy not be neglected, because almsgiving delivers from death and itself cleanses sins.

“May the grace of Christ be our protection. Let us sing our sweet sailor’s song, ‘Alleluia,’ so that joyful and secure we may enter our eternal and most blessed homeland. Let the soul not fear this great sea, namely the world, whose waves and storms we experience as the hostile powers of the world. Many saints, trusting in God, have already despised these waves; many have trampled them; many, walking securely upon their waters, have reached the homeland.

“But a strong wind arises, and each person’s desire becomes a great storm. Is faith wavering on the sea? Let Peter cry out within you, ‘Lord, I am perishing!’ He will extend his hand to the drowning man; nor will he allow to perish the one who, for our sake, deigned to walk upon the waters.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 200. “The topsail stood; it made the ship’s sails. Water, etc.”** —Thus the Roman friend aptly read the passage, whereas previously it stood: “If little stood, or the ship made sails, water.” Likewise, in Isidore’s Rule 20, where the keeper of the sacristy is discussed, an ugly corruption of a similar kind has remained. For where the text has “or to sew clothes,” it should be read, from the Cologne manuscript containing the rules of various Fathers, “sacred veils and vestments.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 201. “Having drained the moisture that had been drawn in.”** —The same friend suggested this reading, whereas previously the passage had only *ore* in place of *humore*. Formerly they wrote *umore* for *humore*. Scribes omitted its first two letters because of the similar ending of the preceding word, just as elsewhere they were accustomed to double a word by repeating the ending of the preceding word and attaching it to the beginning of the following one. Antiquarians have noted this hundreds of times.

Thus in Paulinus an initial syllable was omitted because of the similar ending in the preceding word; likewise two syllables seem to have been omitted in Sidonius, book IX, Letter 15:

> Smoothing every graceful poem  
> So that it may challenge Mantua with Venetian favor,  
> And himself match the glory of Homer.

What is *paret* here? Savaro is silent. Our Sirmondus printed *par et*. But then *que* will be redundant in *Homericaeque*. I would read:

> And himself match the glory of Homer.

That is, *aequiparet*, “let him be equal to,” as in Plautus, *Trinummus*, act 5, scene 2. You can clearly see that *aequi* has been omitted from *aequiparet*, because *aeque* would have preceded it in *Homericaeque*.

A similar error through the omission of one letter occurred in Lampridius, in his *Life of Alexander Severus*, where Casaubon and Salmasius labor in vain: “A singular memory of events, which no one except Acholius almost had reinforced.” The Palatine manuscript, as well as the old Milanese and Venetian editions, reads: “Which no one except nicoa holius had reinforced.” The initial *m* of *mnemonici* was omitted because of the similar final letter of the preceding word *quam*. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 202. “Which is daily in our hand, both of the apostles and of the martyrs.”** —Thus the first edition and the manuscripts; Gravius has: “Our Immanuel of the apostles.” The Roman friend suggested: “the good Emmanuel of the apostles,” etc. But the transmitted reading is unquestionably and most truly *manus*, “hand,” that is, “power.” Paulinus uses it very frequently in this sense. In poem 27, *Natale* 9:

> By the hand of the blessed one I shall recount what was wrought for us.

In the same *Natale*:

> But wherever the part of the body may be, the hand is present.

Likewise in a fragment of *Natale* 11:

> The divine hand, with healing power,  
> Has worked there through every path.

So also Acts 19:2: “God performed through the hand of Paul powers of no ordinary kind,” that is, as through an instrumental cause. *Hand* is rightly used for *power*, because the hand is the instrument of instruments, as Aristotle says, *On the Parts of Animals*, book IV, chapter 10: “For it is, as it were, an instrument of instruments” (*Ἔστι γὰρ ὡσπερεὶ ὄργανον πρὸ ὀργάνων*). ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 203. “Like the nycticorax.”** —The passage comes from Psalm 101:7: “I became like a nycticorax in a dwelling” (*Ἐγενήθην ὡς νυκτικόραξ ἐν οἰκοπέδῳ*). The manuscript read *nocticorax*, incorrectly; similarly, that most learned man whose letter is now published for the first time from a Nolanean manuscript insisted, incorrectly, that it should be written *nycticora*. Although that letter otherwise seems scarcely to depart from Paulinus’s style, this feature could arouse suspicion that it is falsely attributed. It is cited by Antonius Agellius in his commentary on the Psalms.

It is certain, by the common agreement of all authors, that *νυκτικόραξ* means something like “night raven,” and that *κόραξ* derives not from *κόρη*, meaning “pupil,” but from *κόρος*, a word signifying blackness.

Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book VIII, chapter 3: “Some nocturnal birds have hooked claws, such as the nycticorax, the owl, and the horned owl” (*Τῶν νυκτερινῶν ἔνιοι γαμψώνυχές εἰσιν, οἷον νυκτικόραξ, γλαὺξ, βύας*). Gaza translates *νυκτικόραξ* as *cicuma*, and likewise in Aristotle, book IX, chapter 34, in the description of the *otos*, he translates it as *ulula* instead of nycticorax.

Ulysses Aldrovandi thinks that Gaza did not translate it correctly in either case, in book VIII of his *Ornithology*, chapter 6, and believes that it should rather be *otos*. Yet he unjustly suspects that Gaza invented the word *cicuma*, which Festus and Isidore mention in their glossaries.

Others think that the owl is some eastern bird. Jerome, Letter 135, testifies that Symmachus translated the Hebrew word as “hoopoe.” It is plausible that it was a species of those birds that are generally at times called owls and that wander and move about at night.

Apollinaris:

> Or the raven of night, inhabitant of bare pavements.

DUC.

**Note 204. “The whale, avenger and guardian, received the prophet fleeing from God.”** —Thus reads the Regius manuscript, together with the Badian and Gravian editions. The same words occur in poem 21 to Cytherius, on the shipwreck of Martinianus, verses 195, 217, and following, and in poem 19 to Jovius, verses 105 and 113.

Well said. The following passage of St. Gregory’s *Moralia*, book VI, chapter 14, also comes to mind: “The storm finds the fugitive from God; fate binds him; the sea receives him; the beast encloses him; and because he resists obeying his creator, he is carried, guilty, in his own prison to the place to which he had been sent.” SACCHINUS.

**Note 205. “In the tents of a man.”** —Psalm 146:10: “He does not take pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor is he pleased by the legs of a man” (*Οὐκ ἐν δυναστείᾳ ἵππου θελήσει, οὐδὲ ἐν κνήμαις τοῦ ἀνδρὸς εὐδοκεῖ*).

Jerome likewise translates from the Hebrew: “He does not delight in the strength of a horse, nor is he pleased by the legs of a man.” But the Roman and Old Psalters, Hilary, and Augustine, together with Paulinus, translate it “in the tents of a man,” as though they had read in the Septuagint not *ἐν κνήμαις* but *ἐν σκηναῖς ἀνδρός*.

Ambrose’s Psalter has: “He will be pleased with the greaves of a man.” Hence Jerome also says in his commentary: “He seems not to call them legs, but *periknemides*,” because he had described a warrior, and whatever covers the legs. Yet Jerome is mistaken here. Neither Chrysostom nor Euthymius read it otherwise; the Septuagint now has *κνήμαις*, not *περικνημίδας*, namely greaves with which the legs or shins are armed.

For in the Greek text of Chrysostom there is likewise nothing other than *ἐν κνήμαις*; and Euthymius says that the legs themselves are intended: “For just as the strength of the hands resides chiefly in the arms, so the abundance of strength of the feet resides in the legs” (*Ὤσπερ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς βραχίοσι τῶν χειρῶν, ούτω καὶ ἐν ταῖς κνήμαις τῶν ποδῶν ἡ περιουσία δυνάμεως*). DUC.

“In the tents of a man,” instead of “in the legs of a man,” crept into the text. The error was easy for scribes because of the ambiguity of the abbreviations they used so extensively, when they mistook abbreviations that were not actually present. SACCHINUS.

This is not entirely satisfactory, however, for the variation seems to have arisen from the differing Greek readings *κνήμαις* and *σκηναῖς*.

**Note 206. “Elijah’s melote.”** —Thus in 3 Kings chapter 19, verse 13, and 4 Kings chapter 2, verses 8, 13, and 14, the Septuagint calls Elijah’s cloak a *μηλωτή*, “melote.” Eucherius, book II, chapter 10 of *Instructions to Salonius*: “In the Book of Kings, a melote is a simple hide, which the Egyptian monks still use, hanging down from one side.” Jerome, Letter 28: “Elijah, carried to heaven in a fiery chariot, left his melote on earth.”

Athanasius, in the *Life of Antony*, translated by Evagrius, chapter 58: “Having given to Bishop Athanasius the melote and the worn cloak on which I lie.” The manuscript Glossary of Claromars: “Melotes: a simple sheepskin, which monks use, hanging down from one side.” It is also called a *pera*, “satchel.”

Cassian, book II, chapter 8, *Institutes of the Coenobia*: “The last parts of their dress are a goatskin, which is called a melote or satchel, and a staff.” Here our Fronto Ducaeus, in volume I of his work on Chrysostom, p. 12, suspects that *diphthera* should be written instead of *pera*, because Sozomen says of the Egyptian monks: “They clothed themselves in skins in imitation of Elijah the Tishbite” (*Διφθέραι δὲ ἀμφιέννυσθαι κατὰ μίμησιν Ἡλίου τοῦ Θεσβίτου*).

Alardus Gazaeus, the careful commentator on Cassian, thinks that *penula* should be substituted for *pera*. But since Cassian again joins *pera* and staff in Conference 11, chapter 3—“And so, taking up the staff and the satchel”—and since Isidore, book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, expressly says, “The melote, which is also called a satchel,” and the oldest manuscript books of both Cassian and Isidore likewise prefer this reading, *pera* should be retained, because the melote also served in place of a satchel.

The Camberon Glossary: “Melota is called a woolly garment and a satchel. It is a goatskin hanging from the neck, fastened around the body down to the loins.”

It is remarkable what other manuscript glossaries suggest. The Claromars Glossary: “A melota is a garment made of camel hair. *Melus* is an animal, the badger, whose hide is called *mellota*.” Stewechius’s Glossary: “*Melos* is a kind of beast from which the ancient Fathers made melotes.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 207. “A xenium.”** —Franciscus Juretus, in his notes on Book I of Paulinus’s *Life of St. Martin*, reads it as *encaenium*, following the trace of the Badian edition, which has *enxenium*. He wants the word *encaenium* to indicate that this old man—who had previously been a pagan—had now been newly reborn in the Christian faith and dedicated to God.

But *xenium* seems to me sound, although scribes very often wrote *exenium* for it. See what I noted in the *Lives of the Fathers* under the *Life of St. Antony*, and there also in the *Onomasticon*.

Just as Victor here is sent as a *xenium*, so Christ is called by Rufinus in the creed, alternately sent as a *xenium* to Pilate and Herod: “As a *xenium* of his reconciliation, they sent Jesus to one another.” This is figuratively expressed in Hosea 10:6: “And having bound him, they carried him to the Assyrians as gifts for King Jareim” (*Καὶ αὐτὸν εἰς Ἀσσυρίους δήσαντες ἀπήνεγκαν ξένια τῷ βασιλεῖ Ἰαρείμ;*). He translates: “And binding him, they brought him as a *xenium* to King Jareim.” The common version has: “For he himself was carried away as a gift to the avenging king.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 208. “Although both a higher and this interpretation may be found.”** —It is not unreasonable to wonder whether *ethicus* should be written instead of *et hic*, so that the moral sense is understood; for immediately afterward he speaks of the literal sense. Thus Jerome, Letter 151, question 10: “The Psalms marked by letters lead us through ethical matters to theological matters, and make us pass from the elements of the killing letter, which is destroyed, to the life-giving spirit.” Likewise, above, in the letter to Sidonius, I noted that our Sirmondus most happily restored *ethica* instead of *et hic*. ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 209. “A little dust from those very places.”** —Theodore the Studite, *Dogmatic Treatise on the Veneration of Images*, volume III of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*: “The places in which Christ was born are holy and worthy of veneration. If anyone receives from there either a little dust or a stone, he adorns and embraces it as though it were a particular treasure or some sacred relic.” ROSWEYDUS.

**Note 210. “To take and possess a piece of the wood of the cross is a blessing.”** —In former times men and women regarded it as a sign of blessing and magnificence to wear even the smallest fragment of the wood of the cross around the neck. Chrysostom, in his *Demonstration against the Gentiles, That Christ Is God*:

> But that very wood on which the holy body was laid and crucified—why is the whole world so eager to possess it? Many take a small piece from it, enclose it in gold, and both men and women hang it from their necks, adorning themselves with it.

That is: “The very wood on which the Lord’s holy body was placed and crucified—why does the whole world strive so greatly to possess it, so that those who have even a small piece of it enclose it in gold and attach it to their necks, both men and women, thereby becoming greatly honored and splendid, fortified and protected?”

Thus the virgin Macrina, sister of Gregory of Nyssa, wore around her neck an iron sign of the cross and a ring fortified with a fragment of the Holy Cross, as Gregory himself relates in his encomium of Macrina. Likewise, the great confessor wore around his neck a little cross marked with the Holy Cross, as is recorded in book II, chapter 9, of his *Life* by Theodore the Hermit. ROSWEYDUS.

### Note 211. “And without a myoparo.”

Previously it read, “and without my own boat.” Jacobus Billius, a man of distinction, in book I, chapter 6 of his *Sacred Observations*, thinks that light will be shed on this passage if we read: “and without a myoparo, practicing piracy on land,” and so forth. He adds that in the islands near La Rochelle and throughout all those maritime regions there prevails a cruel custom: if a severe storm drives a ship onto the shore, those to whose territory it has been carried treat the shipwrecked as enemies and immediately seize everything that the fury of the waves has left them. From this passage of the procurator Posthumianus, a senator, he concludes that this right was exercised even in better ages.

In the edition of the appendix to the *Library of the Fathers*, a note had been added at the end of this letter of Paulinus: “Better: without a myoparo.” A *myoparo* is a type of vessel, as Gellius explains in book X, chapter 25; Isidore says in *Origins*, book XIX, chapter 1, that it was so called because it was used by pirates; Turnebus, in book III, chapter 1 of his *Adversaria*, derives the name from the island of Paros and says that *myoparones* were pirate skiffs; and Nonius Marcellus writes: “A myoparo is a pirate’s little boat.” Thus our French dialect calls a certain swift type of vessel a *brigantin*, as if it were a pirate skiff.

Those, however, who plunder the property of shipwreck victims are practicing piracy, even if they do not roam the sea in a skiff. Cujacius, in book I, title 6 of the Justinian Code, says: “Wherever it floats, it is property of the treasury.” In England, Sicily, and Italy as well, the property of shipwreck victims is said to belong to the treasury. The emperor Antoninus establishes a more merciful law concerning the shipwrecked in book I: “If at any time a ship, driven out by shipwreck, has been cast upon the shore, let it belong to its owners; let my treasury not intervene. For what right does the treasury have in another’s calamity, that it should seek profit from so grievous a misfortune?” And in book V: “If anyone is discovered to have taken something from sunken ships, the judge, at the complaint of those who are being stripped, shall have power to fine and proscribe him.”

Again, in the Theodosian Code, book XIII, title 8, the emperor Valentinian says: “If any shipmaster claims that he has suffered shipwreck, let him hasten to approach the judge of the province and prove the event before him by witnesses.” Finally, in the Henrician Code of our kings, book XX, chapter 14, article 6, it is decreed that if within a year a merchant reclaims property lost in a shipwreck, he need repay only the expenses incurred by those who recovered that property from the wreck. Many decrees of the supreme Senate of Paris likewise declare the plundering of shipwreck victims to be theft; La Rochelle and the neighboring islands are subject to its jurisdiction. — DUC.

For varying opinions concerning shipwreck victims, according to the character of each nation, see the most learned Fridericus Lindebrochius, in his *Glossary of the Code of Ancient Laws*. — ROSVEYDUS.

## IN LETTER L

### Note 212. “They were filled with swine’s flesh.”

Here Paulinus cites a double reading from Psalm 16:14: “They were filled with swine’s flesh,” or, as some Psalters have it, “They were filled with sons.” Augustine explains the origin of this variation in his exposition of that psalm: “From an ambiguity in the Greek,” he says, “a twofold interpretation arose.” Indeed, there was formerly a twofold spelling among the Greeks. Some read **ὑιῶν**, that is, “of sons”; others read **ὑῶν** or **ὑείων**, that is, “of swine” or “of swine’s flesh,” as Euthymius also testifies.

Augustine explains both readings above. “They were filled with swine’s flesh,” that is, with impurity, trampling underfoot the pearls of God’s words. A Greek scholion belonging to the Septuagint interpreters, attached here to the word **ὑῶν**, “of swine,” explains it as **ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀκαθαρσίας**, “instead of impurity”; another has **παρανομίας**, that is, “of iniquity.” The Roman Psalter likewise has “swine’s flesh,” as do Arnobius and Cassiodorus, who also interpret it as impurity.

Jerome—or whoever after him compiled the *Commentaries on the Psalms*—seems formerly to have read both of those Greek scholia. He says: “They left behind remnants, impurity and iniquity, trampling underfoot the pearls of your words.” You can see that Augustine too used these final words, or that they were taken from him by another writer.

If one reads “sons,” Augustine above understands “sons” as evil works; he develops this interpretation more fully in letter 59, in which he answers Paulinus’s questions.

Nor are there lacking those who understand “swine’s flesh” literally, as though the meaning were that the Jews would not abstain from forbidden foods. Thus Apollinarius, in his paraphrase:

> Filled with swine, they left to their sons  
> the remnants of the feast.

For since **δαίτος**, “of the feast,” refers to the remains of a banquet, he seems to have understood the passage as concerning food; our Marianus follows him. — ROSVEYDUS.

“Swine’s flesh”: **ὑῶν**, “of swine,” or **ὑιῶν**, “of sons.” Jerome translated from the Hebrew, “of sons.” Nobilius, on this passage: **ὑείων**, “of swine’s flesh”; this is the reading of the Vatican manuscript.

Since in older books the word was written without accents, and it was customary for scribes to add **ε** to **ι**, and conversely **ι** to **ε**, it seems that the twofold spelling arose from this practice—as Saint Augustine also suggests. Thus in Greek manuscripts one finds in some places **ὑιῶν**, which means “of sons,” and in others **ὑείων** and **ὑῶν**, which mean “of swine’s flesh” and “of swine.”

In the scholion written in the margin of the Vatican manuscript, the following words are attached to **ὑῶν**, “of swine,” in place of “impurity”: “For they themselves were not only impure, but also communicated impurity to their sons.” Other commentaries likewise have **ὑῶν**, and the passage is read there as follows: **ἐχορτάσθησαν τῶν παρανομοῦντων**, “they were filled with those who transgress.” Elsewhere: “They were filled with every transgression and transmitted it to their sons.”

Apollinarius, in his paraphrase, has: “Filled with piglets, they left the remnants of the feast to their sons.” In the Roman and Arabic Psalters, and in Arnobius and Eucherius, the reading is “swine’s flesh.” In his final letter to Saint Augustine, Paulinus acknowledges both readings: “They were filled with swine’s flesh, or, as I hear it written in certain Psalters, they were filled with sons.”

Saint Augustine notes the same variation in letter 927, in which he replies to Paulinus, and cites the following passage concerning this psalm: “Certainly, in that verse where it says, ‘They were filled with swine’s flesh,’ some copies have, ‘They were filled with sons’; for from an ambiguity in the Greek a twofold interpretation arose.”

In Greek manuscripts, the reading **ὑιῶν** is by far the more common. In the manuscripts of Theodoret, some have **ὑῶν**, some **ὑιῶν**, and some even **ὑιοί**, “sons,” a reading also found in Theodore of Antioch. Theodoret immediately adds to this reading a very similar interpretation by Symmachus, which Eusebius also reports.

### Note 213. “You will winter at Carthage.”

The fifteen manuscripts correctly have **exhiemarem**. Others, along with the printed editions, have **hiemarem**. We believe, however, that one should read **hiemares**. For Augustine, answering this request of Paulinus in letter 149, section 2, writes: “At the same time I had sent, as you had ordered, a copy of that letter which I had written at Carthage to your Charity concerning the resurrection of the body, where the question had arisen concerning the use of the limbs.” By these words he appears to designate letter 95, in which, in section 7, he discusses the functions of the limbs after the resurrection. That letter was written to Paulinus, who was living in Italy, around the end of the year 408.

This is the judgment of the Reverend Benedictine Fathers in their new edition of the letters of Saint Augustine.

### Note 214. “The punishment of the passion placed before her eyes blinded her to belief in the wonder that would follow.”

Saint Paulinus aptly explains how the sword could have passed through the soul of the Mother of God: namely, because she did not turn her thoughts toward those things that could have lessened her grief. Without doubt, if she had wished to think more intensely about the resurrection, or to fix her mind upon the supremely just and wondrous plan of human redemption and upon the fruit of Christ’s passion, she could have greatly alleviated her sorrow. But because this was neither appropriate to the moment nor seemly—since, while her son was voluntarily undergoing such bitter torments, she herself would have shunned participation in his suffering—she instead contemplated those things that could intensify her grief: namely, that her own son, attentive and dutiful toward her, had been so grievously and unjustly tortured.

In this way, the punishment of the passion placed before her eyes blinded her to belief in the wonder that would follow; that is, it concealed from her the wonder and joy arising from the glory and majesty of the resurrection. Here it is elegantly said that she presumed nothing concerning his resurrection, as though she considered it unjust to presume upon, anticipate, or somehow prematurely taste the joy of triumph while he, covered with blood and still dying, was yet engaged in the struggle. — SACCHINUS.

## IN THE PASSION OF SAINT GENESIUS OF ARLES

### Note 215. “Genesius.”

The memory of this saint is celebrated in the ecclesiastical calendars on 25 August, by Prudentius in hymn 4 of *On Crowns*, and by Fortunatus in book VIII, poem 4. He served in the office of a shorthand writer.

This homily on Genesius is commonly attributed to Paulinus of Nola. I have serious doubts about this. Perhaps it belongs to Paulinus, bishop of Béziers, who lived somewhat earlier than our Paulinus. I see Papirius Masson, in his description of the rivers of Gaul, attributing it to Patientius, bishop of Lyons.

There survives an account by Hilary, bishop of Arles, of a miracle performed in his own time through the merits of Saint Genesius, when a bridge over the Rhône collapsed. There is also a sermon by Faustus, bishop of Riez, or by Eusebius Gallicanus, which is incorrectly attributed to Eusebius of Emesa.

Gregory of Tours mentions certain other miracles in book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapters 68 and 69. There was another Genesius, a mime and master of the theatrical art, whom the martyrologies also commemorate on this same day. Savaro, in book I, chapter 17 of *On the Church of Clermont*, incorrectly confuses him with the former. For the theatrical Genesius was at Rome, whereas the shorthand writer was at Arles.

There was also another martyr named Genesius, known from the Roman Martyrology on 11 October, together with the presbyter Anastasius, Placidus, and other companions.

There are still two other Genesii, outside the Roman calendars, though celebrated in their own churches in Auvergne. The first is Genesius the martyr near the fortress of Tigernum, who, clothed in white, passed through martyrdom to heaven. Gregory of Tours speaks of him in book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 67. According to Savaro, mentioned above, his feast is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

The second was bishop of Clermont, and his memory is celebrated on 3 June. On this subject see the most learned Savaro in his *Origins of Clermont*. — ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM II

### Note 216. “Sphondylus.”

Previously the text had **funditus**, but the correct word is **sphondylus** or **spondylus**. It is a kind of shellfish regarded as a delicacy.

Seneca, letter 95: “I remember that there was once a famous dish, into which the cookshop, hastening toward its own ruin, had piled whatever among luxurious foods usually lasts through the day: Venus-shells and spondyli, oysters cut around the part by which they are eaten, and, placed between them as separators, sea-urchins; mullets, twisted and stretched out, were spread beneath without any bones.”

A little later in the same work: “The dishes that are usually arranged are all covered with the same sauce. It makes no difference whether oysters with sea-urchins, disturbed spondyli, or mullets that have been cooked are served.”

Pliny, in book XXXII, chapter 11, places **sphondylus** alphabetically in his catalogue of fish. In the same book, chapter 10, he says: “The spondylus, tied on by itself, is said to cure tertian fevers.”

Macrobius, in book II of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 11, quoting from the fourth catalogue of Metellus, the chief pontiff, counts among the delicacies of the pontifical dinner: “Before dinner, sea-urchins, raw oysters in whatever quantity they wished, *pelorides*, spondyli, and so forth”; and again, “spondyli, glycomerides.”

Galen, book III of *On Foods*, chapter 33:

> The small clams, the spondyli, the “nails,” the purple-shells, the trumpet-shells, and all the other creatures of this kind have hard flesh.

Galen, book II of the *Aphorisms*, section 18:

> Beef nourishes very slowly and little by little, as do snails and sea spondyli.

Thus the learned Nonius, in his little golden book *On Fish-Eating*, prefers to retain the Greek word rather than what Martinus Gregorius translated in the first passage as “vertebrae,” and Nicolaus Leonicenus in the second as “little whorls.”

Columella, book VIII, chapter 16: “A muddy region is especially suitable for shellfish, murexes, and oysters, and for the little shells of purple-shells, mussels, or spondyli.”

Those whom others call spondyli, Athenaeus says are *tracheli*. Posidippus, quoted by him in the section on the Locrians:

> Pinnas, tracheli, myae.  
> Pinnas, tracheli, mussels.

Dalechampius, Rondeletius in book XI of *On Shellfish*, chapter 34, and Robertus Constantinus understand the passage in this way.

According to Hesychius, *tracheli* are purple-shells:

> **Τραχήλους, τὰς πορφύρας, ἔνιοι τοὺς σπονδύλους τῶν κογχυλίων.**  
> “Tracheli”: purple-shells; some interpret the word as the vertebrae of shellfish.

Here “vertebrae” means the necks, or the callus and inner flesh, of oysters. See Hesychius under **Ταραντίναι**, where he says that these parts were sought after as food.

Petronius: “Then, fed with stronger foods—that is, bulbs and the necks of snails without sauce—I drank unmixed wine more sparingly.”

So also with **spondylus** in Pliny, book XXXII, chapter 11, where, speaking of the *perna*, he says: “Inside, in place of the spondylus, there is a large mass of flesh.” Again, in the same book, chapter 6: “Oysters should be judged by their thickness rather than their breadth. They should be taken neither from mud nor from sandy places, but from a solid seabed, with a short spondylus, not fleshy and not divided into fibers, and entirely within the shell.” — ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM III

### Note 217. “Libya.”

That is, Africa. Sallust, in the *Jugurthine War*: “In dividing the earth, most people placed Africa in the third part; only a few held that there were Asia and Europe, but Africa belonged to Europe.” — ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM V

### Note 218. “Almighty, whom I worship in my mind.”

This morning prayer was published under the name of Ausonius in the first edition of his works, printed at Milan in 1490. There the following nine verses, namely those after the first seven beginning with “He himself, the creator,” were missing. Mariangelus Accursius, in his *Dissertations on Ausonius, Solinus, and Ovid’s Metamorphoses*, advised that they be inserted from the ancient parchment manuscripts of Hieronymus Aleander. In those manuscripts this prayer is also attributed to Paulinus, and the first verse is worded as follows:

> Almighty, known to me through the worship of my mind alone.

This prayer subsequently appeared in both the editions of Ausonius and of Paulinus. — ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 219. “And he added Adam, who had been deceived.”

This expression of Paulinus—namely, that Adam had been deceived—is shared by him with many Fathers who lived both before and after him. See the most learned commentaries of our Benedictine, Benedict Justinian, on 1 Timothy, chapter II, verse 14, explaining how this manner of speaking agrees with the Apostle’s statement: “The man was not deceived.”

Augustine briefly reconciles the two statements in book XI of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, at the end of the final chapter: “Therefore he too was deceived in some other way; but I do not think that he could in any way have been deceived by that serpentine deceit by which the woman was deceived, in the manner in which she could be deceived. The Apostle properly called this ‘deception,’ because what was being suggested, although it was false, was believed to be true.”

Eve, then, was truly deceived and led into error by the devil’s art; but Adam yielded to Eve, not through error, but—as Augustine says in the same place—through a certain friendly affection, lest he grieve her deadly delights, for which she was wasting away and dissolving. — ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 220. “Elijah, carried away, penetrates above the ether on a four-horsed chariot.”

Bede, in question 27 on the Books of Kings, conjectures that the poets’ story of the chariot of the Sun arose from the history of Elijah; indeed, that among the Greeks the name **Ἥλιος** was derived from **Ἡλία**.

John, bishop of Constantinople, thinks that the attribution of a chariot and horses to the Sun was taken from the miracle of the prophet Elijah, who was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses.

The Greeks also call the Sun **Ἥλιος**, as Sedulius likewise shows when he sings of Elijah’s ascension:

> How well the path of heaven, shining before him with lightning,  
> suits Elijah, who was radiant even in his name  
> and worthy of this aid. For if in the Greek language  
> one letter is changed by the accent, he is the Sun.

When the Greeks heard this, and so forth. See Chrysostom’s homily *On the Ascension of Elijah*. — ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM VI

### Note 221. “In the reproach of mothers.”

It should also be noted that *mater*, “mother,” may signify not only a woman who has given birth, but also a childless woman, and may therefore be understood as “nurse,” as Nonius observes. Barthius, *Adversarial Commentaries*, book XXXII, chapter 3.

### Note 222. “And may the one born grant this too.”

Previously it read: “The one born granted this.” Paulinus now expresses Elisabeth’s prayers at the coming of the Mother of God, **τῆς Θεοτόκου**.

But even then that fetus to be adored had not been born—much less was there anything that the holy matron could say had already been granted by the one born. Nor does Paulinus call him “born” because of a birth from eternity and before the beginnings of things, since he acknowledges that the benefit was given by him at that very time, although before he was born.

The statement concerns a prayer and a future event, not an accomplished fact. Write: “And may the one born grant this too.” Let him be favorable after he has been born, just as he was before he was born, when he deigned in his mother to visit these abodes. — JO. FED. GRONOVIUS, in chapter 10 of his *Ecclesiastical Observations*.

## IN POEM IX

### Note 223. “Jerusalem will dwell.”

In the same passage, “Jerusalem” occurs three or four times with its first two syllables shortened and its final three lengthened, as elsewhere in the same author, following the example of the Greeks.

Certainly, in Apollinarius’s paraphrase of the Psalms, one repeatedly finds **Ἱερουσαλήμ**, **Ἱερουσαλής**, **Ἱερουσαλήν**, and, in the vocative, **Ἱερουσαλή**, with the same treatment. See his paraphrases of Psalms 136 and 147.

## IN POEM X

### Note 224. “From the name.”

The grammarians teach that a syllable is strengthened by aspiration. Hence Saint Paulinus seems to use aspiration as a consonant, as below, in the passage addressed to Cytherius:

> An exile of the soil and a stranger of the salt.

And elsewhere. — SACCHINUS.

Aldhelmus likewise uses aspiration as a consonant, concerning Silvester:

> This priest performed many signs of virtue.

Concerning Agnes:

> This illustrious woman was aflame with the virtue of modesty.

### Note 225. “Living on the provisions of death.”

Tertullian likewise spoke of “living death” in *On the Pallium*: “Thus far, Sodom, and no Gomorrah, and ashes everywhere, and the nearness of the sea lives together with the soil in death.”

In Prudentius, hymn 13, verse 32: “To live righteousness in Christ,” which means to express the divine law through life and conduct.

### Note 226. “Snow-covered Pyrenees.”

That is, the Pyrenean mountains covered with snow. *Ninguidus* means the same as “snowy,” for the ancients used **ninguis** for “snow.”

“Ninguid passes” occurs in Ennodius, in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius*. Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 2, verse 54: “Snowy Pyrenees.” In the same work, hymn 5, verse 97: “Then also snow-covered.”

In Ausonius, letter 23: “The snowy peaks of the Pyrenees”; and in letter 25: “The snowy lodgings of the Pyrenees.” In an ancient epitaph in Gruter, inscription 1169.6: “The snowy hills of the mountains.”

### Note 227. “You lavish your leisure.”

The leisure which Paulinus reproaches Ausonius for having, Ausonius himself desired in old age in the *Mosella*:

> There will be a time when the honor of my subject  
> will commend me, soothing my cares with the uncelebrated leisure  
> of study and warming me in the sunshine of old age.

The same author, epigram 33:

> To this I assign the uncelebrated leisure  
> that remains for us, whether he reads what I shall give him  
> or whether he reads.

— ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 228. “The fur-clad Bigerri.”

According to the *Notice of the Provinces*, Bigorra was a fortress in the territory of Tarbes, in the province of Novempopulania. Bigerra was a city.

Gregory of Tours calls it “the city of Beorra” in book IX, chapter 20 of his *History*, and also mentions it in book I of *On Miracles*, chapter 74, and in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 49.

From this city came the Bigerri, the people whom Caesar assigns to Aquitaine. Sidonius, in book VIII, letter 12, speaks of a “Bigerrian storm,” that is, a wind blowing from the Bigerri.

That Bigerrian wind is cold because Bigerra lies beside the snowy Pyrenees. Hence the Bigerri are wrapped in *mastrucae*, rough and shaggy garments, and gave their name to garments of this kind, which were called *Bigerricae*.

Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 1: “From the nearest shops he buys a Bigerrian garment, short and rough, for five silver coins.”

Fortunatus, book III, chapter 1, concerning Saint Martin:

> The saint is clothed in a shaggy Bigerrian cloak.

An old manuscript glossary has: “Bigerra, a thick garment, that is, a woolly one.” The natives commonly call such garments *marlotas*, from a Greek word meaning woolly or fleece-covered garments. Savaro gives this learned explanation in his notes on Sidonius. Could *marlotae* be derived from **μαλλωταί**?

Isidore’s glosses have: “Bigera, a coarse or shaggy garment.” Read: “Bigerra, a thick garment.” — ROSVEYDUS.

Here Paulinus notes that the Bigerri customarily clothed themselves in skins or shaggy garments. Hence, in Papias, *Bigerra* means a reddish garment, that is, a garment with a fleece; it is also called *bilis*. *Bilis* is used for *vilis*, “cheap” or “common.”

Ugutio: “Bigerra is a shaggy garment,” and so forth. — CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume I, p. 554.

### Note 229. “The sandy Vasates.”

Hence Sidonius, book VIII, letter 12, to Trigetius: “Does the city of the Vasates, set not on turf but on dust—does the Syrtic country, its shifting soil, and sands flying in contending winds—hold you so entirely in their possession?”

— ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 230. “Rauranum.”

The manuscripts of the Royal Library, the Vossian manuscripts, and the old Lyons manuscript collated by Vinetus, as well as three printed editions in their margins, have **Raraunum**.

VINETUS: “It can certainly be Rauranum. And *Rauranum*, with the diphthong transferred to the first syllable, is read in that itinerary of Antoninus between Mediolanum, Santones, and the Bituriges Cubi at Argentomagus, where the route from Aquitaine into Gaul is described.”

— VINETUS.

### Note 231. “Curule.”

The Vossian manuscript has **secures**, “axes.” Not incorrectly. Axes are indeed found among the insignia of senators or consuls in Prudentius, hymn 10, *On the Passion of the Holy Martyr Romanus*, verse 143:

> Do they not swiftly pass by—  
> the fasces, axes, curule chair, praetexta, and toga,  
> the lictor, the tribunal . . .

## IN POEM XI

### Note 232. “Owls.”

While writing this, Paulinus seems to have had in mind Theocritus’ poem from Idyll 5, in which the goatherd Comatas mocks the unequal challenge of the shepherd Lacon and shows how similar it would be if a magpie challenged a nightingale, or a hoopoe a swan:

> It is not right, Lacon, for a magpie to contend with a nightingale,  
> nor a hoopoe with swans.

Paulinus, using antithetical diction, no less appropriately opposed black coots to swans, and the owl to the nightingale, a bird utterly unlike it in song. The owl is a bird of ominous and ill-omened chattering. Thus Mariangelus, in his *Dissertation on Ausonius*. — ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM XIV

### Note 233. “To spread their breasts before the thresholds.”

In former times the faithful, when approaching a temple, would prostrate themselves before the thresholds of the temples with great reverence.

Paulinus, below, in *Natale* 6:

> He lies prostrate before the doors and presses kisses upon the doorposts;  
> he waters the whole ground with tears,  
> lying on the earth before the holy threshold.

Sidonius, book I, letter 5, to Heronius: “Having cast myself before the triumphal thresholds of the apostles, I immediately felt every bodily illness expelled from my strong limbs.”

Evodius, book II of *The Miracles of Saint Stephen*, chapter 2: “Prostrate before the threshold of the glorious martyr, she expressed the griefs poured out from her heart.”

A little later: “Prostrate before his sacred threshold, weeping day and night.” — ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 234. “The thresholds are adorned with veils.”

It was formerly customary to hang veils from the doors of thresholds. Paulinus, above, in *Natale* 6:

> Those who carry beautiful veils  
> for covering the doors.

Indeed, the entire façade of the temple, together with its doors, was decorated.

1 Maccabees, chapter IV: “They adorned the front of the temple with golden crowns and small shields, renewed the gates and the chambers, and fitted doors to them.”

There is frequent mention of veils before the royal or principal doors of a temple in Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Leo III and the church of Saint Peter: “He made three large white silk veils, which hang before the royal doors at the entrance.”

Likewise, concerning the church of Saint Mary at the Crib: “He made another, larger white veil, which hangs before the greater royal doors at the entrance.”

Again, concerning the church of Blessed Mary: “He made over the royal doors a small veil embroidered with foundation work,” and so forth, “and other Tyrian veils over the greater royal doors at the entrance of the basilica, with a border of embroidered work.”

Again: “A red veil, which hangs before the greater royal doors.”

Veils were not placed only at the threshold, but also before the sanctuary. Thus in the temple of Solomon there was a veil before the Holy of Holies. 2 Chronicles, chapter III. Josephus, book VIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2, calls it **καταπέτασμα τοῦ ἀδύτου**, “the veil of the inaccessible sanctuary.” Paulinus refers to it in poem 15:

> Then, when the veil had been removed and the altars lay exposed,  
> they lost the sacred sanctity of the sanctuary.

Clement, if the letter is genuinely his, in letter 2 to James: “Let the doorkeepers take care that no negligent or ignorant person improperly wipes his hands on the veil of the door of the house of the Lord, because the veil of the court of the house of the Lord is holy.”

Jerome, letter 3 to Heliodorus: “Nepotianus was concerned that the altar should shine, that the walls should be free of soot, that the doorkeeper should be frequently at the door, that the veils should always be in place at the entrances, and that the vessels should be bright.”

Chrysostom should be understood as speaking of veils before the sanctuary in Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> When you see the curtains at the doors being drawn back, then believe that heaven above is being opened and that the angels are descending.

Here **ἀμφίθυρον** should be understood as “the veil of the door,” or *velothyrum*. The latter word is frequently used in the *Lives of the Popes* by Anastasius and William the Librarians; **βηλόθυρα** is also known from Codinus, *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*, and from the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Frogs*.

Perhaps **ἀμφίθυρον** should likewise be explained in this way in Evagrius, book VI, chapter 20, concerning the gift sent by Chosroes to the martyr Saint Sergius:

> A Hunnic **amphithyrum**, decorated with gold.

That is: “A Hunnic veil, gleaming with gold, for covering the doors.”

Christophorsonus translates: “A unique object, open on both sides, gleaming with gold,” which seems to refer to **θυμιαματήριον**, “a censer,” which precedes it.

Musculus translates: “And a unique object open on both sides, adorned with gold,” and adds in the margin: “**Οὐνικόν** is a type of garment. See Suidas.”

But although I consult Suidas, I find nothing there about a type of garment. Under **οὐνικόν** he refers to **ἀπόνοια**, where he cites passages from Procopius referring to a type of hairstyle customary among the Massagetae and likewise among the Veneti, which they called **οὔννιον**—or perhaps **οὐννικόν**. I believe that hairstyle was customary among the Huns.

Theophylact Simocatta has words parallel to those of Evagrius in book V, chapter 14 of his *History of Maurice*. Our Pontanus translates there: “A Hunnic object, open on both sides and adorned with gold.”

Our Gretzerus, in volume II of *On the Cross*, where he reproduces from Simocatta the history of the cross sent by Chosroes, reads **ἀμφίθυρον οὐρανικόν**, and preserves the same words in his Latin translation.

I have often thought that **οὐνικόν** may be an abbreviation used by Greek scribes for **οὐρανικόν**. A basis for this reading could be found in the passage from Chrysostom cited above, where, when the **ἀμφίθυρον**, the veil or curtain, is drawn back, it is said that **οὐρανόν**, “heaven,” is opened above.

In Nicephorus, book XVIII, chapter 22, where the same story concerning Chosroes is found, the translator Johannes Langus renders the phrase: “And a Hunnic amphithyrum, adorned with gold.” He adds this scholion: “The Hunnic amphithyrum, in my judgment, consists of barriers or railings surrounding the more sacred table of the altar or keeping the people away from it; on each side there is a door, with an entrance leading to it, made in the Hunnic manner.”

I agree with Langus concerning Hunnic or Unnic workmanship, for objects were named in this way from the craftsmanship of the nation. And, to remain with sacred objects, Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17, in his account of Nicetius, speaks of a “Sarmatian covering for a chalice,” that is, one artfully made by the Sarmatians. Gregory the Great likewise says in book XII of the *Register*, letter 7, to Adulowaldus: “The Gospel enclosed in a Persian case.”

It also seems quite possible that **ἀμφίθυρον οὐνικόν** refers to a sacred diptych, customarily placed on altars during the sacrifice, as I have elsewhere noted in my *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers*.

Johannes Meursius is not correct in his *Greek-Barbarian Glossary* when he understands the words as bifold panels of the kind that, he says, are now placed on altars, evidently meaning an altar panel.

There were also veils and cloths on the altars. 1 Maccabees, chapter IV, verse 51: “They placed loaves on the table, or altar, and hung up the curtains.”

Clement of Rome, as the letter is commonly attributed to him, in letter 2 to James: “Let the altar cloths alone be washed in that basin.”

Theodoret, book I of his *History*, chapter 31:

> The divine altar was also adorned with royal curtains  
> and golden gifts set with precious stones.

Fortunatus, book II, poem 3, concerning the chapel of the cross erected at Tours by Gregory of Tours:

> Finally Gregory offers this temple to the holy cross,  
> while he covers [the altar] with cloths bearing signs of the cross;

that is, as his meaning shows, he covers the altar with cloths marked with crosses; these cloths he soon calls veils:

> And the veils placed in honor of the dedicated cross are pleasing.

Anastasius, in his account of Stephen IV: “Over the altar in the church of Saint Lawrence he made a covering, and between the columns of the altar, on the right and left, white veils.”

Again: “Around the altar he made eight double veils, four of white cloth and four of scarlet.”

The Thirteenth Council of Toledo, chapter 7: “Those seized by insane recklessness strip the altars and remove their sacred vestments.”

The veils of temples were often marked with images of the saints, especially of those to whom they were offered. Evodius, book II, chapter 4 of *The Miracles of Saint Stephen*, mentions a veil miraculously offered with an image of Saint Stephen carrying a cross and trampling a dragon underfoot; it was hung in memory of Saint Stephen.

Venantius shortly before this speaks of cloths or veils marked with crosses. — ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 235. “The fragrant lights are burned in waxed papyrus.”

The same author, *Natale* 7:

> How smoky was the chamber that gave off  
> the scent of waxed papyrus.

Papyrus was used in lamps and candles in place of a wick. Johannes of Genoa: “Papyrus is so called as if from *parans pyr*, ‘providing fire,’ because it is placed in candles and lamps for burning.”

The same author: “*Funalia*, ‘torches,’ are called *licinia*, ‘wicks,’ from *funis*, ‘rope,’ because before the use of papyrus our ancestors surrounded with wax the cords that they had used.”

Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8: “In it—the lamp—there was neither papyrus nor even a drop of dripping oil,” and so forth.

Drepanius, concerning the Paschal candle:

> The shaping wax confines the papyrus of the sea.

Gregory the Great, book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 5: “He filled all the lamps of the church with water and, according to custom, placed papyrus in the middle.”

Fortunatus, book II of the *Life of Saint Hilary*, near the end: “As long as the candle had been, the wax was found lying there, consumed down to the papyrus,” and so forth.

Papyrus is a plant that grows in the marshes of Egypt or in the still waters of the Nile. From its inner bark—or perhaps one should read “fiber”—veils, garments, and ropes were woven, as Theophrastus teaches in book IV, chapter 9 of his *History of Plants*, and Pliny in book XIII, chapter 11.

Hence we often read of mats and floor coverings made from papyrus for the use of monks. — CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume III, pp. 132–133.

### Note 236. “They shine night and day.”

It is clear from the sacred Scriptures, in the case of the golden lampstand, that lights were kept burning for religious reasons. Josephus too, in book XVIII, chapter 6 of the *Antiquities*, testifies that a lamp was lit every day before the high-priestly robe while it was kept in the Tower of Antonia.

Lights were also lit during the day, as Paulinus says here. Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 3: “Even without the relics of martyrs, throughout all the churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, they light lamps while the sun is already shining—not, of course, to dispel darkness, but to show a sign of joy.”
