Vigilantius himself, quoted by Jerome in the same work, chapter 2, *On the Practices of Various Churches*: “We see that, under the pretext of religion, something close to a pagan rite has been introduced into the churches: while the sun is still shining, great masses of candles are lit.”

Epiphanius, in his letter to John of Jerusalem: “When I had come to a village called Anablatha and, passing by, had seen a burning lamp there, I asked what place it was and learned that it was a church.”

Consult Baronius, volume I, under the year of Christ 58. — ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 237. “Scatter flowers over the ground; cover the thresholds with garlands.”

It was customary to adorn the tombs of the saints and the thresholds of churches with flowers.

Saint Augustine, book XXII, chapter 8 of *The City of God*, relates two miracles produced through flowers that had been offered and brought to the relics of Saint Stephen.

Jerome, in the epitaph of Nepotianus: “He shaded the gathering places of the martyrs with various flowers, the foliage of trees, and the tendrils of vines.”

Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 50, concerning Saint Severus: “He was accustomed to gather lily flowers in their season and hang them along the walls of this building.”

Fortunatus, book VIII, epigram 9:

> You have woven festive altars with varied crowns,  
> so that the altar is painted with new flowers threaded together.

Even among pagans, nature itself taught them this honor; they were accustomed to adorn and entreat their false gods in this way. This rite is frequently found in profane authors. — ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM XV
[Source anchor: Col. 0910C]

Not. 238. **He first served as a lector.**—Here I observe that Felix served for several years in the office of lector in the Church, and from there was raised to the ministry of exorcist. Formerly, those who had been approved after several years in the office of doorkeeper were promoted to the ministry of lector, and so to the other orders, as the needs of the Church required. Nor do I see why, now, in most dioceses, the four minor orders are conferred on one and the same day. Today clerics are ashamed to serve for three or two years in these lower orders of the Church; once they have reached their twenty-fifth year, they immediately rush into the priesthood, for the sake both of honor and of profit. Formerly, and in the age of Cyprian—as can be seen in his Letters 33 and 34 and several others—the office of lector was entrusted only to men of advanced age who were distinguished for merit and learning, and even to confessors who had publicly confessed Christ before tyrants and torturers. Later, however, minors and little children were admitted to it.

[Source anchor: Cols. 0910D, 0911A, and 0911B]

**Not. 239. “The Church would be battered by war.”**—So the manuscripts read. Correctors changed it to “the rule would be battered.” In the *Epithalamium of Julian and Ia*, Cauchius read a similar verse:

> A great sacrament, by which the Church marries Christ.

Tertullian, Book II *Against Marcion*:

> Thus also the Church proceeds in the apostolic word.

The sacred poets do not observe Greek orthography in words of this kind. Fortunatus, Book III to Felix:

> You married the Church; you joined blessed vows.

Again, in his *Life of Saint Martin*:

> But founded upon this rock, the Church reigns.

Nor do they regard it as contrary to religious usage, in such Greek or Hebrew names, to employ a varying quantity of syllables. Thus Tertullian, in *Genesis*, wrote:

> Here Adam was set as guardian, with his faithful wife.

And again in the same work:

> Therefore, when faithful Adam had already joined himself in marriage—

**DUC.**

**“The Church would be battered by war.”**—This should be the reading; for it is written thus in two German manuscript codices. Some, not understanding the passage, corrupted it and, against the testimony of the manuscripts, substituted: “the rule would be battered by war.” Our Paulinus too, by eliding one of the two *c*’s, shortens the first syllable in *Eclesia*, in Letter 32 to Severus, no. 5, verses 13–14:

> A double-roofed hall, as the Church of the Testaments.  
> The joyful mother Church, as she brings forth new offspring in twins.

And in the poem to Cytherius, verse 766:

> And he will steer the ship of the Church.

In the *Epithalamium of Julian and Ia*, verses 167 and 196:

> A great sacrament, by which the Church marries Christ.

And in *Natale* 9, with all the manuscript codices, it should be read:

> Here may the love bind you with which the Church binds Christ,  
> and within, the Church marks the offspring conceived for God.

Tertullian uses the same license in Book III *Against Marcion*:

> Christ is the head, whose members make up the Church.

It was therefore permitted to the ancient Christian poets to make the first syllable of *Eclesia* short. I have no doubt that this word was altered by bad critics in other ancient verses as well, as can be discovered by collation of the manuscript codices. In these passages it should be written *Eclesia* with a single *c*.

[Source anchor: Col. 0911B]

**Not. 240. “He cherished an heir.”**—The very learned Cauchius reads this for *vovebat* (“he vowed”); but the received reading may be retained, since it is customarily used when heirs are concerned. For example: “Nature and the parents’ common vow alike admit children to their parents’ goods.” *Digest*, “Unde liberi,” law *Scripto*. Thus *vovebat* means that he desired, by vows, that an heir be given. **DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0911C; printed p. 934 begins within this note]

**Not. 241. “And they stiffen in the sinew.”**—Eusebius describes a similar procedure among the punishments of Christians, Book V, chapter 1 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Sigonius, Book III, chapter 15 *On Judgments*, thinks that this was the torture of the horse, by which the limbs were stretched with cords. Bede likewise expressed this passage in the *Life of Saint Felix* as follows: “He is sent into a prison of darkness; iron chains bind his hands and neck together; his feet are tightened with a cord, and fragments of pottery are spread beneath him.” Hence Usuard’s Martyrology, January 14, should be corrected and should read: “After the torments, he was sent into prison, and, bound with screws and pieces of pottery placed beneath him, he lay there.” For the matter is likewise related by Ado: “Bound with no ordinary chains, he is stretched out with screws and pieces of pottery placed beneath him.” Eustratius suffered the same torture in Nicephorus, Book VII, chapter 14. **DUC.**

## IN POEM XVI

[Source anchor: Col. 0911D]

**Not. 242. “In a chamber.”**—*Cubile* here means the same as *cubiculum*, “bedroom” or “chamber.” Jerome uses the word in the same sense, Letter 22: “And because at night, outside the public prayers, each person keeps vigil in his own chamber,” etc. Cassian likewise, Book IV, chapter 12: “Sitting within their chambers and devoting themselves to work and meditation.” See Cassiodorus, Book VI, Letter 13, and Leo of Ostia, Book III of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, chapter 26.

## IN POEM XVII

[Source anchor: Col. 0911D]

**Not. 243. “Of Nicetas.”**—This Nicetas—whom you may call *Vincent* or *Victor* in Latin, as Paulinus does in this poem: “Nicetas, rightly named, victor over the body”—was bishop of the Dacians. His memory is celebrated in the Church calendars on January 7: “In Dacia, Saint Nicetas, bishop, who rendered savage and barbarous peoples gentle and tame through the preaching of the Gospel.” He was a most learned man and admired by the Romans, as Paulinus writes in Letter 10 to Severus. Paulinus also mentions him in *Natale* 9.

This is a different Nicetas, a confessor, from another Nicetas, a martyr, who was put to death under the emperor Gratian by Athanaric. The Roman Martyrology mentions the latter on September 15, as do the Metaphrast on the same day, the *Suda* under “Athanaric,” and Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 48. **ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0912A and 0912B]

**Not. 244. “Merrha.”**—Thus corrected from a German manuscript. Earlier editions had *myrrha*.

It should be corrected to *merrha liquores* (“the waters of Merrha”), for it alludes to the story of Exodus 15:23:

> And they could not drink the waters from Merrha.

Origen’s translator, Homily 7 on Exodus: “They could not drink water from Merrha.” Thus it should also be written in Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 56. The Latin Vulgate printed *Mara*. Jerome, Letter 127: “Marah received its name from bitterness. Marah: understand the waters of the letter that kills; when confession of the cross and the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion are added to them, everything that seemed unbearable, sad, and harsh is changed into sweetness.” Ambrose, *On the Institution of the Virgin*: “The fountain of Mara made sweet through wood.” Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 13: “For that wood was then present in a sacramental figure, by which Moses sweetened the bitter water; and we, drinking the water of baptism through the wood of Christ’s Passion, have been restored to life by faith in Christ.” Paulinus himself uses a similar expression in *Natale* 8:

> Divider of the sea and sweetener of the bitter spring,

and Theodoret recognizes the same figure of the Passion in question 26 on Exodus.

Our author also touched upon this very story in Letter 27: “Just as that *merrha*—for so it should be read, not *myrrha*—in Moses’ hand was changed through the wood of the mystery, so the holy and sweet address of your Blessedness changed it into the sweetness of spiritual joy.” **DUC.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0912B, 0912C, and 0912D; printed p. 935 begins within this note]

**Not. 245. “And with a ship armed with the sign of salvation.”**—Our Gretzer, *On the Cross*, Book II, chapter 26, and after him Jacobus Bosius, *On the Triumphant Cross*, Book VI, chapter 9, interpret this as referring to a cross placed on a ship for protection. They think Chrysostom alludes to this in the *Demonstration against the Gentiles, That Christ Is God*:

> It may be seen that the cross is celebrated everywhere: at sea, on ships, and on islands.

Likewise Ephraem, sermon *On the Cross*: “The cross is the guidance of those who sail.” Ambrose, on Psalm 47: “Those who carry the cross of Christ like a mast on their ships sail well.” From it they observe the breaths of the winds, so that they may direct their bodies toward the grace of the Holy Spirit, safe and secure in the Lord’s wood.

Although Ephraem seems rather to be understood of the ship’s rudder, as will follow shortly, and Chrysostom, together with Ambrose, of the mast and yardarm—for Paulinus here also speaks of the yardarm, as do other Fathers. Justin, *Second Apology for the Christians*:

> For the sea is not cut through unless this trophy, which is called the mast, remains safe in the ship.

Origen, Homily 8 *On Various Subjects*, or whoever the author may be in Jerome, volume IX: “The masts of ships, the horns of their sails, fly beneath the figure of our cross.” Minucius Felix, *Octavius*: “Certainly we naturally see the sign of the cross on a ship, when it is carried along with swelling sails, when it glides with its little outspread palms, and when the yard is raised: it is the sign of the cross.” Ambrose, or Maximus of Turin, sermon 56, volume IX:

> When sailors cut through the sea, the mast is first raised by them and the sail is spread, so that, once the Lord’s cross has been formed, the streams of water may be broken, and, secure in this saving sign of the Lord, they may seek the harbor of salvation and escape the danger of death. For the suspended sail upon the mast is a kind of figure of the sacrament, as though Christ had been raised upon the cross. And therefore, receiving confidence from the mystery, people disregard the storms of the winds and undertake the vows of travel. Just as the Church cannot stand without the cross, so the ship is helpless without its mast. For immediately the devil disturbs it, and the wind dashes it about; but when the sign of the cross is raised, the devil’s wickedness is immediately repelled and the storm of the winds is stilled.

Jerome, or whoever the author may be, on Mark 15: “The ship is driven across the seas by its mast, which is likened to the cross.” Various coins depicting ships, on which the mast and yardarm form a cross, may be seen in Jacobus Bosius, *On the Triumphant Cross*, Book V, chapter 12. **ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0913A]

**Not. 246. “You will go upon the waters as the yardarm of the cross.”**—This is a figure of speech; Paulinus should have written *cruce antennae* (or *antemnae*, “by the cross of the yardarm”). The *antenna* is the wooden beam on ships to which the sails are fastened; tied crosswise to the mast, it forms the shape of a cross. Cyprian, *On the Tree of Life*:

> This form of a tree rises from a single trunk,  
> and soon extends its arms into twin branches,  
> as the heavy sails stretch the full yardarms.

**BARTHIUS, *Adversarial Commentary*, Book XXXIII, chapter 3.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0913B]

**Not. 247. “The sailors’ cry.”**—*Celeusma*, or *celeuma*, is the sailors’ cry, expressed in rhythmic song. Sidonius, Book VIII, Letter 12:

> Here, with measured sailors’ song, sing your praises; the rowers among the thwarts and the helmsmen among the stern ornaments shall sing.

The same author, Book II, Letter 10:

> From here the chorus of the bent-backed haulers,  
> with the banks answering “Alleluia,”  
> raises a river-song to Christ.

Sailors especially resounded with it when they were already near the harbor. Jerome, Letter 1 to Heliodorus: “The sailors’ song of rejoicing must be sung as a finale.” Fortunatus, Book IV *On the Life of Martin*: “And as he seeks the harbor, the sailor fills the waters with his song,” where the form is *celeuma, -ae*. Those who trod grapes in the winepress also used a *celeusma*. Jerome on Jeremiah 25: “A work-song will be sung like that of those treading in the winepress.” **ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0913B]

**Not. 248. “With the rudder of the cross.”**—The rudder of a ship resembles the form of a cross. Hence Chrysostom, sermon *On the Cross*:

> The cross is the guidance of those who sail.

The same is found in Ephraem, sermon *On the Cross*. Various coins of Fortuna exist with a rudder, in which the shape of a cross can be seen. See Jacobus Bosius, *On the Triumphant Cross*, Book V, chapter 12, where he reproduces an impression from a coin of Trajan and a certain carnelian gem. **ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0913C]

**Not. 249. “You will go also to Scupi.”**—In Ptolemy, Book III of the *Geography*, chapter 9, among the cities of Dardania in Upper Mysia, one finds *Σκοῦποι* (“Scupi”); likewise in Trebellius Pollio, under Regillianus, *Scupi*, and in the codex, Book VIII, Title 45, *Scuppi*. Others, I think, are the *Σκόποι* mentioned by Stephanus, who says that it was a city of Thrace. Lepidus mentions it in the eighth book of his historical epitome; in Zonaras, volume III, it is called, under Basil Porphyrogenitus, the “city of the Scopians,” and likewise by Nicetas Choniates and Nicephorus Gregoras, “the little town of the Scopians,” which the latter says belonged to the Triballi. **ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0913D]

**Not. 250. “Pilleatus.”**—Thus corrected from a German manuscript. Earlier printed editions had *pelleatus*. **ROSVEYDUS.** Jerome, who will be cited shortly, joins “the fur-clad peoples of the Bessi.” This was the ancient dress of the first Fathers. Prudentius, *Psychomachia*:

> Venerable Adam assumed fur-clad garments.

Propertius, Book IV, elegy 1:

> The Senate-house, which now shines lofty in senatorial purple,  
> once had rustic hearts as its fur-clad fathers.

Prudentius, Book II *Against Symmachus*:

> Or let them wear a cloak made from the hide  
> of a Libyan bear, with its shaggy body.

Cicero, *For M. Scaurus*, as quoted by Asconius: “Let it be pardoned to the filthiest and lightest of peoples, and, I might almost say, to fur-clad witnesses.” Ovid, Book IV *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 8:

> The shores lying too close beneath the fur-clad Coralli.

**ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0913D]

**Not. 251. “Pilleatus.”**—Among the Goths, *pilleati*, or *pileati*, were chiefly those who stood out among them as nobles; from their number, as Jornandes says in *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapters 5 and 11, their kings and priests were appointed. Paulinus here seems to use the word to designate the chief men among the Getae or Dacians. **CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume III, p. 278.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0914A and 0914B; printed p. 936 begins within this note]

**Not. 252. “And the Bessi.”**—Thus corrected from two German manuscripts and the Regius manuscript. Earlier editions had *versos*. **DUC.** It should be corrected from manuscript P.: “And imitate the Bessi in these very things.” For he says that the Bessi, gold-gatherers, are changed into gold; of them he had previously said:

> And their Bessi, harder than snow,  
> have now become sheep.

Strabo, Book VII:

> The Bessi occupy most of Mount Haemus; and because of their brigandage they are called brigands, dwelling in huts and leading a wretched life.

Solinus likewise, following Herodotus, counts them among the peoples of Thrace. Latinus Pacatus calls them seekers of gold, just as Paulinus here calls them gold-sifters. In the *Panegyric on Theodosius*: “He considered that gold not very precious which a Bessian seeker, or a Callaician explorer, had extracted from the veins of mountains or the gravel of rivers; he thought that gold purer and brighter which mourners had given, which human tears, not the waters of rivers, had washed.” **DUC.**

The received reading, *versos*, seems preferable, especially since other manuscripts agree with it, and *vertis* and *versos* answer each other well. Thus the passage formerly read: “You turn brigands into monks.” Claudian also mentions the Bessi as gold-sifters in the *Consulship of Manlius Theodorus*:

> Whatever, probing the veins far from daylight,  
> the skill of the pale Bessian digs from hidden places.

The Bessi as monks are mentioned in the *Life of Saint Theodosius the Coenobiarch* in Cappadocia, January 11. Jerome, Letter 3 to Heliodorus, on the Bessi converted to the faith: “The savagery of the Bessi and the crowd of fur-clad peoples, who once sacrificed human beings at the funerals of the dead, have broken their shriek into the sweet melody of Christ.” Among the Christian epigrams in Gruter’s *Inscriptions*, p. 1169, there is an epitaph of Saint Marcellinus, a priest born among the Bessi. **ROSVEYDUS.**

## IN POEM XVIII

[Source anchor: Col. 0914C]

**Not. 253. “Let them hang curtains at the doors.”**—Since the holy doors were latticed, they were generally covered with curtains, so that the sacred rites performed at the altars might not be seen by everyone. Epiphanius, Letter to John of Jerusalem: “I found a curtain hanging at the doors of the church.” Finally, the Council of Narbonne, 589, canon 13: “Younger clerics are ordered to lift the curtains at the doors for their elders.” Such curtains at the entrances of sacred buildings and at the royal doors are mentioned more than once by writers; Rosveydus collected several of their passages in his notes on Paulinus (Not. 234). **CANGIUS, *Constantinople Christian*, Book III, p. 63.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0914C]

**Not. 254. “With wax.”**—In Bede’s time it was read *cereis* (“with candles”), as is clear from his book *On Metres*, in the chapter on episynalepha or diaeresis, where he says that in this poem of Paulinus the *e* and *i* are joined. **ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0914C]

**Not. 255. “Betrothing souls with dowries.”**—*Desponsare* means to join by a fixed pledge; *sponsare* is certainly not common, but Paulinus uses it here. Nevertheless it is found in that excellent *Onomasticon* of Strasbourg: *sponso, sponsas*, “I betroth,” “you betroth,” Greek *μνηστεύω*. It also occurs in Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 11: “How much more will the time veil them, without which they cannot be betrothed, and under whose pressure virgins cease to be virgins without betrothal.” **BARTHIUS, *Adversarial Commentary*, Book XLII, chapter 21.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0914D]

**Not. 256. “In very humble things.”**—The printed editions have hitherto read incorrectly *servilibus* (“servile things”). He calls the widow’s small offerings *pervilia* (“very cheap things”). The word is known from Livy, Book I of the *Macedonian War*: “The grain supply was also very cheap that year.” **ROSVEYDUS.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0914D, 0915A, and 0915B; printed p. 937 begins within this note]

**Not. 257. “He fixes kisses upon the doorposts.”**—In ancient times the thresholds of temples were reverently greeted and worshiped with kisses. Prudentius, hymn 2 *Περὶ στεφάνων* (“On Crowns”), on Saint Lawrence:

> Even the lights of the Senate,  
> once luperci and flamens,  
> kiss the thresholds  
> of apostles and martyrs.

The same author, hymn 11 *On Crowns*, on Saint Hippolytus:

> They imprint kisses upon the shining metal.

Either because the doors were bronze, or because they were covered with bronze or silver plates. Arator, Book II of the *Apostolic History*:

> The whole city gathers,  
> each one seeking to be first to approach the new building,  
> or to fix kisses upon the doorposts,  
> and to consecrate the place touched by his lips.

Chrysostom, Homily 39 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> We are the temple of Christ. Therefore we kiss the vestibules and entrance of the temple, when we kiss one another. Do you not see how many people also kiss the vestibules of this temple—some bowing their heads, others holding them with their hand and bringing their hand to their mouth? Through these gates and doors Christ both entered and enters to us whenever we share in communion.

Gregory of Tours, Book IV of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 14: “So that they might kiss the thresholds of the basilica of Saint Martin.” Fortunatus, Book IV *On the Life of Saint Martin*, on the basilica of Saint Apollinaris at Ravenna:

> Again, Apollinaris, lick the precious threshold,  
> lying prostrate on the ground as a suppliant.

Hence thresholds were adorned with curtains. See above. Hence also the expression arose, “to proceed to the thresholds of the Apostles,” that is, to the basilicas of the holy Apostles. Claudian, or whoever the author may be, to James, master of the cavalry:

> By the ashes of Paul, by the white-haired thresholds of Peter.

The *Acts of Pope Alexander*: “If you had led him to the threshold of Saint Peter.” **ROSVEYDUS.**

## IN POEM XXII

[Source anchor: Col. 0915C]

**Not. 258. “The monster vomited him from its vast belly.”**—As he said in the *Propemptic for Nicetas*: “That it might receive him submerged and then give him back after drinking.” Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 58: “Jonah, swallowed by the sea-monster, in whose belly shipwrecks were digested, was vomited out unharmed after three days.” John Chrysostom, Homily 5 on the Epistle to the Colossians:

> How did the beast have Jonah in its belly, and he did not perish? And how did it vomit him up unharmed?

And Homily 56 *On Various Passages of the New Testament*:

> For just as the sea-monster vomited him after three days, having found in him no food proper or suitable to itself.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0915D]

**Not. 259. “The Three Fates.”**—There was a place at Rome called *The Three Fates*, which Procopius mentions in Book I of the *Gothic War*, near the end. Anastasius, under Honorius: “He built a church to the blessed martyr Hadrian at the Three Fates, dedicated it, and offered many gifts.” The same author, under Hadrian: “In the church of the blessed Saints Cosmas and Damian at the Three Fates, he made a garment of *stauracin*.” Again: “He restored the basilica of the holy Cosmas and Damian situated at the Three Fates.” Hence Friedrich Lindenbrog, in a most courteous letter to me, suggested that in Cyprian, Letter 21, instead of *usque ad Trian facta*, one should read *usque ad Tria Fata* (“as far as the Three Fates”). A very sound conjecture, if only it were certain that that letter was written at Rome. There are reasons why it may appear to have been sent from Africa to Rome, and thus the received reading could be retained. There are many barbarous place-names there. **ROSVEYDUS.**

**“The Three Fates.”**—Thus the Romans were accustomed to call the Parcae; a place at Rome was consecrated to them. See Procopius at the place cited above.

## IN POEM XXIII

[Source anchor: Col. 0916A]

**Not. 260. “He lashes the clamorous enemies.”**—Thus corrected from a German manuscript and from Schott’s edition in the margin. Five editions—including Rosveydus’s edition and the common editions—incorrectly read *cum nosset*.

The very learned Cauchius suspects that *damnosos* (“harmful”) should be read, or at least that the reading should be *clamosos verberat* (“he lashes the clamorous”); but by following the traces of the received reading, one might write *cunctantes verberat hostes* (“he lashes the hesitating enemies”) instead of *cum nosset*. He evidently indicates that the demons are pressed by punishments when they delay and hesitate to depart. Thus John Chrysostom, Homily 26 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> Though no one is seen, though no one presses against the demon’s sides, voices and rending, blows and tortures, tongues set aflame are heard, since the demon cannot endure that extraordinary and marvelous power.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0916A and 0916B; printed p. 938 begins within this note]

**Not. 261. “It is sacred, and does not slip back over the face.”**—The very learned Cauchius restored this ancient reading from a manuscript, whereas the earlier reading was *nefas est ignorare* (“it is impious to be ignorant”). It is confirmed by Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* 3, *On the Life of Saint Martin*: “Whenever Saint Martin undertook the task of exorcising demons, it regularly happened that several people, their feet lifted into the air, hung suspended, yet their garments did not fall over their faces, lest the exposed part of their bodies should cause shame.” Shortly afterward Cauchius correctly changes *tegmine membris* to *tegmina membris* (“coverings for the limbs”), since garments are coverings of the body and are so called by Theodulf in verses that older Missals contained for Palm Sunday. But from a manuscript it should be corrected as follows:

> Thus let us spread our bodies as coverings for the soul,  
> so that through us the way may always be safe for you.

He says that bodies are the garments of souls, because the limbs are covered and, as it were, veiled by the soul. **DUC.**

That verse had been variously interpolated in printed books. Together with Rosveydus, we corrected it from Belgian and German manuscripts: “It is sacred, and does not slip back over the face.” What could be clearer? He says that the garments did not slip back over the face; Sulpicius Severus also indicates this in Book III of the *Dialogues*, section 6, in these words: “You could see wretched people hanging with their feet raised aloft as though from a cloud, yet their garments did not fall over their faces, lest the exposed part of their bodies should cause shame.” We certainly read that it was frequently customary, at the memorials and tombs of martyrs and confessors, for demons to be exorcised by snatching the bodies of the afflicted upward, with their feet turned above, yet in such a way that the garments covering the private parts of the limbs did not fall back—as our Paulinus reports that he himself witnessed.

[Source anchor: Col. 0916C]

**Not. 262. “The lamp.”**—We corrected this from a German manuscript. Earlier it had incorrectly read *lignum* (“wood”).

There is no doubt that *lychnum* (“lamp”) should be corrected in place of *lignum*. Thus shortly afterward:

> But the boy who had taken away the lamp after the light was extinguished.

And elsewhere:

> And, suspended in place of a lamp, he hung in the open.

Lamps customarily hang fastened by ropes or chains, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> Lamps hang from the golden ceilings.

Lucretius, Book V:

> The bright lights of hanging lamps glitter.

And our author again:

> Hanging lamps are held by bronze spirals.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0916D]

**Not. 263. “As was his stature.”**—*Status* here means *statura*, “stature.” Gregory of Tours, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 24: “He honored Celsus with the dignity of the patriciate, a man tall in stature, strong in the shoulders, powerful in the arm, etc.” The Bavarian Law, title 1, chapter 11, §1: “Let a leaden tunic be made according to his stature; whoever killed him shall pay as much gold as it weighs.” **CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume III, p. 953.**

*Status* for *statura*. Thus *jactus* for *jactura*: “to bear a loss” (*jactum ferre*) for “to bear damage” (*jacturam ferre*) in Paulinus, poem 21 to Cytherius, on the shipwreck of Martinianus, verse 339. Saint Cyprian likewise used *statum* for *statura* in *On Mortality*: “tall in stature,” as J. F. Gronovius notes from manuscripts in *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 3. In Statius: “the short stature of dwarfs.” In Columella, concerning Gallic roosters: “a greater stature is sought.” Ambrose, sermon 10 on Psalm 118: “For a man is tall in stature and handsome in face.”

[Source anchor: Col. 0917A]

**Not. 264. “Like a youth with a pole.”**—P. Scriverius has observed very aptly at verse 150 that among the ancient *θαυματοποιοί* (“wonder-workers” or “jugglers”) there was a kind of entertainment in which boys standing at the end of a piece of wood wrestled. Martial says that they carried unstable weights balanced on the forehead—on the forehead, not on the shoulders, as did the class of porters called *phalangarii*, mentioned by Nonius, who carried burdens on poles, as they still do today. We add to this learned observation that Paulinus called these *θαυματοποιοί* *contigeri* in *Natale* 7 of Felix. **J. F. GRONOVIUS, *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 10.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0917A]

**Not. 265. “With his marrow touched, this brother safe.”**—This correction came from a Roman friend. Earlier it read: “With his marrow covered, this guest-brother.” The manuscript also has this reading. It may perhaps deserve consideration whether one should read “with the marrow covered,” as here, and whether the man cured by Felix had been Paulinus’s guest, from the people of the Medulli in Gaul. I do not see why he calls them *Tecti*, unless he alludes to the neighboring Tectosages. **ROSVEYDUS.**

## IN POEM XXIV

[Source anchor: Col. 0917B]

**Not. 266. “We give right hands.”**—To give right hands is to enter into a pact. Claudian, *Against Rufinus*, Book I:

> He joins right hands in a covenant destined for death.

And Book II:

> Are you giving your right hands, excellent leader?

That the ancients, like Germans today, gave one another their hands in greeting is clear from this passage of Paulinus. We customarily do this when departing; the ancients did likewise. See Xenophon, *Education of Cyrus*, Book V: “When we enter into friendships.” The same was the custom of the ancients. Valerius Flaccus, Book II:

> When he sees them, he himself first runs forward of his own accord toward the waves;  
> he marvels at the men, and, embracing them and clinging to them with his right hand,  
> he begins.

**BARTHIUS, *Adversarial Commentary*, Book XXV, chapter 8, and Book XLVIII, chapter 18.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0917B and 0917C; printed p. 939 begins within this note]

**Not. 267. “With the ship gliding safely through the gentle waters.”**—So the Regius manuscript and Rosveydus’s edition read. We formerly corrected it by conjecture. Earlier it read *lambente* (“lapping”). It was taken from Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> The well-oiled fir slips along the waters; the waves marvel.

And Book X:

> It glides on, cleaving the deep, with the wave and favorable tide.

From the same source comes the familiar poetic expression “he cut a path,” as in *Aeneid* VI:

> He cuts his way to the ships.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0917C]

**Not. 268. “That soon the little boat may be safe.”**—Isidore, Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “A barca is a vessel that carries all kinds of merchandise to the shore. In the open sea, because of the excessive waves, the larger ship receives it into her own bosom.” Thus it should be corrected from a manuscript of our Paris college. The old glosses: *Ἀκάτιον, ἡ βάρκα, τὸ λέμβος*—“a small boat, the barca, the skiff.” It is therefore a kind of small vessel, which he previously called a skiff. A fleet of *barcarii* is mentioned in the *Notitia of Both Empires*. **DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0917D]

**Not. 269. “Death was powerless against virtue.”**—Thus Virgil:

> With the defeated struggle, and with heaven’s powers exhausted,

*Aeneid* XI. Nevertheless the other Latin syntax of this word, which manuscript P. offers, is no less good: “Death was devoid of power.” Thus Statius, *Thebaid* IX, verse 629:

> Alas, why should I be utterly a false prophet of the future?

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0917D and 0918A]

**Not. 270. “He panted after heavy sleep.”**—*Anhelare* with the accusative is shared by Paulinus with the ancient poets. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 685:

> Nor does it always pant after the wave.

The same work, verse 923:

> Nature pours forth her work, for which little vessels pant.

And the same *Apotheosis*, verse 843:

> Now the heat, exhaled, pants after the warm breath.

Statius, *Thebaid* XI:

> Jupiter, exhausted by the battles of Phlegra, pants.

Cicero also says that Catiline “panted after crime.” The same Cicero, in the *Aratea*, on Capricorn:

> Then, panting cold from his powerful breast—

[Source anchor: Col. 0918B]

**Not. 271. “Within the sea, and outside the sea.”**—Our Paulinus elegantly calls Jonah “outside the sea within the sea,” and uses the same word in the same poem to Cytherius, verse 507:

> Now he remains a stranger to you and yet your own.

The same poem, verse 816:

> He was a stranger to Egyptian soil.

And *Natale* 8 of Saint Felix:

> But a stranger in character.

Likewise Letter 11 to Severus, no. 3:

> A stranger to my brothers.

The same word is found plainly in Tertullian’s poem *On Jonah and Nineveh*. Thus he speaks of Jonah:

> Though not drenched by the waters, an outsider in the depths of the sea.

Or, as Philip Robert prefers:

> Between the sea and outside it.

[Source anchor: Col. 0918B]

**Not. 272. “Brotherhood.”**—Here understand *fraternitas* not as one person, as in Letter 35, “I beseech your brotherhood,” but as a group of several persons, that is, an assembly of brothers, as in Letter 3: “And let him fill the monastic brotherhood with softened spelt.” Jerome, to Theophilus, Letter 31: “The whole brotherhood greets you humbly.” It is the same as what appears at the end of Letter 32: “The brothers who are with us in the monastery greet you.” **DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0918B]

**Not. 273. “Generous in what is small.”**—This passage too admitted a conjectural correction, since earlier editions had *largos* (“generous things”), so that both the sense might be more harmonious and the law of the verse more carefully observed. The meaning is that, if the gift should happen to be small, its meagerness is compensated by the generosity of the affection. Something similar is said of the widow in *Natale* 6:

> Whom God regards not by the value of the gift but by the worth of her heart.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0918C]

**Not. 274. “Avaricious little beggars.”**—Here Paulinus excellently portrays the wandering monks, who, having abandoned their monasteries, wandered among various cells under some empty appearance of piety. The Rule of Saint Benedict speaks of them as follows, chapter 1: “The fourth kind of monks is called the gyrovagi: they spend their entire lives lodging in various cells, always wandering and never stable,” etc. The Rule of the Master, chapter 1; Peter Damian, Book V, Letter 9; Saint Bernard, Letter 68; Odo of Cluny, Book I of the *Collations*, chapter 23; and the *Statutes of Hugh of Cluny*, p. 1465, also discuss such gyrovagi. **CHARLES CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume II, p. 683, no. 1.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0918D]

**Not. 275. “Centumcellae.”**—Thus manuscript P. reads, whereas earlier it had *Centumcellis*. Correctors may perhaps have altered the case because they did not know the customary usage of authors of that age, who sometimes expressed indeclinable names of cities with the accusative and sometimes with the ablative, as learned men have recently observed. Thus in Frontinus: “Colonia Veros,” “Colonia Graviscos,” “Cassinos,” and “Agninos”; and in Vopiscus, in the *Life of Probus*: “Besides Copto and Ptolemais, cities rescued from barbarian servitude”; and again in Frontinus: “Puteoli, a colony; Fundi, a town.” **DUC.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0918D and 0919A; printed p. 940 begins at this note]

**Not. 276. “Equals into one.”**—He alluded to 2 Corinthians 4:14: “What fellowship has light with darkness?” and to Ecclesiasticus 13:21:

> What fellowship can a wolf have with a lamb?  
> So a sinner with a godly person.

To these are comparable the following pagan passages. Horace, *Epodes* 4:

> How great a quarrel, allotted by fate,  
> has fallen between wolves and lambs—  
> and between you and me.

Homer, *Iliad* 22:

> Neither wolves nor lambs possess a mind at one.

And:

> Before a wolf shall mate with a sheep.

Aristophanes, *Peace*. But the present passage concerns birds flying together in a flock, from the same book of Ecclesiasticus, 27:9:

> Birds will settle with those like themselves.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Cols. 0919A and 0919B]

**Not. 277. “Let him adorn it with nourished hair.”**—Earlier it read *passis*, “spread out.” But it is more correct to say that the Nazirite adorns his head with *pastis crinibus*, “nourished hair.” Thus in Letter 4 to Severus: “Let us consecrate our life to God in chastity and moderation, nourishing it like Nazirite hair.” Pagan authors likewise said that those who grew their hair in honor of the gods “fed the hair for the gods.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VII:

> to nourish sacred hair for you.

In Euripides’ *Bacchae*, this is *πλόκαμον τρέφειν*, “to nourish the lock,” and in Homer, *Iliad* 23, *χαίτην τρέφειν*, “to nourish the hair.” In Pausanias’ *Arcadica*, *τρέφειν κόμην*, “to nourish the hair.” The ancient Greeks used to dedicate their hair to a particular god. Valerius Flaccus says “to nourish the hair” in the *Argonautica*, Book VI. Pliny, Book IV, chapter 15, says “to feed the hair.” 1 Corinthians 11:14: “If a man wears his hair long,” Greek *ἀνὴρ ἐὰν κομᾷ*. Horace uses a similar expression in Book II of the *Satires*:

> to feed the beard of a wise man.

**DUC. See Not. 290.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0919B]

**Not. 278. *Postea fiat hostium* (“Afterward let him become [something] of the enemies”).**—The printed lemma is incomplete or corrupt; it seems that this should be corrected to *praeda fiat hostium* (“let him become the prey of enemies”), for Samson was captured after being ensnared by Delilah’s tricks. Hence Paulinus himself, Letter 4, on Samson: “Would that he had been as prudent in guarding against a woman as he was strong in strangling a lion! But, overcome by carnal allure, when weakness prevailed against strength, he was defeated.” And shortly afterward: “Let us choose to become the prey of this lion, lest we become the prey of the hostile lion.” **DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0919C]

**Not. 279. “Let the strong soul mortify its own ass.”**—He calls the body an ass because it is naturally inclined toward lust by its own impulse, as Saint Jerome relates of Hilarion in his *Life*: “I shall make you, little ass, stop kicking; I shall not feed you with barley, but with straw. I shall wear you out with hunger and thirst; I shall load you with a heavy burden; through heat and cold I shall track you, so that you may think of food rather than wantonness.” Gregory Nazianzen, *Against the Flesh*:

> An untamed beast, sprung from matter engaged in combat.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0919C]

**Not. 280. “Let him consume the fires of crimes.”**—So manuscript P. reads, not *igne criminum* (“with the fire of crimes”). The same Gregory, using a similar expression when discussing the chastisement of the flesh, supports this reading:

> So that you may cool my flame  
> and wipe away the foul decay  
> of the grievous passions.

Our own Paulinus likewise says in *Natale* 7:

> May he temper the fires of battles.

**DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0919D]

**Not. 281. “And the iron of ruin.”**—If I am not mistaken, once the metalepsis has been removed, it should more correctly be read: “And let him know no damage from iron.” In Letter 4 on Samson, he says the same thing: “May that hostile razor not rise upon our head and strip us of spiritual grace, as it stripped that Nazirite of his hair—hair which, while it remains with those who guard it, is beneficial, but when carelessly cut away becomes destructive.” **DUC.**

[Source anchor: Col. 0919D]

**Not. 282. “This strong rib for you.”**—He calls Cytherius’s wife a “rib” by metonymy, because the first man’s wife was created from his rib. Gregory Nazianzen likewise used “rib” for “wife” in poem 1, *On Matters Concerning Himself*:

> And of the solitary life, the first-fruits  
> of the life that is still to come,  
> which loves its own body,  
> though it lacks a rib.

“Of the heavenly life and of this life, which is led without a wife, recalling the beginnings of the eternal age.” Nor does it seek a rib.

**DUC.**
### Note 283. *Agitator Israel*

He calls God the charioteer of Israel, as Elisha says when Elijah was carried up into heaven, [Col. 0920A] 2 Kings 2:12: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horseman”; and again in 2 Kings 13:14, concerning Joash, king of Israel, at the death of Elisha. In Greek it is: *Ἄρμα Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ἱππεὺς αὐτοῦ*—“the chariot of Israel and its horseman.” Ambrose, however, in *On Naboth*, chapter 15, rendered it thus: “Father, charioteer of Israel and its horseman,” that is, “you who guided the Lord’s people with good leadership.”

For *agitatores* were called the charioteers who directed the races in the circus games and drove the four-horse chariots. See the final law of the Code, *On Sorcerers*: “If anyone of the *agitatores*, that is, charioteers, should attempt to act contrary to [941] this enactment.” Glossary: *Agitator*, ἡνίοχος, ἐλάτης—“driver, charioteer.” Cicero, *Academics* 4: “I shall hold back the horses as a skillful charioteer.” Pliny, book 34, chapter 5: “Whose four-horse chariot, together with its charioteer, a fly covered.” In the *Nomocanon*, title 13, *On the Laity*, chapter 21: “Οὐκ ἔστι δὲ παιγνικὴ τέχνη ἢ ἀτιμοποιὸς ἡ τῶν ἀθλητῶν, καὶ τῶν ἡνιόχων”—“The athletic profession is not a sportive or dishonorable art, nor is the profession of charioteers.” The translator omitted this last clause.

Council of Arles I, canon 4: “Concerning charioteers who are faithful: it was decided that, so long as they drive, they should be separated from communion.” [Col. 0920B] DUC.

### Note 284. *Partis senectam panibus*

The learned Cauchius conjectured that it should read *Partim*; but I would more willingly correct it with the smaller alteration to *Patris senectam panibus*—“the father’s old age with nourishment.” For he said a little earlier: “He would be the nourisher of his father and brothers.” The example of the eagle, which he adds, confirms the point.

Gesner reports of eagles what other writers relate of storks, citing John Tzetzes in the *Chiliads*: “The young of eagles and storks feed their aged parents and assist their flight.” John Tzetzes, *Chiliads*. Aldrovandus likewise relates this very thing from Athenaeus in book 1 of his *Ornithology*; but he was misled by an earlier translator, who incorrectly rendered the passage in book 13, chapter 10:

> When old age soon presses heavily upon them,  
> the young, flying about, seek food, driven by hunger.

For the Greek is:

> Ὅταν δὲ γηράσκωσιν, ἤδη δὴ τότε  
> Ἐπὶ τοὺς νεὼς ἵζουσι πεινῶντες κακῶς.
>
> But when they grow old, then indeed they sit upon the temples, grievously hungry.

[Col. 0920C] The more accurate later translator, Dalechampius, has: “They sit upon the roofs of the temples, miserably hungry.” On storks, see Pliny, book 10, chapter 23, and Aelian, book 3, chapter 24. DUC.

### Note 285. *Coelitis*

Cauchius rightly conjectured that *coelitis* should be read instead of *coelestis*. Paulinus likes to use a similar expression, saying *coelite regno*—“the heavenly realm”—instead of *coelesti regno*. Earlier in this very poem:

> That with a pure heart he may drink  
> the draught of heavenly wisdom.

And below, in *Natalis* 9:

> You who cultivate the sacred, heavenly gardens of paradise.

Likewise:

> For even the ashes of the apostles are beneath the heavenly table.

There is a similar expression in Ovid, *Fasti* 1:

> You had been driven from the heavenly realms by Jupiter.

Conversely, Q. Catulus, in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* 1, used *coelestes* for *coelites*:

> May I be permitted to call you heavenly beings in peace.

[Col. 0920D] DUC.

### Note 286. *Explicant instar crucis*

What Paulinus says here—that birds spread out their bodies, suspended on their wings, in the form of a cross—was also expressed by the author of the Commentary on Mark cited by Jerome, chapter 11: “When birds fly toward the ether, they assume the form of a cross.” Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*: “We saw the sign of the cross on a ship when it is carried along with its sails swelling.” Tertullian likewise speaks of the cross in the *Apology*, chapter 16, as does Justin in the *Dialogue with Trypho*. DUC.

### Note 287. *Sic iste pullus*

Proverbs 5:18: “The most beloved hind and the most pleasing fawn.” The Greek text which Paulinus is expressing reads:

> Ἔλαφος φιλίας, καὶ πῶλος σῶν χαρίτων, ὁμιλείτω σοι.

“Let the hind of friendship and the fawn of your graces converse with you.”

Ambrose, *On Duties* 3, chapter 1, and Jerome, *Homily 3 on the Song of Songs*, citing Origen, have: “Let the hind of friendship and the fawn of graces converse with you.”

[Col. 0921A] The word *σῶν*—“your”—is omitted, as here, in the Roman edition. Ambrose again, book 1 of *Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapter 7: “Let him cling to the most excellent, as it is written: ‘Let the stag of friendship and the colt of graces converse with you.’”

Vatablus has: “The hind of loves and the doe of grace,” that is, the wife, who is like a most pleasing hind.

Glossary: *Πῶλος* means “young horse, foal, offspring.” The Greek word *πῶλος* does indeed signify the young of a donkey, horse, or elephant, and of other four-footed animals. But if we follow the propriety of the Hebrew language and the meaning of this passage, it seems to designate a kid, not a foal. The Latin word *pullus*, although it is also used of eagles and other birds, cannot in this passage of Proverbs be understood of young birds, since the Greek word *πῶλος*, which the Latin translator renders, is not applicable to birds, whereas the Latin word can apply both to quadrupeds and to birds. DUC.

## In Poem XXV

942

### Note 288. *Juliani*

This is that Julian, son of Memorius, [Col. 0921B] whom Augustine mentions as a deacon in Letter 131 to his father Memorius; from that letter it is evident that Julian was very dear to Augustine. Later he was bishop of Campania—that is, in Campania—as the better books read, not “of Capua,” as it is found in the common text of Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45. [In the very ancient manuscript, a thousand years old, Germ. 1000, he is called neither a Campanian nor a Capuan bishop.]

He was also infected with the Pelagian error and eventually became a fierce opponent of Augustine, who answered him in various books. Prosper also attests that he lived in Campania in his poem against Augustine’s detractor:

> Either the Britons by the sea fed this man on their own grain,  
> or this Campanian’s heart swells on Campanian grass.

The common text of Prosper’s *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Festus, makes him Atellan. Atella, however, was a town of the Campanians in Italy. The oldest manuscript books instead have *Eclanensis* or *Heclanensis*. The Eclanian district is known from the book *On Boundaries*, in Calabria [Col. 0921C]—or Apulia. Bede, in his commentary on the *Song of Songs*, calls him the bishop of Celanum in Campania. In Virgil, *Aeneid* 7, Celena or Celenna is a place in Campania sacred to Juno, according to Servius. He wrote various short works, concerning which see Bede on the *Song of Songs* and Gennadius above. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 289. *Iae*

*Iae* is a woman’s proper name. Arnobius, book 5, *Against the Pagans*, concerning Ia, the bride of Atis:

> The virgin who had been his bride—Valerius the pontiff records that her name was Ia—covers the lifeless breast with softer wool, sheds tears with Agdestis, and kills herself; the blood of the murdered woman turns purple into violets.

The Roman Martyrology, 4 August: “In Persia, the holy martyrs Ia and her companions, who, together with nine thousand Christian captives, suffered martyrdom under Sapor after being afflicted with various punishments.” Justinian restored a temple that had almost collapsed from age and bore her name. Procopius, book 1, *Buildings of Justinian*. This name has remained among our people in the forms Ida, Iye, and Iyken.

Fridericus Lindebrochius, learned in many subjects, in his notes on Terence’s *Adelphoe*, cites *Titia* for *Iam*; I do not know whether from a manuscript. Our Schottus conjectured *Aetia*. [Col. 0921D] ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 290. *Pastis cumulatum crinibus*

Thus reads the Schott edition, on the basis of a manuscript. The edition of Rosweydus has *passis*, incorrectly. They do not heap the head with *passi*—that is, with loosened and scattered—hair. It should be written *pastis*, from Virgil, as Ducaeus noted on that passage, formerly numbered 13 and now 21, verse 536:

> And the Nazarene, sacred to Christ,  
> adorns his head with nourished hair.

Here too *passis* had become established in usage. Ambrose, *On Fasting*, chapter 7: “So that not one of their head-hairs should be burned, because they had nourished that hair as well.” And in Hegesippus, book 4: “To dissolve the sex by the flow of the body, to nourish the hair, to whiten the face.” Prudentius, *Peristephanon* 1: “Whether they nourished their hair long and uncut.” J. F. Gronovius, *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 10.

See Note 277.

### Note 291. *Memor*

He is now called *Memor*, now *Memorius*. Augustine’s Letter [Col. 0922A] 131 to Bishop Memorius survives, in which he also mentions Julian. He likewise mentions him in book 1 *Against Julian*, chapter 4:

> Certainly I am not forgetful of your father Memorius, of blessed memory, who had entered into no small friendship with me through literary conversation and had made you yourself exceedingly dear to me.

ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 292. *Aemilius*

Palladius mentions Bishop Aemilius in these times in his *Dialogue*, while discussing the delegation from the Roman council to Constantinople:

> After receiving the letters of the holy men Aemilius and Gaudentius, bishops, together with the presbyters Valentinian and Boniface; the letters of the emperor Honorius, Pope Innocent, and the bishops of Italy—Chromatius of Aquileia, Venerius of Milan, and the remaining bishops—together with the memorandum of the whole council of the West, they proceeded to Constantinople under public guarantees.

Metaphrastes calls this Aemilius the bishop of Beneventum. See Baronius, volume 5, under the year of Christ 405. ROSVEYDUS.

## In Poem XXVI

[Col. 0922B] 943

### Note 293. *Roscidus*

Here he calls it a “dew-bringing spirit,” because in Daniel 3:50 there is *πνεῦμα δρόσου διασυρίζον*—“a whispering wind of dew”—from Gregory Nazianzen’s *δροσερὸν νέφος*—“a dewy cloud”—in Poem 1:

> And in the Assyrian flame a dewy cloud  
> covered the three courageous youths,  
> when they stretched out their hands.

> And a dewy little cloud covered the noble youths  
> as they extended their arms upward into the Assyrian flames.

In the *Paraphrase of Psalm 136*, even the latest Cologne edition contains an egregious error:

> There, amid the Assyrian walls, the cities—

instead of “the city.” For he calls Babylon itself an Assyrian city. DUC.

### Note 294. *In quibus iste feras*

[Col. 0922C] Here too he may seem to have imitated Gregory, whose words are closely parallel, in the poem *Concerning His Own Affairs*. There he compares his sufferings with the ancient dangers of Daniel and Jonah, and then adds:

> Καὶ γὰρ δὴ θῆρές τε καὶ ἄγριον οἶδμα θαλάσσης  
> Καὶ δῆρις στονοέσσα, καὶ αἰθομένου πυρὸς ὁρμή,  
> Πάντα κακοὶ τελέθουσι βίου δηλήμονες ἄνδρες.
>
> For savage beasts, the wild surge of the sea,  
> lamentable war, and the assault of blazing fire—  
> all these are the most certain scourges  
> of a wicked man’s life.

DUC.

## In Poem XXVII

### Note 295. *Sic aeque divina*

Baronius, volume 1, under the year of Christ 58, number 42, after discussing the three feasts of Christ—the Nativity, the Epiphany, and the Ascension—which are believed to have been instituted by the apostles, although no record of their institution is found, as is found for other feasts, cites the poems of Paulinus, by which he seems to imply that these feasts were divinely instituted.

Baronius teaches that this should be understood in the following sense: God, who gave the law prescribed in the Decalogue, by which he commanded that feast days be observed, [Col. 0922D] subsequently declared those days to be the days on which he himself had bestowed certain great benefits upon the Hebrew people. He wished these benefits to be fixed in their minds by a thousand other memorials, so that their memory would not perish. But when afterward he bestowed far greater gifts upon the whole human race through his Son, sent into this world, and added immeasurable benefits, why should it not likewise be considered that he ordained that their memory should be honored with an equally solemn annual celebration?

We think no one would deny this, unless he were wholly devoid of the reason implanted in human beings by God—especially since, as has been said at greater length, those earlier events were types of what later occurred. In this way, by that very reasoning, they were foretold as being legitimate and perpetual: although the former were observed typologically and for a time, the latter would afterward, in accordance with the truth, be celebrated perpetually by all. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 296. *Grande sacramentum*

“*Sacramentum*,” says Hugo of Saint Victor, book 2 of the *Mirror of the Church*, chapter 12, “is used in two senses. Sometimes *sacramentum* means the sign of a sacred thing, as in baptism, where the outward washing signifies inward cleansing. Sometimes *sacramentum* means a sacred secret, as in the sacrament of the Incarnation and similar matters.”

[Col. 0923A] In this latter sense, the Council of Carthage I, chapter 5: “The sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation.” The Council of Carthage of the year 595: “We announce that the sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection will take place on the seventh day before the Ides of April.” Likewise Saint Jerome speaks of the sacraments of the cross, resurrection, and ascension in Letter 48 to the deacon Sabinian: “The sacrament of the creed, the sacrament of the resurrection from the dead.” Rufinus, book 1 against the same Jerome, and in his preface to Origen’s *On First Principles*: “The sacrament of the Lord’s birth.” Saint Gregory the Great, in the *Sacramentary*, part 6. See Saint Augustine, Letter 118 to Januarius. Cangius, *Latin Glossary*, volume 3, pages 659 and 663.

### Note 297. *Verba suis aliena loquens*

[Col. 0923B] He hints at one and the same speaker being understood by different people as though he were speaking in each person’s own language; on this matter the Fathers held various opinions. See Baronius, volume 1, under the year of Christ 34, number 242. ROSVEYDUS.

944

### Note 298. *Sic Deus omnisonae modulator et arbiter unus harmoniae*

Augustine likewise recognizes, in Letter 28, something like God’s perpetual song in the governance of this world:

> If a human composer of song knows what durations to assign to which notes, so that what is sung proceeds and passes most beautifully through the sounds that depart and follow one another, how much more does God permit none of the periods of time in things that are born and die—periods which, like syllables and words, belong to the parts of this age—to pass by, in this wondrous song of fleeting things, either more briefly or more protractedly than the previously known and predetermined modulation demands?

ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 299. *Adorat*

That is, “honors.” Thus below:

> And he honors the brief throne of the great confessor.

See Dungalus, page 884, where he shows from Genesis, Joshua, and the Psalms that in Sacred Scripture *adorare* is often understood as “to honor.” Hence Jerome, commenting on “Worship his footstool,” [Col. 0923C] explains:

> In Scripture, *adorare* is used in two ways: worship is spoken of as directed toward God, and *adorare* is also used in the sense of honoring.

ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 300. *Unctus adest Domini*

Here too it would have been easy to correct the text to *Unctus adest Domini*—“The Lord’s anointed is present,” that is, “the Christ of the Lord,” as the learned Cauchius also corrects it, when he adds: “Christus, accompanied by friends,” namely Nicetas, bishop of Dacia, accompanied by other priests.

For *Χριστός* in Greek means *unctus*—“anointed”—in Latin. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 28: “If, nevertheless, the name is Christ and not rather an appellation—for it signifies ‘anointed’”; and *On Baptism*, chapter 7: “Aaron was anointed by Moses, whence he is called Christ from chrism.” Jerome, on Hosea 12: “Prophets, priests, and kings were anointed with the oil of anointing.” DUC.

### Note 301. *O mihi fulminea Cherubim*

In Isaiah 6:6 the reading is *seraphim*. Therefore this appears to be a *μνημονικὸν ἁμάρτημα*—a mnemonic error. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 302. *Conceptosque Deo notat intus Ecclesia fetus*

He understands the sacrament of confirmation, in which [Col. 0923D] the forehead is marked outwardly and the soul is marked inwardly. Take this as referring to the character of confirmation; he had already spoken of baptism when he said:

> Thus, in the triune name of grace,  
> it renews sterile souls.

Likewise Prudentius, in the hymn before sleep:

> Worshiper of God, remember  
> that you have undergone  
> the holy dew  
> of the font and bath,  
> and that you have been marked  
> with chrism.

Theodoret, on Song of Songs 1:

> Those who are initiated through baptism, after renouncing Satan and confessing the faith, are anointed with the chrism of spiritual ointment as with a royal sign and mark. Under the visible appearance of the ointment they receive the invisible grace of the most holy Spirit.

ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 303. *Hinc sterilis peperit septem*

This is taken from 1 Samuel 2:5, where the Vulgate has “many,” while the Hebrew and the Septuagint have “seven.” ROSVEYDUS.

[Col. 0924A]

### Note 304. *Fulgentis solii pro limine*

*Solium* means “threshold,” especially the threshold of the confession, where those who visited the tombs of the saints out of devotion would stand. Among later Greek writers this was called *σολέα*, since the sanctuaries themselves were open only to presbyters.

Sidonius, book 4, Letter 18:

> Thus also, honoring the threshold of the beloved Felix.

Cangius, *Latin Glossary*, volume 3, page 895. See Note 319.

### Note 305. *Ecce vides quantus splendor*

The use of lamps and candles in the Church is very ancient. Lamps and circular hanging lights, as well as several circles made in the form of a crown, hung from the ceilings. They were placed one above another in stages, so that the lowest was larger than the middle one, and the middle larger than the highest; each was adorned with glass lamps. Such arrangements are elegantly described by Paulinus, *Natalis* 7. Cangius, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, page 39.

### Note 306. *Camera crispante lacunar*

Sidonius, book 2, Letter 10, concerning the church at Lyons built by Bishop [Col. 0924B] Patient:

> Within, the light gleams, and the sun,  
> so enticed toward the coffered ceiling,  
> wanders through the golden metal in matching color.  
> Marble, marked with varied brilliance,  
> runs through the chamber, the floor, and the windows,  
> and beneath its many-colored designs  
> the flowering grassy crust,  
> through green glass, bends sapphire-colored stones.

Hence comes the portico.

ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 307. *Metallo*

That is, “with marble columns.” *Metallum* means any material dug out from the earth’s interior. Thus the stone of an altar is called *metallum*. The Bertinian manuscript Pontifical, in the rite for consecrating churches, contains the following prayer concerning the altar-table or altar-stone:

> We pour forth humble prayers to you, Lord God the Father, that you may deign to enrich with the abundance of your sanctification this polished material, which is to be imbued with heavenly sacrifices; you who once wrote the law on stone [Col. 0924C] tablets.

Another prayer:

> Almighty God, rational craftsman of all things, who, forming creatures, established the stony material for the service of your sacrifice, so that an altar might be prepared for the offering of the law: graciously grant that whatever is offered and consecrated here to your name may rise up for religion, advance hope, lean upon faith, and be devoted to honor.

Thus also *metallum* is used of mineral pigments. Pliny, book 33, chapter 7. Likewise book 37, chapter 7, concerning the sard gem:

> It was first found at Sardis, but the most highly esteemed examples are found near Babylon, when certain quarries were opened, clinging to the heart of the rock.

In this way, it is said, the mineral deposits had been exhausted among the Persians. Likewise Silius, book 8, *snow-white minerals from marble*:

> Then those whom Luna drew from the snow-white marble quarries,

which in Strabo, book 5, is *μέταλλα δὲ λίθου λευκοῦ*—“quarries of white stone.”

Fortunatus, book 3, poem 25, concerning the eucharistic tower of Felix:

> Let Solomon’s temples yield to these golden materials.

Anastasius the Librarian, in his life of Sylvester: “He offered a singular cup made of coral [Col. 0924D] mineral.” In the same place: “porphyry mineral.” ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 308. *Didymus cognomine*

A *cognomen* properly means a family or clan name added to a praenomen or personal name. Here, however, it signifies merely a name, as though he were saying that the Apostle had a double name. Yet, as far as Scripture establishes, he was called Thomas in Hebrew; among the Greeks this word is rendered *Δίδυμος*, and both signify “twin,” as in Genesis 25:24:

> Καὶ τῇδε ἦν δίδυμα ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ—“And she had twins in her womb.”

And Genesis 38:27.

Theophylact, on John 20:24, teaches that *Thomas* is the interpretation of the name when it says:

> Εἶπεν οὖν Θωμᾶς ὁ λεγόμενος Δίδυμος—“Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said.”

For just as we interpret *Cephas* as “Peter,” so Thomas is also interpreted—namely, when translated, it means “Didymus.”

Leontius observes that the Evangelist translated the name of no apostle except Thomas. Euthymius says that he was called Thomas because he was [Col. 0925A] born together with another brother. Maldonatus, however, rightly warns that this was not necessary, since it could have been customary in his family, just as the cognomens *Gemini* occur among the Roman families Rubellia and Fusia. In the same way, the Romans were called *Spurii* and *Fusci*, although they were neither dark in complexion nor illegitimate by birth.

Thus, finally, in John 5:2: “A pool which is called Bethesda”—*Κολυμβήθρα ἡ ἐπιλεγομένη βηθεσδά*, that is, “which is called Bethesda”; and Romans 11:17: *Σὺ Ἰουδαῖος ἐπονομάζῃ*—“You are called a Jew.” The translator of the Vulgate rendered it, “You are named a Jew.” DUC.

### Note 309. *Chalcidicis*

*Chalcidicum* here means *Chalcedonian*, so that you do not err. Euphemia suffered martyrdom at Chalcedon in Bithynia, not at Chalcis in Euboea. Stephen does indeed testify that *Chalcidium* is formed from Chalcis among the Greeks, just as *Chalcedonium* is formed from Chalcedon. Paulinus, however, formed *Chalcidicum* from the river Chalcis, which gave its name to Chalcedon, according to the same Stephen.

Sidonius does the same in poem 2 of his *Panegyric on Anthemius*, [Col. 0925B] speaking of Byzantium, toward which the east wind blows from nearby Chalcedon:

> The nearby trumpet gradually moderates the blast of the Chalcidian east wind.

Other Latin writers do the same, including Jerome, the translator of Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, and Cassiodorus in the *Fasti*. They call Apollonius the Stoic *Chalcidicus*, whom Capitolinus, in his life of Marcus, and Eutropius, book 8, call *Chalcedonius*.

Our Sirmondus, in his notes on Sidonius’ *Panegyric*, advises that *Calchidicum*, not *Chalcidicum*, should be written. He wishes to support this from the oldest copies of the ecumenical synod, in which it is called not *Chalcedonensis* but *Chalchedonensis*, and also from ancient coins, which, he says, never represent it otherwise.

But all the ancient writers defend the spelling received up to the present, and Stephen expressly does so under *Καρχηδών*. Nor should the ancient copies be allowed to carry much weight, since it is certain that many names containing *h* are written in different ways and that the *h* is often transposed. Thus, even in the oldest [Col. 0925C] copies, one finds *Chartago* for *Carthago*, *Phyton* for *Python*, *Cherintus* for *Cerinthus*, and likewise *cheruci* for *ceruchi*.

Nor can any certain argument be drawn from coins, since their spellings too vary. In the *Treasury of Antiquities* of Hubertus Goltzius, on a coin of Sabina Tranquillina, one finds *ΧΑΛΚΗΔΩΝΙΩΝ*; on another coin, *ΧΑΛΚΕΔΩΝΩΝ*; and on a coin of Annia Faustina, *ΚΑΛΚΗΔΩΝΩΝ*. In Goltzius’ *Greece*, the form *ΧΑΛΚΗΔΟΝΩΝ* appears on two coins. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 310. *Corpora transfixos trabalibus inclita clavis*

A *trabale* is a piece of wood that passes through wheels. Thus Cicero, *Against Verres* 5, said “to fasten with a beam-sized nail.” The *Life of Saints Ferreolus and Ferrutio*: “Into the heads of the blessed martyrs beam-sized nails [lacuna] were driven with iron hammers.” Cangius, *Latin Glossary*, volume 3, page 1158.

946

### Note 311. *Mare*

[Col. 0925D] “The sea of the holy table” means nothing other than a receptacle for water, or a hollow in the table shaped like a sea (*θάλασσα*). Such a basin used to be constructed around altars for washing the victims among the Jews, as in 1 Kings 18 and 2 Chronicles 4:6. Cangius, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book 3.

### Note 312. *Liminibus*

Writers frequently use this word when speaking of sacred buildings or of those who travel to sacred buildings as a matter of devotion. Paulinus below:

> Depart, serpent,  
> from the sacred thresholds.

Hence the familiar expression “to go to the thresholds of the saints,” or “to visit them,” used by writers when speaking of those who undertake pilgrimages to the tombs or memorials of the saints.

Since the relics and bodies of the saints were placed within apses or bemata, in the confessiones—that is, beneath the altars themselves—and since only presbyters were permitted to enter the bema, from which the Latins called it the *presbyterium*, the faithful stood at the thresholds, or in the *solea* of the bema, and there fulfilled their prayers and vows.

Pope Nicholas I, Letter 8:

> So many [Col. 0926A] thousands of people, hastening from every part of the world to the protection and intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, wear themselves out daily and intend to remain at his thresholds until the end of their lives.

And so throughout the works of Victor III, *Dialogues* 3; Leo of Ostia, book 3, chapter 49; and others. In these places, *limina* means the sacred building itself—that is, the part stands for the whole.

Nevertheless, some maintain that *limina* should be understood as the first portico of the building, or even the doors themselves. Pilgrims stood there, since they approached the martyrs with such reverence that they were afraid to enter the sacred building itself and considered themselves unworthy. Paulinus, *Natalis* 6, verses 442 and 444:

> Standing in the midst of the thresholds,  
> he reports his vows.

Sometimes, moreover, they kissed the doors [Col. 0926B] themselves. Thus, in Chrysostom, *Homily on the Epistle to the Corinthians*: “to kiss the fore-doors of the temple”; in Arator, book 2 of his *Sacred History*; and in Paulinus, *Natalis* 6, “to plant kisses on the doors.” Prudentius, hymns 2 and 11, speaks of kissing the thresholds of apostles and martyrs. Finally, Gregory of Tours, book 4 of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 14, speaks of kissing the thresholds of Saint Martin.

Paulinus, in the passage just cited:

> He lies prostrate before the doors,  
> spread out upon the ground.

Cangius, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book 3, pages 64–65.

### Note 313. *Mensa Petri recipit, quod Petri dogma refutat?*

Thus Cauchius conjectured that it should be read. Previously it was *Mensque Petri*. He understands “table” as the altar, as in the following verse:

> One chalice of the Lord everywhere, and one food, and one  
> table and house of God.

Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2: *Τὴν ἱερὰν ἀσπασάμενος τράπεζαν*—“after kissing the sacred [Col. 0926C] table,” that is, the altar. In former times, altars used to be placed upon or beside the bodies of martyrs.

Prudentius, hymn 11, *On the Crowns*, concerning the tomb and altar of Saint Hippolytus:

> Beneath such coverings the body of Hippolytus is entrusted,  
> beside which an ark dedicated to God has been placed.  
> That table, giver of the sacrament, and likewise  
> faithful guardian, has been placed beside its martyr.

Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 3:

> The Roman bishop therefore acts wrongly, who offers sacrifices to the Lord over the bones of the dead Peter and Paul—bones venerable to us, but, according to you, mere worthless dust—and considers their tombs to be the altars of Christ.

Nevertheless, *Mensque Petri* could be retained, so that it would mean that the mind or soul of Peter does not receive or admit these banquets, which his teaching condemned. ROSVEYDUS.

Concerning this same abuse, Augustine, then a presbyter, wrote to Alypius, bishop of Thagaste, in the year 395. The letter appeared for the first time in the new edition of Saint Augustine as Letter 29. He relates how, after various exhortations, he finally persuaded the Catholics of Hippo to abhor the luxurious banquets which it had been customary to celebrate in the African churches on the feast days of the saints.

There survives a canon of the Council of Hippo, held in 393, inserted into the Third Council of Carthage: [Col. 0926D] 947

> Let no bishops or clerics feast in the church . . . The people also should, as far as possible, be prohibited from such banquets.

This canon was issued, certainly through the efforts of Augustine, then a presbyter. For shortly beforehand he had urged Aurelius of Carthage, in Letter 22, to confront by every means this evil, which had long been spreading throughout Africa; and he had suggested that it could not be removed except by the authority of a council. The Benedictine Fathers, in their note on Letter 29 of Saint Augustine.

Augustine explains there how these practices had arisen in the Church, Letter 29, section 9:

> After so many [Col. 0927A] and such severe persecutions, when peace had been established and crowds of pagans wishing to enter the Christian name were hindered because they were accustomed to spend their feast days with their idols in abundant feasting and drunkenness, and could not easily abstain from these most destructive and deeply rooted pleasures, it seemed to our predecessors that this weakness should for the time being be spared, and that, after the feast days they were abandoning, other days should be celebrated in honor of the holy martyrs—not with similar sacrilege, though with similar luxury. Once they had been bound to the name of Christ and subjected to the yoke of such great authority, the saving commands of sobriety could be delivered to them, commands which they would no longer dare resist because of the honor and fear owed to the one who commanded them. Therefore the time had come for those who did not dare deny that they were Christians to begin living according to Christ’s will, so that, once they were Christians, they would reject those things which had been permitted to them so that they might become Christians.

For this same reason, Gregory Thaumaturgus, according to the account of his life by Gregory of Nyssa, instituted feast days in honor of the holy martyrs and allowed the faithful to rejoice at them.

Gregory I, pope, was led by the same policy to recommend the following to Mellitus, abbot traveling to Britain, in book 9 of the *Register*, Letter 71: [Col. 0927B]

> And because they are accustomed to kill many oxen in sacrifice to demons, this observance too ought to be transformed for them, so that on the day of the dedication or on the feast days of the holy martyrs . . . they may celebrate the solemnity with religious banquets . . . so that, while some outward joys are reserved for them, they may more easily consent to inward joys.

But Saint Augustine praises Saint Ambrose in book 6 of the *Confessions*, chapter 2, because at Milan he forbade food to be brought to the memorials of the saints, so that no opportunity for drunken gluttony might be given, and because such practices were almost identical with the pagan ancestral rites. The Reverend Benedictine Fathers.

See Ambrose, *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapter 17, and Augustine, *Sermons on Various Subjects* 5 and 101.

### Note 314. *Aquae caecator Amalec*

He touches upon the history related in Genesis 26:14:

> The Philistines, out of envy, stopped up all the wells which the servants of his father Abraham had dug at that time, filling them with earth.

The Septuagint said *ἐνέφραξαν φρέατα*—“they blocked up the wells.” Paulinus uses the verb “to blind,” just as among the Greeks one speaks of *τυφλὴ πίδαξ*—“a spring that does not appear”—and of [Col. 0927C] *τυφλούμεναι πηγαί*, “springs that become blind” and are obscured, or dry up, or seek other channels beneath the earth.

Ovid, *Epistles from Pontus* 4, elegy 2:

> Surely, just as mud blinds the veins amid the waters.

But Scripture says that Isaac suffered this injury while he was staying with Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar—not that he was harassed by the Amalekites, who lived far from the borders of the Philistines.

For Josephus, *Antiquities* 3, chapter 2, says:

> Οἱ τὴν Γοβολίτιν καὶ τὴν Πέτραν κατοικοῦντες καλοῦνται Ἀμαληκῖται.

“Those who inhabit the region of Gobolitis and the city of Petra are called Amalekites.”

Therefore the Amalekites were inhabitants of Arabia Petraea, or lower Idumaea. Hence Jerome, in the *Hebrew Traditions* on 2 Kings:

> Amalekite and Idumaean are one and the same.

DUC.

## In Poem XXVIII

[Col. 0927D]

### Note 315. *Istic porticibus late circumdata longis*

The spaces between the columns of these porticoes were generally secured with railings and parapets, against which one could lean and look out into the atrium. Paulinus:

> But to walk about within the surrounding porticoes.

The Romans called such atria *paradisi*; the Gauls called them *parvis*. Writers commonly use this word, taken from the Greek *παράδεισος*. It is a place enclosed by porticoes in which people take walks. Cangius, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, page 20.

### Note 316. *Impluvio*

Cauchius had restored this word in the margin of his book. I do not know whether from conjecture or from a printed book. Previously it read *in clivo*, which I prefer to retain until something more certain is established by the evidence of manuscripts. ROSVEYDUS.

See Note 167.

### Note 317. *Trinaque cancellis currentibus ostia pandat*

Access from the nave to the bema was open through three doors set in the railings: a large or central door, and two smaller ones on either side. Greek writers commonly call such doors of the bema *ἁγίαι θύραι*, “holy doors.” Cangius, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book 3, chapter 3, page 63.

[Col. 0928A] 948

### Note 318. *Agmina concharum*

A *concha* is a vessel suited for holding horses. Eucherius, in his commentary on the Book of Kings: “Troughs, basins, or water jars.” The *Martyrdom of the Four Crowned Martyrs*: “They began, in the name of Christ, to hollow out basins, fountains, and couches, with seals and cups, with great delicacy of craftsmanship.”

Anastasius, in his life of Leo III, concerning the Lateran Patriarchium:

> In that place he also placed couches, and in the middle a porphyry basin pouring forth water.

By *couches* I understand the railings and barriers constructed all around, against which people leaned, as Paulinus says here:

> But to walk about within the surrounding porticoes.  
> There is abundant space, and, with railings placed between the columns,  
> to lean upon them when weary, and from there  
> to watch the games flowing past.

ROSVEYDUS. See Note 320.

### Note 319. *Vicit brevis astula flammam*

Paulinus uses this word frequently. In Letter 11: “And in an almost atom-sized [Col. 0928B] fragment, a small splinter.” In Letter 12: “A small splinter as a pledge.” Most writers spell it *hastula*, as though it were a diminutive of *hasta*, “spear”; but it should be written *astula*.

Isidore, book 17 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 6:

> *Astula* is named from *tollere*, “to remove,” as if it were *abstula*. A *fomes* is a splinter, which is shaken from trees by cutting, or a charred splinter, or a piece hollowed from wood. It received its name from fungi because it catches fire in this way.

Concerning this Virgil says: “And he snatched up the flame in the tinder.” This is almost certainly taken from Servius Danielis on *Aeneid* 1 and should be compared with him.

The same author, book 19 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19:

> *Ascia*, “axe,” is named from *astulae*, the pieces which it removes from wood.

The Spaniards today call those pieces which the Greeks call *κάρφη* “astillas.” Other authors use *assula*, perhaps from *absilire*, “to leap away,” when material is cut.

Pliny, book 16, chapter 11:

> Raw resin, torn off in many thin and short splinters, is cut into pieces small enough for a sieve.

The same author, book 29, chapter 2:

> Others light the sapwood after placing splinters of torch-pine beneath it and layering them between the pieces, sprinkling them with oil.

Vitruvius, book 7, chapter 6:

> Marble fragments, or *assulae*, are what marble-workers remove from their works.

Festus:
