> *Fomites* are *assulae*, shaken from trees while they are being cut.

[Col. 0928C] This almost reproduces Isidore above; hence it is evident that in Festus *astulae* was formerly read for *assulae*.

From *assula*, Pliny, book 22, chapter 22, forms *assulose*:

> The better reed is the less brittle one, which breaks more in splintered fashion than in the manner of a radish.

Plautus uses *assulatim* in *The Captives* and *The Two Menaechmuses*, as does Naevius. See Nonius. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 320. “The recessed cell, far away,” etc.

Among learned writers there is no agreement at all about what the *concha* was. The *concha bematis*, or the principal part of that portion of the church in which the sacred rites are performed, was apparently this: from several ground plans reproduced by Goar, pp. 13, 26, and 27, one can see in the part where the altar stands, or is intended to stand, several recesses shaped like semicylinders and closed above—at least, as one must reasonably believe—in the form of a shell or apse.

In most churches the *concha* was constructed in such a way that, although only one shell appeared above, it nevertheless covered three recesses and consequently formed a triple *concha*, as the Silentiary observes in part 1, verse 272. There he sufficiently shows that below, or under the curvature of the shell, there were three conches contained and covered by a single quarter-sphere. Paulinus has finely described these three recesses in *Natalis* 10:

> There is also . . . .

And in Epistle 32 to Severus:

> The view of the basilica . . . receives those who pray.

The *concha*, therefore, had a triple recess beneath the same vaulted covering: the larger central one, in which were the sacred table and the seat of the priests, or *synthronus*; and two other smaller ones, one on the right, or northern, side, which they called the *prothesis*, and the other on the left, or southern, side, called the *diaconicon*. Salmasius indeed wishes the *trichora apsis* mentioned by Paulinus to have received its name from this triple *concha*. CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book III, p. 44.

See Notes 150 and 159.

### Note 321. “Beautiful with its starry dome.”

A *tholus* is a rounded structure, compactly formed in the manner of a sphere. Greek writers commonly call this a θόλος (*tholos*). In Isidore and Papias, *tholus* is a prominent rounded elevation and summit of a temple. For Ugution, however, *tholus* properly means something like a short cupola, situated in the middle of a roof, where the beams meet. Some also call it a *trullus*. CANGIUS, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, p. 29.

### Note 322. “Then also, when it shall be given,” etc.

Paulinus admirably begins to transfer the material structure of the temple to the structure and adornment of the spiritual temple. A certain panegyrist had preceded him in this, in a speech which he delivered at the dedication of the temple of Tyre, built under Paulinus, bishop of that city—not so much restored as newly constructed on a larger scale. From this, as Baronius observes, one may understand that in the year of Christ 314 the structures of churches were customarily erected by the ancients not carelessly or without spiritual interpretation, but with the greatest religious devotion: every part of the structure was intended to signify something mystical. Indeed, even the thrones and benches, and the windows of the temple itself, represented something divine, their places being arranged and beautifully ordered according to the dignity of each.

Certainly, anyone who compares these two temples, the Nolan and the Tyrian, will find great similarity between them, and will see that both were constructed in emulation of Solomon’s temple. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 323. “Who devours the Ethiopian.”

Here too the author departs somewhat from the meaning of Scripture when he says that the dragon devours Ethiopians, whereas in Psalm 73:14 David says the opposite: “You crushed the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians.” Some understand this passage literally, taking it to mean that the corpses of the Egyptians, together with their prince Pharaoh, were cast upon the Ethiopian shore of Africa. Pharaoh, therefore, is that dragon given as food to the Ethiopians.

But our author says that the dragon devours peoples of spiritual Ethiopians—that is, those who have been scorched and darkened by the heat of their vices. Cyril of Alexandria embraces both interpretations in his commentary on Hosea, chapter 8:

> “For those who have within themselves a mind exceedingly black and deprived of light may rightly be understood and called Ethiopians, both by us and by God. These feed the many-headed dragon, and they themselves in turn are fed by him.”

DUC.

## IN POEM XXX

### Note 324. “Antioch and Ostia for Luke.”

It is strange that Paulinus asserts that Luke’s relics were preserved at Antioch and Ostia, since the Roman Martyrology says on 9 May that his relics were transferred from Achaea to Constantinople; this is also demonstrated elsewhere in the following note. On 18 October, moreover, the same Martyrology says that the bones of Saint Luke were transferred from Constantinople to Padua.

Unless Paulinus merely means that Antioch and Ostia possessed an outstanding disseminator of the Gospel in Luke, perhaps they had obtained some of his relics from elsewhere. Pope Gregory too, when he was serving as a deacon and legate at Constantinople, obtained from the emperor Tiberius the arm of Saint Luke. Baronius, year 586. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 325. “For Constantine,” etc.

What Paulinus says here about the relics of Andrew and Timothy being transferred to Constantinople by Constantine is also found in Jerome’s work *Against Vigilantius*, where he joins Luke to them:

> “Was Constantine the emperor sacrilegious, because he transferred the holy relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy to Constantinople?”

It is nevertheless strange that Jerome himself and all the other authors attribute the transfer of these relics to Constantius. Jerome, in his addition to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, under the nineteenth year of Constantius: “The relics of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople.” Again, under the twentieth year of the same emperor, when Constantius entered Rome: “The bones of the apostle Andrew and of Luke the evangelist were received by the people of Constantinople with extraordinary enthusiasm.”

The oldest manuscripts also assign this transfer to that year, including the Amandine manuscript, written in capitals—not to the twenty-first year, as Scaliger stated. Jerome likewise says in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, concerning Luke:

> “He was buried at Constantinople, to which city, in the twentieth year of Constantine, his bones were transferred from Achaea together with the relics of the apostle Andrew.”

Ado, in his *Book of the Feasts of the Apostles*, under 24 January, after discussing Timothy’s feast day:

> “His body was transferred to Constantinople, together with the relics of Blessed Andrew and Luke, in the twentieth year of Constantius.”

The *Menaea* likewise refer the transfer of these relics to Constantius: on 30 November, in the office of Andrew, and on 18 October, in that of Luke.

Could Constantine have intended to do what his son Constantius later completed? Certainly, he had built the Church of the Apostles for that purpose. Socrates, book I, chapter 26:

> “He was placed in the church named after the Apostles, which he had built for this very reason, so that emperors and priests might not be deprived of the relics of the Apostles.”

See Baronius on the Roman Martyrology, 9 May. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 326. “Alpha likewise, and Omega, are Christ to me.”

Revelation 1:8: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord.” And chapter 22:13: “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”

Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book I, chapter 6:

> “Rightly does the Lord again promise milk to the righteous, so that the Word may plainly be shown to be both Alpha and Omega, beginning and end.”

That is: “Rightly does the Lord promise milk to the righteous, so that it may clearly be shown that the Word is both Alpha and Omega, beginning and end.”

Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, chapter 5:

> “The Lord has taken upon himself the two letters of Greece, the first and the last, the figures of beginning and end meeting in him. Just as Alpha rolls onward to Omega, and Omega folds back again toward Alpha, so he showed that in himself there is both the course of the beginning toward the end and the return of the end toward the beginning; so that the whole order of things, ending in him through whom it began—namely, through the Word of God, who was made flesh—should end in the same way as it began.”

Isidore copies this in *Etymologies*, book I, chapter 3. Epiphanius, in the *Ancoratus*, derives from it the twofold nature of Christ. Origen does the same in volume I of his commentary on John.

Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 9:

> Born from the Father’s heart before the beginning of the world,  
> He is called Alpha and Omega, himself the source and close  
> Of all things that are, that were, and that afterward shall be.

Various coins of the emperors are found inscribed with Alpha and Omega. See our Gretzer, volume III, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 9, concerning Constantius; chapter 10, concerning Magnentius and Decentius; and chapter 11, concerning Jovian. See also Lipsius, *On the Cross*, book III, chapter 15, concerning Decentius. See also our Gretzer, volume III, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 30.

Taking these letters as their starting point, the heretics Marcus and Colarbasus constructed their heresy from the Greek alphabet. Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 50:

> “After these there were also a certain Marcus and Colarbasus, who composed a new heresy from the Greek alphabet. For they deny that the truth can be found without these letters; indeed, they say that the whole fullness and perfection of truth is arranged in these letters. For this reason, they claim, Christ said, ‘I am Alpha and Omega.’”

Hence, on a coin of the Basilidians mentioned by Duke Arschoianus, appears the inscription “Alphaeto,” that is, Alpha and Omega. For formerly Omega was also written with the Ionic omicron, as is clear from Scaliger, p. 102, *Annotations on the Greek of Eusebius’s Chronicle*. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 327. “And he fixed the banner of the cross above all the stars.”

It is strange how the banner of the cross could be fixed above all the stars. Most of the Fathers, from Matthew 24, assert that the sign of the cross will appear in heaven on the day of judgment: “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” But it is uncertain whether this sign is to be formed from the air, or whether it will be the very cross on which Christ hung.

Saint Paulinus seems to favor the latter opinion, and Chrysostom agrees with him in his homily *On the Cross and the Robber*:

> “Do you wish to learn how the cross is a sign and symbol of the kingdom, and how venerable the thing is? He did not leave it alone upon the earth, but led it up into heaven. How is this evident? It will come with him at his second and glorious coming.”

Our Gretzer, book I of *On the Cross*, chapter 92, believes that Chrysostom regarded as already accomplished something that was at some time to occur. Certainly, since Chrysostom and Paulinus in other passages speak of the cross as existing on earth, one must say, according to the opinion of both Paulinus and Chrysostom, that what had already been eternally destined is described as having taken place; otherwise one would have to admit a new repetition of the cross by miracle.

That the cross itself of Christ will appear in heaven, as I have stated, on the day of judgment is attested by many writers. The Sibyl, book VI of the *Oracles*:

> O blessed wood on which God himself was stretched,  
> The earth shall not contain you, but you shall behold the dwelling of heaven,  
> When the renewed, fiery face of God shall flash.

Ephraem, sermon *On the Cross*:

> “The cross itself will again be the first to appear at Christ’s second coming, as the precious, venerable, and holy scepter of Christ the King, according to the word of the Lord, who said: ‘The sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.’”

That is:

> “This cross will appear again in heaven at the Lord’s second coming, first of all, as the precious, venerable, and holy scepter of Christ the King, according to the Lord’s saying: ‘The sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.’”

Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 13, appears to hold the same opinion. For, when delivering his catechesis at Jerusalem in the presence of the cross, or trophy, of Jesus the Savior, he says:

> “This will appear again from heaven together with Jesus; for the King’s trophy will go before him.”

That is:

> “This will appear again in heaven with Jesus; for the King’s trophy will precede him.”

Because of the passage of Chrysostom already cited, Thomas Waldensis adopted this opinion in volume III, *On the Sacraments*, title 20, chapter 158. He thought that Isaiah 65:22 referred to it: “According to the days of the tree shall be the days of my people,” as though the elect were to be gathered when the wood of the cross had been lifted into heaven. But interpreters assign another meaning to that passage.

Our Franciscus Suárez, in the third part of Thomas Aquinas, question 59, article 6, disputation 57, section 2, reports that some writers, in addition to the privilege by which Christ’s own cross will appear in heaven on the day of judgment, add that it will be preserved perpetually in heaven and granted incorruption, like glorified bodies, because in a special manner it was the instrument of our redemption and the altar on which Christ sacrificed himself. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 328. “To you, venerable cross of God.”

The heretics are wrong to dislike the custom of the ancient Church of saluting, addressing, and adoring the cross. Greek and Latin Fathers frequently used similar expressions.

Ambrose, *Oration at the Funeral of Theodosius*:

> “Helena approaches Golgotha and says: ‘Behold the place of the battle; where is the victory? I seek the banner of salvation and do not find it. I,’ she says, ‘am in royal palaces, while the cross of the Lord lies in the dust. I am in halls, while that triumph of Christ still lies hidden among the ruins. Does the palm of eternal life still lie hidden? How can I think myself redeemed if redemption itself cannot be seen? Let the earth be opened, so that salvation may shine forth.’”

In the Greek *Menologion*, under 13 September, on the eve of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, there are splendid praises of the cross, in which the cross is greeted and adored:

> “Hail, life-bearing cross, unconquerable trophy of piety, gate of paradise, support of the faithful.”

Augustine explains how such expressions are to be understood in *Tractate 1 on John*:

> “We do indeed call the wood life, but in the understood sense, the wood of the cross from which we received life.”

The scholastics warn that these expressions are to be understood tropically or relationally. ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM XXXI

### Note 329. “Concerning the Goths,” etc.

Dungalus cites this nativity poem with that inscription. This victory, sent from heaven, occurred in the year of Christ 406, the fifth year of Pope Innocent and the twelfth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, when Rhadagaisus, king of the Goths, invaded all Italy with two hundred thousand of his people, as Marcellinus records in his *Chronicle*.

But, terrified by divine intervention, he was defeated and captured without a battle, so that the captive Goths were sold like the most worthless beasts, as Orosius reports in book VII, chapter 37. Augustine also mentions this victory in *The City of God*, book V, chapter 23, and in sermon 29 on Luke. ROSVEYDUS.

## IN POEM XXXV

### Note 330. “That, inexperienced in years and new, he might go to the waters.”

“To go” (*ire*) signifies “to die” when used of secular learning. Papinius Statius, *Silvae*, book I, poem 2, the *Epicedion for Glaucia*:

> We shall all go.

Statius:

> We shall go; Aeacus shakes the urn amid the immeasurable shades.

BARTHIUS, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 14, and book XLIII, chapter 3.

### Note 331. “I rejoice that he has died . . . in an age.”

Among Christians, *seclum* does not always designate a fixed number of years, but also the span of someone’s life. Everything here is excellent, and the passage could be punctuated as follows:

> I rejoice that he has died, having completed his mortal life in a brief age.

“I rejoice that he has died in an age,” because he now lives in heaven. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 14.

### Note 332. “To undergo mortal things and to enjoy.”

“With an uncommon usage.” The first expression is Lucretian, *On the Nature of Things*, book III:

> And the mind undergoes many evils from its contact with it.

The second occurs in a fragment of Lucan cited by Lutatius:

> The Theban Alcmena, whom the ruler of Olympus enjoyed.

BARTHIUS, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 14.

### Note 333. “Doing all things as man.”

This is a Greek usage, and one owed to Virgil: *cuncta*, meaning “with respect to all things.” Our own Paulinus, in verse 83 of this panegyric:

> He willingly obeyed, God being in all things harmonious with the Father.

The only distinction is that *cuncta* should be separated as *per cuncta*—“through all things.” Everyone can see the order of the passage in this interpretation. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 14.

### Note 334. “Without the law of faith.”

So reads the old manuscript; previously it had read *sine lege fideli* (“without the faithful law”), as it does frequently elsewhere. The second syllable is long, not short, as it has wrongly been printed until now, in the following line:

> Or the Father receives him in the nurturing lap of faith.

For, as Cauchius testifies, the old book gives the line differently:

> Or he cherishes him, received into Abraham’s bosom.

Or *Abramian*, as earlier:

> Whom you, rival of Abraham’s love, [cherish].

The following passage should likewise be corrected:

> For Christ is the end of the law, foretold by the law of faith.

And again:

> Prescribing for the ancient law an end and the law of faith.

And in *Natalis* 5:

> He scattered them in triumph with helmet and shield of faith.

And in poem 5, *On Saint John*:

> The mother listens to her newborn; such is the power of faith.

These lines escaped the excessively diligent hands of the correctors. DUC.

**“Without the law of faith.”** Badius, Gravius, Grinaeus, Poelmannus, and Schottus corrupted this genuine reading when they replaced it with:

> And the human race everywhere without the faithful law.

In the same *Panegyric*, verse 351, in place of:

> Prescribing for the ancient law an end and the law of faith,

they substituted:

> Prescribing for the ancient faith the law and the measure.

It is characteristic of Paulinus and of the most ancient Christian poets to lengthen the middle syllable of *fidei*. Some, not understanding this, often altered passages recklessly and corrupted them against the evidence of manuscript copies. This has happened in very many places throughout the works of our Paulinus.

Thus, in the ode to Nicetas, where the best manuscripts, the Regius and the German, read at verse 50:

> When a pious part of holy faith was in the world,

some printed editions substituted:

> When a fortunate pious part of faith was in the world.

In *Natalis* 4 of Saint Felix, verse 67, two German manuscripts and the edition of Rosveydus read:

> *Prodidit, ut nobis esset pia vena fidei* — “He revealed it, that for us there might be a pious vein of faith.”

For this Badius, Gravius, Grinaeus, and Poelmannus substituted:

> *Prodidit, ut fidei nobis esset pia vena* — “He revealed it, that for faith there might be for us a pious vein.”

And at verse 127:

> *Fidei quoque solus* — “faith too alone,”

in place of *solusque fidei* (“and faith alone”), as the two German manuscripts and the edition of Rosveydus prefer.

Likewise, at verse 129, in place of *Tantum quia causa fidei* (“only because [it is] the cause of faith”), they substituted *Fidei tantum quia causa* (“because [it is] only the cause of faith”).

In *Natalis* 5, verse 45:

> He strengthened [it] by love of faith,

the two German manuscripts and the edition of Rosveydus read this way, whereas Badius and Gravius substituted:

> He strengthened faith by love.

Bede cites a similar example from the same Paulinus:

> He scattered them in triumph with helmet and shield of faith.

This is verse 125. The line is read this way in *Natalis* 5 of Saint Felix, in two German manuscripts, and in the editions of Rosveydus and Schottus in the margin. In other copies it is corrupted and appears as:

> He scattered them in triumph with the helmet of faith and also the shield.

Likewise, in *Natalis* 8 of Saint Felix, verse 106:

> *Virtute fidei / Fortior Ezechias* — “Hezekiah was stronger by the power of faith.”

Thus it is read in the German manuscript and in the editions of Grinaeus and Rosveydus, and in Schottus’s margin. Others altered it to:

> *Fideique vigore / Fortior Ezechias* — “Hezekiah was stronger by faith’s vigor.”

And at verse 285, in place of *Simul atque fidei* (“and at the same time as faith”), Badius, Gravius, and Schottus substituted *Fideique probatae* (“and of tested faith”).

Moreover, in poem 6, *On the Praises of Saint John the Baptist*, verse 143, Paulinus lengthens the middle syllable in the word *fidei*:

> The mother listens to her newborn; such is the power of faith.

Certainly, so many examples show that this was peculiar to the poets themselves. Fabricius also touched on the matter in passing in his commentary on the Christian poets.

### Note 335. “See how no seeds rise in their fields unless they first perish, dissolved in rotting decay.”

The ancient Christian philosophers demonstrated the resurrection of the dead by comparison with seeds, from whose putrefaction new grains arise, as can be seen in Aeneas of Gaza, *Theophrastus*. The following lines of Tertullian, book II *Against Marcion*, point to the same idea:

> In the grain the tree lies hidden; but unless, buried in the earth,  
> It decays, it does not produce fruits adorned upon the tree.

Barthius thinks the passage should be emended:

> Unless it yields its fruit in rotting decay, it does not produce fruits destined to adorn the tree.

The same Tertullian, in *On the Judgment of the Lord*:

> Thus dry seeds are restored to the empty earth,  
> And, fixed deeply in the furrows, decay in death.  
> Is the stalk not thereby given life again, with ears restored?

BARTHIUS, *Adversaria*, book XXXV, chapter 18.

Prudentius discusses the resurrection of the dead by comparison with seeds of the earth in book II *Against Symmachus*, verses 306 and following.

### Note 336. “You cast bare seeds, clothed fields, dry grains.”

A field is called “clothed” when it contains crops, and the term is opposed to “bare” or “uncultivated.” Charter of King Conrad, year 967, in John Columbus, book II *On the Bishops of Sisteron*, no. 3:

> Everything, in cultivated and uncultivated places, in clothed and deserted lands, in things sought and to be sought, etc.

Another document from the same year, in the cartulary of the Abbey of Beaulieu in Limousin, no. 68:

> Namely, our estate called Candidas, with its occupied and soon-to-be-occupied holdings, fields, meadows, etc.

Another from the year 1298, in the *History of Guînes*, p. 128:

> A certain land covered with woodland, in a place called, etc.

CANGIUS, *Latin Glossary*, volume III, p. 1291.

### Note 337. “Poor in Abraham.”

Thus the old book gives the true reading, whereas previously it had *Abrahamo*. Likewise in *Natalis* 9:

> Whom pious Abraham, holy Isaac, and gentle Jacob [receive].

And in *Natalis* 4:

> Thus Father Abraham, following the commands of the Lord.

Sidonius Apollinaris, book VII, letter 7:

> Abraham, rightly to be joined with the holy patrons.

And again:

> Abraham already has you as a fellow pilgrim.

DUC.

### Note 338. “And he will be food for his own worms.”

The future worms of hell are mentioned in Isaiah 66:24: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.” Ecclesiasticus 7:19: “The vengeance of the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worms.” Judith 16:21: “For he will give fire and worms into their flesh, so that they may burn and feel it forever.” Mark 9:43: “Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.”

Most interpreters take fire literally but the worm figuratively, as the dissection of the conscience. But what prevents both from being understood literally, with actual worms existing in hell? Basil, commenting on Psalm 33:12 and discussing the punishments to come in the abyss, says:

> “Then there will be a kind of poisonous and flesh-eating worm, eating without satiety and never being filled.”

That is:

> “A poisonous and carnivorous species of innumerable worms, always eating but never satisfying itself.”

Augustine, *City of God*, book XXI, chapter 9:

> “It is written in the ancient Scriptures: ‘The vengeance of the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worm.’ It could have been said more briefly, ‘The vengeance of the ungodly.’ Why, then, was it said, ‘of the flesh of the ungodly,’ unless because both fire and worm will be punishment of the flesh?”

Prosper, book III *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 12, is cited by Father Cornelius on Isaiah in support of this opinion, because he speaks of being torn apart forever by devouring worms and never coming to an end. Yet that passage seems to be understood of the worm of conscience, since he had prefaced it by saying: “and the worm of consuming conscience gnaws immortally.”

Ribera, commenting on Revelation 19, since Scripture frequently mentions sulfur and joins it with eternal fire, thinks that sulfur too should be understood literally, just as fire is. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 339. “Joined by the burial-bond to the martyrs who are near.”

He means the martyrs Justus and Pastor, whose memory is celebrated at Complutum, where he had committed his little son to the earth. Prudentius mentions them in hymn 4, *Peristephanon*:

> The blood of Justus, to whom Pastor clings,  
> A double offering and a twofold gift,  
> Will gladly carry to Complutum’s embrace  
> The bodies of the two.

A church had also been erected for them two miles below Terranum in Lusitania. Its inscription can be seen among the Christian monuments in Gruter, p. 1053, no. 2. Their feast day is assigned in ecclesiastical calendars to 6 August. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 340. “That from the neighboring blood of the saints.”

It was a religious practice among the ancients to seek a place of burial near the memorials of martyrs, so that the dead might be helped by their patronage.

Augustine, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 4:

> “I do not see what assistance there is for the dead in arranging that their bodies be buried near the memorial of the saints, except that, when people remember where the bodies of those they love have been laid, they may commend them in prayer to those same saints, as patrons, to be helped by the Lord.”

Constantine wished to be buried in the Church of the Apostles, which he had built at Constantinople, among the twelve shrines of the Apostles:

> “With extraordinary eagerness of faith he took thought that, after death, his body might share in the appellation of the Apostles, so that, when dead, he might also be deemed worthy to participate in the prayers that were to be offered there in honor of the Apostles.”

He adds:

> “Believing that the memory of these men would bring his soul the most beneficial assistance.”

There is no doubt that those shrines were ennobled by the relics of the Apostles. For Socrates relates in book I, at the end, that this church was built by Constantine for the Apostles so that emperors would not at some time be deprived of their relics. Later kings considered it a great favor if they were buried even before the doors of the Church of the Apostles.

Chrysostom, in the homily *That Christ Is God*:

> “At Constantinople too, our kings thought it a great favor, not to be buried near the Apostles, but even to have their bodies buried outside their vestibules, so that kings might become doorkeepers of the fishermen.”

James, a disciple of Maron, collected various relics of holy martyrs, according to Theodoret, *Philotheus*, chapter 21, so that he might be buried among them, like a poor and wandering man among wealthy merchants.

Among Gruter’s inscriptions, in the Christian epigrams, especially those of the city of Rome, p. 1167, no. 2, there is an epitaph of Satyrus, buried in the church of Saint Nazarius beside the martyr, composed by his brother Ambrose:

> To Uranias Satyrus, his brother Ambrose  
> Paid the final honor at the martyr’s left.  
> This is the reward of merit: that the moisture  
> Of sacred blood, penetrating nearby, may wash  
> The remains laid beside it.

In the same author’s *Christian Monuments*, p. 1055, no. 6, there is an epitaph of Marcellina, found at Milan in the church of Saint Ambrose:

> When life released your limbs, Marcellina,  
> You rejected joining your body to ancestral tombs,  
> While you hoped for the pious fellowship of your brother’s sleep  
> And desired to rest, beloved, in the earth of the saints.

And on p. 1170, no. 2, among the sacred epigrams, especially those of the city of Rome, there is an epitaph of the presbyter Silvius in the city of Jureia:

> Silvius rests in this tomb, commending through grace  
> Soul and body to the Lord’s martyrs for their protection.

Likewise, on p. 1167, no. 4, the epitaph of Marina:

> A tomb wholly adjoining the remains of the saints  
> Was deserved by Marina, worthy of the sacred ground.

On p. 1169, no. 7, the epitaph of the presbyter Sarmata in the city of Vercellae:

> Learn, you who read, that by divine gift  
> The reward of merit is given: to him whom God grants  
> A dwelling near the holy martyrs, a welcome bed.  
> Sarmata earned this by his revered priesthood;  
> Here he passed seven times ten years of bodily life,  
> Living in Christ, with the place’s help.  
> For blessed Nazarius and Victor alike  
> Make him safe at their sides and crown him with their merits.  
> O happy man, who deserved, with two martyrs as guides,  
> To be led to the Lord by the better way  
> And to earn his rest.

I have brought forward all these examples all the more willingly so that our heterodox opponents may see what the ancient Christians understood by the merits of the saints. ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 341. “Bind the infants with pure intercessions.”

* Suffragium* with its second syllable shortened also occurs elsewhere. In the sacred epigrams of the city of Rome in Gruter, p. 1166, no. 2, in the epitaph of Pope Boniface:

> These are the pious intercessions of the blessed.

Paulinus, poem 13, verse 293:

> These things now, interceding through his letters.

ROSVEYDUS.

### Note 342. “We shall be able to live in the lofty place.”

The editions read *possimus* (“we may be able”). Cauchius gives the ancient reading from a manuscript: “We shall be able to live in the lofty place.” This is confirmed by the correction of another passage near the end of the *Propempticon* to Nicetas:

> And wherever you strive, we shall be your companions.

And again:

> Now we may hate those roads,

in place of *licet execremur* (“although we may curse them”). Tertullian uses the same construction in book II *Against Marcion*:

> Thus you will be able to see what the true Passover is.

Catullus, addressing Lesbia, in an archaic construction:

> Then, when we have made many thousands.

Ennius, quoted by Cicero in *On Duties*:

> I ask neither gold nor a price; you will not have given me one.

DUC. Add *noverimus* (“we may know”), with its third syllable lengthened, in Prudentius’s preface to the *Psychomachia*, verse 58.

## In the Year of Our Lord 426

# Claudius Marius Victor, or Victorinus

## Notice

*(From Gennadius, Catalogue of Illustrious Men.)*

Victorinus, a rhetorician of Massilia, composed a commentary on Genesis in the person of his son Ethereus—or Etherius—covering the book from its beginning through the death of the patriarch Abraham. He published four books in verse, with a Christian and pious interpretation; but, being a man occupied with secular literature and trained in the divine Scriptures under no teacher, he fashioned interpretations of rather slight weight. He died while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning.

Honorius discusses him further in his *Catalogue*. Among more recent writers, Sixtus, Eisingrenius, Possevinus, and others report that he flourished under Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian III.

# Three Books of the Commentaries of Claudius Marius Victor on Genesis

## Preface to God Almighty

Most high and holy God, source of every virtue,

almighty, whom it is not permitted for human minds to comprehend through subtle investigation of things, yet whom it is impious not to know—for by profound reasoning we believe that you are God in three persons, yet three in such a way that one substance makes the three persons, preserving, through a pious bond, their undivided covenant—

you are without beginning and, equally, everlasting without end. You alone are, and are the same, subject to no age.

You surpass the extent of things, however far the mind’s retreat may stretch; no extent confines you. There is no place capable of containing you, for you are boundless.

Indeed, it is forbidden for the human mind even to attain to what your image is, unseen by the eyes, unless by a special divine power you show yourself to someone for contemplation. Nor is there any created force by which you are animated or moved, through which we exist and move.

You are mind and the innermost substance of sacred mind; you are reason and the wise source of complete reason. You are virtue, the summit of virtue, and truly life itself, the author of life and of deep light.

You are the true light, God; you are the cause and strength of things. Whatever suddenly sprang forth from nothing drew its beginning from you. Filled by so great an author, it either possesses the power of mind or has received form in limbs.

Nature, preserved among mortal fathers, proves you Lord, and the order that has been given acknowledges the sequence you commanded.

You distinguish teachable numbers, balance weights, vary measures and rhythms, and govern motion. You command the alternating changes and constant return of things to remain, and the world to roll through ages already known to you, full of the image of the mind.

You are not content to endow created things with a single gift; whatever you do, you bestow for varied purposes. Indeed, you accomplish everything for a reason, benevolent God, although the reason and manner of your works are unknown to us.

Those things which the clever idleness of the human mind considers contrary, while they contend with one another, possess greater peace. Thus you, rich Creator, join together even elements related through opposition, and fill them with the powers poured forth from you.

And yet, although these things belong to the majesty of creation, you lack none of what you bring forth. You are wholly in need of nothing belonging to the completed world, which remains stable through your ordered structure of things.

Nor does your glory consist only in this: that as a good author you accomplish what ought to be accomplished; it also consists in the fact that you do not disdain to enable secondary causes to accomplish what they can.

Whoever recognizes these things as your gifts is himself also your gift, so that humanity alone may rightly and must refer all things back to you alone.

For the sole reason why you commanded all things to be created for yourself was goodness. When you first commanded the spirits to live and to enjoy the world that you held in mind, and granted them to recognize in you the causes of all things, you gave them leave to fly above the earth and waters.

You assigned the heavens as a settled dwelling for some, and bestowed free hearts and control of themselves upon all, so that they might be able to turn themselves in either direction, whichever they wished.

You would thus grant inheritance to the just and rewards to the righteous, and you would also confer this distinction: that you should become a debtor.

For when one of those first created in the heavenly dwelling—while he envied the Lord of his light and life, his own creator, and coveted that title—preferred to become the author of evil and to introduce the first death, he was cast down from lofty heaven with his companions in crime; yet this did not prejudice your virtue.

Your virtue is satisfied with having made what is good. Yet this is the summit of your praise: although it was a crime and a great sacrilege to exalt oneself above the power of the divine summit, and although no completely indelible flood could erase it, you nevertheless did not deny life and sensation to the ungrateful.

Indeed, you granted them also the joy of the mind’s free choice.

Nor should we accuse the nature of free choice, which is powerful in either direction. For the possibility of destruction was given to all so that life might be sweeter, and so that the mutual balance of alternating danger might yield to merit, when a punishment worthy of stern judgment doubled the rewards of the saints.

Moreover, if I may say this while preserving reverence for you, Father, perhaps in your sight not to have sinned through life’s slippery course is a greater good than to have sinned is an evil for the wretched. But how this stands you will see; we entrust all causes to you alone.

Meanwhile, it is enough for us that, while you breathe sacred reason into the lowly burdens of earth, shape them by your virtue, and fashion them in your likeness, you make them nobler.

You raised humanity, with its countenance turned broadly toward the stars; yet the cruel deceit of the tyrant dragged it into the snares of death and impious Tartarus. You redeemed it by the poured-out blood of your only-begotten Son.

And from the lowest wilderness you restore, to greater gifts, one who had sought them, greater than he had been made; you return him to everlasting life and to heaven, after the ancient enemy has been overcome.

Let no one now recklessly accuse Father Adam because, by loosening the slight restraint through violation of the commandment, he opened the path to death. The parent’s fault has been sufficiently compensated, because conquering death is greater than never having known how to die.

Now, joyful from the hall of heaven, he looks down upon the heavenly axes and treads upon the stars. He calls his descendants, already appointed for the coming kingdom—those whom the rich wisdom of the eternal Father formed again through water and taught to be born again.

I pray to you, benevolent God, who by your gracious divine power grant minds the ability to perceive, and to you, most beloved of the Father—
Son born of the Father, pour your honey-sweet word into our hearts,  
and infuse our tongues with eloquence,  
while we prepare to shape tender minds and hearts  
toward the path of true virtue in their childhood years.

Now open the renowned archives of Moses, the lawgiver:  
what is the origin of heaven, what the beginnings of the world;  
[Col. 0939B] what shook secret faith throughout the whole world,  
by what force the plague, grown strong, gained power in uncertain minds,  
and how ancient customs gave way to vice.

Grant, O God, that I may describe the mysteries of eternal life;  
grant also understanding, grant fitting times for understanding,  
grant diligence, lest care fail such a great labor,  
and grant good success to the study which surpasses all prayers by right  
(the mind of the writer is pure),  
lest you condemn the gift which I, now guilty, dare to offer,  
but look mercifully upon my crimes and spare me in your kindness.

And if the order should have erred against the law of meter,  
if unsuitable speech should have erred, or wavering meaning,  
let no measure of faith thereby suffer harm.

Through the Lord Christ, who, born with you,  
lives in the same majesty,  
as likewise the gracious Spirit, incomprehensible to minds,  
lives through the ages of the ages.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0939]

Before the heavens, before the day of heaven and the darkness of the world,  
before the forms of works, and things, and the seeds of things,  
there exists an eternal Being without past and without end of the future.  
With him there was always the one God,  
with whom the begotten Word, God, lived,  
and likewise the gracious Spirit, the sum of hidden vital power.

The Three, whom concordant substance, joining them in a supreme bond,  
blessed eternally with supreme power,  
reigned in the majesty of creation;  
already seeing things, the causes of things, and future events,  
and perceiving with capacious mind the ages,  
and whatever the times roll onward,  
always holding the present:

[Col. 0939C] His own kingdom was the immense realm of blessed substance;  
nor did his kingdom lack a witness—  
the triune God, who, first giving bodies to things without seed,  
while compelling things to exist,  
made our gift from what he alone possessed.

And when his rich wisdom made this world,  
he brought forth everything at once;  
but afterward adorned the shapeless seeds of things  
with forms superimposed upon them,  
and, with a well-ordered arrangement, brought the times into sequence.

For it was not—as the tongue of sacrilegious madness has believed—  
that a mindless accident, turning ignorant seeds,  
twisted together so prudent a work;  
nor is it lawful to say that it was made before the age,  
since things born in time are moved by time.

Nor is it lawful to believe that the world is eternal  
and coeval with the heavenly powers,  
or that it has always possessed enduring strength:  
for whatever consists of bodies must be confessed to have begun.

[Col. 0939D] A body that blows wear away,  
that time dissolves and destroys,  
and that stretches toward its ultimate end  
reveals a beginning.  
Whatever things are shown to have received such a fate  
must either be believed to have been made  
or be judged to have been born.

Therefore it is established that the world was made—  
a conclusion to which everyone submits  
and which, convinced by the true doctrine, believes,  
acknowledging that God made it:  
he, powerful through the divine Word and through power,  
arranged, commanded, and set in motion whatever is thought to be nature,  
and sustains the created gift through successive revolutions,  
always restoring what is fleeting,  
and drawing back and turning the swift-moving orb.

If he should also wish to dissolve everything suddenly,  
[Col. 0940B] he will immediately restore it to similar forms.

So great is the Father’s power, and so great the glory of the Word.

To touch once upon the beginnings of things:  
the vaulted heights of heaven and the earth lying below  
were the first part of the work.  
But water covered the earth,  
and the air in the midst was wet with a foul cloud,  
while the vast abyss cloaked itself in black darkness.  
And the sacred Spirit, hanging over the outspread waters,  
gave life to the nourishing waters  
and supplied the seeds of things, not yet arranged,  
to be poured forth into the earth for germination.  
Then light, sent from above, flashed forth when God spoke,  
and, drawing back its black veil,  
the shadow departed from the highest Olympus.

[Col. 0940C] Then divine wisdom called the light “day,”  
and gave the darkness the name of obscure “night.”  
Thus the wet day was made from morning and evening, the first.

Again, a new morning, after the first evening had been driven away,  
restored the light.  
Then the most solid mass, withdrawing from the midst of the waves  
with a body made firm,  
rose up and, solidified far and wide by rigid hardness,  
suspended the divided waters  
and set the cold deep against the fiery axes.  
Relying upon the sea enclosed around it,  
it spread above the things which, in a vast circuit,  
the ethereal region covers;  
from this name it was called “heaven.”

Perhaps someone might argue with learned error:  
“Will there not be nourishment for the ethereal flames?  
And will not excessive heat, descending toward the depths  
and following its nourishment, burn up mortal humanity?  
Will not earthly things endure the flashing heaven?”  
The firm structure of the heavens is set below,  
and, while it protects us with its shadow,  
it is cooled by the waters placed above it.

But let our mind flee far from seeking the causes  
of the divine will.  
Let it be enough for you always to believe  
that God can do whatever is thought impossible,  
and that the great sea can be carried above the stars and constellations.  
Prove this by the reasoning of those themselves  
who refuse to believe it,  
yet wish the world to hang there,  
borne by the Creator himself,  
and to revolve, sustained by its immense weight.

The third light was astonished when the swollen waves withdrew,  
as God, having driven back the remaining waters,  
[Col. 0941A] opened a great emptiness through the airy spaces.  
Then, for the first time, the lowest part of the world, the dry land,  
revealed its uncovered face;  
and, shaken by the power of the Word,  
the blue waters encircled the bared lands.

These lands, commanded to bear varied fruit,  
were swiftly covered by luxuriant new growths rising from the mud.  
The forest, rough yet springing from tender turf,  
displayed its joyful foliage;  
each tree and green herb produced its own appearance,  
and the earth was clothed with fruit and seed and grass.

When three days had passed, the first day of the sun,  
set alight by rapid motion,  
was commanded to gather itself into flames and a globe of fire.  
The seeds of light, established there,  
scattered their purple locks with rosy fuel.

And the moon, the glory of night,  
shining with a borrowed light,  
hung beneath the sun in a lower course,  
reflecting the rays it had received from him.

The stars, painting heaven with distinct zones,  
were astonished as the blue night  
caused them to flash varied colors  
with ethereal flowers,  
and to shine more brightly amid its adorned darkness,  
while dark shafts of flame glimmered with ruddy fire.  
The new stars eagerly pressed onward in their courses,  
whose open rays cover the sun’s radiance,  
measuring the four seasons of the divided year.

The sun also, although the moon’s course is monthly,  
completes the turning year in a single course,  
and by its wondrous structure bears witness to the sacred Artificer.

The fifth day stirred breathing creatures in the sea.  
The moisture that wets the sea brought them forth  
and scattered delights throughout the deep,  
which nature fashioned in wondrous ways  
with varied growth, being commanded  
to draw forms and parts from the whole empty body.

It also gave life to brute shapes,  
and produced the vast whales that lift their rough backs  
through the swell of the salt sea,  
filled with soft fat.  
The same fluid preserves their bodies,  
and itself nourishes the offspring of our bodies  
and the growths of the earth.

From this source the gentle race of birds also drew their vigor.  
While it fashioned the liquid waters  
and life entered the sea,  
the swollen waters seethed with abundant birth.  
Nor was it enough that every kind of fish should rise,  
and that the scaly throng should emerge from the brine  
into the upper waves,  
unless, flying through the waters, it should gradually swim  
in the pure ether,  
[Col. 0941D] taught to reach the ethereal retreats as a winged creature.

Therefore birds and fish have one material.

Now the sixth day had shone upon bright Olympus,  
the third after the generative gifts of the warm sea.  
The earth, now warm, had loosened its pregnant limbs,  
when God, bringing forth greater works, commanded the earth  
to produce every animal which the principle of motion alone animates,  
to which it was given to serve according to the needs of things.

There was no delay: living pledges burst forth from the fertile earth,  
each taking on the forms of its own kind.

Here it is now lawful for me to touch upon some matters,  
to pass deeply and anxiously over others in hurried course,  
and to report certain things transmitted in altered sequence.

After the appointed order had produced all things according to their kinds,  
full of the blessings of spring and richly endowed,  
which God would cherish so that they might endure through a long succession,  
the structure appeared exceedingly beautiful to its Author.

But what would the world be—what would the stars, their rising,  
the ether, the glassy sea, and the green earth be—  
if there were no spectator whom the glory of so great a mass might fill  
and lead with eager eyes through each of its parts?

What purpose would such broad boundaries and such extensive possession serve  
if the possessor of things were absent?  
The Ruler of Olympus revolved this in his mind  
and weighed it by the power of the Word.  
He established the sum of the work:  
all things he had created were good.

“Now let us make humanity,” he said,  
“to rule in the world and to be the image of God.  
It is fitting that the creature resemble its Creator,  
free in its will,  
enjoying with its mind the things that have been created.”

[Col. 0942B] He had spoken, and the human being was made—  
whether in the whole body,  
or in soul and form,  
perhaps according to the manner of future things,  
by which he makes what is to be made,  
and by which he always held what was made,  
even though the past age had not yet arrived.

Therefore he commanded this being, set over created things,  
to grow with a spouse through offspring  
and to fill the vacant lands.

Then nature, once granted to created things,  
especially to those which life appears to animate by movement,  
multiplied whatever had first been produced in its forms.

When the seventh light saw that the great Parent had ceased,  
and that he had only finished creating the number of species,  
and had kept his rest,  
then it was rightly consecrated,  
because it saw the completed work.  
For this too is full of power:  
that God ceased and laid down his labors.

[Col. 0942C] For the Son, having fashioned the Father’s form  
which the right hand had prepared,  
was sufficient for the Lord to complete in six days.

The seventh light taught examples of venerable rest,  
which we are all commanded to hope for in the heavenly court,  
provided that the good works of the righteous are not lacking.

This light also signifies the day on which Christ  
released the underworld  
and, having conquered, opened a return from Avernus,  
while he, victorious and destined to return once to the Father’s court,  
now rests in human flesh, free from evils.

Thus God knows how to cease,  
thus he knows how to take leisure—  
ceasing in order to do more,  
resting without end and likewise working without end,  
mixing sequence and time.  
By ceasing, he completes whatever work he had created.

But what sort of material God used,  
and in what manner he formed Adam,  
it is lawful to take up briefly here with Moses.

[Col. 0942D] Humanity, first in merit but last in the whole order,  
was made so that it might know itself superior to created things  
and therefore render fitting praises to the Lord.

Accordingly, the excellent hand of the supreme God,  
when it made humanity,  
took clay easy to handle,  
well suited to yield,  
and to follow the shape and form into which the art directed it.  
It unfolded into visible form the human figure  
which it already held in mind.  
Then, when life was breathed into it as vapor,  
the breath moistened the earth;  
the soil, softened by the fluid,  
was changed into flesh,  
and the blood, that slippery liquid,  
filled the soft veins through their familiar channels.

Then, once full of mind, the human being,  
leaving the earth, sprang up  
and, wise in reason, worshiped the Lord.

In the same way, when Christ’s majesty descends  
through the open heaven,  
it will cause bodies, commanded to rise from opened tombs,  
to spring forth,  
and they will worship the Lord of earth and heaven.

For what the body did not possess when it was compacted  
from poor dust into honored human form,  
it will be very easy for God to restore whole again from dust—  
what the earth has already held, engraved, for many years.

Thus, commanded to rise from ancient tombs,  
the bodies will each take up their own parts again.  
Thus nothing of the past exists that is not a form of the future.

But now it is time to reveal the dwelling and habitation  
of the first human being,  
where the whole wound was received as a seed.

The fortunate earth opens its eastern recesses;  
on a higher globe, the paradise of a pleasant grove is disclosed  
[Col. 0943B] and marked out in ordered ranks of smooth forest.

Here, where the boundary of the sun is already distinguished  
by equal spaces,  
and eternal spring moderates equal hours,  
each tree stands rich in its own fruits,  
and ripened fruits are driven forth by succeeding fruits.  
Pleasant for feasts and full of wondrous vigor,  
they nourish limbs and souls,  
and feed them with taste and fragrance.

Here the earth flashes with varied colors,  
always leafy with new blossom and fresh fruit.  
Here fragile stalks release their scents,  
animated by the vigor of an ambrosial gift,  
and cinnamon breathes its fragrance.

Nor should you think that everything fragrant among the Medes,  
or everything that the Achaemenian land exhales  
with loosened hair,  
or everything with which the Assyrian, rich in soft amomum,  
is fragrant,  
or the Mareotic harvest, red with nard,  
or the shrubs of Tartessus,  
or the branch of Saba,  
or the Palestinian branch that weeps from a wounded bark—  
that all these were separately gathered into this garden.

For here God brought together everything which nature,  
having received each thing in its particular place,  
had distributed separately.

And while a gentle breeze moves through the grove  
with soft motion,  
it mingles into one nectar the fragrances from different sources,  
and a new gift is formed,  
which no single tree can claim as its own.

And wherever the trembling grove is gently shaken  
by a pleasing rustle,  
the whole forest trembles with stirred leaves;  
the trees resound,  
and the breeze, singing in measured tones,  
whistles out hymns to God.  
Nor does an empty motion beat the air with a vain sound.

For in the presence of the Author,  
who holds the whole mass under one structure,  
binding things to things and retaining them by alternating law,  
it is not right to believe that anything happens by chance or in vain.

[Col. 0943D] Indeed, the beautiful grove and the glittering forests  
are proofs of his works,  
and nurseries of created things.

Nor is it doubtful that, before the first parent’s sin,  
the following likewise fixed their tents there with him:  
glory, simplicity, devotion, wisdom,  
the steadfast goddess Truth, prudence, grace, honor, and salvation,  
the noble affections of the soul, renowned virtue,  
and whatever beauty the world possesses.

Why should I wish, in a few words,  
to enumerate so many gifts?

This alone is sufficient for faith:  
that, rising here from blessed seed,  
the tree of life reaches the air with lofty fruits;  
while elsewhere harmful knowledge, with a different fruit,  
hangs knowledge of things from the tree of law.

At the lap of the sacred grove, which the forest crowns,  
a spring gushes forth,  
and, rich in power, joins itself to a fruitful offspring,  
dividing its swollen head into a fourfold stream.  
It is richer than Ocean:  
for Ocean, flowing in its perpetual flood, gives its waters,  
while this receives them all and yet does not swell.  
The lesser stream is the one less able to grow  
from waters poured into it  
than the one unable to diminish from waters poured forth.

Of these, in the first order, Phison leaps forth exultantly,  
the fourth part of the blessed spring,  
bringing forth the gifts of nature  
which wisdom grants.  
It fills the peoples of the Ganges  
and stretches through the Indian kingdoms,  
rolling mud and seeds,  
sowing the fields it makes,  
where the bare sands bristle amid the glittering fragments  
of shining gold.

Here the carbuncle glows with lightning-like fire,  
and the emerald shines radiant with green light.

[Col. 0944B] No less is Geon,  
but gentler in its peaceful waters.  
It raises the waters of the Nile  
and widely covers the parched fields with a blessed flood,  
tempering, in opposition to the sky,  
the waters that flow back through the pools of Ethiopia.

From here the third river, the Tigris,  
runs through a swift current.  
It comes together with the Euphrates,  
and the earth, overcome by their rushing mass,  
absorbs them into an opened hollow chasm,  
until it vomits forth the rivers into the hills of Armenia  
and the Median Tempe—  
places which it could not sustain and can no longer contain.

But the Tigris, as though indignant at the black Avernus,  
springs forth beneath the ethereal airs with greater force.  
Then it enters its caves again;  
submerged in caverns, it drives its roar within,  
and, made stronger by the barrier,  
multiplies its waters.  
Swifter from the dark cavern,  
it emerges and cuts through the Assyrian fields  
in a rapid course.

[Col. 0944C] More justly, the Euphrates,  
generous in its rich flood,  
waters the parched fields of the Persian land below.  
Drawn out through gentle streams,  
it serves everyone equally  
and gives itself wholly for human use.  
At last, exhausted of waters,  
it expends even its own name upon the lands—  
a name which it owed to the waters of the sea.

This, then, the first possession of the first human being:  
a dominion rich in every fruit of nature,  
and delights filled with so great a wealth of powers.

Brought into it, the inhabitant was commanded  
to exult in everlasting life.  
Placed amid such delights  
and the richly fertile Tempe,  
while he was still becoming worthy  
and learning to earn his reward by labor,  
he lived free from sorrow and ignorant of care.

So great is the Author’s judgment:  
that the highest name of merit is  
not yet to have deserved any evil.

What, then, do we suppose the Father could pay back  
when the times of life should return—  
the Father whose pure generosity toward his servants  
was already paradise, not a wage?  
And when he received the decree of the strict law  
and was about to test the danger of freedom,  
he received life by obeying the command.

He who establishes a cause according to merits  
still promises greater things to the good  
and preserves rewards.  
He said:

“Eat from all the trees,  
but remember to fear this one alone,  
which bears beneath its bark  
the storehouse of different things  
and holds the knowledge of right and wrong.  
For savage and dreadful death will follow transgressors.”

Given such a law, sound reason teaches  
that God did not make the mortal human being  
in the beginning with death as an original condition,  
unless the human being brought death upon himself voluntarily.

For even in this there is great indulgence  
from the supreme God:  
what he grants to his servants,  
not on the basis of merit but solely from generous will,  
he wishes to be the result of our labor,  
and prefers to appear to owe what he gives.

But you, whom the guardianship of sacred law binds,  
do not complain that, within narrow limits,  
your permission is partly deprived of its own scope.  
Nothing has been cut away from you by this law.

Before, you had received power only over the earth and sea;  
now you also possess the kingdom of life everlasting  
and, further, death.

Then, so that the inexperienced inhabitant of the world  
might believe that everything obeyed him,  
God summoned every animal  
which the earth, commanded to create,  
had already produced by pouring forth silent seed  
from its flowering body,  
and ordered it to appear and obey its own tyrant.

The purpose was plainly that he should give fitting names  
to all things  
and call each created thing by its own name,  
according to the nature that had arisen by its own movement.

There was no delay.  
Nature, not ignorant of obedience, brought forth every kind of living creature.  
Animals came together from every part of the new world  
at that brief moment of time,  
whether they were slow with gentle steps,  
most ready with rapid running,  
accustomed to glide through the air in sudden flight,  
to swim through the waves,  
or to move with slippery weight.

When these had been summoned by almighty God  
in Adam’s presence,  
he generously endowed each with its own gift  
and armed it with hand, horn, foot, tooth, poison,  
and other defenses,  
so that an animal lacking skill, inferior in mind,  
and devoid of reason might protect itself  
and preserve itself from adverse things.

But no living creature flourished  
with a form, face, and bearing equal to humanity.

Rather, God added to the human being  
almost divine honors.  
Among so many creatures whose lives were adorned  
by the double distinction of sex,  
he alone was incomplete,  
and for a long time, unaware,  
possessed within himself the suitable material  
for producing a spouse.

Therefore God undertook the familiar work.  
He struck the man’s heart  
and swiftly dissolved his limbs in such deep sleep  
that, while he was without awareness,  
he could remove one rib.

The flesh was then commanded to follow:  
with the skin withdrawing of its own accord,  
it made a smooth path for the departing rib,  
while the limbs remained entirely unharmed  
and the body sound.

When God had arranged the rib through the various limbs,  
it received a form,  
and, given life through its warm marrow,  
was changed into the work of life,  
now pleasing as the second sex.

Thus Eve, formed, was entrusted to her husband.

Now, most foolish crowd, cease at last  
to torment your mind with empty questions,  
and do not ask why woman was fashioned  
from the limbs of a human being,  
when she could have been formed from soft dust  
in the beginning, even from nothing.  
Cease searching out hidden causes.

Yet, if conjecture is permitted,  
woman was made from man  
so that there might be a certain kinship,  
and so that mutual and reciprocal love might mingle them,  
each compelling the other to recognize itself  
in the other’s limbs.

Thus Adam immediately understood  
that Eve was part of him.  
As he touched her, a new grace filled his exultant mind;  
his affection rushed into his familiar flesh  
and penetrated his bones with such warmth  
that he now recognized what a spouse and wife were,  
what sweet children were,  
why parents must be placed after spouses,  
and what it meant for two people  
to remain together in one flesh  
while living an equally eternal life.

Moreover, while they were free from the world’s vices and stain,  
strong in divine minds and lacking nothing,  
while the substance of the world and all the wealth  
which the earth bestowed were in their possession,  
and while they bore bodies entirely free from disease,  
hunger, ignorant of pause, did not compel them to eat.  
If they had preserved the commands of the supreme God intact,  
they would never have known the cruel authority of death  
or the dreadful pains of death.

But the crafty serpent, intending to break the Lord’s law,  
persuaded Eve, off her guard, with such deceits:

“O race of human beings, deprived of a better life  
and ignorant of good things!  
For one who is ignorant of evil  
cannot be thought to know good,  
since such a person does not even know  
by what boundary good things differ from one another.

And therefore God did not wish it to be lawful  
for humanity to pluck the august fruits,  
lest, with the cloud removed from the mind,  
they should lift their eyes to heaven,  
know the highest things,  
and become like the gods.”

Here it may be permitted to digress a little  
and lament the shameful ruins of former times.

Ah, how wretched are the gentiles,  
whom madness drove into various rites,  
to invent many names for gods  
and to add a plural voice to the one God.

The serpent’s impious voice first uttered this claim—  
the serpent who then became the cause of death.  
After credulous Eve broke the commandment  
with sacrilegious bites,  
she, now taught by experience and acquainted with evil,  
sought a companion in guilt.  
Poorly aware of the deception,  
she sought her unwary husband  
by the art through which she herself had perished.

Thus, overcome by the enemy in both,  
wretched Adam yielded to sin.  
He tasted the fruits, filled with the sacred juice,  
but because the commands of the severe law  
were contained in them,  
they would bring death more surely  
than viperous poison.

As soon as they violated their mouths  
with the forbidden taste,  
they immediately felt the crime.  
The deed grew before them  
and struck their breasts with unwonted awareness.

From this arose fear; from that, shame—  
their first beginnings.

For while human beings, conscious of lofty things,  
carried hearts intent only on heaven and righteousness  
and turned their breasts toward the exalted Father,  
while they discerned the wonders of divine secrets  
with the bright splendor of incorporeal mind,  
they had not yet experienced concern for their limbs.

But when that everlasting vigor left them,  
and they were touched by death,  
then cold and heat entered upon their aerial alternations.  
The human beings first felt themselves without clothing,  
and secretly blushed at their sex,  
silently lamenting their misery.

Therefore, after their guilt,  
they plucked new coverings from the leaves of the shady fig tree  
and wove garments,  
that, with the body clothed, they might conceal the shame  
which their minds had received.

Nor was this enough.  
They did not know what they were doing,  
nor how to flee the crime branded upon them  
and themselves.  
If it had been possible, they would have wished  
to hide themselves in the abyss.  
So closely does their guilt border upon punishment  
that now the image of mortal death,  
which they feared in their misery,  
pleased them.  
They hid behind forests and shadowy groves,  
offering themselves false comfort in empty darkness.

But where can you lawfully withdraw  
your frightened body?

You yourself, I say, whom the living power of the Father,  
the most hidden presence of the world,  
created from lowly dust,  
fill and pervade,  
extending into the innermost recesses.

Can you flee from the Lord and escape?  
Did you hope to hide from the One who sees everything,  
so that you might lie concealed in vast darkness?  
You will never be hidden.

Therefore, when the shame born of sin  
had touched Adam as he sought hiding places,  
he soon heard:

“Hey! Where are you, Adam?”

What does it mean that God asks for you?  
Is he ignorant, or does he perhaps ask whether you are there?  
You cannot withdraw from the supreme Lord—  
not even death can do so,  
the death which you entered through a fragile mind.

Why does he ask where you are,  
unless it is because he confesses  
that you, having fallen by your own will  
through the grief of death,  
are no longer with him,  
and that you have fallen from sacred heaven?

But the holy Father’s piety forbids despair.  
His mercy—for it is lawful for me to say this,  
and may it also be lawful to approve what I have said—  
surpasses justice.  
He does not so much terrify me  
by the severe voice with which he asks where I am  
and questions what I seek in my trembling breast  
as restore me,  
because, although I have fallen after my crimes  
and am immersed in fear, hidden and almost buried,  
he summons and recalls me.

And, so that examples need not be sought farther away,  
he displays the gentleness of forgiveness toward guilt.

After the cause had been shaken out  
and had exposed the guilty parents,  
heaven, sea, and earth began to tremble  
as God spoke,  
and, shaken, opened their vast recesses.

While the sentence punished the guilty,  
it built Tartarus.

“Since it has seemed right to us  
that you have departed from our commands,  
now a just judgment shall strike new offenders.

“First, among all the living things of the world,  
you shall be accursed,  
O serpent, more wicked than the envious mind you conceal within,  
who cast down the human beings created to enter heaven  
and, by your deceit, drove them to touch forbidden fruits;  
you are the hard source of death.

“Therefore, so that a punishment worthy of the crime  
may follow in due measure,  
since you plunged humanity into the earth,  
you shall lie stretched upon the unjust ground  
and furrow the hard earth with your breast.

“And because you made them attempt forbidden food,  
you shall always eat the wretched entrails of the earth.

“And because you were pleased to be the first inventor of death,  
worthy of that punishment,  
you shall die in everlasting death.

“Upon you in particular, and upon all your kind,  
you shall experience the hatred of the human race  
in mighty war.

“I shall give perpetual fear of you, as death is prolonged for you.  
You shall crawl upon your feet  
and with your breast prone.

“And the woman shall destroy you with her offspring.  
You shall lie in wait only for her heels,  
while she, trembling, shall also set her steps upon your head.”

He spoke, and then began in this way against bloodless Eve:

“And you, who were not content to destroy yourself  
by a small fruit,  
but recklessly drew your husband into similar ventures,  
shall be like a servant,  
subject to your husband's harsh rule  
and experiencing his authority;  
you shall endure labor.

“And because you first dared to multiply the offense,  
you shall always be tossed among many misfortunes.

“Then, in childbirth, you shall be tortured  
by repeated offspring,  
so that those whom your guilt causes to be born mortal  
may sometimes be the cause of a mother’s grievous death.

“And you also, who dared to place my warnings  
and the first bonds of salvation after feminine deceit,  
and who willingly chose to die,  
receive as a guilty person the following fate:

“Let the earth which you shall furrow with the plow  
be accursed because of your crimes.  
Let it bear thorns and threatening thistles  
among cultivated fields,  
and let wicked hope deceive your desire.

“Let the earth no longer keep faith with you.  
You refused of your own will  
to live joyfully amid these delights  
and to live through all ages.  
Now live by harsh labor;  
live forever in misery,  
until slow old age restores you to the earth  
and hides you again in the earth.”

He spoke, and, pitying them lest the violence of heaven  
should harm them in their ignorance,  
he clothed them in the skins of animals  
and taught them to preserve their lives.  
And, so that Adam would not again attempt similar things,  
he struck him with the fear of death.

But lest they prolong everlasting life  
from the life-giving tree,  
and lest more severe punishments await the wretched guilty,  
as they passed too long a time amid such dangers  
and remained subject to dreadful penalties,  
winds immediately expelled those commanded to depart from the sacred light.  
The forest of the deep grove stirred those winds,  
and the air, carrying them bound  
in a balanced whirlwind,  
drove them away from the seat of sacred paradise.

Therefore, expelled from there and returned to the earth,  
the young pair, dismissed into the lost light,  
sighed for the joys they had lost.  
They were deprived of so vast a space,  
deprived of its dangers,  
but not deprived of the grief  
that agitates their hearts.

They pondered in sorrow where they had fallen,  
what they had lost,  
what life would follow,  
and what things had been silently revolving in their troubled minds.

They also anxiously considered what would happen  
at the ultimate end:  
whether worse things remained for them,  
whether no hope at all survived for the wretched,  
whether they would lose what remained  
through everlasting death;  
or whether, when the bitter road of death  
should come upon the world and future peoples through the wood,  
life might still return through a wood.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0947]

Thus far I have traversed the hidden sequence,  
the beginnings of the world,  
as sincere faith taught it, without deception,  
while earthly things were still free from vices  
worthy of death.

Now, as I begin to treat human customs  
and mortal affairs in verse,  
add strength, almighty God, to the poet.

After each of the two had been commanded  
to depart from the sacred dwelling and the kingdom  
and had reached the fields of their birth,  
[Col. 0948D] and after the exile had stood upon his native soil,  
how strange the land must have appeared  
to the unrefined settlers,  
so savage and uncultivated,  
not green with fruit-bearing fields  
or distinguished by trees.

No appearance of the soil pleased them,  
for a confused heap lay there,  
a mingled mass pressed together by weight.  
The heights were stiff with ruggedness,  
the lowlands labored beneath forests,  
the plains lacked grass,  
and the elevated places bristled with thickets.

[Col. 0949A] Alas, with what eyes did they behold these things,  
with what breast did they see them—  
they whose minds contained paradise,  
and whose only cause of grief was this:  
that the face of all things, now filled with every evil,  
had revealed itself in deepest sadness  
after so many delights?

Paradise, your fertile joys and pleasant places  
were gone.  
Their emptiness was now ever present  
and wearied their sorrowful minds.

Now the honor of the sacred grove  
shone upon them in a greater brightness;  
now the blessed forest recalled to them  
the riches that had been taken away;  
now the sweeter use of the fruit  
and its nectar-like taste returned to memory;  
now the earth, breathing out its scent  
through living flowers,  
grieved the absent ones with its fragrance.

“O paradise,” they exclaimed,  
“how unlike those gifts are the things you now return to us!  
Indeed, how much worse these gifts are  
than those blessed delights!”

Thus, in their sorrow,  
the gracious love of life began to perish;  
poverty introduced the sweetness of death,  
lest greater want encounter an even heavier evil.

For a savage hunger compelled them  
to search the bowels of the earth  
and to seek what food the barren forest might give.  
They were driven to examine everywhere  
the uncertain nourishment of roots,  
so hostile were the plants,  
and to fill their barking bellies.

At last, when they were needy and destitute  
of everything required by necessity,  
their final misfortune taught them  
to hope for the aid of the supreme Father.

Then, each lying with his limbs upon the ground,  
they asked through tears and silent grief  
for consolations which they could not request in words,  
praying in supplication,  
while shame held back their inner complaints.

When Adam recognized that the gifts of speech  
had been restored to them for mutual use,  
he rose and prayed in this manner:

“Almighty One, author of the world and creator of things,  
whom, while life remained,  
I once, in my happiness, made hostile to me  
by the stain of evil and my audacious deeds—  
you who had granted that my swift minds  
might follow your vision above the stars,  
spread widely through all things—

“Why do I no longer possess these eyes,  
which once gazed upon your hidden things,  
or possess them only diminished in great part  
and shut within the foul cavern of the earthly prison?  
Now I am permitted to see nothing true  
except certain mortal and fleeting things,  
and the world sinking toward worse conditions.

“And therefore, Almighty One,  
who are always wholly present everywhere,  
we flee to you;  
with trembling mind we beseech you.  
Hear the wretched, whom you always see and hear.

“When that chief of crimes,  
the world’s most hostile enemy,  
wished once to attach me to the condemned side,  
he dared nothing alone,  
lest he yield defeated.  
Taking the form of a serpent,  
he fashioned the weapons of my wife  
with a hard wound;  
thus the unexpected fraud of the criminal artificer  
overcame us.

“And when I was condemned to a just punishment  
for my crime,  
my mind, struck by such grief,  
recognized the guilt so deeply  
that I thought I must impose punishment upon myself.

“Therefore I did not reject the groans and tears of punishment;  
I embraced in my heart the sweet consolations of punishment,  
and afterward placed this very punishment  
among sacred offerings in exchange for forgiveness of my crime.  
I no longer refuse whatever labors you may add.

“Yet meanwhile, best of judges,  
if it pleases you, hear us,  
who ask nothing contrary to your commands.

“We do not now pray with tears and mournful voice  
that the sentence of your judgment should dissolve;  
we pray only that the sentence may retain  
its full force.

“You commanded me to seek food from the tilled soil,  
and said that sterile thorns were to be plucked  
instead of sown grain, and thistles instead of fruit.  
Therefore the crop sought by labor must be sown,  
though it disappoint my hopes.

“Grant me to know what the crops are,  
in what manner they should be sown,  
which plants are fruitful,  
and what form the labor should take.

“Grant aid, Father, in your mercy,  
and imbue these senses.  
Then, possessing knowledge of things  
and certainty of salvation,  
Eve will serve me.  
Having experienced the savage punishment of the parent,  
she will bear peoples,  
so that they may be punished for our crime  
and cleanse the sins of their fathers  
by the deaths of their descendants,  
making the succession an eternal punishment.”

Meanwhile, as they prayed in this way,  
the serpent’s form appeared to them,  
moving along its path  
with a silent sign of fear,  
gently through the soft grass  
on creeping coils.

This sight turned the frightened pair toward it,  
and, shaking off the languor of dreadful grief,  
drew them into kindred anger.

Eve first said to her husband:

“If the supreme cause of our evils moves you,  
take up stones in your hand.  
Look, the opportunity is given  
to give death to the author of death.  
Let that crafty creature learn through its own punishments  
and bloody death  
how sad it is to die—  
the creature that wickedly destroyed me and you.”

She spoke, and followed the fleeing serpent  
with stones hurled from a distance.  
They also threw hard rocks against the trees  
where the crafty snake hid itself by crawling.

One of these, released by a rigid arm,  
struck a bare flint and rebounded.  
It raised a spark,  
which, born from dry tinder,  
burst into flame.  
Extending its fire crowned with flames far and wide,  
it soon set the whole forest ablaze.
