They shuddered and sought hiding places  
with trembling steps,  
but astonishment itself held the frightened pair  
and awakened their attentive concern  
for the unfamiliar flame.

They wished to see it again  
and to watch it in fear.  
They therefore withdrew a little  
and marveled, upon the barren back of the earth,  
that its dark locks had flowed downward,  
that the ashes of the groves bristled,  
that the day had darkened,  
that the whole earth shone,  
and that a new light appeared beneath the sun.

Nor could their minds calmly receive  
the crackling heard everywhere through the hissing forests,  
or the surging globes of flame  
rising broadly toward the stars.  
Nor did they yet understand  
that the devouring fire, sunk into the depths,  
stretched its roots below,  
and that, overcome by the heat it had taken in,  
the earth opened its generous veins for gifts.

When it had been dried of all its moisture,  
the earth soon began to become fluid  
and pour forth metals through their own channels.  
From this, gold’s highest glory gleamed in a tawny stream;  
silver flowed out, shining with white brilliance;  
the slippery rigidity of bronze ran about  
and, its body dissolved, gathered itself into a soft mass.

Do you wish me to capture briefly  
the form of the burning forest?

Sulfurous ashes flew through the dark places of the grove,  
just as when dry Etna, its chimneys split open,  
drives out hissing sulfur mixed with flames.

Then the earth, made exceedingly rich  
by the cooked clods, stirred itself into varied offspring.  
As it gave birth, it dissolved the fertile fields  
with a husbanding rain flowing through them.

[Col. 0951A] Then its swollen hollows cracked,  
the harvest rose up,  
and, as the ears were moved,  
the undulating grain trembled.

He might discern the appearance of a newly cultivated crop.

Yet let no long habit claim anything for itself here, nor chance, lacking all power. When God gave all good things with the light, and willed whatever the greater world possesses to become known to the lesser world through sacred understanding, He also willed Himself to be known through these things. If the mind had remained undefiled, as it was given to humanity and subject to no fault, neither appearances nor the bodies of things, neither the order of the stars nor the number and softness of the sand would deceive it; nor would it fail to grasp how far the earth extends through the vast depth, or what measure has been completed by its mass. What harmony’s vocal melody resounds in the movement of the sevenfold axis is now learned through practice

[Col. 0951B] and acquired through constant study, although whatever we grasp by art or practice we always hold because the Lord grants it.

But now, so that our lyre may return to the first parents after it has departed from them, attend, I ask, to a few words.

After Adam had been driven from the august dwellings of Paradise, he had no prior duty except the use of his wife and to devote all his labor to begetting children. Thus, when the first household was already filled with two children, and amid such varied labors each parent brought much consolation and each saw himself newly made a parent, their multiplied offspring relieved their heavy sorrows, and hope now arose that they might rejoice in their own servants for the work of the countryside. Of these, the elder in years, Cain, turned the rich fields with hard rakes; but Abel, most worthy to rejoice in living profit, pastured harmless sheep on bare hills and the offspring of the dry land, and supplied his parents with milk.

[Col. 0951C] But when they experienced the joys of the expected harvest, they perceived that their vows had been surpassed by divine favor: each soon resolved to dedicate to God the first offerings of his own produce. The former first heaps the sacred altars with fresh crops; the latter offers a snow-white lamb. Abel is the first figure of priests, and soon the impious victim of his brother, yet a figure long beforehand signifying Christ: for He was to be the perpetual priest according to the order of the Most High Melchizedek. When that saving victim hung upon the tree, envy and the hatred of His own brothers were at once kindled against Him.

Thus long ago the radiant Abel sensed beforehand his brother’s envy. For when one had offered from his harvest and the other a snow-white lamb, immediately the smoke from the lamb, once consumed, rose high into heaven.

[Col. 0951D] But, flying through the empty air, the smoke from those crops returned to earth, fleeing from Olympus—either because he had consecrated inferior things to the Lord, or because what he had offered was not pleasing to Him, having been produced by a greedy heart.

Thereupon Cain was inflamed with insane rage, drawing poison from that source of envy from which the serpent had offered the draught; and he slaughtered his brother, who was ignorant of the need to beware, striking him down in savage murder.

Alas, the crime! To what can frenzied desire not drive wretched men? To what can anger, fresh hatred, and wicked force not compel them? What did the innocent brother deserve? Did he deserve to be killed because he was more holy? Now the descendants of the parents have no ground for accusing anything they did; we ourselves have added to their offense. And now there is something the cunning serpent might bring against us, if we should wish to accuse him for the fact that we die: for, to crown that first offspring, he added death, and made the guilt brought into the world by the parents—horrible to say—into a new crime by his impiety. Thus, impious Cain, thus you first stain the new world with murder. For this you will pay perpetual penalties, once freed from death, and eternal ones, far worse than the wicked serpent, if we measure your crimes. He brought death upon us; he did not inflict it. We accepted what was brought, but you are the first to inflict it.

[Col. 0952A] He was therefore much worse, although a public enemy who could have been avoided; you, a private enemy, could not be guarded against by any device. For who would fear a beloved brother?

Yet there is no crime of so wicked a human being that God, in a merciful spirit, does not forgive it, provided that he repents of the deed. We learn this from Cain, whom God—such is His mercy—did not deem unworthy of Himself as reprover, even though Cain was drenched in his brother’s blood. He gently questioned him about where his brother was, convicted him when he denied the deed, and punished him lightly for so great a crime.

For He merely sent him away as a fugitive and exile from both parents, banished him to distant and desolate regions, and ordered him immediately to leave his ancestral lands. In this too He graciously benefited the wretched man: for it is a far heavier punishment to be seen living after punishment and bearing the shame of one’s deed among the happy and those blessed with a pure mind.

[Col. 0952B] And, to make his exile lighter, a faithful wife was added as a companion to the guilty man, perhaps lest despair alone seize him; and also so that she might soften the hard cares of his troubled heart, and restore by her embrace his body weakened by grief. Subject to no guilt, honoring the Lord with prayers and a pure mind, she might draw forth whatever could suffice for the two of them.

Thus much grace accompanied him in exile: God multiplied his progeny through the names of a thousand descendants, and made Cain king over peoples whom He taught to surround cities with walls, foreseeing those born for ages far into the future.

[Col. 0952C] Meanwhile Eve, once again a grievous burden to her sorrowing husband, had compensated for the loss of the first sacred child, and, now that offspring had been born, had once more given the parents many cares of the spirit and joys mingled with labor. They named the boy Seth, whom almighty God gave them in Abel’s place. From him descended a posterity from whose seed Enos arose. He was the first priest, recognized for his quiet virtue; he hoped and deserved to call upon the powerful God with pious prayers and vows, and he instructed the people who followed him to maintain the worship of the eternal Father.

From his line descended Enoch, powerful in virtues and not inferior in merit to his ancestors. Restored to his ancestral dwellings and to the blessed world, he still lives and already possesses the future kingdoms of life.

[Col. 0952D] He was the ancestor of the righteous Noah. In Noah’s time, frequent guilt infected the whole world with united efforts, and posterity, following ancestral vices, added vice to vice. Therefore, although their forefathers had been accustomed to live for a thousand years, or nearly so, lest the perverse customs of human beings receive increase as the years increased, and so that there might be an end to vice, the maximum span of human life was reduced to twelve lustrums.

For when the youth joined to the Cainite race in profane marriages had condemned itself and, inclined toward worse things, abandoned the favor of the heavenly powers, it rushed into various crimes and recklessly ran headlong into every kind of fall. Then God, angered at the world because of so many crimes, immediately uttered these words:

[Col. 0953A] “Never hereafter will that Spirit of mine remain in the human race, nor will it prolong life further. Let the sinful life of human beings be content with one hundred and twenty years, because, pursuing earthly things, they have more flesh than mind.” Thus, by the severe sentence of the unchanging Judge, He fixed a definite term for the age of life, lest the length of life provide opportunities for increasing crime.

For what would the wicked human race not dare now? Giants, born from an immense substance, dreadful monsters of humanity, born from varied seed, dared everything; they possessed no virtue except that, ultimately, they would not be wicked—yet fierce desire dragged them into every crime and allowed them to pass no night without bloodshed,

[Col. 0953B] nor any day without murder. Forgetful of divine law, of human beings, of themselves, of pious affection, of their mothers and fathers, and of God their creator, they advanced so far into the highest crimes that it displeased the Lord to have formed human beings. Therefore God wished, because of the perverse sins of the guilty, to roll up even souls free from crime and immerse them in the waters poured over the earth, while the world returned to its ancient form.

Noah alone was righteous. On his account God delayed coming forth in anger. A faithful life had kept him free from crime for five hundred years and had proved him as one living according to holy law. To him God revealed the sacred mysteries in this way:

[Col. 0953C] “Since the whole air, together with the lands fallen into worse things, has been infected by shameful vices, it has seemed good to wash them away and submerge the world beneath the swelling sea. When it rushes down and covers everything, and, commanded, settles in the precipitous flood, let it cleanse the polluted world, and roll together in the swollen deep the entangled human beings and everything that has been ordered to live because of humanity.

“But because you alone have taken our will to heart, because you have led a life devoted to holy laws, always resisting the perverse with a better purpose, I shall so govern the laws of my decrees that, when the wicked race has paid just penalties to me and the dregs of the world have been purged, the mortal race may begin again more worthily through you, and the peoples who live after these times may count you their supreme ancestor.

[Col. 0953D] “Therefore let an ark be prepared for you, constructed of squared beams. Let it be three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high, adorned with a cubit-high window. Let a door also be placed on its left side.

“Then let hot bitumen, penetrating the absorbent joinery, seek out and coat every fine crack. When the space has been divided into three parts by a double partition, let the living creatures be separated into their own compartments, lest, mixed together, they violate their kind, fight when joined, and confuse their food. You must store only enough of this material for them; for it is my responsibility to ensure that what is distributed among those received does not run short.”

Noah conceived these words with faithful mind—God Himself supplying the understanding and disposition to will and to do whatever He commanded His servant—and undertook the ordered work. He began to cut down dense forests and fell ancient oaks. The groves admitted the rays of light; the plain was relieved of shadow, and the valleys were stripped of their age-old timber.

[Col. 0954A] But although the upper part of the work begun had been hastened by so much labor, it was prolonged for a hundred years, so that the good life that followed might amend the sins of the former life and the wicked race might change its savage ways.

O wretched people, whom the delay of so just a punishment makes still more guilty! They will be punished not merely for the past crime, but much more severely for that very interval of time granted to them, and for the mercy they neglected, while the Lord, by postponing the time, testified that He preferred to spare those who returned.

When the structure had at last been completed, the vessel stood, capacious, with its sides joined together—a final refuge that the Father Himself had prepared for your shipwrecks and rushing waters of nature. Then God, from lofty Olympus, deigned to warn His servant Noah by a voice that the final moment had arrived: he was to hide himself with his sons, wife, and daughters-in-law, rescue them from impending destruction and the darkness of death, and restore all the animals to life-giving enclosures.

[Col. 0954B] Whether the earth nourished them or the bright air sustained them, he was to take seven of each of the clean animals, and two each of those less suited to sacred things and called unclean. There was no delay: whatever is born beneath the vaulted hinge of heaven, unknown in the various regions of the world—whatever the East marvels at, whatever pale Iberia dreads, whatever southern Libya nourishes on its hot sands,

[Col. 0954C] whatever divides the Hyperborean nights with marvelous light—all hurried trembling into the open ark, as though they had already foreseen the Flood and were obeying their creator God, and as though beasts without reason were wiser than human beings, who were more senseless than they, even if the beasts themselves knew nothing.

Therefore, as soon as God ordered the ark, pregnant with every seed of life, to be closed, night rushed upon them, and sudden darkness covered the sky. A cloudburst fell, struck the earth from the poured-out air, raged, and stormed equally throughout the world.

[Col. 0954D] Nor was the rain pouring from the clouds sufficient for destruction. The ancient waters were released, and now, with the ether opened, heaven rained into empty clouds; the celestial world flowed down from the opened abyss into waters and opened new springs equal to torrents.

As all this rapidly joined together in a single flood, whatever heaven vomited, whatever earth, whatever clouds poured forth, it engulfed the submerged fields with their inhabitants, tangled flocks in their stalls, and cities with their citizens, and buried them beneath the waters. As the peoples were destroyed in a floating ruin, no appearance of things remained: the flood covered everything, and even the rivers lost their names as they grew.

[Col. 0955A] Soon Ocean, never satiated by any rivers, sensed the waters rushing toward him in such an enormous mass. He drove them onward with an increased flood and forced the waters returning into a heap to rise still higher.

At last, as the deep raised the swelling waters, the wave, drawn together from every side, joined the shores in a supreme circle, and the seas converged over the overwhelmed lands. And now the ark was carried fifteen cubits above everything,

[Col. 0955B] for this measure rose above the highest mountains. The fury of a single rain and a single death lasted forty days. Then, for one hundred and fifty days of clear weather, the sea remained at a similar level and measure.

Meanwhile, the almighty Father, long since pitying the people confined in their prison, ordered the great sea gradually to withdraw from the lands and slowly to recede, lest, fleeing too suddenly, it overturn everything, and lest the earth, once dry, fail to return to its stable place.

Finally, when the air had spread out flat, the summit gradually began to reveal itself, and the highest ridges could be seen; the waves descended from the rocks into the plains, while, as the waters slowly subsided, forests emerged from the sea and hidden hills gradually rose.

[Col. 0955C] Now the black raven, sent out as a lookout from the open ark, had found clear air and, having found prey, no longer cared to return to its accustomed enclosure. Therefore, once the dove had been sent out from the seat of life, since it brought back nothing certain, it was sent out again and returned bearing a small offering of the peace-bringing olive.

Such a great cry of those shut inside arose for this judgment, with praise of their great Father, by which they revealed their joy—like the cry when a harsh victor assaults the walls, if sudden aid should happen to be brought to the besieged; like the cry when, with a mild judge, a sentence restores those condemned to life; like the weeping in which life returns from an uncertain death amid the tears and rejoicing of mourners.

[Col. 0955D] After the lookout announced that the fields were once again open, since she did not return when sent out and received by the earth, they grew weary of enduring their sluggish hiding place,

[Col. 0956A] and were glad to breathe the winds of the open sky and feed their spirit, released into the heavenly air. But no one was permitted to leave the open enclosure until He who had ordered the remnants of the world to enter it ordered them to leave the sacred enclosure.

Warned from heaven, faithful Noah, with his wife, his household, his sons, and his chaste daughters-in-law, was ordered to go forth and once again give the fields to new settlers, and to release through open doors all the animals that had been preserved for their future offspring, which the good maker of human beings had preserved for human use.

After the gate was opened, they rushed forth: some on wings through the air, some into the woods and forests, some sank into open caves, while others, freed upon the fields, rejoiced in the dry earth and flourished in the open meadow.

[Col. 0956B] But Noah, having obtained the kingdom of a second world, surveyed everything with his eyes and received it with an embracing mind, wishing to fill and satisfy his spirit by taking in all things. He rapidly looked over everything and drank it in, marveling at it as new. The sun shone more brightly than at its familiar rising and smiled more deeply red; the face of the sky was happier in greater serenity, and fields thought lost became green with new offspring. Yet the image of so great a ruin still remained before his eyes, ever worthy of remembrance.

What they had endured amid the waters, and what they had not also endured through sacred grace, when the sea raged with savage blows and the ark scorned the waves striking against it! As Noah reviewed with his people how prompt and generous the largesse of the supreme Father had been toward him, he compelled them, astonished, to wonder and consider among themselves

[Col. 0956C] where enough food for their souls had come from for the entire year, and what drink there had been—for it is clear that, even if the other necessities of life had been supplied, those shut inside could have perished from thirst while the ark floated amid the waters, unless the ruler of Olympus, without human aid or gift, had sustained them by that same will by which he created all things.

He deprived souls destined to perish during the long imprisonment of night of the use of light, but filled them with strength. So that they might endure such sluggish rest, he infused them with a tranquil love of torpor.

For what could the hand of the Almighty not accomplish? When He wished, He could make those suddenly submerged beneath icy waves burn, and those driven into the very flames grow cold. He who now taught human beings that they could perish in a brief time beneath engulfing waters will show that they can be born again through flames and waters.

[Col. 0956D]

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0955]

[Col. 0955D] Carrying such thoughts in his mind and seeing the ages to come, Noah, preserved, resolved to undertake no duty before returning sacred praises and thanksgiving to God for escaping the danger.

Soon sacred altars rose from snow-white stone, and the newly restored world recognized these as its first altars. Previously, the whole world, along the vaulted course of heaven, had itself been a temple. Then, from the flocks prepared for sacrifice, a victim hurried forth—either from the species of birds supported by the gentle air,

[Col. 0956D] or from those creatures that the earth produces; for every seventh animal was laid upon the altars, devoted to sacred rites.

Then fire sent down from heavenly Olympus consumed the fragrant offspring upon the sacred altars, and the whole burnt offerings blazed forth an ambrosial vapor for God.

Although He, Lord and God of the whole world, has need of none of our gifts, nevertheless He delights to be honored by the service and offering of His own.

When the waters had at last been removed, He addressed Noah in this way:

Although the punishment may have been small in relation to so great a crime—the vengeance of avenging rains and the sky poured out upon the guilty, and the cleansing of the sinful dwelling place of earth by the more widely spread deep—I shall not, because I was offended, strike the mortal race with such a blow again.

[Col. 0957A] Although I see human minds and profane peoples rushing once more into various crimes and former offenses, nevertheless my avenging hand will not cease to return punishments to the unjust and rewards to the just.

Therefore, you whose life is most righteous in my sight, multiply, secure in yourselves, and fill the fields with fertile offspring; stretch out your [F. “new”] flocks across the broad lands. The elements will maintain their cycles, and on every day the due harvest will be returned to the scattered seeds.

The work of the world will run in equal measure through discordant seasons: winter will contend with summer, and the year, balancing the periods of spring and autumn, will turn as it departs.

[Col. 0957B] And you, to whom we have entrusted the kingdom of the solid earth, everything in the substance of the greater world will tremble and fear you. Behold, we give you dominion over all things and over every kind of creature. Whatever moves of its own accord, whatever possesses fleshly limbs, we grant for your use.

Yet I will that you abstain from blood while it is still living. If anyone eats it, a severe judgment will punish him no less than if he had drained human blood in slaughter. I shall always pursue and demand this blood as avenger, so that not only the human being, rich in reason, may pay the penalty, but even the brute creature. Let human blood be sacred to all alike.

But so that no one afterward may fear a flood, let him be secure under such a covenant. When the light moisture hanging in the clouds has turned into mist and heaped black waters into hollow clouds, I shall pour forth rays, and the image of the sun will form for me a beautiful curved bow at the highest circle, painting the vault of heaven. It will display various colors in its light and scatter the rains into the air; the shining fire will be greater and the rain now less.

[Col. 0957C] Posterity, secure in such a covenant, may take this as a sign of what is to come, so that afterward it may believe that a flood need not be feared.

Attentive to these commands, Noah and his wife, after giving thanks and returning praise to the Lord, eagerly worked the fields, made joyful with mud and sweet moisture. The father and his sons together soon subdued the land with rakes and married the fields to seed.

Then, in spring, the thick green grass spread widely across the fields. When the golden ears had hardened, the heat of the sun returned a multiplied harvest, the grain’s milk having congealed and been gathered into abundant increase. And now the vineyard, heavy with swelling clusters, luxuriated in sweet fruit; the entire tree produced nectar, and cups were born from the hard wood.

Perhaps Noah, joyful, was celebrating honors for God, indulging in sacred feasts and offering new wine from the first vine. When he had drunk too freely, he became heavy with deep sleep, his limbs relaxed, and, lying with his clothing not properly arranged, he lay prostrate on the ground, exposing to his sons his private parts.

[Col. 0957D] Ham, most foul, your own nature alone moved you to laughter. Nor, believing that it was enough for you alone to have sinned, did you refrain from trying to stain your brothers with a sprinkling of your guilt. But those whose judgment and mind were much better, when the father’s nakedness had been revealed, taught them to conceal his private parts with a cloak. Turning their hands away, they covered their father’s shame.

Then Shem and Japheth, pledges worthy of such a father—whom for this reason the father made masters of their younger brother by right—approached while he was released from sleep and wine. Soon, when he awoke, he learned of the good deed of his sons and repaid Ham’s offense with such a reward.

[Col. 0958A] “You, Ham,” he said, “will be accursed, and you will become the servant of your own brothers forever, throughout the ages to come.

“But Shem will be blessed, and he will make his younger brother share with him in the common seat of blessings, whose possession will extend far and wide.”

Having spoken these words, the elder, when he had lived nine hundred and fifty years, rested in peace.

Meanwhile, while the posterity of the Lord remained strong in holy law, already increased by many descendants and committing itself to the one Lord of heaven and earth, everything obeyed the holy commands of human beings: the heavy earth, the liquid sea, and the life-bearing air. They had no need of skill, for under a heavenly teacher they learned everything.

[Col. 0958B] But after the world went forth into crimes and hid itself deeply in vices, this distinguished gift was lost by the condemned race. Many did not blush to fashion gods, forgetting God. Such is the consequence of forgetting the supreme Father.

Then the grave inventor of death, unwilling to let a fruitful supply of deceit lie idle, subjected everything to his malign rule, by which he might bring fate upon the world and persuade it either that God no longer existed or that He despised these lower functions of the world.

Thus he persuaded human beings to assign all human affairs and the outcomes of events—which it was fitting to assign to the supreme Lord—to wandering stars; to inspect the entrails of birds and the movements of flying creatures; and, with immense zeal, he introduced the crime of magical art. He persuaded them to pray to many gods, and to adore mute idols—or rather, the one hiding behind the idols within them—though he deserved much more to be burned.

Nimrod first descended into such wicked crimes, the pinnacle of impiety, born from the servant Ham’s seed, a giant in body and mind, ruling the Babylonian kingdoms.

[Col. 0958C] Capturing the minds of the Persians, this wicked hunter led them away from the true sacred rites of the Lord to fire.

Not content with deceiving those excessively greedy through this cunning art, that chief of crimes and most hostile enemy of the world attacked the cares of human beings; but he also rushed into their minds, descended deeply into all their senses, and soon into their emotions.

For when his only offspring had carried away with it in bitter death the hope of his line, unhappy Nimrod continued his tears night and day and dragged out complaints in dull lamentation. While he raged and searched everywhere for his stolen son, he consoled his mournful grief with an image he had made, and, in his misery, believed that the form of his son, fashioned from Parian marble, lived with enclosed consciousness and heard his complaints.

[Col. 0958D] Soon he dedicated it, raised altars, and added divine honors; he ordered it to take the place of God. Immediately all the peoples embraced and followed this crime. Each held dear parents as his own gods, and later placed kings in similar honor and called them gods.

Under their name, deceitful Greece, while striving to insert falsehoods among true things, added obscure shadows to vain explanations, excusing burial mounds and the names placed upon tombs, until madness revealed itself in every form and, while the world laughed, gave the empty name of God to the smallest objects and even to shameful body parts.

To provide fuel for such thickets of error, the ambiguous inventor of death summoned oracles, using for his snares either fire, or a hot spring, or earth breathing talkative winds from caves, and attaching to himself the false name of the vain Apollo.

Through such snares that savage being captured nations removed from the Lord, leading them wherever he wished. Such is the cost of departing from the holy worship of the Lord.

But let us return to the line of our ancestors from which we have come. In a few years it grew so greatly that, soon leaving the East behind, they were compelled to seek new settlements elsewhere. They reached an open plain, which the ancients called Shinar. When the youth were also forced to leave these lands and be scattered in various directions, they began to voice their grief in these mournful and most sorrowful words:

[Col. 0959A] “Alas, how uncertain is the condition of life for human beings once they have begun their course! How prosperity deceives those who do not know what is to come through varied events! How the culmination of the wish we seek tends toward the opposite!

“Now, if it is lawful to say so, we are distressed that the multitude of descendants hoped for in our fathers’ prayers has grown. For the band of us, amassed in exile, must be scattered across the world and will perish far from our ancestral boundaries. Shall we then, exhausted by long poverty and dishonored in our bodies, give ourselves to be buried here and there in unknown tombs? Shall we wretched people not even be enclosed in our ancestral graves? Will no fame of us survive after death?

“Come, therefore, young men: while the crowd supplies its strength, leave behind through eternal deeds the outstanding fame that remains for you and knows no end.

[Col. 0959B] “Let us build a city, and beneath its walls raise a tower ever higher, until it reaches the stars that paint the sky and the vault of lofty Olympus, so that our descendants, not knowing otherwise, may think that we have migrated from the abandoned earth into heaven.”

Thus aroused, the youth scorned the rocks and whatever flowed down when the mountain was cut away. From the bowels of the earth they bound together, by fire, bricks they had shaped, and preferred the material of the future work to owe its existence to their own labor. They joined each layer on both sides with bitumen, so that the surrounding walls might imitate solid cliffs.

Soon the hastily built tower rose; soon, with its summit, it crossed the clouds and enjoyed the clearer air nearer to heaven.

Then the Almighty Father summoned the angelic council with a heavenly voice. Astonished at the deeds of the insane and arrogant crowd, He said to the companions of His kingdom:

[Col. 0960A] “Behold, you see where this earthly phalanx is now recklessly proceeding, and what great undertakings it unwisely attempts. It believes that something built by mortal hands can touch the lofty poles and lead to our ether, although no one clothed in an earthly body ascends to heaven unless he has descended from heaven above.

“But because the people are one and have the same form of speech, they will persist in building the tower and will not stop before mutual agreement has completed the work begun. Such is the insanity of the human mind.

“Come, then, let us descend, so that they may know that what is forbidden cannot be done.

[Col. 0960B] Let us disturb their swollen hearts and proud agreement with the varied sounds of their mouths, so that what they have committed through the crime of harmonious minds, the better discord of their confused language may condemn.”

He spoke, and, while they were intent upon the work and raising the mass, forgetfulness first entered their astonished minds, followed by the imperfection of an unknown language.

The overseers, seeing the zeal for the work cease, rebuked their hesitating companions, but no one answered with words they did not understand. If anyone attempted to speak, he hissed emptily or gasped with the growl of broken speech.

When frustrated hands abandoned the vain labor undertaken with a perverse mind, no one followed a neighbor or father, whom he could understand. Each added to himself and gathered together companions, seeking to join a fellow worker.

[Col. 0960C] As the kinship of this people was divided and perished, language made a people. They were scattered in equal groups and sought lands separated beneath different stars.

No differently do the birds of the fields range across the soft plains, when secure daylight has persuaded them to wander in mixed flocks and seek food. As night approaches, they seek leafy shelter; the crowd, freed from the flock, follows its own kind, and in wild flight they mingle according to whatever color or voice has led them.

So then one people divided itself into regions, and each appearance became a separate race. They settled in distant lands and filled the world with nations.

Yet this sacred gift was not wholly without benefit, even though it was the punishment of the guilty. Although this was a just vengeance upon those untouched by reverence for heaven, the proper dwelling of the world's and all things' Parent, so that they did not recognize one another while speaking unfamiliar words, nevertheless this much was secured by the breaking of the covenant: the guilt that the persuasion of a few had brought about would not again affect everyone through the agreement of all, nor make the crime common.

[Col. 0960D] Thus hard battles and war, by which death would be summoned upon peoples in raging fury, would not become a civil war among them. Their first division of language therefore benefited them and was turned to good, although the Hebrew custom of speech was not entirely abolished. For the sound of Hebrew speech and the ancient language remained among those who were free from guilt.

A considerable and righteous portion consisted of the sons whom Shem begot, whom the guardianship of the just preserved and the reverence of the Lord also guided.

[Col. 0961A] But after madness, driven throughout the whole world—leaving aside the unspeakable crime of the magical monster—had driven the human race into trunks and rocks, into hollow forms fashioned by the art of hard metal, and into empty images devoid of light; after it broke minds directed toward heavenly things and brought them down to inert earth, and the contagion of foul corruption enveloped everything, no differently from clouds of disease stirred up in the burning lands of the Ethiopians, as they ran through the corrupted course of heaven: whoever, struck by the lightning of death, groaned, fell at once himself; whoever saw another falling, fell too; and the dreadful plague scattered heaps of corpses everywhere and left the fields empty.

[Col. 0961B] Thus madness, having seized them in its headlong mass and wishing to leave nothing uninfected throughout the world, returned and seized those whom error had already released.

At last a righteous man of Chaldean descent, from the seed of Terah, fearing God, sought another city, new customs, and a new dwelling for himself and his descendants; finally he remained a newcomer in the Assyrian city of Harran. After he had lived there for forty-one lustrums, he redeemed this unhappy life by a fortunate death.

His son Abram succeeded him, equal or superior to him in merit and holy virtues—a man worthy of heaven. From the very beginning of life he reverenced the true God in his mind and always rejected pagan rites. After his father’s death had made clear that he could now follow God’s commands,

[Col. 0961C] the Lord deigned to approach His servant because of these merits:

“Since throughout the entire world we have found you alone who delight in sincere faith and reverence for us, leave far behind your ancestral dwelling and the guilty land, your polluted household. Your entire kinship is profane and must be fled by you. Under my guidance you will reach the fields of a better land. Do not remain part of an unrighteous people, for you can become the head of a holy one.

“Then I shall establish sacred promises that will remain for you, blessed one. I shall make your name magnificent among all peoples, repaying you with every good thing. Whoever blesses you will be blessed; whoever heaps curses and insults upon you will immediately be accursed. Through you blessing will be spread among all tribes and into the age to come.”

[Col. 0961D] He spoke and implanted in him a mind that would obey His commands and believe His holy promises. No delay intervened after the Lord’s word. Immediately Abram departed with flocks of various kinds, his father’s servants, his faithful wife, and his dear brother’s child, whose name was Lot. He took the unknown road directly.

The most fertile fields made pleasant paths for them, and the air, smiling under favorable south winds, was disturbed by no storm. When he reached the lands of Canaan and the most fruitful kingdom of Shechem, he learned that these regions would fall by lot to himself and his descendants as a future dominion.

Therefore, suppliant before God, he built devoted altars and, as a new worshiper recalling ancient rites, increased their honors.

From there he sought Bethel, the dwelling chosen for the lodging of the blessed man, a place that surpassed all lands in its proud merits and would one day be counted second only to heaven. For this seat of God seemed more worthy than the heavenly dwelling itself, since it would receive the pledge of salvation sent into the world, prepared while the whole world marveled, and would send the human being back to the stars.

Here too Father Abram built solemn altars and established dwellings in the fields that he would later have to leave. For once again forced by famine to change his dwelling, he moved his camp, taking his whole household, servants, and flocks with him. Repaying fair commerce in his dealings, he entered Egypt and preferred to call Sarai his sister rather than his wife, lest savage desire incite barbarian hearts to murder the holy guest.

[Col. 0962A] Then Pharaoh was struck by the radiant image of her beauty and burned with desire. He prepared a marriage chamber and a binding contract according to law, intending to carry out this union for many years, unless the author of marriage, to whom such things were displeasing, arranged matters very differently.

Behold, a terror mixed with dread overwhelmed the king; sudden tumult shook his wicked heart, black horror frightened his mind and entangled his limbs. Thus the king of the sacrilegious people perceived that God had condemned such an evil desire. God had surely inspired His servants with the plan that the barbarian enemy should recognize Abram as Sarai’s husband without fear, once he had learned how little safety there was in approaching with profane violence one whom he was not permitted to make a widower.

[Col. 0962B] Therefore Pharaoh voluntarily returned her to her husband, untouched by any stain, and sent Abram, laden with abundant grain, back to Abram’s own Shechem and Bethel. There the father, received again with his flocks and household and with his wife safe, worked the fields and widely enjoyed the rich pastures among mingled flocks.

While frequent quarrels arose between the shepherds of uncle and nephew, and the fields were too narrow to contain the herds of the two, Abram, filled with justice and most observant of fairness, divided the allotted fields, as the elder, in order to settle the disputes and remove greedy quarrels.

The younger chose the region where the countryside is watered on every side by sweet streams, where the Jordan flows between shaded banks and beautifies the smooth groves. Thus, to escape the shepherds’ quarrels, Lot turned away from Abram and migrated into the fields adjoining Sodom.

[Col. 0962C] Then God, strengthening Abram’s grieving heart with this hope, said:

“Do not be moved because, having left your brother’s offspring, you now seem to be alone. You alone will be for me an innumerable multitude, and likewise the progenitor of a friendly people.

[Col. 0962D] “Look attentively upon the regions of the fourfold world,”

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete.]

Look now toward the south and the north,

where the sun rises, where at evening it sinks in the utter west:

these lands I shall grant to you, to your offspring,

and to your peoples, for them to inhabit through endless years—

lands which you too shall enjoy far and wide.

Rise, and traverse on foot the regions that first received you as a guest.

So he spoke; and Abram gladly obeyed. Leaving that place,

he migrated and entered Hebron, and beneath the dark holm-oak

the father pitched his tents beside the oak-groves of Mamre.

Here too he built solemn altars to the Lord, that he might worship him.

[Col. 0963A] Meanwhile an enemy arrives, amid great, tumultuous disturbance—

an enemy hungry for plunder, whom a land rich in varied wealth

provokes; the hoof resounds against the fields,

and the marauder wanders with loosened reins

against the rich pastures of the people of Sodom.

But Lot bursts out through the open gates with the king,

and allied forces of neighboring kings, bearing their weapons,

draw horsemen and foot soldiers along with them. The army stretches out;

the battle-lines clash together, and they strike down and fall.

But Sodom’s shameful youth, softened by luxury,

as soon as renewed shouting flares into rage,

turn their backs in fear. Some seek the walls at a swift run,

some the mountains and forests; others stretch out their idle hands

to the grim bonds enclosing the prisoners.

[Col. 0963B] But when Abram, the uncle, heard that Lot had been captured,

he prepared to rescue his captured brother—not with tears

(for what would useless weeping accomplish?), but with courage.

Accordingly, he selected three hundred men fully equipped

from his entire company, and twice nine servants. He followed them,

with these men going ahead, little by little, along the route

where the enemy had revealed that he was proceeding,

slowed by the weight of his booty. In the silence of night

he attacked their bodies—already exhausted by the hard fighting,

while sweet sleep refreshed them and bound their weary limbs—

as they expected nothing of the kind:

just as the fury of a fasting lion, when it has entered

a sheepfold in a swift leap through the enclosure,

kills the flock with tooth and paw, and its eager anger

to devour overcomes hunger, while the final limit of bitter anguish

has already emptied the last folds of their sheep.

[Col. 0963C] In the same way he struck down the leaders buried in sleep and wine,

and slaughtered the peoples and kings who opposed Abram,

yet in such a manner that no tumult threw the camp into confusion.

No one perceived a movement except the man whose mind and voice failed him;

no one heard the sound of slaughter except the man whom death awakened.

Everything was drenched in blood. The earth, dissolved in the clear calm,

clotted with gore, and footprints slipped and stumbled

in the blood standing across the field and impeding the tread.

Yet not every living creature fell beneath drawn swords;

some of the booty was preserved. Such was the restraint of the righteous

victor. Shameful flight scattered the rest,

and the terror that pursued them pressed on as far as Damascus.

But the victor, unmoved by the glory of so great a triumph,

amid horses, flocks, and the people recovered—

[Col. 0963D] whether captured or rescued—and amid the treasures

(which by their greedy weight move both conquered and conquerors),

desired absolutely none of these things.

Rather, gentle amid such great rejoicing,

he pondered beneath his heart the varied circumstances of human beings,

and reserved all the booty and spoils of war,

taken from the peoples everywhere, for the king.

He made clear that he had not fought for himself, yet he offered a tenth

of the booty wrested from the enemy—the true sacrifice—

to Melchizedek. That king of Salem had offered him wine and bread

when he returned from the slaughter; by such a gift

he had sent beforehand the mystical offerings of the supreme Christ,

whose living body the Church receives from his hands as bread

and, drinking heavenly blood, is refreshed.

But when Abram returned weary from the enemy’s death,

the Almighty consoled him with these words.

[Col. 0964A] “Since no enticements of booty have overcome your desire,

the reward of faith and recompense for your labors

are fully with me for you; and I shall protect you and all that is yours,

to be preserved for your heir, whom you shall beget late in life

and whom, as his loving father, you shall love all the more.

There is nothing for you to fear: Damascus shall not be your heir. You shall see one born from your own seed, whose infancy shall kindle your paternal affections.

Look up and see how the sky, joined by a dense radiance,

sparkles across the painted night; see how many stars are piled upon stars,

stars that, when set before you, refuse to be counted.

Here you have an image of your seed, a likeness

of the future form of your multiplied descendants.”

Having spoken thus, he ended. Abram believed,

and the sole assent of his naked faith was reckoned

as a full crown of righteousness and merit.

[Col. 0964B] Thus from Abram we learn by so great a reward

how great is the merit of believing the divine Word,

and, conversely, how great the demerit of not believing.

For because he believed, he again deserved to be comforted

by this divine voice, as the Almighty began with these words:

“I am that God and Lord who brought you and your people

out of the land of Chaldea, and, after rescuing you

from your ancestral vices, settled you in a better land,

so that the people born from you might inhabit blessed fields

and extend their line far and wide,

after the peoples whom the shameful error of their ancestors

once made profaners of sacrilegious rites have been expelled.

But because you delay too long, hesitating to believe,

take for me a three-year-old heifer, facing me with its stern brow;

with it, a she-goat of equal age, chosen from a gentle flock,

and a ram of the same age shall be sacrificed in my honor.

Also, a chaste turtledove paired with a domestic dove—but among the birds let no victim feel the iron.

Take care only to cut apart the animals in the middle,

and, having thus divided them, set the clean sands between them,

so that corresponding limbs may lie opposite one another.”

He spoke; and Abram, accustomed gladly to observe

the commands of God when warned, hastened to carry them out.

But when he had spread the sequence of offerings upon the earth

in the order commanded, suddenly a black swarm of birds

attacked the prey, intent on plundering it.

Abram, watchful on every side, anxiously guarded against them

and kept looking around, lest they profane the sacred things

by their contact.

But while he was stunned by so great a task,

and while the sun was already setting,

the burden of the duty he had undertaken overcame him.

[Col. 0964D] Behold, black terror, dreadful trembling, and sleep entered him,

bearing prophetic commands and shaping the ages to come.

I believe he seemed to see the Nile enclosed

for the people of the Hebrew nation, and their distant descendants,

and to recognize immense crowds beyond number.

Then he saw fierce movements, the camp of his people drawn out,

the sea crossed on dry foot, the armies submerged in the depths,

a shipwreck following no fleet,

the Hebrews rescued from the sea, and thereafter

all the kingdoms of blessed Palestine opened to the returning people.

When he was stunned by such visions, the gracious interpreter was not absent:

“Know beforehand your people and the offspring of your people,” he said,

“who for four centuries in foreign lands

shall endure the harsh commands of that tyrant of the Nile.

But when it has completed so many years of exile,

I shall free it from servitude and avenge the unjust nation,

and I shall restore it to the lands encircled

by the gentle currents of the Nile and the Euphrates.

But when the sins of the guilty nation of the Amorites,

the people possessing these kingdoms,

have reached the full measure of their crimes,

and they have become worthy to be expelled

from the dwellings of their fathers, then nevertheless,

after a long life has happily reached its appointed limit,

he shall depart in peace, lamented by his children,

and with our gift shall migrate to his holy ancestors.”

Having spoken thus, when night was already clothing the earth

with dense shadows, he gave a sign from the mountain.

At once a smoky furnace appeared there,

and a burning torch seemed to be present.

Then the sacred offerings and the prepared center,

carried in, were consumed by a flame sweeping through them

at headlong speed.

Meanwhile, certain of the future kingdom and offspring,

Abram desired to undertake the office of father.

But his chaste wife refused the duty, since barren old age

had already made her womb empty.

Believing, however, that her husband’s sweet pledge

and the new hope issuing from whatever concubine

would be hers, she substituted for herself a maidservant—

a girl of younger age, named Hagar,

whose origin was the land of the Nile.

By entreaties she prevailed upon her husband

to entrust the seed to a servant’s womb.

Shame upon such servile outrage! As soon as Hagar perceived

that she was carrying the burden of pregnancy,

swollen with proud arrogance she despised her mistress—

the mistress to whom she owed the affection and status of a mother—

and, maddened by the cause of her own swelling, insulted her.

Therefore the supremely just man Abram rightly subjected her

to the whip of his wife. Ashamed by these deeds,

she hid herself far away in the deserted and secret haunts of wild beasts,

indignant, yet even as an exile she did not cease her disdain.

But again, depriving her of the obedience she owed,

she despised her in whatever manner she could,

and preferred to endure the dangers of the desert road.

Had not an angel sent from heaven met her,

restored the maidservant to her former dwelling and gentle mistress,

and, refreshing her with kindly encouragement,

bidden her return with better hopes,

telling her her son’s name, character, and might,
and that countless multitudes would descend from such a stock.

Returning with greater hope, now certain of the future,
she herself first made her master a father by giving birth.

When, after the happy courses of his life,
he was completing more than eighty-six years,

[Col. 0965D] and, as a righteous man, had added twenty-one more years—the gracious Father again approached him

with his customary address, and ordered him to lead

a happy old age. He repeated the promises,

and, while expecting his reward, Abram prostrated himself

with bowed body and worshiped the Lord in supplication.

From him he soon heard, in a firm voice,

that he would become the father of an innumerable and widely extended nation,

and that kings too would come from his seed.

Yet he was ordered to distinguish the Hebrew people from the others

by this sign: that, by cutting away the unnecessary flesh,

it should circumcise itself, and that all present and future offspring

of the male sex should be circumcised.

He commanded that boys newly removed from their mothers,

still inexperienced in life and ignorant of pain,

be consecrated on the eighth day after being stripped

of the foreskin.

[Col. 0966A] Whoever dared to violate so sacred a covenant,

ceasing to serve the law that had been enjoined,

would be disinherited from the kingdom and the life to come.

But when he wished to give him a sign that he should truly believe

that innumerable nations would someday come from his seed,

the Lord changed the name of each of them:

“Your wife shall not be called Sarai,” he said,

“but Sarra. And you shall no longer be called Abram;

with your name enlarged, you shall henceforth be called Abraham

for the nation that is to come.

This name is shared by you with your true wife

because she shall be the mother of the promised race—

nothing is more certain than this—

and, when the sun has completed another year,

she shall make you a father, although you may think

the promises of my power laughable,

and although your old age might seem to prevent it.

Yet I shall forgive your doubts,

and I shall give the future child a name

that will accuse this fault: Isaac.

He will unquestionably be the heir of our covenant,

which has been preserved, together with all the offspring of his line.

Nor shall Ishmael, born from Hagar’s seed,

be without distinction. Supported by my gift,

he shall beget from himself many thousands of powerful men,

and they shall establish kingdoms ruled by twelve leaders.”

He spoke. But Abram, eager to hasten the covenant he had received,

already striking a hundred years of age while his son had reached puberty,

marked himself, his firstborn son, all his dependents,

and all his servants with the prescribed sign.

Thus he made the people a new people and a source of the righteous.

Such was his devotion in receiving the law and fulfilling faith

by one and the same path.

What would such immediate and swift faith not merit?

For this was not fear, but sincere love

and the proof of a righteous servant—

to submit to every command with a tranquil mind.

Thus he won God’s favor. Previously God had been accustomed

only to being heard by him; after such service,

he now allowed himself to be seen by his minister.

And when righteous indignation stirred him to vengeance,

he nevertheless did not reject the sight of mortals,

for, as he was preparing to condemn the crimes of the earth

and destroy the guilty by fire,

he revealed to Abraham either his true form

or whatever form he knew he could be seen in,

and disclosed his name and number.

For while Abraham sat at home in the valley of Mamre,

three beings suddenly appeared, gleaming in the narrow light.

Abraham, stirred by the appearance of so great a presence,

ran out and, prostrate upon the ground, worshiped the Lord.

He also reverently venerated the three in a single form,

and prayed that they might permit him to serve them with a devout mind,

and, as the hours moved toward the height of the heat,

might not disdain to be refreshed by his household and his food.

So greatly did the appearance wander between his active senses

that he doubted whether it was a human substance

whom he knew in his mind to be God.

Nevertheless, the visitor assented, did not reject

the service of his devoted pupil,

and consecrated the food and hospitable tables offered to him.

When the meal had been taken away and the tables removed,

and the guests decided to depart from that place,

the host at once moved his steps from there

and clung as a companion to their side as they went,

rejoicing as their guest, yet shaking his breast,

which was shaken by mournful fear,

and drawing reverent terror upon himself in astonishment.

[Col. 0967A] For he saw the Lord direct silent faces and stern looks

against Sodom joined with Gomorrah,

and saw servants sent forth in peace as ministers of wrath.

When he learned what the Lord was preparing with so great a purpose,

as God disclosed the secret and explained the reason,

he dared of his own accord to question the Lord

whether he would destroy the city, guilty in all its crimes

because of its erring people, if it contained

fifty people tested by moral integrity.

When he said to him, “If I find such a number,

I shall certainly spare it for their sake,”

he continued: “What if five are lacking?

What if there are only forty?

What if perhaps ten fewer than that number?

What if twice five innocent people are found?

Will you too, best of gods, spare the city?”

And when he had said that he would forgive it even for that number,

he left the servant in the midst of his speech,

while the latter continued to plead,

and withdrew into his own kingdoms.

Meanwhile, the angelic beings dismissed from their heavenly seat

came to the land of Sodom. They found Lot sitting

before the gates of the city, with the sun already near the earth.

When he saw the angelic men shining with wondrous brilliance,

he thought they had descended from the highest heaven,

and, prostrating himself upon the earth, worshiped them.

He invited them into his house and, by entreaties,

prevailed upon them to avert the night beneath his roof.

He also urged them to share a meal,

and served innocent food and modest cups.

While they were preparing to indulge in sleep after eating,

behold, as the light was setting and night returning,

a foul, manly hand—or, if it may be said, a hand of the mob—

sprang out, along with youths.

Boys and old men alike burned with mad passions,

and they compelled Lot to hand over the guests

so that they might abuse them. What would insane lust not dare?

But he, wishing to soften the madness of the frenzied people,

offered his daughters, whose virginity remained undefiled,

for whatever use they might desire.

But the unbridled crowd, having fallen into deeper evil,

thought it a small disgrace to mingle itself with a lesser vice

unless it also involved itself in the greatest.

Therefore, to commit the unspeakable crime,

it attacked Lot, and now drove him with greater force

than human strength could repel.

At once both guests stripped away the angelic powers

concealed beneath their assumed bodies,

and, from the people raging in blinded madness,

they pulled Lot back and received him within the inner rooms

of the house. They urged him to leave immediately

the land that was destined to perish.

They no longer concealed in plain speech who they were,

why they had come, and what commands they intended shortly to fulfill.

They said that he could escape safely from this disaster,

and ordered him to gather his household,

his sons-in-law and his relatives,

and take them away with him.

But those men, touched by the same guilt as the crowd,

were enveloped by the same sentence.

They refused to believe a sound warning,

although there is little wonder that they refused to believe

when they thought it ridiculous that Lot should leave

after giving such advice.

Seeing him slow and dragging out endless delays,

both guests seized him by the hands with his wife,

led him and his daughters far beyond the walls,

and ordered him to hurry and climb the high mountains.

[Col. 0968A] Such was the law given: no one, heedless of the warning,

was to look back at the cities blazing with heavenly fire.

But Lot, fearing that the swift wrath of heaven

might overtake him more quickly than he could climb

the high mountains he had begun to ascend,

begged Segor for himself with tears—

a safe retreat and secure cave.

His tears were not empty: he obtained for many

the special gift of deliverance granted to him,

and made his merit greater by the gift.

By then the clouds that normally cover the sky in haste

were no longer ordinary clouds, but, through the Father’s power,

clouds thickened by the mixing of the elements—

such as Etna turns,

such as Inarime vomits forth,

such as Aponus exhales with its boiling waters,

such as the earth, shaken by nearby Vesuvius, belches out,

and such as the savage mouth of the Lycian Chimaera

breathes from the vast hollow of its triple furnace.

And wherever swift spirit, igniting deceptive sulfur,

flowing through a narrow passage,

escapes into the light, vaporous after the earth has burst open,

it gathered there.

Not because he could not also turn rains into fire—

he who could create the whole world from nothing—

but, as a good judge, he preferred to condemn

those whom he pitied for the ruin of their city and morals

with greater preparation, punishing them as an example.

Soon the harsh elements threatened;

they rushed together in a surging mass,

each enclosed by its own wind,

and joined the fuel of the flames into one body.

A curved shell of sulfurous metal covered

the impious lands and guilty cities.

The spirit, swift, gathering its strength through the narrow passage,

drove the mass that had been struck

to roar with such tremendous crash,

and, with repeated lightning driving the thunder,

terrified the minds of all who saw such spectacles.

Indeed, Lot’s wife—alas, pitiable woman!—

whether stunned by so great a fear,

or seized by foolish desire to rise up against the forbidden command,

a desire born in women’s minds—

whatever the cause may have been,

as she looked back at Sodom collapsing by force,

immediately suffered punishment for violating the law.

She was changed into a pillar of salt

and deprived of light; thus the unhappy woman

lost her soul together with her entire body,

so that no corpse remained with its form preserved.

[Col. 0968D] From there Lot entered Segor more swiftly,

fear forbidding grief, and horror at the disaster stunning him.

Then the sun rose, hotter with its entire fire,

sparkling with the radiance of wrath,

and directed its severe rays upon Sodom.

After they enveloped its lights in their flames,

the dissolved sulfurs dragged fires along with them,

and the conflagrations, distributed through the dry substance,

dripped onto their own torches.

A thunderbolt-like cloud fell headlong through the dense air,

enveloped the cities and raged across all the fields.

With mixed hissing it thundered,

and the fiery storm overcame all cries.

When it had found fuel in the burning earth

and settled upon the very sands,

fire raised an immense heap by joining its fuel,

and the flames returned from the earth to the stars.

[Col. 0969A] At last, when the rocks and echoing earth passed into ashes,

and the sands, utterly submerged, dissolved,

and the fields, their turf consumed, opened their hollow plains,

the moisture that had gripped the earth,

now poured out through open channels

and joining its forces, produced a separate sea.

What are we to think it was,

when a lake, swiftly formed and filled by sheer power,

was found where previously there had been a conflagration?

Thus the omnipotence of the supreme Judge

can turn fire into cold waters,

[Col. 0970A] and again turn waters into burning fire.

Nor are hidden mysteries absent here.

For the fact that waters are present where there was fire,

and that what was fiery above was extinguished by waters sent down,

perhaps signified the hot fires of lust,

the fuel contracted from the first father’s sin,

which would one day be extinguished by heavenly waters;

and that, in place of the fierce fires of justice

by which the former harsh law once prevailed,

there would be purification by saving and cleansing waters.

[Col. 0969]

CLAUDIUS MARIUS VICTOR’S LETTER TO SALMON, ABBOT, ON THE DEPRAVED MORALS OF HIS AGE. (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969B] If, as a suppliant petitioner, you have approached the Lord’s temple—

or rather, the temple’s guardian and the people’s teacher—

because there you see so many human beings,

so many altars of Christ;

but if it is pleasant to indulge in shared conversation,

your old guest lives here, my inmost Thesbon,

for whom, in the cave of the leafy vine,

grassy seats have been built upon living turf

for the rest of the brothers.

Tell me, then, Salmon, what fortune is now yours?

What is the state of your homeland? What pleases you in it?

For now, for the first time, while the treaty of peaceful life is disturbed,

the barbarian bears down upon the fields,

the wealth of men, and the cultivators of the land.

Neither villas built of solid marble,

nor rocks cut away and consumed for empty theaters,

are of use for a long life through the ages.

[Col. 0969C] But the inward plague and profound war

has long wearied us beneath a dense cloud of weapons—

all the more savage because the enemy is hidden.

And yet, alas, if the Sarmatian has devastated anything,

if the Vandal has burned anything,

or the swift Alan carried anything away,

we attempt, despite uncertain hopes and feeble efforts,

to restore something resembling the former state.

But the things that were lost through our own peril

we neglect, and through long neglect

we allow our minds to grow squalid.

We have given our necks over to chains,

and as prey we are bound by the shackles of sin.

It is sooner to cleanse the vine, cut away the thorns,

tear out the shattered doors and renew the broken window,

than to cultivate the broad fields of the soul,

the heart’s inner chambers,

and the fallen dignity of a mind held captive.

[Col. 0969D] No enemy, no dreadful famine, no disease, in short,

has brought this about. We were what we now are,

and, tested by these dangers, we are never made any better.

We remain beneath our vices, with no end to our guilt.

Nothing is sacred to us except profit;

and whatever is useful is called honorable.

We give the name of right to our vices,

and the miser takes the title of frugal.

But those who, through confessed vices and open crime,

could not conceal their frauds beneath the appearance of virtue,

nursed their wounds with hidden injuries—

people whom earthly wisdom draws,

ignorant of the truth.

Certain unhappy men are deceived and incited by error

while they investigate the causes of things and the courses of the stars:

what the shape of the heavens is,

why rivers do not perish through their long courses,

and along what boundary the sea lies spread.

They wish to know—alas, great sacrilege!—

things hidden from everyone and known only to God,

and they appear to know them.

These, Salmon, are the sins of our sex.

But your city’s disease of vice is slight

if feminine passions have not burned more fiercely.

Before dawn, Salmon, the damp night will bury us in darkness

before I can pass through the morals of this crowd,

which, though living under God’s law,

lives under the law of men.

Shame! They never sin without our guilt,

for unless they were easily drawn into crimes,

we would not wish them to live by our vices.

Nor would they buy rigid garments embroidered with gold,

nor Serian fleeces,

nor stones brought by the merchant from the whole world,

at the price of the sad sighs of their estates.

[Col. 0970C] Yet, shamelessly, we add empty anxieties.

If Lesbia has appeared weighed down with unfamiliar gems,
and Pessina has shone tenfold in new purple,

each woman immediately demands the same adornment for herself.

Thus, when they strive to confront one another with varied appearances

and to set different faces against men,

is this not the man’s fault?

What are white lead, vermilion,

and a hundred poisonous colors doing upon a chaste body?

The honor of the mind and the dignity of character

are the bonds of holy marriage.

If beauty is pleasing, love will yield as the years come;

honesty alone is ignorant of old age.

For that they inspect everything through endless wanderings,

that they feed, that they carry many things,

that they speak of many things—

is this not our vice?

Leaving aside Paul and Salmon,

what of the songs of Maro about the Phoenician woman,

and Naso’s about Corinna,

and the applause received by Flaccus’ lyre

or by the stage of Terence?

We are the cause of these things;

we shamefully supply fuel to such flames.

Are we free from blame?

For just as excellent mirrors reflect the forms presented to them,

so wives follow the examples presented by men.

But why is the unhappy woman alone at fault

when a vicious wife pleases a foolish husband?

One enemy rages everywhere in a spreading storm,

and it is no wonder that those subdued by the terror of war are defeated.

But if, corrected, we possessed sound understanding,

and if the mind, freed from black clouds and cleansed by Christ,

lay open;

if we pressed the sickle of the Word into our hearts

and wished to cut away the knots of ancient vices,

no force could prevail against Christ’s servants.

[Col. 0971A] The Alans’ Rhiphaean bow would not overthrow us,

nor would servile war overturn everything,

nor those who now rage proudly amid our ruin.

Nevertheless, in your people a considerable crowd of good men flourishes,

and the Church nourishes many devout souls.

There are certainly many innocent men,

best of fathers, whom I would wish to resemble.

Nor are there lacking in our flock those whom each sex

may return victorious, crowned with its own crowns.

[Col. 0972A] And if anything commends the homeland,

if there is anything in it that gives pleasure—

what is it? This one thing: these are the consolations of life.

Come now, dear Father, tell me in turn

what repose worthy of you has received you.

Ever since I departed, carrying you in my heart

and disputing with you, I shall recall my joys,

Salmon, certainly not unwillingly,

nor shall I praise you by the evidence of good bulls.

But now the hour that closes the day reminds us

to rise and hasten to the sacred assemblies of the holy.

Tomorrow’s light will come free to our words.

YEAR OF OUR LORD 427.

MEROBAUDES THE SCHOLASTIC.

[Col. 0971]

NOTICE.

(From Galland.)

[Col. 0971]

[Col. 0971B] I. There is very little that can be said about Merobaudes the scholastic,

and even that is not wholly certain.

Nevertheless, it seems established that some people have wrongly confused

our author with Flavius Merobaudes,

who first became consul with Gratian in the year 377

and again with Saturninus in 383.

The Latin Pacatus [Note: [Col. 0971C] Latinus Pacatus, Panegyric, chapter 28, p. 334, Paris edition.]

and Philostorgius [Note: [Col. 0971C] Philostorgius, Ecclesiastical History, book VIII, § 1.]

remember him.

Yet I would agree with Sirmond [Note: [Col. 0971C] Sirmond, on Sidonius, p. 1235, note b, works, vol. I.]

that Sidonius sang the following lines about our Merobaudes

[Note: [Col. 0971C] Sidonius, poem 9, lines 293–298.]:

“Nor shall that third man now be read,

who, once leaving his native Baetis,

sought the thirst of watery Ravenna.

For him the citizens, who applauded,

and the prince dear for his popularity,

placed a statue in the Trojan Forum.”

You may read corresponding testimony in Hydatius,

who, under the nineteenth year of Theodosius the Younger,

has the following [Note: [Col. 0972C] Hydatius, Chronicle, p. 302, works of Sirmond, vol. II, Paris edition.]:

“Merobaudes, Asturius’ son-in-law, is sent as his successor—Asturius being master of both military commands—a man noble by birth and, above all, comparable with the ancients in eloquence and in the pursuit of poetry; he is also distinguished by the testimony of statues.”

This passage did not escape Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0972C] Tillemont, History of the Emperors, vol. VI, p. 231.].

[Col. 0972B] II. Merobaudes, then, of whom we are speaking,

was perhaps Spanish by nationality.

He left his native land, disturbed by barbarian incursions,

and fled to Italy, where he was highly cultivated

in humane letters and was held in especially great esteem

among the Romans, who honored him with a statue.

Boethius praises the rhetor Merobaudes,

perhaps our author, once and again

[Note: [Col. 0972C] Boethius, works, pp. 807 and 835, Basel editions of 1540 and 1570.].

Concerning the Merobaudes of whom we are speaking,

see more in Nicolas Antonius

[Note: [Col. 0972C] Nicolas Antonius, Bibliotheca vetus Hispana, book III, chapter 3, p. 191.].

Nor would I have you overlook the learned men

who are engaged in composing the Literary History of France

[Note: [Col. 0972C] Literary History of France, vol. II, p. 338.].

III. A poem on Christ is also circulated under the name of Merobaudes.

By that title he must surely be considered worthy

to be counted among the sacred company of Spanish poets,

Juvencus, Prudentius, and the others.

We know, moreover, that this poem of twenty-nine verses

has been printed several times

[Col. 0972C]—both by Georg Fabricius among the Christian poets,

and by Andreas Rivinus together with the poems

of Rusticius Helpidius, Lactantius, and others—

as well as in the Paris, Cologne, and Lyons libraries of the Fathers.

[Col. 0971]

THE POEM OF MEROBAUDES THE SPANISH SCHOLASTIC ON CHRIST. (C, S)

[Col. 0971]

[Col. 0971D] “True offspring of God, older than all the years,

now begotten, though you have always existed,

discoverer of life and light,

[Note: [Col. 0971D]

He imitates Juvencus, Gospel History, book IV, line 482:

‘Discoverer of life and light.’

[Col. 0972D] He also says in book I, line 35:

‘Lord, discoverer of heaven and earth.’

Nor does Prudentius speak otherwise, Cathemerinon, hymn 4, line 9:

‘Creator of things and discoverer of the world.’

This is plainly in the Virgilian phrase, Aeneid, book XII, line 829:

‘He, smiling, discoverer of men and things.’

[Col. 0973A] Moreover, this use of the word ‘discoverer’ in the sense

of ‘creator’ is absent from the latest complete dictionary

of the Latin language published at Padua.]”

parent before your mother,

the Father of equal age who sent you from the stars,

and, poured into the seed of the Word,

ordered you to dwell in a virgin’s womb

and enter the limbs of a body,

to remain in a small dwelling.

No dwelling contains you;

you, who at the first light saw what you would create

when the world was coming into being,

yourself the maker, yourself your work,

deigned to undergo the adverse changes of age

and to endure the differing conditions of this body,

to assume humanity,

so that you might reveal God,

lest slippery error and the deceiving skill

of the varied world, long practiced in deception,

allow mortal hearts to remain for so many ages

in such great delusion.

Your mother, conscious of her childbearing,

knew you to be God the Creator;

the astonished fears of the animals perceived you as such.

The Magi, scanning you with anxious eyes

under a new star,

first saw you in heaven and, following the light,

found you.

You release guilty hearts,

and restore souls that have escaped

to bodies already dead.

Pure, you penetrate to the shades

and, immortal, enter the hiding places of death.

For you alone there was no beginning or end

in dying;

but, when night has been driven back,
you ascend to heaven, to the Father,
and in eternal order remove contamination
from purified lands.

You alone are the Father’s companion;

you are the innocent Spirit,

and, though so often one,

you are simple in the threefold light.

Who, unless for all, could believe otherwise? Who could believe that you were able to die, you who were able to restore life?”

YEAR OF OUR LORD 450.

SAINT ORIENTIUS, BISHOP OF AUSCIUM.

[Col. 0973]

[Col. 0973]

PROLEGOMENON.

(From Galland.)

[Col. 0973C] I. There is a remarkable disagreement among scholars

concerning Orientius’ homeland, profession,

and the period in which he flourished.

Baronius considers him a native of Tarragona

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Baronius, under the year 484, § 138.],

who later became bishop of Illiberis;

he also identifies him with Oresius,

to whom a letter of Sidonius is addressed

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Sidonius, book IX, letter 12.].

“That opinion,” says the distinguished man,

“is easily persuaded by the name of his homeland,

his devotion to poetic ability,

and the sweetness of his writing,

which are praised equally by Sigebert

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Sigebert, On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 34.]

and by Sidonius.”

Many others agreed with Baronius:

Delrio [Note: [Col. 0973D] Delrio, preface to Orientius’ Commonitorium.],

Nicolas Antonius [Note: [Col. 0973D] Nicolas Antonius, Bibliotheca Hispana vetus, book IV, chapter 1, vol. I, p. 206.],

Cave [Note: [Col. 0973D] Cave, Literary History, vol. I, p. 503.],

Schurtzfleisch [Note: [Col. 0973D] Schurtzfleisch, preface to Orientius’ Commonitorium.],

Leyser [Note: [Col. 0973D] Leyser, History of Medieval Poetry, p. 77.],

Basnage [Note: [Col. 0973D] Basnage, on Canisius’ Thesaurus, vol. I, pp. 164 ff.],

and others.

Fabricius dissents from them

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Fabricius, Bibliotheca Latina medii aevi, vol. V, pp. 508 ff., Hamburg edition.].

He acknowledges Orientius as bishop of Auscium,

but persuades himself that the author of the Commonitorium

was a different man.

We pass over the others who hold different opinions,

among them Sammarthanus,

who, relying on an ancient document of the Church of Auscium,

composed at the beginning of the twelfth century,

asserts that Orientius occupied that see from 323 to 344

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Sammarthanus, Gallia Christiana nova, vol. I, p. 973.].

On the other hand, after examining the matter much more carefully,

the very learned authors of the Literary History of France

have transmitted a more coherent account,

following Martene [Note: [Col. 0974D] Martene, on Orientius’ Commonitorium, vol. V of Thesaurus novus anecdotorum, p. 19.]

and Oudin [Note: [Col. 0974D] Oudin, Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers, vol. I, pp. 1068 ff.].

Accordingly, when speaking about Orientius,

we shall chiefly follow these authors

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Literary History of France, vol. II, pp. 254 ff.].

II. First, the author himself calls himself Orientius,

not Oresius, Orentius, or Orontius,

as he says [Note: [Col. 0974D] Orientius, Commonitorium, book II, line 417.]:

“So that Orientius may conquer all sinners.”

Venantius Fortunatus, who wrote in Gaul

in the middle of the sixth century,

likewise calls him Orientius

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Venantius Fortunatus, book I of The Life of Saint Martin, line 17, Bibliotheca Patrum, Paris, vol. VIII, p. 753.]:

“And he touched on a few things with Orientius’ flourishing voice.”

Nor do the manuscript codices from which his little work was taken

give any other form.

But Sigebert of Gembloux says

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Sigebert of Gembloux, cited work.]:

“Orentius wrote the Commonitorium in heroic meter,

to delight the reader with its sweet brevity.”

Moreover, that Orientius was a Gaul by nationality,

or at least lived in Gaul,

and that he witnessed the disasters inflicted on the Gallic people

by the Goths in the middle of the fifth century,

he himself clearly testifies in these verses

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Orientius, Commonitorium, book II, lines 181–184.]:

“Through streets, villas, through fields and crossroads,
