through villages, along all the roads on either side,

death, grief, destruction, slaughter, fires, and lamentation—

all Gaul smoked upon a single pyre.”

[Col. 0975A] From this we infer the period in which our author flourished,

namely around the year 440.

Fortunatus and Sigebert are indeed silent about his episcopate.

But their silence should not be considered so weighty

that anyone could derive from it a sufficiently firm argument

for denying Orientius episcopal dignity,

especially if we consider that the earlier Fortunatus

disposes of the matter in a single verse.

Nevertheless, the Acts of Saint Orientius,

bishop of Auscium, are thought to remove

whatever difficulty there may be in this matter.

They were first published by Philip Labbe

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Labbe, Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum librorum, vol. II, section 3, pp. 596 ff.]

and were later incorporated into the Bollandist Acts of the Saints

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, May, vol. I, pp. 61 ff.].

Although they do not belong to the earliest antiquity,

they nevertheless recount in them certain deeds

that are clearly understood to correspond

with various passages of Orientius’ Commonitorium.

Therefore, as the learned men mentioned above rightly judge,

no one can fairly deprive those Acts altogether of credibility

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Literary History of France, cited passage.].

### III

These Acts accordingly report [Note: Bolland., *Act. SS.*, cited above, p. 61, no. 1] that the most blessed Orientius, having laid aside the squalor of worldly vice, devoted himself wholly, with a chaste mind, to the divine Majesty; and, having attained higher dignities, ascended to the episcopal dignity of the see of the city of Auch. Here we must first reject the conjecture of Basnage [Note: Basnag., cited above, p. 164, § 2] and Fabricius [Note: Fabric., cited above, p. 509], fabricated from a mistaken understanding of the words that follow—namely, that Orientius had initially been devoted to idolatry.

The same Acts continue:

> For, being thoroughly instructed in ecclesiastical doctrines, he corrected the people entrusted to him by sacred preaching, and **destroyed the perversity of the pagans**; and, having taught them most fully with such instruction, he led them, **despising the vileness of idols**, to recognize their Creator and to attain his law by receiving the grace of baptism.

These words, to speak with Martène [Note: Marten., cited above, p. 19], how well do they agree with what Orientius writes [Note: Orient., *Orat.* 24, lines 56 ff., below, p. 196]!

> We too have risen from the dregs of the heathen,  
> and at last have broken through that darkness,  
> when we heed the spiritual angels.

A very sound interpretation by the learned man. For who, after all, does not see that Orientius is speaking here not in his own name, but in the name of his neophytes, for whose instruction he composed this Oration? When they heeded the spiritual angels—that is, the bishops, whom we know to be called by that name in the Apocalypse [Note: Rev. 1:20; 2:1, 8, 12, 18; 3:1, 7, 14]—they rejoiced that they had risen from the dregs of the heathen and at last broken through that darkness. Let the empty fiction of Orientius’s idolatry therefore be dismissed.

### IV

Moreover, from the same Acts we learn [Note: *Act. SS.*, cited above, no. 3] that, when Orientius had already reached an advanced age, he undertook an embassy at the request of Theodoric, king of the Goths, who at that time resided at Toulouse and ruled extensively throughout Aquitania and Novempopulania, so that the holy bishop was subject to him. His purpose was, by his prayers, to avert from the Gothic king the terrible attack of the Roman generals Aetius and Litorius. Salvian gives an excellent account of this embassy [Note: Salvian, *On the Government of God*, book VII, chapters 9 and 10], entirely consonant with what is related in our Acts.

This provided Orientius with the occasion to describe the slaughter and fires by which all Gaul smoked, as we learned above. The war unsuccessfully conducted by Litorius against the Goths is reported by Hydatius, Prosper, and Cassiodorus in their chronicles to have occurred in the year 439 after Christ; consequently, Orientius’s embassy to that same Litorius must also be assigned to that year. In what year the blessed bishop later departed this life is entirely unknown.

His memory is commemorated in ecclesiastical calendars on the first of May. In the *Genuine Martyrology of Usuard*, his epitaph on that day reads as follows [Note: Usuard, *Genuine Martyrology*, p. 74, Paris edition of 1718]:

> At Auch, Saint Orientius, bishop, who, adorned with virtues, rested in a holy death.

To this we may add the following from Sammarthanus [Note: Sammarth., *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. I, p. 974]:

> “The very rich monastery of Saint Orientius in the city of Auch,” he says, “which we read was founded by Bernard-Otho, count of Fézensac, glories in possessing his sacred relics. At least, he was resting there in the year 1068.”

### V

As for some particulars concerning the literary monuments of our author, it will be preferable to present them in the words of the distinguished Martène [Note: Marten., cited above, p. 17]:

> “Here, reader,” he says, “you have the *Commonitorium of Saint Orientius*, one of the most celebrated among the ancient Christian poets. Learned men had hitherto lacked this poem, and especially the most illustrious compiler of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, Cardinal Baronius [Note: Baron., under the year 484, § 138], who lamented that every monument of a noble intellect had perished and that even the name itself had almost been buried in oblivion. At last it has been possible to excavate it and return it cleansed of the rust that covered it.
>
> “The learned Martin Delrio, a priest of the Society of Jesus, partly fulfilled his wishes. Having discovered the first book of the *Commonitorium* in a manuscript codex of the monastery of Anchin, he rejoiced as though he had found a precious treasure and took care to have it printed as quickly as possible, in the year 1600, together with all the errors and lacunae with which it abounded. Nevertheless, he believed that his codex did not contain the complete work of Orientius, but that several portions were missing—at least those concerning the other sins, gluttony, sloth, pride, and perhaps more.
>
> “Nor was his opinion mistaken. For in fact an entire second book was missing. I later made it public, together with other verses by the same author—on the Nativity, the Trinity, the names of the Lord, and prayers—copied from an extremely old codex of the distinguished church of Saint Martin of Tours, written about eight hundred years ago, through the kindness of the distinguished Gatian de Galiczon, then precentor of that church and now bishop of Agde. This manuscript, cleansed of the rust covering it, I published some years ago, in 1700; and I now issue it again, corrected against the manuscript codex, in 1717, with the errors found in Delrio’s edition corrected and the lacunae filled, although I have scrupled to alter those passages in which the author at some point violated the exact rules of poetic art. For even in ancient authors we ought to venerate the very errors themselves.”

Thus far the learned writer. We omit here the remaining judgments of scholars concerning the value of the work, as well as the various editions of it; they can readily be found in Leyser, Fabricius, and the authors of the *Literary History of France* at the places cited.

[Col. 0977]

## The *Commonitorium* of Saint Orientius

(From the manuscript codex of the distinguished church of Saint Martin of Tours.) (C, S)

Whoever hastens toward the rewards of eternal life,  
and desires what is to be perpetuated rather than what is to perish,  
the life that will unlock heaven, drive away death, avoid hardships,  
and run along a fortunate path—learn the way.

[5] For we, overcome both by the vices of the flesh and by time,  
travel an earthly road, or rather a road of sorrow.  
Our only joy amid these mingled prayers is this:  
that, although we do not do it ourselves, at least others may do it;  
so that, since we now spend this age—which immediately flees—  
captured by its treacherous enticements.

Lascivious, wretched, deceitful, brief, changeable, vain—  
alas, the origin of evils rushes headlong.

Having abandoned all these things, which are destined to die quickly,  
hold fast with strong faith to what will not perish.

[15] Come, then: lend attentive ears and an unoccupied mind.  
I must teach life to you; you must seek life.

But, so that the teaching of our little book may be better  
and the order of the poem may keep to the right paths,  
we ask you, almighty God, with heart and voice.  
Without you, Christ, it is not pleasing to unloose the tongue:

[20] You who remove darkness by recalling light to the blind,  
insert hearing into deaf ears,  
drive away the savage diseases of body and mind,  
and in your mercy are accustomed to loosen the mouths of the mute.

[25] The task of our heart and mouth rests with you.  
Grant me understanding; grant me the power to speak,  
so that your gifts may invigorate our tongue  
and, through you, speech concerning you may be pleasing to you.

When, at your command, your order had surpassed all nature,  
and the she-ass, using our voice,

[30] had spoken, and had terrified Balaam,  
who was subduing his own back with goads,  
with the marvelous speech of a four-footed creature—

he who, at the repeated and urgent requests of the trembling king,  
was preparing dreadful words against the holy people—

[35] could not properly subdue the tongue that had been moved against him,  
saying one thing with his mouth and desiring another in his heart.

For although he had intended to curse, he began to bless,  
offering words prepared for one purpose to another.

Therefore, unless you, Christ, supply eloquence and understanding,  
unless you, Christ, govern the soul’s efforts,

[40] all human mouths, mute and brute alike, will be held back;  
and what they are even able to do, they will not be able to do.

First you must recognize a twofold life,  
granted by the Lord with reason to humanity:

[45] because, although the body is brutish under the weight of earth,  
the soul is brought to life by the breath of God;  
otherwise the soul would feel no end to its loss,  
and life in this frail body would be brief.

The principle of birth first brings one life to everyone;  
care, and one’s own merits, bring the other.

[50] Birth is not ours, nor is prolonged life ours;  
but one can prepare the life that follows this life.

Although by the Lord’s will we receive both,  
neither comes to us unless God commands it,

[55] the first is nevertheless carried swiftly along a downward course;  
the life that follows is granted for all time.

Into the first we come ignorant, without reward;  
the other is attained through supreme labor.

We are born so that, awake with all our devotion,  
we may seek the Lord of heaven, earth, and sea;

[60] we seek him in order to know who he is, what he is like, how great he is, and what he does,  
so that we may be able to know him by judgment.

We know him so that, once we have discovered what is worthy of praise, we may honor it;  
we honor him so that he may grant everlasting life.

[65] And we honor him not with incense offered, nor with blood poured out,  
not drunk with wine, nor swollen with feasts.  
Gold, clothing, perfume, cattle, libations, jewels,  
and whatever human beings consider rare or precious  
lie before God as worthless masses of earthly weight,

[70] as filth, as refuse, dishonored.

Everything belongs to him whom we confess ourselves to be.  
Nothing is our own: he possesses it; he gave it.

For behold, the prophet proclaims in a holy mouth:

> I do not want your goats; I do not want your calves.

[75] “The appearance of the field is mine, and the glory of heaven;  
for the world is mine, and whatever is in the world.

“Let the vows owed to the Holy One be paid with a devoted heart;  
let a sacrifice of praise and a pure voice celebrate me.”

Therefore, my reader, you will not be able to plead anything  
that is difficult for you in these instructions.

[80] It is not far away; it need not be sought elsewhere.  
No deed, expense, or price is required.

It is enough that you believe with a devout heart  
and ask with a trusting mouth  
the Lord of the world, the Father of all things,  
in whose power are both good and evil,

[85] who surpasses the words of one who speaks in surpassing greatness,  
the one, incorporeal, everlasting, holy,  
embracing all things and always one in everything.

But why do I use only such bare words,  
as though God had given no instructions concerning this?

[90] First, remember what was ordained under the ancient Law,  
which long ago was written on solid tablets,  
and which grace, given through the Lord Christ, now renews,  
as the venerable voice of the Gospel proclaims:

that what the stones formerly held, our hearts should now hold,  
and that faith, repeated twice, should be more abundant.

[95] Love the Lord with your whole affection and all your inward being,  
and love your God with your whole heart.

And rightly so: what could you ever more justly  
repay for such great gifts laid upon you?

He who, when you lay as clay in the earthly dregs,  
removed from you the mud of merely temporal existence;

[100] who gives you the fact that you are composed of limbs,  
that you are moved by the mind,  
that you speak with the tongue,  
that you understand through reason,

that you touch with your hands, walk with your foot, see with your eyes,  
hear with your ear, smell with your nostrils, and taste with your mouth;

before any merit of yours, in his own mercy he supplies these things,  
as Father and Lord of body and soul alike;

[105] and, not content with this gift alone, by which he furnished you with limbs  
and enriched you with the senses—

he who grants life and bestows the comforts of life,  
so that everything may be provided for you with delights:

behold, heaven hangs above you, earth withdraws beneath you,  
the air is balanced, the ocean heaves;

[110] nights and days succeed one another, months follow the years,  
the sun shines, the stars give light, the moon glows red.

Spring, gentle with varied flowers, pours itself out in budding growth;  
summer, already heavy with fruits, ripens the fields;  
autumn, wet with new wine, is rich in olives;  
winter, with fires kindled, knows no cold.

[115] You strengthen hanging roofs against the rains;  
you keep the winds outside by setting houses against them.

Combing the shaggy backs of wool-bearing sheep with the two-toothed shears,  
you cover your chilled limbs with soft wrappings.

[120] Nor are smooth coverings of snowy linen lacking;  
there are also cloaks made from Eastern fleeces.

The fertile earth, once seed has been cast, will return it to you;  
the Seres gather those [fleeces] from lofty trees.

Finally, throughout the whole revolving year,  
whatever you possess, all of it is given to you by God’s care.

[125] The field grows green with its harvest, the hill is clothed with vines;  
from different trees you gather ripe fruit.

By carefully tending a fertile garden,  
you take useful vegetables whenever the season permits.

You kindle whatever fat pinewood you choose for lights;  
a waxen flame shines upon noble tables.

[130] Nor is earth alone commanded to serve humanity,  
subjected to it for various uses.

Whatever is carried near the clouds, whatever  
is drawn up and moves across the deep sea,

you seek from here and there by countless arts—  
now with deceptive bait, now with linen woven into nets.

[135] Now a fish is drawn up for you from the bottom of the whirlpool;  
now birds are caught in the highest air.

Dense ranks of wild animals burst forth for the hunter,  
struck from afar by javelins or caught in nets.

You attack fleeing creatures with the point of a weapon;  
you stop the fierce horse with dogs and crush its mouth with a bit.

You force oxen beneath the curved yokes and goats to the milking pails;  
sweet honey drips from the curled honeycombs.

From rocks you produce gems, from sands gold,  
and you cook sluggish metals from the earth in fire.

You distinguish grasses that heal grievous diseases;  
with diligent skill you drive away deadly evil.

[140] Moreover, so that you may receive merchandise from a foreign shore,  
and give your own goods to others and seek what belongs to others,  
you traverse rivers by oar and seas by sail;  
there you travel long roads without labor.

Or, if you fear the sea, you will move wagons,  
and the earth, marked by your wheels, will be spread beneath you.

Then, if your tossed-about body seeks gentle leisure,  
moist baths will receive it, covered with dust;

the whole body is stripped of its clothing in the hollow bath,  
and you warm your weary limbs in subdued waters.

[145] With so many and such great blessings granted to you  
as a gift from the Lord, what worthy thing at last do you return  
for his devoted love?

By what resources, by what gifts,  
or through what degree of service could you repay these things?

Yet the Lord, to whom everything belongs, does not seek these things:  
it is enough that the beloved servant love the Lord.

[150] This too follows as the form of the second commandment:  
that your neighbor should be to you as you are to yourself.

I know the law that brings salvation, with its lasting gift,  
which looks to everyone through one duty.

For when the care of another is entrusted to me,  
my own care must likewise be entrusted to another.

[155] Behold, animal leads animal to fertile pastures;  
the happy little cow lowing calls to its own herd.

They answer with a murmur and speak in whatever voice they can;  
in turn, the obedient tongue is accustomed to lick.

The sea does not lack affection for what it hides beneath the waves;  
the bird has affection for the bird, and the wild creature gently for the wild creature.

[160] Then, whenever a predator comes from any herd,  
pressing the weaker with stronger claw or mouth—  
whether the matter concerns birds or wild beasts—  
help is summoned from every side.

They stretch out aid for their captured companion through running,  
herd, voice, and flight;  
and, if they cannot rescue it, they nevertheless wish to do so.

[165] When they thus preserve themselves by nature’s gift alone,  
though they possess neither counsel nor reason,  
what wonder is it if, following the Lord’s revered commands,  
human beings bind one another through mutual care,

and a brother, skilled through use, ingenuity, circumstances, and reason,  
acts for another’s benefit as for his own?

[170] Hence comes that deservedly pleasing saying,  
which binds the human race by equal condition:

> Do not do to others whatever you do not want done to you;  
> and do to others what you want done to you.

Whatever a person’s kind, sex, religious practice, or age,  
who could deny that this is right, who could deny that it is good?

[175] What does this compact commandment not embrace broadly?  
What could be conveyed more fully in such brevity?

For I would simply not wish evil things to be done to me, just as, conversely, I wish good things to be done to me.

No judge is needed, no teacher is sought:  
we know for ourselves what is good and what is evil.

[180] You will certainly rejoice if someone, when you are traveling by night,  
kindly leads you to a neighboring lodging.

You too, concerned for him, receive into prepared shelter  
the one who will be a traveler late at night.

If naked, you wish to be covered with clothing;  
if thirsty, you wish to be offered cups;  
if hungry, you wish to be satisfied with food.

[185] Let the similar cause of your own need also move you:  
share cloaks, cups, and food with the poor.

Behold, when you fall, you ask for a hand;  
when sorrowful, consolation;  
when frightened, help;  
when uncertain, advice.

Offer these things to the sorrowful, uncertain, frightened, and fallen;  
in a similar situation, act so that, as one who loves, you may be loved.

[190] Certainly you do not want to be accused of a false crime;  
do not accuse others of a false crime.

You hate a thief: beware of theft.  
You do not want to lose by force what is yours: do nothing violently.

You do not want agreements made with you to waver in uncertain preparation;  
return the faith once promised with a steadfast heart.

[195] If someone has slandered you, you would wish to cut out his tongue;  
take care that your envious words mark no one.

Whenever you ask for a loan, you want to receive money immediately;  
let a ready hand help the one asking for a loan.

You condemn those puffed up with pride: then put down your own swelling;  
let your inferior not know what you flee from among the heights.

[200] Certainly, if she is your sister, mother, or beloved wife—

[Col. 0983D] Line 264. Earlier editions read *aut arvum* (“or the field”), a reading that strangely tormented the ingenuity of learned men. Delrio, who first published this poem, conjectured that the passage should be restored as *aut arvum solidum* (“or the solid field”). Lipsius thought it should read *aut carnem solidans* (“or solidifying flesh”). Fabricius judged that the first reading should be retained. A recent anonymous corrector believed that *aut artus* (“or limbs”) should be read instead of *aut arvum*, as though the author were alluding to the embalmed bodies of the Egyptians, which spices solidify. Jacobus Sirmondus—what does the republic of letters not owe to his learning?—more successfully emended the verse in his notes on Sidonius’s *Letters*, book IX, letter 13: “or Arab dust and perfume hold it firm.” This emendation agrees entirely with our manuscript, in which *aut Aravum* is read. For the ancients frequently used the letter *v* for *b*.

At the same place Delrio reads: *tenet* (“holds”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 265. Another reading: *formanda* (“to be formed”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 268. Delrio: *excussit* (“shook out”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 275. Another reading: *animarum* (“of souls”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 283. Delrio: *Aspiceus*, and he thinks it should be read *Aspicis ut densi* (“you see how dense”). Lipsius instead proposes *Spiceus ex densi* (“spiky from dense”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 286. Delrio: *virent* (“are green”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 290. Delrio: “this departs, that arrives.”

[Col. 0984D] Line 294. Another reading: *succedit* (“succeeds”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 298. Another reading: *vivet* (“will live”).

[Col. 0984D] Line 307. The martyr Pionius uses the same argument to prove the eternity of punishments:

> “You see and recount the conflagration of that people, the flame boiling among the rocks. Consider also the fire of Lycia and of various islands flowing from the deepest bowels of the earth; or, if you could not recognize these things, consider the use of hot water—not, I say, water that is made, but water that is born. Look at the warm springs, breathing out there from which flames are accustomed to be extinguished. From where do you think this fire comes, unless because it is joined to the fire of hell?”

See also, if desired, what the martyr Methodius observed concerning this matter in his book *On the Resurrection*, preserved by Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 234.

if she attempts, under this revered name, to stain their lives  
with the stain of a grave reputation,  
you act as a son, brother, or husband  
with watchful devotion to perpetual chastity.

[205] If an adulterer attacks this revered woman,  
you do not think the sword sufficient for vengeance.

Are you not guilty of the same punishment  
if you too secretly try to seduce chaste marriages?

For this reason the Lord commanded under the first Law  
that crimes should be weighed out with equal punishments:

[210] loss for loss, wound for wound,  
a tooth torn out for a tooth, eyes for eyes.

And likewise, so that before the judge the bold man might pay back his own life,  
the one who had desired to seize another’s life—  
and, though guilty before the judgment, could not call it unjust—  
vengeance was decreed for crimes.

[215] And although the grace of Christ has changed these things for the better,  
teaching what is gentle rather than what is violent,  
nevertheless whatever either law commands is right,  
whether you restore quickly or act patiently.

Yet the better person is the one who rejoices in Christ as his avenger:  
let him preserve for the Lord what the Lord gave him.

[220] Therefore complete by pious vows and holy deeds  
what this present life and the future life approve:

so that you, whom honor recommends while it swiftly flees,  
may be received after death by everlasting glory.

Remember, assured by our instructions,  
that everything now thought by fools to be destined to perish will remain;

[225] and believe that souls, their same limbs returning,  
will receive again the body’s own covering.

Face, color, blood, veins, skin, bones, and hair—  
as they now pass away, so they will come again.

Not only what stones carefully placed over tombs preserve,  
or what Arab dust and perfume hold solid,

[230] but, sooner than speech can say, a portion will return to firm limbs from tombs,  
a portion from rivers.

What the wind diminishes with its breath, what the beast consumes with its bite,  
what flame burns up, and what collapse crushes—  
all will be present; all will come together from different parts:

[235] one part from a bird, another from a fish, another torn by wild beasts.  
And what long age now gradually dissolves,  
the Lord’s trumpet will restore in an instant.

Thus, according to the merits of their deeds,  
in the same body in which they performed good or evil,

[240] when flesh has returned for the movements of their souls,  
punishment will receive the guilty and glory the righteous.

Why then do you doubt, when what precedes demonstrates  
that faith in what is to come should be clear to you?

Look at the woods stripped bare by winter’s cold,  
now luxuriating in hair that had seemed lost.

[245] The vine that stood mourning, its branches stripped,  
is clothed with leaves and dressed in fruits.

The spiky reed grows yellow with dense ears,  
the grain that only recently was rotten in the earth.

The fields that now lay rough beneath dreary dormancy  
laugh with fresh growth and blush with flowers.

[250] The year itself, enclosed in its various months,  
has the appearance of death when the season changes:

when spring comes, autumn departs; heat drives away cold;  
and, as with human affairs, one thing arrives and another departs.

Yet this continues in an eternal cycle,  
as long as God permits it,  
and revolves in alternating service;

[255] while the moving wheel of the long year follows itself,  
it is born and dies, falls and returns.

For our end does not receive an end,  
and the death by which we first die dies forever.

While movement and sensation remain forever for the one who will live,  
every human being lives through everlasting time.

[260] Humanity will live—but here tears follow my words.

For I think the human lot would have been better  
if, with the awareness of life, it laid down the awareness of punishment,  
and the one born became like the unborn,

than if now, with sins ruling throughout the entire age,  
life is extinguished while punishments continue.

[265] Do not believe, for the sake of shortening punishment,  
that the swift springs consume the appointed flame.

Look at hills immersed in eternal fires,  
burning continually and yet not diminishing;

and behold cold springs and blue rivers  
always pouring out their waters, yet always possessing them.

[270] Thus the avenging fire will always ravage the wretched,  
yet always preserve its rich fuel for itself.

If you think these things false, you will rightly learn them after the truth;  
but you will escape falsehood if you fear the truth now.

Therefore, if after death life follows—everlasting life,  
bringing joy to the righteous and torturing the guilty—

[275] strive with all your strength and all your prayers  
to continue along the paths that lead to righteousness.

Trample down the world together with the ruler of the world,  
and flee from trusting in wanton pleasures.

Above all, always despise celebrated faces,  
and take judgment away from your eyes.

[280] No one will bear gleaming fires without his clothing being touched by them.  
No one amid trumpets will fail to draw their sound through his ear.

No one amid flowers and the alluring circles of perfumes  
will fail to pluck a rose continually with his nostrils.

No one long thirsty and scorched by much sun  
will lean over cold waters without drinking.

[285] No one traveling on foot through winter weather will fail to be sprinkled by rain and drenched.

No one, even amid the walls in wartime,  
will act either wholly secure or wholly safe.

A meeting offers the sight; soon the eyes  
conceive flames from the sight and give birth to wickedness.

[290] Just as, when a fisherman casts his hook with deceptive tricks,  
the mind is first caught and afterward dies,  
so, alas, woman, the serpent’s deceit first defiled you with evil and, through you, drove humanity back from the Lord.

You were the cause of the good that was taken away;  
you are the gate of death;  
you were quickly deceived, and you quickly deceive.

[295] Come, then: since you strive to keep your heart unstained by any blemish  
and to be pure in a pure spirit,  
you will thus flee a praised face as you would snares, powerful fires, and sharp poisons.

I shall not now recount how many peoples, over so many ages,  
pleasing female faces have destroyed.

[300] I pass over the Spartan disasters, the Trojan wars,  
and the near destruction of Rome that followed swiftly,  
when nations subject neither to the law of the Lord  
nor subdued by any admonitions of the saints  
were led wherever furious passion drove them,  
and whatever had been desired was considered permissible.

From the sacred books, I say—from the sacred books learn  
how many times shameful love has brought disgrace.

[305] Dinah’s beauty destroyed Shechem, who rushed to ruin beneath excessive love, together with his father and his homeland.

For the pious concern of her brothers  
does not permit their sister, shamefully violated, to remain in the marriage bed;  
it vindicates her with the sword.

[310] David too, praised in the song of the Psalms,  
was brought down by an attractive form from his lofty station.

When he discovered the crime,  
he covered his wanton body with sackcloth  
and beat it with ashes.

[315] Tamar’s beauty, at the same time, drove two brothers  
to the crime of incest and the sword.

One corrupts her; the other avenges the corrupted woman.  
The vengeance that is just ceases to be pious.

[320] Solomon himself, whose wisdom was famous in ancient times  
and throughout the whole world,  
is led into crime, caught in the snare of forbidden love,  
submitting his shameful neck to a woman’s yoke.

And the praises of the Lord, which had adorned the young man,  
rightly abandoned the old man who had forgotten the Lord.

[325] Pleasing beauty handed Haman over to death at the king’s command;  
beauty carried off your head, commander Holofernes.

That Samson, celebrated for his marvelous strength,  
a beautiful form handed over to the savage Philistines.

A holy and victorious soldier through so many battles—  
alas!—is wickedly subjected to women’s arts,

[330] so that, now polluted, he would give kisses to virgins  
and backs to swords, since crimes produce punishment.

You too, beloved only by a Levite and not his wife,  
subjected to the marriage bed in the mad night of young men,

gave yourself wholly to war in your desire for vengeance,  
content either to destroy the tribes or to perish.

[335] Thus Gibeah, through the scattered limbs in that mutilated corpse, became a funeral pyre, burned in dreadful fires.

Even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,  
I could not explain how much pleasing beauty harms.

The blessed Apostle proclaims this loudly to the world,  
giving strict rules even for lawful marriages:

[340] the man who possesses a wife and the free man who has rejected a wife  
do not have the same reason for religious service.

The care of his wife holds back the married man;  
the celibate wishes to have earned God alone.

But because eyes sometimes yield to beauty,  
the upright man slips at a fork in the road.

[345] If the impious enemy prepares to stain a pure mind,

always rejoice in and cultivate chaste faith.

Receive weapons with which you may guard the holy walls of your heart.  
Let the cross be your shield; let the cross be your sword.

[350] With supplicating tears, groaning, prayer, and a stricken heart,  
seek the God who brings salvation night and day.

And lest hope gradually caress an easy love,  
go on withdrawing your foot from the precipice.

For, not ignorant of how to help the wretched,  
I seek to help, having endured everything that I say must be avoided.

[355] Do you look toward beauty? Then look toward savage punishments;  
look at what you praise; look at what you fear.

See with inward eyes and true light,  
from earth to heaven, and from humanity to the Lord:

here, pleasure is brief and must be enclosed by a tiny end;  
there, devouring flame burns in perpetual sulfur.

[360] Hear the prophet crying out in a loud voice,  
whether you read the earlier commands or the new ones:

“What praise is there in a face? Believe that all flesh is grass,  
since the glory of flesh will be like the flower of grass.”

For just as a blow cuts down flowers, heat crushes them,  
rains confound them, and a stronger wind carries them away,

[365] so time, swelling and envy, can strip away  
and consume any face that pleases.

And, to say nothing of death itself, which crushes everything,  
how much power do diseases, fevers, and ulcers possess?

Those who now grow gray with dirty white hair—

[Col. 0987C] *[The supplied text ends here.]*
Once, when brought together, they did not fear magpies:

[425] The drooping faces, disfigured by ugly wrinkles,  
Had displayed a vain beauty for men to behold.  
The trembling skin that now totters upon loose flesh  
Had scarcely given signs marked on the thin surface.  
The neck, throat, hands—those things that now horrify everyone—

[430] Alas! were once the causes of wretched passion.  
The eyes, which watery moisture washes disfiguringly,  
Once shone like the gleaming torches of the stars.  
Consider what blooms for a few years and does not endure,  
Yet guilt remains through eternal tears.

[435] Therefore, with turned or lowered head,  
Despise youthful faces and attractive forms.  
And, so that you may be pure in heart as well as in body,  
So that you make no one guilty through suspicion,  
Apply care and concern, and always wisely desire

[440] That no woman be joined too closely to you:  
The wind loses its strength if nothing lies in its path.  
If fuel is lacking, the fire will be useless.  
And lest this be thought to apply only to men,  
Who are urged toward the upright paths of life:

[445] Whatever men learn, let a woman believe that it is said to herself as well;  
This sex too has both merit and punishments.  
Let the bold woman hate to fix her gaze upon unfamiliar faces,  
Yet also avoid attaching herself to familiar eyes.  
For eyes that play with a mingled glance

[450] Often speak gently while the mouth remains silent.  
And love, like tears which injury compels one to shed,  
Rises from the eyes and seeks the depths of the heart.  
Therefore, by the same law of instruction by which young men are warned,  
Let the chaste woman flee all men.

[455] Now, if bodily allurements spur you despite a chaste body,  
Shake off the remaining burden of your heart.

## ON ENVY

For envy, mother of manifold crime,  
Often rises from the black gall of poison.  
Unhappy envy prepared death for one destined to die:  
By it the angel fell from the height of the lofty heaven;

[460] And while he hastened to drive man from the heavenly kingdom,  
He himself first deserved to be thrust into darkness.  
From this came the Lord’s avenging judgment upon all:  
For all other deaths, this alone is guilty.  
This is the madness of war; this is the discord of peace;

[465] It harms itself more than the one whom it savagely wishes to injure.  
This was the cause that, under the excessive charge brought by his brothers,  
First made Joseph a slave and soon afterward a ruler.  
It stained Cain with the blood of his righteous brother.  
It was almost the cause of David’s death,

[470] When the war had been finished by one man's strength,  
His father-in-law did not wish his son-in-law to be exalted by praise.  
Compelled by this, the laborer of the first hour, groaning,  
Strives to surpass the digger of the eleventh hour.  
This finally handed Christ over to the mockery of the cross,

[475] While envy carried out its work of cruelty,  
And the headlong crowd saw with its eyes the signs and wonders  
Yet did not receive them into its heart.  
So wickedly did envy turn everyone, in frenzied zeal,  
Ah, toward a truly criminal deed:

[480] They did not fail to know, but were unwilling to believe, that at that time  
The man was to be glorified by the Lord.

## ON GREED

Nor, from now on, remember to avoid with any lighter care  
The countless crime of one thing: Greed.  
In all lands that the sun beholds, that the seas enclose,  
That the daylight visits and darkness covers,

At verse 549: Here Orientius seems to have had in mind those words of Saint Jerome in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*: “You drink from a gem; he satisfied nature with hollowed hands.”

Whatever is spread throughout the world unknown to us,  
In every kingdom and among every people,  
With the minds of many infected by disease, this is  
The root, cause, head, source, and origin of evil.

[490] Whatever the Lord had fashioned for harmless uses,  
Greed destroyed by turning those uses to evil purposes.  
Why do you complain of dreadful harbors and raging winds,  
Of gloomy seas notorious for shipwrecks?  
You fell the oak, its aged timber cut from the forest;

[495] If it is not useful for wood, add it to the fires.  
Be content with what is yours; whatever grows in some remote part of the world,  
Patiently reckon it as denied to you.  
You will safely observe from the secure shore  
Both the movement of the sea and the savage blowing of storms.

[500] Greedy men, you have made nature’s use a vice;  
You have made good things evil through corrupt uses.  
Iron, born from the earth for earthly gifts,  
Curved into sickles and rigid into plowshares,  
We arm for slaughter and the dreadful deaths of war,

[505] With spears, missiles, and swords.  
We received fire to drive away violent cold,  
And to dispel darkness and cook food;  
But in our madness we began to send flames into houses  
And apply them to bodies destined to burn,

[510] As though it were a small crime in the crime of plunder,  
Unless the plunderer carried away riches scattered with blood;  
And the utmost violence compels wretched people, under various punishments,  
To say whether anything hidden remains, after they have lost what they possess.

[515] Greed made brothers hateful to brothers  
And made the life of parents hateful to their children.  
By countless treacheries it teaches how to fashion falsehood from truth  
And truth from falsehood.  
Through it, while he fraudulently withheld part of the money,

[520] Ananias passed wholly into death;  
And he was not alone, for he joined his wife to the wretched man  
In the foul crime of falsehood, with an equal punishment.  
It has made wretched people, at the hour of death,  
Trust badly in their final wishes.

[525] Documents are substituted, and witnesses are sought everywhere,  
Bearing falsehood on their lips while suppressing truth in their hearts.  
Similar seals are engraved: a wicked hand learns  
Alas, to make hands falsely resemble one another:  
So that another man may be believed to be the father,

[530] And the heir may be unable to be the son of his true father.  
Under its guidance, the adulterer, safe among the guards,  
Reaches the chaste bridal chambers by means of gifts.  
Every wickedness is attempted with hearts and hands prepared,  
If you set gold as the price of crime.

[535] Tell me, I beg you, what madness loosens the reins so greatly  
That what is already enough for you is not enough?  
You hasten to join vast lands to lands,  
Though you will be enclosed in the marble of a small sarcophagus?  
Do you desire to become richer through another’s loss?

[540] What you seize from others will soon belong to someone else;  
And after what you have lost, you will grieve so swiftly  
As those grieved who possessed it before.  
You build vast citadels as though they would never fall,  
Yet you yourself will soon die.

[545] When you go to sleep, you have a bright chamber  
With glass thinned almost to transparency and slippery with varied marbles,  
As though a secure rest would not also enter  
A dwelling joined together with timbers, safe in a well-protected heart.

[550] Surely the thirsty mouth is not refreshed otherwise  
Than by what the palm offers or what a hollow gem pours out;  
Nor does the ravenous stomach receive its fasts  
With foods other than those crystal vessels or a dish will provide.  
Would not rough wool from sheep serve you better

[555] To drive away the icy cold of winter  
Than a garment weighted with metal, which, stretched through slippery threads,  
Breaks the alternating steps?  
Why do you need a translucent garment  
That, with its scant covering, exposes to unfamiliar eyes limbs that ought to be covered?

[560] Silver, masses of gold, and glittering gems  
Are from the world and belong to the world: from it they come, and there they remain.  
You came into the world naked, and naked you will return;  
You brought nothing with you and will be able to carry nothing away.  
Yet you can carry away the world’s despised gifts from here:

[565] Send ahead, intending to follow, the wealth that will be doubled.  
For possessions hoarded too closely, though they will soon cease to be yours,  
Will be yours if you do not keep them for yourself.  
Gifts bestowed by a dying man are not really gifts,  
For he gives what has already ceased to be his.

[570] Whoever, while sound and fearing nothing, with a tranquil mind,  
Takes something away from himself while he lives—that person has given it.  
What he has taken away from himself will be restored to him more perfectly:  
He who gives what is destined to perish will soon receive it intact.  
For what is stored up in heaven no thief or enemy will take away;

[575] Neither moth nor rain nor devouring flame will consume it.  
But in heaven you shall store whatever, in Christ’s name,  
Looking toward Christ, you give to the poor.  
For he says, after the mysteries of the assumed flesh:

“I am clothed in the naked, lifted up in the wretched,  
Visited in the imprisoned, healed and comforted in the sick,

[580] Helped in the little ones, protected in widows;  
And whatever you do for the wretched, or fail to do,  
Believe that it is done to me, or not done to me.”

And lest, being poor, you be able to plead poverty,  
And so furnish a pretext for unjust greed:

[585] If you lack the expense that the needy person asks for—  
Neither food nor warm water with which he may be comforted—  
When the thirsty beggar, cold, asks in Christ’s name,  
The cup offered to him will be able to bear its reward.  
With whatever you can, comfort the wretched petitioner;

[590] And if gifts are lacking, you will give prayers.  
For before God the will itself does not perish,  
If the one who desires to do well cannot do so, but wishes to do well.

From this it came that the Lord, through blessed instructions,  
Wished all human beings to be joined by love of peace,

[595] And that what he had previously foretold through the holy prophets  
He should deliver to his disciples with his own mouth:  
That love of peace, guarded in a chaste heart, should be able  
Neither to do nor to say anything unjust, harsh, violent,  
Trivial, greedy, burdensome, or fickle,

[600] In deeds or in words.  
From this the harmony of peace restrains the whole world,  
A harmony granted even to beasts along with reason;  
And, with flaming things, cold things; with soft things, hard things;  
With dry things, moist things; with slow things, swift things—

[605] Through unknown causes, by silent governance,  
It joins every work into one covenant of peace.  
Thus, if you wish to compare great things with small,  
Love of peace restrains the bodily population,  
So that, joined beneath an earthly ruler,

[610] It may learn together to pay its vows to the King of heaven.

Therefore, sinner like me—indeed, lesser than I,  
For I surpass everyone in my crimes—  
Whether appeased or injured, love peace;  
Let peace be in your inmost parts, and peace in your mouth.

[615] Drive away hatred, despise threats, lay aside severity;  
Let no time retain your offense.  
So may the sun, when it sets, leave you keeping  
The gentle bonds of peace, and find you keeping them when it returns.

# BOOK TWO

[Note: [Col. 0991D]

At verse 7: Another reading is *At si* (“But if”).

At verse 28: Read *Si male* (“If wrongly”).

At verse 34: Perhaps *properes* (“you hasten”).]

If you walk according to my instructions, most faithful reader,  
You will safely tread upon the blue necks of the serpent.  
And when Christ the Judge arrives, you will soon go to meet him  
Straight through the air on gentle, favorable paths.

[5] Only take care that, at whatever time, in these commands  
No portion of your concern be absent.  
Or, if the glory of a wind-filled tongue should move you—  
The glory that Tullius recommends in empty eloquence—  
If jokes, banquets, conversation, and pleasure are to be avoided,

[10] And if you must also be separated from your equals,  
With what zeal will you preserve the words of this little book,  
So as to be joined to God by the merits of your life?

## ON VAIN PRAISE

The chief labor is to despise flattering praise,  
Which draws ambitious people headlong to destruction,

[15] And always hastens inward by a silent movement,  
With its bitter plague seated in their very vitals.  
While we wish everything we do to be approved,  
We act so that no one fails to favor his own vices.  
The miser, under a softened title, calls himself frugal;

[20] Cruelty is veiled under the name of severity;  
And with all our zeal and all our skill we strive  
To make whatever we say or do pleasing.  
But if you wish to be approved by Christ alone,  
Seek no glory from human beings.

[25] For when you have been cast down, you will soon be raised up;  
And, small for the Lord’s sake, you will be great with the Lord.  
Let no injury distress you when you are despised;  
If you have suffered something similar, return an equal evil.  
Behold, Christ prays to the Father for those who tear him apart;

[30] Stephen prays, and James prays as well:  
Though they suffered the final punishments with gentle and noble courage,  
They do not wish to become the cause of anyone’s punishment.  
Let no savage sentence make anyone guilty;  
Let no ruler punish with severe judgment.

[35] You see a tiny speck in your brother’s eye,  
Yet do not know that a beam is in your own eyes.  
He unjustly wishes to describe another’s life,  
Who cannot be the defender of his own life.  
But we, condemned by our vices, persist in them,

[40] And soon do the very things we persecute.

## ON GUARDING AGAINST LYING

Believe that deception is wicked: the sentence remains which says,  
“The lying mouth destroys the soul by death.”  
And remember always to speak what is true,  
So that your speech may not echo what is not.

## ON GLUTTONY

[Note: [Col. 0993D]

At verse 67: Read *oblatum* (“offered”).

At verse 71: Perhaps *saucia* (“wounded”).

At verse 93: Read *perfragiles* (“very fragile”).]

[45] Moreover, impose reins upon your sweet palate,  
Lest that ancient flavor rage through its allurements.  
Ambitious gluttony made those who had obtained  
The gifts and kingdoms of heaven mortal,  
While we rush more eagerly toward what is forbidden and desire what is denied,

[50] And prefer whatever is difficult precisely because it is difficult.

## ON DRUNKENNESS

Above all, reject flooding your veins with abundant wine,  
Lest wine suddenly become poison.  
Just as, whenever the dry earth thirsts beneath excessive heat,  
The farmer prepares it for fruits,

[55] If, before the sun destroys the herbs you have pulled up,  
Dense clouds water the soaked days,  
It will immediately yield both thorns and harmful grasses  
Among the defeated seeds—alas!—in an evil abundance.  
So the bodies that have surrendered themselves to much wine

[60] Perish in judgment and luxuriate in vices.  
And what will ever be dirtier or more disgraceful  
Than if drunkenness should rob you of yourself?  
When your head turns this way and that, your steps stagger,  
Your mind refuses understanding, and your tongue cannot hold its sound,

[65] When your heavy, sleep-laden eyes close,  
You do not know what you are doing even while you do it.  
Why should I speak of the heat removed, your face steaming,  
And words loosened in badly ordered rhythms?  
Of cups slipping from your hands, and, across the very tables,

[70] Food mixed with wine often returning?  
Of you, when your wounded mind is stirred, through countless movements  
Either rejoicing too much or suddenly weeping too much;  
Now whirling limbs bent in dance,  
Now moving your arms in wanton choruses?

[75] You might wish to shout, buried beneath wine and feasts,  
Perhaps even forgetful of your own name.  
When will the pious care of praying to God  
Enter your mind, when he who gives you such things so generously is remembered?  
How many needy people could you feed at such great expense,

[80] And how many joyful days could this one day provide?  
But now, while you are full, the hungry poor wander about:  
You vomit wine, while another scarcely has water.  
And if a needy voice should perhaps ask for food, you will deny it  
To those who have nothing, though it is surplus to you.

[85] I sense that for a long time you have been silently saying, reader:  
“These things are true, but what you prescribe is difficult.”  
We are commanded to do difficult things: to climb from earth to heaven.  
Do not suppose that this can be accomplished with little effort.  
For the labor is great, but great is the reward of labor:

[90] Whoever hopes for rewards must flee idleness.  
No one will carry off the palm unless he has first competed;  
The gentle crown is given only to the victor.  
Or are you seeking the fragile honors of the world,  
By whose gift you hope to have earned the favor of a human being?

[95] Whatever it is that torments bodies with various savage trials,  
While we hurry through life in a swift racecourse—  
Contempt, rain, cold, fasts, quarrels—  
You will be able to endure with a steadfast spirit.  
You may spend whole days traversing the city,

[100] And return home exhausted only in the middle of the night.  
Then rise again at first light,  
So that you may be the first to approach the closed doors.  
And when thin sleep has compelled you, weary,  
To lay down your head on hard seats,

[105] Perhaps the one who arrived later, before you,  
Will knock at the entrance, known for his foolish complaint.  
Or, if a louder voice reaches the lictor, hope  
That you may depart after being properly pushed aside,  
And not badly beaten.

[110] But suppose—something rare—that the doorkeeper, overcome by gold  
And prayers, finally says: “You may enter.”  
You enter with a flattering tongue, a modest face,  
And a submissive body; yet none of these things help.  
Every honor has its price: there, according to the weight of money,

[115] The document is either on leaves of paper or powerful tablets.  
For if the rich hand ceases, the matter is useless.  
And if he gives words, you too will receive words.  
Did the honor smile upon you, which custom always requires one  
To take up late, but to lay down quickly?

[120] For what you had given will soon be passed to another and another:  
What many desire, no one held for long.  
But suppose that enduring honor inflates you and drives you onward;  
Will it truly have no end?  
Imagine, come now, that proud titles record your name as lasting,

[125] And that a fortunate year passes under your title:  
What good does it finally do when your power ceases to exist?  
Where is that in which what was and has gone away is felt?  
And what will the succeeding age, gradually arriving, not know—  
And if it does know, what reward will that be for you?

[130] But you who depend only upon earthly honor  
And now court human beings with such great ambition—how will you please  
The Lord, Christ, to whom all things belong,  
And moreover deserve the kingdom of God?  
Preferring truth to falsehood, great things to small,

[135] Magnificent things to worthless things, and everlasting things to perishable ones.  
What injury, then, will overcome a devoted heart?  
And what will be lofty? What will be difficult for you?  
For nothing is hard when hope follows, and every labor  
That has been overcome reaches the fruit of honor—

[140] A fruit that endures through all time,  
Which neither the ambitious, the wasteful, nor the impatient can take away.

[Note: [Col. 0995D]

At verse 155: Perhaps *vernanti* (“blooming”).

At verse 167: Another poet of Gaul, the author of the poem *On Providence* among the works of Saint Prosper, describes a similar devastation of Gaul, which occurred in the year of the Lord 407, in almost the same manner. I gladly transcribe this verse:

“Neither castles set upon rocks, nor towns imposed upon high mountains,  
Nor cities placed beside level-flowing rivers,  
Could overcome the barbarian deceits and weapons of fury …”

At verse 179: Perhaps *Hi* (“these”).

At verse 184: So also the author mentioned above in the book *On Providence*:

“And when the image of the smoking homeland entered his mind,  
And whatever was perishing everywhere stood before his eyes.”

At verse 215: Perhaps *Interdum* (“sometimes”).

At verse 232: Read *dubio* (“uncertain”).]

You hear the Lord promising new rewards to the righteous,  
Who will always give things better than those he has promised.  
Things not seen by the eyes, not conveyed to the ears,  
Not previously imagined by sensation itself.

Not for you do drops of myrrh distill from precious bark,  
Nor does the earth swell with fragrant turf of incense.  
Add thyme, violets, cassia, melilot, and saffron,  
And join white lilies to crimson roses.  
Since on earth a sinner receives so many gifts,

[150] What good things will you, a holy person, receive in heaven?

Imagine, come now, whatever you think is bright, beautiful, precious,  
And everything great that you consider great in the world.  
Let these be given to the blessed according to their merits: golden dwellings,  
Gem-studded doorposts, and purple pavement,  
And fields always fragrant with flowering growth,

[155] With rivers drawn full of milk and honey together.  
Nor, because these things raise the mind and appear in thought,  
Believe that the good things above them will be inferior.  
Yet do not fear that, overcome by the long duration,  
You will be found unequal to God’s commands.

[160] Nothing here is long-lasting, though it proceeds in a long course,  
Compared with the brief span of life in which we now rejoice.  
All things, weary, look down upon their aging end;  
And now the final hour of the day is turning.

Consider how swiftly death has pressed upon the whole world,  
How many peoples the violence of war has struck.

[165] Thick forest, rugged heights of lofty mountains,  
Rivers strong in their rushing currents,  
Castles in their locations, cities safe behind their walls,  
Places inaccessible by sea, desolate wildernesses,  
Hollows, nor even caves beneath fearsome cliffs,

[170] Were able to withstand the sport of barbarian hands.  
For many, false trust; for many, perjury; for many,  
Civic betrayal was the cause of death.  
Ambush did much, and public violence did much.  
Those whom strength did not overcome were overcome by hunger.

[175] The unhappy mother fell with her offspring and husband;  
The master, together with his slaves, entered slavery.  
Here people lay as food for dogs; for many, burning houses  
Provided the pyre that snatched away their lives.  
Through streets, estates, fields, crossroads, and every village,

[180] Along all the roads on this side and that,  
Death, pain, destruction, slaughter, fires, and mourning—  
All Gaul smoked from one single pyre.

[185] Why, however, should I enumerate the funerals of the declining world,
Which always proceed along their accustomed path?
Why recount how many die throughout the whole world,
When you yourself see your own day hastening?
I pass over how much power belongs to swords and falling ruins,
[190] To fire, poisonous plants, and rivers;
[Col. 0995D] How many war, famine, and raging diseases destroy,
And how one death rushes along many paths;
How many guilty people, even in the midst of peace,
Are tormented by deserved punishment, so that peace may exist.

[195] Every hour gradually brings us toward death;
[Col. 0996A] Even during this time when we speak, we are dying beforehand.
Through deceptive courses, with silent effort,
The last stretch of life presses on toward the final days.
While food and sleep, words and cups delight us,
[200] Whether you sit at home or seek foreign lands,
And while you do whatever you do, or even leave it undone,
Death advances step by step without delay.
As a candle set in the darkness of night
To make up for daylight by the service of its light,
[205] While we do not notice, is consumed by a slow fire,
And its devouring flame always hastens toward its end,
So it is with human affairs: whatever is done perishes;
[Col. 0996B] The span life draws out for itself advances and dies.
But suppose this span of long-lived old age so great
[210] That you yourself, untouched, watch the world’s funerals.
Though the end may come late, it must nevertheless come:
It cannot remain absent altogether.
What is born then grows and becomes old,
And for those worn out with age nothing remains but death.
[215] One who has lived ten times three years dies,
And likewise one who has lived a thousand [the second verse is corrupt as printed].
Once the final end holds them both,
At the ultimate moment of death it is certainly the same.
What good is it to have prolonged life if you cease to live?
[220] What reward is there in good things if you are held by evils?
[Col. 0996C] For only while you enjoy the fruit ... [corrupt phrase: *tangere fruendi*, “to touch ... of enjoying”];
And this life lives in the service of life.
What once was is now nothing if it ceases to be;
What you do not feel brings no benefit merely by having been.
[225] What good is it, then, if fasting torments you,
To have heavily laden your body with yesterday’s food;
And when constant thirst grips you today,
To have drenched yourself the day before with excessive food?
When the day, never to return, snatches from our awareness
[230] What has run its course amid swift revolutions?
But we, when the first bloom of youth has run its course,
Are already unsteady in step, sight, voice, and hand;
It is painful to remember whatever we were,
And what follows takes credibility from all that went before.

[235] Are never sufficiently satisfied by this life, burdensome though it is,  
Bent and complaining as our bodies are worn away.

Hence it is that, as though wholly removed from the entire world,  
We watch whatever perishes throughout the world.  
Nor does another’s death fail to warn the wretched,  
Who live as though beneath another sun, of their own death.

[Note: [Col. 0997D]

At verse 249: Instead of *illud*, *quo*, a form not uncommon among medieval writers.

At verse 265: Here *aurum* (“gold”) is elegantly used for a golden dish, as poets sometimes use the material for the vessel itself; thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

“He eagerly drained  
The foaming cup, and bathed himself in the full gold.”

At verse 276: Perhaps *tenue* (“thin”).

At verse 301: This verse seems to be restored as follows: “The right hand guilty of slaughter, the tongue ready for insults.”

At verse 320: Perhaps *Qui* (“who”).

At verse 331: Perhaps “which is the first glory for the conquered.”]

Before our eyes and far away alike, we are bereft of friends;  
From one side grief reaches us through our eyes, from the other through our ears.  
As age declines, beloved parents perish,  
And a spouse is snatched from the very embrace.

[245] Death takes brother from brother’s arms,  
And perhaps the younger was the one taken.  
Nor is the older generation withdrawn in the order of life,  
When a father sees the savage funerals of his child.  
Yet no cautious person believes what he sees,

[250] And, seeing what he does not want, sees that he too can suffer it.

This nevertheless comes from the fact that, because of our unjust deeds,  
We always regard death as a perpetual evil;  
And we believe that receiving later the punishments  
Which holy law threatens for crimes is a gain.

[255] Blessed is the one who regards death as the permitted end of labors;  
Fearing beforehand, he has avoided what punishment he might fear.  
Blessed is the one who wishes, with steadfast spirit and serene face,  
To await the great judgment, which must be set in motion  
With great investigation over cities and peoples,

[260] Secure in the uprightness of his life.  
A good conscience, conscious of its certain causes,  
Keeps his head fearless beneath such a great burden.  
There the once powerful in command and kingdom,  
There the conspicuous in fasces and robes of office,

[265] For whom gold was used at banquets, Falernian wine in crystal,  
And purple, spread beneath, was customary for loading couches;  
Those famous for strength, praised for the gift of beauty,  
And badly trusting in bodily resources—  
Whose belly was their lord, lust their desire,

[270] Hope their present possession, and wealth their glory—  
Who, wretched, neglected to seek the Lord even at death itself,  
When their eyes were about to be closed,  
Will await punishment enclosed. Now learn  
What punishment: punishment corresponding to deeds remains.

[275] Everlasting darkness will hold them beneath blind night;  
Then a severe flame will provide them with light.  
Burning in sulfurous fiery furnaces,  
They will be compelled to climb with mangled bodies.  
Hard ice will bind them, infused with violent rigidity

[280] By blasts of winter.  
And although the nature of hell fights with itself in such discord,  
The force of one name nevertheless has various forms.  
Nor could you distinguish such diverse punishment  
Whether the torment is fire or more grievous cold.

[285] Not, as with us here, where those killed by earthly death  
Are received by one death, though many crimes may cause it;  
For however savage the judge may be according to the weight of circumstances,  
He can do nothing other than snatch away the soul,  
And, as though by a profit from crimes, if many remain,

[290] The first vengeance may deny punishment to the rest.  
But there every offense will be paid in its proper order,  
With a punishment corresponding to the deeds that follow.  
And one body will be displayed through its individual members,  
With as many punishments as it was capable of vices.

[295] One law will punish the cruel, another the greedy;  
They will pay for their deeds in one way and their intentions in another.  
There is one punishment for perjurers, and another for the proud;  
Another will be the punishment for the cause of spilled blood.  
The envious, the impatient, the effeminate, the forger, the adulterer,

[300] And the man wholly given to wine, wholly to seduction;  
The right hand guilty of slaughter, the tongue ready for insults;  
The violator, the boaster, the impious, the unteachable—  
Before the day of judgment, each will pay the punishments,  
So that the delay of judgment grants no small interval of punishment.

[305] Serpents will coil around some in winding folds;  
A glowing chain will grind down others.  
Everything there is full of tears, terror, and pain,  
And there is no voice except one produced by groaning.  
Why should I run further through each crime,

[310] And the terrible tortures by which they will torment the wretched,  
When even if, now, you speak something carelessly with your mouth,  
The account of your speech must be examined?  
Among these will be whoever denies the Lord of all things,  
Bowing his head beneath rocks and stakes.

[315] He will truly be wretched and pitiable to no one;  
Alone he will receive whatever harms from every side.  
Countless worms will live in his dying body,  
Nor will the fire’s smoke provide an end.  
But on the other side, the gentle band of the pious—

[320] Those who, though afflicted, did not repay evil with evil,  
Who gave help and food to the poor,  
Affection to those they knew, and service to their parents—  
Will shine like the eyes of the blazing sun,  
Their splendid limbs veiled in snowy robes.

[325] Especially those whom the nights find prepared  
In Christ’s law and the days receive;  
Those whose desire it was never to stain  
The snowy garment of baptism in female beds;  
Those cautious not only in body but in their whole heart,

[330] Such as I wish you, my reader, to be.  
Or already blessed are those whose first glory was won when the allurements  
Of light and of the treacherous body had been conquered: they did not fear  
To pour out their devoted souls, seeking true life,  
For the name of Christ.

[335] And this holy company will contain priests  
And monks withdrawn from the crowds of men;  
Those who now disdain the delights of flattering fame  
And hope for the rewards of the judgment to come.  
Living in gentle leisure amid secure circumstances,

[340] They now live well according to their merit, and afterward better.  
For they themselves will surround the King in a dense throng  
When the Lord the Judge stands upon the earth,  
And wherever the Lamb turns, they will all go,  
Bathed in the true light, the light of God.

[345] And they will receive so much of their quickened beauty  
That their faces cannot be looked upon by the eyes of those who see them.  
Therefore, when the hollow trumpet gives its terrible sound,  
To bear witness at last to the coming of God,  
The earth, split open by long fissures, will immediately lie exposed,

[350] And flames, lightning, and hail will fall everywhere,  
While the whole world is shaken from its deepest foundations,  
And all paths are kept open on every side [the transmitted sense is uncertain].  
Here there will be sad groaning, there the holy joys of life;  
One voice will arise from the two different companies.

[355] And with all their steps swiftly hastened,  
The father will go, leading his offspring and lineage.  
The whole line will be led in a continuous course,  
When the ancestor stands midway among his descendants.  
I will not tell you of famous cities, distant peoples,

[360] Or kingdoms that now exist or once existed;  
Nor of peoples sluggish from cold or scorched by the sun,  
Nor of those whom the setting or rising day possessed,  
But of everyone born from the world’s first beginning  
To the day that will now be the world’s end.

[365] The first command will establish all souls, righteous and guilty,  
In one place from every land.  
Yet among those countless thousands not one will proceed from there  
Who is not counted by his own Lord.  
Then, in the same flesh that he had carried into heaven, he will ascend the shining tribunal,

[370] Glorifying human nature;  
And he will set in order all things that slip away  
In the successive ages, whatever was then or afterward done  
Under the enduring law. Sacred, high upon his throne,  
Visible in terror, conspicuous yet scarcely able to be seen, he will act.

[375] And amid the courses of flame, the sounds of trumpets,  
The angelic choirs, and the sacred army,  
Amid the pallors, tears, joys, prayers, and fears  
Of infants, mothers, young men, and old men,  
The final sentence will be given to the suspended crowd,

[380] And it will resound from the holy mouth of the holy Judge.  
“Go, company of the righteous, into rest and praise,  
Never to be separated from my kingdom:  
The Father, knowing your merit and your future life,  
Now gives you gifts prepared long ago.”

[385] “But you, impious throng always opposed to our commands,  
Be shut up in Tartarean places.  
There your teeth will gnash and your eyes shed tears,  
To be tortured by unmeasured fires.  
And yet, so that whatever is commanded may truly remain,

[390] This will be the formula of the eternal judgment:  
Glory will hold the righteous, death removed;  
And the guilty person will not die, though condemned to punishment.”

I ought to have handed these things over to you, reader, through deeds,  
So that a life proven good might give weight to words.  
But since, wretchedly, we neglect whatever we are warned,

[395] And it is easier to learn than to do,  
If you entrust to your heart all that has entered through your ear  
And been set out in my writings,  
I shall confidently say that, received into heaven’s dwelling,  
You will break the harsh bonds of savage death;

[400] And even though you had previously been a son of hell,  
You will begin to be a son of the Most High God.  
One thing remains, without which nothing else is of any benefit:  
Believe Christ to be from the Father and with the Father,  
And the Holy Spirit joined with them without distinction.

[405] Let the three names complete one God.  
But you, whoever you are, when you read our little book,  
Whether it is bad or good, remember me.  
And whenever, after reading the poem, you pray to the Lord Christ,  
Let us always be upon your lips.

[410] And lest you believe that I impose this upon you with mere words,  
Or think that you may safely disregard it,  
May no day prick you with bitter cares;  
May whatever you do please Christ entirely;  
May you receive the holy crown, given as a gift.

[415] May concern for my name not depart from you,  
So that I, Orientius, overcoming all sinners,  
May deserve forgiveness through the prayers of the saints.

**THE SECOND BOOK OF SAINT ORIENTIUS ENDS.**

## BEGINNING: ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD (C, G, S)*

A light more splendid than light shines, and the day is greater than day.  
The bright day gleams, more festive than the whole year:  
It is the natal day chosen by God, on which he is born,  
He who, with the Father, always reigns in heaven’s fellowship.

[5] The great power of the Father, soon bearing the first beginnings of our flesh,  
As a man, back into heaven, death having thus been accomplished—  
He who wished to assume flesh, yet does not grow old in flesh.

## ON THE EPITHETS OF OUR SAVIOR

Door, Virgin, Lion, Power, Wisdom, Word,  
King, Staff, Prince, Leader, Rock, Shepherd, Man,  
Nets, Sun, Bridegroom, Seed, Mountain, Star, Teacher,  
Pearl, Day, Lamb, Sheep, Calf.

Treasure, Fountain, Life, Hand, Head, Fire, Plow,  
Flower, Cornerstone, Right Hand, Column, Child.  
Gentle Adam, Finger, Mirror, Way, Cluster of Grapes, Bread,  
Offering, Law, Reason, Rod, Fish, Eagle,

Just One, Offspring of the King, and Priest of the King:  
Great names belonging to God—but he himself is greater, God.

## FURTHER MATERIAL ON THE TRINITY

What existed through the ages and exists through the ages of ages  
Will always be, because it always was, remaining without end:  
And above everything that exists, without whom nothing exists, to whom all things belong,  
The all-parent Word, the omnipotent Word, God.

Alone with the Father, with whom the Father and God alone  
Was this [Word], which had not yet received birth as its beginning. [The printed syntax of these lines is irregular.]  
For Christ is the seed, Christ the beginning of created things,  
Christ the honor of earth, the dread of the world, the glory of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1001D]

At verse 21: Add *est* (“is”).

At verse 22: Perhaps *unus* (“one”).

At verse 30: Read *Ex toto totus* (“wholly from the whole”).

At verse 34: Perhaps *mysteria* (“mysteries”).

At verse 35: Read *sibi dedita* (“given to itself”).

At verse 58: Perhaps *piorum* (“of the pious”).

At verse 59: Perhaps *vivit* (“lives”).

At verse 60: Perhaps *Plecteris* (“you are punished”).

At verse 89: Read *depingit* (“depicts”).

At verse 91: Perhaps *gratas mirator* (“an admirer of pleasing things”).

At verse 101: Something such as *videtur* (“it seems”) or a similar word appears to be understood.]

From the reigning God, King and Ruler in the heights,

the Only-Begotten, begotten before all others by that Begetter

whom no one begot, through whom all things that beget came into being:

we beseech, desire, fear, venerate, and love him.

[30] Wholly from the Whole, diffused as the Whole throughout the universe.

Not the same, yet wholly the same, alike and together,

[Col. 1001B] altogether equal and coextensive: thus Son and Father are one.

The name is divided in designation, but the substance is mingled,

completing the holy fullness of the profound sacred mystery.

[35] The powerful Fullness, given to itself and mutually joined,

the threefold unity of powers is made equal.

The Spirit also, wholly perfect, moves above.

Therefore honor is in Christ, praise belongs to the Father, and Christ is in the Father.

He himself is the Father’s mind, speech, witness, and heir:

[40] he himself recognizes how much the Father dares accomplish in him;

he himself is our head, wisdom, grace, and life;

he himself is mankind’s guardian, watcher, and judge;

he himself is the way of salvation and the unchanging light:

[Col. 1001C] true splendor from the True, light from Light,

[45] goodness from Goodness, fullness from the Full and Rich;

provident, indulgent, merciful, compassionate, and abounding;

perfect, patient, just, and undefiled.

The eternal gift of the Eternal One, the earlier generations’ protection;

the soul’s firmament, the demon’s flight, the weapons of faith;

[50] reigning forever, censor and judge of what is to come;

not enclosed by time, yet by command destined to close time;

beginning and end, giving life both within and without;

holding willing, powerful in ability, gentle yet severe;

the world’s peace and joy, director of the wicked and the good.

[55] While God proved what is mortal to be immortal.

[Col. 1001D] O blessed dominion of the Lord, noble death!

O hard heart and treacherous error of the wretched race!

Impious condemner, your death hangs upon this stake;

believing confessor, may your life live by this blood.

[60] You are brought low while God judges—the one whom you seemed to punish;

he saved the peoples—the wicked people hate him.

This is the one previously rejected by his own and accursed,

the spitting of men, the reproach of the doomed crowd.

This is the one upon whom a savage hand poured gall mixed with vinegar,

[65] whom the blows of a palm wounded with blind striking.

Look, mad executioner, upon the venerable wood;

see the victorious signs of blood profaned.

Is he not the living God, the God whom the enemy cannot overcome,

vengeance, refuge, rest, light, life, faith, and hope?

[70] From the Father he must be recognized as creator and giver of life;

from the cross, as avenger and repeller of hell,

cleanser of errors, faithful peace, and abundant forgiveness.

Born through love for humanity, he suffered for the sake of salvation;

having fulfilled the law of death, he rose again, exalted into heaven;

[75] seated in his native throne, bringing salvation above every age,

from which he deigned to come down to humble earth, returning thither again;

the price of sin, himself knowing no sin,

making his servants participants and conforming them in glory.

[Col. 1002B] Behold for you how beautiful a trophy shines through our portals,

[80] O Christ; how brightly it bears back to the Father its standards,

still bloodstained, yet as before and forever

powerful in might and everlasting in majesty.

But why does the cross retain this form, raised aloft?

The whole design displays the character that must be worshiped.

[85] Because the visible sign is divided into four projecting parts,

it makes known the Lord of the world and all the archangels.

The King himself has as many wounds as the cross sees regions of heaven.

The cross imitates pious palms in the image of a worshiper praying;

[Col. 1002C] the cross, testifying to God’s peace, depicts it, and itself is peace—

[90] the peace given through the wood, the peace preserved in writing upon the wood.

Do you wish also to look upon the forms that arouse wonder and gratitude?

Look upon the complete enigma of the richly meaningful sign.

You may see a Greek P: it is the head, or the arms of the crucified one.

The upright Iota is here the hanging of the body.

[95] The letter continues the punishment, and the punishment brings salvation:

then Alpha stands beside it, and another letter is close at hand, Ο.

The first is the first here; the last is the last here.

These are the elements of letters: God here is above every element:

all the insignia converge in the heavenly sign.

[100] [Col. 1002D] When he mounts the wood, God indicates that the wood is

the material of fruit; when he extends a branch on high,

the Lord, higher than the lofty heavens, towers above all.

He is the middle of the crucified ones: the number three gives him honor.

He is struck; blood comes out, and water flows from the wound made;

[105] it comes forth, and immediately afterward blood from the wound itself. Indeed:

the blood claims martyrdom, the water claims the cleansing bath.

Thus, through divine power, death and life come from the tree.

Through the fruit, first-formed man, you fall; through the cross Christ heals:

there the destructive dragon brought the death-dealing food.

[110] Nor is it surprising if a thousand names, scarcely worthy of God,

draw forth abundant praise—praise unequal to so many virtues—

as the miracles of Christ have produced titles.

## EXPLANATION OF THE NAMES OF THE LORD

“Door,” because he remains in heaven and opens what is hidden.

“Virgin,” because he is the source of the birth of the undefiled mother.

[115] And “Lion”: he is King of kings; the lion is called king of beasts,
and he too is called Strength: nothing is stronger than he alone.

Why, then, is he called “Wisdom”? He is the rule of life.

How is he “the Word”? Because he flowed forth from the Father’s mouth.

Why is he now “King,” now likewise “Son of the King”?

[120] [Col. 1003B] Because with the Father he holds the shared throne of heaven.

Why “Staff”? Because he raises the fallen and lifts up the sick.

Why “Prince”? Because he governs all things subject to his throne.

Why “Leader of the heavenly host”? Because he comes from the holy army.
