Why “Rock”? Because he establishes firmly upon a strong foundation.

[125] Why “Good Shepherd”? Because he keeps blemish away from the sheepfolds.

Now “Man”: for he was born and took flesh from a Virgin.

Why “Nets”? Because he gathers peoples scattered everywhere.

Why “Sun of righteousness”? Because he illumines every righteous person.

Why “Bridegroom”? Because the Church, betrothed to God, is a virgin.

[130] [Col. 1003C] Why “Holy”? Because by his word he sows blessed kingdoms.

“Mountain”: because it offers an ascent not arduous for everyone.

“Star”: because by the light of his guidance he directs uncertain journeys.

Why “Teacher”? Because he loves to teach hearts devoted to service.

“Pearl”: for what can be found more precious than this?

[135] Why “Day”? Because he shines more brightly than light—he alone.

Then, because he is holy and innocent, he is held to be the Lamb,

who alone was able to take away the world’s sin.

And now he is called “Sheep,” because he offers himself to those slaughtering him.

He is also called “Calf”: his passion demonstrates this.

[140] “Fountain,” because he purifies defilement through abundant baptism.

“Life,” because he gives eternal life to those whom he makes alive.

He is “Hand”: the rich working of virtues comes to meet us.

[Col. 1003D] He is “Head”: it is plain that we are created by him, our author.

“Fire”: because in this our testing still remains.

Why “Plough”? Because he subdues hearts and makes them fruitful.

“Flower,” because he is the confessor who himself crowns the martyrs.

Why “Cornerstone”? Because he joins the two peoples together.

“Right Hand,” by which he sits beside the Father’s side, adorning and honoring it.

[Col. 1004A] Often “Dove,” because he knows no deceit and is without gall.

[150] Why “Child”? Because he proceeds pure toward the citadel of his Begetter.

“Vine,” because through his adopted heir he propagates himself.

Why “Second Adam”? Because he himself is the head of those reborn.

He is “Finger,” this “Stylus”: God’s law is written through him.

Now “Mirror,” because the image of the Father shines through him.

[155] Now “Way,” because he goes before the saints in paradise.

“Cluster of grapes,” because he waters the world with heavenly juices.

“Bread,” because in him are the nourishment of our faith.

Why is he himself, the Supreme Priest, a living offering to God?

Because, sanctifying himself, he offers himself upon the ancestral altars.

[160] [Col. 1004B] Now “Reason”: this Reason is the one through whom the structure of the world stands.

“Rod,” because with a blow he corrects the actions of those who go astray.

“Fish born from the waters”: he himself is the author of baptism.

Often “Eagle,” because he flew back from the earth like a bird.

## PRAISE

Finally, so that we do not delay over so many great matters at length:

[165] He is “Eye”: I know that God sees every heart.

Why “Prophet”? Because in brief he reveals what is to come.

Why “Angel”? Because he himself became his own messenger.

He is called “Arm,” from the embrace with which he holds all things.

Whatever it may be, recognize this: what you are called in holiness belongs to you.

[170] [Col. 1004C] The greatness of his works conceals the names of so many things;

but these honors are judged according to his own merits.

The cause creates the titles; virtue makes the names known.

You sit on high: Holy One (*Agios*), our blessing.

You, God Emmanuel: a name meaning “God dwelling with us.”

[175] You, Lord of Hosts (*Sabaoth*), protect with your hand everything that exists anywhere.

The house of Israel and the blessed confessors worship you;

all the patriarchs worship you, and all the angels worship you.

You flash above the unknown cherubim, above the stars;

you who were promised to Abraham from the seed of David,

[180] you hear in heaven the glorious, praise-worthy cry “Hosanna” (“save, we pray”).

[Col. 1004D] Look upon us, O Crucified One, Advocate, Christ,

Nazarene; God whom we believe in, and Galilean,

and God of holy father Abraham, and God of Isaac,

and gracious God of Jacob—from whom our faith and hope arise.

[185] Look upon your own, O Christ, and long protect those you have redeemed.

I, unworthy, beseech you; deign to hear the one who prays.

Almighty, have mercy on me, have mercy on my loved ones:

grant that grief may depart, and that care and fear may withdraw,

[Col. 1005A] [Note: [Col. 1005C]

Verse 2. For *moles*, according to the observation noted above.

[Col. 1005C] Verse 31. Perhaps *furva* (“dark”).

[Col. 1005D] Verse 41. Perhaps *quem laedit* (“whom he injures”).]

and join me to your holy servants, and let me fear you,

[190] and please you while I live, nor be guilty at that time

when I shall stand before your tribunal, mindful of my merit.

Christ, your name: and truly may I honor the name I proclaim.

May your cross rest upon my forehead, in my hand, upon my lips; may the cross rest within me.

May my household be shielded by the cross; may the cross be the breastplate of salvation.

[195] By this sign the shining tower will gleam more brightly,

than when it was drenched with sacrilegious, polluted blood.

## EXPLICIT

## THE PRAYERS OF ORIENTIUS BEGIN (C, G, S)*

## NUMBER XXIV

To you, Lord, the lofty Cherubim has been dedicated,

[Col. 1005B] and that four-sided structure of the massive machine—

they confess you in an everlasting song,

and we, an image of the concordant song,

[5] sound “Amen” and say “Alleluia.”

The seven first angels entreat you,

or the seven men, princes of the city,

near the throne, the nearest gatekeepers.

And we, an image of the concordant song,

[10] sound “Amen” and say “Alleluia.”

The sun’s star, with its monthly sister,

the Pleiades, the Hyades, the Evening Star, the Morning Star,

and all the drops that shine before them invoke you:

and we, an image of the concordant song,

[15] sound “Amen” and say “Alleluia.”

The watery or cloudless air in turn,

and likewise the winds, rains, hail, and rivers,

sing together to the Creator in their own manner:

and we, an image of the concordant song,

[20] sound “Amen” and say “Alleluia.”

The stationary earth, together with the moving produce

that obeys humanity, and whatever is taken from one,

sings to you alone and is silent to the others:

and we, an image of the concordant song,

[25] sound “Amen” and say “Alleluia.”

O Ocean, who restrain the enclosed expanse,

and the central trench of the inner abyss,

[Col. 1006A] with sea creatures sounding forth God:

and we, an image of the concordant song,

[30] sound “Amen” and say “Alleluia.”

The flame of the infernal seat, tawny Tartarus,

and the savage angels presiding there likewise,

sing “Amen” in a threatening song:

and we, an image of the concordant song,

[35] sound “Amen” and say “Alleluia.”

## XXIV BEGINS

Finally, I speak the song of entreaty;

I do this as I have done through the twenty songs,

but let no bold person interrupt anything:

I denounce the serpent, master of falsehood,

[40] so that he may neither add nor remove a letter.

But if a spiritual reading offends anyone,

let that person be permitted to reject the reading,

but not to alter the form of the reading:

I denounce the serpent, master of falsehood,

[45] so that he may neither add nor remove a letter.

If a scribe errs in changing a letter,

he errs through ignorance; let Christ’s pardon be granted, if it is available:

for it is not the will, but the hand, that slips.

I denounce the serpent, master of falsehood,

[50] so that he may neither add nor remove a letter.

This prohibition concerns those men

who are truly called physicians:

if you do not approve, you are free to pass it over.

I denounce the serpent, master of falsehood,

[55] so that he may neither add nor remove a letter.

[Col. 1006C] And we have emerged from the dregs of the pagans,

and at last broken through that darkness,

while we listen to the spiritual angels.

The malignant serpent [lacuna].

[60] Concerning the sixth sign: [a thing] to be guarded against by the spirit

of death—God’s prophets, instruments of demons,

Numa and death forever unto the age [text corrupt].

Holy God, we beseech you, Father of the Only-Begotten;

Christ God, we implore you, living Son of God;

[65] Holy Christ, we entreat you, true judge, God.

## EXPLICIT PRAYER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 1006C] Orientius composed twenty-four prayers from their titles. Our manuscript codex, however, contains only the first and the last.]

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 470

## SAINT AUSPICIUS, BISHOP OF TOUL

[Col. 1005]

[Col. 1005]

## LETTER OF AUSPICIUS, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF TOUL, TO ARBOGAST, COUNT OF THE TREVERI (C)

[Col. 1005D]

To the most exalted and distinguished Count Arbogast,

Auspicius, who love you, sends abundant greetings.

[Col. 1006D] With my whole heart I offer great thanks to the heavenly Lord,

because recently we saw you great in the city of Toul.

Previously you had made me joyful through many of your actions,

but now you have caused me to exult with the greatest joy.

For you alone have appeared greater than all,

[Col. 1007A] so that by an illustrious mind you might surpass the rank of your power.

The honor due to you, not yet bestowed in name with our greater rejoicing,

has already been conferred through your merits.

For it is more praiseworthy for a man to shine through his deeds

than to display a lamp without the light of a flame.

But you, who in all your steps are more than you are said to be,

will, I believe, more swiftly receive what your merits return.

For illustrious in birth and illustrious in the conduct of your life,

you are shown to be just, chaste, sober, and wholly distinguished.

Your father Arigius was noble in every respect;

his noble reputation you either renew or surpass.

But your honor is his, and his remains yours,

and thus, with doubled radiance, you shine upon everyone.

Nor should anyone doubt that fortune granted you this gift:

that your mother should survive for you, worthy of praise by all,

[Col. 1007B] she who fills and adorns you equally with every resource,

so that you are abundant in your uses and honorable in your deeds.

You, city of the Treveri, ought to be congratulated,

for you are governed by such a man, comparable with the ancients.

Your name’s lineage descends from a great stock;
certainly it shares that man’s valor, as we read of Arbogast.

Let this man’s triumphs likewise be recorded in the annals,

just as those of the man mentioned above have also been recorded.

But let us add this merit to the one who is truly greater:

that he invokes the name of Christ, devoted to religion.

That ancient man was vigorous in arms, it is true;

but he died an unbeliever and lost everything through death.

This man, however, our own, is energetic, warlike, illustrious,

and—greater than all these qualities—the worshiper of the divine name.

Now, wise son, I ask you to receive graciously

[Col. 1007C] the page of one devoted to you, which I offer out of affection.

First I ask that you desire to preserve intact within yourself

the great blessings bestowed upon you, and to abound in many good things.

Drive away one vice, lest it stain pure hearts,

the one that sacred writings call the root of all evils:

namely, greed, which rages against its own dependents,

and that savage madness spares not those on whose love it feeds.

This, I say, always devours, enduring a hunger that must be fed

[Note: [Col. 1007C] *Edendi* (“of consuming”).]

and, like a fire kindled by added fuel, grows as its food is supplied.

[Col. 1008A] But I have not said these things as though I condemned you for this crime.

Nevertheless, I earnestly ask that not even a spark wound you.

For if, perhaps unwary, you should at some time be entangled by it,

the conflagration, growing excessively, will quickly blaze up.

Turn your eyes throughout the world; look upon the leading men of the age:

either the greedy perish or they live amid dangers.

They scrape together, seek, and gape after gain like greedy dogs;

yet they neither possess these things themselves nor leave them to their descendants.

Still, I would not say these things universally of everyone,

but so that the disgrace of a few may be an influence upon many.

[Note: [Col. 1008C] Perhaps *emendatio* (“correction”).]

But you, eminent man, prudent judge of many,

suddenly examine as judge the hidden places of your own heart.

If you should sense in it any small drop of this poison,

pour sweet oil over it, lest it spread through your entrails.

Nor are you ignorant, in your wisdom, of this oil:

it is the provision of all the poor, acquired through almsgiving.

Exercise yourself in these pursuits; perform all these good deeds,

so that my joys may remain yours and persevere for you.

For you should know that it is little if someone seizes nothing

and, with a hardened heart, closes off his own possessions from the needy.

He does not provide much for himself who avoids the madness

of greed only to fall at the same time into avarice.

For these two crimes, as if related by nature

and doubled in appearance, remain closely joined;

those wretches who pursue them differ in this single respect:

one of them is bad, and the other is worst of all.

Therefore, my dear dignity, you, unique son, I ask you:

keep yourself from what belongs to others, so that you may give your own to everyone,

and remember above all to retain this in your heart:

I already regard you as marked out for the priesthood.

Preserve this grace, I beg you, and increase in those merits,

so that the people’s previously spoken voice may come as a sacred thing to heaven:

“Holy, first among all, and our Pope Jamlychus.”

Honor him in your heart; love him, so that you may later be loved.

Whatever you give to him, you restore to yourself in Christ;

you will later receive those things which you yourself have sown.

## IN THE YEAR 490

## PAULINUS OF PETRICORDIUM

[Col. 1007]

[Col. 1007]

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 1007D] Paulinus was a Gaul by nation, from Pericorius or Petricordius, that is, Vesunna, if Sirmond’s conjecture is reliable. He flourished in the year 461. For he dedicated his work on the Life of Saint Martin to Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, who presided over the first Council of Tours in the year 461, not 480, as Labbeus incorrectly states, followed by his copyist Oudinus. Paulinus wrote six books in heroic verse on the Life of Saint Martin; in them he did nothing more than render, in a rough and unpolished meter, with a few omissions, what Sulpicius Severus had expressed in graceful and elegant prose. This work was attributed to Paulinus of Nola not only by nearly all later writers, but also explicitly by the ancient Gregory of Tours (*Book I of the Miracles of Saint Martin*) and, less openly, by Venantius Fortunatus (*On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, Book I). Hence it happened that it was often published under the name of Paulinus of Nola, first edited by Juretus at Paris in 1585, and afterward in the Paris and Cologne libraries of the Fathers, in the Bignean appendix, p. 852, and in other collections of ancient Christian poets. It was finally restored to Paulinus of Petricordium and published in the latest *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume VI, p. 297; and separately by Christian Daumius, together with the commentaries of François Juretus, the observations of Caspar Barthius, the notes of Joh. Fr. Gronovius, and his own *Spicilegium of Notes*, at Leipzig in 1686, octavo. Furthermore, there exists a fairly short poem of our Paulinus, *On the Visit to His Little Nephew*, customarily appended to the *Life of Saint Martin*, as well as certain fragments of other lost little works, which are found in the same place. In addition, Gennadius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 68) mentions a certain Paulinus contemporary with our Paulinus of Petricordium, who composed treatises on the Beginning of Lent, Easter Sunday, Obedience, Penance, and Neophytes. Of these little works, whoever their Paulinus may have been, nothing survives today.

## ANNOTATION ON THE FOLLOWING BOOKS

These six books on the *Life of Saint Martin* are not by Paulinus of Nola but by Paulinus of Petricordium, who lived approximately thirty years after the death of Paulinus of Nola and dedicated that work to Perpetuus, archbishop of Tours, who presided over the Council of Tours in the year 480. See Sirmond’s notes on Letter 11 of Book VIII of Sidonius Apollinaris.

## BELLARMINE, ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS, IN THE EDITION OF 1617

[Col. 1009C] The six books on the *Life of Saint Martin* cannot be by Saint Paulinus of Nola; for the author of those books mentions Paulinus of Nola and declares that he bears the same name, and he writes the sixth book to Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, who held office around the year 470.

## FRANCIS JURETUS TO PETRUS PITHOEUS, MOST DISTINGUISHED JURIST

I read with pleasure and with vexation the books of Paulinus on the Life and Deeds of the holy Martin, which you recently sent to me, most distinguished Pithoeus. It was a pleasure to recall a most holy and learned poet, and to see the tablets of his genius surviving as though from a shipwreck; but the countless number of errors and faults provoked my vexation, for the parchments had been so disgracefully corrupted that, while reading, I often called down punishment upon the hands of the scribes who had committed the crime of falsifying them. For what happened? Scarcely a single verse remained without being overturned; there was more verbal matter than sense; syllables tottered, words tottered; with the feet crippled, nothing stood at all. In short, scarcely any meaning remained, as though there were as many erasures as letters. I believe the copyist wanted to make the poet resemble himself in everything. For just as Paulinus, while he lived, cast away the greatest riches of fortune and poured them out himself, becoming rich for the poor and poor for himself amid riches, so the scribe saw new riches in Paulinus’s writings and at the same time begrudged them. Thus he betrayed and destroyed what he feared might betray or destroy the Lord. But what could be more unequal than this equality? Paulinus once rejected the goods of fortune willingly and deliberately. The goods of his genius—by which I mean his little books—he can relinquish only unwillingly.

[Col. 1010B] For he regarded the former as foolish things, but the latter as substantial. As for me, I neither ought nor wished to endure the repeated stripping of one who was already naked. Therefore, using the judgment of your old manuscript, I pursued the traces of the lost passages and finally restored many things to Paulinus; I would have restored all the embellishments if a second copy had come to my aid. Nevertheless, I hope, Pithoeus, that through your singular diligence I shall someday obtain a second exemplar by which the work may be completely restored. For why should I not hope this, since you were born with the destiny of seeking out the books of the ancients shrewdly, finding what you seek successfully, and generously sharing what you find with scholars? Proceed, then, I beg you, proceed eagerly, and rescue the remaining relics of Paulinus from darkness. Thus we shall have a sacred poet who will receive an eloquent lyre in his hands, pale ivy upon his brow, fresh laurels, and palms bound with ribbons. As for me, I shall give whatever assistance I can to writers of this kind. Although others have labored on them until now, many things nevertheless remain to be corrected, so that a person who diligently does again what others have done will not seem merely to repeat their labor. More on each matter elsewhere. For now, I speak of Paulinus, whom I dedicate to your virtues, since you wished one or another from the number to be selected to undergo the hazard of judgment. It will be yours, Pithoeus, to extend a hand to the returning man and gently embrace the guest who, sent to you naked and shaggy, will return from me adorned and polished, proceeding more boldly if you approve his new clothing and appearance. Farewell, most distinguished man; and since you love scholars because they deserve it, love me also so that I may deserve it.

[Col. 1010D] Dated the Kalends of July, 1585.

[Col. 1009]

## THE SIX BOOKS OF PAULINUS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MARTIN (B, C, S)

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009D] Christ had spread a venerable light throughout the whole world,

revealing the mysteries of the kingdom proclaimed by the Gospel.

But because the working of virtues had not moved all peoples,

and they hesitated to believe with their fragile understanding

[Col. 1010D] whatever the messenger had proclaimed from eternal lips

(for present realities move when discovered through words;

things unseen are urged upon belief, but things seen are proved),

he therefore to whom compassion for the whole world was equal

[Col. 1011A] wrought very many miracles in our lands,

granting the distant Gauls the distinction of Martin.

Fruitful Pannonia sent him from afar for our salvation;

he was born of no humble stock, for his father was a tribune,

renowned for the praise of his merits—but Martin himself

was nobler than his ancestors, so renowned that, with Christ as his father,

he rejected sacrilegious rites, nobly degenerate from his father’s practices.

For scarcely had he reached his tenth year

when, already advanced in character, he turned with steadfast heart

to the sacred law and marked his forehead

with the holy protection of the cross.

His mind was not fickle in his youthful breast:

his entire will was to preserve or learn God’s command.

To avoid gatherings of men, to know the secrets

of the blessed wilderness, and, having despised the world, to know God,

to abandon earthly cares with an exalted heart—

[Col. 1011B] while he was scarcely attempting these things at twelve years of age,

the sublime glory of so great an achievement was cut short,

though God, rewarding his merit, approved his desire.

The Augustus ordered the whole offspring of veteran stock

to arm themselves, preparing for the chosen wars.

What can envy not do? His father informed against him and thrust arms upon his son—

alas, piety had forgotten such great danger.

But if your stony mind receives any understanding,

increase your titles; for it is a greater praise that you are defeated.

See all that he accomplished through his pious resolve.

If these things are good, willingly imitate them. If difficult, rejoice.

The soldier of Christ is defeated in place of the soldier of the age,

but his mind is not dragged along, nor is his heart bound together with his flesh.

Empty are the names of military service. Long ago he served,

captured by his own king through many battles:

[Col. 1011C] he conquered avarice and defeated arrogant

luxury; now ambition lies prostrate, stripped of its strength,

and madness flees from his steadfast mind, as does anger,

and destructive pride, surpassing every other fault.

He scarcely permits one companion to proceed with him,

not bound to him by service, but a servant in name alone.

O blessed man, for whom circumstance prepared such a pleasing yoke,

so that, in place of your lot, the competing vows of noble men

could contend with you—if only it were permitted still to serve.

But you too are compelled to a harsh law, released by the law of your birth!

For the devotion of a holy man serves you as your subordinate;

the same clothing, and the frugal abundance of a common table.

Here he was first in acts of service, so that not even by chance

could any skill recognize the servant as superior to the Lord.

[Col. 1011D] Here already, among his equals, there was a grace and modesty

that had subjected even the foremost themselves to him through genuine affection;

and how strict was the regulation governing the food they consumed,

lest their swollen entrails corrupt their swift understanding,

or the burden of their limbs weigh down their wakeful minds,

so that an abundance divided might provide a portion for the needy,

and what would overwhelm one might better sustain both.

For he had divided everything among the needy who begged

so that nothing remained except coverings for their bared limbs.

Then suddenly, in the icy cold of a harsh winter,

a naked man hurries to meet him, scarcely able to form words

through chattering, broken sounds; but suffering makes the cause clear

and cries out the words his tongue cannot express.

[Col. 1012A] Everyone passes by, and the madness of the rich,

laughing with contempt, looks down upon the rejected complaint.

The holy man stopped, uncertain, with troubled heart

what he should do: the will was present, but the means were lacking.

At least his hesitation delayed the deed for a moment.

Only one garment remained to cover his blessed body,

the cloak always doubled, which by its doubled covering

warded off the cold and rain, the winds and their fury.

For the hanging part thus compensates for the shortened portion,

if the head should feel that whatever was lacking had increased warmth,

the body being warmed by the added fleece.

But this happy decision, bound by a strict vow,

drives the thought away, as though condemning the heart’s expenditure—

that the cautiousness of his trembling faith had preferred

to give one person a portion of the doubled covering for his limbs

rather than divide it between two.

Nor does delay hinder the deed; his hand passes beyond his intention,

and the invincible sword is drawn without the guilt of a wound.

Generous compassion cuts away the middle part,

choosing, I believe, the worse part for himself;

then he covers the trembling limbs,

and, handing over some warmth from the garment,

he now receives a lighter share of the cold in his clothing.

O blessed man, surpassing through your virtue all miracles

and exceeding the commands of the Lord who orders them!

For he commands us to be content with little;

he commands us not to keep two garments, but you divide one.

Everyone else looks on and laughs at the unsightly coverings,

and does not perceive the greater beauty truly present in the heart.

[Col. 1012C] But others, inwardly pierced in heart, complain

that justice could have assigned to a needy poor man what abundant resources had denied to a rich man.

Nor is there delay before the palm of victory is granted for so great a triumph.

For scarcely had he, exhausted, thrown his limbs upon the bed,

allowing a thin sleep while his heart remained watchful—

indeed, it was not sleep, because his attentive mind remained awake—

when suddenly, before his eyes, Christ, benign with abundant reward,

stood there, clothed in the poor man who had received him,

and fitted the blessed garment to his own limbs.

O truly precious cloak! What garment of purple,

or what robes distinguished by gold drawn out into shining thread,

could have deserved anything like this? What silks,

smooth to the touch or made vivid by skillfully rendered designs?

He, the God of humanity, earth, sea, and sky,

who bestows all things, without whom nothing exists,

and whose gift and giver are both what we have given and the one who gave it—

if he reckons the profits of salvation, he is enriched by this service.

Yet not even from this did boastfulness disturb his steadfast mind,

nor did he feel any empty swelling in his heart.

O virtue close to God, to regard as no praise

the praiseworthy deeds you perform, and not to attribute to our own action

what we accomplish, nor to seek less praise for a holy deed.

By then he was certainly secure concerning so great a judge.

But he is not exalted; rather, through fellowship with Christ,

the things seen increase faith. Renewed in holy baptism,

his limbs shine and take on a beauty equal to that of his heart,

and the mysteries of the fountain bring forth a new body.

[Col. 1013A] And yet, although he had this maturity of character,

he had completed fewer than four five-year periods,

lacking two years. I certainly believe that earlier

the holy Spirit had enriched his whole heart

with the flowing stream of its gift.

Thus, once, holy Peter saw the blessed gifts

already sent by the Lord in such a soldier.

Who, I ask, will be able to complete so well

what blessed Martin began in his tender years?

And yet, in doing these things, he did not think that he had even begun,

although he had scarcely delayed a little beyond two years.

Already a monk in merit, but a soldier in name alone,

he was already breaking the empty terms of the world beneath his feet.

The sacred fellowship of the tribune’s companions awaited him,

so that, after a small and proper delay, before Christ the Judge,

the doubled salvation of two men might be weighed through their vows.

[Col. 1013B] Meanwhile, once the barriers had been broken

and the gates burst open, a savage enemy had begun

to ravage the Gallic countryside.

The commander prepares to go out against him,

and summons all the companies to war by command, exhortation, prayer, and gifts.

For those whom fear holds back are persuaded by rewards,

and gifts overcome fear.

But the mind filled with God fears nothing, despises everything,

laughs at terror, and tramples earthly gifts underfoot.

Thus, after those who had gone before had received their gift

and the order had been passed through, the holy man was summoned according to custom.

He rejected the gifts offered by the approaching king,

and opposed the tyrant’s words with these words:

“Give these earthly gifts, prince—the money—to others.

Greater rewards of a greater king await me;

this is the payment of war: let those who wish to fight receive it.”

[Col. 1013C] At these words the commander is inflamed with savage anger

and accuses him of cowardice in a time of war,

claiming that he has invented excuses of fear, forgetful of glory.

But he has no fear of the danger that threatens,

nor do steadfast hearts fear an easy death.

Finally, what his words declare, his deeds will prove.

“I myself, first, advancing before the columns,

will approach without weapons—not taking up the weapons of a man,

but the standards of salvation;

trusting neither in the covering of a shield,

but in the name of Christ,

and placing the cross upon my forehead as aid instead of a helmet,

I will meet every danger with fearless heart.”

He assented, and, so that the proof of his statement might demonstrate his faith,

ordered that the pious man be kept under harsh guard.

Already the first dawn was scattering the earth with a new lamp,

when a suppliant embassy came to the king,

submitting its necks beneath the rule of the one who commanded.

What, I ask, do we see here accomplished by arms?

What did the iron battle line avail, what did terror and the sword?

What wedge fell beneath spears, what troop beneath arrows?

One man, and the sole trust of the eternal King,

defeated countless peoples without the wound of slaughter.

Here, Martin, is your triumph, with Christ victorious—

lest he violate the face of the holy with blood,

or afflict his pious mind with the deaths of the dying.

Therefore, joyful at his deserved success and made more vigorous by it,

he hastens to conquer the world after crushing its enemies.

He seeks Hilary, the teacher of the faith,

proved by so many examples, lest the wound of boastfulness

inflict itself, or his heart’s judgment raise him up improperly.

[Col. 1014A] Now the disciple acts as teacher and is proved greater,

while he desires to be lesser, for to scorn praise is itself praise.

Thus, already worthy of the honor of the highest chair,

he refused even to seek the dignity of a deacon,

a position from which he had long surpassed through his deeds.

He accepted lower duties, asking for the office of an exorcist,

though already a priest in virtue.

Then, so that not even earthly piety might mark the man

whom divine piety guided with such distinction,

he desired, with eager purpose, to visit the authors of his birth

and to turn their minds, which had been turned away, back toward the better.

For reckless and wayward error had oppressed his father and mother,

worshipers of sacrilegious rites and of stones or bronze,

with a death far too powerful while they lived.

[Col. 1014B] Therefore, as he undertook the journey, piety accompanied him,

and the angel sent by the Lord had made all the roads passable,

so that the difficult ascent over the sunken hill might be easy

and steep, hollow descents might not pull travelers forward.

And while he was hurriedly crossing the cloud-bearing Alps,

he happened to be intercepted by the ambush of savage robbers.

They came upon him with drawn swords, while his hands were bound behind his back;

he laughed and despised the dangers with an unmoved face.

Indeed, to recall the mystery of so great a deed,

he is said by his admonitions of salvation to have saved his captor—

he was a truer guardian of the other’s soul than that man was of his body.

For one had no control even over his own limbs,

while the other bound the inner chambers of his mind against the enemy.

Nevertheless, both wisely showed the road that was to be followed.

The one pointed out the path over the embankment and learned the way of salvation.

[Col. 1014C] Thus he completes the journey he had begun and approaches his homeland,

entering the fields of Hesperia after crossing the Alps.

Here again the enemy, opposing his unceasing holy endeavors,
fashioning a human appearance in a feigned body,
He presented himself in opposition, daring to ask where he was going and what this haste required. He replied: “Christ is my sole guide on this road; in him the fulfillment of my vow has been accomplished, from whom the will was granted.” But the demon, offended by such an undertaking, went gnashing his teeth and doing everything he could to oppose him. The saint said to him: “The Lord defends me; the enemy does not harm me. With God as my helper, no opposing power can be feared. Fearing the Lord, I despise danger; that fear itself makes me unafraid.” After he had spoken these words, the shadow was driven from his sight and vanished.

[Col. 1014D] But when, with the Lord as his guide, he reached the region of his parents, and found his father hardened by long habit and resisting the words of the salvation that had been offered, he at least received his mother through Christ’s gift.

O happy birth, and happy travail, by which she gave birth to a child through whom she herself was born to God; mother and child alike became, in blessed childbirth, a mother who was to be born again. Before, she bore him from the womb; now, through him, she was born from the laver.

Nevertheless, many were won over by this salutary example, rightly marveling at the marks of such great virtues. At that time, too, the evil error of a disastrous teaching had spread among peoples heedless enough to follow it: the poison that Arius had poured forth from his insane mouth. Above all, this plague held Illyricum in its grip, raging everywhere with its full venom.

[Col. 1015A] There, strong in steadfast virtue, he dared to stand against it and to break the waves upon his opposing breast. Often he restrained the priests, and often the people; oppressed by the plots of all, suffering blows, and driven at last from his earthly dwelling, he departed. Yet with his mouth he retained the faith, and with his heart, salvation.

Therefore, thinking that he ought to withdraw, lest the madness of a world thrown into ruin overwhelm the saint while he lingered, he sought the fields of Gaul and retraced his former steps, mindful of his faith. But when the disastrous error raged throughout the whole world, and these crimes pressed even upon the farthest Gauls, and when the faction of the mad world had driven out Hilary himself, the wall and mighty pillar of faith, he decided to rest awhile in a cell he had built,

[Col. 1015B] here where beautiful Milan depicts Italy rejoicing beneath the shades of the grove or the vine.

From here, too, he was driven away and left the lands and cities, making for the sea and its waves, because the tide of popular welcome and the storm of the mob were fouler and more to be feared than the sea’s waves. A presbyter of equal merit and similar danger accompanied him.

An island was found as a place of refuge, far from every host. Grass was enough for food; using its roots, the saints doubled their fasts on such barren fare. While indiscriminately searching for some scant nourishment—whatever the untried entrails of the earth brought forth—they suddenly experienced the grass of hellebore spreading deadly poison throughout all their limbs.

They continued to the Lord with every effort of prayer.

[Col. 1015C] But mercy anticipated the prayers: human arts accomplished nothing; the only hope of salvation was the medicine immediately present. Let us consider those who seek life with their entire fortune and habitually pour out prayers upon physicians in exchange for payment, so that the length of their lives may be increased by their money. What did the cups of selected juices accomplish here, or the medicines once read in ancient books? Here, certainly, the heart earned swift salvation without expense or art, and the word granted it—let us rejoice and marvel.

The voice is silent, and the cause is established by the cry of those who are silent. The physician is perceived though unseen; every limb admits the cure into its pure inward parts according to its causes.

Meanwhile, at last, the holy priest is reported to have returned from exile by the king’s command, with whom he had shared the splendid companionship of life

[Col. 1015D] while the teacher of the Pictavians flourished in the regions of Poitiers, handing the peoples, still untamed, the precepts of salvation.

And although swift affection had hurried the rejoicing saint away, yet he, impatient of delay, had already left the lofty heights and walls of Rome, to be brought back more quickly to the lands of the Pictavians.

Thus, retracing the earlier footprints with devout haste, he earned the fulfillment of his heart’s desire and the end of his labor. Here he built a cell, a solace for his weary limbs. For his mind remained in a heavenly dwelling, filled with God.

Here now, if we recall the songs of the ancient poets, when miracles suddenly struck astonished senses, senseless madness would have cried out for the wretched Phoebus and would not have allowed even the false Muses to rest.

[Col. 1016A] The temples of Delphi would have been shaken by their false Apollo, the whole crowd of deaf sisters would have been swept away, and monsters, roused by force, would have filled the entire scene with madness.

But we, who seek from Christ both understanding and words, pray, Martin, that you inspire the worshiper of Christ for a little while. You who were able to restore life to the dead, by the Lord’s help restore health to my face. I shall be the first to recount the miracles of the life granted; I shall be the first to break open the tomb of him who confesses. With all my heart I rightly implore you, my patron who is dead, that a living mind may speak the titles of such great praise.

Therefore, although lofty deeds surpass the powers of speech, and the measures of my prayer cannot equal their praises, I shall begin. Whoever you are who, while laughing at the words, despise these wretched verses as you read them, you will marvel at the deeds.

[Col. 1016B] A certain man, seeing the miracles of so glorious a life, chose to join himself to so great a teacher, although the mystical wave of the font had not yet renewed him. Fever, having completely consumed his marrow, tore away his slender life from his wasted body.

At that time the teacher was absent, but the brothers’ diligent religious devotion mourned the lifeless corpse with sorrow, grieving over the brother’s punishment, not over the burial of his flesh. When the saint arrived, he drenched his generous face with tears, pitying the dead man’s sad fate; he filled the whole place with his cries, and, once the witness had been sent away, he rushed into the cell saddened by so grievous a death.

Then he threw himself upon his lifeless friend. He embraced the limbs frozen in every member and breathed a slender breath over the rigid mouth.

[Col. 1016C] Yet his entire hope was directed to the Lord. He prayed to the accustomed mercy, sought the compassion he knew, and, by believing, earned the reward of faith. The confidence of a pure heart saw God present; his devout inward parts felt the effect.

Nor was there delay: scarcely had the prayer been delayed for two hours when the linens began gradually to move as the limbs stirred, and the dry limbs were watered with the moisture of the veins. Through the breath of life the icy chest grew warm. The eyes, covered over, opened as light was poured into them.

Happy those who, at the dawn of this sublime event, were granted to see Martin at the beginning of his illness.

The entire body suddenly raised itself with a unified effort. The skin, long yellow and wasted upon the exhausted limbs, recovered a purple color through a better flow of blood.

[Col. 1016D] His voice was easy, his step steady, his hand effective, his heart vigorous. The whole human being, formed from various bodily causes, received one life for its several functions. Immediately, the greatest joys drew forth a great voice. His tongue sounded praises, the messenger of a grateful mind; the cry of his mouth announced the feeling of his heart.

At once the crowd burst through the doors and filled the cell, and a harmonious chorus sang holy praises. But he, in order to renew his life completely after what had happened, immediately shone forth, renewed by the eternal wave, and, happy, prolonged his old age for many years, as a witness of this great event.

For he often used to tell many people that he had trembled before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, assigned to worthless crowds and sunk in darkness,

[Col. 1017A] until a prayer expressed in angelic words offered his vow to the Lord and restored his life.

He was the first to make Martin known to our regions; through this entrance the glory of his other praises reached us.

Not much time, certainly, had passed after these miracles when a new glory had brought forth another illustrious deed. For as Martin was passing the neighboring estate of Lupicinus—not the estate of an insignificant and obscure man, but of a man distinguished by virtue throughout nearly the whole world, so that his glory might appear all the more securely established through such a witness—he heard from afar a pitiable cry of the unlearned populace. He stopped, asked the reason, and learned the circumstances in turn.

[Col. 1018A] Just compassion aroused his devout grief. A servant had broken the limits of life, having gone mad when a noose tightened around his throat.

He hurried up and embraced the sad corpse: its eyes were forced from their sockets, its throat was dry with blood, its gaze terribly fierce, and its face threatening even in death. Again, tears rose to the Lord, sighs upward, groans and cries from the heart, the loud voice of one who had been silent.

The one faith of merit and the no less remarkable grace of the gift were received by a grateful choir and an accompanying crowd, displaying to all the miracles of the Lord Christ and the glory of the believing people in the enemy’s spoils.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 01017]

[Col. 1017B] Behold, a new sea opens before me, and favorable breezes draw a creaking vessel into the midst of the waves. While the calm joys of the sea carry me forward, a reckless skiff plunges into the vast deep.

I scarcely skim the shores near neighboring lands. What am I doing, and where in fear do I steer my doubtful prow? The winds trouble my course; I fear the return. Let us proceed, since the land is far away, wherever the wave may carry us.

Let Martin, the bishop, spread such a calm breeze and make the wave so gentle for the traveler that the rotten sail may bear favorable winds.

Until now, in recounting the customs and deeds of the monk, the riverbank was my setting; now it will be the sea of episcopal teaching. I shall unfold anew the renowned deeds of the great priest.

[Col. 1017C] Once, in the regions of Gaul, the city of Tours flourished greatly, spread among fields and filled with peoples. Yet, desiring to prosper still more under such a bishop, it burned with every prayer to obtain Martin.

But his humble mind, wholly banishing pride from the holy heart, remained unmoved by frequent prayers. At length, carefully composed words and constrained tears overcame his excessive firmness with righteous deception.

For someone, conscious of such great piety, prayed and pitied the sad distress of his lowly wife. He begged that the saint deign to see the prayers of the petitioner: that by coming quickly he would either be the cause of salvation or, if a harsh judgment delayed the prayers, of death. Sighs were joined to words by deeds as well.

God compelled him to follow, for he would have exposed his deceitful purpose more fully if he had not approved what had to be done.

[Col. 1017D] A crowd of people came out to meet him, exercising a kindly force, and a numerous riot of suppliants filled the road: a peaceful movement, a tumult without bitterness. Even a vigilant guard arranged night-long watches and preserved the master whom it was their duty to preserve.

Hearts rejoiced in harmony with one another. They went out to meet him; eager expectation poured from every gate, and the people’s favor contended with itself. There was one will among all, and no division of mind in their devotion.

Some were infected by devouring envy, blackened with the gall of poison; burning the hearts of the wretched with its goads, their carnal opinion drew them back to the opposing side.

[Col. 1018B] Some even—an abomination for learned people to believe—are said to have drawn a similar madness into their minds, laughing at what should have brought them joy: that no grace had adorned the venerable face; that, with his hair cut, his uncovered forehead displayed the full sign of the Lord; that he did not veil his eyes beneath the cloud of trembling locks; that his filthy clothing, testifying to the brightness of his heart, revealed the devotion of one praying, because, with his limbs turned toward the ground and his body prostrate, dust had clung to his rough, dirty wool.

Rightly, then, such willing devotion yielded to the people, and the sounder judgment of the common crowd overcame the leading men. For no one was permitted not to recognize the judgment of Christ, proved by so many signs.

[Col. 1018C] Among the others, whom a savage faction had wickedly joined to itself in its desire for something different, one bishop was the more violent defender. By his name they perhaps thought that the efforts of their false policy ought to be defended, although God rejected the plan and approved what was just.

The devout people celebrated the customary honor in the holy assembly, observing the mysteries in a solemn gathering. The altars were crowded by an even denser throng, and the frequent worshipers waited upon the vows of their supporter; nor could the reader pass beyond the barriers that had been placed before him.

But a deacon who happened to be present, scarcely having snatched up the book, seized the verse that the first page of the psalm, suddenly opened at the right moment, had immediately offered him.

[Col. 1018D] He hastily sang these words of the ancient prophet:

“From the mouths of infants, and from the small murmur of sucklings,  
you have caused their tender tongues to pour forth praise.”

This praise, uttered by little ones, destroyed the perverse defender of those who hated God.

A cry was raised to heaven, and the judgment was approved: the sentence of Christ was proclaimed by God himself. The thunderbolt of the words overwhelmed the opposing side. The same verse approved the words of those who praised and restrained the livid hearts of those who resisted.

Nor was the monk’s labor lessened by this, since his glory increased. The deeds that must be done are taught by the priest’s example; an action persuades more powerfully than the favor of a word.

[Col. 1019A] Thus he was clothed in a worn and worthless garment; thus humble modesty of heart was precious to the saint. Thus the blessed judgment of his life remained constant.

At first his cell was joined to the sacred altars. Then, so that he could avoid the crowds and his constant prayer could be secluded from continual throngs, he withdrew two miles from the city. The great distance did not harm the cell’s secluded lodging for the monk, the little road for the master, the nearby house for the teacher, or the distant place for the wanderer.

Here, along the natural edge of a cut rock, a curving cliff enclosed a modest recess. Here the Loire, with banks bent into a small curve, surrounded the land that had been entered, stretching its deep waters before it. A single entrance opened between the narrow rock and the river,

[Col. 1019B] passing a little way inward, where, separated by a constricted threshold, the river’s flow touched the mountain’s boundary.

Here he preferred to weave a small cell from a pile of wood, recognizing the mysteries of the holy Wood. The most exalted guest took his place beneath the humble roof, so that the learned modesty of the gathered brothers might learn to despise splendor at little expense, imitating their master’s example in eager competition.

But others had no liking for wood; the neighboring rock, hollowed out, offered them recesses dug into the mountain. Eighty brothers had been drawn there by a proper admiration for such great virtue, so that, by observing him, they might happily take on his way of life.

No one possessed anything special; everything was common to all. Love took its share from the common store, and no one was allowed the power to sell anything.

To prevent the shameful hunger for gold from growing through the taste of it, he prohibited the practice of a trade. Only the study of writing was permitted, occupying mind, eyes, and hand, and holding all three together at a single point: the gaze in sight, the heart in perception, and the right hand in its ordered task.

[Col. 1019C] Yet only those of younger age were occupied with these tasks. For the mature, prayer at the appointed time was sufficient, so that one whose understanding was confirmed by an elder’s judgment might strive for purity of heart and keep watch, cleansing the inward eye in seclusion, lest, covered by the mist of sin, it should be deprived of Christ’s light.

No one had freedom to advance beyond his own cell; only for the purpose of association was the community permitted to assemble, when the customary harmony of voice and heart brought praise to God in prayer.

Or they assembled when, breaking their fasts for weary limbs, they returned at an appointed time to the common tables and, having brought the subdued flesh to the end of the completed day, divided the briefest periods of the modest supper before the labor of the coming night watches.

[Col. 1019D] Only the sick were allowed, under a relaxed rule, to taste unmixed wine, so that the scent of wine sprinkled into their cups might sustain the wasting body of the ill.

For many, their clothing was woven from camel hair, which touched their wakeful limbs with light prickles, excluding sleep from the pierced flesh. They did not allow soft fleeces to nourish the body’s sluggishness,

[Col. 1020A] nor did a delicate garment float loosely around them in indulgence. Such was the abundance of their former life, since prudent judgment had drawn many distinguished by ancient lineage into this way of life. It is therefore all the more remarkable that, after silken cushions and couches, this clothing and such severity pleased those who entered.

Finally, neighboring peoples and nearby cities, amazed at the marks of such great conduct, opened themselves to the saints in a contest of devotion, so that the teaching of God, flowing from such a fountain, might pour irrigating streams into the inward parts of the thirsty.

But now the time has come, after so great a mass of mighty virtues, to touch at least a small part.

And although they adorn his disciples with the titles of upright virtue and teach through their deeds what ought to be done, I shall nevertheless touch upon a very few of his own deeds, displaying the greatest praises through brief signs.

[Col. 1020B] There happened to be nearby a tomb which vain superstition, deceived by error, had falsely consecrated as renowned for martyrdom, continually rendering it honor. Earlier priests had even dedicated an altar to it, so that this religious observance, strengthened by the added cult of sacred rites, might remain more firmly established.

But after Martin took up the reins and received the holy governance of the people entrusted to him, he immediately asked the name and titles of the one being worshiped, and whether he had earned the marks of so glorious a victory by the passage of time or as if under judgment.

[Col. 1020C] But when no history was available that could reveal the truth, and all antiquity had preserved ignorance of the matter, he refused to believe such great claims on doubtful words. The tale of the lying crowd was not sufficient for faith.

Therefore he decided that, in matters doubtful and without the weight of witnesses, an inquiry should be sought from the Lord, to whom all times are subject and before whom the present age of the past stands.

He hurried to the mound with a few companions, so that miracles might attest the faith of the few to the many. When he had approached the mass of the neighboring tomb, beside the cold ashes dissolved from the flesh, prayers rose to heaven. The traces of the flesh remained joined to the tomb, but the mind passed to the stars.

Then he prayed to the Lord with the full strength of faith, asking that he reveal the merit and name of the buried man to those who did not know them.

[Col. 1020D] Suddenly he saw on his left a foul shadow, black, with a face that revealed sorrow; it bore the most grievous fate of the punished guilty and showed a confused and conscious countenance. Its voice, given to mournful words, expressed frequent sighs in complaints such as these:

“Let the ancient error of mourning the Manes cease adding punishment by giving an alien title, lest, when one person’s crimes are enough for his penalties, a doubled burden grow for him through the added honor.

And would that the holy men to whom this service is wrongly attributed might deign to sprinkle even a few drops upon the unceasing flames of the wretched. They enjoy perpetual light. No dreadful chaos encloses them in eternal darkness.

[Col. 1021A] The confusion of night is far from the merits of light.”

This voice reached the ears of many far and wide, but the appearance was disclosed to Martin alone, whose mind, lighter than the frail burden of flesh, passed beyond bodily weight through the light of the heart.

Immediately the altar was removed and every vain superstition, which had falsely imitated sacred rites, was driven away. The mysteries were transferred to true objects of worship.

What could magic, infected with deceitful tricks or stained with poisons, finally offer comparable to these titles? It weaves lies in composed words, searches through examined veins for things that hang hidden, and, seeking them through the silences of Tartarean night, makes the mad demon bellow with deceptive muttering, assuming a false face beneath a slender appearance.

[Col. 1021B] Here, certainly, the simple mind and the solitary devotion of one who prays dissolve the bonds of the infernal law.

And although his limbs lay pressed down in the tomb, nevertheless his confession lived on into the present time.

Nor is this the end of his titles, nor do the marks of his virtues cease even when interrupted for a short time. For grace always accompanies the saint inseparably. It is not confined within a fixed boundary of place; it follows his progress and remains undivided with him who remains. If he is glad to set out upon a journey, it accompanies the one who goes.

For when he was quickly crossing the remote paths of the countryside, where wild Gaul lies spread across broad plains, he saw a Gentile crowd following a wretched corpse, its thin cloths trembling in a light breeze and stretching far across the open plain. He judged the funeral procession to be the worship of a wicked demon and the rites of miserable sacred observances, the frenzied devotees bowing their necks beneath idolatrous images.

[Col. 1021C] At once he carried before them the holy and venerable sign, and, by presenting the cross, quickly blocked those who were approaching. The weight of the banner halted their unsteady steps.

Then it was possible to see the wretched held in numbness placed upon them, their limbs stiffened and bound by rigid sinews, their many efforts frustrated by intertwined members, their steps delayed as if fixed in place. The crowds were enclosed within a boundary imposed by command, and barriers like a wall presented an immense enclosure against their attempt to pass from every side.

At last, when the honor borne in the funeral rites gradually became clear to their nearer sight, freedom was restored again by the same banner and by the sign itself. Thus, by the authority of the cross and the power of faith, he had the right both to bind the wandering and to release the bound.

I pass rapidly over these things, selecting them as I read them because the abundance of material urges me to touch upon virtues worthy of praise in brief signs, lest a most insignificant page delay minds hastening toward such great miracles with lengthy words.

Again I am met by the weight of greater matters.

Once he had thrown down a sacrilegious temple from its summit, laying it upon the ground. He crushed the idols after breaking the beams and buried the images beneath the entire ruin.

Near this place a pine tree, spread out with green branches, extended its aged limbs far and wide and, at its leafy crown, had woven together a green forest.

[Col. 1022A] With a lattice of leaves it kept off the heat, and the dense grove of a single tree, in its perpetual shade, offered a constant coolness, pretending that spring was present.

He also undertook to join this pine to the ruins of the temple, wishing to roll it into the same destruction. He wished to remove whatever drew the hearts of the wretched into error.

But then the senseless madness of the inflamed crowd rose up and opposed his entire devout undertaking. Reason does nothing for the mad; holy words benefit profane minds nothing; a voice does not help the deaf, nor light the blind.

They shouted that a man could not bring salvation to things that could not help themselves; that wood could not be aided by wood; that the masters of the wood should serve the nods of the one who wished to serve them, himself subject to things subjected to him, gathering from the forests what should be burned and leaving what they revered.

[Col. 1022B] The others shouted back, desiring something altogether different, their hearts deeply soaked in idolatrous poison:

“Stop trying to compel us with lengthy words. If you prove these laws by facts, the condition that will bring faith will please us. We ourselves will immediately undertake to cut down our pine.

“If you bring forward true proofs of faith, receive it as it falls and joyfully meet its desired ruin. Trusting in the Lord, fear nothing difficult. The just Lord does not reject a just mouth that trusts in the power of God, to whom it is easy, by a word, to prevent the fall that is already at hand.”

At once bonds were fastened around his limbs, and he was placed beneath that part of the tree where the trunk, leaning forward under its entire weight, was already about to be struck. Its branches, bending under the burden and swaying downward, undoubtedly threatened the earth below with their fall.

They pressed on with all their strength, their joy contending with their prayers, striking repeatedly with frequent axes. Vengeance drove out affection, and anger banished pity.

The monks grew pale and lifeless; the greater danger was that their faith, confused by such terror, might fail.

At last, slowly overcome by the blows, the tree gave a crash as it fell forward, and, driven by its entire leap toward the saint, it rushed ahead of the rapid fury of the eager prayers. Its limbs were already shattered and near to contact, whirling in a broken storm.

[Col. 1022C] But faith drove fear away from him. He stood firm-hearted beneath the impending ruin, lest, seeing the pine suddenly turned back, unbelief should recall the undertaking at the moment of its fall and deny the merit by supposing the outcome accidental.

When the danger came nearer, he raised his right hand armed with the protection of the sign and opposed the cross. Immediately the whole force of the attack was broken, and the pine, violently whirled in a swift rotation, was carried in the opposite direction toward the authors of the crime. The jubilant people, now facing their own destruction, feared it in terror.

Those who thought they had carefully chosen a safe place from which to watch so great a spectacle scarcely recovered their senses when they saw their seats broken and pierced by the branches.

A cry rose to heaven, and the astonished factions echoed it; voices were repeated by the entire assembly. The monks testified their joy; conquered by the miracle, they sang Christ with their tongues. The ignorant and the learned alike sang Christ with kindly mouths. One group recognized his favor; another sought faith.

[Col. 1023A] Thus, in haste, a harmonious will arose among those who had been divided, Christ uniting them. When they had earned the gift of faith, they were also authorized to believe.

For certainly no one in that whole group failed to report that he had received the gifts of the salvation he had hoped for, once he had been added to the flocks under the protection of the sign of the Lord.

And the places that had reeked, covered with grim shrines, were soon covered with true churches by the Church once destitute.

Thus you conquer your enemies, Martin; thus you overwhelm them: a severe judgment crushes the oppressed, and your merciful victory made brothers of those whom it had made savage.

The event sharpened his mind, and fortunate victory constantly nourished his zeal to overcome the rebellious. For scarcely were the fallen idols smoking amid the flames, with fine ashes flying about in the neighboring fire,

[Col. 1023B] when his most righteous hand, rejoicing, renewed the fire of the temple with repeated flames.

But while a whirlwind struck the vapors of the blazing fire far and wide, and the fierce fire boiled with repeated waves, vomiting a swift cloud of flames and increasing its gathered fury through the neighboring destruction, it attacked a house that stood not far away, licking its nearby roof with mournful flames.

When the saint, trembling, saw that the danger was pressing upon him, and that the fire, mixed with the beams that had not been fanned, had already enclosed the house in a whirlpool of flames, he swiftly climbed the roof by a dangerous leap, where the thick mass of excessive fire pressed most heavily upon the house, and offered his limbs against the advancing flames.

Then, with the wind blowing against them, the flames bent backward toward the breeze. Although a greater force, driven by the storm, was pushing them forward and compelling them to advance violently, the wind immediately yielded to the fires as they turned back.

[Col. 1023C] Thus nature, overcome, obeyed the commands of merit. The flames were not driven by the winds; rather, the winds were driven by the flames. Fire, following the command, thus performed both tasks: it seized the decrees assigned to it and left the defended structure unharmed.

After the temple had been destroyed by these righteous fires, they went to destroy another, which a prosperous village happened to worship with a leprous, perverted mind.

But when the repeated madness of the crowd, in its senselessness, recalled the attempt it had made, and the violent whirlwind of the tumult opposed its entire fury, the saint returned to the remote solitude of deserted places.

There he pressed more urgently upon the Lord with prayers, continuing his earnest supplication for three days and joining to them an equal number of nights spent in vigil.

[Col. 1023D] Moreover, wrapped in a garment woven from hair, he afflicted his worn limbs with constant prickling, so that the excessively rough clothing might scour his delicate skin and the skin, touched by the stretched bristles, might tremble. He struck the rocky ground with his still harder bones, prolonged the daylight into late fasts, and drenched his entire face in a river of tears.

Thus he prayed that the perpetual mercy of the Lord Christ, deeply moved by the labor of his innocent servant, might grant effect to his vow and accomplish what he had attempted, completely removing the efforts of the opposing party.

Meanwhile, he saw armed men standing nearby, shining with angelic brightness. Recognition was not delayed: the familiar confidence of their faces was immediately apparent. Their words also explained the reason for their coming. He was told not to tremble, not to fear force, and not to dread their weapons; by such signs they would recognize the favor present, whatever crowd might rise against them in tumult.

He was to believe that God’s help was sufficient, since God could immediately defeat every band by the power of his word; the two had come together to bring assistance and convey commands.

[Col. 1024A] Therefore, his spirit, strengthened by the virtue it had received, grew more ardent, and he returned to the undertaking begun. With courage restored to his trembling heart, he burst into the midst of the crowds.

The temples were utterly overturned and lay in ruins. The fallen images received the entire mass of the buildings, and the broken idols collapsed beneath the roofs they had thrown down.

[Col. 1024B] Dust mixed everything together: beams, altars, statues, mortar, stones, and metal.

No one in the advancing crowd prepared to go to meet him; he remained undaunted, seeing the hearts of the terrified men defeated. The people stood motionless, awaiting what would happen; the breasts of the threatening men grew rigid, and their inward parts were stupefied with astonishment.

They could not set their limbs in motion or find words for their tumult. Their limbs stiffened, and the voice of the wretched caught in their throats. The hands of those who had attempted to strike fell useless, and the cry of those whose mouths gaped died away.

It was like the sea when a storm, stirred from the deepest bottom, presses upon the waves amid a violent gale, strikes the whole cliff with foaming spray, and surmounts the opposing banks with a hoarse roar.

The broken masses beat upon the hollow shores,

[Col. 1024C] mixing the shallows and the neighboring deep throughout.

Soon, when the winds grew silent after laying down their motion, an immense plain of calm waters was spread out. The smooth, marble-like waters settled when the wind subsided, and the changed appearance of the unmoving element invited slender boats over its level surface.

In the same way the madness of the raging crowd fell silent. It laid aside its storm and relaxed its posture.

Only this much did it proclaim, subject to truthful words: that Martin’s Lord was to be worshiped throughout the entire world; that he alone was known as God; that idols could never grant salvation to one who sought it from deaf objects; that they could neither keep for themselves nor give to anyone a gift of which they were themselves deprived, and that the one who asks from a needy beggar is even more destitute.

[Col. 1024D] Thus, having truly received the light’s full radiance, this crowd too was added to the worshipers, dedicated to the Lord’s camp.

With his heart continually strengthened by such triumphs, he again desired battle. Increased faith removed fear, hope gave him courage, and fear of danger yielded to the reward of merit, for a similar cause soon stirred a similar tumult.

As he hastened to assist in the overthrow of a temple, the excessively mad rustic population increased its customary resistance and its precipitous fury with an immense mass of rage.

Finally, madness had so overwhelmed the whole mind that one man came running with a drawn sword, daring to brandish the iron sacrilegiously at the saint’s wounds.

When the saint joyfully cast aside his covering and offered his bare neck, the man held nothing back. He rose high with the sword, lifting his furious right hand,

[Col. 1025A] raising his whole body in a swift effort and stretching his steps upward in a headlong leap, so that the blow, descending from higher up, might fall with greater force.

Suddenly, however, his inward parts stiffened with constricted sinews. His slight motion stopped, exhausted in the air; his outstretched right hand held the sword suspended as commanded. The entire blow perished in his torpid limbs, and his hand remained fixed after its futile effort.

Thus his limbs, collapsing backward with their entire weight, fell headlong in a swift ruin to the ground. His bones resounded as they were buried beneath his shattered limbs, and he lay face downward upon the mound of rocky earth.

Only then did groans break forth and forced tears appear. His ambition to pray for forgiveness, having laid down his weapons, turned toward salutary pardon.

[Col. 1025B] “What, I ask, drew your eager hand back from blood? Why spare one whom no one asks you to spare? What holds back the blow if your anger remains? Certainly you do not wish to forgive.

“Why do you retain the sword? Look, the innocent neck is exposed, bare to your wounds. Why do you delay your desire? If you have the mind of one who strikes, why is vengeance delayed while the crime remains? You do it; and if your right hand saves him, if your will has not changed, what you wished to do remains your guilt. The judgment of your heart is enough for your merits.”

Nor did the astonished breasts of the crowd see only here the gifts of salvation that had been preserved. Soon, when similar madness brought a similar death with a drawn weapon, the blade suddenly slipped away from the striker in a futile blow.

[Col. 1025C] The madman’s right hand sought the weapon that had been torn from it, and his eyes, deprived of the sword, saw all the desires of his collected fury vanish.

Nevertheless, Martin often used to persuade people through salutary conversation, change savage minds with words, and soften hardened hearts by holy speech, illuminating the ancient night with the light of teaching.

Moreover, it was easy for him to bring salvation to the sick, to the lame in their steps, and to the blind in their eyes. Certainly no one was overwhelmed by a disease so violent that he did not bring back the desired remedies of salvation, rejoicing to recover under the saint’s healing gaze, as the present deed will be able to make clear.

Once, within the walls of Trier, there was an unmarried maiden

[Col. 1025D] whose limbs were numb and deprived of every movement. She had been robbed of their functions; her flesh already seemed to have been abandoned, and a faint breath stirred in her cold breast.

Her relatives, terrified by the approaching death, grew pale. They watered her drying limbs with a fountain of tears, and the sorrowful company of attendants had assembled to offer the honor due at her funeral. Amid the murmur of the weeping, a messenger suddenly rushed in with open mouth, bringing the news that Martin had arrived and possessed the ready power to grant what was desired.

He threw himself at the saint’s feet, imploring aid, and sprinkled his footprints with abundant tears. Sighs broke through their sobbing voices; tears spoke more through their prayers than words could speak.

But the saint, rich in restrained compassion,

[Col. 1026A] joined himself to their feeling, denied his merit, and rejected the claim that he possessed the virtue by which he offered help. Yet in his heart he shared their grief; he refused display but mourned the affliction.

By avoiding any claim to merit, he proved it all the more; thus he stood higher through his humble heart and assigned to praise what he removed from honor.

Seeing this, the father pressed his request with still greater force, until persistent and just pleading moved him. The devout entreaty of the parents, joined to the prayers of the priests, compelled the saint, though gently refusing, to visit the sad inner chamber of the grieving father.

The people stood before the doors, their astonished hearts awaiting the miracles of Christ.

When he saw the girl, half-dead and wasted, pitying her, he saw her limbs consumed by decay, her eyes weakened by their wasting disease, her skin clinging to the bones of her dried body,

[Col. 1026B] her skin discolored by a diseased gall-like hue, the murmurs and sighs of her constricted tongue almost wholly withdrawn, a tiny breath issuing from her icy breast, and the threads of her veins perishing as the pulse failed, seeking to abandon their interrupted course.

Immediately he prostrated his whole body upon the ground, asking the Lord in words for medicines—for the Lord, to whom it is enough to command and whose nod overcomes every art.

He perceived that God was present and asked that olive oil be brought. When it had been offered, holy blessing approached the liquid.

Then, rejoicing in the oil whose substance had been changed, he touched each limb with the consecrated chrism. His devout right hand, applied to her, drove away the former pain, and the blessed gifts of the salvation obtained gradually returned, infused at the physician’s touch.

[Col. 1026C] Thus, with the diseases driven away from every part of her limbs, strength returned to her restored body.

Soon the girl rose vigorous, while the people marveled, and, placing her steady steps through the divine gift, she gave praise to the Lord and to Christ through the holy altars.

After this deed of virtue filled the city with renown, the entire crowd hurried together, since either a demon had afflicted their minds or disease their bodies—
Overwhelmed, they prayed in their hearts and remembered the healing:

Some departed steady in step, others sound in mind.

Yet above all, among everything that the grace of Christ deigned to accomplish through his servant, one healing stood out: that of a servant whom the demon held completely captive in his power.

At last, when the saint, moved by the great insistence of those who begged him, ordered the wretched man to be led to the holy threshold,

[Col. 1026D]

no one could bind the frenzied man. He had driven everyone away, raging with savage mouth; gnashing his teeth, he had covered his torn body everywhere with blood, and wounds bristled upon his naked limbs.

Then the master, exceedingly exalted in the splendid honor of the proconsul’s fasces, forgetting this dignity, came forward and fell at the saint’s kindly knees. Bending down, he wrapped his arms around the saint’s feet and pleaded that, since neither force nor chains could draw the servant, raving with an insane heart, to him, the saint himself should visit the house beneath which the servant had long been kept confined under unbroken guard.

But the saint refused to tread upon the threshold of the profane man, and the righteous man would not enter beneath idolatrous beams, distinguishing the stench of the temple from the chrism of Christ.

[Col. 1027A]

The other, however, clinging violently to the saint’s knees, promised that he wished to trust such a holy servant, whatever instruction so great a teacher might deliver.

At last, moved by the suppliant’s wholly justified plea, he carried his desired steps to the threshold of salvation. And to the Lord who sought such just assistance, both gave thanks for the medicine that had healed the servant: the one rejoicing that faith had been received, the other that it had been accepted into his heart.

Immediately after these miracles, another new wonder was performed, and it raised the astonished people to such loud praise. For as the saint happened to be entering the threshold of a neighboring house, he cried out against the dreadful shadow of the frenzied demon.

Without delay, the exposed enemy began to rage against the cook, to stir up turmoil within the innermost chambers of the house, and to bare the threatening teeth of his captive mouth, exercising his inborn fury through another’s bites, while he shook the body possessed by mingled madness.

The demon’s frenzy raged through a human mouth, armed with another’s tooth for its own savage fury. The terrified people fled, and no one dared withstand him; the examples before them sharpened their utmost fears.

But the saint, trusting in the Lord, laughed at the deceitful ranks and swiftly offered himself to meet them.

[Col. 1027B]

When the man, in his madness, shook his trembling jaws, clashing his wretched teeth with a savage growl and repeatedly snapping his head forward to bite, the saint steadily thrust his fingers into the gaping jaws, restraining the fiercest power of the opposing robber.

The greedy cheeks remained fixed in the opened wound; the wicked fury of the gaping mouth stiffened, suspended. The tongue beneath rejoiced at the healing touch, and the soft lips pressed the hand inserted within them.

Then, since no escape lay open through the obstructed mouth, the expelled spirit left the emptied entrails by a flow of the belly, drawing only stench from the body.

Meanwhile everything was suddenly thrown into confusion by an uproar. Evil rumor brought news of barbarian disturbances to the city, scattering unbelievable fears through credulous hearts.

Yet no messenger of this rumor appeared, so that the report might be confirmed by an unmistakable source. Therefore, when he saw people changing their minds amid such uncertainties and being held by unconfirmed terror,

[Col. 1027C]

he ordered the demon, shut up within the captive body, to disclose where he had spread the new rumor.

Immediately compelled by the torturing word to confess, he cried out that he himself was the cause, the crime, and the source of the evils; that he, together with his fellow spirits, had stirred up these lies, so that they might oppress the terrified people with fear.

Thus this true confession of the deceitful robber freed the sorrowing minds from torment, once the demon had been tortured.

But if I should now unfold the deeds of such great compassion, neither my barren mind nor my poor page would suffice.

O truly kindred good, compassion that is ready at hand! A humble heart despises no one, because it loves everyone.

For a certain man had been seized by a dreadful disease of leprosy, infecting all his flesh with a covering of spots and scattering dense blotches across his diseased body.

When the frequent disgust of healthy people marked him out, and the utterly unjust mind, ignorant of its own condition, despised the grievous diseases in another’s body, the saint entered through the gate, preceded by a crowd.

[Col. 1027D]
