As was fitting for the attendance assembled for so great a patron, they crowded the thresholds of the walls in dense throngs. The saint embraced the wretched man’s face and mouth with kisses.

Nor did he fear that his face would be stained by such a touch: he pressed upon the man’s joined lips the tokens of peace.

The others were astonished in their hearts; but the man rejoiced. Through the touch he perceived the gifts of divine grace, and perceived swift health hastening back through his limbs, as renewed radiance spread through his restored flesh.

[Col. 1028A]

O truly precious condescension of your peace, and healing that flowed from the pious mouth! Whether you touch limbs with your lips or hearts with your words, your kisses heal the sick, and your words those who must be taught.

Would that a similar mercy might touch our diseases, and that Martin, praying from so holy a mouth, might drive away the stains of our wretched hearts! Then, I believe, I would be recalled to the joys of true peace, lifting a healed face toward the holy mysteries.

And after the estate which my portion had given has been squandered, may my hope hang upon the mouth of the merciful Lord. Leaving the food of swine and the pleasures of the flesh, may I receive the sure tokens of true faith.

Indeed, merely a touch—or even the fringe of a garment, and threads torn from a genuine fleece—

[Col. 1028B]

has brought swift healing in every circumstance.

For, to pass over deeds no less clearly performed for humble people, who, I ask, could fail to know of Arborius, a man who had discharged the world’s highest office, distinguished because he had governed Rome with the authority entrusted to him as prefect, and no less eminent for the integrity of his pious character?

His limbs had been completely consumed by wasting illness. His only daughter had been laid upon her bed with languid limbs; fever, returning at fixed intervals on the fourth day, had stripped her of the garment of the flesh, repeatedly bringing her low, so that her afflicted body could feel no healing, even during the days midway between the fevers.

While one seizure claimed its period of agitation for itself, she trembled beneath the next, which was destined to come.

[Col. 1028C]

As the father therefore tended such a girl with sorrowful affection, running his warm breath repeatedly over her delicate limbs, a letter from the pious bishop to his grieving friend was placed in his trembling right hand.

Delighted by the gift when he had read the letter through, he joyfully pressed kisses upon the absent man’s hand, quickly closed the venerable pages, and hurriedly brought them to his panting breast.

O truly precious faith! The fever was driven away, and the flame of the burning heat was removed. The present blessing entered the dry veins and watered the exhausted marrow with the dew of the words,

[Col. 1028D]

restoring swift health through the mercy of the Lord. To his praise we shall rightly refer, exulting, what we now marvel that faithful servants could accomplish.

Nor did this healing grant health only to the limbs; faith, increased in the heart, added true salvation.

Immediately the devout virgin, consecrated to God through him by whom she had been rescued from disease, was offered to the Lord.

Thus the grace of this gift was bestowed upon three at once: the bishop consecrated her, the father offered her, and the virgin was made sacred.

Moreover, a similar healing restored health to Paulinus, whom the glory of his conspicuous faith had widely exalted. A cloud had covered his sight, and darkness, poured over it, stretched out its gloom, shutting out all light beneath a covering of spots.

[Col. 1029A]

A light sponge, suspended by the gift of the nearby blessed hand, gently drove the darkness away with its delicate touch. Scarcely had it been brought to his eye when his sight learned to bear the restored light, and, amazed, received a new brightness.

Would that the healing of such a holy patron might also wish to touch the darkness of our hearts with this light, restoring once more the mysteries of the ancient deed: the same name, the same physician, and the same cause of healing.

We marvel as we see so many great things accomplished so swiftly by the remedies of the holy chief physician; let us also marvel at the healing that the physician deserved, with Christ acting as healer.

Through him, generous in the gift and grateful for the gift, the good man rejoices both in what he spends and in what he retains.

For, striving to climb toward an upper part where a lofty house was supported upon high columns, he placed his slippery feet upon the stairs, fell headlong, and, renewing his repeated fall upon the steps, struck the ground and crushed it beneath the weight of his collapse.

[Col. 1029B]

But behold: while his shattered limbs groaned from their savage pain, an angel appeared beside the saint with a venerable face, bringing sudden consolation to the afflicted man. Hastening to wash his wounds with poured-out water, he gradually touched them with the offered healing ointment, leading the thin liquid along with a gentler touch.

From it the limbs were watered and immediately felt a silent healing, while the dampened body softened the veins. At once his limbs grew strong and steady; at the Lord’s command, the pains that had been driven away withdrew everywhere.

His steps were swift, his mind lively, and joy shone in his heart and mouth, his face in harmony with his grateful breast.

While he praised the Lord, he claimed nothing for himself; indeed, he revealed his merit by denying that he had deserved it.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1029]

Why do you call forth sterile reeds and the whistling of a broken voice, sound emitted from stalks? This glory is surely worthy of increasing the voices of our ancestors’ trumpets.

Such a voice could not burst forth from little stems, nor could such a great sound fill the lofty praises as they deserve.

But if a narrow pipe is helped even by a thin breath, such as the blessing sent from the holy mouth, then, although it cannot speak great things, it will at least utter what is pleasing.

The first part of the book, therefore, will be occupied by the ambition that was conquered; this gate will unlock the remaining praises, through which, after many ages of degenerate fears, lost freedom shone forth again into a corrupted world.

Once exalted by the fortunate conduct of wars, Maximus was proud of having brought about the death of one lord. The exile of another, together with a crime clinging to his evil character, had increased his guilt through the outcome; and unhappy prosperity, with its proud heart, had often cut back the wounds of his nature, only to fall more heavily amid favorable circumstances.

[Col. 1029C]

To this king, then, came frequent shepherds of God from different regions, whose constant care was either to preserve the pious master or to feed the people.

They strove to release the guilty, loosen the bound, restore rest to the weary, offer consolation to the sorrowful, pray for exiles to regain their homeland, and seek pardon for those whose wealth had been prescribed, earning life even for the wretched.

While they hastened to accomplish these things with benevolent zeal, the sacred dignity of the Fathers gradually began, with fearful assent, to submit to the swelling ruler. Devoted to flatteries, it became exceedingly base—not the ancient dignity of priests, which it had been accustomed to display, but the shameful ambition of clients, cast down at the nod of the haughty patron.

[Col. 1029D]

Among them Martin alone, steadfast in heart and speech, stained no pious inward part with deceit. Nor did cowardly sloth mark with a shameful blemish his mind, humble toward Christ yet exalted above the world’s contempt.

Indeed, whenever there was some reason to petition the swollen king, he steadfastly persevered in his prayers and accomplished the petitioner’s wish as though he were commanding by right.

The king’s ambition often tried, by repeated entreaties, to move the holy man, asking him to come, however late, to the royal banquets to which he had so often been invited.

But Martin, scorning his arrogance and recalling his deeds, utterly refused to join himself to his table, since he thought it sacrilegious even by the slightest assent to connect his holy mind with a man whose crimes included the slaughter of rulers, power won through the blood of Fathers, the king’s death, and a tyrant’s kingdom.

Yet when the king wearied his pious heart with continual petitions, washing away his guilt and purging the charges brought against him, he said that the rule of the empire had been imposed upon him by fear, and that it was wrong for a power won by sword and arms to be burdened by the weight of hatred.

He said that he had been free of ambition, and that the Lord had surely sent no small signs of his favor in so great a triumph. No one, however lukewarm and weak in faith, should be ignorant that the outcome of war hangs upon God’s nod; but when one inferior in numbers, strength, and men conquers one more confident in these things, it is clearer that the victor has won with Christ as judge.

Nor, he insisted, had he afterward conceived any bloody intention or done anything after the wars; fury had achieved nothing after the battle, arms, and trumpets; innocent swords had ceased from the crime of slaughter; and the peace was entirely unstained by blood.

[Col. 1030A]

Repeating such arguments often and praying more insistently, he softened the holy man’s repeated severity by his reasoning, until Martin, forgiving his guilt and overcome by his earnestness, went to the royal banquet that he had previously despised.

Now hope, more nearly at hand, exults in so great a gift. [Note: [Col. 1031D] Perhaps “more near.”] The festive day rejoices to grow bright amid a joyful assembly.

Nobles are added to the couches, joined by the splendor of neighboring honor beside the royal heights: men distinguished by their trabeae, holding authority over laws and arms, jurisdiction in the courts or command in war. Metal woven into threads is mingled with purple.

[Col. 1030B]

Among them, where the rounded couch bends inward, the presbyter reclined in the middle. On his right and left was the order of powerful commanders; their limbs rested upon golden supports, and they pressed the purple beneath them, made of precious fleece.

At the king’s right sat the venerable elder with his holy face, like Moses, returning with the sacred laws, descending from the summit of the holy mountain, his changed face flashing with excessive radiance, when the splendor of his heart shone forth from his countenance and the veils could not contain the new light.

The silent attendants looked on in amazement and joy. The court vied in devoted and modest service; everyone had one concern: to serve so holy a man. The desired service was greater even than their reverence for the king.

The king himself, who was present, preferred to honor Martin’s excellence.

[Col. 1030C]

Royal dishes crowded the tables below. Rich purple shone upon the lofty couches; soft silks moved in crimson hues, and the threads gleamed skillfully, drawn without fleece.

Curtains stretched across splendid thresholds murmured; at the doors a movable barrier of hanging cloth nodded. Everything glittered above and below in varied decoration, raised with pigments, resting upon marble, roofed with metal.

Capacious crystal vessels held clear water; since the very form seemed both shell and wave, one might think the enclosures could not contain the liquid they had received.

Cups were poured from gems and drunk from gems. Gold, in a mass of amber-colored metal, marked off the electrum. The workmanship itself was precious, and the value of the work more precious still.

Some vessels gleamed with gems; others stood out with figures. Certain pieces were rough to the eye but smooth to the touch. Upon shining platters and broad dishes were fruits of the air, the woods, the earth, and the sea.

[Col. 1030D]

When hunger had been removed by the banquet, only the desire remained to reveal their parched thirst. The attendants brought out ice and snow-cooled water enclosed in gold; others offered dew-covered bowls to those who requested them. The servants’ care and energy anticipated their master’s wish.

Then the king ordered the attendant to offer the cup to Martin, yielding his own precedence and reversing the order of service. He eagerly wished to follow immediately after so holy a hand, so that the cup, made more precious by contact with so great a mouth, might imbue the liquid within it with heavenly dew.

But when Martin had sprinkled his throat with a little water, scarcely moistening his mouth by the touch, the king was reaching out his right hand for the cup.

Martin, measuring the honor due to faith, handed it to the presbyter. The merit of his heart, not the king’s purple, prevailed; the diadem yielded to the faith that had been preferred.

[Col. 1031A]

The spectators’ astonished hearts were fixed in wonder. The man’s constancy, even when the king had been spurned, pleased the king more than the marvel itself, and envy did not inflame him as he weighed the significance of so great a deed.

Who, even if great, would dare so much for a holy priest under a lesser judge?

Fear did not conquer the steadfast man; favor did not conquer the righteous; neither the pleasure of the banquet nor the anger of the powerful prevailed.

O virtue near to God! Thus, with your heart withdrawn, be as though you yourself were far away, and overcome the present world.

[Col. 1031B]

Nor did Martin fear to reveal to the king whatever the kindly Spirit had disclosed to him, filling his pious inward parts with its gift: the varying outcomes of war, first successful battles and afterward a sorrowful defeat in another conflict.

When his fiery mind saw all these things with pure insight, their swift fulfillment proved them as though they had been seen. For in the first battle he routed the defeated king; soon afterward he bowed his captive neck to the returning commander.

Nor is it surprising that so discerning a mind saw so much, having abandoned every care and flying wholly above the stars upon an ethereal perception.

For the faithful monks standing outside the doors were often astonished to hear him mingling words with angelic speech, so that he perceived nothing bodily or earthly, and the weights of the flesh, not yet subdued, did not hinder his spirit, which already enjoyed the freedom of the soul.

[Col. 1031C]

Even the transparent demon, whatever appearance he might have attempted in order to deceive him, was exposed by his futile effort and was not allowed to play with changing forms.

Finally, when no avenue of escape remained for the frightened spirit, it breathed out savage poison through its raging words, wishing to kindle the uninjured man with treacherous speech, to tear him with the poison escaping from its teeth and tongue, and to pour out its empty anger now that its movements had been broken.

Shaking its hand, wet with pitiable blood, and displaying a bloodied horn as evidence of slaughter, rejoicing in evils and laughing at grief, it burst into the holy cell with a deadly growl, pouring forth a hellish voice through insolent words,

[Col. 1031D]

so that he might see at last the proof of his fury fulfilled.

“Perhaps chance furnished these arms; this weapon drove the beast’s obedience into violence, yet it prevailed because of our sin. That man of yours and your band, a greater prize of wickedness, fell to soothe my anger, restoring depleted strength with the blood I desired.”

“Immediately he orders all the nobles who have been summoned to inspect the monks’ cells with swift concern, lest the deceitful robber’s lying words should at least have spoken the truth about his own crime—such as the voice of defendants in sorrow is accustomed to be when, secretly under the torturer, they confess what must be punished.”

Then they reported that no indication whatever pointed to any of the brothers. Before them, the whole flock of the saints had at once been counted: shut within the sheepfold, they were keeping away the furious, gnashing wolves from the enclosure, Martin feeding them for the eternal King.

[Col. 1032A]

Nevertheless, they reported that one man had departed after receiving payment, to keep the cold away from wood carried upon a wagon.

Martin hurried to him and ordered that he be brought to the monks as a companion, believing that the robber’s treachery had been exposed through the man’s confession.

Nor was there delay before the conjecture was proved. They went out and saw, not far from the threshold, a half-dead wretch breathing his final breaths.

As he released his languishing eyes to death, he scarcely drew a thin voice from his icy breast through the broken murmur of his gasping tongue,

[Col. 1032B]

explaining the causes of his wound. It happened that, when the bonds were loosened and tightly wound straps were being fastened, a young bull, freer in the neck and rebellious toward its master, had pierced its tender groin with its infernal horn.

After he had explained this and fallen silent with his mouth pressed shut, he laid his head down, exhausted by death, and a saffron pallor spread over his face and limbs from his frozen body.

This was how he died. Yet in this death also Martin’s merit was revealed to us: he was permitted to know the future in such a way that no veil of flesh or earthly weight could delay his swift mind.

Although the deceitful and cunning enemy attempted either to conceal his frauds through trickery or to deceive by assumed forms, repeatedly wasting these efforts in vain, he dared to imitate the appearances of false gods,

[Col. 1032C]

fashioning the image of those whose honor he imitated: now the incestuous face of Jupiter and the fury of Mars; Mercury bound with false winged feet; Vulcan with tongs; Phoebus with strings or a plectrum; Minerva represented with shield and plumes in her madness; lustful Venus; Diana shaking the wildernesses; the incestuous sister under the unlawful law of marriage chambers, even losing the name of sister through her brother’s crime.

Displaying himself in such forms, with deeds worthy of his kind and revealing his own crimes through a counterfeit face, he could not escape. Once his fraud was exposed, the mocked demon lost his cunning designs, breathing out his final poison through insolent words and assailing the uninjured man with vices, even in speech.

[Col. 1032D]

The saint endured all these things with a face unmoved by patience, scorning flatteries and laughing at insults and abuse. Recognizing the enemy’s deceit in both of his inventions, he could be wounded neither by its crime nor moved by its praise.

He opposed the darts of its words with the tokens of salvation and shattered the robber’s weapons by presenting the cross.

The impious spirit had often attempted, through harsh complaints, to reproach the pious man for his love of piety. Alas, it dared to speak out before witnesses, so that many might hear its deadly words:

“Why do you receive those whom the Lord hates, if you condemn crimes? Why do you seek the company of the guilty? Perhaps the deeds of your own people are hidden from you—deeds done at my urging, which I often counseled and in which I played a large part. Who, I ask, will prove that a man hostile to such deeds can make them right?”

[Col. 1033A]

He replied:

“Serpent, swollen with your ancient poison, this is not Christ’s judgment concerning wretched human beings.

“If he sees that guilt has come to an end, he casts away anger, appointing no fixed period for guilt except the time of new guilt. He warns that sins should not remain; once they have ended, he forgives them.

“When present correction is gentle concerning past offenses, he recalls those who stray, forgives the crimes of those who have returned, and is patient with the perverse, merciful and calm toward those who turn back.

“He is the life of human beings and the death of faults; merciful toward both, he orders the destruction of crime to become the cause of salvation.

“Trusting in proven goodness, I would not despair that, although your crimes surpass all wrongs, if you should grieve over what you have committed, even after a long delay or at the last moment, mercy might snatch you from the midst of the flames.”

[Col. 1033B]

O happy piety, by which someone dares to trust so greatly in the goodness of the Lord God that he benevolently promises even what he admits has not been promised!

While he tries to recall the author of crime from his accustomed crime, removing sin from its source and cutting off the hated stock from its first root.

But since, in striving to sing repeated triumphs, our murmurs have touched the infernal tyrant, and since, wishing to repeat the titles of praise, we have sounded the name of our enemy through the sequence of wars, we shall also tell, in the speech Christ has granted, what happened in that time—something we greatly marvel at.

A young man named Clarus had once been added to the companions of the saints and the ministers of Christ. He had established his cell not far from the holy teacher.

[Col. 1033C]

He gathered several brothers into that fellowship, so that a harmony modulated by the pious might sing hymns and united glory resound through interwoven tongues.

A crafty young man once sought him out, pretending to possess a composed and disciplined character, deceiving everyone by assuming the appearance of an innocent monk under that name. Beneath a sheep’s clothing, however, he came with the mind of a wolf, breathing ancient poison from his corrupted heart.

At first, mingling with the saints in body alone, he acted the part of one sharing their common life.

Then, accustomed to boast of angelic speech, he raised his empty mind to false heights. About to fall from the summit of his exalted heart, he even persuaded the unwary through alleged miracles,

[Col. 1033D]

forcing them, as though his merits had already been proved by demonstrations, to believe his swollen words more than his slight signs.

He sometimes boasted that he had spoken with the Lord, as though a frequent messenger continually brought him reports from the heavenly seat, displaying through conversation with his companion the greatness of the Lord’s favor.

Nor did he fear to compare himself with the holy prophets, breathing out the lying words of the deceitful robber.

By this point he had driven many to believe his invented words. Only Clarus, steadfast in heart, rejected the deceitful murmurs from his holy understanding.

Although the madman pretended that the Lord was angry, he could neither terrify the serious man nor deceive the cautious one, promising that his power would be proved through many signs.

For, so that miracles might capture the deceived minds, he wished to confound the astonished men with words such as these:

[Col. 1034A]

“This night, I say, God—so that the grace he has determined to grant to our merits may not be thought vain—will clothe me in a fleece of snowy garment.

“When this gift becomes manifest and visible to your eyes, then, if you hesitate to believe my words, at least believe what you see, and praise the sight with ready approval.”

As vigilant expectation awaited so great a marvel and the course of the promised event proceeded, behold, at nearly midnight—when the divided day looks toward both ends, not far from the coming dawn and not far removed from what has been left behind—the earth was shaken and trembled.

A vast crash thundered everywhere through the darkness, and an even more dreadful fire flashed with a terrible lamp and deceptive light.

[Col. 1034B]

Suddenly terrified hearts were frightened by the sight.

Then the man, made eager by the result and more emboldened by the very success through which the course of the predicted fraud had advanced, gave someone the fleece to touch and inspect.

That person quickly summoned the others, lest anyone be deceived by the novel form of the contrived trick. Those who were called stood astonished at close range before a garment remarkable for its whiteness and purple sheen, while its inward parts yielded softly to their anxious hands as they passed over the delicate threads of the fabric.

Yet, although the garment shone when brought close, it could not be recognized from what fleece it had been drawn. The garment appeared to the eye and, when touched, was believed by the hand; in both respects the deception maintained the form it had assumed.

Then Clarus urged all his companions to return to the Lord in prayer amid such monstrous confusion, because he alone could reveal the hidden tricks and bring the robber’s fraud out from its darkness.

[Col. 1034C]

Immediately the whole vigilant company flew to the customary melodies of the sweet psalms and sought consolation in holy hymns, to drive away sluggish sleep from their strengthened bodies and overcome the silence of night with sacred songs.

Tears followed the psalms, and sighs followed the voice. When the tongue fell silent, a cry rang out; every moment was joined together in praise of the Lord, in turn through mind and mouth.

Meanwhile, as soon as they saw the darkness of night begin to thin and the approaching light draw near—when the dawn, heralding the sun, spread its received redness and veiled the paling stars with saffron color—they struggled to lead the seized man to the cell of the holy Martin.

[Col. 1034D]

At last, once the cloud had been scattered and driven away, the demon would lose the fabrications of its deceitful ingenuity, exposing the fraud uncovered before so great a judge.

But the demon resisted. With danger now close at hand, it strove to refuse and escape the holy hands of those present, stopping its steps and resisting in its voice.

It cried that it was forbidden to approach Martin’s holy cell and to bring that garment from the threshold.

Then they pressed forward. Its agitation betrayed the fraud, and its pallid cowardice exposed the contrived deception.

The image of the garment vanished in the hands of those holding it, and its appearance slipped away from their attentive eyes.

As the threads of air dissolve the wool of clouds that had woven hollow valleys with a deceptive flood, when the gleaming sun raises its pure orb higher, so the uncovered expanses reveal themselves once the scattered darkness has been dispersed.

[Col. 1035A]

This too, holy Martin, affix as a trophy to the cross: strip the savage tyrant of his counterfeit garment, tearing apart the false coverings of the airy fabric and scattering the floating wool of the hollow cloud.

O fury that will never cease, are you rising again, struck down so many times and so often losing your efforts? Do you rush onward as you fall, and does your audacity set no limit, nor success bring your desire to an end?

Impious one, do you attempt to counterfeit the Lord’s face and deceive the light with darkness? Can senseless madness, arranged in such forms, deceive the saint in this way?

Although you breathe out your final poison without a wound and exhale your exhausted rage through empty jaws, you do not pierce the pure understanding with foul darkness, lest the shadows of clouds shut the sun away from the truth.

[Col. 1035B]

And although you shine in purple and glitter with gems, and place gleaming gold beneath lying feet, imitating the true king with a false diadem, alas, traitor, you proclaim yourself the eternal Christ.

You do this so that, perhaps concealed beneath a pious name, a false impiety might persuade those who believe that God is blessed to trust a deceitful appearance under the name of Christ, and bend pious limbs in honor of a demon.

Thus, alas, religion, believed holy, would become sacrilegious, and faith would lose the merit of believing. It would conceal the deceitful cups of poison meant to be handed over, hiding their bitter juice beneath the sweetness of honey in a jar.

Stretch these things before ignorant minds; lay such snares for inexperienced men who have not yet tested the weapons of war, men who attempt to bar the battle standards with untried darts.

[Col. 1035C]

But the man accustomed to sweat beneath no untested arms, accustomed to close the fortunate standards within an extended rampart, hides his veteran gray hairs beneath a venerable helmet.

Instructed by long experience, he carefully examines every place—those suitable for setting ambushes and those again to be suspected and avoided. He considers how to guide the shield, with what force to hurl the weapon, what titles may capture the king, and what crimes may wound him.

Such a man will resist ambushes with steadfast seriousness and guard against deceit with such reason that an enemy broken by conflict will not accomplish through fraud what it cannot achieve by strength.

Such was Martin in his flourishing power, when the battle standards of Christ utterly overthrew the crimes of the corrupted world.

He knew how to recognize the sign of his King and to trample these displays in the name of the crucified one.

[Col. 1035D]

Now you counterfeit Christ in purple clothing and adorn this appearance with gold and gems, with foreign silk thread. Wretched one, you do not know how to deceive.

Thus, frustrated and repeatedly losing the efforts of your schemes, you slip once more into thin air, dissolve, and confess your flight through foul stench.

But you, holy man of God, stand firm and triumph in unmoved virtue, joined forever to him by your strength.

Unconquered, you established your character against every crime: gentle, patient, just, pious, upright, fair; mild, trusting, humble, endlessly kind; instructed, courteous, approachable, forgiving, yet ardent.

Holy bishop, good teacher, beloved host; wondrous in signs and likewise worthy of imitation in character;

[Col. 1036A]

humble in heart, exalted in mind, venerable in both, you gain praise by fleeing it and deserve honor by avoiding it.

You led the adjacent days into late fasts, always exceedingly sparing in the scanty food that relieved your weary stomach without burdening it with flesh.

Thus you expelled the pleasure of food and rejected the pleasure of sleep, lest this earthly burden weigh upon your vigilant mind, and so that the body might more easily become accustomed to the lightness of the spirit, keeping watch in devotion to prayer and in devotion to reading.

You passed your continuous days in these cares. This alone was your rest: to change one labor for another, succeeding in an unbroken course of prayer.

Let us all praise with wonder that nature itself yielded to such a man, although even the lowest cleric, forgetful of so great an honor, had wounded him.

[Col. 1036B]

He did not swell with bile because he had been wounded, nor did he ever burn with a judge’s love of vengeance against his subjects. Hatred did not kindle fury in him; joy did not provoke laughter, nor sorrow grief, in the holy gravity of his character.

An angelic face shone in his venerable body,

[Col. 1037A]

a face capable of displaying the holy heart and bringing forth the light enclosed within his sacred breast.

God was always on his lips, and mercy always there as well. In counsel and desire he held to peace.

For envy often armed tongues stained with poison against him, and priests themselves, inflamed by dreadful bile, preferred to tear at the pious man with their tongues rather than equal him in deeds.

Yet even then anger did not force the holy heart to fulfill their wishes.

Indeed, for so great a crime he poured out fraternal tears, his compassionate mercy wetting his face. He implored the Lord Christ, through a flood of tears, to spare them by granting pardon for their deceitful words.

Thus, with a heart always steadfast against every wound, hatred did not stir fury; the cause alone produced grief.

[Col. 1037B]

So was the martyr seen receiving the Lord’s footsteps, when a savage rain of stones fell upon him and he breathed out his fragile life from a blessed breast. He asked that the crimes of the insane crowd be forgiven, grieving more over the people’s sins than over the wounds of his flesh.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1037]

The translation that had been begun had completed its undertaken volume, proceeding through the pure copies of the holy book, when suddenly the glory of a hidden history was offered to us, spurring the efforts of our purpose—not so that something better might shine forth from a wretched mouth than what the page of so clear a heart had recorded.

[Col. 1037C]

For the living force of the words, flashing with vigorous power, would lose its innate strength when softened by meter.

But since not everyone seeks to examine inwardly the depths of the clear spring, a great part of those who seek often drinks its own streams, neglecting the coldness.

We too, who can produce nothing worthy for the learned, may cleanse our turbid cups with books not far away. Often, what is uttered in a tangled book strives to match the voices of sounding trumpets.

And what is accustomed to rest beneath a lofty pine sometimes enters the lowly thickets of the willow grove.

You too, who would gladly enter the freely offered light, if the road through a distant forest should weary you, hurry to enter the thicket offered close at hand.

The saint was proceeding to the threshold of the blessed temple, to offer the customary mysteries to eternal Christ.

[Col. 1037D]

Behold, a poor man, trembling with icy cold, clashed his wretched teeth beneath his uncovered head and held his hands against his pale cheeks, seeking the slight warmth breathed out by his breath.

His breath repeatedly hardened into ice. His voice, not always able to resound, was broken into tearful words; it spoke through mournful sounds and groans, proclaiming the whole complaint by its cry.

Although such things might perhaps have softened a harsh severity, Martin’s compassion had already been moved and could no longer conceal the misery of the weeping wretch.

Immediately he commanded the deacon standing beside him—whom, following the custom of his predecessors, the bishop had appointed guardian of the holy treasury—to prepare quickly, at the Lord’s expense and with money, a garment for the freezing body.

Thus he left behind what he wished to have done, as though it had already been done.

[Col. 1038B]

Then, entering the secluded dwelling of the cell where the saint was accustomed to join the neighboring crowds before proceeding to the sacred mysteries, he received the monk who was soon to send out the serving attendant.

But what do the wretched not dare, when misery compels them to expose the worn-out shame of their forehead?

Poverty breaks through what even priests could not penetrate, offering a complaining explanation for the delayed gift.

Then compassion seized his whole mind, and he did not wish to bring back the danger of the command.

He covered his head with the amphiballus, once the witness had been removed; then, rejoicing, he gradually drew his arms away from his limbs, shaking out the garment gathered against his bent breast.

[Col. 1038C]

The naked body did not become visible beneath the clothed poor man. So swiftly did the outer garment cover the body stripped beneath it that, anticipating the poor man’s eager wish, it made the man who had been made joyful by the gift unaware of what had happened, while the needy recipient alone knew the hidden deed.

Tell me, you who, spurning and trampling the joys of the world,  
chose to seek life after casting wealth aside:  
who clothed the naked man by stripping off his own covering?  
Who, though grieved to see another bear something, did not himself shrink from bearing it?  
Who, willing himself to be wretched, restored the wretched man through pity?

You surpassed the examples of the men of old, Martin;  
and you yourself, too, were wondrous then in a poor garment.  
Or when a portion of your garment remained divided,  
by this gift you doubled your ancient palm of victory.

Meanwhile, as was customary, the deacon reminds him that the hour had come  
for the solemn duties to be performed in the assembly of the people.  
He says: “The teaching of the holy prophet must be fulfilled:  
[Col. 1039A] Let compassion precede the Mass, for this sacrifice is more pleasing;  
first obeying the commandment, cover the naked.”

He goes out for a little while and again seeks the poor man,  
but reports that he is absent and has not been found for the giving of the gift.  
“Come now,” says the saint, “bring the gift; the needy man will not be lacking.”

Then the other, in anger, throws at the saint’s feet the garment  
bought for scarcely an eighth of a solidus,  
woven with knotted threads of shaggy wool.  
When the deacon had withdrawn a little, he quickly and joyfully  
draws the costly garment tight around his limbs beneath so cheap a covering.

Thus, as the hero approaches the altar, much more splendid in this attire—  
such as a soldier, wet with sweat and dust,  
meets a king returning after battle—  
he is more beautiful by this title, though his limbs are more shamefully exposed.

For the appearance of virtue is preceded by the deed,  
just as the strength of a deep root outlasts the seasons of the leaves.

[Col. 1039B] Nor did uncertain conjecture long fail to prove this vow.  
For while he heightens his holy gifts with solemn prayer  
and accompanies them with immortal words of worship,  
a shining flame flashed from his bright crown,  
pouring radiance upon his head.  
Harmless, it rose upward in a transparent stream,  
cleaving the clear air with a fiery furrow.

Go on, then; urged onward by the continuous sequence of titles,  
let glory proceed in the easy course of virtues,  
so that, racing with loosened reins through the open arena,  
you may enter what must first be begun before you leave what has been closed.

A certain wealthy man, Evanitus, was indeed bound by these things  
with the world’s tenacious chains of cares;  
yet he preserved the pure feeling of an unblemished faith  
and a kindly heart, keeping his mind undefiled by earthly crime.

[Col. 1039C] The violent fever had utterly consumed his marrow;  
his trembling entrails were repeatedly shaken by his breath,  
and his sobbing pulse broke his sighs.  
As a suppliant, with the confused murmur of a parched tongue,  
he applied the plectrum of his voice to his dried and glued palate;  
striving often through broken utterances to signify his feeling,  
he begged that the saint’s arrival at his house  
might be obtained for those who prayed pitifully—  
if ambition, the stimulus of care, or the love of piety  
seeking remedies for health urged anyone to seek him—  
so that Martin alone might visit him in order to restore life,  
for Martin’s presence surpassed every remedy.

Nor did delay long deem his prayer unjust,  
once signs had been offered by divine grace;  
and the event itself soon proved that this faith was sufficient.

[Col. 1039D] Scarcely had half the journey’s labor been completed;  
a large part of the road still remained,  
when grace anticipated the traveler and sent ahead the gifts of hoped-for healing,  
its swifter power preceding his sluggish limbs.

He met the physician in good health; both rejoiced  
that salvation had been poured into his heart together with the healing of his body,  
while the healing of the flesh increased through the merits of faith.

Therefore, once every cause of delay had been removed,  
wishing immediately to return, he yielded to the whole prayer  
and granted the distance of a single day that had been entreated.

But what had been brief in duration was great in virtues;  
a mighty deed compensated for the confined time.

For a boy whom, by chance, a deadly serpent had struck,  
infecting him with the gall of its poison,  
when already the venom was distending his livid limbs  
and, having been absorbed even into his vital organs,  
the serpent’s deadly evil—almost as though death were complete—  
was loosening his failing eyes into infernal sleep,

[Col. 1040A] his master, bending his pious heart to the proper labor,  
carried him to the holy footprints of the true patron.  
He did not doubt that one whose proven merits had given so many demonstrations  
could, by his present touch, drive away the poison—  
he who, by his mere terror, had made diseases flee.

Without delay, his healing right hand touched the wound  
and cleansed the limbs fixed by the foul poison.  
Wherever the holy hand moved across the body,  
death fled and life returned; soon the gathered pestilence  
withdrew into a single place. Then, through the wound alone,  
he confined the poison, ordering it immediately to burst forth.

[Col. 1040B] And the boy, bracing his steps with fearless effort,  
ran with unafraid strides, to the joy of his master.

With this reward you return, rich man; these are the gifts you receive,  
as you enrich others with the happy gifts of added salvation.  
What time did he spend empty of virtues?  
What road did he not make for heaven, although it was a guest upon earth?

He was inspecting the folds of the entrusted flock,  
where the pious Church enclosed the rustic people,  
lest perhaps the fury of thieves or the cunning of wolves  
should seize the unsuspecting sheep when the shepherd was away.

Meanwhile, perhaps leaving his companions for a little while,  
he went ahead along the road where the public embankment  
raises its straight mass across the level ground.

So that the road, strengthened and elevated with laid stones,  
might slope the poured-down rains toward the hollow depressions below,  
and so that the heavy wheel-track might not sink into the hard roadway,  
nor the wagons, sunk down, swallow the muddy depths,  
but the turning of the wheels might scarcely scrape the road’s upper ridges,  
leaving no trace in any furrow.

[Col. 1040C] But, far away, the clatter of striking iron revealed the approaching vehicle.  
Martin, having gone a little ahead along this road, was proceeding  
when suddenly he saw coming toward him, in a huge swirling rush,  
a chariot that happened to be carrying men swollen with military arrogance.

Neither rank could restrain their fury,  
nor reason compose their deranged minds.  
Ambition, drunkenness, shouting, rage, anger, and tumult  
mingled their uncouth hearts into various monstrosities.  
Among the mules, lifeless with exhaustion, and the terrified drivers,  
the blows of those striking resounded together with the words of those shouting.  
No rule of stopping existed, nor any concern for danger  
delayed their swift course across level ground or steep places.

[Col. 1040D] To such men, different in appearance and bearing,  
the saint came directly to meet them.  
The animals feared the venerable face confronting them; trembling,  
the mules withdrew from the middle of the embankment,  
their bodies, bound in tangled reins, shuddering  
with minds, as it were, more sound than those of their masters.

As once, according to the sacred reading, an ass, forbidden to curse the holy people, is said to have despised its profane master, crushing the foot of the man who pressed against it with his leaning body.

Then, their hearts flooded with insane poison,  
they leap down. The fulfillment of their wish gives them cause for madness,  
and they dare to stretch sacrilegious hands against the saint,  
striving together to beat the holy body to death.

The innocent man alone, gentle, calm, and patient,  
they—angry, unstable, numerous, swollen with pride, and furious—  
strike, hold, and knock down, though he offers no words in reply.  
His face grows wet with blood; they break the breath from his battered chest;  
his throat, bruised and livid, blackens.

[Col. 1041A] His failing eyes, deprived of every light but Christ’s,  
weigh the darkness present to them as the darkness of night.  
His sight fails, but hope shines in his heart.

When his companions then saw their master in such a state,  
the crowd, seeing its patron, grew pale and lifeless.  
They stretched out humble hands to support him  
and pressed gentle kisses upon his bloodied limbs.

Then they hasten to leave the dreadful, mournful place of slaughter.  
A submissive little ass received the venerable burden,  
accustomed to carry such a load. But with its body bent,  
the half-dead pack animal, leaning beneath the weight, nods  
and threatens every moment to collapse beneath its uncertain burden.

[Col. 1041B] Meanwhile, the men, their hearts sated with the completion of their fury,  
returned to the chariot. From there, more swiftly,  
they force the animals to burst forward in a headlong leap,  
so that whatever delays had occurred in the fatal assault  
might immediately be repaid by the whirlwind of their speed.

But these efforts are in vain: the animals, fixed in place,  
rebel against their savage command. The mules, bound to the will of their master,  
stiffened as though in the form of statues.

Then their anger burns hotter in its insane tumult.  
Neither shouts nor whips avail: the battered flanks rebound;  
they seize the neighboring woods for blows.  
Stones, stakes, clubs, goads—whatever weapon each man finds while searching—  
their anger consumes in striking.

[Col. 1041C] Yet none of this can loosen their rigid muscles  
or alter their fixed limbs. You would think they were frozen bronze,  
or figures pressed into stone and hardened there.

At last, when their fury had been utterly exhausted and broken,  
mad folly admitted sound understanding,  
so that they recognized that the mules, despite so many blows,  
were paralyzed by God’s judgment,  
and that the cause of their delay had come upon the wretched men  
not without divine command.

When at last they were warned by these marvels,  
and their fury had been laid aside,  
they remembered their sin and asked who that man was  
whose venerable body had received the blows of sacrilegious attackers.

But behold: when they heard Martin’s name,  
they rush forward prostrate, their hair disheveled  
and defiled with dust. Wetting their cheeks  
with a stream of tears, they clasp humble arms  
around his blessed feet,

[Col. 1041D] asking forgiveness and confessing together.

Nor was the pitiable ambition of those who prayed long delayed:  
mercy cut short their prolonged tears,  
and the gift of pardon anticipated the prayers of those asking.

Without delay, freedom to depart was restored;  
with a swift word, he loosened the reins of the delays he had commanded.

Tell what the swift conveyance of your king can accomplish  
when God causes delay. Set beside it your brows flashing  
with the rays of gems, your coverings bristling with hairs,  
your titles of virtue, and the pomp of your commands.  
Then, at least instructed by the weight of the saint’s merits,  
place his authority above your king’s more rightly.

Go on, then; carry out the succession of virtues in continuous sequence,  
composing and recounting the history.  
Turn the course toward the narrative, priest, and with your aid touch my talent—the strings of my heart or mouth—  
lest the Muses, speaking madly, seize my foolish breast.

Let Martin lead us. Such a change of feeling  
is welcome to me; my inmost being thirsts for such a champion.  
Let thirsty hearts ask for the waters of Castalia;  
other cups befit men reborn in the Jordan.

Again the holy man was traveling along his venerable road  
where the walls of Chartres lie across the open fields.

Thus, while he passed through the byways of the fertile countryside,  
proper admiration filled the neighboring village.  
Countless people of every sex and age gathered from all around.  
So great was the fame of the man that every farmer  
stripped the fields, leaving them empty of cultivators.  
Care for their houses now seemed less important:  
it was enough to have seen Martin; even the name itself  
was rightly marveled at by the uninitiated as a title of praise.

[Col. 1042B] And although they had not yet received the virtue of faith,  
they hurried in crowds to the renowned master.

A dense column of country people surrounded him.  
Proper admiration had covered the exposed fields.  
You would have rejoiced to gather into enclosures those eager for salvation, the fruit of so great a sowing,  
looking back at stalks emptied of their grain.

Suddenly a mother arrived, embracing the lifeless corpse of her child,  
beating her empty lips against the child’s body,  
pressing her plaintive breast to his frozen lips,  
and uttering trembling words amid sighs,  
while streams of tears drenched her pallid cheeks.

The mind of the man, filled with God and close to the favoring God,  
perceived the gifts of God. Grace quickened his pure understanding  
so that he might trust that such a people could be called  
to divine rewards, at least when it had seen the Lord’s power.

[Col. 1042C] Therefore, when the suppliant mother placed  
the pitiful corpse of her dead child in his blessed arms,  
the limbs began to tremble, the eyes opened,  
and gradually grew accustomed to the light poured into them.  
Striking the plectrum of a moist tongue against the palate,  
he distinguished a voice in words forced from his throat.  
Joyfully clasping Martin’s neck with his arms,  
he sought Martin’s embrace, leaving his mother neglected.

Open your spacious bosom to the peoples enriched by those received;  
joyfully embrace the people added to you,  
bride of God, drawing the whole world to your heart.

But you idols, once putrefying in miserable tombs,  
must at last mourn the triumphs that should bring joy.

What hearts did not yield to your teaching, holy man?  
What savagery was not made gentle,  
when the preceding mercy of the Lord Christ  
always softened, even in kings themselves,  
the opposing harshness that resisted your prayers?

But Valentinian alone acted more cruelly than the rest,  
terrible in his vice, swelling pride, and anger.

When Martin often approached him as a suppliant,  
bringing before a harsh ruler a difficult case,  
the king, offended by the persistent ambition of the petitioner,  
lest he repeatedly strike his obstructed ears with requests,  
ordered the saint to be kept away from the doors.

Repulsed, Martin left the troubled inner chambers  
of the hostile king, preferring to knock at the threshold of eternal Christ  
and to enter that court which grants authority even to kings,  
enclosing their times within fixed boundaries  
and binding their rigid mouths with strong reins.

[Col. 1043A] Therefore his mind returned to its accustomed vigor,  
afflicting the slender flesh in his exhausted body.  
He irritated his worn skin with a rough garment,  
passing the day in fasting, the nights in keeping vigil,  
and joining both periods together with unceasing tears.

If at times his eyes yielded to brief sleep,  
the bare ground was sufficient beneath his slight slumber,  
until Christ sent comfort to the afflicted friend  
of his grieving servant through a pious message.  
For an angel, having descended from above, spoke these words  
of the Lord’s command:

“Go on, then, and enter the barred palace without fear.  
Nothing is closed, by God’s mercy, to the one for whom the heavenly court  
has opened when he prays; these earthly barriers will open as well.”

[Col. 1043B] Without delay, his faith, made certain by so great a pledge  
of divine favor, led him fearlessly to seek the tyrant’s threshold,  
which he had to enter. The proud king’s guard yielded,  
and the weapons placed at the posts to enforce dreadful threats were removed.

When the king suddenly saw him from his lofty throne,  
he was stunned and terrified by the sight,  
and from his royal seat he looked grimly at his trembling, threatening ministers.

Meanwhile, wishing to obtain consolation from the saint whom he had spurned,  
he did not deem the man standing nearby worthy of any honor,  
but pressed his body unmoved upon the seats beneath him.

But behold: a fierce, avenging fire,  
sent by divine favor in a swift, crackling whirlwind of flame,  
wrapped around the king’s throne and part of the seated king.

Then, leaping swiftly away from the fire,  
he sprang up in terror, shaking his limbs,  
and rejoiced to restore the honor he had extorted from the holy man.

[Col. 1043C] With gentle affection he removed the reason for the saint’s petition,  
submitting his harsh heart to holy commands  
and bending his conduct, now teachable, to words of instruction.

Indeed, he offered royal gifts in sufficiently lavish abundance.  
But the mind rich in God wished to take nothing from worldly wealth;  
leaving earthly rewards behind, it stored up the gifts of eternal Christ.

Now, since very humble verses in plebeian words  
have entered lofty palaces in a lowly poem,  
we shall speak in connected discourse, as Christ grants,  
of the exalted matters made subject to the merits of the saints.

After, as the page of the completed book records,  
Maximus had cleansed the crimes of the kingdom entrusted to him,  
he wisely strove to preserve the favor he had begun to maintain  
through constant services. For thus he rejoiced to summon the saint,  
desiring to drink faith watered by the stream of divine speech,  
and to draw from the fountain of the blessed mouth  
the nectarous liquid of teaching;

[Col. 1043D] to learn the titles and deeds of holy people:  
what battles they fought with sweat, what rewards  
the victors received, what glory welcomes the just,  
what punishment the guilty, and how much the Father’s mercy  
may cherish them, and how much the king’s judgment may afflict them.

The saint rejoiced with him in his questions,  
opening each matter and bringing light back after the darkness had been driven out.

Nor was the queen inferior to so great a husband.  
Devoted to service, she diligently surpassed the king,  
always hanging upon the sacred mouth of the speaker  
and sprinkling his footsteps abundantly with tears.

She matched in merit the woman who, with blessed hair,  
wiped the Lord’s feet after first washing them with tears.

Yet this woman, girded with a special and singular devotion,  
thought it a small thing to serve,  
preparing, as a happy queen, to set the tables alone  
with the servants removed.

Nor did she stop, often pleading beside her husband,  
until her repeated tears, through constant entreaty,  
compelled the saint to yield.

She set the table, placed the chair,  
voluntarily brought towels for drying hands  
and water for washing them.  
The foods she had prepared with joyful service  
she herself hurried to carry in shining baskets.

And although she was never weary of her duties,  
she supplemented the continual labor of standing by her strength,  
for the reward of so great a task,  
gathering the fragments of crumbs,

[Col. 1044B] so that the holy hunger of faith might be filled  
by the precious touch of food.

O happy woman, who by your virtue place these things  
before royal treasures and riches, preferring to serve the blessed  
rather than to surpass the entire world utterly,  
referring the honor of a reigning woman to the name of a servant.

The gems shining at your temples did not change your mind,  
nor the silks stiff with glittering threads,  
nor gold more precious than woven purple.

In merit, O queen, you equaled that woman  
who, with honor as exalted as a throne,  
came from the ends of the earth to acknowledge Solomon,  
capturing by attentive hearing what she retained in her mind  
and sought by advancing a long way to possess within herself:

a woman who, by subduing the obstacles of the trampled world,  
was made equal in distinction to the men of old.

[Col. 1044C] For often, by herself refusing the yoke,  
deadly pride has conquered kings invincible in many a struggle.

Rightly, therefore, you received the special gift of the saint,  
so that, once your hardness had been softened and laid aside for a while,  
the gentle secrets of his heavenly heart might be opened to you.

How many times, when her pious brow relaxed into a brief calm,  
did she mercifully command the waves to settle?  
How many storms did a gentler breeze calm?  
And how briefly, though shining, did clear weather appear amid the clouds!

How many guilty people did this table make glad,  
this little permitted freedom that loosened bonds?  
How many chains did that brief hour break apart,  
relaxing its own short-lived severity?

For time, person, and place stand beside wise counsels  
and govern the mind with sudden judgment.

Do not, envious man, put forward the name of the female sex;  
it is not sex but the merit of the heart that prepares these things.  
Nor is human nature inferior in a human being [the text is uncertain here: “natura humani F homini”],  
nor do nation, sex, or age differ in the merit of faith—  
man, woman, slave, free person, stranger, or heir.  
It is the merit of the believer, not the glory of the flesh, that prevails.

Finally, wishing to touch briefly upon what I have learned  
this sex deserved through faithful devotion,  
I shall unfold it in whatever account Christ grants.

As the holy man advanced along his journey,  
with the day declining into night he sought nearby roofs,  
and, received beneath the welcoming height of the joyful village,  
hurried to the inner sanctuary of the holy church.

There, as always a guest of the blessed threshold,  
he allowed his tired body a little rest,  
loosening his weary eyes in brief sleep,  
so that, refreshed by a short and moderate slumber,  
his very frail limbs might suffice for unceasing labor  
and support his watchful mind.

[Col. 1045A] But when he had passed through the darkness  
and, with night shining, the light of his labors had quickly  
solemnly completed all its duties,  
he again hastened along the road.

Then a faithful band of maidens, whom holy virginity  
had consecrated to the Lord—untouched in body and chaste in heart—  
joyfully burst into the inner sanctuary of the holy cell,  
though the fragile corruption of the flesh might press down to earth my mind hastening toward heaven’s heights,  
blessed by its pious hospitality.  
They drank in the fresh air  
and absorbed the untainted breath of the atmosphere.

[Col. 1045B] Then, with humble service, the band reveres the teacher’s seat.  
With learned devotion they hurriedly mark each place  
touched by the feet of the standing man,  
each place where the reclining limbs had lain,  
each place blessed by holy food,  
each place pressed by the seat,  
and each place beneath the limbs of the praying man prostrate on the ground.

But when, by seeing the blessed straw bed,  
they had magnified the hay warmed by his pious body,  
violent modesty contends for the discovered treasure.

As each snatches a portion for herself and fills her bosom,  
the smooth stalks prick their crowded breasts,  
and they repel the thin garments from their stimulated chests.

What cannot true faith accomplish? A single company of virgins,  
chaste no less in heart than in body,  
when a demon, violently retaining a certain wretched man by force,  
compelled him to break out in commanded frenzies,  
shaking sound understanding from the captive breast,  
trusting in God’s aid and the patron’s merit,

[Col. 1045C] wisely and lavishly attaches a small portion  
of the suitable treasure to the unhappy man’s throat  
and hangs the pressed hay, touched by the blessed body,  
around the neck of the raging man.

Without delay, terrified by the contact,  
the enemy fled the dry stalks as cruel fires flee,  
unable to withstand the stalks that had touched Martin’s body.  

[Note: [Col. 1045D] Thus the old manuscript correctly has *arentes stipulas*, not *saeva*, because the ancients often lengthened a letter even when a vowel followed.]

And yet, beaten back so many times and so often driven away,  
do you, madman, dare to confront the man who has tested you,  
changing your forms, and to attempt him again,  
to bring your fearful eyes before him in person  
while concealing your appearance and displaying your madness?

For sitting upon the back of a beast,  
shaking the animal with wanton fury  
and plunging himself into its entrails,  
he had driven the nature of the beast out with deadly rage.

Or when he stood upon the back of a captive heifer,  
so that the monster he had mounted  
might carry not merely a body upon its body,

[Col. 1045D] filling the possessed limbs with the infused frenzy  
and adapting his service to bacchic movements,  
sprinkling bloody dew as he shook his head,  
while red drops ran over the smooth horns  
and fiery horns preceded the angry brow,  
he breathed out, while rapid panting scarcely alternated the air,  
stirred up a dusty cloud with his bent knee,  
and his trembling foot scattered fine sand upward.

Indeed, when he had raged among the fleeing herds,  
the fleeing maddened creature ceased at the sight of the gentle saint.  
It stood there, and, casting off its burden while regaining its mind,

[Col. 1046A] joyfully joined the allied herds as a heifer.

Cease now, at least, to plunge yourself among Christ’s flocks,  
since the saint has left you no authority even over beasts.

We yield: the glory of his virtues surpasses the trembling words of the speaker,  
made clearer by illustrious deeds than by sounds  
which the poet’s obscure tongue could hand down.  
We are overcome by the light of his praise  
and, crushed beneath so great a splendor, lie hidden.

Would that the glory of so illustrious a patron,  
though veiled, might make our darkness grow a little thinner,  
lest we cover the light of history with a dark heart  
and the sins of the speaker diminish the title of praise.

What heart was not gentle toward the saint,  
what rebellious anger, what savagery was not made mild?

The mastiffs felt his authority  
when, during the hunt, a wanton band of young men  
crossed the open stretches of the fields,  
leaping rapidly over level and steep ground.  
The horn-footed horses quickly grew wet with much sweat  
and breathed out thin air through their wide nostrils.

Their hooves, driven by terrifying blows, resounded,  
leaving behind their swift tracks a dusty cloud.

Nor was the horses’ course, so swift as that of birds, sufficient.  
Their hanging chests so matched their lowered heads  
that the delay of the horn-footed animals hindered the riders’ hopes,  
and the movement of the drivers passed beyond the course of those they carried.

The eager mastiffs strove to equal the winds,  
and, intent on victory, to satisfy the fury of the spectators.  
Their tongues hung far out through open throats,  
and their trembling mouths were shaken by alternating breaths.

What great labor was this, and what expense, alas, to what end?  
What fruit or benefit is there in catching fleeing little beasts  
and rejoicing in the flight of frightened hares?

[Col. 1046C] You scorned such madness, prudent Martin,  
pitying the sad fate of the innocent,  
the gaping mouths of the dogs,  
and making their terrified steps grow numb.

Whenever he had relaxed the continuous severity of his brow,  
he used the salt of words to release his companions from their cares  
and briefly warm their attentive ears,  
clever with gravity, witty with religious feeling,  
sprinkling the virtue of his heart with the flower of humor.

Seeing a herdsman covered in a skin garment, he said:

“Behold, another Adam clothed himself in such a covering,  
wrapping the cold limbs of his naked parent  
and offering new consolation to his modesty,  
when, after the deadly poison of the infernal serpent,  
he perceived the slippery hissing had deceived the body.

But may new grace once again clothe us,  
stripped utterly and buried utterly in ancient sin.”

Then, smiling, he looked upon a sheep  
whose wool had been cut away. Immediately,  
taking from this deed examples for instruction, he said:

“See how the two-toothed creature has fulfilled the command.  
When asked for one of its two garments,  
it gave away one and, as another grew in,  
was unwilling to retain the former.

But it is shameful if human beings yield to a brute sheep,  
if that creature surpasses us in lavish generosity.”

On another side, the backs of the meadows lay exposed,  
stretched out in a different condition. One part had endured  
the devouring swine, whose rooting had dug it up,  
and its blackened ridges had lost their green color.

[Col. 1047A] Another part, shorn by herds stripping away  
the sad turf in their hunger, had been laid bare;  
the mouths of the grazing cattle had widely removed  
the earth’s covering.

While dewy grasses were seized by open bites,  
the tongue, drawn toward the curved jaws by roughness,  
first licked together the tender herbs,  
so that the avid teeth might suck down the compacted fodder.

The hoof, driving its horn into the ground,  
had no less crushed it, destroying the green shoots  
with repeated blows.

But another part of the field, untouched and flowering in its turf,  
was adorned by nature with varied beauty.  
A light breath made the green grasses undulate  
and gently moved the grasses it touched.

Moreover, countless flowers across the level ground  
painted the fields with gems set among them.

Purple stained some with a rosy dye;  
others, distinguished by snowy whiteness, shone.  
Among them, marking the grasses with saffron hues,  
the golden grace of yellow flowers glittered.

Purple drops bent the gemlike shoots,  
and amber-colored dewdrops bent the grasses with their moist weight.  
A gentle fragrance strove to equal the pleasing color,  
and harmonious concord mingled joys in matching forms.  
The sight fed the eyes; the breath, the nostrils.

Rare leafy branches offered very welcome shade,  
and blue-green limbs nodded among intertwined boughs.  
Birds, hidden beneath the leaves, strove to renew spring,  
modulating their whistles with melodious tongues.

A clear stream fed the nearby grasses  
and nourished the turf by touching it with flowing water.

[Col. 1047C] Beneath it, little stones visible through the transparent water  
rippled the glassy liquid through its pleasant barriers.  
The beauty concealed by the stream could not be taken from the eyes;  
its appearance was open to vision even beneath the depths.

Why do I try to describe such forms in unskilled speech?  
These things cannot be brought forth in words,  
which the grace of nature, through Christ’s gift,  
has painted better by shaping them.

Beholding this beauty, marked by contrasting forms,  
Martin said:

“Compare for a little while the several places of the meadow:  
those grazed down, dug up, and untouched,  
with the wickedness of prostitutes;  
with wives joined to husbands by a lawful bond;  
and with virgins who vow their bodies holy to Christ,  
adorned with the gems of rosy modesty.

As the beauty of the field does not remain there  
where the ground has been dug up,  
so the image of Christ does not shine in one forgotten in vices.

As the root remains here when the grass has been cut,  
so for married women faith is secure  
even without the flower of modesty.

As color and brilliance give splendor to a flowering field,  
so the glory of pure flesh shines with brightness.

These things offer clear signs of vigor  
to hearts attentive always to divine rewards.”

A certain monk came, his name neglected,  
who had been taken away from military service.  
After the bugles and trumpets of war,  
he had preferred to surrender himself to the standards of the true king,  
following more worthily the great banners of the holy cross.

Indeed, drawing his wife into the fellowship of this life,  
he had instructed his companion to live among holy virgins,  
renouncing the rights of marriage and the flesh.

[Col. 1048A] But when revived pleasure again began  
to stimulate his wanton mind  
and to implant deeply in his marrow  
the mortality of the despised world,  
he wished, scarcely having tasted his renunciation,  
to relax its severity and return again  
to the embraces and vows of married people,  
recalling the name of husband after the title of monk.

He even began repeatedly to assail his teacher with tumult,  
mixing such complaints into his prayers:

“If Christ grants me the consolations of marriage,  
deigning to join a different intention to the marriage bed,  
who will take God’s gifts away from me?  
Who will dare, by a new law, tear up the Lord’s ancient law?”

As he shattered his mind in such reckless murmuring,  
the medicine of the holy patron approached him more gently.

[Col. 1048B] “Tell me, come now: do you recall the times of your former life?  
Did you ever join battle in drawn ranks against a savage enemy?”

Since you remember that this happened very frequently,  
consider whether, amid the bugles and trumpets of war,  
the javelins aimed by the terrifying arms of fighters,  
the drawn swords, and the sails swollen by the received wind,  
imitating the breath or rage of serpents,  
the female sex ever disgraced the ranks of war.

What place have shields beside spinning wool?  
What place have weapons for girls?  
Did a sprinkling of dust suit their smooth faces?

But if such things are not appropriate to earthly camps,  
what is there that is feminine which can suit the standards of men?

When you wage war with continual sweat,  
will the mixture of the sexes not be still more shameful to you  
during a time of idleness, when wanton pleasure  
finds such a ridiculous company?

But when manly ranks hasten into the fields,  
when armored troops shine,  
let the walls defend the female crowds,  
and let the women strive to shut themselves behind barred gates,  
let the man who hastens to war reject consolations.”

By such words he healed the pleasures of the unrestrained mind  
and, restoring order, gave the heart new joys;  
then he sent the fighting man back to war in peace.

Who could now worthily traverse this episode,  
or describe how much patience adorned so teachable a gentleness?

Perhaps among holy girls, holy in heart and flesh,  
ever precious through the flower of perpetual modesty,  
whom virginity devoted to Christ had joined to the Lord—  
by a bond of mind, not a compact of flesh—  
one had advanced beyond all the rest  
through devotion to virtue, adding this special distinction  
to her titles of modesty:

once removed from the sight of all men,  
she preserved her undertaken rigor with steadfast heart.  
No fickle woman wavered in unstable feeling;  
she conquered her innate sex by the weight of virtue  
and surpassed the rare examples of men who had gone before.

[Col. 1048D] Proper admiration for her purpose impelled the saint  
to approach her, reverencing her rightly,  
drawn by the girl’s great flower of virtues.

Yet the faith already fixed so steadfastly in her heart,  
now devoted to the Lord, remained so firm  
that the barriers of modesty—enclosures guarding  
the titles of her illustrious palm from men—  
could not be opened even for so great a patron.

Nor did she blush to offer a vowed refusal.  
Her faith rejoiced in its purpose; rather, the kindly man  
reckoned as his own honor all the things  
that had given rise to hope, attending more to the soul’s gains  
than to the joys of the flesh.

What portion of your fury, what portion of yours, O holy man,  
lay in that breast—ambition inflated  
by the winds of insane pride—now lies utterly prostrate?  
Christ can have nothing in common with vices:  
those who swell with praise desire to be exalted.  
He approves sufficiently the one who wishes to remain hidden  
and scorns the heights of the world,  
attributing the honor he avoids to the Lord alone.

But because you preferred to become lowly for Christ when praised,  
adding this judgment also to your blessed titles,  
the praise you flee by avoiding it, you merit by avoiding it.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1049]

[Col. 1049A] Once your tongue has been brought forth in praise  
of so great a patron, why are you silent?  
Why, closing your uncouth murmurs and untrained sounds  
within long silence, do you suppress your voice?

If shame prevents you from speaking of such great matters,  
the law should have been established earlier;  
you are attempting too late to spread these coverings  
over a brow already far too worn.

But if you are held by the cheap torpor of sloth,  
so that the sad image of gloomy death may depart,  
shake off your languor and rise again from your deathly depression.

If you lie depressed with good reason, trust in your patron.  
Why, though guilty of a vow, do you fear punishment as though guilty?

Come, then, and entrust your extinguished ember to the Lord,  
so that the rigor of your intellect may grow warm  
when Christ breathes upon it,  
and Martin’s prayer may melt the ice of your heart  
and make the brutish voice burst forth as soon as possible,  
so that it may once again deserve miracles like those of the former deed.

Where the walls of Chartres lie across the open fields,  
Gaul stretches widely over immense plains.

Here a daughter, already twelve years old,  
who had remained mute and had opened her mouth  
to no words at all,  
the most grievous care of her sorrowing parents,  
caused them continual pain by living on.

[Col. 1049C] Her wounds grew with the passing of the years.  
Alas, how often they grieved that the powerful gifts of God,  
granted to others, had perished for them,  
when they often saw little children, scarcely yet crawling,  
break into words,  
and names emerge, broken, from shadowed lips.

When piety, preceding their speech,  
noticed an uncertain murmur,  
recognizing an indistinct voice through an interpreter of affection,  
receiving the sounds as though they were words  
and seizing upon what was to be said—

these gifts, granted to others after their first cradles,  
a rival piety had mourned for twelve years,  
while, grieving through two lustrums and two years,  
she longed for a first voice by the time of marriage.

[Col. 1049D] Until the father, lifeless with grief,  
clung and adhered to Martin’s knees  
and unfolded his whole complaint in a groan,  
drawing deep sighs from the bottom of his chest,  
cutting his lamentable murmur with frequent sobbing,  
and drenching his breast with the rain of his cheeks.

The love of accustomed piety had also shaken Martin’s kindly mind,  
but the cause of his delay was concern for precious modesty  
and for the modesty that must always be joined to illustrious deeds,  
lest boasting destroy the merit he had bestowed  
and presumption of heart corrupt the work of virtue.

Therefore he said:

“I consider myself unworthy of so great a miracle,  
and I fear the weight upon my trembling neck.  
I am too weak to bear it, lest the burden become too great  
and, unable to endure so heavy a load, I labor beneath it.”

But no cure is difficult for Christ,  
who rightly entrusts such signs to other ministers,  
so that the merits of the saints may reveal the Lord’s miracles.

Behold, two men distinguished in character, faith,  
and virtue stand here—men whom such a life  
has rightly raised to this position.  
Will not the Lord’s medicine more readily give this to them,  
a great thing beyond our merit  
but not difficult for the saints?

Repeating these proofs of humble heart,  
and showing his merit by refusing the honor,  
he proves himself more worthy,  
because precious modesty accompanies all his other qualities.  
He avoids envy because he fears comparing himself with others.

When the father saw this, he pressed the saint more forcefully,  
joining in his prayers those whose faith,  
as Martin had said, was to be concealed,  
so that it might not be permitted even to delay  
what a devout will, breathing through Christ, had advised,  
together with the favor of equal and harmonious right.

[Col. 1050C] Therefore, after the crowds had been removed,  
lest the confused murmur of the people interrupt the man praying  
or boastfulness display their own powers,  
he added only those companions whom he had made his equals  
in honor, and who had equal concern for prayer,  
equal devotion, united faith, and joined intention.

The father, too, was added, trembling;  
the gifts of Christ, which he desired more ardently,  
made his prayers more faithful.

Then, upright in exalted spirit but bent in body,  
he set his holy heart above while his limbs lay below.  
He lies down in the flesh but lives vigorously in the mind;  
his mind, joined to God, ascends on high,  
while the boastfulness of the flesh is pressed down.

Thus dissimilar paths are joined together in a common deed.  
Thus the humble man hastens where others have gone before—
the faithful.

No delay, and the holy man perceived the familiar signs of favor,

[Col. 1050D] rejoicing continually in Christ as his guest, often opening the doors of his heart to such gifts.

Then he ordered that the olive oil be brought, and, blessing it, infused the offered liquid with the nectar of his words; through this, the medicine entered the transformed fluid.

After it had been poured into the girl’s grateful mouth, at once the bonds of her entangled tongue were loosed, and, filling her moist throat with a sudden breath, the long-awaited voice of her sweet speech revived.

At first she timidly began to form a proper utterance and took up uncertain sounds in her father’s name. This was the first word, and from the first mouth of the speaker the father seized it and buried it in his heart.

Then he prostrated himself and clasped in supplication the arms of the man who alone had offered prayers while the girl remained silent; now he repaid the Lord with more than one voice of thanks.

Nor was there less wonder at another deed, of which the infusion of the healing liquid, remembered by me, and the blessing of the oil once sung about have made me mindful.

And whenever medicine called for the help of piety, grace sanctified alike things arising from different causes. For, as the faithful often do with cautious heart, she had been led to preserve a vessel filled with oil as an instrument of salvation, either to offer it to righteous men or to store it in consecrated places—places where present workings reveal patrons who have earned the power of martyrdom; or where manifest faith recalls, or reading discloses, that the Word came into blessed swaddling clothes; or where the preceding age, trembling at the crime of a dreadful people, inserted sudden darkness between us; or where the fortunate hollows of the broken rock, rejoicing at God’s touch, opened beneath the limbs soon to rise, without the law of a tomb.

Or from here, the earth that rejoiced at Christ’s return to the stars happily received his final footprints. Whatever an inventive hand had prepared and adorned, she, disdainful of her own sands, cast far away, preserving these gifts of so holy a touch; she broke apart the fragile barrier by means of the scattered dust,

[Note: [Col. 1051D] “Immediately dissolving the extended [barrier],” etc., so that the limping verse may scan in the poetic composition.]

dissolving the barriers of the extended metal.

In these places, where proximity affords this privilege, they pour the peaceful liquid into pure vessels, so that, infused from above with the nectar of dew, it may be changed; through it heavenly grace flows into the sacred liquid.
