[Col. 1051C] Or those whom the intervening distances of long roads keep completely apart in a different region, believing that the Lord is not confined by the limits of places and that the help of his mercy surpasses all boundaries, with unhesitating faith ask for the present gifts of the present Lord. For, according to the power of his favor, he does not weary the prayers of those who come to him from afar; when approached, he touches those who ask everywhere, and he does not avoid the slow. He stands nearer to those who hasten, and the effort of the traveler becomes itself the only end of the journey.

Those who carry these things in their hearts, wherever they have been called, possess the Lord’s gift, whether they entrust their vows to sacred men or store up whatever they have consecrated in holy places for sanctification. What Christ did not visit in his body, he protects by his power, although he returned long ago and now reigns in the height of heaven in his body.

As she often turned these matters over in her mind, urged on by faith, surpassing her frail sex by the strength of faith, a woman of exalted rather than womanly courage believed that the olive oil, once sent forth, would then be offered to the holy man; and that the piety of so great a minister, near at hand, would favor her prayers to Martin no differently than if, swiftly carried on rapid wings, she had borne her vows within the very tomb of the Lord, embracing the standard of the cross and the wood of salvation.

Filled with such faith, and singing diligently, she poured the green oil into the glass with careful hands. The descending liquid changed its snowy color,

[Col. 1052A] and, silently flowing into the hollow beneath, gradually increased by the growth of the shining fluid; without a sound, the mute thickness swelled.

Yet, so that the mouths of the vessels might remain open and her hand might not falter beneath the excessively full stream, where the neck rises from the rounded base the opening of the still-empty vessel remained wide.

Then the boy, taking the oil, hurried away and carried to the holy man both the vows and the words of the one who prayed.

The work of piety did not delay: swift grace commended the righteous zeal, lest by lingering it either postpone the faithful woman or make the favor doubtful through a brief delay.

At once God proved by the signs he granted how great a gift the present blessing would confer, lest faith should falter through a trembling mind.

[Col. 1052B] The men present were astonished that Christ had commanded the chosen witnesses to be present at such miracles.

Thus, while Martin prayed, the liquid increased: the swelling mass of the rising fluid, lifted upward, filled the empty part with suspended depth; rising continuously toward the top, it did not leave the bottom bare. It boiled over and yet remained full as it settled; it grew as more was poured in, but was not emptied by what it received, until the servant, carrying the blessed gift back to his mistress, went rejoicing and, celebrating such mighty signs, offered the proof of the blessed man’s merit with his right hand.

Such was the holy blessing of the illustrious prophet: when the widow had exhausted her scanty supply, it filled the empty vessels with gifts that would remain,

so that she who had offered proofs of generous faith

[Col. 1052C] might, secure in what she had asked, become richer through her expenditures.

Nor, indeed, should I fear to touch upon the remaining praises and virtues of the man; at least I shall be able to recount these deeds, in which a similar blessing of the same liquid rightly demands the praise of many voices.

One faith, often medicinal, does not differ in its action, but another, equal in signs, differs in the number of its gifts.

The witness is Severus, marvelous in learned speech, who followed Christ with the whole strength of his heart. He was distinguished by the honors of the world, but more distinguished by that virtue of holy faith with which he despised the world; powerful in nobility, he was much nobler still in the worship of Christ than in his origin from blood.

He compressed the sacred canon, and, shortening the written history that had been extended at length, enclosed in two little books everything that had been handed down from the earliest ages.

[Col. 1052D] The same man, carefully investigating the truth and faithfully reporting it, brought forth into the open the distinguished features of so illustrious a life as he rewove the deeds and honors of Martin. Thus, maintaining a just balance with equal judgment, he neither asserted what was doubtful nor was silent about what was certain.

He had often remained closely associated with the holy man in piety, as the mind’s reflection in the mirror of the heart usually joins similar figures of kindred character.

For this reason the witness is all the more trustworthy: he teaches what he discovered in the man’s presence when he speaks of what he saw.

Therefore, among the other proofs of his affection, he asked to receive a special gift of the holy liquid.

[Col. 1053A] After the blessed man had given it to his faithful friend, rejoicing in the aid of its power and the memorial of its favor, he carried it in the religious faith of the Lord, believing that he was conveying a salvation granted to him. He placed it high in a window whose glass, set across it, closes off the clear daylight, exposed to the blasts of the winds and open to the light.

There he covered the bottle with a snowy cloth, so that the stretched fabric might prevent wandering eyes from seeing what would meet them, though it could not shut out the mind.

Then an ignorant boy, in the hurried motion of his hand, snatched the coverings with careless force and threw the glass vessel down upon the marble beneath.

The servant stood bloodless with astonishment, his master pale. Struck by the swift impact, the vessel sprang again to the heights, filling everything with its wandering ringing sound; it struck, was caught, and rose from the ground.

The bottle, though struck with such great crashes, suffered none of them: unbroken, it remained, and its glass covering stayed intact.

Thus the liquid within, enclosed in its fragile covering, hardened the outer drums of the hollow framework, so that one might have thought that the marble, changed completely into feathers, had received the fall upon soft supports.

Thus, Martin—thus does sanctified grace piously receive your gift; thus does what has been blessed protect it.

When the fierce violence of a savage mastiff rushed upon someone, shaking furious jaws, drawing back its wrinkled nostrils from the covering of its mouth, and repeatedly striking its bared teeth with a growling sound,

[Col. 1053C] the person, terrified by such sudden dread, closed the rabid mouth not with a stick or a blow, but only with the name of Martin. As soon as it sounded, the restrained barking clung to silence; the erect mane fell, and the threatening, protruding eyes—flames suffused with blood—laid aside their threats and closed. Then the animal began more gently to caress the air, sweep the ground with its twisted tail, and lower its head with bent neck.

Why, Martin, should such things not yield to your power, since you conquer so great a madness by your name alone?

What wonder is it now if the hearts of savage men yield and human passions grow gentle before you?

Thus once people were astonished that the dreadful power and cruel force of Avitianus should yield to you. His savagery was joined to threats, and his sole delight consisted in claws, executioners, torturers, whips, chains, the death of men, the voice of mourners, the pallor of the accused, the devouring prison, the destruction of those who confessed, the tortures of those who denied—a most savage beast of Tartarean heart, breathing innumerable slaughter with a furious breast.

Fierce with pitiless cruelty, he had entered the city ruled by the bishop Saint Martin.

[Col. 1053D] The sorrowful and pallid company of the unhappy accused remained there, chains tied around their filthy necks, striking the brothers’ limbs with clanking bonds and dragging slow steps with bent bodies.

Offering such spectacles to Martin, Phalaris prepared different executions at nearby benches.

The swift crowd of frenzied attendants hurried to seek out instruments for savage punishments.

[Col. 1054A] Some brought out vessels for Tartarean flames. In them, with the fierce heat of the enclosed vapor, dissolved pitch would call for the crackling of fire, which, boiling up from afar in a torrent of deadly flame, would roast the body enclosed in a sulfurous pit.

Others raised beams of wood and, with furious hearts, prepared a sorrowful service: so that the flesh, soon hanging miserably from stretched limbs, might expose its torn members to the torturer for punishment, while he drenched his Tartarean right hand with blood and scattered sad gore through repeated wounds.

And, so that the same punishment might satisfy a twofold fury, the striker shook the limbs of the mangled body, tearing apart the bonds of the members at their broken joints.

Others brought torches and soaked the long, woven bonds of papyrus in abundant oil,

[Col. 1054B] not so that light might defeat the darkness, distinguishing the obscure night with fire-bearing brightness, but so that they might kindle funeral fires for the wretched, applying flames to their wounded limbs.

Should such things have been seen by Martin in his city, and his peaceful mind pierced by so great a wound, so that at least the report of them might reach his holy ears, or even the rumor alone shake his pious heart?

Therefore, when his mind had been struck by the funeral preparations, and a messenger had spread beforehand the signs of the cruel tyrant’s dreadful plan and approaching fury, rightful compassion ran through his entire being and scattered the swift warmth of pity.

Although humane clemency, recalling the fate of men, compelled him to weep for the deaths of the wretched accused,

[Col. 1054C] there was no less a cause for his present grief: the same man who had supported the crime, while acting as the avenger of the offense, was first making himself guilty by punishing the guilty.

A denser darkness had wrapped the covered world. Welcome rest had spread peaceful sleep through all the elements, and everything languished in moist slumber; the murmurs of silent voices were suppressed.

The deep silence of midnight bristled terribly; the darkness, diffused with its own color, had covered everything and carried away the distinguishing marks of all forms.

But Martin was not concerned to obtain rest. Sacred prayers for human salvation stood beside him, urging his mind through affection. Therefore he approached with rapid steps the deadly threshold of the bloodstained judge,

[Col. 1054D] alone and fearless through the vast, dark silences of night and the hidden darkness of the terrifying roads.

I believe that all the troops of shadows, which the evil demon urges toward nocturnal crimes, gave way, and that the other savage mastiffs were silenced, their terrible jaws’ barking stilled by a gentle word.

When he had reached the blocked threshold of the dreadful judge and the fatal enclosure of his savage fury, he prostrated himself before the house, midway in the approach enclosed by barriers. He was kept from the doors, but struck the stars with his weeping.

The savage beast was breathing heavily in sleep from its swollen breast, and, with its limbs spread out in the image of death, had thrown its utterly numb body upon the bed. Suddenly an angelic terror shook its entrails, and a voice also burst upon its astonished ears.

[Col. 1055A] “Has heavy sluggishness, unhappy beast, oppressed you in deep sleep? Are you belching cups of spoiled wine, while the burden of your raw stomach stretches you in sloth? And here lies the servant of the Lord before your doors upon the bare, dry earth, covering his pious body with much dust. Do you put the barriers of sleep before your doors as an obstacle to the foul silence of nocturnal slumber?”

At the sudden sight it stiffened and quickly ordered the servants it summoned to hurry rapidly to the enclosure, so that they might report the truth in messages of words.

But, as often happens when limbs are bound by torpor, welcome rest binds and overcomes the pressed senses. The servants advanced a little, scarcely reaching the first threshold; their sight was excessively dull and their steps faltered. They returned deceptive murmurs in confused words, saying that nothing had been found before the doors after careful investigation.

Again the pleasure of sleep, though it had been driven far away, immediately closed their languid eyes.

Then a new terror shook their trembling hearts, and the threatening sentence of the angelic voice compelled them to rise at once by repeating the command. He did not choose to risk a second violation of the command.

The judge himself hastened quickly to the threshold of the enclosure, and, when the master opened them, the blocked doors stood open.

The venerable bishop shone forth with a radiant face, displaying upon his holy countenance the marks of his virtues. His grace, bright with many signs, flourished in religion, faith, affection, piety, and modesty; his mind was joyful in hardships, steadfast and serious in joys, neither hardened by savagery nor having its austerity dissolved in laughter.

[Col. 1055C] In every way he shone with steadfast integrity, so that anger did not make him fierce and favor did not make him sluggish.

Such a venerable appearance met the pale tyrant and tore apart the clouds of the gloomy night.

His mind, conscious of so great a crime, had already revealed without words the cause of the holy man’s labor.

Nor did he need to open the matter with prayers. He himself first brought forth a voice, trembling and confused in his fearful heart:

“Why, holy man, do you trouble my heart, long wearied by fear and torpor, after sleep has been wholly shaken off?”

“Though you are kept far from the doors, by your holy merit you rightly break into the inner chamber: you stand there in bodily form and lawfully enter, terrifying me who dwell in the flesh.”

“Nor would I deny that these things are deserved by my deeds, since with a hard heart I breathed innumerable slaughter in your city. Therefore, I beg you, forgive me as I confess. Use your right; if you wish to spare me, be merciful. Release the accused from punishments, and free me from guilt.”

No delay: the chains were quickly loosened and fell—chains that had just bound the pale necks of the accused, preserving their dying bodies for dreadful death.

Suddenly hope, restored to the wretched, rejoiced in its fulfillment. With joy mixed with fear at so great a change, they trembled and doubted whether to believe, but preferred to believe.

They vied with one another in thanks, falling at the holy man’s knees and gently clasping his feet with supplicating arms.

He urged them rather to give thanks to God and reminded them that Christ was the author of this salvation, who pardons crimes only if a change of heart at least reveals true sorrow for the offense,

[Col. 1056A] for punishments remain in store for the guilty so long as guilt endures.

With such words of admonition, and by laboring together in piety, he absolved the prisoners from punishment and released them from their crimes.

Now what tongue could worthily speak of this gift? What mind, terrified even to touch it with astonished understanding, is large enough for the honors of so illustrious a patron?

Thus the merit of the holy man made all the troops of demons tremble, and thus the signs of such great fear were revealed: whenever he advanced from a distance toward the city, leaving the threshold of his own cell, to visit the people entrusted to him under holy governance or to offer the mysteries of sacred worship, grace, moving swiftly with rapid flight, tormented the trembling spirits in their captive bodies.

[Col. 1056B] Scarcely had he left the inner sanctuary of the holy dwelling when the demons, already far in advance through their torments, saw that he was at hand; and the punishment of the guilty cried out the judge’s arrival with a shrill sound.

When he had placed his first footprints at the doors, one could see bodies, their limbs swiftly snatched upward, lifted and bound in airy chains.

Their heavy masses of flesh, wavering through empty space, left the neighboring earth in a rapid whirl, hanging in their own punishment but free from physical bonds, bound by the merits of prayers, suspended in their proper penalties, and crying out the crimes they had committed before the silent judge.

Nor did a confession extracted by the questioner’s words reveal their crimes through a trembling voice.

For the holy man passed by, bent toward the stars in a prayer that alone was his, touching the Lord in hope, but bent in body, humble in heart, lofty in merit, crying without complaint. The judge was hidden from sight but proved by power.

Before his merit such miracles were opened: a guilty man hung in empty space, while his torturer in the air stretched upward his feet, clothed in a stiff fleece fastened around him and clinging to his covered limbs,

[Col. 1056C] lest, bent by their own curve or slipping backward, they should expose the shameful limbs of the suspended body.

Thus, Martin, was your merit; thus holy power and the glory of Christ, to be revealed by God’s servants, reign above the earth in the honors of heaven and air.

It is also certain that, when you prayed, you dried up the clouds and caused the suspended fall of hail to cease, holding back the ruin of the storm within the densely gathered mass of the cloud,

[Col. 1056D] which, heavy and joined with the cold of the rigid wind, hardened the waters into stones and, in repeated whirlwinds, hurled rocks of solid liquid upon the earth. They struck down crops, shrubs, gardens, orchards, and vines with the repeated ruin of storms, and the earth was shaken by the powerful blows.

This plague had spread widely through the fields of the Senones and, accustomed to fulfill the laws of punishment every year, had beaten the fields bare with continual devastation.

The farmer, pale, reported the lost harvest, lamenting the completely shattered traces of the stalks; the digger reported the empty vine, without fruit or shoot, and often, groaning after the yearly hopes of labor, counted the losses in the already swelling clusters.

[Col. 1057A] The most sorrowful mother showed the branches, their fruits—her children—accustomed to creep among the tender apples; and beside them were the pale shoots of the parched field, while stones echoed to the lowing of cattle.

The withered vines searched their empty recesses, declaring their plaintive cause by whatever lament they could.

Therefore the whole people, pierced and driven by this disaster, desiring to obtain so illustrious a patron for themselves, humbly entreated Martin through a delegate and interpreter to strive to appease God and ask pardon for the wretched, and at last drive away the grievous plague.

Let punishment be enough; let Christ’s mercy, after the blows, remove at least the excessive destruction. Nor did the expected hope deceive the wretched.

For as soon as Martin, always joined and clinging to the Lord, asked for the gifts of his customary piety,

[Col. 1057B] they felt the holy aid; the storm was driven away and fell silent, the day shone with clear serenity, and the shoots were moistened by the desired rains.

Nor was the grace confined to a brief period; for a long time it commended its gifts to the extended fields, and it remained for four full five-year periods.

They did not experience the damage of the mad storm again before the Lord, at the close of the present life, took his blessed friend to true rest.

Thus he spent the periods of both pious lives: once salvation for the earth, but now exalted among the stars.

Now the long page of a book that has become too languid weakens the honors and deeds of the illustrious patron. While I, a small voice, speak of great things and, a trembling narrator, of lofty signs,

[Col. 1057C] I diminish the splendor of his praise.

But what am I to do? I know how to run through history in verse; what is narrated fears judgment, while what is suppressed incurs guilt.

Perhaps the reader will more rightly leave these things behind in weariness than the pious listener will seek what has been wholly withdrawn.

The earlier discourse already reached the savage Avitianus; now the order of the work returns to him.

Here he overcame tyrants savage in dreadful cruelty, thirsting for the grievous torments of sorrowful accused men; yet he showed some mercy to the city of Tours.

Here, revealing only traces of human feeling, he subjected his rebellious face to holy restraints, suppressing his inborn fury at Martin’s commands.

And certainly the manifest proofs of this healing appeared one day in this way. The venerable Martin approached the dreadful tribunal of such a judge, so that cruelty might be softened by such services, constrained by the duties owed to a holy patron.

The man happened to sit upon a high seat, conspicuous upon a throne, rising above all in his exceedingly proud ambition. Suddenly the holy man, looking at him, saw the bloody appearance of a dreadful and loathsome mad demon reclining upon his neck, lying prone with all its weight attached to him.

From a distance, as soon as the holy man touched it with the breath of his blessed mouth, he drove it away with the terror of his word.

Unaware, Avitianus believed that he had received from his companion a grave punishment in the form of a curse.

He said:

“Do not suppose that you have been marked by my judgment, or that this is the sign of some sudden movement. This was pity, not anger, that raged against the enemy. Pitying the wretched man, it grieves for him and bursts upon him.

“This breath of ours came from the very depth of my breast. I saw it pressing with terrible force upon this lofty seat, and lying prone upon your neck.

“Cease now to maintain such fellowship with a robber. Trust more in pious counsels; once exposed, let cunning be driven away, and let caution, having learned the deceit, repel it.

“Be ashamed now to obey the guilty man and serve one who has been driven out.”

By such words, when the demon had been expelled, the door of the heart was closed against it and the power of its seat was shattered. From then on the judge became gentler, without his own judge, and the heavy burden was cast from his shaken neck.

Thus he drove all enemies expelled from their seat,

[Col. 1058B] freeing human hearts; nor did he leave the temples to the fugitives. Whatever empty error had built as shrines was now burning, widely destroying them in collapsing ruins.

Not far from the city mentioned above there was a village, once bearing the traces of an ancient fortress, then inhabited by servants of God and ministers of Christ.

Its first inhabitant gave it the ancient name Ambacia.

Here a sacrilegious gathering, in its foolish madness, had once built a lofty temple of immense workmanship. Rising high in the form of a cone, the towered mass extended its marvelous structure upward, so perfectly joined throughout, despite the repeated arrangement of the stones, that the lofty burden would not sway and no crack would appear; instead, a beautiful bond held the fitted stones together.

The more the skill of the craftsman, by means of a rational design, astonished minds deprived of reason,

[Col. 1058C] the more shamefully stupid religion prevailed, venerating as a god only the builder’s intelligence and the genius named after the craftsman.

Therefore the holy Martin ordered that this building be overturned. He reproached the faithful presbyter for having long neglected the command, but the man modestly denied that the order could be carried out: it was too difficult for weary monks, he said, and too much for the few servants of God, since only assembled groups, gathered from the emptied countryside, or laboring cohorts could scarcely accomplish it.

His words made the justice of his excuse entirely clear.

Yet hope was not broken. He did not prepare vows by summoning the peoples, nor did he hurry to Ambacia to lead there troops gathered from the whole world.

He calls upon heavenly aid; all his hope is in the one who rules heaven and earth, whom the air serves and for whom the elements preserve enduring awe.

[Col. 1058D] Therefore again, in his hairy garment, reclining upon the prickles accustomed to pierce the skin, with their hardness joined into stiff threads that wounded the rebellious fleece, he renewed sleepless groans, renewed fasts with meals postponed, and joined the labor of the night once more to the sun that would soon rise.

The prayer did not suffer a long delay. Behold, as day returned, a violent storm roared around the building; the clouds, torn into streams by the whirlwind of the winds, were split apart, and the gathered masses of water, hurled down from the lofty heights, struck the structure with a thunderous blast.

[Col. 1059A] The battle of the clouds returned the sound that had been forced from them.

The earth trembled and, shaken from its deepest foundation, cast off the hanging foundations of the burden imposed upon it.

It scattered the ruin far from the jointed structure and rolled the fragments of the shattered mass down the slopes.

“O you exceedingly beloved of God! Through your prayer Christ has thus dried up the rain clouds in the lofty air.

“At your prayers once again the swift storms returned, and the black clouds girded with heavy winds, ordered to spare what was sufficient, broke apart their powerful masses—soft toward the grasses, but merciless toward the hard rocks.”

This merit too was no less, nor was its cause different: glory, resembling itself, imitated equal triumphs.

The highest supports of a column raised an idol’s image, lifted high by stones joined together from afar,

[Col. 1059B] so that its appearance, higher and loftier than that throne, might look down upon the wretched people before the manufactured deity.

When Martin also desired to overturn this mass, all human aid had failed for such prayers, but hope in the Lord always remained swift.

Therefore, when his thought flew swiftly to heaven and he asked the King of heaven for speedy help, a fiery force, similar in appearance but different in light, descended and shattered the fragile structure, rolling sulfurous flames and crackling embers, raising a smoking cloud from the burnt dust and vapor from the consumed mass.

Thus, Martin, beneath the shining sky, thus in the whirlwind of the wind, you join together twin triumphs, whether through cloud or fire.

Nor is it surprising that the Lord fulfilled his promises to a faithful servant, a holy minister who had once told servants astonished by such great miracles that he would give them proofs of true faith, so that believers might confirm greater signs than these.

What wonder is it that the Lord fulfilled this same promise through servants, to whom he deigned to promise greater things and whose lofty hearts he had prepared for pious ministries?

For, as the heavenly book reveals, it bears witness to the woman’s faith: after rivers of blood and the sad wasting of her body, swift healing returned at the touch of a garment.

So the glory of the same deed was given to Martin, but with God as healer—the God who is now shown to be touched through his members, lofty in the citadel of the starry throne, by those who are joined to the eternal head in holy unity.

[Col. 1059D] What was not gentle toward the pious man? What monsters did not submit to the faithful man? Serpents often obeyed when commanded, and their kindred ferocity did not remain in the conquered venom.

A venomous serpent swam across near the adjacent ford and furrowed the glassy waters. Its head rose from the waves with its neck exposed; it split the surface with its breast, hastening across the river, while it bent the remaining length of its body through the blue waters in slippery curves, twisting curved coils and waving its trembling tongue, prepared for wounds.

When Martin had scarcely seen it in midstream, already hurrying toward the neighboring bank, he compelled it with these words:

“Quickly return backward, restrained by the power of God, or by the name of Christ.

[Col. 1060A] “I order you not to advance farther toward the forbidden bank.”

The evil beast stopped in midstream, and rigid torpor bound together its shattered limbs. Its members gradually clung to the captive swimming, until, when the current of the restrained stream had been blocked, its languid neck floated in the promised depths, and the sluggish channel carried the half-dead serpent backward.

Would that, through a similar power, the faithful compassion of our holy patron might also transform the poison in us, which, having wrongly crossed its course, has corrupted the slippery path of life, continually immersing my sins in a swift age!

May he compel us to remember salvation once forgotten, lest our limbs, bent downward, sink into the muddy depths and our polluted body grow wet in the flood of vices; but may steady steps stand on the bank of virtues,

[Col. 1060B] stand upon faith, trample earthly joys, and strive with swift effort to escape whatever flows away.

With this one prayer I shall linger a little beside the river, while recalling the honors of the illustrious patron, to whose merit the rejoicing flood of waters obeyed, submitting itself to the commands of the holy man.

The fasts continued throughout the entire year, but the solemnities of Easter relaxed them somewhat; on those days alone he tormented his limbs more gently.

Then alone he took a small fish for food.

But while the customary time was being kept for the signs to come, the expected catch disappointed the vow of his service.

When he learned that the fishermen’s labor had flowed away in vain, and that their nets had been stretched through the empty depths,

[Col. 1060C] he recognized it from the complaining words of those who mourned.

For on the remaining days the deacon was present with sufficiently faithful speech and served as his assistant. His more urgent care for this service kept him watchful through the preceding night and, when part of the present day had passed, made him a witness to the common labor, though exhausted.

When the holy man’s pious heart was moved by his anxiety, stirred by compassionate grief, he said:

“Go, then, and carefully search the river, quickly crossing its streams. Your nets will already enclose captive prey.”

No delay: confused by the words of so great a master, the deacon hurried. Hope was restored to his trembling prayer, and the delayed catch did not disappoint his swift effort.

For as soon as he enclosed the nearby shallows with a small net, the rope’s bark-covered float trembled when struck, revealing prey entangled upon the trackless blue waters.

[Col. 1060D] He quickly dragged the entangled fish to the neighboring shores, rejoicing in the pike. Then, bent over with his whole heart, he wrapped his arms around the slipping, wet fish.

The slippery prey scarcely clung to his bare arms; shaken, it almost escaped from his wet embraces.

At last, gradually leaving its kindred element, it breathed out its slight life in the air as it died, and tremblingly opened its mouth in a feeble gasp, while its rejected tail applauded with a waving motion.

The monks were astonished at the joy that fulfilled their prayer. They had come out from the neighboring cells to witness such a spectacle, and, rejoicing in the fulfillment through such a guarantor, had believed that the word spoken from the holy man’s heart would be fulfilled:

“O true mirror of eternal virtue! These gifts flow to you from the one who once commanded his disciples, wearied by their fruitless labor through the night, to draw their nets, sending abundant prey into them; enclosing for holy banquets the chosen fish whom holy teaching of the faith would draw from the world’s whirlpool to the Lord.”

Often God wished to bring forth the sublime merit of the blessed man through illustrious men, so that the signs of his virtues, made to shine more brightly through those witnesses whom the glory of the world had raised to prominence, might gleam before the peoples.

For Arborius, famous at that time by the rank of prefect, saw Martin’s hand shining with the light of glittering jewels while he was performing the sacred rites for God. He saw it glow, and a flashing light clothe the fiery right hand in precious purple,

[Col. 1061B] while the stones struck together with a rattling sound.

Such stones did not decorate the standards of generals, nor do such jewels encircle the foreheads of kings with diadems; rather, they were like the gems that the Lord’s judgment inserts into the bright crowns of the saints at the end.

There is no doubt that, through the exceptional integrity of his faith, he shone beyond mankind with the varied flower of virtues. The fortunate page of the historical book bears witness to his merit through the comfort of angelic speech given before his eyes.

For when he was returning in deep sorrow from the city of Trier, where, fearing from the angry king the death of the wretched people whose lives he sought from that king, he had been compelled somewhat to relax his own severity,

he had looked more gently upon Ithacius’s offense, moved by clemency to spare the condemned cause

[Col. 1061C] and restore again the new bonds of peaceful piety.

An angel visited him, so deeply afflicted with grief; manifest before him in speech and face, the angel brought gentle comfort to his sorrowful friend, soothing his anxious heart with words joined together, teaching him by counsel what must be changed and dissolving what had been committed.

Thus, marking the praises of the eminent prophet, the heavenly messenger made Zacharias announce with holy mouth the beginning of the holy child, promising that a voice would come after the commanded silence.

Finally, an equal merit revealed an equal sequence.

As a son had been given to the former, so grace came to the latter, shining more brightly with the added light of virtues.

For often the spirits expelled from a captive breast, though not yet compelled by the words or voice of the present man,

[Col. 1061D] were terrified by the blessed proximity of his holy cell, and his virtue, extending far away, exceeded the dwelling it had blessed.

Thus, stretched far and wide, the signs shone brilliantly, bearing witness to the Lord’s present favor.

Nor was it content with remaining on land alone. More often, sailors saw the waves themselves, breaking in from afar through Martin’s honors, tossed about in an immense whirlwind while the mad storm’s wave raged with greater violence, showing how much the holy man could accomplish by his name alone.

A ship hurried across the middle of the Tyrrhenian sea, its sails spread over the blue waters.

Its driven prow cut through the depths below, splitting the whitening waves with its opposing breast and leaving long tracks through the foam.

Suddenly clouds stretched over the covered sky;

[Col. 1062A] wet, black wool spread a dark curtain, and the light enclosed in the pitch-black cloud disappeared entirely.

Strong winds pressed upon the sea and overturned it; the wet sands were mingled with red waves; lofty masses were shattered by the violent whirlwind; waves lifted higher raised unstable hills far above, and, returning in repeated collapses, they broke apart in ruins and sent countless crashes from afar.

The sails fell, and the ropes resounded with a trembling shriek.

Now the ship lies hidden amid clouds divided by a mountain of water; again, badly suspended upon a lofty ridge, it rocks, fearing a twofold fall into either depth.

Other waves struck the resistant sides, and, broken against the ship’s framework, rebounded from the shattered timbers,

[Col. 1062B] filling the torn vessel with repeated spray.

The violence of the sea tore away the helm, its steersman cast aside. Fear shook the hearts of the terrified and convulsed their entrails with trembling movement.

Their pallid cheeks were wet not only with spray. Groans born of dismay and tearful voices, with the broken sighs of those continually sobbing, lamented a death that seemed near.

Meanwhile one man, compelled by the extremity of terror but not yet instructed in the knowledge of true faith, called for heavenly help with these words:

“O God, unknown to me but rightly known to your holy servant Martin, whom I venerate and through whom your glory shines: have mercy; drive away the danger; rescue us! For, as I remember, the holy bishop has repeatedly proved by his power that all things are subject to you.”

No delay: the seas fell as the waves were spread flat, and a level plain of tranquil waters lay still.

With a gentle breeze he guided the torn ship,
The west wind, driving [the ship] toward the desired anchorage, brought it safely to rest.

Thus Christ demonstrated his servant’s merit throughout all the elements, and extended the titles of his holy friend, glorifying the renowned name of Martin across the pathless seas.

Nor is it surprising that, with God’s favor, Martin’s faith could accomplish so much, if, whenever he kept watch in blessed vigils, he brought to the Lord auspicious prayers with all the strength of his devotion; if grace, through his name alone, deserved to shine even for one wholly ignorant and far removed.

Although, striving toward this supreme praise, my page draws back in astonishment and fears to rise in lowly words

[Col. 1062D] to such a height of virtues, it is nevertheless proved that the saint healed not one person only, but an entire household at once through his healing intercession.

A lofty witness to the deed is Lycontius, holding the office of prefect and assigning these gifts with grateful speech. A pestilence, spreading in manifold ruin, had overwhelmed one household: everywhere half-dead bodies, rejected in various stages of decay, filled the weary thresholds with their dreadful limbs. Everywhere there was sad pain, frequent sighing, continual weeping, and groans torn from the innermost cavern of the breast; breath convulsed the flanks, constant trembling shook the body, the skin was dry, and a fire implanted in the marrow kindled the stomach; a heavy flood of terror prevailed.

The dying bodies of relatives, already pale and mournful, looked toward the nearby corpse; but the crowd of those who were dying feared even more sadly at such an example. Others, lifeless, were afraid to touch their dear ones, however much their wretched duty compelled them, lest they should sow the grievous contagion of disease. Fear had withdrawn them from attendance, but grief had barricaded their anxious hearts with repeated mourning. Those who had buried the bodies of the dead in the final tombs, delayed only a short time, carried similar diseases to the grim threshold of death.

No medical hands were of any avail, nor herbs with their juices, though they had often brought great cures to the sick.

Thus the master of the household, confounded by such a calamity among his own people

[Col. 1063B] and distrustful of his own prayers, labored to appease the Lord through the intercession of the saint. He presented his grievous calamity through Martin, his worthy patron and interpreter.

Although Martin, already wearied by the burden of his office, felt the weight of the case too heavily, nevertheless, in his mercy, he received the petitioner’s prayer with anxious concern. Nor did he cease before, tormented by constant labor, he had worn away his exhausted limbs to the marrow, struck the hard earth with prostrate effort, doubled his accustomed fasts by added punishments, and, scarcely closing his eyes even in a light sleep, tortured his weary flesh with a bristly scourge.

Then the Lord, moved by the zeal of so great a friend, at last caused his anger wholly to cease and returned the desired gifts of healing. The grateful household embraced the Lord and received him, proclaiming its joy with every prayer and recounting the honors and deeds of its renowned patron.

After the destruction of the calamity through Martin’s prayer,

[Col. 1064A] the master hastened to return worthy gifts to the saint. He carried one hundred pounds of silver to the aforesaid threshold, repaying the benefits with an offered gift, so that the physician’s merit might be acknowledged even by a small reward and that his grateful, generous devotion might become evident.

The saint, rejoicing in the service of his dear friend, did not refuse these rewards, witnesses of the devoted heart’s affection; yet, mindful of the giver’s expense, he considered that the gifts, offered beforehand, should bear the fruit of faith. Nor did he receive them for his own use, lest the saint’s mind should be stained by the desire to possess. Rather, he entrusted them to God and enclosed them in the heavenly treasury, so that, now loosening captives from harsh punishments, and given to the redeemed who had been excluded from holy thresholds, when accepted, they might preserve faith; when rejected, severity.

[Col. 1064B] Proceed, therefore, following what has been begun and seeking what has been promised, O bishop who have won a glorious place in the lofty citadel of heaven, a starry dwelling and shining crown—who were able to bind all the rage and fury of the dreadful demon into a tiny fly.

But we shall always venerate your present remains until you return with your body to eternal life, joined to the tombs of the saints and destined to be united with their crowns.

You have scarcely been able to hide your face from us, remaining with us through your devotion. Our frequent eyes visit you; healing lives in your presence.

The desired gifts of healing are immediately present. The words are silent, but the signs shine: thus you are withdrawn for a little while from bodily sight, yet you are seen as present through your power.

[Col. 1064C] I pray that you may always be present to the request made with a manifest and afflicted heart, so that, when meditation has finished its song, the prayer committed to writing may retain its praise.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 1063]

You summon my care back to renewed murmurings, while you prepare life through your virtue, O priest not closed away by the law of death; surviving your flesh without flesh, you are seen, sought, touched, and held.

While you grant present aid, you display your honor: you stand beside the one who seeks you, never hidden from the one who prays. How well the spirit nearby embraces your limbs and grace pours over the holy stone.

[Col. 1063D] Nothing is far away when faith knocks. Hearts that cry out plead their causes without voice or murmur. He who looks within the mind reads its words, visits the heart, and examines the breast’s secret chamber.

Earlier I recorded deeds in five little books, choosing only a few from many. What portion of such great honors, one of which has come to our knowledge, has fallen to us? How small a labor is weighed against so great a reward?

Again, though I am unworthy of such proclamations, the goodness of my patron permits me to offer whatever praise my ability allows. Merit goes before me, kindly grace is held out, and I do not feel the burden. My concern for labor has not yet been sampled, since the earnest of the gift already commands me to wish for it.

O how many tongues greater eloquence could have adorned with the excellence of this work! It does not allow accustomed songs to be rejected; it believes good things that it recognizes as its own. For it is certain that he himself commanded what his associate and adherent, sent by him, considers worth attempting, continually bringing back the instructions of so great a master:

**PERPETUUS**, blessed, destined to live through a learned age.

He does not report uncertain rumors, nor, trusting the breeze, hasten to spread hearsay through attentive ears. He approves what he has seen face to face; he stands as a most faithful witness; he reveals miracles of proven faith, offered to his own eyes and entrusted to prayer.

From different regions of the world crowds come here in competition. Thousands multiply their many causes and repeat their prayers. Swift grace gives the aid of the desired mercy, and they rejoice, exulting that they carry away the speedy fruit of their labor.

Now, too, he summons here the senses possessed by a mad demon; here swift healing seizes them. The accused are brought forward and tremble. Confession cries out, forced by command. A salutary punishment is seen under judgment, and, in another person’s body, a voice speaks its own words.

[Col. 1071A] The voice sang and praised God in hymns to the saints. Scarcely anyone dares immediately to believe what he sees.

He consults his trembling eyes with doubtful prayer. Faith is not broken by terror; they hurry to the river. New grace promptly restores their vigorous strength. They do not wish to change their clothing: in the same garments they rejoice, and faith does not grow cold in their dripping covering.

Thus the farther bank, rejoicing in so great a triumph, said: “Let us sing joyfully and trustingly to the Lord.” The unharmed prey sings; the submerged predator remains.

Behold again, through the cleft of the divided Jordan, the Lord opened a path through the division and commanded the people to join themselves closely to the ark that had gone before them. As the whirlpool returned toward its source, it turned its waters back to the fountain; and, stopping its course, the returning stream hurried toward its beginning.

[Col. 1071B] The people trampled these places upon the sands, where the frightened sailor had traveled with oar and sail.

Through what routes of land and sea has the glory of this name not penetrated in its swift leap, passing beyond the sea-routes and those accessible to sailors, and across the back of the vast sea seized by powerful storms?

A ship carried far into an unknown depth, beyond the paths of men and fleets, had rushed headlong into the sea, bound fast in the torpor of a whirlpool. No hope of escape appeared. For the sea, standing still like a thick mass of liquid [reading uncertain], held the planks motionless, while the storm’s violence frustrated the desires of those aboard.

Yet the wretched were given no power to escape. A shipwreck so sluggish held them without any movement: what floats upon the sea does not rise out of it but clings to the waves. The sea’s detestable stillness opposed what it supported; it neither carried the ship forward by its force nor swallowed it into an opening.

No path of escape lay open, for the torpid guard kept its prey bound amid the waves.

There is one hope: God, alone the creator of all things. The elements preserve the command of their creator and obey his rule. At the Lord’s nod, they are suddenly stirred and then rest; inert things quickly learn unfamiliar movements, and, once matters have been arranged, the command gives the law.

A certain man, following a report with better understanding, had learned of Martin’s honors as fame proclaimed them throughout the world, and of the many miracles accompanying holy deeds. Driven by necessity, he judged that salvation lay only in crying out to the true God, and thus perhaps prayed:

He raised his eyes toward heaven, seemingly wet with a fountain of tears,

[Col. 1071D] and, joining the innermost places of his heart to his eyes, said:

“Look upon the wretched, O one and true hope of salvation. God, have mercy on Martin, through whom you have scattered among the peoples so many signs of divine favor, and, proving his merit by his virtue, commanded that his renowned honors be extended even across the seas.

“Let him release or loosen his ship’s bonds through his intercessions; let him compel the divided waters to yield,

[Col. 1072A] and let him make so great a surge grow thin in the sea’s whirlpool.”

There was no delay: the immense force of the winds, quickly gliding upon them, expelled the ship that had been seized and broke through the divided whirlpool. It carried the ship easily over the pathless blue waters, and soon restored it to the desired harbor and anchorage. It had been carried out and carried back under Martin’s name.

With unceasing faith they sang the gifts obtained through prayer. Who could grasp these things in understanding? Who could depict them in song? Who could count or express them? Every intellect is defeated; praise restrains tongues pressed into silence.

Nevertheless, I am inferior to the honors that glory accompanies. I have learned of these events many times, or reread them in writing; though I cannot speak of them as worthily as I should, I shall try at least to touch upon them.

A certain man, returning from the holy temple to his home and believing that he was bringing a safeguard of salvation to his household, had carried with him holy wax into its inner rooms.

[Col. 1072B] He had carried with him holy wax into its inner rooms,

trusting that the blessing joined to so great a patron would be present for such just faith through the merit of his power.

Now the time had come for the proofs of favor to emerge. By chance, a serpent, having carelessly escaped, carried fire onward. The devouring flame, increasing its strength among the fuel of the wood, was already pressing its ruin upon the house. Everywhere a great vapor gathered a swelling mass into the air in a whirling cloud; the fire seized and licked everything dry and near at hand, leaving only ashes from so great a disaster.

No hope of escape remained as the danger blazed nearer. Encroaching terror had surrounded the inner rooms and the prey exposed to such neighboring peril.

Prayers returned to the saint. He was invoked with faithful cries, and voices repeatedly uttered his name [sic]. The master himself quickly seized the shining lights of the burning wax,

[Col. 1072C] pouring forth a gentle radiance through its blessed ointment, and with trembling speed carried it into the inner rooms. Setting it amid the raging flames, he drove back the huge fire with the protection of fire.

The raging whirlwind halted; the destructive enemy immediately turned its back, and a spark scattered the fire’s fury.

Even if clouds had poured down whole storms from above, those tempests could not have helped so much. Or if groups had striven to carry away rivers, no one could have caused fountains, with their waters exhausted, to provide such a swift benefit as true power did: the trembling fire fled from its own fuel, and, by natural kinship, feared the neighboring waxes and honeycombs.

By its virtue it destroys the flame that its clear light nourishes, while the fragrant fat, rich in transparent nectar, feeds the liquids.

[Col. 1072D] I, unlearned, have dared to run quickly through these events in a few words and record them for the faithful people to read again. Such great joys strengthened my humble voice. You will not be surprised that the deeds you seek have been described only briefly: it is enough that the poem, disdaining the proclamations of praise, makes clear that death had no power when life was plainly proven.

The city of Tours rejoices forever in Bishop Martin.

## LETTER OF PAULINUS TO PERPETUUS, BISHOP (C)

[Col. 1071D] To the holy and most blessed lord, patron, and bishop Perpetuus: Paulinus.

You have opened again the mouth of the she-ass, granting me confidence to speak, when, confronted with the matter, I would have fallen silent in more bashful silence than I would have chattered in unskilled verbosity. But you ask about the petition of constant intercession. In speaking my prayer, I have revealed it, holy and most blessed lord, special patron before God, whose way of life is angelic and whose dignity is apostolic.

Pressed by conscience, I had believed that even this was too much: that I could be judged rash for approaching such clear brilliance of virtues, as though I needed illumination, and for restricting so bright a light with the cloud of my darkness. But, kindly judging what I had written, you doubled my boldness by your command, so that even now those consecrated walls may bear the strokes of my verses, though we are being instructed for the remedy of our weakness.

As you ordered, I sent the verses through my lord the deacon, so that the opened page on the wall might receive them. I added to them those concerning the visitation of my little nephew, remembering so great a favor: the inscribed letter of virtues, subscribed by the hand of your blessedness, had healed him.

May your prayer cause faith in these aids to grow, so that, since we are permitted to write what we desire to obtain, we may attain it.

## HERE BEGIN THE VERSES OF PAULINUS ON THE VISITATION OF HIS NEPHEW (C, S)

[Col. 1073B] **[Note: These verses were very corrupt in the old manuscript.]**

For how small a drop do you repay with how great a torrent,

holy God, although even that little drop of dew

was given or granted by you to a barren heart.

Such service did not require so great a stream,

nor should moisture that fell from light leaves

make such a copious increase as it slips into the river,

when rather the moisture would rise toward the branches from the rock,

while the green torrent pours out the threads of clouds,

and the thirsty neighborhood snatches the nearby coolness.

And when this drop, so lavish, touched my throat,

you were touched, like marble by the crystals of a solid stream.

How great a gift this single endurance would bring me,

if fortunate boldness incurred no fault!

But now grace would double itself even through these signs,

so that I may sing of you without any end, venerable priest.

The work by which I am raised does not end; when more is added, it grows.

What virtue commands me to remember stands forth and remains.

Then you saw my tears; then, moved by pity, you brought help to those weeping.

The highest author of life, when you pleaded, restrained the severe laments of old age.

Salvation itself restores life. So great a force of illness had cast down my sick and almost lifeless nephew,

and the girl joined to him by the law of marriage,

so that their bodies scarcely breathed with a faint breath,

and even the skilled touch could not detect the veins,

their pulse hidden beneath a weakening thread.

Piety also kept me, removed as I was, from every service: my eyes avoided the hated light, since whatever they saw was punishment.

The one hope of the frightened young man touched his heart: to entrust the matter to his patron and remember the favor so often granted and made his own.

Recently I had happened to unfold and reread a letter that had reached us as an indication of so great a favor, shining with countless wondrous signs. Through it the Lord, bearing witness to the merit of his true friend, adorned the saint’s tomb with immense gifts.

The bishop had marked this letter with his gracious hand:

**PERPETUUS**, rejoicing in the praise of so great a master.

Thus, scarcely with a small murmur of the tongue, with faith that did not hesitate, the young man asked for this letter as a hope not uncertain.

Confidence in speaking gave strength to the lifeless youth and grace loosened his weary tongue.

[Col. 1074B] Therefore, amid the fires stirred by fever, he joined the palms of the virtues to his panting stomach, and, recalling the faith that had written them, seized whatever the closed page held concealed in its very entrails. Swift medicine ran to meet the prayer.

At the command of so great a miracle, the sweat leapt away. The order of the gift also grew to such a degree that, by writing, I may give faith to the face which the writing preserves.

Amber does not suspend a neighboring blade of hay with so swift a leap from the vaporous mass [reading uncertain] as the moisture of the sweat-soaked body hastened to the letter, celebrating the command. Often life returning sought its grandfather through affection, as though announcing so great a gift, and ordered me to join the remaining signs.

The matter must be entrusted to such a patron: mercy stands nearer to the saints and the protection of favor lightens the offense of guilt.

There was no delay. The remedy, preceding the number of days by which hope has often deceived the ignorant when they counted them, was present through the aid of the one who prayed. True grace is not confined to any place, nor is the power God accumulates restricted by any limit. Healing touches wherever the Savior is present.

A little chamber far removed from the tomb received what the attentive mind had asked; and the request itself entered the place in which it had been entrusted at that moment.

The sick man, fearing death for his beloved wife, becomes a physician and urges faith by sending salvation. She too asks from her bed for whatever he had perceived.

There is a struggle to retain the aid and to seek what has been obtained. He fears to let go of what he possesses; she, convinced by the signs, hastens in faith to be saved as well.

[Col. 1074D] Both pray and both retain it in turn [sic], and the devotion clinging to one comes to the aid of both.

As long as breath governs these limbs, and mind and tongue sing, I shall give you thanks, holy one. Now, mercifully, look upon the rest of the household, bringing back the nourishment of swift healing, and, coming nearer, comfort the old age entrusted to you, quickly granting what is desired or preserving what has already been granted.

## ON THOSE WHO PRAY

You who, bent down to the ground, have sunk your face into the dust and pressed your moist eyes upon the unharmed earth, lift your eyes and receive miracles with trembling sight; entrust your cause to the excellent patron.

No page can contain such praises, even though these stones and masonry themselves are marked with such honors. An earthly work cannot enclose what the palace of heaven receives and what the stars inscribe with shining jewels.

If you seek Martin’s aid, rising beyond the stars, touch the heavens. Search the angelic assembly in the ether; seek there the patron joined to the Lord, following always in the footsteps of the eternal King.

If you doubt, behold the miracles placed before your eyes, by which the true Savior honors his servant’s merit. You will join the others as a witness among so many thousands, while you carefully see what must be told and recount what you have seen.

[Col. 1076A] Whatever the page has recorded in the books of the saints, God renews and restores through this gift. The blind, the lame, the needy, the mad, the anxious, the sick, the weak, the oppressed, the captive, the sorrowful, and the poor rejoice.

Every healing rejoices in apostolic signs. Whoever comes weeping returns joyful. All clouds yield; what troubles the merit, healing makes serene.

Seek protection: you do not knock at these thresholds in vain. Such lavish mercy will proceed throughout the entire world.

## AT THE END OF THE FIFTH CENTURY

## AMOENUS

## HANDBOOK OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT (G, S)*

## ON THE OLD TESTAMENT

### ADAM AND EVE

Eve was a dove, first white, then made black. Through the serpent’s ill-advised deceit she stained innocent Adam with filthy spots. The victorious dragon soon gives the naked pair fig-leaf coverings.

### ABEL AND CAIN

God, distinguishing the sacred offerings of the two brothers by his will, evaluates them, accepting the living and rejecting the earthly. The farmer, through envy, strikes down the shepherd. In Abel the form of the soul is expressed; in Cain, our flesh is offered.

### NOAH’S ARK

The dove brings to the ark, in its beak, a branch of green olive as a report that the receding flood has ended. The raven, captured by its gluttony amid foul corpses, had remained behind; the dove brings back the new joys of peace.

### THE OAK OF MAMRE

This is the Lord’s lodging: where the leafy oak of Mamre protected the old man’s pastoral roof, Sarah laughed in that hut at the late joy of offspring and at the possibility that her aged husband could still believe it.

### SARAH’S MONUMENT

Abraham purchases the field in which he may bury his wife’s bones, since justice and faith dwell as strangers upon earth. This is the cave purchased for so many thousands, where the holy ashes found rest.

### PHARAOH’S DREAM

Pharaoh saw in sleep twice seven ears of grain and the same number of cows. Their differing forms foretell seven years of abundance and seven years of famine to come. The patriarch explains this, with Christ as interpreter.

### JOSEPH RECOGNIZED BY HIS BROTHERS

The boy, sold through his brothers’ treachery, secretly orders a cup to be placed in his brother’s sack. When Joseph holds them guilty of theft, the false accusation is exposed; they recognize their brother and blush at their empty shame.

### THE FIRE IN THE BUSH

God, fiery, flashing from the burning bush, addresses the young man, then perhaps a shepherd of sheep. At his command Moses takes up his staff; the staff becomes a serpent. He loosens the bonds of his people’s feet and hastens to Pharaoh’s palace.

### THE JOURNEY THROUGH THE SEA

The righteous man travels safely, even across the great sea. Behold, for God’s servants, the Red Sea splits open, while the same waters drown the raging sinners. Pharaoh is overwhelmed, and a free path lies open for Moses.

### MOSES RECEIVES THE LAW

The summit of the mountain smokes with divine fires. There the written page of the Ten Words is handed to Moses on stone. Having received the law, he returns to his people. But the calf is their god, and gold their god.

### MANNA AND QUAIL

The tents of the fathers gleam white with angelic bread. The golden jar thereafter preserves the stored manna as a sure testimony. Another cloud comes upon the ungrateful and fills the greedy with piled-up quail.

### THE BRONZE SERPENT IN THE WILDERNESS

The dry road of the wilderness seethed with black serpents. Their poisonous bites were already consuming the people through livid wounds. But the prudent leader hung a polished bronze serpent upon a cross, so that it might restrain the serpent’s venom.

### THE BITTER POOL OF THE DESERT

The harsh pool, tasted by the thirsty people, held mournful waters in its stagnant bitterness. Holy Moses said: “Take wood and throw it into this pool; the bitter waters will be changed into sweet flavors.”

### THE TWELVE SPRINGS AND SEVENTY PALMS

The men came to the place, led by Moses, where there were six springs—and perhaps six others—which watered them with glasslike dew, and seventy palms. This is the mystical grove of Elim, which also represents the apostolic number in the books.

### TWELVE STONES IN THE JORDAN

The Jordan is said to carry them in its returning current while leaving dry for God’s people the fords they must cross. The twelve stones, set in the river itself by the fathers, are witnesses in the likeness of the disciples.

### RAHAB’S HOUSE

Jericho fell; only Rahab’s halls remained standing. The harlot, hostess to the saints, shows how great is the power of faith. Safe in her unharmed house, she offers a conspicuous slipper (*soccum*) amid hostile fires as a sign of blood.

### SAMSON’S LION

Samson, invincible through the strength of his hair, attacks and breaks the lion. He kills the beast, but honey flows from the lion’s mouth, and the jawbone of an ass freely pours forth a spring. Folly overflows in waters; virtue in sweetness.

### SAMSON’S FOXES

Samson captures three hundred foxes, arms them with fire, ties torches around their tails, and sends them into the fields. The foreigner’s crops burn. Such a clever fox now scatters the flames of heresy through the fields of vices.

### DAVID THE SHEPHERD

David was small, the youngest of his brothers, and, as Jesse’s servant, cared for the flock while tuning his harp beside his father’s fold. From there he went to the king’s pleasures; soon he joined terrible battles and struck down Goliath with his whistling sling.

### DAVID THE KING

The royal insignia of wondrous David shines: scepter, oil, horn, diadem, purple, and altar. All these belong to Christ: cloak and crown, rod of power, horn of the cross, altar, and olive oil.

### THE BUILDING OF THE TEMPLE

Wisdom builds the temple through Solomon’s service; the queen of the South heaps up heavy gold. The time comes when Christ builds the temple of the human heart, which barbarian Gaza enriches with its worshipers.

### THE SONS OF THE PROPHETS

While the sons of the prophets were cutting wood beside the river, an axe-head flew off and fell. The iron sank in the current, but wood thrown into the waters soon made the recoverable iron light again.

### THE CAPTIVITY OF ISRAEL

The Hebrew people, captured through repeated sin, wept their exile beside the rivers of dreadful Babylon. Then they refused the command to sing their ancestral songs and hung their bitter instruments upon the branches of the willow.

### THE HOUSE OF KING HEZEKIAH

Good Hezekiah deserved to extend the appointed day fifteen years and lengthen the term of his life by as many steps as the evening shadow had covered. The sun, flooded with light, taught that it was returning toward the east.

## ON THE NEW TESTAMENT

### GABRIEL AND MARY

As God approached, the messenger Gabriel descended from the Father’s high throne and suddenly entered the virgin’s dwelling. “The Holy Spirit,” he said, “will fill you, Mary; you will bear Christ, holy virgin.”

### THE CITY OF BETHLEHEM

Holy Bethlehem is the head of the world, for it brought forth Jesus, the beginning of the world and the very head of beginnings. The city gave birth to Christ as man, though Christ had acted as God before the sun existed and before the morning star.

### THE GIFTS OF THE MAGI

Here the Magi bring precious gifts to Christ, the child beneath the Virgin’s breast: myrrh, incense, and gold. The mother marvels at so many honors of her chaste womb, and that she has borne God, man, and the supreme king.

### THE ANGELS TO THE SHEPHERDS

An angelic force fills the wakeful eyes of the shepherds with light, celebrating Christ born of the Virgin. They find him lying in a shelter, wrapped in cloths; a manger served as his cradle. They rejoice eagerly and worship the divine power.

### THE MASSACRE OF THE INFANTS IN BETHLEHEM

The impious enemy Herod rages through the slaughter of countless infants while seeking Christ among them. The cradles smoke with the milk-white blood of the little ones, and the pious breasts of the mothers are wet with hot wounds.

### CHRIST IS BAPTIZED IN THE JORDAN

The Baptist, nourished on locusts and the honey of the woods and clothed in camel’s garment, immerses him in the river. He had baptized Christ, but the Spirit sent from heaven bears witness to the One baptized, who grants forgiveness of sins to those baptized.

### THE PINNACLE OF THE TEMPLE

The first surviving structure rises above the destruction of the old temple. Built of that stone, the stone rejected by the builders, it remains forever and ever. Now it is the head of the temple and the joining of the new stones.

### WINE MADE FROM WATER

They were celebrating the marriage covenant with the company gathered as witness. By chance the servants in Galilee had already run out of wine. Christ orders the water jars to be filled quickly with water; from them the flow of old wine is poured.

### THE POOL OF SILOAM

The water is a medicine for diseases, which the spirit of the mouth, exhaling through various means, pours forth according to a hidden design. It is called Siloam, where the Savior commanded the blind man’s eyes, gathered with spittle, to be washed in the spring.

### THE DEATH OF JOHN

The dancing girl, a virgin, asks as her funeral reward for John’s head. The severed head, which she carries back on a platter, is brought into the lap of her incestuous mother. The royal gift is borne by the dancer, her hands spattered with the blood of the just man.

### CHRIST WALKS UPON THE SEA

The Lord goes through the middle of the sea, treading the flowing waves with his foot, and commands the disciple to descend from the unstable boat. But mortal fear sinks his feet; Christ takes his hand and makes his steps firm.

### THE DEMON SENT INTO THE PIGS

The demon had broken the iron bonds of his prison beneath the tomb. He bursts out and throws himself at Jesus’ feet. But the Lord claims the man for himself and orders the enemy to drive the herd of pigs mad and plunge them into the waters.

### FIVE LOAVES AND TWO FISHES

God breaks five loaves and two fish and abundantly feeds five thousand people with them. Twelve baskets are filled with the smallest fragments of crumbs: such is the abundance of the eternal table.

### LAZARUS RAISED

The place in Bethany bears witness to the remarkable deed; it saw you, Lazarus, return from the seat of the dead. The tomb appears with its doors broken and torn apart, from which the limbs of the buried corpse returned.

### THE FIELD OF BLOOD

The field of Acheldemach, purchased with the price of atrocious crime, receives the funeral rites of the buried dead. This is the price of Christ’s blood. Unhappy Judas tightens his neck from afar with a noose, paying for such a crime.

### THE HOUSE OF CAIAPHAS

The lofty and impious house of Caiaphas fell through blasphemy, the house in which Christ’s sacred face was struck with slaps. This is the end awaiting sinners, whose life, crushed beneath ruined tombs, will lie forever.

### THE COLUMN TO WHICH CHRIST WAS SCOURGED

Bound, the Lord stood in these buildings, fastened to the columns, so that he might offer his back to the scourges. The venerable column still stands and bears the temple; it teaches us to live immune from every scourge.

### THE PASSION OF THE SAVIOR

Pierced through both sides, Christ pours out water and blood. The blood is victory; the water is a bath. Then two robbers, separated upon adjacent crosses, disagree: one denies God, the other receives the crown.

### CHRIST’S TOMB

The stone did not hold Christ, nor did the bars of the tomb. Death lies conquered beneath him; he has trampled the abyss.

[Col. 1080A] The people of the saints went together to the regions above and offered themselves to be examined by the touch and eyes of many.

### THE MOUNT OF OLIVES

From the summit of the olive-bearing mountain Christ rose upward and returned to the Father, marking the footprints of peace. From the everlasting leaves rich moisture flows, proving the gift of chrism poured into the earth.

### THE PASSION OF STEPHEN

Stephen, the first, receives the reward of blood, struck by a rain of stones. Though bloodied, he purchased Christ amid the twofold wickedness of his suffering.

Now act steadfastly; restore the honor of your virtue. Recall yourself, lest harmful things break your courage, lest glory perish or prosperity, slippery as it is, destroy you. Use your accustomed way; then relearn yourself as a teacher,

[Col. 1080B] with the courage of a strong athlete. Error does not overwhelm the saints.

This hand pursues the enemy more fiercely through suffering. A wound once fixed tends to arm manly minds; virtue, renewed by shame, grows from the wound, and victory is granted to the warrior through repeated wounds.

Thus the angel explains in brotherly address:

“So great is God’s care to snatch Martin from his fall.”

Afterward the innocent man no longer took part in the synod and gained new profits at the cost of his virtue.

## AN EGYPTIAN, INVOKING MARTIN’S GOD, ESCAPES THE DANGER OF A STORM (G, S)*

[Col. 1079C] When a certain sailor was crossing the Tyrrhenian Sea, bound for Rome, the violent force of the wind rose, impatient of the ship’s sailing flight. The waves leaped up and struck the hollow sails and ropes. The idle pine mast nodded; the ropes were torn away; the joined horns of the yardarm groaned softly.

Unskilled in the art, the stunned master sprang back from the ship’s deck. They stood helpless while the ship’s equipment fell and the roar of the sea pressed upon them. The prow drank water; while the sailor vomited, skill perished, experience lay useless, hope fled, anger oppressed them, daylight was snatched away, and death threatened amid doubtful circumstances as certain safety declined.

[Col. 1080C] While everyone trembled, one Egyptian said this—and he had also felt the gifts of Christ, though formerly without them:

“God of Martin, save us!”

Immediately the dreadful storm collapsed, and the high swelling of the sea sank to the depths. The wave lay flat around the ship; the surface of the liquid plain stood still, and the murmurs of the sea lay motionless in that place.

The ship travels across the desired waters, now friendly. The sails, given to favorable breezes, follow the line of the shore. As he seeks the harbor, the sailor fills the waters with his cry.

Thus Christ rightly grants honors to his servant according to his merits, whose faith, as it passes through the lands, fills the sea and stars.

## ACROSTIC ON LEONTIUS, BISHOP RESTORED TO THE BORDEAUX CHURCH (G, S)*

[Col. 1079D]

Let every age acknowledge  
the bishop Leontius,  
the reward of Bordeaux,  
restored by heavenly gift.

With a clever, forked tongue,  
he fostered envious crime,  
bringing a bitter report  
that this man had already been buried.

He could not endure to hide himself,  
he who had announced the sad funeral;  
and when he ceased to do harm,  
his insane life was exposed.

[Col. 1080D]

Deceived by harmful craft,  
he mourns crimes now annulled,  
while what he had thought grievous  
has been turned into joys.

He produced savage examples  
to be trampled upon for all time,  
so that he might already write for himself  
decrees against the living bishop.

This painted affair occurred,  
to be avoided by a chaste heart,  
so that he might presume, while the bishop survived,  
upon what scarcely failed after his death.

[Col. 1081A]

The priest disgraces his order  
who seeks the episcopate in this way.  
He who embraces the commands  
flees the ambition of honor.

If this office is owed to someone,  
let him ascend the rank under compulsion,  
not by cunningly seeking it himself,  
but by receiving it as Christ’s gift.

He is unfit who wishes  
to place himself before the Church.  
For the sacred office must be received  
through divine election.

The dear priest Hilary did not seek the office;  
Martin avoided it;  
Gregory scarcely endured it.

[Col. 1081B]

The laws reject ambition;  
every usurper is driven out.  
What civil courts reject,  
let the Church avoid as sacrilege.

The contests were wicked,  
though the struggle concerned not his own seat.  
What the upright mind does not wish to suffer,  
let it not inflict.

The matter does not remain  
in this murmur for long.  
While they are considering succession,  
the priest who had been there returns.

At the prayer of the people,  
when no one believes it, he is restored.  
These joys, which follow the sorrows,
are greater.

The city supported him with applause;  
happiness was restored to it.  
It had mourned the one of whom it had been deprived,  
and in anxiety received him back.

[Col. 1082A]

The man whom it scarcely thought restored,  
anticipated by a prosperous prayer,  
when the marvelous event is seen,  
sight itself is accustomed to marvel.

The shepherd gathers back the flock  
captured by the error of the path.  
Recognizing the shepherd’s citadel,  
the sheepfolds rejoiced.

He assumed the rank at the very time  
when he returned. On that day,  
who would not proclaim  
that this had occurred through heavenly favor?

The people had never before received  
so great a reward when he was made bishop  
as the joy they then felt  
when they received their prelate back.

[Col. 1082B]

Come, citizens, applaud,  
and add vows to vows.  
Since miracles have been performed here,  
may heavenly things preserve him.

May Christ, with serene light,  
hover around the man he restored,  
so that triple grace may increase:  
reward, life, and glory.

Let everyone who does not begrudge God  
resound deeply in song.  
His is the praise—he who restored  
the bishop from the mouth of death.

With a faithful heart zealous for truth,  
we are no longer ashamed to speak it.  
These small verses we give  
to the most noble Pope Leontius.

## AT THE SAME TIME

## SECUNDINUS THE IRISH BISHOP

## HYMN IN PRAISE OF SAINT PATRICK, STILL LIVING (S)

*(See this hymn in our Patrologia, volume LIII, column 837.)*
# As the Fourth Century Drew to a Close

[Note: According to Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 8 May, and Possevinus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, who believe that this Drepanius is the man mentioned by Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, Letter 11.—Ed.]

## IV

# Drepanius Florus

[Col. 1081]

## Notice

(From the Lyons Library of the Fathers)

[Col. 1081]

[Col. 1081D] Drepanius was a Gaul by birth, as we gather from his letters; he was called Florus, as appears from his letter to Moduinus, [Col. 1082D] the thirty-seventh bishop of the Aedui, who was the eleventh after Saint Syagrius the martyr, brother of Brunhild, queen of the Gauls, who lived in the age of Pope Gregory the Great, around the year of Christ 590. Since Magnus, or the Elder Theodosius, to whom Latinus Pacatus Drepanius delivered his panegyric at Rome, ruled around the year of Christ 390 and somewhat thereafter, it seems entirely clear that this poet, our Drepanius Florus, lived about two hundred and fifty years, [Col. 1084A] more or less, after Latinus Pacatus Drepanius, and therefore lived around the year of Christ 650. He himself testifies that he wrote hymns, in a letter to Wulfinus the grammarian:

> Once the finest voice of my cithara fell silent,
>
> and my friendly lyre pressed its sweet-toned melodies.

I cannot assert what else he wrote.

[Col. 1083]

# Psalms and Hymns of Drepanius Florus

[Col. 1083]

## Psalm XXII

[Col. 1083A]

[Col. 1083B]

My almighty Father governs me by his merciful law;

no cruel hunger, no want of any kind, will harm me.

Grassy hills and pleasant pastures are here;

clear springs and abundant rivers are here.

Nourished by these, always richly refreshed by these,

I shall strive to tread the straight paths of righteousness,

which the guide of my mind reveals to me by secret light,

so that his name may be celebrated with everlasting praise.

Following him in my heart, I shall trample fearlessly

the darkness of death and the realm of the grave;

I shall fear no evil:

for your chastisement, O pious King, corrects me with your rod,

and your staff, merciful Father, strengthens and guides me.

You have prepared delights for me, a table, and a feast;

satisfied by these, I shall gain unconquerable strength in my heart,

and in noble combat shall overcome the opposing ranks,

[Col. 1083C]

so that, after the fierce struggles of victorious battle,

my head may be sprinkled with the rich olive of joy,

and the light-bearing cup may wash me with a full draught.

Kept by your mercy through all my days,

may I deserve to ascend into Christ’s starry temple,

beneath which I may live happily through unending years.

## Psalm XXVI

God is my pure light; God is my living strength.

Therefore I shall fear neither darkness nor the laws of death.

With him as my guardian, my life is finally secured,
