so that no dreadful fear can disturb me in this place.

Rather, with powerful strength I shall despise all the enemies

who hasten to consume our flesh with evil.

Behold those who strike my heart with so great a storm:

their strength broken, they have perished in grievous ruin.

[Col. 1083D]

Whether, then, they sit in camp or attempt battle,

I shall put away fear from my heart and take up hope with my whole mind.

There is one thing I have earnestly asked of the Lord of heaven,

one thing I seek with the burning fervor of an ardent prayer:

that I may remain all my years beneath the walls of Christ,

always kindled by love for him,

and often behold the sacred thresholds of the eternal temple.

For here, when I was surrounded on every side by savage wars,

he hid me beneath his own canopy and, covered by sacred veils,

cherished me in a shadow most welcome.

Here he established me upon the mighty heights of a lofty rock,

and in his goodness raised me above savage enemies,

so that my head, set above them, might despise the conflicts below.

Therefore I shall go through the venerable courts of the sacred temple.

And, devoted to Christ at the altar, I shall render the offering of praise;

[Col. 1084A]

rejoicing, I shall sing melodies and songs:

[Col. 1084B]

O God, most merciful ruler of the heavenly kingdom,

open your saving ears to mournful cries,

and, in pity, look upon the groans I pour out.

My face desires you, my mind and heart pray to you;

I seek your sight and your face, merciful Father.

Do not withdraw your pious eyes or your holy countenance,

and do not, O Lord, abandon your servant when war presses upon him.

Rather, be merciful to me and a faithful protector;

do not abandon me, despised, to savage monsters.

For once my cruel parents left me;

but this good Lord revived me with tender mercy.

Show me the straight path through the tangled wilderness,

and grant that the splendid lamp of the law may shine,

so that, unaware, I do not encounter enemies armed with iron.

With you as my guide, I shall walk safely through hostile ranks;

[Col. 1084C]

for false-speaking witnesses have surrounded me on every side.

Yet their empty lies will harm no innocent man;

the lying tongue will bear its own guilt.

But I trust that, in the living homeland, I shall joyfully behold

the Lord’s abundant joys without end.

Wait for the merciful Lord with steadfast heart;

always fight manfully with weapons against adversity,

for the patient man will bear the illustrious blessings of the everlasting kingdom.

## Psalm XXVII

To you, creator of the heavens,

with the innermost pleading of my cry,

I direct my vow and prayer:

in your kindness, lend me your ear.

For if I bear a heart

unworthy of your utterances,

[Col. 1084D]

I am already like those

who are devoured in the pit.

Hear the anxious murmurs

of one who prays,

supreme Father,

while I raise my arms aloft

toward the lofty temples of heaven.

I beseech you, do not drag me down

with the wicked and criminal assemblies

into the lowest depths

of ravenous punishment.

They speak peace to their neighbor

with tongue and deceitful mouth,

but conceal a dreadful war

in their savage hearts.

Therefore, excellent judge,

[Col. 1085A]

repay them with equal favor:

bring crafty torments upon the cunning,

and cunning punishment upon the malicious.

May fitting vengeance punish

their hands for wicked deeds

and their life devoted to deceit;

may deceit bring down deceit,

and may their life collapse.

May the house smeared

with the cosmetics of the deceitful

fall forever.

May the mind that does not know God’s works

dread dense darkness.

Thanks to the ruler of the heavens,

who in his mercy has blessed

the prayers and tearful voice

of his suppliant servant with so great a gift.

[Col. 1085B]

He protects, helps, and raises up

the one who fights;

by his favoring power

I attain glorious triumphs.

Then, after harsh dangers,

the flesh, freed from pain,

will flourish and put on

the new beauty of salvation.

Therefore, with willing spirit,

I shall consecrate due praises

and sing sweet hymns

to this prince of my honor.

For here is the glorious strength,

the reward of the blessed people;

here he himself preserves

the flowing joys of salvation for Christ.

Save, excellent Creator,

the people redeemed by blood,

and enrich them with the rewards

of the glory of your inheritance.

With your powerful right hand

always govern and protect them;

raise them up with the highest blessings

through the ages of everlasting life.

# Hymn of Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael, the Three Holy Men

Let everything that the eternal Creator made through the Word

celebrate the Creator’s name and echo his praises;

let it exult in its parent through all the ages.

Angel hosts, bless your King,

[Col. 1085D]

and let the lofty voice of heaven resound together with you.

Let the waters that the lofty ether sustains sing to him;

let every power sing of him with holy love;

let the shining sun praise him with silver radiance;

let the moon, gleaming with icy light, praise him;

let the entire fire of the stars sing together for him.

Let abundant rain proclaim you,

and let the conflicting winds echo with harmonious voice.

Let the fairest flame speak of its creator,

and let the swift heat breathe forth the Lord’s name as well.

Let icy winter and scorching summer resound with this.

Let the dewy mildness of the weather, the seasons white with frost,

the fearful ice and the immense force of great cold,

and the ice turning the waters into monstrous crusts,

[Col. 1086A]

and the snows enclosing the earth in a dense fleece

sing their songs to God the Creator through the ages.

Let night, wrapping everything in sleep-bearing darkness,

and day, distinguishing its changing colors with light,

praise the flashing bolts that scorch mortal hearts,

and the clouds that enrich the earth with their abundant breast.

Earth, sower of life, established upon immense waters, praise you;

you also, mountains rejoicing in your lofty summit,

and hills looking upon the stars with humble necks,

let the airy forests resound with joyful murmur,

and let every offspring of the fertile earth celebrate you.

Then let the springs, tempering the heat with their cool drink,

and the seas, shaking the shores with dreadful waves,

and the river’s flowing course sing with sonorous cry.

Let the enormous sea-creatures, and everything that creeps in the waters, praise you;

[Col. 1086B]

let the sweet harmony of birds praise you in the fields.

Let the gentle and famous flock of cattle resound for you,

and let the savage might of raging beasts echo as well.

Let every race of human beings, powerful in mighty reason,

sing of him in countless tongues;

let the beloved people of the Israelites themselves

echo his praise to the Thunderer.

And you priests, whom the noble offspring of Aaron produced,

and you Levites born of sacred blood,

whom God willed to be ministers of his own temple,

render everlasting praises to the King on high.

Let spirits and souls summon him through the ages of the devout,

and let the holy and humble throng him with pure devotion.

Let holy Ananias raise him to the highest honor,

and let Azariah likewise proclaim him with reverent voice,

and let holy Mishael praise him with beautiful love,

[Col. 1086C]

who rescued them safely from the midst of the furnace’s whirlwind

and cherished them with the breath of the cooling wind,

when, surrounded by swift flames, they sang these songs,

and the fire, forgetting its power, did not harm the holy men.

A marvelous deed, never to be erased through any ages:

neither flesh, nor clothing, nor even a hair of their heads

felt the pitchy heat or the flame’s vapor.

Indeed, joyful and eager, at the tyrant’s own command,

they came forth into praise of the true God

and subdued profane mouths;

at their singing, astonished at the sight,

barbarian hearts trembled with immense terror.

Therefore let us too exult with continual praises

in this supreme and holy Father,

who established the heights of heaven with his Son,

and with the sacred breath, the powerful source of virtues.

[Col. 1086D]

You, Lord, the eternal axis of heaven proclaims;

the army of heaven praises you with its most holy voice;

the vast structure of all things glorifies you;

it exalts, fears, cries out, blesses, and adores you.

# Hymn to the Archangel Michael

Let the exalted festivals of the angelic day shine forth,

bringing blessed gifts to the devout soul.

For Michael, fosterling of the heavenly court,

consecrates this day for us with his conspicuous voice,

deigning to visit the seat of Peter and Paul,

and cherishing your dominion, famous Rome,

he shone among the leaders amid the pious walls,

with splendid face in a renewed world,

when God drew forth light after the shadows had been banished,

[Col. 1087A]

and established the steadfast day as night fell.

Here, beside the waters of the peaceful Jordan,

he revealed himself to the eminent prophet

as commander of the Lord’s armies,

when he stood in the sacred field with drawn sword

and overthrew the impious barriers with pious trumpets,

striking down seven nations with victorious thunder

and bringing mystical kingdoms as offerings to God.

Gabriel confesses that Michael alone brought him aid

in defending the pious camps of the heavenly God,

when he carried into the courts of heaven

the prayers which Daniel had poured forth with holy, unfed mouth.

The blessed Zachariah saw him with the eyes of his mind

among the myrtle trees, on a rose-red horse,

walking with snow-white feet toward the heavenly temples

and praying for the people with pious concern before God.

[Col. 1087B]

When four chariots rushed down from the double mountain,

snatched onward by horses of different colors,

while red, black, white, and varied steeds

traversed all the vast fields of earth,

they reported everything accomplished to God’s supreme minister

and hung upon the pious commands of their prince.

He, promising hope to the fallen and consolation to the sorrowful,

commands the prophet’s spirit to echo these words:

“The Lord will revisit Jerusalem with abundant mercy,

so that it may now be an eternal dwelling for God.

Such a multitude of human beings and flocks has filled it

that no circuit of walls can contain it.

But God will surround it with the protection of perpetual fire,

consuming its enemies and bringing light within.”

[Col. 1087C]

Here, at the end of time, when that ancient serpent

brings empty warfare against Christ God,

desiring to cut down the heavenly seat with weapons

and tear the holy people with savage tooth,

the heavenly host will rise in the full whirlwind of battle

and crush the impious camps with globes of flame.

Then Christ’s people will enjoy perfect peace

and forever sing their melody with angelic voice.

# On the Paschal Candle

Merciful God, whose law governs the heavens,

whose custody of the world causes the universe’s mechanism,

driven by perpetual motion, to revolve

according to eternal laws:

the heavens and whatever the golden vault of heaven covers,

the chorus of stars, the sun, and the monthly moon,

[Col. 1087D]

the rain-clouds and mists, and the winds that turn the seas,

the alternations of light and night, the four seasons

returning to themselves after their appointed courses;

the earth and whatever surrounds and covers the earth,

the straits, the rivers wandering along their curved banks,

the swift springs, the marshes commanded to stand,

the grazing flocks, and the birds allotted the heights,

the silent fish, and the poisonous serpents—

each in its own way trembles before you.

Come, supreme ruler of all things:

turn upon your servants the starry ranks of gently watching eyes,

and with serene face look upon the people

gathered for such mysteries,

who celebrate one God under a threefold name.

Not so do the Galli imitate the rites of Dindyma on Ida;

nor do Greek brides keep vigil at Attic Eleusis;

[Col. 1088A]

nor does Theban Cithaeron perform nocturnal orgies.

There is nothing frenzied in the noise,

nothing of incense and vapors,

nothing drenched in blood,

nothing immoderate in running.

This night is to be devoted to your sacred rites

only through pure prayer,

with simple vows and hands raised high.

We worship you and your Son, who watches over all things,

whom you, Father begetting by the Word, created as your companion.

When he left the fiery walls of lofty heaven

to see his own lands beneath the appearance of a human being,

an unmarried mother, pregnant yet untouched,

gave him to the world.

So that we may speak of him throughout the whole night,

we bring bright fires to the holy altars.

Fashioning wax—the house of honey—flows in a smooth circle

and encases the sea-like papyrus in countless coverings.

Now the whole company of worshipers

thins the blackening darkness with varied splendor,

makes the flaxen wicks abundant,

and kindles harmonious rivalry,

so that, while sacred mysteries are performed

according to pious ritual,

the competing torches may keep watch

with flames like those of the stars.

This undivided offspring of your Father,

shining with abundant light,

makes the night bright throughout every land;

the night is brighter than the clear day.

No nation beneath the snowy heavens

is so oppressed by cold

or by the harshness of everlasting winter

that it denies you, O Christ, radiant as flame.

Wherever the fiery sun drives across the globe,

wherever lies the second boundary of the setting day,

and wherever the first gate of returning light opens,

you are worshiped.

You will be worshiped while there is an end,

while the earth remains;

the heavens will turn, and the months of the year will turn,

but your honor, name, and praises will always be sung.

# Drepanius to Moduinus, Bishop of Autun: Exhortation to Read the Sacred Books

[Col. 1088C]

Father, I offer flowing thanks

from a joyful heart,

because you open gracious lips

to your Florus.

From them the sweetness of honey drips,

and an ambrosial liquor refreshes our hearts.

You had often heard the pious words

of the Lord who commands;

if you open your mouth, I shall satisfy it.

Thirsting, you drew heavenly breath

into your inward parts,

from which a sweet and nourishing fragrance

now breathes forth.

You drank the gentle waters from Jesus’ springs,

whence, O teacher, you richly refresh my thirst.

I pray that your heart may burn with divine flames,

which Christ sent to the fathers from heaven’s citadel,

[Col. 1088D]

when a violent breath suddenly sounded from heaven

and a red tongue of flame shone upon every head;

when two men’s hearts burned intensely,

and Christ wished to visit them midway,

revealing the mystical oracles of the sacred prophets,

and teaching that all had spoken with one voice.

Believe me, Father: my inward parts rejoice with abundant movement,

and, as my soul celebrates, my tongue can scarcely be silent,

because you deem me, though unworthy, worthy of so great a love,

and address me in poetry so pious and so sacred;

because it is not polluted by the waters of the Assyrian river,

nor fouled, troubled Nile, by your waters,

but instead flows clear from the river Jordan,

by which Christ’s beautiful field is gladdened.

Now let the sand of the Castalian spring dry up,

[Col. 1089A]

and let no pipe sound in the grove of Aonia.

Let the laurel of Apollo’s woodland finally wither,

and let the white privets fall with their berries.

May Christ’s victorious palms flourish forever,

the palms which the jubilant singing crowd gave him,

cutting peaceful branches from the olive’s crown

and spreading a sacred, shining garment along the road,

over which the young foal of a gentle she-ass

carried the Lord,

so that he might gently place his innocent feet upon it.

If we seek the life-giving water of a peaceful spring,

behold, the healing stream of Siloam is present for us,

which can remove natural darkness

and restore day to blind eyes.

If mountains and hills, and holy poets, delight us,

behold, the summit of Zion will offer sacred walls.

[Col. 1089B]

Thabor and Hermon exult in Christ’s praises;

Lebanon itself applauds with its lofty cedars.

Holy Carmel is powerful with Elijah’s lightning;

from its lofty summit it bears God’s holocausts.

Sina, also called by the twofold name Sinai and Horeb,

itself shows us the old man who gave the law,

his fiery eyes flashing beneath his horned face,

and carrying the heavenly laws upon sacred tablets.

Job first unfolds his heroic struggles in song;

David himself resounds upon his divine lyre.

How shall I speak of Solomon, swelling in the splendid buskin,

who sings of the bridal chambers of Christ and the Church?

Let these men, reverend Father, be followed with full love;

from them let all our thoughts and words flow.

Let the pious tongue sing and echo its own author;

let the devout mind celebrate its proper author.

Let the speech of Christ’s worshipers summon Christ

with faithful mouth.

This is worthy, this is just;

this is sweet, wholesome, and pious.

# Drepanius to a Friend: Thanksgiving for Undertaking His Defense

O how sweet a fragrance leaps forth

from the chamber of your heart,

O brother mighty in the love of Christ.

The senses are soothed, the entire inward being is soothed;

a heavenly power delights every mind.

Not so does the vine blaze beneath the springtime star

when the jeweled glory emerges from its joyful branch;

nor does the fresh grace of the fields smell so sweet

when it pours forth white lilies mixed with crimson roses.

Even the gifts of the flowering forest are surpassed by this,

[Col. 1089D]

and the fragrance of every fruit is overcome.

You love equally when present and when absent,

and cunning deceit does not alter your chaste mind,

whether the others are enemies or dear companions without stain.

Your heart nurtures us; your tongue sings for us.

To the former you return gratitude;

the latter you refute by reason.

One love fights with different weapons,

and because truthful affection is victorious,

it will always bear bright trophies forever.

Only one blackened by hatred, and malign in wishes and deeds,

is rightly overtaken by ruin in a headlong storm.

But sincere love shines like eternal light;

it does not yield to darkness,

but drives away the darkness.

What is more, you often send words of saving goodness,

and burden us, both here and at home, with many gifts.

This is true love; this is pure affection;

this is everywhere the pious gift of the Father and of Christ.

The Spirit flowing from heavenly seats

spreads such gifts through chaste minds.

Now it pleases me to repeat the words of the ancient old man,

who, though deprived of sight, was serene in mind and said:

“So now my son smells to me like renowned fields,

whose gifts are known to be blessed by God.

May the Almighty give you from heaven’s wholesome dew

and from rich fields abundant gifts:

namely, choice heaps of grain,

overflowing oil, and exceedingly fine wines.”

With these words I gladly repay you, dear patron,

with perpetual thanks and benevolent prayers as well.

For it is fitting, and returns entirely by a beautiful reasoning,

that divine gifts should be sung in divine words.

May you be happy, preserving the love you have begun through the ages,

and may you always be an accepted friend of the lofty God.

# Drepanius to Wulfinus, Grammarian of Orléans: An Exhortation to Write Back

A year has passed as the revolving months complete their circuit.

Your voice sounded in our ears,

adorned on such polished pages,

with such clear figures,

that the beautiful page offered a likeness of your heart.

Thus a well pours out clear waters in abundance,

and swift heat leaps rapidly from fire.

Thus a glowing carbuncle vomits glowing fire,

[Col. 1090C]

and the hard, pure cup bears lovely wines.

From the beautiful crown of the olive,

beautiful fruit too is plucked,

and from it an even more beautiful liquid flows.

But envious fortune has stolen my honey-sweet song

and an unjust hand has broken the sweet cup.

It is as if someone should take cold cups away from a thirsty man,

or snatch pleasant food from a hungry mouth.

In place of grief has come what I often feared,

and that fear of mine is now plainly shown by events.

Once the finest voice of my cithara fell silent,

and my friendly lyre pressed its sweet-toned melodies.

What are you doing, brother, maintaining such a long silence?

Or why has your love for us been so quickly driven away?

Certainly your Muse’s flourishing songs were so great

that they needed no small delay to reveal themselves.

[Col. 1090D]

Yet your power has scarcely shaken out the verses it completed,

while you command the winged letters to fly back in this way.

Therefore be faithful to your undertaking:

write, and ask for written replies.

For sweet love commonly grows in this way.

Speech binds minds; speech caresses hearts;

it joins the absent and reconciles those torn apart.

Thus the beautiful mind of David clung to Jonathan,

and could not be cast down even by the father’s terrible threats.

For prudent speech burns like glowing amber

and seizes modest hearts with its own touch.

Bring forth, I beg you, the songs customary to your honeyed throat,

and, sweet friend, relieve our thirst.

# Anonymous Author

[Col. 1091]

## Poem on the Praises of the Lord

(C, G, S)

[Col. 1091]

[Col. 1091A]

Who complains of being helped only late by the gift of virtue?

Who complains that God’s promises advance with a slow step?

Who measures the judge’s urn by human limits

and thinks that the ages owe haste

to the day when he will repay merits with rewards?

Noble glory bears witness through a mighty deed.

For where the slow Saône glides along with sluggish current

past its stagnant banks,

and the Diuvix unfolds its lazy stream,

where the youth of the Aedui is born from the Rhine of brothers,

I remember a marriage joined in supreme devotion and fidelity.

Yet divine law increased the reward of love.

There was one vow for both:

to precede the companion in death

and entrust the care of the tomb to pious grief.

But the decree of fate read the wife first.

Then the anxious husband ordered, with generous words,

that stones be hollowed out after death,

[Col. 1091B]

so that, coming to receive them, you might join eternal covenants—

thus [sic] the same little bed that had held them while alive

might, in accordance with God’s commands,

raise their common tomb.

The wife perceived the prophetic vows of her husband

and granted great miracles to chaste times.

For when arms are joined to the limbs of the dead,

and a returning hand binds its bonds to the trunk,

lest what fulfills the duties of human life

should suffer some shapeless dissociation when separated,

a marvel beyond words occurred.

When life had been completed,

the husband had foreseen that he would be joined to his companion

in the appointed place.

After the husband’s death had opened the joyful gate,

and unwelcome daylight had uncovered the dreadful dwelling,

the woman was found extending her left hand,

[Col. 1091C]

inviting her companion with the gesture of living love.

Who gave affection to the tomb?

Who loosed the bonds?

From where did she see the shadow of her future husband buried there?

You do these things, Christ God; your signs are at work,

and little by little you teach sleeping limbs to rise again—

you whom the holy prophets sang as one who would come.

Undecaying offspring of God,

ruler of the Ruler,

without whom the Father undertakes nothing great or mighty:

at whose command the sea stood within fixed shores,

and the boundless deep is not permitted to run over the lands;

the level shores enclose the mountain waves.

You endowed the steadfast earth with varied gifts,

for our use, generous in fatherly mercy.

To you mortals entrust their seeds to the furrows,

and a new offspring rises from the dry turf.

[Col. 1091D]

You command the vines to flow with fertile nectar;

from the trees you draw juices pleasing for human feasts

and healing for health;

you force sweet honey to emerge.

You command every kind of living creature to serve mankind;

you also bend the groves beneath heavy fruits,

and cause new growths to arise from no seed.

[Col. 1092A]

You make varied rivers useful for our labor

and renew the age blessed by sacred springs.

Under your guidance the seas opened to sailing beaks,

and the sailor explored harbors divided by straits.

After you had set the elements in their fixed forms,

lest the heavenly mechanism should begin to languish

with a raw and undistinguished appearance,

you marked the world with varied gifts.

Whatever shines in heaven, your right hand fashioned.

With these signs you were pleased to weave the Lord’s palace.

Now, lest the seas lie barren and inhospitable to every land,

and lest the eager sailor lack a harbor to receive him,

many islands are fixed in sufficient number

in the swelling ocean.

Yet, surrounded by the raging waves,

an island does not fear them;

resting upon its little circle amid the straits,

it withstands them,

confident under your guidance,

whose venerable covenant

equalizes the highest and the lowest

by an equal law

and does not permit those set in place

to overstep their boundaries anywhere.

[Col. 1092B]

And lest the earth lie too flat or bare,

you commanded hills to rise,

fit for vines,

and great groves to spread their abundant shade.

Then, lest vast terror prevail through motionless forests,

you add countless offspring to the lofty woods:

so that the forest might have inhabitants,

and the hunter might not lack prey;

so that many birds and a thousand swarms of voices

might resound in the woods with mortal harmony.

Thus you were pleased to weave the year with varied forms

and to add fruit to mortals in pleasant alternation.

Lest the prolonged day always burn the world too fiercely,

or the short day snatch an unseasoned fire from those being born,

and lest unceasing labor shake everything with perpetual effort,

[Col. 1092C]

the dewy night gives rest to weary human cares.

And so that human well-being might lead a secure life,

health-giving herbs rise spontaneously from the turf.

The Father himself sows these by his nod,

rich without the plow.

Even if I were enclosed in an iron wall,

and had an iron voice and a thousand tongues

with which to sing,

I could not recount all the gifts of your mercy.

But that Father of yours, placed in a secret dwelling,

not easily seen by anyone and dreaded by all,

sent you as lord of the earth and master of life.

And whoever venerates the Son with fitting honor

should offer his vows to both

and pray for everlasting life.

You, steadfast in chastity and righteousness,

are ready to bend the laws after sin,

if reckless folly has driven anyone

from the boundary of life prescribed by you both.

Your Father clothed you in human form

and in frail limbs,

so that our mouths might endure to behold you.

[Col. 1092D]

For who would attempt to raise fragile eyes

if he wished to set you upon the trembling earth

as you are when, with mighty right hand,

you hurl the thunderbolts,

and especially when you command

that the appointed punishment be feared;

[Col. 1093A]

or when, appeased, you divide rain over thirsty fields

and draw uncertain ears of grain through the furrows?

Yet, lest no event display your distinguished birth,

you were conceived by a virgin;

it is not enough that she be merely chaste.

Nor could one who was married unite a brother to the Lord,

lest any shameful contagion be far removed from the womb.

As soon as blessed age ripened through its course,

you undertook to preserve unteachable minds

by paternal warnings,

and offered a straight path to those who were falling.

And so that the commands sent by God

might be completely clear,

you took authority away from death,

and, once disease had been released,

commanded the desperate to take up the duties of life.

You restored the day to the blind,

and, so that nothing should remain entirely unattempted

by which perfidious error might perish,

you announced understanding to the tombs

and commanded limbs long buried

[Col. 1093B]

to rise again into the upper air.

The beloved corpses recognized their own names.

But after the suitable follower had received the law,

so that the heavenly spirit might strip itself

of the mortal dwelling,

and so that, intent upon the law,

you might teach all things

to be endured for the supreme God,

and that each person should rightly take up everlasting life

through contempt of death,

you returned, bearing out the commands of your Father,

[Col. 1094A]

to the secrets of the highest heaven,

where the shining ether prevents sluggish clouds

from setting fire to their own sky.

And so that the appointed provision might exist

for the perishing crowd

that shuts its ears against the commands of the merciful God,

and so that new laws might no longer hold the dead:

free us from the deadly prison of hell,

and command the innumerable people

to rise from the darkness,

except only those shut in

whom impious life has marked.

You divide the places of punishment

among the souls to come—

those who will not believe you

or who pretend to believe.

Holy God, venerable pledge of the supreme God,

at whose name souls, driven away by violent death,

cry out and grow pale,

having entered their own bodies and those of others,

and are ordered to withdraw,

as many miracles previously performed by you reveal,

[Col. 1094B]

when they are held suspended between earth and heaven,

because through you nothing is permitted to the enemy

while he is restrained.

But now make Constantine for me

a victorious lord, distinguished by merits,

a father in mercy,

gentle in authority,

a teacher by the law of life,

and equal to the decrees sanctioned by the law established for you.

You have given nothing better than this offspring to the world before,

nor will you give anything better afterward.

May his children equal their father.

## List of the Manuscripts Used to Establish the Text of Saint Paulinus’s Works

[Col. 1099]

### Manuscript Codices

**BARTH.**—A Belgian codex collated by Barthius, containing poems 18 and 20 of Saint Paulinus.

**BELG.**—Another Belgian codex of Saint Paulinus’s letters and poems, collated by Cauchy.

**BIG.**—Two codices from the Bigot library, six hundred years old, containing nine letters of Saint Paulinus to Saint Augustine and letters of Saint Augustine to Saint Paulinus. Another Bigot codex, seven hundred years old, contains Saint Paulinus’s Letter 4 to Augustine and Augustine’s reply to Paulinus.

**CLUN.**—The Cluniac codex, containing Letters 40, 41, and 51.

**C. ROT.**—A lectionary codex of the Cathedral Church of Rouen, containing the middle portion of Letter 18 to Victricius, bishop of Rouen.

**GERM.**—Two very ancient codices, nine hundred years old, of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, written in Saxon letters. They contain ten poems on Saint Felix and the *Ode to Nicetas*, from which many corrupt and mutilated passages are corrected and restored. Another codex of the same abbey, eight hundred years old, contains the exhortatory poem addressed to his wife.

**JOL.**—A codex five hundred years old belonging to Claude Joly, precentor of the Church of Paris, containing the exhortatory poem addressed to his wife. Another, three hundred years old, contains the letters to Marcella and Celantia.

**LUGD.**—The Lyon codex, collated by Vinet, containing Ausonius’s poems to Saint Paulinus and Saint Paulinus’s poems to Ausonius.

**MARIANG.**—The codex of Mariangelo Accursius, containing poem 25 of Ausonius to Saint Paulinus.

**M. ROTUND.**—A lectionary codex of the collegiate church of Saint Mary of the Rotunda at Rouen, containing the middle portion of Letter 18 to Victricius, bishop of Rouen.

**NOL.**—The Nolan codex, containing Letters 40 and 41.

**POELM.**—The codex of Poelmann, containing Ausonius’s poems to Saint Paulinus.

**REG.**—An eight-hundred-year-old codex of the Royal Library containing Saint Paulinus’s letters and poems and Ausonius’s poems to Saint Paulinus.

**VAT.**—A Vatican codex of Saint Paulinus’s letters. Two others contain Letters 25 and 26. Four more contain Letters 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 50.

**VICT.**—Two three-hundred-year-old codices of Saint-Victor in Paris, containing Letters 25 and 26 and two letters to Marcella and Celantia. Two other three-hundred-year-old codices of the same abbey contain the exhortatory poem addressed to his wife.

**VIEN.**—A Vienna codex of Saint Paulinus’s letters, of excellent quality.

[Col. 1100] **VOSS.**—The Vossian codex in England, containing Ausonius’s poem 24 to Saint Paulinus and Saint Paulinus’s poem 10 to Ausonius.

### Printed Editions

**BAD.**—The first edition of the works of Saint Paulinus of Nola, by Badius Ascensius, printed at Paris in 1516.

**BARTH.**—Barthius’s *Emendations and Illustrations from Sixty Books of Adversarial Commentaries*. Frankfurt, 1648.

**BENED.**—The book of the Letters of Saint Augustine prepared by the Benedictine Fathers, containing Saint Paulinus’s Letters 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 45, and 50 to Saint Augustine, and Saint Augustine’s Letters 27, 31, 95, and 149 to Saint Paulinus. Paris, 1679.

**B. ROT.**—The Rouen Breviary, folio edition, 1491, containing the middle portion of Letter 18 to Victricius.

**CHIFFL.**—*Paulinus Illustrated*, prepared by Chifflet, Dijon, 1662, containing Letters 13, 33, 34, 40, 42, and 51.

**ERASM.**—The book of Saint Jerome’s Letters, revised by Erasmus, containing Saint Paulinus’s Letters 25 and 26 and two letters to Marcella and Celantia. Lyon, at the press of Gryphius, 1530.

**GRAV.**—The works of Saint Paulinus of Nola, prepared by Gravius. Cologne, at the press of Maternus Cholinus, 1560.

**GRIN.**—Grinaeus’s works of Saint Paulinus of Nola, volume I of the *Orthodoxographi*. Basel, 1569.

**LATIN.**—Observations and Corrections on the Works of Saint Paulinus of Nola, Bishop, by Latinius of Viterbo. Rome.

**LUGD.**—The Lyon edition of Saint Paulinus’s poems to Ausonius and Ausonius’s poems to Saint Paulinus, at the press of the heirs of Hugo a Porta, 1603.

**M. VICT.**—The book of Saint Jerome’s Letters, prepared by Marianus Victor, containing the letter to Celantia. Paris, 1600.

**MOG.**—The Mainz edition of Saint Jerome’s letters, containing Letters 25 and the letter to Marcella, 1470.

**POELM.**—Two works prepared by Poelmann: one of the poems of Saint Paulinus of Nola, Antwerp, at the press of Christopher Plantin, 1560; the other of Ausonius’s poems to Saint Paulinus, 1568.

**PONC.**—The book of Saint Jerome’s Letters, printed by Poncet le Preux, containing Saint Paulinus’s Letters 25 and 26 and two letters to Marcella and Celantia. Paris, 1512.

**ROM.**—The book of Saint Jerome’s Letters, containing Saint Paulinus’s Letters 25 and 26 and two letters to Marcella and Celantia. Rome, 1468.

**ROSV.**—The works of Saint Paulinus of Nola, with notes, prepared by Rosweyde. Antwerp, 1622.

**SACCH.**—Notes and corrections on the works of Saint Paulinus of Nola by Sacchini, S.J., at the end of Rosweyde’s edition. Antwerp, 1622.

[Col. 1101] **SCHOT.**—The works of Saint Paulinus of Nola, prepared by Schott, volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume I. Cologne, 1618.

**TOLL.**—The works of Ausonius, prepared by Tollius, from which his poems to Paulinus are taken. Amsterdam, 1671.

[Col. 1102] **VINET.**—The book of Ausonius’s letters to Saint Paulinus and Saint Paulinus’s letters to Ausonius, with annotations, prepared by Vinet. Bordeaux, at the press of Simon Millanges, 1575.

[Col. 1101]

## Index of Words with Unusual Meanings

[Col. 1103]

### A

**Abigere**, used for *rapere*, “to seize.” P. 390.

**Abraham**, with the second syllable lengthened. P. 616, 630, 682.

**Abscidere**, for *abscindere*, “to cut off.” E. 4, 48, 53.

**Abscisio**, “cutting off.” E. 122.

**Abscisus**, “cut off.” E. 123.

**Abuti**, for “not to use.” E. 62, 224, 285, 310. A. 717.

**Abysus**, with the second syllable shortened, for *abyssus*, “abyss.” P. 661.

**Accubitus**, that is, a table or reclining couch. E. 72.

**Aerial princes**, enemies, the same as demons. E. 156. P. 389.

**Aeternum**, for “forever.” P. 606, 686.

**Agitare**, for “to do frequently.” P. 368.

**Amalec**, with the second syllable lengthened. P. 611.

**Ambitio**, in place of *ambitus*, “circuit” or “extent.” A. 727.

**Ambitus**, for pomp and honor. E. 193.

**Amnis**, for *cantharus*, “basin.” E. 205.

**Amplum**, that is, breadth or amplitude. P. 665.

## Index of Notable Persons and Things

[Col. 1107]

E. designates Letters; P., Poems; A., Appendix; V., Life and following sections.

**Alpha and Omega**, Christ. P. 661; A. 949, 940. In imperial numerals, A. 950. On tombs, ibid. Heretics abused them, ibid.

The letter **A**, woven from three strokes, signifies the mystery of the Trinity. P. 484.

**Abel**, slain, a type of Christ. E. 229. After he was taken away, Seth was substituted for him in the holy lineage. E. 59.

**Abella**, a city of Campania. P. 544. Praised by Paulinus, ibid. Tomb of a certain saint, ibid. Praised by Paulinus, P. 548.

Self-denial is preferable to abandoning all external things. E. 247.

**Abraham**, a rich and perfect patriarch. E. 149. As a pilgrim, a type of Christ. E. 229. By overcoming four kings with three hundred servants, he mystically signified the victory that the Christian is to win over four enemies. E. 162; A. 897. He receives angels as guests and washes their feet. E. 144. How pleasing his blind obedience was to God. E. 181. How he became God’s friend. E. 77, 78. Why he mourned his wife Sarah. E. 67. What he indicated to us by buying a field for his burial. E. 68.

**Absalom**, or Abessalom, weighed down by the hair of his head, signifying the burden of sins. E. 129. Why his father mourned him after his death. E. 69.

**Apse**, the larger conch of an altar. E. 202; A. 906. Apses and conches, the same, ibid. Various kinds in churches, A. 906.

**Abstinence** is an aid, not the perfection of holiness. A. 739. What sort is commended, A. ibid. It assists all virtues. A. 740.

**Abuti**, that is, to consume by not using. E. 64; A. 879; V. 191.

Acceptance of persons is prohibited by the Catholic religion. A. 739.

The **evangelical needle**, faith and the word of the cross. E. 176.

**Adam**: whether he was deceived. P. 332; A. 929. By sinning he lost the likeness of God, not the image. E. 156; A. 896. His sin closed the eyes of the mind to innocence and opened them to iniquity. E. 186.

**The second Adam**, Christ. P. 672.

To cleave to God through love is a work of great labor. E. 154.

**Church doorkeepers** are *aeditui*, whose order is most ancient in the Church. P. 474.

The innumerable gods of the Egyptians. P. 454. Their particular deity was Jupiter Ammon. P. 451. Their superstition in the rites of Isis. P. 455 and following.

**Adonis** is Thammuz. E. 190; A. 903. Bethlehem was profaned by the emperor Hadrian through his shrine, E. ibid.

**To adore**, in Scripture and among the Fathers, means the same as “to honor.” P. 628, 664; A. 944.

**Hadrian, emperor**; see **Hadrianus**.

Why adversities often befall human beings. E. 91.

[Col. 1108] The vice of flattery disguises itself under the name of humility and benevolence. A. 776.

The flatteries of flatterers are harmful to those striving along the path of virtue and must therefore be avoided, ibid.

The building of the spiritual temple in the soul is eloquently commended by Paulinus. E. 211, 212.

**Aemilius**, bishop. P. 607. Father of Ia, the wife of Julianus, P. ibid. How Paulinus calls him the father and brother of Memoris, ibid.

**Aequiparet**, “is equal to” or “is comparable with.” A. 924.

Of **Aeschinus** it is said, “He hears, ‘I send’”: a proverb. E. 37; A. 877.

Youth should be an occasion for no one to delay conversion to God. E. 165.

The benefit of affliction. A. 717.

African bishops greet Paulinus by letters and by clerics sent by them. E. 25; A. 873.

**Agabus** foretold the impending famine and the passion of the Apostle Paul. E. 291.

The use of **agapae** among the ancient Christians. P. 502.

How the field of our heart is to be cultivated. E. 236, 237.

**Agilis**, bearer of Paulinus’s letters to Augustine. E. 32.

**Aginnum**, a city not far from Bordeaux and the Santones. P. 354.

**Driver of Israel**, God. P. 596; A. 942.

**Lambs**, the newly baptized. A. 908. The faithful, ibid. Lambs and kids, a hieroglyphic of the righteous and the reprobate. E. 206, 207.

The **paschal lamb** in the ancient law, a type of Christ. P. 610. Likewise in paintings. E. 203, 207; A. 908. It emits five streams, signifying the five wounds of Christ, ibid.

**Heavenly farmer**, God the Father. E. 236.

The relics of the martyr **Agricola** were placed in the Basilica of Saint Felix. P. 638.

When **Alaric** destroyed Rome. P. 440.

**Alethius**, brother of Florentius, bishop of Cahors. E. 212; V. 121, 156. A presbyter. V. 121. Praised by Jerome as a most learned man, ibid. By Paulinus regarded as a guardian of faith and religion. E. 276; V. 85. Bishop of Cahors. E. 212, 276; A. 918. His letters wonderfully refresh Paulinus. E. 212.

**Alfia**, or Appia, sister of Philemon. P. 509, 515.

**Alinganiensis**, a village. A. 887.

**Alingonum**, a town belonging to Paulinus. E. 65, 107; A. 887, 888; V. 3. There, at his expense, Delphinus built a church. E. 107; V. 54, 65. Its clerics were called Alingonenses. E. 65; V. 54.

Flying with wings in the form of a cross. P. 599; A. 943.

**Allophyla**, the woman who deceived Samson; mystically, the poem signifies … P. 585.

[Col. 1109] The altar was formerly unique in churches, A. 906. Altars and temples were already adorned with veils on the solemn festivals of the saints, P. 382, A. 931, 932. The *trichora*, E. 202, A. 906, 907. Let no one approach the sacred altars inflamed with the fire of bodily desire, E. 262. The relics of the saints were enclosed in them, P. 637 ff., A. 905.

Altars were formerly furnished with the relics of martyrs, P. 471.

Altars were formerly closed off by a veil, P. 485.

Altars were adorned with crosses according to ancient custom, P. 485.

In the earlier periods of the Church there were several altars in the churches, not merely one, P. 471.

**ALYPIUS**, converted to the faith by Ambrose and ordained to the priesthood, E. 11, 12, V. 8. Most closely united with Paulinus in charity, E. 9, 10, 11. He shares with Paulinus the five books of St. Augustine against the Manichaeans, E. 10, 11. He writes him a letter, E. 35, 36. He receives from him the *Chronicle* of Eusebius of Caesarea, E. 10, 11. Paulinus asks him to send him the history of his life, E. 10. Augustine writes this and sends it to Paulinus, E. 19.

Amalek, the blinder of the waters, P. 644, A. 947. His being killed signifies sins that must be killed, P. 589. His defeat shows what prayers can accomplish with God, P. 611.

Haman, hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai, declares what prayers can accomplish with God, P. 611.

**AMANDA**, wife of Aper, E. 234, 257, A. 920, V. 132. She frees her husband from domestic cares and civil affairs, E. 259 ff., V. 132. She professes continence, E. 234, 259 ff., V. 131. She is greatly praised by Paulinus, ibid.

**AMANDUS**, presbyter of Bordeaux, E. 7, V. 10. Serving Christ from childhood, E. 64. And nourished on the sacred Scriptures, ibid. Preserver of baptismal innocence, ibid. How gracious he is in writing letters, E. 220. St. Paulinus’s catechist and sponsor, E. 9, 45, V. 10. Delphinus’s successor in the episcopate of Bordeaux, E. 7, 276. Guardian of faith and religion, E. 276, V. 85.

**AMANDUS**, another person to whom Paulinus writes, F. 239, 248, V. 45, 46. He receives letters from Paulinus, E. 238, 248, V. 45, 46. Paulinus commends himself to his prayers, E. 139.

Ambition must be avoided, E. 39.

**AMBROSE** is elected bishop by the people, V. 31, 131. He baptizes Alypius at Milan, E. 12, V. 8. And ordains him priest, E. ibid. He invites Paulinus to the faith, E. ibid., V. 8. He receives him at Florence with great affection and honor, E. 1, V. 30. He wishes the man initiated into the priesthood to be enrolled among his clergy, E. 12, V. 8, 30. He loves him exceedingly, E. ibid. He is asked to write against certain persons who claimed that Christ had learned from Plato’s books, E. 35. He discovers the bodies of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, E. 207. Likewise that of St. Nazarius the martyr, P. 638, V. 53, whose relics he sends to Paulinus, ibid. He designates Simplicianus as his successor in the see, V. 30. He rests in Italy, P. 661.

**AMBROSE**, another, bearer of Paulinus’s little gift and letters to Jerome, A. 770, V. 43.

The praises of Ambrose, pastor of Milan, P. 459. At what time he delivered the speech on Basil, ibid. When, being harassed by the empress Justina, he restrained her fury by a miracle, P. 468. He was likewise the discoverer of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, P. 468.

Amen. What the use of this word was in the primitive Church, P. 449.

How fragile human friendship based on intimacy is, E. 138. Christ’s friendship is strong as death, ibid. Carnal friendship affords no rest to the soul, E. 165. Spiritual friendship, unlike secular friendship, is not to be measured by time, E. 66. It begins from fullness, having arisen through Christ, ibid.

A good friend is medicine for the heart, E. 96.

Ammon: Jupiter, the particular divinity of the Egyptians, P. 451.

A river troubling the basilica of St. Felix was diverted elsewhere through his merits, P. 622.

Self-love is an unlawful affection, E. 217. The self-love of those who seek to please without Christ must be feared, E. 228, 229. It is worshiped by the pagans as a god in an image, E. 87.

The Ana, a notable river of Spain, passing through Mérida, P. 354.

**ANASTASIUS**, pope, most devoted to Paulinus, E. 106. He invites him to his birthday celebration, E. ibid., A. 886, 887, V. 57, 63. He commends him to the bishops of Campania, ibid. He kindly receives him when he comes to Rome, E. 106.

**ANDREW**, the apostle, suffered martyrdom at Patras, P. 637. He was buried there, P. 659. Constantine transferred him to Constantinople, P. ibid. His relics are preserved in the basilica of St. Felix, P. 637. Likewise in the basilica built by Paulinus at Fundi, E. 207.

Andrew completed his martyrdom at Patras, P. 450. He was likewise buried at Patras in Achaia, P. 451. The bodies of Andrew and Timothy were transferred to the city of Constantinople, P. 468. His relics, together with the bones of Luke, were transferred from Achaia to Constantinople, P. 451.

[Col. 1110] Angels steer a ship, E. 278. Whether they have bodies or a tongue.

An angel, in one night, E. 180, strikes down thousands of Assyrians from the camp of Sennacherib, P. 614. He announces to Zechariah the conception and birth of St. John the Baptist, gives him his name, and unfolds the whole course of his life, P. 339 ff. He announces Christ to Mary, P. 339. He frees St. Felix from chains and prison, P. 396.

The Anician family, V. 1, 2.

The soul ought to be virginal and second—how this is so, E. 248. Adorned with virtues, it is a most pleasing dwelling-place for God, A. 737. Its care must not be placed below that of the body, E. 167. It must not be subordinated to the household, A. 739. How we ought to lose it, E. 117, 247. Paulinus aptly applies to its passions Joel’s words about the caterpillar, locust, grub, and blight, E. 236 ff. Bodily expansion kills its sobriety, E. 291. Its remedies are afflictions of the body, A. 725. Its garment is fasting, by which we abstain from everything forbidden, E. 176. Its life is the virtue of God; its death is the covering over of virtue, E. 169. Death is friendly to the life of this world, E. 62. By what blindness it is illumined, E. 131, 132. It is weighed down by sins, E. 131. Through mortification of the limbs it is raised to heavenly things, E. 61. Even after death it remembers deeds performed in life, P. 578. It will be restored to the body at the resurrection, P. 428, 429. It is immortal, P. 428. How it dies eternally among the dead, E. 247. Paulinus commends the soul of his deceased brother to the prayers of Delphinus and Amandus, E. 219, 220.

Which souls are called “black fir trees” and “good,” E. 134. The poor are patrons of our souls, E. 72. The souls of the dead are aided by the good works and prayers of the living, E. 67, 72, 76, 80, 219, 220.

The union of souls is more important than the union of bodies, E. 105.

The mind should be cultivated like a field, E. 234, 235.

Anna, the mother of Samuel, is compared with Melania, E. 181. Marcella is compared with Anna the widow, A. 727.

In what design Christians’ rings should be engraved, A. 909, 910.

The ring of Polycrates, bearing a lyre in its setting, A. 910.

The bones of St. Luke the Evangelist preserved at Antioch, P. 658, A. 949.

**APER**, to whom Paulinus writes, E. 227, 234, 258. He passes from the forum and tribunal to Christ, E. 228, 233, V. 130, 131. Paulinus fortifies him against the persecutions of the world, V. 232, 233, V. 133, 134. He is advanced from the people to the priesthood, E. 233, V. 131. He withdraws into solitude, not pursuing leisure but preparing himself for the greater interests of the Church, E. ibid., V. 132. His wife frees him from domestic cares and civil affairs, E. 260 ff., V. 131. How gracious he is in writing letters, E. 258 ff. Whether he was bishop of Toul? 129, 130. He was enrolled among the saints, V. 134.

Apis, a celebrated Egyptian divinity in the form of an ox, P. 45.

**APOLLINARIS’S** error—that Christ assumed from the blessed Virgin merely a body without a soul—is refuted by Victricius, E. 225.

To invoke Apollo was familiar to poets, P. 363.

At the prompting of Endelechius, Paulinus writes an apology for the emperor Theodosius, E. 175, V. 44. He sends it to Severus, ibid., and to Jerome, A. 773, V. 51.

*Apophoretum*, a small dish, E. 30. A gift customarily taken away from a banquet, A. 875. At the distribution of gifts, ibid. At the triumphs of emperors and on great occasions of thanksgiving, ibid.

What it means to be ordained *ἀπολελυμένως* or *ἀπολύτως* (“absolutely,” A. 870).

The apostles are the mountains of God, E. 45. The feet of the word of God, E. 98. They were wavering about the resurrection and were confirmed by Christ, P. 671. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they speak in all languages, P. 626, A. 943. Paulinus invites them to concelebrate the birthday of St. Felix, P. 630. Each year, when he is going to celebrate their solemnity, Paulinus travels to Rome, E. 93, 106, 196, 199, 254, 264, V. 41. He visits their memorial shrines, ibid.

The Appian Way, E. 183, P. 583.

Apollo Pythius, famous for his oracle, P. 455.

Water in pitchers at the entrances of temples, E. 205, A. 882, 883, 916. Among the Greeks, water was blessed on the vigil of Epiphany, A. 916. The people washed with it before performing the divine offices, ibid. Why this was done, A. 883, 916. Hence fountains and pitchers are still found before the principal churches, A. ibid. Hence also the lustral and blessed water at the doors or vestibules of temples, A. ibid.

The aqueduct at Nola constructed by Paulinus, P. 543, 544.

Eaglets feed their parents, who have become featherless through old age, P. 596. When their parents have regained their feathers, they teach them to fly, ibid.

A spider’s web is a wall for those with whom Christ is present, P. 405.

Noah’s ark, a type of the Church, E. 282, 283, A. 910.

The ark in churches, the treasury, the *tronc*, A. 918.

**ARCHELAIS**, a noble and holy widow, dear to St. Felix, P. 410.

The narrow way of salvation explained, E. 246.

The arch, court, atrium, or vestibule of a temple, E. 204, A. [Col. 1111] 915. Likewise the portico of a church, ibid. Public penitents stood there, A. ibid. In which churches of Gaul this holy custom still endures, A. 916.

The pagans tell the fable that the ship of the Argonauts can still be seen in the sky, E. 282.

The persecution of the Arians against Catholics broke out in the time of the emperor Valens, E. 182.

**ARIUS’S** heresy was cut off at the beginning of the Gospel of St. John, E. 111.

Weapons need faith, not faith weapons, P. 613.

The armor of the Christian soldier, E. 6.

*Ἀρμελαύσιον*, *armilausa*: a military cloak, a surcoat, E. 93, 113, A. 887, V. 191.

Asahel is praised in the sacred Scriptures for the swiftness of his feet, E. 109, 111.

The festival of Christ’s Ascension is of very great antiquity, P. 625, A. 943. Helena adorns the place, E. 192. It cannot be paved, E. ibid., A. 903. The earth is not diminished, even though something is removed from it each day, ibid.

Balaam’s she-ass, speaking in a human voice, is a figure of the conversion of the Gentiles, E. 58.

Paulinus calls the body an ass; why, P. 590, A. 940.

What *assula*, *assulatim*, and *assulose* mean, A. 948.

The Assyrians try to prevent the Jews from rebuilding the Temple of Jerusalem, E. 107.

Asterius, named from *astrum*, “star,” P. 535.

The movements and courses of the stars impose no necessity upon human affairs, E. 86.

What *astula* and *astilla* mean, E. 189, 203, 647, A. 948.

The continence of athletes, E. 153, A. 896, 897.

Atlas, a mountain at the farthest boundaries of Spain, P. 371.

Avarice is the root of all sins, P. 656. Together with pleasure and luxury, it is the source of all evils, P. 342. Its disease easily creeps into the inmost heart when it is protected by no safeguards of mercy, E. 214. What forms of it are to be praised and what forms condemned, E. 74, 218. Fear of the Lord drives it out, E. 231. Paulinus prays to be delivered from it, P. 330.

A beautiful description of a fowler deceiving birds and hunting those he has caught, P. 329, 330.

**AUGUSTINE** sends Paulinus the life of Alypius, written by himself, E. 20. He commends Licentius to him, E. 20. He had once taught him letters, E. 39, 20. He desires that he cross over to Africa, E. 21, 37. He sends messengers to Paulinus, E. 264, 296, V. 79, 80. The book *On the Care for the Dead*, A. 780, V. 92. He writes letters, E. 206, A. 778, V. 90. Paulinus receives letters from him, E. 13, 26, 28. He asks how the will of God, which must be preferred to ours, may be known, A. 778. He strengthens Valerius, bishop of Hippo, against the Pelagians, A. 780, 901, V. 90. He greets Therasia, E. 37. He praises Melania’s constancy at the death of her only son, E. 264, 265. His letter against the Pelagians is addressed to Paulinus, not to Boniface, A. 780, 901. Paulinus praises his wisdom and holiness, E. 266. His five books against the Manichaeans, E. 11, 13 ff. They seem to have been dictated by divine inspiration, E. 11.

**AUGENDUS**, a monk of Lérins under St. Honoratus, E. 313. He was sent by Honoratus, then a presbyter, to Paulinus, ibid.

Gold: *Cephas*, E. 133, A. 891; *Ophas*, A. 892; *Pas* and *Phas*, ibid.

The friendship of Ausonius and Paulinus, in the Prologue.

Ausonius was Paulinus’s closest friend, P. 553.

**AUSONIUS**, professor of grammar and rhetoric, V. 3. Paulinus’s teacher, P. 365, V. 3. Tutor of the emperor Gratian, V. 3. Praetorian prefect of Gaul and Italy, ibid. Roman consul, V. 3. He praises Paulinus greatly and compares him with Cicero and Virgil, P. 376, V. 4. He recalls him, already converted, to poetry, V. 23. He attacks him sharply, V. 23, 24. He calls Therasia a Tanaquil, V. 23. Was he a Christian? V. 3, 23. His parents and those of Paulinus were closely united in friendship, V. 3.

**B**

Babylon means confusion, P. 390. Its daughter is the flesh, ibid. Paulinus calls Rome the daughter of Babylon, E. 184, 276, A. 900.

Baptism wipes out sins and renews the human being, E. 198, P. 344. Why it was not immediately conferred on St. Genesius when he sought it during the persecution, E. 316. The vow of Christians who receive it, E. 128. The effect of the baptism of St. John the Baptist, P. 344.

Description of the baptismal-font basilica of St. Felix, E. 198, 199.

The baptistery built by Sulpicius Severus, E. 195. Adorned with paintings of St. Martin and Paulinus, E. 195, 196, 200. Enriched with inscriptions by Paulinus, E. 196, 197. Baptisteries and pitchers before temples, E. 206, A. 882, 883, 916, 917.

*Barca*, a kind of vessel, P. 572, A. 939.

Barcelona, a very celebrated city of Spain, E. 371, P. 372. There, by the force of the crowd, Paulinus was seized and initiated into the presbyterate, E. 7, 12.

The basilica at Alingon, E. 107, V. 54, 65. The basilica at Fundi, E. 206, 207, V. 76. In the basilica of St. Felix, a fragment of the holy cross was preserved from fire, P. 656. It was enlarged by Paulinus, P. 646 ff., V. 74, 75. Its structure is graphically described, E. 203 ff., P. 646 ff., V. 65, 72 ff.

Basilicas facing east, E. 204, V. 73. In building them, Paulinus celebrates the saints already enrolled in heaven, E. 203 ff., P. 937 ff., V. 65 ff.

**BASIL**, a presbyter of the Church of Capua, E. 82, 83, V. 54. A most holy man, E. 84, V. 54. Exiled from his own house, E. 82, V. 54. Through Paulinus’s intervention, he again enjoys possession of it, E. 65, 82, 83, V. 54.

**BASSULA**, mother-in-law of Sulpicius Severus, E. 23, 29, A. 872. She receives a fragment of the holy cross from Therasia, E. 189.

How blessed our condition would be if we feared and took care to please God as much as we fear and take care to please human beings, E. 75.

After the resurrection, the blessed, already possessing spiritual bodies, will praise God with tongues and voices, E. 268, 275, 280.

Before the final judgment, the blessed enjoy the vision of God, P. 542. What Paulinus’s opinion on this matter is, ibid.

Paulinus shows that Ausonius compared him somewhat inappropriately with Bellerophon, P. 369.

War between human beings and God is abolished through Christ, E. 62. In wartime Paulinus implores the help of St. Felix, P. 610, 614, 616. The enemy is not to be feared, but God, P. 610. We must trust in God, not in weapons, P. 610, 611.

An ancient rite of blessing: placing a hand upon the head of someone being blessed, P. 401.

**BENEDICTUS**, a deacon, E. 166, V. 8. A preacher of the word of God, E. 166, 167, V. 68. Brother of Sebastian the hermit, E. 166, V. 68. He supplies him with what is necessary for life, ibid. Paulinus and Therasia commend themselves to his prayers, E. 165, 167, V. 68.

Beneficence toward the poor, E. 72 ff., 244 ff.

The Bessi, a people converted by Nicetas, P. 419, 421, A. 936. Gold-miners, P. 421, A. 936. Monks, ibid.

The *beta* is to be seasoned with pepper, A. 885. Half-cooked, E. 236, A. 885.

Bethlehem was profaned by the emperor Hadrian with a shrine of Adonis, E. 190.

The Baetis, a river of Spain flowing into the Ocean, P. 371.

*Betissare*, A. 885.

In which part of the church the library was located, E. 204, 206, A. 913, 914, 917.

*Bigerra* and *Bigerrica* cloak, A. 930.

The shaggy Bigerri, P. 371, A. 929, 936.

Bilbilis, a city of Spain, P. 370.

The Boii, a people of Gaul, P. 370.

Boethia, or Achaia: the tomb of Luke, P. 451.

The goods of the Church must be preserved and increased, A. 895. Heavenly things must be preferred to earthly things, E. 182. It is exceedingly pleasing to think of the good things promised by Christ to the faithful after this life, E. 80.

It is not enough to have begun good works; it is praiseworthy to have completed them, A. 741, 742. They are necessary for salvation, A. 728. The uncertainty of death commends the pursuit of them, E. 257. By them heaven is taken by force, E. 215, 216. Just as good things are commanded, so evil things are forbidden, A. 729.

**BONIFACE**, a bishop in Africa, E. 297.

**BONIFACE**, a presbyter accused of a crime, is sent by Augustine to the tomb of St. Felix at Nola to be purified, V. 79.

Oxen driven away by thieves are restored to a peasant through the merits of St. Felix, P. 433 ff., V. 57.

Brevity is charming, P. 360.

The grub, blight, caterpillar, and locust listed by Joel are applied to the passions of the soul, E. 236, 237.

*Burdicus*, *burdo*, *burdus*, *buricus*: what they mean, A. 779. Melania the noblewoman enters Naples seated upon this animal, E. 183.

Bordeaux, a very celebrated city of Gaul in Aquitaine, P. 361. Not far distant from Aginnum and the Santones, P. 355. Paulinus was born there, A. 957, V. 2.

Bordeaux, the most illustrious city of Aquitaine, the fatherland of Paulinus, P. 538.

**C**

The blind are illuminated by Christ, P. 569, A. 888.

How Samson’s blindness is to be desired, E. 131, 132. Also the blindness by which iniquity is not seen, E. 187. The executioner who attempted to behead Victricius is punished with blindness, E. 101, V. 122.

Those who hope for heavenly things despise earthly things, P. 368, A. 747, 748. The former are to be believed; the latter are to be seen, P. 673. What must be done to obtain them, E. 275.

Heaven is open to all, E. 81. It was closed and opened again by Elijah’s prayers, P. 615.

Heaven is counted among the elements, V. diss. 462.

Caesaraugusta, a celebrated city of Spain, P. 371.

Calagurris, a city of Spain, P. 370.

Calamina, a city of India where Thomas suffered martyrdom, P. 550.

A cup in the aqueducts, P. 545.

**CALIPPIANUS**, a presbyter of Sulpicius Severus, V. 120.

Calpe, a mountain at the farthest boundaries of Spain, P. 370.

[Col. 1113] *Καλύψει*, or *κάμψει*—which should be read in Ecclesiasticus 38, A. 879.

Campania was devastated by the Goths, V. 89. The bishops of this province were exceedingly well disposed toward Paulinus, E. 26.

The Campanians were formerly called Osci, P. 409.

Screens at the tombs of the saints, P. 537.

Screens around the altar, P. 645, A. 947.

Seven-branched candlesticks, E. 23, A. 872.

Candles lit in the churches on the solemn festivals of the saints, P. 385, 636, A. 932, 938, 944.

Candlesticks in sacred buildings, P. 472.

How candles were formerly fashioned both by pagans and by Christians, P. 472.

**CANDIDIANUS**, small in stature, E. 222. Bearer of Victricius’s letter to Paulinus, ibid. Paulinus praises his speed, ibid.

Candidates could not approach the voting assemblies wearing a tunic, P. 480, 481.

Why they are rightly called dogs, E. 75, E. 301. Christ thus calls the Gentiles in the Gospel, E. 290. Whether any others should be called so, E. 290, 301.

Pitchers for washing the mouth and hands at the entrance of temples, E. 71, 205, A. 882, 883, 916, 917, V. 74.

Wax-coated pitchers, P. 476.

The name *cantharus* persists in the rituals of the Ambrosian Church, P. 476.

The *cantharus* is a type of lamp, P. 476.

Chapels in churches: their origin, E. 204, A. 913.

Christians ought to let their hair grow for Christ, and how this is to be done, E. 133, 134, A. 914. See *Coma*.

Paulinus gives money for the redemption of captives, A. 798, V. 90. Whether he handed over himself as well, V. 139 ff.

**CARDAMAS**, formerly a mime, E. 104, V. 56. Addicted to wine, E. 8, 104, V. 56. A servant of St. Paulinus, E. 84, 102, 111, V. 56. Paulinus himself hands him over to Amandus of Bordeaux, E. 84, 102, 111, V. 56. Completely changed under that teacher, E. 84, 102. He becomes sober, E. 84, 112, V. 56. A cleric, E. 84, 111, V. 56. An exorcist terrifying to demons, E. 102, 112, V. 56, 64. Married, E. 85, V. 56. Bearer of Delphinus’s and Amandus’s letters to Paulinus, E. 81, 82, 103, 105, 117, 112, V. 56, 64. Of Paulinus’s letters to the same men and to Venerius of Milan, E. 81, 82, 104, 102, 109, V. 56. How swift he is in carrying letters, although old, E. 109 ff., V. 56. Received most warmly by Paulinus, E. 87, V. 56. Commended by Paulinus to Delphinus and Amandus, E. 102, 112. Paulinus plays amiably with him in his continence, E. 48, 85, V. 56.

Charity is the fullness of the Gospel, E. 21, 56, 155. What Christ’s charity is like, E. 46. Its imitation and the sharp incentives toward it, E. 146 ff. Nothing is more commanding than it, E. 9. It is strong as death, E. 239, 287. It teaches us to undergo an evangelical death, E. 266. Spiritual charity, unlike secular charity, is not to be measured by the passage of time, E. 65. It is to be perfected toward one’s neighbor in Christ, E. 118. The true sign of perfect charity, E. 20.

Paulinus’s poem on the figures of St. Martin and himself painted in the baptistery built by Severus, E. 196. Another poem on the baptistery built by Severus, E. 197. On the painting of the basilicas erected by the same Severus, ibid. On the relics of St. Clarus the presbyter, E. 198, 199. On a fragment of the holy cross enclosed in the altars together with the relics of the martyrs, E. 201. On the same relics of the martyrs, E. 203. Another in which he exhorts Licentius, having despised the world, to dedicate himself to Christ, E. 38.

Carnal weakness is the material of spiritual virtue, E. 168.

The executioner who attempted to behead Victricius is punished with blindness, E. 199.

The flesh of Christ is the boiling pot seen by the prophet Jeremiah, burning and consuming sins, E. 120. It joins earthly things to heavenly things, E. 82.

The flesh is the daughter of Babylon, the mother of sin, P. 350. The foreign woman who deceived Samson, P. 587. Christ taught the resurrection of the flesh both by word and proved it by example, E. 81.

To satirize someone is the practice of poets, not of parents, P. 372.

*Καρπός*, the joint of the hand with the forearm, and “fruit,” E. 79, A. 884.

Chastity is to be nourished by fasting, P. 590. Bodily expansion is hostile to it, E. 195. In praising it, the apostle Paul does not prohibit marriage, E. 19. Its path is arduous but its rewards are great, A. 743. The more chaste one is in one’s limbs, the more vigorous one is in one’s senses, E. 255.

Priestly chastity and purity, P. 532.

What “chance” signifies, E. 87. It has no power over human affairs, ibid.

A catechumen is not affected by the disadvantages suffered by Christians, E. 24.

Chains miraculously fall from the hands of Victricius, who was already about to be executed, E. 99. Likewise from those of the imprisoned St. Felix, P. 397.

The Catholic religion knows no respect of persons, A. 16.

Among the Hebrews, *cedar* signifies darkness, E. 69, 184.

**CELANCIA**, a noble matron, is instructed how to lead her life holily and religiously amid honors, riches, and the burdens of marriage, A. 728 ff. She is urged to read sacred Scripture, A. 734. With her husband’s agreement, she vows chastity to God, A. 741.

*Celeusma*, the chant of sailors and of those treading the winepress, P. 417, A. 936, V. 191.

**CELSUS**, son of Pneumatius and Fidelis, P. 665, 686. A relative of Paulinus, P. ibid., V. 1. At eight years old, distinguished for intellectual teachability, P. 666. Of what illness he died, ibid. Paulinus honors him with a panegyric, P. 665 ff.

Martinianus reaches Centumcellae safely, P. 582, A. 939.

The evangelical centurion who had built a synagogue for the Jews was heard by Christ; he supplies Catholics building churches with a sure hope of eternal reward, E. 207, 208.

**CEREALIS** is commended by Paulinus to Rufinus, E. 276.

Wax candles are kept burning day and night in the churches, P. 385, 637, A. 932, 938, 944.

On wax tablets, or to impress something in wax, E. 316.

To paint with wax, or on wax, A. 901.

The ancient custom in the Church of painting with wax, which still continues, P. 463.

How we become spiritual deer, E. 43.

The whale as Jonah’s avenger and guardian, E. 283, A. 924.

Chalcedon, or Calchedon? A. 945.

The *chalcidicum*, that is, the *chalcedonium*, P. 637, A. 945.

Christians have been freed through Christ from the yoke of the ancient law, P. 592. They alone possess knowledge of the true God, P. 330. All have been saved from a certain shipwreck, P. 573, 574. Why the dead are to be mourned less, P. 679. In wartime they are instructed to trust not in weapons but in God, P. 611, 612. It belongs to them to invoke God, not Apollo or the Muses, P. 330. Ephrem is a type of those who are to be called from the Gentiles, E. 144. What their banquets ought to be like, P. 602. What marriage ought to be like, P. 601 ff. The attendance and devotion of those celebrating the birthday of St. Felix, P. 383, 384. Formerly they washed their hands before the doors of temples as a reminder of inward purity, E. 205, A. 882, 883, 916. In what way absent and unknown Christians are said to be present and known to other Christians, E. 30.

A Christian who loves perfection ought to follow Christ, E. 161. A Christian does not live by bread alone but by faith, E. 55. Whoever has faith without works is close to an unbeliever, E. 222. A Christian must differ from a pagan not only in faith but also in life, A. 731. To be a Christian is an argument for piety, P. 331.

**CHRIST** is prefigured by Abel who was killed, E. 229; by Abraham who wandered, E. 229; by Isaac who was to be sacrificed, E. 181, 229; by Joseph who was sold, E. 229; by Noah who was mocked, ibid.; by Moses who was exposed and driven into exile, ibid.; by the paschal lamb, P. 611; by the lion who conquered, ibid.; by the lion’s cub, E. 129; by Samson, E. 125; by Jonah, E. 284; by the evangelical Samaritan, E. 125; by David, E. 111, 112. He is the second Adam, P. 672. Priest and victim, E. 51. Lamb and shepherd, E. 51, 252, 253. He carries the sheep back to the fold on his shoulders, E. 52, A. 877, 878, whose image was formerly represented on sacred chalices, A. ibid. In paintings he is represented by a lamb, E. 201, 205, A. 908. Living and true bread, which the sluggish laborer cannot eat, E. 52. The true vine, E. 238. The fountain, P. 185. The fish of living water, E. 69, A. 880. The solitary sparrow, E. 244, 245. Life, P. 678. Giving life and killing, E. 241, 242. Consuming fire, E. 172. Illuminating the blind and blinding the seeing, E. 188. The rock, E. 202, A. 912, against which the tender offspring of sins must be dashed, P. 350. Refuge of the poor, A. 726. For the humble, E. 42. Foundation, tower, and gate of the heavenly Jerusalem, E. 172. The city, E. 172. Alpha and omega, P. 662, A. 949, 950. Head of all the faithful, P. 419, 599. End of the law, E. 65, 291, P. 590, 677; and of the prophets, E. 292. Turning the yoke of the ancient law away from us, P. 591. The razor of saving circumcision, E. 123. The evangelical pearl, to be acquired by the expenditure of all one’s goods, E. 138. His various epithets, P. 364. Made human for our sake, he had nothing in common with other human beings in the manner of his birth, E. 127. Made sin for our sake through the likeness of sinful flesh, E. 224. Taking the form of a servant, he restored humanity to freedom, P. 382, 669. Hence he makes us participants in his glory, E. 46, 56. How he sanctified both sexes, E. 125. Mediator between God and humanity, P. 331. He alone could aid the human race infected with the stain of sin, E. 56. In what manner he accomplished this, ibid. How greatly he loved the world, P. 669. He seeks our love in return for his own, E. 147. Through his incarnation he joins earthly things to heavenly things, E. 79. The hand and wisdom of the Father, the source of all things, E. 49. He shows himself both God and human, P. 669. From his birth he illuminates the blind, P. 568. As examiner of hearts, he prefers the widow who offers two small coins to all the others, P. 428, 433. By his own example he rebukes those who disdain the poor, P. 683, 684. He is found in every poor person, E. 209, 214. He is refreshed, E. 217 ff., 261. He is anointed, fed, and lent money at interest, E. 119, A. 889. He closes his kingdom to no one, [Col. 1115] E. 80. In the Gospel he summons all to the narrow way that leads to life, A. 733. He greatly commends John the Baptist, P. 735. In the one Lazarus he mourns the sins of the entire human race, P. 421, 422. What fruit he desired on the fig tree that he later withered by his curse, E. 255, 256. Why he sought fruit on it before the proper time, E. 256. He shares his names with his apostles, E. 146. Why, when washing his disciples’ feet, he did not wash his own, E. 142, A. 894. How he erased the record of death, E. 127. He destroyed sin, E. 59. He wished to be fastened to the cross’s gallows out of pure compassion for the human race, not compelled by necessity, E. 105. When already near death, he commended affection toward parents by his own example, E. 198, 199. He laid down his soul by his own power, ibid. Why he emptied himself so greatly, E. 57, 58. On the cross he overcame the devil not by divine power but by human weakness, E. 217. Judas the betrayer had no share in the price of his blood, E. 140, 141. He bought it at a great price; he did not sell it, E. 141, A. 894. How he overcame death, P. 669, 670. He suffered and rose not for himself but for human beings, A. 746. By his own power he took back his soul, E. 105. Rising from the dead, he declares that there will be a resurrection of bodies, P. 332. He teaches it by word and proves it by example, E. 78. He displays his wounds for the apostle Thomas to touch, since Thomas doubted the truth of the resurrection, P. 671. At the final judgment he will repay everyone fitting rewards, P. 373. He appears seated at the helm to an old man tossed about by a storm at sea, E. 282. He comforts and refreshes him, ibid. What his passion and resurrection teach us, E. 60. His humility is especially proposed for imitation by Christians in Saints Peter and Paul, E. 60, A. 733. His praises are recounted most beautifully, E. 252. His life and actions are an example of conduct and morals for us, E. 259. Paulinus commends his sacred warfare to a certain soldier, E. 163 ff. Those who reject his counsels are swallowed up in the whirlpools of worldly anxieties, A. 905. For those burning with love of him, neither labor nor pleasure is an impediment, A. 747. By his power we escape the devil’s deceits, P. 590. Paulinus shows by various examples that from the beginning Christ was hated and despised by his own people in the world, E. 229, 230. By his example he also shows that nobility of birth is praiseworthy even among saints, E. 180. Paulinus invokes him while adorning the birthday of St. Felix with a votive poem, P. 558, 559. To lend money at interest to him is meritorious, E. 214, A. 889, 893. To serve him is complete freedom, E. 38. Eternal rewards are reserved here for those who serve him, P. 373. Those who strive to imitate him must despise riches, A. 727. What rewards are promised to those who follow him and abandon the things of this world, P. 365. Christ is represented standing upon a rock from which four fountains flow—that is, the four rivers of paradise, or the four Gospels, E. 202, A. 912. Certain people asserted that Christ had learned from Plato’s books; Ambrose refutes them, E. 34. Apollinaris taught that Christ assumed from the holy Virgin only a body without a soul, E. 226. Christ’s body was placed on the altar beneath the cross, not among the sequence of images, E. 201, A. 905, 911. It was kept in a golden or silver tower, A. 905. In a dove, A. 909, 911.

How the name “Christ” is formed by the Greeks, P. 482.

Christ’s food is whoever does his will, E. 51, 129.

The piety of storks toward their parents, A. 942.

*Cicuma*, the night raven, A. 924.

Paulinus correctly interprets the sackcloth sent to him by Severus as appropriate for himself, in need of penance, E. 175, 176. The prophet Elijah used it, E. 175, 187, A. 924. John the Baptist likewise, ibid. King David the prophet, E. 175. It was formerly the monks’ undergarment, A. 899.

The circle, a symbol of eternity, A. 912.

A city fortified with surrounding defenses, A. 901.

Nobility of birth is praiseworthy even among saints, E. 180.

**CLARUS**, a presbyter, E. 171, 199, 200, A. 899. His relics were preserved in the basilica built by Severus, E. 199. Paulinus adorned them with verses, E. 199, 200, A. 899.

Bodies of martyrs pierced with large nails, P. 638, A. 945.

Paulinus is merciful toward the accused, A. 959.

**CLEMENT’S** works translated from Greek into Latin by Paulinus, E. 218, A. 922.

Certain Roman clerics hostile and envious toward Paulinus, and why, E. 24, A. 873. Clerics of the lower orders were sometimes married, E. 85, P. 604, V. 56. They were ordained to a definite title of a particular church, A. 871. They must serve for some time in each of the Church’s orders, A. 933. Why they hasten immediately to the priesthood, A. ibid.

**CLOVIS**, while opening the sacred Scripture, receives an omen of victory, A. 897.

*Κνῆμαιαι*, or *σκηναί*, in Psalm 146, A. 924.

Augustine was Valerius’s co-bishop in the Church of Hippo, that is, his coadjutor, E. 36, A. 876.

Knowledge of oneself: whence it arises, E. 91.

What “cognomen” means, A. 945.

[Col. 1116] Evil conversations corrupt good morals, E. 68.

The dove, a symbol of simplicity, A. 915, 916. A type of the Holy Spirit, E. 203, A. 909, 910. Overspreading the lamb—that is, the Holy Spirit over Christ, E. 207, A. 917. Doves were customarily suspended above baptisteries and altars, A. 910. Christ’s body was kept in one, A. 909, 911. A dove bringing back an olive branch in the flood is applied to the mystery of baptism, A. 910. Doves sitting upon crosses or flying over them, E. 202, A. 912. Twelve around the cross, a type of the twelve apostles, ibid. Doves were sacrificed at the tombs of the dead, A. 909. They were placed on the funerary poles of those who had died abroad, ibid.

Absalom’s hair, the weight of sins, E. 130. Hair that is light or heavy signifies different human works, E. 138 ff. What the hair of saints or of the impious is like, E. 128. What kind of hair is becoming to women, E. 132.

**COMES**, sent from Alypius to Paulinus, E. 10.

Comes, who had condemned Victricius to death, was converted to the faith by miracles and became a confessor, E. 101.

Feasting and drinking at the tombs of martyrs, P. 642, 643, A. 946, 947. Their origin, ibid. How they were abolished by the churches, P. 642 ff., A. 946, 947.

How useful fraternal compassion is to the afflicted, E. 64.

Paulinus’s son, an eight-day-old infant, buried at Complutum, P. 685, 686, V. 11.

Complutum, the birthplace of Paulinus’s wife, according to conjecture, P. 529.

A shell, used for a water vessel, A. 947. The part of a temple where sacrifice is offered, E. 203, A. 912, 913, 949. A type of Bethlehem and of Christ’s tomb, A. 913. Shells and apses are the same, E. 202, A. 906, 913, 948, 949.

Deacons as preachers in Gaul in Paulinus’s time, E. 167, 168, V. 68.

The *confessio*, the place where the bodies of the saints rest, A. 881, 882. It is in the apse, A. ibid.

Confessors: who they are, A. 885. Their bright purple, E. 191, A. 885.

The sacrament of confirmation, P. 392, A.

944.

Confusion is called Babylon, P. 350.

Pauline reminds married couples of their duty, P. 604, 605. The diligence of the wife of Aper, later Amanda’s sister, is praised by Paulinus: while managing the household affairs, she provided her husband leisure for divine pursuits, E. 260 and following, V. 131.

Marriage is not prohibited by the Apostle, but chastity is preferred, A. 742. Christ’s marriage: what it is, P. 602 and following.

“To be sealed,” E. 82, A. 884.

Pauline illustrates the evangelical counsels by his own conduct, A. 781.

Consolation for mourning the death of a good wife, E. 69.
