The steadfastness of Paulinus after his conversion is sharply attacked by Ausonius, P. 358 and following.

Constantine deserved primacy among Christian rulers no more by his own faith than by that of his mother Helena, E. 191, A. 903. Why he transferred the relics of Saints Andrew, Luke, and Timothy to Constantinople, P. 659. Or was this Constantius? P. 659, A. 949.

Constantinople was called by Constantine “the second Rome” and “the new Rome,” P. 469.

The bishop of Constantinople obtained privileges of honor after the Roman bishop, 478.

Constantine’s care concerning the veneration of the apostles’ bones, 469.

Constantine and other pious emperors enacted laws against the pagans, 463.

Consul in the colony of Astigi, 521. In Barcelona, 521.

The habit of vices makes the path of virtues difficult for us, A. 732.

Contempt for human judgments: a virtue of Paulinus, V. 23.

Pauline attempts to persuade Licentius, in prose and verse, to despise the world, E. 38 and following.

A woman cannot vow continence without her husband’s consent, A. 741, 742.

Controversies were once customarily settled by an oath made at the tombs of martyrs, V. 80.

Conversion to God should not be postponed because of the flourishing period of life, E. 164. To whom Paulinus owed his conversion, V. 8. Its author is God, V. 9, 10. What movements occurred in it, V. 21 and following. Paulinus himself shows that Sulpicius Severus was a greater miracle than Paulinus’s own deeds, E. 20, 22.

What Christian banquets ought to be like, P. 603.

The basket of manure placed beside the barren fig tree in the Gospel indicates the usefulness of humility, E. 176, 264.

A pure heart is more acceptable to God than abandoning all external things, E. 154. It must be watched with complete vigilance along the way of the Spirit, E. 247, A. 744. The purer someone is in heart, the more capable he is of receiving Christ, E. 255.

The crown: ecclesiastical and pontifical dignity, E. 11, 83, A. 871. Bishops were greeted by it, ibid.

One who desires the crown must contend, E. 204.

The body of Christ was placed on the altar beneath the cross, not [Col. 1117] among the order of images, E. 201, A. 906, 907. It was kept and hung in a golden or silver tower, A. 906. In a dove, A. 909, 910.

The body is the vessel and garment of the soul, P. 676, A. 909. The deceased Paulinus’s body shone with snowy brilliance, A. 960, V. 94. Afflictions of the body are remedies for the soul, A. 719. The mortification of the body is an indication of humility, E. 60. Its relaxation is hostile to chastity, E. 290. Its abstinence strengthens the spirit, P. 590. It is better to hunger in the body than in the spirit, E. 67. What the resurrection of bodies will be like, E. 267, 268, P. 674, 675, A. 769, 770. Whether angels have bodies, E. 267, 268. The bodies of saints are buried in tombs, not their merits, P. 427 and following. Buried beneath the altar, E. 201, A. 906. By them the earth is adorned as the heavens are with stars, P. 659.

In Scripture the raven sometimes expresses the form of sin, sometimes that of grace, E. 134, 135. Thus its color is sometimes represented among the saints, sometimes among the impious, ibid.

The creation of the whole universe and its governance must be attributed to God, E. 86, 87.

No creature should be called evil, E. 88.

Crete: the episcopate and tomb of Titus, 451.

Crete: the kingdom and tomb of Jupiter, 452.

The hair of Christ consists of the saints, E. 140. Hair: see Coma.

Crumilus, E. 121, A. 890, 891.

The cross of Christ overcame death, P. 575. Kings and princes submit their scepters to it, P. 585. Paulinus extols and worships it with numerous encomia, P. 662. Whether it was placed, or is to be placed, above the stars, P. 662, A. 766, 767. By the power of the Crucified One and of the cross, the enemies of the Christian are overcome, E. 162, 163. The wood of the holy cross is a defense in the present life, a title and pledge of eternal salvation, E. 189, P. 417, A. 934. Buried in the earth by the Jews: how Constantine’s mother Helena found and recognized it, E. 192, 193. It is kept by the bishop of Jerusalem and every year at Easter is displayed for the people to worship, E. 193. The same is done for pilgrims who come there out of devotion, ibid. A portion is taken from it daily, yet it is not diminished, E. 194, A. 906. Paulinus sends Sulpicius Severus a fragment of it enclosed in a golden tube, E. 189, 190. And why, ibid. Its entire power is present even in the smallest fragment of it, E. 189, 194, 288. The faithful customarily carry fragments of it about for daily protection, E. 194, 288, A. 926. A fragment of it extinguished a fire, P. 650, 651. Whether the cross can be greeted with “hail,” P. 661, A. 952. Crowned at the top, E. 203, A. 911. With a rainbow, sphere, or circle, E. 202, A. 912. A ship’s yardarm, P. 417, A. 936. Used as protection on ships, A. 934. From the steering-oar, P. 419, A. 934, 935. Birds represent it in flight, P. 599, A. 755.

In ancient times crosses were placed on altars, 485.

Crosses were customarily painted encircled by a crown, P. 486.

Description of the cross, P. 475.

Chambers in churches: what are they? E. 203, A. 913. From this arose the custom of being buried there, ibid.

Desires weaken the virtue of faith, E. 153. Their allurements are our Lotus-eaters and Sirens, E. 93.

While caring for souls, what Paulinus thought about this responsibility, E. 6, 7, 8, 14, V. 28, 29.

Curtis: what it is, A. 889.

CYPRIAN, the martyr, rests at Carthage, P. 660.

CYTHERIUS receives letters from Paulinus concerning the shipwreck of Martinianus, P. 569 and following, V. 66. Also concerning the education of his own son Cytherius, whom under Severus he had dedicated to God, P. 586 and following, V. 66. Cytherius is compared to Abraham, while his son is compared to Isaac, P. 586, and to Samuel, P. 589. Paulinus prays for his son to possess Samson’s virtue, P. 588, 590. He prays that he be kept from vices, P. 587, 588, 589. He compares him to Joseph sold into Egypt, P. 586, 595, 596. He vows that the same son should imitate Joseph in other respects, ibid. He compares him to an eaglet, P. 597, 598.

## D

The Dacians were converted to the faith by Nicetas, P. 421.

DADUCIUS is summoned by Paulinus through a letter, E. 63.

The demon envies the redemption of humanity, P. 670.

Why demons are called “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places,” E. 245. They were expelled from possessed bodies at the tomb of Saint Felix, P. 383. Especially around the day of his birth, P. 559.

The Delphic demon fell silent when Christ was born, 453.

By which emperors the worship of demons was prohibited, 464.

Dagon, “the belly-god,” worshiped among the Philistines, 461.

The condemned will be tortured forever after the universal resurrection, P. 685.

The prophet David used sackcloth, E. 175. When praying to God, he put forward the merit of humility, E. 175. How he exalted his soul while preserving humility of heart, ibid. In laying low the giant, he is a type of Christ, who was to triumph over the devil, E. 109, 110. What he signified by meeting the death of his most beloved son with joy, but that of Absalom with lamentation, E. 78. Why, knowing that his life had been divinely prolonged, he groaned, [Col. 1118] E. 69, 70. He mystically signifies the humble man, P. 590. An example of repentance, P. 680.

“Defender,” in place of “avenger,” A. 896.

DEFENSOR resisted his election as bishop of Saint Martin of Tours, ibid.

The souls of the dead are aided by the prayers and good works of the living, E. 67, 72, 76, 80, 220, 221. Tombs are defended by various examples from Holy Scripture, E. 68. Beside the bodies of martyrs, P. 686, A. 768, 769, V. 12. To what extent one may mourn them, P. 68.

DELPHINUS, bishop of Bordeaux, E. 45, V. 78. He baptized Paulinus, E. 80, 45, 46, 108, V. 10. Paulinus’s brother, V. 2. For this reason Paulinus called him “father,” “Peter,” and “fisherman,” E. 108, V. 10. He is praised for founding the church at Alingon, E. 107, V. 55, 66. He rests in Aquitania, P. 660. He was numbered among the saints, E. 46, V. 80.

Delphi was formerly called Pythus, 454.

The Delphic demon fell silent when Christ was born, 454.

Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, baptized Paulinus, 459.

The number ten was represented by the letter X among the Latins, 482.

“The belly-god,” that is, Dagon, was worshiped among the Philistines, 461.

Shrines: what they are, A. 883.

DESIDERIUS, a presbyter awaiting from Paulinus an explanation of the patriarchs’ blessings, receives an exposition of the curse pronounced by the Lord upon the fig tree, E. 256 and following. Who he was, A. 910.

Detraction must be avoided, A. 734, 735. Paulinus prays to be spared it, P. 330. This vice is extremely widespread, A. 734, 735. And why, ibid. Why it must especially be hated by those who wish to live a holy life, ibid.

Every occasion must be removed from detractors, A. 739.

GOD THE FATHER is designated by a voice, E. 203, A. 908. A hand extended through a cloud, ibid. The Son by a lamb, ibid. The Holy Spirit by a dove, E. 203, A. 909. He is both loved and received in his smallest ones, E. 20. In order to test our charity, he sometimes tempts us, E. 22. Insofar as it depends on him, he wishes all people to be saved, E. 153, 216, 281. He is a consuming and illuminating fire, E. 110. He is not a respecter of persons, ibid. By the good of the rich he made the poor and needy, E. 217, 218. He did not make death, E. 281. Creator and governor of the whole universe, E. 88 and following. This is confirmed by various examples drawn from Holy Scripture, P. 556, 557. Giver of all spiritual and bodily gifts, E. 91. What he demands from a human being, P. 364. He sets forth commandments to be observed so that he may have grounds for rewarding, A. 729. Christians must invoke him, not the Muses, P. 333, 334. He must be moved by prayers, P. ibid. He assumed flesh from a virgin mother, P. 605. Source and origin of every good, P. 684. He equates intention with deeds, P. 381. In wartime he must be appeased, not the enemy feared, P. 611. How great his compassion toward human beings is, E. 181. Paulinus most elegantly describes his kindness and the height of the divine plan for the salvation of the human race, E. 59 and following. It is his work to change a human being, E. 233. His will is better than human prayers, E. 71. His wondrous providence in the creation of the whole universe, E. 90. His worship must be preferred to the profane military service of Caesar, E. 163 and following. Observance of his commandments is especially necessary for those striving to pass their lives holily, A. 727. Confession of him without works of faith and justice is invalid for attaining salvation, ibid. A beautiful description of him, P. 368, 369. Likewise of the Son of God, P. 331. Invocation of the same, P. 331, 332. See Christ. One who serves him is subject to no one, E. 62. One who clings to him easily overcomes nature and himself, P. 555. He must be served with the same devotion with which the world was previously served, E. 234. One who does not serve him becomes entangled in various errors of idolatry, E. 91, 92. One must always trust in him, not in weapons, P. 610, 611. That all things perceive and live for him is established by the example of the fish that swallowed Jonah and vomited him out again onto the land, P. 417. That he renews all the things he made from the beginning is shown by examples, E. 58. Those who recognize him are called human beings, E. 244. Those who do not recognize him are compared with beasts, E. 245. Those who do not observe his commandments neither honor nor fear him, A. 729. No one sees him as the source of every good except in Christ, P. 364.

The devil, the ancient serpent, E. 99, P. 392, A. 810, 885. Enemy of humanity, E. 156. How he is its defender, E. 134, A. 897. The razor of a deadly cutting, E. 122. He is driven away by the destruction of the subjected flesh, E. 13. He attacks us through our vices, ibid. After the fall he was punished by God more severely than the human being, E. 146, 147. He attempts in various ways to impede Melania’s journey to Jerusalem, E. 171, 182. On Christ’s cross he was overcome not by divine power but by human weakness, E. 246. He was overcome by humility, E. 230. He is destroyed by almsgiving, E. 74. He leaves nothing unattempted in order to harm human beings, E. 218, 219. He is overcome by human beings through the power of Christ, P. 590. He thirsts not so much for the destruction of bodies as for that of souls, P. 394.

[Col. 1119] The deacons in Gaul during Paulinus’s time were heralds of the word of God, E. 167, 168, V. 70.

The diaconicum was the sacristy in which ecclesiastical vessels and ornaments were kept, A. 913, 914. What else it was, A. 914.

Traces of the ancient diaconissarium remain in the rites of the Ambrosian Church, 494. What these were in ancient churches, ibid.

The Egyptian gods were innumerable, 455.

Days distinguished by some miracle or mystery are honored each year with a more solemn celebration, P. 625.

Mutual love is the sign of Christ’s disciples, E. 19, 148. Genuine love is extremely powerful, A. 717. Christian love must be stronger than human love and perpetual, E. 313. Christ demands love of himself alone for the entire work of our redemption, E. 147.

DIOGENIANUS, bishop of Albi, E. 276, V. 86. A man of the greatest faith and piety, ibid.

Pauline loved discipline, yet was kind, A. 958, 959, V. 94.

The method of divination by opening Holy Scripture, A. 897.

All things are subject to divine Providence, E. 85 and following, P. 553 and following.

Why the rich banqueter, wholly immersed in the fires of hell, asked for refreshment only for his tongue, E. 76. The antithesis between him and the Gospel’s Lazarus, P. 183.

The rich of this world are needy before God, E. 5. Who are the true rich? E. 4. To the poor, the rich are the substance of their sustenance; to the rich, the poor are the material of their justice, E. 209. God made the poor for the benefit of the rich, E. 216. What sort of rich and what sort of poor God loves, E. 76, 77. Why the names of rich sinners are suppressed in Holy Scripture, E. 77. Why their hearts are filthy, A. 726. The rich are inwardly filthy, while the poor are outwardly so, P. 683.

To abandon riches is the first training of the Christian soldier, E. 151. Riches are not blameworthy, but people misuse them, E. 77, 78. It will profit nothing to lack riches, but to lack vices, E. 247. What sort of riches should be sought, E. 217, 218. Certain pagan philosophers also perceived that riches are harmful to those who pursue wisdom, E. 92. A portion of them, E. 164. How great is the vanity of those who hunger after them, A. 725. They must be scorned by those attempting to imitate Christ, A. 726. They must not be cast away but stored up in heaven, A. 871. One must not trust in them, A. 746, 747. Paulinus possessed very considerable riches, V. 3.

Who should teach? E. 3.

Grief, joy, hope, and fear are the four principal incentives to vices, E. 237. Excessive grief is useless for the devoutly dead and harmful to the living, E. 70, 71. Proceeding from an affection of piety, it pierces the soul like a sword, E. 295, 296. The most immediate solace for the sorrows of this life is the resurrection, P. 672.

“Dominaedius”: Saint Felix was so called by Paulinus, as though “lord of the house,” E. 25, A. 874.

No one can serve two masters, E. 40, 163.

The dominion given to masters over the remaining animals, lest it become a cause of arrogance for human beings, is exposed to various adversities, E. 91.

DOMNIO: Paulinus supplies him with the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea to be sent on to Alypius, E. 10, 11.

A certain house obstructing the view of Saint Felix’s basilica was miraculously consumed by flames, E. 157 and following.

Pauline desires Augustine to be the exterminator of the Donatists, E. 36.

Why the Apostle calls the dead in Christ “sleeping,” E. 70. Sleeping beside tombs in order to obtain dreams, A. 895.

The two women grinding, one of whom is taken and the other left, are a type of the Synagogue and the Church, E. 51.

DUNGALUS wrote against Claudius of Turin, A. 790. His praises of Paulinus, ibid.

Who Dungalus was and when he wrote, Prolegomena and p. 447. His error, ibid.

DYNAMIUS, bishop of Angoulême, E. 279. A man of the greatest faith and piety, ibid.

## E

Ebromagus, a town belonging to Paulinus, E. 57, A. 878, V. 3. Where it was situated, A. 878, V. 4, 5. Paulinus commonly lived there, E. 57, V. 3. He abandoned it for the sake of paradise, E. 57, V. 3.

The district of Ebruica is distinct from that of Nervica, A. 885, 886.

The Church is Christ’s bride and the mother of the faithful, P. 126. As though a widow of the law, she married Christ, E. 122. The sinful woman who washed and anointed Christ’s feet is a type of her, called from the Gentiles, E. 140. Noah’s Ark is her type, E. 285. Why her children are said to have neither age nor sex, P. 605.

The church of Nola suffered persecution during the episcopate of Maximus, P. 391.

The two women grinding, one taken and the other left, are a type of the Church and the Synagogue, E. 51. Those who attempt to hinder the construction of churches, E. 110. Those who build them here prepare dwellings for themselves in heaven, E. 109.

The ancient custom of dedicating churches, 471.

Edicts condemning people to death were impressed on wax tablets, E. 319.

[Col. 1120] Ἐλάτη (“fir”) and *abies* (“fir”), and the fruit of palms, A. 893.

Eleazar, the son of Aaron, succeeded his father in the priesthood, E. 264.

Pauline proclaims and commends almsgiving, E. 72 and following. By the example of Lazarus and the Gospel’s rich banqueter, E. 74, P. 683. How useful it is to distribute alms to the poor, E. 208 and following, A. 894. How generously Saint Felix distributed them, P. 411. By them we escape the snares and traps of demons, E. 219, 220.

The prophet Elijah used sackcloth, E. 287, A. 924. He was carried away in a fiery chariot, P. 392, A. 929. The angel foretells to Zechariah that Saint John the Baptist will be like him, P. 337. In his prayers he closes and opens heaven, P. 615.

What Elizabeth, the mother of Saint John the Baptist, was like, P. 336. In old age she conceived miraculously, P. 337, 338. She joyfully went to meet Blessed Mary when Mary visited her, ibid.

Eulogies by the holy Fathers concerning Saint Paulinus of Nola, A. 773 through 789.

Elusa, Elusio, Elusa: a city, E. 7, A. 870. How far it is from Barcelona, ibid.

ENDELECHIUS, the rhetorician, A. 899.

SAINT ENDELECHIUS persuaded Paulinus to write the Panegyric to Theodosius, E. 175, A. 899. Whether he is the same as the saint to whom Paulinus wrote Letters 40 and 41, V. 46.

Enoch was transferred while still alive, P. 332.

Ephraim, son of the patriarch Jacob, is a type of the Gentiles who would be called to Christianity, E. 145.

EPHREM, bishop of Jerusalem, preserves the holy cross and every year at Easter presents it to the people for worship, E. 194. He does the same for pilgrims who come to Jerusalem out of devotion, ibid. He alone has the authority to give a portion of it to someone, ibid.

The temple of Diana at Ephesus, 454.

Ephesus, the city where John died, 450.

The feast of Christ’s Epiphany is extremely ancient, P. 143, A. 943, V. 72.

The bishops of Campania were especially well disposed toward Paulinus, E. 26. So too were the Africans, ibid. They are called fishers of human beings, E. 253, 254. What sort of bishop Paulinus was, A. 735 and following, V. 89, 90.

How highly Augustine esteemed Paulinus’s letters, E. 15, 16, E. 32. Sanctus and Amandus compiled a catalogue of them, E. 250.

Martinianus unwittingly preserved the Epistles of Blessed Paul the Apostle from the shipwreck, P. 579, 580. It is credible that Martinianus preserved the same letters together with his companions, P. 580.

The epitaph of Saint Clarus, composed by Paulinus and sent to Severus, E. 200, 201.

Pauline’s epithalamium for Julianus, the son of Bishop Memor, and for his bride, P. 602, A. 755, 756.

Feasts at the tombs of martyrs, P. 641, A. 761.

By the example of the Gospel’s rich banqueter and Eleazar, Paulinus commends mercy toward the poor, E. 76, P. 684.

Pammachius provided a banquet for all the poor of Rome in the basilica of Saint Peter, for the soul of his deceased wife, E. 71 and following.

The locust, grasshopper, caterpillar, and mildew mentioned by Joel are applied by Paulinus with great skill to the sufferings of the soul, E. 227, 228.

The story of Esther was painted in the portico of Saint Felix’s basilica, P. 647.

Pauline was a remarkable despiser of pagan learning, V. 6, 14.

Pauline introduces sayings of pagan men while asking pardon, E. 115. The agreeableness of their speech, not the ravings of their doctrine, deserves admiration, E. 90.

When and how paganism was pierced through, 449.

By obeying her husband, Eve overcame the troubles of marriage, P. 605.

The evangelical law dispelled the darkness of the old law, P. 676.

The four Evangelists are represented in Paulinus’s basilica by four springs flowing from a rock, E. 201, A. 912.

Why Paulinus calls Saint John’s Gospel “super-celestial,” E. 111. Its beginning is magnificently described by Paulinus, A. 769 and following. By this one passage all heretics who bark against Christ’s deity and humanity are refuted, E. 110, 111.

The deacons in Gaul during Paulinus’s time were heralds of the Gospel, E. 167, 168, V. 70.

The Eucharist, called *Eulogia*, A. 814. Bread, E. 30, A. 815, 816. Instituted under the symbol of the customary bread and wine, A. 815. Whether it is necessary for salvation for everyone, A. 892. In former times given to newly baptized children under the appearance of wine, A. 892, 893. It was also kept in churches in antiquity, E. 199, A. 905. On the altar beneath the cross, A. 905, 911. In a golden or silver tower, A. 905. Likewise in a dove, A. 909, 911.

EUCHERIUS withdrew with his wife Galla and daughter to the island of Lérins, E. 313, 314, V. 93. He writes to Paulinus, E. 313, [Col. 1121] V. 93. From Paulinus he receives a letter, ibid. He sends some of his own people to visit Paulinus, ibid. He becomes bishop of the Church of Lyon, V. 92. He urges his relative Valerianus toward perfection by the example of Paulinus, A. 783. His testimony concerning Paulinus’s works, ibid.

Eulogies were customarily sent to friends, E. 12, 15, 30, 37, A. 812, 814, V. 43. That there were two kinds, A. 814, V. 43. The Eucharist was given this name, A. 814. Thus the blessed bread distributed to the people in church on the Lord’s days was called, A. 814.

EVODIUS was sent by Alypius to Paulinus, E. 11.

EVODIUS, an African bishop, visited Paulinus at Nola, V. 82.

The relics of Euphemia, virgin and martyr, were deposited in Saint Felix’s basilica, P. 638, V. 75.

Pauline sends the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea to Alypius, E. 10, 11.

EUSEBIUS carried Paulinus’s letters to Jerome, A. 776.

EUSTOCHIUM, the sister of Paulina, the wife of Pammachius, E. 81.

To blind the fountain, P. 644, A. 762.

A most beautiful exhortation to pass this life holily and devoutly, A. 743 and following.

Paulinus wishes Sanemarius to be commended by Amandus to the presbyter EXSUPERIUS, E. 65.

EXSUPERIUS, bishop of Toulouse, E. 276, V. 86. A man of the greatest faith and piety, ibid.

King Hezekiah, having pleaded against the death already threatening him and lived fifteen years longer, declares that fate is nothing and that God can do everything, P. 555. Fortified by faith and prayer, he overthrew the camp of Sennacherib, P. 615.

The prophet Ezekiel foresaw the future resurrection of the dead, P. 676.

## F

Torches made from pine at weddings, 525.

To abandon one’s possessions is the first training of the Christian soldier, E. 151.

How Paulinus used his possessions for sacred purposes, A. 958, 959, V. 88, 89.

The famine during the three years of Elijah prefigured the hunger of the Gentiles for the food of life and faith in the Trinity, E. 122.

Here famine of bread is less to be feared than famine of the word of God, P. 682.

Pauline shows by the examples of John the Baptist and Christ that even distinction of family is praiseworthy among the saints, E. 179, 180. Concern for it does not exclude care of the soul, A. 740, 741.

What sort of companions are suitable for monks, E. 113.

Dangerous intimacies must be avoided, E. 3, V. 6.

The pagans believed that the Fates spin out the lives and affairs of human beings, E. 87. Among them was Plato, ibid.

Pauline shows that Fate and Fortune—powers to which certain philosophers entrusted the governance of some human affairs—are nothing, E. 85 and following. What this signifies, E. 88.

FELIX was of Eastern origin, P. 388, 389. He lived at Nola, distinguished by his wealth, P. ibid. He had a brother, Hermias, very unlike himself; therefore Paulinus compares them to Jacob and Esau, ibid. In the Church of Nola he became lector, exorcist, and priest, P. 391, A. 934. When Maximus, bishop of Nola, withdrew to avoid persecution, Felix became prominent, P. 391. Boldly resisting the persecutors, he was captured and cruelly imprisoned, P. 393. He was freed by an angel like the Apostle Saint Peter, P. 394. He found Bishop Maximus worn down by various hardships and resembling a corpse, P. 394, 395. A grape miraculously found restored him, P. 396. Felix entrusted him, after he had been lifted from the ground, to a certain holy woman, P. 397. After fulfilling these duties of charity, he was blessed by the same Maximus, P. 398. He hid for a short time in his own house, P. 399. Once peace had been restored to the Church, he exhorted Christians to constancy in the faith, P. 399, 350. Sought for death by the unbelievers, he was not recognized through God’s agency, P. 350. While avoiding the fury of the persecutors, he was divinely preserved by spiders’ webs, P. 351. He was buried at Nola amid a vast gathering of the people, P. 429, 430. In heaven he was adorned with a double crown, P. 430. The radiance shining from his body was an indication of a life well lived, P. 431. His tomb, adorned with five great basilicas, became renowned for miracles, P. ibid. He restored stolen oxen to a certain rustic who was grieving bitterly, and restored the man’s sight, weakened by excessive tears, P. 432 through 85, V. 432. The day of his birth was extremely dear to Paulinus, P. 558, 628. He saved Therdadius, whose eye was endangered by an iron hook driven into it, P. 561 through 99. He is compared to the patriarch Abraham, P. 389. He is compared to Isaiah interceding for King Hezekiah, P. 614. Likewise to Daniel in the lions’ den and to the three boys divinely preserved in the furnace, P. 617. Also to Moses’ staff devouring the magicians’ dragons, P. 618. How he subdued wild beasts and fires, P. 617. Through his merits flames and waters yield, P. 620. Ursus, the companion of the deacon Paschasius on his pilgrimage, was restored to health through him, E. 97. There Paulinus also attributes to him the fact that Martinianus, thrown from a mule, remained unharmed, P. 584. On what day his feast is celebrated, P. 380, 381. And with what great attendance and devotion of the people, P. 380, 381, 383. Demons are driven away at his tomb, P. 382 and following. Paulinus graphically describes the structure of his basilica, E. 203 and following, P. 156 and following, V. 66, 73 and following. The same fragment of the holy cross was preserved from flames, P. 622, V. 70. Likewise from a torrent, ibid. The principal author of Paulinus’s conversion, V. 8. Paulinus called him *Dominaedius*, that is, “lord of the house,” E. 26, A. 873. A martyr by will, P. 379, 381. He appeared to an old man endangered by a shipwreck, sitting at the steering-oar, E. 279.

FELIX, bishop of Bourges, made a sacred chest for preserving the Eucharist, A. 905.

Felix of Nola was worthy of the title of bishop, 484. He refused the episcopate, 517. Expeller of demons, 464. Renowned for miracles, 489. The opinion of others weakens this claim, ibid. He did not complete his martyrdom through bloodshed. A martyr without blood, 517. How great his veneration and the people’s attendance upon him were, 503. A feast day was assigned to him, 517. His tomb was opened, 538.

A certain woman fed Saint Felix while he was hiding in a cistern, though she did not know his hiding place, P. 407. Felix is also compared to the raven that fed Elijah and to Habakkuk feeding Daniel, ibid. An encomium of a wise and virtuous woman, E. 68.

Women were given masculine names because of their manly courage, E. 177, 189. How Christian women ought to adorn themselves, P. 603, 604. What sort of hair is fitting for them, E. 132. They are commanded to pray with covered heads, and why, E. 133, 134. Why they are forbidden to teach in church, ibid.

The windows through which death enters must be closed by the fear of God, E. 248.

The feasts of Christ’s Nativity, Epiphany, and Ascension were instituted in antiquity, P. 388. Why they are celebrated in the Church at distinct times, P. 626, V. 72.

Feast days in honor of the saints were instituted in antiquity, 516.

Pauline sends several fig-peckers to Gestidius, together with a poem excusing their small number, P. 328. He sends him oysters as well, with a poem, P. 329.

Pauline wisely explains the curse pronounced by the Lord upon the fig tree, E. 255, 256.

The fig tree on which Christ, when hungry, found no fruit is the Synagogue of the Jews, E. 256.

All the faithful are one body, and Christ is the head of this body, P. 605.

FIDELIS, mother of the boy Celsus, whom Paulinus honored with a panegyric, P. 665, 686.

Faith is weakened by desires, E. 153. It is greater than the law, E. 161. Its praise comes not from human beings but from God, ibid. It uproots the roots of sin, ibid. It is the fuel of good works and therefore must be preferred to mercy, E. 141. It is the bread of Christians, E. 56. Faith itself and the word of the cross are the evangelical needle, E. 176. If firm, it is the necessary expense for constructing the evangelical tower, E. 210. What it is, P. 674. It needs no weapons, P. 613. The excellence of Paulinus’s faith, A. 774, 785, 786, V. 15, 16. One who has faith without works is close to an unbeliever, E. 221. He announces the faith of Christ to the Morini and other barbarian nations, E. 98, 99, V. 125, 126. Through faith in the cross the kingdom of heaven is stormed, E. 190.

Pauline’s confidence arising from poverty, E. 56, V. 15, 16.

How the children of this age are wiser than the children of light, E. 4. The sons of Aaron offering strange fire are extinguished by divine fire, E. 110, 111. What sort of education of children Paulinus approves, E. 263.

Pauline shows from Scripture that one should weep with those who weep, E. 66.

Florentius, bishop of Cahors, deeply affects Paulinus through his letters, E. 253 and following, A. 770. Paulinus commends him, E. 254.

Florens: the relics of Saint Stephen, when offered, perform several miracles, A. 932. Churches were adorned with them, P. 386, A. 932. The tombs and relics of the saints, A. 932.

To lend to Christ, E. 118, A. 890.

The baptismal font was octagonal, signifying the mystery of the eighth day, the resurrection of Christ, A. 908. Description of the baptismal font of Saint Felix’s basilica, E. 198, 199.

Fountains for washing the mouth and hands at the entrance of temples, E. 73, 202, A. 882, 883, V. 75. Four springing from a rock, a hieroglyph of the Evangelists, E. 20, A. 912.

The opening of the evangelical needle is the way of the cross, E. 176.

Church doors were decorated with curtains, P. 386, 426, A. 386. With garlands and flowers, P. 931, A. 932.

What Fortune signifies, E. 50. How the pagans worshiped it as a goddess and depicted it, ibid. Paulinus shows that Fortune, together with Fate—which certain philosophers entrusted with the governance of human affairs—is nothing, E. 87 and following. He confirms the same through various examples drawn from Holy Scripture, P. 556.

Brotherhood: an assembly of brothers, P. 580, A. 910. Women’s foreheads covered with hair, not curled, E. 132, 133.

Pauline proscribes all cosmetics among Christian women, P. 603, 604.

How fleeing is said to take place in winter or on the Sabbath, E. 43.

Who must be fled from? E. 3.

Pauline had estates at Fundi in Latium, V. 4. There he built a basilica, E. 206, V. 77. Description of its construction, E. 207, 208, V. 77.

Frenzy is accorded divine honor by the pagans in an image, E. 90.

Gabriel, sent to Zechariah, announces that John the Baptist will be born from Elizabeth, P. 336, 338. He announces to Blessed Mary the Virgin that the Son of God will be incarnated from her, P. 338.

Galardo, a city four leagues from Chartres, A. 904. What should be noted there, ibid.

GALLA, the wife of Saint Eucherius, E. 313, V. 94. She withdrew with her husband Eucherius to the island of Lérins, ibid. She receives a letter from Paulinus, ibid.

The Galli were priests of Cybele, 453.

Pauline shows from Holy Scripture that one should rejoice with those who rejoice, E. 66.

Joy, grief, hope, and fear are the four principal incentives to vices, E. 237.

The treasury in temples, E. 213. Alms were stored in it, E. 213 and following, A. 918.

GELASIUS, a monk of Lérins under Saint Honoratus, E. 313. He was sent by the same Honoratus, then a presbyter, to Saint Paulinus, E. ibid.

GENESIUS, a citizen of Arles, E. 315, A. 928. In the flower of youth he entered military service, E. 315, A. 928. He performed the office of recorder, ibid. Refusing to receive the sacrilegious edicts of persecution, he cast the wax tablets at the judge’s feet and fled, E. 315. Avoiding persecution, he wandered through various places, ibid. Perceiving the danger of persecution to be imminent, he sought baptism, E. 316. Fleeing his executioner, he leapt into the Rhône as into another Jordan, to be mystically cleansed, E. 316. Having already crossed the river, he was beheaded and gained the martyr’s palm, E. 317, A. 928. The place of his passion, renowned for miracles, was adorned by the faithful with a double city, E. 316, 317. His relics were transferred from the other side of the river, E. 317. Paulinus describes the acts of his passion, E. 316, 317.

Other various GENESII, A. 928.

GENNADIUS’s index of the works of Paulinus, A. 784.

The Gentiles, who were to speak God’s praises, are prefigured in Balaam’s ass speaking with a human voice, E. 58.

A pagan ought to be distinguished from a Christian not only by faith but also by life, A. 731. Pagans think that the Fates spin out the lives and affairs of human beings, E. 88. They once fashioned gods and idols for themselves and worshiped them, ibid. In the Gospel Christ calls them dogs, E. 291.

Whether pagans can be said to accomplish any good by the light of nature alone, 522. By which emperors their rites were prohibited, 463.

GERMANUS was raised by the people to the episcopate, E. 128.

The body of GERVASIUS was discovered by Saint Ambrose, E. 206. His relics were enclosed in the altar of the basilica built by Paulinus at Fundi, ibid.

The Getae were converted to the faith by Nicetas, P. 421.

How the sword of sorrow passed through the soul of the Virgin Mary, E. 296, A. 927.

In Holy Scripture the sword of the Spirit is called the word of God, E. 9, 99.

The reward of heavenly glory is to be bestowed on victors, E. 91.

The GNOSTICS are refuted by the beginning of Saint John’s Gospel, E. 111.

The Goths devastate Italy, P. 607 and following. Their army was routed, and their king killed through the prayers of the saints, P. 661, A. 766.

The Goths were defeated in Italy in the year 405, 513.

How necessary divine grace is to those walking in virtue, E. 246 and following. What it is, P. 671, 672. Its freedom is to be preferred to the severity of the law, E. 134. Its efficacy, V. 8, 15. Paulinus prays to God for the grace by which he may avoid sins, P. 331, 332.

Paulinus’s gratitude toward his benefactors, V. 8.

The Greeks were infected with Egyptian rites, 461. Their madness concerning the article on the Holy Spirit, 459.

Gregory of Tours, by opening Holy Scripture, understood that his adversary Leudastes was to be drowned, A. 897.

## H

HADRIAN, the emperor, placed an image of Jupiter on Mount Calvary in order to eradicate the memory of Christ’s Passion, E. 190. He profaned Bethlehem with a shrine of Adonis, ibid.

The garments and frenzy of the haruspices, 461.

[Col. 1124] Hebromagus, Paulinus’s native place, 529.

Ivy was used to crown the head in Dionysiac festivals, 465.

Heretics who bark against both Christ’s divinity and his humanity are refuted at the beginning of John’s Gospel, E. 113. How they are said by blessed Paul, Colossians 2:18, “not to hold fast to the head,” E. 292.

Harmony of the world, P. 626, A. 944. God is its arranger, ibid.

**HELENA**, mother of Constantine, reigning jointly with her son as Augusta, E. 191. She cleanses the holy places profaned with idols by the emperor Hadrian and adorns them with basilicas, E. ibid., A. 904. How she found Christ’s cross and by what means recognized it, ibid.

**HERACLIUS**, when the sacred Scriptures were opened, understood that he was to winter in Albania, A. 898.

How hedgehogs protect themselves against pursuers, E. 44. How we may become spiritual, ibid.

**HERMIAS**, father of Saint Felix, was a Syrian, P. 390.

**HERMIAS**, brother of Saint Felix, devoted to the world, follows a course entirely different from Saint Felix, P. 390. He is compared with Esau, ibid.

Herod, boasting in royal clothing, is punished by God, P. 604.

How Herodias, the dancing girl, brought about the death of Saint John the Baptist, ibid.

The Ebro, a river of Spain flowing into the Tyrrhenian Sea, P. 372.

Whose flight winter should impede, E. 43.

Hierapolis, a city of Phrygia where Philip was buried, 450.

**HIERONYMUS** teaches Paulinus and Therasia how they ought to conduct themselves, A. 774, V. 6, 21. He writes to the same man, A. 774–776. He receives letters and little gifts from him, A. 776, V. 44. The panegyric of Theodosius, A. 774, V. 52. He honorably receives Vigilantius, who had been commended to him by Paulinus, V. 52. He enters into controversy with him, ibid. He replies to the book published against him, ibid. He urges Julian toward perfection by the example of Paulinus, A. 775. His eulogy of Paulinus, A. 774–776.

Hierotheca, or sacred tower in which the Lord’s body was kept, A. 906.

Jerusalem called “daughter of Zion” by Paulinus, E. 184.

Several cities of Spain listed, P. 371. Paulinus remains there for some time after baptism, E. 66, P. 371, V. 25, 27.

Ἥλιος, *hēlios*, “sun” in Greek: whether it was derived from the prophet Elijah, A. 929.

Kids and lambs, a hieroglyph of the reprobate and the righteous, E. 107.

Holofernes is beheaded by Judith, P. 613.

In Genesis, man is sometimes called the image of God and sometimes the likeness of God, E. 153. After the Fall he was punished less severely by God than the devil, E. 146, 147. How, having been bound through Adam, he is released through Christ, E. 241. Unless he gives himself to God, he sells himself to the devil, E. 110. In what his true rest consists, E. 282, 283. By reason he rules the other animals, E. 90. So that he may not become proud because of this, he is exercised by adversities of various kinds, ibid. For all spiritual and bodily gifts, he has nothing more pleasing to repay God, their giver, than himself, E. 92. Turning away from God’s service, he is swallowed up in countless whirlpools of error, E. 93, A. 908. Clinging to the true God, he can overcome both nature and himself, P. 555. Since he consists of body and soul, he must also be nourished with a twofold food, E. 169. Why he is to be resurrected before the other creatures on the last day of judgment, P. 676, 677. Faith is the Christian’s bread, E. 56.

The ruin of the outer man is the resurrection of the inner man, and conversely, E. 190. To change a human being is God’s work, E. 232. Paulinus writes most beautifully to Severus about the inner and outer man, E. 188 ff.

**HONORATUS**, priest and abbot of the monastery of Lérins, E. 313, 314, V. 93. He sends religious men to Nola with letters to visit Paulinus, P. 313, V. 93. He is appointed bishop of the church of Arles, V. 93.

The age of the emperor Honorius, 514.

Horus, son of Isis, 456.

The gardener is called the Holy Spirit, E. 238.

A garden once stood where the basilica of Saint Felix now stands, E. 162, 163.

The enemy is not to be feared in wartime, but God is, P. 610.

Human judgments are to be considered nothing in comparison with divine judgments, P. 373 ff. Contempt for them was Saint Paulinus’ virtue, V. 24.

The human race, infected with the taint of sin, could be healed by Christ alone, E. 59.

That the humble are exalted is shown by the example of Joseph, P. 594. Christ is a refuge for them, E. 44. The humble heart is Christ’s heart, E. 121.

Humility is a basket of dung that makes a sterile tree fruitful, E. 176, 263. Its sign is mortification of the body, E. 62. Above all by it we become imitators of Christ, E. 64. By the same virtue the devil was overcome, E. 230. What it can accomplish before God is shown by the example of the Gospel publican, [Col. 1125] E. 290. It is the guardian of the virtues, A. 737. It makes us pleasing not only to God but also to human beings, A. 737. If feigned, it is detestable, ibid. Paulinus seeks opportunities for it everywhere, V. 18 ff. For this reason he declines the explanation of the patriarchs’ blessings proposed to him by Desiderius, and explains the curse inflicted by the Lord on the fig tree, E. 255 ff. Saint Felix likewise declines the bishopric of Nola, P. 410. There is a certain evil humility and a good pride, E. 62, 63.

## I

**IA**, daughter of the bishop Aemilius, P. 607, 608, A. 944, 945. Wife of Julian, son of Memor, P. 607, A. 944. Paulinus adorns her with an epithalamium, P. 602.

Idols are erected by the emperor Hadrian at the places of Christ’s birth and Passion, E. 190, 191. They were once devised by pagans and worshiped with divine honors, E. 88. In the presence of the relics of the saints they fall silent, P. 662.

Paulinus rebukes idolaters, E. 40.

The cause of idolatry is neglect of God, E. 91.

The excesses of idolatry, 461.

God is consuming and illuminating fire, E. 109. What is alien to God is avarice, the desire of the eyes, cravings, and worldly allurements, ibid. Who are said to kindle what is alien to the Lord? E. 263. The fire that Christ came to cast upon the earth enlightens our senses and burns away vices, E. 263. It is called the word of God in the sacred Scriptures, E. 298. After this life it will test each person’s work, P. 346. A fire consuming a house near the basilica of Saint Felix was extinguished by a fragment of the holy cross, P. 649, 650 ff. The fire of purgatory, E. 172, P. 686.

The sign “I.H.,” 18. Also the sign of the name Jesus, A. 898.

Ilerda, a city of Spain, P. 371.

Only the image of God remained in Adam, E. 153, A. 897. The image of Christ carrying the sheep on his shoulders in sacred chalices, A. 877, 878. Also the image of Christ standing upon the rock from which four rivers flow, E. 203, A. 912. Likewise formerly represented in the form of a lamb, E. 203, A. 908. The image of a dove pouring water over the lamb, that is, of the Holy Spirit over Christ, E. 207, A. 920. The images of lambs signify either the faithful or the newly baptized, A. 908. Images of the saints in Paulinus’ time were also fashioned in human form, E. 29, A. 911, and painted on the curtains of churches, A. 932. When Severus asks for an image of Paulinus, Paulinus cleverly evades the request by interpreting it as a request for the inner man, E. 186, 187 ff., V. 73.

Immunity of churches, 474. Also the extent to which it was granted by the emperors, 474.

The impious will not rise to be judged but to be punished, P. 346.

Impluvium: what part of a church was it? P. 646, A. 916.

The incarnation of the Word is the foolishness of this world’s wisdom, E. 160. How Victricius preached its mystery to the Gentiles, E. 97, 98, 226. To believe it is the price of the evangelical pearl, E. 160. The site of it is honored by a basilica built by Saint Helena, E. 188, A. 904.

A fire extinguished through the merits of Saint Felix, P. 621, 622; by the power of the holy cross, P. 649, 650. A house obstructing the view of Saint Felix’s basilica is consumed by fire, not without a miracle, P. 622, V. 70.

To become drunk for sobriety, E. 83, A. 884.

The punishments of hell are expressed not only in the poets’ tales but also affirmed by the Gospel, P. 681–683.

The dead who lack faith are to be mourned, P. 679. Paulinus rebukes the madness of the unbelievers persecuting Saint Felix, P. 392. A Christian who has faith without works is close to an unbeliever, E. 222, A. 732.

Paulinus’ remarkably gentle and kindly character, V. 8.

To love an enemy is heavenly vengeance, E. 159, 162. The enemies of man are various, E. 157. Christ taught us to overcome spiritual and invisible enemies, E. 224. They are overcome by the power of the cross and of the Crucified One, E. 262, 263.

Iniquity is the glory of the wicked, E. 131. It cannot accomplish as much against the patronage of the saints as justice can in defending sinners, E. 64, 65.

Who is truly called innocent, A. 730.

Innocence is especially necessary for those who desire to live holily, ibid.

Paulinus sends Severus the inscriptions and paintings of his basilicas, E. 202 ff. He sends inscriptions to be affixed to the images of Saint Martin and Paulinus painted in the baptistery built by Severus, E. 195, 196.

The snares of demons must be avoided with the greatest caution, E. 217.

The intercession of the saints, P. 616.

“In the dining room Coan, in the bedroom Nola”: an old riddle explained, 460.

Envy and hatred are seeds of many sins, A. 730. They are nourished by presence but removed by absence, E. 25.

Invocation of the saints, P. 379, 380, 685, 686.

God’s anger proceeds from mercy, E. 180. By it one person is punished as an example to others, a pious act, E. 100.

[Col. 1126] Isaac, destined for sacrifice, a type of Christ, E. 181, 229.

What Isaiah threatens those excessively devoted to luxury in clothing, P. 602. His prophecy concerning John the Baptist, P. 345.

The priests and worshipers of Isis and Serapis, with shaven heads, 456.

Israel and Israelite: “seeing God,” E. 284.

So that the Israelites would not forget God’s commandments, they wore on the fringes of their garments insignia with scarlet and hyacinth-colored thread.

Paulinus wishes himself a prosperous journey by land and sea when he is going to visit Saint Felix’s tomb, P. 379.

Ithamar, son of Aaron, succeeded his father in the priesthood, E. 216.

Ἰχθύς, “fish”: Christ, A. 880, 881.

## J

The patriarch Jacob, after all his possessions and impediments have been set aside, wrestling with God, is to be imitated by Christ’s soldier, E. 152. Serving as a servant, he is a type of Christ, E. 229. In honorably burying his deceased wife, what he prophetically signified, E. 68.

The doors of churches adorned with curtains, P. 386, 426; with garlands and flowers, P. 386, A. 932.

Januarius and Martin appear to the dying Paulinus, A. 958.

Fasting, by which we abstain from everything forbidden, is the garment of the soul, E. 176. How Paulinus observed the Lenten fast, E. 85. The fast of vigils, P. 562. It nourishes the soul through the body, E. 67. It is an aid, not the perfection of holiness, A. 778. What kind is praised, ibid. It assists every virtue without exception, A. 779. It fosters chastity, P. 590.

Jerusalem: see Hierusalem.

The name of Jesus is to be worshiped by all, A. 752, 753. How many miracles he performed, A. 752.

**JOHN THE BAPTIST** used a hair shirt, E. 174, 175, A. 925. By his example Paulinus shows that noble lineage is praiseworthy even in the saints, E. 179. He is celebrated in a poem by Paulinus, P. 336 ff. God gave him his name, P. 337. An angel foretells to Zechariah the course of his life, ibid. ff. He prophesies in his mother’s womb, P. 339. He is born, P. ibid. When a dispute arises between his mother and relatives over naming him, his father settles it, P. 340. His infancy is grave and serious, ibid. What his boyhood was like, ibid. When he is more advanced in age, he seeks solitude, P. 341. His food and clothing, ibid. He threatens to leave the solitude so that he may baptize in the Jordan, P. 341, 342. Preaching around the Jordan, he baptizes in it, ibid. Isaiah the prophet’s prophecy concerning him, P. 343. His praise confirmed by Christ’s own words, ibid. His relics are deposited in the basilica of Saint Felix, P. 638.

**JOHN**, by the evangelical swiftness with which he outran Peter to Christ’s tomb, prefigured the spiritual swiftness by which he surpasses the other evangelists, E. 110. Left by the dying Christ to the Virgin Mother of God as a consolation, he demonstrates that she neither had nor has sons besides Christ, E. 296. He wrote the Gospel last, ibid. He rests at Ephesus, P. 659.

John, bishop of Jerusalem, sends Paulinus a portion of the wood of the holy cross, E. 190.

John, bishop of Naples, appears to Paulinus after the latter has become blessed, A. 962, V. 96.

John imposed silence on the oracle of Ephesian Diana, 454. He died at Ephesus, 450.

The prophet Job, rich and perfect, F. 152, 153. He shows the usefulness of humility by his example, E. 179. Paulinus wisely explains why so many evils befell him, E. 83. How he triumphed over the devil, E. 77. When tested, he is represented in a painting in the portico of Saint Felix’s basilica, P. 647.

Jonah, swallowed by the sea creature and cast alive onto the land on the third day, is a type of the suffering and rising Christ, E. 283. Through him it is shown that God, not fate, is the governor of all things, P. 556, 557. Martinianus, endangered at sea, is compared with him, P. 575, 576.

The Jordan, providing passage for the people of Israel, is described by Paulinus and painted in the porticoes of Saint Felix’s basilica, P. 641.

Why Joseph of Arimathea is named in the Gospel before the other rich men, E. 78.

The shipwrecked Martinianus is compared with the patriarch Joseph fleeing from a woman after leaving his garment behind, P. 576. The son of Cytherius, dedicated to God, is compared with Joseph sold into Egypt, P. 594.

The patriarch Joseph, transformed into Serapis by Egyptian superstition, 454.

Joshua, trusting in God and making the sun stand still at his command, showed that everything is subject to God, not to fate, P. 556. How he conquered Jericho, P. 612.

Jovinian equated marital intercourse with continence, A. 741.

Hadrian, the emperor, places a statue of Jupiter on Mount Calvary to eradicate the memory of Christ’s Passion, E. 190, A. 903, 904.

**JOVIUS**, a relative of Saint Paulinus, P. 557. Most distinguished by birth, offices, and knowledge of literature, E. 92, 94, V. 59. Ascribing, with certain philosophers, the governance of some human affairs to the necessity of Fate and Fortune, he is taught by Paulinus that all things are subject to divine Providence, E. 85 ff., V. 59. He is also urged by Paulinus to abandon the writings of the philosophers and turn to reading sacred Scripture, E. 81, P. 553, 554 ff., V. 61.

Judas the traitor, more agitated at Mary anointing Christ, betrays his own perfidy, E. 140, 141. Why did Christ receive a kiss from him? E. 158. He had no share in the price of Christ’s blood, E. 141.

Judas, Thaddaeus, and Lebbaeus are synonyms, 450.

The Jews are enemies of Christ’s resurrection and of the holy cross, E. 192. Once called the people of God, P. 556. Christ’s miracles moved them not to believe but to blaspheme, E. 289. By God’s just judgment they were scattered among all nations, E. 290. How, in Romans 11:28, they are called enemies of God and beloved, E. 291. They are rebuked for not believing the prophets, P. 339. By eating unleavened bread at Passover, they recall to mind the flight of their fathers from Egypt, P. 609. They and the schismatics perish in a shipwreck while the Christians are saved, P. 573. They mourn Paulinus’ death; Manasseh is their type, E. 145. Their synagogue is mystically represented by the fig tree struck by Christ’s curse because it bore no fruit, E. 256.

The salutary remembrance of the final judgment, P. 374, 375. Its ancient likeness displayed in Martinianus’ shipwreck, P. 574.

After Judith killed Holofernes, she put the army to flight, P. 575, 576. Her story is painted in the portico of Saint Felix’s basilica, P. 634.

Why the Lord’s yoke is called easy and his burden light, E. 64, 117, 118.

**JULIAN**, a member of Saint Paulinus’ household, E. 9, V. 42. He delivered Alypius’ letter to Paulinus, ibid.

**JULIAN**, son of the bishop Memor, A. 755, 756. Friend of Augustine and Paulinus, P. 602, A. 755, 756, V. 85, 91. A cleric of lower rank, P. 604. He is already entering marriage, P. 604, V. 85. He becomes a deacon, A. 755. Infected with the Pelagian error and a bitter opponent of Augustine, ibid. He is expelled from his see because of the Pelagian heresy, V. 92.

Jupiter Ammon, a native deity among the Egyptians, 451. Driven from Crete while Titus preached the Gospel, ibid. King of Crete, where he was buried and counted among the gods by the pagans, 452.

One must abstain from oaths, A. 880.

**JUSTINUS**, a priest, rests in the village of Sexciacum, V. 122. Many miracles occur at his tomb, ibid.

Justice is stronger in defending sinners than iniquity is against the patronage of the saints, E. 64, 65. Past justice should make no one more lenient, A. 741. He who shakes off its yoke serves every baseness, E. 662.

The empress Justina, filled with hatred toward Ambrose, is restrained in her fury when she sees the miracle of the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius discovered by Ambrose, 468.

A righteous person who has died is in refreshment but leaves grief to the survivors, E. 69. Who the righteous are in Matthew 9:13 whom Christ says he did not come to seek, F. 989. Paulinus wisely explains why evils happen to them, E. 81.

**JUSTUS AND PASTOR**, martyrs, rest at Complutum, A. 768.

## K

Kethem: a lump or mass of gold, A. 891.

## L

Labara bearing the monogram of Christ’s name, 482.

The form of the labarum, 483.

The lips of God are the two Testaments, E. 76.

Milk and wine given to the newly baptized, A. 892, 893.

Λαχανίζειν (*lachanizein*), “to eat vegetables”; *lachanissare*, A. 919.

Excessive tears are useless for the piously dead and harmful to the living, E. 70. What sort of tears befit a Christian, P. 680. Paulinus desires for himself the gift of tears to wash away the filth of sins, E. 240. To what extent it is permissible to accompany the dead with tears, E. 68.

Joy at the death of a righteous person is more pleasing to God than complaining sorrow, E. 70.

In ancient times lamps were also hung in churches, P. 562. A beautiful description of glass lamps customarily hung in churches, P. 562 ff.

In Paulinus’ time lamps were also hung beside the altar, P. 474.

Lebbaeus, Thaddaeus, and Judas are synonyms, E. 450.

**LAMPIUS**, bishop of Barcelona, initiates Paulinus into the priesthood, E. 11, V. 27.

Paulinus prays to be preserved from lust, P. 328.

The thief crucified with Christ, believing in Christ, attains salvation, E. 174, 17. His faith is praised, A. 774, V. 15, 16.

Lauah, “to lend,” A. 934.

Paulinus chastises those who praise him, E. 240, V. 38, 46, 47.

What the self-praise of Paulinus’ works consists in, A. 774, 775, 777, 788, 797, V. 4, 5, 6. Paulinus despises self-praise, [Col. 1128] E. 240. He elaborately celebrates Melania’s praises, E. 180, 265, 266, V. 85, and those of her only son, already dead, E. 265, 266, V. 85. Whoever desires to be truly praiseworthy should despise human praise, A. 737. He fears it, V. 38. He uses the praise attributed to him as an occasion for humility, E. 20, 21, 245.

The antitheses of the Gospel account of Lazarus and the rich man, P. 683.

Lengo, a town belonging to Paulinus, A. 886, V. 4.

The evangelical law dispelled the darkness of the old law, P. 678, 679. It is inferior to faith, E. 164. It breaks off the branches of sin, ibid. Freedom of grace is to be preferred to the austerity of the law, E. 134. Good works must also be added to observance of it, E. 224. The Law and the Prophets are contained in this one commandment: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them,” A. 734. What they could not accomplish is carried out by the Son of God, P. 668.

Paulinus wonderfully praises Pammachius’ generosity toward the poor, E. 72 ff.; what in it is praiseworthy and what blameworthy, E. 75.

True freedom is not to serve sins, A. 739.

Fear of the Lord drives out lust, E. 232.

Sacred books kept in churches in ancient times, E. 203, 206, A. 913, 914, 917.

**LICENTIUS**, son of Romanianus, had Augustine as his teacher in literature, E. 37, 38. In prose and verse Augustine and Paulinus urge him to despise the world and dedicate himself to Christ, E. 37 ff.

The thresholds of basilicas greeted by prostrate pilgrims and worshiped with kisses, P. 383, 434. Adorned with curtains, P. 386, 426, A. 930, 931; with garlands and flowers, P. 386, A. 938.

The outermost line, E. 92, A. 885.

A man’s tongue is a mirror of his mind, E. 66. Its careful guarding is especially necessary, E. 75. Paulinus commends this to Celancia, A. 770.

The smoking flax, E. 24, A. 813.

Paulinus most beautifully praises Aprus’ letters, breathing the power and sweetness of divine grace, E. 259 ff. Paulinus’ letters are praised by Augustine, E. 16, 17, 31, V. 35, and by Jerome, A. 774, 775, V. 40.

Paul makes his body livid, E. 158.

The holy places profaned with idols by the emperor Hadrian are cleansed and adorned with basilicas by Saint Helena, mother of Constantine, E. 191. The site of the basilica of Christ’s Ascension, from which he ascended after being taken up in a cloud, cannot be paved, E. 192.

The locust, caterpillar, grub, and blight listed by Joel are splendidly applied by Paulinus to the sufferings of the soul, E. 238, 239.

Lot, rich and perfect, E. 150, 151. How he escaped the fire of the Pentapolis, E. 78, P. 615. He saved the city of Segor by his prayers, P. 615.

All the forms of temporal goods are Lotophagi for us, E. 91.

A description of lamps, called *lumiere* in Italian, made at Milan with remarkable craftsmanship, 474.

Groves notable in ancient times for superstition, 461.

Luconiacus, Lugagnac, A. 878, 879.

**LUKE**, twice a physician, P. 637. Called by a great name, E. 206. Why? A. 916. Whether he was a martyr, A. 916, 617. His relics are kept at Antioch and Ostia, P. 659, A. 764, and also in the basilica of Saint Felix, P. 637. They were brought into a basilica founded by Paulinus, E. 206. *Luca*, “ox,” A. 918.

Lucretia, not Tanaquil, should be called Paulinus’ wife, P. 30.

To what extent it is permissible to mourn the dead, E. 71, 7.

Lights are kept burning day and night in churches, P. 386, 636, A. 932, 933.

Luxury, pleasure, and avarice are the sources of all evils, P. 342. Christians must avoid luxury in clothing, P. 603. Paulinus teaches this by the example of the first-created humans and Rebecca, P. 604. What Isaiah threatens those excessively devoted to it, P. 603.

## M

**MACARIUS**: who was he? A. 925. Friend of Rufinus, A. 922. Paulinus asks him to protect Secundinianus from the importunity of certain people, E. 277, 286, 287.

**MACRINA**, a virgin and sister of Gregory of Nyssa, wore a fragment of the holy cross around her neck, A. 926.

Just as evils are forbidden, so goods are commanded, A. 729. Evil deeds of one’s neighbors, once heard, should be committed to oblivion, P. 372.

Paulinus wisely explains the curse inflicted by the Lord on the fig tree, E. 255, 256.

Manasseh, a type of the Jews, E. 145.

Those who do not observe God’s commandments neither honor nor fear him, A. 729. God commands a human being to observe them so that he may have grounds for rewarding him, ibid. Their observance is enjoined on all, A. 739. There are two kinds: one forbids evils, the other commands goods, ibid. They must not merely be committed to memory but also fulfilled in action, A. 734. Paulinus rebukes those who babble that they are impossible, ibid.

**MANICHAEUS**, denier of the true Creator and inventor of a false one, is crushed at the beginning of Saint John’s Gospel, [Col. 1129] E. 111. He condemns marriage, A. 742.

Mannus, A. 720.

A hand extended from a cloud signifies God the Father, A. 908. In greeting one another and departing, the ancients customarily gave one another their hands, P. 569, A. 959. They also laid a hand on the head of those being blessed, P. 400.

**MARCELLA** made great progress in the practice of piety through tribulations, A. 717. Paulinus compares her with the holy widows Judith and Anna, A. 727. An epitome of her life, V. 137.

**MARCELLINUS**, consul and grandfather of Saint Melania, E. 179, A. 909.

**MARCION**, distinguishing the God of the Law from the God of the Gospel, is extinguished at the beginning of Saint John’s Gospel, E. 110, 111.

Mark rests at Alexandria, P. 659.

Mark, pastor at Alexandria, underwent martyrdom there and received his burial place there, 451.

The Red Sea, providing a passage for the people of Israel and swallowing the Egyptians, proves that the governance of all things is to be attributed to God, not to fate, P. 556.

The sea of the holy table: what is it? P. 639, A. 946.

The evangelical pearl, to be acquired by the expenditure of all possessions, is Christ, E. 136.

**MARIA**, the Virgin, is greeted by the angel Gabriel and is foretold to become the mother of the Son of God, P. 330. She visits her kinswoman Elizabeth, ibid. Entrusted by the dying Christ to John as his mother, she is shown to have had and to have no children besides Christ, E. 295. When the sword pierced her soul, in accordance with Simeon’s prophecy, E. 94, 295.

How husband and wife ought to conduct themselves and how they should order their household, P. 602 ff. A husband does not have authority over his own body, A. 742. He is to be honored by his wife, A. 741. He should love his wife, P. 604.

The famous baths of Marojalica, P. 372.

**MARRACINUS**, a member of Severus’ household, E. 6. He entrusted letters from Severus to Paulinus to Soriano for delivery, and why, E. 113, V. 62, 66. Paulinus censures him, E. 113, 114, V. 62, 66.

**MARTINIANUS**, shipwrecked after Cytherius’ letters were lost at sea, comes to Paulinus, P. 170, 171. Sleeping in the ship like Jonah, he is awakened by the cries of those perishing, P. 574. How he escaped imminent death, P. 575. He is compared with the patriarch Joseph fleeing from a woman, ibid. He is awakened near the harbor and is astonished to find the letters of blessed Paul the apostle in his possession, P. 577. He reaches Massilia, P. 578. Why, although he had suffered shipwreck, he again entrusted himself to the sea, P. 579. He reaches Centumcellae safely, P. 580. From there he is carried to the harbor of Pharos and proceeds on foot to Rome, ibid. He is received amicably by the brothers, ibid. Paulinus clothes him in the garments of his fellow guest Theridius, ibid. He travels toward Capua along the Appian Way, P. 580, 581. From there, going on to Saint Felix, he is thrown unharmed from the mule on which he was riding, P. 582. Saint Paulinus receives him at Nola with great affection, P. 513, V. 66.

**MARTIN OF TOURS** was thrown into prison because he no longer wished to serve under arms, V. 123. At Vienne he sees Victricius and Paulinus, E. 101, 124. At Chartres he sees the same bishops, Victricius and Valentinian, V. 124. He heals a girl, ibid., and Paulinus, who was suffering from an eye ailment, A. 781, V. 9. Sulpicius Severus frequently visits him at Tours, E. 94. He rests in Gaul, P. 660. He appears to the dying Paulinus, A. 958. His Life, written by Severus, E. 119, 889. Paulinus circulates it at Rome, E. 185, A. 900, V. 55, and throughout Italy and Illyria, A. 781, V. 55. His likeness is painted in the baptistery built by Severus and adorned with inscriptions by Paulinus, E. 195, 196.

At what time Bishop Martin flourished and died in Gaul, P. 459.

A martyr is one who suffers much for Christ, even if he is not killed, E. 279. Why Paulinus calls Saint Felix a martyr without bloodshed, P. 379, 382. Paulinus invites the martyrs to celebrate jointly the feast of Saint Felix, P. 630. They are painted in the central position in the portico of Saint Felix’s basilica, P. 646. As the stars adorn heaven, so the martyrs’ bodies adorn the earth, E. 165. Paulinus visits their memorials and tombs at Rome, E. 92, 264, V. 42. Why Paulinus placed his dead son in their tombs, P. 686. Various customs for adorning their tombs on their feasts, A. 932.

*Martyr*, Greek; in Latin, “witness,” 516.

Martyrs who suffered at Utica, 459.

In the primitive Church the name “martyr” was also given to those who survived tortures, 466.

Countless assemblies of martyrs, even in a single city, 514. Their bodies or bones were once customarily placed beneath every altar, 471.

Martyrdom is equivalent to baptism, E. 315. The martyrdom of Saint Genesius of Arles, E. 314 ff. Likewise that of Victricius, who transferred from Caesar’s camp to Christ’s camp, E. 117 ff.

Massilia, a Greek colony, receives and supports Martinianus and his fellow shipwreck survivors, P. 593.

The apostle Paul does not prohibit marriage, although he prefers chastity, A. 742. God instituted it, P. 602. Its various cares are described by Paulinus, P. 426, 427.

**MATTHEW** rests among the Parthians, P. 659.

Matthew’s evangelization and death, 451. His bones were transferred to the city of Naddavera in Parthia, ibid. He wrote the Gospel in the Hebrew language, ibid.

Paulinus’ morning prayer to God, P. 330. Another prayer, P. 330.

**MAXIMUS**, bishop of Nola, avoids persecution, P. 391, 392. Hiding in the mountains, he suffers terribly, P. 395. Found by Felix resembling a corpse, he is restored by a miraculously discovered grape, P. 395, 396. He explains to Saint Felix why he avoided his persecutors, P. 398. The same Saint Felix carries him on his shoulders and entrusts him to a certain woman, ibid. He blesses the same Saint Felix, P. 399. He dies an old man, P. 406.

Physicians opposed to medicine, 500.

The uncertainty of medicines and remedies; complaints against both this uncertainty and these remedies, 500.

What the true physician and true medicine are, 500.

The Medulli, a people, A. 938.

**MELANIA**, called *Melanius* on account of her virtue, E. 189, 402, A. 922. Related by blood to Paulinus, V. 2. He calls her holy, E. 174, 178. When she returned from Jerusalem, E. 183, 184. Paulinus elaborately celebrates her praises, E. 179 ff., 265, 266, V. 179. Born of consular stock, E. 85, A. 900. She marries while still a young woman, E. 179. She suffers several miscarriages, ibid. Within one year she is deprived of her husband and two sons, ibid. She is chastised by God so that she may be crowned, E. 180. She entrusts her surviving son not to her relatives but to God, E. 181. How she is compared with Anna, the mother of Samuel, E. 180. The devil tries in various ways to impede her journey to Jerusalem, E. 181, 182. While supporting Catholics driven out by the Arians, what she suffers, E. 182. During the Arian persecution she feeds five thousand monks with her own provisions for three days, E. 183. Returning, she enters Naples riding a donkey and is received there by her children and grandchildren, ibid. With what pomp she comes to Nola to visit Paulinus, ibid. Her exercises of piety are recounted, E. 183. She brings Paulinus a fragment of the wood of the holy cross received from John, bishop of Jerusalem, E. 192, 193. Augustine praises her steadfastness in the death of her only son in letters written to Paulinus, ibid. The son himself is also greatly praised by Augustine and Paulinus, E. 267, V. 85.

Melotes, E. 286, A. 924.

Melus, A. 924.

**MEMOR**: how he is called both the son and the brother of Aemilius by Paulinus, P. 606. Paulinus writes an epithalamium for his son Julian, P. 602.

The ancient custom of visiting the memorials of the apostles and martyrs, E. 92, 196, 199, 255, 265, 264, V. 42.

Lying must be avoided, A. 737.

The frauds of beggars who pretend to be monks or shipwreck survivors, P. 581.

The table in churches is the altar, P. 643, A. 761. The treasury is a chest, A. 918. Paulinus’ table is humble and very frugal, V. 33, 34. On whose authority and why the table of the poor is placed in the courts of the Lord’s house, E. 213.

**MEROPIUS**, Paulinus’ first name, E. 239.

**MEROVEUS**, when the sacred books were opened, understood that destruction threatened him, A. 897.

Metatorium: what is it? A. 914.

Fear, hope, joy, and grief are the four principal incentives of the vices, E. 39.

A certain distinguished soldier is admirably urged by Paulinus to pass from the profane service of Caesar to Christ’s sacred warfare, E. 162 ff.

The armor of the Christian soldier, E. 5.

*Milium* used for a mile, or a thousand paces, 547.

Paulinus beautifully derives the miracle of Christ’s feeding many thousands in the desert with five loaves and two fish, E. 72. The immense miracles by which an old man whom God named Victor was saved from shipwreck are described by Paulinus, E. 278 ff. The miracles of both the Old and New Testaments most clearly declare that all things are subject to God, not to fate, P. 556. Christ’s miracles moved the Jews not to believe but to blaspheme, E. 289. Numerous miracles occurred during the transfer of the relics of Saints Andrew and Timothy to Constantinople, P. 659. For those customarily performed at Saint Felix’s tomb, see Saint Felix. Miracles performed through flowers offered to the relics of Saint Stephen, A. 932.

Mercy is to be placed after faith, because faith is the source of good works, E. 140, A. 894. Paulinus extols God’s wondrous mercy, P. 344. Christ is anointed and fed by works of mercy, E. 117, A. 889. Paulinus commends them brilliantly, E. 207 ff.

**MISILINUS**, a priest, rests at Talva, V. 122. At his tomb remarkable miracles are performed, ibid.

[Col. 1131] Paulinus considers embracing monasticism, V. 11, 14.

Paulinus vividly depicts wandering monks, A. 939. The conduct of monks and dissolute men is elegantly described, E. 113, 114. Their former inner clothing, the hair shirt, E. 175, A. 899. Melania feeds five thousand monks with her own provisions during the Arian persecution, E. 181. What kind of associates are suitable for them, E. 113.

Monasteries founded by Victricius, bishop of Rouen, E. 98.

What rewards are set before those who pursue the monastic life, P. 365. Those who pursue it reject the allurements of the world, P. 592. Their goal, P. V. 395. Paulinus embraces it, V. 11, 14.

Beautiful admonitions embracing the perfection of Christian life, A. 747, 748.

The monogram, an abbreviation of Christ’s name, on ancient labara, and its form, 482, 484.

Mount Calvary on the northern side, A. 903.

The apostles and prophets are the mountains of God, E. 45.

Illness makes Paulinus more illustrious, E. 25, 27, V. 47. The illnesses of the strong are incentives to virtue for the weak, E. 81. Why they often befall the humble, E. 81, 90. Not only human beings but also animals are healed at Saint Felix’s tomb, P. 433.

The conduct of monks and dissolute men is admirably described, E. 113, 114.

The Morini are converted to the faith by Victricius, bishop of Rouen, E. 97, A. 885. Who they were, ibid.

How Samson’s death and blindness are to be desired, E. 131, 132. The death of the soul is fond of the life of this world, E. 64. The covering over of virtue, E. 71. Death and life are in the power of everyone’s tongue, E. 76. Why the death of the righteous should never be called premature, E. 69. How it should be mourned, E. 70, 71. It does not bring the soul forgetfulness of what it did in life, P. 377. It was subdued by Christ’s cross, P. 669, 670, 672. The death of children deserves both tears and joy, P. 668, 669. Paulinus’ death stirred almost the whole world; the second death is the life of punishments, E. 250. The uncertainty of death commends devotion to good works, E. 257. Charity is equated with death in Christ, E. 240, 388. When we should put death into the pot of our heart, E. 122. Only charity teaches us to undergo evangelical death, E. 266.

Through mortification of the members the soul is lifted toward heavenly things, E. 62.

A dead man raised by contact with the holy cross removes every doubt that had arisen during its discovery together with the crosses of the thieves, E. 193.

How the dead will rise incorruptible, E. 249. Why those who died in Christ are called “sleeping” by the apostle, E. 71. Many were raised at Jerusalem after Christ’s Passion, P. 677.

Saint Felix is compared with the staff of Moses devouring the dragons of the magicians, P. 619.

Moses exposed and driven into exile, a type of Christ, E. 229. When God threatened to destroy the Israelite people, with what purpose he offered his own removal from the book of life, E. 64. Praying for the people, he is heard, P. 616.

A woman cannot make a vow of continence without her husband’s consent. A certain woman feeds Saint Felix while he is hiding in a cistern, unaware of his hiding place, P. 408, 409. He is compared with the raven feeding Elijah and Habakkuk feeding Daniel, ibid.

Praise of a virtuous and wise woman, E. 69. The head of a woman is the man. Christian women: a most beautiful institution, and the following matters.

What sort of hair is becoming for women, E. 733. With uncurled hair they covered the forehead, E. 134. They are commanded to pray with covered heads, and why, E. 133, 134. Why they are forbidden to teach in church, ibid. How they should honor their husbands; how they ought to adorn themselves, P. 602, 603. Among the Jews, the reproach of women was failure to bear children, P. 341, A. 929.

The world, the enemy of humanity, E. 155. From the beginning it despises and hates Christ and Christ’s imitators, E. 229, 230. Created for humanity, it supplies human beings with every means of advancing both bodily and spiritually, E. 235. The whole universe was created by God for human use, E. 90. What rewards are promised to those who abandon it and follow Christ, P. 365. How greatly God loved it, P. 668. It must be fled if we are to attain heaven, P. 657. The creation and governance of the whole world are to be ascribed to God, E. 87. Those striving to escape its deceptions must imitate the cleverness of Ulysses, E. 90. Love works contempt for the world and its death in our hearts, E. 268. Paulinus tries to persuade Licentius to despise it, both in prose and in verse, E. 38 and following. Its sadness is to be preferred to all worldly joys, P. 681. Paulinus wishes to be foolish in the world so that he may be wise in Christ, P. 374. In the world, not to be stained by its vices is praiseworthy, P. 597.

It was customary for poets to invoke the Muses, P. 365. Christians ought not to invoke them, but God, P. ibid.

[Col. 1132] Nothing in nature is mute, P. 361.

A *myoparo*, a small vessel, especially a pirate vessel or brigantine, E. 288, A. 925.

## N

Why Nebuchadnezzar, with uncut hair, was likened to a lion; with hooked claws, to a vulture; and with fodder, to an ox, E. 130. Having lost his kingdom through sin and recovered it through repentance, he became an example for Christians, ibid.

Naddaver, a city situated in Parthia, to which Matthew’s bones were transferred, 451.

Narbo, a city of Gaul, E. 7, 30, V. 4. Paulinus owned estates there, E. 30, V. 4.

Paulinus sends Severus the *Natales* of Saint Felix, E. 173.

“Birthday” (*natalis*): the annual day of a bishop’s consecration, E. 106, A. 887. The birthday of Saint Peter’s chair was celebrated everywhere, ibid.

Paulinus composes a birthday poem for Saint Felix every year, ibid.

What the birthdays of the martyrs are, P. 518.

How many birthdays of Paulinus there are, and when they were written, in the Prolegomena.

Whether it is permissible to curse the day of one’s birth, P. 519.

The feast of Christ’s Nativity is extremely ancient, P. 625, A. 943, V. 71.

No nature is to be called evil, E. 86.

The prayer of a shipwrecked person in danger, E. 281. Those saved from death through the merits of Saint Felix after a shipwreck, P. 621. To whom the possessions of shipwreck victims belong, A. 925.

Paulinus describes Martinianus’s shipwreck most beautifully, P. 569 through 585. In this account he asserts that none of the Christians perished, P. 586. He compares it with the Last Judgment, P. 587. The shipwreck of the Apostle Paul explained mystically, E. 283.

The ship, a type of the Church, A. 910. A most beautiful description of the spiritual ship floating above the waves of this world, E. 137, 138. The ship in which a certain old man, named Victor by God, was carried was miraculously saved from shipwreck, E. 283. It is compared with Noah’s ark, E. 282. And with Jonah’s ship, ibid. It was tossed on more than one sea, E. 281. At last, on the twenty-third day, it reached Lucania and was seen full of armed soldiers, E. 282. It was seized by the procurator Posthumianus, E. 288. The ship perished through Therasia’s misguided anxiety, A. 786, V. 16. The pagans fancied that the ship of the Argonauts could still be seen in the sky, E. 282. They also venerated the ship that carried the dragon to Epidaurus, ibid. Ships celebrated in the sacred Scriptures, which are these, ibid.

The sailor carrying Martinianus, realizing that his ship was sinking, drowns himself, P. 575.

The duties of a sailor explained spiritually, A. 923.

The relics of Saint Nazarius were enclosed in an altar in the basilica founded by Paulinus at Fundi, P. 638, V. 54. Paulinus received them from Saint Ambrose and deposited them in the basilica of Saint Felix, ibid.

Neapolis, near Nola, E. 183.

Nemesis was worshiped by the pagans as a goddess in an image, E. 88.

Necessity likewise, E. 88. How it was depicted, ibid.

The neophytes wore white garments for eight days, E. 199, A. 904. In former times milk and wine were given to them, A. 892, 893.

Who the Nervii were, A. 885, 886. Their apostle was Victricius, E. 99, A. 885.

The Nervian coast, A. 894, 895.

The Nervian region and boundary, ibid.

The sinew in punishments, P. 394, A. 933, 934.

NICETAS, bishop of the Dacians, E. 185, A. 934, V. 58. Distinct from Nicetas the martyr, A. 934. Admirable to the Romans for his teaching, E. 185, A. 900, 934. He converted the Riphaeans and Bessi to the faith, P. 419, 423. Likewise the Scythians, Getae, and Dacians, P. 420, 423. He came from Dacia to Nola to venerate the relics of Saint Felix, P. 635. Arriving for Saint Felix’s birthday, he filled Saint Paulinus with the greatest joy, P. 412, 622, 635. Why was he called a true Israelite? P. 418. He is compared with the patriarch Jacob, who placed three rods before the mating flock, P. 418, 629. His return to Dacia is celebrated in a poem by Paulinus, P. 412.

What *nigellatum* is, E. 30.

Nineveh, condemned to destruction at God’s command but spared after repentance, shows that God, not fate, is the ruler of all things, P. 441. Its preservation commends the power of prayer, P. 624.

The Ninevites teach by their example the effectiveness of repentance, E. 178.
