Nobility is also praiseworthy in the saints, as Paulinus shows by the examples of John the Baptist and Christ, E. 179. It must be scorned in preference to serving Christ, E. 40. True nobility is to be illustrious in virtues, A. 738.

Noah alone was preserved during the Flood as the seed of the whole destroyed human race, a figure of Christ the Redeemer, E. 59. Laughed at by his son, he was a type of Christ, E. 329.

Nola, a famous city in Campania and a maritime city, V. 32. Near Neapolis, E. 183. Eight leagues distant from Capua, P. [Col. 1133] 583. Famous for the tomb of Saint Felix, P. 386, 387 and following. Captured by the Goths, A. 780, V. 90.

Description of the basilicas built by Paulinus at Nola, E. 204 and following. And of their decoration at Saint Felix’s feast, P. 387.

Nola had a brothel of Venus, 460. It denied water to the sacred buildings of Saint Felix, P. 547. It is the mother of Abella, P. 549. Paulinus reproves it sweetly, ibid.

With what relics of the saints the Nolan basilica was decorated, P. 470.

Nolan wantonness transferred into a proverb, P. 460.

Christ gave the apostles their names, E. 146, A. 895. The names of the rich whose crimes or punishments are reported in the sacred Scriptures are suppressed, E. 76.

Spiritual knowledge is to be preferred to bodily knowledge, E. 152, 153.

Christ is the razor of salutary cutting for us, E. 125. The devil is the razor of deadly cutting, ibid.

In the spiritual sense, “night” denotes Christ’s Passion, E. 141. Likewise the present age, ibid.

Nuceria in Umbria, 478.

Nuceria in Picenum, which belongs to the pagans, 478.

How weddings are to be celebrated among Christians, P. 601.

What the *nycticora* and *nycticorax* are: birds, E. 242. They mystically signify the repentant sinner, ibid.

## O

How pleasing blind obedience is to God, E. 184.

Votive offerings were formerly contributed for the support of the poor, 502.

Oil customarily carried to the tombs of the saints, made illustrious by miracles, 539.

Paulinus dispels the reproach cast upon him by Ausonius concerning forgetfulness of his homeland, P. 370.

Service arising from love is more pleasing than service arising from fear, A. 940.

Those possessed who were freed at Saint Felix’s tomb, P. 559, 560. Some of them are lifted high into the air, P. 560, A. 937. Others are suspended in the air with their feet turned upward, P. 560, A. 938. Yet their garments did not fall back over their faces, ibid.

The criticisms of wicked people must be scorned by those pursuing the discipline of perfection, E. 2 and following.

Paulinus endures detractors and despises them, V. 22 and following.

Opportunity was worshiped by the pagans as a goddess; how they depicted it, E. 89.

We are put to death and given life by Christ, E. 241, 242.

Octocorum, A. 907.

A beautiful description of the eyes, P. 564.

Saint Felix restores the eyes of a certain rustic, weakened by excessive tears, P. 552. Saint Martin restores Paulinus’s eye, A. 784.

Hatred and envy are seeds of many sins, A. 730.

OLYMPIUS informs Paulinus of the death of Paulina, the wife of Pammachius, E. 65.

The letter Omega, composed of three rods, signifies the mystery of the Trinity, 484.

Riches are not to be cast away, but stored in heaven, A. 870.

The work of each person will be tested by fire after this life, E. 172, P. 346, A. 726. Whoever performs a good work for the sake of human notice sins gravely, E. 294. Good works must be added to observance of the Law, E. 224. They force their way into heaven, E. 215, 216. They are necessary for salvation, A. 728. Faith is their fuel, E. 141. To think on the rewards of good works promised by Christ to the faithful after this life is delightful, E. 80. Paulinus commends works of mercy, 26 and following. Through them Christ is lent money at interest, anointed, and fed, E. 119, A. 889, 893.

Why so few works of Paulinus survive, E. 253, P. 613 and following.

The workers of unity, who they are, A. 893.

To work means to show mercy, ibid.

“Work”: mercy, or almsgiving, E. 140, 181, A. 892.

Ophas, A. 891.

Towns ending in *-magus*, A. 878.

The Delphic oracle, 454.

Prayer must be offered for the dead; this is shown by Paulinus’s example, since he asked Delphinus and Amandus to pray for the soul of his deceased brother, E. 219, 220, V. 79.

The poor person’s prayer penetrates the clouds, E. 74. The protection of prayers is especially necessary for human beings, E. 217.

Paulinus shows that prayer is obtained chiefly through almsgiving, E. 218. What prayer can accomplish before God, P. 612, 766 through 776.

A prayer of one in danger from shipwreck, E. 281. Paulinus’s morning prayer to God, P. 330. Another, P. 330, A. 929. To Christ for the successful outcome of a marriage, P. 607.

What it means to be ordained absolutely, A. 870.

The four minor orders were to be conferred separately, according to the intention of the Church, P. 391, A. 933. On whom they were formerly conferred, A. 933.

The appetite of monks, E. 121, A. 889.

Why the Phrygians worshiped the orgiastic rites, P. 453. They were celebrated by vintners in Paulinus’s time with detestable abuse, P. 460. Whether *Ὄροι* (“boundaries”), *ὄρη* (“mountains”), or *ὀραῖα* (“beautiful things”) should be read in Psalm 64, A. 921.

Oroth: lights and vegetables, A. 891.

Moderate adornment was permitted to women, but excessively elaborate adornment was forbidden, A. 940.

Orpah, following a different path from her sister Ruth: what she signifies mystically, P. 641.

The Oscans, formerly so called as though they were “obscene,” 460.

When kisses were customary among ancient Christians at the doors of churches, 455.

Osiris was the son, not the husband, of Isis, 455.

The office of porter was the first clerical rank in Paulinus’s time, 474. Their ancient ministry in the churches was to sleep there at night and keep watch, 475.

The Ostian church claims to possess the remains of Saint Luke the Evangelist, P. 659, A. 949.

Paulinus sends oysters with poems to Gestidius, P. 329.

Christian leisure for acquiring Christian wisdom, E. 276.

## P

The pagans: their worship under Constantine and the other pious emperors, V[itae?] titi, 464.

Pagan Nuceria, 478.

The episcopal pallium, A. 878. Its meaning, ibid. Why it is marked with crosses, ibid. Paulinus rightly interprets the pallium, sent to him by Severus and made of camel hair, as appropriate for one in need of repentance, E. 176, 177.

PAMMACHIUS, to whom Paulinus writes: what sort of man he was, E. 65, A. 774, 879. He mourns his deceased wife Paulina with many tears and almsgiving, E. 66 and following, V. 56. For her sake he provides a banquet for all the poor of Rome in the basilica of Saint Peter, E. 72. His generosity toward the poor, E. 73, 74.

Paulinus’s panegyric on the death of the boy Celsus, written for his parents Pneumatius and Fidelis, P. 665. Likewise his panegyric of the emperor Theodosius, E. 174, A. 899, V. 46.

*Panicium* and *panicum*, A. 890.

The bread of the Christian is faith, E. 56. And the word of God, E. 9. Blessed bread distributed to the people in churches, A. 874. By whom instituted? ibid. By whom distributed? ibid. To whom? ibid. In what form received? ibid. At what time? ibid. “Bread” used for the Eucharist, E. 30, A. 875, 876. Bread sent among friends as a *eulogia*, a symbol of unity, E. 28. One to Augustine from Paulinus, E. 15. One to Alypius, E. 12, A. 872, V. 43. In which the fullness of the Trinity was contained, E. 12, A. 872. One sent to Severus with a boxwood dish, as an indication of monastic poverty, E. 29, A. 874. Five loaves sent to Romanianus and Licentius, E. 37, V. 43.

Pope Urbicus: who he was, E. 26, A. 773. Formerly every bishop was called “pope,” E. 7.

Papyrus used in wax candles and lamps, P. 386, A. 932.

*Par*: companion, E. 98, 206, A. 885.

Paradise: a place before a temple; in French, *parvis*, A. 882.

The origin of altar furnishings, A. 905.

The wall of separation between us and God is sin, E. 61. How Christ destroyed it, E. 61, 62.

Parra, P. 376, A. 930.

Parthia, the place of Matthew’s martyrdom, 451.

The smallest fragment of the most holy cross can accomplish the same thing as the whole cross, E. 189, 194, 289.

How ancient the feast of Easter is, P. 625, A. 758, V. 71.

PASCHASIUS, a deacon of Saint Victricius, retained for a longer time by Paulinus at Nola out of hospitality and excused to Victricius, E. 97, V. 126. His virtues are enumerated, E. 96, 101, V. 126. Through the merits of Saint Felix he obtains the restoration of his former health for Urso, his companion on the journey, E. 98, V. 126. He baptizes him in bed, ibid. He delivers Paulinus’s letter to Victricius, ibid.

The solitary sparrow mystically signifies Christ in the sacred Scriptures, E. 244, 245. It also signifies the repentant sinner, E. 245.

How Christ’s Passion is called night, E. 140. What it teaches us, E. 62. Samson, dying, prefigured its power, E. 125. Helena, the mother of Constantine, adorned the place of Christ’s Passion, E. 193.

Paulinus applies Joel’s words about the caterpillar, locust, grasshopper, and mildew most aptly to the passions of the soul, E. 236, 237.

The combed hair, P. 588, 630, A. 939, 913.

Christ, the shepherd carrying the sheep back to the fold on his shoulders, E. 54, A. 877, 878. The duties of shepherds, E. 9, 272, 273.

A spiritual father: one who baptizes another, A. 885.

Patrae, a city of Achaia where Andrew was crowned with martyrdom, P. 450. Paulinus was of the noblest rank, ibid. Born in Gaul, P. 528. He married Therasia, P. 529.

The homeland and lineage of Paulinus, A. 797, 798, V. 2, 3. Paulinus dispels the reproach cast upon him by Ausonius concerning forgetfulness of his homeland, P. 369.

[Col. 1135] Paulinus invites the patriarchs and prophets to join in celebrating Saint Felix’s birthday, P. 630.

Among Christians, the saints who protect them are called patrons, E. 26, A. 874.

The pavement of the churches strewn with flowers, P. 386, A. 932.

PAULA, the mother of Paulina, Pammachius’s wife, E. 81.

PAULINA, daughter of Paula and wife of Pammachius, E. 81, V. 56. Pammachius mourns her death with many tears and almsgiving, E. 66 and following, V. 56. Her praise, ibid.

The two PAULINI who were consuls under Constantine, V. 2. They had the surname Anicius, V. 3.

PAULINUS, father of Saint Paulinus, also called PONTIUS, V. 3. Founder of Bourg-sur-Garonne, ibid. Prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, ibid. He too was a Christian, E. 65, V. 3. He had sons and a daughter, E. 218, 219, V. 3. He lived a long time, V. 3. After his death he was buried at Bordeaux, E. 65, V. 3. Saint Paulinus his son sent one of his freedmen to his tomb to serve the Church, ibid.

His wife, Saint Paulinus’s mother, was a Christian, E. 65, V. 3. After her death she was buried at Bordeaux, ibid. Saint Paulinus his son sent one of his freedmen to her tomb to serve the Church, ibid.

PAULINUS, also called PONTIUS MEROPIUS, E. 238, V. 1. Born of a senatorial family on both his father’s and his mother’s side, A. 775, 961, V. 1. Related to the elder Melania, E. 178, V. 1; to Pneumatius and Celsus, P. 686, V. 1; and to Jovius, P. 557. From the Anician family, V. 2. His father was Pontius Paulinus, ibid., founder of Bourg-sur-Garonne, ibid., prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, ibid., and a Christian, E. 65, V. 3. Born at Bordeaux in the year 353, A. 957, V. 3. He had a brother who led a secular life, E. 219, 220, V. 3, and a sister to whom he sent several letters on contempt for the world, V. 3. He also possessed a very large patrimony, A. 774, 775, 781, 782, 783, 784, 786, V. 3, 4. He lived on his estates at Ebromagus and Fundi, E. 57, 204, V. 39. His teacher was the Gaul Ausonius, V. 4. He was an excellent poet, P. 590, 591, and also a distinguished orator, A. 773, 775, V. 4. He possessed an extraordinarily gentle and kindly intellect, P. 354, V. 8. He was cheerful and gracious in writing letters, V. 35. Humble, ibid. Merciful, E. 289, A. 960, V. 8. Helpful, ibid. Thinking well of everyone, ibid. He was frank in admonishing his friends, E. 272, 273. Grateful toward those who were helpful, V. 8.

At first he was occupied with the bustle of the courts and secular affairs, E. 22, V. 7. Ausonius advanced him to the highest offices, V. 4, 5. He became a senator, E. 121, A. 774, V. 7, and consul, ibid. Not an ordinary consul, V. 7, but a suffect consul after Valens’s death, V. 7. He formed friendships with many people, V. 7, 26. He saw Saints Martin of Tours and Victricius of Rouen at Vienne, E. 101, V. 9. Suffering from an eye ailment, he was healed by Saint Martin, A. 782, 783, V. 9. He married Therasia, F. 9, 17, 30, 31, 35, 168, 180, 234, 238, 259, 268, 271, P. 667, 607, A. 786, V. 67. How he conducted himself in secular life, 363, 364, 379. Through various labors and hardships, and also through the prayers of Saint Felix and certain other saints, he was converted to God, V. 9. His wife Therasia also helped and encouraged him, V. 7, 9.

He was baptized at Bordeaux by Saint Delphinus the bishop, E. 11, 45, 46, 110, V. 10. He asks God for the honorable conduct of a secular man, P. 329. Paulinus thought that even bad Christians would attain a certain salvation, provided that they preserved their faith intact, P. 346. He prays for a happy future for himself and his family, P. 329, and for grace by which he may avoid sins, P. 330, 331. He celebrates the praise of Saint John the Baptist, P. 332 and following.

Paulinus withdrew with his wife to Spain in order to renounce the world, E. 22, P. 355 and following, V. 10. How he conducted himself there, V. 11, 12, 13 and following. There he received a son by his wife; the child died on the eighth day after birth and was buried at Complutum beside the bodies of the holy martyrs, P. 685, 686, V. 12. How devoutly he endured the loss of this son, ibid. He devoted and consecrated himself wholly to God, E. 13, 42, P. 364, 368, 375. He bade farewell to his homeland, the senate, the secular world, and the Muses, P. 362, 363, 365, 366, A. 774, 775, V. 14. He embraced the monastic life, A. 773, V. 14. With his wife Therasia he professed continence, E. 7, A. 776, 783, 971, V. 6, 16. He sold his estates and distributed the money to the poor, E. 22, 56, 150, 208, 247, P. 336, A. 772, 775, 783, 786.

His excellent teaching on contempt for human judgments, E. 2. His humility in renouncing his possessions, E. 149 and following, 175, 196, 206, 242, 248, P. 634. His astonishing poverty, E. 56, V. 15, 16, 54. His remarkable faith, E. 56, 57, 149, 206, 245, P. 375, A. 773, 783, 786, V. 15, 16. He is praised by the holy Fathers of the Church, A. 773 through 789 and 957 through 963, V. 20, 21, 22. He is despised by secular men, E. 29, 48, A. 775, V. 22, 23. His steadfastness, P. 363 and following, V. 25, 26. Ausonius attacks him fiercely in letters, V. 24, 25, which, by God’s action, were returned only after four years, ibid. and P. 363. He professes his love and reverence for Ausonius, P. 365, V. 25. He firmly refutes Ausonius’s complaints, P. 365 and following, V. 25, 26. He defends the honor of his wife Therasia, P. 362, 368. He confesses Christ with complete freedom in words and deeds, P. 363 and following, V. [Col. 1136] 25, 26.

He forms an exceptionally close friendship with Sulpicius Severus, E. 50, V. 24, 25. At Barcelona, seized by the force of the crowd, suddenly constrained and compelled by the multitude, through the violence of the inflamed populace, he is ordained a presbyter against his will, E. 6, 8, 10, V. 28. He is ordained by Lampius, bishop of Barcelona, E. 11, V. 28, in the year 393, on the Sunday of Christ’s Nativity, E. 6, V. 28, 44. This was nevertheless on the condition that he would not be bound to the church of Barcelona, E. 5, V. 28. For he had decided to retire to Saint Felix at Nola, E. 6, P. 375, and there to serve as a church custodian, E. 6, P. 375, V. 28.

He remains for some time at Barcelona, E. 6, V. 27. He explains the dignity and burden of the priesthood, E. 6, 8. With what devotion he received and exercised it, E. 6, 7, 8, 14, V. 28, 29. He writes to Sulpicius Severus about his promotion to the priesthood, E. 6, V. 30; to Amandus of Bordeaux, E. 8, V. 30; and to Alypius, E. 10. He commends himself greatly to their prayers, ibid. He arms Sulpicius Severus against the insults of the profane, E. 2 and following. He teaches to whom an account must be rendered concerning one’s way of life, E. 2 and following. He recalls him from his homeland, E. 6, inviting him to withdraw to Nola, V. 28, 30.

He writes his first birthday poem for Saint Felix in Spain, P. 375, V. 29. From there he comes to Italy, V. 31. Saint Ambrose receives him affectionately, E. 10, V. 31. He is received honorably by the Roman people and leading men, V. 31, 32. He is treated badly by Siricius, the Roman pontiff, and by certain clerics of the Roman Church driven by jealousy, E. 25, 26, V. 31, 49. He hastens his departure from the city and comes to Nola, E. 26.

What manner of life he established there, E. 29, 85, 114; 121 and following. He is assiduous in singing God’s praises, A. 958, V. 95. How devoted he was to poverty, voluntary bodily affliction, solitude, and silence, E. 29, 56, 238. He greatly despised pagan learning, E. 112, P. 363. He suffers the troublesome assaults of carnal desire, E. 154, 155. He invokes God, E. 155, 187, 188, V. 37. He fears praise, E. 240. He rebukes those who praise him, ibid., V. 38, 46, 47. He despises himself, E. 29, 64, 103, 104, 118, 170, 173, P. 634, 681, V. 37, 39. He considers himself unworthy to expound sacred Scripture, E. 255, 276, V. 39.

How devout he was toward the saints, E. 93, 94, 107, 196, 199, 254, 265, V. 42, 55. Every year he visits their holy memorials at Rome, E. 93, 107, 196, 199, 254, 265, 272, V. 42. How devout he was toward his holy patron Felix, E. 26, 96, 175, 203, P. 387, 561, 644, V. 41, 42, 47. He shows the saint’s power against demons, P. 384 and following, 558, 665. He makes him more illustrious through poems, E. 174, P. 377, 380, 381, 387, 400, 425, 557, 608, 622, 645, 657, 662, 663, 666, V. 29, 42, 47, 54, 57, 65, 70, 71, 83, 84, 85, 153, 160 and following. The magnificence of the basilicas, P. 203, 208, V. 66, 73, 74, 75, 76. His authority and holiness, E. 26, 185, P. 414, 622, 636, 643, V. 58, 71, 72, 80, 81. His lineage and origin are described, P. 388, 389 and following. His miracles, P. 433, 437, 438, 439, 620, 648 and following, 664.

He forms a friendship with Augustine and other saints in Africa, E. 9, 10, 16, 30. He sends small gifts and letters to Jerome, A. 774, V. 44. He celebrates the panegyric of Theodosius, E. 174, 175, V. 45. He is joined in friendship with Sanctus and the layman Amandus, E. 238 and following, V. 46, and likewise with Endelechius, E. 174, V. 46. He falls ill, E. 23, V. 47. He is visited by the bishops of Africa and Campania, E. 26. He glories in his illnesses, E. 23, V. 48. He sends Vigilantius with letters and small gifts to Sulpicius Severus, E. 23, V. 48.

He receives Romanianus, sent by Augustine with books and letters, V. 50. Augustine commends Licentius to him, V. 50. Paulinus replies to Licentius, E. 30, V. 50. His power over demons, V. 50. He learns by letter of Augustine’s promotion to the episcopate, V. 51. He expresses his extraordinary joy on this matter to Romanianus, V. 51, 52. To Romanianus he sends letters with *eulogia* and also a letter to his son Licentius, V. 51, 52. Likewise he sends Vigilantius with the panegyric of Theodosius and letters to Jerome, V. 52. From Jerome he requests a rule of monastic life, ibid. He desires to travel to Jerusalem, ibid.

He writes to Delphinus and Amandus, V. 53, 54. He receives relics of Saint Nazarius from Ambrose, bishop of Milan, P. 638, V. 54, and from Sulpicius Severus receives the Life of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, with letters, E. 55, V. 54. He pleads with Amandus on behalf of Sanemarius, so that Sanemarius may receive a small garden in the Church’s house from which to obtain his livelihood, E. 65, V. 55. He prevents violence done to Basil, a presbyter of the church of Capua, E. 82, 83, 84, V. 55, and obtains the restoration of his house, ibid. For this reason he writes to Daducius, E. 65, V. 55, and to Saints Delphinus and Amandus, E. 82, 83, V. 55, 56.

He consoles Pammachius for the death of his wife Paulina, E. 66 and following, V. 56, 57. From Delphinus’s illness he draws an occasion for humility, E. 81, 82, V. 67. He is joined in friendship with Theridius and Posthumianus, E. 168, P. 561, 669, 682, V. 58, 60. He receives them most affectionately, ibid. Through them he sends letters to his kinsman Jovius, E. 86, P. 553, 558, V. 58, 60. While ill, he invites Sulpicius Severus to visit him, E. 94, V. 62.

He receives Paschasius, deacon of Saint Victricius, bishop of Rouen, with the greatest hospitality, E. 97, V. 63. He excuses to Victricius the fact that he retained him longer than expected, ibid. Through Paschasius he sends Victricius letters full of reverence, E. 96 and following, V. 63. Pope Anastasius invites him to the annual commemoration of his consecration, E. 106, V. 64. He cultivates the friendship of Jerome and Rufinus, V. 64.

He tells Delphinus of his joy at the basilica at Alingon, built at his expense, E. 107, V. 66. He receives Martinianus, shipwrecked, with the greatest hospitality, P. 95, 96, V. 66. He describes the history of that shipwreck to Cytherius, P. 570 and following, V. 66. He praises Cytherius for entrusting his son to Sulpicius Severus for education, E. 108 and following, V. 67. Paulinus receives Victor, Severus’s companion, with great affection, E. 118, V. 67. Through Victor he sends Severus several letters, E. 115, 147, 185, V. 68. He urges a soldier to renounce the world, E. 163 and following, V. 69. He congratulates the hermit Sebastian and the deacon Benedict on their piety, E. 167, 168, V. 69. He commends himself and his wife Therasia to their prayers, E. 167, 169, V. 69.

He trusts in Saint Felix’s protection while the Goths invade Italy, P. 608, V. 70. He burns with desire for martyrdom, P. 633, V. 71. He is visited by Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, P. 627, 634, V. 72, and by Melania, E. 179, V. 72. When consulted by Sulpicius Severus about certain more difficult passages of history, he refuses to give an opinion, E. 174, 176, V. 73. He refuses an image of himself when Severus asks for one, E. 186, 187 and following, V. 73. Through Victor he sends Severus a fragment of the holy cross, together with a tunic of lamb’s wool and the panegyric of Theodosius, E. 189, V. 72, 73.

He orders a basilica to be built beside Saint Felix’s tomb, E. 202 and following, P. 616 and following, V. 73. He adorns it with various paintings, ibid. He makes the ancient basilica of the same saint larger and brighter, P. 636, 646 and following, V. 75, 76. He adorns it with paintings and epigrams, ibid. He addresses the people concerning the treasury, or almsgiving, E. 212, V. 78. He commends the soul of his deceased brother to the prayers of Saints Delphinus and Amandus, E. 219, 220, V. 79.

He receives letters from Alethius, Victricius, Aper, Augustine, Sanctus and Amandus, Severus, Desiderius, and Florentius, E. 211, 222, 228, 238, 249, 252, 254, 255, 259, V. 78, 79, 80, 84. He replies to them, ibid. He translates Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions*, E. 274. He obtains from Rufinus, for Desiderius, an explanation of the twelve blessings of the patriarchs, 255, 276, E. 84. He praises Publicola, Melania’s only deceased son, E. 265, 266, V. 85, and Melania herself, ibid. and E. 179 and following. He also praises many bishops of Gaul, E. 276, V. 86.

He is made bishop of the Nolan Church, E. 285, 397, V. 87, 88. How he conducted himself in the episcopal office, A. 957 and following, V. 88, 89. He was adorned with outstanding virtues, ibid. He loved discipline, yet was kind, A. 958, 959, V. 88. How he used ecclesiastical resources, A. 787, 960, V. 88.

He receives Valgius, shipwrecked, whom he commends to Macarius, with the greatest hospitality, E. 285, V. 90. He receives Paulinus the presbyter, E. 313, V. 91, and another Paulinus, a layman, E. 312, V. 91. He receives Saint Augustine’s letter against the Pelagians, V. 91. Whether he offered himself as a substitute for a captive, V. 140 and following. He suffers no harm during the devastation of Nola, A. 780, V. 90. The emperor invites him to the council at Ravenna to settle the schism of the Roman Church, V. 92. How highly he was esteemed by the emperor and other leading men, ibid.

Through Candidianus he receives Augustine’s book *On Caring for the Dead*, V. 93. Paulinus receives the letters and envoys of Saints Eucherius and Honoratus, E. 313, 314, V. 93. Through them he replies to the same men, ibid. He is afflicted by a very severe pain in the side, A. 958, V. 94. He is visited by Saints Symmachus and Acyndinus, A. 957, V. 94. With them, before his bed, he offers sacrifice to God, A. 958, V. 94. He restores to the Church’s communion those excluded from the sacred mysteries, ibid.

Saints Martin of Tours and Januarius, bishop of Beneventum, appear to him, ibid. Bishop Exsuperantius and his brother Ursatius send him silver for the poor, ibid. He gives it to the presbyter Posthumianus to distribute among creditors, A. 958, V. 94, 95. Even while dying he recites the morning psalmody, A. 958, V. 95. He gives peace to his clergy, ibid. At his death his little cell is shaken by an earthquake, ibid. He gives his soul back to God on 22 June in the year of Christ 431, at the age of seventy-eight, A. 959, V. 95. His face and entire body shine with snowy brightness, A. 960, V. 95. Pagans and Jews, weeping greatly and tearing their garments, gather with the Christians for his funeral, ibid. He is buried at Nola in the basilica of Saint Felix, A. 957, V. 95. His body is transferred to Rome and kept in the church of Saint Bartholomew, V. 96. Saint John, bishop of Naples, is summoned by him to heaven, A. 961, V. 96. Paulinus’s likeness was painted in the baptistery built by Severus and adorned with inscriptions by Paulinus himself, E. 96, 196. His Life was formerly read during the solemn celebrations of Gregory the Great, A. 789. Few of his works survive because very many have perished, V. 135 and following. Why he did not write large works, V. 90.

PAULINUS’S brother was baptized by Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, E. 220, 1, V. 3. He led a secular life, E. 220, 221, V. 3. He left children behind him, ibid. After his death, Paulinus commended him to Delphinus and Amandus, ibid. His sister was the recipient of several letters that Paulinus himself wrote on contempt for the world, V. 3.

PAULINUS the presbyter, a member of the household of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, E. 313, V. 3, 91.

PAULINUS the layman, oppressed by a certain calamity of fortune, took refuge with Saint Paulinus, E. 313, V. 2, 91. How many thanks he gave God for this mercy, ibid. He was dear to Augustine, whom he often consulted about being formed in the Christian life, E. 313, V. 91. He was greeted by Augustine, E. 18, V. 91.

PAULINUS, bishop of Béziers, V. 3.

PAULINUS, a disciple of Saint Ambrose of Milan, whose Life he wrote, V. 2. At that time, when he was a deacon, he accused Caelestius, who was condemned at the Council of Carthage, ibid.

PAULINUS, a Roman citizen, P. 582, V. 67. He kindly receives Martinianus, shipwrecked, into his home, ibid. And gives him his own clothing, ibid.

Another PAULINUS, who wrote certain homilies around the middle of the fifth century, V. 2.

PAULINUS OF PETRICORDIA, who composed the Life of Saint Martin in verse, A. 785, V. 3.

PAULINUS, the grandson of Ausonius, whose *eucharisticus* poem survives, V. 3.

PAUL the Apostle: why he always had the angel of Satan, the thorn of his flesh, as an adversary, A. 718. He summons all to the narrow way that leads to life, A. 734. He did not discipline his body on account of chastity alone, A. 739. In praising chastity, he does not forbid marriage, E. 18. He is believed to have rescued Martinianus and his companions, who were preserving his letters from the shipwreck, from their present danger of death, P. 580.

PAUL, bishop of Nola, E. 205, A. 917.

The Apostle Paul, expeller of Python by his prayer, P. 454.

The poor person’s prayer penetrates the clouds, E. 73. Tobias, preferring a poor man’s burial to his own meal, is praised by the voice of an archangel, E. 67. The poor are material for justice to the rich, and the rich are the substance of nourishment for the poor, E. 209. They are patrons of our souls, E. 72. What sort of people does God love? E. 76, 77. How serious a crime it is to despise them, E. 78. In feeding them, Christ is fed, E. 79, 214, 215. God made them for the benefit of the rich, E. 216. How, while neglecting themselves and their children, they pray for their benefactors, E. 219. That they are dear to God is shown by the example of the old man saved from shipwreck, E. 284. Their poverty supplies an opportunity for doing good, E. 168. Christ is their refuge, A. 726. Their share is what overflows from the rich, E. 187. Those who despise them are reproved by the example of Christ humbling himself, ibid. How useful it is to give alms to them, E. 208 and following. That they must be helped is shown by the example of Lazarus and the rich man at the Gospel banquet, E. 75, 76, P. 683. Pammachius provided a banquet for all the poor of Rome in the basilica of Saint Peter for the soul of his deceased wife, E. 72 and following. Paulinus’s poverty was remarkable, E. 56, V. 54. The excellence of evangelical poverty, E. 5, 57. Heaven awaits its followers, P. 586. Saint Felix was its distinguished lover, P. 411.

The poor were customarily fed from the revenues of the churches, P. 494.

Poverty is the ladder to heaven, P. 534.

*Paz*: refined gold, A. 891.

The sinner is compared most beautifully with Samson, E. 124 and following, and with a beast of burden grinding at the mill, E. 124, 125. The penitent is most aptly called a pelican and a *nycticorax* or *nycticora*, E. 242, 243, and a solitary sparrow, E. 246. He must not despair, A. 743, 744. He is the earth which the serpent—that is, the devil—is commanded to eat, P. 655. Sinners are called “darkness” by the Apostle, E. 243.

The sinful woman, an image of the Church of Christ, E. 138, A. 893. See “Sinful woman.”

Adam’s sin closed the eyes of the mind to innocence and opened them to iniquity, E. 186, 187. Sin is a wall, a rampart separating God and human beings, E. 61. How Christ destroyed it, E. 61, 62. How heavy its burdens are, E. 64. Its weight is represented by Absalom’s hair, E. 131. How it is called a servile work, E. 43. Solomon advises that it be fled, P. 655. Its way is easy and downhill, P. 628. Sins are overcome by almsgiving, E. 76. The soul is entangled and oppressed by them, E. 132. They must now be put to death, lest afterward we live under punishments, E. 248. Their allurements are our Lotophagi and Sirens, E. 91. The Stoics taught that all sins are equal, A. 730. Even the smallest must be guarded against, lest we gradually fall, ibid. Those that counterfeit the appearance of virtue are always more shameful, A. 738. They are blotted out by baptism and repentance, E. 198, P. 341, 342. Not resisting their beginnings is extremely dangerous, P. 351, 352. But destroying them is glorious, ibid. To lament them is Christian, P. 681. Their various forms are the ruins and thorns of the heart, P. 656. The root of them all is avarice, ibid.

To lend money to Christ at interest is meritorious, E. 213, A. 889, 893. Indeed, it is more useful than storing it at home, E. 215. Certain pagan philosophers too perceived that money is harmful to those devoted to wisdom, E. 91. Its exaction for the burial of bodies is detestable, A. 913.

Paulinus allows Victor to wash his feet, following apostolic example, E. 120.

The custom of washing guests’ feet is approved by the example of Abraham and Christ, E. 143.

[Col. 1139] The apostles, and apostolic men, are called the feet of the Word of God, E. 99.

PEGASIUS, bishop of Petragoria, E. 278, V. 86. A man of the greatest faith and piety, ibid.

The pelican, an Egyptian bird, is described by Paulinus, E. 242, 243. It mystically represents the repentant sinner, ibid.

The Pentateuch of Moses was represented in paintings in the porticoes of the basilica of Saint Felix, P. 640. For Augustine’s Pentateuch and the Pentapolis, see V. 194.

How ancient the solemnity of Pentecost is, P. 625, A. 943, V. 71.

“Pera de tua” [phrase uncertain], a proverb, E. 73, A. 881.

Pilgrimages to the holy places of Jerusalem, E. 287. That pilgrimages to the relics of the holy apostles and martyrs were already customary is shown by the examples of Paulinus and Severus, E. 94, 105, 196, 199, 254, V. 42.

PEREGRINUS, deacon of the Church of Hippo, a companion on the journey of Bishop Urbanus when he took possession of his episcopate, E. 315.

The discipline of perfection must not be abandoned because of the slanders of wicked people, E. 2, 3. Those who pursue it should not give an account of their undertaking to the profane, E. 3 et seqq. In what respect they ought to be compared with a mustard seed, E. 5.

How great are the dangers for those living in the world, E. 173.

Persecution of the Arians against the Catholics broke out during the reign of the emperor Valens, E. 182. It was stirred up against Christians at Nola, P. 391.

Perseverance is necessary for those entering the way of virtue, E. 244. Likewise for attaining salvation, A. 743, 744.

The Persians are located in Parthia, P. 451.

Partiality toward persons is unknown to the Catholic religion, A. 738. It has no place before God, P. 585.

Distinguished persons of both sexes to whom Paulinus recited the poem of the thirteenth Nativity, P. 508.

Persons of three kinds praying in the ancient churches: old men, the poor, and gray-haired mothers, P. 494.

Christ is called the Rock, E. 202, A. 913.

Why the apostles Peter and Paul were assigned by God to Rome, P. 450.

PETER and PAUL: why they were buried at Rome, P. 659, 660.

The Pharisee who invited Christ, but anointed neither Christ’s head nor feet, is a type of the Synagogue, E. 139. The antitheses between him and the sinful woman, E. 144. Why the evangelical Pharisee could not enter through the needle’s eye into which the publican had inserted himself, E. 175, 180. His example shows that the proud are rejected by God, E. 289. Christ reproves the Pharisees for enlarging their fringes, A. 734.

Phas, A. 892.

Among the ancients, phallus and male genitalia were synonyms, P. 462.

What the Pharocanthara are, P. 476.

The apostle Philip was buried at Hierapolis in Phrygia, P. 451.

The Philistines were worshipers of Dagon, P. 462.

PHILIP rests in Phrygia, P. 659.

Certain philosophers who assigned the governance of some human affairs to Fate and Fortune are refuted by Paulinus, E. 88. Why they do not deserve to understand the true God, E. 93. Why Paulinus says that they merely train tongues, P. 364. It belongs to the philosophers of this age to obscure the light of truth by fabricated assertions, E. 60. Paulinus praises their eloquence, but not their vain wisdom, E. 93.

PHOTINUS is refuted at the beginning of Saint John’s Gospel for saying that Christ was merely human, E. 113.

Touching pitch, one is defiled by it, E. 69.

Paintings of Saint Martin and Paulinus were placed in the baptistery built by Severus, and Paulinus supplied them with inscriptions, E. 195, 200. Paulinus sent paintings of his basilicas to Severus, E. 201, 202. Paintings representing the whole history of Moses’ Pentateuch can be seen in the porticoes of the basilica of Saint Felix, P. 640. Paulinus explains why he had them made, P. 641. Paintings are books for the uneducated, ibid.

Piety toward parents is commended to us by the example of the dying Christ, E. 295, 296. It must not be absent from a Christian, P. 365.

A pine torch was customary at weddings among the ancients, P. 525.

Pinianus was Paulinus’s spiritual son, P. 525. Likewise, the time at which this illustrious man lived, P. 520, 521.

The disease of the pine is called Thaeda, P. 525.

The pine is an evergreen tree, P. 524, 525. It was under the protection of Cybele, P. 453.

To paint with wax, or to paint a picture in wax, A. 910.

Bishops are fishers of human beings, E. 253. Some people see the ship in which a certain old man, called Victor by God, was traveling alone, surrounded by armed soldiers, E. 284. They escort that same ship into port after being received and refreshed by the same man, ibid.

Christ is the fish of living water, E. 72, A. 880. Christ, roasted, is Christ who suffered, A. 880. In former times a fish was engraved on rings in memory of Christ or of baptism, ibid.

God’s will is better than human wishes, E. 71.

[Col. 1140] The error of the philosopher Plato, who regarded the Fates as the sole determiners of lives and human affairs, E. 90.

PNEUMATIUS, father of the boy Celsus, whom Paulinus honored in a panegyric, P. 666, 686.

Podium ad Lertium, Puech-sur-le-Lers, a town on the borders of the diocese of Toulouse, V. 27. Podium Paulini, Le Puy-Paulin, a place in Bordeaux believed to have been Paulinus’s residence, V. 3.

The punishments of hell are eternal, P. 683 et seqq.

David’s repentance is to be imitated by sinners, P. 681. The efficacy of repentance is proved by the example of the Ninevites, E. 178. By it sins committed after baptism are erased, E. 199, P. 341, 342. The prayer of one seeking the gift of repentance directed to Christ, P. 681, 682.

The verb *poeniteo* among the ancient Latins, P. 549.

Paulinus was an excellent poet, P. 590, 591, V. 5.

Why Paulinus says that poets merely train tongues, P. 364. They were accustomed to invoke Apollo and the Muses, P. 363. Their tales express the torments of hell, P. 682, 683.

Public weight, A. 891.

PONTIUS, Paulinus’s praenomen, P. 353, V. 55.

The doors of churches were fitted with grilles, A. 936. They were decorated with curtains, P. 386, 426, and with garlands and flowers, P. 386, A. 932.

The portico of the basilica of Saint Felix was adorned by Paulinus with very beautiful paintings, P. 646, A. 947. He gives the reason for this act, P. 642.

POSSIDIUS, bishop of Calama, went to the emperor on behalf of his Church, E. 272, V. 85. He visited Paulinus and Therasia, ibid. He brought them a letter from Augustine, ibid.

Paulinus prays that posterity may be happy for himself and his people, P. 330.

POSTHUMIANUS, presbyter, Saint Paulinus’s household companion, V. 82.

POSTHUMIANUS, Saint Paulinus’s friend, V. 58. Known to Jerome, whom he had met at Bethlehem, ibid. Originally from Aquitania, ibid. He left his homeland and came to Nola, ibid. Sent by Severus to Paulinus, V. 82. He was received by Paulinus with great affection, V. 58. Likewise by Sulpicius Severus, V. 70, 82. He composed dialogues with him, V. 71, 82. He carried Severus’s letters to Paulinus, Paulinus’s to Severus, and Paulinus’s to Jovius, E. 86, 169, 184, V. 58, 59, 70. Paulinus commends him to another, ibid. Whether he is the same as Posthumianus, Saint Paulinus’s household companion, V. 82.

POSTHUMIANUS, a senator, E. 288. His procurator seized the ship of Secundinianus after it had been miraculously saved, ibid.

What “potionatus” means, E. 246, A. 920.

Observance of God’s commandments is especially necessary for those aspiring to live a holy life, A. 726.

Preachers of the Gospel were deacons in Gaul in Paulinus’s time, E. 167, 168, V. 69.

What sort of prefect should be chosen, P. 592, 593.

It is exceedingly delightful to consider the rewards of good works promised by Christ to the faithful after this life, E. 79. What has been prepared for those who serve Christ here, P. 373.

“Praereptor,” or “praecerptor”: one who pre-empts, or plucks beforehand, works, E. 120, A. 889.

How presbyterae, that is, the wives of presbyters, lived, E. 261 et seqq., A. 920. Whether they were permitted to associate with their husbands, ibid. Whether, after their husbands’ death, they were permitted to marry a second time, A. 920. What clothing they wore, ibid. Older widows were also called by this name, ibid.

Presence consists more in the union of minds than of bodies, E. 66.

Prayers; see Prayer.

Primuliacum, a town in Aquitania where Severus built a basilica, E. 1, 189, 200, A. 901, 902.

Saint Priscus, patron and martyr of Nuceria Paganorum, P. 471.

The relics of the martyr Proculus are preserved in the basilica of Saint Felix, P. 639.

Profane people must be avoided, E. 3. The faithful should not give them an account of their discipline, E. 2 et seqq. One ought to rejoice at displeasing them, E. 4.

PROFORUS, a member of Paulinus’s household, E. 29.

PROFUTURUS, bishop of Cirta, greets Paulinus by letter, A. 754.

The prophets are the mountains of God, E. 44. What sort of people the prophets mentioned in Ephesians 4:11 were, E. 293, 303, 304. The prophets and the Law are contained in this one commandment: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them,” A. 734. What the Law itself could not accomplish is carried out by the Son of God, P. 669.

Paulinus’s prose works that have perished, V. 135, 136.

The body of Protasius was discovered by Saint Ambrose, E. 206. His relics were preserved at Fundi in the basilica built by Paulinus, ibid.

The bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius were discovered by Saint Ambrose, P. 468.

Who is a protector? E. 166, A. 898, 899.

Adam and Eve are the first-formed human beings, E. 123, A. 890. In Paradise they retained eyes illuminated by God for as long as they remained closed to sin, E. 186, 187.

[Col. 1141] Everything is subject to divine providence, E. 87 et seqq., P. 152 et seqq.

The first Psalm was explained in verse by Paulinus, P. 345. Likewise the second, P. 347. Likewise Psalm 136, P. 349.

Paulinus desires for himself the grace of the evangelical publican, E. 176. His example shows that God grants grace to the humble, E. 290.

How the word “boy” should be understood in Paulinus’s usage, P. 520.

The ancient Christian custom of dedicating boys’ and girls’ virginity to God, P. 526.

Dust carried away from the tombs of the saints, 540.

Pulvini, a port in Sardinia, E. 283.

The dust of holy places is to be honored, E. 288, A. 925, 626.

A beautiful description of the pupils of the eyes, P. 564.

The existence of purgatory is evident from the fact that alms are given for the dead, E. 67, 68, 72, 74, 81. The purgatorial fire, E. 172, P. 686, A. 726.

The Pyrenees are covered with snow, 369, A. 929. From Narbonne the route leads through them into Spain, E. 7.

What it meant to have the Pythium within oneself, P. 454.

Pythian Apollo, famous for his oracle, P. 455.

“Pythus” for Delphi, or for the inhabitants of Delphi, P. 455. Πῶλος, “foal,” A. 755.

## Q

How Paulinus was accustomed to observe the Lenten fast, E. 84.

Complaints against physicians, P. 500.

Paulinus proposed nine questions from different passages of Scripture to Augustine, E. 287 et seqq. Augustine answered them, E. 297 et seqq.

Both the integrity and the corruption of the five human senses are signified by the five wise and five foolish virgins, E. 248.

QUINTUS, deacon who carried Augustine’s letters to Paulinus, E. 265, A. 921. He was a presbyter in the year 414, E. 296.

QUINTUS succeeded Maximus in the Nolani episcopate, P. 409. Saint Felix was his vicar, P. ibid.

## R

What Rachel’s honorable burial by the patriarch Jacob mystically prefigured, E. 68. In life she often represented the Church, but in death the Synagogue, ibid.

Radagaisus, king of the Goths, terrified Italy in the year 405, P. 513. He was defeated with his army, P. 509, 513, 514.

Avarice is the root of sins, P. 656.

Why Rahab the prostitute was spared in the destruction of Jericho, P. 613. By lowering a scarlet cord, she foreshowed the nations to be redeemed by Christ’s blood, ibid.

How Rebecca came adorned to Isaac, her bridegroom, P. 606.

What authority the governors of the provinces of the Roman people possessed, P. 530.

The redemption of the already-perished human race belonged to Christ alone, E. 59.

A single meal toward evening was very customary among the early Christians, E. 86, A. 884, V. 33.

Kings and rulers bend the knee at the name of Jesus, and submit their scepters to the cross, P. 585, A. 868.

The royal gate, that is, the principal gate, E. 72, A. 889, 890, V. 194.

The Queen of Sheba, representing the Church, marvels at Christ in Solomon, E. 20.

How highly people value familiarity with an earthly king, E. 285.

Paulinus rendered metrically the history of the kings written by Suetonius, P. 329.

Barbarous and uncultivated regions bring no stain upon people of approved character, P. 369.

The kingdom of heaven is invaded by faith in the cross, E. 189.

What rewards are proposed to those entering religion, P. 365.

Religious people should not give an account of their undertaking to the profane, E. 3 et seqq. In what respect they ought to be compared with a mustard seed, E. 5. Despising earthly things, they await heavenly things, P. 368, 369.

The relics of the saints are spread throughout the world, P. 657, 658, 659. They are necessary for dedicating a new church, E. 200, A. 905, V. 75. The ancient custom of enclosing them in altars, E. 200, P. 638, 639, A. 905, V. 75. They were transferred to Constantinople by Constantine, P. 658. The relics of John the Baptist, Andrew, Thomas, Luke, Vitalis, Agricola, Proculus, Euphemia, and Nazarius were placed in the basilica of Saint Felix, P. 637, 638. They were adorned with flowers, A. 932. Paulinus celebrates the gathering and adornment of them, E. 106, P. 644 et seqq. Jacob gathered some of them so that he might be buried near them, A. 769.

The relics of the saints were appointed by God for the protection of provinces and cities, P. 447. In former times they were placed in litters when they were transferred, P. 469. They are the bulwarks and towers of kingdoms, P. 468.

Evidence of the holiness, continence, and age of Remigius, bishop of Reims, P. 526.

[Col. 1142] What true human rest consists in, E. 283.

RESTITUTUS, a member of Paulinus’s household, E. 30.

The resurrection of the dead is proved by the example of Christ risen again, E. 80, P. 331, 671. It is the most immediate consolation for the pains and labors of the present life, P. 671, 672. It is represented in various ways both in heaven and on earth, P. 672. What it will be like is beautifully shown, P. 673, 674, A. 767, 768. It is confirmed by the testimony of the prophet Ezekiel, P. 675. Likewise by that of Christ the Savior, who manifested it not only in word but also in deed, P. 675, 676. What the resurrection of the condemned will be like, P. 685. What Christ’s resurrection teaches us, E. 62. Saint Helena adorned the place of Christ’s resurrection with a basilica, E. 192. Those who mortify themselves here will share in it in the future, E. 268.

Why Paulinus says that rhetoricians merely train tongues, P. 364.

Saint Genesius, fleeing from his assailant, crossed the Rhône and was mystically baptized in it, E. 319.

The peoples of the Riphaean region converted by Nicetas, P. 420.

Rome is called by Paulinus the daughter of Babylon, E. 184, 278, A. 900. Paulinus visited it every year, E. 92, 106, 196, 199, 254, 265, 273, V. 42. It was ravaged by the Goths, V. 90.

ROMANIANUS, a relative of Alypius, E. 19. Closely connected with Augustine, E. 35. Recommended by Augustine to Paulinus, E. 71. He carefully preserved Augustine’s writings, E. 34. From a congratulatory letter of Paulinus he learned that Augustine had been given as colleague to Valerius, bishop of the Church of Hippo, E. 36. His name occurs in the book *On True Religion*, E. 17.

The Roman clergy were unjust and envious toward Paulinus, E. 25, A. 873.

ROMANUS, bearer of Paulinus’s letters to Augustine, E. 32.

Rotomagus, a metropolitan city on the Seine and the capital of Normandy, V. 149. It became renowned through its bishop Victricius, E. 98. Paulinus highly commends it, ibid. He also compares it with Jerusalem, ibid.

The rust, caterpillar, locust, and grasshopper listed by Joel are excellently applied by Paulinus to the passions of the soul, E. 236, 237.

The ruins of the soul that must be removed are sins, P. 656.

RUFFINUS, a holy presbyter learned in both Greek and Latin, E. 174. Very dear to Paulinus, E. 242, V. 64, and to Augustine, V. 64. He traveled in the East, E. 242. He had a controversy with Jerome, V. 64. At the end of 397 he returned to the West, ibid. He stayed in Rome for a year, ibid. He went to Aquileia, ibid. From there he returned to Rome; Paulinus asked him to teach him Greek, E. 275. Paulinus also asked him to explain the blessings of the two patriarchs, E. 275, 276, and to visit him on his journey, E. 278.

RUFFINUS, a deacon who carried Augustine’s Letter 149 to Paulinus, E. 299.

Why Solomon says that agriculture was created by the Most High, E. 235.

RUSTICUS, bishop of Clermont, V. 86, 87. Successor of Saint Venerandus, ibid.

A certain Rusticus, bitterly mourning the oxen taken by thieves, recovered them through the merits of Saint Felix; at the same time his sight, weakened by excessive tears, was restored, P. 433–553, V. 58.

What the story of Ruth mystically signifies, P. 642.

## S

Whose flight is impeded by the Sabbath, E. 43.

The blasphemies of Sabellius are nullified at the beginning of John’s Gospel, E. 113.

SABINUS, a relative of Sulpicius Severus, E. 93, V. 62. Paulinus received him very affectionately at Rome, ibid.

Paulinus was compelled to accept the priesthood against his will, E. 6, 8, 10, V. 28. With what piety he accepted and exercised it, E. 6, 7, 8, 14, V. 28, 29. Its burden, E. 6, 8, 9. Christ is its victim and priest, E. 53. Its antiquity is preferred to the seven days, P. 409. Ambrose, Aper, Paulinus, and Germanus were compelled by the people to accept the priesthood, V. 132, 133.

Christ is the victim of all priests, and priests are victims for Christ, E. 53.

The priests of Isis and Serapis wore shaved heads, P. 456.

In former times the name “priest” was applied only to bishops, P. 540.

The priesthood must always be chaste, P. 534.

A sacrifice must be offered to God from our very selves, E. 52. The sacrifices of the Old Law are explained allegorically, ibid.

A sacred rite was celebrated in the evening during the Vigils that were formerly kept as fasts, P. 561.

From what Christ prepared the medicine of our salvation, E. 223.

The evangelical Samaritan is Christ, E. 126.

Samson was invincible while his hair was preserved, but became a captive when it was cut off; he is a type of the sinner, E. 125. Yet in dying he killed more enemies than when alive, and thus represents Christ the Savior, ibid. His killing of the lion represents the Jews, E. 127. He lost his bodily eyes, but not his spiritual ones, E. 129. His hair signified strength, [Col. 1143] E. 130. How his death and blindness are to be desired, E. 131, 132. What his dying while killing several thousand enemies mystically signifies, P. 589. Some of his deeds are praiseworthy and to be imitated, but others are blameworthy and to be avoided, P. 588 et seqq.

Paulinus wishes Cytherius’s son to follow Samuel’s example, P. 588, 590. Samuel’s hair signified sanctification, E. 130.

The first degree of holiness is to pursue virtue daily, P. 627. The second is to practice it at least on feast days, ibid.

Why the saints are called good black fir trees, E. 134. They are called the hairs of Christ, E. 130. Their carnal weakness produces a twofold benefit, E. 167. They are the mountains of God, E. 44. Their glory in heaven, where they reign with God; their hearts are the temple of God, A. 737. They will go out to meet Christ when he comes for judgment, P. 375, 599. Their deeds are to be imitated by us spiritually, P. 591. Their blessedness after the universal resurrection, P. 684, 685. That they should be invoked so that they may pray for us is asserted on the example of Paulinus, P. 378, 379, 685, 686. That they pray for sinners is shown by various examples, P. 616. Their bodies are hidden in tombs, but not their merits, P. 427 et seqq. Their relics are necessary for the dedication of a new temple, E. 200, A. 905, V. 75. In antiquity they were enclosed in altars, E. 200, P. 637, 638, A. 915, V. 75. They perform miracles not only where their whole bodies are present, but also where even the smallest bodily fragment is preserved, P. 638. Their merits are celebrated perpetually, P. 657. Earth is adorned by their bodies as heaven is by the stars, P. 658. They are especially beneficent toward people wherever their bodies rest, ibid. How Paulinus honored them, E. 202 et seqq., P. 644 et seqq., V. 66 et seqq.

The ancient veneration of the saints, P. 467.

SANCTUS was joined to Paulinus in friendship even before his conversion, E. 239, V. 46. He sent him Christian hymns composed by himself, E. 248, V. 46. Whether he is the same as Saint Endelechius, V. 46.

SAINT ENDELECHIUS was responsible for Paulinus’s writing the panegyric of Theodosius, E. 173, A. 899, V. 46. Whether he is the same as the Sanctus to whom Paulinus wrote Letters 40 and 41, V. 46.

SANEMARIUS, bearer of Paulinus’s letters to Amandus, E. 65. Paulinus granted him his freedom and commended him to Amandus, ibid.

The price of Christ’s blood was not paid for Judas the betrayer, E. 139, 140.

Heavenly wisdom is to be gathered from every source, E. 141, 142. The wisdom of the flesh is the foolish virgin, E. 250. It is also foolishness before God, E. 228.

The flavor of the mind is tasted in speech, E. 46.

Sarah is an example of a virtuous wife, P. 605. She called Abraham her lord, A. 728.

To attack someone satirically is the work of poets, not of parents, P. 372.

Saul mystically signifies the proud man, P. 590.

What the rocks split apart in Christ’s Passion should remind us of, E. 189.

Schismatics and Jews perish in shipwreck, while Christians are saved, P. 574.

The graciousness of the speech of pagan writers, but not the ravings of their doctrine, should be respected, E. 99.

How negligent Paulinus was concerning his own writings, E. 248.

God willed the obscurities of the divine Scriptures for the sake of our exercise, E. 312. In explaining them, many interpretations are found that should be admitted if they agree with sound faith and doctrine, E. 312. Sacred Scripture is to be opened in order to seek God’s will, A. 897. It is compared to a pleasant and budding field, A. 734. Its reading provides the greatest help to those walking in the way of virtue, ibid. Whom it suits, P. 579. Paulinus tries to persuade Jovius to read it, E. 90, 92.

Who the Scupi are, P. 420, A. 936.

A box of boxwood sent by Paulinus to Severus, E. 29, V. 49.

The Scythians were converted to the faith by Nicetas, P. 421.

A *scyphus* is a sacred vessel; for what use, P. 476.

SEBASTIANUS, a hermit, E. 166, V. 69. He lived in Aquitania, V. 69. He devoted himself to prayer and fasting, E. 167, V. 69. Paulinus praises him, E. 166, A. 58. Whether he is the same as the Sebastianus mentioned by Sulpicius Severus in the *Dialogues*, V. 69. Or the one mentioned by Augustine in Letter 248, V. 69. Paulinus and Therasia commend themselves to his prayers, E. 166, 168, V. 69.

Retreat for meditation, E. 233, A. 919. Of Aper, ibid. Of Paulinus, E. 21, P. 363, V. 10, 11, 30. Of Gregory of Nazianzus, A. 919. Of Augustine, ibid.

How this age is called night, E. 140.

SECUNDINIANUS suffered shipwreck in Sardinia, E. 279. Paulinus commends him to Macarius, asking that Macarius protect him from human harassment, E. 287, 288.

Segor was saved from the fire through Lot’s prayers, P. 616.

[Col. 1144] What venerable old age is, F. 69.

A certain old man, whom God called Victor, was miraculously saved from shipwreck, E. 278 et seqq. Paulinus proclaims his good fortune, E. 284. He is compared with Israel, Moses, and John the Evangelist, ibid. For what merits he obtained the privilege of being anticipated by so many benefits from God, E. 284, 285.

“Senior,” that is, presbyter, E. 8, A. 870.

Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, threatening the city of Jerusalem with destruction, was driven away by divine power, P. 614.

The human senses are windows through which both death and life enter, E. 249.

The custom of burying people in churches: whence did it arise? E. 203, A. 919. The ancient religious practice of being buried among martyrs, P. 686, A. 931, 932.

Where the tomb of Saint Felix is situated, P. 429, 430. It is adorned with five very large basilicas, P. 431. It is famous for miracles, P. ibid. et seqq. Paulinus visited the tombs of the apostles and martyrs at Rome every year, E. 93, 97, 196, 199, 264, V. 42. The tombs of the saints are famous for miracles, P. 423. They are adorned with flowers, A. 932.

The religious honoring of the dead through burial is supported by various examples from sacred Scripture, E. 68.

Serapis was substituted by Egyptian superstition for the patriarch Joseph, P. 455. When his temple was destroyed, P. 456.

A man’s speech is an index of his mind, E. 67, 252.

To serve God is freedom, E. 40.

God and divine things must be served with the same zeal and affection with which worldly and human things were formerly served, E. 234.

Anyone devoted to sin is a slave, E. 43.

Seth is substituted for Abel in the holy lineage, E. 59.

SEVERINUS, a presbyter; whether he is the same as Sulpicius Severus, V. 121. Miracles occur at his tomb, ibid.

SEVERUS, bishop of Milevis, greets Paulinus by letter, E. 35.

SEVERUS, also called SULPICIUS, Saint Paulinus’s friend and presbyter of Primuliacum in Aquitania, E. 1, A. 859. He was from the Nitiobrigi, A. 869. He had a wife named Bassula, E. 22, 27, A. 871. He lived at Elusa and Primuliacum, A. 869. Following Paulinus’s example, he renounced the world, E. 2, 149. He became a disciple of Saint Martin of Tours, V. 120. He gave his possessions to the Church, E. 149, A. 895. He distributed the revenues from his property among the poor, E. 2. Paulinus prefers him to the Queen of the South, E. 19. Paulinus shows that he was converted through a greater miracle than Paulinus himself, E. 149 et seqq. He wished to write an apology for himself and Paulinus against certain detractors, E. 3, 4. In his letters he refreshed the sick Paulinus, E. 24, V. 48. Paulinus invited him most earnestly, E. 6, 7, V. 27, 28, 48, 49. From Paulinus he received rye bread and a little boxwood dish, E. 29, 47. Paulinus rebuked him because he had written that he was Paulinus’s slave, E. 29. He is numbered among the saints Job, Abraham, and Lot, E. 149, 150. Because he wrote the *Life of Saint Martin*, E. 120, A. 889. Paulinus calls him blessed, E. 55. When Severus requested a portrait of Paulinus, Paulinus cleverly evaded the request by interpreting it as a request for the inner human being, E. 185 et seqq. He sent Paulinus a cook, E. 116, 118 et seqq. Paulinus praises his charity, E. 117, 118, A. 870. He wrote annals, E. 174. He built a basilica near Primuliacum, E. 188. He requested from Paulinus the relics of saints necessary for its proper dedication, ibid. He received from Paulinus a fragment of the wood of the holy cross, E. 189, V. 72, 73. He built a baptistery between two basilicas constructed by him, E. 195. He often visited Saint Martin at Tours, E. 95. He accepted Cytherius’s son, dedicated to God, for instruction, P. 586 et seqq., V. 64. He received Posthumianus and Theridius, sent by Paulinus, with great kindness, V. 70. Whether he was bishop of Bourges, V. 120. Whether he is the same as the preceding Severinus, V. 120. Whether he was a saint, V. 121. Whether his feast was celebrated, V. 121, 122. And on what day, ibid.

SEVERUS ENDELECHIUS, E. 174. Who was he? A. 899. He was responsible for Paulinus’s writing the panegyric of Theodosius, E. 174.

“Let him keep it for himself,” a formula of speech familiar to Paulinus, E. 115, 231, A. 888.

The royal *siclus*, that is, the public weight, E. 131, A. 891.

Sigma and its shape, P. 482.

SILVIA promises Severus relics of numerous martyrs from the East for the dedication of a new basilica, E. 188.

SIMPLICIANUS was designated by Ambrose as his successor in the Milanese episcopate, V. 31.

Heaven is open to simplicity, A. 916.

SIMPLICIUS, bishop of Vienne, E. 277, V. 88. A man of the greatest faith and piety, ibid.

Christians ought to be compared with a mustard seed, E. 5.

All forms of temporal things are our Sirens, E. 91.

SIRICIUS, pope, was hostile to Paulinus, E. 25, 26. Why, A. 873, V. 31, 32. In the year 398. He died, V. 57.

Sisera, commander of the army, was killed by a woman, P. 613. He was transfixed with a stake, ibid.

[Col. 1145] The Christian solemnities listed by Paulinus, P. 625, 626, A. 943, V. 71. Those of the saints were celebrated in ancient times with an all-night vigil, P. 642.

The *solium* is a raised place where the bodies of saints are placed, E. 73, A. 881. It also means the threshold of a church, E. 73, P. 636, A. 881, 944.

The floor of a church was sprinkled with flowers during solemnities, P. 386, A. 932.

SORIANUS, bearer of Severus’s letters to Paulinus, E. 113, 114. Paulinus praises him, ibid.

To stage spectacles, E. 73, A. 881.

A man’s speech is the mirror of his mind, E. 278, E. 67, 252.

SPES, a layman accused of a crime, was sent by Augustine to the tomb of Saint Felix of Nola to be purified, V. 80.

Hope, fear, joy, and sorrow are the four principal incentives to vice, E. 238. Hope was worshiped by the pagans as a goddess in an image, E. 90. When placed in God, it will not disappoint, A. 719.

Thorns that restrain an evil tongue and preserve faith are useful, E. 46. But those that choke the word are useless, ibid. The thorns that restrain the devil are the word of God, E. 230. The thorns of the heart are sins, P. 653.

Christ taught us to overcome spiritual and invisible enemies, E. 223.

The Holy Spirit is represented in paintings as a dove, E. 202, A. 909, 910. He is called the gardener, E. 237. Descending upon the apostles in the form of fire, he enabled them to speak in all languages, P. 626, A. 943.

How brides are to be adorned among Christians, P. 603, 604, 605. They do not have authority over their own bodies, A. 741.

The movements and arrangements of the stars impose no necessity upon human affairs, E. 88.

Barrenness was formerly a disgrace, P. 342, A. 929.

The error of the Stoics, who assert that all sins are equal, A. 730.

Suetonius wrote the history of the kings, P. 328. Paulinus rendered it metrically, P. 328, A. 792, 793, V. 6.

“Suggillata”: parts around the eyes that are discolored and livid, A. 896.

Whence knowledge of oneself arises, E. 91, 92.

SULPICIUS: see SEVERUS.

What the *sumen* is, P. 502.

Paulinus’s household furnishings breathed humility, E. 29.

Holy pride consists in despising everything that belongs to the world, E. 62. Pride is the dissipator of all good works, E. 290. When disguised under signs of humility, it is much more deformed, A. 738. There is a kind of good pride and a good humility, E. 62, 73.

Why unbelievers add punishments to martyrs by delaying their death, P. 394.

The Pharisee who invited Christ, but anointed neither Christ’s head nor feet, is a type of the Synagogue, E. 138. The two women grinding are types of the Synagogue and the Church: one is taken and the other left, E. 51.

## T

The letter T, or Tau, displaying the shape of the cross, 300. What it signifies, E. 162, A. 897, 898.

“Tabernaculis” for “tibiis”: how it entered Psalm 146, V. 10, E. 286, A. 923, 924.

Ausonius called Paulinus’s wife Tanaquil by way of slander, V. 24.

A beautiful description of a sea storm, E. 280 et seqq.

The magnificence of the temple of Ephesus, P. 454.

The hearts of the saints are called the temple of God, A. 737. “Octo rhorum” [reading uncertain], A. 907. The tearing of the temple veil during Christ’s Passion indicates that the Jerusalem temple was to be profaned, P. 678. Paulinus strongly commends the building of the spiritual temple in the soul, P. 154 et seqq., A. 948. Who try to obstruct the building of temples, E. 108. Their dedication takes place with relics of the saints, A. 905. Temples adorned during solemnities, P. 382, A. 931, 932: with flowers, P. 386, A. 932; with curtains, A. 932. Their thresholds were likewise adored with kisses, P. 383, 434, A. 930, 936, 937, 945. They were adorned with curtains, P. 386, 428, A. 930, 931, and with garlands and flowers, P. 386, A. 932.

Paulinus shows from sacred Scripture that there is a proper time for everything, E. 237, 241.

Darkness arose at the time of Christ’s Passion, P. 678.

The various and deceitful temptations of demons must be avoided with great caution, E. 218, 219.

The earth left for the serpent—that is, the devil—to devour is the sinner, P. 155.

During his transfer, an earthquake shook Paulinus’s little cell, A. 958.

Earthly things are to be seen; heavenly things are to be believed, P. 676. Earthly things are sordid to those who delight in heavenly things, P. 368, A. 747, 748.

Paulinus calls the two Testaments the lips of God, E. 77.

The Old and New Testaments were represented in paintings in the basilica of Saint Felix, P. 651. Paulinus explains why he had the former painted in the old building and the latter in the new building, P. 652.

[Col. 1146] The location of Thaddeus’s tomb is disputed by various opinions, P. 451.

Thaddeus, Lebbaeus, and Judas are synonyms, P. 451.

Thamnus is Adonis, A. 903.

THEASIUS, bishop in Africa, visited Paulinus at Nola, V. 81.

Paulinus wrote an apology for the emperor Theodosius at the prompting of Endelechius and sent it to Severus, E. 176, A. 899, V. 45.

THERASIA was betrothed to Saint Paulinus, E. 10, 16, 30, 31, 166, 189, 234, 239, 258, 263, P. 608, A. 785, V. 6, 7. During his conversion she helped her husband, V. 7, 9. She withdrew with him to Spain, V. 6. What life she led there, ibid. She had a son who died eight days after birth and was buried at Complutum, P. 685, 686, V. 7. She sold her estates and distributed the money to the poor, A. 775, V. 6, 7, 15, 16. Through her excessive anxiety a ship was lost, A. 785, V. 7, 16. She professed continence, E. 16, A. 781, 971, V. 6, 14. She avoided the companionship of noblewomen, V. 6. She was content with modest clothing, ibid., and with poor and simple food, V. 7. Ausonius contemptuously called her Tanaquil, V. 24. Paulinus defended her honor, P. 369, V. 7, 26. She came to Nola with her husband, V. 6. What life she established there, V. 33. How highly she was esteemed by Ambrose, A. 775; by Jerome, V. 6; and by Augustine, E. 16, V. 6, 7. Several letters were written and answered in her name, E. 9, 30, 31, 166, 231, 239, 258, 263, 269. She died before Paulinus, V. 93, 94.

Therasia, Saint Paulinus’s wife, P. 529. Her homeland, ibid. Out of a desire for chastity, she consented to separation from the marriage bed, P. 523.

THERIDIUS, Paulinus’s friend, V. 58. Originally from Aquitania, ibid. He left his homeland and came to Nola, ibid. There Paulinus received him with great affection, ibid. He carried Severus’s letters to Paulinus, ibid., and Paulinus’s to Severus, by whom he was received with great kindness, V. 70. Likewise Paulinus’s letters to Jovius, E. 84, V. 70. Paulinus commended him to another, ibid. He returned to Nola and dedicated himself to Saint Felix, P. 565, V. 58, 70. In danger from an eye ailment, he implored and obtained Saint Felix’s help, P. 565–570, V. 58. Paulinus praises him, P. 565.

THERIDIUS, another, very dear to Paulinus, P. 582, V. 67. He stayed in Rome, ibid. and V. 58. He visited Paulinus at Nola, ibid. Martinianus, shipwrecked, was received at his house in Rome, ibid.

Tolus in the church: what is meant? P. 652, A. 948.

THOMAS the apostle, surnamed Didymus, P. 638, A. 945. He doubts Christ’s resurrection, P. 638, 671. Why? ibid. He is reproved by Christ, P. 638. He is confirmed, P. ibid. He rests among the Indians, P. 659. His relics were deposited in the basilica of St. Felix, ibid.

Thomas crowned with martyrdom in India, P. 451. His bones were transferred to Edessa, ibid.

TIGRIDIUS, a monk of Lérins under St. Honoratus, E. 319. He was sent by that same Honoratus, then a presbyter, to St. Paulinus at Nola, E. 315.

To fear God is complete security, P. 611, 612.

The fear of God closes the windows through which death enters, E. 249. It drives out avarice and lust, E. 231.

TIMOTHY was buried in Asia and transferred by Constantine to Constantinople, P. 659.

The transfer of the bodies of Timothy and Andrew to Constantinople, P. 468.

When Titus was preaching the Gospel in Crete, Jupiter was driven from there, P. 451. Titus was bishop of Crete, where he was buried, P. 451.

TITUS rests in Crete, ibid.

Tobias, by his example, commends to us the care of burying the dead, E. 68. He is depicted in the portico of the basilica of St. Felix, P. 647.

Victor performs the barber’s service for Paulinus, E. 123.

A torrent rushing into the church of St. Felix is diverted elsewhere, P. 622, V. 70.

The bodies of martyrs pierced with beam-like nails, P. 638, A. 945.

Tracheli, A. 929.

Transenna: what is it? E. 202, A. 914.

The three hundred companions of Gideon signify the cross, E. 163, A. 897. The three hundred and eighteen companions of Abraham signify the same, ibid. The three hundred cubits of the Ark signify the same, ibid. The three hundred denarii in John XII signify the same, ibid.

The Three Fates, a place in Rome, P. 556, A. 937.

Tribulation is more useful than praise, E. 5. Its benefit, A. 717.

Altars with three apses, E. 203, A. 906, 907. *Trichora* and *trichorium*, ibid.

THE MYSTERY OF THE HOLY TRINITY: how it was depicted in the basilica erected by Paulinus, E. 203. How it was represented in churches, A. 908, 909. How Victricius preached it to the pagans, E. 225. Its mystery represented in the three loaves, A. 872.

Sorrows in this world are to be preferred to joys, P. 682.

There is a kind of sadness that is salutary and another that is harmful, E. 70.

*Tritorium*, A. 907.

*Tropaeum* and *trophaeum* used indiscriminately, P. 485.

With mutilated senses, E. 43, A. 884.

The tombs of the saints surrounded with silver plates, P. 538.

[Col. 1147] A description of the common tunic among the ancient Romans, P. 480.

A military tunic, in French *cotte d’armes*, A. 887. Paulinus sends Severus, as an innocent man, a tunic woven from lambs’ fleeces, E. 190, V. 72, 73.

The city of Tours, famous for the relics of St. Martin, was frequently visited by Severus out of devotion, E. 95.

The tower in which the Eucharist was kept slipped from the hands of an impure deacon and flew to the altar, A. 905.

TYCHICUS, Victricius’s messenger to Paulinus, E. 97, A. 884, V. 125. He makes St. Victricius’s life known to Paulinus, ibid.

U

The cunning of Ulysses is to be imitated by those striving to escape the waves of this world, E. 90, 91.

With what ointment Christians ought to anoint Christ, E. 144, A. 895.

“‘One’” is said not only of a single body but also of the unanimity of many, E. 51.

URANIUS, bearer of Delphinus’s letters to Paulinus, E. 104, V. 65. Negligent in his duty, ibid. Paulinus rebukes him before Delphinus, ibid.

URANIUS the presbyter describes Paulinus’s episcopate and death, A. 957, 960, 961. Whether he is the same as the preceding person, V. 97.

URBANUS, bishop, a friend of St. Augustine, E. 316.

Pope Urbicus: who was he? E. 26, A. 863.

URSUS, a catechumen of the Church of Rouen, E. 96. The companion of Paschasius, Victricius’s deacon, on his pilgrimage, he fell ill at Nola in Paulinus’s house, ibid. There, while confined to bed, he was baptized by the deacon Paschasius, ibid. Through the merits of St. Felix he was restored to health, ibid.

Utica, a famous city of Africa, P. 459.

What a wife ought to be, P. 602 and following; A. 739 and following. Her duties toward her husband, P. 605, A. 740. She does not possess authority over her own body, A. 741. Paulinus’s description of a good wife, P. 593 and following. Consolation for one mourning a good deceased wife, E. 69, 70.

V

VALENS, emperor, a supporter of the Arians, persecutes the Church of God, E. 182.

VALENTINIANUS, bishop, is present when St. Martin heals a girl at Chartres, V. 124.

VALERIUS, bishop of the Church of Hippo, receives Augustine as his colleague, E. 33, 36.

Valerius Publicola was among Rome’s first consuls, P. 521.

VALGIUS, also called VICTOR, is miraculously saved from shipwreck, F. 278 and following, V. 90. Paulinus extols his good fortune, E. 286. He is compared with Israel, Moses, and John the Evangelist, ibid. For what merits he obtained from God that so many benefits should precede him, E. 284, 285. Paulinus commends him to Macarius, E. 278, V. 90.

Whence came the vessel of holy water at the entrance to churches? A. 883.

Paulinus loved earthen vessels, and why, E. 29, V. 34.

The Vasates are sandy, P. 372, A. 930.

Paulinus shows that the uncultivated thickets of Vasconia are not harmful to Probus, P. 370, 371.

What the veil of the Temple, torn at Christ’s Passion, teaches us, E. 288, P. 679. A veil used as an altar hanging in the church of Galardon, A. 905. Veils at the thresholds of churches, P. 386, 426, A. 931, 932, 936. Likewise inside churches, ibid. Adorned with images of the saints, A. 932.

VENERANDUS, senator of Auvergne, V. 86. The seventh bishop of Clermont, E. 276. Successor of St. Artemius, V. 86. A man of the greatest faith and piety, E. 276, V. 86. He died on 24 December, V. 86. Where was he buried? ibid. Many miracles occurred at his tomb, ibid. His relics were transferred to the church of St. Alyrius, ibid.

*Venerarium*, A. 903.

VENERIUS, bishop of Milan, E. 106. Successor of Simplicianus, V. 65. He expresses his attitude toward Paulinus in a letter, E. 106, V. 65. He receives a letter from Paulinus, ibid.

*Veneventum* for *Beneventum*, P. 502.

Venus worshiped on the island of Cos, P. 460.

How the Word became flesh, E. 111.

The Word of God is the ancient and living bread, E. 8. It is sometimes called a sword in Holy Scripture, E. 8. At other times, fire, ibid. The words of God are either defenses or darts for us against the devil, E. 45. The deacons in Gaul during Paulinus’s time were heralds of the Word of God, E. 186, 169, V. 69.

A description of spring, P. 557.

Recognition of the truth is the fullness of wisdom, E. 229.

Will there really be worms in hell? P. 685, A. 768.

A remarkable palindrome verse, A. 883.

The evening office, A. 958.

Fasting is the garment of the soul by which we abstain from everything forbidden, P. 175.

The harshness of Elijah’s and John the Baptist’s clothing commended by their example, E. 175, 285, A. 924.

[Col. 1148] Christians must avoid luxury in clothing, P. 603. Paulinus teaches this by the example of the first-created humans and Rebecca, P. 604. What Isaiah threatens those excessively devoted to it, P. 604.

Mount Vesuvius, P. 478.

VETUSTINUS is sent by Augustine to travel to Nola and is commended to Paulinus, E. 34.

The two ways named by the Savior in the Gospel, and their antitheses, A. 731.

The way of the rich man and the way of Christ, P. 536.

Roads were formerly called *stratae*, whence the Italian word *strada*, P. 504.

Christ, both the victim of his priesthood and the priest of his victim, E. 53.

VICTOR, formerly girded with a sword, E. 162, 163, V. 67. The spiritual son of St. Martin of Tours, E. 118, V. 67. A companion of Sulpicius Severus in the wilderness, ibid. Severus sends him to Paulinus as a cook, E. 116. Paulinus receives him with intimate affection, E. 118, V. 67. He is greatly praised by Severus, E. 118 and following, V. 67, 68. He is adorned with virtues, E. 118, 119 and following, V. 67, 68. An imitator of Saints Martin and Clarus, ibid. An excellent and spiritual cook, preparing food for the monks, Paulinus, and his household in the monastic manner, E. 116, 119, 120, V. 68. An outstanding barber, E. 123, V. 68. Also extremely dutiful, E. 118, V. 68. An energetic bearer of Severus’s letters to Paulinus, E. 116, V. 67, 80, 82; and of Paulinus’s letters to Severus, E. 116, 148, V. 68, 80, 82. He carries letters to Alethius, E. 211, V. 78, 79, and Alethius’s letters to Paulinus, ibid. He carries Paulinus’s letter to Desiderius, in which Paulinus excuses Victor for having been detained with him for a long time during the winter because of illness, E. 253, 254. He visits the thresholds of the apostles with Paulinus, E. 254. Through him the hermit Sebastian, the deacon Benedict, and a certain soldier become known to Paulinus, E. 162, 166, 167, V. 69.

VICTOR, also called VALGIUS: see VALGIUS.

VICTRICIUS, born within the imperial frontiers, E. 94, V. 122. Younger than St. Martin, bishop of Tours, E. 101, V. 122. A soldier, E. 99, V. 121. Converted to Christ, he rejects military service, E. 99, V. 122. Why, V. 123. He lays down his arms at the tribune’s feet, E. 99, V. 123. He is stretched out for scourging, E. 100, V. 123. Beaten with clubs, ibid. Rubbed with a sharp fragment of pottery, ibid. Condemned to death, ibid. The bonds fall of their own accord from his hands, ibid. The executioner who insults him is punished with blindness, ibid. Victricius is released by the emperor, E. 101, V. 123. Rich in graces, E. 101, V. 124. Powerful in merits, ibid. Equal to Martin, ibid. He is made bishop of Rouen, E. 99, V. 124. Eighth in succession, A. 885. He is present at Chartres when St. Martin heals a girl, V. 124. Likewise at Vienne, E. 101, V. 124. He makes the Church of Rouen illustrious through his piety, E. 98, 99, V. 124. He preaches the faith in Belgic Gaul among the Morini and Nervii, E. 97, 98, V. 125, 126. He converts them, ibid. He receives letters from Paulinus, E. 95, 222, V. 125, 126. He refutes the error of Apollinaris, E. 225. He is accused concerning the faith, E. 224, V. 126. He comes to Rome, E. 222, V. 126, 127. Returning to Rouen, he sends Candidianus to Paulinus with a letter, ibid. He receives from Pope Innocent of Rome a decretal letter concerning moral discipline, V. 127, 129. He makes it known to the suffragan bishops, V. 128.

The food and clothing of St. John the Baptist living in the wilderness, P. 342.

The widow who put two small coins into the treasury, praised by Christ, commends benevolence toward the poor, E. 17, P. 428, 433.

Paulinus meets Victricius at Vienne, E. 101, V. 124.

How necessary vigilance is for those who walk the way of the spirit, E. 247. Likewise for attaining salvation, A. 743.

VIGILANTIUS suffers for a long time from fever at Paulinus’s house, E. 24, V. 48. He carries Paulinus’s letters to Sulpicius Severus, ibid., and to Jerome, V. 48, 52. Paulinus strongly commends him, V. 52. Jerome receives him honorably and with great affection, and he remains with him for some time, V. 52. He takes the side of John of Jerusalem and Rufinus against Jerome, ibid. He asks Jerome’s pardon, ibid. and finds favor with him, ibid. Returning from Palestine to Gaul, he publishes a book against Jerome, ibid. From there he rises against the teaching of the Catholic faith, ibid. He spreads various errors, ibid. and becomes the leader of the heretics of Gaul, ibid.

How the vigils of the saints were celebrated in Paulinus’s time, P. 338. Fasting, ibid.

To conquer and to be conquered in spiritual combat are equally necessary, E. 157.

VINCENTIUS rests in Spain, P. 660.

Vincentius, a martyr in Spain, P. 459.

The bonds restraining Victricius’s hands, when he was already condemned to death, are miraculously loosened, E. 100, V. 23.
