One who does not seek vengeance is more severely avenged by the Lord, E. 95.

St. John the Baptist did not drink wine, P. 337. New wine was formerly given to the newly baptized, A. 892, 893, and mixed with milk, [Col. 1149] ibid. It was also formerly consecrated and offered to them in place of the Eucharist, ibid.

Violence is pleasing to God when the kingdom of heaven is seized, E. 164.

A man does not possess authority over his own body, A. 742.

The three rods placed by the patriarch Jacob before the mating flocks, explained mystically, P. 633.

Paulinus quotes Virgil, but with a request for pardon, E. 115.

What the wise and foolish virgins of the Gospel signify mystically, E. 249 and following. Virgins will cling to God more familiarly in heaven, E. 393.

The ancient Christian custom of dedicating boys’ or girls’ virginity to God, P. 535.

The male organs worshiped with a shameful rite in the Isiac rites and Orgies, P. 462.

VIRINUS brings Severus’s letters to Paulinus, E. 113, 114, V. 65, 67.

How strength is perfected in weakness, E. 27, 28. Carnal weakness is the material of spiritual strength, E. 168. Its path is arduous, P. 629. The weaknesses of the strong are incentives to virtue for the weak, E. 82. The habit of vices makes its path difficult for us, A. 731.

How eternal life is to be acquired, E. 274. The present life must be despised in order to attain the future one, P. 657. Friendship with this world is death to the soul, E. 62. Life and death are in everyone’s tongue, E. 76. The Life of St. Martin of Tours, written by Sulpicius Severus, E. 119, A. 889. The Life of Paulinus was formerly read at the solemnities of Gregory the Great, A. 790. The brevity of human life, A. 747. Changing one’s life is very often praiseworthy, P. 373.

The relics of the martyr Vitalis were deposited in the Basilica of St. Felix, P. 638.

Vices imitate and counterfeit virtue, A. 737. Their habitual practice makes the way of the virtues difficult for us, A. 731. Their blandishments are our Lotus-Eaters and Sirens, E. 90.

God the Son is called the true vine, E. 238.

To live for the world is death, E. 42. To live for God is life, ibid. And so is observing his commandments, A. 729.

We are made alive and put to death by Christ, E. 241, 242.

God’s will is not easily known, V. 80. The former practice of investigating it by opening a book, A. 897, 898. Good will is above the law, E. 160.

Pleasure, luxury, and avarice are the sources of all evils, P. 342.

The Christian’s vow at baptism, E. 130. It must be fulfilled to the Lord, A. 743. God’s will is better than human vows, E. 71.

The voice signifies God the Father, E. 203, A. 908.

X

*Xenium*, E. 383, 386, A. 925.

᾿Υπωπιάξω, “I bruise; I make black and blue”: a technical word belonging to athletes, E. 158, A. 895, 896.

Should *υἱῶν* or *ὑῶν* be read in Psalm XVI? A. 926, 927.

Z

*Zabulus*, “the devil,” E. 6, A. 869.

Zabulon: “dwelling-place of strength,” or “flow of night,” A. 869.

What sort of man Zacharias, the father of St. John the Baptist, was, P. 336, 337. Because he believed the angel’s words only imperfectly, he was made mute, P. 338. Consulted about the name to be given to his son, he writes “John,” and the bond on his tongue is released, P. 341.

Zeal is kindled by presence but grows cold through absence, E. 24.

[Col. 1149]

## TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

[Col. 1149]

Dedication letter, 9. Preface, 11. Another preface, from the Paris edition, 13. LIFE OF ST. PAULINUS, compiled from his own writings and the records of the ancients, 15.

CHAPTER I.—St. Paulinus’s birth, family, and wealth. Various persons named Paulinus, ibid.

CHAPTER II.—Paulinus’s studies and learning. Ausonius, his teacher, 18.

CHAPTER III.—Paulinus marries Therasia. He is honored with the consulship and the highest offices. He forms friendships with many people, 21.

CHAPTER IV.—How Paulinus lived in the world. Through various labors and hardships, and also through the prayers of St. Felix and other saints, he is converted to God, 23.

CHAPTER V.—Paulinus withdraws to Spain in order to renounce the world. At what time he was initiated through baptism, 25.

CHAPTER VI.—How Paulinus conducted himself immediately after withdrawing to Spain. Concerning his deceased son, 27.

CHAPTER VII.—Paulinus dedicates and consecrates himself wholly to God and embraces the monastic life, 29.

CHAPTER VIII.—He sells his estates and distributes the money to the poor, 30.

CHAPTER IX.—Paulinus’s humility in renouncing his possessions, 33.

CHAPTER X.—The praises of the holy Fathers concerning Paulinus’s conversion and poverty, 37.

CHAPTER XI.—Nobles and worldly men call Paulinus foolish. He steadfastly and courageously endures the mockery reserved for him, 39.

CHAPTER XII.—Ausonius accuses Paulinus of having changed frivolously and reproaches him for interrupting his letters. Paulinus attests his love and reverence for him, 42.

CHAPTER XIII.—Paulinus firmly refutes Ausonius’s complaints, 43.

CHAPTER XIV.—Paulinus’s closest relationship with Severus, 44.

CHAPTER XV.—At Barcelona, Paulinus is unwillingly initiated into the presbyterate, 46.

CHAPTER XVI.—Paulinus invites Sulpicius Severus to withdraw to Nola. He writes to Amandus about his promotion to the priesthood, 48.

CHAPTER XVII.—Paulinus comes to Italy. He is received affectionately and honorably by St. Ambrose, but poorly by Pope Siricius, 49.

CHAPTER XVIII.—Paulinus settles at Nola. The life he established there, 51.

CHAPTER XIX.—What love of poverty, voluntary bodily affliction, solitude, and silence existed in Paulinus. St. Augustine’s judgment on his letters, 53.

[Col. 1150] CHAPTER XX.—Paulinus suffers the troublesome distress of lustful flesh, invokes God, and despises himself, 55.

CHAPTER XXI.—He considers himself unworthy to expound Sacred Scripture, 58.

CHAPTER XXII.—Paulinus’s devotion toward the saints, especially toward St. Felix. Each year he goes to Rome to venerate in person the sacred bodies of the apostles, 60.

CHAPTER XXIII.—Paulinus forms friendships with Augustine and other African saints, 62.

CHAPTER XXIV.—Paulinus writes to Jerome and receives a reply from him, 64.

CHAPTER XXV.—Paulinus’s relationship with the saints and with Amandus, 66.

CHAPTER XXVI.—Paulinus falls ill and sends a reply to Sulpicius Severus through Vigilantius, 68.

CHAPTER XXVII.—Augustine writes to Paulinus, who sends him letters again. Paulinus’s power over demons, 70.

CHAPTER XXVIII.—Paulinus is informed by Augustine himself of Augustine’s promotion to the episcopate and testifies his joy to Romanianus, 72.

CHAPTER XXIX.—Through Vigilantius, who handles the matter badly, Paulinus writes to Jerome. He devotes himself to sacred reading with the greatest humility, 73.

CHAPTER XXX.—Paulinus writes to Saints Delphinus and Amandus. Severus sends him the Life of St. Martin, 75.

CHAPTER XXXI.—Paulinus wards off violence inflicted on a most holy presbyter, 76.

CHAPTER XXXII.—Paulinus consoles Pammachius over his wife’s death, 78.

CHAPTER XXXIII.—Concerning Theridius and Posthumianus, Paulinus’s friends, and Jovius, his kinsman, 80.

CHAPTER XXXIV.—Paulinus writes an outstanding letter to Jovius, urging him to embrace Christian faith and piety, 82.

CHAPTER XXXV.—Paulinus, ill, strongly invites Sulpicius Severus to visit him, 84.

CHAPTER XXXVI.—Paulinus writes to Victricius. He cultivates the friendship of Jerome and Rufinus, 85.

CHAPTER XXXVII.—Paulinus writes to St. Delphinus of Bordeaux, Venerius of Milan, and Severus. He describes the history and martyrdom of Martinianus, 88.

CHAPTER XXXVIII.—Through Victor, a disciple of St. Martin, Paulinus writes several letters to Sulpicius Severus, 91.

CHAPTER XXXIX.—Paulinus urges a soldier to renounce the world. He congratulates the hermit Sebastian on his piety, 92.

CHAPTER XL.—The Goths spread terror in Italy. Paulinus writes to Severus through Posthumianus, 93.

CHAPTER XLI.—Paulinus is visited by Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, and by Melania. When consulted by Severus about certain points of history, he humbly refuses to give an opinion, 95.

CHAPTER XLII.—Near the tomb of St. Felix, Paulinus orders a new basilica to be built and adorns it with various paintings, 97.

CHAPTER XLIII.—Paulinus adorns the old basilica of St. Felix with paintings and surrounds it outside with numerous buildings, 99.

CHAPTER XLIV.—Paulinus likewise orders a basilica to be built on estates and sends Severus poems for the basilica at Primuliacum, 101.

CHAPTER XLV.—Paulinus writes to Alethius and Florentius of Cahors. The death of his brother, 103.

CHAPTER XLVI.—Victricius, Aper, and Augustine write to Paulinus; he replies to them. Pelagius also writes to Paulinus, 105.

CHAPTER XLVII.—Paulinus writes to Severus and Desiderius. Severus urges Posthumianus to visit Paulinus, 107.

CHAPTER XLVIII.—Paulinus obtains from Rufinus an explanation of the blessings of the twelve patriarchs. He writes to Aper and praises Melania’s son, 109.

CHAPTER XLIX.—Paulinus writes to Augustine about Melania and receives a letter from him through Possidius. He praises many bishops of Gaul. Concerning St. Venerandus of Clermont, 110.

CHAPTER L.—Paulinus is made bishop of Nola. How he conducted himself in the episcopate, 112.

CHAPTER LI.—Valgius, also called Victor, is the sole survivor of a shipwreck. Nola is captured by the Goths. The other Paulinus takes refuge with St. Paulinus. Augustine writes to St. Paulinus against the Pelagians, 116.

CHAPTER LII.—Paulinus is invited to the synod at Ravenna to resolve the schism of the Roman Church. Saints Eucherius and Honoratus form a friendship with Paulinus, 118.

CHAPTER LIII.—St. Paulinus’s final illness and death, 120.

CHAPTER LIV.—After Paulinus has died, St. John, bishop of Naples, is summoned to heaven. Uranius writes the history of St. Paulinus’s death, 123.

EPITOME OF THE LIFE OF ST. PAULINUS, 125.

PRAISES OF ST. PAULINUS from various writers, ibid.

## FIRST PART OF THE WORKS—LETTERS

LETTER I.—Paulinus urges Sulpicius Severus not to abandon his pursuit of perfection because of the slander of wicked people, 153.

LETTER II.—He announces to the presbyter Amandus, who later succeeded St. Delphinus in the bishopric of Bordeaux, that he was made a priest against his will, 159.

LETTER III.—He writes to Bishop Alypius about the books of Augustine that he had received. He wishes to be informed about Alypius’s origin and life, 161.

LETTER IV.—He writes to Augustine, adorning him with elaborate praises for his five books against the Manichaeans, 164.

LETTER V.—He praises Severus and shows that he was converted to God through a greater miracle, etc., 167.

LETTER VI.—Having received no reply from Augustine, Paulinus writes to him again through another letter, 178.

LETTER VII.—Writing to Romanianus, he congratulates the Church of Hippo that it has deserved Augustine as a fellow bishop, 179.

LETTER VIII.—Paulinus urges Licentius, Romanianus’s son, to dedicate himself to Christ, 181.

LETTER IX.—Delphinus had been urged by Amandus to ask Paulinus for some salutary teaching. Paulinus complains to Amandus about this, 185.

LETTER X.—With the greatest piety, he excuses himself to Delphinus as being insufficiently qualified to discuss passages of Sacred Scripture, 188.

LETTER XI.—He shows the superiority of Christian charity over human necessities and, allegorically explaining the ancient sacrifices, teaches that a sacrifice must be offered to God in himself and concerning himself. He also praises Severus for writing the Life of St. Martin and finally, by inviting him to visit, reminds him of the excellence of evangelical poverty, 190.

LETTER XII.—Amandus had requested longer letters from Paulinus; therefore Paulinus writes this letter on God’s grace, no less pious than elegant, 200.

LETTER XIII.—Paulina, daughter of St. Paula, had married Pammachius. After she died while still in the flower of youth, Pammachius mourned her with many tears and also consoled himself through abundant almsgiving to the poor. Paulinus consoles and commends him in both respects, 207.

LETTER XIV.—He congratulates Delphinus on the restoration of his health, 223.

LETTER XV.—He congratulates Amandus that Delphinus has been freed from a serious illness, 225.

LETTER XVI.—He teaches Jovius that all things are subject to divine providence, 227.

LETTER XVII.—He complains that Severus has not come to St. Felix, 234.

LETTER XVIII.—He excuses to Victricius of Rouen the deacon Paschasius, who had been detained with him for a long time. Then he vividly describes Victricius’s praises, 237.

[Col. 1152] LETTER XIX.—He describes his joy at receiving Delphinus’s letter. He says that he is Delphinus’s planting and asks to be watered by his words and cultivated by his prayers, 243.

LETTER XX.—He writes to Delphinus about the affection shown toward him by Anastasius, the Roman pontiff, and Venerius, bishop of Milan. He congratulates him on the foundation of the church at Alingon, 246.

LETTER XXI.—The praises of Cardamatis. The beginning of John’s Gospel is magnificently explained, 250.

LETTER XXII.—He describes the conduct of dissolute men and teaches what sort of people are suitable companions for monks, 254.

LETTER XXIII.—Severus’s charity is praised. He also commends Victor, whom Severus sent to him, and Victor’s service in preparing food according to monastic custom. An elegant discussion of hair, 256.

LETTER XXIV.—Severus had praised Paulinus for distributing his possessions among the poor. Paulinus replies that it is not a matter of great importance if someone renounces riches without renouncing himself, 286.

LETTER XXV.—He advises an unknown nobleman to pass from Caesar’s profane service to the sacred service of Christ, 300.

LETTER XXVI.—He praises the hermit Sebastian and the deacon Benedict together and asks them to intercede for him and Therasia before the Lord, 304.

LETTER XXVII.—He rejoices at receiving news from Severus; he clears himself before him concerning the people who had been taken away and develops Severus’s praises with the greatest charity and humility, 306.

LETTER XXVIII.—He praises Victor, through whom they exchanged letters, to Severus and excuses Victor for having been sent back late. Beautiful figures concerning Christ—as fire, foundation, door, and so forth—are interwoven, 308.

LETTER XXIX.—He rightly interprets the cloaks made of camel hair sent by Severus as appropriate for him, a penitent in need. He sends Severus, as an innocent man, a tunic made of lambs’ fleece, which he had received from Melania, whose praises he develops at length, 312.

LETTER XXX.—Severus had asked for a portrait of Paulinus. On the occasion of this request, Paulinus corrects Severus’s excessive affection and cleverly evades the request, discussing the inner and outer person, 322.

LETTER XXXI.—For the consecration of the basilica, he sends Severus a fragment of the most holy cross, adding the history of the discovery of the cross, 325.

LETTER XXXII.—He remonstrates with Severus, by whom he had been depicted with St. Martin at the sacred font. He sends verses to be inscribed. He describes the basilica of St. Felix that he founded, 330.

LETTER XXXIII.—He writes to Alethius, who had requested some work from Paulinus, and says that he is too inadequate to satisfy Alethius’s desire, 343.

LETTER XXXIV.—A sermon on the treasury, 344.

LETTER XXXV.—Paulinus commends the soul of his brother and himself to Delphinus’s prayers, 350.

LETTER XXXVI.—He commends the soul of his brother and himself to Amandus’s prayers, 351.

LETTER XXXVII.—He grieves that, because of his sins, Victricius did not reach him when he came to Rome. He praises Victricius for his apostolic ministry of evangelization and for the persecutions he endured from adversaries, 353.

LETTER XXXVIII.—He praises Aper’s notable passage from the forum and tribunal to Christ and supplies him with various exhortations, 357.

LETTER XXXIX.—He teaches Aper how the field of the heart should be cultivated; there he applies Joel’s words about the caterpillar, locust, grub, and mildew to the four passions of the soul, 363.

LETTER XL.—Saints Sanctus and Amandus had heaped great praise upon Paulinus in a letter. In replying to them, he adds sharp incentives to perfection, 367.

LETTER XLI.—Paulinus had been warned by Sanctus to tend his lamp carefully while there was still time. He develops the parable of the five wise and five foolish virgins, 377.

LETTER XLII.—He rejoices that he has obtained the friendship of Florentius, bishop of Cahors; he commends him and seeks his prayers, 379.

LETTER XLIII.—He excuses Victor for having returned late. He refers back to Desiderius the presbyter the explanation of the patriarchal blessings that had been proposed to him, 382.

LETTER XLIV.—He praises Aper’s letter and at the same time celebrates the industry of Amanda, Aper’s former wife, now his sister, 385.

LETTER XLV.—Giving thanks to Augustine for a book or letter received from him, he continues with praises of the elder Melania and of her only son Publicola, recently deceased, 391.

LETTER XLVI.—He asks Rufinus to teach him Greek letters. He admits that he did not translate Clement correctly. He requests an exposition of verse 11 of chapter XLIX of Genesis, 397.

LETTER XLVII.—He commends Cerealis to Rufinus and asks that he be visited in passing, ibid.

[Col. 1153] LETTER XLVIII.—He praises the most illustrious bishops of his age, 398.

LETTER XLIX.—He describes the great miracles by which the old man Valgius, later called Victor, was saved from shipwreck. He asks Macarius to protect both him and his patron Secundinianus from the importunity of men, 399.

LETTER L.—He proposes to Augustine several questions concerning the Psalms, the Apostle, and the Gospel, 408.

LETTER LI.—He writes to Eucherius and Galla, living on the island of Lérins, as testimony to his affection and love, and extols them with many praises, 417.

VARIANT READINGS in the letters of Paulinus of Nola, 419.

## SECOND PART OF THE WORKS—POEMS
**POEM I.**—While Paulinus was still living in the world, he sends birds to Gestidius. 437

**POEM II.**—While still living in the world, he sends oysters to Gestidius. 439

**POEM III.**—On the kings collected from Suetonius. Same place.

**POEM IV.**—Shortly after his conversion from the world, he asks God in prayer for honorable conduct and prays for a happy posterity for himself and his own. 439

**POEM V.**—He enumerates various attributes of God and prays for grace from God by which he may avoid sins, so that he may meet God’s judgment securely. 440

**POEM VI.**—On Saint John the Baptist. 442

**POEM VII.**—A paraphrase of Psalm I. 449

**POEM VIII.**—A paraphrase of Psalm II. 450

**POEM IX.**—A paraphrase of Psalm CXXXVI. 451

**Ausonius’s Letter to Paulinus.**—Ausonius writes to Paulinus, living in Spain, and attributes his conversion to fickleness of mind. He reproaches him for interrupting their correspondence and invites him to come to him. 452

**Ausonius’s Letter II to Paulinus.**—He again complains about Paulinus’s silence and lays the charge of violated friendship upon his wife Therasia. Same place.

**Ausonius’s Letter IV to Paulinus.**—When Paulinus had given no answer, Ausonius complained a third time in a letter written in the year 392, which has been lost. He now writes this fourth letter to him on the same subject. Same place.

**POEM X.**—After Paulinus had been living in Spain for four years, he received four letters from Ausonius; this poem answers the first, the third—which has been lost—and the fourth. 453

**POEM XI.**—He answers Ausonius’s second letter. 461

**POEM XII.**—In this poem, which he wrote in Spain on 14 January in the year 394, shortly before he set out for Nola, he implores the aid of Saint Felix, so that he may arrive safely at his tomb. 462

**POEM XIII.**—He gives thanks to Saint Felix because, through his aid, he arrived safely at Nola; and he describes the crowd’s gathering at Saint Felix’s tomb on his feast day. 463

**POEM XIV.**—He shows Saint Felix’s power against demons and implores his intercession with God. 464

**POEM XV.**—He describes Saint Felix’s family and origin, and his sacred offices in the Church. 468

**POEM XVI.**—He continues the history of Saint Felix. 476

**POEM XVII.**—He follows with remarkable praises Saint Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, who had come to Nola for Saint Felix’s feast and was now departing. 483

**POEM XVIII.**—On the death, tomb, and miracles of Saint Felix. 490

**Muratori’s Prolegomena to the following three Natalicia.** 501

**Joannes Mingarelli’s Preface to Paulinus’s Natalitial Poems.** 503

**POEM XIX.**—Poem XI on Saint Felix. 509

**Muratori’s Preface to Paulinus’s Twelfth Natalis.** 551

**POEM XX.**—Poem XII on Saint Felix. Same place.

**Muratori’s Preface to Paulinus’s Thirteenth Natalis.** 567

**POEM XXI.**—Poem XIII on Saint Felix. 571

**POEM XXII.**—He teaches Jovius that everything is subject to divine Providence, while fate and fortune are nothing. He urges him to read Sacred Scripture. 603

**POEM XXIII.**—Saint Felix frees those possessed by a demon. He restores Theridius’s eye. 608

**POEM XXIV.**—He writes to Cytherius about Martinianus’s shipwreck, praising him because he had entrusted his son to Sulpicius Severus for instruction. 615

**POEM XXV.**—Paulinus teaches Julianus, the son of Bishop Memorius, and Iam how they ought to conduct themselves in marriage, how to establish a household, and so forth. 633

**POEM XXVI.**—While the Goths are ravaging Italy, Paulinus trusts in Saint Felix’s protection. He recounts some of his miracles. 638

**POEM XXVII.**—He treats of the solemn festivals of Christians. He receives Saint Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, who is coming to Nola for Saint Felix’s feast for the second time, with remarkable praises. 648

**POEM XXVIII.**—He enlarges the old basilicas of Saint Felix with new buildings, constructs a new one with a baptistery, and adorns them with paintings and epigrams. 663

**POEM XXIX.**—On the basilica of Saint Felix at Nola, enlarged by him. 671

**POEM XXX.**—A fragment of Natalitial Poem XI on Saint Felix, published by Brunius in his Paris edition. Same place.

**POEM XXXI.**—A fragment of Natalitial Poem XIII on Saint Felix, published by the same Brunius. 674

**POEM XXXII.**—A fragment of Poem XIV on Saint Felix. Same place.

**POEM XXXIII.**—A fragment of Poem XV on Saint Felix. Same place.

**POEM XXXIV.**—A Natalitial poem on Saint Felix: a fragment by an uncertain author. 675

**POEM XXXV.**—A panegyric on the death of the boy Celsus. 676

# CORRECTIONS

[Column 1155]

At column 671, the title of Poem XXX should apparently be read as follows: “A fragment of Natalitial Poem XI on Saint Felix, as it had previously been published by Brunius Desmarètes.” At column 674, the title of Poem XXXI would better be read: “A fragment of Natalitial Poem XIII on Saint Felix, as it had previously been published by Brunius.” In the same place, in the title of Poem XXXII, “Poem XIV” should apparently be read instead of “Poem XX”; and in the title of Poem XXXIII, “Poem XV” instead of “Poem XXI.” For in these matters, as also in the Indexes and in comparison with the order previously published by us, Muratori’s edition appears to contain some obscurity—not to say some defect—although it is otherwise highly commendable.

In gathering 28, which, through the printers’ excessive haste, was sent to press before the correction had been completed, please restore the Greek text as follows:
